Ekalasañcikā (Varḍa) Lakṣmīnārāyaṇasaṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga),
Chapter 1.
[Author: Chapter 002.
Salutations to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Second [Part]: The Continuation of the Tretā Yuga. Śrī Rādhikā said:
Oṃ, salutations to the venerable Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self; to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the ruler of the imperishable realm;
to the true father of the lineage of Tretā, the lover of Rādhā, the yogi. || 1 ||
Salutations to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the glorious Māṇikya;

salutations to the Lord who is his own sovereign light, whose locks of hair are beautiful, who dwells within the self, and who is the lord of Īśā and Pāravatī, possessing a form endowed with qualities. 2–3.
Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is the light of the *haṃsa*, who is endowed with power, sovereignty, and the like, and who is manifest in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
salutations repeatedly to the Lord of all abodes, the inner controller.
Salutations to You, the giver of heaven, liberation, and other blessings; salutations to Śrī Hari.
(5) Salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣara), who possesses the majesty of infinite and equal sovereignty and qualities, and who is served by countless liberated souls. (6)
Salutations to that Lord Śrī Svāmī, who, though one, is seen as many— manifesting as Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and others, and in the forms of Īśa, Īśānī, and so forth;
he who is the presiding deity of the supreme knowledge (paravidyā) and who reclines upon the beloved of Brahmā.
Salutations to the Lord of the Gītā-Upaniṣad, salutations to the Lord of Jayantī.
(8) Repeated salutations to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is dear to Ekādaśī, who delights in worship, the Lord of Mahālakṣmī, and the Master of Devotion. (9)
Salutations again and again to the Lord of Muktā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Gaṅgā;
salutations to You, the Lord of devoted wives and the Lord of Rukmiṇī.
You are the sovereign of the wish-fulfilling cow, You are the Lord of the Earth, and You are the Lord of Rati.
You are the Lord of Sovereign Powers, the Lord of Consciousness; may He grant welfare to those who serve Him.
(11) O Beloved of Kamalā, Lord of Goddesses, Consort of Mohinī, Master of Siddhis, Lord of Urvaśī, Lord of Buddhi, Lord of Pārvatī—bestow auspiciousness! (12)
O Lord of initiation, O Lord of pastimes, O Master of Nārāyaṇī!
O Beloved of Virajā, O Blessed One, O Lord of Vṛndā, grant me peace!
O Beloved of Sarasvatī, O Beloved of Svarṇarekhā, O Lord of Sitā!
O Devikeśvara, establish the Tulasī grove and grant peace.
May you be Vibhāvaryadhinātha, Mūrtīśvara, Jayeśvara, Gomatīśa, and Mauktikeśa; may you be the bestower of gold. (14–15)
O Lord of the beloved friend, O Lord of the Godāvarī, O Lord of Kapilā!
O Lord of Dhātrī, O Lord of Svarṇagaurī, be the bestower of all things.
O Lord Laliteśvara, O Lord of Raṃbhā, O Lord of Kumudvatī, O Master!
O Lord of Śītalā, O Beloved of Umā, grant us constant well-being!
(17) O Lord of Hemanta, O Lord of Nanda, O Master of Peace, O Lord of the Arts, O Lord of Nandinī, O Lord of Durgā, O Lord of Vijayā, grant us peace! (18)
O Lord of the twilight hour, lover of musk, sovereign of the fortunate, bestower of boons upon Sāvitrī, you who mount the swing and partake of the fragrance of flowers;
O Lord of the Sun, Master of the celestial paintings, salutations be unto you!
O Lord of the full moon, O Brahmā, O Mādhava, beloved of Śāradā;
O Lord of the *mañjarī*, O Beloved of the circle of Yoginīs, grant me peace!
O Lord of the Beloved, O Lord of the Auspicious, O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Lord of Aruṇā! 2.1.20–21.
O Lord of Joṣṭrī, O Lord of Śabarī, O Lord of Pampā, O Lord of Gālavī!
O Lord of Yājñasenī, O Lord of the Earth, may victory be yours, O Keśava, protector of Padmāvatī and Lord of the well-yielding cow! 22.
O Acyuta, who took Bhārgavī by the hand; O best of lotuses; O Lord of Śrīmatī; O husband of Jaratkārvī; O Lord of Līlāvatī;
O life-breath of Kalāvatī; O Lord of Kadalī—may victory be yours! (23–24)
O Lord of Kāntimatī, O Lord of the Yamunā, O Lord of the Revā;
O Lord of Vardhinī, O Lord of Sumitrā, O Lord of Puṇyanaidheyikā;
O Lord of Bandulā, O Lord of Suśīlā, O Lord of Mānasā, O Janārdana!
O Śarmavatīśvara, O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhavīśa, homage be to you!
(26) O Karṇotpaleśa, O Lord of the Dīrghikā, O Lord of the Akṣamālā, O Lord of Udumbarī, O Sovereign of Ṛtambharā, may victory be yours! (27)
O Lord of Badarī, O Lord of Kubjā, O Lord of Haimī, O Consort of Maṅgalā!
O Lord of Mahāvedī, O Lord of Kṛṣṇā, I meditate upon You within my heart.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
And He who exists in the divine imperishable abode, indeed divine, being served by infinite liberated souls,
shines resplendently in that supreme imperishable realm.
Thus, he descended upon the earth;
for He is the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, known by the names Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He, who is meditated upon in the heart by the residents of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha during their morning worship,
has now [descended] upon the surface of the earth through his mercies.
Indeed, in the land of Surāṣṭra, at the pool named Kuṅkuma,
he attained the state of being the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇā in the home of the virtuous Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī. (3.1)
Since I, though most perfect, have become Kṛṣṇa, the ancient Lord of Rādhā,
and since I have indeed become the Lord of Lakṣmī as well;
The high-souled Lord of the abode of Vaikuṇṭha,
from whom even the residence on Kailāsa originated, and from whom even the abode of nectar originated.
From whom even Avyākṛteśa arose,
from whom Hiraṇyagarbha also arose,
and from whom Śrī Badrikeśa was likewise born.
For it is from him that the dweller in the Ocean of Milk was born,
and from him also was born Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the abode called Śveta, who is indeed the husband of Kamalā.
O Rādhā, since even the lords of countless abodes become [subordinates] of Hari,
the God who is the Self, one should chant the praises of His qualities.
I say, O Rādhā, of the Supreme Lord:
"The glorious Puruṣottama, who is higher than the highest and the cause of all causes, has been praised by you. (36)
I remember that ancient Lord Puruṣottama, the sovereign of all incarnations;
and that which was declared as the one hundred [verses] joined with the twelve [syllables]. //36//
I always bow at the feet of the divine women, the principal consorts of the Supreme Lord; salutations again and again to their husband. 37.
Having first appeared before me, you were gazed upon by me along with the Supreme Lord;
indeed, the abode known as Goloka was bestowed upon me for our dwelling.
O Rādhā, salutations to you for the sake of this pastime.
After that, he by whom Nārāyaṇa was made well-united with Lakṣmī and beheld— [to him I offer salutations].
Salutations to that Supreme Soul, the Giver, who bestowed upon him the abode known as Vaikuṇṭha;
and yet, having assumed the form of Śambhu—
Salutations to the one who possesses all virtues, the bestower of a dwelling, who again bestowed that abode known as Kailāsa which was gazed upon by Satī with equanimity. 2.1.40.
Śrī Rādhikā said: O Kṛṣṇa, O Beloved, O Ocean of Mercy, O Supreme Lord, O Eternal One!
You who are known as the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Soul, higher than the highest. (41)
Where the Upholder of Dharma descended upon the earth, served by his qualities, lordship, opulence, and so forth, as well as by his beloved associates and ornaments;
there, one perceives his form, his qualities, his appearance, and even his sovereignty.
Tell me of all those divine pastimes that bestow liberation and grant the welfare of the world.
I wish to hear about that Lord who resides in Goloka, where our own birth shall take place upon the surface of the earth. ||43-44||
I wish to hear about that cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), that world, and that supreme, purifying place, together with all His own consorts; please speak of that,
as well as of the wives of Śrī Hari, who are His very forms and serve Him.
The discourse concerning those whose very nature is manifestation leads to liberation for embodied beings.
He who knows his own form does not know the Root; he knows nothing at all. Therefore, O Beloved, tell me about that. (46–47)
"I am Māyā by nature, bearing half of your body.
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of that Supreme Person who reclines upon you;
I always behold that Supreme Lord within your form at dawn."

Tell me of that Supreme Person, Kṛṣṇa, who dwells in your heart, who laughs with exceeding brilliance, who draws my mind away, and who is an ocean of beauty and loveliness, though you yourself are dark-hued while he is white-complexioned. (2.1.49–50)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā! I shall describe Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), into whose very form millions of Kṛṣṇas like me are indeed absorbed. 5.1.
He in whose form millions of Nārāyaṇas are dissolved—
such is the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Parameśvara. Indeed,
from the hair-pores of whom the primordial oceans and the earth arise.
Innumerable incarnations arise from His form;
infinite manifestations known as *vyūhas* remain merged within Him, Hari;
and infinite glories likewise abide in His sovereignty. (53–54)
O Rādhikā, within whose splendor the abodes such as Goloka and others always reside, having been brought together in equal measure;
and from a single ray of whom all manifestations come into being.
O Rādhā, how can I describe that form which is directly witnessed by the eyes?
Even if he were to enter my abode by chance while I am alone, the entire Goloka, along with me, would have its splendor eclipsed by him. (56–57)
Her one wife— whether Lalitā, Jayā, Muktamāṇikī,
Prabhā, Lakṣmī, or Pārvatī— has arrived in your presence.
Because her splendor has eclipsed you with its own brilliance, you have become my wives.
O Rādhikā, how can I describe such a form among all forms, a form that transcends all forms? It is beyond the reach of the eyes and not within the range of words.
Even the jewel of His crown outshines the body from which it arises. (2.1.60)
He alone is capable of bestowing splendor upon all luminous beings;
I constantly meditate upon that beginningless, infallible Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, even the other inhabitants of the celestial realm meditate upon that Lord.
O Rādhā, I meditate upon that Supreme Person, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, who is an ocean of the waters of great bliss,
the causal source of all incarnations, and higher than the highest. (62–63)
In the corner of whose single eye, in her side-glance, and in the center of her lips,
all aesthetic flavors, all desires, and all joys abide;
and in whose belly dwell the supreme abodes of the Great Lords.
The cosmic arrays (vyūhas), manifestations (vibhavas), and descents (āveśas) dwell there as the refuge of happiness;
and his infinite qualities, which abide in the state of unsurpassed excellence, exist in embodied form within his heart and other limbs. (65–66)
I meditate upon that Hari, whose fingernails are the source of creation, within whose nails resides the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and from whose hands the lords of the world emerge;
O Rādhā, you too should always meditate upon Him, the Beloved who is even dearer than your own lover.
He who is my beloved is your beloved; that very Lord is your husband.
Meditating upon Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, become a bestower of good fortune.
By serving that Supreme Lord, become a possessor of unbroken prosperity.
Having worshipped and served him, become one who is wise regarding your own true nature;
you are his imperishable abode, while I am the Supreme Abode itself.
His residence is always in me; therefore, he has been seen by you within me.
He alone is in my heart, and I dwell within your heart.
O Rādhā, if you are the eternal will residing in the hearts of all,
then you are indeed said to be composed of all things, and I too am composed of you.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is composed of the mind and is beginningless, is thus described.
The one Reality, the Supreme Brahman, is established in this way as twofold;
it is also established as threefold, fourfold, or even infinitely manifold. (73)
That which is woven by the Lord with that thread does not exceed it;
for there is no separate existence for it, since he is its inner self.
Yet, in the supreme abode, when there is distinction, he is the sovereign of all.
Knowing this, one should worship and meditate upon that Supreme Lord,
the Blessed One among the blessed, the Deity of deities,
the Great Sovereignty among lords, and the Incarnator of incarnations. (76)
He who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the protector of protectors;
the creator of creators, the supreme protector of protectors;
the destroyer of destroyers, and the very object of meditation for those who meditate upon Him. (77–78)
The supreme goal of all that is to be attained, the consciousness of all forms of knowledge, the source of all lords, the protector and abode of compassion for the merciful,
the most gracious among the gracious, and the stainless among the stainless.
He is the most pure among the pure, the divine among the divine, the Lord;
the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the highest dharma among all dharmas;
the ultimate peace among peaceful things, and the source of joy among all joys. (2.1.80–81)
The foremost of festivals among festivals, the most beloved among things dear,
the most charming among lovely things, the auspicious abode for those rich in love;
the supreme object to be worn among things to be worn, and the best of the virtuous among the righteous.
The foremost of ornaments among ornaments, the highest perfection among perfections;
the supreme virtue among virtues, the best vow among those who observe vows; the ultimate truth among all truths, and the most cherished among all that is desired. (82–84)
One should contemplate the highest truth among truths, the reality of the real,
the foremost of the imperishable, the preeminent essence among essences,
the supreme food of the Vedas, and the highest recitation of all recitations. (86)
The supreme recipient among all gifts, the supreme oblation among all burnt offerings;

the highest austerity among those who practice austerity, and the most excellent sacrifice among all sacrifices; the great-grandfather among the ancestors, and the radiant Vedic seer among the ṛṣis. (86–87)
One should worship the illustrious Puruṣottama, the most transparent essence among the pure;
the supreme Rādhā among those who are Rādhās; the highest prosperity among the wealthy;
the imperishable substance among riches; and the eternal abode among dwellings. 88.
One should worship Him, the eternal support of pillars, the seed of seeds;
the inexhaustible ship among ships, the inexhaustible mine among mines;
the fierce strength among strengths, and the supreme eye among eyes. (2.1.89–90)
One should always remember the Lord, the Knower of All, the observer of celibacy, who is the supreme state of meditations, the pervader, and the unifier;
he is the supreme vigor among all powers and the source of all majesties. 91.
He is the supreme lord who attracts all things that attract;
he is the giver of refuge among those worthy of refuge, and the forgiver among the forgiving.
Likewise, he is the courage and invincible heroism of the steadfast, the brave, and the unconquerable. (92–93)
One should always worship Śrī Hari, the supreme measure among measures, the mother of those who give birth, the nourisher of those who sustain,
the dissolution of dissolutions, and the highest treasury of all treasuries. (94)
O Rādhikā, I always worship the self-restraint of those who possess self-restraint;
from whom Mahākāla was born as the ordainer of limits, and from whom indeed Prakṛti and Puruṣa arose by His divine play. 95–96.
Because the name "Mahāpuruṣa" was first applied to him in ancient times; because Vāsudeva arises from dwelling [in all];
Aniruddha is the progenitor; and Pradyumna is the bestower of nourishment.
I bow to that Saṃkarṣaṇa, the drawer-away, who is my Lord.
Indeed, all beings are His feet, subject to the control of Saṃkarṣaṇa; the entire creation rests in the hand of Saṃkarṣaṇa like a flower. (98–99)
By whose grace the measurement of the body exceeds the creation itself,
and by whom the entire creation shines forth like the tip of a mace within its scabbard;
he whose servant’s servant is such a Gadādhara (the Mace-bearer).
I worship that Supreme Lord, the Lord of all, the husband of Rādhikā.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even speaking of this, one shall become a dweller in the supreme abode; therefore, O Rādhikā, always worship Him! (101–102)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Universal Sovereignty of the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama-Nārāyaṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 2 Section 2 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*: The Tretā-yuga-santāna.
Chapter 2.
[Author: Chapter 003.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe Māṇikīśvara, which bestows peace.
From me you arose, and from you the golden Puruṣa was born;
from him Mahāviṣṇu was produced, and from him the Virāṭ was born.
From the Virāṭ, the cosmic eggs endowed with eightfold repetition were produced.
From the navel region of Vairāja, a stalk joined with the Creator of the Universe emerged there in the water; that egg was then entrusted to Brahmā. That single egg measured fifty crores of yojanas.
The golden [egg], joined with its pedestal, was pervaded by splendor and possessed an auspicious exterior.
Then, through his yogic power, Brahmā fashioned the worlds within it—numbered fourteen—situated one above the other. (4–5)
In the center stands Mount Meru, the great mountain, which is also called the supporting pillar;
Brahmā himself fashioned it, for it is considered the support of all other worlds.
Just as the spinal column is in the body, so is Meru the sovereign in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
And from the body of Vairāja,
water was produced there; from his navel, a lotus arose, and within it, Brahmā along with the cosmic egg developed for a full thousand divine years in every respect.
And when the water produced from himself had become his disciple, Vairāja remained for a thousand years.
Now, because he was born from the Golden One (Hiraṇmaya), that Vairāja is so called;
and that Golden Womb (Hiraṇmaya-kośa) also emerged from the middle in two ways.
Those two were born as portions of the beard and remained in the great waters.
Just as a young bird, once mature and with fully developed limbs,
emerges from outside after breaking the egg, so too did the Virāj emerge from that [waters].
Having cast [the embryo] into the water, he sleeps there while remaining within it; at that time,
the two portions of the eggshell that remain in the water as tufts [of membrane] become moistened and cooked by the water for many thousands of years.
Then two Asuras were born from the two tufts of grass that had been cooked in water:
one named Hiraṇyakūrca and the other called Hiraṇyaṇḍa. Their bodies were like silver, yet they possessed frames larger than the cosmic egg.
Hungry, rich in strength and vigor, firm and equipped with maces and armor,
they roared with great sounds, brandishing their own maces,
churning the waters, and tearing asunder the thighs. (15)
Thundering in all directions and terrifying even the great lords,
laughing and emitting loud bursts of laughter with playful ease,
they then looked about there in the ocean for things to eat.
Running about and seeing their reflections in the water and other surfaces, they mistakenly took them for food; yet, failing to find it, they fell into despair.
Even upon searching, the two did not find any food produced from the water.
Then they approached to devour the sleeping Vairāja;
at that time, he was held by one on the head,
while he was held by the other from the feet in the midst of the water.
Having lifted them up from that place, both were prepared to depart. But Vairāja, beholding those two great asuras who resembled himself—
both of them dark in nature, invincible, and striving to devour him— [reflected].
He remembered his own progenitor, Mahāviṣṇu, the refuge of all;
and, tormented by those two who were emaciating him, he praised Him with supreme devotion.
Then Vairāja struck them both with maces and discs.
He struck them with great force using his palms and fists;
nevertheless, disregarding that, they both seized him within the water.
Then, being under their control, this Vairāja [addressed] his own father.
Becoming one-pointed in mind, he meditated for the very purpose of protection:
the lotus of Brahmā, its stalk, and the entire cosmic egg were all submerged in water, as if at the time of universal dissolution. (25–26)
Brahmā, overcome with fear, remembered for his protection the Supreme Lord, his own great-grandfather, the golden Mahāviṣṇu:
"O Blessed One, who are these two Daityas, destroyers of great rains? (27)
"Protect, protect, O Mahāviṣṇu! Destroy both of them quickly!
(28) Thus was Mahāviṣṇu—armed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and spear—repeatedly remembered by Virāja and also by Brahmā. (29)
Accompanied by iron arrows, mallets, tridents, and *śataghnī* weapons,
the Lord mounted his divine vehicle and approached the presence of the Daitya.
By him were seen two firm fragments that had arisen from the two halves.
Desiring to slay their son Vairāja, who was reclining in the water,
the powerful Viṣṇu let out a roar;
that sound pervaded the worlds of Īśa and spread throughout Goloka.
Then the unmanifest abode (avyākṛta-dhāma) was pervaded on all sides by Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, the abode known as Amṛta was completely pervaded by the one who awakens the battle.
By that sound, O Great King, the powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa [was awakened].
Having understood the battle and meditated for a moment for the sake of protecting the universe—
for the protection of Vairāja Mahāviṣṇu and Brahmā— he,
possessing a divine body, went forth as soon as he was remembered, equipped with his divine mace.
There, while the two Daityas, Mahāviṣṇu, and Virāṭ remained in the waters,
Mahāviṣṇu— having bowed down— praised the protector of creation and the destroyer of the wicked,
and requested his protection.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa assumed a terrifying form,
during which he possessed ten thousand arms;
his topknots, moreover, rose upward, pervading the entire realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Ten thousand of his feet sank into the great waters even beneath the tortoise, while in the midst [of the ocean] were millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Those stones became like balls of hail, and they turned into weapons.
Having hurled those cosmic eggs at one another with their hands,
Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others then fought with the two Asuras; indeed,
many cosmic eggs were destroyed as they were thrown against each other.
Being struck by maces, those [eggs] then shattered like powder;
yet the two Daityas, seizing those very eggs,
hurled them with great force at the mighty Mahāviṣṇu and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, moreover, struck those [weapons] as well with his mace.
Thus, a terrible battle took place between the two of them in the path of the sky.
Then Mahāviṣṇu, leaping up, struck Hiraṇyakūrca on the forehead.
Struck on the head by Hiraṇyāṇḍa, he fell into a swoon;
struck with a mace,
Saṃkarṣaṇa was filled with rage and struck Hiraṇyāṇḍa violently upon his broad forehead with the mace.
Hiraṇyāṇḍa fell into a swoon for a moment, but having risen again,
he became composed; just then, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa struck Hiraṇyakūrcaka in the chest with his mace.
His heart was indeed shattered and he died from that single blow of the mace.
Then Hiraṇyāṇḍa struck Mahāviṣṇu on the head;
Mahāviṣṇu, springing up, struck Hiraṇyāṇḍa with his fist.
Leaping up, he ran toward Saṃkarṣaṇa from behind;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa struck that asura with his mace,
and the asura likewise struck him with his mace.
Accepting that blow, he indeed let out a loud, boisterous laugh;
whirling his mace in the sky— which resembled ten cosmic eggs—
he hurled it with his hand, desiring to slay Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Mahāviṣṇu struck that mace with his own mace in the middle;
that mace broke there in the water and indeed became a hundredfold.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, equipped with his mace, rushed toward the asura.
The Asura, for his own protection, seized a massive egg consisting of fifty-six stars and hurled it at Saṃkarṣaṇa;
that [egg] was then reduced to powder by Saṃkarṣaṇa’s mace.
Then, running further, he seized another great cosmic egg;
struck by the mace of Mahāviṣṇu, it shattered into a hundred pieces.
Then, running even further, he took a third egg in his hand at that time.
Having seized it, he quickly hurled it into the heart of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
though it struck his heart, it pierced through and was reduced to powder.
Then the god Saṃkarṣaṇa became enraged at that destroyer of creation.
Desiring to kill him as he was fleeing there, the Lord struck him with his mace. Saṃkarṣaṇa pursued the Daitya’s back across the great waters,
while the Daitya also fled, seizing the cosmic egg that was nearby.
That which is situated within the Brahmā-stalk, together with its covering and Mount Meru,
along with the shell of the cosmic egg, remains within the lotus together with Brahmā; and he [Viṣṇu],
having indeed taken hold of the entire earth out of fear of Saṃkarṣaṇa, [remains there].
He fled by way of the sky, and Saṃkarṣaṇa then pursued him.
Then the asura entered the depths of the great waters,
and Saṃkarṣaṇa, following closely behind, indeed entered the water as well.
And while Saṃkarṣaṇa was seizing the great asura by the hair,
the asura then assumed a subtle form within the vast waters;
indeed, he did so out of fear and exhaustion from battle, being truly deprived of assistance.
Having entered through the eight enclosures, he went into the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
There, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the sovereign who assumes a subtle form, arrived in a mere instant, having taken Brahmā along with him. (64–65)
He established Brahmā in Satyaloka, on the highest level;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa playfully assumed a fierce form,
while Mahāviṣṇu then assumed a subtle Viṣṇu-form.
Then those three inhabitants of the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) searched for the Asura who had become invisible on Mount Meru.
Hiraṇyāṇḍa, being in the form of an egg, remained situated upon the waist of Meru.
Even though he was being sought, Viṣṇu could not be seen by the body at that time; indeed, Viṣṇu employed his yogic power and beheld him with his form concealed,
staying on a hidden part of Mount Meru’s slope, appearing terrified and greatly exhausted.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa-Rudra, assuming a subtle atomic form,
entered the flank of Mount Meru by means of his yoga-weapon;
he then seized that great Daitya, who was living in disguise.
There, by means of his illusory power, the Asura quickly became massive;
having emerged from the hand of that trident-bearing Saṃkarṣaṇa,
he circumambulated Mount Meru and fled.
Saṃkarṣaṇa also pursued him from behind with great speed.
Thinking Mount Meru to be his refuge, the Asura wandered like a wheel;
indeed, he performed one hundred and more such revolutions.
Then, by that Mudgala, who was exceedingly exhausted and desirous of death, Saṃkarṣaṇa was turned around and struck;
and Saṃkarṣaṇa, in turn, hurled his mace, which was released from his hand.
Then, indeed, the Daitya, with great force, seized the golden egg in order to destroy it;
grasping the Saṃkarṣaṇī mace, he struck Saṃkarṣaṇa.
He then fled toward Mount Meru and wandered about in terror.
Saṃkarṣaṇa followed behind him wherever he ran;
grasping his mace, Saṃkarṣaṇa struck him on the back.
As they were thus running about, the trembling of Mount Meru occurred.

With the placement of his feet, the sounds of his mace, and his roars, he caused the earth, the seven worlds, the heavens, and even the nether regions to tremble; yet Saṃkarṣaṇa’s mace, having been taken [by the opponent], fled away. (2.2.80)
Saṃkarṣaṇa took up a golden mace from Mahāviṣṇu;
with their two maces, those two fought each other upon the slope of Mount Meru.
From the blows of the two maces, Meru, the king of mountains, trembled.
All the sides of Meru were agitated on every side.
An earthquake, a trembling of Mount Meru, and a shaking of its peaks occurred;
for when the striking of Meru’s waist proceeds, it is fruitless.
Then a fragment of Mount Meru was shattered again and again from its waist;
thus, through that state of being shattered and by friction,
a fire arose there, blazing like a world-consuming conflagration up to the heavens.

Then, streams of flames produced by the blow of the mace reached as far as the rim of the cosmic egg on all sides; and together with the celestial chariots of the gods, everything blazed up on every side. (85–86)
Mahāviṣṇu extinguished the fire with nectar.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among all the inhabitants of the worlds.
Then, by the blows of his mace, fragments from the sides of Mount Meru fell on all sides.
Struck and separated, they fell individually into the sky;
some were a hundred thousand yojanas long, some ten thousand yojanas,
others twenty thousand yojanas, and others twice that.
Some were twenty-five thousand yojanas, thirty thousand yojanas,
and forty thousand yojanas; likewise,
other fragments were then sixty thousand yojanas in length.
Some were fifty thousand yojanas long, while others were eighty-seven thousand; indeed, they became so extended. Thus, the planets, dark in color, were scattered all around Mount Meru.
In the lower region of the heavenly world (Svarloka), some fragments fly up into the atmosphere;
some remain in the water, while others indeed exist in the air.
By means of attraction, they all fly upward according to their respective dispositions.
Then all the planets, along with the comets, became like stars.
On the southern side of Mount Meru, that great asura Hiraṇyāṇḍa was struck;
it then fell upon his chest, his sides, and his head.
Saṃkarṣaṇa, however, struck him with his mace while he was still breathing;
then, by the blows of that mace and by the many fragments of the mace,
the southern portion of the earth split open and flowed down from Mount Meru.
A region measuring one hundred thousand *krośas* is joined by salt waters;
therein are the Haima, Māhendra, Ūrala, and Āmrakācala mountains, as well as the king of mountains, Abrikta, and other mountains that extend forth. (97–98)
By means of the yoga of constant attraction, situated beneath that in the intermediate space are the regions of Uttarakuru, Kimpuruṣa,
and Pradeśaka; likewise, the regions named Nara are located in the southern salt-water ocean.
In that western region, indeed, there are uninhabited territories;
islands situated in the midst of the salt ocean measure ten thousand yojanas,
while others are one thousand yojanas, and still others are thousands in number but very small.
Those three southern divisions are equal in extent to Meru in terms of their prosperity.
The salt-water ocean extends for sixty thousand *krośas*,
while the portion belonging to the earth measures forty thousand *krośas*.
Thus, for a hundred thousand *krośas*, the planet remained in the intermediate space.
There, due to the passage of time and the shifting of water and land,
the middle oceanic regions were repeatedly overturned by the force of time.
Water becomes land, or water on land; a forest becomes a house, or a house a forest.
Thus, by the power of time, transformations indeed arise upon the earth.
By the conjunction of time, even oceans come to exist within the divisions of the continents.
He separates the water and the food from Ajanābha in the west (106).
He also separates Siṃhāraṇya, which is submerged in water and uncovered;
and Śukla-kuru, submerged in water, and Kinnarīyaka in the north (107).
Within this golden terrestrial sphere, they divide the world into the regions of Kiṃpuruṣa, Rāmaṇīya, and Jambū;
in the center lies the depressed region of Akhātadeśa, along with the intermediate territories. 108.
Wherein they divide the world within this golden earthly globe.
O beloved Rādhā, where Nara-Nārāyaṇa shines upon the Himālaya mountain, there,
on this very earth which is the jewel of Cānūra,
in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in Saurāṣṭra, resides Puruṣottama.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the boy Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa appeared,
born from the goddess Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, O beloved Rādhā, go there and become Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇī.
By serving Him who gave you away and to whom you belong, you shall obtain happiness;
then, by His permission, you will return again to my abode, Goloka. (112–113)
The golden egg, having perished on Mount Meru by the hand of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
that golden earth indeed came forth from within the middle of the egg.
And [the mountain] named Hiraṇyakūrca is outside the Lokāloka mountain.

And having died in the water, the earth born from that body became golden there. O Rādhā, this ancient narrative of yours regarding the earth has been told for the sake of conviction and for the sake of providing familiarity with the cosmic egg (aṇḍa).
It was there, in that sphere which is the abode of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, that the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, manifested himself.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Two Asuras, Hiraṇyakūrca and Hiraṇyāṇḍa—born from the tuft of hair on the Cosmic Egg—and the Presentation by Śrī Kṛṣṇa of Himself to Rādhikā, Occurring through Saṃkarṣaṇa, within the Extensive Genealogy of the Lord of the Imperishable Supreme Abode in the Second Section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. There are always millions of Bhūmans and also millions of Sadāśivas;
indeed, the number of Brahmāṇḍas is truly neither found nor even known.
[4] [He likewise created] the gods, the Daityas, the Rākṣasas, the Munis, the Ṛṣis, the virtuous men, and the virtuous women.
The sun, the moon, the planets, the nāgas, the mountains, the rivers, and the reptiles;
the immobile and the mobile, as well as the worlds and the guardians of the worlds; the abodes, the protectors of the abodes, the lords of the abodes, and those who dwell within the abodes.

Although the Supreme Brahman, as the inner controller (antaryāmī), exists in every way within all that has been created— including the lords of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), their protectors, and their dwelling places—
the Lord remains beyond the range of vision.
"As long as this [truth] does not shine forth for them, so long peace is not born.
(7) Having reflected thus upon the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, these incarnations, lords, and gods offered their prayers. (8)
Then, for the sake of being seen directly by those in their own abodes, worlds, and respective realms, Śrī Puruṣottama— though situated in the supreme abode—
was entreated by the inhabitants of the imperishable realm (Akṣaradhāman).
Having become the Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣarādhipati),
the two-armed Lord of the Imperishable dwells upon the great lion-throne called Akṣara, possessing a second form in the imperishable abode, and is worshipped by the Imperishable One.
The Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣarādhipa) accepts the worship, food, and other offerings made by those liberated souls who abide in the Imperishable and follow their meditative cultivation;
that Blessed One, possessing a divine form, shines resplendent in the abode of the Imperishable.
In His second form, through the desire to inscribe the imperishable [Veda],
for the purpose of bestowing bliss upon His devotees, and out of a desire to grace those who are liberated,
Puruṣottama shines forth among the imperishables and the liberated ones.
Then, O Rādhā, at my request, that blessed Lord,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, shines in Goloka according to my will.
That beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa is eternally worshipped by me.
"O Rādhā, behold my eternal form in the temple!
(16) Reciting the mantra: 'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā,' I perform japa and meditate upon Puruṣottama. (17)
For my sake, for your sake, for the sake of the cowherd women, for the sake of the cowherds, for the sake of my abode, and assuming a third form, the Supreme Person,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, indeed dwells here.
The Supreme Lord manifests in order to receive the worship of His devotees residing in Goloka and to grant them His vision;
this Śrī Bhagavān is the manifest bearer of the fourth form.
In Vaikuṇṭha, he shines, worshipped by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
Puruṣottama was requested by Nārāyaṇa for the sake of worship.

It shines in the house of Saṃkarṣaṇa, in the house of Pradyumna,

in the abode of Mahākāla, in the seat of Māyā, and in the temple of Sadāśiva.
The Lord shines in the abode of Viṣṇu, and likewise in the abode of Mahāviṣṇu;
he shines also in the house of Prakṛti-Puruṣa,
in the dwelling of Pradhāna-Puruṣa, and he shines in the splendor of Bhūman.
Thus, in the abode of Mahāviṣṇu, within the Vairāja-dhāma,

Hari remains there, worshipped, saluted, and served by them.
In the worlds and abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa,

That Blessed Lord was entreated by the sages as well as by the ancestors.

Likewise, He shines in the abode of Pṛthu and in the abode of Dattātreya as well.

and in the capital of the king of kings, the Lord resplendent.
He shines in the abode of Vyāsa, in the abode of Buddha, and in the abode of Īśa.
He shines resplendent in the city of Varuṇa, in the abode of Kubera, and in the dwelling of Indra;
in the realm of Yama, in the world of Nirṛti, in the abode of Anila, in the world of Vahni, in the residence of Sūrya, and in the world of Candra.
Likewise, in the abode of Dhruva, in the residence of Śukra, in the residence of Maṅgala,
in the residence of Budha, in the refuge of Bṛhaspati, and in the orb of Śani;
there you were propitiated by the planets and likewise entreated by the constellations.
Adored by the stars, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent upon Mount Meru, on all the continents, and on the islands of the ocean;
in the higher worlds, in the lower worlds, in the intermediate space, and among those who dwell in the sky. (37–38)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shines even among those dwelling in the mountains,

(49) as well as by others such as creepers, trees, shrubs, and grasses—
this Supreme Self, Hari, shines in that house, being entreated by them all. (2.3.50)
In the remaining houses— those of Kamaṭha, the Dānava, and the Daitya—
the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa shines, worshipped within those dwellings.
O Rādhā, He dwells in the abodes of devotees and within the hearts of devotees.
The beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendently in the abodes of the liberated women, in the homes of the maidservants,
in the realms of the sovereign ladies, and in the palaces of the goddesses. (52–53)
She shone in the palaces of devoted wives, in the hermitages of virtuous women,
in the dwellings of householders, and even among beautiful caves;
she resplended in the hermitages and homes of holy yogis.
In the hearts of maidens, in the dwellings of yoginīs,
in the abodes of the Mothers, and even in the pavilions of her friends—
the beloved husband shines resplendent upon the couches of his wives.
Requested by those inhabitants of each respective world, the Blessed Lord Hari— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—
manifested as the two-armed Supreme Lord in accordance with their desire and for the sake of fulfilling their wishes. (57)
Just as he is the locus of the forms, character, and qualities desired by his devotees,
the divine Lord Śrī Mahāprabhu shines forth assuming a celestial form.
He is worshipped by all, and he is propitiated by all.
Everyone remembers him in the morning; everyone always worships him;
and everyone entrusts to him whatever they themselves desire.
Therefore, everyone seeks from him prosperity, power, and wealth.
Without him, no one’s effort can succeed when directed toward anything else.
He alone is remembered as being present in both adversity and prosperity.
In every creation that arises, lords, gods, and humans are born.
During a great calamity, they pray for the protection of the cosmic eggs;
then, for the sake of destroying their misfortune, He is born there.
At times, out of compassion, He who is subservient to His devotees is born in the world.
Compassion, however, is the primary cause that bestows yoga upon living beings and upon himself.
Through compassion, he goes before, shines forth, and becomes manifest to embodied beings.
Having acted thus, the Supreme Person [manifests] through compassion throughout all the universes.
At the beginning of creation, he appears resembling the entire cosmic egg;
sometimes among gods, sometimes in a lineage of sages or humans,
and sometimes among the movement of animals, assuming a form at will.
On land, in water, in heaven, in a shrine, in a forest, in a house, or in the expanse of the sky;
even in a palace or on a battlefield, he manifests as he desires.
For the sake of his devotees’ welfare, he takes up residence according to their mental inclinations.
O Rādhā, where the Yamunā is, where the Gaṅgā flows,
where Mount Raivata and the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa are located;
where the three divisions formerly existed within Goloka when it was divided.
There, out of compassion, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari took birth in the first age at the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, in the house of Gopāla and Kaṃbhārī. (2.3.70–71)
I was born in the house of Vasudeva, and you were born in the house of Vṛṣabhānu in Kalāpura. Goloka, which consists of hundreds of thousands of krośas, is divided into Khaṇḍagoloka.
Indeed, he was purified by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. In the month of Āśvina, during the first fortnight, on the eighth day of the dark half,
the Lord Hari was born there upon the bed of Kaṃbharā.
For the sake of providing all forms of protection, for the attainment of all prosperity,
for the purpose of bestowing auspiciousness and for the purification of embodied beings—
there, the Lord Hari desired to go out of compassion.
He dispatched his attendant Ānarta to the earth and commanded me to give him the jewel. Consequently,
I presented the jewel to that high-souled Ānarta.
By him, the western region of Saurāṣṭra on earth was made divine.
At that time, I, Kṛṣṇa, a twice-born man devoted to his wife, was sent there;
likewise, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāviṣṇu were also sent.
And you, O Rādhā, became the embodiment of Mahālakṣmī—
devoted to your husband, highly fortunate, and one who has practiced austerities for many years.
And I too am devoted to the vow of a husband, known by the name Gopālakṛṣṇa.
There, a divine brāhmaṇa was born, a promulgator of the Vedas and Śāstras.
O beloved, at that time, I bestowed the embryo upon Kambharā for you.
Indeed, that divine bestowal of the embryo was merely for the purpose of filling the wind.
At that time, Kambharā bore only what was visible as her womb-dwelling.
In that age, creation arose from mere volition;
what need is there to speak of dwelling in a womb? My description follows the conventional method.
O beautiful one, Hari, who had been so intended, arrived there;
he took up residence in the heart of the father and the womb of the mother,
just as a child receives its first sight upon birth.
There, the bed became brilliantly radiant, and the quarters of the sky grew luminous.
(85) The principal incarnations, having arrived, respectfully showered down flowers, sandalwood paste, and parched grain. (86)
Then the female friends dwelling in each of the celestial abodes arrived there;
with their voices sweetened by song, they sang while their eyes were closed in rapture.
They magnified the Lord of the Goddess, the Sovereign of Brahman, the Perfect Master.
And all the goddesses and maidens of creation arrived there;
having beheld the face of Hari, they, with hearts full of joy, repeatedly offered their blessings to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The lords, the world-protectors, the liberated ones, the lords of the gods, and the gods,
as well as the Apsarases from the lake of Brahmā, all arrived.
Having paid homage to their beloved Lord, they performed a dance with great devotion.
The Gandharva women, the celestial Gandharvas, the forest-dwellers, the hosts of Kinnarīs, the Vidyādharīs,
and even the Gopīs and other liberated women arrived;
they played musical instruments and rejoiced upon beholding that Lord.
The Mānavī women dwelling on the earth, having arrived and performed auspicious rites,
beheld that Supreme Person and addressed him with gentle words.
So too did the Nāginīs, other goddesses, and those born of animal and human wombs.
Other divine and non-divine beings, including those dwelling among the grasses and other plants, gathered together.
Beholding their beloved, the supreme and most lovely Great Lord in the form of a child,
they all attained bliss and honored Him with unblemished offerings.
On that earth, a most magnificent festival took place there,
renowned everywhere throughout the universe and in other creations.
[There were beings] with infinite heads, with a hundred thousand heads, and with ten million heads.
The Parameṣṭhins, with hundreds, tens of thousands, and millions of heads,
as well as the Viṣṇus and Rudras, and their wives by the millions,
came to Kuṅkumavāpikā to behold the Lord. || 97-98 ||
Having received his vision and obtained his blessings, they returned happily;
then the Blessed Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
revealed himself to the people as residing in the supreme abode of Akṣara.
Possessing a divine form, situated in the supreme abode, two-armed, and most excellent;
having the nature of ten million Kṛṣṇas, consisting of ten million Nārāyaṇas,
having the form of ten million Vairājas, and equal to a thousand Mahāviṣṇus.
He revealed Himself as the Lord, endowed with infinite power, capability, and qualities, charming, two-armed, and youthful.
O Rādhā! Having thus displayed His divine form in the state of a child, He manifested His boyhood.
And once again he revealed himself, and the great lords of the gods worshipped him.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord Nārāyaṇa Puruṣottama’s Existence in Embodied Form within All Creations and His Manifestation through Grace in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in Saurāṣṭra," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 4 [Author:
Chapter 005 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā: a truly great festival has taken place there in the house of Kambharā, as well as in the homes of those residing in Saurāṣṭra.
Having learned of this, the guardians of the universe, the lords of the directions, Īśvara, and the others [have arrived].

Mānavas, gods, and goddesses, all moving through the sky, arrived by way of the celestial path in their aerial chariots for the sake of seeing [the event]. The sky became completely covered with those divine and radiant vimānas.
In the house of Kambharā, there occurred a rain of flowers, a shower of sandalwood paste,
and indeed a rain of unbroken grains (akṣata) for those who had gone to the divine abode.
Then, drops of divine saffron fell from the sky.
Shouts of victory, sounds of musical instruments, and songs arose in the sky.
It was as if another Goloka, or another Vaikuṇṭha,
or the unmanifested second realm, or another imperishable abode had appeared.
Likewise, the sacred field named Kuṅkumavāpī became equal to the realm of Kāma;
there, the incarnations, the lords, and the gods offered hymns of praise.
Having prostrated and beheld him in his supreme form, they presented their offerings.
We bow to that Supreme Lord, from whom we have arisen, by whose sovereign power we enjoy our dominion, and under whose control we always remain;
who is the true essence and the transcendent form, dwelling within all abodes. (8–9)
Out of compassion for the protection of the world, we bow to the Lord, the possessor of Dharma, the Supreme beyond the supreme,
the Child, the son of Kambharā-Lakṣmī;
he whose sovereign glories have no end whatsoever.
We bow to the Lord who was born from the condensed essence of all beings out of compassion.
We bow to that Supreme Person, the giver of liberation to all worlds, the giver of abodes to those endowed with merit, and the giver of heaven to those possessed of passion. 11–12.

Driven by compassion, you abide with an equal vision toward the Daitya, the Deva, the Rākṣasa, and the human; toward the Piśāca, the Nāga, the mountain, the sage, the woman, the animal, the tree, the grass, and even the Caṇḍāla.
We pay homage to you, that best of men, who shares the same father as us.
(14) Furthermore, although other sacred fields and pilgrimage sites will indeed exist on earth in future ages, they shall certainly not be equal to this one. (15)
Henceforth, the incarnations beginning with the Fish (Matsya) shall indeed come into being;
having reached this sacred field, they will dwell in your presence.
For it is here that you, the Supreme Lord, abide as the cause of these incarnations.
That field shall always be worthy of worship among all abodes.
Indeed, this cosmic egg is more auspicious than other eggs,
since within this fragment you shine as the indivisible, perfect Lord.
Even an emperor, if devoid of your grace, is considered most wretched;
but one joined with your grace, though lowly, acts like a sovereign.
But even the celestial realm, if bereft of your lotus feet, is defiled.
Indeed, even the earth, joined with your lotus feet, O Kṛṣṇa, has become radiant.
Blessed is this Lakṣmī, Kambharā; blessed is Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa;
blessed is the land of Surāṣṭra; and blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Blessed is Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara; blessed are those trees and creepers;
and blessed indeed are the men and women here, even down to the insects and moths, for they possess an eternal union with the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
"Victory to you, O Lord! Victory, O Primordial One! Victory, O God! Salutations be unto you! (23) Having thus praised the Lord, O Rādhikā, they all observed silence.
Then the Blessed Lord, smiling, [addressed] those gods, goddesses, and others. (24)

"Choose a boon," said the Blessed One, the abode of compassion. Vakra, having prostrated to all, [requested that his] birth be in the region of Surāṣṭra, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, where his two lotus-feet [might remain]. (25)
The goddesses dwelling in every abode likewise chose this boon:
"May we take birth as maidens and dwell by your side.
And they obtained hundreds of millions and billions of such births in Saurāṣṭra and other regions.
And likewise, O gods, the Kumāras then became manifest;
deities were born by mere volition in every house.
All those trees and creepers were indeed infinite goddesses.
Cows, bulls, and likewise other elephants and horses,
as well as deer and sacrificial animals, then possessed divine bodies. At that time, there were wish-fulfilling trees, wish-fulfilling creepers, and wish-fulfilling pillars.
In Kuṅkumavāpikā, there were always millions of wish-fulfilling gems and cows of plenty;
and there were swans, cranes, ruddy geese, cuckoos, parrots, and peacocks, as well as deities in their true forms. || 3.1 ||
Ascetics, sages, and others, as well as seasons and other virtuous beings,
were present there among the trees and other features; birds were everywhere, and rivers, streams, and sacred fords made their dwellings in its vicinity.
Embodied and unembodied beings, even those in the form of insects and moths,
having arrived on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, made their dwelling there.
Gandharvas, female singers, other goddesses, and daughters of the Nāgas also settled there.
There, possessing divine bodies, they joyfully made their dwelling in that water.
That place became a divine land, Svarṇasthala, filled with jewels— indeed,
whatever jewels exist in the ocean or in places such as heaven were present there.
Whatever riches belong to the gods on mountains such as Meru and even in their hermitages, whatever prosperities belong to the Siddhas, and whatever splendors belong to the lords of the earth—
all of these have come to the feet of Hari at Kuṅkumavāpī.
To the east of Mount Raivata, to the west of Śatruñjaya,
to the south of the Bhadrā river, and extending fifty *krośas* in circumference,
the supreme abode of the Kuṅkumavāpikā field shines resplendent. (38–39)
There, the Supreme Lord Hari shines with the behaviors of a child.
On the first day of his own birth, Brahmā arrived there, and the station of Parameṣṭhin was bestowed upon him by Śrī Hari. (2.4.40)
For the sake of protecting the worlds, Vaikuṇṭha was offered by him to Viṣṇu above the waters;
likewise, Śvetadvīpa was offered to Nārāyaṇa,
and Kṣīroda was offered by him to Śeṣanārāyaṇa.
Then Śrī Hari entrusted the sovereignty over the ancestors (Pitr-rājya) to Aryaman;
he, in turn, bestowed that supreme Vedic station upon Sanatkumāra.
Then, the status of a celestial sage (Devarṣi), born of the mind, was granted to Nārada.
The station of Mahendra was granted to Indra as king in heaven;
the station of Yama was offered by him to Dharmarāja;
and wealth-abundance was given to Kubera, while the station of Varuṇa was given to Varuṇa.

To Vāyu, Agni, Īśāna, and likewise Nirṛti, the guardianship of the directions was bestowed; and to Sūrya, the realm of light was given. To Soma, the lordship over medicinal herbs as well as the sovereignty over the constellations was granted.
To Meru he gave the sovereignty over the mountains and the sovereignty over the rivers in the ocean;
the supreme sovereignty over the principles (tattvas) was established within each respective principle.
Thus was the order in the world ordained by that Supreme Self.
Seated upon the jeweled lion-throne, the Lord offered crowns;
and they, having accepted those sovereign commands, worshipped Hari.
Indeed, prior to midday in his birth, he established the order that sustains the world.
Composed in the past by Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa: || 2.4.50 || Then, for the occasion of his birth and for the occasion of his kingdom, the father and the gods bestowed countless gifts. || 51 ||
Rudra, the performer of destruction, having attained his divine station (dhiṣṇya), bestowed gifts;
Gopālakṛṣṇa gave away gifts consisting of tens of millions of cows,
as well as jewels, golden vessels, gems, and houses.
He indeed gave away beautiful and glorious palaces as gifts;
he bestowed golden-colored vehicles equipped with canopies,
as well as divine aerial chariots drawn by elephants and horses.
With joy, he gave daughters in marriage to the Brahmins,
as well as wealth, various kinds of food, well-refined ghee,
sugar, divine garments, and ornaments set with diamonds.
He gave bodily treatments, ointments, Viṣṇu-oil, and other such preparations;
he gave rings, divine bracelets, beds, couches, and bark garments;
as well as water-pots, cooking vessels, water-jars, and coverlets.
He gave divine vessels for worship, inexhaustible vessels,
suitable draft-oxen as vehicles, and heaps of food;
with joy he gave wish-fulfilling trees, wish-granting gems, and wish-yielding creepers.

he then gave female buffaloes, yaks, cows, and black antelopes.
He gave all the household utensils suitable for domestic use;
he gave all the sacrificial vessels to the Brahmins;
and with joy, he gave divine vessels for liberation and images of the deities.
And so, at that time, he gave gifts of fearlessness and various forms of satisfaction;
he gave beautiful sacred threads, instruments for seeing from afar,
instruments for hearing from afar, and cooling pearl necklaces.
Then he gave countless sun-stones (*sūryakānta*) and magnet-stones (*ayaskānta*); he gave wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), gems that provide enjoyments, and gems that bring about destruction.
He gave flower-arrows, graceful charms, fruits, leaves, and fragrances.
He bestowed rain-bearing punishments for offenses against the earth, which were as wondrous as liquid marvels.
He gave divine mantras that possess perfected power and assume forms at will;
he gave the wonders of the *Kalpajāla* that function like the creative resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of Brahmā.
She gave radiant and auspicious Śāradā-kanyās,
as well as those suitable for Brahmins and those appropriate for sages;
and then she gave to the Kṣatriyas those things that nourish the duties of the warrior class.
Then he gave sound-machines, wind-machines, and likewise medicinal pills;
all the instruments suitable for Vaiśyas,
as well as those appropriate for servants and fixed for the various classes.
Whatever things were desired, those very things he gave at that time;
during that great festival, there was nothing whatsoever that he could not give.
[It included] that which is born of supernatural powers, that born of yoga, the divine, that arising from the mind, and that produced from the ultimate reality.
Whether it be material, elemental, mental, born of mantra, or even self-born—
whatever was desired or wished for by anyone at that time,
I have indeed granted it as inexhaustible, because that [gift] is truly imperishable.
Thinking, "May the thread of all world-dwellers attain inexhaustibility," he gave that which increases prosperity and bestows wealth. He gave beautiful wish-fulfilling dolls that grant all desires.
He indeed gave even golden rings set with jewels.
Thus, on the day of the birth of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
the illustrious Gopāla Kṛṣṇa bestowed gifts throughout the night.
And Kambharā Mahālakṣmī gave gifts from her heart:
garments, combs, mirrors, bodices, water-pots,
tunics, saffron, and lac-dye.
He gave fragrant oils, bracelets,
and chains to the women, the maidens, and the young girls;
as well as bangles, anklets, *natthīs*, and *cibūkabindvikās*.
Moon-shaped earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and anklets;
silken garments and substances that bring good fortune;
various kinds of foods and toys for children. (85)
She gave children’s seats, swings, hammocks, and cradles;
small stools, low couches, and little beds, as well as wooden bowls.
She also gave soft garments for infants and clothes for young girls. (86–87)
Water-pots, ewers, wooden troughs, jars, small vessels,
bowls, ladles, sacrificial spoons, cooking pots, and various other utensils;
as well as ornaments for the forearms bound with networks of tiny bells.
The virtuous woman gave ornaments made of charming ivory;
at that time, she also gave fields, groves, villages, gardens, and forests, as well as crops of excellent grain and delicious foods. (2.4.89–90)
Sindūra, parched grain, threads, and even golden cīpiṭa ornaments;
golden necklaces set with jewels and garlands adorned with diamonds; armlets, crowns, crest-jewels, and veils. || 9.1 ||
She then presented copper boxes, trays, chowries, and fans;
she gave blankets, cotton balls, protective cords, and so forth;
and she offered milk, curd, ghee, clarified butter, sweets, and mixed delicacies.
Having prepared the drinks and solid foods, she took up fragrant substances;
she offered ground rice, parched grains, and *jārikā* and *barjara* sweets.
She also gave wheat, mung beans, black gram, kidney beans, and other such grains.
He gave barley, rice, chickpeas, grain-particles, and horse-gram;
at that time he gave jaggery, honey, sesame seeds, and honey-mixtures (madhuparka).
He then gave clarified butter, fresh butter from a cow's first milk, and milk-rice porridges.
Whatever came to his mind at that time, he gave that very thing as a gift.
The gods, the Daityas, the sages, and human beings were filled with wonder;
even the lords and the guardians of the world, having seen this, were struck with amazement.
And he gave him golden juice-vines and medicinal herbs such as *sandhinī* and others.
Having taken the divine vines and the pills made from divine seeds and other ingredients—all of which grant the power to assume any form at will—the women obtained those pills. (98–99)
The masters rejoiced exceedingly and bestowed their blessings;
a great festival arose through the distribution of food and expressions of praise.
Beholding Śrī Hari, the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds were filled with joy.
Having accepted gifts and offerings according to tradition,
and having partaken of food and drink together to attain eternal satisfaction,
they took with them the gifts and honors they had received and went to their own worlds at evening.
Then, after birth, the cutting of the umbilical cord and other rites were performed;
Mahāmāyā herself acted as the wife of the Great Being.
She also performed the purificatory rites of bathing, the sacraments, purification, and even the service of the sacred fire.
Like the world of the gods, Janaka also made the entire interior of the lying-in chamber suitable for bathing and other rites;
the Blessed One, though born like an infant, slept in yogic slumber (yoganidrā).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnations of the Supreme Lord, the Arrival of the Lords, World-Guardians, and Subjects, as well as Various Gifts, on the Birthday of the Supreme Lord," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
