Chapter 5 [Author:
Chapter 006 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā: the goddess who is the mental service of the Supreme Lord is renowned by the name Ṣaṣṭhī; she is considered the protector of children.
She, possessing a divine form, is eternally present and performs [her service].
She is like Rādhikā in beauty, like Lakṣmī in nurturing;
she is like Pārvatī in love, like Ramā in dalliance;
she is like Kamalā in touch, and indeed like a mother in affection. (2–3)
Equal to Dhanvantari in medical science, she serves Hari;
for one who exists in a state of childhood and is powerless,
her protection— like that of one who is truly incapable— is according to the reality of the elements and other principles.

The goddess Ṣaṣṭhikā provides protection against obstacles consisting of both the formed and the formless. (5) Since there is no obstacle for one who is already free from obstacles, how could an obstacle exist for him? Nevertheless, being born of the mind and acting by the will of the Blessed One, she imitates the worldly custom. (6)
On the sixth day, he caused the worship of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī to be performed by Brāhmaṇas;
and his father indeed had the protective rite (rakṣā) performed by the sage Lomaśa.
There were gifts of food and also sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) of gold.
And Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa performed the worship of the planets arising from the cause of Para-Kṛṣṇa; furthermore, the Brāhmaṇa caused the worship of the gods, the worship of the Brahmins,
and also the worship of the Mothers to be performed.
The Brahmins from Saurāṣṭra, having eaten that which grants infinite satisfaction,
bestowed blessings upon the boy and, having received wealth,
performed the sacrificial rites on the auspicious thirteenth day of the sixth fortnight, and they celebrated a festival.
At night, the goddesses performed a dance in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The Lord, possessing a divine form and having assumed the state of youth,
watched their dancing, service, songs, and so forth, smiling indeed.
Then, when the night had passed, in the morning that child became [asleep];
though ever-watchful, he slept upon his mother’s very bed.
Ṣaṣṭhī protects her beloved Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Every day, the mother gratified her son with the drinking of milk.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, she laid him to rest upon her side on a divine,
enchanting, and moon-bright golden couch.

The sixth [mother] remains awake for the sake of protection, while the mother sleeps with slumber. Then, during the night, the Daityas dwelling in Pātāla arrived, assuming forms at will in the likeness of women, like young maidens. (16)
Having become divine goddesses, they went to delight the child.
Meanwhile, those who had gone to Pātāla and were informed by the Daityas—who had arrived for the birth festival and then departed—concerning the form of the Blessed One, [remained there]. (17–18)
Then, filled with fear, they indeed made this representation:
"O lords of the Daityas, all of you, know that there is a great lord upon the earth,
who is the cause of all incarnations and who abides in the supreme state beyond all abodes."
And he took birth upon the earth for the sake of eternal residence.
Indeed, that Hari will strive from time to time for the destruction of our forces, and he will assume incarnations again and again. (2.5.20–21)
And the destruction of our family shall come about through his disguise;
he will provide protection for the gods and bring about the destruction of the Daityas upon the earth and other realms.
He alone is the primary cause and the reason for all these manifestations.
Upon the destruction of that [tree], there will always be the destruction of the enemies of the Daityas.
When the root is destroyed, how can there be branches? Therefore, one should cut down the root.
As long as this [tree] remains a mere sapling, its cutting will be possible. (23–24)
Disease, the enemy, and fire must indeed be destroyed while they are still small;
once they have taken root, these three destroyers become difficult to overcome.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the cause of our enemies.
The enemies are merely gateways for that Supreme Person.
This Supreme Lord is the root of all incarnations; in every kalpa, he indeed becomes the cause of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and the others. (26–27)
Upon his destruction, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Paraśurāma,
Hayagrīva, Vāmana, Vāsudeva,
and the others will never again appear; therefore, he must certainly be slain.

Even though one who possesses unfailing power is not slain even when he ought to be killed, nevertheless, for those who have exerted effort, some auspicious fruit may still arise. Thinking thus, one should apply effort in order to kill him. (2.5.30)
"May the host of Daityas neither be born nor perish"—
having thus formed this resolve, Kalmaṣa, Kajjala,
as well as Kaccara, Mala, Kardama, and Kledana likewise [remained]. (3.1)
Mehana, chikkana, kṣuvana, and likewise pardana;
lālana, haṃgana, ṣṭhīvana, and likewise meṣana;
mardana, nodana, kampana, and likewise sphurjatha. (32–33)
Khañjana, Śoṇaghoṇa, Kudarśa, Kucelaka,
Khātanāsa, Durgajaṅgha, Araṇyaromā, Darīśravas,
Giryaṅguṣṭha, Ayutahasta, and likewise Rasātalodara. ||34||
These and other great Daityas, having consulted with one another,
approached through that opening where Mount Raivata stood behind them;
armed with their hands as weapons, they were full of enthusiasm and intoxicated by the desire for battle.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, they were as if fearless despite being full of fear;
though stationed in the underworld, they possessed weapons, arrows, and the power of *indrajāla*;
and they were densely crowded with armies created through the magic of mantras and the sciences of the Daityas.
They lived in the Aśvapaṭṭasara forest to its west;
having gathered there in disguise, they repeatedly sought to kill the boy,
watching for vulnerabilities during the night of the fourteenth day.
Some assumed the form of cuckoos, while others took the form of owls;
some took on the form of jackals, and others the form of cranes;
some had the form of female ospreys, and others the form of cats.
Likewise, others were in the form of serpents and had the appearance of making terrible sounds;
some had the forms of variegated leaves, while others assumed the forms of *civarīs*.
There were those with the forms of mongooses and the like, as well as those having the appearance of dogs.
Taking the forms of cats, house-lizards, gadflies,
and mosquitoes, they arrived there; the Blessed One, the beginningless and supreme among the glorious Puruṣas,
remained hidden within the interior of the maternity chamber.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa knows them as well. Ṣaṣṭhī, like a child, induces sleep; she too knows them. So too do gadflies, mosquitoes, lizards, and the like, as well as cats, serpents, and dogs. (44–45)
And on that very sixth day, they were slain at night by the will of Nārāyaṇa;
through the prowess of Manasā, they died as if already dead.
Meanwhile, owls, cuckoos, jackals, cranes, and other birds were in the sky.
Those who had come to kill Hari were also dispatched by the sixty [Gopīs].
Seeing them destroyed, others then took their corpses during the night and went to that forest where their dwelling was located.
In the morning, having observed the blood-stained marks in the maternity chamber,
he purified them on the day of Dīpotsava at dawn;
then Gopāla, Kṛṣṇaka, and others had the recitation of peace-mantras performed.
Then, having fallen into distress because their friends and family members had died, they arrived on the night of the Dīpotsava festival bearing weapons;
yet, being concealed, they were indeed unable to kill Śrīprabhu out of anger. (2.5.50–51)
They led away that goddess Manasā, the destroyer of the sixty [demons].
Even as she was being carried off by the great asuras, she meditated in her heart upon her beloved husband, Mahākānta, the illustrious and most excellent lord. (52)
Then the Lord, abiding within himself, ordained her protection.
On the sixth lunar day, the Blessed One released the power of the Mahākāla fire—burning and reducing everything to ashes; by that, they were consumed.
Having abandoned that goddess, they all fled far away.
Then, from her own body, the goddess manifested an army;
likewise, there was an army of hundreds of thousands of maidens traveling in celestial chariots.
The army of those stationed on swans numbered one hundred thousand; that of those on tigers, ten million;
that of those on lions, one hundred million; and that of those on śarabhas, one hundred million.
It was adorned with weapons such as spears, javelins, and nooses, as well as various mechanical engines. (56–57)
Desiring to slay the Asuras, these maidens of fierce prowess then engaged in battle with divine weapons, their limbs remaining unhurt. By them,
many lords of the Daityas were slain there in that great forest.
Those who were thrown open [into her mouth] died, but other eminent Daityas,
grasping blades of grass in their mouths, bowed to the great and virtuous Ṣaṣṭhī;
having truly sought refuge in her, they were not slain at that time.
With their minds bent upon Natakaṇṭha, they went to that forest.
Then, millions of goddesses were repeatedly praised there as being worthy of choosing Hari as their husband for the sake of victory. (61)
She brought them all and presented them to Bālakṛṣṇa.
On the bank of the lake, her husband, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, addressed them, saying, "Choose a boon. Vakrā [spoke] to them all.
"Grant us residence, service, liberation, and likewise a husband at the sacred site named Tīrtha"—
to this Hari replied, "So be it. Thereupon, those maidens made their daily dwelling in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The Blessed Lord gave them the beautiful name Dīpāvalī;
he created for them forms composed of divine splendor, appropriate to himself. Having fashioned their two-fold divine forms within his own abode, || 65–66 ||
He sent others away, while he himself remained protected in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having bowed down, the sage Lomaśa spoke to Hari with great compassion:
"By your own will, these goddesses shall become your wives."
"Let them stay in my hermitage at the Kuṃkumavāpikā field.
They, being greatly delighted, took up residence in Lomaśa’s hermitage;
there in that hermitage, they celebrated the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava), which was equal to heaven.
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, early in the morning,
they celebrated a great festival for the divine-formed Lord in every house with various kinds of fresh grains and cooked foods.
(2.5.70) Having prepared diverse dishes of cooked food for Him whose form is celestial, they offered them.
The noble ladies offered [the offerings], played musical instruments, and performed dances.
They partook of the *prasāda* and held a great festival at night;
they indeed worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then, while they were all asleep at night, Ṣaṣṭhī protected the child.
Then the Daityas arrived once more to kill Hari;
however, they were all driven away by Ṣaṣṭhī through the power of Hari.
Then, having taken that demon Sūtaka, they went to their own abode.
Śrī Rādhikā said: "Who indeed was this demon Sūtaka, and where did he dwell?"
"What happened after that, O Kṛṣṇa? Tell me, for I am filled with curiosity.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, this great Daitya Sūtaka was born from the lineage of the Asuras."
Listen to how he appeared and where he dwells by virtue of that boon:
formerly, when there was a battle between Hiraṇyakūrca and Saṃkarṣaṇa, a lotus belonging to Brahmā repeatedly fell there. (76–77)
Then the unborn [Lord] was indeed shaken by that asura who had seized him;
trembling, he became afraid, and from the heart of Brahmā there then arose a son named Kampa, and a second one named Bhaya.
The third is named Sweat (sveda), and the fourth is named Grief (śoka). The fifth is called Distress (vihvala), while the sixth is the Cry of "Hā Hā" (hāhākāra).
The seventh is the Unsupported (nirāśraya), and likewise the eighth is the Dependent (parāyatata). (2.5.79–80)
Having gathered around Brahmā, those lords said:
"O Father, how have we come to be born from you here in this ocean?
Tell us what must be done; let us perform it quickly."

Then Brahmā said to his sons, "Go quickly against the great Asura Brahmakūrca for the sake of his destruction, so that he may become devoid of courage. Thus commanded, the sons then went swiftly to the great Asura.
Then, due to Saṃkarṣaṇa, he indeed met his death by the club while leaping toward that Brahmakūrca; however,
from the pores of his body and his senses, impurities issued forth under the influence of his agitation caused by Māra.
From his emission of semen, there arose a man named Janman;
from his emission of urine, there arose a man named Sūtaka;
and from the discharge of his waste, there arose a man named Nidhana. (85–86)
From his piteous wailing, a man named Garjana appeared in the water;
and from his groaning, a man named Durgandha then came into being.
From his womb was born an inauspicious son named Rakta.
That which was called "corpse" (śava) became impure and then turned into what is known as pus;
these undesirable elements became the arrogant Asuras. But his auspicious elements then became gold.
These sons born of Aśura, indeed filled with fear, bowed down to and praised the venerable Mahāsaṃkarṣaṇa, the refuge of all:
"Protect us! Protect us, O great hero, O powerful one who brings about the destruction of all! (2.5.90)
"We are your sons; grant us the gift of life.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa granted them the gift of fearlessness, as well as excellent clothing and food to those who requested it.
Saṃkarṣaṇa granted ten days for the birth of Nara;
let the period of impurity (sūtaka) remain in the house of that woman who gives birth.
He gave the woman who has recently given birth a dwelling apart from blood, foul odors, and pus.
Birth, impurity, blood, foul odor, and pus—
these always dwell together within the womb.
Then, after ten days have passed, they depart through the birth canal like a net into the ocean.
Thus, birth-impurities (*janmasūtaka*) and other such *āsura* states exist as sources of suffering.
This one, known as Sūtaka, then resided for ten days in the house of Kambharā according to worldly custom. (96)
Then others— namely Nidhana, Śava, and Malinaka—
then requested a dwelling, food, and so forth.
Saṃkarṣaṇa then gave all of them over to Death.
And at that time, O Kālaputra, wherever Mṛtyu may be, there these abide:
Nidhana, Śava, Mṛtyu, Malina, and likewise Sūtaka;
they remain right where the command of Kāla resides.
Therefore, all these Asuras are givers of fear and likewise givers of suffering.
(2.5.10) Now, those other sons of Brahmā, such as Kampa and the rest, having previously gone to that place where Death arrives, [remained there]. (101)
When a corpse arises, they dwell within it and then emerge from that ground;
thus have these sons been described to you as those who bring about the state of death.
Now, even there, a person named Śrāddha was created by Brahmā.

Indeed, he took up residence with his family at the place where the funeral rites were performed. Because Nimi had previously performed a śrāddha for the destruction of his own son Ātreya, he subsequently became established in the world through that śrāddha.
Thus, O Rādhā, this demon named Sūtaka has been described to you;
he dwells in the maternity quarters together with his brothers.
Indeed, those Daityas have placed this Sūtaka within the house of Kṛṣṇa.
On the tenth day, they forcibly led him to their own camp.
Those fierce-born ones deliberated for the sake of Śrī Hari’s destruction;
they gave the order to Sūtaka: "Bring the boy here quickly."
"Having taken that Lord Śrī Hari, we shall enter Pātāla;
right there we shall kill him and cause him to be slain by our own hands.
Otherwise, O best of Sūtas, we shall slay you yourself."
"Go quickly and perform your task; bring the child here at night.
You must provide assistance to the Daityas, for the bull is yours.
Having been addressed thus, Sūtaka went to the lying-in chamber.
When midnight had passed, her circle of friends fell asleep;
and Ṣaṣṭhī, too, there for a moment attained yogic sleep (yoganidrā).
Yet, by the will of the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he [remained awake].
In the darkness of the night, Sūtaka carried Śrī Hari from His place on the bed and led Him to the camp inhabited by the Daityas. The Daityas rejoiced in many ways and raised shouts of "kilakila."
Having raised their entire camp, they went to Pātāla in an instant to slay Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. They then led him to the execution hall belonging to Yama, the lord of death.
The great messenger named Śrāvaṇa, omniscient, all-pervading, and all-seeing, has come to inform Śeṣanārāyaṇa:
"O Lord of lords, O Lord of the world, O Support of the universe, O Keśava! (1.15–1.16)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is being harassed by the Daityas;
the child has been taken to the Ghātakī hut in Pātāla.
Thus addressed, the powerful and majestic Lord, who reclines upon Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk,
quickly arrived in Pātāla within a moment, accompanied by his chariot of discus-power,
and then blew his conch shell with a piercing sound.
Then, by the sounds made by the blowing conch shell,
the women of the Daityas miscarried their fetuses, and their ears were split asunder.
All the serpents, together with Śeṣa, assembled and set out for the battlefield.
Then, having taken up their weapons, they went forth to wage war against the Daityas.
At that time, the Daityas also abandoned the child and arrived to fight;
Sūtaka, devoted to the child and overcome by compassion, protected him.
Before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa were Lakṣmī, Sudarśana, Garuḍa, Nanda and Sunanda as attendants, Pārvatī, Prabhā,
Rādhā, Ramā, Māṇikyā, Mañju, Haṃsā, and others.
Saguṇā, Lalitā, Muktā, Jayā, Haimī, Devikā,
Dayā, Campā, Mauktikā, Śānti, Śāntā, and Manu—
these and other friends, having heard the sounding of the conch, were likewise liberated. (124–125)

They arrived there in Pātāla, where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was; for Sūtaka had become like a wretched man because he had committed an offense. Yet, Hari protected him in disguise, since he was indeed His devotee.
He was led away by force out of fear of the Daityas, and not by his own will.
Thus, this best of men was protected there by Hari as if in sport.
Such was the desire of Hari; who indeed is capable of warding it off?

He related how the abduction had been carried out from behind while he was in a state of ritual impurity due to birth, and how he had ensured the protection of everything; by this, Lakṣmī and the other goddesses were gratified.
They offered him their congratulations and then placed their lovely forms upon his lap.
Then, during another moment of the night, they indeed served him. A terrifying battle took place between the Daityas and Śeṣanātha;
the Daityas were pierced by the discus, rendered incapable of rising again or being reborn.
"Those who have died have all gone along with the magician;
they have reached the city of King Yama, while all the survivors have fled.
And Sūtaka, having taken Hari, departed together with Lakṣmī and the others."
Where the Lord Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Master beloved by Śeṣa, [resides]—
[there] Śeṣanātha gave the young Lord to Śrī Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa; and having bowed, he departed for Kṣīroda along with Ramā and the others.
Together with the birth-impurity, they went to the lying-in chamber on the ground floor;
meanwhile, at dawn, the roosters began to crow.
Having abandoned their sleep, they awoke to find the child Hari still sleeping.
These very beings— Mātṛ and the others— awakened the Supreme Lord;
for they were unaware of Kṛṣṇa’s nighttime activities,
since Lakṣmī had reported everything regarding the period of ritual impurity.
Then the father indeed caused the recitation of peace-chapters (*śāntiprapāṭha*) to be performed;
the members of the household considered their son to have been born anew. And on the morning of the eleventh day, for the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) attendant who was devoted [to him]...
The Blessed One indeed granted him a boon: "You shall receive divine worship.
On the eleventh day, people will truly gratify you with devotion through special divine offerings, such as ritual baths, drinks, and excellent food. (2.5.140)
"You shall become my divine narrator in the form of a Sūta.
Wherever I am, there shall be your dwelling, even in another form.
Your residence shall be among all people; of this there is no doubt. (141)
"From this day forward, your demonic disposition shall come to an end.
Thus addressed, Sūtaka became a devotee under the power of Hari; though he remained in the state of a charioteer, he proclaimed verses that grant liberation.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been described how the wonder of Hari occurred.
On the tenth day, the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) took place; I shall now tell you of that.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Protection by the Sixth-Day Rite in His Child Form, the Abduction by the Daityas through the Medium of the *Sūtaka* Man in Pātāla, the Origin of the *Sūtaka*, the Protection by Śeṣanārāyaṇa, and the Devotion and Status of the *Sūtaka*," in the second section, the Tretā Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 005 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 6 [[Author:
→ Chapter 007
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the account of Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. When the eleventh day arrived, the great sages headed by Lomaśa [approached]. (1)
Virtuous people devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, who were observant of moral conduct and vows,
arrived at the home of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa when summoned by his father. They performed the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa-saṃskāra*) according to the prescribed rites.
They performed the initial worship of the planets, the adoration of the deities, and so forth;
they reverently performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the worship of Īśa and the other [deities];
and those lords performed the worship of the Mothers and the worship of the Sages.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, known as Ūrjāṣṭamī, while the moon was situated in the sign of Gemini, he was born; therefore his name is indeed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Since he has neither beginning nor end, he is thus Anādinārāyaṇa.
He who is the Lord of incarnations is called the Incarnate One (Avatārī).
He is designated as Hari because he removes all suffering;
he is Kṛṣṇa because he draws away (karṣaṇāt) sorrows; and he is Nārāyaṇa because he resides within men (narasthatvāt).
Since he does not abide within *nara*, he is also called *Nārāyaṇa*.
He is the Lord of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and is said to be beyond the Imperishable.
He is the most excellent among persons and is therefore called *Puruṣottama*.

He is always called the "Supreme among Men" (Pumuttama), for he is indeed the most excellent of men. Because of his vastness, his all-pervasiveness, and likewise his transcendence over everything, Kṛṣṇa receives the designation "Supreme Brahman" (Parabrahma). || 2.6.10 ||
Because he is always endowed with Śrī, he is himself the beloved of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa;
he is the Lord of lords and is called the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
He is the Lord of Māyās and, as their husband, is called Mādhava.
Since Svāminārāyaṇa is the Lord of all souls,
he is therefore always dark as a rain-cloud, adorned with a parasol, and accompanied by his preceptor Śāli;
he is the Lord who is the husband of Jayā, Ramā, Lalitā, Māṇikī, and Lakṣmī.
He will be the husband of Prabhāpāravatī, Mañjuhaṃsā, and Saguṇikā;
he will be the supreme lord of one hundred and twelve noble queens, and he will also be the husband of many other millions and billions of women. (13–14)
In his hand, the bow, fish, banner, and svastika shine resplendently;
the thunderbolt, arrow, trident, and the mountain peak are upon his feet.
There are clear and auspicious lines of these sixteen marks.
On his forehead, a golden line shines as a mark of the tilaka.
At the corners of his eyes, there are enchanting red lines.
His eyes extend to the ends of his ears, and his face is radiant like ten million moons.
His lips are naturally red, and there is a sesame-like mole on his throat.
On his chest, there is a clockwise curl of hair.
Furthermore, he possesses the auspicious golden *lakṣmī* line and the *maṇi* streak.
A golden thread-garland remains upon his heart;
his nails are like the moon, while the palms of his hands and soles of his feet resemble the interior of a lotus, and he possesses four wheels.
His own auspicious conch-mark of Hari is present;
moreover, there is a wound-mark at the root of his left thigh.
Furthermore, upon his left knee and thigh, there is also a white moon-mark.
For he possesses the consciousness of lordship over ten million wives.
On his hips—that is, on the lower part below the navel—there exists the female sign;
thus he is Ardhanārīśvara, possessing the nature of both husband and wife.
Moreover, the arms of this Lord extend down to his knees;
indeed, there are three lines on each of his feet.
On the middle of his right thigh, there is the sign of a chariot.
A Garuḍa stands there, and from that line comes Nārāyaṇa.
This Lord of the Supreme does not possess a thousand arms;
rather, upon his *liṅga* there is a black sesame seed situated on the side.
Then that powerful one [placed] many [seeds] at the root of his left thigh;
he had four testicles, two on the sides and two situated below.
Thus, unshakable and strong, he was the provider of satisfaction for ten million women.
Within his abdomen, indeed above the navel, there exists a jar-like line;
like a jar, this line obstructs the breath through prāṇāyāma.
Consequently, that king of yogis may even assume many forms. (28–29)
Even in darkness, his eyes shine like the sun;
therefore, that Supreme Lord possesses divine vision.
The tip of his tongue is red, and the tip of his *liṅga* is likewise red.
The tips of his fingers are naturally red. (3.1) Consequently, he shall become a king of kings, a supreme lord. The hairs on his body are golden in color, fine, and soft. (3.2)
They shine like flashes of lightning appearing in the darkness;
then that Blessed One, Puruṣottama, abiding in the supreme abode,
[manifests] such a wondrous whiteness in his teeth.
And because he is seen to bestow luster upon his smile and other expressions, he is Narāyaṇa.
(34) Behold, both hands at the base of Gopālakṛṣṇa’s arms shine with divine golden lines; therefore, he is Narāyaṇa. (35)
A brilliant triple-fold line extends from his navel to the middle of his body;
his forehead is prominent, his eyes are long, and there is a slight curvature at the tip of his nose. His incisor buds are even and complete in number.

And his fragrance is always like that of the pārijātaka flower. It manifests in his form, in his breath as saffron-scented perfume, and even in his sweat; there is coolness, whiteness, purity, and sweet fragrance.
Even in his urine and other excretions, there is not even the slightest foul odor.
There is brilliance in the inner parts, and redness in the belly;
there is a dark hue in the spaces between the hairs and blackness in the roots of the hair.
His veins are curved, dark, red, and likewise tawny;
his vital points (marmans) are white, and his loveliness is captivating. His tenderness is like that of a land-lotus. (2.6.40–41)
Speech is his Vedic song; the musical notes and resonances belong to Śaradā.
This Supreme Self, the Sovereign Lord, is the treasury of all knowledge.
His names are infinite, and likewise his qualities are innumerable.
Indeed, his sovereign powers are infinite and beyond all calculation.
This beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shall forever attain renown upon the earth through the sages and the Saṃhitās in every way.
With many stories, as well as with hundreds of millions of accounts of wives,
with numerous incarnations, and likewise with marvelous deeds—
having spoken thus, Lomaśa, the best of sages, ceased speaking.
Then other sages as well offered auspicious blessings.
The young maidens also eagerly waited upon the beloved one.
Then his father proclaimed the names of Acyuta.
The excellent women played musical instruments and sang songs;
the female dancers performed dances accompanied by rhythmic clapping.
Then, the goddesses of all the worlds offered blessings to increase his prosperity.
They delighted [him] exceedingly during the great festival of Kṛṣṇa’s name.
The subjects and the people feasted on sumptuous foods;
and then the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa bestowed gifts.
The lords worshipped Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa and presented Him with offerings worthy of the celestial abode.
Having performed such various rites, Lomaśa and the others returned to their homes.
All the gods departed to their respective abodes, and the people went home.
Listen here, O Rādhikā: at this great festival of the Name, a great asura who dwelt in the tiger-infested forest arrived to behold the Lord. (52–53)
The asura named Sāṇa had made his abode in a mountain cave;
at that time, even the mountains where Sāṇa dwelt came to be known by the name "Sāṇa’s Mountains. Thus did they acquire their fame.
This *sāṇa* (flaxen garment) was produced previously from the urine of the Asura Hiraṇyāṇḍa at the time of his death, in the presence of Saṃkarṣaṇa. And he,
having observed the power of Karṣaṇa which is the cause of universal dissolution—
Overcome with fear, he offered praise and sought refuge;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa granted him the gift of life.
Indeed, seeing the earth divided into fragments and separated [from its stability], he [acted].
Then he went to Samaraṇyaka to take up residence there.
Having seen that vast forest extending for a hundred *yojanas* with dense trees, and within that land of a hundred *krośas*, [he saw] mountains as high as [great peaks]. (58–59)
The demon Sāṇa made his dwelling there, free from fear;
and he arrived there on the day of the naming ceremony (*nāma-saṃskāra*),
when the beginningless Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was indeed present in the house.
Sāṇa, having arrived in the form of a Brahmin and received food,
took various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and departed for the cave of Mount Sāṇa.
On the twelfth day, an exceedingly dark-minded thought arose within him.
He remembered his enmity toward his father and that child who was the cause of his death;
having identified Mādhava as Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is Saṃkarṣaṇa,
the Asura took up his missiles and weapons and arrived fully armored.
O Rādhā, in order to destroy Kṛṣṇa, his enemy in the form of a child, he became a brāhmaṇa during the day and remained there in the guise of a guest;
searching for a way to seize him, he found no vulnerability during the day. (64–65)
Those sixty maidens, having gathered together, delighted, caused delight to, and took pleasure with their beloved Acyuta without ceasing.
At night, they left him and went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then, finding a great opportunity when half the night had passed, the Asura, assuming the form of a tiger and possessing a cruel appearance,
became for a moment one of cruel deeds, cruel eyes, and a cruel roar, in order to devour the child. (67–68)
Having arrived at the maternity chamber, he let out a roar;
other roars were likewise made, causing the forest to tremble.
The entire earth shook, and the worlds, overwhelmed, fell into terror.
The mother was distraught and terrified, and the father fell into fear.
Out of dread of the tiger, the people there hid even within their houses.
At that time, there was only the cry of "Alas! Alas! at the place where Kṛṣṇa lay.
"Aha! A tiger, the very embodiment of death, has come from the forest for the child!
"May the gods and goddesses protect the Lord! thus cried the people.
"May the Protectors guard the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!"
Thus the mother spoke there repeatedly with cries of lamentation.
Just then, a tiger leaped up and seized the maternity bed;
as the beast of prey strove to seize the infant with its paw, [the child vanished].
At that moment, Kṛṣṇa appeared there as a young boy accompanied by Sudarśana.
Seeing this, his mother fell into a swoon, believing her son had been carried off by a tiger.
Indeed, Sudarśana is the supreme discus belonging to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

Released from between his fingers, it was filled with fire, intensely blazing, and possessed a thousand revolving spokes; it surpassed a hundred suns in brilliance. Then it became fierce and agitated as soon as it sought to kill the tiger.
Then, out of fear of death, the tiger leaped from the house to the outside and fled into the forest, eager to save his life.
The discus struck him on the back and burned him again and again.
Touching his back here and there, he cut it into pieces.
Being struck, that tiger leaped with great speed;
then, distressed and miserable, he cried out with a terrifying voice.
Having traveled only a *krośa* toward the southern direction,
he was slain by Sudarśana along with his tiger-bodied son.
That place where the tiger was killed is the sacred site (*tīrtha*) established by Sudarśana.
It is well known that to the south of the Aśvasarovara lake and near Kuṅkumavāpī, Sāṇa was destroyed;
his body, a yojana in height, then blazed up and was reduced to ashes by the Sudarśana fire through that very merit. ||82-83||
Having emerged from that, he then became four-armed;
indeed, he was a divine attendant, devoted, purified in soul, and freed from sin, uttering from his mouth the words, "O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! (84)
Then, under the command of Sudarśana, he quickly went through the sky toward the beginningless Kṛṣṇa;
having merged into the Lord, he then vanished.
Next, the liberated souls of the Imperishable (Akṣara), seated in celestial chariots, arrived to lead him away.

Then, at the sacred field of Śrī Hari, this [discus] emerged from the form of Kṛṣṇa and went to the eternal, imperishable abode along with Aṇa. Then the Sudarśana became peaceful and merged into the finger of Kṛṣṇa.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also slept happily. Then, at dawn, his mother and others, as well as the lords such as Lomaśa, entered into yogic sleep and performed rites for the pacification of obstacles. (88–89)
Hearing that the demon Vyāghrāsura had been slain, ordinary people recognized him as the Lord; they made the child their god and offered him worship.
And hearing this, all the maidens wept with intense distress.
Having heard of the protection and the strength [of the city], they rejoiced and arrived before him;
they beheld their beloved with profound devotion, offered auspicious blessings, and considered him as newly arrived. (91–92)
The father performed fire oblations and recitations for the sake of pacifying the obstacle;
he gratified the virtuous and others with food, drink, and excellent wealth.
The chaste woman gave gifts of clothing, ornaments, and other items to the young maidens.
He gave fodder to the cows and also abundant sweet foods;
he gave grains of flour and the like even to tiny creatures such as ants.
Having thus performed the propitiatory rites, he delighted Mādhava.
O Rādhā, thus have I described the heroic deeds of Bālakṛṣṇa, including his mother, father, other members of the family, and the group of young maidens;
by reading or even hearing this, one attains supreme liberation and heaven.
It bestows sons, wealth, and prosperity; it destroys disease.
It removes grief and obstacles, being delightful, protective, and bringing happiness.
It dispels the sorrow of women, auspicious, and increases good fortune. (97–98)
This supreme purifier, the life-story of Kṛṣṇa which ensures freedom from widowhood,
should be constantly heard with reverence by those who desire prosperity.
Within six months, the supernatural powers (siddhis) attend upon the listener.
The divine qualities beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the celestial prosperities (*samṛddhi*).

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Naming Ceremony of the Supreme Lord, the Destruction by the Discus of the Asura Sāṇa who had assumed the form of a tiger and desired to kill Hari, and the Bringing of Peace," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 6: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)*

Chapter 008 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
And listen, O Rādhā, to the wonderful marvel that occurred on the twelfth day for the beloved of Kṛṣṇa during his naming ceremony. On that day, the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇaka—
For the sake of his son, he had a beautiful swing made of sandalwood (2).
And there, he prepared a soft couch as a bed,
adorned with the finest jewels, pearls, diamonds, and other precious gems (3).
Abounding in the splendor of golden mirrors, adorned with various jewels and ornaments, beautified by golden peacocks, starlings, and other birds, and possessing excellent quadrangular courtyards;
it stands with four forms of Garuḍa situated at its four swan-like entrances.
It was draped with diamond threads and supported by pillars of pearls;
it possessed four divine creepers of flowers pleasant to the touch,
and was shaded by a central canopy from which nectar-rayed [moonlight] flowed.
By the force of the natural wind, it was enchanting with the song of the flute;
without being pulled, its movement was guided by the will of the Child.
In some places it was in the sky, in some on the ground, and in others it touched the low-lying earth.
In some places it was white and rising upward, and in others it had the appearance of gold;
in some places it moved to and fro, and in others it was naturally still.
It was endowed with the power of determining desires at will and possessed the perfection of attainment.
On the day of the naming ceremony, at an auspicious moment, the father summoned Viśvakarman and had him construct such a beautiful swing, adorned with exquisite ornaments, for his son Hari.
They placed the lordly son upon the swing with his head toward the east;
once the swing was adorned, they laid the supreme being to rest upon it.
Then the gods arrived, bringing new swings as well. ||| 11-12 ||
O Rādhā, you went there for the sake of the sleep of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, taking with you a supreme,
divine, and highly precious swing born of Goloka, adorned like the finest celestial chariot.

Lakṣmī also arrived there upon a beautiful, divine swing born of Vaikuṇṭha, which was rich with the essence of divine manifestations, fixed in the path of the sky, and supreme. Likewise, the wives of the Imperishable One came upon a most splendid swing. (14–15)
Then the goddesses,
the sovereign consorts of Mahāviṣṇu and Vairāja,
as well as the wives of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa— all of divine splendor— took up the form of a celestial lion-throne and presented it.
Those women indeed gave various swings to Bālakṛṣṇa:
square ones, circular ones, fashioned in the shape of lotuses, as well as auspicious ones in the shapes of fish, tortoises, and conch shells. (17–18)
There were couches shaped like elephants, horses, and beds;
swings in the form of single pillars, double pillars, and those with many legs;
as well as those supported by wheels or feet, made of wood or fashioned from gold.

There, Śacī arrived at a beautiful celestial vehicle made of silver, gold, moonstone, ruby, and pearl, which was supported by a single chain and remained suspended in the sky by the power of Dhruva’s attraction. (2.7.20–21)
Having brought forth that supreme [throne] made of the essence of adamant,
fragrant as the *pārijāta* tree,
flowing with nectar, auspicious, and moving like a celestial chariot, he presented it to Kambharādevī. (22)
Tārā, Rohiṇī, Menā, Siddhi, Vasundharā, and Satī [were there].
They brought various swings that were enchanting to Kṛṣṇa;
they were furnished with divine materials and produced by divine resolve. || 23–24 ||
Wherein, in every single region, the heavenly realm of Vaikuṇṭha,
Goloka, and the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma) are seen as the terrestrial sphere;
and wherein, within every single jewel, there exists [the earth] together with its oceans and forests.
There the earth is seen, as well as Mount Meru and other mountains.
At that time, in one jewel the sun appears, in another jewel the moon;
in one it shines as fire, and in another the sky is beheld.
In one place Satyaloka and the assembly hall of Brahmā are seen; in another, however, the multitude of Gopīs is beheld within a jewel;
and in yet another place there, the vast circle of the Rāsa dance is visible.
In some places, the seven oceans are seen within the gem;
likewise, in other gems, vast forests are perceived.
And within yet another gem, the great and radiant Nandana grove is beheld.
O beloved, in other jewels the netherworlds (pātālas) are seen;
in some, the ocean of milk, and in others, the circle of the nāgas.
Celestial chariots (vimānas) and all the abodes of the gods and so forth are also beheld.

In some places, the supreme assembly of one hundred and twelve wives of the Lord of the Supreme Abode is seen, who are solely intent upon His service; as well as the circle of the seven sages, the pole star, and the planets and so forth. 22–33.
Marvels are seen within certain diamonds;
indeed, in some, pure gardens are visible.
Thus, taking women who were endowed with divine splendor upon swings, [he proceeded].
They arrived and gave those very things for the sake of Bālakṛṣṇa.
The daughters of the forest-spirits, the Gandharvas, and the Kinnaras also came,
intent on dancing and singing, for the purpose of providing a swing for Kṛṣṇa.
The cowherd women gave her blankets, and the wives of the cowherds gave her small couches;
even the daughters of men gave her small rocking-horses adorned with rays of diamonds and resounding with clusters of tiny bells. (37)
The musical instruments produced pleasing sounds, and the knots of their garments were tied. (38) Having obtained this, that mother became exceedingly delighted;
and Kṛṣṇa simultaneously established his abode within all of them. (39)
Hari assumed as many forms as there were swings;
appearing himself in the form of a child, he rocked them while laughing repeatedly.
Seeing this marvel, the women were overwhelmed with great wonder.
Placing the beloved Kṛṣṇa in their hearts, they meditated upon Him as their husband and lord.
This glorious, beginningless Lord is the sovereign of the imperishable;
He fulfills all desires—what wonder is there in this? (41–42)
Then, having beheld that radiant Hari, the Supreme Brahman, those women—
whose hearts were filled with love— took hold of the Lord as he moved about tending his own herd,
shaking him to amuse Hari.
For so long as he assumes manifold forms through the resonance of the jewels fastened to the swings;
and for so long as, upon each swing, one perceives the Lord as consisting of many forms, that shall become a reflected image.
Kṛṣṇa, the performer of wonders, was not at all within their grasp;
then, having reached a state of despondency, the beloved remained as if inert.
Thus, they [perceived] Hari in many forms upon all the swings.
The charming girls remained unable to grasp it, wondering, "How is Kṛṣṇa not being found? Then,
for the sake of providing proof to them, Lalitā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Pāravatī, Jayā, and Māṇikyā— the eternal yoginīs— appeared.
He said to them all: "Listen, sisters, to the truth regarding Ādhava.
If you wish to grasp him, we shall state the evidence of Hari:
on his right hand are found a fish, a trident, a bow, and a banner."
The images should be in the right hand, while the reflections are in the left.
Do not touch the reflection with your left hand bearing its mark; instead, seize that true Śrī Hari with your right hand bearing its mark. (2.7.50–51)
Thus addressed, they held him up in that manner and lifted the Supreme Lord;
seating the Beloved of Śrī upon their hips, they laughed and made the Lord laugh again and again,
kissing the young and handsome Kṛṣṇa.
Placing you repeatedly upon their palms as if on a swing,
they lifted you up and held you, delighting you with total devotion.
Thus, having attained bliss, they made Hari partake in the swing.
Then the Lord, having withdrawn his various forms, became single-formed once more.
As for the empty swings that had been produced,
Kambharāśrī returned them all to those [deities] according to the prescribed ritual of restitution.
One swing, consisting of syllables and fashioned by Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, was left behind for the child;
it was auspicious, made of sandalwood and wood.
Those divine swings were of a gracious nature and most purifying. ||56-57||
Having taken the maidens, the goddesses of the northeast were filled with joy. Then there was one daughter of the Daitya who dwells in the Siṃhāraṇya forest;
that maiden, named Talājā, resides on Mount Tala.
Having heard of the festival, she then arrived and assumed two forms.
One was in the form of a maiden, like the daughter of Indra, richly endowed with the beauty of every limb and radiant with divine loveliness. (2.7.60)
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing golden garments and the like,
she was mounted upon a divine elephant and seated beside a divine young woman.
She then assumed a second form called Dolā, which was set with many diamonds.

It was endowed with many wonders, possessed many jewels and fine pearls, and was beautified by countless garlands, necklaces, and flocks of birds. Two lamps traveling through the sky were seen moving upward. (62–63)
That swing, supported by that [lotus], was without support, moving through the atmosphere;
its movement was produced by the heat of lamps, and it had celestial silk as its ropes.
Of such a kind, it was shaped like a lotus flower and perfectly circular.
Provided with a comfortable bed arranged in the middle, soft, and white as milk,
that swing— moving through the sky— descended toward the earth from the elephant's trunk by the gentle movement of his hand. ||65-66||
Although she had been brought down to the ground, she nevertheless remained at that time in the sky,
staying firm one cubit above the earth and not touching it.
Seeing such an auspicious swing, the celestial women then—
They were bewildered, they rejoiced, and they praised [Him] again and again.
Then Talājā, having honored Hari with saffron and unbroken rice grains,
placed Him upon the swing while standing in the presence of Kambharā.
Filled with mental impurity, she slowly took up Hari, who was sleeping on a sandalwood swing, and placed him upon her own swing;
then, striking with her palm, she sent him forth to kill his enemy, Kṛṣṇa.
Assuming such a form, that wicked woman slowly lifted the boy who was seated on the swing,
and quickly fled through the path of the sky into the atmosphere.
She traveled eight yojanas away to her own hermitage in the forest.
Then that four-armed Lord became manifest in the cave of Talājā, having recognized that this deer was desirous of killing him.
He also appeared in a second form as a child to [the goddess] who had come to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
And having resorted to a sandalwood swing, he remained there, demonstrating his state of being beyond the perceived world (cetya).
There, the goddesses delighted the Supreme Lord on the swing; since no sorrow could arise for them during the festival of the swing, he acted accordingly. //74-75//
Although he bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, that Lord, possessing the form of a child and exceedingly radiant,
caused the Rākṣasī to laugh with various jests, gestures, and the shaking of his limbs.
Seeing Hari, who was like the moon, that Rākṣasī fainted.
"This child with such tender limbs has been brought by me to kill;
how can I kill him, who is so perfectly suited for being delighted? (77–78)
"And he must not be killed; rather, he must be delighted.
Once he has grown up, he will become my firm and youthful master.
Having thought thus, she [placed him] upon a beautiful bed in the cave.
He always nourished him there with fruits, honey, juices, milk, and so forth,
and he protected him constantly.
Even as a child, he acted at all times in such a way that she remained delighted.
At that time, her resolve to belong to Kṛṣṇa became a source of merit for her.
Considering his own devotee thus purified by that, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
Mādhava, brought about the destruction of the sins of that sinful woman through her service.
She constantly accepted service and repeatedly drank the milk of love.
In this way, eight days passed; Tala waited for his daughter, who had not returned from the forest to his hermitage. (83–84)

Thinking, "I have learned that she is dead," or "she is staying in Kṛṣṇa’s house," or "she has been assaulted and abducted by another powerful man," he abandoned the hermitage and wandered from forest to forest.
When he was walking along, looking at a tree, a peak, the ground, and a mountain, he saw the footprints of a woman at the entrance of a cave.
He called out to her by name; hearing him, she was overcome with fear.
"Because he thinks, 'She was brought here by me for the purpose of execution and yet she is being protected,' my father will fall into a rage and kill me along with the child.
Having fallen into such fear, she remained silent and offered praise.
I have sought refuge in every way with the lovely, four-armed Kṛṣṇa.
"Protect me, protect me, O Hari, O beloved, O Supreme Lord, O Keśava!
My mind is fixed upon you; my father will kill me. (2.7.90)
Having thus praised that boy and placed him upon her breast, the beautiful woman then shed tears; Kṛṣṇa became firm as a youth,
nourished for the sake of destroying the Dānavas, and he held the discus.
Upon seeing him, Talajā immediately kissed her husband.
But the Blessed One, having bestowed upon her momentary bliss and rendered her divine, merged her into his own body and assumed a dark form. ||92-93||
He came out from the cave to where Tala was stationed;
Tala, however, wielding his mace, became apprehensive for his life.
Thereupon Hari blew his conch, and Tala fled in fear.
At that time, Hari vanished into the depths of the earth;
having left him there, Hari himself, accompanied by the maiden, went regularly to the *kuṅkumavāpikā* at the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having assumed two forms as maidens at that very moment,
he sent his beloved away on a swan-vehicle to her own abode;
he preserved the second maiden-form, known as Lājā.
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, she was together with other maidens;
and she, having offered the parched grain (lāja) to Kṛṣṇa, became one of divine form.
She became the auspicious essence in all worship, appearing in the form of lāja.
The celestial women constantly honor Śrī Hari with parched grain offerings;
thus that swing, which was made of *talāja*, likewise became composed of *lājā*.
By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, it remains forever in the form of a swing.
In the form of a maiden, she is the consort of Kṛṣṇa, abiding among the young girls and others;
likewise, possessing a divine form, she shines in the supreme abode.
Through her union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she assumes fourfold forms.
She remained engaged in the service of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
she was Lājā, the maiden Preṅkhā, a beautiful woman of liberated form.
Just as water from a street becomes the Ganges through contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, through union with Kṛṣṇa from time immemorial, the Rākṣasī attains liberation.
(104) But what great wonder is there here, O Rādhā? I shall indeed tell you of Hari: she who is like you will become the wife of Hari through marriage. (105)
Then the Blessed Lord, assuming the form of a child once more, approached the boy in the presence of his mother and became absorbed within him.
This was told to the great sage Lomaśa by Tālajaṅgha.
Lomaśa also related that divine matter to his parents.
When eight days had passed, the miracle was recognized by everyone;
they considered it a great wonder and performed recitations for peace.
Then, during the festival, the gods and goddesses who had arrived were fed,
saluted, honored with gifts, and sent back to their own abodes in peace.
On the thirteenth day, having gone home eight days after [the festival], [he departed].
Having understood the supreme majesty and extraordinary wonder of Kṛṣṇa, those gods and goddesses rejoiced within their hearts through their lineage;
they bowed and remembered Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in their hearts. (2.7.110–111)
Thus, O Rādhā, has this great and auspicious festival of the swing been described;
and the miracle, which grants liberation to both the listener and the speaker, has also been told.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Miracle of Liberation and Other Wonders," concerning the daughter of Talaja, the Rākṣasī Talajāra, who, though she had approached with deceit during the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s festival of ascending the swing, was nonetheless enchanted by Hari, within the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O fortunate Rādhā, listen to this narrative concerning the Supreme Person. Following the festival of the swing, the supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa..."
Thinking, "He is the one who took my daughter," the Rākṣasa named Tālajaṅgha became greatly enraged at Bālakṛṣṇa in the house of Kambharā.
Yet, for the Supreme Lord there was no suffering; rather, the suffering belonged to the Rākṣasa.
Having gone there by way of the surface [of the earth], they searched for the cave;
and those Rākṣasas who were stationed there were awakened to their own kindred nature and consulted together with joy to destroy Kṛṣṇa at Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra. (3–4)
Having heard the entire account regarding the seizing of the talisman and other matters,
they returned with the talisman and stayed in the Siṃhāraṇya forest.
Wandering through villages at night, they remained intent on searching for a vulnerability.
