coming on in disguise, they would depart after failing to find even a moment's opportunity,
leaving them hopeless and filled with fear of the Lord’s discus.
In this way, the first month of Bālakṛṣṇa passed. Then, on the very first day of the second month from His birth,
the mother, the father, and Lomaśa [approached] the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama.
Then Hari desired to have them drink divine milk.
On the morning of the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having risen, he played and laughed upon a swing, manifesting his grace. (2.8.10)
His mother was exceedingly devoted to making Hari drink milk;
she milked a cow named Maṅgalāgaurī, who was like a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadughā).
He caused Hari to drink cow’s milk, purified by a cloth and drawn through a conch shell.

Knowing it was the festival of milk, the auspicious cows— capable of assuming any form at will, endowed with divine characteristics, and possessing speech as discerning as that of humans— [approached].
They said to their mother, "Make the cowherd drink our milk.
Having heard the request for a thousand cows, the mother then said to the cows:
"How could this boy be worthy of drinking all the milk? (14)
"All that would be unwholesome; what indeed shall I do? Please tell me.
The cows said: "What such misfortune could be ours?
We are cows belonging to you, yet we have not attained the service of Hari."
As soon as the Mother heard the cows' supplication,
a hundred thousand cows arrived from Goloka via the path of the sky;
likewise, they came from Akṣara, from Vaikuṇṭha, and from the unmanifest heaven.
From the land of Vṛṣāraṇya, crores of cows also arrived;
by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they came together—
some traveling in celestial chariots through the sky, and others moving through the intermediate space.
Those dwelling in the water and others dwelling on the earth stood before Hari and bowed with joy;
they caused milk to flow, and from that a river of milk arose,
like the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, its milk mingled with the water.
That place became known as Dugdhatīrtha, which destroys both sin and suffering.
At that moment, Hari, knowing the desire of the cows, said to his mother:
"O Mother, tell them all: my son shall drink their milk."
The cows offered praise to him, saying: "O Acyuta, drink our milk!
O Universal Soul within the belly of the universe, grant us fulfillment!
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [responded] to that prayer.
Having accepted them with grace, he indeed became ten million-fold;
for each cow, that boy stood ready like one who yields milk upon being milked,
and having reached the udder of each cow, he released a natural stream of milk.
Hari took for himself the most delicious food prepared with ghee;
he drank water to his heart's content and caused the cows to suckle their milk.
He likewise offered pleasing oblations to the gods, the maidens, and the ancestors.
Afterward, Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa became one with them.
Then those cows petitioned Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the virtuous:
"O Protector, always protect us; indeed, we wish to serve at your feet. (27–28)
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, smiling, said, "So be it.
Then the God assumed two forms for the cows:
one in the form of a cow and the second in the form of a young girl.
The Lord Hari first protected those girls from the hairy demon;
all the cows, possessing divine bodies, returned indeed to their respective places.
Having witnessed this great festival, the gods and goddesses were filled with wonder.
Then those asuras, having observed the festival of milking the Samayā,
assumed the forms of cows and approached to provide milk.
Likewise, Arjuntī and the other women among them took on the forms of cows.
Then, having become tawny, reddish-brown, crimson, dark, and others variegated in color, they approached the presence of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa. At that time,
the venom collected within their bellies became like white milk.
Having understood that deed of the rākṣasas, the goddess Vasundharā herself became a cow and first approached Śrī Hari;
she said to the boy, the master of the cows, "O Lord, drink my milk."
"Drink all my milk as much as you desire until you are satisfied.
These cows, dwelling in the forest, have come seeking liberation;
drink their milk up to the throat and grant them liberation. (36-37)
Having heard this, the Blessed One, Śatarūpa, who bore the affection of Vasumatī,
said "Om" and again became manifest through his divine play.
The Blessed One firmly grasped their garments with both hands.
Placing their breasts against his mouth, he drank the exceedingly potent poison-milk.
But that poison, having reached the mouth of the Blessed One, attained the state of nectar; he forcibly drank all that milk along with the poison as if it were mere breast-milk. (2.8.39–40)
When this was done, those Daityas and Daitya women then cried out, "Save us!
Save us, O ocean of mercy! Release us! Release us! Protect us!
Appearing in their true Daitya forms, they then begged for forgiveness.
The mother, the father, and the young maidens were seized by fear and agitation;
they trembled at the Daitya’s evil deed, the act of attempting to kill Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the Daityas, they wept, and Lomaśa consoled them.
Arjuna and the other Rākṣasas praised the Supreme Lord:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; O Supreme Lord, let there be salutations to you!
O Compassionate One, we are your sons, and these women are your maidservants."
A virtuous person does not give way to anger at the misconduct of scorpions.
O Acyuta, do not yield to wrath toward the nature of the asuras.
Protect your life, O Lord of Liberation; you have turned their venom into nectar.
Likewise, ordain us as those who have taken refuge in the Kṣveḍa [mantra] and as those who are immortal. May the incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, the sages, the gods, the seers,
the ancestors, mortals, the Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas [be so ordained].
Kinnaras, Cāraṇas, Sūtas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and the attendants of Yama;
animals, domestic beasts, trees, creepers, reptiles, and wild deer;
shrubs, grasses, birds and the like, insects, and the various species of mosquitoes. 48–49.
The Daityas, Dānavas, those of mixed castes, the Asuras, the deceitful,
the Nāgas, the serpents, the dull-witted, the Caityas, men, and women—
all these, O Lord, are your sons, endowed with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
"O Kṛṣṇa, may you have equal affection for all of them.
"A father's and a mother's affection is equal even toward children who are different;
protect, protect us, O Great King; do not deprive us of our lives!"
We were born as killers of our father, poisoners, and evil-minded;
do not count our offenses, for we were ignorant doers of cruel deeds.
Again and again we bow down, indeed placing blades of grass in our mouths.
"Protect us, O Lord; give us life; do not deprive us of our lives!
Having thus entreated Hari, the Daityas fell at the feet of Hari.
Hari, wishing to liberate them, protected them from the vicinity of the earth.
Through the excellent union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their sins were consumed by fire.
Then Arjuna, the best of the Daityas, having understood the cause of his birth from a Rākṣasa womb,
described it with a pure and truly heartfelt mind.

Formerly, we resided in a desert region at the hermitage of Gālava. We were Brahmins learned in the Vedas, devoted to pure sacrifices, following the dharma of non-possession, and subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits. (57–58)
They subsist on wish-fulfilling trees, wish-granting creepers, and wish-fulfilling gems; they assume forms at will, travel through the sky, and possess the luster of the sun.
They undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords and remain free from worldly attachments.

Nevertheless, due to the asceticism of a Śūdra in the desert land, there occurred a drought; by that, the roots, fruits, and other provisions were destroyed. Having all become mendicants, we nevertheless came to possess property again. (2.8.60–61)
Those who receive gifts have become greedy for food and forcibly seize wealth;
indeed, those sinful ones, being hungry, have become eaters of what is unfit to be eaten.
Likewise, the trees and the wish-fulfilling creepers have perished.
Then we wandered through the forest as we pleased, acting contrary to dharma.
Whosoever we encountered on the path, we would seize their wealth and clothing,
as well as their food and water at that very moment.
While fifteen householders were living in this manner,
once a pair of Brahmins arrived in their presence;
they were endowed with righteousness, possessed of compassion, and likewise devoted to the path of Brahman.

He was perfected in the study of the Vedas and devoted to the six duties. His wife was a devoted spouse, dedicated solely to her husband; she was a virtuous woman who performed service to her husband and attended to his bathing, worship, and other needs.
The vow of eating once a day and likewise the vigil during the two [monthly] observances—
these two, when performed with devotion for the worship of Brahmins, are pleased and bestow all things. Endowed with a spirit of faith, they are devoted to their gurus and their fathers.
Having arrived, they rested right here in our hermitages near us.
Before them were placed parched barley-flour, barley grains, and unhusked rice; these were taken away by us, as was their food. (2.8.69–70)
Their garments were stripped away and their wealth was plundered;
at that time, only two pieces of cloth suitable for loincloths remained.
Even as that wealth was being carried off, the husband continued to remember Hari alone.
That virtuous woman also said nothing; she merely repeated the name of Hari again and again.
Thus, those two Brahmins were then forcibly plundered there by us—who were devoid of compassion—acting like thieves in the guise of Brahmins.
Seeing those two most righteous ones being oppressed, an earthquake occurred;
there was a rain of stones and a shower of dust at that time.
These two remained taking refuge in a tree, mindful of Hari.
Thinking that it was all by the will of Hari, that devoted wife massaged her husband and rubbed his body. Even when there was a rain of stones and a shower of dust, she continued on. (79–76)
They did not experience grief, nor did they harbor any desire for protection;
reciting "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," they performed their *japa* while remembering Hari, their Guru.
Just then, another Brāhmaṇa arrived there, carrying an umbrella, wearing fine garments, and provided with food; he was adorned with a *tilaka* mark and graced by the *śrīvatsa* on his chest.
Radiant like the moon, he inquired after [the others] and gave them excellent food. (78–79)
He gave garments and likewise an umbrella to that couple; we witnessed that even as the rain was falling. Having gone there, however, all of that was taken away once again.
Then the donor, whether he was a divine deity or a sage, vanished.
He cursed us: "O sons of Brahmā, because you are cruel and merciless eaters of your own kinsmen, therefore become Rākṣasas! (81–82)
Those who possess not even a trace of compassion toward women, men, or indeed brahmins—
whatever barley, clothing, or other items were previously obtained by them have now been acquired [by others].
Due to the disparity of place and time, the turning away from sin has been endured.
Again it was seized and again taken away by merciless and evil-minded men.
Therefore, having met their death through showers of stones, let the Rākṣasas become subject to the nature of the wind and dwell upon barren mountains.
"May they be eaters of raw flesh, consumers of meat, and deprived of happiness.
Thus were we cursed by him at that time through a voice from the sky.
As he was pronouncing the curse, we entreated him for forgiveness, liberation, and happiness once more.
Then that sage Gālava himself, his true form having become manifest, was our former preceptor; out of compassion, he spoke again:
"In Saurāṣṭra, [is the abode] of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. (87-88)
"Through yoga, liberation will come to you; go to him.
Then we paid homage to the sage and likewise to that couple;
we begged for forgiveness, offered wealth, and honored them in return. (89)
Then, having returned the clothes and food, we were indeed struck by those showers of curses;
having died there, we entered the womb of Rākṣasīs.
Today, all of us are Rākṣasas with families, earning our living.
Having made our dwelling on a mountain or similar place, we meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, thinking: "When will the Blessed One, the bestower of liberation, appear?
Indeed, through the words of Tala, we have all become rememberers of our past lives.
The possessors of knowledge [declare that] the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of liberation, shines here.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, we have achieved our purpose, having been liberated from our demonic nature;
yet through your yoga, our sin has been set ablaze.
O Lord, we who were evil-souled Brahmarākṣasas have been delivered;
yet for our sake, poison has become nectar for those who were offenders.
There is no limit to your compassion, nor is there any end to our suffering.
"May He who acts for the sake of others indeed lead those dependent on Him across the ocean of worldly existence.
Having spoken thus, the Daityas, remembering their former births, wept again and again;
they prostrated themselves like a staff before Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and sang His victory.
The Blessed One quickly looked upon them with compassion;
he caused them to cast off those bodies and caused the deities to fashion them anew.
Then those maidens came to possess two forms.
A hundred maidens were protected in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Divine goddesses, sent by means of celestial vehicles to the abode of Brahmā, [were there].
Thus, through that yoga of those practicing Brahmins who were practitioners of yoga, [they attained their goal]. (2.8.100)
By His grace, liberation was indeed bestowed, and Pṛthvīgau vanished from sight.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa became a child;
cherished by young maidens, He played upon the Rañjanā swing.
During that festival on earth, the true nature of the cow was made known;
the activities of Kṛṣṇa were understood by the mother, the father, and the maidens.
O Rādhā, I have told this to you; it grants liberation both when read and when heard. 1.02–1.03.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Milk-Drinking Festival at the Beginning of the Second Month of Bālakṛṣṇa’s Life in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna; wherein the Lord, through various forms, partook of the milk of divine cows, and brought about the destruction and liberation of the deceitful Rākṣasas who had assumed the forms of cows along with their wives by causing the living milk to flow away. Chapter 9 Section 2: The Tretā-yuga Continuation of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Chapter 9.
[The Author: Chapter 10.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to another account of the Supreme Soul.
When the second month had passed and the third bright fortnight arrived,
the mother indeed brought her son out from the house;
there, the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the Nāndī-śrāddha, and other rites were performed.
The father had him initiated by the brahmins and joined him with their blessings;
having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he indeed touched his feet for his well-being.
His guru then applied a tilaka of saffron-moon on his forehead.
Having joined his own hands and placed them [before him], he whispered the mantra into his ear:
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my refuge; obeisance!
Oṃ namaḥ Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇāya Svāmine svāhā. || 4-5 ||
Having heard it, the boy repeated the mantra three times again;
Lomaśa Ṛṣi, his mother, Janaka, and the others were filled with joy.
He placed the two-fold Tulasi necklace around his neck.
The sage Lomaśa placed a garland of flowers around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
With his hand, Lomaśa placed a grain of sugar in Kṛṣṇa’s mouth,
made him drink milk, and repeatedly touched him with his palm.
Then the mother gave the child to the maidens staying in that hermitage, who were beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of play.
Eagerly, they repeatedly kissed their beloved and made him laugh.
They led him to a garden nearby, into a bower of flowering creepers.
Then a quarrel arose, each saying, "I first!
I first!"—a dispute over which single beloved youth among the maidens and women should be enjoyed.
Having observed the inclinations of ten million maidens,
the Lord assumed ten million forms specifically within that garden,
so that he might become a source of happiness for them like the crescent moon.
The beloved Kṛṣṇa was always under their control.
One woman delighted Kṛṣṇa by kissing him again and again; another, placing him upon her breast, spoke words laden with affection. (13–14)
A certain woman, placing her charming child-form upon her lap, makes her beloved laugh;
touching his cheeks repeatedly with the tips of her fingers, she delights his steady heart. (15)
One woman, placing excellent fresh butter upon his head,
gently massages the child-form with the palm of her hand;
another applies a reddish drop of *bindu* to his forehead with a small stick.
One woman applies a beautiful, captivating, and sovereign saffron tilaka with a golden rod; it is passionate (rājasa) and alluring. Another applies a charming mark on her cheeks and chin. 18.
She makes a soft, red garland that brings joy to the mind. Another, having fashioned a fresh garland of land-lotus petals, soft and of tranquil fragrance, places it upon his neck. (2.9.20)
Another woman, however, applied auspicious collyrium made from ghee to his eyes for the sake of brilliance, while another, beautifying him, applied pigment for the sake of beauty.
Another then raised the child up in her hands in the sky.
Another [strikes] him repeatedly on the chest and likewise on the belly;
with her mouth, lips, and breath, she makes the sound "bhaṃbhaṃbhaṃ.
Another gently plays upon his neck and coos "kil-kilā."
One woman rejoiced while placing her feet upon his chest;
another, having placed her hand upon his waist, held the Lord with her arm.
And she indeed indicated a dancing peacock by her gestures.
Another woman applied a charming, slightly reddening substance to his feet and hands,
which were beautiful to behold;
another [applied it] to this very cuckoo as it warbled, joined with mango trees.
One girl shows her teeth, another coos in response, and yet another makes Hari laugh;
one adorns Kṛṣṇa’s nose with a cloth,
while another quickly brushes away the dust clinging to him with a breeze.
Another points with her finger toward a monkey perched on a tree branch;
likewise, another, holding clusters of ever-fresh white flowers,
respectfully offers their fragrance to Bālakṛṣṇa.
One makes him hear a faltering sound and rejoices;
another indeed offers a slight taste of sweet honey.
Likewise, one sings a song while another dances upon the ground.
Another whirls the child like a wheel and is whirled about as well. (3.1) One woman kneads *saugandhika* and Viṣṇu-oil;
likewise, another mounts a swinging cradle and swings it. (3.2)
The second also gives him a woolen blanket for the sake of dispelling the cold;
another, having kindled a fire, stands by his side joined with him;
and yet another beloved woman causes him to mount the back of a deer.
Likewise, she takes another [child] before the young deer and places it near her beloved;
she leads the calves toward the cows and shows them to her dear ones.
Another, seizing two rabbit ears, shows Kṛṣṇa in the sky.
And his beloved likewise shows him his own face in a mirror;
while others announce to him the various marks [of her infidelity],
the newly arrived women indeed look upon them with joy.
Seeing the sky, Śrī Kṛṣṇa utters "Kilkile!
and opens His mouth to some, showing them even the entire universe;
to others, He shows primordial Goloka, as well as the imperishable Vaikuṇṭha.
There, the Blessed Lord also reveals Himself within their own bodies;
thus all the maidens rejoice in the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa. Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have become those whose desires are fulfilled.
Then the Blessed Lord withdrew those forms.
He became four-armed once again in the hand of Lakṣmī,
and likewise, he became two-armed in the lap of Māṇikī.
Then, having beheld the entire majesty upon the waist of the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī,
they became satisfied; thereafter,
the father worshipped the sage Lomaśa, his preceptor, according to the prescribed rites.
He worshipped [him] with sandalwood paste, adorning his forehead with a tilaka.
He caused a crescent moon to be fashioned with unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, beautiful flowers, necklaces, sandals, fruits, leaves, and lovely stalks. ||43-44||
With roots, the finest skins from deer, milk, clarified butter,
rice, garments, bark-cloths, and other excellent articles used in the sacrifice,
he gratified Lomaśa and received his blessings.
And the mother gave auspicious articles of fortune to the young maidens;
likewise, garments, bracelets, and household utensils, as well as foods to be chewed and eaten, drinks, savory delicacies, and clarified butter. (46–47)
Then the mother indeed gave her hair ornaments;
she gave all those infinite things that were dear to her.
The mother protected all those daughters as they were in their maidenhood.
Indeed, that great second stage of life, the stage of celibacy (brahmacarya),
was like Vaikuṇṭha itself, free from illusion (māyā) and other such defects by the grace of Hari. And there was the hermitage of Lomaśa, resplendent with liberated maidens.
Day and night, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa were meditated upon here;
all were beloved of Nārāyaṇa, and none were otherwise.
Lomaśa remained there eternally liberated, free from Māyā.
He is indeed imperishable and immutable, the liberated self who has reached the further shore of Brahman.
(52) When there is no desire in his stage of life, nor anger that shines forth, when there is neither greed nor delusion, how then could there be pride and the like? (53)
Where there is no transformation of gender, where there is no activity of the womb,
and where desire indeed does not exist— such is the hermitage of Lomaśa. There, the great abode is situated above, hidden, where peace is eternal.
And Lomaśa indeed [spoke] four auspicious syllables.
When the father honors such a knower of Brahman,
then the maiden named Prabhā [honors] the dear Lord Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having led her to a tree born in the garden to sport and delight her, he went there;
and having taken refuge at that royal campaka tree, the young girl’s dear friend sat down and indeed offered all her worldly activities to Hari. (57)
Just then, the Asura Krodhanaka arrived there through the sky—
he who was indeed born from the forehead of Rudra amidst the waters.
For when Rudra was manifested from the forehead of Brahmā, [he emerged] from his own forehead.
Then, for the sake of creation, he indeed became agitated in mind;
staying within the water, he felt a momentary distress as he reflected.
By him, a drop of sweat was produced on the forehead of that Rudra.
Born from that drop, he became a cruel being, a hater of the gods, and one other than the gods (an asura).
Wrathful and powerful, he performed most formidable austerities.
Having attained perfection through his penance, he became a traveler of the sky, assuming forms at will.
Having thus realized through yoga on the grounds of Kuṅkumavāpikā that the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the adversary of the Daityas,
was present in the garden at the hand of the maiden, he then indeed understood this.
Desiring to seize the boy there, the demon arrived with impetuosity;
having assumed the form of a maiden, he came to amuse him.
Then, without asking permission, he took Kṛṣṇa, who was held in his hand by Prabhā.
Bālakṛṣṇa, perceiving his wicked intention,
took hold of his two hanging hands for the sake of his destruction;
and for the sake of granting him liberation, the Lord came into his grasp.
Prabhā, having recognized him, gave the boy to a certain female companion.
That girl, Krodhanā, took the boy and in a moment quickly vanished from sight among the trees and creepers. (67–68)
Prabhā did not see her, so she called out to her;
then Krodhanā, having carried her into the sky, quickly went along the path of the clouds. She made repeated efforts to kill that boy.
She placed the noose around his neck,
but then, as she was being consumed by fire, she released the boy’s throat.
Standing in the sky, scorched by the flames, she was then enveloped by crests of fire.
Her body consumed by the flames arising from Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body, she cried out "Hā! Hā! and then threw herself upon the ground. Yet, the fire born from Kṛṣṇa’s body did not release her at all.
The fire blazed in many ways like a smoke-bannered comet in the sky;
that cruel fire consumed the girl, and no protection was found.
Then she quickly leaped up and descended after the boy.
But Prabhā quickly seized Bāla by the hand;
having caught Hari as he reached her, she ran toward Lomaśa.
Then, filled with anger, she said: "Extinguish the fire that is equal to yourself!"
"I am burning because of my karma; protect me here, you wicked and sinful woman!
Having spoken thus, she blocked the path before him and praised the boy:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa, ocean of compassion, deliver me from this distress!"
"I am indeed the son of Śaṅkara, and my name is Krodhanaka. I am the hater of the gods, sent by the asura named Tāla for the purpose of your destruction, and sin has been accumulated by me."
"Since my mind, though directed toward one who is not to be slain, has resorted to the intent of killing him, I therefore beg for forgiveness; protect me and grant me liberation.
Thus addressed, Bālakṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, [responded].
Then, filled with innate compassion, he spoke to the angry one:
"O proud woman, how have you become a maiden for my destruction?
You do not know me at all—I am the inner self of all, the Supreme Lord."
"The channels and vital breaths are in my hand; they belong to both creation and liberation.
Tell me, O beautiful one, what offense have you committed against me? Declare what punishment I should impose upon you, and I shall carry it out."
The wrathful one spoke to that charming lord, Kṛṣṇa:
"O Lord, allay the burning of my body in such a way.
O Lord of Gods, become my beloved; I, a maiden, choose you. (84)
"O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my mind runs toward you.
Grant me liberation, and likewise, at the end, destroy my state as an Asura.
Hari said, "So be it; all this shall come to pass for you."
"By my touch, your body shall always be divine and youthful;
for my sake, let it become beautiful and endowed with the qualities of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
And you, O beautiful lady, must remain among the maidens in the form of a maiden!"
May your second such form attain liberation, the imperishable state.
May your third such form be of a manly nature, resembling fire—
wrathful, entirely cruel, and known as Krodhana upon the surface of the earth.
"May you indeed take the form of a sage, yet remain forever prone to anger.
Thus did Kṛṣṇa grant these three forms to Krodhana.
Furthermore, in another birth, this Krodhana shall become Durvāsas.
"O Rādhā, this most excellent Vaiṣṇava shall always be equal to Nārāyaṇa in his qualities;
he will become the instrumental cause for the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus to the auspicious girl who was angry, the Blessed Lord [departed]. 91–92.
Having fashioned an eternally beautiful maiden and likewise a second maiden-form for her that was easily released,
he instantly dispatched her from his abode to the imperishable realm by means of a celestial chariot.
The third form, consisting of *puruṣa* and characterized by *tamas*, became his son.
He performed supreme austerity in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage,
and [he established] the great holy site named Krodhana on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.

O Rādhā, it should be understood that what was born is auspicious and bestows liberation. Then Prabhā and the maiden Krodhanā took Bālakṛṣṇa and went to the place where Lomaśa’s worship was being performed.
When asked, "Who is this new girl?", Prabhā replied.
Indeed, having heard of the miracle of Nārāyaṇa, they were filled with wonder.
Then the mother, the father, and Hari performed the worship of Lomaśa.
The other maidens went home, but that girl remained among the maidens out of a desire for Hari;
she always made her dwelling there and became the beloved of Kṛṣṇa’s consort. Then, at the time of evening twilight, she performed the worship of the Moon according to the prescribed rites.
The father and mother caused [the rites] to be performed; they had him chant the Vāmadevya hymn. The mother caused the son to perform the Saumya rite, which is indeed like the sight of lightning.
And the wives of the Moon, as well as the Moon himself, rejoiced upon beholding Mādhava.
Upon seeing Hariścandra, he then pointed with his finger and said to his mother,
"O Mother, bring the moon here into my presence," thinking thus within his heart.
The Moon, perceiving Hari’s intention, arrived accompanied by twenty-seven [attendants].
Accompanied by the chariots of his twenty-seven wives,
he arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, which, when the moon reached it, became entirely divine, resembling the lunar orb itself. (10.3–10.4)
Candra brought various kinds of jewels,
as well as divine garlands endowed with celestial luster that bring forth cool nectar;
these were then offered there by Candra’s mother to Hari.
Auspicious hospitality, beginning with a welcome, was extended to his wives;
water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), honey-mixture (madhuparka), food, and drink were given.
Having honored Hari and offered blessings, Candra [departed]. (106–107)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to his own abode in heaven and became joyful. Then all the others, beginning with his father, having prostrated like a staff before Lomaśa, the best of sages, with devotion, offered him gifts.
Having accepted the excellent prasāda and likewise having received blessings,
and having bestowed blessings upon the maidens, they departed toward their own abodes.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, is the nature of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
This purifying narrative is wondrous and brings happiness;
it bestows liberation upon those who hear it and grants prosperity to those who remember it.
For those who desire worldly status, sons, and wealth, it bestows heaven, progeny, and riches.

O Rādhā! I have described to you that supreme purifier in the form of a child, which bestows the perfection of knowledge upon those who desire learning, sovereignty, and the like; it grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and bestows good fortune upon women. 11.2–11.3.
By merely thinking of this, one shall indeed obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
likewise, one obtains the merit born from the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of all sacrifices.
Furthermore, one obtains the fruit of all gifts as well as the fruit of all yogas.
"O Rādhikā, [this account] concludes with the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇakānta.

(2.15) Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section on the Tretā Age, during the third month of the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa’s life, on the bright fortnight, while the sacrament of the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa-saṃskāra*) was being performed by women, there occurred His play of fondling and His manifestation of many forms, as well as the divine vision. Then, Prabhā took Kṛṣṇakānta to the hermitage of Lomaśa; there, the demon Krodhana, having become a girl named Krodhanā, carried off Hari.

In the sky, she was consumed by Hari; he released her, and having made that divine being threefold in form at the hermitage of Lomaśa, he manifested her as Citrā during her liberation and in her future birth as Durvāsas. This concludes the ninth chapter, titled "The Vision of Lightning and the Manifestation of Wonder," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga), Chapter 10.
[The Author: Chapter 11.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Furthermore, there is another account of the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you that which bestows the nectar of the bliss of Brahman.
(1) In the fifth month, on this earth, the father indeed performed the *upaveśana* sacrament for his son and then gave various gifts. (2)
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, having risen early in the morning, the father bathed, performed his daily obligatory rites, and near the courtyard of the palace,
had a pavilion constructed adorned with plantain leaves.
He had auspicious archways constructed from the leaves of the *aśoka*, cloud-tree (*abhrādipa*), and other species;
he fixed water-pots and placed them upon [the arches];
he hoisted banners and draped them with cloths. (4–5)
He prepared a canopy and fastened up small banners;
he arranged creepers all around the sacrificial posts and pillars,
and then he set out trees laden with fruit and flowers that were swaying in the wind.
In the pavilion, he placed lamps and luminous gems in their proper places,
as well as pearls set in strings;
likewise, he suspended variegated canopies from the ceiling.
In the pillars, in the middle, and in the corners,
he bound the captivating goddesses and the gods in embodied forms;
beneath that floor, he [filled it] with soft, golden sands.
Having prepared the heart-pleasing and unsurpassed seats,
both variegated and beautiful, made of wool and silk,
he spread small and long mats all around there.
The noble father placed a cushion upon the excellent lion-thrones;
he established a divine seat for Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the center, rich with the finest gold.
He also protected the beautiful divine ground within the pavilion, which consisted of black earth,
for the purpose of seating the children;
and he had a pure, square altar constructed.
Having placed there a long golden band adorned with the essence of excellent jewels, and having laid upon it linen, woolen, and white cloth,
as well as red garments, he then placed them among the wheat.
A water-filled pitcher at his side, rice, saffron and the like;
flowers, sandalwood, camphor, garlands, collyrium and so forth; various kinds of food offerings, drinks, as well as betel leaf with cardamom and other ingredients. (16–17)
The father indeed set out five vessels, a cooking pot, water for rinsing the mouth, fruits,
all the implements for worship, those made of *tulasī* leaves,
and all the articles for the offering.
He caused two images to be fashioned— those of Dharādevī and the Lord Varāha— which were beautiful in every limb, adorned with ornaments and garments,
gentle, divine, and possessing the form of gods.

He visualized the goddess Pṛthvī, beautiful in form, possessing the appearance of Lakṣmī, and most splendid; she was seated, clearly manifesting the svastika posture. Her two feet were the netherworld (Pātāla), and her two shanks were Rasātala.
Her knees were Mahātala and her two thighs were Talātala.
The root of her thighs was Sutala, both her hips were Vitala, her loins were Atala, and her womb was Bhūtala. (22–23)
He fashioned her belly as Bhuvarloka, her heart as the auspicious Svarga,
her throat as Mahas, her mouth as Jana, her eyes as the highest Tapa,
and her forehead as Satyaloka; thus he formed her embodied form.
There, the ocean, mountains, and forests are indeed seen directly;
likewise, the form of Varāha is seen seated upon a throne, two-legged, white in complexion, and radiant with firm hair. (25–26)
With a long nose, tawny hair, fine eyes, and a tuft of hair,
she stood upon the ground with her two hips, having bent both her feet;
holding a mace and a discus with her two foremost hands, she was most excellent.
Wearing a forest garland, having likewise lifted up the earth with her supreme tusk, she stands upon the waters,
adorned with a crown, bracelets, earrings, a sacred thread,
a waistband, and a girdle.
Gopālakṛṣṇa likewise had a beautiful and charming golden image of Varāhikā fashioned;
he then established the various articles for her worship and other offerings within the pavilion.

Then, when an auspicious and pleasant moment had arrived, his father respectfully summoned the great seer Lomaśa with the sounds of musical instruments and other offerings. Having brought him and seated him upon a throne, he performed worship for him.
Then the auspicious words and songs of the women were set in motion; and at that time, musical instruments were played all around.
Milk, curd, ghee, water, sugar, and fresh honey [were offered].
Having brought the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the father established himself before [the child].
After having the son purified, the mother was summoned to the pavilion;
placing him on her lap, she stood there upon that most excellent vacant spot of ground.
Lomaśa caused the auspicious worship of Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, the gods, the brahmins, and likewise the virtuous ones to be performed.
Then, with Vedic mantras, Lomaśa [performed the rites] for the Earth and Varāha.
He caused the couple to perform an auspicious worship. Then the divine maiden Pṛthvī, having approached Hari, sang songs of praise regarding the virtues of Bālakṛṣṇa. ||37-38||
Having bowed down, she became steady in the invocation within her own image;
and Hari, when the invocation was completed, assumed a four-armed form.
Then, having arrived before the Lord, he remained stationed within the Boar.
Lomaśa, having thus invoked them both, offered the beloved water for sipping (ācamana);
he gave the respectful offering (argha), water for washing the feet (pādya), and a seat that brings auspiciousness;
and he performed their bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with pure water.
Then, having performed a thorough cleansing with garments, he offered fragrant perfumes.
He presented priceless ornaments consisting of cloths enriched with mineral threads,
as well as a sacred thread, a moon-shaped forehead mark, and saffron.
Then he gave collyrium, vermilion, and Viṣṇu-oil;
he gave lac-dye, saffron, sandalwood, flower petals, Tulasī leaves, garlands, and beautiful necklaces.
He offered every kind of erotic adornment and excellent fragrant unguents;
he gave him chains, gentle bracelets, rings, and so forth,
as well as saffron, *abīr* powder, unbroken grains of rice, *gulāl*, and other such items.
Having offered incense as well as a lamp, he presented an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa).
He gave water mixed with sugar for drinking, along with all kinds of grains and most delicious food. He also offered betel leaf with cloves and cardamom.
The sage Lomaśa presented a fruit, fragrant substances, a beautiful golden seat, and a sacrificial fee consisting of gold, silver, and other items;
he also performed the *ārārtika* rite for the Goddess Dharā and the Lord.
He offered salutations, praise, circumambulation, blessings, and a handful of flowers;
he performed prostrations like a staff, prayers, and requests for forgiveness.
Having thus worshipped the God and the Vedic Brahmins at that time, [he departed]. (2.10.50)
Then the father honored those who were seated in his presence;
musical instruments were played and there was most excellent dancing.
The goddesses and the Kinnarīs sang beautiful songs.
At the conclusion of the worship, according to the procedure taught by Lomaśa,
the mother placed her son upon a consecrated spot of ground in the presence of the Earth-goddess,
who had been worshipped, saluted, and entreated for forgiveness. (52–53)
Then the goddess Earth appeared in personified form;
placing Hari Kṛṣṇa upon her lap, she honored him with blessings.
She gratified Hari with saffron and other substances, as well as with sweet milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then the other goddesses and maidens offered worship and performed obeisances.
The Goddess Earth placed her joined palms in supplication before Śrī Hari to ward off his sorrow,
and he lowered them onto her own head.
Then the divine four-armed Boar, Viṣṇu himself,
became manifest before the eyes of all and bowed down to Bālakṛṣṇa.
The Boar presented a golden throne to Bālakṛṣṇa.
Dharā gave them an eternal golden bed and the earth itself.
Then, having gradually established Bālakṛṣṇa there for those two,
the sage Lomaśa performed the dismissal of the ritual worship.
Then Kambharā-lakṣmī indeed fed Lomaśa,
as well as the brahmins, the foremost ṛṣis, the virtuous women, and the maidens.
Having given sacrificial fees in every way, she bowed down and offered her salutations.
He dismissed everyone and laid his son down to sleep.
Thus the father celebrated the festival of Bhūmipraveśa;
then the son made an excuse, saying, "I am sleeping peacefully."
Then, at that time, a certain female mendicant arrived there with a desire for food;
she was of wretched appearance and miserable voice, yet possessed a divine form and great pride.
Never seen before, she desired to see the son.
Questioned by her mother, "Who are you? What do you desire? I shall give it to you," she replied: "If you are truthful, give me here your son;
I am a maiden named Siṃhikā, a cave-dweller and daughter of the Earth. (64–66)
"I dwell upon the mountains and I roam even in the forests.
The goddess Earth is my mother, and she has been honored by you today.
Knowing this, I have come here for the sake of seeing your son. (66)

This charming youth, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, has taken up residence in my heart the very moment he was seen; he is the destroyer of my sorrow. Enveloped by darkness, I perform austerities in the forests for the sake of my beloved.
Without food, lacking luster, and unadorned,
there are thousands of other sisters of mine upon the mountains;
for all those maidens perform penance to obtain a beloved husband.
"If you think so, O Mother, give me your little son.
Having obtained peace and joy here, I shall delight your son;
and having attained the supreme fruit of my asceticism, I shall return your son to you. (2.10.70–71)
"I shall go to the place designated by my beloved, and I shall remain there.
O Mother, if you have favor toward me, tell me: give me your son.
I swear this truly; I am the daughter of the Earth, reflecting upon my beloved. (72)
Having heard this, the mother Bhikṣukī said to the two maidens:
"O daughter of the Earth! If it is so, then delight him and take him as your husband.
Upon hearing this, Kandara was satisfied, serene, and filled with joy.
She quickly took the sleeping boy in her hand to carry him away;
seeing that he was still asleep, she looked at him repeatedly with love and kissed him.
Then the maiden ate the food given by her mother.
And having placed Bālakṛṣṇa upon a swing,
that beautiful woman rocked it and repeatedly cast her gaze upon him. Then, out of affection for her sister, she honored the virtuous Kambharā.
Having received the command, her sister then went to bring you;
she summoned all those female ascetics who were residing on Mount Meru and other mountains, wherever they might be,
and having gathered them together, she returned once more.
All the auspicious female ascetics, the deep caves, and the foremost mountain ravines,
along with ten thousand maidens, arrived to behold the Supreme Lord, the Mother Satī, the presiding deity of Kuṅkumavāpī. (2.10.79–80)
They praised Kambharā with love and entreated Acyuta; they petitioned Acyuta, saying, "O Mother, grant us [our son].
Hearing those sweet voices, the child quickly awoke.
The Mother, a treasure-house of compassion, gave them milk after first making them drink;
meanwhile, they were intent on [claiming] "mine first, mine!
and in her grasping for this or that one, he repeatedly assumed a second form.
While it was thus with her beloved, as long as she remained the giver of the child, so long did he come into the grasp of the seizer in a second form;
and that [child] along with Bālakṛṣṇa entered ten thousand caves.
He became peaceful and took delight in them;
at that time, all those maidens considered their birth to have been fruitful.
They worshipped him, the youth who captivated the mind and enchanted the heart.
Then Hari, smiling, spoke to them for the sake of granting boons;
they then requested the eternal, sinless service of this very Lord—
service, glory, fame, devotion to the virtuous, and being beloved by Kṛṣṇa.
"So be it," Hari replied, and he granted those maidens residence in the hermitage of Lomaśa. Furthermore, Hari spoke to them:
"In all the mountain caves that are always suitable for your purpose..."
"Virtuous practitioners of yoga, free from passion, will dwell with me.
You shall always have the company of the righteous.
Fame, renown, and service to the virtuous shall ever be yours."
"Through devotion to the virtuous, my own devotion and purity shall arise.
And for you who always remain here in these caves, may there be eternal union with me; I shall grant you everlasting liberation."
"And I, O virtuous lady, shall dwell in your cave;
that cave shall become known as Siṃhagahvara (the Lion’s Cave), where eleven maidens will take birth within that cavern. (93)
"By my grace, the people will always perform that vow of your daughter Ekādaśī in mountain caves, sacred fords, and mountain clefts; they shall become saviors [from saṃsāra]. (94–95)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, in the presence of his mother,
addressed them and summoned the preceptor Lomaśa, and gave them to him. Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and having eaten and drunk, they departed for the hermitage.
Kṛṣṇa remained alone in his true form, and his mother was filled with wonder.
She considered those who had performed meritorious deeds to have fulfilled their purpose through her very self;
for when the supreme goal to be attained has been reached, what else remains? || 97-98 ||
O Rādhikā, the Lord of Compassion indeed meets [us] by showing mercy;
the manifestation of the Supreme Self is for the sake of attaining His compassionate grace.
By reading, hearing, remembering, and even causing others to hear this, [one attains that grace]. || 99 ||
One shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, the fruit of ten million sacrifices, and a beloved [spouse].

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Daughters of the Earth, Siddhikā and Others, Attaining Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as Their Husband during the Consecration of the Earth for the Seating of Lord Bālakṛṣṇa," in the second section, the Tretāyuga Lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 10: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (Tretāyuga Lineage)*
Chapter 11 [Author:
Chapter 12 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Listen, O Rādhikā: indeed, Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, being constantly nourished by his mother and others, grows like the young moon. That Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is eternally served by those maidens.
Stainless, pure-hearted, the Supreme Self, and without support;
bringing joy to his mother, with eyes as radiant as the reflection of his father—seeing that dark child, who was the perfect embodiment of all forms. (2–3)
Indeed, the subjects, upon seeing him, considered it their own merit;
and the yogis, having seen him, considered him to be the Supreme Lord.
Once, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇaka, his father, summoned Lomaśa.
In the sixth month, he had the piercing of the ears performed with a silver needle.
With a double-stranded thread, for the sake of increasing nourishment,
longevity, and prosperity, on that very day at dawn, his father Gopālakṛṣṇa bathed.
Then, having had a silver image fashioned, his father, through the hand of Lomaśa, caused the worship of the Aśvinīkumāras to be performed;
at that time, when the father worshipped, he invoked the divine physicians there.
Then he arrived there in person, resembling the sun and adorned with earrings.
Having accepted the performed worship, he touched Hari’s ears with his hand—
ears that were very soft, beautiful, and graced by the circular shape of the earlobes.
Both ears have been made a permanent seat for the accomplishment of all hearing and other faculties;
first, both ears are smeared with a medicinal paste of a healing flavor.
Then, a fine, new, golden needle is honored.
Then Karṇa was pierced by her with firm force at the very spot; however,
because of his skill, ease, and gentleness,
the touch of the needle was not perceived by the young boy due to the intensity of the sensation.
Then, as the two ears were pierced according to requirement, a needle appeared there;
it was a goddess in embodied form, adorned with divine garments and ornaments, rich in the beauty of every limb, radiant as the moon, and tender. (13)
Then that goddess joyfully said to her mother and father:
"For her who has touched Nārāyaṇa, the destruction of Māyā is certain.
My Māyā has perished today; protect me in the presence of Kṛṣṇa."
Having heard her, the mother said to her: "Whose daughter are you?
Tell me here, O Kanakī, O Goddess; what desire of yours shall come to pass?
Having heard this, Sūcī related her own history exactly as it had occurred.
"I am indeed the mind-born daughter produced from Brahmā.
My task is to reach the further shore and to create openings;
likewise, while alone, it is the destruction of the Daityas such as Kaṇṭaka."

The tailor is my father-in-law, and he is the son of Viśvakarman. To the son of the tailor, Doraka, has been entrusted my task— the reunion of us two who have been separated, I together with my beloved.
I am inert, having the form of the elements, and yet I am the conscious deity. My family is likewise twofold: always consisting of both the effect and the cause.
The cause is of the nature of the deity, and the effect is also material.
Thus have I told you here: "I am the beloved of the cord;
O Mother, from this day forward I have become devoted to your son. Having manifested myself here in a particularly divine form, indeed possessing a celestial nature.
"Protect me, Nārāyaṇa, in the service of your son.
Having heard this, Kambharā-Lakṣmī then spoke to her again:
"O Queen of the Gods! Dwell here in this hermitage of Lomaśa together with your husband."
"Residing here on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake together with your husband and family,
dwell contentedly with a joyful heart to serve Kṛṣṇa.
Having been addressed thus, she bowed to the twin Aśvinīkumāras and rejoiced greatly.
Having quickly consulted with her mother, Śrīharī, she went to her father-in-law’s house;
then, having deliberated, she returned swiftly with her family to the former site on the shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Indeed, she dwells there with her family, devoted solely to the worship of Kṛṣṇa;
her daughters take Kṛṣṇa with them and go to that place to sport.
From there, on the eastern bank, arose the holy site of the Tuṇṇavāya hermitage.
Then one day, having placed Kṛṣṇa upon her hip, she rejoiced. She reflected, "When will the Blessed Lord truly become my husband?
Knowing what was in her heart, Kṛṣṇa spoke to her while smiling.
I grant you success, which is of a manifold nature;
become a maiden in form and dwell indeed in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
O sinless one, my arrival shall take place for you at the proper time.
As soon as this was said, that goddess, a maiden of divine form,
possessing the beautiful hue of the campaka flower and assuming a second body,
appeared in the presence of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa on the bank of the lake.
She went with her beloved Kṛṣṇa to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Known as the wife of Doraka, she remained in the house of Doraka.
And by means of the supernatural power bestowed by Kṛṣṇa, she assumed the form of a crore [of women].
In the worlds, she, appearing in the form of a needle, pervaded everything with her clear connection.
Thus, through the attainment of grace, she always obtained Kṛṣṇa as her beloved.
The two physicians, the sons of Aśvinī, were indicated for the granting of boons.
They both also requested a dwelling for the sake of propitiation;
and Kṛṣṇa, with a gracious mind, said to them, "So be it.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) then became known by the name Āśvinīputrārāma.
On the eastern shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, among the trees,
Lord Kṛṣṇa thus granted a dwelling to the two of them and to her as well; then,
attended by the maidens, he himself went to his own supreme abode.
The sage Lomaśa also received there, from Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, extensive worship and sacrificial fees at the excellent shrine named Karṇavedha;
thereafter, the divine king of sages, Lomaśa, departed for his own hermitage.
On the full moon day of the sixth month, in the bright fortnight of Caitra,
his father summoned Lomaśa to that very place and performed the auspicious annaprāśana ceremony according to the prescribed rites.
Having first performed the auspicious bathing ceremony for the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa with curd, ghee, and honey, and having performed the worship of the Mothers,
he established a pure fire and performed the oblation of sacrificial porridge (caru-homa).
He performed the worship of Brahmā and the other deities and also fed them with excellent food.
Likewise, he gave wealth to the Brāhmaṇas, to the virtuous, and to the poor and the blind; he also gave it to virtuous women, to maidens, and to young boys.
Then he gave mouthfuls of food to the cows and deer, flour to the insects and such, and grains to the leeches, tortoises, and fish; at that time,
his father also gave grains to the crows, pigeons, and other birds.
Then he offered water from trees, creepers, grass, and other sources;
he then gave [offerings] to the ancestors, the gods, and human beings,
as well as desired foods and various utensils.
To all the maidens, [he gave] wealth, ornaments, and garments; articles of adornment suitable for the body and implements for practice;
as well as food, seats, vehicles, and leaf-shelters.

His father gave him divine texts on the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*) and on the practice of devotion (*bhakti*), as well as various kinds of enjoyments. Then there were medicinal herbs growing on the earth, appearing as grain and yielding kernels.
They are givers of oblations, givers of fruits, givers of roots and tubers, and givers of wheat and other grains;
they are givers of juices, sweet, givers of the essence of sugarcane, and givers of sugar;
they are givers of leaves, givers of flowers, and givers of foods that are chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked. (5.2)
The trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth— which destroy disease and bring about nourishment—
assuming the form of young maidens, took all the various items to be tasted produced by each of them, such as fresh grain and other foods, and placed them in platters. (53–54)
Adorned and resplendent with the brilliance of fire, they arrived to feed Kṛṣṇa,
performing songs accompanied by musical instruments in the western Kuṅkumavāpikā garden, which extends for one yojana.
Having guarded the vessels, they remembered the Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
Knowing that they had arrived in the Kalpa-garden, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa assumed a hundred thousand forms and stood before each of them.
The beloved Lord was seated upon a golden throne by each [of them],
fed, honored, delighted, and kissed again and again.
Then the Blessed One, having assumed youthful forms, [proceeded] from there.
Then, out of affection, he ate the well-prepared foods;
and to all of them, a platter filled with his own prasāda was given.
Whatever he ate at that time, all of it was through the power of Śrī Hari. (2.11.59–60)
Nothing was seen to be lacking, as everything was increased by Lakṣmī.
All of them fed their husband, the lord, with their lotus-like hands.
And the Blessed One ate again, bound by the affection of their devotion.
Again and again he was fed, given drink, and likewise honored;
assuming a divine form, he fulfilled their desires.
And on that first day of the *annaprāśana* ceremony, he ate the foods.
Beholding all that sovereignty, they were bewildered there at Keśava.
And the Blessed One, having drunk the water, assumed the form of a child;
he repeatedly took up satisfying belches and rejoiced.
Then Hari was saluted there by them for the sake of service:
"Act in such a way that we may constantly perform service unto you;
you are our self, you are the supreme self, you are our essence, and you are our strength. (65-66)
You are the fruit, you are the leaf, the flower, the inner core, and the bud;
you are the root, the central trunk, the branch, and even the sprout.
You are the vital breath, you are life itself, the food, and the eater as well.
You are the enjoyer and you are indeed the object of enjoyment; likewise, you are our inner self (antarātman).
You alone are the creator, the sustainer, the protector, the nourisher, and the ground of dissolution.
You alone are the Supreme Brahman, the Master, the one dearer than life, and the Lord.
"O Puruṣottama, accept our innermost heart;
O Lord, protect us in your service so that we may perform service unto you.
Thus addressed, Viṣṇu, taking them onto his lap, laughed and spoke to the deities.
"O forest goddesses, may you dwell here in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
You shall certainly remain in the form of maidens, as well as in the form of trees and creepers—
taking the form of vines and the form of trees, bringing auspiciousness to this garden abode."
"May you remain forever for the sake of my service with fruits, flowers, and other offerings"—
having been addressed thus, and perceiving the supreme love of Nārāyaṇa,
they accepted his excellent grace and became double-bodied.
In the form of trees and creepers, they dwell in the Kalpa-grove.
Then, as soon as those maidens saw Keśava again and again upon his lap, Lomaśa withdrew [the vision]. || 74-75 ||
Having assumed a single form and holding the maiden Śrīvallī on his lap,
he smiled and remembered his eternal preceptor, the sage Lomaśa. As soon as he was remembered, that sage appeared instantly in a divine body.
And he praised the Supreme Lord. "What is your command? Tell me, O Lord! [He asked]. (77) Hari joyfully gave those maidens, who were forest goddesses, to him.
Lomaśa, having bowed to those deities, led them to his hermitage. (78)
The female attendants became devoted to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and attained the nature of Brahman. Thereupon Hari vanished and went to his own abode.
And Lomaśa reported the prowess of his son to his father.
Having understood all incomparable sovereignty, he attained joy.
Then, at that time, Gopālakṛṣṇaka said to Lomaśa:
"This one appears to be a child; yet in reality, he is certainly no mere infant."
Marvels occur for him that are characteristic of the deeds of a divine being;
therefore, some inconceivable Lord and Sovereign of all must exist.
What indeed could be his primary mode of subsistence or primary activity?
"Whether he be a king, a preeminent deity, or even a generous guru—what single, certain mode of conduct, based on an auspicious refuge, should be adopted by him?
Thus addressed, Lomaśa replied: "Clothing, alms-bowls, wealth, and so forth... (83–84)
"Place these before him, so that you may know whatever he might take.
Having been told this, the father quickly placed before him a garment,
a vessel, a weapon, wealth, a book, and a pen, in order to ascertain his livelihood.
A staff, *darbha* grass, a diamond, a garland, a handful of grain;
(86) a *sruva* ladle, a betel nut, a thread, a fruit, a conch shell, a cowrie shell;
a water vessel, a mirror, a crop of grain, and a carved swan. (87)
A lamp, an umbrella, a stone, ghee, wood,
as well as medicine, a flower, a clod of earth, sandals, a needle, and a sword— these thirty-two objects he placed down again.
Having observed these thirty-two things, the Blessed One also [proceeded].
Having manifested with thirty-two arms, the Lord touched all things simultaneously.
For the treasury of arts knows every single object;
since he consists of all modes of existence, what could be unknown to the Supreme Self? (2.11.89–90)
"What indeed is impossible for Hari to achieve, what is there he cannot do, or what is unknown to him?
His father was struck with wonder, and Hari then truly laughed.
Lomaśa then said, "The sixty-four arts are unsurpassed."
They abide right here in the Lord of Gods, the Ancient Person, the Guru.
He will be the creator of all, the giver of all livelihoods, and the sustainer. This eternal Supreme Self is the performer of all actions. (92–93)
The mother rejoiced upon hearing of it and seeing her son’s splendor,
while all those who were watching; meanwhile, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, smiling,
held a book and a rosary in two hands, and a pen and *kuśa* grass in the other two.
Holding [the two other objects] with his other two hands, he became four-armed;
then, holding a garland and a book, he became two-armed.
Having placed the book on his lap and cast the garland around his neck, [he remained as two-armed].
Taking a blade of grass in his hand, Hari, who possessed the form of a child, laughingly placed it upon his own head; he then smelled that flower.
At that time, he was indeed seen bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Even as a child,

Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as strength itself—and nothing else; sin, merit, and all strength—no other purpose exists for him.

"This one may be harmed, this one not"—thus is dharma established in the world.

Mārtaṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and likewise Bhāṇḍaka;

Women, wealth, and land nourish their own refuge;

They donned armor that was impenetrable, inseparable from their bodies, and filled with vital strength;
it was both soft and hard, pleasant to the touch, and protective.
Having taken up this armor along with water, they drank the mantras of weapons and missiles.
Simultaneously, through their grace, they became enriched with the Kanyakāvarman mantra:
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, devour this for the sake of my beloved! Oṃ kṣaḥ phaṭ svāhā!
Then they chanted that very mantra one hundred and eight times.

"He who is indeed remembered as the protector everywhere in battle and elsewhere—this mantra was then held and recited by them. Furthermore, Lomaśa bestowed upon them the supernatural powers (siddhis), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. (2.13.70)
He bestowed thousands of invincible sovereign powers (aiśvaryas),
as well as the Sandhinī, Yojinī, Kṣatavāriṇī, and Śūlahāriṇī [vidyās], along with the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Indeed, he gave these thousands of vidyās together with the water for rinsing the mouth.
Then she bestowed all the sciences (vidyās), including the ability to assume many forms, the maintenance of both falsehood and truth, invisibility, and reappearing;
as well as armies of maidens dressed in military attire, numbering in the hundreds of billions.
By sprinkling drops of water,

the sage Lomaśa instantly created vehicles drawn by musical instruments, as well as those drawn by elephants, lions, and horses; he also fashioned vehicles drawn by swans and Garuḍas from that very water.

At that moment, musical instruments were sounded and young maidens flew up into the sky. By means of a moment’s meditation, they went to where the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the infant master, was staying inside the house; having reached the heavens, they stood before him.
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Śrī, Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Prabhā, Maṅgalā, Manasā, Revā, Bhārgavī, and Sarasvatī stood ready to ward off the armies of the rākṣasīs. (77)
Gaṅgā, Mañjulā, Bhakti, Muktikā, Ekādaśī, Rati;
Haṃsā, Saguṇā, Tulasī, Kamalā, Virajā, Satī; Mūrti, Gomatī, Svarṇarekhā, Jayā, and Nandinī. (78–79)
Durgā, Lalitā, Sāvitrī, Dolā, Puṣpā, Kalāvatī, Badarī, Mādhavī, Pampā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Prīti, Ṛtadhvajī,
Mauktikā, Lāḍakī, the Goddess Manu, Kastūrikā, and Sitā. 2.13.80.
Haimī, Śānti, Praśāntā, Campā, Godāvarī, Yamī;
Ojasvatī, Savitrī, Ratnā, Miṣṭā, Amṛtā, Dhani;
Caturā, Vajrikā, Muktā, Suśīlā, Śyāmikā, and Amalā. (8.1–82)
Santuṣṭā, Candrikā, Kānti, Kuṃvarī, Śivā, and others—
these and another four hundred and ten who were foremost among them,
numbering in the crores, became the leaders of the army, possessing great strength. (83)
Then they raised shouts of joy: "Victory to Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa!
Victory, O Beloved, Great Beloved, Supreme Lord! Victory!
Victory, O Master, Victory, O Protector! And may Lomaśa also be victorious here! (84–85)
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā.
Reciting this mantra, the demonesses blocked [the path].
"Oṃ kṣaḥ phaṭ svāhā! May Kṛṣṇakānta swallow this for the sake of his beloved!"
Then, while performing the recitation of mantras, they warded off the demonesses.
Seeing the army of rākṣasīs suddenly approaching through the path of the sky, the parents, the residents, and others [prepared for battle]. (87–88)
Then, having become a young calf, Bālakṛṣṇa said to his parents, "Do not fear at all, do not fear, do not fear!
The widowed Rākṣasīs have come to fight out of enmity; they are coming forth. (89)
"Women must never be harmed by me anywhere, nor indeed ever by any man;
nor must they ever be harmed even by Lomaśa, since that preeminent teacher protected the hermitage with fire. (2.13.90–91)
Frightened by that, they have indeed come here to kill me;
let these maidens, sent by Lomaśa, fight them—
equipped with armor, spells, weapons, and missiles, and emboldened by their delight in battle.

"O Mother! These [goddesses] by the millions, stationed in the sky in the form of an army, desire to fight according to my wish; there is nothing at all surprising in this. When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, [he summoned] Garuḍas and swan-vehicled [deities].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara gave divine elephants, celestial chariots,
and aerial palaces to the maidens in the sky;
and the great army of the heroes' daughters was adorned with mounts.
Meanwhile, the rākṣasīs rushed up from all sides;
they then struck that group of Vīra’s daughters most fiercely,
while those maidens, fierce in battle, returned their blows.

The trumpeting of elephants, the neighing of horses, and the cries of swans and Garuḍas, as well as the roaring of lions and the thundering of celestial chariots, completely overwhelmed the fierce clamor of donkeys,
camels, cocks, and Rākṣasas.
There, the barking of dogs and the howling of jackals resounded in response;
indeed, there were repeated falls of missiles, weapons, and arrows, as well as the striking of one another’s bodies by the murderous women. (2.13.99–100)
Some struck with javelins, some struck with small swords;
some, seizing them by the hair, threw them down upon the surface of the earth.
Others struck with maces, and likewise others with clubs.
Some struck others with *bhindipāla* slings, and others with swords;
some with scimitars, others with stones, rocks, and projectiles;
likewise, others with chains, staffs, iron arrows (*nārāca*), and shafts (*śara*). || 102–103 ||
There the rākṣasīs were slain, yet the young girls were not killed;
some were struck with spears and mallets, while others were hit with *bhūśuṇḍī* weapons.
Consumed by the fire of their wrath and enraged by the gnashing of their lips, they slaughtered [the enemies].
With clubs, tusks, tridents, mallets, and sharp-edged spears (paṭṭiśa),
they struck down the deluded Māras; with white swords,
lances, small spears, arrows, discuses, and pestles.
With knives, stones, clubs, and piercing instruments,
the apertures of the Brahma-crevice are pierced; the thighs and arms are cut asunder with spikes,
*kuśaka* arrows, *bhalla* shafts, bamboo, and hands tipped with fire.
Their hearts, breasts, and heads are torn asunder;
they are bound with nooses of cords and cast down by hooks and the like;
and their headless trunks are split apart with axes and hatchets.
Then they were beaten with chains and scorched by fires;
the Rākṣasa women struck the maidens against one another with blinding blows.
Thus, indeed, a tumultuous battle broke out there.
Not a single sound was heard here amidst the roars of battle.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Tumultuous Battle between the Rākṣasīs and the Maidens in the Vicinity of Aśvapaṭṭasara," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 13: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (Tretā-yuga Lineage)*

Chapter 15 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the terrifying battle of fierce women— of rākṣasīs who were the wives of jackal-kings— a battle that was dreadful in every way,
destructive, and involving the surrender of their very lives. (1)
"Since their husbands have died here, they must die there in the ashes.
Thinking thus, they fought as if already marked for death;
having seen Hari, they cast aside all fear and cried out, "Kill! Kill!"
"Let them be cut into pieces and portions like tufts of grass! they cried out, like the surging flood of the ocean on the day of the full moon;
even so did the army of the Rākṣasīs fall upon the house of Bālakṛṣṇa.
At that time, the great army of maidens was not separate, as they were mingled together;
for those cruel women, even after death, desired to rescue Bālakṛṣṇa by force,
just as before, however they might.
"He must be captured; he must be killed! While alive, he shall not remain a living being!"—thinking thus, and placing death right before them, they rushed forward to slay him.
Like locusts falling from the sky to the earth at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya), [they descended].
In that manner, all those rākṣasīs fell upon the child’s chamber.
Seeing this reversal of fortune, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa then,
smiling, caused them to dissolve into the field of the Kuṅkumavāpī pool.
Seeing everything in that forest dwelling— both on land and in the water— to have suddenly vanished, the rākṣasīs departed into the sky in despair.
Filled with intense rage, they engaged in a great battle with the maidens.
Those maidens of divine bodies are struck by millions of weapons;
yet their bodies are not pierced, remaining like masses of fire, and no pains arise, nor do they experience any lacerations. (11–12)
Protected by the armor of their Lord and shielded by protective mantras,
the wives of Kṛṣṇa do not die, whereas the wives of the Daityas perish.
At that time, the maidens were cut into many pieces by the fierce weapons [of the demons].
That Rākṣasī who had become twofold was indeed not one and the same again.
Having been slain, she departed from the living; once gone, she does not return.
The sky was completely pervaded by the battle, adorned by the fierce fury of the fray.
He became filled with joy and granted many spaces;
indeed, at a distance of a thousand *krośas*, there was then room for battle.
Throughout Surāṣṭra, there was space for crores, hundreds of millions, and tens of billions of women on all sides.
At that time, not even a single man remained there in the midst of the battle;
instead, the headless trunks, heads, arms, breasts, thighs, and hips of the rākṣasīs fell from the sky onto the earth.
A rain of blood, a rain of flesh, and a rain of lumps occurred;
indeed, there was a rain of hair, a rain of weapons, and a rain of corpses.
A rain of limbs and a rain of moon-like fragments occurred.
Their bodies, as delicate as fresh butter, are torn apart;
for the sake of their husband-gods, they are cast down by the throngs of their beloveds against one another.
Hearing of this, King Yama himself arrives to witness the battle for a moment. (2.14.20–21)

The gods, who move through the sky, observed the battle but did not perceive that it was caused by a living being. When the hosts of Daitya women realized their own destruction and the eternal nature of the maiden, they then consecrated her with mantras.
Indeed, divine weapons capable of destroying living beings were released;
first, the Rākṣasīs discharged the weapon of tears,
and as the vapor rose into the sky, not even a blade of grass could be discerned.
The weapon of rays discharged by Lakṣmī became a destroyer of tears.
Then Śukrajīvanī indeed released the smoky weapon (dhūmrāstra).
The sky was shrouded in smoke, and a burning sensation arose in the eyes.
Then, having prepared everything— including collyrium and the inhalation of smoke—
the [prince] discharged the fire-missile there, which produces the nature of a Rākṣasa.
Śukra, however, discharged the cloud-missile there, which restores to life.
Then Vṛndā discharged the great Śālagrāma weapon;
indeed, those Śāla-mountain [missiles] struck the rākṣasīs in the sky.
At that time, the rākṣasī Koṭarā swallowed the Śālagrāma weapon.
There, Śukrajīvanī released the dust-weapon (*pāṃśvastra*), which was thick with dust.
Then Añjanī indeed released the wind-mantra weapon (*vāyumantrāstra*).
And there, Ṣaṇḍhikā discharged the serpent-weapon (*nāgāstra*) in every direction.
Then Kamalā discharged the Gāruḍa weapon, which brings happiness;
at that time, the Rākṣasī Vikhātā discharged the scorpion weapon;
and then Garutmatī again discharged the Cillikā weapon.
The life-taking Śukrajīvanī unleashed a shower of fire,
but Śāradā then effortlessly swallowed that shower of fire.
Then those wives of the Rākṣasa engaged in a battle of illusions.
The Maruts created stones, trees, flesh, blood, and pus,
as well as streams of liquor, arrows, and all kinds of weapons;
they rained down these most fierce things, along with blisters and powders mixed with fire.

Then, as sharp weapons, as well as filth, urine, and so forth, [fell] from all sides upon the group of maidens on the earth, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. At that time, the circle of Yoginīs, consisting of sixty-four groups, [manifested].
Having assumed forms as large as mountains,
all those illusions born of falsehood repeatedly swallowed [the world];
yet, overcome by the power of the Yoginīs, they met their destruction from the very roots.
Then those illusions, which had the nature of a rain, dissolved once more.
A shower of corpses was then released from the mouth of the one named Pherucita;
indeed, millions of corpses, as well as women, fell from the sky.
And there were the corpses of female chickens, vultures, crows, and female parrots;
likewise the corpses of female hawks, female herons, female pigeons,
and flesh-eating female owls.
They fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth, which was completely covered.
Then, beholding that, the great and virtuous Bhairavī, the consort of Śambhu, assumed her own form, ten yojanas in length.
He seized all those hundred thousand rākṣasīs who were emitting corpses from their hundreds of thousands of arms simultaneously, and then he crushed them. Then,
with their hundreds of thousands of feet, those bewildered women raised a tumultuous outcry.
The creation of Śiva has gone to dissolution; false illusion has gone to its end.
(44) Then, at that time, the wives of the Daityas fell into the hands of Bhairavī;
they endeavored to escape from her hands in order to deceive her. (45)
Each one of them indeed assumed countless forms in her hands;
some took ten, some fifty, and others a hundred.
Just as they could not be counted by my hand, so did those arts move about.
Then Bhairavī brought about the increase of her own hands;
likewise, those rākṣasīs also then assumed their own growth.
Thus, there was a great burden in the creation of innumerable bodies.
Having emerged from the fist of Bhairavī,
those countless Rākṣasa women, stationed in the path of the sky, roared repeatedly and struck Bhairavī violently upon her head. 49.
Standing on the brink of losing their lives, they did not even consider the fear of death.
Then Mahālakṣmī beheld those innumerable Rākṣasīs, who possessed countless forms and assumed infinite appearances. (2.14.50–51)
Mahālakṣmī herself, remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
assumed a form equal to the universe, endowed with ten million arms;
indeed, the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and other celestial bodies hung from the hairs upon her head.
She, however, was most terrible and struck with every kind of weapon;
seizing them again and again, she repeatedly slew the rākṣasīs.
Others had four hands, and still others had eight hands.
Others were sixteen cubits tall, others thirty-two cubits,
and others possessed sixty-four arms; there were hundreds of thousands with excellent hands,
and ten thousand-cubit-tall forms created by Mahālakṣmī.
Leaping up again and again into the sky, they struck those rākṣasīs down.
Many there were slain, perished, and fell, tormented and deprived of life;
once dead, they remained truly dead, forever deprived of resurrection.
Then they all attained absorption into Mahālakṣmī; however, more than half of the strength of the Rākṣasa women was destroyed.
Mahālakṣmī, Bhīru-lakṣmī, and other Lakṣmīs [remained] for a moment thereafter.
Beholding their own victory, they sounded the war-drums;
then the maidens, together with Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, attained great joy.
Now, there was a certain Rākṣasī named Rūḍhikā who stood there in the form of a mountain.
Having become so, it fell swiftly from the sky upon Bālakṛṣṇa;
at that moment, indeed, heaps of parched grain appeared like a great mountain-dwelling.
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā was thus protected by the mountain-like heaps of parched grain.

The maiden became pregnant, and from that point on, her fear departed. (62) Just as Ruṇḍhikā fell with great speed upon the Talāja mountain, she was cut, pierced, and torn apart by its peaks, and she died. (63)
Then another [form], consisting of the earth itself, entered the surface of the ground;
it indeed became long in shape, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Having assumed the form of a lizard, it was ten yojanas in height.
The lower lip was fashioned from the surface of the earth, exceedingly beautiful;
and the upper lip was fashioned from heaven, endowed with all the stars as its ornaments, where indeed no confusion or fear could arise for anyone. (65–66)
Having acted thus through deceit, she placed all those maidens,
as well as the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
and even the hermitage of Lomaśa, within her own mouth.
Then Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, having understood that wicked deed,
assumed the form of a maiden among the maidens himself, for the purpose of destroying the Rākṣasī and likewise to create a spectacle.
Placing the divine Sudarśana discus in his hand and standing at the throat,
Kṛṣṇa and the maiden named Kṛṣṇā shone brilliantly for a moment.
Then he released the Sudarśana, which was endowed with great splendor and fire.
With a wheel joined by fire, he instantly cut the throat, mouth,
and belly of that Maṇḍūkī into pieces;
from her fat and bones, the Cākacakyaciroṭikās were born.
Then another rākṣasī named Dāminī, seeing that Dardūrikā was indeed dead,
herself assumed a form composed of splendor,
pervading the sky and filled with garlands of flames from great lightning bolts. 73.
Opening her mouth wide, she swallowed the Sudarśana of Viṣṇu;
but that Sudarśana instantly burst through her and emerged,
falling to the earth just as flashes of lightning descend.
The Rākṣasī Dāminī, composed of sugar-candy, fell to the earth;
then another, Dyuhanā, having assumed a body there like the sun,
placed Bālakṛṣṇa in her mouth and leapt up toward the sky and heaven.

Having observed the sage Lomaśa there for only a moment, Vīraśi placed him in his mouth and leaped upward; he traveled far into the sky. Then the boy Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lomaśa, the king of yogis, [remained behind]. || 77–78 ||
Indeed, two terrible beings in the form of fire were born there within the womb;
they blazed up with fire, and the two Rākṣasīs likewise perished.
Having torn open the womb, Lomaśa and Acyuta emerged.
Then another woman, Dāminī, became fire in that hermitage.
She quickly burned the entire hermitage of Lomaśa and the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā with fire until nothing remained. (2.14.80–81)
Bālāhakī Mahālakṣmī assumed the form of rain;
