she obstructed the fire and extinguished it with her showers.
Then, seizing a lightning bolt there, the virtuous goddess struck him to his very life.
There Dāminī died, having stretched out her hands and feet.
Then another rakshasa woman, named Dhībhakṣyā,
took the goddess Kambharālakṣmī upon her shoulder and went into the sky.
Seeing that, the virtuous woman then struck the wisdom-devouring demoness with her fist;
the wisdom-devourer died instantly and fell down at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).
Then Śauṇḍī, assuming the form of a tigress, [attacked] Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Just as he was about to seize his father, Pārvatī became a tigress and devoured her;
then the father became restored to health.
Then others, daughters powerful in every way and fierce in battle, [seized him]. || 86-87 ||
There, all those who were struck down died, leaving only about a hundred remaining;
at that time, Kuṇṭha, Diṣṭi, Damā, and the others sought refuge with them.
Deprived of their weapons, they were bound in fetters by the maidens.
Remembering Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, those widows bowed down to him. Overwhelmed by fear, they wept and entreated the Lord:
"O Kṛṣṇa, our protectors have indeed been slain; we have come to you for refuge. (2.14.90)
O Supreme Lord, O Great Master, deliver us from this great suffering!
Perform the salvation of the hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of root and artificial women,
of the Rākṣasīs who have died.
But we, O Kṛṣṇa, your beloveds, are indeed weak and have been slain.
Where shall we go? O Ocean of Mercy, take us under your protection as your own!
May we become Lakṣmī, Ramā, Rādhā, Śrī, Satī, Pārvatī, and Prabhā. || 92-93 ||
O Lord, make their maidservants charming with rubies;
or rather, O Mādhava, appoint maidservants for those maidservants as well.
Without you, no other house is considered to be a source of happiness for us in the future.
But we, fallen from both [paths], how indeed shall we obtain happiness?
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, forgive our most terrible transgression;
having consumed our karma, protect us and bestow upon us a divine state.
The gods, the enjoyers, the Daityas, the Dānavas, the Rākṣasas, the birds, the sages, the seers, mortals, trees,
and so forth— these are your progeny; born from your lineage, they have attained union with you.
"How shall we live through sin, having come to this lovely place that was unattainable?
Make us all pure and free from the nature of *rākṣasas*. Thus entreated by them, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [acted]. 98–99.
By means of divine vision and divine sprinkling,
through her own state of aversion toward them, and by her constant remembrance [of the Lord],
she then rendered them all cleansed of sin and free from the influence of the *rakṣas*.
Having been placed inside the bellies of cows that were like wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu),
they were then expelled through the urinary passage by Lomaśa right there;
possessing divine bodies like Lakṣmī, they became fit for the status of Brahmins.
Then they forgot their own births, conditioning, and bodies;
they became like divine goddesses, just as the digits of the moon are born [from it]. All those maidens were [born] by the desire of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhikā, by the power of Kṛṣṇa, those twelve-year-old girls became gentle, endowed with the marks of Viṣṇu, and otherwise transformed;
and those who had died then on the battlefield were absorbed into the form of Kṛṣṇa.
And all those divine maidens emerged from the body of Kṛṣṇa;
numbering one hundred thousand, they were stainless and their garments were as radiant as the sun.
They were adorned with bracelets, crowns, armlets, earrings, and girdles.
In an instant, beloved wives were born for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
(1.07) Śrī Lomaśa bestowed the mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," upon them in the presence of Śrī Hari. (1.08)
Having caused the oblation to be performed for them and for others as well, Lomaśa gave them sacred threads, yellow garments, and garlands;
he then also gave them tulasī leaves, rosaries for chanting, and necklaces.
He then gave them the emblems of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
All those who were there in the battle— Ramā and the other ten million maidens— were fed, initiated, and protected at the hermitage of Lomaśa.
There, the Lord of Kṛṣṇa bestowed upon them the bliss that is higher than the highest;
embracing them with his arms and pressing them against his own chest, the Master gave them words of auspicious blessing and kisses. (11.2)

Then, the exhaustion from battle and the fatigue from handling missiles, weapons, and so forth—all ceased in an instant; not even a single hair was harmed. A great cry of victory arose there for all of them. (11.3–11.4)
All were fed, honored, embraced by the compassionate one,
kissed upon his chest, pressed close, and rendered immortal.
A great festival was celebrated there and here on account of the victory.
The gods and others arrived; they were honored and fed.
Having departed as they had come, Lomaśa, the sovereign sage, then indeed bestowed new names upon the hundred thousand maidens.
The sage Lomaśa gave her auspicious names such as Suśīlā, Susahā, Vidyut, Kiraṇā, Candrikā, and Dyuti; then,
by the command of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he led them all to his hermitage.
Then Pṛthvī was summoned by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
at that time, the Earth herself leveled the battlefield.
She removed all impurities and made the ground pure.
Then that auspicious ground, washed by the rain from the sky,
became known as Lakṣatīrtha, honored by Kṛṣṇa.
And those weapons which the Blessed Lord had kept in his own palace—
In that battle, divine and material weapons fell.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, did that battle take place there in ancient times; it was never before, nor will it ever be again, a battle that grants women such a divine destination.
By the will of Hari, two forms were produced from each of the hundreds of thousands of maidens; one by one, they ascended into celestial chariots and,
accompanied by the attendants, were led to the supreme, imperishable, and true abode.
And the second [incarnation] was in the form of a maiden, residing in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this most wonderful and supreme divine narrative of Hari, consisting of a battle between women, has been told to you here. || 125–126 ||
"By reading this, by hearing it, by reflecting upon it, and likewise by offering it [to others],
one shall attain the state of being beloved by Kṛṣṇa and find a destination in the world of Brahmā.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how, at the conclusion of the battle between the Rākṣasīs and the countless maidens capable of fighting, the Rākṣasīs face defeat and destruction, and finally seek refuge in Bāla-Kṛṣṇa’s grace, thereby attaining the state of liberation and the status of maidens," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 014 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 15 [[Author: → Chapter 016
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to the most purifying account of those women who attained the state of Ramā through union with the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 1.

Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa entrusted them to Lomaśa for the purpose of their residence and protection in his hermitage. Having attained divine forms, they reached the state of celestial maidens.
For this very reason, even those who have not yet obtained the lamp of knowledge remain devoid of aesthetic flavor during the narration or the explanation;
with their intellects unrevealed, they remain silent in the assembly like simpletons. (3–4)
They did not know self-knowledge, nor did they know the austerity of dharma;
being ignorant of the principles of liberation, they were like lamps hidden beneath coverings.
Yet, they were rich with the desire for liberation and devoted to the arising of wisdom.
All of them questioned Lomaśa, the sun of knowledge:
"Just as a female bee makes moths her own by stinging them,
so too does the wise man, the bestower of knowledge, make the blind possessors of sight."
"O Guru, grant us that knowledge which bestows liberation and grants peace.
A woman’s form is always devoid of knowledge and is a locus for latent impressions (vāsanā).
It is indeed a locus for defects; therefore, liberation does not arise from it. (8)
"O Kṛṣṇa, please instruct us upright men who bear our duties, as well as these women, so that we may attain liberation and so that the destruction of our faults may come to pass. (2.15.10)
Thus entreated, Lomaśa, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, instructed all of them in the auspicious duties of the vow.
"O daughters, the Ekādaśī vow is supreme and removes all sins! (11)
It was performed without water, without food, and likewise with constant vigilance;
it included the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the performance of śrāddha, accompanied by the propitiation of Kṛṣṇa,
the company of the virtuous, and the restraint of the senses— indeed, that [observance] destroys sin and bestows liberation.
Go this morning and perform the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, during his vow; for it grants the grace of Kṛṣṇa and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Perform the rite with flowers and other offerings, fruits, water, and sandalwood paste.
Through self-surrenders, circumambulations arising from the heart that are most enchanting;
through gifts of food and gifts of drink, as well as by means of swinging in a palanquin;
and through repeated dancing, singing, amorous gestures, pleasing expressions, and services. (15–16)
"By restraining the senses and observing silence, perform the vow of Kṛṣṇa, entirely devoid of sense-objects, for the sake of his very grace.
Thus addressed, those young maidens undertook the waterless vow.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣ�ṭha, they performed the vigil.
Bālakṛṣṇa, being pleased, caused them to behold Vaikuṇṭha and granted them his own vision in his beautiful four-armed form.
He bestowed [the boon] attended by the splendor of a vast assembly and other such riches;
and those beloved consorts of Śrī Hari considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose.
They kept a vigil at night and performed the breaking of the fast in the morning.
They questioned the seated Lomaśa regarding the compendium of dharma:
"What is that which should always be practiced, which destroys sin and bestows merit,
which grants liberation and heaven, and which wards off the sufferings of Yama?"
Then Lomaśa said to him: "Cows of such a kind are to be served;
cows consist of all the gods, they are goddesses, and they are oceans of nectar.
They are deliverers, they are the very form of sacred fords, they are pure, and they are bestowers of nourishment. (23)
Their service should always be performed, for it bestows all gains.
By offering cow products even once, the deities and others are pleased;
indeed, all the thirty gods are gratified by curd, and Maheśvara by milk.
With clarified butter, Pāvaka is always pleased; with milk-rice, Pitāmaha;
by giving a cow and drinking its milk, a man becomes pure and dear to the gods.
Pañcagavya is supremely purifying and bestows the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
The Maruts are in the tips of the cow's udders, and Sarasvatī is on her tongue;
the Gandharvas are in the middle of her hooves, while the Pannagas are on the tips of her hooves;
the Sādhyas are in all her joints, and the Moon and Sun are in her two eyes.
All the kṣatriyas reside in his hump; Dharma is established in his tail.
All sacred fords are in his anus, and the river Gaṅgā is in his urine.
The oceans are in his udders, while the great ṛṣis dwell in the pores of his skin.
Lakṣmī resides in the cow-dung of the cow; all powers reside in its hairs.
(2.15.30) Fortitude, steadfastness, peace, nourishment, growth, as well as memory, intelligence, modesty, physical form, fame, learning, intellect, and progeny—(31)
The cows, who are the wives of Dharma and embodiments of devotion, always abide among cattle.
Cows given to a worthy recipient follow the deceased.
Where there are cows, there is prosperity, righteousness, knowledge, and the gods.
Even the immortals were fashioned by means of the rays (or cows) bestowed [by me].
Therefore, worship the wish-fulfilling cows (Kāmadhenu) as daughters within the hermitage;
this auspicious and great dharma has been proclaimed by me here in the forest.
Having heard this, those young women performed the auspicious service of cows;
then they also questioned another upholder of dharma regarding what brings welfare:
"Is there any other service equal to the service of cows, or is there not?"
"By which [service] both worldly enjoyment and liberation may become sources of auspiciousness for women.
Then Lomaśa said: "Such is the service rendered to a husband;
through service to one’s lord, heaven, liberation, and happiness are indeed obtained. (36–37)
Having drunk the water used for her husband’s feet, she is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The husband alone is the Supreme Brahman; the husband is the gift, the vow, and the sacrifice.
The command of the husband is the highest dharma; through him, indeed, women attain liberation.
Indeed, all the gods and the ordinances abide within the word of the husband.
For those whose husband-god is pleased, the Supreme Lord is pleased;
she who sleeps when he sleeps and certainly wakes when he wakes. (2.15.40)
O daughters! she who eats only after her husband has been fed certainly conquers death. She who remains silent when he is silent and stays where he stands—O daughters!
she conquers death; there is nothing else that brings victory over death.
Single-minded in her vision, focused on a single thought, and carrying out the words of her husband—those messengers of Yama fear her; that virtuous woman is honored by the gods.
When addressed with love by her husband, she would never refuse him. (42–43)
A woman who is dear to her husband does not go to another deity other than her husband;
that devoted wife, equal to Lakṣmī, does not enter the mouth of death.
He is my mother, he is my father, he is my kinsman, and he is my supreme deity.
She who serves in this manner certainly conquers death.
Constantly meditating upon her husband, following after her husband, and thinking only of her husband, she never beholds the realm of Yama. (45–46)
She who does not look upon another with her mind while bathing, sitting, traveling, or grooming her hair, does not see Yama at all.
Nor does she see him when he is worshipping a deity, eating, or sleeping comfortably.

She who does not abandon her husband when death comes shall conquer Time itself. That woman who always cleans the house before the sun has risen and remains devoted to the service of her husband shall not behold the realm of Yama.

Endowed with purity and proper conduct, she who gazes upon the face of her husband lives indeed without seeing the door of death for her lord. Devoted to their husbands, truthful in speech, unconquered, and serving their masters— such are the faithful wives.
Those who are free from violence never go to the world of Yama.
Maidens devoted to celibacy, widows established in righteousness, devotees of Hari, and female servants of the virtuous do not go to the city of Yama. (51–52)
Likewise, those who are the refuge of knowledge, who have attained supreme wisdom, and who are composed;
those who give up their lives for the sake of their master; and those who serve and attend upon their mother, father, husband, and true guru—these do not go to the city of Yama. (53)
Those who give sesame seeds, cows, and gold do not go to the abode of Yama.
Those who observe the Cāturmāsya vows, those who follow the intentions of their gurus,
and those who constantly listen to sacred discourses do not go to the residence of Yama.
Through austerity (tapas), heaven is attained, as well as fame, long life, happiness, and so forth;
through austerity, one also attains knowledge, realization, health, beauty, good fortune, and prosperity.
Through austerity, worldly enjoyments are obtained, and through devotion to Viṣṇu, the supreme state is reached.
Those who subsist on milk go to heaven; those who give wealth attain abundance of riches.
Through service to the guru one attains worldly enjoyment, and through meditation, liberation.
By performing śrāddha rites one obtains progeny, and for those who subsist only on leaves, heaven shall be their reward.
For those who subsist on fruits and roots, sovereignty is attained; for those who serve cows, liberation occurs.
Through the gift of flavorful juices, good fortune arises.
Through the giving of food and drink, eternal satisfaction is achieved.
By the gift of a *saugandhika* lotus, one is satisfied with sensual enjoyments;
by fruits, one obtains a son; and by flowers, supreme good fortune.
By the gift of fearlessness, one shall attain all desires. (2.15.60–61)
He who bestows fearlessness upon a living being gives them freedom from fear;
by means of that worthy recipient, both shall achieve liberation.
This occurs through association with the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Through service to the virtuous, evil is brought to an end;
therefore, a pure intellect that bestows liberation and its own fruit arises.
Furthermore, auspicious action—which destroys afflictions and removes sin—is produced.
Heaven is the attainment of auspicious fruits, while hell arises from sin.
One should always strive to acquire that which is excellent and productive of fruit, never that which is inauspicious.
Non-violence toward all beings is characterized by being free from craving and anger.
A woman who commits no evil certainly saves those of universal sovereignty.
She who always remains free from hope regarding desired objects and is not greedy, who possesses dispassion and is fixed on Hari—that woman crosses the ocean. (66–67)
A woman who is faithful, free from malice, devoted to serving her teacher,
of noble character, and rich in righteousness crosses the ocean.
She who performs auspicious deeds and avoids those that are inauspicious [crosses it].
Abiding in auspiciousness, she is liberated from all sins.
With a pure mind, she frequents sacred sites—both stationary and moving—and by constantly serving the virtuous, she attains the supreme goal. (2.15.70)
The illustrious young maidens said: "Tell us that which involves little effort and is easy in every respect, regarding the various births arising from inauspicious actions. (7.1)
"O one rich in asceticism, tell us that which is capable of shattering [our doubts].
Śrī Lomaśa said: "When Hari, the bestower of liberation, has been attained, and when the virtuous person and the guru have been attained... (72)
That service which one performs with a pure inner self is indeed a straightforward means for the destruction of evil deeds. Having seen holy men, she who bows down to them is liberated from sins.
Whatever impurity has been committed through thought, action, or speech—
by offering that to Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved, one becomes pure and attains liberation.
One should perceive Kṛṣṇa in the sun, Kṛṣṇa in the moon, and Janārdana in the cows.
She who beholds Kṛṣṇa in her spiritual preceptor shall be liberated from bondage.
Having seen a virtuous husband, a preceptor, a deity, a cow, one's parents, a chaste woman, or a twice-born brahmin,
she should bow down, meditate upon them, and perform circumambulation.
Having quickly abandoned her misdeeds, she is released from that bondage.
Cows are purifying, auspicious, and even the deities of the gods;
she who serves them with devotion is liberated from sins.

She who drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during an auspicious moment is liberated from all sins committed throughout her life at that very instant. That virtuous woman who receives upon her head the water drawn up by the tail [of a cow]—
Having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords, she is liberated from sins.
That virtuous woman who receives upon her head the stream of milk flowing from the udder of a cow is liberated from sins.
Having properly served a virtuous person and fed them according to the rules, one should worship them;
all of that person's sin perishes at that very moment.
Having placed *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward, one should establish the bull in front.
One who has bathed in the water from its tail becomes pure in every respect.
By bathing with water contained in a right-spiraling conch, one becomes purified.
By bathing with water mixed with black sesame seeds, one becomes pure at that very moment.
Having bathed with water from a flawless lotus leaf and with water containing all kinds of jewels,
as well as with the water used for washing the feet of the virtuous, one is liberated from sins.
By observing the *bodhinī* [Ekādaśī] in the month of Kārtika, and likewise by observing the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), [one attains liberation].
The practitioner of the vow swiftly destroys the sins committed throughout ten million lifetimes.
O Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Consort of Lakṣmī, through the chanting of the names Māṇikyeśvara and Haṃseśa, one attains absorption into Him. (86–87)
Having propitiated the Supreme Lord over thousands of other births,
some woman attains the status of a Vaiṣṇavī upon the destruction of all her sins;
that [status] has been attained by you through the grace of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
O sons! This state of being a Vaiṣṇava, obtained through grace, is indeed difficult to attain.
For the highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas purify the entire world—whether remembered, praised, seen, or even touched, O sons! (2.15.90)
The Blessed One, the purifier of thousands of births, purifies instantly.
Knowing this, you should worship him with special care.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa possesses the form of a child.
Having spoken thus and given them water for sipping (ācamana), Lomaśa bestowed upon them radiant self-knowledge (ātmajñāna) and then became silent; those young maidens as well,
having abandoned both dharma and adharma, remained established in eternal wisdom.
Free from fear and beyond reproach, they undertook various religious observances,
filled with supreme affection and constantly meditating upon Kṛṣṇa.
Lomaśa, too, every evening [meditated] upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He caused them to hear those stories that bestow devotion such as *pātivratya* (devotion to one's husband) and others;
and he caused them to hear the entire *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* in its entirety.
He had all of them listen while they remained established in their vows during the *cāturmāsya* period.
The hundred thousand new maidens, as well as other lakhs of maidens,
always chanted the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with great reverence;
they did so while awake, during sleep, and even in deep slumber.
Eagerly, they held their husband, Śrī Svāmin, within their hearts;
with their hearts, they chose Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharā.
They enjoyed that beloved Lord as the Self within themselves and as the Inner Self of the self.

Thus, O Rādhikā, those divine women, though born of darkness (tāmasa), became so through the yoga of the Supreme Lord; what wonder can I tell you? Kṛṣṇa, who assumes birth solely out of compassion, is the possessor of grace.
Having destroyed his own terrible sins, he made men, women, animals, trees, creepers, Daityas, and others his own;
likewise, he indeed made the reciters and the assembly of listeners his own. (10.1–10.2)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Service Rendered to the Husband, Cows, Gurus, and Others by New Maidens through the Ekādaśī Vow as Revealed by Lomaśa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 15. [Chapter 16 follows]. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 16.
[Author: Chapter 17.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, you have not previously heard this divine narrative.
I shall relate a marvel; listen to me with attention.
(1) In the month of Āṣāḍha, all the maidens indeed performed the Cāturmāsya vows as instructed by Lomaśa for the pleasure of Bālakṛṣṇa. (2)
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
having bathed early in the morning, meditated upon the Lord of Compassion, bowed down, and worshipped Lomaśa,
[they offered] sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, flowers, saffron, garments, and garlands.
Having brought cow’s milk enriched with sugar, cardamom, and saffron, as well as boiled [milk],
they— adorned with ornaments, garments, necklaces, and finery— approached to behold the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (4–5)
With their minds fixed on the glorious Lord, they sing songs with sweet voices; they carry water-pots upon their heads adorned with girdles bound with pearls;
holding vessels for fruit-offerings in their hands, their eyes are fixed on Mādhava.
With Kṛṣṇa held in their hearts and having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony, they proceeded forward,
each vying with the others to be first, as they remembered the Lord of Śrī.
Then, in the morning, a miracle was displayed by Bālakṛṣṇa.
"Ten million maidens will come to my house for the sake of worshipping me;
there will be a great crush here, so I must go to the edge of the lake.
The worship must be accepted simultaneously so that there is no crowding."
Having thus resolved, the Blessed One, whose nature is that of an eternal youth, assumed ten million forms at that very moment;
laughing, he proceeded along the path toward them.
Thus, one was seen by one woman, while another was not seen by her.
One [woman] knows: "The Lord approaches me with a smile;
because of his overflowing love for me, he did not go toward the others.
Another [woman] knows: "He comes toward me alone, not toward the others. (12)
Each one perceives him approaching as if he were directed solely toward her, appearing full of compassion.
Thus, indeed, every single woman beholds her own beloved; considering his fortune to be incomparable, they quickly embrace him to their chests. (13–14)
Śrī Hari bowed to Lomaśa, and Lomaśa also joyfully bowed to Hari;
then, with those two crores [of attendants], the earth became like the heavens.
Kṛṣṇa, inquiring after their welfare, proceeded ahead.
The maiden proceeded slightly to the side, to the side, or behind, and to the left.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, which was many yojanas wide,
possessing the shade of a cloud-like umbrella, and adorned with flowering trees and creepers— (16–17).
In that place abounding in auspicious and tender crops, and filled with cool, fragrant breezes,
they set out the vessels for worship, arranged a beautiful seat before them,
and honored them all with offerings consisting of sincere devotion and material substances. (18)
They applied leaf-patterns on their foreheads with fragrant sandalwood paste.
They applied collyrium to their eyes and a tilaka mark upon their foreheads.
Having placed a red dot on the right cheek, they eagerly kissed them.
They placed a flower crown with a peacock-feather plume upon his head, clusters of flowers and various crests upon his ears, and garlands of flowers,
lotus-fiber ornaments, bracelets, and likewise waist-bands.
They presented the Lord with garments adorned with floral patterns;
they applied lac and saffron to his feet and hands,
and they gave him anklets with small bells for his ankles and forefeet.
They gave him yellow garments made of linen and silk;
they placed a flute and sprouts upon his ears and offered clusters of flowers.
They placed a lotus petal in his right hand and gave him a fragrant sprinkling.
They gave cool, sweet water, food, fruits, juices, and milk;
they offered cardamom, cloves, seeds, and leaves for cleansing the mouth.
Having thus worshipped that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa again and again, [they honored him]. (25–26)
They offered the nightly lamp-offering, water from a conch shell, and the wiping with a cloth;
they performed prostrations, hymns of praise, circumambulations, and the offering of the right hand.
They made the offering of their own selves, the handful of flowers, and the request for forgiveness.
They drank the water used for washing his feet and placed it upon their heads.
Placing Kṛṣṇa’s feet upon their chests, they were filled with bliss;
being thus gratified, they requested vows from their own Lord.
For four months, one requested a diet of fruits;
another, a diet of roots; another, a diet of leaves; and another, a diet of milk.
One requested food consisting of a single grain, while another requested the food of sages.
One ate only barley; another ate only wheat. One took mouthfuls of rice; another food devoid of flavor.
One ate food without salt; another food devoid of sweets. (31–32)
One [portion] was devoid of bitter [flavors], and another was free from pungent ones;
one was uncooked by fire, while another was dried and roasted;
one was even without grain, and another was devoid of vegetables.
One [offering] was devoid of split pulses; another was without stalks.
One was lacking meat, and another was deprived of milk. One consisted of food without clarified butter, and yet another was likewise without oil. (34–35)
Some [practice] eating only at night, some eating only once a day, and some every fourth period; others eat at six periods, or even once every seven days;
likewise, there are those who eat once a fortnight, once a month, or follow the Cāndrāyaṇa and other such observances.
They undertook various types of arduous vows, lasting for one, two, three days, and so forth, out of a desire to please Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard this, Śrī Lomaśa said: "Listen, O maidens! Hear what is beneficial. (37-38)
Whatever vow may cause Kṛṣṇa to be pleased is the most excellent of all;
whether by vow, austerity, worship, or by the restraints (yamas) and so forth—
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is to be propitiated by millions of such spiritual practices.
Even in the absence of a vow, if one is serene, that very state is indeed a vow.
(2.16.40) If there is no serenity even when a vow is observed, then that vow is merely a non-vow.
Therefore, O daughters, you must inquire into that by which Hari may be pleased. (41)

"Knowing this, perform that vow during the Cāturmāsya which bestows satisfaction. Thus addressed, those delicate women, sitting comfortably, questioned Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa: "Tell us that by which you are pleased."
Having heard this, Hari laughed and said: "I am pleased by devotion, and not otherwise.
Not by vows, nor by gifts, nor likewise by restraints or observances;
not by sacrifices with their sacrificial fees, nor by the emaciation of the body. (43-44)
I am not pleased by deliberations, nor by wealth, nor by considerations of delicacy;
rather, I shall be gratified only by sincere and unswerving love.
You yourselves must perform the vow of love for my sake.
He is to be worshipped with love, to be saluted with love, and indeed to be remembered with love.
Service characterized by *kaiṅkarya* toward me must be performed with love—in bathing, in meditation, at the beginning of meals, and in all bodily functions whatsoever. (46–47)
I am Kṛṣṇa who should be propitiated; that vow shall grant liberation.
I am the strength of the weak and the portion of strength for the young.
I bring happiness (kaṃ sukham) to maidens; I am Nārāyaṇa, the giver of liberation.
During the Cāturmāsya, let there be circumambulation and prostration for my sake;
let there be the chanting of my garland-mantra, meditation upon me, and the beautiful recitation of my names.
Let songs of mine, stories of mine, and a life dedicated to my sake be dear to you. (2.16.49–50)
"Indeed, the offering of everything to Kṛṣṇa is that most excellent vow which has been performed by me for your sake—a divine rite directly empowered by my yoga.
No other vow is equal to this; through it, the bliss of liberation shall come to pass."
"I am indeed that very person who was to be attained through the vow; I have attained it in every respect.
"What then is that vow, and what other vow is there?"—saying this while remaining in his state of observance, the Blessed One accepted their articles of worship.
Assuming ten million forms, He bestowed upon them the pleasure of seeing and touching Him.
Then, having bowed to Hari, they all spoke to the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord, having come together here, we shall perform Your worship eternally."
"In this very way, grant me happiness through the favor of accepting my worship. "So be it," Hari replied. O Rādhikā, listen, dear one, as I tell you what wonderful thing occurred there. (55–56)
Indeed, the mountain named Śatrūñjaya is situated in the south-eastern direction;
there, in Saurāṣṭra, the Daityas known as Kaṅkatālakas resided.
By the thousands, those Kaṅkatālakas were devoted to liquor and meat.

Resembling mountain peaks, with teeth and hair like ploughs, they were as tall as heated palm trees and touched the very path of the clouds. They subsisted on sea-fish and likewise devoured human flesh. (58–59)
Then, having learned of the festival for the worship of Kṛṣṇa, those Asuras—who subsisted on the flesh of wild and forest animals and who preyed upon birds and living creatures—all arrived;
they were all vow-breakers, wicked, and armed with various weapons and missiles. (2.16.60)
They descended from the path of the sky to slay Bālanārāyaṇa:
"Kill him! Strike down this opposing child-Kṛṣṇa, the great enemy of the asuras and the supreme slayer of hundreds of thousands! || 61-62 ||
"Quickly kill the lord who steals the wives of our husbands;
furthermore, swiftly destroy Lomaśa by binding him around the neck with a rope.
Then, perform the killing of the Brahmins and utterly demolish their refuges."
Having spoken thus, as those intent on killing were about to fall from the sky,
Lomaśa indeed paralyzed them in mid-air;
for he was the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself.
Having gathered all his own forms in a mere instant,
he assumed the form of Vairāja and shone like the king of mountains.
He remembered the divine Garuḍa, and he indeed arrived in an instant.
With his two wings spread wide,
he likewise protected the hermitage and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake; having guarded this sacred field extending ten yojanas, the king of birds covered it as if with a canopy.
With his wings spread wide, he stood there fearless by the command of Acyuta.
The Lord, bearing weapons, swiftly mounted his back;
then, as if in sport, he spoke and released the Sudarśana discus.

"O Kaṅkatālas, conquerors of enemies, why do you remain inactive? Let you who have lost your wits strive with all your life-breath! And here stands Lomaśa, dragging away your state of dullness. (2.16.70–71)
When their state of dullness had thus been withdrawn, those demons were then consumed by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; their fortune destroyed,
they again exerted their strength and rushed forward with great speed to bring about Kṛṣṇa’s destruction.
While Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Garuḍa were first preparing their weapons for the purpose of striking, at that very moment the Sudarśana discus—
resembling the fire of universal dissolution, whirling with sharp spokes, and unbearable to behold— [fell upon them]. (73–74)
He cut off the heads of the Kaṅka and Tāla Asuras;
their bodies, split in half, fell from the sky on all sides,
and even their severed heads, dripping [blood], fell down at that time.
Hands, feet, and hips fell all around upon the ground.
Though armed with weapons, they were as powerless as if their hands had been severed by a discus;
they were then unable to strike either Kṛṣṇa, Garuḍa, or Lomaśa.
Then, a thousand of them met their destruction, cut down by weapons; the rest fled, and the club Kaumodakī herself—
embodied, mountain-like, and endowed with many weapons in her hands— [pursued] them.
Blocking the path and running about on all sides,
that terrifying mace of many forms, the great virtuous one, stood ready wherever the Daityas fled in whichever direction. (2.16.79–80)
Leaping up, he stood before me, but then he struck them down; those others were slain by the mace, and only five or six remained.
Assuming the forms of maidens, they took refuge with Garuḍa.
Having entered the maidens, they protected them from the Lord.
Then Nārāyaṇa, along with his discus, mace, and Garuḍa,
having slain the Daityas, assumed their own subtle form once more.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord Śrī Hari there,
Garuḍa quickly departed for Vaikuṇṭha with the Sudarśana discus now in his hand.
And the Blessed Lord, bestowing courage upon each of the maidens, then remained alone.
He laughed and said to Lomaśa: "Five or six new maidens are present here;
look, O Guru! Out of fear of death, the Daityas have become deceitful women for the sake of saving their lives. (85–86)
"I, being compassionate, must effect the preservation of their lives.
When he had spoken thus, they wept, prostrated themselves, and entreated him:
"Grant us protection and guardianship, as well as the status of perpetual slaves. (87)
Kṛṣṇa said, "Let it be so; let this female form of yours remain forever.
Let your eternal form as maidens abide here in my abode.
Hari then caused their residence to be established in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
And Lomaśa gave him the Vaiṣṇava mantra, the garland for the neck,
the Tulasī, the tilaka, the name-mantra, and a divine form:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā."
The virtuous young maidens, remaining unperturbed, received the mantra;
they became devotees of Viṣṇu and thereafter took refuge in Śrī Hari.
They prayed to the Lord of Lords for the sake of liberation for those who had fallen in battle.
Those Daityas who died in battle by the will of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arrived by the thousands with subtle bodies, free from all taint;
for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, had utterly destroyed their state as Asuras.

Then, having granted them divinity, all the inhabitants of Śatruñjaya were led to Vaikuṇṭha by means of celestial chariots and divine attendants. Thus, those who had taken refuge in Hari attained liberation on the Ekādaśī day.
Then, having led all those maidens away, the sage Śrī Lomaśa went to his own hermitage; Kṛṣṇa indeed became Bālakṛṣṇa.
That sacred site named Kaṅkatāla is located within the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Born and renowned on the right side, where worship of Hari was performed;
having thus brought joy to the women observing the vow, Bālakṛṣṇa vanished at the end of a moment and went to his bed in the house. ||97-98||
O Rādhikā! By knowing, hearing, reciting, or even remembering this auspicious account of the God of gods, one will certainly attain liberation.
One shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, illustrious, and an inhabitant of infinite heavens.
The woman shall become enriched with good fortune and fame, and she shall grant progeny to her lineage.

(2.16.10) Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of Lord Bālakṛṣṇa’s worship performed by the maidens on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha in the Tretā-yuga section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including His assumption of many forms, the vows, the battle with and liberation of the Kaṅkātāla demons residing on Mount Śatrūñjaya, and the dwelling of the remaining maidens in the form of girls at the hermitage of Lomaśa. 16.
← Chapter 016 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 17 [Author: Chapter 018 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; when those Daityas did not return home, their wives came forth in search of the Daitya army. (1)
Then, in the month of Śrāvaṇa during the rainy season,
ten thousand demon wives arrived from the region of the sky at that auspicious site of Kuṃkumavāpikā, which was flooded with water and other elements. || 2 ||
They beheld a vast and delightful hermitage situated in the forest,
which was the refuge of ten million maidens and frequented by the sage Lomaśa.
Among them, some were forest-dwelling Vaikhānasas, while others remained without seats.
Some were Yāyāvaras, others were forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), and still others were householders (śālīnas); some had adopted the pigeon-like mode of life (kāpotī vṛtti),
while others had resorted to the auspicious practice of compassion toward all living beings.
Some subsist on gleanings of grain, while others likewise eat from wooden bowls;
some do not cook their food, yet others cook it at times.
Some possess various kinds of wealth, while others have conquered their own selves.

Some were observers of the vow of silence while standing; likewise, others were sleepers in water, others slept on their heads, and others lived like deer. Some were practitioners of the five-fire penance, and some subsisted on leaves and fruits.
Some subsisted on water, some on air, and others likewise on vegetables.
Others still undertook most intense ascetic practices in that forest where millions of virtuous men and women dwell.
In that hermitage dwell ten million maidens who are the wives of Hari;
there resides the divine Kuṅkumavāpikā, which bestows liberation;
and there flows the divine Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
That region brings about divine perfection,
wherein stands the great and beautiful palace of Hari, more radiant than Goloka; there resides the goddess Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī, and there dwells Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

The subjects, accompanied by the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, shone brilliantly on all sides. That great, divine region, possessing the splendor of the Nandana grove, was thus beheld by those demonesses from the path of the sky. (14)
It is composed of diamonds, crystal stones, coral sprouts, and gravel;
it is rich with blue, pure clay and graced by waterfalls.
It is endowed with various flowers and bears clusters of creepers. (15–16)

There, the plateaus shone even more brightly with the outpourings of various minerals, appearing as if painted on all sides and endowed with diverse flowers, while the tall trees seemed to scrape the very sky. (17)
In them, clusters of *ketakī* and blossoming thickets of *kunda* shine as if they have opened their eyes, alongside the rows of *dhātakī* forests;
[all this is washed] by the waters of the springs, clear as polished sapphire and pure. (18–19)
That radiant region was graced by various carpets of minerals covered with flowers,
where divine couples sported and throngs of apsarases danced,
while intoxicated peacocks warbled.
It was filled with white water-lilies and frequented by swans and cranes;
it abounded in lakes of clear water covered with blooming lotuses, and was graced by herds of lions as well as by deer and birds. (21–22)
Adorned with vessels served by hosts of sages, made lovely by the songs of *kinnaras* and resounded by the calls of cuckoos;
crowded with hundreds of *vidyādharas* and frequented by gods and *gandharvas*. (23)
By the downpours of rain from the clouds and by thousands of sparks,
the soft and charming green meadows were repeatedly illuminated;
it was a place of groves and gardens of all seasons, beautifully adorned with the bloom of spring.
It is the abode of the *yajña-kimpuruṣas* and the refuge of the *guhyakas*;
it is the beautiful dwelling place of liberated attendants and Vaiṣṇavas.
Therein resides the Lord, the boon-bestowing Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Lord Hari, the teacher of all the immortals, is eternally present there.
Compassionate toward his devotees, that glorious one dwells together with his attendants.
All those who travel in celestial chariots [worship] that god, the Supreme Lord.
The gods come to serve the one who is most excellent, unborn, and immutable;
other hosts of deities also fall down to serve him.
This region, which is his very abode, has been beheld by women.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the region was beheld by the Daityas as exceedingly enchanting.
Hari, their Lord, was seen swinging on the branches of trees;
the Supreme Lord was watched as He swung upon a swing suspended from every tree.
Seeing Hari, who had caused the destruction of their husband, they were struck with amazement; they became exceedingly enraged at Kṛṣṇa and rushed from tree to tree to kill him.
Whichever branch of a tree Kṛṣṇa’s swing hung upon—
Each of those trees became a deity in the form of a tree, a servant;
and each of those trees instantly became a divine man bearing weapons, in order to protect that Blessed One and to slay those demonesses. (33–34)
Then the rākṣasīs waged war with the gods in the very sky,
using *bhindipālas*, *tomaras*, clubs, and weapons made of bone;
with fierce tree branches, bamboo poles, and stones and thorns.
Then again, with stones and even with sticks, they fought hair-to-hair;
the gods fought with trees against the rākṣasīs, yet they did not kill them while they were still alive, nor did they strike them in their vital organs or their tender limbs.
Thinking thus, they did not harm the female species, considering them as their own life; yet those fierce women destroyed [the others] by means of virgins alone.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇa, having learned of this, remembered [his power] against the women who were crushing the battle.
Instantly, the Lord arrived there, having manifested himself in two forms.
The Master, assuming the form of Kāla and Lakṣmī, equipped with all weapons,
possessing a thousand arms, and mounted upon an elephant, came through the sky.
When the white elephant, endowed with wings, roared in the sky, the rākṣasīs, their ears pierced by the clear resonance of the echo, then became distraught;
they fell into a swoon in the air and collapsed onto the forest floor.
Others, however, fled to destroy the elephant;
but Hari, who was the very embodiment of the Fortune of Time (Kāla-lakṣmī), then struck them down while they were still alive.
As they died, the women fell cut in two, shattered, and broken, already dead.
Their very selves repeatedly underwent dissolution into the splendor of Time;
yet at that time, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, appearing in a youthful form,
shone resplendent in the hermitage of Lomaśa, situated in the midst of the maidens.
Some wives of the leaders of the Daityas were struck by the trunk of an elephant;
others were slain by weapons. Deprived of their splendor, they perished utterly.
Having died, they attained a divine state and shone like goddesses.
Having beheld the youthful Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord of lords, the Mubhuhus entreated him most fervently:
"Be forever our beloved and the protector of us who are helpless."
"Deprived of the qualities of Daityas, we have died and been reborn through your majesty.
O compassionate one, grant us residence among your daughters in the presence of Lomaśa; we always desire to perform service for you. (48–49)
"So be it," Hari replied; "let there be ten thousand divine maidens.
By the power of Kṛṣṇa, they became less than twelve years of age, possessing limbs proportionate to their beauty, dear to him, and equal to Rādhā and Ramā.
And Lomaśa gave to them the supreme Śrī-Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," as well as a tulasī garland for their necks and an auspicious tilaka upon their foreheads.
He placed yellow garments in their hands and a rosary for the practice of chanting;
he bestowed knowledge and wisdom upon them and gave them residence in his own hermitage.
And all of them [washed] the feet of Bālakṛṣṇa with a stream of milk.
Having washed their hands, they drank the water of his favor and ate the food, fruits, and so forth.
Then, with great affection and a spirit of service, they partook of it at that time.
And Lomaśa then granted refuge to all of them.
He indeed awakened [them] in six ways, consisting of the complete surrender [of all things]:
"O maidens, listen all of you, who have resolved upon the purpose of Kṛṣṇa!
A woman’s body exists for the sake of another, and the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama) is that other. (56)
For that purpose, women devoted to their husbands must cultivate this state in every way.
(57) The husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, the savior who bestows liberation.
Through merit accumulated over a hundred births, a virtuous daughter is born. (58)
Through the merit of a thousand births, she becomes one dedicated to Kṛṣṇa;
through the merit acquired over a hundred thousand births, a virtuous woman becomes the wife of Kṛṣṇa.
By my grace, you all shall undoubtedly become the wives of Kṛṣṇa.
From what cause and by what means, then, would merit be acquired?
Through union with Hari, the ocean of merit increases like a treasure-store;
yet through desire, anger, attachment, greed, or even delusion toward the Lord, [merit is lost]. (2.17.60–61)
If they were absorbed in Him and dependent on Him, all merit would have been earned;
thus you women have today come into the hands of Lakṣmī.
Indeed, even through enmity toward Hari, eternal merit has been attained.
By the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, no delusion whatsoever enters my hermitage on all sides. This place belonging to me, Lomaśa, is beyond the reach of Māyā. (63–64)
Indeed, the defects such as lust and anger blaze forth for those who possess them;
yet, for those who travel through the sky above my portion of the hermitage,
even as they go overhead, their hearts truly perish.
Defects such as passion and the like exist even among beasts and birds;
they exist among gods, dānavas, daityas, and women;
and for all transmigrating beings, saṃsāra consists of false mental impressions.
By resorting to my hermitage, one attains dissolution from the very root;
those embodied beings who have made their dwelling in this hermitage become divine.
By the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I shall grant them eternal peace.
"All of you, take refuge here in Hari Kṛṣṇa and depend upon him.
Apart from attaining Hari, nothing else is to be specially desired.
Indeed, practice devotion to him, meditate upon him, and truly follow his path. (2.17.70)
"Serve him alone constantly and always without sloth.
Your sin has gone, your [demonic] disposition has gone, your state as a Daitya has gone, and your old age has gone.
Fear has gone, and even death—which causes you such affliction—has gone."
"Everything that was to be gained has been gained, everything that was to be attained has been attained;
indeed, what was to be done has been done, and nothing else remains.
"O maidens, keep this in your hearts and practice the sixfold service! (72–73)
Faith in Mādhava should be cultivated just as one does toward a child’s mother;
the granting of boons and the choosing [of him] must be performed by you alone for me.
For embodied beings, renunciation of the body unto that Kṛṣṇa should be practiced in every way.
One should practice self-sacrifice and service toward the Supreme Self like a servant;
one should always maintain steadfastness in both happiness and sorrow, and nothing else but devotion to the husband.
To be in accordance with my beloved is my own desire. (75–76)

"I have no aversion toward him, yet that which is undesirable to him is not desired by me"— thus should a noble woman consider her own happiness to be in the happiness of her husband. But she who is not at peace when her husband suffers will certainly herself become sorrowful.
One should behave toward that beloved Lord, the Supreme Self, as one would toward oneself.
Whatever refuge one desires should be offered to Him;
He alone is the father here, He the protector, and He alone is the mother and the source of birth. (78–79)
Kṛṣṇa alone is my great kinsman; Hari himself is my brother and my sister.
Kṛṣṇa alone is my younger brother, my younger sibling, and even my daughter.
Kṛṣṇa alone—Hari—is my husband, my wife, my daughter-in-law, and my bride.
Kṛṣṇa alone is my father-in-law, mother-in-law, maternal uncle, and daughter;
Kṛṣṇa alone is always my son, daughter, female friend, and male friend.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my brother, king, servant, and attendant.
Kṛṣṇa is my servant, my teacher, and my priest; He is my guide, my caravan-leader, my home, my master, and my lord. That Mādhava is my refuge, the bestower of fruits, and my supreme one.
"My field and my garden, my wealth—Hari himself!
My kinsman is Keśava; he is my boy, and she is my girl. He who is dear to my heart is Mahīmāna; the Lord is my guest. (84–85)
"O Kṛṣṇa, my co-wife is always [there], and my rival is within my very self.
Janārdana is the seer in me, the hearer in me, and the toucher in me.
Kṛṣṇa is the smeller and the taster; Hari indeed is the thinker within me. (86)
He is the goer, He is the grasper, He is the speaker, and He is the one who gladdens me.
Kṛṣṇa is the one who dismisses, He is the awakener, and He is the thinker within me. He is the decider, He is the one who causes attainment, and He is the knower and the wise one within me.
Hari is my satiator, my delighter, and He is the one who bestows jewels upon me; He is my protector and the one who draws [all things] toward me. He is within my womb, in my belly, and in my heart;
He is my vitalizer, my life-giver, my inner self, and the Supreme Person.
"Kṛṣṇa is the witness, the conscious one, and the husband; I am his wife, consisting entirely of Him. Everything belongs to Him, and I belong to Him—the glorious Supreme Soul.
Thus, O little daughter! have you been described by me here. (2.17.90–91)
Whatever is sweet to me, whatever is dear to my heart, whatever is delicious, and whatever is cool—
all that belongs to me; and may Bālakṛṣṇa and these maidservants likewise protect it,
just as Lord Hari, the most secret of secrets, protects that which is to be hidden.
This very beloved one must be concealed; nothing else remains to be done.
All concealment is for the sake of the beloved; there is no concealment in the presence of the beloved.
Kṛṣṇa is perceived as the beloved, and therefore he indeed behaves like the beloved.
Just as a woman who longs for her lover acts like a lover toward him,
so too does Kṛṣṇa act like Kṛṣṇā toward Kṛṣṇā, who longs for him. The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dwells within you.
The substance remains undivided; for it is eternal and indeed imperishable.
That very same one has come here, united [with his consort], into the house of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa;
he is the son of Kambharā-Śrī, and he has indeed arrived because of your vow.

In eating, lying down, bathing, meditating, traveling, sitting, wandering, sporting, drinking, resting, and in exertion; in agitation, in well-being, in gentleness, and in despondency—enjoy that [state]. 98.
And when he turns away from sleep, attend upon that beloved husband.
Thus, indeed, surrender your entire range of activities to him.
Such is the extent of the expansion of the scriptures, and such is the instruction. (2.17.100)
"Oṃ! May there be peace and detachment from you toward Nārāyaṇa;
may the dissolution of all desires occur for you within the Supreme Self.
Having thus instructed them, the king of sages, who possesses the true power to wash away illusion, [proceeded].
And he provided dwellings for the maidens in leaf-huts;
he himself became absorbed in meditation, while those maidens were fed,
honored, saluted, and entertained with words of welcome and the like.
Then they too listened daily to the supreme discourses of the *Śrī Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, morning and evening, day after day.
Every morning, they would constantly worship their beloved husband, Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Day and night they truly make their births fruitful.
Thus, O Rādhikā, I have here related this divine account, which bestows divinity,
which grants life for the sake of a husband, and which is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
In those [women] in whom there is no virtuous conduct, in whom there is no service,
in whom there is no devotion, worship, or meditation upon Kṛṣṇa— Hari,
who is devoted to bestowing grace, is pleased with them as well. (1.07)

Accomplished through compassion, the Great King rained down [blessings] beyond all boundaries. Capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise, he who is higher than the highest indeed creates the races of Daityas, the races of Devas, and the races of Brahmas.

"Even from one who is more sinful than the most sinful, by reading or even by hearing [this], one becomes like a god, like a liberated soul, or like a wife of Kṛṣṇa. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Daitya Wives of Kaṅka and Tāla Attaining the State of Being Wives of Kṛṣṇa in Battle at the Field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and the Instruction on Self-Surrender to Bālakṛṣṇa given by Lomaśa," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 17: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 18 [[Author: → Chapter 19

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā; in the month of Bhādrapada, during the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa), the daughters [of the gods] offered a house for Hari to the ancestors, beginning with Aryamā. || 1 ||
The maidens arrived together, accompanied by sweet milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds,
along with fruits, flowers, agallochum, musk, saffron, and rice grains;
they were provided with golden vessels and other items joined with camphor and similar substances.
Adorned with every kind of finery for the purpose of worshipping the ancient deity,
and overflowing with love, they all arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa on the day of the new moon in celestial chariots filled with divine provisions. (3–4)
Having first bowed to Lomaśa and their supreme father, the Guru,
they remembered there indeed Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
At that moment, Bālakṛṣṇa arrived at Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Out of compassion, for the purpose of receiving the worship and offerings presented by the maidens,
[Kṛṣṇa], under the influence of mercy, saw his own daughters approaching— brilliant, captivating, and youthful— and quickly rose up. (6–7)
They approached with great joy, bowed, and honored him with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings;
they congratulated him most heartily and fell at the feet of Hari. Having addressed one another with inquiries concerning their welfare and health, [they remained there].
A thousand maidens placed flower garlands upon his neck;
placing the dust of his feet upon their heads, they established his form within their minds, fixed his beauty within their eyes, and placed their affection within their hearts. (2.18.9–10)
Then, having gathered together, they themselves offered it and arrived at the hermitage;
that supreme realm of Satyaloka was presented by the maidens who were like celestial lakes. First, the divine throne of the Swan-seated Lord (Brahmā) was offered, resembling a celestial chariot.
It was adorned with a hundred moons and graced by a golden frame;
it flowed with nectar on all sides and was endowed with fragrant cascades;
it swayed of its own accord and was enchanting with the melodies of song.
It moved according to its will and was adorned with pillars of sentient beings;
it shone with jeweled staircases and was flanked by crystal sides,
resplendent with soft, magnificent cotton-padded mattresses.
And the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa ascended it.
At that time, the splendor of Hari was a hundredfold greater than that of the lion-throne.
Then, with the Apsarases and maidens, two very soft sandals [were presented].
For the sake of Makhamalla, two soft sandals, resplendent with streaks of gold and silver and adorned with lightning-like flashes, moonlight, and stars, were offered at the feet of Hari by Bharata.
These beautiful sandals, resembling the celestial cow Surabhi, were placed at the feet of the Lord.
They were surrendered to you according to your desire, for the sake of providing support as you wished.
And when those two sandals were worn by Kṛṣṇa with great joy, a vast and divine splendor was manifested through them. || 18–19 ||
Then, that [parasol], resembling ten million moons, pervaded the very ends of the quarters.
Subsequently, the daughters of the suns beginning with Aryaman offered a parasol adorned with golden fringes and cloth, and joined with silver bells. (2.18.20)
A golden pitcher with a jeweled handle, radiant and brilliant;
adorned with clusters of silk and shimmering with variegated sun-like patterns—then a footstool was presented by the daughters of Kubera. (21–22)
Inlaid with soft gold and fashioned from sandalwood trees,
it was richly adorned with beautiful lion legs and possessed eight corners;
as clear as a lotus petal, it was cool yet endowed with brilliance.
Inlaid with mirrors on its sides and adorned with a moon in its center,
Śrīpati— the Lord of Lakṣmī and Supreme Person— placed his feet there. Then,
by the daughters of the mountain, two chowries made from the hair of white cows [were waved].
And two staffs made of jewels and gold were offered to Kṛṣṇa for his satisfaction;
then a golden cane was presented by the daughters of Indra.
It graced his conch-like neck, which shone like the crown of Brahmā, and rested upon his chest.
Then, there was the auspicious interior of the creeper, adorned with various bracelets;
it was bound at its edge with yellow cloth and possessed the hoods of Śeṣa,
while in the middle it was studded on all sides with pearls, diamonds, and gems.
And then a sacrificial ladle was offered by the daughters of Dharmarāja;
it was made of gold, with its tip possessing the power of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti-śakti*) and its base the power of sustenance (*jīvana-śakti*).
Its middle possessed the power of concentration (*samādhi-śakti*), and it was endowed with the face of the embodiment of Dharma (*dharmamūrti*).
In the center, she was joined by the assembly of Yama; at the periphery, she was accompanied by hosts of messengers.
Then, for Vāyu, there were two fans with jeweled handles held by maidens, bound with golden bands and adorned with silken fringes.
Upon the casting of a golden cloth, which was adorned with both the sun and the moon, circular, radiant, set with jewels, and naturally resonant,
the daughters of the Seasons then offered two clusters of flowers as crests for Kṛṣṇa.
Then the daughters of Viśvakarman gave him a ball of flowers, necklaces, and arches filled with fragrances—
unfading, of divine form, sweet, desirable, and sweet-smelling—
as well as a radiant crown. (33–34)
And ornaments made of gold, garlands, signet rings, girdles, finger-rings, and waist-bands; bracelets,
armlets, chains, anklets, and small bells.
They gave various neck-ornaments to Nārāyaṇa. Then the daughters of Druma gave him garments with devotion:
a protective undergarment, a washed cloth, an upper garment, and a head-cloth.

They gave a shoulder-cloth, a loincloth joined with gold and silver, a small garment, a handkerchief, a fine cloth, and an excellent sari. Then there were the daughters of the ancestors of Śravaṇa, known as the Śrāvaṇīs.
They gave auspicious golden jars filled with water to Śrī Hari. (39) Then the daughters of the year-god offered cooked rice, fried cakes, milk-rice, vegetables, and various foods to Hari. (2.18.40)
The daughters of Kāla gave him a divine wheel of fearlessness in his hand,
and the daughters of Agni and the Pitṛs gave him many vessels—
both cooking pots and frying pans, as well as jars and small water-pots.
Then the female spirits of the deceased, the ancestors, and the daughters gave betel leaves, as well as water-vessels made of gold, silver, and other metals. Furthermore,
the daughters of the ancestors born from the earth presented auspicious articles.
They placed various liquid substances arising from mineral transformations and possessing beautiful colors,
as well as other offerings suitable for Hari, both those belonging to the ancestors and others, before him.
And the Vārkṣyas offered caṭanyā and other items mixed with bitter, sour, and pungent flavors.
Thus, on the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, all the ancestors worshipped the Lord Hari exceedingly with their own extraordinary offerings;
having fed him again and again, they gratified him most abundantly.
The Blessed Lord Viśvaṃbhara, assuming many forms, partook of milk-rice and other foods, various fruits, and sweet, cool, delicious, and flavorful drinks. (47)

Assuming a million forms, Hari, following the intentions of all the ancestors and their hundred thousand daughters, accepted the śrāddha offering they had performed. Then the Blessed Lord summoned the ancestral deities to that place.
Brahmā and the other principal gods, as well as Brahmā and those of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas), sages, seers, deities, the guardians of the world, the lords of the directions,
the ancestors of Śrāvaṇa, the ancestors of Yama, the ancestors of the deceased, and the ancestors of Kālaka. || 2.18.50 ||

Hari gratified the ancestors of the year, as well as all those who are to be honored in every way— the Ājyapas, the Somapas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas— according to their respective karmic dispositions. (51–52)
With water, sesame seeds, fruits, clarified butter, milk-rice, sweet foods,
vegetables, honey, curd-rice, various kinds of edible substances,
as well as with food, clothing, drinking water, mouth-powders, and the like.
Mādhava offered libations to all the ancestors who had arrived;
Keśava offered libations to the ancestral deities by the millions and,
with devotion, fed them sumptuous and highly meritorious food.
Then the Blessed One himself bestowed gifts of ten million jewels upon all those maidens, numbering in the hundreds of millions;
he fed them all according to the prescribed rites with milk-rice and other foods in every way.

The Lord also gave many sweet foods and various kinds of drinks, as well as betel leaves and other items that were pleasing to the palate. All those maidens, the daughters of the eastern and western [kings], were completely satisfied. (57–58)
Then, in the evening, they worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with devotion;
thereafter, they performed the lustration ceremony (ārātrika) and offered salutations as desired.
Those daughters of the Pitṛs who had arrived made their formal requests.
"In order to grant the attainment of service to Kṛṣṇa for as long as they live," Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said, "So be it.
All of them remained constantly in the hermitage of Lomaśa with eager anticipation.
By the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, they became eternally devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa;
and those ancestors who had been satisfied departed for their own celestial realms and so forth.
The Lord, in the form of a child, having duly honored Lomaśa—
Having fed and honored him, Hari, assuming a single form, went to his own palace—
the abode of Kambharāśrī and the refuge of all prosperity.
Then, at the time of twilight, Śrī Hari remembered the son of the Sun (Yama).
Indeed, for the sake of liberating the sinful beings dwelling in hell,
as well as those remaining there whose [karmic] fruits are still being experienced,
and in order to grant fearlessness to the servants of Yama within the realm of Dharma, [he spoke].
At that moment, Dharmarāja arrived in the presence of Hari.
Accompanied by Citragupta, Naya assumed a second form, appearing as old age, disease, great time, and death. (66–67)

The Lord said to them: "Today is the great day of the ancestors, which bestows satisfaction; therefore, I command you in every way that all those who have gone to the realm of Yama must be fed with milk-rice (pāyasa)."
"By my will, they shall be purified by my prasāda, such as vegetables and other foods.
Let everyone become pure today; go to heaven and attain liberation.
Having said this, Kṛṣṇa gave them the prasāda milk-porridge. (2.18.70)
There, Yama and the others accepted [the offerings] and ate them with devotion;
having partaken of the water for drinking and other refreshments, they indeed considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose.
Then Kṛṣṇa gave to them an abundant supply of milk-rice (pāyasa).
And for the purpose of making offerings to those of the southern quarter, Yama and the others accepted it.
By the command of Śrī Hari, Dharmarāja and the rest, having worshipped him, bowed, praised him, and prostrated at his feet, departed for the abode of Yama.
Having summoned the Yāmya dramas, they went forth with perfect composure;
according to the command, they caused them to eat the *prasāda* of Hari’s milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having quickly consumed it, they washed away their inner sins as well.
Then, by the command of the King of Dharma, they became stainless;
at that time, they went to heaven, the true world beyond, and even to liberation.
Thus, indeed, through the majesty of Hari, the groups of ancestors, beginning with the *pretas*, attained [these states]. (75–76)
The fathers of the worlds, who abide by the law of karma, were delivered by Hari;
even those who had attained realization were delivered by that compassionate one.
For his birth upon this earth was for the sake of bestowing grace upon living beings.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is higher than the highest.
Under the influence of his compassion, he leads living beings to the supreme abode; intent upon the resolve of his devotees, he bestows his own yoga upon them. (78–79)
From reading and hearing this, the liberation of one's ancestors becomes certain;
likewise, through hearing it, the female ancestors indeed attain liberation.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
The Pitṛs, however, are heard of as the Devapitṛs, the Śrāvaṇas, the Pretas, the Yāmyas, the Sāṃvatsaras, the Kālās, and the Khāneyakas;
as well as the Agniṣvāttas, the Bārhiṣadas, the Ājyapas, and the Somapas.
Aryaman and the others, who are of the form of sages, possess sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), and are divine lords;
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, along with humans, Rākṣasas, birds, Yakṣas,
messengers, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and likewise Kūṣmāṇḍakas.
The Vaināyakas, the Vetālas, and those who have gone to the lower realms—
all these ancestors have been heard by me from you in this context.
However, as for the daughters whom Kṛṣṇa gratified, they are yet to be mentioned by you.
O Lord of the Rasa dance, ocean of mercy, O Kṛṣṇa, show me those who were the ancestors here at the time of the Śrāddha feast;
where and how do those women who became ancestors now dwell? (85–86)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, you have asked well out of a desire to show favor to the world.
Although you indeed know everything, listen; I shall speak it as well. (87)
The class of women was created by me in Goloka to my left:
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and others;
Virajā, Śrī, Yamī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, and yet others.
Those beloved ancestors of the father's line, born before him, eat at the śrāddha when they have been satiated.
Then, at the śrāddha, Pitāmahī becomes Sāvitrī, Prapitāmahī becomes Śrī, and Praprapitāmahī becomes Durgā; these women come then. (2.18.90)
The mother, Lakṣmī, the maternal grandmother, Sarasvatī, and likewise the paternal great-grandmother, Satī, all come to the śrāddha ceremony in every way.
And those who are daughters-in-law, daughters, young girls, widows, or maidens— [they too come].
Or else, they may be unmarried, virgins, aged, or possessed of latent tendencies (vāsanās);

they may be insane, those who have made verbal gifts [of themselves], or those who have been cast out; they may be independent women, those without lineage, those without family, and those without support or refuge. (92–93)

Those for whom the water-rite and *śrāddha* have not been performed, as well as those for whom the cremation fire has not been offered; those whose bodies were carried away without reaching a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and those corpses touched by unrelated persons;
those who met with untimely death and those who passed away suddenly—[these are the ones who remain].
Those who died through the fault of pregnancy or childbirth, those killed by malevolent spells (abhicāra),
those who died from such spells, those who died by force,
those who died during forced sexual intercourse, and those carried off by yakṣas and rākṣasas— [these are the ones who remain]. 95–96.
Those who died from defects of the womb, those who died while devoid of the duties of widowhood,
those who met with many calamities, and those who met their death under the power of others;
those who met their death through the influence of the shadows of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like.

Furthermore, O Rādhikā, those who are devoid of merit and have not performed meritorious vows or festivals— all such daughters born into a lineage-less family become the property of the ancestors (pitṛs). These lineage-less maidens reside in the realm of Yama within Satyaloka.
In the world of humans alone are those others born of untimely death;
in heaven dwell the hosts of Apsarases who have performed meritorious deeds, yet they are without lineage.
In the world of the earth (Bhūrloka) dwell Bhūtī, Pretī, and Piśācinī.
O Rādhikā, [the goddesses] are Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Kūṣmāṇḍinī,
Vaināyakī, Vaitālī, Bhairavī, Raṇḍā, Kṛtyā, Ṣaṇḍhā, Sūtakī, Śavī, Citānanā, and Śmaśānī. || 101–102 ||
These belong to the ancestors (Pitrya) and reside in the worlds of Bhuvaḥ and Bhūḥ:
the Nāginī, the Bhikṣukī, the Pipīlikā, the Matsyī, and the Rākṣasī;
as well as the Kākī, the Gṛdhrī, and the Makarī, who dwell in the netherworld (Pātāla) and in the water.
O Rādhikā, those who are born of the lineage of death become the ancestors (pitṛs).

Even those mothers who are deities and characterized by goodness (sāttvika) are likewise women; whether they have cruel eyes or belong to a noble lineage, they remain so even after death. || 1.04–1.05 ||
The ancestors exist according to their own sins, dwelling in accordance with their respective karmas;
therefore, one who is wise and knowledgeable should always offer the *śrāddha* rite to them.
And by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [it was ordained] for them alone.
Then water, food, and other provisions were given by Viśvambhara for their satisfaction.
Having accepted all of those and attained his grace, they, accompanied by the bull, went to heaven and other abodes of bliss and joy. (107–108)
Listen, O Rādhikā, a great marvel occurred there.
At midnight, the rākṣasas arrived at the preceptor’s residence;
among them, one was headless and another was eyeless.
The third was noseless, and the fourth was earless;
the fifth was footless, and the sixth resembled a blade of grass at the waist;
the seventh had feet on his back, and the eighth likewise had his face on his back.
The ninth was blind and deaf, lame and mute, and afflicted with leprosy;
the fourteenth suffered from wind-disease (vāta), had dropsy, and was a eunuch;
the seventeenth was filthy, with flies clinging all around him.
The eighteenth was Galapāśa, and likewise another with a spear;
the twentieth was Śvaphāṭita, Kroḍatroṭita, and others as well.
These and other such hosts arrived at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Crying out various cries of reproach and confessing their evil deeds, deprived of food and water, with their throats, lips, and palates parched,
and with their bellies sunken, the pretas then arrived there in great numbers.
Then they wept bitterly before Lomaśa for the sake of their own liberation.
Lomaśa asked, "How indeed did you come to this state of being ghosts?
Thereupon, one of them said, "In the past, I severed the head of a brahmin."
"By that very sin, O sage, I was born here as a headless Rākṣasa.
Another said: 'And by me, during a theft in the house of the master, the eyes were gouged out;
therefore, O sage, I became eyeless.'"
The third said, "I indeed cut off my wife's nose;
because of that, I have become a wretched ghost, deprived of a nose and full of suffering.
The fourth said, "I indeed cut off the ears of a brahmin."
"Adorned with ornaments, I committed the theft of those very ornaments;
because of that, I have become a suffering ghost (preta) deprived of ears.
Then the fifth spoke: 'Formerly, while I was traveling abroad...'"
"Furthermore, while in the forest, my two feet were struck by a thief for the sake of plundering my goods;
consequently, I became footless and must always walk with my face cast downward.
The sixth said: 'My waist was struck by Māra with a staff.'"

"Because of that previous sin, I have become one with a broken hip. And the seventh said: 'By binding my wife's feet, I caused her suffering though she was without fault; by that transgression, O Rākṣasa, [I am thus afflicted].'"

"In this matter, I have become one whose feet are turned backward and who is devoid of the power of movement. The eighth [son] said: "Furthermore, I twisted the neck of Ajabāla and subsequently killed the young goat. (125–126)
"Because of that fault, I was born with my face turned backward, deeply distressed. The ninth said: "And in the past, while I was engaged in hunting, I plucked out one eye of a living deer."
"Because of that fault, I was born blind from birth, suffering in misery.
The tenth said, "In the past, I heard a censure of Viṣṇu; because of that, I am deaf from birth. The eleventh also spoke to him: 129.
"I was struck on the foot by a dog, and because of that, I have become lame.
The twelfth said, "By censuring holy men, I have become mute.
The thirteenth then said, "I have become a leper due to approaching those who should not be approached."

The fourteenth was a sufferer of wind-disease (vāta-roga) and a betrayer of trust. This fifteenth was a fish-eater and suffered from dropsy; he declared, "There is no one like me. The sixteenth was a lecher and a eunuch who destroyed his own seed. (131–132)
From that, he was born as one who performs the work of a *caṇḍāla* among bulls;
then, being completely covered by flies, he was born in that state and spoke thus:
"This [being] who provided the noose for my neck became a noose for my neck. (1.33)

"Because he inflicted the spear upon living beings, he has therefore become afflicted with the disease of colic (śūla). The twentieth said: 'In the past, I tore apart hares and other creatures with dogs and beasts of prey; being a great sinner, I am now torn apart myself. (134–135)
We eat most wretched food and find nothing to eat;
we are thirsty and distressed today. If the compassionate Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, would deliver us.
"O Brahmin! We shall attain liberation; grant us liberation!
Thus addressed, Lomaśa gave them a mantra accompanied by water:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (1.37–38)
Kṛṣṇa then remembered Bālakṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa arrived there instantly.
Having made them drink the water from his own feet and having endowed them with divine bodies in the form of four-armed beings, Hari— 139 — [did so].
He sent them by means of celestial chariots to Vaikuṇṭha, the eternal abode.
Having thus granted liberation, Hari returned to his own residence.
Victorious is this Supreme Lord, the giver of liberation even to sinners!
From reciting and hearing this, the deliverance of one's ancestors will certainly occur;
as well as fame, renown, wealth, grain, cattle, and even health.
Sons, grandsons, daughters, gold, liberation, fortune, and all prosperities [shall be attained].
All perfections shall belong to both the listener and the speaker; of this there is no doubt.
(143) Homage to that Blessed One, who is compassionate toward all and uplifts them, who bestows liberation even while disregarding the karmic deeds of sinners. (144)
Salutations again and again to the purifier of the Daityas, Dānavas, and sinful Rākṣasas, and to the one who grants liberation to the Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas.
Even for the compassionate Śrī Hari, there is no limit to his compassion.
"Moreover, for sinners, there is no end to their faults anywhere.
(146) Thus, O Rādhikā, having known Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Lord, those who constantly worship Him are established in liberation; of this there is no doubt. (147)
"Kṛṣṇa is in the mind, Kṛṣṇa is in the heart, Kṛṣṇa is in the eyes, and Kṛṣṇa is in the self;
