he in whose *brahmarandhra* Kṛṣṇa resides shall certainly attain liberation.

(148) Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Hari performed by the Daughters of the Pitṛs on the Pitṛ-pakṣa in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including the libations for the ancestors performed by Hari, the liberation of those in hell, the acquaintance with the species of the Pitṛ-women, and the deliverance of the *pretas*. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, when his first year had passed and the auspicious second year had begun,
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika, his father commenced the birth festival.
Then he performed the worship of his guru Lomaśa as well;
he fed the brāhmaṇas and gave abundant gifts.
O Rādhikā, I shall relate all of that to you in brief.

Of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person. On the seventh lunar day, having risen in the morning, O Rādhā, the illustrious Ropālakṛṣṇa remembered Kṛṣṇa Hari, bathed, and worshipped Keśava.
On the great festival of the first anniversary, he had a document prepared:
"May my auspicious year for Nandana be fulfilled at dawn on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
and then, upon the occasion of the second year, may it be complete. (5)
On that very auspicious day, during the joy-bringing great festival being performed by me and augmented by you who have arrived,
let the increase of splendor be carried out, considering this [festival] as your own self. (6–7)
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, the treasury of blessings, bestow auspicious benedictions according to your affection; may they be brought and given.
Considering this home as your own, I entreat you all to come.
[He should offer oblations] to those gathered with his family, servants, good people, friends, and relatives;
to the gods, sages, ancestors, elders, and the virtuous who practice the Veda; and to devoted wives, noble women, goddesses, and the wives of Brahmins. (2.19.9–10)
For those who follow the dharma of the Brahmins and who associate with saintly devotees,
the dark-complexioned child Hari becomes as dark as a rain cloud through their auspicious blessings.
[This occurs] at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā and on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Everyone must come to my house on the land of Saurāṣṭra.
(12) To its north is the Bhadrā river, to the east the Śatrujit river, to the south lies the Vyāghrāraṇya forest, and to the west is the mountain. (13)
In the center is a divine lake, circular and surrounded by the ten wrathful deities (krodhas).
In the middle is a great island, where stands the temple of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Therein shines my own abode, that of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
"O highly fortunate ones, you must come to the second annual festival of the Supreme Soul,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. By your arrival, I shall become blessed and one who has fulfilled his purpose."
"By your arrival, this earth shall become equal to Vaikuṇṭha;
and by your arrival, the birth of my son shall attain its fulfillment. Bowing down again and again, I bid you farewell for your journey."
A gathering of those residing on the fourteenth level shall take place here;
through mutual association, gains that are otherwise unattainable will be achieved.
And with a concentrated mind, I shall serve the great ones according to my ability.
Thinking "this one is wretched," a slave indeed should be shown favor;
likewise, according to the scriptures, a woman such as Kambharāśrī should be favored by women. Furthermore, I also request the principles endowed with all mental faculties.
I invite all things—substances, qualities, actions, and universals—as well as all sentient and insentient beings, with sincere intent:
"May my son be your son; may he be nourished by auspicious blessings."
But regarding the future, my thought is always centered on the future:
may that [thought] arise so that my compassion may not be diminished.
Perpetuity must be preserved for the eternal great festival.
Having thus entreated him, he ceased, for he was extremely eager for the fulfillment of his prayer.
O Rādhikā! In this manner, the father wrote a letter of saffron paste, filled with deep emotion, and sent it to the Lord in a distant land.
Having taken all of Kṛṣṇa’s weapons, they departed toward heaven;
his qualities went to the worlds of the Lord, and his splendors to the circle of sovereign powers.
Having taken the ornaments from Pātāla and elsewhere, they departed along with the messengers.

O Rādhikā! Just as those personified messengers of Kṛṣṇa departed, they were invited to go and joyfully set out on their journey, taking with them the most excellent and beloved objects from their respective worlds in every respect. (27–28)
They brought forth divine articles worthy of offering, made of gold and silver, as well as woven and dyed cloths, and placed them upon the celestial chariots and other conveyances.
They regarded the great festival of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as a source of supreme bliss.

Thinking that their desired fortune had arrived, they became eager. On the seventh lunar day itself, Gopāla, Kṛṣṇa, and Lomaśa prepared the collection of all necessary materials in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
O Lord of All, with joy they prepared streams of ghee, streams of curd, streams of molasses, and sugar-candies; various kinds of honey and sweet foods, as well as drinks and mouth-perfumes. 32.
And with that same splendor, the Kāndivika women of the gods, as well as Lakṣmī and other ladies,
and the maidens who were devotees of Hari, prepared the kitchen provisions— whatever various kinds of food there were, both for the journey and to be offered to their stomachs. (3–34)
All varieties of condiments, augmented by sour gruel and the like; as well as what is to be licked, sucked, eaten, desired, chewed, and even roasted;
boiled, cooked, heated, and likewise moistened. (35)
They thoroughly prepared the *pepita*, the *kūrcita*, the burnt, the *sārīkṛta*, and the *prapeceta*;
likewise the *chūṃkārita*, the steamed, the mixed, and the churned—whatever was appropriate, they performed all of it entirely during the night. (36–37)
Darvī, Cullī, Kaṭāhī, Sthālī, Kuṃbhī, Mahānasī, Cipiṭī, Gargarī, Bhrāṣṭrī, Āgaminī,
Vardhinī, Mūśalī, Vallarī, and others are goddesses who provide assistance in cooking. (38)
The virtuous women performed the service of Rāmā and the others with great devotion.
(39) Furthermore, the twelve zodiac signs were then assigned from every region to fetch articles; they brought them back with due respect. (2.19.40)
Wherever the movements of the zodiacal signs occurred and wherever they resided,
people arrived there with great eagerness, taking along various objects.
The sign of Aries resides in places such as granaries and treasuries of jewels.
He constantly roams everywhere upon the earth covered with fresh green grass, as well as on the flowering banks of lakes;
he frequents flocks of goats and sheep, wealth and grain, and various kinds of crops. (42–43)
And she [gave] grains and flavorful juices from her own dwellings,
as well as jewels, pearls and the like, diamonds, and gems;
likewise, footwear, headgear, armor, and shining ornaments.
Hand-guards, waist-guards, blankets, and woolen cloths;
from the womb of the Earth, he drew forth riches, leaves of the *śāka* tree from all sides, blossoming flowers, necklaces, and likewise grains both ripe and unripe. (45–46)
She brought forth abundant fruits, tubers, and face-powders;
and that divine Goddess Meṣā presented them to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then there is the one named Vṛṣī, who wanders through Gokula and other places.
Her residence is among farmers, the earth, and so forth;
she also dwells in the house of Śaṅkara in the form of the Goddess of Dharma (Dharmadevī).
She likewise resides in Goloka during its festival as that divine one.
And from Goloka he brought thousands of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus),
as well as grains such as rice, barley, and wheat, along with milk and clarified butter; and in abundance, fresh butter, curds, and buttermilk of every kind.
He brought from Kailāsa vehicles, carriages, palanquins, and all manner of articles for enjoyment, as well as innumerable jewels;
he gave an abundance of these materials there to Śrī Hari for the sake of the festival.
The Gemini (Mithunī) lunar mansion is associated with singers, dancers, and artisans;
it also pertains to the taking up of beds and seats by couples,
as well as to the playing of lutes and other instruments, play, and sexual union.
Her residence was located among householders on the road and other such places;
she stayed everywhere—in crowds, with elders, in great public spaces, and among large assemblies.
She, too, brought divine objects as gifts.
She brought sixty-four types of arts, including song, dance, and crafts,
as well as young maidens, and presented them to Śrī Hari during the festival.
She also provided beds resembling the foam of milk and radiant seats.
Having brought together all the materials for the assistance of the household, he indeed gave them;
he brought all the lutes and musical instruments, as well as the magnificent articles fit for royal enjoyment, and having brought the various splendors suitable for teachers and gods, he gave them.
Having brought forth from the sites of his own hermitages all the glories suitable for mortals as well as those suitable for all embodied beings, he offered them to Śrī Hari.
Furthermore, that zodiac sign named Cancer has the lizard as its presiding deity.
Dwelling in the waters, residing in fields, wells, and riverbanks,
and established upon secluded lands, she brought forth water-born pearls,
diverse lotuses, and various essences.
She brought and offered to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, during the festival, well-ripened pods of grain from the new fields.
Siṃhī, however, [sought] in the mountains, forests, difficult terrains, and mountain caves—
She dwelt among the hunting lodges, in thickets, and in caves.
And from her own dwelling place, she brought two fine chowries,
as well as musk, fragrant minerals, camphor, and sandalwood.
Silken garments, those made of elephant-ivory,
woolen blankets and soft cloths that ward off the cold,
as well as beautiful deer skins and likewise lion skins.
Tiger skins, elephant hides, ivory, and diamonds; 66.
celestial elixirs, metallic essences, and mineral ores; likewise, medicinal pills, divine herbs, and inexhaustible creepers that cause paralysis. 67.
She brought celestial fragrances, divine fruits, as well as *kalpa* trees,
and divine lamps and leaves, and gave them to Hari. Then, indeed, there was a multitude of maidens, beautiful with every kind of auspicious grace.
The most auspicious of all auspicious things, radiant as a golden campaka flower,
she is the very embodiment of the Kalpa-kanyā and always bestows the fruits of one’s meditative aspirations.
Holding a grain of rice and a lamp in her hands, she dwells upon the bed of the divine couple.
She bestows betel, the essence of the speech of the *Gaṇadharas*, and grants bliss; she dwells likewise in reed-thickets,
in auspicious chowries, in lotus buds and the like, in cities,
and in the abodes of the gods.
The maiden dwells everywhere— in heaven, in the world of mortals, in Pātāla, and in the abode of Hari— and she brought auspicious substances:
saffron, unbroken grains, tokens of good fortune, ornaments, and jeweled baskets.
At that great festival, there were bodices fastened with moonstones, turbans like the autumnal moon,
golden ornaments for the womb,
vessels, bracelets, and countless, infinite golden bowls.
She brought forth water-jars, pitchers, bowls, small pots, and cooking vessels;

as well as various necklaces, beautiful bracelets, and captivating gems such as sun-stones (*sūryakānta*), moon-stones (*candrakānta*), fire-stones (*vahnikānta*), and divine stones (*devakānta*). || 75–76 ||
Chowries with jeweled handles, golden umbrellas, cane staffs, walking sticks,
*velaṇas*, and the like, as well as *vardhanīs* and *kaṇḍanīs*;
various betel leaves, and clusters of *campaka* filaments.
She brought *kādamba* flowers, *kaunda* flowers, *kalpa* stalks, and golden ones;
long vessels of sweet food, natural lamps, perfumes, flavors, and sandalwood paste, and presented them to Hari. (78–79)
The divine zodiac sign of Libra is indeed the beautiful woman named Tulā.
She dwells and moves about in streets, marketplaces, shops, cities, on roads, in houses,
and in places of business for the wealthy.
She too, for the sake of her beloved Kṛṣṇa, conducted that divine festival.
Therein, she provided an abundance of foods and delicacies, free from any deficiency;
indeed, she offered a divine scale upon which what was placed remained truly inexhaustible.
She gave him wealth— gold, silver, coins, and nooses—
and having brought many riches from the abode of Kubera, she bestowed them upon him then.
And that fierce scorpion which was in the pit and on the ground became a heap [of jewels].
It dwells and moves within anthills, cow dung, fissures in the ground, and likewise within the interior of the earth;
it resides in stones and the like, and moves through thin-skinned plants and similar things;
it is found in house walls, forests, fields, wildernesses, refuse heaps, and even in minute fragments.
And that divine maiden, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, brought forth from the mountains juices from stones,
juices from trees, as well as earthy tubers and radishes;
juices produced by battle, juices produced by the earth, and those known as salts.
She also gave her pungent, sour, and sweet tastes, as well as those that destroy poison.
A divine maiden, whose form was that of a horse, appeared with a heap of bows;
she was equipped with a bow, arrows, and quivers, a hero, and the most eminent among those skilled in missiles and weapons.
He stands or moves upon elephants, chariots, horses, vehicles, celestial palaces, on the ground, in carts, and in palanquins;
he occupies those various places and mounts, such as elephants, horses, chariots, and the like.

During the festival, she gave to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa celestial aerial chariots and tens of millions of divine sky-gardens— fresh vehicles indeed, adorned with swans, horses, elephants, and other [beasts]. (2.19.90–91)
The zodiac sign named Makarī is a divine maiden with the face of a deer;
she dwells in rivers, the ocean, great lakes,
and the like, as well as in excavations such as moats surrounding the gods.
He gave to Hari the various jewels produced from those respective places.
[There was] the one known as Kumbhikārāśi, who dwells upon the shoulders of men;
she exists in the form of empty jars and in the guise of a maiden within the houses of vintners.
She dwelt and moved about in gambling houses and halls;
then she gave crores of golden jars to Hari.
She, who was of the sign of Pisces, wandered with love through the oceans of sacred pilgrimage sites.

She dwelt at sacred fords and in the abodes of gods and brahmins. Then the divine Mīnī, in the form of a maiden, arrived and presented to Hari all the vessels for worship and the most excellent materials for worship.
He joyfully bestowed sixteen types of offerings upon Hari.
Thus, at that time, the twelve-fold Sun-god, along with his host of divine maidens,
gave the most excellent treasures extending from Satyaloka to Pātāla to Śrī Hari.
Viśvakarman, having been summoned, arrived at the marvelous pavilion.

He constructed a hundred-storied palace situated within the sacred field, extending to the ends of the quarters, featuring celestial pathways and carriage-roads, and beautifully adorned with gardens. (2.19.99–100)
The assembly hall of Dharma, the assembly hall of Indra, and the assembly hall of Bṛhaspati; the assembly hall of Śukra, the assembly hall of Brahmā, and the assembly halls of Viṣṇu and Śiva—
these were all present at that time, having entered into that very pavilion.
There were divine lion-thrones and likewise golden banners;
there stood one hundred jars fashioned from gold,
and [the mountain] was enriched with a thousand peaks, appearing like a natural sun.
It is resplendent with a mass of luster shining like the natural moon;
it possesses the beauty of millions of lightning-lamps and is adorned by ten million stars.
It is embellished with ponds, wells, lakes, and the like, as well as houses and other means of enjoyment.
It is resplendent with divine substances such as couches, drinks, and carpets;
it possesses walls of divine rubies adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and the like;
and it is enriched by divine pearls, gems, necklaces, and other such jewels. (105–106)
It possessed many gopura-gates and enclosures, eternal and fixed for a thousand ages;
in its center was a great divine altar naturally provided with clarified butter,
resplendent with rows of pillars numbering hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions.

Adorned by all the gods, ṛṣis, and sages—the auspicious protectors of the worlds—the pillar was topped with a divine parrot and peacock; it was provided with celestial hearing and sight, as well as divine food, dwellings, and other such amenities. (108–109)

It was resplendent with divine gardens, monasteries, and the like, as well as celestial food and houses; it shone with divine bathing areas and excellent courtesans. Moving through the sky and traveling at will, it was adorned by billions of maidens.
The divine arena for the wrestlers was pervaded by celestial displays;
it was graced by the science of divine music and delighted by divine drama.
It was adorned with the sounds of divine musical instruments and the conversation of those who had attained the desired state. (11.1–11.2)
Resembling an elephant, a lion, and other such beings, and adorned by all the gods—
whatever indeed does not exist within the Egg of Brahmā or in the world of Īśvara,
that truly does not exist there in the pavilion constructed by Viśvakarman.
In the creation of living beings, in the creation of the Lord, and in the supreme realm of Brahma’s creation—
whatever is renowned as existing there has been fashioned here in this pavilion.
Viśvakarman performed the craftsmanship, and Brahmā performed the ritual design.
Vāsudeva manifested forms that were renowned as substantial entities, and at that time, he made the imperishable Brahman the manifest state of those forms.
O Rādhikā, you are Mahāmāyā; you yourself removed all deficiency.
Lakṣmī established fullness, and Jayā brought about victory.
(1.17) Thus, on the evening of the seventh day, the pavilion became magnificent;
for when the eternal abode had arrived, night was no longer seen there. (1.18)
Nidrā resides at Kuṅkumavāpī; Ānandinī is located one *krośa* away from that sacred field (*kṣetra*); Mahābrāhmī is situated in Saurāṣṭra as the Śakti;
and the first rising of the Sun consists merely in the sight of its orb.
The arrival of night was signaled solely by the blackness pervading the horizons;
the departure from the horizons was determined by the radiance of light.
And the sunrise was inferred only by the arrival of the Bālakhilyas.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sending of Invitation Cards to All Worlds, the Presentation of Offerings by Rāśi, and the Construction of the Great Pavilion," on the occasion of the celebration for the commencement of the second year of the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 20 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 20.
[Author: Chapter 21.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When such a pavilion had been constructed there by hundreds of thousands of artisans, [the Lord spoke].
It was beautified with colorful patterns, svastikas, and creepers;
it was auspiciously adorned with pillars decorated with curd, goads, parched grain, and *lāja* seeds;
and on all sides, within the center of cymbals (*jhallarī*), were placed verses that awakened understanding.
Upon the principal deities placed at the top of the pillars,
each with their respective banners and their characteristic vehicles positioned upon them;
and in the sky above the guardians of the various gate-towers, [he saw] the encirclement of the necks [of the demons].
[This occurs] through the pleasing of the minds [of the devotees] by means of the names of those respective principal deities.
(4) In a circle of pillars draped with divine golden cloths, and with staffs encircled by garments rich in the seven forms [of precious materials]. (5)
On that ground made beautiful by the tops of pillars adorned with images of celestial goddesses,
there was land where there should have been water, and water where there should have been land; O lady with eyes like fire,
it was further graced by waving fly-whisks shining like reeds amidst the flames.
Surrounded on all sides by lightning-vines, it was as clear as liquid mercury;
in its circular central pavilions, it shone with the splendor of a *rāsa*-circle,
possessing the beautiful luster of fresh saffron from whose origin it could not be discerned.
In which the new spectacles of dances upon screens of lightning delight the eyes,
which is beautifully variegated by the wonders of the divine hosts descending in their formations,
and which consists of the playful grace of millions of Kṛṣṇas and their beloveds.
In that place of all prosperity, where desires are fulfilled at will, a deep pit of longing,
where truth is present through desire, and which is a pavilion of true resolve—
on such a morning of the eighth day, the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa appeared. (2.20.10–11)
He sprinkled the ground with cool waters scented with sandalwood and other fragrances; he perfumed it with incense and various kinds of delightful aromas.
He drew svastikas, sarvatobhadras, and circular wheels.
He had various mandalas drawn with colored powders (13).
He adorned those auspicious [sites] with unbroken grains, flowers, saffron, curd, and young sprouts, as well as with gate-towers and arched portals (14).
With the leaves of mango, *aśoka*, and other trees, as well as with the leaf-sheaths of plantain trunks,
he beautified the garden paths with fruit-bearing plantain stems and branch-tips laden with fruit,
as well as with clusters of blossoming flowers. (15)
He caused banners to be raised, resounding with sounds that signaled the festival;
he also had flags fastened everywhere upon the pavilion.
Likewise, divine glass and other mechanical instruments, as well as electric lamps and the like, were installed.
It illuminated the pavilion and its surroundings on all sides.
In every pillar of that exceedingly beautiful pavilion, the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhis),
appearing in forms that fulfill desires, fulfilled every wish.
The fixed instrument, the time-measuring instrument, and the immensely great piercing instrument;
instruments for seeing from afar and for hearing from afar; and image-projecting instruments in every place and every house. (2.20.19–20)
In the divine pavilion, there were pillars and woven hangings;
indeed, very long woolen carpets resembling green meadows were present.
There were also grass mats, straw mats, cushions, lion thrones, and altars.
There were elephant-thrones, swan-mouthed seats, and vulture-mouthed seats at the crossroads;
there were thrones inlaid with gems and sands of gold, as well as various kinds of swings and long couches on all sides. (22–23)
There are many costly items, as well as sandals and mattresses,
enriched with gold, gems, and jewels, which shine on all sides. There,
the fields made of clay are adorned with cotton and *sīdru* trees.
Various species of noble flowers, such as the *anagha*, *śārṅga*, and *campaka*, grow there;
auspicious and compact trees stand within the pavilion, and the ground of golden sand shines forth on all sides. (25–26)
Soft, suitable for young girls, thin, and exceedingly delicate;
the sacrificial enclosures, the small streets, and the pathways were circumambulated clockwise.
There, in the pavilion, the paths shone with sprouts, creepers, and other such adornments.
The seats for the spectators were provided with couches and benches;
they were arranged all around, higher and higher, even reaching up into the sky.
These were for the servants, bards, ritualists, soldiers, heralds, and panegyrists.
The high seats of the learned brahmins, the wise women, and the poets, eloquent singers, shone like streaks of lightning;
and within that area, there were rows of seats for human beings.
They shone on all sides with great expansion, like moonlight.
Then, within [the city], there were yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas;
likewise, kūṣmāṇḍas, vaināyakas, vetālas, and kinnaras.
The Kimpuruṣas, the Vidyādharas, and likewise the hosts of Yoginīs;
then those dwelling within, possessing divine bodies, radiant with crowns and bracelets— the gods, goddesses,
guardians of the gods, lords of the gods, and the followers of the Suras.
At various places, quadrangular platforms were likewise constructed.
There stood four-legged, eight-legged, and sixteen-legged thrones for the foremost gods and lords of the divine realm.
Then there were lion-thrones with canopies and parasols made of gold, exceedingly divine, presided over by the ancestors.
Then within [the hall], there were sages who were reciters and contemplators of Brahman.
There were reciters of the Vedas as well as reciters of the Lakṣmī-saṃhitā;
some were reciters of the Saṃhitās of Rudra and Brahmā, and others were reciters of the Saṃhitā of Agastya. (37–38)

Then the great sages stood upon woolen seats spread with cloth; thereafter, the maharṣis who dwell in Satyaloka as well as those who reside in Vairāja took their places upon the pedestal below the inner pavilion.

They were devoted to the celibate life and dedicated to the chanting of sacred prayers (brahmajāpa). The officiating priests (ṛtvij), who were the most eminent among the knowers of Brahman, were intent upon the performance of sacrificial rites;
these included, in their respective order, the Brahmā, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, and the Adhvaryu.
There were chanters of the Sāmaveda and others who sang songs, as well as those engaged in the recitation of mantras;
there were the Bhārgavas and others, skilled in their respective duties and accompanied by their Śaktis.
There were sacrificial vessels, sacrificial porridges, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and likewise liquid offerings.
The sacrificial wood, rice, and other grains became abundant;
then clarified butter, oblations, and various offerings were all present in full measure.
The sacrificial pit was vast, and Viṣṇu was the deity of the sacrifice.
There the Vaiṣṇava fire, the Āhavanīya, shines resplendent;
and preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana), the sacrificial rite proceeds.
His mother is Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī, and his father is Gopālakṛṣṇa.
In that place where the sacrificer stood, Lomaśa and [the other] shone forth before him.
There, Lomaśa performed the worship of Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites, and thereafter the fire-oblation (havana) was commenced.
To the south of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), auspicious beings liberated from the syllable (akṣara-muktas) reside;
on one side are the inhabitants of Goloka, and on the other side dwell the residents of Vaikuṇṭha.
Beyond them are others who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and those who inhabit Kṣīroda and Śveta-dvīpa.
Those residing in Badrī, those on Kailāsa, and likewise those dwelling in other abodes,
remain on the southern side, fully devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Upon the altar is the Supreme Brahman himself, Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Lord who assumes the form of a youth, shines forth visibly as a child. Although, according to worldly convention, he appears to be in his second year of life.
Nevertheless, the Supreme Lord, rich in the form of light, shines forth.
On the sacrificial altar, upon a beautiful throne in a celestial chariot, the Blessed One himself was present;
by his side were Rādhikā and I, Kṛṣṇa, your beloved. (52–53)
By my side dwells Śrīpati; by his side is Nṛnarāyaṇa;
by his side is Śvetavāsī, and likewise Kṣīravāsī;
after that are Bhūmā and the others, Vāsudeva and the others, and thereafter Kapila and the others.
They sit upon the altars, lion-thrones, and celestial palaces (vimānas).
Their wives, their daughters, and those released by them stand all around them as staff-bearers, umbrella-holders, and attendants at their sides. (55–56)
And musical instruments were sounded behind the altar,
while ten million goddesses shone resplendent upon their seats, some equal and others slightly inferior.
Those who delight in the great festival of Kṛṣṇa sang charming songs.
Containing within them the beginningless divine and enchanting pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
a true fire-offering (homa) takes place therein, and the Lords and others are satisfied—
the gods, all the ancestors, the incarnations, and millions of liberated souls. (58–59)
All of them indeed accept, under the guise of fire, the ever-fresh sacrificial offerings presented by the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa—
various kinds of milk-rice, as well as fruits, flowers, and honey.
Rice and coconuts were also offered repeatedly.
Then, when the ritual dismissal was performed and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) had likewise been made,
the assembly rose up there in the pavilion and offered divine, excellent flavors as oblations.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā, the planets, Gaṇapati, the Mothers, the water-jar, the guardians of the quarters, and the lords of the deities—
whosoever were established there, each in the form of their respective sanctuaries.
Worshipped in person, they assembled for the sacrifice;
having witnessed the oblation, they then accepted it through the mouths of the fire.
Satisfaction arose, the sacrificial rite was completed along with the ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Satiated by the giving of infinite sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), those deities of the Brahmanas then prepared to perform the worship of the primordial Bālakṛṣṇa.
Likewise, the incarnations, the liberated ones, the celestial sages (*brahmarṣi*), and the great sages (*maharṣi*) [did so].
And the inhabitants of those various worlds set forth,
bearing offerings; musical instruments and trumpets that produced sharp and purifying sounds were played,
as were mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and other drums, along with water-organs.
Stringed instruments, drums, conchs, bells, and likewise cymbals, as well as lutes, kettledrums, and horns, were sounded by the *tumbiras*.
There were also those who play with the throat (*gālavādya*), those who play with tone (*svaravādya*), those who play with the lips (*phudvādya*), and those who play with touch (*sparśavādana*).
Then the sweet sounds of Vedic mantras, such as had not been heard before, were intoned by the twice-born;
and streams of blessings flowed forth toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.20.70–71)
Lord Hari-Kṛṣṇa was sprinkled with the waters of the ocean’s holy bathing places,
with the waters of the Brahma-lake, and with the waters of the Gaṅgā, Virajā, and Yamunā,
as well as the waters of the Sarasvatī, Svarṇarekhā, and Gaṇḍakī.
Then the youthful Kṛṣṇa shone, exalted by his splendors;
upon his head a crown gleamed like ten million suns,
adorned with ten million moons and resplendent with the dharma of the Kali age.
Adorned with a divine peacock-feather ornament, the two beautiful golden earrings, set with jewels and shaped like ears,
shine resplendently upon the ears of Bālakṛṣṇa.
The head is adorned with a topknot of matted hair fashioned with oil;
the forehead is resplendent with an upward-pointing sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) made of kesar powder;
and the moon [on the forehead] is auspiciously marked with sandalwood paste and saffron.
Likewise, the radiant collyrium in his two eyes shines forth;
even his forehead, though anointed with sandalwood paste, is marked by a long vertical streak.
Adorned with beautiful lines and central dots, it is resplendent upon his brow. (78)
On the right cheek there is a subtle, pale spot that appears very permanent;
there is a mole on the chin and also a mole on the throat.
Endowed with splendor, his two round cheeks shine beautifully. (2.20.80)
Having attained the state of lotuses, their eyes filled with love shine most enchantingly with lines like red coral.
Their ears, reaching as far as the corners of the eyes, are equal and capable of hearing from afar. (8.1)
With conch-like necks and prominent throat-joints, their red lips were enchanting.
Resembling the curves of bows and marked by unblown lotuses, those two seeds of Rati shone forth as the attractors of Hari’s heart. (82–83)
With well-developed shoulders and full arms, adorned with folds on their forearms,
they possess broad palms and are beautified by the three joints of their fingers;
though not stained with red lac, they are marked by fine crescent-moon lines.
Adorned with the marks of the wheel, fish, bow, trident, swastika, and thunderbolt, they were captivating with the lines of longevity upon which the ring fingers rested;
always as clear as a mirror, they reflected and revealed all things. (85–86)
His arms, with rows of hair growing upward and fingers as delicate as lotus stalks, were turned toward his sides, pale and resembling autumnal [lotuses].
His flanks were the dwelling place of desire, and his beautiful chest was the abode of Śrī.
In the midst of its hair, it shone with a beautiful rightward curl;
it was resplendent with excellent gems gleaming alongside golden lines, and it appeared radiant with two lovely, stringless pearl necklaces.
Her two breasts shine with the beauty of two blue stars,
likewise joined by a cluster of golden-threaded body-hair.
The garden of her body-hair shines forth, manifesting the quality of guilelessness.

Between the two thighs, at the junction, there is a long, golden line of hair (*romāvalī*) extending to the hips, as if it were the beauty of a painted entrance; and from his navel, this [line] shines like the water of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) flowing downward. (9.1–9.2)
The male organ is brilliantly radiant, adorned on the left with the beauty of sesame seeds;
the two thighs possess the splendor of the interior of a plantain tree or the moon, covered with fine hairs.
With their extremities having the nature of gold, they shine as they extend toward the imperishable.
Possessing the beautiful hue of the campaka flower, well-nourished, filled with vigor, and auspicious;
[the calves] extend from the heels to the malleoli, reaching up the backs of the thighs; and on the hips, two distinct lines of hair appear, extending to the end of the pelvic region. (94–95)
The two beautiful channels of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha exist;
they descend two finger-breadths from the root of the left thigh and extend for more than one finger-breadth, marked by the scars of the stake-wounds. (96)
On the upper part of the left knee, on the thigh, there is a white-colored mark, an eight-petaled lotus, the abode of Śrī Kamalā;
it exists, rich in great beauty, as a manifest resting place for Kamalā. (97–98)
The two jewels Akṣayavīrya and Kośa are external and rest upon the bull;
the other two are hidden within, situated on the sides of the *liṅga*.
The navel-pool, shining with the three-fold line, is resplendent. (99)
Her two hips are as white as the moon, soft as fresh butter.
(2.20.100) Adorned with skin resembling a golden girdle, she shines like an elephant;
her back appears as a temple, while her front is the abode of Kama. (101)
The calves are rounded and globular, golden-hued, and adorned with hair.
On the right calf, at the side of the *nalikā*, there is a black spot.
Likewise, on the right arm, there is a spot, and three ankle-bones shine forth.
On the surface of the feet, which have the form of a workman, there are lotuses;
they are endowed with upward lines, marked by the peaks of palaces and mountains, and adorned with lotuses, water-pots, vajras, barley-corns, and other such signs. (103–104)
Adorned with sixteen, thirty-two, and eight auspicious marks and lines; beautiful with soft fingers graced by moon-like nails;
auspicious, resembling a white lotus, gentle, and worshipped by ten million gods. (1.05)
Victorious are the two feet of Hari,
placed upon a golden pedestal, which have been touched by ten million maidens, adorned with the splendor of ten million sovereigns, and beautified by anklets, necklaces, and saffron-dyed garments.
His auspicious hips shine, marked by a golden girdle;
his body is adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, rings, and finger-rings.
On the two middle fingers there are conch-marks, and on the eight [fingers] there are wheels.
On the palm of the left hand there is a large line extending upwards;
it hangs from the base of the middle finger down to the wrist.
His form is adorned with flower clusters, beautiful balls, garlands, and wreaths.
Adorned with golden ornaments, jewels, gems, and pearl necklaces,
as well as with the decorations of amorous grace,
the exceedingly beautiful Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent during His own great festival.

He was resplendent in the midst of the assembly hall, seated upon an elephant-throne within the pavilion. At that time, Śrī, Ramā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Padmā— though distinct in form— all shone forth together, united with the beloved Hari.
Such is this Blessed One, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
on His annual birthday, O Rādhikā, the All-pervading Lord shines resplendent.
[He shines] in that place rich in beauty, possessing all splendor, and which increases the glory of the world.
In the center of that beautiful and divine pavilion, Hari shines resplendent.
Sprinkled with fragrant waters of the Vedas by the great sages,
Kṛṣṇa stands alone as a child before all embodied beings.
He was the object of the eyes and of the minds, even of the hearts;
he alone existed both within and without, just as in the transcendent state of Brahman.

(2.17) Thus ends the chapter titled "Description of the Splendor of the Great Pavilion, the Seating Arrangements for the Assembly, and the Description of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa’s Adornments and Form," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Twenty. 20.
Chapter 20: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 21.
[Author: Chapter 22.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how [the Lord] shines within the supreme abode.
The Supreme Self, the Incarnate One, Hari became manifest in such a form.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is superior to ten million forms of Kṛṣṇa, is enriched with forms corresponding to His own nature; He possesses a supreme essential form that transcends all.
He alone is the object of the vision of all living beings;
he alone is the object of the mind, the ego, the intellect, and the self.
Possessing a divine form, he is like a youth slightly less than sixteen years of age. (3)
Radiant and exceedingly effulgent, his garments were like a blazing fire.
His waistband was golden in color, and he wore a beautiful waist-cloth (kaṭikañcuka) enriched with golden bells and tassels, as well as a lower garment (dhautra) adorned with golden filaments.
An excellent lower garment (*kāṭeya-paṭa*), pervaded by rows of golden stars, was positioned at his waist as well as upon his shoulder; likewise, an upper garment of great luster was worn.
A crown rested upon the head of this glorious Supreme Soul.
Pervaded by every kind of fragrance and endowed with divine scent,
he sat down upon his own suitable, lofty, and auspicious pavilion.
There, upon the great altar, were excellent slabs of sandalwood.
There are four auspicious golden pitchers with firm feet,
each indeed weighing as much as a thousand wrestlers.
They are [the images] of Garuḍa, Narasiṃha, Śarabha, and likewise Kūrma.
At its feet shine the powers, adorned with strength.
(2.21.10) There, sixty-year-old elephants, mounted by four drivers and adorned with four girth-bands, stand resplendent, reaching toward the sky as they rise up. (11)
Wearing all kinds of ornaments and garments, those of golden complexion shine forth;
they have white bellies, white trunks, and white tusks, resembling the color of milk.
Seated upon the backs of elephants are auspicious, golden lions, beautifully adorned.
There were four lions with trunks that touched the sky.
(13) Upon the backs of those four lions shone a great tortoise, green in color and possessing a long, circular shell. (14)
Behind her is the Māṇikī-śakti, Aśvinī, possessing a divine form;
she sits with a straight back, enriched by the beauty of all her ornaments.
Upon her back is an auspicious, soft, golden-colored covering.
There shone a silver couch, covered with a variegated silken cloth (16).
It was most beautiful, with divine pillows placed at its sides and back;
it was adorned with sacrificial carpets and was auspicious for the seven steps (of marriage) (17).
Above it is a parasol formed by the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa,
auspiciously bestowing divine splendor with its celestial diamond-like eyes.
There, upon the couch, Hari placed his feet upon a footstool.
The great king, the sovereign over the kings of kings, sat down.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa both stood at his sides,
accompanied by two chowries, while the Imperishable (Akṣara) stood at the tips of his feet.
Lomaśa stood by the side of the tree holding a vessel for worship,
while his mother and father sat near Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
While they were thus situated, ten million celestial chariots then appeared in the sky.
Divine beings, supported by celestial powers, remain stationed there in pairs to behold [the scene].
For the purpose of worship, a beautiful and lofty ladder has been constructed from the surface of the earth,
consisting of a succession of steps.
On the ground, however, seven steps were fashioned for the silk bands;
then there were two [bands] hanging down like the trunks of elephants,
touching the silk bands and serving as supports for the steps, standing like the rungs of a ladder.
And up to the level of the temples of the two trunks, reddish steps were fashioned, very firm and secured with chains;
right there at the temple-bases, resting-shelters were constructed. (25–26)
Above that, other very beautiful staircases were constructed upon the two lion-trunks, which shone like staffs; then,
a ladder was fashioned all the way up to the head of the lion.
A four-legged frame with lion heads is supported by a tortoise base.
(28) Two auspicious swans are positioned at the sides of the tortoise’s neck; between them, and between their arms, another ladder is fashioned. (29)
The face of Māṇikī is in contact [with the central figure], and on both sides are two Garuḍas; with their outspread wings, there are peacock-feather whisks upon the backs of swans,
touching the steps which indeed consist of wings in due order.
Attached to the sides of the ruby [throne] and with peacock feathers above, there the worship of Hari is performed by the gods and others;
thus the Lord sits upon a divine, expansive, lofty, and beautiful seat. (3.1–32)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is worshipped by all;
yet neither had His seat been heard of nor seen before, O Lord of Śrī.
There, He was resplendent with the glory of the King of Kings.
To perform worship, Kambharāśrī first arrived;
holding a golden vessel in her hand, she was equipped with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, sandalwood, musk, birch-bark substances, and tulasī blossoms. (34–35)
Filled with colored powders, sprouts, parched grain, flower garlands, ornaments, fruits, water, sugar and other sweets, and the essence of perfumes,
Lomaśa then, at that moment, uttered words of blessing.
Oṃ! May the liberated souls of Bālakṛṣṇa grant well-being and may they move about in peace.
May the imperishable Brahman grant well-being and long life.
Oṃ! May Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa extend well-being to you. (37–38)
May Vāsudeva and the other lords grant well-being;
may the incarnations of the lords of gods, such as Śaṅkara and others, grant well-being.
May the ṛṣis, the ancestors, the Siddhas, the virtuous ones, and the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga [grant well-being].
May the gods and human beings grant well-being to the child Hari.
May all the sacred fords (tīrthas), the Ādityas, and the Rudras likewise grant well-being.
May the Vasus, the Nidhis, and the Vidyās indeed grant well-being to Hari.
May the truthful women, the virtuous, the maidens, and the wives devoted to their husbands;
may the goddesses dwelling in the forests grant well-being to Hari.
May the trees, the creepers, the celestial singers, the kinnaras, and the tree-spirits [grant it as well].
May the attendants, the servants, the rivers, and the streams indeed grant well-being to Hari.
May the yakṣas, the bears, the gandharvas, the māgadhas, the kimpuruṣas, the śakas, the vidyādharas, and likewise the sādhyas indeed grant well-being to Hari.
Mountains, mines, sacrificial posts, excavations, battlefields, and forests;
the netherworlds, serpents, daityas, dānavas, and likewise asuras;
rākṣasas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, and piśācas.
May the Mothers, the Kṛtyās, and those who dwell in water,
on land, in the forest, and in the world, grant well-being to Hari.
May the Caityas, the Mantras, those of divine bodies, and the manifestations such as weapons and missiles [grant him well-being].
Boys and groups of girls, the elderly, Brahmins, and those born from a womb;
those born from eggs, born from sweat, and born from sprouts, as well as those who bestow well-being;
Vināyakas, Gaṇeśa and the others, Hanumān, and likewise Garuḍa.
May the attendants, headed by Nanda, bring well-being to Hari.
Rādhā, Ramā, Lalitā, Padmā, Jayā, Sarasvatī, Māṇikī, Śrī, Kamalā, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Rati—[may they also grant well-being]. 2.21.50–51.
May Śāradā, Virajā, Gaṅgā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Narmadā, Sāvitrī, Mañjulā, Haṃsā, Amṛtā,
Durgā, Maṅgalā, Saguṇā, and Dvādaśā— these twelve beloved goddesses— grant us a hundred blessings. (51)
There are sixteen thousand other powers (śaktis), numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions;
may the sun, moon, planets, and so forth, bring well-being to Hari.
May the principles (tattvas), the beings born of the elements (bhūtajā bhāvāḥ), and Māyā—along with that which stands beyond Māyā—be auspicious.
May the ornaments of Hari—those practitioners of yoga established in celibacy, who are the embodiments of the qualities of the Vairāja [Puruṣa]—be auspicious;
likewise, may the various forms of erotic grace, the musical notes, and the songs be auspicious. (54)
May the divine musical instruments always bestow auspiciousness upon Śrī Hari.
May Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Dharmarāja, and Dharmadeva,
endowed with devotion, grant you auspiciousness from Hari.
May Janaka Kambharāsvāmī, the inner self and supreme self of Hari, grant us well-being; may he grant well-being to himself.
Muktā, Campā, Jayā, Haimī, Ramā, Śāntā, Vrajā, and Dayā— [may they likewise grant us well-being]. ॥57॥
May Bhānu, Dīpāvalī, and Ūrjā bestow well-being upon Hari.
(58) Oṃ! May there always be perfect peace, and may there be long life free from end;
may there be health, eternal happiness, and indeed the permanence of Hari. (59)
Thus Lomaśa, having sprinkled [him] with water and other substances accompanied by words of blessing,
performed an auspicious tilaka and a crescent-shaped mark (candraka) with barley sprouts and flowers;
together with his mother, he conducted the worship along with its constituent rites.
The mother, the destroyer of sorrow, repeatedly placed sweet food in his mouth and pressed his hands together in *añjali*;
the mother also bestowed her words of blessing upon his head:
"May you indeed possess eternal life; may you become the Lord and Master of all. (6.1)
Having spoken thus, she placed a garland of divine flowers and *kalpa* blossoms around his neck.
Scattering unbroken grains (*akṣata*) upon his head, she performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and bowed, the mother returned to her own seat.
The father performed worship in this manner: "May you be possessed of well-being, my son;
may you be the one who joins the thread of the lineage and be endowed with eternal life.
Then Śrī Lomaśa, joyfully worshipping the Lord of the Gods, [spoke].
With all the mantras of ritual service, he bestowed an auspicious blessing:
"By means of your intellect, virtues, reflections, self, devotion, and learning;
through dharma and the most excellent yogic powers—may you attain eternal prosperity. (66)
By means of divine lifespan, conduct, splendor, and strength,
through compassion and dispassion, may you become eternally exalted. Likewise,
through service to your mother and father, and through devotion to the venerable Guru.
Be one who protects those who have come for refuge and brings about eternal prosperity.
Be ever devoted to the path of Brahman, fulfilling the desires of the mind;
be one of equal vision, a great merchant, and dedicated to the virtue of giving.

"Be a giver of all contentment and one who possesses eternal prosperity! (6.9). Thus, with these blessings, the delighter of children was honored by Lomaśa; he was Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, over whom parched grain was scattered. (2.21.70)
Then, the opportunity for worship was granted to others;
the beloved wives of Śrī Hari, who had gone to the supreme abode, [returned] for the sake of worship with divine means and materials, such as fragrant sandalwood waters. (71)

Then they performed worship with necklaces of jewels, beautiful garlands, and likewise with flowers accompanied by heart-mantras; they performed the *ārātrika* rite which destroys suffering. Bringing their joined palms to their heads, they also offered water for the feet.
Having drunk [the nectar], offered their gifts, and applied the saffron of grace,
they repeatedly touched their necks with love and gazed upon their beloved of life;
then Akṣara and the others departed for their own celestial chariots.
Likewise, those established in the Imperishable (akṣara), as well as the liberated ones, worship the Lord who is distinct from the liberated;
so too do Śrī Kṛṣṇa joined with Rādhikā, Nārāyaṇa joined with Śrī, all the inhabitants of Goloka, and likewise the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. (75–76)
The residents of the four Vaikuṇṭhas, those dwelling in Amṛta and Avyākṛta, those residing in other abodes, the liberated ones (muktas), as well as the others— the Vyūhas,
the incarnations (avatāras), and the Lords (īśvaras) headed by Sadāśiva.
Equal to Mahāviṣṇu are the Māyā-pradhāna-puruṣas;
likewise the Vairājas, the Brahmadevas, the Īśas, the Munis, the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, and millions of gods who dwell in the Bhuvarloka. (78–79)
Led by Bṛhaspati and led by Śukrācārya,
the rivers and streams, humans, mountains, trees, creepers, and so forth,
as well as pillars, sacred fords, shrines, men, and bards and panegyrists. (2.21.80)
Grass-eaters, forest-dwellers, cattle, and likewise birds;
elephants, the best of the Gandharvas, the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra, and those dwelling on the earth;
those of the sea, those traveling through the sky, and crores and arbuds of maidens.
Likewise, all the world-protectors, the sovereign lords of the quarters,
the kings, the divine monarchs, and the Brahmins and Kshatriyas among the denizens of heaven—
all of them worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme among men, with exceeding devotion.
They applied the *tilaka* and the crescent moon-mark, and presented various offerings.
"Be one whose life is eternal," they repeatedly offered such blessings.
Then all the goddesses of the entire universe assembled and formed a circle ten million times as large.
They performed the *ārārtrika* rite for Hari, revolving [the lamp] one hundred and one times;
then they offered handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and subsequently drank the water from His feet.
Having received the *añjali* that removes all suffering, they departed for their own celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
Thus, when the worship and the benedictory words had been concluded,
Lomaśa then offered every honor and spoke these words:
"Śrī Harikṛṣṇa himself bestows upon you an auspicious welcome."
"By the blessings of you, the illustrious and all-honored ones, may I too attain eternal prosperity; thus does Hari pray.
I have become one who has fulfilled his purpose, for Bālakṛṣṇa is now your son."
Furthermore, I must be gazed upon every year, at every vow,
and especially at every festival, accompanied by auspicious blessings.
Here I am, with my young son, indeed bowing down with reverence.

"O lords, any offense committed by me, my father, the great sage Lomaśa, or even my mother regarding the rites for the guests and other matters must indeed be forgiven. Having spoken thus, Lomaśa said, "The auspicious time for the meal has arrived."
"Food is being served; he will come to your dwellings.
There will also be an exemption from the assembly. May victory be yours!
When this was said, Kṛṣṇa rose up, and the assembly likewise rose at that moment.
They went to their respective dwellings, taking with them food appropriate for each,
as well as various kinds of drink and maidens numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Bearing many forms, they became female servants and led [the guests] to those residences.

Having gratified the assemblies and provided beds for rest, they likewise offered excellent service after midday; then, having received their leave, they departed for their own abodes with eager anticipation. (96–97)
Then the father gave this triad as a reward to Viśvakarman:
the Kalpahāra, the Kalpasūtra, and the Kalpavallī;
and he also gave gifts to the other workmen.
He gave the Kalpa maiden, born of the eternal thread, to Lomaśa.
He bestowed the supreme grace of Hari upon all those who were departing.
Then, he indeed caused the dismantling of the pavilion to be carried out.
Furthermore, whatever objects remained there,
those he gave away on all sides to the destitute mendicants;
and to the dancing apsarases, he gave the finest unguents.
Having gathered necklaces, ornaments, the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and other priceless things,
the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa, the Blessed One who had assumed the form of a child, concluded the evening festival and attained supreme peace during the night.
Lomaśa sat as if mounted upon a swing, in accordance with worldly custom;
and the maidens also went to Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Thus, O Rādhikā, [is the nature] of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa indeed.
On the first day of the second year, a divine and great festival was celebrated,
which increases all auspicious fortune and likewise bestows liberation upon those who remember it, recite it, and listen to it with devotion. (105–106)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Seat in the Pavilion during the Grand Festival at the Beginning of the Second Year of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and the Narration of All the Offerings and Benedictions," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 22 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 22: The Arrival of the King of Vaidarbha and the Marriage of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa with the Princess of Vaidarbha. Śrī Nārada said: O great sage, please describe the arrival of the King of Vaidarbha, as well as the marriage of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa with the princess of Vaidarbha. Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O sage, listen attentively; I shall relate the wonderful account of the arrival of the King of Vaidarbha and the marriage of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa with the princess of Vaidarbha. Formerly, there was a king named Sudarśana who ruled over the city of Vidarbha. He was a devotee of Viṣṇu, virtuous, and a protector of his subjects. His wife was named Padmāvatī, who was endowed with all auspicious qualities. From them was born a daughter named Vaidarbhī, who was beautiful, radiant, and possessed of all virtues. She grew up in the home of her father, becoming a source of joy for her parents. Once, the King of Vaidarbha heard that the son of Nanda, the descendant of Yadu, had become the Lord of the three worlds and the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He thought, "I am fortunate indeed, for my daughter has attained such a husband. Having thus reflected, he summoned his ministers and spoke these words: "The son of Nanda, the descendant of Yadu, has become the Lord of the three worlds and the Supreme Personality of Godhead. I wish to give my daughter Vaidarbhī to Him in marriage. Therefore, O ministers, go quickly and bring that son of Nanda here. Hearing these words of the King of Vaidarbha, the ministers were delighted and set out immediately for the city of Mathurā. They traveled by chariot and reached the city of Mathurā within a few days. There they saw the son of Nanda, who was adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by His friends. Seeing Him, they were filled with wonder and bowed down, offering their obeisances. Then, having related the King's message, they informed Him of the King's desire. Upon hearing this, the son of Nanda smiled and spoke to His ministers: "I shall go to the city of Vidarbha tomorrow morning. Hearing these words, the ministers were overjoyed and returned to the city of Vidarbha. They reported everything to the King of Vaidarbha, who was then greatly pleased. The next day, the son of Nanda, accompanied by His friends and attendants, departed from Mathurā and arrived at the city of Vidarbha. There, the King of Vidarbha, along with his ministers, came forward to receive Him with great honor. He offered Him a grand welcome, including water for His feet, Arghya, and other respectful offerings. Then, the King led Him into his palace and seated Him upon a magnificent throne. After honoring Him with various offerings, the King spoke these words: "O son of Nanda, O descendant of Yadu, please accept my daughter Vaidarbhī as Your wife. She is endowed with all auspicious qualities and is worthy of You. Please accept her with favor. Hearing these words, the son of Nanda smiled and replied: "O King, I accept your daughter as My wife. Let the marriage ceremony be performed according to the sacred rites. Thereupon, the King of Vidarbha arranged a grand wedding festival. He invited all the kings, sages, and citizens. On an auspicious day, the marriage of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and the princess of Vaidarbha was celebrated with great splendor. After the marriage, the son of Nanda remained in the city of Vidarbha for some time, enjoying the company of His beloved wife. Then, taking leave of the King of Vidarbha, He returned to the city of Mathurā with His wife. Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Arrival of the King of Vaidarbha and the Marriage of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa with the Princess of Vaidarbha," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Author: Chapter 23.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, once in the past, there was indeed a great treasure-house of austerities.
The most excellent of sages named Cyavana, the lord of the Bhṛgus and a man of great asceticism,
while visiting sacred fords, went of his own accord to Pātāla by chance.
Thence he reached Rasātala, where he beheld a beautiful sight.
He entered that great city of the Dānavas;
being honored on all sides by the daughters of the Nāgas, he moved about within that city.
Beholding this Cyavana, the lord of the Rasātala named Prahlāda [approached].
He performed the highest worship for the son of Bhṛgu, according to his merit.
They both inquired after each other's mutual welfare and freedom from illness.
Having bowed to the sage who was seated, Prahlāda spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Today, by the sight of you, I have attained the fulfillment of my purpose;
for the sight of the virtuous removes sin, bestows merit, and is auspicious.
Virtuous people such as you deliver worlds like mine.
Those compassionate ones wander about for the sake of delivering the sinful.
O holy one, since you have come here intent on my deliverance, I, who dwell in the midst of Daityas and Dānavas, am purified by you, O Sage. (7–8)
"Stay here, practice righteousness, perform sacrifices, and recite prayers and the like.
This kingdom is yours alone; I shall serve you like a slave.
The sage said, "O devotee, this is indeed fitting for you, since you are a Vaiṣṇava."
While you, O lord of devotees and worshiper of gods and brahmins, were ruling, kings on earth always performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites;
and the brahmins and others practiced austerity, dharma, and made pilgrimages to sacred fords. (2.22.10–11)
The gods exist and are free from anxiety, and the laws of righteousness abide among the subjects.
O Daitya, while you remain established in the kingdom and steadfast in dharma, the Bull of Virtue (Dharma) remains present.
Whether in the netherworld, on earth, or in heaven, my state is the same.
"O King, wherever there is devotion, all that place is considered by me to be heaven.
Indeed, for the sake of fulfilling your wish, I shall remain here during the northern solstice;
thereafter, I shall certainly go to behold the youthful Lord."
Then Prahlāda said: "Even though I have heard this from the mouths of the Daityas— that Hari, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
shines as a youth upon the earth— nevertheless, tell me more."
Who is Puruṣottama, how does he exist, and of what nature is that sanctifier?
I desire to see this Anādi-Puruṣottama;
tell me of his wonders and speak to me of other sacred fords (tīrthas).
"Which are the most excellent sacred sites (tīrthas) on earth, which are in the sky,
and which might be in the netherworld (rasātala)? Tell me this,
and then I shall set out to go on a pilgrimage and behold them."

Then Cyavana spoke to Prahlāda, the foremost among devotees: "In Saurāṣṭra, there is a supreme sacred site, the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, belonging to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul. (2.22.20)
On earth is Naimiṣāraṇya, in the intermediate space is Puṣkara;
in Rasātala is Cakratīrtha, and in Pātāla is Hāṭakeśvara. On the mountain is Badarītīrtha, and in the forest is Nārasiṃhaka.
"In the waters [lies] the one reclining on the Ocean of Milk, and on Meru in heaven is the abode of Hari.
(22) Thus there are sacred fords that purify even sinners.
Having heard these words of Bhārgava, O Rādhikā, the king of the Daityas— (23)
Desiring to go to the sacred fords (*tīrthas*), he spoke this to the Dānavas:
"Arise! We shall go to bathe at the sacred fords on earth;
we shall behold the Supreme Self, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa."
Thus addressed, the Dānavas, Daityas, Āsurās, and likewise the Rākṣasas,
made incomparable preparations and emerged from the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Together with Cyavana, they went to Śrī Hāṭakeśvara.
Having performed the ritual bathing, worship, and other rites according to the prescribed rules for the illustrious Lord Hāṭakeśvara,
they emerged from Pātāla to the surface of the earth through fissures in Saurāṣṭra,
at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Filled with joy, they performed their ablutions in the waters to the east of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
There, Cyavana and Prahlāda, together with all the Daityas,
[beheld] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the form of a child.

He beheld, worshipped, and meditated upon that which was endowed with all incarnations, served by liberated maidens and others, and enchanting to all. Then, having bowed to the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa...
Having worshipped Lomaśa, he went to the Puṣkara lake;
having bathed in the Sarasvatī, he proceeded to Dharmāraṇya.
After visiting the excellent holy sites of Meru, he then went to Śrī Badarī.
There, Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed supreme austerity,
their minds intent on penance and bearing the weight of their uplifted matted locks;
those two sages were exceedingly gentle in appearance and wore black antelope skins.
He beheld the two stainless gods and worshipped them most fervently with devotion.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā at a śāla tree near the Naimiṣa forest,
that very lord of the Daityas went there and saw them once again.
Those two best of men were ascetics dwelling in a residence made of *śāla* trees;
and at their sides were two divine bows endowed with auspicious marks—
the Śārṅga and the Ājagava— as well as two inexhaustible quivers.
He beheld a great-branched *śāla* tree covered with arrows and weapons;
he saw other arrows stuck together at their tips.
Then he saw those arrows of wondrous form, serving as sacred threads for the serpent.
Seeing this, the Daitya became filled with incomparable rage due to the sight of their two forms;
seeing those two ascetics armed with weapons, he considered them to be hypocrites.
Overcome by pride in his own strength, he spoke to the two Supreme Persons.
"Have you two commenced this hypocrisy that destroys righteousness?
Where is asceticism, where is the mass of matted hair, and where are these two excellent weapons?
Then Nara said to the Daitya: "What concern is yours regarding the deeds of others?"
Whatever one can do when possessing the requisite power, that is fitting for him;
we two are indeed ascetics who provide protection and are the slayers of Daityas.
O Lord of Daityas, we shall accomplish both tasks; do not harbor pride.
Then the Lord of Diti said to them: "What power do you two possess here, while I, the protector of dharma, remain as the destroyer of the Daityas?
Nara replied: "O Lord of Daityas, power has been acquired by us two."
No one would be able to defeat Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle,
for they are the Supreme Lords whose very selves are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Then, out of pride, Prahlāda made a vow in their presence.
"In some way or another, I shall conquer Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle.
To him, Cyavana then said: "Do not speak thus regarding Śrī Hari;
for this Blessed One cannot be conquered by you, who are subject to decay, at any time."
The Daitya said: "That vow which was uttered by me shall not be otherwise.
I will certainly make every effort; indeed, I shall surely conquer those two.
Having spoken thus, he bowed to Cyavana and, having strung his bow, drew it taut.
He let out a roar and struck his bowstring with a thunderous sound.
Having stationed his own forces in a compact formation within the forest, he prepared himself for battle.
Then Nara, having bent the Ājagava bow, [discharged] arrows.
The bull among the Daityas released those [arrows] and cut them down with his own shafts.
Then, seeing his arrows severed by the Daitya at that very moment,
Nara discharged great arrows in succession, capable of destroying the Daitya.
The man discharged one arrow, the son of Diti two, the man three, and the asura four.
The man discharged five, the son of Diti six, and Bāṇa released arrows that were incapable of causing destruction.
The man discharged seven, the son of Diti eight, the man nine, and [the others] six.
Then the Daitya released ten arrows and the Nara eleven;
the Daitya [released] sixteen and the Nara thirty-two shafts.
Then the Daitya released sixty arrows, the Nara a hundred, and the Daitya again two hundred.
Nara discharged three hundred arrows, and the Daitya discharged six hundred;
Nara [discharged] a thousand, and the Daitya brought forth more than a thousand.
In this manner, out of pride, the two of them mutually released countless arrows at one another. (55–56)
Nara covered the surface of the earth with volleys of arrows from his quiver;
the Daitya, too, with countless shafts, severed them despite great effort.
Then Nara and the Dānava fought with excellent weapons accompanied by mantras.
The fire-missile, the water-missile, the Daitya-missile, the mountain-missile,
the serpent-missile, the Garuda-missile, the smoke-missile, the radiant-missile, the woman-missile, the man-missile, the eunuch-missile, and the youth-missile. (58–59)
Thus, with a desire to kill one another, the two of them hurled [missiles] at each other.
That best of Daityas released the most terrifying Brahmāstra,
and at that very moment, Nara released the supreme Nārāyaṇāstra.
When those two [discuses] had been withdrawn, Prahlāda, overwhelmed with rage,
seized a mace and swiftly leapt down from his excellent chariot.
And Nārāyaṇa, seeing him approaching armed with a mace, [prepared for battle].
Placing Nara behind him, he went forward to fight.
The Daitya, having whirled his mace, struck Kṛṣṇa violently on the head.
From the two eyes of Hari, who had been struck, much water fell.
Even though the mace fell to the ground broken into a hundred pieces and fragments,
the Daitya quickly stood upon his chariot and took up his bow;
he released sharp, bee-like arrows that possessed the luster of half-moons.
Hari pierced that Dānava with arrows,
and the Dānava also struck Hari with feathered shafts.
Thus, out of rage, they both pierced each other in their vital organs.
Then, in the sky, there was a gathering of embodied beings— the gods— who desired to witness the sight; great-sounding drums were beaten in the heavens,
and likewise, a rain of flowers fell upon those two.
Then, having thus attained such power, both the Daitya and Nārāyaṇa covered the sky with showers of very sharp arrows;
as they fought, they obscured all directions, making it difficult to discern.
Nārāyaṇa, for his part, pierced that Daitya in his vital organs with arrows;
the Daitya, in turn, struck Nārāyaṇa in the heart, the arms, and the face.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, Nārāyaṇa severed the Daitya’s bow.
The Dānava, having strung another bow, rained arrows upon Hari;
Hari, having cut those down, overwhelmed the Daitya with his own shafts.
Then, with a razor-headed arrow, he severed his bow and yet another as well.
He cut through the third and the fourth, and the fifth bow as well.
Then the Daitya seized a firm iron club and whirled it about,
but the Blessed One cut it down with his arrows.
Prahlāda whirled his mallet and hurled it at Nārāyaṇa;
when Hari cut that mallet with ten iron arrows,
the Daitya quickly fled toward Śrī Hari, carrying a noose.
Hari, however, cut the noose into many pieces with his arrow.
The Daitya, seizing a spear as long as seven palm trees, hurled it at Mādhava; Hari, for his part, cut that spear apart with razor-headed arrows.
And the Daitya hurled a mountain peak at Mādhava;
Hari, having torn that apart with his spear against the breast of the Dānava,
the Dānava then swiftly hurled a trident equal to the spear at him.
With his heart shattered, O Rādhā, he fell down in the midst of the chariot.
Knowing him to be unconscious, the charioteer carried him away from the battlefield.
Meanwhile, the Asura Nārāyaṇa regained consciousness and rested.
Taking up his very firm bow, he returned once more to fight.
Then, seeing him at evening, Hari replied to the great asura:
"Go, O Lord of Daityas; we shall fight tomorrow morning. Perform your daily rites."
Having been addressed thus, he bowed and departed for Naimiṣa, where he performed his daily rites (82).
In this manner, that great battle proceeded daily on those days;
even at night, during the time of rest, the Dānava would reflect upon it (83).
"How shall I conquer that heroic, deceitful Lord who is so difficult to subdue? Then the Dānava fought with him for many years;
yet he did not defeat the unconquerable Hari even at the end of a thousand years.
Approaching Nārāyaṇa, the Dānava spoke these words:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, for what reason am I unable to conquer you, the Sādhya Lord? Tell me the cause of this. (85–86)
Nārāyaṇa said to him, "I am invincible to gods and asuras,
even by means of all kinds of forces, including millions of missiles and weapons.
Prahlāda then replied, "If you are indeed unassailable and invincible,"
If I were to fail to conquer him, my promise here would become false.
O Lord, how could I live on, infamous as one whose vow has been broken?
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, in your presence I shall renounce my life.
Having spoken thus, Hari sat before him chanting the eternal Brahman. Then the compassionate Lord spoke to his supreme devotee, who was filled with faith:
"Go; you shall conquer me through devotion alone, never by means of battle."
Then Prahlāda said: "The three worlds have been conquered by me;
however, you alone remain unconquered, for you are the protector of the world who has undertaken the practice of austerity for the sake of setting forth the Dharma."
O Lord of Gods, I shall perform supreme and auspicious devotion to conquer you in truth;
I shall offer service, worship, attendance, and so forth, by means of which battle you may suffer defeat. (93)
"That battle which I have vowed will indeed bear fruit for me;
henceforth, I shall employ the weapon consisting of devotion toward Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus, that best of Daityas, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, [addressed] Andhaka.
Having summoned him, the observer of vows, being delighted, said:
"O Andhaka, both the Daityas and the Dānavas must be protected by you.
Accept this kingdom relinquished by me and protect it. (96)

"By means of battle, austerity, devotion, and likewise through worship, I shall conquer Śrī Hari, the Lord of gods, that deceitful sovereign. Having spoken thus, the demon Andhaka seized the supreme kingdom. (97–98)
Prahlāda went to the holy hermitage of Hari at Badarikāśrama,
where he beheld those two very deities, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who were formerly the two lords residing in the field of Naimiṣa and at Śālagrāma.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he paid homage at their feet.
Nārāyaṇa said to him: "O great Asura, why have you bowed here without first defeating me? Tell me what it is that you desire."
Prahlāda said: "O Blessed One, what man is capable of conquering you?
What man is superior to you? You alone are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
You alone, radiant with ascetic power, bear the matted locks and the bow."
Yogis meditate upon you, and the wise offer you worship.
Snātakas chant your names, and those who perform sacrifices offer you oblations.
Women delight in you, and devoted wives revere you. (103–104)
Those who possess the senses seek refuge in you alone, the Supreme Lord.
You are the immortal Hṛṣīkeśa, the wielder of the discus, and the upholder of the earth.
You alone are the Great Fish, the Horse-headed One, and the one in the form of the Tortoise.
You are the boar, you are the lion, you are Brahmā, the Lord of Śrī, and the husband of Satī.
You are Kubera, Varuṇa, the wind, the sun, and the moon.
You have become the self of all beings; who, O Mādhava, shall conquer you?
"If you have come here to practice devotion, then submit yourself to me with devotion.
Having said this, he bowed again at his feet.
Nārāyaṇa then said to him, "O sinless one, I am well-pleased with you."
"But by your unswerving devotion, you have today defeated me.
And a man who is defeated must pay a penalty to his victor;
for the sake of that penalty, I shall grant you a boon—choose whatever you desire."
Prahlāda said: "May my physical, mental, and verbal sins—whatever was committed by me while fighting—come to destruction.
O Viṣṇu, whatever thought arises in me, let it be centered upon you."
"May I be exceedingly devoted to the worship of the gods, with my mind fixed on you and having you as my supreme refuge;
and may there always be the highest delight for me in your lotus feet.
Nārāyaṇa said to him, "So be it for you always."
Furthermore, by my grace, O lord of devotees, you shall forever be imperishable, undecaying, ageless, and immortal. Depart from here to the most excellent and supreme Lake Aśvapaṭṭa.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, where Puruṣottama resides—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord— having beheld Him, having meditated upon Śrī Hari, and having placed that Lord within one's heart; || 1.15–16 ||
Then, having received the great mantra from Lomaśa, Pāvana said:
"O tiger among devotees, go to your own abode and remain devoted to your duties.
Governing all the Daityas, protect the kingdom eternally."
Practice deceit and devotion toward the teaching that is consistent with your own kind.
Since your mind is fixed on Me, there shall be no bondage of karma for you.
Become the instructor of what is beneficial and the preceptor of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to Hari and asked forgiveness from Śrī Hari Nara;
then, accompanied by Cyavana, he went to Lomaśa’s hermitage in Saurāṣṭra.
In the sacred field of Kumkumavāpikā, he beheld Puruṣottama.

Having bathed in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and worshipped Keśava, he received the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance. Having stayed there for only a month, he departed for his home.
He ruled over the city named Aśmaka and the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
He was seen and honored by the Dānavas, including Andhaka and others.
He practiced the ninefold devotion consisting of meditation, worship, and other such rites.
"By worshipping the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Rādhā, Janārdana is thus said to be conquerable through devotion;
even by a demon, through supreme devotion, the Supreme Lord has been conquered. (1.24–25)
In the second year, during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Daitya Cyavana dwelt at that great holy site, Cyāvana, on the southern bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
it is likewise called Prāhlādika.
Prahlāda instructed the Daityas and Danujas in that mantra.
Having descended to the netherworld (Rasātala), they too became devoted lords;
day and night, they took refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Thus has this been told, O Rādhā, which destroys all sins;
it is the supreme means of practice, the deliverer of the Daityas, imperishable and firm;
it bestows victory, peace, prosperity, and eternal bliss. 129.
"Bestowing the feet of Hari through recitation and hearing, it is the supreme giver of liberation.

(2.22.130) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Prahlāda’s Arrival on Earth from Rasātala for the Purpose of Pilgrimage by Means of Cyavana’s Yoga, His Battle with Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the Defeat of Nārāyaṇa through Devotion, and the Arrival of Prahlāda and Cyavana at the Hermitage of Lomaśa," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
