Chapter 24 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then those Dānavas, O Rādhikā, desired to see Kṛṣṇa immediately—
that child who is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
by whose prowess this lord of the Daityas conquered the Lord Hari.
Instructed by Prahlāda, they desired to practice that devotion.
Listen, O Rādhā, to that story of how those lords of the Dānavas,
having come together, became devotees of Hari and engaged in his worship.
And those belonging to the lineage of Andhaka, those born in the lineage of Prahlāda,
those born in the lineages of Kujambha, Jambha, and Śaṅkukarṇa;
as well as those born in the lineages of Maya, Dundubhi, and Śambara.
The Dānavas and others, born of the lineage of Ayaḥśaṅku and Vṛtra,
remembered the brahmin Cyavana, who showed them the path to Prahlāda.
Cyavana quickly appeared before them.
Having been saluted, honored, and questioned regarding his welfare, Sukeśin, the eldest son of Vidyutkeśin, spoke to him:
"I wish to ask you something; this doubt resides within my heart."
"What indeed is the highest good in the next world, and what is it in this one, O best of the twice-born?
By what means may one become worthy of honor among the virtuous, and by what does one increase in happiness?
Thus were Cyavana questioned at that time by those born of the lineage of the Daityas.
Having reflected, he spoke for the sake of the highest good in this world and the next:
"Merit is the highest good, as is righteousness; it is beneficial in every way, both here and in the hereafter.
When one is established in righteousness and honors the virtuous, one shall always be happy. (2.23.10)

Dharma is one’s own virtuous conduct, which bestows peace upon oneself and others and brings happiness. (11) It also grants peace to one’s own self and is always meritorious, providing constant bliss.
For human beings, the supreme Dharma consists of ritual acts such as sacrifices performed at all times. (12)
Vedic study, the knowledge of reality, and the worship of Viṣṇu—
by the acquisition of what do men become happy both here and in the hereafter?
Also, the protection of the devotees of the gods and the acceptance of their worship.
By that which was acquired by him, your protection of subjects and so forth became sources of happiness;

by that which was acquired by him, the Daityas' possession of mighty arms, their warfare, and even their worship, as well as policy, devotion, and surrender, became sources of happiness for you. (14–15)
For the Siddhas, there is the perfection of yoga, self-study, contemplation on Brahman, devotion, worship, and peace; by that which they have acquired, they are happy.
For the Gandharvas, there is song and dance, instrumental music, and speech that flows with sweetness.
And by that which was earned through the service of the great ones, you have attained happiness;

[so too] the auspicious knowledge of the Vidyādharas, their specialized sciences, manly prowess, and intelligence—by constant devotion to Nārāyaṇī and what was earned thereby, you have attained happiness. (17–18)
The Kinnaras attained skill in devotion to the Sun, in the Gandharva arts such as singing, and in the expression of humor and other emotions; through that merit they became happy.
The artisans attained skill in their crafts and the constant contemplation of Nārāyaṇa.

Through that which you have earned, you possess the quality of benefiting others; by that which you have earned, you find happiness for your ancestors. The restraint of the senses, freedom from pride, and constant devotion to the Supreme Lord—by that which you have earned, you find happiness.
The sages possess virtue, truthfulness, sacred recitation, wisdom, forbearance, compassion, and a stainless inner heart; by means of these acquired qualities, they are happy.
Furthermore, there is the service of their husbands performed by those who are renounced, virtuous, and noble women.
Dedication to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is free from attachment. (23) Devotion to Hari should always be practiced; by that which is earned, you shall obtain happiness.
Guarding wealth, the giving of enjoyments, and service for the sake of others [are the means]. (24)
May they have devotion to Hari; by that which has been earned by them, may they be happy.
For the greed of Rākṣasas is directed toward the property of others and toward the humiliation of others.
Or rather, may they have devotion to Hari or to a devotee; by that which has been earned by them, may they be happy.
Lack of discrimination, the consumption of impure food, untruthfulness, and eating the remnants of offerings—by what they have earned through these, those [Pretas] are happy.
Serving others, like animals—by what they have earned through this, those [Tiryag-yonis] are happy. (26–27)
Thus have been described these sixteen meritorious dharmas that grant liberation.
Abiding in dharma according to their respective castes, people are always happy.
Among all dharmas, these are the most excellent, common to all, and the very bulls of virtue.
Visiting sacred fords, worship of the Lord, service to others,
austerity, non-violence, contentment, and the chanting of Hari’s names when obtained through righteous conduct—
whatever embodied beings may rely upon these dharmas, [they shall attain the supreme goal]. (2.23.30)

Those who take refuge in Brahman certainly attain eternal liberation; those who walk the path of righteousness are happy, while those who have not removed their sins are miserable. Having heard these meaningful words of Cyavana, the Daityas, seeking happiness, [acted accordingly].
Those who have taken refuge at the feet of Prahlāda consider the holy ford (tīrtha) to be the highest good.
They then asked Cyavana about that which is the most excellent among all holy fords;
Cyavana then told them of the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara Tīrtha.
The Badarīvana forest, the supreme among holy sites, and Śrī Puruṣottama;
the sacred field of Śrī Gaṇḍakī-tīrtha, as well as Māthura and Puṣkara;
and the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake, which stands as the most excellent of all supreme holy sites.
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and likewise the hermitage of Lomaśa;
Saurāṣṭra, which is most excellent in every respect and graced by the Supreme Lord;
and the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of a child.
The Blessed One resides there, the Supreme Lord, the most excellent of persons, the sovereign lord of all abodes, the cause of all causes, the Lord of all incarnations,
and the true master of all Lakṣmī and the other goddesses. (37)
He is the bestower of all liberation and supernatural powers, and the abode of equal compassion toward all.
That sacred site is the most excellent among all sacred sites;
having performed one's desired rites there and attained one's goal, one rejoices in all states of peace.
Having heard this from Cyavana, the Daityas, desiring a sacred bathing place,
then took Cyavana with them and went to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
There were Daityas and Dānavas, as well as their wives, sons, and others.
They joyfully set out for the holy site of Kuṃkumavāpikā to visit the sacred ford.
On account of Cyavana’s discourse and through the instruction of Prahlāda and others,
they arrived there to behold the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Descending from the sky to the hermitage of Lomaśa, those Dānavas,
together with their families, bowed before Lomaśa along with Cyavana.
Observing the supreme devotion of the Dānavas, the sage Lomaśa—
He offered a most excellent welcome to them along with Cyavana;
he gave them the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), seats, water for drinking, and so forth.
He provided them with beautiful dwellings fashioned from the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
And from the city named Aśmaka, [he brought] more than a hundred most beautiful,
highly prosperous palaces, rich in all kinds of articles, resembling the moon in luster,
and adorned with assembly halls and reception rooms, well-provided with baths, food, and beds.

The sage gave [them] attendants devoted to service, who were stationed throughout the garden groves where cool, pleasant, and comfortable breezes blew; who were gladdened by the fragrant perfumes of sandalwood, agallochum, and musk; and who were provided with all necessary requisites. (47–48)
Cyavana became very pleased because of Lomaśa’s state of distress.
He then spoke to the Daityas and Dānavas: "The sages are without possessions;
they are free from partiality and the like, and devoid of attachment and aversion."

Beneficial to all living beings and tranquil, they indeed liberate people from sin. (2.23.50) He in whom an equal disposition toward enemy and friend is observed—he alone should be known as the giver of liberation, the supreme purifying shrine. (2.23.51)
"By the grace of Lomaśa and by means of this water, all the masses of terrible sins born of your previous lives shall indeed come to an end.
Therefore, serve the brahmin Śrī Lomaśa with joyful hearts."
Dwelling there for some time, he acquired spiritual instruction.
(53) Among all holy places (*tīrtha*), a moving one is more swiftly purifying;
indeed, a perfected saint (*sādhu*) is the supreme holy place, destroying sin through mere touch. (54)
Through prostration, service, massaging the feet, pleasing them,
and by giving desired objects, they rescue even sinners.
Service to the virtuous is the burner of great sins and transgressions.
For the virtuous are indeed to be fed, honored, and beheld;
the virtuous are indeed to be touched, bowed to, and gratified.
The virtuous are indeed to be served with the offering of all one’s possessions.
Meeting with anyone at all is easy, but meeting with the virtuous is difficult.
Indeed, the virtuous must be gratified through body, mind, and speech.
They are devoted to meditation, are treasuries of merit, and shine with the radiance of austerity.
Devoted to the Supreme Brahman, dedicated to the welfare of their disciples, and beloved;
such virtuous ones, who bestow all auspiciousness, should be served for the sake of one's own liberation.
Whether they possess the nature of a Dānava, a Daitya, a human, or the lordship of the gods—(60).
Indeed, that [suffering] arising from the birth of a body and so forth does not belong eternally to the selves;
for upon the dissolution of the body, everything adventitious perishes.
"This family and so forth is mine," "the kingdom is mine," "my kinsmen"—[these are all such adventitious things].
"Son, wife, and husband—these are falsely constructed by the ego.
When the seed consisting of the ego has departed, the latent impression will also depart.
And when the storehouse of karma is destroyed, where is there 'demonhood' and where is there 'discipleship'? (62–63)
The Self, however, through its association with a illusory body, possesses the etymological derivation of names:
since he was born from Diti, he is a Daitya; and since he was born from Danu, he is a Dānava.
That conscious being who is unborn is said to be "born" by virtue of being born [into a body].
The body that is born is certainly not the Self; therefore, the Self does not possess a name.
In whatever place one is born, it is right there that [the notion of "I"] arises for him;
this attachment is like a mold within Māyā, due to the power of the sense of "mine-ness."
Therefore, you are not inhabitants of Pātāla or Rasātala, nor are you Daityas, nor indeed are you heroes; for all that is merely a portion of the body.
And by the yoga of the virtuous, the virtuous have been born here in this lake.
"O dust-born ones, having bathed and drunk water here at the site of Lomaśa,
you are purified by this connection with the sacred ford (tīrtha). Now receive the supreme mantra,
honor this Guru, and thereafter worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
"We shall go indeed for the sake of seeing [him]; you will certainly attain the highest good.
Having been addressed thus, ten thousand Dānavas and Daityas bathed at the Aśvapaṭṭasara tīrtha and proceeded to the region of Prāhlādika.
Having bowed to the brahmin Lomaśa, they honored him with respect.
Having drunk the water used for washing his feet, they prostrated before the sage Lomaśa;
they worshipped him with devotion using sandalwood paste, flowers, and garlands.
And they received the great mantra, purifying and bestowing all happiness:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Having taken this mantra, those Vaiṣṇavas indeed began chanting it.
Having taken a garland of *tulasī* upon their foreheads and likewise a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with a dot (*bindu*),
they stood in rows and partook of the excellent food— consisting of what is chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked— which had been offered by Lomaśa. (74–75)
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, they took sweet drinks and betel;
Cyavana too, having performed his twilight devotions, ate with joy.
Then they all went to their own dwellings to obtain rest.
Then, in the evening, they all took their offerings and,
desiring a vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
went to the seven-storied palace of Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī.
There, the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa shone upon the swing;
and Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, the father, having taken his son by his own hand,
arrived at the throne and sat down there appropriately.
Both Lomaśa and Cyavana arrived accompanied by their disciples and hosts of Daityas.
Their father himself then offered them seats and personally extended a welcome and hospitable reception to the Daityas as well.
Having been granted seats, those Daityas, overwhelmed by their prostration,
considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose upon beholding Lord Hari;
for a moment they remained steadfast, with steady eyes and composed conduct.
And they beheld that supreme wonder of the Lord;
having seen for a moment Bālakṛṣṇa, who then assumed the form of a youth—resplendent, most excellent, and beautiful, possessing a divine form corresponding to his true nature. || 83-84 ||
There, in the form [of Viṣṇu], he saw Prahlāda, then Śukrācārya,
and after that Kaśyapa, Diti, Danu, and the patriarch Dakṣa;
as well as Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu— his ancestors.
Then Brahmā, likewise Rudra, and Viṣṇu with four arms;
then the form of Vairāja and the fourteen worlds (bhūmikās).
Therein is Rasātala, and there the excellent city of Aśmaka.
There they all quickly beheld their own dwellings, their own family members,
and their own forms.
There, five thousand maidens of purified souls—
They chose the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa as their youthful husband.
Thus they gazed upon Him; then Hari, who had previously appeared in the form of a child, once again assumed His adolescent form.
Thus, having beheld this, they were overwhelmed with supreme wonder;
they worshipped Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe.
They placed offerings before Him and water for washing His feet.
Then all those Daityas and Dānavas, as well as their wives, drank [it].
Their daughters, numbering five thousand and possessing divine forms, became enchanted by Śrī Hari; absorbed in meditation upon Him, they remained steadfast at that time.
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, they chose him according to their desire:
"O Lord of the Universe, grant devotion at Your lotus feet;
O Lord of the Universe, grant liberation and eternal bliss. (94)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said, "So be it for you:
the station has been granted, as well as devotion, liberation, and happiness.
Having spoken thus, those women of divine form indeed became so at that very moment.
Those five thousand wives quickly became the wives of Hari;
having obtained their lord, the powerful Hari, they stood there holding his feet. Protected by the Beloved of Śrī, they remained in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then both Lomaśa and Cyavana, having worshipped Śrī Hari,
joyfully protected their own daughters in their hermitage.
By the command of Śrī Hari, those girls were established among the daughters of Arbuda.

Ten thousand Daityas, desiring to go quickly to Vaikuṇṭha by the grace of Śrī Hari, chose that abode there. Then, having been transformed into divine forms, they were led to Vaikuṇṭha by Hari. (2.23.100)
Then the Lord Śrī Hari himself gave all the gifts that he had bestowed upon the maidens to the two sages;
and having assumed the form of a child, he returned from Dvārakā.
Having bowed to Lomaśa and given auspicious blessings to the maidens,
Cyavana departed on a pilgrimage to the supreme Puṣkara forest.
Prahlāda, the long-lived one, indeed went to Rasātala.

Thus, O Rādhikā, the exceedingly divine life-story of that Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe, was narrated during the month of Śrāvaṇa. By reading and hearing it in the second year, it bestows supreme liberation.
It bestows prosperity and longevity, grants sons, grandsons, and wealth, and brings about unbroken good fortune; for Hari is to be attained through grace.

(106) Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Ten Thousand Daityas and Dānavas Residing in Rasātala and Other Regions, and the Choice of Bālakṛṣṇa by the Five Thousand Maidens," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 23: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 24 [[Author: → Chapter 25
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; at the beginning of his third year, his father performed a great festival according to the prescribed rites, even more excellent than that of his second year. (1)
On the thirteenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he performed the *caula* sacrament; having first performed the auspicious bath, the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*),
and so forth, as well as the *nāndī-śrāddha*, the recitation of the *svasti* hymns, and the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the domestic fire (*sabhyānala*).
Having placed the vessels for the ritual, on a spot to the south of the fire (3),
one should then place twenty-one auspicious bundles of *darbha* grass; subsequently,
having placed red cow-dung and other materials on a spot to the left of the fire (4).
Then the father set down the pot of *kṛsara* rice;
having performed the *vyāhṛti-homa* and other rites, he took an iron razor and shaved off the small tufts of hair situated on the right and left sides.
Then, having gradually performed the shaving of the hair from the womb,
the father had his son's head shorn with a tuft of hair remaining by a barber.
He gave gifts of cows and other offerings, fed the Brahmins, and honored the yogis.
He gratified the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds;
he honored Lomaśa and fed the maidens.
On that day, he fed the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the guests.
He caused morsels of cow-meat, flour-cakes, and grains to be given to living beings.
In this way, he performed the *caula* sacrament which destroys sin.
[The sages asked: "How indeed could there be sin for Śrī Hari, the destroyer of sins? (2.24.10)
Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world and for the preservation of the Vedic path,
his father indeed performed that auspicious and appropriate sacramental rite.
Then Rādhā, filled with humility, heard of this and questioned Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, let it manifest clearly for boys or girls who are pure,
whose hearts are like a clean mirror, who do not know much,
and who delight in acting as they please, eating what they desire, and wandering wherever they wish. (12–13)
"What indeed is that sin of theirs which is destroyed by the *caula* ceremony?
O Rādhikā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: 'Listen, O child, to the transgression [of those who undergo it]:
the sins committed in previous lives and other births truly follow them. (14)
Whether from heaven or even from hell, that which remains as a residue follows him.
That very dwelling of the self within the womb—in the receptacle of urine, amidst the fire of falling, and in the element accompanied by *rajas*—is produced solely through sin. (15–16)
The emergence of the body there arises from merit and demerit;
dwelling in water during a state of swoon results only in demerit.
Indeed, the great suffering of birth and the state of dependence arise from demerit.
Life, such as the drinking of milk and so forth, arises from merit and demerit.
Likewise, contact with excrement, urine, and the like, as well as being bitten by gadflies and other insects, muteness, and incapacity, arise solely through sin. (18–19)
Indeed, those very sins committed by him in the past manifest during the course of this birth, bestowing nothing but suffering in every way.
But for those who possess no sin, O beloved, that Self is like Rudra himself.
The wise one born of the mind (mānasa) is equal to Sanaka and the other [mind-born sons], not so the one born from a womb.
Now, the removal of impurity occurs only through purification rites (saṃskāra);
for one whose body has not been consecrated by such rites, purity must be achieved through its very nature.
Indeed, the sins of previous births, together with impurity, grow upon the head in the form of black-colored hairs;
these are the "womb-hairs" (*garbhakeśāḥ*), which are the growths of sin, and their destruction brings about the destruction of sin.
Therefore, the *caula* sacrament is indeed prescribed for children.
Because sin (*cūm*) is dissolved (*līyate*) by it, that tonsure is known as *caula*.
Now hear another thing, O Rādhā: hair that has been cut... [25]
There is a cause for why matted locks (*jaṭā*) grow with such speed;
indeed, the roots are the cause in the case of new hair.
Furthermore, by means of action known as "white" (*śukla-karman*), that matted lock comes into being.
Therefore, the matted locks or the topknot must always be protected according to the Śukla-saṃhitā. Just as a child grows, so too does merit, demerit, or mixed karma arise through action. (27–28)
In this context, it is indeed declared that [the debt] up to five years is to be borne by the father;
beyond five years, it is to be borne by oneself, for it settles upon the very body hairs.
Therefore, hair and body hairs are indeed the seats of sin.
All those who cleanse the mud of filth are the fathers of Kaccara.
Therefore, one should especially perform the shaving of the head at a sacred ford (tīrtha);
that cutting of the hair should be understood as the removal of sin.
Thus, after shaving the hair in the third year,
they may thereafter shave it as desired all around, except for the *brahmarandhra*. Alternatively, the sacred matted locks (*jaṭā*) should be preserved, consecrated, beautiful, and pure.
As long as people's hair remains black and visible,
so long do objects of the senses cause embodied beings to commit sins; but when the hairs have become white reaching to the ears, the aged are no longer defiled.
Therefore, for one who is old, there is no longer any traditional injunction regarding merit and sin;
all of that is specifically declared to apply to one in the middle stage of life.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the purifying rite of tonsure (caula-saṃskāra) has been performed.

Rādhikā said: "O Blessed One, how does the accumulation of sins from previous births reside within the body hairs of a child still in the womb? Śrī Kṛṣṇa replied: "O Rādhā! Listen, I shall tell you that."
In ancient times, there arose from the back of Brahmā a man named Adharma;
he was joined with his wife Hiṃsā, and from them was born their son Pāpa.
This Pāpa was devoted to his father and likewise to his mother.

He does not leave for a moment, nor even from afar, at any time or in any state. (3.9) Where there is unrighteousness and violence, there the wicked man exerts himself; where there is neither unrighteousness nor violence, there the wicked man does not exert himself. (2.24.40)
But for those souls who are situated in the womb— unripe, inactive, powerless, devoid of qualities, and enveloped by the amnion— for them there is no unrighteousness in being harmed.
How indeed could there be sin in that case, given the prior accumulation of karma?
If, having abandoned the sinner, sin departs far away without being endured, then where can it remain without a support?
For that which is produced by one does not stay elsewhere, but rather goes away. (42–43)
"Whatever has been done by someone remains with that very person in every respect;
its destruction occurs only after the experience [of its fruit], as is determined by the extent [of the karma].
By this principle, the son named Pāpa informed his father.
"In that womb where there is neither unrighteousness nor violence—how can I remain within myself without those two? Having reflected, Adharma spoke to his son, who was known as Pāpa. (45–46)
"Son, come with me; I shall petition the Grandfather.
Whatever he grants you for the sake of a dwelling, there you shall reside.
Having spoken thus and taking his son with him, Adharma indeed went to Brahmā.
Having paid homage to his father, he sat down before him.
Brahmā questioned that son regarding his arrival with his sons and his purpose:
"Tell me quickly, why have you come here with your sons?"
Adharma said: "O Blessed One, this son of mine is named Pāpa (Sin).
For wherever there is violence and likewise myself, there I am always intent on dwelling.
However, those two do not exist for living beings who are still within the womb."
"In that regard, tell me how they should remain there due to their past sins.
Having reflected thus, Brahmā spoke to him who was indeed within the womb:
"By my command, he must remain in the form of hair [or a lock of hair] as a consequence of his sin."
Then the wicked one, remaining in his own abode, attained supreme satisfaction,
even though he remained there for three years without his parents.
Then Brahmā, by his own resolve, [created] sixteen purifying sons.
He performed the *saṃskāras* for the sake of destroying sin.
Therein, the *caula-saṃskāra*, which consists of the hair and destroys evil, was performed; and in this same manner, other [rites] that cause the destruction of sin were carried out. (54–55)
Thus, O Rādhikā, for the sake of protecting the creation, Brahmā performed his duties in accordance with the previous creation;
so too did Hari act in that very same manner for the purpose of instructing the worlds. (56)

The father performed the auspicious sacrament known as *caula*. (57) Now, I shall tell you of the marvel that occurred there at that time—a marvel never seen nor heard of by those who came before, nor even by their predecessors. (58)
O Rādhā, when I arrived there at that time,
I saw all those hairs which had been removed from the head by the barber being thrown into the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (59)

Thousands of divine, auspicious Nārāyaṇas appeared, four-armed, bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses; their brows were adorned with frowns, they wore golden earrings, were clothed in fire-like garments, and were attended by Ramā. (2.24.60–61)
Mounted upon the daughter of Vinatā, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
those blessed lords shone forth, adorned with the Kaustubha gem and forehead marks (tilaka).
At that time, they all appeared there as entirely equal and identical.
From that very source appeared those with eight arms, then those with sixteen arms;
afterwards, those with thirty-two arms and those with hundreds of thousands of arms were seen by the thousands— Nārāyaṇas of divine form.
Thus, that mass of a hundred thousand head-hairs was indeed of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
at that time, those short hairs were seen as four-armed [beings], and thereafter,
the long ones appeared as eight-armed Nārāyaṇas.
Then there were those with sixteen arms whose hair was longer;
then indeed those with thirty-two arms whose hair was longest of all.
Thus, with hundreds and more arms, the hair became increasingly long and exceedingly long.
And thousands of Nārāyaṇas with a thousand arms were seen;
along with them, those Śrīs with equally many arms were likewise seen.
Those pairs, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, praised the Supreme Lord.
We, the Nārāyaṇas, abide within your hair;
you are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the source of innumerable incarnations, higher than the highest. (2.24.70)
We remain merged within your form by your will;
and at the proper times, we emerge as the protectors of the universe.
We become lords for as long as your command endures.
And by Your will, O Kṛṣṇa, we indeed undergo our dissolution;
we worship You, we bow to You, and we carry out Your command.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, though we appear as separate, we are Your very form.
"Where should we go and where should we dwell? O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Akṣara, please give us instruction; we shall do exactly as you say.
Furthermore, those other multitudes of hairs upon your form—"
For they are liberated from the beginningless [bondage], and likewise those who are adventitious;
they become liberated, as do the female Brahmas and the male Brahmas.
And those divine qualities, O Hari, which dwell within your form— //75-76 //
All the Viṣṇus are served by the maidservants of Lakṣmī;
and those ornaments which exist upon your form are your own Śaktis.
By the command of Rādhā and Ramā, they are Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Lalitā, and Prabhā.
Indeed, Māṇikī, Mañjulā, and the others dwell there in the form of divine love;
they are ornaments personified, pearls distinct from other pearls.
And Vāsudeva and the others are the very principles of your erotic sentiment.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, there exist manifestations such as Nakhā and others who are lords of lords;
they are non-different from you, their specific attributes being established as not separate from your incarnations. All of them dwell within you, hidden within your very form.
We are of the nature of hair, yet we have become separate by Your will.
Having received the *caula* sacrament, we have taken on the forms of Your incarnations;
therefore, grant us permission to dwell [there], for we shall act accordingly.
Thus spoke the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; and being requested by their command for the sake of their welfare, he was pleased and summoned them into his presence.
He then [bestowed] upon them the *tilaka* marks, consisting of dots of saffron and *kesara*.
Having placed [his hand] upon their foreheads, the Lord of Akṣaras spoke:
"You are my incarnations, the auspicious bearers of my sovereign power.
Understand this: by me, multitudes of cosmic eggs are perpetually produced. (84–85)
"O venerable Narāyaṇas, by my command go now to those who have today produced *golās* and those partial [followers] numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
Likewise, O four-armed ones, go to the fourteen worlds (*caturdaśatalāṇḍa*). (86)
Likewise, having reached twenty-eight levels of the earth, he became eight-armed;
having reached fifty-six star-eggs (*tārāṇḍa*), he became sixteen-armed;
and having reached one hundred and eight levels of the earth, he became thirty-two-armed. (87–88)
Go to the five hundred egg-worlds with a hundred or more arms;
go to the thousand-layered egg-worlds with a thousand arms.
In each individual egg, I appoint only one person here.
In that very manner, a new and ever-fresh universe proceeds one by one.
Behold with your own eyes: whatever egg (universe) is seen by anyone, it enters into that very [new] one through the power of my yoga. (2.24.90–91)
Having been addressed thus, those embodiments of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa bowed and departed;
having surveyed their respective universes, they rested for as long as their lifespan allowed.
When they had all gone, Lomaśa spoke to Keśava.
"Show me those very cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) within which you [dwell].
Having heard this, Hari smiled and then, with his finger and the application of water, touched Lomaśa’s eyes; he then became divine.
With divine vision, he beheld these incarnations and the spheres;
overcome by supreme wonder, he indeed realized the majesty of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as it truly is. (95)
He performed the exemption from the rite known as the *caula*;
having given many gifts, Hari returned to the palace. Seeing this marvel, his father and mother attained great joy.
Lomaśa went to the hermitage accompanied by a group of maidens.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been described the activity of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, which is entirely inaccessible to worldly people and perceivable only through divine grace. (98)
By both reciting and listening to it, this [work] bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it grants cattle and sons, provides grain and wealth, destroys sins, confers devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and likewise grants the state of Nārāyaṇa. (2.24.100)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sins in the Hairs and the Nature of the Hairs as Being Nārāyaṇa Himself," concerning the *Caula* sacrament of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 25 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga Santāna*) [Chapter 25 begins]
[The Author: Chapter 026.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to the purifying story of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
In his third year, on the first day of the month of Phālguna,
Gopālakṛṣṇa celebrated the great festival of the flower-swing in the sacred precinct of Kuṅkumavāpī during the bright fortnight of Phālguna. (1–2)
When spring arrived there, the *kiṃśuka* trees, glowing with the brilliance of fire,
shone constantly with their leafless branches, beautifying the surface of the earth.
It was as if they had torn apart the elephant named Śiśira with their claws.
O beloved, the spring lion arrived with *palāśa* flowers;
then the jasmine blossoms laughed constantly with their bud-teeth. The forests of *karṇikāra* trees, in full bloom, shone resplendently. (4–5)
The red Aśoka groves shine, suddenly ablaze with blossoms;
swarms of bees, turning the thickets golden-brown, gleam within the dense forest.
(6) Along the riverbanks, the reeds resplend with clusters of flower-stalks.
Rādhikā has hands like red aśoka flowers, a slender form, and feet like kiṃśuka blossoms.
She is dark-complexioned with hands like blue aśoka flowers, a face like a blooming lotus,
eyes like blue water-lilies, and breasts like bilva fruits from the middle of the tree.
Her teeth are like blossoming *kunda* flowers, her hands are adorned with flower-clusters (*mañjarī*),
her lower lip is like the *bandhujīva* flower, and she possesses the fresh sprouts of the white *sinduvāra*.
Her voice is like the song of the male cuckoo, she is divine, and she is auspiciously clothed in *kaṅkola* garments.
With a mass of *barhi* grass as her hair-tuft, the cry of cranes as her anklets,
the sacrificial hall (*prāgvaṃśa*) as her girdle, and the graceful gait of an intoxicated swan;
adorned with a garment of *putrajīva* wood and shining with a line of hair like a row of seeds.
The splendor of spring has arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara;
the lotuses, with their eyes of water, gaze with affection.
The waves, like hands of water, repeatedly beckon those who wish to bathe.
The thundering laughter of the water announces its joy;
the parrots dwelling on the banks announce the arrival of the rainy season, and the winds carrying cool sprays of mist draw the mind toward it. (13–14)
The water-fowls invite even the sky, rich with stars;
and the Rohita fish, submerged in the water, bring to mind the virtuous who have been drenched by floods.
Here, the cry of the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird alone [encourages] the children who long for a bath.
He performs and delights in the most excellent peacock dance.
When the youth of spring has arrived, the cuckoos on the flowering branches repeatedly call out to Hari with their warbling, as if inviting him for his bath. (16–17)
Beholding such a serene and blossoming forest on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, all the Brāhmaṇas,
as well as thousands of boys, girls, and women, were there at that time. (18)
With eager minds, they went to celebrate the Flower Swing Festival (puṣpadolotsava).
Having tied comfortable swings to the branches of the kadamba trees, the young boys, girls, maidens, and others swung back and forth. (2.25.19–20)
In the springtime at the Setu, men and women delighted themselves with colors,
filling jars and other vessels with saffron, as well as yellow, red, green, and brown pigments derived from the leaves of the *pālāśa* tree.
On the shore of the lake, they took delight in throwing dust, splashing water, scattering colored powders, and using *gulāla* paste;
with saffron and red powders, they played with one another in the morning, seizing each other by force and casting each other down. (22–23)
Anxiously, they repeatedly sprinkle the water from the gargara-vessels;
they smear their faces and other parts with the sacred clay of the lake.
They pour streams of water over their heads by means of mechanical contrivances.
Some, holding clusters of flowers to their ears, dance;
others, filled with joy, sing the songs of Kṛṣṇa;
and still others wash away their soiled bodies and garments.
Shaking their heads, they clear away the dust and grime;
wiping the dust from their eyes, they enter the waters of the lake.
Crossing over by means of various rafts, they bathe together in the waters.
Men and women wash garments dyed with colors;
young boys and girls sport in the bowers of flower clusters.
Men and women take delight in their own groups and sprinkle one another with water.
Having played musical instruments, they also worshiped Vasanta,
having fashioned a golden image adorned with yellow garments,
honored with red flowers, and endowed with earrings and a crown.
Adorned with a girdle and anklets, wearing a beautiful bodice,
she had attained the state of youth; she was captivating, casting sidelong glances, seated upon a flower-chariot, gentle, and crowned with a crest of blossoming sprays.
Her ears were adorned with clusters and bunches of flowers, and she was anointed with fragrant unguents;
her shoulders shone with a mass of matted hair, and she was resplendent with a golden parasol. Her upper garment was the moon situated in the center between the edges of bound sun-gems.
Adorned with a crown embellished with diamonds, gems, and fine pearls; wearing a flower as a crest-ornament, flowers at her waist, and clothed in floral garments;
richly adorned with garlands of *kadamba* flowers and a forehead-mark of *campaka* blossoms. (34–35)
Her forearms were like *karṇikāra* flowers, her arms graced by *pālāśa* blossoms; she was lovely with clusters of *japā* flowers, and her beard-like mustache was like blue water-lilies (*aindīvāra*).
Her eyes were like *citraka* flowers, and she shone with teeth as white as *kunda* jasmine.
Her nose was as beautiful as a sesame flower, adorned with a cluster of *kādamba* blossoms;
her forehead was richly decorated with plantain flowers, and her thighs were like plantain trunks. Her hips possessed the luster of *kālhāra* lotuses, and she had a navel of exquisite beauty. (37–38)

All human beings worshipped the form of the god Vasanta, which had shanks like the trunk of an elephant, feet with soles like lotuses, nails with the subtle appearance of the moon, and was pale-complexioned and smiling gently. (39)
With beautiful flowers, saffron and other substances, grains of rice, and fine *śigru* plants;
with saffron, *abilā* powder, and *gulāla* that shines as brightly as the pure sky;
likewise with flower-clusters, red leaves, and various kinds of fruits. (2.25.40–41)
They worshipped Śrī Vasantaka with milk-based preparations and very liquid offerings;
having also bathed Śrī Vasantaka with various melodies,
they honored him with spring garments and the like, ornaments, and flowered cloths.
And with garlands of flowers they worshipped Vasanta, the Lord of buds;
the Master of blossoms and sprouts, the Sovereign of shoots, the Lord of flowers, the Master of stalks, and the Season. (43–44)
On the bank of the lake, they worshipped Śādvaleśa, the beautiful youth,
as well as other beloveds of Vasanta: the female cuckoo, the female swan, the female crane, Sumanā, Menā, the peahen, and the female bustard.
The sixteen beloved wives worshipped both Śukī and Gāruḍī;
all of them were embodiments of Lakṣmī, beautiful with variegated colors, maidens with the luster of gold and faces filled with the radiance of the moon. (46–47)
Some wear white garments, some yellowish-brown garments, and some wear green garments; others are clad in tawny garments, as well as those wearing variegated clothes.
Some wear garments with a golden luster, and others wear tawny-colored garments.
Clad in blue garments, dressed in white, and preeminent in variegated robes;
adorned with saffron-colored attire and wearing pale white garments—
these women of Spring, possessing every grace of amorous beauty, paid their worship.
They worshipped with sandalwood, aguru, musk, saffron, unbroken grains, and water,
as well as with milk-preparations and betel leaves.
Then, the Blessed Lord, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, was there.
Assuming the form of a youth on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
he established the season named Śrī Vasanta, accompanied by sixteen noble ladies, upon a swing and worshipped it with various ritual offerings. (52–53)
Then Vasantaka performed the nightly lamp-offering there;
accompanied by his sixteen wives, he appeared visibly before him. Possessing the form exactly as described, he spoke to his lord, the worshipper.
To the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved and enchanting one;
O Supreme Lord, Puruṣottama, you perform my worship by adopting worldly custom, being worshipped by all the gods and others. (55–56)
"Today I have become purified, having become your servant along with my wife.
I desire to worship you; please sit upon this excellent seat.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Vasantas, together with his beloved, [arose] from his own seat.
Having descended and stood upon the earth,
Ṛtu, together with all his wives, placed the Lord Puruṣottama upon a swing and worshipped him with devotion using the sixteen articles of worship. ||58-59||
There he worshipped Śrī Hari, who had assumed the form of a youth;
beholding that Supreme Person, whose every limb was in perfect proportion to his beauty, Vasantasena and the other people were likewise enchanted by His divine form. (2.25.60)
All the women of spring became infatuated with the Lord;
the sages and the wives of the sages were bewildered by the Supreme Lord.
Thus, for a moment, they remained motionless, stunned, and filled with bliss.
Then, by the side-glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which was filled with laughter and grace,
they immediately regained consciousness of their own selves and praised Śrī Hari— the beloved Supreme Lord who grants all desires.
You alone abide as the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all worlds;
you are the Supreme Person from the beginningless past, manifestly endowed with all sovereignty.
O Protector, grant me always your station, your feet, for the sake of service.
"Without you, everything indeed exists as fruitless and devoid of happiness.
Having spoken thus, the people and women fell at the feet of Hari.
Hari said, "So be it; it shall happen exactly thus, there is no doubt."
Then Keśava again displayed a marvel:
his own pervasive, divine form within the body of Vasanta. Śrī Hari himself was seen by all the beautiful women of spring.
In the spring, while the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was their master and protector,
Kalikā and the others were enchanted upon seeing him as their husband and lord;
they chose this youthful Puruṣottama as their own.
These sixteen beloved ones purified themselves and offered praises once more;
they presented garlands and then fashioned the *candraka* ornament.
Hari, perceiving in his mind their well-cultivated desire for self-surrender, [accepted it]. (2.25.70–71)
"So be it," said the Lord Hari, assuming the form of a youth; and then the glorious Lord created two forms for each of the sixteen maidens—
one divine and one non-divine.
That which was divine, equal to a god, was indeed that sixteenth form.
Then he gave those sixteen divine and beautiful maidens to Vasantaka,
keeping them for his own beloved wife.

There, in that hermitage among millions of maidens, he gave [himself] to Lomaśa for the sake of his residence; thereafter, Kṛṣṇa became a child once more. His mother went to the shore of a lake to bathe Hari, who was wet with the colors [of the arena].
Meanwhile, that great Daitya, staying within the water in the form of a fish,
seized the boy Kṛṣṇa, who was thirty cubits in height.
At this, the mother became distraught with the apprehension of her son’s destruction.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa! Who was that great fish, the king of demons, who arrived there and stood ready to devour the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa? (78)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The great Daitya Sālamāla, born from the skin of Hiraṇyakūrca,
dwelt in the forest of Sālemāla and was a source of terror to the world.
In the eastern region of Saurāṣṭra, there was a great asura who subsisted on forest fare;
he was seven palm trees in height and one palm tree in width, resembling a mountain peak.
Carrying a mace and a mallet, he danced while remembering his ancestral enmity.
Then, in the middle of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the Daitya appeared in the form of a crocodile;
indeed, that crocodile was thirty cubits long and could assume any form at will.
At that time, he dragged the boy, who was bathing on the bank, by means of his tail.
And seeing him standing on the beautiful and enchanting staircase by his mother's side,
the ocean of compassion— the child— knowing that he had come swiftly to slay him as was fitting for an Asura, and was leading him down to the bottom of the water, [acted]. (83)
Then Bālakṛṣṇa became twofold: a boy and a crocodile.
Having become a boy, he quickly took his stand upon the steps on the shore of the lake;
having become a crocodile, he stood in the middle of the water, measuring fifty cubits in height.
In order to swallow the great fish, he quickly turned onto his back;
out of fear of death, the fish fled across the surface of the water.
The crocodile abandoned its own form and seized that fish.

The great Daitya Sālemāla, having become a man holding a mace, swiftly struck the crocodile; the crocodile then met its destruction. But that man, the wielder of the mace, became seven palm trees tall.
A great battle took place there between Sālamāla and Nārāyaṇa, both of whom were exceedingly powerful; it was fought with maces.
Then, by force, Sāla struck the mace against the head of Hari.
Then Hari, firm as a thunderbolt, shattered it into a hundred pieces.
The great lord struck that Daitya with his very mace;
struck on the chest, he quickly fell down unconscious.
Rising again, he forcefully hurled his own mallet;
however, it was shattered against Hari’s staff-like fist by the mace.
Deprived of his weapon, that Śālāmāla leapt into the sky like a mountain peak.
Taking up the tip of a mudgara, he hurled it at Keśava.
The Blessed One, the Great Lord, crushed that mudgara with his own mace and released the Sudarśana [cakra] to destroy him. (93–94)

Resembling a hundred suns, filled with garlands of blazing fire, and whirling rapidly, it fell upon the head of Śāla and severed his head. A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there, and all the gods became delighted.

This Sālemāla, who was dead and possessed a body as large as a *krośa*, fell to the ground, destroying trees and shaking the earth. Through the application of Hari’s discus, his soul attained liberation. (96–97)
By means of a most divine celestial chariot, Sālaka reached Vaikuṇṭha;
Garuḍa, however, seizing his body with his feet from the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
carried him away and released him along the path of the sky.
After Yaśodā had departed for the mountain forest called Śaileśamāla,
those foremost Daityas born of his own lineage who were assembled there,
as well as even his hundred wives, fell into supreme grief. (2.25.100)
Seeing their beloved fallen from the sky, they wept most bitterly; they performed his funeral rites according to his caste. There were five hundred Daityas and one hundred women belonging to him.

Even though they had a thousand sons, they found no happiness due to their grief; they all constantly brooded over the means of avenging their enmity. Then, the Blessed One, having become a boy, appeared there in the vicinity of Aśvapaṭṭa.
Having celebrated the festival of the flower-swing, she returned home with her parents;
by his command, the maidens then went to the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
Thereafter, the sages and those women departed for their respective abodes.
And the father tied a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*) made of *caurṇaka* grass upon Hari’s hand.
Thus, during the festival of the swing, O Rādhikā, this miracle was displayed by Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul, and the demon was slain. (105–106)

Whether by reading or even by hearing it, a man, a woman, a maiden, a child, an ascetic, or even a youth shall attain all auspicious fortune. By listening to that narrative with devotion, one shall attain the supreme abode.
O Rādhā, beloved of the Lord of Pāravatī, [you are] attainable through the grace of Hari.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Blossoming of Spring, the Festival of the Flower Swing, and the Destruction by Hari of the Asura Sālamālā—who had assumed the form of a *timiṅgila* fish and arrived for the purpose of destruction," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 27 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Listen, O daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, to another wonder of Hari arising in his third year, which bestows happiness; I shall relate it. On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, all the brāhmaṇas residing at Kuṅkumavāpikā—
On the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, during the sacrificial festival of the Brahmasūtra,
nine thousand sages led by Lomaśa, holding darbha grass, assembled for the purification of the Brahmasūtra through the nine sacraments. (2–3)

Together with their vessels and accompanied by offerings for the gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*), they performed the purification of the body with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other rites, as well as the libations to the *pitṛs*.
They also performed the worship of the gods and the fire-oblation (*havana*) and other rituals.
They put on a new, radiant sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
For that purpose, they performed the Great Rudra rite and the daily Viṣṇu sacrifice on the bank with great festivities, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and dancing.
Through the instruction of the narratives of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
the cooks, at the foot of a banyan tree on the shore of the lake in the kitchen,
[prepared] powdered sweets, pearl-like *laḍḍukas*, *pūrikās*, *apūpas*, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Dishes of sandalwood paste, boiled chickpeas, and various side dishes;
likewise, soups with rice, sweet and bitter liquids, mustard-based curries, sour gruels, and fried cakes. (8–9)
They caused food to be cooked in great abundance for the sake of tens of millions and hundreds of billions of twice-born brahmins;
there were mountains of cooked foods, lakes of clarified butter, and pools of milk.
There were also rivers of buttermilk and lakes of milk-rice porridge.
All that was required had already been prepared by the great sages who were like wish-fulfilling trees.
While the oblation was being offered into the sacrificial fire at midday,
an army composed of Daitya beings arrived from the sky.
That distance from the sacrificial ground was but a single *krośa*.
Upon hearing their cries,
the sage Lomaśa quickly surveyed the Dānavas with his divine vision.

Accompanied by female demons (dānavī), bearing weapons, missiles, and armor, those exceedingly cruel ones had assembled for the very purpose of avenging their enmity; they stood there desiring to fight. (14–15)
"This is the territory of our enemy, and this very place is the black palace.
This is Lomaśa, the foremost of the twice-born. Let them strike them down; let them kill them!
By this Bālakṛṣṇa, our lordly father has been slain."
"Let them crush Bālakṛṣṇa, his parents, and Lomaśa!
Let this village of hermitages and even the trees of the Brahmins be split, cut down, set ablaze, and destroyed in an instant! (17–18)
A thousand Sāla-sons, servants, female slaves,
and kinsmen of Sālamāla fell upon the shore of the lake;
others, moreover, descended with great speed along the path of the sky.
While these maidens, wives of the Daityas— whether young, old, or in the prime of youth—
had not yet reached the sacrificial ground,
Lomaśa paralyzed them in the sky by means of Atharvan mantras.
At that very moment, Lomaśa paralyzed those standing on the bank and at its sides,
so that the sacrificial offerings would not fall into ruin.
Having done this, he then remembered the Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
Bālakṛṣṇa, though still a youth, arrived at the sacrifice in an instant.
Honored by the brahmins and worshipped, Kṛṣṇa— accompanied by Sudarśana and requested to repel the army of the Daityas— took his place along with Garuḍa.
Having quickly bowed to the sages, the wielder of the conch, discus,

Having reached the vicinity of the army, Hari himself blew his conch.
Then Lomaśa warded off the Atharva mantras with that much power.
The conscious army fell upon Śrī Hari to fight;
Śrī Hari crushed the army on all sides with his mace.
Then Garuḍa struck him in many ways with his two wings, his talons, and his beak, and cast him down upon the earth;

Then the routed Daityas, seizing rocks and trees,
turned back and struck Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.

He cut down all those asuras born of the Salva lineage;

Standing at Vaṃśavaṭa, they all cried out for the granting of a boon:

Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, seated upon the divine Garuḍa,
burned away their sins with the splendor of his discus.
Having fashioned them with bodies like those of celestial beings, he endowed them with divine forms.
The Blessed Lord, the refuge of all, joyfully granted them His own protection;
the Supreme Controller directed them to stay in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having sprinkled them with water and bathed them in the waters, Lomaśa [tended to them]. || 35-36 ||
After having performed purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then offer the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," as well as a garland of *tulasī*, a forehead mark (*tilaka*), and other such offerings.
He initiated them all and indeed made them Vaiṣṇavas.
Then he fed one hundred and five hundred of them,
and he sent the mothers and the maidens back to the hermitage.
Then the sages, headed by Lomaśa, having performed the ritual procedures for the sacrifice,
having donned the sacrificial threads, and having completed the final oblation,
fed the maidens by the tens of millions to their heart's content.
The wealthy householders likewise fed their guests;
they gave various excellent gifts,
such as cattle, fields, forests, jewels, garments, ornaments, and houses.
Having given away vehicles with their furnishings, as well as mounts, food, and water— having thus bestowed these gifts and completed the sacrificial rites—
they returned to their respective homes with joy, speaking of the supreme wonder.

Then Gopālakṛṣṇaka, accompanied by Bālakṛṣṇa, went to his own abode; thereafter the bird departed for Vaikuṇṭha. At that time, Lomaśa and the others, filled with joy, returned to their own hermitages.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, all those foremost of Daityas from Sālamāla were slain by Śrī Hari, and they went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Their daughters, staying in the hermitage of Lomaśa, chose Hari as their husband.
Then their mothers—the wives of the Daityas who had entered the state of widowhood—questioned Lomaśa, the bull among sages, regarding their own welfare:
"O learned one, by what action here might there be well-being for us in both worlds? (47–48)
In that same way, O bull among sages, Lomaśa then out of compassion spoke to the wives of the Daityas and to their daughters all manner of dharmas that are ever-beneficial and bestow prosperity.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, charity, forbearance,
self-control, compassion, absence of pride, purity, austerity, celibacy, auspicious speech, and service to the virtuous— these bestow the highest good. (2.26.50–51)
This dharma, protected by men and women, consists of thirteen parts;
it bestows worldly happiness as well as eternal spiritual welfare.
It includes the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the tending of the sacred fire, and ritual bathing.

Alms-gathering, service to the guru, and bringing about the guru’s pleasure (53)—these indeed bestow both worldly happiness and eternal spiritual welfare. One should dwell constantly in the guru’s house, [serving] his wife, his sons, and so forth. (54)

Regarding them as gods and likewise regarding the goddesses as divine, she should always worship them; serving them without pride, that virtuous woman certainly conquers death. Through the contemplation of the Self, she [should serve] the ancestors, the gods, and guests as well.
One who properly gratifies [the deity] with devotion certainly conquers death.
Good conduct must always be maintained by Daityas, gods, and humans alike;
for one devoid of good conduct, there is no well-being either in this world or the next.
In this world, sacrifice, charity, and austerity always lead to prosperity;
yet for one devoid of right conduct, even these become utterly fruitless.
Indeed, a woman of evil conduct finds no joy either in this world or in the next.
Effort should always be exerted in right conduct, for that is the destroyer of misfortune.
Right conduct is indeed a tree that dwells within the body of a woman, and it descends even into the bodies of her offspring, bringing them happiness. (2.26.60)
Dharma is the root of that tree; Artha is its well-provided branches;
Kāma is its lovely flowers; and Mokṣa is its fruit endowed with flavor.
This very [tree], when cultivated by a woman, bestows auspiciousness both in this world and the next.
One should first awaken during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and remember Hari.
One should also recite the morning auspicious verses for the gods, the sages, and the virtuous women;
Śaṅkara, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, has indeed spoken this supreme auspiciousness. (62–63)
That which a mortal recites at dawn is released from the bondage of sin;
listen as I relate that morning auspiciousness.
By hearing, remembering, and reciting it, one is liberated from all evils.
From the auspicious sound of this [conch], many have attained liberation.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is the source of all incarnations, beyond the imperishable, without beginning, and the Supreme Lord.
May those liberated souls, existing throughout countless creations, grant me a beautiful dawn that bears the fruit of liberation;
[may He too,] accompanied by Rādhā and the countless cowherds and cowherd girls— || 66 ||
May Kṛṣṇa, who is served and resides within the lotus of my heart, as well as Lakṣmī, Ramāpati, and his attendants and others, grant me an auspicious dawn that bears the fruit of liberation. (67)
The supreme lords accompanied by Śrī Vāsudeva,
the various Nārāyaṇas residing in diverse abodes, and the liberated souls possessing the splendor of rubies, coral, and lotuses.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Sun, and the Moon; Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Dharma—make my auspicious dawn bear the fruit of liberation. (68)
May the sages, Śani, the Pitṛs, and the lords of the Gaṇas and Īśa grant me a beautiful dawn that bears the fruit of liberation.
May Raibhya, Gautama, Pulastya, and Marīci likewise do so.
May Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Lomaśa, Gālava, and others,
as well as Vasiṣṭha, Bhārgava, Ribhu, Cyavana, and the rest, grant me an auspicious dawn that bears the fruit of liberation. (2.26.70)
The illustrious attendants— Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, Sounaka, Piṅgala, Sanātana, Nārada, and others;
as well as Indra and the other guardians of the directions, and tens of millions of gods.
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation.
May the seven musical notes, the surfaces of the earth, the subtle elements, the gross aggregates of principles, the mountains, and the oceans [be favorable].
May sacred fords, excellent rivers, and women devoted to their husbands make my auspicious morning bear the fruit of liberation.
[Rukmāgada, Dhruva, Suyajñaka, Puṇḍarīka...]
May Prahlāda, the hundred sons of Suvrata, Ambarīṣa, Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha, Divodāsa, Śuka, and others grant me a beautiful dawn that bears the fruit of liberation. (73)
Thus, at dawn, one should hear, recite, or remember with devotion this supreme and most purifying *Suprabhāta*; there is no doubt that it will surely come to pass.
Having remembered Hari and performed the purification of the body, one should bathe according to the prescribed rules.
She should perform libations, as well as the twilight prayers and the worship of Śrī Hari.
She should apply the sectarian mark (tilaka) and the crescent mark (candraka), and also perform the worship of the gods.
She should bow to the Sun and prostrate before her parents and her husband.
Having bowed to the Guru, having bowed to the virtuous woman, and having bowed to the Earth, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
In the morning, one should look upon curd, dūrvā grass, clarified butter,
a cow with its calf, a water-pot, a bull, gold, a svastika, and honey.
Cow dung, unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, earth, and Brahmin maidens; white flowers, crops, fire, sandalwood,
the Arka plant, the Aśvattha tree, a virtuous man, a mirror, and an image of Hari.
One should honor a guest with sincerity and cultivate the company of the virtuous.
One should certainly not perform an oil massage on Sunday, nor consume milk on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, one should not approach a woman; and on a festival day, one should not approach one's own wife.
One should never sleep with one's feet toward the north, nor with one's head toward the west.

One should perform a circumambulation—keeping it to the right—around a temple, a sacred tree, a learned man, a crossroads, a teacher, and an elder; such a person bestows the merit of a bull-sacrifice.
One should never wear clothing that has been worn by another or that is soiled.
One should bathe daily, especially at the commencement of planetary periods and the like, and perform offerings to the gods and acts of charity.
One should dwell among the virtuous, but not among the wicked, and one should reside in holy places.
One should never dwell among people who harbor enmity, nor even among those devoid of dharma.
Those whose food should not be eaten are: women recently delivered, eunuchs, cats, mice, and cocks;
as well as the fallen, the outcaste, the naked, the Cāṇḍālas, and those who are base.
A Brahmin woman and a Brahmin who are both unfaithful are called "birth-bringers" (sūtikā); the food of those two is censured.
He who does not offer oblations at the proper time, nor bathe, nor give gifts—
One who is deficient in the worship of the ancestors and the gods is proclaimed to be a eunuch (ṣaṇḍha). He who mutters prayers, performs austerities, or even studies for the sake of hypocrisy,
and does not strive for the sake of the hereafter, is celebrated as a cat (mārjāra).
When wealth exists, he neither eats, nor gives, nor offers oblations;
they call him a rat, and his food must not be eaten by one who possesses dharma.
He who, being a member of an assembly, resorts to partiality toward those who belong to it [is likewise condemned].

They call him a cock; his food of water is greatly censured. One who abandons his own duty and adopts the duty of another is considered fallen. So too is one who abandons the gods, the ancestors, and the teacher, or one who harms cows, Brahmins, and women.
That food which has been cast away, or which is defiled by sin, should not be eaten.
Those families in which there is no Veda, no sacred discourse, and no religious observance—they are declared to be naked; their food is defiled by the lack of consecration.
One who is distressed by desire yet does not give, one who forbids another from giving, and one who abandons those who have come for refuge—he is a Cāṇḍāla, the lowest of men.
One must not eat the food of such people; otherwise, one will partake in their sin.
Furthermore, whatever action one performs such that the self does not feel any reproach whatsoever—
that should be done fearlessly, for it is supremely conducive to well-being.
And for a woman of such conduct, whether in the home or in the forest, [there is no difference].
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa indeed come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, self-realization through austerities, the total renunciation of all attachments, and constant remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—[these are the means]. (96–97)
The total surrender to Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Guru, the inner self of all—
by performing this, one is never tainted by actions born of the body.
You [should likewise offer yourselves] in every way to Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
For those who serve the form of the Child, supreme liberation will come.
Moreover, for that woman by whom self-surrender has been performed here, supreme liberation certainly occurs in her abode; of this there is no doubt. (2.26.100)
Whether in sleep or waking, in dream or in the waking state, whether gross or subtle, within the heart, or in states of passion, darkness, or goodness— let them remember Mādhava.
Let them serve Hari through the self, the senses, the body, or through ritual service.
"Let them propitiate that Lord with their inner senses and through their actions.
Having been thus addressed, they received the name-mantra from Lomaśa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (1.02–1.03)
Thus they recited this [mantra] day and night without weariness.
Having attained divinity through the constant practice of japa, those hundred women reached the celestial realm.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, appearing as a child, traveled in a celestial chariot.
Accompanied by a hundred celestial chariots, Mādhava approached them; he caused them to ascend the foremost of those chariots and led them to the supreme abode,
which is indeed higher even than the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Then those maidens, having received instruction from their preceptor Lomaśa and considering the boy Kṛṣṇa to be their own husband,
stayed right there among the girls by the thousands at that time.
"By reading or even by hearing [this], a virtuous woman shall attain Bālakṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Daityas of the Sāla and Mālava Lineages at the Yajñasūtra Festival on the Shore of the Lake during the Śrāvaṇī Month in the Tretā Era, the Battle with the Lord, Their Destruction, and the Mokṣadharma taught by Lomaśa," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Listen, O Rādhikā: the gods, the daityas, millions of dānavas, humans, sages, and the virtuous are all equal sons of Hari.

Intrinsic natures arise and pass away, following the influence of purpose;
that purpose is pleasure, and it follows from the specific type of body one possesses.
(4) The body is considered to be of three kinds: female, male, and neuter.
The child, the youth, and the old man; the householder, the renunciant, and the ascetic.

In childhood one plays, in old age one attains tranquility, but the youth does not. (6)
