she performed such penance that she obstructed the setting of the sun.
O Rādhikā, the vision of my beloved and union with him did not indeed cease even for a night;
for even during the night, O Rādhikā, the performers of sacrifice, together with their officiating priests, continued their rituals in the sacrificial halls.
The great devotees of the Lord perform worship of Viṣṇu with devotion. (35) Other people worship the Sun, others the Moon, others Brahmā, and others Hara;
indeed, all creatures perform worship day and night, regarding [these deities as supreme]. (36)
The discerning, however, know the rising of the sun by the blooming lotuses, and the rising of the moon by the blossoming night-lilies; likewise,
they know that the city of the night-stalkers has come under his majesty by the bulls.
But Sūrya, unable to endure that, contemplated how to thwart it.
(38) Then, gazed upon by Bhānu with eyes inflamed by anger, Sukeśī together with the village blazed up in the sky. (39)
The Sun swiftly released his own solar disc toward him;
that disc indeed shattered the city of that night-stalker.
Fallen from the sky along with Keśin and the Rākṣasas, it plummeted down. (2.27.40)
Sukeśī cried out loudly, "Obeisance to Śambhu! (41).
Hearing that lamentation on Kailāsa, the Lord Śaṅkara, through meditation, realized that the city of his devotee had been struck down by Sūrya. (42)
Enraged, Śambhu gazed at the sun with his third eye;
the sun fell from the sky and descended to the surface of the earth.
[This occurred] starting from the time of Yogiśāyin until the appearance of Keśava.
The auspicious ground extending from Prayāga as far as Keśava is this holy field of Hari; it is the city named Vārāṇasī. He fell within that very space between the Varaṇā and the [Asi]. ||44–45||
Then, having scorched her for a moment and plunged into that lake,
as well as into the Varaṇā and the Gaṅgā, he became known by the name Lolārka.
Thereupon, that Sun-god entreated the Earth through Hara.
Hara also, taking Bhānu by the hand, placed him upon the chariot;
he likewise placed Sukeśin and Pura upon it like a god in heaven.
Thus, even a Rākṣasa becomes powerful through righteousness.
Śambhu became his ally, and Sūrya obtained the fruit of his wrath.
Thus Lomaśa spoke of auspicious and beneficial bovine bulls to the daughters of the Daityas,
and they questioned him again with great respect.
"O Lord, Sovereign Guru, tell us: whose worship is to be performed and how?
Lomaśa replied to them: "Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, sleeps upon the body of the serpent from the morning of the eleventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha."
Having prepared a couch of the coils of the serpent Śeṣa and having worshipped Keśava,
one should cause the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to rest for a moment.
On the thirteenth day, Kāma himself indeed sleeps upon his auspicious bed.
There, at that time, in a place fashioned with the fragrant blossoms of kadamba trees, Kāma— the lord of delight and passion—
should be especially worshipped in the form of Kṛṣṇa as the bestower of happiness. (53–54)
Then, on the fourteenth day, the yakṣas sleep in comfort and coolness upon golden lotuses provided with soft pillows;
there the Lord of Yakṣas, accompanied by yakṣas and joined by Maṇibhadra and others, [rests].
He is to be honored with food, drink, and other offerings, and especially to be gratified. On the full moon day, the Lord of Umā sleeps upon a bed of his own skin,
having tied up his mass of matted hair with another hide, specifically that of a tiger.
And there Śambhu is to be worshipped with the flowers of the dhattūra and other offerings.
Then the Sun enters the zodiac sign of Cancer;
by that, it becomes night for the immortals and the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
Then, O beloved, on the first lunar day (pratipad), Brahmā sleeps upon a bed made of blue lotuses with the desire for the welfare and auspicious thoughts of the worlds;
on the second day, Viśvakarman; and on the third day, Pārvatī. (2.27.59–60)
Vināyaka sleeps on the fourth day, and Dharmarāja also on the fifth;
Skanda sleeps on the sixth, and the Lord Ravi on the seventh;
likewise, Kātyāyanī on the eighth and Kamalālayā on the ninth.
On the tenth [lunar day], the lords of serpents sleep, subsisting on air;
on the eleventh dark lunar day, the Sādhyas and the gods sleep. On those respective days, a virtuous woman should perform the worship of those deities.
Therefore, being observant of her vows, she should follow you in every way for the sake of her welfare.
On the second lunar day, Viśvakarman Prajāpati sleeps;
at that time, an image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī should be fashioned.

An image of Kṛṣṇa made of gold, marked with the Śrīvatsa and possessing four arms, should be fashioned. On a couch provided with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Kṛṣṇa together with Lakṣmī on that bed, and one should also place excellent fruits there.
Having thus offered fragrant substances, one should pray to the glorious Hari:
"O Lord, just as You shine with Śrī upon Your unempty bed, so may my bed also remain unempty;
and may this always be so. (67)
"Just as your bed is never empty of Lakṣmī, so too, O Blessed One, let my household life not be empty. Having uttered, "May Lakṣmīdhara be gracious," one should perform the vow. (68–69)
During the four-month period, the observer of the vow should eat food free from oil and alkaline substances.
Having uttered, "May Lakṣmīdhara be pleased with me," he should bestow upon a twice-born man gifts of fruit,
gold, clothing, a bed, and a cow.
By that merit, the practitioner of vows rejoices happily in the life of a householder.
(71) When the sun reaches the month of Āṣāḍha and faces the sign of Gemini,
from that point until it shines while situated in Scorpio— (72)
O Rādhikā, during the intervening period of four months, those who seek the vow of awakening awaken the gods in succession;
and when the sun is situated in Libra, Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa first awakens.
One should perform his worship with great gifts, offerings, and so forth.
Then, Kāmadeva awakens there; one should worship him.
On the second [tithi], however, there is a golden image of Lakṣmīdhara.

A bed provided with a coverlet, according to one's own means, should be given here by this vow; there shall be no separation between the husband and wife. Now, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is considered Kālāṣṭamī.
On this day, conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, Śaṅkara sleeps within the Liṅga.
One should bathe [the image] with cow urine or even with water, and likewise perform an ablution for Śiva.
Thereafter, one should worship him with flowers of the Dhattūra plant and with sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense made from saffron resin, as well as food offerings of honey and clarified butter, while reciting the prayer for his gratification: "May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me.
Then, during the month of Āśvina, one should perform the bathing ritual or bathe oneself, and subsequently worship him with cow dung.
One should offer incense made from lotuses and the resin of *sarja* trees,
and one should feed honey-sweets while praying, "May Hiraṇyākṣa be pleased with me.
In the month of Kārttika, one should perform a bath with milk and worship with *karavīra* flowers.
One should offer incense made from the resin of the *śrīvāsa* tree and an offering of honeyed milk-rice (*madhupāyasa*).
Reciting "May Sthāṇu be pleased," one should present a gift of silver.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is a bath with curd, and the food offering consists of rice mixed with honey.
One should request, "May Śarva be pleased," while offering incense made from the resin of the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree.
In the month of Pauṣa, there should be a ritual bath, worship with sacrificial oblations (*havir*), and likewise with *bilva* fruits;
the incense is the resin of the *madhuka* tree, and the food offering consists of honeyed barley flour (*madhusaktu*).
One should offer a ring while praying, "May Tryambaka be pleased.
In the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath with *kuśa* water and worship Śiva with a white water-lily (*kumuda*).
The incense should be the resin of the *kadamba* tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) should be rice mixed with sesame seeds.
"May Mahādeva be pleased with me"—thus one should pray with salutation (namaḥ).
In this way, this vow lasting six months always bestows good fortune. Then, in the month of Phālguna, one should perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 86–87 ||
One should worship with *kundapuṣpa* flowers and offer incense made of sandalwood.
One should present as an offering (*naivedya*) rice mixed with jaggery and ghee in a copper vessel.
Having said, "May Rudra be pleased with me," one should cause a pair of garments to be given.
In the month of Caitra, one should perform a ritual bath with the waters of the Udumbara tree, worship with Mandāraka flowers, offer incense made of guggulu, and present sweetmeats (modakas).
One should also give the gift of a deer skin, saying: "May Nāgeśvara be pleased with me."
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform a bath with fragrant flowers and worship with *abhra* (mica) flowers;
the incense should be the resin of the *sarja* tree, and the food offering (*naivedya*) should be ghee along with fruit.
One should offer a water-pot while saying, "May the Slayer of Śālva be pleased."
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should bathe with *āmalaka* fruits and likewise perform worship with *arka* flowers.
One should eat curd and barley meal (*saktu*), and offer an umbrella and sandals.
With sandalwood incense, one should say: "May the Destroyer of Bhaga’s Eyes be pleased with me. (92–93)
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform a bath with bilva fruits and worship with golden flowers.
One should incense the deity with jasmine and offer cakes as the supreme food offering.
With the prayer, "May the slayer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice be pleased," one should give gifts such as barley and grain-particles.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform a bath with *bhṛṅgarāja*, worship with *śrīdru* leaves, offer incense of *aguru*, and present as an offering curds and sweetmeats (*modaka*).
By the giving of gold, cows, and clothing, may Gaṅgādhara be pleased with me. (95–96)
With these six months [of practice], worship grants the fulfillment of vows;
then, when the year is complete, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the ninth day.
Furthermore, there is always fasting on the eighth day of each of the twelve dark fortnights.
Thereafter, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to the word of Maheśvara.
From this meritorious vow, the couple obtains imperishable happiness;
it bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and it is exactly so and not otherwise.
The lotus emerged from the navel of Prajāpati and originated with the Aśvins;
therefore, in the worship of Brahmā, a lotus should be offered, which increases his pleasure.
The Kadamba tree is for Kāmadeva, and the Vaṭa tree is for Yakṣa.

The *dhattūra* tree arose from the heart of Śiva; indeed, the *khadira* tree emerged from the middle of Brahmā’s body. From the central torso of Viśvakarman, the *kaṇṭakī* tree was born, and from the palm of Girijā’s hand, the *kunda* bush sprang forth.
The Sinduvāraka tree situated in the pitcher of Gaṇādhipa shines resplendent;
on the right side of Yama, a Pālāśa tree indeed grew forth.
To the south-east of Yama, a black Udumbara tree was born.
For Skanda, the Bandhujīva tree was produced; for Ravi, the Aśvattha tree.
For Kātyāyanī, the Śamī tree appeared; for Lakṣmī, the Bilva tree appeared in her hand.
In the mouth of Nāga, the Śara-reed appeared; on the back of Vāsuki, the Dūrvā grass appeared.
O Rādhikā, sandalwood was born upon the heart of Sādhya;
this story belongs to another kalpa and originated at the beginning of creation.
Through worship with these [leaves], the gods' satisfaction shall be supreme in every respect.
"When they are propitiated, they bestow virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), desire (*kāma*), and liberation (*mokṣa*).

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Sukeśī, the Aśūnyaśayana Vow, the Śivapuṇyaka Vow and others, the Sleep of the Gods on Different Lunar Days, and their Worship," within the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in this way the sage Lomaśa indeed instructed the daughters of the Daityas in the principles of dharma and various vows.
And they performed the practices of the bull (the *vṛṣācāra*), as well as the observance of vows (*vratācaraṇa*),
the vow of the unempty bed (*aśūnyaśayana*), the Cāturmāsya vows,
and the meritorious Śiva-Kālāṣṭamī vow lasting for a year.
They performed service to their venerable guru and took refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having become pure-bodied and pure-souled,
they were carried by excellent attendants in celestial chariots to the imperishable abode.
Having gone and seen him, those maidens of divine form arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa; there they all worshipped Lomaśa, the preceptor of Hari,
having recognized the full majesty of Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
They attended upon that beloved Lord Harikṛṣṇa as their husband and master.
(6) Thus, when the third year had passed and a great festival was held, at the commencement of the fourth year, the grand festival of his birth was celebrated. (7)
Then his father fed millions of living beings and caused gifts made of jewels and gold to be distributed.
O Rādhā, listen; I shall tell you of a single marvel that occurred there.

From Pātāla, the Nāga named Svastika— possessing the body of a serpent and the head of a human, with hands joined in *añjali*, measuring a *tāla* in height, and deeply distressed— stood weeping in the presence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.28.10)
Crying out, "Save me! Save me! he approached, his household now empty;
meanwhile, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa sat upon the elephant-throne. Having arrived there, he fell repeatedly at the feet of Śrī Hari.
He said, "O Blessed One, protect me, a serpent who has come to you for refuge!
(12) Apart from you, no protector exists for me in the three worlds.
Śrī Hari said, "What sorrow has come upon you? Describe it. (13)
While everyone was listening and the festival had arrived, the Naga described his own suffering born of battle in Pātāla, just as it was:
"O Blessed One, many species of Nagas dwell in Pātāla."
Those born from Śeṣa become kings;
those born from Vāsuki become ministers; and those of the lineage of Takṣaka indeed become esteemed royal officials among the Nāgas. (15–16)
I am a Brāhmaṇa of the Svastika lineage, devoted to the service of my gurus;
those Dhṛtarāṣṭras are Kṣatriyas, belonging to the Karkoṭaka lineage, and are engaged in military service;
while those of the Kuhaka lineage are merchants.
Those of the same lineage as Suṣeṇa are cultivators of vegetables and other crops;
they are known as Hāritas, forest-dwellers, and indeed they serve as guardians of the wilderness.
The Kārburakas always perform servitude within the royal circle.
The black-colored *nāgas* become commanders of armies;
likewise, the *puṇḍīka* *nāgas* become gardeners.
The *ambarīṣas* perform the duties of midwives and serve as protectors of vehicles.
Those *godhūmīya* nāgas are wandering minstrels who awaken the lineage;
these wise nāgas of the *bhadra* breed are like learned brahmins, for they recite the sections of the narratives and instruct the children. (21–22)
Those of the *kumuda* class become servants of enjoyments, falling under the power of others;
those of the *piśaṅga* class invariably become attendants performing the work of cooks.
Those of the *keśīya* class are skilled in drama; they are actors who perform dances.
The Āmṛtikas are singers of songs; the Ḍāṇḍikas are esteemed by the elders. The Bhūphālas are gardeners; the Śukas seek out stories.
Those of the Kapardaja class are always the purifiers of the village. (24–25)
Thus there are many others with various names who dwell there;
their great king today is named Kāraṇḍava. His minister, known as Sumadhu, resides in that circle of serpents.
He is honorable, worthy of worship, wise, and possessed of great strength and prowess.
Though he may act unjustly even for his own sake, he indeed conducts himself for the benefit of others;
he is a benefactor of the subjects and one who honors those who seek his protection.
Therefore, the subjects honor him properly, just as they would a king.
There, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the king performs a great festival for the trident-bearing Lord Hāṭakeśvara, worshipping with bilva leaves and other offerings.

And he gives a gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee for the satisfaction of the twice-born. This year, indeed, at the request of that king’s minister, brahmins were invited there for the recitation of the Śatarudrīya.
There were thousands there—reciters and readers alike, as well as worshippers and performers of fire-sacrifices; among them, I was a reciter. I have one hundred sons and likewise twenty daughters.
And by the power of the mantra-grace, they became reciters there.
Young girls, daughters of Brahmins, constantly came and went;
they departed for the sake of worshipping and beholding Hāṭakeśa.
I have twenty daughters who are beautiful and have reached the prime of youth;
they were all born from a single womb and all possess the beauty of Urvaśī.
Adorned with every limb, they were beheld by Sumadhu.
In form, they possess the luster of the campaka flower; their long eyes are like those of Śrī.
Their eyes are tawny, and around their heads there is a halo of radiance. Their bodies are visible from every side, and they are endowed with nails that are jewels of light.
All of them could assume any form at will, possessed slender waists and beautiful hair;
they wore garments of fire, had lovely voices, and were filled with sweetness.
Their bodies were suffused with fragrance, and these pure daughters of the twice-born were sanctified.
Having observed that all [the women] possessed the characteristics of a *padminī*, Sumadhu summoned me and said: "Give me twenty maidens;
they are suitable for me and worthy of a king—grant them to me. (2.28.40)
Having reflected upon this, O Lord, I then said to the excellent minister:
"If my daughters should desire [to go], I will certainly give them; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is desired by their minds must always be done by me."
Then I questioned them all, and their mother was also informed:
"Are you indeed worthy of choosing a husband? Speak, which suitor do you desire?
They replied, "O father, O mother, we have heard [of one] on the earth of men."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all and the Sovereign,
dwells in the house of Śrī Kambharā as a young cowherd boy;
his form and every limb are exceedingly beautiful and captivating.
And we have heard from our friends right here that, in every respect,
you are worthy to choose as a husband the Blessed Lord Śrīpati, Puruṣottama;
and other daughters of the Nāgas as well [have sought] that Supreme Lord.
"By the thousands they desire to make a husband through marriage;
therefore, if you wish for our welfare, we do not wish to choose anyone other than the Lord of Śeṣa, the Lord of Śrī, the Bearer of Śrī. (47)

Thus addressed by the maidens, Svastika and I, their father, then informed the minister of the maidens' intention. Thereupon the chief minister said angrily to me: "The daughters are dependent on their father; they are not independent."
"Give [them] to me; I speak thus because you shall obtain all happiness.
Otherwise, suffering will be yours here, and your entire property will be seized.
Or else, by the method of a Rākṣasa, I shall carry off your daughters."
"Therefore, let the maidens follow me out of humility;
tell them, 'If they do not consent, I shall take them tomorrow on an auspicious day.
Having spoken thus, I later [addressed] those maidens of mine again.
I told them all that, yet they did not believe it.
Then I went to the king and reported it to him.
The king, being partial to their side, declared that gain to be mine.
"Give those maidens to that minister and be happy!
I did not report this to the king, nor was my approval granted; however, having heard everything myself, I have informed the maidens. (54–55)
They spoke with a solemn vow: "We choose the Lord Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the form of a child.
Otherwise, O father, we shall resort to death. (56)
I reported that matter in every way to my circle of kinsmen;
and the kinsmen likewise gave their consent, saying, "So be it.
Hostility toward the king and his people is not the path to prosperity. (57–58)
"Therefore, the maiden must indeed be given to the minister; he will be the destroyer of obstacles.
Then I told all this to my wife, and she said to me:
"She must certainly not be given by you to that leper minister!"
"Whatever may happen, let it be so; he must not be given to a leper, my lord.
I asked, "How was he known by you as a leper, my dear?
My beloved replied, "A maidservant named Karaṇṭikā told me."
She who is a servant and attendant of Sumadhu performs his service—
massaging his feet, bathing him, and applying oil massages and the like.
She constantly attends to the excellent minister and beholds him in private.
In the secret parts of that body, red leprosy resides.
During a conversation about diseases, she described the leprosy of the minister;
therefore, the maiden must certainly not be given to that leprous minister.
Having spoken thus, she ceased, overcome by the sorrow of her impending fate;
I, Svastika, was seized with grief, thinking, "A reversal of fortune is about to occur.
And that hardship, having arrived through destiny, must be endured.
But the divine Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the Supreme Ruler;
may He, from whom this Hāṭakeśa has arisen, protect me.
Having reflected thus and having accepted my sacrificial fee, I indeed— || 66–67 ||
Even though he had gone home, he found no sleep, neither with his wives nor with the maidens.
Then, at dawn, the ministers and soldiers arrived there;
for the minister desired all twenty of the maidens.
"Let them mount the divine chariots for the sake of the wedding, as directed by the minister.
By these words of the king and the speech of the minister, we royal officers say this; otherwise, we would have taken them away by force. (2.28.70)
Since their daughters, fathers, mothers, sons, and humble folk were there,
they wept and once again became intent on fighting.
During that hour, we were all captured by the soldiers in the battle.
The daughters were bound and the sons, having been taken away, were held in prison.
Indeed, in the month of Bhādrapada, I was released along with my wife;
however, those daughters do not wish to be married and remain dwelling in prison.
"O Blessed One, save us! Sent by our wife, we have come here.
O Keśava, uplift those who have lived solely for your sake!
Thus addressed, Bālakṛṣṇa, smiling, granted him fearlessness.
And he called to mind Garuḍa, whose *sudarśana* discus was terrifying.
Both of them arrived instantly, their strides equal to ten million suns;
commanded, they departed, taking Svastika with them. (75–76)
"In Pātāla, where those serpents dwell having established their kingdom, Garuḍa said to the king: 'Let the King of Serpents act with justice;
the minister’s forcible abduction of the maiden is a violation of dharma.'"
"O King, give the daughters of the brahmins to Svastika!
Everything should be accomplished through conciliation, for enmity is indeed endless.
[Let this be done] here on earth by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (78–79)
Sent for this purpose, I, Garuḍa, the devourer of serpents, have arrived here;
the Sudarśana weapon has indeed been given to me by Nārāyaṇa.
If you do not release the maiden, then engage in battle with me.
Thus enlightened, King Kāraṇḍava, blazing with rage,
summoned his minister and became intent on war.
So too did the remaining Vāsukis, Takṣakas, and Kuhakas.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Suṣeṇas, Hāritas, Karburas, and others;
the Kṛṣṇas, Puṇḍarīkas, Ambarīṣas, and Bhadrakas;
as well as the Kumudas, Piśaṅgas, Keśīyas, and Amṛtas.
The Śailūṣas, Kapardas, Bhūphālas, Ḍāṇḍikas, and Śukas— these and others,
at the command of the king, took their armies and arrived for battle, all intent on engaging in combat with weapons, missiles, and arms. (84–85)
Then, perceiving that the bird was small and the discus possessed little power,
Śrī Garuḍa thereupon remembered the Supreme Lord;
he then assumed a vast form that pervaded the ends of the quarters.
Then, with his two wings, he covered all the netherworlds (pātāla) with their feathers;
he filled the sky with his body and the surface of the netherworld with his two feet.
With his beak, claws, and wings, he then brought about destruction.
The king, along with his minister, was quickly seized and devoured by the beak of that bird, which struck down weapons against the elephants who had initiated the battle;
his armies were slaughtered by that sharp-beaked bird.
Likewise, hundreds of thousands were slain by his sharp claws and wings;
others fled to the far shore of the Ocean of Milk. They reported the remainder of that battle to the one known as Ananta.
Śeṣa arrived there and saw Garuḍa in that state; upon beholding Sudarśana, he bowed with supreme devotion. He then warded off the serpents and the warriors, yet when they [still] persisted, ||| 92 ||
The wheel indeed did not turn back; Garuḍa released it in the battle.
Pātāla blazed up, as did all the families of serpents.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and there was a great commotion at that time.
Śeṣa praised that discus and Garuḍa with great devotion. For the sake of Śeṣa’s satisfaction, Garuḍa pacified the discus and even offered the sovereignty of Pātāla to Ananta-Śeṣa.
Having entrusted the position of his minister to Svastika,
Garuḍa then liberated Svastika’s sons and daughters from their bonds.
Śeṣa, Svastika, and Garuḍa then remembered the Lord, the Discus-bearer.
To that primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who exists in the form of a child,
the Blessed Lord Hari then assumed the form of a youth;
mounting the Brahma-elephant, he descended into the netherworld (Pātāla).
Those devotees of Kṛṣṇa indeed offered a welcome;
then Hari performed his consecration into the sovereignty of Pātāla upon the skull of Ananta-Śeṣa. (2.28.99–100)
The minister Svastika also joyfully offered twenty daughters of his own to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
and taking the discus and Garuḍa, the maidens were then seated upon elephants.
Having quickly led [them] to the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake, the glorious Lord arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā by means of yoga; there,
he caused the maidens to bathe in the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara.
He instructed the sage Lomaśa to stay at his hermitage;
likewise, Lomaśa gave the mantras and a garland to them at the hermitage.
Having received the command, Garuḍa protected them and went to Vaikuṇṭha.
The peaceful discus remained in the hand of Hari, and likewise the girls stayed in the hermitage.
O Rādhikā, thus did the Blessed Lord, that treasure-house of divine and noble qualities, perform this miracle at the beginning of His fourth year.
Then, in that netherworld (Pātāla), Śeṣa’s wife Sunandī indeed remembered Bālakṛṣṇa so that he might appear during the month of Kārtika.
Knowing her thought, Śrī Hari went there, assuming the form of a youth.
Having been worshipped by her, he gave her his own mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. He also gave her a garland and a tilaka; she, a devotee, then worshipped Hari.
There were ten thousand daughters of the deceased serpents;
to them Manu gave Sunandinī and bestowed garlands and other gifts.
All of them became the most excellent Vaiṣṇavīs and beloved of Hari.
All those auspicious women arrived on the earth together with Śrī Hari;
indeed, they were presented by Ananta while seated in celestial chariots, accompanied by gifts.
And they were protected by the Supreme Soul in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Blessed are those women, O Rādhā, who have been offered to Kṛṣṇa;
for in them the Supreme Brahman Himself, the bestower of true liberation, shall take delight.
In their case, indeed, everything is to be given; nothing remains that ought not to be surrendered.
And if that which is declared as the goal to be attained is indeed grasped by means of this [work],
what gain in this world could be greater than that? If Hari is pleased with one’s body,
the Lord will become a bestower of bliss through the reading and hearing of this.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation from Suffering for the Naga Svastika of Patala through Garuda, and the Bringing of the Naga Maidens to Lomasha’s Hermitage," occurring during the celebration of the Lord’s commencement of His fourth year in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Listen, O Rādhikā: in the fourth year, during the month of Māgha, the brāhmaṇas, sages, maidens, and others residing there undertook the vow of the Māgha bath in the waters of Aśvasaras. (1)
Beginning at the hour of Brahmā, people bathe in the lake.
Five or six young boys and girls immerse themselves in the water daily;
yet suddenly they are no longer seen by those performing their ablutions while standing in the water.
Even by the people standing on the shore, no cause whatsoever is perceived. People imagine there that there are predatory crocodiles (*makara*) present;
others say that sharks (*grāha*) have gathered here.
But others conjecture thus: "There are Piśācas living here;
surely these murderous Rākṣasas are devouring these children.
What the cause of this may be is not known through direct perception. (5–6)
At that time, there was a cry of distress throughout every direction in the land of Saurāṣṭra:
"The waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake are devouring five or six living beings.
Therefore, one must not perform a ritual bath there, for children are dying because of it.
"Indeed, some person was carrying away the girls in the water of the Aśva-sarovara.

"Tell me the cause of that; what happened to the children? Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhikā, I shall tell you all of it in brief."

In the western region of Āraktadeśa, there was a king named Śāvadīnaka. Because his soul resided within a corpse (śava-deha), he was "corpse-born" (śāva); and because he behaved like one who is wretched (dīna) therein, he lived according to the mode of ignorance; thus he bore the name Śāvadīna. (2.29.10–11)
He had a hundred wives, yet no son was born;
indeed, he had a thousand daughters, but not even one son.
Thereupon the king, overcome with grief, questioned his own preceptor, the ascetic.
"How may a son be born? Tell me the cause for this.
To him, his teacher, who was very distressed, replied after reflecting for a moment:
"A son is born through the bond of debt and out of a desire for [discharging] that debt."
If death occurs for someone in this world while their debt remains unpaid,
then due to the bondage of karma, a son is born in his house as a bull, a horse, a camel, a goat, or even a donkey.
Or if the creditor should become a son in the house of the debtor, he goes to his death free from debt after taking back the wealth previously given.
O King, you do not sit as anyone's debtor; indeed, you have never been so before.
Therefore, you had no creditor who lent you wealth;
you have no such debt, so what son could possibly exist for you here?
Freedom from debt is in every way superior, desired, and bestows liberation.
Nevertheless, if you have a desire for a son, perform worship.
When the great goddess Śāvarī Mahākālī is worshipped with the offering of a sacrificial victim,
she will grant you a son who is a sovereign ruler and long-lived.
By offering a sacrifice (bali) to Śāvadīnā Mahākālī, one obtains a child; therein, the sacrifice is declared to be most excellent.
If the child is under five years of age and possesses auspicious characteristics, [the rite is performed].
"If it were given to a woman who has recently given birth, then she too would burn her son.
The king said, "How so? Of what characteristics must the boy be endowed when he is offered? Tell me those characteristics by which my son shall become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth."
The ascetic Yati-dīna said: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you that.
He in whose hand there is the line of a fish, or one endowed with a bow, a string, and arrows;
or who has a banner, a trident, a svastika, a wheel, or even a barley grain—[he is a king]. (24)
He whose feet have three lines or the design of a palace;
he who has a single line on his forehead or a dark mole on his throat;
and whose form has the luster of a campaka flower with eyes that extend like petals—[such a one is a king]. (25–26)
That doll which shines in the form of lines upon the buttocks,
or that white lotus which may be on the left thigh—
that child indeed should be offered as a sacrificial oblation (bali) to Mahākālī according to the prescribed ritual.
"Because of that, you shall have a son who will be a great king, a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Having heard this from the ascetic Dīna,
King Śāvadīna then employed perfected ones (siddhas) for the purpose of searching for such a boy.
Siddhas and ascetics who travel through the sky, who examine the lines on the hands,
and who wear blue garments, wandered upon the earth for the sake of obtaining children;
they behold the lines of children as well as the luminaries, planets, and so forth.
At that time, O beloved, ascetics were wandering through all the regions.
Among them, one named Kāsadīna then went to Saurāṣṭra;
he arrived at the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and reached the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then he heard from Lomaśa that the child bearing the aforementioned characteristics was named Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Kambharā;

He traveled swiftly through the sky toward the region of Ārakta to reach the king.
He said: "In the region of Saurāṣṭra, there exists a boy in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; he is the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa. (34–35)
Then, having heard what he desired, the king gave five villages to the ascetic;
and furthermore, he dispatched five ascetics who were experts in the art of *indrajāla* (magical illusions) to Saurāṣṭra and to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
In that auspicious water where people devoted to the ritual bath in the month of Māgha bathe,
those ascetics were constantly moving along the bank, beyond the range of sight, intent on making an effort to seize that child. (37–38)
They constantly submerge five or six children within the water and swiftly lead them to the execution ground in the presence of the king.
The king's servants, who provide comfort, protect those children while they are still alive.
Thus do the ascetics pass their days and nights on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa.
Indeed, those ignorant men seize children for the sake of obtaining one marked with lines;
being themselves unacquainted with the lines, they carry off many boys.
The ascetic, however, gazes at the lines;
yet that line is not seen at all, and he does not let go of it.
The children there are being carried away, and indeed a cry of "Alas! Alas! arises.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was bathing inside the house. He did not come into the hands of the ascetics and heard of the destruction of the boy.
Then that Blessed Lord, together with his mother, forcibly [departed] from the house.
Having departed, he went to bathe in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
While his mother was bathing on the bank and the boy remained nearby, an ascetic,
desiring to seize him, arrived there swiftly and invisibly.
Having assumed the form of a water-man, he seized the boy;
possessing two forms, the boy came into his hands,
while with his second natural form, he remained playing in the presence of his mother.
"Māṃ! Māṃ! O Mother, look! O Mother, look at this formidable water-demon, who is repeatedly looking at me while taking up another boy;

Look, look! That long-bodied one, together with the boy, is entering the water—measuring three *tālas* in height, moon-like in luster, with a head of tawny hair, and his eyes shining like those of a lion, with tawny pupils. (2.29.50)
All the fingers of both arms are as long as ropes;

His face is like that of a monkey, endowed with a red beard.
On its side, four formidable fangs are seen like blades of grass;
and above its skull, there is a horn shaped like a goad. There are two tails upon its shoulders, and two tails at its hips.
He possesses four cords that are exceedingly long;
he has chronic diseases in his heart and on his back,
and there are webbed membranes between the toes and fingers of his hands and feet.
And at his navel there is a moth-like creature that shines like a lamp;
it possesses webbed feet and long fingers,
and within its belly there is a stomach-cavity resembling a child’s hut.
He makes his feet into hands and his hands into feet;
he is breastless and earless, covered in fiery hair, and terrifying.
Uttering the sounds "ciṃciṃ-huk" and "ciṃciṃ," he has gone beneath the surface of the water.

"O best of sages, what must be done to destroy this water-demon?

The Asuras, the Kārmaṇakas, the violent, and the merciless— Kṛṣṇa himself will bring about their destruction.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa knows their nature.

"Since the manifestation of Śrī Hari was for the purpose of destroying the Asuras, He Himself will act as the remedy for the Rākṣasas. Having spoken thus, Lomaśa then remembered Bālakṛṣṇa. (2.29.70–71)
The Lord Hari, assuming the form of a youth, arrived laughing, mounted upon Garuḍa and holding his discus; he spoke to Lomaśa and the others:
"Tell me quickly, how have I been remembered?"
Then Lomaśa and the others, having bowed, spoke of the calamity involving Bāla and the rest;
having heard everything regarding the presence of Rākṣasas in the lake in the form of water-men, Hari spoke to the one bearing the fish, the trident, and the bow.
Standing in the water, they search for the boy who bears the banner;
they strive on my behalf in the worship of the corpse, the wretched woman, and the arrow, fish, trident, and bow.
The boy must be surrendered along with the fish, the trident, and the bow-banner.
By means of this sacrificial offering, the king shall indeed obtain such a son.
It was for this very reason that I did not come into their hands;
therefore, they employ children in the act of seizing [the victim], and I shall instruct them.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, appearing as a child, went to the shore of Lake Aśvasaras;
at that moment, O Rādhikā, while thousands of worlds were looking on, he seized Kṛṣṇa, having assumed the form of a water-man.
Then a great cry of "Alas! arose from everyone there on the shore of the lake.
Hari, assuming a divine form, entered the water with his discus;
he was seized by the asura and fought with him within the depths of the water.
With his discus, the Blessed One severed his four cord-bindings,
as well as his head, horns, hands, feet,
and forearms; then Kṛṣṇa, equal in height to three palm trees, bound him with ropes.
And he brought forth from the water, still alive,
that white water-man who was three palm-trees in height.
Upon seeing him, the people were struck with great wonder and fell into a state of amazement.
Then four other ascetics who were staying there in the water also emerged outside in the forms of water-men;
they entreated him most earnestly for the sake of saving their lives.
"The children have not been killed at all; they are all alive," they said.
"We shall certainly bring them here; however, grant us the gift of life.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, [responded]. (85–86)
The Lord granted them the gift of life and spoke to them again:
"Come with me through the sky upon Garuḍa to where these children are, who have indeed been protected and restored to life."
Then those Mlecchas, who were water-beings, having heard the words of Kṛṣṇa,
traveled through the sky taking Hari to a region that was glowing and intensely red—
a realm of red color, red waters, and a circle of red men.
Where everything is generally reddish-brown, including the ground-cover;
where the great king is as wretched as a corpse, and likewise the teacher is as wretched as a mendicant;
and where Mahākālī is as wretched as a corpse—there he dwells in the abode of the protector of the earth.
There, those ascetics departed, having been well-honored by the king.
There, fifty happy and untroubled boys were shown;
indeed, the king and the others beheld the beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having learned of the supreme and auspicious wonder from the perfected ones (siddhas),
the wives and daughters of kings massaged Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person,
with northern oils as well as fragrant powders. (93)
Then they thoroughly bathed him with tepid waters.
Beholding him, whose limbs were proportionate to his form, bearing a fish, a trident, and a bow, and holding a hand with a banner, they were both bewildered and filled with joy.
"Aha! This man is worthy of the sacrificial offering; by good fortune he has arrived here.
Thus did the women quickly inform the king.
The king, having reflected, immediately dispatched his soldiers and generals.
Indeed, laughing, he gave the order to imprison him in a jail.
Those maidens, charmed by his beauty, did not wish for the death of Hari;
rather, the queens, desiring a son, wished for Hari as a sacrificial offering there.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa, assuming the form of a child, was seized by the soldiers;
musical instruments were sounded, and the king considered his purpose fulfilled.
Then Sudarśana and Garuḍa became children with beautiful faces.
And the two protectors, having gathered together among the children, bestowed courage upon them.
Then Kṛṣṇa was placed in prison by the soldiers while bound in chains;
at that time, the thousands of maidens fell into a state of swoon.
Śāvadīnā and Mahākālī joyfully undertook a vow, saying:
"If this boy is released and becomes our husband, then we shall observe for one month the vow of subsisting solely on milk. || 102 ||
We shall perform the worship of Śāvadīnā day and night.
From this day forward, sweet honey, *śṛṅgāraka*, and other such offerings are abandoned;
we shall instead offer five garlands to the goddess Śāvadīnādevikā. 103–104.
Thus they accepted that rule as a protector for the children.
Then, while the subjects, the king, the soldiers, and others were fast asleep at night,
Śrī Hari, who displays the world’s play, lay down in his prison.
In his second form, the Lord dwells in his own abode;
Hari, who brings joy to all, resides in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and relates news from the region of Ārakta to the venerable sage Lomaśa.
Everyone heard [the sound] and marveled at it as something originating from a distant land.
Thus the night passed and dawn broke.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s Journey There for the Sake of Releasing the Bound Children Intended as Sacrificial Offerings to the Goddess Śāvadīnākālī by the King of Āraktadeśa for the Purpose of Obtaining a Son, and the Infatuation of the Thousand Maidens with Lord Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

He caused all of them to drink the nectar of Śrī Hari’s feet;
then, after having the worship of Nara-Nārāyaṇa performed,
Hari went to Kurukṣetra, which is ten krośas in extent.
"It is supremely purifying and most excellent, situated at the foot of the Himalayas.
Śrī Rādhikā said: "When and by whom was Kurukṣetra created? Tell me that in detail."
"How indeed is that place considered always to be a praiseworthy purifier?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"There was a king of great strength named Ṛkṣa, born of the Lunar dynasty."
At the beginning of the Kṛta age, Saṃvaraṇa was born from Ṛkṣa.
He was consecrated by his father in his own kingdom while still a child;
even in his youth, he was devoted to dharma and was always a devotee of me.
His priest was Vasiṣṭha, the son of Varuṇa;
that noble-minded sage taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs.
On days when study was forbidden, the king would go to the forests to observe them.
He entered the vast, delightful, and beautiful Vaibhrāja forest;
he then entered Dvaitavana, where the two Rudras had gone.
Thereupon, he beheld the edge of the forest covered with blossoming red lotuses.
There he saw the daughters of the gods,
and among them he beheld Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun, who surpassed all others in beauty.
With his mind fixed upon her, the powerful king proceeded toward Mount Meru.

The beautiful city of Pratiṣṭhāna remained standing, indeed, as he dwelt there remembering her. When he had not yet returned home, the family priest learned that he was staying on Mount Meru, his mind fixed entirely upon Tapatī.
Vasiṣṭha, having ascended, proceeded toward the solar orb;
Sūrya bowed to him, and he in turn honored him.
The sage asked the reason for his arrival, and Sūrya spoke to him.
"I have come, O Lord of Gods, O you of great splendor, to entreat you:
you ought to give Tāpī to Saṃvaraṇa as his daughter.
Having been thus asked by Sūrya, [Indra] gave Tāpī, and he rejoiced.
The sage returned after having taken the kingdom, and Samvaraṇa also arrived.
Upon seeing him, Tāpī desired him; she was bestowed upon him by the great sage.
In due time, a son was born to her, who was indeed named Kuru.
At sixteen years of age, he married the daughter of King Sudāman.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to one named Kīrti, the king entered the forest.
Together with his wife, the daughter of Sudāman, the monarch practiced austerities in the Dvaitavana forest.
There he beheld the goddess Sarasvatī, whose tongue is like a lion’s;
the mother of Sudarśana, the daughter of Brahmā, born from the Plakṣa tree.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, he approached the Brahmavedī altar.
That northern [site] is called the Brahma-altar, the sacrificial ground.
The middle Brahma-altar is said to be Prayāgarāja.
The eastern altar-ground is Gayā-vedi, while Virajā is indeed the southern one.
The western lotus is the sacrificial altar (vedī), adorned with three pits (kuṇḍa);
the Dharmasthāna at Syamantapañcaka is the northern altar (uttaravedikā).
It extends five yojanas on all sides, reaching five yojanas in every direction.
The royal sage considered that field to be holy and of great fruit.
Having created a lake and constructed a leaf-hut, he took up residence there.
He fashioned a plow with the bull of Rudra and likewise the buffalo of Yama.
Having arranged for a plowman, he himself prepared to plow;
as he was plowing, Mahendra arrived and asked him the reason:
"O King, why are you intent on performing this agricultural labor here?"

The king said: "Austerity, truthfulness, purity, charity, compassion, forbearance, yoga, and virtuous conduct—this is the eightfold set found here. Indra replied: "O King, may your desire be fulfilled accordingly."
When Indra had departed, that king plowed incessantly;
he made the land more than seven *krośas* in extent furrowed by the plow.
Then, O Rādhikā, having become a Brahmin, I went into the presence of the king.
And I asked, "O King, how indeed is suffering endured?
Then the great eightfold dharma was fully explained to me by the king. Thereupon, O King, I said to him, "Where does the seed of this [suffering] reside? (2.30.90)
He said, "Indeed, within my body here lies the seed of my mind.
I said to him, "Extract that seed from your body and give it to me;
I shall surely sow it in a garden, and you yourself must plow with a plow. (9.1)
Then the king extended his right arm;
it was severed by me with the discus and there it became a thousandfold.
In the same way, his left arm and both feet were cut into two pieces from the waist.
Those seeds grew up in abundance on all sides, numbering more than ten million.
Then he gave me his head, and I was pleased with him.
When he said, "I am a granter of boons," I then requested a boon from him.
"Let this field of Dharma, which has been cultivated by me, belong to you.
For those who bathe here and for those who die here, there shall be the fruit of great merit;
likewise, fasting, giving, bathing, recitation, and worship [shall yield great results]."
O Lord, may all acts such as the *homa* sacrifice become inexhaustible here;
likewise, O Lotus-eyed One, may you dwell here together with the gods, Brahmā, and Śambhu,
in this place which truly manifests my name.
When he had spoken thus, I then said "So be it" to him:
"And so may you once again possess a divine body and be well;
at the end of this long time, you shall attain dissolution into my own form."
"By my grace, your fame shall be eternal;
here you shall perform thousands of sacrifices as the officiating priest.
[I shall also grant] the guardians of the field: the yakṣa Candra and the serpent Vāsuki."
I give to you here eight thousand powerful archers: the Vidyādhara Śaṅkukarṇa, the Rākṣasa Sukeśa, King Ajāvana, and Mahādeva Pāvaka.
In the midst of Kurujāṅgala is the great lake Pṛthūdaka,
and there also flows the auspicious and purifying river Sarasvatī.
Between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī lies Kurujāṅgala.
The auspicious Brahmasaras is a sacred ford (tīrtha) extending half a yojana on all sides.
This was originally the altar of Brahmā; from that place, the Rāmahrada is remembered [to have arisen].
Beyond that, Kurukṣetra is proclaimed—the purifying field of Dharma.
That which lies between Tarantuka and Ārantuka,
and that which indeed lies between the five lakes of Rāma—
that is the vast Kurukṣetra, known as Samantapañcaka.
Then, O Rādhikā, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived through the sky;
having bathed the women at the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, and the Brahma-lake, he traveled by vehicle in a mere moment. || 107–108 ||
He went to the Lomaśa hermitage in the region of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Then the boys, the girls, the women, the Goddess, Garuḍa, and Hari descended to the earth there, and shouts of "Victory! arose.
Musical instruments were sounded, and the conch of the Goddess was also blown.
Lomaśa and the other sages arrived swiftly, as did the subjects;
the brahmins and others, having addressed one another with auspicious greetings, performed the rites of benediction.
Having bathed in the lake and partaken of all kinds of foods, they,
weary from the fatigue of their journey, created a garden.
A festival of victory was celebrated at night, and the destruction of the king was proclaimed.
Then Hari entrusted the boys to their own fathers;
all the girls and women were presented to Lomaśa for the purpose of protecting the hermitage and for the imparting of sacred mantras.
And Lomaśa gave them purifying mantras and garlands:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā.
By the spiritual splendor of Brahman, those women became divine in form and devoted to Viṣṇu.
By the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, those mothers performed worship;
with divine bodies and celestial chariots, they went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
By the will of Śrī Hari, those maidens remained there forever.
Thus were the children protected and the barbarians likewise destroyed.
From reading and hearing this, the fruits of heaven and liberation shall accrue.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Performance of the Animal-Sacrifice Ritual for the Goddess by the King, the Destruction of the King and Others by the Goddess, the Return to Badarī, Kurukṣetra, and Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Restoration of the Children to their Fathers, and the Liberation of the Mothers," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Rādhikā; the goddess Śāvadīnā is indeed Kālikā.
She dwelt on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, having taken refuge under a divine banyan tree.
The beloved eighteen-armed goddess, the consort of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is mounted upon a lion, indeed provides protection for the sacred field;
she of divine form always protects young maidens.
It is visibly seen by the people through the will of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
That holy place, the Kālikā-tīrtha, is situated at Aśvasaras;
it is indeed on the western side of that bridge, in the vicinity of the constructed temple.
Upon the completion of the Māgha bath, the subjects, the brāhmaṇas, and the maidens worshipped the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa most intensely.
A great festival took place, for it was divine and indeed bestows liberation.
Then that news spread everywhere with the speed of the wind.
(6) People came from afar to see the water-man;
seeing this great marvel again and again, they marveled at the power of Śrī Hari. (7)
Then, sprinkled with water by Hari,
that man of the waters attained a divine form, with hands, feet, and all his limbs restored.
He praised Śrī Hari and requested eternal service at His feet.
Śrī Hari appointed him as the guardian of the sacred field (kṣetrapāla) right there at the lake.
He said to him: "Your lineage shall spread everywhere from Mānasa; it will become a creation of water-demons (jalamānuṣa). (2.31.10)
Then he cast his inert body into the midst of the water;
from that, a hundred divine male and female water-beings (Jalanaras and Jalaris) came into existence.
Then the people would behold Mahākālī and proceed [to worship her].
They proclaim the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord; and many attain liberation through the power of the Lord of Śrī, the Master.

Since Hari, the beloved Lord, had arrived there at that hermitage, those maidens observed the vow of consuming only milk; for they had previously honored it for His sake. O Rādhikā, at that time, cows that yielded all desires were provided for the fulfillment of their vow.
The maidens constantly offer milk and observe their vows;
in the early morning, they bathe Śrī Hari with pure milk,
and afterwards, having bathed the Lord with water, they honor Him with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
They adorn the Lord’s body with emotion, perfume it with excellent unguents, massage it, and delight him with beautiful songs;
they cause him to laugh with great sweetness and please him with exquisite dances.
They gladden them with pleasant touches and satisfy them with excellent food;
they praise and exalt them with lustrations (*nīrājana*) and requests for forgiveness (*kṣamāpana*).
Thus, those who observe the vow of Kṛṣṇa drink only milk. (18–19)
Having observed the vow for a full month, they offered it unto Kṛṣṇa.
Having performed the festival of charity, the fire-oblation, and the concluding rite (udyāpana), they attained completion.
They remained right there and worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
[She meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Master of her life.
Śrī Rādhikā said: "How is it that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman [yet married] the daughters of barbarians and rākṣasas?"
The purifying Lord accepted her, who had arisen from a state of low birth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you my divine story."
In the past, I was manifested as a partial incarnation (svāṃśa) by the Supreme Brahman;
at that time, Rādhā was made his wife as a partial incarnation of her. That she obstructs my majesty is indeed not surprising here, for such is the nature of those possessed of splendor.
By the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa was made four-armed;
and Lakṣmī, arisen from the Supreme Brahman, was made his beloved by him. That nobility does not cause any obstruction in the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa.
Brahmā married Sāvitrī, who was born of his own lineage.
Gāyatrī, born of his lineage, was made his beloved daughter by Brahmā;
likewise, Sarasvatī was honored as his daughter and accepted as his wife. (26–27)
The daughters born of Dakṣa to the grandson of Brahmā were all of noble birth,
and they were married to the sons and grandsons of Brahmā.
In former times, Kaśyapa made those born of animal species his own beloved wives.
Danu and Diti—these two Rākṣasīs were the wives of Kaśyapa.
Arundhatī and Śvapacī were married to Vasiṣṭha.
Kālī, Bhairavī, and Durgā are the Tāmasī consorts beloved by Śaṅkara.
Vṛndā and Tulasī were the two wives of the Daitya, wedded by Viṣṇu.
The Mlecchas were born from the hair of the cow; they are remembered as the lineages of cows.
The Lord, being all-powerful, purifies everyone at that very moment.
In his presence, there is no state of birth, nor highness, nor lowness.
For the Blessed One is to be realized through being; when he is cultivated, he in turn causes [others] to cultivate [him].
He is everything in all things, and he alone is of that very nature.
The enjoyer of all, the creator of all, the lord of all, and the sovereign of lords— by his command, Brahmā formerly created pairs;
those pairs were in the form of brothers and sisters, and they numbered a thousand.
Consequently, creation indeed occurs during the Kṛta Yuga; there is no fault in this.
At that time, there was no custom of giving daughters to others.
Then, for the sake of ensuring the continuity of the lineage for those who were without daughters—
A rule was established that the gift of a daughter must be given to another;
furthermore, there was a subsequent rule that she must be given to one belonging to a different lineage.
There was also a rule that she must be given to one who is not a sapinda and belongs to the same caste.
In this way, indeed, all obtain a daughter who perpetuates their lineage.

Other duties were established in the primordial creation, and others at the very beginning of the world; other righteous laws prevailed in the first Kṛta age, while different ones existed at the start of the Tretā age.

In the Kali age, O beloved, those who were considered unrighteous at that time became righteous; yet all those who follow the dharma in the Kali age are not regarded as such by virtue of their inherent nature.
Due to the differentiation of energy (*tejas*), distinct dharmas prevail in each successive age.

Therefore, there is no fault in Kṛṣṇa; that action is indeed dharma. That supreme tradition established by him always governs the entire world, yet that tradition is never able to govern Kṛṣṇa himself.
The ritual action of Kṛṣṇa exists as the great mother of the sacred tradition (āmnāya).
Therefore, all the rituals of Kṛṣṇa have the nature of the self and the sacred tradition.
Therein, there is no desire, no anger, no sexual intercourse, and indeed no violence.
Neither that theft nor that confusion which is performed by Kṛṣṇa is truly theft or confusion;
for divine desire as well as divine anger, divine sexual union, and even divine violence, theft, and confusion— whatever is performed by Kṛṣṇa is eternally divine.
Rādhā is divine, Rati is divine, and the enjoyment of her splendor is divine;
everything there is divine, consisting of the Supreme Brahman, and thus there is no defect.
Where there is a mass of light, darkness is not found there.
Darkness is said to be a defect, but it cannot exist among those who possess light.
Defects are perceived by those dominated by darkness through their limited vision;
however, through the vision of Brahman, those very same things indeed become ornaments.
Whatever affection one has for a wife, a son, a daughter, or one's parents— the same affection, when directed toward the virtuous, bestows liberation, being itself free from worldly qualities.
In the presence of the virtuous and the holy women, faults are reduced to ashes through the power of yoga.
Indeed, through union with Hari, the virtuous become divine and saintly.
O Rādhā, just as your sons, though born from the salt ocean, have in every way become purifying, like sacred fords, and truly possess divine forms. (2.31.50–51)
Just as the *liṅga*— which is rooted in desire and characterized by defects— is indeed worshipped among the worlds through the yoga of Śaṅkara like Brahmā himself;
so too stones and other materials, when they take the form of an image, are worshipped through their union with Brahman.
O Rādhā, all of that must be honored by you on my account.
O beloved, through union with Kṛṣṇa, even barbarism attains purity;
indeed, through union with Brahman, the *bhaga* is seen within the sacrificial fire-pit.
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, an image of Aśvaliṅga is given into the hand of the wife.
O beloved, in every case, purity is established through union with Brahman.
Therefore, no doubt should be entertained as to how the daughters of Mlecchas can be dear [to you].
Whatever is dear to Śrī Hari is indeed pure; of this there is no doubt.
Now, however, I shall proclaim this principle of dharma; learn it from me, which was perceived in former times by the high-souled sages who were knowers of dharma.
O fair-faced one, it is said that in former times women were unconfined;
O lady of lovely smiles, they moved about according to their own will and were independent.
O fortunate one, as they transgressed against their husbands from the time of their youth—
"O lady of beautiful hips, there was no unrighteousness; for that indeed was the law in ancient times.
Even the creatures born of animal wombs always conform to that very ancient law, following the dictates of their seasonal nature."
This dharma, established by authoritative means of knowledge, is honored by the great seers;
it prevails in the northern regions and among the Kurus as well.
Among the mountain-dwelling peoples, this dharma permits polyandry.
That very same dharma exists even among goddesses in heaven and other realms;
that very same dharma exists everywhere, even among female slaves.
Indeed, that eternal dharma is attained through favor toward women.
Now, listen also to that boundary established out of anger by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, on one occasion.
It is said that formerly, in the presence of Śvetaketu’s father, [he spoke] to his mother...
The Brahmin took her by the hand and said, "Let us go.
Then the son of the seer, incited by indignation, became filled with anger upon seeing his mother being led away by force in front of his father. (65–66)
Seeing his son enraged, the father said to Śvetaketu:
"Do not give way to anger, my son; this is the eternal dharma.
For on this earth, women of all social classes (varṇas) are indeed unrestrained."
Just as cows remain under their respective owners, so too do women;
yet Śvetaketu could not at all tolerate that practice,
and he established this boundary between men and women on earth.
Listen, O beloved Rādhikā: from this day forward, among humans alone and not among others,
the sin of a woman who transgresses against her husband shall be as terrible as the murder of a fetus, bringing only misery.
Likewise, for one who commits adultery with a wife who has observed lifelong chastity from her youth,
this very same sin shall exist on earth; and so too for a wife who,
being appointed by her husband, is engaged solely for the sake of obtaining a son.
And he shall not do so; for that very thing shall indeed come to pass.
A righteous boundary was established by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka;
therefore, that dharma remains firmly settled.
Furthermore, during every fertile season, a husband must certainly not be bypassed by his wife.
In other remaining times, a woman is indeed entitled to independence; for instance, Saudāsa was commissioned by his own wife regarding the procreation of a son. (74–75)
Madayantī went to her own preceptor, the sage Vasiṣṭha;
from him she obtained a son renowned by the name Aśmaka.
Now, in former times, there was a wise sage known as Utathya.
He had a wife named Mamatā, who was highly esteemed by him.
Now, Bṛhaspati, the younger brother of Utathya and the priest of the gods, possessed of great splendor, pursued Mamatā.
Mamatā said to her husband’s brother, the best among speakers:
"O brother-in-law, I am pregnant by your brother; therefore, O brother-in-law, since you are one whose seed is never in vain, there can be no conception from two fathers for one womb."
Even though addressed thus, he was not able to restrain his passion. He then took delight with her, even while emitting his seed.
Then the son of Utathya, staying within the womb, spoke to him: "There is no possibility of this [birth] here."
"There is no room for two; you ought not to cause me pain.
But even before hearing those words of the one dwelling in the womb, Bṛhaspati nonetheless discharged his semen.
That semen became a child within the womb.
Struck by his feet, he fell to the earth; thereupon the enraged Bṛhaspati cursed the embryo:
"O fool, you shall enter into long-lasting darkness.
He was indeed born as the seer Dīrghatamas, blind from birth.
But the wise man thereafter obtained a wife named Pradveṣī;
he begot sons such as Gautama and others who were ascetics.
Dīrghatamas, like a bull, engaged in sexual intercourse in public.
In the presence of people, he acted in such a way as to destroy the boundaries of propriety.
The sages then shunned him, for he had indeed transgressed those boundaries. He, being full of hatred, did not serve him; therefore, the sage spoke to her.
"O wife, tell me why you do not serve me at all; state the reason.
The wife spoke to her husband with resentment:
"A husband is so called because he supports (bharana), and also because he protects (palana); yet neither of these two qualities exists in you."
On the contrary, I, along with my son, shall become a sharer in your miseries during our maintenance;
moreover, being incapable [of providing for you], I shall take another husband.
Do as you wish, O best of Brahmins; I am going elsewhere.
Dīrghatamas said:
From this day forward, I shall establish this law in the world:
for a woman, there is but one husband who is her sole refuge as long as she lives. (9.1)
Whether her husband be dead or alive, she shall not obtain another man;
should she obtain another, she would become an outcaste—thus it is ordained.
Having heard this, she spoke with anger to her sons regarding their father.
"Let us cast this blind man, who speaks such unpleasant words, into the boat!
Having bound their father, the sons set him adrift in the boat upon the Ganges; and he floated along with the current, carried away by the flow. (93–94)
When the boat, having fallen into the current, reached a distant land,
King Bali saw the blind man alone on board, who was engaged in the chanting of the name of Śrī Śiva;
he seized him and took him away.
Knowing him to be a householder, the king, desiring a son, appointed the sage to his wife. That queen, Sudeṣṇā, did not accept the sage;
instead, she then sent her own nurse’s daughter to that old man.
In her, the sage fathered eleven sons, Kākṣīvat and the others; thereafter, Sudeṣṇā took a liking to him.
Then five princes were born to Sudeṣṇā as his sons.
Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Puṇḍra, and Suhma were his sons;
their respective lands shall be known by those very names.
Thus was the lineage of Bali formerly proclaimed by the great seer.
Parāśara united with Matsyagandhā, the daughter of a fisherman;
such was the dharma of former times—what need is there to speak of Nārāyaṇa?
Everything is to be enjoyed by Nārāyaṇa, and everything is the very body of Nārāyaṇa.
Everything is the form of Nārāyaṇa’s wife, and the husband is Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhā, do not entertain any doubt regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he who bestows offspring within Māyā bestows offspring even within that which is composed of Māyā.
He alone is the Supreme Lord—the creator, the protector, and the destroyer.
Indeed, he may always accept all maidens, for that is ever appropriate for him.
By reading or hearing this, one attains the ancient truth of Dharma.
"By this it shall be known, and doubt shall dissolve; one shall become a partaker of merit.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Milk-Vow of Maidens, the Boundary Established by Śvetaketu Regarding the Principles of Ancient Dharma, Aśmaka Born of Vasiṣṭha’s Son upon the Wife of Saudāsa, Utathya’s Wife Touched by Bṛhaspati, Dīrghatamas Begetting Sons upon the Slave-girl and Queen of Bali, and the Subsequent Establishment of Boundaries," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
