Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa himself performed the worship of the planets and other deities when obstacles arose during the month of Māgha.
In the month of Phālguna, he caused the Viṣṇuyāga to be performed by the Brahmins for the purpose of pacifying obstacles within the sacred field (kṣetra) and also for the propitiation of the planets,
so that the welfare and security of the children residing in Saurāṣṭra might be auspicious.
And just as he had given countless gifts at that time,
so too did his father perform worship for the various deities;
likewise, he caused worship to be offered to his mother and others, and had the most excellent sacrificial offerings presented.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, who are those planetary spirits and child-seizing spirits that afflict children here? What is the form of these spirits? Tell me this. (5)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, Skanda became the son of Rudra, born from his seed,
as well as from Pārvatī, Vahni, Gaṅgā, and Darbhaka.
At that time, the infant Skanda became the husband of the six wives of the sages;
he was born as the commander-in-chief of the gods (Devasenāpati), and thereafter Lakṣmī took refuge in him.
Endowed with Śrī, Skanda [was worshipped] on the fifth day; therefore, it is remembered as Śrīpañcamī.
Because he attained his purpose on the sixth lunar day, therefore the sixth is a great tithi.
Then the six goddesses, the wives of the seven seers, approached Mahāsena, the commander-in-chief of the divine army, who was endowed with splendor and had been appointed to that office.
Abandoned by the sages, they spoke to their son Kārtika:
"O son, we have been abandoned by our husbands for a trivial reason.
Indeed, it was declared according to the Vedic tradition that you were born from us."

We have been freed from that fault; therefore, you ought to save us. Having fallen from our station in heaven and being censured by the sages, make it so that our heaven becomes imperishable through your grace.
"We desire you as our son; having done this, become free from debt.
At that time, the high-minded Mahendra spoke to Skanda:
"A sister named Abhijit has gone to the forest to perform austerities."
"That younger sister of Rohiṇī desires the status of the eldest through her ascetic penance.
That place remains vacant; O Skanda, fill that spot.
Indeed, complete the number of lunar mansions with Kṛttikā."
Skanda appointed those six mothers in the form of the Kṛttikās;
thus that constellation named Kṛttikā indeed shines with Agni as its presiding deity.
But how is it that there are six Kṛttikās there, while [the constellation] is considered to have seven heads?
If you wish to hear the reason for this, I shall tell it to you.
Vinatā spoke to Skanda, "Include me there as well," and Skanda then granted her that auspicious seventh station.
Thus, that constellation Kṛttikā is considered to have seven heads.
Then those Kṛttikās spoke again to Skanda as they desired:
"We are Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Nārāyaṇī."
Gāyatrī, Durgikā, Māyā, and these who are the seven Mothers—
those who were fashioned for the world from time immemorial—
let our abode be there, but let it not be theirs. (2.32.20–21)
"O Kārtika, may we become worthy of worship by the world; for they are not the ones to be worshipped, since it was by them that our separation from the sages was brought about.
We desire these mothers whose offspring are the ancestral deities."
"May they always be the providers of our enjoyments, like the Ṛṣis.
Skanda said, "Let them indeed become the wives of Candra as you have given them;
and may you always protect our others as well, as if they were your own sons. (23–24)
Then the Kṛttikās said: "O son, we shall do so;
however, these offspring will be youths sixteen years of age.
Grant us the right to consume [the offerings] through various forms of mortal progeny. (25)
Skanda said: "Let it be so; may you all be endowed with happiness.
I, however, shall grant you my own imperishable and fierce self.
United with that supreme [self], dwell indeed in bliss in heaven."
Having spoken thus, Kārtika produced from his body a personage with the brilliance of fire in the form of a planet, and gave him to them for the sake of attaining happiness.
Taking that one of fierce form, they went to the lunar realm.
Those who know the truth call Skandāpasmāra a seizing spirit (graha).
Vinatā, however, is said to be the most terrible; she is called the Śakuni-graha.
They speak of Pūtanā as a Rākṣasī; one should know her as the Pūtanā-graha.
The night-stalker of terrible form and painful aspect is called the Piśācī Śītapūtanā, who is of a cruel appearance; she,
of fearsome look, carries off the fetuses of human women.
They call Aditi Revatī; her graha is Raivata.
That most terrible great graha indeed afflicts children.
They call Diti, the mother of the Daityas, Mukhamandikā. (32–33)
Exceedingly delighted by the flesh of porpoises and difficult to approach,
all those male and female children born from Skanda—
those great grahas who consume fetuses and perform cruel deeds— are [present].
The women of the Kumāras, the maidens, and those men who perform terrible deeds seize the newborn infants. Furthermore, there is Surabhi, the mother of cows, who resides in the abode of the gods.
Then, having mounted that bird, he eats the children on the ground together with her.
O Rādhikā, she who is the goddess Saramā, the mother of dogs,
also constantly takes up the fetuses of human women.
Now, she who is the mother of trees, known as the Dwellress-in-the-Karañja, is alone the bestower of boons, the protector, and compassionate toward all beings;
men seeking sons worship her in the Karañja tree. (38–39)
Moreover, other mothers and grahas who are fond of meat and honey constantly dwell in the lying-in chamber by day and by night. Then Kadrū, assuming a subtle form, enters the pregnant woman.
There she consumes that embryo and gives birth to one equal to a *nāga*.
And the mother of the *gandharvas*, having taken the embryo, departs;
therefore, a human woman is seen by people with her pregnancy dissolved.
The mother of the Apsarases, however, remains holding her embryo;
when such a thing occurs, people say, "The embryo has perished.
And she who is the daughter of the Ocean of Blood is known as the nurse of Skanda.
She, known by the name Lohitāyanī, is worshipped by people at the Kadamba tree.
As Rudra is among men, so is Āryā among women;
Āryā, the mother of Kumāra, is worshipped separately for the sake of fulfilling desires.
All these great *grahas* are indeed devourers of children;
they are indeed inauspicious for infants until they reach sixteen years of age.
So too are the groups of Mothers (*mātṛgaṇas*) and the *grahas* belonging to the groups of men.
In this world, all those called *skandagrahas* bring suffering to awakening (bodhi).
Their pacification must be performed through ritual bathing, incense, and collyrium; furthermore, there should be offerings of bali-oblations and especially worship (*ijyā*) of Skanda. (47–48)
Thus worshipped, they all bestow longevity, vigor, and strength.
Now, O Rādhā, listen as I describe those planetary deities who preside over men after the sixteenth year; they are indeed considered to belong to Maheśvara.
The man who sees the gods, whether awake or even while lying down, quickly becomes insane; they know that to be possession by a deity (devagraha).
And the man who sees the ancestors, whether sitting or lying down, [is likewise possessed].
Then he quickly goes mad; that is known as the Pitṛ-graha.
He who insults the Siddhas and is cursed by the virtuous in their anger quickly goes mad; that is known as the Siddha-graha.
He who repeatedly sniffs at fragrances and even tastes flavors,
and who quickly becomes intoxicated, should be known as possessed by a Rākṣasa spirit.
Furthermore, that beloved man into whom divine Gandharvas enter is likewise possessed.
He indeed quickly goes mad; that is the Gāndharva spirit.
That man whom Piśācas constantly ascend—that is the Paiśāca spirit;
he indeed quickly goes mad.
And when yakṣas enter a man at the turn of time, he quickly becomes insane; that should be known as a yakṣa-graha. There is derangement, seizure, agitation, fear, and a terrifying appearance. (56–57)
One indeed desires to play, another likewise desires to eat, and yet another desires sexual union; such is this threefold *graha* (seizing force).
These *grahas* of men persist until they enter the state of old age.
Henceforth, fever shall be like a planetary seizure for embodied beings.
(60) Planetary seizures always avoid one who has restrained his senses, who is devoted, pure, free from pride and sloth, and who is a believer and full of faith. (2.32.60)
Planets do not afflict those who are devoted, chaste, virtuous, and well-behaved.
Then Svāhā said: "Skanda, you are indeed my dear son.
O son, grant me a permanent dwelling to reside with Agni."
Skanda said: "The twice-born shall always offer oblations to the gods (*havya*) and to the ancestors (*kavya*), which have been consecrated with mantras, saying 'Svāhā!
into the fire; may you always have a dwelling there.
Wherever there is no house and no sacrificial offering, there you shall dwell in the form of a planet."
"You shall become the devourer of the five in the group of five; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus by Vahni, Svāhā dwells with him eternally.
Thus have those *grahas* been described, which cause destruction here and there.
Therefore, they are indeed worthy of worship; when satisfied, they are remembered as bestowers of happiness.
On the eighth day of the month of Phālguna, Gopālakṛṣṇa caused their worship to be performed with mantras and the offering of various oblations.
With milk-rice, fried cakes, vegetables, and parched grains,
he devoutly gratified all the planetary deities with offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Then Skanda, having likewise dealt with Vinatā, Pūtanā, and the others, [proceeded].
Diti, Aditi, Piśācī, Surabhi, and Śakuni;
Saramā, Kadrukī, and the mothers of the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
Dhātrī, Raktāyanī, as well as the Deva-pitṛs and the Siddhas and Grahas.
The Paiśācas, Rākṣasas, Gāndharvas, Yakṣas, Kāmas, and likewise Jvaras,
as well as others such as the Svāhās— these were the twenty-six classes of lineages.
They arrived visibly through the sky and descended into the lake.
Wherever this worship took place, they assumed gentle forms.
Having received the worship, the offerings, and the milk-preparations and other gifts in every way,
they were satisfied and praised Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord.

O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, we are planets who perform wicked deeds; since we were created exactly so, we shall not reach the further shore of sin. Therefore, show us Your grace so that we may cross the ocean of illusion.
"Forgive us always for the offenses committed by those of evil intent. Where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa resides, there is no oppression by us;
we shall never enter this sacred field for the purpose of causing harm."
O Kṛṣṇa, purify us by granting the nectar of Your feet;
You are the God who is the seizer of the planets, their controller, and the Supreme Lord.
Grant us residence at Your feet, making us eternally auspicious and pure.
"We have sought refuge at your lap; accept us as your own servants.
Having thus entreated him, they then fell at the feet of Śrī Hari, who had been consecrated with water by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Sprinkled, purified, and satiated by the drinking of water,
and touched and fed, they all then attained a divine state;
radiant and possessing the forms of gods, they were indeed like the attendants of Hari.
Then Hari spoke to them on the shore of the lake:
"O gods, dwell here forever— free from fear, free from disease, free from affliction, and always bringing about prosperity."

"Here on this southern bank, there shall be a famous pilgrimage site known as Grahatīrtha. Those people who always worship your images here—even those residing in other lands—their children born into their lineage [shall attain success]. (82)
"Let them not be oppressed by you, even though you have traveled to other lands.
Now, with your second forms, roam this earth;
perform your respective duties as the task of the planets has been assigned."
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā extends for ten yojanas;
let them commit their assault elsewhere, provided there is some other opening.
Even there, however, let them not commit an assault upon my devotees.
May they not commit an assault upon those who observe the vows of Brahmanic conduct;
may they not commit an assault upon the virtuous, the chaste, the Brahmins, and those most devoted to the Veda;
nor upon those who practice austerities, who observe their vows, and whose deeds are meritorious.

They must never, under any circumstances, commit an act of assault or inflict suffering upon those who serve cows, gods, and the virtuous, nor upon pure yogis or householders who are devoted to the Divine. //88//
Let them practice the subjugation of atheists, revilers, and slanderers;
let them act against those who are violent, envious, and wicked.
Let them also practice the subjugation of those who do not honor the gods, the ancestors, or the sacred fires. (2.32.89–90)
May they repeatedly inflict humiliation upon thieves, drunkards, those who cause suffering to others, the wicked, and those devoid of righteousness;
likewise, upon the unrighteous, those who consume the deposits of others, and those who create dissension.
May you ladies show defiance toward those who oppose the true purpose [of this place].
(92) The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā is supremely divine and blissful;
it is equal to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself and is free from both merit and sin. (93)
Consisting of the offering to Brahman, it is the ground of liberation and my own abode; let those whose nature is liberated dwell there in my refuge.
My guru Lomaśa will bestow the mantra upon you here.
"Having reached that mantra, let the Vaiṣṇava planets remain there.
(95) Thus addressed, all those planets—both auspicious and inauspicious, existing in two forms—became shadow-selves causing unhappiness through the resolve of Kṛṣṇa. (96)
Those divine beings, in their original forms, went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Lomaśa bestowed upon them the mantra dedicated to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
And he placed a garland of tulasī upon their necks and gave them excellent sectarian marks (puṇḍraka).
Having thus become Vaiṣṇavas, they remained on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake; then, as shadow-selves, they departed for whatever other regions they desired.
In this way, the Blessed One brought peace to all the seizing spirits;
they became givers of happiness to devotees, ever-liberated and always bestowing the highest good.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this divine marvel has been recounted.
Whoever should hear or recite it, for them there shall be the bliss of liberation.
(10.1) There shall also be abundant wealth, grain, cattle, birds, and riches;
and sons, grandsons, daughters, and granddaughters, along with their lineages, shall be free from disease. (10.2)

"They shall become equal to the gods, overflowing with all bliss; they will be free from all [worldly] things, devoid of dualities, and possess bodies like those in heaven. (1.03) Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifest Appearance of the Child-Spirits and Others upon Worship, and the Description of Their Names, Forms, and Other Attributes," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada in my fourth year, I performed [the vow]; I shall now relate to you the life and deeds of Śrī Hari-Kṛṣṇa.
The noble ladies of Kuṅkumavāpikā and millions of maidens likewise observed the vow of Ṛṣipañcamī and performed the worship of the sages (ṛṣipūjana),
in order to avoid the defect of contact while they remained in their menstrual state.
Thereafter, they all performed the worship and acts of charity as auxiliary parts of the vow (vratāṅga). On the sixth day, they performed the Gaurī-vrata, having invoked her and worshipped her;
on the seventh day, they fed her with offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa) and other foods.
On the eighth day, they indeed worshipped Gaurī with *dūrvā* grass;
they performed the worship of eight-year-old girls in the form of Gaurī with sandalwood paste and other unguents, saffron and other pigments, and fragrant *akṣata* rice. (5)
With various types of perfumes, garments, ornaments, and decorations;
with fruits, flowers, sweet foods, drinks, and betel leaves; and by the offering of desired objects, they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites. (6–7)
Then they performed songs and dances, and subsequently, all the women and maidens went to Lake Aśva to perform the ritual dismissal of Gaurī.
Carrying an earthen image of Gaurī upon their shoulders, they were surrounded by all the women.
Richly adorned with every kind of ornament, seated upon the back of a divine lion, and carried in a celestial palanquin by women holding chowries and an umbrella—
thus carrying the image of Śrī Gaurī, the women sing. (9–10)
The sounds of musical instruments arose, signaling the commencement of the festival.
Thousands of men and women went there to behold Gaurī at the northern bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa.
Kambharāśrī, the mother of Hari, went together with the cowherd women.
Taking the child Hari with her to the festival for the dismissal of Gaurī, the eager women went to the bank and installed Gaurī there. (12–13)
Then, having placed [the image] upon the ship, they performed worship and offered this prayer:
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be like Śaṅkara to us;
may he be as radiant and beloved as you are. Be gracious to us!"
Having thus offered their prayers, they then presented a handful of flowers;
amidst the sounding of musical instruments, they performed the ritual immersion in the water.
Then, as the women reached the gateway to heaven, there arose shouts of "Victory! (15–16).
They gladdened the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the best of sages.
When the dismissal of Gaurī had been performed, a marvel then occurred:
there was a certain very well-fed tiger, as tall as the height of a banyan tree.
Suddenly he arrived there where the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa was;
opening his eyes wide, gaping his mouth, and manifesting his inner intent,
he pricked up his ears, wagged his tail, and bristled his hair and skin.
Displaying his anger and scratching the earth with the tips of his front hooves,
he quickly leaped up to seize the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
All the men and women stood stunned and motionless out of fear.
Then, by that roar, the atmosphere became trembling;
the trees shook, and for a moment the wind became motionless. The earth turned into a state of quaking, and hearts trembled. (21–22)
Then, as the tiger sprang up, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose;
the people, beholding its terrifying form, fled in all directions.
But Kambharā-Lakṣmī, the mother, said, "May Gaurī protect [us]."
And other maidens there then made a vow:
"When Kṛṣṇakānta is protected here, we shall perform worship at the onset of night to Gaurī and Durgā as well, with all ritual offerings. (24–25)
Thus they made this vow and indeed chanted the name of Śrī Narāyaṇa;
unable to look upon Him, they stood with their eyes covered by both hands.
(26) Śrī Rādhikā said:
"Who was that great tiger? Why did he arrive in the evening?
For, having abandoned the others, he was indeed intent on seizing only that child.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
He was born in the land of Rakta and was the younger brother of Śavādīna;
indeed, he was a Mleccha and a Rākṣasa, desiring to avenge the enmity against his brother. He could assume any form at will, move through the sky, and even travel upon the water.
Even though he has made his dwelling in the forest, he acts like a tiger here and there;
among humans he behaves like a common man, and among birds he acts like a bird.
For such a person is indeed defiled, possessing a truly impure intention.
When his brother was slain by Śrī Hari in the land of Avrikta, he then went abroad to the ocean.
In the land of Avrikta, not far from the bank of the river Nāvila—
In order to purchase gold-bearing earth and other minerals from a distant place,
he took some of that golden soil and returned to his own home;
there he heard of the death of his elder brother and the abduction of his daughters.

Beholding the death of his guru, the upheaval, the kingdom falling under the power of Jalla, and the reversal of fortune following the child’s festival— even during the offering festival— resulting in misfortune,
he witnessed this total calamity and became exceedingly angry and deeply grieved.
Sovereignty, an army, the power to travel through the sky, a preceptor, a queen, and the reputation of an ascetic—
(35) even when these capable things exist, the writing on one's forehead is more powerful.
Even when there is a capable brother, abundant wealth protected by the ocean, (36) [the destiny ordained by fate prevails].
There is grief that the destruction will occur specifically in the house while the country is occupied by soldiers;
yet a person born in a foreign land, though unaccompanied by an army, arrives and destroys him completely,
leaving not even a trace.
The abduction of a maiden’s mother is indeed a cause for lamentation.
Alas! Having heard this, neither my death nor my valor increases. Of what use is the life of an embodied being who has been thus humiliated? (38–39)
"I shall slay that enemy, or I shall bring back my daughters;
otherwise, I shall give up my life. Fie upon this strength that is but useless strength!
Having reflected thus, he abandoned the golden ship, his home, and all else.
Taking with him his own people and ascetics who could assume many forms,
he went to Saurāṣṭra to slay the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
And he beheld the vast and auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa;
he observed it all repeatedly, looking for a way to kill him.
He constantly moved among the thickets and even dwelt within the trees.
Accompanied by his retinue, he indeed wanders through the field assuming many different forms.
Among them, some act like crows in various trees here and there;
others act like vultures, and likewise, others act like wolves near the lakes.
Some acted like parrots, while others acted like cows;
some acted like bulls, and even some acted like cats.
Some acted like mosquitoes, looking for a flaw again and again.
And having found the opportunity to slay the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
some act like fish in the water, while others act like children;
and still others, assuming the forms of young girls, become his assistants.
Even though they acted in this way, they could find no vulnerability to slay Kṛṣṇa.
Then, becoming utterly despondent, they spoke with anger to the King’s younger brother:
"Indeed, no vulnerability can be found even in hundreds of years."
"Therefore, he must be killed by force; let whatever will be, be.
Having thus reached an agreement, those hundred heroes went to the shore of the lake and, having assembled, said: "We shall kill that murderer of the king! || 50-51 ||
"Each one should gradually assume the form of a tiger, slowly;
first, indeed, let them enter among the women in the forms of young girls.
Thus, a hundred girls then entered into the girls.

With cruel intentions, they sought to kill that glorious Bālakṛṣṇa at twilight. Seeing Nārāyaṇa among the women, they perceived him to be innocent and alone without a protector; then the king’s younger brother himself [acted]. (53–54)
For the purpose of exacting vengeance, that first tiger was a demon;
as soon as the demon leaped up and went to seize the boy Kṛṣṇa,
Janārdana himself became a śarabha there.
Hari assumed the form of a tiger and seized the younger brother of the king, who was distressed by the creeper.
Grasping him by the throat, Hari swiftly slew the asura.
There, shouts of "Victory! arose for Hari, accompanied by a rain of flowers.
The gods brought about the destruction of his suffering, and the women lowered their heads;
Mahākālī, appearing as a young girl in the form of Gaurī,
arrived herself at Śarabha’s feet and bowed down to him.
But at that time, the Blessed One became a youth among women as he had been before.
A tiger, having produced other tigers there, then died;
thus, the Śārabha Tīrtha was born there at the Aśvasaras lake.
Where Kṛṣṇa bathed after having slain that asura at that time,
the goddess Mahākālī, acting as his servant, praised Kṛṣṇa:
"O Blessed One, I did not know that this obstacle had arisen for you."
The Guardian of the Field did not know how or why this had come to pass.
Śrī Hari said, "O fortunate one, such was my will:
'This wicked one must be slain by me so that the virtuous woman may not find out.'"
I acted in such a way that the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) would not know;
likewise, that entry was not noticed by you, the guardian of the field.
Now, behold these hundred very young maidens.
Those Asuras who were his companions indeed remained in disguised forms.
Having come here in succession to kill me, they took the form of tigers;
when that leader was slain by him, they became terrified and hid themselves.
When the Goddess and the Guardian of the Field saw the maidens,
they became tigers; and having joined together among the tigers,
they then sprang at once toward the Goddess, the maidens, and Hari in order to kill them.
Having made the firm resolve that "either we must die or they must be slain," Kṛṣṇa quickly blew his terrifying war-conch.
And Siṃha, the vehicle of the Goddess, arrived instantly.
There, the roars of tigers arose, shattering the universe;
the entire tiger-infested forest was filled with those cries.
The planets trembled, the trees shook, and the earth and the lake likewise quaked.
The lion also let out a roar, and froth fell upon the earth.
From that roaring, masses of foam flew up into the sky;
from them, indeed, five hundred lions were born in an instant.
Upon seeing the lions, some of the powerful tigers then became lions; indeed,
a terrifying battle then took place there between the two lion-armies,
with the slaughter occurring through the mouths and claws of both sides.
The pulling out of entrails and the sucking of throats occurred in great abundance.
"A woman must certainly not be killed"—such was the vow of righteousness (*dharmasaṃgara*).
Lions fell in the battle, and those that were artificial were slain as well.
The enemies who rely on their manes, being the very root, are slain;
though they may be fewer in number, once dead, they are dead for all time.
And then the lionesses of the Goddess, born from the dead, multiply once again.
To witness the battle of the lions, even the Lord Nṛsiṃha came from his abode to that place,
roaring toward the realm of heaven.
Leaping from *krośa* to *krośa* in the sky, the sons of the lion fought.
The Blessed One also beheld him and roared while stationed in the sky;
the lion of the Goddess went forth and welcomed him in the heavens.
Then the lions born of the lion struck down the remaining asuras.
All those hundred who had previously been dead fell down lifeless before Hari.
Then, by the grace of Hari, through their own selves becoming one with the essence of Śrī Nṛsiṃha,
they attained dissolution there, rendered sinless through their union with that sacred field.
Both the artificial and the natural ones died at Narasiṃhaka;
they then attained dissolution and went to the abode together with Nṛsiṃha.
Those others who were born from the lion of the Goddess, as well as the remaining ones born from the foam, [did likewise].
Śrī Hari gave them a forest in the south for the purpose of their residence;
that became Siṃhāraṇya, which has always been a dwelling place for lions.
Furthermore, Hari granted it so that their lineage might remain unshakable.
He granted a boon and gave him forest fare and a herd of animals.
Then, the tiger who had died, as well as those who were emaciated by the creeper, were born as tigers;
indeed, they became those who possessed the forms of lions and were formidable.
Even though they were struck down and appeared dead, the Lord Nārāyaṇa did not [desert] them;
he bestowed upon those who praised him the gift of life, health, and freedom from disease.
He granted them the Vāsā forest eternally, yet that very place became a tiger forest for them.
The lineages of tigers suited for the forest were indeed intermingled with lions;
likewise, there were lions in the tiger-forest and tigers in the lion-forest—this Hari ordained.
And by virtue of a boon granted in Saurāṣṭra, they dwell perpetually in that forest.
Those asuras are tigers and those divine beings are lions.
Thus they dwell in Saurāṣṭra and indeed in the southern forests,
on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, where there is a great battle between lions and tigers.
Where Narasiṃha appeared and from where he then descended from the sky—
that purifying great holy site of the lion and the tiger is thus proclaimed.
Following the battle, at the onset of night, there occurred an excellent rain.
The earth attained purity, and everyone went to their respective homes.
(92) Then those maidens performed vows, worship, and a night vigil for Durgā and Gaurī for the sake of protection from Kṛṣṇa. (93)
At the end of the night, having worshipped Durgā and Gaurī and asked for their forgiveness,
they performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana) of Durgā and Gaurī toward Hari.
Then they all went to see Him and considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose.
Then, having given gifts and honored their preceptor Lomaśa,
and having likewise honored their parents, they indeed performed the ritual breaking of their fast.
Kālī went to her own abode, and the lion also vanished from sight.
O Rādhikā, Saurāṣṭra then became healthy and free from fear;
this is the miraculous power of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Supreme well-being shall accrue to whoever hears or recites this.
"And there shall also be worldly good fortune arising from the thread of progeny.

(98) Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Worship and Dismissal of Gaurī, and the Destruction of the Asura Vyāghra named Vallīdīna along with his hundred demon hosts assuming the forms of tigers and lions," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 35 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O highly wise Rādhikā, to this wondrous account of the fifth-year celebration of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self of all selves.
When the fifth year had arrived, the father celebrated the Lord’s birth festival.
He caused the worship of all the gods to be performed according to the prescribed rites;
he organized an assembly of musicians for the singing,
and he had a pavilion constructed adorned with golden garments.
Adorned with the splendor of many puppets and graced by all manner of visible wonders,
Viśvakarman himself fashioned the deities there;
both Maya and Śambara also rendered him assistance.

The sight of dry land in water, and of water on dry land; the sight of the earth in the ocean, and of the ocean on the earth (5). Likewise, the sight of members of an assembly within a wall, and of women in a gathering; and the sight of gardens in the corners of the canopy in the sky (6).
Seeing a staircase on a royal road or at a river, or seeing a pit;
seeing a gatehouse in a long enclosure, or an enclosure within a gatehouse—by such observations, even those who are masters of technical science may indeed become confused. (7)
And they became unable to proceed without a guide.
In entering, going, standing, sitting, or looking about, the members of the assembly were rendered motionless without their guides. (8–9)
Having seated Bālakṛṣṇa upon a beautiful, divine throne within such a pavilion as this, the supreme lords worshipped him.
They presented divine offerings, which the Father accepted.
Exceedingly delighted at the festival of his son’s birth, he bestowed gracious gifts upon them.
(11) Having thus performed the worship, the men remained seated in the assembly hall; then the goddesses arrived there for the purpose of worshipping Hari. (12)
With saffron, unbroken rice, perfumes, and the like, as well as flowers, darbha grass, and so forth;
with various sprouts, fresh grains, and the like;
and with garments, ornaments, decorations, and other beautiful objects. (13)
They worshipped [the Lord] with lustration rites (*nīrājana*) that remove suffering and with ritual offerings (*avatāra*).
Those women of the city presented gifts and placed vessels of food before him; they set down sugar, fruits, seeds, and juices in his presence. (14–15)
Then the inhabitants of the city worshipped the Supreme Lord;
the maidens also worshipped Him, and the twice-born brahmins bestowed their blessings.
So too did the ascetics, the sages, and other virtuous women who were faithful and devoted to their husbands.
They bestowed blessings upon that Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
(17) Then, following the worship, the singers remained there, as did the musicians, including those born of divine and human lineages. (18)
Hāhā, Hūhū, Nārada, Parvata, Citradarśana,
Sudarśana, Tumburu, Viśvāvasu, Parāvasu,
Meghasvana, Tāranāda, Dharaṇidhra, and Anugālava.
Vaṃśadhara, Taraṇika, Jalaghoṣa, Vaiṇika, Āmramañju, Alaṃbuṣa, Rāṃbheya, and Śaṅkhakarṭaka—
these were the celestial Gandharvas, led by Cūḍavarman. (2.34.20–21)

Those staying in the pavilion performed singing at that festival, accompanied by musical instruments and adorned with rhythmic timing (*tāla*), tempo (*māna*), scales (*grāma*), and modulations (*mūrcchanā*).
Then the Blessed One, pleased with them, [bestowed] garlands of diamonds and pearls.
Then he gave [gifts] to the humans; thereafter the Gandharvas arrived at the assembly hall:
Citraratha, Pratola, Sāraṅga, Maṇirañjaka, Tāmareru, Tānasainya, Jagannātha, and Harītaka.
Bāṣpavarṣin, Dhūmramedhas, Śaśakunda, and Kapardaka—
these and other Gandharvas performed singing and instrumental music. To them, Hari gave delightful and diverse rewards.
There were ornaments of gold and silver, gold coins, and garments.
Then the Gandharvas of the Dānavas and Daityas arrived at the assembly hall:
Kambukīrti, Gālavāda, Nassvana, and Bhujaghoṣaṇa. (26–27)
Khātadhvaja, Golabhūpa, and others performed songs of praise;
to them Hari gave garlands of pearls, gems, and coral.
Then the elephants, bards, heralds, panegyrists, and eulogists—
The Brahmabhaṭṭas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and Kiṃpuruṣas arrived swiftly at the assembly with their poetic compositions;
they displayed their skill in their respective works before the gathering. (2.34.30)
They described the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the highest terms.
The father gave them suitable gifts of purified and auspicious objects.
There were also dancers and singers, along with vocal and instrumental music and rhythmic dancing.
To please Hari, they performed [these acts], and Hari, being pleased, gave them wealth:
ornaments, vessels for decoration, various articles, divine garlands and garments, and rewards suitable for women. (32–33)
Thus were the supplicants satisfied there during the birth festival;
when they had all departed, the residents of the Abode were released—
the inhabitants of Akṣara, Amṛta, Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the other realms.
They offered blessings to him, their own beloved Supreme Soul.
Śrī Harikṛṣṇa rose from his seat again and again, and placing them all simultaneously upon his chest, he embraced them many times over.
Assuming many forms, Kṛṣṇa took the flower garlands,
the sandalwood paste, the unbroken grains of rice, and the moon-like [ornaments], as well as the worship performed all around him with them.
Having given them pleasing gifts in return, he dismissed them.

At the conclusion of the assembly, his father gave them various kinds of food, as well as drinks, betel, and gifts of satisfaction; having celebrated that festival, they all returned to their own respective abodes. (38–39)
Thus, when the great festival had commenced, a mighty cry of victory arose:
"May the child Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be victorious throughout all the worlds!
In this way, the voices of the people were heard everywhere upon the earth.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa remains as a great lord of generosity;
he bestows whatever is desired upon supplicants, even exceeding their requests—
whether it be food, drink, nourishment, wealth, clothing, or vehicles.
"Whatever desired object a seeker takes from the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa—
such fame as this arose in the world and spread among the people.
Having heard this on the Himālaya mountain, Baka Dālbhya and likewise Gavāyana [set out].
Sālāyana was a sage devoted to the dharma of well-being, dwelling in the forest.
There were a thousand Brahmins practicing austerities, reciters of the Vedas,
established in the dharma of the virtuous, wearing bark garments, matted hair, and deerskins.
Wearing garments made of the skins of lions, tigers, deer, and elephants,
they arrived for the purpose of a pilgrimage after having performed ablutions at Kurukṣetra;
having visited Puṣkara and Siddhabhūmi, they came to Saurāṣṭra.
Some among them were divine beings, virtuous celibates;
others were forest-dwellers, as well as householders who resembled saints.
They were devoted to the dharma of austerity, experts in the scriptures, and practitioners of yoga.
They arrived at the supreme purifying field of Kuṅkumavāpikā,
a sacred site of the Lord renowned throughout the three worlds as the bestower of liberation.
There lies the delightful Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, extending for many krośas.

Having previously beheld that beautiful forest, filled with flowers and fruits, which was dug by the gods, possessed of most desirable water, lovely, and radiant as the moon; which was the abode of all sacred fords and rested upon the earth itself. (2.34.50–51)
In the region of Lomaśa’s hermitage, where no illusion exists, they attained firm peace— peace that is unfading and enriched by all seasons.
Then, in the mango grove, the sages prepared their seats.
Having bathed and performed their worship and other rites, they ate fruits.
Then they circumambulated the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and came to see the sage Lomaśa, the great devotee of the Lord.
And having bowed to him as he sat in the hermitage at the foot of a rose-apple tree,
a thousand sages felt themselves to be blessed.
Lomaśa welcomed them with offerings of water for the feet, seats, salutations, and other honors.
With fruits, drinks, golden plantains and other fruits, and excellent foods—
thus they accepted all the hospitality prepared by the sages.
Then they arrived at the palace of Hari to behold the glorious Supreme Lord.
Kṛṣṇa, assuming a thousand forms simultaneously, embraced those who were the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the form of a child.
At that time, the sages, including Dālbhya and others, attained supreme wonder.

Some beheld the Lord as a child who had entered the abode of Brahmā, possessing four arms, eight arms, or even a thousand arms. Having performed worship, offered water for His feet, and paid obeisance to Him, they [proceeded]. (2.34.60)
Then they went by way of the eastern direction to their own seat, the mango grove; thereafter,
on the second day, those sages came to the temple of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of alms,
while Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was there.
Then Hari placed a vessel of ghee, a vessel of wheat flour, sugar, side dishes,
a vessel of oil, asafoetida,
and split pulses along with rice on his side. (62–63)
With his own hands, he gave them abundant food according to their desire;
what was given from each individual vessel did not diminish.
And for the sake of feeding more than a thousand holy sages, [he provided the meal].
Then those who knew the majesty of Kṛṣṇa experienced great wonder.
Having departed and taken with them a vast quantity of raw grains, they cooked them and ate; then they attained a nectar-like peace.
Then in the evening, Hari went with his father to that assembly of holy men to see them, where the auspicious sages sat upon lion-skins,
shining as they were intent on meditation upon Brahman. (67)
Then Bālakṛṣṇa spoke insistently to his father:
"O Father, give me a lion’s skin for a seat.
Having said this, he repeatedly extended his long finger toward his father. (68–69)
He made a persistent request for the sake of obtaining a lion’s skin.
Seeing that, the seer Dālbhya said to his father with a laugh:
"What does this boy desire, and what is he saying again and again?"
The father said: "This boy indeed acts with mere obstinacy in vain;
he desires a lion's skin, which is simply not to be obtained.
Dālbhya said: "O Prince! You wish to mount a lion!"
"This is a lion; no one else is able to mount it.
The prince said, "O Sage, give that to me for my seat.
Dālbhya replied, "That is indeed suitable for sages dwelling in the forest."
"Therefore, my son, nothing exists that should be given to one who is not a fit recipient.
Having heard this, the illustrious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "Give it to me.
Then the illustrious Narāyaṇa, the sage, replied, "This must not be given."
He let out a lion’s roar, a formidable sound of intense thundering.
Upon hearing it, those who were in the form of skins— lions, tigers, deer, and the like—
all regained their life through the will of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The sages, who were standing upon the hides, fell down all around onto the ground.
They were seized with terror upon seeing those fearsome tigers, the lions of truth;
yet the tigers fled in every direction, driven by the roar and other sounds [of the sages].
They filled the forest and the lofty sky;
their cries shook the earth as far as the edge of the ocean.
Running by the hundreds were those lions, as well as deer and other wild animals.
Those whose skins had once been used [as drums], having now become these very creatures with life, bowed at the feet of Kṛṣṇa and departed for the forest;
even the sages such as Dālbhya were unable to restrain them by means of yogic powers. (2.34.80–81)
Having thus witnessed that wonder of Hari once more,
they took refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa and offered praise:
"That which they declare to be the supreme Brahman, the one without a second— " || 82 ||
To you, O Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Self, we bow; be gracious to us.
(83) O sole Sovereign, ocean of the true Dharma, beginningless source, abiding in the heart, Viśvaksena, Vṛṣāvarta—we bow to you; be gracious to us. (84)
O Śuciśravas, O ocean of nectar, eternal, imperishable, and indestructible;
O consumer of oblations, Mañjukeśa, O Unborn One, we bow to you—be gracious unto us.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, O First-born, O Flower-Smiling One, O Bāla Janārdana.
O Ruler of the moving and the unmoving, we bow down to you; be gracious to us!
(86) You are the most excellent of the Sun, abiding as Hiraṇyagarbha;
O Vāsudeva, ocean of compassion, we bow down to you; be gracious to us! (87)
O you whose faces are infinite, whose feet are infinite, and who are the refuge of infinite power and qualities;
O Hotṛ, Potṛ, and cause of the oblation, we bow before you—be gracious to us!
O Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Brahman, glorious Gopāla-Bālaka!
O Lord born in the house of Śrī Kambharā, we bow to you; be gracious to us.
O Supreme Person, Soul of the Universe, Lord of exalted deeds, Ruler of Heaven, Witness of all, Lord of Surāṣṭra, we bow to you; be gracious to us.
O Lord, you are the giver of all that is most auspicious, the great deity of the gods;
be our protector, sustainer, nourisher, and refuge.
You are the one whom even seers like us do not perceive, despite seeing everything else.
Beholding them, you who possess the form of a child, become our refuge, O Lord!
We bow to that auspicious youth, by whom the entire world— from the earth up to the pillar of Brahmā— is pervaded as the moving and the unmoving, and by whom this net of illusion was fashioned.
We bow to that Child of Compassion, whose two eyes are the sun and moon, whose two arms are the earth and Śiva, and whose two feet are the white ocean of milk.
(94) The thrones have been destroyed; the lions have gone to the forest.
"O Bālakṛṣṇa, let our desires be fulfilled for the sake of a seat.
Thus praised, the Blessed One then said to the sages,
"O fortunate ones, come and touch my toenails."
"Seats shall appear for you; let them be provided here.
Thus addressed, those sages—Dālbhya, Baka, and the others—then touched the big toe of Śrī Hari’s left foot in succession.

From the nail of his thumb, whatever [item] belonged to each—such as the lion’s skin and so forth—appeared there; the sovereign sage took hold of them all. Indeed, those skins were offered by Śrī Hari to everyone.
Then they all joyfully worshipped Hari Nārāyaṇa and received the mantra from Gopālakṛṣṇa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Having applied the *tilaka*, the *tulasī* mark, and a garland, and having taken the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the Vaiṣṇavas then became sages endowed with divine vision;
having completed their pilgrimage, they returned once more to the Himālaya mountains.
That sacred bathing place (tīrtha) came to be known by the name Dālbhya-tīrtha on the eastern bank;
through hearing or reciting [this account], it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Songs of the Gandharvas, the Revival of Lions and Other Animals from the Skins of Lions, Tigers, and Others by the Thousand Sages such as Dālbhya and Baka, and the Manifestation of Those Respective Skins from the Big Toe," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the great festival in the fifth year of the Lord.
