Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen to the beautiful, wondrous pastime of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Once, however, actors from the region of Kailāsa arrived there;
they were experts in many dramatic performances, capable of captivating the assembly,
possessed of many instruments, and skilled in the arts of illusionists.
There were one thousand young men and five hundred maidens;
a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, and likewise a hundred gayals;
a hundred camels and donkeys, and ten lions. (3–4)
There were twenty tigers and ten bears as well;
there were exactly one hundred monkeys, and one hundred each of swans and parrots.
There were exactly three hundred dogs and ten gaṇḍakas as well.
And there, twenty Mallas joined together to form that vast [circle],
known on the face of the earth as the preeminent circle of dance (nāṭyamaṇḍala),
which was presided over by the dancer named Ardhanārīśvara.
There were a hundred Garuḍas and a hundred fire-birds,
all capable of assuming any form at will and sustained by the food of the Kalpavṛkṣa tree;
they moved through the atmosphere and showed them the cities of the sky.
Where there exist practitioners of the art of lightning, performers who display many forms,
and even beasts and birds that have been thoroughly trained—
that circle of dancers is at the field of Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra. (2.35.9–10)
He stayed on the northern shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara;
having established his camp, he drank water and performed his ablutions in the waters.
On the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, he performed that dance at night.
There, a vast and beautiful pavilion, measuring one *krośa* in extent, was erected.
Hundreds of thousands of people from Saurāṣṭra arrived there from all sides to witness the event and sat down for the sake of a clear view.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the sage Lomaśa, the mother, the father, and the daughters— both men and women— sat down;
the lamps were like lightning, their natural radiance blending with the rays within the pavilion.
They shone like the moon, and at that time there was the illusion of being daytime. Meanwhile, musical instruments played naturally within the pavilion,
and sweet sounds resonated from the tops of the pillars, resembling the assembly of Brahmā.
And there, from the pillars and the jars, auspicious songs emerged,
taking the form of celestial voices, accompanied by singers and instrumentalists.
Within the middle of the pillars, tens of thousands of maidens were seen.
The Lord of All beheld forms equal to Śrī, Ramā, Kamalā, and Gaurī.
Then, within the canopies, he saw the celestial realm of Svarga, as well as Sudharmā;
and the cities of Alakā, Amṛtā, Svarṇā, Hiraṇyā, and Aśmakā.
The assemblies of the Kalpas are seen, resplendent with supreme beauty;
upon the walls of cloth are seen the gods, the Daityas, and the Dānavas;
as well as the Ṛṣis, the Pannagas, the Īśas, the Pitṛs, and the best of men.
And these natural sights were seen on all sides. But this entire [display] was artificial, like a magician’s performance;
having beheld it within the pavilion, the assembly stood motionless for a moment. (21–22)
Then, after the benediction had been pronounced, auspicious songs of joy and celebration were heard, consisting of hymns of praise to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"Victory, victory to you, beloved of the world! Victory, victory to you, beloved of the world! (23)
Victory to you, O one honored by the people, whose countenance brings joy; victory to you, the subduer of the pride of enemies!
Victory, victory to you, who are desired by the world!
Victory, O Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who are well-honored by the liberated and who gladden those who have come to you for refuge!
Victory to you, O Lord of Rādhā! Victory to you, O Lord of Kamalā! Victory to you, O Mādhava, the husband of the Ganges!
Victory to you, who have made yourself the refuge for both the inert and the conscious, and who are the bridegroom of the Pāravatī!
Victory to you, O Nārāyaṇa, whose dwelling is the nectar of immortality, and whose heart is fixed on the Supreme Brahman! 25–26.
Victory to you, O Lord of Māṇikya, protector of the imperishable, sustainer of gods, sages, and ancestors!
Victory to you, O Self; victory to you, O Lord of Light; victory to you, the son of the illustrious Kambharā!
Victory to you, the infant born from Gopāla; victory to you, the sustainer of the universe!
Victory to you, who offer your own self through the deeds of Śaṅkara; victory to you, the remover of the suffering of Vaiṣṇavas!
(28) Victory to you, O beloved Lord of Lakṣmī, Master of the Padma lake and the Arbuda mountain of maidens; victory to you, the bestower of happiness!
Victory to you, whose feet rest upon the Kuṅkumavāpī; victory to you, the one who crosses over the Aśvasaras lake! (29)
Victory to you, O Lord of the Abode, O Sovereign; victory to you who bear a beautiful form!
Victory to you, O Treasure of Bliss, O Lord of Attributes, the bringer of well-being, the one who is easily attained!
Victory to you, O Jewel of Saurāṣṭra, the Avatārin, who moves upon a swan and sports among the people!
"Victory to the creator, the protector, and the destroyer; victory to the one who dwells within the bodies of both the insentient and the sentient!
(31) Thus, auspicious words were heard there from all sides.
Following that, the director, dressed as Kṛṣṇa, appeared in the midst of the stage. (32)
The members of the assembly bowed to me as I was bowing to the Lord of the Assembly.
Then I spoke, encompassing the beginning, middle, and end of the dance:
"The Supreme Brahman, the source of the world, the primordial Lord of the world, who is beyond the quality of rajas."
He is the supreme among the high and the low, the teacher of the Teacher of all the worlds.
Out of compassion, for the sake of the welfare of the world, this Lord—the highest among lords—has indeed descended to the surface of the earth, having entered the womb of Kambharā. (34–35)
"Here comes this child-souled one; let them behold that Supreme Lord!
Having said this, O Rādhā, I stood there pointing out the child.
At that moment, the child, dressed in the attire of Kṛṣṇa, arrived upon that stage.
And the assembly beheld him, resembling ten million times ten million suns.
Then, from his body, there issued forth Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Narāyaṇa by the tens of millions, as well as the Vāsudeva and other vyuhas by the hundreds of millions.
The Bhūmans, Mahāviṣṇu, Vairāja, and Vedhas, as well as Sadāśiva and other incarnations, emerged from the body of the child;
likewise did the ancestors, the sages, the gods, the principles (tattvas), and human beings.
The Nāgas, Daityas, Dānavas, trees, mountains, and likewise rivers—
mobile deities created from the steady mind— all these were displayed at that time before the child Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa. (2.35.40–41)
Upon seeing him, the entire assembly, having attained supreme wonder toward Nārāyaṇa, uttered shouts of "Victory! Then,
having presented an offering, I spoke to those spectators at that time.
This very child, the Supreme Self, shines resplendent in your midst.
As soon as I had said, "Beside the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa is the glorious Supreme Lord," everyone there realized that he was indeed Nārāyaṇa. ||43-44||
Having performed obeisance to the assembly, he departed, carrying [the image] on the back of a cloth.
Then Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and Prabhā arrived before him.
At that moment, Bālakṛṣṇa appeared in the form of a youth.
Those four performed a prostration before their husband, the supreme among men.
They washed his feet and drank that water from his feet;
thereafter, they honored him and likewise performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
There, Śrī Hari shone, his palms joined in reverence upon a golden throne;
then all four of them merged into the form of Śrī Hari.
Furthermore, the people beheld them re-emerged from the body of Śrī Hari.
One hundred and twelve [gopīs] also arose as beloveds of Śrī Hari.
Likewise, the people beheld the great hermitage of Lomaśa, where the wives of Hari—countless maidens numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions—were present. (2.35.50)
They emerged from the form of Śrī Hari and sported upon the stage of the dance.
Standing on the stage, they were filled with wonder upon seeing their own forms in the dance.
Then the goddesses and apsarases emerged from the lake of Brahmā for the sake of Hari.
Seeing this on the stage, the members of the assembly, filled with joy, raised shouts of "Tāla" and "Jaya";
they were delighted all around, and consequently, there was a great celebration.
Then, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa arrived upon the stage.
Accompanied by Kambharāśrī Mahālakṣmī, Bālakṛṣṇa gave his blessings to the gods and, together with his sons, went home.
Having thus manifested himself on the stage, the Lord of the Raṅga returned once more to the back of the curtain.
Thus, O Rādhikā,
having displayed this entire conduct which makes known His state of being an avatāra, He performed its concealment;
then He beheld another sight within the pavilion in the path of the sky.
Bound within nets of cords, dancers dressed in firm and beautiful costumes descended by the hundreds; for every cord,
there were birds [of actors] that flew up a hundred cubits from one ray to the next.
They also travel by means of two parasols, with garments of a thousand cubits.
Having grasped the end of a rope, when cast forth he goes a hundred [yojanas] more;
when cast like an arrow from a bow, he went a thousand [yojanas] more.
Though thrown by his feet, he goes again to a height of a hundred cubits;
without support, he descends and then takes hold of a rope.
He travels from one bamboo pole to another, and from one spot to another in the sky.
And when there is a single ray [of light] for many who are moving toward one another,
having placed their feet within a vessel and with their bodies situated in its midst—
without even touching one another, they are driven away from the front of that very ray. (61–62)
Then, after flying up at the edge and alighting upon another edge,
he kissed the space between people as he suspended himself in the midst of the sky;
then followed the flight from the seat of the rope in every direction.
Without support, even with their hands, feet, or other parts of their bodies,
they performed the *uḍuyana* dance in this manner;
then, those fifty trained in the art of dance constructed a beautiful gateway.
Then they constructed a second gate, rising one hundred cubits high;
thereafter, they built a third gate, three hundred cubits high, above the second.
At that time, fifty men were visible within the pillars.
Thus, fifty men constructed the beautiful gateway of Sudharmā, which was provided with three architraves (kampa-nikā). On all sides, young maidens stood there like statues. (67–68)
All those goddesses, assuming divine forms, were exceedingly beautiful;
they shone at that city gate, devoted to all spiritual perfections, graced by chowries in their hands and bearing seven jars upon their heads. (69)

Having thus caused the gatehouse to be built, O Rādhā, Naṭeśvara stationed the elephant army along with Ambālikā within it; and whenever an individual elephant entered and then emerged again, [he would strike it]. (2.35.70–71)
At every elephant there, the women of the city gateways leaped up high and slowly descended as each elephant passed;
yet the army of elephants came to an end, and even the gateways no longer existed.

Seeing such great effort and such great skill, there was a cry of victory for the sake of the Lord of Dancers and his dancing partner. "Never before has such a gateway been seen, nor will one ever be seen again. (73–74)
However, some are unable to perform *kuṃbhaka* (retention) without *āyāma* (expansion).
For those who move through the sky, the form of the gate-tower (*gopura*) is simple.
Then, palaces for elephants, camels, and horses were constructed there.
There, on stable palace grounds, men and women from all sides swing back and forth upon swings seven stories high;
and in the middle, there are stairways and animals such as gayals, goats, and bulls.
The rungs were fashioned from fire, birds, and *garuḍa* birds;
the parasol was made of the finest serpents, and the rays and the serpents themselves [formed the rest].
Parrots and swans, perched upon the ropes, let out their warbling cries.
And then, around the gardens, they created illusions like those of a magician:
masses of fire in the forest, masses of rain in the sky, gusts of wind within the palace, and artificial sun and moon. (2.35.79–80)
There, monkeys were eating the fruits of the garden upon the palatial buildings;
having displayed the mansions in this manner, he then granted the exemption.
Then the wrestlers arrived, eager for the wrestling match.

Then those men and women engaged in various forms of wrestling, performing supreme and most humorous feats. Indeed, the army of the monkeys was excellent, while that of the bears was even greater. (82–83)
There came into the midst of the arena soldiers clad in human attire and bearing weapons, riding upon lions, donkeys, rhinoceroses, and tigers; there, too, were dogs and jackals. (84)
Then, amidst the sounding of war-drums, the buffalo-riders and the commander Śarabha,
along with their respective armies, divided into two factions and began a great battle upon the surface of the cloth. (85–86)
Then, in that battle, most of the bears and monkeys were slain;
the black bears, donkeys, dogs, jackals, and lions were destroyed. Whatever was killed at that time was like a mere feat of sorcery.
"The monkeys, bears, and bhallukas and others were indeed real; they were certainly not killed.
Then Naṭeśvara provided him with a solution:
"The aerial battle of the maidens was created by means of sorcery (indrajāla)."
Slain and shattered, the young maidens fell indeed from the sky to the earth;
the entire army of maidens lay slain and sleeping upon the ground.
Then the commander-in-chief, the lord of women, wept profusely.
"Alas! My daughters are lost; my entire army has been slain!
(91) Then the boy Kṛṣṇa himself restored the girls to life—those thousands of fierce maidens who were the very embodiment of Rudra’s shadow-form. (92)
The Lord, the Master of Women, created entirely new magicians; having attained great wonder and casting off his pride,
he then fell at the feet of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then the Lord of Actors provided a remedy for this visible [illusion]:
those thousand illusory daughters of the magician, resembling Rudras, were enchanted by Śrī Hari there and chose a boon from him. (94–95)
“You are our protector and lord; be the guardian of our lives at all times.
Hari said, “So be it,” and reported this to Lomaśa.
The Blessed One himself protected them in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then, lions were brought onto the stage in rows by that preeminent trainer. At that time, men who were actors caused the presentation of their faces within the mouths of those lions. (97–98)
They offered their own heads, and that was indeed a great marvel.
Then the Lord of Women himself, having resolved that matter,
caused the lion’s head to be severed.

He placed his own head in his mouth, performing a feat that caused great wonder. (2.35.10) Then, perceiving his immense pride, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resolved to destroy that pride and gave his command to the lion. (101)
"This protector of mine remains here and constantly causes me pain;
therefore, I shall forcibly devour his head!
Having thus resolved, she seized the head in her mouth with fury.
The lion forcibly crushed his face, having firmly closed it.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; an ocean of grief was seen, and hundreds and thousands of actors and actresses wept.
And although Rudra himself is the Lord who is half-female,
Naṭeśvara then gave his own head into the mouth of Kāla;
yet even though he became fearless and attained perfection, he remained subject to another's will.

Then, having been recognized there by the gods themselves, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arose quickly from his seat and went into the presence of Hara; Satī, however, remained grieving, holding Śambhu upon her lap.
He said to Satī, "Give me this matted head;
by the touch of my hand, I shall indeed restore it to its former state.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Narāyaṇa touched it with his left hand.
O Rādhikā, the head of Śambhu quickly became as it was before.
Then Śambhu, having risen, bowed down to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord; being pleased, Hara himself cast away his pride.
Then the boy said to Hara, "O Hara, grant me a vision!
Become Ardhanārīśvara even before the attendants.
Thereupon, Śambhu himself became Ardhanārīśvara right there.
Half [of the body] took on the form of a woman, beautiful from the nails to the hair.

Then, the hair became matted locks (*jaṭā*), the beard grew, breasts appeared, and there was a vulva (*yoni*) and a phallus (*liṅga*). There was one testicle, and the body became both hairy and hairless.
At that time, his form became one adorned with a silken garment and a hide, yet devoid of ornaments;
seeing him thus upon the stage, and likewise seeing Śrī Hari within him,
the assembly was suddenly and exceedingly delighted at that very moment.
Śambhu himself is Naṭeśvara, and these Gaṇas are his dancers. Indeed, animals and others who are his devotees have come for the sake of the performance in order to please Hari;
consequently, Hari himself was pleased. (11.5–11.6)
The Lord granted them residence on the northern shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
he bestowed divine bodies upon all those male and female dancers,
and as a desired reward, he granted them passage to the supreme abode.

That supreme holy site (tīrtha), known as Naṭanāṭya, which effects the upliftment of all, became the savior of sinners, a bestower of heaven, and most excellent. Indeed, through hearing it or reciting it, both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise. (118–119)
Then, having offered his salutations, Hari went to his own abode;
the men of Saurāṣṭra, as well as the gods, sages, and ancestors,
and all other spectators, departed joyfully for their respective homes.
Having thus performed this dance himself, O Rādhikā,
Śrī Śaṅkara took up residence there with his three classes of attendants (gaṇas) in the forest to the north of the Aśvasaras lake, along with all living beings.
He took up residence in the forest of *vaṭa*, *bilva*, and *kadamba* trees;
he shall dwell there as long as the earth remains stable.
O Rādhikā, having assumed the guise of Kṛṣṇa, he became invisible to you.
And at that time, the artificial theater-hall vanished.
Then, bestowing grace upon Śrī Śaṅkara, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke regarding those embodied beings who were here in the drama: || 1.25 ||
May you—the Gaṇas, men, women, maidens, beasts, and birds—all become twofold through my grace in every way:
possessing divine forms as my liberated ones in my abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara). || 126 ||
Established in the fourfold liberation, they indeed depart by means of divine vehicles.
Out of compassion, I grant this supreme reward:
may you dwell here forever in the grove of *vaṭa* and *bilva* trees in other forms.

Thus spoke the illustrious Hari; Hara and the others always resided there. Śrī Hari dwells in the palace, and he constructed the palace for Śambhu. Thus did the god Śaṅkara [speak] to Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
And he performed a supreme, divine festival of dance in order to please [him].
Then the Blessed One, the soul of all, also stood upon that stage of dance, having become a spectator, in order to please Śambhu.

Hari fulfilled the desire of his devotee Śambhu, for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is subservient to his devotees, O Rādhikā. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Satisfaction through Various Unworldly Dances Performed by the Ardhanārīśvara Dance-Company of Kailāsa in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpī, His Dispelling of Śaṅkara’s Pride, His Bestowing of Liberation, and the Naṭanāṭya Tīrtha," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 35: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 36 [[Author:
→ Chapter 37
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you another marvel of Hari; listen.
Having observed the strength of his preceptor in the month of Māgha during his fifth year, || 1 ||
Having gone before Śrī Lomaśa, his father duly performed the auspicious commencement of Bālakṛṣṇa’s education;
he also worshipped Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, Sarasvatī, and the Vedas.
Having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, he offered oblations of clarified butter. He fed the Brahmins and gave gifts of cows.
Then Sarasvatī herself, being pleased, truly appeared before him in person.
Abounding in the splendor of the peacock posture, with a lute held in her hand,
she was worshipped by fourteen maidens of learning;
endowed with the beauty of all ornaments, garments, and decorations.

Having worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Śāradā, the beloved of Hari, attained a state of invisibility within Bālakṛṣṇa. Then her companions— the Śrutis as well as the Smṛtis— [did likewise].
Narratives, poetic compositions, the power of logic, and the sections [of the Vedas],
as well as the Mīmāṃsā, meditative absorption, solitude, and stories; likewise,
that which pertains to mantras, to tantras, to machines, and to the elements.
The arts, calculations, and arrangements, as well as ritual actions; the science of elixirs, strategic planning for war, and sorcery;
the sciences of the stars, of the Rig Veda, of the Sāman, of the Atharva, and of the Yajus.
The verbal, the metrical, the etymological, the genealogical, the epistolary,
as well as the oceanic, the aerial, the dream-like,
the delusive, the ornithological, the physical, the mental, the pertaining to the living beings, and likewise the celestial.
The Sañjīvanī, the Vaivartī, the Ārtavī, and likewise the Dhātavī;
the divine Cikitsā consisting of weapons, the Saṃhāriṇī, and the Poṣaṇī;
the Śilpinī, the Bhūstarī, the Tattvaśodhinī, and the Khanimārgiṇī. (12–13)
Vaidyatī, Bahubhavanī, Sīvanī, Garbhavedinī,
Drāviṇī, Mūrchinī, and others such as these were the maidens who were *vidyās*. They were young girls possessing the luster and beauty of whiteness, with complexions like the campaka flower.
Following the Sarasvatī, they entered into her as her very image.
(15) Thus, O child, at that time the acquisition of knowledge occurred through the Guru;
nevertheless, in accordance with worldly custom, she then practiced the drawing of lines. (16)
He likewise practiced the repetition of syllables and words;
he was seen by people as a treasury of the sciences of the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth.
Then all those maidens attended upon him even outside.
Remaining hidden, they always serve Him in secret;
yet when manifest, they also serve that very Beloved.
Those friends of Śāradā chose Śrī Narāyaṇa as their Lord.
Those auspicious personified sciences always resided in the hermitage of Lomaśa, serving the Supreme Lord, the Master, and the Sovereign, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇabāla; indeed,
by the command of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, those most beautiful sciences remained there.
The boy would always go to his teacher for the purpose of practice. Lomaśa taught him meaningfully every morning;
Kṛṣṇa grasped it like an ordinary person, and the teacher was exceedingly pleased.
He accepted the service of the maiden and thereafter went to his own home.
Then one day, the preceptor of the gods arrived at Lomaśa’s hermitage;
Bālakṛṣṇa bowed to him, Bṛhaspati, who is praised by the gods.
Then, for the purpose of testing Hari’s intellect in the very presence of Lomaśa, Bṛhaspati indeed asked a question consistent with logic:
"Tell me, what would be the value of a bhāra of gold measured by guñjās? || 24-25 ||
The fool said: "If it were permanent, even a single *guñjā*-berry's worth would not be subject to buying and selling in manifold ways;
for as many times as ownerships are transferred therein," (26) so many [transactions] would there be.
An object that is distinct and separate bestows exactly as many qualities [as its weight].
(27) As long as it remains in one's possession—for a hundred thousand years or ten million years—its value shall correspondingly increase;
therefore, its price is infinite. (28)
A single *guñjā*-measure of gold remains that very same gold even as it is transformed;
whatever new object is purchased with it will appear ever more new.
O Guru, in this way that gold is measured as having infinite value.
Having heard this reply, the Guru was pleased with that logician.
The omniscient one, the knower of all things, bestowed blessings upon him: "May you become all-knowing and all-seeing;
may your childhood remain full and nourishing until the end of the fifth year."
May your childhood last until the tenth year, endowed with the dawning of knowledge;
may your youth, until the fifteenth year, be devoted to great spiritual prosperity.
Beyond that, may your youth be filled with infinite bliss.
"May your life be eternal; may you possess the nature of the Sanātana.
Having thus bestowed these blessings and received the worship then performed, he, about to depart, questioned the great asura Varāṭaka regarding Śrī Hari.
He was situated on the shore of the western ocean, performing supreme austerity;
he spoke the truth, practiced non-violence, and was established in the vow of non-stealing.
He was devoted to celibacy and was entirely free from all possessions. (39)
He was filled with sorrow yet remained contented, always devoted to the study of the Vedas (svādhyāya),
intent upon Brahman, and desiring the kingdom of the land of Saurāṣṭra— rising from the ocean, adorned with rows of *sāla* trees, protected by the son of a god, and preeminent in strength. (36–37)
"O Blessed One, here in Saurāṣṭra, near the shore of the western ocean,
Varāṭaka, the son of Sāla, performs fierce austerities for the sake of obtaining a kingdom.
In summer he practices the five-fire penance, and in winter he stands in the water."
During the rainy seasons, he likewise remained there continuously subsisting on air alone. Placing his head upon the ground and his feet in the air day and night,
that great asura sat reciting "Oṃ" for the sake of sovereignty.
"Indra, having recognized this austerity, has sent me; therefore I am departing.
I shall instruct him in such a way that he turns away from his penance.
"Instruct me in that manner so that there may be a cessation of it."
You are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
You are the protector of the gods and the subduer of the Daityas;
therefore, act in such a way that this Devaśūla shall not attain the kingdom. (42–43)
"Instruct me, O Blessed One; having gone, I shall do exactly as you say.
Upon hearing this, the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa said:
"I desire that the obstruction of the Daitya’s asceticism be accomplished."
"O Guru, the Daitya should be restrained with conciliation that awakens him to what is appropriate for him.
I shall describe the duties of the Daityas, as well as their knowledge, ritual actions, and so forth;
indeed, let instruction be given by you in the form of a Brāhmaṇa."
For the most part, the Daityas, Āsurās, and Dānavas, who are gratifiers of the senses,
abide by the doctrine that the body is the self and act according to their own whims. Indeed, for the Daityas, their strength lies in righteousness and the acquisition of wealth through battle.
Having committed an act of violent abduction and likewise brought her under his own control, Daityadharma displayed his prowess; whereas the dharma of those free from passion is austerity (tapas).
Therefore, having caused him to fall away from that austerity, instruct him in the duties pertaining to the body.
"Promote opposition to the dharma of the gods, atheism, the voidness of sin, and violence; instruct the lowest of the Daityas thus:
'Perception alone is the valid means of knowledge; indeed, no world beyond exists. (2.36.50)
Understand that the fruit of asceticism is always meager;
likewise, realize that the Lord is partial and acts for the benefit of the gods, while he remains opposed to the Daitya by assuming a guise of deceit. (51–52)
"Even in the granting of boons and even in sovereignty, you must make him understand that the destroyer of the Daityas and the Supreme Lord himself is indeed to be slain by the Daitya.
Having been thus instructed, the preceptor Bṛhaspati himself—
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and placed him in his heart, and having paid homage to Lomaśa,
the great sage descended from the sky and, assuming the form of a brahmin, went toward the Daitya Varāṭaka who was stationed on the shore of the western ocean.
Blazing with splendor, gentle,
and endowed with serenity, the Daitya Bhūmika— whose feet reached the sky— became absorbed in meditation.
For a moment, the Brahmin gazed upon him, who was capable of enduring the trials of faith.
Then he spoke to him slowly: "O Varāṭaka, behold me!
I have come from the sky for the sake of fulfilling your desire.
Look upon me; choose a boon, O auspicious one—tell me now what you wish."
Everything resides within you who are powerful; behold me, a twice-born.
What is dear to you that could not otherwise be accomplished by force must indeed be achieved through austerity—what need is there for this [bird] which bestows such terrible suffering? (59)
"That which is to be accomplished by strength must be attained by strength alone by one whose nature is strength.
Having been addressed thus, he looked at the twice-born man and bowed mentally;
he said, "Tell me everything, and grant me my desired boon."
Then, O Rādhikā, Vṛhaspati enlightened him:
"Tell me, what do you desire? How indeed is this suffering to be overcome?
I have come to grant a boon; I am the eternal Brāhmaṇa."
Having heard this, Varāṭaka said: "Welcome indeed to you, O twice-born one!
For the sake of a kingdom, I am performing this most formidable austerity. Instruct me as I practice it, and likewise grant me such a boon. (63–64)

"Listen, O Daitya, you are powerful; how is it that you endure such hardship? For penance is the dharma of those who are dispassionate, yet you seek the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra which bestows happiness. (65)
War is the duty of kings, while for the weak, it is the bull-like penance of austerity.
You are powerful; therefore, abandon austerity and practice valor.
Indeed, the desires of the strong are fulfilled through exertion.
By austerity for those who are weak, by dharma for those who perform sacrifices,
by an army for kings, and by knowledge for the learned;
by weeping for children, and by enchantment for women.
For those whose livelihoods depend on others, success against enemies comes only through great hardship involving service and the like;
for subjects, it comes through fasting unto death directed toward the king;
and for foes, it comes only through the slaughter of their enemies. (2.36.70)
Having thus observed everything, you, being strong, should exert yourself;
abandon the thought that there might be someone else to grant me the fruit of my asceticism.
For, having become the best among the powerful, you endure this hardship in vain.

The body would become devoid of strength and would certainly not be fit for enjoyment. One who subsists on what is given by another is not praised at all; for the entire collection of sense organs quickly succumbs to weakness when afflicted by hunger. (72–73)
Old age arises quickly, or else even destruction occurs.
Therefore, having abandoned hunger, you must indeed nourish the body.
Nourishment alone is the supreme dharma; here, enjoyment is indeed the supreme liberation.
Joy is known as the abundance of happiness and indeed as heaven for one who lives;
but a life devoid of enjoyment, or a day that has passed in vain, is truly useless.
When the body perishes, how can there be happiness? For that which has vanished brings no benefit.
The fruit imagined by mere words does not come after death;
for what has not been seen by this person cannot possibly be seen by another.
Even if it were possible here, it would not have been experienced; and how could it be experienced if it were impossible?
The fool seeks the primary object of his desire at the very time it must be abandoned.
Disregarding his own body, senses, and life-force, that evil-souled person endures hardship for the sake of his own pleasure; he is indeed called a self-destroyer. (78–79)
The destruction of happiness is the destruction of the self, which leads to hell and the experience of suffering.
Abandoning hell, turn back from the destruction of the self.
By whom was this ascetic cord, consisting of austerity, fastened upon you here?
Self-harm is futile; it is a treasure-store of sin and agitation.
(81) An embodied being should consider that which is conjoined with the body as truly real, whereas everything devoid of conjunction with the body is entirely unreal. (82)
For indeed, the festivals of passion and enjoyments exist only when the body is present;
the absence of enjoyment is penance, which arises naturally in the aged.
Prosperity is attained through strength, and the earth is won through battle.
A woman is obtained through fortune, while prosperity is considered to result from effort.
From birth until death, life is seen by no one to be a rebirth; therefore, abandon your asceticism and go in peace.
From birth one is called a *jīva*, and at death one is said to be liberated (*mokṣa*).
Between these two lies heaven, which is happiness; and the body is considered the locus of the self.
O Asura, there various objects of sense are to be enjoyed perpetually.
A day that passes without enjoyment brings only loss;
once gone, it is truly gone, and it will never return again.
That which has passed unenjoyed is lost, and that which is lost through giving away is one's own fruit rendered futile. (87–88)
That which bestows its own happiness is fruitful, for it grants one's own well-being.
If one does not exert effort oneself, who else will grant it?
Therefore, O Varāṭaka, rise up from your misery and make an effort!
Virtue, however, is considered to be action that bestows happiness and consists of enjoyment.
Perform indeed such action that grants happiness; do not perform austerity that grants suffering.
A morsel of food does not enter the mouth of one who is fast asleep of its own accord. (2.36.90–91)
Wealth and other blessings inevitably come into the hand of one who exerts effort;
there is no giver of fruit, nor is there any Supreme Lord.
There is no one other than oneself—whom else do you wait for?
Abandon all this illusion and don your formidable armor.
Having assembled a vast army, bring the earth under your control.
Who is one's own and who is a stranger? That which is to be enjoyed is considered one's own.
A wise person should acquire by force that which is the supreme object of enjoyment.
Those factors that are conducive to prosperity are considered in reality to be dharma;
among them, those that are contrary should be avoided with great effort.
"Winning over the Daityas who are well-disposed toward you, acquire the kingdom.
Enjoy supreme and excellent happiness, and make the Daityas happy as well.
O Daitya, if this speech pleases you, consider [the matter of] subduing [your enemies]."
Having joined with Śukrācārya and others, and having gained strength, conquer Īśa and the others; practice the bull-like conduct of the Dānavas.
Worship is false, meditation is false, and even self-restraint is indeed false.
Vows are false, sin is false, and that which is useless to oneself is false.
(99) The Lord is false, attachment is false, and everything after death is utterly false.
Hope that is fruitless is false, for speech that is purposeless is indeed false. (2.36.100)
Strength without valor is false; valor without wisdom is false;
wisdom that bears fruit only in sorrow is false; and everything is false in one who is impotent.
If you are indeed a man, do not become a follower of falsehood.
Accomplish what must be achieved through effort quickly; do not make my words false.
Even ants and insects exert themselves, relying on the season; afflicted by the cold, they gather grains with great effort and consume them.

Lions, having attained prowess and seized wild elephants and the like, enjoy the fatness of the earth by their own strength; you too should enjoy it in that same way. For land, women, and wealth are not obtained without effort.
Fame, purity, goodness, and austerity cannot be attained without [this]. (105) Reality is not indeed obtained through other means nor by any other practice.
Having reflected upon this as you wish, O best of Dānavas, act accordingly. (106)
The swans, having left Lake Mānasa, go with effort toward the ocean;
they obtain meals of pearls and fly about.
Even the crows, though exerting themselves, obtain only stale food.
Like indolent men, those who have entered their nests do not obtain [their goals].
(108) But farmers, through exertion, obtain the fruit born of the grain;
for neither food, nor kingdom, nor the fulfillment of desires is obtained merely through asceticism. (109)
Ghee held in the mouth indeed bestows nourishment through its sweet flavor;
yet ghee cast into the fire, having turned to ashes, provides no satisfaction.
How is it that you offer your youth, vigor, and strength into the void?
What fruit will you obtain there in that saline soil of asceticism? Therefore, arise and rely upon the wisdom granted by me;
accept the dharma of the foremost among the Dānavas and abandon that of the sickly.
Thus addressed by his preceptor, O Rādhikā, the Dānava reflected for a moment,
abandoned his asceticism, and said, "I have achieved my purpose," since I have been awakened to the truth that stands as an obstacle to all hope.
"Grant me a boon; show me such grace that I may become a king.
"So be it," said the Guru. O Dānava, the Brahmin Bṛhaspati, satisfied by the excellent fruit of his penance and the restraint of his senses, abandoned his asceticism.
Accompanied by the Dānavas, he said: "Commence the effort to bring the earth under your own control from this very place, so that the kingdom may come to be yours;
may there be welfare for all, and may you attain whatever you desire. (116)

"By virtue of my boon, you shall become a king," having said this, the brahmin took his offerings and departed for heaven. Varāṭaka, for his part, gathered the lords of the Daityas and held a council.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Acquisition of All Sciences upon Beginning His Education, the Examination of His Intellect, Bṛhaspati’s Instruction on Diligence to the Daitya Varāṭaka, and the Daitya’s Abandonment of Austerity," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 37.
[The Author: Chapter 38.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhā, the Daitya spoke to the most eminent of the Daityas.
Pāvadurga, Makhkhana, Saiṃhikeya, and Coṭila;
Dhāreya, Viśvasana, and other mighty chief warriors;
as well as Airaka, Thūraka, Nīmba, Eraka, and Barbura. (1–2)
Śālmali, jhimpaṭa, kūrci, karkaśa, gṛñjaka, as well as tamalāka, garlic (laśuna), palāṇḍuka,
bhaṅgikā, ahiphena, mahājihma, vatsanāga, and phenaka.
He spoke to these leaders of the Daityas— Hiraka, Viṣakanda,
Karka, Kṛkalāsa, Śillaka, and likewise Godhaka— for the sake of obtaining the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra and for the purpose of war.

The powerful Varāṭaka spoke of Ghorakhāda, Vṛka, Dvīpa, Śītadhāra, and the leaders, for the sake of mantras and for the sake of battle. A certain brāhmaṇa, however, said to me: "Austerity is a most grievous hardship."
That is the duty of those who possess nothing, especially of those who are weak.
For those who are strong, however, battle is their duty, since through it they may obtain a kingdom;
therefore, [the conquest] of the Saurāṣṭra regions was brought under his own control.
"O best of Daityas, act swiftly so that it may be so for us!
Without battle there is no land; without a herd there is no victory.
Without exertion there is no prosperity; the herd, exertion, and battle bring happiness."
"We must also seize the wealth by force;
likewise, let the kingdom of the land of Saurāṣṭra be free from thorns.
Then they all, being immersed [in devotion], said: "Om! So be it! May victory be yours! (2.37.10–11)
Then, beginning from the western ocean, those asuras began to harass the inhabitants of the villages and seized their household wealth.

With spears, arrows, excellent swords, blades, mallets, and the like;

with water-bombs, poison-bombs, tear-gas, and poisonous winds.

Then, by means of those employing illusions, artificial puppets made of air,

To the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,

to the Lord who is a treasure-house of compassion, the refuge, the Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign.

"O Lord, the armies of Khaṭvāṅgada are indeed destroying us on all sides. Therefore, grant protection to us who have sought refuge with you, even though we are the perpetrators of offenses,

Then, in their presence, at the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa—

On the western shore of the ocean, however, there was a mountain named Varāḍa,

Then, having fashioned a reed-stalk complete with leaves upon the ocean, he granted a boon: "The attainment of Kṛṣṇa shall occur somewhere.

Thereupon, security and well-being arose for the subjects.
Bṛhaspati went to Mahendra, and Varāṭaka spoke:

Having been transformed into a mountain, he indeed waged war for the sake of the kingdom.
Other Daityas as well were firmly restrained by the rod of punishment;
then, having heard of peace, he departed, and Saurāṣṭra became happy.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the auspicious sovereignty of the Lord has been described to you. By the power of visiting sacred sites, those virtuous ones shall indeed attain liberation.
Now, I shall tell you another account that purifies even the most sinful.
O Rādhikā, listen to [the account] of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The Mlecchas of the Ḍaphphara caste, having followed the forest path and traveled by sea routes, settled in Surāṣṭra. (67–68)
Wicked ones of sinful conduct, who likewise eat the flesh of animals, who consume birds and fish, who are devoid of the duties toward wife and husband,

Constantly engaged in acts of theft, devoid of charity, righteousness, and other virtues;

Constantly devoted to the nature of hunters, dwelling forever in the forest, they were wicked men— robbers, murderers, and plunderers of all, who moved with cruelty;

Those who destroy crops and oppress those engaged in agricultural work;

Those who consume intoxicants anywhere and those who destroy their own human kin; 73–74.
Cruel, full of deceit, and revilers of the gods, the sacred law, and so forth, the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra oppressed everyone on all sides.

But the people, oppressed by them,

Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (76–77)
They reported their own suffering, born of that [demon] and destructive to all.

"Act in such a way that they shall not do so again, or else slay them on all sides"—

Then, having beheld the self-luminous Sudarśana discus,

He swiftly severed the heads from the headless trunks;

Saurāṣṭra remains happy through the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;

(103) Thus, O Rādhikā, this auspicious account of Bālakṛṣṇa has been told to you; by hearing or reciting it, one is granted heaven and liberation. (104)

"I shall go to the hermitages of those who perform austerities with wicked intent.

"An offense against my husband has been committed by you most cruelly;
therefore, may you Rākṣasas be deprived of your own characteristic marks.
Thus were those three principal sages swiftly cursed. (94–95)
In that forest region, there was a *vanaspati* tree, a *sarja* tree; for even that *rākṣasa*, though possessing the power to assume any form at will, had taken the form of wood.
At that time, he also became a mountain in the forest of trees, appearing as a lord of the sky.
Though possessing the power to assume any form at will, that Rākṣasa took the form of a black stone.
Then he became a boar with tusks,
yet he remained a Rākṣasa devoid of a penis, even while maintaining his capacity for shape-shifting.
Three of those *rākṣasa* trees were born within the forest of wooden trees;
others, the *vālakhilya* trees, being cursed, became clusters [of flowers] upon the water.
Though they possessed roots, they were devoid of branches, flourishing only with leaves.
Those Vālakhilyas, who were without physical marks, dwelt in the water with their heads submerged;
they did not eat anything other than earth, living solely on water like clusters of flowers along the Brahma-putra river and others. (2.38.100–101)
At the time of the curse, submerged in sorrow, they praised Satī with their minds:
"May that be ordained so that our deliverance may come about;
we do not know the true disposition of the high-souled Śaṅkara. (102)
"Therefore, we have committed an offense; let an end to our curse be ordained.
The wives of the sages wept and praised their mother Satī.
Then Satī spoke: "Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord."
In Saurāṣṭra, in the western region, the Lord— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Hari— is present as the son of Kambharāśrī.
Through union with Him, one’s liberation will come to pass.
"That Lord will bring about the complete deliverance of the sages.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman, deeply distressed, vanished from sight.
Then, those sons of the sages and others who were free from offense— ||| 107 ||
Other sages as well, including the Brāhmaṇas and others who were spectators there,
seeing that great upheaval which portended the dissolution of the universe,
remembered Brahmā and sought refuge in Brahmā.
The gods and others offered prayers for the pacification of the fire from the *liṅga*.
Being enlightened by Brahmā with various forms of spiritual instruction,
they [approached] the radiant one, established in Brahman, whose form is eternal Brahman.
Having recognized that you, though bound by the qualities of desire, are one who follows the ways of the vulgar, they have committed an offense; therefore, this great agitation has arisen.
It shall be pacified through the practice of the worship of the *liṅga*, and not otherwise.
"Alas, those sages are deluded, having fallen under the sway of anger!
For that Brahman which is eternally pure within the body and the self—even for one whose heart is purified by austerity or ritual action—that [Brahman] is obscured. (112–113)
Indeed, purity is the expulsion of states such as desire and anger;
therefore, the wise man should purify that mind through the practice of the yoga of knowledge.
When his mind is thoroughly purified, the person attains purity.
The sages dwelling in the hermitage were overcome by anger and desire.
For those overcome by desire and anger, sacrifice, charity, virtue, austerity, vows, penance, fortitude, and meditation—all go to fruitlessness. (115–116)
Therefore, let them go to that place, abandoning desire and anger, and worship that god Śaṅkara, who illuminates all desires. Let them indeed propitiate the Liṅga; from that, peace shall arise.
Having been addressed thus, they all departed and worshipped the *liṅga* with devotion.
That *liṅga* remained fixed in its proper place, and Śaṅkara became present there along with the *liṅga*.
Wherever this [fragment] fell, there the *jyotir-liṅgas* came into being.
"Divided into twelve forms, that divine [power] indeed bestows liberation.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the entire world attained peace.
Then those three sages also became indeed Rākṣasas born of a curse.
Then, remembering their former births, they came to Saurāṣṭra for the sake of their own liberation.
Vanaspati was born in the form of wood as the essence of the cart,
while Nabhaspati was born as a mountain in the form of stone.
Bṛhaspati became a boar with tusks;
through the yoga of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, they were then liberated from the curse.
Those divine sages, whose wealth was their austerity, praised Hari.
Furthermore, for the sake of the deliverance of all the remaining sages, the Blessed Lord spoke again and again: "Let them go there as well;
I shall come to the Dāruvana forest and deliver them from their curse."
Having mounted Garuḍa, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari himself, rescued the Vālakhilyas who were in the form of a pillar. O Rādhikā, all of them, born in the forest of wood, were performing penance.
Then all those who were in the form of sages became peaceful;
their lineages, the Vālakhilyas, became pillars within the waters.
Hari, having lifted them up and received their worship with reverence, [departed].
Accompanied by Garuḍa, he came to his own domain, the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
O Rādhā, through reciting or hearing [this], the sin of the curse is pacified.
It is indeed a marvel that even when the state of a rākṣasa had arrived, those endowed with devotion remained so.
"Indeed, liberation comes through the state of hatred; such is the illusory power (*māyā*) of the gods.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disturbance in the Garden of the Great Sages Vanaspati, Nabhaspati, and Saraspati—who had attained the state of Rākṣasas due to Satī’s curse—the Liberation from the Curse by the Lord, the Wandering of Nagna-Śaṅkara among the Hermitages of the Ascetics, the Offense Committed Against the Sages, the Falling of the Liṅga, and the Cause of the Curse," in the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 38: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 39 [[Author:
→ Chapter 40
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to this knowledge by which no austerity remains.
Formerly, when the terrible single ocean had arisen and all moving and non-moving beings had perished; (1)
There was one great egg, containing the seed of all beings,
produced from Mahāviṣṇu, within which Virāṭ shines. Having split that egg, the Blessed One brought forth the Vairāja outside.
From Vairāja arose the threefold gods: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. At that time, Brahmā, endowed with the quality of *sattva*, beheld the world as a void;
then, through his *rājasa* nature, he indeed undertook the work of creation.
He remembered the divine Darśaka, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond the senses, transcendent of the qualities (guṇas), all-pervading, and the Supreme Person;
by whom this entire universe—designated as both the stable and the conscious—is pervaded. (5)
He who knows that Great-Souled One certainly knows everything.
(6) He who knows that Supreme Self—the Puruṣa beyond the qualities, the eternal Supreme Brahman—is a knower of liberation and knows everything. (7)
What need have they for all the sacred fords or hermitages,
whose infinite mind is established in the Self alone?
The Self is a river with virtue as its bathing-ghats, truth as its water, and endowed with tranquility.
Having bathed therein, one becomes pure and meritorious; the self is not purified by mere water.
(9) The highest duty for a person is to abide in the bliss of self-knowledge. That alone is to be known by the virtuous, upon attaining which all desire ceases. (2.39.10)
There is no wealth superior to this for one who is fixed in Brahman:
equanimity, truthfulness, virtuous conduct, straightforwardness, and likewise renunciation.
Upon attaining these, one certainly reaches the supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
O Rādhā! Having known that Lord, one shall obtain the fruit of dharma.
He who is established as the all-pervading, eternal Lord within this body of water—He is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest.
That glorious young Gopāla, the son of Kambharāśrī,
exists as Bālakṛṣṇa in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
O beloved, when his fifth year was complete, [people came] to behold him.
Thus addressed, the goddess Rādhikā, full of enthusiasm, donned a brilliant attire,
rich in all splendor, fashioned from gold and rubies,
and beautifully inlaid with pearls, diamonds, and gems.
Having assumed various amorous adornments mixed with the essence of fragrances, augmented by dots, leaf-patterns, body-paints, red lac, and collyrium;
and endowed with ornaments such as strings of beads, chains, rings, garments, and cloths. (17)
Adorned with a mass of braided hair decorated with clusters of flowers and gold dust, she—
holding in her hand a vessel containing articles for the night worship—
beautified her husband Kṛṣṇa, making him splendidly radiant, consecrated, and auspicious.
He quickly drove the celestial chariot and the bull-vehicle;
its vessels were filled with fruits, flowers, delicious foods, and nectar.
Kṛṣṇa himself was the charioteer, and Śrī Rādhā herself was the rider.
Having crossed over the worlds of the lords from the glorious abode of Goloka,
and having transcended the layers beginning with Brahmā, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa descended from the sky onto the earth in Surāṣṭra, at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, in the courtyard of the temple of Bālakṛṣṇa, that splendor first pervaded the entire universe at the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s chariot;
the sun and moon were no longer visible, having been overwhelmed by its brilliance. (23)
By the splendor of Rādhā, the earth and the directions were exceedingly magnified.
Even the hermitage of Lomaśa became like the world of the Moon.
And all the maidens were endowed with forms surpassing even that of Rādhā in beauty. (24–25)
Upon seeing Rādhikā, each of those hundred Rādhās shone with a splendor exceeding her own;
yet when Rādhā saw those maidens, she became free from pride,
and in that moment, her pride in her own beauty and form melted away.
Rising up and looking toward Bālakṛṣṇa, she said to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Lord, you have indeed made my person fruitful, since I have obtained the vision of this Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (27–28)
At the commencement of the sixth year, on the morning of the eighth lunar day,
Rādhikā worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with various offerings.
Rādhikā bathed the child with the milk of Goloka.
She performed an ablution with the waters of all sacred fords and other holy sites.
Having worshipped [him] with the essences of liquid sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and the like,
she adorned him with ornaments, garments, and finery.
Then she performed the *ārārtrika* ceremony, beautiful with peacock feathers;
she placed a crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa,
gave a flute into his hand, and placed her right arm around his neck.
Having made Sutilaka laugh, Rādhikā placed a beautiful, auspicious crescent moon adorned with unbroken grains upon his forehead; she then performed the rite of *nīrājana*,
offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and prostrated herself in salutation.
He bestowed blessings, saying, "O beloved of Kāntā, may you be as handsome as Kānta.
Then Rādhā, raising her hands in a difficult-to-bear *añjali* gesture from her head,
offered food such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) brought from Goloka.
He gave balls of milk, ice-cream, and *pūrikā* made from the essence of milk;
[he offered] sweet, divine [food] and excellent curd, for he did nothing that was not pleasing to him.
Then, having fed him, he gave him delightful and auspicious betel leaf.
Then, having thus completed the worship, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself ceased;
he then reverently worshipped that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with a yellow garment, a jacket adorned with golden stars, and a crest-jewel. (38)
He gave him a helmet, a sword, and two auspicious flower-ornaments for his ears;
he placed garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers around the child's neck,
and likewise gave him two soft sandals adorned with gold.
She gave him a beautiful parasol, lovely whisks, a girdle, and earrings;
she gave him a supreme jewel of the Kaustubha variety, a pearl necklace,
and she gave the sweet-sounding flute to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
He also gave him a staff composed of supernatural power and an excellent lion-throne.
Having thus honored the young Lord, Kṛṣṇa offered this praise:
"O Witness of All, obeisance to You, the cause of all incarnations. (42–43)
O Supreme Person, Lord of the Liberated, Abode of the Supreme, salutations be unto You! From whom the present, the past, and the future shine forth in every way—
harmonious, gentle, well-ordered, and following a sequential progression.

O Unattached One, You are the Sovereign; obeisance to that Divine Being! Obeisance to You! 45. Your infinite powers are manifested here in the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Nṛsiṃha, as well as in the natures of Rādhā, Ramā, and Śrī; I bow down to that Supreme Lord. 46.
I am my own abode, Goloka, as well as Nārāyaṇa and Ramā;
from me proceed Śrī, Vaikuṇṭha, the nectar of immortality, and the state of the Truth (Satpadam).
Before me is the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma), which is eternally embodied and serves as my servant.
The lords and their incarnations are adorned by His portions and qualities;

the manifestations (vyūhas), the guardians of the lords, the world-protectors, and the great seers, as well as the gods who preside over sacrifices, are each embodied forms of a single portion of His qualities. 48–49.
I bow to that Supreme Lord who exists here in this cycle of existence;
O Inner Self, O Infinite Self, O Self of my own self, salutations, salutations to You! O Supreme Self, Witness of the world, Infinite Lord, let there be obeisance to You!
O Omniscient One, O Supreme Lord, O You who are both knowledge and the object of knowledge, homage be to You!
(5.1) O Primordial God, difficult to propitiate, O Supreme Lord, homage to You!
O Great Master of Yoga, O Holy One, O Compassionate One, homage, homage to You! (5.2)
O supreme light, O *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, O *svāhā*-utterance, homage be to you!
O all-seeing one, O creator, O you whose essence is Agni and Soma, homage be to you!
O Mahārājika, O one worshipped by the Siddhas, O Hiraṇyavāha, homage to you!
O you with beautiful hair, O you with child-like locks, O you who teach compassion—salutations be to you!
(54) O All-pervading Lord, O Performer of Sacrifice, O Lord of Sacrifice, O you who have compassion for your devotees—salutations to you!
Be gracious, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations again and again unto you! (55)
Having spoken thus, the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā bowed to the Lord and went together into the interior of the world to the presence of the venerable Kambharā.
Having bowed to her and likewise having bowed to the illustrious Rūpālakṛṣṇa, they departed.
Having received the welcome they offered and having praised the festival for their son,
Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā departed for Goloka by means of a celestial chariot.
Then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā, arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, for the sake of worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord Vāsudeva and Bhūmā arrived, filled with joy, mounted upon Garuḍa. Likewise, Mahāviṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Nara also arrived.
Śeṣanārāyaṇa, as well as Matsya and Kūrma, arrived;
Vārāha, Kapila, Hari, and Pṛthu also arrived;
likewise Dattātreya, Haṃsa, and Nṛsiṃha arrived. (2.39.60–61)
Ṛṣabha, Vāmana, and Paraśurāma arrived;
Yajña, Rāma, and the Kumāras, as well as Hayagrīva, arrived.
Nārada, the King of Kings, and the supreme lords arrived.
"Victory to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! they sang.

(63) They performed the consecration of the child’s big toe with the five nectars and the nectar of immortality; thereafter, they carried out the sprinkling with water from darbha grass and the nectar of immortality. (64)
With devotion, they honored her forehead with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains;
they fashioned a tilaka enriched with saffron and offered fragrant substances.
They placed flower garlands upon her neck and presented crowns and floral wreaths.
They offered tulasī leaves, ornaments, and chowries;
they presented an umbrella, divine sandals, and various garments as well.
They performed the nīrājana ceremony with camphor and other substances and with lighted wicks.
All the incarnations offered incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, nectar-like rice, and fruits; they also presented water and betel leaves.
They offered these most abundantly, including items produced in their own respective worlds.
Thus, for the sake of worship, even the women residing in that abode arrived with many excellent articles and honored the Lord. Having thus performed their worship, they departed for their own homes.
Then the gods, the ancestors, the sages, the seers,
and human beings beginning with the Brāhmaṇas indeed arrived for the worship of Kṛṣṇa;
having ascended divine celestial chariots, they came to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having rested on all sides along the paths of the sky, they arrived at the temple of Kṛṣṇa (72).
They worshipped Him with various offerings and gratified Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, exceedingly (73).
Then there were other lands, mountains, rivers, lakes, and oceans;
sacred fords, celestial trees, creepers, and flower-clusters;
forest goddesses, shrubs, and various other elements as well.
They arrived for the sake of worshiping Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and performed the rites of honor.
Then the Yakṣas, Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, Kimpuruṣas, Bhāṭas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and celestial women [also came]. (75–76)
The Māgadhas, bards, heralds, Vidyādharas, Pannagas,
and others came for the sake of worship at the festival of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
They performed worship, and the dancers executed their dances.
Fine musical instruments were played and singers sang at that time;
storytellers recounted his story, and dancers performed their dances.
The officiants performed the sacrifice, and the virtuous engaged in silent recitation.
The noble elders gave blessings and auspicious benedictions;
and then Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, the sage Lomaśa,
as well as the other sages present there and the daughters of Brahmā [offered their prayers].
They performed the worship of Śrī Hari and joined him with blessings.
Then the father gratified all those honored guests from every side with excellent foods such as milk-porridge and sweetmeats (laḍḍukas).
And after Hari had fed all those who had arrived,
he then caused gifts to be given to the brahmins, the female servants, and the attendants,
as was appropriate for worthy recipients and according to what each mendicant had requested.
He gave jewels, gold, silver, sweet foods, and even garments;
rings, ornaments, vessels, and wealth—giving all these repeatedly and according to the desire of everyone who had arrived. (84–85)

Then, when everyone had departed for their own respective abodes and homes, Lomaśa, accompanied by the maiden, joyfully returned to his own hermitage. Thereafter, other Brahmins and others belonging to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī [also departed].
Having arrived, they worshipped the Supreme Lord, Hari, with love.
Afterwards, they went to their respective homes, and a great wonder occurred.
Listen, O Rādhikā, a certain couple had also arrived there.
The woman was the color of collyrium and the man’s body was covered with leprosy.
Having bowed to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the boy said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, perform the deliverance from sin for us two, who have fallen and are devoid of lineage."
Although Hari knew [the truth], he questioned those two, who were dejected in mind:
"Who are you? Speak; what sin was committed, and how did this pain come about?
Nara replied: "I was a brahmin, Devāyana by name. (2.39.90–91)

In Gaurjara and in the city of Śrīpattana, this beautiful woman of mine and I were both devoted to the worship of the gods and dedicated to our daily rites. Afflicted by the cold, yet intent on worship, we performed our rituals without bathing. ||92||
Then, due to that fault, their lifespan reached its end.
They died suddenly from fever and were both born together in the house of a dog-cooker (outcaste). There, in that very same city, they were married once again.

O Destroyer of Sin! Knowing through the power of our dream that we two, Kuṣṭhika and Kṛṣṇa, are suffering and remember our past births, [we recognize] that you are Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava. O Lord Nārāyaṇa, shake off our sin and grant us liberation!
"O Lord, today is the day for you to grant liberation to those who are bound.
You are known among the people as the remover of the sins of sinners.
Having heard this, we have indeed come on foot to seek refuge in you. (96–97)
Having heard this, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is supremely compassionate and the destroyer of sins, spoke with mercy to those two oceans of grace: "O Rādhikā,
having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and having drunk that water..."
"Then, having performed a circumambulation, drink the nectar of our feet.
Having become purified, you two shall go to the world of Brahmā, O you who are beyond human measure.
Having heard this, they then followed exactly what was said.
Instantly assuming divine bodies and mounting celestial chariots,
they attained the fruit of a hundred thousand and more than a hundred thousand sacrifices and ascended to heaven.
[101] Starting from Śrīpattana and extending as far as Kuṅkumavāpikā—
For as many steps as one takes in circumambulation, so much indeed is the fruit of sacrifice obtained.
Such is the fruit gained even by approaching holy men who are beloved by Śrī; how much more so, then, in the presence of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa? (10.2–103)
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari is to be served, and His saintly devotees are also to be served.
Holy fords, sacred fields, and religious observances that bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices are to be served;
by approaching them, the merit of a horse sacrifice is produced at every step.
Thus were those two made and released by Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
On the auspicious festival day of the eighth lunar day at the commencement of the sixth year,
through both reciting and hearing this, liberation and ultimate release shall likewise come to pass.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival and Worship Performed by Devas, Humans, and Others for the Manifestation of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa on the Eighth Day of the Lord’s Sixth Year, as Well as the Liberation from the State of a Cāṇḍāla of the Brāhmaṇa Devāyana and His Wife," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, regarding that Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, they took up residence in the presence of the Lord on the western bank of the lake at Setukocchraya. There they established Dattātreyatīrtha and likewise Vārāhatīrtha.
Kūrmatīrtha, Matsyatīrtha, and Kapilatīrtha; likewise Haritīrtha, Pṛthutīrtha, and that named Vāsudeva;
Haṃsatīrtha, Dattātreyatīrtha, and Nṛsiṃhatīrtha.
The holy ford named Ṛṣabha, the holy ford called Yogeśvara,
the Vāmana holy ford, and thereafter the auspicious Paraśurāma holy ford;
the Yajña holy ford, the Rāma holy ford, and the holy ford known as Hayaśiras.
The Sanatkumāra-tīrtha, the tīrtha known as Nārada,
the Vyāsa-tīrtha, the Kṛṣṇa-tīrtha, and likewise the supreme Buddha-tīrtha;
the Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha, the Viṣṇu-tīrtha, and Śrī Puruṣottama.
There is the holy ford created by Mahāviṣṇu, known as Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
the Ardhanārīśvara Tīrtha, and the supremely auspicious Lakṣmī Tīrtha,
where I bathed together with you, O Rādhikā.
Rādhātīrtha and Kṛṣṇatīrtha are located at Aśvapaṭṭasara;
they destroy the heat of sin, grant liberation, and bestow residence in the divine abode.
O Rādhikā, in this way these holy places originated there.
Then, in the sixth month of the year, the sages dwelling in Mahākālavana and the holy men (tīrthikas) arrived at the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭa.
They were Samīraṇa, Pavamāna, Santāraṇa, and Barbura.
Voḍhu, Ghanabheda, Dyuviśrāma, Paṅkila,
Nīlakarṇa, Alarka, Puṇḍarīka, Kalāyana,
Vītihotra, Camasa, Parṇakutsa, and Aśvapāṭala. (12)
Bhāllaveya, Corjavrata, and also Āśvalāyana;
Pārṣṇi, Ada, Sumantu, Aśokākṣa, Abhayākṣaka, Brahmastamba, Kūpyavāla, and also Cetanabrahma. (13–14)
The goddesses are Śrī, Kamalā, Pṛthvī, Rāṇikā, Amaraputrikā,
Dhanyeśvarī, Satīśā, Devānikī, Kṛṣṇikā, Pampā,
Nārāyaṇī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gaṇḍakī, and Kuśā. 15.

Then, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, Sarasvatī, Hiraṇyā, Svarṇarekhā, Gomatī, Gautamī, Vallī, and Vṛkṣā— concentrated in mind— nourished even the principles (tattvas). || 16–17 ||
In the morning, the deities performed their ablutions in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having returned home, they bowed to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then they bowed to the Ṛṣi Lomaśa, and the maidens bowed to them as well.
All were fed, honored, saluted, and likewise worshipped.
[They reached] the western shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, adorned with kunda flowers,
devoid of groves and thickets, and possessing the majesty of its vast expanse.
Devoted to their daily rites, they went at midday to that place, which was rich with *pārijāta* groves and charming with fragrant trees;
there, it was beautified by *gundraka*, *dāḍima*, and *tintiḍī* trees.
On the beautiful ground shaded [by trees] near the temple of Bālakṛṣṇa, they took supreme rest in the evening; then the sage Urvajavrata recited the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. (22–23)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Kālajit, Pañcaśikha, Lomaśa, Āsuri, Jamadagni, Hanumān, Jāmbavat,
Vibhīṣaṇa, Vyāsa, Prahlāda, Bali, and Ṛbhu.
Gālava, Kṛpa, and others who possess a lifespan of a hundred kalpas—
those who live for seven kalpas and those who live for ten thousand kalpas—
sat in the assembly, seated at the head of the listeners of the discourse.
There, the Lord Kambharānanda, together with his parents,
sat upon a central throne surrounded by knowers of Brahman and shone resplendent.
The gods, the celestial beings, along with the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and humans [were present].
Accompanied by a multitude of goddesses, they listened to the auspicious narrative.
And the great sage Ūrjavrata, a lord whose lifespan was a hundred thousand kalpas,
recounted the primordial auspiciousness of the perceptible Hari.
When there was no single imperishable syllable, nor even the abode of the cows,
nor even Vaikuṇṭha, that place of immortality;
When even the abode did not exist,
and when the creation of the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth had not yet occurred, He was already present.
May that beginningless one, who possesses the beautiful form of Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Bāla, be mine; salutations to the Bhūmikā.
He who, in his own supreme abode, is accompanied by liberated souls and others who are his powers—

May the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be the ground for the setting forth of my speech—He who is served by seekers with manifest qualities, attributes, and divine manifestations; He who, though delighting in both ways, is perceived here as one, like a child. (3.1)
If the Inner Self is present here within this discourse of the sages,
then this child of Kambharā— who appears like a human being—
is one whose play is free from clamor and who bears the weight of the entire universe within his belly.
May he who resides at Gopālakṛṣṇālaya grant fruitfulness to all people.
May this beautiful Kuṅkumī tank, the Aśvapaṭṭa lake—the foremost remover of the world's sins—be victorious upon the earth. ||32||
May Lomaśa, honored by the sages and foremost among the virtuous, be victorious;
and may the Lakṣmī-saṃhitā, the bestower of liberation, be triumphant.
From the beginning, through the middle, and unto the end, [resides] the eternal Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa.
May this Supreme Brahman, who is sung of here, bestow auspiciousness.
May the venerable elder brother, the contented sister Satī, the wise brother Śuka, and likewise the younger brother Śrīvallabha, grant blessings. (34–35)
May his mother, Kambharālakṣmī, his father, Gopālakṛṣṇaka,
and his one hundred and twelve wives, together with their children, be victorious!
May Svayaṃprakāśa himself be the preeminent disciple within the circle of disciples.
There were other hosts of disciples numbering ten million, and women numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion;
Lomaśa, the chief among gurus, and other sages who know Hari;
we bow to those born of the lineage of Brahmā, who are moving embodiments of sacred pilgrimage sites and are honored by all seekers of truth. (37-38)
Manifest and yet transcendent, this child who is greater than the vastness of the non-child—
may Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, grant us our desired welfare. May the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Māṇikī, the Lord of Pārvatī, and the Lord of Prabhā [bestow it upon us].
May the beloved of Śrī Rādhā and Rukmiṇī always grant auspiciousness.
Let the sages know him as the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest, Kṛṣṇa, the Master, the Supreme Controller, who is without beginning or end. 2.40.40–41.
For by him, in ancient times, the Vedas were recovered from the ocean;
likewise, in former times, the goddess Earth was lifted up with the tip of his tusk.
Furthermore, Śeṣa is indeed supported upon his back by him.
By him, Nārāyaṇa himself was borne upon his own couch;
by him, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya was offered for the sake of self-illumination;
and by him, in ancient times, knowledge was offered to Brahmā by Śrī Hari.
The Daityas were also utterly destroyed by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
he, Hari, has assumed this form consisting of the military array (vyūha).
By him the earth was protected, and indeed, he became the king of kings.
Having performed such ascetic penance, he indeed became this very Haṃsa in former times.
He was that very Keśarī, the slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
devoted to virtuous conduct and intent on compassion, he lived as a forest-dweller.
The one of short form is the seizer of the earth, and he is indeed the younger brother of Mahendra.
Here, these protectors were wounded by this wise man with a blow from a rib-stick.
This one is indeed the consumer of clarified butter in the fire, and this one is also the bestower of the yoga of rain.
"For he shall indeed lead the Daityas dwelling in the southern region to the realm of Yama.
He who was formerly the son of Brahmā, the best of the virtuous, appearing in the form of a child—
he is that very same supreme among men who now exists here in the guise of a youth."
He is the great sage Vīṇāmagna, the distributor of Vedic knowledge;
he is indeed Rādhākānta, served by Satī, and an ocean of awakening.
He is the Lord, the Beloved, the Husband, the Protector, the Guardian, the Progenitor, and the Father.
The King is the witness and the inner self; this child is honored by the sages.
Therefore, worship him with heartfelt devotion, for he is the giver of the eternal abode.
I take refuge in that Supreme Lord, the unborn one who is dear to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Salutations to that Supreme Brahman, the Great Soul, the Lord of the entire universe;
salutations to Him who is served by gods, daityas, lords, liberated souls, and others.
Salutations to the one who possesses all senses, whose self pervades all, and who is the inner controller.
To him whom the singers of the *gāyatrī* sing, and whom those who are fully dedicated worship;
to him in whom everything—the cause, the effect, the action, and the means, as well as the deity and the assembly—resides; salutations to that Playful One! (55–56)
Salutations to the peaceful one, the supreme lord, who holds the conch, the discus, the banner, and the lotus;
salutations also to the wielder of the trident, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the wielder of the spear.
Salutations to you, the possessor of auspiciousness, the one marked by the fish, the all-powerful lord.
Homage be to the peerless one who bears the banner of his own true nature!
(58) Homage to the one who is delightful in manifold ways, and homage to the most skillful one!
Homage to you, the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya, and homage to you, the proclaimer of Yoga! (59)
Salutations to you, the proclaimer of the Vedas; salutations again and again to you, the proclaimer of logic (Nyāya).
Salutations to you, the proclaimer of liberation; salutations to the bestower of instruction. Salutations to the proclaimer of Mīmāṃsā; salutations to the bestower of the nectar of immortality.
Salutations to the one of golden form; salutations to the one with the splendor of the campaka flower.
Salutations to the one worthy of praise, to the mantra, to the embodied soul of all beings.
Salutations to the priest (hotṛ), to the one established in virtuous conduct and vows, to the one of supreme beauty.
Homage to you, O long-eyed one, the bestower of all desires;
homage to you, whose eye is within the sky, the eye of all.
Homage to you who are distinguished by both difference and non-difference, the transcendent one.
Salutations to you, whose form is both shade and heat, and who are the essence of tranquility.
Salutations to Brahman, the single-formed one who delights in the sacrificial portion. Salutations to the protector of the daughter of Pañcāla and the bestower of Bhaguputrī.
Salutations to the Lord of the daughter of Anaraṇya, salutations to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī.
Salutations to You, the giver of food, the Lord of food, whose very self is the treasury.
Salutations to Him who belongs to a lineage suited to children and who delights in the playful pastimes of a child.
Homage to you who are both child and elder; homage to you with beautiful hair!
(67) Homage to you who delight in the six rites and who possess a thousand ornaments;
homage to you, the refuge of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa! (68)
Salutations to the one who is the refuge of infinite qualities, sovereignty, and majesty;
salutations to you who possess the splendor of clouds and the radiance of the moon, sun, and stars.
You are the food and the eater of food, the consumer of the ripened, and the purifying fire.
You are water, you are satisfaction, and you are bliss; O Ānanda, salutations to You!
(2.40.70) The viviparous, the oviparous, the sweat-born, and the soil-born—all these have been created by You.
O Lord of Incarnations, You alone are the fourfold multitude of living beings. (71)
You alone are indeed the creator of this world of the moving and the unmoving, its protector, and its destroyer;
the wise call you Brahman, the supreme goal of those who know Brahman.
You are the supreme light of the mind, and you are the light even of lights.
The exponents of Brahman call you the swan, the tree, and the honey-bee;
likewise, the sages say that you are the performer of sacrifices and one who delights in their fruits.
You are eternally recited in the hymns of the Vedas and the collections of Upaniṣads.
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the universe, you alone exist as men, women, the stationary and the moving, and even as animals.
You alone are the masses of clouds, the lightning, the thunderbolt, and the roar of thunder.
You are the year, the seasons, the month, and even half a month;
you are the ages (yugas), the moments (nimeṣas), the divisions of time (kāṣṭhās), as well as the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) and the planets.
You are the one who bears the spear, the mace, the discus, the sword, the thunderbolt, and the bow.
You are the cutter, the breaker, the striker, the thinker, the leader, and the eternal one.
The oceans, rivers, mountains, trees, lakes, and the earth;
creepers, grass, medicinal herbs, climbing plants, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds—[all these are You].
Time is the undertaking of vast deeds and qualities, and the source of flowers and fruits.
You alone are the seed, the sprout, the leaf, the stalk, and the node; the stem, the flower, and the fruit as well; and you are indeed the sap, the fragrance, and all else. (2.40.80)
O Supreme Lord, you alone are the ground of all that is ground, the sweet, and the beloved;
you are the purity of purities and the auspiciousness of auspicious things.
