You alone are the foremost of all risings and the supreme goal.
You are the vital breaths, the winking of eyes, yawning, sneezing, and likewise the impact [of sound];
you are the teacher and the awakener of Brahmā, Kāla, Yama, and Agni; you are the four ages, the four Vedas, and the one who sets in motion the fourfold sacrificial office.
He is the leader of the four stages of life and likewise the creator of the four social orders;
he is the master craftsman, the calculator, the mother, and the initiator of all arts.
He is *svāhā*, *svadhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the salutation, and likewise praise.
You alone are the prayer and that which is to be prayed for; salutations, salutations to you!
(85) You alone are the one of hidden vows, the one of secret penance, the savior, and the supporter of the earth;
you are the creator, the ordainer, and the uniter; salutations, salutations to you! (86)
You alone are Brahmā, Śambhu, Viṣṇu, Virāṭ, and Bhūmā;
you are austerity, truth, celibacy, rectitude, and contentment.
You alone are the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, as well as the creation of individual souls and the creation of the Lord.
You are the creation of Brahmā, the cosmic order (*ṛta*), initiation, and self-restraint; you are Janārdana.
You alone are the beloved, the dear one, the husband, and the master—Nārāyaṇa.
You are also the point (*bindu*), the resonance (*nāda*), the sound (*dhvani*), Brahman, reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and the sudden flash of intuition (*sphoṭa*).
You alone are Paśyantī, Parā, Madhyamā, and the distinguished Vāk;
you are Gaurī, Bhūmi, the devotee of Brahmā, the virtuous one, Satī, and the servant.
You alone abide as everything that is subject to control; apart from you, there is nothing, indeed, nothing at all.
O Janārdana, you are the moon, fire, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, old age, disease, mental anguish,
physical illness, peace, and medicine. You are the drinker of Soma, sweetness itself, the Lord of the Maruts, and the Lord of the Universe.
You alone are Amṛtāśī and Jagannātha, and you are indeed Kuṅkumeśa;
you are Akṣateśa and Gaṇeśa, and you are Mukteśa, the Supreme Lord.
You are the drinkers of poison, fire, and Soma, as well as the drinkers of milk and butter.
You are the drinker of clarified butter, the drinker of honey, and the consumer of all things, O Grandfather.
You alone are the golden-seeded one, the foremost of persons, and the solitary one.
You are the female, you are the male, and you are the third state, devoid of the two conditions.
Though you transcend the three states of existence, you manifest within those very three states;
you are the child, the youth, and the elder, the creator of the universe with decayed teeth.
The moon and the sun are your two eyes, and Sarasvatī is your tongue.
Day and night, as well as both moments of blinking, are their dwellings and abodes.
O child, neither Brahmā, nor Śiva, nor Viṣṇu, nor those ancient seers are able to know their majesty in its true essence.
You abide encompassing millions upon billions of liberated male lords and sovereigns;
you alone are both the internal and the external.
You are eternally beyond the great darkness (mahat-tamas) and even beyond the Imperishable (akṣara).
In the supreme abode you shine as the Supreme Lord; here, you manifest in embodied form.
Salutations to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, who have conquered their vital breaths, who abide in purity, and who dwell in Brahman, perceive as the Supreme while practicing yoga.
Those subtle forms which are yours cannot be shown;
salutations again and again to all those forms of yours here.
O Lord, compassionate toward devotees, you always abide among your devotees.
Salutations to You, whose hair is the clouds, whose channels are the rivers, and whose belly contains the great oceans;
salutations to You who lie upon the golden waters and perform ascetic penance. Salutations to those conscious beings, both stationary and moving, who are the size of a thumb.
Those who [dwell] in rivers, in oceans, on mountains, and in caves;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in dense wildernesses;
at crossroads, on carriage-roads, in squares, and in assembly halls.
In elephant stables, horse stables, and chariot sheds; in dilapidated gardens and dwellings (1.06);
and those who are also among the five elements, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, in the moon, in the sun, in Satyaloka, and in the fourfold realm known as Vaikuṇṭha (1.07).
Those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and those who have gone beyond that—
O Keśava, they are your devotees, your servants, and your attendants. O Mādhava, the female slaves are truly your devotees and your handmaidens.
Salutations to them, salutations to those women, and salutations to both, O Acyuta!
To those whose number, measure, and even form do not exist—
to those innumerable hosts of liberated souls, let there be constant salutation.

"Be gracious, O you who possess the form of a child; reveal your own true nature. Let our hearts be fixed on you alone—may this be the fruit of your sacred teachings. Thus, O Rādhikā, was Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa praised by him.
At the commencement of the discourse, being pleased, he granted his own vision [to them].
Indeed, every single hair-pore of him was filled with the radiance of ten million divine suns;
all his incarnations were within his form, and all abodes of light resided in him.
All the lords, sages, gods, and millions of humans;
the Daityas, who are the armor of the universe—all move within a single hair of Him.
There are millions of liberated ones, millions of beauties, and millions of great lords who protect Him.
In whose womb all splendors shine, and in whom all dissolutions and all creations reside;
in whom all classes of souls appear through divine vision. (1.15–1.16)
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself revealed that supreme, divine, embodied form, beautiful in its youthful splendor.
Smiling and inquiring after their welfare, he bestowed upon them his divine vision.

Having observed this, all the sages and others who were intent on hearing [the scripture] beheld the Lord in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. Having seen that heart-pleasing form never before seen, they placed Hari within their hearts.
Having demonstrated this, he again offered a rebuttal:
"Just as a child behaves here, so did the child become once more.
Seeing it thus, the eminent sages considered themselves to have accomplished their purpose.

They attained supreme bliss, as if they were constantly dwelling in nirvāṇa. Thus, having directly beheld the venerable Supreme Lord, the worthy recipient of the Saṃhitā, they then eternally listen to the nectar of his discourse.

In this way, for three months, that most auspicious Pārāyaṇa took place in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; O Rādhikā, it then became the bestower of liberation. At the conclusion of the narration, having performed the Phālgunī rite and established all the holy places in their entirety, [he departed].
The sages also took up residence right there, each by his own name.
This very place is celebrated as Saṃhitātīrtha and Koṭitīrtha;
it is likewise known as Ṛṣitīrtha, Kathātīrtha, and Divyatīrtha.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Divine Vision, the Hymns of the Sages, and the Holy Places Originating from the Dwellings of the Sages," occurring in the context of hearing the narrative of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā* performed by the sages during the *Ūrjavrata* in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 41. Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 41.
[The Author: Chapter 042.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to [the account] of that very Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
This supreme, divine, purifying, and wondrous narrative:
There was a righteous king named Kanthādharā who ruled his own kingdom in Saurāṣṭra. 1–2.
For that king was a devotee of Śambhu and a worshiper of Sthāṇu;
dwelling in the Siṃha forest as the powerful lord of Koṭīnārā,
he propitiated Śambhu through austerity and obtained the Kāladaṇḍa weapon.
Where there is punishment, the noose of Yama does not exist.
Likewise, seeing punishment, the messenger of Yama and Time himself turn back.
A king [should worship] Śaṅkara, the lord of the earth, constantly with a thousand lotuses.

Having performed worship at dawn, he recited the mantra "Oṃ namo kālakālāya saṃkarṣaṇāya śambhave | mṛtyave yāmyavārāya nirbhayaṃ padam arpaya ||" one hundred times while standing on one foot. || 6 ||
Thus he mutters the mantra, repeating it constantly.
Then, with a single repetition, he offers one hundred and eight oblations.
In the afternoon, however, he eats only cooked vegetables, devoid of seeds.
He accepts only what is necessary for the maintenance of his body, always sleeping on the ground at night;
even while in the prime of youth, he never desires a woman.
While the king was thus conducting himself, he remained full of majesty.
In the kingdom, there was no theft, fear, disease, or adultery.
The subjects partook of sacrificial offerings, avoiding liquor, meat, and forbidden foods.
On both the thirteenth days of the lunar fortnights, they performed the ritual bathing at Somatīrtha.
Likewise, he performs the auspicious sight and service of Bhavanātha,
bathes in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, beholds Lomaśa,
and thus completes his pilgrimage before returning home.
He causes the water from his pilgrimage to the sacred sites to reach the millions of people in Koṭīnārī again and again for the sake of the welfare of the subjects. Furthermore,
on the full moon day of every month, he provides sweet food to the people.

He gives water to all, from children and the elderly down even to beasts and birds, as well as to fish, insects, winged creatures, and trees. Thus, for one devoted to dharma, both the kingdom and the subjects are free from fear.
But when he had gone elsewhere himself, no fear remained in the kingdom.
There was no untimely death, nor likewise any fear of spirits.
When time had passed in this manner, a desire arose in him toward Puṣkara.
He went there to perform a sacred ablution (*tīrtha*), and a month passed while he was there.
The king propitiated Vasiṣṭha with excellent service.
Vasiṣṭha said, "May you live long," and the king replied, "So be it."
Having attained supreme longevity and having obtained infinite welfare,
the king, after bestowing gifts at the sacred fords, bathing, and worshipping Brahmā,
then bathed in the Sarasvatī and worshipped the Siddhas. (2.41.20)

Having bathed at Aśvapaṭṭasara, he quickly returned to his own home. On the way, he saw in a dream a Brahmin’s son being led away by someone of dark complexion; the king thought, "I shall protect him. (21)
As soon as he reflected and ran with haste to protect him,
his sleep dissolved and he perceived that nothing remained;
filled with apprehension, he quickly returned toward the kingdom.
Upon reaching the village boundary, his entire dream turned into reality;
for in that kingdom,
the son of a brahmin who was the village priest had met his death at the end of his lifespan while his father was still alive.
Seized by the messengers of Yama and led to the realm of Yama in an instant—
just then the king arrived there immediately after completing his journey.
Upon learning of the weeping and lamentation, the king was indeed overcome with grief.
Having fully understood the account and realized that death was indeed death,
and having taken up his staff and Śaṅkara, he consoled that brahmin; then,
the performer of desired deeds departed behind him to bring back both the son and the brahmin.
Wherever he goes taking his staff, there his path exists.
Since the movement of one who holds the staff extends across the earth, water, fire, air, ether, darkness, and the planets—throughout the fourteen worlds. (28–29)
Without the staff, he would have no way to reach the surface of the earth;
with the staff of Śiva, that king traveled through the sky to the abode of Yama.
When his human body was indeed restrained by the messenger of Yama, [he departed].
Touched by the king’s staff, the messenger of Yama fell far away.
Having fallen and then risen again, the follower of Yama, overcome with fear, ran toward King Yama and reported his own defeat. (3.1–3.2)
"O Lord, some being possessing a human body has arrived from the city of Yama;
he was traveling with his staff, but I blocked him with great speed.
Nevertheless, he was not stopped at all, for he touched me with his staff."
"I was so utterly defeated that I felt as if struck by a thunderbolt.
Falling to the ground and then rising again, O Lord of Yama, I have come here to report what has occurred: who is this person, and for what reason has he arrived? (34-35)
"I do not know, O Great King; consider therein as you wish.
Having been addressed thus by the messenger of Yama, Dharmarāja then summoned the one named Mṛtyu and commanded him to exile [him].
Death went and swiftly seized the king with his hand.
He said to the king, "Go! If Death is not yours here," and upon hearing this, the king raised his staff against Death.
Mṛtyu leapt down onto the ground and fled swiftly;
he reported the man’s strength to King Yama.
Then, at that very moment, Yama dispatched Mahākāla.
"Who is this, and from where has he come? Bring him into my presence.
Being thus addressed, Kāla himself approached his presence.
Having bowed, he said: "Who is here? The Dharmarāja desires to know."
The king said: "I am the lord of Koṭīnāra in Saurāṣṭra, and I have come here to see the young Brahmin.
Where does he stay, and how was he brought here by a messenger of Yama?"
"O giver of honor, it is for this reason that I have come here to inquire.
Time said: 'Come, inform King Yama;
he will give you an answer, for I am indeed not the one suited for that.'"
Having spoken thus, Kāla took the king along with him and presented him before Yamarāja; Yamarāja also received him.
Having offered a welcome, he asked the reason for his arrival.
The king bowed to Dharma and spoke to the young brahmin:
"I have come seeking him; where is that young brahmin?
His father is weeping most piteously on account of his son. (46–47)
"He has but one son, and he likewise met his death.
To dispel his grief, O protector of the earth, I spoke thus to that priest:
'O King of Dharma, I wish to bring back and give him his child again.'"
"That corpse remains guarded until I go to him.
Therefore, give back the son of the twice-born; grant my request.
Yama then spoke to the messenger standing there and to Yama himself with haste.
"Summon Citragupta along with his records for the sake of this Brahmin.
Thus summoned, Citragupta arrived there with the records.
[The king asked: "Behold, how much lifespan remains for this young Brahmin?"
Citragupta said, "Since his full lifespan has been completed and he is therefore dead,
there is not even the slightest bit of life remaining for him to enjoy within the body of this brahmin.
King Yama, having heard that, informed the king.
O King, there is no life-force remaining in his body to stay or to experience [the fruit];
he is dead, and you shall not obtain [it]. No principle of karma applies here:
"Whatever was done by whom, of what nature, to whom, for whom, from whence, and in what manner. || 54 ||
"Whatever is intended for whatever purpose, all that shall be exactly so and not otherwise.
The King asked: "What sinful deed was committed by this boy, by which his life-breath became a messenger of Yama?"
Then Citragupta spoke at the command of King Yama:
"This man was a brahmin and a constant worshipper of the Lord;
indeed, he performed his ablutions in the cool [waters] within the temple of Vāsudeva. (57)
He caused the god to rise up; yet by that very sin, his destination in the world of Yama was certain. Without punishment, he is not purified.
He possesses no merit for the sake of humanity, nor does he have a future life.
"How will you take him away, O Indra among kings, without the labor of the brahmin boy?
The king replied, "I shall give him my own renewed life;
through the blessing of Vasiṣṭha, long life was obtained by me at Puṣkara."
"From the midst of that [account], I grant him ten thousand years of human life.
Having said this and released water from his hand, he granted him life;
Citragupta then recorded for him ten thousand years of excellent living.
The two Dharmarājas gave him a child who was to live for ten thousand years.
Then he asked the king, "From where did you obtain this strength,
that you have arrived here through the sky in a human body?"
"Yama, Death, and likewise Time, who are invincible, have been overcome by you.
Tell me, by what power was this supreme sovereignty attained?
Having heard this, the king then replied, "By the power of Śaṅkara."
"The power has been attained by the King of Dharma, by whom I have been seen here;
and even though I am but a child, this has been obtained through the grace of the great ones.
Then the King of Dharma said, "O Lord of the Earth, give me my staff."
The king said: "Indeed, all my power of truth resides in this staff.
O Bull, if the staff is lost, I have no means of moving through the air.
Therefore, I will not give up the staff; for this staff belongs to Saṃkarṣaṇa."
"Time itself remains as the destroyer; what then can be said of another?
If I were to apply my staff to you, your destruction would be certain.
Having spoken thus to Dharmarāja, the king prepared to apply that staff.
He let down his own hand, and at that moment the bull fell into agitation.
His seat also shook, and Dharma bowed down to that king.
Strength is the strength of the gods; it is long-lasting, for true strength is indeed not mere physical power.
Then the King of Dharma thought thus and consoled the monarch:
"Do not act in this way, O Indra among kings; you are worthy of honor, for the gods have looked upon you.
By the grace of the Destroyer of Time (Śiva), everything is now at your disposal."

Therefore, O Indra among kings, I give you my daughter Hṛdḍakāyinī—this lovely woman, beautiful of form, whose every limb has blossomed with youth—who, upon seeing you, desires you; accept her as your beloved. (73–74)
Having spoken thus and ascertained his strength, the king gave him that maiden Hṛdḍakāyinī,
who was to become his wife, as well as the son of the Brahmin;
and taking them both, he traveled through the air by means of a vehicle provided by Dharma.
He arrived at the city named Koṭīnāra in Saurāṣṭra.
That celestial chariot, equal to the sun and full of splendor, slowly descended from the sky near the house of that very brāhmaṇa. || 76-77 ||

Having seen the virtuous wife and the Brahmin’s son, who were accompanied by celestial women, adorned with divine furnishings, perfumed by various sovereign powers and spiritual attainments, and fearless of Yama, the people [were amazed]. (78)
They joyfully raised shouts of "Victory! and cries of "Hail! toward the king.
The king gave his son to that brahmin and bowed down before him;
at that time, he became known there by the name of the sage Vṛṣaparvan.
Vṛṣaparvan rose up; he entered the dead body.
The brahmin became pleased with the subjects and gave them his blessings.
The son of the brahmin rose up, but he did not bow to the elders again and again.
The king performed a sacrifice for his parents and himself;
having placed his own queen, the daughter of Yama, at the forefront as Hṛddhakāyinī,
the monarch offered oblations, gifts, sacrificial fees, and meals.
Seeing whatever was given, the queen blazed up within;
she was dark-natured, arrogant, and intent solely on her own self-interest.
She was radiant with her own splendor, exceedingly greedy, and opposed to the welfare of others.
During the acts of giving, feasting, and fire-offerings, Hṛddhakāyinī repeatedly said to the king: "O King, do not incur such expenditure.
You are the Supreme Brahman; you are indeed Nārāyaṇa himself. (82–86)
You are Viṣṇu, you are Śiva, you are Brahmā, and you are indeed Prajāpati.
You are the enjoyer, you are the creator, you are Agni, and you are the Lord of Heaven.
You are the vessel, you are the supreme teacher, you are the sacrifice, and you are the ultimate refuge.
You are the Lord of *svāhā* and the Lord of *svadhā*; you are the ground of the *vaṣaṭ* call.
You are the *hotṛ* priest and you are the sacrificer; what other god is superior to you?
Therefore, O Lord, you alone exist as the supreme reality of all. (88–89)

Having abandoned the Lord himself, who is present here before one's very eyes, as well as one such as you traveling in a celestial chariot, and the husband of Yamarāja’s daughter whose sovereignty has increased—who else in this world is worthy of worship? Maheśvara! [2.41.90]
Therefore, recognize yourself as the supreme reality, the Lord of Sacrifice.
You are capable of slaying Time and likewise slaying Death;
you exist as the Lord, able to restore the dead to life.
Neither Indra, nor Varuṇa, nor Pavana, nor Kubera, nor Agni, nor Nirṛti—nor indeed any of the guardians of the quarters or the protectors of the world—are there any like you, O beloved.
Everything in this world is under your control; whom else, then, do you serve?
Abandon sacrifice as well as charity; abandon attachment to the world beyond.
Cherish your own happiness, for know that it is indeed granted by me through service.
Service to one's own Self is merit, and the tormenting of one's own Self is sin.
"Know that the sweet words of your own beloved are one thing, while any other is bitter and brings destruction.
Knowing this, rule over the supreme kingdom gathered within your own mind.
Thus did she, whose body was of pure love, constantly speak to him, O Rādhikā.
He too, through the fault of association with her, gradually fell into atheism.
Virtue departs from one’s side in stages—during sleeping, eating, traveling, touching, holding breath, looking, and acting. (97–98)
In living together, in conversation, in study, in kissing,
in eating what is prescribed for the learned, and among people, the sin of men is transmitted.
[99] Also in inhaling air from above and in wearing wet clothes.
When water for drinking is given, the intellect proceeds to a state multiplied by that [number].

Through the influence of hunger, the intellect becomes cruel; through the influence of enemies, it becomes ruined; and through the influence of a beloved, the fluctuating intellect becomes an object of enjoyment. (2.41.100–101)

Through association with the virtuous, the mind always attains a state of goodness; through association with the teacher, it attains humility; and through association with servants, it attains the nature of a master.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, the king’s mind underwent a complete transformation.
She became intent solely on her own self-interest, as Hṛṅkukāyinī said.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of King Kaṇṭhādharas attainment of Kālayaṣṭi through devotion to Śaṅkara during the Tretā Age; his long life through service at Puṣkara and the blessing of Vasiṣṭha; the bringing back of the Brahmin’s son who had gone to the city of Yama; the granting of his own lifespan; his marriage to Hṛṅkukāyinī, the daughter of King Yama; and, in connection therewith, his atheism," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-Sattva*. 41.
← Chapter 41 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 42 [[Author: → Chapter 43
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! King Kaṇṭhādhara was indeed constantly devoted to women; through his association with them, he became an atheist intent only on his own self-interest. (1)
The evil-minded reviler of the Vedas caused a proclamation to be made in the city:
"Never shall anything be given, never shall sacrifices be performed, and never shall oblations be offered.
I alone am here to be saluted; I am always to be worshipped by you."
"Indeed, you have been protected by me; dwell, O subjects, in happiness.
There is no other god besides me who is your ultimate refuge.
To me alone must the oblation, the sacrificial offering, the gift, and the priestly fee be given. (3–4)
"I am the king; I am the guardian of the world, and I alone am the protector of the subjects.
I alone am the giver, the sustainer, and the ordainer of all creatures.
I alone am the giver of life, the giver of crops, and the giver of grain."
I alone am the giver of happiness, the giver of punishment, and also the provider of protection.
(6) Fire itself is my mouth; what is to be given must be placed therein, not in one who is unworthy.
My hands are the recipient and the head; it is only there that a gift is properly applied. (7)

"Give gifts, but do not give alms; for that which is born of policy must be given. Clothes, livestock, cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth—all my wealth should be bestowed upon you, provided it is for the sake of the subjects. (8)
"In times of famine and the like, he should be employed for the sake of the happiness of the subjects.
Having heard these words, the Brahmins who perceive Brahman, the elders of the people, the learned, those whose eyes are the Vedas, and the most excellent of the wise— [2.42.10] — [spoke].
Having come together in harmony for the sake of the king’s instruction, they prostrated before the monarch; being thus honored, they spoke these words:
"The Veda is the authority for dharma; upon it the sacrifice is established."
Without sacrifices, the gods who bestow crops do not remain pleased in heaven.
(12) And when the gods are displeased, famine arises;
O King, there would be the destruction of subjects as well as the ruin of the country. (13)
Therefore, O King, the pacification of elemental spirits and the pacification of the planets must always be performed,
as well as the gratification of the gods and the ancestors through great sacrifices. A sacrifice must never be obstructed, for the ritual is rooted in the sacred revelation (Śruti).
"The gods, who bestow happiness, are always to be gratified by means of the mouth of fire.
(15) Although addressed thus, King Kaṇṭhādhara did not believe it at all; he censured the Vedas in many ways, saying they were intent on deception. (16)
The Brahmins, intent on their own interests, are masses of Vedas devised by rogues;
these twice-born ones, greedy for sweet food, regard the fire as a deity, cast something into it, and then eat sweets themselves. (17)
They themselves take the sacrificial fees, the vessels of wealth, and the cows, horses, and elephants for their own sake;
therefore, they are indeed intent on self-interest.
There is no deity residing in the image, nor does it eat, nor does it have any preference. (18–19)

The Brahmin is indeed a manifest god; whatever pleases him, that is all [he receives]. Invoking the deity as the cause, the earth-dweller (Brahmin) enjoys sweet food, sweet water, ornaments, flower garlands, and fragrances.
The gift of a cow, the offering of milk to drink, the gift of a bed, and the donation of a house;
the Brahmin who enjoys everything, including the garden intended for the deity;
as well as vehicles, beautiful vessels, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, and a mount—[all these he may accept]. (21–22)
The Brahmin who performs worship enjoys soft bedding and all manner of objects of enjoyment;
he partakes of juices, fruits, and the finest cooked foods.
The twice-born worshipper also enjoys male and female slaves and servants.
Therefore, Brahmins, intent on their own interests, eat while pointing toward a sacrifice.
For this reason, one should certainly not perform sacrifices, nor should one give gifts at all;
such is the firm command of my queen, the daughter of Hṛdika.
"Having transgressed this, one who acts according to their own will shall incur my punishment"— thus were drums sounded by the king everywhere throughout the kingdom.
From that time forward, neither the worship of the gods nor sacrifices took place.
There was famine, and by that the subjects were oppressed with suffering.
The powerful forcibly seized the property of the weak,
and the king, being addicted to sensual pleasures, did not perform his duty of protection.
Then, indeed, the kingdom became utterly overturned by the force of time;
the staff of Śambhu, which bestows success, vanished from the king and disappeared.
Then the king grieved excessively, thinking, "My very life is lost."
His sovereignty was also lost due to his contempt for the gods.
The subjects, enraged over the matter of grain, besieged the king’s courtyard;
having seized the grain, they then departed with wealth such as cattle and other goods.
The prosperity of the kingdom vanished, and the subjects became exceedingly destitute.
Then Kanthadhara and his wife Hṛḍḍakāyinī,
both deeply distressed by fear, departed for the forest.
And between those two was a boy, about one year old and exceedingly delicate.
The Brāhmaṇas took him to their own home for the sake of protection,
along with a celestial chariot, a divine staff, and divine implements.
When they had departed, his own place, the kingdom, then became empty.
Indeed, when a mass of merit increases, prosperities increase;
but when merit is destroyed, they perish—what need is there to mention even the gods? (35)
O Rādhikā, that king met his end in the forest.
And Hṛdḍakāyinī, having abandoned food and water, died as well;
both of them, being atheists, obtained birth as barbarians on the shore of the ocean.
By the turn of fate, those two were born nearby as partakers of suffering.
The prince named Raṇaṅgamā reached the age of twelve;
having received the sacred thread and learned of his father’s conduct from the words of Brahmins, he [acted].
He reflected repeatedly upon the miserable state even in the forest.
Having completed his studies, he became the bearer of the burden of the kingdom;
for they considered him supremely worthy and devoted to the performance of dharma.
The brahmins consecrated him as king, the protector of the earth;
thereafter, protecting his subjects with righteousness, he brought them joy.
That righteous-souled one performed sacrifices and established the worship of the gods.
Then, standing in the midst of the brahmins, he prostrated himself before them and said:
"O twice-born ones, my father and likewise my mother, who caused the sacrifice to be interrupted, have died in the forest; how should their funeral rites be performed by me?"
"Announce [this] thus in the presence of the Brahmins," he said.
Then, shining with splendor and known by the name Svayaṃprakāśa,
the disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa traveled through the sky.
While proceeding toward Somakṣetra, he indeed descended at Koṭīnāra.
Upon seeing those brāhmaṇas, he suddenly approached them;
they offered him a seat and, having prostrated before him, questioned him.
Blessed are we, having arrived at this time to behold the Great Sage.
Your conduct is for the sake of destroying the suffering of the worlds and for their ultimate welfare.
O Blessed One, you know the auspicious and inauspicious of all the world.
You are the beloved direct disciple of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa.
This wicked-souled father of the king, a reviler of the gods and Brahmins, devoid of his own dharma, has taken refuge in the forest together with his wife. (48–49)
"Having met death in the forest, where does one who has committed evil deeds abide?
How might he attain liberation? Tell this, for a child asks you.
[The Lord replied: "The self-luminous, divine soul, having known by means of his divine eye—"
Remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who resides at Kuṅkumavāpikā, he spoke these words:
"On the shore of the western ocean, there is indeed a king accompanied by his queen;
born among the Mlecchas, he is afflicted with consumption and leprosy. (51-52)
And his rescue must be effected by this son in every way;
for he alone is called a "son" in the world who protects his fathers from fear.
Let this son go there, taking the Mleccha along with his wife.

At the holy ford of Aśvapaṭṭasara, which is presided over by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, let him purify his body in the waters of that sacred site; then, freed from sin, he shall attain liberation along with his beloved—of this there is no doubt. (54–55)
Having heard the words of self-luminosity, the brahmins and the subjects said to Kumāra, who was on the field of battle, "Go!
And that Kumāra, accompanied by a limited number of brahmins leading the way—
Accompanied [by his followers], he set out for the shore of the ocean where his father was staying.
Having reached that western region, a refuge for barbarians (mlecchas) abounding in trees and rich with the name Makarālaya, he searched for him through his servants.
The servants saw him, afflicted with leprosy and consumption;
they also saw that Hṛḍḍakī, likewise suffering from leprosy and consumption.
Both were rememberers of their former births (*jātismara*), waiting for their son.
Having heard that their rescuer had arrived, the Mleccha and the Mlecchī were then exceedingly joyful; full of longing, they quickly came with their servants to where the prince,
the warrior, was staying.
Seeing him, they wept again and again for the sake of deliverance;
they entreated him there and remained in his presence.
Seeing those two lepers likewise afflicted with consumption, their son—
Tormented by great grief himself, he spoke these words:
"Taking the command of you two, my parents, I shall lead you to the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara; I will restore you both to health."
Then, having gone to his circle of ancestors, the king said this: "Alas, O ancestors!
I bow to you; here are two men afflicted with leprosy.
For the sake of their medical treatment, I shall lead them back to my own home."
"In that regard, I shall bring these two to an end, if it is your wish.
"So be it," said the Mlecchas from all sides to the prince who was supremely compassionate;
with all their limbs bowed, they said, "Do as you know best."
Then, having brought men equipped with a palanquin,
the king seated his two paternal ancestors upon it.
And at the very dawn, the king, his attendants, and the brahmins [prepared for the journey].
They departed in haste and reached Aśvapaṭṭasara in the evening.
The sage Svayaṃprakāśa also went to the hermitage of Aśvapaṭṭa,
while the king and the others took up their positions near a banyan tree.
On the western shore of that lake, in the region of the wind-quarter,
they all took excellent rest at night on the sacred ground.
Then, in the morning, the king and the brahmins went to bathe those two in the lake.
Then, as they were about to set out, Vāyu spoke these words from the sky:
"O King, do not commit this rash act; protect the sacred ford with great effort.
These two are enveloped by every kind of terrible sin. (72–73)
These two sinners, who revile the Vedas, who hate the gods, who destroy sacrifices,
and who cause the destruction of Dharma— there is no end to their sins.
When these two fall, the lake will surely dry up.
"These two fierce ones, having bathed at this great sacred ford, will cause its destruction.
Therefore, do not immerse them both in the water on the shore of the lake.
Having heard these words from the sky, he was overcome with great sorrow. (75–76)
Afflicted with grief, he spoke to the voice from the sky: "O Lord!
If these two, most terrible sinners, are by no means worthy of bathing, then tell me, O Lord, what expiation I shall perform for their sake."
Then Vāyu and the gods, as well as the sacred fords (tīrthas) from all sides,
having observed the king, all spoke these words:
"Having bathed repeatedly in the sacred fords situated at Aśvasaras," ||| 78–79 ||
Constantly bathe yourself with the waters from the jars of the sacred fords,
as long as it takes for the destruction of their sins to be accomplished—
especially those people who promote their own interests at the expense of others and who corrupt the gods. (2.42.80)
Purification does not arise anywhere by bathing only once.
Therefore, having bathed with devotion at these sacred fords (tīrthas) for their sake, sprinkle them repeatedly with water; then they will become pure.
Having heard these words, the king then established a hermitage there;
bathing repeatedly at various sacred fords (tīrthas) and filling jars with water,
he performed ritual ablutions at those holy sites day after day.
He constantly consecrated his own parents with the water of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Thus, having been repeatedly consecrated with the waters of all the sacred fords,
they were purified by their son through the greatness of Aśvatīrtha.
"When they have become free from sin, O King, then one speaks of sacred fords;
bathe these two supreme purifiers in the lake.
Thus addressed, the king went to the battlefield and had them bathe in the month of Vaiśākha.
At that moment, they were born endowed with divine bodies;
their state as barbarians vanished, and their divine splendor increased.
Kanthadhara, seated in a celestial chariot together with his wife, became a deity. (87–88)
Seated in the celestial chariot, exceedingly joyful, he praised with supreme devotion the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama:
"O Supreme Brahman, O embodiment of supreme compassion and grace for the sake of liberation!"
O Lord, those two sinners were delivered by your disciple, the Ṛṣi;
they were delivered by your son, and they have been delivered by you as well, O Hari.
Those two wicked ones were also delivered by waters that are ever intent on helping others.
We two have been delivered from the terrible darkness born of the power of ignorance by the Brahmins;
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, we have been saved from hell through taking refuge in You.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Lord, who dwells in the heart and resides within the Brahmins.
Salutations to You, whose nature is self-luminous, who are the very soul of all sacred fords.
Salutations to the God who is the refuge, who bestows life even upon the sinful;
salutations to You, the Child, the youthful Kṛṣṇa, who grants liberation to those who take shelter in Him.
By your majesty alone, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas cross over; likewise the daityas,
dānavas, the wicked, the asuras, and those of tamasic nature— those who employ illusion, those possessed by latent desires, the most arrogant, and the conceited.
Those who engage in sexual misconduct, those who eat meat, thieves, those who drink intoxicants,
those who cause the intermixture of castes, and likewise those who commit the slaughter of cows or women—
all these indeed cross over by means of you, a treasure-trove of compassion and grace. (96–97)
"O Lord, we two have been delivered; let us go to your immortal abode.
Having spoken thus and prostrated themselves, they said, "O son, may there be well-being for you," and having bestowed their blessings, they departed toward the hermitage of Lomaśa.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. Having received this mantra and a garland of *tulasī* from Lomaśa, they became supreme Vaiṣṇavas and went to the abode of Viṣṇu. (2.42.100)
The non-Buddhist ascetics and householders have attained supreme wonder,
for by merely bathing here, eternal liberation has indeed been achieved.
This is the supreme compassion of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

O Rādhikā, the intense longing and the profound compassion of Hari [were such that] where the two became liberated, a heart-shaped mark appeared upon the hem of his garment. That supreme sacred site, known as Kanthādhra, attained fame throughout the earth.
Then that goddess Hṛṇḍakāyinī assumed two forms;
her shadow-form went to her own father, Yamarāja.
By the command of Yamarāja, she became the personification of hiccup.
The Yoginī established her permanent residence among all living beings.
(105) In her second form, she, the divine one who dwells within the heart, attained the path of liberation together with her divine Lord. (106)
Having attained the state of liberation and following the path of her father,
she, in the form of *hikkā*, became a shadow-form through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus ends the [section] in the second book, the *Tretā-saṃtāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter Forty-Two, titled "The Description of the Atheism of Kanthādharas due to his association with the wife of Hṛḍḍakāyinī, the loss of his sovereignty through the cessation of Vedic rites and other duties, his death in the forest and birth as a Mleccha, and his subsequent liberation at the Aśvapaṭṭasara Tīrtha by his son Raṇaṅgama.
[From] the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga), Chapter 43.
[Author: Chapter 44.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen to this most purifying account of a devotee.
Then this king, at this sacred ford on the battlefield,
constantly performed the funeral rites, the *śrāddha*, and the libations according to the prescribed rules;
he also fed the brahmins, the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the maidens.
To children, sages, gods, mendicants, and likewise to servants,
he gave various gifts of gold and silver with devotion.
He quickly received from Lomaśa the supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
(4) He performed his vow according to the rules and duly observed the rites of pilgrimage.
He took up a garland of *tulasī* and the image of the Supreme Lord. (5)
Then he sent Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
there he dwelt with great affection along with brahmins, servants, and others.
And he engaged in the company of holy men day and night.
Remembering his ancestors there, he desired to perform a sacrifice.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"Who was this king? In whose lineage did he arise? Who were his ancestors?"
"Tell me here: how did he perform the sacrifice, when, and where?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"The son of Candra was Ṛkṣa; he had a lifespan of one hundred million years and was a knower of the yoga of dharma."

His son was Saṃvaraṇa, a sovereign ruler of the whole earth. He married Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun, a maiden of excellent character. From them, after some time, was born the dispassionate Kuru king.
Since his father had bestowed the ancestral kingdom upon his elder brothers,
he, having received his own portion, went to the Dvaitavana forest and performed excellent and auspicious agriculture with a plough,
indeed through the vision of Brahman.
Having directly worshipped Viṣṇu in a sacrifice, he indeed went to the world of liberation.
The auspicious younger brother of Kuru, named Kanthādharā,
who was the son of Saṃvaraṇa, also received the portion of the inheritance known as Surāṣṭra.
Having obtained only a fragmentary kingdom for the sake of mere livelihood,
he resided in the city of Koṭināra in the Siṃhāraṇya forest.
Thus, his son Raṇaṅgama was likewise of the Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśa).
The pilgrim remembered his ancestors at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
he gratified Brahmā, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Candra, Ṛkṣaka,
Saṃvaraṇa, and Kanthādhr̥ with offerings of sesame seeds and water.

He offered libations with water mixed with sesame seeds to Sāvitrī, Kalā, Aditi, Rohiṇī, Ghaṭikā, Tapatī, and Hikkā. Then, on a grassy mat to the west of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he performed a sacrifice.
The exceedingly righteous king, who had gone forth to battle, desired to perform [the sacrifice];
in the sixth year of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
during the Cāturmāsya, he wished to conduct a great Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
He quickly brought all the necessary materials from his own kingdom;
he prepared the *kuśa* grass and various kinds of sacrificial fuel.
He constructed a magnificent central pavilion and several other beautiful pavilions.
He had artisans construct leaf-huts suitable for dwelling,
as well as sacrificial pits, smaller pits, altars, wooden boards, seats,
excellent sacrificial vessels, and a preeminent vessel made of udumbara wood.
He quickly had fine silken garments manufactured. He caused beautiful juice-halls, cooking halls, dining halls, and drinking booths to be constructed among the trees.
He caused cowsheds, horse-stables, wives' quarters,
and places for religious observances to be built according to the prescribed rites; and he had unbroken grains brought—
wheat, barley, rice, sesame seeds, fruits, and sugar.
All sacrificial substances and whatever materials for coloring,
the most excellent articles for worship, as well as abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
all implements for chanting and recitation, and all garments.
He had water-pots, colored cloths, and five kinds of leaf-plates prepared;
likewise, he had vessels for clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru) for the gods,
and ritual seats made according to the prescribed rule, accompanied by auspicious benedictions.
The Nāndī-śrāddha, the purificatory rites, the sprinkling for purification,
and so forth were performed; then one hundred and eight, and then a thousand Brāhmaṇas likewise stood ready— those learned in the Vedas, as well as others beginning with Brahmā.
The Hotṛ, the Pratyudgātṛ, those who know the Sāmans, and those skilled in the Yantras;
the Āhartṛ, the Pratihartṛ, the sacrificers, and the reciters; the readers, the meditators on Brahman, and likewise those who perform the duties of the subordinate priests.
Adorned with deer-horns and other ornaments, the sacrificial rites proceeded in the pavilions;
the fire, the consumer of oblations, was established there.
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord—
He was worshipped before him along with his twenty-four incarnations.
Brahmā, Muktā, Rādhikā, and other liberated women, as well as the consorts of Viṣṇu—Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Satī, Kamalā, and others—were present. (33–34)
The Haṃsas, Paramahaṃsas, Saguṇas, Mañjulas, and Priyas;
the honored Mothers, as well as Śambhu, the gods, and the Lord of the Gaṇas;
the Brahmacharas, other Ṛṣis, and likewise the attendants and Śaktis.
The silk-clad maidens, Durgā and the others, the planets, the gods, the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas),

the protectors of the directions (dikpālas), the protectors of the worlds (lokapālas), the supernatural powers (siddhis), the host of yoginīs, and the virtuous classes of ancestors (sāttvika-pitṛvargas) have been established within the divine mandala. (36–37)
The creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of the individual soul (jīva)— whichever is most excellent—
is that which is worshipped there in the pavilion and which desires a share of the sacrifice.
Even those who are rajasic and tamasic speak of them as servants of the gods.
She was honored here by Lomaśa during the great festival of the Viṣṇu-sacrifice.
The sacrificer was Raṇaṅgama, and the preceptor was indeed the sage Lomaśa;
the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was the foremost deity of the sacrifice. (2.43.39–40)
Everything there was perfectly accomplished during the four-month sacrifice performed day after day; this entire ritual, from beginning to end, was constant and complete according to the rules.
Its commencement took place in the month of Āṣāḍha, and its conclusion in Kārttika.
There, the daily fire-sacrifice was performed, along with the feeding of ten thousand Brahmins;
for others, there was no end to the feeding of ten million maidens and the like,
nor to the constant giving of garments and food for ten million children and others.
Thousands of streams of ghee, streams of curd, and streams of milk;
streams of juice, streams of honey, and the splendor of offerings such as *madhuparka*;
countless sweet drinks and the finest delicacies.
There, food is given and embodied beings become satisfied.
The Lord Vahni, eternally possessing a form, consumes the oblation with his own two hands; self-luminous, he himself offers it with a stream of clarified butter. 45–46.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Fire-god, receives [the oblation] in his lotus-like mouth;
the deities who constitute the sacrifice attain supreme satisfaction in that most excellent rite.
Ten million gifts are constantly bestowed by Raṇaṅgama.
Thus, while this sacrifice is perpetually taking place, the inhabitants of the three worlds come and depart for the purpose of beholding it and for the purpose of offering oblations.
The gods constantly worship Hari with thousands of lotuses.

Where that Kambharā-Lakṣmī and Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa shine forth, and where their parents provide the materials for worship and offer the sacrificial requisites— what deficiency could there possibly be there? (2.43.50)
"The great sage, devoted to his wife, presides here as the supervisor of all.
What deficiency could there be therein regarding all honors, drinks, and foods?
Thus, O Rādhikā, the sacrifice proceeded day after day.
Rain falls constantly, and all varieties of crops rejoice;
indeed, a sacrifice was performed by the son on account of Kanthādhara.
The son Raṇaṅgama gave everything in charity, even without Kanthā.
Saying, "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased and be present in person," he placed [the offering] in a fine vessel.
Then the gods, having descended from heaven and smelled the smoke of the clarified butter, assumed the forms of boars and spoke to one another in divine speech: ||| 54-55 ||
Blessed is he who enters the field of battle in this world, and blessed is he who wears a patched garment;
blessed are the elders such as Candra and others, in whose lineage there is such an expansion of sacrifice.
In their sacrifice, even the twentieth syllable was lost—a nasalized one.
In that sacrifice, everything is given away, even down to one’s loincloth and upper garment;
indeed, in that sacrifice, the goddess Hunger has met with defeat,
while Satisfaction reigns supreme— blessed indeed is the sage Lomaśa!
Blessed is the brahmin devoted to his wife, and blessed is the self-effulgent one, for whom the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa acts as a helper.
O gods! During the Cāturmāsya, you must always reside here by all means.
Constant effort in coming and going is not desired as it is in vain.
(2.43.60) A sacred pilgrimage site is difficult to find; likewise, association with the virtuous is difficult to find;
constant worthy worship is difficult to find, and refuge in Hari is difficult to find. (61)
Fame for merit is difficult to attain, and hearing the sacred narrative is difficult to attain;
the constant sight of dear friends is difficult to attain.
Devotion to Śrī Hari is difficult to attain, and the nectar of His feet is difficult to attain.
The constant enjoyment of that [divine] grace is difficult to attain;
likewise, everything that is difficult to obtain becomes easily obtained there. Blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā, and blessed is the holy site of Aśvasaras where the sacrifice proceeds.

O gods, there is no lake like this in the presence of Śrīpati himself that bestows satisfaction upon the three worlds; neither is there a Brahmāsaras such as this, nor indeed a Puṣkara lake such as this;
nor is there a Mānasa lake such as this, nor a Nārāyaṇa lake such as this.
Nor is there such a lake as Pampā, nor is there a place where the Supreme Lord does not dwell.
Indeed, here all trees and creepers abide as liberated beings;
indeed, all stalks, shrubs, and those consisting of grass abide as liberated beings.
Beasts, birds, aquatic creatures, species of winged insects,
terrestrial beings, worms, and mosquitoes— all indeed dwell here liberated.
Blessed is the dust of this land, for its touch destroys sin.
Blessed is the water of the lake, for even a single drop of it bestows liberation. (69) We who partake of the sacrifice are blessed, for we have obtained this supreme gain.
May he who has gone to the battlefield be blessed, and may he become the very body of the God of gods. (70)
"May he be endowed with divine accomplishment, may he be laden with divine prosperity,
and may this warrior on the battlefield possess the gait of a god.
Thus was this king of devotees, Raṇaṅgama, joined with these blessings.
At that moment, a magnificent divine chariot, richly adorned for his sake, arrived.
It was a granter of desires, joined with a wish-fulfilling creeper, filled with bliss, and stood ready for constant service; it had been offered by Indra and was equipped with a charioteer.
Accompanied by male and female servants and attendants, provided with lakes of edible nectar,
illuminated, and endowed with all kinds of beds and articles for enjoyment—
thus did King Raṇaṅgama [attain this state] through the great favor of the gods.
Having obtained an imperishable celestial chariot that always bestows inexhaustible objects,
he constantly gave gifts in the amount of billions and trillions after making formal vows. He likewise summoned Viśvakarman, Śambara, and Maya.
At that sacred site, near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, he caused to be built a seven-storied palace made of divine materials, ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference;
it shone like heaven, and likewise, he installed deities within it.
And for the sake of worship, he indeed gave gifts of houses to the Brahmins;
at that time, he gave a wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpavallī*) to each individual Brahmin.
Everything desired and enjoyable bears fruit upon that creeper eternally.
At that time, there was no need here for fields, nor for crops, nor even for cattle;
it was only for the sake of grain, for the sake of seeds, and for the sake of fat.
Even though that king’s realm was small, he possessed a most pure radiance like that of the moon.
Then he attained fame in the world, beginning with the status of a sovereign emperor.
O Rādhikā! For my devotee, nothing whatsoever remains unfulfilled.
To him who gives me everything, I give everything.
Thus, while the sacrifice was being performed and tens of thousands of temples were being constructed,
Raṇaṅgama and Divaṅgama were born from him during the seventh auspicious year of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
When the year had arrived, on the eighth day, he celebrated the festival of Hari’s birth.
There, he seated the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa upon a jeweled throne and worshipped him with numerous divine offerings and gifts.
He fed hundreds of thousands of Brahmins and even children;
he worshipped the gods and had songs sung;
and with devotion, he caused various auspicious rites to be performed.
The king indeed honored the virtuous sages and the chaste, noble women.
He caused gifts to be given: gold, silver, and diamonds;
clothing, ornaments, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, chariots, and servants.
Then, at night, Lomaśa recited a delightful discourse from the second section of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. At the conclusion of the discourse,
ten million maidens performed the worship of their beloved.
At night,
the Supreme Lord Hari himself, assuming ten million forms, performed the rāsa dance together with ten million beloved women in an expansive garden of land-lotuses. (2.43.90–91)
Then, having brought joy to the circles of her friends, she offered a formal response;
and at dawn, the king performed the sacrificial oblation as was his custom.
And for the gods who had arrived to celebrate the birth festival, the king [acted].
He performed service in many ways and offered his dismissal.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, following the sacrificial oblations,
the king granted him leave from the rite and bestowed sacrificial fees upon him.
He gave gifts many times over— ornaments of gems, diamonds, rubies, gold, and silver, as well as clothing, food, vehicles, mounts, and so forth. Then,
together with the sages, he performed the ritual ablution (*avabhṛtha*) in the lake.
Likewise, the incarnations were liberated, as were the other lords;
the gods, the ancestors, mortals, and all things mobile and immobile, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, departed eagerly to their respective abodes. (96–97)
Worshipping the eternal Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the king,
accompanied by the brāhmaṇas and his servants, ascended a divine vehicle.
[98] He [beheld] the sages, Kṛṣṇa, his father, his mother, the gods, and the celestial abodes.
Having bowed to the sacred fords, trees, and creepers, he departed for home.
Honored by the people, he entered his own city named Koṭīnārā and rested in his own dwelling.
Then a yakṣa named Citramālā heard of that king—
who was majestic, deeply devoted, illustrious, and in the prime of youth—
and he came to Saurāṣṭra, to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.

He beheld the sacrificial ground of the king, with its magnificent palaces (102). Having recognized, again and again, the supreme majesty wrought by the monarch, he went to Raṇaṅgama to offer his own daughter, Kṛtamālā. (103)

The preeminent Yakṣa beheld the city, which had been renewed by Raṇaṅgama like a celestial wish-fulfilling tree; it was a city that rivaled the city of the gods. Then he descended from his celestial chariot into the king’s residence from the sky.
He gave his daughter, as well as female and male servants, to Raṇaṅgama.
The king performed the taking of her hand according to the marriage rites;
the son-in-law of the preeminent Yakṣa shone upon the earth like a god.
Having given his daughter, the Yakṣa departed for the city of Kubera.
O Rādhikā! The listener and the speaker of this [account] shall partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fame Gained in Battle, the Seventh Birth Festival of the Lord, the Marriage of Raṇaṅgama with the Yakṣa Maiden, and the Attainment of the Celestial Car," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
← Chapter 043 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 44 [[Author: → Chapter 045
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! Afterwards, the king, having attained perfection, constructed a great city named Somavelā. 1.
There were ten thousand golden palaces,
as many silver palaces, and thousands of jeweled palaces;
there were wonderful gardens, groves, and lotus ponds.
He caused [the temples] to be built in many ways and established the deities within them.
Then, he provided a *kalpavallī* (wish-fulfilling creeper) for each individual temple,
as well as Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas, bards (*bandins*), wandering singers (*cāraṇas*), and Brahmins (*bhūsuras*).

He settled millions of men who were like unto gods. Having thus established the city named Somavelā with twelve gate-towers (gopuras) on the western side, it became as enchanting as the Soma-tīrtha itself.
Then he had the dilapidated golden temple of Śrī Somanātha demolished and constructed a new, magnificent one;
it featured a seven-storied gopura rising to a height of a thousand cubits.
The spire, fifty cubits in width and resembling a mountain, stands there;
the Lord Somanātha, stationed in the sky, shines forth supported by it.
There, a bell, recognizable by its golden chain, resplendently gleams.

It could be heard from ten yojanas away, weighed a hundred bhāras, and was perceptible at a distance of a hundred mānas; it resounded by means of a mere mechanical device. Its pinnacle and its pinnacle-vase were made of gold and consisted of seven parts. (2.44.10)
It was fifty cubits in height and radiant like the sun;
its staff was one hundred cubits long, and its banner fifty cubits.
Upon it, clouds would rest continuously during the four-month rainy season.
Wherever a man stood, he appeared like a swan;
there he provided enjoyments and engaged the Brahmins in worship. In particular, that king established a continuous feast of food (annasatra).
There, ten thousand women and likewise ten thousand men,
as well as fifty thousand boys and girls,
constantly partake of foods mixed with sweets and clarified butter.

Thus, by the power of the merit of his sacrifices and through the majesty of the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, King Raṇegama became like a world-protector on earth and traveled in a celestial chariot. (15–16)
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, he indeed traveled toward the southern direction by means of a celestial vehicle across the ocean to observe it.
The mighty one then went further ahead to behold the Southern Pole Star.
Taking with him food, drink, his retinue of servants, his attire, and likewise the Kalpalatā— the instruments of his practice— he traveled through the sky in a celestial chariot.
Having observed the southern region from Saurāṣṭra, he beheld Siṃhāraṇya.
Having traversed a region of a hundred yojanas, the king proceeded further ahead;
he beheld the ocean situated toward the southern direction.
There he saw the beautiful island of Lākṣādīpa.
Then he proceeded further through the sky and beheld Māladvīpa;
having seen it, he traveled through the air and beheld his own desired island.
Having observed that [island], he subsequently saw the auspicious place named Muraśeṣa on all sides.
And he surveyed the island where the demon Muru resided;
he had indeed come through the sky by way of the battlefield to fight.
Having fashioned from the Kalpavallī a formidable noose of Varuṇa, [he stood ready].
Then the king had the Daitya bound and cast into the ocean;
somehow retaining his life, he went to his own abode.
Thereafter, the king proceeded further and reached Kurujaṭa on the island.
Then, from there, Mānava saw Jaṭāyū all around him;
he proceeded ahead by means of his celestial chariot and beheld the island of Antarabījaka, which is composed of coolness, where the people indeed have the faces of crocodiles. (26)
And mostly dwelling in the water, they were beheld by that king.
Then he departed through the sky in a celestial chariot toward the southern direction;
there he saw the earth, white and perfectly circular.
There are water-basins covered with moss, beautiful and radiant;
there the earth consists of water, and embodied beings are brilliant white.
All those who eat from the water-basins dwell upon the mountains in the water.
Men and women there are always shaped like fish, enduring water and mud.
Drinking cool water and eating water-crystals,
they subsist by consuming moss and aquatic plants.
There, people dwell in houses made of water and stone;
they possess a radiance equal to the cool moon, are born from water, and subsist on nectar.
Beholding such beings, he saw the Southern Pole Star (Dakṣiṇa Dhruva).
First he turned toward the Kārakī region in order to see it.
From his position in the celestial chariot, the king beheld that circular earth;
the entire surface of the world appeared like water, made of silver, and devoid of trees. (33–34)
There, clouds are ever-present and the heat of the sun is not found;
there are oceanic stones and minerals consisting of hailstones.
Indeed, the desired essence of water, which is nectar, arises from those hailstones.

Water, clusters of *śaivāla* moss, water-leaves, and creepers—[36] these are white in color, with white fruit, resembling fragments of the moon. These aquatic vegetables are fit for consumption, and there are houses made of water-stones. [37]
The salt of the ocean, water-crystals, sweet sugar,
water-stones, and tubers— these were enjoyed with pleasure by the people there.
Having beheld all this, as well as the abode of Varuṇa, [he departed].
Having observed the site situated at the central point of the southern fixed celestial sphere,
the king returned once more to the bank of the battlefield; there he saw the region of Kampa and then Kaṭisara before him.
Having looked all around, he then beheld a region characterized by passion (rājasa);
and having gone forward, he saw before him a place that was the abode of maidens.
Then, further ahead, he saw a fine location with one-eyed men.
Beyond that, he saw an excellent region together with Sugrīva.
Then he beheld a land free from mountains, born of water and rock;
and he indeed beheld the region of Yāta, a place where enemies have departed.
Then he saw a region empty of summer heat and a region of foul diseases;
having beheld the *dhruvabindu* (the polar point), he saw the circular path of the sun at its end.
Thus he saw that subterranean place, which serves as a mere abode for cold.
O Rādhikā, just as he was about to turn back upon seeing that it was cool,
a certain man, resembling a white mountain, emerged from the interior of the earth and arrived via the path of the sky. (45–46)
Possessing infinite valor, he dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg and has a family;
he is white-complexioned, clad in white garments, and endowed with the radiance of white light.
He has a white beard, possesses white nectar, and holds a mace made of white stone.
Clouds rest upon his head, and white mountains at his feet;
white moss is upon his waist, and thundering clouds are in his mouth;
his sound proceeds, pervading as far as the southern pole.
His gait possessed the speed of lightning, his breath caused the ocean to tremble,
and his loud laughter returned after pervading the ends of the quarters.
Upon seeing him approach the field of battle, he was indeed seized by fear for a moment.
At that moment, that white man summoned him to the field of battle:
"Come, come, O divine deity, you who move through the sky!
What fear can you have of me, for you are surely resting upon the Kalpa-valli tree?"
O King, you in whose heart the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa resides—
such a great devotee as you shines forth powerfully upon the earth.
You are blessed, O King, for you have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord.
Although you are composed of the elements, O Lord, you shine like a god by virtue of being beheld by the Lord;
for you yourself have reached the further shore of the ocean of existence.
Come to my abode and purify my home, which is always perfumed by the excellent fragrance of the earth;
that which is ever worshipped by me is indeed to be worshipped by you as well.
The Lord of Lords was propitiated on the field of battle.
For I am a man born of the noble lineage of Śeṣa, dwelling here within the womb under the name Lakṣmaṇa.
Together with all my kinsmen, I eternally worship the child Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning;
please accept this unsurpassed hospitality from me. 56.
Thus, having performed [the task], grant me your audience;
I shall present the offerings suitable for worship,
and you ought to give them to Bālakṛṣṇa.
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O devotee of my Lord; obeisance, obeisance to you, O knower of the Supreme Self.
Obeisance, obeisance to you, O devotee of the Supreme Lord; obeisance be to you, the performer of great sacrifices.
Thus, O Rādhikā, was he duly honored by that Lakṣmaṇa.
Having gained confidence through these words, the warrior became steady on the field of battle.
Meanwhile, Śrī Lakṣmaṇa assumed there a human form—
gentle, handsome, inspiring trust to his devotee, and adorned with a sectarian mark (tilaka).
Raṇaṅgama bowed with supreme love and intense devotion to the Vaiṣṇava, who was accompanied by Tulasī and chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Lakṣmaṇa said, "Behold this here, for the sake of conviction within my heart."
The Lord Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa shines forth resplendent.
Raṇaṅgama beheld the Supreme Lord within his heart—
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa seated at the Aśva lake.
To the Lord of Rādhā, the Master of Light, the Lord of Pāravatī, the most enchanting one;
to the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Sovereign of the Swan, the glorious Son of the Cowherds;
to the Lord of the Possessor of Attributes, the one cherished by Kambharā, the delighter of His devotees.
Adorned with divine bracelets, crowns, rings, and necklaces;
endowed with a form that rivals the supreme beauty of ten million Cupids;
radiant and abiding in a gentle smile, he was beholding the battlefield.
Beholding his beloved Mādhava in such a form within his own heart,
the great devotee Raṇaṅgama attained renewed confidence.
Then he [beheld] Lakṣmaṇa, the serpent in the form of a human being.
Taking his hand, he quickly helped him ascend the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Guided by the path shown by him, his own chariot was driven until it reached Pṛthvīguptabindu, situated within the waters, stones, and earth. (68–69)
Near the mouth of the southern fixed celestial sphere (Dakṣiṇadhruvagola),
there is a great opening through which one may enter the interior of the earth;
it is circular, measuring one *yojana* in extent, and well-guarded by white serpents.
With its cool stone steps and protected by cool ramparts,
the aerial chariot entered the opening of the cavern in an instant along the path directed by Lakṣmaṇa, where shouts of victory then arose. (71–72)
Amidst the great clamor of the gatekeepers, within the womb of the earth and in the intermediate space,
[the chariot] was illuminated by the light of lightning-jewels and made radiant by the splendor of the moon;
it was honored with parched grain by maidens and worshipped with flowers and gems.
Having traveled through the intermediate region, the celestial chariot descended to the earth.
There, indeed, the ground was delightful, white, black, and pale;
there were various medicinal herbs and trees beautifully adorned with fruit.
