which was capable of pulling out iron— and released it into the belly of the asura.
Having pierced her, it entered the intestines and became fixed there;
then the powerful Asura, having bound his split abdomen with chains and other means,
extracted the Śakti and fell unconscious for a moment.
Stationed in the sky itself, he consecrated a long arrow with the *vidyut* mantra and launched it to destroy the one who had entered the field of battle; meanwhile,
the one who had entered the field of battle dispatched a thunderbolt born from the *kalpalatā*.
Having destroyed the arrow, it entered the heart of the Daitya;
the Daitya fell from the sky into the waters of the ocean, having lost consciousness.
For him who was thus unconscious, the ocean rose only to his waist.
Then, having encountered that coldness, he fainted;
with his face bowed down in shame, he reproached himself.
Thereupon, he indeed created a terrible Rākṣasa illusion.
Then the Daitya became a thousandfold, and he struck the army engaged in battle on all sides with arrows, staffs, mallets, clubs,
pestles, spears, javelins, stones, and other weapons.
With spears, swords, and weapons of many forms,
he then became invisible from the midst of the battlefield in an instant by the power of the Kalpalatā, and stood at the front of the celestial chariot.
Then the Daitya, overcome with rage, abandoned his position on the battlefield;
when he extended his arms to seize the celestial chariot,
those two hands were instantly consumed by the fire arising from the Kalpalatā.
With his hand burnt, the asura was unable to grasp the vehicle;
moreover, though full of pride, he was unable even to seize his weapons.
The mountain became a flaming mouth, overwhelmed by the forest fire.
Nevertheless, he indeed resolved to burn the battlefield;
yet the battle-ground, like a wish-fulfilling creeper raining nectar,
protected its own self and those situated upon the chariot with streams of ambrosia.
The asura blazed there, yet his celestial chariot was not consumed by the fire.
Lakṣmaṇa recited benedictory prayers for his own protection—
those auspicious rites which are meritorious and the most excellent of all blessings.
Oṃ! May Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, grant us well-being.
May Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Brahmā—the Infallible One—grant us well-being.
And may Śaṅkara, accompanied by Śivā, also grant us well-being. (38)
May the lords, the world-protectors, the planets, and likewise the great seers;
the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the hosts of Sādhyas and Maruts, the fires, and the suns;
the Yakṣas, the Vasus, and the Kinnaras and others—may they all grant well-being. (2.46.40)
The Nāgas, Suparṇas, rivers, lakes, and likewise the oceans;
the Sudarśana discus, the mantras, and the weapons of Hari;
the devotees, the liberated ancestors, and the powers such as Rādhā and Ramā.
May the elements grant you well-being, as may the radiant ones such as fire and the rest.
May there be well-being for those with two feet and for those with four feet;
may there be well-being for us from those with many feet and from those with no feet, and may there be freedom from disease.
May there be well-being for the celestial chariot, and may there be well-being for him who enters the field of battle.
May there be auspiciousness for the inhabitants of the celestial realms, and may there be well-being and prosperity as well.
May there be well-being for those with flaming mouths, and likewise for those whose flames are composed of illusion.
"May the Inner Self likewise grant us well-being from the Asuras.
Thus did Lakṣmaṇa there remember Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the auspicious Śrī Puruṣottama, the bestower of blessings.
Bālakṛṣṇa appeared visibly on Mount Anala, smiling and saying,
"May there be peace, coolness, and freedom from ailment for your celestial chariot.
Then the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [acted] for the sake of reducing the asura to ashes.
He commanded his own attendant, the personification of great splendor.
That personification of great splendor forcibly set ablaze the Dānava Jvālāmukha, just as fire consumes a moth.
The Blessed One himself protected the celestial chariot along with the food;
he reduced the Daitya to ashes in a great fire consisting of flames.
At that time, the area covered in ashes extended for ten yojanas.
Having thus destroyed the Daitya named Mātrāgaskara on that island,
Śrī Hari, Lakṣmaṇa, Āryaraṇaṅgama, and the others returned to Surāṣṭra by means of their celestial chariot. || 51-52 ||
Having beheld the Kuṅkumavāpikā field, the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, and Lomaśa, as well as that city resembling heaven,
they descended happily to the earth accompanied by Nārāyaṇa.
Having first bowed to Lomaśa, they went to the cowherd’s dwelling.
There, honored with joy by their father Bālakṛṣṇa and also by their mother Kambharā, they attained great delight, being well-received.
Then Lakṣmaṇa and the others— having been offered seats, having taken up residence, having finished their meals and rest, and having engaged in conversation and learned the news—
[approached] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
And they came to Kambharā’s house with offerings to pay their respects.
By her will, the child Hari shone upon the throne;
first, his two feet, which grant happiness, were washed with waters of nectar.
All those maidens of divine form worshipped Śrī Hari;
and by the command of Lakṣmaṇa, they received the nectar of his feet,
as well as flower garlands, jeweled necklaces, and strings of pearls.
They presented him with a crown, earrings, a sword, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and diamonds; they offered bracelets, waist-bands, ornaments,
garments, fruits, drinks of nectar, vessels, and saffron.
They gave various articles to that Bālakṛṣṇa;
likewise, they performed the ārātrika rite, circumambulated him, and offered salutations.
Placing his feet upon their chests, they attained supreme peace.
Having thus fully honored the maidens, they placed the Beloved of Śrī within their hearts.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved, indeed entered into their hearts;
and Mādhava drew the hearts of them all toward himself.
Having understood Śrī Lakṣmaṇa’s disposition toward his beloved Kṛṣṇa,
he gave those women, along with wedding gifts consisting of many jewels and other valuables, to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; thus he attained fulfillment.
Then all the princes performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Thereafter, Lakṣmaṇārya performed the supreme worship of the Lord;
Raṇaṅgama and Mālinī also performed the worship of Hari.
Then they performed the worship of the glorious Lakṣmī Kambharā;
they performed the divine worship of the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
They went to the brahmin Śrī Lomaśa and performed his worship as well.
Bālakṛṣṇa gave the girls to Lomaśa for their protection.
Lomaśa protected those wives of Kṛṣṇa, who were devoted to Viṣṇu, in his own hermitage.
In this way, everyone attained fulfillment in the presence of Hari.
They experienced exceeding joy through the hospitality of food and drink;
then, at dawn on the full moon of the month of Māgha, they performed the rites for the sacred ford (tīrtha).
They gave divine gifts, including gold, jewels, and garments.
Then, having made his departure, Lakṣmaṇa desired to go to his own kingdom;
but Raṇaṅgama spoke to him:
"This Lomaśa is a great yogi who bestows even upon princes [the power of flight]."
"O King, cause the mantra that grants liberation to be bestowed in their presence.
Thereupon, the noble Lakṣmaṇa caused the mantra to be given to his sons;
Lomaśa, having remembered Śrī Hari, [bestowed it] upon the five hundred youths.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā.
(75) Having purified them with this mantra, He adorned them with garlands of tulasī and bestowed upon them divine knowledge that brings about the destruction of latent impressions. (76)
Sons, listen: this world is considered to be born of the bondage of karma.
Service to the virtuous is auspicious action; the worship of Śrī Hari is auspicious.
One’s own spiritual welfare is the most excellent good; the destruction of craving is the supreme happiness.
The predominance of the body, senses, and so forth is considered the arouser of latent impressions (vāsanā).
When knowledge is powerful, that [predominance] becomes secondary and takes the form of restraint.
For yogis, this restraint serves to burn away the latent impressions. (78–79)
The strength of her body and senses becomes ineffective for him;
though the body is female, the life-force (jīva) dwelling within it is male.
The male life-force experiences the body, and his experience consists of the perception of pleasure and pain.
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) must indeed always exist in the form of Brahman.
Its attainment of the state of Brahman is considered to depend upon its taking refuge in the Supreme Brahman;
and here, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself abides as that Supreme Brahman.
Union with Him has now arisen for you; nothing further remains to be done.
Indeed, this Kṛṣṇa is attained through the merits accumulated over ten million births.
Through association with the virtuous here, His attainment occurs swiftly.
For this king, who is of virtuous form, a friend of yours, and one who goes to the field of battle,
has brought you here and bestowed upon you the highest welfare.
Therefore, O sinless ones, cultivate devotion toward him, who is Nārāyaṇa.
O sinless ones, practice therein that state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) which consists of total surrender;
for without direct perception, the goals of human life are not accomplished here.
Through the yoga of direct perception, the supreme goal of human life has been achieved by you.
For those who possess supreme devotion to Kṛṣṇa, as they have toward Kṛṣṇa, so too toward the guru—for them all the goals of human existence are surely accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, those knowers of Brahman depart for the Supreme.
Complete surrender, trust, magnanimity, contemplation, mindfulness, and affection for one's own [teacher]—these six bestow the Supreme Brahman.
Tranquility, faith, lack of craving, absence of agitation, and a fearless state of being; ||| 89 ||
And freedom from dependence—these six bestow great bliss:
saluting the elderly, service, enthusiasm, performing one's duty, seeking recourse through justice, freedom from possessiveness, and gentleness. (2.46.90–91)
These six, in every respect, increase the merit of people in the world:
enduring all forms of pain, relinquishing the conceit of a body, not seeking after fame and the like, and living without possessions. (92)
Freedom from longing for anything whatsoever and the total renunciation of the activity of passion—
these six, in every respect, increase one's liberation while living in this world;
as do the constant vision of the gods and likewise the vision of discernment.
The vision of the *lakṣyabindu*, the vision of the *phalgupradarśana*,
the vision of the *avighna*, and the vision of the vision—
these six bestow liberation as well as victory.
Those who are free from desire, those who do not seek their own self-interest, those who seek their own self-interest, and those who act for the sake of others;
those whose virtuous conduct is never lost, and those who are wise—these six are indeed "non-blind.
Furthermore, those who perceive only virtues and those who bestow only virtues [are also non-blind]. (96–97)
Those who practice with a vision of qualities engage others in those very qualities;
those who rejoice in the knowledge of reality remain indifferent toward what is other than the qualities.
These six, being stainless, exist as bodiless ones within their physical bodies.
Those for whom the womb, childhood, youth, old age, death,
and even the state of being a ghost are all equal, are liberated and devoid of the qualities of nature.
Body, home, wealth, field, ornaments, clothing, and food— [are likewise seen as equal].

For that person who treats these six like guests, there is indeed a foothold in the Imperishable (akṣara). Those men here who act for the sake of the virtuous, for the sake of their master—whether they be women, sons, fathers, mothers, daughters, female servants, cattle, or others—[attain that state]. (101)
They possess two feet within the Lord’s abode of the imperishable.
Whatever is dear to oneself, one should indeed give that for the sake of the virtuous;
he who gives his life, gives his husband, or gives his beloved, partakes in liberation. (101–103)
"One should give away wealth for one's own sake; for one's own sake, one should give away a beloved wife;
for one's own sake, one should give away a kingdom; but for the sake of liberation, one should surrender everything.
Having been thus instructed by Lomaśa, the princes regained their sight.
Endowed with divine knowledge, they prostrated before Lomaśa; then,
having bowed to all their sisters and addressed them with words full of affection,
they ascended the celestial chariot together with their father and the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa.

They went joyfully to the city of Koṭīnāra, the capital of Raṇaṅgama, and likewise visited the holy site of Someśvara with great devotion. Having accepted the worship offered by Raṇaṅgama, they departed by way of the sky.
All of them went together by means of the celestial chariot to the circular region of Antārka.
Having brought them to the interior of the earth and having entrusted that kingdom to them,
Raṇaṅgama returned again to his own city of Koṭīnāra by means of the celestial chariot.

Thus has been described, O Rādhā, the conduct of the devotees of the Lord—excellent, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and bringing auspiciousness to both the listener and the speaker. (2.46.110) Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Raṇaṅgama and Mātrāgaskara, the Victory of Raṇaṅgama, the Arrival at Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Worship of the Lord, and the Offering of Two Thousand Maidens by Lakṣmaṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (46)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Lomaśa explained in truth that the two thousand maidens were the beloved wives of Lord Hari, Lakṣmaṇa. (1)
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, and the life-force is transitory;
even volitions are momentary, but the Lord Hari is eternal.
His abode is said to be the self, and Hari resides within that very self.
The Lord of the house, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, is indeed the protector and the master.
Water was created, and from that came the embryo (kalala), then the karkandhu stage, then the peṣikā; then the puttala, and finally the body with fully formed limbs was fashioned by Him.
O sons! Childhood and youth were created by Him alone;
likewise, old age, separation, and death were created by Him.
Indeed, one who has entered the realm of the measurable should take refuge in the Mother of all that is to be measured.
Then, indeed, through union with the immeasurable, the Self also becomes immeasurable.
(6) And here, O daughters, that which has made its dwelling in your hearts shines forth as immeasurable, yet it appears like something measurable, as does an object to the ignorant. (7)
He indeed is to be served; He indeed is to be worshipped; He indeed is to be meditated upon incessantly.
Having attained Him, that which was to be attained has truly been attained; nothing remains to be attained.
With this impermanent body, one should accomplish the eternal liberation.
One should propitiate the beloved Kṛṣṇa with impermanent activities.
Kṛṣṇa is the vow, Kṛṣṇa is the recitation, and one should offer gifts to Kṛṣṇa;
austerity is service to Hari alone, and restraint and discipline are directed toward Hari. (2.47.10)
Every sacrifice is the offering of all to Kṛṣṇa; that indeed is eternal wealth.
Samādhi is the state of relishing Kṛṣṇa; yoga is union with Kṛṣṇa.
Devotion is service to Him, conversation is discourse with Him, and glorification is the recounting of His qualities. (11)
Beholding Him is indeed direct perception; touching Him is the perfect union. Following His will is considered self-restraint that bestows liberation.
O sons, His grace alone is eternal merit, and nothing else. (12–13)
One should indeed perform the hearing and the reflection upon Hari;
one should sleep there and always awaken within Hari.
He in whom yogis delight is Rama himself; he is indeed Rāma.
This is the true cessation for those who are weary; any other cessation is meaningless.
(15) And here, Hari eternally relishes the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) for those who possess it.
O fair daughters! Without that, any other tasting is meaningless. (16)
In the fifth year, she should in every respect be treated as a daughter;
in the tenth year, she should in every respect be treated as a female disciple;
thereafter, until the end of the fourteenth year, she should be treated as a maiden.
Therefore, O sons, you must become wives of the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In that regard, listen to how your status as daughters, your discipleship, and your maidenhood are rendered authentic, and how your wifehood becomes meaningful and purposeful. (18–19)
She is celebrated here as "Putrī" because she protects one from the hell named Put;
she is a disciple who removes the remainder of sins, for she indeed removes the sin from the head.
After five years of age, the sin committed by her passes on to him.
That which did not exist on the heads of her parents—namely, the five things born before [her]—is what she possesses:

the *kuṃ-sūtra* (the thread), the *māṃ-gāyatrī* (the Gāyatrī mantra), and that which she bestows (*rāti*). She is the maiden (*kumārikā*) who possesses the *sūtra*, the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), and the *gāyatrī*, the knowledge born of reality (*tattva*).
The maiden who accomplishes this is proclaimed as a "Kumārikā";
she is said to be one who has bathed in knowledge (*vidyāsnātā*), and she alone is called a celibate student (*brahmacāriṇī*).
She who leads her husband into the womb is indeed the wife (*patnī*), for she is the very self of the embryo. 23.1–2.
She who has been led away according to her husband’s duty is a wife dear to the fallen.
(24) Listen now to the names of the hells, and indeed to that which causes distress for a couple when they remain childless. (25)
That suffering and that first hell dissolve away when one has offspring;
even the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the libations of water for the ancestors become only lukewarm when performed by one who is childless. (26)
That suffering is called the second hell, to be experienced by the ancestors.
However, when the ancestors have offspring, that suffering indeed dissolves.
In a house without offspring, there are neither purificatory rites nor festivals. (27–28)
The first sixteen [days] do not arise, nor are the deities satisfied;
the sixth and subsequent [days] are not worshipped, and no gifts are given.
This, indeed, is the suffering of the deities and the obstruction of merit.

The third hell is said to cease upon having offspring. For one without offspring, prosperity—devoid of lineage and heirs—is a fortune whose trust is destroyed; lacking enthusiasm, it does not bring joy. (2.47.30–31)
This fourth hell, which obstructs the fortune of wealth and happiness, is said to cease upon having offspring.
In a childless household, there is neither a son-in-law nor likewise a daughter-in-law.
There is no pavilion, nor pillars of rubies, nor the circumambulation of fire;
the Gārhapatya fire does not exist, nor would the deity presiding over its limbs be pleased.
Indeed, this misery of sacrifice obstructs the expansion of one's lineage.
The fifth hell has been described; it ceases upon having offspring.
In a childless household, there is not even the slightest fruit of desire or dharma.
There is no fruit of the seasonal rites (*ṛtudharma*), nor is there any fruit of the seasonal gift (*ṛtudāna*).
The destruction of seeds is fruitless and becomes a source of sin;
that sin brings about suffering and obstructs the goals of human life.
That is declared to be the sixth hell, which ceases upon having offspring.
Even guests do not find pleasure in a house without offspring,
nor do men wish to see the face of one childless in the morning.
Furthermore, those who possess children do not desire to have a residence for the childless situated beside them.
This indeed is human suffering, which obstructs the respect of the people;
it is declared to be the seventh hell. It ceases upon having offspring. A couple who are dear and beloved, yet childless, are as utterly contemptible as two ghosts.
Even while living, those two are as good as dead; no distinction exists here between them and the deceased, for their funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika) have been performed by the hands of others.
Such rites neither grant a higher rebirth nor do they obstruct the path to the world of the departed.
The eighth hell has been described; it ceases upon having offspring. Understand that these are the faults that exist in a childless household:
there is the intrusion of others and the service of sinners. 43.
Harshness consists in the fruitless acquisition of wealth through the giving of gifts and religious duties;
discontent always exists as the destroyer of worldly prosperity.
It is also the falling away from one's own duties and the fear of death.
Even eating sweet food alone, false accusation and the like,
consorting with another's wife or another man, greed, as well as covetousness, censuring those who have sons, and transgressing against the disciplined; 45–46.
The destruction of the conduct of the cultured, the abolition of virtuous rites and the like, the loss of refinement, delight in the ruin of others,
the forfeiture of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and the remoteness from liberation. 47.

And it is declared that for everyone, failing to act as a protector against these [evildoers] leads to hell. (48) Furthermore, a person who is childless and constantly enveloped by these sins—which are called "sons"—indeed dwells in terrible hells. (49)
Offspring utterly destroys the terrible hell;
for this reason, heaven is considered to consist of sons and daughters.
Just as a male disciple and a female disciple likewise remove sins.
He shall become a disciple, a slave, a servant, and an attendant of the learned;
or likewise, she shall be a female disciple, a female friend, a female slave, or a female attendant of the learned or the gurus; both of them shall be providers of assistance. (5.1–5.2)
Service to the gods, service to the ancestors, service to the sages, and even service to guests—these are interrupted somewhere during a calamity if one lacks a disciple.
Such an obstacle is declared to be caused by sin; therefore, the disciple indeed saves [the teacher].
Furthermore, for a person who is neither a householder nor free from disciples, no undertakings whatsoever succeed in this world; indeed, that leads to hell.
Knowledge, arts, skill, mantra, and eternal method—these [are the means]. 95.
Instruction, the sequence, the method, the lineage, and the commonality—all of these perish without a disciple.
Their destruction is said to lead to hell; it is averted when there is a disciple.
A disciple is fit for the transmission of consciousness, while a son is the heir to the inheritance.
A wife is a partner in half the duties and the destroyer of hell;
without a wife, there is no standing anywhere, not even in one's respected home and possessions.
There is no trust, no refuge, and no peace; for that is indeed hell.
There are no fire-offerings (homa) and the like, nor is there any purification; that sin leads eternally to hell.
Indeed, there is no accomplishment whatsoever in this world, nor even in the next.
That hell, which consists of all that is perceived, ceases upon attaining the state of having a wife.
Ignorance is said to be hell; it is the perpetual lack of knowledge regarding the Imperishable.
However, it perishes through the possession of wisdom in those who are celibate from youth.
This cycle of existence (saṃsāra) was fashioned in such a way that, without assistance,
no task can be accomplished here among the social classes (varṇas) or even the stages of life (āśramas).
Furthermore, lack of assistance leads to hell, since it causes the failure of one's undertakings.
For since heaven is accompanied by assistance, it brings about the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Indeed, in many undertakings, a son, a disciple, and a wife are protectors from hell and providers of help. (63–64)
Whatever various kinds of evil there may be— whether physical, vocal, or mental, whether born of one's own nature, or even committed without an assistant—
all that goes to dissolution through [the presence of] a son, a disciple, a beloved, and so forth.
Therefore, a wise man should indeed appoint both a son and a disciple [as heirs].
Six heirs and six kinsmen are proclaimed to be the offspring;
likewise, three disciples and three wives are proclaimed.
And three types of sons have been declared who follow according to their respective actions;
listen, O daughters, for I shall describe them to you here in brief:
the legitimate son of the body (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the given son (datta), and the adopted son (kṛtrima).
The son born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*), as well as the son brought home (*ānīta*)—these six are the heirs and kinsmen.
While these six exist, there shall be the performance of debt-repayment, funeral rites, and the distribution of wealth;
the lineage’s renown, its sustenance within the family, its stability, and the expansion of the clan [depend upon them]. (2.47.70)
Among these, the *aurasa* (legitimate son) is one born of one's own body, being the very reflection of oneself.
That which is begotten upon another's wife by one's command is the *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).
He who is given by his mother and father is indeed proclaimed as the *dattaka* (adopted son).

One who considers a son born of a friend or others as his own is called a *kṛtrima* (artificial) son. One whose origin in the house is not known is a *gūḍhaka* (secretly born) son. And one who is brought from outside is indeed called an *ānīta* (brought-in) son.

The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the son born of a woman of lower caste (nimnavarṇaja)—these are merely bearers of names.
The son born of an unmarried girl is a kānīna; one born from a woman who was pregnant at marriage is a sahoḍha.
One who is taken with a price is indeed a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), and [the son born of her] is a *paunarbhava*.
A girl who, though given to one man, is given again to another, is a *punarbhū* woman; and the son of such a woman is a *paunarbhava*. 75–76.
One who arrives of his own accord during a famine or similar crisis, or one who has been abandoned in the forest by himself,
or one found in the woods without a protector, is declared a *svayamdatta* (self-given) slave.
A person born of a woman of lower caste from a man of superior caste is of lower caste.
Among these, there is no mention at all of debts, funeral offerings, or the like for those born of the lineage.
These three types of disciples—the initiated, the servant, and the attendant—as well as the heir, are those whose means of livelihood have been made one's own. (78–79)

Wives are of three kinds: the lawfully wedded (*vidhyūḍhā*), the remarried (*punarvyūḍhā*), and the clandestine (*nigūḍhikā*). In legal affairs, they are respectively superior, middling, and inferior. Husbands are likewise of three kinds: the wedded, the twice-wedded, and the paramour (*upapati*).
In legal proceedings, these are respectively superior, middling, and inferior (8:1).
Instruction, the sacred thread, and gifts should be given to them alone;
furthermore, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should be performed for them in order to remove the state of childlessness (8:2).
Just as there are heirs and kinsmen, so too are those related through kinship;
just as there are sons such as the son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna) and others, so too are daughters of that same kind.
Just as there are three types of male disciples, so also are there three types of female disciples.
In that regard, there is also worldly convention consisting of the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
Indeed, by means of the mantra, you ladies become my disciples;
likewise, the wives and daughters-in-law of the disciples also become vessels of knowledge.
Therefore, my knowledge, which constitutes the inheritance, must be bestowed;
indeed, this inheritance must be received from the Guru by millions of disciples.
Knowledge, liberation, as well as devotion, service, the worship of the Deity, and so forth—
The yoga of the Self, the attainment of Hari, and the merit of serving sacred fords and other holy sites—
these, indeed, are the portions of inheritance that purify the circle of disciples.
Now I shall further describe the Sudarśana with its sixteen spokes.
Having known that which is the Sudarśana, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, nothing further remains to be known.
He is the most excellent Beloved, dwelling within your hearts and yet existing outside as well.

I shall describe to you the supreme yoga whose essence is the Beloved within your own bodies. O most excellent maidens, come forward; take water in your hands and receive from my mouth the mantra of the Beloved Kṛṣṇa. 2.47.90–91.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā"— thus, O Rādhikā, they received this mantra from the mouth of Lomaśa;
and for its purpose, he then taught them the sixteen-petaled yoga.
The syllable *oṃ* resides in the hair; this is the illustrious Puruṣottama.
The syllable *na* is in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and it is the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
The syllable *ma* has entered the mouth; it is the Lord Māṇikyāpati. (93–94)

The syllable *śrī* resides in the eyes as Śrīpati, the Lord of Kamalā; the syllable *kṛ* is indeed Kṛṣṇa himself, established in the nape of the neck (*kṛkāṭikā*). The syllable *ṣṇa* dwells in the heart as this Lord Bālakṛṣṇa.
The letter *ma* resides at the navel, consisting of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
the letter *rā* resides in the locations of the body hairs as the Lord of Rādhikā;
the letter *ya* resides on the seat of the womb, reclining upon the waters of yoga.
The letter *ṇa* resides in the circle of the channels (*nāḍīmaṇḍala*) for the Supreme Man;
the letter *ya* resides in the mind as Hari, who grants the meaning of one's intentions.
The letter *pa* dwells in the two feet as the Lord, the Master of Pāravatī.
The letter *ta* is situated upon the pustules; he is the Lord himself, whose splendor is radiant.
(99) The letter *ya* resides at my knees; he is the Lord, the sovereign master of sovereignty.
The letter *sva* shines within all my limbs as his own beautiful essence. (100)
The syllable *hā* is the soul of the *haṃsa*; through service, it attained the *homa*.
The Lord with qualities (*saguṇeśa*) is indeed the fifteenth [digit], while I am the sixteenth digit (*kalā*). Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the possessor of all digits, is the lord of all digits.
"Knowing this supreme truth, my Lord shall indeed no longer be subject to birth.
O Rādhā! Thus did those maidens receive the garland of mantras;
they chanted them and worshipped their beloved Lord, who is non-different from their own Supreme Self.
But those men and women who, having realized this supreme truth, worship Śrī Narāyaṇa— who shines resplendently and is directly manifest— within their own bodies,
will undoubtedly attain the supreme state at the end; of this there is no doubt.
"From reading and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.

(105) Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by Lomaśa to the Daughters of Lakṣmaṇa Regarding His Sons, Disciples, Wives, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 47. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Age).

Chapter 49 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to this beautiful and wondrous tale concerning the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa in the month of Caitra; I shall relate it to you.
The daughters of the Grandfather (Brahmā), eternally youthful and established in their vows—
Constantly devoted to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*), they were reciters of the Sāmaveda.
Endowed with forms like the sun, the three maidens— Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā— became virgins upon the earth by the command of the Creator.
Driven by pride and impelled by the force of their own minds, they went there with a desire for the holy ford.
Indeed, in the past, they had heard from the mouth of Nārada in Satyaloka that on earth Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, shines as Nārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī.
(5) Then, desiring to know [more], they questioned Nārada:
"What are the qualities of that Blessed One, for whom you are so intent on praise? (6)
Then Nārada said: "O sisters! He is indeed the Blessed One—he who is the father of our father, Vairāja;
he whose father is Mahāviṣṇu, who is the Pradhānapuruṣa."
His father was Prakṛtīśa, and his father was Śrī Hari himself.
That youth is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
on earth, he is the son of Śrī Kambharā and the joy of the illustrious Gopāla.
This world, along with the world of the ancestors (Pitṛloka), and beyond that the layer of earth;
beyond that is the covering of water,
and beyond that, Vaikuṇṭha shines forth, which is considered to be a mass of radiant light.
And there are the worlds named Vairāja, where the Lord named Vairāja shines; therefore, that is the station of Mahāvaiṣṇava. Mahāviṣṇu resides there, and it is indeed the primary abode.
Therein lies that which is designated as the unmanifest (avyākṛta), where the Infinite (bhūman) shines forth;
that indeed is the lower Vaikuṇṭha, inhabited by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Beyond that, in the world of Prakṛti-sāttvika, is the supreme abode of Goloka.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines here; Vāsudeva, the Lord, shines in the unmanifest.
Beyond that is the imperishable abode where Brahman shines, accompanied by infinite liberated souls and resplendent with divine sovereignty. (14–15)
Beyond that is declared the supreme, auspicious abode of Hari;
it is eternal, enriched with all splendors, the great and highest of all abodes.
Residing in that supreme abode is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
He is the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, who is without beginning;
from whom indeed arise the Vyūhas such as Vāsudeva and others, as well as the incarnations, the lords, the gods, and the best of sages. (17–18)
He possesses infinite powers, such as Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, Śrī,
Lakṣmī, Pāravatī, Haṃsā, Kṛṣṇā, Vṛndā, Jayā, and others;
even among those, there are one hundred and twelve who stand by His side as the most excellent.
Prabhā, Pāravatī, Rādhā, and Lakṣmī—these four are indeed [his consorts].
(2.48.20) They are eternally non-different from his own form; Rādhā resides within his heart, while Lakṣmī is situated upon his chest in the form of a line. (21)
The radiance, appearing as a halo of splendor, is situated upon his dark face;
Pārvatī, whose essence is marked by the lotus, resides on his left thigh.
In this manner, other [goddesses] also abide, embodied within the various limbs of his body.
And those other goddesses, numbering in the hundreds of billions, who reside in every pore of his body,
being youthful, worship him as their husband—
he who is a treasure-trove of all charm, beauty, bliss, and good fortune.
Ten million billion young maidens residing in the realm of Brahmā worship him; fourteen thousand Nālas and impure beings also worship him.
There are ten million Dīpāvalyas and likewise sixty of his daughters.
Talājā, the daughter of a Daitya, and the daughters of Gopa worship him. A hundred foremost maidens serve that Supreme Lord;
a maiden named Krodhanikā also worships that Nārāyaṇa.
Caves and maidens by the tens of millions also attend upon him;
likewise, the Brahmaputrī, the Sūcī, and Vanadeva attend in their hundreds of thousands.
A hundred thousand daughters of Rākṣasas attend upon him as their husband.
There were five or six thousand, as well as ten thousand, belonging to the Kaṅka-tālīya class;
there were Apsarases from the Brahmasaras lake, Devakoṭikas, the daughters of Aryaman,
and likewise the daughters of Kubera.
The daughters of Indra, the daughters of Yama, and thousands of daughters of Vāyu;
the daughters of the Seasons, the daughters of Viśvakarman, and the daughters of the Trees (3:1);
and the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas, numbering five thousand.
They worship that Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Likewise, the sixteen wives of Vasanta worship Him, as do five hundred daughters of Sāla and Māla. (32–33)
Ten thousand Naga maidens, a thousand daughters of Śava and Dīna,
and thousands of fierce maidens of the Aindrajālika class;
sixty young maidens and fourteen who are of the nature of Vidyās.
The daughters of Vahni, the daughters of Śravaṇa, those born of the Year, the daughters of trees,
and those born from the earth worship that Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, two thousand maidens of Lakṣmaṇa worship him.
The Lord of Yogis, who possesses innumerable forms, is the eternal youth and sovereign Master.
Through union with Him comes liberation and the generation of an ocean of bliss.
Since this state exists eternally through Him, those seeking liberation worship Him.
"I always go there in the morning to behold him;
I sing his virtues, and Sarasvatī sings of him. Having been addressed thus by Nārada, these three sisters indeed— ||| 38-39 ||
With their minds fixed upon Him, they traveled by celestial chariot from Satya-loka to the Himalayas, following the path of the Mandākinī;
having beheld the Lord of Śrī-Badarī, they descended and worshipped Him.
Having beheld Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, Arbuda, and the Sarasvatī,
as well as the mountain Catuṣtila and the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
they arrived by means of their celestial chariot, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
From the path of the sky, those beautiful women beheld the earth ablaze at the moment of moonrise on the evening of the full moon of Caitra;
through the air, they saw that field of Kuṅkumavāpī like another sun.
And they beheld him shining, without even the slightest darkness.
Then they reflected that this was the field of Puruṣottama;
and they saw a lake and a vast city.
In the center, however, they beheld a magnificent golden palace, circular like the sun, proclaiming its own self as if it were the solar disc;
and there were various wonderful gardens filled with celestial flowers.
They beheld delightful celestial abodes and thousands of hermitages of sages;
they saw divine beings and deities, as well as forest deities,
and likewise the hermitages of incarnations and the dwellings of the Lord.
They beheld the divine and auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa, radiant as the moon,
spread with celestial herbs and inhabited by maidens;
and they saw the bridge of holy fords extending all around through the sky.
Having performed four circumambulations of that sacred field,
and having reflected upon the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa which resembled the sun,
they offered a rain of flowers accompanied by shouts of victory.
The cry of "Victory! from the goddesses pervaded the sky on all sides.
Hearing those sounds mingled with cries of victory, the people looked up into the sky.
[It was] like the moon pervaded by moonlight, yet in form resembling a lotus.
A celestial chariot that brings joy to the eyes, rich with exquisite fragrance, composed of light, wonderful, and beautified by various colors;
having entered within, it was auspicious, visible to the eye, and occupied by maidens. (53–54)
Filled with divine objects, enriched with cloths and archways,
adorned with golden jars, possessing three peaks and provided with three seats—
human beings and others beheld it, overcome by supreme wonder. (55)

The celestial chariot remained steady in the sky above the temple of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. There, three maidens heard the sounds arising from all sides produced by the waving of lights (nīrājana). ||56-57||
Amidst numerous sounds and innumerable supreme hymns of praise,
they became absorbed in Him at that time and attained supreme peace.
Then, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, knowing those daughters of Brahmā to be devoted to Him as His bhaktas—
He himself appeared in the celestial chariot in the form of a youth.
He bestowed upon them for a moment the bliss born of his divine appearance, the supreme joy of touch, and the great happiness arising from their embrace.
There, Śrī Hari brought the celestial chariot down to his own abode;
he then became invisible within the vehicle and entered the golden palace. Those maidens descended from the chariot into Kṛṣṇa’s mansion.
They stood for a moment upon the moon-chamber (candraśāla) near the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Taking those divine and radiant offerings from the chariot,
they placed them upon the moon-chamber, awaiting the one who would show them the way.
Knowing the male servants and female servants, as well as the descent [into the palace],
and the porters and attendants for the purpose of entering within,
those daughters of Śrī Kambharā remained in the upper chamber (candraśālā).
Santoṣā quickly arrived together with her friend Suśīlā and with Amṛtā, the wife of her divine brother.
Then those divine maidens, whose bodies were composed of splendor, who resided in the moon-chamber, [appeared]. || 65-66 ||
Having seen them, they quickly spoke words of welcome and comfort: "Come, O illustrious ones, toward Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
[and see] your mother and father, resplendent in the seventh heaven. (67)
Thus addressed, Suṣumṇā, Iḍā,
and Piṅgalā likewise [brought] flower garlands, sandalwood, camphor, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as saffron, fragrant essences, and the finest filaments.
Jeweled necklaces, jeweled ornaments, a crown, and likewise earrings;
divine betel, divine fruits, and unguents;
divine and lovely collyrium, and the most excellent *brāhma* oil.
Saugandhika flowers, water-essences, and garments purified by fire;
necklaces of excellent gems and diamonds, golden vessels,
mirrors of divine appearance, and celestial powders for rubbing the body.
And taking divine offerings suitable for the gods, sweet foods prepared with grain,
nectar-like substances, the essence of milk, countless seeds and fruits, as well as vessels filled with excellent divine drinks; ||| 73 || and having likewise taken these once more.
Taking divine beds and coverlets as well as celestial garments to wear,
they descended slowly with vessels in their hands; and by means of staircases suitable for noble descent, they reached another level of the earth.
In front was the maiden Santoṣā; in the middle were three daughters of goats;
and behind them were Amṛtā and her sister-in-law Suśīlikā.
Then, descending to one spot upon a vast expanse of ground, [they sat] on a spread of earth.
They entered the seventh floor where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
There, the virtuous mother Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī shone resplendent.
Having prostrated before their mother and having prostrated before Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, [they remained there]. (77–78)
When divine seats had been offered, they sat down as was appropriate;
and they were addressed by their mother regarding auspiciousness, well-being,
and likewise the purpose of their visit toward their father and mother.
They spoke of their entire acquaintance, saying, "We are the daughters of Brahmā—
Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and the maiden named Piṅgalā.
By the instruction of our own brother Nārada," [81]
Having recognized this glorious son as the beginningless Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself— the lovely, eternal youth—
we have come here to behold him; we are blessed today by his vision.
"Today our birth has become fruitful, and our maidenhood is fruitful as well;
even our status as goddesses is fruitful, O Mother, by the sight of you.
Having spoken thus, she questioned Amṛtā, Santuṣā, and Suśīlikā. (83–84)
Those who were dear to Keśava, Bālakṛṣṇa, performed worship;
first they worshipped Kṛṣṇa’s feet with water from the Gaṅgā,
and they placed the nectar of the Lord of Śrī’s feet upon their faces and heads.
Then they applied drops of sandalwood paste and other substances to the forehead of Hari;
they applied fragrant unguents and gave him scented water.
They also gave him camphor, collyrium, saffron, and other such items.
They gave flower garlands, jewel necklaces, various types of crowns, as well as bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments;
they also gave garments, beds, fruits, food, and drinks.
They placed chowries and other articles before him;
they also offered food offerings and various sweet drinks.
They presented betel leaf and then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
They performed circumambulations and placed a great garland around his neck— an eternal signifier of their innermost feelings.
And the beloved, having accepted with his hand that worship performed by his beloveds, [proceeded].
Kṛṣṇa, who understands their inner feelings, touched their hands to awaken them to what was to come;
laughing and looking repeatedly at their faces,
they too rejoiced greatly because of the arrival of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Rādhā.

Then, like that, they offered those unfading flower garlands around the necks of their mother, as well as Santoshā and Amṛtā. Bowed down before them, they paid their respects; having been fed and made to rest, they were refreshed.
They were given drink, laid down to rest, and massaged upon their beds;
they were attended by female friends and maidservants, and then fell asleep. Rising in the morning and bathing in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, ||95-96||
Having performed the supreme ritual for visiting sacred sites and gone to the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa,
he took up the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," along with a rosary and Tulasī, and beheld ten billion [manifestations].
Having worshipped the circle of maidens with devotion and a serene mind,
they bowed and quickly returned once more to Kṛṣṇa, their beloved.
Having obtained his sight, those women, who were under the sway of Kṛṣṇa, remained satisfied again and again.
As if insatiable, they gazed upon their lord and master, holding him within their hearts;
for they had been accepted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself within his own heart. When they expressed no desire to go toward their own homes, Nārāyaṇa then spoke.
Having again received her father’s command, she returned here in haste.
"I shall fulfill the hearts' desires of you all, of this there is no doubt," she said;
having spoken thus, she offered all the articles before Hari. 101–102.
Having made the palace empty of people and having worshipped Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Rādhā, then,
after eating, bowing down, and receiving His permission,
you should propitiate your beloved Śrī Hari by bowing to Him again and again.
Having obtained the fruit and flowers born of their serene devotion, they ascended celestial chariots.
Having repeatedly bowed to Aśvapaṭṭasara, Kuṅkumavāpikā,
and the temple of Kāntadeva, they traveled through the sky by means of a vehicle in the atmosphere.
Having uttered shouts of victory again and again, he vanished in an instant.
By reading or hearing this, one becomes possessed of the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Three Daughters of Brahmā—Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā—arrived by means of an aerial chariot, regarded the Lord as their husband, worshipped Him, and departed," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
