Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Beloved! Why was it that Suṣumṇā and the others, though accepted by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, were not commanded to stay in the hermitage of Lomaśa? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Seventy-two thousand other daughters of Brahmā,
who were his mind-born offspring, desired Kṛṣṇa as their beloved and supreme lord.
They were dwelling in Satyaloka and awaited with devotion that the three elder sisters would arrive upon seeing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. "We shall go there together with them to behold Him."
"We shall serve Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Mādhava.
While they were thus waiting for His arrival,
they were not permitted to remain now in the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
"Sent by Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa will protect them once again.
Then, by means of their own celestial chariot, they [departed] toward the western and southern directions,
as well as the ocean and uninhabited islands with excellent regions.
Beholding [the earth] while traveling by way of the sky toward the north with the desire to circumambulate it,
they saw a vast region completely free of clouds. Turning back again and again, they traveled fearlessly through the air in their vehicle.
Having seen the great island of Āra-bīja and the battle-field ahead of him,
and having seen the ocean of blood, he beheld the river Nārāyaṇī upon the ground;
and on the southern side, he saw the Rudrabāṣpa lake.
Likewise, having seen the excellent lake named Vijñaturīya,
as well as the Tuṅgānīka lake and the Nyāsasara lake,
and having beheld the Liṅgarasa mountain and the Drākṣābīja mountain.
Having seen Kālahari and the Raṇa, as well as Umāśambhugiri;
having seen the river Karmāṅgī and likewise the mountain Karmaghna;
then having seen Caṇḍasara and beheld the river Naṣṭajarā.
Then, having observed the battle known as Hari-Hara,
he likewise beheld the mountain Ataleṣṭa, the mountain Tanmukha,
the Trirāśi mountain, and the Līlābīja battle.
Śrī Rāmā, having seen the battlefield and beheld the kingdom of Turu,
and having seen the ocean-like Kaśyapāyana and Mount Coral,
and having looked toward Mount Kukkeśa in the west and the blue ocean; || 15 ||
And the river Nīparā, as well as Mount Kārpaṇthāyana;
having seen the river Dīnayūpā and Mount Ailaparvata; and Mount Īpīnāsana and the island Śāradīdvīpa. (16–17)
Having beheld Madhyavāhin and his own father’s mountain,
and having seen the river Tegirā and the regions situated in the midst of the ocean,
he saw the river Lukvārā, the Senānadī, and the Khāḍikā.
And having beheld Jarāmauna-pradeśa and Bālayama-pradeśaka,
as well as Iṅgadvīpa and Āyadvīpa,
and Khāḍikā, Koṭadvīpa, Svedadvīpa, and thereafter Phenadvīpa. (2.49.20)
Then, having observed the Piṣṭavargas, as well as the mountains,
the earth, Ālīśāmṛtapṛthivī, the heavens, the islands beginning with Nadvīpaka,
and the Khāḍikā islands, they went to the land of Vikturīya.
Having crossed the Khāḍī river, they then entered the Northern Kurus.
Among them, they saw the great Mahābṛhat lake, the great Sulu-named lake, the Ayābāṣka lake,
and the Vinipātagacchaka lake.
The Haṭṭāsana mountain, the ocean, and also the island of Dviphena; the earth beginning with Lambodara, the lake situated high above it all,
the region of Santaluyī, and the region extending as far as Atala.
Having crossed the Mākṣika mine and beheld the island of Kyubā, he then surveyed the Vargi islands;
thereafter, he looked upon the Grīya islands, beheld the Āmārjunā river, and saw the region of Śāntārāma. (25–26)
Beholding the earth as far as the Brahmīla region, they gazed upon the lands of others; and having observed the regions of Ārjayaṇtī, they looked toward the two islands of Koka.
Having seen Grāhāma and Cārakoṭa, as well as Antārkivartula, [they proceeded further].
Having observed regions of water and stone, as well as the Binduka cave in the earth,
they turned back and beheld Tirodeva,
Paṭṭoga, Cīllikā, Perukā, Pṛthvī, Pan-nāmī, and likewise Nirjhara. (28–29)
Having beheld the Mākṣika mountain, the Bhūtala region, and having observed Nimnaphorna;
having seen the Kīṭa mountain, the Rokiśaila mountain, and the Ilāsana mountain;
and having beheld the Raṅgila mountain and the Alāṃśukā land.
Having crossed the ocean at Dvirika, he beheld Kāmacāṭaka;
then the river Kālimā, the Yāmas, the Bīnas, the regions of Tandrā, the river Yāneśī,
and after that, the river Obī.
Having beheld Mount Urala and having observed the island of Nāva,
and having observed the islands of Phiyojāna and Āsana with their flourishing populations,
and having observed the great mountain Skandanābha and the White Ocean (Śvetavārdhi).
Having seen the Devī river, the Valgā river, the river named Valgā, and the mountains called Valgā;
having seen Lake Urala as well as Bālakṛṣṇa-saras;
and having seen the regions of Śveta and Rakta, as well as Sāvari-araṇya.
Having seen the land of Kimpuruṣa and the lake Dvikala,
having observed the mountain Prabhālunā and the mountain Stenāvāsa,
and having looked upon the ocean where there are places for drinking water and so forth, [they proceeded].
Having beheld the Piśaṅgavārdhi and likewise the Akṣiga mountain,
then having seen the Gopīraṇa and the Āpatāyika mountain,
as well as the Triyānāsana mountain and the Kunalīna mountain.
Having beheld Mount Kārukora and the radiant Cipiṅga country,
the river Śikṣāṅgī with its limbs of training and its subsidiary streams,
the Phullipāna islands, and the Vāraṇīyaka islands; || 3.9 ||
Having beheld the island of Navagīti and the islands born of the ocean,
they surveyed from the sky the earth known as Uṣṇālayā;
then, having looked upon Cāṭadeśa and the mountains of Divādika, they proceeded further.
Having seen Okadvīpa and Navajīvadvīpa situated within the ocean,
and having seen the Trāsamāna island, they saw the Murā river at the abode of the camels;
[they saw] the Turu river, the Aita river, and Mount Mekadāneya.
And having seen Maśakagrīvaśaila, the Mahāraṇa forest, as well as the five lakes, Mount Dārāliṅga, Bālādri,
the Hemashālā mountain, and the regions of Ārṇahemapradeśaka.
Having seen all of Sumātra and the land of Malaya, he then saw the islands of Annada, the Śyāma regions, the river Mikāṅganā,
the river Irāvatī, Mount Cārākarṇa, and the lands of Brahmadeśaka.
Having seen the forest named Sundara, the great river Hutalinī,
the Gaṅgā, and the Brahmaputrā, as well as the Khāsī mountains,
the great mountain Patatkārya, and the regions of the Himalayas.
Having seen Lake Mānasa and the region of Śrī, as well as Trivartana;
having seen the Indukuśa river and Mount Kṛpālupa;
and having seen Thararaṇa, Kaccha, and Lake Sābharaka.
And having seen Mount Āravallī and the river Narmadā;
the mountain named Saptapuṭa and the great river Tapatī;
having seen Mahābaleśvara as well as Mount Malaya. || 2.49.50 ||
Having beheld the Sahya mountain and the southern regions,
and having sighted the island named Siṃhala situated in the ocean, they turned back.
[They also saw] the river Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇā, and the great river Godāvarī.
Having beheld the sacred field of Jagannāthapura, as well as Kapilāśrama,
Vaṅga, Aṅga, Vihāra, Bhūtāna,
Nipala, the Gaṇḍakī, Kurukṣetra, and Gaṅgādvāra, they [departed]. ||52-53||
O Rādhikā! Having gone to Badarī, they dwelt there happily through the night after performing service to Nārāyaṇa and worshipping that Lord.
Then, having beheld Gaurīśṛṅga, Śivaśṛṅga, and likewise the celestial river (Svardhunī), [they departed].
Following the path of the celestial Gaṅgā from the world of the gods (Svarloka) to Satyaloka,
they went into the presence of the venerable Brahmā, overflowing with great bliss.
Then Iḍā, Suṣumṇā, and Piṅgalā likewise paid homage to their father.
Overwhelmed with great joy, they described the ritual performed at the sacred ford as it had been done:
the nectar of the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They offered garlands of flowers and chanted the mantra again and again.
And they spoke to one another about Nārada’s kindness.
Upon hearing the news, seventy-two thousand other maidens also arrived there to learn the details of what had occurred. ||58-59||
Then, for the sake of a welcome, they approached in the presence of Brahmā:
the illustrious Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, Viśvodarā, Kuhū, Alambuṣā,
Gāndhārī, Śaṅkhinī, and Payasvinī.
Sarasvatī, Vāruṇī, Tejasvinī, and Raktinī;
Purītat, Vīryavāhā, Prāṇavāhā, and likewise Ārdrikā—these and others, numbering seventy-two thousand, are indeed present there. (6.1–6.2)
The sixteen divine maidens, each less than sixteen years of age,
repeatedly offered their affectionate welcome to the three of them.
They drank the water from the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with reverence, they took up the flowers from the garlands of grace;
they heard the news of Śrī Hari concerning his form and beauty,
which was entirely composed of wonder, as well as that of the city itself.
They also heard that at the hermitage of Lomaśa and at the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa, there was the service of hundreds of millions of maidens;
as well as Yaśasvinī and others, the daughters of Brahmā born from the Nāḍī lake.
They beheld the supreme beauty and splendor of the three sisters,
both their divine nature bestowed by the beloved Kṛṣṇa and their worldly form;
they reflected deeply upon that most excellent fortune of Kṛṣṇa.
They considered it their own misfortune that the vision [of the Lord] did not arise;
they thought, "We have not even gone for the sake of seeing Him—how indeed could there be a vision?
For by the command of their father, they must certainly go to see Acyuta.
"Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved, the Supreme Lord"— thinking thus, they spoke eagerly to their father:
"O Father, please cause us to have a vision of Him, just as you have done for these others."
"We shall choose that very one, the Lord of lords, the Supreme Person.
When this was said to Brahmā by them, Brahmā rejoiced in his mind:
"What other supreme gain could there be than this—that Hari should become my son-in-law? (72)
Blessed are those maidens in this world whose maidenhood is thus made fruitful;
blessed is their father, blessed is their mother, and blessed is their family.
Blessed are Bhṛgu, the Ocean, Kedāra, and Anaraṇyaka.
Sūrya is none other than Nārāyaṇa;

those whose daughters will be the wives of Kṛṣṇa, and those whose auspicious sons will become the husbands of Kṛṣṇa’s consorts—such as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and others—those people shall be blessed in the world. (75)
If that which is to be attained through devotion, knowledge, austerity, detachment, sacrifices and the like,
or through hardships, yogic practices, charity and so forth,
or even through service to the virtuous, can be obtained through affection— [then what need is there for other means]? (76–77)
If the Supreme Person should meet with delusion, youth, latent impression, desire, beauty, or the force of the senses,
then that delusion, youth, desire, latent impression, beauty, and the sense-organ [are all overcome]. 78.
Everything is of the nature of Dharma and must be understood as such; even desire and anger are composed of that.
In Kṛṣṇa, desire as well as greed and delusion always bring about liberation.
Liberation is eternal bliss, and that resides in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Whether something blameworthy or praiseworthy has been done for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa, it should all be understood as venerable, for it is indeed purifying and salvific.
Oh, daughters! I am truly blessed and fortunate forever.
"What gift shall I bestow upon Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is a worthy recipient? What is Kṛṣṇa’s desire? Having ascertained this, I shall give so that it may be auspicious.
Having said this, Brahmā himself called to mind the sage Nārada.

In an instant, he appeared there, bowed down, and took his place upon a seat. Brahmā said: "Your three sisters, Suṣumṇā and the others, having worshipped Nārāyaṇa where He was, have now returned here."
In this regard, there are other maidens here who are eager to go and see him;
therefore, you must take them there by means of celestial chariots.
When the proper occasion arrives, I shall give these maidens to Kṛṣṇa.
Seventy-two thousand auspicious channels (*nāḍī*), such as Yaśasvinī and the rest, which are like the waters of a lake, desire to behold Keśava.
He possesses ten levels, a single peak, and moves according to his will.
Take this Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), which is a circle one *yojana* in length and breadth.
Plant here the creepers of desire, the trees of desire, the wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) that bestow wealth, and the nectar that provides desired food and other enjoyments. (88–89)
Indeed, here there are armories, barracks for the army, and dining halls;
there are also halls for counsel and collections of medicinal herbs and the like. Furthermore, there are alchemy laboratories, clothing workshops, and guard stations here as well.
The supernatural powers (*siddhis*), the divine energies (*śaktis*), and the female servants (*dāsīs*) and attendants (*kiṅkaras*) exist here by the hundreds of thousands.
Likewise, these various weapons, the four Vedas,
and even the ritual applications for death and other ends are truly present here in embodied form.
For the purpose of destroying Indra’s net, for the purpose of destroying illusion,
and for the purpose of destroying the Daityas and Dānavas, there exist here personified mantras.
In the end, I myself am Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and also Nārāyaṇa.
Just as we, being conscious beings, dwell here directly in embodied form,
so too you should accept this celestial chariot (vimāna), which is uncuttable, indivisible, untarnishable, indestructible, unburnable, and eternal. (94–95)
O Sage, O son, together with the seventy-two thousand channels— namely Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā— along with those [other] maidens,
proceed indeed toward the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who resides upon the earth.
Taking various kinds of desirable gifts of divine splendor—
auspicious articles of utility such as ornaments, necklaces, and decorations—
bring them along in this vehicle and offer them happily to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 97–98 ||
Thus addressed, Nārada there requested Sanatkumāra—
the virtuous form, the form of Brahman, the protector, and the embodiment of spiritual luster—
as well as Rudra and Dharmarāja, indeed requesting them for the sake of protection. (99)
Then Brahmā bestowed the Dharma upon Sanatkumāra and Rudra.
The maidens ascended a celestial vehicle laden with divine objects;
adorned with every ornament and beauty, they uttered cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Auspicious signs occurred there again and again at the start of the journey;
then Sāvitrī called out from behind as they were departing:
"O daughters, go with care, taking provisions and garlands!"
Saying, "Take it," Devaśivā then gave this most excellent auspicious object to them. With a melodious voice, she invoked victory;
even Devahārīta, who had previously been turned away, now stood before her.
As the vehicle was moving along, Nārada’s lute fell from his hand; it became an inauspicious omen, for it broke into two pieces. "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Thus spoke Nārada for the sake of pacifying the inauspiciousness.
That celestial chariot descended from Satyaloka toward the earth in the western direction, reaching the Lokāloka mountain in an instant. (106–107)
Having found a moment’s rest upon the golden ground,
she proceeds slowly from the path of the sky, having fixed her direction toward the east;
the maidens behold her as she approaches the earth.
"They rejoice together upon the oceans and in various lands"—
thus, O Rādhikā, the demons of cruel mind saw that vehicle, which had arrived above the clouds and was as radiant as the sun.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Suṣumṇā and Others Viewing the Regions of the Earth by Means of a Celestial Vehicle and Then Departing for Satyaloka, as Well as the Seventy-two Thousand Maidens Setting Out through the Sky in a Celestial Vehicle for the Sake of Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 50: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Tretā-yuga Lineage) [Chapter 50 begins]
[Author: Chapter 51.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! To this divine wonder of Hari as well.
And at that time, the fruit of the breaking of the lute occurred for those dwelling in vehicles;
likewise for those who dwell in uncultivated lands, the Mlecchas born of the Rākṣasa womb, and those who live in the forest, in villages, or on mountains. (1–2)
Standing at a distance of a thousand yojanas, they then gazed upon that celestial chariot in the sky,
which was equal to a hundred suns and possessed a radiant canopy;
it surpassed the splendor of the sun by ten times in its majestic power.
He emitted rays into the sky that were neither hot nor cold, but temperate;
they were beautiful to behold and pleasant to the touch, laden with a mass of exquisite fragrance.
They were producers of bliss, bestowers of peace, and wondrously radiant.

O Rādhā, whatever has been offered by Brahmā for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—what indeed could be lacking there? In that celestial chariot, everything becomes like that of humans: streams of ghee, milk, and yogurt, and excellent lakes of nectar-like water.

There, within the eternal wish-fulfilling trees, there are always found pills made from the essence of sandalwood paste, the essence of powders, and the essence of other substances; as well as excellent betel rolls containing the essence of mercury, the essence of fragrance, and exquisite chewing spices. (7–8)
The jewel-islands are worthy of being seen, resplendent with many colors and other qualities,
enchanting to the hearts of maidens with the hue of golden campaka flowers;
they possess groves of golden arches and bowers of green foliage.
There, beautiful plateaus shine forth, adorned with lush meadows serving as delightful seats within the gardens; they are auspicious, resembling the surface of the moon.
The beauty of the maidens has the form of celestial chariots, and their appearance is like moonlight.
Indeed, all forms of light are likewise produced from material objects such as lamps;
and the forms of jewels, gems, and so forth, though distinct from one another,
attain a mutual superiority, each shining most excellently.
Whose minds among the people would not indeed become agitated with rivalry,
drawn by such divine rays,
by celestial maidens, and by divine splendors? (13–14)
Incited by them, the Mlecchas and Daityas dwelling in Abhrīkta,
wielding illusory spells and mantras, obstructed that celestial chariot in the sky.
They were swift, filled with hope and greed for gain, and considered themselves successful.

Without deliberation, they fall even into that which brings fierce suffering ending in death. Just as moths, seeing fire, fall with the desire, "Let us seize it," so too do people fall for the sake of enjoying forms, only to be consumed by its extreme brilliance.
Even those unworthy of the vessel exert themselves for a meager fruit;
casting themselves into what cannot be reached by their power, they meet with death.
These are the Asuras, the Kālasīdas, and the Mlecchas, who imagine their own strength to be sufficient.
Greatly incensed and acting with haste, they donned their armor and came to the battlefield.
Raktavārdhi, Raudrabāṣpa, Vijñaturīyaka,
Tuṅgānīka, Nyāsasāra, and the exceedingly fierce Liṅgarasa [also arrived].
Dhvākṣabīja, Mūśalāmba, Karmāṅga, Karmahā, Caṇḍasāra, Naṣṭajara, Sahāra,
Cātaleṣṭaka, Tuṅgamukha, Trirāśi, Līlābīja, and Bhayaṅkara.
Phalgubīja, Gambhīrākṣa, Senāgola,
Sphuṭārdana, Jīvala, Ketaṇḍa, Kumeru, Sthānali, Tumbāsura, Līnāpa, Cāliviṣṭa, and Kimūṣaka. (22–23)
Tūnāya, likewise Ābāla, Rukvāsana, Māvura,
Bāṅgivali, Dinolūka, Kuvaṃśaja, Kurenṛka,
many Dhodhasādas, Ambikāsa, and Śirvama.
Deṣala, Kakrala, Ījyāpāta, Nabījaka,
Sudāna, Sumāli, Kāṇima, Trigoṇika,
Rudraśiras, Triṣvāla, Pilipa, and Namākuva. (25–26)
Dinamera, Aṅgulāda, Phenaga, Kāmanāruṇi, Nimnajhara, Lālavāra, Hrīyoḍha, Mārakarkaśa, Alijīra,
Roṇḍega, Śāhuda, and Phakarāṇaka. (27)
Pārṣṇi, Kṛkāṭaka, Piṇḍanala, Randhrapramoṣaka;
Bhujahā, Jatruśamana, Lāmaka, Mūrdhabhāmaka;
Prakoṣṭhaka, Pṛṣṭhavaṃśa, and likewise Nitambaveṇuka. (28–29)
Āsavāpa, Amīṣapa, Kukkuṭāśa, and Kṛkāśaka—
these powerful ones, moving through the sky by means of their illusory power,
all arrived at the battle arrayed with the speed of lightning.

Thereupon, King Jumāsēmla dispatched a messenger named Raktavārdhika to the front of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to convey his desired message. The king said: "O Raktaka, go to the front of the chariot and announce this!"
"Let there be a celestial chariot for us here, and let our maidens become women [of that realm].
Let men situated in the chariot go to heaven and find happiness elsewhere.
Otherwise, we shall simply seize the maidens by force."
"And we shall slay you; therefore, do whatever you wish in this matter.
Having bowed, the messenger went before the celestial chariot and spoke exactly those words.
Nārada said to that messenger: "Speak thus to the king of the asuras on my behalf."
The maidens who are here are indeed the daughters of Brahmā, and you are born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, the grandson of Brahmā. Daitya Hiraṇyacakṣus had a son named Sukālika.
Añjana, Kālamegha, Jāsuśeṣa, Malīnasa, Hāvuka,
Bhāvuka, Dāuka, Dhāvuka, as well as Kvaśmaka and Ajamāla— these and others, such as the Saireyas, number more than a hundred. (37–38)
When the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa had been slain by Viṣṇu in his boar incarnation,
they fled in fear of him, yet they were obstructed by the mountains of the battlefield. Having arrived at this region, they made their dwelling here.
Indeed, you who belong to that lineage have likewise become devoid of virility;
born from the lineages of my brothers and others, you are unrefined and behave like barbarians (mlecchas).
Here I am, as is Nārada, and likewise the sage Sanat resides here.
For here the King of Dharma shines as the wielder of the staff;
and here Rudra, the supreme Lord who effects the destruction of the worlds, resplendent.
Formerly, in the forest, Rudra was indeed [worshipped] by the childless Hiraṇyākṣa.
It is said that in former times Lord Hara was propitiated for the sake of a son;
by his power, your grandfather became possessed of offspring.
Let them not obstruct that Rudra here, nor let them obstruct Yama, the lord of the dead.
All those mothers shall indeed become your daughters;
for without conquering Yama and Rudra, the fulfillment of your desire is difficult to attain.
Only one who could cross the ocean with his arms or cast the sun to the earth [could achieve this].
He might even uproot Mount Meru and conquer Yama and Śaṅkara.
O King, have you not heard how in former times the demon Andhaka, deluded by his lust for Pārvatī, met his destruction along with his Daitya hosts? (46–47)
Mahiṣa, as well as Jambha and Kujambha, met their destruction;
likewise Śaṅkhacūḍa and Jālandhara also perished.
Muru was reduced to ashes, and others too were destroyed, slain by delusion.

In former times, King Daṇḍa, deluded by lust for another's wife, met his destruction along with his entire kingdom after taking pleasure with the daughter of Śukra. Listen, O messenger! Having heard this, you must report it to the lord of men.
Daṇḍa was a great king, possessing abundant forces and vehicles;
that monarch, protected by Śukra, performed various sacrifices.
And Śukra served as his priest again and again at those sacrifices.
Once, Śukra went to the netherworld (pātāla) at the counsel of the Daityas.
Śukra had a daughter named Arajā who resided in his house;
she was alone in a leaf-hut, tending the sacrificial fire.
The king, having come to the house made of leaves to see her,
and having bowed to the fire, beheld a single maiden of beautiful form;
at that very moment, the monarch was consumed by desire.
But these [ascetics] did not recognize her as the preceptor’s daughter, though she was endowed with full youth.
When he arrived, that maiden, whose wealth was her asceticism, rose to meet him,
honored him as if he were a brother, and gave him a beautiful garland.
Then the king said to her: "O girl, gladden me here, who am tormented by the fire of desire, with the water of your embrace.
She then said to him: "But my father would surely burn you and me."
"You are capable of reviving the gods and even slaying them;
since you are my brother by dharma and a disciple of my father,
O King, you ought not to harbor such a thought in your mind in private."
He said, "O timid one, Śukra will consume me in due time;
but today the fire of passion burns me here—quench it!
She replied, "O King Daṇḍa, wait for a moment."
"Entreat that very Guru; he will undoubtedly grant it to you.
Daṇḍa replied: "O Araja! There is no room for delay at all.
Indeed, at every single moment, a succession of obstacles is found everywhere."
Virajā said: "O lord of men, I am not able to give myself away;
for women are utterly lacking in self-control regarding sensual pleasures.
What can I say to you, O King, who are thus treading upon a wrong path?"

Your kingdom, your realm, your family, yourself, and whatever else belongs to you—all this, joined with you, shall go to destruction by the curse of Śukra. Do not do this, O King; do not cast yourself into the fire, for this is not righteous.
The king said: "If you do not agree, I shall surely devour you by force!
O Arajā, taking the sacrificial fire in her own hand, she hurled it over the king, saying:
'Go, O evil-souled one, depart from here with your mind shattered!'"
Having spoken thus, as she was running outside to leave the leaf-hut,
that dull-witted man, his mind and soul overcome by lust, seized her, pressed her against his chest, and violated her. (67–68)
Having caused her to fall from her virtuous conduct, he departed and went home.
That young girl, Arajā, who had been leaped upon by Śukra, was herself now overwhelmed by passion (rajas).
Then, having emerged from the hermitage, she stood outside with her head bowed down.
Thinking of her father and weeping again and again,
she remained there without bathing or eating, taking refuge under a tree.
At the end of the third watch, her father Śukra arrived at the hermitage.
He beheld his own daughter, resembling the twilight, yet stained with menstrual blood.
He asked, "O daughter! By whom have you been violated, or how has this come to pass?
Where has that wicked, sinful man gone who has defiled a maiden?"
Weeping out of shame, that daughter of a spy said to her father:
"Though the king repeatedly tried to stop me with punishment,
I, being helpless and weeping, was forcibly brought to such a state."

Having heard this and touched water for purification, the pure Śukra cursed him: "Since you, disregarding my command and my authority, have caused Arajā—of auspicious conduct and fallen from her duty—to be deprived of her husband. (75)

"Therefore, let the staff of ashes fall upon him, along with his kingdom, his army, his servants, and his mounts, within seven nights, together with his followers. Then Śukra spoke to his daughter, who was ascetic and of pure conduct:
"When the monthly period of menstruation has arrived at its end, you will become pure.
Until then, O daughter, perform penance as you desire and as is fitting for you.
There is indeed no fault in you, my daughter; there shall be no embryo within you. (78)
"Drink the warm *pañcagavya*; do not be afraid, my daughter.
Then, O Asura, within seven nights, King Daṇḍa, along with his kingdom, army, and vehicles, was reduced to ashes by the curse.
Thus the formidable Daṇḍaka forest became a field of ashes.
In this same way, all those people who violate the wives of others are reduced to ashes, along with their kingdoms, armies, and vehicles.
Those who are virtuous in character, disciplined, and established on the path of justice are indeed fearless.
But those who forcibly violate the wives of others are not fearless, neither in this world nor in the next.
The sun is endowed with *dharma*, and the Brahmin is *dharma* itself, as well as one devoted to his wife.
Agastya, Manu, Svayaṃprakāśa, and other lords of sages— resplendent, capable of granting boons and releasing from curses, and honored by the gods— [intervened].
But those established in unrighteousness, including Candra, Indra, and Andhaka, became miserable.
Therefore, dharma must not be abandoned, for dharma is the supreme refuge. (85) Dharma is the highest means of deliverance, while falling occurs through unrighteousness;
therefore, one must always strenuously avoid consorting with the wives of others. (86)
But those who approach the wives of others are led away by terrible great sins;
those who dwell upon the wives of others for the sake of another are always considered deserving of hell.
Therefore, the wise should avoid the wives of others from afar.
Those whose wisdom has been destroyed by violating another's wife do not attain prosperity.
"Listen, O messenger, I shall relate another story in brief," having said this, Nārada spoke an ancient, divine tale. (88–89)
The virtuous daughter of Viśvakarman was named Citrāṅgadā;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, like Kamalā or a lotus-lake.
Accompanied by her companions, she went to the Naimiṣa forest to bathe.
While she was bathing, King Suratha, the son of Sudeva, beheld her.
She too was filled with desire and wished to offer herself to him.
Her friends said to her, "O girl, this is certainly not appropriate."
"You have no independence here regarding the giving away of yourself to another;
for the father may give away his son, since the son is under the father's authority.
O King, it is not proper for you to give yourself away here of your own accord."
In the meantime, King Suratha, afflicted by desire, said to her:
"O intoxicating-eyed one! O charming girl, you seem to bewilder me.
Therefore, you ought to lay me upon the bed of your breast."
Then, tormented by desire and repeatedly entreated by the king,
she— though being dissuaded by her friends— gave herself away of her own accord.
Having thus given herself out of her own free will, he then [accepted] such a daughter as she was.
But his father, having been insulted, cursed him as he was departing at will:
"Since you have abandoned dharma out of a desire for wealth and given yourself to a foolish king, therefore your marriage shall not take place. (97–98)
"Deprived of marriage, you shall never obtain happiness from a husband;
you shall have neither the fruit of sons nor union with a spouse.
As soon as the curse was uttered, the Sarasvatī swept her away.
When the king had been drawn away thirteen *yojanas* without having accomplished his purpose,
she too, her desire unfulfilled,
fell there into a swoon; then her friends [revived] her with water.
Having become chilled, they were overcome with extreme suffering in an instant;
nearly dead and their vigor destroyed, she slowly regained consciousness.
Not seeing the king, she then fled with great speed.
She fell into the Sarasvatī, being bewildered by its waves.
Having emerged into the great forest teeming with lions and tigers,
a Guhyaka saw her and led her to the bank of the Śrī Yamunā.
Having eaten there, he threw it into the water in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Emerging from the water with her head bowed, she remained standing at midday.
Then a certain ascetic named Ṛtudhvaja beheld her.
He said to her: "O daughter! Whose daughter are you, and how have you come here? (106) Then she related the entire account exactly as it had happened.
Having heard it, the sage became enraged at her father, the best of artisans. (107)
"O Tvaṣṭṛ, since you, a sinner, have joined her— who is worthy of being given away—
with one who is not her husband, therefore become a monkey! By this curse, Viśvakarman immediately became a monkey.
Due to the cause of that curse, he fell from the peak of Mount Meru to the surface of the earth.
Wandering the world, he came to Śrīkaṇṭha Ṛtudhvaja and entreated him: "My most terrible curse has been given; let it be revoked."
Regard me as Tvaṣṭṛ, the father of Citrāṅgadā.
Indeed, even sins have been committed by me in the form of a monkey;
let them come to an end through me. Have mercy on me, O Ṛtudhvaja!
Then Ṛtudhvaja said,
"The end of the curse will come once he has procreated a son of great strength upon Ghṛtācī.
While he was longing for the gentle Ghṛtācī, he beheld her.
Desiring a child, she too conceived on the bank of the Godāvarī;
when the time arrived, she gave birth to a powerful son, Nala.
That monkey, having abandoned his monkey form, became Viśvakarman in an instant.
Citrāṅgadā went to the Saptagodāvara Tīrtha;
because she was always immersed in the worship of Hāṭakeśvara,
the monkey there then assumed the form of Viśvakarman.
Having understood all this, the daughter realized that the misery of independence is such as this.
Then Viśvakarman, having summoned King Suratha there once again,
gave his own daughter Citrāṅgadā to him.
Then she became happy, having endured a hundred years of suffering.
Therefore, O messenger, great messenger, you who possess excellent intelligence,
report to King Jumāsmlā what has been spoken by me in the ocean of blood.
"Go home with everything as it truly is according to the prescribed rites and dwell there in happiness.
However, without conquering the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), you shall not obtain the maiden.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Abrikta’s Blocking of the *Sarvakāma-vimāna* by His Army Commanders, the Messenger’s Speech, Nārada’s Reply, and the Narratives of Śukra, Araja, Daṇḍa, Viśvakarman, Citrāṅgada, and Asura," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the great asura Raktavārddhi, acting as a messenger, went toward King Jumādagni of the land of Abhīkta.
He recited it in its entirety, step by step, exactly as it was told;
yet that evil-minded one, impelled by his impending destruction, did not accept it.
Then the mighty one, having armed himself, became enraged at all those who were in the sky.
Taking up his mace, he stood before the front of the celestial chariot.
First, making both heaven and earth resound with a roar,
he agitated the winds intensely and spoke these words appropriate for the occasion.
"Who is this leader of a celestial chariot standing before me?
Leave the chariot and go far away if you wish to live!
If you desire life, then do as I say. (5)
"And let all these maidens here be given to us immediately.
Who is this Rudra, or Dharmarāja, or Sanatkumāra? Who are these mendicants who have come here for the purpose of destroying our lives?"
Having all become ascetics, they took their place in celestial chariots,
lusting after throngs of maidens and following a path of deceitful conduct. Occupied with enjoyments that were not to be enjoyed, they were merely instructors in the bait of sin.
The wife of mendicants shall be distinguished by her lineage;
the wife of Mlecchas who follow the dharma shall be distinguished by her milk.
Indeed, we shall take these maidens as wives, distinguished by their fields. (2.51.9–10)
Hiraṇyākṣa indeed had a hundred wives;
from among them, thousands of daughters and thousands of sons were born. They were all produced by the seed of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Then those whose milk had been mixed were married to one another.
Indeed, those born of the same mother do not become husband and wife;
however, those born of the same father but from different wombs may be married.
"This has always been considered the custom for those born of our lineage:
whether they be daughters of Brahmā or others, we do not favor those who have no mother.
Nārada said: 'Only after conquering him will you obtain her; therefore, do what is beneficial.'"
Having heard that, the lord of the Dānavas, his eyes blazing with anger,
commanded his attendant to strike the war-drum for battle.
With great force, the servant struck the drum.
He let out terrifying roars like a mad female donkey;
and upon hearing that sound, a hundred thousand great asuras,
equipped for battle and longing for combat, quickly arrived at the field of war.
The previously mentioned army commanders also, with elephants, camels, horses, chariots, vehicles,
and small celestial chariots (*vimānas*), as well as various weapons, formed battle arrays around the *vimāna* in the sky and on all sides of the earth. (18–19)
Anxious, they quickly obstructed him and roared.
Then Rudra remembered Agni and Nandin;
both arrived swiftly and said, "Give us your command."
Hara said to Agni:
"O Fire, having fashioned a brilliant rampart consisting of flames of fire in the sky, protect the vehicle and remain steadfast.
Thus addressed, Agni guarded the celestial chariot on all sides.
And Rudra said to Nandin, "Quickly summon the Gaṇas here.
Having touched water for purification, Nandin called to mind the leaders of the Gaṇas.
By the thousands, the Gaṇas and lords of the Gaṇas arrived, adorned with various weapons and missiles.
Ten thousand of those belonging to the class of Rudra arrived there;
six hundred and sixty-six six-faced ones also came together,
and six thousand elephant-faced lords of the Gaṇas arrived.
Then other hosts with black faces, fighting with swords as their weapons,
naked and resembling collyrium in hue, arrived by the tens of lakhs.
Śambhu quickly gave the command for those black-faced ones to go forth to battle.

With four eyes and four arms, their chests marked with the Śrīvatsa, they arrived mounted upon birds; firm and bearing discs and tridents, twenty-one lakhs of Vaiṣṇava hosts were present there. (27–28)
Four-faced Brahmā hosts, numbering one million, arrived by way of the sky; they were experts in the knowledge of missiles, weapons, and other arms.
Then, a most terrible battle commenced on all sides.
With blackened faces and extremely terrifying, they slaughtered those of Mleccha descent.
Being struck down by the powerful foremost of the Gaṇas, the Daityas and Dānavas,
with sledgehammers and mallets in their hands, set out to kill the Gaṇas.
Then, the gods—including Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Grandfather (Brahmā), as well as Sūrya, Candra, Varuṇa, and others—were summoned into the sky; desiring to witness the event, they arrived.
Then, those with dark faces began slaughtering the army of the Dānavas.
The fourfold army consisting of Mleccha tribes was indeed crushed.
The Mlecchas, who wore beards, [attacked] with *gola*, *mahāgola*, and *tūpaka* weapons, with *dhūṣkṛtī*, *vajraghāta*, *bhūśuṇḍī*, and *chūraka* weapons. ||33-34||
With swords, scimitars, shields, and the like, as well as with crescent-headed arrows,
spears, darts, and iron clubs, they furiously struck those whose faces were like Time (Kālānanas).
And the Kālānanas [struck back] with moon-like arrows, spherical missiles, and clusters of fire.

Then, with arrows, javelins, firebrands, slings, and many types of mechanical weapons, they struck those Kālānalas in every way. The Kālānanās, falling and springing up with speed along the paths of the sky, [attacked them].
They placed nooses around the necks of the Mlecchas and applied fire to their beards;
meanwhile, those hundred thousand elite soldiers perished and fled at that time.
They sounded trumpets to summon the fresh troops.
Then, ten hundred thousand asura armies arrived there from all sides,
traveling by means of aerial chariots. At that time,
having filled the balls with sawdust and powders, [he set them ablaze].
Then they indeed hurled [weapons] at ten million hosts of Brahmins;
the hosts of Brahmins then struck the Dānavas with lightning-arrows,
and the Dānavas also [struck them] with mountains, trees, water, stones, and so forth.
And with blows from their breath, they struck down those whose deity was Brahmā.
Those Dānavas fell upon the field of battle, deprived of life;
by the strikes of lightning, they went to their death everywhere, their vital breaths departed.
With cocks' plumes upon their heads, adorned with conch-shell chains,
wearing garments of fierce tiger-skins and blue-bordered cloths around their waists,
and richly dressed in yellow-colored robes— ten hundred thousand of them died.
Then, seeing the destruction of his great army, the lord of the Dānavas, the king,
caused the sound of kettledrums to resound like a roar in the sky; indeed,
with cries like those of cranes amidst flashes of lightning, he summoned ten million troops.
That sound pervaded the great sky as far as the four oceans;
by the force of the wind, it surrounded the army of the Abhīra country.
Gathered together in the center, it indeed spread out on all sides.
From the mechanical device of Vijaya’s chariot, long trumpeting sounds arose.
Upon hearing them, the gods rejoiced, while the Mlecchas fell into extreme terror.
Indeed, the armies of the gods were roaming all around there.
At that time, resting upon the top of the celestial chariot with their subtle powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest,
the Daityas arrived from all directions toward the chariot like millions of locusts from the sky.
Let them kill, destroy, and devour those who dwell in celestial palaces;
let them carry off and seize their maidens and their wealth as well;
let them perish, cause destruction, and utterly annihilate the deities.
"Let the soldiers facing them cut, pierce, and obstruct [the enemy]!
Whichever divine maiden has come into the hand of one, all that shall belong to him as the victor; this is certain. (53)
Thus shouting, those great asuras, numbering in the tens of millions,
struck from all sides with various weapons known as yantramāras and with ballista-discharged projectiles the celestial chariot protected by Vahni. (54–55)
Having reached the region of the fire, the pellets scatter;
becoming liquid in form, they blaze like clarified butter.
The Daityas do not know that at all, yet they certainly perceive the discharge.
They create a rain of pellets for the purpose of destroying the celestial chariots (vimānas).
Others kill [the enemies] with *tūpī* engines and *śataghnīs*;
they strike them down with *ātaṅka* engines and hurl triple-jointed pīḍās.
Thus, for four watches of the night,
those Daityas did nothing but gaze at Māra’s aerial chariot; it was reduced to powder, its timbers destroyed,
its spherical ornaments shattered, and the fire consumed everything.
The celestial chariot, firm and unbroken, remained suspended in the sky.
Then there was the army of the Vaiṣṇavas, numbering twenty-one lakhs,
beautifully adorned with discuses, nooses, maces, spears, mallets, and other weapons.
By the command of Rudra, twenty-one hundred thousand Sudarśana discs fell upon the millions of the Daitya army;
impelled by his wrath, they indeed remained unimpeded at that time.
For that single division of the Daitya army was indeed split in two.
Some had discs [pierced] in their throats, shoulders, hips, and backs; others in their thighs, hands, knees, and likewise in their forearms.
They rendered the two [demons] lifeless by cutting them in half at the middle of their feet—right and left, or left and right—dividing them into two parts.
They fell from the sky to the earth; even a single army of theirs numbered ten million.
Just as moths meet their end in a fire, so indeed did they go to their destruction.
Then the king, overcome with grief, fell into a swoon for a moment,
remembering the many slain women who were now left protectorless.
"Among those who come to fight, not even a single one returns alive from that battle-storm; thus I am distressed.
Then, in a moment, he regained consciousness and spoke to his army commanders:
One must never retreat from battle, for the duty of a king would be violated.
Whether there be defeat or victory, death or life,
I do not accept retreating from the field as a base course of action here.
Then he summoned another army numbering ten million;
even during the night, there was no cessation of the battle.
The heroes, clad in tiger skins and protected by iron armor, [advanced].
Moving through the sky by means of fire, lightning, and mechanical engines,
those warriors— numbering in the tens of millions and standing seventy palms in height—
arrived on all sides at the place where the celestial chariot was located.
They indeed fled in order to destroy the celestial chariot (vimāna) in its presence;
however, being set ablaze by the protecting Fire, they retreated.
Then, they realized their own great incapacity.
"Even birds fly in the sky, and we too are like them here;
yet, since we are not able to endure even the slightest burning caused by fire, how shall we achieve victory?"—thus they fell into doubt. (75–76)
Nevertheless, thinking "the king's command must be obeyed by warriors in every way," they too, from a distance, targeted the chariot with lightning-balls and struck it;
yet those balls, like sparks in fire, fled away.
Indeed, it was a second marvel to behold upon the top of that celestial chariot:
they stood above and rained down globes that cause destruction;
yet those very globes melted and blazed even as they remained in the sky.
The celestial chariot was always protected by Vahni himself and remained uninjured;
yet, in order to slay those six thousand lords of the Gaṇas,
[he created] gods with trunks like elephant-snouts, wielding nooses, axes, and bows.
And Rudra dispatched those [demons] who were equipped with spears, javelins, and iron balls, and who held mantras, kusha grass, and vajras; in an instant,
they rose up from them and quickly traveled through the atmosphere, striking [the enemies] with their weapons and iron balls.
Then millions of Mleccha-Daityas fell into the fire;
being struck on all sides by the lords of the Gaṇas, they were indeed unable to flee,
and so they fell into the fire which was their protector.
Then, by the mere falling [of the powder], they became known as ashes in the very sky;
with nothing remaining but their names, they did not even return to see the king.
In this manner, those ten million warriors met their destruction there once again.
They were devoured by Mahānala until nothing but their bones remained; yet they did not attain [their goal].
Alas! The hope of the arrogant is powerful and brings about their destruction;
it is as if it were the daughter of Time herself, the elder sister of old age.
And when the total destruction was known, the king indeed lost his fortitude.
Just as he desired to depart from that place for his own palace,
there appeared the army commander Raktavārddhi and another.
Both Raudra and Vāṣpa spoke to the king for a moment:
"The king must not go, he must not go! Having withdrawn from battle, let him stay as long as the army exists and as long as there is strength on both sides. (89)
"As long as there is strength in our arms and the army commanders remain unhurt,
we must by no means go from the battlefield to our homes.
Rather, we shall fight and conquer those maidens."
Having spoken thus, those fierce warriors caused the battle-instruments to resound; they sounded many terrible lightning-drums and numerous lightning-pipes,
which served as signals to summon the armies.
Having heard this, the army, numbering ten crores,
gathered on all sides in an instant there in the central region around the lake,
as far as the Karmaghna mountain and likewise up to the Caṇḍasara lake.
From Karmāṅga as far as the river Śvetanārāyaṇī,
and as far as the Trirāśi mountain which was the refuge of ten koṭis of warriors,
there arose at that time a vast plain, a great field of battle.
From Tuṅgānīkasaras to Nyāsasara,
his entire army of ten million was reduced to ashes in the sky in an instant;
even before that, Kālahari had already reduced Āsāmbaparvata to ashes.
O Rādhikā! On the bank of the Vijñaturīya river, ten hundred thousand [demons] were slain;
previously, to the west of the Drākṣābīja mountain and on the bank of the Vāla river, one hundred thousand Daityas were indeed killed.

Thus these ten billion soldiers, skilled in the creation of lightning-weapons and experts in fire-mantras, arrived to meet their destruction. They fought with fire-engines, lightning-balls, and various missiles. (2.51.99–100)
By the god of fire, all those artificial puppets created through mantras were reduced to ashes in the sky near the celestial chariots.
Then they dispatched radiant celestial vehicles.
There were great globes of lightning and mechanical dolls;
there were mechanical horses, mechanical drivers, and chariots made of copper,
as well as weapons for those machines, likewise fashioned from lightning and copper.
By means of those practices performed by them, these ten crores of warriors fought fearlessly, situated within the middle of the fire-walls;
and having leaped over the fire, they then went there into the celestial chariots.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; then Śambhu, having risen, spoke to the Vāḍava fire: "Go, O best of beings, and reduce these to ashes.
At that moment, the Vāḍava fire rose up like that at the time of universal dissolution.
Spreading his crests in all directions, he assumed the form of ten million points;
licking up all those warriors as well as the puppets,
he reduced ten million soldiers to ashes in an instant by his mere touch.
Just as Jvālāmukha appeared in the sky like a mountain or a planet, so too did that vast, fire-filled mass resembling the cosmic egg meet its destruction; thus the visible became invisible. (108–109)
Ten billion soldiers there were consumed by the submarine fire (vāḍavavahni);
desiring to protect their lives, they fled from that place.
Then, for the sake of restraining them, [he summoned] the mighty Kārttikeya.
He bound six thousand five hundred [demons] with serpent-nooses.
They were unable to escape there and were consequently reduced to ashes;
they had neither bones, nor hair, nor heads, nor veins.

O Rādhikā! During that conflagration, it is said that something accessible and obtainable indeed arose; thus were the warriors, who prided themselves on their heroism, destroyed. Then, O Rādhā, at dawn, they appeared once more, assuming illusory forms.
By the king’s command, well-prepared and with mantras, they approached to fight.

(1.14) Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of how the Warriors, the Nagas, the Mlecchas, eleven crores and eleven lakhs [of beings] perished in the land of Abrikta by means of the Brahma-vimāna," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 53 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! Thus, upon the destruction of ten crores of asuras, a great cry of "Alas, alas! indeed arose among the hosts of asuras.
Even in other regions, an invincible terror then manifested.
Indeed, our king, devoid of righteousness and grasping at what is unjust,
being ignorant, invites the destruction of the provinces, the kingdom, and the householders.
For both wealth and sovereignty are the very grounds for the pride of embodied beings.
Pride born of justice brings happiness, whereas that born of injustice leads to destruction.
Oh, how wondrous is the variety of the Lord's illusion, by which [this occurs]!
Even when one possesses wealth as vast as the lotus-seated Brahmā and a kingdom extending to the ends of the ocean—
Even though the king is ignorant and even though he has beloved wives, his greed for the wives, wealth, and prosperity of others increases;
his power, strength, and sovereignty are in reality regarded as being like an enemy. (5–6)
If power and the like were such [as they claim], they should be understood as enemies that bring suffering;
yet pride is the messenger of Time, it is the son of Wealth, it is the adopted child of Strength, and the disciple of the Retinue. (7)
Wherever wealth, power, and attendants reside, there indeed do prideful thoughts arise for the sake of accomplishing one's aims;
through such pride, a person thinks, "I shall conquer everyone. (8–9)
Time quickly destroys even the most arrogant in an instant;
injustice, lurking by the side of pride, incites human beings.
Then, in seizing the wives and wealth of others, they sacrifice themselves to their own destruction.
For even though a dog has been satisfied by those living in houses along its own street with gifts of food and the like,
it still wanders through other streets out of pride due to its lingering thirst;
consequently, it is bitten on all sides by the fierce teeth of other dogs.
A buffalo, having found satisfaction with grass and other fodder in a field or similar place,
yet out of thirst and pride desiring the forest,
is torn apart by lions in the woods; for indeed, thirst and pride are the causes of destruction.
Blinded by pride and devoid of stars, he does not even know how to cross over.
Possessed by intoxication, he alone casts himself into the current;
submerged by bees, he will surely die without a doubt. (14–15)

Food, clothing, shade, and water are indeed the enjoyments for embodied beings; the maintenance of life is supported by them. If that [maintenance] proceeds with ease, why would a wise person, deluded by falsehood, undergo useless exertion? (16)
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, the home is momentary, and so are kinsmen;
sovereignty is momentary, life is momentary, and detachment from the body is momentary.
Having realized this, one should strive for the supreme good and not fall back into the lower state. (17–18)
Fall occurs due to pride, thirst, the desire for enjoyment, and undertaking tasks beyond one's capacity; therefore, one should abandon these through contentment.
O Rādhikā! Many have perished, and others will likewise meet their destruction.
Even those things existing in the present perish; the earth itself did not go along with them.
(20) Wealth, prosperity, home, wife, husband, son, and family—there is no real bond here; rather, the bond consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) toward them. (21)
That [suffering] persists eternally for the enjoyer who is unpeaceful and devoid of dispassion.
Attachment and lack of peace arise and increase in one who is destitute of knowledge;
wherever there is indeed an absence of knowledge, there it always shines forth.
Having entered the dwelling, the enumeration of desire, anger, and the rest is completed.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, and pride—all these brothers are devourers even of the master of the house. (23–24)
O Rādhikā, what need is there even to speak of others devouring them?
All the lumps of flesh there are pecked by vultures with their beaks;
and the powerful vultures peck at and carry off those who possess flesh.
In all worlds, the Piṇḍikās have been created by the Lord;
they were fashioned by the Lord and bestowed for the sake of attaining satisfaction.
Those who are dissatisfied therein perish like moths in a fire.

For those who have purified their food and practice solitude, this auspicious reflection arises, which yields the fruit of peace; for those dominated by darkness (*tamas*), such talk does not exist. Indeed, the *asuras*, *daityas*, *mlecchas*, and *dānavas* are preponderant in darkness.
Resorting to a tamasic disposition, they cause agitation to the stable world.
Offered as oblations into the fire of anxiety, they summon Death itself.
O Rādhikā! That which is called "kingdom" is that wherein one shines through righteousness.
In whose realm the subjects are always peaceful and happy through food, wealth, and other necessities; where the calamities of war do not exist and the rain falls well—[that is a virtuous land].
Envy of others is said to be evil, and its fruit is considered to be suffering.
War should be waged for the purpose of protection, and not for the sake of aggression. War rooted in hostility toward others leads to destruction.
Dharma, Artha, and Kama—these goals of human existence grant liberation if they are pursued as ends in themselves.
If they do not bring about one's welfare, those who dwell in their homes are hell-beings; for those who have no contentment with either wife or husband,
they are to be considered nothing but hell-dwellers, being perpetually dissatisfied and scorched by heat.

Those for whom there is no contentment regarding their courtyard, house, field, wealth, prosperity, or cattle; nor regarding food and clothing obtained as they may come, which merely sustain the body—they indeed stand in the Vaitaraṇī river of craving. (35–36)

Even while living, there is no hope for peace; once dead, what peace will come? For those whose thirst increases with taste and touch, hell indeed shines forth, having taken its place within their very bodies.
The thirst for sensual pleasure quickly casts one into the shackles called "the pair";
the thirst for greed quickly casts one into the current called "exertion"; and the thirst for delusion quickly casts one into the exile called "acquisition. (38–39)
The thirst for anger casts a living being into the affliction called dispute;
the thirst for pride casts an embodied soul into the affliction of "I-ness" and "mine-ness.
For humans, insects, and moths, sense objects are entirely the same. (2.52.40)
Those who are immersed in excessive exertion surely go to their destruction.
Having approached the king, the female messenger (dūtī) desires her own victory;
messengers and female messengers should be understood as being equal, whether they possess bodies or are bodiless. 42.
They desire their own victory, yet they seek the defeat of the king;
the fool, being deluded, does not recognize the invitation to his own end.
Indeed, the merchant understands the supreme profit consisting of usury.
A deceitful person knows the wealth, yet he never truly repays the principal.
Furthermore, when lending on interest, one should not lend less than the principal, nor indeed an equal amount.
Therefore, having received [the loan] again and again, one should not proclaim the failure to repay. 44–45.
Thus the deceitful merchant always triumphs, while the honest man is ever subdued.
Indeed, the deceitful enjoy the preeminence, while the honest man hangs upon them.
Hanging, he surely falls; for how can there be a fall for one who is not hanging?
One who runs surely falls; when one is already seated, how can there be a fall?
A warrior perishes even while fighting, having pursued pleasures that are as false as a mirage.
One who is submerged may lose his life while swimming across, but one who is not submerged does not lose his life.
One should reflect: "For what purpose is one fighting, or for what purpose is one drowning, or for what purpose is one falling? How much of that is truly mine?
O beloved, such discernment must be exercised by the king or by the subjects.
Even a boar acts as the king over its own body and senses. All these beings, from insects upward, are considered kings within their own domains.
Humans dwell in houses while disregarding those very insects.
Spiders make their dwellings on the walls and webs in the corners;
ruddy geese make their nests in the hollows beneath the pipes in the walls;
mice live in the conduits of the house, and insects dwell upon the ground.
Crows and pigeons dwell even upon the heights of houses;
whose house indeed is this to be known, which is enjoyed equally by all?
Yet they all consider themselves, by force, to be the masters of the house.
Indeed, they all become utterly bewildered upon the destruction of their home;
for whatever the nature of one's attachment, such is the sorrow that belongs to them.
This is not so for one who is free from the sense of "I" and "mine," even if he dwells in the house of another.
Just as a snake dwelling in a mouse's hole feels no portion of grief even when its home is destroyed,
so too, if a king understands this, why would he bring about his own destruction? (56–57)
One who knows the dharma of kings would produce a pretext and speak falsely;
O Rādhikā! everything false is considered in every way to be a source of suffering.
Therefore, that which is well-knowing should avoid falsehood and embrace truth.
One should not fight for the sake of destruction; one should fight for the sake of the eternal.
Even beasts fight for the sake of sense-objects and for the sake of their bodies.
Therefore, the battle of the ignorant against the wise for such purposes would be equal to theirs. (2.52.59–60)
If those possessing knowledge, having attained wisdom, should nevertheless fight for the sake of sense objects, that knowledge is indeed like husks—devoid of grain and fruitless.
Whether it be a king or a subject, a god or even a human being... [61]

It is called an *viṣaya* because poison (*viṣa*) goes (*yāti*) into it; the Self (*ātman*) is poisoned therein. (62) They are called *viṣayas* because they bind (*visinvanti*); those things which bind the mind to themselves.
And the Self, when dependent upon such a mind, is designated as the *viṣayin* (the subject). (63)
In former times, Citraketu had ten million wives;
nevertheless, by sprinkling his thirst with sensual enjoyment, he did not attain satisfaction in the end.
"Hundreds of millions of crores of my wives could not endure separation from me."
And enjoyments consisting of hundreds of billions of forms were incessantly offered by me to them.
Even though I was thus constantly bestowing that treasury of bliss,
they were never seen by me to be satisfied, due to their state of constant agitation.
Yayāti was not satisfied and chose youth from his son;
Nahuṣa also was not satisfied and set his mind upon Paulomī. Only Nara and Nārāyaṇa remain eternally contented, established in asceticism.
Dattātreya, Kapila, Lomaśa, Sanaka, and the others are eternally satisfied; they do not desire even the slightest assistance from the senses.
Satī is eternally satisfied; she desires no one other than Śambhu.
The saintly, the virtuous, and those who are eternally satisfied with Lord Hari become enchanted by Him, and no others.
If that very body for whose sake the embodied soul exerts himself should perish, what kind of effort is that said to be? It is like the exertion of a female scorpion over her young.
If that kingdom by which this king is adorned should perish, what kind of kingdom has been established by him? It is like a spark of fire upon cotton.
Even the celestial stars fall; they see [this] constantly with their eyes.
Those who stand upon the branches do not see the fall of their own roots;
he by whom a gift was made far away and he by whom a debt was held before him—
desiring little but facing much that is undesired, such a person will come forth in two ways.
By whom [the debt] has been made distant, and by whom that which was to be given has been placed before [him], to him a vast and desired fruit will come of its own accord.
O Rādhikā! Once Viśvāvasu [offered] three hundred maidens.
He arrived to offer [the gift] to the self-luminous sage;
with supreme affection, he bowed to that best of munis, who was radiant as the sun.
Having received a welcome, Viśvāvasu spoke what was in his mind.
"O Sage, you are a great yogi who assumes manifold forms;
likewise, you abide as one whose vital seed is drawn upward, a follower of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, these hundreds of daughters here are truly suitable for you. (77–78)
"Accept them, if you consider it to be for their supreme welfare;
for the cherishing and protection of those who possess splendor is not difficult to bear.
He, the Self-Luminous One, said to him: "That which is in your mind is indeed true."
The welfare of the daughter must be ensured; this is indeed the duty toward the ancestors. She should always be given in marriage to a worthy man who desires her;
however, giving her to one who does not desire her results only in the suffering of the girl.
I have no desire for maidens; give them to another great sage.
I am the Self, free from dualities, while the body is a burden of excessive dualities.
[This applies] at dawn, at dusk, at midday, and during the middle watch and so forth.
Urine, excrement, as well as saliva, phlegm, and even sweat;
spitting, sneezing, the movement of wind, urination, and so forth—manifesting these suddenly, it indeed renders me powerless. (83–84)
I always perform service for the sake of his purification;
I provide rest for the sake of alleviating his fatigue.
[This applies] during travel, eating, drinking, fire-offerings, recitation, and likewise while seated.
Whether standing with the body turned to the side, or while walking and so forth, when I have undergone extreme exhaustion, my teacher frequently becomes heavy [to carry].
To alleviate that, no extra time is available for me. (86–87)

"O King of Gandharvas, for the sake of the three hundred maidens, why should I not, having found the opportunity, please them through service and other means as they seek happiness? Indeed, I am unable to perform service here for only a single body. (88)
How could I possibly complete the service of three hundred and one embodied beings?
Therefore, O sinless one, I must not strive for this, nor should you grant it;
that Brahman is understood as incomplete when there is a longing for happiness from anything else. (2.52.89–90)
That Brahman is to be understood as fullness, which is the state of being filled with the bliss of the Self.
For that attainment, people strive toward others out of a longing for pleasure;
yet they perish midway, like oyster shells seeking pearls from the ocean.
Then Viśvāvasu, with devotion, offered three hundred maidens to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
the stainless Kṛṣṇa, the supreme among persons. (92–93)
Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa gave them all to the abode of Lomaśa;
and by his command, the divine Lomaśa protected them.
Therefore, those endowed with knowledge do not become attached to things that are embodiments of suffering.
O Rādhikā! Wealth, wife, prosperity, kingdom, and the like are embodiments of suffering.
For King Jumāsena, who was attached to them, total destruction has arisen; he awaits only a moment’s delay. (95–96)
"When shall I take a celestial chariot? When shall I touch young maidens?
When, having ascended a celestial chariot, shall I bring the earth under my control?"—thus did his craving become manifold; it does not decay even as he himself decays.
Having become a young woman, she drew the king aside for a private consultation.
Then the king repeatedly commanded the commanders of his army for the purpose of investigating the destruction of the celestial chariot, or its subjugation.
The bugle, signaling for counsel, quickly resounded;
and the commanders of the armies, having been summoned, arrived swiftly.
"Either the vehicle must be destroyed, or it must be brought under control."
Therefore, let the protectors devise means to destroy the fire.
This final battle must be fought for our welfare or our ruin; whether we survive or not, there is no cause for fear here, O fishermen.
Having been addressed thus, the eighty-two brave asuras, led by Raktavārddhi— who had not been slain in battle— conversed together;
they were stationed at a distance with their army mounts, observing the combat of the troops.
Adorning the station of generalship, he then practiced discernment.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Knowledge of Discernment and Non-discernment Performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Listen, O Rādhikā! Afterwards, King Jumāsemla himself, his mind filled with grief, spoke these words to the leaders of the demon hosts, such as Raktavārḍhya and others, numbering eighty-two: || 1 ||

On all sides of the celestial chariot is a fire such that it is impassable and fierce;

Therefore, what should be done here so that the celestial chariot is not destroyed,
and those inhabitants of the chariots who dwell within it are not likewise destroyed?
"O Raktavārddhi, you must speak to me only after having deliberated upon this;

if they are to be rendered motionless by those [weapons] created through great illusion."
"What would happen then? Therefore, let another means be sought.
Then a certain man of fierce resolve spoke of a new plan:
"Let us go to that place, having assumed the form of the wind."
By which [path] and in whatever manner that celestial chariot shall depart from here in an instant, as long as it proceeds among us who have taken the form of wind, so long shall we,
in our own nature as winds, [accompany it] with fierce and violent gales.
Indeed, this celestial chariot will suddenly meet its destruction.
Having separated and divided all the maidens and their limbs,
and having broken everything down into its constituent parts, we shall bring it to dissolution.
Then the one who knew the fourth [Veda] spoke this further reply to him:
"Even though he is worthy, this Maheśvara is situated upon a celestial chariot;
for if he were to swallow us all with his breath, he would be like Agastya."
"Then, consider what our condition will be.
At that time, Aṭaleṣṭaka also said: "Wherever the vehicle goes, let it maintain the beauty and charm of that region's own form. (17-18)

Seeing the beautiful island in the midst of the ocean and thinking it to be his own land, he will then trustingly and happily make his descent. There, we too shall manifest in forms identical to theirs to fulfill their desires.
"When it is time to sleep at night, dissolution shall take place. 2.53.20.
Following that, the commander-in-chief Nyāyasāra said:
"Even when everything has been created, the gods remain devoid of sleep. 21.
"If they do not fall asleep, what means indeed remains for us?
Then the Daitya Rudraśiras spoke words full of reason:
"In every way, we must seek refuge; there are deities who grant protection."
And those who have come for refuge to an ascetic become objects of trust;

The mantras belonging to him and the initiations bestowed by him should be received by householders;

Having set down the celestial chariot upon the earth, we must perform supreme and auspicious service with the devotion of servants, so that they may gain our trust; then,

"Having become the guardians of the celestial chariots, let them bring about destruction there.

"At this time called Vijaya, by means of weapons that inspire confidence, we must indeed assemble our forces here; otherwise, the enemy will overcome us.

Those of deceitful intent awakened him excessively and prostrated on the ground;

Like a rat perched on a swan’s wing, he tears away its feather;

Indeed, this impurity must be endured by us for the sake of our own faction. Having made the Mlecchas our disciples, we must act so that our goal may be successfully achieved.
We must remain mindful of them here and stay vigilant regarding them.
When water is poured upon a fire, it certainly blazes up while it is still burning;
likewise, these Mleccha fires are such that one must not sleep near them. Therefore, one must remain vigilant so as not to suffer defeat at their hands. ||52||
Having heard these words of Hara, Sanatkumāra said:
"Whatever Hara speaks is indeed entirely appropriate;
for there is no destruction of the powerful, as it is the one of inferior power who perishes. (53-54)
Dharma said: "For we are indeed those who provide refuge and ward off evil.

Those who have come for shelter must be protected according to their fitness, even if they are under the control of others—whether they be elephants, lions, thieves, or guards—and must be guarded with vigilance. (55)
The King of Dharma and the King of Men were attentive even toward those under their control;

The king replied: "Let the chariot, however, touch the surface of the earth."
"We shall become your servants here, worthy of initiation and your eternal attendants.

Tuṅgānīka, Pratāraka, Supāla, and Vīrakesara—

Then they led them by vehicle a great distance of a thousand yojanas,
as far as the city of Murārka, which lies on the opposite shore of the Araṇa ocean.
Nārada, Śaṅkara, and Sanatkumāra, as well as Yamarāja and his messengers, went to the city of Murāri; likewise,
the king named Jumāsela and twenty army commanders [went there].
They went to the city of Murārka, while the Dānavas remained behind.
In a moment, they were joined by those army commanders stationed in swift celestial chariots,
as well as by new hosts of Rākṣasas consisting of both women and men.
Calamities were set in motion, causing the destruction of the celestial chariots;

Furthermore, fire was ignited in one of the celestial chariots.

in that very moment, the plundering of objects was carried out there, and a battle took place in the celestial chariot with the Gaṇas, gods, and others. (83–84)
Then the Rudras and others, as well as the sons of the Kalpalatās, were remembered;

on the head with his mace and crushed him, leaving him lifeless.

"I am your devotee and I have sought refuge; I have not committed even the slightest offense," he said there to the Gaṇas. Then those Gaṇas protected him, while they rendered all the others lifeless with their terrifying fire-spears.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; at that moment, hundreds of thousands of demon women, skilled in warfare, followed along the path of the sky.

some were armed with swords and scimitars, others held daggers at their fingertips;

they encountered there the Suṣumṇā and other female spirits who had touched the wish-fulfilling creepers and trees;
these were the armies of the Daityas' magical spells (kṛtyās) for the purpose of destroying the women.

Without repeatedly forming the thought, "Let them arise on all sides," there emerged from those creepers thousands and tens of thousands of extremely fierce *kṛtyās*, whose eyes were like the fire of cosmic destruction. (2.54.10)
Some followed the path of the sky, some were subtle and short, while others were as massive as mountains;
having searched for one another,
they then engaged in various battles, grappling hair-to-hair and staff-against-staff.
Having seized the female Daityas who were Kṛtyās, they were crushed;
they were broken, pulverized, split apart, and even destroyed.
They were urinated upon in their faces and torn asunder in their hearts.
Their breasts were pierced and their vital organs tormented by arrows;
they were torn apart, reduced to ashes, and slain by flames of fire.
Indeed, ten lakhs of women were destroyed by means of magical spells (kṛtyās).
The maidens remembered their beloved Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Immediately, that Great Lord arrived mounted upon Garuḍa;
having come at the start of the battle, he truly appeared before them in person. (15–16)
The Lord dwells in the celestial chariot and dwells within their hearts;
standing invisible at the commencement of battle, he surveys the conflict.
Seeing the Lord arrived before their very eyes, the maidens were filled with great agitation.
Overwhelmed by the weight of their love, they offered worship, prostrated, and embraced one another.
Hari sat upon his throne in the midst of the circle of maidens,
and likewise he shone within the circles of Śrī Śaṅkara and the other sages.
Worshipped by Śaṅkara and others, by the Gaṇas and others, and by the sages,
the Lord sat upon a beautiful, excellent, worthy, and radiant throne.
Nārada then related the account of the battle that had taken place.
And with human-like grace, she also gave her introduction to the king.
Then the king wept profusely and begged for forgiveness;
likewise did those who were his army commanders and those who had gone far away with him.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, granted them fearlessness;
the king and the others beheld within the belly of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa the worlds,
oceans, nether regions, and all things stationary and moving.
The Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, as well as the hosts of Viśvedevas;
the Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas, and the multitudes of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
the sages, humans, and Sādhyas, as well as beasts, insects, and ants.
Reptiles, trees, shrubs, fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs;
those dwelling in water and those dwelling on land; those with unblinking eyes and those with blinking eyes;
the unmanifest and the manifest; bipeds and quadrupeds. (26)
The Daityas and Dānavas, as well as the Rākṣasas and Uragas;
the coverings of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), the Īśvaras, and the Parameśvaras; the liberated souls (muktas) and those who dwell in liberation, and the consorts such as Lakṣmī and others. || 27–28 ||
He also saw the attendants of Śrī Hari and other forms of Hari;
then the king, bowing with devotion, beheld his own country, his kingdom, his celestial chariot, and his army—indeed, everything. || 29 ||
Recalling his own states of being and those past actions, he spoke:
"Alas! Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
yet, being greedy for worldly existence, I did not recognize his devotees."
I have always committed sins, as well as those that are great sins;
even where there might be their destruction, I have committed evil there as well.
How and when shall there be liberation from this sin, which is like an adamantine coating?
"O Devajya! May it not be so! O Mādhava, deliver me from this sin!
(33) For this is the very nature of the Daityas: a lust for the wives of others and the consumption of liquor and meat; therefore, O Mādhava, deliver us! (34)

"O Mādhava, it is by means of this human body acquired through the accumulation of millions of merits that liberation itself is attained here through the power of *prapatti*. That *prapatti* has been obtained by me through the command for battle."
Although I have committed evil by engaging in battle, the fruit of my merit has come to pass: namely,
this union with those who perform deliverance and the vision of the Blessed Ones today, amidst my own lands where embodied beings were struck down in war.
"May the Blessed One himself, having wandered forth, perform my deliverance;

"O lord of men, let your evil deeds— whether physical or mental, or even ill-conceived thoughts— as well as your demonic disposition, depart from you."

O King, listen: that which is certain is to be accomplished, but that which is uncertain is never to be achieved.
Prosperities are always to be understood as transient; however, that which is to be accomplished through them is eternal.

And another, wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
mounted upon a white elephant, rich in goodness, and possessing a white form;
and yet another, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
