Śvetā stands facing the Moon and Brahmā, representing the quality of *sattva*.
The red [form] attended upon Indra, the king, and the Manus, the sovereigns;
the yellow [form] went to the Prajāpatis and the very righteous Vaiśyas;
while the blue [form] [attended upon] the Dānavas, Daityas, Śūdras, Rākṣasas, and others.

The Brahmins and others accepted Sarasvatī of white complexion, as well as the sacrifice, the mantras, worship, and other auspicious divine rites. The Kṣatriyas accepted Rājasī, who is red in color and the goddess of victory.
The Vaiśyas accepted her everywhere as Nīlā, whose nature is the mode of livelihood;
the Śūdras took up the goddess of service, Nīlā, in the form of servitude.
Thus was Lakṣmī divided, for as long as fortune endures.
The essential natures of these are the imperishable treasures (nidhis):
the Vedas, narratives and the like, the Saṃhitās, the virtuous practices of the scriptures, and the sixty-four arts; these are white, and the treasure Mahāpadma is established therein.

Jewels, gold, silver, elephants, horses, chariots, ornaments, weapons, missiles, and other such objects—these are known as the treasure Padma; likewise, cows, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, gold, garments, and lands [are associated with it]. (54–55)
Herbs and animals are known as the Mahānīla treasure when they are consumed;
the constant service of all species is established therein.
Nīlā is pervaded by both pleasure and pain, and she is known as the Śaṅkha treasure.
I shall describe to you the forms assumed by these [goddesses] for the sake of awakening those humans and others who have taken refuge in them:
they appear gentle, endowed with the splendor of goodness (*sattva*), and as upholders of truth, purity, and other virtues. (57–58)
They are handsome, performers of righteous deeds, and givers of delight upon being seen;
they have long eyes and long arms, and are endowed with laughter, contentment, and other such qualities.
Their bodies are unimpaired, and their families are likewise undivided.
They possess unbroken food, drink, and other necessities, and their stainless fame remains undiminished.
They are endowed with truth and purity, delighting in the festival of giving strength; they are distinguished by faith, the purity of charity, and the performance of services for others.
O King, those people who dwell near the Great Lotus become fortunate;
they are performers of sacrifices, blessed, proud, adorned with garlands, and givers of many sacrificial fees.
They possess great enjoyments, manifold forms, and they abide under the sovereignty of many kings.
Radiant with the splendor of all their requisites and possessing great renown;
as long as they possess material things, they enjoy the fruits of their kingdoms and fields; honored and bestowing honor, they are joyful, robust, and long-lived. (63–64)
People with lotus-like eyes, brows marked by pride, bearded, with hair as long as a year’s growth,
with red nails and red complexions, dwell there supported by lotuses.
They are characterized by a mixture of truth and falsehood, and they perform acts of charity, seek refuge, and offer sacrifices.
Devoid of both justice and injustice, they bring satisfaction to all.
Their acts of charity are neither excessive nor deficient; their clothing is not overly fine, yet it is not unattractive.
These people have coarse bodies, are moderately well-nourished, and are devoted to the Mahānīla mountain.
They were atheists, devoid of purity, wretched, and deprived of enjoyments;
they were speakers of theft and falsehoods, doers of harm to others, and deceitful;
they were intent solely on their own self-interest, black-hearted, ugly, and lacking in noble qualities.

O King, those who dwell in that [city]—whether men, women, or eunuchs—are devoid of fragrance, possess evil natures, and have formed friendships with flies; they tolerate filthy garments and take refuge in conch shells. (2.54.69–70)
Moreover, others— modesty, fame, splendor,
radiance, power, progress, forbearance, prosperity, knowledge, policy, compassion, and intelligence—
as well as sacred revelation, tradition, strength, renown, fortitude, peace, action, and accomplishment, all take refuge in him. (7.1)
Prosperity, contentment, and likewise others, all subsist upon primary fortune (śrī).
O King, that fortune is subject to its lines; for as long as the line remains, so does that fortune.
When the line disappears, fortune and all forms of prosperity depart.
All forms of prosperity come according to the arrangement of past karma;
O Lord of Daityas, those joys and sorrows must indeed be endured for the sake of sons,
friends, and wife, as well as for the enjoyment of sovereignty and wealth.
In the coming and going of fortune, let no despondency enter the wise man anywhere.
Seeing the arrival of calamities, the self-controlled man should not become dejected;
and having obtained vast prosperity, he should not become elated. (75–76)
They are not deluded by the loss of wealth, nor do they become corrupted by the arrival of wealth;
those alone are called steadfast, wise, and the best of men.
Furthermore, O mighty-armed one, listen to this other beneficial teaching of great significance.
Go for refuge to that Puruṣottama, the worthy protector.
Those who take shelter in Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person—
those who are honored by hundreds of their own lineages— cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
O best of Dānavas, fix your mind on Him and be devoted to Him in every way;
that very Nārāyaṇa will ordain your welfare.
Offer all actions—whether auspicious or inauspicious—to Him alone.
Offer here to Mādhava all those things born of passion and hatred.
(8.1) For indeed, no karma remains unexhausted even after the passing of ten million kalpas;
yet, if it is offered to Nārāyaṇa, it need not be experienced, for nothing remains to be suffered. (8.2)
Just as a thief undergoes punishment according to his offense such as theft, if the king were gracious, he would not impose any punishment at all;
rather, he would forgive everything done by him and forbid him from doing it again. (83)
Thus, the illustrious Lord, having fully recognized the sins committed by living beings who possess life,
inflicts punishment in every case;
however, if Kṛṣṇa is pleased, he indeed does not inflict punishment at all.
One should forgive everything done by him and refrain from doing it again;
his favor must be won even through various means.
However, whatever he says when he is present and acting directly, that one should carry out.
"Right here resides the glorious Puruṣottama, manifest before our eyes.
Come, go to him for refuge; do whatever he tells you to do.
Having spoken thus to the Mleccha king, the sage Sanatkumāra—
He led him to the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The king said: "O ocean of compassion, deliver me as you desire!
I am a sinner, I am a doer of evil deeds, I am a sinful soul, and I am born of sin. (89)
"O Abode of Mercy, uplift me, who have committed the offense of associating with the wicked!
Śrī Hari, smiling, said: "You have become pure in every way;
by the direct association with the virtuous, you have been liberated from your demonic nature. (2.54.90–91)
"You— servants, generals, men, and women—
all shall undoubtedly become purified through my virtuous yoga.
Your country, its cities, its ponds, and likewise its rivers," ||| 92 ||
"Mountains and battlefields become pure through association with the virtuous.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa ceased speaking.
And Nārada, having bowed to Hari, took the wish-fulfilling creeper in his hand.
He wandered repeatedly through the seven-storied palaces;
indeed, by means of his martial prowess, he treated them like mere refuse wherever he went—broken, shattered, crushed, overturned, and turned upside down. || 95 ||
Having made all the arrangements quickly and according to the rules, he had everything properly executed.
Having sprinkled water for purification over all the grounds,
he approached before Hari and stood there, bowed down and filled with joy.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle Fought by the Daitya Women, the Destruction of the Daityas and Others Created by the Kalpavallī as Kṛtyās, the Vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the King’s Prayer, and the Instruction," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, on the seventh floor of the Vimāna in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 55 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Continuation of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 55.
[Author: Chapter 56.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! At that time, the king petitioned the Supreme Lord.
Show compassion and act so that there may be liberation for those who have died.
O Keśava, having arrived by means of your celestial chariot, visit the sacred fords (tīrthas) wherever the battle took place, wandering through each of those places. 1–2.
"And may the worlds yet to come become vessels for liberation.
Thus, O Lord, show supreme compassion toward sinners that brings them across.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said:
"O King, blessed is your stainless intellect that has now been awakened.
I shall make this entire region, in every respect, a sacred site (*tīrtha*).
Those rivers, the daughters of Brahmā, have attained the state of *daityas* through their association with the Daityas."
"Having arrived here, I shall indeed purify those purifying rivers once again today.
As soon as this was said, the rivers, the lakes, and likewise the mountains,
having assumed embodied forms, arrived then to entreat the Lord.
They said, "O Lord, ocean of compassion, purify us on all sides!
Hari replied, "So be it; I shall indeed purify you all very soon.
Then, having worshipped those rivers, he went to see the daughters of Brahmā.
To see their own sisters in the celestial chariot situated on a higher level,
they went there together, having repeatedly taken leave of and spoken with them;
then, they suddenly vanished from sight, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa departed from that place.
He traveled by means of a celestial chariot to visit the purifying holy sites (tīrthas) in order to uplift his deceased soul, proceeding indeed in a clockwise circumambulation.
First he went there by the celestial chariot, and thereafter [he proceeded] further.
He went to purify the auspicious Caṇḍanadī from the field of battle.
Having likewise bathed in the Caṇḍanadī and at the Caṇḍasaraḥ, Hari,
all those traveling in celestial chariots, as well as men and women, [worshipped] the Most Great One.
Having established a sacred bathing site (tīrtha), they then went to the mountain of the three heaps (trirāśiparvata).
Having performed a circumambulation of that mountain and bathed in its waters and other sites,
they established a sacred bathing site on that mountain at the second [spot] of Nārāyaṇī.
Having bathed at Dhodha on the third day, and having bathed at Dhodha on the fourth;
having bathed at Dhodha on the fifth, and then having bathed at Dhodha thereafter;
and having bathed at Antavairāsaṅgama on the sixth Dhodha.
Having bathed in the Tūyāna lake at the confluence of the two Nārāyaṇīs, who possess white and blue forms respectively, the Lord established sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having bathed in the ponds known as Ābālā, he indeed made them bestowers of liberation.
Then, after [visiting] four ponds of pure water,
the Lord summoned those various deceased spirits who had died in the great battle at the aforementioned excellent holy sites (tīrtha) and effected their liberation.

By means of divine vehicles, they all indeed went to the eternal heaven, where Hari—the ocean of boundless compassion and the giver of liberation—resides. In that place, what need is there for a destiny dependent on karma? What need is there for a state arising from compassion? (19)
Then, having touched the river Jubvā and the Rudrabāṣpa lake,
having bathed in the Mārkaṇḍa ocean and the Ālāvarta lake,
and having bathed in the Antāvarta pond and the Kimu lake; || 2.55.20–21 ||
Having bathed in the Vijñatūrīya lake, as well as in the Nyājāsarovara,
the Tuṅgānīka pond, and the Rukvasarovara lake (22),
he then bathed in the Raphijyā and immersed himself in the Rovumā.
Having bathed in Nyājāsarovara, he then [bathed] in Śivāsarovara;
then, having bathed in Jāmbūjā, he bathed in Baṅgavyālīsarovara;
having bathed in Māvūrasaras, he then performed his ablution in Kaṅgū. (23–24)
In each of those places, the Lord, the abode of compassion, liberated the pretas who had met their end,
and likewise made those sites sacred fords (tīrthas).
Thereafter, the Blessed Lord Hari went to Dinolūka-Ṭaḍāga.
And having understood the fourth state of consciousness at Kubaṅgikā-taṭa,
he bathed in the lake born there, and then immersed himself in the Limpa river.
Then, having bathed in the Bāla river, he [proceeded to] the Dakṣiṇāvarga mountain.
Having ascended high into the sky by means of the celestial chariot, they went over the ocean of artisans.
Then, descending from the chariot, they all bathed in the sea.
Thereafter, mounting their vehicle again, they proceeded to the Orañjā river.
Having bathed, the Blessed Lord Kālahari liberated from the jaws of death those demons who had died in battle, as well as those who had perished in the aforementioned places. Then,
having bathed at Kunayanā, he immersed himself in the Kurenṛkī river.
Having gone and bathed at the water-reservoir named Sthānala, which belongs to the Kuvaṃśa lineage,
and having bathed at the confluence of the great river Karmāṅgī,
and likewise having bathed in the Limpā lake and the Tumbā lake; || 31 ||
Having bathed at the lower portions of Sthānalī,
at Āruva-mījala, at Karmāṅgī, and likewise at Uveṇī, and having bathed at the confluence of those two,
as well as at the meeting of the ocean, one effects the liberation of ten million deceased spirits.
There, Śrī Hari, the bestower of eternal welfare, established holy sites for those who had died;
having created those tīrthas, he then departed for Āgīvyā.
Having made the mountain on the bank of the Venajayā a tīrtha that destroys all karma, [he proceeded].
And bathing at the confluence of that [river] where old age is destroyed,
likewise in the Keḍaṇḍā river, in the Caṇḍasara lake,
and having bathed in the Phalguvipīnasaras lake at the meeting of rivers; || 35–36 ||
Having bathed in the Gambhīrā, the Sphuṭā, and the rivers Senā and Gola,
and likewise having bathed in the Phalgubīja, Hari indeed crossed over the battlefield.
Having bathed in the Raṇasarovara lake and [visited] Mount Ataleṣṭa.
He performed his ablutions in the five lakes of Alajāli-saras;
then, having gone to Mount Tanmukha and Mount Trirāśi,
and having gone to Līlābījaraṇa, he indeed visited the sacred fords (tīrthas) within the water.
Then, having bathed in the ocean at the center of the earth, in the sea belonging to Nārāyaṇa,
and indeed having bathed at the confluences of the oceans in the primordial Dhodhasāraka;
and having seen Navabījaraṇa, one should bathe in the Raktasamudraka.
Having performed all those purificatory rites with sacred waters—rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, reservoirs, and watercourses;
as well as regions, battlefields, mountains, great rivers, and canals. (41–42)

Having purified and sanctified as sacred fords the villages, cities, and houses born in those various regions, as well as royal capitals, reservoirs of water, forest retreats, and lands, the glorious Nārāyaṇa—
Together with crores of attendants, celestial maidens, and holy men,
and accompanied by Dharmarāja, Skanda, Śambhu, Vināyaka, and others,
he sported upon the dry land and performed the rite of liberation for the departed spirits.

"O King, this desire of yours has indeed become fruitful here.
Now we shall go to the Aśvasarovara on Mount Raivata.
Having heard this, the king said, "O Blessed One, I desire eternal liberation. (47-48)
If one does not find liberation even while meeting a giver of liberation,
then saṃsāra will certainly remain fixed upon his head.
(49) I have enjoyed a vast kingdom for a period of ten lakhs of years.
"Previously, the Daityas who lived for ten million years went before me;
these [women] have not gone together with anyone else, nor will the earth, its wealth, and its subjects go along with me. Therefore, O Blessed Lord, [I am distressed]. (2.55.50–51)
Having shown compassion, I shall uplift the Kurus and attain that eternal state;
my family will be purified, as will my earth,
and all my subjects shall be sanctified, and likewise the departed spirits shall be delivered.
Even though sacred fords such as rivers and the like have been made purifying, I shall go with my wife to your eternal abode;
therefore, O Lord of Life, show me the favor that arises from your grace. (53–54)
"These thousand maidens of mine, all sixteen years of age and possessed of beautiful limbs, are here; become their husband, O you who are accessible to friends!
There are other sons of mine as well; do with them as you wish."
"And for your family members and servants, O Kṛṣṇa, do as you wish.
(56) Having heard these most affectionate words, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said to the king, "O Indra among kings, your sins and merits have been exhausted. (57)
"You are worthy of liberation; I shall grant you liberation in a mere moment.
Thus addressed, the wise one then took water in his own hands at that very instant and offered it into the hand of the Lord of Śrī.
"O Kṛṣṇa! I give you these thousand maidens as your wives;
let them be endowed with all auspicious fortune, and may my lineage be happy.
Having said this, he gave him a divine dowry of ten billion [coins]. (2.55.60)
He gave golden ornaments, silver, strings of pearls, diamonds, and precious gems;
divine garments and ornaments, as well as vehicles and mounts;
and he also gave male and female servants by the thousands.
He gave elephants, horses, camels, gayals, cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having taken the maidens and their dowry onto a celestial chariot, placed them in the vehicle and spoke to the king. (62–63)
O King, receive here the nectar of the feet from the illustrious Nārada;
let your three hundred queens receive the nectar of his feet;
and let your sons and your family receive the nectar of his feet.
Thus addressed by Nārada, they indeed accepted the nectar of his feet;
they joyfully drank that water which had washed the feet of Śrī Hari.
Instantly, they all entered into samādhi, their channels merged into Brahman.
At that time, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, all these indeed became twofold in form:
those who were the Maruts and the gods became shadow-forms in the world of the gods;
others, assuming divine bodies, came to dwell in celestial chariots.
Then they went to the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
(68) Then these maidens prepared his grave-pit; having caused the earth-sealing ceremony (*bhūsamādhi*) to be performed, as well as the subsequent rites (*uttarakriyā*) and so forth. (69)
And having caused everything to be performed according to the rules as was appropriate, the Lord, when the sixth month had passed at the confluence of the Nīlā and Śvetanarāyaṇī rivers,
completed everything according to the rites and divided the two kingdoms.
Then, from the city of Jīmūta on the bank of the Adanākhāta river,
to the west is the port of Embāga, containing the water-vessel of Tūnāya;
it is at the source of the river called Uṣṇāṅgī and to the west of Mount Karmāṅga.
Having shown and marked the boundary from the middle of this region all the way to the ocean,
and likewise having delineated the southern and northern limits,
he bestowed the southern portion upon Rudraśiras, the yogi devoted to Bhakti.
To the devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Keśava [granted] the northern kingdom; and likewise, Nārāyaṇa himself, Keśava, gave the kingdom called Dinamera to his own devotee. 74–75.
The two powerful generals, named Rudraśiras and Adinameru, were devoted to Nārāyaṇa; they remained free from worldly attachment during the battle.
When the kingdom was offered to them by those two, they were then consecrated by him in person. (76)
Hari made him equal to a god and bestowed a crown upon him.
Then, the capital was established in the great kingdom of Dakṣiṇa;
it became renowned as Rudraśirā, situated on the fourth side of Vijñapura.
In the eastern [portion], it is ten yojanas long and exceedingly beautiful;
likewise, in the northern section, it was fashioned by Dinamere.
And the royal capital is situated on the western ground near Caṇḍasaras.
By name it is Dinamerā, extending ten yojanas;
having constructed a temple there one thousand dhanus in height, [he established] the supreme image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (2.55.80–81)
The auspicious golden [image] was installed by him together with Hara;
it was honored by Sanat, Nārada, and Dharmadeva.

yet the clubs and mallets were shattered against those [bodies] which were indeed like adamantine cement.
Then those fierce ones fought in the sky with maces.
There, maces were reduced to powder by maces themselves.
Then, seizing their spears, they struck one another with great fury;
grasping each other's spears, they broke them and hurled them into the sky.
Then the Dānavas struck them with mountain peaks;
the Yamas, however, effortlessly shattered those mountain peaks with their thunderbolts.
Then [the Dānavas attacked] with arrows, bhalla-tipped shafts, and many swift tridents.
They struck one another for the sake of killing, devoid of any compassion.
Grasping and seizing their weapons, they repeatedly broke them against each other;
they all hurled [their arms] at the ground and cut arrows with arrows.
Then, having cast aside their weapons, they struck one another like fools;
they fought fist-to-fist, grappled throat-to-throat, and crushed one another.
At that time, there was combat foot-to-foot and hair-to-hair.
Having struck down Adrimālī upon the earth, and having brought Ilāka down; having indeed struck down the Asura Damana with the noose of delusion,
and having struck down the Daitya Kālakarṇi from the sky onto the earth.
Even with his hand used for crushing, he cast the seeds of sport upon the ground; then,
with knees that possessed strength equal to the wind, he pressed the Daityas against their chests, and at that time,
he reduced the bones of their chests to powder, piece by piece.
Uttering repeated insults, those intoxicated with the fury of battle gave up their lives.
Wherever they were crushed by the messengers upon the earth, there pits formed, a yojana in width, due to the repeated blows of Yama’s agents. (77–78)
The streams became flows of blood and the water turned red;
the earth then became crimson with the blood from the mountain-like bodies of the daityas.
O Rādhikā, the battlefield indeed took on a blood-red hue.
Then other excellent Daityas followed at their head: Pāka, the wretched Trirāśika,
Alīthaka, Śirodhā, Piṇḍitāyu, Vāyuja, Trithuka, Baṃsura, and Ūrdhvamīna.
Then they fought with the Yamakas, beginning with Bindumāla; Garvagandha,
Yamaka, Bindumāla,
Vibhūtika, Gaḍeḍa, Khañjana, Haḍeḍa, and Bhaṣakānana.
Śārdūla, Dhaḍaghāta, Kaṭakaṭa, and Dahanāśana—
these and others struck down the Daityas of terrible pride;
lifting them up again and again, those lords beat them upon the earth.
They indeed tore those Asuras apart at the middle of their thighs;
they indeed split them in two at the middle of their hips.
All those who had fallen into the hands of the Yamas were truly dead.
Others, seeking to save their lives, fled from afar from the one who belonged to Vaidiśa.
The army of the Daityas became destitute, its enthusiasm destroyed and its leader gone;
it was shattered, cut to pieces, and broken, as if already conquered on all sides. (86–87)
Then the messengers of Yama blew their conchs, kettledrums, and large drums.
But all of them, victorious and free from fatigue, were cheerful of countenance;
they were dancing, laughing, and making others laugh, full of joy.
Having seen Vijaya approaching from the southern quarter in this manner, Raktabīja,
perceiving his own defeat, stood for a moment bowed with shame.
Then he halted the fleeing army with the sounds of battle-drums.
With battle-signals and shouts, he restrained the army commanders;
mounting his elephant himself, he went to the front for the sake of combat.
At that moment, the army and the army commanders, filled with great wrath, rushed forward.

In an instant, they surrounded King Yama in the sky on all sides of his celestial chariot for the purpose of destroying him; they seized King Yama just as millions of moths and millions of parrots seize a cage.
In that manner, the hosts of Dānavas instantly obstructed Yama, the Lord;
his celestial chariot was no longer visible, being then shrouded by the clouds of the Daityas.
Then King Yama himself, out of wrath, released the Staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
From staff after staff were born by the hundreds and thousands.
Any Daitya whom it touches instantly perishes through contact with the staff;
he turns to ashes right there, and not even a bone remains.
Thus, indeed, many thousands of Daityas were slain then in the sky;
scorched by the staff of Yama, they went to the abodes of Yama.
But those among them who desired to live, having seen their destruction in an instant, [fled].
They all fled and departed, abandoning Pātāla itself.
Taking their sons, grandsons, daughters, wives, animals, and even birds, as well as their own excellent and fitting wealth, they entered Pātāla. (98–99)
O Rādhikā, even though Raktabīja has died, in another period of time he will become a great Daitya named Dhundhu;
other Daityas will also become his allies in that future age.
Then the Ṛṣi Bakadāna, having realized that it was the destruction of the Asuras,
emerged from the water and approached Dharmarāja.
He offered him hospitality and likewise spoke words of praise.
When Dharmarāja requested a messenger for the sake of protection,
he gave him his own messenger named Arava, as well as a female messenger named Aravī;
and for the very same purpose of protection, he gave a hundred male servants and a hundred female servants.
In the Bakadāna hermitage, they and those women took up residence.
From them were born ten thousand sons named Āravas in that age;
and from them, ten thousand daughters were born through their union with the Dūtīs.
From them, millions more offspring were born there.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Yama, having destroyed the dānavas there,
gave the kingdom to his own messenger and established protection for the sage.
Having ascended a celestial chariot, he went to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. Yamarāja, having become a Vaiṣṇava, dwelt in the presence of Kṛṣṇa along with his soldiers in his second form.
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and having caused his servants to bathe as well,
he constructed a great palace and established a residence at that sacred site (tīrtha).
Rudra was there with the hosts of Rudras, and Nārada together with Sanat.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they each went to their own dwellings.
The seventy-two thousand maidens bathed in the house of Hari;
having bowed to Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī, they were honored and then fed.
By the command of their beloved, they remained constantly in the hermitage of Lomaśa;
and the celestial chariot always remained there, accompanied by the dowry.
It was like a divine heaven within the garden of the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa.

Upon seeing the house of Hari, those maidens, who had previously been filled with desire, became absorbed in that celestial chariot which was situated in its corner. By reading or hearing this account, one becomes meritorious. (113–114)
His obstacles shall be destroyed and his impurity shall perish;

he shall have no fear from the messengers of Dharmarāja. (1.15) Thus ends the account in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna: the destruction of the ten thousand Daityas led by Raktabīja by means of Yamarāja, the granting of the kingdom to the messenger named Arava, and the protection of the sage Bakadāna.
The fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage Beginning with Āravavaṃśa," [from] the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga),
Chapter 58.
[Author: Chapter 059 → Śrī Rādhikā said: O Kṛṣṇa, who was this demon Raktabīja in a former birth?
"But how was that Dhundhu born, who is he, and what will he do?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhikā, to this auspicious and excellent narrative concerning an ancient creation."
When the previous kalpa had passed away during the night, the Great Fish Nārāyaṇa placed a boat upon his own horn in the water, together with Satyavān,
for the sake of preserving the seeds of the world and likewise for the purpose of future creation. (2–3)

Holding onto a boat, he moved about upon the surface of the frost-like water. There, at dawn, a great ocean-born fish that had arisen from the waters arrived there to fight with Nārāyaṇa in the form of a fish.

Desiring to devour the seeds situated on the boat, he then fought with Nārāyaṇa in the form of a fish. The Sudarśana [discus] was then hurled by Nārāyaṇa at the head of the fish, and the fish split into two parts. (5–6)
From his blood-drops, millions of fish were born in the water as the ocean-fish was being torn apart by the discus. Then,
drops of blood, having flown from his body, fell into the boat.
Then, while those seeds were still clinging to some of the trees,
at dawn, when they were cast from the boat into the water by the king,
those ten thousand Rakshasas known as the Raktabijas [emerged].
But immediately, by their very nature, they were born there in the water as sons of fish, all of them dwelling in the ocean waters;
and they searched for an island, a high ground that would serve as a permanent dwelling.
At that time, the water, which had been like frost, indeed became dry by morning.
There, the earth with its mountains was seen standing amidst the waters.
Then the Blessed One, having descended as a fish, [spoke to] King Satyavān.
Having commanded, "Sow seeds upon the earth," he suddenly vanished in an instant; the king likewise cast that treasure of seeds upon the earth,
in water, in the sky, in the wind, and in fire.
Having cast all the seeds [into the boat], he indeed abandoned the vessel in the water.
Those very fine seeds that had become stuck to the cracks and the joints of the wooden planks of the boat remained there.
Indeed, the Rakshasas known as Raktabijas rushed forward to devour him;
having boarded a boat, they then consumed his minute seeds.
From that consumption, children were born who were called Aravijakas.
And likewise, daughters were born from the *āra* seeds who became very youthful.
When all of them had been born, even the boat vanished from sight;
all those offspring of Raktabīja were called by the name *ārabīja*. (17–18)
Assuming any form at will, moving through the sky, and remaining without support,
they flew up from the ocean and searched the earth for a place where they might dwell and where water would be available on all sides. (1.9)
And all around that, there shall be the earth, as well as forests and the like;
battlefields, wilds, men, seeds, flowers, and fruits;
and various caves shall exist there on every side.
Thinking, "We must dwell there," and considering that such a terrestrial realm was entirely occupied by the *raktabīja* demons and their subjects—
those very seeds who had seized the earth which is like unto a continent— [they departed].
In ancient times, there was a great king named Raktabīja, born from the seed of Matsya.
From among his subjects, a king was then born who likewise originated from him;
he became the great king Ārabīja, who acted as an adversary to the gods.
Having slain him, King Yama duly gave the kingdom to his own follower, Arava,
for the protection of the sages.
Raktabīja, killed in battle, went indeed to the world of Yama.
There, the legitimate son of Kaśyapa shall enjoy the fruits of his karma;
born from the womb of Danu, he will become known by the name Dhundhu.
Having propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance, he will attain invulnerability to the gods.
He will swiftly conquer heaven and himself become Śakra;
meanwhile, the kingdom of the Asuras will then be established in Triviṣṭapa.
Out of fear of him, the gods (Tridaśas) will indeed depart for the world of Brahmā.
Dhundhu will say to the Daityas:
"O Daityas, how indeed shall we go to Satyaloka to conquer the gods and others?
Having heard this, the Daityas will say: "There is certainly no way for us to go there."
Beyond this lies the world of Mahas, frequented by hosts of great rishis;
there the Daityas burn with wrathful glances upon seeing women.
Beyond that is Janaloka, where the Janas, who are gods, dwell.
Then there is Tapas, where those devoted to Brahman abide in truth;
upon hearing the sound of the Vedas, the gods and others blossom,
while the asuras and those who share their nature undergo contraction.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, do not resolve to go there;
the palace of Vairāja is agitated and difficult for the Dānavas to ascend.
Having heard their words, Dhundhu will speak to the Daityas.
Desiring to go to the abode of Brahmā to conquer the lords, [he asked:
"By what action is it reached? How does one go there, O Dānavas?
How indeed does Indra set forth, and how do the gods proceed? (36)
"O Daityas, speak here to me, and we shall do exactly as you say. Then Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, will explain the means of accomplishment.
"In ancient times, the thousand-eyed Indra performed one hundred and one sacrifices."
By means of those most excellent horse-sacrifices, he shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Having heard Śukra’s words, he will indeed perform sacrifices;
and having addressed Śukra, the Daityas and Dānavas [departed] toward the earth.
Then that best of rivers, the Devikā, which bestows success, will flow there;
he will perform sacrifices with the Bhārgavas, the disciples of Śukra.
At that time, Svarbhānu and others shall be the partakers of the sacrificial portions there.
Hayagrīva, Trātṛ, Agnidhūma, and Asura shall come to be;
and Gandha shall roam upon the earth and indeed go to heaven.
Having smelled it, the gods, being dejected, will address the Creator.
They will go to the Supreme Lord residing within the milk and offer their petition;
O Janārdana, let it be heard:
"The lord of asuras named Dhundhu is powerful and surrounded by a vast army."
The Lord of the Three Worlds remains, yet no protector for us is to be found.
Now he is intent on conquering even those dwelling in the world of Brahmā;
having adopted the counsel of Śukra, he performs hundreds of sacrifices.
He desires to ascend to the world of truth (satyaloka) and to conquer the Creator (Brahmā).
Therefore, O Supreme Lord,
consider at once a means for the destruction of the sacrifice, by which we may attain perfect peace.
Having heard this, the Blessed One will say: "You go to Ketana.
Having said, "I shall go to conquer him," he will depart;
the Blessed One, having become Vāmana, will bathe in the waters of the Devikā.
He will fall into the waters of the Devikā in the vicinity of the sacrifice;
sinking for a moment and then surfacing, he will perform movements in the water.
Thinking that the sacrificial victim was drowning, they will quickly [seize] him.
And they will set out to rescue him, having lifted up one who stands upon the bank.
Then the priests of Dhundhu will question that dwarf Brāhmaṇa:
"Who are you? From where have you come? Why and what is your purpose?"
Then that brahmin will say: "I am suffering, deprived of my home.
My father is named Prabhāsa, and by lineage he belongs to the Vāruṇa gotra.
My brothers are Netrabhāsa and Gatibhāsa, and I myself am [Gatibhāsa]. (52)

Having abandoned our delightful dwelling, our father has since passed away. At the end of the year, my elder brother said, "Let us divide the house between us. He replied to us, "There is no share for you whatsoever. (53–54)
For those who are humpbacked, dwarfish, or lame; for the impotent, as well as for those afflicted with leprosy, the insane, and the blind, there is no share of the inheritance.
[They are entitled only to] kind words, residence in the house, food, clothing, and so forth.
Only this much is given to them; they are not heirs to the inheritance.
(56) Then, having been expelled from that house with great hardship, I arrived here after hearing of a sacrifice and entered the water to bathe. (57)
Since I have been submerged, I do not know how I was brought down;
who are you who have arrived here, appearing like affectionate kinsmen?
And who is this person, resembling Śakra, who shines resplendent in your midst?
"May they show compassion if a refuge can be found here.
Having heard these words of Vāmana, the Brahmins will speak to Dhundhuka for the sake of alms, and Dhundhu will give them what is beautiful.
Vāmana [bestowed] a magnificent residence, female slaves, various jewels,
all kinds of household utensils, male servants, cows, vehicles,
gold, chariots, horses, and likewise elephants.
At that time, he will not grasp at worldly possessions while proclaiming the true Dharma.
Having renounced female and male slaves, servants, his home, jewels, and furnishings, he will indeed attain perfection by then, using only three steps of ground as his seat.
When Dhundhu shall grant him three paces of land, then,
assuming the form of Vairāja, he will cover this earth with one pace,
the shell of the cosmic egg with the second, and the Dānava with the third.
Hari will seize him and lead him down to the netherworld of Pātāla.
Having given his own kingdom to the gods, he will become invisible.
Later, when Bali has grown in power, Hari will take back the kingdom from him, making it diminished.
Then Dhundhu will also provide assistance to Andhaka;
a great battle between Andhaka and Śaṅkara will take place.
At that time, Śambhu, having cast Śukrācārya into his mouth, will swallow him into his belly.
Having grasped it again with his penis, he will then cause it to emerge.
Taking the form of semen and known by the name Śukra, he shall become the son of Śambhu.
Then, Mahendra too shall go forth to fight with Indhaka.
When he shall strike Andhaka, whirling the thunderbolt above his head, the thunderbolt will be reduced to powder upon Andhaka’s very skull. Then Vahni will surely grant him a terrifying spear.
And likewise, the gods and Gandharvas will provide a svastika-shaped chariot. At that time, when the earth is trembling, the wife of the sage Śamīka will indeed place the child upon the ground.
At that time, those two boys shall become one;
of them, one indeed named Mātali will go to Mahendra.
Then, having become his charioteer, he will provide assistance.
Then Rudra, Mahendra, and likewise the other deities together with Śaṅkara,
the benefactor of the world, will slay Andhaka. From above the forehead of Śaṅkara, drops [of sweat] shall fall due to the blow of the mace.
They will fall even upon the blood and shall become terrifying;
[they are] Vidyārāja, Rudrarāja, Caṇḍa, and also Pracaṇḍa;
Kapālin, Ekakapālin, and likewise Lalitarājaka.
Vighnarāja shall be the eighth, and those Bhairavas will arise from them.
From the forehead-slab of Śambhu, one daughter shall be born;
she is the virtuous Carcikā by name, who dwells upon the Hiṅgulā mountain.
Then, having slain Andhaka, Śaṅkara will make his own host the one named Bhṛṅgi; thereafter, Dhundhu, filled with fear,
will quickly go to the netherworld (pātāla), and later, after some time...
"When he provides assistance to Bali,
then Hari shall slay Dhundhu while he is still alive with the Sudarśana discus.
Thus, O Rādhā, has the narrative of Raktabījaka been told.
Śrī Rādhikā said: O Kṛṣṇa, how was the fish in the water slain by Viṣṇu’s disc? Why did he not attain purity, since there were demons in his lineage? (82)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the water-fish, severed by Viṣṇu’s discus,
was instantly cleansed of sin and attained the status of Mahendra in heaven.
He alone, born of a mere resolve, became the Lord of the Devas;
then, for the sake of initiating the first age, he descended upon the earth.
In this world, he became a devotee of Viṣṇu, renowned as Suvarṇāṅgada.
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s devotee, the supreme human being,
then went from there to the divine, supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā. Now,
as for those Raktabījas, Ārabīja, and the others...
Since they all became destroyers of seeds at the beginning of creation,
they fell into the state of Rākṣasas due to the curse of Satyavrata.
They were slayers of the primordial seed and destroyers of things that ought not to be destroyed.
"They are great sinners, even exceeding sinners, since they are the destroyers of the lineage.
Having reflected thus, the king then cursed those destroyers:
"You shall indeed become Asuras who bring about the destruction of seeds."
Thus they became *asuras* because of their demonic inclinations;

for those *rākṣasas* were indeed devourers of the embryos of birds, from the stage of the *kalala* onwards, as well as destroyers of the seed of cattle and annihilators of passion and virility. (2.58.90)
Those who destroy the seed-vessels are considered to be *tāmasa* asuras.
Indeed, a great sin arises from the destruction of unobtained seed;
first [this occurred] when the goddess Pārvatī was united with Śaṅkara. (91–92)
At the opportune moment for obtaining an offspring, the gods created obstacles;
with a distressed heart, he cursed his virtuous beloved:
"The gods, for the sake of achieving their own ends, have destroyed my desire for a child. (93)

"Since you have indeed become destroyers regarding Hara by withholding the seed, therefore I have been made childless and barren by you. For you too shall be childless, and your wives shall likewise be barren. (94–95)
"May they always remain childless," she cursed the gods.
Therefore, O Rādhikā, the first sin is the destruction of seeds;
even greater than that is the sin of a woman who destroys her fertile season.
Even more sinful than that is said to be the destruction of an embryo. The killing of a child is a sin more intense than all others;
and the slaughter of those who have just been married constitutes ten million times the sin.
The sin of killing one who is pregnant is greater than ten billion times ten million sins;
indeed, if the couple has not yet completed their union, that killing is equivalent to the destruction of creation itself.
Therefore, such sin is produced, and those who destroy the seed are certainly not liberated.
Therefore, the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) is considered to bestow both merit and liberation.
In that state, the seed is not destroyed but is preserved by its very nature;
there is great merit in such preservation, and it is even granted through righteousness.
"O Rādhikā, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves have always proclaimed that there is great merit [in this]; thus has the reason for being born as a rākṣasa been told.
Kṛṣṇa himself does not come within the range of sight of those who destroy the seed (of their lineage)."
The Lord brought about their destruction through the gate of Yama.
(103) The giving of a daughter in marriage (*ṛtudāna*) is declared by the gods to be a source of great merit for householders;
and the giving of a lineage (*vaṃśadāna*) is proclaimed as an even greater merit for those who establish a lineage. (104)
"Those without lineage do not rescue at all; they do not cross the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
Ancestors who possess a lineage, being satisfied, rescue [their descendants] from the sea.

Thus ends the section on the origin of the Asuras beginning with Raktabīja and Ārabīja, the origin of the Daitya Dhundhu, and the sin consisting of the destruction of seeds, in the second part, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
The fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Mityā and Others," [ends].

Chapter 59.
[The Author: Chapter 60.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen; when Caitra has passed, the second [month] follows.
The life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone bestows liberation.
(1) There is a region renowned as Bhālladeśa, honored by Vaiṣṇavas;
there is a famous city named Dhavala, an excellent locality. (2)
In that place, there lived a merchant named Godhana, engaged in the business of trade;
he was full of wealth, intelligent, and had reached the further shore of mastery in the arts.
Once, he prepared to travel from his own kingdom to Saurāṣṭra.
Accompanied by a vast caravan and laden with many goods and merchandise,
as he was traveling, he encountered a band of thieves at night on a waterless,
parched stretch of land, at a solitary spot where fishermen had cast their nets.
Then that merchant, having had all his wealth stolen and being constantly afflicted by grief,
wandered here and there until he came into the vicinity of the Jālikā tree.
Seeing the Jālikā devoid of deer, birds, and insects, [he approached it].
Patiently enduring hunger and thirst with his throat parched, he approached the side of a tree.
Having rested, he sat down and fell asleep; thus did his rest come to pass.
Then, having risen at midday, as soon as he did so, he beheld a *preta*.
Surrounded by hundreds of hungry ghosts (*preta*s) and being carried on a comfortable seat by those *preta*s arriving from all sides toward the tree of the net,
he reached that very tree where the merchant’s son was located.
The King of the Pretas beheld that merchant’s son, whose inner mind was steadfast.
The Preta offered him a welcome, and the merchant did likewise;
having exchanged greetings concerning their mutual welfare and saluted one another, they sat down.
Then the two merchant-pretas sat comfortably in the shade.
The lord of the pretas asked: "O merchant, from where have you come?
Where is your dwelling? Where will you go from this place?"
"How is it that you have taken refuge in this desolate place?
Thus questioned, the merchant replied: "Though I was once possessed of wealth, my riches were seized by thieves in the forest; now I wander about, exceedingly distressed."
Due to the merchant's suffering, the preta became distressed for a moment;
he spoke to the merchant as if to his own kinsman: "Do not grieve;
wealth shall come again if you possess the power of fortune. (15)
Wealth perishes when fortune declines, yet it arises again when fortune flourishes.
For this body that has already decayed, no new birth can come about through mere anxiety;
for the sun, both its rising and its setting occur perpetually.
The trees become withered and yet again put forth new sprouts;
likewise, there is brilliance in the moon during one fortnight and the waning of its luster in the other.
The rivers are dry in the summer and filled with water during the rainy season.
In some places there was an abundance of crops in the fields, while in others there was a total lack of grain.
At times the eyes were dull and heavy with sleep, yet at other times they experienced the splendor of lotus petals.
And the sky was turbid at certain times, while at others it was stainless and radiant.
A lamp burns at night but produces no light by day;
sometimes one is a king, sometimes a merchant, and sometimes a servant.
Sometimes one is a teacher, sometimes a student, and sometimes one is free from both extremes.
In some places he is the glorious Lord of Fortune, and in others he is destitute of fortune.
(22) Indeed, all embodied beings are by nature free from possessions in childhood;
in youth they are pervaded by craving, and in old age they are devoid of power. (23)
They are born by the force of time and by their previous karma;
for whatever wealth was previously obtained from various sources in the form of debt,
if it is not given back to those [creditors] afterwards, that debt indeed follows one along.
Through the bondage of debt, they become your givers, your sons, your wives, and your householders;
likewise, they become kings, servants, and attendants.
Or, assuming the form of thieves, they even strike you by force. (25–26)
Neither given away nor enjoyed, nor even sufficiently accumulated, it increases through effort yet seeks its own destruction.
Wealth diminishes the master of wealth; your mastery over wealth is but a falsehood.

Because you did not perform that exchange with the worthy person, death awaits you in his presence; O merchant, you will depart having abandoned [your wealth]. Therefore, your lordship lies in the property, and true lordship does not reside in you.
Oh, the greatness of greed! Even one who possesses wealth exceeding seventy-seven crores still desires to accumulate more, even from his hair.
Indeed, the acquisition of wealth brings supreme suffering, arising from servitude and other such labors.

Even in guarding wealth there is supreme suffering, as the tigress of anxiety leaps about (3.1). In its expenditure there is the suffering of depletion; in its enjoyment there is the suffering of disease;
in pride there is the suffering of war and the like; and from wealth, death itself arises (3.2).
Therefore, wealth that is not employed for the sake of dharma is said to be suffering;
but when wealth is applied to dharma, there is happiness from dharma and no more misery.
From dharma comes peace; through the practice of dharma come the destruction of craving and discernment.
Contentment with whatever is obtained, conduct such as service to the gods,

a disposition of goodness toward one's family, freedom from passion, hatred, and the like, absence of fear from thieves and other dangers, and even sleep that occurs with ease— [these are the signs]. //34-35//
O merchant, such virtues as these bring happiness when one is poor, but when one possesses wealth, they repeatedly give rise to the defects of suffering.
In this regard, there is nothing particularly wonderful; [the cycle of life] comes and goes like the waters of the ocean.
All wealth is indeed flickering, for fortune is always unstable;
life itself is also transient, so do not grieve over prosperity.
By fate everything may come about again, even through diligent effort. (37–38)
Having spoken thus and summoned his servants, the deceased said to them:
"Today this excellent merchant has arrived as a guest at our house;
he is my childhood friend, worthy of honor, born in the same land as I. (39)
"In this [state] I perceive that I have seen my own kinsmen;
now that he has arrived, incomparable joy has indeed arisen within me today.
Having spoken thus, the deceased spirit recollected his excellent meal.
Just then, a new, sturdy, and auspicious vessel arrived for him,
filled with sweet food as well as curd-rice,
and indeed complete with vegetables, soup, sour gruel, and other items for his meal.
Likewise, seeing a new, sturdy earthen pot filled with cold water, as well as a water-jar and a cooking vessel, the Lord of the Dead then said:
"Arise, O best of merchants! Wash your hands and your face."
Having spoken thus and offered water, the King of the Pretas seated him upon a splendid throne; he gave him sweet food, curd, and water.
The merchant ate the rice, sour gruel, and vegetables.
He gave every kind of food to the worthy recipients and the birds.

The hungry ghosts (pretas) ate the delicious food and delicacies with great respect; thereafter they drank water, and the Lord of the Hungry Ghosts (Preteśvara) consumed the remainder of that very same [food].
They ate and drank water, and thereafter they all became satisfied. Then, even as the merchant looked on, the cooking pot, the water-vessel, and the remaining food entirely vanished instantly.
Having seen this wonder and marvel, the merchant indeed asked:
"O bull among the spirits, tell me how this vessel full of food and this water-jar filled with water came to be found here in the forest? || 2.59.50 ||
"Nevertheless, how is it that your servants are altogether emaciated, while you yourself are not at all well-nourished? Tell me, how is this weakness?
While he was speaking thus, a beautiful, new white garment arrived there.
And at that time, the ghost gave those clothes to the merchant there out of sincere devotion.
Seeing that wonder— how the garment had come to be—
and questioning the ghost as to how it had arrived, the merchant was told by the ghost exactly as it happened.
"O merchant, in former times I was a Brahmin named Prabhānātha in the city called Dhavala; I was always a cook.
And I had a wealthy merchant, Dhanāḍhya by name, who increased his merit."
The patron who worships Viṣṇu is my master and provider of wealth. Named Dharmavardhana, he always commands me for the sake of righteous deeds,
for the purpose of dharma, and for expenditure as he desires.
He issues unimpeded commands for the sake of giving and for the sake of helping others;
yet I, being miserly and greedy-minded, even though I possess abundant wealth,
do not give to the gods, nor to the Brahmins, nor do I perform acts of charity.
I do not perform any service for any living being who is without a protector.
I do not take account of ascetics, holy men, or those devoted to dharma in any way whatsoever.
I do not eat to my full satisfaction; being greedy myself, what need is there to speak of others?
It is certain that the splendors of one who lacks merit end in destruction;
likewise, I did not possess such merit at that time, for I have not yet exhausted it.
If, through negligence, I should consume curds, milk, ghee, and so forth—
Whether it be sweet food or sweet water, sorrow then arises:
"Alas! Today I have made a vain expenditure that has caused me loss;
sleep does not come at night for me, who am preoccupied with thoughts of my expenses. (61-62)
In the morning, whatever it may be, I obtain this way or that;
thus, as such a greedy person with excessive thirst, I live on meals of rice, sesame, oil-cakes, husks, vegetables, and the like. (63)
"When shall I exhaust myself by passing the time with mere food?
Thus, although I possess wealth, a great deal of time has passed for me without merit gained through giving; now, however, a solar eclipse has arrived. (64–65)
Likewise, when the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī arrives in the month of Bhādrapada,
people go day after day to the Sābhramatī river for the sake of pilgrimage.
And I, having fasted on the Ekādaśī, was together with the merchant.
On the day of Ekādaśī, he went to the Sābhramatī river to bathe;
from that day until the solar eclipse, I remained steadfast at that sacred ford (tīrtha).
During that time, the merchant gave away wealth by the millions on the day of Ekādaśī.
Having seen this, I was overcome with great shame and gave there, according to my means, gifts such as garments, excellent vessels, and cows;
and I also gave a single new pair of washed clothes to a brahmin who was learned in the Vedas.
A new cooking pot, filled with food and full of sweets, was offered;
likewise, it was provided with curd, rice, sour gruel, and vegetables.
Then a water-jar was given, and a wooden vehicle was also presented.
At that time, an umbrella was indeed given to the brahmin for the sake of shade;
and the merchant's groups of servants were employed by me for the sake of the brahmin.
O best of merchants, only this much was offered by me at that time.
Not even the slightest thing was given by me, even for ten thousand years.
Then, in the course of time, having met my death, I went to the state of a preta.
These people, indeed, had not given gifts themselves, yet they subsisted on the food provided by me.
The servants of that merchant named Godhana have come under my control;
this wooden vehicle has been obtained, and those servants have been acquired by me.
A vessel filled with sweet food and a large pot of water have also been obtained.
That which was given returns to me day after day, even at midday.
As long as I do not eat food, it does not dissolve;
but once I have eaten and drunk, everything becomes absorbed into me.
"By the gift of an umbrella and other such acts, this tree has indeed been acquired by me eternally;
I dwell here for the sake of shelter, and the *pretas* perform service for me.
All this that I have told you concerns how [the merit] is obstructed through giving. (78)
"In the past, because of that sin, I fell into the state of a preta.
Through greed and craving, though I was a brahmin, I fell into the state of a preta;
for even water and food given but once are consumed [by me]. (2.59.80)
Indeed, having given [alms] once every day, I always eat;
for one who constantly bestows gifts, heaven shall indeed become eternal.
O merchant, I shall likewise act for your benefit in every way.

"O merchant, go quickly to the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, to the hermitage of Lomaśa, and there to the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; perform your ablutions and offer oblations there. (82-83)
"Perform the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) with my name in mind.
By that gift of the rice-ball, I shall be instantly released from the state of a preta and, being liberated, go to the same world as the donors. (84)
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is meritorious and auspicious;
when joined with Wednesday and the Śravaṇa asterism, it brings me supreme benefit.
Alternatively, perform a śrāddha for me on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika.
"On the day of the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my liberation will certainly occur; reflect upon this.
Having said this, he gave him gold, diamonds, and other such treasures.
Placing that merchant from Surāṣṭra upon his shoulder, he abandoned him there.
On the eleventh day of the month of Bhādrapada, he went to Lake Aśvasaras;
there, he performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased ancestors in due order.
Then he duly performed a great śrāddha for his kinsmen, his ancestors, and himself, without the use of sesame seeds. He likewise offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for others born of his lineage.
The merchant indeed liberated them all through the giving of *śrāddha* offerings and other rites.
Once freed from their karma, they all arrived in his presence,
possessing divine forms and divine attire, and resplendent with a brilliance more intense than the sun.
There the merchant gave them water and a meal of sweet food;
then he led them, now possessing divine bodies, to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
At that time, Lomaśa caused them to hear the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
(94) He gave them garlands of tulasī and the nectar of His feet.
Then the merchant departed, taking with him all those who had been liberated. (95)
They all bowed down to Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the palace with beautiful golden pinnacles, and worshipped him with great reverence.
Having drunk the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet, they became ten million liberated souls.

Having ascended a divine chariot by the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they went from there to the realm known as Goloka, and then to the supreme, imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma). Then, O Rādhā, this merchant went from there to his own place.
In that city named Dhavala, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
having practiced the ninefold devotion, he met his end.
Then, indeed, he became a god, a Gandharva, and also a Guhyaka.

Then, having become King Virāṭ, he— who was indeed a supreme devotee of the Lord— worshipped the primordial Supreme Brahman, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. At the end of his body, having praised Him again and again, he went to the abode of Hari.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been described the miracle of Hari,
by the sight of whom the *pretas* attained liberation and became possessed of divine bodies.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the *Pretas* through the Śrāddha at Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake on the Eleventh Day of Bhādrapada in the Tretā Age, and the Dialogue between the *Preta* and the Merchant," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Sixty Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga),
Chapter 60.
[The Author: Chapter 61.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, listen now to another marvel of Hari at that time.
There was a righteous king named Udaya, a worshiper of the gods.
(1) His vast kingdom lay within the region of Mount Aravali, and his auspicious capital city was indeed named Udayapura. (2)

The king undertook a supreme vow: eating but once every four months, daily giving gifts, feeding Brahmins and virtuous men, tending cows, and providing food and clothing to the helpless, children, and chaste women. (3)
Likewise, wealth for the gift of knowledge and excellent riches for temples;
always the fire-sacrifice in the morning, the Vedic recitation, and the immersion in water in the evening— thus,
while one is performing these vows well in every way during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
The desire arose in him to bathe for one month in the lake,
just as in the month of Āṣāḍha he [visited] the Dhīravīra lake.
With only a few followers, the king went to the forest of the sage Āryāyaṇa.
And he made his own dwelling in the hermitage on the bank of the river.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, rising every morning with haste,
he would constantly pay homage to Nārāyaṇa and meditate upon the infallible Śrī Viṣṇu.
Having bathed and worshipped Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Light,
and having worshipped with devotion Pārvatī’s husband, Rādheśvara,
he then performs the daily worship of the sage Āryāyaṇa.
Then, afterwards, he would always come specifically to see the holy fords (tīrthas):
Satītīrtha, Śambhutīrtha, and after that Cakratīrtha,
Kṛṣṇatīrtha, Svāmitīrtha, and also Mañjulātīrtha.
Sūryatīrtha, Indratīrtha, and beyond that Brahmatīrtha;
Muktatīrtha, Ṛṣitīrtha, and Dharmatīrtha situated by the water—
having established these and other such holy sites all around the lake.
Having circumambulated the lake and having given gifts of all kinds—
gold, silver, garments, various vessels,
edible foods, and gifts of alms— he then proceeds to his own abode.

Having done this, he then performs the fire-sacrifice (homa) and the Vaiśvadeva rite. Having distributed food among the Brahmins, sages, virtuous and chaste women, holy men, children, and the helpless, and having fed the guests as well as his own followers, [he proceeds].
Then the king himself ate, having bowed to the noble sage Āryanamṛṣi. Thus, by the power of the king’s merit, whatever sins he had committed in the past were entirely consumed.
Furthermore, a great mass of merit has been offered by him to Kṛṣṇa;
consequently, only the grace of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa remains for him.
He considers that grace to be the great merit, and no other merit.
Hari-Kṛṣṇa became pleased, having entered the heart of the noble sage.
And the sage said to the king: "O King, come near me;
receive the supreme mantra, which is Lord Puruṣottama himself."
Then the king sat down before the sage,
and the sage instructed him in this mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," as well as a garland of *tulasī*.
Then the sage Ārṣyaśṛṅga spoke the mantra also to his followers.
(22) Having received the mantra and bowed to the seer, the king, together with his attendants, went home;
there, on the riverbank, he sat down in his own leaf-hut. (23)
Then the youthful Lord himself arrived there, adorned with a flute in his hand,
attended by Rādhā, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, and Pāravatī;
he was the Supreme Blessed One, whose form was the very embodiment of beauty corresponding to every form of beauty.
Laughing repeatedly and making his beloved laugh, he was filled with joy;
divine and surrounded by wives of divine form, he was adorned with a golden crown richly decorated with peacock feathers. || 25–26 ||
Wearing garments purified by fire and resplendent with divine ornaments, his hand marked with the fish-banner, the svastika, the bow, the trident, and other signs;
and slightly to his side, Lakṣmī, Śrī, and the virtuous Kambharā. (27)
A short distance away on another side, the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa was present;
other female and male servants likewise gathered there in leaf-huts.
There, a blissful splendor shone forth, equal to the light of ten million times ten million suns.
Beholding that beautiful form, the king stood firm there; his eyes closed, their rays obstructed by the splendor. After a moment, having opened them, he gazed upon Keśava.
At that moment, Śrī Hari himself became one with Kṛṣṇa’s form;
he then revealed Saurāṣṭra, as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā,
Aśvapaṭṭasara, and the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
Likewise, having shown Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of maidens, as well as all the sacred fords (tīrthas) from every direction,
the Blessed Lord caused everything to dissolve once again.
Then, in an instant, he showed him his own feet;
below them was Pātāla, and above that, Rasātala;
beyond that was Mahātala at his calves, and Talātala at his knees.
Below the earth is Sutala, and Vitala is beneath the thighs;
Atala is at the base of the thighs. Therein dwell the Daityas, Dānavas, serpents, Nāgas, and other living beings, as well as rivers, mountains, and the expanses of land.
He showed him his supernatural powers, as well as Śeṣa and the Tortoise;
the earth upon his hip, the Bhuvarloka upon his loins, and beyond that, Svarga in his navel, Maharloka in his belly, and Janaloka in his heart.
He showed him the world of austerity (tapoloka) in his mouth and the world of truth (satyaloka) on his forehead;
he also showed him the seven coverings within his skin. Having thus displayed them, he then caused them all to vanish in an instant.
Then he showed him his own Vaiṣṇava form—
beautiful, with a thousand heads and a thousand hands and feet.
There, indeed, he showed him water at his two feet.
One should meditate on fire, wind, and space, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, at the feet;
likewise, one should meditate on Jala-Vaikunṭha and Vairāja at the shanks;
then Mahāviṣṇu at the knees, and Bhūmā at the thighs.
He showed Pradhāna at the base of the thighs and Puruṣa likewise at the penis;
he showed Prakṛti on the buttocks and Vāsudeva at the navel;
he showed the person Kāla on the hip and Saṃkarṣaṇa on the side.
And on his side Keśava showed Pradyumna, while on his belly he showed Aniruddha;
in his two flanks Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, and on his chest the attendants of Ananta,
as well as the powers such as Rādhā and Ramā.
In his throat, he revealed millions, billions, and hundreds of millions of liberated souls whose nature is Brahman;
in his mouth, the world of nectar; in his eyes, the Imperishable;
and on his forehead, a mass of splendors, he manifested Brahman.
There, Hari revealed his own supreme abode at the *brahmarandhra* to Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī and the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
There, a divine throne was situated, and upon it, Hari likewise.
And as he was performing his service there, the king observed him;
then once again, all of that became invisible.
[The king saw] him standing in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in the form of a child.
The king beheld his own glorious self, served by ten million embodied beings;
there, the monarch again saw himself standing nearby.
Then, in an instant, everything dissolved, and the king was struck with wonder.
Then, after a moment, he beheld his own beautiful hut.
Having become composed and bowed to the quarters, he remained established in meditation and offered praise:
"Om, salutation to Śrīnivāsa, the sleeper of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti)."
Salutations be to you, the unconquered and great-souled god;
salutations be to you, the unattached, the peaceful, and the desireless.
Salutations to the primordial god, who consists of all the gods.
Salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the primordial form of the Ṛṣis;
salutations to you, who are without end, unique, and eternally manifest.
Salutations to you, the hidden one, the light, and the Lord of the Guṇas.
Salutations to you who are inconceivable, immeasurable, and incomparable;
salutations to you who are free from anxiety, primordial, and eternal.
Salutations to that ancient one; let there be salutations to you who are devoid of qualities.
Salutations to You who are the foundation of the world; salutations to You who are established in Brahman.
(58) Salutations again and again to Padmanābha, to Yoga, and to Govinda.
Salutations be to You, the Lord of the Universe, who is to be known through Sāṃkhya. (59)
Salutations to you, Hari, the protector of Śiva, Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the giver of the immeasurable, whose strides are immeasurable.
Salutations again and again to you, who are adorned with the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Salutations be to the Mahoraga, to the Lion, and to the dweller in the Vedas (61).
Salutations to you, the Great Fish, the Beloved, and the Tortoise;
salutations to you, the Dwarf, the Long One, and the Four-Armed One (62).
Salutations again and again to him who is praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas; salutations to Acyuta, to the All-pervading One, and to Him who reclines upon the king of serpents.
Salutations again and again to the milk-colored one, to Kṛṣṇa, and to the one with a golden luster.
Salutations to you who wear yellow garments and who destroy the Daityas and other foes.
Salutations to you, the imperishable one, the lord of the imperishable, whose navel is a lotus.
Salutations to you, the four-faced god, and salutations to you, the five-faced one.
Salutations to you, who dwell in the milk-ocean, who are glory, and who are beauty; salutations to the giver of boons, the Lord of all, the beloved, and the sovereign of those who desire.
Salutations to you, the most excellent, the remover of obstacles, and the lover of devotion.
Salutations again and again to you who have long, lotus-like eyes, whose nose is like a parrot’s beak, and who bear the Śārṅga bow;
salutations again and again to you, the Lord of Yoga, the Tree, the one with branches.
Salutations again and again to you, the Sage, the path of the gods, the virtuous one.
Salutations to You who appear in the form of the Enchantress (Mohinī) and who dwell within all living beings;
salutations to You as the Boar, the Man-Lion, and the Śarabha. Salutations to the immutable, the cause of all, the Supreme Person, and the Ancient One.

I bow to the beloved of Māyā, the beloved of Īśa, and the beloved of all. [2.60.70] [I bow to] the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Lord of Time and Māyā, the Lord of the Vyūhas, the liberated soul, Vāsudeva, the beloved of Satī, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. [71]
I bow down to that Kṛṣṇa, the delight of Yaśodā, the dark youth who is the protector of the cowherds; to him who dwells in the supreme abode, the best of persons,
whom the celestial sages declare to be the eternal form of Brahman.
I take refuge in Hari, the Lord of the Imperishable and the Lord of Liberation.

(73) I take refuge in my Master, who is marked with the Śrīvatsa, whose chest bears the lines of white lotuses, who wears necklaces of the three qualities, and who is adorned with the sixteen auspicious marks. (74)
I take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the source of all beings, possessed of divine qualities, in whom the universe resides, who is the universe itself, and in whom everything is established;
He who is the supreme goal of the virtuous who are free from attachment.

With devotion, I take refuge in the Blessed One, who dwells within the self, whose abode is the woman, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is worthy of refuge, and who is compassionate toward his devotees—
he who, when the time of death has arrived, reveals his very self.
The Supreme Lord indeed leads His own devotee to His own abode;
I bow to that Supreme God, the Best of Persons, the bestower of liberation.
Indeed, everything from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the realm of truth (satya) is contained within Him.
I take refuge in that supreme Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, in whom all of Mahāmāyāntaka is contained, and in whom the abodes and millions of liberated souls abide within that Supreme Lord.
O Lord, I do not know how to praise you as you truly exist;
I do not know your true nature, but I know it only from the perspective of an outsider.
O Kṛṣṇa, that which has been made by you through your grace is of the essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
My form has been revealed to me—the fruit of my penance and the fruit of [your] compassion.
My abode has also been shown, as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā, Aśvapaṭṭasara, and the hermitage of Lomaśa. //82-83//
"O Protector, I desire to behold you again and again through service;
I long for your favor—thus, be the granter of boons to me.
Thus was the beginningless and glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa praised.
And immediately the Lord, the lotus-eyed one who holds the discus and the lotus, compassionate toward those who seek refuge, arrived there full of affection;
he spoke sweetly to that high-souled Udaya. (85–86)
O King, I am repeatedly pleased by your hymn of praise. O King, through the influence of Āryāyaṇa, everything you desire shall be yours;
moreover, before long, your residence shall be in my own field.
"O King, I shall lead you to my field by way of the waters of Varuṇa.
Through your yoga and through my yoga, this place shall become a sacred ford on a river.
And those who, O King, shall recite this hymn in their home or in the forest," [88–89]

Those people who, at this sacred site of the Dhīravīra lake, as well as beasts, birds, insects, trees, creepers, and the like, shall attain the supreme perfection that consists in the realization of my own nature. (2.60.90)
They shall drink the water and attain purifying liberation.
(9.1) Those who here offer śrāddha, charity, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, food, and water according to the prescribed rite, for them there will be liberation. (9.2)
Having spoken thus to the king, the Blessed One assumed an invisible state.
The king repeatedly chanted the names of the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
he sang, danced, meditated, laughed, and wept.
He stayed with him, served him, honored him, and gazed upon him in every possible way.
He dispatched his own servants to Udayapattana and commanded his son Nāgadeva to bestow the kingdom upon him.
There, the king, the best of devotees, conducted himself virtuously.
While he was sleeping at night on the eighth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the lord of clouds poured down rain;
the lakes, rivers, and wells took on the appearance of water like the ocean.
Then, due to excessive rain, the leaf-hut was submerged in the water.
More than a hundred people also met their end, having been drowned in the water;
they remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with great intensity.
Immediately, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the ocean of mercy and the protector, took the eternal boat and departed;
assuming a thousand forms, he went wherever there were people in the water. (99)
Men and women, including children and the elderly, as well as animals, were all submerged;
yet he rescued them all, and not a single one met with death.
He also rescued the great seer Āryāyaṇa, who had entered the water while absorbed in meditative concentration.
Taking them up onto the boat, the Blessed One, the abode of compassion, held them;
that boat was then placed by the Supreme Self upon the great river.
Having supported those two hundred and more who were submerged, he protected them.
At that time, he protected the beasts and the flocks of birds as they lived;
and all the human beings, remaining alive, worshipped the illustrious Narayana with single-minded devotion, just as a boat remains upon the surface of the water.
"O Rādhikā, she was carried slowly upon the water by Kṛṣṇa; protected by Kṛṣṇa, what pain indeed could there be for her? (105).

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Udayapura’s Vision of the Lord while staying on the shore of Dhīravīra Lake during the Cāturmāsya, His Being Submerged in Water Due to Excessive Rainfall, and His Rescue by the Lord in a Boat," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
