Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! Our boat, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and occupied by two hundred men, was upon the waters of the earth.
The Blessed One carries her along with his previous momentum and protects her;
the waters that have gradually merged into the great river [flow on].
At the confluence of the great river, the boat was then among the bees.
Tending toward the bathing place, the river was protected by Kṛṣṇa upon its waters.
(3) Indeed, that river in Gurjara was long, unfathomable, and terrifying;
driven by the force of the flood, it then flowed for a hundred krośas. (4)
Then all those who had traveled by boat, overcome with great wonder, saw that the city named Lūnāpaṭa was not very far away;
and they then beheld a forest ahead as the boat moved with great speed toward the shore.
When they had traveled fifty *krośas* while being carried along,
the people on the boat beheld the great holy ford of Devīkoṭa;
and beyond that, at a distance of fifty *krośas*, they saw Bhadrāyana.
Then, ahead, there is the city of Kaṭhina; likewise, the great pilgrimage site of Stambhapura and Kāvyatīrtha are nearby.
In the middle, the great river Mahī shines like the ocean.
There, that boat, manned by men, traveled upon the water in a place where no channel had been dug.
Protected by Śrī Hari, it moved toward the ocean as the waters of the Sābhramatī river merged with those of the unchanneled sea.
The boat, which had previously been at the front of the dry land, then crossed the confluence of the ocean and reached the supreme island;
by the power of the illustrious Lord, it became vast, providing shelter for a thousand men. (11)
Having crossed the Narmadā ditch, she reached the shore of Saurāṣṭra.
At the confluence of the river Śatrujit and the ocean, she was made to stay steady.
There, everyone indeed partook of food and drink with great ease.
Then the boat, propelled by Kṛṣṇa, went first to Gopanātha;
after that, it went to Mādhuka, and then to Jāphalita.
Then, having made the sky auspicious, it went to the city of Kṛṣṇāvatī.
From there he went to Somanātha, and from there also to Makarālaya.
Having seen the confluence of the Bhadrā and the ocean, he went to the city of Svarṇavatī.
Then, entering Kacchākhāta, he proceeded to the vicinity of Camatkārapura.
Then that boat, having assumed the form of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*),
soared into the sky by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
It arrived swiftly through the air at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
A divine vehicle, equal to the moon and radiant with the splendor of the sun,
adorned with gold, worshipped by the gods, and protected by Kṛṣṇa—
yoked with two hundred men— it descended near the lake. (18–19)
There, shouts of "Victory! and "Hail! arose again and again;
the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā appeared full of enthusiasm.
The entire field was beheld by all, and the golden palace was seen.
He beheld the auspicious and lofty spire of the temple, the great abode of the Bhāgavatas; he saw Kambharā-Lakṣmī, and he saw Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, the sage Lomaśa was seen, and the city was surveyed.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they descended from the celestial chariot,
as did others known as Udaya, both male and female devotees.
At that moment, the chariot created by Kṛṣṇa vanished from sight.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, along with his caravan, also vanished.
Having witnessed this supreme wonder— the state of becoming invisible—
all those pilgrims questioned people again and again.
The gods went to where Bālakṛṣṇa shines resplendent;
having all been granted a vision by this Kṛṣṇa, they were protected by him.
Remembering this, filled with joy, they shed tears of love.
Bālakṛṣṇa gave them a great mansion suitable for residence,
furnished with all necessities and graced by male and female servants.
Then all the holy men duly performed their rites around Aśvasaras.
Then the Blessed Lord himself gave sweet foods and drinks—
edibles, consumables, things to be licked, and things to be sucked, as well as flavors;
also mouth-fresheners and powders, and those things which are to be rubbed.

The Blessed One, who is compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees, caused [the gifts] to be given out of mercy. Furthermore, the Blessed One protected them all until the end of the Cāturmāsya period.
Lomaśa also gave to them mantras and garlands of tulasī.
Having attained the divine Vaiṣṇava splendor in the presence of the Lord of Śrī,
they were beheld by Kṛṣṇa and became divine, endowed with divine qualities.
Having realized this very Bālakṛṣṇa to be the Great Lord (Mahāprabhu) through direct perception—
They attained that Supreme Lord, the abode of the bliss of the Supreme Brahman.
Lomaśa instructed them daily for the sake of liberation, saying:
"Listen to this beautiful and supreme means for attaining the highest good."
He whose body is everything and who exists within all— by praising him, one obtains eternal protection from saṃsāra.
Today I shall recite that hymn of praise dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord whose weapon is the discus, be present to my east.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the mace, be with me always in the south.
May Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, be with me forever in the west.
May Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, holding a sword, be ever with me in the north;
may Hṛṣīkeśa be in the corners, and Janārdana in the center of each;
may the Lord Narahari be in the sky, and Varāha in the earth.
The Sudarśana [discus], with its razor-sharp edge exceedingly keen on all sides, strikes down the hungry ghosts (pretas), spirits (bhūtas), and night-roaming rākṣasas;
the mace, with its thousand edges pointing upward, slays the wolves and piśācas. (2.61.39–40)
May Hari’s Śārṅga bow strike down the Kuṣmāṇḍas and others crosswise;
may it destroy the Yakṣas, Daityas, Jṛmbhakas, cruel birds, and Vināyakas.
May Viṣṇu’s conch shell, by its roar, slay the wicked serpents.
May the lotus of Viṣṇu, through its fragrance, render my enemies gentle— those lions, tigers, śarabhas, venomous serpents,
and beasts that seize the fluctuations of the mind, snatch away memory, and rob one of strength and vigor.
May the chanting of Hari’s names also pacify those [obstacles] that carry away prosperity and enjoyments, those that steal auspicious marks, and those that take away wife, sons, wealth, and home;
and through the glorification of Hari, may my sensory faculties attain well-being.
May there be well-being of the intellect, well-being of the mind, and well-being of the body, which brings happiness.
May Hari be at my back, in front, on both sides, and in the corners;
may He be in my crest-lock and in my nails; may Hari be for the welfare of my skin.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
O Rādhikā, in this way the sage Śrī Lomaśa first gave this protective hymn to all of them, and then he spoke this illustrative example.
In the past, there was a king named Krūrasimha in the city of Vaṭāsīnapura.
He was a betrayer of gods, brahmins, and virtuous women; a slanderer, the lowest of kṣatriyas, an oppressor of others, mean-spirited, and by nature merciless. (48–49)
Deprived of the gift of Dharma and shunning the service of the virtuous,
he was indeed born at the end of his life as a fierce night-stalker in the forest.
Whatever animal, bird, or human he encountered in the wilderness, [he would devour].
"He performs acts of cruelty, thinking, 'This one is to be eaten, this one is to be killed.
Devoid of compassion, whatever animal or other creature he sees, he seizes it quickly and devours it as soon as it comes within the range of his arms. (51–52)
Thus, after a long period of time had passed, old age came upon that wicked man as he was wandering somewhere on the bank of the Narmadā.
Then, within his sight, there appeared an ascetic, a sage devoted to yoga.
A Brahmin named Jitaśravas, who had conquered his senses, arrived there.
Seeing him, the lord of the Rākṣasas rushed forward quickly to devour him.
The twice-born man quickly repeated the protective mantra over and over again.
Upon hearing this, the Rākṣasa immediately became paralyzed and rendered senseless;
overwhelmed by the hymn of praise, he was unable either to advance or to retreat.
His momentum suddenly shattered, the Rākṣasa stood right there, motionless.
Thus, as the twice-born one was reciting his prayers, the end of the day arrived.
Then, at the conclusion of his recitation, he beheld that night-stalker—miserable, with his strength and vigor destroyed, fleeing in all directions, and stripped of his luster. (57–58)
Filled with compassion, the twice-born brahmin consoled the Daitya again and again,
and asked him the reason for his state as a Rākṣasa as well as for his arrival there. The Rākṣasa [related] his former history and how he came to be born as a Rākṣasa.
He said all this, including that he had come for the purpose of devouring him;
then, despondent and deprived of happiness, he said to the brahmin, "Be gracious!
I have committed many sins and have killed many virtuous beings."
He forcibly enjoyed many women, even widows;
he caused the destruction of many innocent beings;
and he constantly consumed liquor and meat in great quantities.
Therefore, through your grace, I desire liberation from this sin.
For the pacification of that sin, provide me with a means for dharma;
quickly grant me that which causes the destruction of this evil and bestows liberation.
Having heard the words of Niśāṭa, Jitaśravas said to him:
"Protection has been granted to me here, and you too have been purified.
O Rākṣasa, the desire for liberation has been instilled in you; go to Kuṅkumavāpikā."
In Saurāṣṭra, having bathed at the Aśvasarovara of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and gone to the venerable Lomaśa, you must by all means offer prayers;
Lomaśa or another brāhmaṇa will bring about your deliverance.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed through the path of the sky;
the rākṣasa arrived at the field of Kuṅkumavāpī and dwelt in a mango grove.
With a dejected mind, he pondered: "How might my liberation from this place come to be?"
Even though he was oppressed by hunger, he did not devour living beings;
rather, at every tenth interval of time, he consumed a single creature.
Having wandered through the tiger-infested forest, he returned once more to the mango grove.
Once, while wandering in the forest during a great rainstorm, he became hungry.
He saw a religious student (brahmacārin) who had come for the sake of gathering fruit;
the Rākṣasa then attacked him, whose name was Brahmaprakāśa.
Then the religious student addressed that rākṣasa with conciliatory words:
"Tell me, forest-dweller, what is the reason for this assault upon me?
The rākṣasa replied: 'My meal occurs at the eighth watch.'"
"You have arrived here in this forest before me, who am hungry and harsh; yet you are a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). He said to him: "Listen to my auspicious words:
O night-stalker, I am going to give fruit to my teacher!"
"Having given that to you, I shall return, provided indeed that I am fit to be your food.
Therefore, wait for me right here for just a moment, until I have informed my teacher and return; then eat me. (75–76)
Then the night-stalker said: "Go, but listen to what is for your benefit.
Tell this to your teacher so that he may effect my liberation;
I shall certainly not devour you, for which purpose I have come. (77)

"O Brahmin, grant me liberation in such a way that it is not contrary to my guru, does not obstruct dharma, and does not cause you to lose your vows; for I am by nature [low-born], and especially so due to the defect of my birth. (78–79)
With a mind full of sensual objects, sinful karma was constantly accumulated;
from my childhood, my mind was not even slightly inclined toward dharma.
Indeed, unrighteous deeds were especially committed.
"Having reached the bank of the Narmadā, I was sent here by a Brahmin;
I have come here with sincere devotion for the sake of washing away my sins.
Since you have met me here, O sinless one, liberate me from my sin."

Thus addressed, the brahmin said: "Through the power of my guru, I shall certainly effect your liberation by burning away all your sins, provided that the fire has been served by you following the service of your guru.
Or let there be liberation for the Rākṣasa through the vows well-performed.
(84) If I pay homage with reverence to my father, the god, and my teacher, and to Hari, my mother, let there be liberation for the Rākṣasa. (85)
"If I do not cause my guru Hari to be treated with disrespect by thought, word, or deed, let there be liberation for the Rākṣasa.
O Rākṣasa, chant the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person and Lord of Gods."
I bow down to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, the Lord of the World; may he grant me liberation. [I bow to] the Teacher of the moving and unmoving, the Protector, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
I bow to Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who bears the conch, the discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the banner; may he grant me liberation. [I bow] to Dāmodara, the lotus-eyed one, who reclines upon Śeṣa.

I bow to Govinda, and may he grant me liberation. (2.61.90) I bow to Nārāyaṇa, to Nara, to the upholder of the earth, who dwells in the abode; I bow to the Lord of Light, and may he grant me liberation. (91)
I bow to the Lord of Śrī, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the glorious husband of Pārvatī, the beloved of Ramā; may He grant me liberation.
The ascetics meditate upon Him, and Rādhā delights the Lord.
I have gone for refuge to Him whose form is the embodiment of all objects of perception;
(93) to the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of countless gopīs, the son of Śrī Kambharā, the support of all and the omnipresent; to Him I have gone for refuge. (94)
I have gone for refuge to that Supreme Self, who abides within the self, who possesses the power to wash away karma, and who is the shatterer of rebirth;
[to Him who is] the Lord of gods, sages, ancestors, humans, and reptiles.
He creates, sustains, and protects trees, water-born beings, and those born from sweat.
To him who bears the form of Brahmā, the source of the universe, the protector, the infallible one,
and the youthful Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, I have gone for refuge.

I have gone for refuge to Him, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Ender, the inner controller of all, the Supreme Lord, than whom nothing else is higher. Whatever auspicious or inauspicious deeds were performed by me in previous births—
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dispel them.
Whatever sin has been committed by me at night, in the morning, at midday and afternoon, or during the two twilights—may all of that perish. (2.61.99–100)
Whatever painful karma has been committed by me while standing, walking, or indeed lying down— whether through body, mind, or speech,
whether out of ignorance or knowledge, or with a mind disturbed by intoxication— [may it all be purified].
May that [sin] quickly go to destruction through the chanting of Bālakṛṣṇa’s names—
[the sin] arising from longing for another's wife or another's wealth, from malice,
from reviling great-souled ones, and from causing suffering to others. (102–103)
May that evil committed through words that pierce the vitals be destroyed;
and whatever [evil] was done in food, drink, solid food, what is to be sucked, or what is to be licked;
and whatever sin of mine was committed in childhood, in youth, or in my prime.
Whatever [karma] was committed during the transition of age or in another birth—
may that immediately go to dissolution through the chanting and glorification of the name "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," who is without beginning, by the power of Him who bestows liberation.
Salutations to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, to Hari;
salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharā-Śrī.
Salutations again and again to the child of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
O gentle one, I have related to you this divine hymn, which destroys all sins, bestows heaven, and grants liberation— exactly as it was spoken by my preceptor. O Rākṣasa, worship Bālakṛṣṇa with this!
Every day, by remembering Lomaśa as well as your guru, the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama,
and by praising Him with this hymn and establishing firm devotion, you shall then be liberated from sin.
Hari, who is subservient to his devotees and the destroyer of all sins, was thus praised with devotion.
Upon hearing this, the Rākṣasa said: "Lead me to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
show me my guru, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation."
Thus addressed, the religious student gave that protective hymn to the cruel lion-demon; by means of it, he became freed from sin.
Then, having been born [renewed], he departed together with that very religious student.
Having come here to my hermitage named Lomaśa, that Rākṣasa was instantly freed from sin; for, having gone into the presence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he obtained His vision and drank the nectar of His feet.

Having visited all the sacred fords, he indeed became possessed of a divine body; mounting a celestial vehicle, he went to the abode of the Imperishable. You, Āryāyana and the others, were likewise protected from the dissolution by the waters.

Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (1.17) Take refuge in this Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, the Savior, by whom those rescued from death shall be delivered from the cycle of worldly existence. (1.18)
Having spoken thus and remembering Śrī Hari, Lomaśa remained silent;
Āryā, Ayanodā, and the others attained supreme peace. Through the recitation and hearing of this hymn, there is worldly enjoyment, protection, and the destruction of calamities.
"O Rādhikā, there shall be liberation and peace; everything will be attained, of this there is no doubt.

(2.61.120) Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*: Having taken two hundred men who were submerged in the water onto His boat, the Lord crossed the Stambha mound by way of the Mahī river. He circumambulated Somanātha, Svarṇapura, Camatkārapura, and other sites, and by means of His boat-like celestial vehicle (*vimāna*), He brought them to the holy field of Kuṅkumavāpī. [This was achieved] through the protective hymn (*rakṣā-stotra*) instructed by Lomaśa, and through the demon Krūra Siṃha’s attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa via a brāhmaṇa.
The sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation," ends.
Chapter 62 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2: The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga.
Chapter 62.
[Author: Chapter 63.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, those two hundred men and women indeed [saw] Śrī Lomaśa.
Having bowed and worshipped with devotion ten million times ten billion times one hundred trillion maidens,
and having fully honored the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, they went to their auspicious dwelling;
there they attended upon the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
"O Lord of ten million maidens, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord of the universe, O Lord of all, protect forever those who have no other support and who have taken refuge in You.
Having spoken thus, they joyfully performed their worship together.
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Light!
O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, O Lord of Mañju, O Lord of Śrī Pārvatī!
Thus did those protected by the boat perform the rhythmic clapping of their palms.
There, filled with devotion for Kṛṣṇa, they observed the Cāturmāsya vow.
Then came the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
it was the festival marking the manifestation of their chosen deity, which occurs every eighth year.
The gods, the lords, and the sages made heaven exceedingly beautiful.
Beholding that, they were filled with joy and performed worship to Hari.
O Rādhikā, a supreme wonder then occurred; listen, for I shall tell it to you.
The Blessed One, the King of Kings, having been worshipped early in the morning on the eighth year of his own birth, gave many gifts;
he fed the Brahmins, the holy men, the virtuous women, and the girls.

Children, maidens, the wretched, and the helpless; likewise young boys, the lame, the one-eyed, the deaf, the maimed, the blind, and the dull-witted; as well as those who are insane and those afflicted with leprosy—all of whom had come from various regions to the sacred ford (tīrtha). (2.62.10–11)
Seeing the diseased embodied beings who were crippled and deformed, the compassionate Lord himself spoke to those with lameness and other infirmities after their meal at midday:
"Let those with deformed bodies and those who are diseased and suffering come here."
"May even those who are maimed in their limbs and deficient in their senses come here!
On the occasion of my birth festival, I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, bestow upon you today an unprecedented gift that grants happiness."
Having spoken thus, she placed a golden vat of sugar by her side and sat upon an elephant-throne to distribute the sugar. Then,
groups of people with lameness arrived, and she gave them fine sugar.
In the portion of those who were lame, Hari-Kṛṣṇa touched them with his left hand.
Their lameness quickly vanished, and they became possessed of perfect feet.
Then, having given sugar to those who were one-eyed, he departed from them.
He touched his eyes with his left hand for the sake of liberation from blindness;
at that moment, one-eyedness, blindness, and all defects of vision were instantly destroyed,
and his eyes were indeed restored, filled with a full abundance of rays.
Then those who were deaf arrived; having given them sugar-candies, he touched their ears with his hand and called them by their names. Their deafness vanished, and they regained the power of hearing.
Then, when those who had been cut were brought together, Nārāyaṇa gave them sugar and, with his hand,
touched their wounds on the forearms and fingers; in an instant, he removed their state of being mangled.
Just as they had naturally been born with hands, so too did they become clear-minded.
Then those who were dull-witted and senseless arrived in their presence;
sugar was given to them, and indeed their bodies were touched by hand.
Likewise, by touching their heads, dullness, mental confusion,
diseases such as wind-disorders (vāta), and even insomnia were destroyed in an instant.
Then the maidens arrived, and those afflicted with leprosy also arrived.
Having given them sugar and likewise the nectar of his feet,
and having sprinkled their limbs with water, he destroyed their diseases and leprosy.
Then there arrived those whose wings were struck down and whose bodies were broken.
Having given them sugar and touched them with his hand,
he mercifully destroyed their disease of the blow at that very moment;
and by means of yoga, he quickly healed the fractured parts.
Then people suffering from oozing leprosy came to the Supreme Lord.
Hari, having given them a sprinkling of sugar-water, personally applied it to the areas affected by the oozing leprosy. || 28-29 ||
All their impotence vanished, and in an instant their whiteness turned to brilliance.
They became free from disease, radiant, and endowed with merit.
Then the eunuchs said: "Our eunuchhood was caused by great sin."
O ocean of mercy, you, the illustrious Puruṣottama, have been born for us.

You, who are capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise, proceed [in this world]. If we, having attained union with the Blessed One, were not to possess the seed [of our former nature], [then this would not be so]. (3.1–3.2)
"O Blessed One, what benefit would there be for you in seeing him?
Having heard this from them, Śrī Hari himself gave them sugar-candy and then issued the command to bathe at Aśvapaṭṭasara."
All the eunuchs went quickly; they bathed and then departed.
Those men, who had appeared like men in their virility, were yet fit for women; though endowed with strength, they possessed male characteristics and became full of seed at that time. (34–35)

Women who resembled men became women in their female state, yet remained endowed with the qualities suitable for men; and those women who possessed the characteristics of men became full of the abundance of *rajas*.
Thus, indeed, by his grace, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [acted] through his own powers.
He created eunuchs from males and women from the same elements.
Having witnessed this marvel, they were struck with supreme wonder;
the sacred bathing place where they bathed is called Ṣaṇḍoddhāra.
Then all the women and men offered hymns of praise to Hari,
their hearts full of love and their mental dispositions steady.
"Salutations to You, the Supreme Abode, who shines as the Self beyond the supreme."

Salutations to the one who instructs the countless virtuous women, the chaste wives, and the holy men. Salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable, who instructs those liberated in the Imperishable. Salutations to the dweller of Goloka, who instructs the cowherds and cowherd-maidens.
Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the cows, the husband of Śrī Rādhā;
obeisance to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha, the husband of Śrī Ramā.
Obeisance to the Lord of many Vaikuṇṭhas, the husband of Lakṣmī-Śrī.
Salutations to the Lord who possesses the qualities of a beautiful swan with glorious radiance;
salutations to the Lord of Vṛndā, Tulasī, Kamalā, and Pārvatī. Homage be to You, O Lord of the World; salutations be to You, O Vāsudeva. 43–44.
O Śrīnivāsa, salutations to you; O Viśvaksena, salutations to you.
O Garuḍadhvaja, Lord of the Gopīs, O Viṣṇu, O Vaikuṇṭha, salutations to you.
O Puruṣottama, Lord of Gods, Sovereign of All, salutations to you.
O you who are without beginning, middle, or end, salutations to you, O beloved of the lotus-born.
Salutations to you, the womb of creation; salutations be to you, O Śatruñjaya.
Salutations to the one of golden form; salutations to you, the destroyer of Time.
O you of the great navel, O you of the great root, O abode of the root, homage be to you!
O abode of dharma, O abode of the heart, O you of pure hearing, O you of vast renown!
O supervisor of dharma, O supervisor of creatures, O supervisor of time, homage be to you!
O wielder of the mace, O wielder of the lotus, O you who are questioned by the Vedas, salutations be unto you!
O support of Śrī, O wearer of the forest garland, O Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto you!
O Puruṣṭuta, O Great Kalpa, O Soul of All, O All-pervading Lord, salutations be unto you!
O Supreme Lord, whose nature is the twelvefold Time, whose nature is the Sāman,
you who are the essence of the sky and the sun, the essence of the moon, most subtle of all— salutations be to you!
O Nīlakeśa, Guḍākeśa, Mahākeśa— salutations be to you!
O Mañjukeśa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Sarvakeśa, homage be to you!
O Śveta, Rakta, Pīta, Citra, Kṛṣṇa, homage be to you!
O Kuśeśaya, O Giver of Joy, O Govinda, O Haṃsa, homage to you!
Salutations to you, the eye of Dharma; salutations to you, the thousand-limbed one.
Salutations to you, whose form is the universe; salutations to you, whose form is the abode of light.
Salutations to you, the banyan tree, the holy fig tree, the one of great branches.
Homage be to you, whose branches, leaves, sprouts, creepers, and shoots [are the Vedas].
You are indeed Viṣṇu composed of the Vedas, the all-pervading Lord who transcends the deities of the sacred fords;
you are the very embodiment of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—homage to you, the enjoyer of the sacrificial portions.
O Supreme Brahman, salutations be unto You; O Word-Brahman, salutations be unto You.
You are knowledge, You are the object of knowledge; O Worthy of Veneration, salutations be unto You.
You are the very essence of speech in women, and You are the embodiment of compassion toward men.
"Out of affection for our son, we have come to you for refuge.
O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, deliver us from this cycle of existence!
Having spoken thus, they fell silent; then the sage Āryāyaṇa—
With supreme affection, he praised the beloved of Śrī, the Supreme Person:
"I bow to the Fish and I bow to the Tortoise; I bow to the Horse-headed One (Hayaśīrṣaka);
I bow to Trivikrama and I bow to the Lord Mādhava."
I bow to Īśāna and Hṛṣīkeśa, and I bow to Kumārila.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa; I bow to the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
I bow to Narasiṃha, and I bow to the protector of desires.
I pay homage to Śrī Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes resemble white lotuses;

I pay homage to Him who bears the banner, the discus, the lotus, the bow, the fish, and the beautiful trident. I bow to the Lord of the cows, the son of Kambharā, the omnipresent one, the joy of the cowherds.
I bow to the wielder of the mace who dwells at Aśvapaṭṭasara;
I bow to the Lord Ardhanārīśvara, who bestows happiness upon the multitude of women.
I bow to him who holds a lotus in his hand and whose thighs are like lotuses.
I pay homage to him whose rays are like lotuses and who possesses a broad expanse of upward-pointing lines;
I pay homage to the one garlanded with forest flowers, whose hips resemble the goddess Lakṣmī.
I pay homage to the Lord of the Earth; I pay homage to the Consort of Śrī.
Salutations to you, the protector of the helpless, who abide upon the boat and in the celestial chariot.
Salutations to you, who dwell in the heart, who sport among your devotees, and who stand as the guardian of the wretched.
I pay homage to the Brahman of great splendor, the one who has mastered the three Nāciketa fires.
I bow to him who destroys all diseases and satisfies the sense of smell;
I bow to Rukmakavaca; I bow to Puruṣottama.
I bow to Vanaspati, Madhupati, and Sudhāpati.
I bow to Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus, whose glory is his wealth.
I bow to the Supreme Lord, who dwells within all beings, who is peaceful, the embodiment of Dharma, the giver of liberation; O Protector, I go for refuge to You, the worthy refuge.
Thus the illustrious sage Āryāyaṇa praised the Lord of Gods.
Then, in the evening, the gods and men performed the ritual dismissal of the worship.
There on the bank, the sage Āryāyaṇa spoke thus.
The men and women who had disembarked from the boat intensely entreated Hari to look upon their own lands.
At the end of the month of Kārttika, Hari there remembered his supreme vehicle.
A divine celestial chariot, endowed with divine qualities, arrived there;
having seated them all within it, the Blessed One reached Dhīravīra Lake through the sky in an instant with great speed.
Wherever their birthplace was— on the Aravalli hills or elsewhere—
they were all then brought there in comfort; having returned to their respective homes, they all related the news of their family to one another.
Filled with wonder, they took refuge in Hari, the beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Then the Blessed Lord, together with his chariot, quickly vanished;
he returned to his own auspicious abode at Aśvapaṭṭasara.
And the royal sage named Udaya, devoted solely to the name of Hari, performed a sacrifice of japa at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
he repeatedly addressed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa from within his heart. (2.62.80)
"O ocean of compassion, grant me liberation; may I attain the eternal state.
"So be it," Hari replied. Then the king entered into meditation and, with the movement of his vital breaths and channels stilled, gradually relinquished his life-breaths.
Then, liberated, he became endowed with a celestial, radiant chariot;
he went to the glorious, supreme abode characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Thus did the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa uplift them.
Those well-bodied beings who were born as the lame, the deaf, the blind, and so forth,
each went to their own country and home and lived there in happiness.
Seeing them, the subjects and the onlookers were struck with wonder.
Recognizing his supreme majesty, they took refuge in the Supreme Person.
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Supreme Brahman, Lord of Śrī! Thus they worshipped him, saying: 'O Master, protect us always. (85–86)
Śrī Hari showed Himself to them as they were far away in a dream;
they beheld His beautiful, youthful form, exceedingly radiant.
Having remained absorbed in that for a mere moment, they then [awoke].
Awakened, they remembered Nārāyaṇa, the cowherd boy;
and for the sake of seeing him, thousands of men and women arrived from all sides at the temple of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (88–89)
They beheld him with a form exactly as it had been seen in their dream;
they worshipped the Lord of Śrī exceedingly, with their whole being.
Having performed various rites at the sacred ford and having received the mantra from Lomaśa, [they proceeded].
The Vaiṣṇavas, beloved of the Lord, returned to their own regions. To those who come there to the lake during the Cāturmāsya vow in order to bathe, Hari indeed grants his own direct vision.
Having made the elders, whose lifespans are complete, divine and established in celestial chariots,
He sends them to His own abode, the imperishable and supreme state.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, are they protected by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
And people who had been submerged in water were rescued and restored to their own lands;
eunuchs were made free from disease, with nourished bodies and restored virility.
Thus, his incomparable majesty was proclaimed throughout the surface of the earth.
Through chanting, remembering, praising this marvel,
and even hearing it, all sufferings truly come to an end;
diseases perish quickly, and even great calamities are destroyed.
Times of calamity always perish by listening to the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
O Rādhā, protection is obtained in every way by reciting hymns of praise.
O Rādhā, by performing pilgrimage, people attain their heart's desire.
Everything undesirable dissolves away and good fortune increases;
one shall possess wealth, grain, progeny, sons, attendants, and so forth.
Having attained worldly enjoyment here and heaven thereafter, one is glorified in liberation.
"For one who is devoted to the Supreme Brahman, no duty remains.

(2.62.10) Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise Offered by Those Rescued from the Waters, the Restoration of Health to the Sick and the Maimed on the Eighth-Year Festival, the Hymns Sung by Them, the Hymn of Āryāyaṇaka, the Return of the Water-Rescuers to Their Own Country, and the Liberation of King Udayana," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 62: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 63 [[Author:
→ Chapter 64
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the deeds of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa—those which protect His devotees and others that occurred in His eighth year, including the one born from the ocean. 1.
On the bank of the Revā, however, there was a beautiful city named Candrodaya,
inhabited by all devotees and supported by subjects devoted to righteousness.
There lived a great merchant, prosperous with wealth and grain.
Known by the name Vasumedha, he was a devotee of Viṣṇu and pure in mind. (3) Constantly intent on serving the virtuous, he performed the worship of the deities:
Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Satī, Śambhu, Śrī, and Hari. (4)
Having bathed in the morning, he reverently worships with ritual offerings;
he always eats after sharing [the food] and constantly gives gifts.
He performs service to cows, service to the virtuous, and the satisfaction of the ancestors.
His business dealing in merchandise increased with great profit.
(6) He had five sons who were skillful, and his wife was devoted to dharma;
she was named Suśīlā and always observed the vow of eating only once a day. (7)
Having worshipped the Śālagrāma stone with offerings mixed with *tulasī* leaves,
he partakes of the food that has been touched by the water used for washing the Lord’s feet— the food born of divine grace (prasāda).
All his sons are indeed Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to wearing garlands, meditation, and the chanting of mantras.

Desirous of liberation and having properly heard the discourses of the scriptures, [they remained there]. (9) Now, there was a great seer named Śatānanda; he was the son of Uddālaka and had established his hermitage in the forest. (2.63.10)
Śatānanda would always arrive at will in the evening, not far from the vicinity of Candrodaya, at the hermitage of the brahmin;
and in the morning, he would recite the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
Having delivered the discourse and received alms, he would go to his own hermitage.
People from the village would always come there to listen to the discourse.
That which was heard there was [later] heard in Saurāṣṭra at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, within the Śrī-gṛha of Kambharā, Hari—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Gopālā—
is indeed present as the Lord Puruṣottama in the form of a child. (14)
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, fish-banner, and trident,
and having hands marked with signs such as the bow, svastika, and thunderbolt—
the imperishable Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign of All— is present before our very eyes. (15–16)
The Supreme Lord, the life-master of hundreds of millions of crores of cowherdesses,
having heard this wonderful narrative, and having heard of Śrī Somatīrtha,
the meritorious Svarṇapurī, and likewise Camatkārapura—
Having made a firm resolve to visit the sacred fords, accompanied by his family and followers,
and having gathered provisions such as food, water, fruits, roots, and grains, he— possessing an abundance of wealth and grain— embarked upon a spacious ship. (18–19)
Accompanied by a company of thirty men and following the waters of the Narmadā,
he set out, standing upon a boat propelled by the sailors;
for the sake of his journey, he traveled by boat to the confluence of the Revā and the ocean.
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Supreme Brahman, Supreme Lord!
(2.1)" Thus he constantly proclaimed, and along with his caravan, he recited the rosary.
Having rested on the banks of the Revā during the month of Māgha, he bathed there together with his followers. (2.2)
He gave gifts of clothing, food, gold, and silver with devotion.
Then, having boarded a boat, he reached the unfathomable ocean.
Having bathed at the confluence of the river and crossed the unfathomable [ocean], he arrived.
At the confluence of the Śatruñjaya and the ocean, he bathed there according to the prescribed rites.
From there, he went to the Gopanātha Tīrtha, which is frequented by both Hari and Hara.
Then he proceeded to Mūla, the city of gold, where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, he went to Somanātha;
then, having bathed at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā and performed the rites for the sacred sites,
he visited the Makarālaya-tīrtha and the confluence of the Bhadrā and the ocean.
Having performed the rites for the sacred ford, he went to Kṛṣṇasvarṇapurī.
Then, having seen the island at the shore, he went to Nārāyaṇasaras; and returning by boat, he went to Camatkārapura.
Then, turning back by an unexcavated path toward the ocean and abandoning Svarṇapurī, he proceeded by way of the water.
At that time, as he was at Somanātha, a maritime obstacle arose.
A great, tumultuous wind blew with extreme velocity, causing great agitation;
it was as beautiful as the ocean yet like frost.
In the midst of it, the boat was dragged about by the adverse wind.
Then, by the waves, surges, and billows as high as palm trees,
many boats were submerged, shattered, and destroyed, and men perished.
Even the boat of Vasumedha rose up and moved in a zigzag course.
Falling on both sides and filled with water by the surging waves, the boat became overwhelmed;
even the sailors were rendered powerless to protect it.
Vasumedha, the eminent merchant, his wife, his sons, and the others [were all in peril]. (33–34)
They remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
and they lamented in many ways for the sake of Him for whose purpose they had come.
Having heard about that Bālakṛṣṇa through the words of Śatānanda—
"O weak women, if we do not look [back], we shall die here in this ocean water.
Water fills the boat, and it overflows even more than it can hold; it is tossed by the wind and repeatedly struck by the waves. (36-37)
Struck by the water, she forms whirlpools on her sides;
and these other merchant ships have gone to their destruction.
Our ship, too, in their presence, desires to settle at the bottom.
Let them remember that Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Controller (39).
May He, for whose sake we have come, protect us from the affliction of the heart;
may that Blessed One, who pervades the boat, make the boat steady. (2.63.40)
May Kṛṣṇa, who stood amidst the stormy wind, quell the wind in an instant;
and may Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, standing upon the water, grant stability to the waters.
Or rather, may He reveal His own self here to those who have met with death.
In every way, O Lord, we have indeed come to you for refuge.
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, son of Gopāla; O Śrī Kumāra of Kambharā, O Lord of the gopīs, O Master, protect us!
Thus, all those devoted to Kṛṣṇa, their enthusiasm destroyed and deeply distressed,
became hopeless regarding their lives as the boat was tossed by the force of the wind.
The water filled it to the brim, and it was bent by the lashing of the wind.
As soon as she had quickly gone to the bottom of the water, the Blessed Lord himself immediately arrived there in the form of a tortoise;
he placed the boat upon his back and carried it across the water.
In his second form, the Lord became the helmsman of the ship;
in ten other forms, he became the one who drew [the vessel] out of the water.
And in twenty other forms, he [rescued] those men who were submerged in the water.
Lifting them up one by one, he cast everyone into the middle of the boat.
Whatever goods were on the boat and whatever had fallen into the water,
he also lifted those with his hands and threw them back onto the boat.
By his grace, the storm was halted and the water became still;
the boat also became steady, and the devotees were protected by the Blessed One. As for those other devotees who were on another boat during the storm...
He effortlessly rescued them as they were submerged in the water.
Having thus provided protection for his devotees and assuming a single form,
the youthful Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa vanished from that place.
Slowly propelled by the sailors, that ship moved forward;
it reached Śrīsomanātha and there it was moored for a fortnight.
Having stationed the boatmen there, Vasumedha remained with his caravan.
Hurrying with his wagons, he went toward the eastern Sarasvatī.
Having bathed there and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he thereafter proceeded to the auspicious Arkatīrtha and the site of the Balamakha sacrifice.
Then, after bathing at Svarṇarekhā, he went to Vāmana’s Stalī, as well as Vastrāpatha and Rāṣṭrasarovara; afterwards,
he went to Vaṭasthalī and then to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Beholding that sacred field from afar, he prostrated himself upon the ground like a staff.
Having gone to Aśvapaṭṭasara, bathed, and performed the rites prescribed for a holy ford,
he circumambulated it and paid homage to all the sacred sites.
She went to the great palace to behold Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord;
she beheld Hari in the golden temple, seated upon a divine throne,
possessing the luster of the midday sun, with a moon-like face and a cooling radiance.
With limbs proportionate to his form, clad in pure fire-colored garments,
wearing a golden crown and garlands of gems, diamonds, and pearls,
he was praised and worshiped by gods, humans, and celestial musicians. (2.63.60–61)
Having bowed down, Vasu, together with his family, praised [Him] with love;
shedding tears from his eyes and overwhelmed, he spoke with a faltering voice:
"By those rich in merit, who have acquired the fruits of virtue over many births, is this attained. (62)
That Supreme Lord has been attained by me; protect me, O Parameśvara!
(63) He who is attained by yogis through the efforts of yoga over many years—that Lord has been found by me today; protect me, O Parameśvara! (64)
He who is attained by devotees through devotion and the surrender of all one's possessions—this very Lord Śrīkānta has been reached by me; O Hari, protect me!
Though He is difficult to achieve even for those performing austerities over a long period of time, that very Hari [has been reached].
"Today I have attained the Lord of Life; protect me, O Puruṣottama!
Having been rescued by you from drowning in the ocean along with my family, O Lord of Gods, rescue me once again from the ocean of saṃsāra."
Without you there is no life; though the vital breaths remain, they are not eternal.
Without you, all prosperity indeed becomes calamity.
You shine within the heart, you in the eyes, and you within the self.
"You shine in the family, on the boat, in the water, and on the land.
Today my birth has become fruitful; my pilgrimage has become fruitful; my family has become fruitful, and everything has attained success. (2.63.70)
All those sacred sites for the sake of which you abandoned your home and departed with a desire for pilgrimage are contained within this very foot of yours.
Whatever was to be attained has been attained here; no duty remains to be performed.
"Protect me, O Lord, ocean of compassion; I have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, he worshipped him and fell repeatedly at his feet, offering jewels, ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as fragrant sandalwood and other perfumes.
His entire family honored that Hari;
standing before Śrī Hari, he then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
By the command of Śrī Hari, he partook of sweet food, fruits, water, and so forth.
And then he placed it first into the vessel before Hari.
The Blessed One ate that nectar-like remnant with affection as a divine favor, and out of great grace, he gave it to Vasumedha, who was accompanied by his family.
Vasumedha and all the others then ate their food, drank water,
and dwelt in the palace of rest provided by the Blessed One.
In this manner, they passed ten days.
On the eleventh day, in the morning, Vasumedha and his beloved wife Suśīlā likewise beheld Nārāyaṇa in the very early hours,
who had arrived in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to lead him to his own abode. (78–79)
Then, at that time, Dharmamedha and Suśīlā quickly awakened their sons and others, and related to them in its entirety that excellent dream-event which indicated the attainment of liberation.
The sons attained supreme joy; having bathed and worshipped the deities, they all then quickly went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa. Hari granted them his own vision and spoke to them.
"Receive from Lomaśa the mantra, the initiation, and likewise the garland;
then this very evening, the liberation of your parents will be attained.
Having been addressed thus, they went quickly to the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
They received the Vaiṣṇava mantra and a garland of tulasī:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Having taken up the mantra, they partook of food and gave various kinds of gifts.
They returned to their own abodes and took refuge in the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa.
At that time, during the afternoon, the parents became absorbed in meditation.
Their sons requested forgiveness and performed service as was appropriate.
In another moment, a celestial chariot arrived with a divine retinue.
Having transformed Vasumedha and Suśīlā into divine bodies, they were led to the abode of Brahmā; thus, at that time, their sons performed a meritorious deed.
With concentrated minds, his sons performed the funeral rites for him;
thus, those two devotees who had taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa attained the path of liberation.
Then the sons performed the śrāddha ceremony and other duties as was appropriate.

They traveled by way of the cart-road to where the boat was operating. Having boarded the boat, they all went to their own country; and upon reaching the land of Camatkāra, they indeed spoke of Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard this, people took refuge in Hari, the manifest Śrī Puruṣottama. Thus, O Rādhā, I have narrated to you the purifying life-story of Hari,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the listener and the speaker, and always grants protection.
It bestows the fruit of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), grants heaven, bestows prosperity, and is auspicious.

(93) Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of How Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Rescued the Merchant Vasumedha and His Family—who were living in the city of Candrodaya and had gone by boat on the Saurāṣṭra ocean to visit sacred fords via the Narmadā river, only to be submerged in the waters by a storm—and Granted Them Liberation," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Rādhikā said: O Supreme Brahman, ocean of mercy, O Hari, you have described the auspicious holy place called Gopanātha on the shore of the ocean in Saurāṣṭra.
"How and when was it born? How is its name meaningful?
Tell me truly, O Kṛṣṇa, my beloved Supreme Lord.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to this divine narrative within my sphere of knowledge:
in former and earlier kalpas, many Śrī Kṛṣṇas have appeared.
This occurred in the forenoon, at the very dawn of the first year of Brahmā.
On the first day, O Rādhā, I arrived here from Goloka along with you.
Indeed, this cosmic egg was produced by the prayer of Brahmā;
I came there to see the jewel that belongs to me.
And that region of Saurāṣṭra was deposited within this sphere.
Having arrived there, I beheld a divine chariot made of gold,
frequented by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, endowed with cattle, and enchanting.
And upon the expansive surface of the jewel, I descended from the sky.
O Rādhā, the cowherds, the cowherd girls, you, and I dwelt near the water;
we partook of nectar as well as the milk of the cows.
Cows roam there, and cowherds play in that forest;
the gopīs and gopas take delight in this divine place created by me.
There, O Rādhā, I am with you among the trees on all sides.
Accompanied by cows, cowherds, and cowherdesses, I wandered about, leading my life there.
At that time, Sanatkumāra and other sages arrived at that place;
and Śrī Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu, knowing me to be a devotee, also came then.
By the cowherds, by me, and by you as well, those two were highly honored;
they were worshipped, saluted, fed with sweet foods, and served with joy.
In that place where the two gods, Śrī Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, had made their dwelling—
While the two gods, whose natures are Hari and Hara, were being worshipped there by the cowherds,
Brahmā arrived there quickly upon learning of it.
He too was honored by the cowherds and received with hospitality by both me and you.
Then other attendants of Viṣṇu, Hara, and Brahmā, having learned [of this],
arrived with their goddesses and female servants and stood there on level ground.
Then, on that auspicious spot upon the earth, I questioned them.
"Manifestation is desired quickly for the sake of the world's welfare.
(16) Just then, Dharaṇi and Meru arrived there and, while the virtuous were listening, they both entreated me for the sake of sons. (17)
"I shall do so," I said then to those two auspicious mind-born children of Brahmā. They were born as a human couple in Surāṣṭra;
the cowherd was named Merudhara and the cowherd-maiden was Kṣamādevī.
Near Somanātha, the two of them took up their divine residence.
(19) Then the cowherds, the cowherd women, and the cows, having worshipped Hari and Hara, all departed together with the Goddess Kṣamā and Meru. (20)
Residing in the Siṃhāraṇya forest, they remained there filled with joy:
Śambhu, the illustrious Gopanātha, Viṣṇu, and likewise Gopīśvara.
In that place where they were worshipped, they became the very embodiments of their respective forms.
There, O Rādhā, cowherds and cowherd girls constantly come and go.
That sacred ford (tīrtha), consisting of the essence of Hari and Hara, became known as Gopanātha;
it is supremely purifying, O Rādhā, and sanctified by the dust of my feet.
O Rādhikā! Where Meru itself abides and where the Earth is my mother, there I was born as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the mental son [of Brahmā].
You, the other gopīs, and all others were likewise born from my mind.
And they were born right there in the city called Merukoṭi. Wherever the Hiraṇyā river flows, wherever the Prācī Sarasvatī is found,
and wherever Someśa resides— that is the land of Merukoṭika.
And that region became filled with my divine play for me at dawn;
O Rādhā! pervaded by your feet, the door to liberation was opened.
There, the venerable Sanatkumāra was my guru.
The cowherds, the cowherd women, and the cows always dwelt there with me.
At that time, I was the cowherd, and that place was my primordial root. That Dvārakā of mine is known here as Merukoṭi. ||28-29||
In the past, my sacred field extended from Śatruñjaya in the east to the Sarasvatī in the west,
and the Mahābhadrā river in the north;
it contained Mount Kṛtasmara and the great forest of Siṃhāraṇya.
The tiger-infested forest and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake were my lands;
O Rādhā, there was also the supreme land of my pleasure-grove,
where the cowherds, the cowherdesses, and the cows moved through the path of the sky.
They always dwelt there indeed by the power of the god Merudeva.
There, my attendants— the gods and goddesses— having established their dwellings,
all remained in various places at all times out of a desire to serve me.
At that time, Saurāṣṭra was filled with cowherdesses devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, Rādhā, the cowherds, and that very abode of Goloka were present there.
Furthermore, the Gāruḍī Saṃhitā, which discerns my divine majesty, was also there.
There, on the bank of the Madhuvatī, was my grove;
and in the midst of Siṃhāraṇya, there was formerly my divine abode.
It was surrounded by a moat and adorned with a natural inner pond.
Situated in the midst of a garden two yojanas in extent,
there all my wives— excellent queens who were dear to me and traveled through the air in celestial chariots— used to perform their excursions. (37–38)
O Rādhikā, all my attendants— both gods and goddesses— resided at various places in Saurāṣṭra by my command;
likewise the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, and both Aśvins.

The eight Vasus, the nine treasures, and likewise the eight supernatural powers; the seven sages, the five arrows, the Manus, and the deities of the lunar days; the digits, the principles, the circle of constellations, and millions of qualities. (2.64.40–41)
The Maruts, the circle of Yoginīs, the Kalās, the Nāḍīs, and the Dāsikās;
the Vālakhilyas born of the primordial creation—all have taken refuge in me.
Virajā, Kamalā, Gaṅgā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī.
Durgā, Rādhā, Padminī, Pārvatī, Mañjulā, Prabhā, Saguṇā,
Śāradā, Haṃsā, Suśīlā, Subhagā, Śrī,
and others like them, having come from my Goloka to my abode, [dwell there]. ||43-44||
Likewise, the rivers, sacred fords, and divine lands made their abode there;
as did the wish-fulfilling trees, the wish-fulfilling creepers, and the wish-fulfilling pillars, grasses, and so forth;
along with the wish-fulfilling vehicles, the wish-fulfilling jewels, and the wish-fulfilling garlands.
And there are wish-fulfilling vessels and wish-fulfilling utensils;
even wish-fulfilling sandals, wish-fulfilling pills, wish-fulfilling necklaces, and divine wish-fulfilling bracelets—these indeed dwell there in embodied form. (46–47)
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā! I have reminded you of my previous births in Gurjara, Maru, Kaccha, the south, and likewise the north;
for my births in the east as well are truly infinite.
In some divine realm, in some [state] pertaining to the sages, and in some human lineage—
whether born as a twice-born brahmin or in another family— I have been born out of a desire for my duty;
yet you never abandon me, remaining ever present within my heart.
O Rādhikā! Wherever I may be, I am always with you alone—in Goloka, in the cow-pastures, among the gopīs, and even among the gopas;
O Rādhā, I never leave you at any time.
Just as I am the Self, so too are you; you are considered my supreme power (śakti).
Those who thus worship me, the Supreme Lord together with my power, go to my abode, Goloka, and dwell by my side. ||52-53||
Thus, O Rādhā, have my birth and previous lives been told;
by remembering or even hearing this, enjoyment and liberation are produced.
Those who will restore what is decayed or cause it to be restored at my sacred site—
"They shall dwell by my side in My world; of this there is no doubt.

(55) Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of All Primary Sacred Fields and Pilgrimage Sites of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Saurāṣṭra," within the section on the Greatness of Gopanātha, in the second part, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 64: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)*
Chapter 65 [Author:
Chapter 66 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Moreover, O Rādhā, listen to the Vedic injunction regarding Kṛṣṇa, the purifier of all purifiers, who followed the path of the world; he who,
as the author of the Vedas himself, indeed instructed Brahmā in ancient times.
Having relied upon this world and protected his own duty,
he— being of primordial nature like the protector of the Veda— receives the Vedic consecration (brahmasaṃskāra),
by which the state of being twice-born was fashioned at the beginning of creation for the sake of eternal welfare. (2–3)
But he, having grasped the Sūtra, becomes a twice-born one even if he was not twice-born;
by his touch, women, men, trees,
and creepers, as well as animals, ghosts, piśācas, and others, become pure and behold the Self.
Through union with whom even those such as the Kāmas always attain divinity;
having attained whose yoga, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, or those born of Mleccha wombs become divine in an instant— he has become this very Brahmagraha.
O Rādhikā, Lomaśa said to the father and mother of Hari:
"This Yajñapāvana is now fit for the sacred thread ceremony;
the *brahmasūtra* should be given to him, the Supreme Soul who provides the thread."
Then, having heard these auspicious words from the mouth of Lomaśa,
the parents were delighted and bowed to the sage who was worthy of their devotion. Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa also offered him divine seats in the form of elephants.
He offered the madhuparka, pearl necklaces, sweet food, and water;
he also presented betel, fruit, and auspicious garments.
He said to Lomaśa, "O Lord, make this a moment of auspicious celebration."

This month of Vaiśākha is now approaching; if it pleases you, a festival should be celebrated there, for I consider it entirely appropriate. Please point out a day that is auspicious and suitable for the sacred thread ceremony (yajñopavīta).
Then Lomaśa spoke to the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa:
"The third lunar day is inexhaustible, supreme, and bestows imperishability.
Through the purity of the moon and the constellations, all auspiciousness prevails. (13)
And issue an invitation throughout the three worlds to all [beings]: "Grant that it be so!

Accumulate the provisions and divine enjoyments that are exceedingly difficult to obtain—those which are suitable for those dwelling in various worlds, and which are the most excellent of the excellent to be served. (14–15)
Having heard the words of Lomaśa, the illustrious Gopāla Kṛṣṇa dispatched divine auspicious letters everywhere,
along with his attendants and servants residing at Aśvapaṭṭasara.
He dispatched [messengers] in every direction by means of celestial chariots and divine vehicles.
"In the eighth year from my birth, in the month of Vaiśākha, on the auspicious Akṣaya-tithi of the bright fortnight,
the sacred thread ceremony for my son Śrī Hari shall indeed take place."
Together with the incarnations and those who have been liberated, along with the liberated female abodes;
together with the Brahmas, the male attendants, and the female attendants in every respect;
and likewise with the virtuous female servants and those who have themselves taken incarnations.
Together with lords, sovereigns, sages, and householders; with virtuous men, ascetics, and male devotees of the Lord;
and with female devotees of the Lord, you should all come with great respect. (2.65.20–21)
Together with the Pitṛs accompanied by their wives, the gods accompanied by the goddesses,
the guardians of the directions and the guardians of the worlds, the circles of planets and constellations, the stars,
as well as the principles (tattvas) and those who dwell in the intermediate space (bhuvarloka).
[It was filled] with humans, trees, creepers, and the like born from the lineage of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa);
with grasses, shrubs, and other beings born from the soil; with birds; with singers;
with Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and Kimpuruṣas skilled in the art of dance. (23–24)
"O dancers, bards, and those born of the lineages of Dharma, Adharma, and the rest; and you, the families of gods and asuras, and the lords of the directions from all sides—
you must surely come to the festival of the sacrificial thread for my son."
All the holy fords, rivers, streams, forests, groves, and lakes;
the oceans, excavated ponds, wells, and so forth; the mountains and birds situated upon the earth—all must come from every direction, as well as all the winged creatures. (26–27)
With qualities and the substrates of qualities, both manifest and unmanifest, with reverence;
together with times, seasons, primordial powers, and years;
as well as with wish-fulfilling cows, treasures, and spiritual accomplishments.
[He was served] by the treasures (Nidhis), by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others, and by Brahmā and those with many heads;
likewise by the eminent kings beginning with Indra, by human beings, and by sages;
as well as by Brahmins, eminent Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and servants.
Those of the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
as well as those consisting of *māyā* and the *prakṛtis*, should come to the sacrificial enclosure (*upavītaka*).
So too should the *daityas*, *dānavas*, and *asuras* residing in the subterranean realms beginning with Atala.
Together with nāgas, serpents, kinsmen, friends, family members, and their physical forms;
with vehicles and means of accomplishment, as well as with the rasas; and with both divine and non-divine vidyās, arts, and so forth, you must come here. (32–33)

"By the power and essence of your splendors, and through your blessings, may my child surely increase like a sacrifice and become a mass of merit. Having thus dispatched letters by means of servants, [he departed] from there.
And whatever foods there are in the abodes of the manifestations of pure beings—
in the supreme Brahman, in the imperishable [Vaikuṇṭha], in Goloka, in Vikuṇṭhaka, in the world of the Immortal, in the world of the Lord, and in Satyaloka— those are nectars.
He quickly had piles of divine Brahmajāla cloths, as well as various kinds of foods to be licked and sucked, prepared there;
and likewise whatever [articles] existed in the worlds of Bhuvaḥ, Mahaḥ, Janaḥ, and so forth.
As well as their stores of food and drink and their dwellings—
whatever edible, chewable, and drinkable items there are, and whatever dwellings exist in heaven, in ascetic retreats, on Mount Meru and elsewhere, on earth, or in the seven netherworlds. (38–39)
Whatever things are fit for crushing, serving, or enjoyment; whatever is suitable for embodied beings; whatever is appropriate for moving or stationary entities;
and whatever objects are manifest or unmanifest—for all those things, he likewise [perceives] their accumulations and their inexhaustibility.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa caused many things to be made:
Brahma-lakes, Kalpa-lakes, the juices of the Kalpa-trees and so forth, inexhaustible vessels, and likewise banana trees that yield an endless supply.
He gathered around him inexhaustible treasuries of lotuses, the most excellent vessels for attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the eight *siddhis*, medicinal pills,
thousands of vessels that grant a thousandfold, and many wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*).
And those that produce wonders, as well as the supreme *brahmapuṣpa* flowers;
the excellent *devamāyā* [mantras] and those which are the *devīsūtra*; the nooses of the illusionists (*aindrajālika*) and likewise the *maṇika* gems that bestow a hundred thousand [merits].
He gathered from all sides mantras, yantras, tantras, and likewise seeds of wonder; the channels of the nectar of yogic sovereignty;
the hearths of yoga, the ladles of yoga, and the courtyards of the cauldrons of yoga.
He gathered together from all sides yogic vessels and lamps for yoga;
all the yogic seats and universal ambrosias;
as well as kalpa-cloths, kalpa-necklaces, and kalpa-bracelets with their ornamental ends.
He made various kinds of accumulations for the sake of hospitality:
material foods and material drinks,
as well as foods and drinks produced from subtle elements.
Edibles produced from the manifest and drinks born from the manifest;
edibles produced from the unmanifest and drinks born from the unmanifest;
all those produced by Māyā, as well as those which are Brāhma.
He gathered from all sides every kind of divine syllable, those consisting of the Self,
those born of affection, and all those arising from the principles of merit;
indeed, he collected all things that are objects of enjoyment.
Charming channels of juice, channels of ghee, and channels of curd;
channels of honey, channels of molasses, and lakes of sugar-candies;
channels of sugarcane, lakes of nectars, and sweet ponds.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa gathered [offerings] all around;
he constructed mountains of thousands of offerings,
as well as towering heaps of gems, jewels, and pearls.
At that time, he indeed caused mountains of gold,
silver, and diamonds to be made, as well as mountains of rubies, pearls, and ornaments, along with heaps of garments and jewelry. (56–57)
Likewise, heaps of aromatic powders, fragrant oils, ointments,
collyriums, and dyes;
and collections of sandalwood, saffron, and filaments.
He also made inexhaustible heaps of musk and medicinal herbs,
as well as mirrors, combs, purifying substances,
and earth; and he provided beds, swings, and seats for those who turn the wheel of sovereignty.
He created countless accumulations of vehicles and conveyances;
thus, when all objects of enjoyment and the like had been produced and reached completion,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa indeed remembered [his devotees] in due order.
[He sees] those liberated ones residing in the supreme abode and their female counterparts in every respect;
the groups of liberated souls situated in the Imperishable (akṣara) and the Imperishable itself; the incarnations and their female counterparts, as well as the foremost attendants.
And indeed all the male and female attendants, as well as the male and female devotees;
likewise, the twenty-four Viṣṇus and the fourfold emanations (caturvyūhas) in their proper order;
and all the supreme lords and their consorts, and the lords and their consorts in every respect.
The Vairājas, the Brahma-Śambhus, the Rudras, the Viṣṇus, and likewise the sages;
the saints, the saintly women, the chaste wives, and the beloved goddesses beginning with Ramā;
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Haṃsā, and Māṇikī. (65–66)
He [brought] his own and other principal wives, numbering one hundred and twelve; likewise, millions of female and male servants, the cows and other animals residing in Goloka,
those situated in the four Vaikuṇṭhas, and the inhabitants of Badarikāśrama.
He remembered those established in truth who dwell in heaven, as well as those who have gone to the highest heaven;
he remembered the ancestors, the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, the lords of sages, gods, and humans;
and he remembered the guardians of the quarters, the kings who protect the gods.
Those dwelling in the intermediate space, those situated on the earth, and those residing in the seven netherworlds;
all those staying in water or on land, both the immobile and the mobile;
as well as the Apsarases of Brahma’s lake and the most excellent maidens.
He summoned the bards, wandering minstrels, and gandharvas; the kimpuruṣas, kinnaras, and māgadhas; as well as the cāraṇas, instrumentalists, singers, and dancers;
the actors, playwrights, and those who exhibit theatrical troupes. (71–72)
[He summoned] wrestlers and artisans, as well as great magicians; likewise, sweet-makers, cooks, preparers of food, and servers;
[and] those fit for the sacrifice, knowers of the sacrifice, and those devoted to the ritual section of the Veda.
He summoned the Brahmins and the great seers, the guardians of the fields, gates, and other sites;
he summoned those possessing divine principles, divine beings of human form, and the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas who dwell in water and on land. (74–75)
The wretched and the destitute, the virtuous practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, devoted wives, maidens, goddesses, those of noble birth, and the yoginīs honored by their families;
those dwelling on Kailāsa and Badarī, and those residing at Kṣīraśveta.
Then Śrī Hari remembered those dwelling in the regions upon the earth—
his devotees, the cowherds, and the cowherdesses, who were as many as millions, billions, and trillions—
as well as his own disciples, the Vālakhilyas, who were ascetics taking refuge in knowledge. (77–78)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Narāyaṇa,
who is affectionate toward His devotees, remembered His devotees with His divine mind.
On the morning of the third day of the waxing moon, all of them assembled.

They arrived by means of vehicles that travel through the realm of Brahmā, as well as aerial and mental vehicles; likewise, they came by means of self-propelled vehicles, vehicles of yoga, vehicles of meditative absorption,
wind-borne vehicles, and vehicles consisting of the sky itself.
Garudas, as well as swans, parrots, peacocks, and mongooses, along with Vināyakas,
Gaṇeśas, and Vighneśas, arrived there;
[they came] on elephants, horses, fire-breathing creatures, rhinoceroses, cranes, and other such beings.

Clouds, planets, as well as lightning-garlands and rays—Sūrya, Candra, and the others, bearers of splendor, arrived swiftly. Those borne by mind, those borne by the cosmic age, and those borne with speed all assembled together. (83–84)
The liberated souls, as well as the incarnations, the manifestations, and likewise the lords—
all have gone to the abode of Brahmā, and likewise to the abode of Īśa.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, and the others are likewise there.
Accompanied by the Fortune of the Treasures such as *koṭi*, *koṭya*, *arbuda*, and *abja*;
likewise accompanied by servants such as *koṭi*, *koṭya*, *arbuda*, and *abja*—Rāma, Mādhava, Govinda, the cowherds, and the cowherd-maidens [are present]. (86–87)
The Viṣṇus, headed by the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, the deities of the earth, the Vairājas, and those beginning with Brahmā and Rudra numbering hundreds of millions;
the virtuous ones established in truth, the gods, the ascetics, and the celibate students—[all these were present]. (88)
The Vedas, the sciences, as well as the mantras, the sacrifices, and whatever oblations there are;
the fires and the Maruts, appearing in divine forms; all splendors as well, the ancestors, the seers, and the immortals—[all these] arrived. (2.65.89–90)
The lords of sages, virtuous men, truthful women, chaste wives devoted to their husbands,
those dear to Brahmā, those dear to Kṛṣṇa, and those dear to the gods are present everywhere.
There are also queens and kings of the fourteen worlds.
Daughters of Brahmā, daughters of sages, daughters of the waters born from the ocean;
daughters of gods, daughters of nāgas, and daughters of kings by the millions;
and kumārikās, gāndharvīs, and vidyādharīs in their entirety. ||92-93||
Orators and musicians came, as well as those who sang his praises;
vendors, bards, and the like, as well as porters, actors, and dancers;
storytellers, historians, narrators, and even jesters.
Brahmins, mendicants, those seeking renunciation, and likewise those bearing shaven heads;
Avadhūtas, celibate students, and practitioners of yoga arrived there,
accompanied by their wives, kinsmen, children, and others, resting with their second [wives].

The lineages of those devoted to their wives and the families of those faithful to their husbands, along with the associations of kinsmen and relatives— all of whom were highly disciplined through that yoga—
arrived there; for indeed, all of them, though born of various lands, possessed bodies of equal stature.
The hosts of Viṣṇu, the hosts of Rudra, and the hosts of Brahmā are innumerable.
There are rows of lamps, no impurities, the goddesses of the sixth day, those with parched grain, the cow-maidens, as well as the Arjanyas, the young women, and the hundred maidens.
Kandarā had ten million daughters, as did the virtuous Krodhanikā;
there were a hundred thousand Rākṣasa maidens, and five or six Kaṅkatālīs.
Indeed, thousands of Kaṅkatālī maidens presented themselves.
There were thousands of daughters of Brahmā, daughters of the Waters, and daughters of Aryaman;
likewise, daughters of Kubera, daughters of Indra, and daughters of Yama;
as well as daughters of Vāyu, daughters of the Seasons, and daughters of Viśvakarman. (10.1–102)
Five thousand daughters of the *drumakanyās* and *dānavas*,
as well as the sixteen wives of Vasanta, were likewise present;
and there were daughters of Agni, along with a thousand daughters of the *sāla* and *māla* trees.
Thousands of Śravaṇa maidens and thousands of Śāvadīna maidens; likewise, thousands of fierce Aindrajālika maidens; and sixty maidens—Vidyā-kanyās and Kiśorīs—were present. 104–105.
The daughters of Saṃvatsara and the innumerable daughters of Vārkṣya,
as well as the daughters born from the earth, arrived with their water-pots.
Two thousand daughters also presented themselves before Lakṣmaṇa.
Then three hundred daughters of Viśvāvasu presented themselves;
seventy-two thousand daughters of Brahmā presented themselves;
and a thousand daughters of King Jumāsemla also stood there.
Twelve hundred Kārṣṇī maidens arrived for the sake of the auspiciousness of their beloved Hari;
they indeed performed the kīrtanas of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The father provided dwellings for the congregations who had arrived and bestowed various honors, such as the *madhuparka* offering, according to their merit. Furthermore,
O Rādhikā, great sages also came there.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Arrival of All by Means of Invitation Cards on the Great Festival of the Sacred Thread in Vaiśākha, during the Lord’s Eighth Year," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 65. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Listen, O Rādhikā: divine great sages arrived—Samīraṇa, Pavamāna, Santāraṇa, and Barbura;

Nīlakarṇa, Alarka, Puṇḍarīka, Kalāyana,

Kauṇḍinya, Kauśika, Pautimāṣya, and likewise Gaupavana;
Śāṇḍilya, Gautama, Agniveśya, and also Amlāna. (5–6)
Saitava, Prācīnayogya, Dhārāśarya, Maindava,

Panthā, Ayāsya, Ābhūti, Tvaṣṭra, the Aśvins, Dadhīcaka, Viśvarūpa, Vipracitti, Prādhvaṃsana, Ātharvaṇa,

Śāṇḍilī, Pautimāṣī, Kātyāyanī, and Gautamī;

Vāmadeva, Śṛṅgin, Kratu, the ascetic Āruṇi,
