Pāribhadra, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Rudra arrived;
as did Kubera, Varuṇa, Mahendra, Agni, and Anila;
Yama, the Grahas, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the Śeṣa serpents. (31)

Thus all those great beings, worthy of worship and honor, arrived. Gopāla Kṛṣṇa bowed his head to them upon the ground with devotion and then praised those respective lords of creation with supreme affection.
Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa said:
The Supreme Lord, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who shines in the supreme abode of the Supreme Brahman, is higher than the highest and is accompanied by those who are eternally liberated. 34.
"Today indeed the Supreme Lord of the worlds resides in my house!
Oh, what great fortune it is for me that Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has come here!
Oh, what great fortune it is for me that Vāsudeva and the others have arrived!"
Oh, what fortune! The incarnations of the Supreme Lord have arrived. The Īśvaras, the liberated ones of the abodes (dhāma-muktas), and other liberated souls have assembled.
There is Bhūmā, Virāṭ, Viṣṇu himself, Vidhātṛ, and the Lord who is the creator of the universe.
The great sage Patnīvrata has also come to my house;
he is himself the teacher of teachers, worthy of worship by perfected beings, virtuous women, ascetics, and yogis.
Brahmā himself dwells in my home; indeed, today is a day of great fortune for me.
By worshipping him, people attain enjoyment, liberation, and residence in the same world [as the deity];
moreover, by his majesty, all calamities are destroyed.
This Gaṇeśa, whose form is the glorious Kṛṣṇa, resides in my abode. (2.66.39–40)
I am the foremost among the gods, worthy of worship, and in every way blessed upon this earth;
so too are the Lord Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Rādhā is the mother of the worlds, and Pārvatī is the primordial form.
She is the primordial root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), the first cause, and identical in essence to the Supreme Brahman.
By fully worshipping her feet, the observer of vows obtains his heart's desire.
That auspicious mother is herself present today in my house. (42–43)
The daughters of the *dhāma*, the most excellent among those liberated from the *dhāma*, and the *sādhya*s dwell in my house.
Blessed is this Kambharā-Lakṣmī, for whom this vision has been attained today— indeed,
the direct fulfillment of the destiny of women created by Brahmā.
There is the vision of the virtuous women created by Īśa, as well as of the Īśānas themselves;
blessed is Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā, and blessed is the land of Saurāṣṭra, where the glorious Supreme Lords reside. ||45-46||
The ancestors, the seers, the gods, and the goddesses, as well as the fundamental principles (tattvas), dwell in my house;
all those who reside in the netherworlds, both embodied and unembodied, are in my home.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and this age has been made successful by me.
Today my creation has borne fruit, and today my life is fruitful,
since today indeed the great beings dwelling in the three worlds are in my home;
the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of Jīva are all within my house.
Having thus paid homage to them all, he caused them to be seated according to protocol on appropriate thrones in the great hall of Śatābhauma;
there, for ten *yojanas*, he worshipped them in due order and according to the prescribed rites.
The Father, assuming forms at will and bearing millions upon billions of forms,
chose each of the supreme lords—
the gods and others— as well as the hosts of sages, seers, holy men, liberated beings, deities, and the twice-born. (51–52)
And with devotion, he chose the sage Lomaśa as his own domestic priest (purohita),
honoring him with jewels, corals, necklaces, ornaments of pearls from the Kalpa tree,
garments, perfumes, garlands, and gems such as rubies, emeralds, and diamonds.

Seated upon a lion-throne of jewels, he chose Śrī Gaṇeśa, who was situated in the very center for the purpose of worship— the elephant-faced god established for the auspicious rite— honoring him with waters and with sandalwood, the essence of fragrance. (94–95)
And with the waters brought from the heart of Brahmā, as well as the waters brought from Virajā;
with the waters of the ocean-covering seas, the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā, and the waters of Mount Meru;
and with the waters of the seven oceans, as well as the waters of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
With [water] cooled and infused with the fragrance of flowers and sandalwood and mixed with nectar,
and likewise with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he bathed [the deity] with devotion. (57–58)
He worshipped Gaṇeśa, who is the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of all obstacles,
and the god who bestows all auspiciousness, with various offerings,
as well as with *pārijāta* flowers and divine lotuses.
With *durvā* grass from Vaikuṇṭha, as well as ornaments of precious gems;
with garments pure as fire, and likewise with vermilion from the Brahma-world;
with fragrant sandalwood, flowers, and golden finger-ornaments.
Having thus worshipped Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rites, one should thereafter worship Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Ramā,
Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Haṃsā, Jayā, Lalitā, and Dayā.
Likewise, he saw other illustrious and virtuous chaste women residing in the abodes of the Lord,
as well as the goddesses Kārṣṇī, Mahālakṣmī, Sāvitrī,
and Sarasvatī; Gaṅgā, Diti, Aditi, and the wives of the sages who were devoted to their husbands.
Kambharā also worshipped the goddesses who possess lordship, the wives of the ancestors,
and the beautiful women; likewise, she honored the Yoginīs, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, Lopāmudrā and others, as well as those devoted to their husbands and those esteemed on earth.
Likewise, Arbuda, Abja, and Kanyā, though graced with great beauty,
embraced Arbuda again and again in the form of Kambharā;
and having conversed with one another, they all indeed clung to each other.
Kambharālakṣmī caused all of them to dwell in the palace;
she honored them with garlands, garments, and jeweled ornaments,
as well as with the flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa and the blossoms of the Pārijāta tree.
Likewise, she was adorned with dots of vermilion upon her parting hair,
with beautiful crescent-moon designs on her forehead, and with sandalwood marks;
as well as with fragrant substances such as musk, saffron, and red lac.
Having honored them, she fed them with various appropriate delicacies.
Then Śrī Kambharā gave nectar-like water and betel leaf, exquisitely scented with camphor and other fragrances, to the wives of the sages in due order.

She worshipped, according to the prescribed rites, those virtuous women who possessed husbands and sons, as well as the enchanting daughters of the Sun, the daughters of Śiva, and the daughters of the Pitṛs;
the daughters of the gods, the daughters of the Nāgas, and the daughters of Manu, all of whom were devoted to the Bull (Dharma).

She honored the daughters of Bandhu, the daughters of Bhakta, those born of the Gandharvas, and likewise those born of the Asuras according to the prescribed rites; she fed them with respect and lodged them in palatial mansions endowed with magnificent gardens.
The musicians played auspicious musical instruments;
she caused auspicious rites to be performed and fed the brahmins.
She worshipped the goddess Śrī Devī, the Mistress of Kuṅkumavāpī.

With all those materials, he devotedly worshipped the goddess of the sixth day as well as the deity of auspiciousness; the father worshipped the village deities and the lake deities with all his being, and indeed worshipped the local dignitaries with every possible means.
Then he had auspicious rites for merit and well-being performed;
he caused the Vedas to be recited and had songs sung.
And with the waters of the Gaṅgā held in golden jars, [he bathed] Acyuta.
And his mother bathed the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
She adorned him with beautiful attire, sandalwood paste, garlands, and other ornaments;
she dressed him in divine garments and jewels, and anointed him with divine sandalwood unguents.
Then, Hari indeed became the presiding presence there for the lords who had descended to the assembly, for the ascetics,
the seers, the gods,
and embodied beings from the three worlds.
And when Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arrived together with his father,
then the incarnations, the lords, the gods, the Manus, human beings, sages,
and others all rose up and paid homage to the Supreme Lord.
You are indeed the manifest Supreme Brahman, shining forth as Bālakṛṣṇa;
you are the one who assumes incarnations, the witness, whose form is attained through grace.
You are untainted, resting in the Self, and the cause of the creation and all else of the universe.

O Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa, Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭ, Bhūman, Brahmā, Śeṣa, and the others abide within you, like gnats in the cosmic egg. And we, though being your portions, exist as virtuous beings and gods throughout all creations.
Indeed, innumerable cosmic eggs reside upon the coils of Śeṣa;
Śeṣa rests upon the Tortoise, and the Tortoise moves within the waters.
The water, by the power of fire, always remains above like a cloud.
Fire has its support established by air; air moves within space.
This space resides in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and the space of consciousness shines within the Imperishable (akṣara).
The Imperishable shines within the state of Brahman, and that shines within the Supreme Lord.
"You are this glorious Supreme Lord; you exist as the son of Yaśodā.
You are indeed the cowherd boy manifest before our very eyes.
Thus was Kṛṣṇa himself, in the form of a child, praised.
In the midst of the assembly, the Lord of the splendor of Rādhā and Ramā shone exceedingly;
he was two-armed, rich with white luster, golden-hued, and captivating; his face was bright with a gentle smile, and he was resplendent with ornaments. || 91–92 ||
First, for the sake of purifying his body, Acyuta performed three *kṛcchra* penances;
then, when an auspicious moment had arrived and a favorable *lagna* was reached,
with the lord of the *lagna* remaining awake and being aspected by benign planets— (92) — he [proceeded].
He undertook the ritual action when it was not within the range of inauspicious planetary aspects and the like.
For the sake of purifying the faults of eating and drinking at will,
he gave three cows as a gift and had the benediction of "svasti" recited.
By the command of Lomaśa, he gave a thousand pieces of gold and a treasure of jewels as a gift to the Brahmins, and paid homage to the deities;
having worshipped Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Pārvatī, and Sūrya.
Having worshipped the fire according to the prescribed rite, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa performed the consecration of his son with Vedic mantras in the assembly hall;
likewise, he worshipped the gods, the planets, the guardians of the quarters, and the Mothers.
Having performed the Nāndī-śrāddha and the Mahāśānti rite immediately thereafter,
he offered oblations into the fire produced upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Then, having offered a stream of wealth (vasudhārā) seven times with clarified butter, he proceeded.
He performed the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and the *daiva-śrāddha*, and offered libations to the ancestors. To his son, who had been shaved, bathed, released from his vows, and adorned as a *brahmacārin*,
his father gave a waistband, a loincloth, and a sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*).
Having tied the three-stranded muñja-grass girdle around his waist and [the sacred thread] upon his ear,
the hairy sage imparted the Gāyatrī mantra three times into his right ear.
After causing the oblation of clarified butter to be performed, the sage instructed him in the duties of dharma.
Then Śrī, Arādhikā, Prabhā,
the sovereign goddesses, the liberated ones, the Sādhyas, the goddesses, the maidens, Mahālakṣmī, Prakṛti, Haṃsā, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī gave alms to him. (103–104)
Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Dhāmakanyā, and likewise the daughters of Īśa;
the daughters of gods, nāgas, and kings, as well as the daughters of the three worlds and others—all these dark-complexioned women with divine forms resided in the hermitage of Lomaśa. (1.05)
Kambharāśrī, Amṛtā, and the mothers of the gods, Daityas, and others;
the wives of the sages and the consorts of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; and the beloved wives of the guardians of the directions—all these gave alms separately and individually. (106–107)
Having taken alms in a divine golden vessel set with priceless jewels, the Blessed One gave a small portion to Lomaśa.
[He also gave] the staff reaching to his crown, the sacred thread, the deerskin, and the upper garment.
Lomaśa gave him the ritual of worship, the twilight prayers, a water-pot, and virtuous conduct;
all the other venerable sages gave him highly precious gifts:
alms, strings of jewels, necklaces, gems, and articles fashioned from gold.
The beings of divine origin gave him various kinds of nectars and objects of enjoyment, which they had brought from their own worlds.
Then, having thus completed his ritual duties and given a sacrificial fee to Lomaśa, [he departed].
Gopālakṛṣṇaka gave gold, diamonds, and jewels; the father gave his son a diamond necklace that provides protection.
The auspicious goddesses, the maidens, and likewise the mothers [gave their gifts]. (112–113)
They bestowed auspicious blessings with white flowers and *durvā* grass;
whosoever came to the sacrifice, each and every one gave them auspicious blessings.
Songs were sung and musical instruments were played.
And his father taught him the lineage (gotra), the excellent Veda, and the Vedic branch (śākhā).
(1.15) The lineage consists of the Supreme Brahman; these three ancestors are as follows:
Akṣarabrahma, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Śrī Nārāyaṇa himself. (1.16)
"The Veda is the single, all-encompassing essence, and the Sāman emerged from the mouth of Śrī;
the Patnīvratīya is its branch, and you, O Supreme Lord, are the tree itself.
Having thus completed the rites of honor for Rādhikā, [he spoke].
And Gopālakṛṣṇaka provided a resolution for the assembly.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Bestowing the Sacred Thread (*yajñopavīta*) and the Worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 66] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)
Chapter 67 [Author:
Chapter 68 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
After the sacred thread ceremony for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā was completed,
the great honors departed from that assembly hall to their respective residences.
Then indeed Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa and the virtuous Śrī Kambharā [departed].
Likewise, there are those who have transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), as well as liberated souls and innumerable maidens;
the sages dwelling therein, the sacred fords (tīrtha), the personified creepers, the divine principles (tattva), and the glorious primary powers (śakti). (2–3)
When the time for the meal had arrived, they signaled to the doorkeeper, the Brahmanāda,
to announce [the arrival] there for the purpose of summoning him; and in an instant,
he [struck] the sweet-sounding Brahma-bell, which resounds throughout the three worlds.
He caused a sweet-sounding announcement to be made regarding the meal.
At that time, there were rows of the Lords who have descended, of the Blessed Ones, and of the liberated souls established in their abodes, as well as of the liberated women.
Hundreds of rows of divine and sovereign goddesses belonging to those whose bodies range from Vāsudeva up to Vairāja appeared;
at that time, they produced divine arbudas, abjas, and padmas of maidens.
The serving of nectars to be enjoyed by themselves, which had been brought from their own abodes;
likewise, divine foods—both solid and soft, as well as those to be licked and sucked—and other sweet drinks, along with various cooked dishes and vegetables. (8–9)

Divine juices, divine soured gruels (*cāranāla*), and similar divine liquids— suitable [for consumption], originating from the Lake of Brahmā (*brahmahrada*) and produced in the Garden of Brahmā (*brahmavāṭī*),
which were cooked and well-prepared by the beloved wives of Brahmā, auspicious [in nature].
And they respectfully served them in abundance:
auspicious ghee, curd, milk, milk-based preparations, honey, and sugar, presented in platters, golden vessels, and various bowls. || 11-12 ||
Rice, split pulses, soups, sweetmeats,
and all kinds of milk-rice— none of these are auspicious for me in any way.
Even the sweet vessels of delusion, as well as cakes and pearls [are likewise unsuitable].
Sūtraphenī, laḍḍukas, catuṣkas, and likewise śaṣkulis;
śāṭakas, ghṛtapūras, and sweet antaḥpolikas; phulavaṭīs, rājatṛptas, kvathikās, and likewise bharjikās. (14–15)
They also respectfully served *kalikās*, *sevikās*, *saṃyāvas*, *bhājikās*,
and various kinds of *caṭanīs*,
as well as foods prepared with a dry seasoning and those enriched with bitter and salty flavors.
They gave sweet drinks, whey, fresh butter, fruits, seeds of fruits, and fragrant plantains;
then, deeply immersed in devotion, those lords made their own bodies into vessels [for the offering]. (17–18)
Then those liberated female lords, who were themselves the supreme sovereigns of the liberated,
forcibly gave him food and other offerings as companions of Brahmā;
they fed him until his throat was full, and being satisfied, they took up handfuls of water for him.
They drank water and took betel leaves;
thereafter, they took the desired powders for their mouths. Then those created by Brahmā and Īśa departed for their own dwellings.
Then, beginning with Brahmā, [there were] Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and their progeny;
the gods, goddesses, and the ancestors, from Satyaloka down to Bhūrloka;
as well as the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the guardians of the quarters, Sureśvara, and the others.
All the divine maidens sat there in rows.
To them and to those [others], the daughters of Brahmā and the daughters of Kṛṣṇa joyfully and repeatedly offered seats and served food again and again. (23–24)
They indeed gave vessels of sweet food and drink born of truth;
those various foods and drinks—sweet as nectar, fit for eating and chewing, as well as all that is to be licked, sucked, tasted, and drunk. (25)
He repeatedly gave them food, vegetables, juices, powders, and other such items.
After they had eaten, those gods drank water;
they took betel and other refreshments for their mouths and returned to their abodes.
Then the ṛṣis and the human kings seated upon their thrones,
having emerged from the four mouths, quickly took their places in rows.
Likewise, those divine and non-divine, embodied and formless, as well as mobile and immobile beings [assembled].
Filled with joy, they sat down in the circular rows of the dining hall.
The maidens of the hermitage of Lomaśa, full of eagerness, gave them vessels and seats and served them their food.
Then the daughters of the eightfold divine creation,
eager for the feast,
prepared the food consisting of endless nectars and radiant, sweet delicacies.

Then they gave them various juices— eatables, foods to be chewed, licked, and drunk— all imbued with flavor, suitable for each of those classes of gods. Having eaten and being satisfied, they drank beverages and used mouth-fresheners.
They took betel leaves and other offerings and departed for their dwellings with eager anticipation.
Then, at that time, there were rows of inhabitants from the worlds below,
such as Atala, belonging to the Daityas, Dānavas, Asuras, and likewise the Rakṣasas.
There were rows of hooded serpents dwelling in the water.
There were various kinds of foods fit for the enjoyment of those respective worlds—eatables, things to be licked, things to be sucked, and things to be tasted in every way. (35–36)
And with eager anticipation, the maidens served the side dishes, the gruels, and the essences of flavors upon suitable vessels and other utensils—
[the offerings] of those who possess excellent qualities, both embodied and unembodied, and supreme in their essential nature. (37)
They became suitable handmaidens for those seeking purification through virtues, rituals, and all sacred fords;
for the wretched, the blind, and the miserable; and for men, women, and eunuchs;
as well as for the ranks of both moving and unmoving beings. (38–39)
The servants and the Brahmins served them exceedingly;
they fed them most abundantly and gave them very cool drinks.
[They offered] the essences of the forest, the essences of water, the essences of fire, and the juices of the earth.
Those whose essence is milk, those whose essence is grass, those whose essence is tubers, and those who are very fatty;

those whose essence is the body, those whose essence is mud, those whose essence is flowers, and those consisting of juices and the like; those whose essence is leaves, those whose essence is roots, and those produced from the essence of craftsmanship.
Those whose essence is in the bark, those whose essence is in the pith, those whose essence is in the seeds, and the finest fruits;
those whose essence is in the flower-clusters, those whose essence is in the stalks, and likewise those produced from the stems;
those whose essence is in the mines, those whose essence is in the sky, those whose essence is in the clouds, and those produced by the seasons.
Those whose essence is rain, whose essence is merit, whose essence is faith, and who are born from the heart;
those whose essence is dreams, whose essence is time, whose essence is material substance, and who arise from qualities;
those whose essence is action, whose essence is yoga, and who have assumed forms through their sovereign power.
The maidens gave all kinds of excellent foods to those who were worthy;
for where Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Haṃsā, and Ramā are the givers, O Rādhā, what deficiency could there be in the food and drink that provides such assistance? (46)

Where Kṛṣṇa himself is the host and Lakṣmī is the one who bestows [hospitality], what indeed could be considered a deficiency? There, the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavallī*) are the gatherers [of offerings]; all abodes and worlds, as if personified, truly offer their devotion there. (47–48)
Where the principles of reality (tattvas) abide, what indeed could be called "depth"?
Where fire itself is the cook and satisfaction is the server,
where the foods are the imperishable nectar— what indeed could be called "depth" there?
O Great Lords, since you are eternally blissful and perfectly satisfied,
where all the wonders of sovereignty and supernatural powers exist like wish-fulfilling trees and thought-gems, what indeed could be considered a deficiency? (2.67.50–51)
Thus, O Rādhikā! After the refusal of the food, Lomaśa himself ate first, and then Bālakṛṣṇa;
thereafter, the cooks and those who served the meal also ate.
Then Kārṣṇi ate, and after him the cowherd kinsmen;
then the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa himself ate,
and thereafter the glorious Śrī Kaṃbhārā ate together with her sons.
The mother gave excellent foods to the servants,
as well as to insects, fish, birds, and even those who live by their luck;
Kambharā gave edible foods to those whose intake is uncertain.
He gave away gold, silver, and jewels by the millions as sacrificial gifts.
Having rested for a moment, in the afternoon, the assembly hall— which increases the honor of men—
became the gathering place for the supreme lords among gods and for all embodied beings.
Resplendent upon a golden throne, filled with millions of gods and sages,
the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shines in the midst of the sky.
Upon a high seat enriched with the splendor of elephants, his father likewise sits by his side.
The Mother Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, as well as Śrī and Nārāyaṇa;
both the Lord Hemanta and [his consort] stood holding His two chowries.
The incarnations and female incarnations, the lords and the hosts of goddesses. (2.67.60)
The gods and goddesses, the ancestors and their progeny, the sages and the seers,
the asuras and the female asuras, and likewise human beings and women;
the beasts, birds, plants, serpents, daityas, and their females.
That long and spacious assembly hall shone, filled with beings of dull intellect and with various principles,
both divine and non-divine, possessing excellent bodies.
Then, a most beautiful dance by the female dancers commenced.
The songs of the Apsarases and the sweet music of the Gandharvas proceeded;
the most excellent and auspicious dance of the Gandharva women took place.
When the dancing was concluded, the wrestlers displayed their skill in combat.
They displayed the various terrains of the battlefield to an extraordinary degree;
then, through the performance of actors, they were made visible as if enacted in a drama.
Furthermore, feats such as swinging from the skillful use of aerial ropes began to take place.
Then, indeed, there were displays of flying through the air, celestial battles, and the exhibitions of magicians;
sights of the power of lightning were produced,
and songs arose that were filled with the weight of Kṛṣṇa’s glory.
There arose the most excellent expositions of the Vidyādharas,
and the instructions of the Siddhas were deeply moving to the heart.
Those skilled in the arts of bards, wandering minstrels, and panegyrists, renowned as poets, offered their praises.
The women sang of this festival as it truly was.
At the command of Śrī Sanatkumāra, Nārada praised that supreme, divine festival— one such as had never occurred before, nor would ever occur again.
Wherein resides the supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
who is the worthy recipient of the sacred thread, as well as His incarnations and manifestations of glory;
and from whose greatness the three worlds have arisen, bestowing upon them excellence.
Where all flavors and all fragrances, as well as all forms of bliss, exist in every way;
where all truths reside, along with the manifestations of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā—such a greatness shall never be again; this greatness is superior to everything.
One must practice its recollection (smaraṇa), as well as hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana);
indeed, through meditative absorption (nididhyāsana) upon this very [reality], there is direct liberation at the feet of Hari.
Therefore, that alone should be performed in this world by which one may enter into liberation.
By performing that through which no bondage whatsoever arises in saṃsāra—
these great festivals of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa should always be observed by devotees, so that one is liberated from bondage. (75–76)
For those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence and sinking under the burden of family life,
the refuge here is Śrī Hari, who takes the form of a boat and is the savior.
Those who have taken shelter of Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Guru, and the Supreme Lord—
They do not go to Kamaleśa, the region of Dharmarāja.
That alone is a tongue which praises Hari; that alone is a mind offered to Mādhava.
Those two hands are indeed praiseworthy and worthy of honor which are devoted to the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Otherwise, one is like a withered branch of a tree, devoid of service;
that throat is merely the throat of a jackal which does not sing of Mādhava.
That indeed is a great disease wherein there is no remembrance of Hari.
He alone is to be pitied while still alive who does not worship Keśava.
This Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, is worthy of worship by all incarnations; He is the most excellent of persons (Puruṣottama) and must be adored. (81–82)
Those worshippers are not to be pitied; for even when dead, they go to liberation.
All that is moving and unmoving here shines within Bālakṛṣṇa.
By whomsoever His worship is performed, by him the entire world of moving and unmoving beings has been honored.
Just as the qualities of the ocean of jewels are innumerable, so too are the qualities of Śrī Hari.
Because they have taken refuge in the Lord of Lakṣmī— the husband of Rādhā, Prabhā, Pāravatī, and Śrī—
they are not afflicted by suffering in saṃsāra, since they are destined for liberation.
This boy, whose seven hands are marked with the trident, banner, bow, arrow, fish, svastika, and wheel,
and who possesses sixteen marks— consisting of upward lines and others— on his feet and palms, is worthy of worship. (86)

He by whom this Lord Bālakṛṣṇa is worshipped together [with his companions]—he who bears all weapons and is an ocean of skill in all arts—that child, by whom this youth is worshipped, becomes a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. (87–88)
In whose inner organ Kṛṣṇa resides, and in whose self Nārāyaṇa dwells—
he who is pervaded by both Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa has no fear of death anywhere. For those who have taken refuge in the Supreme Goal and who delight in Bālakṛṣṇa, there is never any cause for fear.
For those qualified for the supreme abode, there is no downward descent.
Those who are devotees of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa attain the liberation of the virtuous, which is higher than the highest and proclaimed by Rādhā, Ramā, and others. (2.67.90–91)
For those who engage in battle, who are righteous, sattvic, and great-souled, and for those who know the Blessed One, there exists a supreme and auspicious goal beyond all other goals.
Devotees behold Kṛṣṇa, who is subtle, omnipresent, and dark; others do not.
In this way, those great-souled ones who are abodes of compassion behold that Kṛṣṇa.
He whose every action is directed toward Kṛṣṇa and offered to Him—though he is the doer of all, yet he is a non-doer; he is not bound, but is liberated.
Those for whom Hari is eternally dear are always dear to Hari as well;
and he who meditates upon Hari meditates upon Him who has taken refuge at his feet.
Having risen at dawn, this Bālakṛṣṇa should be remembered with devotion.
He is indeed worthy of being heard and proclaimed, for he is the deliverer from difficulties. Those who drink the nectar of the stories of this Kṛṣṇa cross over [all obstacles],
provided they possess unwavering devotion toward this glorious Bālakṛṣṇa.
They shall perform [these deeds] and they shall go to where Hari himself resides;
that goal which belongs to those devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa in the supreme abode cannot be attained even by a thousand births or by austerities.
What is the use of mutterings, what use the words of mantras, or what use diligent efforts at spiritual supports?
What is the use of sacrifices, what use of gifts, what use of religious duties, or what use of fame?
What need has he for many other things, if he has attained Śrī Hari? (2.67.100)
"Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā.
If this mantra, the bestower of all goals, is recited, what need is there for other knowledge?
For those who have Hari, they possess victory; for them, there is liberation, the highest of the high.
Blessed and auspicious are those in whose hearts dwells the Supreme Lord.
(102) Thousands of millions of holy fords and hundreds of millions of acts of charity do not equal even a sixteenth part of bowing to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (103)
By the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) is attained;
through meditation on Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the yogi achieves the supreme goal.
Those who perform the worship of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa even with water alone [attain this].
They too shall go to the supreme abode of the virtuous who have performed meritorious deeds.
(105) For those women who remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband at the three junctions of the day, there is liberation even while remaining in their bodies; of this there is no doubt. (106)
Men and women, gods and goddesses, lords and even those who rule over the north-east—by serving Bālakṛṣṇa, you shall attain the supreme goal.
Blessed are Rādhā, Ramā, and the others; blessed are Kālindī and the young maidens.
"Blessed is Kuṅkumavāpī, for its beloved is the Blessed One himself!
We, the inhabitants of Mahīmā, are blessed, since we have met him at this great festival!
Having said this, the glorious Nārada bowed down again and again.
Having placed jeweled garlands around the necks of the Blessed Bālakṛṣṇa, Śuka, and Śrīvallabha, Nārada bowed down.
Looking once more at the assembly with a long-drawn gaze, Nārada—
Raising his hand, he spoke again to all who were listening:
"Let those who honor the earth listen! I speak the truth, the absolute truth:
in this world, there will be thousands of incarnations of Kṛṣṇa."
But such a Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the Avatārī, the most perfect, the highest of the high,
has appeared somewhere today at the commencement [of this age], and shall never be born again. (11.3)
Others will take refuge in his divine play with devotion.
From the feet up to the crest-lock,
there are thousands of marks of this Supreme Self upon every part of his form.
One hundred [tufts] are on his feet, ten likewise on each of his shanks, twenty on the region of his thighs and private parts, five on his anus,
thirty on his buttocks, and twenty-five on his abdomen.
On his chest there are one hundred [marks], and on his back and sides three hundred;
two hundred on his throat and shoulders, one hundred on his face, and three on his neck;
there are one hundred marks on his two hands, and likewise fifty on his two palms.
Ten on each forearm, twenty-five on the two eyes,
sixteen on the cheeks, five on the forehead, and likewise six on the two ears;
ten on the tongue, twenty on the two lips, and [ten] on the mouth, respectively.
On his nose there are ten lines, and on his brow a hundred times as many.
There are twenty on his hair and four on his chin;
throughout all his body hairs reside heaps of the qualities of gold.
The qualities, intrinsic natures, lines, spots, and joints;
the conjunctions, configurations, structures, and excellent arrangements—of each single limb, it is impossible for me to describe them all. (122)
Everything possesses the nature of all things, and excellence exists here in every direction.
By taking portions of this form, other forms will come into being—other gods, lords, and supreme lords. (123–124)
"O you who stand in this assembly, there is nothing more to be said by me as proof;
for you are incarnations and liberated souls, supreme lords.
In the Vāmana incarnation, within the universal form (Viśvarūpa), between every two hairs..."
Countless marks remain; they would not be capable of being numbered.
Indeed, the very nature of the three worlds resides within the form of the Blessed One;
for the marks of all creation exist upon His body alone. (126–127)
Above the throat and in the head, the subtle creation is established;
below the throat and above the hands, the creation of effects is situated.
Below the hips, the inferior creation is established, extending down to the tips of the nails.
"Indeed, marks of ten million, hundred billion, and one hundred trillion [lotuses] exist upon his body.
Having spoken thus, Nārada ceased, by the command of Sanaka. Then, O Rādhikā, her father presented him with rewards.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Feeding of the Great Beings (*mahīmānas*), the Subsequent Assembly Gathering, and the Instruction on the Supreme Knowledge (*parāvidyā*) Spoken by Nārada," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 67. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 68 [Author:
Chapter 69 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Kubera, Vasava, the wish-fulfilling trees, the earth, Lakshmi, the treasures, and the wish-granting gems stood before Krishna Narayana,
O Radhika, as if to offer them as rewards for his satisfaction.
To the liberated ones, those born of divine opulence gave celestial garlands;
to the incarnations themselves they gave crowns and earrings,
and by the command of Kṛṣṇa, they then gave divine necklaces to the lords.
They indeed gave golden thrones to Brahmā and the others,
and at that time they presented inexhaustible vessels to the ancestors;
they also gave sacrificial vessels and seats to the sages.
They gave suitable jewel-necklaces to the *asuras* according to their respective ranks.
Then they gave vehicles, mounts, ornaments, and wealth to the *dānavas*, *asuras*, and *daityas*, as well as to human beings. (5–6)

They gave jewels from the elephants, the nectar-like food from the cattle, and substances such as juices of fruits and flowers from the birds; and they gave wealth to all beings, both sentient and insentient, whether embodied or formless, according to what was appropriate for each. (7)

Then they gave gold, silver, and so forth to the Brahmins; diamonds and such to the kings; clothing, patched garments, and the like to the virtuous; and ornaments, fine clothes, and other articles of adornment that increase good fortune as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the chaste women. (8–9)
They bestowed gifts there until they were satisfied; "Give more" was not said again.
And they gave so much that they were unable to carry away as much as they desired. Whatever was wished for by whomsoever, that very thing was immediately presented there.
The word "na" (not) was not employed, nor indeed was the word "gṛhṇa" (take) used.
In this manner, they gave much wealth as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and also as rewards (*pāritoṣika*) to those worthy recipients, such as the Brahmins and others.
They gave abundant wealth to the cooks and the confectioners;
they even gave gold necklaces and diamonds to the laborers.
They also gave wealth to the porters, the bards, and the artisans.
They gave wealth to the cymbal players, dancers, and actresses;

to the singers and female servants, they gave necklaces, ornaments, garments, and the like; and to the male servants, the destitute, and the wretched, they gave clothing, jewelry, and so forth. (14–16)
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, they gave ornaments, garments, wealth, and vessels of gold and silver to the daughters of the three worlds;
whatever would bring satisfaction to each of them, in whatever manner and by whatever means it might be.
Whatever was given at those times, there was no hesitation whatsoever.
To virtuous women, to chaste wives, and likewise to those devoted to their husbands; to those in distress, to the elderly, and even to mothers—in every way [he gave]. (17–18)
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, they gave ornaments, garments, and wealth to their sisters, daughters, and granddaughters, as well as to the goddesses, each according to her rank; indeed,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself bestowed these honors upon the guests of honor.
And she caused excellent rewards to be given; indeed,
Śrī Kaṃbhārā gave ornaments of every kind, truly priceless, through Kuberavasu and others, to all the women.
Likewise, Gopāla gave to all the people golden necklaces of gems, jewels, and pearls; he also gave them abundant wealth consisting of gold,
excellent jewels, necklaces, and so forth, according to their needs.

Thus, at that time, Śrī Lomaśa gave to all the great sages the *kalpātmagūṭikā*, by means of which their every desire was fulfilled moment by moment. She was the sister of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, named Santopā, and his elder sister.
He gave auspicious threads, dyeing substances,
combs, golden ornaments, bodices, and likewise silken garments; he gave water-pots, tunics, and other such items, as well as necklaces and Bangiḍī ornaments.
"Girdles, bracelets, and rings that bestow satisfaction—
having thus bestowed such gifts and rewards, the father spoke words of favor to those who had assembled at the festival. (26–27)
Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa said: "O you who have always come to the great festival of my son Kṛṣṇa’s sacred thread ceremony, bringing with you an increase of splendor."
I offer a welcome and give my thanks;
with humility, I confess that any service I have rendered here has been deficient.
Considering this a matter for forgiveness, O Lord, may I be forgiven. (29)
Of the liberated ones and those who have descended [as incarnations], of the female Brahmās and the female practitioners of celibacy;
of the lords and the sovereign goddesses, of the gods and the celestial women;
of human beings and human females, and of the Daityas and the Daitya women.
Through the presence of the nāgas and their wives, of those with inert and conscious bodies,
of the world-protectors, of kings, and of the ṛṣis and their wives,
the festive rite became greatly magnified.
By your arrival, I have been made a vessel for all glories;
my son, too, has been nourished by the splendors within your own domain.
You must understand this once more, and my transgression must be forgiven.
Having spoken thus, he repeatedly offered words of thanks to those who had performed the work;
together with his family, he requested their blessings.
At that time, a cry of "Victory! was raised by the assembly.
Then, at the outset, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa arrived for the sake of worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa;
they honored him with divine offerings,
presenting him with a crown, cowherd attire, a flute, and cintāmaṇi jewels.
He gave away wish-fulfilling cows and worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Then Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa worshipped Śrī Hari with a crown,
earrings, a conch, a discus, a mace, and likewise a lotus.
He gave a *garuḍa*-flag, a celestial chariot, and divine *kaustubha* necklaces to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; he worshipped him with saffron and other offerings.
Vāsudeva, as well as his other incarnations, the Lord of Prakṛti, did likewise.
Pradhāneśa, Bhūman, Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭpuruṣa, and Sadāśiva, along with their respective Śaktis, arrived joyfully;
they indeed applied the sectarian mark (tilaka), collyrium (kajjala), and the forehead dot (bindu), and donned their crowns.
They gave them earrings, necklaces made of pearls and gems, signet rings, waistbands, and staffs;
they also gave them divine treasures fashioned in their respective abodes, in the forms of swans, lions, and elephants. ||42-43||
They gave excellent seats upon the ground to the embodied child;
likewise, the lords established in the eight enclosures,
the seven sages, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as the celibate ascetics.
They gave golden necklaces, flower garlands, golden vessels, and sandals;
water-pots, jars, and numerous garments;
and they offered Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa ever-new, divine wealth. (45–46)
The ancestors, sages, and gods; likewise, the parasol and the fly-whisks; celestial chariots and vehicles; swans, male servants, and female servants;
a staff fashioned of gold, a mirror, Śuka, and Menakā.
Various musical instruments and likewise jars of nectar;
the wish-fulfilling vine of desire and so forth, as well as sun-stones and moon-stones;
the garments of the lords of the directions and other ornaments, such as garlands of jewels.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras gave divine riches to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; they also presented their opulences.
The Nāgas, Sarpas, and Bhogins offered gems, rubies, and pearls.
At that time, they indeed gave necklaces, distinguished riches, and various articles;
the oceans gave jewels and pearls,
while the rivers and streams, such as the Varuṇā and others, gave even the finest substances and essences.
The mountains and the mines also gave various kinds of jewels:
gems, diamonds, pearls, rubies,
emeralds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, and topazes.
They gave him, in particular, karketanas, bhīṣmakas, pulakas, those called rudhiras,
crystal, coral, and puṃkharājas;
and the men indeed gave him auspicious garments from their own lands.
They also gave radiant blankets, vessels, ornaments, and towels;
as well as elephants, horses, bulls, cows, and buffaloes.
With sincere devotion, they gave gold and silver objects to the boy.
The trees and creepers offered sweet juices and worship with garlands and other offerings.
They also provided couches, excellent cushions, mats, four-legged stools, and the like;
as well as beds, lutes, carriages, and grinding stones.
They joyfully gave forth hearth-stoves, threshing-floors, and water-jars; they gave brooms and secret chests with handles.
They also gave pestles, spinning-wheels, and beautiful, priceless chests and boxes.

Then they joyfully gave water-jars, milk-pails, and vessels for churning buttermilk; as well as wooden troughs, curd-bowls, granaries, and ear-ornaments; along with flour-mills, grinding stones, bells, and oil-presses. (2.68.60–61)
They gave swings, hammocks, small riding horses, and four-legged couches;
silken garments as well as woolen clothes;
and excellent, richly adorned attire along with sugar and other sweets.
Then they gave fruits, fruit-bearing plants, as well as garlands of dried *elā* and other flowers;
they offered various kinds of cool sandalwood,
and indeed they gave leaf-shields, body-armor, and helmets.
Bowls, pairs of pots, cooking vessels, jars and the like;
water-pitchers, various vessels, and those used for baking in sealed containers;
water-sprinkling vessels, large basins, and plates for serving food.
They also presented spears, pikes, and various weapons and missiles;
at that time, they gave away countless riches of gold and silver.
[They honored him] with sandalwood, *abīra*, saffron, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and liquid *gulāla*.
With flowers, filaments, and fragrances, as well as with musk,
various camphors, dyes, coloring agents, and decorative leaf-patterns;
and with clusters of *tulasī*, as well as the leaves and blossoms of *kunda* and *ketaka*.
They worshipped the Lord, their master, with *campaka* flowers and fragrant oils.
(69) The deities and others, as well as the incarnations and lords, performed the *ārārtika* rite for Hari with one hundred and one excellent offerings. (70)
They joined him with blessings, circumambulated him, praised him, prostrated before him, and sat down upon their seats. Then, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, possessing grace, in an instant—
Then he granted them a vision of his own fundamental nature as the Self.
First, the members of the assembly beheld the supreme abode;
they also saw the liberated men and the liberated women right there.
They beheld the abode of Brahman, the Imperishable, as well as the liberated males and liberated females upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa’s form;
and they saw thousands of incarnations of Hari upon his forehead.
They beheld Goloka in the right eye and Vaikuṇṭha in the left eye;
they also saw Amṛta and eternal Kailāsa in the two ears,
Mahāviṣṇu in the nose, and Kāla on the forehead.
At the two corners of the forehead, they beheld the Supreme Lord and the Lord of Nature;
at the base of the nose, they saw the emanations (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva;
and in the middle of the face, those members of the assembly beheld the Vairāja form.
And in his fangs, they beheld the creators beginning with Śatānana;
and in his teeth, they saw the Rudras beginning with Śatanetra;
and situated upon the lines of his beard, they saw the Viṣṇus beginning with Sahasrahasta.
The members of the assembly beheld Mahāmāyā upon his upper lip and Pradhāna likewise upon his lower lip; they saw Śrī Lakṣmī upon his chin,
and on the hairs of his jaw, they beheld the lords of the eight enclosures of Māyā.
And upon her cheeks, they beheld millions of goddesses;
truly, in the roots of her hair they saw the world presided over by Brahmā and the other gods,
in the middle of her hair the heavens, and at the tips of her hair the nether regions beginning with Atala.
Those members of the assembly saw human beings upon his head and back;
thus they beheld the entire creation, consisting of the nature of Brahman, characterized by its causal essence,
subtle, eternal, perpetual, and indeed existing in the form of a seed.
Then they beheld again the gross creation, both the primary (kāraṇa) and the secondary (vaikṛta),
which had emerged from the region below his throat;
in his throat was the Supreme Brahman, and in his heart was the Imperishable Brahman.
They beheld Goloka upon his two breasts, Vaikuṇṭha on his right and left [shoulders], nectar on his shoulders, and eternal Kailāsa on his shoulders as well;
they beheld Mahāviṣṇu in his heart and Kāla in his throat.
And in the two armpits, they beheld the Lord of Pradhāna and the Lord of Prakṛti;
in the upper part of the heart, they beheld the manifestations (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva; and below the heart, as well as in the ribs, they beheld the Vairāja and the Creator (Brahmā).
One should place the Viṣṇus in the joints of the head, the Rudras in the joints of the back,
Mahāmāyā in the belly, and Pradhāna in the navel.
One should place Śrī and Lakṣmī at the sides of the navel, and the desired Āvaraṇas (enclosures) in the hips.
They beheld the Īśvarāṇīs below the hips and the Satīs at the base of the liṅga;

they saw Satyaloka and the other worlds within the body hairs, and the Guptas below in the regions beginning with Atala; and in those respective places, they also beheld the oceans and the mountains. (2.68.90–91)
Moreover, they saw the remainder of the tortoise upon his hips, as well as the great waters within his channels and vital constituents;
they beheld Kāmadeva at the tip of his organ, and the Daityas and Dānavas in his thighs.
And in their body hairs they beheld the sages, the ancestors, and the gods;
at their knees they saw human beings, and in the pair of their shanks they beheld the asuras;
and once again, at their feet, they beheld the nāgas, serpents, and others.
Beholding this great wonder—the form consisting of the three worlds and yet again consisting of Bālakṛṣṇa—they realized their own cause:
that Supreme Person from whom all incarnations arise. (95)
Then, having understood this, they meditated upon Bālakṛṣṇa for a moment.
(96) Then, at the conclusion of the assembly, the sound of bells arose;
accompanied by shouts of victory, the members of the assembly rose and departed for their own abodes. (97)
Honored with sweet drinks and the like, betel leaves, and sweet speech,
and further distinguished by celestial chariots and other marks of high esteem,
all those honored guests departed for their own homes and regions, as well as foreign lands, filled with happiness.

The principles (tattvas), the embodied beings, the insentient qualities such as taste and the rest, other groups of servants and so forth, having been honored, went to their respective homes; thereafter, these sages and ancestors departed for heaven and other realms. (2.68.99–100)
Then the supreme lords went to the worlds of Brahmā, the lords who dwell in the realm of Īśana; the Daityas and Dānavas went to their own abodes in Pātāla and other regions;
and the mountains, trees, creepers, rivers, sacred fords, and streams likewise departed. (101)
They also went to the lakes, fields, forests,
and groves; and having bowed down again and again to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they departed from the great palace pavilion that had been fashioned by the architect.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa made his departure;
and the venerable Sanatkumāra and Nārada also, having bowed down, departed for Badarī. Then the young women went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.

And thus, O Rādhikā, the most magnificent festival of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) for the Supreme Soul was celebrated in the month of Vaiśākha during His eighth year. By reading, hearing, or remembering this, one shall become a partaker of liberation.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Rewards upon the Great Beings, the Worship of the Lord, the Presentation of Gifts, the Divine Vision, the Dispelling [of Doubts], and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 68. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Age).
Chapter 69 [Author:
Chapter 70 → Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa! How should service and worship be performed for You? O Kṛṣṇa! Through what form of adoration does Your pleasure arise?
What gifts should be given for Your gratification, O Hari?
Which meritorious acts are praised, and which bring satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
All gifts are praised for the complete satisfaction of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Through devotion and worship, this Śrī Kṛṣṇa becomes fully satisfied. Whatever one desires should indeed be offered to Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of pleasing Him;
O beloved, every meritorious offering made therein brings satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa.

Those gifts which are bestowed by the faithful and those devoted to devotion, dedicated to the Lord of Śrī, truly never undergo decay. Those lunar days alone are most excellent upon which Kṛṣṇa is indeed encountered.
Among those [days], other lunar days are inferior compared to those on which service is rendered to the virtuous.
When the holy ones are honored, the Supreme Lord is honored;
he who hates them is a base soul and goes to a low birth.
Whether it be a man or a woman who, being mindful and devoted to Kṛṣṇa, worships with devotion, she is indeed my own body;
for I possess a Vaiṣṇava body.
Wise men or even those who are ignorant—sādhus must never be disregarded.
Therefore, those holy ones are my divine bodies;
one should always worship them with action, mind, and speech, through offering, service, food, and even through acts of reverence; the virtuous are to be satisfied in these ways. (2.69.10)

Rising early in the morning, remembering Me and bathing with auspicious substances, one should perform the worship of My form; for the service of the virtuous is indeed worship. Devotion to Me is true propitiation, and servitude is always the most excellent.
"O beloved, meditation must be performed by me for the sake of the virtuous and for the cause of liberation. The massaging of the feet of the virtuous must always be performed;
for I am present within their senses, and their satisfaction is my own satisfaction. (12–13)
They indeed should be worshipped with flowers endowed with fragrance and sap.
These are: the *campaka*, the *kunda*, the mango (*āmra*), the white *khadira*, the *śatapuṣpa*, as well as the *aśoka*, the *bakula*, and the *karavīraka*.
The *tilaka*, *japā*, *jātī*, *yūthikā*, and likewise *padminī*;
*kamalī*, *sthalapadmā*, *tulasī*, and likewise *kaumudī*;
*sūryamukhī*, *cammilikā*, *pārijāta*, and *sukesara*. (15–16)
O Rādhikā, these flowers— the ketakī, the hāraśṛṅgāra, the kadamba, the devadāruka, the sarjataru, and the kalpavallī—
should be offered by you to me during my worship, with the exception of the ketakī.
The bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the bhṛṅga leaf, and the tulasī leaf,
as well as the tamāla and mālatī leaves, are recommended for my worship.
One should also worship me with the tender sprouts of creepers and with darbha grass.

O beloved, I always worship with coral, the fibers of lotus stalks and the like, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, as well as buds, sandalwood, saffron, *uśīra*, and filaments; and I satisfy [the deity] with fragrant wood and incense.
Barley, wheat, and rice that have been consecrated with oblations;
sesame, mung beans, and the like, as well as black gram and paddy—these are dear to me.
Also, the pure gifts of cows and the gifting of land are dear to me.
O Rādhikā, gifts of clothing, food, and gold should be given for my pleasure;
in the month of Māgha, sesame seeds and fuel should be offered so that Hari may be pleased.
In Phālguna, rice, clothing, deerskins, and the like are recommended.
In Caitra, one should give very fine garments, beds, and seats. In Vaiśākha, fragrant and sweet-smelling substances should be given,
along with a cow accompanied by a water-pot, a palm-leaf fan, and excellent sandalwood.
By him [who does so], a son, wealth, a wife, a daughter, and a cow shall be obtained.
He should constantly listen to the story with devotion and worship Hari.
For him, there is the fruit of that horse-sacrifice accompanied by its sacrificial fees.

The merit arising from the gift of gold, land, horses, cows, elephants, and chariots is indeed supreme; of this there is no doubt. Whether a woman or a man, whoever listens to even a single verse of the narrative of Hari [attains that same merit]. (27–28)
He is pure and meritorious in this world, for he has resorted to all sacred fords:
at the Gaṅgā, in the Naimiṣa forest, at Puṣkara and likewise at Mānasa;
at Nārāyaṇa, Aśvapaṭṭa, Kokāmukha, and Prayāga.
Whatever preeminent merit exists in the month of Māgha shall arise from hearing this narrative.

Whatever fruit results from the Rājasūya sacrifice, whatever great reward is found in heaven, and whatever fruit is obtained in the world of mortals—all that shall arise from hearing this narrative. (2.69.30–31)
Whatever fruit is obtained from the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, and whatever fruit arises from the gift of sweet food;
whatever fruit comes from the gift of jewels during an eclipse of the sun or moon;
and whatever fruit is gained from protecting one's kinsmen and people during a famine— [all that is attained by this]. (32)
Whatever fruit arises from protecting and guarding the gods, the sacred fire, and virtuous brahmins;

whatever fruit comes from service to one's parents and parents-in-law, and to one's elder brother; and whatever fruit may be born from service to children and a cow—[all that is obtained by him]. (33–34)
O Rādhikā, may the fruit of that [merit] accrue to me here from listening to this narrative:
a pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt, myrobalan and the like, cool water in the month of Jyeṣṭha, fine clothing, and buttermilk. (35)

O beloved, curd, sandals, and an umbrella should be given for my pleasure. In the month of Āṣāḍha, O Rādhikā, a fan, milk, sugar, and garments should be offered, as well as vehicles and mounts for Hari’s abode.

O beloved, for my pleasure, one should always give all kinds of gifts— food, clothing, utensils, juices, and so forth— in their entirety during the month of Śrāvaṇa. In Bhādrapada, one should give milk-rice, salt, and rice mixed with jaggery.
Likewise, for my pleasure, one should offer nine grains, as well as honey and clarified butter;
in the month of Āśvina, one should present new grains, a bull, a horse, gold, copper vessels, garments, lamps, and so forth. (2.69.39–40)

In the month of Kārttika, one should indeed offer gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth, as well as lamps, new grain, and delicious food for my pleasure. In Mārgaśīrṣa, one should give vehicles such as donkeys, camels, and mules.

For my pleasure, in the month of Pauṣa, one should with great devotion give elephants, horses, sheep, goats, carts, and wagons; as well as houses, clothing, and the like, palaces, cities, and so forth, along with food endowed with the six flavors. 42–43.
One should indeed give female and male servants and ornaments for my satisfaction;
whatever is most cherished, whatever is possible, and whatever is pure in the home—
that which fulfills all desires should be given for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama.
He who causes a temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be built shall go to the imperishable realm (akṣara).
He who gives pleasure groves rich in flowers and fruits shall go to the imperishable realm;
he [delivers] eighty-four generations of ancestors and descendants of his lineage.
The builder of a temple for Viṣṇu shall cause himself, along with others, to cross over [saṃsāra].
And these virtuous ancestors and gods sing this song:
"Will there be someone in our own family who will become a devotee of Kṛṣṇa?"
May he who builds a temple for Hari surely grant us happiness;
may he who anoints the abode of Kṛṣṇa be ever with us, as well as the devotee who sweeps the temple—by whom we have been uplifted. (48–49)
Will one born in our lineage offer a banner, a lamp, incense, flowers, and ointment in the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa? Will he appear in our family and perform the Ekādaśī vow? (2.69.50)
The concluding rite, my worship, the fast, and the act of giving—[all these are accomplished].
Even one burdened with great sins, who paints the temple of Kṛṣṇa, becomes liberated from sin; blessed is the birth of him who belongs to me.
Blessed was the ancient King Manu, who in this world constantly established the supreme Mānavas as devotees of Viṣṇu;
he caused temples to be constructed in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He decorated the temples of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa with pure, beautiful paintings in five colors. He constantly placed lamp-vessels in the temple of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He joyfully gave golden vessels and indeed vessels for clarified butter; he gave garlands of victory in various colors, necklaces, and divine strings of beads dyed with deep saffron.
|| 56 || He also gave flower wreaths and divine neck-ornaments colored with great red dye.
Mañjiṣṭhā plants, Navaraṅgīyas, and white Pāṭalikās were situated there.
There were various beautiful groves, rich in flowers and abounding in fruit, covered with climbing vines and sprouts, and surrounded by Devadāru trees. (57–58)
He had enchanting, divine lakes constructed, adorned with pavilions and groves;
he gave them to the temple and placed around them decorated platforms presided over by skilled craftsmen. (59)
He caused to be constructed auspicious and divine palaces, comparable to the abodes of the gods, adorned with jewels and fashioned by those skilled in the Gandharva arts and the knowledge of passion;
in these, ascetics and celibate students were constantly honored. (2.69.60–61)
Vedic scholars, the best of Brahmins, sages, virtuous and stainless men; truthful women, chaste wives, female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and women devoted to Brahman—
thus were they all established by that very Manu in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
And Bhakti, together with his wife, went at the end to the abode of Hari.
Thus King Jyāmagha also, like Manu, performed [these acts] on earth;
through supreme devotion to the Supreme Lord, he attained the highest state of Brahman.
Therefore, O Rādhikā, you must indeed build a temple for me; worship me with diligence, as well as the saintly men and women who have taken refuge in me,
who follow virtuous conduct, who narrate sacred stories, and who bring about the welfare of the world.
O Rādhikā, properly honor my devotees by offering them garments, ornaments, jewels, cows, land, gold, and so forth;
by providing food, water for drinking, and services such as massaging their limbs. (66–67)
"Since wealth exists, perform the propitiation of the Lord in every way.
Thus addressed, Rādhikā also caused a supreme temple for the god Kṛṣṇa to be built in Goloka—
a mansion as beautiful as the moon.
Having duly consecrated the auspicious image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
Rādhā performed service and other duties for it,
including sweeping, smearing [with unguents], decoration, and feeding. (2.69.70)
Rādhikā herself offered sugar and other sweets, as well as lamps, incense, circumambulations, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and the festival celebrations;
the large-eyed lady also performed the cleaning of the vessels in Kṛṣṇa’s temple.
Rādhā herself indeed performed singing and chanting.
In this way, Rādhā always practiced devotion according to her husband's word;
for if a virtuous woman acts upon her husband's word, it is indeed the word of the elders.
Whether it be ill-spoken or well-spoken, that [advice] which is affectionate becomes like clarified butter for one bitten by the serpent of calamity who is otherwise devoid of mantra;
indeed, only the medicines of the words of the elders bring about the total neutralization of the poison.

Having drunk the nectar of the words of the elders and having assented to what they have said, the satisfaction that arises in men is not found even in drinking the Soma juice. Those for whom the elders are not teachers are indeed dead, even though they are living. (75–76)
They alone are to be pitied and will be ruined at every step,
where the elders do not provide guidance for those seized by the crocodiles of calamity;
nor are there any deliverers for them, and thus no peace exists for them.
For those submerged in the ocean of calamity and sinking amidst the waves of misfortune, there is no way whatsoever for their rescue except through the words of the elders.
Therefore, one should listen to the words of the elders or act upon them. (78–79)
He immediately attains perfection through the repeated blessings of the elders.
O Rādhikā, you must always act in such a way that I may be pleased;
I meditate upon my own fundamental form, Puruṣottama.
The followers of Kapila and others meditate upon me; other men meditate upon Kapila. The manifestations (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva meditate upon Puruṣottama;
and Nārāyaṇa, residing in Vaikuṇṭha, meditates upon Vāsudeva.
Śrī Viṣṇu meditates upon Nārāyaṇa, and the multitude of beings meditate upon Viṣṇu;
thus has this meditation been set in motion, handed down through the lineage of gurus.
Within the guru resides Viṣṇu, and within Viṣṇu shines the Infinite (Bhūman).
In the infinite, the vast and truly great Supreme Brahman shines forth.
Thus, through inquiry into one's own self, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; one should serve that Supreme Lord, salute him, and worship him as well. (84–85)
One should offer everything to this Supreme Self, who is the inner self;
through yoga, the illusory self and the inner self become possessed of the Supreme Self.
For the individual soul situated within Māyā, its qualities [are transformed] over a long period of time.
The impurities such as desire, anger, and the like, produced by *māyā*, belong to this [individual];
having arrived from one birth after another, he is said to be defiled by them.
His very nature (*svabhāva*) is pervaded by *māyā*, even throughout many successive births. (87–88)
One should conform oneself to the self; one ages through the yoga of the virtuous.
By taking refuge in the Supreme Lord as well, one indeed ages [in that state];
therefore, O Lord, there is the attainment of the path to liberation consisting of devotion through His grace.
By that [path], one goes to the Supreme Brahman, just as Jyāmagha did.
By reciting, hearing, remembering, or even causing others to hear this, O Rādhikā, heaven and liberation shall indeed be attained; there is no doubt in this matter.
"As Rādhā is, so shall a woman attain the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa;
and as Garuḍa is, so shall a man attain [His] service.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Fruits of Service, Worship, Giving, and Adoration of the Lord," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
