Śrī Rādhikā said: How did King Jyāmagha, though filled with his former nature, later attain liberation through the fruit of his worship? Tell me that.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to this ancient narrative that bestows detachment;
I shall relate the story of Jyāmagha, which spans many lifetimes.
The son of the sage Dhanurmagha was named Kauśika;
his son was Jāḍyamagha by name, who was dull-witted in appearance.
Like a fool, he did not speak, and like a blind man, he did not see. (3)
Having placed him on a swing at the door of the house,
his mother then went indeed to fetch water from the village well;
meanwhile, the crow-eyed Rākṣasī played with the boy from the swing.
Taking a handsome, tender child, she gave him to her own *rākṣasa*.
Upon seeing him, the *rākṣasa* asked, "My dear, what have you brought?
She replied, "This boy has been brought by me from Kauśika."
The Rākṣasa said: "O blessed lady, you have certainly not done what was right.
The powerful Kauśika, being enraged, will surely curse us quickly.
Therefore, place him swiftly upon a swing and bring him to his house."
"Or rather, go and place him right where she goes for the purpose of fetching water;
having seen him there, his mother will take him.
Having said this, the Rākṣasī quickly seized him and went to the pond.
Seeing that Satī had arrived there, he released the child before her.
Having reached her son, Satī also returned home carrying water;
considering it the good fortune of her son, she caused the worship of the planets to be performed.

He performed the pacification of obstacles and offered gifts with sincere devotion; yet, due to contact with the hand of a *rākṣasī* and from drinking the milk of a *rākṣasī*, the nature of a *rākṣasa* persisted in the child upon touch. (12)
This boy grew up and received the sacred thread (yajñasūtra).
Sent by his father to the house for the purpose of studying the Vedas, he encountered dullness;
because of his stupidity, he did not recite them, even though his father provided instruction.
Out of fear of being beaten and the like, he fell into a well at the boundary;
there stood an *āmalakī* tree, which had borne fruit for his nourishment.
Having eaten the *āmalaka* fruits and gone to the water in the well, [he drank] the auspicious water.
He constantly drinks from the tree and comes and goes by way of its root.
In the well concealed by trees and creepers, where the descent is by way of the root, this boy dwells happily, moving about unnoticed. (16–17)
Thus nourished, he would also go outside every night to eat grains, tubers, fruits, and other such things. Consequently,
his father and the others realized that he was either dead or had simply vanished.
However, once the mother, desiring sacrificial wood,
went to that boundary to fetch *āmalaka* logs;
having gathered the branches of trees, she was making a heap on the bank.
Just then, a boy happened to sneeze at the base of the well;
hearing the sneeze of a human being, he approached to look, and upon seeing his own son, he was overcome with extreme joy. (21)
The mother, distressed, called out to her son who was situated within the well.
Seeing his mother, the son’s voice became choked with emotion from love;
emerging from the well, he prostrated at his mother’s feet with lotus roots.
Having approached her own son and quickly gathered firewood,
she went to her own home accompanied by her son and bowed to her husband.
She then related all of her son’s actions to him.
Then that brahmin, having regained his son, was filled with joy and asked him:
"How did you leave the house, and how do you still live?
Why do you not speak, my son? Tell me the reason in every way. (25-26)
Then Jāḍya spoke of his own former history:
"Listen, dear father, to the cause by which I have resorted to muteness;
I shall tell you truly of my blindness and my dullness."
Formerly, I was a brahmin, an astrologer who could read the lines on the palms.
Through my incidental examination of the hand-lines of women, I fell into delusion and repeatedly developed a longing for the wives of others. (28–29)
And once, insulted by people with bitter speech,
I died by hanging and then went to the city of Yama. When a thousand years had passed from that time, and my remaining sin had been exhausted, [I returned].
He took birth in the forest as a tiger possessing a human body.
Then, having been seized by the king from his youth, he was placed in a cage;
though bound and remaining within the cage, he continued to exist in the state of a tiger.
My former knowledge was not lost, yet my desire increased;
though I am a tiger, I do not kill, nor do I even commit cruelty.
Along with the king and queen, I constantly sport in the garden.
I stood before the lion-throne and followed behind it;
I entertained him like a child, and I dwelt in that garden.
Thus, as the days passed, I attained youth.
Having become tranquil, I sit near the queen’s bathing pool;
whenever the king and queen have bathed, I then behold them with focused attention—
the queen bathing, sporting, and repeatedly becoming naked in the water.
Because of that, my desire, arising from past habitual tendencies, arose repeatedly.
King Sudarśana, having bathed, went to his own city for the sake of royal affairs,
leaving the queen behind in the garden.
Accompanied by her friends, she repeatedly delighted me— who was like a beautiful, auspicious tiger, well-reared as if I were her own son.
And I wandered again and again with them in the garden.
They would sometimes climb quickly onto my back;
at other times, standing by my side, I would perform a kiss upon her thigh with my mouth.
In this way, my desire for the queen grew rapidly.
Then, while all my friends were asleep in that dwelling during the night,
I lay upon the side of the bed and thought of the king’s beloved.
Due to former habituation, the god of love grew within my heart toward her.
By my touch, even her state of passion increased.
(43) I said to her: "O Princess, you who are endowed with fresh youth, you steal my heart, O Queen; tell me, for I have fallen under the power of love. (44)
She said, "O dear one with the body of a beast,
how can there be a union of pleasure between us here, you being a human and I a tiger?
Then I replied, "O Queen, it shall come to pass through skillful means."
Then, having embraced me, she set about to enjoy herself with me.
At that moment, I was spotted by a certain female friend;
she went quietly to the armed gatekeepers and informed them.
Having personally heard this news thus reported, the king said:
"I was indeed killed by the king and went to the realm of Yama.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, I became a white donkey."
I was employed as a bearer of burdens for people by a potter.
Even there, all my previous knowledge appeared clearly to me.
Once, however, the lords of the earth arrived at the potter’s [dwelling].
Then, beautiful maidens and women remained there for two days.
Among them, one beautiful young woman, while at her father's house,
desired to go to a village situated nearby at a distance of one *krośa*.
Her husband said to her, "Go, having mounted this excellent donkey.
You must return tomorrow; you should not remain there beyond that.
Having been addressed thus by her husband, the slender woman mounted the donkey.
He proceeded quickly, but halfway along the path, a river arrived there.
Full of water, she descended from behind me to bathe.
The potter and his caravan also went to the bank for the purpose of purification.

Seeing her, who was beautiful in every limb, alone and wearing a wet garment, I approached her under the pretext of drinking water. Having gone up to her as she was bathing, I fell upon her and embraced her out of desire. (95–96)
Under the influence of my past conditioning, I had her touch the *liṅga*.
At that moment, I was seen by the caravan people;
I was severely beaten with a staff and fell into the midst of the water.
Rising in an instant out of fear, I fled toward the south. As I was running away, a rope became tightly fastened around my neck; by means of that noose, my life came to an end at midnight.
Then I was born again in hell; from there I was released as a parrot. Thereafter, in a great forest, I was captured by a wicked Śabara, placed in a cage, and sold there to the son of a merchant.
I dwell constantly in the house in the company of young women.
Those young women always nourish me with rice-porridge made of fruits and other foods.
Once, however, there was a merchant’s daughter, a young woman named Candrikā.
She grasped me with both hands and took delight in speaking to me again and again;
placing me upon her breast on the couch, she made me recite a song.
Then, from the touch of her breasts and by the force of my former impressions, I—
Out of desire, he indeed flew up and repeatedly touched her in the secret place with his claws. Her hip was wounded by them, and she became enraged;
she struck me with a slender rod, and I fled from there out of fear.
By fate, her firm waist-knot became entangled around my neck;
a tight knot was formed by it, and consequently, I died in an instant.
Having suffered great misery in the world of Yama, I then became a bull.
I lived in the house of a caṇḍāla as a carrier of wooden carts. (67) Then the husband and wife went into the forest to fetch firewood;
at midday, the caṇḍāla went to the river to fetch water. (68)
A young Caṇḍālī woman was standing in the shade near a cart.
Out of lust and driven by the force of past habitual tendencies, I licked her.
Thus, those two were always on the riverbank for the purpose of gathering wood.
The rainy season arrived there; it had passed away and was returning once more.
One day, however, the Caṇḍāla became afflicted with fever at home.
The Caṇḍāla woman went into that forest for the purpose of gathering wood.
Then, having loaded the wood previously gathered onto a cart,
she led me to that river to give me water to drink. There, as she was bathing, I saw her naked, endowed with perfect beauty.
"Due to the influence of my past impressions, desire was established in my heart.
She put on her garments and, having bound me with a girdle, fastened me to the yoke of the cart with a thong. (73–74)
At that moment, I stood for a brief instant at the front of the yoke;
then, flying up, I alighted upon it along with the yoke itself.
Due to the blow from my forefeet, she then fell far away.
Bound by the yoke and dragged down by the cart, I was then cast into a pit by the two wheels which had sunk low;
falling with the cart, I was helplessly submerged in that bottomless hole. (76–77)
Bound by that very tether, I then met my death;
and that beautiful woman, having risen slowly, went back home.
Thereafter, by the command of Dharmarāja, I was plunged into hell.
"O father, born in your house, I am entirely one who remembers my former births.
I remember all those very same births today in their proper sequence;
and because of my previous practice, I have consequently experienced great sufferings. (2.70.79–80)
In this life, I shall indeed neither speak, nor hear, nor desire that by which sin might arise; I will not practice such a thing under any circumstances.
And the cause of my muteness and deafness is my memory of the past.
Even though it is insentient, consciousness alone is the cause, and nothing else.
Whether it be terrible sins committed through mind, action, or speech, or even that which is auspicious or inauspicious, whether it be bondage or even death—[consciousness is the cause]. (82–83)
Even such things as desire arise through previous habituation;
therefore, one who possesses discernment and knows this is never deluded by them.
But when a human being here remembers his former birth, [he is no longer deluded].
Then he will indeed attain cessation from those evils:
generosity, austerity, study, theft, sin, fame, virtue, wealth, knowledge, and the burning by fire—all these are indeed governed by the force of prior habituation. (85–86)
Non-violence, devotion to the Lord, steadfastness, tranquility, desire, affliction, suffering, and the attainment of a mate— these indeed arise through the power of prior practice.
Affection, natural disposition, faith, service, learning, arts, and wealth [likewise follow from past impressions].
"O householder, you are my teacher and I am your disciple, for we are bound by our former practice.
Therefore, dear father, I shall go to the forest for the sake of auspiciousness and the removal of sin.
Having said this, and having bowed down, Jāḍyamagha then departed for the forest.
Having previously gone to Kurukṣetra and then to Badarikāśrama, O Rādhikā, he performed various kinds of penance for the removal of his sins. In time, he met his death in the Gaṅgā.
Having had his sins destroyed by austerities, that ocean of merit, along with his latent impressions,
was thereafter born as the son of Raji in the city of Śrīnagara in Gaurjara.
He became Jyāmagha, the righteous and pure son of King Karkamagha.
At that time, even in Jyāmagha, there arose the impressions of his former animal births, a disposition toward asceticism, and devotion to Nārāyaṇa.
The prince became a rememberer of his past lives, yet he said nothing at all.
He does not hear, he does not laugh, nor does he direct his mind [to these things]. Being without a mental state (nirmanaska), he eats his food and likewise drinks water;
he wears clothes, ornaments, and decorations just as one who is without a mental state would. (94–95)
His kingdom, the enjoyments of sovereignty, wealth, servants, attendants, male slaves,
female slaves, elephants, and horses— all these indeed became equal for him. Even his bed of flowers and the rough earth were truly the same to him.
Whether the food is sweet, savory, richly fragrant, dry, or equal;
whether there is praise or blame, honor or contempt; and whether one is greeted with a salutation or treated with disregard—one has attained equanimity toward all of this. (97–98)
While he was living in this manner, youth arrived; and his father established him in the life of a householder through marriage.
He had no curiosity as to who his wife was or who his husband might be.
"What is desire? What is volition? What is pleasure, and likewise, what is cessation?
(2.70.100) And all this became equal for him at once; then, during the night, his beloved asked her husband the reason for his indifference. (101)
Then, remembering his wife Rādhikā, he spoke to her with composure:
"Whatever auspicious duty ought to be performed here in this rare human birth...

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Following One's Previous Nature and the Examination of Stupidity through the Example of Agha over Six Births," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to that which Jyāmagha spoke to the beautiful woman—
a knowledge that bestows liberation from everything, by the attainment of which nothing remains.
Jyāmagha said to his beloved: "Listen, O Goddess, you who are indolent regarding wealth!
Māyā, which causes delusion, is considered the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
It is Māyā, whose form is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by whom this entire world is sustained. (2)

By her alone does the Lord of Śrī himself create, nourish, and swallow this entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans. It is by presiding over her portions that the gods became possessed of power. (3–4)
By this power, all the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, [are sustained].
She alone is the source of the entire universe, the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa).
Neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor human beings, nor even Indra himself are capable [of creating it].
And those other embodied beings on earth who wish to cross over this illusion—
by worshipping Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, with blessings upon him, salutations to him, intent upon him, and devoted to him, such a person crosses over it. (6–7)
Once, the supreme devotee Indradyuti,
a brahmin who was ever devoted to Viṣṇu, set his mind upon beholding Māyā.
While he was thus longing, at one time, the Supreme Kalā appeared before him.
She revealed her divine form, born of Nārāyaṇa.
Having seen that virtuous lady, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, he bowed his head in salutation and then,
filled with humility, praised the Goddess and questioned her.
"O Mother, O large-eyed one, O auspicious lady marked with the signs of Viṣṇu—who are you?
O compassionate one, tell me now your true identity as it really is.
Having heard this, Lakṣmī said to him: "I am Śrī, the beloved of Śrī Hari."
The sages do not see me, nor do the gods, much less human beings.
I alone am Māyā whose essence is Nārāyaṇa; I am supreme and composed of that.
There is no difference between me and Nārāyaṇa; being composed of him, I am the Supreme Goddess.

And He is the Lord of All, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. Those who worship the Supreme Lord through knowledge and the yoga of action are absorbed in Him, are worthy of His grace, and are servants of Puruṣottama. (14)
They are His supreme devotees; I am not their master.
(15) By worshipping the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa through the surrender of everything and through knowledge, a devotee will certainly attain liberation. (16)
Having heard this, Indradyumna then asked Śrī again:
"Tell me how that Blessed Lord Īśa is to be known.
Thus addressed, that Māyā [then] took the Brahmin by both hands.
Having touched him, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "O sinless one, He will speak to you.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished. That brāhmaṇa remained there in meditative absorption (samādhi) in order to behold Śrī Hari.
Bestowing grace through that devotion, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself appeared— clad in yellow garments, a youth, and the embodiment of the universe.
Beholding Hari, Indradyuti bowed and praised that Lord.

O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Puruṣottama, O Keśava! (21) O beginningless Śrī Hari, O Lord, O Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations to You! O Soul of the Universe, O Creator, O Kṛṣṇa of infinite power, salutations to You! (22)

O Puruṣottama, whose form is full of infinite divine qualities that are themselves beyond all attributes, who is attainable through knowledge and accessible through grace— to You, I offer my salutations.
(23) Salutations to You, the one of infinite forms, whose nature is supreme bliss.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.
You are the father of all beings, the mother, the kinsman, the well-wisher, and the friend.
You are the imperishable, supreme abode, pure consciousness alone, the vast ether.
Your servants behold You, the Supreme Self— the support of all, unmanifest, infinite, and beyond darkness— by means of the lamp of knowledge.
I take refuge in Him whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Wherever the Blessed One resides is indeed the supreme abode of Śrī Hari.
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, you alone lead me there;
grant me knowledge, grant me Your state, and let not Your Māyā come near me.
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, smiling, repeatedly touched with his own hand that man who was falling at his feet.
As soon as he was touched by the Blessed One, he then attained divine vision.
Having known the supreme reality exactly as it is through his grace, [he] said:
"By your grace, there has arisen in me a knowledge that is free from doubt, eternal, focused solely on Brahman, and which bestows the perfection of bliss. (2.71.30–31)
"O Blessed One, instruct me here as to how you are to be served in every way;
and what must be done by me, your devotee in this world, O Supreme Lord?
(32) Having heard his devotee, Hari spoke to those devotees who are endowed with righteousness.
I alone am to be worshipped through knowledge and the yoga of devotion.
Having realized Me as the supreme reality, the manifestation, and the cause and effect, and having understood My supreme activity, one who seeks liberation should worship Me. (33–34)

Having abandoned all attachments and knowing this world to be my illusory manifestation (*māyā*), one should meditate upon me alone within one's own self; such a person shall behold me, who am higher than the highest.
O twice-born, having cultivated the threefold contemplation, worship me always.
Therein, one [consciousness] has me as its object, while the other has the Supreme Brahman as its sphere.
By way of distinction, the Blessed Lord shines in the supreme abode—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master of the Lord, the Sovereign. (36–37)

The Self-Ruler (Svarāṭ), the possessor of all powers, is the cause of all incarnations. Therein lies the second contemplation: that everything—both the insentient and the sentient—is the body of the Supreme Soul (Śrī Paramātman). All that is inert and all that is conscious is pervaded by the glorious Supreme Spirit.
Everything is dependent and subject to the control of the Supreme Lord Śrī Paramātman.
Within all those principles (tattvas), He shines as the inner Self;
He is this very Śrīmat Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Without that, not even an atom exists; that which is of its nature is composed of it.
Apart from that, there is neither the insentient nor even the sentient.
Therefore, everything is its form, and for that very reason, it is the possessor of form.
Just as the Divine dwells in the divine, so too does the Divine abide even in the insentient.
Boundless, stainless, unattached, and established as the inner controller,
He shines forth everywhere— in you, in me, and likewise in all else.
Thus, having perceived me in every reality, serve me;
then there is the third contemplation, which consists of one's own nature as Brahman.
One who possesses a body should think: "I myself am indeed of the nature of Brahman. (44)
That Brahman, transcending the qualities of its own nature, manifests [as follows]:
"I am Brahman. The individual self (jīvātman) is the state of being a living soul, which consists in being joined with karma.
Karma does not exist at all within Brahman; for that [Brahman] is the very nature of the Self (ātmatā).
Every action should be performed; by that, one is not smeared by Brahman.
Having contemplated in this threefold way, one shall attain the supreme state.
Even if incapable or like one who is deluded, one should take refuge in Hari.
Therefore, with every effort, being devoted to that and having that as his supreme goal, one should worship the Supreme Brahman; by that means, liberation will certainly be attained.
[This is] of that glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
All sovereignties together are called eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*).
Through the propitiation of the Lord, manifestation is attained by the devotee.
I am also present in the manifest world of effects, as well as in the unmanifest, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
I am the cause, the imperishable Brahman, and I am distinguished in every way.
(5.1) I am Nārāyaṇa, the inner controller (antaryāmī) there, worshipped by the Lord; I am the agent of creation, preservation, and dissolution. Knowing this, worship me. (5.2)
Therefore, through knowledge and action, you shall attain me by means of yoga.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; formerly I was the Great Virāṭ.
From me, the four-faced Brahmā, the Grandfather, was then created.
In that manner, Rudra was created by me from my own body, and likewise Viṣṇu; then Śrī,
the power of Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed Kamalā,
was created— she who is beautiful, gentle-faced, and enchanting to all embodied beings.
She of pure smiles, most serene, possessing divine luster and exquisite beauty;
wearing celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments, she is the abode of majesty.
She is Nārāyaṇī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti) of Viṣṇu.
Having seen her, Brahmā then spoke to me again and again:
"O Keśava, employ this one of beautiful form for the delusion of all beings, so that this vast creation of mine may increase. (57–58)
Thus addressed, I then spoke laughingly to the goddess Śrī:
"O Goddess, having deluded this entire universe—including gods, asuras, and humans—cast them down into the cycle of worldly existence at my command. (59)
Confine within yourself those who would devote themselves to you alone—

those who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge, self-controlled, most firmly established in Brahman, exponents of Brahman, free from anger, and dedicated to truth. But keep far away from those [others].
Keep far away from those Brahmins who have stilled their doubts through the knowledge of the Vedas and Vedānta, and who are devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
Those who worship the Supreme Lord through recitations, fire-offerings, and devotional services— [keep them at a distance].
Avoid with effort those who [engage in] Vedic recitation and sacrifice from afar.
Keep at a distance those stainless ones who are endowed with the yoga of devotion, whose minds are offered to the Lord, and who perform the surrender of all things unto Me.
Avoid those whose minds are attached to me, those who are devoted to meditation on my form, my virtuous servants, my devotees, and those who are most righteous.
What is the use of saying more here? Avoid the virtuous men and women.
Do not delude those who are fully absorbed in my worship by means of my own command.
Thus, this Māyā of mine, my beloved, being impelled by me, acts according to my direction; she does not bind my followers.
My devotee should worship her; he should honor Lakṣmī and Śrī.
When worshipped, she bestows abundant fortune, nourishment, intelligence, fame, and strength.
As the consort of the Blessed One, when honored, she grants auspicious riches.
She bestows service to Kṛṣṇa; therefore, one should worship Lakṣmī.
Indeed, by its very nature, an embodied being does not remain without action.
Action arises as twofold: that which is engaged (pravṛtta) and that which is withdrawn (nivṛtta).
That which is preceded by knowledge is "withdrawn" (nivṛtta), whereas that which is otherwise is "engaged" (pravṛtta). By practicing the withdrawn path, one attains that supreme state.
Forgiveness, self-restraint, compassion, charity, non-greed, and renunciation—these too [are part of it].
Straightforwardness, freedom from envy, and likewise visiting sacred fords;
truthfulness, contentment, faith, devotion, and restraint of the senses;
the worship of the deities and, especially, the honoring of the virtuous. (72–73)
Non-violence, pleasant speech, absence of backbiting, and great humility—
this dharma leads to liberation for all classes of human beings.
However, the realm of Prajāpati is the heavenly abode for Brahmins who perform ritual actions.

The station of Indra belongs to the Kṣatriyas who proceed according to their duties; likewise, the station of Marut belongs to the Vaiśyas who abide in their duties. The station of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who abide in service. (75–76)
That which is the station of the eighty-eight thousand ascetics who have drawn up their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) is indeed the Vairāja station for those who serve their guru.
And that which is the station of the seven seers (saptarṣi) is the station for those forest-dwellers who abide in righteousness.
The realm of Prajāpati is said to be for householders who abide in their duties,
as well as for ascetics, renunciants, those of sublimated vital energy, and virtuous givers;
and for chaste women who are devoted to Brahman, the Vairāja station is declared.
The immortal abode of yogis is that which is the unmanifested state of the Infinite;
but for devotees, it is above that, known as the sky, the supreme imperishable,
the blissful domain of the Lord from which one does not return again.
For those who have surrendered their souls to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī,
there exists the supreme abode, ruled by the Supreme Lord,
which is filled with all that is of the nature of Brahman and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. (8.1–8.2)
Listen further, for I shall proclaim another supreme knowledge that bestows liberation:

it is held that among all the stages of life (āśramas), there is a twofold division within the student stage (brahmacarya). These are the *upakurvāṇa* student and the *naiṣṭhika* student who is solely intent upon Brahman.
He who, having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules, enters the stage of the householder (gṛhasthāśrama) is to be known as an *upakurvāṇaka*. The *naiṣṭhika* remains until death.
Furthermore, the householder is considered to be of two kinds: the *sādhaka* and the *udāsīna*.
Devoted to the maintenance of his family, this practitioner becomes a householder.
Having discharged the three debts, he should become detached and indifferent.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and the ascetic (tāpasa) are considered to be of two kinds: those seeking liberation (maukṣika).
The ascetic (*tāpasa*) is one who is devoted to austerity, fire-offerings, sacrifice, and the study of sacred texts (87).

Beyond that, the seeker of liberation (*maukṣika*) is one devoted to meditation and service to Kṛṣṇa; the first type of renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) possesses knowledge, while the second also possesses devotion (88).
The monk who possesses discernment between the body and the self proceeds toward knowledge;
delighting in the self and satisfied with the self, this renunciation belongs to the portion of knowledge.
Endowed with right vision, he is solely devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa.
Delighting in Kṛṣṇa and satisfied with Kṛṣṇa, he is indeed a renunciant seeking liberation.
But the yogi exists as an āśrama within all āśramas at all times;
even while at home, the first [type] is unattached, for he is a man of discrimination and a king among yogis.
"I am Brahmā, of imperishable form and untainted; he, however, is the king of yogis.
I have taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman alone; he, however, is the king of yogis.
(92) Thus, the yogi who pursues the path to liberation may be of three kinds.
In this way, I have indeed entrusted to my subjects the means for liberation.
Everything was taught to Brahmā, and Brahmā then gave it to his sons, the sages; through those paths, they attained liberation.
These three qualities, which are for the benefit of the world, have been taken up by me alone;
they are mutually attached, they subsist upon one another, and being devoted to each other, these manifestations of the Supreme Lord sport in play. (95)
Due to the association with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, three forms of mine alone, the Supreme Self, have been proclaimed:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
I am Brahmā and I am Mahādeva; we are not distinct from one another in the ultimate sense.
Having divided myself by my own will, I abide as the Inner Controller;
therefore, Mādhava is to be worshipped in all three ways with every effort, if one desires that imperishable state known as liberation without delay. (98)

A twice-born man should serve me with devotion according to the dharma of his caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama). With a mind full of devotion and a lifelong vow, he should worship me, even while remaining in the Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, or Śāmbhava stages of life.

Bearing those marks, self-restrained, and affectionate toward His devotees, he should meditate upon Me, worship the gods, and be devoted to the supreme knowledge. He who has taken refuge in the Lord Nārāyaṇa as a seeker of protection—
One should wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead with sandalwood paste and other substances.
Śambhu resides at its top, Viṣṇu in the middle, and Brahmā at its base.
One who has taken refuge in Brahmā, the supreme lord and seed of the universe, [attains liberation].

One should maintain that great *bindu* on the forehead, situated in the middle of the brow. The upper line is *Śāṃbhavī*, and in its center Viṣṇu is established. The lower line is *Brāhmī*; thus the three gods reside there.
A devotee who has taken refuge in Śambhu should indeed wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash on the forehead,
equal to the moon and occupying half its space.
Śambhu resides above, Viṣṇu in the middle, and the Unborn (Brahmā) below.
From that, this [universe] evolves, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Rudra’s forehead is like the sun; Vaiṣṇava [the forehead of Viṣṇu] is indeed like the moon;
and Brahmā’s forehead is like fire, always radiant with its sectarian mark (tilaka).

When the *tilaka* is applied, the abode of the gods and the Lord itself truly comes to be [on one's forehead]. (108) Having thus borne this supreme mark and having cultivated discernment within yourself, offer yourself at the feet of the Lord and attain the eternal state. (109)
Thus, O Rādhikā, Jyāmagha gave to his wife this knowledge centered on the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which was perfected with realized wisdom (vijñāna).
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa gave it to Purandrayuti.

"All this knowledge, even for those engaged in ritual action, bestows liberation. Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of how King Jyāmagha told his wife Dhanālāsā everything previously spoken by the Blessed One to the Brahmin Indradyuti," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 71: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 72 [[Author:
→ Chapter 73
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! Understand this most wonderful knowledge.
[It concerns] the celibate student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic. || 1 ||
The stages of life (āśramas) are established in their proper sequence, though they may also be undertaken otherwise for a specific cause.
Having attained knowledge and realization, and having reached supreme detachment,
one should go forth into the life of a wandering mendicant either from the stage of the student (brahmacarya) or from that of the householder (gṛhastha), as is appropriate.
Having taken a wife according to the prescribed rites, he should perform various sacrifices.
He should procreate sons through righteous means, and when dispassion arises, he should renounce.
Now, if by the force of his dispassion he is unable to remain at home— (3–4)
One should first become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and later take recourse to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*);
however, one who possesses the force of extreme dispassion (*ativairāgya*) should take recourse to renunciation alone.
Whether having gone through the stage of the forest-dweller or directly to renunciation, [one should proceed].
He should not return to his home, nor should he enter into union with a wife.
Detachment is prescribed for all [stages] regarding renunciation;
however, one who is not detached falls from renunciation—of this there is no doubt.
Or else, he may live properly in a single stage of life until the end of his mortal existence;
being devoted to that object of knowledge and its knower, he is fit for immortality.
One who is perfected in both knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*) is fit for becoming Brahman.
(9) Having surrendered all actions to Brahman, free from attachment to desires and the like, performing them with a serene and unattached mind, one attains that state. (2.72.10)
That which is to be given is given by Brahman; indeed, it is Brahman alone that is given.
The gift is given to Brahman; this is the supreme offering of Brahman.
I am not the doer; Brahman alone performs all this in such a manner.
This is the offering of action to Brahman; it is dedicated within Brahman.
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī be pleased by his own action.
Thinking thus, that which is performed is this supreme offering to Brahman.
One should also renounce the fruits to the Supreme Lord;
thus, the offering of the fruit to Brahman is unsurpassed.
Whatever obligatory action is performed as a duty alone, free from attachment—
Action performed by the wise may indeed become a giver of liberation.
(15) If the renunciation of the fruits of actions is not directed toward Brahman, then one would be bound by that fruit; from that, there would be an obstruction to liberation. (16)
Through this offering, sin or merit that leads to liberation—
whether of this life or of previous lives— is destroyed, and there arises clarity of mind. Furthermore, self-knowledge arises, and from that, the knowledge of Brahman is born.
From knowledge conjoined with action, right yoga is born.
From yoga, one attains the presence of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, by every effort, whether devoted to this or that stage of life (āśrama), [one should practice]. 18–19.

One should perform actions for the sake of pleasing the Lord so as to attain freedom from action (naiṣkarmya); having attained the realization of Brahman through His grace, one becomes free from action. Immersed in the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, which is one's own self, such a person has conquered the senses.
Solitary, free from possessiveness, and peaceful, even while living he is like one who is liberated.
He beholds the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord. Ever-blissful and free from limiting adjuncts, he attains absorption in Śrī Hari. (21–22)
Therefore, O Rādhā, one should practice that state of actionlessness which consists of offering [all deeds] to Him;
through that, for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord, one shall attain the supreme state.
Such steadfastness as is thus established bestows eternal perfection.
But no human being attains perfection by transcending this [duty].
(24) Thus Jyāmagha, having reflected upon all that was beneficial for himself, explained his entire realization, preceded by wisdom, to his wife. (25)
Having realized through wisdom that his own beloved wife was of the nature of Brahman, and having bestowed the kingdom upon his younger brother Śrī Magha, Jyāmagha— the beloved of Hari—
along with his wife, prostrated at the feet of his parents.
Having embraced his brother and inquired after his welfare in every respect,
and having received the blessings of the subjects on the bank of the Sābhramatī river,
he established a constant association with the virtuous in that hermitage frequented by the holy.

His brother proclaimed that city as Śrīnagara, together with his own name. Thereupon, Jyāmagha caused a most auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice to be performed on the bank of the Sābhramatī through the agency of his brother.

Out of devotion to him, at the time of the *homa*, the glorious and imperishable Narayana arrived there at the sacrificial pavilion in embodied form. Agni himself appeared in person, and Brahma and Shambhu likewise came there.
The deities consumed the oblation offered by Jyāmagha.
Śrī, being pleased, said to him: "By your devotion, Janārdana is gratified;
indeed, he has given me the command to remain in your kingdom."
"I shall not dwell alone in your city;
I have become satisfied by the sacrifice along with my husband and the gods.
Therefore, cause a beautiful temple to be built here, where I may dwell forever."
Having heard this, Jyāmagha, the king of devotees, rejoiced along with his brother.
Having spoken thus, he said again: "Go to Kuṅkumavāpikā;
there lies the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, where I dwell eternally."
Devoted to the service of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, (36) through the service of that couple, joined with the spirit of servitude, I shall behold my Lord; of this there is no doubt. (37)
Having spoken thus, she vanished from the sight of the gods and men along with Nārāyaṇa.
The sacrifice reached its completion, and prosperity increased in the city.
Jyāmagha, having bowed to his parents and bestowed the sacrificial fees, [departed] Śrīmagha.
Accompanied by his wife, he departed by boat upon the Sābhramatī river. Śrī Magha had a seven-storied temple constructed at the Nārāyaṇa ghat, which was as high as a cloud and possessed a spire.
There, at the very outset, the King had Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Lakṣmī installed through Vedic rites; a garden was offered to him,
and worship, food offerings, ornaments, and festivals were also ordained.
In this way, Śrīmagha also worshipped the glorious Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa.
Having enjoyed that kingdom for a hundred thousand years, he departed for the supreme abode.
Jyāmagha also returned from the path of the river to the ocean at Stambha.
Then, having visited the holy site of Śrīgopanātha and thereafter,
he abandoned the boat and traveled by carriage to Kuṅkumavāpikā;
there he beheld Aśvapaṭṭasara and gazed upon the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
Beholding the ground, richly endowed with divine splendor, he attained supreme bliss.
Seeing the magnificent palace of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
its peaks kissing the heavens, and beholding the banners, he spoke with a faltering voice.
First, he prostrated like a staff and then performed a circumambulation of him;
at that moment, a Brahmin in the form of a youth arrived there—
Śrīnivāsa, who was beautiful and the vessel of all loveliness.
With eyes like the petals of a lotus and fingers endowed with subtle lines,
his chest adorned with a radiant gem and graced by an aura of splendor,
he welcomed them while showing them the sacred sites. 48–49.
The brāhmaṇa led him to the temple where the Beloved of Śrī resides—
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, seated upon an elephant throne—
and having shown Him to him there, he vanished.
Jyāmagha and his queen were filled with supreme wonder;
having obtained the direct vision of the drama of Mānava,
and furthermore, having obtained the vision of Bālakṛṣṇa there.

Having realized that there was oneness between the two in their essential nature, their inherent disposition, their virtuous conduct, and even in their physical forms, and having thus attained their purpose, they thought:
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for Jyāmagha and his wife! (53)
Then Bālakṛṣṇa appeared directly in the form of a young brahmin boy. He brought [him] to his own home and then vanished.
His favor was attained through the service of merits accumulated over many lifetimes.
Because the Blessed One himself had come to his own home,
they then beheld Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous mother Kambharā,
and the Blessed One with great joy. (56)
Upon seeing Śuka and beholding the beloved circle of gods,
they rejoiced exceedingly and worshipped the Supreme Lord with sandalwood, unbroken rice, saffron, ushira, and water mixed with clay.
With flowers, *tulasī*, *kalhāra*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *sukeśara* blossoms,
as well as with necklaces, ornaments, garments, and other articles, the two of them indeed performed worship. Then, they placed offerings such as golden vessels and the like before him.
They both gave sweet cooked food, vessels, betel-leaf, water,
and other offerings to Śrī Hari, as well as to their mother and father;
they performed the ārātrika rite and prostrated themselves like a staff.
Bālakṛṣṇa, however, asked whether their journey had been auspicious, and likewise inquired about their welfare during their travels, their lack of affliction, and their arrival in comfort.
Then Hari led the couple away for the purpose of performing the rites of hospitality.
He provided them with food, water, betel leaves, and other such items.
Hari granted them an independent mansion for their residence, and he gave the couple male and female servants and all manner of goods. (63–64)
Then, at evening, that king rested by the Aśvasarovara lake;
he went there to bathe according to the prescribed rites, and having bathed, he performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā).
[He visited] the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, which is endowed with ten million sacred bathing sites (tīrtha).
He performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with one hundred and eight wicks.
Having drunk water, he returned to his own palace accompanied by his followers.
The king spent the night in comfort and, after performing his morning ablutions, [resumed his duties].
Having worshipped his lord, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the husband of Śrī,
and having performed the *ārātrika* and other rites, he bestowed gifts of every kind:
gold ornaments, garments, wealth, pearls, and many gems.
He fed the brahmins, sages, and noble maidens residing at the sacred site.
He also undertook a pilgrimage to all the gods.
Having performed a circumambulation of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he returned home.
Blessed indeed is the guṇḍraka tree, blessed is the auspicious tintiḍikā;
blessed is the pomegranate tree, and blessed are the two jambu trees.
Blessed is that bael tree where the Blessed One shines resplendent.
Blessed is that Kuṅkumavāpī, the most excellent among the best of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Blessed am I, Jyāmagha, and blessed is my beloved Dhanālasā, who have taken refuge in the primordial Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (72–73)
"Indeed, a dwelling exists for you, for you shall dwell in the world of Brahmā.
As he was reflecting thus, the queen spoke to him with urgency:
"Have a most magnificent palace built here, as Śrī has shown it to you."
"Where the god Nārāyaṇa may always receive our worship.
Having heard this, the king reflected for a mere moment: "What kind of vast and lofty temple should be caused to be built? (75–76)
He beheld a supreme, most excellent, white, and expansive radiance;
therein, within that space, he saw a single vast peak.
There, in its center, was an auspicious form consisting of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
On his left, he beheld those wives of divine appearance— Rādhā, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Māṇikī; and on his right,
he saw his father, his mother, and his sister Santuṣā.
He beheld the Blessed One, Śuka, and his beloved kinsmen of the monkeys; he saw this entire circle and beheld his queen. And as she remained there in service, all of that vanished from sight.
Then the king summoned the preeminent artisan there and spoke to him.
That best of artisans fashioned a painted cloth exactly as it had been described.
Then, to the west of the horse-stable, he built a beautiful temple.
He caused the entire installation to be performed according to the prescribed rites,
and had thirteen images fashioned by the brahmins.
Having summoned Lomaśa, he also caused his own palace to be constructed.
And he received the auspicious initiation (dīkṣā) endowed with the principles of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
In his own magnificent palace, that great and supreme Vaiṣṇava, together with his wife, worshipped the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with devotion. || 84-85 ||
Through devotion, he exhausted the tendencies from his previous births by means of constant vows, austerity, meditation, and a spirit of service;
having become a great devotee of the Lord, he performed everything with sincere feeling.
He composed the twenty-four principles for the sake of Hari;
the king offered his consciousness to Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa and employed his goodness (sattva) for the manifestation of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then Śrī Hari appointed *rajas* for the purpose of his manifestation so that Hari might be pleased; he assigned *tamas* to the elements for the purpose of dissolution.
He then employed the *mahat-tattva*, which is of the nature of intellect (*buddhi*), for the sake of discernment.
He made the *citta* his faculty for reflection and his faculty for self-conceit;
he made the *manas* his faculty for deliberation, the ears his faculty for hearing the narrations of Hari, the skin his faculty for touch, and the eyes his faculty for seeing him. (2.72.90–91)

His tongue was for tasting its grace; his speech was for its glorification; his nose was for the fragrance of its flowers; and his voice was for the description of its virtues. His two hands were always employed in service, in attendance, and in devotion.
She performed obeisance at his feet during her approach and likewise circumambulated him;
she offered water for his feet when he took his seat, and she served as his emblem during his delight.
She provided strength for bearing his burden and skill in attending upon him. (93–94)
He offered everything pertaining to his body to Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and the queen likewise offered everything to Bālakṛṣṇa—
those very elements, the objects of the senses, and even that which is auspicious and inauspicious.
She herself became a guest of Hari and gave everything to him;
she likewise offered all her bodily actions to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
She constantly performed his worship, remembering him, and offered him salutations and hymns of praise. (96–97)
He always performed the massaging of Viṣṇu’s feet, His worship, and even servitude;
friendship, play, playful speech, laughter, and even mirth;
as well as chanting and the offering of everything to the glorious Kṛṣṇa.
And the queen also became a highly devoted Bhāgavata.
She performed the sweeping and smearing [of the temple], as well as the preparation of cooked offerings, the fetching of water, and the washing of garments and other such tasks. (2.72.100)
The washing of the vessels, as well as the fetching of flowers;
the stringing of garlands, and likewise the bringing of *tulasī*;
the fanning of the breeze, and also the swinging of the cradle.
With her own hands, she performed everything, even the spreading of the bed. She constantly massaged the feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; like a maidservant, she then offered herself entirely to him.
Thus associating together, those two auspicious ones, relying on divine merit,
became cleansed of all taint through the grace of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And they were initiated by Lomaśa into the supreme Śrīvaiṣṇava mantra.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations.

(1.05) Having received this mantra and having worshipped Hari on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha at sunrise, one should remain steady for a moment, absorbed in meditation. (1.06)
Then a divine, imperishable, and auspicious celestial chariot arrived,
accompanied by its attendants and possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Jyāmagha and Dhanālāsā, having cast off their bodies, ascended that celestial chariot.
By the command of the attendants, the two of them, possessing divine forms,
ascended the celestial chariot and quickly went to the imperishable, supreme abode.
And shouts of victory arose in the abode of Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Rādhikā, those two attained liberation through devotion.
The reader, the reciter, and even the listener of this shall go to the state of liberation.

(2.72.110) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Jyāmagha and his wife Dhanālasā through the devotion of self-surrender at Kuṅkumavāpī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The seventy-second chapter.
Chapter 72: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 73.
[Author: Chapter 74.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to another auspicious marvel of Hari.
In Gaurjara there flows a beautiful river named Dhṛdhara.
To the south of its bank stands the auspicious city of Āmoda,
a dwelling for many eminent merchants and devoted to the service of the gods.
It was inhabited by people devoted to their endeavors and endowed with wealth; there,
many kinds of men dwelling on the banks of the river Hrādhara resided as devotees of Śambhu,
excellent ones who were intent upon devotion to Śambhu.
And others on the banks of the Dhrādharā were devoted to worship and recitation;
they went to and returned from the city after having beheld Śambhu.
There, on the bank of the Dhrādharā, was an auspicious Vaiṣṇava temple.
Where Hari Nārāyaṇa, endowed with splendor,
shines forth assuming the form of an image, he is worshipped and honored by people;
he is also saluted and served by Vaiṣṇavas at all times, especially in the early morning.
Pure holy men dwell there on all sides of the temple.
Through association with them, a merchant named Sudhana became a Vaiṣṇava;
he would always first bathe and worship the deities. (7–8)
Having bowed to the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, he then proceeds to the abode of Śambhu,
which is filled with excellent gardens, adorned with trees and creepers,
and graced by noble trees resplendent with fruits, flowers, and the like.
Adorned with water-tanks and beautifully graced by the abundance of crops upon its pillars,
it was free from all affliction for devotees and bestowed peace even by its mere sight.
And within that great enclosure (mahālaya) was the Āmodeśvara Liṅga in its garden.
It shone with the brilliance of pure crystal, divine and captivating.
In its service, O best of Brahmins, was the great seer Varcakāyani,
who was devoted to celibacy and dedicated to the performance of sacrifices and fire-offerings.
Eating only fruits, sleeping in the open air, possessing divine vision,
he was a supreme Vaiṣṇava devoted to the dharma of service toward Śambhu.
He was a master of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and various sciences, and was dedicated to sacred discourses and narratives.
Having attained emaciation through his vows, his body possessed veins that had become visible;
devoted to the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
he would daily take refuge in a bower of trees in the Śiva-grove at evening.
The gods deliver this discourse, which humans and others hear.
Men, women, birds, and all embodied beings dwelling there listen to it constantly; Sudhana, filled with devotion, goes there every day to hear it.
There, indeed, the learned one [heard of] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī,
the son of Śrī Kambharā in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra—
the Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the child Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (18)
It is endowed with every power, served by Śrī Rādhā, Ramā, and others;
it shines within the Mahālaya near Aśvapaṭṭasara,
as well as the hermitage of Lomaśa and many sacred fords (tīrthas).
Then, for that merchant Sudhana,
there arose a desire to behold the primordial God Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa— who had assumed the human drama— in person; a desire that bestows liberation.
Day and night he constantly meditated upon the beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa.
From that sage Śrīvarcakāyani, he received the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (22–23)
He recited that supreme mantra and meditated on the form within his heart.
Even though he desired to see Satī, he considered a distant location;
indeed, he found satisfaction in worshipping her at home through offerings and other rites.
He constantly worships Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. He offers food oblations in the morning, at midday, and at the onset of night;
he also performs the waving of lights, recites hymns of praise, and engages in the chanting of mantras.
He also performed auspicious festivals with wealth acquired through righteous means.
His wife, sons, grandsons, and others were devotees of Viṣṇu who took refuge in Śrī Hari;
indeed, they were intent on the service of the gods and devoted to the service of the virtuous.
They were intent on hearing the sacred narratives, with their intellects dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
They constantly served saintly men and women with wealth and other gifts, as well as with vehicles, carriages, food, and by massaging their feet and similar acts. (28–29)

While Sudhana was always living in this manner, Lord Hari himself manifested visibly within the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in his home, and there, in person, He accepted the food and other offerings presented to Him. (2.73.30)

Then, smiling, Bālakṛṣṇa granted his grace to that devotee; he thus acted constantly, vanishing from the physical form. Once, the merchant Sudhana, for the sake of his grandson's wedding, [prepared for the ceremony].
Having adorned his own army with wealth, ornaments, garments, and the like, accompanied by excellent men, women, and kings, and traveling on vehicles such as chariots,
he proceeded out of joy toward the city of Kanyā, which was filled with the sound of golden bells.
Having crossed the river by boat and traveled to Jāmbusāra,
when he had performed the marriage rites and was returning,
twenty notorious thieves were on the bank of the river named Dhṛtadhārā. (34–35)
Those fierce-looking men, armed with weapons, rushed into the thicket of trees;
those formidable ones struck the drivers of the carts as well as the protectors of the army with clubs and other implements.
The horse-thieves, who were actually robbers, carried away gold, ornaments, silver, garments, and other such excellent wealth;
they also seized food and other provisions, so that Sudhana became deeply distressed.
Then his family became like a caravan abandoned by its wealth;
the women were devoid of ornaments and stripped of their finery and fine garments;
likewise, the kinsmen and relatives were overwhelmed with grief.
The army was dispirited, destitute of wealth, and devoid of luster.
The womenfolk and the circle of female companions became overcome with grief and agitation;
and at the time of the wedding, the daughter-in-law was seized by inauspiciousness. (2.73.40–41)
"The loss of my fortune was surely a sign of impending poverty.
Reflecting thus, Sudhana established firmness in his heart;
taking refuge in himself by means of the Self, he remembered Bālakṛṣṇa.
With supreme devotion, he praised his own beloved Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the best of men and his personal deity:
"O Lord of Grace, Ocean of Compassion, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence! (43–44)

O protector of those who have come for refuge, you previously provided protection for an elephant here within the forest; indeed, you also provided protection for Prahlāda amidst the host of Dānavas in the midst of the waters. (45)
And by you, O Marut, protection was afforded within the inner sanctum.
You are the protector, you are the creator, the eternal Supreme Self.
Protect, protect us, O Lord, ocean of compassion, from the terror of thieves! 46–47.
The thieves have seized all the possessions and the livelihoods of householders;
therefore, rescue them from their suffering—their gold, silver, ornaments, and the like.
For householders, wealth and property are their sustenance, while for women, ornaments are their very substance.
Peace and wealth belong to the virtuous, and the food offered to them is Hari himself.
(49) Indeed, without wealth there is no standing at all in this world;
O Lord, grain, clothing, and worldly dealings are all established upon wealth. (2.73.50)
Even if there are many defects in a substance, its qualities are the granters of life;
therefore, wealth is always a source of support.
In that regard, O Kṛṣṇa, for merchants, gold, ornaments, and the like [are essential].
All my possessions exist, yet they have been entirely stolen by thieves.
O Lord, this severe humiliation has come upon me because of my devotion to you;
those who lack devotion have become objects of ridicule.
O Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, deliver us from calamities;
make Your name "Protector of Devotees" meaningful.
Otherwise, O Janārdana, people will [censure] You for the shattering of their hopes.
Thinking that their Lord provides no protection, they will abandon their devotion.
Indeed, those who are distressed worship Kṛṣṇa, the remover of distress, only as long as they are in distress;
and those seeking wealth worship Kṛṣṇa, the giver of wealth, only as long as they have need of wealth.
Those who desire to know worship Śrī Hari only so long as their desire to know persists; once He is known, they indeed desist.
But for those who are intent on their own self-interest, there must also be a means of deliverance.
O Lord, however one may hope for You and however one may take refuge in You,
so do You fulfill the desires of Your devotees; O Master,
grant me protection as well, so that I may cultivate devotion.
Having thus entreated him there in the forest, he, distressed, shed tears.
But having heard his request, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari quickly went to where the thieves were, disguised in the form of a brāhmaṇa.
The thieves, having sat down together in the shade of a tree on the bank of the river,
divided the gold, the silver, and the wealth; and while the distribution of the ornaments and other items was taking place, a beggar— || 61–62 ||
Having become a wandering mendicant (*vicitta*), Bālakṛṣṇa, like a pauper,
wandered about with his body covered in dust and clad in nothing but the sky;
wearing only a loincloth, he went forth to beg for food.
"I beg for food here; it is pleasing to me who am hungry.
O fortunate and auspicious merchants, may you give to me.
Wealth is not desired by me; I require only food. (64–65)
The thieves said, "There is wealth here; take it, sir!
If it pleases you, we shall give you a silver coin—tell us so.
But the mendicant then replied, "I have no need for wealth."
For there are indeed many faults in wealth; it bestows suffering and creates enmity.
Wealth causes one to abandon righteousness and quickly incites violence;
indeed, wealth summons sudden calamity.
There is exertion in the acquisition of wealth, great anxiety in its preservation,
and constant worry regarding its depletion during enjoyment, along with the defects of being plundered by thieves and the like.
Therefore, a mendicant seeking happiness should not desire wealth.
"O sirs, you who possess wealth, give food here!
Even one who possesses a silver coin does not find peaceful sleep before him, because he is always afraid of separation for some reason or other. (2.73.70–71)
Devoid of wealth, birds beg only for fruit;
having eaten upon the branches, they wander there itself, free from ailment.
And children, having eaten their meal, sleep happily upon the ground.
But anxiety devours these: the elderly, the young, and the wealthy.
(73) Gems such as pearls and diamonds are by their very nature stones; yet they serve as invitations to death. (74)
Gold, silver, ornaments, garments, and wealth—whether earthly or of light—are always causes of anxiety and agitation;
they bind one to the notions of "I" and "mine," giving rise to passion and hatred. (75)

In the end, they bestow birth and death, being the very nature of latent impressions and greed. I do not desire wealth consisting of that [worldliness], for the property of others leads to destruction.
O great people, why is so much wealth acquired here? 76–77.
Thus questioned and addressed with "Go! Go! in anger, they spoke there;
meanwhile, one of them took up an iron staff and rose up to strike the mendicant who stood there like a wretched man.
At that moment, the mendicant vanished from that place.
Beholding this display of power, they were struck with supreme wonder; yet, deceived by the illusion, they thought it must have been either a spirit or a *piśāca*.
Just then, a crow arrived and spoke from atop the tree;
perched upon a withered branch, it then became an inauspicious omen.
Then, they indeed divided the gold and wealth among themselves.
When they were dividing the jewels, such as necklaces and garlands, Śrī Hari was mounted upon a horse, as were his other royal servants;
fifty cavalrymen, armed with weapons, followed swiftly behind them. (82–83)
Dressed as royal messengers and the like, they arrived there from all sides, uttering sounds of "shame! and shouting, "Let them be attacked!
Let them be killed! Let them be seized! These are thieves! (84)
Speaking thus, they then formed a defensive array around [the city] like a rampart,
beautified by horsemen. Those thieves were seized with fear and then fled in all directions.
Having cast aside their gold, silver, garments, diamonds, and pearl necklaces at that very moment,
yet unable to find a path and powerless before the array,
they truly fell into the hands of the soldiers.
Helpless, they were made into hand-cuffs and nooses of rope by them.
Some were struck with sticks, some were beaten with whips;
some were struck with clubs, with hands, and with creepers. (88–89)
Punished by his soldiers, they entreated the Lord;
placing blades of grass between their teeth and touching the ground with their heads,
wretched and with hearts faltering, they begged for forgiveness for their offense.
The compassionate Blessed One taught them once more for the sake of turning away from their faults. They all then made a vow:
"From this day forward, we shall never again commit theft. || 91-92 ||
"O Great King, grant forgiveness and release them from their bonds.
To those who were thus entreating him, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
having placed water in his hand, made a vow regarding that act of theft.
Indeed, one must never commit theft, nor cause such a thing to be done.
Then, on the lovely and enchanting bank of the Dhṛtadhārā river,
the Blessed One released them and took back the wealth that had been stolen.
Taking all that gold, silver, jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth which had been there,
Sudhana went to where Keśava resided with his assembly, along with his cavalry. ||96||
He gave all the wealth seized from the hands of the thieves to Sudhana.
Sudhana and his caravans rejoiced at the recovery of their riches.
The king’s officers returned all the gold and silver to the caravan.
The soldiers of Hari gave back to each person those very ornaments, garments, and so forth, as well as gems, pearls, and diamonds, which had belonged to them;
and Sudhana also bestowed wealth upon them as a reward.
Then the commander of the troops said: "There is a reward for dharma.
Always practice devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who grants liberation;
this alone is the reward here, and not otherwise. (2.73.100–101)
Having heard this regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Sudhana fell into doubt:
"Has the Blessed One himself arrived for the sake of protection?
Having thus doubted, he rose and indeed prostrated at his feet.
Others also indeed bowed down, following the example of those who had already done so.
Then the commander of the soldiers, accompanied by his cavalry,
led the army across to the other side of the river and caused it to be rendered free from fear.
He indeed reached that beautiful garden of Śaṅkara;
then, the soldiers of the commander-in-chief became invisible.
There were no horses, no royal soldiers, and likewise, the commander-in-chief was not there.
And the people of Sudhana were struck with supreme wonder.
Then Sudhana quickly summoned that lord,
raising a great cry toward the sky with all his might.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmin, O upholder of compassion!
You have provided protection for me in the forest; my good fortune increases today.
O Kṛṣṇa, I have a desire to see you; grant me your vision once again.
Speaking thus, he rolled repeatedly upon the earth in a field of dust;
dancing and clapping his hands, he again rolled in the dust.
And having beheld the devotion of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [he was moved].
Bālakṛṣṇa quickly became possessed of a divine form and great beauty,
radiant with a splendor surpassing that of ten million suns, fires, and moons;
he was adorned with divine golden ornaments and wore a divine crown and earrings.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, with a divine celestial chariot as his vehicle;
his limbs are proportioned to his form, and he is resplendent with the Kaustubha gem and other jewels; he is served by Śrī, Rādhā, Māṇikī, Pāravatī, Prabhā, and others. (112–113)
Worshipped by Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Haṃsā, Lalitā, and Sujayā, Hari himself became visible in this manner.
Beheld by Sudhanā and the others, he spoke from his celestial chariot: "You all..."
Having made them stay there in the celestial chariot for a mere moment,
and having shown them in an instant the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the temple, his parents, the sage, and all the lakes and holy fords; (15–16)
Having brought them to that garden by means of his celestial chariot, he vanished from sight.
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, Sudhana and the others attained happiness;
they became possessed of divine vision and became devoted solely to divine bhakti.
Indeed, all of them were made successful by Hari during the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
Then, on the eleventh day at midday, on the auspicious shore of the Dhṛtadhārā river,
the Lord bestowed upon them the supreme abode after some time.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the protection of his devotee was performed by Śrī Hari.
By reading and hearing this account, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained.

(2.73.120) Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Protection of the Devotee Sudhana—who resided in Āmodanagara and had attained the state of devotion to the Bhāgavata through the great sage Varcakāyani—from thieves, as well as the Lord’s divine vision and other graces," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 73: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 74 [[Author: → Chapter 75
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Queen of the Rāsa, during the festival of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
in the ninth year, on the eighth lunar day, a great assembly of the inhabitants of the three worlds took place.
Likewise, the liberated ones and their incarnations; the liberated lords and likewise the sovereign goddesses; the gods, the goddesses, the ancestors, and the sages;
the ṛṣis, those of the lineage of Kaśyapa, the descendants of Kaśyapa, and likewise the human beings.
Nāgas, Daityas and others, trees, creepers, beasts, and birds;
those born of water and those born of land, as well as the immobile and the mobile; virtuous men and women, the arts, rivers, and oceans all arrived. (3–4)
The seasons, the Vasus, the mountains, millions of holy fords,
the lords of the directions, kings, and the poor, the blind, the wretched,
and others all came to Bālakṛṣṇa and worshipped him with reverence.
They offered blessings and presented gifts before Hari.
An auspicious worship was performed by Lomaśa as well as by the other sages;
and Gopālakṛṣṇa honored those who had arrived.
Kambharā offered sweet foods— edibles, snacks,
and things to be licked— as well as drinks, honey-mixtures, water, and betel leaves.
A lustration ceremony was performed by everyone using a hundred wicks.

Praised thus, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign, granted His grace to them; having bestowed His blessings, He allowed them to rest. Then they departed in their own celestial chariots to their respective lands and regions at the ends of the quarters. (2.74.9–10)
Then, in the evening, after the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), a wonder occurred; listen:
on the auspicious northern bank of the Narmadā in Gurjara, there is a beautiful city named Kuśāmbā, inhabited by people of the four castes.

There lived the great seer Kauśika, a mighty sage (12) devoted to meditation on the gods, devoted to sacrifice, and devoted to yogic practice; he possessed the power of moving through the sky and was perfected in the practice of breath-retention (kumbhaka). (13)
He is devoted to the meditation upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, He bestows the knowledge of liberation.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and even those of the lowest castes—
He instructed whoever came to his own hermitage [as follows]:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
And he constantly bestowed this mantra upon the disciples who had approached him.
Once, however, a man of the lowest caste named Tryaṣṭakāru, who was destitute,
arrived at dawn accompanied by his wife for the purpose of seeing the sage.
He was childless and afflicted with dropsy.
His wife became afflicted with leprosy and was extremely distressed.
Meanwhile, the great sage Kauśikāmbo would constantly deliver discourses on the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in that assembly hall. (18–19)
Having gone there, the outcaste sat down in the shade of a tree.
Right there, he listened with devotion to the story being told by his wife.
He heard that in Saurāṣṭra there is the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord of the supreme abode, the Sovereign of all, Śrī Puruṣottama—
the beloved son of Gopāla— resides in the form of a child within the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara as the Supreme Brahman, the Most Excellent Person. 21–22.
By the mere act of saluting him and by holding his name-mantra, all illnesses, wretchedness, poverty, as well as childlessness and the like,
surely go to their dissolution, and good fortune increases.
"Indeed, for one who has come for refuge to him, the attainment of the desired goal shall quickly occur.
(24) Having heard this at the conclusion of the discourse, when the assembly of listeners had departed, he remained beneath a banyan tree at the edge of the hermitage until midday. (25)
He thought to himself, "How shall I question that sage?
But the sage, having known his mind through the power of inner knowledge (*antarveditva*),
summoned that *antyaja* from Kauśāmbī, who was a believer (*āstika*).
Knowing that he was a devotee of Brahman and desirous of true knowledge, and seeing him arrived at his hermitage like one come from a sacred pilgrimage site,
Sarvamitraka offered him food, water, fruits, and the like; he also extended a warm welcome and performed every mark of hospitality.
When he had rested, he asked that outcaste: "O devotee, from where have you come, and how did you arrive here? Tell me what is in your mind.
That devotee, who was skilled in the three and eight [limbs of yoga], spoke while showing humility.
Then, prostrating like a staff while uttering these words, [he said]: "May there indeed be victory for the great seer!
May there be security, well-being, and constant happiness for the sage.
O compassionate one, knower of the heart, O God of gods, may he live long! (2.74.30–31)
"O Guru, virtuous ones such as you are the saviors of sinners here;
since I have come here for the purpose of washing away my sins, my task has become fruitful and this place has thus become my supreme sacred site. (32)
Through the direct vision of one whose very form is divine, my purpose is fulfilled. By obtaining this discourse, the fruitfulness of my birth exists for me today;
by your grace, my fortune increases this day.
"I am a sinner and an outcaste, yet I have been delivered by you, O Guru.
Having said this, he repeatedly placed the dust of the hermitage upon his head.
Afterwards, he said to the sage: "If you have a command for me..."
“I conceal my mind wherever it finds delight from hearing your stories.
The sage said: “Ask with ease; I recognize your desire for liberation.
This is no common man; he is pure, ever composed of *sattva*, and nowhere subject to the final state of decay. (36–37)
"Indeed, his body as an outcaste was born due to his past karma.
Having heard this, the outcaste said: "How did I become such?
And how is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa attained?"

"What must I perform here for the sake of attaining liberation? What divine rite should I undertake for the sake of destroying my childlessness, and likewise for the sake of destroying my disease? O Lord, please tell me out of compassion what I must do. (2.74.39–40)
Thus questioned, the sage said: "Listen to your history as an outcaste. Formerly you were a Brahmin who dwelt in the seven cities and mountains;
your name was Devapriya, and this woman was then your wife, Dyumatī."
Therein was the temple of Viṣṇu, containing Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
You performed worship there constantly like a servant, and your wife then prepared the kitchen for the sake of the food offering (naivedya). || 42-43 ||
Even while it was cold, you bathed without [using] water; you were soiled and dressed in dirty clothes, yet both you and your beloved performed my worship and touched me.
At that time, you performed the cooking and other tasks with water that had not been strained.
Then, without having bathed and without having washed her clothes, she offered the *naivedya*;
she even offered me water that had not been strained for my drinking.
Your beautiful wife constantly touched me while her body was impure.
At that time, she did not consider menstruation and such matters to be of great consequence.
Thus, having long consumed the sin born of impurity,
you two went to the world of Yama, and there, in the Vaitaraṇī river, you attained the state of cats.

Therefore, you two, now residing in the bodies of outcastes, by virtue of your service to the Divine and the remainder of your merit, have become sinless and have attained the company of the virtuous.
Service rendered to parents, the Divine, or a guru over the course of time—[this is the cause]. (48–49)
In another birth, however, that merit stands ready to bring about one's welfare.
Whatever has been offered in sacrifice, given in charity, performed, or recited—all of it follows one into another existence.
Violence, affliction, injury, censure, deceit, fraud, and cruelty—
Deception, killing, and everything else returns in another existence.
Merit, sin, one's own nature, mental formations, latent impressions, the mind, the sense faculties, hatred, and passion indeed proceed to another existence. (51–52)
Practice, recitation, devotion, service, altruism,
virtuous conduct, vows, and surrender surely carry over into another birth.
So too do knowledge, realized wisdom, faith in the scriptures, discernment, and the worship of the Divine.
Blessings as well as curses surely follow one into another existence.
Likewise, a debt, a devoted wife, a husband devoted to his wife, and even deeply rooted enemies—all these pass over into the next life. (54–55)
Fortune, accumulated karma, and the water-offering given later—
the funeral rite (*śrāddha*), austerity, and contentment— truly pass over into another existence.
But the service and devotion performed by you two were filled with impurity.
In the course of time, she obtained as the fruit of that [action] the birth as a human being.
Thereafter, due to the fault of impurity, her birth became that of an outcaste (antyaja).
Indeed, leprosy is the fruit for a woman of defects such as menstruation during an impure state. || 57–58 ||
Because you offered unstrained water to Mādhava for his drink,
this dropsy has arisen within you, which will be a constant source of great suffering for you. (59) Furthermore, because you offered unrefined food as an oblation to Hari...
As the fruit of that [action] in this world, poverty overcomes you.
Sin is the fruit of lack of faith, and from it arises atheism (*nāstikya*).
And because of that atheism, you became devoid of *śrāddha* rites and other duties there.
Therefore, O best of the low-born, you remain childless here;
thus has your previous history been told to you, so listen now to what follows as well.
Even though you are of the lowest caste, since you perform service to the virtuous and undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords—
Since you both listen to this discourse and practice its devotion,
by the power of that merit and likewise through the blessings of the Guru,
[may] disease, childlessness, poverty, and suffering likewise [be removed].
Other afflictions as well will swiftly come to an end through the remembrance of the Lord of Śrī.
Quickly take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
who shines resplendent in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī on the shore of Lake Aśva.
In the house of Yaśodā, the child Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of the cowherds, resides—
he who maintains all incarnations, the cause of all causes, the controller of all lords, and who abides as the inner witness within all. (66–67)
He is the bestower of the fruits of all actions and the giver of liberation;
he alone is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise.
He possesses the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of cause and effect.
The Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Pāravatī, and Māṇikya-śakti; the Sovereign of the Earth who possesses the grace of the beautiful swan;
the Lord of Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Padmā; and the Master of power, sovereignty, and majesty. (2.74.69–70)
