The Lord of the virtuous, such as Nanda, Nārada, Śaṅkara, Sanaka, and others;
the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer of the worlds; the bestower of liberation upon his devotees;
possessing all desires, all tastes, and all fragrances; and the seer of everything.
The embodiment of all bliss, the protector of all, the lord of all, beloved by the virtuous;
the husband of the chaste, the friend of the righteous, the foremost among renunciants, and the teacher of teachers;
the eternal, supreme reality, the transcendental Brahman, the ancient one. (72–73)

Worship daily, together with your wife, that Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, whom the wise— the gods devoted to celibacy, the renunciants, the yogis, and those who practice self-restraint— behold through the cessation of mental fluctuations.
[He meditated upon] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Śrī Svāmī, the husband;
the primordial human form known as Pārameśvara, who is born age after age and thus possesses many forms. (75–76)
He is the form of compassion and the form of ferocity; the form of knowledge, the son of Vṛṣa;
the form of learning, the form of royalty, the ruler, and the ascetic.
He is the form of the cosmic array (vyūha), the manifestation (vibhava), the representative image, and that which dwells within.
Worship that Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), whether in His essential nature (svarūpa) or in a virtuous form;
or as a partial incarnation (aṃśa), as a digit-incarnation (kalā), or as one characterized by divine immersion (āveśa);
or as a manifestation of power (vibhūti), or as the full form, the perfectly complete Supreme Lord.
Whether as an incarnation of the Lord, or as Viṣṇu, or as Mahāviṣṇuka;
or as the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman, the most excellent among the perfect—
thus he is this beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa in many such forms.
Worship [him] together with your wife; then you shall attain liberation.
Come, come here; take this water, that nectar from his feet.
Drink it, hold it upon your head, and perform the sprinkling over your body.
"May your sins, along with those of your wife, be swiftly destroyed here.
Having spoken thus, he gave them the auspicious water arising from the grace of the worship. Tryaṣṭakāru drank of it, and his leprous wife also drank.
Through the sage’s drinking of water, by his own power and a fragment of Kṛṣṇa’s grace,
those four great diseases— ascites, poverty, leprosy, and childlessness— departed from his body. (84–85)
Standing at his side, they wept and bowed to that Kauśikāmbaka, saying, "O Brahmin, where shall we go? Grant us our lives! They entreated him thus.
The sage [bestowed] water-belly upon the Earth, Kadali, and Śrīphala.
He also gave portions for the sake of drinking forbidden liquors;
he gave to the thirsty, to the greedy, and to those deprived of the bath of giving; he gave to the addicted, to the poor, and to the lecherous.
To one who lusts after improper unions, who causes the mixing of castes,
who hates the Dharma, and who commits theft, he granted leprosy.
To those who kill the offspring of others and who cause abortions, [he likewise granted it].

"To those who have been consecrated [as officiants], he granted childlessness for having omitted the *śrāddha*. (2.74.90) Having been told this, those four defects departed into such a worthy recipient.
That outcaste became stainless, accompanied by his wife, and free from disease. (91)
The sage gave him the purifying mantra of the Supreme Lord:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Then, performing its recitation, he remained in the hermitage like a servant.
He performed cleansing and other rites as was appropriate, and enjoyed the gardens.
Having heard the discourse, his latent impressions of affliction were completely destroyed.
This occurred during the month of Kārtika, in the lunar fortnight, on the eighth day of the dark half.
The sage indeed celebrated the birth festival of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
There, a divine celestial chariot, radiant with a splendor equal to a hundred suns,
arrived at the place where Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was resplendent.
The divine attendants and women such as Rādhā were shining there;
from that place, Hari suddenly descended.
The Blessed One himself accepted the great worship performed by the sages.
He gave him a graceful woman with eighteen arms,
and having placed the sage in a celestial chariot, he went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Then Hari became visible, having reached the celestial chariot in the expanse of the sky.
It was beheld by the inhabitants of the Kuṅkumavāpikā field.
That celestial chariot descended upon the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having descended, he then performed his evening bath and offered oblations to the three groups of eight ancestors.
His wife also performed her bath in that very lake at that time.
Their two bodies fell away, and they instantly became possessed of divine four-armed forms, adorned with celestial ornaments. (101)
Possessing divine vision, divine movement, and endowed with divine knowledge,
the two of them quickly beheld Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, their mother, their father,
and the sage Lomaśa, and performed extraordinary worship.
They both rejoiced as they traveled by that celestial chariot to Brahmaloka, the supreme abode.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, the sage remained here until the conclusion of the month of Kārtika.
Afterwards, at Kṛṣṇa’s command, he departed for Kuśāmbā; was it because [Kṛṣṇa] was not present?
Instructing his devotees, he dwelt there for a hundred thousand years.
Every year, the sage celebrated the birth festival of Hari.
Having gone to the bank of the Anadyā, Śrī Narāyaṇa performed that rite at that sacred ford.
Having taken the water of the river made holy by the sages and being worthy of honor,
he bathes and returns in a moment upon a divine celestial chariot.
Thus does the Kauśikāmba Tīrtha shine upon the Anadyā river.

"O Rādhikā! [This was] born from the descent of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (1.08) Then the sage went to the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord, which is even beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara) and is the refuge of the liberated souls. (1.09)
Thus, O Rādhā, this wonder of Hari has been told to you.
By reading or hearing this, one shall attain supreme liberation.
Liberation is the most excellent fruit, surpassing children, wealth, wives, and the like.
"What indeed has been gained by that devotee through his offspring and the like?

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the State of Liberation by an Outcaste, a Sick Man Accompanied by His Wife, through Devotion to the Lord via the Yoga of the Sage Kauśika at the City of Kuśāmba on the Bank of the Yamunā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 74: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)*
Chapter 75 [Author:
Chapter 76 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, I shall tell you of another marvel as well.
Long ago, on the banks of the Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun, in the city of Kāmapura,
there was a Daitya named Santāpana, the lord of the hosts of Daityas.
Endowed with great strength, he roamed the banks of the Tapatī;
eating meat, he made his dwelling upon the Seven Cloth Mountains (Saptapaṭṭādris).
Having gone again and again as far as the distant limits of the eastern direction, he [seized] children.
Having reached the vicinity of the source of the Tāpī,
even the very few Daityas who feed on human flesh gather together and devour them with great merriment.
To the east of Bhūśāvālaya, however, there was a great [encampment] on the bank of the Tāpī.
There was a school there belonging to the sage Hiraṇyakeśaka.
He was the best among those who know the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and was the most eminent of sages.
At that time, students of knowledge and practitioners of celibacy took up residence in his hermitage.
Thousands of Brahmins belonging to the Hiraṇyakeśī school were there,
as were others in the presence of their preceptor named Hiraṇyakeśa;
and those residents of the hermitage, students of the Veda, [performed rites] in the waters of the Taptī.
At that time, when the Brahmins go there to bathe, the Asura Santāpana arrives, well-concealed,
and carries off the sons of the Brahmins—
always two or five, sometimes six, or even nine or ten. (8–9)
Among thousands of children, those who perish are not even noticed by those dwelling in the hermitages as to where they go;
indeed, where there is no counting, there the loss is not perceived.
Thus, when a great deal of time had passed, five hundred offspring of Brahmins were indeed brought to destruction by the Rākṣasas; likewise,
hundreds of other offspring born of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were destroyed.
Thus, as the abundance of youths came to an end thereafter,
people perceived a decrease in the number [of students] engaged in study and meals.
Indeed, on the banks of the Tāpī, children were constantly diminishing.
They sink in the water and are surely carried away by sea-monsters (makara).
Thus, having fallen into such danger, they go to bathe together;
for the Rākṣasas, having become children, enter among the children.
Those who go far for the sake of purification, they seize and carry away;
and when they do not return, people realize the truth:
it is not crocodiles that carry them off, but rather demons.
There was exceeding grief in the hermitage for the children;
then the sage named Hiraṇyakeśin lamented in many ways:
"Alas! My children are lost—more than six hundred in number. (17–18)
Until this very day, it has not been known what has become of my ancestors, nor what must be heard as the harsh reproaches of those related to them.
Alas! I have offered my meditation, yet until now, at the time of its exhaustion, nothing at all has been granted.
"How might these very people survive? For they would surely have been killed by the Rākṣasas, or perhaps devoured—alas, fate destroys the weak!
Having thought this, he placed both hands upon his head and wept piteously.
Then the other residents of that hermitage wept with great piteousness;
the hermitage became desolate, even though its inhabitants were men of pure intellect.
The sage himself became devoid of luster, and grief arose even toward the trees.
The herds of beasts and flocks of birds also wept, knowing of his destruction.
The deer and other animals did not graze on grass; the parrots did not take fruit;
even the ants, overcome with grief, did not take a single grain.
The creeper did not reach the water, even though it had been placed in the fields;
the breeze did not blow pleasantly, nor did the fire blaze in the hearth.
The peacocks did not utter their cries, and even the sages were like corpses.
In the hermitage, the women became lusterless like widows. (26) A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the region of the hermitage:
"The Daityas, stationed on the seven-peaked mountain, are carrying off the sons of the brahmins! (27)
They kill and devour us—alas, what misery!—impelled by Time.
Oh, there is no protector for us, nor any slayer of these Rākṣasas!
Is there anyone remaining other than Kṛṣṇa? And where does Kṛṣṇa abide? (28)
I have previously heard in a narrative that, near the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Blessed One himself resides.
And I have likewise heard this from the mouth of the sage Kauśika.
Likewise, I have heard from other brāhmaṇas that Kṛṣṇa shines forth,
having become a human being in embodied form, the glorious son of the cowherds;
and in the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Hari himself was heard [to speak].
"That Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beginningless God, shines forth.
May He indeed grant us protection from this great calamity of time.
Thus did they speak while immersed in grief within the hermitage of Hiraṇyakeśa.
Then the great seer Kauśikāmbaka arrived there;
having perceived through the power of yoga the cries of distress uttered by the sages,
he came to the hermitage of Hiraṇyakeśa on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa.
Honored and treated with hospitality by means of offerings such as the *madhuparka*, the sage sat down upon the seat offered to him. He then asked about the cause of the weeping.
Hiraṇyakeśaka replied that it was because of the Rākṣasas and the children of the Brahmins.
O Sage, many who were devoted to the study of the Vedas went to bathe on the bank of the Tāpī during the Brahma-muhūrta, but they were seized by Rākṣasas;
indeed, upon investigation, it is known that six hundred were thus slain.

While ten thousand brahmins were indeed living in the family of their preceptor, a great calamity of the Asuras arose. "What shall we do? Where shall we go? What has happened? And where have they gone? [they cried]. (38–39)
"If such a decline in the number of brahmins proceeds in this way, what would become of the stage of life (āśrama) here? Alas, it would surely perish!
If there exists some means here to prevent this destruction," [he said].
"O Yogi, tell us the cause for the attainment [of realization] by the ignorant; we shall act accordingly.
Having spoken thus, that sage Hiraṇyakeśaka fell silent.
Then Kauśikāmba, remembering Hari, addressed him, O Rādhikā: || 42 ||
"Do not fall into despair, O Brahmin; I know everything through my yogic power.
Previously, a great calamity occurred even in my hermitage.
Indeed, the Rākṣasas and Daityas were repeatedly destroyed by me."
Having been born anew, they do not go toward that direction;
rather, they cause havoc in your hermitage on the banks of the Tāpī.
Indeed, those who dwell upon the Saptapaṭṭa mountain devour even human beings.
Having understood that great calamity through the power of yoga alone,
I remember the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless God,
who dwells in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī and resides in the heart of all.
"Let us go for refuge; He will provide protection.
Welfare and well-being are within His grasp, and they shall be ours.
There is no one else capable [of this] except for the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (47-48)
"Having said, 'In order to protect [him] from the cycle of suffering and from calamities in the ocean of existence,' the king of yogis, having remembered Śrī Hari, traveled by way of the sky and,
taking Hiraṇyakeśa with him, went to Aśvasaras."

Resplendent like the sun and moon, or like two luminous spheres of moonlight, they descended from the path of the sky onto the edge of Lomaśa’s hermitage. Having first bowed to Lomaśa and then honored one another, [they remained there]. (2.75.50–51)
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā,
drunk its water, and bowed to the deities,
they both went to the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the temple.
Therein shines the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, higher than the highest (53).
Upon a golden elephant-throne adorned with jewels and gems,
he is attended by sacred fords, sages, gods, Lakṣmī, and others (54).
Beholding Bālakṛṣṇa— the Supreme Brahman— consisting of divine splendor, adorned with celestial ornaments, garlands, and garments,
worshipped with beautiful fragrances, and possessing a serene lotus-face,
they bowed down to him again and again.
Tearful, filled with affection, and gentle, they prostrated themselves like staffs.
(56) Honored by Hari, they were quickly presented with the madhuparka offering;
given seats and questioned comfortably, they sat down nearby. (57)
When questioned regarding the cause for their arrival, they spoke to the Supreme Lord:
"O protector of Brahmins, cows, the earth, holy men, virtuous women, and righteousness;
O refuge for the wretched, the afflicted, the miserable, the helpless, and those without support. (58)
"Many Brahmins have perished, as well as students and celibate seekers of knowledge;
whoever falls into their hands is constantly carried off by the Rākṣasas.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, grant us protection from them! (2.75.59–60)
O Kṛṣṇa, the restoration of life for the deceased shall arise from Your resolve;
act in such a way that it may be according to their happiness and as is appropriate.
O Protector, inflict the ultimate punishment upon the Rākṣasas.
You are the Sustainer, you are the Ordainer, and you are the One who ordains what is difficult to achieve, O Supreme Person.
With You as their refuge are the Bull (Dharma), the Sacrifice, the Veda, Knowledge, and the Brahmins;
the stages of life, the yogis, and the ascetics all depend upon You for their very livelihood.
Upon hearing this, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa remembered his own discus, Sudarśana, as well as the god Śaṅkara, the goddess Pārvatī, Vīrabhadra,
the Mṛtasañjīvanī lore, and Sandhinī, the giver of life.
The wish-fulfilling creeper, the celestial chariot that moves through the air and is eternally imperishable,
as well as Lakṣmī, Siddhi, and Gaṇeśa, quickly appeared before him;
they prostrated themselves like a staff before the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord said: "O Mahādeva, Gaṇeśa, Siddhi, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Vidyā, Kalpavallī, Vīrabhadra, and Sudarśana!
Many children have been slain by the Rākṣasas, such as Santāpana and others. (67)
Thousands of Rākṣasas dwell on Mount Saptapuṭṭaka.
They must be slain by you today, and the Brahmins must be protected.
For that purpose, we shall go there equipped with weapons.
"May you all ascend this celestial chariot along with me.
Thus addressed, they ascended together with the Lord of Śrī,
accompanied by Kauśikāmba and joined by Hiraṇyakeśin.
As soon as it was meditated upon, that celestial chariot went there through the air;
it performed a circuit in the sky above the mountain of seven layers of cloth.
Seeing that divine vehicle, the rākṣasas came out.
Armed and capable of traveling through the sky, they came to seize the divine celestial chariot;
some were like mountains, while others had noses like mountain caves.
Some had thumbs as large as palm trees, and some had ears like ponds.
Some had eyes like lightning, and others had nails like the sun;
others had hair like bamboo, while still others had faces like clouds and mist.
Bearing many forms and many guises, they were masters of illusion.
Ten thousand inhabitants of mountain caves came forth.
Seeing them, Śrī Hari quickly blew his most formidable conch shell;
he produced a terrifying sound that announced the onset of battle.
Then, surrounding them on all sides, they let out a loud, mocking laugh.
Powerful and intoxicated with pride, they roared as they prepared to seize the celestial chariot.
At that moment, the Blessed Lord spoke to his beloved, the virtuous Kalpavallī.
"Rouse indeed powerful armies for the sake of battle!
Having heard this, Kalpalatā immediately dispatched ten thousand warriors who then engaged in combat.
They all emerged from their celestial chariots and gathered around the Rākṣasa.
A most terrible battle then took place in the sky between the Kāleya Rākṣasas;
blinded by the heat of combat, they struck one another for the sake of victory.
With maces, swords, scimitars, javelins, iron clubs,
as well as pillars, trees, stones, pestles, spears, and darts;
with iron arrows, sharp-edged spears, and crescent-headed shafts, they struck one another.
Suddenly, that battle with the Rākṣasas broke out upon the earth.
There, the heads of the Rākṣasas fell to the ground like rain;
the severed limbs of the Daityas fell to the earth like mountain peaks.
Some were deprived of their hands, others were bereft of their feet;
some had their waists severed, others were split in two, and still others had their shoulders cut off.
These terrible Rākṣasas fell to the ground, their lives destroyed.
From their destroyed bodies, new and fresh ones are born.
Having assembled in the sky, those of great strength engage in combat.
In this manner, the army of the Rākṣasas indeed increased by the tens of millions.
Then, a terrifying and boundless darkness was seen in the sky.
And the Kalpa-warriors, seizing them again and again by the hair with swords,
cut them in two, splitting them from the shoulders down to the hips.
They fall down headless, yet they rise up and fight again;
struck by the millions of hands, feet, and other limbs produced from the *kalpalatā* at the front of the battle, they rise up repeatedly in their fury. (2.75.89–90)
Flying up into the sky like living beings, they strike the soldiers of the aeon;
yet the warriors of Time are slain while remaining as divine consciousness alone,
for their weapons do not even reach an obstruction in the ether.
Then the Daityas created an illusion there that produced mountains;
mountains appeared in the sky and fell from above upon the celestial chariots with great force, for the purpose of their destruction.
The celestial chariot was indeed divine, as were the gods and the goddesses;
they were all untouchable like the sky, and no one was able to overpower them.
The chariot remained steady in the sky, situated there just as the sky itself is.
Mountains fell from it, covering even the surface of the earth.
Seeing this, the Daityas and Rākṣasas were struck with supreme wonder, saying,
"This celestial chariot is surely not fit to be seized or destroyed."
"Indeed, these gods and warriors are not fit to be slain.
Thinking thus, others, devoid of valor, fled from the battle.
They too were struck down by iron arrows discharged by the warriors of Kālī.
With their bodies split asunder and their heads severed,
they were deprived of life and met their end, even though they had been born in every way.
Others, out of delusion, continued to fight with the soldiers of Kāla on all sides.
The fire arising from the *kalpalatā* reduced them entirely to ashes;
the army of Rākṣasas, consisting of tens of millions upon tens of millions, was turned to ash.
Indeed, five thousand of the principal Rākṣasas met their destruction.
"And about five thousand others were commanded to engage in battle.

(101) Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Efforts and Battle Undertaken by Śrī Hari for the Destruction of the Rākṣasas," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the destruction of the six hundred boys staying in the hermitage of the sage Hiraṇyakeśin by the Rākṣasas. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 75.

Chapter 77 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen then, O Rādhā! There were also five thousand remaining rākṣasas, possessed of great strength and speed,
who engaged in aerial combat with trees, stones, and mountains.
Then those Rākṣasas surrounded the celestial chariot on all sides.
Having boarded the chariot, they struck Śambhu, Gaṇapati, Sudarśana, and Vīrabhadra with javelins and other weapons.
Then the hero Gaṇeśa, as well as Sudarśana and Śiva,
repeatedly seized the Daityas who were inside the celestial chariot with their tridents and struck them all until they were breathless; Vīrabhadra, moreover, struck them in the face.
Having cast them down, he chewed up the hosts of living Rākṣasas.
And those who were born from the dead, possessing illusory forms, Hara reduced to ashes with the submarine fires arising from his great Māyā.
Those four thousand Daityas were indeed destroyed, reduced to ashes;
then those numbered in the thousands fled by way of the sky and entered the caves and other recesses of the mountain Saptaputaka.
The warriors born from the Kalpalatā, following that sequence,
entered the caves and other places and seized them on all sides;
[the Lord] cut Sudarśana, the great discus, at the region of the throat.
The fire, having gazed upon them from all sides, completely reduced them to ashes.
Thus were the great Daityas dwelling on the Seven-Peaked Mountain destroyed.
Then the wives of the Daityas, along with their children, became terrified and sought refuge in Hari.
Indeed, they returned weeping for the sake of protecting their life-breath.
Then the compassionate Śrī Hari warded off his own Sudarśana discus from them and granted them the gift of life.
Then they showed the bones of the deceased Brahmin boys who had been devoured by Rākṣasas, which had been cast into a pit;
likewise, [the remains] of six hundred twice-born men and a thousand women.
And for ten thousand men, birds, animals, and children, no count of bones could be found;
having seen them all around within that great pit extending for a *krośa*. (14–15)
He commanded Lakṣmī, who was present there as the Kalpavallī creeper,
and the Sañjīvanī and other vidyās to restore him to life.
Then Lakṣmī [brought] the auspicious water from the feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
She herself took [the bones] into her own inexhaustible jar made of gold.
Then, seated upon a swan, she departed from the celestial chariot carrying the jar of nectar.
Having circled the entire earth, she repeatedly searched for the bones through the sky.
He performed a ritual sprinkling over it with drops of nectar from that water;
the bones were thus nourished and immediately became possessed of life.
Then the Kalpavallī arrived, having filled an inexhaustible jar with essences.
He performed a consecration over that essence with drops of nectar.
By that, bodies were produced, endowed with flesh, marrow, and skin— namely,
boys, men, women, as well as beasts and birds.
That very *saṃjīvanī* vidyā, commanded to restore to life all those embodied beings— more than a hundred thousand— who had died and been devoured,
descended upon all living creatures in the form of rain.
Then raindrops, possessing the form of living beings and endowed with consciousness, entered [the earth].
All those born from the bones in the pit arose from their terrible slumber,
according to the nature of their bodies and as they were during the year.
That men and women born from improper wombs, as well as those of other species,
were born endowed with life— this was a great marvel.
All the beasts and birds fled toward the depths of the forest.
Having bowed down again and again to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
those men, women, boys,
and girls then emerged from the pit by way of the uneven ground and came outside.
In that place, Śrī Hari indeed caused a celestial chariot to descend;
he then gave them food and water that brought complete satisfaction.
He also gave them garments and whatever other things they required.
He bestowed upon them the power of recollection regarding their birth,
for that which belongs to those whose kinsmen reside in a certain village manifests clearly to them where they may be.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord to the yogi Kauśāmbika.
"O Sage, grant me this supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra from among these.
At his command, Kauśāmbika gave him the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Then Hiraṇyakeśa received that mantra from the sage.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord, having gathered everyone together in a vast celestial chariot, said to Śaṅkara: "O Śambhu, these indeed are your own abodes."
"By this very celestial chariot, cause them to arrive in a mere instant.
Śambhu, becoming absorbed in meditation, beheld their various levels;
having manifested hundreds of thousands [of beings], they moved through those respective regions of the sky.
He brought them all to his house in a mere instant.
Those householders became joyful upon regaining their own kin;
and having heard of this supreme marvel, they thereafter became true Vaiṣṇavas.
The disciples of Hiraṇyakeśa were then brought to that hermitage;
the hermitage became happy, devoted to Viṣṇu, and filled with the Lord.
Then there were five thousand Rākṣasa maidens.
Beholding Bālakṛṣṇa, they were infatuated by his form and chose him as their husband.
The Blessed One accepted those girls who were offered by their mothers;
meanwhile, the sage recited a mantra over the children and wives of the Rākṣasas.
"Oṃ, obeisances unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Then the Lord himself issued a command to the wives of the asuras:
"From this day forward, no one must ever commit violence."
"Having cultivated this field, may you indeed live and dwell here.
I shall be the giver to you of water, food, clothing, and wealth.
Having spoken thus and granted them freedom from fear, he led the maidens away and entrusted them [to others].
Having bathed there at Tapatī and established that most excellent holy site (tīrtha),
Śrī Hari proceeded toward the southern direction for the sake of visiting other sacred sites.
Thereafter, he performed his ablutions at Pūrṇā and then at Ambikā.
After wandering by means of his celestial chariot over the Sahya mountain,
he then went to Mahābaleśvara and performed his ablutions in the Bhīmā;
thereafter, he bathed in the Kṛṣṇā and then in the waters of the Tuṅgabhadrā.
Having bathed at Vārdhi on the western ridge, he went to Śrīparvata;
then, having beheld Nīlagiri, he proceeded to Elādri.
Then, having bathed even in a natural pool, he went to Siṃhaladvīpa.
There, having touched the Puṣpanadī, he performed his bath in the Kāverī.
Then, having bathed in the Kaṭunadī, he performed his bath at Pannārī.
Then, having gone to Droṇācala, he performed his bath in the Kṛṣṇā.
Having bathed in the Kolāra lake, he then went to the Godāvarī;
having bathed there in the Mañjirā, he then went to the Candrāvatī.
Having bathed in the Indrāvatī, he then went to the Cilasaras lake.
Then, having bathed in the Mahānadī, he went to the Huhūgalī;
then, having bathed in the Gaṅgā river, he went to the Brahmaputrā.
After bathing in the Kāñcanagaṅgā and then bathing in the Kuśī, he proceeded further.
Then, having bathed in the Gaṇḍakī, he performed the ritual bath at Gograsnāna;
then, having bathed in the Nandā, thereafter in the Yamunā;
then, having bathed in the Chambalā, and having bathed in the Śambhara lake.
Having bathed in the waters of Śatalājā, and having bathed thereafter at Rāvi;
then, having bathed at Cīnāpā, he performed his ablutions at Jhelam.
Then, having bathed at Kābilā, he performed the ritual bath at the Indus.
Then, having performed the *luṇī* bath and gone to the Nārāyaṇa lake,
he crossed the Akhāta and performed the Gomatī bath.
Then, having bathed in the Bhadrāvatī, he went to the Aśvapaṭṭasara.
In the sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā, at the hermitage of Lomaśa,
Hari stationed his celestial chariot; thereafter, having bowed to his preceptor,
he returned home, prostrated before his parents, and spoke to them of what had been done.
Mādhava announced five thousand maidens; he fed them and provided them with all necessary articles. He then settled them in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Śaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and Vīrabhadra went to their own abodes,
and the Sudarśana celestial chariot vanished as well.
Lakṣmī and the others remained in the sacred field of Śrī Hari, at their own holy site, and in their own temple.
Having enjoyed their devotion, Bālakṛṣṇa returned to his own abode; attended by all his devotees, O Rādhā, he rested happily there.
On the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, which corresponds to the month of Candra, the Supreme Lord [remained].
Having protected and sustained [the world], and having established sacred fords upon the earth,
the Lord, the bestower of life to all beings, returned to his own field.
By reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Restoration to Life of the Disciples of Hiraṇyakeśa Who Were Killed by the Daitya Santāpana, the Destruction of the Daityas, and the Consecration of the Southern Rivers as Holy Tīrthas," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

[Author: Chapter 78.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to another marvel of the Supreme Soul.
[This was] for the sake of devotees, gods, and holy men, as well as for the protection of cows and those who uphold the sacred threads.
1. Long ago, in the city of Anaṅgapura, there was a king named Bṛhadvarcas.
He was constantly devoted to the service of the gods and dedicated to the service of the virtuous. 2.

Devoted to the performance of religious duties, dedicated to sacrifices, long sessions of recitation, and burnt offerings; endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom, he was intent upon storytelling and the chanting of sacred names.
He was a benefactor to the helpless, the wretched, and the poor, and his character was defined by generosity.
His wife was a virtuous and faithful woman, devoted to serving the righteous;
she was constantly intent on devotion and service, and her speech was always truthful and consistent with the Sāṃkhya philosophy.
From her, the king had three hundred wise sons.
Two hundred maidens as well were all devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
On every festival day, that king would go to the bank of the Tapatī,
perform the ritual of bathing at the sacred ford, and bestow excellent gifts.
Gold, silver, copper, wealth, goods, and rings;
(7) jewels such as pearls and the like, diamonds, corals and so forth, gems with the color of rubies, elephants, horses, cattle and the like; (8)
Goats and sheep, as well as mounts, vehicles, palanquins, and carts;
likewise, various celestial chariots and steam-powered trains;
and those which have two wheels, three wheels, or even many wheels.
On the auspicious festival days, he gives excellent aerial vehicles as supreme gifts to the brahmins, according to their merit, following their worship. Then,
during a solar eclipse in the month of Phālguna, on the banks of the Tapatī, [he likewise gave].
The king, accompanied by a great abundance of wealth, went there for the purpose of bathing. Hundreds of thousands of people arrived at Tapatī to bathe;
there were Brāhmaṇas and village-dwellers from lands extending five yojanas.
Those who perform sacrificial rites and those who teach the Vedas—
worthy recipients (satpātra) devoted to austerity, knowledge, vows, and dharma— along with their wives and children, all came there for the purpose of bathing. (13–14)
Having bathed during the solar eclipse, they performed their recitations on the riverbank;
and the king began to bestow gifts upon the brahmins.
He gave elephants, palaces, fields, gardens, and jewels.
He gave pearls, diamonds, milch cows, and likewise buffaloes;
horses, vehicles, food, mung beans, and figurines of copper;
he gave his own iron figurine and garments of leather.
He gave gold, silver, coins, vehicles, and even draft animals;
he gave female and male servants, goats and sheep, villages, and houses;
as well as black garments, black grains, and black liquids.
He gave black necklaces set with gems, well-fastened with black threads;
he also gave a gift of black men accompanied by ten million coins,
reaching a depth of four cubits as a continuous flow.
Out of greed, those best of Brahmins accepted that supreme gift—
a great donation laden with weight and endowed with more than a hundred thousand coins.
At that time, the Brahmins, numbering in the thousands, each accepted their share.
One elephant, likewise one horse, one cow, and two bulls;
(22) one milch buffalo, one house for habitation, one field, one garden, a gem, and a black pearl. (23)
A diamond, the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), mung beans, a statuette of copper, an iron statuette of one's own making, black skin as well as clothing;
a black thread, a black-colored servant, and a maidservant who is also black.
A black goat, a black necklace, a black Madra woman adorned with collyrium,
black beans, gold worth a hundred thousand, and silver worth a hundred thousand—
the king gave all of this to each individual Brahmin. (25–26)
A thousand greedy brāhmaṇas indeed seized it;
those gods upon earth bathed again at Tapatī on the occasion of the sun’s purification.
They were exceedingly satisfied by the acquisition of the gift, their minds being filled with great joy.
Out of great affection, they bathed in the water until they emerged outside;
at that moment, due to the fault of accepting a gift, they became black and deformed.
Indeed, a fault is incurred by accepting a gift from one who is black-complexioned.
O Rādhikā, listen; I shall tell you that by which there may be fault:
for a king, the giving away of an elephant in battle is indeed a stain of injustice, and whatever deceit there may be is sinful and a great defect.
The killing of women and children who are free from fault,
as well as the slaughter of charioteers, domestic animals, draft animals, and those performing the duties of messengers— all that is purified by the gift of an elephant. (3.1–3.2)
This sin shall fall upon the head of the one who accepts the gift of an elephant.
However, for a king who has given a horse, there is a great merit performed by his cavalrymen:
the warding off of harm in battle through the protection of horses and the like. (33)

The fruit of the gift shall belong to the king, while the recipient shall be the partaker of the fault. (34) As for the killing of bulls and other animals in battle and the like, as well as the castration of bulls and other such creatures that may occur during the reign— [the consequences follow]. (35)

That sin of the king shall perish and pass upon those who accept the gift. By the gift of two bulls, however, those who died in battle—whether they were cowards, those who fled from their backs, or those who died while fleeing under duress—[are liberated]. (36)
The sin arising from their slaughter perishes for the king;
however, it remains fixed upon those who accept the two bulls, until it is removed by the gift of a buffalo and the taking down of the noose and the stake. (37–38)
Whatever sin arises for a king from unjust punishment,
that very sin of the king born of such killing is destroyed when the noose is bestowed by those wearing black garments who act as the givers of the noose.
One attains [the merit] specifically through the act of bestowing a gift of a buffalo.

And by the gift of a house, [one gains merit] regarding the king's kingdom, the people on earth, and whatever arises from palaces and the like constructed by artisans, as well as villages, roads, and so forth. (2.77.40–41)
The entire sin of the slaughter of innumerable living beings is averted;
O Seizer of Planets, all that becomes attached to you at that very moment.
By the gift of a field or a garden, the infinite sin of agriculture [is removed].
Whatever belongs to the subjects becomes the property of the king; its cessation occurs when it is restored to the subjects.
[Theft] regarding the seizure of fields, groves, gardens, and so forth, as well as from brahmins and others, is addressed therein.
Furthermore, regarding the excavation of mines and the like, [the rule applies] through the offering of a black gem.
Whatever sin of kingship may accrue to the king, all that shall be averted;
yet for the one who takes the jewels, every sin of the excavations shall prevail—
whether in the giving away of the pearl or in the destruction of the sea creature.
Whatever sin arises from the production of pearls and from the production of salt,
as well as that which arises from the killing of creatures such as fish and from the operation of mechanical engines,
and whatever sin originates from the sea and other sources— that sin of the king is averted.
O pearl-catcher, everything becomes exceedingly unbearable for you:
the sin arising from the giving of diamonds,
that which arises from poisons, medicines, and the like, and that which is produced by the heat of the summer.

The sin arising from poisonous winds, which causes the destruction of living beings, ceases for the king and instead falls upon the one who seizes him. Likewise, whatever [sin] arises from the killing of living beings by means of vehicles or the wheels of those vehicles is likewise [transferred]. (2.77.49–50)
The sin of the king perishes when the charioteer departs;
and by the gift of a *māṣa* every year, whatever affliction from the planets the king may suffer [is removed].
However, the sin arising from the failure to protect the wretched, the helpless, and the miserable remains.
That [sin] of the king ceases, and it passes to the one who took the beans (māṣagrāhiṇī).
But by the gift and offering of a copper statuette to the king,
the king's sin arising from association with a courtesan likewise ceases.
O you who seize the effigy, a marriage [of fate] occurs that brings terrible suffering.
Through the gift of an iron effigy to the king, whatever sin arises from the six calamities within the kingdom and originates from the subjects [is removed]. (54)
That [calamity] becomes lost for the king, but it falls upon the one who seizes the statuette.
Excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots, and earthquakes—these are declared to be the six calamities (ṣaḍītayaḥ). ||55-56||
By the gift of a black antelope skin, the great sin of hunting is averted for the king, and it accrues to the seller of the skin.
By the gift of a black garment, the great sin arising from the operation of a water-wheel [for irrigation] is removed.

The sin arising from the destruction of innumerable living beings belonging to the king is indeed destroyed; yet that very sin continues to persist. By the offering of a black thread, the sin produced by the rope in the kingdom is indeed eliminated. (58–59)
Whatever sin known as the slaughter of living beings is committed for the sake of wool, for the sake of woolen cloth, or for the sake of silk, that sin falls upon the king within his kingdom;
O Rādhā, all of that is averted for the king by the gift of thread.
All of that [sin] is set aside for a Brāhmaṇa and others who uphold the Sūtras.

By the gift of a Kṛṣṇapuruṣa, however, whatever arises from the killing of a child, as well as that which arises from the killing of a fetus, and likewise that which arises from a futile killing, [is removed]. 61–62.
Whatever sin belongs to the king regarding his subjects is entirely averted;
however, all that [sin] proceeds fully against the one who accepts the gift of a slave-girl.
Likewise, by the gift of a Kṛṣṇa-slave-girl, the sin arising from the killing of a maiden is likewise removed.
Indeed, whatever sin arises from the killing of a woman or a widow, and the evil arising from attachment to another's wife, is removed for the king;
however, all that [sin] accrues to the Brahmin and others who take a slave girl as a wife. (64–65)

Whatever sin arises from eating the flesh of goats, whatever sin arises from eating sheep, and whatever sin arises from eating goats— all that is removed for the king by the gift of goats. Furthermore, when one who seizes goats arrives, [the merit] arising from the slaughterer’s rice-grain [is transferred].

By the offering of a black garland, the king’s cruel and concealed sin is averted as soon as the one who receives the garland departs. By the gift of a black coin and the like, [the sin] arising from wealth among the subjects [is removed]. (67–68)
Whatever sin may arise from the treasury, whatever may arise from the hand [of the king],
the evil produced by forcible seizures, and that which is caused by punishments—
all that ceases with the king and passes upon to the one who takes the wealth.
By the gift of black beans,
whatever affliction has been inflicted upon the king by Śani passes entirely to the one who receives those beans.
Through the gift of gold, there is the favor of the ancestors and the belovedness of the gods.
Through the gift of silver, Lakṣmī becomes composed of *sattva*;
such is the fruit of giving for a king. However, his sin and suffering go to the recipient;
along with the objects [given], the king departs from his faults.
But the recipient suffers; he becomes bereft of luster.
If he is not rich in merit, capable of meditating upon Brahman, and devoid of the power of virtue, he is quickly tormented by sins. (73–74)
Those with deficient merit are born dark-complexioned merely by the influence of the planets;
or they become misshapen or devoid of knowledge due to the fault of a curse, like certain people;
or they are mentally deranged, afflicted by chronic diseases, with broken limbs and ruined fortunes.
Those whose vigor is broken, as well as those whose household affairs are ruined, are born [as such];
deprived of happiness and filled with suffering, they are born from the accumulation of gifts.
Therefore, one who seeks to protect their merit should not accept a gift that is more terrible than this. (76–77)
The hand that extends skillfully to receive a gift is the same hand that reaches out to bestow merit; it is also the hand that reaches out to take away evil.
Therefore, one who is a treasury of merit should indeed accept a gift.
For the sake of destroying the defects of giving, one should perform acts such as offering [the merit] to the gods.

Otherwise, one becomes a consumer of sin and goes again to a place of experiencing suffering—the realms of Yama, the physical body, and the womb—from which there is indeed no swift liberation. (2.77.80)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the brāhmaṇas eagerly accepted the gifts;
in an instant, they became dark-complexioned and ugly, like outcastes. Like cāṇḍālas, they became discolored and devoid of luster.
Just as collyrium bodies are [consumed] by fire, so too were they reduced to ashes in a mere moment after bathing in the Tāpī;
for the fruit of that terrible gift was then indeed difficult to avert. (82–83)
The merit of bathing at the time of an eclipse was not able to protect the Veda-reciting Brahmins from the terrible consequences of accepting forbidden gifts.
Then, seeing them thus possessed by sin, Śrī Suratāyana—
The great sage, dwelling in a sandalwood tree, was an ascetic of extreme austerity.
He was a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, a supreme Vaiṣṇava, a perfected soul (siddha), endowed with sovereign powers, and devoted to knowledge and meditation.
He who previously remained established in meditative absorption for a thousand years—
over whom tree trunks grew as anthills at their bases—
and who was scorched by the force of the waters caused by excessive rain; 87.
When the washing of the clay was finished, the great sage, who had been hidden from view, emerged;
his body remained entwined at the foot of a sandalwood tree,
yet he himself stood right there at its base, departing from that very spot through the power of meditative absorption.
Having reached that tree with his consciousness, he dwelt there with his mind fixed on the Blessed One.
And the Blessed One, having assumed a physical form, beheld him through meditative absorption:
"Now he resides upon the earth near the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake."
In the field of Kukumavāpī resides the glorious son of Gopāla,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the supreme among men, the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kamalā, and the husband of Haṃsārādhā. (91–92)
The Lord of the virtues of Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Mañjulā, and Prabhāsā;
the beloved of infinite liberated goddesses and hundreds of millions of virtuous wives;
this son of Kambharāśrī, Bālakṛṣṇa, shines forth resplendently.
Knowing [Him] to be eternal, he indeed goes forth every morning for the purpose of beholding [Him].
By means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) lasting but a moment, he attains the sandalwood [tree];
he worships the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa perpetually. (94–95)
The compassionate Śrī Hari imparted His own mantra to him:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
Chanting that mantra, he remained beneath a sandalwood tree on the riverbank.
Then he saw those thousand Brāhmaṇas who had accepted the gift of Kṛṣṇā; they were filled with impurity,
overcome by grief, and deliberating among themselves on how to destroy their transgression.
They all approached that great Lord of Yoga, the illustrious Suratāyana,
and having sought refuge in him, their eyes then filled with tears.
For the sake of pacifying their faults, they made this petition in his presence.
Having prostrated like a staff while remembering Śrī Hari, the great sage sat down.

Then [the Lord] bestowed upon him knowledge that grants the pacification of sins, serves as a basis for spiritual practice, and grants the attainment of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (2.77.10–101)

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Sage Suratāyana with the Thousand Brahmins Who Had Become Black Monkeys Due to Accepting Terrible Gifts from King Bṛhadvarcas on the Banks of the Tāpī," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 78 [Author:
Chapter 79 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, that knowledge which the illustrious Suratāyana Yogīndra bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas, I shall now relate to you. O Rādhā,
previously I gave that [knowledge] to Suratāyana Yogī.
Therefore, I shall relate that very matter to you here, since it brings benefit to the worlds.
O Brahmins, listen as the sage Suratāyana speaks:
"The Lord of lords, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī... (2–3).
He who is indeed the manifest Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and the Supreme Lord, shines in the region of Saurāṣṭra at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpī;
endowed with all powers, he is the destroyer of the sins of the wicked.
Go for refuge to that supreme Lord, the highest deity.
Worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇa with unwavering devotion;
through meditation, through the yoga of action, through devotion, and indeed through knowledge, he [is attained]. (5–6)
O twice-born ones, go for refuge to the illustrious Supreme Lord, who is to be attained.
Whatever action consists of charity and righteousness, and whatever pertains to the system of castes and stages of life,
when accompanied by knowledge of the supreme self, leads to liberation, O twice-born ones.
In the past, I proclaimed the supreme Dharma, which consists of the knowledge of Brahman.
(8) When everything is offered and cast into Me, the agent is never tainted.
This Dharma—consisting of knowledge and devotional service as a servant—shall reveal the Supreme Brahman. (9)
Having renounced all attachments, they have gone to Him alone for refuge;
established in the yoga of the Lord, they worship Him always with devotion.
Free from all attachments, peaceful, self-controlled, and devoid of envy— || 2.78.10 ||
Free from pride toward Hari, they have surrendered everything to Him and act for His sake.

With their minds fixed on Him, their lives dedicated to Him, and delighting in the narration of knowledge concerning Him—whether women or men, children or youths—all who have renounced everything to Hari [attain liberation]. (1.1–1.2)
The Supreme Lord Hari himself is indeed the remover of their bonds;
with knowledge alone, they have thoroughly shaken off darkness and become one with Him.
Ever blissful in this world, they are not born again into rebirth.
O twice-born ones, let them go for refuge to Him through action, mind, and speech.
A yogi must always protect his childhood as well as his state in the womb;
so that, whether in childhood or in the womb, no latent impression, desire, or thirst [remains]. (14–15)
Effort, thirst, and passion do not exist at all, like branches [of a tree];
likewise, one should remain steadfast in youth as well as in old age.
Just as even a conscious person in deep sleep does not attain the fruit of cognition.
Likewise, O Brahmins, one should always abide in such a way that one possesses the state of a sage even within knowledge.
Just as there is no perception of objects graspable by the senses for one whose mind is fixed elsewhere,
so too the mental activity of a Brahmin whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa leads to liberation.
Just as a child, having taken clay from the earth,
smears it [upon himself] and feels neither great sorrow nor joy regarding that very thing,
so too are all objects within the scope of action and activity.
Having cast that [body] into the god like a lump of clay, the wise man, even upon gathering it,
should feel neither sorrow nor joy, nor should he find fault therein;
for at that time, his perception of the fruits of action does not manifest excessively.
In the state of non-perception there is no status as an enjoyer, and no impurity arises.
That which is the stainlessness of the eternally pure is indeed liberation.
(22) Objects, the body, the senses, and likewise the mind—
The object of cognition is also distinct from that [Self], and therefore the Self withdraws from it.
(23) Indeed, the agent enters into bondage if he becomes attached to those [objects];
being unattached, he does not become attached at all, and thus he does not enter into bondage. (24)
Just as objects existing in their own form remain far away, they do not exist when they are in contact [with the senses], provided the Self does not become attached to them here.
Even the flowers situated in a garden, though full of honey for the bees, [do not intoxicate one who is detached]. //25//
They do not cling to him, nor do they go to his abode;
likewise, all those sense-objects do not envelop the knower of the Self, the Puruṣa. Therefore, he must certainly not be bound.
Having constructed its dwelling upon a stake, the female insect (kīṭī) resides in that house;
yet, having pulled down the house, she constantly departs from there to wherever else she may go. In the end, both the house and the body—all things—indeed go to destruction.

Thus, this ignorance, having led [the soul] to that body, wanders everywhere bound upon the surface of the earth; likewise is the bondage of the body. Bound by ignorance, they wander from place to place, leading the body along.
The suffering and pleasure born thereof arise at every moment;
however, yogins who know its power, by means of *saṃyama*, [leave] the body and indeed depart for another world even from within this one. (3.1)
No firm bondage of the body exists for them anywhere.
(32) And having returned there, they dwell according to their own will;
like birds dwelling upon the branches of a tree, they live there merely for the duration of their stay. (33)
Just as birds depart even after leaving behind their nesting branches, so too do those liberated ones dwell within the body like birds; it does not serve as a bond for them,
becoming like the sloughed-off skin of a serpent.
The sense organs always depend upon the body in every respect.
(35) Accompanied by the mind, they lead to bondage; devoid of the mind, they lead to liberation.
The mind should be employed only as long as there is a purpose. (36)
When this which is purposeless must indeed be withdrawn,
then the senses would no longer be bound, nor would they cause bondage.
And when the mind is also withdrawn and rendered unbound, it certainly does not produce bondage.
That intellect which serves as the witness should likewise take refuge in her husband and her own self;
but a virtuous woman should never, under any circumstances, take refuge in her son, nor even in her mind, nor in her senses which are like sons, nor in servants, nor in sense objects. (38–39)
This very absence of reflection within it is the purity of the intellect;
likewise, when the stream [of mental fluctuations] is blocked, the Self shines forth by itself—unwounded, sinless, stainless, and free from evil. (2.78.40)
One who is not deluded by the state of fruits, who is unattached and liberated, does not partake in suffering.
Where the mind is free from the pairs of opposites, there indeed is pure intellect;
where the wife is pure, there the master of the house rejoices.
One who is always content with one’s own possessions does not desire the possessions of others;
why then should sorrow and delusion arise for such a person?
Indeed, for the yogi who is self-contented and perpetually satisfied by bliss, [neither sorrow nor delusion arises].
The union with ultimate satisfaction proceeds indeed from its own nature.
Therefore, like liberation, he eternally goes, stays, and rejoices;
having known in every way the fullness of bliss belonging to the Supreme Lord. (44–45)
He is properly attached to that alone and does not desire attachment to anything else;
his mental fluctuations are blunted, and his intellect has become characterized by contentment.
For him whose wife is a giver of happiness, liberation resides within the home itself.
For him whose wife is a source of suffering, hell indeed resides in his very home.
Therefore, that wife-like intellect must be made serene here through all means of purification, just as a king is made gracious [by his queen]. (47–48)
One should strive for the Supreme Self in order to attain eternal grace—
that state wherein there is neither action nor the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
Through union with that, one shall likewise become free from all dread.
Immersed in the lake of eternal bliss, what indeed is the use of mud for him?
There was a most excellent Brahman-sage named Śvetāśvatara;
his disciple was the grandson of Pṛthu and the son of Śikhaṇḍin.
Named Suśīla, having relied upon detachment since childhood,
that knower of dharma resolved to take up renunciation through the power of his fortune.
Remaining on the slopes of the Himalayas, he indeed performed service to his guru.
There, in the Forest of Dharma, dwells the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
there flows the most meritorious and pure river named Mandākinī,
filled with groves of lotuses and water-lilies, and frequented by perfected beings and holy men.
Having bathed in her waters, offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
and worshipped Nārāyaṇa— who is joined with Nara— with beautiful flowers,
he once bowed to his preceptor named Śvetāśvatara and said:
"Oh, how great is my fortune! My austerities have borne fruit, since a true guru such as you, like the omniscient one himself, is manifest before me.
O Lord, grant me knowledge, devotion, dispassion, and renunciation. (56–57)

Thus addressed, that divine Guru bestowed the supreme renunciation (*sannyāsa*). He granted the complete surrender of all actions into the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which consists of total self-surrender (*prapatti*). ||58||
He taught the great mantra for the sake of all accomplishments:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
It pacifies all sins, is the essence of all things, and bestows supreme liberation. (2.78.60)
He also bestowed upon King Suśīla the knowledge of universal surrender:
"Nārāyaṇa resides in me, and I abide in Nārāyaṇa;
I am Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa is indeed I. (6.1)
Thus, the Guru first imparted the knowledge of abiding as Brahman.
Then he said: "You are not the body; the body does not possess the form of the senses.
The senses are not the mind, nor is the mind the Great Principle (mahat)."
The principle of Mahat is not the Self, nor is the Self ever of the nature of Māyā;
Māyā is not the essential nature of the Self. Your Self is the Supreme Lord.
Nārāyaṇa is Your Self, and You indeed are considered to be Nārāyaṇa.
For Nārāyaṇa is indeed untainted, free from the bondage of karma;
he is eternally pure, enlightened, liberated, and devoid of māyā.
Realizing your own true nature to be thus, worship the illustrious Supreme Lord.

Perform the morning bath upon your own body, making the Supreme Lord perform it. Perform the donning of garments upon your own body, making the Supreme Lord perform it. Perform the application of ornaments, sandalwood paste, and so forth upon your own body, making the Supreme Lord perform it. (67)
Perform the offering of the *ārārtika* lamp and other rites upon your own body as Him. O Supreme Lord,
manifest that embodied Being within your own person as the food, the meal, the drink, and the fragrant betel.

Offer sandals, shoes, and an umbrella for your own body; with devotion, offer all vehicles and the like to Him, the Supreme Self. [2.78.70] Seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and so forth—[offer these as well].
Bestow upon Him desire, affection, and the vital force within the body;
likewise, offer to Him lying down, walking, livelihood, awakening, reflection, as well as laughing, weeping, and agitation. (71–72)

Offer to the Divine within the body: rest, refinement, stumbling, exhilaration, as well as pleasure, the practice of meditation, yawning, melting away, suffering, happiness, and the deliberation of action. (73)
Offer discernment, breath, and devotion within the body to the Lord of Śrī.

In this way, offer to that Kṛṣṇa the entire collection of your actions—whether material, subtle, or consisting of the elements—as well as those arising from the senses and those arising from mental conceptions. (74–75)
Offer this collection arising from yourself to the Supreme Lord.
This very renunciation is indeed what is designated by the term "liberation.
And its fruit, having been offered to Hari, must not be enjoyed by you at all.
For one who conducts oneself in this manner, all action indeed becomes divine.
Desire, anger, greed, thirst, affection, attachment, injury,
compassion, cruelty, and impurity— all these become divine because they are offered to Hari.
This very renunciation is indeed the ultimate Vaiṣṇava path;
neither sin nor merit residing therein can obstruct him.
Thus, being of virtuous character, he performed penance while practicing austerities at Badarī.
Worshipping the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, he, freed from all impurity, attained the supreme abode at the end of his life;
he became four-armed, possessing a divine form like that of Nārāyaṇa. (2.78.80–81)
"In that very same way, O twice-born ones, you too should worship this Nārāyaṇa on the bank of the Tāpī with a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
thus freed from all affliction, the Lord, being pleased, will destroy even your sin. (82)
Thus addressed, those brahmins performed a most Vaiṣṇava sacrifice on the bank of the Tapatī,
which was thick with sandalwood trees.
On the seventh day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, there appeared one in the form of a child.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa appeared in person and said to them, "I am pleased; choose a boon, O brāhmaṇas!
Having beheld the Lord of Liberation, who was as radiant as ten million suns, the brāhmaṇas—
They bowed to him, praised him, and chose as their boon the destruction of their sins.
At the end, having prayed, "Grant us Your supreme abode, grant us Your vision which brings peace to the heart,
and grant us eternal service," they observed a vow of silence.
"So be it," laughed Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and he remembered the two physicians, the sons of Aśvinī, who bestow beauty. Suddenly, the two sons of the Sun, possessing excellent luster, arrived there.
Handsome, endowed with youth, adorned with ornaments and crowns,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and possessed of the Kaustubha gem—
those two, served by Śrī and Ramā, bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.78.90)
They both bowed to Śrī Hari and said, "Command us, O Lord; what shall we do here?
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, burdened with compassion, replied:
"O brāhmaṇas, these two have fallen into sin due to accepting gifts from a wicked person."
"Act in such a way that they may become free from blemish; provide the medicine accordingly.
Upon hearing this, the two sons of Aśvinī bowed to the Supreme Lord and said:
"O Blessed One, you alone are the master capable of accomplishing everything."
O Supreme Lord, you exist as one who is to be worshipped through your incarnations;
within your will lies the state of great creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
Nevertheless, out of compassion, you cause us to perform service and remain mindful [of you].
"There is no other supreme medicine here for them than the nectar of your feet.
Their crookedness and impurities will dissolve through the fire [of that nectar].
Having said this, Aśvinī then took her own water-pot from the two boys.
Having moistened the lotus-feet of Śrī Hari with the water of the Tāpī river and washed them,
they took that water into another pitcher;
having added a small amount of medicinal juice to it, they caused the twice-born to drink it.
As soon as those twice-born ones had sprinkled [the water], they instantly became free from sin through that drinking;
their dark complexion vanished and they immediately became golden-hued. (98–99)
By that sprinkling, however, their deformity was destroyed entirely within a moment;
they became endowed with beauty as before, possessing the power of Brahman.
With divine faces like the gods, they became even more auspicious than they had been previously.
Thus, in an instant, Hari caused their sin to burn away.
Having stayed for a moment on the bank of the Tāpī, Hari established a divine holy site (tīrtha);
that most auspicious tīrtha is where these brahmins were purified.
There arose the famous and supreme Aśvinīkumāra-tīrtha, where Śrī Hari indeed resided and bathed in the waters as if performing penance;
that became known as Haritīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Other gods also came there for the sake of seeing [the Lord], and likewise bathed in the water. Many sacred bathing places (tīrthas) were produced there;
having bathed there and drunk the water, as well as having cast in the bones of the deceased, [they attained their goal].
Even a man of great sin would attain liberation by performing this.
Then, O Brahmins, having performed the worship of Hari and the worship of the two Kumāras,
they bowed there and repeatedly begged for forgiveness.
O Rādhikā, having then established the two Aśvinī-bālakas and installed Śrī Hari— being free from all blemish— they indeed departed for their homes.
Thus, in that month of Phālguna, he provided protection for the brāhmaṇas there.
From reading and hearing this, the destruction of sin will certainly occur;
even by merely hearing it, a human being shall obtain the merit born from bathing in the Tapatī.
Then the two divine Aśvinī-kumāras departed from that place, becoming invisible.
Śrī Hari arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī in an instant.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction Given by the Sage Suratāyana, the Manifestation of the Lord, the Arrival of the Aśvinī Kumāras, the Purification of the Brahmins, and the Clarification of Sannyāsa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 80 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! Although the brāhmaṇas had returned to their own homes, they continued to contemplate that Lord day and night;
for that vision which was so difficult to obtain had now become easily accessible. (1)
By means of the yoga of the path of devotion (*suratāyanayoga*), from that very moment they behold the Supreme Self, Bālakṛṣṇa, at the edge of their vision;
they see him constantly in dreams, and it does not cease even in deep sleep. || 2-3 ||
For once the divine form of the Lord of Ramā has been seen,
it is placed within the unfathomable heart and never departs;
it shines forth with such firmness as if acquired through long-term practice.
This very compassion of his was manifested without prior practice.
(5) Then, when the auspicious period of Cāturmāsya arrived, the gods on earth (brāhmaṇas), eager for it, came to bathe in the waters of the Tāpī at that sacred ford. (6)
All of them gathered together and remembered the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, their own protector and the destroyer of great sins.
Having assembled on the Ekādaśī known as Devaśayanī, the brāhmaṇas [proceeded].
They indeed performed the chanting of the names of Nārāyaṇa:
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Inner Self, O Hari, O Supreme Brahman, O Lord of Śrī, O Master!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of all incarnations, O son of Gopāla Kṛṣṇa, O beloved of Kambharā! (8–9)
