O Lord of Haṃsā, Lord of Mañjulikā, Lord of Śrī Dayā, Lord of Śrī Lalitā—O Master!
O Lord of Vital Energy, O Lord of Śrī and the Possessor of Qualities, O Lord of Musk, O Lord of Peace, O Lord of Victory!
Victory to You, the Imperishable, the Supreme Person! Victory to You, the Lord of the Liberated, the Most Excellent of All!
Victory to You, the Supreme Lord, the Highest Self! Victory to You, the Witness, the Best of Divine Incarnations!
Victory, O Blessed One! Victory, O delighter of the self! Victory, O one beyond qualities! Victory, O truly desireless one!
O Śrī Bhagavān, destroyer of impurities, always protect your devotees.
Thus they performed kīrtana on the southern bank of the Taptī.
They became absorbed amidst the sounds of clapping cymbals.
At that moment, a light appeared there, and in its center was a supreme celestial chariot (vimāna).
Therein shone the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, attended by his devotees.
Together with their sixteen attendants, they all beheld that Supreme Lord,
whose excellent chest shone with rows of necklaces set with fine gems,
and who was adorned with a crown embellished with gold, jewels, and precious stones. (16)
He was resplendent with two golden earrings shaped like sea-monsters (makara), and was beautifully adorned by dark, fine, tawny hairs flickering at the edges [of his face].
His broad forehead was graced with a saffron tilaka mark possessing the luster of fire. (17–18)
Adorned with two frowning brows that have made ten million abodes tremble,
and graced by large eyes whose red corners flicker like fish;
beautified by a halo of radiant luster arising from his gentle smile.
It was exquisitely adorned with a nose like a full-blown sesame flower; it was exceedingly beautiful with a right cheek where a black mole was formed;
and it was resplendent with a cluster of cheeks shining with a stream of radiant luster. (2.79.20–21)
His upper lip was drawn upward in a fine line resembling a delicate golden thread;
it was shaped like the curve of a bow and pulled taut.
His lower lip was enchanting, its ruddy hue enriched by the sweetness of nectar. (22)
His chin and jaw were graced with the beauty of very fine black spots;
his broad forehead was singularly beautiful, adorned with a long, shining line;
and his two ears were exceedingly radiant, as lovely as the circles of a pair of earrings. (23–24)
His eyes are a treasure-trove of love, more resplendent than the sun and moon;
his supreme face is the abode of the glory of all beauty and tranquility.
It is adorned by two bees that have taken up residence in the station of ten million sovereign powers.
His teeth are like the foam of curdled milk, causing great delusion;
his heart is captivated by the corners of his face, rich with a broad, smiling gaze.
He displays maternal affection through a subtle dimple on his cheek. (26–27)
His white eye perceives all other sights by overpowering their light;
Śambhu resides in his throat, and the conch is situated at the nape of his neck.
The Kaustubha gem rests upon his heart, accompanied by a garland of forest flowers.
And indeed, he in whose middle of the throat a black point shines;
in the hollow of the throat, the wheel of wind (vāyucakra) remains supported by the year.
In the fold of his throat, the imperishable Brahman shines forth.
In his heart there is indeed a pearl necklace devoid of gems, and upon his skin a *cāmpeka* flower;
the bee named Śrīnivāsa shines as a clockwise curl upon him.
The two auspicious shoulders of Hari are firm like the shoulders of a tiger.
Hari’s two arms are like the coils of a serpent—plump and soft.
Covered by the garment of moonlight, his two eyes are radiant and captivating.
Upon his belly are two tufts of hair, dark and tawny in hue, thick with fine down.
Upon seeing [Him], affection and devotion are produced in the beholder.
His two beautiful arms are golden-hued, and his chest has the luster of campaka flowers.
The marks of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus are also visible upon his forearms.
On the two forearms there are three lines, and on the right hand there are auspicious marks:
a fish, a trident, an arrow, a banner, a svastika, and a bow; these beautiful line-marks are indeed eight wheels. (35–36)
A vajra, which destroys enemies, is also present;
his two palms shine with the luster of lotuses, brilliantly radiant.
His nails gleam like the moons situated on a full-moon night.
Her belly is adorned with three folds; her navel is a treasure-store of consciousness.
Her hips are rich with the likeness of the Goddess Śrī; her organ is the abode of desire.
Her beautiful waist shines all around like a garland of stars. (38–39)
Her hips are radiant and beautiful, delighting the hearts of her friends;
the roots of her thighs are white in color, pervaded by splendor, and exceedingly lovely.
A girdle made of gold rests upon the region of her waist.
The *ūrmikā* resides on the fingers, and the *śṛṅkhalā* serves as an armlet.
The *kaṭaka* is likewise worn on the golden forearm and the upper part of the arm.
Between the thighs, the splendor of the syllable Brahman shines forth. 41–42.
On the left thigh, below the root, is the mark of Kailaka;
above the thigh is the mark of Lakṣmī, white in color,
as long as the palm of a hand, and beautiful, where even yogins become bewildered.
Hari’s auspicious knees are lovely, rounded, and beautiful.
His shanks possess the luster of lotuses, are charming, and are adorned with a line of hair; his thighs are as splendid as the root of a plantain tree, cool, and auspicious. (44–45)
The feet are shaped like tortoises and resemble the interior of a lotus;
they are endowed with the sixteen marks and the like, and likewise adorned with upward-pointing lines. The mountain peak, the wish-fulfilling creeper, the wheel, and the vehicle as well— || 46 ||
His lotus-feet were marked with signs such as a palace, a bull, an elephant, a horse, a moon, and a garuḍa;
they were beautified by the upper portions of his feet shining with golden lines of hair. || 47–48 ||
With a pair of arms reaching down to his knees and fingers extending to his feet, the Lord Hari—
possessing a gentle form yet pervaded by splendor— became truly divine and auspicious;
such was he as he released a gentle smile.
Hari descended from his celestial chariot into the midst of the brahmins.
The brahmins bowed at his feet and praised the Supreme Lord;
all of them became exceedingly joyful in their hearts upon seeing him.
Then the great sage known as Suratāyana, having approached from a sandalwood tree, worshipped Śrī Hari with devotion.
"Oh, may we have such fortune again that there is the sight of Hari within our home! ||52||
Having spoken thus, he then performed a prostration at the feet of Śrī Hari.
All the brāhmaṇas, filled with devotion, repeatedly offered worship;
they were all successful in their purpose and well-versed in the performance of sacred rites.
Standing in his presence, they fervently prayed to Śrī Hari:
"O Lord, grant us a vision of the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
Thus praised, Hari spoke at the Aśvinīkumāra Tīrtha.
"Having bathed again and ascended the celestial chariot with me,
you, my servants, must come to my field.
Then, having bathed together with Hari at the Aśvinīkumāra [tirtha], they departed.
And the foremost among those seeking the path of devotion settled upon that celestial chariot.
Taking all of them along with him by way of the sky,
Hari arrived in a single day with five thousand brahmins and others.
Having crossed the Akhāta and reached the mouth of the Śatruñjitā river,
he bathed them there and proceeded to Gopanāthaka.
Having established a shrine at that sacred ford, he went to Mūlasvarṇapurī.
Having emerged from that sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), they then went to Somanātha;
having bathed at the confluence of the Bhadrā and the ocean, they proceeded to Camatkārapura.
Having performed their ablutions in the Devikā, those inhabitants of Vanasthalī departed.
They prayed most fervently to purify the forest region.
Having accepted their request, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [arrived] on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the lunar month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Sunday.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself went to the forest grove;
having purified all his devotees and fed them with *prasāda*, he gave them supreme instruction that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence. (64)

Listen, my devotees: for those who do not offer everything unto Me, there is never any end to the experience of the fruits of their sins and merits. But for those who practice the discipline of offering everything, I am Nārāyaṇa.
I myself bring about their purification and lead them to my own abode;
whether they be man, woman, boy, girl, or even a eunuch,
by a mere fragment of my grace, they quickly become liberated.
Therefore, worship me with love and build a beautiful temple here.
Install my image and worship me constantly.
And I am the savior of you who seek refuge in me.
Having spoken thus, having pointed out the ground, and having bestowed the nectar of his feet,
he destroyed the diseases of worldly existence as well as the ailments of the sick;
and having purified the forest regions, he blessed the men and women with auspicious benedictions.
Having joined him in his own devotion and having offered the water for his feet,
and having granted him sight and touch while accepting his service at his feet,
and having accepted the worship performed, [the Lord] ascended the celestial chariot.
In a mere instant, he went to the auspicious city of Saurāṣṭra,
where dwells the illustrious Lord Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa himself,
the sovereign ruler, in a vast and most magnificent palace.
The youthful Lord Hari shines with a radiance white as milk, overflowing with smiles.
The Lord, who possesses a form like that of the people of Saurāṣṭra, is to be worshipped and adored by yogis, men, and women alike. (74–75)
In the Mahālaya temple, which was resplendent with divine golden jars,
he touched his own form and addressed his beloved Lakṣmī,
the mother of the worlds, while beholding Dharma and Bhakti.
Then Hari, having embraced Sūrya, Śeṣa, Praśāya, Dattātreya, Śiva, Vidhi, Hanudāsa,
and Gaṇadāsa, departed in an instant upon a bright celestial chariot through the air.
Mādhava established the Kuṃkumavāpikā field and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake there in the sandalwood grove; having placed his celestial chariot there,
he showed Lomaśa’s beautiful hermitage from the vantage point of the chariot.
Having bathed the followers of other sects in the waters of Lake Aśvatāṭaka,
and having obtained the beautiful vision of his preceptor Lomaśa,
he also beheld crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of the dark-complexioned daughters of Kṛṣṇa.
Having had it constructed, Kṛṣṇa went to his own excellent palace and showed it to his mother, the great and virtuous Śrī Kambharā,
as well as to his father, the divine and illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
On the seventh floor, the Lord showed them his own elephant-throne.
He offered them hospitality, providing food and lodging as well.
Then, after the rites of hospitality were concluded, they all rested there.
In that spacious celestial chariot, they spent the night full of longing;
in the morning, having performed the ritual of bathing, they paid obeisance to the Supreme Lord.
They then offered a hundred maidens to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
Keśava protected them in the hermitage of Lomaśa. Then, having been honored by him, they departed for their own homes together with the glorious Nārāyaṇa in a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Having led them to those regions, Hari returned again on the sixth day to the divine field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the abode of the Imperishable Lord.
Thus, having granted his vision and having caused the holy site to be established, [he departed].

Having caused his own people to reach their respective lands by means of the celestial chariot, the compassionate Lord, O Rādhā, brought fulfillment to the minds of his devotees. Therefore, the Supreme Person from time immemorial is himself to be attained through grace alone. (2.79.89–90)
Neither by vows, nor by gifts, nor by fire-offerings,
but rather through love for the goal, devotion to the Name, and acts of self-surrender;
for He Himself remains present in the service of those devotees who engage in such service.
O Rādhikā, I always remain in your service;
O beautiful lady, in Goloka there is no other servant like you for me.
In the service of a servant, a lover becomes like a slave. (92–93)
Likewise, the illustrious Lord also, for the sake of his servants,
suddenly becomes a servant himself and becomes intent on protecting them.
Service performed with the body is considered superior to all other forms of worship.
Then there is mental service, and after that, service consisting of material offerings.
Indeed, the offering of one's entire self is the incomparable service toward Rādhikā, for it is understood to bring about her favor; it consists of acting in accordance with her will.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is pleased with one who offers service;
He indeed bestows the supreme abode that grants eternal happiness at the end,
as well as wealth, grain, sons, a beloved wife, a husband, and the expansion of one's family.
He bestows health, prosperity, fortune, daughters, cows, buffalo-cows,
elephants, horses, female slaves, progeny, male servants, grandsons, and even heavens. O Rādhā, this wonderful power of Hari has thus been described to you.
"By reading this, by hearing it, by causing others to hear it, and even by remembering it,

one shall attain enjoyment and liberation at the end, and reach the feet of the Blessed Lord. Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Five Thousand Brahmins, headed by Suratāyana, at the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha and the Auspicious Instruction," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen to this supreme wonder of Hari:
in ancient times, devotees were delivered from suffering on the bank of the Bhīmā river.
In the southern city known as Pauṇḍraka, there was a king named Baleśavarman, a bull among Kṣatriyas and lord of Khaṇḍadharā;
he was a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu and highly skilled in the practice of yoga.
Kapila had a disciple who possessed the discernment of the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
On the mountain not far from Bhīmātaṭa, in the hermitage of Kapila,
he brought about the union— the coming together— of the Sāṃkhya practitioners and the yogis.
Formerly, O Lord, when the deity Kapila, who had mastered the yoga of sacred fords,
stayed right there in that beautiful and auspicious forest for ten years,
in a most excellent mountain region that was peaceful, secluded, and pure.
Then, having served the sage Kapila,
that Baleśavarmā attained the Sāṃkhya and Yoga systems, as well as the wealth of supreme sovereignty, the supernatural powers (siddhis),
invisibility, the ability to assume many forms, birth, and so forth.
Kapila, having thus bestowed such sovereignty, departed for another place.
The king came daily to that hermitage to behold him;
after meditating for a moment and repeatedly recollecting his teacher, he would indeed depart from that spot.
Having worshipped this sacred seat (pīṭha) and then bowed to the supreme practitioners of yoga and the virtuous ones dwelling in the forest, he returns to his own home.
Thus does he, devoted to Sāṃkhya and Yoga, act daily.
Then once, the king, accompanied by his wife, went to the hermitage of Śrī Kapila to observe a vow; during the month of Kārtika, he resided outside.
Taking refuge in the shade of a tree, sleeping on the ground and subsisting on fruit, he remained there.
He was devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and his beloved wife remained steadfast in difficult vows.
He was dedicated to the duty of hospitality and maintained a continuous distribution of food;
he was constantly intent on the fire-oblation (*homa*) and daily fed a thousand destitute people.

Devoted to the dharma of giving and intent upon the vows at the end of the four-month season, many virtuous ones were there— perfected beings, those seeking perfection, and yogis. Pilgrims and forest-dwellers also constantly arrived for the sacred observance.
He gives food to those seeking food, and likewise clothing to those seeking clothing;
he gives vessels to those seeking vessels, and wealth to those seeking wealth.
Whatever may be desired by any seeker, that very thing he gives to him.

The Lord of Bali indeed grants [their wishes] and bestows sacrificial fees upon him who observes the excellent vow in Kārttika and whatever he may request. That very thing should certainly be given to him; the word "no" must never even be uttered.
There, the king had a son who was twelve years old and exceedingly tender.
The queen, named Śīlavatī, strictly protected her devotion to her husband,
while the son, named Puṇḍraka, indeed practiced devotion to Brahman.
Indeed, three of them are devoted to the service of the virtuous in the world.
There dwells a great Vaiṣṇava sage named Tārakāyana,
a yogi dedicated to yoga and meditation.

Moving through the air with divine gait, the ascetic assumes any form at will; he dwells as the locus of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), free from all desires. Having perceived Kuṅkumavāpikā through the yoga of meditation, that sage— 21–22. [He] moves through the air with divine gait, the ascetic who can assume any form at will. He remains as the locus of the eight siddhis, devoid of all worldly desires. That sage, having known [the location of] Kuṅkumavāpikā through the yoga of meditation, [proceeded].
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, which was directly inhabited by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and having beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
he received from the Lord of Śrī, Mādhava, the mantra that bestows liberation.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (24) Remaining within his own hermitage, he chanted this constantly in that secluded place. Every morning, he would regularly travel through the sky to the Aśvapaṭṭa Sarovara lake. (25)
Having beheld Hari, this great sage named Tārakāyana returned once more to his hermitage; he descended from the sky to the earth,
and at that time the king went quickly to see him.
Becoming humble, he questioned the sage, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him:
"O Sage, where do you go every morning? If it brings about auspiciousness, I wish to know; please tell me if there is no obstacle. (27–28)
The company of the virtuous is considered always to bestow heaven and likewise to bestow liberation; it is held to be the destroyer of suffering and the dispeller of calamities.
[This applies] even to yogis, lords, the virtuous, and the good.
A monastery exists wherever Nārāyaṇa is present as its object of perception.
(2.80.30) The feet of the virtuous are to be worshipped; the water from their feet is to be drunk as nectar;
their food is to be eaten as a divine gift; and the speech issuing from their mouths is to be accepted. (31)
Service to the virtuous is service to Hari; indeed, association with the virtuous is association with Hari.
The body of the virtuous is the body of Hari; the virtuous are truly the very forms of Hari.
The virtuous should always be meditated upon in meditation; the virtuous should always be held within the heart.
The saintly should always be served with all kinds of gifts; for within the saintly, Lord Hari shines resplendent.
(33) The vision of the saintly is the vision of Hari; the touch of the saintly is indeed the touch of Hari.
Embracing the saintly is embracing Kṛṣṇa, which destroys all sins. (34)
The dust from the feet of the virtuous should be borne upon the head, the heart, and the face;
the water from the feet of the virtuous should be borne upon the mouth, the head, and the body.
The favor of the virtuous should be attained through one’s own body, home, children, and so forth.

By bestowing wealth and prosperity, and by surrendering oneself in every way—(36)—the body is impermanent in all respects; even when protected, it perishes. Therefore, service should always be performed, and the favor of the virtuous should be sought. (37)
Wherever there is a longing for a particular sense organ or object, and where one’s own impulse is exceedingly strong,
service should indeed be rendered to that sense organ for the satisfaction of both.
In the hearts of the virtuous, the Supreme Self shines forth directly.
Therefore, all the auspicious actions of the virtuous arise from their senses and bodies.
For the virtuous, their actions are divine, their bodies are divine, and their collection of senses is always divine; indeed, the constituent elements of the virtuous are divine. (2.80.40)
The deliberation of the virtuous is divine, and the intellect of the virtuous is always divine.
The dream, sleep, and pleasure of the virtuous are likewise entirely divine. Among the virtuous, no work produced by *māyā* exists in any way whatsoever.
In those [realms], merit as well as sin rests upon the Supreme Lord.
They are eternally free from taint, divine, and bestowers of perpetual bliss; they are mines of merit for the virtuous, where indeed not even a trace of sin exists.
Such a divine one as you, O sage Tārakāyana, exists;
indeed, just like Viṣṇu, you are the savior from the ocean of worldly existence.
Tell this to those who have attained union with you, for our fortune is truly great.
Having spoken thus, the king stood waiting for the words of the sage.
Tārakāyana said to him: "Listen, O King, Lord of Bala!
That Blessed One who is celebrated in the world as Puruṣottama..."
And the Supreme Brahman exists in the Veda as the Lord who assumes all incarnations;
he who resides in the supreme abode has appeared in Saurāṣṭra, in the house of Kambharā,
in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, on the grounds of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
That glorious Gopālabāla shines resplendent upon Lomaśabhūmi.
There, there are crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of beloveds of Brahmā, as well as all the Śaktis, crores of sacred fords (tīrthas), and embodied beings. ||48-49||
In human, plant, animal, and elemental creations alike,
where the beloved of Brahmā dwell, longing for Brahman;
there are those who are liberated, who have reached the abode, and those who reside in various celestial realms.
Wherein the yogis dwell, concealed and with their forms transformed—
I go there constantly to behold that Lord, the Supreme Self.
Having worshipped that God in the morning and having drunk from His lotus feet...
"Then, having visited the holy fords, I shall return to my seat.
Thus addressed, the king said: "O Brahmin, tell me, O virtuous one, show me your grace; when will that vision of you be mine? (53)
The sage said, "Accept this mantra and be devoted to its recitation:
'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
O Rādhikā, having given him this mantra, he also gave him a garland of tulasī."
Having bestowed the nectar of Hari’s feet, which is to be served by the great Vaiṣṇavas,
the sage departed for his own abode; thereafter the king, queen,
and son chanted that supreme mantra and remained absorbed in meditation.
They remembered that beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
(57) Then, for the sake of testing the king, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa arrived in the guise of a guest at midday, after his meal. (58)
On the seventh day, a man of dark complexion, wearing an iron bangle, with red eyes and clad only in a loincloth like a forest-dweller, appeared.
Seeing him, the king said to him: "Come here, O forest-roamer! (59)
"Take this food and water, and then go as you please.
The Jaṅgamī replied: "I never eat what has been left over, nor do I eat what has been cooked by another;
how then can you give me food?"
"I am indeed a forest-dweller, and my food is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
I never eat that which originates from other living beings.
If you are true to your promise, let not the word 'no' be spoken by you. (62)
"O King, give me food that is dear to me and which may bring peace.
The king said, "I am able to give you whatever food you desire. Tell me what you wish; I shall give it here. There is nothing that I cannot give you in this matter."
"Whether it be *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, or even *tāmasa*, tell me which of these pleases you here.
If you do not desire one arising from another, then state what arises from yourself and I shall give it to you.
Whatever I am capable of, that I shall surely grant; my vow is to [fulfill] Kārttikeya."
"If it is obtainable, it must certainly be given; tell me, O forest-dweller, and I shall give it to you.
The beggar said: "Listen, O King, I am a meat-eater living in the forest;
yet even in the month of Kārttika, this very vow has been observed by me."
"Only meat that has not been solicited shall be eaten by me from the king's son;
furthermore, if the king himself should give it, it must be from his own heart and nothing else. Such is the vow I maintain: blood is to be drunk only as it comes from the heart.
"I shall not drink water at all, for my vow is of a dark (tāmasa) nature.
O King, I do not beg from you; my vow has been made public, and one must never make a request, as it causes the breaking of a vow."
Having spoken thus, he looked back toward the forest from that spot and began to take steps to depart, so that he would not truly be one who makes a request.
The queen, looking at him, said: "Stay! Remain firm."
"I perform the washing of the feet for this guest who is the Supreme Self.
After a moment, this king offers you your desired food.
Accept this woolen seat and remain here in tranquility.

The woman said: "I have a vow that I must always remain [in this state] during the month of Kārtika. If the naked thigh of a young maiden is obtained, I must remain upon her thigh, and never otherwise."
Then the queen said to her daughter, "Be seated on an auspicious throne, my daughter.
There were three daughters of that king by name— Kṛṣṇā, Bhīmā, and Tuṅgabhadrā— and all three were present there.
Kṛṣṇā, casting off her garment, gave him her thigh as he desired;
she sat there in the forest and became absorbed in meditation.
Then, O King, the son said to his father: "My heart is indeed failing me quickly."
"Having pierced [him], give [the heart] to the Supreme Lord, the Guest, so that there may be liberation.
In an instant, the king indeed split his own body from shoulder to hip with a sword;
having torn open his son's heart, he gave the blood at that very moment.
Then the second daughter, Bhīmā, also, being naked,
placed her own thigh here in the forest for the forest-dweller after setting down some meat;
meanwhile, Tuṅgabhadrikā ate it and drank his blood.
Then those forest-dwellers, though unclothed, repeatedly massaged his hands and thighs;
they massaged his face and his loins, and they also repeatedly performed the massaging of his feet and the rubbing of his body. 81–82.
Then, as soon as the mendicant rose and endeavored to depart,
the king spoke these auspicious words for the sake of a gift:
"The mendicant replied, 'I have a vow that meat must be eaten.'"
Therefore, her mother alone should indeed be accepted as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and never anyone else.
As soon as she had said, "I am a forest-dweller," the queen quickly appeared and said, "Here I am; I shall be your servant. Accept me as the sacrificial fee, O Lord. (84–85)
Having made that forest empty of trees, he stood beneath a tree;
for a moment, he sported in the sky without even touching the earth.
Seeing her held up in the air, the king then reflected:
"Oh, what supreme fortune is mine, as well as that of my son and my daughter-in-law!
What great good fortune for these daughters! We have been employed for the sake of Hari.
Whether one be a forest-dweller, a forest-recluse, a wanderer of the woods, or even one who does not wander the woods," ||| 87-88 ||
The inner self, Hari, is satisfied with my impermanent body and so forth, provided that [the sacrifice] for the sake of others is fruitful; though it is impermanent, it meets its end.
What fortune could be greater than this, by which Mādhava is indeed gratified?
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; everything I have done has become fruitful.
Having come here for the sake of a vow, the forest-dweller has taken away my physical body, yet not even the letter 'Na' has found a place within my mouth. (2.80.90–91)
"Whether it be my wife, my daughters, or my son—victory is mine!
Blessed are those daughters, and blessed also is my dear son.
Blessed too is my queen, for they did not take up this vow. (92)
I have been delivered by my family; truly, my family [is mine].
Having personally caused this auspicious [food] to be accepted for the sake of a guest, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa now stand within my hand by virtue of this vow.
"Today, by the grace of my guest, the world has indeed been conquered by me.
Thinking thus, he became joyful in mind.
Meanwhile, the forest, the trees, and the rest remained there, as if having already feasted upon the queen.
Having completely abandoned his female form, he was then seen indeed accompanied by Mahālakṣmī; joined with Śrī Lakṣmī Rādhikā, he appeared with two arms.
Mahāviṣṇu held the umbrella over him, and Viṣṇu held the vessel of food.
There the Supreme Lord was seen devouring the food;
he was enriched with the splendor of ten million Cupids and as radiant as ten million suns.
He is praised by infinite liberated souls and worshipped by gods and ancestors.
Worshipped by the lords and their incarnations, adorned with ornaments, served by ten million Brahma-priyas, and saluted by the Supreme Imperishable;
he was beheld shining in the supreme abode of the divine void. (2.80.100)
Seated upon his elephant throne in the midst of a divine celestial chariot,
the Divine One— appearing sixteen years of age, smiling, and manifesting love—
looks all around at the devotees, the King, and his virtuous beloved. (101)

The three maidens, with great intensity, repeatedly deluded his mind. There, in the presence of Śrī Hari, the prince remained, divine, adorned with celestial ornaments, possessing his former auspicious form.
Puṇḍraka, laughing, suddenly approached his father from the side of Hari, appearing as pure as one who has just awakened from sleep.
The gods and liberated lords showered down a rain of flowers.

The king praised the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with devotion. (1.05) Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of King Baleśvara’s State of Supreme Devotion through the Yoga of Lord Kapila; the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Forest-Dweller for the Purpose of Testing King Kārtika during the Vrata by the Great Sage Tārakāyana; and the King’s Vision of the Lord through the Surrender of His Sons, Daughter, Wife, and Family," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (80)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to how King Baleśvara, with supreme devotion, praised Mādhava, the Lord of Śrī and the Supreme Controller. 1.
You are the God of gods, the eternal Supreme Self;
you abide in the supreme, imperishable abode.
You indeed are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord.
You alone are the one to be saluted by the liberated, for you are indeed the one to be saluted by the imperishable [Brahmā].
You are to be worshipped and propitiated through all your incarnations, since you are the source of those incarnations;
you are to be saluted by all the lords and propitiated by the divine manifestations (vyūhas) who are intent upon your service.
He is worthy of worship even by those whose nature is Viṣṇu, and by the great lords such as Brahmā and others;
likewise, he is to be honored by the gods, the ancestors, the guardians of the quarters, men, and the Siddhas.
He is also praised by the Daityas, the foremost of the Dānavas, the Asuras, and the Rākṣasas.
You are to be meditated upon by the Nāgas, the spies, and the moving living beings; you are hidden by the sword and reside within the heart of the sword.
5. You became Vāmana, you became Narasiṃha, you became Nārāyaṇa, and you became the son of Vṛṣa (Kṛṣṇa).
You are Viṣṇu in form, you are Haṃsa in form, and you likewise became Matsya and Kūrma (the Fish and the Tortoise). 6.
You are the form of the Boar, you are the form of Kapila; you became Datta, the wielder of the axe.
You are the form of the Sacrifice, the form of Rāma, the form of Kumāra, and the form of the horse-faced [Kārttikeya].
You are the form of the divine sage, the form of the king, and the form of Vyāsa, O Lord of Rādhikā.
You are the very nature of knowledge, the very nature of Hari, the very nature of the Master, and the very nature of the Lord.
You exist in a concealed form as a young student, and you exist in the form of a householder and a forest-dweller.
You are the very embodiment of the virtuous, the embodiment of the chaste, and you are the embodiment of the Brahmin; you are born of the Kṣatriya caste.
You are indeed the form of the Vaiśya, you are a servant, and you are the beautiful form of the dharma of the devoted wife.
You are affectionate toward those who protect their devotees; O Lord, you are the one who assumed the form of Mohinī.
You possess millions of forms, you are the refuge of all virtues, and you are approached with divine and delightful blessings.
You possess a divine body; you are indeed our examiner, and you are our deliverer—protect us! You are the beggar, and you are the devourer of your own son.
You are seen here as the protector and the giver of life; you are the enjoyer of that which is to be enjoyed and the creator of divine play; you are the Lord here, free from all attachment. 1-2.
How was this performed, and by whom? Here, it was indeed accomplished by you, the radiant Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
That which was offered by me has become fruitful through you; O Viśvamūrti, be gracious toward me.
Blessed is Satī, endowed with virtuous character, who is dear to you.
All three of those maidens are blessed;
blessed is your son Pauṇḍraka, and blessed am I, your servant, O Balarāma. (14)
Blessed is your true nature as a forest-dweller;
blessed is the delight of you who have gone to the celestial realm;
and blessed is your meal upon the lap of your son.
Blessed is your son, who is the very form of food; blessed is the Guru, the foremost of yogis and a savior;
and blessed is this land on the banks of the Bhīmā.
Blessed is your most divine action;
blessed is the fortitude of your servants.
The surrender of one's son is the most blessed of all.
The month of Kumuda is a blessed vow;
you are the beginningless Lord of Fortune, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and here, too, King Kambha is blessed. (17)
You are the cowherd boy and the youthful Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Light and the Lord of Pāravatī;
you are the Lord of Rādhā and the Lord of Māṇikikā, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of the Earth, and the Lord of Lords.
You are the Lord of Haṃsā and the Lord of Mañju, the Sovereign of the Gods.
You are indeed the Lord of Māyā and the Lord of all attributes;
this form of yours is equal to many millions of suns, which one cannot truly behold with ease.
He is endowed with many rays of light like ten million suns, and likewise accompanied by numerous incarnations;
he is surrounded by lords and masters, by ancestors, gods, and others, as well as by Daityas and Nāgas;
he is joined with Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Rādhikā, and likewise joined with the discus-weaponed Viṣṇu.
Likewise, he is joined with Mahālakṣmī and is well-worshipped by Mahāviṣṇu.
My eyes are not capable of beholding him here; therefore, diminish your splendor so that you may be worthy of being seen.
Be gracious, O Lord of Life, and make your own form beautiful in the form of a child.
Salutations, salutations to You who deliver [beings] from worldly existence; let there be salutations to You who are devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
To Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, to Nārāyaṇa—salutations, salutations to You again and again. Salutations, salutations to You of infinite forms, with countless faces and indeed innumerable eyes.
Salutations to the Supreme Lord, whose names are infinite, the husband of ten million lotus-eyed maidens.
(24) O Kṛṣṇa, everything I have done has indeed been offered to You; please act in such a way that You remain pleased.
Whatever was to be attained by me, both here and in the hereafter, has now been obtained; nothing remains to be desired. (25)
Having thus praised Rādhikā, O King, the monarch ceased for a moment.
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to the lord of the earth:
"O King, he who is seen here is Mahāviṣṇu himself; you are he."
And she who dwells as Mahālakṣmī is this Śīlavatī of yours;
this Śrī is your Bhīmā, and Lakṣmī is your daughter Kṛṣṇā. Know indeed that Rādhikā, Tuṅgabhadrā, and [Kṛṣṇā] are your three daughters. (27–28)
"This Viṣṇu here is your son Pauṇḍraka himself;
he is Tāraka, and I am your guru, O King, the Lord who bestows liberation.
Behold me here with these divine eyes that have been granted to you."

Behold within your heart my own forms, endowed with all possible appearances, as well as those forms which are my incarnations. O King of kings, this son of yours has not died; he is [here] by means of my illusory power (māyā).
And it was demonstrated by you during the ritual of total surrender for the sake of examination:
"In this Kārtika vow, one must never say 'no' to a petitioner.
O King, accept your son according to his appearance and according to his pleasure.
My wife was enjoyed by me; that which was displayed was not for the sake of testing her. The maidens were made naked; that was done indeed not for the sake of testing them.
I have become pleased, and even most exceedingly pleased.

"You are my incarnations; that indeed shall be your knowledge. From this day forward, all of you shall always be excellent deities here in this world for the sake of liberation, through portions, sub-portions, and further subdivisions of My own. (35)
Your incarnations have been sustained on earth in the form of a family.
By my power, let six of you each assume two forms here; let twelve forms remain here, equal to me.
"Let them come; let them stay there in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
Let the auspicious maidens stay at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Īśa made his own divine form disappear.
He became the very embodiment of Bālakṛṣṇa, especially beautiful to behold;
full of loveliness and the vessel of all beauty, he was a magnet for the eyes and a ground for the steadiness of vision. (2.81.40)
Resembling the campaka flower and possessing a golden luster, he was clothed in garments as pure as fire;
adorned with ornaments set with excellent gems, he was more beautiful than ten million gods of love.
Rich with the fullness of fresh strength, his limbs were firm and filled with vital essence.
He is beautiful in every limb, captivating to the mind, and enchanting;
his gentle smile radiates splendor, and he bestows a stream of love.
He is attainable as a treasure-trove of affection and is the ocean of compassion.
Thus he became a child in form, as delicate as the filaments of a lotus;
with his two eyes like white lotuses, he repeatedly captivated that entire family in order to grant them a boon. (44) He spoke to that whole household for the sake of bestowing the favor.
"The king’s desires are fulfilled and his family is indeed content.
Since the direct presence of the Lord has been attained, what other boon remains here?
Having reflected thus, they said: 'Employ us as you desire. (45–46)
Then Hari, smiling, spoke to the three maidens who had taken refuge with him:
"And as for the maiden named Bhīmā, let her become the river Bhīmā;
let her dwell here in this place within the Bhīmā, taking the form of my own sacred ford."
May the maiden Lakṣmī, named Kṛṣṇā, become the river Kṛṣṇā;
may she dwell here within this Kṛṣṇā, who is the very embodiment of my sacred ford (tīrtha). And may the maiden Rādhā become the river known as the Tuṅgabhadrā. ||48-49||
"Here, she is the very embodiment of my sacred ford (tīrtha), taking the form of the Tuṅgabhadrā.
Thus, these three maidens remained established there within the rivers themselves;
he thus ordained it out of compassion for the sake of performing the upliftment of the world."
The Lord himself, the founder of the holy site (tīrtha), dwelt there together with them.
On the bank of the Bhīmā, Hari shines there as Bhīmākṛṣṇa;
on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā, Hari shines as Nivāsa, named after his residence.
On the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Lord of the Tuṅgabhadrā shines resplendent.
Thus the Blessed One himself created these three delightful sacred sites (tīrtha).
Then he said to the king: "As for you, you shall be Mahābaleśvara."

"O King, you who possess the very form of Mahāviṣṇu and are always equal to Śaṅkara, dwell here as an embodiment of a sacred ford, bestowing the fruits of pilgrimage upon me. Stay together with Mahālakṣmī and your wife Śīlavatī. || 54-55 ||
Thus, having granted an auspicious dwelling to those two, Kṛṣṇa established the holy site of Mahābalēśvara together with Mahālakṣmī.
The king and queen remained forever at Mahābalēśvara.
Then Hari himself spoke to his son Viṣṇu Puṇḍraka:
"O Puṇḍraka, you shall always build a city with a divine form; and you, being the very embodiment of Viśvasthala, shall dwell forever in the city of Puṇḍra."
"And always be the bestower of liberation upon the people who depend on you.
Having thus commanded Viṣṇu to remain in Puṇḍrapura,
and thereafter having established various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and entered into each of them respectively—
Especially Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of all,
took those six divine forms which had been assumed by his command,
and having placed them in his own celestial chariot, he then [took] that Guru Tāraka.
Having summoned the meritorious Tārakā, he entrusted her to the divine hermitage:
"O you who are the very form of a sacred ford, you must remain in this holy place along with Tārakā;
and my mantra must be imparted to any embodied being who comes to you for refuge."
Having spoken thus, he established the lineage of Tāraka upon Tāraka.
And having taken that second form of his onto a divine chariot and bestowed blessings upon all, the blessed Lord Hari was pleased.
Having established seven sacred fords (*tīrtha*) as the foremost on the surface of the earth,
and having bathed in those various locations within those fords, Mādhava,
the leader of the three worlds, created the most excellent of all sacred fords.
When Śrī Hari assumed those seven divine forms within his celestial chariot, the gods—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others— as well as the sages and the ancestors, [gathered there]. (66–67)
The Sādhyas, Siddhas, Vasus, Īśvaras, and the best of men arrived there suddenly and repeatedly uttered cries of "Victory!
They raised shouts of joy and honored him with unblemished offerings.
They let fall a rain of flowers and sprinkled sandalwood water;
they honored him with parched grain and gladdened him with hymns of praise.
They bowed down, paid their respects, and offered him hospitality with their very selves.
Having offered various articles, they likewise gave words of praise and said to the venerable Supreme Self: "O Lord! There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be given by you to a devotee;
the Lord of Bali is an illustration of this. (71)
Such an examination should not be performed anywhere else;
for in some cases, it might destroy the vow of those who are unripe through deceit.
O Kṛṣṇa, since you are free from deceit, your examination must likewise be free from deceit.
"By one devoid of *māyā*, that which is difficult to overcome can be mastered by one who possesses *māyā*.
Having said this, and having worshipped the Supreme Lord with flower garlands and other offerings,
he then likewise honored those seven great liberated ones (*mahāmuktas*).
All the other gods and their hosts vanished from sight.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa directed his celestial chariot through the sky; it swiftly arrived at Āśvasārasa.
In the field of Kuṃkumavāpikā, in the vicinity of the hermitage of Lomaśa,
he descended in the evening after having wandered ten yojanas, blazing with eight forms and possessing a splendor like that of ten million suns.
In the midst of a grove of kadamba trees, within a most enchanting garden,
those men and women then descended upon the earth all around;
they ran forward for the sake of a vision and beheld the Supreme Lord.
In an instant, even the people beheld the celestial chariot, which was accompanied by seven divine and highly fortunate devotees and had become invisible;
they then uttered cries of "Victory! and prostrated before the auspicious group of eight.
Hari led his mother and father to their residence;
then, having shown them Śrī Lomaśa,
he led them to Aśvapaṭṭasara and subsequently to other holy pilgrimage sites.
He gave an excellent mansion for the permanent residence of Kudamba,
and he granted a hermitage at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā to Tāraka.
He provided hospitality, food, drink, furnishings, and all necessary articles.
Śrī Puruṣottama granted everything desired that was divine;
and Hari said to the king: "Indeed, through my power, your vow of Kārtika has attained completion in every respect."
Fame, charity, the food-sacrifice, water, clothing, wealth and the like;
chanting, fire-offerings, service to guests, and subsisting on fruits for a month—
all this has reached completion for you through a mere fraction of my grace.
"O King, there remains nothing else for you to do.
Devote yourself to service here and offer everything to me; thus, the vow of ten million Kārtikas has reached completion for you. (87–88)
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, had spoken thus,
the king offered his three daughters there to that beloved wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
he then sent the maidens to the hermitage of the sage Lomaśa.
Śrī Hari caused Bali’s lord Tāraka, the virtuous Satī,
and his son Puṇḍraka to perform ablutions there;
thus those places became sacred fords (tīrthas) like the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Those divine stars, indeed well-known by their respective names,
then rested themselves in his exceedingly soft abode;
thereafter, he slept at night, and then, at dawn on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha.
On the birthday of Śrī Hari, Tāraka performed worship;
so too did Mahābaleśvara, the three maidens, the young girls, the ṛṣis, the munis, the siddhas, human beings, the gods, and others. (93–94)
All the goddesses, the mistresses, worshipped the Supreme Lord.
On the first day of the tenth year, in the pavilion, Hari, the Supreme Person,
sat upon a magnificent, divine elephant-throne.
The guardians of the Lord, the guardians of the worlds, and the guardians of the kingdom all arrived.
They worshipped him with exceeding love, and Lomaśa performed the ritual of adoration.
Then he performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, and the gods and others presented offerings.
The father and mother provided a feast and extended hospitality to the families of the gods and goddesses with great honor, wealth, and other gifts.
Then he arranged for their departure and held a grand festival at evening.
Other Vidyādharīs and skilled women performed dancing and singing;
their father himself gave them rewards and other gifts, while Hari bestowed blessings, happiness, excellent food, and so forth. (2.81.99–100)
Having thus completed that most excellent ten-year festival,
he fed the brahmins and others residing at Kuṅkumavāpikā;
he gave gifts of jewels and cows for the satisfaction of his supplicants.
Having thus celebrated a great festival, the gods and others departed for heaven.
All the other cowherds and Kṛṣṇa returned to their respective worlds;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa also rested comfortably in his palace.
Accompanied by the maiden, Lomaśa, having received worship, went to his hermitage;
the honored guests returned to their own country, praising the festival.
Then, eager for the service of Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—
The two divine Hemanta and Bhagavān, attendants of Śrī Hari, remained constantly in the service of the Lord with their whole being like servants;
they served Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with royal offerings. (1.05–1.06)
O Rādhā, by reading or hearing of the deeds of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa,
enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained through the majesty of the Beloved of Prabhā (the Sun).

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of King Baleśvara with his Family Praising Śrī Hari and Attaining Two-fold Divine Bodies," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lasmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe the manifest Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
who was indeed instructed by Viśvāmitra to Jayadhvaja during the sacrifice.
There was a king of the lunar dynasty named Sahasrārjuna;
he possessed a thousand arms, was radiant, and was the foremost among those skilled in the science of archery.
He had five hundred sons, all of whom were great chariot-warriors.
Skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and worshippers of the gods—
some of them worship Rudra, some the Sun, others the Sacrifice;
others worship Fire, others Viṣṇu, and others Satī.
Others worship Aja, while others worship Gaṇeśa and Candraka;
Jayadhvaja was the youngest, who was indeed the last-born of all.
He became devoted solely to the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
That wise one constantly takes refuge in the Lord Nārāyaṇa-Hari, Viṣṇu, the deity who is higher than Brahman. To him, his other sons said: "Listen, O righteous younger brother! (6–7)
"Our father worshipped the god Vahni, Śiva, Datta, and likewise Muni;
worship them here, do not worship Nārāyaṇa.
Jayadhvaja said to them, "But my supreme duty is considered to be [him]."
On this earth, kings have arisen as portions of Viṣṇu.
The Lord Puruṣottama is the protector of their kingdom;
Viṣṇu, the unconquered Hari, is the worshipful guardian of the worlds.
Indeed, Śrī Hari is to be worshipped by you in every way;
for Brahmā, whose form is rajas, creates, and Hara, who is characterized by tamas,
destroys, while the Lord Viṣṇu, whose nature is sattva, nourishes all at all times.

Therefore, for kings protecting their kingdom, this Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Sovereign Nārāyaṇa, must be propitiated. By means of *sattva*, a living being is liberated; Lord Hari is the very soul of *sattva*.

The quality of *sattva* is always the most excellent, as determined by the practitioners of yoga. In the purification of all things, the purification of *sattva* brings about clarity and fearlessness. That *sāttvika* purity in Viṣṇu is indeed eternal fearlessness.

In Śambhu, Vahni, and likewise Sūrya, the quality of Tamas is predominant; in Kratu, Satya, Gaṇeśa, and Aja, Rajas is predominant; and in Candraka, Sattva is predominant. In Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods, Nārāyaṇa, Sattva is especially distinguished.
O brothers! He is always to be honored by you as well;
for there, Viṣṇu is the nourisher and the teacher, and the duty of kingship also resides therein.
One's own duty (svadharma) is conducive to liberation, but no other [duty] leads to the complete liberation of kings.
[She is] the great power Nārāyaṇī, who always bestows [blessings] upon kings.
Having heard thus that the supreme worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the highest dharma and virtue of a father, his elder brothers spoke. (18–19)
"Your father propitiated the Fire-god, and likewise Lord Śambhu was granted [to him].
Therefore, these very deities should be accepted for worship according to the duty toward the ancestors; through this, liberation is attained.
Jayadhvaja then said to them, "What has been spoken by my elder brothers is indeed appropriate."
The duty toward one's father must be protected, both according to expectation and even more so.
However, regarding this matter of sacrifice, which involves the assembly of all the gods, as to who is to be honored and worshipped, Acyuta gave this answer: [21–22]
For in this matter, whatever the bull-like sages of valid authority might say, that shall indeed be so.
Then the sages Vasiṣṭha and others, the bulls among progenitors,
were summoned and questioned regarding the dispute over dharma concerning the form of worshiping the gods.
"Tell us, which deity is to be propitiated at a sacrifice, or at any other time?
To them, those sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, spoke according to the truth:
"Whichever [deity] is favored by a person, that indeed is his own deity. (24–25)
However, even a mere stone is worshipped due to a specific purpose and because it grants desired results;
for there are many deities, as they are indeed the very forms of Brahman.
Furthermore, seekers of various goals exist, and just as the goals differ, so too do the deities.

Due to the exigency of business, the force of time, a command, or likewise a royal decree: (27) A servant may be attended upon by a king somewhere due to the exigency of business; and a servant may also attend upon another servant for the sake of business as well. (28)
Even the most excellent serve those who are inferior for the sake of a particular task.
Furthermore, castes are differentiated according to the configuration of their bodies;
whatever purpose arises from a particular [body], that body is discarded for the sake of that very purpose.
For the sake of excellent and desired fruits and the like, they worship the crops;
for the sake of obtaining flavor, they worship the earth and water;
and for the sake of the ripening of flavors, they worship the sun and the moon.
For kings, Viṣṇu as well as Purandara is the deity;
for Brahmins, Agni, Āditya, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the gods [are the deities].
For the gods, Viṣṇu is always the deity, and for the Dānavas, Hara.
Soma is said to be the deity of the Gandharvas and the Yakṣas.
Vāgdevī is the deity of the Vidyādharas, and the blessed Lord Hari is the deity of the Siddhas.
Śaṅkara is the deity of the Rākṣasas, while Pārvatī is the deity of the Kinnaras.
Among the sages, Brahmā is the deity; Śiva, the ancestors, and the gods;
as are the Sun, Agni, the Viśvedevas, and likewise Janārdana.
Among women, the deity is Lakṣmī; and for those devoted to their husbands, it is Rati.
The husband, the Supreme Lord, Śambhu, and even the Goddess of Good Fortune (Śrī) [are the deities].
For householders, the gods and goddesses are the deities as required by their respective circumstances;
for ascetics and celibate students, the Supreme Brahman himself is the deity. (26, 37)
For the virtuous, the goddess Kṣamā (Forgiveness) is their deity, as is Śīla (Good Conduct);
for children, their parents are their deity; for animals, the Protector is their god.
For the hosts [of attendants], Śaṅkara is their deity; for devotees, the Supreme Lord is their deity.
Among lords, Vāsudeva is the deity; among trees, water is the deity.
The inner controller, the glorious Supreme Lord, is the deity of all things.
For the sick, medicine is the deity; for thieves, punishment is likewise the deity.
Thus, whether it be insentient or sentient, whatever one's own chosen deity may be,
Śrī Hari, who exists everywhere, is the deity of all. Therefore,
Jayadhvaja certainly deserves to perform the worship of Viṣṇu.
One should realize the identity of Hari with Rudra, Viṣṇu, and even Brahmā.
Having understood this, Hari—the Lord of the lords of all—is always to be worshipped;
likewise, all the incarnations, such as Vāsudeva and the others, are contained therein.

Mahāviṣṇu and others who are Vairājas, as well as those who are partial incarnations (aṃśa), or even those who are manifestations through possession (āveśa) or portions (kalā)— the gods and all such beings—
attain perfect union with Śrī Hari, the Supreme Self.
"The gods, goddesses, the guru, the virtuous, the brahmins, the cows, and devoted wives"—
having spoken thus, all the sages performed his sacrifice,
a supreme Vaiṣṇava rite in which the sacred rites were completed over seven days.
There, all the lords, the sages, and likewise the deities— all the inhabitants of heaven, including the planets, humans, and brahmins—
enjoyed in every way various kinds of cooked foods and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
The fires and all the Maruts attained supreme satisfaction through the consumption of Soma and the drinking of nectar at that sacrifice performed with great devotion;
they partook of the offered oblations and other offerings, which brought contentment to the three worlds.
And the divine-form Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, arose visibly from the fire and partook [of the offerings].
Thus, when the sacrifice was successfully completed and the rite of giving the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) had been performed—
When the remaining oblations had been offered and the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) was completed,
all the brahmins and others took their meal in rows.
Just then, a rākṣasa named Videha arrived there.
Terrifying with his fangs, with blazing eyes, and bearing a trident, he roared in all directions.
Seeing him, mortals fled in fear toward the forest.
Then all the great and powerful sons of Arjuna prepared themselves.
They fought the Dānava with spears, mountain peaks, swords,
and mallets. There, the lords of the earth hurled at him the weapons of Prajāpati, Varuṇa, Rudra, Vāyu, Kubera, Indra, and Agni.
Taking up a trident that shone like the sun and whirling it around,
the Dānava brandished it and shattered those weapons on all sides;
by means of the fire residing in the trident, he drew them back in every way.
Then the fierce kings struck him with maces;
yet as soon as they touched his body, which was like a mountain of clay, all the maces shattered.
Even those lords were unable to move the Dānava with their maces.
Then, overcome by fear upon witnessing his prowess, they fled; their enthusiasm was shattered when they beheld his extraordinary valor. Thus occurred the flight of the five hundred princes.
Upon seeing him, Jayadhvaja remembered Hari Nārāyaṇa—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the Supreme Person.
Having meditated for a moment, he recited this mantra: "Protect me, protect me, O Supreme Person! (2.82.60–61).
"O Protector of those who have come for refuge, come here, O Supreme Lord!
Being thus remembered, the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari himself quickly arrived there, bearing the discus, conch, lotus, and mace as his weapons.
Viṣṇu—the victorious, the source of the worlds, the immeasurable, and free from all affliction;
Śrī Hari, the protector of devotees, the primordial and supreme Person—bestowed his own Sudarśana discus upon Jayadhvaja. (63–64)
Having bowed to Śrī Hari, the king took the Sudarśana discus in his hand;
he then hurled it at the Rākṣasa on his shoulders,
and it quickly struck off his head from the shoulders onto the ground.
"The Rākṣasa there, possessing a body as large as a mountain, has been destroyed.
Knowing this, the seer Viśvāmitra arrived to see him;
and his brothers, being delighted, praised that banner of victory.
They offered an excellent seat to the sage Viśvāmitra.
The sage sat there and then inquired after his welfare.
Jayadhvaja said to the sage: "By your grace, the asura..."
There, the great Dānava Videha was struck down by my discus.
Because of your words, I have always worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa;
I sought refuge in him, and he has bestowed his grace upon me.
Thinking, "I shall perform a sacrifice for the sake of destroying the sin of killing a rākṣasa," [he asked:
"How and by what ritual procedure is Hari, the Lord, to be worshipped?
Who is this Nārāyaṇa who is to be honored here in the sacrifice, and what is his power?"
"Explain all of this to me; I wish to propitiate that Lord.
Having heard the words of Jayadhvaja, Mani spoke to him—Jayadhvaja, who was a foremost devotee of the Supreme Lord and had sought refuge in Him. (72–73)
Worship that Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, from whom the activity of all beings proceeds, in whom everything is, and from whom the universe arises; him who is without beginning,
whom they call the one beyond the imperishable, residing in the secret cave of the heart.
[He is] Ānanda, the supreme ether, the Lord stationed in the highest abode;
higher than the high, the Supreme Brahman, higher even than Para-Nārāyaṇa;
the sovereign of the Imperishable, the bestower of liberation, for he is indeed the Lord of the liberated. (75–76)
He who is the cause of thousands of incarnations, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),

who assumes the fourfold manifestation (Caturvyūha) and yet remains without manifestation (Avyūha), the stainless one (Nirañjana); he is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), the supreme abode (Parandhāma), the supreme ether (Paramavyoma), and the supreme state (Paramapada).
The exponents of Brahman declare that the imperishable Brahman consists of three quarters;
[it is] Vāsudeva, the Lord, the perfected one of yoga, the illustrious Puruṣottama,
from whose portions the lords Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have arisen.
Vairāja, Mahāviṣṇu, Bhūman, and Kāla are those born from his portions; he who is the Lord of Pradhāna, the Lord of Māyā, and also Puruṣa—
he is known as Mahāpuruṣa, whose portion likewise exists within her.
And that Supreme Person, the Lord who is himself the highest among all the Blessed Ones,
is to be propitiated through selfless surrender (*prapatti*).
O King, therefore, once again propitiate that sacrifice, the Supreme Lord.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra ceased.
Thereupon, the sacrifice was commenced by the king; and there, Viśvāmitra, together with the brahmins, [worshipped] the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva.
He caused the sacrifice for the Lord of All, the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest.
When the sacrifice reached its conclusion, the Blessed Lord Hari himself appeared there in person, repeatedly consuming the oblations.
"Choose a boon, O Lord of the Earth, whatever dwells in your mind.
Thus Hari spoke, and the King said:
"O Compassionate One, lead me to Your eternal, supreme, and divine abode."
Hari said, "What you have requested is excellent; let it indeed be so.
Having spoken thus, he vanished from sight. At that moment, four ascetics arrived there, saying, "Give us alms. (87-88)
The king gave them alms consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) for their meal;
they accepted it and ate, and the king gave them a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
At that time, those monks were dark-complexioned, coarse, and hairy.
Assuming various forms, they were forest-dwellers of hideous appearance.
Having eaten, they drank water and then sat down, taking refuge under trees;
for those four were like fools, yet tranquil, resembling calm clouds.
When the sacrificial rites were perfectly completed, all four of them went together to the Narmadā for the purpose of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*).
All the sages, gods, and Vaiṣṇava devotees likewise bathed there.
The humans there were full of majesty, as were the brahmins, who were truthful and virtuous.
(13) But those four, having bathed in the lower part, were of dark complexion;
by the power of the merit of their bathing, they became white-complexioned. (94)
Resplendent like the sun and moon, possessing forms equal to those of Mahendra,
with bodies as magnificent as Viṣṇu, and divine like the gods of heaven—
seeing them, those who had performed their ritual ablutions after the sacrifice (avabhṛtha) questioned them regarding their lineage.
They spoke their respective names: "This first one is Śrīśaila;
this second is Nīlagiri; and this third is Elādri.
This fourth is Droṇācala. We are born from the lineage of Meru. (96–97)
We are mountains capable of assuming any form at will, desiring to bathe here;
we are steadfast mountains, Vaiṣṇavas who wish to wash away our sins.
Indeed, there are those who seek to harm us in the forests and in the caves.
Whatever sins even the heretics dwelling here commit,
by transferring those sins to us, they indeed depart purified.
Through those sins we became black of complexion, but by bathing, we have become fair.
Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself came there for the sake of receiving his portion of the sacrifice and also for the sake of bathing;
by that grace of the Vaiṣṇavas, every single sin was destroyed.
"Then, O mountains, we shall go to our own abodes; salutations be unto you!
There, where the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself resides, his devotees bathed in the water, for this is indeed the Narmadā Tīrtha."
And Jayadhvaja said to them, "I shall perform the rites of hospitality;
may you, O best of mountains, indeed take up residence here in my home.
Having spoken thus to the mountains, who were like gold in color, O King, O Rādhikā—
At the conclusion of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he led them all to their respective abodes with great affection.
All the other honored guests, having partaken of food and received worship, departed for their own homes; Jayadhvaja, however, remained there to rest.

The subjects— including the helpless, the wretched, servants, male and female slaves, and even insects such as ants— were satisfied by that excessive food. Whoever hears this with devotion, causes it to be read, or reads it themselves, [attains the highest goal].
"By the power of Nārāyaṇa’s grace, for him there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(108) Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Jayadhvaja’s Attainment of Śrī Hari at the Sacrifice through the Power of the Worship of the Supreme Brahman Taught by Viśvāmitra, the Destruction of the Videha Rākṣasa, and the Avabhṛtha Bath at the Four Mountains," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
