→ Chapter 84
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, in this way that king Jayadhvaja, a true Vaiṣṇava, [installed] Droṇa, Elā, Nīla, and Śrīśaila—all four—in his own abode. || 1 ||
Having honored them with seats and other offerings, he extended a most excellent welcome;
he gave them delicious foods, various drinks, and even diverse kinds of edibles,
as well as articles for enjoyment, beautiful utensils, and water.
Jayadhvaja also gave the articles for the worship of Śrī Hari.
(3) Those mountains, having accomplished their purpose, questioned Jayadhvaja:
"How are sins destroyed? How is one liberated from material nature? (4)
How may one remain forever untainted even when accused of sin?
Through the company of whom does liberation arise, and from what comes eternal peace?
What is one's own interest, what is the interest of others, and what activity brings about auspiciousness?
By what karma is either dullness or divinity attained?
O Great King, you remain like an omniscient one, a sovereign among devotees, by virtue of even a fraction of the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (6–7)
"Therefore, tell us the supreme good by which it may be attained.
Having heard this, Jayadhvaja said: "In my forest dwell many great sages who are divine and enriched with realized knowledge. (8)
I go constantly for the sake of seeing them and for the attainment of knowledge.
Whatever I have heard from them through the opportunity of conversational discourse, as well as during the hearing of the stories of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, [is as follows].

Listen as I relate what I have experienced myself: sins are destroyed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), whether that ford be stationary or mobile. Having rescued the one who has come for refuge from the ocean called latent impressions (vāsanā)— 11. Listen as I relate what I have experienced myself: sins are destroyed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), whether that ford be stationary or mobile. Having rescued the one who has come for refuge from the ocean called latent impressions (vāsanā)—
It sends forth even the supreme abode of the Supreme Lord.
That sacred site (tīrtha) should be understood in every respect as being either insentient or of the nature of consciousness.
The insentient consists of waters, shrines, and material objects composed of the elements. || 12–13 ||
Indeed, even those sacred sites that are devoid of qualities become divine through divine yoga;
such holy places invariably deliver even the sinful in every way.
The Self is declared to be the great sacred site, and Kṛṣṇa is the most excellent among all sacred sites.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the most excellent holy ford (tīrtha). Through union with that holy ford, all devotees—saints, virtuous women, and yogis—become embodiments of the holy ford and saviors. 15–16.

Those who are devoted to the character of Brahman, the character of the household, and the character of the forest; those who are dispassionate, devoted to renunciation, and devoted to meditation—they are indeed considered to be the true tirthas of Kṛṣṇa.
They are the servants of Kṛṣṇa, the devotees of Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the associates of Kṛṣṇa.
Holy places, both inanimate and animate, have attained their status through their connection with Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, a person enriched by Kṛṣṇa’s qualities, a virtuous woman, and even beasts, birds, trees, and creepers—through union with Kṛṣṇa, they are all liberators. (18–19)
Gardens, village halls, rest-houses for travelers,
riverbanks, lake shores, forest clearings, mountains, and wilderness tracts—
these stationary and moving things are the sacred sites (tīrtha) of the yogi Kṛṣṇa.
Villages, cities, towns, capitals, market-towns,
hamlets, settlements, and dwellings— wherever Kṛṣṇa shines forth,
all that is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha), a savior that has attained divinity. (21–22)
That which is directly touched by Hari becomes a liberating *tīrtha*.
For as is Hari, so indeed are his holy men; they are truly *tīrthas*.
By bestowing knowledge, they constantly enable people to cross over [to liberation]. (23)
And having destroyed ignorance, they bestow divinity.
Having destroyed desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, envy, thirst, and latent impressions, they perform purification. (24–25)
By association with them, those who abide by the virtuous cross over illusion as if by means of boats.
The virtuous are eyes; the virtuous are lamps.
The virtuous are boats for those in the ocean, and they are islands of nectar for those in the forest fire.
Indeed, among those overwhelmed by poison, the virtuous are the destroyers of venom, taking away the sting;

for in this ocean of worldly existence which is like Hālāhala poison, the holy ones are the blue-throated Śiva; and in this ocean of worldly existence which is like a sea of great diseases, they are the very embodiment of Dhanvantari.
For the virtuous are like rains for those scorched by the fire of sense-objects;
indeed, they take the form of shears for those bound by the net of latent impressions.
The virtuous are the supreme sacred ford, a ford fashioned by the Supreme Self.

Where Nārāyaṇa himself always dwells in embodied form—(2.83.30)—and where those who have renounced the life of a householder for the sake of Hari have completely abandoned all worldly ties; indeed, such saintly persons are embodiments of sacred pilgrimage sites, bound to Śrī Hari. (31)
Hari is the supreme sacred ford; from Him come the saintly, who are themselves sacred fords;
and the saintly women are likewise sacred fords like the saints. By means of these, even sinners cross over [suffering].
These three constitute the supreme sacred ford, while the assembly of brāhmaṇas is the fourth.

The guru is a sacred ford (tīrtha), the best of all sacred fords, and the eternal bestower of liberation. The mother is a sacred ford; the father is a supreme sacred ford; likewise, the husband is a sacred ford.
A chaste wife is a sacred ford, dharma is a sacred ford, and righteous people are indeed sacred fords.
A son is a sacred ford, as is one endowed with righteousness; a daughter is a sacred ford when possessed of virtue;

a sister is a sacred ford when joined with dharma; and a wife is a sacred ford if she is chaste. A righteous family is a sacred ford that delivers others; it is the most excellent of all sacred fords.
A temple is a sacred ford, and the nectar of sacred stories is a sacred ford. (36) The speech of the elders is a sacred ford, and the eternal scripture is a sacred ford.
The gift of a cow is the supreme sacred ford, and the giving of gold and food is a sacred ford. (37)
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, freedom from passion is a sacred ford;
likewise, freedom from hatred is a sacred ford that produces purity.
Service to Kṛṣṇa is the supreme sacred ford, and devotion is likewise the highest sacred ford.
Dedication to Kṛṣṇa is said to be the supreme among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
From the perspective of discernment, initiation, mendicancy, and right observation constitute the triad of sacred fords.
Thus, indeed, the mountains become sacred fords through their connection with Hari.
What need is there for many words here? The virtuous are in every way holy places of pilgrimage;
they bestow everything upon living beings seeking dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Having sought refuge with the virtuous, one certainly crosses over [suffering]; of this there is no doubt.
One who has taken hold of a piece of wood certainly crosses the ocean of waters.
In wood there is indeed lightness, and Hari dwells among the virtuous.
Wherever Hari is, there is everything that is most desired.
The wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpavallī*) is in the hands of the virtuous; the wish-granting gem (*cintāmaṇi*) is in the mouths of the virtuous;

the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) is in the hearts of the virtuous; and the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*) is in the minds of the virtuous. Furthermore, the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) beginning with *aṇimā* roll at the feet of the virtuous.
Indeed, the lordly powers that bestow happiness reside upon the lips of the virtuous. Purity dwells in the gaze of the virtuous, and righteousness likewise resides in their speech.
Liberation, having come for refuge, abides in the service of the virtuous.
Nature is said to be *māyā*, and its practice consists of engagement with sense objects.
This latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which persists in its state, is worn away by the practice of [meditating on] Kṛṣṇa.
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa; Nārāyaṇa," [one should recite] at all times.
For indeed, by means of recitation (*raṭana*), the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) come into being.
Through the "black yoga" (*kṛṣṇayoga*), those divine [impressions] destroy the illusory ones;
having destroyed the material ones, they purify the interior of the heart.

That illusion (māyā)— whether it takes the form of delusion, or consists of ignorance (avidyā) characterized by the sense of "I" and "mine," or consists of attachment and aversion, or is doubt consisting of falsehood—
goes to dissolution through the power of Hari by means of the method of knowing things as they truly are. (2.83.50)
If, having reached the moment of death, the mind is not fixed upon Kṛṣṇa;

|| 51 || and if the mind is instead directed toward a woman, a man, a son, wealth, or anything else—that illusion, which is the very cause of bondage, perishes through the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa. || 52 ||
Thus let the mountains listen: for the yoga of Kṛṣṇa is indeed the savior;
even the yoga of the virtuous is a savior, by which Māyā is turned back.
Just as iron, through its union with wood, truly floats upon the water.
Likewise, even a sinner crosses over the ocean of worldly existence through union with the virtuous.
(54) Just as a lotus, by its very nature, is not stained even when in water, so too the man of knowledge who is endowed with devotion is not stained even by sin. (55)
Just as oil thrown into the midst of water floats upon its surface,
so the man of knowledge, though situated among the sinful, floats above sin.
Knowledge burns away actions, and devotion burns away the fruits of action.
In this way, he burns away both other types of karma— the black and the white— that have been performed. That self which was held within the supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, now exists as the self,
separated from the internal organs.
The internal instrument [of cognition] is thereby divided by the internal effort;
it does not perceive through the senses, being devoid of power and parched without its Lord.
Consequently, the senses do not go toward objects when they are abandoned by Kṛṣṇa.

For sin that has entered into the objects of the senses does not remain there once they have been withdrawn. (2.83.60) When the sense organs of the yogin no longer have their objects, his mind likewise becomes forever free from objects. (2.83.61)
The self, devoid of objects, is considered by Kṛṣṇa alone;
at that time, it indeed becomes one who has turned away from sin and is destined for liberation.
If, having become thus, it were to create a body and sense organs, [it would not be liberated].
Whatever action it may be, this [state] does not lead to bondage for the yogin—
whether it be an action performed according to scriptural injunctions, or one devoid of such injunctions;
whether it be an action recognized in the world, or one not so recognized and thus excluded from worldly convention.
Whether performed with discernment or not performed with discernment, whether devoid of discernment,
sinful, or free from sin— whatever action a yogi may perform, however it may appear in the eyes of the world, let it be just so. (65)
That which is innate does not lead to his bondage.
He who has no attachment to pleasure and no aversion toward objects of suffering,
whose self is free from both elation and dejection— he is not defiled by evil.

For one whose intellect is free from the desire "may I have happiness" or "may I not have suffering," there is no need for effort; indeed, the state of effortless action does not destroy what must be done.
Thus, he by whom both the desirable and the undesirable have been forever abandoned from the perspective of the Self— (68) —[he alone is liberated].
For him, indeed, the subjugation of the three qualities never occurs.

For one by whom everything—the object of enjoyment, the act of enjoying, and the state of being the enjoyer—is of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, and by whom every action arising from the body and senses is offered to Kṛṣṇa. (2.83.70)
Whether it be sin or merit, its fruit is likewise offered to Kṛṣṇa;
though he may be smeared by all things, he is not tainted in the slightest.
Indeed, this is the state of one who acts for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
For one who has accomplished what was to be accomplished, whose nature is always virtuous, and who is untainted—through association with such a person, liberation that destroys bondage shall arise.
Indeed, bondage is said to be latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is characterized by the notions of "I" and "mine. (72–73)
That which is the birth of false knowledge and the latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of insentience—that is indeed saṃsāra, the bondage; it perishes through union with Kṛṣṇa.
It perishes through association with the virtuous whose nature is Kṛṣṇa.
Then there is indeed liberation for the living one, free from the bondage of the elements;
it is beyond dualities, devoid of effort, free from thirst, and devoid of passion;
it is a state established in the eternal Self, overflowing with eternal bliss.
For one who is ever peaceful, peace arises through union with Kṛṣṇa, the Imperishable;
that eternal peace which is experienced through the self by means of the self in its steadfastness is born from Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. (77)
This is liberation; it is the supreme liberation, for there is indeed no peace higher than this.
Immersion in the Supreme Self amidst an immeasurable mass of bliss—that is the true purpose of one’s own self, for that is the ultimate goal. (78–79)
For one who desires liberation, the goal of the world of living beings is indeed one's own true interest (*svārtha*).
When that goal is known, one should seek it within one's own self; that is one's true interest, and here it is liberation.
That interest which provides momentary pleasure should certainly not be pursued by those seeking liberation.
Those seeking liberation should regard their own true interest as consisting of eternal bliss.
(81) Thus, it is precisely by perceiving one's own interest that activity bestows what is auspicious;
the auspicious is merit, the heavenly world, and the truth of the divine abode. (82)
That which is associated with destruction is said to result from the creation of Prakṛti;
liberation (mokṣa) is indestructible, auspicious, and the attainment of the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
The attainment of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is auspicious and the most supreme of all.
Kṛṣṇa is divine and eternally so, whether he appears as he is or otherwise.
Through actions that identify with him, a human being attains a divine state;
for even the body, the senses, and their activities, though insentient, [become divine] through the grasp of Hari.
Inanimate things attain divine states, and the divine attains insentience. O mountains! In the same way, you too shall become divine through the practice of devotion.
Abandoning this state of inertia, may you become possessed of divine forms.

The Lord and Master Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, who is without beginning, resides in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī near Lake Aśvasaras. Let them practice union with Him and worship Him; through that, let them attain divinity. (87–88)
"You shall indeed depart quickly by the power of Nārāyaṇa’s grace.
While Jayadhvaja was speaking thus to the mountains,
four other tranquil persons arrived there.
Having bowed to Jayadhvaja and the others, they then stood behind him.
"From where have you come? Where are you going? What is your purpose? They replied to him, "We are the Vinatas; having heard of your sacrifice... (2.83.90–91).
Having arrived here with joy, let us go to the Aśvasaras lake to bathe and to behold the Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Master. Indeed,
the countless sins offered by the pilgrims [are destroyed there].
Let us go to the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā to perform our ablutions.
This king of holy places (tīrtharāj) is renowned by the name Kolārasara;
this second one is indeed known by the name Cilasarovara.
This third king of holy fords is named Śambhala-saras;
I am the fourth, the person Nārāyaṇa-sarovara.
Having gathered together today, we have gone to Lake Mānasa.
Then, having heard that there was a divine lake on the Golden Mountain for the purpose of seeing [the Lord],
we have come here from there to this sacrifice;
now we shall go to that very place where the Supreme Lord shines.
Having heard this, those mountain deities and King Jayadhvaja,
together with their families, all traveled through the sky to the city of Hari;
[they went] to the holy site of Kumkumavapika and the Ashvapat-tasarovara lake.
They descended from the sky and bathed in the Aśvasarovara lake.
Then, having seen the sage Śrī Lomaśa in his divine form, they [uttered]:
"Oṃ namas śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (2.83.100)
Having received the supreme mantra, they went into the presence of Bālakṛṣṇa;
then, having worshipped Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites,
they drank the nectar from his feet and, being honored, sat down before him.
They prayed most fervently: "Grant us liberation, the supreme state!
(102) Śrī Hari, out of compassion, caused those three forms to assume the appearance of liberated devotees of the holy places, and then sent them forth as sacred pilgrimage sites. (103)
Indeed, for the sake of purifying embodied beings, he settled his various respective dwellings there like a lake of faith;
having appointed the great devotees as his own servants within his own refuge.
From that time forward, he resided at that sacred ford (tīrtha) along with eight other holy sites:
Kolāṭatīrtha, the excellent Cilatīrtha,
Śambhalatīrtha, and likewise Nārāyaṇasaraḥ.
Droṇatīrtha, Nīlatīrtha, Śrītīrtha,
and Cailatīrtha shine with divine forms at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having assumed liberated forms, the Lord sent them by celestial chariot to the imperishable realm (Akṣara).
"O Rādhikā, [this is] the abode known as the dwelling place of the liberated; [it belongs to] the ocean of compassion.
Having thus witnessed that wonder, Jayadhvaja also, remaining there for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, prayed for liberation from Hari.

Hari granted him liberation, and he departed by means of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to the imperishable abode, the divine state filled with eternal bliss. Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge Imparted by Jayadhvaja, the Divine Nature of Droṇa, Eilanīla, Śrīparvata, Kolāṭa, Cila, Śambhala, Nārāyaṇa, and the Lakes, the Liberation [of those], and the Final Emancipation of Jayadhvaja," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to this wonder of Nārāyaṇa—the devotion shown by the wife of Pulastya, the son of Brahmā. (1)
The beloved and auspicious wife of Pulastya was the daughter of Tṛṇabindu, named Ailavilā;
by her, Viśravas was born as their son.
He became a knower of many scriptures and was devoted to righteousness.
Once, Cailavilā asked Pulastya regarding the virtues (*vṛṣa*):
"O Lord, tell me, what were the duties of the ages (*yugadharma*) like in ancient times?
Thereupon, Pulastya spoke of all the virtues in brief.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
In the Kṛta age, meditation and austerity are paramount; in the Tretā, knowledge and sacrifice;
in the Dvāpara, sacrifice alone; and in the Kali age, charity is the sole means.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the god Brahmā was omnipresent;
in the Tretā Yuga, the sun became the means of movement, capable of uniting [all things];
and in the Dvāpara Yuga, the deity Viṣṇu himself became the means of movement.
In the Kali age, the god Rudra manifests in the form of Time itself;
wherever he prevails, there is great suffering, for in the Kali age he is the destroyer.
In the Kṛta age, however, girls and boys were equal in number.
Their conduct was characterized by the pair of equanimity and lack of greed.
All the subjects were always satisfied, possessed of every joy, and abiding in happiness;
there was no distinction between high and low, and the women were without difference [in status]. || 9–10 ||
Their lifespan, happiness, form, strength, contentment, and intellect were equal;
they were free from sorrow, possessed abundant knowledge, and were likewise devoted to solitude.
Established in meditation, established in austerity, they were dedicated to the Supreme Brahman.

Always acting without desire and with minds eternally joyful, they dwell upon mountains and in the ocean; indeed, they are homeless, taking refuge on the earth. Their food is produced by mere thought, and they subsist on water arising from their thought alone.
Born of their own volitions, they were ever full of divine essence and tranquil like lords;
everything was attainable through their own selves, for all had been surrendered to Brahman.
Indeed, in the Kṛta Yuga, they always experienced the overflow of aesthetic bliss and were fulfilled in every purpose.
Upon the passing of four thousand years, the transition arrives.
Therein, for eight hundred years, the surge of passion (*rasollāsa*) is not intense; indeed, both passion (*rāga*) and playfulness (*vilāsa*) arise only gradually. (15–16)
When the accomplishment of truth has been exhausted, another accomplishment proceeds:
when the water has reached its limit of pleasure, then from the sky, in the form of a ram, a discharge of rain proceeds from the thundering clouds. (17)
Once touched by that rain upon the surface of the earth,
water remained for twelve months filling the dry land.
There, trees and creepers appeared, laden with sap.
Then indeed, all objects of enjoyment arose from them;
at that time, living beings subsisted upon trees and other such things known as the *kalpa* tree. Those trees then served as both dwellings and landmarks for the people.
All houses were likewise devoid of walls.
All living beings took refuge in trees, oppressed by passion, greed, and other such afflictions;
and they occasionally resorted to disputes over what was their own and what belonged to others.
Then the affliction born of passion and greed gained a foothold;
by that, even those celestial wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadrumas) met their destruction.
When they had perished, the subjects became bewildered and filled with grief.
From the earth, they obtained wish-fulfilling trees that were devoid of power yet yielded fruits born of service;
these trees fell within the range of what arises from seeds, providing garments known as bark-cloth and fruits for food. (24–25)
Flowers and ornaments were produced from them with great effort;
from those very flowers arose for them a greedy desire and their food.
In every leaf-cup there was honey of great potency, free from bees.

From the fruits, sweet juices flowed forth in streams. With these, the subjects sustained themselves—contented, free from suffering, and without affliction. Then, in the later period of the Tretā age, the subjects were shrouded by greed.
In particular, having used their own trees by force, they became equal;
and they took possession of the honey, the beeswax, and the fruits.
Thus, there was suffering for the weak in obtaining honey.
Then, observing the partiality shown by the people toward the trees,
even those trees born from seeds perished along with Madhu.
At that time, suffering arose among human beings due to cold, heat, and rain.
Afflicted by the pairs of opposites (dvandvas), they indeed constructed shelters;
they built house walls, leaf huts, and devised means of subsistence.
And wherever there were rivers formed by the waters produced by the rain, [they settled there].
They settled at the sites of streams, in hollows, and by lakes.
There they established their dwellings, subsisting on trees, grain, and other such resources.
Then, through the union of water and earth, medicinal herbs came into being.
In some places they ripened without being ploughed and even without being sown;
in other places they were sown, and there they became full of grain and fruit.
There, the trees and shrubs produced flowers and fruits according to the seasons.
At the end of the Tretā age, people became filled with passion and greed, possessed by the sense of "I" and "mine," and were inevitably burdened by impurity;
they forcibly seized fields and vegetable gardens through their sheer presence.
Out of passion, the subjects forcibly claimed for themselves, according to their strength, trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs; they also took possession of rivers, fields, and mountains as their own.
Even there, powerful Kṣatriyas arose in ancient times to act as protectors.
Indeed, they were appointed by Brahmā for the protection of the distressed and for performing other such duties.
In the Tretā age, the Unborn (Aja) established the system of the social classes and stages of life;
for the sake of stabilizing the boundaries of conduct, he then created the rod of punishment.
The initiation of sacrifices and the avoidance of injury to animals—
these were the regulations established at the end of the Tretā age, which the Brāhmaṇas, together with the Kṣatriyas,
protected according to what was appropriate; from that, a divergence of opinion arose.

Passion, greed, partiality, war, and the plundering of prosperity—indeed, all these began among the people when the Dvāpara age arrived. Cities, kingdoms, boundaries, fields, and gardens [all came into being]. (42–43)
O beloved, at that time even the grains ripened on plowed land [only to wither],
and there occurred drought, death, as well as the afflictions of disease.
Sufferings born of speech, mind, and body arose in every single household.
And during the period following half of the Tretā age, offspring were produced through sexual union;
however, O beloved, at various times there were also offspring born of mere volition.
Indeed, in the Dvāpara age, offspring arose entirely from the seed of desire.
With their foundations corrupted, their vigor became false and their fruits likewise false;
pervaded by the force of latent impressions and devoid of self-power,
all creatures grew up empty of accomplishment and afflicted by pride.
In the Dvāpara age, there is the suddenness of miseries and of death.
Out of fear of these, there arises in them the contemplation of liberation from suffering.
From such contemplation come detachment, knowledge, devotion, and liberation. (48–49)
Thus, at that time, the duties of the Dvāpara age arose for the social classes, and likewise the specific duties of the stages of life (āśramas) emerged separately.
When the Kali age arrived, characterized by the acquisition of suffering, the people became agitated by affliction.

Under Tiṣya, people, intoxicated by pride and shrouded in darkness, constantly practice deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics. In the Kali age, there will be a pervasive disease and constant fear of hunger.
There will be the terrible fear of drought and the ruin of countries;
people will be unrighteous and ill-behaved, full of great anger yet possessing little luster.
In the Tiṣya age, greedy people of wicked progeny will speak falsehoods.
Through ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, wicked conduct, and false scriptures, as well as through the ritual faults of Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects.
That is not true dharma, nor is it the Vedic dharma; rather, it is merely a fabrication.
The duties of Śūdras will become uniform for all, as people— devoid of the system of castes and stages of life— will share the same beds, seats, and food.
Kings will engage in the deeds of thieves, and Brahmins will live on wealth acquired through deceit.
Even gurus and those who carry disciples become fond of strife.
O Lord of Men, there shall be the killing of embryos, the killing of heroes, the killing of women,
the killing of the virtuous, the killing of chaste wives, and the destruction of dharma among the subjects.
In the Kali age, bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, charity, worship of the gods, and remembrance of Hari are abandoned by men who are devoted to desire and greed.
They even revile the gods, the virtuous, the dharma, liberation, and the Lord of Śrī.
Those following the path of base conduct perform unjust deeds. (2.84.60) People of evil character, surrounded by heretics and vain practices, all become beggars in abundance during the Kali age. (61)
The lands will be as desolate as wildernesses, and the villages as barren as cowherd settlements.
Men and women alike will be harsh, devoid of affection, and dependent on others.
There will be thieves of grain, thieves of husks, thieves of clothing, and violent assailants.
There will be thieves who steal from other thieves, and others who kill those very thieves.
In the Kali age, people will be beset by much suffering, afflicted by disease, destroyed, and short-lived; because they are intent upon unrighteousness, the progeny will be pervaded by darkness.
In the Kali age, the distinction between high and low seats, propriety, honorability, and right conduct— along with the respect due to men and women— surely perish. In the Tiṣya age,
kings and subjects act like dancers of deceit.
The twice-born indeed become Śūdras, and likewise Śūdras become Cāṇḍālas. But there is only one single dharma regarding food, drink, clothing, and ornaments;
there is no distinction between what may be drunk and what may not, nor is there any state of being fit for enjoyment or unfit for enjoyment.

They lack discrimination between truth and falsehood, they transgress the boundaries of what is acceptable and unacceptable, and they possess the qualities of imagination and women who cater to their desires; likewise, their beloveds cater to their delusions, and these ascetics behave like rogues. (68)
In the Kali age, the glorification of deities through worldly songs is devoid of dharma;
knowledge and action are always utterly destroyed. In the Tiṣya age, there are stings from insects, mice, and serpents. (2.84.70)
All those who follow wicked vows and conduct, being solely intent on their own self-interest,
delude all people by displaying [false] fruits.
Indeed, they are performers of mantra-rites, practitioners of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and slayers.
In the Kali age, men will be merciless, deceitful, rogue, and murderous;

they will be meat-eaters and drinkers of liquor, forming unions merely for the sake of sexual intercourse and alliances merely for the sake of the phallus, and committing murders for the sake of wealth. (72–73)

In the Kali age, people will be identical in dress and conduct yet devoid of respectful treatment toward others; they will be betrayers of trust, slayers of friends, and betrayers of those who have sought their refuge.
In the Kali age, they will be destroyers of homes, destroyers of families, and even destroyers of their own kin.
Those who destroy the Dharma, those who kill the upholders of Dharma, matricides, patricides, killers of daughters-in-law,
killers of daughters, killers of sisters, and killers of brothers—
those devoid of the sixteen and other purificatory rites, and excluded from the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka)— [75–76].

In the Kali age, men and women will be devoid of purity, devoid of ritual bathing, and devoid of vows; they will be without sacred threads and excluded from the rites of marriage and other ceremonies.
They will be without the sacred fire, without pavilions and the like, and deprived of burnt offerings.

In the Kali age, all will be devoid of good conduct and devoid of domestic propriety; they will eat what is unfit for consumption and consume everything. Brahmins, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and gods will all become like Rākṣasas.
In the Kali age, dog-cookers and piśācas indeed become equal;
they cause fear for one another and bring about each other's destruction. They are shameless, utterly devoid of modesty, and stripped of all sense of reverence.
The youths, maidens, and women possess all enjoyments as they desire.
The maidens have hair, a vulva, and breasts, and are richly adorned with garments.
Furthermore, there are female weavers and male weavers who perform secret crafts in public.
In the Kali age, people will have bodies only a cubit in height, wearing garments made of hair; at the end, even the five-cubit trees will cease to exist.
There will be no king, no subjects, no one to be ruled, and no ruler.
There were no houses for residence, nor halls for the preparation of cooked food.
There was no one in the house to provide food, nor anyone to provide water and drink;
there was no bed for the woman, nor did the husband dwell in the house.
In the Kali age, yoga practiced according to the traditional rules certainly does not endure.
A woman of eight years has a moderate vitality, while death occurs at the end of twelve years in the Kali age. Those who have conceived for five years and more may dwell even without a village.
Then that woman, like a female monkey, was a mother without a midwife;
and on earth, she gave birth to a boy without a labor-pain.
At that time, Gaurī [reached maturity] at two years of age, and Rohiṇī at the end of two years.
In three years she becomes a maiden; at four years she reaches puberty.
Beyond that, she conceives, and within six months she gives birth.
For two years she indeed gives birth, while her menses appear only once, remaining stable for a moment.
Death may come in the span of a single *ghaṭikā*, and the life-force does not endure for long.
(2.84.90) Children roam upon the earth like young deer;
they are nourished by the essence of grain, while their mothers provide milk from their wings. (91)
In the Kali age, there is no mention of the father’s name, nor anywhere the mother’s name;
there is the loss of initiation, the loss of the guru, and the loss of mantras, as well as the absence of festivals.
Furthermore, in the Kali age, there are no assemblies of either gods or men.
In the Kali age, there is no renown for "this family," nor is there any household. At the end of the Kali age, the word "father" and the word "teacher" do not endure;
neither is there a king with royal ordinances, nor are there punishments or a ruler at that time.
There was no god, no temple, no tradition, no scripture, and no ancient vow; there was neither celibacy nor the state of an ascetic recognized as a householder.
There was no renunciation at all, nor conduct, nor indeed any dharma at that time.
In the Kali age, neither widowhood nor the state of being husbandless is considered dharma. At that time, neither the status of a virtuous wife nor the status of a chaste woman is dharma.
In that age, the pursuit of desire is the supreme dharma; self-restraint is merely heresy.
Men and women were of equal form, equal dress, and equal conduct;
they shared equal status and received equal portions from the common store.
At that time, there was no counting of years, nor even any counting of numbers.
Even the practice of knowledge does not exist for those born under the influence of darkness during the Kali age.
Indeed, at the end of the Kali age, the Lord, the Sovereign King, manifests;
having utterly destroyed the power of Kali, he establishes the state of the Kṛta age.
"O wife, thus have I described the dharmas for the four ages,
and how they all exist among embodied beings through the conjunction of time.
At the end of the day of Brahmā, the cosmic sphere (golaka) is indeed being shaken."
O King, by its speed and by its revolution, the earth becomes very small;
at that time, the days and nights indeed become short,
and the ghaṭikās, kalās, kāṣṭhās, months, and divisions of time also diminish.
Everything moves toward diminution, and when life is exhausted, it undergoes transformation;
thereafter, decline and dissolution occur at the end of the day.
O son of Ilavila! we shall then go to that truth which has the unborn as its refuge.
"O Rādhikā! Thus did Pulastya speak to his own wife.
(1.05) But the virtuous Ailavilā, having heard those duties, said to her husband:
"In that [lineage] where all the duties of the ages exist, such a grandson shall be born. (1.06)
"And I wish to see right here, O Sage, that which rests upon the four yugas!
Pulastya said to his own wife, "So be it;
by way of his grandson's visit, the Blessed One will also assemble there."
Knowing him to be her gain, Satī, the daughter of Viśravas, chose that son who bestows the yoga of Kṛṣṇa; he thus became Rāvaṇa. Ailavilā performed penance directed toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord Himself,
came to the Sahya mountain to behold the penance of Ailavila.

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Four Yugas as Spoken by Pulastya, the Granting of Boons to Ailavila, and His Performance of Penance," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Ailavilā, the wife of Pulastya,
performed austerities that were difficult to endure for the sake of obtaining a son who would possess the virtues of a bull among men throughout the four yugas.
The beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
assuming the form of a brahmin, was on the peak of the Sahya mountain in her hermitage (2).
He was richly adorned with matted hair, bark garments, and ashes, and was devoted to wearing garlands and the recitation of prayers.
He arrived and stood nearby on a shaded spot beneath a tree.
Subsisting constantly on a diet of roots, tubers, and fruits, and performing his ablutions at the three periods of the day,
he appeared like some charming young son of a seer.
Having arrived, he stays there for a while, and then at another time he goes into concealment;
sometimes becoming a parrot in a tree, and likewise becoming a cuckoo,
or even a peacock, a swan, or a deer.
In some places, assuming the form of Agastya, he observes that asceticism;
in some places, becoming Viśravas; in some places, [assuming] the forms of Pulastya’s wives;
and in some places, indeed, assuming the forms of Pulastya’s sons.
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa repeatedly gazes upon her austerity.
Rādhikā said: "O Kṛṣṇa, what is the merit of women?
And how indeed does the Blessed Lord [behave] in her presence in various ways? (8)
The Lord Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa assumed various forms.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to Rādhā: "O Rādhā! [I gave] Brahmā the son Pulastya [the mantra]:
'Om, obeisance to You, Śrī Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; svāhā. (2.85.10)
Thus he bestowed the great mantra; then he also entrusted his own beloved, Ailavilā, to him, and she chanted that mantra incessantly.
Her heart drawn by that chanting, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [appeared].
Hari, who is subdued by devotion, appeared in that very form near her.
O Rādhikā, I then beheld Kṛṣṇa in the form of a black deer,
wandering about— Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the beloved, the Lord of Śrī, the Master.
Beholding the asceticism of Ailavila and hearing his recitation, she shines forth;
for that wife of Pulastya, wearing matted hair and bark garments,
strives as a virtuous female ascetic for the sake of attaining the Supreme Lord.
Having fashioned an altar of earth upon the ground for the one who dwells in the sky,
she places the fire there and performs her worship in the morning;
then [she worships] Rudra, Satī, Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī, Aja, and the Son of Savitṛ.
Having daily worshipped the Sun, Prabhā, Gaṇeśa, and the virtuous goddesses with excellent offerings, he indeed performs a hundred-fold recitation of mantras with a rosary.
Then, having brought fruits and other items at midday, he himself [offers them] to Hari.
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) along with water, he performs penance and remains standing.
Indeed, gazing at the sun on one foot, he stands firm until evening;
then, having bathed, he performs the ritual waving of lights (ārātrika).
At night he performs worship, chanting "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
After midnight, he sleeps for only a single ghaṭikā.
Rising up and meditating on Hari, he bathes at dawn and performs the worship of Hari.
She continued to subsist on bulbs, roots, and fruits as if it were her constant practice.
Having done so for one year, she thereafter became one who subsists only on water.
Beginning at sunrise, she remained standing constantly until sunset.
Thus, she performed penance for a full year, remaining steady on her big toe alone;

thereafter, maintaining steadiness day and night, she remained standing with her heart devoted to the worship of Śrī Hari. (23) She then subsisted on air alone, worshipping the glorious Hari within her heart.
Within a single year, her body became like wood, rendered insentient;
(24) there, birds perched and insects built their earthen nests;
thus, within four years, she became covered by an anthill. (25)
In her fifth year, however, the growth of stalks appeared upon her head, and the emergence of grass was seen; she was not a human being.
Then Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Gaṇapati, and the goddesses [approached].
The goddesses, beginning with Devī, arrived, distinguished by the excellence of their virtuous austerities.
(27) The goddesses cleared away the stumps, grass, and other obstacles by means of heaps of earth;
Gaṇeśa and Sūrya also cleared the earth far away. (28)
There, Brahmā gave auspicious water for sprinkling with his joined palms;
Rudra then caused the movement of the vital breaths through that sprinkling;
and Viṣṇu invoked consciousness into her entire body.
Then she arose, regained her consciousness, and bowed before the gods:
"Oṃ, obeisance to you, Śrī Svāmikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; svāhā!
The virtuous woman, composed, spoke thus to her own Lord who was protecting her.
She remembered the Lord of the gods of gods, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The gods said: "Speak, O virtuous lady, what dwells in your mind?
We shall grant you your desired boon right here; choose it today, do not delay."

Thus addressed, she replied: "I choose a boon from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone, and from no other; may there always be well-being for you, O gods! For you have been constantly honored by me, since you are indeed Dharma itself."
"May there be well-being for you all since you have come for the sake of protecting and sustaining the world.
O goddesses, may there always be well-being and likewise prosperity for you.
Having spoken thus, he welcomed them with a heart that was deeply gratified.
He chanted the name of Śrī Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī.
At that moment, the Blessed Lord who had been stationed there within the pillar—Hari himself in the form of a tree—manifested from the anthill. (36–37)
The Lord has two arms, is the color of a campaka flower, and is resplendent with golden ornaments; he possesses a divine form pervaded by the brilliance of millions upon millions of suns.
He is enriched with divine golden ornaments and adorned with celestial garments.
The Beloved of Śrī shines with garlands of divine jewel-strings;
he is enriched by the splendor of divine bracelets and possesses a divine crown and earrings.
He is resplendent with the divine Kaustubha gem, a girdle, rings, and a staff-like ornament. 2.85.40.
He is worshipped by Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Haṃsā,
Mañjulā, Guṇā, Māṇikī, Śāntā, Vijayā, and Lalitā;
and by Hemanta, Bhagavat, Deva, Prakāśaka, Keśava, and others.
Accompanied by his attendants, the youthful Hari took his place there.
With his limbs proportionate to his form, holding a handkerchief in his hand,
chewing betel, and smiling, Hari remained standing.
Touching her head with both hands, he spoke words of blessing and,
requesting a boon, looked toward the gods.
Hari was seen directly by the gods and praised with hymns by those who chant the Sāman.
Having been honored with supreme devotion, the lords of the gods then stood there.
That virtuous woman worshipped her own Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the Highest Sovereign; she offered leaves, flowers, water, and her whole being to the Lord of Śrī.
He requested a boon from him: "O Blessed One, may my grandsons be the locus of the qualities of the four ages, so that through them there may be union with you;
and may this come about through the devotion of my grandsons and their family, a devotion unattainable by any other."
Due to the defects of the age, as well as by faults and even through hatred, your devotion may quickly arise;
for it is more enduring than affection and constant in its remembrance.
Without union with you, liberation does not occur for embodied beings.
"You are obtainable through other means only after a long time, but you are obtainable quickly through acts of hatred.
Death at your hands would certainly grant me liberation.
O Lord, for the sake of my family, I thus desire this boon."
Upon hearing "Give it to me," Keśava replied, "So be it.
(5.1) Then, by the command of Hari, the gods departed after being duly honored; and Ailavila, having abandoned his asceticism, enjoyed the favor of Hari. (5.2)
Having bathed in water, fruit, juice, and honey, and having performed purification,
the virtuous wife of Pulastya questioned her husband Kṛṣṇa.
Ailavilā said:
O Blessed One, Omniscient One, you ought to sever my doubt in this matter;
no one else is capable of severing the doubts of a noble woman.
Some [advocate] meditation, others the bull [dharma], and others discernment as the means for yoga.
Others praise celibacy, austerity, devotion to the husband, and fidelity to the wife;
likewise, others praise truthfulness, renunciation, non-violence, chastity, and even total renunciation, as well as charity, compassion, and study. || 55-56 ||
Pilgrimage, restraint of the senses, association with the virtuous,
total surrender, seeking refuge, dedication to the guru, detachment,
and knowledge consisting of Brahman— O Lord, tell me which among these is the highest good!
"Or if there is anything else hidden that exists, you ought to speak of it.
Having heard the words of Elavilā, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke the supreme divine truth, which bestows the highest good and is higher than the highest.
For the benefit of all living beings, this was composed by those of former and even more ancient times.
It is unspeakable, containing all hidden meanings—a knowledge excluded by the ignorant.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī said:
The most supreme and secret field, the highest bestower of the supreme abode—
my field called Akṣara, wherein lies Kuṅkumavāpikā,
which carries all embodied beings across the ocean of worldly existence by virtue of their dwelling there.
Delightful with the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and adorned by the hermitage of Lomaśa;
there, O Ailavila, high-souled devotees dwell, established in my vow and relying upon supreme devotion to me. (62–63)
That which is the best of all holy fords (tīrtha), the best of all sacred fields (kṣetra),
and the best of all abodes— that field known as the Imperishable (akṣara) is not at all attached to the surface of the earth; indeed, it is situated within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
The non-divine do not see it; the liberated see it with their heart.
(65) That is my most beloved place, secret and swiftly bestowing final liberation, where my devotees abide and indeed worship me alone. (66)
The men and women who go there also proceed to my own abode;
having merely seen other dwellings, they enter into me alone.
Whatever has been given, chanted, performed, desired, practiced as austerity, meditated upon, offered in sacrifice, or heard—[all that becomes perfect].
Whatever is served, fed, or known there shall all become inexhaustible.
Whatever accumulated sin has been committed over thousands of other births—
all of it quickly goes to total destruction for one who has entered this imperishable field (akṣetra).
Mānavas, men, women, and those of mixed castes who are exceedingly sinful;
wicked women born of impure unions in sinful wombs;
Mlecchas, those born of Caṇḍālas, as well as insects, ants, and wild beasts.
If cattle, birds, reptiles, grasses, trees, creepers,
and all species of insentient beings die within the Imperishable Field (akṣara-kṣetra),
they indeed become possessed of the moon as their forehead mark and ride upon great elephants and other such vehicles.
In my beautiful, imperishable state, those divine ones attain final liberation. Indeed, no one who has died in the Imperishable, even if burdened by sin, goes to hell.
Having received my grace, they all go to the imperishable station.
What need is there to speak further regarding my place, which is covered with rags?

Having realized that liberation is extremely difficult to attain and that worldly existence is most terrifying, one who has destroyed rebirth through knowledge may dwell in my imperishable field. (74–75)
For one who has perished anywhere, this place indeed bestows liberation;
through my grace, sin is burned away, and by residing here, one attains divinity.
Moreover, from the mere sight of me, liberation arises in the imperishable state.
Through my yoga, great liberation arises for me in the supreme state.
Those devoid of merit do not see it, their eyes veiled by the film of māyā;
shrouded in darkness, they do not behold my divine, imperishable field.
They indeed repeatedly enter the body that bears feces, urine, and semen; yet the embodied soul who, even while being struck, enters [the field] despite hundreds of obstacles—
the imperishable, supreme field surrounding the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.

He goes to the supreme abode, reaching which he does not grieve. That supreme field, my own domain, is free from birth, death, and old age; it is declared for those who desire liberation and do not die again. (2.85.80–81)

Neither by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by knowledge is that supreme goal attained which is obtained in the Imperishable. Those of various castes, those of faded caste, and the despised such as Caṇḍālas and others— [all attain it]. (82)
Their bodies are filled with impurities and joined with base transgressions.
For them, the supreme state is the imperishable field, which is the potent medicine;
that is the imperishable supreme knowledge, that is the imperishable supreme state. (83–84)
That which is the supreme syllable (*akṣara*) is the imperishable Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). Having taken up the lifelong vow of initiation, those who dwell in that imperishable state—
having received the supreme knowledge from Me— go to My highest abode.
Prabhāsa, Svarṇanagarī, Vastrāpatha, and the Narmadā; Nārāyaṇasara, Puṣkara, and the Kaurava region;
Gaṅgā, Badarikā, Śālagrāma, and Śrīśaila as well. (86–87)
The Himalaya, Kedāra, Gayā, and Gokarṇa;
the Kṛṣṇā, Godāvarī, Sindhu, Gomatī, and Brahmaputrī;
the river Nārāyaṇī and the lake Vijñaturīyaka.
The Tūṅgānīka lake, the Nyāsa lake, and likewise the Caṇḍa lake;
the Naṣṭajarā river, the Raktavārddhi ocean, and also the Nīlābdhi ocean; the Nīparā, the Dīnayūpā, the Senā, and the Mahābṛhatsaras.
There is also the circular lake Antārkivartula, situated one above the other;
then Pannāmnī, Kālimā, Yāneśī, and Śvetavāridhi;
the mountain Uralā, the Mānasa lake, and the Brahma-lake.
Also the Bālakṛṣṇa lake and likewise the Dvikala lake;
the Aṅgaśikṣāṅgikā, the Murā river, the Turu river, the Eitā river, the Mikāṅgā, and likewise the Irāvatī river. (92–93)
And the Gaṅgā, having entered [the lake], also flows into the great lake named Ābhara.
These are indeed the famous sacred sites on earth;
they all constantly flow into the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara.
Therefore, those who die there do not attain supreme liberation as they do in the Imperishable (Akṣara).
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, I, the Supreme Lord, am personally present;
having taken up the Brahma-lake, I abide there eternally.
The Brahmahrada destroys the sins committed over infinite births.
Elsewhere, the Ganges, ancestral rites (śrāddha), charity (dāna), recitation (japa), and vows (vrata) are easily obtained;
however, all of these are exceedingly rare within the sacred field (kṣetra) of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Whether he be a sinner, a rogue, or even an unrighteous person, having attained that imperishable state, he purifies seven generations of his lineage.
He may constantly sacrifice, offer oblations, give gifts, and likewise perform acts of worship. (98–99)
But for the devotee in this imperishable field, the fruit is of infinite quality.
Those devotees who, having gone there, worship and praise me—
freed from all sins, they are to be known as my personal attendants (pārṣadas).
Except through sacrifice, knowledge, renunciation, or yoga,
that supreme state is attained after a thousand births;
but those who dwell in the Imperishable attain it in a single birth.
In that regard, I am the uninterrupted yoga, austerity, knowledge, and vow for my devotees; having attained me, there is no further goal to be reached.
That alone is considered the secret of secrets, the bestower of the supreme good. (103)

To those who are established in knowledge and meditation and who desire supreme bliss, I grant there the mantra within my imperishable field (*kṣetraka*). That which is the most transcendent reality is I myself, and that field is mine. (104–105)
Whether from the middle of the eyebrows, the middle of the navel, the heart, or the head—
from whichever [place] the life-breath departs, one is liberated here into the Imperishable (akṣara).
I, the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, dwell herein.
Even those of extreme sin, having approached me, attain the supreme goal.
Among all the Nārāyaṇas, I am the preeminent Supreme Lord;
likewise, other Nārāyaṇas as well as Śambhu and others are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
All the abodes as well as the millions of liberated ones residing in those abodes,
the foremost lords of the cosmic eggs, the gods and others, and millions of sacred fords—
all of us dwell there in my imperishable field around Aśvasara.
Kuṃkumavāpikā is the very form of Brahman, the city of the liberated and the virtuous.
Those whose intellects are struck down by sin do not perceive its divine nature;
for them, it is impossible to behold my imperishable ground.
Those of meritorious conduct remember this city with their divine eye,
and those perfected in yoga perceive it even while dwelling in other worlds.
Let those who desire liberation come to dwell in this place.
If these have died on the path, there is no rebirth for them.

Whether one is a yogi or not a yogi, whether a sinner or the most virtuous of doers, [this is known] neither from the words of the world, nor from the father, nor even from the words of the guru. (113–114)
And he directly awakened her auspicious mind, which was focused upon the imperishable field [of Mathurā], saying:
"O Rādhikā! The Lord himself has thus awakened Cailavilā, who dwells at Kuṅkumavāpikā and bathes in the waters of Aśvasara. || 1.15 ||
She too paused for a moment, and upon hearing this, she was filled with wonder.

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Imperishable Syllable as Told by the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to Ailavilā," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 86 [Author:
Chapter 87 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhikā! Afterwards, Ailavilā said to Hari:
'O Blessed One, I have a desire to behold that imperishable abode.
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [led her] from the Sahya mountain..."
Having mounted Garuḍa in the month of Caitra, he traveled through the sky to the imperishable realm;
[he reached] the divine field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, known as Akṣara,
which shines like the abode of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, where men are eternally blissful.
It was pervaded by divine beings, frequented by gods, ancestors, and others,
and joined by the Aśvapaṭṭaka lake mingled with the waters of the ten Brahma-lakes;
it was brilliantly radiant, having been made a dwelling place for thousands of groups of sages.
It is the purifier of purifiers, the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
the supreme among those that grant liberation, the bestower of liberation, and the destroyer of all sins.
It is beautified by hundreds of thousands of palaces and by forest creepers.
It was surrounded by thousands of divine trees and pleasure groves,
with auspicious lakes and gardens fragrant with fruits and flowers;
it was enriched by wish-fulfilling trees and illuminated by the radiance of the *cintāmaṇi* gem.
It was constantly nourished by sages through sacrifices, Vedic study, and devotion;
it was inhabited by beloved guests seeking the abode of Brahman;
and it had its auspicious marriage-rites performed for the beloved consort of Lord Hari.
It was joined by lakes of nectar, frequented by all created beings,
and filled with righteous Vedic scholars skilled in the language of the gods;
it possessed a thousand long banners shining with golden staffs.
It was resplendent with peak-palaces that were seven-storied mansions;
there, men and women, having been liberated, fly up by means of celestial vehicles.
There, even the birds go to heaven, such as parrots and others who are conversant in refined language.
Even cows, elephants, and other animals speak the Vedic language there along with the twice-born,
where the blazing sacrificial fires abide upon the altar-ground,
and where gifts are bestowed day and night by the guardians of creation. (13)
Where there are hundreds of thousands of pilgrims who partake in liberation;
where there are thousands of assembly halls for listeners and narrators, and hundreds and thousands of temples containing divine images. (14–15)

There exist trees adorned with golden jars that beautify the peaks of the sky; groves belonging to householders are visible, and the hermitages of the most excellent sages shine like those of the denizens of heaven. (16)
Where there are ascetics by the millions all around Aśvasara,
where holy men perform devotion to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the worlds,
and where virtuous women, beloved of Brahman, are ever devoted to the vow of Brahman. (17–18)
They dwell for the sake of serving Kṛṣṇa, taking refuge in the imperishable field;
they become performers of the sacrifice of knowledge, the sacrifice of the Veda, and the sacrifice of charity.
They become performers of the sacrifice of service, the sacrifice of liberation, and the sacrifice of contentment.
The brahmin-sages constantly dwell [there], performing sacrifices through discourse (kathā-yajña).
They perform sacrifices through vows (vrata-yajña), sacrifices through sacrificial sessions (satra-yajña), and are renowned for the rites of concluding ceremonies (udyāpana-vidhi).
They perform sacrifices at sacred fords (tīrtha-yajña) and always conduct sacrifices consisting of the chanting of Hari’s names (kīrtana-kratu).
Where the methods for worshipping the gods are practiced constantly;
where embodied beings dwell with divine and pure hearts;
[where] they proclaim, "O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman."
"O Kṛṣṇa, who brings joy to Yaśodā; O Mādhava, son of Gopāla;
O Lord of Śrī, beloved of Rādhikā, the soul of all—be dear to me!
Thus worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa, they dwell there. (23–24)
In the delightful hermitage of Lomaśa, inhabited by those dear to Brahmā, he beheld even animals free from enmity; there,
the personified forms residing therein were resplendent with abundant radiance.
Then, having been observed by her from the sky by those seated in the vehicle,
she completed a circumambulation of the sacred field with that celestial chariot and descended into the temple of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Together with Śrī Svāmin, she went toward Śrī Kambharā;
she beheld her, worshipped her, paid homage, and bowed down.
Then she went to Gopālakṛṣṇa and bowed at his feet.
Then, having approached his Lord,
the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— who was traveling with him, who had performed great exertion, who appeared in the form of a child, and who is the Supreme Brahman— he served Him by massaging His body.
Then, like a maidservant, she massaged the feet of Śrī Hari;
she went to the holy sites located at Aśvasaras and bathed there according to the prescribed rites.
She drank the water from the Kuṅkumavāpī pond and held it upon her head.
Then, having bowed to the venerable Lomaśa and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites,
all the maidens, beloved of Brahmā, gathered together and went to the temple.
There, Bālakṛṣṇa fed Elāvilā with milk-rice (pāyasa).
He caused her to drink the sweet water that was the nectar of his own feet;
he purified his own devotee and delighted her with his true being.
Then, having beheld that imperishable realm, she set her mind upon dwelling there.
When Satī constantly prayed for the Supreme Soul as her eternal abode,
Hari then granted her two equally auspicious forms;
he then sent Chāyā toward Pulastya.
He always protected Ailavilā, who possessed a divine form, near him;
she was a virtuous woman observing the vow of Brahma, endowed with the dharma of the righteous, and chaste.
Then, the granting of the boon to her became fruitful.
Viśravas had four wives who increased his lineage:
Puṣpotkaṭā, Vākā, Kaikasī, and Devavarṇinī.
Devavarṇinī gave birth to Vaiśravaṇa, the eldest of the Yakṣas.
Kaikasī gave birth to Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
as well as Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Puṣpotkaṭā also bore auspicious sons to Viśravas.
Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva, and Khara;
likewise Kumbhīnasī, Śṛṅgī, and hundreds of other daughters;
Vajrajā, Triśiras, Vidyujjihva, and Dūṣaṇa.
There were also one hundred cruel daughters born of the lineage of Pulastya, as well as ten thousand who possessed the nature of *rākṣasas*. They all relied upon the *dharmas* of every age (*yuga*);
they were devoted to austerity, devoted to charity, yet possessed of passion and impurity.
Those who are endowed with truth, untruth, or both, and possessed of strength and pride—
even those who resort to the dharma of the Kali age— for their destruction Hari himself assumes the form of Rāma and slays the Rākṣasas.
Having washed away their sins, they attain residence in Vaikuṇṭha; yet,
by the power of the boon granted to Ailavila,
Kṛṣṇa’s discus slays the Rākṣasas born in that lineage along with their armies in age after age.
O Rādhikā, whether it be my discus, water, a tulasī leaf, or even my footstep— whosoever has obtained any of these becomes liberated,
whether they be a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a dānava, or even a daitya. ||47-48||
Then Viśravas went to Siṃhala Island together with his lineage;
there, at the site of Ailavila’s asceticism where Hari himself was present,
he performed both protection for that place and a test of his penance.
That sacred site on the Cailavaileya peak of the Sahya mountain range is graced by a water-filled pool and a flowing spring;
it is purifying and imbued with the dust from the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
There, Hari appeared in the form of a tree-trunk, bestowing liberation upon those born there.
For one year he remained as such, and for one year Śuka and the others likewise;
they were sustained by Hari in that form and became his Vaiṣṇava descendants.
On the Sahya mountain, those born of the female offspring of the Sahya bird and descended from the Harivaṃśa reside;
they are divine, possess celestial forms, and dwell endowed with great happiness.
There, the purifying trees likewise originate from the Harivaṃśa. (53–54)
Where there is never even a trace of drought on the Sahya mountain;
where there are no forest fires and likewise no harm from predatory beasts;
and where the elephants are white, four-tusked, and of great stature.
Where there dwell the mounts of the gods born of the lineage of Hari;
where there reside auspicious Śarabhas born of the lineage of Hari, white in color, with two trunks, and belonging to the species of lions. (56–57)
The white, auspicious serpents, as well as the purifying ones, are free from venom;
those born of the lineage of Hari are white, as are those of the peacock species.
Possessing divine forms, they indeed originate from the lineage of Hari.
The Sahya mountain is in every way the best of holy places, as are its forests.
O Rādhā, for five years these were purified by the yoga of Hari;
by reading or hearing [this account], they grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Ailavilā’s Arrival at Kuṅkumavāpī, Her Two Forms, and the Residence of the Descendants of Harivaṃśa on the Sahya Mountain," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
(Chapter 86, Section 2: The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
