Chapter 88 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: devotees of Hari perceive His true virtues, whereas the wicked, having superimposed faults upon those virtues, perceive only evil qualities.
Indeed, [this was seen] in the case of the Rākṣasa Khara, the son of Viśravas.
To Khacaryā was born a son named Adharmajīva.
He had a crooked waist, a bent back, and a pimple on his cheek called "lizard.
His eyes were like those of a matted-haired ascetic, he always suffered from asthma, was full of foul odors, and was fond of children.
He was tainted by sin, his conduct excessively fickle, and a betrayer of trust.
By birth he was a "slayer of his mother," for he had struck her with his feet while she was dead.
He had the voice of an owl, a black complexion, and hair like peacock feathers.

Having a mark on his back, with blunt ears, protruding tusks, and being exceedingly envious, he became a tormentor of children, causing them pain as soon as they were born. Once, he went to the bank of a river to play together with some boys. (5–6)
In the dwellings of leather-workers and in the houses of outcastes,
where the children were left alone while their elders had gone out for work,
she struck those children and devoured them in those houses.
He ate dog meat and drank wine, and he drank water.
Then, having gathered together with the children, the outcastes forcibly seized and bound him,
and threw him into a foul-smelling pit of alkaline mud.

Covered there by a stone slab in the pit, he remained in that vessel day and night; indeed, in that vessel, he acquired the odor of the vessel itself. For half a month, hungry and distressed by thirst, he sought to preserve his life.
Water produced from washing leather is also called *cārmakardama*.
That evildoer ate food produced by tiny insects in a pot;
he was a Rākṣasa by birth who ate the food of a Cāṇḍāla household.
Making his dwelling in a leather bag, subsisting on leather and mud, a killer of his mother, and a crocodile—who could be more sinful than he?
O Rādhikā! Such was that great demon, a life of unrighteousness, known by name.
Clad in the dyed garments of the outcaste leather-workers,
that wicked man was expelled, castrated, beaten, and likewise emasculated;
he remained on the island of Siṃhala at the edge of the battlefield, subsisting on forest roots.
Sometimes, seizing domestic animals, flocks of birds, and even the children of his own household,
he would kill them and eat them as well.
Once, the king of devotees, Vibhīṣaṇa, who was dear to Lord Hari, was there.
Chanting "Rāma," "Kṛṣṇa," and "Nārāyaṇa" as he traveled,
he went along that path to wander and behold the forests. There, he caused him to see a great demon who lived by unrighteousness.
He said: "O son, how do you remain here in this desolate place?
Come home; worship Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of happiness.
Do not carry this sorrow in this parched, lonely forest."
Having heard Vibhīṣaṇa, he who was full of pride spoke to his paternal elder brother:
“Who is Hari? Who is Kṛṣṇa? And who indeed is Nārāyaṇa?
I do not know him; who is he that exists, and for what reason should I worship him without reflection? (2.87.20–21)
The devotee Vibhīṣaṇa said: "That Hari is the remover of suffering;
he is the Supreme Brahman himself, divine, and the abode of the divine syllable.
But the Rākṣasa, whose life was unrighteousness and who was a plunderer of wealth, spoke.
He who steals property is indeed one who steals women and other such things.
But he who steals the prosperity of others may be a thief, yet someone might call him "Hari.
Since black is sin and evil action, he who performs such acts would indeed be "Kṛṣṇa" (the Black One).
He may be some fisherman dwelling on a river, moving neither by land nor by water;
or he may be a servant carrying water, or an attendant to someone.
Or perhaps he is a serpent dwelling in the water, or else a fish. (25)
The supreme enemy is the Great Brahman; indeed, he is the great adversary.
He is divine, a rogue, an expert in gambling, and a certain addict to vice.
He delights in dice and snares, and he seizes the coin.
And suppose there were someone of sinful nature dwelling in a gambling house;
Vibhīṣaṇa, however, said to him:
"This is indeed the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord, the Lord of lords. (28)
"O son, the Lord of Muktā shines resplendent in the supreme abode.
But this one, O father, is a Rākṣasa who lives by unrighteousness; he is not like that, for he himself takes pleasure there in drinking liquor. (2.87.30)
Greedy for drinking intoxicants and the like, he becomes a supreme drunkard;
as a lord, he causes suffering to others who are wretched people.
Enveloped by excessive darkness, he binds himself with many sins.
He would be one characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*) and a doer of evil; yet he is indeed Puruṣottama.
His secret organ (*bhaga*) would surely be marked with the sign of a woman;
that Blessed One (*bhagavān*), though disguised as a woman, would be one who wears the appearance of a man.

Even the Lord of Lords would not be able to protect himself if he were slain by the misfortunes of warriors like me, who are themselves lords. Those women who have been abandoned by their husbands and those who have been driven out from their homes—
He would become their lord, the crest-jewel of transgressors.
O Father! He dwells eternally in another's abode or house, residing in the property of others; or he may become a mendicant who has no door to his own home.
And Vibhīṣaṇa said to him: "O son, who assumes the form of the military array!
He is the Lord who is the cause of all incarnations and the possessor of all powers.
He is the Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, indeed the Supreme Person. (37)
"Venerate him who is accessible to yogis, the inner self, and the bestower of liberation.
Even he who protects the lives of the unrighteous—I believe he is a deceiver;
for the sake of deceiving the world, he assumes various guises, repeatedly adopting one form after another. (38–39)
In one place he is an actor, in another a cowherd, in another like a prince; in yet another he becomes a Brahmin, a deceiver who possesses various manifestations.
Indeed, among all his incarnations in this world, his actions are truly humble.
O Father,
I truly believe that some person of low caste, born of an inferior lineage, who acts as the instigator of the power of weapons among all living beings, would indeed be the slayer. (41–42)
Someone who is wicked by nature becomes a source of suffering through force;
he indeed becomes a great leader among the herds of cows and bulls in this world,
or he may become a great bull himself, or one who drives bulls.
One who dwells in a place devoid of splendor, such as a house or a hut, and is free from [worldly attachments],
may indeed become a supreme man among the Rākṣasas, appearing like an enemy. Friendship,
established by walking seven steps together, is to be sought with those of similar character who are endowed with yoga.
Therefore, O father, I consider that there is indeed some person who is not a true gentleman—
one whose internal state differs from his outward appearance, whether in his desires,
his mind, or his speech; for such a person would be a betrayer of trust.
I believe that some cruel person, a slayer of the weak, acts to destroy the weak by cutting off all their means of liberation; who indeed would resort to such a wicked man,
devoid even of the highest virtues?
Vibhīṣaṇa, however, spoke to him— he who was wise, a refuge of virtues, a knower of the Vedas, the author of the Vedic scriptures and other works, possessed of good character and vows,
the locus of all dharma, a performer of righteous deeds, and endowed with tranquility. (49)
Then the Rākṣasa, who lived by unrighteous means, replied: "O learned one, he does not exist.
He knows nothing of the *raṃbhaṇa* rite, nor does he know song;
he knows nothing of malevolent spells (*abhicāra*), nor does he know illusion (*māyā*). (2.87.50–51)
Therefore, O father, he could never truly be a wise man,
even if he possesses a rope with which to milk cows.
For that reason, O father, a cowherd is indeed one who relies upon a rope around his shoulder.
A potter knows how to construct that altar or pedestal made of stones or clay by people at a crossroads in a village;
indeed, he would be a potter who is an expert in the craft of making altars.
Indeed, by means of the weapon [of the razor], this barber effects the shearing of the hair on the head;
moreover, he possesses the sharp weapons that are the enemies of body hair.
(55) Furthermore, *śīla* is non-lapse, *dharma* is the law, and *vrata* is austerity such as the *kṛcchra* and other penances.
He eats and devours both [of them]; such is the destroyer of the Dharma. Indeed, some person may become a consumer of moral conduct and vows;
for all such things are the dharma of beasts, and whoever possesses them becomes a beast.
The act of destroying a house is contrary to the duty of virtuous householders;
one who performs such an act would be a renunciant (yati) by nature, characterized by renunciation and the like.
He may be dull-witted or distracted, yet he remains solitary and filled with peace.

And Vibhīṣaṇa said to him: "O son, there is a Brahmin named Mādhava, who wears the sacred thread, who pacifies the heat of suffering, who takes refuge in the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), and who himself is the author of the scriptures. (2.87.60)
"This one who undertakes pilgrimages is truly alone and without a second, O Acyuta;
he is a Rākṣasa living by unrighteousness, for he would not be a Brāhmaṇa.
He who seizes a bird is like a hunter.
Therefore, someone might become a hunter, or a bird-catcher, or even a beast;
or someone might be a Mādhava who approaches his mother, or one who has animals for offspring—[that person] for whom there is no restrainer and likewise no husband. (62–63)
There was a certain forest-dweller who had lost both his mother and father.
A bird arrived here from somewhere in the vicinity of that very sacrifice;
a bird-eater seized it for the sake of food. (64)
One who pacifies through afflictions, torments, and excesses is a destroyer of the world.
Therefore, such a person would be a perpetrator of chaos and a murderer;
[he employs] great spells, spells of desire, and those that cause eradication and destruction. (65–66)
O Father, if he knows [the truth] regarding that which deludes and infatuates,
then he would indeed be a dog-cooker, an outcaste, or a filthy man;
for he is the author of deception within the scriptures.
Someone might be a deceiver, for he is not the author of the scripture.
Wandering alone in the forest or the wilderness, devoid of family, this man is solitary and destitute; he may even be one who has shaved his head at a sacred ford.
O Father, wealth does not diminish when given in charity, yet he who gives it becomes poor;
he is devoid of virtuous dharma, a hypocrite, a slanderer, and a villain.
He is a secret thief and an increaser of women's fickleness.
He shall be a wearer of disguises who deludes countless women;
he shall become a performer of perfected mantras who renders the gopīs invisible;
he shall be a fulfiller of the desires of amorous women and a doer of unjust deeds. (71–72)
A destroyer of dharma and a destroyer of his own family, he is indeed attached to vulgar sights;
he is a mine of defects such as anger and greed, a treasure-trove of ignorance, devoid of proper conduct, lacking in intelligence, and utterly enshrouded in darkness. (73)

Whether he be a beast, a snare, a thief of maidens, or fond of children—whatever he may be, what need have I for him? I cannot endure his qualities, whether they be divine or non-divine, under any circumstances. (74–75)
"Therefore, O father, there is no one else for me to meditate upon or to worship;
I am the most excellent, and there is no one more excellent than I.
To this, Vibhīṣaṇa replied: "O son, do not treat him with contempt."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Kamalā;
the Lord of all, the Supreme Lord, the inner witness, and the controller—he indeed is Hari, capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise. (77–78)
He exists in the form of a child; worship Him with your whole being, my son.
Divine qualities reside within Him, each one of which indeed bestows liberation:
truthfulness, purity, compassion, forbearance, renunciation, contentment, and straightforwardness.

Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, equanimity, forbearance, cessation of activity, and sacred learning; knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, heroism, splendor, strength, memory, independence, skill, beauty, fortitude, and likewise gentleness. (2.87.80–81)
Boldness, humility, good character, patience, vigor, strength, majesty, profundity, steadfastness, faith, fame, self-respect, and freedom from egoism;
having performed beneficial deeds, lack of malice, absence of worldly striving, and likewise the state of possessing nothing.
"Loving-kindness, omniscience—these qualities reside in the Supreme Self.
The Rākṣasa, who lives by unrighteousness, said: 'I consider him to lack those qualities;
I regard him as a eunuch, devoid of zeal for action.'"
I believe that in him alone exist these traits: being devoid of virtue, wealth, and desire; being inactive and powerless;
subsisting on the fortune of others; coveting the prosperity of others;
and even following an improper path. (85)
Therefore, O Rādhikā, you ought not to speak of his virtues to my father. In this very way, this asura, who lives by unrighteousness,
spoke of hundreds of faults regarding Hari to his father.
Then Vibhīṣaṇa, enraged, struck him with a mace;
he fled from Siṃhaladvīpa and,
becoming a deceitful man, arrived in Saurāṣṭra.
On the bank of the Śatruñjaya river, at a place on earth named Trivaṭa,
that wicked man, a hater of the virtuous who bore malice toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, took up residence having assumed the guise of an ascetic. (2.87.89–90)
Having become a wicked hypocrite, he deceived many people;
harboring enmity toward the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, he spread atheism throughout the world with his words. (91)
With his life-force already spent, he arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī;
having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he began to revile the Supreme Lord.
Then, hearing this, Śrī Śaṅkara spoke to his attendant Bhairava.
"O Bhairava, by means of these [powers], slay that wicked asura who lives by unrighteousness;
indeed, let him be destroyed by the piśācas through his own karma.
Thus addressed, Bhairava took up his trident and went forth with the piśācas.
Having seized him alive and bound him with leather thongs,
they then threw him into a place of filth upon ground covered with excrement.
At his sacrifice, the Piśācas urinated and defecated.
They all slew the stubborn, deluded Asura;
they cut off his limbs and cast them into the waters of the Lāvaṇa ocean—
those very ones who were haters of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then, by means of a continuous line of rope, they tied him to a branch within the tree where the vultures dwelt; he hung there with his face turned downward,
and the excrement of vultures, crows, and other birds fell directly into his mouth.
Thus Śrī Bhairava inflicted punishment upon the asura for two months;
thereafter, overcome by hunger and thirst, he indeed perished from his life-breaths. That asura, who lived by unrighteousness, went to the abode of Yama.
There he fell into the Kuṃbhīpāta hell for a thousand years.
Then, in this place, Lord Bhairava bathed in the Aśvasarovara lake indeed for the sake of washing away the sins arising from the fault of his association.
Thus, having met his destruction, that demon who lived by unrighteousness,
though fond of his children, died due to his own sin and entered upon the path of an evil destiny.
O Rādhikā, for those who commit offenses against Me, there is no auspicious destination.
If one has taken refuge [in Him], then I grant him a destination.
But if he has not come for refuge to the Supreme Lord even when dying,
then indeed there will be no true happiness for him even after hundreds of billions of years.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, that Rākṣasa, who was like a Daitya and a great reviler, died. Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having heard of the death of that unrighteous soul,
took his mother there to Saurāṣṭra by way of the sky.
He arrived and prayed for a good rebirth from the Supreme Lord.
Hari said, "In another birth, he shall attain a [good] state;
having met his death at my hand, he will go to a good state."
Thereafter, the sage Lomaśa gave a mantra to his mother;
he then gave the Śrī-Pārameśvara mantra to Vibhīṣaṇa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrī-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Having stayed for one month, the two of them, Rādhikā and [her companion], went to their own abode;
they both worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
And Vibhīṣaṇa and the celestial woman (khacarī) became divine at the end.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Atheism of Kharaputra Adharmajīvana, His Imputation of Faults to the Qualities of Hari, His Hatred toward Hari, His Bad End, and the Subsequent Granting of a Boon for a Good End in a Future Time," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 88 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 88.
[The Author: Chapter 89.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen once more to the divine wonder of Hari.
At Prayāga, during the Kumbha Yoga, millions of embodied beings departed [for liberation]:
humans, Nāgas, Daityas, gods,
hosts of sages, ancestors, Munis, and Siddhas all arrived there in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Within ten krośas everywhere, there was indeed a new city;
outside of it, divine trees and creepers dwelt in eager anticipation. There were also divine sacred fords and divine lakes.
Divine rivers, wells, ponds,
and oblong lakes came from all directions to that confluence to bathe during the *kumbhayoga*—
at the junction of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, and at the meeting of the Sarasvatī.
In the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, they bathed at the holy ford;
indeed, their own sins were washed away by those pilgrims at Triveṇī.
Then, there at that place, was the saint Sanatkumāra, a man of great renunciation.
The son of Brahmā arrived, appearing as a five-year-old boy.
Seated in a divine, atomic-sized celestial chariot, he was resplendent like ten thousand suns,
illuminating the entire surface of the earth, the quarters, and the sky on all sides.
A miracle occurred; the embodied beings, including the gods and others, attained great satisfaction.
That celestial chariot, which had assumed a subtle form, expanded once again, wherein that yogi was seen in the form of a divine child.
He slowly descended to the ground in the vicinity of the Akṣaya-vata tree.
There the great yogi stood for a moment and then quickly vanished from sight. He appeared at the Triveṇī and, remembering Hari, bathed there immediately.
Becoming invisible, he arrived in an instant at the place where the celestial chariot was;
then, having touched the banyan tree, he bowed to the One who reclines upon the banyan.
He worshipped Him with divine flowers and paid homage with Vedic hymns.
Then, having learned of this, the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans arrived there.

Having come together for the purpose of seeing him, they worshipped him with flowers and other offerings. Then, after they had inquired of one another regarding their welcome and welfare, [they sat down].
They stood and sat upon the vast surface of the earth and in the sky;
meanwhile, the sacred fords (tīrthas), rivers, and streams arrived there,
as did Prayāga in embodied form, along with lakes, wells, and ponds.
Pūṣā, Kaṭvī, Pannārī, Candrāvatī, and Mañjirā;
Indrāvatī, Kuśī, Mahānadī, and likewise Huhūgalī;
Gaṇḍakī, Kāñcanagaṅgā, Śatalājā, and Gogarā. (16–17)
The Cambalā, Cīnapā, Nandā, Jhelamā, Kābilā, Luṇī, Sindhu,
and other rivers, having united,
bowed to Sanatkumāra— the son of Brahmā and destroyer of sins— and questioned him. (18)
Whatever sins of embodied beings exist for twelve years, O Sage, they are indeed washed away upon coming into our presence;
yet all those [sins] remain within us for twelve years. (2.88.20)
In the course of the ritual bath at the pitcher (Kumbha-snāna), we abandoned [our sins] elsewhere at Prayāga;
then, freed from evil, we attained happiness and peace.
But, O Sage, how is it that this occurs every year, month after month?
May there be the destruction of our sins so that peace may always prevail.
(22) Show us the place where, by going there month after month, as well as during the fortnights and on days of terrible sin, the pacification of sin may occur. (23)
O Brahmin, O Lord, show us that burning place where the conflagration of great sins and even greater evils arises.
[Show us] Prayāga, Haridvāra, Puṣkara, and likewise Nāsika.
"In Kumbha, all those who are sinful become free from sin.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying their sins, they go to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Gomatī.
This was previously heard from Nārada on the banks of the Godāvarī. (25–26)
"In this regard, is there a place of pilgrimage, or perhaps the most excellent, the supreme holy site on earth?
O Sage, tell us all this; it is known to you within your mind.
Thus questioned, Sanātana Hari himself, the son of Brahmā, [replied].
He who was named Sanatkumāra spoke of such holy places (tīrthas) as being superior to the most superior, which instantly burn away sins every day—
[the sins] of great and even greater transgressions belonging to all those existing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
He who is the Lord of lords, the sovereign Master of incarnations, the Supreme Soul, the Great Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of the imperishable liberated ones, higher than the highest. (2.88.30)
He dwells in the supreme abode; he is the Lord, the sovereign of the lords of his own.
(21) He is the Blessed One among all blessed ones, to whom none is equal, nor indeed any superior, wherein lies the ultimate limit and the supreme goal. (32)
This very king and emperor, in an instant, manifested from his own form the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Satī;
he gave them abodes to dwell in.
He bestowed the perfections of sovereignty and likewise granted his own divine qualities.
This very one, the son of Śrī Kambharā and the delight of the illustrious Gopāla,
first manifested like a child at the beginning of creation.
He dwells in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, served by the liberated ones,
served by the Muktānīs, and served by the beloved of Brahmā;
he is attended by sages such as Lomaśa and others, as well as by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
It is served by the incarnations of Viṣṇu with his thousand arms,
as well as by Vāsudeva and others who possess a hundred thousand heads;
there, on the ground known as Akṣara, it is served and worshipped.
Mādhava sports all around the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake in this sacred field;
he dwells everywhere, even in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage,
where the wives of the gods exist as trees and creepers in the form of pearls.
Liberated and yet possessing the very nature of pillars, they remain there with a desire for vision.
By whose grace the gods, having become the likeness of ants, and even swans, sparrows, and other birds, wander about the Aśvasaras lake. (2.88.40–41)
A field measuring ten yojanas is considered to be the Imperishable Brahman (akṣarabrahma),
pervaded by whose dust even insects attain the supreme goal;
that divine ground, which exists within every atom, is auspicious and bestows liberation.
Even the wind, through union with the Supreme Lord, bestows liberation. Indeed,
even creepers and trees purify the worlds,
for the Blessed One is eternally present within them, just as he is in the horse-dung lake.
One bathes and sports with devotees here at the Brahma-hrada;
the Ganges and other excellent holy fords (tīrthas) exist within its waters.
There is also the lake called Amṛta, as well as the Virajā, Yamunā, and others.
In that lake dwell those who are intent upon the yoga of Śrī Hari.
Such a purifying place does not exist in the world, nor in heaven, nor in Satyaloka, nor in Rasātala, nor even in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms; no rivers there are superior to it.
Through its union with Puruṣottama, that lake has attained the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara), supreme excellence,
and the power to dispel the heat of sins.
Having gone there constantly, one must bathe at that very place even in the evening.
Sins committed during the day are burned away by association with that [practice].
Having gone there at dawn, one should perform an ablution; by that, all sin arising from the night shall dissolve for the bather in the Aśvasarovara lake. (2.88.49–50)
Embodied beings— whether divine or non-divine— should travel there at every sacred juncture (*parvan*) and bathe in that place which removes the impurities of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
This should be done either month by month, or annually, or seasonally, or even during the solstices (*ayana*).
Having gone there, one must indeed bathe; for that [act] burns away all sin.
There resides Kuṅkumavāpī, whose water Hari himself always drinks along with the food offerings (naivedya) from within the waters of the pool. || 52-53 ||
For this Aśvapaṭṭasara always bathes in the early morning;
it is this very Kuṅkumavāpī, considered the heart of Śrī Hari.
Indeed, there is no other holy place (tīrtha) superior to it anywhere in the worlds of the Dhāmas.
It does not exist in the worlds of the gods, nor in the abodes of Īśvara and others;
how then could it be found on earth except at Kuṅkumavāpikā?
Kuṅkumavāpikā itself is equal to [any other] Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He is equal to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; he is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself. He is equal to the virtuous Kaṃbharāśrī; he is the virtuous Kaṃbharāśrī herself.
And he is equal to Gopālakṛṣṇa; he is indeed Gopālakṛṣṇa.
The Imperishable is equal to the imperishable; there is nothing superior to it that is equal.
It is equal to this entire universe, for it is indeed this very universe wherein the beginningless Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, truly resides. (58–59)
Let the rivers there go and perform their ablutions;
and at early dawn, let them drink the divine water of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
the saffron-water of the Kuṅkumavāpī pond, and the nectar from the feet of Hari.
May they worship Bālakṛṣṇa directly day and night;
may the Goddesses dwell there always in happiness in their primary forms,
and may they sport in various regions in their functional forms as the embodiments of water.
Through the yoga of Bālakṛṣṇa, you shall attain true happiness—
ineffable, indescribable, and characterized by limitless bliss—
which is the supreme bliss residing in his form, and which does not even exist within the imperishable Brahman.
But from where else could that happiness surely be obtained?
Only by serving Bālakṛṣṇa with the offering of one's entire being will Hari, being pleased, grant all happiness and his own beloved state. (64–65)
Wherever even the slightest distinction exists, there is also a distinction within that bliss;
where no distinction exists, there is no distinction within that bliss.
When the two are unified, streams of happiness indeed manifest.
The illustrious Kṛṣṇa is the best of men; O Cit, may you be His servant.
This is the very bliss of those two; what talk can there be of suffering therein?
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, sins dissolve moment by moment. (67–68)
There, mountains of merit arise moment by moment, and streams of bliss flow forth from every side like oceans.
These are born through the power of Śrī Hari; let those who serve Him go unto that Hari.
As the rivers were being described in this manner, minute black insects emerged from all sides from the circle of his body hair. Then they asked them: "Who are you that have emerged here?"
The insects said: "We are the sinful defilements of the wicked, manifesting as their very sins. Indeed, having cast us off from you, the sinners go to their homes.
We have emerged from your bodies because of the recollection of the Aśvasaras lake."
“We shall go to other rivers, on mountains, and so forth;
otherwise, by merely bathing there, our destruction will occur. Having fallen into such fear, they departed for other places while still alive. (73–74)
Those who, having remembered Kuṅkumavāpī, Bālakṛṣṇa the Supreme Lord, and the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, go toward that Imperishable One— by them,
when the bridge [of devotion] is established, all sins are swiftly destroyed in every way. (75)
Therefore, we who desire to live shall go to another place.
Life is superior to death, whether attained through austerity, hunger, or even some other means;
for while living, one may inevitably behold auspicious things.
"Human purpose shall also arise, and one's desired goals will be attained again and again.
Having spoken thus, all the holy fords (tīrthas) then departed from the multitude of rivers,
their very names bringing about a wondrous result upon being heard.
"Evil deeds indeed go far away; what kind of sacred ford (tīrtha) must that be?
Having thus resolved, "Therefore, one must go there and attend upon it, and indeed dwell there," they praised the sage again and again. (2.88.80)
They worshipped him with supreme devotion and spoke repeatedly to the sage:
"O Blessed Sanatkumāra, lead us indeed to that sacred field;
grant us this favor by accompanying us there at least once."

At that very moment, the sage exclaimed "Om! regarding all the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) whatsoever that exist upon the earth; they all rejoiced exceedingly on every side. As soon as the news was made public, it quickly reached those who had arrived at Kumbha.
The venerable Sanatkumāra proceeds indeed toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa for the purification of all sins,
taking with him all sacred fords along with Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Where Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord Hari himself, resides,
and where the sage Lomaśa dwells in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara— let us indeed go there, taking our water-pot with us, for the attainment of divinity. (85–86)
Having thus made this resolution and taken up their requisites,
they then set out for the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) in order to perform the rites of pilgrimage. All the rivers situated in every region, as well as all the lakes in every region, [also departed].
All the wells situated in every region, the ponds, the natural lakes, and the oceans;
all the springs, the tanks, and the oblong pools; as well as the confluences of rivers and the meeting points of seas and streams. (88–89)
Having beheld the water-tirthas and whatever tirthas there are on the earth—
mountains, plateaus, caves,
and heights; forests, excellent wildernesses, river-fords, and likewise rivers.
Those from the various continents and even the rivers, having arrived for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites,
met with their respective companions and fellow practitioners according to their stations;
likewise, the mountains, the peaked hills, and the deities of those regions did so as well.
All the lakes and ponds likewise undertook the journey on foot.
A hundred thousand holy sites (*tīrthas*), as well as others by the hundreds of thousands,
[proceeded] with musical instruments, wind instruments, flutes, *trāsakas*, and cymbals.
Accompanied by mṛdaṅgas, dvimṛdaṅgas, bherīs, and musical instruments that produce notes,
as well as lutes with high-pitched strings, and by Tumburu and others, they sang the glories of Hari with excellent musical accompaniment. (94–95)
Having reached the month of Āśvina, they departed comfortably from Prayāga;
on the way, having visited Puṣkara and likewise Siddhāśrama,
they bowed to Satī, Bahucarā, and Mount Catuṣṭila.
Having seen the sacred fords (tīrthas), the gods, the Siddhas, and the great seers (maharṣis),
as well as the ancestors and the mountains and others who indeed bore divine forms,
they joyfully approached the vicinity of the boundary of the Kuṅkumavāpī field.
The sages and great seers, together with Sanatkumāra,
as well as other yogis of divine bodies, arrived there.
They then took rest in the region of Śaṅkara to the north of the sacred field.
Then they arranged the procession, which signaled the commencement of the festival assembly.
O Rādhikā, goddesses dwelling in heaven and even celestial nymphs—
truthful and virtuous women— arrived, longing to behold the sacred pilgrimage site.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Pilgrimage from Prayāga to Kuṅkumavāpī by All the Tīrthas through the Majesty of Aśvapaṭṭasara as Revealed by the Sage Śrī Sanatkumāra," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 88. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 89 [Author:
Chapter 90 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In the eastern part of the field known as Kuṅkumavāpī, O Rādhikā,
there is the auspicious Pārijātaka forest, worthy of being the abode of the immortals;
it is vast, measuring one yojana in extent, and situated in the northeast direction.
There is an excellent forest of *kādamba* trees extending for three *yojanas*.
To the north of that, the divine Bhadrā river shines resplendent;
in its various places, Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa bathed. (2–3)
Having rested well on its bank, bathed, and partaken of milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
the assembly of pilgrims then proceeded along the road while chanting praises to Hari.
At their head was a golden elephant, adorned with various ornaments such as gold and jewels, moving upon the earth.
Resembling a mountain of red chalk and carrying a drum like a cloud,
he indeed goes at the front, making a loud, thundering sound.
Following behind him goes the śarabha named Vairājāvarta.
Carrying on his back two resonant drums, the personage followed behind them;
upon the back of Māṇikī was a banner extending a hundred cubits,
adorned with silk and gold stars, and graced by the five deities.
The Vindhya mountain moves along, carrying clouds as if they were banners;
behind it, the sound of conchs resounds through the ten directions.
This wind, created by the gods, shines forth and is experienced by the inhabitants of heaven.

After that, the Blessed One Vāmana, laughing as he went, held up the flowing Sudhātu mountain and made both heaven and earth resound. Following him, Śrī Nṛsiṃha himself indeed roared in all directions.
Adorned with the splendor of a divine lion’s mane and possessing tawny eyes, he proceeds.
Behind him, the two gods of the Aśvinī constellation, both resembling the sun and the moon, beautiful in form and mounted upon horses, proclaim his victory. (11–12)

After that, the powerful Śvetavārāha, white in color and exceedingly handsome, proceeds for the sake of the sacred ford, shaking the ends of the quarters and roaring. Then the Gandharvas follow, skilled musicians who know how to play their instruments.
And they play the jhaṅkāras, cymbals, and mṛdaṅga drums;
the vīṇā, mayūraka, tantrī, and instruments sounding like the roar of water; the prāṇapāśas, the sounds of the throat, and the tālikās and tālapaṭṭakas. (14–15)

Then, after that, various musical instruments were played: drums of diverse shapes, kettledrums, flutes, reed-pipes, *sṛjihvikā* pipes, *trāṭaka* horns, *citraghoṣa* trumpets, *śalākā* pipes, and likewise *rāgiṇī* lutes.
|| 16 || Indeed, such instruments as these were sounded thereafter.
Then indeed the performers of *kīrtana*, the male holy sites (*puṃtīrtha*), proceed;
then the divine *siddhas* go forth, as do the truthful, the virtuous women, and the virtuous men.
With their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, they chant the name of Hari, which is accompanied by musical instruments.
Then the ancestors depart with shouts of victory and hymns of praise;
then indeed all the deities go forth—the gods who dwell in heaven.
Then the sages depart, both those established in truth and those dwelling upon the earth.
And likewise, chanting the mantras of the Vedas as well as the Sāman hymns,
the Cāraṇas, Bhaṭas, Gandharvas,
and singers then proceed with the sounds of musical instruments, proclaiming his name.
After them proceed the kings of the gods and the world-protectors;
after them follow all the rivers, streams, springs, lakes,
and ponds, as they proceed and proclaim [his name].
Then the wives of the sages go, followed by the goddesses and the celestial women;
filled with love, they sing the verses concerning Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then they proceed to the circle of forests, wildernesses, mountains, sacred sites, and pilgrimage centers.
Then the male servants, likewise the female servants, and then the men departed;
thus the flow of the procession and the assembly extended for the distance of a yojana. At that time, there was a long and divine rain of flowers.
And seeing that the majestic holy places were approaching him, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, desiring to offer a welcome, went forward with great joy;
likewise did Gopāla Kṛṣṇa. (26–27)
The virtuous ones such as Kapila, the great sages such as Lomaśa,
the truthful ones such as Rādhā and Ramā, the Vaiṣṇavas such as Śaṅkara,
the brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas, and even crores, billions, and trillions of maidens.
Brahmapriyā, Kambharāśrī, and likewise all the Vallikās;
the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpī, as well as other auspicious oblong ponds;
the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, and the trees of the hermitage.
The guardians of the fields, all the sacred fords on the banks of the Aśvasaras lake,
whatever deities dwell there, as well as the rivers, streams, and mountains—
all of them wore garlands and were provided with the madhuparka offering and other honors.
Accompanied by singing and instrumental music, they approached the followers of other sects.
Brahmahrada, Aśvataṭāka, and likewise Kuṅkumavāpikā went ahead of Hari; then Viraja and the others followed by his side.
Having beheld the temple of Hari and another seven-storied palace made of gold, those great-souled ones arrived;
they prostrated themselves like a staff and placed their heads upon the dust.
Overwhelmed with full enthusiasm, they uttered cries of "Victory!
When they had entered the sacred precinct at a distance of one yojana, they met together, beheld [the deity], and raised shouts of victory again and again. (35–36)
They exchanged greetings with one another and likewise offered words of welcome.
Then the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa himself performed the rites for those who are the very soul of sacred pilgrimage sites, saying:
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! That the arrival of these holy places has come to me!"
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari gave them the madhuparka and other offerings;
others gave flower garlands, sandalwood, and floral wreaths. Having gathered together, they inquired after each other's welfare and embraced one another as was appropriate.
Seekers after sacred fords and those desiring the holy sites, intent upon chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa,
arrived near the Kuṅkumavāpī lake as quickly as a crane.
Indeed, they repeatedly rolled in the dust of the path to the sacred field.
Considering it a great fortune, the gods, goddesses, and likewise the sages—
some were dancing, some were singing, and others were playing instruments at that time;
they placed the dust upon their heads and rubbed it upon their bodies.
Some bowed their heads to Hari, some joined their palms in reverence,
some applied the dust from his feet to their chests, and others to their faces;
the Lord himself, appearing as a child, rolled about at Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Some, having recognized the majesty of the lotus-born goddess, wear upon their heads the foot-dust of her devotees,
as well as that of the sages and all sacred fords;
others likewise carry her leaves, flowers, stalks, and even blades of grass.
They take [the water] by holding it in their mouths and consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose;
they drink the water from a spring, thinking it to be a destroyer of sins,
and after drinking it cup by cup, they consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose.
Some, having repeatedly drawn into their mouths the wind that has come from being touched by the waters of Lake Aśvasaras,
then attain supreme bliss;
some remember the divine abodes, and some remember those who have descended there.
Some whose hearts are fixed on Him remember the liberated souls, as well as His divine opulences and perfections,
His weapons such as the discus and conch, and likewise His attendants and female servants;
they quickly grant whatever desired honors one wishes for on the path.
Thus, with musical instruments, hymns of praise, and vehicles filled with love,
accompanied by shouts of victory, they all reached the lake named Aśva.
At that time, the sins of those embodied beings were as hard as adamant.
All those [sins], indeed innumerable, that were abandoned at the sacred ford (tīrtha) are instantly consumed there by the mere sight of Aśvapaṭṭasara, which is like the sight of Hari;
not even a trace remains.
Whatever [impurities] go far away when a bath is taken at another sacred site, they are all burnt away by the mere sight of Aśvasaras.
Oh, the great majesty of Kṛṣṇa is seen directly before our eyes! || 53-54 ||
"Whatever dust, whatever water, and even whatever leaf belongs to that field [of Lord Hari] burn away all sins; what then need be said when it is in Hari himself?
Thus praising him, those lords of the earth remained on the shore of the lake.
In the northern region of Śiva, which was exceedingly vast and a most excellent location, they rested, bathed, drank water, and offered salutations;
they performed the rites of the sacred ford (tīrtha), washing away all their sins. ||56-57||
Then, having bathed the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with those waters,
the holy sites and others performed their own ablutions and drank the water born of His grace.
By means of the divine waters, they became divine in form and attained the state of liberation.
Having thus performed the ritual at the Aśvasaras tīrtha according to the prescribed rules,
they then proceeded to the vast Śrī-kuṅkumavāpī, which is the very embodiment of light.
They all drank that water and bathed repeatedly in its waters.
Then, by the will of Hari, those great-souled ones attained *sārṣṭitva* at the sacred fords and other sites.
Thereafter, having gone to the Brahma-lake, they bathed and drank its water.
Then those illustrious beings attained the state of *sārūpya*.
All were equal to Bālakṛṣṇa in their abundance of virtues and beauty;
they became fit for liberation and were freed from rebirth.
Then they all proceeded further to the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa.
Lomaśa welcomed them with sweet foods, fruits,
and water; he fed all those honored guests from the holy places with nourishing meals and satiating offerings made from the essence of milk brought from the abode of Brahmā.
He caused them to be satisfied and offered them mouth-fresheners.
(65) The gods, sages, ancestors, and humans went to all the sacred fords, as did the rivers, streams, mountains, and whatever forests and wildernesses there were. (66)
And all those great souls went to the auspicious abode of Bālakṛṣṇa,
which is divine, enriched with divine splendor, frequented by liberated souls,
served by those of inconceivable and infinite power, and is the refuge of the Lord.
Always graced by incarnations, it is auspicious and bestows liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*).
There, in that divine and most excellent Brahma-lake, whose waters were bathed by the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the great sages (*mahīmānakas*) bathed. (68–69)
Possessing divine bodies and endowed with divine vision, they all beheld their own eternal selves stationed in that supreme, divine abode beyond the Imperishable.
Then, those who were once proud of their greatness realized their full majesty.
Sālokya, Sārṣṭi, Sārūpya, and Sāyujya indeed exist here [in this place].
Liberation from sin is found at other holy sites, but Aśvasaras burns away all evil.
Kuṅkumavāpī bestows Sārṣṭi, while Brahmahrada grants one’s own true nature (Svarūpa).
Indeed, the divine hermitage of Lomaśa exists here, which bestows the liberation of *sālokya*;
and this abode of Bālakṛṣṇa is truly the giver of *sāyujya* liberation.
Oh, by the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, indeed everyone [attains their respective goals] one by one!
And they increase in supreme power, bestowing liberation in every way—oh!
One should either make one's dwelling here or proceed to the Imperishable;
once the Supreme Brahman has been attained, what sinner would dwell elsewhere? || 74-75 ||
Thus conversing, they celebrated a great festival at night,
during the dark fortnight of the seventh lunar day in the month of Kumuda.
They did so with songs, hymns, dances, devotional worship, and praises.
They passed the night happily through meditations and listening to sacred discourses.

In the morning, having bathed in the Aśvasaras lake, they all went for the worship of Kṛṣṇa on the great festival day of the eleventh lunar day—the anniversary of His birth—on the eighth [lunar day]. || 77–78 ||
In the vast pavilion constructed by Viśvakarman, Hari himself shone forth at night in the center upon an elephant-throne;
there were also various other thrones and lion-seats everywhere.
And upon them were established the lords of lords, the supreme lords;
likewise, the incarnations, the liberated ones, and other liberated souls, as well as virtuous women, virtuous men of Brahmanic character, gods, goddesses, and great sages. (2.89.80–81)
Brahmā and the other sages, the ancestors, and tens of millions of gods shone forth; so too did the sacred fords, rivers, streams, and lakes.
The world-protectors, the guardians of kingdoms, the mountains, forests, and lands were all present.
The forest trees, creepers, grasses, and ponds likewise,
as well as all things insentient and sentient, shone brilliantly upon their seats;
divine musical instruments were played, and auspicious sounds resounded at that time.
The sound of the Vedas arose and there was a rain of flowers;
the king of sages, Lomaśa, freed from all illusion, worshipped Hari.
He applied a *tilaka* and a *candraka* mark upon the forehead of the Supreme Soul.

He placed a beautiful garland upon his head; he also placed a golden one, as well as garlands of *tulasī* and flowers made of gems, around his neck. He offered a handful of flowers and placed sprouts of *dūrvā* grass upon his ears. (86–87)
She placed an excellent *śrīphala* fruit in his hand and offered other fruits before him;
she then honored his feet with sandalwood paste and increased his prosperity with unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*).
She performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) for Hari and bestowed auspicious blessings.
Then the illustrious Queen Kambharā worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa.
Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa placed a necklace upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck,
and the Lord Śukadeva, along with Vallabha and others, offered garlands.
Hemanta and the Blessed One, as well as Haimī, Upadā, Samuttamā,
Santopā, Amṛtā, Dugdhā, Jīvantī, and the others, offered excellent gifts of woolen cloth and garlands.
Then they applied saffron *tilaka* marks upon their foreheads and [placed] a drop [of it] on the forehead of Hari.
Then the lords, the incarnations, the liberated souls, and other goddesses,
having worshipped Śrī Hari with the *ārārtrika* rite, [stood there].
So too did the sages devoted to the vow of Brahman, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
The gods and goddesses, the male rivers and female rivers, the lakes and even the small pools;
the mountains and the unexcavated plains, the sacred fords and the forests, and the wildernesses—all these principles worshipped the Supreme Lord. ||93-94||
They offered nightly lamps, handfuls of flowers, and gifts;
likewise, ornaments, garments, and various utensils;
as well as rings, fruits, flowers, gems, and diamonds.

For the sake of worship, they gave celestial vehicles and wish-fulfilling trees. After such worship and after the dismissal of the assembly, Hari fed all those honored guests who had come with their families.
To all those who were guests and visitors, as well as to all embodied beings,
he gave pleasing sacrificial fees with a sincere heart.
Then, a request was made by the holy fords there in the presence of Śrī Hari.
Having obtained the gain that bestows liberation, who would desire any other gain?
Therefore, O Ocean of Compassion, grant us liberation, the eternal bliss.
Then Hari, out of compassion for them, indeed assumed three forms.
Keśava then sent the divine Mūla, as well as Chāyā and the forms of the Mūlas in their respective abodes, along with his attendants (pārṣadas) in celestial chariots; thereafter,
he kept his own divine forms in his own presence.

They dwelt at will in the region of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ, which consists of sacred fords (tīrtha), in embodied forms within temples constructed by Viśvakarman; they were contented and desirous of serving Hari. (102–103)
At that time, whatever shadow-forms of the holy fords (tīrthas) were present there,
the Lord spoke auspicious words to them for the sake of purifying the world:
"O lords of the holy fords, your birth upon the earth is solely by my will."
"O Lords, you must indeed go for the sake of purifying the worlds!
You should remain right there where my presence has been established in this world in the form of activity— where I have created the rivers, streams, and lakes."
Indeed, one must dwell there in that very manner for the burning away of the sins of the wicked.
One should come every year on my birthday in every respect,
as well as during the festival of Ekādaśī, in the month of Kumbha, in Māgha, and in Kārtika.
"At the transit [of the sun], in Śrāvaṇa, and also in Vaiśākha at Puruṣottama"—
having been addressed thus, those embodied Lords of Tīrthas bowed down and departed for their own regions; likewise, the great ones departed.
Having worshiped Hari, their beloved, O Rādhikā, all those people— Brahmā’s dear ones and others— went from Lomaśa’s hermitage to their respective abodes.
Even during the night, an excellent festival was held with dancing and singing.
Through both recitation and hearing, this [work] shall bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of All Holy Places, Deities, and Others at Kuṅkumavāpī, and the Festival for the Birthday of Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. 89.

Chapter 90 [[Author: → Chapter 91
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to another wonderful account of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; I shall relate to you this supreme narrative which protects the world. (1)

In ancient times, the two divine sons of Dharma, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, while at Badarī on the Himalayas, meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, those two ascetics [saw] the Lord who had manifested from themselves.

And on the bank of the Gaṅgā, eager for a vision [of Him], they meditated in their own hermitage. (3) On the western edge of the earth, in Saurāṣṭra, in the field named Kuṅkumavāpī belonging to Ajanābha, Hari dwells in the house of Śrī Kambharā. (4)

"When will He— the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, who dwells as a child, and who is the cause of all incarnations— grant us His vision? As the two brothers, who were themselves Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were thus remembering Him, [the Lord appeared].
To fulfill that resolve, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself,
having spoken to the devotees residing in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ,
departed by means of a celestial chariot for the Badarīvana forest on Mount Hemādri. (6–7)
Having taken Lomaśa with them and leaving the rest there,
and having entrusted [the others] to Hara and the Guardian of the Field for protection,
the two kinsmen went to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa on the eleventh day.

In the fortnight of Kārtika, they both worshipped him with water, flowers, and fruits. They, as well as the ṛṣis and the ascetics, performed service to the Lord and practiced devotion to dharma every single day.
Seeing that the month of Mārgaśīrṣa was the most excellent for sacrifice, those great sages, the ascetics, performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice at Badarī.
He constantly provided leaf-huts as suitable dwellings for them.
To Lomaśa and likewise to Bālakṛṣṇa, Śrī Narāyaṇa [spoke].
(1.2) In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, this great and auspicious festival of sacrifice took place;
there, Lord Hari himself—the Supreme Soul, the Supreme Controller—was present. (1.3)
Then the Lord of Sacrifice, stationed within the fire, consumed the oblations; likewise,
the liberated souls who dwell in Goloka,
those liberated ones who reside in Vaikuṇṭha, and those dwelling in other abodes were present in person.
Desirous of obtaining the grace of Hari, they gathered there at the sacrifice:
the gods, the great seers, the goddesses, the sacred fords, and likewise the ancestors;
as well as the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, the Brahmins, and those who travel through the sky.
Then the Daityas and Dānavas, his devotees, arrived at the sacrifice;
for thus did the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, shine forth there.
At that very time, in the month of Kārttika, in Surāṣṭra—
At night, by the command of Śambhu, Mahāmārī, the messenger of Śambhu, stands at the boundary and protects the region of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ;
indeed, she does so having remembered her brother’s son from Siṃhaladvīpa. (18–19)
Kubhīnasī, Śṛṅgī, and two hundred other rākṣasīs—
traversing the sky, able to assume any form at will, and experts in the web of illusion—
learned that the one who lived by unrighteousness had indeed died in Surāṣṭra.
Armed with weapons and missiles to exact their vengeance, they arrived;
having leaped over the lion-infested forests, they reached Saurāṣṭra through the sky on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika. || 21-22 ||
Then, on the night preceding the Festival of Lamps, they descended from the sky,
displaying firebrands and flames of fire issuing from their mouths; indeed,
they displayed tridents blazing with fire from their hair.
Kill these, devour these—the beloved young maidens of the enemy!
Divide them, chew them up, and bring them for the sake of the Rākṣasas!
Set them ablaze, overpower them—all of them, the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa—by force! 24–25.
"There is no protector for them here, and this is our time for victory," saying thus,
those cruel female Rākṣasīs quickly descended upon Lomaśa’s hermitage in order to assault them.
The protectress of the boundary, the messenger, Mahāmārī herself, Bhairavī—
having perceived the sudden conflict and the calamity of war,
she assumed a thousand forms and, bearing weapons, rushed forward. (27–28)
In all the maidens' quarters, there arose at night a terrible outcry,
causing great terror due to the harassment of rākṣasīs.
Bhairavī, having taken up a noose and performed incantations with serpent-binding spells, [acted].
He released the rākṣasīs from their bonds amidst the assembly of rākṣasīs.
Then they were bound with chains by the nāgas like thieves, upon their hands, as well as on their hips, bellies, and necks. (2.90.30–31)
All the nāgas were indeed bound by nooses and rendered motionless;
they fell to the ground and became scorched by poison.
Then that Bhairavī approached Śambhu while he was asleep and [honored him] with hymns of praise.
He quickly awakened her and reported the assault.
Upon hearing of the calamity, Īśāna went to Lomaśa’s hermitage;
seeing the Rākṣasīs equipped with the serpent-weapon (nāgāstra), his mind was filled with satisfaction.
"Having become free from bondage, let us make this Bhairavī our messenger;
having waged war, let us all look toward her destruction.
Thus commanded, that Bhairavī bowed at the feet of Śaṅkara.
By the command of Śaṅkara, he rendered those Rākṣasīs free from their bonds.
He spoke to those Rākṣasīs, who were proud of their strength, to engage in battle;
bearing weapons, they fought with various martial maneuvers.
With spears, mallets, staffs, and likewise with stones;
with swords, blades, daggers, fists, and so forth, and by trampling with the feet;
with bodies as large as mountains, and by means of showers of malevolent spells (abhicāraka).
Moving through the sky, they fought incessantly with the Bhairavīs.
By the power of Rudra, those Bhairavīs then became possessed of adamantine bodies;
born of his will and assuming many forms, they fought there with their weapons.
With swords, axes, hatchets, and tridents;
with discuses, spears, pillars, thunderbolts, staffs, and nets;
with spikes, slings, explosive balls, and trees.
And those Bhairavīs, exceedingly enraged, struck down those Rākṣasīs violently.
Letting out cries, they leaped into the air and fell upon one another;
the Rākṣasīs, assuming many forms through their illusory power (*māyā*), struck the goddesses.
The masters struck the Lord with tridents and spears empowered by mantras;
indeed, they struck and pierced his hearts with Sītās and bhalla-arrows.
Then a great artificial army of rākṣasīs appeared.
Then those artificial women of Bhairava bound them with nooses of lightning and set them ablaze, uprooting the very roots [of their existence].
Thus, while that most terrible battle was unfolding by the thousands, || 45–46 ||
And headless trunks, resembling mountains, fell from the sky;
likewise, Kumbhīnasī and Śṛṅgī fled outside out of fear.
The others, numbering in the hundreds, were devoured by the Bhairavīs.
There, hundreds were repulsed; some were slain, and others fled alive.
Then victory was achieved by the Bhairavīs through the power of Śaṅkara.
Śambhu became pleased with them because the protection of the sacred field had been accomplished.
Having fought a great battle at night, he protected the hermitage of Lomaśa as well as the maidens, fulfilling his word. Being pleased, the bestower of boons spoke thus to those Mahāmārīs:
"I am pleased; ask for a boon and I shall grant it to you.
Then the Mahāmārīs, having bowed to the illustrious Śaṅkara, spoke likewise to that supreme Mother, the progenitress, the worshipful Mūla-Bhairavī.
O Śambhu, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to us,
then let there be food that shall alleviate our hunger and thirst,
as well as dispel our exhaustion. (53)
"O Lord, give us that which provides nourishment and strength, for we are of the nature of *tamas*.
We are all born of *tamas*, intoxicated by battle, and subsisting on the flesh, blood, and other substances born of combat, which grant us great nourishment. (54–55)
"We desire that very same food and drink if you will give it to us.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara replied at Dharmakṣetra in Surāṣṭraka—
this abode of the Supreme Brahman— "That gift is exceedingly difficult to bestow here."
"How could that indeed be possible here in the land of the Compassionate Lord?
Then they all replied, excluding the devotees of Hari:
"Only those who are tamasic, sinful, cruel, atheistic, and devoid of devotion. (57-58)

Those who are devoid of proper conduct, those of wicked conduct, those bereft of worship and recitation, those who do not bathe, those who avoid pilgrimages and the like, the hypocritical, the deceitful,
those lacking the grace of Hari, and those deprived of the *tulasī* garland; //59//
We shall indeed devour those who are not devotees of Śambhu, who are devoid of courage, who are not Vaiṣṇavas, who cause suffering to others,
who steal the property of others and so forth, who are destitute of merit,
and who are fit for the journey to Yama. (2.90.60–61)
"Such women— impure, devoid of dharma,
and lacking in worship— we shall indeed devour.
When this is done, the Blessed One will not fall into anger."
The city of Yama was created by Him alone for the purpose of punishing the unrighteous and the sinful.
Why then would the Lord not be satisfied when those wicked ones have been devoured? We consider Him to be our Master and Sovereign. (63–64)
"We shall satisfy him with our service as female servants.
Having said this, they ceased; but Śambhu, overcome with compassion, said to them, "So be it," and provided them with food and drink, which he had not given to his wicked subjects.
Then Mahāmārī, having bowed again and again to him who is dear to Hari,
and having bowed to Kuṅkumavāpī, having bowed to Aśvapaṭṭasāra,
having bowed to Śrī Kambharālakṣmī, and having bowed to Gopālakṛṣṇa— ||66–67||
Remembering the son of Gopāla, the Lord of Śrī, their Master and Sovereign,
they departed joyfully from that sacred field ten yojanas away.
Having raised up the bodies of the deceased rākṣasīs, they stood behind them.
Having cast them swiftly into a great pit among human beings,
they quickly entered into those who were not devotees of Viṣṇu— specifically those alienated from Śiva,
as well as the unrighteous, the wicked, the hypocritical, and the atheists.
Toward those who are deceitful and devoid of dharma, who wear external marks yet are internally filled with impurity—
toward such people who are renowned as devotees but are sinful both outwardly and inwardly.
They entered among such men and even among women.
That thousandfold multitude of thousands of great plagues [spread] in Saurāṣṭra,
Gūrjara, Mahārāṣṭra, and the South.
In the center, in the east, in the north, and in the west, throughout all the grounds,
the Mahāmārīs appeared, pervasive, invisible, and having the form of wind.
Having swiftly entered into bodies, they remained within the hearts.
They eat and drink flesh and blood that is warm and melting;
in a mere moment, men and women become devoid of life.
Having gone again and again throughout all the people as far as the edge of the ocean, [they devour them]. (75–76)
They devour wicked men, women, and others by the hundreds of thousands;
at that time, men and women die visibly in every village.
Indeed, for every thousand people, there are twenty who remain.
Then that cruel great pestilence spares no children;
it spares neither maidens nor brides, nor the young, nor the old, nor pregnant women;
it spares neither the destitute nor guests, nor those honored by the earth, nor spiritual guides. (78–79)
Neither kings nor queens, neither the wealthy nor the destitute; neither those wearing saffron robes nor those in a state of birth-impurity;
neither those engaged in sacrificial oblations nor those performing worship and recitations.
Upon merely beholding men joined with sin, women devour them.
Every day, women and men die by the hundreds of thousands on this earth;
having seized one, they go outside, and meanwhile another becomes dead.
But as soon as they had carried out the deceased and were returning home,
at that very moment five others had died;
and as soon as they had carried out those five and reached the village gate—
At that time, there were ten others who had died, or even more than that.
For some, the entire family residing in their house had met its end; for others, half of the members of the human family had perished. (84–85)
In some places a child remains; in others, a young bride;
in some places an aged old man; and in others, merely a beast.
In one city, out of a hundred thousand, only a thousand remain.
In some parts of the village, however, half the village was entirely dead;
in other places, the villages became terrifying, deserted by men.
And for the people who were dying, there was no one to provide water.
Where there is no one even to point the way, how can a giver of food be found?
Thus there was great destruction, and many were crushed.
Within a month, half of the people had indeed died from hunger.
Tens of millions of great Mārīs devoured sinful people;
likewise, Rākṣasas, Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras [devoured] those who were deceitful,
cruel, atheistic, and devoid of dharma.

Indeed, at the end of the month, as they were not being fed, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the quarters of the earth. At that time, the people, abandoning their villages and even their homes, fled in fear from the towns and cities to the forest.

Afflicted by the fear of the [time of] destruction, they made their dwellings in the forests like forest-dwellers. At that time, due to the fear of the great pestilence, the forests became cities and the cities became forests; all was turned upside down.
In the land of Aśvapaṭṭākṣara, extending for ten yojanas,
O beloved, there was no fear of the great pestilence among those who were devoted;
even those non-devotees residing there were spared by their respective fortunes.
Those who had gone outside, having abandoned the sacred field (kṣetra), met their death.
"Save us! Save us! the subjects cried, and they remembered the Supreme Lord.
For the sake of destroying this disease, the subjects indeed performed acts of devotion.
We shall offer various kinds of food offerings in the temple of the deity;
we shall present garments, ornaments, fine cloth, and gold in the presence of the God.
We shall establish perpetual endowments of food, perform complete recitations of the scriptures, and conduct virtuous sacrifices.
We shall perform religious duties and practice the service of the Dharma;
we shall worship Hari and his holy devotees, serve the gods, and cultivate devotion; we shall abandon all sin and transgression. (2.90.99–100)
We shall worship Sūrya, Śiva, Satī, Lakṣmī, and Īśinī;
Gaṇeśa, Mahākāla, the Mātṛkās, and the ancestral deities.
We shall also undertake a pilgrimage to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Where there was no great pestilence due to the power of Bālakṛṣṇa,
the people everywhere, being extremely overwhelmed by the fear of death,
made a solemn vow to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (102–103)
O Bhairavī! O Great Plague! We shall tremble when our lives depart, yet we shall surely remain [in this world]. You have an oath before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"If you touch me, do not touch me there. 104.
The subjects gave their command thus, and a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose upon the earth:
"O Great Plague, do not touch us! Here we give you roasted barley meal (saṃyāva) as an offering; this is the oath of Śaṅkara, and likewise the oath of your parents."
Thus did the people of Rādhikā offer their salutations;
then those truthful, virtuous, twice-born ones departed through the sky for Śrī Badarī.
Let there be repeated obeisances to Sadyojāta Mahādeva.
Salutations to Mahākāla and to Kālabhairava; salutations to you repeatedly. Salutations again and again to Ajāpāla and to Vīrabhadra;
salutations repeatedly to Mṛtyuñjaya, to Mahākālī, and to Caṇḍī.
"Salutation to Durgā!"—thus did the wretched subjects cry out at that time.
Śrī Hari had already known all about this impending calamity beforehand.

(2.90.110) Thus, in the second section, the *tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described are] the Lord’s departure for Badarī, the arrival of the rākṣasīs at Kuṅkumavāpī, the destruction of the rākṣasīs by Mahāmārī, and thereafter, among the sinful subjects...
The Ninetieth Chapter, titled "The Pervasiveness for the Purpose of Consumption and the Description of Cetya," etc.,
