Chapter 91.
[The Author: Chapter 92.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O virtuous Rādhikā, listen! Having gone to Śrī Badarī, the twice-born [sages]—
The truthful, the virtuous, and the saintly bathed through the sky in the waters of the river.
Having performed their ablutions in the Gaṅgā, they chanted the names of Hari together and went to where Nārāyaṇa was.

Having bowed to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and having repeatedly prostrated before the assembly of great sages, they were honored by those present; they received a warm welcome and worship, and accepted the *madhuparka* offering from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (3)
Having inquired where Lomaśa was staying, they went to his leaf-hut.
Seeing that his devotees had arrived with distressed minds, Lomaśa quickly asked after their welfare and the purpose of their sudden visit.
Having offered seats, they all spoke to the sage Lomaśa after beholding Śrī Hari and likewise performing worship.
Then we shall explain the reason for our coming here.
Having spoken thus to Śrī Hari, who was staying in the leaf-hut,
Lomaśa immediately went inside the house, announced the arrival of his kinsmen,
and taking the affectionate Hari with him, he went outside together.
When Śrī Hari arrived at the courtyard of the hall beneath the sacred Badarī tree,
those pilgrims then prostrated themselves like a staff;
out of love, Hari inquired after their welfare, their welcome, and their well-being.
Then, shedding tears, they spoke to Śrī Hari:
"The Bhairavī Mahāmārī, who protects the borders,
has slain countless rākṣasīs of Siṃhaladvīpa."
Those who had arrived at the region of Aśvapaṭṭasara for the sake of battle—
in order to avenge the enmity of the Daitya who lives by unrighteousness—
have protected the maidens and likewise protected the hermitage. (12)
Then, at night, Śambhu himself was pleased with that Mahāmārī and spoke for the sake of granting a boon; she too then made this request:
"O Mahāmārī, those born from me who wage war and are afflicted by hunger—" || 14 ||
"O Śiva! We desire that he be a consumer of human flesh.
When this was said by Śambhu, Bhairavī replied:
"We shall certainly not accept those who have come for refuge to the glorious Hari."
Those who abandon devotees of Śiva and devotees of Hari—
those sinners, atheists, those devoid of dharma, those who are indeed enemies of the gods,
the deceitful, the revilers, those who harm sacred sites, and those possessed of hypocrisy. (16–17)
"Men and women who are devoid of bathing, worship, recitation, and devotion—
we shall devour them here, from ten yojanas outside.
"So be it," Hara said, and Mahāmārīs came by the tens of thousands.
They swiftly devoured people excessively— children, the elderly, pregnant women,
old women, young women, and even the young. Thus, indeed, a total upheaval occurred, and the villages were left devoid of human beings.
There are people living like crows, deprived of their families; some dwellings have become half-occupied, and some are even entirely without descendants.
But this calamity, O Lord, persists by relying upon its own strength.
O Lord, by the force of Mahākāla, human beings die;
indeed, there is no counting those who have perished, nor do even their carriers meet again. The forest has become a city, and villages have become forests.
"O Lord, come quickly and protect us from that dissolution!
Having spoken thus, they all wept; but the compassionate one, overcome by pity, arose immediately and called Narayana to mind.
Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa stayed in a leaf-hut.
Having bowed before the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest, they sat down in front of him and asked for his permission: "O Lord, why is there such agitation? (25–26)
Hari said: "In the region of Ājanābha on the earth, there arose a great pestilence among men, through which many sinners perished.
Even those devotees who had taken refuge there died, despite having very few faults."
This destruction of the Rākṣasa who lived by unrighteousness occurred through the extermination of Khara’s son in the lineage of Pulastya;
indeed, it was brought about by those very Rākṣasīs who were the sisters of Khara. ||28-29||
An affliction has been wrought upon our field,
and Bhairavī, the Great Plague and the dark emissary of Śambhu, acts as its remedy;
in the form of a reward, she indeed devours the sinners.
Even those of little sin and great merit, as well as my devotees, will be devoured by the wicked in their company. Therefore, for the sake of protecting them,
I shall go quickly to that region of Surāṣṭra along with these devotees.
Thus addressed, Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the ocean of mercy, said:
"Indeed, whatever is the will of the independent Supreme Lord shall come to pass.
For my part, I have constantly remembered the Blessed One during the month of Kārtika for the sake of worship."
Every day during the month of Kārttika, he was worshipped by me five times;
he was constantly saluted and served with the massaging of his feet and other such acts, as well as being fed fruits and honored with devotion, righteousness, and the like. (34–35)
The sages were gratified, and the Badarī forest was purified;
all the sages were purified, as was the Himālaya.
The celestial Gaṅgā was purified, and the hermitage of Parṇaśālā was purified.
This [hermitage] shall always remain here in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
All our intentions have been fulfilled; you have shown us the state of an ascetic woman, O Lord, and from you we have acquired the conduct attainable through self-restraint.
Everything has become complete for me; my own desired sacrifice has been born.
That Vaiṣṇava rite is fulfilled and proceeds according to the rules.
So too do the Supreme Lords, the Īśas, the gods, and the great sages.
O Lord, the ancestors have been gratified by you as you established yourself in the sacrifice;
and as you directly accepted the oblation through the radiant mouth of Agni, what more remains for me today? For they have been satisfied and set free. (2.91.40–41)
"O Lord, my heart has been completely fulfilled by you.
Having dwelt here for one month and more, Badarī has been sanctified.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Nara and Nārāyaṇa [departed], while the great sages remained devoted.
Gharma and the other gods likewise worshipped the Supreme Lord;
they performed the *ārārtika* rite, circumambulated Him, offered flowers with joined palms, and then sought His forgiveness, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (43–44)
He bestowed blessings upon them and said: "Bring Nara and Nārāyaṇa, devotion, righteousness, and the great sages to my home;
[bring] the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake."
"Let them also visit the purifying hermitage of their preceptor Lomaśa.
Let them make this supreme, imperishable field a source of purification for me.
For the sight of you who dwell in the golden realm is difficult to obtain on this earth."
Having spoken thus, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the others, their minds filled with joy,
bathed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa and set out on their journey.
Then the sages, stationed in the path of the sky, proceeded by means of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Dharma, Bhakti, and Lomaśa— these virtuous ones,
along with the saintly women and the liberated souls, arrived at the house by means of a celestial chariot.
In the evening, they reached Saurāṣṭra, where the people were distressed by the passing of time.
With its household customs ruined and lost, and abandoned by men whose wealth had vanished,
it was no longer as it once was, though it possessed its former splendor;
and in that same manner, various countries were beheld along the way, such as Saurāṣṭra.
The Kurus, Śūrasenas, Maravas, and Gaurjaras—
bereft of offspring and wealth, withered and devoid of luster like empty houses—
were devoured by the great pestilence and destroyed by the force of Time.
Human beings, forest-dwellers, and householders; Piśācas, corpses, and those dwelling in death; animal existence as their way of life;
houses that are cremation grounds, and mice who are messengers of death.
Indeed, inconceivable portents were seen in the cities like the dissolution of the world.
Having understood all this, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person,
reflected for a moment and then remembered Śaṅkara from his vehicle.
There, on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, Śaṅkara, the guardian of the field, quickly arrived and bowed to the Supreme Lord.
Śrī Hari said to Śaṅkara: "Since it is by means of these very great plagues..."
"Destroy the entire world; ward off the great pestilence! 98.
At once Śaṅkara let out his own roar from his throat, and the entire cosmic egg and the fourteen worlds trembled. 59.
They trembled instantly as Mahāmārī summoned these women from all directions; bearing forms like millions [of beings], they,
who devour liquor and meat, arrived in the presence of Hara.
Then Śaṅkara spoke to them, as did Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord:
"The compassionate Blessed One, the protector of the world,
the illustrious destroyer of the sins of the wicked, himself forbids this."
Let not the wicked devour them, nor let they be devoured through association with the wicked;
let the devotees and even the families of devotees be protected by me in every way. Let them abandon that which leads to their destruction.
Thus addressed, those great plagues ceased out of fear of Hari;
they begged for his forgiveness and also requested service at the feet of Hari.
Hari said to them all: "Go everywhere upon the surface of the earth."
May I have a *tilaka* on my forehead and a garland on my neck;
having bestowed life, power, and consciousness upon those who possess these,
O Devajīva, restore the lives of those who promote the path of devotion.
Then he said to them, "O blessed ones, we are indeed not capable of bestowing consciousness and life in that manner; what shall we do here by your command?
Then Hari gave to them the *kalpalatā* plants known as *sujīvanī*.
Taking them all, they went and restored the bricks to life;
by the command of Śrī Hari, they revived all his devotees who had been afflicted by half-sins.
Then, indeed, joy was born once again upon the earth among human beings.
"Those who indeed possess a forehead mark (tilaka) and a necklace (kaṇṭhī) become possessed of life.
When this proclamation was made, even for those who were dead,
people would place a necklace upon the corpse and look for signs of life.
At that time, some indeed apply a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead of the corpse,
and they place a *tulasī* garland around its neck for the sake of restoring life.
Thus, in all regions, corpses were seen wearing such marks and garlands.
Still alive, they rose from the ground and gazed on in wonder.
At that time, those men became Vaiṣṇavas in the realm of Anjanābha, crying out:
"O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, O Viṣṇu, O warder-off of death! (73-74)
"Protect, protect us always in this manner, and pray thus toward Śrī Hari.
Then Śrī Śaṅkara spoke to all those auspicious Bhairavīs:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇakārpaṇyāya svāmine svāhā."
"Let the Bhavas also receive this mantra from me alone;
let them cause all living beings to hear it in their ears.
Having been addressed thus, all the Manovegas immediately took hold of him.
Having become mantras themselves, the Vaiṣṇavas bestowed mantras in every way;
having caused the Vaiṣṇavas to arise from the Kalpavallī trees,
they brought the world back to life and dispelled the grief of their devotees.
And they performed such a feat as has never occurred in the world nor will ever occur;
except for the Supreme Brahman, who else would be capable of doing such a thing?
For only he in whose hand the channels and the vital breaths reside can truly accomplish it. (2.91.80)
Festivities broke out throughout the entire universe, in every village and every home;
indeed, those who had died were restored to life by the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained new life, they all came for the sake of visiting the sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having seen the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī as well as Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa and the hosts of Mahāmārīs, the people were struck with wonder;
they continued to arrive even during the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra.
Having all achieved their purpose, the men and women, numbering in the tens of millions, then departed for their own abodes, having been restored to life by Hari.
Then those goddesses, Rādhikā and the Mahāmāris, [also attained their goal] through Mādhava.
They indeed chose the service of the feet of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then Hari granted them a dwelling in a forest in Saurāṣṭra, saying:
"May you all become jujube trees (*badarī*) of divine form. (85–86)
In the fields and even in the forests, they are indeed short-lived;
they possess two thorns and are beset by dark thorns.
In Saurāṣṭra, they are completely covered with the dust from my feet.
"May they remain for as long as an eon, receiving rewards equal to those who serve at my feet.
In the form of Rāma, I shall devour your fruits;
even the women of the Śabara caste here will give you fruits. (88–89)
Thus, having been made into devotees on the surface of the earth,
they instantly became small jujube trees (*badarī*) that live for a long time.
[This was done] for the sake of devotion and dharma among the sages, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and the others.
"Welcome," said Śrī Hari; both his mother and Lomaśa were also welcomed.
Hari provided them with lodging in his own golden palace, and the Lord gave food to the ascetics as well as sacrificial offerings and other provisions. (91–92)
Then they all rested there; at dawn, they bathed in the Aśvasaras lake and then all proceeded to behold the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa,
which was vast, of divine form, and radiant with the beloveds of Brahmā.
Where there is neither illusion nor even [worldly] existence, that which is auspicious and equal to the divine syllable (akṣara);
having performed the ritual at that sacred ford (tīrtha) and taken up the worship, and having met with the deities of the ford, you two assumed two forms. 94–95.
Then, having assumed the form of various holy places (tīrthas),
they all departed for the sacred forest of Śrī Badarī after receiving the command of Hari.
[They went to] Dharmatīrtha, Bhaktitīrtha, and likewise the supreme Naratīrtha.
The holy site of Nārāyaṇa and likewise the auspicious Ṛṣitīrtha—this Badarītīrtha came into being at Aśvasaras. Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, a great miracle occurred there. || 97-98 ||
"Bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and removing death through mere remembrance, the entire world was indeed made Vaiṣṇava for the sake of protecting the maiden.

Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, when many men were destroyed by great pestilences, a group of virtuous women, holy men, and brahmin sages went to Badarī; having informed the Lord, they caused Hari to come. Hari—
The ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of How He Revived the Dead Living Beings of the World," etc.,
[Chapter 91] from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga),
Chapter 92.
[Author: Chapter 93.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others.
The three lords of lords questioned Jñāna, who imparts the knowledge of Brahman:
"O elder brother, tell us that which produces devotion in living beings and lords;
who is the Self, what is liberation, and what is the cause of saṃsāra? (1–2)
What is saṃsāra, and likewise, what is Brahman that is higher than that?
You know everything, O Blessed Lord, the supreme secret;
you are Nārāyaṇa himself, the ancient, inconceivable Puruṣa.
"For there exists no other knower than you, O Supreme Person.
Having spoken thus, Aniruddha, Pradyumna,
and Saṃkarṣaṇa meditated within their respective hearts upon that certain Supreme Person, the Lord.
Then they beheld Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
who had abandoned His supreme causal form known as Vāsudeva—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, Lord Hari.
Resplendent, adorned with pearls, divine and wonderful;
with the Śrīvatsa on his chest, lovely, and graced by a halo of light;
bearing all weapons, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, endowed with wisdom. (7–8)
He is the refuge of eternal bliss, qualities, sovereignty, prosperity, power, and happiness;
he has two arms, and his lotus feet are served by millions of liberated souls;
laughing and causing others to laugh, he is as beautiful as ten million gods of love.
A youth, rich in divine splendor, enchanting to all creation,
radiant, endowed with a gentle disposition, and possessing long eyes;
the Supreme Lord seated upon his divine elephant-throne in the highest abode.

Then they beheld the imperishable abode of Brahman, which is beyond all limits; and they saw millions of charming beings known as the Imperishable (Akṣaras), who are liberated from all bonds. Then they quickly beheld Goloka, inhabited by cowherds.
Adorned by hosts of gopīs and presided over by Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa,
they then beheld that beautiful Vaikuṇṭha, which resembles the abode of Brahmā,
is the dwelling place of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, and is inhabited by ten million attendants. || 13-14 ||
Then they beheld the divine Mount Kailāsa, the abode of Sadāśiva and Śivā; and thereafter, they saw the radiant realm called Amṛta belonging to the Infinite One (Bhūman).
Then they beheld Viṣṇu’s Vaikuṇṭha and the Ocean of Milk.
Then, at Śvetadvīpa and Badarī, while Vāsudeva was their elder brother,
they beheld there, in each place, the various forms of Hari exactly as they were; indeed, within Vāsudeva they saw the entire illusory creation.
Then, at the end of that moment, the creation vanished and they beheld there a mass of light, as if the divine Saurāṣṭra were present exactly as it is.
There, the field named Aśvapaṭṭasara appeared, brilliantly radiant.
Therein lies the Kuṅkumavāpī lake as well as the illustrious hermitage of Lomaśa;
all of that is the supreme abode, divine and resplendent with pearls and other jewels,
pervaded by the beloveds of Brahmā and inhabited by the yoginīs of Sāṃkhya.
It is perfumed by the devotion of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
it is graced by the divine Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa;
and it is attended by Prabhā Pāravatī Lakṣmī and Māṇikī Rādhikā.
It is resorted to by Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Haṃsā, Vijayā, and Lalitā;
it is perfumed by one hundred and twelve beloved ones; it is presided over by infinite millions of lotuses and possesses divine splendor. (22–23)
They beheld palaces adorned with divine jars;
they beheld this great palace of Anādi-Kṛṣṇa,
the supreme, divine support of His own self, wherein the Blessed Lord Himself resides.
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Nārāyaṇa, possesses the brilliance of a youth.
He is the Supreme Person among all Nārāyaṇas, the glorious Supreme Lord; and he is the Supreme among all lords, the manifest Śrī Puruṣottama. (25–26)

O Rādhā, they beheld that Hari, who is the cause of the multitude of incarnations and the one who takes those incarnations; who is the Kṛṣṇa among all Kṛṣṇas, and the Lord who creates the manifestations of the divine arrays. They saw Him within Vāsudeva, within Hari.
They beheld Hari, shining brilliantly upon a stainless throne of gold and ivory;
having seen Him as Vāsudeva—within whom all this exists and from whom this entire world is non-different—they attained supreme bliss. (28–29)
Then, in another moment, they saw everything dissolved before them;
they beheld Vāsudeva and their minds became tranquil. Having thus caused them to attain direct realization, he then— || 2.92.30 ||
Vāsudeva spoke this secret, eternal knowledge,
which neither the gods nor the twice-born sacrificers fully comprehend.
Having known that Supreme Lord, the great seers have become one with Brahman.
Even those who formerly dwelt in the abode of Brahmā do not enter into saṃsāra.
This Self is possessed of bliss, translucent, pure, subtle, and eternal;
yet within it resides that which is the innermost of all, higher than the highest.
He is the Inner Controller, He is the Puruṣa, He is Prāṇa, known as the Lord.
From Him the universe is born; into His abode it dissolves.
Grasping Māyā through His reflection, He creates diverse bodies.
For him there is no bondage, nor its absence, nor is he dependent upon the qualities of *māyā*.
(35) Just as the identity of light and darkness is not possible, so too there can be no relation of oneness between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). (36)
Just as in the world shadow and sunlight are mutually distinct,
so too, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the phenomenal world and the Puruṣa are separate.
The Self is by its very nature pure, eternally awakened, and liberated.
The Supreme Self is exceedingly pure, omniscient, and well-established in itself.
The Self and its Inner Self are both free from modification, beyond dualities, perpetually immersed in bliss, united, and endowed with divine, auspicious qualities. (38–39)
The two are eternally united, friends, witnesses, and controllers.
The Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) enjoys the fruit of the action performed by the self, yet remains devoid of personal experience.
Just as a supervisor bestows the reward upon the master at the proper time, [so does He bestow the fruit upon the individual soul].
"I am the doer, happy, miserable, thin, and fat"—
through such egoism (ahaṅkāra), the individual becomes the enjoyer of these states due to the power of ignorance.
Through ignorance and through misapprehension, it becomes joined with the mind.
Having repeatedly joined the unstable mind with the association of the qualities of nature (guṇas), it indeed makes itself rich in its own dharmas;
through the lack of discrimination caused by egoism, it conceives the thought, "I am the doer."
The defiled person indeed forgets their own self, which is the imperishable Brahman.
One who perceives the self in that which is not the self becomes a treasury for all suffering;
furthermore, passion, hatred, and the like, born of delusion, take hold therein.
Just as one experiences merit and demerit born of one's own nature through those defects, so too,
upon the destruction of delusion and the disappearance of defects, he remains alone, free from the manifold world (niṣprapañcaka), dedicated to the Divine Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

Through union with *saccidānanda*, he always possesses *saccidānanda*, just as the Supreme Lord does by the grace of the Supreme Lord. Indeed, just as the sky is never soiled by contact with smoke, [so too is he]. 47–48.
Likewise, untainted by mental defects and designated as the Immutable (akṣara),
free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), pure, and stainless in nature, it shines forth. Then,
having abandoned the object of knowledge, as well as the act of knowing and even the latent impression of knowing—

Having abandoned [all else], one should become self-luminous, just like Nārāyaṇa himself. Therefore, the Self—which is imperishable, pure, and eternal—should be resorted to by those seeking liberation; it must be meditated upon, reflected upon, and heard.
When the Supreme Brahman shines within the self at all times and in all places,
then it manifests of its own accord to the faithful devotee.
When one perceives the entire multitude of effects as being within oneself alone—
Then Hari attains his own self within the multitude of effects;
when, established in meditative absorption (samādhi), he perceives nothing as distinct [from himself],
the self becomes one with the Supreme and is then liberated.
When his mental states dissolve into the supreme Hari, then,
having become immortal, he attains liberation to the abode of Hari.
When everything that appears as separate is perceived within Him alone—
Then, furthermore, there is the expansion of his fitness for Brahman.
When he perceives himself as the Self alone, then occurs his attainment of Brahman; then, moreover, there is the cessation of the illusory.
When the knowledge of the Self, the individual soul, and Brahman— which is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease— arises, then this [Self] is eternal and auspicious.
Just as rivers and streams attain oneness with the ocean, so too [do all things].
The self should attain oneness with the Imperishable (akṣara), and that [Imperishable] with the Supreme Brahman.
Then there would be the direct perception of the Unmanifest (aparokṣa). That non-duality of distinction—that is, non-dualistic difference—is well-established by the Śrutis. (2.92.59–60)
That consciousness, known as upāsanā, bestows the supreme good;
where it arises, there is neither the phenomenal world (prapañca) nor latent impressions (vāsanā).
Where ignorance persists, there is delusion and latent impressions.
Therefore, having abandoned delusion and having burned away all latent impressions (vāsanās),

the wise one, having become Brahman— which is the perfect transcendence of all scriptural learning— should cross over. Indeed, having firmly accomplished higher knowledge (vijñāna), devotion to the Blessed One, and yoga, he shall cross.
Having meditated upon the form of Brahman, one shall attain the supreme Hari.
This unmanifest Self is I; this is the abode of Brahman for the devotee.
He is the supreme Lord within Brahman; He is the Imperishable Puruṣottama.
That non-duality characterized by distinction is Hari, the Supreme Lord (65).
He is all-taste, all-form, all-fragrance, ageless, and immortal;
his hands and feet are everywhere, he is the self of all, and his faces are on every side (66).
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is also the inner controller;
though without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper, abiding within all.
Though without eyes, he sees; and though devoid of ears, he hears.
I know this ancient Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord,
who dwells in the highest abode— the auspicious son of Kambharāśrī,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, and that very Naranārāyaṇa. (68–69)
The sages who possess His grace behold Him as Vāsudeva, Hara, Viṣṇu, Hari, and the one dwelling within all;
the ascetics do not see Him at all, for only His servants behold Him.

When those who perceive subtle principles and the like behold the Lord—who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and whose nature is stainless—He is known as the Imperishable (akṣara), which consists of His sovereignty.
That which even the gods do not know, being deluded by His Māyā, [is revealed to them]. || 71–72 ||
What need is there to speak of the world of living beings? Listen to me, O brothers!
Aniruddha, in you resides the supreme sovereignty over all creation;
it is born from but a ten-millionth part of that Imperishable Brahman.
O Pradyumna!
That sovereignty over nourishment which resides in you should be understood as arising from but a ten-millionth part of the Imperishable Brahman itself.
O Saṃkarṣaṇa! That sovereignty over withdrawal which resides in you likewise [arises from that same source]. || 74–75 ||
That which is to be understood as arising from a ten-millionth part of the Imperishable Brahman resides within me— namely,
that sovereignty, dwelling, and divine play. Indeed,
that which was attained by Hari is to be understood as belonging to the Imperishable alone.
In that syllable (akṣara) whose nature is non-duality, there is no qualification of "I.
Indeed, this non-dual distinction exists as the imperishable Brahman;
that alone is the one imperishable, and there is nothing else equal to it designated as the Imperishable.
Wherein the qualified, the Imperishable (akṣara), is subsumed within the non-dual Śrī Paramātman—
that Supreme Lord is Viśeṣādvaitādvaita.
He is beyond Māyā, he is the Imperishable, and the Supreme Lord is even beyond that.
Having abandoned *māyā*, living beings indeed go to that imperishable state.
Those practitioners of devotion who have entered it and transcended all *māyā*, which takes the form of the entire universe, attain union (*sāyujya*) with Him. (2.92.80–81)
They attain the abode of the Imperishable; there lies my supreme station.
For them, there is no return, whether by the power of the Lord or through *māyā*. This is by the grace of that Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, Hari, the Sovereign.
This is the instruction of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa:

O Brahman-woman, this should be given to His sons, disciples, and holy men; it must not be given to others who are unworthy vessels, for that would be as unwholesome as medicine to one who cannot digest it. 83–84.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this knowledge has been revealed to you by me,
which was previously proclaimed by Vāsudeva to his younger brothers.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of That State through the Knowledge of the Supreme Brahman and the Distinct Non-dual Advaita," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna, concerning Vāsudeva’s teaching in the Gītā.
← Chapter 92 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 93 [[Author: → Chapter 94
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Vāsudeva spoke to Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others concerning the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Time, known as the power of elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka-śakti*), is the son who effects dissolution;
he takes away everything, and it is said that he also removes the imbalance of *māyā*.
Furthermore, at that time, this agitator of *māyā* causes agitation.
Through union with the Great Puruṣa, Māyā brings forth this uneven state. Māyā, Kāla, and Puruṣa are the powers of the Supreme Lord;
from them all this has arisen, and therefore they are of the nature of Brahman.

That which is born from Him is the form of Brahman, and indeed the entire universe is His body. For in all those places, there truly exist the hands, feet, eyes, ears, mouth, head, and navel of this imperishable Brahman. (5)
Therefore, that very Imperishable remains, pervading everything.
It manifests as the qualities of all the senses, yet is endowed with divine senses;
it is the support of all, the great bliss, and its sphere transcends the means of valid cognition.
Devoid of all comparisons, the abode of all, the supreme nectar;
undivided yet existing in diverse forms, eternal, constant, and imperishable;
without qualities, the supreme light, free from conceptual construction, and limitless.
That Self of all beings stands both outside and inside;
there dwells the omnipresent, peaceful Supreme Lord, whose very nature is that [Self]. By Him this entire universe is pervaded, permeated by the liberated souls who have realized the Lord.
By His will, I too was born as Vāsudeva, the Supreme Lord. From me arose you three alone—the Mūrtis—who are the very essence of the Japa-mantra:
first Bhūman, then Mahāviṣṇu, and then Virāṭ, the creator of the universe.
Then the great sages and the gods [praised] the world, both the stationary and the moving.
The Mother of the World is Mahāmāyā, whose fundamental form is Will (icchā).
She is called Amṛtā, the creator of defects, as well as Pāragā and Pūrikā. || 12–13 ||
That which is accepted as *prakṛti* gives birth to the entire universe, beginning with the *mahat* and ending with the *viśeṣas*; she is like a beloved, enchanting, and dear wife.
But the *puruṣa*, having fallen into delusion (*moha*), is the self (*ātman*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*).
Those who practice friendship based on egoism have the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) as their closest kinsman;
having placed their trust in the mind, they are destined for rebirth. For one who has no desire for primordial nature (prakṛti), delusion does not exist.
There is truly no friendship in the ego, nor kinship in the Great Principle (mahat-tattva);
there is no trust in the mind that conduces to the attainment of liberation.
Indeed, these [faculties] exist as benefactors only when they remain favorable to him.
Māyā, time, and the Puruṣa—these too are auxiliaries;
they lead one to the divine Imperishable for whom the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who dwells in the supreme abode, is the desired goal. (18–19)
Through union with that [Self], however, there arise for the devotee divine forms, as well as knowledge, will, and action, and the mental states of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
the sheaths of merit and demerit, and the mind, ego, intellect, and feeling. (2.93.20)
Beings of divine form are born, as well as the qualities of *sattva* and the impurity of *rajas*.
The subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the group of sense organs, the six sheaths, and the five gross elements—
all these modifications arise through divine conjunction.
Their actions, their worldly dealings, their exertions, and even their conduct—
all this becomes divine, bestowing liberation, and is of the nature of the attributeless Brahman.
Time has no power here, for it is time that creates and destroys living beings.
All are subject to Time, yet Time itself is indeed subject to the devotee.
In the devotee resides the Imperishable, and in the Imperishable resides the Omniscient One, the Beloved of the Lord.
There is nothing higher than the Omniscient One; by worshipping Him, one is liberated.
In this world, there is nothing— whether stationary or moving— that is eternal,
except for the glorious Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Puruṣottama.
Neither by various austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can [this state be attained].
Indeed, it is possible for embodied beings to know Śrī Hari—who dwells within all beings and everywhere—without supreme devotion to that which is beyond;
yet the worlds, though they are the lords of others, do not know Him, the witness of all. (27–28)
In whom all this is contained, and who abides within all— He is the Sustainer and the Ordainer, Time, Fire, and the one whose face is turned in every direction.
Sages who are characterized by passion, as well as the ancestors and the gods, do not behold Him.
Brahmā, Virāṭ, Bhūmā, and whoever else is even beyond them—somehow I know that Lord to be inferior in meaning to Him;
for He is neither the end nor the imperishable, so what need is there to speak of others? (2.93.30–31)
Māṇikī herself does not know Him at all while He is constantly pervading her body;
what then can be said regarding her knowledge of the other Śaktis?
The Vedas eternally proclaim that one Supreme Lord.
Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas sacrifice with various sacrifices;
those established in yoga meditate and strive to behold the further shore. Yet, without his grace, they do not see it at all, even through the highest austerity.
He alone is the enjoyer of all oblations and the bestower of their fruits;
he is the embodiment of all deities, the soul of all, and the abode of all that is auspicious.
Only the wise and the virtuous behold him through his grace.
He is present for those who constantly worship Him;
He grants them that abode, the state of supreme bliss. Whether they be high, middling, or even low-born from sinful wombs, [they all attain it]. (36–37)
Through devotion to Him they are liberated when they are united with Him;
His devotees do not perish, nor indeed do they go to a low state.
Standing on His path, the virtuous truly bring about their union with Him.
The fool who indeed censures them censures Bālakṛṣṇa;
he who worships them with devotion worships that Lord.
[He offers] a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, clothing, and a liquid. (2.93.40)
He who gives to Him with devotion shall always be dear to Him. Indeed,
for the sake of destroying the suffering of His circle of devotees from the very beginning,
He manifested His power by means of Rādhikā at His left side.
Requested by her, Kṛṣṇa indeed came to abide in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman).
He resided in Goloka for the purpose of accepting her devotion;
previously, he had done so solely for the sake of bestowing prosperity upon the multitude of his devotees.
He manifested his power, Śrī Lakṣmī, from his own chest;
thus entreated, Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha indeed became manifest.
For the sake of the prior arrangement, he remembered the creation just as before.

He manifested from his loins the supreme Prakṛti, who is Śakti. Requested by her, that Blessed One, Vāsudeva, became "I" within the unmanifest, which rests upon the Imperishable (akṣara), bestowing consciousness upon Prakṛti.
Requested by him, the Great Emanation— which possesses the nature of birth, stability, and dissolution—
arose from his own body as you three alone:
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṃkarṣaṇa, who possess exceeding majesty.
The glorious Supreme Lords, who manifest and perform the functions of the *guṇas*, appeared. Requested by Him, that Principle (*nyāya*), which is the Abundance (*bhūman*) arising from His heart,
shines forth as the ordainer of justice for the Lords in the immortal abode.
Requested by him, that modification of Māyā which is the cause of the sprout was released from his frown; from that, this Puruṣa arose.
At that time, this Puruṣa of Prakṛti sported with Māyā.
And from that [Prakṛti] was born the pair known as the Great Intellect (Mahat);
and the Spirit (Puruṣa) is its beloved, the one who delights in union.
Both Pradhāna and Puruṣa are eternally celebrated as the body of Hari.
From those two, that which is called the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) arose as the ultimate reality (tattva).
He indeed became Mahāviṣṇu, attended by Śrī, for the purpose of creation. From him was born the one known as Virāṭ, and from him the gods, Hara and the others.
Through the lineage of the Pitṛs, Hari indeed caused the Vedas to reach them.
He, the Supreme Lord, shining in the highest abode,
assumed the form of Nara-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of performing austerities.
For the sake of the peace of the world of living beings, for the destruction of suffering,
and for the pacification of the demons, the Lord of Lakṣmī shines in the white abode within the Milky Ocean as a mere fraction of His essence.
He is the supreme teacher of yogis, of the virtuous, and of noble women;
he is the protector of the righteous and the slayer of those who hate the Vedas.
He is the destroyer of the illusions of the deceitful; he is the Supreme Lord. (57–58)
When that supreme power, Māyā, is celebrated as *vidyā* (knowledge), it is indeed considered the supreme power;
when that same Māyā is *avidyā* (ignorance), it is considered the inferior power.
And Mādhava, the bestower of liberation, destroys that Māyā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the initiator and the withdrawer of all powers;
he is the support of them all and the storehouse of immortality.
That which is the single power of Keśava is the imperishable Brahman and his abode.
There is another vast power which indeed sustains the universe;
that other power of His is precisely His state as the Inner Controller (antaryāmitā).
Through the two wings of knowledge and devotion, one propitiates the Lord.
Having indeed transcended all sin, he goes to the abode of Hari;
having transcended all powers (śaktis), he who performs my desired service approaches me.
Through the worship of me, some men even become Nārāyaṇas.
Accumulated through my own states of being, they deliver embodied beings;
by the power of His grace, some become lords of the worlds, such as Viṣṇus, while others become Haras and the like, and still others become lords such as Brahmā. (65)
In all of them, the Blessed One is the impeller and the one who causes cessation.
He is this very Brahmā of those who know Brahman, the self-existent one whose face is turned in every direction;
he is this ancient, imperishable Lord Hari, the master of illusion.
For yogis, he is Śambhu; for women, the goddess Girīndrajā;
among the Ādityas, he is Viṣṇu; and among the Vasus, he is Pāvaka.
Among the Rudras, he is Śaṅkara; and among those who fly, he is Garuḍa.
Airāvata is the king of elephants; this Rāma is the foremost among those who bear weapons.
Among the sages, he is Vasiṣṭha; among the gods, he is Śatakratu (Indra).
Among artisans, he is Viśvakarman; among the enemies of the gods, he is Prahlāda. (2.93.70)
Among the sages, he is Vyāsa; among the hosts, he is Vināyaka.
Among heroes, he is Vīrabhadra; among the perfected ones (siddhas), he is the sage Kapila.
Among mountains, he is Meru; and among the lunar mansions, he is the Moon.
Among weapons he is the thunderbolt, and among vows he is truth itself.
Among serpents he is Ananta, and among generals he is the son of Agni (Kārttikeya).
Among stages of life he is the householder, and among the ages he is the Kṛta Yuga, truth itself.
Kubera is the foremost of all yakṣas, Nirṛti of all rākṣasas;
Dakṣa is the chief of the Prajāpatis, and the lion is the king of beasts.
Among the Vedas, he is the Sāmaveda, and among those to be chanted, he is this very syllable Om (praṇava).
Of hymns, he is the Puruṣasūkta; for among those possessed of wisdom, he is Manu. Of sciences, he is the science of the Self; for among principles, he is consciousness.
Among goals, he is liberation alone; but among bonds, he is latent impression (vāsanā).
Among the twice-born he is the one devoted to his wife; among virtuous women, he is the virtuous Kambharā;
and among all prosperities, that Puruṣottama has the form of Mahālakṣmī.
One should indeed contemplate Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in this way in each respective instance.
Therefore, the Lord Nārāyaṇa bears fruit there in every respect.
O younger brothers, He exists in all worlds in the form of an image;
likewise, the venerable Supreme Lord exists in the form of the Preceptor.
He alone is the one of virtuous form, he is the divine body, he is the purifier; Mādhava is indeed the form of the father and also the form of the mother.
He alone is the best of men, the form of the wife and the form of the husband.
For these eight are gurus, saviors, and perfected by divine nature.
Indeed, no recompense whatsoever exists for them;
one should always do what is pleasing to them through action, mind, and speech. 81–82.
These very beings are essentially the beginningless, glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
those who worship them with this realization attain the supreme goal.
He is the manifest Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Śrī Puruṣottama.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the teacher of all incarnations;
he is the Blessed One, beyond the imperishable (Akṣara), the inner controller, and the Lord of lords.
Having descended, he dwells in the house of Śrī Kambharā in the form of a child.
That illustrious Gopālabāla resides in a golden palace at Akṣarakṣetra, near the hermitage of Lomaśa, at Aśvasārasa,
at the holy site known as Kuṅkumavāpī, and upon the divine ground.
He exists in human form, served by those dear to Brahmā.
Out of compassion, for the sake of liberating living beings and for the protection of the universe, Mādhava—who is beyond the reach of mortals—exists in human form. (87–88)
"By good fortune, he who is visible to you— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa— who are the very forms of his portions, has become the object of our sight as well.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Vāsudeva paused for a moment.
"Even those three desired that divine, human, and infallible [state].

(2.93.90) Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Means of Attainment and His Glorious Manifestations," in the *Vāsudeva-gītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 93. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 94 [Author:
Chapter 95 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; awakened by the words of Vāsudeva, those three, possessing knowledge of His majesty, beheld that which was born before the cosmic egg.
"In previous festivals, we went for the sake of seeing Kṛṣṇa. [1]
Now, desiring to see Him, we who are endowed with the knowledge of His majesty wish to go together with you, O You who have assumed the form of a child,
in order to behold His unique divine play, being delighted by the realization of that very truth.
Thus addressed by his brothers, the Lord Hari Vāsudeva went from that world into the interior of the cosmic egg along with his brothers.
From the world of Vāsudeva, atoms resembling those of the Vairāja world [emerged].
Having become so, they entered the worlds of Virāja, and from there as well;
having become even more minute, they then entered the world of Satya.
Having become even more subtle than that, they reached the celestial realm (div).
Becoming even more minute than that, they entered the world of men;
for previously, in their own abode, they had resided as the form of Śrī Vāsudeva.
Now, in this human realm, they occupy a portion equal to the tip of a single hair of that [divine] body.
Even a ten-millionth part of that [splendor] is assumed by those who have taken human bodies;
they are four in number, known as the Vyūhas, radiant with brilliance,
and having become like children, they abide in the sky above the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Extremely radiant celestial swans arrived in a most brilliant celestial chariot;
there, Vāsudeva appeared four-armed and exceedingly resplendent,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as his weapons, and shining with a crown.
The other three were two-armed, bearing the discus and mace as weapons;
they were youthful, of divine form, auspicious, and equal to Vāsudeva.
Resplendent like many suns, they were adorned with golden earrings. || 11–12 ||
Wearing forest garlands, the Kaustubha jewel, and other ornaments, they are resplendent with crowns;
possessing divine bodies, they shine with the power and sovereignty of divine siddhis. [13] And the brilliant splendors of thousands of millions of gods—

Those upon whose hairs such [jewels] were found appeared in their celestial chariots situated in the sky; it became as if evening had turned into midday. All the subjects of Saurāṣṭra, having beheld them even during the day, [were amazed]. (14–15)
The Lord himself reflected upon those exceedingly great splendors:
"Is he traveling through the sky to another place in his celestial chariot for the sake of recreation?
Or perhaps the gods are arriving repeatedly to worship Hari? (16)
Thinking that these [others] might likewise arrive there, they waited.
Then, at that time, the people of Kuṅkumavāpī who were devotees of the Lord went quickly from their own homes for the sake of a vision [of Him]. (17–18)
Then, indeed, a beautiful celestial chariot descended from the sky onto the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Those four Kṛṣṇas, having formed a military array, emerged from the chariot.
Their forms were like an ocean of nectar pervaded by a splendor as radiant as ten million moons.
Having walked slowly on foot to the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, those beings in human form bathed and proceeded to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
The sage performed the rites of hospitality, including a welcome and honors;
he offered the *madhuparka* and worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Having understood the reality of the cosmic array through his divine vision, he prostrated himself like a staff.
Then the sage Lomaśa performed the *ārārtrika* rite for the military arrays;
thereafter, the sages dear to Brahmā performed the rites of salutation. Having risen and bowed to those sages, they went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa informed his parents of the arrival of the Vyūhas;
full of enthusiasm, the parents quickly went there for the sake of honor.
Upon hearing this, the other gods, the sages, and even the lords [also arrived].

Holy fords, collections of essential truths, virtuous men, saintly women, and great sages—those who possess forms of divine manifestation—approached him there for the sake of honoring him, repeatedly [shouting] cries of "Victory! along with unbroken grains, sandalwood, and flowers. (26–27)
Having been nourished and honored, they went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa;
then Bālakṛṣṇa assumed his own form for the sake of that [attainment].
Indeed, the multitudes of Vāsudevas attain dissolution into his very form.
The lords of Koṭi, Goloka, and Vaikuṇṭha attain dissolution [into Him].
He assumed such a divine form residing in the supreme abode;
Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, sat upon a divine elephant-throne.
Attended by hosts of liberated souls numbering in the millions, He shone with His form established therein.
At that moment, having abandoned their various manifestations, the eyes of others instantly turned toward Śrī Hari;
indeed, overcome by His splendor, they could not function elsewhere.
Then the gods and others, their lotus-eyes overcome with dejection, departed from there;
they all went to their respective abodes. Thereafter, Hari likewise [dismissed] the battle arrays, and his parents affectionately welcomed him on the courtyard of their palace.
Accompanied by their Lord, they entered the palace of Bālakṛṣṇa;
they bowed down to their beloved one seated upon the elephant-throne, and Nemi paid homage as well.
Prostrating themselves on the ground like a staff, they joyfully performed his worship.
Vāsudeva placed a divine crown upon the head of Hari;
Saṃkarṣaṇa applied sandalwood paste mixed with the essence of oil to his forehead;
and Pradyumna offered him a tilaka-mark made of the finest fragrance.
Vāsudeva applied beautiful collyrium and cosmetic dyes to her eyes;
he gave her earrings, clusters of flowers, ear-ornaments, and crest-jewels for her ears;
and he placed auspicious golden necklaces upon her neck.
Saṃkarṣaṇa gave him beautiful necklaces adorned with diamonds, rubies, pearls, and the Kaustubha gem, as well as bracelets, chains, signets, rings,
and wrist-ornaments. (38–39)
Aniruddha gave him a girdle with beautiful golden bells,
two divine and soft sandals, two chowries, and a parasol;
he also gave him a golden staff inlaid with jewels and a hand-glove for his hand.
Saṃkarṣaṇa gave a fragrant bundle of flowers, leaves, and other offerings;
Pradyumna presented a beautiful golden vessel filled with sweet food like nectar, and stocked with fruits, seeds, and other delicacies.
Aniruddha gave him a drink of nectar as well as betel-leaf;
then the Lord Vāsudeva himself performed the *ārārtrika* rite.
The lords then performed circumambulation, prostrations, and the *daṇḍavat* salutation.
The supreme lords offered handfuls of flowers and praised Kṛṣṇa:
"You are the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama; you shine in the supreme abode as the two-armed one served by the imperishable. (44–45)
The Supreme Lord is served by those liberated from that [state] and by those liberated by you;
you are the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the transcendent Blessed Lord and Master.
From you the liberated ones shine forth and dissolve into your form.
And they stand in your presence, overflowing with bliss for you;
innumerable are those in the state of Brahman, beloved of Brahman, and equal to you. They are indeed your powers of sovereignty, born from your very form.
Those liberated ones who possess the form of Brahman perform service unto you;
from you we have arisen as the Vyūhas, the Avatāras, and likewise the Īśvaras. (4.9) So too have the Īśvarīs, Māyā, the Puruṣas, Kāla, and the years.
The Vairājas, the Vaiṣṇavas, as well as the Brāhmaṇas and the Śāmbhavas—
these great seers (maharṣis) have indeed arisen from the very form of your body;
so too have the ancestors, the sages, the Siddhas, the virtuous ones, and those disciplined in yoga.
The truthful ones, the virtuous ones, those who have taken vows of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and beloved wives;
likewise, the devoted wife and the husband devoted to his wife, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; the ancestors, those clad in celestial garments, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
In Pātāla dwell the subterranean chambers, and in the milk-ocean resides Śeṣa, who is Nārāyaṇa.
[His consorts are] Śrī, Līlā, Bhū, Satī, Padmā, Gaṅgā, Prabhā, Sarasvatī, Māṇikyā, Saguṇā, Premā, Pāravatī, and Mañjulā. (53–54)
Vibhūti, Rādhikā, Sītā, Amṛtā, Santoṣikā,
Ramā, Haṃsā, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, Dayā, Jayā, Tulasī,
Haimī, Śāntā, and Sāvitrī— these are the Vṛndās, who are indeed the Śaktis.
Campā, Lalitā, Kastūrī, Ojasvatī, and others likewise;
Kapila, Datta, Īśāna, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Hari, Haṃsa, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, and Jiṣṇu as well. ||56–57||
Hari, Pṛthu, Gopāla, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Īśitā, Rāma, Paraśurāma, Bala, the blessed Śuka,
Vallabha, Hemanta, and Devaprakāśa— these are they.
The sacrifice and the yogas of the Kumāras are indeed manifestations of your own portions.

The principles (tattvas), the consciousness of the principles, the qualities, powers, and flavors—all these, O Blessed One, are your portions, in which you are likewise woven as the warp. (2.94.59–60)
Everything is woven within you; you alone are the supreme Lord.
Eager to behold your child for the sake of obtaining a vision of you, we have now attained that vision, O Lord, and our purpose is fulfilled.
Having spoken thus, they bowed down, offered a handful of flowers, and remained there at ease.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa said to Rādhā to request a boon:
"O Vāsudeva, may I always have my dwelling at your feet. (62–63)
"O Lord, O ocean of compassion, grant [this] and completely fulfill my desire for the manifestation.
"So be it," the Lord replied, and he created two bodies for them;
one was fit to dwell in Kuṅkumavāpī, while the other resided at Vyūhatīrtha.
Then, by the command of Śrī Hari, that second primary form and the fourfold manifestation (vyūha) departed for the White Island;
from there they went to Satyaloka, and from there to the unmanifest abode (avyākṛtadhāma).
Thus, O Rādhikā, those great lords known as the Vyūhas— Vāsudeva and the others—
who are the masters and creators of the individual souls, always took up residence before Śrī Hari at the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake.

On the bank of the waters of that sacred ford, a most auspicious and supreme temple named Vāsudevālaya was constructed by Viśvakarman; and there, by the command of Śrī Hari, those brothers shine resplendent. (68–69)
They are absorbed in Svayaṃprakāśa, the crown disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; they are known as the Vyūhas,
the four Lords whose forms consist of the embodiment of consciousness.
That very manifestation of the Vyūha is the self-luminous Lord;
Vāsudeva himself abides, endowed with four qualities. And men [perceive] him as divine, four-armed, and self-luminous. 71–72.
Those who worship Him shall obtain the merit resulting from the *vyūha*—the fruit born of that manifestation.
Listen, O Rādhikā, to Vāsudeva, who is self-luminous;
His beloveds always go forth in the early morning for the purpose of worshipping Him.
Lakṣmī is indeed the wife of Vāsudeva, while she who is Hariṇī is [the wife] of Saṃkarṣaṇa; that great chaste woman Sunandā is the wife of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and Dhī, the nourisher of all, is the beloved of Pradyumna.
O Rādhikā, these four women of Aniruddha, who possess excellent character,
always travel by means of a celestial chariot of the fourfold splendors;
behold, this is now the Brahma-hour, the time for their departure.
At that moment, their celestial chariot emerged before Rādhikā.
Upon seeing them, Rādhikā descended from the chariot;
she then rose up, bowed, and embraced them with deep emotion.
With a serene mind, she offered a welcome, as well as the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and a seat;
she gave her worship, performed the rites of hospitality, and made it complete.
She also inquired after their welfare, and likewise that of Rādhikā.
Rādhā said: "O beloved ones, where will your departure take place tomorrow morning?
They replied: "Our Lord, the Blessed One known by the name Svayaṃprakāśa, has manifested as an incarnation from his own expansion (vyūha) and resides at Aśvasarovara."
The great lord is the disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, four portions of our husbands reside within him.
Abiding in human form, he is endowed with the vow of a youth-brahmin (brahmacarya).
"The prince indeed comes here constantly for the sake of worshipping him.
Therefore, O Rādhā, being remembered by you, we have come here joyfully.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, they, full of eagerness, began to worship her.
They indeed gave all the articles of adornment to Rādhikā;
then, having received her command, they quickly departed for the Aśvasarovara lake.
These were Hariṇī, Sunandā, Dhī, and Suśīlā.
Having fully honored her husband with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sandalwood paste,
and having drunk the water from his big toe, she should then feed him; thereafter,
having performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) and other rites, she should obtain his favor.
Having massaged her feet, they then bowed to the glory of Śrī Kaṃbharā,
and after joining together and offering worship, they received her auspicious words;
thereafter, they proceeded toward Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

Having worshipped the Lord of lords, having bowed and praised him again and again, and having performed the *ārārtika* ceremony for Hari, they stood and meditated upon Hari for a moment. The Lord said, "I am pleased; choose a boon that you desire. (2.94.90)
Then we said to them, "In such a way that our residence may be here,
and our devotion to our husbands (*pātivratya*) may be protected while serving both [of you],
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, always grant the fulfillment of our desire. (91)
"So be it," Hari replied, and having assumed two forms,
he established four forms in the shape of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) at Vyūhatīrtha.
The Lord then caused them to dwell within images in a temple.
Just as the service of the self-luminous [Lord] occurs through divine forms,
so indeed was it performed by them when Nārāyaṇa had acted;
then, having received his command, they assumed other primary forms.
They departed for the unmanifest abode (*avyākṛta-dhāma*) inhabited by Vāsudeva and the others.
Thus, O Rādhikā,
the wondrous sovereignty of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has come before your eyes as something difficult to comprehend.

What can I say of the majesty of that Supreme Lord, by the chanting of whose qualities both worldly enjoyment and liberation are eternally secured? Therein, sovereign powers abide perpetually through divine forms. //97//
Where even the lords of lords dwell with divine forms;
where the Hari incarnations dwell with divine forms;
and where all the lords of creation and the gods dwell with divine forms. (98–99)
In that place where the beloved of Brahmā dwell, liberated and possessing divine forms,
for the sake of attaining the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—
the majesty of that sacred field cannot be described.
On the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha, that Vyūhatīrtha became a lake.
And on the second day of Āṣāḍha, the Śrīcatuṣṭayatīrtha and the purifying Svayaṃprakāśatīrtha likewise came into being at that time.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Arrival at the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha by the Fourfold Vyūha and the Fourfold Śrī, and the Description of Svayaṃprakāśa Tīrtha, Vyūhacatuṣṭaya Tīrtha, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 95 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) [Chapter 95]
[Author: Chapter 96.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to another marvel of Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul.
And by means of the performance of the Ekādaśī vow on the full moon day of Rādha, the region was well protected.
Indeed, while Dakṣiṇa Khaṇḍa, known as Uṣṇālaya,
was present there in the battle at Astrālaya, [it was protected] from the terrible oceanic winds.
When the calamity arose, the land was buried in the midst by sands,
while its periphery was overwhelmed and devastated by the waters of the ocean;
it was covered over and destroyed by the rains in the month of Bhādrapada.

Then, protected by his own Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of his devotees— listen to this most meritorious narrative. In the eastern Mahākhaṇḍa of Uṣṇālaya, there was a great sage named Pūrvaṅga.
In former times, Agastya traveled through the sky to purify that land,
traversing many regions even after bypassing the ocean.
He proceeded to that great continent, to the mountain named Hemaśāla.
Then he went from the sky to Bālācala,
Rāvāsanādri, Dārāliṅgagiri, Maṣīgrīvādri, Bhekadānaka,
as well as the mountain Śālavīnagiri, and then to Grāmācala. (7–8)
Having likewise gone to Mount Ācāla, Mount Divādi, and Mount Cāṭa, he then arrived at Hemaśālaka.
There he reached its auspicious valley, which was covered with trees, creepers, and grasses in full leaf.
He dwelt there for a year, observing the land abounding in fruits and flowers due to the excellent rains.
Day and night he remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, reciting:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."

Dwelling on the Hemashalacala mountain, he constantly recites the mantra; Lopamudra, devoted to her husband, likewise recites that very mantra with him. Together with her, the sage then constantly went to make the rivers sacred.
He constantly traveled through the air to bathe on the banks of various rivers:
repeatedly in the Murā, Turu, and Aita rivers, as well as in the Gośaṅku and Bālā rivers. (13–14)
He bathed in the Marcāśanā river and also in Lake Māka;
he bathed in Bālāsarovara, in Māṅgisarasa, and in the waters of Śvānikā.
He bathed in Kuvana lake and also in Lābharucisarasa.
He bathed in the Jhinku River, the Rinku River, and likewise in the Phinku River;
he bathed in the Uttuṅga lake and likewise in the Āra lake;
he bathed in the Turū lake and also in the lake named Grāgi.

The sage bathed in the Maurī river, the Turā river, and the Bhurā river; likewise, he bathed in the Kavindumā river and at the Gaurānarasara lake. He also bathed in the Kāruliṅgī, the Dāruliṅgī, and the Cāruliṅgī rivers.
Then, at the Kuvīlpīṇā, the Laviṅgā, and likewise the Pāvanā;
at the Mīcalā and the Philañcā, the sage Agastya bathed;
as did he at the Ghelī, the Helī, and the river Vitūrī.
In the Phījarā river, the Cāpagā, and even in the mountain cascades,
the virtuous Lopāmudrā performed worship and the adoration of their respective deities.
The lakes and rivers as well paid homage to Agastya.
Then, in these various regions— on the banks of rivers in some places,
in mountainous districts in others, and on the shores of lakes in yet others—
there were Brahmins who were fierce ascetics, as well as Vaiṣṇavas and those whose deity was the Sun.
Upon seeing Agastya, whose prowess was renowned, all of you, Vāsanta,
Hemaśālāyana, Bālāyana, and Rāvāsanāyana, with hearts full of joy, affectionately offered him a welcome and other greetings. (24)
Also Dārāliṅgāyana, the ascetic Bhekadāneya,
the great seer Masigrīva, as well as Śālavanāyana,
the seer Ācāla, Grāmāyana, and likewise Vāṭāyana. (25–26)
Thousands of ascetics who knew the Veda, such as Divāṅgāyana and others, as well as other Brahmins dwelling in hermitages and forests,
and female ascetics who were wise and devoted to great renunciation, [were present].
Truthful and virtuous women dwell there, devoted solely to meditation upon the Self.
Agastya, however, bestowed upon them the supreme knowledge of the Lord—
knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, which transcends the imperishable and shines within the highest abode.
He who is served by infinite liberated souls, known as Śrī Puruṣottama;
who is the Supreme Self and the Inner Self, and who is even darker than Kṛṣṇa;
from Vāsudeva comes Mahāvāsudeva, the illustrious Supreme Lord.
The Blessed Lord is endowed with divine sovereignty, majesty, and other such powers;

He is the controller of time and *māyā*, the teacher of the cosmic manifestations (*vyūha*) and incarnations (*avatāra*), the Lord of the lords of lords, and the bestower of power upon the gods. (31–32)
He is the protector of the sages and the ancestors, abiding within their hearts;
He is the inner witness of gods, humans, and nāgas, higher than the highest.
He is the beloved who cherishes all Brahmas and the bestower of splendor upon all abodes.
The sustainer of all incarnations, the witness of all, and the stainless one;
self-luminous, possessing boundless splendor, as beautiful as the limitless god of love;
possessing a divine form, known through the Vedas, and known by yogis within their inner self. (34–35)
He is to be known by those with the eye of the heart, yet unknowable by external faculties; unapproachable to those shrouded by *māyā*, yet approachable by those endowed with devotion.
Though situated at the furthest distance, He dwells in extreme proximity as a friend who bestows happiness.
Hari is the giver of all, eternally blissful, and the bestower of all joy.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Rādhā and Ramā; the Lord of Prabhā, Pāravatī, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, and Saguṇā. (37–38)
The Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Māṇikī; the true Master who is cherished by his devotees;
the sovereign of sages, full of compassion; though not a child, he assumes the form of a child—he who resides in the region of Surāṣṭra, in the district of Ājanābha.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, in the Akṣara-kṣetra that bestows liberation,
in the divine city known as Kuṅkumavāpī, and in his own abode,
dwells that glorious child Gopāla, the son of Kambharāśrī. (2.95.40–41)
He who is the Supreme Brahman himself exists today as Bālabrahmā;
he who is the inner self (antarātman) indeed exists today externally as Bālātmā.
He is the bestower of the fruit of yoga for yogis, and the object of realization for the wise.
He dwells in the minds of the liberated; He is the upholder of truth for the virtuous.
In the form of fire, He is the consumer of sacrifices and the devourer of oblations.
He is the Lord who exists as the very embodiment of faith for the ascetics whose conduct is penance.
Among the virtuous, he is the essence of dharma; among policies, the expansion of justice; among noble deeds, the hospitality shown to guests; and among devotees, the object of their worship.
Though formless and possessing infinite forms, he shines as a child.
Out of compassion, he is an ocean of mercy who grants liberation even to sinners. (46) By his grace, even insentient principles, though they be created, become uncreated, conscious, and divine. (47)
By his meditation, those who are unliberated attain liberation; the sinful become pure;
and the unperfected, having achieved perfection, go to final release. By his majesty, even those devoid of virtues become possessed of virtues.

Even by his mere remembrance, illusory things born of *māyā* become empty; even by the sight of his form, impurities go to their destruction. Once the vision of him has been attained, nothing further remains to be done. (2.95.49–50)
"Nothing further remains to be attained; indeed, he is now a child.
O Brahmins, receive that mantra which grants liberation and bestows all perfections.
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, the Brahmins received the supreme mantra.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
(52) They chanted this constantly and beheld Him indeed in His divine form.
Within their hearts, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa truly shone forth. (53)
A youth of divine form, as beautiful as ten million gods of love,
they then constantly performed the worship prescribed by Agastya;
desiring liberation, they practiced the eightfold devotion to Śrī Hari.
In this way, thousands and lakhs of Brahmins worshiped Hari.
Then, through the power of Agastya, they became devoted to Him in the great region of Uṣṇālaya, on the land where the weapons were stored.
At the end of the rainy season, the sovereign sage Agastya, having visited all the holy fords (tīrthas) in every direction,
traveled through the air together with Lopāmudrā to the region known as Aśvasārasa;
there he established his residence at the sacred field named Śrī Kuṅkumavāpī.
Then, in the month of Bhādrapada, a great planet appears there in the sky at night (vv.
58–59), with a crest of fiery flames extending for a thousand yojanas;
it rises daily indeed as a portent of calamity for the land.
The comet, which brings great terror and destroys the world—
seeing it, all creatures became overwhelmed with the fear of destruction;
O Bālakṛṣṇa, they sought refuge in that most excellent of men.
I performed devotion toward him, consisting of various forms of worship.
(61) Then, at the end of the month of Bhādra, on the full moon day, right in the morning, a flooding of the waters of the ocean occurred on all sides. (62)
The tides, which bring fear and cause the dissolution of all lands,
became violently agitated along with fierce winds and rains;
thus the earth surrounding the region of Uṣṇālaya was submerged by the waters of the ocean.
Indeed, the regions extending for a *yojana* were submerged like at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).
Villages, hamlets, market towns, dwellings, and extensive cowherd settlements—all of them, reaching as far as a *yojana* with the ocean as their limit—[were submerged]. (64–65)
Then, by the force of the surging waves of the ocean during the dissolution of the waters,
the trees, creepers, forest regions, gardens, and groves were destroyed;
as were the moorings for ships, embankments, and the lands of the fields.
The roads, the houses, and the mountain peaks were seized for the purpose of protecting those who traveled;
and the sites of activity were lost to the force of the surging tides.
All the foundations of the aerial chariots and the grounds of their moorings were destroyed by the floods of water.
Likewise, all the river mouths, as well as the dwellings of living beings, cattle, birds, and other creatures, even the mines, went to their destruction.
When this dissolution by water had thus occurred, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Then even the rivers were agitated, and the lakes as well;
the waters of the rivers and lakes flowed out toward the fields on all sides.
With their overflowing banks, those regions along with their inhabitants went to destruction.
On dry land there was water, and in water there was dry land; everything became inverted.
Due to excessive rain and fierce winds, embodied beings met their destruction. Neither those dwelling in the mountains nor those living in the forests were to be seen anywhere.
In the currents of the waters, corpses of humans, birds, animals,
reptiles, deer, and so forth, were seen by the thousands being carried away by the waves. (73–74)
Trees and the branches of trees are seen in the waters of the flood;
houses and leaf-huts float upon the waters of dissolution.
Rivers, lakes, other ponds, and even wells [are likewise submerged].
Filled with water, they appeared like ocean trenches or excavated pits.
When such a cause for destruction— a deluge of water— had thus arisen,
the sands on the battlefield were then swept away by violent winds.
Then those [visions] appeared in the sky just like clouds;
their eyes, filled with sand, fell into blindness.
With their eyes struck by the sand, those embodied beings [could not see] one another.
Indeed, those blinded by dust and struck by the wind do not see anything there at all.
Likewise, trees, houses, creepers, and even the coverings of pavilions are tossed into the sky by the force of the wind.
Ceilings, canopies, garments, and birds alike were cast with great force by the wind, both upon the water and upon the land.
Houses were utterly shattered, as were trees and leaf-huts.
Dwellings, hermitages, mansions, palaces, and even leaf-huts were destroyed;
the villages were indeed covered beneath a shower of sand by the showers of sand that arose from the battlefield and fell. || 82-83 ||
Trees, groves, gardens, living beings, birds, animals, and even ascetics— their forms were covered by sand;
in an instant, they were buried within the sand and placed inside the womb of the earth.
Deprived of breath, they died by the thousands of millions.
Even the ṛṣis and munis, whether dwelling on mountains or standing upon the earth, having restrained themselves in meditative absorption (samādhi), beheld that most terrible calamity. (85–86)
Having drawn back the vital breaths through the channels, they sat in the practice of *kuṃbhaka* and other yogic techniques;
they remembered the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa within their hearts.
But those who were not devotees wept, trembled, and cried out with choked voices.
The children cried out "Hā! Hā! and wailed, "O mother! O father! (88).
Lamenting, the men called out to their wives with choked voices; the wives, in turn, called out excessively to their children and their fathers. (89)
The cries and roars of beasts, birds, camels, and elephants, as well as those of lions and fires— all bearing great suffering— were repeatedly shattered by the violent storm at that time. (2.95.90)

Where one's own protection is not heard of and is difficult to achieve, by whom or where can the protection of others be found except through Hari? For those who have become morsels in the jaws of Time, who here is their protector? (9.1–9.2)
Mountains, battlefields, rivers, and lakes,
forests, lofty regions, wildernesses, and agricultural lands—
all the surface of the earth was then oppressed by violent winds.

He was born on the full moon of Bhādrapada, and on the night of the first day [of the new moon], before evening, the subjects died without those great portents. At that time, the stainless great sages, headed by Hemaśālāyana, [were present]. || 94–95 ||
Beholding the unappeased force of the wind and the dissolution caused by water and air,
they remembered Bālakṛṣṇa alone for the sake of peace—
Him who is an ocean of compassion, the protector of devotees, and a treasure-house of mercy.
[He meditated on] the Protector who disregards all sins, the Lord Kṛṣṇa who protects those who have come for refuge; the Lord who protected [the child] in the womb,
the Master who is the protector at the time of dissolution, and the Sovereign who guards against illusion.
To Hari, the protector of the vital breaths, the beloved, the performer of all protection;
to the Lord who protects children, the husband who effects the preservation of creation;
to Nārāyaṇa, the Master and Supreme Lord, the protector in yoga—to Him [I offer salutation]. (99)

The eleven sages, while the dissolution remained present, remembered within their hearts the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the life-sustainer of embodied beings; they all praised Him mentally for the sake of protecting the land. (2.95.1–2)
For the sake of pacifying the stormy wind, for the sake of pacifying the rain,
for the sake of pacifying the rain of sand, and for the protection of all beings, O Rādhikā,
they indeed praised the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest.
When destruction was imminent, the great sages [sought] the compassionate Bālakṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya’s Departure, the Storm and Turbulence of the Ocean Waters, and the Remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa by the Assembly of Sages Therein," in the Uṣṇālaya-khaṇḍa of the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
