Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, then all those hosts of celestial beings (vaimānika-gaṇas), numbering indeed billions upon billions, were the servants of the primordial Bāla-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Śaṅkara, the king of sages Agastya, and the goddesses also took leave of their own Lord and descended at the site of Hemaśālāyana.
Hemaśālāyana indeed offered them a warm welcome.
Having seen his preceptor Agastya, as well as Śambhu and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he attained supreme bliss and offered them a welcome. Prostrating himself on the ground like a staff, he cried out, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa!"
Then he offered them seats, honey-mixture, water for the feet, and the respectful offering (arghya).
He danced before those compassionate protectors.
Seeing that devotee dancing, Śrī Hari rejoiced.
The Lord, overwhelmed with affection, placed his feet upon the chest of his devotee;
he laid his hands upon his head and embraced him again and again.
He then swiftly bestowed divine vision upon Hemaśālāyana.
Hemaśāla, with his divine vision, beheld the abode of the camels;
indeed, the entire ground all around was well-guarded.
Men, birds, and even the conscious animals [were there].
Seeing that they had indeed been restored to life, he attained great joy.
Then he remembered the ten Vaiṣṇava sages;
for the sake of beholding Hari, they were instantly remembered there and immediately arrived.
By way of the path of the sky, auspicious Vaiṣṇava yogins, shining like the moon, descended upon the hermitage of Hemaśālāyana;
all of them wore garlands of *tulasī* and were chanting the name of Śrī Hari.
Having seen their guru Agastya, as well as Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa,
Śaṅkara, and the physician Sukha, they bowed with great joy. They all honored them with mental offerings.
Hemaśālāyana, Bālāyana, Rāvāsanastha, Dārāliṅgāyana, and he who bears the name Bhekadāneyana;
Maṣīgrīvāyana, and likewise Śālavanāyana.
Ācāla-Ṛṣi, as well as Grāmāyana and Vāṭāyana,
Divā, Diṅgālaya, and these eleven great sages were solely devoted to their own chosen deity, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (15–16)
The most excellent and highly fortunate devotees, perceiving the supreme emotion [of their teacher], rejoiced upon seeing their chosen deity, Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as their preceptor Agastya;
they prostrated themselves like staffs before those who had granted them the gift of life.

Then Keśava spoke to the great sages who were seated upon their seats: "Is all well with you in every respect regarding your hermitages and other matters? Is there prosperity in your asceticism, and likewise, is it well with all embodied beings?"
Is all well with all living beings among the subjects?
Is there welfare for the lands, and is there happiness for the ascetics? Is there perhaps happiness for the male and female devotees?
"Is all well in all regions and among all classes of people?
Having asked this, the venerable Lord Parameśvara fell silent.
Agastya then replied: "Does any sacred field exist here?"
Śaṅkara likewise inquired after the welfare of the ascetics, the subjects, and the male and female disciples;
and Satya also questioned them, and they in turn replied that they were free from affliction.
All the great seers spoke in succession of that most terrible dissolution,
which was painful and brought about their own destruction,
as well as the re-creation [of the world], the ruin of countries, and likewise their upheaval.
"O Blessed One, from the sight of you, Hemaśālāyana has spoken again concerning both the destruction and the protection of subjects.
All is well today, since your arrival has occurred within this realm. (26)
First, this region was submerged by the ocean on all sides; thereafter, it was afflicted by violent storms. By means of wind, rain, and downpours of water, many living beings were destroyed. (27–28)
And you were remembered by the great sages within the womb of the earth through their excavations;
having come here, this terrestrial globe was protected by you.
Beyond this, no other well-being or security exists.
The granting of fearlessness to living beings which has been ordained by your honors,
and the restoration of life to the dead— O Hari, in this sudden dissolution, who else but the illustrious Supreme Lord would be capable of this? (2.97.30–31)
O Lord! A stretch of land one *yojana* in length, situated near the ocean, was submerged on all sides by the waters of the sea and destroyed.
Then, Agastya drank that water with his cupped palms.
O Hari! Living beings have been endowed with life here by the physician [you].
All is well with everyone; what else could be more auspicious, O Lord?
Wherever the regions of the earth were covered with sand, there the people were afflicted. //33-34//
O Hari, by your grace all those who had died were restored to life;
O Hari Kṛṣṇa, at your command, Rudra dried up the waters, and all the separated family members were reunited with their servants.
And just as before, the prosperity was restored by the illustrious Mothers;
this land has been protected, O Kṛṣṇa, and those who had died have been restored to life.
All are indeed well; what happiness could there be beyond this?
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what happiness! Oh, what security! For those who have the Supreme Lord as their protector—what deity could there be beyond Him?
Oh, what merit! Oh, what heaven! And likewise, what sublime state of being!
In whose dwelling Kṛṣṇa himself has arrived— the bestower of liberation, the remover of all sins, the giver of all merit, the Supreme Lord,
and the granter of all bliss— for them nothing remains to be attained. (2.97.39–40)
O Supreme Lord, what need is there for further speech? All happiness proceeds [from you].
O Omniscient One, you know everything; indeed, all that is auspicious for us is in your hands.
You are the controller of the ocean, of battle, and even of the wind.
By you, however, on account of this very cause, the oceans and other elements have been restrained;
(42) so that there shall never again be destruction of living beings here within this cosmic egg.
Well-being and great happiness have been established; what more than this could be done? (43)
Then, having spoken thus to the sages, the seer Hemaśālāyana said,
"O noble lady, listen to my own great hardship and my liberation.
Hemaśālāyana said:
O Lord, I was once a child among the rows of trees on the bank of the river Nandā.
Overwhelmed by excessive rain, I was submerged in the water and driven toward the ocean. While I was thus submerged in that water, [you] indeed [rescued me] by force from the sky.
Thereafter, I arrived at Mount Hemaśālā by way of the path.
Then a rain of sand occurred, in which I was once again submerged.
Following that, I entered into meditative absorption (samādhi), recollecting you and likewise my Guru.
"O Lord, I was nearly dead, buried beneath a shower of sand;
yet you, my preceptor, came and rescued me.
Bālāyana said:
When I had gone to bathe in the waters of the ocean, I was then dragged into the midst of the water by terrifying waves of the sea such as I had never encountered before,
along with the waters, toward the earth.
Just as I had arrived at the bank of the Bālā river,
I was covered by showers of sand and became buried within the sand.
Having fixed my life-breaths in the *brahmarandhra*, I remained established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Until now, I have been saved and brought back to life by you having come here.
O Kṛṣṇa, without your arrival, my destruction on this earth was considered imminent.
Rāvaṇāsana said:
Indeed, I was in meditative absorption on the bank of the Gośaṅkusarīt river;
I did not know what had happened to me when I returned to consciousness.
Then, while there, I realized that I had been buried in sand and oppressed by the earth.
While I was within the womb of the earth, I remembered Kṛṣṇa Agastika.
Then, O ocean of mercy, I was protected by you who arrived;
with my life restored, I emerged from the earth like one waking from sleep. ||54-55||
Dārāliṅgāyana said:
While I was dwelling in the forest of Mount Dārāliṅga, chanting the name of Hari, a branch of a tree there was broken off by the wind and cast far away. (56)
"Cast down by the branch, my body was broken and I died. I do not know what happened after that, O Lord; I have arisen healthy and have obtained a cool draught of nectar while awake. || 57 ||
Then I informed him of the calamity, for I was protected by you.
Bhekadāneya said:
"I was on Mount Bhekadāna, taking refuge in a hollow."
A whirlwind carried my leaf-hut, along with its roots, up into the sky.
At that time, I was fast asleep within the hut upon a wooden floor; thus, I was cast from the air onto the mountain together with the leaf-hut. (2.97.59–60)
On an inaccessible peak, I perished from falling into the sky;
I know not by whom I was revived—by you, or perhaps by Hari?
Remembering you, I have come here; victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
"Who else is there to protect me when death has arrived without you?
Maṣīgrīva said:
"I went from the edge of the battlefield to the southern forest."
That forest which I saw was, in an instant, submerged in waters.
There in the water, I was seized by a crocodile and devoured;
I know not how I subsequently returned to life through your compassion.
"In that case, there exists a cause for survival even after being eaten.
Thus, O Lord, you have certainly been restored to life by the physician Śārṅgin.
Śālavanāyana said:
While I was worshipping you, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), on a mountain in a Śāla grove,
I was swept up by a whirlwind and carried five yojanas away from my place.
Falling from the sky into the ocean, I sank and subsequently died.
"I remember you, O ocean of compassion; protect me, protect me!"—thus [I cried] then.
You were seen by me there, indeed grasping me with your own hand;
I was protected, rescued, and established here by you.
The sage Ācāla said:
"While I was engaged in the Agnihotra sacrifice, a fierce fire broke out by accident; then a forest, overwhelmed by a wildfire, began to burn with heaps of wood."
I was burned in the forest and there I was reduced to ashes;
at that time, I remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
as well as the divine preceptor Agastya, the protector and Lord of the universe.
I was born from the ashes and have been restored by you once again;
nourished and endowed with consciousness by the Gaṇakas,
I have arrived here through your grace and my own aerial power.
Grāmāyana said:
"I was on the mountain near the village, there remembering Hari.
Just as I had bathed and was performing worship, a roar occurred. (73)
A fear born of the earthquake arose; at that moment, when I fell from the trembling peak of the mountain, I was carried far away by a whirlwind and placed within a cloud in the sky. (74)
I do not know what will happen after this; I died from extreme cold in the clouds.
How did I regain life? Such is your compassion!
O Kṛṣṇa, you protect your devotee even in the midst of the sky.
Vātāyana said: "While I was being tossed into the sky by a whirlwind and whirled about with great speed,
I was cast down into a certain forest where I saw a rutting elephant."
"Because of that extreme hunger, I was both held and devoured by him.
Therefore, O Keśava, I do not know why my life remains; you must know the reason.
Divādiṅgāyana said:
Between Mount Divādika and Mount Parvata, on the bank of the Kavindumā,
there was ocean water that had come from the east;
there, the Kavindumā river was flooded by the waters of the sea.
There I was indeed submerged when the water receded far away.
Then a mountain of sand arose even upon my head;
while I remained there absorbed in meditation, that mountain was removed by you.
Then, O Lord, remaining within my own body, I regained consciousness; at that moment,
I saw in the sky a most radiant celestial chariot,
exceedingly distant and resembling the sun, and having beheld it, I approached it.
I have been protected by you, O Kṛṣṇa, and brought back from the jaws of death. Indeed, O Lord, no embodied being can truly live here without your compassion.
For in this land, O Kṛṣṇa, the people who were dying have indeed been restored to life by you.
Furthermore, who is capable of acting otherwise than what has been duly ordained?
Agastya provided protection, and Śaṅkara did so again and again;
here, the child of Aśvinī restored consciousness to the subjects.
By your glories, the lands have been made prosperous and restored once more;
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beasts and birds have been protected by you.
Blessed is this land of weapons, known by the other name Uṣṇālaya.
"Though he was like a dwelling for camels, he has been made like a celestial abode;
having arrived, he has purified us, protected us, and delivered us.
When Rādhikā had been addressed in this way by the eleven sages, [she spoke].
Śrī Hari said: "Indeed, you have been delivered by me through your devotion.
For the sake of my devotees alone, I bestow all things;
indeed, for the sake of the female ruddy goose, I caused water to flow upon the mountain. (2.97.90)
In the past, having flooded the surrounding lands, I brought and gave food to my devotees;
for the sake of my devotees, I abandoned Lakṣmī, who was hostile toward them.
For the sake of my devotees, everything is given by me, and they are protected.
For the sake of one person, I provide protection for countless embodied beings;
for the sake of one person, I bring about the destruction of countless embodied beings.
I do everything for the sake of my devotees, but never for the sake of those who are not devotees.
But those who are not devotees do not obtain even a portion of what is inevitably gained by being near a devotee.
This land was uplifted for the sake of you and my devotees;
furthermore, in the past, I ensured the protection of the offspring of cats.
Out of great devotion, that Mārjārikā placed [the food] into a multitude of fire-heated frying pans.
"Whatever kind of affection one has, such is the protection one provides for it; I constantly observe this vow in the world: the protection of those who are devoted. (95–96)

Chanting my name, remembering me, touching me, seeing me, bowing to me, worshipping me, regarding me as a friend, and even hearing about me—of all these, the supreme act is the surrender of one's self with love; this is what pleases me. (97)
O twice-born ones, for him for whose sake there is nothing whatsoever in this world that should not be given,
I shall relinquish everything on his behalf, both in this life and in the next.
For your sake, O brahmins, I have performed every act of protection.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Supreme Lord ceased;
O Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa, and you all became steady-minded.
For a moment they meditated upon His external form, and then upon that Hari within.

Immersed in an ocean of bliss, they rested for a moment. (101) Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of Lord Hari’s Celestial Vehicle at the Hermitage of Hemaśālāyana in the Land of Uṣṭrālaya, and the Narration of the Account of Their Own Protection," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, after a moment, all the yogīs asked the Supreme Lord: "O Rādhikā! How was the protection of the female cakravāka bird accomplished?"
Just as Lakṣmī was formerly abandoned by the Supreme Self despite being His beloved,
and just as Hari formerly protected the offspring of a female cat;
who were they, how did they become devotees, and what kind of protection was it?
"What kind of merit did they possess that Mādhava provided them with protection?
Śrī Hemaśālāyana said:
"How was your female *cakravāka* devoted [to you], born as she was from a previous birth?"
"How can you sever your affection for my sake? Cut through this doubt!
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said:
"O brahmins, listen to this story concerning the female cakravāka birds that occurred in the past."
He was named Sanatsujāta, the mind-born son of Brahmā;
he was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted solely to the path of devotion,
dedicated to celibacy, and an instructor in the knowledge of Brahman.
Possessing unimpeded movement throughout the fourteen worlds,
that observer of vows wandered upon the earth in the form of a youth, desiring to visit sacred fords (tīrthas).
Once, he went to the Nārāyaṇa lake to bathe on its bank.
With a face like the full moon, gentle, and adorned by a halo of splendor;
(8) a sage whose limbs were proportionate to his form, yet clothed in bark garments;
with every limb robust and flourishing, he was radiant with the beauty of desire. (9)
Charming to women, adorned with extreme patience and gentleness,
with a serene mind, he was solely devoted to meditation upon the One Lord.
Having cast off his bark garments, he wore only a loincloth.
And he descended into the midst of the waters of the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Having plunged in and reached the shore, he recited the Mother of the Vedas;
then he went back into the water and stood once more upon the bank.
Meditating on Hari and chanting the Gāyatrī, he goes again into the water and bathes with ease; having bowed to the Sun, he immerses himself in the water.
(13) Having come outside, he remains in meditation for a period of one ghaṭikā.
Meanwhile, Urvaśī, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, arrived there from the Himālayas by her own will,
accompanied by many female companions.
She had been produced from the thigh [of Brahmā] and was bestowed upon Mahendra.
From that very day onward, she comes to Badarī every fortnight for the sake of seeing her father,
on the days of the full moon, the new moon, and so forth. In Badarī, she beholds the auspicious vision of her father Nārāyaṇa.
Having thus prepared for the sake of pilgrimage to Nārāyaṇa-sarovara,
the great devotee, the Vaiṣṇavī daughter of Viṣṇu,
the goddess who is a supreme Bhāgavata and whose hair is like a host of Apsarases, arrived there. (17–18)
O fortunate one, fickleness is the very nature of apsarases toward men;
thus, though she was devoted, she was longing for a youth due to her fickle disposition.
She beheld him, radiant with splendor and possessed of beautiful limbs, coming within the range of her vision. (19)

Beholding him alone, she was overcome by the god of love; standing before him, she entreated that sage Sanatsujāta for sexual union. Having assumed the form of a young maiden, she danced with many gestures.
She performed a song with seven rhythmic beats (*satāla*) and joyfully sang a little verse;
in her dancing, she whirled many times like a wheel,
making a circular motion to display her own agility.
With her voice she quickly delighted the sage with the dance of the cakravāka bird;
the sage heard her voice and beheld the dance of the cakravāka.
She too, perceiving the sage to be infatuated, danced even more intensely.
With gestures of amorous play (*hāva-bhāva*), movements of her limbs, and glances full of love and affection, she enchanted the sage; the sage, indeed, laughed repeatedly.
Even as she, though afflicted by fever, desired to touch the sage, [she was unable].
Then the discerning sage Sanatkumāra,
the brahmin who upholds the true Dharma, rose up and said, "Do not touch me! Having spoken,
he went a great distance laughing and sat down in another spot.
Then, having fallen under his power, she went to the bank of that very lake and performed a captivating dance once again.
Looking at the sage again and again, she entreated him.
Desiring to sport, she approached him and stood firmly by his side.
The sage said: "O maidservant! Why indeed do you behave here like a maidservant? You who are the daughter of Nārāyaṇa himself, are you not ashamed at this touch? (2.98.30)
"I am indeed the son of Brahmā, while you are but the granddaughter of my grandson.
I alone am one who observes the vow of Brahman; do not exert yourself in vain.
Bathe in the delightful waters of the Nārāyaṇa lake, a sacred pilgrimage site."
"O daughter, do not bring upon yourself this groundless mental anguish!
Thus addressed, she, filled with despair and the exhaustion of her grief,
spoke to that youth with a mind that had abandoned all sense of propriety.
"O Brahmin, we Apsarases grant all common enjoyments;
we are esteemed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and the gods.
Therefore, O yogin, I am not to be regarded by you here as a daughter. (34)
All daughters of Nārāyaṇa are likewise beloved by Nārāyaṇa.
Lakṣmī, born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa;
Rādhā, born from the body of Kṛṣṇa, is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was born in the lineage of Aja;
she is the daughter of Dakṣa, the son of Aja, and the wife of Dharma and the other gods.
Since there is no obstruction in the creation of the gods, I have therefore approached you.
"By you, laughter and contemplation have been shown, which awaken delight.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, accept [this]; otherwise, I shall quickly pronounce a curse.
Having said this, she threw herself into the lap of Sanatsujāta.
But the seer Sanatsujāta, out of fear of a curse or for fear of breaking his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), did not say anything to her at that time;
rather, having immediately practiced *yoga* and withdrawn his vital breaths (*prāṇas*), he departed.
Having entered the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) during his meditative absorption, he dwelt there at ease.
Then, beholding that beloved sage—who was devoid of desire and established in the Self—Urvaśī perceived him to be as unsatisfying as a cat’s behavior. (41–42)
Then he immediately cursed him: "O King of rogues, become a cat!
For you do not pay any price whatsoever for a devoted woman;
you do not know the suffering of a woman, yet you only increase your lust for women."
Having manifested fire, he sees it burning at a distance.
For such a eunuch, there is indeed the fitness for birth as a female cat;
let him become a pitiless female cat who experiences suffering.
"Just as you shall come to know the suffering of women through the various forms of desire,
so shall you, deprived of your cat [husband], become a female cat dwelling in a frying pan.
Having thus incurred this curse, the ṛṣi became a female cat.
And there, on the very bank of the Nārāyaṇa lake, he who remembered his former births suddenly arose from his meditative absorption and beheld his own body;
having fallen into the state of a female cat, he then indeed fell into a fit of rage.
Then, as Urvaśī was bathing, he who delighted in dancing like a wheel said to her:
"With the play of your words, you cause even those like me to fall into delusion;
yet, having failed to obtain your favor, you, full of fault, curse one who is free from fault. (49)
Therefore, in a place devoid of water, you who are possessed by thirst—
remain unsatisfied as a maidservant and as a female ruddy goose (*cakravākī*) afflicted by love;
separated from the male ruddy goose and abandoned by your circle of friends.

Thus was Urvaśī cursed; in an instant, she was born right there as a female ruddy goose (*cakravākī*), richly variegated, winged, and belonging to the species of birds. Then her friends quickly abandoned her and departed by way of the sky.
They went to heaven and to Mahendra, and told him what had occurred:
"Since desire in this worldly existence is a fault that bestows much suffering,
it is not reckoned as a virtue by the wise, even though it is a treasure-trove of bliss."
Then Indra, overcome with grief, went to the illustrious Parameṣṭhin and related the account; Brahmā, too, was seized by sorrow.
Those two [then] went to Viṣṇu in the forest of Badarī, who was the one to effect their deliverance.
They assumed the forms of Nara and Nārāyaṇa for the sake of liberation from the curse.
They bowed down, paid homage, and worshipped Hari;
and Nārāyaṇa himself, having prostrated before Brahmā, the Supreme Lord. (56–57)
Having offered the *madhuparka* and extended a welcome, he spoke:
"O Grandfather, is all well in every respect with the subjects?
Brahmā replied, "O Hari, all is always well with the subjects."
For what purpose do you perform penance here, and how could there be anything unwholesome regarding those women?
However, Urvaśī is your daughter, who was bestowed upon Indra;
Sanatsujāta is my son, a lord of yogis and a knower of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (2.98.60)
Due to the power of a curse, these two have entered the state of animals;
they were both excellent Vaiṣṇava devotees, my daughter and likewise my son.
They were born as a female cakravāka bird and a female cat in the region of Kaca.
"O Lord, on the shore of Lake Nārāyaṇa, you two were caused to be slain by one another through desire;
yet both of you have become rememberers of your former births. Therefore, O compassionate Blessed One, please ordain such a means as that your liberation may come to pass. (62–63)
"The ruler is capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise.
Having heard this, the Blessed One then reflected and said to the Creator:
"I myself shall effect their deliverance in a very short time."
Due to the curse, they will experience some suffering in their state as animals;
yet, by virtue of their innate memory of past lives and their devotion to me, they will remember me. And for the sake of their liberation from the animal womb, I shall manifest a specific cause.
"Then, having gone quickly to their side, I shall grant the release of those two devotees;
let there be no long-lasting suffering for them. Cast away your anxiety, O Grandfather.
When this was said, both Mahendra and the Grandfather were pleased.
Having worshipped Nārāyaṇa and bowed to the lake of Nārāyaṇa,
the two arrived at its shore where the maidservant and the cat were;
and upon seeing Mahendra and the Creator, those two remembered their former births.
They quickly came to their side and wept out of sorrow;
they were comforted by the two of them, who informed them that liberation from the curse would be granted.
"In a very short time, the Blessed One will bring about your release from the curse. (2.98.70)
Worship indeed Lord Anādinārāyaṇa!
For the wise there is no sorrow, since [their] acquisitions are perishable;
for the embodied beings, bodies are indeed equal, being merely objects of experience.
In that state, consciousness alone remains; it is the knowledge that destroys suffering.
That which is suffering for the ignorant is indeed happiness for the wise.
(73) [This is so] despite the transformations of objects and the threefold types of afflictions.
For those who possess discernment, all conditioned things are diverse and bring about suffering.
Youth is entirely corrupt and a source of pain because it is the cause of desire;
craving is its companion, and even one who possesses pleasure shall encounter suffering.
If there were no suffering in saṃsāra, what would be the distinction between it and liberation?
Therefore, saṃsāra is indeed suffering, and liberation is said to be happiness.
In the realm of māyā, suffering always increases, even when mixed with pleasure.
In the destruction of craving there is great bliss; therein illusion does not cause affliction.
(77) A wise person should abandon craving if they desire their own happiness; the destruction of craving is not even a fraction of the value of ten million supreme sensual pleasures. (78)
The enjoyment of sense objects increases new craving;
craving is the defect of sense objects, for its fruit is indeed extreme suffering.
But for the wise, the enjoyment of sense objects leads to their cessation.

When desire is destroyed, the fruit is supreme: happiness that assists toward liberation. (2.98.80) For yogis and the wise, even enjoyments do not cause bondage; on the contrary, they indeed serve to turn back the thirst born of non-perception [of the Self]. (81)

For when that [intellect] is endowed with knowledge and rests at the end of thirst and non-satisfaction, [then it is liberated]. But if thirst increases craving and is possessed by a state of delusion, then delusion is indeed destroyed by knowledge; and the guru is the cause of that knowledge.
The attainment of a guru occurs through the conjunction of merit; merit arises from hearing the scriptures and similar practices.
(83) Hearing the scriptures and so forth arise from faith; faith arises from the desire for liberation and other such qualities.
And the desire for liberation is set in motion solely by the grace of Hari. (84)
The grace of Hari, however, comes from worshiping, serving, remembering Him, and so forth.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the Supreme Lord.
He is indeed to be heard, reflected upon, meditated upon, and sought after. (85)
Those who have gone to him for refuge cross over the oceans of suffering.
In every way, one should offer oneself to him with one's whole being;
love and devotion should always be practiced toward him alone, for he is the one who brings an end to worldly existence.
If we were His [servants], He too would always be ours;
for the Lord of devotees honors the devotee, and the Lord of devotees favors the follower.
By union with the ocean of bliss, even a river attains happiness.
Through contact with the ocean of milk, the water of a river becomes milk.
|| 89 || There is no illusion in the Supreme Lord, nor is there suffering or thirst;
indeed, no defects exist in Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. || 2.98.90 ||
Divine qualities, which are infinite and free from any superior excellence, exist in the Lord Mahākṛṣṇa; indeed, His devotees attain them.
And let the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be remembered by you both.
He himself will bring about liberation from the curse in a short time.
Having manifested a sign, he will come here of his own accord.
Even while in the state of an animal, he performed a bath right here at this sacred ford and remembered Hari. (92–93)
Bowing even with the head, offering fruits, leaves, and so forth,
and even merely chanting the Name— this should never be abandoned.
If such devotion arises even while in the state of an animal, [it is sufficient].
That gain would be most excellent even compared to a human body.
Without devotion, the state of being a mere beast is equal for souls even among the gods. What distinction is there in divinity itself if devotion is not present? (95–96)
Even for one established in sovereignty, the tongue’s perception of taste is the same;
the capacity of all the senses is equal for both the poor man and the king. Indeed, I have ordained this to be the same for both; there is no distinction here.
The body is indeed the same, as are the sense organs;
their tastes are the same, and their satisfaction is likewise equal in every respect.
Since these have been given to all embodied beings, no distinction exists here. (98–99)
Devotion to Hari alone, when practiced, is distinguished here as supreme;
therefore, through such devotion, your liberation shall soon come to pass.
Let us both go to our own abode, and may there be well-being for you both by virtue of your devotion.
Having spoken thus, while both Mahendra and Vedhas were being honored by the maidservant and the female cat, they touched their feet with deep devotion; having been bowed to and saluted well,
they departed through the sky to their own celestial realm.
For both of them, by their father’s command, worship the illustrious Narayana;
day and night they chant the praises of their Lord, the husband of Sri Rama.
Thus did the sages dwell there at the Narayana lake.
"Indeed, both of them have become birds and beasts for the sake of your curse.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa rested for a moment and drank the auspicious water offered by His devotees.

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Births of Cakravākī and Mārjārikā as Asked by Hemaśālāyana in the Land of Uṣṭrālaya," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.

Chapter 100 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how thereafter the beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Lord Hari, performed the deliverance; He related that story.
(1) Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa said:
O Sage Hemaśālāyana, listen now to a further story:
she who was once a female cat on the shore of Lake Nārāyaṇa fled to a nearby village,
having fallen into fear of wolves and other predators.
Wherever the cowherds who are devotees of Śrī Hari dwell—
those men and women who are Vaiṣṇavas and worship the Supreme Lord—
there she indeed wanders constantly, overcome by hunger, seeking alms.
Having obtained food with great effort through theft,
she either subsists on it or does not steal at all;
out of fear of dogs, she sleeps at night upon a heap of husks.
Whether upon a heap of grass or on a pile situated on the roof of a house,
she maintains her livelihood by obtaining food scraps in whatever manner possible;
yet where there is no kind of cat at all, she remains there alone.
Even without a man, the young woman dwells there in her season;
then, by the burning of desire, she is tormented day and night like a female cat.
Yet, due to the cause of the curse, she does not obtain a male cat.
The villages were much farther than the hamlets; she was unable to go there.
In the midst of wild beasts, she remained right there out of fear.
Thus, she was tormented by the burning fire of desire until the limit of eight years had passed.
In the ninth year, there was both rain and excessive flooding upon the earth. By the force of that current, a certain cat, carried by the waves from a distant place,
arrived amidst the waters of the lake.
Clinging to a tree branch by the edge of a lake while still alive, he—
along with that branch— was carried by the water with a swift current to the bank;
thus the cat was brought to shore, and the branch came to rest upon the bank.
When he had dissolved into the water, that cat then went very slowly to the very place where the female cat was, having spotted her there. Having united with him, she became pregnant.
In the potter’s house, she, being pregnant and situated amidst fodder and straw,
gave birth at the full term to five boys;
she then placed them upon a heap of grass in another spot.
Then, in another place, she also protected her own children;
subsequently, at a site where the ground was unbaked, she protected them amidst a heap of raw clay vessels in a fire-pit prepared by a potter for the purpose of baking.
Having hidden the children in unbaked clay pots, she went outside. Later, for the sake of obtaining food for herself, the potter set fire to them to bake the vessels; she saw only that smoke.
Arriving there quickly, she saw fire at her mouth;
her children stood behind her, and there was no path for escape.
There, the fire had grown, blazing intensely with garlands of flames.
She too, out of fear of the dog, remained there on the side among the withered grass;
well-concealed, the young girl wept bitterly.
Indeed, no means whatsoever existed for protecting the lives of the children from the fire.
The potter was not there; who indeed could hear her weeping?
Filled with affection for her offspring, for the sake of protecting her child, she remembered the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (23)
He praised Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, with composed meditations.
Vahni stood encircling the hollow of the sacrificial vessel,
while the offspring of the vessels stood in its center upon that base.
The fire blazed upward, yet it did not reach the ground at all.
With great devotion, Mārjārikā chanted, "O Kṛṣṇa! O Hari! O Lord!
O Kṛṣṇa, protect my auspicious children with effort. (26)
O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, protect those who are faultless yet devoid of knowledge.
If I am devoted to you, O All-pervading One, protect my children—
by whom protection was granted in the womb and whose father [was saved] within the waters.
May that Lord by whom I was protected guard my children;
O Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Master, glorious one, supreme among men!
May He by whom I was formerly brought forth guard my children.

May that God who dwells in fire, water, earth, space, and wind; who resides in the heart, in the left vessel, in the pit, in the frying pan, and in the hearth—He who is eternally all-pervading—protect my children. (2.99.30–31)
"O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Lord! O Kṛṣṇa, protect these children!
Protect my dear ones, who are but small and without a protector, even more than my own life-breaths.
For the sake of your satisfaction alone, I shall perform one hundred thousand recitations."
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World, protect my young ones!
O You who grant protection to those who seek refuge, please guard my calves!
Thus she prayed as she stood in the courtyard of the potter. (33–34)
Having approached the *tulasī* plant, he prostrated himself ten times like a staff;
and considering the tree to be Hari, he performed fifty circumambulations, saying:
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Svāmin! O Lord of Śrī! O Lord of Kamalā!"
Protect me, O Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Brahman, Lord of the liberated, O Sovereign!
O Lord of Pārvatī, O Radiant Master, Lord of Haṃsa, appearing as Mañjulāya!
O Lord of the qualified (Saguṇeśa), Witness of the Self—O Hari, protect my children! 36–37.
O Self, O ocean of compassion, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Victory!
O bestower of nectar to the gods, protect us, O Acyuta, Lord of Peace!
O Lord of Śrī, Lord of the Earth, Lord of Badarī, Lord of Līlā, O sinless one!
O Lord of Prosperity, Lord of the Imperishable, Lord of Power, protect the children!
O Lord of Goloka, Lord of Haimī, Lord of Lalitā;
O You who dwell in the cave, whose mouth is the womb, O Lord of Fire, protect us, O Lord! 2.99.40.

O Īśvara, who dwells in the imperishable field, protect my children.
May the divine Fire protect the children; may all-consuming heat be pacified.
May these children of mine have their bodies made immortal by taking refuge in you.
Where there is no other refuge, you are the Guru, the protector, and the one worthy of seeking shelter; O Lord, protect these children.
Thus repeatedly entreating Tulasī, the female cat bowed down,
took some of her leaves, and went to the place of the fire.

"O Agni, protect my children, who are the very fruit of my old age.

For there is no other means here for protection than the remembrance of Hari.
Thus, with her mind, speech, and actions, that female cat worshipped the Supreme Lord, Śrī Puruṣottama, with leaves;
she constantly chanted His name and remained in the vicinity of the fire of the frying pan.
Clinging to the hope for life, she continued to worship the Lord of the World.
(48) Then, while she remained thus by his side, not a single person came;
no protector was seen at all, and in her despair, she worshipped Hari. (49)
At that moment, she heard the words of the children from within the frying-pan;
possessing hope for life, her mind became serene.
And the fire increased in intensity at the upper part, above the lid of the vessel.
With flames that were blue, green, and tawny on all sides, and with fierce,
variegated red flames whose bases were white, the fire became intensely formidable, pervading the entire space around the furnace on every side.
Inside, outside, on the sides, in the middle, and even beneath— in every respect—
there were unbaked and baked clay vessels, and [the house] was empty by day and night.
Yet that female cat, overcome by hunger and thirst, [sought] her own young ones.
He heard them speaking and likewise playing and crying out from hunger.
One said: "O elder brother, when will mother come?
Hunger afflicts me greatly; please call for mother. (54–55)
The eldest said, "A fire remains, blocking the paths on all sides.
How can our mother come? Remember the Supreme Lord Śiva;
he who provided protection for us in the womb will provide protection here as well."
The Blessed One will indeed bring you back to life by giving you food out of his devotion.
Behold the fire, intensely hot and exceedingly fierce, augmented by garlands of flames!
How could your mother come here? Remember Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
This is the compassion of the Blessed One that we live;
for here, in this cool cave, protection has been provided by Hari.
Even though there is an abundance of fuel, fire does not enter here.
"Behold! The flame does not burn; the smoke causes no fainting.
Come, come, let us go outside quickly from this hollow that is devoid of fire.
This fire appears cold to me, O younger brother, and it does not burn. (2.99.60–61)
Saying, "Let us go toward our mother," they departed quickly;
emerging from the midst of the fire with their body hairs unburnt,
all the boys went to their mother as if they had emerged from a frying pan.
Overcome by joy and overcome by hunger, they drank their mother’s excellent milk.
The mother showed them affection and even licked them again and again.
They told their mother that the frying pan was a cool place of refuge.
Having drunk milk and taken their leave, they entered the bakery once more;
going beneath the floor of the bakery, they rested happily and joyfully.
That fire which indeed cooks raw pots and the like by means of burning—
That very same fire which, having consumed fuel, grass, and other such things, reduces them to ashes—
by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s mercy, it became perfectly cool for the sake of the kitten; at that time, indeed, it was rendered devoid of burning power.
And the female cat, having observed this and being herself fearless,
went toward the opening of the frying pan to enter upon its surface.
At that moment, the fire was touched as such— extremely hot and intensely burning.
Having attained supreme wonder, she remembered Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the Lord! Indeed, that which is but a single thing becomes a source of happiness for one, yet it truly becomes a source of suffering for another. (2.99.70)
Although he was the burner of all,
on this occasion he became the protector; surely my children here have been protected again and again by the Supreme Soul, Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
This is the greatness of my devotion: that children find refuge in me.
Whatever great merit from previous births they may possess, by that power these children sport within my midst as if in their own home. (72–73)
Then, having understood the most perfect greatness of Kṛṣṇa, the cat worshipped Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord, with intense devotion.
Though tormented by hunger and thirst, she made a firm resolve. 74.
"I must not go elsewhere;
Hari will provide food for me and protect my children; He will guard them.
Thinking thus, she chanted: "Oṃ Hare Acyuta! (75–76).
"Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Gopāla, Nārāyaṇa, Narāyaṇa"—
thus she muttered his name with her voice, her mind, and her heart during every inhalation and exhalation.
Then she sat down near the frying pan that was dedicated to Hari.
Two days have passed, yet he neither rises nor departs.
[The Lord] Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the God, the Supreme among men, the Refuge of men—having ascertained his firm resolve and having recognized his devotion that transcends the highest, [he spoke]. (78–79)
Assuming the form of a potter, he who protects those who have come for refuge arrived with milk-preparations and *pūrikā* cakes offered at the *śrāddha* ceremony in the month of Bhādrapada;
holding them in his hands, he presented them to the ancestors themselves.
In the sky he gave [offerings] to the crows and to the cow;
he gave to the spirits and also gave to the cat.
At that moment, those boys emerged from the fire-hearth.
He made them drink milk cooked for the śrāddha ceremony, which bestows happiness.
Having drunk it, they entered there onto the floor of the kiln, which was conducive to comfort.
Thus were other potters invited by that potter.
"Behold, indeed, cats live even in the midst of fire!
Having said this, he showed the boys to the potters;
and the superintendent of the frying-pan makers also beheld them and was struck with wonder.
The unbaked clay vessels were being baked, yet the children were not burned at all;
this was a supreme marvel that became manifest there.
Crowds of people arrived to behold the young sons of the potter.
They worshipped the god of fire and gave food to the female cat.
They gave milk to the children; and those children, having come outside and drunk it, would return again and again through the hollow of the frying pan.
Having observed this, those people, protected by Hari, reached a conclusion:
"These men live and do no harm, for he is indeed the protector of the distressed.
Then the Lord, the creator of the pitcher, himself [proceeded] after the pacification of the fire.
He cleared away the ashes and all other things from the jars and vessels;
he even emptied the floor where the young girls were stationed,
for there he beheld the footprints of the Blessed Lord.
There, a potter constructed a pedestal for the Lord’s feet,
and that place indeed became famous as the holy site known as Mārjārarakṣā (Cat-Protected),
because the children were protected there by the yogi Nārāyaṇa.
He too shone forth at that time in the midst of them all;
none other knew that Lord in the form of a potter.
Then, at that very moment, the Blessed Lord Badrinārāyaṇa himself— ||| 93-94 |||
Out of compassion, He revealed His own four-armed form.
Upon seeing Hari, the potters, filled with faith, worshipped Him.
Mārjārikā also beheld this glorious Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
Instantly, they attained the memory of their forms as Sanatsujāta.
He felt various sorrows arising from his birth as a cat, thinking:
"Where am I, Sanatsujāta, and where have I come to this state of being a cat?"
"Today Nārāyaṇa himself has arrived for the sake of destroying my curse"—
thinking thus, having attained true detachment, he did not bow to Hari, Nārāyaṇa.
Then Nārāyaṇa also quickly emerged from that animal body.
And he gave them the form of Sanatkumāra, consisting of the essence of Brahmā’s son. The children were protected and raised by potters;
under their influence, those forest-dwellers indeed became cats. (2.99.99–100)
Then the god Nārāyaṇa and Sanatsujāta went to the lake to bathe; the potters followed after them.
Then a rain of flowers was released by the gods from the sky onto the lake.
Because Nārāyaṇa himself bathed there along with the gods,
that auspicious sacred site was proclaimed as "Nārāyaṇasaras.
It provides protection, grants liberation, and bestows [the state of] Nārāyaṇa.
Accompanied by Sanatsujāta, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, having bathed,
went to his own vast abode at Śrī Badarī on the Golden Mountain;
and the sage Sanatsujāta also, having bathed in the waters of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā).
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, he then went to Satyaloka in an instant.
A village named Mārjārapura was established there by the subjects.
Thus did Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [speak] to the sage Hemāyana.
He likewise told the story of the protection of the cat's offspring;

O Rādhā, he paused for a moment, and they attained the greatest joy. (107) Thus ends the description, in the second section on the Tretā Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, of how Nārāyaṇa protected the kittens of Mārjārikā from the fire of the potter’s great kiln, and how Mārjārikā was released from her curse, and so forth.
The Ninety-Ninth Chapter:
99. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 100.
[Author: Chapter 101.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! The Lord is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
She related the story to the sage Hemāyana:
"By the curse of Sanatsujāta, Urvaśī, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, became a female ruddy goose (cakravākī) on the shore of Lake Nārāyaṇa. (1–2)
Remembering her past lives, she constantly meditated upon sacred fords;
she would fly far away from one village to another and,
having eaten grains at midday, would rest within the trees.
Flying through the air, she traveled to a distant land by evening.
In this manner, desiring sacred fords and established in a state of detachment,
she gradually left the Kaccha region and swiftly crossed the Khāta.
Having come from the land of Ānarta toward Camatkārapura,
she bathed in the lake and beheld Hāṭakeśvara;
having seen Somanātha, she proceeded to Akṣarakṣetra.
Having bowed to the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa,
she went to Siddhasarasvatī at Arbuda and proceeded to Puṣkara.
Having prostrated before Brahmā, she arrived at Gaṅgādvāra.
Then, having passed through Kurukṣetra and the river Pragaṇḍakī,
and having paid homage to Śālagrāma and prostrated before Mount Śāla,
he flies up into the sky to behold Paśupati.
Then, while she was flying in the sky above the foothills of the Himalayas,
in the region of the Nīpālaya district,
she saw a certain maiden on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī with her gaze directed downward. (2.100.10–11)
With a moon-like face and exceedingly fair, her body was radiant like the sun;
though only eight years of age, she was on all sides equal to Kamalā in the beauty of her form.
Rich with a luster like that of the land-lotus, her eyes were as long as lotus petals.
Her body was pervaded by fragrance, like the divine Nārāyaṇī;
holding the beloved Lord of Śrī in her heart and "Hari, obeisance! on her tongue, she stood as if gazing all around at the Cloud-bearer upon her hips.
With hands adorned with jeweled bracelets, her beautiful neck bound with gems;
her waist encircled by a girdle, her forearms richly set with chains;
her feet graced with anklets, and her nose adorned with a nose-ornament.
Her beautiful ears were adorned with earrings, and she was decorated with garments and jewels glowing like fire.
Abounding in the radiant splendor of jasmine, campaka, and gold, she was exceedingly beautiful. [She cried out:
"O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu! O Supreme Brahman, O Lord! O Hari! (16–17)
"O Blessed One, Supreme among Men, when will you grant me your vision?
Thus she was seen uttering these words in a secluded place.
But Cakravākī, recognizing her as one worthy of trust, [approached her].
Then she descended from the sky while Śrīdruma stood by her side.
And for the sake of attracting her, he sang with very sweet words;
indeed, having heard that song sung like that of an apsarā, the maiden—
She beheld a small female bird on a tree, skilled in song.
In her song, there was this sentiment: "When will Kṛṣṇa meet me?
I am the daughter of Nārāyaṇa; when shall I obtain Mādhava? (2.1)
"Then you too shall meet Mahākṛṣṇa; do not grieve.
O friend, just as I am separated [from him], so do you appear. Who are you? You are in the form of a maiden; tell me, are you human? Speak of your former state. (22-23)
Having heard this sentiment expressed by the singer, the maiden was greatly delighted and said:
"O maidservant, who are you that speak thus in the body of a bird?
Come, O lady of virtuous vows; enlighten me with divine speech."
"Are you Kṛṣṇa, or Kṛṣṇadūtī, or Kṛṣṇā? Why do you remain here? (25) Come, stay by my side; tell me of auspicious and favorable tidings.
I shall listen to your auspicious news; Hari will remove my suffering. (26)
Thus addressed, she descended from the tree onto the ground in her presence;
she beheld a gentle form at her feet, like the feet of Śrī.
She bowed at her feet and drank the water offered by her.
She sat down near her as she was seated on the riverbank.
When questioned for the sake of familiarity, she spoke of the fruit born of a curse:
"I am Urvaśī, the daughter of Hari, [fallen] due to the curse of Sanatsujāta. (28–29)
Even though I am an Apsaras, I have become exposed and I have indeed become a Cakravākī bird;
yet, when I behold Nārāyaṇa himself,
I shall then be released from the curse and become Urvaśī once again.
Having spoken thus, that maidservant repeatedly gazed with emotion upon the maiden,
who was like Śrī herself and adorned with auspicious marks;
she beheld a dark mark upon her heart, resembling the eye of a ruddy goose.
He beheld a streak of the *puṇḍra* mark known as the *tilaka* above her feet;
on her hips, a line like an arrow; and on her forehead, the shape of a crown.
On her right cheek, however, he beheld a red dot upon her brow.
On her chest she saw the line of Viṣṇu, and likewise the mace on her left arm;
on her left thigh a sandal, and the Vaijayantī garland resting upon her heart;
and in her hand she beheld a lovely lotus and the mark of an elephant.
On the right foot are the marks of a conch, a boat, a celestial chariot (*vimāna*),
a mace, a fish, a mountain peak, a large fish, and a betel vine (36).
On the left foot are the lines of a barley grain, a temple, and likewise an umbrella.
An upward line, a lotus, a banner, a goad, and likewise a jar;
(37) a water-lily, a bilva fruit, a land-lotus, and likewise the moon; ten full discs, and fingers adorned with golden lines. (38)
On the forehead, there is a golden necklace, a golden line, and a dot;
on the chin, a dot; and on the upper part of the right breast, a hand-line.
On the left breast, a wheel; on the neck, a necklace; and on the chest, a golden ornament.
He beheld a banner, a fish, and a flute, as well as a svastika, upon his right hand;
he likewise observed a bow, a fish, and a water-pot upon his hand,
and he also beheld a rampart and an archway upon his right hand.
On his crest he beheld a most beautiful plow-sign;
on his feet, a horse, an elephant, a tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, and a javelin;
and on his hand, the lines of a beautiful garland, a lamp, and a fly-whisk.
She showed him the mountain, the earring, the altar, and the discus;
she attained supreme wonder, realizing that this was the power of the Supreme Lord (Śrī Pārameśvarī),
for no other such thing could be seen except for that which belongs to Nārāyaṇa.
"None of these marks exist except in a lotus," she decided,
and asked her name, lineage, and so forth.
Having heard this, the girl told the female ruddy goose (cakravākī) the truth.
"Daughter! What can I say to you in this matter? Destiny is indeed always powerful.
I am the wife of Nārāyaṇa; I have become your mother.
By name I am Lakṣmī, the eternal beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose glory is beginningless."
As the Ardhangana, I always dwell in the realm known as Mahavaikuntha;
never do I go far away, leaving Narayana behind.
But Narayana, for the sake of his devotees, goes far away, leaving me behind.

"If I were to take the form of an obstacle during your father's devotion before Hari, I would have been abandoned by your father from the abode of Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of your devotion. O child, the Blessed Lord, who is dear to His devotees, [has gone] to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (2.100.50)
Having abandoned [her former state] and become a follower of Bhaktā, she arrived here in this universe.
I have come to this earth to search for her;
remaining in human form, I kept my powers unmanifest.
"My father is Śivarāja," said Śaṅkara on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī.
"He is Hara, the lord of Kailāsa, who assumes a human form by his own will;
he is a great devotee of the Lord, a worshiper of Śrī Gopāla, and full of dispassion. (5.2–5.3)
Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, became his wife; she is known as Jānakī and is the beloved of Hara.
She too, by her own will, is a human being and shines in the house of Śambhu.
Those two parents were created by me as mental beings, the most excellent Vaiṣṇavas.
Situated on the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, there exists this most magnificent city named Kailāsadhāma within a mountain valley;
here, Satī and Śiva shine forth in human form. (55–56)
In the city of their own kingdom, in a garden resembling Mount Kailāsa,
those two sons of the king— whose true nature was unknown to the world, though known by all— resorted to the duty of the warrior class for the sake of protecting the people. (57)

In whose house the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa dwells under his control, there Hari comes every morning to the chamber of worship. Having accepted the offering dedicated by Satī and Śambhu, he enters into a state of absorption. ||58-59||

Therefore, for the very purpose of worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I have come from the garden to fetch water for the sake of the ancestors and the gods. By good fortune, my daughter, I have seen you here after being separated from me for so long.
"Come, dwell here in my house and here in my cage.
Conduct yourself according to the nature of a bird so that they do not recognize you at all.
I shall protect you in every way, my dear son, when the time comes. (61-62)
"By the will of Nārāyaṇa, liberation from the curse will come quickly.
Not far from this place, there are many forests nearby;
we shall indeed dwell here and behold Nārāyaṇa."
There is no fear here from Hari’s yoga, nor anywhere from Śiva’s yoga (64).
Likewise, O daughter, there is no fear from my yoga or from Satī’s yoga;
the kingdom known as the abode of Kailāsa and the city itself are also free from fear (65).
Everything indeed proceeds correctly and auspiciously;
yet Nārāyaṇa, your father, though he knows me as such,
always remains here as if ignorant and does not inform Śambhu.
He alone, being compassionate, will uplift [us] when the time has arrived.
Or else, we shall perform secret penance for the sake of our deliverance;
then he will bestow the fruit of that penance, known as his own grace.
Having heard these words spoken by the daughter of Śiva, Cakravākī, the daughter of Nārāyaṇa and Urvaśī, said to her:
"O Mother, by the sight of you today, my sorrow has indeed departed. (69)
"In whatever state she may be, a mother’s lap indeed grants peace.
By good fortune, I have today found and beheld my most venerable mother here.
Whatever you tell me, O mother, I shall do exactly so."
The word of a mother is the Veda; it is dharma, charity, austerity, and sacred vow.
Indeed, for a maiden, all these are considered fruitful only through the word of her mother.
You are the destroyer of my suffering, O Mother, and I am your daughter.
"I shall strive through asceticism and other means for the sake of destroying this separation from Kṛṣṇa.
For the service of her mother is indeed the highest and most excellent virtue for a maiden;
until marriage, the mother is the very everything for a daughter. (73–74)
Throughout her entire life, a mother desires the happiness of her daughter;
indeed, no living being exists for a mother who is equal to a daughter.
Through merit accumulated over a hundred lifetimes, a mother becomes one who possesses a daughter.
A daughter becomes a servant to her mother through the merit arising from a thousand births.
(73) The wealth belongs to the mother alone for a daughter, but the wealth belongs to the father for a son.
A son is an assistant to his father, while a daughter is an assistant to her mother. (77)
Even when a son is present, a mother is considered barren if she lacks a daughter;
for during bathing, cooking, eating, in the house or the garden, by day and by night,
in bed or while traveling, and in solitude, the daughter is one's companion.

Just as a cow with her calf becomes exceedingly dear, so too a mother accompanied by her daughter is considered more worthy of honor in the world. A daughter has her mother for her support; a mother has her daughter for her support. (2.100.80)
Therefore, a mother is always served by her daughter as the bestower of welfare;
the mother is the supreme sacred ford (*tīrtha*), she is Sarasvatī herself,
(81) the mother is Lakṣmī, the constant nourisher, the savior, and the protector.
She indeed instructs even her own daughter in the noble arts for the sake of others;
she protects what is dear as if it were herself and always gives everything away.
Only a mother, and no other, experiences suffering in times of hardship and happiness in times of joy.
Having experienced hardship and considering her daughter to be weak, the mother who bestows strength always provides refuge; no other woman is like her.
A mother should be understood as Sāvitrī, just as Svāhā and Svadhā are.

The Mother is Brāhmī, the Great Power; the Mother is most venerable among all. The word of the Mother is always auspicious and is considered the highest omen. She is eternally composed of the blessing of the *mātṛgālī* and the *ghṛtanālī*. 85–86.
The motherland, the mother tongue, and the mother’s milk are praised;
the mother and the land of the Triveṇī are praised as the savior.
The Ganges is considered the mother’s milk, and the Yamunā river is the mother’s lap.
The mother is declared to be the triad of sacred fords; the mother’s word is Sarasvatī.
The water from the mother’s feet is meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of sins.
The touch of the mother is the touch of nectar, providing nourishment even in the absence of food.
And the food remaining from the mother’s meal is like the grace of the Supreme Lord;
since the daughter consists of the mother’s blood-essence, the mother is therefore highly praised.
Indeed, the body of the daughter is produced from the mother’s body during the ninth month.
Therefore, the mother is equal to Brahman, for she is the cause of the flow of creation.
(9.1) Indeed, the vision of her yields a fruit even greater than the vision of Brahman;
and the remembrance of her yields a bliss even greater than the remembrance of Brahman. (9.2)

Service to her, attendance upon her, and the carrying out of her commands—even these are considered superior to the study of the Vedas; they are held to bestow the world of Brahmā. By whichever daughter one's own mother is satisfied through such service and other acts, [she attains that supreme goal].
Thus colored by her mental, physical, and verbal compliance,
she has no fear born of illusion, time, karma, Yama, and the like;
nor does she have sudden fear, nor any fear arising from disease and so forth.
For her, there is no fear of the three realms, nor likewise any fear of thieves and the like;
she has no fear of obstacles, nor likewise any fear of hungry ghosts (preta) and so forth.
What is the use of saying more here? She has no fear of birth or death.
The mother is ten times more venerable than the father, owing to her bearing him in the womb, giving birth, and nourishing him.
(97) The mother is the Guru, the mother is Hari, the mother is the progenitor, and the mother is the abode of Brahman.
The mother is heaven, the mother is home; indeed, the mother is the eternal state. (98)
Beasts, birds, children, those who have reached old age,
and even youths, when beset by distress, utter "moṃ moṃ moṃ. Affection for one's mother and affection for Brahman are such that there is indeed no liberation higher than them.
Upon seeing her daughter in a dream, joy arises in the mother;
saying, "Today my daughter has been seen by me," she remembers her constantly.
Indeed, if a daughter is a savior to her mother, performing all necessary tasks for her. (2.100.100–101)
By failing to serve her mother, a daughter shall always be devoid of fortune;
through the distress of the mother’s heart, the daughter’s good luck perishes.
Household duties, such as fetching water and cooking food, [must be performed].
The removal of refuse and the like, as well as the cleaning of the alms-bowls;
the raising up of beds and such, as well as the washing of garments; the dyeing of the robes of the younger brothers, and the protection of the house through cleaning and other such tasks. (103–104)
The preparation of grains and other ingredients, the cleaning of spices and condiments, the protection of household goods, and appropriate service to the members of the family;
the performance of worship of the deities and the churning of curds, buttermilk, and so forth. (1.05)
Tending to cows, sheep, and so forth, as well as massaging the mother’s body;
grooming the mother’s hair, massaging her feet, and other such activities—this range of duties constitutes the daughter’s service toward the mother-Brahman. (1.06–1.07)
Having prepared [the offerings] again and again, the daughter, endowed with devotion and possessed of faith,
should offer them. By the merit of her vow to her mother, that daughter attains victory in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as eternal prosperity.
Indeed, she is born in this world like Nārāyaṇī, as one who embodies ten million Brahmās.
What more need be said by me here? My mother has been served;
by her, the eternal Brahman has been served, and heaven has been attained both on earth and in the celestial realm.
Thus, O Rādhikā! the daughter Cakravākī—she who is the Lakṣmī that destroys suffering, who knows His majesty, and who is full of devotion—spoke to her mother:
"The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [bestowed grace] upon the sage Hemāyana..."
And there, on the mountain named Hemaśāla, he told her this story.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Meeting of Cakravākī with Her Mother Lakṣmī on the Banks of the Gaṇḍakī and the Narration of the Mother’s Greatness," during the pilgrimage of Cakravākī in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
