Chapter 101 [Author:
Chapter 102 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā! That female cakravāka bird questioned her mother again:
'Tell me here, for what reason have you been abandoned by Hari?
Thus questioned, her mother Lakṣmī spoke to her daughter."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoke this nectar of a story to Hemaśālāyana:
"Listen, I shall tell it to you for the sake of the devotees—how even the Lord Himself abandons Lakṣmī; what then need be said of anyone else? (2–3)
In the world of Mahāvaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa is constantly served with devotion by the inhabitants of Mahāvaikuṇṭha;
they serve him with even greater affection than Lakṣmī herself does.

A female friend named Kṛṣṇā, who excelled Lakṣmī in her service, constantly protected Nārāyaṇa in her own home; that beautiful woman herself performed his bathing and anointed him with fragrant unguents. (5–6)
That female companion adorns her [with love] through thorough massages of the limbs, along with shaving and other such services, as well as by means of garments, ornaments, decorations,
and the like; and through worship, food, drink, and so forth, as well as by means of bedding and household furnishings.
With constant laughter and various forms of mirth, with diverse modes of service,
and with many varieties of love, she remains day and night offering herself entirely;
Kṛṣṇikā is never for even a moment separated from him, as if he were her own body.

Always crying out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! even during her formal religious observances, she served her beloved husband Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa with three bodies. Thus, her two brothers, Jaya and Candra, became two of his attendants (pārṣadas).
Indeed, they both offered their entire ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and themselves to Hari.
They were eternally great devotees, solely intent upon Nārāyaṇa; finding all happiness in Hari, they were never for even a moment separated from Kṛṣṇa.

The two ascetics were devoted to the recitation of prayers and were dear to Hari; their senses and internal faculties were fully directed toward Kṛṣṇa. Endowed with the ninefold devotion, they were dedicated to the yoga of meditation.
With the disposition of offering their very selves, those two worship the Supreme Lord.
Even there, Kṛṣṇa dwells wherever his brother resides;
in that house, the youthful Kṛṣṇa himself always dwells. (14–15)
Their father, the lord of cowherds and protector of the cows, was like a cowherd himself; he was constantly immersed in the service of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Through his acts of self-surrender, he became, as it were, identical with the form of Kṛṣṇa. (16)
He remained devoted to Hari with love, intent upon serving Him in every way.
(17) Then once, those four came to their own home to present various offerings to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. (18)
Then, in an invisible form, Nārāyaṇa comes along with them to the interior chamber of that divine, magnificent palace;
there, on the bed, Śrī Nārāyaṇa is served by the illustrious Mahālakṣmī.
Receiving the loving service of Mahālakṣmī, he remained utterly absorbed in her.
Mahālakṣmī, immersed in love, united with the body of Nārāyaṇa;
as his beloved, she became submerged in the ocean of the supreme bliss of the Brahman.
Out of a long-standing desire for service and a longing for the eternal bliss of Hari,
she became free from any wish for separation and was united with the embrace of Śrī Hari.
At that very moment, those four excellent attendants—
Having gathered their offerings and quickly come to the door, they cried:
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Supreme Lord Keśava, Hṛṣīkeśa! Grant a vision of Yourself to Your devotees. (23–24)
Thus they uttered the word "bhakta" (devotee) with great devotion.
Hearing that word "bhakta," the Blessed One abandoned his bed and,
rising quickly, immediately commanded Pāla, who was standing at the door.
For the sake of his entry, she then abandoned her own state, which was overflowing with supreme bliss.
Though her beloved had departed, that devoted wife, the servant-maid, did not say anything;
for even though she was pained by separation from Nārāyaṇa himself, she remained dear [to him].

"Keśava will soon arrive and delight me," she thought, full of such anxiety; thus, she remained steady upon her bed. At that moment, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the beloved, arrived bringing his devotees with him.
Accompanied by them, he entered and sat upon the lion-throne situated within the palace.
Nārāyaṇa summoned his own Lakṣmī to that auspicious seat.
Addressed by Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī’s face became radiant with joy.
Then she quickly approached Hari at his throne;
together with Śrī Hari, Lakṣmī sat down upon the seat.
Those four, having brought [the offerings], then presented them with great devotion.
All kinds of offerings—various foods, drinks, and delicacies;
the complete collection of erotic articles, including garments, ornaments, and beautiful garlands; and numerous strings of necklaces filled with pearls from oyster shells. (32–33)
They presented to Nārāyaṇa articles rich in the fragrance of fruits and flowers, endowed with excellent flavors, and worthy of Lakṣmī’s adornment;
and they gave them to Lakṣmī there as well, worshipping her with exceeding devotion.
They stood still, offered praises, and became absorbed in meditation.
When they had performed worship and presented offerings, yet did not rise for a long time,
Lakṣmī quickly became enraged toward those who were forms of obstacles.
She does not manifest her inner anger outwardly; indeed,
she is unable to speak even though she is capable,
nor is she able to rise up, except by the will of Hari and without Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with anger, she thought: "When will these devotees depart?
When shall I again attain Nārāyaṇa upon my comfortable bed?
Meanwhile, those devotees remained absorbed in meditation, fixing Hari before them in their contemplation.
Śrī Satī and Hari remained there for a long time in that state of prohibition;
meanwhile, they arrived from Kailāsa to behold Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
One obstacle had not yet passed when a second one arrived.
Realizing this, Śrī remained steadfast and helpless at the side of Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, Śaṅkara was a supreme devotee, a great follower of the Lord, as was Satī, who was a great devotee; who then could transgress them? (41–42)
Nārāyaṇa himself, rising quickly from his lion-throne,
embraced Śambhu and offered him a welcome;
Lakṣmī also respectfully offered a welcome to Satī.
Then Satī and Śambhu performed the worship of the illustrious Hari. Śambhu, a devotee of the Lord, sat upon a beautiful seat offered by Satī in front of Śrī, and he performed various kinds of dances.
Hara danced for a long time out of sheer love in the presence of Śrī Hari;
his mind was so captivated by Hari that he was unaware of anything else.
Lakṣmī, meanwhile, was agitated with the longing for the bliss of Nārāyaṇa’s touch.
He quickly desires the end of the dance and a state of solitude.
Hari is subject to his devotees; he does not even remember or look toward Lakṣmī.
With his mind fixed on his devotees, he does not permit them to go outside.
Then, abandoning her composure,
she cursed Śaṅkara, Satī, Dhenukā, Pāla, Jaya, Candraka, and her friend Kṛṣṇā— who had pointlessly violated their agreement— saying, "May you all become human beings! (49)
Wherever there shall be the fruit of obstacles, of this there is no doubt.
(2.101.50) They are immersed in untimely dancing and are practitioners of untimely meditation;
for they cause me obstacles by utterly disregarding the proper time. (51)
"May those who possess bodies in the world of mortals encounter obstacles," having said this,
and repeatedly taking Śrī Hari by the hand, he said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, please come to my home and rest for a moment."
O Lord, such a multitude of your devotees exists here, though they are but few;
yet these affectionate ones come repeatedly even without [your] command.
Those beloved devotees truly do not understand your inner mind.
"Come, O Hari, and bring peace to my inner chamber;
for you who have remained seated here for so long, great fatigue would surely arise.
Thus did Ramā insist upon taking Nārāyaṇa with her.
Śaṅkara and the others, being his devotees, were filled with supreme wonder upon hearing this.
Due to Lakṣmī’s curse, they became dejected-faced and as if devoid of luster.
Having quickly bowed to Nārāyaṇa and perceiving that Lakṣmī was distressed, [they acted].
They departed quickly from their own abode, from the presence of Śrī Hari;
they fell into the world of mortals even as the gatekeepers and the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha looked on,
and a great cry of lamentation arose there.
News spread everywhere, in every place, even throughout Vaikuṇṭha:
"By the curse of Lakṣmī, the four sons of Kṛṣṇa, though devoted to Hari, have fallen into the world of mortals like ignorant fools who do not know the proper time. (2.101.60)
Therefore, a moment must never be spent in vain by those who possess splendor;
one should never depart at an improper time from the presence of the great.
Nor should one create an obstacle for a married couple when they are in a private place.
Whether he be a great man, a lord, or even a god, he who causes suffering to another shall himself experience that suffering.
Indeed, he who creates obstacles for a husband and wife shall surely meet with obstacles himself.
Thus, cries of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods and among men alike.
A virtuous king named Śaṅkara-Śivarāja reigned in the city of Kailāsadhāma on the Himālayas, on the banks of the Gaṇḍakī.
In the house of Kṛṣṇasiṃha, he had a mind-born son, like a being of divine origin.
The Lord was Mahādivya, endowed with great sovereignty and possessing the splendor of Arjuna.
And Satī was born as the daughter of the ruler of Ṣaṇmāṇḍavyapura; she became the goddess Jānakī, who was equal to Śivā in both name and virtues. (65–66)
Satī and Śambhu, both remembering their former births, grew up like two gods;
joined together once more by the rites of marriage,
they were united at the most auspicious time, like Speech and its Meaning, as residents of Kailāsa.
Thus, at the foot of the Gaṇḍakī on the snowy mountain, on the riverbank, in their own kingdom,
in the city that is the abode of Kailāsa, the two attained sovereignty.
Then Kṛṣṇā, her friend Dhenupāla, Candra, and likewise Jaya—
They descended upon that city of Kailāsa on the Himālaya mountain.
Śivarāja’s younger brother became Dhenupāla,
and his daughter was the virtuous Kṛṣṇā.
Candrāditya was his younger brother, and Jayakumāra was his younger brother.
Due to the occurrence of a common curse, their family remained as one;
all were devoted to Brahman, established in the Supreme Spirit, and always dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
Devoted to meditation, yoga, and austerity, possessing knowledge of the Dharma and free from passion,
they are constantly engaged in the sacrifice of Brahman, established in the nature of Brahman, and devoid of deceit.
Though endowed with all the outward marks, they remain unrecognized by men.
And those great devotees of the Lord, whose duty was the protection of their subjects,
were always intent upon the service of Kṛṣṇa as if they were in Vaikuṇṭha itself;
they wandered through the regions of Nīpālaya and the snowy mountains.
They exist with divine forms through the perfections of natural yoga;
they exist in human forms through actions such as those resulting from curses.
When they fell due to a curse, at that time Hari entered into their hearts.
The Lord became distressed by the suffering of His devotee;
nevertheless, He was unable to say anything else to Śrī, since Hari is known as the embodiment of pure goodness (sattva).
He endured all the suffering of His devotee and maintained silence for a moment.
Śaṅkara and the others were capable of cursing Lakṣmī in the presence of Hari;
nevertheless, being devotees who regarded him as their servant, they did not curse that Ramā then.
She who is the mother of the worlds [could not endure] anything other than the touch of Hari.
They cursed us who had the form of obstacles; their followers considered that to be appropriate.
Having thus understood the will of Hari as determined by their chosen deity, they accepted it as a source of happiness, even though it took the form of a punishment from their Lord. (2.101.80–81)

Faith in Śrī Hari, the granting of boons by Him, the words of Hari, the entrusting of one's self to Hari, and total dependence upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord— [these must exist] in every way, even when one possesses great wealth or even when one possesses sovereign power. (82)
Day and night, their service was indeed directed toward Hari.
The intellect of devotees remains steadfast even in great calamities;
and theirs, moreover, became firmly established in the Supreme Soul.
Even in the event of total ruin, may the Blessed One not depart from my mind.
For whatever is favorable to Hari is indeed favorability itself;
and whatever is unfavorable to Hari is indeed unfavorability itself.
"Since this is the duty of servants for those who have sought refuge, and certainly not otherwise," thinking thus, Śambhu and the others could not endure the words of Śrī.
Satī, the Vaiṣṇavī devotee, Rudrāṇī, the bringer of dissolution—[she too could not endure it]. (86–87)
How could she endure a curse if she were not indeed devoted to Hari?
For she knows Lakṣmī to be her mother, and she is indeed dear to her preceptor.
One should bow down to the wife of a preceptor and never provoke her to anger.

If the wife of the guru carries out his command without hesitation, she too must be protected to the best of one's ability; the word "no" must certainly not be spoken. In this regard, Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of his master, [is the authority]. (2.101.90)
The Guru is the venerable speaker of the Vedas, and his beloved wife must certainly not be disparaged;
for that virtuous woman knows everything arising from the interruption of their pleasure.
Because she experienced all such suffering in every kalpa, she did not utter a curse.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the remover of distress,
spoke to the one named Hemaśālāyana regarding the cause of his curse;
and Lakṣmī related her own domestic history to the female cakravāka birds.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of the Six—Kṛṣṇa, Dhenu-pāla, Candra, Āditya, Jayāditya, and others—who were servants [of the Lord], as well as Satī and Śaṅkara, into the world of mortals due to the breaking of the pleasure of Lakṣmī’s reclining with Nārāyaṇa and the subsequent curse of Lakṣmī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the Blessed One while He was reclining upon Lakṣmī in Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Chapter 101. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 102 [Author:
Chapter 103 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to what occurred in Vaikuṇṭha after the curse, which took place between Kamalā and Kṛṣṇa; I shall tell it to you. Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [spoke] to the sage Hemāyana.
Whatever the maiden spoke, and whatever the female cakravāka birds spoke—that I shall tell you all; listen with a one-pointed mind. Having heard the curse, Hari, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, Janārdana— [3]

Then Kṛṣṇa, his own soul pained by the suffering of his devotee, did not speak to Kamalā; instead, he reflected within himself upon that which was consistent with justice and auspicious. "Oh, how strange is the diversity of individual manifestation, having reached such a distinct state! || 4 ||
I always gratify this Lakṣmī who dwells within my heart.
Even when I leave her far away for a moment, she is never satisfied with my great joy; indeed, she speaks as if she were restless.
For the sake of my devotees, that virtuous woman cannot endure separation from me for even a moment;
she cannot endure it for a long duration.
Just as I grant happiness to myself, I likewise always grant it to Śrī.
Just as my separation from Śrī is undesirable to me, so too is it for her attendants.
(8) But this is the very nature of women: if their own purpose is not fulfilled, in an instant they become like strangers and yield only evil fruit. (9)
"Even though Lakṣmī is not a devotee, she should never be abandoned;
for she is my most excellent devotee, exceedingly devoted, my wife, and my own dear friend.
Just as Śaṅkara is a devotee, so too are Satī and Kṛṣṇikā devotees. (2.102.10)

Jaya, Candra, Dhenupāla, and then Ramā, the best among devotees. Nevertheless, for the sake of demonstrating affection toward the foremost of devotees, my devotees are always far more dear to me than even Lakṣmī. || 12 ||

Even if Lakṣmī, though dear to me, were to cause suffering to my devotees, I would renounce her for the sake of my devotees; Kamalā herself is the very example for this. In this matter, I shall provide an illustration accordingly.
"May the fruit of my curse befall Lakṣmī as an example;
and may the instruction be true so that she never acts thus again anywhere.
Having reflected in this way, the Blessed One experienced grief. (14–15)
Distressed by the suffering of his devotee, he himself became sorrowful; he neither spoke nor looked upon him.
Having become as if mindless, he did not even smile in the slightest. Greatly agitated, he did not look upward even with his mind, and he appeared utterly despondent.
Just as grief is experienced at the death of a mother, at the loss of a wife,
or at the death of an only son, so too is it felt [regarding this];
as if, in a mere moment, she will leave the house and go away somewhere.
Just as one might become broken-hearted upon the loss of all one's possessions,
so is Nārāyaṇa seen when he has attained dispassion;
he is like one who has conquered the assembly of his senses and subdued his internal organ and the rest.
And Nārāyaṇa remained on the further shore of Māyā;
then Lakṣmī, filled with many playful gestures and amorous expressions, laughed and,
taking his hand in her own, repeatedly pressed him and kissed him.
Having dragged Nārāyaṇa, he desired to lead him into his house; however,
the Supreme Lord then became like a corpse, like a stone,
and like an insentient object due to the grief for his devotee.

"If that house which provides a refuge and happiness for my own devotees should instead become a place where the suffering of a curse arises for those devotees, what would be the purpose of my dwelling there? Having reflected thus, he spoke to her.
"Do not touch me here, O lady of beautiful thighs; do not cause me vain distress.
Where there is a curse upon my devotees in their home, there I have no desire.
Go back to your bed, O virtuous one; this bed of mine brings me no pleasure."
The great devotees have been cursed; what indeed could be more painful than this?
(26) Guests are always to be honored, and among them, those who are my own devotees—those who have surrendered all their possessions for my sake—are always to be worshipped and honored by me. (27)
O Lakṣmī! For the sake of my devotees, I am always spinning this garland;
and for the sake of my devotees, I descend into the worlds at all times. I am Nara and Nārāyaṇa, appearing as ascetics for the sake of my devotees.
In the Ocean of Milk, on the White Land, and in the Imperishable Field (Akṣarakṣetra), I am Nārāyaṇa. And in Goloka, in Vaikuṇṭha, in the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta),
and in the Abode of Immortality— wherever my devotees dwell, O Lotus-born One, there I abide.
I dwell in the homes of my devotees and sport together with my devotees;
Vaikuṇṭha is my abode, for nothing else is pleasing to me.
Even if my own home were the cause of suffering for my devotees, [I would abandon it].
Then indeed, the name "Vaikuṇṭha" attains its true meaning for him.
For if that which is known as my divine abode—which bestows eternal bliss—is a place that gives pain and grants birth, what "vikuṇṭhatā" (freedom from distress) could there be? || 32-33 ||
Even there, the curse of Śaṅkara, the God of gods who is dear to me, and of my devoted wife Satī— a curse that brings birth as a human—
what greater misery than this could there be, so terrible and productive of ill repute?
Of Kṛṣṇā, your friend, and also of Jayacandra and Candrakā,
as well as the slaying of Dhenupāla and his attendant—
O beloved, how is it that your mind has become like this, performing such an untimely dance? || 35-36 ||
"You have spoken what is improper, being opposed to the devotion of your husband;
never before have you acted in this way toward Śaṅkara.
What can I do now in a household joined by a woman who is antagonistic?"
Food, such as sweet and savory delicacies, becomes like poison without rice; (38) a drink rich in coolness and fragrance becomes like fire without rice;
even gentle silk clothing becomes like arrows without rice. (39)

Without a devotee, ornaments such as gold and jewels become like fish; fragrant oils, garments, and the like become like mud when not offered to a devotee. Without a devotee within my heart, every pleasure becomes like a flame.
"O Lakṣmī, apart from Śambhu, I am burning due to the power of a curse.
That curse of mine was a curse from a devotee, and that curse of yours is likewise mine;
because we are of the nature of half and quarter portions [of the Divine], it causes suffering—of this there is no doubt. (41-42)
You do not know the supreme greatness of my devotees;
Sanatkumāra knows the exalted majesty of devotion.
If his two eyes did not behold my devotees standing before me, [he would not know this].
I shall always cast those two [eyes] out from my globes and keep them far away.
If my head does not bow down before this yogi of devotion, I shall cut it off from my neck and hurl it far away; of this there is no doubt.
If my two ears do not hear the words of my devotees, I shall cut them off at the root and cast them far away; of this there is no doubt.
If my nose does not perceive the fragrance of my devotee, then—

O Lotus-born One, if the tongue does not constantly sing the hymns of the devotees, or if the palate does not seek the flavor offered by the devotee, I shall cut off the nose from its root and cast it far away. (47–48)
Then, having pulled it out from its root, I shall forever abandon my tongue,
if the two lips do not receive the betel and other offerings given by devotees,
or if the teeth do not chew what has been offered by the devotees. (49)
Then, having cut off my lips and teeth with weapons, I shall indeed abandon them.
(50) If my two hands are not useful for the service of my own devotees, I shall cut them off at the root and cast them away like pieces of wood. (51)
If my chest were not useful for embracing devotees, then I would tear out my chest and cast it forever into a pit.
If devotees were never to dwell within my heart, [I would do the same]. (52)
I shall indeed pull out my heart along with its blood and consume it.
(53) If you do not permit my stomach to digest the food offered by your devotees, I shall quickly tear everything apart and cast it away; of this there is no doubt. (54)
If the touch of my devotees is not pleasing to you,
I shall quickly tear this body from my frame and cast it into the great fire.
If my virility, strength, and phallus do not bring happiness to my devotees, [then let them perish].
Then, having destroyed all that, I shall bring about my own impotence.
If my thighs are not even for the purpose of being sat upon by devotees,
then, for the sake of my devotees, I shall indeed become a headless trunk (kabandha).
If my feet do not indeed go toward my devotees, then having cut them off with an axe, I shall surely become footless.
If my body does not manifest for the sake of the happiness of my devotees, [then I shall likewise be punished]. 58.
Having thus kindled a fire, I shall surely reduce [the world] to ashes.

(59) Furthermore, if my qualities such as intellect and the rest were not dependent upon devotion to Me, I would abandon those qualities and, being devoid of attributes, dwell in the dense forest. (2.102.60)
What is the use of saying much more to you in this matter?
If you act as an obstructer of devotion, causing distress to devotees, creating obstacles to devotion, or even inflicting suffering upon devotees and opposing their peace; ||| 61 ||
I abandon you; then what else would I not abandon?
I abandon everything, my very all, for the sake of my devotees; I have no desire for this myself.
Know, O Lotus-born One, that if a devotee perishes, everything of mine perishes.
Know that when my devotee is protected, everything is protected by me.
Oh, where indeed will such a human being as Śrī Śaṅkara appear?
Oh, where will his beloved Satī, a human woman, appear?
"Alas! Where will Kṛṣṇā, my dear maidservant and devotee, be born?
Alas, O Rame, even Jaya and Candrā, though they are cowherds, shall by your curse be born upon the earth in a place of misery. || 65-66 ||
"As long as I do not know the state of these living beings, I find no delight;
until then, there is no happiness for me. I shall go where they also go.
Having said this, he abandoned Kamalā and abandoned Śrīkamalākara.
Having abandoned his beautiful lion-throne, his palace, and his radiant abode, Hari completely renounced Vaikuṇṭha and all objects of affection;
becoming despondent, he departed even after leaving Garuḍa behind. (68–69)
Without even looking back, he proceeded toward the earth within the cosmic egg;
he did not see Lakṣmī, his most beloved life-breath, who was crying out piteously, "O Lord!
O Lord! Śrī Hari went to the earth as she continued to call out thus.

Invisible and with an unmanifest body, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, descended here upon this earth at Maṇijanya, in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, that field of the Imperishable. (71–72)
The Supreme Brahman, who transcends the imperishable and is the director of all incarnations,
was then present in the field known as Kuṅkumavāpī, in the house of Śrī Kambharā,
within the home of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, which was endowed with divine opulence.
He descended even for the purpose of Nārāyaṇa’s arrival. Having come and attained absorption in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, he remained near Lake Aśva.
Then, by the command of the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he assumed a disguised form and set out toward the north on earth to search for [him] in the region of Nīpālaya,
situated within the Himalayan foothills.

Having searched for the young prince Śivarāja, the devotee of Śaṅkara, in the kingdom of Kailāsadhāma, he remained there beyond the range of perception. Then, in order to seek out Satī, he went to the city of Ṣaṇmāṇḍavya.
There, that virtuous woman became a maiden by the name of Jānakī.
There also dwells Nārāyaṇa, invisible and fond of his followers.
From their marriage were born Kṛṣṇā, Jaya, and Candraka.
Dhenupāla, the brother of Śivarāja, was stationed there;
and the Lord Nārāyaṇa dwells together with his devotees,
remaining unmanifest, eating, sporting, and staying there constantly.
In one place he comes to the syllable and the field of Aśvasarovara;
in another, he remains there with devotion in the palace of King Śiva.
Thus the Blessed One, having abandoned Lakṣmī, did so solely for the sake of his devotees.
And Brahmā arrived in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) to dwell among the devotees.
Then Lakṣmī, who had gone to Vaikuṇṭha, realized [the situation] and left her own [place];
likewise, Nārāyaṇa abandoned Vaikuṇṭha, his throne, his splendor, and his abode.
He departed for a long journey for the sake of his devotees while remaining in a human birth;
there, in his empty house, he grieved in many ways and wept like one bereft,
praising him repeatedly with his voice and confessing his own faults.
I am indeed the fickle Goddess of Fortune (Lakṣmī), who follows after the faults of suffering;
I am always the cause of pride and other such vices, providing no assistance to the wretched.
My dwelling in the houses of those who commit sins against others is considered by me in many ways to be a source of reproach.
It is the abode of faults such as violence and falsehood, and it nourishes unrighteousness; it is the place of deceit, hypocrisy, and sensual enjoyment, where the venerable are insulted;
it is the loss of virtue, the loss of purity, craving, passion, and excessive greed. (88)
Theft, violence, and verbal abuse—these are the faults arising from my influence.
I am fickle, unstable, and nowhere constant; I cause mental distress and am ever intent on seizing everything. And yet, O abode of compassion! [2.102.90]
The Blessed One, overcome by supreme compassion, protects me within his own heart;
devoted to mercy, he does not even enjoy his own pleasures after casting me out.
Having given everything to me, Kṛṣṇa himself has departed from his home.
And what kind of straightforwardness does he possess that it causes me no suffering?
He does not slight me even slightly; he tolerates my lack of discipline.
Dependent upon my devotion, he always protects me, his devoted one, though I am impure. (92–93)
Although my devotion as a wife was not perfect, the Blessed One himself,
being devoted to his own wife, protects me even more than he does himself;
he eats nothing and drinks not even water without me.

Indeed, wherever cooked food has been prepared by anyone other than me, Keśava neither sees it, nor accepts it, nor eats it at all. O Hari, only when my entry among the cooks occurs will you [be able to eat]. || 95–96 ||
Hari partakes of the food offering only when it is obtained from a worthy person, never otherwise.
[He accepts] clothing, jewels, water, a vessel, betel, food, collyrium, ornaments, sandalwood paste, gold, a vehicle, a mount, and lordship. (97)

"The seat, the bed, the dwelling, the offerings, the fruit, and the water—having offered all these to Me, this My Lord has indeed enjoyed them. Oh, upon reflection, Kṛṣṇa is the most excellent, for He remains steadfast in His vow toward His wife. (98–99)
"Though fickle, she is a vessel of affection; I, a devoted wife, am not like her.
Oh, what universal good fortune! For without my beloved, everything is indeed fruitless—Vaikuṇṭha itself, all wealth, and every object of enjoyment. (2.102.10)
Male and female servants, gardens, palaces, and parklands;
mansions, temple-turrets, elephants, horses, chariots, and cows;
ornaments, garments, and the drinking of nectar—all these are indeed fruitless without a beloved. (101–102)
"My beloved has departed from my home solely because of my own fault.
Alas! Why have I not died? Why do I not become a corpse?
Without my beloved, I am a living corpse, for life is utterly fruitless. (10.3)

This daughter of Nārāyaṇa is Urvaśī’s daughter;
by the curse of Sanatsujāta, she has remained in the body of a female ruddy goose.
Desiring release from this curse, she wishes to perform penance. (2.104.70)
O monkey, I am Lakṣmī herself, and I shall go to that place where Hanumān’s hermitage stands upon a peak with deep caves;
there flows the Golden Gaṅgā, which takes refuge in the Kalpavallī creeper.
"Therefore, I shall go into your presence for the sake of penance, so that Hari may be obtained.
Upon hearing these words of Ramā, Hanumān quickly bowed at his mother's feet and immediately considered it a great fortune.
Upon hearing that Śivarāja’s daughter was Jānakī, he immediately attained great joy and became a devoted servant.
He was the son of Śaṅkara himself, Hanumān, the best of monkeys.
Knowing her to be Śrī, the sister of Śambhu’s daughter, he was filled with an abundance of bliss.
Recognizing her as Urvaśī, the daughter of his own sister, he greeted her joyfully and led her to the entire hermitage there, which was adorned with groves of plantain trees.
On a small mountain plateau, in a cave that was always pleasant,
endowed with wish-fulfilling creepers and possessed of all supernatural powers—
free from fear and like a kingdom— the monkey gave them a dwelling.
He gave him a fire-drill and a sacrificial fire-pit as a source of auspicious refuge;
he also gave him a water-pot, bark garments, a seat, a rosary for recitation, pools of cold and warm water, and fruits, roots, and water. (78–79)
Then Hanūmat gave her an image of Nārāyaṇa with four arms, as well as the entirety of all ritual offerings for his sister. Thus, in that land protected by him, Lakṣmī became a sovereign queen.
From the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, they began their primary austerity, consisting of recitation (japa).
[81] "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā"—with this mantra, they performed its recitation with rosaries day and night. [82]

They both performed their ablutions three times daily in the Kāñcanagaṅgā; indeed, having bowed to the venerable brother, the monkey, they did so every morning. Then, having worshipped Hari according to the regular rites, they proceeded further.
Having performed oblations in the fire, they joyfully practiced their recitations;
for about a month, they took only roots as food once a day.
Sleeping on the ground at night, they performed the worship of Hari.
Then, in the second month, they made fruit their food;
in the third month, they respectfully made leaves their food;
and in the fourth month, they eagerly made flowers their food. (86)
In the fifth month, they both drank the water of the clouds from the sky;
in the sixth month, they joyfully subsisted on vapors;
and in the seventh month, those two virtuous women practiced the consumption of air for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
In the eighth month, they remained endowed with consciousness for a mere breath;
in the ninth month, they stood like trees on one foot;
and in the tenth month, those two bodies became like pieces of wood.
Then, in the eleventh month, the Fire born of asceticism arose,
a terrifying being of great flames through its own power;
causing destruction, it pervaded all directions within the cosmic egg.
With intense burns of a corresponding nature, Hanumān reached the end of his life and met with a miracle while chanting "Rāma, Kṛṣṇa.
There, a servant devoted to Hari was engaged in guarding him.
Having perceived the extreme intensity of Lakṣmī’s asceticism,
and having observed the supreme limit of Urvaśī’s penance as well,
Nārāyaṇa himself arrived there immediately.
He arrived on foot out of love to behold his wife’s austerity,
and he came to bestow the fruit of her penance and to bring it to its conclusion.
And having beheld Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who was like ten million suns—
Hanumān performed a most excellent welcome by prostrating like a staff.
He offered Nārāyaṇa a seat, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), worship with fruits and flowers, excellent food offerings, and cool water.
Śrī Narāyaṇa did not partake of the food offering nor the water,
as long as Lakṣmī and Urvaśī had not yet consumed the fruit and the water.
Then, having quickly gone into their presence, the Supreme Lord spoke.
Oh, what kind of supreme austerity must Lakṣmī and Urvaśī have performed,
that from their bodies flames indeed flow forth like the sun—
capable of burning the cosmic egg and resembling the great dissolution!
"Today the remedy for the curse has been fulfilled; nothing remains.
Having enlightened these two, I shall grant them whatever they desire that bestows happiness.
Thinking thus, the Blessed One spoke to Hanumān.
"Go and bring water from the golden Gaṅgā for the sake of these two;
bring it quickly in this vessel, O King of Devotees, do not delay.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One remained silent for a moment, absorbed in meditative concentration.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
in His very form as Nārāyaṇa, arrived to bestow the fruit [of her penance].
Upon hearing this, Hema, Śālāyana, and the others were struck with supreme wonder.
"Ah! How supreme was the penance of Urvaśī for the sake of [attaining] Lakṣmī!

(105). Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Lakṣmī and Urvaśī’s Departure for the Hermitage of Hanumān on the Himālaya to Perform Penance after Receiving the Command of Their Mother and Father, Their Austerities, and the Direct Arrival of Nārāyaṇa There at the End of the Year to Bestow the Fruit of their Penance," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
