Chapter 106 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall later relate to you what occurred, that which Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke to Hemaśālāyana.
Taking his water-pot, the illustrious Hanumān traveled through the path of the sky and quickly brought the purifying water of the golden Gaṅgā.
He gave it immediately to Nārāyaṇa, who in turn offered a reverential salutation with joined palms.
Meanwhile, as the two ascetic women became emaciated,
the movement of consciousness from the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) occurred in the hearts of both.
Their vital breath (prāṇa) also ceased to circulate in the body, and they then opened their eyes.
They beheld the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, before them;
seeing Puruṣottama, they attained supreme joy.
He wore a golden crown adorned with jewels, gems, and pearls.
He bore upon his own head matted locks that were curved and glossy;
he wore earrings in his ears, a crest and forehead-mark on his sides, a lunar tilaka upon his forehead, and auspicious collyrium in his eyes. (6–7)
Surrounding his face was a white, radiant halo;
his dark complexion was graced by a smiling countenance and adorned with a necklace and the Kaustubha gem.
He was further embellished with waist-bands, chains, bracelets, rings, and other ornaments.
Adorned with rings, bracelets, garments, flowers, and garlands—[I bow to] the Supreme Lord, Janārdana, who is the Supreme Brahman;
the abode of all beauty, delightful, youthful, and golden-hued. (2.105.10)
Resplendent with the luster of a *campaka* flower, adorned with divine garments purified by fire,
and decorated with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, and a forest garland—
the Lord of Kamalā has indeed arrived to bestow his boon.
[He saw] the Lord of devotees, an ocean of compassion, peaceful and enchanting;
(12) again sprinkling him with water, [he saw him] pacifying the fire of his asceticism, and calling out "Kamala! and "Urvaśī! again and again. (13)
"O Kamalā, O dear one, O daughter Urvaśī, I have come to grant you both success; choose a boon!
Indeed, you two have undergone great hardship for my sake. (14)
"I am pleased; today I grant you the boon you desire.
O Kamalā and Cakravākī, desist from your ascetic yoga.
Let this drought end this very day, for I grant you both your most cherished wish. (15–16)
Kamalā said: "O Blessed One, accept me as your own wife according to the rites of marriage; indeed, forgive my transgression.
"Nevertheless, marry me, the daughter of King Śiva, according to the sacred rites.
"So be it," Hari replied. "Go to your father’s house, my dear;
when twelve years have passed, your father, mother, and kinsmen [will be there]."
"These sisters of yours will indeed depart for the purpose of residing in Kāśī.
There, having arrived, I shall take you, O blameless one;
there I shall marry you and lead you to my own abode."
"Drink water, eat fruit, sit on my lap; indeed, I am delighted.
Having been addressed thus, she abandoned her asceticism and went to the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Sitting on his lap, Ramā embraced that beloved for a moment.

Having set aside his daughter, the Lotus-born Lord did not accept the fruit and the water that had been offered. Then he said to Urvaśī, "O daughter, come quickly; eat this fruit and drink the water."
The daughter said to her father: "I shall accept neither fruit nor water.
O Father, if you are pleased with me, and if my penance is complete; if you are the granter of the desires of your devotees, and if there is nothing that ought not to be given. (24-25)
"O bearer of water, here on this peak—a place for ascetic penance—bring me other water; I shall not drink what is offered by embodied beings.
If you do not give me water here in this manner, then I shall not drink."
I would give up my life here on this peak before you, with nothing but water between us.

O Father, your name shall become renowned as "Viśvambhara" (the Sustainer of the Universe), and you shall be known by the name "Bhaktavatsala" (Loving toward Devotees) because of your separation from Śrī for the sake of your devotee.

"My mother Ramā has abandoned Lakṣmī, who resides in her own abode. Therefore, if I am truly devoted and a worthy recipient of affection, I ask: impelled by parental love, what will you do? Let me see. (29)
"I shall collect rainwater here in a vessel;
I will drink that, and by this, O Father, may there be liberation from the curse for me.
Having spoken thus, the daughter Urvaśī did not return to her father's lap for the sake of water. (2.105.30–31)
"He renounces everything for the sake of his devotees; what then would he not renounce for my sake?
If my father has attained such subjection to devotion for me, then the Blessed One himself [would surely come].
Having reflected thus, he did not go near his father by force.
Thereupon the father Nārāyaṇa said to his daughter regarding the acquisition of water:
"When the rain has gathered in the valley, the water will reach the peaks;
once the rainwater has risen, it will flow from the summits down to the lower lands. (33–34)
"O daughter, all living beings would be submerged in waters and a universal dissolution would occur; you alone would incur that sin. Therefore, come here and drink.
Urvaśī said, "O Blessed One, your word regarding the granting of this boon [is final]."
"If your word granting my desire is true, then bring water here.
If your word is not true, go away, O father; I shall perform penance right here, and I will drink water only from this place, nowhere else."
The drink situated in an unworthy vessel is not stable; it is not a drink that remains steady, nor indeed is it the divine drop falling from the sky.
If I am your devotee, then fulfill the word of a devotee.
If you fail to fulfill my request, you will incur the sin arising from untruthful speech.
A false statement that grants what is desired should never be uttered.
O father, why is it that everything done for the sake of Śaṅkara is not likewise done for my sake?
"O Father, everything was done for the sake of Kṛṣṇa; why was nothing done for my sake?
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Janārdana, abode of mercy!
If you do not grant me water here on this peak while I am your devotee," [41]

"I shall perform fierce austerity that reduces all of saṃsāra to ashes. (42) If many embodied beings are destroyed, sin will accrue to you, just as my own sin would have arisen had the world been submerged in water. (43)
What more need be said here? You are the destroyer of sin.
Even so, if you cause fear of sin to prevail here, O Father, who indeed will worship you for the sake of destroying that very sin?

Who indeed will provide for your needs—flower gardens, sacrificial offerings, and delicious foods—to behold you, if your sin is not destroyed? O timid one, if the destroyer of sin becomes afraid, to whom shall the sinner go for refuge? (45–46)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "Drink this, if you wish to drink.
O daughter, the water requested by you will not come there.
Lakṣmī, if you wish to drink, then you yourself must drink this water."
"But I shall go elsewhere; do as you please, O beautiful lady!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished from that place in an instant.
Lakṣmī did not drink even a drop of water without her daughter.
"The daughter did not drink the water as she wished because it was not offered to her.
Thinking thus, they both performed penance once more regarding the non-drinking of the water.
Indeed, the mother was unable to go home without her daughter.
Once again, they performed a fierce and intense penance for the sake of water.
Having resolved, "He gives everything for the sake of his devotees; why would he not give us water?", they remained thirsty while established in their austerity.
Having attained oneness with Nārāyaṇa through the means of self-restraint,
they performed severe austerity until their throats, lips, and palates were parched.
For one month, they practiced intense penance through the yoga of oneness.

Then, due to the thirst of his daughter and likewise his wife, Hari’s own thirst increased day by day, and a burning sensation arose in his throat. Although he was made to drink nectar-like water repeatedly by his male and female devotees, [his thirst remained]. 54–55.
Again and again, Nārāyaṇa drinks handfuls of water;
yet even so, no cessation of his thirst ever occurs.
[Whether] in Śvetadvīpa, in the Ocean of Milk, in Vaikuṇṭha, or in the Badarī forest.
In the syllable, in the immortal, in the unmanifest, and wherever else it may be—
Nārāyaṇa himself dwells there in every way.
Even when drinking an immeasurable amount of strength, his thirst is never truly quenched.

Having drunk the water himself, Nārāyaṇa became exhausted; his belly was filled with waters, yet his throat repeatedly grew parched. Such was the great austerity performed by the thirsty Urvaśī as well as by Lakṣmī.
Nārāyaṇa increases with speed and finds no peace;
scorched by the fire of the fever of thirst, he behaves as if deprived of his senses.
Rising up again and again, he falls down and runs about like one who is mad.
Thirsty, he falls into a swoon and finds no comfort in sleep;
rising at times, he repeatedly falls into water or onto the ground.
Even when attended by devoted servants, winds, and waters, [he remains distressed]. (62)
Even when sprinkled with water, that Supreme Lord does not attain coolness.
And so it is for the Inner Self of all; when extreme thirst and parching have arisen within, all bodies indeed—whether stationary or moving—suffer accordingly. (63–64)
In the three worlds,
the lords, sages, gods, ancestors, humans, birds, animals, aquatic creatures,
and even the Daityas and all others everywhere, underwent extreme dehydration born of thirst. (65)
Stricken by the defects of thirst, they wander in confusion, running about and falling down.

(66) At that time, the entire triple world became parched with thirst and was on the verge of destruction; for when the hunger for water and the act of drinking are frustrated, there is total ruin upon the loss of sustenance. (67)
If there is no drinking of water, there will be a parching of the throat; if there is drinking, there will likewise be desiccation.
In either case, the destruction of the worlds is imminent.
Then Brahmā, Hara, and Viṣṇu, having entered into meditative absorption (samādhi), [acted].
Having understood the cause of their thirst— the heat born of longing for Rāma—
they quickly went to the earth, to Saurāṣṭra, that imperishable land,
to the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, where Anādinārāyaṇa resides.
The Lord resides in his own abode within the field of Kuṅkumavāpī;
he is intensely thirsty, fainting from the thirst for all incarnations.
Even Brahmā and the other gods are thirsty, though they are subject to death.
In whatever way possible, they fell at the feet of the Blessed One;
with their throats, lips, and palates parched, as if they had reached the very moment of death,
they then addressed the Supreme Lord with broken voices.
"O Lord, quickly bring water from the Yamunā for Ramā and Urvaśī—
water that has not been produced by drought, which is not contained in a vessel, untouched by others, and not offered as an oblation. Otherwise, the entire world will surely perish in a moment."
When total destruction has arisen, the loss of a small portion is beneficial.
If that [destruction] is seen to be imminent, then by sacrificing a small part one may perceive the rest;
quickly, through rain, on the peak of the snowy mountain at the monkey’s hermitage.
"O performer of deeds, cause water to reach the place of Urvaśī’s penance.
Thus entreated by the gods, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
quickly summoned the clouds and commanded them to rain.
Those twelve clouds, having gathered together, sent down rain;
they completely inundated the valleys, the foothills, and the fields situated amidst mountain ramparts, with waters reaching up to the very peaks, as if at the time of universal dissolution.
A great and terrible slaughter of beasts and birds occurred within the valley;
the forest regions were submerged, and Hanumān’s hermitage was submerged as well. An entire area ten yojanas in extent was completely submerged.
The water was held to reach as far as the mountain peaks within the vessel of the earth.
During the dissolution, the lowlands, the depressions, the valleys, the ravines,
and the mountain clefts were all submerged by the waters.
Just as water from the ocean reaches the feet of Lakṣmī and Urvaśī,
so too did [the water] reach their peaks and stand before them in the place of penance.
Then the gods went to Nārāyaṇa and entreated him repeatedly.
Then, for the purpose of drinking water, they both drank from it;
and the thirst of the Nārāyaṇas, as well as that of all embodied beings—both stationary and moving—was instantly quenched in every respect. (84–85)
By the desire of Hari, the waters quickly became tranquil;
divine clouds vanished from the earth and dissolved away.
That place of his austerity became renowned as Śrīśṛṅga and Urvaśīśṛṅga.
The forest became renowned as Lakṣmīvana and Cakravākīvana.
The Gaṅgā known as Lakṣmīgaṅgā and Urvaśīgaṅgā became the famous Kāñcanī Gaṅgā.
There was also Hanumadgahvara, which was named Nārāyaṇaguhā.
Then the lake became the Lakṣmīsarovara;
and the Kāñcanagaṅgā-tīrtha became indeed superior even to the Brahmagaṅgā.
Truly, the waters from the Kuśī had entered into the Kāñcanagaṅgā.
In the low-lying regions, the lack of fortitude among the people arose from the sight of the water;
indeed, a dissolution by water would occur there, whereas elsewhere they must depart.
Thus, a great clamor arose in those lands because of the waters of the rivers.
Under that pretext, the people then went to Kāśī, Śrī Puruṣottama,
the Kaurava field, and the Kṣetra, on account of pilgrimage festivals.
Śivarāja, Jānakī, Kṛṣṇā, Jaya, and Candraka—
Having bestowed the kingdom upon Dhenupāla, they then departed for Kāśī.
Those who were male and female servants in other lands became residents of Vaikuṇṭha;
having arrived in Kāśī, they too manifested themselves in the north.
They dwelt on the delightful bank of the Varaṇā in mango groves,
which were filled with fruit-bearing trees, fragrant with flowering creepers and the like,
and beautified by gardens occupied by the armies of the King of Kāśī.
In the golden palace of the King of Kāśī on the banks of the Varaṇā,
provided with every necessity, they were honored by the King of Kāśī and treated with great hospitality through welcomes and hundreds of elephant-drawn chariots. ||96-97||
And also by the Bahuvādins and others, by hundreds of thousands of human beings and gods,
by learned Brāhmaṇas and those belonging to Brahmā, headed by Bṛhaspati;
and also by goddesses, Śaktis, and countless heroic Gaṇas.
The family of King Śiva, protected by men, was honored by all the holy fords, ascetics, virtuous women, and hosts of celestial nymphs;
they had their eternal residence in a seven-storied palace constructed of gold.
In that place endowed with wish-fulfilling creepers, Viśvanātha of Kāśī himself, the husband of Satī, honored Śambhu along with Annapūrṇikā; likewise,
his female servants and male servants were the family members who bore the very form of Śambhu.
Having embraced Śivarāja and Śiva, he offered them a welcome;
he presented the madhuparka and nectar-like foods, and rejoiced exceedingly.
Thus, by the desire of Hari, this family took up residence there.
Everything occurs according to Time, just as Kṛṣṇa desires.
The Vaiṣṇavas, the male attendants (pārṣadas), the other attendants,
and those women who were human became honored by the King of Kāśī.
Honored by Śambhu, they dwelt within the royal palaces (105).
They remained there constantly remembering Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
as well as Nara-Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa (106).
And the goddesses remained there, remembering Lakṣmī and the female ascetic;
Rādhikā, Urvaśī, and Lakṣmī likewise remembered their families.
The maiden, who was equal to Ramā, was released from the curse of Cakravākī.
"Endowed with the very form of Urvaśī, these two did not [abandon] their father Hari.

(108) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, when the life-breath of Lakṣmī and Cakravākī was restored by water consecrated by Nārāyaṇa during their penance, the female ruddy goose (Cakravākī) chose to drink water on the mountain peak and thereafter sought liberation. Hari, having submerged the region with rains, gave water upon the peak; having drunk it, she was released from the curse due to the fear of the rains.

Chapter One Hundred and Five: Description of the Arrival in Kāśī of the Vaikuṇṭha attendants and others in human form belonging to the family of Śivarāja, their residence on the banks of the Varaṇā, in the palaces of the King of Kāśī, and in the mango groves, as well as the honors bestowed upon them by Śambhu.
Chapter One Hundred and Six: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Section Two (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 106.
[The author: Chapter 107.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, in this manner Hari [spoke] to the sage Hemaśailāyana.
And he related the narrative concerning the female ruddy goose seeking water.
That celestial beauty Urvaśī was indeed released from her curse;
having bowed to her father Nārāyaṇa and her mother Ramā, [she departed].
Formerly, she went to the world of Indra because she was entrusted to him;
then Lakṣmī indeed spoke to her own beloved:
"Hanumān protected me while I was established in penance along with my son."
"O Lord, a boon should be granted by you to that Hanumān.
When he had spoken thus, Śrī Hari said, "Hanumān, choose what you desire.
The lord of monkeys chose a name whose meaning would always be true to its essence.
"By your grace, may I possess the nature of a monkey so that I may continuously drink the eternal bliss from the form of Nārāyaṇa—may this be my purpose.
Furthermore, may there be unswerving devotion toward you, O Nārāyaṇa. (6)
Wherever there is a discourse on Nārāyaṇa, there lies the very life of my vital breaths.
(7) The nectar of the stories of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and also the nectar of the stories from the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*. (8)
Wherever it may be, let my presence truly be there;
and wherever those devotees sing, let my abode be there as well.
Wherever your temple may be, let my station be at its doorway.
"May she remain eternal for the sake of service, protecting her devotees.
Thus did Hanumān, the king of devotees, offer his prayer;
"So be it," Hari replied, and He gave him a garland of pearls.
She gave him a pair of sandals and a garland of unfading flowers;
Lakṣmī also declared Hanumān to be her family deity (kuladevatā).
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "Hanumān, remain in my presence."
Dwelling in the region of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ and protecting the land, Hanumān caused a magnificent palace to be built for Lakṣmī upon the mountain;
there, together with Nārāyaṇa, he performs the worship of Lakṣmī. (13–14)
Then, having taken Lakṣmī from there by means of a celestial chariot, Hari went to Kāśikā,
where Śivarāja and others indeed reside.
Having brought her down from the chariot, he bestowed the bridegroom upon her for the sake of marriage.
"I shall return in the twelfth year; then your curse will come to an end.
Wait for me during that time," he said to Śivarāja, "and having arrived, I shall marry you; everything will turn out well."
Having spoken thus and having made known her fierce penance to her, the Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa became visible there on the bank of the Varaṇā.
Then Hari departed by celestial chariot for the Aśvapaṭṭasarovara lake.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke thus to Hemaśālāyana:
"Having married Lakṣmī, He will liberate Śambhu and others from their curse.
In this manner, in the past, Hari abandoned Lakṣmī for the sake of His own devotees. (2.106.20)
Hemaśālāyana and the others, having heard that, attained supreme joy.
Then all the sages, at various places in the camel-stations there,
[performed] the yoga of the beginningless Śrī Hari as well as the touching of His feet.
Having worshipped him again and again, they requested that he make the surface of the earth a sacred ford (*tīrtha*),
and likewise that he purify the people of that region of Uṣṇālaya. (22–23)

O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, may mountains, lakes, rivers, and streams, as well as our homes and forests, be made into sacred fords (*tīrtha*) by Your placement of feet, Your bathing, Your sitting,
and Your wandering. (24)
"So be it," Hari replied; then they all ascended a divine celestial chariot and first surveyed the mountain named Hemaśāla and the house of the god Hemaśālāyana.
Having purified themselves by applying the touch arising from his feet there,
and having received worship performed with gold, they then went to the Bālā river.
Having bathed there, having purified themselves, and having beheld the deity beginning with Bālā, they proceeded.
Having bathed in the waters of the Gośaṅku, they went to Mount Rāvāsana.
Then, having purified that entire mountain with their feet, they [visited] the Marcāśanā river, as well as the Surānadī and the Turūnadī. (28–29)
Having purified the Aita river and made it a sacred ford (tīrtha) by immersion,
and having bathed in the lake known as Mākamānasa as well as in Bālāsaras,
one should then bathe in the Śvānanadī and visit the Dārāliṅga mountain.
Having performed the *supāvana* rite with his feet and bathed in the Kuvans lake (3:1),
he beheld the stream Lābharuci and the southern forest;
then, having bathed in the Turu lake within the Gaurānarasara lake (3:2).
Having bathed at Prāgiri and having bathed at Ārasarovara,
and likewise having purified Maṣīgrīva mountain with his feet;
having bathed at Uttuṅgasaras and beheld the battlefield from the sky.
Having once made the mountain of Añjana pure with his feet,
he then went further north; having performed ablutions in the Viturīya river and bathed in both the Delyā and Ghelyā rivers, he drank that water.
Having gone to Śālavīnaśaila and having purified that place,
they then [proceeded] to the Rinku River, the Jhinku River, and the Phinku River.
Having bathed there and having purified Grāmaśaila, they descended [into it].
Then,
having bathed repeatedly in the waters of the Kāruliṅga river and the Dāruliṅga river,
and having bathed repeatedly in the waters of the Murā river and the Turā river, they reached Mount Ācala.
Having purified themselves with their feet, they proceeded toward Mount Diṅparvata by day;
then, having bathed in the waters of the Kuvindūmā river at Kiṇḍīcā,
they bathed in the purifying waters of the Kvīlpī and Laviṅgā rivers.
Then, having bathed at Micalā and beheld Mount Cāṭa, they purified themselves, crossed the northern region, and proceeded toward the west. Then,
having bathed at the Phijarā and purified those subjects, they continued on.
The servants of Hari accepted the worship offered by the subjects;
they were fed, honored, and saluted again and again.
Agastya, Śambhu, Lopāmudrā, and Ramā likewise [did so].
Pārvatī, the son of Aśvinī, and their attendants likewise—
those who were then the protectors of the people of Uṣṇālaya—
bestowed abundant blessings upon those subjects. (43–44)
They gave them the auspicious, liberating Vaiṣṇava great mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," as well as tulasī necklaces and rosaries for chanting.
They then sought refuge [in him], and a great cry of victory arose.
Then, having gone to the capital city, they performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
the sages residing there became the officiating priests at that time.
Agastya became Brahmā, and Rudra remained stationed at Rudrasthala;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa stayed at the primary deity’s station.
Hotā was Homāyana, and likewise Udgātā was Balāyana.
Āhartṛ was Maṣīgrīva and Pratihartṛ was Ravāsana.
(49) There were others who served as the Hotṛ priests, while the great Mahān was the patron of the sacrifice (yajamāna).
He was the sovereign emperor (samrāṭ) of the region of Rājauṣṇālaya, the son of Dakṣa and Javangara. (50)
The mind-born son of Dakṣa, saluted by gods and daityas—
may whatever sins have been committed through regional calamities and obstacles be brought to an end,
and may such obstacles never arise for us again. (51)
Intending this, all those gods on earth, by the king's command,
performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice; the embodied deities were satisfied,
and the Brāhmaṇas there also performed the *puraścaraṇa* rites.
Some [recited] the Puruṣasūkta, others the Viṣṇusūkta;
likewise, others [recited] the Nārāyaṇasūkta and the Śrīsūkta.
Still others [recited] the Lakṣmīsūkta and the Devīsūkta.
Some were reciting the Rudrādhyāya, others the Sāvitrī of Savitṛ;
others were studying the Gaṇeśādhyāya, and others the chapters of the Sāmaveda.
In this manner, they then performed the recitations of the various Vedas.
From the commencement of the sacrifice, King Dakṣajaṅghara always gives gifts at dawn, and his subjects always enjoy them;
every day, boys, girls, and others partake of sweet foods. (57)
The poor, the helpless, the destitute, as well as the lame, the blind, the wretched, and others—
having completed the sacrifice for seven days,
they then performed the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) near the capital city of King Dakṣajaṅgha. ||58-59||
To the south of the auspicious city named Uṣṇādattāṅga,
at the confluence of the rivers Ārasa and Phiṅkūna,
they performed the ritual ablution on the sixth day of the bright fortnight while traveling in celestial chariots.
The local Brahmins and others returned to their own regions.
The king, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, became joyful and requested Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to construct a magnificent temple.
"So be it," Hari replied; and the king caused an excellent,
lofty temple to be built there for Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari in the capital of the monarch on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina.

The great wise one, Agastya, established [the image] according to Vedic injunctions. Indeed, the king offered devotion to this son of Kambharā; then he, together with his subjects, his family, and the Brahmins, performed the consecration ceremony.
The pious and pure Vaiṣṇava [Vijaya] desired to see the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, the city of Śrī Haripattana, and the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Hari said, "So be it," and he [Vijaya] departed with a hundred celestial chariots.
Taking ten thousand people, both men and women, as his subjects,
he traveled by way of the sky to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also arrived together with him.
In their own celestial chariot, accompanied by their own Vaimānika deities,
the assemblies of the devotees from Uṣṭrālaya also arrived;
on the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, they reached the sacred field of Akṣara.
Honored with words of welcome and other courtesies, they stayed for five days;
they visited all the holy fords and daily heard the nectar-like discourse from the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, which grants eternal liberation.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Ūrja, during the Brāhma-muhūrta,
they bathed in the Aśvasarovara lake and celebrated the festival of Anādikṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
they performed worship and other rites for the occasion of His twelfth birthday.

There, in that constructed golden pavilion—beautified by the God of gods, the Goddess Satī, the virtuous lady, and the king of great sages; presided over by lords and their consorts; and exceedingly vast—the Blessed Lord, the beloved of Śrī, [was seated]. (73–74)
Adorned by the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and hosts of Apsarases,
he shone upon his divine elephant-throne; the lords of sages honored him,
offered blessings, and performed the ārātrika ceremony for the Lord.
The people presented offerings of unbroken rice with moon-shaped patterns;
likewise, music, dance, and instrumental performances took place.
There were hymns of praise by celestial bards, proclaiming divine gains and awakening.
And there, honored by the maidens who are dear to Brahmā,
the divine Lord shone forth, magnified by the ancient scriptures.
There, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa bestowed gifts.
At night, ten thousand camels devoted to their master held a festival for the occasion of the Lord’s birth, placing Lomaśa, Agastya, and Hemaśālāyana at their head. (2.106.79–80)
Having seated the Lord upon a beautiful elephant-throne,
and having bowed to and worshipped their mother and father in due order,
they all worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with various kinds of ritual offerings.
They placed a divine crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa.
They also fastened to the crown, near the ears, beloved crests bound with gold and jewels of the finest gems. || 82-83 ||
They poured fragrant oil and *attara* and other substances upon their hair;
they made a sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) on the forehead with a dot of saffron in its center;
they applied collyrium to the eyes and placed earrings upon the ears.
There were golden ear-ornaments and floral decorations for the lips;
on the shoulders was a royal armor made of gold and set with jewels; and there was a bodice of the *nāṭa* variety, made of silk and embroidered with gold. (85–86)
The two long, auspicious silken cloths, rich with gold, gems, and jewels, were like lamps and moons;
radiant as the sun and moon, they emitted a brilliant luster.
Hanging from her shoulders, they rested upon her breasts and chest.

They placed upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest two glistening sword-hilts, joined with golden waist-bands at the hilt, each worth more than a hundred thousand [gold pieces]. Above his crown, they placed a scimitar whose base was set with pearls. (88–89)
In the center, it was adorned with fine diamonds set within a halo of light;
at its edge, it was endowed with a radiance flowing from rows of golden stars.
It was [marked] on the neck, the cheeks, the forehead, the chin, and the two forearms.
They gave jewels fastened with golden chains, well-settled [in place].
(91) They placed excellent golden necklaces, flower garlands, and wreaths of *tulasī* upon their necks; likewise, they placed armlets and golden chain-bracelets upon their arms. (92)
They indeed gave him bracelets, armlets, and rings;
Mādhava wore golden staffs and golden canopies.
He also wore a golden waist-cloth below his hips and a sun-bright tail-fan.
Abundantly adorned with golden bells, with jewels and pearls for its stars, it was richly decorated with the wonders of the seven netherworlds and variegated with many colors.
Upon her feet and ankles were anklets bound with gold and gems. (94–95)
Those best of devotees indeed gave golden sandals for his feet—
adorned with lion-heads on the big toes, graced by elephants in the middle,
beautified by swans on the sides, and further embellished by Garuḍas at the back. (96)

They applied a reddening substance to their nails, as well as to the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet— [hands] which were shaped like the serpent Śeṣa at the tips, adorned with tortoises in the middle, and resplendent all around with rows of jewel necklaces. (97–98)
They gave him betel-leaf rich with fragrance mixed with lime-powder,
a great upper garment resplendent like the seven heavens,
and golden ornaments endowed with divine splendor, resembling the imperishable syllable (Om).
They gave him a parasol with thirty-two ribs, resplendent with all its ornaments;
two chowries that shone with the brilliance of the sun, moon, fire, and lightning;
and they offered there a canopy with jeweled handles that was like truth itself.

They gave him a single, vast, divine celestial chariot (vimāna), which was richly adorned with images, endowed with splendor, possessed of wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī), and fit for all the worlds. At that time, the king gave golden vessels and bowls set with jewels.
He offered an *ārārtrika* lamp-rite equipped with a thousand excellent wicks and other requisites.
For the sake of ten million maidens, he gave ornaments; for the sake of the beloved of Brahmā (the Goddess), he gave infinite jewels, gems, and other articles of utility.
After the worship, he then joyfully performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
At that time, musical instruments were played and dances were performed;
there were hymns by the great sages and songs by the celestial maidens.
And the auspicious, melodious voices of young maidens were heard.
Thus, those devotees of the Abode of Weapons, together with the king and his subjects, celebrated that wonderful birth festival of the twelve-year-old [child] during the night. (106–107)

Then they performed the ritual circumambulation and slept thereafter. On the morning of the ninth day, they fed those who had bathed and performed auspicious rites to their hearts' content with the essence of milk and the essence of food.

The delighter of the cowherds gave him the essence of juices, the essence of drinks, and the essences of various foods and edibles; he also gave him mouth-fresheners and aphrodisiacs. And likewise, he honored Lomaśa, Agastya, and other preeminent sages.
Those masters of weaponry honored Śambhu, the two sons of Aśvinī, and tens of thousands of hosts of Gaṇas;
they indeed bestowed upon them wealth,
including all kinds of desired articles, fruits, flowers, and garments.
Then they offered their excuses and respectfully accepted the king's command. They then requested liberation for the purpose of returning to their own country.
Hari said, "I shall grant you liberation at the time of the departure of your life-breaths."
Hemaśālāyana and the others were indeed those eleven sages;
from then on, they made their permanent residence on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. Then, the king had one hundred daughters and a thousand subjects’ daughters [to give in marriage].
O Rādhikā, at that time the deluded ones indeed beheld the Supreme Soul who had turned away.
Then the king and those subjects offered them all to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
they were all protected by the Supreme Soul in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then, having received the command of Śrī Hari, they departed for the abode of Uṣṭra in celestial chariots, indeed worshipping Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
while remembering the imperishable realm (Akṣara-dhāma) and praising the Aśvatīrtha.
Roaring with valor, they reached their own country.
O Rādhikā, this is the narrative of the protection of the kitten by the cat,
the drinking of water by the female Cakravāka bird, and the passing of the time through the penance of Lakṣmī.
For one who hears, reads, causes others to hear, or remembers this [work] which wards off the oppression of the people in the great land of Uṣṭrālaya,
there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation according to his desire from Hari.
The attainment of perfections, sovereign powers, and so forth; land, grain, sons, and the like;
the expansion of wealth and lineage, as well as health and the state of a householder—all this indeed comes about through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (121–122)

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, [is described] the granting of boons to Hanumān; in the *Uṣṭrālaya-khaṇḍa*, the holy places (*tīrthas*) established everywhere by the Lord; the Viṣṇu sacrifice performed there by King Dakṣaja Vaṅgara; the arrival of the king along with his subjects at the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara by means of a hundred celestial chariots (*vimānas*); and the twelve [manifestations] of the Lord—

The one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Birthday Festival, including worship and gifts; the King’s hundred daughters and the subjects’ thousand daughters being offered to Bālakṛṣṇa; and the departure of the King and others for their own countries.
Chapter 106. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 107.
[Author: Chapter 108.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen now to another marvel of Hari.
Just as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became a helper to his devotees,
once many daughters of Māna arrived by celestial chariot to see the earth and the people dwelling there who were his ancestors. (1–2)
The Brahmaputrī, the Lavahītā, the Candrāvatī, the Irāvatī;
the Śālāvatī, the Mīnakaṅgū, the Lāṭiśā, and likewise the Kāniśā; the Māpīṅgā, the Śīkyāṅgā, the Aṅgasvāṅgā, and the Harāṅgahā. (3)
Mauktikā, Tārimā, Pannāmā, and likewise Tvāṅgahā;
Mīnāmī, Tānasarimā, Sīnā, Gāndharvavedikā, Nṛtyagāyanakuśalā, Rāgarāgiṇī, and Abhijñikā—[these were the women]. (4–5)
Twenty maidens, endowed with beauty, the fullness of youth, moon-like faces, and radiant as the sun;
clad in garments of cloth purified by fire, adorned with divine ornaments, and possessed of splendor—
these were their maidservants, numbering in the thousands.
Capable of assuming any form at will, they shine with the power and mastery of the perfected ones (siddhas).
These goddesses, who bear missiles and weapons, possess invincible strength;
from their own world, these women of auspicious limbs arrive by means of a divine celestial chariot.
Having offered salutations to the Truth, and likewise to Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and the Unborn,
and having bowed to the gods seated in the assembly of Brahmā, they performed auspicious rites.
First, from the peak of Meru, they proceeded to the valley of Meru.
Having circumambulated Mount Meru and beheld many celestial abodes—
palaces and great gardens equal to the dwellings of the world of Brahmā,
rich with the splendor of heaven and even beyond it— and likewise the residences of the guardians of the quarters; (2.107.10–11)
He saw the exceedingly brilliant palaces of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars,
as well as the abodes of yogins, sages, and gandharvas,
along with the mansions of the daityas and dānavas and the dwellings of the kinnaras.
Having observed the abodes of the Kimpuruṣas as well as the hermitages of the ascetics,
and having subsequently seen Elāvṛta and the land of Jāmbavī,
they traveled through the sky from the earth to the region of the Kimpuruṣas.
Having seen the Āpatāyin mountain, as well as the Gopīraṇa mountain visible to the eye, the Kunalīnādri mountain, the Kārukora mountain, the Triyānaśa mountain, the Cipiṅga mountain,
and the Prācīnabhāga mountain, he beheld the yellow ocean.
Having seen the river of the limbs of training (*śikṣāṅga*), as well as the river consisting of the limbs of training (*śikṣāṅgikā*),
the places for drinking water, the places for drinking fermented liquor (*phulli*),
and the various islands of the taverns, they went to Sumātṛkā. (16–17)
Then, turning back, they went toward the river Mīnakaṅgūna;
they reached Irāvatī, which has moon-like waves, where mountains of falling bodies were descending.
Meanwhile, the rākṣasas of the ocean beheld the maiden’s celestial chariot.
Stationed at the water-drinking place, traveling through the sky in celestial chariots—
tawny-colored, tall, and resembling mountain peaks—
they arrived in the air with weapons in hand to seize the jewels of maidens.
In this way, even the Dānavas born in the land of Phullipāna arrived by means of a vehicle traveling through the path of the sky to abduct the maiden;
they were masters of illusion, terrifying, and capable of assuming any form at will.
They carry missiles and weapons, roam through the sky, and dwell within the ocean;
their bodies are like mountains, they wield lightning as their arms, and they are terrifying.
They are merciless, tawny-colored, with coarse bodies that cause burning. (22–23)
In this way, other terrifying Daityas from the island of Vāraṇī—
cruel devourers of humans, armed with fire, stones, and weapons,
equipped with slings, arrows, and the like, and capable of moving through the sky— [attacked]. (24)
That beautiful and auspicious celestial chariot for the maidens was one *krośa* in length.
Upon seeing Sūryaprabha, these [beings] arrived to carry off the maidens; from Ādamanadvīpa came the Kṛṣṇas and the Kaṣmalas, who were like serpents. (25–26)
Having recognized that group of beautiful maidens,
five hundred and thousands of Rākṣasas arrived; likewise,
Daityas, Dānavas, and even Kṛṣṇa-snakes came by the thousands.
Then all those five thousand [demons] approached from every side;
they obstructed the celestial chariot as it fell upon the great mountain, saying:
"All of you come for refuge, otherwise you will surely perish quickly! (28–29)
Having spoken thus, all the asuras, desiring to enter the celestial chariot,
ran about in haste when they found that the chariot of the essence of merit was forbidden to the touch of sinners.
When that [weapon] could not find a way to obstruct them in the sky, being unassailable by Rākṣasas, Dānavas,
and Daityas, then those Asuras again employed the illusion of their own sins and seized it at that very moment.
The forms of the principle of evil (pāpatattva), the weapons of the principle of evil,
the missiles of the wicked, the arms of the sinful, the nooses of evil,
the iron arrows of the evil ministers, and likewise the bows, swords, and other such implements.
Desiring to seize them, they obstructed their celestial chariot with fire-stones, arrows, maces, tomara-spears, and mudgara-clubs;
with iron balls filled with fiery powder, and likewise with explosive bombs.
With clouds of the nature of sin, they indeed obstructed their path;
they blocked the doors and entered the celestial chariot.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the group of maidens in the chariot.
Not a single protector was to be found, even though the celestial chariot was nearby—whether on the surface of the earth, in the sky, on a mountain, or even in the ocean.
The maidens fell into distress and remembered Aryaman as they were being carried away. (37–38)
Just as he thought of his own father, his protector, his progenitor, and the dispeller of his sorrow,
Tvaṣṭṛ arrived with great haste along with his attendants.
As soon as he was remembered, that deity of a hundred splendors appeared in a celestial chariot.
He warded off the Rākṣasas with showers of thousands of arrows. Then the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Daityas, and black serpents tormented Āryaka from all sides with showers of arrows.
Aryaman produced a fire and dispatched it everywhere;
in order to consume the Rākṣasas and others, it burned in all directions. [The gods] created waters through their *māyā* to protect the waters from the water-dwelling Rākṣasas.
Then their father Aryaman extinguished the fire;
having created tens of millions of Aruṇas, he dispatched them everywhere.
Those lords, with sharp flames as their minute weapons, set [the enemies] ablaze.
Then the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Daityas, and Kṛṣṇa-snakes all became Asuras assuming false forms through their own *māyā*.
Having concealed their original forms, they fought with the sons of Aruṇa.
The red messengers of Aryaman, with their weapons of sharp and scorching rays,
searched again and again for the Daityas and other asuras and set them ablaze.
Many who were burned there were reborn from the ashes.
At that time, there were tens of millions of Rākṣasas;
that entire battle took place in the sky and was destructive to all.
A great and profound conflict then ensued between the Āruṇas and the Rākṣasas.
By means of the mantras of Aryaman and Sūrya, millions of Aruṇas are produced;
and by the mantras of the Rākṣasas, Rākṣasas are produced.
There is no end to the armies; millions of troops continue to multiply.
Weapons also increase, and heaps of arms multiply;
they are split apart, severed, killed, and fall down.
Blood becomes blood-red, and likewise the sky and the surface of the earth become crimson.
Here, tens of thousands of bodily arrays fall from all sides;
the bodies and forms of the slain Aruṇa Rākṣasas, resembling mountain peaks, fall down in heaps and mounds.

Like mountains arisen in the sky beyond the clouds, those corpses of naked men became mountains upon the surface of the earth, which was a hundred yojanas in extent; indeed, they were then like mountain peaks. (54)
With their bodies falling, those mountains became indeed naked crags.
Those who were skilled in battle perished as the tawny peaks vanished.
Thus, the great battle continued day and night for seven days.
There was no cessation there at that time; the noble Sun himself [remained].
Pitṛkakṣa remembered the triad of Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the Unborn (Brahmā)—the lords of the gods of gods, who are the Grandfathers in the form of the ancestors—for the sake of protection. (56–57)
"O Lords of the gods, come quickly in an instant for the sake of protection!
Protect all the maidens and destroy the asuras!"—
at that very moment, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arrived there.
Mounted upon three celestial chariots and accompanied by divine armies,
at that very moment the Daityas, Dānavas,
and Rākṣasas remembered the great Daitya, who was highly skilled in the art of illusion.
He was named Kālaprāleya, accompanied by an army of ten million;
equal to Mahākāla, born of Mahāmāyā, and resembling Mount Meru.
He had a thousand heads, and in every mouth he was chewing a hundred goats.
He indeed arrived instantly, making the worlds tremble.
By his mere loud laughter, the hosts of planets fell down;
all the oceans were agitated, and even the earth shook. (62–63)
The peaks collapsed and living beings surely abandoned them;
the roars became equal to the falling of a great thunderbolt.
Indeed, the peak of Mount Mandara was held up by him with a single hand.
With one hand, Kālaprāleyaka held up banners;
such was that great-bodied asura whose mouth then became wide open and expanded to ten yojanas. (65–66)
Thus, having seen Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
he who possessed a thousand faces summoned the gods along with ten million deities into the sky by cracking his thighs.
Then the gods, beholding him who was like the form of Vairāja—
They remembered Saṃkarṣaṇa, the massive-bodied destroyer of Time.
Swiftly, the god Saṃkarṣaṇa arrived there in the sky;
the three gods praised the Lord, who held a mace, for the sake of protection.
Saṃkarṣaṇa forcefully brought his mace down upon his head;
but Kālaprāleyaka, having quickly dodged that mace,
struck Saṃkarṣaṇa on the top of his head with his own mace.
Saṃkarṣaṇa pulverized that club with his own mace.
Then, with great force, he struck Kālaprāleyaka on the head;
the mace was broken by the blow, but it did not shatter the Daitya’s head.
The Daitya, seizing a trident, rushed at that moment to kill him;
Saṃkarṣaṇa pierced Kālaka in the chest with his own spear.
Then, like a mountain in height, he fell into the eastern ocean.
Then he was struck in the throat with a spear and likewise in the belly with a thunderbolt;
he was crushed by mountains and torn apart by blades of grass. Having fallen like a tree, he fell unconscious in an instant.
Rising up for the sake of protecting his life, he fled;
and when, having circumambulated Mount Meru, he ran outside,
Saṃkarṣaṇa pursued him as far as the Lokāloka mountain.
He went behind the region where that Asura, the destroyer of Time (Kāla), was located.
Leaving behind the Lokāloka mountain, he went outside into the lightless sky;
out of fear of Saṅkarṣaṇa, even Ananta went into the infinite, numberless firmament.

The god Saṃkarṣaṇa also, having bestowed fearlessness upon Śambhu and the others by means of his subtle form, departed for the abode of Īśvara. Then Śaṅkara and the others fought with the Daityas and Dānavas.

They struck the Daityas—who were like the wings of the frost of Time—from all sides with tridents, discuses, lightning-nooses, ordinary nooses, and javelins; likewise with swords, projectiles, mountains, scimitars, and spears. (2.107.80–81)
With the wind-missiles, mountain-missiles, cloud-missiles, and fire-missiles;
with the serpent-missiles, Garuḍa-missiles, lion-missiles, and śarabha-missiles;
with the boar-missiles, lizard-missiles, crab-missiles, and scorpion-missiles.
With the weapons of Yama, the weapons of Rākṣasas, the weapons of Makaras, and the weapons of water;
with the weapons of tigers, the weapons of lamps, the weapons of madness, and the weapons of fainting;
and with the weapons of hunger, the weapons of thirst, and the weapons of insanity, they struck one another.
The armies of Brahmā and the others excessively tormented the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, and finally destroyed them;
those Asuras, numbering in the tens of millions, were slain in battle on all sides.
There were those that were artificial and those that were natural, as well as those that were illusory and those that were non-illusory.

By the bestowal of mantras, they too were made Vaiṣṇavas by Hari.
Then those terrifying Asuras, born from the dissolution of Time (Kāla-laya),
numbering three million, armed and assuming many forms, flew through the sky; they fought against ten million of the Lord's attendants (Pārṣadas) who were devoted to Viṣṇu.
With artificial puppets in the sky, with rapidly bursting balls,
with showers of arrows, with lightning-nooses, with showers of water-jars,
with serpent-nooses, with stones, and likewise with thick iron weapons—
The cruel ones, arrogant with false magic and pride, slaughtered the Vaiṣṇavas.
But the attendants, wearing the armor of the Lord,
stood in celestial chariots in the sky and then fought with them using missiles.
The eldest son of Kālaka, born of Kālī, was named Raṇamadaṅka;
wielding a mace, he slew many foolish Vaiṣṇavas.
Others fell to the earth in a swoon, while some, their hopes shattered, fled away.

The twice-born ones chanted the Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-Varma for the sake of protection. (2.109.40) Of this Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-Varma, Satī Ramā is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the bestower of its desired fruits. (41)

I bow to Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, the all-conquering Supreme Brahman, the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the beloved Master. (42) He is the seed, the youth of the cowherds, the protector of devotees, and the Great Lord.

The auspicious initiation of the Great Bhāgavata is the power (śakti) of Vaiṣṇavī. The Kīlaka is the illustrious son of Kambharā, the increaser of devotion. Having remembered the Lord of Rādhā and Pārvatī, he is employed in the recitation of mantras (japa). 43–44.
May there be the placement of meditation upon the heart of Mañjuhaṃsahari, who is the source of all entries, powers, and splendors, and who possesses all qualities;
and may my head here be the head of Śrī Hari.
O Blessed One, may the eyes of Hari be in my eyes; may his ears be in my ears. May the nose of Kṛṣṇa be in my nose, and the face of Nārāyaṇa in my mouth.
May the throat of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the Asuras, be in my throat.
May the heart of the wielder of the discus be in my heart, and may the heart of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow be there as well.
May the back of Hari, who dwells at Kuṅkumavāpī, always be upon my back.
And may the belly of Him who resides at Aśvapaṭṭasara be within my own belly.
May the navel of Bālakṛṣṇa be my navel, the sustainer of the universe;
may the powerful hip of Hari be my hip;
and may the two private organs of the Creator Hari be my two concealed loins. || 2.109.50 ||
May the two thighs of the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas be my two thighs;
may the two knees of Lord Hari, the worshipper of Śakti, be my two knees;
and may the two shanks of Para-Nārāyaṇa, the refuge of the universe, be my two shanks. (51)
May the entire element of all things reside in my feet; may my feet be the protectors of strength.
May the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be present here in embodied form within me; and may He, the Lord of Brahmā’s beloved, abide in my body, senses, and so forth.
May my Lord, who has attained the abode of the supreme imperishable, protect me from above;
may Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign, protect me from the front;
and may both Kṛṣṇa and Hari, the two excellent brothers, protect me from the sides.
May Nara and likewise Nārāyaṇa protect my back from below;

may the Lord of Lakṣmī protect me on the earth, and may the True Lord protect me in the water; may the Beloved of Śrī protect me in the fire, and may the Lord of Radiance protect me in the atmosphere.
May the Lord of Brahmapriyā protect me in the sky; may the Lord of Māṇikī protect me in the wind. May the Lord of Rādhā, the wielder of the discus, grant me protection in the forest.
May Hari, the wielder of the mace, protect me from tens of millions of demons.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the spear, protect me in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
May Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, protect me from the host of fires;
and may Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, protect me from the asuras.
May the Valiant One protect me from the destruction caused by missiles and weapons;
may He who dwells within my heart protect me from sudden fears.
May He protect me from the fear of Time, Māyā, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous foes.
"May he who bears the trident, fish, banner, bow, and svastika protect us!
(61) Thus did those Vaiṣṇavas, divine beings whose bodies transcend *māyā*, wear the armor of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (62)
They were born with all-black strength and endowed with every power;
for they are indeed the very forms of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
With their Sudarśana great-discuses discharged in every direction, [they struck down the enemies].
They swiftly cut down thirty lakhs of asuras born of the dissolution of Time (Kāla).
Though they were alive, they all fell dead in the great waters of the battlefield.
Even the son of Kālaprāleya, whose mark was the pride of battle, died.
A hundred of his sons were destroyed in the sky by the discus of Viṣṇu;
and Bodhavihaṃgama, the king of the Prācīnas,
also fought a battle on earth with Koṭipiśaṅga, who bore a raised mace.
Accompanied by crores of hosts of Āruṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, and Raudras born from the Kalpa-lattices,
[he fought] in the field of battle with weapons and missiles beyond imagination—
in the sky, in the water, on the earth, on the mountain, and in forest lands. (67–68)
From all sides, his armies fought against him with fire-arms,
lightning-balls, fire-engines, and puppets that explode instantly;
with minute whistles, catapults, arrows, and tunnel-weapons.
With lightning-arrows, fire-nooses, sky-nets, and poisonous fires;
with *śataghnīs*, army-destroyers, carts, and celestial chariots;
and with water-sprays and earth-strikes, those fierce warriors caused slaughter. (2.109.70–71)
The hosts led by Āruṇa assumed a divine armor;
they indeed struck down the armies of Bodha, which numbered tens of millions.
There were lovely effigies made from *kalpavallī* creepers, resembling gods.
Filled with fire-machines, they struck the Dānavas in the sky;
half of that great army, consisting of mechanical puppets, was destroyed by those puppets.
Then, the conscious army numbered eighty lakhs.
Indeed, that [host] of the Asuras was destroyed; ten lakhs fled, while ten lakhs sought refuge with Śrī Hari.
Likewise, King Piṅga, the bird of awakening, met his destruction.
His hundred sons, including the learned Vija and Haṃgama,
sought refuge in Śrī Hari and were indeed made Vaiṣṇavas.
Furthermore, ten lakhs of soldiers were also made Vaiṣṇavas by Hari.
Three hundred thousand Cipiṅgas, warriors traveling in celestial chariots,
were commanded by Piṅgalaka;
they then fought with the Vināyakas and all the Kalpavallī-born beings in the forest and in the sky in a fierce battle.
Hundreds of thousands of soldiers were slain by those destroyers born from the *kalpa*-trees;
they were all killed with axes, balls, projectiles, mountains, serpents, nooses, thunderbolt-jaws, and tridents, both in the water and in the sky. (2.109.79–80)
Whether on the ground or in celestial chariots, wherever they had gone, they were indeed slain;
Piṅgalaka was killed, as was his son Piṅgaśekhara.
Having sought refuge in Śrī Hari, that Vaiṣṇava was indeed made a follower of Hari by Hari himself.
Samaramaṅgala was the king of the Maṅgūjanapada regions;
Hārakirīṭa was the lord of the Mañcūraṇa regions;
and Kṣaṇātmavadana was the king of the Lāśahāna regions. (82–83)
Likewise, King Kāruvarmā and Karvarīdeśaja also fought;
all of them, accompanied by their own armies numbering fifty lakhs,
engaged in battle with Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Then Brahmā, by means of Atharva mantras, brought forth the Jāṭikas;
he swiftly dispatched the gods against the armies of the Daityas.
Endowed with lightning-nooses, they indeed traversed the path of the sky in an instant.
Fifty hundred thousand *jaṭika* [demons] quickly took flight,
while thirty hundred thousand *dānavas* were destroyed by lightning-weapons, nooses,
and lightning-thunderbolts; the remainder fled.
The remaining ten lakhs of Daityas who had been bitten by locusts produced from the Atharvan [mantras] and by the poison-smeared ichor flowing from the horses, like clouds,
all died; thereafter, only ten lakhs of his soldiers remained.
And for the sake of their livelihood, they came there for refuge to Śrī Hari;
all of them were indeed made Vaiṣṇavas there by Bālakṛṣṇa. Hārakirīṭa and Samaramaṅgala likewise died.

Then all ten sons of Hārakirīṭa, who were all exceedingly powerful, went for refuge to Śrī Hari, abandoning all hope for their lives. Prabhāsa and Kirīṭa, the best among them, were indeed made Vaiṣṇavas by Hari.
All the thousand sons of Samaramaṅgala, who were indeed Vaiṣṇavas, sought refuge in Hari and were made his own by Hari.
Then King Kṣaṇātmavadana fought again with Śambhu.

Accompanied by a hundred thousand troops, he was slain by Śaṃkara. Again, Kāruvarmā, joined by a hundred thousand troops, fought with Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and he too was struck down by the Sudarśana discus.
Their sons and grandsons, as well as their allies,
were all slain in battle by Viṣṇu with his Sudarśana discus.
Indeed, the king of Ilādeśa, Maṇḍalākṣi, was possessed of great strength.
Likewise, King Pādasaha was the protector of the region of Pannāma.
Formerly, the king named Prācīnaśāyana fought with Śambhu, accompanied by an army of one hundred million. (97–98)
The king named Śṛṅgaśekhara, [ruler] of the regions of Aṅga, Śikhaṇḍa, and Deśa,
fought with Śambhu accompanied by a hundred million warriors;
they, along with two hundred million combatants, were slain in battle.

By Hara, along with his own hosts, all were destroyed and slain in battle; not even one remained among those who had marched into the conflict with Hara. Thus, those four crores who had entered the fray perished.
O Rādhikā! At that time, the remaining subjects and the soldiers of the army were made Vaiṣṇavas by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
[They were established in the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Hari gave the mantra to them, and the sages did so by the command of Hari.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seeking of Refuge by the Twenty-five Million Remnants of the Fifteen Kings, including Makaraketu and others, who were accompanied by an army of four million troops and had perished in battle with Śambhu and his hosts," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 109: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)*
Chapter 110 [Author:
Chapter 111 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Thus, O Rādhikā, in the past, on this earth near the ocean in regions such as Prāgjyotiṣa, there occurred a battle that brought an end to the Dānavas. Then, for the sake of their purification, he performed once again a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
At the source of the Śālāvatī river, on the bank of the Lāśahāsa lake,
on the northern side of the Brahmaputra and extending for a hundred yojanas,
the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa created a lake all around.
All the subjects were summoned, men who were ready for the field of battle,
arriving in *sarvatobhadra* celestial chariots capable of traveling a thousand *krośas* in an instant.
All the gods arrived, as did the sages and the ancestors.
The sacrifice lasted for seven days, characterized by most excellent oblations and other rites.
(5) There was no end to the number of sacrificial offerings, nor even a count of the juices;
there was no limit to the foods to be eaten—what then can be said of the drinks? (6)
There, the Sāttvika beings were preeminent among those born from lotuses;
the earthly men and women were intent on the purity of battle.
But there was no counting the gods, the great seers, and the hosts of ancestors.
The sacred fords (tīrthas), rivers, streams, and oceans were summoned;
likewise, the lakes Lāṃśaha and Āsara came to the waters and the waters of the Brahmaputra, as did the sacred fords at the source of the river Śālāvatī.
A region of the earth extending for a hundred yojanas became a refuge for the deities;
it was like Goloka, it was like Vaikuṇṭha,
it was indeed like Brahmaloka, and it was even like the Imperishable (Akṣara).

Where the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, shines forth in person; where Brahman likewise resides, as do the Brahmarṣis, the Ṛṣis, the gods, and the progenitors of the worlds. (11–12)
In that place, O Rādhikā, what indeed could be lacking, or what could be devoid of prosperity?
For there dwell the beloveds of Brahmā, and there are indeed the wish-fulfilling vines (kalpavallī).
What loss could there be where Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, and Aryaman reside in person?

Where there is the seven-tongued Fire, the unborn (Aja) who upholds the four Vedas, and Rudra himself with five faces—who could possibly be deficient there? Where the sattvic gods and lords bestow the welfare of the world, [who could be lacking]? (14–15)
Where pure Vaiṣṇava great sages, bestowers of liberation,
have gathered in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha) for the sake of purifying the world;
where the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice is performed by the Vaiṣṇavas and the gods.
In that auspicious place, what ground for deficiency could possibly arise?

(17) There, the wish-fulfilling trees, pearls, rivers, streams, and likewise trees, as well as the gods and the principles (tattvas), brought forth the supreme materials required for the sacrifice. (18)
The lords caused all those sages who were stationed in their celestial chariots together with Nārāyaṇa to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
for the sake of the ritual purification of the bodies of the subjects engaged in battle, according to the prescribed rites.
Out of enthusiasm, they performed the Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge in every way.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (2.110.20–21)
Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
I am Brahmā, bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika;
I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
The first refuge is the mantra, and the second is self-surrender;
the first consists of sixteen syllables, as does the second.
The fourteen sages gave him the third protection-mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables,
as well as the fourth, the mantra of the nature of Brahman which bestows half of Hari’s own body—
thus [giving] the thirty-two-syllable mantra.
Maṅkaṇaka, Maṅkiraya, Kūrma, Prācīnabarhiṣa;
Trita, Prabhūtānaka, Ruśāyin, and likewise Khāsana;
Aṅgaśyāma, Ārakarṇa, Brahmadāsa, and Anāmaya. (26–27)

Then Śyāmala-ṛṣi and Malaya-ṛṣi gave these to the Manus. Following the command of Hari, they indeed gave garlands of tulasī to the subjects after the oblations, to those subjects who were as large as lotuses.
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge.
(29) At the sacrifice, He gave mantras to them, and Pāvanya produced offspring;
Keśava bathed them all in the waters of the Lāśahāsa. (2.110.30)
And likewise at Śālāvatya and in the waters of the Brahmaputrī, the Blessed One purified all beings— women and men, boys and girls—
as well as all the people of every lineage.
Having satisfied the god Agni with the essence of the oblations, as well as the ancestral deities,
the attendants, and the maidens who protected the battle,
the Blessed One fed the sons of Brahmā with sweet foods.

Having attained the grace of the sacrifice, they became fulfilled in their purpose. After performing the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), Bālakṛṣṇa commanded Aja in the assembly hall for the sake of bestowing rewards.
Having bowed to Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā spoke aloud to all the subjects, granting them freedom from fear:
"He is the Supreme Brahman, beyond the imperishable, the cause of all incarnations. (35–36)
From whom indeed the military arrays (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva arise,
whose powers are Time, the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), and Māyā;
and from whose form the incarnations and abodes are born.
This very one is Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Svāmī Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha;
the son of the illustrious Kaṃbharā, the glorious Gopāla-Bālaka Hari, who makes his residence in the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, the field of the Imperishable. || 38-39 ||
The Lord who resides at Kuṅkumavāpikā, the husband of Prabhā, Pāravatī, Kṛṣṇā, Brahmapriyā, Rādhā, Ramā, and Lakṣmī;
the Lord who is the consort of Māṇikī, Lalitā, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, and Saguṇā.

He is the Lord of Jayā, Śāntā, and the other goddesses, and the husband of the golden digit (Haimī-kalā). He is the Master of the virtuous, the Beloved of Liberation, the Lord of Creation, and the Supreme Sovereign.
He is the Lord of all abodes, the Inner Self of embodied beings, and the bestower of fruits himself.
That by relying upon which nothing remains to be known or attained;
that than which there is none higher, with which nothing is equal, and than which no other exists;
that supreme, eternal liberation which is sought even by the followers of Aruṇa.
The giver of that [liberation] is this very Lord, the husband, the beloved, the supreme Hari.
O people, supreme liberation is indeed to be sought from this Śrī Hari;
for our victory always exists through His majesty alone. ||44-45||
He whom we, Nārāyaṇa and the others, constantly worship is indeed He Himself.
Worship His form and revere Him alone.
Render service to Him and abide by His word.
His speech is the great Vedas; his action is the great bull.
His form is always to be served, for he is always to be meditated upon by people. Indeed, through his touch, both the insentient and the sentient become purified.
May all those gods and those who belong to the side of the gods who were slain in battle become alive again here this very moment by his grace.
May those followers of the gods who have died on earth, in water, or in the sky [likewise be restored].

"May they quickly become divine; may they come toward Hari. Having spoken thus, Brahmā took water from the foot of Hari into his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and cast that water into the sky, which became like a cloud.
Increasing rapidly, it spread across the earth, the sky, and the waters;
having then become nectar, it indeed restored to life all those who had died—
the gods, all living beings, and others, both natural and artificial.
That very water became [cool] when touched by the sleeping Dānavas;
nevertheless, the Dānavas did not become alive at that time,
for such was the will of Śrī Śvasvāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Touched by [the weapon] equally, the gods regained their lives, but the Dānavas did not.
Then Brahmā bestowed upon them a fourfold mantra;
there, Hari gave a reward to those who had been restored to life.
Likewise, he gave excellent rewards there to the victors:
one body fit for liberation and another remaining on earth;
he then sent all those fit for liberation to the imperishable state.
With a mind full of grace, the Blessed One himself said to those worthy of honor:
"Accept the sacrificial offering, the favor, the drink, and the sweet, excellent food.
At his command, they all partook of it.
Then Hari, having summoned the princes, the sages, the armies, and likewise all the subjects, said: "Indeed,
the lands have been purified by me through you, who are like sacred fords."
Rivers, streams, lakes, and mountains have been made givers of liberation;
furthermore, the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas has been accomplished here upon the surface of the earth.
These princes are Vaiṣṇavas who have taken refuge in me.
My young sons shall be established upon the very thrones of kings.
And you, my subjects, are likewise my daughters in every respect;
let them proceed according to the king’s command, for this is my eternal decree.
"Let my venerable sages likewise offer their devotion to me;
let them listen as well, according to their respective divisions, to how I bestow that kingdom.
This Brahmā is the grandfather of all creatures and the Lord himself."
"Let him to whom I shall utter the name give him a crown.
The land of Jalapāna-dvīpa is given to Sūryaketu;
the collection of islands of Philīpa is given to Bījajaṅgin. (65–66)
The land of Vāraṇīyadvīpa is given to Sāraketu;
the land of Ārdramānadvīpa is given to Raktakeśa;
and the ancient kingdom is given to Vijñavihaṅgama.
The kingdom of Piṅgacipiṅga is given to Piṅgakeśa;
the land of Maṅgu is given to Āhavamaṅgala;
and the region of Mañcurāṇa is offered to Prabhākirīṭa.
The region known as Lāṣahā shall be given to Trītarṣi;
let that kingdom become renowned by the name Trītavitte.
Let this be the kingdom of the Ṛṣis, and let the Āruṇas dwell there.
And those who possess bodies of shadow-form and know the self-knowledge of Brahman—
let the kingdom of Karu be granted to the great seer Kūrmi;
let that kingdom of sages also be eternally Vaiṣṇava and purifying.
May Brahmā himself rule the kingdom of Ilādeśa;
may Brahmadeśa always remain a sacred site with the river Airāvatī;
and may Viṣṇu forever govern the land of Pannāmanadikā.
May there be a dark region to the east of Brahmapura, and let there be a sacred ford named Pannāmnī. May Śiva always be the protector of the land called Cayaṇa to the east,
and may the Vināyakas be intent upon protecting that eastern region.
May Śaṅkara himself, the king of the limbs, the sciences, and the regions,
rule over that kingdom of the east and south together with his own attendants.
And may the Mothers always abide in this land blessed with excellent mothers.

"May these kingdoms be truly Vaiṣṇava, for the sake of protecting Śiva’s truth and destroying the Daityas of the ocean. O Rādhikā, when Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa had spoken thus, [the gods replied]: "So be it. (77–78)
Brahmā gave him that crown of sovereignty;
and Hari himself likewise gave it to Viṣṇu, the unborn Śambhu,
having fashioned for him a saffron tilaka, a necklace, and a garland of tulasī.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa himself bestowed them upon the newcomers. Then Hari, acting for their benefit, spoke these words to those kings:
"Even my own gurus are being given by me here to you for the sake of devotion."
The preceptor of the Karvarī-jalapānas was indeed the sage Kūrmī;
the preceptor of the Prācīna-philīpas was Śambhu Maheśvara;
and the preceptor of the Prācīnottara-bhāgas was Prācīnabarhiṇa.
The sage Śyāmalaka was the preceptor of the Śyāmalas and the Cipiṅgas;
Malaya-ṛṣi was the preceptor of the Malayas; Brahmadāsaka was the preceptor of Ilā; Trīta was the preceptor of the Lāśahās; and likewise, Lūśaya was the preceptor of the Lūśas. (83–84)
The venerable Mātariśvan is to be known as the teacher of the elephants, and he is dear to the sages;
Brahmā, whose mind is moist with compassion, is the creator of the Brahmas and the teacher even of them.
Maṅkaṇaka is the teacher of the Maṅgūjas who dwell in that region.
Maṅkir was considered the teacher of the Mañcūrās and others;
Anāmaya was the teacher of the Prabhūtānas and the Pannāmas; and Cayanarṣi was considered the teacher of those from the region of Prākcayana. 86–87.
Aṅgaśyāmalaka was the preceptor of the Aṅgas, Śikṣāṅgas, and Deśas;
Ārakarṇa was the preceptor of the Ārakas; and Khāsana was the preceptor of the Khasīs.
These were always the gurus of the kings and the subjects of those respective lands. (88)
The great sages, the most excellent of the great devotees of Viṣṇu, were bestowed by me;
they, in turn, accepted those kings as their Vaiṣṇava gurus.
All those sages, kings, and subjects attained great joy. (2.110.90)
Then the Blessed Lord, who knows the hearts of his devotees and dispels the suffering of living beings,
assumed the form of a lotus and appeared before all embodied beings;
he placed his feet, adorned with auspicious marks, upon the chests of them all.
An eight-pointed star, an upward line, a svastika, a barley grain, and a vajra;
a jambu fruit, a banner, a goad, and a lotus appeared on the right side.
A triangle, a pitcher, a cow’s footprint, and a bow appeared [on the left]. (92–93)
The fish, the half-moon, the sky, the tortoise,
Garuḍa, the peak, the elephant, and the swan— these,
along with the celestial chariot and the sun, were located beneath the ankle-joints on the left foot. (94)
On the right foot of Hari, there appeared at the knee and the direction of the big toe:
on the left side, however, at the hollow of the knee, these five things appeared upon the foot of Hari: Lakṣmī, a palace, a tree, a cow, and a lion-throne. (95–96)

Then, [he should meditate on] the right hand, which bestows success and is endowed with a fish, a banner, a bow, a discus, a svastika, and a trident; it is joined with a lotus, an arrow, and a staff, accompanied by the fearless discus, marked with the line of Śrī, and possessed of a peacock. 97.
