by young maidens, saffron, unbroken grains, and sugar should be offered.
By those of sweet fragrance, auspiciousness consisting of ornaments, garments, and the like should be bestowed.
Indeed, the most excellent [gifts] should be given to the rivers beloved by Hari;
swings, horses and the like, carriages, and even protection [should be provided].
Likewise, wind-vehicles, steam-vehicles, and auspicious fire-vehicles [are to be offered].

A warm vehicle, a radiant vehicle, and the most excellent atomic vehicle should be given for the purpose of a monastery, as well as vehicles for the sky, for water, and likewise for the air. A water-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, and one that travels upon the earth should also be given. (65–66)
One should thoroughly satisfy the daughter of the Pitṛs, who possesses both the form of water and a physical form.
When those wives of the Lord are satisfied, the Lord himself is pleased.
Great festivals for them should be performed during the dark and bright fortnights of the month of Māgha.
In front of them, dancing and the playing of musical instruments should be performed;
there should be recitation, singing of the Lord, and Vedic chanting from the Sāmaveda.
At that time, they should be adorned with ten million diamonds, gems, and other precious things.

The beloveds of Hari should be worshipped with flowers, fragrances, ornaments, and other offerings. On the morning of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is accompanied by the beloved of Brahmā, the daughters of the Pitṛs, and others.
The Blessed One was then to be worshipped with supreme devotion and adorned with excellent objects,
like a sovereign king of kings,
with golden necklaces and the like, as well as garments of golden thread and the like.
Kṛṣṇa is to be propitiated with one hundred and eight kinds of foods, both solid and soft, as well as with services and most excellent songs;
and also with delightful crowds consisting of a beautiful mixture of men and women.
In every city, in every village, in forests and even in dwellings,
in cowherd settlements, in market towns, in ports, and especially in royal capitals—
there Hari, Nārāyaṇa, dwelt together with those various excellent wives.
He should indeed be paraded along with auspicious processions consisting of elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, golden carts,
and silver carts, accompanied by water-pots,
banners, and attendants.
The chariot must be stabilized by attendants at every crossroads (77). At every market, every street, every shop, and at the city gate,
as well as at every royal palace, it should likewise be honored with offerings of *śrīphala* and other fruits (78).
A rain of flowers mixed with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), parched grain (*lāja*), and so forth, should be made;
furthermore, sandalwood and scented water must indeed be offered for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Sweet food and sweet drink should be given from the chariot to the petitioner to drink.
And grace must always be bestowed upon the devotees on the path.
Musical instruments and royal trumpets should be sounded before [the deity].
This is the supreme festival of circumambulation, accompanied by incense and lamps.
The great festival of Kṛṣṇa’s birth should be celebrated during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Having thus paraded the Blessed Lord together with his beloved,
he should be installed at night upon an elephant-throne within a spacious pavilion.
Then, a lustration ceremony (nīrājana) should be performed with one hundred and eight wicks;
there, a dance should be performed with clapping, staffs, and so forth,
as well as with various musical instruments, and at that time, a narrative of Hari should be recited.
Having performed the worship, one should carry out the ritual dismissal (*parihāra*).
At night, the Blessed One should be led to that temple along with his consorts.
Then, the devotees should likewise perform a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*).
Having gone to one's own home, those devoted to celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should sleep there.
In the morning, having bathed, bowed to Hari, and performed the rites of viewing and worship, one should then perform acts such as giving gifts on the morning of the ninth day. 86–87.
There is no end to that merit, for it bestows supreme liberation.
In this way, during such a great festival, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is pleased;
the rivers are also pleased and bestow abundant prosperity.
They bestow ever-new prosperities of wealth, grain, and the like;
health, sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as cows, buffaloes, and riches; horses, elephants, camels, vehicles, celestial chariots, and royal splendors. (2.112.90)
"The best of rivers, when pleased along with the Lord of Śrī, surely grant fame, gold, honor in the world, supreme renown, and stability.
Thus did the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself speak.
"In every house, my image shall be protected along with the river;
it must always be worshipped in the morning, at midday, and likewise in the evening.
I shall fulfill that desire of his and grant him his wish again and again. (92)
Thus spoke the Blessed One to those virtuous women there in the beautiful forest; afterwards, they bathed at the ocean of Brahmā’s daughters,
and traveling in all their celestial chariots, they bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Together with the Blessed Lord Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
they meditated for a moment and worshipped the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
they fixed the form of Nārāyaṇa within their hearts and remained steadfast in meditation.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this account of Hari’s deeds has been told to you by me;
it is auspicious, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation through hearing or even reading,
granting heaven and final emancipation, and destroying sins and suffering.
It should indeed always be glorified by devotees as well as by those seeking liberation.

(98) Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Installation and Worship of the Embodiments of the Sacrificial Ground, the Upalaśa Tree, the Hāsa Lake, and the River," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 112. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Tretā-yuga Lineage).
Chapter 113 [Author:
Chapter 114 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Śrī Rādhikā! those beloved daughters of the Pitṛs asked Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with great reverence:
"O Beloved, our greatness has been increased by You through Your grace."

"And we shall come to know the greatness of the Śrīmata, O Soul of All, so that liberation may be ours at the end; tell us this. Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign who is devoid of birth, destruction, and the like, [spoke].
He said: "From them arises the knowledge of one's own true nature, which is assisted by devotion.
Beyond the world of living beings exist indeed the realms of the lords.
There dwell Vāsudeva and the others, in millions of manifestations."
In Goloka, I dwell as Kṛṣṇa, served by Rādhā;
and in Vaikuṇṭha, I indeed dwell as Nārāyaṇa, joined with Śrī.
Beyond that, in the imperishable abode, I exist as Puruṣottama.

I am known as the one who transcends the imperishable (akṣara), the two-armed Supreme Lord; I am beyond even the supreme imperishable in the abode of the highest. I am served by countless liberated souls and attended by the beloved of Brahmā.
The divine splendor arising from the region of a single hair-pore of mine pervades all lords and appears as if full;
by a mere fragment of my single quality, they become lords with an abundance of qualities.
Indeed, my incarnations come into being by my mere volition;
and countless creations, truly, arise by the will of my Puruṣa.
Therein they are born in infinite numbers, and I abide within them as their Inner Ruler.

I dwell within and without all beings, each according to its proper place. O my beloveds, having assumed whatever form is required— according to the task at hand, according to what is needed, and according to the service of my devotees— I abide among the multitudes of my devotees.
In some places I exist among the lords (Īśas), and in others among the gods in heaven; in some places among the best of sages who are devoted to me, and in others among the human race.
In some places I am in water, on land, in the forest, on a mountain, upon the earth, or in a cave.
In beasts, birds, aquatic creatures, trees, creepers, and grasses, || 14 || I indeed become whatever is required—man, woman, or otherwise;
a king, a subject, or a wretched man; a saint, a virtuous wife, or a passionate woman. || 15 ||
"O beloveds, whether as Gopāla, Gobāla, Gojāla, or the husband of Gopikā, my descent is certain in every kalpa, yuga, day, and hour. Now I am Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of the virtuous Śrī Kaṃbharā."
The beloved of ten million lotus-maidens, who fulfills the desires of maidens—
I am indeed the Supreme Soul, the human Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa Anādi Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa, known by the name Puruṣottama. (17–18)

O ladies, I dwell in the imperishable field (Akṣarakṣetra) near the hermitage of Lomaśa, in the region of Saurāṣṭra, within the sacred precinct of Kumkumavāpī, which is adorned with horse-patterned banners; there, my assumed disguise is fashioned out of compassion for you.
Though immeasurable, I assumed the state of being measured while performing the dance of men.
By bestowing the fruit of the penance of the maidens of the previous kalpa, I became one possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids and infinite valor. (2.113.20–21)
Endowed with the six fortunes, the eight powers, and the eight perfections;
the locus of countless qualities and strengths, possessing the power and form of ten million lotuses;
I have been born here in person as Kāntaka for the sake of fulfilling the destiny of these maidens.
"By the power of my ascetic penance, I am today your husband.
You must perform service for me for the sake of attaining happiness;
indeed, service to me with affection is considered by me to be true devotion."
I am pleased by her alone, and not by any other means whatsoever;
just as a virtuous and devoted wife always serves her own husband, so should one who desires liberation always worship me with undivided devotion. (25)
She, whose nature is supreme devotion, must be cultivated by me in every way.
(26) And the hearing of the stories of my births and deeds must be performed;
for that, heard from the mouth of my male or female devotee, indeed bestows liberation. (27)
The hearing of my incarnations and deeds by one seeking liberation is auspicious;
likewise, the hearing of the wonders of my devotees is auspicious.
Those seeking liberation should listen to the accounts and narratives of these deeds.
Thus, O beloved! My work is the glorification of myself and my saintly devotees as well.
Discourses concerning the stories of my births, deeds, and conduct should be caused to be narrated from the mouths of the virtuous at appropriate times, repeatedly, with faith. (2.113.29–30)
The reading of my devotees' works as well as my own,
and likewise the teaching of the lives of my consorts, indeed bestows liberation. This applies always to both my verses composed in meter and my prose.
With joy,

one should perform my *kīrtana* by singing both Sanskrit and Prakrit texts, accompanied by instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*), or with the clapping of hands (*tālikā*), and with the sounds of flutes and cymbals. (32–33)
The well-proclaimed [song] should be performed accompanied by the sound of small bells (*kikiṇī*) bound to the ankles,
and by the rattling sounds of the cloth-bands fastened around the waist,
all joined with dance. 34.
My praise and my prayer, as well as the chanting of my names,
should be performed with devotion through verses and delightful words. Furthermore, my remembrance should be practiced by contemplating me within the lotus of the heart.
O beloved ones! My form, complete with its primary and secondary limbs, should be meditated upon within your own hearts.
Having contemplated each individual limb, from the hair down to the nails of the feet, you should especially contemplate my smile during the meditation on my form.
My names and deeds should always be remembered. (38) The miracles of my devotees and of myself should be remembered;
the recollection of my qualities should be performed, and likewise, my mantra should be chanted. (39)
Of my supreme abode, the imperishable realm, Goloka, and the immortal [realm],
as well as Vaikuṇṭha, the unmanifest, and likewise Śvetadvīpa;
of my abode named Viśāla and that called Sāketa.
And likewise, O beloved ones! [these are] my eternal Kailāsa and my Ocean of Milk;
my Śrīpura and my Śrī; my attendants and the wives of Brahmā;
and my sovereignties, perfections, and glories.
On festive occasions, one should perform the remembrance of my divine holy men,
of my temples, of my parents and their kin,
of my cows, my vehicles and so forth, as well as of my own attire. (43)
One must always maintain mindfulness of my weapons and of all things related to me;
through that, liberation shall indeed be attained, for they grant me divine liberation. Furthermore, O beloved ones, the massaging of my feet must be performed. || 44-45 ||
"Here, you must repeatedly perform the massaging of the feet of me, Hari, who am present before your eyes as the true Lord Kṛṣṇa from time immemorial.
Remaining there, I shall accept your service, such as the massaging and so forth. (46)
An image of me should be fashioned, complete in all its limbs and beautiful with its marks—
whether made of metal, wood, or clay—
and it should be worshipped at all times and in every way by both men and women. (47–48)
One should perform acts of service filled with affection, as desired by the mind;
or, having fashioned a mental image of me created through meditation, one should touch its feet and all its limbs. (49)
One should touch her with one's whole being and take delight with her. My mind is entirely resolved upon serving her;
she is to be fed, honored, and especially gratified. (2.113.50–51)
"Though I am Kṛṣṇa, residing within your hearts, I shall accept your service.
Having placed me upon your bed, you must indeed sleep with me constantly.
Even in your worldly affairs, that [service] must be performed by placing me at the forefront."
One should eat only after having firmly realized Me, and never otherwise.
I am always present in the body and in every way within the senses;
thus, one should perform all actions while fixing Me in both the enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment.
All that shall be free from qualities (nirguṇa), bestowing liberation and bestowing merit.
One should proceed placing me at the forefront, and one should abide in me in every way.
In this manner, my service should be performed, as well as the tending of my body.
Through my service, the younger brothers of Vāsudeva, who possess the nature of the divine manifestations (vyūha),
attained the powers of creation, emergence, nourishment, and withdrawal.
Purified by my big toe, the Gaṅgā sanctifies the entire world of Goloka.
Time, illusion, evil karma, enemies, treacherous hearts, fear, and so forth—
these quickly perish for those who take refuge at my feet through service.
Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, Pāravatī, Śrī, Māṇikī, and Priyā— [58]
Furthermore, one hundred and twelve other wives of Brahmā attend upon my feet;
indeed, millions and billions of women, as well as even liberated souls, constantly serve those two feet of mine. (2.113.60)
Indeed, countless Devapriyas and countless Gopīs have attained even greater fame by serving at my feet.
Vyāsas by the hundreds of thousands likewise praise those very feet of mine.
Those two feet are to be massaged and served by those who desire liberation.
My two hands are likewise to be served, as are my feet;
my head is always to be served, and my back by means of massage. (62–63)
"O beloved ones! My limbs, as well as my secondary and tertiary limbs, must be served with devotion.
The service of any one of my limbs grants me liberation.
Now, my worship must be performed by the Sāttvatīs and the Sāttvatas. (64)
The external worship should be performed with sixteen or even one hundred and eight offerings that are heart-pleasing, excellent, and delightful.
In the case of my mobile image, one should invoke me and perform the worship.
One should bathe [the image] with ghee, milk, and other substances, and likewise sprinkle it with water;
thereafter, one should have excellent garments prepared and properly offer them.
One should also place various ornaments upon the appropriate parts of the body.
One should apply anointing unguents such as sandalwood mixed with saffron from Kashmir (68).
According to the season, one should affectionately fashion a *tilaka* mark containing a central dot,
as well as fragrant necklaces, crests, and ear-ornaments (69).
One should offer me a lamp, excellent incense, and the finest food offering (naivedya).
One should perform the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana) accompanied by the playing of songs and musical instruments.
One should also perform circumambulation, hymns of praise, prayers, prostrations, and so forth.
One should offer a handful of flowers and perform worship at the five times of the day;
or one may perform it at three times, or twice, or even only in the morning.
On my birthday days, this great worship must be performed here.
On the day of the concluding feast (pāraṇa) of the Ekādaśī vows, virtuous and truthful persons should be fed accompanied by song and instrumental music.
Those who possess wealth should cause firm temples to be built for me.
There, the wealthy patron should have the consecration performed with great festivals.

He should grant a village, a field, wealth, or a house for the sake of the materials for worship. He should establish a beautiful means of livelihood to ensure the continuous success of the ritual worship. (74–79)
One should cause wells, ponds, flower gardens, and beautiful lakes to be made, as well as sacrificial pits and wells, for my sake and for the benefit of the virtuous.
One should also cause the most excellent Vaiṣṇava sacrifices to be performed with abundant sacrificial fees.
One should perform the recitation of mantras, the reading of hymns,
and so forth; likewise, one should repeatedly perform the *puraścaryā* (preliminary rite) for my names,
as well as the *puraścaryā* for mantras and even for sacred texts, with devotion.
The ancestors are deities to be worshipped, as are the sages who possess aged bodies.
Thus is external worship described; mental worship, however, is internal. It consists of one hundred and eight excellent mental offerings performed within the heart.
Worship must be performed for me by those filled with an ocean of love.
(2.113.80) Furthermore, salutation to me must be performed by bowing with the eight limbs—the six limbs, the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, and the eyes. (2.113.81)
"By speech and by mind, men should always prostrate like a staff; likewise, women, having sat down together, must perform obeisance to me with their feet, hands, mind, speech, head, and eyes. (8.2)
One should perform prostrations upon the pure dust touched by my feet;
indeed, those very particles should be placed upon one’s body and head.
Likewise, water and other substances that have touched my limbs, as well as sandalwood paste that has touched my limbs [should be received].
"Even the stage-powder, water, perfumes, and scented dust should be worn.
Oh, how great is my supreme fortune; I have obtained this powder and this dust! Oh, how blessed am I that it has been touched by the lotus feet of the Blessed One! (85)
Speaking in this very way, a person shall be broken within eternal bliss.
(86) Furthermore, service must always be performed, just as the sage Lomaśa did for me;
for in the state of servitude, prosperity ever abides, just like Lakṣmī. (87)
One should certainly not harbor pride in that service, for it causes injury;
at all times, one should remain like a servant in the service required.
Service of every kind—whether appropriate or inappropriate—is in every way to be performed.
I must always be served with devotion by a man, just as I am served by a woman as a maidservant or a handmaid. I, the Supreme Lord, am to be served;
one should personally fetch water for my use in bathing. (2.113.90)
One should also gather flowers and personally weave a garland beforehand;
one should likewise grind *tulasī* and sandalwood into a paste.
A devotee should prepare the cooked food himself and feed me with morsels.
One should offer water for drinking and the like, and even cause me to rinse my mouth with a handful of water.
A devotee should personally offer me betel leaf as a mouth-freshener and should fan me appropriately with palm-leaf fans and other such items.
One should perform the sweeping and the anointing of my temple;
one should carry out restoration of what is dilapidated or construct new temples and the like.
It is auspicious to serve devotees with food, water, fruits, and other offerings.
Abandoning pride, one should act with devotion and indeed bow down to them.
One should perform the surrender of one's body, wife, children, wealth, and so forth into their service.
To me, who conducts myself in this manner, I grant equanimity.
Therefore, let all friendship be established with me as if I were manifest before you;
indeed, one should behave toward me here and in the hereafter exactly as one would toward an equal.
Yet, a greater degree of affection should be shown toward me than toward the body, wife, husband, sons, and so forth.
While I am engaged in human-like dramatic performances, you should not perceive any fault in my actions.
O beloved ones, since I am dependent upon my devotees, you must never entertain any doubt regarding me as an agent, a non-agent, or one who acts otherwise in my various deeds.
"Whether they approach me through desire, anger, greed, delusion, self-interest, or the longing for pleasure—in whatever way people surrender to me, in that very same way do I reciprocate.
One should have no doubt about this; this is my friendship and my benevolence toward them. (2.113.10)
Whatever I do for the sake of my devotees and for the welfare of my devotees,
people do not understand that profound course of mine;
therefore, one should place full trust in all my actions.
Now, indeed, my entire task is this:
the surrender of oneself by a man or even by a woman; the body must be offered to me in every way. Likewise, the senses must be offered, as well as the internal organs.
One's own nature and one's family must indeed be offered to me;
they should be surrendered by the devotee, and one should certainly not remain dependent on them.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, your Lord.
He should always remain dependent on me, performing all his actions for my sake;
he whose every activity is for my sake, being devoted, shall be dear to me.
Thus, you who are so dear to me must always conduct yourselves toward me in this manner.
"I am beloved by you all, and I shall indeed grant you eternal happiness.
Thus spoke Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme Lord.
"O Rādhikā! [I have seen] the various forms of devotion in particular. (107–108)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "An Analysis of the Various Forms of Devotion that Bring About the Lord’s Complete Satisfaction," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 113.
[Chapter 114 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Section 2 (The Tretā-yuga Lineage)].
[Author: Chapter 115.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Thus did the Lord of Śrī, the illustrious Narāyaṇa, speak in particular.
Furthermore, O Rādhikā, listen to that which He spoke:
"One should abandon even one's own kin who create obstacles to my devotion;
one should behold with both eyes the form of my body, complete with its major and minor limbs. (1-2)
One should constantly hear my stories and accounts of my deeds with one's two ears;
one should experience the touch of all my limbs with one's skin;
and one should perform the recitation of my qualities and the chanting of mantras with the tongue.
One should eat the prasāda from my mouth and drink the water;
one should take the prasāda through my nose, as well as a leaf born of the tulasī, flowers, fragrance, and the sandalwood offered to me. (4–5)
With both hands, one should perform the auspicious massaging of my body;
with the head, one should perform my salutation, and likewise, circumambulation with the feet.
With the mind, one should form the resolve for me, and with the intellect, the supreme determination for me.
She should cause my beloved alone to be contemplated by her mind.
She should always maintain the conceit of being my servant;
indeed, she should perform all agricultural labors and virtuous deeds solely for my sake. (7–8)
O daughters of my father, you must indeed exert yourselves for my sake!
Whatever object may be dear to you, that you should always offer to me.
[This includes] perfume, flowers, ornaments, clothing, and likewise unguents.
Having performed this auspicious act of grace toward me, one should thereafter wear it.
Whatever leaf, flower, or even water has not been offered to me, that should not be eaten, nor drunk, nor worn—even if it be a diamond or the like. (2.114.10–11)
One should perform austerity, one should perform sacrifice, one should give charity, and likewise perform recitation;
indeed, for the sake of my grace, one should perform everything for the benefit of others.
One should also serve the Sātvatas and likewise serve virtuous women.
O sinless ones, this must indeed be performed by my devotees for the sake of my gratification.
I am always present within the devoted man, as well as within the virtuous woman;
my limbs and all my senses are ever situated within their bodies.
They indeed dwell there, without a doubt; therefore, they should be served daily.
The virtuous should be served by those who have desires, for in my view, they are like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
The virtuous fulfill all longings and bestow both heaven and liberation.
"Virtuous women and wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavallīs) are to be served by a woman who has desires.
From them, all heart's desires are indeed accomplished; of this there is no doubt. Through their constant blessings, those desires surely bear fruit."
The goals of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa bear fruit;
and among them and within them, I myself, the supreme Nārāyaṇa, truly dwell. And according to their respective needs, I fulfill the heart's desires of my devotees.
And at the end of the body, I grant them the eternal abode of great bliss. There, they indeed obtain their desired happinesses, which are truly imperishable.
[They attain] Sālokya, Sārṣṭi, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and identity with Him (Tadātmatā).
"I indeed grant these very things to them because I am pleased by their services.
There are others who are superior, the most fortunate and my supreme devotees;
they desire nothing other than service to Me, nor do they seek the splendors of supernatural powers. (21)
Nor do they ever desire liberation in its fourfold form;
nor do those devotees desire the supreme and mighty sovereignty granted by me or being granted by me,
just as Lakṣmī does not desire it for them.
Indeed, because they create obstacles, even spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*) are impediments;
you do not grasp even with your heart those impediments, such as worldly powers (*aiśvaryas*).
My auspicious little hut of the self is my heart, completely filled with bliss.

O dear ones! indeed, his beloved ones become completely permeated by the bliss of my form. (25) Those people who thus worship me with a desireless disposition are declared by me to be the best of devotees, because their hearts are filled with me. (26)
For one who thus honors and serves me constantly, affection increases ever more greatly, wherein no obstacle arises—
just as the waters of the daughter of Brahmā, having pierced through many snow-capped mountains.
As these [rivers] come from various regions and enter the beautiful ocean,
so indeed does the love of devotees, having pierced through obstacles born of place,
time, association, and others, enter into me, the Infinite.
All the functions of internal and external principles, as well as their inherent natures and latent impressions, truly find their rest in me alone.
Even when I have become perceptible and am present in close proximity, [they rest in me].
Among those called humans who are equal to themselves and behave like their own kin,
the devotees— having attained a fullness of affection and having entered the ocean of my bliss—
do not find attachment elsewhere; for they never turn away from me to anything else.
People encounter two kinds of objects, for they are indeed twofold: secluded and non-secluded.
The first is considered pleasant, favorable, and a giver of happiness;
the second is unfavorable, unpleasant, and a giver of suffering. (33)
That [pleasure] must indeed be abandoned by its very nature; for what need is there to mention it for all [beings]?
Indeed, although it is always desired by all embodied beings, even then it appears as a source of great suffering to those possessed of discernment. (34–35)
Indeed, for yogins, even the mere maintenance of the body must be undertaken with force;
yet even that appears to their intellect as something distinct and a source of suffering.
This [notion] of beauty never arises in them regarding things that are beautiful.
And wherever I am, there alone is the loveliness of these great-souled ones.
Without me, sandalwood—though lovely, cool, and full of fragrance—quickly becomes like poison when touched; yet when joined with me, it becomes like nectar. (37–38)

Without me, flower garlands, golden necklaces, and the like become nooses when cast around the neck; but when joined with me, they become the hands of a bride. And an ornament devoid of me—be it gold, pearl, or diamond—is likewise [no more than a burden].

Supported by me, it would indeed be like a bed of leather; joined with me, it is as pleasant as the moon. (2.114.40) A beautiful flower-bed, though devoid of me and joined with another lover, even if fashioned with garments washed in fire, acts like the Raurava hell. (41)
The autumnal moonlight, though dripping with nectar, acts like poison and heat when deprived of me; yet when united with me, it acts like milk.
A palace worthy of Indra’s residence acts like a mere cave when devoid of me.
A dwelling place devoid of me becomes like a forest of wild beasts for living beings;
likewise, a fragrant and cool breeze devoid of me acts like fire.
A fine garment devoid of me becomes like a thorny jungle.
To him who is entirely bereft of me, his relatives act like wolves;
his gentle and charming form acts like leprosy;
and even delicious food, when devoid of me, acts like poison to the devotee.
Even a sweet drink, when devoid of me, acts like vomit; even nectar, when devoid of me, acts like poison.
Even a gait full of grace, when devoid of me, acts like an arrow;
even a virtuous woman, though she be a goddess, acts like a forest fire when devoid of me.
Everything that is pleasant becomes painful, and likewise, everything peaceful appears cruel to one who is bereft of me. To a devotee deprived of me, even the sweetest thing turns bitter.
Furthermore, a festival devoid of me always feels as though its joy has been shattered.
Even Ānanda, deprived of me, experiences bitterness in such a way;
even every auspicious association, without me, acts like death.
Indeed, for a devotee, everything auspicious without me becomes as if inauspicious. (2.114.50)
In this way, the devotee’s boundless affection for me should be understood;
indeed, I alone manifest both within and without the devotee. When I am suddenly perceived by the devotee within, I alone am seen.
Then, beholding me, the devotee would sometimes smile with love;
sometimes, seeing me as if departing for afar, he would weep;
and at other times, through the attainment of bliss, he would dance and sing.
In some places he converses with me, who possesses a divine form;
in some places he performs the eight-limbed prostration, and in some places he embraces me.
In some places he kisses me, and in some places he sleeps with me with great affection.
Sometimes, rising up suddenly, he then gives me water;
sometimes here and there he provides me with bathing, food, ornaments, and the like.
Sometimes, becoming absorbed in meditation, he delights within me.
Sometimes, adopting silence, she summons me within her heart;
sometimes, drawing me near out of affection, she leads me indeed into solitude.
At other times, becoming a maidservant herself, she performs service for me.
In some instances he practices loving-kindness, in some excellence, and in some he maintains equanimity (58).
In some cases, considering his own fault, he even says, "Please forgive me.
In some cases he requests an object, and in some cases he becomes subject to another's will (59).
Sometimes becoming unrestrained, he utters only names:
"O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Svāmī-Pati-Prabhu!
O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Self, my Lord, my Beloved, O Hari, O All-pervading One! (2.114.60)
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Kṛṣṇa, O glorious Nārāyaṇa!
O Supreme Lord, O ocean of mercy, where are you? Tell me this!
Having thus addressed me, he served me according to his desire.
In this world, there shall be no shame for him who obstructs my service—
whether he be a devotee of mine, or a female devotee, or even a servant.
Such a person purifies the entire universe and the cosmic egg with his very breaths.
Indeed, by the dust of his feet, evil ways are set ablaze.
By the mere sight of him, people indeed become purified instantly.
Through taking refuge in such a devotee, supreme liberation is attained.
Through service, there shall be service unto Me alone; of this there is no doubt.
There is no difference between him and Me; he is indeed My very body.
His senses are My senses; of this there is no doubt.
I see with his two eyes; indeed, I touch with his skin.
I hear with his two ears and taste with his tongue.
I speak indeed with his speech and smell with the faculty of his nose.
There, with my nose, I perceive various intensities of fragrance;
with my eyebrows I express [my intent], and I grasp it with his very hand.
And with my two feet, I always go to the sacred fields of the gods.
I gratify that very organ with its function of desire;
I likewise discharge waste through that organ, the anus.
Yet, I contemplate that very [organ] with my own mind.
O beloveds! I always perform reflection upon Him with that mind;
indeed, I everywhere maintain the sense of "I" through His heart;
and I always make my determinations regarding Him solely by means of His intellect. (72)
"I perceive sound, touch, taste, form, smell, and even bliss;
yet I remain established in Him, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Thus, all His activities are divine, and they are indeed my own activities. (73–74)
Devotional moods that take the form of liberation are not merely illusory; they are indeed beneficial.
One should perform service to Him, for through that I find satisfaction. By offering everything to Him, there is indeed the offering of all things for embodied beings.
In that way, I am manifest to me as one possessing the nature of the saintly;
likewise, I am unmanifest to me as one separated from the saintly.
Indeed, the saintly are manifest to me as divine forms.
One should perform service to those Blessed Ones through all ritual actions and the like;
there should be no doubt in this matter, for they are indeed my own forms.
Neither the Brahmins, nor the munis, nor the great sages are so preeminent.
And there are no teachers nor gurus like my excellent holy men (sādhus).
Among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the best; among Brāhmaṇas, the Sāttvatas;
and among the Sāttvatas, those who are my devotees and have offered themselves to me are supreme. (2.114.80)
Among those who offer themselves [to Me], the virtuous who have received initiation are indeed the best;
among the virtuous, I am the most excellent—for there is no one else superior to Me or equal to Me.
The virtuous are My equals and the most excellent; therefore, I always chant their names.
I constantly grant my vision to the holy ones who dwell within me;
to those who have offered everything to me and whose minds are surrendered to me, I grant liberation.
I bestow remembrance upon them, as well as servitude and friendship toward those great-souled ones.
I perform the chanting of praises and the salutation of those holy ones;
I massage the feet of the holy ones who are my very selves.
Furthermore, in their worship, I even offer myself as a gift.
I have no greater affection than for the virtuous, because of my contemplation of the ultimate reality.
Those who bear the name of the Supreme Lord are indeed givers of liberation through my name;
they are called Nārāyaṇas, and such virtuous ones are truly dear to me.
I take my food through their mouths and I am satisfied by them;
neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Cāraṇas, nor Guhyakas and the like, nor ancestors, nor sages, nor Brahmins are superior to the virtuous man for me. (87)
The lords, the world-protectors, and others are not superior to the saintly for me. Even those who are liberated and have attained liberation are not superior to the saintly for me.
What need is there to mention Lakṣmī herself, Rādhikā, Kamalā, and the rest? (88–89)
Śrī, Līlā, Bhū, Vibhūti, Pārvatī, and Māṇikī—these, beginning with Prabhā, are not superior to me because of their saintliness; what then need be said of others?
O daughters of the Pitṛs, worship me with such devotion as this!
"I shall deliver you all; purify yourselves, O embodied beings!
Having spoken thus to them, O Rādhikā, Śrī Narāyaṇa then placed his two feet and his very form within their hearts.
Having bathed, eaten, and fed [them], Hari himself gave permission for them to go to their respective abodes and to the purifying holy places (tīrthas).
"Always worship me, your husband and lord, in the manner prescribed by me."
"Even while causing my devotees to practice devotion without effort,
such devotees— and you as well— will, at the end, attain absorption in me without exertion and go to my own abode."
Having attained the divine body of Brahmā by my will in my abode,
you women who possess devotion shall go with me;
all these eternal and supreme things have been granted by me.
Those who, filled with devotion, shall serve me, and those people as well as women who likewise shall practice devotion, will always obtain infinite syllables and divine pleasures. (97–98)
They and they shall go to my supreme state of liberation;
let them know me thus, let them serve me as their beloved.
Indeed, by bestowing my mantra upon them, let them liberate all embodied beings.
"I am going to my own field, the eternal Kuṅkumasthalī.
Having spoken thus to his daughters, to the rivers, to the sages,
and to the gods— the beloveds of Brahmā— he then remained silent for a moment.
He reflected within himself on something to say to Śrī Śaṅkara;
men and women stood ready to carry out his command.

(102) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Demonstration by the Blessed Lord of the Nature of Devotion to His Own Self, His Devotees, and Others, as Well as to the Rivers Consisting of the Daughters of the Ancestors," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The One Hundred and Fourteenth Chapter.
Chapter 114: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 115.
[The Author: Chapter 116.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! Having thus commanded those who are of the nature of rivers—
Then Hari said to the illustrious Śaṅkara:
"O Yogin, these warriors who are your devotees must be granted a kingdom; therefore, let the auspicious Pārvata kingdom be given to them, for it is suitable for them. || 1-2 ||
And here, on this Himalaya mountain in the vicinity of Kailāsa,
let there be mountains for the bhūtas upon its upper levels;
let that great kingdom of the mountains indeed be the seat of the bhūtas.
Having spoken thus to Śambhu, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gave him an auspicious crown;
then, under the name Bhūtanātha, he bestowed upon him the kingdom.
In the form of Bhūtanātha, the Lord is of the nature of Bhairava.
There, Śaṅkara also gave a crown to Bhairava, the great-souled sovereign of all beings, who is the very essence of his own nature.
Having obtained the kingdom, Bhairava bowed to the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed to his father Hara and taken the host of spirits (bhūta-maṇḍala),
he went swiftly to Mount Himālaya, which exceeds sixty lakhs [in extent].
At that time, those mountains were indeed made into abodes for the spirits by him.
Having thus bestowed the kingdom upon him, the Lord Śrī Bhagavān spoke to Brahmā right there:
"May you govern and protect forever this land of Cera-vatī, known as the Brahmadeśa."
"Let Śaṅkara go to Piṅgā on the land of Prācīnarājya;
let Viṣṇu go to Śyāmarājya, which is renowned by your name.
Having thus commanded those gods and dismissed them, he [entered] the rivers.
Then Hari commanded the sages dwelling in those various regions to depart for their respective eternal abodes, and likewise instructed the subjects;
thereafter, he dispatched all the assembled hosts of gods who had been born as warriors.
He said to me: "Let your followers dwell in the region known as Sāmaveda;
those who remain here, moving eastward along the daughter of Brahmā (the Gaṅgā), shall quickly reach the land of Kāmarūpa as far as the Patatkāya mountain."
"In this southern region, as far as the Lūkaśayana,
and the naked mountains extending toward the Lūkahītā river—
let them dwell there, filling that entire Sāmaveda region."
Having thus settled all the hosts of warriors, Hari himself established a Śiva-liṅga there for the king while he was seated. Then the Gaṇa named Śivaliṅgaka led all the soldiers from that place.
The Gaṇa took up residence everywhere in this neighboring region,
having taken with him the goddess Śivā— who is born from the Śiva-liṅga, who is the embodiment of desire, and who is Kāmākṣī of Kāmarūpa. || 18 || He departed after leading her along.
Having constructed that auspicious and lofty temple-mansion on the mountain, the Gaṇa established the virtuous Satī, who could assume any form at will;
regarding her always as his mother, he worshipped her with reverence.
He established an excellent city named after himself on the heights;
thus Nārāyaṇa, having bestowed the kingdom upon the Śiva-liṅga,
stationed all the soldiers and dismissed the gods and sages.
Then, taking ten million maidens entrusted by Prajāpati into the celestial chariot—
ten thousand maidens who were attendants, twenty who resided with him,
twenty daughters of the Pitṛs, and others who were beloved of Brahmā— [he departed].
Having taken [them] with him, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇasvāmī, together with Lomaśa and accompanied by his mother and father, arrived through the sky at Kāśī, the abode of Śrī,
where his own Lakṣmī indeed resides as a maiden in the palace of Śiva.
Indeed, she waited expectantly for Śrī Puruṣottama.
There, in that garden on the bank of the Varaṇā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa brought his own celestial chariot down to the earth and went to his home. 26.
Having bowed to Śivarāja Hara, as well as Pārvatī, his father-in-law,
and likewise to his devotee Jaya, Candra, Kṛṣṇa, and Dhenupa,
he then met with his own virtuous and beloved wife Lakṣmī in a secluded place.
Having caused her to embrace all the maidens in the celestial chariot and to behold them,
and likewise having arranged for her to see her parents and Lomaśa as well,
and having comforted her, let her be settled once more in her father’s house.
Having granted the blessing, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, arrived by celestial chariot at the sacred field known as Kuṅkumavāpī, which is called Akṣara;
on the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, Hari himself came there.
The supreme Lord arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī in the evening.
Seeing that he had arrived at the end of the month, his brothers, kinsmen, and virtuous men,
as well as Rudra, the gods, and the holy fords, came to Aśvapaṭṭasara itself.
Millions of sages, portions of the Lord's incarnations, and likewise devotees arrived in his presence upon seeing that extraordinary splendor in the sky;
they beheld a divine celestial chariot adorned with the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Beautiful, with the radiance of ten million suns and as cool as the luster of ten million moons, it was accompanied by ten million maidens, eighty thousand maidens, and twenty thousand maidens.
Those inhabitants of Akṣarakṣetra uttered cries of "Victory! (Jaya). || 34-35 ||
With parched grains, unbroken rice, and saffron from Kashmir,
they greatly honored the celestial chariot of the Supreme Lord.
And then, it descended from the western side of Lake Aśvasaras.
Then, in the garden near the palace of Anādikṛṣṇa,
Śrī Svāmī Nārāyaṇa Hari descended from his celestial chariot,
accompanied by the beloveds of Brahmā, the daughters of the Pitṛs, and their handmaidens. ||37-38||
Lomaśa, as well as other great sages and his father,
along with his mother and the other virtuous women beginning with Ramā, entered their own abode.
Hari, his mother, his father, and Lomaśa rested there for a moment.
Those maidens gazed upon Hari’s palace, which was higher than the highest;
a great abode pervaded by the wealth of supreme beauty, endowed with divine prosperity, and resplendent with the sovereignty of ten million powers. (2.115.40–41)
It was auspicious, adorned with seven stories and with the statues of the lords,
beautified by the Brahma-pool and the Brahma-lake;
it was divine, endowed with divine qualities, and resplendent with divine mechanical devices and the like.
Then, having witnessed that supreme wonder, all those maidens were filled with astonishment.
At that time, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to his own sister, Santopā: "O sister, let food be given to these [maidens]."
Mādhava then said to the goddess, his brother’s wife, "You are immortal.
He continued, "Let these two be given a drink and auspicious mouth-fresheners and the like.
When this was said, those two suddenly [beheld] a son born from the wish-fulfilling gem of the Kalpa tree.
They gave food of a hundred varieties and many kinds of drinks,
and they showed great hospitality to the wives of Kṛṣṇa.
All of them embraced their sister, who was the wife of their brother.
Likewise, other maidens and the wives of the sages also beheld those divine girls at that time with their own divine glances,
which were offered to Kṛṣṇa.

Likewise, assuming the forms of creepers as well as birds, deer, and other creatures, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, possessing many forms, appeared bringing wonder. Afterwards, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama spoke to Śrī Lomaśa. (2.115.49–50)
"O Guru, these women must be led by you yourself to your own auspicious hermitage;
they should be protected with great care along with Brahmapriyā and the others.
Lomaśa, too, was honored, fed, and likewise saluted."
Having taken the girl to his own hermitage by his own command, he then departed;
the Blessed Lord rested, and the parents went away happily.
Then indeed, O Rādhikā, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself— || 52-53 ||
In the month of Phālguna, he indeed celebrated the great festival of the flower-swing;
having caused beautiful and variegated divine platforms to be constructed, moistened with water,
together with the two lords Hemanta and Bhagavat, their attendants, and other followers.
Having prepared the necessary materials, he then began the performance.
Having worshipped Śrī Vasantaka with excellent golden mechanical dolls, as well as his own image and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, [he commenced]. (vv. 55–56)
Taking the syllable, as well as the liberated ones and the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
in her own hand, she held a golden yantra adorned with colors; then,
while the people remained within their boundaries, she indeed cast the color [upon them].
Repeatedly, he cast his supreme splendor upon his own countless beloveds who were themselves devoted to his devotees;
likewise, he bestowed that same excellent radiance upon his devotees, the Sāttvatas, the great sages, the common people, the cowherd women, and the cowherds devoted to him. (58–59)
He scattered red powder (gulāla) and turned everything into the color of blood; he made all his own dependents red, and he himself likewise became red.
The sky also became red, and the filaments [of the lotuses] likewise turned tawny.
And the water of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, mixed with various colors,
attained a variegated appearance like a rainbow in the sky; indeed,
the surface of the earth became an imperishable field consisting of a colorful arena.
The clay from the Kuṅkumavāpī field, having assumed the form of sandalwood,
attained a tawny hue when thoroughly mixed with colored water.
Then, having thus arranged the play of the flower-swing, he—
Hari bathed along with all his subjects and played in the water.
Then, wearing new garments, the people went into the forests and among the trees,
and throughout the gardens permeated by fragrant breezes.
There, having tied up various and wonderful flower-made swings upon the branches of the trees all around,
they created unsurpassed beauty there with fruits, flowers, and other ornaments.

All the maidens wearing new garments, as did the Blessed Lord and all the subjects, engaged in the auspicious swinging during the great festival of the flower-swing, and they rejoiced exceedingly. (67–68)
All the young women swing back and forth with one another;
the beloved of Brahmā swings her own lover with deep emotion.
They proclaim various wonders through their songs of praise.
Then some danced near Hari as he swayed, while others played beautiful musical instruments in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, others made Kṛṣṇa laugh with humorous words.
Other women gave cool water to that beloved,
and other women gave him ripe fruits.
Then, many of them made their own beloved Kṛṣṇa swing.
Indeed, with her own feet, she repeatedly swings the swing.
Then, Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lords, knowing all the minds present there, manifested in countless forms.
Toward every maiden, every woman, every devotee,
and every tree, the youth became charming, removing the intoxication of ten million desires.
And for all virtuous women, devotees, and the wives of Brahmā—
Having accepted their service, the Blessed One again became one-fold.
Thus, on the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra,
Hari performed the most excellent festival of the flower-swing in the imperishable field (Akṣarakṣetra).
Then he went home and once again fed [them].
In the evening, he held a celebration with singing, dancing, and instrumental music.
Thereafter, they all went to sleep and quickly attained rest.
Then, while he was living in this manner, the month of Śrāvaṇa arrived.
Devotees prepared various swings made of gold and silver, richly adorned with many ornaments and beautified by rows of flower garlands. (2.115.80)
Inlaid with divine diamonds, gems, and other jewels, and fragrant; adorned with divine, soft beds and auspicious seats— there,
having seated the beloved Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
And those beloved of Brahmā caused their Lord to swing.
Then a marvel occurred there: clouds indeed became human beings at that time, and having done so, they came from the sky to that place for the purpose of swinging Hari.
And they gave to that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, a new swing— divine, radiant as lightning, without support, yet resting upon the sky.
Upon each of its individual parts were pearl-like gopīs and attendants.
Incarnations and abodes are seen, as well as lords;
likewise sages, ascetics, gods, ancestors, and even humans;
oceans, mountains, planets, and the circle of constellations. (85–86)
The guardians of the directions, the guardians of the worlds, as well as those dwelling in the netherworlds (pātāla); Kṣīroda, Śvetadhāman, and the inhabitants of Viśālākṣara;
the Unmanifest (avyākṛta), as well as the abode of Amṛta—these too were seen there.
Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Sāketa, and Kilāsaka;
likewise the four-faced Brahmā, and the eight-faced Brahmā;
likewise the unborn one with sixteen faces, and the thirty-two-faced one. (88–89)
He is seen with fifty faces and even with a hundred faces;
he is seen with a thousand faces and even with a hundred thousand faces.
Likewise, Brahmā is seen with ten million faces within the circle of jewels.
Such a divine swing was indeed given by the clouds to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa accepted it;
having ascended the swing, he rocked it and then questioned the clouds.

"Why has this divine, auspicious, and worthy celestial swing, which reveals the entire universe, been brought here for the sake of me, the Lord of All? The clouds replied, "O Great King, we have come from Kāśī."

Then, in the month of Āṣāḍha, for the purpose of a pilgrimage to the banks of the Varaṇā, we saw the daughter of Śivarāja at the beautiful Mahālaya. There, we engaged in pleasant conversation with one another. (94–95)
Having performed both bathing and viewing here,
one must indeed proceed to the Aśvapaṭṭasara tīrtha and the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa;
[then] to the auspicious field called Akṣara, the supreme, eternal bestower of liberation.

Therein shines the Great King, the beginningless Śrī Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person, the Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, the sustainer of all incarnations, and the cause of all causes. (97–98)
Bālakṛṣṇa himself is the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
he is the son of Śrī Kambharā and the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa. If it is indeed our intention, let us go for the very purpose of beholding him.
Having heard that, the maiden said: "I indeed have a swing in my house;
it should certainly be given for its sake if you truly intend to go.
O Lord, this was given by Lakṣmī, the destroyer of sorrow, and has been brought here by me."
"O ocean of mercy, accept her; the burden of maidenhood is too great.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One rejoiced greatly and accepted her. He bestowed blessings upon her and upon them as well, again and again.
Having bowed down, the clouds departed into the sky; Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself personally rocked the swing in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
remembering the goddess Lakṣmī Nārāyaṇī, and he considered it a great festival.

Thus has been narrated, O Rādhā, the auspicious and beautiful life-story of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, which bestows liberation and grants all prosperity. By reading it, by hearing it, by causing it to be heard, and even by teaching it—
"Through meditation, it bestows liberation and grants a divine, spiritual body.

(106) Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord granted the kingdom of Bhūtāsana to Bhairava, and the kingdoms of Nagna and Parvata along with the sovereignty of the Sāmas to distinguished warriors; how he commanded the rivers in the Sundara forest to go to their respective regions; and how, upon returning to the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, he performed the Phulladolotsava and the Śrāvaṇotsava," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (115)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the auspicious birth-month of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; it is indeed the month of Kārtika, consisting of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇapakṣa). 1.
The thirteenth divine day, the eighth [lunar] tithi, has arrived.
To celebrate that festival, the Vaiṣṇava people of Prāgjyotiṣa,
as well as those devoted to the eastern lands and those born in the region of Śyāmabrahma, have gathered.
Those born in the land of Trivitta, as well as the inhabitants of Kāśmīra;
likewise others dwelling in the snowy regions and those originating from the land of Śambhu—men, women, boys, girls, and those who serve the elders. (3–4)
Great sages arrived at Aśvapaṭṭatīrtha by means of celestial chariots,
as did virtuous and truthful men, bringing various offerings;
eager indeed, they came for the sake of worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa.
And likewise those born in the region of Uṣṭrālaya, as well as those born in the region of Abrikta;
those from the region of Ārabīja, and those born in the field of Kumārī;
others indeed belonging to Ajanābha, and likewise those originating from the land of Kaccha. (6–7)
Eager and bringing offerings, they arrived for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa.
In the morning, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa prepared a beautiful pavilion.
Having bathed and put on his garments, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa sat upon the elephant-throne.
Having put on ornaments and other finery of love, he entered the assembly hall.
There were the gods, the ancestors, the sages who have attained liberation in the Imperishable, the lords residing in other realms, the deities, and human beings. (2.116.9–10)
They arrived at that assembly for the sake of worshipping Śrī Hari;
excellent musical instruments were played, and shouts of "Victory! arose. Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa shone resplendent, seated upon His own throne, having been magnified.
In the assembly, the brahmin Lomaśa worshipped Acyuta.
He placed a crown upon him and then gave him two earrings.
Thereafter, he applied a tilaka on Hari’s forehead, adorned with unbroken rice grains and the mark of the moon.
They performed the *ārārtrika* ceremony for Him and placed garlands of flowers around His neck;
thereafter, they offered blessings, and the lords worshipped Him.
Then [they worshipped] Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, and even the beloveds of Brahmā.
Then the goddesses, the Gandharva women, and the noble wives of the sages;
likewise the gods and their goddesses, the progeny of Vaiṣṇavī belonging to the Prāgjyotiṣas, and those honored by the earth who had come from other lands—all [honored] that Lord. (15–16)
They worshipped him exceedingly with all divine articles of offering; they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and presented great gifts before him:
various garments, ornaments, and pearls.
They gave necklaces made of gold and silver, diamonds, and thousands of girdles;
they gave vehicles, elephants, horses, and likewise excellent ornaments; as well as foods, drinks, and fruits that were like nectar.
Having thus worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa,
his mother Śrī, Gopāla, and his father Śrīhari in the beautiful pavilion,
he then bowed to the sage Śrī Lomaśa and the other seers from his elephant-throne in accordance with the custom of the people.
Then, having risen and bowed to the elders assembled in the hall,
Puruṣottama, who was highly esteemed by his father, departed for his own abode;
and Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, having fed those honored guests, likewise retired.
Then he bid farewell to the people and their virtuous wives;
at that time, Lakṣmī and Śrī Kambharā honored them with devotion.
Having fed them, he sent them back to their own homes.

Thus, the thirteenth festival of the birth of Śrī Hari was perfectly accomplished; the great devotees then returned to their own regions. O Rādhikā, listen to the wonder that occurred there on the second day.
Sent by his guru, the blessed Dattātreya, who is the Supreme Self, a certain Śarabha went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He arrived there for the sake of liberation and then offered praise to Śrī Hari.
Having indeed attained a divine body, he went to the abode named Akṣara.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, who was that Śarabha who was impelled by Dattātreya?
"Tell me that entire narrative; I wish to hear it in its entirety.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you the auspicious story of Śarabha."

Samīraṇa became the king, born of the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa). He was the auspicious sovereign of the western region of Ājanābha, and the lord of kings over Gaurjaras, Kacchas, and Saurāṣṭras. (2.116.29–30)
He was compassionate in protecting his subjects and a devotee of Nārāyaṇa;
he was constantly intent on righteous deeds, devoted to giving and fire-offerings,
possessed of unbroken fame, and likewise dedicated to the protection of the distressed.
He was the protector and supreme guardian of cows, the earth, Brahmins, and the virtuous.
In his kingdom, there was never any famine in the past;
likewise, he was the protector of those who sought refuge and the defender of the land. (32-33)
The archer himself constantly performed service to the gods.
His capital was situated on the bank of the river Śatruñjitā;
it was a great, divine city named Kuṇḍalā, adorned with Brahmins.
It was inhabited by gentle subjects such as Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
there, the Brahmins were devoted to sacrifices and offerings and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas;
likewise, there were virtuous ascetics dedicated to meditation upon Kṛṣṇa. (35–36)
Even the forest-dwellers did not experience any hardship anywhere within his kingdom;
both men and women were always happy under his protection.
Indeed, this was the constant distinction in the reign of Samīraṇa.
Every morning, the drum is constantly sounded by the king’s officers:
"Is there anyone—miserable, blind, wretched, without support or refuge;
one who is without food, or an orphaned child, or an old man, or even a beggar? (38–39)
A woman who is without support, aged, a widow, or without family;
a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a female yogi, or an ascetic woman destitute of wealth;
or one who is poor, penniless, a eunuch, or likewise a female eunuch.
"Coming to my door in the morning, let him accept food and sustenance.
In my village, my city, my town, and among my subjects—
wherever indeed there are houses containing my food— " || 42 ||
"Let him come together here and there and receive food and drink;
let him take up his garment and his bowl, honoring the Supreme Person.
Thus does his drum resound at dawn, awakening [the people].
Men without wealth ate his food at every place;
having eaten, they were constantly satisfied and offered words of blessing.
Thus, endowed with merit, the king one day [addressed] his circle of servants.
Having taken them, he set out for the tiger forest, eager to roam about;
his servants, elephant-drivers, and attendants also went along with him.
Then, in the middle of the forest, upon the bank of a pond, among the trees—
Having established a residence for his elephants, horses, and other animals,
that king entered the forest to hunt according to the duty of royalty.
Some servants also went along with the king, accompanied by their mounts.
Having merely sighted the gavaya, the king followed its tracks;
thus, he entered the dense forest in vain.
Armed with a bow and mounted on his horse, the king, who was fond of hunting animals, pursued it with speed.
He reached a beautiful river there, auspicious and overflowing with water. On its bank stood a delightful and most exquisite hermitage,
indeed well-arranged with trees laden with fruits, flowers, and the like.
It was exceedingly beautiful with sages and birds and deer that inspired great trust;
it was supremely pure, bringing peace through the cessation of the predatory ways of violent creatures;
and it was frequented by the disciples and grand-disciples of the sages, like the abode of Brahman. 52.
Where there was no arising of the defects of lust, anger, or excessive greed;
where even among the beasts there were indeed no faults such as deceit or falsehood;
and where the birds sang sweet songs among the trees and other plants.
Then the parrots, peacocks, cuckoos, and royal swans gathered together and sang in their own tongues the words of the Vedas;
indeed, even the gods and goddesses came from the celestial realm and took up residence there.
Having bowed to the sage, they depart indeed, considering themselves to have accomplished their purpose.
And in such a hermitage, the great sage Pārṣṇigraha performs extensive asceticism for the sake of the welfare of the world.

In the summer, he sat continuously in the midst of five fires; during the rainy season, he sat upon the bare ground amidst the downpours of rain. Dwelling in cold water, he remained standing in every way throughout the day.
At night, he indeed remains there at the foot of a tree, completely unsheltered.
(5.9) Sometimes fruit, sometimes flowers, and sometimes even the food of sages; sometimes water, and sometimes drinking water—the cloud gathers for him. (2.116.60)
Without food, he remains wherever he is, worshipping Śrī Narāyaṇa;
he meditates within his heart upon the true Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Such is this sage, beneath whichever tree he may be situated at that time.

Before him, that gavaya approached and, out of extreme fear, became perfectly still there, having sought refuge with the sage. The king, not seeing the hermitage from afar nor the sage likewise, [proceeded further]. (62–63)
With his mind fixed on the hunt, he forcibly struck a gavaya with a sharp-edged arrow that pierced deep into its belly.
With the arrow still lodged within it, the gavaya cried out there in front of the sage.
He fell down just as his son had, indeed for the sake of protection. Seeing the sage then in such a wretched state with a piteous eye,
and beholding him fallen along with his arrow, the sage Pārṣṇigraha [intervened].
The compassionate one immediately touched that animal with his hand and gave water to its mouth; then he saw an arrow lodged in it.
Likewise, he saw deer fleeing in terror.
Seeing them running about on all sides, he fell into great distress:
"Alas! Who is this slayer who has arrived today in my hermitage?
He is wicked, terrifying to the animals, lawless, and exceedingly cruel. (68–69)
"Whoever here has slain the faultless gavaya with arrows while it was breathing"—
just as the best of sages was thus engaged in reflection,
the king arrived there on horseback, following the track.
He saw a beautiful brahmin wearing a garland and possessing matted hair and a beard,
as well as a gavaya fallen there from its steps;
he regarded them with a gentle mind due to his connection with that hermitage.
Tormented and seeing that his rear was being attacked, the king turned back;
having tethered his horse at the foot of a tree, he followed on foot and,
filled with fear, quickly fell at the feet of the sage.
Then the sage said to him: "How is it, O wicked one!
that you, a hunter, have killed this innocent animal who dwells in my forest? You appear to be a wicked king, for you perform cruel deeds."
O lord of men, like a hunter of cruel deeds, do you not feel shame to commit such wicked acts even within the hermitages of sages?
By my arrow, the deer dwelling in my hermitage have been struck down.
This gayal here has indeed died within a moment;
when the arrow reached its full draw, his life-breath did not remain.
Behold, O wicked one, your own son—why do you not kill him yourself? (77–78)
Hunting is truly not appropriate for you among the creatures who trust the sages;
the deer near my hermitage are like my own sons.
Out of fear of you, they have fled, desiring to save their lives.

"O King of kings, you were broken by an arrow from a lion near my hermitage; therefore, become a Śarabha, for dwelling in the forest is extremely difficult. Furthermore, you shall never again inflict such punishment or slaughter upon anyone."
Thus addressed by the sage, King Śarabha right there cast off his human form and assumed the form of a beast.
In this manner, King Samīraṇa was indeed cursed by the sage.
Having become that śarabha beast, he then departed from the hermitage (83).
He did not speak there to request release from the curse,
being exceedingly terrified by the fault and also by the anger of the ṛṣi at that time (84).
Quickly abandoning that hermitage, he entered the forest of lions;
submerged in sorrow upon sorrow, he found no happiness anywhere.
Remembering his past lives, he was constantly intent on bringing an end to his own suffering.
While he was constantly wandering in the forest, thinking of this again and again, the king’s servants indeed learned of that news;
then, fearing for their own lives, they quickly went home. (86–87)
Then, at the Gavaya tree, the sage himself cast the handful of flowers consecrated with mantras together with the cow Sandhinī; by that act, the king was restored to life.
Thereafter, the king wandered through that forest in order to end the curse.
Having approached Pārṣṇigṛha, he requested his release.
The sage said: "In the great forest, at the lake of Pātālī, Mount Raivata will arrive and make it his own dwelling. (2.116.90)
There indeed, on a peak that is devoid of people, inaccessible, and traversing the sky, the Lord Dattātreya himself, the Great Master,
will personally perform intense and formidable penance. (9.1)
For while you were staying there in a mountain valley,
that Blessed One was seen and propitiated by you; out of compassion, he will lead you away,
O sage, and the son of Atri shall reside there at the sacred site known as Kuṅkumavāpī.
Then, on the western shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara, he worshipped Hari— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— through austerity;
by the grace of Dattātreya, [he beheld] the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

"Having beheld him and drunk the water produced from his feet as a favor, you will quickly be released from my curse; of this there is no doubt. Thus addressed, that royal sage, who possessed a body like that of a śarabha, [acted accordingly].
He departed from there for the forest near the great lake.
Then, after some time, Raivataka Mountain arrived there.
It was on that very spot that the venerable son of Atri performed his penance.
On the peak, he saw Śarabha performing his prayers.
The compassionate Lord Dattātreya had come to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, having taken him [Śarabha] with him to his own abode. (98–99)
Indeed, for the sake of his release from the curse, Dattātreya remains there invisibly;
that sacred ford named Dattātreya is located here at Aśvasarovara,
for it exists as a purifier to destroy the sin of the curse.

Having gone there indeed, Śarabha beheld Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; having drunk the water from His feet, he obtained liberation from the curse. Furthermore, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), he regained his auspicious royal form.
Having assumed a divine form here, he went to the auspicious, imperishable world.
Thus, O Rādhikā,
that excellent Śarabha always drinks the water from the feet of Hari at the Aśvasarovara lake in the evening.
He attained the supreme, divine, and eternal liberation of Brahman.
By reading and hearing this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for those with desires, there shall be the increase of their lineage as well as release from suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Thirteenth Birthday Festival of the Lord, King Samīraṇa’s Transformation into a Śarabha in the Forest due to the Curse of the Sage Pārṣṇigṛha while Out on a Hunt, His Liberation at the Kuṅkumavāpī Field through Dattātreya on Mount Raivata, and the Dattātreya Tīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
