[The Author: Chapter 118.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen further, O Rādhikā, to another [holy place], namely the Vārāha Tīrtha.
In ancient times, at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake of Kuṅkumāvā, there was the glorious Lord of Letters, the Sovereign of All, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is the Supreme Brahman itself;
when he began the creation from his own form. (1–2)
As he contemplated the principles (tattvas), fire was born from his mouth;
divine, liberated through the divine syllable, and bearing a divine liberated form.
He then had two arms, was white in color, and possessed a cool touch.
This very one became embodied, radiant with splendor, beautiful in form, and auspicious.
Then the Blessed One looked upon the fire to create it from the essence of the principles (tattva).
And the fire, having perceived his intention, then stood before Hari.
And Hari gave him this command: "Go among the lords and others being created by me;
always remain as the principle of radiance (tejas-tattva).
Having accepted this charge, he entered into Mahāmāyā.
Then Māyā, in the form of the embryo, underwent agitation like fire.
As that Māyā, which consists of the three *guṇas*, though subtle and by nature in a state of equilibrium, repeatedly underwent agitation. (7–8)
In that manner, the fiery quality of Māyā receded,
while by the will of Hari, her tamasic portion indeed increased.
Through Māyā, the aggregate of the principles (tattvas) became the Vairāja.

There, having attained the state of heat, the great fire consisting of warmth emerged from his mouth; he is the Lord named Vahni (Fire). Having taken recourse to the Vairāja [sound] *vaṃ*, he struck the jaw with *haṃ* through the path of the mouth. (2.117.10–11)
The god emerged from all sides and became fire itself;
divine, with a bright face, a brilliant complexion, and fully radiant.
Having relinquished his state as Brahmā, he attained the state of Īśvara.
Vairāja spoke to that Fire, his own son who was in human form:
"O son, create other sons like yourself who are fit for creation.
Placing the command upon his head with the word "Om," Vahni reflected:
"May my sons indeed be worthy of creation and possess my own nature;
may they be born from mere volition, purifying and like the wind.
From *pavi* three were produced: *pavi*, the *vajra*, and the lightning bolt (*vaidyuta*). (15)
The son was entrusted to Indra by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin;
but he who is named Pāvaka was entrusted to the worlds for the purpose of cooking,
being Pavamāna, possessed of great flames, and exceedingly restless.
"Swift and destructive, this burner is also most formidable.
When the people, having realized this, did not accept [the food],
then he, enraged, went to the forest to seek food in the great woods.
That one of great strength wandered through the great forests and other regions.
Thus, while wandering himself through the territory of Saurāṣṭra, Pavamāna was searching for food; not finding any, he became exceedingly distressed.
Extremely tormented by hunger, he set the tiger-infested forest ablaze;
the forest became terrifying, enveloped in garlands of flames.
As it burned, it became impossible to enter and difficult to exit from any side.
There, deer, birds and other winged creatures, wild beasts, and reptiles— along with cattle—
are burned by fire in that dense thicket of trees,
pervaded by clusters of grass and creepers, where the surface of the ground is invisible. (22–23)
All the deer flee, as do the birds blinded by the smoke; likewise, the forest-dwelling animals—
helpless with their young and offspring—
by the thousands, unable to sustain their lives, are overwhelmed by the fire.
There, the trees were burnt and perished by the son of Fire (Agni) accompanied by the Wind;
even the living creepers were reduced to ashes. What need is there to mention the number of grasses, vines, and shrubs? || 25–26 ||
The treetops appeared like mountains of fire;
at that time, the elevated regions of the forest were composed of fire.
Likewise, the mountains with their few peaks, the trees, the forests, and the sky were then [all] made of fire.
Just as the Jvālāmukha mountains were consumed by fire,
so too, when cruelty was unleashed for the destruction of those dwelling in the forest,
a pervasive fire arose, accompanied by the wind.

When the trees on the riverbank were about to be consumed by fire, the hermitage of the sage Picchala was overwhelmed by the force of the conflagration. The sage Picchala, who had been established in asceticism for many years, remained steadfast in his penance.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa in the form of the white boar,
he performed most formidable austerities in the forest among the forest-dwellers,
in that hermitage where the wish-fulfilling cows graze.
The cowherds stood there on the bank and also took refuge under the trees;
they fled toward the river water with the speed of fire.
To protect their lives, the cowherds fell and plunged into the waters.
Then this great seer, Picchala by name, the lord of the twice-born,
beholding the cruel deed of Pavamāna,
became personally filled with compassion and spoke to Pavamāna.
"O Vahni, O you who are exceedingly cruel and more than a great predator!
Afflicted by hunger, [I have come to] this forest and likewise my hermitage, along with the cows, cattle, living beings, flocks of birds, and reptiles. (36)
You burn me without fault, yet you do not release this wretched man.
(37) It is true that one who is hungry becomes evil-minded; it is exactly so.
But why, having abandoned all bounds of propriety, do you destroy everything by force? (38)
Behold, even the offspring of winged creatures and other animals, though footless and wingless, are being burnt;
yet you feel no compassion as you watch.
How have you come to such cruelty that you find no peace at all?
By your power, even the mountains and the elevations of the earth have been consumed.
Having obtained your own food, you have burnt all other provisions;
my forest has been brought to ruin, for all living beings therein have perished. (2.117.40–41)
"Therefore, I shall curse you here as the one who causes destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by Agni, O Rādhikā, the sage Picchala was distressed and cursed Vāyu:
"May you swiftly meet with destruction!"
Having said this, he released the water held in his hand onto the ground.
As soon as it fell, the flames of the fire grew dim;
its power to burn was destroyed, and its power to cook came to an end.
Likewise, the capacity of the taste for eating became latent in an instant;
the whiteness of fire was destroyed, and its heat likewise dissolved.
Furthermore, that which increases by nature then spontaneously underwent diminution.
The state of smoke increased, and the coals became lusterless and black;
they were then like dark-colored wooden brushes, lacking any light.
Indeed, the fire was extinguished without effort due to the cause of the curse. (46–47)
All the essences, seeds, and even the beasts and birds that had been consumed emerged from Pavamāna’s stomach in an undigested state.
He became thin-bellied, dull in luster, and slow in his breath.
On the verge of death and deprived of the power of his feet, he became devoid of the radiance of his senses and empty of their functions;
having reaped the fruit of his karma, he lamented in many ways and wept. (2.117.49–50)
"What must be done? Where should one go? How might the curse pronounced by the great sage be revoked? And how might he become gracious?"—thus he reflected.
Then this Wind-god, free from pride, [addressed] that sage.
Having prostrated like a staff, he went [to him] with his heart, mind, and speech;
desiring liberation from suffering, he praised him who is the very form of Brahman:
"O holy one, you are indeed compassionate, whereas I am merciless and a perpetrator of violence. (92–55)
"O virtuous one, you are devoted to truth, yet truth is not found in me.
You are always sinless, whereas I am most sinful and a bringer of suffering.
I am indeed discontented and greedy, while you are contented and not a hunter."
I am devoted to worldly possession, while you are dispassionate and free from possession.
I am the one who torments living beings, whereas you are an ascetic who does not torment.
You are eternally established in Brahman, while I am deluded in nature and subject to illusion.
I am indeed devoid of forgiveness, whereas you always possess forgiveness; I have not even a trace of the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), while you are here the very locus of those powers.
Like you, I am not capable of destroying the sins of sinners.
You abide as the sacred ford (tīrtha), yet I do not cross over that ford.
I am an individual soul (jīva) possessed of ignorance (avidyā), while you are always the locus of knowledge (vidyā).
You possess the body of Brahman, whereas I possess the body of Māyā.
"You are the bestower of divine liberation, while I am the giver of birth and the destroyer.
You abide as the granter of peace, whereas I am the one who causes agitation.
O gentle one, you here constantly contemplate the supreme Brahman."
He alone is capable of providing relief for the bodies of the destitute.
O high-minded one, grant forgiveness for the offenses committed out of ignorance;
you are the master who can bring back to life that which has been set ablaze by me.
Shining with ascetic power, revive the wilderness— its beasts,
its throngs of living beings, its birds, and its trees;
O one whose wealth is penance, rescue me and all creatures, including the reptiles and the rest.
"May I again become a vessel for the curses of the virtuous and a vessel for their satisfaction.
O holy one, I have received this instruction; do not bring about my death.
I have come into the presence of death; O remover of distress, restore me to life!"
The saintliness of saintly devotees of Kṛṣṇa consists precisely in this:
that having forgiven the offenses of a living being, they bestow virtues upon him.
A scorpion stings with its sting, yet the saint does not release it.
The mouse gnaws at the wing, yet the swan does not let it go.
(67) Guardians provide protection even for wicked beings.
O best of Brahmins, restore me to life; for the virtuous have forgiveness as their very essence. (68)
"I shall never again commit such an offense;
truly, truly, truly, I fall at your feet," O Rādhā! Thus did Pavamāna say repeatedly in his heart.
Having fallen there in the forest, he praised that seer Picchala.
Then the great seer, perceiving that hymn of praise through his state of meditative absorption, was moved with compassion; the ocean of mercy rose up immediately from his seat.
The one who takes refuge in the auspicious departed quickly to Pavamāna, who was praising his own [state]:
"O Pavamāna! May it be well with you; do not grieve, O son of Fire!
You are a god and the son of Vahni; if you were not so, you would not act thus. (71)
"I shall indeed restore you to life; let not the embodied one be consumed by fire.
Having spoken thus, he took water in his hand, consecrated it over the vessel with mantras, and as soon as he had taken it up, he sprinkled it over the wind-god.
Pavamāna became capable; he stood up and bowed down.
Endowed with splendor, he then prostrated himself like a staff before that sage.
Pavamāna then said to him, "O Lord, grant me release from the curse."
The sage said: "I have granted you the power to travel through the sky.
Go to the mountain named Śrīśaila, where the glorious Boar resides—the bestower of liberation and the protector of the life-force of the earth. (76–77)
"The boar, the creator of all protection, will grant you protection.
Having been told this, Pavamāna went with reverence to Śrīśaila;
staying near an anthill, he then continued to remember him.
O Rādhikā, the Lord then emerged from that anthill;
white-complexioned and beautiful, the Wind-god bowed before Him.
Then the Lord said to the son of Agni, "Be happy. || 2.117.80 ||
Then Anala asked him the reason for his arrival there;
he related the entire cause, including the curse.
Vibhāvasu said, "O Viṣṇu, effect my deliverance."

"O Supreme Lord, may you grant me here those qualities of former times: splendor, power, strength, form, divinity, and likewise pervasiveness. Thus addressed, the illustrious Varāha spoke to that Pavamāna.
Come, O Pavamāna, come with me to Surāṣṭraka,
to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake—
where dwells the Lord Himself, the sustainer of all incarnations, the Supreme Person. (84)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, shines resplendent in the imperishable field (Akṣara-kṣetra); He will grant you everything—
He will grant you liberation and divine status, and indeed all things.
Having spoken thus, he led Śrī Varāha by the hand to the realm of the Imperishable (Akṣaradhāman) suddenly through the path of the sky, and likewise to Lake Aśva;
there he quickly bathed him before the presence of Hari for the sake of His vision.
Having led him away, the glorious Lord Bhagavān Vārāha departed.
Pavana prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before him with great reverence.
Then Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa raised up the son of Agni.
Having seated him on his lap, he embraced him to his chest;
he then offered that lion-throne to this boar, who was his own self.
And having understood the reason for this, Hari assumed a human form.
To remove the sage’s curse, the Lord granted him grace.
Pavamāna partook of that grace as the fruit of immortality and drank the water;
as soon as he did so, he was endowed with all excellent qualities.
The Soul of the Universe, the refuge of his former attributes as before, attained [his natural state];
freed from all curses, he became exceedingly joyful and happy.
He worshipped Varāha as well as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

Then, through his union with Hari, Pavamāna became the very embodiment of a sacred ford (tīrtha). By the command of the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, Varāha also took up residence at that lake in the sacred ford.
Thus, that Vārāha-tīrtha came into existence there eternally.
There dwells the Lord Varāha, the Sovereign joined with the Wind-god (Pavamāna).
Those people who perform their ablutions there shall be free from disease.
Through contact with Hari and by sprinkling the waters of sacred fords,
they shall attain liberation and worldly enjoyment, and likewise reach a divine state.
By reading or reciting this, there shall always be health and what is dear.
O Rādhikā, the Lord, having assumed the form of a boar, spoke thus to you on the morning of the full moon day of Phālguna:
"I have indeed granted a dwelling in the sacrificial ground, as well as in the forest and in the great waters. (99)
He gave a dwelling in the water of the rain to Pavamāna;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa granted him a dwelling within the womb of the earth.
He bestowed upon him fearlessness and likewise the status of being a Vaiṣṇava.
He gave him a necklace of tulasī beads, as well as a forehead mark and a crescent-shaped tilaka, along with the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Then Pavamānaka, having offered his salutations, bestowed this mantra upon him.
Having worshipped Hari at the sacred ford, he went to the lake for the purpose of residing there.
Varāha also accepted the hospitality offered in every way;
O Rādhikā, he took up residence in that great Vārāha-tīrtha.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varāha-tīrtha and Pavamāna-tīrtha, and so forth, including Pavamāna’s journey toward Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ after assuming the form of the Lord Varāha for the sake of removing the curse given by the sage Picchala, and the liberation from the curse through the yoga of Hari," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

— Chapter 118 [[Author: → Chapter 119
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to another auspicious wonder of Hari, which is supreme for protecting devotees and destroys both sins and suffering. (1)
In Jayanagara in Saurāṣṭra, there lived a twice-born man named Santāraṇa.
He was devoted to the Vedas and the Dharma, fully intent upon the performance of worship,
dedicated to the six duties, and engaged in the recitation of sacred stories and the glorification of virtues.

He was a great devotee of the Lord, intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa through hearing His narrations, remembering Him, serving His feet, worshipping Him, praising Him, rendering service to Him, befriending Him, and finally, self-surrender. (3–4)
Every morning, the twice-born man himself would rise and go to the riverbank; having bathed in the Bhadrā and performed his twilight prayers and salutations,
he would personally carry a jar of water upon his head with devotion.

That twice-born man always performs the worship of the Śālagrāma with flowers and other offerings brought by himself, as well as with sandalwood paste and other substances ground by his own hand. While that worship was being performed, his wife, who was devoted to her husband, [acted likewise].
Indeed, that collection of materials known as Taraṇī,
out of sincere devotion, offers water, flowers, fruit, clothing, ornaments, ghee, and so forth.
His daughter Taralikā is a maiden, a virtuous young girl.
Always rising quickly before the time for worship, she would bathe, bow to her own parents, and with great devotion prostrate before the Lord;
then, acting with haste, she would prepare the hearth provided with fire. (2.118.9–10)
Having cooked milk-based sweets and *pūrikās*,
she offers this excellent oblation to Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu with supreme devotion.
The second daughter, named Kumudā, always [does so] early in the morning.
Having milked his own cow, he indeed offers the milk for worship;
having prepared the essence of the milk and so forth, he constantly offers it for worship.
His son Vinoda resides among the divine flowering trees.
He indeed performs the service of sprinkling water and other such tasks;
he always stands by his father’s side in the appropriate place, performing the washing of vessels, offering incense, lighting lamps, pouring water, and so forth. (14)

His second son was Vasantarṣi, a Vaiṣṇava who, during acts of worship and the like, offered the gift of air by means of a fan; he also provided the driving away of flies with sugar and *tulasī* leaves. (1781, 16)
They also offer fruits and perform service according to their needs.
Then, after the worship, everyone performs a hymn of praise to the Lord;
they also circumambulate him, prostrate themselves like a staff, and offer handfuls of flowers.
They offer forgiveness and requests for pardon, and then they indeed dance with joy.
They play excellent musical instruments and proclaim songs of praise;
they always sing with various rhythms and measures accompanied by diverse dances.
Having thus worshipped the beloved of Ramā, their eternal Lord,
they then distribute and bestow prasāda upon their devotees; thereafter,
those householders partake of the sugar-rice, water, and other offerings.
At midday and likewise in the evening, they worship according to the prescribed rite.
During the day, however, they strive for their livelihood, seeking only a small amount of what is required.
As time passed in this manner, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), [appeared].
Once,
during the night of the Ekādaśī vow in the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha,
he became visibly manifest through supreme devotion alone, wearing a beautiful crown and an excellent golden face-plate.
He wore the tip of the crest-feather of a preeminent peacock, adorned with jewels and gems;
he bore beautiful crocodile-shaped earrings upon his ears,
and he wore a saffron *tilaka* with a beautiful crescent moon in the middle of his forehead.
With a face of gentle smiles, his mind captivated by a divine radiance;
wearing around his neck the excellent Kaustubha gem, garlands of *tulasī* leaves, and strings of golden necklaces; and bearing a girdle upon his waist.
He also gave golden bracelets for his two arms and forearms,
beautiful golden chains, finger-rings on his hands,
and a staff made of gold set with pearls, rubies, and diamonds.
Wearing sandals fashioned from beautiful gold, Hari,
clad in radiant yellow garments, appeared by chance,
standing in the midst of a circle of splendor and honored by hosts of male and female servants. (29)
The youthful sovereign of kings, served by Rādhā, Ramā, and others,
then concealed his manifest forms from his devotees and became the self-effulgent Lord himself;
he appeared in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa as the illustrious Great Emperor of Emperors.
The youthful Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Master himself, bestowed the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya ravāmine svāhā.
Then, placing his hand upon his head, the Lord vanished from that place.
Thus, beginning from that day,
Śrī Mahārāja Keśava— the youthful Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, served by Śrī and Bhū— comes daily to the worship during the morning service. (33–34)
The Lord indeed accepts all the offerings presented during the worship in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and likewise Āśvina.
Having accepted their sincere worship, Hari spoke to them.

"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, my great festival of birth shall take place on the fourteenth [tithi] on the shore of Lake Aśvasaras, on the ground known as Akṣara. You must come to my abode. (36-37)
"Even my parents, along with their daughters and sons, will come to my abode,
for they are the lords of the three worlds who have come to worship me. Having spoken thus to those devotees, the Blessed One then vanished from their sight.
Then those devotees became eager for the sake of a pilgrimage to holy places.
On the sixth day, having prepared their provisions and secured their homes with locks,
they took auspicious gifts and set out on foot.
On the seventh day, they reached Lake Tvaṣṭṛ Aśvasaras in the evening itself;
they beheld Kuṅkumavāpī as well as the venerable hermitage of Lomaśa,
the sages, chaste women, holy men, many gods, and numerous temples.
The guardians of the fields and protectors of the fields, as well as cities, groves, and the like;
various gardens and divine forests of trees; sacrificial halls, storytelling halls, dharma-halls, and great assembly halls. (42–43)
Having seen the glorious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and likewise Śrī-Gopāla Hari,
and having beheld the divine earth and the maidens beloved of Brahmā,
as well as most celestial chariots and liberated souls on all sides within the palaces; ||44||
They attained the highest wonder at the supreme and marvelous Lord.
Having bowed to and worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
those people were then honored and fed by that Nārāyaṇa.
They entered the exceedingly beautiful palace in the house of Mānagṛha for the night;
overwhelmed with love, they kept a vigil on the night of the seventh lunar day.
They beheld celestial chariots arriving through the path of the sky.
In them dwell the liberated ones of the Imperishable (Akṣara), as well as the inhabitants of Goloka;
likewise the liberated ones of Vaikuṇṭha, the residents of Vairāja and Amṛta;
and the lords such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as the ancestors.
The seers, the celestial gods, the deities dwelling on Mount Meru,
the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and stainless human beings;
the perfected ones (siddhas), virtuous women, noble ladies, and likewise the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Rivers and streams, sacred fords, oceans, and likewise the seasons;
months, qualities, forests, and the asuras dwelling in the netherworld;
divine devotees, as well as daityas, dānavas, and the celestial bards (cāraṇas), and so forth. || 51–52 ||
Indeed, there are kings and celestial beings who reside within them;
such are those celestial chariots, resembling the sun and the moon,
resounded by the auspicious songs of throngs of maidens.
The sounds of musical instruments fell from the sky in an unceasing stream.
By the thousands, they gathered in the vicinity of the Kuṅkumavāpī field;
their splendors and radiance then resembled ten million moons.
In the sky, on the earth, in the city, and in every direction, there was not even a particle of dust; nor was there any darkness there, for it was like a realm of light.
[There appeared] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign.

Likewise, his father was named Gopālakṛṣṇa and his mother Kambharā; his sister was Santoṣā and his brother was the venerable Śuka; furthermore, Vallabha and the venerable Hemantaka were also [his relatives]. ||57–58||
The two charming male servants, the swans, and the group of virtuous female friends offered a welcome,
a place to stay, respectful offerings, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with great pleasure.
Then, at the hour of Brahmā, the great seers recited the Vedas.
Then auspicious musical instruments resounded on all sides.
The sages performed worship, and the virtuous practiced meditation;
the people and the honored guests also went to the lake to bathe.
Santāraṇa was his son, and Taraṇi was his beautiful wife;
they had Taralā, Kumudā, Vinoda, and Vasantaka.
All of them, indeed, remembered Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as their family deity.
Then they went to bathe in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
taking a boat and seeing a Śabara standing on the shore,
they boarded the vessel, desiring to sport upon the ocean.
Having paid the toll, they boarded, and the boatman set the vessel in motion.
When the boat had gone more than a *krośa* into the midst of the water,
other men were then made to board the vessel.
By the hundreds, they sported happily in the midst of the lake, on its banks on all sides,
and even in the great ocean;
indeed, at that time, they did so by their own great will upon that very boat.
Suddenly encountering a violent impact, the boat turned and in an instant its bow went downward; out of fear of that,
those on board then suddenly moved away to one side and fell into the depths of the water.
That boat too, filled with water, sank in the midst of the waters.
Indeed, there was no means whatsoever then to rescue them, even with a large ship or even with many smaller boats. || 2.118.70 ||
Suddenly, they were all searched for there by the fishermen;
however, six of them sank into that bottomless water at that very moment.
This was because they did not possess even a fraction of the art of swimming.
Though submerged in the depths of the lake, they did not fall into the hands of the fishermen.
Submerged in the depths, they drank the water especially and remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Those who were subject to the noose of death praised Hari in their minds— the remover of suffering, the provider of refuge, and the one who exists without support amidst the waters—
He who, as a boar, lifted up the earth submerged in water.
And he who, as a sea-monster (makara), seized a great ship situated upon the water;
he who, as a tortoise, bore a massive mountain submerged in the water upon his back;
and the Lord Hari, who protected his devoted elephant when it was submerged in the water.
The Blessed One who protected the merchant submerged in the water,
who protected the great land of Uṣṭrālaya submerged in the water,
and who in former times protected King Udayana submerged in the water.
He who protected Māñjāmbikā when she was submerged in the ocean—
O Nārāyaṇa, if you consider me to be a true devotee, know that the Lord likewise protected others who were submerged in water in many ways. (78–79)
Then, O Kṛṣṇa, deliver us out of the midst of these waters with compassion;
death is forever subject to you, and time likewise is your prey. Water and the obstruction of life-breath are always under the power of your might.
You abide as the inner self, the remover of untimely death.
O Lord of Gods, remove our sorrows if you indeed intend to protect us;
you are the boat, you are the Great Breath, you are the living soul, and you are the source of life.
In the midst of the waters, you alone were indeed the giver of life to Prahlāda.
There is no time for praise now, as my life-breaths are constricted by the water.
My heart and soul are becoming steady, and my consciousness is ascending toward the crown of my head.
"A moment exists within death; there is nothing more than that.
Thus, O Rādhikā, they became utterly fainting in the midst of the water, and having offered praise, they went for refuge and surrender to the son of Śrī Kambharā.
The omniscient Blessed One, Śrīśa Bālakṛṣṇa, acting with great haste,
assumed the form of an excellent tortoise, Kāmaṭha;
he suddenly took six devotees upon his back and held them above the waters.
The Lord,
assuming the form of a child, brought forth water from the surface of the waterless ocean; and suddenly,
touching it repeatedly with both hands, the Master warded off that delusion at that very moment.
The water they had drunk dissolved merely by the touch of their hands;
their fainting fit vanished, and they became radiant once more.
Bestowing well-being, they saw the great tortoise standing nearby.
They likewise saw the boy Kṛṣṇa, the protector of the cowherds, assuming a divine form;
upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, they attained supreme peace.
While searching, those six were indeed seen by the people atop a tortoise.
"Protected by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," they suddenly boarded the boat from the back of the tortoise at that time. The sailors indeed seized them, and the tortoise vanished from sight.
Indeed, that Blessed One became the bearer of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
For a moment, he was seen by everyone as a man in the form of a tortoise within the water;
then, having gone to dissolution in Bālakṛṣṇa, he was likewise seen by the people.
Having gathered them all together by boat and brought them to the shore, they left them there.
The people marveled at this wonderful miracle of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
they recognized Kṛṣṇa as their protector and thereafter served him with true devotion.
Then, in order to perform the worship for the birth festival,
the liberated lords, gods, goddesses, and embodied beings arrived at the pavilion.
They performed the worship with all kinds of articles and other offerings, and they performed the *ārārtika* rite.
They presented offerings and likewise bestowed blessings;
Śrī Gopāla fed all the great men in every way.
Having given many gifts and considering their service to be supreme, he honored them.
He dismissed all the great lords, and they departed.
Then the brahmin Santāraṇa, knowing that Bālakṛṣṇa was desirous of two maidens, joyfully gave him his two daughters. (2.118.100)
The Blessed One, the Lord of Śrī, accepted the two jewels among maidens;
and the two maidens, having achieved their purpose through the attainment of a husband,
both were given by Hari to Lomaśa at his hermitage.

Mādhava, along with his wives, protected the two maidens together with the beloved attendants of Brahmā. Then Śrī Hari, accompanied by his wife and son, performed the worship and the birth festival; having witnessed these rites, he became one whose desires were fulfilled.
Having received his command, that brāhmaṇa went to the city of Jayanta.
O Rādhikā, there exists that auspicious great tīrtha named Santāraṇa,
where the Lord Kūrma himself shines resplendent.
By bathing on the bank or within the temple, one is delivered from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
By reciting or even hearing this, he delivers one from the torment of sin.
Through the mere remembrance of him, liberation (mokṣa) occurs; how much more so, O Lord, through his service?

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rescue of the Brahmins Submerged in Water by Assuming the Form of a Tortoise at Dawn on the Eighth Day of the Fourteenth Year of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa at Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 119 [Author:
Chapter 120 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to another wonder concerning the devotee of Hari, O Rādhā!
There was a devotee named Devāyatana, a resident of Saurāṣṭra, O beloved, who took refuge in the auspicious [Lord] in a village called Samādhiyāna. (1)
The foremost of the Ābhīra caste, known by the name Devāyatana, was constantly devoted to ritual bathing and took refuge in the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, [repeating]:
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! O Hari, O Master! O Hari, O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (2–3)
O Śrī Gopāla, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kambharāśrī, Rame, and Sati!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama!
O Lord of Akṣara, O Lord of Prabhā, Rādhā, Māṇikī, and Pārvatī! 4.
"O Lord of the True Master, O Lord of the Abode of Liberation, O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare!
(5) Thus he constantly performed kīrtana on the bank of the river—upon the sands, in the water, under trees, and on the ground. (6)
In the house, in the field, in the groves, in the gardens, and even in the wilderness or the forest—
at all times and in all activities— he remembers that Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord;
whether eating, sleeping, traveling, walking, or sitting.
In wrestling, hunger, swimming, purification, and in the house of the indolent;
at the crossroads, in the assembly hall, and at the festivals of one's caste or family; during birth-impurity, in matters of grief, and even always in occasions of joy— (8–9)
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord!
Accompanied by the clapping of hands, he always performs the congregational chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
With faith, he indeed performs worship after his ritual bath. (2.119.10)
And he performs the *ārārtika* ceremony for the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
filled with the love of devotion, he indeed offers the Lord food offerings (*naivedya*) adorned with fruits, rice, and water.
In that village and region, people addressed him by the name Devāyatārṣi. Once, while seated at the foot of a tree,
Devāyatārṣi took a ripe *ṭimburu* fruit— sweet, delicious, and a source of comfort.
He indeed remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in order to offer his petition.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, brought under control by that devotion, arrived at the place where Tumburu stood, where that king of devotees was located. (14–15)
Then, having approached while laughing and disguised as a young cowherd boy,
he took ripe and desirable drumstick fruits from the hands of the deity and ate their sweet juice.
Devoted to the Lord, the sage offered him beautiful fruits;
he ate the grace bestowed by Kṛṣṇa, danced, and praised Him.
Absorbed in Him and immersed in His form, he possessed divine vision and a divine body.
Bālakṛṣṇa became free from bondage and possessed the power to traverse the sky; having eaten the fruits, he went to the river for water. Devāyana also followed after him to the river for water.
With his senses, life-breaths, and body drawn away by Kṛṣṇa, he followed along the path.
Having leaped over mountains, forest trees, and the like, he followed Hari through the path of the sky, his body free from all obstruction. (2.119.20–21)
He arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī and at Aśvasarovara;
meditating upon Śrī Hari with a focused mind,
he bathed in the lake using the steps leading into the water through the yoga of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Forgetting his body, he playfully immersed himself in the water for a moment.
Indeed, while his body remained in the midst of the water, turbid with the liquid, he drank the water and, becoming divine by his own nature, rose above the water. (23–24)
Chanting "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Rām," he emerged onto the riverbank with a divine body; and as soon as he stood there for a moment,
the thought that delivers one from worldly existence arose within him.
"If I cause the people to perform worship and the chanting of Viṣṇu's names with divine bodies, then living beings will attain liberation.
Having reflected thus, he performed the worship of Śrī Hari, Hari. (26–27)
Then, having passed through the tiger-forest and the lion-forest, he went to Saṃyamanī, the city of Yama, and there too he called out:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa! Hare Svāmin! Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! (28)
Śrī Gopāla, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kaṃbharāśrī, Hare Vibhu!
Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of Ramā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī; O Lord of Kamalā, Lord of Prabhā and Māṇikī, O Lord Nārāyaṇa! (2.119.30)
Thus he performed worship by proclaiming the chanting of the Name.
Hearing this, those standing in the fetters of Yama became suddenly pure, freed from their bonds and devoid of the torment of sin. (3.1)
Those worthy of liberation, possessing divine bodies and bodies fit for Vaikuṇṭha,
having assumed meritorious forms and repeatedly heard the name of Hari,
paid homage to Dharmarāja and went to the eternal Brahman.
Devāyana also, having wandered through all the lands of the Yāmyas and repeatedly proclaimed the name of Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari,
burned away the sins of the sinners and sent them to His abode.
Beholding this great marvel, the messengers of Yama hurried toward Yama and reported the undesirable news:
"O King Yama, O mighty-armed one, the prisons for sinners— " || 35–36 ||
But some, having approached and proclaimed the name of Hari, cause those who are empty of merit to perform [the rites]; yet these sinners depart for the realm of Brahmā.
Those with meritorious bodies, meritorious forms, and meritorious souls travel through the sky.
Indeed, they are capable of traveling by means of divine vehicles and thus they proceed;
he does not take account here of us who have been appointed as his staff-bearers.
Disregarding all of us, he shows his thumb and his teeth. (38–39)

"Laughing, these [beings] are departing from us; behold, your city is empty! Thus addressed, as that King Yama looked toward his city, he then beheld the entire realm of Yama and the world of punishment to be completely empty.
He saw that devotee of divine form, the path of the gods for Hari,
chanting his name with his tongue and making it heard by the denizens of hell,
washing away their sins and bringing about their divine liberation. (41–42)
Seeing that most powerful Sāttvata standing there, who was about to depart for the abode of Hari,
Yamarāja bowed down with devotion to this devotee.
He said, "Welcome," and offered him respectful water (arghya) as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
He offered him a seat, and the king of devotees sat down. He inquired after his entire well-being, his health, his name, and the reason for his arrival;
and the devotee indeed spoke auspiciously to the devotee.
Yama said: "The name of Hari destroys the sins of sinners.
You, O foremost of devotees, take it up; indeed, that is what is fitting for you.
This worldly existence, however, is most sinful, a giver of suffering, and enveloped by the fruits of karma."
A living being is born through karma and through karma alone it perishes.
Through karma one experiences suffering, and through karma happiness is attained.
Indeed, the performer of virtuous deeds reaches the sovereign heaven.
Indeed, the doer of evil deeds encounters the suffering of hell;
for the purpose of punishing those sinners who have performed unrighteous acts,
a hall of punishment was built here by Viṣṇu and exists eternally.
There, I am the son of the Sun, appointed as one whose body is Dharma. Hari Nārāyaṇa himself is the son of my form as Dharma;
Kṛṣṇa and Nara were indeed my four sons in former times.
Indeed, in Viśālā-Badarī, my mental incarnations have arisen;
by its name, the sins of all sinners are surely consumed,
and living beings attain liberation through the very power of that land of action.
But this is the city of Yama; it is indeed nothing but a hall of punishment (53).
This is not a place for the exhaustion of karma, nor is there entry here for those who have attained liberation.
Without the experience of the fruits [of one's actions], there is no turning back from this place (54).
Thus, by the command of Śrī Hari, as well as by the will of Manu and the ordinance of Brahmā,
and following that very [command], I bestow the fruit here upon the embodied soul.
No one whatsoever should ever cause any harm therein.
"Thus, O devotee, this very rule has been violated by you today.
Since you have come here disregarding the rule of Kṛṣṇa—
who is the destroyer of sins and the bestower of liberation— " (56–57).
"O devotee, you have not performed what is appropriate; perform the chanting of Hari's names!
Though thus entreated, he did not acknowledge the power of Śrī Hari.
Thereupon, the devotee said to Yama: "Release this man; this is the city of hunters."
"By the name of Hari, I shall indeed grant you dharma and liberation as well.
'O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Lord! Speak, O Nārāyaṇa!'—worship this Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and truly abandon all other speech. (2.119.59–60)
Having realized that, one attains the state beyond death; there is no other path.

Indeed, for the sake of the liberation of living beings, the granting of liberation is considered supreme. [6.1] The release of those who are wretched, helpless, poor, and powerless—this is the highest goal.
"Furthermore, for the sake of the liberation of ignorant Asuras and Rākṣasas, I, who am fully aware that this worldly existence is perpetually crowded with sin, must always act;
thus, having arrived here, I shall diminish the oceans of the sins of the wicked. (62–63)
O Yama, they are burned away by the name of Hari; thus, that which is appropriate is performed.
O son of the Sun, even if but a single human being here were to deliver another from this state by means of the Name, I truly see no end to his merit.
"How is it that these messengers of Yama are guarded like Rākṣasas?
Let them indeed be given by you from this day forward into a state of non-servitude.
And let Citragupta and the others depart for liberation upon hearing [this]."
Proclaim the name of Hari and make the city desolate;
let all the devotees of the Lord dwell there, free from suffering.
Cleanse the mechanical devices and effect the liberation of the sinners.
Indeed, all these compassionate Sāttvatas shall become Vaiṣṇavas.
By the power of Hari’s name, I shall liberate them all; of this there is no doubt.
Let this city of Yama become a heavenly city filled with bliss.
"I shall make myself free from sin here by worshiping Hari;
do as you wish, O Lord of Yama! Worship Nārāyaṇa, Hari!
Having spoken thus and bowed to Yama, he continued to worship Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
Holding Bālakṛṣṇa in his heart, he went to the ponds of the sinners.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa! Hare Svāmin! Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare Kṛṣṇa! Śrīpati! Pārvatīpati! || 72 ||
"O Supreme Brahman, O Imperishable, O Māṇikīśa, O Lord of Ramā!
O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, Lord of Prabhā, protect me, a sinner!
Thus he cried out with his palms and likewise with his voice.
Bringing happiness to the sinners, he went all around the southern city.
Having thus caused countless sinners to hear the mantra and the kīrtana, he completely incinerated their sins and sent them to the imperishable realm.
King Yama, being overwhelmed with agitation, went to Kuṅkumavāpikā,
the imperishable supreme field, and the divine Aśvasarovara. Suddenly, having arrived before Śrī Hari, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
Having fallen down with tearful eyes, he remained there observing silence.
Although the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, already knew [the truth], He questioned him regarding the cause of this through His human-like dramatic play.
Yamarāja also spoke to his devotee who had arrived from the realm of Yama, who was offering liberation from sins through the chanting of the Name.
Having heard that, Hari said: "O Yama, I am subservient to my devotees."
I am the fulfiller of the desires of my devotees and am subject to their will; what can I do?
Neither I nor even Brahmā and the other gods are able to restrain him.
Therefore, listen to my command: do not grieve over this occurrence.
"Indeed, grant me a period of time to empty the realm of Yama once for all;
thereafter he shall depart.
When the city of Yama is empty, he will not find any sinners there to behold."
Thinking his own task accomplished, he will depart of his own accord.
Today is my birthday, marked by the fourteenth year;
O Yama, let there indeed be the release of the shackles of sinners.
Thus addressed, King Yama, having received Kṛṣṇa’s command, performed the worship of Hari according to the prescribed rite; remaining there, he rejoiced in happiness.
Thereafter, the Blessed Lord fed King Yama.
And Hari placed a golden crown upon his head, and a golden necklace adorned with jewels and diamonds around his neck.
[He uttered: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (86–87)
And he gave a mantra and a garland of *tulasī* to Yameśvara;
as a reward, he gave him his own golden image.
Then the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa spoke to the son of the Sun.
"Speak of the devotee as one who has reached the divine abode; victory to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
Grant him this all-pervading celestial chariot, a source of happiness, which is the refuge of the wish-fulfilling tree and other wonders, for the sake of traveling through all the worlds. (2.119.90)
Having ascended, O King Yama, proceed to your celestial chariot;
having granted me your favor, bestow it upon all as well.
May your city become purified and today free from offenders.
"O Rādhikā, when the gods have departed for their journey, it will become full once again.
Having been addressed thus, King Yama then bowed to Śrī Hari, prostrating like a staff; indeed, he became a great Vaiṣṇava. (92–93)
He departed once again in his excellent celestial chariot to his own city in the south,
and he caused everyone there to hear all that had occurred in the presence of Hari.
Devāyana too, having heard it, rejoiced greatly and danced.
Having wandered all around the city, he performed the chanting of the Name;
by proclaiming the name of Hari, he indeed made the city of Yama empty.
King Yama then granted him grace and a celestial chariot.
Then the messengers of Yama ceased their tormenting of the sinners;
they were likewise released from their shackles and bonds at that time.
Having all gone by the name of Hari to heaven—the truth, the refuge of happiness—[they attained liberation].
Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, the unmanifest, and likewise the immortal, the imperishable,
supreme abode from which those who have gone do not return—
such was the wonderful sight witnessed by the people at that time. (98–99)
By the fourteen worlds as well as by the inhabitants of the divine abodes, [it is said]:
"What can Kṛṣṇa, who is capable of bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, not accomplish?
He to whom everything belongs, in whom everything resides, and under whose control everything indeed stands."
"Since He is indeed the Teacher of all, O Rādhikā, what is there that He cannot do?

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Sage Devāyatana, a devotee of Śrī Hari, liberated all those in the city of Yama by chanting the names of Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! Afterwards, you will be honored by the inhabitants of the realm of Yama;
for as a devotee of the abode of the gods, you shall receive worship offered by Yama himself. || 1 ||
From there, he traveled alone toward the southern quarter (the direction of Nirṛti) by means of his celestial chariot.
He beheld a beautiful city made of gold, equal to heaven,
adorned with palaces belonging to the Nirṛtis, the Rākṣasas.
It was surrounded by a rampart extending for a hundred thousand *yojanas*,
filled with halls of false magic and sorcery,
and abounding in the prosperity of families of *rākṣasa*s numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Then, beholding that city— which was frequented by the great gods, comparable to heaven itself, situated in the sky, and radiant like the sun—
the king of devotees began the chanting of Hari's names with a long-drawn voice, accompanied by rhythmic beats and other musical elements.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
(6) Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, Lord of Ramā!
Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Māṇikī, Lord of the splendor of Pārvatī! (7)
O Śrī Gopāla, protector of the virtuous, Lord of Rādhā, son of Kambharā;
O Lord of the Imperishable, Lord of the cowherds, Lord of the liberated, Sovereign of Kuṅkuma;
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Supreme Lord, Janārdana!
"O Muktinātha, O Mahāviṣṇu, O Śrīpati, O Puruṣottama!
(9) Thus, wandering through the sky in the city of the Nairṛtas and chanting these names, he likewise caused the mantra to be heard by the Nairṛtas. (2.120.10)
And the Nairṛta beings of the world, having heard that auspicious speech again and again,
became free from sin; the hosts of Rākṣasas also assumed divine forms,
being divested of their demonic nature and endowed with the bodies of celestial attendants.
Having assembled and cast off their physical forms, they abandoned their own city and departed by means of the power of the devotee alone, on vehicles produced from the wish-fulfilling creeper,
as well as on elephant-vehicles and celestial chariots offered to the path of the gods.
Some went to the imperishable world of Brahmā, others likewise to Vaikuṇṭha;
similarly, others to Goloka, while still others went to the immortal realm or the unmanifest.
Having become attendants according to their desire, they departed for those respective abodes.

By hearing the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they became oceans of great merit and indeed went to the eternal Brahman. Then, from that region, he [departed] through the sky toward the city of Varuṇa.
Chanting the names of Hari, he proceeded toward the west;
wandering through the sky in his celestial chariot, he beheld from all sides that city which had taken refuge within a rampart extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
He caused the people of the eastern region to hear [the names] again and again.
And all those divine beings, having heard the name of Manu and having become celestial,
departed for the abode of Īśvara in vehicles fashioned from the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavallī).
Men and women, possessing divine bodies and entirely celestial forms,
departed for various abodes upon meeting with the gods. Then, from that region, they indeed traveled through the sky to the city of Vāyu.
The devotee Devāyana went forth, repeatedly chanting the name of Hari. Likewise, all the deities of the winds and the creations of the Maruts,
whose bodies were composed of wind, heard the name of Manu, the progenitor of Hari.
Then the inhabitants of that city, situated within a hundred thousand yojanas,
having assumed divine bodies, indeed departed for the abode of Hari.
A celestial chariot, however, wandering through the sky, [circled] the entire city of Pracetasa.
He caused the subjects dwelling there to cry out, "Hare! Hare!
Devāyana then sent them to the abode of Hari, as well as others to various other realms, by means of celestial chariots adorned with wish-fulfilling trees.
Then the sage Devāyana proceeded toward the northern direction; from there,
chanting the mantra of Hari’s name, he beheld through the path of the sky the beautiful city of Kubera, which possessed fortifications extending for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Wandering through that region in his celestial chariot, he caused the assembly of yakṣas residing there to hear the names of the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"Hare! Brahmā! Supreme Brahman! And he rendered those yakṣas liberated.
The sins of those Yakṣas, who were rich in merit, came to an end;
their merits increased by the power of hearing the name of Nārāyaṇa.
Thereupon, having attained divine bodies, they were liberated from their [former] bodies on all sides.

Leaving that city, they traveled in celestial chariots produced from the wish-fulfilling vine (*kalpavallī*), which move through the imperishable realm (*akṣara*). By the power of Śrī Hari, they abandoned Vaikuṇṭha and the abode of cows (*gavāṃ sthalī*) and attained the supreme, imperishable Brahman.
Then the devotee Devāyana went toward the direction protected by Īśāna; there he beheld the city ruled by Īśa,
situated within a fortress a hundred thousand yojanas in extent and adorned by Rudra.
There are hundreds of Rudras, ten million Rudras, Śaṅkaras, and forms of Īśa;
there are Īśānīs and wives of Rudras, numbering in the tens of millions of Arbudas and Abjas.
There are also Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Vināyakas.
Vetālas and Kumāras, Bhairavas and crores of Gaṇas;
Vīras and Bhadradevas, as well as hosts of Ḍākinīs and Śākinīs;
Yoginīs and Yogins, and ascetics free from passion.
There dwell Vetālas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Kṛtyās, and hosts of Pūtanas;
Durgās, Nandins, Caṇḍas, Caṇḍīs, and throngs of Satīs—indeed, these and countless hosts of male and female servants reside there. (36–37)

Indeed, having been seen by Devāyana, that celestial chariot of Īśāna, the very Hara, was then made to circle in the sky by that king of devotees. He loudly uttered the name of Hari: "Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!"
O Viṣṇu, delight of Kambharā; O Mādhava, child of the cowherds;
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Puruṣottama, Keśava; O Inner Self, beloved of Prabhā, beloved of Śrī, Supreme Lord. (2.120.40)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin, Hare Nārāyaṇa Prabhu;
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Nārāyaṇeśvara, O Rameśvara;
O Māṇikyeśvara, O Māyeśa, O Pārvatīśvara, O Bhūpati!
O Lord of pastimes, O Lord of manifestations, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of the virtuous;
O Beloved of Śrī, O Lord of the lotus of Śrī, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa;
O Śrī Rāma, O Lord of Kamalā, O Lord, the abode of auspiciousness! 42–43.
Thus chanting the names of Kṛṣṇa and the mantra of Hari,
he caused them all to hear it and liberated them from karma;
having transformed those auspicious hosts into divine bodies fit for his own abode.
He sent servants equal to Viṣṇu, who were devotees of Śambhu, as well as female servants equal to Ramā,
to Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and likewise to the imperishable (Akṣara) realm,
the divine abode called Amṛta, the unmanifest (Avyākṛta), and Kilāsaka. ||42-46||
He also dispatched to Sāketa those who were fit for that place;
having secured their liberation through the chanting of the names of Hari,
he sent them off in celestial chariots and then departed toward the eastern direction.
He beheld the auspicious city of Indra, radiant with the splendor of ten million suns;
it was encircled by a wall a hundred thousand yojanas in extent, filled with every prosperity,
the delightful capital of heaven, and the supreme abode of the world-protectors.
It was filled with palaces made entirely of gold, consecrated by the guardians of the quarters and others;
it was brilliantly adorned with the palaces of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars,
and surrounded on all sides by the abodes of the comets and the hosts of gods.
It was endowed with temples of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*), beautiful abodes of the Vasus,
as well as temples of the treasures (*nidhis*) and dwellings of the Seven Sages (*saptarṣis*); it was joined by the great palaces of the Kṛttikās and the majestic mansions of the quarters of space.
It was joined by the abodes of the Rudras, the Suns, and the Kāmas;
it was endowed with the temples of the Manus, the Kalās, and the lunar days (tithis);
and it was filled with the dwellings of the Maruts, the Vālakhilyas, and the Āruṇas.
It was adorned with the abodes of goddesses, apsarases, and Brahma-lakes;
with well-arranged gardens of the principles (tattvas) and kalpa-trees on all sides;
and with channels of nectar and groves of Brahman.
It was attended by charioteers, Magadhan people, and bards;
it was filled with professional singers, wandering minstrels, Gandharvas, Kimpuruṣas, and Kinnaras;
and it was joined by the Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, Siddhas, and kings.
Having beheld the preeminent royal capital,
so abundantly filled with various beings of diverse castes and delightful,
the seer Devāyana, full of longing, attained great joy with exceeding speed. (57–58)
He indeed recited the mantra of the names of Bālakṛṣṇa:
"O Hari-Kṛṣṇa! O Lord of Hari! O Nārāyaṇa, O Master!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Rāma-Kṛṣṇa, O Janārdana! (59)
O Śrī Gopāla, protector of the virtuous, son of Yaśodā, O Lord!
O Consort of Brahmapriyā, Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Ramā, O All-pervading One!
O Lord of the Self, Lord of the vital breaths, Supreme Brahman, Supreme Sovereign! 60–61.
O Lord of all worlds, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord of light! O Māṇikyeśvara, O Lord of Māyā, O Lord of the lords of the gods of the gods!
O beloved of Śrī Bhūpāravatī, O Master, O Lord Nārāyaṇa!
O Lord of the Imperishable, Lord of the Liberated, Bestower of Liberation, Great Master!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Beloved of Lakṣmī, Lord of Heaven!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! (63–64)
O Lord of Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Kṛṣṇa, O true Master beloved by Kṛṣṇa!
O Lord of the incarnation as Vidyāvyāsa, O Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa!
Thus chanting these names in many ways and clapping his hands, he played the cymbals.
Then, causing his own celestial chariot to whirl all around the city of Indra,
Rādhikā’s beloved— the king of devotees, the abode of the gods, and the foremost of the Sāttvatas—
liberated the deities who dwell in Mahendra’s city.
Having rendered them possessed of divine bodies, liberated from their physical frames, and fit for the [divine] abodes,
he dispatched them by means of celestial chariots produced from the wish-fulfilling trees to Vaikuṇṭha,
Amṛta, Avyākṛta, Goloka, and Akṣara.
The supreme abode of the liberated, worthy of their residence, obtained from the son of Kṛṣṇa; that supreme abode,
endowed with righteousness and devotion, presided over by the Supreme Lord, the Master of All,
and served by the Supreme Ishvara.

The gods were of many kinds, as were their goddesses; they possessed divine bodies with four arms, two arms, eight hands, and likewise sixteen arms. Having assumed these forms and heard His names, they went to the abode of Hari.
Having thus established those dwelling in heaven as liberated through the chanting of the names, he,
a devotee of the divine abode, then went to the city of Agni,
where countless millions of distinct fires reside. (72–73)
The fires of the womb, the fires of digestion, the digestive fires (jāṭharāgni),
the fires of heat, the fires for oblations (homa), the fires of poison (kṣveḍa),
the fires of thought, the divine fires, and the fires of the funeral pyre.
The forest fires, the groups of cool fires, and likewise the digestive fires;
the fires of the departed spirits and the fires that are the mouths of the gods;
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, Pavi, and those born of the cremation ground. (75–76)
The fires of the jars, those that consume all things, the sacrificial fires that consume oblations,
those in the form of the submarine fire, as well as the fires of the clouds and so forth;
the seasonal fires, the cruel ones, and likewise the gentle groups.
And there are the fires of the elements, fires of diverse origins:
white, red, black, blue, yellow, and green-hued; tawny, seven-tongued, and many-tongued, they are the burners. (78–79)
Beholding them all situated in their celestial chariots in the sky, the Lord of Devotees loudly proclaimed the names of Hari in many ways:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare! He caused the mantra to be heard by them.
O Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman; O Lord of Māṇikī and Rādhikā!
(81) O Yajñanārāyaṇa, Beloved of Kṛṣṇa; O Lord of Śrī Satī!
O Supreme Lord, Lord of Gods; O Hari, Lord of the Abode of the Liberated! (82)
O Lord of radiant splendor, O Consort of Ramā, O Beloved of Kamalā, O Mādhava!
O Lord of Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā; O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Satī!
O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of the wretched, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā! 83.
O Lord of Pārvatī and Lalitā, protector of the splendors of Vṛndāvana;
