Then, descending from the chariot and bathing in that ocean, they [proceeded].
Having settled the subjects there and causing them to hear the chanting of his name,
he then bestowed mantras upon them at that temple of the deity.
Then, indeed, having ascended a celestial chariot, he went to the great confluence of the Lāsa.
There, all the supreme lords were honored by the sage Kumbha.
He also caused them to perform a purifying circumambulation of his own abode.
Devāyana, having caused the people and subjects to hear the name-mantras, [proceeded].
Having given those mantras to them, the sage subsequently traveled by celestial chariot to Mount Āpa;
he also went to the river named Trivalā, which has many banks.
Then they bathed at the confluence of the Irā, Trīśā, and Trivalā.
The sage then caused the people of that region to hear the name of Hari at the temple of the deity; and then the king of sages bestowed names upon the subjects as commanded by Siṃharṣi. (2.122.40–41)
By them Pradyumna was honored, and Devāyana was also honored;
all others were likewise honored as they departed on the celestial chariot to the north,
proclaiming the name of Hari and the union with the power of the three syllables (Om Bī Tribala).
They descended from the celestial chariot and bathed there in the great waters.
Then the great sage Dhanāyana and the subjects as well worshipped with supreme devotion those people who remained in the chariot.
Having repeatedly honored the temple of Hari known as Devatāyatana,
and having bestowed names and mantras upon the subjects, he caused the local king,
Vīrajāra, to hear the name-mantra as well as the Manu-verses.
Having caused his sons, daughters, and their wives to hear those *mantras*,
he took them all together in a celestial chariot and went to the confluence of the Oghavatī and the ocean.
They descended from the chariot and bathed at the confluence of the Oghavatī and the ocean.
Causing the people to hear the name of Hari, we beheld them;
thereafter, the sage Devāyana gave the mantra to them.
Then, on that very mountain named Coru, the sage Kanyāyana [did the same].
Having led them all by celestial chariot to his own abode, he honored them;
then, having accepted their worship, he departed toward the eastern direction.
Upon reaching the confluence of the ocean of terror, they descended from the chariot.
They caused the subjects to hear [the glories] of Hari-Kṛṣṇa exceedingly;
then, having bathed themselves and bathed the Manus, and having given them gifts,
they all departed for the confluence of the Yāmunī and the ocean, traveling by celestial chariot.
Having caused the people to hear [the teachings], they bathed him and performed his ritual ablutions.
And the king of devotees, the sage Devāyatana, bestowed the Name-mantra upon him;
he also gave the Mantras to the subjects who were like thieves and those of similar disposition.
In the northern regions and the higher plateaus of the Śibi kingdom,
along the banks of the rivers Tuṅgā and Asiknī, he bestowed the Manus upon the people.
Then the sage Devāyana, honored by all, went to the country of Tandra.
Having caused the beings born of the snowy regions there to hear the name of Hari,
the sage Devāyana gave them the Manus; then, having caused those born of the three cities to hear it, he gave them the mantra of the Name.
The sage Rendī and Meṣāyana honored those who were traveling in their celestial chariots;
he made his own abode pure by being covered with the dust of their feet.
Pradyumna and the others were thus worshipped by the sage Meṣāyana.
Chanting the names of Hari, they went to the Anāvarā river.
Having caused the people to hear the names and having bathed them,
they themselves bathed at the confluence and gave the *mantras* to those subjects.
In the past, they traveled by celestial chariot toward the Ālanaukā river;
at its confluence with the ocean, all the subjects also bathed.
King Śaktyakṣi, together with his family, bathed at that junction of the ocean.
Having heard the names Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa,
they received the mantra of those names from the great sage Devāyana.
Having received the worship offered by the king and the subjects, Pradyumna and the others [departed].
They proceeded along the Bīna river toward their former locations as directed by Tandra;
then all those traveling in celestial chariots bathed where it meets the ocean.
There the subjects gathered and performed the chanting of His names.
Then they received the name-mantras from the abode of the deity. Thereupon, the sage Vṛṣabha of that place honored them;
and having received that worship, they all departed by means of a celestial chariot.
There, together with the subjects, they bathed in the river Askanadī;
then Devāyatana bestowed the Manus upon the subjects.
While proclaiming the name of Viṣṇu, they then proceeded to the river Yānā.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Yānā and the ocean, and having bathed the people,
they caused them to hear the name of Hari and bestowed the *mantras* upon them.
Then, by means of their celestial chariot (*vimāna*), they went to the river Kālimā.
Having bathed in the waters of the ocean and having caused the people to bathe,
and having made them hear the name of Hari, they then bestowed the *mantras* upon them.
And the great sage Tulāyana [dismissed] them as they traveled in their celestial chariots back to their own abodes.
He led [them] and worshipped Pradyumna, the deities, and others. At that time, King Kāliya also became a true Vaiṣṇava;
with supreme devotion, he worshipped the lords of the gods seated in their celestial chariots.
The devotee of Viṣṇu, together with his family, indeed ascended the celestial chariot;
from there they went to the regions of Alāñchuka,
and beyond that to the regions called Dviraṅga and the banks of the Anādīra river.

Having caused the proclamation of that name to the people dwelling on that earth, they then bestowed the *mantras* upon them and departed at their will. Thereafter, they purified those subjects by means of the name of Hari.
Having bestowed the mantras upon them, they returned to Akṣauḍhābhū;
having caused all the inhabitants of the thieves' quarters to hear the mantra of Hari,
and having bestowed the mantras upon them as well, they went to Mount Prabhālu.
Having caused the name of Hari to be heard by the people dwelling on that ground,
the deities, beginning with Devāyatana, then gave the mantra to them; thereafter,
they all departed for the western region of Vilīnāyupradeśa.
And all the people there, filled with eagerness, were made to hear [the names]:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Svāmin, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
They also gave them these mantras, as well as the offerings presented by them.
Having gathered them, they all went to the regions of the sixfold wombs (yonis).
There, having caused all the inhabitants to hear the name of Hari,
they bestowed mantras upon them and then performed worship for their sake.
Having taken them all along with them, they went to the regions of Oṃ by means of their celestial chariots.
Having descended there, they caused all the subjects to hear the name of Hari;
they gave the mantras of Hari to them and established those auspicious Vaiṣṇava rites.
Then, O Rādhikā, the sage Devāyana,
accompanied by Pradyumna as well as the twelve preeminent ṛṣis,
likewise traveled through all the lands along with the kings of the regions of Rāśiyāna.

Having wandered through the eight divine delusions, he indeed made living beings Vaiṣṇavas. In every place, people—men and women, children, the elderly, and those of middle age—became devoted to the chanting and recitation of Hari’s name. (84)

The daily bathing and worship of Bālakṛṣṇa were performed constantly at all times. At that time, the abode of the God of gods was indeed established in every house; then they made a formal request for a temple for the deity.
The sages beginning with Meṣāyana, as well as the kings beginning with Tharkūṭastha—
we, indeed, through our union with you, have become devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Today all of us, your subjects, have been born anew, having been turned away from the path of sin.
They have become devoted to Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, and a great service has been rendered;
you have now brought about the fulfillment of this human body.
You alone are the Guru, the Supreme Brahman, and indeed our savior.

Through the Guru’s door, Hari indeed meets one face-to-face; of this there is no doubt. Grant us such a means that we may have direct union with Hari. [2.122.90] It is the vision of Bālakṛṣṇa, of Kṛṣṇa, one's own chosen deity.
In that same way, may you perform such an arrangement so that it becomes manifest to us.
(91) If even a mantra, which is a mere name, is capable of incinerating sin, why indeed should its direct perception not bring benefit to embodied beings? (92)
Hearing of whom is auspicious, remembering whom repeatedly is auspicious,
and chanting his name is auspicious— what indeed does the sight of him not bestow?
Just as grace has been extended here by you through your arrival, so [may it continue].
May our chosen deity appear; likewise, grant us your grace.
May there be a vision of Śrī Hari for children, girls, men, and women alike, as well as for those who are incapable, through his coming [to them]. || 94–95 ||
If, by the grace of a devotee, one happens to attain the desire for liberation,
then the wise Vaiṣṇavas worship him here upon his arrival;
indeed, even the land, its rivers, streams, lakes, and oceans would attain a state of divinity.
Through the arrival of Hari,
forests, mountains, villages, cities, and waters— whether natural or man-made— shall attain divinity upon the earth. (97–98)
Furthermore, the battlefields and the lands of the continents,
as well as regions that were both difficult and easy to traverse, will thereafter attain a divine nature.
Indeed, the hearts of human beings, which were filled with impurity, [will likewise be purified].
"Through union with Hari, they shall become pure by virtue of great merit.
Thus do we pray here for the sake of the high-souled Pradyumna;
and we also offer auspicious blessings to the temple of the deity.
Thus requested, O Rādhā, Pradyumna and his divine consort both gave them a firm assurance of "Oṃ" as consolation.
Then, with everyone, they went to the Bālakṛṣṇa lake by means of a celestial chariot.
On the northern bank of that river, they were brought down for the sake of their return.
Having performed their meals and other duties, they all rested;
and during the night, they worshipped and remembered Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of How the Maharṣis and Kings, after traveling by celestial chariot through the regions of Rāśiyāna, proclaimed the name of Hari among the subjects, bestowed the mantras, and established temples for the gods and ṛṣis," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 122. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 123 [Author:
Chapter 124 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rāseśvarī Rādhā! in the morning, having bathed, the people of Hari worshipped the form of Bālakṛṣṇa and also Pradyumna;
they also visited the temple and engaged in beneficial deliberations. || 1 ||
The sages beginning with Meṣāyana, the kings beginning with Tharkūṭastha,
and the foremost devotees among the Sāttvatas residing in the regions of Rāśiyāna—
having heard this, the Blessed One formerly performed a sacrifice on the bank of the Lāśahā. (2–3)
On the banks of the Śālāvatī and in the Piṅga regions,
Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, purified his subjects out of compassion,
having come there in person along with the gods, Brahmā, Pārvatī, and others. (4)
Together with his two parents, he also made that land a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
Furthermore, it was said: "In this place, one should come together so that these lands may become sacred sites—pure, bestowing happiness, and possessing the power to destroy all sins."

May all rivers become worthy of the abode of all gods, worthy of worship by all, and bestowers of liberation, sanctified by the feet of the Blessed One. Therefore, we shall perform five auspicious Śrīvaiṣṇava sacrifices.
The first sacrifice was held in the kingdom of Śibi on the bank of the Bālakṛṣṇa lake;
the second auspicious rite was performed in the kingdom of King Tharkūṭastha;
and the third sacrifice took place in the realm of the great king Vīrajāra.
In the kingdom of King Śaktyakṣi, we shall perform the auspicious fourth sacrifice;
and in the kingdom of King Kālimāśa, we shall perform the excellent fifth sacrifice,
offering wealth and all manner of ritual requisites.
Likewise, the liberated ones and the non-liberated, the lords and their attendants;
the goddesses and the wives of the gods, the ancestors, and the preeminent perfected sages; and all embodied beings, whether human or consisting of both the insentient and the sentient. || 11-12 ||
We shall indeed summon the holy fords (tīrthas) and the world-protectors (lokapālas),
and we shall perform the most excellent sacrifices for the gratification of Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, is Janārdana.
"And may you come together in our regions; let devotion be practiced in this manner.
Thus addressed, the sage Devatāyatana, who resembled a god, then said "So be it, so be it" to those Vaiṣṇavas seeking liberation.
The king of devotees then gave the command to rest for a moment;
having gone to the shore of the lake known as Śrībālakṛṣṇa, he [instructed] the kings and others, the sages, and the sage Devāyatanaka. (16)
They traveled by way of the celestial path to Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara. They descended to the ground with their aerial chariot on the northern bank;
there were all four kings and also the twelve great sages.
Likewise, thousands of prominent leaders of the people, endowed with wealth and devoted to Viṣṇu, descended there, having resolved to perform the sacrifice.
Pradyumna then said to the sages: "Make a proclamation throughout the earth."

A sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu should indeed be performed on the shore of Lake Bālakṛṣṇa. First, on the northern side; afterwards, the second, which is the most excellent of sacrifices, on the shore of the lake named Dvikalā, by the mountain Tharkūṭa.
And the third sacrifice is to be performed by King Vīrajāra at the confluence of the rivers Obīrā and Trīśan on the expanse of the earth. Furthermore,
the auspicious fourth sacrifice is to be performed by King Śaktyakṣi.
Likewise, on the vast surface of the earth where the ocean meets the land at Ālanaukā, the fifth sacrifice is to be performed by King Kālimāśa.
Indeed, let the Vaiṣṇavas come there at the confluence of the Kālimā and the ocean. ||23-24||
Therein dwells the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama,
the Lord of Akṣara, the glorious Supreme Soul, the Supreme Controller. Indeed,
the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa is our chosen deity.
He will come in person from the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Indeed, one must certainly come for the purpose of seeing him and for service.
Initiation has been granted at various locations until the full moon.
Now, on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the commencement of the first Makha sacrifice will duly take place;
Kṛṣṇa will perform the rites of this seven-day sacrifice.
But for the second sacrifice,
the commencement and completion indeed took place on the fifth day and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight;
and the commencement of the third rite was on the third lunar day.
The conclusion will take place on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa;
the commencement of the fourth sacrifice, however, will be on the eleventh day.
And its conclusion will occur on the second day of the bright fortnight.
"The commencement of the fifth sacrifice shall indeed take place on the fifth day, and its conclusion on the eleventh; this is certain.
Thus they proclaimed in every way throughout the villages.
Thus addressed, the royal classes as well as those great sages quickly made proclamations throughout their respective regions. Then,
by means of aerial vehicles, the king and the others departed.
They thoroughly purified various auspicious materials;
they likewise had pavilions, halls, dwellings, and campsites constructed there, gathered from every direction. (35–36)

And on ground ten *yojanas* in extent, they eagerly had [the city] constructed; Pradyumna, acting as supervisor, had it built according to what was appropriate. And those twelve sages likewise [constructed] the temples of the deities.
They traveled by celestial chariot toward the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
They prayed to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the lords of lords;
and Hari, being pleased and urged by his father, said, "So be it."
Thus commanded by Lomaśa, the sage Devatāyana took thousands of ṛṣis in a celestial chariot and went to the sacrifice.
They all caused it to be performed on the bank of the Bālakaṛṣṇa lake.
Various sacrificial pits and altars for the purpose of installation, as well as altars;
halls for the sacrifice, dwelling-halls, and likewise shelters for the great measures;
beautiful temples for the liberated souls and likewise temples for the incarnations.
The abodes of the lords and likewise the abodes of the goddesses;
those of the ancestors and likewise those of the seers; the abodes dear to Brahmā, as well as the abodes of the lakes of Brahmā and the abodes of the celestial nymphs.
Likewise, he saw the various abodes of the many classes of gods,
as well as the dwellings of the servants who inhabit the Bhuvarloka,
and the abodes of human beings, of sacred fords, and of stationary beings.
Then they constructed many-storied palaces for the inhabitants of Atala and the other netherworlds,
both upon the vast surface of the earth and in the sky;
and they built a spacious pavilion with seven stories, extending ten yojanas.
By the command of Pradyumna, the artisans constructed [the dwellings].
At intervals of fifty yojanas, they built the foundations for the residences; and at every residence, lamps were placed that were produced from the natural radiance of jewels.
Likewise, there were natural channels of water for both cold and warm [baths],
as well as natural channels of milk, curd, and clarified butter.
There were also natural channels of the juices of honey and sugar.
There are lakes known as Amṛta (Nectar), containing delicious drinks and cool waters;
likewise, the Brahma-lakes, Gopa-lakes, Nārāyaṇa-lakes,
Satya-lakes, and Deva-lakes are established there eternally.
Just as desired, blunt fire-sticks were fashioned into water-pots;
there were naturally occurring preparations of milk and the essence of milk produced by nature.
There were herds of wish-fulfilling cows, and groves of trees and creepers laden with nectar.
There were auspicious alchemy laboratories providing all kinds of created foods and drinks;
chests containing garments, ornaments, cosmetics, and articles of enjoyment; and vessels for storing fragrant essences, powders, collyrium, and lac.
There were displays of instrumental music, singing, dancing, and the like;
various means of mental entertainment; and firecrackers accompanied by flames and wind.
There were also vehicles, mounts, palanquins, and [images of] Garuḍas, swans, cows, and bulls.
Walls adorned with beds, couches, canopies, hangings, and cloths;
diverse gardens containing groves of every kind of medicinal herb; and heaps of food, drink, and other articles like mountains. (56–57)
Likewise, there were heaps of sacrificial offerings, grains, and fruits;
as well as piles of leaves, juices, and fuel-sticks;
and especially stores of rice, barley, and the various foods of forest hermits.
Heaps of sesame seeds, portions of clarified butter, and cooked foods;
[heaps] of distance-hearing instruments, of those that produce distant vision, of moons, of long-range piercing devices, and of those that produce the perception of touch. (2.123.59–60)
And at various places, there were indeed appointed stations for those who announce the seasons, those who inform of events within the palace precincts, and those who carry news across the houses;
as well as for female servants, male attendants, and natural scribes.
There, upon that sacrificial ground, royal highways were fashioned at every spot—
roads for the gods, and paths for elephants, horses, swans, and garuḍas—
which were then constructed so that they might proceed with ease.
Halls for sacrificial fees, a pavilion for the sacrifice, a temple for alms-bowls,
clothing halls for the purpose of giving, and shrines worthy of divine worship,
as well as halls for all ritual services, were constructed by the Viśvakarmas. (64)
In every place there were wish-fulfilling creepers, and in every corner the luster of jewels;
the dwellings, preeminent with *cintāmaṇi* gems, bestowed all happiness. Against the white sky of pearls and within the atmosphere of the gods, [they shone].
Dwellings providing comfort were constructed for the inhabitants of the earth upon the ground, and for other embodied beings upon the trees, during the festival of Bālakṛṣṇa’s sacrifice.
Thus, in every way, the earth was adorned with magnificent pavilions.
At the top of the pavilion, a banner eight hundred cubits long was raised;
a thousand golden jars were set up,
and Vedic mantras were inscribed upon the cymbals and the archways.
The splendors of the colored decorations were made equal to the celestial gardens;
thus, while those dwellings shone brightly all around the sacrifice,
the great lords arrived, having been invited by messengers.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself is performing this sacrifice through King Śibi Deva; everyone should proceed with reverence. This is now on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Behold the commencement of the sacrifice on the shore of Lake Bālakṛṣṇa!
The great drum of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, auspicious and commanded by Hari, resounded throughout all the worlds. (73)
On the tenth day, all those residing in the worlds, having heard of the sacrifice, arrived; indeed,
all those liberated from the world of the Imperishable Brahman arrived,
as did all the divine abodes inhabited by the Blessed Lords.
The Blessed Ones arrived, as well as innumerable Muktānyas;
likewise the Īśvaras, the Īśvarāṇīs, the Pitṛs, and the Munis;
the Siddhas, those devoted to the study of the Brahman, and the Suras and Surāṇīs.
The celestial nymphs of the Brahma-lake, the goddesses, the preeminent guardians of the quarters,
the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, as well as the gods of the Bhuvarloka,
human beings, sages, Brahmins, and the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (77–78)
Those born in the open air, those born from the navel, those dwelling in the hollows of trees and the like,
those living in the depths of the earth, and those dwelling in subterranean cavities;
as well as rivers, streams, oceans, trees, and even creepers— all arrived there.
Holy fords, beasts, winged creatures, and species born of animals;
beings of earth, water, fire, and air—all embodied beings arrived there, having resolved to participate in the sacrifice. (2.123.80–81)
The gods, dānavas, and daityas, as well as the Rudras and Vasus;
the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Manus, and the sons of Brahmā;
Sanaka and the other virtuous ones, and the great ṛṣis headed by Nārada.
The sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of Brahmā arrived at the sacrifice of Hari. All the quarters resounded with the gathering of celestial chariots;
and kings and groups of ministers respectfully presented garments.
Meanwhile, the sage Devāyana was in a beautiful, wish-fulfilling celestial chariot (vimāna),
which was filled with every prosperity and highly magnificent in its hundred stories;
there he beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Likewise, all those dear to Brahmā, as well as the entire family;
the seven ṛṣis beginning with Lomaśa, the brāhmaṇas, men, and women;
mother and father, the gods and others, the sacred fords, and Śaṅkara and the rest. (86–87)
Having taken the guardians of the fields, the serving goddesses, the deities such as Īśvara and others, and those possessing divine bodies belonging to that place, she arrived through the sky.
At that time, beautiful musical instruments were sounded and shouts of "Victory! arose.
All of them indeed honored that [deity] with parched grain, flowers, and unbroken rice;
and they all bowed down from every side to the auspicious celestial chariot of the Supreme Lord, which was as radiant as ten million suns, exceedingly brilliant, and equal to the Imperishable.
Abounding in the great beauty of divine weapons, adorned with divine swans,
and graced by divine banners and auspicious jars, it moves at will and is full of bliss;
by its side, thousands of excellent celestial chariots proceed.
And from the cloud, a soundless voice came, reaching up two and five yojanas into the sky;
having attained stability there in the atmosphere, the Blessed One himself suddenly descended, resplendent with a multitude of tens of millions of lotuses.
The sounds of electric machines and other instruments were played as indicators;
the sky, having assumed a physical form, sang the song of Kṛṣṇa.
The *rāgas* and *rāgiṇīs*, as well as the Sarasvatīs and Śāradās, [also sang].
Then all the goddesses of learning (Vidyās), eager for him, sang for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Virajā, Sulalitā, Vijayā, Jayā, Suśīlā,
and the others then performed a captivating song.
Then the Gandharvas sang for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa.
The sages produced the resonant sounds of the Vedas with deep thundering voices and the like, while the deities, beginning with Agni, also uttered cries of "Victory! (97–98).
The disciples, the sages, and all others offered him honor by prostrating themselves like a staff before him;
they all cried out, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
At that moment, Hari indeed arrived at the assembly pavilion upon the earth.
They gave him flower garlands; they gave him crests and clusters of flowers.
With heaps of flowers, they all honored Acyuta, as well as their mother, their father, and the blessed Śuka. (2.123.100–101)
O Rādhā! [I bow to] Santuṣṭā and Amṛtā, as well as the sage Devāyatanaka;
to the blessed Hemanta and Lomaśa, and to Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Ajā;
to the beloveds of Brahmā and others, O Rādhā, and to the offspring of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
The subjects repeatedly and exceedingly increased the heaps of grain.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Construction of the Sacrificial Pavilion and Other Structures on the Shore of Bālakṛṣṇa Lake, the Arrival of the Mahīmānas, and the Arrival of Bālakṛṣṇa and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā! Thus the great Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, having descended from the celestial chariot, proceeded to the sacrificial pavilion. 1.
Then, having observed this, the lordly sacrificer quickly performed his ablutions in a small pond; he himself, together with his wife, his devoted brahmin Lomaśa, and Devāyatana, [proceeded].
Accompanied by his mother, father, and others, he sat upon an auspicious seat.
Meanwhile, the brahmins, eager for the recitation of blessings, chanted the *svasti-vācana*.
Then, having caused him to perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), the sage Lomaśa [proceeded].
Having recited the purification mantras and offered the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having performed a sprinkling with water, one should take the thread in the hand. (5)
The sage Lomaśa bound Bālakṛṣṇa in the fore-arm of the patron of the sacrifice;
likewise, he bound the king who was the nominal patron, together with his wife,
as well as the one named Śibideva.
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also bound Lomaśa, the knower of sacrifice,
as the primary officiant there, and likewise the secondary vow of the wife;
having appointed this pair of teachers, he then [appointed] twelve brāhmaṇas.
In the presence of Rudra, he bound fierce beings of the very form of Rudra,
and near Brahmā, he bound others numbering ten thousand.
And there he bound the sages who were engaged in recitation and fire-offerings;
by the command of Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā himself took his place upon the altar of Brahmā.
Then the Vedas and the Upavedas likewise became the singers.
And at that time, there were also Udgātṛ priests who were embodiments of the [Vedic] branches.
Then there were the Hotṛs and Upahotṛs, beginning with Sanaka;
likewise the Siddhas who are masters of yoga, such as Kapila and others, who are forms of Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, there were the Āhartṛs and Pratihartṛs, auspicious lords.
Bhūman and others likewise became the Vairāja and other [Prajāpatis];
and there the great sages, Vasiṣṭha and the rest, became the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
and at that time the Vālakhilyas became the reciters of the Vedas. ||13-14||
Vyāsa and others who were knowers of the Vedas, as well as Bṛhaspati and others, became reciters of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (15)
Then all those Nārāyaṇas became the carriers of oblations among the fires;
indeed, they were the incarnations with fire-faces at that sacrifice. ||16||
And there in that assembly, the fires, possessing divine forms, shone forth;
the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*), accompanied by the wish-granting creepers (*kalpavallī*), offered oblations.
Indeed, they then gathered all the materials that had been mentally intended.
Thus, those who were to assist at the sacrifice were appointed there for that rite.
Then followed the worship of the Earth, the worship of Vārāha,
the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the worship of the altars (vedikās).
Then Śrī Lomaśa and the others performed the worship of Gaṇeśa;
at that time, the twice-born ones performed the worship of the manifest Gaṇeśa,
as well as the worship of the conch and the worship of the discus.
The worship of the water-pot (kalaśa) and likewise the excellent adoration of Lakṣmī;
the worship of Rudra and likewise the worship of Durgā;
the installation of the water-pot and likewise the worship of the Mothers (Mātṛkās). (21–22)
The worship of the guardians of the directions and likewise the adoration of the planets;
the worship of the lords and likewise the worship of their powers (śaktis);
the worship of the attendants and likewise the worship of the Vasus.
And likewise, the worship of the Ādityas and the worship of the gods. ||24||
Also the worship of the world-protectors, as well as the honoring of virtuous women;
the worship of the gods, the worship of the ancestors, and the worship of the sages. (25)
Furthermore, there is the worship of the spirits who announce what is desired and undesired, as well as the worship of the quarters and the worship of the Viśvedevas. (26)
Likewise, there is the worship of the two sons of Aśvinī, as well as that of the Rākṣasas;
and similarly, the worship of the fields, the guardians of the fields, and the Yogins. (27)
And likewise, there is the worship of the yoginīs, the worship of the kalās, the worship of the mantras, and also the worship of the tattvas. (28)
There is also the worship of the Maruts, as well as the worship of the sacred fords (tīrthas), and likewise the worship of gods who are characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa). ||29||
Likewise, there is the worship of the Vighnas and the Vighnarājas, as well as the worship of the Brāhmīs,
the Vidyās who are the wives of Brahmā, and the consorts of Dhāman; indeed,
there is the worship of all of them there in their embodied forms.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa performed this for their great satisfaction. ||31||
Then Harikṛṣṇasvāmī himself, Śrī Puruṣottama, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, remained at the site of the principal deity. (32)
Śibi-deva indeed performed his worship and the great worship;
when the principal deity was worshipped, ten million musical instruments resounded.
Then Nārāyaṇa himself spoke to Agni, who had assumed a physical form.
"Stay in my sacrificial pit as my own form for the satisfaction of the gods in this sacrifice. (34)
Having spoken thus, the Fire-god was worshipped and became gracious; seated within the sacrificial pit, the carrier of oblations manifested there in the form of flames amidst the fuel-sticks.
Then the sages performed the worship of the sacrificial vessels and other implements.
Having worshipped the Kuṇḍadevas, the Samiddevas, and other deities as well. || 36 ||
Having offered them worship according to the rites, he proceeded with the fire-oblation (homakārya).
There, the goddesses beginning with Svāhā were indeed his companions, possessing divine forms. ||37||
And taking sacrificial offerings in their hands, they offered them into the mouths of the fires;
so too did the deities, the lords, the liberated ones, and even the Nārāyaṇas. (38)
There were those dear to Brahmā, the liberated ones, the sovereign goddesses, the divine women,
the human women, the sages, and those beloved by the sages;
there were also gods who were characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa).
The bodies of Hari are also composed of sattva, rajas, and tamas. 40.
Manifest and embodied, they took their portions at the sacrifice—those who belong to the creation of the Jīva, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of Brahmā. ||41||
All those [deities] residing upon the leaves of the Veda consume the oblations offered in the fire during the sacrifice; thus Hari becomes fully satisfied. 42.
Thus, for exactly seven days, the sacrifice proceeded according to the prescribed rites;
it was a supreme Vaiṣṇava oblation, a sacrificial rite that grants satisfaction to all.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
I desire to hear everything regarding those deities whom one must remember at that time so that the fire sacrifice may be properly performed in that Vaiṣṇava rite. (44)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to how the fire-offering (homa) is indeed performed there: *Anādi-śrī-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā* ||45||
Svāhā to the Imperishable Brahman, and svāhā also to the liberated ones;
svāhā to the beloveds of Brahman, and svāhā also to the female liberated ones.
Svāhā to Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved, and svāhā to the multitude of gopīs.
Svāhā to Rādhā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, and to the host of cowherds;
svāhā to the abode of Goloka, and svāhā also to the cows;
svāhā to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā to Lakṣmī, and likewise svāhā to Śrī.
Svāhā to the glorious female companions, and likewise svāhā to Vaikuṇṭha;
svāhā to the assembly of attendants, and svāhā to the multitude of maidservants.
Svāhā indeed to Vāsudeva, and svāhā to Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Svāhā to Pradyumna, and likewise Svāhā to the one known as Aniruddha;
Svāhā indeed to Mahākāla, and to the one known as Mahāpuruṣa;
Svāhā to Māyā, and likewise Svāhā to Tatpuruṣa.

Svāhā to the Primal Person (Puruṣa), to the Unmanifested Source; svāhā to the Dweller in Immortality, svāhā to the Vast One, svāhā to Sublime Intelligence; and svāhā to Ego-consciousness, to the Great Viṣṇu, and likewise to the Mind.
Svāhā to Viṣṇu in the form of Vairāja, and likewise to Śambhu;
svāhā to Brahmā, and svāhā to Sadāśiva;
svāhā to the Īśvaras, and also to the Īśvarīs. ||53–54||
Likewise, "Svāhā to the subtle elements," "Svāhā to the sense organs," "Svāhā to the vital breaths," and also "Svāhā to the elemental beings";
"Svāhā to those who dwell in the eight enclosures," and "Svāhā to Īśa-Īśvara."
Svāhā to Matsya in the form of Kūrma; svāhā to the one having the form of Vārāha;
svāhā to Kapila and Hari; likewise svāhā to Śrīpṛthu; svāhā to Dattātreya in the form of Haṃsa; svāhā to the one having the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Svāhā to Ṛṣabha and Vāmana; svāhā to the wielder of the axe.
Svāhā to Yajña and Kumāra; svāhā to Rāma, the archer.
Svāhā indeed to Hayaśīrṣa; svāhā to Nāradanāmin.

Svāhā to the King of Kings! Svāhā to Vyāsa Kalki! Svāhā to Mohinikā! Svāhā likewise to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin)! Svāhā to those who dwell in Truth! Svāhā to the venerable Parameṣṭhin! ||59-60||
To Sarasvatī, to Gāyatrī, to Sāvitrī, the consort of Brahmā;
to Asiknī, to Paliknī, and to Svadhā, the consort of Vīriṇa. 61.
And also to Sṛṣṭi, Sandhyā, and Mohinī, [he says] "svāhā";
likewise "vaṣaṭ" to Dakṣa and the others, and also to the Prajāpatis;
"vaṣaṭ" to the Manus, the Vālakhilyas, and also to the Ṛṣis.
"Also *svadhā* to the ancestors, and *svāhā* to the clouds;
*svāhā* to the host of lineages of dharma and adharma, who possess forms at will; *svāhā* to the seasons, the years, and so forth, and also *svadhā* to the ages."
Svāhā to the directions, and svāhā to the qualities, and also to the substances;
svāhā to the actions, to the classes, and also to the yogas. 65.
Svāhā to Indra and the other lords of the directions, and also to the inhabitants of the worlds; svāhā to Truth, to Penance, to the People, and also to the Great One (Mahas). ||66||
"Oṃ svāhā to heaven, to the inhabitants of heaven, svāhā to the gods;
svāhā to the hosts of Apsarases, and svāhā also to the goddesses;
svāhā to the Siddhas, to the Vasus, and svāhā also to the Nidhis. ||67||
Svāhā to all the Grahas, to the Suns, and to the lunar days (Tithis);
likewise, Svāhā to the Kalās, and also to the Nakṣatras;
likewise, Svāhā to the Tārakās, and also Svāhā to the Maruts.
Svāhā to the Rudras and the wives of the Rudras, and to Śrī Śaṅkara;
svāhā to the Kalās and the Yoginīs, and likewise to the Khanis;
svāhā to Nara-Nārāyaṇa, and to the one who reclines upon Śeṣa.
Svāhā to the one whose nature is the descent [into the world], and likewise to the self that is the embodiment;
svāhā to Gaṅgā and the others, and also svāhā to the sacred fords (tīrthas);
svāhā to Kailāsa-gaṇakeśa, to Gaṇeśa, and to Śiva.
Svāhā to Mātṛ, to the circle of Yoginīs, and to Hanumān;
to Kārtika, to Haṃsa, to Garuḍa, and to Aruṇa.
Svāhā to the circle of Fire, and likewise Svadhā to the one belonging to Yama.
"Let there be *svadhā* for the *śrāvaṇas*, and indeed *svadhā* for the *pretas*.
Likewise, let there be *svadhā* for the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and *kūṣmāṇḍas*;
and for the *vināyakas* and *vetālas*, let there be *svāhā* and likewise *svadhā*. (74–75)
"Oblation (svadhā) indeed to the ḍākinīs and śākinīs, and to the wives of the ancestors; vaṣaṭ to the sūtas, māgadhas, and bandīs, and likewise to the sacred fords (tīrthas);
likewise vaṣaṭ to human beings, and vaṣaṭ to trees and shrubs."
Vaṣaṭ to the creepers, and vaṣaṭ likewise to the grasses and climbing plants.
Vaṣaṭ to the animals, to the beasts, and likewise to the birds;
vaṣaṭ to the reptiles, to the insects, and likewise to the small creatures.
Svāhā to the deities of the house, the village, and the field, and to the Earth.
Vauṣaṭ to the forests, the wilds, and the rivers, and also to the oceans;
vauṣaṭ to the stages of life, the social classes, and also to the mountains.
Svadhā to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather.
Svadhā to Mātrādyā and also Śrauṣaṭ to Viśvādhivāsin;
Śrauṣaṭ to the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the Kiṃpuruṣas. ||81||
To all the Viśvedevas who are to be propitiated, Svāhā! Also to the Maruts, Vaṣaṭ!
To the Cāraṇas, Vauṣaṭ! And to the women and courtesans, Ā! 82.
To the virtuous women, likewise *śrauṣaṭ*; and to those who have renounced everything, in every way.
To the aquatic creatures, *vaṣaṭ*; and likewise to the *nāgas* and serpents, *vaṣaṭ*.
To the *daityas*, the *dānavas*, and the *rākṣasas*, likewise *vaṣaṭ*.
And one should offer the *vaṣaṭ* call to the Yakṣas and likewise to the Kāśyapas, each according to their respective order. //84//
Svāhā to all the gods who create the universe, and likewise to the Inner Controller;
svāhā to Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, who is dark as a rain cloud. ||85||
And to Bālakṛṣṇa, Svāhā! And to Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha;
to Gopālabālakāya, and to the son of Kaṃbharāśrī. 86.
Svāhā to Śrī Hari, the illustrious Lord of Māṇikī;
likewise, svāhā to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who consists of love.
Svāhā to the Lord of Pārvatī, svāhā to the Lord of the Queen of the Rāsa dance.
Svāhā to the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, Duḥkhahā, and Lakṣmī;
svāhā to Jayā, the Lord of Lalitā, the Haṃsa-yogin;
and svāhā to the Inner Controller, the true nature of all, the Lord of All. ||88-89||
"Oblation to Yajña-Nārāyaṇa, Svāhā! Likewise, oblation to Śrī-Vahni!
Om, oblation to the Supreme Brahman, Svāhā!"—thus they offered the oblation to the Blessed Lord. (90)

Then all living beings were satisfied with the charming offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya and kavya). Having thus performed the oblation, they respectfully fed the honored guests as well as the inhabitants of the land, numbering in the tens of millions and hundreds of millions.
Both humans and conscious beings, as well as inanimate objects, were provided with articles of enjoyment.
Indeed, at that sacrifice, millions of humans arrived there;
they received the remaining portions as well as the Śrī-Vaiṣṇava mantras.
In this way, even though they are eternal, the oblations and other rites are performed;
and millions of men are born as Vaiṣṇavas.
The auspicious sacrifice, which was to be completed in seven days, came to an end.

Then they all performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the Bālakṛṣṇa lake. Indeed, all embodied beings—whether divine or non-divine—who had gathered there became purified through the power of Bālakṛṣṇa. (95–96)
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa bestowed exceedingly great sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā).
Then King Śibi-deva also gave away his entire possessions in that sacrifice;
indeed, he gave his own hundred daughters to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa.
And there are vehicles and celestial palaces made of elephants, horses, chariots, and gold. 98.
At that sacrifice, the king then gave gold, silver, diamonds, and so forth, as well as houses and gardens; he also gave many male and female servants. 99.
The king gave gifts of food, clothing, and cows numbering in the millions;
O Rādhikā, he then indeed gave his entire personal possession to Hari.
Thereafter, they made preparations for rest, and everyone went to sleep at night.
Śibi had a beautiful palace constructed there, where Bālakṛṣṇa shines resplendent together with his six wives:
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Kamalā, Śrī, and Ramā. (101–102)
They always serve their beloved in a celestial palace;
by reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the fruit of sacrifice. (103)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrangements for the Sacrificial Rites, the Conclusion of the Sacrificial Work, and the Gift of One Hundred Maidens by the King to Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 124. [End of] Section 2 (*Tretāyuga-santāna*) of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 125.
[Author: Chapter 126.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having thus performed the sacrifice on the bank of Lake Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari—
Bālakṛṣṇa created a lake named Bālakṛṣṇasaras after his own name.
Having bestowed both the mantra and his vision upon those who had assumed countless bodies,
and having subsequently purified them, he then fed the people as well.
On the third day, the Lord himself informed the people in the evening:
"The great king Śibideva is living on earth like one who is liberated.
Indeed, by the power of my grace, the kingdom of Śibi has become Vaiṣṇava."
May the subjects of Śibi be endowed with prosperity, wealth, enjoyments, and all that is necessary for life;
may they be vessels of happiness, and may there never be any deficiency among them. May they never experience suffering anywhere, but rather always possess true advancement.
May there always be well-being for you, for the subjects, and for the king.
May my devotion always remain toward the royal lineage and the subjects.
(6) Now, let the subjects proceed to perform the second sacrifice.
"Let the servants, the sages, and also Tharkūṭastha, Nṛpa,
and the others go for the sake of assistance to the kingdom of King Tharkūṭastha.
Your own duty must be protected by you with devotion."
The qualities of the virtuous should be acquired; they bestow happiness and grant divine peace.
One must indeed always remain established in one's own true nature, which is the nature of Brahman.
Truth—speaking according to reality—should be maintained, for it grants welfare.
Purity consists of the constant purification of one's own self through the cleansing of the internal senses.
This must always be maintained by devotees, remaining free from the turbidity of sins. Furthermore, compassion should be practiced toward all living beings to remove their suffering. (2.125.10–11)
Patience is to be guarded as forbearance even toward those who have committed offenses;

it consists of the restraint of the mind and is always characterized by freedom from agitation. Generosity is to be guarded as constant giving, arising from the state of having one's desires fulfilled.
But indifference toward illusory objects of enjoyment bestows tranquility.

(13) Freedom from grasping toward those who seek [one's help], lack of greed even when wealth is obtained, contentment, and the state of being completely filled with one's own bliss—these too [are signs of peace]. (14)
Contentment with whatever is obtained and freedom from craving—these, as well as freedom from the afflictions (*kleśa*), must always be guarded by people.
Furthermore, there is uprightness, straightforwardness, and the uniformity of these three. (15)
The single-minded unity of mind, speech, body, and inner dispositions must always be diligently guarded by devoted followers of the Lord (bhāgavatas).
Tranquility is eternal peace, the turning away from sense objects. (16–17)

Restraint, which is the control of the senses, must always be practiced for the sake of the highest good, without interruption, toward those things known as vulgar that cause suffering. People should always exert effort for the attainment of wisdom through austerity.
One should observe vows and fasts, and attend upon the elders.
One must maintain equanimity toward both the auspicious and the wicked, and always remain indifferent toward the illusory.
One must preserve forbearance and endurance when confronted by the suffering known as the pairs of opposites.
One should indeed abide in the form of the Self with a state of non-resistance;
cessation must always be guarded, which is the avoidance of futile activity.
The knowledge heard from the scriptures, the true guru, and the deity is that which must be attained.
It must be experienced by oneself and by others in particular.
(22) Detachment from all objects, constant freedom from longing, and the state of having an unattracted mind must likewise be guarded with special care. (23)

Sovereignty is attained through union with the Blessed One, reaching equality of power in the presence of Hari; valor is the victory over one's own nature, which must be practiced by people in every way;
and splendor must be protected by devotees so as to remain invulnerable to others.
And one's own strength is always to be protected through union with the All-Pervading Controller. Indeed, the power of Bālakṛṣṇa is my grace;
mindfulness regarding what is to be done consists in constant reflection upon the auspicious refuge. (25–26)
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord, one's independence and freedom from dependence on others must be protected with great effort by the followers of the Sātvata path;
likewise, skill and excellence in all undertakings must be preserved as the highest priority. (27)
Radiance, born from the power of celibacy and characterized by beauty, must be protected.
(28) Fortitude is the avoidance of agitation even in adverse circumstances.
Gentleness must always be maintained, consisting in the avoidance of harshness and rigidity. (29)

Boldness and presence of mind, which grant insight into liberation, must be preserved; humility and modesty must be preserved, for they produce virtuous conduct. Patience should be practiced by the mind, such that one remains unharmed even when all things are struck down.
Vitality (*ojas*) is to be protected in all respects within the organs of perception, beginning with the eyes (verse 31).
Likewise, power (*prabhāva*) and strength (*bala*) are to be protected within the organs of action.
My sovereignty (*bhaga*), which consists in the state of being preeminent over all else and so forth, is to be protected. (Verse 32)
One's profound depth must be guarded, as must the inner counsel that is difficult to grasp; steadfastness must always be preserved by devotees, free from fickleness.
There must be faith in dharma, liberation, and so forth, as well as a mind fixed steadily upon me, Hari. (33)
There should be conviction in the meaning taught by the scriptures and faith in the Supreme Self (34).
Auspicious fame, devotion, renown, and the granting of light are to be attained by people;
silence should be maintained and idle talk avoided at all times by the followers of the Sāttvata path (39).
The absence of pride must always be guarded, as it is the state of being free from egoism regarding one's virtues and the like;

likewise, the absence of conceit must be guarded, for it is the non-destruction of one's true nature. Similarly, the absence of hypocrisy must be guarded, as it is the state of being devoid of deceitfulness.
Likewise, one should adopt suitable food that yields the fruit of liberation.
Skillfulness, the teaching of beneficial words, and nothing else, should be preserved;
and friendliness toward all embodied beings, as well as being a foundation for their trust, must be maintained. (37–38)
One should perform service for all with great longing;
one must always protect one's composure, even at the cost of intense thirst.
Those of sattvic nature who are devoted yogis should never become agitated by sense objects.
Vaiṣṇavas must never, under any circumstances, inflict suffering upon living beings.
They should practice universal hospitality toward all and ensure that they are free from the occurrence of undesirable events and humiliation.
One should dwell together with those who know Brahman and with the virtuous;
one must preserve goodness and protect those who have come for refuge.
One should maintain freedom from desire for rewards and remain devoid of possessiveness.

O Sāttvatas, you must offer total self-surrender and devotion unto me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. Just as devotion is to be performed toward me, so too should it be performed toward my virtuous devotees. 43–44.
Likewise, one should serve the guru with a spirit of sincere love;
service to the guru is service to me, which always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should perform my worship as well as the worship of the virtuous, for they are my own worship.
This bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it is the destroyer of all sins.
(46) A wife is always to be protected for the sake of happiness; she must never be oppressed.
A husband is always to be honored by his wife; he must never be oppressed. (47)
Those in middle age, such as sons and others, must always serve their elders;
likewise, cows and virtuous people must always be protected, for they inspire devotion and wisdom.
Deities in the form of icons, which purify the sight, should be protected within the home.
The gurus, who deliver one from the cycle of worldly existence, must always be protected in the home.
One must always perform devotion to me, Nārāyaṇa;
and one must take refuge in me, Puruṣottama, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The command of the guru—whether auspicious or bestowing liberation—is always to be obeyed;
the words of the guru are to be honored at all times by his younger disciples, for they bring peace to them.
Worship of me, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, must be performed at all times.
The Supreme Brahman alone is present here in this form of mine; therefore, O best of devotees,
a bath in this lake for Bālakṛṣṇa should be performed on the eleventh day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the new moon day, and on the second day.
This rite, which destroys all sins, should be performed over seven days.
Here, the gift of cows should be given, which bestows liberation.
Furthermore, the offering of my own image shall accomplish all goals.
The gift of an elephant, the gift of a horse, and the offering of a bull;
the gift of a buffalo-cow, the gift of a ram, and the gift of a goat-ram and a bull; and the offering of a cart, a vehicle, and a celestial chariot. (55–56)
The gift of palanquins, the gift of vehicles,
the gift of garments, woolen blankets, and fine cloths should be performed; likewise,
the gift of bodices should be given for the sake of ten millionfold merit.
The gift of gold, the gift of silver, and the gift of copper bestow prosperity.
One should perform the gift of worthy recipients and the gift of food, which is most excellent.
The gift of water, the gift of sweets, and the gift of desired objects bring about auspiciousness.
One should perform the gift of vegetables and the gift of a maiden, which bestows the status of a divine day;
likewise, the gift of knowledge and the offering of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Similarly, there is the gift of a house and the gift consisting of household utensils and the like.
A gift of a garden or a gift of a field should be made.
Whatever one holds dear, that indeed should be given here as a gift.
Food should be given to the virtuous, and honor should be paid to the great seers.
One desiring spiritual welfare should offer food, bark garments, and other such items;
for the satisfaction of the ancestors, the offering of *piṇḍas* and other rites must be performed,
which will grant eternal satisfaction just as at Lake Bālakṛṣṇa.
The worship of the gods should be performed on the shore of Lake Bālakṛṣṇa;
likewise, temples for the deities, as well as abodes for the liberated incarnations and lords, should be constructed on that shore. (64–65)
Auspicious palaces that grant liberation to the sages and the ancestors should be constructed;
likewise, dharma-halls and halls of devotion that bring about auspiciousness should be built.
Gardens, groves, and the like should be established for the sake of Hari.
To those devotees who, having constructed a temple here, shall install the gods together with my own image, I grant a dwelling place,
as well as a livelihood, a means of subsistence, and a continuous stream of offerings for worship.
Those devotees who cause [this] to be made shall possess infinite merit.
I myself, Puruṣottama, shall grant everything to him in my abode.
All the gods, as well as the liberated ones, the lords, and the Nārāyaṇas [are there].
May the incarnations, the goddesses, the liberated ones, and the foremost of gods;
may the goddesses, the gods, the sages, and the sacred fords dwell here.
For Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, dwells here himself.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
every year, all the sacred fords, the gods, the virtuous,
and the liberated lords must come here incessantly for the sake of the world.
For the sake of attaining all purity, for seven days it shall possess the nature of a sacred ford (tīrtha). Indeed, millions of people will bathe here in this lake;
their sins shall be destroyed, and their merit shall likewise be infinite. (73–74)
This is the most excellent of sacred fords, the highest among all the best of tīrthas;
having established my residence here permanently, I shall dwell here.
Indeed, the diseases of those who perform rites at this tīrtha shall go to their destruction.
Poverty shall go to destruction and misfortune shall meet its end.
Prosperity shall dwell in their homes, and likewise, they shall increase their good fortune.
Furthermore, the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth shall belong here to those who visit these sacred sites (tīrthas).
For those who perform pilgrimage even in months other than Mārgaśīrṣa, the attainment of whatever they desire among the four aims of human life shall occur;
their sins are destroyed, and merit that bestows heaven arises.

Indeed, for those who have died here in this ocean, even by the casting of their ashes and bones, there shall be the destruction of all sins and eternal liberation. Furthermore, any person who drinks even a single drop of the water of this lake [shall attain the same]. (2.125.80)
Even for one who has reached the state of death, his liberation shall be eternal.
I, the Supreme Lord, have become his master;
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Through union with the lake, my yoga shall become certain. By bathing in it, drinking from it, beholding it, sipping its water, touching it,
and even by remembering this sacrifice and the lake, there is liberation.
It is indeed so; there is no doubt that I, the Supreme Person, shall bestow [the fruit].
Asceticism, pilgrimage, vows, and fire-offerings must be performed here by those seeking liberation.
Furthermore, the dedication of all actions to me, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, must be performed.
For that which is offered unto me, merit shall certainly be eternal.
Herein also are the Muktatīrtha, the Brahmatīrtha, the Tīrthas of Brahma’s beloveds and others, the Tīrthas of the incarnations and so forth, as well as the Bhūmatīrtha. ॥85-86॥
The holy site named Vāsudeva, as well as the Prādyumna-tīrtha; the Devāyatana-tīrtha, and also the Vairāja-tīrtha;
likewise the Kṛṣṇa-tīrtha, the Rādhā-tīrtha, and the Śrī-tīrtha.

Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha is the supreme sacred site, and Lakṣmī-tīrtha is the most auspicious and supreme. There is Brahman-tīrtha, Viṣṇu-tīrtha, and Śiva-tīrtha accompanied by Satī; likewise, there is Rudra-tīrtha, Rāśi-tīrtha, and the excellent Ṛṣi-tīrtha. (88–89)
The sacred ford of the ancestors, the sacred ford of the gods, and the sacred ford of the guardians of the directions;
the sacred ford of Indra, the sacred ford of Agni, and the most auspicious sacred ford of Dharma;
the sacred ford of Vāyu, the sacred ford of Yama, and the supreme sacred ford of Kubera.
The Īśāna-tīrtha is preeminent, as is the Bṛhaspati-pratīrthaka;
there is the auspicious tīrtha named Lomaśa and the most excellent Yajña-tīrtha;
furthermore, there is the Kambharā-tīrtha and also the Santoṣa-tīrtha.
The illustrious Gopālatīrtha, as well as Māṇikītīrtha; likewise Sabhātīrtha, the auspicious and beloved Pāravaśantīrtha;
Vedatīrtha, Gāyatrītīrtha, and that called Sāvitrikā.
The Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha, the Bālakṛṣṇa Pratīrthaka,
the great Kalpavallī Tīrtha which bestows all desired blessings,
the Graha Tīrtha, the Sūrya Tīrtha, and the Devāyatana Tīrtha. (94–95)
Vasutīrtha, Sādhyatīrtha, Viśvetīrtha, the auspicious Śubhāspada, as well as Sāmudratīrtha, Kailāsatīrtha, Vaikuṇṭhatīrtha,
and Gaṇeśatīrtha. (96)
The Gaṇatīrtha, the Satītīrtha, and the most excellent of all excellent Sādhvītīrthas;
the Vratatīrtha, the one called Vimānatīrtha, and the Śibitīrtha;
the Avabhṛthatīrtha, the great Tīrtha, which is the abode of all holy fords.
Indeed, all these and other embodied forms dwell here;
by my command, from this very day forward, they shall be purifiers for embodied beings.
Therefore, religious duties must always be performed here by human beings.
Then all shall surely depart from the kingdom of Ṭharkūṭastha.
Wherever fame is to be established, let them establish their presence there;
I myself shall come there either tomorrow or the day after.

Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, the deities of the holy fords assumed a second form; indeed, they remained there forever in the form of those very holy fords. Then they all went to that lake known as Dvikalā.
Indeed, in the kingdom of the great king Tharkūṭastha,
all the lords, gods, and humans came by means of celestial chariots for the sake of the sacrifice;
they numbered in the millions, billions, and hundreds of billions, being virtuous, chaste, and beloved of Hari.
Bālakṛṣṇa stayed for a day in the royal palace of Śibi for the sake of rest as well as to accept the service of the king.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instructions and Blessings bestowed by Śrī Hari in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa, the Command for the Second Sacrifice, and the Sacred Tīrthas of Bālakṛṣṇasaras," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
