Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; a great wonder occurred there in the presence of the assembly, where thousands of emaciated bodies were present.
Men and women of coarse complexion, dark,
and devoid of luster arrived there like wretched people, suffering and without refuge.
Indeed, they sought their own liberation from the bonds of the ocean of misery.
Upon seeing them, a great wonder then arose among the subjects. "Who are these, and from where have they come? the people wondered, and they sought to know.
Having understood the intention in Hari’s heart, he asked them, "Who are you here?"
Weeping then, they spoke while men and women listened:
"We were previously deceased ancestors, born from the womb of ghosts;
all of us, by the thousands, have gone to this miserable state upon the shore of the lake. (5)
"We dwell here in this great forest, hungry and likewise distressed.
We are the fathers of these creatures, yet they do not recognize us.
O Blessed One, please grant us deliverance by providing water. (6–7)
To them who had spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having made his own consecrated water *prasāda*, gave it for their drinking alone;
and having repeatedly given sweet *prasāda* and rendered them satisfied, [he departed]. (8)
He granted them the supreme and most excellent liberation that leads to the world of Brahmā.
Indeed, they all became auspicious, liberated, and possessed of divine bodies there;
equal to the liberated, they departed in celestial chariots to the eternal Brahmā.
Thus, on the shore of the lake, Hari granted liberation to them;
having witnessed this supreme marvel, the subjects performed śrāddha rites.
Through that, both the liberation and the satisfaction of the ancestors were produced.
Thus, O Rādhikā, that Pitṛ-tīrtha came into being.
In the garden, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, dressed as a king and surrounded by his army and retinue, was worshipped by King Śibi. (12–13)
The Supreme Lord, resplendent in royal attire and accompanied by Ambālikā,
was seated upon a white four-tusked elephant;
having traveled indeed by means of a celestial chariot named Svāmipālāśa.
And again, Kṛṣṇa was paraded through his own capital city on a four-tusked elephant along the royal highways and other streets; thereupon,
Acyuta was honored by the subjects with flowers, parched grain, and parched rice.

Kṛṣṇa was honored, saluted, and entreated with great devotion by King Bhūpāla, together with Queen Bhūprabhā, for a long time in the royal palace. Then, having traveled by way of the celestial chariot (vimāna), he went to Tāmrakaśā.
Having granted his vision to the queen, the Lord, honored by her parents,
departed in a celestial chariot together with King Śibi, Mādhava,
to the kingdom of King Ṭaṅkūṭastha on the shore of the lake named Dvikalā.
On the western land as far as the river Bīnā,
having seen the pavilions that had been constructed and the new encampments,
he caused the aerial chariot to circle the lake and then descended it.
On the western shore of the lake, near the pavilion, auspicious musical instruments were sounded; there were indeed shouts of victory and cries of "Well done! (21-22).
With flowers, sandalwood, parched grain, unbroken rice, saffron, and other offerings,
the people honored Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. There,
on the shore of the Dvikalā river, there were millions of men.
Eager for a vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
and desiring purification, ten million men and women— human beings from children to the elderly— have gathered to witness the sacrifice. (24-25)
Beholding the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa shining like the sun,
as well as his mother, father, two brothers, sister, daughter-in-law, and Śibideva—
the foremost of devotees— they rejoiced with eager excitement.
Lomaśa, the deity Āyatana, and Patnikāvrata;
the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha gave necklaces to Śrī Hari. Also, King Tharkūṭastha and his four queens likewise [gave offerings]. (27–28)
The sages, beginning with Meṣa and others, also placed pearl necklaces around Viṣṇu’s neck.
There, at a distance of fifty yojanas, a great pavilion stands.
In its center, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa went after bathing in the lake.

On a golden central throne, he sat and shone resplendently. On the morning of the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, Hari himself appointed a circle of sages, each according to his fitness, for the performance of the sacrifice.

The gods, the lords of the gods, the liberated ones, the incarnations, the twice-born and others, as well as virtuous wives, saintly women, male servants, and female servants, were all present just as they had been at the first sacrifice.
Then the great king Ṭharkūṭastha, accompanied by his beloved wife, became the performer of the sacrifice.
Then, with the binding of the forearm-thread (*prakoṣṭhabandha*), he chose Brahmā and the other officiating priests (*yājñika*).
Lomaśa bound the king and Bālakṛṣṇa as the patron (*yajamāna*); Kṛṣṇa bound [the thread] on his own forearm and also bound Lomaśa.
He bound even the secondary preceptor, the wife’s vow-keeper, Hari, and the twice-born;
indeed, he bound others by the thousands and even beyond a hundred thousand.
There was purification, the recitation of auspicious benedictions, the installation of the deities, and so forth.
Worship, fire-sacrifice, and giving occurred just as they had in previous rites.
Worship, feeding, gifts, sacrificial fees, and hospitality—all these were fulfilled exactly as they had been in former ceremonies. (36–37)
This very Vaiṣṇava sacrifice was completed within seven days. All the sacrificial fees— consisting of gifts of food, clothing, gold, silver, and so forth—
were indeed performed here by Tharkūṭaka exactly as before.
And on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
on the second watch of the night, those eager ones performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) there in that western lake.
The liberated Lords, the incarnations, the gods, the ancestors, and human beings [all gathered].

Likewise, those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), as well as other embodied beings, both insentient and sentient, bathed at the root of the bīnā tree; furthermore, people accompanied by Kṛṣṇa did so again.
And thus, for two kalās, Kṛṣṇa remained even in the waters of the Bīnā river.
Having bathed at the sacred fords and performed the honors due to the earth, he fed those devoted to him;
he was intent on feeding the wretched, the helpless, the poor, and others,
and thereafter he fed all his subjects with various kinds of sweet foods.
Afterwards, Hari fed those who served the meal;
he satisfied the groups of both sentient and insentient beings with fresh water.
There, the sage bestowed mantras upon all the seekers of liberation who had arrived.
Lomaśa said: Śrī Hari himself bestowed his own manvantaras [upon him].
Thus was the sacrifice completed by that mountain-like king;
and Hari gave his own lotus feet to that monarch to be held within his heart.
May your kingdom be unshakable, may your subjects be joyful,
may you be endowed with all prosperity, and may you be the sustainer of your lineage.
Just as there are sacred pilgrimage sites within the waters of Lake Bālakṛṣṇa, [so too shall these blessings abide].
Likewise, let all sacred fords (tīrthas) dwell here in this lake;
as well as the liberated lords, the incarnations such as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Ramā;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others; and likewise the ancestors and the sages. 48–49.
"Wherever the gods, goddesses, and humans bathed during that interval,
let them all dwell there in divine form, possessing celestial bodies. Thus commanded by Hari, they resided there continuously.
"All those sacred fords (tīrthas) have been created by the Supreme Self," he said;
"they shall serve as aids for bathing, giving gifts, recitation, sacrifice, and fire-offerings,
and they will bestow infinite rewards numbering in the tens of millions."
A śrāddha ceremony should be performed here at this auspicious tīrtha during the seven-day festival of sacrifice;
for here, the abode of all tīrthas, it shall grant liberation and fulfill one’s desires.
On the fifth and eleventh lunar days of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—
An assembly should be held there on the auspicious bank of a lake.
And a temple should be constructed here, containing my auspicious golden image,
which bestows the gift of fearlessness and is likewise adorned with a garland.
The excellent Rādhā, accompanied by six maidservants and joined by Lakṣmī, Brahmavidyā, Ramā, and Śrīmāṇikī, should be installed here in this temple.
Furthermore, Vaiṣṇava sacrifices such as the Sarvamedha and others must be performed right here.
Just as this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which honors all the gods, has been performed,
so too should auspicious sacrifices be performed by devotees according to their means.
Indeed, through the libations offered here, there shall surely be liberation even for those destined for evil states.
Śrāddha, giving of gifts, and other rites should be performed here at this sacred site (tīrtha) by reciting the names of one's ancestors.
For the sake of the complete destruction of sins, one should certainly bathe here in every way.
Those whose death is imminent should dwell here on the shore of the lake.
"I am Lord Nārāyaṇa; I shall grant the mantra that brings liberation. The divine stories that reveal my power must be recited by those who know the truth—the stories of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā."
In this matter, she who bestows liberation and grants the primordial awakening should be consulted;
for my scripture is indeed the Veda itself, heard by Lakṣmī and Rādhā,
as well as by Māṇikī, Ramā, and Vidya.
It was heard by Mañjulā, Haṃsā, and likewise by Sadguṇā;
it was heard by Jayā, Lalitā, Bhūlīlā, and others, as well as by the liberated ones.
It was heard by the sages, the ancestors, the gods, Nārāyaṇa, and the inhabitants of the earth. (63–64)
Because my deeds performed by me in body after body have never been heard by others dwelling below the netherworld (atala) and outside,
they are worthy of being heard, worthy of being proclaimed, and should be listened to again and again.
I am Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣottama. I alone am the one to be worshipped, the inner self, higher than the highest.
Thus must my resolve be made—firm and free from doubt. (66–67)
Devotion to me must always be practiced, preceded by the offering of all one's possessions.
My devotees should always be honored with divinity, just as I am.
One must not commit an offense against a devotee; such an offense is a violation of my own essential nature.
Likewise, my constant assembly with my devotees must be maintained.
My vision must always be sought by bathing in the morning at the temple;
and the devotion of a servant and the devotion of a slave must likewise be practiced toward me by the virtuous.
One should dwell in my abode for the sake of ceasing the faults of suffering;
one must not commit violence against anyone, nor should one enjoy another's wife.
One must not eat meat, nor drink liquor and such.
One must never commit a breach of moral conduct toward an unworthy person (72).
One should not even commit suicide, nor should one ever engage in theft.
Furthermore, one must never cast false accusations or stains of infamy upon another (73).
Neither the gods, nor goddesses, nor embodied beings are indeed to be reviled.
For revilement gives rise to sin and consequently destroys merit.
That which is unfit to be eaten must never be eaten, and that which is unfit to be drunk must never be drunk.
Since that which is devoid of divine grace is considered unfit for consumption or drink,
one must not associate with atheists, for such association obstructs liberation. One should always serve the virtuous, for the virtuous are indeed my own forms.
Whether a man or a woman, one is indeed liberated from sin through service.
Those who are my holy ones (sādhus) are the bestowers of liberation.
Their body is in every way meritorious, a giver of merit, and supremely purifying.
There is no partiality there; as it is with me, so it is with him.
Service to one’s mother and father must be performed in every way on this earth.
Those who will obey my command shall indeed possess certain success.

In their homes there will always be streams of lightning from the cosmic age (*kalpa*), as well as the subtle essences of the cosmic age and the juices of the celestial wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpavallī*).
Their dwellings shall possess the power of resolving desires at will, and they shall expand through the lineage of their own volitions.
All the collections of truths that grant all desires shall become universal in the homes of those who carry out my command;
I shall always be the giver of whatever they desire, just as I am in the Imperishable.
One should enjoy pleasures, but not excessively; one should practice devotion, but in an extraordinary measure.
One should sleep, but not excessively; one should perform service, but in an extraordinary measure.
The mind should not be drawn toward what is base; one should employ the power of *māyā* to delude [the enemy].
One should not harbor excessive thirst, nor should one entertain desires that exceed my [the Teacher's] intent.
One should not form attachments here; rather, one should practice that which grants liberation hereafter.
Agitation must be abandoned in every way, and eternal peace must be attained.
One should not exert effort in manifold ways; rather, one should apply oneself to the supreme task of self-knowledge.
One must not remain dependent on others, but should instead abide in the reality of the Self.
One should certainly not live as the body-self, but should live as one's own true Self.
Devotion should not be placed in the household; it must certainly be placed in the true Master.
For I am indeed the Master of all devotees in every respect;
I alone am the supreme Master known as the Supreme Lord. 87–88.
Water is a sacred site (*tīrtha*), land is a sacred site, and the self is the ever-supreme sacred site.
Holy people are always a sacred site, and my Lord Hari is the sacred site.
Wherever I am and wherever my image is, that is a sacred site that bestows divine liberation.
Thus, in every way, you people of Tharkūṭastha,
acquire wealth and cultivate devotion to me with daily reverence;
and receive from me alone my mantras, which grant excellent liberation.
Thus instructed, those millions of devotees approached the presence of Śrī Hari for the sake of receiving the *manus*. Hari bestowed the *manus* upon them:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."

"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times. (93) "O Lord who bears the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika, [protect me] from the fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and malicious hearts. (94)
"I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
"Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband."
"May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian.
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa-vallabha-svāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge"—in this way, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa indeed bestowed the mantras upon them. (96-97)
Then, having made his excuses, he went home for the sake of rest. At that time, the great king of Tharkūṭastha, as well as the queens and their sons,
massaged the feet of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Honored and fed by the king, they all rested. On the second day in the capital, the subjects, filled with joy and eager anticipation,
beheld Bālakṛṣṇa mounted upon an elephant as he was being paraded about.
They increased [the offerings] exceedingly and, full of eagerness, performed worship.
Having arrived at the royal palace, Keśava spoke in the assembly:
"Tomorrow, let them depart only after having eaten, for the meeting with the Lord of Obīrātrī."
In the kingdom of the great king Vīrajāra, the third sacrifice shall take place. (102) The commencement of the sacrifice will be on the third day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa;
it must last for seven days, until the ninth lunar day. (103)

"I shall come there on the very morning of the second day. Having been addressed thus, all the lords of the gods and the sages, traveling by celestial chariots and possessing the majesty of the entire creation, went to the bank of the river Oṃ.
Having attained well-being, Śrī Hari resided at Tharkuṭasthaka.
O Rādhikā! While dwelling in that house, Hari—the Lord who grants liberation, the treasure-trove of all desires, and the fulfiller of every aspiration—brought happiness to them. (105–106)
"By reading this, by hearing it, by causing others to hear it, and even by reflecting upon it,
a person shall obtain the merit of bathing at Dvikala as well as the merit of [attaining] fame.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Second Viṣṇu Sacrifice in Lake Dvikala during the Reign of the Great King Tharkūṭastha, and the Bestowing of Mantras upon the Subjects," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 126: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 127 [Author: Chapter 128 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! A great wonder indeed occurred there.
Previously, by means of an earthquake, those who had died attained the state of the celestial nymphs (apsaras). || 1 ||
More than a hundred thousand *preta*s, who resided upon the Samāna mountain,
came to the Dvikala Tīrtha in the presence of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of liberation.
Some indeed had crooked faces, while others had withered bodies.
Others had broken hips, while others had bellies clinging to their backs;
some were covered with hair and swarming with flies, while others were infested with nets of mosquitoes.
Some suffered from the pains of hunger and thirst, and others were blind, lame, or maimed. (3–4)
Those afflicted with leprosy, those with impaired limbs and so forth, those suffering from asthma, cough, and other ailments;
others with hanging bellies or dropsy, those without eyes, and those deprived of ears;
those with backs for feet, those with backs for faces, the hideous, and the impoverished—(5).
In their thousands, those suffering ones approached the presence of Hari;
for the sake of destroying their misery alone, they prayed to Acyuta—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Indeed, in the past, we were destroyed by earthquakes through the crushing of our homes;
we were also struck by the falling of trees and fell even as the earth split open.
We sank into water-filled chasms, perished, and died at that time.
Indeed, we are hungry ghosts suffering from sudden deaths;
you alone, and no others, are capable of delivering us here.
Therefore, deliver us from this most sinful womb and show us compassion. (2.127.10)
Thus entreated, the Blessed Lord indeed cast water upon them with his cupped hands; it was gracious and they received it. Their sins were burnt away, and they again requested water.

For the sake of drinking, Kṛṣṇa gave them water from a lake; the Lord made them drink that water which he had brought for his own purpose. Having drunk again and again until they were fully satiated, they then requested food.
The Blessed One gave them auspicious sweet rice mixed with sugar,
along with milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared from the wish-fulfilling cow (kalpadhenu) and accompanied by ghee.
Having eaten and become satisfied, they were born anew and requested freedom from disease.
Hari granted them a delightful state of health and a gentle form.
Then they requested liberation and service with divine bodies; Hari granted them liberation, and they departed with those divine bodies. (15–16)
To the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha, by means of celestial chariots resplendent like the sun,
the men became attendants with four arms, exceedingly radiant;
and the women also became female attendants with four arms, endowed with great fortune.
"Indeed, they have become liberated in form and dwellers in the abode of liberation.
Thus, out of compassion for them, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī,
by means of his own yoga, granted Vaikuṇṭha itself to them this very day in an instant.
In this matter, neither merit nor even devotion is the cause;
rather, the state of being a protector of those who have sought refuge, imbued with compassion, is the cause. Therefore, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa—the Great King and Lord of Ramā—[is moved by that].
Māṇikyākānta, the Lord of Lords, spoke to Tharkūṭastha:
"O Great King Tharkūṭastha, listen to that which is to be known here:
dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and devotion—this is the fourfold [path]."
Indeed, four duties must always be fulfilled by you on this earth;
they grant happiness in this world and bestow bliss in the hereafter.
You must protect the subjects, and you must show compassion toward the people and others.

One should perform service for others— which brings happiness to both the other and oneself— toward the poor, the helpless, women, the virtuous, the elderly, and so forth. One must never inflict pain upon others at any time, except in accordance with the duty of war.
You must always provide protection for those living beings who have taken refuge [in you].
He in whose mouth the name of the Blessed One resides is worthy of honor and is indeed exempt from punishment.
Vaiṣṇavas are to be honored in every way with gifts, marks of respect, and worthy offerings.
One should indeed associate with the Sāttvatas with a gracious heart, through disciplined conduct, speech, and service characterized by the nature of a servant; however,
association with the Rājasicas should be performed merely through the body.
One should indeed cultivate association with those characterized by tamas in a manner that appears false,
so that the kingdom may not perish and one may not suffer bondage. Furthermore, one must always act in such a way that obstacles are overcome.
One should indeed place trust in all respects in virtuous devotees of the Lord.
One may trust a queen, a son, or a chief minister, but with vigilance;
one should not consider them as one's own until they have been thoroughly tested.
One should not place trust in those who are greedy for power and intent solely on their own self-interest;
rather, one should with devotion trust those people who are free from desire and established on the path of the virtuous.
One should not meet anyone alone, for a solitary place is indeed a source of fear.
One should not accept food without first offering it to another;
nor should one accept anything to be drunk or touched if someone else offers it without reflecting upon it.
One should not accept any objects of enjoyment that are insentient without first dedicating them to another. (33–34)

One should never, even for the sake of one's own interest, consume so much as a grain of [the king's property], not even a brother or a son; this must be observed with vigilance. Subjects must not be provoked to agitation, nor should living beings be harmed.
One should never trust someone who bows down while their eyes are slightly meeting;
one should never dwell in an empty house, nor indeed dwell without a weapon. One should never dwell with a maidservant, nor even with a queen in a secluded place.
One should certainly not have many wives, nor should one indulge in sexual pleasure with a female slave.
One should not go to another's wife except for the sake of dharma or for the purpose of a specific task.
One should not sleep without being vigilant; one should protect virtuous people at their side.
One should never apply desire to the place of dharma;
nor should one apply knowledge to the place of desire, which leads to dispassion.
One should not apply longing to the place of dispassion or austerity. (2.127.40)
One should employ spies in the territories of others, as well as within one's own kingdom, in the home, and on the ground;
one should also employ spies born of righteousness within the kingdom of the body, senses, and so forth.
Having made discernment the primary factor, one should carry out all affairs.
If the leader should become despondent, he ought to consider the obstruction of his purpose.
Having gained experience from the elders, he should act for eternal peace;
he should not rely on a newborn infant even in a great matter.
For the sake of liberation, one should resort to whatever is beneficial, whether it be small or great;
one should cast away the intellect that causes exhaustion as if it were a she-wolf,
but one should cherish the short-lived intellect that bestows peace as if it were a virtuous wife.
One should protect even a dull-witted person like a pillar in a place of calamity.
One should also protect a learned man, provided he is not intent on the actions of an assassin.
A king should not wander alone in the forest or on a hunt. (45–46)
One should not trust one's own people at a reservoir, a well, or similar places;
rather, having placed the family priest at the front, one should traverse the forest with the army. Even there, one should always have a person experienced in the forest walk ahead.
During the rainy season, one should not travel through the forest, nor during a festival or a time of upheaval.
At night, even while disguised, he should examine the welfare of his subjects.
[He should protect them] from the barber, the weaver, the tax-collector, the flatterer, and the thief.
Having personally assumed that form, he might at times manifest great majesty;
having learned all the circumstances, he should act for the welfare of his subjects.
First, he should dispatch his own servants, such as barbers and others, in those various guises.
Then, having himself assumed that form, he should go, and not otherwise.
Having become a woman, at the time for the Brahma-rite,
she should go to the water-source with her own female servants who are fetching water.
He should ascertain the welfare of his subjects through them and through reports;
likewise, he should provide for the maintenance and livelihood of his own servants, dependents, and wives.
Having learned of the sufferings of the wretched, the helpless, and the poor, he should destroy them.
He should likewise destroy atheism, deceit, and crookedness.
Through the means of discourse and the means of punishment, he should instruct his subjects;
being devoted to compassion, he should provide widows with food, clothing, and shelter.
The king should cause the gift of knowledge to be bestowed and cause the imparting of training and wisdom; he should always cause the arts, sciences, and crafts to flourish.
Furthermore, he must not cut open the scrotums of men or humans.
One should not have women perform tasks such as the protection of children through another person's agency.
One should have them perform the protection, nourishment, and education of children through their mother.
Furthermore, one must never, under any circumstances, suppress their menstrual flow by means of a command.
One should not cause seasonal changes, such as fruits and flowers, to be altered by means of medicinal drugs;
nor should one drive away a human being who is dependent on others, like a domestic animal. Furthermore, one should not kill an innocent person without purpose or without reason.
One should never impart the Dharma of Liberation to an unworthy person who acts as an obstacle;
rather, for the sake of their own welfare and for the benefit of the worlds, one should entrust such matters to the divine works.
One should never treat the human being as worthless as chaff;
one should achieve new blossoming and never destroy that blossoming.
One should cultivate agriculture, which takes the form of the highest of all blossoms.
One should also develop craftsmanship as well as authentic higher knowledge (vijñāna).
One should develop alchemy, tantric science, mechanics, and likewise incantations, as well as divine power and aeronautics, according to one's strength. (63–64)
One should never cause a superior part to become mixed with the inferior, which would result in its degradation;
rather, one should make the inferior part superior, bestowing upon it the power of manifestation.
One should indeed cause the transcendental reality to blossom forth as distant hearing, vision, and so forth.
Like a yogi, one should expand the path for entering the earth and so forth;
one should also expand the ability to travel through water, fire, the atmosphere, and other realms,
yet one should never ever neglect the journey to the supreme egg (parāṇḍa).
He should convene an excellent assembly of sages, ancestors, gods, and others— including Daityas, humans, and Rākṣasas— for the purpose of mutual acquaintance.
From that [assembly], the king himself should perform the Sarvamedha sacrifice.

And he may have acquaintance with those who dwell in all the worlds; yet he should not neglect the proper sequence of honoring the worshipful through offerings and other marks of respect. The king should, in every way, increase the state of venerability of his gurus.
One should protect all things as if they were treasures hidden for the sake of heaven;
one should act in such a way that all subjects rejoice like the gods.
Just as I, the Supreme Lord, am the bestower of happiness upon my subjects, so should the king be.
O Queen, I, who abide by the duties of a king, always act as your residence. Therefore, the king, being of my own nature, shall protect his subjects like his own children;
he shall then cause them to attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
One should never cause subjects to fall from the worship of the Supreme Lord.
Falling results in the loss of liberation, while rising leads to the non-abandonment of liberation.
Considering the human state to be the primary object of meditation, one should practice righteousness.
One should meditate and cultivate a pure disposition in such a way that there may be no lapse in devotion.
Without that, what is known as "royal" on earth becomes known as "profligate.
You are Thakūṭarāja by name; become filled with the bliss of Thura.
If you should ever violate the Dharma spoken by me, suffering will surely befall you;
therefore, being vigilant, protect my teachings.
The two essentials are devotion to Hari and auspicious association with the virtuous.
In every way, a king who seeks the true purpose of kingship should cause these two to be performed.

Herein lies the protection of subjects, which bestows liberation in this world and the next; indeed, it must be carried out by one who follows the dharma of a king, for it also grants his own liberation. (78–79)

The ruler of the kingdom must exercise authority over those who act contrary to the duties of protection, encourage those who are devoted to divine dharma and seek the welfare of others, and pursue the contemplation of liberation as the ultimate goal. 2.127.80. This is what must be performed by one who follows the dharma of kingship.
Those endowed with such wisdom should be appointed to the administration of the kingdom.
(81) The king must achieve liberation as the fruit of his human body;
for by refining that which is impermanent, one will certainly not attain the permanent fruit. (82)
Having ruled the kingdom according to the prescribed law, he should practice the teaching of liberation.
Then, having entrusted the kingdom to his sons and others, he should depart for the religious life.
Even if renunciation is not desired, he should nevertheless [remain] engaged in royal duties.
One should prioritize action that consists of propitiation.
Victory over a foreign kingdom is not considered a certain victory;
victory over the realm of Brahman is considered a certain victory. (84–85)
Lying down upon the body, senses, and so forth is not a permanent happiness;
it is called lying down upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Indeed, lying down [upon the Self] is the permanent happiness.
When the impressions of things experienced have dissolved and the residual trace (*saṃskāra*) has reached a state of dissolution...

The destruction of craving gives rise to a happiness equal to the bliss of the Self. That kingdom of Brahman, that great sovereignty, is to be attained by the king—a state that is neither finite, nor subject to seizure, and never a source of agitation. (87–88)
A merchant should engage in such business as increases his profits;
however, a person seeking prosperity should abandon any enterprise that causes loss.
One should conduct oneself in such a way that one may attain a kingdom superior even to the best of kingdoms.

One should not perform that which, upon the destruction of one's kingdom, bestows the state of a denizen of hell. (2.127.90) The merit that leads to the station of the virtuous, the supreme heaven, and union with my lotus feet;
the enjoyment of union with my own form—these indeed are to be attained by the Vaiṣṇavas. (2.127.91)
Suffering, the bondage of sovereignty, hell, the multitude of latent impressions (vāsanās), negligence, laziness, and death—these must indeed be abandoned by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Sovereignty for me is the attainment of the Imperishable; my family is the circle of liberated souls.
The palace shall belong to me alone, liberated in my abode of the Imperishable (akṣaradhāman).
That kingdom which is my own imperial sovereignty—that kingdom shall belong to him who is mine;
I grant my kingdom to that devotee who has offered himself to me.
"O King, worship me with devotion alone, as a servant always serves her master.
I shall grant you liberation at the proper time; cause devotion toward me to be established on earth. Build a beautiful temple for me and install me as the presiding deity. (95)
Endowed with Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Brahmavidyā, Śrī, and Māṇikī,
continue my unbroken flow of worship. Remaining established in the image, I shall accept your service.
Thus did the venerable Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa Svāmī Śrī Puruṣottama instruct the householder named Tharkūṭa, O Rādhikā!
And the king caused a most magnificent temple to be built. 98.
Having established those images there, he served them like a servant.
At the end of every night, at dawn, the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Master, [worshipped] the one known as Tharkūṭa. (2.127.100)

He said, "For the sake of the third sacrifice in the kingdom of Vīrajārā, we must go this very morning; I shall go with you. Having spoken thus on the second day, Hari himself set out that very morning.

Then the king and queen offered their own fifty auspicious daughters according to the prescribed rites; having accepted them along with their dowries, and having received worship and bestowed beautiful, auspicious blessings, they departed. (102–103)

By means of his celestial chariot (*vimāna*), he went swiftly from Prajā and the others to the union with the Lord of Night (Śiva); he also beheld various regions provided with pavilions (*maṇḍapa*). Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Deliverance of the Preta, and the Instruction on Royal Policy and True Dharma to King Tharkūṭastha," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 127: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 128 [Author: Chapter 129 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! The Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arrived in the sky upon a most radiant celestial chariot. 1.
A white radiance appeared, like the light of ten million moons,
upon the earth in all directions and intermediate points at the confluence of the two rivers.
There, millions of humans, gods, and sages cried out, "Victory to Mādhava!"
"Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to the Lord! Victory to Bālakṛṣṇa, O Master!
(3) "May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious!
Thus, with great joy, they uttered shouts of victory with unrestrained voices. (4)
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke, and with unblinking eyes, they gazed; meanwhile, Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot, having circled five times through the sky,
bestowed its auspicious sight upon the people from the heavens itself.
He descended upon the ground in that beautiful vehicle which moves at will;
it was in the most excellent middle region, at the junction of the Irā and Triśauṣikā rivers,
fifty yojanas from a lovely pavilion.
On the banks of the Irāvatī river, Kṛṣṇa descended from the celestial chariot;
likewise did Śrī Gopāla, Śrī Kaṃbhārā, and the kings as well.
Lomaśa and the maidens also emerged from the chariot.
They were honored by the common people with parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.

(9) Then the Blessed Lord, having bathed in the waters of the Irāvatī and Īśānī rivers, and having inspected the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, the altar, and so forth, went to his own residence. (2.128.10)
Then, honored and served by the king, the royal family, Vīrajarā, and the others, Kṛṣṇa rested in the palace.
Thereafter, in the morning, Bālakṛṣṇa bathed and went to the sacrificial ground.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, he beheld the sacrificial altars adorned with celestial sages and ancestors,
as well as sacrificial pits and golden pedestals;
there were also countless materials for the performance of the sacrifice, all devoid of human presence.
Then, on the sacrificial ground, Hari beheld ten million brahmin-sages and deities; there, in the pavilion, he sat upon his own throne for the purpose of choosing [a bride],
and likewise the king, the lover of Vīrajā, sat together with his beloved.
And he arrived for the sake of the sacrifice, and Lomaśa also arrived.
Then the great Vasiṣṭha, a devotee of Viṣṇu who was devoted to his wife, as well as Brahmā, sat down upon their respective seats; at that time, auspicious songs were sung.
The learned brahmins, filled with joy, sang the Sāmaveda;
and there the goddesses sang songs that proclaimed auspiciousness.
Various musical instruments and diverse types of trumpets were indeed sounded.
The binding of the wrist-threads, the recitation of benedictions, and so forth proceeded.
There was the installation of the deity in the limbs and worship for the removal of obstacles;
indeed, there was the worship of the principal vessel and the worship of the ritual materials.
At that moment, the worship of the God and Goddess began in the sky;
the gods and others arrived for an instant to shower sandalwood paste and other offerings. The god of fire (Vahni) was indeed established within the sacrificial vessel (*kuṇḍa*).
Then those gods, beginning with Brahmā, assuming embodied forms, offered their invocation.
Lomaśa and Vasiṣṭha commenced the sacrificial rites;
there the mantras were recited and the oblations were offered.

Those whose faces are fire—the incarnations of the liberated souls of the Supreme Brahman—namely the lords, the divine sages, the celestial sages, the ancestors, humans, and the twice-born, attain satisfaction through the sacrificial offerings;
indeed, those with fire-faces partake of them. (23)
The creation of individual souls, the creation of Brahmā, and the creation of the Lord—O Rādhikā!
all these creations were satisfied there at that former sacrifice with the consumption of countless offerings of sacrificial oblations, just as they had been before. || 24-25 ||
Inanimate beings, as well as stationary objects, sentient beings capable of assuming forms at will,
sacred fords, mountains, rivers, insects, moths, and birds—
all these indeed were the bodies of the Blessed One, and they were satisfied there at that great sacrifice.
In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the primordial Lakṣmī;
the Blessed One who is the inner self of all, the foremost among those who are never satiated, Hari—thus indeed for seven days there is the vow consisting of the festival of satisfaction. (27–28)
On the ninth day, the dismissal of the sacrifice took place with the ritual sites for the gods;
the conclusion of that rite was performed with sacrificial fees excluding the *aṅka* [mark].
And there were meals for everyone, fresh as always.
Just as there arose foods that were wholesome and suitable for embodied beings according to their needs;
then, at the confluence of the Vyāsa and Irāvatī rivers, the youthful Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, performed the supreme avabhṛtha bath.
He performed [the rites] together with all the sacrificial priests and ten million people.
At that time, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) there became manifest in embodied form;
indeed, all the Muktatīrthas as well as the Brahmatīrthas were present.
Those which are the descent-tirthas and those which are the liberated-tirthas;
all the Kṛṣṇa-tirthas belonging to Nārāyaṇa, as well as those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, the ancestors, and likewise the yogins. (33–34)
And for the sages, the gods, the twice-born, and the virtuous;
for the chaste women, the goddesses of the gods, the guardians of the directions, and the ascetics;
and even for the virtuous wives and the holy men—the sacred pilgrimage sites became incarnate. (35)
Then they dwelt at the confluence of the Obyā and Irātri rivers.
There, one should perform a ritual bath starting from the third day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa until the ninth day; this [practice] for seven days bestows the merit of a sacrifice.
Thus spoke the Great King at that time during the avabhṛtha bath: "I was then standing by the side of that Hari, having bathed;
Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, was also present there by my side. (38)
The learned one heard that which was spoken by Hari, and it was likewise repeated again and again. Indeed, it was spoken here by all the Nārāyaṇas, by all the Kṛṣṇas,
by all the Vāsudevas who are incarnations, and by millions of Lords.
One should dwell here also in the form of a sacred ford for the welfare of men; and likewise,
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and all other goddesses should always remain here in the form of sacred fords together with their respective beloveds.
Thus, at that very place— the sacred ford of the sacrifice at the confluence—
the gods [performed their rites] during the night of the new moon, at the Trivalā [conjunction], and in the waters and other sites such as ponds,
portions of wells, and even in large oblong lakes in every way.
"O beloved, by the command of Śrī Hari, we all dwell there in ponds, on sacrificial grounds, and in various places.
Hari spoke again there concerning those who commit sins and even the most heinous crimes:
By bathing here, indeed, mountains of sin shall be destroyed.
One's sons, grandsons, and family members will become partakers of merit;
they will be prosperous, enjoyers of pleasures, free from disease, and long-lived.

Whenever people come together from anywhere to bathe here, drink the water, touch these waters, or even while residing in another land, remember this sacred ford (tīrtha) of the sacrifice; [for them, it shall be as if they have bathed there]. 47.
To them I shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation, of this there is no doubt. [I shall grant the fruits of] bathing, giving, austerity, fire-offerings, service to others and the like,
as well as the building of temples, almshouses, and the planting of trees.

Those people who shall establish schools for the gift of knowledge, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the cultivation of medicinal herbs and rice-fields, their merit shall be infinite. They shall also establish alchemical laboratories, observatories for the planets, laboratories for piercing gems, and sacrificial halls.
For those who frequent it, it is a hall for the virtuous, a hall for discourse, a workshop for machines, and a house for bulls; it is a hall for food,
charitable feeding houses, a hall for water, a house for milk,
a maternity home, and even a hall of knowledge.
To those people who shall cause a service hall, as well as houses for feeding guests and so forth,
and a hall for the spirits to be built at the site of the sacrifice,
I shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did Śrī Hari speak at the site of the avabhṛtha bath, O Rādhikā.
He himself immersed himself and bathed repeatedly in the waters;
he was bathed by all with their cupped hands, and they were all bathed by him as well. || 54-55 ||
I have repeatedly bathed you with showers from my cupped hands during the final purificatory rite;
this pleasing water has been held by me for your sake.
Drink from the jar this pure, supreme, and sacred water of the Lord.
"I shall drink," saying this, Rādhā drank the nectar from the feet of Śrī Hari.
Nārāyaṇa gave it to Lakṣmī, and she too drank the water.
Thus, O Rādhā, the Supreme Lord, having completed the avabhṛtha bath, [departed]. (57–58)
Having gone outside and put on his garments, ornaments, and so forth,
Hari went to his own seat situated within the pavilion.
There he obtained a moment’s rest, and then, in the evening, he proceeded to the auspicious assembly hall.
The Blessed One caused [this] to be performed for all the inhabitants of the world.
The great king Vīrajāra performed worship with devotion;
by the command of Śrī Hari, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Vāsudeva, the Infinite, Vairāja, Parameṣṭhin, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Aryamā, Sanatkumāra and the others,
all the beloved consorts of Brahmā, as well as Indra, Sūrya, and the Prajāpatis.
The king worshipped Vasiṣṭha, Gālava, the sage Devāyata who was devoted to his wife,
and the sages Śrīgopāla, Kambharā, Śrī, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; likewise,
he worshipped other goddesses and those worthy of worship.
Then he offered various kinds of gifts for that worship;
he asked for forgiveness, saying, "My service was deficient, please forgive it.
"I have been purified by your very grace, and the circle of the earth has been purified."
And having arrived here, the lords proclaimed me throughout the quarters:
"Blessed is the king named Jāra, who has attained true heroism; for I, though a *jāra* (paramour) in every respect, have destroyed my state of being a *jāra*. (66–67)
What indeed could be a greater fortune for me than this?
That here, in my own home, I have obtained the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
My kingdom has become meaningful, and my enjoyments as well.
Today my family has become meaningful through the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Today my subjects have become meaningful, and even the men and women have become meaningful;
my very life has become meaningful because here resides Puruṣottama.
All my wealth, including my elephants, horses, and palanquins, has become meaningful today;
indeed, everything of mine has become meaningful now that the Supreme Person is here.
I am blessed, my mother is blessed, and my family of a hundred members is blessed.
In whichever lineage and in whichever house Kṛṣṇa— the glory of all incarnations— resides,
the attainment of Śrī Hari occurs here through merit accumulated over ten million births; that attainment has arisen solely by the power of His grace, so what can I say of such good fortune?
Blessed indeed is the river Obī, and likewise blessed is the auspicious river Irātriśā;
blessed too is the Tribalā, for in its waters dwells Puruṣottama.
Blessed indeed are the sages of the Rāśi clan, in whose home resides Puruṣottama.
Blessed are the trees, the creepers, the shrubs, and the multitude of grasses;
blessed are the beasts and the birds, since Puruṣottama dwells in their abode.
Likewise, blessed are those in whose house Nārāyaṇas and Kṛṣṇas have arrived today.
Liberation is theirs, victory is theirs, and they possess the wealth of good fortune;
all glory belongs eternally to those in whose home Puruṣottama dwells.
Blessed is King Śibi, and blessed also is King Ṛthakūṭaka.
Blessed is King Vīrarāja, in whose house dwells the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Blessed are those who dwell in the netherworld, and blessed are the mountain-dwellers;
blessed are the maidens and the youths who have the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
"Let all those remaining men who desire liberation receive from us, from Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the mantra that bestows liberation.
Having spoken thus, the king prostrated himself like a staff before Śrī Puruṣottama.
He prostrated himself like a staff before the assembly and rolled eagerly in the dust.
Hari placed both his feet upon his head;
he also placed his feet upon his heart and then embraced him.
Hari himself gave the king a gift of flower garlands,
and his four queens worshipped the Supreme Lord.
His sons and daughters likewise worshipped Kṛṣṇa with great devotion.
The subjects worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (84).
Men and women, the local inhabitants, and those of great honor worshipped Him; guests also worshipped the venerable Lord, the Supreme Controller (85).
Śrī Hari took his own crown from his head and gave it to the king.
Then, millions of subjects arrived for the sake of the mantra.
Hari gave them the mantras preceded by the remembrance of His names.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations to Him.
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times, from the fear of time, illusion, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and wicked-hearted beings. (87–88)
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika, I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my Master.
"Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; he is indeed my eternal Lord.
May he be my venerable father, my well-wisher, my friend, my protector, and my guardian.
I am indeed his body, and may he truly be my embodied self. (2.128.90–91)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī Śrī Hari is my refuge"—
thus did the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa give these mantras. He then had his own people partake of the gracious water for drinking.
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself granted his vision, together with the great Muktas and others, to those gathered from the divine abode. The people took refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.

At the conclusion of the assembly, the Blessed One, having fed the people who had arrived, rested for a moment; everyone likewise rested during the night and at dawn. Having bathed, Hari spoke to the sages, the gods, and the others.
Let everyone indeed go quickly for the purpose of performing the fourth sacrifice. At Ālanaukā, where the ocean meets the land, in the year thirty-six hundred and sixty-one,
let them swiftly prepare the fitness for the commencement of the rite.
"However, on the eleventh day, we shall indeed arrive in the morning.
Thus commanded by Hari, the celestial sages, ancestors, and humans,
along with all the officiating priests, went to the confluence of the Ālana river and the ocean.
Requested by him, Bālakṛṣṇa remained in the palace of Vīrajārā;
served thus by the queens, the king, and the princes and others, Hari, together with his family, dwelt happily, finding delight in his mind. (2.128.99–100)
But the king, perceiving that his hundred daughters were infatuated with Kṛṣṇa,
