For one who bathes at the site of the *avabhṛtha* rite, the worlds of the hereafter bestow happiness.
(63) In the world of the *avabhṛtha* site, there is the month of Śrī Puruṣottama, and the three images of Bālakṛṣṇa, which are the supreme granters of liberation. (64)

In this world, the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas are indeed known as Sāṃkhyayoginīs. The three *saṃhitās*—the *Brahma*, the *Priyā*, and the *Muktā*—along with the *Brahmakuṅkumavāpikā*, are the three forms of Hari. (656)
These three are indeed the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) of Brahman and the concluding purificatory rites (*avabhṛtha*) of all sacrifices:
the constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the heart, a garland of *tulasī* on the hand, and a *tulasī* wreath around the neck. (66–67)
These three are bestowers of the imperishable abode by means of mere acceptance [of devotion]:
a tilaka on the forehead, the drawing of the discus and other marks on the arms, and the name of Śrī Hari upon the tongue; these three are destroyers of Yama.
He in whose house there are Vaiṣṇavas, and in whose garden there is Tulasī;
he among whose cattle even are cows that have crossed to the further shore of existence;
he whose wife is devoted to her husband, and who possesses the grace of a true guru. (2.130.70)
Knowledge of the scriptures coupled with devotion— by him who has offered his entire body and physical existence to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, he becomes one who has crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
A peaceful disposition and freedom from desire— these three bestow the state of stainlessness.
He for whom the night dwells in Hari, whose morning is spent in worship,
and whose midday is in the portion of knowledge— he indeed is liberated here, though possessing a physical form,
through association with the virtuous, through the yoga of sacrifice, and through yoga that makes the wielder of the Śārṅga bow manifest.

Neither a man nor a woman becomes superior to the *avabhṛtha* bath by [merely] bathing in a river. However, having remembered sacred fords (*tīrthas*), one should perform the ritual bath with sesame seeds or with *āmalaka* fruits; this becomes superior even to the *avabhṛtha* bath.

At the time of death, the sacrificial ground, as well as Nārāyaṇa Hari, and virtuous men and women are remembered; the fruit of that is indeed greater than the merit gained from giving away ten million maidens or performing a thousand sacrifices. (75–76)
The fruit that is obtained from a thousand fields of grain is attained through the avabhṛtha bath;
likewise through the Cāturmāsya vows, through those devoted to the study of the Vedas, through austerities for a thousand years, and through the gifting of a thousand cows. (77)
Whatever fruit is obtained on earth, that same fruit shall result from the avabhṛtha bath.
[This is attained] by pilgrimages to all sacred fords, by service to one's father and mother,
by service to one's husband, by service to cows, and by service to the gods.
Whatever fruit is obtained by residing in a divine sacred field and likewise by the service of the *tulasī* plant, that same fruit shall be attained by serving the feet of a saintly person.
A man or woman devoid of intelligence, having heard this narrative, should worship Hari.
One should constantly serve the virtuous, for through their power even liberation may be attained.
(8.1) He before whom there is indeed no wealth, nor land, nor even a garden, and whose livelihood consists merely of labor, such as that of a servant or slave; (8.2)
Therefore, one should indeed serve the temple of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa by means of sweeping, smearing, and washing with water;
by removing refuse and the like, and by means of flower garlands, artistic decorations, and so forth. (83)
And by means of craftsmanship, such as the constant washing of clothes and so forth;
by the scrubbing of vessels, the rubbing of walls, the removal of spiderwebs, and the clearing away of dust. (84–85)
And by the orderly arrangement of objects, by the lighting of lamps at the crossroads,
by the act of opening the gates, by the sounding of musical instruments,
by chanting, by rhythmic clapping and the like, and by the recounting of virtues.
With shouts of "Victory!", cries of "Hare!", with acts of worship such as [offering] garlands and the like,
by bringing forth vessels, by the purification of grains,
by the fetching of water, and with hymns of praise and circumambulations; 87–88.
The temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be served with prostrations like a staff, with the grasping of His qualities,
with divine states of being filled with the weight of love that cause the mind to rejoice,
and even by the carrying of earth [for the altar].
Whether by a woman, by a man, or even by either one of them according to their understanding,

whatever may be possible according to their strength, according to what can be accomplished, and according to what is appropriate— that service to the temple should be performed in that manner, even by the virtuous. (2.130.90–91)
Thus, that servant who is a great devotee of the Lord is indeed purifying and superior to all ritual ablutions (*avabhṛtha*). Therefore,
at the time of the *avabhṛtha*, the sage Devāyatanaka went there.
Having thus instructed him, the illustrious Puruṣottama then became silent.
He said: "I am pleased with this sacrifice in which much has been offered by the king;
I am also pleased by his service. May the king be ever victorious here!"
Then the king fell at the feet of the Supreme Lord, Śrī Hari. A golden necklace was placed around his neck by Hari.
The king honored all the guests with gifts and other offerings.
Having accepted the blessings, he then granted leave;
the people returned to their own dwellings and rested for a moment.
The king fed the embodied beings of the three worlds.
There he gave sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and all embodied beings were gratified.
During the night, the people and the celestial sages (*devarṣi*) performed a great festival for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One with *rāsa*-songs,
recitations, and dances.
Then, having fallen asleep, they arose at dawn and performed their daily rites.
They then entered that assembly hall, where they were honored by Śrī Hari with the presentation of priceless offerings, including the deities and others.
Then, having been fed by Hari, they were all commanded:
"In order to perform the fifth sacrifice, you must go this very evening to the region on the shore of the Kālī ocean, in the land of King Kālimān. (101)
"On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the commencement of the sacrifice will take place.
I shall arrive there on the fourth day, at evening itself.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One bestowed upon the worlds those Manus who seek liberation.
For men, women, or anyone else desiring liberation who has taken refuge in Śaktirājya: "May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge always.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!"
"Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends, one should bear the marks of the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika.
I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (105–106)
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my Lord and my husband.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, truly be my eternal husband.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and sustainer. (107)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge. (1.08) Thus, Hari himself gave these mantras to those seeking liberation. Then, commanded by him, they all departed for the Pañcama sacrifice. (1.09)
O Rādhikā! For the sake of a sacrifice on the bank of the Kālī river in the kingdom of Kālīmaśa, Śrī Hari— served there by King Śaktyakṣi—
dwelt for two days, delighting the eager king.
Out of compassion, the beloved Lord bestowed knowledge upon the king and others.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of the Fourth Viṣṇu Sacrifice in the Kingdom of King Śaktyakṣi during the Tretā Era, as well as the Glory of the Manifestation of the Purpose of the Avabhṛtha Bath," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 131 [Author:
Chapter 132 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! On the morning of the third lunar day, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Earth, spoke these beneficial words to Śaktyakṣi:
"The sacrifice has been performed by you perfectly; all embodied beings have been satisfied. (1)
I, Śrī Hari, am manifestly pleased; nothing remains to be gratified.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa is satisfied, all embodied beings become satisfied.
The Blessed Lord, the inner self of all, who dwells within the heart—He is satisfied.
"Tell me what you desire here, and I shall grant you the most excellent of boons.
I am pleased with your devotion; I give you whatever is wished for in your mind.
Thus addressed, the king said: "Dwell here in this palace forever."
"I shall have a beautiful golden temple made of gold constructed.
May you dwell there forever as my likeness for my own welfare.
Hari said, "So be it; I shall dwell in your temple."
"Install there my beautiful golden image,
accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Brahmavidyā, Śrī, and Māṇikī.
Residing eternally within that image, I shall accept your service and other offerings."
Just as I am directly devoted to you there in every way,
so shall I dwell within your form as your inner self, becoming perceptible just as I always abide as the inner self within the hearts of all people.
Just as I shall become perceptible here in the imperishable great field, in the abode known as the Imperishable, and in the Kuṅkumavāpī pond;
so too is that divine form of mine, which acts as the inner controller, intended for service.
"Your power is understood to be subject to the will of your devotees for the welfare of the worlds.
In this first age, fashion my form to be seven *tāla*s in height,
so that I may appear as tall as the men of that time."
Just as there is indeed a decline of embodied beings during the times of other ages,
so too is my form approved by them according to their mental essence (tanmānasāra).
Just as [it is used] for worship, for travel, for recreation, and for being drawn as a chariot.
It should be made so that it is easy to traverse, neither more nor less than the measurement of a man.
There can be no single measurement for human beings due to differences in time;
the settled conclusion is that each person's own body is seven spans (vitasti) in length.
Just as the body may be long, so too may the arm be long;
likewise, his fingers are long according to the arm.
Even the finger-joint is long in accordance with that respective part of the body.
In childhood I was short, with limbs like those of a child; in youth, I was like a youth and so forth.
(17) And today, in your house, I am measured by my own limbs to be five and a half cubits in height, handsome in form. (18)
He possessed the luster of a golden campaka flower and white jasmine, and his arms reached down to his knees; he was endowed with eyes extending to his ears and curved eyebrows,
and he shone with a row of teeth resembling jasmine buds.

"O King, my auspicious form should be fashioned by you with a broad tilaka on the forehead, a body endowed with fullness, a wide and elevated chest, and beautified by well-developed thighs and other limbs. (2.131.20–21)
To my right side indeed are Lakṣmī, Brahmavidyā, and Ramā.
Lakṣmī is sixty finger-breadths [in height], Brahmavidyā is fifty-seven, and Ramā, the third, is fifty-four finger-breadths. (22)
All are radiant, with the luster of gold, and sixteen years of age. (23) Now, on my left side are Rādhā, Māṇikī, and Śrī.
Rādhā is considered to be sixty finger-breadths [in height], and Māṇikī fifty-seven. (24)

The third [deity] is Śrī, richly endowed with great beauty, measuring fifty-four finger-breadths according to my own fingers; she should be fashioned adorned with the moon. She is beautiful of form, with a slender waist, and holds vessels for worship and other implements in her hands.
All of them were radiant, with the luster of gold, sixteen years of age,
enriched by the beauty of every kind of auspiciousness, and possessed of limbs perfectly formed;
they were well-nourished, with cheerful countenances, adorned with ornaments of liquid [gems].
I, Hari, four-armed and endowed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem, should be installed by you in the center—
charming, youthful, eighteen years of age, and bearing the marks of royalty. (28)
"He must be fashioned with all the marks and limbs complete, and not otherwise.
Having thus installed me,
O King, perform my worship perpetually in the central temple, and then in the right-hand temple.
Establish me together with my father and mother before Bālakṛṣṇa, who is dark as a rain cloud and beautiful at twelve years of age.
Here, this glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa shines as my father.
"O people of this world, behold my mother Kambharālakṣmī!
Likewise, through the medium of the arts and crafts, fashion three images;
and furthermore, in my left-hand temple, construct a beautiful bedchamber."
Adorned with the splendor of golden balls and equipped with all necessary furnishings, have an elephant and a garuḍa fashioned; place them in the vicinity of the central temple.
Indeed, install those two likewise in the middle of the magnificent palace at the front.

O Indra among kings, install my two auspicious feet within the central parasol at the crossroads; and install my attendant named Raṇaṅgama, who is devoted to the temple of the God, at the city gate. 35–36.
And appoint those two most excellent auspicious ones, equipped with all weapons,
as the doorkeepers for both Hemanta and Vasanta.
Appoint Svaprakāśa and Dyuprakāśa as their attendants.
On the front sections of the temple, place those who produce the sounds of victory;
and on the side sections, install the auspicious and gracious Lord together with Śuka and Vallabha, accompanied by the *arghya* vessels.
Have the twelve zodiac signs constructed upon the temple;
there should be auspicious images of the sages, ascetics, and Vaiṣṇavas,
as well as one hundred and forty of the foremost devotees dear to Brahmā.
"Arrange all my wives and the men separately, one by one,
in the form of a *rāsa* dance within the upper circular palace.
Taking up musical instruments, form a circle with me at its center."
Whether by the craft of artisans or by the knowledge of painters,
with me in the center and twenty-four hundred wives at my sides—
O King, O gentle one, always arrange such pleasant service.
"There, you shall be my field of activity; I will dwell here, of this there is no doubt.
(44) Then the king, desiring a divine vision of him, said to Kṛṣṇa:
"Grant me a divine vision of you once you have been installed in the palace. (45)
"Indeed, having seen [the Lord] so beautiful together with his six wives, I shall perform the *pitṛ-mūrti* rite; likewise, having seen the *rāsa*, I shall even prepare the bed.
Thus was the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, addressed, O Rādhikā.
Instantly, he revealed his image and temples;
the Blessed One, possessing a beautiful form pervaded by a splendor like that of many millions of suns, appeared auspiciously accompanied by his sixteen-year-old wives.
Having indeed displayed his own forms residing in the divine abode,
he gratified the king as well as the king’s family—
the sixty princesses and likewise the hundred princes.
And the queen was bewildered upon seeing Puruṣottama directly before her eyes.
Then the king, perceiving that the minds of the maidens were drawn toward Hari for the sake of attaining him as their husband,
and the queen likewise understanding that to be so, [acted accordingly].
He gave sixty young maidens to Śrī Hari;
having obtained Hari as their husband, they all indeed became fulfilled.
Having obtained Hari as their son-in-law, the king and queen attained great joy.
Then, considering themselves especially fulfilled, the maidens, overwhelmed with love, performed the worship of Śrī Hari;
eager and excited, they offered the garland of choice upon Hari’s neck. ||53-54||
There they served Hari with food and other offerings with great devotion. The king also gave them an unexpected and vast amount of divine dowry,
including necklaces of celestial jewels numbering in the millions and billions.
He also gave sixty excellent celestial maidservants;
then the king presented four-tusked white elephants and a divine chariot of great speed, carrying a thousand men.
He gave the land to be consecrated for the gift intended for the construction of a nunnery;
and Śrī Hari, having thus obtained the gift, dwelt there happily.
Having performed the fourth-day rite there, he spoke to the lord of men at evening.
"In the evening, you must go to the sacrificial ground for the sake of the fifth sacrifice.
O King, come with your family and together with me to the sacrifice.
Having been addressed thus, the lord of the earth prepared himself along with his servants.
While Hari was drinking water,
a certain Piśācī, who had fallen into a wretched state and was accompanied by a hundred servants,
arrived there; she then wept profusely in the presence of Śrī Hari.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Hari said: "Who are you, and why do you weep?
What is your sorrow, and who are your friends? Speak; I shall bring you happiness.
Then, filled with shame, she did not say anything at all.
Just then, Śaktyakṣi arrived there before Hari.
Seeing him, she wept once more, wailing repeatedly.
And the king, having seen her, asked: "Who are you, and why do you weep?"
At that moment, she assumed for a brief instant the form she had held in her previous birth.
She was the king’s eldest sister, a young maiden who had died and,
through the defect of the poison of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), had attained the state of a *piśācī*.
And she said to the king: "Without my sacred thread, I am sick and have died before my marriage, though I was still in the bloom of youth;
for my heart was filled with latent desires and thirsted for a man. (67)
"Having quickly attained the state of a preta, I indeed dwell here in this forest.
And those other maidens who, possessed of desires in their hearts, have met with death—they are these women. (68–69)
"For my friends are indeed *piśācinīs*, the wives of *piśācas*;
our husbands are *piśācas*. Having consumed the remnants of the sacrifice (*yajñaprasādaka*), they were cleansed of sin and attained liberation, heaven, or that supreme state. (2.131.70)
Since we remained at home, devoid of faith,
we did not come here to the sacrifice due to the obstruction by the Piśācas;
thus, we have not even obtained the sight of this beautiful ritual.
If our state as *piśācīs* has not perished despite such a sacrifice,
then those *piśācas* have attained liberation while we, unfortunate women, remain behind.
For women have no strength without a protector who is infallible.
"Deprived of both offspring and husband, we have come here from that place.
O King, O brother Hari-Kṛṣṇa, act for our welfare out of a desire for our liberation.
I am your sister, as are these daughters of the subjects who have died. (74–75)
"Therefore, we have come for refuge to the God of gods for the sake of liberation.
Grant us great liberation so that there may indeed be no more suffering.
The King said: "And by what karma, O female Piśācas, have you come to this state?"
"Tell me how she came to be here; may there be well-being for you, and from that, may it be auspicious.
The sister said to the king, "Listen to the origin of this female piśāca:
there is a girl who is merciless and extremely wrathful, residing in her father’s house. (77–78)
She who causes excessive strife and dies shall become a *piśācinī*;
she who disregards her own mother, acts independently, and destroys her virtue;
and she who is submerged in sinful deeds—having died, she shall become a *piśācinī*.
Engaged in secret sins and devoid of meritorious dharma,
intent on serving her mother, and not a purifier of the home—
if she is devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa, that female spirit (piśācinī) shall not remain dead. (2.131.80–81)
Just as a mother, sister, or brother’s wife who has been provoked to anger,
or a family stained by sin, she becomes a female spirit (piśācinī) upon death;
likewise, one who is devoid of ritual bathing and worship, and likewise one who is in her menstrual period.
One who is impure, who has sexual intercourse with animals, or who dies [as such], becomes a *piśācinī*.
She who commits suicide, she who destroys her family, and she who kills her father and others—she, upon death, becomes a *piśācinī*. (83–84)
That girl who, under the sway of anger, repeatedly strikes children,
and who commits theft in the house, shall become a dead Piśācinī.
She who kills living beings by seizing them by their hair or their clothes [shall likewise become one].
Even if she knows [the truth], if she dies while standing over the hearth, she shall become a *piśācinī*.
Or, if she is a killer of mice, cats, or other living beings, or a slayer of calves, she shall become a *piśācinī* upon death. (86–87)
She who does not give milk to drink to the calves of buffaloes, or even gives buttermilk to their mother,
shall become a female Piśāca upon death.
She who harms birds and cattle is a killer of living beings.
A woman who is wanton, unchaste, lustful, or likewise a courtesan;
one who consumes liquor and meat, or is a destroyer of embryos—she indeed becomes a *piśācī*.
If she dies in water or likewise in fire while afflicted by hunger and thirst, [she becomes a *piśācī*]. (2.131.89–90)
If she dies submerged in the earth, in a cave, or similar places, she becomes a *piśācinī*.
Whether she was unconsecrated at death, or whether she was intact or even mutilated;
if she dies devoid of devotion and possessed by passion, she becomes a *piśācinī*.
"Thus indeed these Piśācikās have been born possessed of such faults.
O Indra among kings, effect their deliverance by bestowing the grace of Hari.
A sacrifice has been performed by you here, and likewise the gift of a maiden."
By that merit, may our physical sin be destroyed by its portion;
but the mental [sin] shall go to destruction through your grace—grant this to us.
Then the Lord Hari, the master and lord of all living beings, shall grant us liberation.
Thus requested by them, O Rādhikā, the king himself gave the grace of Hari and the water that had touched his feet;
they indeed drank and ate it out of love at that very moment. ||95-96||
Then they were born with divine forms, like the goddesses of the Lord of the Gods;
those pure maidens fell at the feet of Hari.
And Śrī Hari, immersed in compassion, bestowed mantras from his own mouth.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
(98) "May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times, from fear of time, māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and wicked-hearted beings. (99)
Bearing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika, I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my Master.
"Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; He is indeed my eternal Lord.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian.
Śrī Hari, the beloved Lord Kṛṣṇa, is my refuge. (101–102)

Thus he bestowed these mantras and gave him the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Having introduced him to all his paternal kinsmen and his own family, Śrī Hari sent all those women away to their respective homes.
For that long, all of them remained infatuated with Hari and did not wish to go;
leaving behind their handsome, beloved husband, Śrī Puruṣottama, they chose Harikṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, and Narāyaṇa. (104–105)
Those maidens, numbering in the hundreds, as well as the princesses,
all possessed faces resembling ten million moons; they were beautiful, radiant, and all sixteen years of age, holding garlands in their hands.
Out of love and with the desire for the status of wife, they placed [garlands] around the beautiful neck of Kṛṣṇa.
Hari accepted them all out of a wish to please them.
O Rādhikā, having thus taken them along with those others in His own celestial chariot, [He departed].

Taking the princess with her, he traveled swiftly through the path of the sky at evening and quickly reached the land of Kālīmā, having bestowed the auspicious marriage-thread. Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the giver of the *maṅgalasūtra*.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord and the Supreme Person from time immemorial,
purifying the hearts of his own devotees, then descended from the sky and,
having gone to the kingdom of King Kālimāśa, beheld the earth.
By reading or hearing this, one shall become a partaker of the fruit of liberation;
and he who causes it to be read or heard shall likewise obtain the fruit of liberation.

(11.2) Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispatching of the Celestial Sages for the Fifth Sacrifice after the Sacrifice [of the King], the Offering of Sixty Maidens by the King to Hari, the Causes of their State as Piśācīs, and the Liberation of One Hundred and One Piśācinīs," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the reign of King Śaktyakṣin.
← Chapter 131: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 132 [[Author:
→ Chapter 133
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! The Lord Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Nārāyaṇa, beheld from his celestial chariot in the sky the land of King Kālindī.
During the conjunction with the ocean of blackness (Kālimāsāgara), he beheld a vast pavilion,
auspicious and fifty yojanas in length, extending as far as the Yānā river.
He saw it by means of his celestial chariot upon the surface of the earth, as well as in all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Indeed, a light equal in radiance to ten million suns shone everywhere.
At that time, musical instruments were sounded and shouts of "Victory!
arose from humans, gods, and embodied beings who are lords.
Then the spectators also quickly ran toward that auspicious ground, which was worthy of the descent from the celestial chariot; they carried parched grain, unbroken rice, and flowers.
On the shore of the ocean, Kṛṣṇa brought down the celestial chariot.
He descended from that [vehicle] himself, and then the king and the others did likewise.
Thereafter, all those beloved of Brahmā descended from the celestial chariot;
they were honored with gifts of necklaces and other offerings, and their prosperity was increased with parched grain and unbroken rice.
Then all those brothers of Śrī Kṛṣṇa were honored by the common people with shouts of victory and welcomed with prostrations;
they were seated upon thrones and refreshed with offerings of madhuparka.
They were gratified with drinks of water and the like, and likewise fed with sweet foods;
they were rested at night and massaged so that they might be comfortable,
and were put to sleep in palaces provided with priceless beds and such.
Then King Kāliya, together with his family,
served and honored Kṛṣṇa and His family in a fitting manner.
In the morning, Hari awakened him who had fallen asleep with the sounds of musical instruments and songs.
Listening to the hymn of praise offered by bards, Nārāyaṇeśvara performed the cleansing of his teeth. He bathed with fragrant water and other substances,
put on ornaments, and donned a pair of garments.
The kings and others performed the worship of Śrī Hari with the splendors of their royal power;
likewise, the beloved wives of Brahmā performed the supreme worship of the Lord.
Then, on the fifth day at an auspicious time, he went to the sacrificial pavilion.
He saw that everything was suitable and had it prepared by Lomaśa;
likewise, he caused King Kālimāśa— who was devoted to his wife— to make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the commencement of the sacrifice.
He had his forearms bound according to the ritual of *svastivācana*,
and he chose the Brahmins and sages for the purpose of reciting mantras, performing oblations, singing hymns,
and so forth; likewise, he chose the gods, the lords and non-lords, whose abodes are in heaven.
He chose sages, virtuous men, chaste women, noble ladies, and divine maidens;
the essential principles of sacred fords, the sons of Diti, the offspring of Kaśyapa, and worthy deities who had manifested in bodily form. (18–19)

At the site of the principal deity, the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was present; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others were manifest as the presiding deities of the place. There, the guardians of the quarters and the Mothers likewise took their respective positions.

The guardians of the house, the guardians of the fields, the planets, and other dark (tāmasa) beings—these also were present there, stationed in their appropriate places within the field of vision. Likewise, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and those born of the Sādhyas and Siddhas [were there]. (21–22)
The Brahmins learned in the Vedas, those of the seers, the gods, and likewise the ancestors;
the ṛṣis and the lords, as well as the goddesses and the hosts;
Gaṇeśa and the attendants, the perfected ones (siddhas), and the millions of liberated souls.

Likewise, all the incarnations and the women who were their consorts appeared in person at the sacrifice and shone resplendent in their respective places. At that time, even the four Vedas themselves became manifest in embodied form.
The *ṛc* verses became manifest there, as did the mantras in embodied form;
likewise, the fires appeared in personified forms, embodying the offerings to gods and ancestors.
Indeed, all these were present within that supreme Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
The ritual acts, the procedures, and the personified forms appeared;
the injunctions, the applications, and the most worthy recipients were present in embodied form.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements became manifest with bodies, as did the *darbha* grass, the rice, and the barley.
Wheat, wild rice, juices, and molasses from sugarcane—
all these appeared there at that time, fully formed and ready. Fuel-sticks, ritual circles, sacrificial installations, and altars were also present.
At that time, the sacrificial pits, the protective enclosures, the ritual stalks, and so forth, all became manifest with form.
O Rādhā, where Hari himself resides, endowed with all bodies,
what deficiency could there be regarding food, enjoyments, activities, and the like?
Then, when the worship of Gaṇeśa had taken place, the worship of Rudra and others,
as well as the worship of the Mothers and so forth, was completed, Śrī Hari himself,
by means of the King’s hand, performed the formal installation of the fire in the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules.
And as he caused [the rites] to be performed then, the Vedas resounded;
then Agni himself shone in the midst of the flames within the sacrificial pit.
The offering of oblations, accompanied by mantras, proceeded as desired in the fire.

Once the rites for the gods, sages, and ancestors were completed, even the eating of food, as well as sweetmeats, water, betel-leaf, and so forth, ceased. There, at night, the recitation of stories and other such activities performed by the Sāttvatas took place.
Furthermore, the daily rites and the fire-oblations and so forth proceeded.
Thus the seven-day sacrifice, a great festival, unfolded;
indeed, it was completed on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa.
At midday, after the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) had been given, the final oblation was likewise performed;
and at the conclusion, the Fire-god was satisfied by countless *śrīphala* fruits.
Then indeed, Śrī Hari fed all the liberated souls (muktas).
Those who are dear to Brahman, as well as those who delight in the avatāras;
those who dwell in the various abodes, the male and female attendants, the masters and mistresses, and the Nārāyaṇas and Narāyaṇīs. (2.132.40)
The principles (tattvas), primordial māyā, Brahmā and the others who are the forms of the Vyūha,
the ancestors, the gods, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the sages, the ascetics,
the practitioners of yoga, the virtuous men and women, and those who have taken refuge in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as the divine beings.
[He created] human beings and the guardians of the directions, the planets, lunar mansions, and stars;
the Brahmins residing within the body, as well as the [other] castes and those dwelling in the stages of life (āśramas);
trees, creepers, clumps of grass, rivers, streams, and lakes.
He saw the oceans, both natural and excavated, the islands, the caves, and the mountains;
the inhabitants of the worlds from the nether regions upward, situated in water, on land, or in the air;
those dwelling in hollows and within the earth, and all the great beings who had assembled there.
Keśava fed even the insects, moths, and other such creatures. There was no one who did not eat—not the dull-witted, nor even the immobile beings;
neither those whose consciousness was like that of the insentient, nor the wise, nor even the strong. (45–46)
Then Hari fed those embodied beings— whether they were of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)— thinking, "They are my own sons.
He gratified them by giving them water to drink and other refreshments, and satisfied them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then all of them, together with Śrī Hari, took rest. Thereafter, the Blessed Lord Hari went to perform the avabhṛtha bath,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, as he entered the waters of the ocean which had turned black.
Accompanied by songs, all the goddesses went indeed for the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
Kālī entered the water, as did others who had come in vehicles to the water.
Others [entered] the waters of the ocean, and those of wells, ponds, and lakes.
Then the guests bathed there at the concluding purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice,
having remembered the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— beloved, the bestower of peace, and shining eternally within their hearts. (51–52)
To the Lord who bestows liberation, the giver of freedom, the master of Nārāyaṇa and Īśvara,
the Lord of the abode of Brahman, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, the Sovereign—
there the king bestowed gifts of treasuries, camels, and horses.
Of those traveling in palanquins, vehicles, and aerial chariots—[drawn by] elephants, swans, and garuḍas—as well as gold, silver, rubies, diamonds, and pearls;
houses, household utensils, gardens, forests, and groves. (54–55)
Kālimakeśvara gave fields, worthy recipients, and all kinds of food;
he bestowed every kind of great gift.
Having thus performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), they returned to their own abode.

In the evening, King Kālimeśa, filled with joy at the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, provided various kinds of foods and drinks. At night, Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī, in the form of maidens, [related] the stories of Hari.
Seated upon the throne of Vyāsa in the assembly, she recited the beautiful *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa.
There, the wives of the ocean and the divine rivers arrived.
Then they honored the virtuous Mahālakṣmī and Śrī Kambharā with various objects such as jewels, with enchanting necklaces,
and also with auspicious, divine garments and ornaments. (2.132.60–61)
Then the forest goddesses also performed the *ārātrika* rite;
likewise, all the wives of the sacrificers, the wives of the gods, the wives of the ancestors, the wives of the *siddhas*, the wives of the lords, and the goddesses of prosperity did so as well. (62)
Then the wives of Brahmā and likewise the wives of the [other] guardians performed worship.
They joyfully performed the worship of Kambharā, the mother of Hari, who is Lakṣmī;
and all the goddesses residing in every creation performed auspicious worship.
He offered an excuse for both his conversation and his worship by means of various names:
"The Lord of Śrī," "the son of the cowherd of Śrī," "the cause of all incarnations," "the child of Kaṃbhārā," "Kṛṣṇa," "Nārāyaṇa," and "the husband of Ramā."

We worship Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved lord of Brahma’s beloved, the husband of Rādhā, the husband of Śrī Māṇikī, the lord of Brahmavidyā and Ramā, the husband of Lakṣmī, the lord of the virtuous, and the beloved. 66–67.

Thus all the members of the assembly performed this delightful recitation. Then, for the sake of obtaining rest after receiving the divine favor, they performed the *ārātrika* rite with hymns and departed for their own homes. (68)
Indeed, they all fell asleep as if still engaged in wakefulness.
On the twelfth day, having performed his daily rites, the king came for the purpose of worship;
he worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, who is his own self, with devotion. (2.132.70)
They also worshipped the queens with one hundred and eight substances;
twenty queens performed a grand *ārārtika* ceremony.
At that time, two hundred of their maidens became enchanted by Hari.
To that lord of divine form, as beautiful as millions upon millions of Kandarapas, these queens placed the bridegroom’s garland around his neck;
and all those maidens there likewise offered it. (72–73)
To the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self,
Śrī Hari accepted those [gifts],
and the king also gave him as a wedding dowry a celestial chariot one *yojana* in length and four-tusked elephants.
He gave him Garuḍas as mounts— winged beings that travel through the sky—
and at that time he gave him natural jewel-lamps, male servants, and female servants;
the son of Kambharā accepted two hundred of each.

Having obtained that enchanting Supreme Lord as their husband, all the maidens rejoiced exceedingly; nothing further remained to be attained. Thus, after the sacrifice and following the worship on the twelfth day, Kṛṣṇa—
Hari placed his own feet upon the king’s heart and his hands upon his head.
To the queen as well, Hari gave a beautiful garland of flowers;
and to all the other queens, he gave necklaces set with diamonds.
He desired to grant his own vision, which reveals the Supreme Lord;
immediately and suddenly, a circle of light manifested.
Indeed, streams of splendor issued forth from all sides of Śrī Hari.
Then, in the sky, sounds as loud as ten million billion suns pervaded all space.
At that time, Hari bestowed upon the eyes of everyone— upon all those gathered together— the divine vision known as Sudarśana, which is capable of enduring that brilliance.
Then the royal family, as well as the subjects,
beheld the Lord Śrī Parameśa, the all-pervading Sovereign who transcends the supreme imperishable (parākṣara),
and who is served by those liberated in the various abodes (dhāma) such as the realm of Brahmā and others.
By means of incarnations, lords, gods, perfected beings, and humans—
[He who is] possessed of forms corresponding to every form, the youthful, the dark and beautiful,
the remover of desire and pride, the beloved, served by Rādhā and Lakṣmī. (84–85)
Two-armed, beautiful, dark-complexioned, the enchanting Bālakṛṣṇa,
filled with the fullness of youth, endowed with all powers,
wearing a crown of peacock feathers and adorned with golden earrings.
The all-pervading Lord, whose broad chest shone with the Kaustubha gem and a necklace, was adorned with golden ornaments; he held a flute and had a slightly tilted face.
Then [he appeared] with four arms, beautified by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Then, having seen him with two arms, served by his own daughters and others,
residing in his own kingdom, dwelling in a palace, and shining resplendent in their presence—
having seen him thus, they all quickly abandoned their meditative absorption.
They beheld Śrī Hari before them and were utterly bewildered by that wonder. The queens, the king, and the subjects considered themselves to have attained self-realization.
Then, other kings indeed arrived for the purpose of seeing him.
Ruling over the five kingdoms together with their queens, they worshipped Lord Hari most intensely; and thereafter, the great sages as well,
the virtuous ones, the gods, mortals, and even the Daityas who were masters of devotion [did likewise].
And the inhabitants of all the worlds, having arrived, worshipped the Imperishable One (Acyuta).
Those from the regions of Rāśiyāna and also from the kingdom of Śibi,
as well as the people of other islands, likewise worshipped the Lord of Lords (Īśvareśvara).
The people of Kāmacāṭaka-deśa, the Ālāyutāyanas,
and the inhabitants of Pūrvabhū-deśa worshipped the Supreme Lord;
likewise did the people of Riṅgajala and the people of Pakṣavāta.
Those dwelling on the island of Māloṣṭha, those dwelling on the island of Sphuṭākṣa;
those dwelling on the island of Thurāyasa, those residing on the island of Kūṭalāna; those dwelling on the island of Svairanārī, and those residing on the island of Kṣemīyāna. (96–97)
In this way, other beings as well worshipped the Supreme Lord.
O Rādhā, a certain saintly person named Lālāsana,
residing on an island in the midst of the eastern ocean, came through the path of the sky to behold Kṛṣṇa.
Falling at his feet, he also begged for food from Hari.
Hari gave him excellent milk-rice (pāyasa), fried cakes (pūrikā), and other delicacies.
That best of virtuous men ate them, while at that moment drums resounded in the heavens.
The conch shells resounded, and there were natural outbursts of sound;
having drunk water, he let out a belch indicative of his satisfaction.
At that moment, all the musical instruments were sounded naturally.
This wonderful marvel was seen by the people incessantly, even though it was not being prompted. Then King Kālimeśa said:
"O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord Hari, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! || 103 ||
"What is this that arises so suddenly? Cease the musical instruments! O Kṛṣṇa, fear arises within me upon hearing these sudden roars!
Hari said, "There is no fear; he is my virtuous devotee, the foremost among them."
Having known that I had arrived here, he sat upon a seat of foam in the midst of the ocean for another kalpa, performing penance while seated in yoga;
his sacrifice reached completion when he ate it, and thus five sacrifices were performed by me.
When a single person of sattvic nature is satisfied, indeed the three worlds are satisfied.
He is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and he indicates the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Because such a liberated one dwells with me, the musical instruments truly resound with joy.
Having spoken thus, that Hari created a suppression of the sound of musical instruments.
And the virtuous one, clad in the directions (naked), having eaten, went to the island of Lalāsana.
By reciting and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.
Even insentient things offer honor to those whose minds are solely devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, all principles of reality sing together, just as musical instruments play in harmony.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifth Viṣṇu Sacrifice, the Concluding Bath, the Feast, the Narrative, the Worship, the Gift of Two Hundred Maidens, the Divine Vision, the Worship Performed by the Subjects of Many Islands, the Feast with the Sages Seated on Lālāsanas, and the Natural Resounding of Conchs and Drums," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the kingdom of King Kālimeśa at the confluence of the Kālimā and the ocean.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 132.
Chapter 133 [Author:
Chapter 134 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord,
having fed the participants of the sacrifice at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite on the twelfth lunar day,
and having subsequently eaten all embodied beings as well, attained rest.
In the evening, he indeed prepared a great assembly hall within the sacrificial pavilion.
In an instant, he was seen in the assembly hall seated upon a throne,
wearing all saffron-colored garments and bearing a garland of tulasī.
With limbs proportioned to his form, like one who has repeatedly practiced the sacred syllables,
he is indeed the very embodiment of great liberation, resplendent through his observance of the vow of Brahman.
Chanting and glorifying Kṛṣṇa, may Bālakṛṣṇa be victorious here!
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the virtuous, be victorious! (5) Victory to You, O Master Bālakṛṣṇa, O Supreme Self; obeisance be unto You!
Victory to the son of Śrī Kambharā; victory to the delight of the cowherds! (6)
This land has been purified by the performance of sacrifice and made sacred to Viṣṇu.
Blessed are those men in this world in whose presence you have appeared here!
Blessed are all the women and men in whose home Puruṣottama resides.
I am blessed; though seated upon a stool of saliva, I am a king among yogis, being Saccidānanda.
Since I have obtained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, [O] Refuge-giver, grant me the mantra as well as the Bhāgavata initiation.
"Grant me the imperishable abode, your station at the end of death.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One bestowed upon him the Vaiṣṇava initiation,
O Rādhikā, for that yogin dwelling on the island who was desirous of liberation.
There, the Blessed One caused a pavilion to be constructed, [shaped] like a plantain tree;
it was richly adorned with leaf-shaped arches, beautified by altars and water-pots,
provided with sacrificial pits, furnished with canopies, and graced with offerings of cow-products and other oblations.
Hari also caused that devotee, who was seated on a swing, to perform purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
he performed the purification of his body.
Then Hari, facing north, [purified] him who was facing east.
He first gave water into his hand for the fulfillment of his resolve (saṃkalpa).
Having announced the place, time, and other details, and having released the water onto the ground, Hari then caused it to be sprinkled upon his head. (14–15)
The ocean of compassion gave him that refuge-mantra into his right ear:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times.
Having thus bestowed this mantra, he gave him the mantra of protection.
"Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends—
[be protected] by the one possessing the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika.
Having thus imparted the mantra, he then gave the mantra of dedication.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
"Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal Lord.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (1.9)
Having bestowed these mantras and caused him to apply the vertical *puṇḍra* mark, Hari placed a double-strand garland of *tulasī* around his neck. He then instructed:
"Wine, meat, adultery, and theft must never be committed under any circumstances."
In this manner, Mādhava caused him to hear the restraints (yamas);
he then bestowed upon him assistance, detachment, knowledge, and devotion.
Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, [then taught] the observances (niyamas) that grant liberation.
"Association with the virtuous should always be cultivated, for it bestows liberation," he said to him.
"Service to the guru, service to Hari, service to one's parents, and service to one's family members—service must be performed," the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama said to him. (23–24)
"Nothing on earth is ever to be feared or gratified;
the truthful and the virtuous are to be saluted, for they are indeed the powers of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus instructed him, the illustrious Puruṣottama [departed].
He enjoined him to observe a fast for the purpose of bestowing the great initiation (mahādīkṣā).
At that place of fasting, he caused the gift of a cow to be performed.
Thus, having provided the proper rite of fasting, he did so for the sake of purifying the body.
Lord Hari himself caused the *nāndī-śrāddha* and the *svastyayana* rites to be performed.
In the pavilion, he had a *sarvatobhadra* mandala fashioned, adorned with grain;
and in its center, he had a golden pitcher placed.
In the eight directions, he placed eight water-pots filled with water, gems, and fruits;
he set them upon the jars, adorned with sprouts and cloth.
Having placed a beautiful vessel full of sesame seeds, he established the image of Hari.
Having placed [the image] upon a pedestal made of precious stones, he worshipped it with a golden one as well—
[an image] joined by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Brahmavidyā, Ramā, Śrī, and Māṇikī. Then, in the eight directions, [he placed] Satī and Śaṅkara in the eastern pitcher.
In the south, Bhāskara and Saṃjñā; in the west, Gaṇeśvara together with Siddhi and Buddhi; in the north, Śrī Narāyaṇa;
in the southeast, the Caturvyūha; and in the southwest, Garuḍa and Gaja.
In the northwest he installed Hanumān, and in the northeast the host of Brahma’s beloved attendants;
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Supreme Lord, performed these installations.
Following this, he recited benedictions, performed the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* rite, and then carried out the purification of the elements (*bhūta-śuddhi*).
Having likewise performed the invocation and other rites for the deities of the limbs (aṅgadeva),
and having performed the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa), he worshipped Acyuta with the sixteen services (upacāra) and with both mantras and Vedic hymns.
Then, he established the deity Agni in the sacrificial pit to the south;
he caused the Vaiṣṇava *caru* to be cooked and worshipped Hari.
At that time, he also had the *homa* performed with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and the *caru*.
He caused [the offerings] to be presented with one hundred and eight mantras of dedication;
he offered a single oblation to each of the deities of the limbs.
Then, having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he executed the great lustration ceremony (mahānīrājana).
Then Kṛṣṇa also caused the auspicious handful of flowers to be offered to Hari;
having seated the disciple facing eastward, Hari himself, facing north,
gave him divine saffron-colored garments as well as an upper cloth.

[He gave him] the sacred thread and the four marks, such as the discus and so forth. Then he imparted the mantra, together with its meaning, into the right ear of Lālāyana three times, bestowing the state of Brahman.
"I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my Master.
Śrī Hari, the beloved Lord of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, is my refuge. (42)
Afterwards, he indeed gave this mantra for the worship of his own form;
for the sake of liberation, he gave his golden image together with his six beloved consorts.
He also bestowed the saving knowledge that awakens one to Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
This self is indeed of the nature of Brahman, radiant with being, consciousness, and bliss.
O sage, you should contemplate Me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, within your heart.
From this day forward, you are My own, having offered yourself to Me; indeed, you are equal to Me.
Thus addressed, that sage rose and prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, offering as the fee for the initiation rite leaves,
flowers, fruits, water, and his very heart.
Hari bestowed upon him auspicious blessings that grant liberation:
"O devotee, by my grace here, your heart's desire has borne fruit;
and by serving me, you shall attain supreme happiness in both worlds."
"May the attainment of the goals of human life belong to him who possesses supreme devotion to Kṛṣṇa and to his guru, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; may that come to you through my grace.
(2.133.50) Then Śrī Hari himself performed the dismissal of the gods.
Then Hari said to him: "Worship me, Nārāyaṇa.
Grant me the instruction consisting of my own worship;
O Sage, bestow initiation according to this rite upon me, who am desirous of liberation."

You, named Saccidānanda, wearing the saffron robes, are my preceptor; please accept my command for the initiation of people—women, men, animals, birds, those who remember their past births, and even grass and other such things. (53)
Make them all capable of assuming any form at will and purified by initiation.
I am Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all embodied beings;
let everyone constantly worship me, Hari, the Supreme Brahman, as their husband.
"O virtuous one, cause devotion to me to spread among every person on earth—
among children, youths, and the elderly, and among men, women, and eunuchs.
Thus addressed in that assembly, Saccidānanda, the king of yogis, [replied].
Having bowed to his master Bālakṛṣṇa, he instructed the people:
"He bestows divine knowledge and even washes away sins;
such is the will of Hari, known by the name Dīkṣā, the great virtuous one. (57–58)
Since the Brahmaputrī bestows the abode of Brahmā and grants liberation,
it should be accepted by people— whether it be common or special— as auspicious.
Hari does not eat the food or water offered by one who is uninitiated.
Śrī Hari does not abandon even a leaf belonging to one who has been initiated. (2.133.6) The initiate is the king of devotees; he himself is the holy ford, the best of all holy fords.
All holy fords reside there at the tips of his toes. (2.133.61)
All the deities and even all the lords dwell eternally within the body of one who is initiated in every respect; therefore, one should indeed become initiated.
For the fruit of serving one who is initiated is liberation.
The merit born from touching one who has been initiated destroys great sins and other evils.
(6.3) Through the grace of the initiated, his food is purifying, and so too is his water.
Dwelling together with the initiated bestows liberation and grants the divine abode. (6.4)
For one who has been initiated, association with the virtuous is equal to association with the Blessed Lord.
All the ritual acts of the initiated are divine, consisting of offerings unto Hari.
Indeed, the merits of all sacrifices reside within the initiated.
Having drunk the water from the bath of one who has been initiated, his ancestors are satisfied.
The seers, sages, perfected ones, yogis, ascetics,
as well as the virtuous who possess the nature of Brahman, indeed bow down to the initiated one.
The house to which one who has been initiated goes becomes like a divine abode;
she who serves the initiated one should indeed be known as a possessor of merit.
He who serves the initiated one is born as an attendant of Hari.
The Earth constantly prays before Hari for one who has received initiation:
"I am indeed purified by the feet of those who have attained the initiation of the virtuous;
by the mere act of bathing one who is initiated, water becomes a sacred pilgrimage site. (2.133.70)
I am indeed Sādhulālāsana; I speak the truth repeatedly.
By the initiation of Hari, I have truly become known as Saccidānanda.
Even from childhood, one should take up the mantra of him who has come for refuge.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the provider of that [protection], is where there is truly no fear.
Therefore, the mantra for protection should indeed be received from childhood onwards, [for it guards] against time, the bondage of māyā, sin, and the bondage of karma. (72–73)
From enemies, from the suffering of Yama, and from the fear caused by bad friends and the like— Mādhava, whose marks are the trident, the fish, and so forth, truly protects from that.
He who holds in his hand the mark of the trident, the mark of the fish, and the insignia of the banner.
The mark of the bow, the sign of the wheel, the mark of the svastika, and the thunderbolt— among these,
the divine trident indeed destroys the fear of Time (Death).
Likewise, the divine fish destroys the fear of illusion and bondage.
Likewise, the divine banner-mark always destroys the fear of sin;
the divine bow-mark likewise destroys the dread of karma.
The great divine wheel-mark destroys enemies and the fear thereof.
Likewise, the divine svastika mark destroys the fear of Yama;
this divine vajra indeed destroys the fear of those with evil hearts.
Even the hand of one who bears these seven marks, when it merely touches the body, [brings about such results].
In his body, however, even the possibility of the aforementioned fears does not arise.
Therefore, one should indeed take up the mantra of surrender preceded by knowledge:
"Oṃ, I always offer salutations to Hari, who is beyond names. (2.133.80)
It has been offered to my Master, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
From this day forward, I belong to no one else; I am indeed under His control alone.
O Hari, from this day forward, I become Your servant, Your slave, and the servant of Your poor devotees.
Thus, my entire being, known as the gift of self, is offered there;
just as clarified butter is poured into the fire, so am I offered into Hari.
From this day forward, there is no separate existence for me apart from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my Beloved.
Realizing this, one should understand that just as Śrī Harī exists within one's own body and inner being,
so too does Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa eternally abide here within the Supreme Brahman;
He is to be known as the eternal husband, the father, and the kinsman.
Friendship, amity, and likewise the state of being a protector, as well as the state of being a guardian— these are to be known as eternally present in Kṛṣṇa. Thus,
when such knowledge of offering has become mature and firm, [one attains the goal].
Therefore, one should receive that auspicious and excellent initiation which bestows the state of Brahman;
for I am indeed of the nature of Brahman, and not truly the body, senses, and so forth, since I am the eternal devotee who performs service with love for Hari. || 87-88 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone is my everything:
he is my husband, my protector, my enjoyer, my master, and my controller;
he is my inner self, my supreme self, and even my external self. (89)
"The self of the senses, the self of the body, and the self of the physical frame—all that is mine alone.
(2.133.90) Thus, I am never separate from Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; I am eternally immersed in His form, possessing His qualities, and being a portion of Him. (91)
Thus, indeed, having realized one's own true nature as Brahman, goodness shall bear fruit;
one shall then attain the eternal bliss of Śrī Hari in the supreme Imperishable.
In this way, by quickly accepting initiation, embodied beings become divine.
Therefore, the supreme *sādhvī* initiation of Hari should be received by the wise;
others should receive the *rakṣiṇī*, *śaraṇī*, or *samarpaṇī* initiations.
Without receiving an initiation, human beings must not remain here [in this world]. ||93-94||
One should never abandon a favorable place, time,
or company when one has reached the abode of the Supreme Lord, which is gracious and bestows liberation.
For that fool who does not renounce *māyā*, there is loss at every step.
The human body, the supreme means for attaining liberation, is difficult to obtain.
Having acquired it, one must strive for liberation here; for he who does not do so is a destroyer of his own self.
Therefore, men should not destroy their own selves, even though they are capable of attaining liberation.
"May the virtuous receive initiation— either this one or another— according to their fitness,
for this very Śrī Bhagavān grants it to me directly. Having spoken thus, that king of yogis, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, fell silent.
Having heard [this], hundreds of thousands of men arrived for the sake of initiation.
Bālakṛṣṇa granted them refuge and protection;
and to those who possessed knowledge, he gave the mantra of surrender and the Brahma-mantra.
Divided by five thousand, they then indeed became holy men;
they were the teachers of the people of the world and the very ones who bring about liberation.
They were dispatched for the purpose of instruction to regions such as Rāśiyāna and others.

By the command of Hari, those dear to Hari departed for various lands. (102) O Rādhā! Hari rested and held an assembly; having gone to their respective dwellings, the embodied beings also took their rest. (103)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, having bestowed the Vaiṣṇava initiation of a *sādhvī* upon the yogi Sādhu Lālāsana, subsequently bestowed the initiation of a *sādhvī* upon five thousand others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 134. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 134.
[Author: Chapter 135.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the Lord is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed at dawn on the thirteenth day, he summoned the king,
the great sovereign Kālimeśa; and that king, having quickly arrived,
bowed to Hari, performed worship, and sat down before the Lord.
The Blessed One said: "O King, at the conclusion of the meal today, give to all a gift known as *vidāyā* upon the dismissal of the festival.
Thus addressed, that great king quickly had it prepared.
He caused various foods to be brought, as well as excellent wealth:
diamonds, rubies, and gems; gold, silver, and signet rings;
ornaments, decorations, and garments; cows, palanquins, and vehicles.
At midday, he caused Śrī Hari to be fed to all the great lords of the earth,
and he joyfully bestowed sacrificial fees upon them.
Those who were fed were the liberated ones, the non-liberated ones, and others— the manifestations of the imperishable Brahman.
The Śaktis, Pārṣadas, male servants, female servants, attendants, and ministers of the Lord of the Earth;
the male and female incarnations and their consorts, all well-fed;
as well as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and all others, and likewise Vāsudeva and the rest. (7–8)
Bhūmi, Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, Vairāja, Śambhu, and their attendants;
Māyā and her Puruṣas—these are the abodes and those who dwell therein. The Vairājas are the sages and seers belonging to Satyaloka.
The Siddhas and Sādhus, the Pitṛs and the celestial deities;
the guardians of the quarters and the guardians of the worlds, those who dwell on Mount Meru;
and the Maruts and Viśvedevas residing in the Bhuvarloka.
The Vasus, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, Nidhis, Mānavas, Gaṇas,
Gaṇeśas, Gaṇikās, as well as Bhūtas, Pretas, and Mātṛs;
the Daityas, Dānavas, Rakṣases, Asuras, and those created by devotees.
The suns, Rudras, planets, stars, and constellations belonging to Kaśyapa;
trees, creepers, clumps of grass, bamboos, bulbous roots, fruit-bearing trees;
rivers, streams, oceans, lakes, waterfalls, and so forth. (1.3–1.4)
Ponds, wells, tanks, excavated and natural lakes, oceans, sacred fords, mountains, forests, and groves;
as well as insects, birds, reptiles, and those dwelling in the netherworld.
Others, including various regional deities, even insentient principles,
sacrifices, fires, sacrificial vessels, and the finest oblation-liquids—
all these were worshipped by the king at that time through their union with Hari in embodied form. (16–17)

Likewise, they were honored and fed by all the kings; they were gratified with sacrificial fees and granted exemptions from taxes and other duties. Those who had been in the service of the sacrificial rites as groups of slaves and laborers [were also so treated].
The Bhaṭṭas, Bandins, Sūtas, Bhāṭas, Cāraṇas, Guhyakas, Gāndharvas, dancers, those skilled in the art of drama,
actors, singers, female dancers, female singers, goddesses, hosts of Apsarases, and others likewise [were present]. (2.134.20)
There were also foot-massagers, servants performing service, attendants, washers, sweepers, and even those who carried [loads];
as well as coppersmiths, garland-makers, carpenters, and weavers. (11)
There were also washermen, barbers, and artisans skilled in their crafts;
likewise others such as torch-bearers, staff-bearers, and the like;
as well as those who proclaimed victory, guards of the horses, and protectors of the palaces and gardens. (22–23)
Cowherds, householders, and guardians of forests and wilds;
millions of men who protect vehicles and mounts;
likewise, those fond of women, women, eunuchs, and jesters. (24)

There were those of many forms, performers on stage, jesters, and storytellers; members of the assembly who knew the arts of the court, manifesting the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) with gestures (*hāva*) and expressions (*bhāva*);
as well as those who performed displays and those who produced fire-sparks.
Those who possess knowledge of lightning, those who operate machines, those who transport water and so forth, as well as other artisans of visible crafts and whoever else are engaged in manual labor—
both men and women, all of them were honored by the kings.
They were gratified with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and articles of reward, with garments, clothing, wealth, and so forth, as well as ornaments, utensils, and the like;
likewise with gold, grain, jewels, necklaces, and other such valuables. (28–29)
Beggars, the destitute, the helpless, and those afflicted by poverty were fed, gratified, and repeatedly inspired with great faith.
Men and women— chaste and virtuous— as well as holy men free from passion, were likewise honored.
Ascetics who are homeless, guests, and forest-dwellers;
beings born of many species, those who remember their past lives, and those born from non-womb sources;
likewise others who are indolent, as well as those of passionate and ignorant natures. (3.1–3.2)
All were satisfied with every kind of gift by the command of Acyuta;
they were gratified there at that festival by the kings with all manner of gifts.
Then, O Rādhā, they also performed the worship of Hari in the afternoon.
They requested a parting gift, and Hari gave them a parting gift.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī and supreme among men,
and having received the command of the Supreme Lord, they considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose.
Having offered forgiveness to the king for the failure of their service, they requested his blessings; then,
by means of their own celestial chariots, vehicles, and carriages,
they departed for their homes according to their respective power, wealth, and status.
They [depart] from their respective worlds by means of portions of the earth, paths of wind, and celestial chariots;
likewise by means of Garuḍas, elephants, horses, swans, lions, and the like; as well as by means of fires, rays, mental resolves, and supernatural powers (siddhis). || 37–38 ||
They went home by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as through the powers of sovereignty characterized by various forms,
through the contemplations of invisibility, and likewise through the dissolution of sovereign powers;
furthermore, they went home through the sovereignties of creation and through the states of the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*).

Thus, on that thirteenth day, all the great honors departed from there for their own worlds and regions, with the exception of the Saurāṣṭra district; Hari, accompanied by crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of Brahmā’s beloved daughters, remained behind. (2.134.40–41)
Together with the sages headed by Lomaśa, as well as those from the Aśvapaṭṭa Tīrtha,
the guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapālas), the incarnations and others, and likewise with his two parents; accompanied by devotees, servants, family members, Vaiṣṇavas, and sages.
Together with virtuous women, virtuous men, and all the maidens;
together with the subjects dwelling in Akṣarakṣetra, along with the Sāttvatas, and with the Devāyanas and others, Śrī Hari [reached] the full-moon limit. ||43-44||
The Compassionate One resided in the palace of King Kālimeśa for the welfare and satisfaction of King Kālimeśa’s family.
All the royal families remained there until the full moon.
I am Kṛṣṇa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa; by the will of that Lord, we two, accompanied by you, Lakṣmī, have dwelt here until the full moon.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, having performed this act of hospitality.
Having attained rest during the night, Śrī Puruṣottama himself,
Hari, bathed at dawn on the fourteenth day, summoned the kings,
and instructed his own heart’s secret to the members of the assembly in that royal gathering.
"Let all the Vaiṣṇavas, the kings, and their families listen!
The king is the refuge of dharma, and I dwell within that king.
Indeed, the powers of the guardians of the quarters have been deposited by me in the monarch. (2.134.50)
All subjects, being dependent on the king, protect the auspicious virtues:
non-stealing, non-violence, celibacy, and likewise justice;
as well as truthfulness, protection [of the weak], and service to mother and father. (5.1)
Likewise, the wife is dependent on the husband, and the husband is dependent on the wife.
Servants are dependent on their master, and the protector is dependent on his servants.
Just as people abide in proper conduct out of fear of the king, so too do they act out of fear of punishment.
Therefore, the king is my form and he abides by my command.
Indeed, by the king dharma is protected, and likewise artha is also protected.
Through the welfare of his subjects, the king performs sacrifices and festivals.
He establishes food-offerings for the gods and temples with heaps of wealth; the king who is a devotee of the Bhagavat practices devotion himself and causes it to be practiced throughout the kingdom,
and he also delivers his subjects.
Therefore, you kings on earth should cause proclamations of devotion to Hari to be made everywhere by messengers and even by drums.
And let the subjects become devoted to Hari and well-initiated.
May those who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in every way become Vaiṣṇavas.
Let them accept the purifying and auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
and let them also receive initiation (*dīkṣā*), the mantra, and the name of Hari, which grants liberation.
And let them observe the vow on the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī in the month of Kārttika;
likewise, let them observe the vow of Ekādaśī with great devotion during the dark fortnight.
Furthermore, let them perform pilgrimages to the sacred sites on the days of sacrifice.
Let them also perform the chanting of the Name day and night;
let them celebrate various festivals together with assembled Vaiṣṇavas, and let the subjects also engage in the recitation of sacred stories and other such practices.
"Let them perform worship and other rites for Śrī Hari during the Cāturmāsya;
let them cause such proclamations to be made throughout their respective kingdoms.
Thus commanded, the five principal kings and the others did accordingly.
Śibi Devanṛpa, as well as Tharkūṭastha-nṛpa;
Vīrajāra Mahārāja, and likewise Śaktyakṣi-nṛpati; Kālimāśa-nṛpa, and other regional rulers as well. (64–65)
Placing their hope in the head [of the Lord], they bowed to Śrī Puruṣottama; saying,
"We shall do so," they had a proclamation made by the best of messengers throughout their respective kingdoms in every direction.
And Śrī Hari fed them all in his own palace in many ways with delicious food at the request of King Kālimāśa.
In the evening, he ascended the celestial chariot and went to the house of the sage Lālāyana.
The illustrious Blessed One went to an island situated in the eastern ocean;
having made it beautiful, he returned by way of the sky and reached the palace of King Kālimāśa for rest during the night.
Śrī Hari spoke to the virtuous sage Lālāyana, who was known as Saccidānanda and had been initiated: "Go to the Northern Kurus;
from your island, go to the eastern regions together with Keṇāṭa Island."
"Reveal the regions of the immortals and my devotion as well.
Having been addressed thus, that ascetic, endowed with great power, departed by way of the sky through yoga for the Kuru country of Kenāṭaka. (72)
Then, at night, Hari obtained rest;
and then again, having risen in the morning when the moon was full, he bathed and became intent on meditation.
At that moment, O Rādhā, a great marvel occurred there before Hari.
Then, a celestial chariot, brilliant and joined with liberated souls,
descended from the abode of the Imperishable and stood firmly in the presence of Śrī Hari.
The attendants, having descended from that chariot, [approached] Puruṣottama.
"O Rādhikā! Devoted to devotion, they worshipped and spoke [thus]:
'By Your command, for the sake of the liberation of Śūrajāra and likewise for the liberation of his wife, named Devavarūthinī. (76–77)
"Remembering exactly what was promised, we have come together;
O Kṛṣṇa, give us your command, for we are devoted to serving you as you direct.
He then reported all of that to the King, Śrī Hari.
Having joined the benedictions for King Kālimeśa Śakti,
accompanied by Vīrajāra and joined by Śūrajāra and others,
[he established] the kingdom of Śrī Harivīrajāra on the bank of the Cobī river.
Then Hari, served by his own circle [of attendants], arrived in a magnificent celestial chariot; he brought Śūrajāra and the divine host of gods to the eternal,
imperishable, and divine abode that grants liberation.
Then the illustrious Lord quickly returned by means of that celestial chariot to Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara,
and from there once again to the royal palace.
Having received the command of Hari, Tharkūṭastha returned to his own kingdom.
Then a marvel occurred there: sixteen maidens arrived, all possessing divine forms, bearing tridents and having three eyes.
Likewise, four youths also appeared, likewise bearing tridents and having three eyes.
Divine, endowed with the arts of yoga, and possessed of great sovereignty and other such qualities;
then other divine men arrived there—four white-complexioned ones, bearing tridents and [many] eyes, restless, tall, and stout. (85–86)
And five other men, dark-complexioned, bearing tridents, three-eyed, of divine form, tall and lean, arrived;
one among them, though weak and unarmed, also arrived.
Though his complexion was coarse, he was happy and free from anxiety, even while being restless.
Thus, these thirty having come together into the presence of Hari, fell prostrate like staffs at the feet of Kṛṣṇa, filled with devotion. (88–89)
"We are blessed, we are blessed! We have been uplifted by the Supreme Soul.
Having spoken thus, they worshipped the Supreme Lord with many jewels and other offerings.
Honored by Śibi, they performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and other rites.
Then, having been questioned, they sat down: "Who are you, O ones of divine form?
They replied: "We were created by Rudra in the past as his sons;
we have lived here in concealment for the purpose of destroying Rudra's creation."
"O Supreme Soul, today we always abide purified by you;
grant us the Vaiṣṇava mantras, O Śrī Parameśvara!
Thus entreated, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa bestowed the mantras.
Among them, those who were maidens and fierce daughters were as follows:
Uruḷā, Bālikā, Irātriśā, Obī, Māniśī, Bīnā, Tribalā, Trāsā, Tuṅgāsikā, and Anāvarā. (94–95)
Ālanaukā, Uṣṭrīyāskā, Yānā, Anādirā,
Anāṃśukā, and Kālimā— these were the Vaiṣṇavīs at that time.
Now hear their names, O Rādhikā, as they were the four Kumāras.
Bālakṛśa, Dvikala, Alpa-mātra, and Yurālaka—these too, having then received the mantras, became auspicious Vaiṣṇavas. Listen, O Rādhikā, to the names of those other tall men. (97–98)
Akṣoḍha, Kāraka, Kaśyapāya, and Dviriṅgaka—
they too received the mantras and became Vaiṣṇavas at that time.
O Rādhikā, hear now the names of those other five men!
Ūrlaśca, Samāna, Stenāvāsa, Prabhāluna,
and Āpatāyin— they indeed seized the Vaiṣṇava Manus; and thereafter,
those who were weak individuals also became Vaiṣṇavas.
Named Śivaraṇa, he then received the *mantras*;
all became Vaiṣṇavas, servants of Śrī Hari.
Having received his command, those maidens departed for their destination in the form of rivers.
The four youths indeed departed in the form of lakes;
the four men also departed in the form of oceans;
and these five men departed in the form of mountains.
Then one who was harsh, weak, and warlike departed;
meanwhile, the stars, appearing like sacred fords (*tīrtha*), always resided there among embodied beings.
Seeing that family of Śibi and Devaka, everyone indeed became filled with wonder.
"From reading and hearing this, the fruit of each respective sacred ford (tīrtha) shall be obtained.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Honoring of All the Great Beings, the Proclamation of the Vaiṣṇavīs, the Dispatching of Saccidānanda-lālāyana to Uttarakuru, the Liberation of the Couple Śūra and Jārā, the Transformation of the Thirty Raudrī-Raudra Sons into Vaiṣṇavas, and Those Sacred Fords," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī Saṃhitā*.
