Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! I am Kṛṣṇa, the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having resided in the palace of Śibi and having accepted the service rendered by him, [I have come here]. || 1 ||
Having passed the night, on the morning of the first day of the month of Māgha,
having performed the daily and divine rites and instructed the excellent Sāttvatas in their duties,
he received the great worship, food, gifts, and other offerings presented to him.
Having greeted everyone with auspicious benedictions and having gratified them—
namely, the devotees of the temple of the God, as well as Śrī Lomaśa and others,
all those dear to Brahmā, and all the inhabitants of Akṣara-kṣetra— (3–4).
The guardians of the fields, the deities of sacred fords, his family, the attendants and others, as well as his mother, father, brothers, and sisters-in-law;
his sister and her female companions, and even the maidens presented by the king. (5)
Having seated his own people of Saurāṣṭra in new celestial chariots,
he traveled through the path of the sky by means of his own vehicle;
passing beyond Indukuśa and crossing the Sindhu-vyoman.
Having gone to Badarikāśrama and beheld Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and having seen the sages and ascetics, he then went to Śrī Kāśikā.
On the bank of the Varaṇā, [he beheld] his own Lakṣmī, the virtuous daughter of Śiva.
Having seen Śivarāja, Kṛṣṇā, Candra, Jaya, and Jānakī,
and having all gathered together, they then bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
thereafter, having beheld Viśveśa and all the gods, they worshipped them in every way.

Accompanied by all his celestial chariots, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), arrived at his own auspicious Aśvapaṭṭakṣetra, O Rādhikā! The performers of the pilgrimage were greeted with cries of "Victory! by the subjects.
The celestial chariots, however, circled that imperishable field seven times,
beheld the Kuṅkumavāpī lake and the garden groves, and having informed everyone of their arrival, they then departed toward the west.
Then they descended into the great garden, having indeed attained stability;
they were honored by the people with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and parched grain.
Having all emerged from their celestial chariots and having repeatedly taken leave of one another, they departed.
Having bestowed upon them safety, well-being, and freedom from disease, along with garlands and other gifts,
and having honored and embraced them, the people departed for their respective places;
Hari then settled them in palatial residences worthy of their dwelling.
He fed them quickly, and they likewise rested there;
then he sent forth all the maidens together with the beloved wife of Brahmā to the delightful hermitage of Lomaśa, which was forever free from illusion.
The supreme sage Lomaśa, who had been liberated from the divine [realm], protected them all. The sages, the deities and others, and the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla) residing there,
having eaten their own food and stayed in their dwellings, departed and attained rest.
Hari, together with his family, ate and attained rest.
On the morning of the second day, having performed his daily obligatory rites,
he devoutly fed the honored guests from Surāṣṭra.
Kanṭhādharas and others, as well as Raṇaṅgama and his followers;

the Brahmins such as Śīlavrata and others, and even the great sages who were virtuous—all these, having received the command of Hari, departed for their respective villages in every direction. (21–22)
With a serene mind, Hari said to Devāyatanaka:
"O devotee, you have performed every Vaiṣṇava rite, including the Rāśirājyaka.
Such a great deed as this does not come to pass without a devotee. (23)
The *kiṃpuruṣas*, men, women, and even eunuchs have indeed been purified.
(24) "I am pleased; tell me what you wish for, for there is nothing that cannot be given to you by me.
Listen, I shall grant you everything that dwells in your heart. (25)
Having spoken thus, he drew [him] close and embraced him with his own chest;
for a moment, Śrī Hari placed his hands upon his head,
and Śrī Puruṣottama placed his divine feet upon his heart.
O Rādhikā, this Devāyana is also a devotee whose desires are fulfilled.
Therefore, that king of devotees chose: "I shall indeed become your servant in every place where you reside, O Supreme Form, the Lord Hari himself. (27-28)
The nature of an incarnation may exist in a divine, celestial, or human form; it may be known as a *vibhava*, or take the form of a *vyūha*, or be a partial manifestation (*aṃśaka*).
Alternatively, it may take the form of an image (*arcā*), or possess the nature of an *āveśa*, a *kalā*, or a *vibhūti*.

"Wherever you, the Blessed Lord, who are the form of power and the form of the gods, reside, there let my home be; dwell forever in my house. Hari said, "You are blessed; may I dwell daily in a house that has you as its soul."
Just as I dwell here in happiness, so may you become my home.
You are conscious, of the nature of liberation, and the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
likewise, though possessing the form of an object, become my temple.
I shall always dwell within the temple in the realm of creation.
Let my temple indeed become worthy of being a temple;
wherever I am, let that place everywhere become a sanctuary for the gods.
Endowed with manifold powers and assuming manifold forms,
become like an insentient object, appearing as the visible form while you are its presiding deity.
Strengthened by Tvaṣṭṛ, become the presiding deity of all the divine abodes.
"Indeed, as a supreme deity of exceeding beauty, you shall be most pleasing to behold for all embodied beings.
And I shall manifest to you forms consisting of divine abodes. Having spoken thus to him, the Blessed One [assumed] a body consisting of divine temples.
He showed him a beautiful temple endowed with peaks;
then, even within his own form and within the temple of the deity's form,
he showed him such a temple of the gods in every limb.
The altar-railing, the base-platform, the plinth, the pedestal, and likewise the upper pavilion;
the pinnacle, the lotus-stone, the water-pot, and the banner; as well as the front pavilion, the elephant-throne, and the circumambulatory path. (2.135.39–40)
Then Hari repeatedly showed everything within his own essential form;
he revealed that which consists of the abode of the deity for the sake of the abode of the deity,
and likewise bestowed clear, divine knowledge.

Having attained divine abode and knowledge, as well as the nature of existence, he became one who had fulfilled his purpose; he was humble and possessed a dual form. Thus, being liberated in form, he appeared in the form of a divine temple, exceedingly beautiful.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, a divine temple arose;
that palace, measuring a thousand cubits, stood in the sky.
Its domes, adorned with banners, were constantly bathed by the waters of the clouds.
The Blessed One indeed made his own abode auspicious in such a manner.

Having understood this, the ṛṣis, the siddhas, the goddesses, and the deities—both those born from the waters and those born from the land, as well as those produced from the four oceans—[assembled]. (45–46)
The Īśas and the principal Īśvaras, as well as sentient principles;
trees and creepers, forms, Garuḍas, elephants, and horses;
Yoginīs, flowering vines, pillars, and likewise those seeking liberation.
Dwellers of the forest, dwellers of the sky, and others as well who were devoted to the Lord,
having realized that the temple was the very embodiment of the abode of the Divine, came into the presence of Hari, desiring to dwell there. (48–49)
Desiring service to Śrī Hari with their very bodies and filled with the spirit of devotion,
they indeed worshipped Hari and prayed most fervently:
"O Lord of Mercy, Ocean of Compassion, Soul of All, Protector of All!"
You are the provider of all dwellings; grant me a residence in your own abode.
You are known as "Affectionate toward Devotees," for your entire body belongs to you alone;
without you, the world provides no dwelling place for happiness.
Devoted to the temple of the deity, through devotion he has become your own abode.
"By your grace, may we be your servants dwelling in your abode"—O Soul of the Universe, we hold this hope; grant it to us.
To them the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, the ultimate refuge of all that is most auspicious, said:
"Considering that which is difficult to attain as easily attained, you have indeed requested this here.
My abode shall surely become yours, where I dwell in three forms. (54–55)
The Imperishable (akṣara) is the supreme Brahman, the abode of liberation, and my own dwelling place.
Wherever that Imperishable Brahman exists, there indeed I dwell.
For it is there that the liberated ones reside, and never elsewhere.
And for those who have reached the further shore of illusion, the knowers of Brahman, and the yogis—there, in that place, dwell the ancient Sādhyas and gods as eternal residents;
having abandoned the state of being individual souls (jīva) and having relinquished the state of being [limited] lords (īśa). || 57–58 ||
Having burned away the latent impressions of illusory karma, being intent on my worship, and becoming supreme in meditation upon me, they have washed away all causal impurities.
Pure, consisting of consciousness and bliss, they have taken refuge in me and exist solely for my sake. (59)
Those who are intent on self-restraint within my form go to the imperishable Brahman.

(2.135.60) Those who, by a mere fragment of my grace, have become divine and are of my own nature, and whose state of being is absorption into nothing other than me—they go to my imperishable Brahman. (2.135.61)

For those who crave illusory transformations, for those whose nature is the taste of desired illusions, for those possessed of the illusion of ego, and for those characterized by the nature of illusion;
for those striving with effort to achieve their own ends, and who always exert themselves for the sake of passion. (62)

For those devoid of meditation upon me, there is no place in Brahman anywhere. (63) Likewise, for those devoid of devotion to me, those ignorant of my path, and those lacking my mantras and so forth, there is no place in Brahman anywhere. (64)
Thus, this supreme state has been described by me as my imperishable [abode].
But that other, second state of mine is the heart of the virtuous,
wherein I always make my dwelling in the abode of consciousness.
I am the liberated, the great liberated, and also the imperishable Brahman.
Indeed, we all dwell together eternally in the hearts of the virtuous who are liberated and living here in this world; we reside within the hearts of those who are established in truth.
There indeed there is no latent impression (vāsanā), nor is there any transformation through illusion (māyā).
There is truly nothing other than Me; therefore, I dwell therein.
My form is eternally divine, residing in the imperishable abode.

Therein, endowed with the dharma of devotion, she shines within the hearts of the virtuous. (69) That lineage of dharma which is my own personified form, consisting of divine qualities—those very qualities always shine there within the hearts of the virtuous. (2.135.70)
Faith, tranquility, compassion, intelligence, contentment, nourishment, as well as progress, modesty, friendliness, forbearance, wisdom, form, action,
and excellence— these, who love righteousness, always dwell within the hearts of the virtuous.
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, fearlessness, austerity, uprightness;
truthfulness, security, happiness, purity, steadfastness, fortitude, and gentleness; self-restraint, renunciation, faith, contentment, forgiveness, and mindfulness. (72–73)
Self-restraint, sacrifice, tranquility, yoga, cessation of activity, worship, serenity, auspicious splendor, Vedic study, humility, and joy;
meditation, equanimity, the knowledge of Brahman, attainment, capability, and exertion.
Devotion in the form of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth dwells in the hearts of the virtuous.
Therein I always reside, peaceful and with a gracious heart.
You are my eternal abode; dwelling there is difficult for others to attain.
Never shall there be a dwelling among my true devotees for those who are unreleased, who are devoid of my mantra, or who lack devotion to me. Indeed,
only those who dwell in my Imperishable and whose hearts belong to the virtuous have such a place.
"Their dwelling shall always be auspicious and worthy within my temple.
Now this excellent devotee has today become the very abode of the God; though he possesses the form of a temple, he is conscious even as he appears like an insentient object. (78–79)
If you desire to dwell there in my temple, a shrine for the dull-witted,
then accept my mantras and become my devotees.
No others are worthy to remain there except for my Sāttvata devotees.
"This Lomaśa, the best of sages, will impart the mantras to you.
Let those who are Vaiṣṇavas be born here; therefore, let them dwell in my house.
Having spoken thus to the deities and other embodied beings, Śrī Hari then—
Having bowed down, honored, and fully worshipped Śrī Lomaśa, they departed by his command;
Lomaśa, for his part, bestowed mantras upon them and made them Vaiṣṇavas.
Then they went to the abode of the gods, the temple of the Lord.
They bowed down at the feet of Hari.
By the command of Hari, those Vaiṣṇavas residing in the temple became initiated; then the temple spoke: (84–85).
O Blessed One, the gods are fickle and so too are embodied beings;
they are always filled with fear when a time of calamity arrives. If, upon learning of the assault by the Asuras, they were not to flee— || 86 ||
From time to time, they should simply pass through and not remain in another place.
(87) If they should make a vow to dwell permanently in your presence, then you must grant them a residence; establish this as the rule. (88)
Having heard those auspicious words of Devālaya—words that were beneficial, wholesome, and true—Bālakṛṣṇa then spoke as he was being entreated:
"If you think it right, let it be exactly as Devālaya says. (89)
"Take oaths right here, and I shall grant you residence:
as long as the temple stands, whether it be dilapidated or reduced to mere walls, and as long as the deity remains, so long must you remain in that temple. (2.135.90–91)
"When a deity leaves its abode and rises for the sake of all time, then one may approach; otherwise not.
Having made this very vow there at that time, I [acted accordingly].
"I shall always provide a dwelling in a temple, a divine abode.
Having been addressed thus, they made that vow continuously:
"As long as the temple stands, and as long as the deity remains," || 94 ||
"You must certainly remain here even during this great period of calamity.
Having spoken thus, and having drunk the water that was pleasing to the ground,
the gods and others released the water from their feet and touched the feet of Hari.
Having thus taken this oath, they obtained residence in Mahālaya.
Indeed, those Vaiṣṇavas are worthy of dwelling in the temple of Hari;
therefore, as long as the temple remains, so too does that deity remain there.
O Rādhikā, as long as the limbs of a temple remain standing—
even if they are broken or shattered— O Rādhikā,
the restoration of that dilapidated temple is beneficial for human beings.
Those who have attained clarity are portions of the divine; as companions, they bring happiness.
Having thus attained such clarity, the sage Devāyatana became the very embodiment of the temple of the gods, and likewise, the gods found their dwelling place in him. (2.135.100)
Out of compassion for Śrī Hari, one should indeed bow to those [images] even from afar;
for just as I always dwell within a *śālagrāma*, even when it is broken, so too do I dwell in a temple even when it is ruined, dilapidated, or its images have fallen apart. (101)
I indeed dwell [there] as long as even a small shrine exists.
He who bears my command upon his head shall surely dwell there;
by reciting or hearing this, the fruit of building a temple shall be attained.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s Threefold Abode—namely, His arrival at reaching the field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ in the second section on the continuity of the Tretā Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; His threefold residence in the Akṣara-dhāma, within the hearts of the virtuous, and in the form of the temple-image; the nature of the Devāyatana-ṛṣi as the temple itself; and the stability and other qualities of the deities who are limbs of the temple. Chapter 136 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Continuity of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 136.
[Author: Chapter 137.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen once more, O Rādhikā! [I shall tell you of] Devāyatanaka, the king of devotees.

Then, in order to understand the construction of the temple for the benefit of the world, he questioned Śrī Hari regarding the measurement of its parts and all the internal dimensions of the sanctuary.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, please describe how the various parts, beginning from the base up to the flagstaff, are situated within the temple,
so that I may know my own limbs and where the deities reside. (3)
"And these internal [powers] shall also dwell within my body.
Having understood the true nature of this temple and other excellent temples, there will arise others of the same kind.

When artisans, who are masters of craft, shall design temples of manifold forms based upon their own intellects, that will be the future. Therefore, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, explain the analysis of the constituent parts of a temple.
"Since the expansion of the arts has its root in that which brings benefit to the dwellers of heaven," thus questioned,
Harikṛṣṇa spoke to that sage in brief:
"The temple of the gods indeed has as its essential form the lines and the marks."
A middle finger-joint (aṅgula) is said to be measured by seven barley-corns;
twenty-four such finger-joints are proclaimed to be one cubit (hasta). This cubit is known as the "elephant" (gaja) measure, used for the temples of the gods.
In an image, a linga, a pedestal, and likewise in a pavilion; in a royal palace or even in a very long residence;
and in a long mansion or upon the ground—one should measure with this [same] cubit.
The measurement should be taken for the temple of the deity, the pavilion, and the exterior of the walls; likewise for the pinnacle and the main structure of the divine abode.
Indeed, the length of the ground shall be measured in as many cubits as there are [units].
That [measurement] should be multiplied by the number of cubits of the diameter (vyāsa).
The resulting number of cubits should be divided by eight;
the remainder will indeed be known as that which is called the *āyana*.
A single mark on the flagpole (dhvajāya) is auspicious, while five marks on the bull-pole (vṛṣāyaka) are likewise;
seven in number on the elephant-pole (gajāya) are considered excellent in a temple.
Indeed, a mark on the flagpole brings the acquisition of wealth, whereas a mark on the bull-pole bestows riches and grain.
These are considered auspicious for elephants, horses, temples, and so forth.
[16] In a palace, in an image, in a linga, on the earth, in a pavilion, on a pedestal, on a throne, on an altar, in a sacrificial pit, and in a fly-whisk; [17]
On a parasol, a pond, a lake, a well, a divine throne, or in the sky;
on an ornament, a pedestal, a necklace, or likewise a crown—the flagstaff is in every way the most excellent and should be accepted by one who knows the arts of craftsmanship. (18)

In the remaining case of three [types of pillars], the lion-pillar is considered auspicious for a throne. (1.9) In a temple, the banner-pillar (dhvajāya) is excellent; of this there is no doubt. Neither the bull-pillar nor the elephant-pillar should be used in a temple. (2.136.20)
If the Dhvaja (Banner) does not occur, then the Gaja (Elephant) is taken there.
The Lord of the East is Dhvaja, while the Bull is the Lord of the West.
The Elephant belongs to the North, and the Lion belongs to the Southern direction.
One should multiply the length of the site by its width; then,
having divided that number by twenty-seven, whatever remainder there may be,
the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the house shall correspond to that numerical value.

Having indeed divided the asterism by the number eight, the remaining number is designated as the expenditure (*vyaya*). If that [expenditure] is less than the income (*āya*), it is excellent; it is known as "human" (*narasaṃjñā*) and bestows wealth, grain, and so forth.
Expenditure that is excessive is *rākṣasa*; when it is equal, it is *piśācaka*.
These two should always be understood as inauspicious, for expenditure on men indeed brings profit.
Those eight types of expenditure should be known; the remaining one is named *śānta*.
Equal to Dhvajāya, the expenditure named Śānta should be given as it yields fruit;
equal to Siṃhāya, the second expenditure named Pauro should be given;
and equal to Vṛṣāya, the fifth expenditure named Śriyānanda should be given. ||27||
The Śrīvatsa and the Vyaya should be given together with the Gajājya.
These are proclaimed as the Kṣetrapas; when worshipped, they destroy obstacles.
Temples made of gems, jewels, gold, and other materials are dear to the deities. (28–29)

Auspicious temples should be constructed on a riverbank, in a city, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a hermitage of the perfected ones (siddhāśrama), in a cave, in a garden, and by a pond. Palaces facing toward the city are excellent and always bestow happiness.
Among them, both within and without, the deities are always bestowers of happiness.
Śrī, Kubera, and Gaṇeśa are always bestowers of happiness at the gateways;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas are bestowers of happiness in the center or within their own abode.
Having placed a lamp upon the ground at night,
the wise man should draw a line of alignment using the polar star as a reference and a plumb-line.
That direction is the pure north, determined by means of stakes.
One should construct a retaining wall and level the ground to the extent of the share of the site.
One should install the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) either at the edge of a rock or at the edge of water.
One must not perform the excavation on that side where the serpent’s mouth is located.
Indeed, one square must be made for each of the sixty-four squares;
having formed it as a symmetrical four-cornered figure with openings on both sides,
one should write the eight days beginning with Sunday there in sequence.
One should draw it in such a manner that the sun moves within the four corners.
In that square, in the row of Maṅgala, there is the great Nāgamukha;
indeed, his body is considered to be in the row of Śani and the row of Maṅgala.
The tail should be placed gradually in the row within the square known as Nāgāsya;
moreover, no excavation whatsoever should be made in the region of the body.
When the Sun is in Virgo, Libra, or Scorpio, the face should be directed toward the east.
In the months of Bhādrapada and Mārgaśīrṣa, the mouth of the serpent (nāgamukha) should always face the east;
then three [houses] to the south, then three to the west,
and then three to the north— one should not cause a pit to be dug there.
Just as it is considered auspicious to excavate on both sides of the two "bellies," if there is no serpent’s mouth in the east, one should perform the excavation in the northwest (Vāyavya).
If there is a serpent’s mouth in the south, one should perform the excavation in the northeast (Aiśānī).
If the Nāgamukha is in the west, one should perform the digging in the southeast;
if it is in the north, one should perform the digging in the southwest.
In all temples, one should bury [the object] in the left side of the belly.
In a temple measuring one *gaja*, the tortoise [pedestal] should be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) high;

from that point up to ten *gaja*, one should increase the tortoise by two finger-breadths for every additional cubit (*hastaka*). That which is thus proportioned is considered suitable as the *kūrmaśilā* (tortoise-stone).
From ten [aṅgulas] up to twenty, one should increase it by one aṅgula;
from twenty up to fifty, one should take half an aṅgula for each [increment].
This is known as the "Brick-Tortoise" (iṣṭakākūrma) for bricks in a temple.
Regarding stones used for temples and other structures, one should fashion a tortoise from stone;
on the lower portion of this tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), one should execute a lotus measuring one-eighth of the whole.
This [lotus] should be one cubit in length and eight fingers high, and its shape should be square.
In a stone mansion, that [stone] known as *svasthā* should be given as an aid.

But in brick mansions, having made the tortoise-stone according to the measurement of half a finger-breadth in thickness, it should be placed; by its stoutness, it shall be a bestower of stability. || 2.136.50 ||
Then, nine square compartments should be made upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā).
In the compartment situated in the southeast (Agni), the sign of the water-jar (vāridṛśya) is seen; in the south, the fish (matsya);
in the southwest (Nairṛta), the frog (maṇḍuka); and in the west, the crocodile (makara).
In the northwest is the mouth of the vessel; in the north is the sight of the conch;
in the northeast is the sight of the serpent; and in the east is the sight of the pitcher.
It is the established rule that in the ninth central portion, the tortoise must be fashioned.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, as well as Ajitā, Aparājitā, Śuklā, Saubhāginī, and Dharaṇī is considered the ninth.
A tortoise should be fashioned with one cubit [in height], measuring half a finger-breadth in the temple.
It is considered best if made of gold or silver.
Thereafter, from one cubit up to fifteen cubits, this tortoise should be increased by half a finger-breadth [at each stage]. (55–56)
From fifteen to thirty-one cubits,
an increase of one-fourth of an *aṅgula* per cubit is always prescribed for the tortoise-shaped altar (*kūrma*).
From thirty-one to fifty cubits, however, [the same rule applies].
An increase of one *doraka* (finger-breadth) is to be added for each successive tortoise.
Then, together with the tortoise, it should be bathed with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar;
thereafter, it is to be installed, for that [tortoise] is indeed named Dharaṇī.
The leaf-patterns must not be made at all; rather, they should be made free from defects.
In the center, there should be a hollow space devoid of any parts.
It should be worshipped with gems and covered with corals.
The eight auspicious stones located in the eight directions, beginning with Nandā, are as follows:
in a temple of one cubit [in height], the stone is considered to be seven finger-breadths thick;
from that point up to five cubits, those stones are considered to decrease by two finger-breadths each.
Therefore, for a [pillar] of ten cubits, those stones are considered to be three finger-breadths thick;
for twenty cubits, they are three-quarters of a finger-breadth;
and up to fifty cubits, they are one-and-a-quarter finger-breadths.
Nine stones should be made with right angles and as thick as one-fourth [of the measurement].
Upon these stones, one should place the Śakti in the southeast corner,
the Daṇḍa in the south, and the Khaḍga in the southwest.
In the west one should place the noose, and likewise the goad in the northwest;
one should place the mace in the north and the trident in the northeast.
One should place the thunderbolt in the east, and the sacrificial altar for them outside as follows.
The garments should be red, dark blue, cloud-colored (grey), pale, and white;
one should clothe [the deity] with green, white, and yellow garments in sequence.
In the excavated pit, nine stone caskets for the treasure should be placed beneath.
Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara,
Kundana, Alaka, Kacchapa, Mukunda, and Kharva are the nine treasures (nidhis).
From the northeast corner toward the southeast, or on the right side, the eight stone slabs (śilās) are to be offered.

In the center, the Tortoise Stone (kūrmaśilā) is placed; afterwards, with Vedic and auspicious songs, Nandā should be established in the east, and then the other [stone], Dharaṇī. The interior of the eight stones, leaving sufficient space, should be protected like a sealed casket.
Having fashioned small bowls on all sides, they should be placed on top like a *puṭa* [seal].
However, the navel-base of the earth should be left with space above it;
one should lead [the channel] up to the lion-throne, for that indeed bestows happiness.
Upon the installation of the tortoise and the installation of the foundation stone (śilā),
one should offer sweet food cooked in ghee to the deities and sweet cakes to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas).
One should present a divine garment, accompanied by a bilva fruit, to the artisan.
One should offer food and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas. The foundation of temples is considered to be the *jagatī* and the altar (*vedikā*).
As long as there is a corner, so too should the temple of the deity have a *jagatī*.
A vedikā (altar-platform) that is square, octagonal, circular, or oblong,
and which takes the form of a temple, is indeed highly praised.
The terms *vedikā*, *jagatī*, and *pradakṣiṇā* are synonymous.
The jagatī (pedestal) should be made six times the height of the prāsāda (temple), which is considered auspicious;
however, for the temples of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, it is seven times [the height].
Alternatively, it is sometimes considered to be twice, four times, or five times [the height].
The *jagatī* with three circuits is the best, while that with two circuits is middling;
that with one circuit is the smallest. In the temple of Viṣṇu, the second circuit is reduced by one-third of the height.
The third enclosure should be less than that by one-third of its height;
thus, the total height of the enclosures should be made according to this threefold division.
They may be four-cornered, twelve-cornered, or twenty-cornered.

The [mandala] with twenty-eight corners and those with thirty-six corners are indeed the most excellent. If the temple (prāsāda) is twelve cubits in length, then the base (jagatī) is considered to be half that measure in length and equal to it in height.
When the length is twenty-two cubits, the height is considered to be one-third of that;
when the state of length is thirty-two [cubits], the height is held to be one-fourth;
and when the length is fifty [cubits], even in the fourth case, it is four parts.
In the case of a heightening [of the structure], equality is also always the cause of freedom from obstacles.
(85) First, for that which is being raised in the world, the parts should be made equal;
then there are twenty-eight [parts], and the *jāḍyakuṃbha* consists of three parts. (86)

The pericarp (karṇikā) should be made with two parts; the fillet-band (sarapaṭṭikā) within the three-part division should be provided with lotus petals. The base (khuraka) is considered to be two parts.
The pitcher (kuṃbha) shall consist of seven parts, and the vase (kalaśa) shall be three parts.
The *antarapatrī* shall consist of one part, and the *kapotālī* shall be produced from three parts.
The *puṣpakaṇṭha* should be made with four parts; these [proportions] are conducive to happiness.
Indeed, for the projection (*nirgama*), the *puṣpakaṇṭha* is taken as four parts.
Likewise, a jar for the dull-witted (or a jar of dross) is also taken as one-fourth part.
Starting from the east among the pericarp petals and proceeding clockwise,
auspicious and beautiful images of the eight guardians of the directions should be installed.
The stones that support the palace should be long, thick, and without gaps;
they should be firmly set with well-prepared mortar and the like, free from any intervening spaces.
Above the base (jagatī) and the foundation (dāśikā), there should then be the entablature (bhīṭa).
Having constructed the *bhīṭa* (the upper story) of the elephant-palace with a height of four *aṅgulas*,
and extending it up to fifty elephants [in length],
the *bhīṭa* should be raised by half an *aṅgula* for each successive elephant.
One, two, or three *bhīṭas* should be constructed one above the other according to measurement;
they must in every respect be made with a measurement reduced by one-fourth.
The *nikāsa* (projection) shall also be one-fourth [of the height] according to the measure of its own respective height.

Having divided the *bhīṭa* into three parts, one should fashion *puṣpaka-cippikās* on the uppermost portion, which constitutes half of that part; one should then place the pedestal (*pīṭha*) upon the *bhīṭa*.
In the case of a temple measuring one cubit, the pedestal should indeed be twelve finger-breadths in height.
Up to five cubits, the increase for each elephant is five finger-breadths;
beyond that, up to ten cubits, the increase is by four finger-breadths;
and beyond that, up to twenty cubits, an increase of three finger-breadths is considered auspicious.

The increase in height reaches up to thirty-six [parts], measured at one and a half *aṅgulas* per unit; the total height extends up to fifty [units] for elephants, being reduced by one-quarter. An increase in the pedestal (*pīṭha*) exceeding one-fifth [of the height] is considered auspicious and excellent.
The height of the palace consists of twenty-one parts;
the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is five parts up to nine parts, according to one's preference.
Likewise, the Sarvatobhadra, Padma, and Vasundhara [plans] bestow auspiciousness.
The lion, the void, the garuḍa, the swan,
and the bull constitute the ninefold pedestal (pīṭhaka), for the pedestal is that which supports the temple.
Beyond that, fifty-three parts should be made for the height of the pedestal.
Twenty-two parts are to be assigned according to the rule during the exit [of the breath].
Nine parts are to be understood for the jar of dullness (jāḍyakubha), seven parts for the ear (karṇaka), and likewise seven parts for that which is accompanied by the blind woman (andhārī). 103–104.
Likewise, the *grāsapaṭṭikā* (the band for the mouth) is considered to be accompanied by six *chajjikās*.
The elephant-stall (*hastistara*) should be made in the twelfth part, the horse-stall (*vājistara*) in the tenth part,
and the human-stall (*narastara*), which is auspicious to behold, should be made in the eighth part.
Or else, there may be a bedding even for the principal vehicle of the deity on a horse-bedding.
Indeed, by the power of the tip of the *karṇaka*, the emergence of the five parts occurs;
for the *jāḍyakuṃbha* should be made with a *karṇaka* measuring three and a half parts.
The intermediate space shall be half a part, and beyond that, four parts;
then a beautiful *chajjikā* with a pair of *grāsapaṭṭīs* should be constructed.
The elephant-projection shall be four parts, or it may be the same as the horse-projection.
The first layer should indeed be made with one part, and the second layer with two parts.
Between the layers, as well as above them,
a *karṇikā* (pericarp) and a *chajjikā* (coping stone) should be fashioned, O Rādhikā, which provide great beauty.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description and Measurement of the Components of the Temple, Beginning from the Excavation and Ending with the Pīṭha and Karṇī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 136. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 137 [Author:
Chapter 138 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke to the sage Devāyatanaka:
"Listen, O Rādhikā! [I shall describe] the pavilion and so forth exactly as they are.
A pavilion is traditionally defined as being above the corner line of the temple."
The *maṇḍovara*, *udayinī*, and *ubhinī* are synonymous terms.

Indeed, the height (*udaya*) of a palace should be five times its [width] starting from the hand-cubit; that height should be made equal to the length of the palace, for such a proportion bestows auspiciousness. (2–3)
Up to ten cubits in length and fourteen finger-breadths in height,
it should be constructed for each cubit, extending up to thirty cubits;
beyond that, a pavilion twelve finger-breadths high should be made.
Up to fifty elephants [in height], it is considered to be nine *aṅgulas* thick.
The sections of the pavilion (*maṇḍovara*) should be constructed by the artisan as follows:
the pavilion consists of one hundred and forty-four [parts]. (5–6)
These [elements] are considered to extend from the top of the pedestal (pīṭha) to the top of the dome (śikhara).
The *khuraka* occupies five parts, and the *kuṃbhaka* likewise twenty.
The *kalaśa* occupies eight parts, while the intervening space (*antarāla*) is two and a half parts.
The *kapotikā* occupies eight parts, and the *mañcikā* nine parts.
The *jaṅghā* consists of thirty-five parts, while the *udgama* is fifteen parts. The *bharaṇī* is eight parts, and the *śirāvaṭṭī* is ten parts.
The *kapotālī* (dove-cot) is eight parts, with an interval of two and a half parts;
the covering is thirteen parts, and the projection is ten parts.
The *khuraka* (pedestal) is five parts in height, and its projection is two parts.
The inner leaf (antarapatra) shall be half a part, while the fillet (karṇaka) shall be two parts.
The shoulder (skandha) of the pond (vāpī) shall be one and a half parts, and the excellent fillet (kaṇakottama) shall be one part.
The tip of the fillet (kaṇakāgra) should be made beautiful with two bands (paṭṭikā), making it well-pleasing to behold.
The *paṭṭikā* should project out by one part, neither more nor less;
the *kaṇaka* should project out by one and a quarter parts.
In the great row of the *kumbhaka*, there is the projection of the *apaskandha*.
It should be constructed up to the *karṇaka*; now listen to the description of the *kumbhaka*.
There, the height of the *kumbhaka* is twenty parts, divided into sections:
the *skandhapaṭṭa* is half a part, and the *cippikā* is one part. (14–15)
The shoulder-band (skandhapaṭṭa) should be made very graceful, circular, with variegated leaf-patterns, and beautiful, so that what is seen upon it may indeed be lovely.
One should cause the cippikā to be fashioned beautifully with lotus leaves.

In the eastern, middle, and western sections of the pitcher, one should install the images of Brahmā, Hari, and Hara according to their forms, worthy of being seen, along with their emblems (Heti). Furthermore, there should be auspicious splendors for the three junctions of the day and various kinds of paintings. || 17–18 ||
One should indeed fashion the shoulder-band (skandhapaṭṭa) as it appears [in the model], beautiful to the mind;
the nostrils are placed at the ears, and on the petals of the *pratirathikā* [the secondary arches],
in the corners and in the center of the interior, auspicious images with their deities should be made.
On the pillars, an archway should be fashioned like a lotus leaf;
likewise, it should be beautifully formed and adorned with lotus stalks and other such elements.
This pinnacle, possessing a manifold and wondrous form, is considered the most excellent *kumbhaka*.
Above the *kuṃbha*, a very beautiful *kalaśa* should be made, consisting of eight parts;
its middle portion should be made very ornate, consisting of six parts. Above that, a circular form should be fashioned, and upon it, an auspicious *cippikā*.
On one side, a beautiful head-band (*paṭṭabandha*) should be fashioned;
it should be adorned with jewels and made across two and a half parts (*aṃśaka*).
An intermediate space should be fashioned, beautified with divine flowers and the like. (23–24)
Then, the *kapotālī* (dove-cornice), which brings auspiciousness, should be made with eight parts;
the *skandhapaṭṭī* (shoulder-band) with half a part; the *skandha* (shoulder) with two and a quarter parts;
the *mukhapaṭṭī* (face-band) with one-quarter part; and the *karṇapaṭṭikā* (ear-band) with two parts.
The *skandha* (shoulder-piece) is auspicious, consisting of two and a half parts; it should be joined with the neck-band (*galatā*).

A *skandhapaṭṭa* (shoulder-strip) measuring half a part should be made, and below that, the *mukhapaṭṭī* (face-strip) should be fashioned, with *gagārakas* (ornamental projections) at its front and rear. ॥26-27॥
The two facing [parts] are considered beautiful when they are four finger-breadths wide and symmetrical.
The upper shoulder (ūrdhvaskandha) should be made with the interior of the petals recessed.
Above the interior of the *kapotālī* and the *aṅga*, a *ṭhagārikā* should be constructed.
Above the *kapotālī*, a pedestal (*mañcikā*) consisting of nine parts should be constructed.
Beyond that, the inner panel (*antarapatraka*) shall be one and a quarter parts;
the *kāmarūpa* shall be three-quarters of a part, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) shall be one part. (2.137.30)
The shoulder (skandha) is divided into two parts, and the face-band (mukhapattī) follows that;
likewise, the ear-piece (karṇaka) is with one-quarter [of a part], and the shoulder is also with one-quarter.
The inner leaf (antarapattrī) is with one-quarter, and the ear-piece is likewise with one-and-a-half parts.
A beautiful and auspicious *nirvāṇa-ṭṭikā* should be fashioned at the base. From the openings of the *kapotālī* lines, *gagārakas* should be made;
the pillars of the *jaṅghā* should be richly projecting, with circular *lumbikās* beneath them. (32–33)
Above that, the *jaṅghikās* (pedestals) should be made, occupying thirty-five parts;
they are auspicious when provided with a globular pillar (*golastaṃbha*) and a nose-projection (*nāsāphala*).
In all cases, for every primary nose-projection (*mūlanāsā*), four pillars (*staṃbhī*) should be constructed.
They are joined with elephants, lions, garuḍas, crocodiles, and horses.
On the ears are the eight guardians of the directions, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.
Rudra is dancing in the fifth part, and the slayer of Andhaka is on the right.
In the north, there is the goddess Daṃṣṭrānanā, who destroys the power of Caṇḍa;
likewise, at the *pratiratha* positions, one should place the deities of the threads as well as the lords of the directions.
On the paths of the waters, the lords of sages should be depicted, established in austerity.
And windows should be made upon the *bhadra* projections, provided with openings;
they should be adorned with five types of pillars, coverings, and *tilaka* ornaments, beautifully graced by the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva, and be most pleasing to behold. (38–39)
Above the window-frames and pillars, they should be adorned with half-globe arches (*ardhagola-toraṇa*).
On the *jaṅghā* (lower) sections, one may likewise depict couples, groups of birds,
or beautiful clusters of blossoms (*mañjarī*) and creepers (*pallava*), arranged in such a way that they are highly decorative.
The *bharaṇī* should have a height of eight parts; below it, the *chanda* is in the form of a sphere.
The *nirgama*, the *grāsapaṭṭī*, and the *bharaṇiskandhikāvaṭī* should be circular;
it must not be made [otherwise], and at the *nirgama* it should have six equal petals.
The *kāmarūpa* is three-quarters [of the height], and the *skandhapaṭṭikā* should be one-quarter;
the *cippikā* is half a part, and likewise the *kaṇaka* is one-and-a-quarter parts. The *paṭṭikā* and the *antarāla* are always remembered as being one-quarter each.
The shoulder (skandha) should be made two parts; half a part for the ear-lotus (karṇaka-utpala);
the fillet (paṭṭikā) and the interval (antarāla) are likewise considered to be one quarter each;
the shoulder is half a part, and the molding (bartna) is three-quarters of a part. ||44–45||
The inner leaf should be made half the size [of the outer] to bestow all desires.
Auspicious sprouts should be fashioned on all the sides of the nose;
for those aśoka sprouts indeed grant all wishes.
In the golden parts, the shoulder-bands should be fashioned in the form of *tāla* leaves.
Furthermore, above the *bharaṇī*, they should be merged into the spherical portion (*golabhāga*).
A beautiful, elevated neck-opening (*śirāvaṭṭi*) should be made in the tenth part.
In that [structure], auspicious load-bearing figurines (bhāraputtalikā) should be made occupying three parts;
the shoulder (skandha) should be one-quarter less, and likewise the ear-part (karṇaka) one-quarter less.
The space between them should be half a part, and within that interval, there should likewise be a fillet (paṭṭaka).

The circular neck-ring (*śirāvaṭī*) should be made with five parts and provided with a central thread; it should be adorned with pearls and set with diamonds. Above that, a pigeon-ornament (*kapotālī*) should be well-proportioned at one-quarter part.
The intermediate space, however, must indeed be made to measure two and a half parts;
therein, the covering should be made according to thirteen parts.
The shoulder-band is half a part, and the shoulder itself is three parts.
The face-band (mukhapaṭṭī) is half a part; the height of the cornice (chajjā) is four parts.
The pillar-shaft (daṇḍikā) is one part, and the interval (antarāla) is four parts. The fillet (kaṇaka) is one and a quarter parts, and the shoulder (skandha) is two parts. 53–54.
The shoulder-band (*skandhapaṭṭī*) measures one quarter [of the width] and fulfills all desires.
The egress for the covering (*chādyanirgama*) is considered to be one-tenth [the width];
the lower shoulder (*adhaḥ-skandha*) is four parts, while the wrist-connection (*maṇibandhaka*) is one and a half parts.
The *agrecippi* should be half a part; it bestows all desires.
The *kāmarūpa* is one part, while the *skandhapaṭṭikā* is a quarter-part.
The *cippikā* is also half a part, and the *mukhapaṭṭikā* is a quarter-part.
The *kaṇaka* is two parts, and the *daṇḍaka* is half a part;
at the location of the wrist (*maṇibandha*), the *sārilambana* is three parts.
The *nikāra* is ten parts, while the *praveśa* is six parts.
The water-channel shall be one-sixth [of the width], and the entrance shall also be one-sixth.
Furthermore, the width of the hand (pāṇi) and the length of the star (tārā) shall each be one-sixteenth of a part.
When established in this manner, the temple will indeed be firm and conducive to long life.
All the elements beginning with the *kumbha* (pitcher) are stable, and their projections are equal in measurement.
The projection of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) on the exterior is likewise that of the covering (*acchādaka*).
The measurement of the *kumbha* and the width of the platform (*tara*) is equal to the length of the temple (*prāsāda*).
The artisan should understand [the proportions] according to what is appropriate by means of the primary measurements (mūlanāsā).
Indeed, the emergence of the five, three, seven, and nine secondary parts (upāṅga) should be understood by the artisan of beautiful craft as being located precisely on the exterior. 62–63.
Karṇa, Pratiratha, Karṇikā, Nandikā, Uparatha, Bhadra, and Subhadra— these are the [parts] in the exit.
It should be so arranged that they lie outside the boundary of the root.
Seven noses should be fashioned in the auspicious half [of the temple], specifically in the sixth part.
The first [nose] consists of eight parts, the second is ten parts,
the third is eight parts, and at the end, it is four and a half parts.
The auspicious half-measure (bhadrārdha) shall indeed be one-sixth [of the width], while the full measure (pūrṇa) is twelve parts.
In a temple, the site for the building (vāstukṣetra) should be made with eight corners.
On the level of the sight-lines (dṛṣṭikā), the wall is always considered to be one-quarter [of the total height] thick.
The stone wall should be understood as being limited to six parts;
the wooden temple wall is considered to consist of seven parts;
the wall made of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as that of rubies and other gems, consists of ten parts.
The circumambulatory path (*bhramaṇī*) should also be made as one-tenth the size of the palace.
From the middle corner of the circumambulatory path, [the lines] should be led upward according to that sequence.
And in a palace of fifty elephants (in height), the upper part of the circumambulatory path is like the *bhadra* [projection].
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should also be constructed with circular rotation and supported by pillars.
A lamp-chamber should be made in the southern portion of the temple (prāsāda).
Furthermore, the lintel (kolikā) should be made half the width of the temple's breadth.
Above that, a very beautiful *śukanāsa* (gargoyle) should indeed be constructed.
The door should be made in the east, west, or north, but not in the south.
In a temple shaped like an elephant (*gajaprāsādaka*), the door should be sixteen finger-breadths in height.
Up to four *gaja*s, sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) should be increased for each cubit (*hasta*);
at eight *hastas*, three finger-breadths [are added per cubit].
Up to fifty *gaja*s, two finger-breadths should be increased for each cubit.
The width of the door should always be half of its length for it to be auspicious.
If one-sixteenth part of its height is added to that half, the door becomes excellent;
indeed, such a door bestows all prosperity and happiness.

In the temple, for the various species of celestial flower-decorations, an auspicious Nāgara-style door with nine branches should be constructed; indeed, that is the Vaiṣṇava door. A banner should be placed at the door according to the measurement-line of the temple.
One should divide the door-frames according to the proportions of the base;
indeed, in a nine-part [structure], there should be nine branches, while in a three-part [structure], they are auspicious.
For the sake of purifying defects in the dimensions, both reduction and increase are also considered appropriate.
In the middle panel, the door-keepers (dvārapālas) should be fashioned, being most enchanting.
On the side branches as well, delicate creepers are considered to be beautiful.
At a height of one-fourth the span of the branch, two auspicious door-keepers are prescribed.
On the left is the Yamunā and on the right the Gaṅgā;
likewise, both Gandharva women and Gandharvas should be fashioned together with musical instruments.
Elephants, Garuḍas, swans, and horses are also the attendants.
Or, wherever the gods may be suitable [to be placed], they should be fashioned on the nine-fold branch (navaśākhaka).

There, eleven long divisions should be made for that branch. Furthermore, two form-pillars (rūpastambha) should be constructed, consisting of two parts each and joined with corner-projections (koṇikā).
In that [structure], an extension measuring one and three-quarter parts is auspicious.
The first branch is the *patraśākhā*, the second is the *gandharvā*,
the third is the *rūpastaṃbhā*, and the fourth is the *khalvaśākhā*.
The Gandharva is the fifth, and Rūpastambha is the sixth;
the seventh is Rūpaśākhā, and Khalvaśākhā is the eighth; the ninth is Siṃhaśākhā, or alternatively, it may be whatever is beautiful according to one's desire.

The expansion of the side-panels (śākhā) and the frames (peṭaka) should be one-fifth of the width of the entrance; the image of the deity to be installed should be on the northern beam (uttaraṅga), accompanied by the deities of the side-panels.
Alternatively, Gaṇeśa may be the principal deity, along with the gods and their retinues.
The goddesses, who are dear to Brahmā, should also be fashioned upon the northern projection (uttaraṅga).
According to the measurement of the root-ear (mūlakarṇa), the Udumbara [projection] should be made equal to the pitcher (kumbha).
Five jewels should be placed within the lower layer.
In the middle of the third part from the door, the *mandārikā* is considered to be situated;
it is shaped like a half-moon and joined with lotus stalks and leaves.
Below the lotus stalks is the *jāḍyakuṃbha*, followed by the *kaṇālī* and the *kaṇapīṭhaka*.
On both sides of the lotus stalk, at the mouth of the two corners, there should be *koṇikās*.
On the side of the *udumbara* [pedestal], there should be *tilas* in the form of branches. The auspicious height of the *udumbara* should be made one-quarter less than that of the *kumbha*. ||92-93||
The height of the half-moon is always equal to the *khuraka* (pedestal).
Its projection outward should be equal to the width of the door, or half of that.
In the half-moon design, there are two parts; within those, at the half-and-half portion, are the *gaga* and *araka* elements.
On both sides, two beautiful and well-formed [deities] should be fashioned.
Between the moon and the sun, a conch shell adorned with a campaka creeper should be placed;
on the moon as well, a lotus should be made, for that indeed bestows prosperity when it is beautifully adorned.
"O Rādhikā! Thus has everything regarding your inner passion been revealed, which Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke concerning the temple.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Dome, the Pitcher, the *Chajju*, the Nasā-Maṇḍapa, the Door, the *Udumbara*, and so forth, in the form of a Palace," in the second section (Tretā-Santāna) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 137 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 138 [[Author: Chapter 139 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall tell you what the beginningless Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, spoke to His devotee Devāyatanaka. 1.

An auspicious pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed according to the dimensions of the temple (prāsāda). The central axis (kolikī) is established by the cord reaching from the corner of the temple's base; likewise, the courtyard (catuṣkī), the pavilion, and the spire (śikhara) should be fashioned accordingly.
Whether hidden or open, having one door or three doors,
a pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be well-constructed at the front of the temple in the deity’s abode.
To the north, south, or east of the pavilion, there should be four small chambers (rūpacatuṣkikā).
A dance pavilion (nṛtyamaṇḍapa) should be constructed, and porticos (balāṇaka) should also be made;
it is considered beautiful when its length is one and a half parts greater than that of the temple (prāsāda).
It should be provided with a quadrangular courtyard (catuṣkikā) and be twice as large, thus very grand.
Above the pavilion, a dome (ghūmmaṭa) should be constructed, possessing a long and extensive measurement;
it should be rich in height and shaped like a half-globe.
The pavilion is best when its dimensions are divided into eight parts and is enclosed by walls.
It is enriched with staircases and archways, with water-spouts shaped like the mouths of sea-monsters (makara),

and with windows provided with lattices or, according to some authorities, without lattices. In the main temple, there are the plinth (jaṅghā), the girdle-moldings (mekhalā), the pedestal (pīṭha), and so forth.
They should be constructed in such a way that they fall along a single thread within the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
The projections of the petals are considered to be half, or one-quarter, of the size of the petals.
Having divided the pavilion into nine parts, four of those parts [are used for the construction]. 2.138.10.

The central hall should be understood as the essential form, and the *pada* (architectural module) must indeed be constructed. The stage (*raṅgabhūmi*) is variegated and beautiful, consisting of *pada*s.
A pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) provided with sixty-four pillars is always dear to me.
Twenty-one steps should be constructed in front of the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
richly adorned with jewels and featuring the forms of elephants, horses, and Garuḍas.
On both sides, beautiful four-sided platforms (catuṣkikā) should be made, with appropriate width.
Nine beautiful quadrangular pavilions should be constructed on all sides;
they should be auspicious, enriched with the splendor of many canopies and endowed with variegated beauty.
Indeed, this pavilion named Ākṣarabrahma is very dear to me.
A pair of pillars should be constructed, never a single one at any time.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be understood as being shaped like a kādamba flower, or like a lotus, or having the form of the sun's face, or lunar, or even resembling a rainbow. || 16 ||
The *jagatī* and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) are considered to have projections according to the measure of the *bhadra*.
The *jagatī* of the gateway (*pratolī*) is also considered to have projections like those of the *bhadra*.
In front [of the shrine], the *pratihāra* (side-chambers) should be constructed on both sides of the principal image.
From the top of the *narapiṭha* up to the summit of the *bharaṇī*,
ten and a half *padas* should be made; beyond that,
one part is considered the *rājasena* and two parts the *vedikā*.
The pillar has four parts, with its capital (paṭa) nearly half a part;
the neck-ring (bharaṇa) is half a part, and the sacrificial vessel (caru) is likewise one part.
The fillet (pāṭa) is one and a half parts, and after that comes the covering (chādyaka).
Likewise, the archways and other beautiful structures should be fashioned from wood;
to the east of the colored pavilion, pavilions for dancing should be constructed,
as well as pavilions for storytelling and pavilions for the fire oblation (homa).
For the concluding ceremony (udyāpana), pavilions and dance-halls (rāsamaṇḍapas) should be constructed.
Indeed, neither the ritual piercing of the site (vāstuvedha) nor the piercing for the pillars (staṃbhavedha) need be performed.
The thickness of the pillars should range from one-tenth to fourteen times the [length of the] base.
It depends on the thickness of the palace and follows the solidity of the stone.
(24) In a palace of one cubit [in width], the pillar should be four finger-breadths;
in a two-cubit [palace], seven finger-breadths; and in a three-cubit [palace], nine finger-breadths. (25)
Then, from twelve cubits, there is an increase of two finger-breadths for every cubit up to sixteen cubits; and beyond that,
there is an increase of finger-breadths until reaching the limit of forty cubits.
Up to fifty cubits in length, the pillars should be increased by three-quarters of an angula [per cubit].
The pillars should have a svastika at the top and be eight-sided with auspicious features (bhadra).
They should be enriched with figures, leaves, and beautiful creepers, and likewise, the base-pedestals (kumbhikā) should be endowed with auspicious features.
In the supporting structure, there should be rafters joined with creepers and accompanied by *kinnaras*.
My excellent palace must indeed be constructed with seven peaks. A *kolikā* should be understood at its front, and in front of that, a concealed pavilion (*gūḍhamaṇḍapa*).
Then there was the dance pavilion, and beyond that the pavilion known as the assembly hall;
then indeed the Rūpacokī, and then the staircases.
There were fifty-six pillars on the right side and fifty-six on the left.
Temples for my wives must be constructed everywhere;
I shall occupy the central temple, and my six wives shall be on the sides.
In the pavilions and the domed chambers, there shall be seven floors each.
The [shrines] should be made very beautiful, provided with a *rāsa* circle, archways, altars, and so forth.
To the west is the chariot-hall; to the south, the monastic quarters and storehouses;
to the north, the kitchen; and to the east, the armory.
In the northwest (vāyu) is the storehouse, and in the southeast (agnikoṇa) is the kitchen. In the northeast (īśāna) is the flower hall, and in the southwest (nairṛtya) is the utensils room.
In the west is the water hall, and above is the recitation hall.
The residential quarters should also be constructed in dependence upon the temples on all sides. (36) In the third part of the height of the door, two parts should be occupied by lattices;
likewise, windows should be made, either short or full-height. (37)
Above the pavilion (maṇḍapa) there is an octagon, and above that a sixteen-sided figure.
Above that is the dome (ghūmmaṭa), which is spherical; its height is half the measurement of its length.
Having divided the total height into sixty parts, [the measurements] are assigned to those initial sections.
The *karṇadardarikās* should have an equal height and projection in seven parts;
the *rūpakaṇṭha* is considered to be in four parts with a projection in two parts. Sixteen *vidyādharas* should be made, measuring twenty-four cubits [in total]. (2.138.40)
The projection is considered to be one-seventh [of the width] due to the broadness of the *vidyādhara*s.
Above that are the *citrarūpa* figures, the female dancers (*nartikā*s), and those dancing with musical instruments (*rāsanartana*).
Of these, the first occupy six and a half parts, while the second occupy six parts.

From that, the *kolās* (crossbeams) shall be five parts, and the central dome (*madhyagola*) shall be four and a half *gavālakas*. It is adorned with figures performing music, song, dance, and so forth, which possess the splendor of wonderful tales. ||42-43||
Adorned with various depictions of the world of living beings, the world of the lords, the world of Brahmā, and so forth,
and featuring canopies the color of the sun set within a bed of jewels—
the first sixth part should be fashioned with these ornaments.

Those same [images] from the second onwards should be made with increments of one-fourth [of the previous size], up to twenty-five, each adorned with ornaments in due order. In the first [image], five bells should be fashioned that are exceedingly beautiful.
From the second [section] onwards, they should be made with an increase of four [units] each in the subsequent sections.
On the left and right, in the Bhadrārdha and Rakṣārdha, there is a nine-bell [structure].
The length of the chariot-pavilion (rathikā) is half [a unit], and above that chariot-pavilion, it occupies one part.
Bells and pinnacles should be fashioned; from that, indeed, the pinnacle-vase (kalaśa) arises.
The first small bell should be made, beautified by five vases.
In this manner, even according to a single count, beautiful bells should be placed in front.
At intervals of one, two, three, four, five, six, or seven steps,
a four-sided platform for the vehicle of the deity of the palace should be constructed;
it should be well-adorned, auspicious, and take the form of the vehicle’s station.
The divine form should be divided into nine parts from the feet to the crest;
alternatively, the height of the vehicle may extend to five, six, or seven parts.
Or else, it may extend to the eyes of the vehicle, and [the body] to the secret organ, the navel, and the breasts.
The two lines should be equal, and the height of the pedestal (vāhana) should likewise be equal;
alternatively, the pedestal should have lines equal to the foot, the waist, and the knee.
The pedestal of the Śiva-liṅga should have a height equal to the reservoir for water (jalādhārī).
The *sūryavāha* is considered by the Lord to be equal to the *skandharekhā*.
Around the main temple, there should be temples numbering according to the count of the *garbha*;
having established the *garbha*, one should then perform the work, but one must not cause a piercing of the navel.
The palaces of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, facing east and west,
are auspicious and always bringers of welfare when they face toward the city. However, if all three gods have their faces turned away from the city, they destroy it.
Gaṇeśa, Bhairava, Caṇḍī, Nakulīśa, the nine planets,
the Mothers, and Kubera are auspicious when facing south;
Hanumān alone faces southwest, and no other deity does.
The most excellent image is one-third the height of the interior of the temple;
that which is less by one-tenth is proclaimed as the middling;
and that which is less by one-fifth is the smallest, seated in the *svastika* posture. (59)
When the height of the door is divided into nine parts, leaving aside one part from the top,
the remaining eight parts are considered auspicious when the [pedestal] has a height of four parts;
likewise, the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is considered to be four parts in height.
Alternatively, among the thirty-two divisions of the height of the door itself,
having omitted the four above, in the twenty-eighth division is the lion-throne, and in each of the fourteenth [divisions] is the image.
The lion-throne is prescribed for the thirteenth [part], and the image for the fifteenth;
the lion-throne for the fifteenth, and the image for the thirteenth.
If the lion-throne is in the twelfth, then the image is in the sixteenth part.
In a temple of one cubit, the image shall be eleven finger-breadths;
it should be increased by ten finger-breadths up to four cubits.
It should be increased by two finger-breadths up to ten cubits.
It should be increased by half a finger up to a limit of fifty fingers.
The medium [size] should be reduced by one-tenth, and the smallest by one-tenth of that.
The sleeping form [of the deity] should occupy five out of seven parts within the inner sanctum.

Two parts should be avoided; [the remaining] two parts within the interior of the palace provide comfort for those lying down, excluding the portion of the doorway. In the remaining section, five parts should be made, each being half the size of a seat.
In the first section adjacent to the wall, the seats of the Yakṣas and others are located;
in the second section, indeed, are the seats of all the gods;
and in the third section, the seats of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are situated. (2.138.70)
In the northeast, at one-fifth [of the width], the seat of Śiva (śivāsana) is one barley-corn in measure.
For all temples, the division is considered to start from the womb-chamber (garbha).
Indeed, the seats of the deities are located sequentially from the central part of the womb-chamber.
One should fashion them as quadrangular, oblong, or oblong-circular, and likewise as circular or even octagonal, according to what is appropriate.
There should be exactly twenty-eight mandalas situated upon the walls.
Śiva is in the center; in the second maṇḍala, however, there is Viśvasṛj;
Nakulīśa is in the third, and Sāvitrī is considered to be in the fourth.
Rudramūrti is in the fifth, and Svāmī Kārtika is in the sixth.
Brahmā is in the seventh [mandala], while Vāsudeva is in the eighth;
Janārdana is in the ninth, and the Viśvadevas in the tenth;
Agni is in the eleventh, and likewise Bhāskara in the twelfth.
Durgā is honored in the thirteenth [chapter], and Vighneśa in the fourteenth;
the nine planets in the fifteenth, and the mother-deities in the sixteenth;
the Gaṇas also in the seventeenth, and Bhairava is held to be in the eighteenth.
In the nineteenth [year], the Kṣetrapālas; in the twentieth, the Yakṣarāja;
in the twenty-first, Hanumān; likewise, in the twenty-second, Bhaga;
in the twenty-third, the Aparadevas; and in the twenty-fourth, the Daityaka. ||78–79||
In the twenty-fifth [year] there is a Rākṣasa, in the twenty-sixth a Piśāca;
in the twenty-seventh the class of Bhūtas, and in the twenty-eighth it is empty (riktam).
They are served by their respective wives, servants, female slaves, family members, and dependents.
The deities should always be installed in their respective abodes as is appropriate.
[Their vehicles may be] an elephant-seat, a lion-seat, or likewise a swan-seat;
or a celestial chariot (vimāna) supported by liberated souls, or an exceedingly excellent one with a parasol.
Just as the Śaivaliṅga is, so too is the Yonikāsana.
The yoni should be made with eighteen parts according to its height:
the *kaṇa* (bud) should consist of one and a half parts, and the *paṭṭikā* (band) should be half a part.
The second fillet is equal [in measure], and the shoulder is known to be three parts;
another fillet is half a part, while the inner leaf is one and a half parts.
Another fillet is half a part, and the corner is two parts. (84–85)
Another band is half a part, while the leaf is one and a half parts;
another band is half a part, and the shoulder is three parts.
Furthermore, there are two bands, each measuring two and a half parts.
The *karṇaka* (ear-ornament) shall consist of one and a half parts; from that, the manifestation of the *liṅga* [is formed].
Whatever material the *liṅga* may be made of, the *yoni* (base) is considered to be of that same material.
It may be square, circular, provided with a girdle (*mekhalā*), or having many corners. || 87–88 ||
The thickness of the liṅga should be measured with a thread, for that constitutes its circumference.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be made as long as the thread and indeed wide as well.
The thread should be divided into three parts; it is considered that the yoni occupies two of those parts.
The wise should always understand that the height of the Śiva-liṅga is one part.
The outflow-channel (praṇāla) is considered to extend from the liṅga as measured by the same cord;
the length of the cord for both [the liṅga and the channel] is exactly two parts, and the yoni-liṅga is not greater than this.
The entry into the *liṅga* is desired from the top of either the incomplete or the complete [channel];
or indeed, the entry into the *liṅga* from above occurs from the completely full *koṣṭhala*.
And the conduit (*praṇāla*) on the north or left falls into the secret *caṇḍamukha*.
Among many deities, there should indeed be a water-channel on the ground in the four directions.
Six parts of the door-jamb should be made, specifically at the auspicious fifth [section].
The gaze of Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and others should always be directed toward this auspicious [spot].
In the third part of the form of Śiva, and likewise for the illustrious Śeṣaśāyin,
one should divide the door-jamb into eight parts; thus, by dividing [the whole] with those eights,
there will be exactly sixty-four parts in total.
The aspect of the deity is determined when there is a single [odd] portion, but not when there is a pair.
(96) The aspect of the deity is prescribed for a single one among the thirty-two portions;
even-numbered portions are strictly prohibited for the purpose of the deity’s aspect, as they cause loss. (97)
Through the ripening of the fault of [wrong] views, there is the destruction of one's position and the loss of wealth;
whatever is struck down by the fault of views does not grow again.
Through an upward gaze, there is the loss of possessions; through a downward gaze, there is the loss of enjoyments.
Equanimity (*samadṛṣṭi*) bestows happiness at all times, according to the circumstances.
Among the sixty-four divisions, the first pertains to the primordial principle (*āditattva*);
creation (*sṛṣṭi*) is in the third, and the principle of sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is in the fifth and the seventh. (2.138.100)
Longevity is considered to reach one hundred thousand years in the ninth and likewise in the eleventh [year];
in the thirteenth, one is wise, and in the fifteenth, one is considered learned.
In the seventeenth, the principle of peace (śāntitattva) is attained, and in the nineteenth, the unmanifest (avyakta).
The Manifest and the Unmanifest are in the twenty-first [ring], while the Manifest alone is in the twenty-third.
Śeṣanāga is in the twenty-fifth, Hari lies in the twenty-seventh,
Garuḍa is in the twenty-ninth, and the Mothers are in the thirty-first.
In the thirty-third [chapter] is Kubera; in the thirty-fifth, Varāhaka;
in the thirty-seventh, Umā and Rudra; in the thirty-ninth, Buddhaka;
in the forty-first, Aja; and then in the forty-third.
Durvāsas, Nārada, and Agastya—these three are other great sages (maharṣis).
In the forty-fifth [section] are Śrī, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and others;
and in the forty-seventh is Dhātṛ, followed by the deities.
In the forty-ninth [digit], Śāradā and Gaṇeśa;
in the fifty-first digit, Brahmā seated upon a lotus throne;
in the fifty-third, Siddhi and likewise Harasiddhi and others.
In the fifty-fifth [incarnation], Viṣṇu was born as Aja; in the fifty-seventh, he was Sūrya, free from passion.
In the fifty-ninth, Śukrācārya appeared, as did others;
and in the fifty-ninth, Caṇḍikā and other goddesses appeared. (108–109)
In the sixty-first [digit], the deities Bhairava and others are proclaimed;
in the sixty-third, the Vetālakas and others; beyond that, however, is indeed the void.
The gaze of the vehicle should be directed toward the feet or the waist of the image.

Thus, O Rādhikā, by establishing oneself in these states, the four goals of human life are attained; conversely, if one acts otherwise, the opposite result will surely follow. Kṣayakṛt spoke to the sage Devāyatanaka regarding Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurement of the Temple, the Pavilion, the Dhūmaṭa, the Throne, and the Deities therein, along with their respective parts," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
