That which begins with the *śikhara* has been described; now I shall explain it in brief.
(1) Now, I shall describe in summary the auspicious *prāsāda-śikhara*, along with its various divisions and its manifold types of artistic construction. (2)
It has many peaks, many smoke-houses, and many projections;
it possesses many auspicious windows and is indeed manifold in form and eternal.
It has many altars, many pedestals, and is covered with many creepers and leaves.
That householder’s [temple] has many lines, many paintings, and many corners (4).
It may have seven stories or a hundred stories, a pinnacle, many sons,
a moon-chamber at the top, many finials, and be of the forest-dweller type (5).
The single-pronged [type] is dedicated, while the hornless one belongs to the virtuous caste;
likewise, the long-globular and the globular types may have limbs according to one's desire.
In its width, it is four parts, and in its length, five parts.
Above, there is a triple-vase (trikalaśa) joined with lions and a hanging globe (lambagolaka).
On the right and left sides of the hanging globe, each is one and a half units in width.
The emergence from the forehead constitutes the eight-fold auspicious (aṣṭabhadraka) hanging globe.
A single egg-shaped dome (ekāṇḍa) forms the pinnacle, while the rows of egg-shaped elements (śreṇyaṇḍakāni) are placed at the corners;
beginning from a fourth part and increasing by twelve up to one hundred and twelve,
having displayed the various levels (talānāṃ), these indeed become the pinnacles (śikharāṇi).
Indeed, above even a single floor there may be many pinnacles.
A blow [of the chisel] should be made upon the covering (chādyam) for a pinnacle; that which is higher than that is a crest (śṛṅgam).
Pinnacles numbering one, two, or three are indeed formed by means of a single line alone.
A line forming a peak within the interior of the womb is not at all praised;
however, one that is broad and expansive on the exterior bestows all happiness.
Indeed, the verticality of the peak-line is determined in relation to its length.
It should be accepted as being one and a quarter or one and a half [units] in height, but never less;
a bell should be placed upon the top of the horns and the shoulder, which is auspicious and bestows fruit.
Furthermore, one should provide a portion for the handle, and there, the horns should be fashioned again.
The beautiful images are considered to be joined with musical instruments at the base of the *śṛṅga*;
likewise, the *śṛṅgikās* are beautiful on the sides and above the *śṛṅga*.
Nine large *śṛṅgas* should be fashioned in a straight line.
From the base of the first *uruśṛṅga* up to the limit of the shoulder (*skandha*) of the subsequent *uru*,
thirteen parts should be made; having formed the first *uruśṛṅga* with seven parts, one should then diminish the second *uruśṛṅga*.
Thus, indeed, nine parts should be made from the base of the *mṛdya* upwards. Having divided the base of the line into ten parts, the upper portion shall consist of six parts.
The beautiful *skandha* (shoulder) should be fashioned; it must not have more than [six] parts, for [more] is defective.
If it is not less than five parts and is well-proportioned, it does not bring misfortune.
If the flagstaff enters the root or the trunk, it causes the destruction of the master.
Furthermore, for every elephant, the base of the flagstaff should extend outward by one finger-breadth.
A window is recommended at the first peak, and a *māḍha* (pavilion) at the second;
up to the third summit, the placement of lions is considered auspicious.
Up to the fourth summit, it is called the "parrot-lion" (*śukasiṃha*).
Alternatively, there may be nine such divine forms beginning with the others;

the deities should be placed in the windows, while Śuka and Hari are to be installed at the front in the three [sections] of the Bhadra. By this, all happiness arising from the spire shall be attained.
From the *chādyā* up to the end of the *skandha*, there are indeed twenty-one parts.
Between the ninth and the thirteenth [parts], the *siṃhas* and the *śukanāsas* are located.
There, the *śukanāsas* should be made fivefold; they are considered auspicious.
From nine to nineteen cubits in length according to the measuring line, one should construct pillars for the pavilion in accordance with the central sanctum.
The bell should be made equal to the *śukanāsa* (the gable-end) or otherwise slightly lower. ॥25-26॥
One should indeed provide as many *eraṇḍa* plants as there are horns, humps, horns, and minor limbs.
On the ears and the nine corners, one should place a *tilaka*, the ornament of the white palace.
Water-channels should be made between the parts according to their number; these bring about auspiciousness.

Alternatively, from the base stone to the pinnacle, twenty parts should be made for the total height; among these, the *maṇḍovara* (dome) is best when it occupies eight parts, middling when it occupies two and a half [parts] plus eight [parts], and smallest when it occupies nine [parts]. (28–29)
The emergence of the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be directly above the maṇḍovara.
In a temple, the emergence of the spire (śṛṅga) is always considered to occur at the second, third, or fourth part, or at one-quarter, one-half, or one-third of the ten divisions.
Having divided the peak and the base into ten parts each,

one should then [arrange] two parts for each of the two ears, and one and a half parts for each of the six pillars. Furthermore, the *bhadraka* should be made as three parts, even at the top of the binding.
The nine divisions (navāṃśas) should be fashioned such that there are two parts each with two corners;
the two side-arms (paḍharau) are each one and a half parts, and the central auspicious portion (bhadraka) is then two parts.
From the corner, the pinnacle (śikhara) is one and a quarter parts, or alternatively, the pinnacle is one and a half parts.
Between the two ears, there should be twenty-five lines.
At the rising [of the breath], between the two ears, there are also twenty-five lines.
From eight to sixty-eight, there are sixteen lines.
In the upward direction and in the state of the five expanses (āyatana), there are five; thus, there are twenty-five.
An increase by one part (aṃśa) constitutes a digit (kalā); by that [method], the divisions are likewise formed.
Starting from eight and ending at sixty-eight, there are sixteen [divisions] through an increase of four.
Eight, twelve, sixteen, and twenty [lines] are likewise drawn upwards and downwards;
or alternatively, eighteen upwards and sixteen downwards.
Thus, there are indeed two hundred and fifty-six lines.
From the three sections, there is an increase of sections up to eighteen;
each one has eight parts, and by that, there are sixteen equal divisions.
The first [section] consists of twenty-four, and the second consists of twenty-seven.
The third [measurement] is thirty parts, and there too, sixteen;
having fixed a cord fourfold from the line like the interior of a lotus bud, the height of the dome (golā) should be made with a length equal to the pinnacle plus one-quarter. 2.139.40–41.
The five parts shall be six, seven, eight, twelve, and sixteen;
now, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed describe the *dhvajapuruṣa* (the banner-man),
starting from the line of the pinnacle up to the height of the binding.
Having divided [the structure] into six parts, one should set aside four parts in the sixth division;
leaving aside the upper portion, the support for the banner (dhvajādhāra) should be constructed using the remaining three parts on the right side of the *pratiratha*.
Alternatively, starting from the line, having made two parts (aṃśa) up to the end of the shoulder of the pinnacle,
one should divide the upper part into three portions;
half of that [portion] should be made as the support for the beam (vaṃśādhāra), and on its left side, the banner (dhvaja) should be placed upon the hand.
The flagstaff should be offered, and it should indeed be offered on the right side.
On the right side of the back of the temple, on a pedestal,
the support for the flag should be constructed in the southwest of the one facing east.
In the north-eastern direction, the flag-bearer of the western-facing temple should be placed at the shoulder-level of the temple,
midway between two rows of pillars.
Like the row of pillars, the *āmalasāraka* (dome) should be constructed as circular.
Its beautiful height should be made half of its width.
Of that height, there should be four parts; among them, the neck above should be three-quarters of a part, and the amalasaraka [capital] should be one and a quarter parts. (2.139.50)
The moonlight-pattern (candrikā) occupies one part, and the jhāṃjharī-pattern likewise occupies one part.
Thereafter, I shall describe the measurement of the pitcher (kalaśa) in brief:
there are seven parts for the lotus-bud (padmakośa), and its neck (grīvā) consists of one part.
The *āmalasāra* is proclaimed to have a height of one and a half [units].

Then there is the five-petaled [lotus] measuring three-quarters [of that], and from that, the *jhāṃjharī* measuring three-quarters. The auspicious *kalaśa* has a height of three parts and an extension of two parts.
The pinnacle (kalaśa) is one-eighth of the length of the temple's spire (prāsādakarṇa).
When increased by one-sixteenth part of its width (vyāsa), that pitcher (ghaṭa) is considered the best;
when increased by one-thirty-second part, it is indeed considered the middling.
Alternatively, the height of the pitcher (kalaśa) should be made beautiful, measuring one-fifth of the diameter of the base-line;
or else, it should be one-fourth of the height of the *amalasāraka*.
The length of one part is proclaimed to be that of the *kalaśa* (vessel).
From there, a fourth part should be increased by half; thus it possesses height.
The height is nine parts, and likewise, its thickness is six parts.
By the measurement of the standard sūtra, the pitcher (kalaśa) grants all desires.
(58) The neck and the pedestal occupy one part each, while the egg-shaped dome (aṇḍaka) likewise occupies three parts.
The two ear-ornaments (karṇikā) each occupy one part, and the ḍoḍala occupies three parts. (59)
The tip of the ḍoḍala shall be one part, the thickness at its base two parts,
the karṇikā three parts, and the chajjī four parts;
the neck shall be two parts, and likewise the half-pedestal (ardhapīṭhaka) two parts.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is one part, and the dome (cāṇḍa) is four parts, with its height being six parts.
Indeed, the golden pinnacle (dhvaja) is the best among all excellent things.
The amalasaraka (the pinnacle finial) of the temple is proclaimed to be the abode of the life-force (jīva).
In that case, the person within the temple is considered to be the deity;
that person should be installed as the inner self endowed with consciousness.
And in a temple of one cubit, the person is half a finger-breadth in size.

Up to the limit of fifty elephants, one should increase the size by half for each subsequent one. His bed is indeed made of silver; there is a lotus in his right hand, and in his left a banner with three pennants, held as if against his chest.
Just as the portion of the flag and banner is situated upon the shoulder [of the pole],
so too should a vessel of ghee made of copper or gold be placed within the *āmalasāraka*,
as well as the golden *prāsādapuruṣa*.
And he should be depicted as reclining on a silver couch; this is considered auspicious.
On each of the four legs of the couch, there should be four jars, adorned with gold and gems, and beautified by the signs of treasures. (67–68)
Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, and Makara are the names [of the four types].
Listen as I describe the measurement of the flagstaff:
it should be exactly as long as the temple extends from its corner.
The flagstaff should be made long according to the superior measurement;
the medium one is reduced by one-tenth, and the smallest is reduced by one-fifth.
Alternatively, it may extend from the top of the base (jagatī) up to the top of the dome (ghaṭa).
The height [of the staff] is divided into three parts; among these, one part constitutes the long handle.
The superior [staff] should be so, while the middle one is considered to be reduced by one-eighth.
The inferior one is declared to be reduced by one-sixth in every respect.
Alternatively, that which measures one line (rekhā) is called the smallest;
then, by an increase of one-twelfth [of a line], it becomes the medium;
and by an increase of one-sixth [of a line], that staff (daṇḍaka) indeed becomes the best. ||73-74||
The boundary for the corners of the temple is considered to be seven cubits;
the boundary for the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be twenty-five cubits;
and the boundary for the measurement of the lines (rekhā) is considered to be fifty cubits.
The length of the flagstaff shall also be according to those respective proportions.
In a temple of one cubit [in height], the staff shall be four and a quarter fingers wide;
from that point on, for each subsequent elephant [unit], one should maintain a width of half a finger.
A measurement up to fifty *gaja* in thickness is considered auspicious.
It should be made of bamboo, *añjana*, *mādhuka*, *śaiṃśapeya*, or *khadira* wood;
it must be circular and provided with a series of steps.
It should have a single joint and be provided with two knots.
The *markaṭī* and *pāṭalī* [rope] should be as long as one-sixth of the length of the staff.
It should be wide by half of its length and thick by one-third of its width. (2.139.79–80)
It is equipped with small bells (*kiṅkiṇī*) and *ghaṇṭikā* ornaments, and beautifully adorned with *kāṅgarī* motifs.
The height of the pinnacle (*kalaśa*) is five parts of the length of the *markaṭī*.
Below the *markaṭī*, it has the appearance of a crescent moon, with *gagāraka* ornaments on both sides.
The water-pot (kalaśa) adorned with the tips of *kuśa* grass should be placed directly upon the staff.
A banner (*patākā*) should hang from the staff, its length being one-eighth of that [staff],
or else beautifully adorned with three or five cloth bands of various forms.
On the right shoulder [of the temple], at Paṇḍharāya, the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) should be situated.
On the right rear part of the temple, at Paṇḍhara, it is auspicious;
the kalaśa, which serves as the support for the flagstaff, is considered beautiful.
The length of the *kalāba* (the neck) should be made according to the measure of one-sixth [of the width];

the height of the *kalāba* is considered auspicious when it is equal to the height of the bell (*ghaṇṭā*). Furthermore, it should correspond to as many cubits as there are in the width of the temple (*prāsāda*). || 85-86 ||
The width of the pit for the staff should be equal to its length in finger-breadths.
In a temple with four faces, the installation of the staff is in the northeast;
one should examine the *pāṭalikā* slightly to the northeast of the staff.
From that, there shall arise the prosperity of the kingdom, the advancement of one’s status, and the happiness of the subjects.
(88) In a great mansion devoid of a banner, Rākṣasas desire to dwell;
however, by the gift of a banner, the deities as well as the ancestors are satisfied. (89)
The merit of ten horse-sacrifices shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage.
In the restoration of what is dilapidated, one should not discard the original structural layout;
rather, the building should be constructed with superior materials in accordance with the previous ones.
In an auspicious conjunction occurring at dawn or other such times, one should carry out the restoration of a dilapidated temple.
The restoration may be performed using gold, silver, ivory, or the tusks of elephants.
One should not entrust the work of restoring a temple to a deity other than the one for whom it was originally built. (9.1–9.2)
Shaking a deity that has been consecrated causes the destruction of merit;
however, this does not apply to householders, virtuous ascetics (*yatis*), or celibate students (*brahmacārins*).
The raising of an image is considered permissible during a *cara* lagna by means of a fee (*lañca*).
The price for an elephant or a horse is one silver coin or a diamond.
The door-panels must be aligned with a level line; one should not allow the rows to be broken.
All stone foundations and other structural bases are approved when they are aligned with a level line.
"Beautiful side-streets and large gate-towers (gopuras) should be constructed;
likewise, a pillar of fame (kīrtistambha) and such things as water-lifting machines (vedhayantra) should be made.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Nārāyaṇa spoke to his own devotee.
And he spoke that very thing to Lakṣmī, who was devoted to the temple of the God.

(97) Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Detailed Description of the Specific Features such as the Spire, the Lotus-Bud, the Finial, and the Banner in the Form of the Temple," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 139. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 140 [Author:
Chapter 141 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Listen, O Rādhikā! Hari spoke to Devāyatana concerning the temple, its divisions, and its golden domes (*cāṇḍa*) which were as beautiful as those on Mount Meru. (1) Within the temples, there were indeed hundreds of golden domes.
Indeed, even thousands minus one exist within the divine palace (prāsāda).
Meru is considered the king of palaces, the refuge of all the gods;
that palace is celebrated as being called both the Imperishable (akṣara) and Goloka.
Vaikuṇṭha, the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta), the Immortal (Amṛta), and Hiraṇmaya; Vāhneya, Vairāja, Bhūman, and Vaiṣṇava;
Kailāsa, Vaiśāla, Śvetadvīpa, and Mandara.
The one named Sarvatobhadra, Śrīvatsa, and likewise Svastika;
Haima, Haṃsa, Gāruḍa, Gaja, and Vṛṣabha;
as well as Mandira, known as Brāhma—these are the twenty-five types.
The king of mountains, Meru, is proclaimed to be circular with infinite peaks;
it has a thousand corners, is imperishable, and is crowded with infinite abodes.
Goloka is held to be enriched with nine hundred and ninety-two pillars.
In every respect, that which is rich in peaks is proclaimed as Vaikuṇṭha;
in every respect, that which is rich in smoke is proclaimed as the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta);
and in every respect, that which is rich in mere houses is proclaimed as Amṛta.
In every respect, Karmānikāḍhya is proclaimed to be golden;
in every respect, Vāhneya is proclaimed to be the support of the quarters.
In every respect, Vairāja is proclaimed to be rich in the splendor of elephants.
In every respect, a palace abounding in the splendor of horses and other [attendants] is celebrated as a *bhūma-saudha*.
One filled with female servants and messengers of Viṣṇu is called *vaiṣṇava*.
However, one entirely pervaded by the *gaṇas* is celebrated as *kailāsa*. || 11-12 ||
Vaiśālī is indeed proclaimed to be entirely pervaded by sages; the region called Śvetadvīpa is said to be entirely pervaded by ascetics.
It is four-cornered, auspicious in every respect, and marked with the Śrīvatsa like a diagram of fortune.
The *svastika* is equal to the *svasti*, while the *haimaka* consists of many sections. The *hāṃsaka* contains many swans, and the *gāruḍa* is enriched with eagles.
That which has five parts is called the "elephant," and that which has four parts is named the "bull."

The Śatapāda and the Mandira, as well as the Daśapāda and the Brāhmaka—these are indeed the primary [types], distinguished by various subdivisions of their limbs. They are further differentiated by variations in craftsmanship, variations in form, and variations in appearance. (16)

According to one's intelligence, according to one's power, according to the light [of the site], and according to one's pleasure (17). Indeed, palatial mansions (*vaimānika-prāsāda*) arise in many ways, produced by the intellect of artisans and free from human effort (18).
As many as there are embodied beings, so many shall be such dwellings;
moreover, other palaces of manifold forms will also come into being.
It has eight floor-sections, five *aṇḍas*, and it is the *kesarī*.
The *sarvatobhadra* has nine eggs (*aṇḍa*), for it consists of eight *talatila* [cells].
The palace named *nandana*, however, is joined with thirteen eggs;
the *nandiśālika* mansion is recorded as having seventeen eggs.
There, ten *talabhāga*s constitute four *tilaka*s;
ten *talabhāga*s and twenty-one *kāṇḍa*s constitute the *nandiśa*;
and twelve *talabhāga*s constitute twenty-five *kāṇḍa*s.

Adorned with eight *tilakas*, it is called the Mandira type. (23) Having fourteen sections for the stories and nineteen divisions (*kāṇḍa*), and possessing twenty-four *tilakas*, it is called the Śrīvatsa type. (24)
The *Amṛtodbhava* is said to have fourteen parts for its floor-levels, thirty-three auspicious *śubhāṇḍakas*, and sixteen excellent *tilakas*.
[25] It has fourteen parts for its floor-levels and thirty-seven auspicious *śubhāṇḍakas*.
And Himavat is proclaimed as being twelve *tilakas* high; likewise, Hemakūṭa is said to have fourteen terrace-sections, eight *tilakas*,
and forty-one *daṇḍas*.
The sixteen square units (tala-bhāga) and the four tilakas constitute the forty-five-cubit Kailāsa; it is thus celebrated.
The forty-nine cubits and sixteen square units [constitute the next].
That temple is celebrated by the name Pṛthvīvijaya. Furthermore, there is the Indranīlaka temple, which has sixteen parts for the floor, eight tilakas, and fifty-three daṇḍakas. (2.140.30)
With sixteen parts of a *tala* and likewise eight *tilakas*,
and with fifty-seven *daṇḍas*, it is called Mahānīla.
With sixteen parts of a *tala* and sixty-one *daṇḍas*, it is Bhūdhara.

With eighteen parts for the floor-levels (*talabhāga*) and sixty-five *aṇḍakas*, as well as forty-four *tilas*, that is called the Ratnakūṭa. With eighteen parts for the floor-levels and likewise forty *tilas*... [33]
The great and auspicious [pillar] called Vaidūrya is said to have sixty-nine eggs (aṇḍakas),
eighteen floor-sections, and to be endowed with thirty-six tilakas.
The great and auspicious Padmarāga is said to have seventy-three eggs.
The Vajraka temple has eighteen floor-sections, thirty-two *tilakas*, and seventy-seven *aṇḍakas*.
[Its dimensions are] eighteen floor-sections and twenty-eight *sattilas*. (35–36)
That which consists of eighty-one segments is called the *mukuṭojjvala* (radiant crown);
it has eighteen *tila*-parts and twenty-four *sattila*-parts.
This one consisting of eighty-five segments is called the *airāvata*.
With twenty-two floor-divisions and four *tilakas*, it is declared to have eighty-nine *aṇḍakas* and is named Rājahaṃsa.
Likewise, with twenty-two floor-divisions and eight *tilakas*, [it is another]. 38–39.
The auspicious one named Garuḍa is said to consist of ninety-three *aṇḍakas*;
it has twenty-two divisions of floors and four *tilakas*.
Furthermore, this Vṛṣabha is declared to consist of ninety-seven *aṇḍakas*.

With twenty-two parts of a *tila* and one hundred *aṇḍakas*, this Meru palace is described; for it is the abode of all splendor. Furthermore, the square-based structure with one *aṇḍaka* is named *tilaka*. 42.
The Gaurī-tilaka temple is octagonal with eight sections and possesses one egg-shaped dome;
its base consists of eight parts and it has four tilakas and a single egg.
The Rudra-tilaka temple is to be understood as the most excellent, bringing happiness.
With eight base-sections, four *tilakas*, and five *aṇḍakas*, that temple known as the *Śrītilaka* is also auspicious. It likewise possesses eight base-sections and four *tilakas*. (44–45)
The spire known as Haritilaka is indeed considered to consist of nine eggs (aṇḍas);
that same [spire], when consisting of thirteen eggs, is called Lakṣmītilaka.
Likewise, it has a base of ten parts and is supported by twelve tilakas.
That which has twenty-nine *aṇḍakas* is called the *bhūtilaka*.
That same [structure] with thirty-three *aṇḍakas* is known as the *raṃbhātilaka*.
The *tala* consists of twenty-four *tilakas* and twelve divisions (*bhāgas*).
The Mandiratilaka is considered to have thirty-seven bays (daṇḍas) and twelve sections of floors, with twenty tilakas.
The Hemavat-tilaka is considered to have forty-five bays.
The Kailāsa-tilaka is considered to have twenty-four tilakas and twelve parts for its base;
it possesses forty-nine daṇḍas and is endowed with twenty tilakas, with twelve parts for its base. (2.140.50–51)
The one known as Pṛthivītilaka is considered to have fifty-seven pillars;
Tilaka has thirty-six, and Talabhāgaka has twenty-eight.
That which is called Tribhuvana is said to have sixty-five pillars.
That same [structure] with sixty-nine eggs and consisting of sapphire and sesame seeds (53),
having twenty-eight tilakas and thirty-two talabhāgas,
is declared to have seventy-three eggs and is considered the Sarvāṅgatilaka. (54)
The temple named Suravallabha has twenty-four *tilakas*, thirty-two parts for the floor, seventy-seven *aṇḍakas*,
twenty-five *aṇḍakas* [for the spire], eight parts for the floor, and four *tilas*.
This auspicious *siṃhatilaka* has been designed by artisans.
[56] The *makaradhvaja* is considered a beautiful ornament, consisting of twelve *tilakas*, seventy-seven *aṇḍas*, and ten *talas*. [57]
Adorned with one hundred and forty-five eggs,
with a floor consisting of ten parts and eight *tilas*, it is named Maṅgala.
[58] It consists of one hundred and seventeen eggs and is composed of four *tilas*.
That which consists of ten parts of the base is indeed called *tilakākṣa*.
That same [structure], with forty-nine *daṇḍas*, is named *padmatila*. [The structure] consisting of one hundred and sixty-five *daṇḍas* has twelve parts of the base. (2.140.60)
The *Somatilaka* is said to have twenty-four *tilakas* and one hundred and eighty-nine *aṇḍakas*,
with twelve stories (*talas*).
The auspicious one known as *Vijaya* is considered to have twenty *tilakas*.
The auspicious [temple] consists of four hundred and twenty-five *aṇḍakas*.
On the base, there are twelve *tilakas* in the twenty-fourth [section], and the three worlds (*tralokanam*) consist of thirty-two *talabhāgas* and four *tilakas*.
The temple named Ṛṣabha consists of three hundred and thirty-seven eggs (aṇḍakas);
it possesses two hundred and sixty-nine eggs,
and its twelve floor-sections are called the Ajita-prāsāda.

The temple named Svayaṃbhū is said to bestow happiness; it consists of one hundred and thirteen *aṇḍakas* and eighteen *sattalas*. [65] The temple of auspicious form consists of one hundred and seventy-seven *aṇḍakas*. [66]
The portion consisting of eighteen stories is named Abhinandana;
the portion of fourteen stories consists of fifty-seven *daṇḍakas*.
That indeed should be known as Sumati, the bestower of all peace.
It has twenty storey-sections and two hundred and nine cubits;
that temple is known by the name Padmavallabha. It also has ten storey-sections and fifty-seven cubits.
This temple is celebrated as Supārśvavallabha;
it should have two hundred and twenty-nine eggs (aṇḍakas).
The temple named Śītala has thirty-two parts for its stories (talas).

Possessing twenty-four *tila* divisions and endowed with twelve *tilakas*, it has forty-nine *daṇḍas*; that is called a portion (*aṃśaka*) of Śrī. It possesses twenty-four *tilas* and contains twenty-four *sattilas*. (71–72)
That which has thirty-three sections is called Śītalā;
it consists of eighteen parts for the floors and is endowed with twelve *tilakas*.
This one, having seventeen sections, is called by the name of its own family.
The Vasupūjya [kalpa] consists of two hundred and fifty-seven *daṇḍas*, possesses twenty-two *talabhāgas*, and is endowed with sixteen *tilakas*.
It comprises twenty-four *talabhāgas* and seventy-seven *kāṇḍakas*. (74–75)
This temple, named Vimala, possesses auspicious characteristics;
it consists of twenty stories and measures fifty-three hundred and four [units].
That temple which has such eggs (aṇḍas) is called Anantamāyā.

Consisting of twenty-eight storeys and endowed with twelve *tilakas*, this is called the Dharma [egg], containing two hundred and twenty-five eggs. Likewise, it consists of twelve storeys and one hundred and eighty-nine [eggs]. (77–78)
This excellent temple named Śānta is considered to have eight sections on its ground floor and is endowed with twenty *tilakas*.
With sixty-nine *aṇḍas*, it is called Kanthādhara.

That palace named Kamalakanda, which has eight parts for the base and twenty-one domes (aṇḍakas), is beautiful. Likewise, that which has twelve parts for the base and eight tilakas [is also beautiful]. (2.140.80–81)

This [city] named Mahendra consists of one hundred and eighty-one eggs (*aṇḍa*) and has fourteen sections of floors (*talabhāga*), as well as eight *tilakas*. This one named Mānasatuṣṭi consists of eighty-five eggs.
It has twenty-six parts of the floor and is endowed with sixteen *tilas*.
Indeed, that one of excellent intellect [has] four hundred and seventy-three *aṇḍas*.
It has twenty-two parts of the floor and consists of forty *tilas*. (83–84)
This one named Nemi has one hundred and ninety-three eggs (*aṇḍaka*),
twenty-six talabhāgas, and eight *tilakas*.
That one called Pārśva indeed possesses one hundred and thirteen eggs.

That which has twenty-four parts for its base and two hundred and twenty-one eggs (aṇḍas) is to be known as the auspicious one named Vīra. It consists of a single unit, a single temple, is square, and possesses a single egg. (86–87)
There are those with three parts and three pavilions, as well as those with five parts and five;
likewise, there are those with seven parts and seven pavilions, and those with nine parts and nine.
Their forms are of various spire designs, produced through the creative ingenuity of artisans.
That which is square and consists of a single *aṇḍaka* is indeed called Vairāja.
That which has a floor of four parts and thirteen *aṇḍakas* is named Nandana; it is said that Śrīnandana consists of twenty-nine *aṇḍakas*. (2.140.89–90)
That which consists of six *tala*s and twenty-five *daṇḍa*s is called the Mandira; that which consists of twenty-nine *daṇḍa*s is said to be named Malaya;
and that which consists of thirty-three *daṇḍa*s is called the Vimāna.
The Viśālaka is thirty-seven daṇḍas and eight tilakas;
the Trailokyabhūṣaṇa is considered to be forty-one daṇḍas;
and the one of forty-five daṇḍas is equal to one-eighth of a *tala*.
That which is joined with four *tilakas* is considered to be named Mahendra;
indeed, through the increase of the *aṇḍas*, seven varieties of it arise.
[In this,] there are ten parts for the base and forty-one *aṇḍakas*.
"Endowed with sixteen *tilakas*, that is called a *mahīdhara*.
Furthermore, this [type] becomes manifold through the various divisions of *tilakas* and *kāṇḍas*.
Thus, O Rādhikā, he then explained those varieties of *śikharas* to him. (95–96)

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Temples Made of Meru-like Materials, Akṣara-like Materials, and Other Various Materials," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 140. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 141 [Author:
Chapter 142 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! I shall describe to you exactly as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has spoken it, the abode of the devotee, according to its true nature.
It consists of one thousand and one cosmic eggs and is endowed with seventy-two layers.
This very one, known as Jyeṣṭha-Meru, is considered the most excellent among all.
When the field is made square and divided into seventy-two parts,
the wall consists of four and a half parts, and the *abhrāntikā* (the space between the wall and the parapet) consists of three and a half parts.
Then, one should divide the square field into ten parts;

one part is to be made for the circumambulation path (*bhramaṇī*), and one part is considered for the wall (*bhitti*). A corner (*koṇa*) consists of two parts, and likewise, a *pratiratha* consists of one and a half parts.
This *bhadra* consists of three parts, equal in all directions.
(5) Then, one should again divide the square field into eight parts;
there, a corner consists of two parts, and the *bhadra* consists of two parts. (6)
Thus, there are three types of Meru palaces on earth:
those consisting of seventy-two stories, beginning with the Kaṇa and ending with the Bhadrakānta.
Among them, one should understand that there are two groups of six, two groups of six, two groups of six, and two groups of six.
Having extended [the base] to the ears of the *bhadra*, there is the arrangement of the various body-parts (*aṅga*) and so forth.
(8) The half-*bhadra* consists of eight parts, with a projection of six parts;
above the *bhadra* are the windows (*gavākṣa*) as well as the body-chariots (*aṅgarathikā*). (9)
Likewise, five "great-horned" (uruśṛṅga) pillars should be erected in every way.
In the corner, however, the Sarvatobhadra, Nandīśa, and Pṛthivījaya [pillars] are to be established,
one above the other, in due order, being firm in nature.
The *Bhadraka* has nine pillars, and the *Nandīśa* has twenty-one pillars.
The *Pṛthivījaya*, which is highly esteemed, has forty-nine pillars.
Likewise, the *Keśarī* and the *Bhadraka* have pillars arranged in equal proportions on both sides of the ears (*karṇa*).
There, a five-egg-shaped *keśarī* should be provided as the *nandīśāla*;
for the *bhadra*, it is seventeen egg-shaped and nine egg-shaped.
Then, above the *nandikas* situated on the left and right of the *bhadra*—
Keśarī, Keśarī, Śrīvatsa, and likewise the Śrīvatsāṇḍakas—[these] should be placed there; however, the Śrīvatsa with a single egg-cell (aṇḍaka) is to be used, while the others are as before.
Then, above the Nandikas situated on the left and right of the corner: || 14–15 ||
Keśarī, Keśarī, Śrīvatsa, Śrīvatsāṇḍaka, and likewise Nandikā— these six are to be understood there, whether they be small or indeed large.
Dhruva is situated above the Nandikā located on the left and right of each ear.
Only the Keśarī [style] should be given, and never otherwise.
But in the Bhadra style, having made the nose, there is the Śrīvatsa-egg [ornament] there;
and on the left and right ears of the Bhadra, there are the Pratikarṇas.
In this manner, eight subsidiary parts (pratyaṅga) are to be assigned to each of the four [directions];
thus, there are indeed thirty-two subsidiary parts in the four directions.
In a palace of seventy-two *pada*s, there are fifty-four *aṃśaka*s.
Thereafter, the lines of the summit (śikhara) and the neck (namaṇa) should be drawn.
In this way, it becomes endowed with one thousand and one eggs;
indeed, it is known as the Great Meru, the abode of the Supreme Brahman.
I shall describe the central Meru, the field which is square,
divided into sixty-four parts, extending from the center to the corners.
One should divide it by seven, two, three, four, six, four, and six [units].
The auspicious *nirvāha* is three parts; this [structure] consists of seven parts and is auspicious.
The first *nandikā* is two parts, while the other is three parts. The *pratikarṇa* is four parts, and the *prātirāthaka* is six parts. (23–24)
The *pratikarṇa* is one-fourth [of the width], and the corner (*koṇa*) likewise arises from six parts.
In this manner, it should be constructed in the four directions; the rotation is considered to consist of six parts.
The walls consist of six-sixths, and the lines are twenty parts.
Keśarī, Sarvatobhadra, Nandana, and Nandaśālika— these should be established in order in the corners. Trayodaśāṇḍanandana,
two Śrīvatsas, and Keśarīs should be situated in sequence at each corner.
The Śrīvatsa, the Keśarī, and likewise the Sarvatobhadra—
these three ornaments of the temple should be placed upon the pedestal.
One should also apply the Śrīvatsa and the Keśarī to the Nandikā.
The second [section], Nandikā, should be made, adorned with two Śrīvatsas. On the Ṣaḍara,
the Pratirathaka, the Karṇa, and likewise on the Nandikā,
and also on half of that, on the left and right, the Pratyaṅga itself should be placed.
The *aṇḍakas* are to be understood as before, and the measurement of the peaks (*śṛṅga*) is also as before.
This central Meru consists of five hundred and five *aṇḍakas*. It is characterized by the peaks known as Muni, Vidyādhara, Siṃha, Gaja, Ghaṇṭaka, and Kūṭaka. (3.1)
Endowed with the concealment of the *varālikā*, it is consecrated by Śiva.
It has sixty-four stories and five hundred and five *aṇḍakas*;
this is proclaimed as the middle Meru. Now I shall describe the smallest.
In a square field divided into fifty-five parts,
the arrangement should be made in sequence by six, three, three, six, three, and six [parts].
Starting from the *bhadra* (the projection) up to the corner, half of the *bhadra* consists of six parts.
There are two parts in the projection, and likewise the *nandikā* consists of three parts;
the second [projection] is also three parts, while the *paṭhara* possesses six parts.
The third *nandikā* is enriched by three parts, and there are six corner-projections (*koṇaka*).
In the exit [of the rays], they possess an equal state; from that, the arrangement of the limbs should be performed.
The wall is four and a half parts, and the circumambulatory path is likewise extended.
But the lines of the bowing [deities] are fixed like the central Meru.

On each *pratiratha* and at each corner (*koṇa*), three *śṛṅgas* known as *keśarīs* should be placed above them. On each *nandikā* and on each *pratikarṇa*, there should likewise be three *śrīvatsas*.
Having made the nose beautiful, there should be two Śrīvatsa-marked sections;
there are four thigh-ridges on each limb, left and right. Meru, with its smallest [scale], consists of two hundred and ninety-three eggs (aṇḍakas).
It possesses the splendor of the Gaṇas, the Vidyādharas, and so forth, and is indeed dear to the gods.
Now, the temple named Merumandira is described: when the field has been made square and divided into thirty-eight parts. 41–42.
The *bhadra* shall consist of four parts, and its projection shall be two parts.
The *nandikā* shall be one part, and the second likewise two parts;
the *paṭṭa-raśmi* shall be five parts, and another shall be two parts.
Furthermore, the *nandikā* and the corner (*koṇa*) likewise consist of five parts.

All of these have equal petals; the wall is considered to be three and a half [parts], and the circumambulatory path (*bhramaṇī*) is also considered to be three and a half, equal in all four directions.
The ground floor of the central temple is considered to consist of twelve parts;
it should be constructed in all four directions,
with three lions at each corner and one Śrīvatsa as well, followed by that upon the pedestal.
Three *śrīvatsas* and one *tilaka* must indeed be made.
On the *sarvanandika* and the *ūrdhvaka*, three *aṇḍakas* for each of the *śrīvatsas* should be fashioned; on the *bhadra*, four *śṛṅgas* are to be made.
One should likewise place the secondary limbs (pratyaṅgas) on the right and left sides respectively.
Above the lines, one should install the forms within twelve divisions;
furthermore, there are thirty-eight parts for the base and eight for the tilakas.

Thus, this Mount Meru is considered to have eighty-five *aṇḍakas*. The circumference of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍamaṇḍala*) consists of one hundred and forty-nine *talas*, sixty-four *tilas*, and one *aṇḍaka*. (2.141.50–51)
This temple known as Lakṣmīkoṭara is called Meru;
it has twenty-four tilakas and thirty-six floor-divisions.
Kailāsameruka has one hundred and nineteen domes (aṇḍas).
Abounding in seventy-two *tilakas* and possessing eighteen parts of the base, it has one hundred and sixty-one *aṇḍas* and is named Pañcānana.
It possesses twenty-four *tilakas* and seventy-seven *aṇḍas*. (53–54)
That Meru-vimāna is said to have twenty-six parts on its base;
while that which has one hundred and sixty-four *tilakas* on its base possesses thirty-six parts and two hundred and nine sections (*kāṇḍas*).
This Meru, named Gandhamādana, is considered beautiful.
It has twenty-six parts for its floors and twenty *tilakas*;
it consists of one hundred and twenty-five *aṇḍas* and is free from corners.
Furthermore, there are one hundred and thirty-six *tilakas* on the base;
that which has three hundred and thirty-two parts,
as well as forty *aṇḍakas*, is known by the name Giriprāsādaka.
The Meru named Tilaka has eighty-four *tilakas*, eighteen parts for its tiers,
twenty-one *aṇḍakas*, ninety-two *tilakas*, and one hundred and nine *aṇḍakas*. (2.141.59–60)
The Meru temple named Candraśekhara has thirty-four storeys;
Tilaka has fifty-six, and Kāṇḍaka has seventy-three.
The temple named Mandiratilaka has twenty-eight storeys. (6.1)
It has thirty-three pillars and is endowed with sixteen *tilakas*;
it consists of twelve sections for the floors, and that very [structure] is the Meru of Good Fortune (*saubhāgyameru*).
Indeed, there are forty-nine eggs (*aṇḍas*) therein.
Where there are forty-eight *tilakas* and twenty-two parts for the floors, that is indeed the beautiful Meru.
Where there are twenty parts for the floors and thirty-six *tilakas*, [that is the other form].
It consists of exactly one hundred and forty-nine eggs;
this auspicious temple is known by the name Śrītilaka.
Furthermore, that which possesses one hundred and fifty-seven eggs— ||| 65-66 || |||
The temple named Viśāla, which has forty *tilakas* and twenty-eight *sattalas*, is considered to bestow auspiciousness and should indeed be understood as such.
Likewise, the *ekāṇḍa* [type] possesses forty-four *tilakas*.
That mountain-peak indeed has twelve parts for its terraces;
it has forty *tilakas* and fifty-seven *daṇḍakas*, and with twenty-two parts for its terraces, it is called Nandivardhana. (68–69)
Thus have all my palaces and abodes been described;
now I shall speak of the images exactly as they are conceived by me.
The stone should be dense, free from flaws, soft, fragrant, and sweet.

The stone intended for the image should be endowed with luster and beautiful to behold. Whatever mark there may be made of pure gold, bronze, or iron, as well as any diverse deformity upon the image, is a source of fear. (71–72)
A stone that resembles a bee, a pigeon, a night-lotus, black gram, green gram, or snow;
which is pale white or has the luster of ghee or a lotus—is auspicious for all types of images.
An image smaller than twelve finger-breadths is considered fit for worship in the home.
In a temple, [an image] from twelve *aṅgulas* up to nine *gajas* should be worshipped.
An image exceeding ten *gajas* may be worshipped provided it is not in a temple (*prāsāda*).
In a quadrangular hall (*catuṣkī*), that [image] may be up to forty-five *gajas*.
An image made of the eight metals, of stone, of jewels, of excellent wood,
or even of coral and other materials, bestows auspiciousness.
That which is more than a hundred years old and has been consecrated by gods or men [is likewise auspicious].
Even one that is broken or cracked is worthy of worship; any other [image] bestows faults.
In sacred sites and forests, deities—even those that are broken—should indeed be worshipped as they grant fruits, but never elsewhere.
An image made of precious gems or metals, even if smeared with ointments or difficult to repair,
may be restored through re-consecration and thereafter become worthy of worship.
However, an image made of wood or stone that is broken is not considered fit for restoration.
She should never be made with extra limbs or missing limbs.
Whether she is fashioned from wood, plaster, stone, ivory, or even from clay, iron, and other materials,
an image of the Goddess that exceeds the prescribed measurements, even if it includes her retinue, is not to be worshipped in the home.
Where the gods manifest roaring, weeping, laughter, the opening and closing of eyes, or cruelty, there is great danger.
When a stone that was sleeping upon the earth is buried outside, then [this occurs].
Having remembered the southern and western sides, one should fashion the head [of the image].
(83) One part is for the crocodile face; likewise, the bird has two parts;
the elephants and others have three parts, and the kinnaras have four parts. (84)
The auspicious gods should be made by the artisan with five parts;
Gaṇeśa, Vāmana, and Kroḍa—these are considered to have six parts.
However, the bull, the boar, and the human [forms] should be made with seven parts.

Pārvatī is the power (śakti) with eight parts; likewise, the other goddesses (devikās) have nine parts. Other deities have ten parts, while Śiva-saṃkarṣaṇa has eleven parts. Caṇḍī, Bhūta, Hanumān, and Kārtika have eleven parts.
The Vaitālas occupy twelve parts, the Rākṣasas thirteen parts,
the Daityas fourteen parts, and Bhṛgu fifteen parts.
The cruel deities, beginning with Devikā, are always considered to occupy sixteen parts.
Ganesha, mounted upon a mouse, holds a tusk and a battle-axe;
he has the face of an elephant, is adorned with serpents, and carries a lotus and a sweetmeat (modaka).
Two parts of his body are his face, and likewise two parts are his belly. (2.141.89–90)
The hips are four finger-breadths; from there to the knees it is seven finger-breadths.
The knees are three finger-breadths, and likewise the shanks are seven finger-breadths.
The feet are three finger-breadths; such is the measurement for the six-part form.
I shall now declare the measurement in seven parts; listen to me.
The hairline [from the top] consists of three parts, while the face is likewise one part.
The neck is three *aṅgulas*, and the wing [side] is ten and a half *aṅgulas*.
The abdomen is said to be nine finger-breadths; the interval between the navel and the genitals is indeed seven and a half finger-breadths; the thighs are eighteen finger-breadths;
the knee is three finger-breadths; and the shank is eighteen finger-breadths.
The feet should be known as three *aṅgulas* each, and the body as seven *vitastis*.
(95) In the eight-*tāla* proportion, the face is one *tāla*, the hairline likewise three *aṅgulas*, the neck should be known as three *aṅgulas*, and the heart as nine *aṅgulas*. (96)
The navel is twelve finger-breadths in measure, and the penis is nine finger-breadths.
The thigh is considered to be twenty-one finger-breadths, and the knee three finger-breadths.
The shank is twenty-one finger-breadths, and the foot likewise three finger-breadths.
This form, enriched by eight vitastis, is declared for a skilled artisan. (98) Now I shall describe the nine-tāla [measure]: the distance to the hairline is three aṅgulas;
the face should be known as twelve aṅgulas, and the neck is three aṅgulas. (99)
The heart is ten finger-breadths [in width], and the navel is twelve finger-breadths;
the abdomen is four finger-breadths, and the distance to the private parts is eight finger-breadths.
The thigh is twenty-four finger-breadths, and the knee measures four [finger-breadths].
The shank is twenty-four finger-breadths long, and the foot is four [finger-breadths] in measure.
The width at the center of the breasts is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
likewise, the beautiful belly extending from the breast is four finger-breadths in length. (101–102)
The space between the belly and the arms is considered auspicious at one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The forearm from the shoulder to the elbow is seven fingers broad and well-fleshed;
its length is sixteen fingers, and the wrist is ten fingers long. (103)
The length of the forearm is three finger-breadths;
the palm of the hand is twelve finger-breadths in height and five finger-breadths in width;
the middle [of the body] is fourteen finger-breadths in length, and the waist is likewise.
The root of the thigh is twenty-four finger-breadths;
likewise, the shank and the forearm are each ten and one finger-breadths in length. Furthermore, the foot is fourteen finger-breadths long, extending from the toes to the heel.
The portion from the armpit to the breast is four *aṅgulas* above [the breast].
Likewise, the portion from the belly to the top of the shoulder is considered to be eight *aṅgulas*.
The neck is eight parts, and the foot is six parts in length; such is the measurement.

Thus, O Rādhikā, although pride may arise in many ways, it is indeed in accordance with the age (yuga), just as Lord Hari has declared. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Measurement and Proportions of the Meru Temples of the Highest, Middle, and Lowest Orders, as well as the Images of Gaṇeśa and Others," in the section on the Festival of Installation within the second book, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The One Hundred and Forty-First Chapter.
141. ← Chapter 141. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 142.
[Author: Chapter 143.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! I shall describe to you other forms of the Divine.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said to His devotee:
"One should discard into water an image whose major or minor limbs are broken; however, one should not discard an image that is merely broken in its nails, ornaments, garlands, or weapons. (1-2)

Indeed, the four-faced Creator of the universe [is so called] because of the fourfold division of the Vedas beginning with the Ṛgveda, because of the divisions of the ages beginning with the Satya Yuga, and because of the distinctions of the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
His right half [shows] above the hand a rosary as well as a sacrificial ladle (sruk).
The lotus-seated one, possessing a beard, holds a book and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
(4) Sāvitrī, who possesses four faces and brings joy to those learned in the Vedas, holds a rosary, a book, a lotus, and a water-pot. (5)
The Ṛgveda is white in color, two-armed, and has the face of a donkey;
he holds a rosary and a water-vessel, and is devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
The Yajurveda has the face of a goat, is yellow in color, and holds a rosary.
In his left hand he holds a goad; he is the bestower of prosperity and the bringer of auspiciousness.
Sāmaveda has the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and the face of a horse;
he holds a rosary of beads in his right hand and a conch shell in his left. || 7–8 ||
The Veda known as Atharvaṇa is white in color and has the face of a monkey;
bearing a rosary and the Khaṭvāṅga staff, he indeed bestows victory.
Viśvakarman has four arms and holds a rosary and a thread.
He holds an elephant and a water-pot, has three eyes, and is mounted upon a swan.
With the Sudarśana discus in his right hand and a lotus in his left,
this is proclaimed to be the form of the Sun under the name of Viṣṇu.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments, he has two arms and wears a single garment; his hand holds a white lotus.
He is a circular orb of splendor, situated in the center, and clothed in red garments.
Yoked to a chariot drawn by seven-faced horses and joined with Aruṇa—Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Śakti, and Rudra are the deities;
they should be understood as the forms of the Pañcāyatana, auspicious in every respect. (13–14)
In that [mandala], the ninefold portion of the form of Nārāyaṇa should indeed be fashioned;
it holds the conch, lotus, mace, and discus, and is adorned with a crown.
Hari likewise bears the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace.
Kṛṣṇa holds the Pāñcajanya conch, the mace, the lotus, and the Sudarśana discus. Garuḍa is green in form, with a nose shaped like that of an owl;
he has four arms, round eyes and face, and is endowed with two wings. (16–17)
With thighs, knees, and feet like those of a vulture, golden-hued and endowed with all artistic refinements,
he should hold a parasol and a water-pot while performing a gesture of reverence with joined palms.
His left foot is bent forward at the front, while the other foot follows behind, resting upon the knee.
Seated upon Garuda, he rests his foot upon the earth. Umāmaheśvara likewise holds a trident in his right hand and a citron in his left, which is embraced by her.

The lord of serpents held the goddess Pārvatī of auspicious countenance seated upon his own lap; her hand was most beautiful upon his shoulder. In another hand he held a mirror, and likewise, a bull stood below.
One should depict Kumāra together with Gaṇeśa, Bhṛṅgī, Raṭa, and others;
likewise, one should represent Umā as two-armed, and Lakṣmī as resting upon Nārāyaṇa.
Hari is established upon Garuḍa, accompanied by his own weapons.
The right hand should be placed against the neck, while the left hand holds a lotus.
Hari’s auspicious left hand rests upon the region of Lakṣmī’s belly;
she, in turn, beautifully bears a boon-granting gesture and a drinking vessel marked with the lines of a trident.
The peacock and the elephant are proclaimed as Mahālakṣmī.
Above the eight-petaled lotus, Lakṣmī is seated upon a lion-throne; she sits like Vināyaka, adorned with auspicious ornaments. (25–26)
The two hands of the Goddess should be raised, holding lotuses;
she bears an amṛta-pitcher in her left hand and a mātuluṅga fruit in her right.
She has one face, four arms, and is resplendent with a crown.
Endowed with a circle of light, adorned with earrings and a crest-jewel, and richly possessed of the rosary, lotus, lute, and book—she is celebrated as Mahāvidyā.
Possessing the auspicious rosary, lotus, and book, she is Sarasvatī, the bringer of welfare. (28–29)
A person whose reflection is attached to a wall is entirely inauspicious;
a flagstaff should never be erected within a house. When the sun is in its northern course (Uttarayana), the installation of deities and other such rites is most excellent.
Consecration, installation, entry, worship, and so forth [should be performed].
(3.1) Likewise, the pavilion should be situated in front of the temple, in the northeast, or in the north;
it should be at a distance of three, five, seven, nine, or eleven [cubits] within the intermediate space. (3.2)
Having first purified the earth through burning, digging, and the pouring of water,
and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and worshipped the Tortoise (*kūrma*),
one should thereafter worship Śeṣanāga and the Earth as well.
One should prepare the eastern direction for the sake of the pavilion as follows:
having drawn a circle with a cord, one should plant a stake in the center;
then, by means of two lines [drawn] at the times of sunrise and sunset, one should determine the directions.
It may measure eighteen, twelve, sixteen, or eighteen cubits;
it may be provided with pillars starting from sixteen [cubits] in height, or even twenty cubits;
its height and width may be one span (vitasti), or equal to the height of an elephant.
When a second pavilion is to be constructed, it should be made according to the measurement of the first pavilion;
having set aside a space of that many cubits, another pavilion should be built.
In the pavilion divided into nine parts, the central part shall be the altar (vedikā).
The central altar (vedikā) is considered to be one-third of the pavilion’s size.
It measures two cubits plus eight finger-breadths.
There are four beautiful doors, radiant with arches (toraṇa) and other ornaments.
Now, furthermore, I shall describe the banners; listen to me.
Eight banners are to be erected in order, starting from the east:
they are two *dvi-gaja* in height and five *pañca-gaja* in length. (2.142.40–41)

That which has an elephant in yellow on the east is called Indradhvaja; that which is red in the southeast and adorned with the face of a thief is presided over by Agni. That which is black in the south and richly adorned with a buffalo is called Yamadhvaja.
In the southwest is the Rakshasa banner, blue in color and variegated.
In the west is the Varuna banner, white in color and having the face of a crocodile.
In the northwest is the Vayu banner, green in color and bearing a deer; it is called the Wind-banner.
In the north is Kubera, white in color and marked with the sign of an elephant;
in the northeast is [Īśāna], white in color and possessing a banner marked with a bull.
Having fixed these upon the tops of bamboo poles ten cubits long, one should indeed offer them.
Indeed, bamboo poles should be planted in the ground for the sake of stability.
In the center of the pavilion, there shall be a pole seven cubits long,
or even three cubits in length, beautiful with a network of small bells.
A beautiful banner, richly adorned with chowries and featuring mixed colors, should be offered; it is considered auspicious.
It should be very firm at the top of its ten-cubit bamboo shaft and be excellent.
Each [banner] should be seven cubits long and one cubit wide.
Having a triangular shape, rich with various weapons, and extending along the lineage;

likewise, the weapons are to be understood in sequence as the thunderbolt (vajra), spear (śakti), staff (daṇḍa), sword (khaḍga), noose (pāśa), goad (aṅkuśa), mace (gadā), and trident (triśūla). 2.142.49–50.
And the banners, endowed with the aforementioned excellence, should be placed on all sides.
The ninth banner, white in color, should be in the middle between the northeast and the east.
Having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings, one should fix it upon the tops of the staffs.
I shall also describe the ritual for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) on the grounds within the pavilion (maṇḍapa). Starting from ten cubits up to sixteen cubits in measurement,
one should construct an altar in the center of the pavilion, as well as the sacrificial pit and other auspicious pits.
One should indeed construct five, eight, or nine [mandalas] in the sequence starting from the east:
a quadrangle in the east, a yoni-shape in the southeast,
a half-moon in the south, and a triangle in the southwest.
In the west, one should make it circular, and in the northwest, a hexagon (55).
In the north, it should resemble an eight-petalled lotus, and in the northeast, an octagon; or it may be circular or square in the center between the east and the northeast (56).
This preceptor, named Kuṇḍa, possesses sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the guardians of the directions and other deities;
or alternatively, he may construct five pits:
that in the east is square, that on the right (south) is semicircular, and that in the west is circular. (57)

In the north it should be lotus-shaped, and in the northeast it should be circular or square, according to the specific distinction of its form. If only one [shape] is desired, that is considered to be square. ||58-59||
It should indeed be constructed in the west, the north, or the northeast;
all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) must be at a distance of one and a quarter times the height of an elephant from the altar (vedī).
Alternatively, they are considered to be at the end of an interval equal to one-fourth of the altar's dimensions.
For Brahmins it is square, while for Kṣatriyas it is circular (6.1).
For Vaiśyas it is indeed a half-moon, and for Śūdras it is triangular;
or else, it may be square for all, or even circular (6.2).
For women, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed considered to be the vulva (yoni), which is auspicious in every respect;
it is joined with a girdle (mekhalā) and the pit itself is one cubit (hasta) in measure.
For ten thousand oblations (homāyuta), the pit is one cubit; for fifty thousand (lakṣārdha), it is two cubits.
A *lakṣahoma* is performed in a three-cubit [mandala], a *daśalakṣa* in a four-cubit one;
a *triṃśallakṣa* in a five-cubit one, and half a *koṭi* (*ardhakoṭi*) in a six-cornered one.
In a seven-cubit [mandala] there are eighty *lakṣas*, and a *koṭihoma* in an eight-cubit one.
For fifty oblations, one should make [the sacrificial pit] twenty-one finger-breadths;
likewise, for a hundred oblations, it should be twenty-two and a half finger-breadths.
For the purpose of a thousand oblations, however, it is considered to be one cubit in measure.
For ten thousand *homa* offerings, the pit is two cubits; for one hundred thousand, it consists of four cubits;
for the purpose of ten million, it is six cubits. However, for the purpose of a *koṭi-homa*, it should be eight, ten, or sixteen cubits in size.
The subtle oblation consists of sesame and ghee; the middling consists of grapes, barley, and so forth;
and the gross is proclaimed to be the *bilva* fruit, coconut, sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), and the like.
Whatever the nature of the substance may be, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) must likewise correspond to it.
Alternatively, one should increase the measurement of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) by one *gaja* for every hundred thousand oblations.
Up to ten million oblations, one should have it constructed as ten cubits (*hasta*).
Alternatively, for the purpose of a sacrifice of fifty lakhs, [the pit] should be seven *gajas*.
For ten hundred thousand oblations, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring five cubits is prescribed;
for twenty hundred thousand homas, a pit six cubits long is considered appropriate;
and for fifty thousand oblations, a pit of three cubits is also [recommended].
The depth of the pit is considered equal to the area [of the mouth], and the girdle is likewise considered equal [to that area].
Even without a girdle, the depth is declared to be equal [to the area].
In a twenty-fourfold division, the neck of the pit (*kuṇḍakaṇṭhaka*) is twelve parts. (73–74)
These girdles may be one, two, three, or indeed two, three, or five;
then, in the eight-part division of the site, one should dig a foundation five parts deep.
Above that, in the three-part division, three girdles should be constructed according to the prescribed rule.
The upper part is four finger-breadths high, while the middle part is considered to be three finger-breadths.
The lower part, enriched by two parts, is considered a beneficial girdle (mekhalā).
It is square, measuring one cubit [in width], and four finger-breadths in height. || 76–77 ||
The sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) or the *homavedikā* may also be one finger-breadth in height. On a spacious altar, one, two, or three cubits in length,
the maṇḍala named Sarvatobhadraka should indeed be constructed.

O twice-born ones, there should be eight, thirty-two, or even sixty-four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are learned in the Vedas, knowers of the ritual procedures, and worthy of being addressed with mantras. One-third of the way toward the north of the sacrificial pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇḍapa*) should be constructed.
There, on a sacrificial mound, a mountain, or in sand provided with shade,
the images should be bathed with the five products of the cow and with decoctions.
One should bathe them with the waters of a hundred jars while they are covered with bark garments.
With Vedic mantras, musical instruments, songs, and auspicious hymns,
one should cover the deities with cloth beneath the pavilion by the side of the altar.
One should cause [the person] to ascend the balance on the altar and place it there, beginning from the north.
One should place the water-pot (kalaśa) at the region of the head and the water-strainer (kamaṇḍalu) at the position of the feet;
the fan at the back and the mirror on the left side.
[Furthermore, there are] diamonds, lapis lazuli, pearls, and very blue sapphires (indranīla).

One should place the puṣparāga, gomeda, and pravāla gems according to the sequence of the directions starting from the east. Then, one should offer the metals—gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, brass, lead, tin, and iron—in order, beginning with the east. (85–86)

One should likewise place the medicinal herbs according to the previous sequence: *vajrī*, *vahniśikhā*, *sahadevī*, *tulasī* leaves, *indravāruṇikā*, *śaṅkhāvalī*, and *udyāvalī*, as well as *tvaritā*.

Barley, rice, millet, and small millet, as well as sesame seeds, akṣaka beans, mung beans, and wheat—these should be offered in order starting from the east. A great festival should be held with dancing, singing, food offerings, waving of lamps, and other such rites. (88–89)
One should also perform the rite of consecration through the placement of mantras on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other such methods.
One should give the garments, ornaments, and so forth offered to the deity to the artisan;
however, one should give everything offered during the sacrifice to the person acting as the preceptor (*ācārya*).
One should cause the placement of deities to be performed upon each part of the palace.
One should place Vārāha on the foundation stone (kharaśilā), the Nāga on the water-channel,
the Water-deity (Jaladeva) on the water-jars (kumbhīs), and likewise the Asuras on the neck of the pinnacle (puṣpakaṇṭha).
One should place Nandinī in the jar of dullness (jāḍyakuṃbha), and likewise Viṣṇu in the two pericarp-cells;
Gaṇeśa on the elephant-throne, and the two Aśvins on the horse-throne;
the mountains on the man-throne, and likewise Medinī on the razor-throne.
One should worship the three junctions (sandhyās) in the auspicious pitcher (bhadrakumbha), and likewise Pārvatī in the water-jar (kalaśa);
the Gandharvas in the pigeon-hole (kapotālī), Sarasvatī on the pedestal (mañcikā),
the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) on the leg (jaṅghā), and the deity Indra at the spout (udgama).
One should know Sāvitrī in Bharaṇī, the Devikās in Śirāvaṭī,
Vidyādharī in Puṣpakaṇṭha, and the Suras in Antarālakā;
Parjanya in Kūṭacchādya, and the Sun and Moon in the two Śākhas.
One should worship the three gods on the upper beam, and likewise the Yakṣa on the Udumbara post;
the two sons of the Aśvins in the cavity of the conch, Śeṣa on the pillar-base, the Earth on the pedestal,
the mountain deities on the pillar, and the deities of the sky on the pinnacle.
In the center, one should worship the principal deity; on the supreme neck, Jāhnavī;
on the broad peaks of the pinnacle, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśvara;
Indra as the fifth of these five deities; and the three lords of the gods within the temple.
On the peak [he worshipped] the god Īśvara, and on the pinnacle (kalaśa) Indra himself; on the neck (grīvā) the immortal [Amararāja], and on the amalasaraka [ornament] the night-walker (Niśācara);
on the lotus-leaf Padmākṣa, and on the pinnacle (kalaśa) Sadāśiva.
One should likewise place the deity Aghora on the left and Tatpuruṣa on the right;
one should also install Bhairava in the temple divided into five parts.
Once the deity has been consecrated, the daughters of Brahmā should gaze upon him.

Then others—virtuous men and women who are free from passion—should perform the consecration ceremony (darśana). Then indeed those following the householder dharma [should do so]. By that means, the patron (yajamāna) should request merit from the architect (sūtradhāra) for the propitiation of the deity. 103–104.
The master builder should say, "O merchant, may there be no loss for you.
One should give the master builder and the craftsmen offerings, gifts, and the like.
One should hold a great festival with food and other provisions, as well as with storytelling and similar entertainments.

"Thus, O Rādhikā, I have declared to you the ritual action according to the intention of Hari. (106) Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Concise Installation and Other Details Concerning the Measurement of the Images of Brahmā, the Vedas, the Gods, and the Goddesses, as well as the Pavilion and the Fire-pit, during the Pratiṣṭhā Festival," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (142)
