Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen then to the great oblations of the final offering (pūrṇāhuti) which Śrī Hari described there; I shall tell you the ritual procedure for them here as well.
"Syonā pṛthivī" for the Earth; "aghorebhyaḥ" and "śambhave";
"indrāya" for Indra, "mahendrāya" for Mahendra, and also "agnim dūtam" for Agni;
"paśūnām" for Paśupati, and "agna āyāhi" for Agni. (2)
One should offer "asi hi" to Rudra in the form of Indra for the sacrificer;
"yāmāya" is indeed for Yama; "ud u tyaṃ" is for Sūrya in his form;
and one should assign "ā vo rudrāya" and "asuṃvantaṃ" to Nirṛti.
"Āpo hi" is for the god of water; "vibhūṣam" is for Bhava; "imaṃ me varuṇāya" is for Varuṇa; "vātā vā" is for the form of Vāyu;
"īśānāya" is for Īśāna; and "ā no niyudbhiḥ" is for Vāyu. || 5 ||
One should offer to Soma, to Sūrya, to Indra, and to Mahādeva; to Hari with "ādiprān", to Bhīma with "mṛgo na bhīmaḥ", and to Īśāna with "abhityam"—having consecrated these with mantras. (6–7)
In a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the Great Master (*mahācārya*) should perform oblations for all [the deities] by name;
he should offer eight thousand, or else eight hundred, oblations.
Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the right ear of the deity, [he should proceed].
After eight oblations of clarified butter, one should perform the touching of the two offerings with the root mantra, and offer oblations numbering one hundred or more. Then,
having offered curd into the *yāma*-pit, one should touch the navel of the deity.
Having offered milk into the western pit (vāruṇa-kuṇḍaka), one should touch the heart of Hari;
having offered honey into the northern pit (saumya-kuṇḍa), one should touch the head of Hari.
In the western pit, one should offer the four substances beginning with ghee mixed together.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should touch all the limbs of Hari.
Having performed the ritual of *nyāsa* upon the image and having worshipped the tortoise-stone (*kūrmaśilā*),
as well as the Brahma-stone (*brahmaśilā*), the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the vehicles, and the attendants (*pārṣada*).
One should worship the attendant deities and their retinues; one should consecrate those attendants of Viṣṇu, beginning with Caṇḍaprabha, on the left side.
Having sprinkled them with honey and ghee and washed them with water, one should worship them.
Having covered the image with a cloth, one should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*).
In the procedure for the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) where Viṣṇu is to be installed, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ paṃ bhaṃ phaṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī," at the heart and the head. (15–16)
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the pedestal with "Śikhāyāṃ kavace netre huṃ phaṭ svāhā" and "namama," one should then place the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) there as well.
One should worship the embodied form (*mūrtimān*) with the mantras upon the image; indeed, one should worship the embodied form in the image.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrāṃ kṣaḥ, salutation to the illustrious Supreme Brahman, the sustainer of all.
Oṃ hrāṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the auspicious one who possesses divine splendor.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), [one performs] the preliminary consecration of the temple.
Having fashioned a mandala of eighty-one squares near the new [image] using unbroken rice grains,
and having placed mounds of seven kinds of grain upon those very squares,
one should prepare eighty-one auspicious, new jars filled with water.
Having brought [the materials] there, one should take the middle one among the nine new [vessels].
(21) Having identified the central compartment among them, one should place the jars according to the sequence beginning with the center.
Then, indeed, twelve twigs should be placed in the central jar. (22)
The śamī, udumbara, aśvattha, palāśa, aśoka, campaka,
kadamba, plakṣa, nyagrodha, āmra, kavi, bilva, and arjuna trees—
leaves from these should be taken and cast [into the fire] with the mantra: "Obeisance to Soma."
Then, in the eastern jar, [one should place] lotuses,
gorocana, dūrvā sprouts, tufts of darbha grass, white and yellow mustard seeds,
as well as red sandalwood, jasmine flowers, and ten *nandāvarta* plants.
Then, one should deposit seven items into the fire-pitcher as follows:
barley, rice, sesame, gold, silver, earth from a riverbank, and cow dung that has not touched the ground; having uttered "Namaḥ," one should cast them in.
Then, one should place eight [substances] into the southern jar according to their respective order:
*sahadevī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *mahauṣadhī*, *śamī*, *śatāvarī*, *guḍūcī*, and *śyāmāka*—these one should cast in. (27–28)
Then, having uttered "Obeisance," one should place in the Nairṛtya pitcher a plantain, a betel nut, a coconut,
a wood-apple, a *nāriṅga*, a citron, a jujube,
and an emblic myrobalan.

In the pitcher belonging to Varuṇa, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with mantras. In the pitcher belonging to Vāyu, one should set down the "five astringents" (kaṣāyapañcaka) derived from the Śamī, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Kapāśa trees.
In a northern jar, one should place the eight roots (aṣṭamūla), which consist of their root forms: śaṅkhapuṣpī, sahadevī, balā, śatāvarī, kumārī, guḍūcī, vacā, and vyāghrī.
In the northeast pitcher, one should place the seven types of earth beginning with that from an anthill.
"O Jātavedas, bring to me Lakṣmī, who is golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver, radiant, and made of gold. (34)
With this mantra, one should consecrate the central jars;
then, having filled the remaining ones with scented water and likewise consecrated them,
one should wrap them inside, outside, and below with threads using the root mantra.
Having sprinkled the upper pinnacle of the temple with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then smear its summit with clay from an anthill while reciting the *divam* mantra;
thereafter, one should smear it with the mantra beginning with *samudrād ūrmī*.
One should bathe [the deity] with the *īśāna* mudrā and the *kuṃbhaka* breath-retention, and with the *kaṣāya* mudrā and the *kuṃbhaka* while reciting the mantra "yajñā yajñā... (Yajurveda 3.61).
One should also bathe [the deity] with the *vāyavya* mudrā and the *kuṃbhaka* while reciting the mantra "payaḥ pṛthivī... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.1).
Then he should bathe [the deity] with a pitcher of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) belonging to Varuṇa;
then with a pitcher of fruits belonging to Nirṛti, using the mantra "yāḥ phalinī";
and then with eight pitchers of water from the Saumya vessel, using the root mantra "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad".
With the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam asi" and the pitcher situated in the east;
with the mantra "somo rājā" and the pitcher situated in the southeast;
and with the mantra "viśvataśca" and the pitcher situated in the south.
Salutation with the serpent mantra (sarpamantra) and by means of the middle kuṃbhaka;
then, one should bathe the pinnacle (śikhara) with eight [mantras] according to the previous sequence:
"Oṃ, O Waters, carry away this, whatever is impure and whatever is filth. (43)
Whatever falsehood I have uttered through treachery, and whatever I have sworn falsely in fearlessness—may the Waters and Pavamāna release me from that sin.
Oṃ! Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods, O flowing ones.
"Purified ones have conquered; I purify this for you.

Having sprinkled [the image] with these words, having wound it with thread, bathed it, and contemplated the temple as having the form of a deity, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). ||45||
Oṃ Hrīṃ! O you who consist of all the gods, O inconceivable one, O you whose form is radiant with all jewels!
As long as the moon and the sun endure, remain firm here!
(46) Then, one should likewise install the horn-shaped pitcher and the banners.

Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) for the deities of the Piṇḍikāvāha with sesame seeds and other offerings, one should then worship four cows facing north at the eastern gate [with the mantra]:
"Oṃ, we know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva. (47–48)
Having churned the milk and cooked the *pāyasa* (milk-rice), and having prepared and offered the *caru* to Nārāyaṇa, one should feed ten Brahmins and recite: "May Viṣṇu be pleased. (49)
One should give cows to the Great Preceptor and gold finger-rings to the officiating priests (ṛtvij). Having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should hold a great festival at night.
The preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) may last for seven, five, three, or one night, ending with the offering of oblations (bali).
Then the Guru, having gone outside, should meditate upon the deity of the temple:
the pedestal stone is said to be the feet, and that which is above the feet is called the shank;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should be known as the belly, and the waist-band as the hips.
The pillars are to be understood as the arms, and the bell is proclaimed to be the tongue.
The lamp is to be known as its *prāṇa*, while the outflow of water is the *apāna*.
The navel is its *brahmasthāna*, and the heart-lotus is considered the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
This person is the image; the foot is likewise the ego (ahaṃkāra).
The light is the eye, and that which is above it is proclaimed to be his primordial nature (prakṛti).
The self is the image; from Nalakuṃbha downwards, the lower opening is the penis.
Its nose is the *śukanāsā* (the gargoyle), its window is called the ear;
its shoulder is the *kapotapāli* (the dove-cot), and its neck is the *āmalasāraka* (the amalaka-bud).
Its head is to be known as the *kalaśa* (the pinnacle), and the *majjākṣiptarasa* is beneficial [for it]. ||56-57||
One should know that its fat is the earth; its flesh is said to be the plastering [of the ground].
Its bones are the stones, and its sinews are remembered as the stakes and so forth.
Its eyes are the peaks, and its hair is proclaimed to be the banners.
In this manner, the sacrificer should meditate upon the form of the Man as the temple;
he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and likewise encircle it with a thread.
He should provide a cloth and a thread, and thereafter perform a salutation.
Having performed this consecration (*adhivāsana*), and having bathed in the morning at the pavilion,
the preceptor (*ācārya*) arrives and worships the image-protectors (*mūrtipas*), the door-keepers, the deities,
and the Vāstu-gods; then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
With the *Vāstoṣpati* mantra, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) from the root [mantra].
Then, having offered the sacrificial gift (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions, one should bow to the deity.
Thereafter, one should sprinkle the patron with the water from the jars located to the north of the pavilion.
One should satisfy the preceptor, the Brahmins, the architects, and others with sacrificial fees and other gifts.
Having specified the place and time, one should perform the consecration of the temple for the pleasure of the deity, saying:
"This temple, this abode of the deity, [is dedicated] for the pleasure of the Lord."
Having declared, "I release [the deity]," and having then cast down the *kuśa* grass and water,
he should bow to the Lord and feed the Brahmins and other virtuous men and women.
For the sake of the rite concerning the image of Acalā, he should do so together with the *mūrtipas*.
Having consecrated the Kūrmaśilā, the Devādhārā,
the Brahmaśilā, and the Piṇḍikā, the preceptor, moving clockwise around the temple while reciting the mantra "Trātāram indram," brings them inside.

With the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," for the destruction of obstacles, he should sprinkle the auspicious dwelling with streams of water and flowers; then, with a blade of *darbha* grass, he should indeed scratch [the ground] while reciting "Oṃ ca mahāṃ indreṇa. (68–69)

Having properly sprinkled the center of the temple door with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should place the Kūrma-śilā— which has been purified by rites such as bathing and is set within five gems— either toward the southeast or the north.
Having placed a golden tortoise upon a pure [surface] with the syllable *praṇava*,
and having brought it facing the door and deposited jewels there,
[one should place the slab] together with thirty-six or forty-five pits.
One should place the consecrated Brahma-stone and worship it with the mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to the all-pervading, stable, immovable, and eternal one; grant us peace!
(73). One should worship it as desired with the mantra: "Oṃ Śrīṃ Laṃ Svāhā."
You alone are the power of the seat; remain here forever, O Stone.

Homage to the path of phonemes, homage to the path of words, homage to the path of mantras, homage to the path of worlds, homage to the path of principles, and homage to the path of the manifest whole.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as having ascended the even path, one should then cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations into the cavity of the *brahmaśilā*,
one should, with a clockwise motion and with a hand adorned with gold, perform the placement of the jewels.
One should construct a stone pedestal with a cavity on a stone surface that is itself free of cavities (77).
In a mansion facing east or west, one should place the pedestal with its channel toward the north;
if it faces south or north, the channel should be toward the east, while reciting the *Dhruva-sūkta* (78).
One should consecrate the pedestal (piṇḍikā) with the mantra of Devapatnī;
then, reciting the Śrīsūkta and the Ca-sūkta, one should install Ramā.
One should also perform the nyāsas of the principles (tattvas), beginning with "Salutation to the principle of the self" (ātmatattvāya vai namaḥ).
Salutations again and again to the Ātmatattva for its power of action and its sovereignty. Salutations to the Vidyātattva, and salutations again and again to the power of knowledge.
Salutations to the Śivatattva, and salutations again and again to the power of will.
One should place the deities of the principles (tattvas), both with and without form, along with the world-protectors (lokapālas).

Having performed the rite of placing the seat of Ananta together with the Fire (vahni) for the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) with the mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ," and having worshipped her, one should pray to that excellent Power (suśaktikā).
"And I establish you here as the foundation for all the worlds.
As long as the earth endures, remain steadfast in this temple.
Having thus prayed, [he should place] the Praṇava and the sixteen vowels outside of that.

Having prepared the various side-dishes and placed them all around, one should then deposit gems and other such items within the hollows; furthermore, one should place barley and rice on the outer perimeter,
as well as flat beans, sesame, mung beans, millet, and wild rice.
Also rice, white mustard seeds, diamonds, pearls, and conch shells;
lapis lazuli, crystal, topaz, sapphire, and emerald; moonstone, realgar, yellow orpiment, and red arsenic. (86–87)
Lead, tin, saurāṣṭrī, yellow orpiment,
red ochre, mercury, gold, silver, copper, iron,
and tin; lead, bell-metal, brass, or even the various types of steel.
One should place white sandalwood, red sandalwood, aguru, and likewise arjunaka;
as well as uśīra, vaiṣṇavī, sahadevī, and lakṣmaṇā.
In the absence of seeds, one should offer barley; in the absence of gems, one should offer a diamond.
In the absence of the [five] elements, one should use yellow orpiment; in the absence of copper, gold;
in the absence of the medicinal herbs, the *sahadevī* plant; thereafter, one should perform the *lambhana* rite.
In the east, [one recites] "Indra, the protector," and in the southeast, "Agni."
With "Yamāya tvā," [one offers] to Yama; with "Asunvantaḥ," to Nirṛti (92).
With "Pañca nadyaḥ," to Varuṇa; with "Vāyo ye te," to Vāyu.
With "Oṃ vayaṃ ca," to the North; with "Tam īśāna," to Īśāna (93).
Having thus performed the placement of the jewels for the Earth, Sumeru, and the Tortoise,
as well as the golden vehicle facing the doors;
and having placed mercury in the central cavity with guggulu resins—

Having stabilized the jewels and so forth, and having smeared the pit with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and honey, and having covered it with cloth, one should then recite "Hūṃ," envelop it with the armor mantra (*kavaca*),
and subsequently utter "Phaṭ" for the weapon mantra (*astra*).
May Manojūti be pleased;
having consecrated the temple and offered oblations to Indra and the other gods,
one should then sprinkle the ground outside the temple with the five products of the cow while circumambulating it clockwise.
Having swept [the area] with tufts of *darbha* grass, one should then proceed in the eight directions.
Then, one should prepare eight square altars (*sthaṇḍila*) made of sand,
each measuring three *vitasti*s in size, starting from the northeast (*īśāna*).
Having placed water-filled jars adorned with fine flowers, sprouts, and excellent fruits,
and wrapped with threads upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and having performed the consecration of the ground,
one should then prepare the fire and bring it forward using *palāśa* fuel-sticks.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī mantra,
one should sprinkle the head of the deity with water from eight jars consecrated by the root mantra, saying "Huṃ Phaṭ," and perform the binding of the directions.
One should pray to him: "Awaken, O God of gods, Lord of the world!
To you who have awakened, O Infinite Vāsudeva, the support of the earth, obeisance be unto you!
[103] Then, one should take rice, sesame seeds, kuśa grass, milk, water, and so forth, which are placed within a conch shell.
"O Rādhā, having offered the *arghya* water to the Lord, one should cause Him to rise with the mantra.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Full Oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the Consecrations (*nyāsa*), the Preliminary Consecration (*adhivāsana*), the Water from the Vessel, the Bath on the Summit, the Cooking of the *caru*, the Meditation on the Form of the Person in the Temple, the Worship, the Tortoise Stone (*kūrma-śilā*), the Brahmā Stone (*brahma-śilā*), the Pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the Jewels, the *arghya* for the Deity, and so forth," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Endowed with all splendor and equipped with the conch, discus, and mace,
I establish here the wielder of the discus, the Supreme Lord who has become a deity.
One should recite the mantras known as the *Puruṣasūkta* according to the prescribed rules.

"O Blessed One, pervaded by that form which encompasses all that is moving and unmoving, please abide within this image in that distinguished form. Having spoken thus, one should then install the deities of its retinue. (26–27)
In the eastern pit, one should offer oblations twenty-one times with the heart mantra; in the southern, with the head mantra;
in the western, with the crest mantra; and in the northern, with the armor mantra.
In the teacher’s pit, one should offer oblations with the eye mantras. (28)
Having offered oblations into the eastern pit with the Astra-mantra and with the mantras of the weapons, and having further offered oblations, one should pray:
"Dwell here always for the sake of protecting the world;
let there be no cessation of progeny, and may this sacrificer prosper."
"May the kingdom of the virtuous be prosperous; may they enjoy inexhaustible happiness.
Having thus prayed, one should install the limbs and deities in their respective shrines.
One should offer the guest-water (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and a seat, saying "Obeisance" (namaḥ).

Having worshipped with "svāhā" and then with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and water, one should bathe [the deity] and recite the Puruṣasūkta; likewise, one should pray and touch the feet, the navel, the head, and the chest, saying: "Be the giver of liberation."
O Lord, may your ritual, whether performed with knowledge or without knowledge, be complete for you. O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, by your grace,
may one offer the name of the God, perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with musical instruments, and offer hymns of praise.
One who has committed an offense should perform an expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) for the sake of destroying that sin.
[This should consist of] *śamī*, *palāśa*, sesame seeds, and other materials, numbering one hundred and eight.
Furthermore, one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*), consisting of wealth, cows, jewels, land, and houses.
One should perform the oblation once again for the pacification of the arrival of what is forbidden:
"Oṃ, for stability, be firm, svāhā! Be established here!
Be immeasurable, awakened, eternal, and all-pervading. (37)
For the sake of complete pacification, one should perform here a fire-oblation (homa) one hundred and eight times:
Oṃ prajāpataye svāhā; this is for Prajāpati, [may it] be mine. Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā; this is for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, [may it] be mine. ||39||
Having offered the oblation, one should perform the consumption of the remnants (*saṃsrava*), the sipping of water (*ācamana*), and the giving of the vessel.
I indeed give this full vessel, dedicated to Prajāpati, to you, O Brahmin.
One should then perform the untying of the *brahmagranthi* with the *sumitri* mantra.
"Oṃ, may the waters and plants be friendly to us.
(41) Having wiped the head of the sacrificer with the water brought forward through the two strainers, he should then cast the two strainers into the fire. (42)
Uttering the mantra "durmitri," one should indeed cause the *praṇītā* vessel to tip over.
Then, having raised it outside toward the northeast and poured clarified butter (*ājya*) into it,
one should offer oblations with the hand itself while reciting the mantra again and again.
Oṃ, O gods who know the way, having found the way, come hither.
O Lord of the Mind, this sacrifice for the gods—svāhā! Place it in the wind, svāhā!
Then, having uttered the place, the time, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij). || 44–45 ||
They should perform the fire oblation (*homa*) in their respective hearths (*kuṇḍa*), concluding with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
The patron (*yajamāna*), together with his wife, should touch the right shoulder of the preceptor (*guru*) while holding betel,
fruits, areca nuts, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Having placed a *śrīphala* fruit upon the *sruva* ladle, one should offer oblations together with the mantras:
OṂ. From the ocean, the honeyed wave has arisen; through the *upāṃśu* [muttering], it has attained immortality.
That which is the secret name of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is the tongue of the gods and the navel of immortality. (48)
Let us proclaim our names at this sacrifice; may you sustain me with a stream of clarified butter through our acts of homage.
May the Brahman hear the hymn being recited; the four-horned bull has bellowed this.
Found by the gods upon the cow was the clarified butter, established in three ways and hidden by the Paṇis.
Indra begot one, Sūrya begot one; they fashioned one from Vena by their own inherent power.
These flow from the ocean within the heart; they cannot be seen by the enemy who possesses a hundred thunderbolts. I gaze upon the streams of clarified butter.
The golden reed is in their midst.
The streams flow together like milch-cows, purified within by the heart and the mind.
These waves of clarified butter flow forth like deer fleeing from a swift hunter;
like the rapid currents of a river on its course, they fly forward, mighty and overtaking the wind— the streams of clarified butter like a ruddy stallion.
Breaking through the barriers, swelling with their waves,
like beautiful women smiling as they go to a gathering, they have approached Agni.
The streams of ghee, continuous like fuel-sticks,
Jātavedas, being pleased, desires;
like maidens going to their wedding, I gaze upon you as they are being anointed.
Where Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is performed, there the streams of clarified butter flow all around.
Flow toward our excellent praise in the contest for cattle; bestow auspicious riches upon us.
Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods; the streams of clarified butter flow sweetly.
Oṃ, I offer consciousness with mind and clarified butter,
so that the gods, who increase the Truth and who are the perfect Hotṛs, may come hither;
I offer it for the Lord of the entire world.
To Viśvakarman, who is invincible at all times, [be] the oblation.
57. Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven the Ṛṣis, and seven your beloved abodes.
The seven hotṛ-priests sacrifice in seven ways;
fill the seven wombs with clarified butter, svāhā!
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again, O leader of wealth, may the Brahmans kindle you again with sacrifices.
Spreading yourself with clarified butter, do you cause us to increase; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.
You are the purifier of wealth, with a hundred streams; you are the purifier of wealth, with a thousand streams.
May Savitṛ purify you with the filter of Vasu, with its hundred streams and beautiful vessel, yielding all desires.
O full ladle, fly away; well-filled, fly back again.
Like two merchants at a market, let us barter food and strength, O Śatakratu! Svāhā!
(61) This is for Agni Vaiśvānara, for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, for Śatakratu, and for the Waters; obeisance!
"Om, this [offering] is for the three lords of the gods, for the incarnations, for the powers, and for the Supreme Brahman; Svāhā! Namas! (62).
Thus one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and offer what remains in the *sruva* ladle.
Then one should perform the rite for bestowing the triple life-span (*tryāyuṣakaraṇa*) by means of ritual placement (*nyāsa*):
"Oṃ, salutations, salutations" is the triple life-span of Jamadagni on the forehead;
"Oṃ, salutations, salutations" is the triple life-span of Kaśyapa on the neck. (63–64)
"Whatever triple longevity exists among the gods, [I place] at the base of the arms; salutation, salutation!
May that triple longevity be ours—thus [one should offer] salutation to Kṛṣṇa in the heart.
(65) Having thus offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) in the northeast.
And one should sprinkle the water from the *śānti* jar upon the patron and his family with Vedic mantras, using *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and mango sprouts:
"Oṃ! The waters are indeed our source of bliss; may they grant us strength. (66–67)
For the great battle, for seeing, and for the peace of the sacrificer—
may you cause us here to partake of that most auspicious sap of yours,
like longing mothers, for the prosperity of the sacrificer.
Therefore, we come gladly to you, for whose dwelling you quicken us;
O Waters, give birth to us for the satisfaction of the sacrificer.
May they be for our health, for our abundance of essence, and for our great longevity. (2.159.70)
O Bhaga, bestower of fortune, O Bhaga, whose gifts are true, O Bhaga, lift up our inspired thought for us.
O Bhaga, bringer of prosperity, cause us to be born with cattle and horses; O Bhaga, may we be possessed of heroes through those who bring prosperity.
O Waters, carry away this which is blameworthy and whatever is impure.

Whatever falsehood I have uttered against one who wronged me, and whatever harsh word I have spoken in anger—may the Waters and Pavamāna release me from that sin. Om! May the divine beings purify me; may they purify me with their mind and their wisdom.
May all beings purify [me]; O Jātavedas, purify me!
Increase, O Soma; let virility come to me from every side.
Be present for the sacrificer at the gathering of strength.
Grant your grace for great prosperity and for the welfare of my great-grandchildren and others.
Oṃ! May there be milk on the earth, milk in the plants, milk in the heavens, and milk in the mid-air;
may the quarters of space be full of milk for me, and may milk-rice be present in my house, not in the forest.
Oṃ! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan,
I place you— the fourth [part] of Sarasvatī’s speech— into the three worlds.
O Bṛhaspati, I consecrate you with sovereign power.

(77) Om! At the impulse of the divine Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the fourth instrument of Sarasvatī, Speech—I consecrate you, O Agni, with sovereign power. (78)

Oṃ! At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I sprinkle you with the healing medicine of the Aśvins for the sake of splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge. With the healing medicine of Sarasvatī, I sprinkle you for the sake of vigor and the enjoyment of food.
With the power of Indra, for strength, prosperity, and glory, I consecrate you.
(2.159.80) The vessel is made of *pālāśa* wood; with it he consecrates him for Brahman.
For the *pālāśa* is indeed Brahman; thus, by means of Brahman, he consecrates him. (8.1)
The Sāman is indeed the essence of all the Vedas;
he thus consecrates him with the essence of all the Vedas.
When he offers the oblations called *devakalpas*, the *kalpas* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
The vital breaths are indeed immortality; with immortality he thus consecrates him.
"For long life, for strength, for splendor, for good progeny, and for vigor—live then for a hundred autumns!"
Heaven is peace, the intermediate space is peace, the earth is peace, the waters are peace,
the plants are peace; the trees are peace, the Viśvedevas are peace, and Brahman is peace.
All is peace; peace indeed, peace alone.
May that peace be mine—the peace of the Supreme Brahman, the peace of the images, the peace beloved by Brahman; peace alone is peace. 84.
The Supreme Brahman is the Imperishable Brahman, Goloka, and Kṛṣṇa-Rādhikā;
likewise, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, this creation consisting of the gods and others, the creation of individual souls, the Śaktis, the goddesses, the Satyas, and the Sādhus. (85)
"May these [deities] consecrate you and grant you well-being and peace.
(86) Then the patron should indeed give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*):
a village, a herd of cows, land, or vehicles such as elephants and horses. (87)
I give you male and female servants, canopies and the like, vehicles, garments, ornaments, gold, silver, and so forth, as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Indeed, with water from a cow's tail, barley, tulasī, sesame, and a pair of kuśa grasses— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the portion given.]
And he should pray: "O Brahmin, may you be the bestower of eternal heaven.
Today my wealth, my birth, and my prosperity have become fruitful; whatever has been given according to my capacity, O giver of merit, be pleased with it. (2.159.89–90)
Whatever has been done by me, whether through knowledge or ignorance, that all may indeed become complete; by your grace, forgive me.
(9.1) And the Preceptor should speak to the devotee with the desire for [the attainment of] Puruṣottama.
May that which was deficient attain completeness; may everything bestow its full fruit.
Whatever was lacking in materials, lacking in ritual action, lacking in prescribed procedure, or born of negligence—may all that indeed become complete through the grace of Śrī Hari unto you.
Oṃ. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya with his unbroken wheel grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ Śrī! Splendor, longevity, and health—
One who performs the rite shines and is honored;
he obtains grain, wealth, cattle, the gain of many sons, and a long life of a hundred years. (95)
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle you again;
may the Brahmans, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] again with sacrifices.
Increase your body with clarified butter; may these [words] be true.
May the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled!
May the meanings of the mantras bear fruit; may his heart’s wishes be complete.
May there be the destruction of the intellect of his enemies, and may there be the prosperity of his friends.
One should also ask the gods for forgiveness, saying, "May they always remain gracious.
Having worshipped the fire and offered words of apology, one should dismiss it, saying:
"O Blessed One, go forth from the midst of the hearth to your own abode."
"Having taken the oblation, give it quickly to the gods; be gracious to me!
Go, go, O best of gods, to your own abode, O Supreme Lord;
go, O Consumer of Oblations, to where Brahmā and the other gods reside. (2.159.100)
"May all the hosts of gods depart, taking my offering,
for the sake of fulfilling their desired wishes and for the purpose of returning again.
(101) One should scatter unbroken rice grains and a handful of flowers upon all the installed deities.
"This very festival of installation is incomplete in terms of faith, materials, and so forth.
By the grace of the Brahmins and Viṣṇu, may the ritual be most complete for me. May those Brahmins be the embodiment of all sacrifice; may the rite be entirely complete in every respect."
They should speak without flaw and receive from him even more;
they should also accept food and speak again thereafter.
By remembering him and by uttering his name during acts such as austerity and worship—

I bow to Lord Hari, by whom that which is deficient immediately attains completeness. Whatever rite performed during sacrifices might fall away through negligence, may that indeed become complete through the remembrance of Śrī Hari; so may it be.
Salutations to Him whose essence is sacrifice, into whom offerings are poured four times, four times, twice, five times, and again twice.
Having caused a great feast to be prepared and having bestowed great gifts, [he offered it].
Having performed a supreme great festival, the patron should provide a feast;
having fed everyone, he should then present gifts.
He should also perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) in a river, the ocean, or a lake.

"Then all the gods come to the sacred fords for the avabhṛtha bath; thereafter, the avabhṛtha rite is performed for the sake of destroying all evil deeds. O Rādhikā, thus has this procedure for installation been described to you.
Thus has been described that which was spoken by the Blessed One regarding the body of the divine abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Installation of the Deity upon the Lion Throne in the Piṇḍikā, the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā and Nyāsas, the Invocation of the Life-force (Jīvāvāhana), the Ārātrika, the Homa, the Offering of the Pūrṇāhuti, the Benedictions, Peace-chants, and the Recitation of Auspiciousness; the Dismissal of the Deities, the Declaration of Completeness, and the Final Bath," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed speak that which was uttered by the Supreme Soul regarding the ritual procedure for the installation of the flagstaff with its golden pinnacle.
Having prepared a svastika mandala on the northern side of the pavilion itself, the preceptor, accompanied by the officiating priests, the patron, and others,
[should proceed] to that hut where the construction of the jars has been completed by the artisans.
Having gone there, having bathed the supreme jar with five jars,

and having consecrated it with the *manas-jūti* mantras, he should likewise offer the *bali* to the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), and after sipping water (*ācamana*) and sprinkling [the area] with oils; || 3–4 ||
Having worshipped [the image] with sandalwood paste and other offerings, having wrapped it with a triple-threaded cord, and having placed it upon the chariot,
one should lead it to the bathing pavilion while reciting propitiatory chants and the like.
Having established it on a seat known as *bhadra* within a *svastika* diagram, one should place it before that [altar].

He should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; having indeed anointed [the body] with ghee while reciting "Ghṛtaṃ ghṛtam," and having rubbed it with a paste of barley, lentils, and turmeric,
he should wash it with warm water, and then smear it with clay from an anthill.
Having bathed [the image] with scented water and likewise with four jars of pure water,
and having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers,
one should cover it with garments and recite the mantras for the rite of pacification (śānti).

Having arisen with the *svasti* mantra and circumambulated the pavilion clockwise, he led [the deity] to the western door, entered, and placed [the deity] upon an auspicious seat (*bhadra-āsana*) in the presence of the God. Then, having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings... (2.160.10)
Having filled [the vessels] with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, and having recited the *Viśvataḥśruti* mantra,
the preceptor, having performed the *saṃkalīkaraṇa*, should offer oblations of honey, milk, clarified butter, and curd one hundred and eight times individually into his own fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having performed [the rite] and poured the residual water (saṃsrava) into the *śānti* jar,
he should then touch his feet, navel, heart, and eyes with that water in succession while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, and thereafter place it back into the jar.
Having worshipped the pitcher and offered the *bali* offering as well as the temple itself,
he then ascends it; having washed his limbs with scented waters,
he performs the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments upon that summit of the temple.
Then, having brought the water-pot and rested for a moment, one should place it upon the ground at an auspicious hour while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra:
"Oṃ, smell the pot; may the gods and the drops enter into the earth. (15–16)
Having installed [the image] with the mantra: "Oṃ, return again with vigor; yielding a thousandfold, let the broad, milk-rich streams flow;
may wealth enter into me once more," one should wrap it with a cloth.
Having uttered "streṇa huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should then offer salutation.
One should then install a golden discus, a lotus, a trident, and a weapon.
Having firmly stabilized them, the artisan should likewise bathe them with water.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, and having descended below and prostrated,

one should give gifts of clothing, ornaments, silver, and so forth, according to one's ability. Likewise, one should cause food and other provisions to be given to the poor, the helpless, and the virtuous.
[This applies] to the families of Brahmin preceptors, to virtuous women, and to those practicing celibacy.
(2.160.20) Now, in the vicinity of the water-pot (kalaśa), a pillar of honor (mānastaṃbha) of great firmness [should be erected];
and there, a flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha) should also be installed according to the prescribed rite. (21)
The *mānastaṃbha* (pillar of pride) is indeed considered to be made of the heartwood of trees, born of the essence of stone, or even of iron;
it is adorned with leaves of *śiṃśapā* wood or copper, and is circular, horn-like, long, or otherwise as is appropriate. //22//
The staff, the pitcher, and the banner should indeed be made according to the measurement of the craftsman.
In the chapter of three hundred and nine verses, their measurements were described;
here, however, only the worship and the declaration of the fruits are intended.
In this worship, the mantras for the banner of the pavilion are to be understood;
both the worship and the fire-oblation are prescribed according to the ritual procedure pertaining to that [pavilion].
Indeed, the banner is the emblem of the Supreme Lord, yet it belongs to all the deities.
Seeing which, wicked beings may come to abide by the teaching;
the virtuous develop a disposition of devotion, and likewise, those of demonic nature feel fear.
A temple devoid of a banner must never be constructed anywhere on earth. (26–27)
For thousands of years, the donor is glorified in heaven;
by the weapon of shaking the banner, the donor’s sin is destroyed.
In whatever village, city, kingdom, or realm there is a banner—
There is no untimely death there, nor misfortune even among those who have committed sins.
There is no fear of calamities there, nor diseases, nor indeed any afflictions.
Adverse conditions do not exist there; there is an abundance of food and a bountiful harvest of crops.
The rain-cloud pours forth at its proper time, the milk-yielding cows abound with milk,
and those who perform the salutation of the banner become meritorious.
(3.1) The sight of the banner and the water-pot is entirely auspicious.
Likewise, the summit [of the temple] bestows auspiciousness and merit (32).
Through the sight of the flagstaff and other features, the sins of the wicked shall be pacified;
indeed, this occurs in relation to the temple, the image, the altar, the sacrificial pit, the flagstaff, and the water-pot (33).
For as many atoms as there are, for that many thousands of years they indeed rejoice in heaven, in eternal heaven, and in liberation— namely,
the sacrificer and all the others, by the grace of the Lord. (34)
I shall now describe briefly the installation of the image of Cala-mūrti as it is prescribed.
On the day of the installation, having constructed a pavilion, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and an altar in a pure location, one should then bring the image into the pavilion.
Having seated himself on a seat, restrained his breath, and marked the day,
he should then perform the formal declaration (*saṃkalpa*) for the sake of the installation and worship Gaṇeśa;
likewise, he should cause the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkārcana*) to be performed.
Then, having performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* and having chosen the preceptor (*guru*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),
one should honor four of them; the preceptor shall perform the installation of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-sthāpana*),
the establishment of the sacred fire (*agni-sthāpana*), the worship of the site (*vāstu-pūjana*), and the sacrifice to the planets (*graha-yajña*).

Then, in the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], one should invoke Brahmā and the other deities; one should worship them, establish them, and then prepare a sacrificial oblation (caru) of wild rice for the presiding deity.
Having cooked it and performed the offering to the planets at the conclusion of the portion of clarified butter, one should proceed with the fire-sacrifice (grahahoma).
One should offer one hundred and eight *samidhs* of *pālāśa* wood and other such woods for each deity individually,
using the mantras of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and others;
or alternatively, one may perform the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* and likewise carry out the *ājya-homa*.
Having offered ten oblations each of fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, and clarified butter to the installed deities, and likewise having offered one hundred and eight oblations to Sviṣṭakṛt,
he should offer sacrifices with the mantras of the principal deities and bow to the Lord.

One should say, "Welcome, O Lord of all gods; we indeed offer you a place here. Then, having raised [the deity] with auspicious mantras saying "Arise," and having placed him upon the altar, one should bathe him with the five products of the cow and the five nectars while reciting the mantras.
Having performed the anointing with ghee, the rubbing with unguents, and so forth, as well as the bathing with jars and other rites,
and having seated him upon the pedestal,
one should place water-pitchers all around and scatter perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains.
In the first *kumbhaka*, [one places] seven types of earth; in the second, auspicious sprouts;
in the third, the seven grains; and then in the fourth, *kuśa* grass.
In the fifth, however, there is water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*), the five jewels (*pañcaratna*), and fruits.
One should scatter flowers into the downward-flowing water on the sixth day, and likewise barley grains;
on the seventh day one should pour in the "sampāta" (remnant) water, and indeed on the eighth day,
having well-poured all the medicinal herbs with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Having bathed [the image] with the *hiraṇyavarṇā* mantras and also with the *pavamāna* hymns,
and having offered two garments and a sacred thread (*upavīta*),
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and lamps made of flour.
Having placed honey and clarified butter in a golden vessel, one should then recite the mantras and apply them to the right and left eyes with a golden probe:
*oṃ citraṃ devānām udagād anīkam*.
The eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
Om! You are brilliance, you are pure light, you are immortality; you are the name of the abodes, the beloved of the gods, the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods. 53.
One should anoint the image with the mantra "añjanti tvā adhvaram.
One may also anoint it with honey, ghee, and sugar.
With the mantra "devasya tvā savituḥ," one should apply the collyrium.
One should show him various kinds of food and mirrors, but one must not look at them oneself.
Having offered a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born and others, one should offer praise.
Then, having placed food endowed with the five colors into a bamboo vessel over a fire, [one should proceed]. 55–56.
One should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the deity with food at a crossroads for Rudra;
one should offer it saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, svāhā! May this rite be auspicious.
Having offered the *bali* oblation upon an *aśvattha* leaf with the words "obeisance to the spirits," [one should proceed].
Having sipped water (ācamya) and worshipped the deities of the mandala in the central mandala,
one should say, "Be established," seat the deity, and worship him.
One should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter ten times into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) while reciting the names of the deities.
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed from the north of the mandala,
he should prepare a bed upon a swastika-patterned couch with the "uttiṣṭha" mantras.
Then, sitting upon that bed, he should recite the *Sahasrasūkta*.
One should perform the ritual placements (*nyāsa*): "Salutation to the Self of Puruṣa at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head);
salutation to the Self of Prāṇa at the mouth; to the form of Prakṛti at the throat; to the principle of Buddhi at the heart; and salutation to Ahaṃkāra at the belly. (61–62)

Salutation to the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*) in the secret place and so forth, and to the mind (*citta*) in the feet; salutation to the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*) in the bladder, and indeed to the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*) in the nose;
salutation to the principle of sound (*śabda-tattva*) in the ears, and to the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*) in the body.
Salutations to the principle of form in the eyes, and to the principle of taste in the tongue;
salutations to the principle of speech in the voice, and to the principle of the hand in the two hands;
salutations to the principle of the foot in the feet, and to the principle of the anus in the anus.
Having performed the worship, one should offer salutations to the Earth at the feet; to the water element at the abdomen; to the fire element at the heart;
to the air element at the nose; and to the space element in the ether.
"Salutations again and again to the principle of qualities (guṇatattva) in the form [of the deity] and to the instruments (karaṇas).
Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsas) with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, he should then say,
'Be one who sleeps happily,' and thus lay the Lord upon the bed."
Having worshipped him, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsa) and present offerings to the deity.
There, one should offer all kinds of food to Brahmā, ghee-rice to the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra),
water to Agni, ghee-rice to Yama, and black-gram-rice to Yama.
One should offer black rice with clarified butter to Nirṛti;
fresh butter-rice to Varuṇa; barley-rice to Vāyu; millet-rice to Kubera; and milk-porridge to Īśāna. (2.160.70–71)
One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to all [the deities], as well as an oblation of wild rice (*naivāra-caru*).
Having set this out, one should present the *bali* offering to the deities of the mandala.
Then, one should pass the night; and having risen in the morning, [one should perform the rites] with the root mantras.
Having cooked the *caru* and sprinkled it with clarified butter, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, and likewise with the names of the deities:
"Svāhā to Agni, to Soma, and to Dhanvantari in his own form. (73–74)
Hail to Kuhū and to Anumati; hail to Prajāpati, the Lord of Creatures;
hail to Agni, whose nature is that of Parameṣṭhin, the Supreme Creator;
hail to Soma; hail to Agni; hail to Food, to Agni.
Svāhā to Agni, the Lord of Food; and Svāhā to Prajāpati.
Svāhā to the Viśvedevas; and Svāhā to all beings.
Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt; obeisance.
At sunrise, having placed the Guru upon the altar facing the deity, and having displayed gems, flowers, and so forth, as well as roots, fruits, and medicinal herbs,
he should take the water of pacification (*śāntijala*) in a copper vessel.
One should consecrate [the deity] ten times with the principal mantra of the deity (pradhānadevamantreṇa).
Having sprinkled water upon the head of the deity, one should cause him to rise with the mantra "Oṃ uttiṣṭha.
One should then mutter "viśvataścakṣuḥ" and so forth, bowing again and again. (2.160.80)
Salutations again and again to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; salutations to the guardians of the quarters.
Salutations to the Vasus, and salutations again and again to the Rudras and Ādityas.
Salutations again and again to the two Aśvins, to the Maruts, and to Kubera.
Salutations to the great rivers, to Agni and Soma, and to Heaven and Earth.
Salutations to Indra and Agni, to Dhanvantari, and to the Lord of All.
Salutations to Brahmā, to the Viśvedevas, and to the Supreme Brahman.
Having thus recited [the mantra] and consecrated the patron, one should meditate upon the deity. Then,
having offered a handful of flowers to the installed deity with the *Puruṣasūkta*,
the *Gāyatrī*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the sacred mantras, [one should proceed].
Having first installed the deity within the image, one should thereafter perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the consecration of the vital breaths). Listen, O Rādhikā, to how this is done:
for this mantra known as *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, there are three sages (*ṛṣis*).
The deities are the three Vedas and the meters; likewise, the body consists of the ritual action.
The deity is named Prāṇa, the seed-syllable is *Āṃ*, and the application of power is *Krauṃ*.
Indeed, in the rite of the installation of vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should offer salutations to the sages at the head.
To the meters, [one offers] in the mouth; to the deity, in the heart, [saying] "namaḥ.
To the seed-syllable *āṃ*, [one says] "namaḥ" in the secret place; to the power (*śakti*), *krauṃ*, in the feet, [saying] "namaḥ.
*Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ*—to the five elements, *āṃ*, in the heart, [one says] "namaḥ. (88–89)
Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, obeisance to the subtle elements (tanmātras); īṃ ca ke svāhā.
Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ oṃ, obeisance to those who produce knowledge; oṃ śikhāyai vauṣaṭ.
O taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ eṃ, obeisance to those who perform actions; eṃ kavacāya huṃ.
Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ; obeisance to the actions (karmas), Oṃ! To the three eyes, Vauṣaṭ!
|| 9.1 || Oṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ; Oṃ! Obeisance to the internal [senses], Aḥ! To the weapon, Phaṭ!
Having thus performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) upon oneself and the deity,
and having touched the deity, one should then recite the mantra:
*oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ*.
The breaths of the deity are here, the breaths.
Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Krauṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Vaṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Saḥ.
The life-force (*jīva*) of the deity is stationed here. ॥93॥
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ, [I invoke] all the sense organs of the deity.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ, [I invoke] the inner [being] of the deity.
"The vital breaths and the organs are established here.
Having come here for well-being, may they indeed remain for a long time, Svāhā!
Having touched the heart [of the image] with the thumb, one should recite the mantra over the image as prescribed. (94–96)
"May her vital breaths be established; may her vital breaths move within her.
Let no one whatsoever cause harm to this deity for the sake of the image.
Having thus restrained [the breath] with the *praṇava* and meditated upon it as truly alive, ||| 96 ||
Having recited the mantra "oṃ dhruvā dyauḥ" and the Gāyatrī verse into the ear, and having touched the feet, navel, and head with the Puruṣasūkta verses, [one should say]:
"Welcome, O Supreme Lord; may you remain firm here for a long time."
"O Lord of Gods, as long as the moon, the earth, and the sun remain unimpeded, so long should you remain here out of compassion for your devotees.
[Perform worship] with the *Puruṣasūkta* and the sixteen *upasad* substances."
Having honored [the deity] and removed the bracelets, as well as the ornaments and weapons from the image;
having meditated upon the vehicle and the retinue and displayed the mudrās;
and having worshipped with the root mantra and recited it one hundred and eight times.

Having offered praise and prostrated, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should complete the rite ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having concluded the ritual and bestowed the gift of a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*),
one should perform the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and the festival, and finally partake of the meal at the conclusion of the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having caused [the image] to be made and having performed the rite, one should personally carry out the ritual.
In this way, one should indeed perform the installation of a mobile [image] during the month of Mādhava.
Thus spoke the Blessed One regarding the body of the temple of the deity.
The procedure for the renovation of a temple whose paint and other features have decayed is considered here in brief:
having constructed an auspicious pavilion with its entrance facing west in the south-western corner of the site,
one should then place a single archway in the center.
Having constructed a circular or square altar (vedī) in the west,
and likewise a Vāstu-pīṭha in the north consisting of a sand mound,
one should proclaim the place and time for the sake of purifying the defects of decay.
One should reflect, "I shall perform the rite for the purpose of extraction.

Then, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana), and the worship of the Mothers (mātṛkārcana); having performed the Nāndī-śrāddha and chosen the Guru, one should thereafter worship them.
Then, having performed the consecration of the pavilion and likewise the worship of Vāstu, one should place the deities upon the Sarvatobhadra diagram and that seat upon the pedestal.
Having worshipped it, [one should say]: "O God of gods, O Vyāpakeśvara, salutations to you!"
*Hṛdayāya namaḥ svāhā*, *Śirase śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*,
*Kavacāya huṃ*, *Astrāya phaṭ*— [these are for] the pervasive wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should worship with the root mantra and recite it one hundred and eight times.
Having established the fire and offered oblations up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* portions, one should present the bali offering.
Then, having worshipped the worn-out deity with the *praṇava*, one should pray as follows:
"O God of gods, you whose skin has grown old and whose form has become decrepit, [forgive] this worn-out and broken [image]."
I shall extract this worn-out body here; grant me forgiveness, have mercy!
Go to your approved abode—either by the side of the image or into the unmanifest (akṣara). After the restoration of the dilapidated [temple], you may indeed depart once again for your arrival.
Taking the nightly lamp-offering, the food, the worship,
and the drinking water— all of it— and carrying them away with compassion to another place,
O Viṣṇu, go to your own desired abode, accompanied by all the gods.
Having spoken thus, one should offer [the image] while forming a *añjali* with flowers and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Then, having again performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other rites, one should worship it.
Furthermore, in the rites for the consecration of dilapidated [images], one should feed Brahmins and others.
"One who causes the expansion of a temple for a deity attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(1.18) Thus, O Rādhikā, Hari—the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—spoke to the deity; and likewise have I related this to you. (1.19)

From hearing this, from reciting it, and from the construction of a temple, one shall obtain the fruit of the rite of restoration (*uddhāra*) and the fruit of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ascending of the Vessel (*kalaśārohaṇa*), the Erection of the Pillar of Honor (*mānastaṃbha*), the Installation of the Mobile Image (*calamūrti*), the Rite of Restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*), and so forth," in the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*. (2.160)
← Chapter 160: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 161 [[Author: → Chapter 162
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, that divine devotee, the sage Devāyatanaka, having heard [this], was filled with wonder and worshipped Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 1.
Having performed the supreme *ārārtrika* rite, he became deeply immersed in love and attained great perfection;
then, by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself,
he spontaneously became a divine temple endowed with a thousand pitchers.
Endowed with all the primary marks and possessing all limbs in their full perfection,
he is present in person during service, being joined with all modes of attendance;
yet even while existing apart from these, he remains as one who bears a liberated form.
That palace became renowned and was worshipped by the gods and others.
Seeing it, Indra resolved to have one built equal to it.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he showed him that masterpiece.
Then he gave the command to construct a magnificent palace in Amarāvatī.
Viśvakarmā, having practiced his craft upon a ground marked with saffron syllables,
then went to heaven and fashioned a peak adorned with a thousand finials.

He installed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, together with his six wives amidst great festivities. Thereafter, temples indeed began to be constructed throughout all the worlds.
In every place, there is indeed a divine being who is the path for the gods among them.
(9) Thus, humans, as well as the gods residing in Pātāla and those dwelling in Satyaloka, come to behold this divine temple. (2.161.10)
Having beheld the Kuṃkumavāpikā field adorned with temples, men and women rejoice and rest in great happiness. Indeed,
having heard from the assembly of Kapardin that the temple is worthy of being seen...
People came from as far as the ocean, eager to see [him].
(12) Even Dhīvara, the fisherman, who lived on the shore of the western sea, hearing [the news], went out from his house with his family to see him. (13)
Having seen the auspicious Vastrāpatha on the road, he went to the goddess Turī,
who was seated in bodily form within a pavilion of tree-shade;
she was the virtuous lady dwelling in a temple on the bank of the Jīvantikā river.
Seeing her standing in the midst of a mango grove, frequented by wood-gatherers and others,
providing shelter to the forest-dwellers, bestowing peace upon those who live in the woods,
seated upon the back of an elephant, four-armed, and beloved by Hari; || 15–16 ||
Having gone near her— who was an embodiment of a portion of Lakṣmī, rich in purity, and worshipped with fruits, flowers, and other offerings—
he stood before her with extreme devotion, his body covered in wealth. He bathed in a river, in a lake, and on the ground beneath a mango tree.
Then, having set aside all the requisites for the journey,
he took up cool water, campaka flowers,
excellent ripe fruits of immortality, and tulasī.
He went indeed to the temple to worship the goddess named Turī Lakṣmī;
together with his family, he prostrated himself in the presence of that deity.
He offered praise according to the prescribed rites to her who protects the forest-dwellers.
He worshipped her with supreme devotion using fruits, flowers, water, and other offerings.
"O Mother! O Mother! O Mahālakṣmī, O Greatly Virtuous One!
That which was given by me in the forest has been brought here; please accept it today. Salutations to you! (21–22)
Be gracious for the sake of my journey and burn away my impurity.
O beloved of Hari, you are the purifier of fishermen; deliver me!
Since I am low-born and utterly impure, I do not know how to perform worship.
Considering your pure heart offered to me, accept this nectar.
Grant me wisdom, as well as devotion, and grant me liberation worthy of me. Bestow upon me, together with my retinue, that which is most auspicious.
Having spoken thus and bowing repeatedly, he swept the temple;
having cast out the dry leaves and removed the dust and other debris,
he washed the temple as well as the broom with water.
He sprinkled it with water and performed a circumambulation.
Taking many fresh leaves and flowers,
he fashioned a gateway and a garland, which he offered as an act of worship.
Having observed that very place to be a peaceful refuge, he stayed there for the night;
and seeing wild food such as fruits, he remained for the next day.
On the third day as well, he stayed and obtained great rest.

Constantly, as if in their own home, they perform all the rites for the Goddess with excellent worship; in the forest, they carry out purification, service, and so forth with true devotion. Indeed, at night, the members of the family perform their adoration with their voices raised.
Having kindled a fire to dispel the cold for the sake of ending their chill,
they gathered together in the palace of that goddess;
thus, O Rādhikā, having passed the night, on the following day—
Taking various kinds of flowers and garments,
they prepare those very flowers for Lakṣmī and offer them:
a crown, blossoms for the ears, ear-ornaments, and a beautiful bodice.
Having prepared a sār̤ī, a girdle, a garland, a cluster of flowers, a waist-belt, as well as sandals and a small bell, they offer them;
and having brought fragrant, sweet honey situated upon a tree.
They offer many delicious foods to the Goddess.
Having gathered auspicious sandalwood from within the forest,
they prepare fragrant incense and serve it with devotion.
"O Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, O Mother Lakṣmī, obeisances unto you!
Thus they constantly perform worship within the forest, in the house of the Turyā [the fourth state].
Although Lakṣmī, who is of the nature of the Turyā state, is invisible, she accepts their worship. (38)
By her very nature of service, she became entirely devoted;
though remaining within the form [of the deity], she partook of the nectar, the honey, and the fruits, drank the cool water, and wore those garlands. (2.161.39–40)
He took up flower-garments and accepted incense with devotion;
he received all the service performed by the devotees while present in the forest.
Thus, even though he was a fisherman possessed of great wealth, he remained together with his family.
He obtained security and well-being in the forest by way of his pilgrimage.
With a pure inner heart, he dwelt joyfully for fifteen days in that forest near the temple of Turyā.
Through the perfection of his daily worship and other rites,
he acquired abundant merit and attained manifold sanctity by the grace of Goddess Lakṣmī.
On the night of the full moon of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, when the moon was positioned at the head [of the zodiac], || 44 ||
He performed a kīrtana with his family members using a mṛdaṅga drum,
in that tranquil royal assembly hall during the pure portion of the night, which was as white as the nectar of the cool-rayed moon and adorned with forest trees and other beauties.
Together with his wife, daughters, and sons, he sang a song;
hearing that sweet melody directly before him, Turī became manifest.
She was exceedingly beautiful, her limbs and every part richly adorned with various forms and splendors.
With a serene countenance, holding a lotus in her hand,
she is adorned with ornaments of jewels and gold, wearing divine garments and the like;
she shines with a splendor surpassing the combined luster of ten million full moons of autumn.
Seated upon the back of the white elephant, that enchanting lady said to him, "Accept this boon; I am pleased with you. "O devotee, you have made your dwelling here in my temple within the forest."
"Service has been performed by you in many ways, as if it were your own home.
Choose a boon—blessings upon you! Name whatever you desire and I shall grant it.
Even for this single instance of sweeping my house here," ||| 51-52 ||
Poverty shall perish, and one shall attain the divine heaven;
by lighting a lamp even once in my abode for a long duration,
the fruit shall be the attainment of the world of the Sun for a thousand yugas.
By offering Tulasī to my head even once,
I grant him the status of a universal emperor (cakravartin) and lasting prosperity.
By offering flowers, garlands, and the like, I grant him golden ornaments.
By offering fruit even once,
I indeed bestow the eternal nectar, the celestial realm of Indra, and the radiant station. By giving water even once, I grant the domain of Varuṇa.
By the surrender of myself, I give my entire being and my eternal abode.
My Lord is the direct, beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa;
I bestow upon this high-souled devotee of mine the prosperity belonging to Him.
I accept what is offered to me and then offer it to my Lord;
ever devoted to His service, I always partake of that grace.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the glorious Puruṣottama.
Through my service, the Blessed One becomes prosperous and gracious.
(2.161.60) Just as I am dear to Him, and just as Māṇikī is dear to Him, so too is the devotee dear to Me; the Lord gives abundantly to him. (61)
“O Dhanamjaya, you are pure because I am pleased with you.
Choose whatever is in your heart; I shall grant it according to your husband’s desire.
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, within a moment, that Dhanamjaya—
Having attained supreme wonder and having found happiness and the highest joy,
he chose servitude for his mother along with her family;
he did not desire wealth, nor kingdom, nor sovereign power.
O Dhana, you are blessed! In servitude, everything proceeds for one’s benefit;
yet such sincere service toward a master is difficult to find in this world.
Indeed, servants long for such service throughout millions of lifetimes in saṃsāra.
Indeed, countless slaves for one’s own self-interest exist throughout the three worlds.
But slaves for the Heart (hārdadāsa) are truly rare; therefore, become here my slave for the Heart.
For within the state of being a slave for the Heart, the perfections and sovereign powers always abide for the sake of accomplishment.
In servitude to the Deceiver, those who steal one's passion exist as mere afflictions;
therefore, one must here perform service that delights the heart, so that I may become a handmaid of Nārāyaṇa, O Lotus-born One. (68)
Just as Pārvatī Satī is here the maidservant of Śiva;

as Prabhā is the maidservant of the Sun, and Padmāvatī is the maidservant of Hari; and just as Māṇikī is the maidservant [of the Moon], Rādhā is the maidservant of Hari, and Jayā is the maidservant of Hari. (2.161.70)
Just as Mañjulā, Haṃsā, and Suguṇā are the maidservants of Hari;
and Lalitā, Akṣarabrahmā, and Garuḍa are likewise His servants—
so too, O God, perform service just as the monkey Hanumān did.
"Just as one says 'the winter slave' or 'the spring slave,' so too these [souls] become slaves of Hari in every kalpa. Therefore,
obtain servitude unto me and my Lord, Śrī Puruṣottama."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kaṃbhārā,
dwells there in human form wherever you go—
in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, in the vicinity of Lomaśa’s hermitage.
In that celestial palace, Śrīkānta shines resplendent;
there, even millions of Lakṣmīs like myself are radiant, filled with bliss through service to him who possesses all heroic power. (75–76)
O devotee, serve that auspicious and beloved field named Kuṅkumavāpikā; all its fruits, endowed with prosperity, shall be granted to you.
Take forest flowers and various kinds of fruits as well.
"Entrust [it] to the Lord there and offer salutations on my behalf.
By His command, I myself abide here at the western boundary of the sacred field in the form of Turī, while Kamalā herself is the Kṣetrapāla. || 78-79 ||
"I indeed serve Kṛṣṇa eternally with my invisible form;
go quickly to Mānasa, and your desire will be fulfilled there.
Having spoken thus, that Turī-Lakṣmī dissolved into the image.
Intoxicated with joy by his wealth, he went with his family in delight to the Kuṅkumavāpī tank during the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
Beholding again and again the gardens and groves, he indeed attained great happiness. (81–82)
Having gazed repeatedly upon the hermitage of Lomaśa, whose dwelling was situated in the sky;
having beheld the beloved abodes of Brahmā and observed the Aśvasaras lake;
and having seen hundreds of thousands of palatial mansions and temples of the gods.
Beholding the divine sacred sites, he rejoiced as his wealth and fatness diminished.
At every station, he and his family performed prostrations like a staff.
Then, to behold the Great Abode (Mahālaya), whose beauty was revealed by Lakṣmī, he departed.
Therein shines the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is beginningless,
resplendent with a crown and ornaments possessing the brilliance of ten million suns;
the Blessed One, whose every limb is proportioned to His form, [is served] by Lakṣmī and others.
Śrī Hari himself, who is served by the gods, the liberated souls, and others, was served [by him].
They did not merely prostrate before Kṛṣṇa like a staff; they offered lamps of ghee and worshipped Him personally with flowers, fruits, and heartfelt sentiments. (87-88)

He drank the water for washing the feet and held the image in his heart. Having received hospitable treatment, including a welcome and other courtesies, and having also obtained food, he took his rest. (89)
In the evening, he went to the bank of Lake Aśvasaras to perform his ritual ablutions at sacred fords;
and during the night, he dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree on the shore. By virtue of his innate nature, he had preferred to stay upon the bank.
At night he performed worship and the chanting of the names of Hari.
In the morning, by his natural disposition, he saw Rohita fish;
seeing them, beautifully adorned with the marks of the discus, he then set his mind upon catching them.
Having gone to the shore, he cast a line with a hook into the waters.
Hari himself, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a fish,
took the hook in his mouth and came under its control.
Through the increase of his merit, the fish attained great size;
in an instant, he became Padmavān, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Beholding that magnificent form, the devotee was then filled with shame.
Hari said: "O fisherman, abandon your own nature and take refuge in me.
By the words of blessing from Lakṣmī and by a fragment of her grace, I have come to you.
Accept my service; go and bring Lomaśa and the mantra. (96–97)
"Be a Vaiṣṇava; stay here and likewise perform service for me, just as you have seen my four-armed form here as a fish.
This is my Matsya-tīrtha, where I exist in the form of the Fish incarnation."
"I have come before your eyes for your sake; accept me.
Fishermen, the givers of fish, surely become affectionate toward the fish.
In the form of a fish, I shall grant you liberation; accept me. (2.161.100)
"Having assumed the form of a fish here beneath the banyan tree, worship me;
this is my holy ford (*tīrtha*) of the Fish Incarnation, which destroys all sins. On the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara lies this auspicious place that bestows both heaven and liberation."
"It will especially grant lordship to the fishermen.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished. Then Dhanameda quickly went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having obtained the mantra, a garland of *tulasī*, and the status of a Vaiṣṇava servant—
