There, the brahmin guest named Ṣaḍguṇa spoke to him.
"Accept from me the mantra of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā'.
Thus did the one endowed with the six divine qualities bestow this mantra upon that farmer.
He gave a beautiful-necked Tulasī plant and named him Nārāyaṇa;
he gave him a garland for the purpose of chanting, as well as an image for the purpose of beholding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

For the purpose of chanting upon the rosary, he then gave them all the name "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. Thereafter, they set out in the morning and arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī, at the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
They also constructed Aśvapaṭṭasara and the Sahasraghaṭa temple;
thereafter, they established gardens and all the sacred fords (tīrthas). Then they all went to Narāyaṇa Bālakṛṣṇa, who was shining within his palace.
Having duly worshipped the holy ford (tīrtha), they returned to their own country.
Dyuviśrāma, the farmer, filled with joy,
set out from the city of Kāmyaka with his family for the purpose of a pilgrimage after due reflection.
Accompanied by cows and bulls, he arrived at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, eagerly chanting the names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
while grazing the cows and bulls in the forest, he reached that place in the evening. (64–65)
He took rest for the night on the eastern bank of the lake;
having given water to the cows and the bulls, he let them loose under the shelter of trees. Those animals stayed happily nearby.
At night, those beasts and humans fell under the power of sleep;
through that sound slumber, they dispelled their exhaustion from the journey.
Free from fear, they slept on the bank of the lake in that sacred place.
When midnight had passed, when the movement of men had ceased,
when the noise of the village was hushed, and when the beasts and birds were overcome by sleep,
a pride of seven lions arrived from the tiger-infested forest.
Suddenly, that most terrifying being seized the bulls;
the cows and the bulls also let out cries of distress and loud bellowing.
Hearing their lamentations, the people quickly became aware of what was happening.
And they remembered the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, for the sake of protection;
the devotee indeed remembered Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa within his heart:
"Come, O Blessed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the one higher than the highest!"
O abode of all living beings, protect, rescue, and preserve us!
(73) The wealth of cattle is my strength, for I am weak and a farmer;
if these are destroyed by lions, I, your servant, shall become miserable. (74)
Act quickly, O Great King, before they are attacked;
for if they are assaulted, neither your cows nor your bulls will survive.
These animals entrusted to your protection are no longer truly mine.
"O Blessed One, you yourself protect [me]; drink the milk as is fitting.
O Great King, I shall give you cows; quickly protect and guard them.
Having spoken thus, he took a large log that had been burnt by fire and was still smoldering.
The devoted one stood there, having forcibly lifted himself up in the presence of the lions.
The lions, however, let out roars again and again with terrifying sounds;
that entire lake and field was filled with those roaring, fearful noises.

And all embodied beings, deprived of sleep by the roarings and other sounds, fled here and there, inside and out, afflicted by fear. Seeing that great log of wood with fire, the lions were filled with terror. (2.163.80)

The cows did not indeed come into his presence; filled with fear, they abandoned the causeway to the lake and fled far away. Behind them, the lions ran, but once they had gone a great distance, the cows stopped.
The best of devotees wept, as did the animals who were devoid of knowledge.
Overwhelmed by the lion-like thunderbolt, he cried out, "What shall I do here?
Meanwhile, Bālakṛṣṇa, the protector of his devotees and a treasure-house of compassion, [remained present].
In an instant, the divine Lord became a cowherd boy bearing a discus;
shouting with joy, Kṛṣṇa released his formidable discus.
Moving with speed and whirling, the discus struck down the circle of lions.
Wherever the touch of the lions' claws occurred at that time—
whether it was the tearing of the skin or the breaking [of bones] caused by the lions— he touched those very parts of the animals' bodies with his own hand. (85–86)
The compassionate Lord Hari quickly dispelled the pain in an instant;
by the mere touch of his hand, he restored the joining of the skin to its former state,
such that no trace of nail-marks remained.
Indeed, blood flowed from here and there even from the new [wounds] of Śrī Hari;
yet, through the touch of his hand, not even a drop of blood flowed.
Just as the body of a god is free from disease, so indeed were those [limbs]. || 88–89 ||
He fashioned the bodies of cows and bulls,
protected the wealth of cattle in this manner, and then sounded his flute.
Having gone into the presence of the devotee, he gladdened the devotee.
Suddenly hearing that the wealth of the gods had been taken by Vaṃśī, the child-harasser,
the Blessed Lord, bearing the discus, arrived quickly at the shore of the lake near Dyuviśrāma and sat upon the seat offered to him.
The bulls gathered together and licked the lotus feet of Hari;
the cows, emitting streams of milk, made a lowing sound.
At that time, the devotee, having caused the Lord Hari to be milked, [offered] the milks.
He caused [her] to drink beautiful, sweet, and excellent milk repeatedly.
Praising the milk offered by his devotee, the Blessed One drank it.
He held a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in his four hands.
He revealed his own form in the likeness of the incarnation of Hari;
he granted liberation from the lions to them and sent them to Vaikuṇṭha. He likewise granted heaven to their wife, their sons, daughters, and the entire family.
Having displayed his divine form, Hari quickly vanished.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, in the middle of the night,
Bālakṛṣṇa protected the cows from lions.
On the twelfth day, the devotee gave various kinds of gifts and worshipped Śrīpati Puruṣottama with sincere devotion. Then Dyuviśrāma gave wealth in cattle to Bālakṛṣṇa.
Hari returned [the cows], and even though he was a devotee, he rejoiced exceedingly. By Hari’s command, having recovered the cows, he went to his own city of Kāmyaka.
That sacred ford became known as Haritīrtha, and it also became famous as Gotīrtha.
Thus, the farmers had a temple for Hari constructed there,
and they installed the four-armed Supreme Lord Hari.
Being eager, they also established Bālakṛṣṇa and the cows there.
From hearing and reciting this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall likewise come to pass.
(103) A gift of a cow should be given there in the southeast corner;
then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa will become pleased. (104)

"O Rādhikā, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of mercy, shall indeed provide protection for the pilgrim from the messengers of Yama, as well as for the giver of cows and the giver of bulls. (1.05) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of Hari-tīrtha and Go-tīrtha," wherein the Lord, in the form of Hari, protected the cattle of the farmer named Dyuviśrāma— which had been attacked by lions— during the second section, the Tretā-santāna, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
One hundred and sixty-third chapter.
Chapter 163: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 164.
[Author: Chapter 165.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen now to another marvel of Hari.
In the city named Bakasrāva, situated in a tiger-infested forest,
densely crowded with many trees, inhabited by ascetics and holy men,
filled with people of the four castes, and located on the bank of the river Vṛkaśāvī.
A man named Nīlakarṇa lived with his family in the Cātvāla forest;
however, due to excessive rain in the great wilderness, the river flooded and the city was submerged on all sides, along with its people and animals. (3)
The food is spoiled and dead; no edible thing can be found anywhere.
(4) Due to seven days of rain, the land appears like the ocean;
the paths are blocked for travel, and one cannot go from village to village. (5)
This Cātvāla, together with his family, hangs from the branches of trees;
having bound pieces of wood with creepers, he lives upon swings made from the branches.
His family as well lives upon the swings among the branches.
It became hungry and death drew near.
And the great seer Vṛkāyana, established in a state of meditative absorption,
was carried by the waves and arrived in the vicinity of the tree.
Then, having encircled it with a long rope from the sacrificial pit (cātvāla) and a branch,
he was confined there beneath the tree, obstructed by the trunk of the tree.
Slowly descending from the tree via the sacrificial pit, Vṛkāyana—

Seized by his matted locks and suspended upon a branch, his body exceedingly weak, he remained utterly absorbed in meditative concentration; he was not even aware of the rain, the carrying away [of the tree], or his imprisonment by the tree. (2.164.10–11)
Touched repeatedly by the sacrificial pit (cātvāla), shaken at his head,
and awakened by many sounds, the sage indeed attained consciousness.
Then he understood that all this was water resulting from excessive rain.
He quickly performed worship of the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
"O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Son of the Cowherd, Lord of Lakṣmī, Son of Śrī Kaṃbharā! (13–14)
O Keśava, who manifested yourself in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
O Lord of Brahmapriyā, O Consort of Ramā, O Lord of Padmaja;
O Lord of the virtuous, O All-pervading One, O Sovereign of the Imperishable Abode, O Supreme Lord! (15)
"Protect, protect the people, O Kṛṣṇa, who are deeply distressed by this excessive rain!
(16) "Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Thus did Vṛkāyana perform worship and offer this prayer. (17)
At that moment, out of great affection for him, the supreme Lord Bālakṛṣṇa arrived by way of the sky, mounted upon a white elephant,
with a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands, and a crown upon his head. (18)
He wore the Vaijayantī garland around his neck and the Sudarśana ring upon his finger.
His face was graced with a gentle smile, and his beautiful eyes shed showers of love.
He was equipped with a chest filled with foodstuffs and caskets containing woolen garments and other fine things.
Served by two attendants resplendent with parasols and chowries,
Kṛṣṇa arrived from the path of the sky and, having settled himself upon a branch within the tree, [took] from the two caskets... [of his own child].
At that very moment, the Blessed Lord himself gave food to Vṛkāyana;
he indeed gave full provisions and garments to Nīlakaṇa and to the family of Nīlakaṇa.
Having seen Hari and seeing that his family was left without refuge, Nīlakarṇa then beheld Nārāyaṇa directly through the power of virtuous yoga;
he indeed became one who had accomplished his purpose and partook of the food born of divine grace.
He offered food and garments, for the cold had departed by then.
Vṛkāyana, the great sage, repeatedly bowed down to Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord,
and indeed offered a hymn of praise to Hari.
Then he performed worship with the leaves of the *śāla* tree;
with the waters of the rain and his own mental dispositions, he worshipped the Supreme Lord,
by whom protection had been granted at the beginning of the creation of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.

By you, protection was granted to me here; salutations again and again to you! (28) By you, through whom protection was previously granted to Satyavrata in the ocean, by you, protection has been granted to me here; salutations again and again to you! (29)
By whom, in the past, protection was indeed afforded to many during the churning of the ocean;
by whom the gods were protected and the Daityas were struck down;
and by whom the earth was milked and living beings were protected in ancient times.
By whom the earth situated at the bottom of the ocean was indeed protected in the past;
by whom this cosmic egg was purified with the water from his big toe—by you, he has provided protection for me here; salutations be to you!
By whom Dhruva and Prahlāda were protected as children in the past;
by whom the demon Sāṇa was slain here, that Supreme Soul;
by whom the daughter of the king was protected and liberated when she had come for refuge.
By that Supreme Self by whom the Daitya Damanaka was liberated,
by whom Kaṅka, Tāla, and the denizens of hell were likewise delivered,
and by whom Sālamāla was destroyed— by him I have been protected. (34–35)
By him the children were liberated, the kingdom was released from its mother,
the creeper was deprived [of its support], the cowrie shell was destroyed,
and the lords of the forest and others were freed from their state as demons. (36)
The deliverance from the womb of a *caṇḍāla* to the path of the gods was accomplished by him;
even Cirajīvin was made to wear a patched garment by him.
By that son who went to the field of battle, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was rescued. (37–38)
Māñjāmbikā was protected and the Mlecchas were likewise destroyed;
Raktabīja was slain by him, and by him I have been saved.
Furthermore, the king named Udaya, who was submerged in water, was indeed protected by him.
Salutations to you by whom Vasumedha was protected in the water;
salutations to me for you, by whom Jyāmagha was rescued from thieves and Sudhana was saved, and by whom Tryaṣṭaka was liberated.
Salutations to him by whom the disciples of Hiraṇyakeśin were indeed restored to life, by whom Vṛhadvarcas was rescued, and even Baleśvara was liberated;
salutations to him by whom Jayadhvaja was also set free. May there be obeisance to me [from you].
Ailavilā was delivered and the one who lived by unrighteousness was destroyed.
Mahāmārī was slain, and those who were dead were brought back to life by him; the people of Uṣṇālaya, who had died from water, were restored to life by him. (43–44)
By him water was offered upon a mountain peak for the sake of the female ruddy geese;
by him the kittens of a female cat were protected within a fire-heated pan.
[He visited] the regions of the Kiṃpuruṣas and the lands of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Salutations again and again to You, by whom [the wind] was purified through sacrifices and other rites;
salutations again and again to You, by whom Samīraṇa was protected and Pavamāna was also guarded; salutations again and again to You, by whom Santāraṇa was protected.
By the Supreme Self, Devāyatana was protected;
by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the deliverance of the *preta*s was accomplished at Rāśiyāna.
The Śūrajāra was liberated, and likewise the *piśācī*s were liberated.
Salutations again and again to him by whom wealth and fatness were bestowed upon you;
salutations again and again to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, by whom the bearer was made wise and the cows were likewise protected— may this be for me a hundred thousand times.
O Blessed One, by my yoga this sacrificial pit has been excavated;
to that compassionate Lord, salutations again and again, ten million times!
O Lord, ward off the excessive rain and cause the clouds to disperse.
"Enter [the waters], fill them completely, and protect the embodied beings who have been submerged!
Having said this, they cast *sarja* leaves upon the head of Hari.
Then he blew his conch shell, and the clouds quickly roared in response.
The waters split apart and their raining ceased;
the waters and the floods dissolved away due to that sound.
Through the occurrence of the Vṛkāyana [mantra], living beings became happy.
The great seer Vṛkāyana went to Mount Kṛtasmara;
Bālakṛṣṇa, having vanished from sight, went to Lake Aśvasaras;
and Nīlakarṇa, together with Cātvāla, [went] to Parameśvara from that day onward.
He propitiated that Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and constantly performed the worship of that very Hari who was ever present before his eyes.
Dwelling among the trees, subsisting on fruits, wearing garlands, and chanting prayers, he remained full of dispassion.
The wise man, possessing deep devotion for Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa within his own heart, constantly worshipped Hari while chanting with hand-claps and other instruments:
"Bālakṛṣṇa! Hare! Kṛṣṇa! Nārāyaṇa! O All-pervading Lord, protect me! (58–59)
"Bālakṛṣṇa, Harekṛṣṇa, victory to Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
Harekṛṣṇa, Harekṛṣṇa, beloved of Śrī Hari, victory to You!
Thus he performed his worship together with his wife, sons, and others.
Content with whatever food he obtained and satisfied with even a small amount of clothing and other necessities,
he worshipped the illustrious Lord Kāṃbhareya, the Great Master.
Indeed, he established a circle of his own kinsmen who were devoted to him.
Always meeting at night, they remain in the maṇḍala and worship;
they chant the names of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, praise Him, and bow down to Him.
They worship with tulasī and other offerings, and feed Him fruits and other foods.

They perform the *ārārtrika* rite, partake of the sacred offerings (*prasāda*), and then go to their own homes; with their minds fixed on Hari, they sleep. Rising [the next day], they meditate upon Hari and then engage in their worldly activities.
Thus conducting themselves, those Cāṭvālas,
who were knowledgeable in the divisions of the Vedas, once reached a decision to go to Kuṅkumasthalī for the sake of pilgrimage,
in order to see the hermitage of Lomaśa and behold Bālakṛṣṇa.
To behold Aśvapaṭṭasara and to perform sacred rites at the holy sites there,
more than a hundred men— both males and females, including children and the elderly— set out with their families, taking provisions for the journey. (67–68)
On the way, they sing songs rich with musical instruments in praise of Nārāyaṇa;
then, proceeding slowly, they arrive at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Some bow down to the trees, while others carry up the dust.
Some, remembering Nārāyaṇa, rolled upon the surface of the earth;
others then performed prostrations like a staff with all eight limbs; and still others, accompanied by circles of musicians, danced with intense emotion.
Some devotees sing the virtues of Hari-Kṛṣṇa,
while others join in singing those very virtues once again.
Remembering Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, they indeed drink and eat on the way.
Then they performed service for the virtuous as they proceeded along the path.
In this manner, all the devotees, whose minds were fixed on Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa amidst the resounding noise of musical instruments and kīrtana.
To see them, all the sages as well as Brahmapriyā and the others went to the side of the path outside; then, seeing them,
the devotees prostrated themselves like staffs and placed the dust [from their feet] upon their heads.

Having washed the feet of the sages and their beloveds with water, they drank the water of grace and applied it to their bodies and heads. Beholding Lomaśa and worshipping him according to the prescribed rites, those dear to Hari [honored him]. (76–77)
Having burned away their own sins and taking up the *lomaśa* mantra— “Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā”—
they chanted it while wearing *tulasī* garlands upon their chests.
Chanting the praises of Bālakṛṣṇa, the eternal Supreme Brahman,
they beheld the divine temple of Hari containing a thousand pitchers;
they bowed before those divine pitchers and the banner situated atop the palm tree.
In the past, they went quickly to bathe on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having bathed, drunk the water of the sacred ford, and rested beneath the shade of mango trees,
they [proceeded] for the sake of beholding the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Taking their gifts with them, they all entered the interior of the celestial palace.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Hari quickly summoned his own disciple, the great yogi Svayaṃprakāśa, and bestowed upon him the nectar of his own feet.
He gave it to them, and they all drank it in an instant;
then Kṛṣṇa bestowed his grace upon them, and they then ate.
Having been gazed upon by Hari with a mere glance, they were all completely transformed.
At that time, they became divine in form, freed from bodies composed of the elements;
indeed, those gods, possessing celestial bodies, became equal to the sun in radiance.
Devoid of dullness, they traveled along the path of the sky.
Free from the obstruction of walls and possessing unobstructed vision,
all of them bear divine knowledge; they are white in color, possess excellent forms,
and have limbs proportionate to their bodies, appearing here as if they were liberated souls.
Whether they have come from the world of the Imperishable Brahman (Akṣarabrahmaloka), or from Vaikuṇṭha,
or else from the abode of Goloka, or from Śvetadhāman—
such [beings] are white in color, with a splendor like the orb of the moon. (88–89)
Having attained the grace of Hari, they reached divine state through devotion;
their childhood vanished, as did their dullness.
Impurity was destroyed, and their human condition came to an end. (2.164.90)
Divinity was manifested and mastery of the scriptures was acquired;
all of them, including Nīlakaṇṭha and the others, became possessed of divine vision.
Then, with supreme devotion, they worshipped the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
At that moment, a divine celestial chariot (vimāna) descended from the sky there.
Then, for the sake of liberation, those devotees of Hari offered this petition:
"We shall carry out your command here; indeed, that alone is considered by you to be liberation."
"Neither a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) nor anything pertaining to the next world is desired here;
O Great King, we shall provide protection right here and serve you in this very place.
To those who petitioned thus, Hari then gave his command. (94–95)
"O devotees, remaining in your divine vehicles, proceed toward the northern direction—
to the great land of Ketumāla, which lies to the west of Mālyavat.
This Mālya, known as Urala, is situated to the east of Ketumāla."
"Even in those regions, let the gift of mantras be given by me to the people.
Having spoken thus, they bowed to Śrī Hari and ascended their celestial chariot.
At that moment, the most excellent sage Vṛkāyana was remembered by Kṛṣṇa.
Arriving by way of the celestial path, Śrī Hari himself gave him the command to go to Ketumāla for the sake of engaging in devotion.
He too, having ascended the celestial chariot along with more than a hundred great sages—
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, he went through the sky together with those possessing divine forms.
He swiftly directed his celestial chariot toward Ketumāla;
having beheld Kaccha, Sindhu, Indukuśa, Kaśyapa, and the ocean, he proceeded.
Transgressing the Kukkeśāsana, he went swiftly to Ketumāla,
where the Kaśyapa people dwell with white bodies due to the cold;
all the descendants of Kaśyapa are indeed equal in their religious duties.
Then,
by the command of Vṛkāyana, Nīlakaṇṭha, the king of devotees, brought his own celestial chariot down from the sky onto the bank of the river Nīparā to rest for a moment. (103–104)
O Rādhikā, Nīlakaṇṭha and others bathed at the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara;
because they bathed there, that sacred ford indeed became known by the name Nīlakaṇṭha.
For merely by bathing there, it bestows divinity upon embodied beings.
"By both reciting and hearing [this], divinity is attained by people.

(106) Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection Granted by the Blessed Lord through the Sage Vṛkāyana during the Excessive Rainfall upon the Family of Nīlakarṇa and Cāṭvāla in the Second Section on the Tretā Age within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; and the Attainment of Divinity by Nīlakarṇa and His Hundred Retainers upon Reaching Kuṅkumavāpī, as well as His Dispatch by the Blessed Lord to the Ketumāla Region. (164)

Śrī Rādhikā said:
O dear one, O lord of my life, O Kṛṣṇa, O beloved, O you who enchant all!
Nīlakaṇṭha, Vṛkarṣi, and likewise other preeminent devotees— [1]
What did they do then on the bank of the Nīparā in the region called Ketumāla?
Since that place is unknown to me, you should tell me all of that.
[Please relate] the story concerning the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Even after hearing it again from the mouth of my beloved life, I do not attain satiety.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, on the bank of the Nīparā river, which is crowded with many trees...
In that place, a delightful abode of cool breezes and many birds,
they all descended from their celestial chariots onto the earth near the edge of the water.
Having gone there, they bathed and then performed worship to the beginningless Lord Hari.
Having offered an oblation of fruits, roots, and the like, as well as cooked food,
and having partaken of provisions for the journey and drunk the water born of grace,
they rested for a mere ghaṭikā and performed the chanting of the Name.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, Hare Hare! Maheśāna, Pareśāna, Sarveśāna, Hare Hare!
Thus, filled with joy, they performed the congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana) accompanied by musical instruments. || 7-8 ||
Then they ascended their celestial chariot to behold Khaṇḍa,
proceeding with skill and in due order along the path of the sky;
from the heavens, they surveyed the regions of Yavakrīta.
Having beheld the river Nistārā, the Pṛthā river whose banks cause the hair to stand on end, the mountain Kṛpāsthala, the river Dinapā,
and the servant [river], as well as the regions of Yugaśāva and the districts of Valgurāya.
Having observed the regions of the Lord of Mountains (Śiva) and the areas where even a small portion of their desires might be granted,
and having likewise seen the Mountain of Nourishment (Āpyāyanādri) and the Minor Mountain (Alpādri),
as well as the regions of their own desired elders and the regions of jackals and serpents.
Having seen the river of the Rāhus and beheld Mount Parījava,
he saw the river Indirā, the river Gavādakavitā,
the river of the Gavādayas, and the regions of Pūrta and Gaṇḍa.
Having observed the Trigrasā river, the Dūrā river, the Mitrā river, as well as the Supāna region, the rivers of the Gurus,
the regions where fruits are eaten, and likewise the Lavavārā river.
Then, having beheld the river Senānadī, and having observed the Cāpagā;
having seen the regions where creepers flourish and the areas of the Jarā and Mauna rivers; and having beheld the river Ālpāpā as well as the Audarī stream.
Having seen the regions of Pālanāda, the river Viṣatulā, and likewise Prapīṭhā among the Niyamā rivers,
and thereafter having seen the regions of Lātavāya and the river Dūnā; ||| 18 ||
Having seen the lake of the anus and indeed the lake of excrement,
having seen the lake of the womb,

Beholding the beautiful union of Kāmā and Vastunī,

Having rested at night, on the second day...

Having performed the six rites and proclaiming [the glory of] the Lord along with their attendants, they wandered about in celestial chariots according to that very same order. And the subjects and kings, having heard the roar of the Supreme Lord, [were filled with wonder]. (25–26)
Attaining supreme bliss, they raised cries of victory;

Having performed their morning rites and seated themselves upon the celestial chariot, those travelers of the sky wandered about in that very same order. And as for that [mark] on the throat of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa form...
Then, having touched the wish-fulfilling gem held in the center of the garland,

In whatever region people were seen,

And the subjects, with cries of joy, received those sugar-candies.
Greatly delighted, they shouted cries of victory;
eager, they exclaimed, "Welcome! Welcome!
Having offered their favor, they presented that very celestial chariot at evening.
At the onset of night, they arrived at the confluence of the Donā, Ajavā, and the ocean.
During the night, they indeed performed worship, chanting "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Just then, twenty-eight maidens arrived there.
All of them were maidens bearing divine forms,

Chanting "Nārāyaṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa" with a gentle disposition, their minds fixed upon the Lord,

One was white, another black, the third swift;

They worshipped him exceedingly with flowers, pearls, and diamonds;
with divine jewels, golden garments, ornaments, fruits, and the like;
and also with divine honey and fragrant sandalwood and other offerings.

Then, with the heart-mantra, they performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) for Hari and for the Mother as well, using the essences of perfumes, all flavorful substances, and meditative visualizations;
they also performed circumambulations and offered prayers. (85–86)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, you are the forgiver of the offenses committed over ten million lifetimes;
please come to our lands and indeed purify them.

"Come here and purify us, who have resided here for a long time.
When our arrival from the world of Satyaloka along with our mother occurred, it was indeed through the effort of Bhagīratha and by the grace of Hara. (88–89)
At that time, our mother was not there to grasp her own matted locks;

and saw here the desolate and uninhabited Ketumāla, free from all affliction.
"By the will of Nārāyaṇa, we have come here and dwell in extreme peace.
Among us are these twenty-eight young maidens;
we are all daughters of Gaṅgā, and likewise, these five are our sons."
"These three children, as well as the twenty youths and the four boys— all of us are born from the Gaṅgā.
Having performed sacrificial festivals here and having summoned the assembly of the gods," ||| 93 ||
"Make Ketumāla, Pāvana, and Kṛṣṇa pure on all sides.
Having heard this, Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, laughed, rejoiced, and accepted their request.
Having bestowed his grace upon them, he vanished within the image;
indeed, the entire retinue also disappeared in an instant.
So too did the great seer Vṛkāyana, Nīlakaṇṭha, and the others.
Having heard the account and seen him, they embraced him with joy in their hearts.
Then they welcomed him with water for the feet, offerings, and food.
This was done for all the descendants of Gaṅgā who were graced by the mercy of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having gathered together in their celestial chariots, they performed the glorification of Śrī Hari and then exchanged their personal introductions with one another.
They also extended invitations to those traveling in the chariots who were born of Gaṅgā.
Then Vṛkāyana and the others accepted the invitation once more to travel and sanctify their own lands again and again;
they also spoke of staying together for sixty years within their own celestial chariot.
And those sixty divine girls accepted [the proposal] exactly as it was spoken.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the union indeed took place by the will of Kṛṣṇa.

(102) Thus ends the [section on] the journey by celestial chariot to Ketumāla, the observation of the land, and the meeting with the sixty offspring of Gāṅgeya by the great sages Vṛkāyana, Nīlakaṇṭha, and others, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Rādhikā said: How and when were these young boys and girls born in the Gaṅgā?
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me all that; I wish to hear it according to the truth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"They were all questioned by Vṛkāyana and the others in exactly that same manner."
They all related the account exactly as it happened; I shall tell it to you:
once in Goloka, Śrī Kṛṣṇa was requested by Rādhā for the sake of offspring, and at that time, he was conceived by me for that purpose. (2–3)
Then, having produced a daughter named Vikuṇṭhā and the seven oceans as sons,
you gave them away and became satisfied in mind.
Seeing that you possessed offspring while Gaṅgā was deprived of offspring, [she was filled with envy].
Desirous of offspring, she requested children from me.
I then granted her as many auspicious daughters as she desired; numbering twenty-eight, they brought her great satisfaction. (5–6)
Then she desired the five princes to be given to her by me;
yet she was not satisfied even then, so four more were given. Still, she did not attain contentment, and thus twenty boys were given.
Then she indeed attained satisfaction; nevertheless, she desired more. At that moment, three children were then offered by me.
In this way, sixty boys were given by me to Gaṅgā in Goloka.

Bestowed through the power of her resolve, she then attained great satisfaction. When she descended into the world, she was accompanied by her offspring; having brought forth her children, she returned together with them, full of affection.
From Goloka she first descended into Vaikuṇṭha;
then into the second Vaikuṇṭha, the covering of water;
and then, having become the foot of Viṣṇu, she descended into Satyaloka.
Protected by Brahmā with the desire for consecration in the world of truth,
she is eternally held within his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and resides in embodied form even in her own home;
thus, in the abode of Brahmā, she shines forth in the very nature of cause and effect.
By the exertion of Bhagīratha, she who consists of cause and effect was offered by the Creator to Bhagīratha for the sake of the ocean’s liberation;
purifying the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods born of Vāyu.
By way of Meru, that goddess fell upon the head of Rudra;
she was held by Śambhu in his matted locks and there attained dissolution. Then, instructed by her mother, the sixty-year-old girl [went] to Himālaya.
Abandoning their abode of Śambhu, they fled swiftly to a great distance out of fear.
Leaving Indukuśa, Kaśyapābdhi, and likewise Kiṃpuruṣa, they went to another region where they remained indeed free from fear. (17–18)
Having established their dwellings in Ketumāla, those sons of Gaṅgā— the sixty Kumāras and Kumārīs— resided there according to their desire;
remaining in comfort, they awaited the lotus feet of the Blessed One.
They worshipped Hari and always remembered their mother. To fulfill their heart's desire, the Supreme Lord sent Śatka as a mere pretext for the sake of his devotees.
Under that pretext, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Himself became visible in the celestial chariot in the form of Rādhikā.
Desiring to fulfill their resolve, He wished to perform a sacrifice.
Having spoken these words there, he then vanished once more.
Listen to the names of the maidens and the names of the youths;
they remain in embodied forms, and they also remain as created [images].
The eldest daughter is named Valgu; the second is Niṣṭhāparā;
and likewise Nistārā, Pṛthā, Dinapā, and Sevikā.
Indirā is considered the seventh, and Gavādakavitā is regarded as the eighth.
The ninth is Rāhūnā, and likewise the tenth is Gavādayānā.
Trigrāsā is Dūrikā, and Mitrā is Lavavārikā. Senā is Sthāyinī, and that which is considered the eighteenth is indeed Alpāpā. || 26–27 ||
Audarī, Viṣatulyā, Prapīṭhā, Niyamānikā,
Dūnā, Trinayā, Hīnā, Pācaurā, Kāmikā, and Donā—

Bālatrika, Śveta, Kṛṣṇa named Kaśyapa, and Ājava as the fifth—these were indeed the elder brothers. After them, there were four brothers; I shall describe them to you.
Parīja, Alpa, Āpyāyana, and Kṛpāsthala as the fourth;
from that point twenty were born—listen, I shall tell them to you by name:
Yavakrīta, Romāyana, and Yugaśāvaka.
Valgurāya, Girīśa, and the sixth, considered to be iṣṭalava;

These sixty youths, the sons of Gaṅgā,
intensely entreated Vṛkāyana to wander through their own lands.
Then all those hundred [youths] once again ascended the celestial chariot.
Then, together with the sixty [sages], they set out in their celestial chariot to wander,
moving through the sky in a clockwise direction according to the ancient sequence.
Descending at various places along the banks of the Gaṅgā, they did so out of a desire for the sons of Gaṅgā.
Indeed, performing acts of purification and offering worship to Hari,
they visited the sixty sacred sites and celebrated festivals there;
and they caused the name of Hari to be heard again and again by kings and commoners alike.
Once again, they all went there to the confluence of the Drona and the ocean;
they all dwelt there happily, recounting the stories of Hari.
Then the descendants of Gaṅgā spoke again to these men, Vṛkāyana and the others.
When will the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari himself in person, come for the sake of the sacrifice? When will he be beheld by our sight?
All the people here in these regions await this festival with great joy. (44–45)
"O great sage Vṛkāyana, proceed toward Śrī Hari;
you ought to petition Him so that the sacrifice may be accomplished quickly.
Thus addressed, the perfected and divine Vṛkāyana, through his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [proceeded].
Swiftly restraining his vital breaths, he reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
By means of yoga alone, he emerged and arrived at the lake of Āśvasāra.
Having bowed to the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, he requested that which was in his heart.

Then, throughout all lands and in every place among kings..."
"You must indeed go during the month of Bhādrapada, in the dark fortnight of Āśvina.
Travel through various regions and make it known so that the people and subjects may know the time for the sacrifice."
O Kuru, having gathered the necessary materials from the sons of Gaṅgā,
take this Sudarśana discus with me and set forth.
Send it by way of the sky to those regions in every direction.
Having wandered for a while, wherever one may find rest upon the ground, there a sacrifice should be performed;
prepare that spot with consecration.
And that place shall be illuminated by a celestial chariot once again during the day.
Having traveled through the path of the sky, cause it to be manifested;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, I shall go by way of a celestial chariot, accompanied by the gods, my family, great sages, and the Śaktis. ||55||
"I shall return together with you immediately after midday.
Thus commanded by Sudarśana, the illustrious great sage,
through his yogic power, suddenly went to the confluence of the Drona and the ocean.
In the morning, he related the auspicious news to everyone;

Having performed their morning rites, they [proceeded] with all kinds of musical instruments and hymns of praise.
Having all ascended their celestial chariots as an auspicious omen,

Having once whirled his great discus and surveyed the various levels of the earth,

"Let the highly fortunate ones come to the sacrifice dedicated to Nārāyaṇa;

The Muktakoṭyas, Īśakoṭyas, and Devakoṭyas, as well as humans;

Let those devoted to giving and oblations there become partakers of the sacrifice. (95–96)
"Kings and royal retinues, guilds of merchants and the common people,
children, infants, women, and the elderly— all of you, receive the merit of the sacrifice! Thus, O Rādhikā, a celestial chariot repeatedly proclaimed this in the sky.
Having indeed wandered seven times through Ketumāla,
he proclaimed the announcement of Kṛṣṇa throughout all lands, from the region west of Urala as far as the shores of the ocean. ||98-99||
Then the celestial chariot descended peacefully upon the site where Yatakrīta lived,
to the east of Prapīṭhā and to the west of Nīpara.
May Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be victorious forever!
Chanting [the mantra], they descended together with Sudarśana.
Those great seers rested in the vast forest during the night free from enemies;
then, the sons of Gaṅgā, including Bāla and Bālādi, attained supreme peace.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Gāṅgeyas and Their Names, Vṛkāyana’s Arrival at the Kuṅkumavāpikā Field, the Invitation to Hari, Vṛkāyana’s Arrival in Ketumāla with Sudarśana, the Determination of Kratusthalī as shown by Sudarśana’s Steadfastness, and the Proclamation of the Sacrifice," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 167: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (Tretā-yuga-santāna).
Chapter 167.
[Author: Chapter 168.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall tell you what happened afterwards.
The Lord of Lords, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī,
dispatched Lomaśa and other great sages who were experts in sacrificial rites,
as well as the eternal great sage Śvetavyāsa, who was devoted to his wife.
And likewise Sanatkumāra, Gaṇeśa, Jātavedas, Satrāyaṇa, Gālava, and Svīyaprakāśa;
Śatānanda, Nārada, and Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.
And Īśāna, Mahādeva, the sage Kapila, Śuka, Vallabha-muni, Vāmana, Suratāyana,
Hemanta, Devaprakāśa, and even the implements of sacrifice. (4–5)
On the day of the first lunar phase (pratipad), after midday, he sent all those sages together in a celestial chariot;
they arrived on the opposite shore of the Niṣṭhā river, where Vṛkāyana and the others were.
Then Yavakrīta and the others offered a welcome;
they honored Lomaśa and the other great sages who had arrived with cries of victory and with offerings such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
The celestial chariot, however, did not collide with the other chariot on the ground;
and Gāṅgeya, Yavakrīta, and the others honored them with great respect.
Likewise, Viśvakarman and the two gods met together.
By Hari’s command, on that very first day, the two preeminent artisans rested,
took their meal, and then proceeded with the clearing of the ground;
they constructed pavilions, dharma-halls, and kitchens.
They constructed sacrificial halls, residential quarters, and fire-offering halls; they built potteries, storehouses, and auspicious pavilions for the great festival.
They also built halls for the distribution of gifts, residences for the incarnations, and temples for the deities.
They constructed hermitages for sages, shrines for the ancestors, and excellent dwellings for yakṣas and rākṣasas;
they also established abodes for both the insentient and the sentient all around within that region measuring one hundred krośas between the two rivers.
They constructed beautiful pavilions, appropriately furnished for the residence of each inhabitant;
Yavakrīta and the others also departed quickly to their respective countries,
bringing with them the subjects and the kings of those various lands.
The merchant’s excellent food offerings were carried by men and women with their families;
they all quickly brought them to the sacrificial ground by means of celestial chariots.
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the principal names of those who sought the sacrifice. || 16–17 ||
The sovereign of the eastern regions, known by the name Uralaketu,
accompanied by the sage Yavakrīta and sixty million subjects,
departed together with his family and all his wealth, including the prosperity of Cīja. (18)
Accompanied by his abundant array of vehicles and mounts, King Kratha arrived for the sake of the sacrifice along with the sage Romāyana;
together with his family, he came accompanied by a hundred thousand subjects. (2.167.20)
King Pṛthu, accompanied by his family and ten thousand followers, arrived for the sake of the sacrifice along with the sage Kṛpāsthala;
likewise, King Uṣṭrāraṇya arrived together with the sage Yugaśāva.
King Haṃkāra, as well as King Jayakoṣṭhala—
these three brothers, the kings, together with their families and accompanied by hundreds of thousands of subjects, arrived there for the sake of the sacrifice. (22–23)
Then King Tīrāṇa, together with the sage Valgurāya and ten thousand men, arrived at the sacrifice as a householder;
likewise, King Alvīnara, accompanied by Girīśa, came with his family.
Then King Jinavardhana came for the sake of the sacrifice together with ten thousand men;
at that time, the householder Iṣṭalavarṣin came to the sacrifice accompanied by five thousand subjects.
Then King Alpaketu set out together with the sage Āpyāyana and his family,
accompanied by ten thousand men.
King Jayakṛṣṇa also went along with his own chosen elder sage.
King Pariśāna, accompanied by his family and ten thousand men,
arrived at the sacrifice along with the sage Pheraṅgu;
likewise, he came together with ten lakhs of subjects and his household.
In the sacrifice, King Indurāya arrived together with the sage Parīja,
accompanied by his family and three thousand subjects;
likewise, King Gaṇḍaka arrived together with the sage Pūrtagaṇḍa.
Then, at that sacrifice, King Nudrāṇḍa arrived together with his family and five hundred subjects,
accompanied by the sage Supāna;
he was accompanied by five hundred thousand subjects and came as a householder.
In the sacrifice, King Līnorṇa, accompanied by the sage Phalāśana and possessing a family of two hundred thousand subjects, arrived; likewise,
King Bṛhaccharas came along with the sage Vallījīvana.
Accompanied by a thousand men, the householder Makha arrived;
together with the sage Jarāmauna, King Balalīna, accompanied by ten million subjects, arrived at the sacrifice as a householder. (34–35)
King Varasiṃha, accompanied by a hundred thousand subjects and joined by his family, arrived at the sacrifice together with the sage Pālanāda.
Likewise, King Rājagāma, together with the sage Lātavāya, [arrived].
Accompanied by a thousand men, the householder Phālanādarṣi came to the sacrifice;
together with him, King Phenatantu,
accompanied by a thousand men, arrived at the sacrificial rite.
In the sacrifice, King Stokahoma, accompanied by his family and joined by a thousand men, arrived together with the sage Svādvadana.
Likewise, in the sacrifice, King Kāṣṭhāsya arrived together with the sage Nārada.
A householder accompanied by five hundred subjects arrived;
Kolaka, the king at the sacrifice, arrived together with Lepanādārṣi,
and a householder accompanied by a hundred men also arrived.

And from the regions of Layadāna, the King of Aṅga arrived, accompanied by his assembly of ministers, joined by a hundred thousand subjects, and attended by his family. And from the land of Śakunta, King Śākuntaka came to the sacrifice.
Accompanied by a hundred thousand subjects and his family, he arrived there.
From the eastern regions, indeed, the subjects came to the sacrifice; likewise, subjects came from the northern parts of the continent.
They arrived accompanied by celestial chariots, elephants, horses, carts, and palanquins,
as well as camels and bulls; they were laden with gold, jewels, and wealth,
along with many articles of food and gifts.

Accompanied by male and female servants, adorned with sons, daughters, and the like, and consisting of groups of married couples, they all arrived there. They came bringing offerings suitable for the sacrifice and all necessary materials. (46–47)
Those twenty-six kings, endowed with countless wealth,
brought the collection of materials for the sake of the sacrifice; filled with great enthusiasm for the ritual,
they arrived and then presented all those various requisites.
To the sage Gālava, and likewise to Sarvādhyakṣa-Īśāna;
Īśāna, the illustrious Mahādeva, the Vaiṣṇava Supreme Lord,
was then the presiding deity over all sacrificial rites and the presiding deity over the elements.
For he indeed became the regulator of the arrangement of the pavilions and other structures.
And there, having arrived, the circle of kings presented [offerings] to Īśāna;
for each member of the royal group was a patron for the sake of the sacrifice.
"Therefore, O King, sacrifices are requested so that you may be able to provide the expenditure;
let there be twenty-six of them, adorned with sacrificial pits.
Having heard these words from the assembly of kings, Vṛkāyana likewise [replied]. (52–53)
Lomaśa, as well as Īśāna, Nīlākarṇa, and others; Svayaṃprakāśa, Kapila, Devaprakāśaka, and the rest—
these leaders took up the words here, with Viśvakarman as the presiding deity.
Having received the command of the ṛṣis, they constructed sacrificial pits there accordingly.
The twenty-seventh was the great preeminent pit for the sake of the Blessed One;
it was designated as the foremost of all oblations, intended for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
There, nine types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) were indeed fashioned by Viśvakarman,
all according to the rules of the Vedas and Ṛṣis, and in accordance with the directions.
Among them was the pit known as Sarvatobhadra-vedi, which was shaped like a lotus.
The altar was made auspicious on all sides and likewise square;
a yoni-shaped pit was also made, as well as a half-moon pit, a triangular pit, and a circular pit. (58–59)
There was also a hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), as well as a six-petaled pit;
an eight-cornered pit, and likewise an eight-petaled pit.
A pit for the preceptor was constructed, and a pit for the Ṛgveda was prepared.
Altars were constructed for the Yajurveda and for the Atharvaveda;
altars for the Sāmaveda and other altars were also made.
The central altar and the side altars were likewise fashioned according to the prescribed rules.
Thus, having consecrated the earth accordingly within the pavilion, Viśvakarman fashioned auspicious sacrificial pits of appropriate size, highly adorned altars,
and even a temple for the deity.

They caused to be built within a range of a hundred *krośas* magnificent pavilions of divine splendor, adorned with beautiful pillars and banners, and graced by excellent archways enriched with directional markers and other ornaments. (64–65)
Natural splendors, natural waters,
cool and fragrant breezes, and naturally occurring garden lands;
small-flying celestial chariots, and millions of lightning-chariots.
There were various swings that provided natural music,
as well as lakes and ponds of cool and warm water possessing natural fragrances.
There were likewise beds, vehicles, objects of enjoyment, and garlands of flowers.
All that is natural has been made from the essence of natural oil;
whether it be heaven, Satyaloka, or even Vaikuṇṭha itself—there, the suns are naturally born and the moons are naturally radiant. (69)
Where lakes and rivers flow, born of their own nature; even so, indeed, everything pertaining to the body— whether divine or natural—
is ordained for kings, subjects, merchants, and ascetics.
Then, for poor men, women, and even eunuchs,
enjoyments, clothes, foods, drinks, and dwellings—
belonging to the divine world and born of eternal splendor— become equally available to them.

Indeed, that which is established is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), devoid of laughter and destruction. (73) The wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) came there from Goloka for the sake of milk;
there were streams of milk, streams of yogurt, streams of ghee, and streams of milk-rice porridge (pāyasa). (74)
Then milk, the essence of that which is milked, and indeed fresh butters became divine and inexhaustible, as did sacrificial offerings from an endless source.
The trees and creepers likewise brought forth honey from the wish-fulfilling vines.

They brought from the infinite distance countless products of sugarcane—molasses, candied sugar, and refined sugar—as well as *gundra* roots, *gundrapāka* preparations, fruits, and leaves; they also brought forest regions, groves, and pleasure gardens. (76–77)
Then the divine herbs eagerly brought grains of rice,
juices, sesame seeds, barley, excellent grains, and sacrificial fuel. The clouds, lakes, sweet rivers, streams, and ponds [brought their waters].
They brought naturally cool and delicious drinks at the end.
Śrī and Lakṣmī, the two wives of Lord Hari, who are the manifestations of the lotus-like play of the earth, namely Ramā, Annapūrṇā, and Kamalā, brought mountains of delicious food. (2.167.80)
Stems, clusters, bunches, thickets, stalks, and trunks,
as well as creepers, grasses, leaves, and finally flowers, [were carried away].
Caverns, pits, mountains, and chasms [were likewise swept clean].
Gairika brought various colored powders and saffron dyes;
Meru brought all the vessels, and Indra brought the carpets.
The deities brought celestial chariots to the great festival of the sacrifice. (82–83)
Vasava and Kubera gave various articles for the sacrifice; Himālaya, Arala, and others indeed gave precious gems and jewels.
The oceans and the regions of the islands gave pearls at the sacrifice.
Then the clouds cast their shade and the seasons became favorable;
all the Gandharvas became musicians and offered autumnal instruments;
and the kings gave male and female servants as well as skilled attendants.
At that time, during the sacrifice, parasols, fly-whisks, vehicles, and mounts were gathered in every house; and from them, multitudes of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) appeared,
which bestowed everything whatsoever one might think of or desire.
The divine drum of Śrī Hari dances and resounds repeatedly;
this drum, which is the very form of the Kalpa, possesses the nature of the imperishable Brahman, and like a treasure to be sought by all, it grants even that which is desired. (88–89)
Whatever ornaments of garments, jewelry, and flowing materials the divine artisan requires for the sacrifice, he promptly provides them all;
indeed, such is the infinity of all things found therein.

Where the goddess of water herself was born in the form of nectar, and the goddess of the earth in the form of food—what more could be lacking there, O Rādhikā? Indeed, this is all by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (91–92)
By the command of Him who dwells within, the *saṃhitā* quickly came into being there;
[it manifested] the sun, the moon, night, twilight, day, wind, and likewise the sky, fire, the gods from the ears, the earth, water, and mountains. (93)
Mādhava issued commands to Megha, Kāla, Vṛṣa, Māyā, and Ājñā.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
[commanded] them all immediately and everywhere throughout the fourteen worlds.
"Let the people be informed that the sacrifice is indeed being prepared;
let those eager for the festival go forth, taking the oblations, toward Ketumāla.
Thus commanded, the residents of the place and the inhabitants of the hermitage were informed.
There they brought sacrificial offerings and gifts that were beyond measure.
O Rādhikā, in this manner, mountains of countless ritual materials had already been prepared for the sacrifice by the great seers; indeed, they were inconceivable.
The twenty-six rulers of the earth were struck with great wonder:
"Oh, the majesty of the Lord cannot be measured!
They have become free from pride and recognize their own insignificance. (99)
"O Rādhā, by reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Sages Lomaśa and Others, as Well as Viśvakarman, the Devas, the Kings of Ketumāla, and the Subjects, at the Sacrificial Ground, and the Presentation of the Pavilion, the Fire-pits, the Oblations, and the Ritual Implements," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 167 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 168 [[Author: → Chapter 169
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; I am myself the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. I immediately remembered my own attendant named Akṣara. (1)
The messenger arrived there at the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
having bowed down, Hari stood before him and gave him a command of auspicious import:
"A great sacrifice shall take place in Ketumāla"—thus was the letter.
"Rich with saffron, bestowing wealth for the purpose of summoning all created beings—send her forth quickly with your divine attendants; do not delay!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One gave that letter to him.

May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious! On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the conjunction of the *sārpapauṣṭha* and *niṣṭhāparā* asterisms in the Ketumāla region, [he performed] the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which fulfills all desires.
"Those who dwell in the three worlds must come there with respect.
Let them consider this the reception of guests and the attainment of Makha;
on the eleventh day, it shall be a full sacrifice accompanied by joyful festivals."
May the incarnations, the lords, the ancestors, the sages, and the deities;
all humans, the descendants of Kaśyapa, and those dwelling in the netherworlds and elsewhere;
as well as the stationary and moving beings—come happily to this sacrifice.
Lomaśa, Yavakrīta, Kapila, Bṛhaspati,
the blessed Sanatkumāra, King Uśīnara, and Īśāna— these we respectfully offer our salutations. (2.168.10)
"Those who dwell in the world of living beings, the world of lords, and the world of Brahmā—all of them must come; I say this even to Nārāyaṇa.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [spoke] three times upon the leaf."
Having made this promise, I speak again: let everyone indeed come to the sacrifice.
On the third lunar day, I shall go from the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā to the sacrifice; you must then attend that sacrifice.
"May the attendants residing in all abodes and the female attendants who are Śaktis come on the previous day for the purpose of service at Mahīmāna.
Having spoken thus, he dispatched millions of such written invitations.
In all worlds, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself [is present] through the ether of consciousness,
the elemental ether, as well as through Māyā, Mahākāla, and Dharma, indeed by means of these, in all creations. (15–16)
O Rādhikā, at the beginning of creation, there was a union, a connection, a meeting, and a movement among all principles (tattvas) and the inhabitants of the worlds, like that of a family.
There is nothing at all surprising in this, for they exist there in the form of gateways.
I too, having gone to Goloka, then came there along with you.
All the Nārāyaṇas arrived there upon seeing the letters;
and all the people of the entire creation came there, filled with affection. (18–19)
Then, the multitudes of people’s celestial chariots were seen in the sky from all directions as they approached the sacrificial ground; by the millions,
billions, and hundreds of millions, they arrived from every quarter.
As many as there are crores of liberated souls, so many are the attendants and others;
likewise, there are that many Śaktis, other liberated beings, and Siddhas.
And all those Īśvaras are adorned by their respective Śaktis and other attributes. (21–22)
There are as many Maheśas and others, as many inhabitants of the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), gods and demons, sentient and insentient beings, substances, qualities, actions,
and so forth; as well as the Vedas, sciences, sacred fords, principles, and the expansions of dharma.
Just as many were the mineral beings dwelling in all the heavens—

those situated in cavities, those in mixed locations, those who were distinct, and likewise those who were combined— all of them, consisting of the Supreme Brahman and endowed with the three qualities, arrived there.
That which is difficult to behold for all who dwell within the created worlds is indeed easily attained here at this sacrifice through the grace of Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhā, what more need be said? At that time, Hari would have acted otherwise [if He were not pleased].
He is established as both the agent and the non-agent; there is no other power such as His.
(27) All causal complexes are kissed by whatever kind of magnet they may encounter.
Here, the Supreme Brahman is the magnet; how then could there not be an attraction of all things? (28)
I am unable to describe how the subjects were drawn to the sacrifice;
indeed, they had never been seen by me before being drawn to such a sacrifice. They come from the festival with hymns of praise, musical instruments, and dances.
And as they were speaking, he indeed addressed us as well, "O, the Supreme Brahman!
While everyone was thus proceeding in every direction,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa set forth.
Together with sages and ascetics, as well as the guardians of the sacred field (kṣetrapālas) and others, with the holy sites (tīrthas) of the Saurāṣṭra region, and with the subjects and householders—
all those beloved of Brahmā, numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions— [he arrived].
Thus, together with his devotees and family, he ascended the celestial chariot (vimāna).
In thousands of such chariots, millions of other devotees also ascended,
and as they traveled along the path of the sky, they raised shouts of victory.
Then the virtuous, the perfected ones, and the truthful followed Hari;
the entire sky resounded with the roar of celestial chariots and musical instruments.
At the front, the Vedas proceeded in embodied form, chanting their mantras.
The female attendants holding canes, Śāradā and the others, sing praises of his virtues.
Then the sages indeed proceed with divine musical instruments and celestial chariots;
thereafter, Niśāna, Dhvajadaṅka, and the others go forth with shouts of victory.
Then there were the countless beloved wives of Brahmā;
then the aerial chariot of Kṛṣṇa, and then the men who were his guards;
then all the attendants (pārṣadas), and then the inhabitants of Surāṣṭra.
Then all the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) arrive at the sacrifice, trailing behind everyone.
Does Himālaya himself actually go into the sky? Or does he come down from heaven and travel across the northern part of the earth? (2.168.40)
"Do the oceans, rich with the splendor of jewels, perhaps go to heaven itself?"—
such was the extraordinary vision of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the sky as his caravan set forth on its journey. (41)
On the third day, after midday had passed and exactly ten *ghaṭikās* had elapsed, the Blessed One himself reached the sacrificial sky; at that time,
shouts of victory arose in the atmosphere and on the ground.
Millions upon millions of bubbles emerged for the spectators to behold;
the sky became pervaded by a unique radiance, wherein the sun, fire, and other luminaries were dissolved and no longer within range of perception. (44)
At that time, the eyes of all people were indeed capable of beholding [the Lord],
solely through the grace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
By the splendor of Śrī Hari, everything then became filled with light.
Even all the black stones shone like jewels;
even the black surface of the earth then became as radiant as the moon.
Even the body hairs and the hair on the head then became the color of gold.
Even the crows, bees, swans, and cuckoos became like [the sounds of] those [divine beings];
even the sky then became as blue as the lunar surface;
and even the inner regions of the worlds became radiant with the splendor of Brahman.
Then that which was material became divine, for it became like the Imperishable (akṣara). The distinction between the principles of heaven, earth, and space also vanished;
all seven forms became white in color. (2.168.50)
Even the dark and passionate nature of Māyā attained the state of purity (sattva).
Furthermore, at that time, all collections of resources became composed of Brahman;
likewise, the villages and houses were then equal to the abode of Brahmā.
Everything became permeated with Brahman by the splendor of Bālakṛṣṇa.
With divine offerings, worship, and other rites, the subjects, kings, and great sages stood ready, full of eagerness, to welcome Rādhikā. (53)
They offered shouts of victory, decorating the effigies;
with palms joined in reverence, bearing offerings, full of devotion, their faces tender with affection, their lotus-eyes blossoming, and their hearts overflowing with love. (54–55)
At that time, women holding infants in their wombs and men holding fallen heads became suspended with their movements turned upward and their faces turned skyward.
Then the Lord, the Master, the Blessed One, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa appeared.
As that fierce radiance vanished, it descended from the sky;
the Lord became visible to all and perceptible to the physical eye.
Then, a rain of flowers released by the gods fell from the heavens.
An auspicious rain of sandalwood and likewise of unbroken grains (*akṣata*) occurred;
then a rain of gold, silver, and diamonds fell from the sky.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa descended slowly by means of the constructed gateways and stairs.
He seated Kṛṣṇa upon a vehicle drawn by four-tusked white elephants.
All the kings presented him with necklaces of gold and jewels and clusters of flowers;
they prostrated themselves like staffs, while the queens, princesses, and maidens offered their congratulations.
He repeatedly honored the Blessed One— the destroyer of suffering— with unbroken grains and other offerings, with sprouts, sandalwood, and flowers; with lotuses known as *netrapuṭa*,
with joined palms (*añjali*), with the hems of his garments, with ritual services (*upasthāna*), and with the *svastika* hand gesture.
They honored him with their hearts, with feelings of love, and with prostrations.
With shouts of victory, parched grain, flowers, and waters from sacred fords, the subjects honored Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, as Nārāyaṇa. (63–64)
With fans, chowries, and umbrellas, with fragrant and cool waters,
and with sandalwood paste, the merchants joyfully brought comfort to Kṛṣṇa.
With coconuts, sugar, saffron, and lotus stalks, [they served Him].
They nurtured Bālakṛṣṇa with auspicious fruits and other such items.
Then the Lord, shining resplendently upon a divine lion-throne within a golden chariot of a hundred wheels,
accepted the offerings presented by the people.
Kṛṣṇa honored the subjects with his gaze, the corners of his eyes, smiles, and gestures, as well as by various expressions;
at that time, Hari, with smiling faces and many forms, [honored] them all.
Out of compassion, he bestowed his own vision upon them for a long time from every side.
Just as he was seen in front, so too was he seen behind; just as on the sides, so too above;
likewise, he was seen in all eyes and even in hearts. (2.168.70)
Out of grace, the Great King, the Supreme Lord, who is so pleasing to behold, gives flower garlands to some; to others he gives clusters of diamonds, pearls, and other precious gems. (71)
And he gives fruits, betel leaves, areca nuts, and so forth;
as well as coconuts and garments brought for the worship, which are like offerings of welcome and are truly pleasing. (72–73)
Having granted his vision everywhere throughout the hundred *krośas*,
Hari returned to his dwelling at night by means of his elephant-vehicle.
All the members of the caravan performed their drinking of water and took their meal.
Then they indeed rested in suitable dwellings that had been provided.
Hari himself, together with his family and accompanied by the beloved of Brahmā,
enjoyed [the offerings] for one hundred and forty-six years.
He drank [the nectar of devotion], attained peace, and then entered into a sleep consisting of yoga;
and until dawn, attended by male and female servants, he remained awake.
During the night, there were kīrtanas (devotional songs) here and there in that place.

Then the great sages recounted stories interspersed with accounts of former events; and at that time, the bards, skilled in traditional history, proclaimed the expansions of their lineages and ancient chronicles within the assembly of kings.
The virtuous ones, possessing knowledge and providing instructions on the path to liberation, engaged in discourse;
the women, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, sang songs filled with passion and other sentiments;
and the young maidens, having formed a *rāsa* circle, wandered in circles.
The dancers perform their dance on the stage amidst a dense crowd of wealthy patrons, accompanied by the sounds of hand-clapping and the jingling of anklets and waist-bells; meanwhile, the musicians,
skilled in their craft, play their instruments and take their delight.
Actors perform dances and display their skill;
poets, immersed in composition, are seen then proclaiming [the glory].
Wrestlers engage in combats that delight the people.
Displays are seen, as well as creations within further creations;
magic tricks are witnessed performed by highly skilled masters;
and there are also humorous performances and jests in comedy theaters. (84–85)
Forms in the shape of fire are manifested by the skilled artisans of lightning-fire using sparks of fire,
along with roars in the sky;
and playful feats through the application of fire are even cast into the atmosphere.

There are thundering sounds in the sky and a variety of bursting substances; assuming many forms, they are manifested by their own skills. Then the jesters and those in disguise delight the people. (87–88)

O Rādhikā, at that time, during the night which took the form of a festival, there were combats between bulls, buffaloes, and arrogant rāṇḍiyas, as well as between elephants, bears, and monkeys. ||89||

The sounds of musical instruments played in duets resounded again and again; at that time, the notes of the lutes of Mura and the others arose, and the songs of the Apsarases and maidens were heard everywhere. (2.168.90–91)
At that time on earth, Vedic sounds as well as those of the ṛṣis were heard;
there were the jests of eunuchs and games with dolls,
and the practical applications of the Garuḍa-mantras also took place then.
In certain places, there was the manifold construction of a web of cosmic cycles (kalpa-jāla).

In some locations, there were the pastimes performed by Kṛṣṇa during the Rāsa dance, adorned by the assembly of gopīs; elsewhere, there appeared forms that captivated the mind through various distinctions of devotion. ||93-94||
In some places, those who know [the truth] manifest the sports of Rāmāditya and Narāditya, and in other places, they display the wonders of Bālakṛṣṇa. Thus, O Rādhā,
at that time during the night for the people dwelling upon the earth, [these things occurred].

Likewise, for others as well, there were indeed festive celebrations of bliss according to their desires. At that time, songs of the glory of the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa and the illustrious Śrī Kambharā were sung among the women in every place. (96–97)
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and Surāṣṭra, which is accessible even to those who are not of noble birth,
were then praised with words of benediction in all the songs.
At that time, the young sons of Gaṅgā as well as the daughters of the mountains [were likewise honored].
The sages and those devoted to Brahman are praised in songs.
O Rādhikā, the confluence of the two rivers, as well as the Sudarśana Tīrtha and the Yajña-tīrtha extending for a hundred krośas, are extolled on all sides. (2.168.100)
Thus that third night passed away in great comfort;
at dawn on the fourth day, Kṛṣṇa abandoned his sleep.
And auspicious musical instruments were sounded on all sides.
The bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists sang songs of His glory. Hearing these auspicious sounds, Śrī Hari abandoned His sleep for Rādhikā’s sake;
the entire sacred field, extending for a hundred *krośas* in every direction, became wide awake.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Announcement of the Auspicious Sacrificial Invitation, the Arrival of All Inhabitants of the Created World, and the Description of Śrī Hari’s Journey to the Sacrificial Ground by Airship along with His Family and the People of Saurāṣṭra, as Well as Their Welcome, Wandering, Resting, and Entertainment," in the second section, the Tretā Continuation, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 169] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Tretā Yuga Continuation) — Chapter 169.
[Author: Chapter 170.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having risen in the morning, the Blessed One performed his ablutions.
Then he performed meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations;
he performed worship of his own true form, the viewing and salutation of his ancestors, and the sight of holy men and virtuous women. (1–2)

Having drunk a small amount of the milk-like nectar, he mounted his elephant to survey the sacrificial ground and departed from his own abode. That elephant with wings traversed all lands through the sky itself.
Having taken hold of Sudarśana, he surveyed the auspicious ground;
seeing the altar constructed by Viśvakarman— hidden in some places and revealed in others— he was delighted and went to that spot.
Then Hari praised the Lord Īśāna, the all-seeing, as well as the devotees, Devāyana, Viśvakarman, Kapila and others,
the preceptor of the gods, Gaṇeśa and the rest.
Then Hari praised all the millions of male and female servants who had provided the materials,
as well as all the kings;
the Blessed One praised all the principles (tattvas) again and again.
Then the kings, sages, the truthful, the virtuous, the attendants and others,
as well as the beloveds of Brahmā and the rest, performed worship to Hari. Having bowed to Lomaśa and the others, Hari obtained rest in the palace.
In the morning, the Lord caused drinks and foods to be distributed to everyone.
Laboratories for medicinal juices were established, and meals were provided according to what was appropriate and desired, so that all might be fully satisfied. (2.169.10–11)

Beginning from morning, whatever food, drink, or other necessities are required are provided continuously in a steady flow until the break of dawn. Just as those principles (tattvas) are, and as their forms and natures are—
The *vallikās* bestow upon them whatever is beneficial for them.

So too do the jewels, the wish-fulfilling cows, the trees that grant every desire, the liberated ones, those who are liberated even further, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), and the goddesses such as Śrī and Ramā. (13–14)
Then, the infinite divine powers, sovereignities, and qualities bestow upon all of them whatever is desired and fit for enjoyment;
they cause these desirable foods to reach them in every house.
For they indeed provide everything that is required, and even more.
O Rādhā, having seen the greatness of Gāṅgeya, you became filled with indignation;
do you not remember how you were pacified by me through skillful means?

O Rādhikā, on the fourth day, you were specially honored there as a guest; you were fed, saluted, and had your feet massaged by Gaṅgā, and you were adorned with her braided hair, for you were then truly gracious.
Millions of men arrived in celestial chariots on that day.
From the regions of Rāśiyāna, sixteen hundred thousand men came,
and from the land of Prāgjyotiṣa, one hundred thousand men arrived at that time.
From the eastern regions, ten lakhs also arrived;
from the land of Brahmā, one lakh people came, and from the land of camels, one lakh.
From Ājanābha, ten million people came, and from Abrikta, millions of people.
From Ārakta and even from the north, people arrived;
at that time, there were four crores of men there.
As for the other worlds, those inhabited by the three classes of beings, [they also came]. (22–23)
There is no counting the number of embodied beings who have come [to him],
whether they dwell upon the earth, in water, in wind, or in the atmosphere;
or in clouds, on mountains, in caves, in the sky, or in all the fundamental principles (tattvas) everywhere.

And they were fashioned by Viśvakarman, the subtle-seer. Then, having attained perfection, they remain in this sacrifice— some becoming minute, some becoming pervasive, and others even remaining latent— all with their minds fixed on Hari.
Then, through the dwelling within the inner state, there occurred a complete immersion of all [beings] into the Supreme Brahman, the imperishable abode; they all merged into that supreme,
directly manifest, imperishable realm.
There is nothing surprising here, O Rādhā, since Hari is the refuge of all;
he is capable of causing all creations to enter into a minute space, and is able to manifest vastness within a very small area. (28–29)
I do not find the limit of his deeds; who else is capable of knowing them?
He alone is capable of displaying creations within an atom and kalpas within a moment, and of satisfying all those born in the three worlds with a mere mouthful of water. (2.169.30)
He alone is capable of granting satisfaction by the mere act of eating a grain of sesame.
For Mādhava, nothing is impossible, inconceivable, irrational, or unattainable;
indeed, all this [universe] previously arose from the very glance of his form.
By whose will it undergoes contraction again, and at the end will return to that very same place:
who am I, who are you, and likewise who are the others— the four-armed Nārāyaṇas—
who indeed became possessed of power before that form?
Enough with excessive words, for Hari is indeed the support of all.
He made everyone happy at the sacrifice through honors and other such gestures.
Then, on the fourth lunar day, when the sun was in the middle [of the sky], that glorious Bālakṛṣṇa—
In the pavilion, he bestowed mantras upon the kings and the common people;
Bālakṛṣṇa appeared everywhere, assuming ten million forms.
At that time, having sat upon a bull-hide seat at every dwelling, he remained amidst the grass-born [Kuśa].
The Lord caused the mantras to be heard by his devotees as they held water to their ears:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge forever.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! (37–38)
"Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends, one should bear the signs of the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika.
'I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.'"
"Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is my master and my husband. (2.169.40) "Bāla Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is indeed my eternal husband;
may He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (41)

"Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my beloved; this Kṛṣṇa is my master and indeed my husband. Thus [one should recite] the mantra of refuge, the mantra of surrender, the protective mantra, the mantra for the state of Brahman, and the mantra that offers oneself to the Master.
And the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa made Manu the recipient of all his possessions.
Having observed everyone— from children to the elderly, both men and women— according to their respective capacities,
He proclaimed them as having attained their life's purpose and established many among the human race as perfected beings.
Then, O people, those who were initiated partook of their meal;
and in the evening, Lomaśa indeed performed the narration of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and conducted the *nīrājana* ceremony for Hari.
And there, after the meal, festivities arose during the night;
O Rādhā, they brought happiness to everyone, and in the latter part of the night, they rested.
Then, on the fifth day, at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta, Śrī Hari himself—
He bathed at the confluence of the two rivers, and thereafter they all bathed as well.
Then, having performed the daily rites and completed the worship of the deities and other ceremonies,
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa quickly went to the sacrificial pavilion.
The kings, all the subjects, as well as the ṛṣis, the munis, the servants,
the officiating priests, the reciters, and others, all assembled there. At that time, the sounds of musical instruments arose, portending auspiciousness.
"Let the gods on earth perform the ritual portion of the sacrifice," [he said].
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa instructed the twice-born;
the Brahmins and others performed auspicious rites with Vedic mantras in resonant voices. (2.169.50–51)
There, the preceptor Lomaśa declared the proper place and time;
and the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having remembered Gaṇeśa and bowed to his guru Śrī Lomaśa, performed the formal selection of the preceptor.
He performed the binding of the ground within the courtyard and the invocation of the earth.
He sprinkled the ground with the five products of the cow and *kuśa* grass; and, for the purpose of expelling malevolent spirits and other obstacles, he scattered white mustard seeds.
Having thus worshipped the ground, he performed the rite of expiation;
