having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma), he carried out the full worship of Gaṇeśa,
who is his own self, with the sixteen secondary offerings (upacāras).
He performed the ritual recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) as well as the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*).
There, the Brahmins, knowers of the Vedas, bestowed their blessings;
the twice-born then chanted peace-mantras (*śāntipāṭha*) and performed the sprinkling of water.
They sang auspicious hymns and performed the consecration of Kṛṣṇa;
they performed the worship of the Mothers and conducted the Nāndī-śrāddha rite.
Then the Supreme Lord gave the sacrificial fee as an ancillary offering.
The selection of individual preceptors and the selection of the Brahmā priest;
the selection of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the selection of the gatekeepers;
and the selection of the reciters (jāpaka)—he then worshipped them all within the circle.
Then, having worshipped the earth, he performed the protection of the quarters;
then, having sprinkled the sacrificial materials with water, he recited the *svasti* mantras.
He performed the worship of the pavilion and the worship of the site (*vāstu*).
He performed the entire ritual of worship for the deities of the site according to the prescribed rules.
He established the water-pot (kalaśa), offered fruits, medicinal herbs, and earth,
presented the sacred grass (darbha) and purifiers (pavitra), and likewise invoked the holy waters (tīrtha).
Then the Supreme Lord performed the rite of transferring the fire and worshipped all the deities; he recited the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantras and,
according to the prescribed ritual, Hari worshipped the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas.
He performed the worship of the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭhas), offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), and prostrated.
He performed the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and indeed carried out the worship of Brahmā;
likewise, he performed the worship of the deities of the pavilion.
He performed the worship of the sixteen pillars and so forth, the external worship of the deities and others,
the thorough worship of the deities of the branches, as well as the worship of the banners;
he also performed the worship of all the ritual jars and the worship of the Veda.
He performed the worship of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa-pūjā) in all the altars and pits;
he performed the worship of Viśvakarman in the center of the pit,
as well as the worship of the girdles (mekhalā-pūjana) and the worship of the gods there.
He performed the worship of the womb, the worship of the throat, and the worship of the navel;
he also performed the worship of the Vāstupuruṣa and the ritual installation of the sacred fire.
He further performed the offering to the nine planets and the offering to the presiding deities.
He performed the worship of the presiding deities and the worship of the nāgas;
he offered worship to the world-protectors (lokapālas), the worship of Gaṇeśa and the bhūtas,
the worship of the guardians of the quarters, and likewise the worship of Śrī Devī.
Hari likewise performed the worship of the deities established in the mandala,
as well as the worship of the water-pots and the worship of the fifty-six gods;
he also performed the worship of the ṛṣis, the worship of the ancestors, and the worship of the siddhas.
He performed the worship appropriate for the time of death, including the veneration of rivers and the ocean;
he performed the worship of the mountain-weapon and the thorough adoration of the Ṛṣi-goddess.
Having established the ritual water-pot (*kalaśa*), he carried out the worship of Varuṇa.
The virtuous Harī worshipped all twenty-four incarnations, beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as the lords and their wives;
he also worshipped all the attendants of the three gods and all those who dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa worshipped all those consisting of the creation of Brahmā, as well as those consisting of the creation of Īśa, and all those consisting of the creation of the individual soul (jīva). Indeed, whatever embodied beings dwell within the fourteen worlds, [he honored them all].
Kṛṣṇa indeed honored all— those who were insentient, divine, sentient, gurus, female servants, and male servants— as well as those born from the four wombs.
And in every sacrificial pit, the kings likewise performed worship.
They performed everything exactly as instructed by their great ṛṣi preceptor.
The Supreme Lord performed the renunciation of the ritual substances into the fire of the sacrificial pit;
he performed the sprinkling with the *prokṣaṇī* water and likewise carried out the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having consigned the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) into the fire and likewise established it in that place, he performed the offering of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* ladle.
He performed the *homa* sacrifice in this manner: "Svāhā to the god [Name]! and so forth.

The Lord offered many oblations to the sacrifices, the gods, and even to the creators of Brahmā, Īśvara, and the individual soul (jīva). He also presented the sacrificial call to the deities presiding over the sacrificial pits, the pavilions, and the sites.
Kṛṣṇa granted an invitation to the Satīs, Sādhvīs, Sevikās, and Śaktis;
and to the Yoginīs who are liberated, as well as to the beloveds of Brahmā;
Kṛṣṇa granted an invitation to the Siddhis who pervade every limb.
He offered an invocation to the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the Aśvinikumāras; he offered oblations to his own [manifestations] accompanied by their respective incarnations.
Hari also offered oblations of sacrificial pap (caru), consisting of nectar, for the sake of their satisfaction.
Then he performed the installation of the sacrificial post (yūpa) and worshipped the deities of the post;
he sprinkled the post and indeed offered an oblation to the post.
After that, Hari caused the worship of the Nidrā-kalaśa to be carried out.
To those living beings invited to the sacrifice, Hari gave their share;
he gave milk-rice, ghee, milk, fruits, and juices.
Just as in the sacrifice, [the offerings] flowed into the fire by the thousands and tens of thousands.
In that manner, as the oblations consisting of sacrificial offerings fall on all sides,
all living beings become satisfied through the grace of Hari.
This includes rice, barley, wild grains, and other foods fit for sages.
Dates were full of juice, and grains were endowed with sweet flavor; medicinal herbs served as sacrificial fuel, and fruits were likewise succulent.
Candied sugar and other such sweets became the oblations.

Fire-gods of every kind arrived and brought satisfaction. Furthermore, there were embodied beings with fire as their mouth, others with Brahmā as their mouth, those with Kṛṣṇa as their mouth, and others with the virtuous as their mouth. (93–94)
The Śaktis who have Satī as their chief, those who have Devikā as their chief, those who have Svāhā as their chief, and likewise others who have Lakṣmī and Śrī as their chiefs,
as well as those whose faces are full of food— all of them brought about satisfaction.
Having satisfied the principles of the insentient and the sentient with various oblations,
he then offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and performed the waving of lights (ārātrika).
Thereafter, he granted rest to all beings, beginning with the gods.
Thus, indeed, in all twenty-seven types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍakas),
the sages performed worship, the offering of oblations (bali), and burnt offerings (homa). Likewise, kings and couples, possessed of the desire to sacrifice, did so as well.
And by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, the acceptance of offerings was undertaken at the sacrifice.
Furthermore, abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) were indeed presented in honor of the worship.
For those who subsist on fruits, those who subsist on juices, and those who subsist on food are indeed very dear [to Him]. (2.169.100)

The wielder of the Śārṅga bow bestows upon all living beings their respective foods; furthermore, he provides delicious edibles produced by the wish-fulfilling gem of the kalpa. Thus was the beautiful and auspicious fifth oblation successfully performed.
Then he fed all those who were liberated— numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions of lotuses and so forth—
as well as the liberated abodes, the liberated lords, their beloved consorts,
and the male and female attendants, with nectar.
And there were divine sweet foods and infinite drinks,
all kinds of edibles and foods, as well as auspicious things to be licked;
likewise, there were devoted women, beloved by Brahmā, virtuous and chaste, who were dear to Hari.
The Blessed One fed the numerous maidens;
Mādhava fed the lords and the non-lords, Māyā and the family of Māyā, and the twenty-four principles (tattvas).

Mādhava fed those residing in the worlds of the eight enclosures who serve Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, as well as the male and female servants of the three gods. All the goddesses of the three gods and the young maidens devoted to celibacy were also fed.

He fed all the goddesses, the maidens, the yoginīs, and the virtuous Sāṃkhya-yoginīs; he likewise gratified the hosts of goddesses who embody the lunar days, such as the Ekādaśikā-vrata, as well as the celestial nymphs (apsarases).
The Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, caused them all to feast together—

the sages dwelling on Meru, those in Satyaloka, and those situated in Mahar, Jana, and Tapoloka— as well as the ancestors, the Ṛṣis, the female ancestors, the male progenitors, and the female progenitors.
Mādhava fed the gods residing in heaven and the secondary deities (devikās) situated in the Bhuvarloka;
likewise, he fed the men and groups of women dwelling on earth, as well as those born from a womb,
from eggs, from sweat, and from sprouts.
Mādhava fed the holy fords, forest rivers, mountains, oceans, and so forth; he even fed the insects, moths, and other such creatures,
as well as those born of Brahmā, the rajasic, the tamasic, and all species of beings.
And the Kāśyapas born of Dharma and Adharma, those born of the Sun and Moon;
the Rākṣasas dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
the seven classes of beings, and the Pretas residing in the abode of Yama.
Furthermore, he fed the Magadhan bards,
the heralds, the *cāraṇas*, those of the Śūdra caste, the Vidyādharas who dwell in the forests,
cruel creatures, and likewise other *ḍākinīs* and *śākinīs*.
Mādhava fed the Cāṇḍālas, the Śvapacas, and the beasts;
Mādhava fed the serpents, the Nāgas, the flocks of birds, the Kuṣmāṇḍas, the Pravināyakas, the Daityas, the Devas, and the Asuras.
He indeed consumed the auspicious and gracious sacrificial portion of the rite— everything, both insentient and sentient, mixed as the container and the contained,
all that is born of the triple creation, eternal and transient, stable and moving.
Having partaken of the remnants of the sacrifice, they indeed attained eternal, perfect satisfaction.
"O Rādhikā! All my beloveds, beginning with Rādhā, have obtained satisfaction born of this grace. Thus did the sacrificial rites proceed on this first day.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Earth, the Worship of the Deities of the Vāstu, the Sacrificial Pit, and the Pavilion, the Worship of Beings Created by Brahmā, the Lord, and the Living Soul, the Oblation, the Offering of the Great Final Oblation, and the Distribution of Food," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 169. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 170 [Author:
Chapter 171 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rādhikā, on the sixth, seventh,
eighth, ninth, and tenth lunar days, they were gratified by Hari at the sacrifice;
and on the eleventh day, they were likewise gratified by as many ritual procedures as were prescribed.
Indeed, all embodied beings are essentially bodiless; for they are designated by names such as "gross" or "subtle.
They are called "insentient," "born of consciousness," "substances," "qualities," and "actions. Likewise, they include the gods and the lords of their respective principles (tattvas). (2–3)
All the inhabitants of every world, as well as all householders—
both the stationary and the moving, women, men, and eunuchs— were satisfied. Indeed,
there was nothing at all remaining for consumption.
Thus, this Vaiṣṇava sacrifice of all desired offerings was performed by Hari.
During the seven-day festival, inhabitants of the various worlds constantly arrive;
having obtained a vision [of the Lord], millions upon billions of men and women depart.
In the sky, however, the crowding of celestial chariots never ceases.
As many as there are gods dwelling in heaven and elsewhere in the sky,
so many are the humans on earth, and so many are those upon the mountains and other places.
There are just as many among the trees and as many among the rivers;
there are as many men upon the boats, on the riverbanks and so forth,
as well as in the pavilions, the halls, the palaces, and even in the mountain caves.
In the groves, at the carts and so forth, and even among the vehicles,
wherever there were men, they gazed upon those very men;
and here and there, the inhabitants of every dwelling were likewise beheld.
And the inhabitants of both the worlds and the non-worlds were seen here and there;
at that time, the dwellers of the lower regions were perceived everywhere.
During the seven-day sacrifice, a constant increase in the arrival of scriptures was observed.
Gold, silver, diamonds, gems in the form of ornaments,
all kinds of beautiful jewels, and wish-fulfilling trees became the peaks;
mountains arose as tribute-offerings, and tens of millions of vehicles and mounts appeared.
Rows of mountains were then formed of garments, riches, and foods;
peaks of pearls and mountains of sweet delicacies; and mountain-treasures of all articles for enjoyment. (14–15)
There were rivers of rice-gruel and oceans of milk;
treasures of wealth were offered in the sacrifice.
Kubera, the Vasus, Indra, Meru, and likewise Bṛhaspati [were present].
Viṣṇu, beholding the splendor of the sacrifice, became bowed down with shame.
(17) Having witnessed the greatness of the Supreme Lord, Annapūrṇā, Lakṣmī, and Śrī also became humble with shame at that sacrifice. (18)
Immeasurable, inconceivable, non-manifest, and beyond thought—
whatever the knower of reality desires, that very thing appears immediately.
O Rādhikā, this is the majesty of Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, in that regard.
For those who were blind, afflicted with leprosy, impoverished, deformed, and suffering—blindness, leprosy, poverty, and deformity vanished;
that which was undesirable met its destruction, and indeed, that which was desired was attained. (2.170.20–21)
In this sacrifice of the Supreme Lord, everything was like heaven;
even the *siddhas*, beholding this, were struck with supreme wonder.
All their powers of sovereignty became bowed down with shame.
At that time, even Māyā was overcome with wonder at the miracle of Hari.
Indeed, millions, billions, and trillions of men came again and again to behold Bālakṛṣṇa, and a great crush of people arose. (23–24)

Then the people, longing for a vision of him, fall into despair. Having understood their supreme state of mind and perceived the exhaustion from their journey, the Lord, who is compassionate toward his devotees, recognizes their hopelessness. (25)
And there, right before the devotees, the Inner Self (antarātmā) became visible on all sides;
he was seen in the space before their eyes in millions of forms at every spot—
exactly as he was present in the pavilion and exactly as he was upon the sacrificial seat (homāsana).
Such [a form] was before other sacrificial pits and on the seats for oblation;
such was he in countless palaces and pavilions;
such was he on the banks of rivers, on boats, and even in vehicles.
In celestial chariots, in trees, in forests and wildernesses, such was he;
among devotees and crowds of devotees, on paths, in streets and the like,
in halls, in attic chambers, and in kitchens, such was he.
In dwellings of great honor, as well as in places for guests;
in dining halls, on mountains, and even in gardens—such was he [the Buddha].
In chariots, in parts of carts, and even upon horses, elephants, and so forth.
He is seen in such a manner even within the depths of visible stage-plays;
Hari is seen everywhere—in water, on land, in the sky, in oceans, in lakes, and even in rivers, as well as in calamities and in difficult terrains. (2.2–2.3)
With a face of gentle smile, radiant and adorned with every ornament,
the gentle Bālakṛṣṇa is seen wearing yellow garments.
The Lord bears divine marks, possessing a bow, a banner, and a trident.
He is seen adorned with fish, svastikas, wheels, and other such symbols.
His dark, curling locks of hair are shimmering; his eyes are as broad as lotus petals.
His chest is beautified by the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, and he is attended by Lakṣmī.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, bearing the luster of ten million suns, was beheld;
thus, the vision of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa appeared in every direction before the devotees during that seven-day sacrifice. (37)
O Rādhikā! He accepts the worship performed by children, the elderly, and others;
He accepts food and joy, and He bestows them as well.
He delights in the states of the *rāsa* dance and He delights among virtuous women.
He sports in all the worlds, assuming every form.
O Rādhā, having seen such a marvel, I was filled with wonder.
Then even Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, spoke to me.
Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, this great wonder that has reached its ultimate limit:
Bālakṛṣṇa shines forth, assuming a form corresponding to every form;
indeed, there is no place where Bālakṛṣṇa is not present.
For those people who arrive at the sacrifice not knowing the way,
he becomes a guide for them by going before them.
But for those whose minds are unwell, that twice-born reciter stands before them.

He tells a delightful and ancient tale that brings great delight. (44) Assuming the form of a physician, he approaches those whose bodies are unwell and gives them auspicious medicine that restores their health. (45)
O Rādhikā, a wonderful marvel was seen by me there:
among millions, billions, and hundreds of millions of worlds, no one at all abandoned their body;
nowhere did anyone perish suddenly, and no one there was suffering.
Not a single householder was separated from his own family.
During that crush, no one’s ornaments or the like were lost; there was no massaging of limbs there, nor any foot-rubbing. ||47-48||
Neither was any vehicle broken, nor did any object disappear;
nor was there any human being who had not beheld Bālakṛṣṇa.
Furthermore, there was no embodied being who had not partaken of the remainder of the sacrifice.

At that time, there was no one who had not received a welcome, nor anyone who lacked honor; there was no one whose desires were not yet fulfilled, nor anyone who had not obtained the sacred mantras of Brahman. (2.170.50–51)
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the Lord! Even Īśāna was deluded;
Vāsudeva and the other members of the divine manifestation were struck with wonder.
They became bowed with shame and lost their pride in their own power. (52)
"Oh, what splendor belongs to Lord Bālakṛṣṇa at this sacrifice!
(53) Thus spoke Mahāviṣṇu, shaking his head in amazement.
Pārvatī said to Māṇikī: "Oh, how wonderful is your husband's miracle! (54)
Kaṃbhārā said to Kamalā, "Behold the majesty of my son!
Kamalā, overflowing with joy, held herself in high esteem.
[She did so] in the place of Kṛṣṇa, as well as in the place of Nārāyaṇa, and in her virtuous deeds.

Hari himself remains the creator; this, however, is a great wonder to me. Oh, Rādhikā! By the attainment of Kṛṣṇa here, the sons of Gaṅgā—the oceans—have been made low by you in this performance of sacred rites.
Today, Ketumāla has become meaningful in its own right through the grace of Hari;
indeed, from this day forward, he has become like a banner (ketu) among all the worlds. Moreover, he shall forever remain like a crest-jewel upon the garlands of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa). ||58||
Constantly purified by sacrifices on account of Bālakṛṣṇa, this place shall become equal to Śvetadvīpa in its supreme sovereignty;
this great, purifying region will become a bestower of liberation. (59)
Even the subtle living beings such as insects who die here,

and even embodied beings who are sinners, shall attain supreme liberation. Furthermore, those people who even merely remember this sacrifice in the form of all-encompassing rites [shall likewise attain it].
For them, the destruction of sins shall occur and liberation will be within their grasp.
Even those who have gone to distant lands, by remembering and bowing to the earth,
will undoubtedly attain the merit born of performing sacrifices.
"Indeed, even those who merely shout out 'Nīpa' and 'Prapīṭhikā' shall have their sins destroyed and obtain the fruit born of bathing. Furthermore,
that man who shall proclaim the twenty-seven sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) [shall likewise attain these benefits]."
He shall attain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and great satisfaction through prosperity and other blessings.
He will even receive the dust from the ground between the feet of Saṅgama;
whether upon his head or his body, he shall become a pure-souled being. (64–65)
Moreover, whoever shall go on foot with faith to that land out of a desire to visit the sacred fords (tīrtha),
shall obtain at every step the fruit of a sacrifice.
Or, by staying for even a week, or even a single day, at the confluence (saṃgama).
Some person shall attain eternal heaven. Even if a man or woman performs the seven-day vow for a single day with fruits and other offerings, they shall obtain the fruit of universal sovereignty.
Furthermore, he who lights a lamp even upon the surface of a leaf and offers it to a deity at a sacred ford (tīrtha) shall attain the abode of the Sun.
Moreover, he who gives an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) to one who is wretched or destitute [shall likewise attain that same state].
Having reached the world of the moon, he shall indeed become a consumer of nectar.
Whether it be a garment, or an ornament, or sandals, or two bracelets;
or a parasol, or a chowrie, or a fan, or even a pair of shoes— 2.170.71.
Whoever gives a bowl, a water-pot, a granary, or even a protective amulet, as well as a loincloth to an ascetic here, shall attain the station of Indra.

[One who gives] Māṇikyā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Śrī, and Rādhikā— (Note: The second half-verse appears to be a fragment; the full verse likely concludes with a statement regarding the attainment of these goddesses or their respective realms.)
One who worships [the deity] here together with Bālakṛṣṇa shall partake in liberation.
One should give mouthfuls of fodder to the cows and auspicious grains to the birds here;
one who gives food to people here shall also partake in liberation.
One should offer water, one should offer fruit, and one should present leaves, flowers, and milk at this confluence on the ground of sacrifice; that man shall partake in heaven.
And those who here, with devotion, give a bed, a ball, or a couch—
By the power of their great merit, they shall go to the great heaven.
Those who provide seats, grass mats, and even small benches here will undoubtedly become worthy of the Brahma-seat (Brahmāsana). || 76-77 ||
Those men who perform sacrifices here on this sacrificial ground shall go to the supreme abode, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
[They shall also attain the merit of] the gift of elephants, the gift of horses, and even the gift of land.
Those who here give gifts of swans, cuckoos, peacocks, and parrots,
as well as gifts of bulls, celestial chariots, and likewise vehicles that move by thought— they shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
The gift of a daughter, the gift of land, and the gift of a son are most excellent;

likewise, the gift of a house, the gift of a field, and even the gift of a garden. Those people who shall perform the gift of trees, creepers, and pillars here— ||| 8.1 || [they shall obtain great merit].
They shall go to the immortal heaven, which is endowed with all flavors and nectar.
By giving wood, by giving stones and the like, by giving clods of earth,
and by giving minerals, they will reach the realm of fire.
Those who give curd, milk, and other such gifts will go to the lunar sphere;
those who give household utensils will attain the abode of Brahmā;
and those who bestow kingdoms here shall reach the realm of Vairāja.
Those who give gold and silver shall go to Goloka.
Those who bestow the gift of knowledge shall become worthy of worship by the gods.
Those who provide the means for agriculture shall become like Kubera.

Those who are skilled in the arts and sciences will indeed become pierced [by the truth]. Even if one takes this water-pot to another land and gives even a single drop to someone else, it shall grant liberation to both. (87)

In this water, if the feathers or bones of animals or birds should fall, they shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme state. Even at the time of death, he into whose mouth water falls [shall likewise attain it]. (88–89)
"O Rādhikā, those whose bodies are liberated here, or even whose bones fall into the water, shall all attain liberation; there is no doubt about this.
Such is this sacred ground, circular for a hundred *yojanas*."
Situated between the two rivers, it is purifying and preeminent in its description.
(91) If anyone indeed receives Vaiṣṇava initiation at Makha-sthalī, he shall become a divine four-armed attendant in Vaikuṇṭha. (92)
A woman who possesses the initiation becomes divine, four-armed, and beloved of Hari;
she is eternally liberated, and for her there is no further rebirth.
As for those people who [hear] the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*...
And those people here who cause [others] to hear and who themselves listen go to liberation. (94) One should by all means give food here to virtuous women and to chaste women;
one should give food to holy men, and the donor shall attain liberation. (95)
In this regard, those who shall perform penance through the observances of fasting—
those pure ones who have attained Brahman, who are liberated, and who seek the meaning of the divine syllable,
O Rādhikā, I tell you: what need is there to speak of them where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself resides?
Likewise, there are other incarnations such as Nārāyaṇa, the lords, and the gods;
the ancestors, the seers, the perfected ones, the truthful women, the virtuous wives, and the masters of ascetics;
the female practitioners of yoga, the classes of those worthy of worship, the sacred fords, and the stars. (97–98)
Having arrived, they dwelt there; they drank the water of the rivers, ate forest produce, and touched [the earth] at every spot.
Merely by remembering those divine pastimes, they become partakers of liberation.
"By reading and hearing this, one shall certainly attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offerings Presented at the Seven-Day Sacrifice (*saptāhayajña*), Bālakṛṣṇa’s Assumption of Ten Million Lotus-Forms, and the Greatness of the Gift of the Sacrificial Ground," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 170.
Chapter 171 [Author:
Chapter 172 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, there, indeed, every night in the assembly of people,
the auspicious narration of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā) takes place;
the Lord Sanatkumāra himself, the master, recites it.
Vyāsa Śvetakṛṣṇāyana also expounds the narrative here.
It is called Śvetāsana after the name of Vyāsa Śveta;
that place is the very essence of a sacred ford (tīrtha), eternally bestowing both knowledge and realized wisdom.
It was at that very spot on the bank where the great seer Yavakrīta, the son of Gaṅgā,
performed most rigorous penance after consuming a mouthful of alkaline water.
That purifying and supreme holy site is known as Kṣārakavala.
There, on that plateau, there arose a famous place that always bestows liberation.
By its name, that region also extended for a hundred yojanas,
reaching as far as the shore of the Black Ocean and extending all the way to Nistārā.
Yavakrīta became renowned as one who took refuge at the banks of the Niṣṭhāparā river.
That great sage Yavakrīta was devoted to the rituals of the Vedas.
On the eleventh lunar day, at midday, he spoke to Bālakṛṣṇa.
"O Hari, at this very moment of Abhijit, please offer the final oblations (pūrṇāhuti).
Having heard that, Lomaśa, with the consent of Śrī Hari,
offered the final oblations there into the fire whose essence is the Supreme Brahman.
Having placed betel leaves, areca nuts, unbroken grains of rice, ghee,
and bilva fruits into the *sruva* ladle, Hari offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblations.
He recited the mantras beginning with "oṃ samudrād" and those taught in the verse "pūrṇād arviḥ."
Having heard the seers reciting these [mantras], he offered the final oblations:
"Homage to Agni Vaiśvānara, to the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, to Śatakratu, and to the Waters."
This [is offered] to the Lords of the three heavens, to the incarnations, to the Śaktis, and to the Supreme Brahman—svāhā! Salutation!
This [is offered] to the four who reside on the seven levels and those who dwell upon the earth.
To the insentient and sentient beings, Svāhā! Salutation to me.
To these seven musical notes, to the eight abodes situated in the enclosure, and to the abodes ending with Īśāna, Svāhā! Salutation to me. (13)
"Om Svāhā! To this Brahman, Svāhā! And Svāhā to the Supreme Brahman!
And Svāhā to Me, the One and Only without a second! Om, salutations!
Having spoken thus, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa offered the great final oblations.
He offered countless *śrīphala* fruits, vessels of ghee by the thousands,
sandalwood, sacrificial fuel, and great oblations of sweet offerings.
Then the primordial Lord himself appeared visibly within the circle of fire.
Laughing, he took up the oblations with particular distinction every day;
likewise, he took up those offered in pairs in all the sacrificial pits.
Then the Lord gave countless golden sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
[They offered] gems such as jewels, pearls, and diamonds, as well as various other precious stones.
(18) Having thus performed the full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*), the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas bestowed blessings upon the patron (*yajamāna*) there with sacred mantras. (19)

"May the Brahmins purify [us] with the waters from the *śānti*-pitcher, using *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā*, and mango sprouts," said those who spoke the words beginning with "punantu. Then, the Brahmins uttered propitiatory prayers on all sides.
Then the sacrificial fees were received, and the priests sang words of auspiciousness.
They offered the gods, beginning with Agni, their respective stations,
and then spoke pleasant words of fulfillment.
Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa bestowed upon all the grace of sacrifice, consisting of cooked food marked with lotus designs, which increased and was inexhaustible.
Mādhava, assuming ten million lotus-like forms, gave this everywhere.
Indeed, at that time, no one remained without the grace of Caru.

Whether in the intermediate space, in the atmosphere, in the sky, in water, on land, in a forest, on the earth, in a cave, in a remote region, in a wilderness, under a tree, or on a mountain—[no one was left without his grace]. (24–25)
In a celestial chariot, a vehicle, a carriage, a boat, and even upon a mountain peak,
Kṛṣṇa, assuming countless forms, bestowed the grace of the sacrificial oblation (caru-prasādaka).
Then, indeed, he fed all those who were honored on the earth.
The great liberated guests who have arrived, the liberated ones who possess splendor, the splendors themselves;
the beloveds of Brahmā, the liberated women such as Rādhā, Ramā, and others;
and all the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lords.
The Vyūhas, the guardians of nature (prakṛtipālas), the lords who are the personifications of time (kālapuruṣakeśvaras), those known as the Vairājas and Bhūmas, as well as the hosts of Mahāviṣṇu;
the three deities, the lords of the enclosures, and likewise their wives and female attendants.

The Blessed One fed his servants and male attendants, as well as the female attendants on all sides— those born of the creation of Brahmā and those born of the creation of Īśa. Then he fed the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, the virtuous ones, the ancestors, and the chaste women.
All the gods and goddesses dwelling in the five heavens along with their families, the hosts of celibate students, the guardians of the quarters, the protectors of the worlds,
and the thirty-three deities residing in the Bhuvarloka. ||32||
Mādhava fed the four classes of living beings dwelling on the earth— both the insentient and the sentient— as well as those residing in the seven netherworlds,
all the hosts of gods and demons, and the descendants of Kaśyapa and human beings.

The Blessed Lord indeed fed at that sacrifice all the moving and non-moving beings created by Brahmā, along with their qualities, actions, and those things dependent upon them, as well as their underlying substratum. Today, I am the Blessed Lord, and I feed that which is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).

"On this Ekādaśī day as well, may everything of mine indeed bear fruit. May all [beings] with devotion partake of everything touched by me, though it be devoid of qualities; let the act of eating itself today become a vow through my will alone. (36–37)
Thus spoke the Blessed One; and then, O Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa,
having fed everyone, took his meal together with his father,
his brothers, and his family.
Then his mother, his other mothers, his sister Santoṣiṇī,
and all those dear to Brahmā enjoyed that family feast.
Having received betel nut, all those lords took their rest.
Then musical instruments were sounded and songs were sung;
indeed, everyone became diligent for the purpose of the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
At the confluence of the Niṣṭhā and Parā rivers, there were infinite numbers of men.
The gods, the liberated ones, the lords, all the incarnations, and all the powers;
the ṛṣis dwelling in the three worlds, the truthful ones, and the virtuous—all these followed the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all lords. (42–43)
Accompanied by the great sages and praised with Vedic mantras, he proceeded on foot toward the riverbank for the sake of the avabhṛtha bath. There,
the Lord Bālakṛṣṇanārāyaṇa stood at the confluence of the waters.
The ancient Lomaśa then caused him to perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):
"In the four-faced Egg of Brahmā, at the commencement of creation at the end of the Kṛta age,
during the first cycle, in the glorious Kāṃbhareya Nārāyaṇa..."
And in this present fourteenth year upon this earth,
while he who has descended here in the form of the primordial man remains,
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, on a Sunday—
This [rite] is indeed the end of the sacrifice at the union of Niṣṭhā and Aparā-prapīṭha;
it is the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) that cleanses all sins and possesses the power to wash away the inevitable impurities of the ritual.
Bestowing all merit and warding off all unknown sins, [this applies] when offering minute insects, seeds, wood, particles of chaff, flowers, or buds into the fire;
when offering the earth; when purifying the ground; and when constructing the pavilion.
In the Rasaśālā, whether at the hearth, the mortar, the water-jar,
the grinding stone, the broom, or even in the cutting of leaves and petals— whatever misconduct or transgression has occurred there; ||| 51–52 ||
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa performed a purificatory bath (snāna) for him to destroy [the sin],
for the sake of completing the sacrificial rites, to please the gods,
and for the sake of nourishing his supreme, unprecedented merit— consisting of the final ritual bath (avabhṛtha).
"Endowed with the three-fold creation, I perform my bath today; Oṃ Namaḥ.
Having thus made this firm resolve, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama submerged himself in that water, O Rādhikā, and emerged once again.
Then, having remembered the three worlds, he performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as an ancillary part of his bath;
he then massaged his body with sesame paste,
with the powder of *āmalakī* fruit, with clay from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and with ashes.
With the powder of turmeric from a sacrificial pit,
with sandalwood and musk, as well as barley flour and the like,
and likewise with powders of five colors and all medicinal herbs.
Then, by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) as well as the water from the Suvarṇatīrtha,
and through the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) via the vessel of Brahmā (*brahmakamaṇḍalu*),
he rubbed all the powders together and performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
When the great king had bathed, then the oceans were there:
the Brahma-lake, the ocean of nectar, Virajā, and Mahājala;
as well as the waters of the Nārā, the rivers, the streams, the lakes, and the ponds.
The waters of the sky, the clouds, and the divine white water;
the great sacred ford of Varuṇa, as well as the waters of the great elements—
all these holy fords, together with their presiding deities, arrived there.
They indeed overwhelmed the Blessed One excessively with their streams;
they were the liberated ones, the abodes, the incarnations,
and likewise the female incarnations— powers, lords, goddesses, and beloveds of Brahman.
The ancestors, the lords of the gods, the seers, the perfected ones, and the holy men;
the stages of life, all the social classes, and men, women, and eunuchs;
those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from a sprout, and those born from sweat. || 64-65 ||
The Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Vahnis;
those consisting of earth, water, fire, and air;
those belonging to the sky and those dwelling on the surface; and likewise the sentient and the insentient.
Everyone bathed there at that holy site during the avabhṛtha rite in the ocean of merit.
Amidst that divine conjunction, possessed of divine qualities yet devoid of [material] attributes, and performing a divine act,
a beautiful rain of flowers and sandalwood then fell there.
Then, from the ether, the divine preceptors, the purifiers who dwell in the imperishable abode of Brahmā, the Supreme Brahman, spoke: "May they purify [us]!
O Lord of Devotees, you who descend as incarnations for the sake of devotees, you who abide in the abode of all abodes! 69.
May the incarnations and their attendants, as well as the lords, likewise purify us;
may the goddesses, the great truths, and the sovereigns of the gods purify us;
and may the great seers purify the sacrificer and those who sacrifice.
O gods, let the divine Mahānārāyaṇa, who is pure by his very nature, purify you;
and let the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) that have come here for the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) likewise purify you.
Gaṅgā, Irāvatī, Menakāṅgī, and the daughter of Brahmā [are present].
Aṅgaśikṣā, Aṅgikā, Harāṅgahā, and likewise Āyūrikā;
Bīnā, Yāneśvarī, Caubī, and likewise Sindhu, as well as Coralikā; Valgu, Niṣṭhāparā, Dīnā, Dinapādyā, and Saridvarā—these are the rivers of the quarters. (73–74)
Nārāyaṇī, Naṣṭajarā, Karmāṅgī, Jāmbujā, Nadī, Murā, Kāruliṅgā, Parīṇā,
Āmajānikā, Miśrasurī, Mahākāñjī, Yūkāsanā, and Saridvarā. ॥75॥
May these and other great rivers purify those who perform sacrifices:
Aśvapaṭṭa, Puṣkara, Mānasa, the lake Nārāyaṇa,
Lake Pampā, Indradyumna Lake, and the excellent Lake Brahma.
The lake Śambhula, the lake Cilasa, the lake Kolāraka,
the lake Mākamāna, the lake Bāla, and the lake Māṅgirā;
the lake Lābharuci, the lake Kuvana, and the lake Prāgira.
Ārasaras, Turusaras, Gairānaras, as well as Suśīla-saras;
likewise the auspicious Mīnakaṅkasaras, Bālakṛṣṇa-saras, and the Dvikala-sarovara. || 2.171.80 ||
And the Yugala lake, as well as the Tryaṅginarasarovara;
also the Phulamaṇḍa lake, and likewise the Lurāsa lake;
the Maśakela lake, and also the Jayeśāna lake.
Udvaśa, Sara, and likewise Yoniga-saras;
Leṇḍuga-saras, Pāyūśa-sarovara, Tūnāya, Rukmavāsa, Āvāla, and Rudanphala. (82)
Also Viśturīyasaras, as well as Ālavārta-saras;
Itivartta-saras, or perhaps Tuṅgayānika-saras;
Mādhura, Vāgviyāla, and Nyāsajayātmaka-saras.
And Śirova, the one known as Caṇḍa, Grātavīra, and likewise Saras;
also Grātaślavasara and likewise Arthavāsa-saras;
Vinipāra-saras and likewise Suparīyāraka. (85–86)
May Klinnavārisaras, as well as the lake Īśasarovara,
the Śoṇabhadra river, and the Ghargharā river,
as well as all the oceans here, purify embodied beings.
May the celestial river purify you; may the millions of sacred fords (tīrtha) purify you.
May Meru, Mount Mandara, the Himālaya, the Vindhya, Kārukarmā, Patatkāya, and Mount Raivata purify you. (88–89)
And thus, throughout the rivers and the waters of the ocean for a hundred *krośas*,
all the kings who were performing sacrifices bathed in those various sacrificial rites.
In each of those places, there was a single divine person, radiant as the sun.
Just as Hari was born there from the confluence of two rivers,
so too did he approach Bālakṛṣṇa, holding in his hand a golden vessel containing sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice, along with a flower garland and a crown.
He worshipped according to the prescribed rite and applied a tilaka mark upon the forehead of Hari with a paste of unbroken rice grains, saffron, and sandalwood.
He then placed a crown upon the head of Kṛṣṇa and a garland around His neck.
He prostrated himself there like a staff and spoke to Bālakṛṣṇa with a voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud, while everyone listened:
"I am the Puruṣa, the eternal son of Yama, who has performed his ritual ablution."
This Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which fulfills all desires, is now complete, bestowing full merit.
Today I have attained nourishment by coming here to this place of all holy fords.
