the king— or those possessed of great wealth— must perform the offering of land, villages, and so forth for the sake of the continuous flow of her worship, according to the prescribed rule; or the offering of wealth [by the wealthy] (57).
For the sake of bestowing upon me the supreme knowledge, indeed, vast schools and educational institutions that grant awakening must be established;
and teachers must be appointed as worshippers even within my temple. (58)
The circulation of these books must also be carried out among human beings,
as well as among the gods, in other worlds, and in all the nether regions (pātālas).
In each of those places, one should effect the dissemination of the respective portions of the compendium (saṃhitā).
Thus the tradition proceeds in its sixfold form:
the Vidyā, the Śāstra, the Guru, the Mūrti, the Mandira, and the group of disciples.
The Vidyā is said to be the Parā [Vidyā], while the Mantra consists of the names, the modes of worship, and so forth.
Another [type of knowledge] is manifold, mixed with worldly convention:
the scriptures, the Vedas, the Saṃhitās, the words of the guru, and the speech of Hari.
The guru, moreover, is a Vaiṣṇava who applies the knowledge of mantras, scriptures, and so forth.
And I myself am the embodiment, the Supreme Lord, together with my consort;
accompanied by liberated devotees and beloved ones, I am the noble one, the favorite of Kṛṣṇa.
All my incarnations and my manifestations are the performers of my work. (63–64)
The portions (aṃśas), the digits (kalās), the manifestations (āveśas), and the glories (vibhūtis) are of His own essential nature;
likewise, there are the perfect worshippers, the devotees, and others who are Nārāyaṇas.
The temple has a hundred pitchers and likewise a thousand pitchers.
One should likewise have a firm [image] made, divine and golden, or fashioned from jewels.
Indeed, the groups of disciples should be those who receive and practice the mantra;
the virtuous members of the household, both men and women, shall be the attendants.
Children, youths, and the elderly; those with spouses and those who are widowed; girls and boys; the wise and those devoid of wisdom;
kings, subjects, and leaders; and those most devoted to Brahman who are free from passion. (68)
Ascetics, practitioners of yoga, and likewise self-controlled mendicants—
even those men who are eunuchs, or whoever else belongs to any religious tradition—
should always worship me with a heart full of devotion, free from all hypocrisy. (2.173.70)
If those free from thirst, passion, hatred, anger, malice, and envy were to resort to me, then the tradition would become eternal. However,
when resorted to by those who are faultless, the tradition shall attain manifestation.
But when those who have taken refuge [in the lineage] are possessed of faults, the tradition will fall into blindness.
Where there is no teacher who is enlightened, eternally contented, and free from desire, and who is endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas)—that tradition perishes. (72–73)
Where there is no guru who is renounced, detached, self-controlled, learned in the scriptures, and virtuous, that tradition perishes.
Where there is no guru who is a knower, a giver of knowledge, and a destroyer of ignorance...
And that tradition which pervades all scriptures perishes [when]:
where the guru is a stealer of wealth, addicted to vices, and likewise untruthful; where he is intent solely on his own self-interest and remains silent—that tradition perishes. (75–76)
Where the guru is devoid of compassion and considers those who have sought refuge as belonging to others,
and casts his disciples into suffering, that lineage perishes.
Where the guru is a destroyer of dharma, an atheist, a rogue, and a cheat—
That tradition perishes where the teacher is an abode of faults, a seeker of sensual objects, and a hoard of thirst, greed, and the like;
that tradition perishes whose belly is never filled. (78–79)
Where those who are merely protectors are actually devourers, where saviors are but mockers, and where betrayers of trust are held as superior— that tradition perishes. There,
those devoted to ritual action are but heretics, thieves, plunderers, and robbers.

Where those who hold the highest positions exist, that tradition perishes. (8.1) Where the members of the assembly, the judges of legal disputes, the mediators, the extortionists, and the consumers [of wealth] prevail, that tradition perishes. (8.2)

Where men are violent, unjust, contentious, antagonistic, and afflicted by suffering, that tradition perishes. Where people betray their teachers and look only for faults in others, [that tradition perishes]. (83)

When [the followers] are devoid of devotion and become critics, that tradition perishes. (84) When they lack discernment, lack foresight, are devoid of love, and transgress the worship of those worthy of honor, that tradition perishes. (85)
Where there are those who delight in acts of violence, who consume the property of the gods,
and who disparage their gurus— there the tradition perishes.
Where people hold false views, harbor evil intentions, and have minds pervaded by bad company.
Where people plunder the houses of others, that tradition perishes.
Where people perceive faults in virtues and cannot endure the excellence of others, that tradition perishes; indeed, such people belong to Yama.
Where there is the doctrine that the effect is non-existent [in the cause], where speech is false, where there is injustice at every step,
and where there is the disparagement of the great— there this tradition perishes. Where there is no image of Me, nor is there any temple of Mine.

"I have no compendium of scriptures; that tradition is perishing. I have no constant narrative; there are no pure *hṛndyas*. There are no pure servants at all; that tradition is perishing. (2.173.90–91)
Where householders are the gurus and millions of renunciants are the disciples;
where the gurus indulge in women—that tradition perishes.
If all enjoyments and luxuries reside only with the gurus, [the tradition is lost].

Where there is no element of renunciation, that tradition perishes. (93) A great void behind the teacher, a demonic disposition in his heart, and blindness in grasping [the truth] before him—that tradition perishes. (94)
If that tradition which men and women indeed breathe forth as their heritage should become its own support, then that tradition perishes.
Where there is no learning, no school, and no wonder, [there the tradition is lost].
Where there are no accomplished masters (siddhas) at all, that lineage perishes.
Where the disciples are merely bellies-fillers, devourers of unrighteousness, and devoid of fear of the gods, that lineage perishes. (96–97)
One thing is spoken, another is seen, and yet another resides in the heart of man;
where such a tradition exists, it perishes.
There is atheism regarding knowledge and action, and the display of false sovereignty.
Where there is grasping after having vomited out [the teachings], that tradition perishes.
O Prajāpati, where learning, scripture, the guru, the deities, and temples do not exist, there the destruction of the tradition occurs swiftly. (2.173.100)
"Therefore, the mantras have been given by me; let them be given to the group of disciples.
Let them establish and worship the Vidyā, the Śāstra, the Guru, and the Devas.
Having spoken thus and bestowed his blessings, he caused him to ascend the celestial chariot.
Amidst the sounds of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, and the exhilarating sounds of machines,
he traveled through the sky with his caravan toward the kingdom of Krathaka.
He had been requested by the sage Romāyana and by King Krathaka.
O Rādhikā, then the subjects, seeing Hari departing into the sky, said: "Please return, protect us, and grant us Your vision.

Thus ends the description, in the second section on the Tretā Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, of how Hari bestowed upon King Uralaketu, the great sage Yavakrīta, and the subjects both knowledge of His own true nature and eternal wisdom.
The One Hundred and Seventy-Third Chapter (173).
Chapter 174 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2: The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga.
Chapter 174.
[Author: Chapter 175.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Lord.
In the capital city of Krathaka, known by the name Oṃkāreṣṭā—
a city resplendent and resonant with the humming of bees named Kṛṣṇa—
it was inhabited by the sage Romāyana and the king Krathaka.
When the many kinds of ways had been shown, he brought the celestial chariot down into the garden, which was filled with people and its green grounds adorned with ornaments.
And when the Blessed One descended from the chariot at the royal palace,
As he entered, a rain of flowers and unbroken grains of rice fell.
Musical instruments were sounded according to royal custom with sweet and pleasing tones;
beautiful songs were sung, and shouts of "Victory! arose.
The entire family of Śrī Hari— the beloved wives of Brahmā and the great sages—
descended from their celestial chariot onto the mountain residence, which was richly adorned with gold,
brilliantly illuminated by flashes of lightning, and filled with fragrant scents.
In that palace, delightful with every kind of luxury, shared by male and female servants (7),
crowded and filled with great bustle by attendants, chief ministers, royal family members, and the common folk, Kṛṣṇa entered the mansion. (8)
At the time of his entrance, he was honored with a welcome;
with prostrations, salutations, affectionate glances, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, he was welcomed by the king, the queen, the princes, the princesses, and their brothers and kinsmen. (9)

Śrī Hari was honored for a mere moment with water, as well as with cool breezes, fruits, juices, and excellent drinks; likewise, all those members of his caravan, including his family, were duly honored. (2.174.10–11)
The Supreme Lord, the Blessed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, was delighted by flower garlands, clusters of blossoms, and the sprinkling of fragrant liquids.
Having rested for a moment in this manner, he was awakened by the bristling of his body hairs.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa went to the royal assembly hall (13).
It was shining even at night as if it were day, due to the lamps,
the rays of the jewels, and likewise the light of the moonbeams [reflected] therein (14).
Having reached that vast assembly hall, which was surrounded by deities stationed upon its wall-surfaces,
rich with the visible splendors of gardens, and as beautiful as heaven itself,
Hari sat down upon an elephant-throne.
In that place, richly adorned with gold and diamonds and decorated with parasols and chowries,
his father and the others also sat upon suitable seats.
The Blessed One [inquired] after the welfare and the abundance of happiness of all the worlds.
He likewise inquired after their health, and all the people became joyful. Having washed the feet of Hari, the king and the royal family then drank the gracious water with fragrant scents. (18)
With sandalwood, flower garlands, and the like, as well as with golden necklaces,
diamonds, and pearls, the subjects worshipped the Supreme Lord;
likewise, the leading merchants and prominent citizens offered their worship.
O Lord, we have been made fulfilled by the sight of Your arrival;
the holy city has been sanctified by the Blessed Śrī Hari.
Having found rest today, grant us Your vision tomorrow morning.
Having spoken thus and offered their salutations, all the subjects departed.
Then all the great lords quickly returned to their own residences.
Śrī Hari, together with his family, remained in the magnificent royal palace.
For the sake of rest, Kṛṣṇa went to the bed shown by King Kratha as well as by the ṛṣi; there he lay down and fell fast asleep.
Having partaken of milk and other refreshments, the great-souled ones rested.
O Rādhikā, the king went to his own palace for the sake of rest.
On the morning of the fourteenth day, the Lord, the Blessed One,
having risen and been awakened by auspicious sounds, heard His own stainless glory.
Having meditated upon himself, he then performed all the daily rites in their entirety.
Lomaśa and the other subjects likewise arrived for the purpose of seeing him.
King Krathaka, the queen, his daughters, and his sons all came together.

Eager with all the necessary materials for the worship of Hari, they washed his feet with water and drank that water; likewise, they honored him with garments, ornaments, decorations, diamonds, and pearls. (28–29)
Worshipping Hari with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, flowers, and jewels,
as well as their mother and father— who were pleased like Śuka and his beloved—
and also worshipping the daughters dear to Brahmā, Lomaśa, and the others; || 2.174.30 ||

Then they performed the *ārārtrika* rite and circumambulated [the deity] like a staff; they then offered various gifts before him with devotion. Then the king spoke to Hari-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World.
My kingdom has been purified, and my own abode has also been sanctified.
My family has been purified here; O Blessed One, dwell here forever.
Together with my family, I am yours, O ocean of compassion.
And the Blessed One said to the king: "O King, I shall always dwell in your house in embodied form, as if visibly present.
Build a temple for me and install me, the Lord, here."
The king asked Hari: "When indeed should the temple be constructed?
What is the proper time—such as the *muhūrta* and so forth—and what are the lunar days, asterisms, and zodiac signs?
For these are most excellent for auspicious undertakings, such as the building of a temple and other virtuous deeds."

"O Lord, tell me now those times when you will establish yourself here. Hari said: "O King, whenever the Blessed One exists upon the earth, having indeed assumed a human form, at that time my command shall prevail. (37–38)
Whether by night or by day, at twilight or even during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), at an improper time or in an unfavorable state, or even amidst grief and affliction—
whatever the time may be, it is considered auspicious for that purpose.
For all times are dependent on Hari; indeed, they are auspicious according to His will.
Every kind of place as well is auspicious when it is resorted to by Hari. And the words of those who are capable and equal to Kṛṣṇa [are likewise authoritative]. (2.174.40–41)
Indeed, whatever time one obtains is entirely auspicious;
however, I shall tell you of the excellence of specific times by their very nature—listen.
These are the years, months, fortnights, weeks, and days.
The lunar mansions, planets, days of the week, four ghaṭīs, and the muhūrta;
the yogas and lunar days (tithis) have been arranged for the sake of accomplishing worldly affairs.
O King, listen first as I describe those things to be avoided, each according to its proper category.

One should indeed avoid those combinations (yogas) born of [inauspicious] lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays that are defiled, as well as the *vyatīpāta* and other such [portents], for auspicious undertakings. Furthermore,
one should avoid ill-omened yogas, the *bhadrā*, the new moon, and the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*).
One should avoid one's birth asterism, the lunar day of birth, and the month of birth.

//46// One should also avoid the increase or decrease of the lunar day in auspicious rites. Furthermore, one should avoid those [asterisms] occupied by or currently being traversed by malefic planets. //47//
One should also avoid asterisms that are designated as "to be enjoyed" (bhogya) in auspicious rites.
One should avoid an asterism marked by a portentous event (utpāta) and an asterism pierced by a malefic planet.
Furthermore, one should avoid an asterism that is pierced by a malefic planet even when it is in its proper course.
One should avoid the lunar mansion of a total eclipse for a period of six months;
the mansion of a partial eclipse for three months; and the mansion of a one-quarter eclipse for one month. (2.174.50)
Three days before the eclipse should be avoided, and seven days after it one should likewise avoid;
if the sun sets eclipsed, three days prior [to the eclipse] should be avoided, and if it rises eclipsed, three days following it.
In the case of a total eclipse (pūrṇagrāsa), one should avoid three days both before and after.
One day at the end of a month, two ghaṭīs at the end of a lunar mansion,
one ghaṭī at the end of a lunar day (tithi), half a ghaṭī at the end of an ascendant,
and the poisonous ghaṭī of the lunar mansions— one should avoid these in auspicious rites. (62–63)
One should avoid the defect of *pāta*, as well as *ekārgala*, the day of burning (*dagdhadina*), and the moment of the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*) during auspicious rites. Furthermore,
when the lord of the ascendant is situated in the house of an enemy or of death...
One should avoid midday, midnight, and the junctions of the twilights (55). One should avoid the intercalary month, as well as the setting of Venus and Jupiter;
one should also avoid the periods of childhood and old age for both Venus and Jupiter (56).

One should avoid the following in auspicious rites: the lord of the birth sign being eclipsed, mental distress, birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the mother’s menstrual period, the onset of disease, portents, and other calamities.
Furthermore, when Jupiter is situated in Leo, one must avoid marriage, shaving, and the taking of vows.
Since travel, initiation, and consecration are beset by obstacles therein;

therefore, that lunar mansion which is occupied by a malefic planet, or which is to be occupied, or which is currently being occupied—should be accepted for all undertakings as it brings about success. (58–59)
However, a lunar mansion conjoined with Rāhu must indeed be avoided in auspicious rites.
But if a lunar mansion afflicted by a planet should be occupied by the Sun,
or if it should be occupied by the Moon, then it will become a bestower of auspicious results.
If a lunar mansion is eclipsed by a planet, it becomes auspicious at the end of six months.
However, if there are two eclipses within one month, the first asterism is purified by the first eclipse,
while the second is purified by the second eclipse occurring six months later.
A well dug in Caitra brings sorrow; in Vaiśākha, it is remembered as bestowing wealth.
In Jyeṣṭha, it causes affliction from malevolent planets; in Āṣāḍha, it results in the destruction of livestock.
In Śrāvaṇa, it increases wealth; but in Bhādrapada, it renders one destitute.
In Āśvina it brings affliction, and in Kārttika it causes the loss of servants.
In Mārgaśīrṣa it bestows wealth, and in Pauṣa it grants the fulfillment of desires.
In Māgha it brings the danger of fire, while in Phālguna it is considered to bestow prosperity.
The commencement of building a house when the Sun is situated in Aries bestows all auspiciousness;
when in Taurus, it causes an increase in wealth; when in Gemini, it brings about death;
when in Cancer, it shall be auspicious; and when in Leo, it increases fear. (66)
If [the Moon] is situated in Virgo, it will cause disease; if in Libra, it will be a giver of happiness.
If in Scorpio, there is an increase in wealth; if in Sagittarius, there is great loss.
If in Capricorn, there will be income from wealth; if in Aquarius, it is considered a bestower of jewels. (67–68)
If [the moon] is situated in Pisces, it will cause fear; therefore, one should undertake an enterprise after due consideration.
The installation of a deity in the months of Māgha or Phālguna likewise bestows wealth;
indeed, it grants longevity and health to the master and brings about fame.
In Caitra, she should be understood as bestowing fear and disease in every respect.
In Vaiśākha and likewise in Jyeṣṭha, she is the giver of wealth, sons, and other blessings.
When the sun is in its southern course, one should worship Vārāha and the Mātṛkās.
One should comfortably install Bhairava, Vāmana, Durgā, and Nṛsiṃha;
in Śrāvaṇa, the Śiva-liṅga; and in Āśvina, Jagadambikā.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, one should install Hari, Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and me, the Lord.
In the month of Pauṣa, however, one should install all the deities.
[One should also undertake] constant singing, agriculture, painting, festivals, and the construction of houses and so forth;
as well as clothing, ornaments, decorations, craftsmanship, the arts, and the like.
On the eleventh, the first, or the sixth lunar day—on these days known as *nandā*—one should cause [the scripture] to be prepared, taught, or studied; this shall be auspicious.
Marriage, the investiture of the sacred thread (*upanayana*), journeys, and the wearing of ornaments and the like [should also be undertaken on such days].

Artisan work, training in the fine arts, and the driving of elephants, chariots, and horses; [the mounting of] a bridegroom and the ceremonial riding—listen as I explain how these grant success. On the second, seventh, twelfth, and auspicious lunar days, || 76–77 ||
The maintenance, practice, and employment of armies, battles, weapons, and the like; as well as military expeditions, festivals, the construction of houses, and activities related to medicine—
listen now to these [to be performed] on the third lunar day known as Jaya, and likewise on the eighth.

On the thirteenth lunar day, one should perform that which bestows all accomplishments. Listen: on the lunar day known as Riktā, the killing of enemies, their binding, the administration of poison, and the application of weapons or fire should be carried out. (2.174.80)
On the fourth, the ninth, and the fourteenth [lunar days], success is attained.
On an empty day (riktā), an auspicious rite must never be performed.
[This includes] royal consecration, a military expedition, marriage, and the investiture of the sacred thread.
Listen to [the rules for] rites of pacification (śāntikarma) and rites of nourishment (puṣṭikarma) on the lunar day called Pūrṇā:
indeed, on the fifth, the tenth, and the full moon, they grant success.
By acting in this manner, the accomplishment of the task is certain. (82–83)
The second, fifth, third, seventh, tenth, eleventh, the first day of the dark fortnight, the thirteenth,
and the full moon— these lunar days (tithis) indeed bring auspiciousness for all undertakings.
Other lunar days, however, are never considered to be auspicious at all.

The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the first day of the bright fortnight, and the day known as *darśa*—these lunar days should be avoided in auspicious undertakings, for they bring about fear. (85–86)
The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn— these are the seven days ordained.
For an auspicious rite, Jupiter, the Moon, Mercury, and Venus are the benefic planets.
The Sun, Saturn, and Mars are malefic planets for cruel deeds.
By their very nature, the Sun is stable, the Moon is mobile, Mars is fierce, Mercury is even, Jupiter is light, Venus is mild, and Saturn is sharp.
On Sunday, the installation of a deity bestows splendor and power;
on Monday, it brings security; on Tuesday, it causes fire and burning;
on Wednesday, it yields desired fruits; and on Thursday, it grants stability.
In [the period of] Venus, it shall bestow bliss; in [the period of] Saturn, she dwells in the imagination.

Royal consecration, auspicious ceremonies, the construction of vehicles and mounts, the marching of armies, the accomplishment of mantras, and the discharging of missiles and weapons [are the results]. 92.
The administration of medicine, warfare, trade and commerce, setting fire [to property], service, and even the work of a goldsmith,
as well as wearing ornaments— these indeed are auspicious activities on a Sunday.
Now, on a Monday, one may fashion ornaments from conch-shells, pearls, and silver,
as well as wear such jewelry; furthermore,
the study of the science of music, the performance of sacrificial rites, and agricultural work [are auspicious].
Eating [rich food], indulging in women, causing the boiling of sugarcane juice,
and the excellent construction of water channels, wells, and storage vessels—
these occur on Tuesday; likewise, there is a sense of division and falsehood.
Theft, deceit, the use of poison, weapons, fire, and even killing;
the collection of taxes and fines, and the wearing of gold and coral—these actions are declared auspicious when performed on a Tuesday (Maṅgala). || 97–98 ||
Furthermore, on Wednesday, learning, trade, the arts and so forth,
forming alliances, service, physical exercise, the chanting of the Vedas,
and the commencement of writing a treatise— these activities are considered auspicious. (99)
On a Thursday, one may perform sacrificial rites, as well as acts of righteousness and hospitality (2.174.100).

Auspicious ceremonies, nourishing rites, the acquisition of knowledge, journeys, the construction of houses, medical treatment, and adornment— all such auspicious activities should indeed be undertaken on this day (101).
Under Venus, there is singing, association with women, and the wearing of jewels;
the preparation of beds and couches, and the wearing of garments, ornaments, and the like;
festivals, the buying and selling of land, agriculture, and trade activities. (102)
The preservation of a treasury—these are auspicious [activities] under Venus (Śukra).
Under Saturn (Śani), there is the entering of a house, as well as the initiation into mantras;
likewise, the acquisition of elephants and the like, and the determination of service. 103–104.
The use of weapons, speaking untruths, and even theft— these,
as well as stable undertakings and indeed auspicious deeds, should be performed during the period of Saturn.
Rohiṇī, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Hasta, Citrā, and the three Uttarās [are the favorable constellations].
Revatī, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Punarvasū, Anurādhā, and Svātī— these lunar mansions are indeed auspicious. All auspicious undertakings attain success under these asterisms.
The three Pūrvas, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Mūla,
and Śatabhiṣaj— in these, the activity shall be common (sādhāraṇa).
Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, and likewise Āśleṣā.

"However, O Rādhikā, that most formidable and wicked deed must indeed be performed during these months. Thus did the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa speak to Kratha then, in the presence of the sage Romāyana.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of How, Having Gone to Oṃkāreṣṭā in the Capital City of Krathaka and Performed Worship and Rested, Hari, Being Questioned by the King on the Morning of the Fourteenth Day, Spoke of the Auspicious Times and Other Matters for the Construction of Temples and Other Structures," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 175 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga)
[Author: Chapter 176.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen later to that which the Blessed Lord himself spoke.
And specifically regarding the asterisms, [one should consider] auspicious and inauspicious actions and so forth.

(1) Since Rohiṇī and the three Uttarās are considered to be designated as "fixed" (dhruva), in them one should perform the construction of temples, the digging of village ponds, and the consecration of kings. (2)
Therefore, one should have all stable undertakings performed under these [lunar mansions], for they are stable.
Mṛgaśirā, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Revatī are known as the "mṛdu" (soft) ones.
Because they possess a friendly nature, one should practice singing and sexual pleasure under them.
One should always wear ornaments, auspicious items, and clothing that grant happiness.
The constellations Puṣya, Aśvinī, Abhijit, and Hasta are declared to be light and swift;
therein one may engage in the knowledge of ornaments and medicinal herbs, travel, craftsmanship, and pleasure.
Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Mūla, and Āśleṣā are said to be sharp and cruel;
therein [are performed] piercing, killing, binding, and the accomplishment of mantras, spirits, and so forth.
Śravaṇā and the triad following it, Svātī, and the latter part of Punarvasu are mobile.
In that regard, [the asterisms] Vāji, Gajāroha, and Vāṭikāracanā,
as well as Bharaṇī, Maghā, and the two Pūrvās, are declared to be cruel and fierce (krūra-ugra).
Therein, one should effect cutting, destruction, and the like by means of poison, weapons, fire, and so forth.
Viśākhā and Kṛttikā are considered mixed or common;
the release of a bull, fire rituals, and mixed rites succeed under these.
When Jupiter is present, Puṣya, the three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, or Mṛgaśiras [are auspicious].
If the asterism Śravaṇa, Āśleṣā, or Pūrvāṣāḍhā should occur,
or if Jupiter should be situated there, the commencement of a house brings forth sons,
bestows sovereignty, and likewise grants all happiness.
If Aśvinī, Citrā, Śatabhiṣā, or Ārdrā are situated in the house of Venus (Śukra),
or if Venus itself occupies the next sign from there, the commencement of a house yields wealth and food.
Likewise, Revatī, Puṣya, Hasta, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Maghā [yield similar results].
If Mars is in the Mūla asterism, or if Mars follows it,
then the house begun will be consumed by fire or will cause suffering to one's children.
[The asterisms] Rohiṇī, Aśvinī, the two Uttarās, Phālgunī, Citrā, and Hastā— || 14 ||
Or, if Mercury is favorable for that, the commencement of a house will grant sons.
[The asterisms] named Bhādrapadā (both), Anurādhā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Bharaṇī— [if] Saturn is favorable for these,
and if Saturn is present here at the commencement of the house, [it is auspicious].
There is no doubt that a house built there will become the dwelling of spirits and *rākṣasas*.
If the sun or the moon should be situated above the Kṛttikās at the time the house is begun, it will immediately turn into ashes through fire. (16–17)
Even when the Moon and the stars are joined with or pierced by malefic planets,
and even when the strength of the Moon and the stars is deficient, rites performed under the Puṣya asterism certainly succeed;
there is no doubt that all auspicious acts indeed bear fruit.
Having reflected thus, one should indeed perform the digging of wells and other such works.
Now I shall declare to you the twenty-seven names of the yogas:
Viṣkumbha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, and Śobhana.
Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi,
Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi,
Vyatīpāta, Varīyān, Parigha, and Śiva. (21)
Siddhi, Sādhyā, Śubha, Śukla, Brahmā, Aindra, and Vaidhṛti—
these indeed yield results according to their names and are considered meaningful.
One should avoid Vaidhṛti and Vyatīpāta in every way for auspicious undertakings.
In the cases of Vajra and Vikumbha, the first three *ghaṭikās* must be abandoned;
in Parigha, half [of the period] is to be avoided; in Śūla, five *ghaṭikās*;
in Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa, six; and in Vyāghāta, nine *ghaṭikās*.
Indeed, in auspicious rites, one must avoid that which produces a hostile yoga.
(25) Now I shall tell you the *karaṇas*: *kiṣṭughna*, *bava*, as well as *bālava*, *kaulava*, *taittila*, and likewise *gara*. (26)
In Bava, one should perform rites for prosperity and rites pertaining to the twice-born; in Bālava, [rites for] merchants, laborers, birds, quadrupeds, and elephants;
in Kaulava, rites concerning women and friends; and in Taitila, that which is pleasing to one's wife.
One should plant seeds on the Gaṇḍa yoga and engage in trade on the Vaṇija yoga.

One should not perform burning, casting down, or similar acts during the Viṣṭi yoga, as it is inauspicious there; however, on the Śakuni yoga, one may administer medicine, practice mantra-siddhi, and perform rites for nourishment.

One should perform rites for the kingdom on the day of Govipra; rites for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) on the day of Catuṣpada; rites for good fortune on Dāruṇa; and auspicious rites on Kistughna and Magala. On the eleventh and fourth lunar days of the bright fortnight, as well as during the afternoon of the Bhadrā muhūrta, [these rites should be performed].
On the eighth and the full moon day, Bhadrā is considered to be in the forenoon;
on the third and the tenth day of the dark fortnight, Bhadrā is in the afternoon;
and likewise, on the seventh and the fourteenth day, Bhadrā is in the forenoon.
That Bhadrā lasts for five ghaṭīs in the mouth and one ghaṭī in the throat;
it lasts for ten ghaṭīs in the heart and five ghaṭīs in the navel.
That Bhadrā lasts for six ghaṭīs in the hips and three ghaṭīs in the tail.
Thus, with thirty divisions, there are likewise six auspicious limbs (bhadra-aṅgas). The results for these limbs in their respective functions are as follows:
destruction of the task, death, loss of fortune, dissolution of intellect, and strife. (34–35)
Therefore, the *viṣṭi* yoga must be avoided, and one should also avoid eating in it when it is mandatory.
If Bhadrā occurs during the conjunction of a lunar mansion with a deity, or on a Monday, Wednesday, Friday, or Thursday,
it is auspicious and brings success in all undertakings.
Bhadra arising from the first half of the *tithi* occurs at night, while that arising from the second half occurs during the day.
It should always be understood that it does not confer any defect, especially when a necessary task must be performed.
[This applies] when the moon is situated in Aries, Taurus, Gemini, or Scorpio. (37–38)
Bhadra indeed dwells in heaven and is always considered auspicious;
so too is she who resides in Pātāla considered ever auspicious when there is Dhana, Tulā, Kanyā, Makara, or Candrikā. (39)

When the moon is situated in Aquarius, Pisces, Cancer, or Leo, it is Bhadrā in the world of men; it should be avoided in auspicious rites. Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, Bhadrā, and Mars [are inauspicious] during the afternoon.
All auspicious [planets] as well as even malefic stars are considered auspicious when the Moon is situated in the birth ascendant (janmarāśi); in such a case, the fruit of nourishment arises.
However, if it is situated in the second house, there will never be any happiness whatsoever.
In the third house there is gain of wealth; in the fourth, the occurrence of disease.
In the fifth, the ruin of undertakings; in the sixth, great acquisition of property.
In the seventh, honor from the king; and in the eighth, death is certain. (43–44)
In the ninth house, fear is to be known; in the tenth, the fulfillment of undertakings;
in the eleventh, the gain of wealth; and in the twelfth, various calamities.
In the second, fifth, and ninth houses, the Moon is auspicious when it is in its bright fortnight.
In the dark fortnight, those stars that are powerful should be seized, for they bestow auspicious results.
Having made a square grid, a long nine-sectioned one,
a large three-sectioned one, and seven and twenty [sections], ||| 46-47 ||
In those [sections], the numbers nine should be assigned in sequence to the first group of nine;
likewise, in the second group of nine, the numbers ten and eighteen [should be assigned] in sequence;
and in the third group of nine, nineteen and twenty-seven.
Having thus bestowed [these gifts] upon the newborn, one should understand that birth, prosperity, adversity, security, wealth, cattle, death,
friendship, and kinship—
these ninefold aspects of birth are presided over by the goddess Tārā. (2.175.49–50)
In the first group of nine, she is that [nature]; but in the second, she consists of action.
In the third group of nine, she is always said to be the "placing" (ādhānā).
Indeed, among all three groups of nine, she is both the first and the second.
The eighth star is proclaimed to yield middling results.
The second, fifth, and seventh stars are indeed considered inferior.
The fourth, sixth, and ninth stars are excellent and bestow excellent results. (52–53)
An inauspicious moon, an inauspicious lunar day, and likewise an inauspicious asterism— having crushed these,
the *tārā* situated in the sixth, fourth, or ninth houses yields its fruit.
In journeys, battles, and marriages, the birth-asterism (*janmatārā*) is not auspicious.
In other auspicious undertakings, as well as during entry [into a new dwelling], it is likewise auspicious.
When the Moon is in Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius, it is always situated in the east;
when the Moon is in Taurus, Capricorn, or Virgo, it is considered to be in the south. (55–56)
The Moon is considered to be in the west when [the sun is] in Aquarius, Libra, or Gemini;
it resides in the north when [the sun is] in Cancer, Pisces, or Scorpio.
When facing the Moon, there is gain of wealth, but when to the south, there is happiness and prosperity.

In the west it brings death; on the left, the moon causes the loss of wealth. (58) One should avoid the *karaṇas*, asterisms, days of the week, transits (*saṃkrānti*), the fourth lunar day (*tithi*), the *kulikas*, the four watches (*prahara*), the four *ghaṭīs*, and the conjunctions of Mars, Saturn, and the Sun. (59)
The moon, when facing forward, removes Rāhu, Ketu, and other defects;
even though the moon is situated in a single zodiac sign, it exists in all directions.
There are seventeen ghaṭīs in the east and fifteen in the south.
There are twenty-one ghaṭīs in the west and sixteen in the north;
again, seventeen in the east and fourteen in the south;
twenty in the west and fifteen ghaṭīs likewise in the north.
Even when situated in a single zodiac sign, he bestows the results pertaining to each respective direction.
In festivals and marriages, Jupiter is indeed considered powerful;
however, in the assembly of kings, the strength of the Sun is desired everywhere.
In battle, the strength of Mars is paramount; for the study of sciences, Mercury is powerful.
(64) The strength of Venus is for journeys, and that of Saturn is for initiation.
In all undertakings, the strength of the Moon bestows full results. (65)
On the eleventh day the Guru [Jupiter] is present; on the sixth, Bhauma [Mars]; and on the thirteenth, Śukra [Venus].
On the ninth, the eighth, or the first day, the Sun shall be the day of the week.
On the second, the ninth, and the tenth, it is Monday.
In that regard, the *bodhya* yoga is the *siddhiyoga*, which brings success to all undertakings.
Nandā occurs on Friday and Wednesday, Bhadrā on Saturday, Riktā on Tuesday, Jayā on Thursday, and Pūrṇā on [Sunday];
this is the *siddhi* yoga, which accomplishes the task and grants the success of one's work. (67–68)
When the Sun is in Hasta, the Moon in Mṛgaśīrṣa, Jupiter in Puṣya, Mars in Aśvinī,
Mercury in Anurādhā, Venus in Revatī, and Saturn in Rohiṇī,
there occurs the Amṛtasiddhi yoga, which brings about the accomplishment of all undertakings and goals.
If the Hasta nakṣatra should fall on the fifth lunar day conjoined with the Sun, it is not auspicious. On the sixth day, even Mṛgaśiras conjoined with the Moon is not auspicious.
On the seventh day, even Aśvinī conjoined with Mars is not auspicious.
On the eighth lunar day, even if Anurādhā is conjoined with Mercury, it is not auspicious;
on the ninth day, Puṣya conjoined with Jupiter is likewise not conducive to welfare.
Even though that [ninth day] is the "attainment of nectar" (amṛtasiddhi), it must be avoided in rites for auspicious purposes.
Other yogas for the attainment of immortality accomplish all undertakings.
(73) One should diligently avoid Jupiter and Puṣya at a wedding; Mars and Aśvinī at an entry; and Saturn and Rohiṇī during a journey. (74)
On a day corresponding to any one of the weekdays of the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus;
on a lunar day (tithi) that is the first, fifth, sixth, tenth, or eleventh;
and under any one of the nakṣatras Anurādhā, Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, or Maghā. (75)
On any one of the asterisms Hastā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Śravaṇa, or Pūrvabhādrapadā, the Kumāra-yoga is most excellent and brings about all success;
it occurs on a day corresponding to any one of the weekdays of Sunday, Tuesday, Wednesday, or Friday. (76–77)
On any one of the twenty-second, seventh, twelfth, or fifteenth lunar days;
under any one of the asterisms Bharaṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, or Citrā;
or under any one of Anurādhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Dhaniṣṭhā, or Uttarābhādrapadā.
The Rājayoga indeed occurs when Jupiter and Saturn are situated in any one of the fourth,
eighth, or ninth houses from each other,
or in any one of the thirteenth or fourteenth lunar days (tithis). (2.175.80)
In any one of the asterisms Kārttikā, Ārdrā, Śravaṇa, Uttarāphālgunī, or Svātī;
or in any one of Jyeṣṭhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śatabhiṣaj, or Revatī—whichever constellation is joined with the *sthavira* yoga is most excellent for accomplishing one's objectives. (8.1)
When Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn is in the second, seventh, or twelfth house [from the Moon], and the Moon is in Mūla, Citrā, or Dhaniṣṭhā, it is the Dvipuṣkara yoga.
This is declared to be excellent, bestowing success upon one's undertakings and bringing happiness when beginning a task. 82–83.
When Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn is in the second, seventh, or twelfth house, and when the moon is in one of the asterisms Kṛttikā, Punarvasu, Uttarāphalgunī, Viśākhā,
Pūrvabhādrapadā, or Uttarāṣāḍhā. (84)

The Tripuṣkara yoga accomplishes all purposes and goals. (85) When the sun is in Hasta on the fifth lunar day, it is an inauspicious death-yoga. When the moon is in Mṛga on the sixth lunar day, it is an inauspicious death-yoga. (86)
On a Tuesday with the asterism Aśvinī and on the seventh lunar day, there is an inauspicious yoga of death.
On a Wednesday with the asterism Anurādhā and on the eighth lunar day, there is an inauspicious yoga of death.
On a Thursday with the asterism Puṣya and on the ninth lunar day, there is indeed an inauspicious yoga of death.
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) when the moon is in the constellation Ārdrā, the Abalā-yoga is inauspicious.
On the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) when the moon is in Mṛgaśiras and accompanied by a malefic planet, the Abalā-yoga is likewise impure.
On the second lunar day (dvitīyā) when the moon is in Rohiṇī and Mercury is present, the Abalā-yoga is inauspicious. (88–89)
On a Saturday in the asterism of Kṛttikā, the conjunction of the five [planets] (pañcāvalāyoga) is also impure.
On a Sunday in Kṛttikā on the twelfth lunar day, there occurs the Viṣa-yoga. On a Tuesday in Śatabhiṣā on the seventh lunar day, the Viṣa-yoga is inauspicious.

On the second lunar day, when the moon is in Āśleṣā and Saturn is present, the Viṣaya-yoga is inauspicious. (9.1) In Bharaṇī, when the sun is present, the Dagdha-yoga is always considered inauspicious.
In Citrā, when the moon is present, the Dagdha-yoga is always considered inauspicious. (9.2)
In Maṅgala (Mars) and Uttarāṣāḍhā, the yoga is always considered burnt and inauspicious;
in Dhaniṣṭhā, when Mercury is present, the yoga is always considered burnt and inauspicious;
and in Uttara-phālgunī, when Jupiter is present, the yoga is always considered burnt and inauspicious.

When Venus is combust in Jyeṣṭhā, and when Saturn is also combust while conjoined with Revatī, it should always be understood as inauspicious, for it causes the ruin of one's undertakings. Likewise, when the Sun is in Maghā, the Yamaghaṇṭa yoga is inauspicious. (94–95)
In Viśākhā, it is Candraka; in Ārdrā, it is Maṅgala;
in Mūla, with Mercury, it is Yamaghaṇṭa; and in Kṛttikā, with Jupiter, it is that same one. In Rohiṇī, with Venus, it is he as well; and in Hasta, with Saturn, it is indeed he.
Yamaghaṇṭa should always be avoided, for it bestows no auspiciousness whatsoever.
(97) When the moon is in the fourth, sixth, thirteenth, twentieth, or ninth asterism from the sun’s asterism, that is the Ravi-yoga, which grants all auspicious results. (98)
"O Rādhikā, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is the eternal destroyer of the multitude of manifold defects and the bestower of auspiciousness. Thus,
everything that I have spoken to you regarding Krathaka is exactly so.
It bestows knowledge regarding auspicious times and likewise brings about the fruits of undertakings.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Nakṣatra Wheel for Auspicious and Inauspicious Deeds and Their Results, the Bhadrācakra, the Auspicious and Inauspicious Lunar Results, the Strength of the Stars, the Moon’s Strength, the Siddhiyogacakra, Auspicious and Inauspicious Yogas, and the Strength of Solar Yogas," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 175. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 176 [Author:
Chapter 177 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to these twenty-eight yogas, beginning with Ānanda, which the Blessed One described to Kratha; I shall now declare them to you.
When the Moon is conjoined with the Sun, Aśvinī, Vanikā, and likewise Mṛga.
When Mars is conjoined with Āśleṣā, and likewise when Mercury is joined with Hasta;
when Jupiter is situated in Anurādhā, and Venus is in Uttaraṣāḍhā;
and Saturn is conjoined with Śatabhiṣaj—this is the Ānanda Yoga, which bestows success. (2–3)
When the Sun is joined with Bharaṇī, when the Moon is joined with Ārdrā,
when Mars is joined with Maghā, and likewise when Mercury is joined with Citrā;
when Jupiter is joined with Jyeṣṭhā, and when Venus is joined with Abhijit.
When Saturn is situated in Pūrvabhādrapadā, that yoga is called Kāladaṇḍaka (the Staff of Death).
Its result is death; therefore, it must be avoided in all undertakings whatsoever.
[This occurs] when the Sun is conjoined with Kṛttikā and the Moon is situated in Punarvasu.
When Mars is situated in Pūrvaphālgunī, when Mercury is joined with Svātī, when Jupiter is joined with Mūla, when Venus is situated in Śravaṇa,
and when Saturn is in Uttarabhādrapada, there occurs the Dhūmrākṣa yoga, which yields the fruit of unhappiness.
One ghaṭikā at its commencement must be abandoned; thereafter, it bestows happiness.
On Sunday, Rohiṇī; on Monday, Puṣya;
on Tuesday, Uttarāphālgunī; and likewise on Wednesday, Viśākhā. (8–9)
Pūrvāṣāḍhā with Jupiter, Dhaniṣṭhā with Venus,
and Revatī with Saturn constitute the Prajāpati yoga, which bestows good fortune. Mṛgaśirā with the Sun, Āśleṣā with the Moon, and Hastā with Mars [constitute another such yoga].
When Anurādhā coincides with Mercury, Uttaraṣāḍhā with Jupiter,
Śatabhiṣaj with Venus, and Aśvinī with Saturn,
that Saumya Yoga bestows good fortune; however, it should be avoided for five ghaṭīs.
Ārdrā is for the Sun, Maghā for the Moon, Citrā for Mars,
Jyeṣṭhā for Mercury, Abhijit for Jupiter, Pūrvābhādrapadā for Venus, and Bharaṇī for Saturn;
that is the Dhvāṅkṣa yoga, which causes the destruction of wealth.
When the Sun is in Punarvasu and Pūrvāphālgunī, likewise in Somaka (Mṛgaśiras); Svāti on Tuesday; Mūla on Wednesday; likewise Śravaṇa on Thursday; Uttarabhādrapadā on Friday;
and Kṛttikā when it falls on Saturday. (14–15)
The Dhvaja yoga indeed bestows happiness and grants victory in every undertaking.
Puṣya and Uttarā-phālgunī on Sunday;
Viśākhā on Monday; Pūrvā-āṣāḍhā on Tuesday; and Dhaniṣṭhā on Wednesday; [these are the constellations for the respective days]. (16)
In Venus, Revatī; in Saturn, Rohiṇī—this is the Śrīvatsa yoga, which brings happiness.
(17) In the Sun, Āśleṣā; in the Moon, Hasta; in Mars, Anurādhā;
in Mercury, Uttarāṣāḍhā; and in Jupiter, Śatabhiṣaj. (18)
When Venus is in Aśvinī and Saturn is in Mṛga, it is the Vajra yoga, which brings about destruction.
It should be avoided for five ghaṭikās; thereafter, it may occasionally be auspicious. When the Sun is in Maghā, the Moon in Citrā, and Mars in Jyeṣṭhā—

When Mercury is with Abhijit, Jupiter with Pūrvābhādrapadā, Śukra with Bharaṇī, and Saturn with Ārdrā, this yoga is called Mudgara; it causes the destruction of wealth. It should be avoided for five ghaṭikās, though it may occasionally yield auspicious results thereafter.
When the Sun is in Pūrvāphālgunī, Svātī in the Moon, Mūla in Mars, Śravaṇa and Uttarābhādrapadā in Mercury, Kṛttikā in Jupiter,
and Punarvasu in Venus— then [these are auspicious]. (22)

That is indeed declared to be the *chatrayoga*, which always bestows royal honor. When the Sun is in Uttarāphālgunī, the Moon in Viśākhā, Mars in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Mercury on Wednesday, [that is the *chatrayoga*]. (23–24)
Revatī with Jupiter, Rohiṇī with Venus, and Puṣya with Saturn—
this is indeed declared to be the Mitrayoga, which bestows nourishment in all undertakings.
Furthermore, Hasta with the Sun, Anurādhā with the Moon, and [Puṣya] with Mars...
Furthermore, Uttarāṣāḍhā on Wednesday, Śatabhiṣaj on Thursday,
Aśvinī on Friday, Mṛgaśiras on Saturday, and Āśleṣā on Sunday— this yoga, known as Mānasa, indeed bestows happiness in all undertakings. (26–27)
When the Sun is in Citrā and the Moon in Abhijit, it is Jyeṣṭhā; on Tuesday it is Mṛgaśirā, and on Wednesday it is Pūrvābhādrapadā; on Thursday it is Bharaṇī, while on Friday it is Ārdrā;
on Saturday it is Maghā—this is the Padma-yoga, which brings about the acquisition of wealth.
A period of four ghaṭikās must be avoided; thereafter, it is considered to bestow happiness.
When Svāti, Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, and Śravaṇa fall on a Sunday; when Uttarābhādrapadā falls on a Tuesday; when Uttarāphālgunī falls on a Wednesday; and likewise Kṛttikā on a Thursday. (2.176.30)
When Venus is in Śukra-yoga and Saturn in Prākphālgunī-lambuka-yoga,
it causes the loss of wealth and must be avoided for exactly four ghaṭikās.
Furthermore, when Viśākhā coincides with the Sun and Pūrvāṣāḍhā with the Moon;
When Dhaniṣṭhā falls on Tuesday, Revatī on Wednesday,
Rohiṇī on Thursday, Puṣya on Friday, or Uttarāphālgunī on Saturday,
that is the "Utpāta-yoga" (the portentous conjunction), which must be avoided because it results in the destruction of life. || 32-33 ||
Anurādhā with the Sun, Uttarāṣāḍhā with Mercury,
Śatabhiṣaj with Mars, Āśleṣā with Mercury, Mṛgaśīrṣa with Jupiter,
Āśleṣā with Venus, and Hasta with Saturn— this is the conjunction of death (mṛtyuyoga).

One should always avoid the full moon, for its fruit is indeed death. [The asterisms] Abhijit on Sunday, Prāgbhadrā on Monday, Bharaṇī on Tuesday, Ārdrā on Wednesday, Maghā on Thursday, and [Śatabhiṣaj] on Friday and Saturday [are to be avoided]. (35–36)
The conjunction of Citrā with Kaṇa is troublesome and should be avoided for two ghaṭīs.
Mūla is [inauspicious] on Sunday, Śravaṇa on Monday, Uttarā-bhādrapadā on Tuesday,
Kṛttikā on Wednesday, Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā) on Thursday, and Pūrvaphālgunī on Friday.
When Svāti coincides with Saturday, it is Siddhiyoga; the fruit shall be the accomplishment of one's purpose.
(38) Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Sunday, Dhaniṣṭhā and Revatī on Monday, Rohiṇī on Tuesday, Puṣya on Wednesday, and Uttarāphālgunī on Thursday are [Siddhiyogas]. (39)
When Saturn is in Viśākhā, that is an auspicious conjunction that brings about well-being;
when the Sun is in Uttarāṣāḍhā, and the Moon in Śatabhiṣaj;
when Mars is in Aśvinī, Mercury in Mṛgaśirā, and Jupiter likewise [in Puṣya].
Āśleṣā with Venus, Hasta with Saturn, and likewise Anurādhā [with Saturn] constitute the Amṛtasiddhi yoga; it bestows royal honor and other riches.
Abhijit with the Sun, and Pūrvābhādrapadā with the Moon likewise [constitute this yoga].
Bharaṇī with Mars, Ārdrā with Mercury, Maghā with Jupiter, Citrā with Venus, and Jyeṣṭhā with Saturn—this is called the Mūlaśalya yoga.
It causes the destruction of wealth; lasting four ghaṭikās, it must certainly be avoided.
On Sunday, Śravaṇa; on Monday, Uttarābhādrapadā;
likewise Kṛttikā on Tuesday; Punarvasu on Wednesday;
Pūrvāphālgunī on Thursday; Svātī on Friday; and Mūla on Saturday. ||44-45||
The *gadāyoga* causes destruction; it should be avoided for seven *ghaṭikās*.
It occurs when Dhaniṣṭhā falls on a Sunday, Revatī on a Monday, Rohiṇī on a Tuesday, Puṣya on a Wednesday, Uttarāphālgunī on a Thursday, and [Śatabhiṣaj] on a Friday. (46)
Viśākhā with Saturn and Pūrvāṣāḍhā with the Moon constitute the Mātaṅga-yoga.
It bestows increase of one’s lineage and is considered always to bring about auspiciousness.
Śatabhiṣaj with the Sun, Aśvinī with the Moon, and Mṛgaśiras with Mars [constitute the Mātaṅga-yoga]. (47–48)
Āśleṣā with Mercury, Hasta with Jupiter, Anurādhā with Venus,
and Uttarāṣāḍhā with Saturn constitute the Rākṣasī yoga.
This yoga bestows great suffering and must always be avoided in auspicious undertakings.
Pūrvābhādrapadā when the Sun is in that asterism, and likewise Bharaṇī when the Moon is there;

Ārdrā when Mars is there, Maghā when Mercury is there, Citrā when Jupiter is there, and Jyeṣṭhā and Abhijit when Venus is there—this is the Cara-yoga, which causes the failure of one's undertaking. (2.176.50–51)

That period of three ghaṭikās should indeed be avoided; beyond that, it may occasionally bring profit. When the sun is in Uttarā-bhādrapadā and the moon in Kṛttikā, and when Punarvasu is with Mars and Pūrvā-phalgunī with Mercury.

Svāti with Jupiter, Mūla with Venus, and likewise Śravaṇa with Saturn [constitute] Sthira Yoga, which brings about great undertakings and increases all prosperity. Revatī with the Sun, Rohiṇī with the Moon, and Puṣya with Mars [are also included]. (53–54)
When Uttarāphālgunī falls on Wednesday, Viśākhā on Thursday,
Pūrvāṣāḍhā on Friday, and Dhaniṣṭhā on Saturday,
that is the yoga known as Vardhamāna; it always brings auspiciousness when used for determining the ascendant.
The first lunar day (pratipad) falls on Sunday and Friday; the second on Monday and Mercury;
the third on Tuesday; the fourth on Saturday; the fifth on Jupiter;
the sixth on Tuesday and Venus; and likewise the seventh on Mercury. (56–57)
If the eighth or ninth lunar day falls on a Sunday, a Saturday, or a Tuesday;
or if the tenth falls on a Sunday, a Saturday, or a Thursday and the Moon;
or if the eleventh falls on a Thursday or a Friday; or if the twelfth falls on a Wednesday. (58)
If the thirteenth lunar day falls on Tuesday or Friday, and the fourteenth on Saturday, and the fifteenth on Thursday, this is the Siddhi Yoga, which brings auspiciousness.
Now, I shall describe to you twelve other inauspicious yogas. (2.176.59–60)
Hutāśana, Dagdha, Viṣa, Krakaca, Saṃvarta, Caturthīgṛha, Mṛtyu, Vajrapātaka,
Kālamukha, and Jvālāmukha— these inauspicious ones are to be avoided.
On the sixth day it is the Moon, on the seventh Mars, and on the eighth day it is Mercury;
on the ninth day Jupiter, on the tenth Venus, and on the eleventh Saturday;
on the twelfth day it is the Sun—the conjunction with Fire (Agniyoga) is always inauspicious.
On the third day Mercury, on the fifth Mars, on the sixth Jupiter,
on the eighth and ninth Venus, on the eleventh the Moon, and on the twelfth the Sun—
this is known as the *dagdhayoga*, always considered inauspicious. (64)
Mercury is in the second [house], the Sun in the fourth, and the Moon in the sixth;
Saturn and Mars are in the seventh, and likewise Jupiter in the eighth;
Venus is in the ninth—where such a planetary conjunction occurs, it brings about fear. (65–66)
On the sixth day Saturn, on the seventh Venus, and likewise Jupiter on the eighth;
on the ninth Mercury, and likewise Mars on the tenth;
on the eleventh the Moon, and likewise the Sun on the twelfth.
That yoga called *krakaca* is indeed considered inauspicious in every respect.
When Mercury is in the first [house] and the Sun is in the seventh, that is the inauspicious *saṃvarta* yoga.
Likewise, when Saturn is in the first, Venus in the second, and Jupiter in the third.
On the fourth day it is Mercury, on the fifth Mars, on the sixth the Moon, and on the seventh the Sun;
the conjunction with the house of the fourth day is inauspicious.
On the first day it is Jupiter and Mars, and on the second Venus and Jupiter.
Mercury is in the third house, Venus in the fourth, and Jupiter in the fifth;
Saturn is in the sixth, as is the Sun and Jupiter;
likewise, the seventh is occupied by the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Venus, while Mercury is in the eighth. (71–72)
The ninth [tithi] falls on Friday and Saturday; thereafter, the tenth follows.
On the eleventh day are the Sun and Mars; on the twelfth, the Moon and Jupiter.
On the thirteenth are Mercury and the Moon; likewise, on the fifteenth is Saturn.
On the fourteenth lunar day, when Mercury, Venus, or the Sun [are present], it is a *mṛtyuyoga*.
This inauspicious configuration that causes death must always be avoided.
Anurādhā on the second lunar day, and the three *uttarā* constellations on the third, [are likewise to be avoided].
On the fifth day, however, is Maghā; on the sixth, Rohiṇī follows thereafter.
On the seventh is Hasta and Mūla, and on the eighth is Pūrvābhādrapadā.
On the ninth is Kṛttikā, and on the eleventh, if Rohiṇī occurs—
The conjunction of Citrā with the thirteenth lunar day is known as Vajrapātaka.
It certainly brings about suffering equal to a thunderbolt strike in all undertakings.
Anurādhā on the third lunar day, and the three Uttaras on the fourth, [are likewise unfavorable]. (77–78)
On the fifth lunar day with Maghā, on the eighth with Rohiṇī, and on the ninth with Kṛttikā—
this is the yoga known as Kālamukha, which always yields inauspicious results. Furthermore,
Mūla occurs on the first lunar day (pratipad), and Bharaṇī on the fifth day.

On the eighth [tithi] with Kṛttikā, on the ninth with Rohiṇī, and on the tenth with Āśleṣā—this conjunction is Jvālāmukha; it is inauspicious and always causes agitation. On the seventh [tithi] with Bharaṇī, on the ninth with Puṣya, and on the tenth with Āśleṣā—[this is another such conjunction]. (2.176.80–81)
On the thirteenth lunar day, Citrikā occurs; indeed, that is an inauspicious conjunction.
On the first [day] there is the Sun and Mars; on the second, Venus and the Moon;
on the third, Mercury and Jupiter; and on the fourth and fifth, Saturn.
On the sixth day, the Sun and Mars; on the seventh, Venus and the Moon;
on the eighth, Mercury; on the ninth, Jupiter; and on the tenth, Saturn.
On the eleventh, the Sun and Mars; and on the twelfth, the Moon and Venus. (83–84)
Mercury in the thirteenth [lunar day], Jupiter in the fourteenth, and Saturn on the full moon—
these are declared to be inauspicious yogas that obstruct all undertakings.
Likewise, at the junction between the constellations Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla, as well as between Revatī and Aśvinī.
The four *ghaṭīs* in the interval between Āśleṣā and Maghā,
as well as two *ghaṭīs* before Pūrvaphalgunī and two *ghaṭīs* after it, constitute the conjunction of *gaṇḍānta*.
This too must be avoided in auspicious undertakings, for the *gaṇḍaka* yields undesirable results.
Between the fifth and sixth [tithis], at their junction,
and between the tenth and eleventh [tithis], at their junction, there is a *gaṇḍānta* lasting for two *ghaṭikās*.
Likewise, there are two *ghaṭikās* at the end of the ninth [tithi] and one *ghaṭikā* at the end of the fifth [tithi].

At the end of the fourth [lagna], half a ghaṭikā should also be avoided as Gaṇḍānta. The interval between Cancer and Leo, the interval between Pisces and Aries, and the middle of Scorpio and Sagittarius are recorded as Gaṇḍānta for one ghaṭikā each. (2.176.89–90)
From Ravi (the Sun) to Śani (Saturn), these Muhūrtas are respectively fourteen,
twelve, ten, eight, six, four, two, and one;
they take the form of Kulika-yogas and should be avoided in auspicious rites.
From Mercury down to Mars, the muhūrta-numbers are indeed those same [as before];
they are to be avoided as they take the form of "thorns" (kaṇṭaka-yoga) in sequence. From Jupiter down to Mercury, the muhūrta-numbers are indeed those same [as before]. (92–93)

Gradually, that very yoga known as Kālavelā must be avoided; likewise, those same Muhūrta-numbers from Śukra up to Guru [are to be avoided]. Yamaghaṇṭa, too, must indeed be avoided in succession for the performance of auspicious rites.
The Kulikas and others have been described for the day; now hear them for the night. From the Sun to Saturn, these Muhūrtas follow in sequence:
thirteen, eleven, nine, seven, five, three, and one. (95–96)
Those forms of the *kulika-yoga* should be avoided in auspicious rites.
From Mercury to Mars, those same figures are the "thorns" (*kaṇṭaka*). From Jupiter to Mercury, those figures are the "time-velocities" (*kālavelikā*).
From Śukra up to Guru, those [periods] known as Yamaghaṇṭakas are to be avoided at all times during the night for auspicious rites; indeed,
on Sundays, the fourteenth Muhūrta is to be abandoned as it is inauspicious.
Likewise, for the Moon, the ninth and twelfth [houses] are indeed to be avoided as they are unfavorable;
for Mars, the seventh at night and the fourth during the day are to be avoided;
for Mercury, the eighth; and for Jupiter, the sixth and twelfth are likewise to be avoided.
In the case of Venus, the fourth and ninth [houses] are [inauspicious]; for Saturn, the first and second.
These are indeed evil moments and must be avoided in auspicious rites.
However, when the Moon is auspicious, all of them become weak and proclaim good fortune.
In the conjunction of accomplishment (siddhiyoga), even bad yogas become powerless and proclaim success.
When the sun is situated in the middle of the sky during the muhūrta called Abhijit,
the two-ghaṭī period known as Jayamuhūrta destroys all defects.
In that [situation], every undertaking begun will be victorious; of this there is no doubt.
Then, a staff seven finger-breadths long should be placed upon the ground, and its shadow should be observed according to the method known as the "shadow of success" (siddhacchāyā).
For the Sun, it is eleven finger-breadths; for the Moon, eight and a half finger-breadths;
for Mars, nine finger-breadths long; for Mercury, eight finger-breadths long;
for Jupiter, seven finger-breadths; and for Venus, eight and a half finger-breadths long. (106)
When the shadow produced by the sun reaches eight and a half finger-breadths during the time of Saturn,
that moment known as Siddhicchāyā makes even the wicked auspicious;
at that time, [one should disregard] the lunar mansion, the lunar day, the day, the star, the moon, the planets, and so forth.
"Having reflected upon these aforementioned [factors], auspicious works such as the digging of wells and so forth should be undertaken.
Thus, O Rādhā, he spoke to King Krathaka at that time.

Thus ends the section on the examination of inauspicious yogas arising from the twenty-eight lunar days (tithis), weekdays, and asterisms (nakṣatras) beginning with Ānanda, as well as the three types of *gaṇḍānta* yogas, *kulikā*, and other inauspicious muhūrtas, in the second part, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Jīva, Chāyā, Muhūrta,
and Other [Time Units]," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 177.
[Author: Chapter 178.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Hari [performed] the higher planetary rites and so forth.
Krathaka said: "I shall speak of that and other useful matters.
[The lords of] Aries are the Sun, of Taurus the Moon, and likewise Mars for Capricorn;
Mercury for Virgo, and indeed Jupiter for Cancer. (1–2)
For Jupiter is in exaltation in Pisces, and Saturn in Libra;
indeed, the Sun is in Libra, and likewise the Moon is in Scorpio.
Mars is in Cancer, and likewise Mercury is in Pisces.
Jupiter is the preceptor of Capricorn; Venus is in Virgo; Saturn has gone to Aries.
(4) These [planets] should be understood as situated in their states of debilitation, and they do not bestow happiness at all.
Kanyā is the domicile of Rāhu, while Mithuna is its exaltation sign. (5)
The bow sign (Sagittarius) should be understood as a debilitated position, and its results are likewise [unfavorable].
If auspicious planets are situated in the second, fifth, eighth, or twelfth houses from a dual, common, or fixed sign ascendant— excluding the eighth and twelfth houses—
and if they occupy other positions [as well], [the results are favorable].
If malefic planets are situated in the eleventh and sixth houses,
the commencement of a house, palace, or temple is auspicious. If Jupiter and the Sun are in the ascendant, and Mercury is in the sixth or seventh house, [the undertaking is likewise favorable].
If Venus is in the fourth house and Saturn is in the third,
then if one should undertake the construction of a house or similar project, that [house] will indeed have a lifespan of a hundred years.
If Venus is in the ascendant, the Sun in the third, Mars in the sixth, and Jupiter is also present—

If one should build a house when [the Moon] is in the fifth house, that [house] will indeed have a lifespan of two hundred years. And if one should build a house or the like when the Sun is in the eleventh house, Venus is in the tenth house, and Mercury is [in the ascendant], that [house] will indeed have a lifespan of one hundred years.
If one constructs a house when Jupiter is in the fourth house, Saturn and Mars are in the eleventh, and the Moon is in the tenth,
its lifespan shall indeed be eighty years. Or,
if Venus is in its exaltation in the ascendant, or Jupiter is in the ascendant or the fourth house.
If Saturn is in its exaltation or in the eleventh house, it bestows prosperity upon the home.
(13) If the Moon in Cancer is in the ascendant and Jupiter is in a quadrant,
and the other planets are in their signs of exaltation or in their signs of friendship, (14)

When that is conjoined, the house built will become eternal and a bestower of fortune. If Venus is situated in the ascendant of the sign Pisces, and Jupiter is situated in the fourth house in Cancer; ||| 15 || [then it is so].
And the *tulāśani* occurs in the eleventh house.
A house begun [under such conditions] bestows prosperity and long life.
All planets are not auspicious when situated in the twelfth or the eighth house.
Malefic planets situated in the ascendant, the trines, or the tenth house are not auspicious.
Furthermore, the Moon in the ascendant joined with Mercury is also not auspicious at all.
The Moon situated in the eighth house is certainly and most certainly not auspicious.

If all the planets should be situated in their debilitation navāṃśas (nine-degree divisions) therein, the house built there will indeed be destitute; therefore, one should by no means undertake any work there.
If even a single planet is in the ninth navāṃśa of an enemy planet... [2.177.20]
Even if [the lord of the year] is situated in the tenth or seventh house, and likewise again [the lord of the ascendant is there],
if the lord of the ascendant is indeed weak,
then that house will be built within the year, but it will certainly fall into the hands of another.
If the lord of the ascendant, the lord of the birth [sign], and whichever planet is the lord of the [current] sign—
as well as the Moon, Jupiter, and Venus— are not set, and if they are situated in their exaltation, their own signs, or their own Navamśas; || 22–23 ||
Then the house commenced will always bestow happiness and prosperity.
Now, if at the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the Sun is in the ascendant or in a kendrā (angular house),
and if it is in the third, sixth, tenth, or eleventh houses— the houses of increase— then [the result is auspicious].
If the Moon is likewise situated in the aforementioned places, it shall be excellent.

A planet of that same nature will be excellent when positioned in Sagittarius (Dhanus) or the ninth house (Dharma), or in even-numbered signs. Mars and Saturn [are auspicious] in the third and eleventh houses, while the benefics are [auspicious] in the sixth house.
If Mercury and Jupiter are auspiciously situated in the second, twelfth, eighth, or sixth houses,
and Venus is in the first, second, fourth, fifth, ninth,
tenth, eleventh, or even the third house, he is indeed most excellent. (27)
If malefic planets—Ravi (the Sun), Bhauma (Mars), Śani (Saturn), Rāhu, and Ketu—are situated in the first, eighth, fifth, or seventh houses, then those [malefics] are so;
likewise, if the benefic planets and the Moon (Śaśin) are in the eighth or the first house. (28–29)
In the sixth or eighth house, these planets become Kuṇḍalīs and must be avoided.
However, the installation of the deity Sūrya is considered auspicious in Leo ascendant;
likewise, for Hara (Śiva) it is auspicious in Gemini, and for Viṣṇu and myself as well, in Virgo ascendant.

In the case of Brahmā, the installation is prescribed in a movable (cara) lagna of Aquarius; for the minor deities, likewise in a movable lagna; and for the Yoginīs, their installation is considered best in a movable lagna. However, for the Goddesses, a dual-natured (dvisvabhāva) lagna is excellent for a stable installation.
When the Ascendant is fixed (Sthira), the installation of all deities is considered most excellent.
However, if the Moon is in the first house during the installation, it brings death;
but if it is in the second house, the sign of Sagittarius, the Moon bestows an increase in grain.
In the third house of valor, the Moon indeed causes affliction.
Located in the fifth house, the Moon causes the destruction of one's lineage and progeny.
In the sixth house, the Moon brings fear from enemies; in the seventh, the Moon bestows suffering. (34–35)
In the eighth house, the Moon bestows death and causes obstacles; in the ninth, it is the Moon itself.
In the tenth, it grants strength, and situated in the eleventh, the Moon bestows wealth.
Situated in the twelfth, it causes expenditure; thus should the Moon in the Kundalī be understood.

Even the auspicious Moon becomes inauspicious if it is situated in the seventh house from a malefic planet. Likewise, even if joined with a malefic planet, it is impure; similarly, if it is situated between malefic planets, it is inauspicious, and if waning, it is also impure. (37–38)
If [the Moon] is in its sign of debilitation or in a division belonging to Saturn, it will be inauspicious;
however, if it is conjoined with or aspected by Jupiter, it will become auspicious.
Alternatively, if it is situated in its own sign of Cancer or in its exaltation, it will be auspicious. (39)

If the Moon is situated in a benefic planetary navāṃśa, or occupies the navāṃśa of its own sign or a sign that is its own or a friend's, then even if it is otherwise inauspicious, that Moon shall indeed be auspicious. [40] Furthermore, if it is located in the first, fourth, seventh, or tenth house from the Moon... [41]
If the planet should be malefic, then by that sequence these following configurations are inauspicious:
Āpīḍā, Saṃpīḍā, Bhṛgu, and likewise Vartitā.
When an action is performed therein, it results in harm to oneself, one's kinsmen, one's wife, and one's work.

Indeed, there would be the destruction of the four; therefore, one should not undertake any task therein. Even if a malefic planet should be in the same zodiac sign where the Moon is located, then that conjunction constitutes a defect and must be avoided in auspicious undertakings.
When the Moon is conjoined with Mercury or Jupiter, there is indeed no fault arising from conjunctions;
nor are there faults produced by the year, solstice, season, month, asterism, fortnight, or the "burnt" day (dagdha-aha).
Furthermore, there are no defects arising from the ascendant being afflicted by blindness or one-eyedness, nor those born of the Moon’s ninth-part (navāṃśa) being associated with malefic planets.
Defects arising from the guru, jña (Mercury), and Śukra (Venus) situated in angles (kendras) or trines (trikoṇas) are destroyed.

Defects produced by the nine divisions (navāṃśa), the planets, the six dignities (ṣaḍvarga), the kṣaṇa, and the ascendant—all these defects are destroyed when the Moon is in the eleventh house, by its power. 46–47.
If Jupiter is in the Lagna in Vargottama, or in the Moon's sign, or in the eleventh house from the Sun, or if he is in a quadrant or a trine, then by his strength all defects are destroyed.
Leaving the seventh house, if Mercury is in a quadrant or a trine; ॥48॥
Among those, Venus destroys two hundred faults;
Jupiter among them destroys a hundred thousand faults, and auspicious results will follow.
(If) the lord of the ascendant should be in the ascendant itself, or if he should be in its ninth-part (navāṃśa), [the result is as stated]. 2.177.50.
Whether in the eleventh house or in a quadrant, it destroys all defects;
and when the strength of the ascendant is excellent, malefic yogas never cause harm.
Having counted from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should determine the number of the lunar day (tithi).
Having added the number of the weekday starting from Sunday to the number of the asterism starting from Aśvinī,
one should sum those numerical values and divide by four.
If one remains as the remainder, the earth situated there brings strife at the commencement of a house.
If two remain as the remainder, the auspicious Kṣiti is seated; likewise if three remain.
If zero remains as the remainder, she is Jāgratī; however, at the commencement of building a house, she bestows what is undesirable.
Having thus observed all this, Krathaka indeed built a magnificent mansion here.
"Explain my purpose to you so that I may obtain worship, service, and the like.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, the Supreme Ruler beloved of Kṛṣṇa, ceased speaking.
Accepting those words, Krathaka worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Likewise, other subjects, their hair standing on end with joy,
offered worship; and full of eagerness, they paraded Hari through that city with auspicious vehicles, mounts, musical instruments, and welcoming ceremonies.
They honored Acyuta with infinite offerings.
Hari, his hair standing on end, gave everything there to that great-souled one;
he also bestowed gracious gifts upon the subjects and upon the king and his family.
Having purified the city as well as the mansions of the merchants,
he returned to the royal palace and partook of food.
Then all those daughters of the king also took their meal.
And the five divine knowers of the Self took the hand of Hari.
The giving away of Kumāra took place at midday;
thereafter, they departed from the kingdom together with Kumāra and Hari.
All the sages, headed by Lomaśa,
who were dear to Hari and likewise dear to Brahmā, departed after receiving leave;
escorted by the king, they went forth preceded by royal honors.
Then, requested by King Pṛthu of Kṛpāsthala,
as well as by the mountain-dwelling king Pṛthu and the sage of Kṛpāsthala,
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by the subjects, traveled through the sky.
By way of the divine vehicle, they beheld from the sky the capital city of Jarasthalī, O Rādhikā, which was adorned with forests,
rich in the splendor of its welcoming arrangements, and situated on the banks of the river Pṛthā.
Having seen the subjects and the celestial chariot, they raised a shout of victory: "Victory!

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Results of High and Low Planets, the Results of the Planets situated in the Ascendant Chart at the Time of Installation, the Results of the Moon, the Āpīḍa and other Yogas, the Defect of Conjunction (Yuti-doṣa), the Strength of the Ascendant, the Examination of 'the Earth is Asleep' and so forth, and thereafter the Wandering through the City, the Worship, the Farewell, and the Arrival at Jarasthalī, the Capital of King Pṛthu," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
