Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Rādhikā, my beloved of dear life and beautiful form;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa departed for Jarasthalī by means of a celestial chariot.
At that time, the family of King Pṛthu was also there with Hari;
for the sake of welcoming Acyuta, they brought him down from his celestial chariot amidst the sounds of musical instruments,
shouts of victory, and the booming of cannons.
Making the air resound with the booming sounds of drums and cymbals,
the king, having received the worship of the *hāra* (necklace), stood upon the ground nearby,
in a great garden on the bank of the Pṛthu river, which was adorned with royal palaces.
The Lord descended from the sky onto the vast surface of the earth.
Then the King himself gave necklaces to Śrīśa, the Supreme Soul;
at that time, the King’s wife Kṛpī gave necklaces to Kaṃbharā, who was Śrī herself.
The young maidens saw twenty necklaces upon the neck of Brahmapriyā; they all worshipped her, and other girls as well did the same.
Likewise, a hundred young princes worshipped the sages.
Having asked after his welcome and well-being, the king,
accompanied by the assembly of people, seated Hari upon a divine throne situated in the royal court.
And Hari inquired after the auspicious welfare of all the people.
Then, on the fourteenth day, in the evening, he paraded Hari through the city.
(9) Thereafter, having gone to the riverbank, he performed the twilight rites at night;
Śrī Hari then partook of a meal together with the sages. (2.178.10)
Having obtained rest during the night, he woke up early in the morning;
having performed his daily worship and other rites, he was honored by the king in the assembly hall.
There, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself gave spiritual instruction.
O King, just as clouds arise in the rainy season and then dissolve,
so too do all beings come into existence and pass away.
Whether it be today, tomorrow, the day after, or even further on, separation from them will surely follow.
There is no doubt that for those who have gathered together in a mass,
bodies will develop within the womb and attain nourishment outside; indeed,
once old age has truly arisen, they laugh only at their own destruction.

Just as the mind is unstable, flickering, and deceptive, so too should the body be understood; there is no difference between them in this regard. A human being wonders: "When and where will this [body] ever be separated from me? (15–16)
One is unable to determine [the outcome], and even that which is protected shall pass away:
the kingdom, the lineage, the family, the kinsmen, the subjects, and the servants;
likewise, women and children exist according to the influence of past karma. (17)
The attainment of the Blessed One arises for these people through great merits.
O King, there is no end to your merit, nor even to that of your family, by which the great sages have today found lodging in your house along with me. (18–19)
"Great indeed is the good fortune of those subjects whose sight is mine;
today your kingdom has become a holy land, having taken on the very form of a sacred pilgrimage site.
Thus did the king himself address Śrī Hari there.
Having bowed to Śrī Hari, he inquired about his own previous births and so forth:
"Who was I in the past, O Kṛṣṇa? Who are these my kinsmen? And what is my entire family and progeny? Tell me, O Mādhava. (2.1–2.2)
Thus questioned, Hari said: "Listen, O King, to your story.
In a former kalpa, you were a sage named Āraṇyaka.
You subsisted on wild fruits and always made your dwelling upon the trunk of a tree. (23)
The eight great highways converge there in the vicinity of your hermitage.
O Mānava, people come and go upon those paths to your hermitage,
resting for a moment and eating the fruits provided by you.
Having drunk water and bowed to you, they depart as they please;
there, service is rendered to them by you with fruits and waters,
and repeatedly for a long time through the provision of seats and other such supports.
You should by no means have them perform service for you;
for since you possess knowledge, no debt whatsoever should be incurred.
One must certainly give to all, but not accept even a speck of dust.
In that same way, a debt arises for them through accepting gifts and taking [possessions].
However, with this human body, one should never incur a debt at all.
The debtor undergoes rebirth; of this there is no doubt.
Through service, liberation is born; through service, heaven is attained. (2.178.3) By means of services, having obtained blessings, they become long-lived.
Whatever was given in the past is certainly obtained later through disciplined practice. (3.1)
Therefore, one should give according to one's ability and should give repeatedly with faith,
whether to a man, a woman, a living being, or to any person whatsoever.
Thinking thus, you have given, and many souls have been propitiated.
At that time, there were twenty-five sages in your hermitage;
they were your equals and devoted entirely to service.
In this manner, all of you [should care for] women, men, and others who are without a protector.
Having served them by providing a dwelling, the foolish forest-dwellers— having seen the happiness and observed the service [rendered] in your hermitage—
lived there continuously, even though they were poor and destitute.
Always abiding by the command of the twenty-six Brahmins, they serve all who arrive and indeed acquire merit. All those servants indeed perform their service with desire. (36–37)

Those who had taken refuge with the sages were born as householders established in hermitages; that circle of humans increased to more than a thousand, and it remained supported by twenty-six [others], like servants and attendants. (38)
And by them, regarding the matter of consciousness and the transition to the next world, you compassionate Brahmins were indeed requested:
"You must not depart for the eternal state, leaving us behind. (2.178.40)
"O Brahmins, we must certainly go after first leading you to heaven or liberation.
Such words were offered out of compassion, saying, "Let it be so for those who have sought refuge. This very compassion, though appearing as a bond, exists for your sake.
The virtuous should practice auspicious compassion that removes the suffering of living beings;
however, they should not act in such a way that it results in their own bondage. Indeed, you have acted here to bring about your own imprisonment. (42–43)
In that place, you twenty-six [disciples] were indeed previously established as repositories of merit through the virtue of helping others;
likewise, there is that maṇḍala which was resorted to by more than a thousand [others] on the far shore.
But during the daily dissolution, or when an accidental dissolution occurs at evening,
all [beings] abandon their bodies and depart from here to the heavenly world; then,
having gone to Maharloka itself, they remain until the night of Brahmā.

Having exhausted [their merit], they were created again; taking refuge in heaven as deities, there arose fourteen Manus and likewise twelve Suns. When that kalpa had passed, those dwelling in heaven became the abodes of happiness.

All those who were formerly his servants became dependent upon him in that same way, and their families likewise came into being. An entire kalpa passed away through the merits of service acquired in the past. (48–49)
Then, in the creation of the gods within heaven, I myself became the Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. In the form of the King of Kings, I am present in all your vital junctures.
And I was the one who conferred the coronation upon each of them in those various places.
At that time, I was indeed the ruler of the Sūryas and the Manus;
and then, through your service, I was entreated by you for the sake of liberation.
Having reflected upon my merit, I [vowed] that after one more birth, may liberation be yours; and the words "So be it" were granted.
For karma that has not been experienced does not perish, even when ten million kalpas have passed.
And that which remains from the enjoyments of heaven must be experienced on the surface of the earth.
Indeed, you have come to this land of the experience of karma for the sake of that enjoyment;
and when the kalpa has ended, at the next creation, it is likewise for the sake of auspicious enjoyment alone.
O sirs, you were indeed born here together with your families;
Bhava was the Araṇyaka Manu, and he was the third.
The first was Uralaketu, and the second was Krathaka Manu.
Uṣṭrālarāja was the fourth Manu in that kalpa;
Haṃkāra was the fifth, and Jayakāṣṭhala was the sixth.
Tīrāṇa was the seventh, and Alvīnara was likewise the eighth. (57–58)
Jinavardhi was the ninth; the tenth was Alpaketuka;
the eleventh was Jayakṛṣṇa; the twelfth was Yajñaśānaka;
the thirteenth was Indurāya; and Gaṇaka was the fourteenth.
These were indeed the Manus who were the lords of the earth here;
then there were twelve Suns. Mudrāṇḍa was the first, Līnorṇa the second Sun, and Vṛhaccharas was the third.
The fourth is Balalīna, and the fifth is Varasiṃhaka;
the sixth is Rāyagāmalaka, and the seventh is Phenatantuka.
The eighth is Stokahoma, the ninth is Ārka, and the tenth is Kāṣṭhayānaka.

The tenth was King Kolaka, the eleventh was the King of Aṅga, and the twelfth was Śākuntarāja; at that time in ancient days, these were the Suns. Thus, the Suns are my own forms as the Lord of the Kings of Kings.
Through my own entry [into them], you twenty-six indeed became kings born here as Manus, Suns, and auspicious refuges. Consequently,
there arose for you the state of being lords over the kings of kings.
And on the following day, the yoga of Vāmana occurred again in heaven.
By the power of my great merit, this yoga has arisen for you once more here on earth, O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (66–67)
Those who were without protectors— whether women, men, boys, girls, or servants— all those members of your family were then in heaven;
yet here on this earth, they have been born as your kinsmen once again.
"In the sacrifice, I indeed bestowed upon all of you the gain that was my sphere of experience.
Therefore, because of what was asked by you, I have related your previous birth;
I know all of that, though it has been forgotten by you. (2.178.70)
But as for you, having enjoyed the kingdoms of Manu and the realms of the Sun through the merit of the service rendered to embodied beings by you while living as forest-dwellers in the wilderness,
you have now been born here indeed as kings for the sake of experiencing the remainder of that enjoyment.
"O great sages, by my yoga, by my ancient merit, and indeed by the power of my latent impressions (saṃskāras), the sons of Gaṅgā and others,
such as Kṛpāsthala, who reside in this region, have been acquired by you. (72–73)
I served [the sages] in every way with love and likewise acquired their blessings; therefore, having remembered all that ancient history once again,
I dispatched Vṛkāyana Nīlakaṇṭha here for the sake of the sacrifice.
For the sake of awakening and for the sake of liberation, I have come here myself, remembering you as well as Lomaśa and the other sages;
and all these subjects who were formerly before you [are likewise remembered].
Those people who have eaten the sacrificial grains and fruits as guests—
the subjects in your territories are indeed meritorious and devoted to you.
I consider their fortune to be supreme, since they have been united with the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, the creator of all beings, cannot be attained by one of little merit. (78) Holy men who know Brahman cannot be attained by one of little merit.
Relatives devoted to service cannot be attained by one of little merit. (79)
A family that serves Hari cannot be obtained by one of meager merit.
There shall be a virtuous wife who serves Him, sons who are devoted and obedient to His commands, and daughters endowed with devotion for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. (2.178.80)
Servants endowed with righteousness, devoted to truth, and bringing contentment;
those who perform their duties, bestow nourishment, and provide assistance in religious works; and those who share in one's sorrows—such people do not meet with those of little merit. (8.1–8.2)
Worldly happiness is obtained through merits for an infinite duration;
the bliss of the Supreme Brahman is obtained through the dharma of service to Hari.
It is incalculable, infinite, and never eclipsed.
That happiness is neither diminished nor transformed; it is free from suffering.
O King, the fulfillment of human existence lies in the dedication to Brahman;
that has been accomplished by you kings during this great festival of sacrifice.
"O you, you have achieved your purpose here by taking refuge in me.
I am pleased and honored by all your dispositions in this great sacrifice.
Today I have been established in your home; your house is forever sanctified. (86)
Worship me with a spirit of love and construct a beautiful temple.
Install me there as the two-armed Supreme Lord, in whatever form you have seen or obtained—handsome and adorned with a ruby. (87–88)
Always serve him who is endowed with Lakṣmī and possesses a divine nature;
he is seated upon an elephant-throne, measuring four and a half fingers in height.
Likewise, he is joined by Śrī and Padmā and accompanied by Ramā while seated upon the great throne.
"Establish me eternally; worship me and obtain happiness.
Having thus instructed [them], and having received their offerings, he then fed the people;
and having himself eaten, he established many [disciples] who were devoted to his own mantra.
Having obtained a brief rest at midday from the circles of kings,
and then being honored by the principal figures and others at the end of the watch, Śrī Hari was thus entreated in many ways by King Uṣṭrālaka.
Requested by the sage Yugaśāva, the Supreme Lord [said]:
"Let that great kingdom of Pṛthu Rāja go to Uṣṭrāla after midday.
At that time, Pṛthu Rāja had twenty daughters. (93–94)
Having gathered together with their mothers, they approached for the purpose of worship,
holding in their hands garlands of choice, unbroken grains, flowers, and fragrant vessels; and thus,
in the form of a *svayaṃvara*, O Rādhikā, [they offered them] upon the neck of Hari.
At that very moment, a bridal garland was offered by twenty [maidens],
and according to the rite of bestowing a maiden upon a youth, they took the hand of Hari.
With great longing, they all gazed at Hari with love.
Having bowed down to their father, their mothers, and the circle of elders,
and having received blessings in every way, those beloved of Brahmā then became [ready].
A festival was quickly celebrated by everyone with the offering of garlands and other honors.
Then there were celestial chariots fully prepared for departure;
twenty maidens indeed desired to go with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the chariot of Śrī Hari, who is beloved by all.
Others set out after closing their eyes, all having ascended the celestial chariot;
likewise, the entire family of Hari, as well as other great sages, departed.
At that time, musical instruments were indeed played, producing auspicious sounds.

They sang songs and the chanting arose. Strengthened by the ritual of the waving of lights (ārātrika) as well as by offerings of handfuls of flowers and other rites, Śrī Hari quickly ascended from that spot into the sky.
O Lord, amidst shouts of victory, the roar of machines, and cries of joy,
the aerial chariot and other vehicles moved comfortably ahead in the sky.
Furthermore, O Lord, by Your grace, the subjects here were indeed worthy of being approached.
Thus they spoke in many words, pleasing the Supreme Lord.
In a mere moment, O Rādhikā, celestial chariots then descended from the sky along the path indicated by Yugalaśāva to the kingdom of Uṣṭrāla.
Having arrived at the city of Viyānikā on the bank of the Dinapā river, Hari, traveling through the sky, beheld the kingdom of Rādhika, which was most beautifully adorned.

(1.07) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, [it is told how] having gone to Jarasthalī, the capital of King Pṛthu, and having received a welcome, Hari instructed [the king]; and [how he described] the former state of those twenty-six kings as Ṛṣis, Manus, and Suns in a previous kalpa.

Thus he spoke; then, having rested, he arrived at the kingdom of Uṣṭrāla on the full moon day—this concludes the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description [of His Journey]," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 179.
[Author: Chapter 180.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, there was a king who was the lord of the city of Viyānā.
And likewise, his younger brother Uṣṭrāla was a king of devotees;
he was gentle by nature, known by the name Haṃkāraka, and was the lord of the city of Guḍākeśī.
Furthermore, his third brother was named Jayakāṣṭhala.
The king of Prayāga city was righteous and possessed auspicious intentions; he was the family preceptor of the three royal lineages and a protector of the world.
The entire family of kings, as well as other kinsmen and friends, [were under his care].
Then all the subjects of the merchant, for the sake of welcoming Hari,
[prepared] on the bank of the Dīnapā river, which was beautifully adorned with a great garden,
at a site not far from the city called Viyāna.
For the purpose of welcoming Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul,
[the people] were provided with banners, flags, insignia, and musical instruments such as conchs;
they were accompanied by vehicles, mounts, carts, celestial chariots, and carriages.
Wearing garlands of flowers, unbroken grains, sandalwood paste, and fragrant scents,
(7) and accompanied by royal armies and circles of subjects who had performed their services for them,
they remained intent upon that [divine presence] in the sky, awaiting the auspicious arrival. (8)
They beheld their own celestial chariot and as many other chariots as there were suns,
all possessing such exceeding splendor;
they raised shouts of victory and displayed welcoming banners in the sky.
Then musical instruments were sounded and the roar of machines arose;
they gave signals to indicate the descent of the celestial chariots.
All the subjects sang cries of victory mingled with hymns of praise.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!
Supreme Brahman, Beloved of Ramā, Beloved of Rādhā, O all-pervading Hari!"— in this manner,
the kīrtana was performed by more than a hundred thousand people.
The riverbanks and the sky indeed resounded with the proclamation of his fame. Then the subjects, like surging ocean waves, were eager to behold the Lord,
the Sovereign of the Lords of Lords, who was like the full moon.

In the vast Mahodyāna grove, the vehicle of Hari descended; then all the other vehicles likewise descended there from the sky. The three kings and their ministers received them with respectful welcome.
Then all the subjects offered auspicious welcomes to Hari.
By the first-born, a necklace of jewels was presented upon Hari’s neck;
by the second, a string of diamonds was then placed around Hari’s throat.
With the third, a necklace of ocean pearls was offered;
and then the queens presented a golden garland to Hari.
Flowers and garlands were likewise placed around the neck by the sons, daughters, and others.
Hari was honored and worshipped with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, sandalwood paste, and other offerings. He was likewise venerated by the subjects, the wealthy, and the assembly of ministers;
as were Śrī Hari’s parents, his brothers, and his sister.

Then the royal family and all others indeed worshipped the sages, the great sages, the devotees, those dear to Brahmā, and all the female attendants. Having bowed to him as he sat upon the elephant-throne, the royal family [honored him].
Having prostrated like a staff and washed his feet,
the king and the other leading subjects then drank the nectar of his feet in due order.
Thus, having offered a most cordial welcome and having caused milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to be prepared, [they honored him].
They paraded through the entire city, carrying drinks and fruit-eatables;
accompanied by armies adorned for the royal occasion and various musical instruments,
they, full of zeal, paraded with hymns of praise and songs of his names.
A magnificent and spacious elephant-vehicle moved forward;
at the city gate, he was honored by young maidens with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, water-pitchers, and hands joined in salutation to dispel his sorrow. (25–26)
On the main road, Hari was honored by wealthy merchants stationed in their shops;
he was sprinkled with pearls before him in the square by throngs of women,
and by all the subjects in every way with sandalwood water.
Hari was worshipped and glorified with flowers, unbroken grains of rice and other offerings, coconuts, fruits, saffron, sugar, and floral garlands;
he was honored by the city women along all the royal highways.
Beheld in many ways, the Lord, whose true nature is beyond form, was a source of satisfaction;
at that time, the Youthful One was known as the most desirable youth to the maidens,
and as the Lord of charming form to the young women.
To the elderly, he appeared in the form of a child; at that time, he was known as being like a son.

To widows, he was known as their manifest Lord, directly attainable. To virtuous women, he was known as the embodiment of the True Being (Sat-svarūpa), and to the helpless, he was known as their protector.
He is known as the teacher of the youths, the ruler of the young,
and the one who is attainable by the elderly;
he is known as Hari, the Lord of his devotees who are worthy vessels of love.
To the spectators he appeared in a beautiful form; to the yogis, as the embodiment of Brahman;
to the sages, as Acyuta bearing the conch, discus, and other emblems, awakened to his true nature;
and to the virtuous, he was then the Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (34–35)
"Thus, by wandering through the city and showing himself, the two-armed Supreme Lord became known to all the worlds;
having captivated the hearts of the people, he returned to his own royal palace."
He rested there for a moment, and Lomaśa gave this instruction:
"O King, this is Nārāyaṇa himself, Śrī Puruṣottama, who has appeared for the sake of you, the solar kings of former births. (37–38)
The Lord, who is directly subservient to His devotees, has come here remembering them;
for sacrifice, fire-offering, chanting, the turning of the rosary, worship, austerity, knowledge, charity, and service all shine forth in their true essence in Kṛṣṇa alone. (39)
Kṛṣṇa is the refuge of all dharmas and himself the treasury of all merit.
For those men and women with whom he has personally united, appearing in the form of a human sage, their service shall bring about the delight of Kṛṣṇa. (2.179.40–41)
Just as one serves a husband, a wife, an aged mother, a guru, an elder, or those worthy of honor, so too should one serve Hari.
[She] was directly perceived in her divine form, the bestower of the four goals of human existence.

Wherever devotion to the Supreme Lord exists, there both the duty of the householder and the duty of the ascetic reside. For one who dwells there constantly, the offering of oneself with one's whole being must be made to the Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest. (43–44)
The Blessed One, the true worthy recipient, is encountered directly through millions of merits.
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, the body is momentary, and wealth is momentary.
That Blessed One, the Supreme Person, must be propitiated in this very moment.
What is the use of sovereignty, or wealth, or family, or people?
(46) What is the use of fortune, or prosperity, or honor, or learning?
What is the use of a field, a wife, women, sons, daughters, and so forth? (47)
What is the use of vehicles and celestial chariots? What is the use of renown or even fame?
What is the use of a well-nourished, handsome body or physical strength?
[48] If [one serves] Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with devotion and service...
Even by means of offering and devotion, He is not truly satisfied in this birth.
One's very self must be given; for whatever belongs to oneself, all of that is indeed to be offered.
Both enjoyment and liberation are to be acquired from Acyuta through the offering of everything.
By you and by these kings, a great and auspicious sacrifice has been performed here;
this young Śrī Kambharā-Bālaka-Kṛṣṇa has been fully gratified.
Indeed, you have all accomplished your purpose and attained every auspicious station.
"Since he has been thoroughly propitiated, nothing further remains to be done.
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa then ceased.
The king, taking hold of the feet of Śrī Hari, placed them upon his own head. (52–53)
The queen, the princes, and the princesses placed [the command] in their hearts;
having received the order, they all departed, and Hari attained rest.
Having prepared food and other provisions, they all took to sleep.
Having risen early in the morning and performed his daily rites, Hari,
who is honored by the assembly of great sages, then sat upon a beautiful seat.
At that moment, the king, the queen, their daughters, and their sons arrived.
Uṣṭrāla, Haṃkāra, and Jayakāṣṭhala also entreated the Lord most fervently for the sake of long-term residence.
Hari said: "Today, indeed, the fruitfulness of your birth has been realized."
"From seeing you and worshipping you, a state of serenity has been attained by me.
O sinless ones, that which would cause me to be fully pleased must always be performed. There is absolutely no time remaining for me to dwell here any longer. (58–59)
It is necessary to go to the kingdom of Haṃkāra’s Ālaya,
and it is also necessary to go to the kingdom of Jayakāṣṭhala.
Here, profit has been gained, and I am satisfied with this honor.
"May the touch of your feet upon the ground take place within the royal palace.
Let this be held in mind: I shall fulfill your desire this very day.
Having drunk milk this morning, you shall travel by means of celestial chariots."
Everyone must certainly go to the kingdom of Haṃkārālaya at the outset;
there, one should take a meal at midday and likewise wander through the city.
Only after midday should one perform the placement of the feet and other such rites.
One must indeed go to his abode in the kingdom of Jayakāṣṭhalara.
Having wandered through that city and purified that abode, one should then eat at night and rest for the remainder of the night. (64–65)

"At the time of dawn, you must go to the kingdom of Ālvīnara; acting according to that instruction, ensure everything is favorable. My command must be observed in every way, for happiness is found right there. ||66||
"Even in a very short time, I shall grant you happiness beyond measure.
Having heard this command of Hari, those three brothers were delighted by the Lord's words and acted accordingly with great reverence.
O Rādhikā, at that time, when the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa had received the hospitality of Uṣṭrālasya and was preparing to depart,
the five sons of Uṣṭrālasya performed worship with great reverence.
The ten daughters took the hand of Hari in marriage, desiring him as their husband.
Delighted by their parents there according to the rites of wedding, they reached Hari and met with great eagerness within the circle of the beloveds of Brahmā.
Having then received those blessings, they set out;
and then the maidens of the mountain king, together with the departed Hari,
ascended celestial chariots and quickly departed through the sky.
In a mere moment, they reached the capital Guḍākeśī, ruled by King Haṃkāra, hearing the proclamations of victory—
augmented with auspicious sounds— announced by those who had gone ahead of them.
[He saw] the city of Guḍākeśī, situated on the bank of a river with poor crossings, beautifully adorned, endowed with great gardens,
and decorated with gate-towers, arches, and finials.
Adorned with colored garlands, svastikas, and other banners and emblems;
swept clean, sprinkled with perfumed waters, and made to resound with the music of instruments; and greeted by the citizens who had come out from the city to welcome him. (76–77)
Haṃkāra, together with his family and his younger brother, went forward; accompanied by his army, he offered a welcome with banners of victory and other honors.
Following its indications, Yugaśāvaka [approached] that celestial chariot.
Then the sage brought down [the chariot] from the sky near the palace;
likewise, other celestial vehicles descended from the heavens at that time.
Then shouts of "Tūp! arose, along with cries of victory and hymns of praise. (2.179.80)
Then Hari quickly descended from his celestial chariot to the surface of the earth. King Haṃkāraka, together with his family,
then honored Hari with shouts of victory and worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Having washed the feet of Hari, the king and the others drank the water.
Then, having placed Śrī Kṛṣṇa upon a horse-carriage,
the king led him toward the city along the royal highway with great festivity.
Bowing to Hari at every station, the subjects honored him with devotion;
they presented offerings, sought his audience, and performed salutations and other rites.
The ministers, having led him to their own homes, performed the arghya and pādya ceremonies for the Lord.
Having led the subjects to their respective homes, they worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Having thus purified the city of Guḍākeśī, they all then proceeded to the royal palace; at that time, Hari descended from his golden chariot.
Having descended quickly and bathed, he performed the midday rites;
having offered food to the deity and having fed all his dependents,
he himself ate and then rested for a moment.
Having made the king well-pleased and having bestowed auspicious blessings,
Hari, accompanied by his retinue, was at the time of the midday meal about to depart by means of his celestial chariot when he was entreated by the queen, the princesses, and the others. (88–89)

Then, having been honored by the king, he took the hands of five maidens; at that time, they were commanded by Kṛṣṇa’s mother. They became fulfilled in their purpose, and the entire family was filled with joy.
Those five, possessing divine forms, were conceived by the beloved wives of Brahmā.
Then, having taken leave of the king, the queen, and their subjects,
Hari ascended his celestial chariot and departed for the sky along with his retinue.
Then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose;
having granted his audience, he quickly departed for the city of Prayāga, the auspicious refuge and capital of King Jayakāṣṭhala. (93)
Then the Lord reached that delightful city, which was endowed with great gardens, in the evening.
King Jaya went forward with his subjects and offered a welcome,
accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and adorned with banners and well-arrayed troops.

Having seen the beautiful city named Prayāga at evening, the Lord of Lords, Śrī Hari, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, then descended from the celestial chariot to the earth through the path described by Yugaśāva.
Then the celestial chariots descended near the palace.
Having washed the feet of Hari with water, the king drank [the water from them];
having offered a welcome with necklaces and other gifts, he gave him excellent water.
Having caused all the waters to become sweet, the king, together with his army,
joyfully led Kṛṣṇa on a tour of his own city;
the Supreme Lord was honored by the subjects and the leading classes.
Having purified the ground of the city with his footsteps and the gift of his sight,
he arrived at the royal palace and partook of food and other refreshments;
then, after having fed everyone, he rested at the onset of night.
The Supreme Lord was gratified by the songs of those royal singers and bestowed upon them offerings and diamonds as rewards.
Having slept at night, Hari was then awakened at dawn by musical instruments.
Mādhava quickly performed his daily rites during the Brahma-hour.
The king, having approached with his subjects, placed offerings before Hari;
he then bestowed all of that upon Yugaśāva for the sake of his three brothers.
Then the queen Vaiṣṇavī, accompanied by her five daughters, arrived for the purpose of worship; having worshipped him, the five maidens,
fallen under the sway of delusion, took Hari as their own beloved.
Having married the Supreme Lord according to the rite for bestowing a daughter upon a youth,
they felt their purpose was fulfilled; thereafter, they indeed drank the milk and caused their venerable household head to drink it as well in great abundance.
Mādhava caused the king and all his subjects to drink [the milk]; likewise, the eternal Supreme Soul caused the sages, the gods and others, as well as the beloved wives of Brahmā and the rest,
to drink the milk and other [substances].
Then Kṛṣṇa, intending to depart, gave his blessings. He quickly became ready and was then sent forth by the subjects and others;
he first swiftly ascended the divine celestial chariot.
Others also swiftly ascended their own celestial chariots, and then they set forth with shouts of "Victory! and auspicious blessings.
King Tīrāṇa, the ruler of the regions of Valgurā, [also departed].
Then the sage Valgu-rāya, accompanied by his family and possessing a household,
previously departed for Hari by means of a celestial chariot. From the sky, Hari beheld the regions of Valgu-rāya.
Then, from the sky, she beheld the most beautiful capital city situated on the delightful bank of the river Sevika;
and Rādhikā, remaining in her celestial chariot, heard the sounds of auspicious music.
The sounds of victory, the shouts of "Tūṣa," and the cries of "Victory! uttered by the people.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Travel by Air-Vessels to the Royal Capitals of Uṣṭrālaya, Haṃkāra, and King Jayakāṣṭhala; the Wandering through the Cities, the Worship, and the Departure toward the Royal Capital of Tīrāṇā on the Morning of the First Lunar Day," in the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.

→ Chapter 181
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhikā, the glorious Lord Hari, together with the sage Valgurāya and King Tīrāṇa, ascended His own celestial chariot.
He brought it down to the earth by the path he had shown;
then the other celestial chariots descended behind it.
At that time, there arose shouts of "Victory! and the sounds of musical instruments.
Then there arose on all sides the joyful shouts of women, the sweet voices of children, and the cries of "Welcome! from the people;
as well as showers of flowers, showers of unbroken grains, and even a rain of sandalwood powder.
At that time, when Hari emerged from the celestial chariot,
other great-souled beings also descended from their vimānas.
There, the king named Tīrāṇa bowed at the feet of Hari.
Neither the family nor the royal attendants washed the feet of Hari.
All the members of the household, however, having washed his feet,
offered him drinks adorned with golden necklaces, jeweled necklaces, and strings of pearls and gems.
They all placed [the garland] upon the neck of Hari, the Supreme Brahman and the Supreme Self.
They offered a welcome with flower garlands and proclaimed cries of "Victory!
Then, on a chariot drawn by seven horses from Reṇḍiyāra, the King [placed] Hari.
He seated Śveta upon the horse, and likewise the others on the steeds.
Honored by the royal armies and worshipped by the foremost monkeys, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shone forth, enriched by the splendor of the parasol and chowries. (2.180.9–10)
In the city named Tīrāṇa, the king indeed caused Śrī Hari, accompanied by His caravan, to be paraded with great honor;
all the subjects worshipped Him exceedingly at every spot along the way.
Having granted an audience until midday, the Lord reached the royal palace,
which was like the assembly hall of the gods and resembled the mansion of Indra.
After resting for a moment, he then performed his ablutions and other rites.
The king caused all [the guests] to drink milk and so forth;
and Hari, having been honored, fed his family members, all the great sages, the Brahmins, and his servants. (14)
And the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself partook of the meal;
then the king and the others received the auspicious remnants (prasāda) of Śrī Hari.
After midday, they all went to the garden.
The king, together with his family, massaged the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
he performed the service of rubbing His body and attained the fruit of such service.
Then, in the evening, the assembly hall became vast.
Where hundreds of thousands of men sat in the presence of Hari,
women and men alike sat around him or even stood there.
Then the king honored that Supreme Lord with offerings.
The king sat upon his seat and, filled with humility, asked:
"O Kṛṣṇa, why does bondage not approach one who has established a kingdom?
I know that through attaining you, all bonds have been severed."
"Nevertheless, O Great King, instruct me so that, despite being in a state of bondage, there may be no actual binding. Teach me how to provide peace for my family.
Having heard this, the Blessed One spoke in the assembly while everyone listened:

I shall declare to you that which leads to the shore of the ocean of existence, so that there may never be any bondage for you anywhere in the midst of it. All this is food for the vital breath (prāṇa), but never for the Self (ātman). (23)
Everything, both stationary and moving, is the food of the vital breath (prāṇa).
When the vital breath remains, there is a dependence on the elements for the maintenance of the body;
indeed, the vital breath is the effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), and once the vital breath has departed, there is no thirst [for existence].
Realizing this, the wise man should engage in eating and enjoyment without longing;
he should not behave like a greedy person, for there is no bondage for one who is dispassionate.
Just as one might climb a great tree, take its honey from it, and [depart].
Having eaten the honey right there, he leaves the tree;
thereafter, he sheds his impurity, and subsequently, the body will be cast off.
Having reflected in this manner, one who conducts oneself accordingly is not bound. (27–28)
Just as a person, agitated by hundreds of hopes, might fall upon a great road and fail to find the fruit, becoming utterly despondent;
so too, the wise man, having remembered everything and realizing it is transitory, is not bound.

Just as even a powerful person yields to gentleness in times of distress, so should one behave with gentleness toward a deceptive person; thus one is not bound by it. And just as one who is overcome by old age, or one who has fallen into the hands of a child, [is powerless].

One who abandons the hope for objects of enjoyment is not bound by such conduct; even mountains and trees are practitioners of perpetual renunciation. Having abandoned the sense of "mine," they exist without possessions.

One who acts in such a manner and governs a kingdom remains untainted and is not bound. (33) All aquatic creatures are solely intent on sustaining themselves; they do not engage in possessiveness. One who acts in such a manner is not bound. (34)
Listen now to this history which brings benefit to ascetics.
In ancient times, certain Vaiṣṇava twice-born men, having abandoned their homes,
came to the forest as steadfast ones devoted to celibacy.
Indeed, they were like ascetics, handsome, and even though they had not yet grown beards.
Then Indra, assuming the form of a bird and becoming filled with compassion, spoke:
"O sirs! Out of childishness, you have indeed resorted to the path of renunciation."
"How did he depart from the life of a householder, O sinless ones, and what was the cause for his renunciation?
Having heard this, the sages said: "To one who is free from desire, the entire world is but a blade of grass;
whether in the household or in the forest, no bond exists for him."
We are indeed free from desire; therefore, we have taken refuge in the path of the forest.
For it is better not to touch mud at all than to wash it off; indeed, he who has become stained by mud certainly requires water. (2.180.39–40)
It is considered better to wash away [impurity] with knowledge whose nature is like water;
or rather, it is considered better to attain dryness through the application of heat.
Let the mud itself become a saw and bring about its own separation.
The propitiation of Hari is of the nature of heat and is purifying.
Alternatively, even the state of dryness [of the mind] through the wind is considered supreme;
for by relying on the wind of the Guru, the mire of ignorance is destroyed.
Therefore, by firmly embracing the knowledge of that Great Guru, the True One, or the Supreme Lord, the wise person should destroy *māyā*.
All ritual action as well— whether worldly or Vedic— [is likewise to be abandoned].
By acting with a state of detachment from action, a human being attains perfection.
O bird, this sacred field of perfection bestows the fruits of karma;
it [purifies] the lineages of gods, the lineages of ancestors, the lineages of Brahman, and virtuous people.
Only that action which is performed in accordance with tradition yields fruit for men.
We abide by taking refuge in the Vedic lineage of Brahmā;
if the life of a householder is joined with austerity, it is fit to bestow liberation.
But that house of obstacles is indeed [the path] for us who are tranquil;
therefore, when there is weakness, one should resort to the simplicity of the path of the Self.
For those who possess strength, the great path is the life of the householder, which involves many austerities.
"We are not capable of bearing the burdens of household life;
therefore, we have taken refuge in the dharma of the virtuous, wherein the highest good is certain.
Between doubt and certainty, one should abandon the former and take recourse in the latter."
Having heard these words of those sages, the king of birds himself spoke to them concerning the household duties that are both rigorous and most excellent;
though submerged in water, he was yet filled with an excess of contact with the water.
Only a rare person in this world, though fallen into fire and yet possessing an abundance of freedom from burning,
and though situated within the nature of desire and yet devoid of any portion of longing,
may be truly capable and endowed with merit. (53)
If such a person should be a householder, he attains the highest good.
By renouncing even his own self alone, a person attains well-being;
by performing the duties of a householder, a person becomes a creator of immeasurable merit.
Just as all rivers find rest in the ocean,
so do all beings find rest in the householder's home.
Even great-souled yogis who possess renunciation and are free from desire [find rest there].
Indeed, birds take refuge in trees that abide by the dharma of the household and bear fruit;
in that dharma of the household, service to others arises.
One who possesses the dharma of the household is truly a refuge for guests, just as such a tree is for birds.
Having acquired wealth through the duties of a householder by means of policy, truth, and reason,
the householder enjoys it only after sharing it with his family members,
mendicants, the king, guests, the destitute, and even ants and other small creatures. (59)
Having remembered them and given to each according to what is appropriate, the householder always eats.
For the gods are satisfied in the morning, guests and beggars at midday, thereafter the ancestors, and finally the small creatures. (2.180.60–61)

All embodied beings eat food cooked by the householder; therefore, the householder is an eater of *vighasa* (remnants), for he takes only after giving, not otherwise. "Ghasa" means sin; it refers to the state of filling one's own belly alone.
But that in which the remnants of the meal are free from evil, where others find satisfaction—
where sacrifice, charity, austerity, fire-offering, self-study, and dedication to the Lord exist, these six being present, that alone is the state of eating the remnants (vighasāśitva). (63–64)

Indeed, among all dharmas, the practice of eating the remnants of offerings (vighasa) is supreme; by observing that dharma, one shall attain the highest welfare. For such people, this world provides enjoyments, and even heaven bestows extreme happiness.
Furthermore, even beyond that, if there is an abundance of fruit, the highest good may be attained.
Through the practice of offering everything, the supreme state is to be reached.
Indeed, on this earth of action, there is nothing else superior to the householder’s stage of life.
"O ascetics, I have attained the status of Lord of the Gods through my own deeds; I am Indra.
Previously, Sūrya, Candra, and all the others were eaters of *vighasa* (remnants of offerings).
But now, even they remain in heaven as mere eaters of *vighasa*."

Hari himself, residing in Vaikuṇṭha, shines as one who eats the remains of the sacrificial offering (vighasāśī). Likewise, Kṛṣṇa shines in Goloka as one who eats the remains of the sacrificial offering;
Vāsudeva with four arms and Viṣṇu are also eaters of the remains of the sacrificial offering.
Hara, Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and the others are indeed eaters of *vighasa*;
though they abide on the path of enjoyment, they are free from the pairs of opposites.
Devoted to the dharma of offering everything to the Lord, they shall go to the supreme state.
In this way, indeed, the ascetics who subsist on the remains of food attain Brahman.
Having divided the food in the evening and in the morning among the family, guests, beggars, the Supreme Lord, the gods, living beings, ancestors, and one's own kin, [they eat].
Toward the helpless and those who have sought refuge, toward servants, and likewise toward dogs and other such creatures;
toward a woman, a cow, a beggar, and even a preceptor;
toward a male slave, a female slave, a laborer, one's offspring, and all elemental beings—[one should act with compassion]. (74)
Having divided all food and other provisions according to what is appropriate and in accordance with dharma,
those who eat what remains are called *vighasāśins*.
Having become teachers of the world, they are born as eternal eaters.
Having attained the great sovereignty of the third heaven, lasting for eternal years,
they proceed to the state of no-return through the merit of offering everything to the Lord.
Therefore, those who eat the remains of the offerings become liberated from bondage.
Many, relying upon the duties of householders, attained that state.
Therefore, may you all, both young and old, be eaters of the remains of offerings (vighasāśinaḥ).
The seven Ṛṣis and others know this to be true austerity, O Brahmins.
Having been addressed thus, those lords of ascetics, hearing his words consistent with dharma,
abandoned the stage of renunciation and took up the life of householders. Those great sages, subsisting on the remains of sacrificial food, offered everything to Kṛṣṇa.
Consequently, all of them took refuge in the dharma of self-surrender;
even with their wives, sons, and families, they eventually attained Brahman in ancient times.
Therefore, O King, although the duty of the householder is difficult, it brings great happiness.
Since you are rich in the merit of helping others, always devoted to the service of the virtuous,
and the bestower of gain through service to the Supreme Lord and other such acts, you are indeed preeminent;
therefore, may you always subsist on the remains of offerings (vighasa) together with those who depend upon you.
"Even amidst all the activities of your senses, O King, meditate on me, Kṛṣṇa, repeatedly.
By my yoga, no bondage shall ever befall you;
by my yoga, there will always be peace for you. (84–85)
"Protect my image here and offer everything to me.
I shall lead you, O King, who are devoted to no other, to the abode of Brahman.
Whatever people here are intent on the dharma of offering themselves to me,"
"I am their deliverer from the ocean of the bondage of karma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One ceased;
those subjects then worshipped the Supreme Self and received the mantras with reverence.
"From that day forward, all of them became observers of the vow of eating only the remains of offerings (vighasāśī-vrata).
Having thus concluded the assembly, O Rādhikā,
the Blessed Lord thereafter performed his bath, twilight prayers, and other rites, followed by his meal and so forth.
All those honored guests, having eaten, rested upon the earth.
The king attended to Hari as he slept together with his family;
then, in the morning, Śrī Hari awoke to the sounds of musical instruments.
Having performed his daily rites, he returned and sat upon the lion-throne;
meanwhile, the king and all the others approached to worship Hari.
Indeed, many foot-stools were offered by King Tīrāṇaka.
The queens and maidens of that king likewise assembled, and holding vessels for worship in their hands, they worshipped the Supreme Lord.
O Rādhikā! And six maidens took the hand of Śrī Hari.
Having received the gift of the prince, they then felt their purpose was fulfilled.
Then, having attained rest and performed their meals and other duties,
they were eager to depart when requested by King Alvinara.
Then Hari, who is worshipped by the Lord of the Mountains and the sages, became ready.
At that time, musical instruments were played and songs were sung; hearing shouts of "Victory! and receiving honors such as respectful salutations, he proceeded. (96–97)
Then Hari ascended his own celestial chariot,
and others likewise mounted their vehicles; at that time, they traveled along the path of the sky amidst auspicious sounds and the clatter of mechanical engines.
Thus honored with blessings by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and the others,
they set out with great speed in their celestial chariots; in a mere moment,
they reached the excellent kingdom of Girīśa, situated upon the earth and joined by the ocean.
Hari became delighted while listening to the shouts of victory and looking about;
Alvinara went forward and stood there to offer a welcome.
"The Great King Hari is coming!"—thus the subjects cried out in great excitement. (101)
They stood ready upon the surface of the earth to behold [Him] and offer Him welcome.
Gazing toward the sky with eager anticipation, the women and men performed a kīrtana, holding unbroken grains, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, O Rādhikā.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Arrival at the Kingdom of Alvīnara on the Second Day, after Having Visited the Kingdom of King Tīrāṇa in the Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, Having Wandered through the City of Tīrāṇā with His Army in the Manner of a Welcome, Having Taken Food and Other Necessities, Having Spoken of the Dharma of Eating Remnants (vighasāśitva) in the Evening Assembly and Described Liberation from Bondage, Having Rested at Night, and Having Performed Worship and Eaten in the Morning and Prepared Himself. || 180 ||
