Chapter 182 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Gopī Rādhikā! On the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādra, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa descended to the earth of Alvinara. 1.
At the place directed by the sage Girīśa, he joyfully descended from the sky while his subjects awaited him, beholding his own celestial chariot;
at that time, other celestial chariots also descended from the heavens.
In the presence of Arthaśrī, Rājadhanyā, and Sannidhi, upon the grounds of a garden,
the king Alvīnara, together with his family, as well as the sage Girīśa,
offered a welcome with musical instruments, offerings, necklaces, and sandalwood paste.
As Hari was descending from the palace onto the courtyard by means of a constructed staircase and ladder, the people placed golden necklaces around his neck.
At that time, shouts of "Victory! and cries of praise from the staff-bearers arose.
At that time, there arose an excellent hearing of verses (śloka) concerning his fame, produced by the voices of bards, panegyrists, eulogists,
and wandering minstrels; likewise, [the people honored him] with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, gold coins, and other such offerings.
At that time, the people performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa with wheat.
Having led Hari, along with his family, into the royal palace,
the king offered him water for drinking, betel, and other refreshments, and he bowed at his feet.
Accompanied by his sons, daughters, and others, the king performed the washing of [the sage's] feet;
together with his family, he also drank the nectar of [his] feet.
After that, he gave milk to drink there to everyone.
He quickly brought a golden chariot with horses for the sake of Hari, so that he might wander through the city accompanied by his army. There,
the Blessed Lord shone with joy together with his parents.
Then his brothers and other sages, such as Brahmapriya and others,
sat upon vehicles, palanquins, chariots, and elephant-machines; and at that time, musical instruments were played along with cries of victory.
The army, rich in every splendor, proceeded toward the city;
it reached the royal highway in the city known as Arthaśrī.
It was accompanied by ministers, royal officials, merchants, and likewise by the common people.
The Lord was repeatedly increased in glory, worshipped, seen face to face, touched, saluted, and thoroughly propitiated with offerings;
then the Blessed One, having wandered all around the city, [returned] once more. (15–16)
Having arrived at the garden and the royal palace, he took rest upon his own seat; others who had become weary likewise bathed. Then they rested in their own residences and ate with ease.
Indeed, they partook of many kinds of cooked foods with the utmost devotion.
(18) At that time, O Rādhā, a marvel occurred; listen, for I shall tell it to you.
There was a great Rākṣasa, a resident of Kītadvīpa, who was very dear to Artha. (19)
Having arrived for the purpose of testing the worldly power of Hari,
he first, in the form of a server, placed stones resembling sweetmeats,
smeared with ghee, upon the food.
Hari quickly understood that, and by Hari's will,
all those stones then abandoned their stony nature and attained the state of sweet food.
Having witnessed this marvel there, he then performed an investigation.
Listen further, O Rādhā: he indeed assumed the form of a bed. Having displayed a beautiful ball upon a lovely couch, he secretly prepared a bed of spikes beneath it for the sake of Śrī Hari.
Hari, showing great reverence, ascended that bed of spears.
At that time, the spears became golden flowers and filaments;
having experienced this marvel there as well, the Rākṣasa departed from that place.
Then the Blessed One also prepared sandals treated with poison; he then performed the third test.
Having put on the sandals, which were indeed rendered into the nature of nectar, [he proceeded].
And there, in that palace, the Lord remained motionless in bliss on all sides.
(27) Nevertheless, the Rākṣasa performed a fourth test: he placed a divine golden throne in the assembly hall and kindled a fire. (28)
Then Hari, having gone to that assembly hall, touched the seat near the fire and made that golden one cool once again.
At that, the Rākṣasa, who was devoid of human feeling, experienced supreme wonder.
He requested Kṛṣṇa to grant him liberation so that he might go to his own home. Hari said, "So be it," and as soon as he placed his two feet upon the head of the Rākṣasa, he became a god.
That divine realm named Tuṣita is a place of eternal celestial residence.
When questioned by the people, he then related his own story:
"I am a god named Tuṣita, who has come here upon this earth by chance."
"I came here to wander and saw Sundarī here.
She was my beloved by name, and formerly, near the ocean, she was suddenly assaulted by me and gave me a curse. (33-34)
"O you of evil conduct, intent on violating maidens, become a Rākṣasa!
But I have immediately become a Rākṣasa dwelling upon purchased land.
By your touch, O Blessed One, I am now freed from the curse."
"O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Master of the Universe, you have been born again.
If I may have your command, I shall go from this place to my own home.
Hari said, "Go to the Kurus situated in the northern direction."
"Lālāyana was previously sent by me after meditating upon the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
having searched for him, give him my message.
O Lord, receive these mantras and depart at my command. (38)
Having spoken thus, he sent the gods to him with the mantras of the tradition. And when the sage had indicated the northern regions by traveling through the sky,
Hari himself arrived in the western region of Ketumāla.
"At the end of this month, the Blessed One will certainly come here as well.
Having gone to the bank of the Pālipāra lake, he spoke thus to that sage who was staying on the eastern shore,
which was joined by the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest and the river.
Upon hearing of the arrival of his own lord, the sage rejoiced exceedingly.
Then the sage offered a grand welcome to Tuṣita;
together with Tuṣita, the sage quickly proceeded to the northern regions.
Then, eager for the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, he told the people; meanwhile,
the two [brothers] wandered everywhere through the various regions,
and the lords respectfully bestowed names and mantras upon the subjects.
Then, O Rādhā, the glorious Lord Mādhava, having arrived at the abode of Aḷvīnara,
convened a very great assembly there during the night;
being honored and worshiped, he gave instruction to the people.
Whether they be subjects, the class of kings, ascetics, or householders,
if they perform their appropriate duties and offer them unto Me,
there shall be no bondage for them, either from those actions or from their fruits.
I indeed bring about their freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) as the fruit of those [deeds].
Those who bestow wealth acquired through dharma upon sacrifices— being self-realized practitioners— they are indeed renunciants belonging to the stage of life of renunciation (tyāgāśramin).

They do not call renunciation "renunciation"; rather, freedom from bondage is called renunciation. That person who, having adopted indifference and dwelling among trees, does not perform any action at all—he is indeed called *tāmasa*.
If one’s dwelling were in the Lord, he would attain freedom from the qualities (nirguṇya).
But performing all actions repeatedly with a desire for pleasure,
if one does not remember the God therein, those actions are indeed rajasic.
The renunciation of actions for the sake of pleasure is considered to be *rājasa*.

He who, while performing all actions, offers his entire being to me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme— whether out of a desire for pleasure or a desire for the fruit [of action]— [is one who renounces].

That action would be characterized by *sattva*, and renunciation as well is *sāttvika* when a person performs it free from desire for fruit and surrenders it unto Me. All that becomes devoid of the *guṇas*, connected with Me, and intended for My sake.
According to the qualities of one's actions, so is the householder bound;
if the action is devoid of qualities (guṇa), one is liberated and not bound.
On one side are all the other stages of life (āśramas), and on the other side is the householder stage alone.
One who follows the dharma of a householder or the dharma of a Kṛṣṇa-bhakta becomes a renunciant devoid of worldly qualities (nirguṇāśramī).
One should offer all action to Me, with its fruit dedicated to My self.
Tranquility, self-control, as well as fortitude, truth, purity, and likewise straightforwardness—these [are the virtues]. 57–58.
Sacrifice, fortitude, and righteousness do not attain any separateness from him;
yet action performed out of egoism, devoid of my remembrance, swiftly causes the noose of death to be placed around one’s neck through the gateway of *yama*. (59)
Therefore, abandoning pride, perform actions with me as your supreme goal.
Even while in the householder stage of life, I shall effect liberation for you, for my sake;
indeed, in the past, Brahmā created all beings by my command.
For the sake of maintaining the continuity of karma, for my own worship,
and likewise for the purpose of sacrifice, [I created] even conflicting trees and medicinal herbs;
as well as juices, fruits, leaves, and sacrificial oblations intended for ritual offerings.
The householder’s life, joined with a wife, is always considered fit for performing sacrifice;
indeed, the union of a husband and wife is praised for the purpose of worshipping the gods and goddesses.
Those householders who attain this state, endowed as they are with wealth, grain, and essence, [should perform these rites]. (63–64)
If they do not worship the gods, they indeed consume their own sin;
for the wise, the sacrifice is knowledge, and for the virtuous, sacrifices are the service of the good.
For the sages, the sacrifice is self-study, while for kings, it is the sacrifice of material offerings.
The sacrifice of food belongs to farmers; the sacrifice of meditation belongs to yogis.
(66) The sacrifice of service belongs to servants; for women, the rite is obedience.
For sons, it is the words of their father; for celibate students, it is indeed the Veda. (67)
For householders, sacrifices consist of giving; for ascetics, they consist of austerity.
Thus, sacrifices are of various kinds according to one's fitness.
However, for all people, sacrifices of devotion to Hari are free from bondage.
Therefore, having beheld me as being centered in that [sacrifice], sacrifices should be performed as is appropriate;
being gratified by these offerings, I shall grant liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, horses, elephants, cows, and other such things ought to be given by kings.
Male and female servants, adorned with ornaments, as well as villages, districts,
groves, houses, fields, and various gardens—
the fruit of these is declared to be eternal, especially for kings.
Kings who fail to give and provide no refuge share in sin;
they are consumers of faults alone and never of happiness.
Having failed to perform the great sacrifices and having omitted the libations and other rites, [they suffer]. (72-73)
If one proceeds on the path without bathing in sacred fords (tīrtha) and without having propitiated the Supreme Lord,
he indeed returns again;
or like a scattered cloud, he goes to his dissolution and perishes.
The two-syllabled word is death, while the three-syllabled word is Brahman and immortality.
"Mine" (mama) is indeed death; "not mine" (na mama) is eternal immortality.
These two always abide either upon one's own head or in the heart.
In this regard, having abandoned all obstacles and attained that which is supreme, this path has been followed by the virtuous; let it be constantly practiced by you, O embodied beings.
Having obtained a kingdom, a noble family, wealth, and likewise prosperity—

He who sacrifices at a rite without honoring the Lord—his sacrifice is indeed fruitless. (78) For one who has not propitiated the deity and lives solely for his own sake, death does not spare even the hair on his head, as he harbors a sense of "mine" regarding wealth and other possessions. (79)

Death releases those by whom the eternal witness of all beings— dwelling both within and without— has been propitiated with offerings in this world. Even a mind that is prosperous and filled with enjoyments remains bound by thirst.
That mind is declared to be impotent which does not find the kingdom of Brahman.
An impotent person neither enjoys the earth of Brahman nor the wealth of devotion;
indeed, in the abode of the impotent, there is no worship of the gods nor any auspiciousness.
Therefore, one should never exhibit weakness in the service of the Supreme Lord;
for Hari is always to be served by the elders, and others indeed follow them.
Since those who take refuge with an elder become perpetually intoxicated through his intoxication.
Therefore, madness arising from illusion, passion, and the like must be abandoned.
Lord Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Lord Nārāyaṇa, should always be worshipped.
Just as a sacrifice was performed [in the past], so too should it be performed at all times in the home.
"The Brahma-yajña must always be performed; I shall grant liberation, of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Lord then bestowed the mantras upon the subjects.
O Rādhikā, thereafter, the assembly was then dismissed.
Having rested during the night, the Blessed One, having performed his morning rites,
then desired to depart quickly, as requested by King Jinavardhana; he was also entreated by Iṣṭalavarṣin to visit the kingdom of Iṣṭāli.
The king, together with his family, brought offerings of food and other honors;
then Kṛṣṇa, the performer of their deeds, accepted them.
After that, all the others also accepted the gifts from Hari.
The queen, together with her five daughters, worshipped Hari. All five maidens there took the hand of Śrī Hari;
according to the marriage rite, Kṛṣṇa gave his own hand to them.
Having received worship and words of blessing, Hari prepared to depart.
The five maidens, including Brahmapriyā and the others, being most devoted,
ascended the celestial chariot and went along with Śrī Hari.
Having received his leave, the Blessed One ascended the vehicle;
all the others likewise ascended their celestial chariots at that time. Then musical instruments were played and shouts of "Victory! arose.
"O Hari-Kṛṣṇa! O Hari-Nārāyaṇa, Lord! All the subjects then chanted Your names in the sky;
their celestial chariots moved over the water in the direction indicated by the fragment of the sacrificial offering."
They crossed the Vārdhikhāḍī river and then reached Rāmapurī.
On the western bank of the Khāḍikā, King Jinavardhana, accompanied by his family, had previously descended from his celestial chariot (vimāna) there to welcome them.
Then the great sage Iṣṭalava and all the subjects were on the bank near the garden to welcome the Lord Hari;
upon merely seeing the celestial chariots, they cried out "Victory! with joy. (98)

"O Rādhikā, the entire kingdom was thus intent on offering a welcome—consisting of those who were well-informed, those who brought gifts, and likewise those whose voices raised songs of praise. There, the earth became crowded and appeared like an ocean of people. (2.181.100)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, on the second day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada in the Tretā-yuga succession of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, went to the kingdom of Alvīnara, wandered through the city of Arthaśrī, ate, granted liberation to the Rākṣasa, sent the Tuṣita deity to the Uttara-kurus, instructed him in the assembly hall, accepted worship, rested, and after breakfast on the following morning, set out toward the royal capital of King Jinavardhin. Chapter 181.
← Chapter 181: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 182 [[Author: → Chapter 183
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having been instructed by his beloved consort, [placed] his own celestial chariot at the designated place. || 1 ||
He brought it down upon the auspicious ground of a vast garden situated on the bank of the river Trivarā, which was thick with excellent trees;
it was near the city of Rāmapurī and resounded with the music of instruments.
King Jinavardhana, together with his ministers, princes, kinsmen,
and subjects, offered a grand welcome to Hari there.
He placed flower garlands and necklaces of gold enriched with diamonds upon His neck.
As the illustrious Hari descended from his celestial chariot outside, all the subjects honored him with sandalwood paste, parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and the like;
they offered shouts of "Victory!", cries of joy, and prostrations with devotion.
They all honored their parents, all their kinsmen, their sister, their elders, the sages,
and those dear to Brahmā with necklaces and sandalwood paste. Then, [they mounted] a golden elephant-vehicle accompanied by an army.
King Jinavardhaka caused Hari to mount [the elephant],
and he caused all the dignitaries to mount upon many vehicles—
on palanquins, carriages, and even on carts.

With the sounds of musical instruments, proclamations, and festive celebrations, he caused Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to be paraded everywhere throughout the city of Rāmapurī. Hari was honored by the citizens at every point along the royal highways.
Having thus granted his audience with fruits, flowers, unbroken grains, silver and gold coins, garments, and other gifts, the Supreme Lord returned to the royal palace;
honored by the crowds of people, he shone with splendor.
With his heart full of bliss, he convened an assembly in the evening.
For the sake of performing what was pleasing to the people, Hari then gave instructions to the subjects after having drunk water, [accommodating] up to a hundred thousand men.
Seated there upon a divine throne with a serene disposition,
those who perform the work of the Lord, who take refuge at the feet of the Lord,
and who are perfected in meditation upon the Lord, attain the supreme goal. (14)
Those who perform service for the virtuous, or those who take refuge at the feet of the virtuous,
and those who travel upon the path of the virtuous, attain the supreme goal. Indeed,
riches produced from the earth eventually dissolve back into the earth.
If those [pleasures] were for the sake of the virtuous, for the sake of desire, and bestowers of liberation,
then the earth would give food, the clouds would give water,
fire would perform cooking, and the wind would produce dryness. (17)
Having prepared all their beds and objects of enjoyment, they indeed offer them for the sake of man;
for men offer these things to the Lord.
But without offering to the Supreme Lord, riches are surely calamities.

Even at the end, they surely become female denizens of hell who deliver others to that same state. Therefore, whatever riches have been given by living beings out of great reverence must all be offered to Hari; indeed, in that way, they truly grant liberation.
By him the ocean was made, and by him the earth was fashioned.
By that god the grain-yielding crops were created;
by him the body was made, and by him the seed was produced.
That which is of the same nature as that [Self] has been made by Him; it is to be enjoyed and is equal to what was given.
That to whom all this was given, to that Supreme Self it must be offered.
He alone is the Blessed Lord here upon the earth for the sake of the world.

He remains within the range of vision of embodied beings as a bestower of happiness for their ultimate welfare (24). Having understood this, one should diligently serve and please Him. Indeed, those people who, knowing this, shall perform service unto Me— (25)
I shall indeed rescue them from the ocean of birth and worldly existence.
I am the dispenser of punishment; punishment has been created by me, for without taking recourse to it, embodied beings would surely become vessels of retribution.
"In this matter, let them seek refuge with me alone, the giver of punishment, in every way.
(27) The punishment which I have cast upon kings must always remain under my control; and the punishment which I have assigned to Yama is the chastiser of those who act contrary to their duty. (28)
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod of righteousness protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep, bringing about virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Grain, wealth, wives, sons, servants, daughters, and gardens—[all depend upon it].
Dharma, justice, and the bounds of social order are maintained through the fear of punishment.
Out of fear of their mother’s punishment, children do not engage in quarrels;
out of fear of the king’s punishment, some sinners do not commit evil.
For the wicked do not resort to injustice out of fear of punishment from the king;
nor out of fear of Yama’s rod, nor even out of fear of the next world;
yet here on earth, subjects are restrained by mutual fear as well. (32)
Thus, by fear, the world established itself in dharma through its own inherent nature.
Out of fear of punishment alone, all do not devour one another.
There is the royal punishment, the punishment of dharma, and likewise the other, the punishment of Yama.
The divine rod of punishment is their primary [tool], by which they protect the various subjects;
for if the subjects were without punishment, they would sink into a great abyss.
Indeed, the rod of punishment subdues even those who are unsubdued and ill-behaved.
I indeed possess the power of the rod of command; for that command of mine is Vedic.
Those who depart without abandoning it reach the further shore of the rod.
I am the leader of all creations, as well as the ruler and the protector.
Entering the king, I abide within him and carry out his governance; likewise, assuming the form of restraint, I preside over all subjects and all kings.
Wherever my rod of punishment proceeds, it moves there always well-prepared.
There, the subjects do not become deluded, nor do they lead themselves astray from the path of the righteous.
(3.9) Even humans, animals, birds, insects, and flies—by the fear of punishment alone, these remain established on the path that accords with reality. (2.182.40)
No one worships without fear; no one desires to give without fear;
and no person desires to abide by their agreement without fear.
Rudra, Skanda, Mahendra, Vahni, Varuṇa, and Yama—
Time, Vāyu, Kubera, Ravi, Mṛtyu, and likewise Śani;
the Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and Rākṣasas—
even these have fallen into fear and abide by the restraint of Daṇḍa.
Thus, living beings, being afraid of these, bow down to them again and again;
for if there were no fear in the world, they would destroy one another.
It is only through fear of punishment that everyone proceeds according to dharma.
For the joy of the four castes and for the protection of good policy,
the fear of punishment has been ordained to always preserve dharma and artha.
Through these two, liberation shall subsequently arise for him who takes refuge in my form.
If beasts of prey and other wild animals did not fear the law,
then cruel lions and other forest-dwellers would devour their own kin;
and even human beings, having gathered together, would surely devour one another by force.
Universal disorder would prevail and the boundaries of moral conduct would be shattered.
People would not perform the duties of their respective stages of life; daughters would not seek marriage;
young women would not rely upon a husband; and a servant girl would not obey her master’s command. (48–49)
A person should not abide in restraint or moral conduct without the fear of dharma;
for dharma is the foundation of heaven for humans and of this world as well. Dharma, when joined with devotion, leads to the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇatva).
Nothing is absolutely possessed of qualities, nor is anything absolutely devoid of qualities.
(51) In all the worlds, both the good and the bad are seen.
Having reflected well, one should act upon what is good and abandon that which is not good. (52)
The assembly of the virtuous is auspicious; may Śrī Hari always be my refuge.
Through the rite of total surrender, I must effect this assembly.
For those people who have placed themselves under me, and under Kṛṣṇa, the inviolable ruler—
They shall indeed not be oppressed by fear of Time, Illusion, and the like.
Therefore, let the subjects protect the Bhāgavata Dharma;
my command, which takes the form of a rod of punishment, bestows happiness and is free from fear.
"May all humans here be fearless, established in their desired goals.
May there be well-being for you, O Jinavardha, who abide in the refuge of your desired lot.
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, ceased speaking.

Then the king and others, filled with great eagerness, performed the *nīrājana* ceremony and the worship of Śrī Hari, as well as of his parents and kinsmen. The queens and others likewise performed the worship of the wives of Brahmā and other gods. (57–58)
And they deposited all their possessions: gold, silver, and diamonds;
ornaments, garments, gems, vessels, and pearls;
as well as jewels and various kinds of utensils. (59)
All the men and women remaining there received the mantras. Then Śrī Hari withdrew from the assembly hall; thereafter, he and all the others partook of milk-based foods, sweets, and other delicacies.
The subjects, filled with great honor, partook of the feast and accepted the king's favor;
then the king and the others returned to their own places, and Hari took his rest for the night. Rising in the morning, he indeed placed [the Lord] within his heart.

Having meditated upon his own supreme form, he heard auspicious sounds. (63) Just as he was becoming composed after performing his daily rites, the king brought forth vessels of cooked food, milk, and other offerings. (64)
He offered food to Hari, and they partook of it as guests;
then, at the time of midday, having eaten, they took their rest.
Indeed, when Hari had finished eating, the queen and the seven daughters likewise did so.
Having come to serve him, they offered garlands of flowers and other gifts;
they wore various wonderful ornaments for the Lord.
Having thus adorned Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, who is of beautiful form— ||| 66–67 ||
The maidens took his hands in marriage according to the rites,
and having obtained the beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they became fulfilled.
The Vaiṣṇava women, filled with joy, were united with the consorts of Brahmā.
Then, O Rādhā, everyone indeed purified their pairs [of garments].
And then a great wonder occurred; listen, for I shall tell you:
a certain wretched person, like one without a protector, came before Hari.
Crying out, he said, "O Blessed One, some rākṣasa has indeed carried off my young son and one daughter during the night.
Other rākṣasas carry away children and daughters of the people. (7.1)
They kill people and even follow behind them;
seizing them on the mountain, the rākṣasas carry off both the old and the young.
Therefore, O Great King, O Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Lord, protect us! (72–73)
"O Lord of Mercy, have mercy upon all the mountain-dwellers!
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari quickly became ready, O Rādhā;
he took his subtle Sudarśana disc and placed it upon his finger like a ring.
Endowed with hidden splendor, he endeavored to go quickly to that place.
At that moment, King Jinavardhana, equipped with weapons and intent on protecting the miserable, also became ready along with Hari.
Just then, the king named Alpaketu, the lord of the small kingdom of Alpaparvata, arrived there; having bowed to Hari, he then said:
"O Śrī Parameśvara, please purify my kingdom."
The great ṛṣi Āpyāyana likewise petitioned the Lord;
Hari said, "So be it," and spoke thus to Udantaka regarding the protection of the helpless Rākṣasa of cruel deeds.
And having heard that, Alpa-ketu, equipped with weapons,
sat upon his celestial chariot (vimāna) to slay the bull among the Rākṣasas;
and then all the armies as well quickly [mounted] their celestial chariots.
Weapons, missiles, and mechanical engines were prepared in the sky for the purpose of battle.
The Lord, honored by the king, the queen, and the subjects,
was proceeding to the house of Alpa-ketu, intending to slay the Rākṣasa.
Having recognized that the offerings had been presented to Śrī Hari,
he accepted them, gave leave to all, and bestowed auspicious blessings upon them;
meanwhile, the sounds of farewell trumpets and the thundering of battle drums resounded.
Having heard [the news] and having taken up flower garlands, they ascended into the middle of their vehicles.
(84) Then all the other groups of guests and merchant caravans, having boarded their celestial chariots (*vimāna*), uttered cries of "Victory! to Hari. (85)
Even a person who was destitute became a spectator from Kṛṣṇa’s aerial chariot;
following the path shown by Him,
their vehicles proceeded until they reached that mountain in a mere moment.
To the west of Pūrvavārdhikhāḍikā is a long mountain range (87),
difficult to traverse due to thorny forests, boulders, and overhanging crags, as well as because it is the dwelling place of predatory beasts and especially of *rākṣasas* (88).
Especially by the obstacles posed by the mountain enveloped in garlands of flames and the [flowing] juices,
there was a great cave on the mountain plateau in the sky;
at its entrance were Rākṣasas, while below it stood a tree that had eclipsed their banners.
Terrifying and naked, they were even eaters of animal flesh;
they were also eaters of human flesh, naked and fearsome,
equipped with weapons made of bone, and likewise skilled in the weapons of mantra-weaving.
Seated in his celestial chariot, Hari, who is devoted to the helpless, showed her that direction;
upon seeing it, he recognized it as the abode of the Rākṣasas.
Although Kṛṣṇa, assuming the role of the human dancer, knows everything, [he acted thus].
Then he said, "A great and terrible battle will take place.
These fierce rākṣasas cannot be slain here without Rudra Śaṅkara. Having spoken thus, he addressed Īśāna.
O Rudra, O Rudra, O mighty-armed one, O arm of mine, O Lord of the Gods!
For the sake of battle and for the sake of protection, you have indeed always been with me here.
You have been protected at my side; your task has now arrived.
"Assume a fierce and great form; destroy these great asuras!
Slay them, O Lord named Īśa; become a wealthy god, O Īśānadeva!"—thus [spoke he] to Hara, the Lord of the Kṣetrapālas, who was seated in his own celestial chariot. (96–97)
Having addressed Mahārudra, the great king urged him to go forth for battle;
thereupon Rudra Maheśāna, abandoning his peaceful disposition,
assumed a terrifying form resembling a mountain.

In the sky, however, Hari caused the celestial chariots to form a formation resembling a discus and secured them firmly in every way. Likewise, King Jinavarddhi and King Alpaketu [remained there]. (2.182.100)
They gave the command for the sounding of musical instruments to announce the battle and to roar; war-drums were beaten, and the heroes became red-eyed.
Conchs, kettledrums, and trumpets were then sounded on all sides.
Then, cries of "Victory! arose from the heroes for the sake of battle.
At that time, ten thousand Rākṣasas were born from Mārīcā;
and they all suddenly recognized those sounds of the battle-cry.
Having prepared themselves, they all set out from the city of Mārīśā and,
traveling through the path of the sky, reached a deep cavern and were filled with wonder.
Desiring victory in the great battle, they became like those who had lost their way.
Then Rādhikā cried out loudly at Rudragomukha.

(105) Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, having purified Rāmapurī, given instruction, eaten, rested, and received worship in the kingdom of King Jinavardhin during the second period, the Tretā-yuga, departed with Vidāya toward the mountain for the purpose of destroying the people-destroying Rākṣasa," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.

Chapter 184 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; having heard the war-drums, the Rākṣasas made terrifying sounds of "kilakila" and the cracking of their thighs. (1)
Making the earth tremble and causing the quarters of the sky to resound,
they let out loud, boisterous laughter, having resolved upon battle;
[they brandished] spears, tridents, swords, scimitars, mallets, and clubs.
Gathering boulders, *sarja* trees, and stones in the sky,
ten thousand of them, all equipped with missiles and weapons and assuming the forms of mountains, leaped up for the purpose of battle. (3–4)
Let them kill, devour, and chew those who dwell in celestial palaces;
let them bind, crush, and even deprive them of their lives.
Let them cut off their hands, feet, and other limbs, and let them strike down their heads.
Let them devour the bodies of men, and let these maidens carry them away!
Let them set the vehicles ablaze and shatter the mechanical engines;
let them crush the heads and seize the celestial chariots!
Thus, with much clamor, those Rākṣasas, resembling an army,
gathered all around in the sky; then, moving upward with catapults,
they made a shower of terrifying stones and arrows.
They unleashed a rain of iron arrows and a burning rain of *golās*.
Then Hari quickly called to mind both the ocean and the moon; both appeared in embodied form and bowed before him.
Hari said, "Extinguish this fire quickly with waters that are like nectar. With joy, the two of them did exactly so;
the ocean then released a shower of water-laden vapors.
There, the Moon, drawn by the Fire, showered down liquid nectar.
Then King Jinavardhana and the two of great strength, Alpaketu and Mahābala,
struck the Rākṣasas with hundreds of thousands of iron arrows.
Cut in two by crescent-headed arrows and broad-headed shafts,
those Rākṣasas fall to the earth, flinging their hands and feet about and crying out "water, water!
as they give up their lives on that mountain fastness.
Then, from the sky, the royal armies on the ground were struck down by Upagolas;
they killed the Rākṣasas and cast them down while still alive.
Having seen this terrible slaughter, those who caused the corruption of the mantra [acted].
Then those rākṣasīs, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, quickly emerged from the cave and soared into the sky. At that time,
they were accompanied by rākṣasas created through mantras— illusory beings bearing swords.
They indeed caused those two kings to fall from the sky to the earth.
Those [women] slaughtered the armies with artificial Rākṣasas;
thus, a crushing destruction of the human armies occurred.
Then, a cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose everywhere in the celestial chariots upon seeing the two kings dying; Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, descending from his chariot with the speed of the wind, [approached] the two monarchs.
Holding the celestial chariot with both arms, Mādhava returned to his own abode. By the touch of his hand, he restored the two kings to life;
he then commanded Candra to distribute nectar everywhere.
"Quickly restore to life those among the human armies who have died. Candra did so immediately, and the troops indeed returned to life.
Then, for the destruction of the artificial demon armies...
Then, having produced from his matted locks the illusion that devours falsehood,
Lord Īśāna released a false army; she went forth,
assuming the form of an incalculable number of Rākṣasīs who acted as counter-Rākṣasas.
Then Śaṅkara devoured all the Rākṣasas and,
having manifested his own Durgā from his left side,
dispatched her for the destruction of the female Rākṣasas; and Durgā, having bowed to Śaṅkara, [set forth].
Assuming a form consisting of ten million [parts], beautiful with eighteen arms,
mounted upon a lion, bearing many weapons, and possessed of great strength and prowess,
she descended from the sky in every direction at that time, accompanied by all her forms.
Seizing each individual rākṣasī by the neck, he led them to the abode of Yama.
At that time, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within the rākṣasa host, while shouts of joy resounded from the celestial chariots, the armies, and among the humans.
Seeing the deed accomplished with difficulty, the Supreme Lord rejoiced.
The maidens, including Brahmapriyā and the others, rejoiced, having attained their long-cherished desire.
At that moment, the Rākṣasas saw that their wives were destined for the abode of Yama.
Exceedingly enraged and distressed, they rushed swiftly toward the army of Durgā;
indeed, for the sake of destroying the women, they charged from the sky toward Durgā herself.
Śaṅkara then spoke to his own attendants, the Kṣetrapālas: "Seize them!"
The Kṣetrapālas then seized the Rākṣasas one by one by the throat as they moved swiftly through the path of the sky;
having reached them again and again, they held them by the throat and indeed slew them.
With their feet, with maces, clubs, and bhallas, as well as with their fists,
blows to the knees, and strikes with their elbows,
those lords killed the great burdened one by breaking his bones.

The attendants of Īśāna deprived some of the Rākṣasas of their lives with weapons such as swords, spears, javelins, and arrows. Five thousand Rākṣasas who had fought as human warriors lay dead. (36–37)
Then hundreds of thousands of Rākṣasīs were slain and deprived of life;
those who remained reflected, "What purpose is there in our living?
Since our entire clans have been destroyed, we must certainly die after them."
Having reflected thus, they were fully prepared in every way in the sky;
they indeed fashioned various nets of illusion (māyājāla) and created countless delusive, illusory devices.
Just as the celestial chariots and the armies of the Vaimānika gods met their destruction here in the sky, so did they make [the enemy's efforts] futile.
The great king of the Rākṣasas was entirely devoted to the power of illusion.
Named Mārīcaśārdūla, his eyes copper-red with rage, he bit his teeth, tongue, and lips, and discharged magical mantras;
for at that time, he did not recognize Mahārudra, Nārāyaṇa, or Satī. (42–43)
Having perceived that the human army was powerful or of such a kind,
he released the illusion-mantras of the other-born Rākṣasas;
first, having protected himself with his own shadow, he dispatched five thousand [of them].
Then he released these terrifying locust-spell mantras.
Indeed, a new ocean of locusts then arose in the sky;
by their weight, the celestial chariots were then pressed down.
And all the warriors, covered by locusts resembling a shower of rain,
could not see one another at that time, as if obscured by clouds in the form of locusts.
For their destruction, Rudra indeed discharged the Kila weapon.
At that time, innumerable birds known as *kilaha* appeared in the sky;
they devoured those locusts from all sides in the air.
And seeing the swarms of *karburī* birds, the foremost of the Rākṣasas—
He set his mind upon destroying those women who were prone to quarreling;
by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), he fashioned nets of hawks with his arrows.
Those hawks, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, devoured them in the sky.
Then, having become mountain-like in body and equal to chariots,
those fierce beings struck the celestial chariots with the strength of their wings.
Some were equal in size to the chariots, while others had bodies like mountains.
Possessing various kinds of great bulk, they shattered everything on all sides;
the broken celestial chariots were cast down and fell from the sky.
While such a diverse slaughter was taking place, Hari himself—
Then he commanded the god Vāyu for the sake of providing support;
the lord of the winds held up even the shattered celestial chariots in the sky itself,
for Viśvakarman was summoned and arrived.
Through his craftsmanship and skillful work, he quickly joined the broken parts together;
having fashioned the vehicles according to their original forms,
he made the Supreme Lord well-pleased and remained right there on the battlefield.
Then Rudra, by means of fire-mantras and arrows,
swiftly produced millions of fire-named birds. Those fierce fire-birds devoured the hawks.
Impelled by Rudra, they rushed forward to devour even the Rākṣasas; however,
the Rākṣasas there vanished for a moment through their illusory power (māyā) and then unleashed fierce serpents with virulent poison.
Having gone to those who were in their celestial chariots, they entered them and bit them.
Then Rudra, by means of the Gāruḍa mantra,
created thousands of crores of Garuḍas, the destroyers of serpents, as devourers [of the snakes].
The Garuḍas pursued them and indeed devoured them.
For the sake of destroying the Garuḍas, the Rākṣasa unleashed fire.
Agni, Agnimāhāgni, and Ālāyamaya appeared in the sky.
At that very moment, Rudra opened his third eye.
Thereupon, the fire of universal destruction (pralayāgni) arose; having drawn in the false fire produced by the Rākṣasa, he indeed consumed it within his own exceedingly terrible form.
Then the fire was quickly extinguished by the Rākṣasas, who brought about fear;
hidden beneath the trees at the edge of the thicket, they released arrows, shafts,
and even broad-headed missiles, having resolved that they must fight.
Then the hosts of Rudra from the path of the sky and the Kṣetrapālas from all sides rained down a shower of arrows to slay those foremost of Rākṣasas. Then,
Then, with mantras over stones, they loosed many arrows;
at that moment, boulders as large as crags rose up in the sky.
Leaping again and again through the atmosphere, they indeed struck down the celestial chariots.
Having understood Rudra’s maneuver, he discharged that thunderbolt weapon (*vajrāstra*).
All the rocks were pulverized and scattered in every direction by the wind.
Then the Daityas vanished and unleashed clouds that rained down hailstones.

Then, by means of the wind-weapon (*vāyvastra*), Rudra caused the clouds to dissolve. Thereupon, those remaining Rākṣasas who had survived fled toward the ocean out of fear; at that moment, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, [intervened].
He released the Gaṇas so that they might hold them back from behind.
Then the Daityas turned back and fought with the Gaṇas once more.
At that time, Rudra then unleashed his trident, which strikes fear into the worlds.
Whirling with speed and emitting fires in every direction,
that lord of Mārīśa slew those Daityas and then vanished.
Having assumed a deceptive form, he took up that very trident of fire.
Then, while everyone was watching, that [weapon] entered entirely into the mouth;
seeing this supreme marvel, Śaṅkara and the other Gaṇas were likewise struck with wonder.
Having observed that supreme feat of the Rākṣasa, Nārāyaṇa—
He praised this deed of the Asura, which struck terror into the worlds.
Beholding Śambhu, Hari quickly released the discus from his hand.
When the discus, resembling a ring, emerged from his finger—
Quickly releasing fire, it grew exceedingly terrifying;
thousand-spoked, like the sun, red in color, and impetuous, it made all the directions resound and set the forests ablaze. (78–79)
Reducing the mountain to ashes, he swiftly devoured the Rākṣasas;
by his force, the earth and the circle of the wind were shaken.
The oceans were indeed agitated, becoming rigid and overflowing their shores.
For a moment, the celestial chariots in the sky lost their stability and equilibrium;
the hearts of all embodied beings trembled and abandoned their fortitude.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the powerless ones were momentarily bewildered. (81–82)
In that moment of extreme velocity, the beings were indeed rendered unconscious;
the Rākṣasas became paralyzed once they recognized the Sudarśana.
Just as the discus reached them, it indeed tore their heads asunder.
The remaining Rākṣasas were slain, and even Mārīca was destroyed.
Then their bodies fell upon the earth like massive boulders.
Thereupon, seizing his discus and his spear which protects his hosts, [he advanced].
It retreated, most terrible and resembling a circle of fire;
having attained great speed, it did not quickly find peace.
It slowly receded through the expanses of mountains and forests.

At that time, the many regions that were the foothills of the mountain were consumed by the fire of the *cakras* and attained the state of mercury (*rasa*). Rich with the ashes of white crystal, they became like black gems. (87–88)
The beloved regions, which were yellow and like gold,
became like stones and mountains, scorched by the fire of the discus.
Once again they attained the state of stone, just like beautiful jewels.
On all sides, stones produced from rasa (essence) consist of the essence of metal (āra).
Born from contact with the discus, they are crackling (*marmara*) and resonant with that friction;
those regions, having undergone transformation, possess bodies fit for artistic work. (2.183.90–91)
He indeed assumed a peaceful form and took on the appearance of his attendant;
he also bore the trident and the form of the Gaṇas, as well as the three-eyed [form].
Having summoned the hosts of Gaṇas and the army of men dwelling in the forest, ||| 92 ||
Both granted him courage and proclaimed his victory.
(93) At that moment, trumpets of triumph were sounded on all sides, and a rain of flowers fell from the sky, offered by the gods and other celestial beings. (94)
The kettledrums resounded, as did the conchs and bugles;
indeed, joy entered the army of Manu as if it were embodied.
And likewise, among all the hosts of celestial beings in their chariots, [joy prevailed].
The joy in the hearts of both kings could not indeed be contained.
From great delight, shouts of victory arose from the celestial chariots.
Then the Discus, the Trident, and the two attendants likewise descended upon Parvata.
The two went to the entrance of the cave, the dwelling place of the Rākṣasa;
having gone inside, they beheld it enveloped in darkness.
Then, having extended their own light into that cave, they [proceeded].
Having beheld the heaps of remaining bones of the men and women who had been devoured,
the two attendants, overcome with grief and filled with compassion, went forward and then looked about there once more. (2.183.100)
Two hundred and a thousand maidens and women who had been abducted by the Rākṣasas then wept;
they both reported the accounts of those Rākṣasas.
And on the side, within a grove of trees in the forest, there exists a city.
In that valley, which is invisible in form, many men, women, children, and even infants have been seized and held in bondage. (1.02–1.03)
Having quickly led them all out from the cave,
they went to the city as it had been built by the Rākṣasas in former times.
There they saw many youths in their prime standing in fetters.
Others who had been liberated were placed within the enclosure;
many men and women there were to be eaten by the Rākṣasas in succession,
but having observed them, [the two brothers] released them, numbering more than a thousand.
Then the discus remained there and the trident went to Hari and Hara;
at that time, Nārāyaṇa and Hara related the entire account.
Quickly abandoning the celestial chariot, they both went swiftly to the city.
Even while weeping, they attained joy upon seeing Hari, the Lord Hara.
Released from their bonds, those subjects bowed down again and again;
there, Hari consoled all the subjects like a father.
The son and daughter of the protectorless one also bowed down to Hara, the Supreme Lord, and wept again and again. O Rādhikā, Hari indeed granted them courage and fearlessness.
Hari spoke to Śaṅkara for the sake of their deliverance, bringing them happiness.

(111) Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Rākṣasas and the Two Kings along with Their Armies, the Battle of the Rākṣasī Women with Durgā, the Destruction of the Rākṣasas by Rudra, the Protection of the Subjects Held in Shackles, and the Transformation of the Mountain into Stone through the Splendor of the Sudarśana Discus," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (183)
