Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, spoke to Rudra, who is capable of delivering others and is the slayer of demons. (1)
"O Śambhu, grant a mantra to this helpless girl and to the boy;
then grant two Vaiṣṇava mantras to those two boys who are likewise helpless.
Śambhu quickly gave the mantra to the girl and to the boy.
Though he was without a protector, he took up the mantra of Śambhu and became a Vaiṣṇava.
Then, considering Kṛṣṇa to be a suitable and worthy protector,
that young girl obtained her father’s permission and took Kṛṣṇa’s hand right there.
Having observed this,
those two hundred and one thousand young women who had been rescued and protected from the abyss all recognized their beloved Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Lord.

Those goddesses, who were of white complexion, chose a worthy Lord as their protector with auspicious hearts intent on marriage; impelled by merit, they took hold of Hari’s hand there in the forest, acting of their own free will. (6–7)
Śambhu first gave the Vaiṣṇava mantra to all of them;
he then established them all in the sky among the beloved wives of Brahmā.
Mādhava [liberated] all the men and women who were situated in the prison.
He placed his own feet upon their heads and made them independent.
Kṛṣṇa removed their miseries and caused them to receive the mantra from Śambhu.
At that time, they became Vaiṣṇavas and took refuge in Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
And to those people who were besieged by the Rākṣasas in the city of Mārīśāna,
Hara gave Vaiṣṇava mantras and delivered them.
Having wandered through that most beautiful city from place to place, [he...]
Then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the God of all, purified everything.
Requested by them all and worshipped within their hearts, Kṛṣṇa was repeatedly entreated to remain there for that very night.
Having seen that meditation, he quickly descended the celestial chariots at nightfall near the city of Mārīśā in the vast Araṇyaka forest; there,
he caused dwellings to be established upon the tree-covered ground.
Having indeed caused all to take their meal at night,
Hari himself caused a most excellent festival of victory to be celebrated there with songs,
dances, musical instruments, and joy-inspiring hymns of praise.
Then he passed the night with plays, stories,
and narrations. Śrī Hari quickly remembered by means of his yogic power all those warriors on his own side who had been killed in battle.
Having all attained the state of living beings, they regained their vital breaths and their bodies;
becoming healthy, they returned that very night to the abode of Hari.
Even those whose bones lay in the depths of the forest or in the wilds, having died there, likewise returned.
Then they fell down in the vicinity of the city; by his yogic power, the Blessed One remembered those embodied beings there.
All who had died were restored by the will of Kṛṣṇa, whose resolve is ever true.
They became alive and healthy, and they arrived there during the night.
Indeed, many men, women, children,
and even infants were seen in their dwellings in the morning with entirely new forms.
In this manner, Śrī Hari restored one hundred thousand men to life within the night through his grace; to them, Śambhu bestowed the mantra.
Having drunk the water from the feet of Hari, they then became Vaiṣṇavas.
Those people from different lands remembered their own native places;
some who were able went to their own countries, while others indeed remained there.
Then the Blessed Lord spoke to the high-souled Lomaśa.
"Indeed, this kingdom is to be handed over to King Jinavardhana;
O Guru, bestow upon him the crown according to the rite of consecration.
Place the tilaka upon his forehead so that he may become the king here."
Then Jinavardhana said:
"O Śrī Parameśvara, that kingdom must indeed be given to the conqueror; it should be bestowed upon Īśāna.
Likewise, Alpaketu and other great sages have also spoken thus. (27–28)
Then Hari spoke to Śambhu, having forcibly seated him upon a golden throne;
having established the moon upon his forehead with unbroken grains of rice and saffron,
he himself, with his own right hand, placed the crown upon him.
Īśāna, the illustrious Mahādeva, became the king of Mārīśā. O Rādhā, he gradually resettled the city of Pārvatībhūmi on the foothills, adorning it with groves and gardens.
This very Lord Īśāna, Śaṅkara, assuming a second form,
together with Durgā and accompanied by his attendants,
established his own residence at the request of the subjects, by the command of Hari.
This very one became the chosen deity, the Lord Īśāna, the Supreme Sovereign (33).
He is indeed the destroyer of the Rākṣasas who are white and fair-skinned;
he is the god who destroys all defects, the eternal bestower of liberation and happiness (34).
On that day, Śaṅkara said to the son of Gaṅgā:
"Only after I have secured the stability of your kingdom will I give this city to you.
Take the garland and the water-filled añjali in the presence of Hari."
Thus addressed there in the morning, he took up the garland. Then, having stationed Hari and the attendants of Śambhu as guards there,
[he departed], after taking leave of Śambhu, Durgā, the wives of Brahmā, the great sages, and his own family.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Blessed One, having assembled the people, instructed them:
"The time is indeed demonic; for just as there was a demon here [before], so too does one exist now. (38)
He, along with his lineage, was slain by Śaṅkara, my devotee.
Likewise, even the Rākṣasa Kāla is destroyed by those who have attained a state of liberation through taking refuge in me alone; of this there is no doubt. (2.184.40)
Let them practice devotion to me and likewise worship Īśāna;
let them indeed take refuge in Śambhu, their chosen deity who provides great protection.
Let them also worship Mahādevī Satī, Durgā, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Yesterday was indeed a Sunday, presided over by the Sun deity.
For the sake of destroying all defects, she who bestows light must be propitiated by me here on this Sunday, accompanied by Śaṅkara and others. (42–43)
The terrible Rākṣasas, who are devourers and givers of suffering, have been struck down;
you too must slay the faults that bestow sin upon the Sun.
All [faults] such as desire and anger must be destroyed, and the Bull (Vṛṣa) must be protected during the time of the Sun.
Disease arises in two ways: either physical or mental.
Mental disease arises from the physical, and physical disease also arises from the mental;
for these two are born of one another, consisting of desire, anger, and so forth.
The *doṣas* are indeed declared to be diseases; they should be abandoned on the day of the Sun.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities of the mind. On Sunday, these three, which possess universal forms, should not be excessively engaged.
Sorrow is overcome by joy, and joy is overcome by sorrow.
But both joy and sorrow are overcome by the quality of darkness (tamas).
Having understood this wheel of the qualities, one should suppress them while the sun of spiritual power shines.
Discontent, negligence, pride, passion, excessive longing,
greed, delusion, arrogance, and agitation— these indeed are the Rākṣasas.
One who is possessed by these evils should never, under any circumstances, even look at the sun.
The pit called the belly cannot be filled by people in a single day.
A wise man, considering it to be unfillable, should not attempt to fill it when the sun [is high].
Just as a fire blazes up when kindled, it is extinguished when not fed with fuel.
When the sun is devoid of food, it indeed subsides by itself;
for people prepare much sacrificial remains (vighasa) solely for the sake of their own bellies.
When the sun becomes the conqueror of the belly, it shall be the conqueror of all evils.
Human desires and enjoyments must be conquered on the day of the Sun (Sunday).
People who do not indulge in such enjoyments go to the unsurpassed abode when the Sun is present.
Yoga, security, and renunciation should always be practiced toward the Sun and toward Hari.
For the sake of a single belly, a tiger produces a great deal of remains;
other dull-witted and greedy animals, such as deer and the like, subsist upon those remains.
Having reflected thus, one should discard at sunrise the useless heaps of remains.
O King, whether by those who subsist on leaves, those who subsist on fruits, or those who eat but once a day,
a king who rules over this entire earth in its totality is not truly distinguished if he is not devoted to renunciation toward the Sun. (57–58)
On Sunday, auspicious intentions should be undertaken without worldly exertion;
those who are free from meat-eating do not grieve, for meat must indeed be abandoned on Sunday.
On Sunday, one may obtain the path of the ancestors and the path of the gods through Śaṅkara.

Through austerity, celibacy, and devotion, the great seers, having liberated themselves from their bodies at the end, go to the stainless world of Brahmā. Worldly gain creates bondage; that karma must always be abandoned in the presence of the Sun.
Therefore, one who is liberated from that and attached to Hari attains the supreme state.
Having ascended the clarity of wisdom, that which is to be abandoned must indeed be abandoned;
and by one who is sighted and possessed of sound intellect, the worship of the Lord is to be grasped.
In this body composed of the six sheaths, the Sun indeed stands as the seventh, distinct [from them].
He who perceives that deity and that Self truly sees;
from that very perception, he gradually attains the supreme Brahman.
On the day of the Sun, those who are self-controlled, peaceful, and patient attain the state of the wise.
On the day of the Sun, devotees of humanity should perform the sacrifice to Īśāna, as well as the worship of Durgā,
the worship of the Guru, and the worship of Hari.
On that day, he should remain unattached, free from worldly ties, and released from all bonds.
Equal toward enemy and friend alike, he will certainly be liberated.
Thus following this dharma, or else devoted to charity and austerity, [the virtuous attain liberation].
Endowed with the quality of compassion, free from desire, anger, and other such passions,
devoted to the protection of your subjects, and established in the vows of Sūrya and Īśāna,
you shall attain the worlds you desire by being intent on honoring your gurus and elders.
"And may there be well-being for you all, and may there always be happiness for those who serve the Sun.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari, having reflected and observed silence, spoke to Alpaketu to go to his city, Jīvanīpura. (2.184.70)
"Let others also be prepared; we shall indeed eat there.
Then, having bowed to Hari, Jinavarddhi Mahārāja spoke, as did Īśāna, Durgā, Āpyāyana, and the sage.
"O Blessed One, after eating here in the city and wandering thereafter,
you must purify the surface of the earth and proceed from there.
The compassionate Blessed One said, "O Rādhikā, let it be so."
Cooked foods had already been prepared there by the local people;
at midday, everyone ate according to the desire of Īśāna.
Then Durgā, Satī, and the wives of Brahmā indeed partook of the meal.
Having rested for a moment in their vehicles, mounts, and celestial chariots,
and having prepared themselves, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and the others quickly entered the celestial chariot after receiving the worship offered to them by the people there in the sky.
Then, many excellent musical instruments were played profusely;
shouts of victory and the sounds of trumpets arose indeed on all sides.
Having thoroughly protected the royal army there, the king, who possessed the splendor of a Jina, [remained].
Śambhu, Durgā, Nārāyaṇa, and the others bestowed a parting gift upon him;
together with King Alpaketu alone, they departed in their vehicles,
and the celestial chariots proceeded along the path shown by Alpaketu.
And the great seer Āpyāyana arrived together with them in a celestial chariot.
Having passed over Mount Apiyāna and crossed the northern mountain,
those situated in the chariot beheld the exceedingly beautiful mountain named Alpa.

With a small chariot, he was the first to arrive at the front. He, along with his own city of living beings, accompanied by musical instruments and his army, quickly [approached] with necklaces, offerings, and other gifts for the sake of a welcome.
Accompanied by the queen, her sons, daughters, and others, he stood before him.
At his command, the musicians quickly sounded their instruments;
the subjects raised shouts of victory, and the bearers of fly-whisks uttered words of praise for his glory. (83)
Mechanical devices produced sounds indicating a welcome;
and upon seeing the golden celestial chariot in the sky, the men bowed, as did the women dwelling on the mountains, the people in the houses on the earth, and those in the air. (84–85)
Beholding Hari’s celestial chariot, blazing with splendor and adorned with a banner—extraordinary, perfectly equipped, and resplendent with an excellence of divinity;
[adorned] with many garlands, archways, and the like, fashioned from pearls and diamonds. (86)
Abundant with the splendor of its form, it shone like the sun with its radiating rays;
it was preceded by swans, Garuḍas, elephants, horses with rubies for manes, lions, and even śarabhas, all appearing in embodied forms. (87–88)
It was adorned on its sides with many other vehicles and celestial chariots;
behind it, the gods and goddesses surrounded it, proclaiming cries of victory.
It was beautifully decorated and highly honored with flowers, unbroken grains, garlands, and other offerings.
Below, it was cooled by moon-like jewels;
its center was graced with gardens featuring rows of *kalpa*-tree blossoms and the like;
and it shone with rich wall-slates inlaid with *cintāmaṇi* gems.
It was exceedingly beautiful with peaks adorned by the splendor of golden jars;
it displayed auspicious svastika patterns fashioned in the shape of lotuses;
and it was endowed with divine fans, umbrellas, and radiant whisks.
The eastern quarter resounded with the sounds of "Victory! and the waving of canes, proclaiming:
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious!
Thus, they indicated their devotion to Mādhava with those golden-colored [words]. (93–94)
Beholding such a beautiful celestial chariot in the sky, they bowed;
and on the auspicious, vast surface of the earth, along the path shown by the king,
the infallible Hari brought his own chariot down.
Other celestial chariots also descended to the surface of the earth.
With cries of "Victory!", the subjects offered a formal welcome with prostrations like well-disciplined staffs;
standing at a distance, they scattered parched grain and other offerings toward the chariot.
Others scattered flowers, some scattered unbroken grains of rice,
and others scattered perfumes, garlands, and the like upon the celestial chariot.
Thus it was on the fifth day of the month of Bhādra, O Rādhikā, regarding Kṛṣṇa.
Nārāyaṇa reached the city of Jīvanī, which was filled with groves.
King Alpaketu, the queen, their daughters, sons,
and others were waiting outside at the front of the palanquin for the arrival of Hari.
"Everyone gazes right there at the gate, wondering when Mādhava might come outside; with steady eyes, they are filled with intense joy.

(101) Thus, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, following the destruction of the Rākṣasas for the sake of rescuing the orphaned children, [the Lord] took the hands of one thousand two hundred girls in marriage; from the bones of those killed by the Rākṣasas...

The one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Reviving of the Dead, the Establishment of the Kingdom of Īśāna, the Majesty of Sunday, the Worship and Benedictions, Resting at Night, and the Departure on the Fifth Day of the Dark Fortnight of Bhādrapada for King Alpaketu’s City of Jīvanī after Breakfast. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 185.
[Author: Chapter 186.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, O Rādhā, this Blessed One [set out] toward the city of Jīvanī.
Having cast his gaze from the celestial chariot, he quickly descended outside.
At that moment, King Alpaketu, Āpyāyana Rishi, and others placed auspicious necklaces around the necks of the sons of Bālakṛṣṇa.
They placed fragrant clusters of flowers— made of gold, silk, diamonds, and gems— in their hands, and they offered blossoms upon their heads.
They honored them with unbroken grains of rice and prostrated at their feet.
Others as well—Īśāna and the rest, as well as the ṛṣis—were honored by all.
The ancestors, together with their families, were highly esteemed with words of welcome.
Then those devotees of Hari, having washed their feet, drank the water.
They seated Hari upon an elephant-carriage adorned with gold;
others they placed upon auspicious vehicles, mounts, and indeed upon chariots.
Having seated them in palanquins and celestial chariots amidst the sounds of auspicious music, [they proceeded].
Overwhelmed with love, the king and others caused [the image] to be paraded through the city.
(7) It was carried by the principal figures—the king and others, the merchant-princes, the officials, the subjects, and likewise by women and men of every caste. (8)
He was honored and worshipped on the main road, at the crossroads,
in the courtyard, at the junction of paths, and in the circular area of the marketplaces.
Hari was repeatedly welcomed and propitiated by everyone with words of greeting.
Nārāyaṇa was worshipped with priceless offerings, all kinds of requisites, fruits, flowers, and auspicious items.
Having thus beheld that city and then granted his vision, [he departed]. (2.185.10–11)
Having come to his residence, Hari drank water;
he then quickly sat down in the assembly hall and gave instructions.
Wherever the Lord himself resides, and wherever the virtuous have taken refuge in Hari—
That land where devotees dwell is called divine.
Indeed, that region is beyond the gunas and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Blessed is this Ketumāla, blessed are its kings, and blessed are its riverbanks.
Blessed are those cities where My feet have come;
blessed are you, the people here, who have attained the state of being Vaiṣṇavas. And this state of being Vaiṣṇavas consists of association with the virtuous and the grace of the Supreme Lord.

Devotion to one's chosen deity and service to the virtuous—these are indeed difficult to attain. For those in whom these have come together, nothing remains to be achieved. Even the inhabitants of the divine realms desire this pentad. (16–17)
For those whose nature is devoted to austerity and sacred study, there exist eternal worlds;
wise ones who have no enemies, through devotion, have attained supreme liberation.
Turning away from sense objects, they go by devotion to the highest state.
Those seeking liberation, endowed with devotion, go to an ineffable state.
(19) But for those to whom the fivefold [discipline] has not been taught, there is only the worldly;
by splitting open the trunk of a plantain tree, no core is found. (2.185.20)
Therefore, having obtained those five [senses], having set the goal of the highest good,
and having restrained the thirst of the mind and abandoned the continuity of karma,
one should remain attached to the Supreme Lord while following the path of the virtuous.
One should meditate upon the God who dwells within; he shall indeed attain the highest good.

Those who delight in ritual action, who are immersed in sacrifice, in giving, and even in the performance of service, yet who cast these aside upon beholding Me—they are considered by Me to go to My world.

Renunciation, contentment, sacrifice to the Lord, the exhaustion of longing, and the dissolution of pride and other such traits— for those who possess these, there is indeed eternal happiness. In this regard, a four-stepped ladder leads to the world of Brahman.
The sacrifice of discourse is for the assembly of sages, while knowledge is the ladder for those who perceive reality.
The ladder of ritual action is intended for householders, and the ladder of austerity for the virtuous.
If worldly effort is directed toward sense objects, then freedom from effort is superior. (25–26)
In worldly striving there are many faults that bring about both destruction and rebirth;
by such striving the self is defiled, and thereby one's spiritual welfare perishes.
He who acquires here what is unworthy and abandons altogether what is worthy [is lost].
And at the end, he would be abandoned by both, becoming thereafter blind.
Having reflected thus, especially by householders among men, let there be the sacrifice of action according to rule, and the sacrifice of wealth with true riches. (28–29)
Nārāyaṇa and I myself must be sought after and propitiated.
In ancient times, Indra became the king of the gods through various sacrifices;
and Mahādeva, having offered himself in the great sacrifice, became that [supreme state].

The God of gods, having pervaded and supported all things, attained the state of the Sovereign Lord. At the sacrifice of Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, he received Śrī as the server of food; and through devotion, she who grants everything attained even my own abode.
In this way, other performers of ritual action in previous kalpas and in other ages,

having engaged in sacrifices of action and even giving wealth, went to heaven. Indeed, through the sacrifice of action, one attains Vaiṣṇavahood, the company of the virtuous, and the pleasing of Hari.
One should perform such a sacrifice as the service of the virtuous; indeed, it becomes that very thing. If one is free from worldly striving and well-contented, one attains the eternal Brahman.
Contentment is indeed the supreme heaven, for satisfaction is the highest bliss.

Nothing whatsoever is praised anywhere as a happiness greater than contentment. Having withdrawn all desires within his own self, the embodied soul becomes serene. From him there is no fear at all, nor does anyone have any fear of him.

When one who is himself deficient in desire and anger perceives the Self therein, he becomes free from malice toward all beings and devoid of all longing. Having offered everything to Hari, he attains Brahman. || 37-38 ||
However, for those beings whose worldly activity flows with passion,
their goal lies in the eternal offering to Hari.
Some praise conciliation (*sāma*), while other people praise effort (*prayatna*).
Some praise meditative absorption, while others praise the auspicious refuge;
some praise sacrifice, and others praise renunciation;
some praise charity, while others accept gifts.

The peaceful, having attained a state of silence, worship the Supreme Lord; the restless desire sovereignty, wherein both are equal. Having reflected upon this, the wise should resort to that which bestows happiness.
The pursuit of what is innate is indeed an auspicious means that bestows the highest good. Living without malice toward all beings is the practice of the virtuous;
that is declared to be the path of the righteous, wherein the self is never bound.
If that king should always abide in his kingdom by a path free from malice—
through truth, through sharing, through self-restraint, and likewise through compassion;
through modesty, through generosity, through devotion to the gods, and through the protection of his subjects.
And by means of self-mastery, by regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant as equal,
(46) by subsisting on the remnants of sacrifice, and by showing favor to the virtuous— through these,
both this world and the next shall become for him a source of the arising of the highest fruits. (47)
Thus, for those who are devoted to dharma, who always resort to the service of the virtuous,
and who fight here solely for the sake of protecting their subjects and for the cause of dharma,
there shall be a most excellent and auspicious state, a heaven beyond even heaven.
In former times, the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the world-protectors,
the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Viśvedevas— having performed such dharma through meritorious deeds, attained the supreme heaven; thereafter, human beings [attained it] here.
Relying upon such a dharma, let them indeed go to the supreme goal.
For the gods, the ancestors, and likewise guests, depend constantly upon the householder;
so too do servants, the virtuous, and all human beings perpetually subsist upon him.
Birds, cattle, and all beings that have taken refuge [in them],
as well as austerity, sacrifice, knowledge, mendicancy, restraint of the senses, meditation, solitude, virtuous conduct, contentment, wisdom, and service— these are [the means]. (52–53)
O Kṛṣṇa, those duties of the brāhmaṇas which belong to the householder must always be offered by me unto You:
sacrifice, learning, exertion, the acquisition of wealth, the wielding of punishment,
fierceness, conduct, knowledge, the protection of subjects, and the giving of gifts.
O Kṛṣṇa, those duties of the householder which belong to the king should always be offered by me unto You.
The acquisition of wealth, enterprise, charity, protection, and so forth, as well as the cultivation of crops and other such duties of the Vaiśya, should be offered unto Me, the Lord. (55–56)
Service, endurance, obedience to commands, eating only what remains, and the state of servitude—these are the duties of a Śūdra; these too must be offered to me, Mādhava.
Chastity, service to the guru, and the maintenance of the household and so forth [are likewise to be offered].
The protection of offspring and the duties of women are to be entrusted to me, their lord.
(58) Study, play, expansion, delight, jesting, and daring—these duties of children are to be entrusted to me, their lord. (59)
Desire, strength, self-interest, vision, victory, lack of reflection, acquisition, application, and the duties of youth— all these are to be offered to me,
my lord. So too are chatter, trembling, dependence on others, incapacity, and ferocity.
Laziness, contempt, and the like are to be offered to me by those who follow the dharma of the elders;
likewise, enduring beatings, suffering, poverty, being treated like cattle, punishment, harshness, and insults are the duties of the lowly toward me as their master. (61–62)
Laughter, pleasure, dalliance, affection, servitude, ferocity, bondage, and even hopelessness— all these feminine qualities are indeed offered to me,
the Lord. For those who abide in this manner, with their minds offered unto me alone—
I indeed effect the deliverance of those sinking in the ocean of death.
Long ago, there were two sages born of brahmins named Śaṅkha and Likhita;
they were brothers and each had his own separate residence.
Once, on the banks of the Bāhudā, there was a hermitage protected by Śaṅkha, which was always endowed with trees bearing flowers and fruit;
however, at that time, Śaṅkha had gone elsewhere in the forest and was not present in the hermitage.
Likhita indeed caused the ripe fruits to fall;
he began to eat them right there when Śaṅkha arrived.
Śaṅkha said to his brother, "Without asking permission, you have [taken] these which truly belong to another."
The fruits have fallen here; your virtue is compromised here.
By taking these fruits yourself, you have committed this act of theft.
Go, approach the king, and confess the deed of robbery.
He too went quickly and reported that deed to the king:
"I have committed a theft; grant me the expiation for it. King Sudyumna said: "If you consider me to be the king..."
"Then, O Brahmin, take my permission and choose another staff.
Although addressed thus, the king of sages did not choose anything else.
Thereupon, the king cut off both hands of the sage.
Having taken up his staff, the brahmin departed and went to his brother.
Śaṅkha said to him, "O most righteous one, brother, go to the Bāhudā river;
satisfy the sages, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rites. (73–74)
Then, once again at another time, you must never set your mind upon unrighteousness.
Having received the command of Śaṅkha, Likhita went to the Bāhudā river.
Having bathed in that holy river, he said to me, "May the fruit of my expiation [accrue] to me."
Just as the Brahmin proceeded to offer water for the sake of the funeral libation,
his two hands suddenly appeared before me at that moment due to my taking possession of them.
Then, having performed the offering of water, he offered everything permanently unto me.
Having realized the greatness of dedication (*arpaṇa*), which destroys all sins, that brahmin performed [his duties] here in this land of action continuously.
Even the punishment that the king had inflicted was surrendered by him to me.
The gift of water and other offerings was entrusted to me by means of a written document;
likewise, the command of Śaṅkha was also entrusted to me.
Thus, by this complete surrender, they have been purified through my power.

"There is no fault of speech for Śaṅkha, no fault of punishment for the king, nor is there any fault of the hand for the scribe, because [the document] was submitted by me. Thinking thus, those men who remember me and offer themselves unto me—
Those who have taken refuge in me enjoy themselves and live free from all obstacles;
at the end, being liberated from the bonds of karma, they surely come unto me alone.
In the same way, you all—the classes of kings and the classes of subjects—everywhere [should do likewise].
Having made the offering of everything to Me and having worshipped Me, go to My abode.
At the end, when life departs, I shall appear before you as an object of perception;
I shall lead My devotees by means of a celestial chariot to My supreme abode.
"Make me your object of devotion; worship me always.
Make me your firm refuge, and I shall lead you to my supreme abode.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the high-souled Lomaśa.
"Give mantras to the subjects, and let the people take their food.
Thus addressed, he gave the mantras that deliver those who have come for refuge.
Then all the subjects went to their respective homes, and thereafter Hari [departed].
O Rādhikā, they all prepared the meal and partook of the food.
Having rested at night, Kṛṣṇa rose quickly in the morning; having performed his daily rites, he sat down upon his own seat. (88–89)
Then the king requested Hari to allow him to drink milk and so forth; Hari did partake of the milk meal,
took betel, and desired to depart.
Others who had consumed milk and other foods also became ready to depart early in the morning; at that time, the queen, accompanied by her daughter,
arrived for the purpose of worship and worshipped the Supreme Lord.
The seven maidens and the young girls took the hand of Hari;
having thus performed the offering of their hands and obtained the Supreme Lord as their beloved,
they received the garland of choice and other honors, and then became fulfilled.

Then those seven beloved wives of Brahmā, having gathered together, ascended that celestial chariot (vimāna). The king then worshipped Hari with devotion; he bid farewell to his subjects, gave gifts, and presented royal offerings.
Then musical instruments indicative of the departure were indeed played;
the honored guests ascended their celestial chariots, and thereafter the Lord,
together with his family and Śambhu, ascended his own celestial chariot.
Then Hari, being entreated by the sage who was filled with devotion even as he grew old,
and by the king named Jayakṛṣṇavana,
bestowed blessings upon Alpaketu and the others in the sky.
By means of his celestial chariot, Hari-Kṛṣṇa made his way toward the kingdom of Jaya-Kṛṣṇa-vara;
having crossed over Alpādri, he reached the land where his beloved Jarā resided.
Thus, Hari-Kṛṣṇa and the others, traveling through the sky on their aerial vehicles, arrived there.
They arrived at the lower reaches of the river Āpagā.
The king and the sage had previously gone there to ensure a favorable reception;
they prepared the ground for Hari’s arrival and welcomed him with musical instruments and other offerings.

O Rādhikā, upon seeing the city of Varaṇā— vast, radiant, and beautifully adorned— the Lord Hari rejoiced at that time. Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section on the continuity of the Tretā Age, concerning the wandering of Śrī Hari through the living city of Alpaketu, His worship, His teaching in the assembly by means of the example of Śaṅkha and Likhita, His meal, and His rest at night.

Chapter One Hundred and Eighty-Five: The Description of the Arrival of King Jayakṛṣṇavana in the City of Varaṇā on the Sixth [Lunar Day], Following His Morning Meal and Homage to His Own Chosen Sages and Deities.
Chapter One Hundred and Eighty-Six: *The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga* — *The Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section Two.
[The Author: Chapter 187.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, from the sky the Blessed One beheld the city of Prāvaraṇā.
By the path commanded by the king, he brought down the celestial chariot;
thereafter, other chariots also descended. Abundant musical instruments were played, and proclamations of victory arose.
There were sounds of victory and joy; the subjects rejoiced and did not weep.
The king himself approached Śrī Hari and worshipped Him with golden garlands, flower garlands, clusters of flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
The king’s servants, the merchants, and the subjects offered him a welcome (4).
Through prostrations, shouts of victory, and auspicious hymns of praise,
the subjects displayed their enthusiasm and showed him honor (5).
Having washed the feet of Śrī Hari with water, he drank the nectar;
the king, together with his family, and the subjects likewise drank that nectar.
They performed the worship of Īśāna and the other deities according to their respective rites.
The queen likewise performed the honors for Brahmapriyā and the others.
Having caused all the armies, adorned with ornaments, to mount their elephant-vehicles, the Blessed One himself ascended his elephant-vehicle.
In the city, with instrumental music and songs, the king joyfully paraded Kṛṣṇa along the great highway and at all the junctions of the streets; he likewise led Hari through the royal palace,
the servants’ quarters, and even the house of the chief minister.
In other settlements as well, the people took him and offered him due honor.
Having purified the city, at midday the Blessed One returned to his own residence; he bathed and took rest.

Then, seeing that everyone was weary, the king indeed caused auspicious meals to be prepared— abundant and excellent foods served in due order. The Blessed One ate, and the others then partook of their meal.
Having rested for a moment in the evening, the Lord Hari convened an assembly.
There, Bālakṛṣṇa himself gave instruction as follows:
"Meritorious deeds and sins are always joined with the embodied soul as its two paths. (12–14)
In due time, it bestows either sin or merit, as well as suffering or happiness.
Indeed, your own merit has borne fruit here in that I have come before you.
My union with you and my service to you are the result of abundant merit.
A mantra bears fruit in due time, and medicine bears fruit in due time.
Rain falls in due time, and trees bear fruit according to the season.
The moon waxes full in its time, and even the rivers swell in their time.
When the proper time has arrived, prosperity comes of its own accord;
and a seed sown at the right time sprouts when the season comes.
Likewise, decay occurs in due time, and the loss of sap in trees likewise happens in due time. (18)
For the transition brought about by Time touches all embodied beings.
(19) Having reflected thus, a wise person should take refuge in the Supreme Lord at the proper time.
This present time is most auspicious for you; it has now arrived. (20)
A true union with me, Nārāyaṇa, has indeed arisen for you here. But those who, having obtained such a one as I in person, remain elsewhere—
whether they be deluded or possessed by ignorance— their loss occurs at every step.
Having abandoned the Supreme Lord, those who remain fixed on other objects due to the impulses arising from thirst and greed become partakers of suffering;
for them, the fruit is nothing other than the suffering born of the affliction of thirst.
Or rather, if a happiness that is momentary and followed by suffering were to be obtained—
wherein suffering follows happiness and happiness follows suffering—
then indeed, happiness ends in suffering and suffering ends in happiness. (24)

Therefore, one who desires eternal happiness should abandon these two. Whatever causes grief, distress, or fainting and the like—that the wise person should renounce here, and thus acquire eternal happiness. (25–26)
In this world, every pleasure is invariably accompanied by suffering and is indeed illusory;
for there is no end to sufferings, as they arise ever more and more. Therefore, [pleasure] exists at all times either through its alternating manifestation or through its inclusion within suffering.
Indeed, for one wandering in saṃsāra, suffering comes mixed with pleasure.

Having reflected thus, one should abandon that which is momentary, perishable, fraught with great exertion, and productive of torment; instead, one should acquire that happiness which is designated as bliss, characterized by permanence, and eternal. (28–29)
Through service, austerity, devotion, and single-minded righteousness, as well as through charity and self-restraint, one indeed attains eternal happiness.
Contentment is truly the highest heaven; contentment is the supreme bliss.
Contentment is nectar and immortality; through contentment, indeed, the highest perfection is attained.
The individual soul who has taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa always fears no one else by virtue of Nārāyaṇa’s power, nor do any fear him.
When one experiences joy at all times through my grace, then one attains Brahman;
when one does not harbor any evil intention toward anything whatsoever,
whether by mind, deed, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
He by whom pride and delusion have been destroyed, as well as attachments and falsehoods,
and who has taken refuge in me— he attains nirvāṇa.
Having realized that accumulations end in decay and that prosperity ends in a fall, he reaches liberation.
One who possesses discernment should take refuge in me alone— the union that ends in separation, life that ends in death, and even happiness that ends in suffering;
for whether it be happiness or suffering, it arises only in succession.
It swiftly robs the embodied being of the very consciousness of the bank.
Even while this is so, one thinks, "I am noble-born," "I have attained perfection," and "I am indeed great.
Thus the mind is deluded, and even one’s memory is lost. (37–38)
One whose memory has failed considers the seizing of others' property to be virtuous;
therefore, the King Yama punishes that man who has transgressed the bounds of propriety.
Thus, having reflected and scrutinized the matter, a wise person should administer medicine.
Or else, it is the refuge of the virtuous and of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa.
Otherwise, a triad consisting of the onset of suffering, delusion, and the experience of the undesirable would arise; a fourth does not exist for him.
For old age and death are the devourers of living beings, just like two wolves;
no one can escape them, not even the sovereign of the universe.
There is no avoiding the suffering that has already arrived.
In the same way, pleasure should be understood [as being subject to change], for it does not exist as something absolute.
Desires do not come to pass in this world exactly as wished;
rather, they present themselves and persist in ways that are always contrary to one's expectations and unavoidable.
Union with those who are unpleasant and separation from those who are very dear—
these two are considered to be the causes of gain and loss, and the givers of happiness and suffering.
Birth, growth, and end— all these are established within them.
Smell, form, taste, and touch exist at a particular time and then pass away.
Seats, beds, vehicles, celestial chariots, drinks, ointments, food, and even the act of rising are born and perish. (46–87)
Even physicians are afflicted by disease; the strong are powerless before women;
even the wealthy are eunuchs—strange indeed is the turning of karma!
Birth in a noble family, great prowess, health, beauty, and uprightness—
Good fortune, enjoyments, and the like are obtained through abundant merit.
Even when these exist, if there is no devotion to Kṛṣṇa, they are fruitless.
Poor people have many sons even though they do not desire them. (2.186.50)
There is no son for those who possess great wealth; the activities of karma are manifold.
Likewise, there is disease and suffering for the learned man, and hunger for the destitute.
Calamities always befall the man of abundant riches, and fever the king.
From whatever emanation [of a being] there arises, from that comes manifold action and activity.
A young man who dies wealthy goes [to his next state], while one who has lived for a hundred years goes forth destitute;
likewise, those with nothing live long, while the prosperous are short-lived.

The capacity for enjoyment exists in the wealthy, not in the poor; the digestive fire is more intense in one with wealth than in one without. The mind is intent on action when there is wealth; the workings of karma are indeed wondrous. Having reflected upon this, a wise person should act for the sake of his own ultimate welfare.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings, nor repeated recitations [can save one];
neither honor nor the prosperity of a noble lineage protects one whose death has arrived.
Just as a tree and a log might meet by chance upon a flood.
Having come together, they depart; such is the meeting of living beings.
Whether they possess a kingdom of women, sons, and wealth, or whether they are destitute and dependent on others' food—whether they are lords or paupers—time acts equally upon them all.

Whether they are learned or blind, diligent or lacking in effort, whether they are devoted or undevoted—time acts equally toward them all. Whether it be unenjoyed or enjoyed, protected or neglected, [it remains the same]. (58–59)
Whether treated with hostility or accepted as one's own, Time acts equally toward them all.
Throughout various births, thousands of mothers and fathers, tens of thousands of wives and sons, and countless wealth and kingdoms have been enjoyed and then abandoned.
Again they are encountered in saṃsāra; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
(6.1) No one will ever belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone; this collection consisting of wife, kin, and friends is merely met upon the path. (6.2)
"Where have I been? Where shall I go? Who am I? And what is it that I am established in here?
How much time remains for me as certain?"—one should reflect thus again and again.
[This world] is impermanent, a dwelling place of suffering, outwardly appearing like happiness, yet inherently impure.
On the path of life, this mother, brother, son, and beloved are indeed encountered by chance;
yet the world perpetually sinks into the deep ocean of time,
where old age and death are its great crocodiles, and no one perceives it.
Even those who study Ayurveda are overcome by disease;
even while drinking medicinal decoctions, they do not transcend death.
And even those who drink elixirs of rejuvenation become overwhelmed by old age.
Even ascetics who are givers, and even sacrificers who have long endured—
even those with divine bodies dwelling in the sky— decay with time.
For indeed, the days that pass away for living beings never return.
Indeed, time and the path— which are infinite and frequented by all the worlds—
drag away even a person who has established firm resolve, as he becomes helpless and excessively longing.
The body approaches the soul, or the soul approaches the body, like a traveler.

Travelers depart after meeting other travelers, as do kinsmen and others. (2.186.70) No one ever finds a truly lasting companionship even with their own body, so what need is there to mention anyone else? (71)
Where have those former performers of ritual actions gone, such as our grandfathers and others?
We do not see them, nor do they see us, nor do we see one another.
They have been devoured by the Piśācinī-like Māyā and have entered the state of digestion.
They do not emerge again from that bottomless pit in which they sleep.
Therefore, having reflected upon time, action, and delusive illusion, as well as the body which inspires confidence and the separation of those who are united— (73–74)
One’s own instability, the world’s being devoured by Time, and its sudden nature— let them all take refuge in me, the Blessed One, as their protector from the noose of Time.
Through my yoga, there is no further death, nor is there any devouring by the serpent of Time.
In my abode, which is the perfection of bliss, there shall be no destruction for you. Those who take refuge in me, whose minds are fixed on me, who offer the objects of their senses to me,
and whose wisdom is established in my true nature, attain my eternal happiness.
Knowledge is said to be nectar itself if it results in awakening;
my service is its food if it is endowed with faith;
and my attainment is indeed satisfaction if it is joined with greatness. (78)
The total surrender of everything to Me bestows upon him eternal bliss.
Reflecting thus, devotees—both men and women alike—should in every way offer all kinds of actions to Kṛṣṇa, who is I, day and night. (2.186.80)

"O Rādhā, having brought about the absence of qualities in this [soul] and the relinquishing of fruits, I shall grant the attainment of fruits whose nature is My own, known as 'liberation' (uddhāra). Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then became silent; thereafter, the people [departed].
They worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with supreme devotion in due order,
using sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken grains, fragrant garlands, *puṣpasāra* perfumes, *rasasāra* essences, and garments of great value. (82–83)
Then, having honored [the deity] with ornaments, fruits, seeds, pearls, gems, diamonds,
and various offerings,
the people performed the *ārātrika* rite and likewise offered salutations and hymns of praise.
Then the king, likewise the queen, and the royal family,
having indeed concluded the assembly, brought Hari to their own abode;
both the king and the queen fed Hari and the members of Hari’s family.
Devoted to the service of the king, they fed the great sages, those of high honor, as well as others who were dear to Brahmā, to their heart's content.
Then the queen herself spoke to her own most beautiful daughter.
"Take that very one, who is alone and without a second, by the hand of Kṛṣṇa.
She too, being desirous, quickly took hold of the hand of Kṛṣṇa and placed upon the neck of Śrī Hari a golden garland inlaid with jewels.
Hari even placed a garland of flowers around her neck;
thus, by the rites of marriage, the princess obtained Mādhava.
Then the king celebrated that festival, and thereafter [he performed] further [rites].
Having rested during the night, the Blessed One himself caused the subjects to hear his own mantra, which bestows the state of being a Vaiṣṇava, in the morning. Then,
having performed his daily rites, the king set his mind on departing.
He fed all the great lords from every side with milk-based foods according to the prescribed rites; then, having granted them leave,
he sent them forth with vehicles, mounts, and armies, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and cries of victory.
Then, with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and joyful gifts, he gave them leave to depart.
Celestial chariots appeared in the sky, and all the people took their seats within them.
Hari, having ascended his own chariot, set it in motion for the sake of departure.
Having crossed the river of the Rāhus in the sky, their celestial chariots indeed proceeded swiftly toward the regions inhabited by Pheruna and Sarṣi.
There, King Parīśāna and the sage Pherunasa were present.
Placing the celestial chariot at their head, they both descended swiftly to the earth.
To welcome Hari, the king mobilized his auspicious army;
he caused the sounds of musical instruments, shouts of victory, and the bursting of firecrackers to resound.

Then the people, filled with an abundance of joy, respectfully awaited the celestial chariots in the sky, equipped as they were with parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings. Thereupon, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa beheld the beautiful grounds.
On the delightful bank of the Senānadī river, [he saw] the auspicious city of Pariśā,
which, by its splendor, made even heaven appear inferior;
it was richly endowed with prosperity, graced by gardens, and resplendent with golden-hued palaces.
O Rādhikā, [we entered] that vast city inhabited by men equal to gods and resplendent with beautiful women like yourself;
[we proceeded] along the path shown by the king to the great garden and the royal palace.
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa slowly descended from the celestial chariot (vimāna).

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari, having descended from the chariot in the kingdom of the royal sage Jayakṛṣṇa during the second period, the Tretā-yuga, wandered through the city of Varaṇā, accepted worship, gave instruction, partook of food and rest at night, performed his morning rites in the morning, and after drinking milk and so forth, went on the sixth day to the regions of the sages Phera and Nasa and the kingdom of King Parīśāna," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna.
