Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Sovereign Lady of Goloka, Bālakṛṣṇa emerged from the midst of the celestial chariot.
At that time, he beheld a wondrous throng of more than a hundred thousand men, all of whom had heads like those of the *cakora* bird. 1.
Just as the function of the eye [is directed] toward the circle of light and power in the moon,
so too did the function of the eyes of all those who offered a welcome turn toward the Supreme Lord, the Giver of Boons. (2)
Just as peacocks, upon seeing a cloud, become utterly absorbed in their cries of joy,
so too do living beings at the sight of Śrī Hari.
Then they were indeed immersed in the sound of victory,
just as flocks of cātaka birds rejoice with great delight when rain falls from the clouds during the Svāti constellation.

Likewise, the flocks of birds were exceedingly delighted and gladdened by the dark, dense fruit; just as children [rejoice] at sweet, well-sugared [food]. 4. But as for the young girl, [she was drawn to] the sweet, well-sugared...
Just as [the gods] became filled with excessive joy upon reaching him,
so too did the subjects then become filled with excessive joy upon attaining their lord, whose face was like the nectar of their own desires. (5)
Just as a virtuous wife rejoices upon finding her exceedingly handsome beloved after being long separated from him, so do all creatures rejoice upon finding Him, the infallible Beloved of others.
Having obtained that which is forever inseparable [from them], they are filled with joy;
for just as moths, deluded, rush toward a fire of extreme brilliance when drawn by it.
Likewise, O enchantress, upon beholding the Lord with his limbs fully radiant, they were drawn out and fell,
just as [bees fall] upon seeing the full moon at night.
Just as oceans flow toward the world,
so too do millions of lotuses of living beings run toward the Lord of the Imperishable, who is full and beholds them with favor.
Just as iron, having encountered a magnet, naturally gravitates toward it from all sides,
so too do many people gravitate toward one who is beloved by the world.
By their very nature, they go toward the Child-Hari;
just as rivers flow toward the ocean,
so do their hearts go toward Him who is obtainable at will.
In that same way, the hearts of all creatures went toward Kṛṣṇa from every direction;
for Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was endowed with immeasurable splendor.
He became like the midday sun;
his subjects, possessing exceedingly beautiful forms of pure white, became like blossoming lotuses. (11)
Then that celestial chariot, presided over by Hari,
became a garden of flowers with hundreds of thousands of lotuses,
a grove of various kinds of exquisite blossoms.
Beholding the peak of Mount Mandara, which was reeling from its whirling motion,
Hari then indeed became a flowering tree, beautiful with clusters of blossoms mixed with all kinds of medicinal herbs.
Emerging from the cave of his own mouth, possessing the splendor of being liberated from the syllables,
he was held by Acyuta, joined with the diamond-like Acyuta.
Having spoken of gold, rubies, and excellent pearls,
he shone like the Lord of Day (the Sun), with his preeminent crown upon his own head and his pair of swords positioned as they were. || 14 ||
Possessing a naturally arisen web of countless rays and a halo of splendor surrounding his face on all sides,
he stands like a thousand moons gathered together.
...even extends the memory of their non-difference.
[Her] forehead is broad; she shines with a mark (tilaka) joined by two upward lines like white filaments, produced from the fire of her anger.
He informs the people that the two eyes of the Lord of the Gods— vast, beautiful, and dear— are the two paths leading to the imperishable abode. 16.
In that state, the exceedingly beautiful and most tremulous weight of love,
which showers forth infinite compassion, is understood as having its limbs distinct from Hari. (17)
At that time, Hari’s lips, with their lower edges as red as coral and filled with joyful, gentle smiles,
captivated the hearts of women.
With all their mental states and likewise with their selves,
[they perceived] the two well-rounded, elevated, and charmingly radiant breasts of Hari, touched by the hue of saffron. || 18 ||
Full of bliss, radiant like jewels, soft, even, heart-pleasing, and auspicious—[his two hands];
while his left hand held a cluster of flowers. (19)
Then he became exalted as the bestower of boons;
his right hand, rich with a bow, a banner, a svastika, a trident, a fish, and an arrow, became the giver of fearlessness. (2.187.20)
Adorned with beautiful flower garlands of fresh and varied splendor that grace his broad chest,
and having come into contact with the Kaustubha gem;
They display the face of Fortune upon their chests;
their shoulders are firm, draped with flower garlands, and likewise adorned with beautiful earrings.
With the luster of jewels and a radiance surpassing the sun, they displayed their arms upon the lap of Rādhā;
then [she showed] her abdomen, adorned with divine, beautiful flower garlands—
It reveals to all creatures the chest of Hari, which was previously concealed;
let those joined in devotion ascend my chest by means of the ladder that is the necklace. 23.
His pair of feet, served by countless maidservants, shone like land-lotuses,
constantly bowed down by the streams of people.
He was a bestower of boons to those who offered even a little.
At that time, Hari was the sovereign emperor among kings,
the king among subjects, and the teacher among disciples.
He is the virtuous one among the good, the beloved among women, the giver among the destitute, and the ancient one among poets;
he is the subtle one attained by devotees and by yogis. (25)
He was a charming actor in the dress of a preeminent dancer for those who delight in form;
he was a beloved husband for virtuous women, a Vedic sage for the seers, and a captivating figure desired by all people. (26)
On the path of the stairs, Hari, smiling gently, descended from the shower of flowers rained down by the Lord,
while being honored with handfuls of parched grain by the women of the city and the people.
Having heard the sound of victory and having his desires fulfilled,
he repeatedly pointed out his own previous births and descended from the stairs.
The king spread out soft silken cloths from the Kauśika region as he proceeded with the placement of his feet during the race,
whereupon there appeared a chariot made of beautiful gold.
It possessed a single peak topped with a hundred golden jars;
it was endowed with eight wheels and great speed, and was joined by seven elephants of four cubits in height. (29)
In the center, surrounded on all sides by beautiful celestial women who were offering garlands and whose faces were radiant with smiles; by those most lovely ladies.
Adorned like a flower-decked celestial chariot (puṣpavimāna),
King Pariśānaka quickly led that Lord Hari, together with his family, away.
He caused the Lord of Lords to mount the chariot and seated him upon a golden elephant-throne;
he honored him with various and diverse necklaces.
With fragrant essences and excellent sandalwood, with parched grain and unbroken rice, with cool and sweet-smelling waters,
with golden ornaments and priceless garments. (32)
And the king gave him an excellent *suravāla* garment, as well as a fine silken robe with a border of superior gold;
likewise, he gave him a radiant bodice.
And he gave him an excellent crown, adorned with rows of gems studded with diamonds, complete with its jeweled fillet, which was to be worn by the great sovereigns.
The Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, accepted all the ornaments fashioned of gold;
he drank the water washed from the feet of Śrī Hari.
Accompanied by his own family, Hari placed [the garland] upon the king's head;
and out of his grace, he bestowed upon the king a beautiful garland and a cluster of flowers that foretold his own mercy.
But the people, with bodies fairer than a hundred thousand [lotuses], did they then become Sugatas from the abode of the gods?
Indeed, they possessed the splendor of the moon's luster and were white in color.
With beautiful tawny eyes and slender, tall bodies—
whether they be fair-skinned maidens, women, young girls, or even the elderly— their forms are small and well-concealed. (36)
Wearing identical garments, holding variegated parasols, with disheveled hair and tawny eyes, they were dressed alike and possessed a soft, reddish radiance. (37)

With their feet protected by the very subtle turning of their heels, and with the colors visible on the hems of their garments that were slightly tucked up, the young women— whether already fair-complexioned or becoming fairer— became exceedingly joyful.
At that time, great kettledrums resounded, along with cymbals, lutes,
and the sounds of flutes.
Likewise, there were lutes, bards, and musical instruments;
indeed, shouts of victory arose on all sides,
along with many proclamations of his glorious qualities.
Then, even the songs and hymns of praise became blended with the voices of a thousand throats;
they were produced by thousands of mechanical bandhukī birds.
The sounds produced by the bursting of the balls were auspicious and pleasant to the ear; they attained the resonance of *oṃ* and awakened the consciousness of the Supreme Lord. (41)
Great roars produced by the vast armies and sounds of exultation went forth toward Kakutstha;
there were the trumpeting of elephants and the neighing of horses.
Those traveling toward the Brahma-world dispersed in the intermediate directions;
hundreds and thousands of vehicles, equal to celestial chariots, quickly followed the elephant-drawn conveyance.
Accompanied by those devoted to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa,
they proceeded slowly, all equally adorned with excellent flags, banners, umbrellas, and other ornaments. ||43||
The chariots, yoked with great sages, shone brilliantly with numerous jars having golden horns and with celestial, most divine arched gateways. 44.
With radiant halos, supreme in color, beloved by Brahmā, and possessing beautiful golden complexions,
they shine resplendently in their golden vehicles.
They lead one to the notion that Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are [separate].
Then those people— both men and women— who have beheld Him, indeed became bewildered regarding Hari.
Then, indeed, a female horse-rider, extending for a *yojana*, [beheld] that Gopāla boy, the son of Aṃbhareya, who was exceedingly beautiful with limbs proportionate to his form. ||46||
It was crowded with the crushing throngs of living beings, and filled with many elephants, horses, female elephants, and bulls;
with swans, Prageṇḍas, Garuḍas, and Gaveyakas. (47)
By means of excellent chariots, celestial palaces, and horse-drawn carriages,
by those who approached on foot with tearful eyes,
and by virtuous kings and princes, the subjects—
By all the people residing in the city;
by the sages, the true gurus, the Sāṃkhya-yogins, the devoted wives, and those in the highest stages of life (āśramas), etc. [48].
Accompanied by the sons of Gaṅgā, the Raudra-gaṇas, and others, as well as the cavalry, the army indeed shone resplendent;
having heard and understood this while staying within the city.
Even the most elegant women, having abandoned all their duties with great haste, go out from their houses to see Hari, the Lord of lords. (2.187.50)
Their minds intensely eager for that sight,
they formed a dense line at the edge of the main road,
their bodies pressed against one another.
They gazed with uplifted eyes;
for even though they stood on the road at a great distance,
they heard the loud sound of musical instruments.
With their eyes fixed upon the arrival of Hari, they stood with uplifted hands joined in reverence and bowed down;
[he was honored] with a golden parasol, beautiful whisks, and other [regalia]. || 52 ||
Resplendent with the emblems of imperial sovereignty,
he beheld the city, which possessed wonderful and abundant beauty, was well-maintained, and was filled with all delights. ||53||
With fragrant waters and the ichor of elephants,
the main roads and crossroads were sprinkled;
and with auspicious golden jars and plantain trees—
The pillars were beautifully adorned with leaves of mango and other trees;
there were flower-offerings and *akṣata* grains, as well as artificial gateways and very high, formidable, and excellent main gates.
It was exceedingly beautiful with lofty mansions and multi-storied palaces accompanied by garden sections,
and with flowering creepers in every house. (55)
It was also endowed with fragrant, budding trees,
and with garden plots rich in grain, which were abundant with clusters of flowers whose roots reached down into the ponds.
There were lakes, a central excellent clothed ground, a park ground, a monastic ground,
a ground for exposition, and a ground for dancers and the like.
And it was endowed with theaters for entertainment,
with schools of arts that were endless,
and with desired medical clinics.
It was exceedingly well-endowed with refectories for juices from Avanti, with halls for the True Dharma,
and with schools for the sciences from Anūpaka.

It possessed a beauty delightful with music halls; it was filled with cherished joy by assembly halls for the virtuous; and it resounded incessantly with the noise of workshops for machines and the like. (99)

By those skilled in the piercing of constellations, those skilled in the piercing of clouds, those skilled in the piercing of the ocean, those skilled in the piercing of planets, those skilled in the piercing of foreign lands, and those skilled in the piercing of the [proper] time—
[She was] accompanied by those who pierce with wind and those who pierce with the true essence,
by those who pierce with heat and those who pierce with coolness, and equipped with the mechanism of the water-clock (ghaṭī-vedhaka-yanttra).
By means of lightning-piercings, mercury-piercings,
and piercings of the vowels and so forth, as well as piercings that demonstrate [the goal]; by means of piercings with vehicles and piercings with carts.

He beheld that city, which was exceedingly beautiful and possessed of a foundation of consciousness, together with its piercing mountain peaks, its piercing fissures in the earth, and its piercing depths within the waters. (62)
Constantly resounding with the sounds of throngs of celestial chariots, filled with beautiful women gathered all around,
its lofty and magnificent halls seem to kiss the very limits of the sky.
And he beheld that other city,
adorned with agallochum incense, lamps, banners, and flags, and filled with all desirable things.
With water-channels and reed-pipes, with wide nets that attract [beasts] by their own sound,
and with far-reaching star-lamps.
In various places,
the Blessed One beheld the city named Parīśā, which was adorned with celestial damsels’ mansions and possessed a mind-stealing splendor.
As he entered that [palace], his limbs were most enchanting,
resembling the full moon and rich with fresh youth;
[he was attended] by a golden parasol and two chowries.
And the subjects beheld him thus honored;
then, having ascended their palaces, the women, abandoning all other activities, looked on with agitation.
With their garments and ornaments disarrayed, they gazed through the windows with steady eyes at that most beloved one;
on every terrace, they stood upon the balconies of the mansions.
Nourished by circles of women with unbroken grains, flowers, and sandalwood paste, the Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign of Lords,
accepted that which was offered from the hearts of those women.
Likewise, at that time, the merchants, casting their eyes upon the tip of the marketplace, paid him honor and reverence with offerings of fresh fruits,
dried fruits, and seeds.
Then the Brahmins honored him with their desired mudrās, garments, and so forth, as well as with unbroken grains, sandalwood paste,
flowers, necklaces, salutations, and other such offerings.
They made her auspicious with Vedic mantras and joyfully sang the Sāman hymns aloud;
and groups of wealthy men [honored her] with gifts of riches.
The poor people offered him mental gifts,
and the devotees then performed a welcoming ceremony for Hari by offering their devotion. || 71 ||
The king, accompanied by his army, caused the Lord to wander all around the city, as far as its outer limits;
and upon merely beholding the city, Hari [issued] his command.
He offered praise for the city of Pariśāna in the king’s palace,
in the hut of the great sage, and in the mansions of the leading merchants and others.
(72) In the king’s palace, in the hut of the great sage, and in the residences of the chief merchants and so forth—
Having made the earth exceedingly pure with his two feet, Kṛṣṇa established the city as a place of excellent holy sites;
thus, after wandering about, he performed his return.
The king of kings, having arrived at the royal palace and descended from his vehicle, entered the palace for the sake of his desired peace. ||74||
He drank water, attained peace for a moment,
and then entered the assembly hall where a high throne had been prepared for the king.
Then Acyuta shone resplendently; thereafter,
the Lord of the high and the low, whose purpose is the preservation and upliftment of the world, gave instruction to the people, beginning with the kings.
All the subjects sat silent,
their minds fixed on Rādhā like cakora birds longing for the moon; they held their mental faculties and the functions of their senses upon Hari.
O beloved of all, who bestows splendor upon Your own devotees;
O showerer of nectar, whose conduct is ever virtuous; O beloved of Your own Self, dear consort of Kṛṣṇa. (77)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Crowding of the People, the Splendor of Hari, His Mounting of the Elephant, the Attraction of the People, His Wandering through the City of Parīśāna, and His Arrival at the Royal Palace," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 187. [End of] Section 2 (Tretā-yuga-santāna), Chapter 188.
[Author: Chapter 189.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa gave instruction to the assembly.
I shall relate to you that which occurred in the city of Parīśāna.
Hari said: "In this cycle of existence, death is indeed certain;
for the body is transitory, the vital breaths are transitory, and riches are transitory. (1–2)
All unions are transitory, and even the entire universe is transitory;
for all beings are indeed transitory, yet the Self shall go elsewhere.
One of perfected intellect will not again encounter such a transitory state.
For eternal liberation is indeed to be attained by one who is himself steadfast;
[thus] the king, worthy of honor from the foremost of rulers as well as from gods and great seers, was strengthened by words of auspiciousness and joined with blessings. (4–5)
And Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, was a great devotee of the Lord;
for the gods, led by Bṛhaspati and including Indra and Varuṇa,
as well as the creators of the universe, came to the sacrifice of that high-souled king.
While he ruled the earth, crops ripened even without being ploughed.
(7) At his sacrifice, the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly, the Maruts were the servers, and the Sādhyas, who are likewise virtuous, were present. (8)
At that time, I was the embodied enjoyer in the sacrificial fire;
having made his kingdom devoted to me and having made himself intent upon me, he went to my imperishable abode. Thus should it be done by kings here on earth.
There was a king named Suhotra who was likewise a devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata).
During his reign, Maghavan rained gold for an entire year;
the earth was true to its name as it became "Vasumatī" (possessing wealth), and the rivers flowed with gold at that time.
Indra rained down crocodiles, tortoises, and various aquatic creatures made of gold; the Emperor presented them all to the Brahmins.
"I am Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa," he said, "and he [the Emperor] placed me within every vessel. || 11 ||
Having performed excellent sacrifices, he became a guest and went to my supreme abode.
King Bṛhadratha of Aṅga was indeed a great devotee of the Lord;
he gave away a thousand times a thousand white horses as gifts.
And a thousand times a thousand maidens adorned with gold,
and a thousand times a thousand elephants of the finest breed,
and a hundred times a hundred thousand bulls adorned with golden garlands.

He gave thousands of gold *niṣkas* as a counterweight for the sacrificial fee (*pratimānavam*) while performing the seven *soma*-concluding rites of the extensive sacrifice; he bestowed such fees even upon mendicant Brahmins. (16–17)

Having made me well-pleased and having worshiped me in the sacrifice, the king became a great devotee of the Lord and, at the end, went to my abode. And Śibi, the king of Auśīnara, became a great devotee of the Lord.
He who covered this entire earth with gold—
whatever cattle, horses, elephants, and gayals existed upon it—
he gave all of that away in charity, which was thus multiplied by countless virtues.
Having attained serenity here and become a great devotee of the Lord,
Śibi worshipped me and went to my eternal, imperishable abode.
Bhagīratha brought down the Gaṅgā for the sake of delivering his ancestors.
Having become the Great Lord, he went to my imperishable abode.
Dilīpa performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice for my gratification;
he bestowed as a sacrificial fee a thousand golden elephants.
Upon that golden sacrificial post, which had a golden *caṣāla* pinnacle,
sixty thousand celestial Gandharvas danced in seven groups.
Having propitiated me, the Supreme Brahman, through devotion and service to the virtuous, he [attained his goal].
He went to my imperishable, eternal abode, which is free from rebirth.
Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, became a great king and a devotee of the Lord;
Indra himself was his nourisher, and he ruled over the entire earth.
He performed a hundred horse sacrifices and likewise a hundred *rājasūya* sacrifices;
he also gave golden rohita fish to the brāhmaṇas.
Having satisfied me with these sacrifices, he rendered his devotion to me even greater.
He attained my imperishable abode and became forever one who has fulfilled his purpose.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was also devoted to me;
having caused a reservoir to be constructed by throwing a clod of earth, he indeed worshipped me there.
He performed a thousand sacrifices as well as a hundred Vājapeyas;
he gave as gifts three most excellent golden mountains dedicated to me.
Having gone to the forest and propitiated me, Kṛṣṇa, he attained the imperishable state.
And Ambarīṣa Nābhāga became a great devotee of the Lord;
he, while performing a thousand times a thousand sacrifices with ten thousand officiating priests,
offered everything in sacrifice unto Me as the sacrificial altar was spread out.
The Sudarśana discus was entrusted by me for his protection;
having propitiated me, the Supreme Lord, he attained the imperishable abode at the end.
And Śaśabindu became a great devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
Having given away his kingdom and all his possessions at a sacrifice, he departed for the forest.
Having propitiated me, he went to my eternal and stable abode.
King Gaya became preeminent, a most fortunate and pure devotee of the Lord.
For a hundred years, that king subsisted on the remnants of sacrificial offerings.
Agni, being pleased, granted him a boon in the form of devotion to Hari.
He performed the horse sacrifice for a thousand years.
Having fashioned the earth out of gold, he bestowed it as a gift upon the twice-born. He gave away as many cows as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
and having propitiated me, at the end of his life, he went to my imperishable state.
King Rantideva was a great devotee of the Lord;
upon seeing me as a guest, he gave water even to a Puṣkasa.
In his house, thousands of millions of crores of twice-born brahmins used to eat.
Having propitiated me, he attained my abode, the imperishable state.
And the king named Sagara, having performed a thousand horse-sacrifices and having given away all his possessions, worshipped me and went to the imperishable realm.
Pṛthu was myself in person; having performed my worship, he entered into my very form. Let the kings do likewise.
So too were the royal sage Rukmāṅgada and his son Dharmāṅgada.
Having propitiated me, they both went to my supreme, imperishable abode.
In the house of Rukmāṅgada, the enchanting daughter of the Creator became his beloved wife;
she who was the wife is called Tithi by the Creator.

King Sudyumna, having meditated upon me as Nārāyaṇa, attained my eternal and imperishable abode through devotion; indeed, he was my very progeny. King Indradyumna became a sovereign among the devotees of Puruṣottama.
Having propitiated me, he went indeed to my eternal, imperishable abode.
Puṇḍarīka became a king and a great devotee of mine;
through devotion, he attained my eternal, imperishable abode, the supreme station.
Prahlāda, Bali, Bāṇa, and the kings dwelling in Pātāla—
though they are Kṣatriyas, they satisfy me day and night through their devotion.
So too do the great king Udayana and Raṇaṅgama.
Citraketu, Nanda, Kanthādhara, Bhadrāśva, Lakṣmaṇa, Mucukunda, Viśāla, Prajāpāla, Durjaya, and Aśvaśiras— these are my devotees (bhāgavatas). 2.188.50.
Camatkāra, Satyasandha, Amitrajit, King Kalaśa,
Puṇyanidhi, Suyaśas, as well as the king of Pañcāla;
Alarka, Toṇḍamān, Nābhi, and likewise Ṛtadhvaja.
Ranti, Vedaśravas, and also Nandasāvarṇi; Nimidhruva, as well as Dharmadhvaja, Kuśadhvaja,
Dṛḍhadhanvan, Divodāsa, Ānarta, Raivata, and others.
These and many other kings who were devoted to Viṣṇu,
having attained my state which is so difficult to reach, have indeed become fully perfected.
Together with their subjects, many of them went there to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
The duty of kings is the protection of their subjects, accompanied by devotion to Hari.
The duty of subjects is the obedience to the king's commands, accompanied by devotion to Hari.
Thus, those who desire righteousness should provide mutual assistance to one another. (55–56)
By the mere succession of my remembrance, they shall be awakened as partakers of liberation.
For the person appointed by me performs both the good and the evil;
he himself should be a stream of goodness, and not a stream of evil.
Having reflected through the vision of knowledge, one should perform only what is right and nothing else.
(58) In all actions, goodness consists in dedication to Me; this is My view.
That which is dedicated to Me is good, but that which is otherwise is not good at all. (59)
One should not commit an act that harms others, nor ever be intent on causing distress; one should not do what leads to one's own ruin, nor should one do what is censured by the world.
A wise person should conduct themselves in this manner, having indeed cast everything upon me.
Then, having attained supreme peace, one should abide in the end, in the imperishable Supreme.
Men and women are bound by action; indeed, they do not become free from action.
Even that innate activity should be cast into the Lord, who consists of "I."
Just as wood, whether dry, wet, or otherwise, when thrown into fire,
becomes ashes either quickly or after a long time— of this there is no doubt—
so too should one cast one’s action, whether auspicious or otherwise, into Me, the Supreme Lord.
"I am capable of reducing [the world] to ashes, and I can even liberate one from the bondage of karma.
Or else, because of the undertaking of that [action], one would obtain the fruit of the karma;
for this reason—that one might obtain it—one should offer [the action] to me, the Lord. (64–65)
Nevertheless, the person, possessing ego through the functioning of ignorance, is the agent of both auspicious and inauspicious actions, and he becomes the enjoyer of their fruits as well.
Indeed, everything is bound together in sequence by the very thread of karma.
That which has been cast upon me—the consequence of the qualities of pleasure and pain—falls away.
For he who, at the commencement of an action, becomes permeated by that state, would be overcome by it; but when [the mind] is set on me, one is not overcome.
Consequently, all impurity is completed within me alone;
for that, there is no expiation, nor does any [karmic] experience exist for it.
By failing to perform prescribed action and likewise by performing what is forbidden—
A person who fails to offer [the fruits of action] unto Me incurs the need for atonement.
(2.188.70) A man should never perform forbidden acts; for indeed, [such acts consist of] the abandonment of one's own duty and the following of the duty of another. (71)
A youth who is beloved by women should never abandon one who has sought refuge, nor the ornaments and such belonging to a servant;
he should not seize the property of others, nor engage in disputes with his father;
and he should never forsake his wife.
A wife, even if young, should never abandon her husband.
It is held that one should always provide for those who depend on them;
one should serve the elderly and offer assistance to the distressed.
One should never speak untruth, nor harsh words filled with deceit;
one should never commit violence against living beings, but remain devoted to compassion.
One should provide for those who depend on one and for animals by warding off their hunger and thirst.
One should perform service for others and always feed the virtuous;
one should practice service to the virtuous and service to me at all times.
One should make oneself happy and never lead oneself into agitation.
One should never, anywhere, cause distress to others through idle talk, falsehoods, lies, and the like.
One should constantly perform the congregational chanting of Hari’s names with both speech and heart.
One should always practice meditation on Hari, which bestows liberation and destroys all sins.
One should perform auspicious deeds and desist from those that are inauspicious.
One should constantly give wealth and other gifts; by this, one is liberated from sin.
The conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭācāra*), applied according to place, time, and other factors, is the supreme dharma. (2.188.80)
He alone should be served here by one who desires happiness both in this world and after death.
One should perform recitation (*japa*) in a sacred place of the gods, as well as fire-offerings (*homa*), fasting, and so forth.
One should seek the vision of the Divine, which is knowledge that effects the purification of the self.
A wise person who is subject to the law of death should never be arrogant.
Having worshipped the gods, the sages, humans, the ancestors, the domestic deities, and Hari as well, the householder is then fit to eat. (82–83)
Acting thus, the king, the subjects, the virtuous, women, the distressed, and the common folk shall all be entirely unstained;
let them always do so by constantly uttering my name and remembering me for even a moment in every situation. (84)
Performing all actions while surrendering them to Me, one is not tainted.
Likewise, let them always act while remembering Me and offering everything to Me;
I shall liberate all those who are Mine—my Vaiṣṇavas who have taken refuge in Me.
May there be well-being for you kings and royal consorts,
for the subjects and their lords, and especially for the wretched;
may there be well-being for the women who have performed deeds for my sake.
"May there always be well-being, and may Hari grant you peace.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
then remained silent for a moment in the assembly of the learned.
The king performed worship with countless pearls and diamonds,
with necklaces and other ornaments, garments and the like, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood.
The queen and the princesses performed a grand *ārātrika* ceremony.
The princes, the leaders, and the subjects also performed salutations and hymns of praise, and they ate the food granted by Hari’s grace; thereafter, the princesses likewise did so. (9.1–9.2)
Then twenty-one young women of charming minds took the hand of Hari according to the marriage rite.
Immediately after the taking of the hands, the king quickly [performed] a great festival at night.
Having fed his honored guests, including Hari and others who had arrived as visitors,
he caused them to enjoy delightful performances such as dance, song, and the fine arts.
At night, all the guests obtained the highest rest.
The maidens, however, served their new beloved with great devotion.
Rising in the morning, the Blessed One performed his own meditation.
The king also arrived and, for the sake of worshipping Kṛṣṇa, he worshipped Him.
Thus, O Rādhā, that great festival of the Supreme Lord took place.
Then, in the city of Parīśāna, the subjects presented gifts;
and King Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa accepted those farewell offerings at that time.
He caused all [the people] to perform the drinking of milk and other rites with devotion;
Lomaśa, moreover, gave the *tāraka* mantra to the subjects.
Then Hari became ready to go to Mount Parīkṣa.
King Indurāya made a persistent request of him.
Then, at the king's command, musical instruments were sounded as Hari ascended his celestial chariot; others likewise ascended their own chariots there.
They traveled by way of the sky to the kingdom of Indurāya. Hari beheld the earth covered with mountains.
And Indurāya, accompanied by his family, went forward to welcome them.
Then, the sounds of the trumpets of honor resounded on all sides.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Instruction upon Parīśāna, Prajā, and Others; Their Worship; and the Arrival in the Morning on the Seventh Day in the Kingdom of Parījara by Means of Celestial Chariots," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 188.
Chapter 189 [Author:
Chapter 190 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari gazed all around at the splendor produced by the trees from the very garments [he wore],
as well as at the auspicious city named Vāyunā situated to its west.
Having observed the people gathered there for the sake of a vision,
[he saw] the king standing before him to offer a welcome; then, by the path shown by the monarch, he caused the celestial chariot to descend.

Then, all the celestial chariots descended from the sky into that most beautiful garden, which was like a forest situated before the royal palace. Bālakṛṣṇa stepped down from his own chariot and proceeded toward his own courtyard.
The king gave necklaces made of fine gold to Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
he also then offered a welcome to the others as was appropriate.
Upon hearing the sound, Hari then became filled with joy.
Having crossed over, he then found rest in the royal palace;
having washed his feet, the king and others drank the nectar of his feet.
The monarch then fed him with various kinds of sweet foods and other delicacies.
He devoutly fed the great king, his family members and others, the great sages, the wives of the Brahmins, and all other distinguished guests. Then, at midday, Hari obtained rest.

King Suśṛṅgāri said to Hari: "O Lord, for the sake of granting me an audience, I desire to wander with my great army through your city, Vāyūnāyā. || 2.189.10 || "O Master, I wish to travel about together with my forces."
"So be it," Hari said, and he sat upon a most splendid elephant-throne. Then Ambālikā and Kāñcanī sat down, and after that, the others sat upon their respective appropriate mounts.
Various musical instruments were played beautifully,
and the sounds of bursting mechanical devices as well as those that bestow honor resounded then.
Women with fair complexions brought milk for Hari-Kṛṣṇa in their own courtyards and other places.
They caused the Lord of Īśā to prosper with parched grain, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
They presented fruits and other gifts, worshipped him, and gazed upon him for a long time;
at that time, those subjects considered themselves to have fulfilled their life's purpose.
Having thus wandered through the city, Hari went to the royal palace.
The king and queen performed a great worship with many articles:
golden vessels, silver ones, coins, diamonds, and so forth.
He presented royal gifts, including garments and ornaments, to Śrī Hari.
Then, by the command of the queen, the two lovely maidens beheld Hari and joyfully took the hand of Bālakṛṣṇa.
There, the festival proceeded perfectly according to the rites of marriage.
Out of compassion, the king beheld his son-in-law as four-armed,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with a countenance full of mercy.
Though situated on a mountain, he praised Him who is without joints with supreme affection:
"You are devoid of the joint of ignorance and are free from the qualities of Māyā. Protect me from the states of composite existence and lead me to Your imperishable abode. (2.189.20–21)
The Supreme Brahman, Bālakṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, is without beginning or end;
you are Harikṛṣṇa, you are Bhava, you are Nara, and you are Nārāyaṇa.
The ṛṣis, the ancestors, the perfected beings, the gods, the gandharvas, and the dānavas— [all these are you].
The serpents, rākṣasas, and yakṣas do not know him in truth;
nor do the yogins, the virtuous, the truthful, the wise, and the lords of ascetics know this Lord of Gods— how then could they know, "This is the Blessed One"?
Therefore, let there be my salutation to You; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
To You, in whom the birth, growth, and destruction of all beings reside—salutations again and again!
O Soul of the Universe, O Soul of Viśvakarman, O You who possess the eye and other faculties of Viśvakarman!
Bestowing even upon actions the state of actionlessness, do you protect me from the ocean.
I bow to the Supreme Lord, the thousand-rayed Viṣṇu, the sovereign whose eyes are everywhere, and whose hands, feet, and other limbs are infinite.

I bow to You, the Supreme Lord, who are Hari—the subtlest of the subtle, the greatest of the great, and eternally present even within the vast; the most venerable, the most excellent, and the highest of all.
You are beyond the actions of the elements and the like, and remain outside the range of the intellect, the senses, and other such faculties.
I bow to you, the ancient Person, the Brahman, the Supreme Lord;
I bow to you, the treasure-house of the universe, the self-born, the eternal Lord of the world, the Lord of all, the golden-hued Supreme Lord. (2.189.29–30)
Salutations to You who shine even for the sake of coolness and illumination;
salutations to You who are the primordial sound (*svara*), the reality of all meanings, and whose form is song.
You are the *oṃkāra*, you are the descent (*avatāra*), you are the manifestation (*vyūha*), and you are the four-armed one.
You are the Infinite, you are Mahāviṣṇu, and you are Virāṭ whose abode is the lotus.
You are action, the instrument, the agent, as well as the deed and the causal factor. You are the seer, the witness, the Great Time, and the devourer; salutations to you.
Salutations to You who possess all forms, who are peaceful, and who are the son of Kambharī; salutations to You, Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and the son of Gopālā;
salutations to the one who pacifies all sins and removes all suffering.
Salutations to the Inner Controller of all, who is the form of the soul’s provisions for the journey.
My home has been purified by you, O Lord, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
and my family, submerged [in suffering], has been uplifted by you through taking hold of me.
"Salutations to You in all worlds, and salutations to You in all souls!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Mahākṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇeśvara, let there be obeisance to You!
Having spoken thus, King Indurāja offered his salutations to Rādhikā.
The beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa spoke these auspicious words to him:
"O King, having observed your supreme and steadfast devotion toward Me,
I have here revealed a small portion of My divine form to you."
When he took the hands of these two maidens of mine, a doubt arose in your minds: "Who indeed is this, and how could it be so?
Out of compassion, he has shown himself to me in order to dispel that doubt.
"Always meditate upon this four-armed form of yours within your heart.
Having spoken thus, he withdrew his form and became a human being once more.
The king fell at his feet, and [the sage] placed his feet upon the king's heart.
With tears in his eyes, he also entreated him, saying, "Please grant me forgiveness.
The entire world belongs to you alone; what then is the value of these two girls?
Having spoken thus according to the prescribed rites, the king then celebrated a great festival.
He fed them all and honored them with sincere devotion. Hari also instructed him:
"O King, everything that is performed as action results in either prosperity or misfortune."
But that action, when directed toward me, transcends [ordinary results], for it accomplishes one's own desired ends.
Such action, having me as its object and support, would otherwise yield a different fruit.
[This includes] the worship of deities, the twice-born, teachers, and the virtuous.
It indeed brings about freedom from debt and likewise honors one's parents.
For kings, their duty is exertion; through that, the divine is produced.
When both arise together, they bestow prosperity as well as liberation.
Human effort is the first task; thereafter, one should rely upon destiny.
Without undertaking an enterprise or exerting effort, one will never be a partaker of the fruit.
And when both human effort and destiny are attained through truth, [success is certain].
That bestows certain success and brings happiness both in this world and after death.
A person rich in virtuous conduct, self-restraint, and gentleness shall be attended by prosperity.
One should contemplate the Supreme Brahman as the cause of one's own happiness.
One should never destroy the cause, for by destroying it, one destroys oneself.
Just as fire arises from water, a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa, and a clod of earth from a stone—
if that which has arisen goes to destroy its own cause, it perishes.
The self, knowledge, action, and karma arise before Hari.
(5.3) If one does not worship Hari, he is a destroyer of the self and becomes a slayer of Hari;
for one intent on harming Kṛṣṇa, destruction shall occur like fire. (5.4)
Therefore, I must always be protected, sustained, and honored with devotion;
I must be remembered and worshipped, for I shall grant liberation from bondage.
Those seeking liberation should avoid worldly vices in vain.

Addiction, eating, drinking, sleeping, jesting, and constant attachment to pleasure— when these exceed what is required by necessity and are directed toward me, they are not called addictions at all. (56–57)
That vice which is merely for the sake of subsistence is not called a calamity;
however, gambling and the like, being both improper and useless, are considered true misfortunes.
Indeed, such misfortunes are the constant abode of suffering and grief.
Where that [desire] exists, how could a human being find his own true happiness?
Therefore, having reflected upon its worthlessness, one should abandon that which is inherently corrupting.
If subjects were to conduct themselves in this manner, they would indeed follow the excellent path.
Then Dharma shall prevail there, endowed with devotion and faith;
and wherever Dharma is, there I dwell perpetually.
Whether manifest or within the heart, I protect my own dependents.
"I protect the ignorant like a mother; I shall protect him who is endowed with virtue.
Therefore, let all subjects and others devoted to dharma worship me.
I shall deliver them from the ocean of desire; of this there is no doubt. (62–63)
"Let them install my image here for the sake of constant vision.
Today I shall go to bathe in the auspicious waters of Indirā.
May it be well with you; may there always be happiness and health free from ailment."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa then rose from his seat.
The king quickly prepared all the vehicles, including those that travel through the sky, and granted him leave to depart.
Having bathed in the great river Indirā, Hari resolved with certainty that he must indeed go to Supānarāṣṭraka by evening;
having prepared himself, he ascended the celestial chariot, as did the others.
Having ascended their vehicles and celestial chariots, they remained in the sky.
The king, the queen, the family, and the subjects begged for forgiveness.
Then there were the sounds of musical instruments for the departure, as well as songs.
Then shouts of victory, cries of joy, and exclamations of "Live long!
arose, along with King Mudrāṇḍa and King Supāna-muni.
Requested by Sahasta, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa went before them.
Honored by multitudes of people with joined palms, he proceeded to the bank of the Indirā.
Then, having descended from his vehicle at that vast location, Hari bathed;
likewise, everyone else bathed, for that place had indeed become a sacred ford (tīrtha).
There, the Blessed Lord Śrī gave a fine drink to the sage;
at that time, the devotees drank the nectar-like water used for Hari’s bath.
Wherever Hari had bathed, there many vetālas appeared.
All those who had performed evil deeds in their previous lives indeed met with misfortune there.
Though they were fair-complexioned, they all arrived bereft of luster; suffering in human form, they reported their miserable fate.

Formerly, we were violent plunderers, wicked men devoid of compassion, thieves who oppressed the subjects; now, through our own sins, we have died here, tormented by cold gale-force winds and afflicted by hunger and thirst. (76)
"Vetālakas have been born here, and we dwell upon the riverbank.
O Lord of Gods, grant us deliverance; we have come to you for refuge.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [took] the water of immortality.
He gave it to them for the purpose of drinking; they, freed from sin, drank it.
At that very moment, having acquired merit, they became divine-bodied like the gods.
They became gods and goddesses, worthy of heaven, with auspicious limbs.
The compassionate Blessed One said to the high-souled Lomaśa:
"Bring Manu here; thereafter they shall become Vaiṣṇavas.
Lomaśa quickly caused them to hear the mantra of Hari.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
Having heard this mantra, those Vaiṣṇavas, possessing divine forms, offered their salutations.
Then Hari spoke to Īśānadeva and to these who had taken refuge in him.
"O Śambhu, send them to Kailāsa; let them be your attendants there.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara quickly sent them all—Hari and all the people—from there to the realm of Kailāsa through the sky.
Having ascended their celestial chariots, they arrived at the kingdom of Supāna,
in the auspicious city of Madriṭa on the bank of the river known as Dūra—
a vast place with hundreds of thousands of halls and many gardens on all sides. (85)
In that city, which was as prosperous as heaven, they beheld the splendor of the sky.
Indeed, the city shone brilliantly, adorned in many ways and sprinkled with fragrant waters, with its excellent archways and gate-towers. (86–87)
Then, by the king's command, the army rested on the riverbank in a great garden for the evening, in order to welcome Nārāyaṇa with satisfaction.
Thereafter, the king brought down his own celestial chariot from the sky.
The seers, the king, and the subjects also stood before him for the sake of welcoming him.
Then musical instruments were sounded, and cries of "Victory! arose from there. There were the sounds of machines, the shouts of the people, and the sounds of conch shells. (2.189.90)
Following the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari brought his own celestial chariot down into the great garden near the royal palace.
At that time, other celestial chariots as well descended from the sky.
Then the subjects, the king, and others greatly honored Rādhikā with shouts of joy, parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings;
they raised cries of "Victory! to the countless presiding deities of the principles (tattvas).

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship and Feeding of Hari in the Palace in the Kingdom of Indurāya, the Wandering through the City of Vāyūnāna, the Instruction, the Farewell on the Seventh Day at Sunset, the Bathing in the Indirā River, the Resuscitation of the Vetāla, and the Arrival in the Kingdom of Mudrāṇḍarāja," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
(Chapter 189, *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2: The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Chapter 191 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: at that time in the month of Mādhava, King Mudrāṇḍa offered flower garlands and golden necklaces and worshipped Hari. Then he donned the most splendid royal attire for Hari.
He endeavored to take Madriṭā on a tour that evening.
There, the lion among kings honored all the dignitaries;
and Supānarṣi applied the *tilaka* and *candraka* marks upon Hari.
Afterwards, the king gave water to drink and settled all the mounts upon their vehicles;
he then caused auspicious musical instruments to resound.
Hari [mounted] a new, bright chariot covered with blankets and deerskins.
He was yoked with sixteen white bulls, possessing the marks of divine beings;
likewise, with one great, foremost, and white bull.
Being praised by bards and honored by the great seers, [he proceeded].
He ascended a chariot resplendent with gold, gems, and pearls;
Maudgalya held the reins, while the prince Trigartta held the goad;
and Gavādana the sage held the parasol.
A large white parasol was held over the middle of the chariot;
it shone like the moon accompanied by stars because of its beautiful ribs.
Two sages joyfully took up the fly-whisks for him.

O Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa’s parents, his brothers, and likewise his sister— those two great ascetics Supāṇarṣi and Mitramaharṣi— are endowed with a luster equal to the rays of the moon and are exceedingly long and beautiful.
Then all those who were like gods were seen stationed upon chariots.
Having mounted a brilliant chariot yoked with the finest horses,
Rudra, the Lord, attended by his hosts, followed behind.
Having mounted an excellent golden chariot yoked with very large horses,
the preceptor Lomaśa himself followed Rudra;
both Vṛkāyana and Nīlakaṇa followed on a yellow chariot.
Then Yayāti, indeed, set out with horses of blue hue yoked to his chariot;
thereafter, all the beloved wives of Brahmā, adorned with beautiful ornaments, proceeded by the thousands in human-drawn carriages and various other vehicles of diverse kinds.
All the sages of the Ganges, as well as others, including maidens,
princesses, and queens, followed on splendid chariots and other vehicles.
Then there were many chariots, elephants, and [mounts] accompanied by camels and bulls.
The foot soldiers followed behind, mounted on horses.
Then the bards, heralds, genealogists, and panegyrists likewise went along with the subjects, singing well-composed verses.
Then, however, there occurred an incomparable vision of Viṣṇu, an unsurpassed sight on earth of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
as Hari entered Madriṭā by the city-dwellers. (19)
The city’s royal highways and other thoroughfares were adorned in many ways;
the earth was graced with white garlands and banners,
while the royal roads were refined and thoroughly perfumed with incense.
Likewise, the city was made beautiful by fragrant powders, various flowers, priyaṅgu blossoms, and closely interwoven garlands of flowers; auspicious,
new jars filled with water were placed at every door.
White and pale-colored flowers were strewn here and there;
the gates were likewise adorned with decorative patterns of colored powders. And so, he entered the city that had been thus beautifully decorated.
At the time of Hari’s entry there, thousands upon thousands of city-dwellers gathered, desiring to behold him.
The royal highway, with its squares beautifully adorned, shone most brilliantly.
Just as the ocean rises at the rising of the moon due to the successive arrival of the tides,
so too did an inconceivable increase of people occur on the royal highways.
All the houses along those royal roads were entirely adorned with jewels.
The full breasts of the fair women seemed to tremble under their weight;
those women praised the son of Kambharā, the Lord of Śrī.
"Blessed are these beloveds of Brahmā who have obtained Puruṣottama."
Likewise, the women praised the vow-observances of the fair-complexioned girls.
O Rādhikā, with their words of praise, expressions of affection, shouts of victory, and hymns of glorification, the city resounded. (2.190.30)
At every street, at every crossroads,
at every square, at every marketplace, and at every palace, the subjects worshipped the Lord. Then, having wandered through the city along the royal highway, Hari—
Adorned and radiant, he approached the royal palace.
There, all the subjects—both citizens and those from the countryside—spoke words pleasant to the ear: "By good fortune you have arrived, O Mādhava! (32–33)
"Your grace and the sight of you here are considered auspicious;
otherwise, O Kṛṣṇa, how could there be a vision of you without such fortune?
Thus, at the gate of the royal palace, he was gratified on all sides with auspicious rites.
Having descended from his vehicle, Hari entered the royal palace (35).
The king, the great sages, the queen,
and the princesses honored the beloved of Kṛṣṇa with perfumes, garlands, and necklaces of jewels (36).
With *sumana* flowers, sweetmeats, jewels, and abundant gold, with various kinds of offerings and diverse gifts according to their desires—
having recognized the right moment there, they fell under the power of the noose of delusion.
The fifteen princesses took the hand of Hari.
Then there arose the proclamation of a holy day (*puṇyāha*) and the chanting of His names,
which brought joy to their friends and was meritorious and pleasing to the ear.
Likewise, the sound of kettledrums and the delightful blare of conch shells arose,
along with the auspicious voices of those proclaiming victory.
Hearing this, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was then filled with a joyful heart.
He sat upon a supreme throne within the royal palace made of gold.
In the assembly, he instructed the king in many ways regarding his duties:
"If a king should become addicted to vices, he is held in contempt by the people. (41-42)
He who causes distress to the world hates it and finds no happiness;
therefore, having abandoned his own personal likes, he should practice what is for the welfare of the world.
A king who brings about the welfare of the world must never abandon steadfastness under any circumstances.
Indeed, excessive joking should not be practiced by the king with his servants.
For, out of rivalry, those who live off the king may treat him with contempt;
they do not remain in their proper place and even transgress his commands.
When sent on an errand, they do not go; they reveal secrets that should be kept hidden.
They beg for what should not be asked for, and they eat foods that are forbidden.
They cry out, they flare up with anger, and they cause tasks to be ruined.
They even practice deception and sometimes resort to extortion;
they establish their own fabricated claims through forged signatures and handwriting.
They conspire with the guards of women and assume their attire.
They even vomit and spit in the presence of the king;
being shameless in the vicinity of the monarch, they destroy his very reputation as well.
They mount the royal horse, the elephant, the chariot, and so forth.
Even in the assembly hall, they speak of the king as ignorant;
when the king is angry, they laugh at him and divulge his secret counsel. They make public what was kept private and they transgress his commands.
They even treat him with contempt and revile him in his very presence;
they say, "The king is right here in our hands," and they speak likewise to the people.
Therefore, one should not be overly cheerful nor overly mild toward servants and others.
And he should always exert effort that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By pleasing the people, a king fulfills his duty; for the duty of a king is indeed to please them.
Furthermore, he must protect the truth and protect the administration of justice.
One must practice the protection of patience and must not deviate from the royal path;
a self-possessed man who remains vigilant in his human endeavors deserves kingship.
Indeed, all men and all duties must be protected by the king.
The elderly should be attended upon, and virtuous men should be served.
A king should bestow gifts upon the virtuous and take them away from the wicked for the sake of righteousness.
Furthermore, the king should honor the learned and their virtuous deeds in every way.
The king should protect the learned, those skilled in policy, experts in the scriptures,
storytellers, upholders of dharma, and instructors of the Supreme Lord.
The king should honor his gurus and worship them with abundant gifts.
He should constantly honor the virtuous, feed them, and listen to sacred stories.
He should cause temples to be built and arrange for the performance of worship. With devotion, the king himself should daily sacrifice to his beloved deities. (2.190.59–60)
He should set aside for the sake of dharma one-tenth, one-twentieth, one-hundredth, or one-fifth of the king’s wealth, grain, and other assets. Furthermore,
the king should protect sacred sites and likewise cause sacrificial rites to be performed.
He should protect cows, Brahmins, women, the destitute, children, and ascetics who have sought his shelter.
He should constantly give gifts after honoring his teachers and elders;
he should always salute the aged and receive their blessings from them.
One should constantly remember the Blessed One during one's activities in the morning and evening;
it shall not produce any fear, nor shall it ever cause the destruction of one's lifespan,
nor indeed ever cause the destruction of one's merit.
One should always eat the remains of the meal and be devoted to the Brahma-yajña.
One should look upon one's offspring with the highest parental affection,
regarding Me, Hari, as residing within all of them, and worship them accordingly.
A king should not engage in harmful acts in vain, even for the sake of his own interests.
He should always undertake virtuous deeds in this world with sincerity;
he should provide assistance in meritorious works and indeed perform them himself.
The king should cause the virtuous to dwell in his kingdom and serve them with the highest respect.
He should cause the Blessed One and his devotees to wander through the cities and other places.
Remaining on his regular throne, the king should perform the ritual turning of the garland (mālāvartana).

The king himself should maintain his family and others in their duties, their work, and their devotions; performing bathing, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and offerings, as well as giving charity, practicing righteousness, worship, and service. (2.190.70)
If a king conducts himself in this manner, he is liberated and not bound.
(71) In whose [house] there is never deceit, hypocrisy, or illusion toward the virtuous;
in whose house there is discourse on knowledge, devotion, and the worship of the Divine. (72)

Even he who follows the path of the virtuous and conducts himself as if he were a renunciant may indeed become a partaker of liberation through service to the Lord of Lords. As is the king, so is dharma; as is dharma, so are the subjects.
The king who seeks liberation must protect the dharma of Kṛṣṇa with extreme effort.
When he himself abides in the dharma of the Lord, his family, kinsmen, friends, and others—including all his subjects—will likewise abide in it in every way. (74–75)
"As the king is, so shall the subjects conduct themselves in the Sātvata dharma.
Therefore, O King, let all the subjects also practice the Sātvata way.
I shall uplift those who have taken refuge in me through my supreme devotion, which bestows liberation."
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, that Bālakṛṣṇa indeed became silent. The king, the subjects, and all others truly accepted his words;
those who were devoid of counsel accepted the counsel of the Lord.
They took up necklaces, vessels, and the chanting of His names;
thereafter, King Mudrāṇḍaka dismissed the assembly.
Hari, as well as the great sages, [dismissed] the meals and the family members.
Īśāna and the other lords, beginning with Brahmapriya, performed [these rites].
Having attained rest at night, they rose and performed their ablutions and so forth;
then, having performed the daily worship, they likewise drank milk and so on. (2.190.80–81)
Hari became ready to go to the regions of Pūrtagaṇḍa;
then the king requested Śrī Hari to go to the excellent city of Śaivāla,
situated on the bank of the river Gavādaka.
Hari said, "So be it," and with shouts of victory and hymns of praise,
he accepted the worship along with [the others] and ascended his own celestial chariot (vimāna).
Others sat down quickly, and at that very moment, Mudrāṇḍaka also did so.
Ascending his celestial chariot, he went ahead to ensure a successful welcome;
other chariots also traveled toward the city of Śaivāla.
In an instant, they reached that region, the vicinity of Gavādaka’s hermitage.
The celestial chariots descended upon the bank of the Godāvarī river.
In his own palace, the king honored Kṛṣṇa and all [the others] with devotion;
the monarch worshipped Hari with garden fruits, flowers, and other offerings.

Then he performed the *ārārtrika* rite and caused the Lord to circumambulate the city. Having thus purified the town, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa partook of milk, fruits, and other offerings, and received worship from the king and others. (88)
Having bestowed all the blessings offered by the subjects,
Acyuta desired to depart quickly with that same measure of time.
At that place, a king named Gaṇḍa had arrived to lead Kṛṣṇa away.
Then Hari, together with Pūrtagaṇḍarṣi, became ready;
having quickly ascended the celestial chariot and offered words of blessing,
he departed while hearing the sounds of victory, heading toward the river Gavādayānikā.
Having leaped over the regions of rivers, Hari traversed through the sky.
Upon reaching the river Trigirā, King Gaṇḍaka indeed descended before him along with the sage Gaṇḍarṣi to offer a welcome.
O Rādhikā, having gone to the auspicious city of Līśavana, which was adorned with ornaments and filled with troops, he offered a welcome in the garden.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wandering in the City of Madrid, Arrival at the Royal Palace, Worship, Instruction, and Feasting; Departure on the Morning of the Eighth Day after Nightfall Following the Morning Rites, Wandering through the City of Śaivala, and Travel toward Līśavana-pattana of King Gaṇḍaka in the Regions of the Pūrta Gaṇḍarṣis," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*. The queen, the maidens, and other princes,
as well as their kinsmen and the assembly of ministers, stood before them to welcome them.

The ten directions were indeed made to resound with the sounds of drums, *vigula* lutes, and excellent *dundubhi* kettledrums,

The king, the sages, and the householders nourished him with flowers and other offerings; they offered a welcome with necklaces, excellent unbroken grains, and parched rice.

He seated the Lord of Gods upon other suitable vehicles,
excellent mounts such as *gantrīs* and the like, as well as on *paṭolas* and carts,
amidst the sounds of musical instruments, [and brought him] to the city of Līśavana.
Full of enthusiasm, he caused [the chariot] to whirl about; the subjects offered their due honors, seeking his vision and worshipping his feet with great respect and many offerings.
Then, having beheld the beauty of the seashore, the Blessed One—
He arrived at the excellent royal palace together with his family.
The beloved of Kṛṣṇa was honored by the king, the queen, and the princesses with sandalwood, the finest fragrances, flowers, and auspicious garments. (2.191.1–11)
The leaders performed the worship of Śrī Hari with cooling offerings, powdered garments, jewels, ornaments and the like, as well as substances and fruits.
Then, there were nine young maidens, the daughters of Gaṇḍa, present there.
They quickly performed the hand-grasping ceremony for Hari according to the marriage rites.
By good fortune, the king and the royal sage also became fulfilled.
He celebrated that great festival with worship and honors.
The king caused a feast to be served, filled with cooked foods; there, the lord of the earth had dancing and singing performed.
The king bestowed many kinds of riches upon Kṛṣṇa.
Then the Blessed One gave those [gifts] to the sage Pūrṇagaṇḍa. Having eaten and attained rest through the chewing of betel and drinks,
the King himself delighted the honored guests with draughts of milk.
Then, in the evening, in the assembly hall, Bālakṛṣṇa directly instructed the subjects in many ways with words of peace:
"Whether in the kingdom, or in a garden, or in the house, or even in the forest... (18)

The embodied soul who is devoted to internal activity and possesses discernment attains peace. (2.19) Having thoroughly severed the thread of craving and abandoned the state of being an enjoyer, he who remains well-established in the abiding of the Self attains peace. (2.191.20)
He whose striving has ceased and whose mark has reached the state of being markless,
and whose tongue has become tasteless— he attains peace.
Sounds are but portions of space, and touches are like forest fires.

He for whom forms are like leprosy attains peace. She whose women are life-destroyers and he whose man is a demon—by the mental renunciation of her, she indeed attains peace; by his, he attains peace. (22–23)
He whose elements are like impurities, whose family behaves like monkeys,
whose servants are like consumption,
and whose disciples are like enemies while his sons are intent on devouring him— he indeed attains peace. (24)
He whose body is always afflicted with disease indeed attains peace.
He for whom detachment prevails, who perceives the sphere of passion as painful and the sphere of affection as unfavorable, indeed attains peace. (25–26)
One who possesses discernment attains peace amidst great enjoyment and great suffering;
"I am not the body, I have no object of enjoyment, and I am indeed not the enjoyer like a wretched man.
Thus, the discerning one, realizing "I am certainly not dependent on the insentient," reaches peace.
In the delightful regions of rivers, in forest groves and gardens, in palaces, in temples,
at sacred fords, or in solitary places, one should abide in peace;
whenever and wherever there are indeed no enemies, whether external or internal.
Whether they are adventitious or eternal, it then attains peace;
for just as one whose pain has been relieved falls under the power of sleep and no longer feels the suffering,
so too the individual soul (jīvātman), though struck by the world, does not suffer when it has entered the fourth state (turya).

A living being whose latent impressions have been destroyed attains the company of the virtuous. (3.1) If one should be devoted to serving the virtuous, he attains auspicious peace. One should adopt the qualities of the good and practice the conduct of the good. (3.2)
One should always avoid that which is not to be grasped and strive for that which is to be grasped as auspicious.
An embodied being should calm the waves of the mind and become tranquil.
Through the grace of the Guru, one should abandon conceptual constructions, doubts, and delusions.
One should abandon arguments, logical reasons, and disputes by means of one's own discernment. Having recognized anxieties and the causes of distress, one should avoid them from afar.
Only after thoroughly considering the future should one act, remaining free from agitation.
Having approached Hari for refuge, one should offer the fruit of one's actions to Him.
He who begins his work after meditating on Hari and perceiving Me as the agent, should perform what is beneficial with a mind permeated by Me;
such action bestows the goal of welfare.
One should practice that which brings about the highest welfare for oneself or for another.
One should contemplate the richness of wealth consisting of knowledge and realized wisdom (*jñāna-vijñāna*).
Being endowed with non-possessiveness and contented, one shall attain supreme peace.
Having reflected thus, the king, the queen, and the subjects should always conduct themselves for the sake of perfect peace, relying on mutual benefit.
They should perform service for the subjects, protection for the kingdom, and protection for one another.
One should act with the thought that they are oneself and the thought that they are one's own son, thereby bestowing perfect peace.
Bṛhaspati, Viśālākṣa, Kāvya, Prācetasa, Bharadvāja, Mahendra, Gauraśiras, and Manu likewise [practiced thus]. (2.191.40–41)
These very exponents of Brahman always praise one another’s protection of the Dharma, which is promoted by kings in every aeon:
charity, service to the virtuous, and likewise the gathering together of the virtuous.
Skillfulness, truthfulness, and straightforwardness, as well as impartiality toward all;
the rescue of those who are suffering, the honoring of those of noble birth, the non-abandonment of the virtuous, and service even to the wise. (43–44)
One should always observe enemies, friends, and those who are neutral, whether they be outsiders or one's own kin; one should always follow the path of ethics and dharma and avoid the ignoble.
In this world, exertion is appropriate in every respect regarding worldly affairs, the worship of Hari, and spiritual contemplation.
These virtues—liberation, renunciation, and dispassion—are devoted to protection;
they must always be guarded by the king and by the subjects who desire immortality.
Through exertion, the gods, joined by Mahendra, attained immortality. (46–47)
For the protection of one who is devoid of exertion indeed departs far away.
One should always practice the exertion of righteousness and perform virtuous deeds;
even if there should be misfortune for this embodied being due to the duty of protection, [one must still persevere].
That vast dharma of his is indeed from me alone, for I am the protection itself.
I am both the protection and the protector, and I am also that which is to be protected;
I always provide protection and I guard it, of this there is no doubt.
I never protect those who are cruel-natured and lack protection;
for on this earth, the class of kings is my own self in the form of a protector.
Therefore, protection is my duty, and that which is performed by me must be upheld by people.
While Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, was being addressed in this way,
King Gaṇḍaka, the son of Rādhikā, questioned Śrī Nārāyaṇa: "How, why, and when indeed was the title 'King' bestowed upon you by you?"
Even though their physical existence is equal, even though they possess the same nature of sense faculties,
even though they experience the same pleasure and pain, undergo the same transformations, and have the same bodily form;
even though their semen, bones, and marrow are alike, and they are composed of the same flesh and other elements— (54)

When life and body are equal, and when they are equally subject to death and existence—how is it that sovereignty belongs to one among such beings? And how is it that one alone excels others who are brave and wise? (55–56)
The possessor of being presides over the earth and protects it alone;
by the grace of that one alone, the entire world becomes gracious.
And in that one alone, the kingdom bows down as before a god.
"O Blessed One, how is it that even though there is equality, this sovereignty transcends all others and exists as supreme over everything?
Tell me, what is the reason for this?
Having heard this, Hari spoke to Rādhā about the discourse arising from the laws of kingship.
In the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was here neither kingdom nor one who ruled a kingdom;
there was no king, nor was there punishment, nor anyone to be punished, nor anyone who inflicted punishment.
By means of truth and righteousness, the subjects, being devoted to Brahman, protected one another.

At that time, all subjects were independent and happy, possessing wish-fulfilling trees, wish-granting creepers, the *cintāmaṇi* gem, and the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*). Then, in the course of time, at the end of the Kṛta age, the powers of conceptualization increased. (61–62)

At that time, when things had reached a state of depletion, the sense of ownership was set in motion; there arose disputes such as "this is mine" and "this is the wish-fulfilling tree," and "this is not yours.
Thus, at that time, the delusion of possessiveness entered among the subjects.
Then their thoughts, consisting of mental constructs, became fruitless.
Through the onset of the defect of craving, true dharma perished; they fell under the sway of greed, coveting what they had not yet attained. (64–65)
Another great defect, desire, took hold among the creatures.
Passion, which brings about the undesirable, indeed touched those people who were devoted to desire.
Deluded by that, they did not understand what ought to be done or what ought not to be done.
There arose sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, as well as the distinction between what may and may not be spoken.
Likewise, there emerged the concepts of what is edible and inedible, and what is fit and unfit for consumption.
When the world of men fell into disorder, the state of Brahmanhood was utterly lost.
Upon the destruction of Brahmā, there was the destruction of Dharma, and the gods were seized with terror.
They went to the unborn Father (Brahmā) and, being deeply distressed, spoke to him after propitiating him:
"O Brahmā, in the world of men, the Truth (Brahman) has indeed gone to dissolution."
"Because Dharma has met its destruction, we have been deprived of the *svāhā* invocation;
we have now reached a state of exhaustion and have become equal to ordinary men.
Therefore, O Grandfather, contemplate here that which leads to our supreme welfare."

Brahmā said, "I shall contemplate for you that which brings about your welfare and removes fear. Then, at the dawn of the Tretā age, Brahmā established the fourfold aims of life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— each distinguished by its own specific quality.
He established the rules of dharma, as well as the regulations for punishment and protection;
he fashioned the forms of sacrifices and other rites associated with the fruits of action;
and he created the objects of wealth, such as fields, gardens, houses, and so forth.
He created the essential forms of the riches of wealth, which communicate ownership and other such relations;

he also created the seasons, which are capable of assuming any form at will and are mutually interconnected. Furthermore, out of delusion, he established the rules of conduct that define the specific objects of enjoyment for each individual.
The dharma of liberation consists of the form of Sāma and the offering [of all] unto me, Mādhava.
Because there is no definitive conclusion even regarding the offering of the three aims of life as being the giver of liberation,
there are indeed many other various types of teachings for which no final determination exists.
Śaṅkara, this very Īśānaka, first received that Nīti;
and the scripture spoken by Śaṅkara then became known as the Vaiśālākṣa.
Indra, for his part, received that very same work as the Bāhudantaka.
Bṛhaspati wrote this, and from it the Bārhaspatya [treatise] arose.
From that, the Auśanasa [treatise] was born, and from that, political science (nīti) was set in motion.
Then Viṣṇu was requested by the gods regarding one who knew the science of polity (nītiśāstra).
Then Nārāyaṇa and I gave him our mind-born son;
his son was Virajas, and Kīrtimān was his son.
Kardama was his son, a highly intelligent man named Anaṅga.
He was a virtuous protector of his subjects, skilled in the science of governance.
His son was Aṅgarāja, who, having married Sunīthikā, the daughter of Mṛtyu, begot a single son, the cruel Vena. (82–83)
The great seers struck that hateful Vena with the tips of their sacred mantras;
the seers then churned the right thigh of Vena’s body and produced the Niṣāda,
from whom the Niṣādas subsequently arose.
Those great seers churned his right hand once more.
From that, I became broad-bodied, armed with weapons and clad in armor;
knowing the science of polity, I obtained the title of "King."
Together with the gods, I caused the earth to be leveled;
by my resolve, the entire prosperity of the kingdom was renewed.
Indeed, in the first cycle of the ages, the kingdom was established by me.
The earth was milked for the sake of the subjects, and the subjects were protected by means of punishment.
Because he delighted the subjects, they called him "Rājā Pṛthu" on this earth;
and because he protected [them] from injury (*kṣata-trāṇa*), I became a *Kṣatriya*, even though I am a twice-born (*dvija*).
I alone established the earth and established the kingdom;
there, as the eternal Viṣṇu, I applied the principles of policy.
Then, from my forehead, a beautiful golden lotus was born.
Then the goddess Śrī was born from it as Kamalā, the wife of Dharma.
In the kingdom, Śrī took the form of Artha (prosperity), bestowing both desire and liberation.
When Vaiṣṇavī Śrī resides in the kingdom, she indeed bestows liberation.

Thus, from that time forward, both the gods and the lords of men have been called equal to the wise, since these kings are portions of myself. In this manner, O Queen, I have established this preeminence known as "kingship."
Therefore, I am to be seen by that king and by his subjects within their own selves.
I am to be worshipped, saluted, and offered with supreme devotion.
Those who have surrendered themselves to me shall attain me alone; there is no doubt in this.
"Those kings who, abandoning me, consider themselves as possessing their own status will surely go to ruin; their royal lineages will become diminished and impoverished.
Having understood this conclusion, people should worship me, Janārdana.
"Having eternally established the fourfold goals of human life within me alone, O Rādhikā, Hari spoke thus to the members of the assembly.
They accepted his words exactly as they were; everyone then bowed and departed. (97–98)
Hari reached his own residence and took his meal in the royal palace;
the other great men also ate with great respect.
Then they all obtained rest, and at night they all fell asleep.
"O Rādhikā, the princesses served that beloved of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure for the Capital of Gaṇḍaka, the Wandering through the City of Līśavana, the Worship, the Meal, the Instruction, and the Resting at Night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 191. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 2 (Tretā-yuga-santāna).
