Chapter 193 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the morning of the ninth day, the Lord was awakened by auspicious sounds of musical instruments and by the words of bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists; likewise,
everyone else woke up and performed their daily rites.
The king brought milk and other foods and gave them to Hari.
(2) They all drank the milk and ate the food as was appropriate.
There, the Lord Śrī Hari bestowed blessings upon the monarch. (3)
Then Hari bestowed blessings, words of honor, and other marks of respect upon the people;
thereafter, he became ready to depart for Līnorṇarāṣṭra.
King Līnorṇa, having arrived there, entreated Acyuta.
Then the Lord spoke together with the sage who subsisted on fruits.
There, King Gaṇḍaka gave many gifts of leave-taking;
and Hari, being honored, ascended his excellent celestial chariot.
Likewise, others also then ascended the path of victory over the subjects; hearing all these sounds, they urged on their birds of the sky.
Having leaped across the Khāḍikā mountain, they went to the city of Vāruṇī.
Having first descended to his own city,
King Līnorṇa welcomed Hari along with the fruit-eating sage;
following the path shown by the king, he brought down the celestial chariot.
Then Hari and the others descended from their vehicles from the sky;
the sound of musical instruments and songs pervaded every direction.
Hari, having alighted from his vehicle, mounted a splendid chariot drawn by men.
When the gold was displayed by the king, it shone amidst shouts of victory.
(11) Having been properly honored with garlands and other offerings by the king, the Supreme Lord, together with his family and others, caused everyone to sport in the western quarter. (12)
Accompanied by the royal army and honored by the citizens, the Blessed One arrived at the vast palace, the king’s residence.
Thereupon he rested, bathed, and took his meal.

Others also took their meal; then the queen, accompanied by four maidens, arrived before Hari for the purpose of worship. Having obtained their beloved Hari, the maidens joyfully performed the ritual of taking his hand in marriage.
Then the queen offered worship and a dowry according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, having rested, the Blessed One quickly became ready.
Having ascertained the king's intention, the Lord made everyone ready.
Before King Bṛhacchara, the kingdom indeed reached the limit of the Khāḍiga forest. Requested by the sage Vallījīvana, Hari departed;
and King Bṛhacchara descended to his own city ahead of him.
He brought along Śrī Hari, who was adorned with the name Dhīvara;
he worshipped the Supreme Lord in a beautiful palace within the city.
The king, the queen, the two maidens, and the subjects all offered a warm welcome.
The two maidens took the hand of Hari with pure devotion.
The king felt his purpose was fulfilled, and Hari passed the night.
In the morning, he wandered around the city, adorned by his army.
Having granted an audience to the subjects and purified that city,
the Lord performed the drinking of milk and other rites, and became ready to depart.
At that moment, King Paścimasāmudra, having heard [of the Lord's arrival], quickly [approached] the Lord.
He arrived there quickly with celestial chariots to lead them away.
Having bowed to Hari, the King of Aṅga prayed to the Supreme Lord. Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready.
At that time, other celestial chariots as well became beautifully adorned.
Having crossed the Khāḍī river, the Blessed One proceeded to the city of Milinda.
Honored by the king according to his capacity with musical instruments, an army, and hymns of praise, [he entered].
Pleased by offerings and gifts, he was made to wander through the city.
At midday, he caused all the people to take their meal;
in the evening, having placed everyone in celestial chariots, he showed them the various continents.
Having again surveyed everything, Hari returned to Milinda and bestowed upon him instruction augmented by the principles of statecraft (rājanīti).
He likewise [gave instruction] to the subjects of Dvilīnā and those subjects who were full of curiosity.
Having arrived there with his attendants, Śrī Śrīdhara Svāmī heard the instruction in the assembly of hundreds of thousands of twice-born men during the tenth watch of the night;
and he, O Rādhikā, imparted that teaching which is beneficial and brings about liberation.
This Īśāna is the Supreme Brahman; he should always be honored by people.
Indeed, supreme devotion should be directed toward Īśāna, who is my very self.
One must never speak untruth, nor should one ever take an oath in his presence.
Sunday should indeed be observed for the propitiation of Hara;
parents must always be served, and violence must never be committed. Theft is to be avoided, as is false testimony even in a court of law. (32–33)
One must never desire the wealth, clothing, or other such desirable things belonging to others; one must not kill another living being, nor should one ever take what belongs to another.
One must never, under any circumstances, commit treachery against anyone.
One must never, under any circumstances, commit an act that destroys the dharma of the subjects.
By thus protecting the dharmas, a king shall attain heaven.
[He should practice] truthful speech, freedom from anger, forgiveness, and impartiality.
Delighting only in one’s own wife, purity, avoidance of malice,
straightforwardness, and the support of dependents— these should always be practiced by all people.
The brahmin classes adopted self-restraint as their ancient dharma.
Vedic study, the practice of yoga, austerity, and the protection of one's progeny;
friendliness, beneficial speech, upholding [dharma], and constant protection—by conducting himself thus, a Brahmin shall eternally attain heaven. (38–39)
A Kṣatriya, however, should give gifts, study the Vedas, and perform sacrifices;
he should protect his subjects and exert his prowess against those who act unjustly.
For the primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the warding off of the Dasyu tribes.
Charity, study, and sacrifice—these bring happiness to kings.
By abiding in his own duty through these, a king should indeed cause all others to abide in theirs.
A king who stands thus in righteousness is called a lord of Kṣatriyas.
Furthermore, others who are engaged in agricultural work or business, as well as people in general,
should practice giving, study, perform sacrifice, and acquire wealth;
they should indeed protect all cattle with the same affection one has for a son.
By the protection of cattle, a Vaiśya shall attain supreme happiness.
(44) In ancient times, Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
he gave all subjects to the king, and he gave the autumnal [Veda] to the Brahmins. (45)
Taking one-seventh [of the produce], he may live his life in every way.
If he is a Kṣatriya, then by offering himself to me, he shall attain liberation.
[He should perform] service, servitude, slavery, attendance, and the duties of a messenger.
Indeed, those groups of servants who perform service shall attain great happiness.
(47) Service is the wish-fulfilling creeper; service is the wish-fulfilling tree;
service is considered to be the cow of plenty and the jewel that grants all desires. (48)
Through service, a lion, a king, a guru, and the planets come under one's control;
through servitude, a master, a husband, a virtuous wife, and subjects become submissive.
Through devotion, enemies, haters, darkness, and the wicked are brought under control.

The world, intent on service, delights its leaders. Because of this delight, kingship, sovereignty, and the like do not indeed exist apart from the one who causes delight. Therefore, one should obtain everything—provided it is filled with jewels—through service.
An umbrella, a turban, ornaments, sandals, fans, and so forth,
as well as garments and excellent food, are given to the attendant. Indeed,
one who is childless must be supported, as must the elderly and the infirm.
The male servant, the female servant, and the group of employees are to be supported by you in accordance with dharma.
Sacrifice is the duty of Brahmins; sacrifice with wealth is the duty of kings;
the support of others is the sacrifice of Vaiśyas; and devotion is the sacrifice of servants.
Among all sacrifices, faith is the foremost sacrifice; it is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Faith is the supreme deity, by which Mādhava is pleased.
Those who perform actions with faith are enriched with all fruits.
Therefore, in all worlds, the sacrifice of faith is ordained.
Where that which is called faith is the supreme deity, there the deity resides.
Having entrusted the accomplishment of the task and the attainment of the Lord to me, it is brought to fulfillment.
Whether he be a thief, or a sinner, or even the worst of evildoers—
if he desires to perform a sacrifice, he is indeed a virtuous man; therefore,
one should always sacrifice, whether to a deity or to a conscious being.
Whether toward the poor, the helpless, or those worthy of protection who have been uplifted through faith, it is the firm resolve that one should always and in every way perform sacrifice for them;
for there is nothing equal to sacrifice as a supreme bestower of fruits and happiness. (2.192.59–60)
Or he may be devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), not practicing the duties of a householder;
by offering oblations into the *brahman* alone, he attains the Supreme *Brahman*.
Or else, even while performing the duties of a householder with his wife, if he possesses the dharma of having me as his supreme refuge, [he likewise attains liberation].
Even one who practices the dharma while remaining within my own refuge is liberated from bondage.
Or, having accomplished his purpose through the vision of knowledge, he may dwell even in the forest.
Such a performer of action, ever devoted to me, attains equality with the Imperishable.
If an ascetic, free from dualities, should attain me by relying on my teachings and their virtuous nature, he is fit for my state of being.
And he who remains self-possessed, without possessions, subsisting on alms, [attains me].
Whether engaged in action or devoid of action, one who is intent on my nature attains me.
Sleeping little, eating little, free from desire, without a fixed abode, and living on whatever is obtained, such a silent sage shall attain me. (65–66)
Free from desire, he is declared to be like Brahman; satisfied, he is the refuge of perfect bliss.
Devoid of enjoyment and free from worldly activity, he attains equality with the Imperishable.
Even while remaining in the householder stage of life, he crosses over Māyā and its illusory women.
Even by casting everything upon me, one is then released from bondage.

(68) One who is content with his own wife, satisfied, free from deceit and crookedness, devoted to the worship of the gods, truthful, self-controlled, and likewise one who makes proper divisions [of wealth]. (69)
He who is devoted to forgiveness and compassion, a giver to all as is appropriate, who practices straightforwardness, honors guests, and supports those who have sought his protection—
he who acts thus, causes others to act thus, and lives accordingly, is a partaker of liberation.
Having attained pure fruit in heaven and rejoiced there for eternal years,
at the end of the body he shall obtain— in no doubt— imperishable and infinite desires existing everywhere, provided he is intent on me and has offered himself to me.
Whatever one performs here in such a manner, one shall obtain a corresponding result; first, having made something belonging to another into a form of service for the festival,
one should then perform that which pertains to the body, then that which is internal, and finally that which is one's own.
Then one should perform the *pārameśa* [rite], which wards off all defects.
(74) Whatever king or even common subject conducts himself in this manner in the world, he obtains the black Meru, strung upon all the threads. (75)
Therefore, having constantly surrendered themselves to the Supreme Lord,
people should remain free from the pairs of opposites and free from [worldly] actions in order to attain the state of Brahman.
[They should be] those whose actions are for Me, who find rest in Me, who offer oblations to Me, and who have Me as their supreme goal.
I shall deliver them from the fullness of the ocean of death; of this there is no doubt.
(77) Having worshipped all the ancestors, the gods, and the sages upon whom they depend, as well as Hari who dwells within, one shall at the end go to the abode of Hari. (78)
Whether not acting, or acting otherwise, or acting at all, one who has taken refuge in me reaches the further shore of the ocean of countless karma through my yoga.
Let them always worship me in the morning and remember me during their ritual activities and the like.
"Keeping me within their hearts at the end, let them go to my imperishable state.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One himself became silent;
and so did the king of Milinda’s capital, his subjects, and the others.
Having attained the Dharma that destroys bondage when combined with discerning knowledge,
they all joyfully accepted the teachings then imparted by Him.
And Lomaśa also gave them there the mantra of Hari.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
(83) Thereupon, the subjects and the king worshipped the Lord with gold and silver coins, as well as with offerings and garments. (84)
With ornaments, sandalwood paste and the like, unbroken grains, flower garlands,
and various other objects suitable for giving, Hari, with a gracious heart, [honored] the Supreme Lord,
those subjects, and the kings.
He bestowed his blessings: "May you be of excellent renown;
may you possess an excellent kingdom, excellent dharma, and be devoted to excellent justice.
May you be intent upon devotion to me, Maheśāna, the Supreme. (86–87)
Having spoken thus, Hari rested in his own dwelling place;
the people, who had realized the nature of the Self, went to their own abodes.
The King of Aṅga offered meals to the glorious Supreme Soul.
He also fed all those who had come from the earth seeking refuge with Hari;
he worshipped Īśāna and honored Lomaśa. Having paid homage to the family of Hari, the king took his meal.
The queen named Raṅgarajā was the wife of Cāṅgarāja;
she was fair-complexioned, possessed of a gracious heart, and accompanied by eleven daughters.
[91] She offered garlands of flowers, golden necklaces, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and fragrant scents.
Having taken them, she came into the presence of Bālakṛṣṇa to worship him.
With affection, she worshipped the feet of Hari and washed them with water;
Gaurī drank [the water], and all those eleven maidens indeed drank as well.
Beholding the beginningless and glorious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, their beloved master,
they took him by the hand according to the marriage rite;
they placed necklaces around his neck, and Hari gave them to them as well.
A great festival arose, and the king felt his purpose was fulfilled.
Then they fell asleep and rested comfortably through the night; and perceiving that the night had passed and hearing the auspicious sounds, the Blessed One [arose]. (95–96)
When Hari, having completed his daily rites, quickly became composed once more,
the king and the virtuous queen immediately brought pure water;
and the Blessed Lord accepted that, as well as food consisting of fruits and other offerings.
The sages, dear to Brahmā, eagerly accepted the family [offerings].
Thereafter, they also took the fruits and betel leaves;
having received that momentary honor, they also accepted their leave.
Hari and the others, having questioned the king, quickly ascended their prepared celestial chariots while hearing the sound of trumpets from the path of the sky; then,
as if by command, they moved ahead.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went forward.
From the sky, Kṛṣṇa beheld the surface of the earth, exceedingly beautiful, with its kings and kingdoms subdued by his strength, and its ground filled with sages who had transcended old age. 101–102.
Then the king, accompanied by the great sage Jarāmouna, went on foot upon the ground with his army to welcome Hari;
it was on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, during the second watch, O Rādhikā.
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose;
the sounds of mechanical devices became garlands of names, and songs of praise resounded upon the earth.
Then, in succession, the celestial chariots proceeded along the path shown by the King.

They descended into the great garden in the vicinity of Vālīnā, within the vast capital city of Viśālā, which was crowded with hundreds of thousands of people. (1.06) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described are]: Hari’s arrival in the kingdom of Līnorṇa; his wandering, worship, dining, and taking leave in the city of Vāruṇī; then his arrival in the kingdom of King Bṛhacchara and his wandering in the city of Dhīvarā; and then the journey of the King of Aṅga toward the city of Milindā.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, then the king [beheld] him descending from the celestial chariot.
She placed a garland of flowers around the neck of the Blessed Bālakṛṣṇa.
She gave him a necklace of jewels upon his throat and a cluster of flowers in his hand;

The king’s family, the ministers, the chief officials, and likewise the subjects,
respectfully welcomed Śrī Hari there with offerings of worship.

At that time, the royal highways were exceedingly crowded with people;

The heights, the dilapidated sections,

Then he was honored by the troops and by the royal people;
likewise, he was honored by merchants, those of noble families, shopkeepers, and residents,

With offerings such as fruits and the like, grains of rice and the like, ornaments and the like,
garments such as woolen blankets, necklaces, and golden garlands;
with unbroken rice, saffron, and strings of gems and diamonds.
And Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was honored with flowers by him with great devotion.
Having thus wandered through the city, he arrived at the royal palace;

On the eleventh day, Hari performed the worship of the vow during the night;
and in the assembly hall, he kept a vigil accompanied by the exposition of dharma,

the vow becomes complete and the state of darkness is restrained.
Even by force, devotion to Hari arises, which brings about satisfaction.
When Śrī Hari is pleased, the entire human birth becomes fruitful.
For that purpose, indeed, a vow must be observed in this world by one who is attentive.
That lunar day which remains at sunrise is the true Ekādaśī for those seeking the fruit of the vow.
Considering the rising of the sun, Ekādaśī should always be observed;
likewise, my Janmāṣṭamī occurs at dawn when the eighth lunar day arises on the day of my birth.
In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, the Śarat-pūrṇottarā (the full moon of Āśvina followed by the first day of the dark fortnight) should always be accepted.
In this way, other lunar days (tithis) should also be accepted when they persist at sunrise.

Men may achieve success by relying on either a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or a day (vāsara), but that is certainly not my primary view; for I hold that the lunar day is defined by its presence at sunrise.
The vow should be observed on that very day upon which the lunar date (tithi) falls; there is never a loss of the tithi. When diminished, it is considered to exist at moonrise;
indeed, the presence of the tithi is certain either at moonrise or at sunrise.
For a festival rite performed at night, the lunar day is considered to be that which includes moonrise;
for a festival rite performed during the day, the lunar day is considered to be that which includes sunrise.
Thus, by my power, those vows must be observed in every way.
The merit-bestowing [vows] become fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.
Māyā, born of Brahmā, and Vedhas—the creator—bring no loss in relation to me.
Thus, having understood my command, one should indeed perform the supreme vows.
Devotees should always carry out my commands, for they bestow fruit.
On whatever day the festival, birth, or dissolution of a particular deity occurs, that lunar day (tithi) present at that moment is always auspicious for a vow (vrata). || 58–59 ||
The rising of the sun, the rising of the moon, or the rising of the stars should be considered secondary (gauṇa) in that context; the primary (mukhya) time for day and night is the moment (kṣaṇa).
If men should perform their vows setting this aside, [they will not be effective].
Divergent opinions will undoubtedly arise regarding that very matter (6:1).
Indeed, those [opinions] will become causes for the interruption of vows;
therefore, one should always seize the opportune moment during a vow or any festival of all-knowing [deities] (6:2).
By that, dharma indeed increases, and never otherwise.
Merit increases through faith, especially when conjoined with the proper time;
it increases even more when conjoined with a worthy recipient, by virtue of the excellence of that recipient.
I am the vessel and the Supreme Brahman; my great vow is that I am to be served.
Service to mother, father, and guru is the supreme vow. Service to the teacher and the virtuous is a great vow that bestows merit. (64–65)
One should devotedly cause public works to be built—water-stations, wells, and auspicious resting places—and perform meritorious vows; for such acts bestow merit.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, righteous livelihood, charity, and protection [of others] [constitute the path].
Serving the elders and supporting one’s sons and wife constitute a vow.
Sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) must be given during sacrificial rites by one who desires prosperity.
Pākayajñas and Kaṇayajñas, which bestow prosperity, should be performed.
For one who constantly honors the Arhats in every way by sharing with them, that very vow shall indeed grant heaven; of this there is no doubt.

This supreme vow always bestows merit and leads to heaven.
For one who performs all acts of hospitality, heaven is certain; of this there is no doubt.
[One should perform] the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), and the honoring of guests and so forth.
For one who performs the sacrifice to the gods, heaven is certain; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, there is the undertaking of initiation, the constant honoring of the learned, the remembrance of the gods, and the protection of those who have come for refuge.
Livelihood free from crookedness and the vow of sacred knowledge bestow heaven.
Furthermore, for an embodied being who acts with compassion toward all creatures and is intent on their protection, this vow shall grant the attainment of heaven. (73–74)

For one who offers a welcome and other courtesies to those who arrive, who performs appropriate services, who honors others with humility, and who remains under the authority of his family and the words of the virtuous, his vow shall grant the attainment of heaven. (75)
For one who abides by the words of the scriptures, the vow shall become a bestower of liberation.
For one established in that dharma, whether in any hermitage whatsoever, the vow consisting of righteousness leads surely to heaven; of this there is no doubt. (76–77)
For one who conducts themselves in the world by honoring status, lineage, age, and virtue, heaven is certain.
Having observed the laws of the land, the laws of kin, and the laws of subjects, [one should act accordingly].
And he who conducts himself in that manner possesses this supreme vow.
Even a householder who is not greedy for prosperity, sensory objects, wealth, the body, or anything pertaining to the body, his vow becomes equal to that of the virtuous. (2.193.80)

Virtuous people, who delight in the Dharma, are devoted to the Dharma, provide assistance through the Dharma, and dwell in the Dharma— even while in the state of a householder— truly become such. And he who always conducts himself toward all beings in the world as he would toward himself, [attains the highest state].
The embodied being who removes the suffering of others obtains happiness in this very world.
Those whose source is Dharma, whose vigor is Dharma, who protect Dharma, who guard the sacrifice, and who rely on the virtue of renunciation, surely cross the ocean of existence swiftly. (82–83)
When his turbulent volition has been severed at its root, the embodied soul,
having attained the state of pure being (*sattva*), then partakes in Brahman. Therefore,
all volitions whatsoever should be surrendered unto Me, the Lord.
"My self is to be offered, and my abode shall grant liberation"—
having spoken thus, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, became silent.
And the king likewise worshipped the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed his morning bath and other rites, and having completed the worship and other ceremonies, the king, with the utmost devotion, worshipped the Great Lord Maheśa, the Lord of Satī,
and then caused the breaking of the fast with sweet foods and other delicacies.
Just as Śrī Hari, having completed his breaking of the fast, was taking rest,
Queen Ratīśā arrived, accompanied by the materials for worship and forty fair-complexioned maidens.
Then he worshipped the Supreme Soul and drank the nectar of His feet;
forty maidens took the hand of Hari in marriage.
At that time, by the king's command, musical instruments were played and songs were sung.
And a festival accompanied by dancing arose, with songs sung by the Gaurīs;
the king also considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Furthermore, the king gave gifts and dowries to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Having received all those pearl necklaces, golden ornaments, blankets, garments, and fine cloths, Hari then quickly became ready to depart at the king's command;
meanwhile, the king fed Acyuta.
He fed all the honored guests with milk-rice and other delicacies.
Then, O giver of honor, the army was made ready for departure;
he sounded the musical instruments and raised a roar of victory.
Then all the celestial chariots were in the sky. Honored on all sides by his subjects, the great king ascended;
likewise, everyone else, urged by the sages, ascended for the sake of protection.
Then they were also invited by King Varasiṃha;
moving through the sky, they proceeded while hearing the shouts of victory.
The aerial chariot of Hari went to the kingdom of Varasiṃha.
Formerly, King Varasiṃha, accompanied by sages,
prepared a ready army before him to welcome the host of Hari on the bank of the river Viṣṇutulyā, at the shore of the city of Vāśīlā.
Beholding the celestial chariot of Hari, the army offered a welcome.
With the sounds of various musical instruments, the thundering of the mechanical engines,
and the songs of fair-complexioned women, the sky indeed became filled with sound.
By the path shown by the King, the celestial chariot descended to the earth;
indeed, the other chariots of Hari also arrived.
A rain of flowers was showered upon the chariot by the subjects.
And the people became overwhelmed with longing to behold [Him], O Rādhikā.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s Arrival in the City of Vālīnā, His Worship, the Vigil, the Instruction on the Vow, the Breaking of the Fast on the Twelfth Day, and the Subsequent Departure for the City of Vāśīlā," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

At that time, fair-complexioned women ascended to their own dwellings;

Having obtained the fruit of their eyes, their minds drawn by the sight of him, the women—
whose vision was granted by one impelled by compassion—
beheld him whose appearance is inaccessible to embodied beings.
Having beheld this Hari, who is most exceedingly beautiful, do not delay; make your own birth fruitful.
[Do not let] the one who is excessively greedy for sense-objects and powerless [be driven away]. 12.
For the mind does not attain stability;
thus, by the mere sight of her, Mādhava himself becomes exceedingly greedy and helpless toward the woman. 13.
The pair of lotus feet, praised by the virtuous, which serve as the seat for the yogis formed by the crest-jewels atop the crowns of the lords of gods, kings, and sovereigns who bow before them;
Hold this one, who is supported by Kamalā, within your minds—
He who, in His supreme abode, possesses an auspicious divine form and is described by the Vedas as the locus of all virtues.
Filled with the qualities of power, prosperity, and beauty, do you now fill this mind with him who is enveloped in radiance; for he is beautiful, endowed with abundant splendor. || 15 ||
This body, well-nourished and serving as the dwelling place for the senses, shall not again be obtained by you in such a state of weakness;

The lotus-face, which destroys manifold afflictions, and which— by its measured, gentle, and beloved smiles— is exceedingly alluring;
it bestows liberation upon this earth and grants liberation in the world beyond.
Let this moon filled with nectar, which bestows happiness, be drunk in;
for this Supreme Person swiftly draws away the heart, as well as the collection of senses and consciousness. 17.
Having realized that Lord here as the eternal Beloved, may they meet within the heart; once met, let the Lord be enjoyed.
For He who dwells in the heart has indeed come forth externally. || 18 ||

O friend! Let him be worshipped with flowers and the weight of your devotion; let him, who has been embraced by the offering of jewels and diamonds of passion, be served now that he has come together with you. 19.
Thus, Kṛṣṇa, whose fame is sung by all, having wandered through the city,
arrived at the royal palace and was honored by the citizens.
The king quickly worshipped the feet of Hari with sandalwood paste.
With unbroken grains and flowers, Hari sat upon the lion-throne (21).
As he sat there, the people showered him with garlands and blossoms;
with hearts overflowing with love, they gazed at him with steady eyes (29).

There, a most magnificent assembly was convened by the illustrious Supreme Self; and then the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ruler who shines in the supreme imperishable, gave instruction for the sake of the welfare of the people. (23)
Out of compassion, he indeed comes for the protection of his own subjects.
The subjects are the daughters of the Blessed One; they must be protected like a mother, nourished, made happy, and led to the imperishable state. (24–25)
I am the sustainer of all incarnations, the beloved of the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇa;
having crushed Māyā, I abide here in this world within the range of your perception.
I am the son of Kaṃbharā, the Lord of Rādhikā, and the husband of Lakṣmī and Padmāvatī.
Māṇikīśa, Ramānātha, he himself the delighter of Gopālā;
the beloved of those dear to Brahmā, the Lord and Master of all creation;
the husband of Lalitā, Vijayā, and Haṃsā, who is beautiful with her excellent virtues. (27–28)
Wherever I may dwell even in this world, let that place be composed of the Divine Abode;
for by the residence of Nārāyaṇa, this earth has become like Vaikuṇṭha.
O Lord, you are the cause of this divine nature in one who is destined for divinity.
Likewise, devotion is also a cause for the acquisition of a good land and other such things.
(2.194.30) If the king should indeed be devoted, then the Kṛta Yuga would prevail there; a king endowed with policy and dharma will certainly cause the Kṛta age to manifest. (31)
There, indeed, among all the social orders, no thought of unrighteousness arises;
for there, security and prosperity always prevail for the subjects. All virtuous deeds are performed by the twice-born.
All the seasons become exceedingly pleasant and free from affliction;
people become gracious in heart, mind, and speech;
diseases do not arise, and no person is born with a short lifespan.
There, no men were miserable, nor were there women without husbands;
even the earth, though without cultivation, produced crops, and the medicinal herbs, nourished by the essence of the soil, bore fruit and bestowed happiness. (35)
Even the bark, leaves, fruits, and roots become potent.
(36) In every house there is indeed righteousness, happiness, and contentment;
in every person there is trust, happiness, and no cause for agitation anywhere. (37)
Thus, when a king endowed with righteousness abandons even a portion of his share for the sake of the true time, then that very portion shall belong to righteousness;
and in this world, among men, the Tretā age shall prevail in every place.
The inauspicious quarter is the fourth part; it causes suffering to that same extent.
Then the earth becomes productive like grain sown in a furrow, yielding a third of its fruit.
Everything yields a third of its fruit when the [inauspicious] portion is in the fourth part. (2.194.40)
When the king—the cause of the Tretā age—is present, everything—be it happiness, the means to achieve it, or even the objects to be attained—is not fully realized;
for when the king indeed abandons righteousness and moral conduct, he remains only half [effective]. 41.½.
When the Dvāpara age has arrived for the king, it proceeds in this manner among the subjects:
[it manifests] in the cloud, the forest, the season, the tree, the sap, and the cows.
At that time, two parts are considered inauspicious, while two parts are considered auspicious.
Everything—
whether external or internal, one's own or another's, fated or unfated,
for one's own sake or for the sake of others— indeed bears fruit in its entirety. (44)

When the king abandons even one-third of the Dharma on earth, half the earth yields grain, while the other half is enriched by mere chaff; likewise, in the season, the sap, the people, the trees, the work, and the fruit, there is only a quarter of their former excellence. (45–46)
One should understand that there is fruitlessness in three parts, and even in the [remaining] part, there is no certainty.
When the king conducts himself in this manner, then the Kali age (Tiṣya) prevails; by improper means, he oppresses his subjects, and at that time, people become devoted to unrighteousness.
Indeed, the minds of all human beings fall away from their own duty (svadharma).
In the Kali age, unrighteousness prevails mightily in every house and among every person.
Monks will be the property of all castes, and servants will belong to all castes as well.
The intermingling of castes will be most prevalent, and there will be no security of person or property anywhere.
Holy rites will not be found; how then could there be Vedic recitations?
All the seasons will be unpleasant, and people will be afflicted by diseases.
Always regarding untruth as victory, they persist in it.
(51) Indeed, the beauty, voice, and minds of human beings decline;
new diseases arise there, and people die at a young age. (52)
For the most part, many people become widowed and destitute;
generally, subjects are indeed contemptible, being utterly devoid of happiness and peace.
While the rain-god pours down on one side, he causes drought on the other.
In some places there is the appearance of mere grain-particles, and in others the sprouts are scorched;
when the juices have gone to ruin and Kali prevails in the kingdom,
kings indeed become destroyers of their subjects' protection and possessors of the treasury of Kali.
The king is indeed the creator of the Kṛta age, as well as of the Tretā and Dvāpara;
the king alone is the creator of the Kali age and the cause for the transition between the ages.
By bringing about the Kṛta age, the king enjoys the highest heaven.
By initiating the Tretā age, a king enjoys a third part of heaven;
by bringing about the Dvāpara age, a king attains half the happiness;
and by setting the Kali age in motion, he experiences suffering and the loss of his kingdom.
Thus, in the Kali age, a king who is indeed like a *rākṣasa* experiences only sin;
he goes to hell and dwells there for many years.
He consumes the impurity of his subjects and experiences boundless suffering. (59)
He incurs both sin and ill repute, and experiences a succession of miseries.
Therefore, a king should always conduct himself according to the principles of policy as practiced from the Kṛta age onwards;
he should practice the dharmas without delusion and cultivate affection free from bondage.
One should act out of compassion for those who are always suffering, even if they are free from greed, rather than for the sake of gain.
One should speak what is pleasant, not out of sycophancy; one should exert effort, not through boasting.
One should give, but not to an unworthy recipient; one should be profound, but not like a shallow river.
One should not accept anything from all types of people, including the ignoble, nor should one do so improperly.
One’s conduct should never be flawed; one should perform one’s duty and not cause harm.
One should not speak of wealth to the wicked, nor should one speak of one’s own virtues.
One should not take from the poor, nor should one seek shelter with the wicked.
One should not inflict punishment without deliberation, nor should one disclose secrets.
One should not bestow gifts upon the corrupt, nor should one place trust in those who have done harm.
He should also be free from envy toward his wives and even toward his offspring.
He should not indulge excessively in women; he should eat what is wholesome and avoid what is unwholesome.
He should honor those worthy of respect and serve his teachers with devotion.
One should worship the gods with devotion if one desires irreproachable prosperity;
one should exercise skill as required and practice gentleness according to the occasion.
One should offer consolation to gain affection and show favor for the sake of success.
One should strike [the enemy] after having ascertained the truth; having done so, one should not later feel regret.
One should indeed manifest anger, but not otherwise, nor should one adopt excessive mildness.
One should constantly serve the virtuous for the sake of peace and liberation.
For the sake of concentration, the king should constantly serve wise men;
thus, having risen early in the morning in a secluded place, he should cultivate his intellect.
And he should serve me, the inner self, who reveals the truth as it is.
A king ought to cause his sovereignty to blossom with forty virtues, as if he were a god;
therefore, he should be endowed with political wisdom (nīti).
O King, you should always and in every way remember me as a witness within your heart.
Therefore, one should perform everything [with faith], for I am the bestower of the Satya Yuga;
I am the deliverer of one who has set out upon the path of unrighteousness.
I, Janārdana, am the one who raises up him who is submerged in the mire of doubt.
I am the liberator of those who have fallen into the snare of unwholesome actions;
I am the one who reaches the further shore for those who cannot reach it.
Therefore, I am always truly present; I am the refuge to be sought.
Whether it be the king, the subjects, a son, or a daughter, even those engaged in [the study of] duties would never reach the end of the details of dharma. Therefore,
when a matter to be performed by them is doubtful and its conclusion is not reached, [one should act accordingly].
The best of gods, who are learned and firmly established in the Dharma, should be questioned.
Having risen to meet them, grasped their feet, and offered salutations, they should be informed of the matter at hand for the sake of recollecting Nārāyaṇa. (78–79)
Men are devoted to one who protects them, who gives, who is constant in righteousness and unwearied, and who is free from desire and hatred;
likewise to one who has me as the supreme goal, who serves the virtuous, and who exerts effort for my sake. (2.194.80)
For all beings indeed follow him upon whom they have placed their entire trust.
Therefore, by means of the path thus described, the king and his subjects must act;
in this way, there will be happiness in this world and a favorable destiny in the next.
Whether he be a king, a subject, or whoever else among embodied beings here,
he who constantly worships me, the giver of bodies, shall be happy, and no other.
He by whom dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa have been directed toward liberation [is truly successful].
He indeed becomes united with me, Mādhava, by his very nature.
(84) Thus, let everyone perform all actions as being centered on me;
enjoyment and liberation will surely follow—there is no need for doubt in this matter. (85)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa then gave his own mantra;
thereafter the Lord, who grants satisfaction to the minds of all, ceased speaking.
The queen and the princesses then worshipped the Supreme Lord.
At that very moment, five maidens respectfully took his hand.
Having obtained their beloved, the five fair-complexioned women attained supreme bliss.
The king rejoiced exceedingly, and the queen considered her purpose fulfilled.
The worship of Hari was performed by the people, and the dismissal of the assembly took place;
having partaken of food, Hari attained rest in the palace.
All the honored guests also obtained profound rest.
The Blessed One spent the night with the ṛṣi, providing him with protection;
then, having given him the collection of gifts and requisites, he prepared to depart.
The king, accompanied by his army and musical instruments, offered him a grand farewell.

Then, in the morning, after Hari had performed his daily rites, the king honored him with garlands of flowers and provided him with milk and other offerings. Following that great worship, he performed the *ārārtika* ceremony and drank the nectar of the Lord’s feet.
Hari, his chest adorned with rows of necklaces, ascended a celestial chariot.
Then all the great-souled ones mounted the sky-faring vehicles; thereafter, musical instruments were played in abundance.
From there, they proceeded by means of vehicles to the kingdom of Rājagṛha-amala.
King Rājagṛha-amala and the sage Lāṭava,
along with the royal family, went forward to meet them in great splendor.
"Welcome to Śrī Hari, who has brought such great splendor to the army!
(96) Thus they all cried out with shouts, hymns, musical instruments, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, seeing Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot arrived in the sky, they [rejoiced]. (97)
They raised shouts of victory and caused the sound of musical instruments to resound;
all the women sang sweet melodies.
Thus, in that place of honor and fortune, adorned with the beauty of a garden—
On the bank of the river Dvyūnāsari, in the vicinity of the city of Rigā,
Hari caused the celestial chariot to descend by the path shown by the king;
at that time, other celestial chariots also descended from the sky.
"O Rādhikā, the people gazed at Kṛṣṇa with steady eyes;
they honored him with flowers and celebrated him with the sounds of songs and shouts of victory.

(101) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of King Varasiṃha’s procession through the city of Vāśīlā, the worship of Hari, his instruction on the Yugas, his meal, his rest, and after sleep, his departure for the kingdom of Rāyagāma on the thirteenth day before midday," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇī Saṃhitā*.
Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Four.
Chapter 194. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 195.
[Author: Chapter 196.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa descended from the celestial chariot.
The king of Rājagṛha placed garlands of flowers around his neck.
The queen washed the feet of the Supreme Soul,
and the daughters and the royal family worshipped the Imperishable One.
Then the king gave him fragrant perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, flower garlands, and scented sandalwood; he also presented necklaces and clusters of jewels,
and seated that Lord Hari upon a beautiful elephant adorned with the splendor of Ambālikā’s choice.
The multitude gazed upon Kṛṣṇa as he sat upon a high [elephant], who was adorned with ornaments, exceedingly beautiful, four-tusked, white,
and excellent; and the princes held a parasol over his head as well as chowries.
He placed all the other great men upon carts.
The King paraded the Lord of Lords through the royal highway of the city.
The subjects of Riga, having bowed to Hari, honored Him with the most excellent offerings.

With fruits, jewels, garments and the like, gold, silver, and woolen blankets; with flower garlands, diamonds and other such priceless objects—at the city gate, in the square, at the junction, in the marketplace, and by the roadside. (7–8)
In the courtyard, the people honored him in every way with excellent offerings;
the auspicious Gaurīs increased his prosperity with unbroken rice, parched grain, lotuses, and filaments, as well as with heartfelt intentions, glances, and joyful minds. (9)
They welcomed him from all sides with their intellects through songs of praise and chanting. Then the exceedingly radiant Kṛṣṇa went to the excellent royal palace;
there, five princesses eagerly took hold of Kṛṣṇa’s hand.
Then the queen joyfully honored the Lord of Gods, her son-in-law;
the fortunate lady gave various gifts and performed worship.
There, she indeed gave five daughters to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Carrying a sense of fulfillment, the king celebrated an auspicious festival.
Then Hari went to the principal palaces, the houses of the subjects everywhere, and the temples, gardens, and residences of the merchants.
The Lord Śrī Hari was worshipped everywhere there;
likewise, Īśāna, the wives of Brahmā, the Gaurīs, and the great sages—
all were joyfully honored by the citizens in that city.
The family of Kṛṣṇa was worshipped by the fair-complexioned women with offerings of heartfelt devotion.
(16) Then Hari, resplendent with his army, returned to his own abode;
he drank water and held a council there. (17)
And Kṛṣṇa’s beloved, Rādhikā, instructed the people:
"Dharma must always be protected by devotees; through it, wealth is produced.
A living being who is intent solely on wealth perishes before long. (18)
Wealth that is given away or deposited in an improper place perishes;
even when employed for the purpose of violence, it leads only to sin, for it either brings about one's own destruction or makes one a perpetrator of violence. (2.195.20)
The udder of Dharma truly exists; one should never cut it open.
If the udder is severed, one who seeks milk will not obtain any.
Therefore, a person possessed of discernment should take the milk for the sake of the udder itself.
Just as excellent milk is constantly obtained by tending a milch cow,
so too one who enjoys the earth through proper means obtains its fruit; likewise, by enjoying a virtuous cow— namely, one's own body— one obtains the fruit of dharma.

One who possesses discernment should protect grain, gold, and that earth which yields [sustenance], and should constantly protect righteousness, regarding it as a cow that milks forth these blessings.
The protection of living beings is righteousness; compassion is considered its supreme form.
Indeed, by the practice of compassion, the doer crosses the ocean of existence.
One must provide protection for those who are afraid; the fruit of such protection is easily obtained:
it consists of a residence in heaven for ten thousand years. (25–26)

The wise person, performing righteous conduct with compassion, conquers those very worlds that one of good sacrifice, good study, and pure penance conquers. The deities, the ancestors, and the virtuous live by the dharma of giving.
Other beings live by the duty of householders through compassion:
they find comfort in shade, water, or wind during the heat;
and they find comfort in fire, clothing, or the sun during the cold. (28–29)
The mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form, and smell;
it seeks the cool in heat as a beautiful form that is to be attained, granting happiness to the heart.
And in cold, it seeks the warm, a dark form that is to be attained, always granting happiness.
One who is not attached to those enjoyments attains supreme happiness. (3.1) The religious duties of those born in cold regions are different from those of those dwelling in heat;
likewise, for those living in hot places, the fruit arising from bathing is that which bestows auspiciousness. (3.2)
For those residing in cold regions, the fruit resulting from sacrifices and gifts shall be even greater than that.
The gift of wealth is considered to bestow nourishment for the satisfaction of the body.
Indeed, wealth here is of two kinds: that in the form of riches which truly grants happiness.
But the benefit for others, consisting of liberation, bestows eternal happiness.
(34) For one who grants fearlessness, the fruit is the most supreme of all;
indeed, there is no gift equal to the gift of life, and the gift of liberation is superior even to that. (35)
I am indeed Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the beloved of Svāmī Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha.
I bestow the gift of liberation, the gift of life, wealth, and so forth.
These three—superior, middling, and inferior—are thus distinguished.
The gift that bestows liberation is the supreme gift; it should be given in every way on this earth.
That gift which bestows eternal bliss must indeed be accepted.
By accepting anything else, disease arises, but in the acceptance of the gift that bestows liberation, it perishes.
In the granting of liberation, the gift of the Veda indeed makes one become Brahman.
When the tree of the Veda is protected, it surely yields honey and gold.
In the realm of creation, there is no gift superior to the gift of the Veda.
The gift of liberation is the gift of Brahman; I am Brahman, and I give myself. I am Dharma, I am in the form of Artha, I am Mokṣa, and I am the giver of Mokṣa.
Being propitiated, I indeed bestow upon the seeker of liberation my very self, which is the essence of liberation.
He who would kill a woman, or Brahman, or kill a virtuous person out of malice—
by the sins he commits, he is made destitute.
Rudra, the Lord God, destroys those who are wicked and sinful.
The Lord Rudra, who is my very form and the self of all, protects the virtuous.
(42) Rudra is declared to be one's own innate Self; when he acts spontaneously, he destroys sin.
He shall destroy sin, hatred, deceit, and the like, as well as self-destruction and other such evils. (44)
Self-destruction is the destruction of liberation; one should never commit it.
One should always be intent on one's own true self-interest, seeking liberation through union with Me.
One should not give rise to the notion of a physical body and should abandon all dualistic states.
If dry wood is mixed with wet wood, even the latter is burned;
likewise, if the self were mixed with the body, it too would become subject to suffering.
However, one who possesses discernment can somehow avoid being mixed with those who commit evil deeds.
One who desires liberation must abandon passion and hatred, which are forms of evil;
one who desires prosperity must also abandon negligence and delusion, which are likewise evil.
The world of merit is heaven itself, and the self is happy when it is considered as being in heaven.
In this context, the world of sin is hell, and the self is considered miserable when it is cast downward. (49) The earth supports both the virtuous and the wicked alike;
likewise, the sun imparts its heat equally to both the virtuous and the wicked. (2.195.50)
Water indeed brings satisfaction to both the virtuous and the non-virtuous;
the wind provides life-force and touch equally to all embodied beings.
Water purifies everyone—both the virtuous and the non-virtuous—with impartiality.
In this world it is thus, but in the world of results there is a distinction:
for one who possesses merit, cool water approaches; for one devoid of merit, the water does not even come within the range of vision. (52–53)
For the sake of the meritorious, the earth is provided with soft carpets;
for the sake of the meritless, the earth is filled with thorns and pebbles.
For the sake of the meritorious, the wind is cool and touched by fragrances.
For one who has committed no merit, the wind becomes exceedingly cruel, filled with intense poison;
yet for one possessed of merit, the sun bestows its heat only as required.
For one who has committed no merit, the sun becomes a burner that reduces everything to ashes.
Thus, in this world abounding in fruits, there always exists such an interval:
a world of merit, rich in honey, where one eats ghee and is adorned with gold;
where one eats nectar, is filled with joy, and is free from old age and death.
The world of the wicked is hell, a place of intense torment and suffering;
pervaded by hunger and thirst, it is a treasury of grief where one falls under the power of death at every moment.
He who desires to go to that world has indeed fallen away from discernment.

Indeed, he who desires to go to the world of merit is one possessed of discernment; and that wise man who wishes to go to the eternal, supreme world, my abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara), is truly the best among those seeking liberation.
The Brāhmaṇa who performs daily worship attains that world. The Kṣatriya who is constantly charitable, performs sacrifices, protects, and worships also goes there.
And the Vaiśya who is industrious, helpful, and righteous likewise goes there. (6.1–6.2)
Even a Śūdra who serves, is devoted, is contented, and eats only the remnants [of the meal] goes [to the highest state].
In each and every instance, constant reflection characterized by devotion to Me is prescribed.
That person who, being self-restrained, carries out the command of the Guru without faltering— || 63 ||
Success certainly comes to him through the power of the Guru; of this there is no doubt.
(64) Furthermore, that which is to be performed should be especially concise and essential, by which success swiftly bestows the highest good upon the embodied being. (65)
Those for whom the Blessed Lord is to be protected, and for whom His glorification is to be protected—my devotees as well as they are to be protected; they are always to be protected by me.
Those whose leaders are my devotees, and who are virtuous and devoted to Brahman—I am indeed their protector.
Those daughters who receive alms in your house must always be protected by me;
for them there shall be no fear from Time, nor from Karma, nor from Māyā, nor from Yama.
And I am ever present in their houses as a woman, and I am always worshipped in their hearts.
The king should always protect the virtuous, for they, when protected, in turn protect him.
May their blessing be a bestower of light and a destroyer of bondage.
[May it be attained] through charity, austerity, sacrifice, devotion, self-restraint, and service.
Whether they be virtuous ascetics or householders, those who desire their own welfare [should seek him].
He is the one who provides a shore where there is no shore, and he who provides a boat where there is no boat;
by depending upon him, people find happiness in this most terrible cycle of existence.
Whether he be a renunciant or a householder, a man or a woman, one should worship that virtuous person, regarding him as a savior and a kinsman;
likewise, one should honor the Supreme Lord, the holy one, the giver of knowledge, and the master who is the Guru.
One should honor a virtuous and faithful wife, for the guru is indeed the bestower of liberation.
What is the use of those bulls that cannot carry loads, or of a cow that yields no milk?
What benefit is there from a barren wife, or what purpose is served by a king who does not protect?
What use have I for that wealth or for this body, when I cannot serve the holy man?
What use for a withered kingdom, or for prosperity seized by bandits?
What use for an object of enjoyment devoid of affection, or for a birth that does not grant liberation? (75)
Just as an elephant made of wood, or a tiger made of leather;
just as a eunuch, or a field of saline soil, or one who is devoid of discernment;
just as the thundering of clouds, or a warrior class (kṣatra) bereft of strength. //76-77//
Just as a vow devoid of charity, a devotee devoid of affection, and a guru devoid of knowledge and so forth—all these are useless.
Everything that is endowed with these is fruitful and bestows liberation; everything bereft of them is fruitless.
Where there is no attainment of the Self, that is indeed called a loss.
The attainment of the Self is the supreme attainment; it is the surrender to the Supreme Self.
Through that, the attainment of liberation occurs, for that is considered the attainment of Truth. (2.195.79–80)
May people always serve the virtuous and constantly worship me;
may they protect their own dharma and also attain my abode.
May there be well-being for you all in this world and in the next.
Having spoken thus, the king then ceased;
he worshipped that Lord, and the subjects honored him with great respect using many articles.
Then the queen, accompanied by her daughter, performed worship to Śrī Hari.
The three maidens, devoted to their husband, took the hand of Hari;
having obtained Śrī Puruṣottama, they made their birth meaningful.
And the king provided a meal for Hari and his family.
Then the king himself enjoyed the great honors [offered] by those very [guests].
Together with his subjects, he held a magnificent festival at night;
he caused dances to be performed along with instrumental music, devotional songs, and other such arts.
Having obtained a fine meal at night, Hari and the others rested; then,
having risen in the morning to the sounds of musical instruments and auspicious chants,
Hari and the others, having performed their daily rites, became ready to depart.
There, Hari quickly bestowed the mantra requested by the subjects.
The king gave much gold as a dowry to Śrī Hari, and he also presented various gifts; and Hari likewise gave wealth at that time.
The king offered appropriate worship to the sage Lātavāya and then granted him leave to depart after he had finished drinking milk.
Then Hari, hearing shouts of victory, quickly ascended his celestial chariot.
And he was in the sky together with his entire family.
At that time, all other vehicles were also in the sky.
The king, along with his army, offered him the honor appropriate for the occasion.
Then King Phenatantu and the sage Phālanāda arrived to bring the Lord of the virtuous back to their own kingdom;
they were quickly entreated by Hari with great respect.
Having offered blessings to all from the sky, he then departed.
Other celestial chariots as well then quickly traveled through the air, crossing over Khāḍikā and the great kingdom of Phenatantu. 94–95.
On the charming bank of the river Tūrṇanayā where it meets [another stream],
in the city named Trinayā, within the garden groves adjacent to it,
the king went forward and honored the army.
Following the path shown by the king, Hari brought down his own celestial chariot into the garden near the royal palace;
likewise, other chariots then descended from the sky. (97–98)
Then musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose;
a rain of flowers fell from the vicinity of the celestial chariots for the sake of the subjects.
O Rādhikā, the people sang songs of praise to Gaurī.
The King offered a most excellent welcome with excellent mechanical substances.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Feeding, Resting, Spending the Night, and the Departure for the Kingdom of King Phenatantu after Drinking Milk and Other Substances on the Morning of the Fourteenth Day," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; then the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, descended from His celestial chariot onto a beautiful and auspicious horse-drawn carriage. 1.
King Phenatantu shone resplendent upon a throne rich with golden luster, adorned with parasols and chowries,
and provided with a woolen, variegated rug and a footstool;
there he worshipped Kṛṣṇa with garlands of flowers.
With sandalwood paste and other priceless, excellent articles that lead to heaven,
the queen, the royal family, the sage Phālanāda,
and the subjects likewise worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the husband of Gaurī.
Accompanied by his army, the king, increasing the welcome,
caused Hari to be paraded all around the city of Trinayā.
At the city gate of the capital, the leading citizens honored him.
On the royal highway, the king’s servants, the guild-leaders at the crossroads and other places,
and the subjects— both buyers and sellers—
at every marketplace, [honored him] with sandalwood, saffron, divine flowers, and ornaments made of bilva fruit. (6–7)
Then, at every spot, the fair-complexioned women greatly celebrated him;
they bowed to Acyuta with unbroken grains of rice and parched grain,
and by the sight of Hari, they then obtained the fruit of procreation.

And upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, the fair-complexioned women obtained the reward of having eyes as long as those of a bull. At that time, the entire city of Trinayanapura became crowded with people; for the purpose of beholding Hari, everyone abandoned all other activities.

Thus, in all places without exception, Mādhava granted his vision; then, having been honored by the king, he departed for the royal palace. There, the Blessed One himself gave instruction to the subjects.
Shining brilliantly upon a golden lion-throne, he was exceedingly radiant.
(1-2) The mind, which is constantly dependent on the latent impressions of saṃsāra, must be conquered;
likewise, the senses must especially be conquered from their objects. (13)
Embodied beings must constantly turn away from sense objects;
they should not engage in vain thoughts, having abandoned the Supreme Lord.
A day should not be spent in vain without devotion to the Blessed One.
Life should not be spent in vain without serving the saintly;
people should not undergo exertion in vain without the company of the virtuous;
and speech should never be rendered useless without the chanting of my glories. (15–16)
One's physical life should not be spent in vain without offering [the fruits of one's actions] unto Me;

indeed, the night should not be passed fruitlessly without meditating upon Hari, my own self. Wealth should not be made useless except for the construction of temples dedicated to Me and similar pious works.
The self must not be employed in vain without me, the Supreme Lord.
(18) All of *māyā* would become useless if I were not present there;
likewise, everything would be in vain wherever I am not worshipped. (19)

When I, Kṛṣṇa, am worshipped, everything becomes worshipped; for when even a small amount of wealth is offered to me, all wealth is thereby offered, since I am beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa). Devotees who possess human bodies should always remain free from the influence of the material qualities.
Freedom from malice, absence of pride, modesty, endurance, self-restraint, tranquility, truthfulness, fortitude, mindfulness, self-control, cessation [of worldly activity],
and lack of greed— these qualities, when dedicated to Kṛṣṇa, lead me to the state beyond all qualities (nirguṇya). (21–22)

By that [devotion], liberation will surely occur; for I am the giver of liberation, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), yet endowed with all sovereign powers, wonders, and divine attributes. Having bestowed this qualitylessness upon the devotee, I deliver them across [the ocean of existence]; of this there is no doubt.

Non-violence, truthful speech, kindness, self-restraint, and compassion—this is declared to be great austerity; by this I am always satisfied. Indeed, the drying up of the mind is far superior to the drying up of the body.
In my view, service consisting of the drying up of the mind is the highest form of servitude;
remaining in accordance with [the Lord’s] command is, for me, superior to all else.
A person marked by that command is indeed always near, even if far away.
It is my view that one who does not carry out orders is far away even when in close proximity.
Therefore, the expectations of the guru, parents, Hari, one’s wife, husband, and the circle of venerable elders who possess specialized knowledge must always be fulfilled. (27–28)
Indeed, the Vedas were composed by me, as were those commands and injunctions;
they are repeatedly remembered by the sages for the welfare of embodied beings.
They are taught to the subjects, and they abide following them.
Those who, having enjoyed numerous heavens, indeed attain liberation—
such sages one should honor and worship both in word and deed;
one should do what is pleasing to them and never perform anything that is displeasing.
The sages and the divine beings are indeed my very own forms;
in every respect, they are treasuries of virtues, identical with my own nature, and bestowers of liberation.
Indeed, neither fault nor virtue can be discerned when examined within them.
He who thus conducts himself constantly within the circle of the assembly of holy and virtuous people—
wherever he may be situated— is here considered to be established for eternal glory.
Having gone to the highest heaven, my own abode, he is indeed deemed to have attained it.
This world is a locus of calamities, bestowing misfortune at every moment;
yet, through the attainment of the yoga of the wise, those calamities dissolve.
Calamities are of two kinds: external and internal.
All [these] manifest perpetually, either by themselves or through another. Those that are internal certainly arise from one's own performed action;
those that are external, however, arise from another and may even exist without [one's own] action.
The internal [enemies] are subdued by endurance, by knowledge, and by perseverance;
the external ones are overcome by conciliation, by compliance, and by gifts. (38) One should constantly give food according to one's capacity, for the giving of material goods is indeed required.
Rectitude, gentleness, great forbearance, honoring [the worthy], and so forth;
even the act of pleasing others serves as a warder-off of external calamities.
However, the blessing of the virtuous is considered the destroyer of all calamities. (2.196.39–40)
Taking refuge in Śrī Hari is considered the bestower of all happiness;
for there, where I am well-worshipped by my devotees, protected, and sustained, I am an ocean of bliss. (41)
There is not even a trace of misfortune where I am the ocean of bliss.
Wherever I am not present, there thieves and evildoers slay the lord of the city;
they slaughter the subjects and destroy the authority of the virtuous when there is no protector.
In former times, there was a sage named Kākalata who dwelt among the trees.
He instructed a crow in living together with humans.
Many crows, however, remained in his tree-cage.
Through association, he mastered the science of crows after a long time;
and gradually, through incidental contact, he came to know all forms of speech.
He discerns auspicious omens and recognizes those that are inauspicious.
Having placed crows in a cage, he wandered through the city;
he went to his dwelling in the city of Kosala, repeatedly speaking to people as one who perceives their fortune and seeks news. (47)
"Study the science of the crow; my crows announce [the future] to me.
"I know the future, the past, and the present.
Thus he wandered for four months through the city, from house to house.
He observed the wicked deeds of all the king's servants:
all those royal attendants were seizing wealth through unjust means;
they consumed liquor and meat, and being devoid of virtue, they committed theft.
And all the subjects, being merciless, oppressed him in secret.
Even his own followers desired to kill the king in order to obtain the kingdom.
Having learned all this through the speech of a crow, he went to the king.
He told the king, "I am omniscient," and spoke regarding the conduct of servants and others.
At the king’s command, Kākapa said to the minister:
"This property was stolen by you, and this other deed was done by you there. (53)
"This royal treasury here has been taken and destroyed by you.
Furthermore, these other followers of yours are also stealers of the treasury.
Thus this crow speaks; what I have said is the truth.
The king, having seized them all, demanded the treasury wealth.
All that was born of his subjects was true; nothing false was spoken.
Thereafter, those leading men and others were punished by that king.
Other servants, seized with fear of the punishment called "the crow's cry," pierced the sleeping brahmin with arrows at night. Then,
other crows emerged from the cage through the broken lattice.
Having observed a dead crow, the brahmin went before the king and said:
"O King, I beg for your welfare and likewise for your safety.
Whatever has been uttered by the crow, I have spoken it to you as the truth at your command. (59)
Your servants have been punished by you, and others have become afraid because of that.
Those wicked servants of yours, who are hostile to me, have killed this crow of mine.
Where there is no powerful king, such is the state I have come to.
"The crow's property has been destroyed here by me, and other crows have likewise departed.
From you, indeed, nothing has been obtained other than the fear for my life.
For kings have many friends, and they likewise have many enemies. (62)
For one who is addicted to attachment to the *rajas* quality, destruction first sets in.
Indeed, a king must not practice heedlessness exclusively;
for he who places his trust in a king who is heedless perishes. (63–64)
For through negligence a king may stumble, and when he has stumbled, there is no life.
A wise man should serve the king, truly thinking, "I am as good as dead.
[He must remain vigilant] against improper speech, lack of instruction, poor conduct, and mismanagement.
A wise man, remaining suspicious of improper sitting, improper walking, gestures, and bodily movements, should conduct himself with caution in the presence of a king;
for if the king is enraged like the fire Vaiśvānara, he might consume one utterly.
Therefore, I shall not dwell here; it is only for my own safety.
But hear from me, O King, what happens where there is no king:
there, calamities incited by the wicked arise among the subjects themselves. (68)
Wherever the king is weak, a non-seer, ignorant, and lacking discrimination,
there indeed heavy calamities befall even the subjects.
In your kingdom, servants dwell who are solely intent on taking.
O King, out of fear of those who desire the destruction of living beings and who steal by means of their ruin,
or those who seek eternal sovereignty through the annihilation of existence,
I shall go to another refuge.
Just as that crow was struck by them with an aimed arrow,
so it may be for me, or for you, or neither of us may have met the course of the shaft.
Having resolved thus— whether it shall be so or not— I have crossed over [the danger] because of my gift to the crows.
Your kingdom is like a wicked river that brings about death, filled with many crocodiles, large fish, and sharks, and teeming with swarms of *timiṃgila* monsters.
Indeed, your kingdom is a dense thicket composed entirely of darkness.
"Even you cannot trust here; how much less can I?
Therefore, there is no auspicious dwelling here where death indeed stands at the forefront. For in this place, the virtuous are slain while the evildoers are protected. (71–72)
It is not fitting for one who desires his own welfare to remain here for long;
for your kingdom is like a honey-trap, your food is mixed with poison, and it is surrounded by venomous snakes and devoured by wicked men. (77)
O King, purify that [body] which is infested with dogs, vultures, and jackals!
Your own followers—nourished by you, appointed to office in your kingdom, and protected by you—are now plotting against you alone, seeking to kill you. (78–79)
"For your sake, my crow was killed by those evil-minded ones;
therefore, O Great King, I am going away, for there is no other reason.
For one who seeks security must break with all enemies who harbor ill will. (2.196.80)
Thus addressed, the king spoke to the truth-telling Kākin:
"I shall provide for your protection with abundant hospitality; I will satisfy you, O protector of crows. Stay further in my house. (8.1–8.2)
To the king who was speaking thus, Kākapā said:
"O King, do not commit such a rash act, nor exert such haste here.
Instead, seize them one by one with a firm staff and weaken them."
"Therefore, slay each man according to his specific fault.
When this is done, victory will be yours; it will not come by acting rashly otherwise.
For many sharp thorns, when joined together, can kill even a mighty elephant."
For many weak men, when united, can harm even a powerful king;
many invisible defects destroy the master of the body.
Therefore, enemies should indeed be destroyed one by one, like individual defects.

When this had been said, the king acted accordingly and indeed struck down his enemies in due order. Having cleared the kingdom of all thorns, the sovereign of Śrīkosala subsequently ruled the earth, having made it beautiful through virtuous deeds.
Having performed vows, austerities, and the rites of sacred fords, and having rendered service to his guru and to the virtuous,
he performed divine worship and departed for the abode that is the source of happiness.
Likewise, there was indeed a king named Kauśala in the city of the body.
This self exists, afflicted by the anger and other passions of the foremost of robbers.
The Guru, like a crow, having led the crows that are the scriptures before the Lord of the City, speaks again and again of the wickedness of anger and the rest. (2.196.90–91)
The defects are destroyers of the scriptures, exceedingly firm and powerful;
united together, they seek to slay the self that is situated within illusion.
Having understood this, the king himself must remain possessed of courage.
The defects should be destroyed by one's own essential nature, gradually and very slowly.
(93) Then, in a kingdom free from thorns, one should perform service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
By that, great bliss arises, and liberation becomes one's kingdom in this very life. (94)
Thus, O Rādhikā, Hari, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having instructed her in this manner, ceased speaking and bestowed the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
At that moment, the two daughters of the king were in the assembly hall together with the king.

Having worshipped her supreme beloved, she took the hand of Śrī Hari according to the marriage rites. Once she had obtained the Lord and both were fulfilled, the king and all the subjects indeed honored Hari.
Then the king had various kinds of food prepared;
everyone rested in the evening, and at night they held a great festival.
Rising in the morning, the Blessed One took Phālanā in every way.
The Supreme Lord gave him his entire possession, including his wife;
having performed his daily rites and drunk milk, he set his mind on departing.
Just then, King Stokahoma approached to take Kṛṣṇa with him.
Having taken leave of Phenatantu, Hari quickly became ready;
accepting the worship offered by Rājadatta, he ascended his celestial chariot (vimāna).
All the other honored guests likewise then ascended their celestial chariots.
Then, the sounds of clarionets mingled with shouts of victory;
joyous cries produced by the subjects pervaded the sky and all directions. Hearing those sounds, Śrī Hari proceeded on his way.
Having left behind a small kingdom with a king, a sweet-faced realm,
and the coastal region of Samudrakhaḍika, he beheld the auspicious land of Saubhaga. Indeed, the king went forward there to welcome Hari.
Then the sage named Svādana also departed from the sky ahead of him.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Phentantu’s Arrival in the City of Trinayā, the Descent of Śrī Hari, His Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Feeding, Resting, and after Nightfall, on the Morning of the New Moon of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, following the drinking of milk, the arrival of King Stokahoma and his kingdom," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
