Chapter 198 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Svādana-Ṛṣi and King Stokahoma,
having descended from the sky, arrived at the vast Mahodyāna grove.
They went quickly to the vicinity of Umāpuri for the purpose of welcoming [him];
taking the army with them, they remained in the garden awaiting him.
Following the path shown by the king, he brought down the celestial chariot.
Hari and the others brought down their celestial chariots into that garden. Then musical instruments were played, shouts of victory arose,
the people raised cries of joy, and songs of praise were sung.
The celestial chariot was made to flourish by the subjects with fruits, flowers, and other offerings.
Hari was honored with parched grain, unbroken rice, and so forth, and received a formal welcome.
Then Śrī Hari emerged from the middle of the chariot and stepped outside.
The king indeed worshipped with devotion using golden flower-crests, necklaces made of jewels, clusters of flowers, sandalwood water,
various types of fragrant essences, and by washing his feet.
Accompanied by his family, he also drank the water from the [Lord’s] feet;
likewise, together with the ministers and the subjects,
the king then indeed honored the parents of Hari.
The queen worshipped all the supreme goddesses who are dear to Brahmā;
the king honored the god Īśāna, and the daughters worshipped Gaurī. The sage honored the great sages, and the king then honored the Lord Hari.
He seated [the king] upon a palanquin adorned with gold like Śeṣa,
resplendent with a thousand hoods and carried by sixty men.
The king then seated the others upon new wagons.
Then, while all the quarters resounded with the blare of trumpets, songs of glory, and beautiful melodies, Hari, graced by a magnificent welcome,
wandered through Umāpurī, purifying every spot.
At the city gate, he was honored by royal officers with ornaments of jewels;
in the middle of the city, by the best of servants and merchants on the great highway;
and in the courtyards of the houses, as well as everywhere else, by the common people at that time.
Honored and celebrated, Kṛṣṇa departed, bestowing his sight upon them;
then, having received worship, he went with his army to his own residence.
Urged by the king, he arrived and performed the drinking of water and other rites.

The family members performed the drinking of water and other rites, as did others as well. (16) Then, having seated himself upon the royal throne in the assembly hall, Kṛṣṇa sat down and gave instruction. (17)
The subjects must always act for the sake of the Supreme Lord;
the kings must always act for the sake of the Inner Controller within the subjects.
Both must always act for the sake of their mutual Inner Controller.
"May they, with concentrated minds, worship me as Virāṭ in both states;
by that, your victory shall come in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should always honor the virtuous and abandon all rivalry toward them. (2.197.19–20)
One should not abandon dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or anger.
One should likewise be free from pride, truthful in speech, and self-controlled.
For one who conducts himself in this manner, there arises eternal prosperity.

Splendor, fortitude, forgiveness, purity, affection, steadfastness, and constancy—indeed, one should abide by relying upon these qualities for the sake of liberation. One who has perfected wisdom, who is intelligent, learned, and who perceives the Self in all things; 22–23.
One who is purified by all good deeds, wise regarding himself and others, whose soul is a friend to all, and who is free from passion, deserves to go to my world.
One who speaks the truth, is endowed with virtuous conduct, is modest, and remembers the Brahman [deserves to go there]. //24//
One who is contented and devoted to the vow of truth deserves to go to the world of Malla.
A person who practices consoling speech, adorned with virtues even in a single word,
shall obtain happiness everywhere throughout all creations.
Sāman is declared to be my praise, and it is also that very same thing as consolation;
even the consolation of people is mine alone, residing within their hearts.
I am constantly pleased by that [sāman] through its recitation, glorification, and practice.
Kindness in a single word always bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Indeed, when kindness—gentle, smooth, and sweet—is properly practiced, I dwell upon the tongue. (28–29)
Through pure conduct, I dwell within his heart;
and by means of both, having come into his presence, I become as if within his range of perception.
Thus, I am ever present and indeed perform what is auspicious for him.
Thus I always abide among righteous people.
(3.1) And wherever righteous people have made their own dwelling, there I dwell in secret for the sake of their protection. (3.2)
One should perform sacrifices with those rituals, and one should give gifts to those worthy of charity.
One must protect the helpless, and one must not do anything that obstructs the Dharma.
[One should likewise provide for] the wretched, the helpless, the elderly, women, and those who serve others.
Indeed, the righteous must provide security, well-being, and a means of livelihood.
(34) At the appropriate times, clothing, vessels, and food should be given to those in the various stages of life by the subjects, as well as by the king and the merchant guild leader. (35)

One who desires his own welfare should indeed honor with beds, seats, and food that virtuous man who renounces all objects for the sake of others, who bestows liberation, and who is grounded in the scriptures;
even robbers and assassins place their trust in such a person.
In the Guru, who destroys sin, is pure, is virtuous, bestows liberation,
and brings about all that is auspicious, even those dwelling in the forest, wild animals, lions, and even cruel beings place their trust. (37–38)
They find peace right where there is the dwelling of the virtuous;
even the seasons become endowed with goodness upon meeting the virtuous.
Beings born in the presence of the virtuous are themselves endowed with goodness.

"Since I dwell daily within the hearts of the virtuous, by serving them, my own auspicious service is accomplished. Whatever fruit arises from their service is indeed the fruit of serving the virtuous."
One who seeks dharma and yearns for liberation should constantly serve the virtuous according to place, time, intellect, and strength.
One should serve those who possess security in such a way that one’s own ultimate good may be attained.
A virtuous person should perform actions in such a way that he may remain contented.
Those who show favor to living beings and instruct them in virtue and other such qualities—
those virtuous ones must always be protected in the kingdom by a wise king.
A wealthy man should constantly honor with drink, clothing,
and food that virtuous person who governs the subjects and is an auspicious teacher of dharma.
Generally, a wealthy and righteous man should honor those endowed with austerity.
A wise man should always protect virtuous persons within his own city.

(46) Those who uphold truth, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, devotion, righteousness, and dispassion are considered virtuous men; they are regarded as the ones who ensure the security of the kingdom. (47)
"What is my flaw? To whom am I attached? What means of practice should I perform?
From where might a fault take hold of me?"—thus should the wise man reflect.
Indeed, the king should protect the virtuous, for they are the removers of all faults.
A king exists for the sake of dharma, for the purpose of protecting the world. (49) If a king practices dharma, he is fit for divinity;
if a king practices adharma, he is fit for hell. (2.197.50)
Living beings abide in the Dharma; the Dharma abides in kings.
That king who governs it well is considered a protector.
A king whose soul is supremely righteous is called a virtuous Dharma.
The accomplishment of one’s goals is seen for those who abide in their own duty (svadharma).
People follow that very same auspicious dharma;
for the virtuous who are endowed with righteousness, there is no sense of "this is mine. (52–53)
The virtuous sages, having observed the well-being of the world on all sides, created that great being [saying]: "This shall indeed be Dharma.
He in whom Dharma shines forth is considered the king, the protector.
When Dharma increases, all beings increase in happiness;
when it diminishes, they decline. Therefore, one should protect Dharma, for Dharma was created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the prosperity of all beings.
Dharma prevails through the virtuous; therefore, the virtuous must indeed be protected.
Since the virtuous are the source of Dharma, one should always honor them.
[One should protect them] from one who is intoxicated, from one who is heedless, from one who is a mere child, from one who is insane, and from one who is addicted to vices.
Because they are pure, the virtuous always remain far away from those who are illusory, deceitful, rogue, lecherous, and fraudulent;
for they rescue those who are submerged and lead even me to the Supreme.
Therefore, the virtuous indeed ought to be protected, honored, and served.
One should avoid excessive renunciation, pride, hypocrisy, and anger.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the fourfold cycle of the ages.
All things are dependent upon the king; indeed, the king alone is said to be the Yuga.
A king who is virtuous in soul is called the Kṛta Yuga;
but when the king becomes unrighteous in soul, the virtuous truly depart.
Indeed, calamities will arise on all sides in that kingdom;
when the king has become unrighteous, all living beings perish.
He who has no teacher in dharma and does not consult the virtuous—
One who does not see beyond himself does not enjoy happiness for long.
A king who makes his teacher paramount in matters of dharma, who personally abides in the dharma of the virtuous,
and who holds dharma as his primary concern, enjoys imperishable happiness.
"Therefore, both the subjects and the king should always abide by the armor of dharma and associate with the virtuous, whereby there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having spoken thus to Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa then indeed ceased speaking.
The king honored them, and the subjects honored him with respect. Then, having fulfilled her mother’s command, the daughter of Stokahoma took the hand of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Gaurī, having performed her duties, celebrated the royal festival;
she fed Hari, her family, and the honored guests.
Then all the subjects took their rest and went to their respective homes.
During the night, the king caused great festivities to take place, including dances and other performances. After that, they took their meals and then rested.
Rising in the morning, the Blessed One performed his daily rites and was well-honored.
Having drunk the milk and other refreshments, Acyuta was ready to depart;
the resplendent king gave him gifts along with an army,
and he also granted him leave, while the sounds of trumpets then arose.
Mounting his celestial chariot and hearing the auspicious sounds of victory,
as well as the songs of fair-complexioned women sung by all the inhabitants of the vimānas,
Hari proceeded swiftly through the sky toward the city of King Kāṣṭhāyana.
The king likewise proceeded ahead with his chariot through the vast kingdom, which extended to the edge of the ocean and was free from the rain of arrows,
toward the vicinity of the city of Tunnayāma,
which was shaded by trees in a grove.
Nāradamuni also went forth to welcome Hari.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the king set out at the head of his army;
likewise, all the subjects arrived for the sake of honoring Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Small Fire-Sacrifice (*stokahoma*), the Descent of Hari in Umāpurī, His Wandering, Worship, Teaching, Eating, Resting at Night, and the Arrival of King Kāṣṭhayāna from his Kingdom on the Morning of the First Day of the Bright Half of the Month of Bhādrapada," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*. [Author: Chapter 199 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhā, King Kāṣṭhayāna [approached] Bālakṛṣṇa at that time.
He commanded Hari to descend together with the celestial chariot.
Hari brought the chariot down from the sky into the garden;
at that time, other chariots as well descended from the heavens.

The military instruments were sounded, and cries of victory then arose. Krishna Narayana, honored by the subjects with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, flowers, necklaces, and other offerings, rejoiced. (3) He was worshipped with sandalwood, *akṣata*, flowers, pearl necklaces, and the like.
Worshipped by the king, the subjects, and the sage,
the Lord descended from his celestial chariot, filled with serenity.
Bestowing fearlessness with love, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa extended his hand.
The great king Kāṣṭhayāna placed a necklace upon the neck of Hari, one enriched with the value of ten million diamonds; he worshipped His feet with sandalwood paste,
drank the water arising from His grace, and honored His entire family as well.
Filled with joy, he seated Kṛṣṇa upon a chariot drawn by dark horses.
Then, at night, he held up the umbrella while the two princes held the auspicious chowries;
at that time, the shouts of victory resounded, amplified by the radiance [of the lamps].
The Lord was honored with garlands of white flowers and unbroken grains of rice;
then the King properly seated the other great men upon various auspicious vehicles, both high and low.
In the city of Tunnavāya, the king led Śrī Hari on a procession;
there, in the midst of the city gate, the Supreme Lord was worshipped by the king,
honored with five principal lamps, and consecrated with the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Honored by the merchants in the central courtyard of the city,
and honored by the subjects at the market stalls with coins for fruit;
and in every house, worshipped by the Gaurīs as the sustainer of life.
Having thus wandered through the entire city himself, the Blessed One came to his own residence, the palace in the royal garden. There,
the Blessed One himself presided over a delightful assembly for the people.
Having received worship from the subjects, he instructed them in what is beneficial:
"The ocean of worldly existence is ever fraught with cold, heat, and other such conditions;
it touches those who are submerged within it with the claws and teeth of the crocodiles that are the defects. (15)
Indeed, the virtuous become like boats for the purpose of crossing over;
holding others by the hand, they ferry across those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
In the hearts of those in whom the Blessed One, the bestower of liberation, dwells eternally, [I too reside].
Those virtuous and steadfast ones are worthy of worship, for they are considered by me to be my very heart;
through the side of the virtuous, there shall be victory both in this world and in the ultimate sense.
Indeed, victory joined with the unrighteous is unstable and does not lead to heaven.
He indeed sinks into the terrible mire of saṃsāra as a conqueror—
[he] who, by violating dharma, by overstepping the bounds of propriety, and by transgressing the words of the virtuous, should seek to bring about his own happiness therein. (2.198.20)
In whose home the people are gracious, guests are honored with worship,
and the family is content, Nārāyaṇa truly resides there.
So too do the virtuous, the elders, the teachers, and others worthy of reverence.
I dwell in the house of him by whom truth is honored.
By the restraint of the wicked, the gathering together of the virtuous,
through devotion, sacrifice, charity, and service, I am always won over.

He who fights for the sake of the virtuous, for the sake of liberation, or for the sake of Hari—having offered himself as a sacrificial post (yūpa)—attains glory with infinite dakṣiṇā. He who has abandoned pride and other such traits for my sake, and who is consecrated for my sake; ||| 24 ||
He indeed attains all desires, imperishable and yielding every object;
having abandoned the wicked, he should always cultivate the company of the virtuous.
One should recognize the wicked through their dispositions and by signs that fall within the range of indirect observation.
He speaks of faults behind one's back and finds fault with one's good qualities;
when others praise them, he remains silent or turns his face away.
He sighs, bites his lips, and shakes his head.

He acts repeatedly with a troubled mind and speaks perversely; he plots behind one's back but does not speak when face to face. Having spoken one way, he tramples it down, saying again and again, "It is not like this. (28–29)
In sitting, lying down, or traveling, he behaves contrary to one’s wishes;

in such a case, his wickedness is to be recognized through living together with him. (2.198.30) Suffering when [the other] suffers and joy when [the other] is dear—this much is the definition of a friend.
But the characteristics of wicked enemies should always be understood as the opposite.
(3.1) The virtuous, who are true friends and excellent companions seeking one's own welfare, who destroy evil and bestow liberation—they should be especially served. (3.2)
One should personally conduct oneself with discernment in his presence;
indeed, one should cultivate discernment within the heart regarding impermanent things.
(33) All this, which is nourished by my egoism, is entirely impermanent.
Whatever name-and-form exists, all that does not exist hereafter.

Thus, one who possesses discernment is never distressed when [something] is lost, nor does he remain joyful when it is obtained; for what cause for celebration is there in that which is transitory? (34–35)

Even when fallen into calamity, one possessed of discernment does not suffer. For that which has been, that which has passed, and that which is yet to come—whatever exists in the present—all goes away as if laughing; none of it shall remain.
Thus, one who has known what is to be known is no longer subject to sorrow. Knowing that what has come must perish, who indeed would grieve?
Having understood that all this has its root in sorrow, one should abandon sorrow. (37–38)
Where indeed have the elders gone—those fathers, grandfathers, and the rest?
Knowing that all things stable do not exist, who would truly grieve?
Children, those of middle age, and the elderly likewise live for long periods.
Hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of years will pass before they die; of this there is no doubt.
Even so, embodied beings do not relinquish their great craving.
Having reflected thus, one should abandon that craving and do what is beneficial for oneself.
The future does not belong to me, nor does the past exist for me;
nothing exists for me upon my forehead. Therefore, one should always be virtuous.
Even those who are not wealthy live, and kings likewise do so.
Among kings there is an abundance of disease, whereas among the poor it is not; therefore, the one without wealth is happy.
Thinking thus, one should not grieve, for time is indeed equal toward all.
Some are enjoyers, others are acquirers, and still others are consumed by anxiety.
Seeing that all enjoyments in this world are thus [transient], one should not grieve;
for it is a fixed law that what was given by another in a previous life will be obtained hereafter.
Furthermore, people desire even what has not been given and long for it without effort.
That person of inferior experience censures the Unborn (Aja) but never himself;
filled with envy and pride, he then experiences agitation.
For this reason, suffering persists even more intensely in the manifest world.
The fortune that does not exist on one's own forehead is to be endured by others;
or rather, one should strive for its sake, since prosperity is the fruit of effort.
Furthermore, those who are skillful always enjoy the fortune found elsewhere as well.
For Fortune indeed flows toward one who is industrious and radiant.
Having produced fortune, sons, grandsons, daughters, and even the earth—things that are ultimately to be enjoyed by others—they themselves surely abandon them. (2.198.50)
Desiring objects that are undesirable, dependent on others, and fraught with calamity,
one should abandon such volitions and become happy like a virtuous man who possesses nothing.
Indeed, misfortunes take the form of prosperity, and prosperities take the form of misfortune.
They indeed come to pass according to one's fortune; therefore, a wise person should not place trust in them.
For some, even the total destruction of everything occurs for the sake of wealth;
for others, even a great gain occurs for the sake of misfortune.
Ignorant and infinitely greedy, he becomes attached, considering [worldly] pleasure to be true happiness;
delighting in prosperity, he later considers nothing else to be the highest good.
But when prosperity is suddenly lost, his entire undertaking perishes.
Then, his desires shattered, he becomes disillusioned with that object.
(55) Some on this earth, born of noble lineage, practice the Dharma alone, desiring happiness in the next world; they become disillusioned with worldly things. (56)
Some, overwhelmed by great greed, merely amass wealth;
for they consider the acquisition of wealth to be the very purpose of life and the true goal of human endeavor.
Having recognized their wretchedness and having recognized their lack of wisdom, [one should feel compassion].
Beholding men devoid of knowledge— who, out of delusion, fix their sights on wealth in this unstable life,
who suffer in vain,
and who are cast into the blinding darkness— who indeed would set his mind upon what is false? (58–59)

Restrain the senses from these objects; restrain your own mind as well; and by means of discernment, restrain your speech from these sense-objects. When you become their suppressors, then victory will be yours.
One who is satisfied with wisdom regarding all things that exist for but a moment does not grieve.
One who is content with little, gentle, self-controlled, and whose character is Brahman does not grieve;
but one who has fallen into a cruel and most sinful way of life is not released from sorrow.
Even one who subsists on roots and fruits may find delight in the lonely forest;
a person who is restrained in speech, devoted to Me, dedicated to all things, and surrendered becomes happy.
By restraining desires through wise discernment, even a householder may become happy.
Just as one who delights alone in the forests is satisfied by the forest life itself,
so the great man, satisfied, finds peace in his own self alone.
For one who conducts himself as a virtuous person, all suffering resides in another.
Having abandoned hypocrisy, desire, anger, joy, and likewise fear,
one should serve the virtuous with one's body and other means, and thereby acquire eternal happiness.
Service to the virtuous is considered the supreme merit, exceeding all other merits.
Without doubt, one of virtuous character attains the supreme goal.
Worship of mother, father, and teachers is highly esteemed by me;
a man devoted to this in this world enjoys great fame and the [higher] worlds. (67–68)
Whatever they may authorize as a duty when they have been duly honored—
whether it be consistent with dharma or contrary to dharma— that must be performed by sons and others.
And one should not practice any other dharma without being authorized by them.
"And whatever they may authorize, that is Dharma; this is the certainty. (2.198.70) These three alone are considered the three worlds and the three fires;
those established in their doctrine—namely the three Vedas and the three stages of life—are indeed victorious. (71)

The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire; this triad of fires is most venerable. By remaining vigilant toward these three, one shall surely conquer the three worlds.
By serving one's father, one conquers this world; likewise, by serving one's mother, one conquers heaven.
By serving one's teacher, one conquers the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
One should constantly attend upon these; that indeed is the highest merit.
All the worlds are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all his ritual actions are fruitless.
He by whom these three teachers are perpetually disrespected—
Neither does this world nor the next come to his security;
neither in this world nor in the next does his fame spread, nor does any other auspicious thing arise for him in either place. (76–77)
Indeed, a virtuous teacher (sadācārya) is superior to ten śrotriyas;
in this world, a sub-teacher (upādhyāya) is said to be superior to ten such teachers.
A father is everywhere superior to ten sub-teachers.
A mother is indeed the best of ten fathers, for she is equal to the entire earth.
As it has been said, the mother is the preceptor; there is no preceptor equal to a mother. A preceptor is always weightier than both father and mother. (2.198.80)
For both parents are the givers of birth and the creators of the body;
the Guru, however, is the divine bestower of knowledge and likewise the creator of divine kinship.
That lineage which is joined with the Guru is divine; it is ageless and immortal. (8.1)
For a mother, a father, and a teacher must never be treated with disrespect by their children and others.
When the teachers are honored, the sages and the gods, together with the ancestors, are likewise pleased; therefore, among those worthy of honor, the teacher is most worthy of honor.
One should never treat a guru with contempt on account of any conduct whatsoever.
Neither mother, nor father, nor likewise the guru deserve such disrespect.
One should not find fault with their actions, but should always offer them honor.
And whatever sin there is in the murder of an embryo belonging to one who commits insults,
for these four— treacherous to friends, ungrateful, slayers of women, and murderers of gurus— there is no atonement, for they are the greatest of great sinners. (85–86)
The virtuous devotees of Śrī Hari, who are renounced and auspicious teachers,
are to be worshipped, saluted, and fed from all sides.
Indeed, when they are served, the entirety of dharma is realized here in this world.

When [the gurus] are satisfied, all sacrifices are accomplished here; of this there is no doubt. (88) Thus, by always honoring and propitiating the gurus, O people, you shall indeed obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation through my grace in this world. (89)
Having spoken thus, O King, the Blessed One ceased speaking to Rādhā; then the monarch,
showing great reverence, worshipped Śrī Hari with the *nīrājana* ceremony and other rites,
and all his subjects likewise worshipped Him then with many offerings.
The queen also performed the worship, as did the princess Kumudvatī.
Then, according to the marriage rites, she took Hari’s hand;
the king held a great festival and indeed celebrated the occasion.
Then the king fed Hari and his guests;
having rested and passed the night, and having performed his morning rites at dawn,
Hari became ready to depart for the kingdom of King Kolaka.
Having drunk the milk and other offerings and performed his worship, Kṛṣṇa ascended the celestial chariot;
then all the sages, along with the king, also ascended into the sky amidst shouts of victory.
Accompanied by the sages, Kṛṣṇa was honored with unguents.
Honored by the people at that time, they went quickly to the region of Lepa.
For the sake of accomplishing a welcome reception, the King, filled with great devotion, went before them.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s wandering, worship, instruction, and meal in the city of Tunnavāya belonging to King Kāṣṭhayāna during the Tretā Age, followed by His departure for the kingdom of King Kolaka at dawn after the night," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section on the continuity of the Tretā Age.

→ Chapter 200
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari himself, beheld from the earth the King of Leperāṣṭra together with his army.
The Lord,

beloved of Kṛṣṇa, descended from the sky to the earth at the edge of the city of Muramāṣā by means of a celestial chariot, following the path shown by the King, into his own vast and magnificent garden where he stood to welcome him.
He caused [the chariot] to descend upon a vast, beautiful, and most splendid spot.
(3) Other celestial chariots also descended nearby.
At that time, musical instruments were played and shouts of victory arose. (4)
There were songs from the fair-complexioned women, proclamations of joy for the subjects;
and from his celestial chariot, Hari quickly descended outside there.
The Lord was honored by the king, the subjects, the queen, and the great sage.
With necklaces, beautiful crests, flowers, sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings,
the other great men there were also honored by the subjects. Having seated Hari in a palanquin, the king placed the others upon elephants and other mounts.
Out of great respect, he caused the royal lineage, the leading merchants, and even the learned scholars to circulate through the city of Muramāṣā; likewise,
men and women gathered at the city gates, on the royal highway, and at major junctions.
And at the crossroads and in the halls, they worshipped with devotion,
[offering] many gifts, ornaments of gold and jewels,
various divine decorations, blankets, and wealth.
At every place, they performed the lustration ceremony and offered worship;
fair women honored Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, with flowers and other offerings.
Having thus wandered through the city, He arrived at the royal palace.
Having convened an assembly, the Blessed One, the benefactor of all beings, said to the people:
"The Supreme Lord, eternal and whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is indeed to be worshipped and adored by men who desire liberation. (12–13)
Truth is the supreme vow; it is most excellent, for nothing exists that is higher than truth.
Even if it results in one's own ruin, truth must never be spoken.
The proclamation of Dharma was made for the sake of non-violence toward all living beings.
They say that *dharma* is so called because of its capacity to uphold; by *dharma* all creatures are sustained.
That which is endowed with the power of upholding is *dharma*: this is the certainty.
That which is endowed with non-violence is *dharma*: this is the certainty. (15–16)
In the case of violence, speaking the truth is considered dharma;
in the case of falsehood, even when there is violence, that is considered dharma.
Whether in truth or falsehood, or in the face of violence, maintaining silence is considered dharma. (17)
The protection of living beings is the remainder of truth; therefore, truth is considered to be Brahman.
(18) One should not speak of one's wealth to thieves; in that case, truth is no ornament.
Truth must not be told to them either—this is the certainty regarding dharma. (19)
If liberation is attained through not crying out, one should not cry out at all.
Or, if one must certainly cry out, it should be done very softly and mixed with falsehood. In that case, even such a falsehood would be conducive to dharma and lead to the highest good.
Even an oath should be uttered if one is released from bandits.
In a life-threatening emergency and in marriage, a falsehood is said to be the truth;
likewise for the sake of protecting wealth or in order to preserve another’s life.
Untruth is indeed truth; the reality of dharma is deeply hidden.
One should not speak untruth to the virtuous, for they are the saviors of embodied beings.
Untruth toward them is always a sin; therefore, one should speak that which is purified by truth.
Truth is indeed the very nature of Brahman; it is considered the most excellent vow.
One should practice truth as one's duty through action, mind, and speech.
For one whose vow is truth, sufferings never arise at any time.
One who has a self-restrained mind and is free from craving crosses over even the difficult fortress of suffering;
likewise, one devoid of hypocrisy and deceitful conduct, and a restrainer of the sense objects, crosses over even the difficult fortress of suffering.
One who is non-violent and does not speak excessively also crosses over even the difficult fortress of suffering.
One who is a donor, free from the state of begging, and likewise a worshiper of guests;

one who is free from malice, a devoted servant of mother, father, gurus, and the virtuous; one who is devoid of sin and lives by righteous conduct—even such a person crosses over the difficult fortress of suffering. (27–28)
One who is devoted to truth, who wards off the suffering of others, who is pure and steadfast, and who is free from deceit,
crosses even the difficult fortress of misery.
Such an ascetic, possessing the splendor of Brahman, is peaceful and transcends the realm of the material world.
Free from fear and bestowing fearlessness, he crosses over even the difficult pass of suffering.
Possessing equal vision toward all and likewise increasing the prosperity of others,
and having turned away from vulgar objects, he also crosses over even the difficult pass of suffering.
One who is devoted to bowing before all the gods, who constantly listens to the stories of Kṛṣṇa,
and whose mind is faithful and peaceful, crosses even the difficult fortress of suffering.
Free from pride, honoring others, worthy of honor, and a worshiper of the gods, sages, and ancestors— ‖32‖
Free from anger and subduing anger, he crosses even the difficult fortress of suffering.
(33) One who has conquered the tongue, conquered the genitals, and even conquered Nārāyaṇa;
one who has conquered thirst, conquered conduct—he too crosses the difficult fortress of suffering. (34)
In that place where I am Janārdana, with eyes as red as lotuses and clad in yellow garments— there I am the friend, the brother, the companion, and the kinsman who bestows happiness;
there I am Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kaṃbhārī, the cowherd boy Acyuta.
I abide wherever I am present in the heart of a devotee as their benefactor;
wherever I am as the beloved husband, the Lord of Śrī, who is dearer than Brahmā;
and whoever takes refuge in me, that Hari, crosses over the difficult fortress of suffering. (36–37)
I am Truth; I am the embodiment of Truth and Dharma; I am also the destroyer of all sufferings.
Having known Me and taking refuge in Me, they too cross over the difficult fortress of suffering.
Therefore, worship Me constantly; you shall attain Me alone in My abode.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One gave the mantra to the king who sought refuge,
as well as to his subjects; thereafter the king worshipped Hari,
and the queen, together with her daughter, then worshipped Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā.
A certain maiden took that beloved of Kṛṣṇa by the hand with deep devotion;
having obtained him through the rites of marriage, she indeed became one who had fulfilled her life's purpose. Having dismissed the assembly and the honored guests, that king—
He caused them to be fed various foods and delicious fruits. The king held a magnificent festival for Arjuna during the month of Bhādra;
thereafter, they rested on the night of the third lunar day.
Having all performed their morning ablutions, they partook of a meal of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
At that moment, the daughters of Gaṅgeya arrived to request a boon from Hari.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, those maidens [requested] the granting of a boon.
Indeed, the best of rivers chose Bālakṛṣṇa in order to be made into sacred fords (tīrtha).
"O Nārāyaṇa, O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, bathe in our waters! Through your immersion, we shall all become of the nature of sacred fords. (45-46)
Hari said, "So be it," and assuming manifold forms,
he quickly went out of compassion to bathe in rivers as well as in lakes and oceans,
taking on many different shapes.
In that same way, Kṛṣṇa shines with a singular form in the presence of kings.
By means of the divine vision granted to him, the great king named Kolaka sees everything right there, even while remaining within a bean pod.
Then Hari bathed in the Nīparā and likewise in the Nistārā;
he performed his ablutions in the Pṛthā, the Dinapā, and the Sevikā.
He performed his ablutions in the Trivarā, the Rāhuṇā, and the Senā.

He performed his bath in the Indirā river, in the Gavādaka-vitā river, and he performed his bath in the Trigirā river, which flows from the mountains. He performed his bath in the Dūrā river, in the Gurūṇā river, and in the Mitrā river. (51–52)
In the Lava-vārā army, he likewise performed a non-plunging [rite] when it was doubled;
in the Sukautukī and Sthāyinī rivers, he performed it with little danger;
and in the Audaryā, which is equal to Viṣṇu, he performed a full immersion at the Prapīṭha.

One should perform a bath in the waters of the Niyamā, the Dūnā, the Adyā, and the Pāyupaśyaka; likewise in a lake, in the Leṇḍuga, and in the Yoniga. One should also perform immersion in the Trinayā, the Hīnā, and the Pañcorā. (54–55)
At that time, the Blessed One simultaneously performed his ablutions in the Kāmā, the Volga, and the Donā rivers,
as well as in the eastern ocean, the white ocean, the black ocean,
the ocean of Kaśyapa, and the ocean of Bālatrika.
The Blessed One, the creator of beings, assumed forty forms;
having fashioned those maidens as sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and lakes,
he likewise established there the primary female attendants (*upakanyā*) who were of his own nature.
Kṛṣṇa quickly vanished and went to the abode of Kolaka;
there, Kolaka came to understand the greatness of Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest, is both the descent and the one who causes descent.
Thus, this Lord Nārāyaṇa himself became my son-in-law. I have indeed accomplished my purpose; O Blessed One, Janārdana, show me your grace and dwell forever here in my abode, which is worthy of you.
While this was being discussed, midday arrived;
then Yavakrīta and all the other great sages dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā came there,
having been summoned by Hari for the purpose of seeing him.
Having bowed down in the presence of Bālakṛṣṇa,
Lomaśa and the others, as well as Vṛkāyana, Nīlakaṇṭha, Īśāna, and other hosts and attendants, were then remembered. (63–64)
They all arrived in the presence of the king of Kolā at his palace.
Hari said, "The task concerning Ketumāla has been accomplished in every respect;
all the lands have been purified, and all the kings have taken refuge in devotion. (65)
Subjects were born devoted and subjects were born [of me], and sacred fords were also created.
Likewise, the sages became satisfied through gifts and other such acts.
Furthermore, I have made the beloved wives of Brahmā and the Gaurīs full of happiness.
The mountains have been purified here, and everything has now become complete.
Now we must go to that place where the circle of sages speaks;
you, the virtuous great seers, are indeed my authority.
Having spoken thus, Bālakṛṣṇa awaited the words of the sage.
At that moment, a rain of flowers fell from the sky along with shouts of "Victory! for the virtuous one known as Saccidānanda. (2.199.70)
The great seer Lālāyana, who had previously come from the north, arrived;
later, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, the deity Tuṣita also arrived. Both of them, seated upon magnificent celestial chariots, came to the abode of Kola.
Worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa, the two of them raised shouts of victory:
"May he who makes Ketumāla a sacred ford conquer, he who is the master of the imperishable abode!
O Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Svāmī Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha! (72–73)
"O Kāmbhareya, O Lord of Brahmanic Power, O Son of Gopāla!
Prosper here, remain for a long time, and make the lands pure.
While speaking thus, those two [ascended] a celestial chariot resembling the sun.
As they were slowly descending into the royal palace garden,
those two sages, the foremost of the Sātvatas, emerged from the celestial chariot,
adorned with flower garlands, filled with devotion, and their minds entirely fixed upon Kṛṣṇa.
Having approached Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, they bowed down near Him and worshipped the Supreme Lord with prostrations like a staff, as well as with flower garlands and other offerings.
Their eyes were filled with tears, their ears were dripping [with moisture], and their limbs were covered in horripilation.
By Hari’s command, they both sat down near the two seats. Hari rose and placed their feet upon his chest;
he set his hands upon their heads and embraced them with his arms.
He inquired after their welfare and the expansion of their devotional activities.
They both replied, "By your grace, O Lord, our well-being and security proceed unimpeded.
By your grace, O Master, even the regions of the Aṭas and Cāmarīs have been subdued."
Those imbued with the desire for liberation await your arrival.
Having come there, you must indeed perform the purifying sacrifice to Viṣṇu;
those subjects born in the region of Amarīka are to be purified by it.
"The kings, the subjects, and even the great sages are intent upon that; they await your arrival. Make those subjects successful in their purpose.
Thus entreated, the glorious Hari [spoke] to Lomaśa and likewise to Śaṅkara.
He questioned the great sages: "Tell me, what ought to be done?
They all replied: "O Lord, it must be done exactly as Lālāyana requests, for you are indeed Tāraka."
Yavakrīta, Nīlakaṇṭha, Vṛkāyana, Lomaśa,
and all of us who are sons of Gaṅgā, as well as Śaṅkara and the others,
shall act according to your command for the sake of delivering the world; of this there is no doubt.
When this reply had been given, the Blessed One, who assumes the dance of men,
said "So be it" to Lālāyana, the deity of the Tuṣita heaven;
and there, at that time, the Ṛṣi named Hārīta spoke to Hari.
"I am going first, O Hari, to my disciples in the eastern region—those known as Garima, Hārita, and Mādhyamsthā; please purify them.
Having spoken thus and received his command upon his head, he departed from the celestial chariot ahead.
And King Dinamāna,
the lord of Āvikāpura,
having lost his preceptor’s disciple, sent auspicious gifts from other regions for the sake of welcoming Hari. || 2.199.90–91 ||
He adorned [the place] with various auspicious rites and preparations.
Then, King Kolaka gratified the Supreme Lord, the sages, the virtuous women,
and the great dignitaries there with supreme foods and meals.
He worshipped him in many ways and offered everything he possessed.
He entreated the Lord to remain in his own abode for one night.
Hari said, "So be it," and the king held a great festival during that night.
He caused a beautiful performance to be staged with displays of dancers and wrestlers.
After the night's sleep had passed, in the morning, Hari quickly performed his daily rites and became ready to depart;
the King swiftly offered him honors worthy of respect.
Honored by the army and honored by the subjects as well,
he ascended his celestial chariot, while others also ascended their own.
Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa proceeded along, listening to reports of his glory, fame, and other virtues.
Traveling swiftly through the path of the sky by means of both his *gāṅgeya* and *nairjhika* powers,
he crossed over the ocean and went to the earth of Garima;
from the sky, he then beheld those regions that had been lost.
To welcome him, King Hārita and King Dinamānārka stood before them in the city of Aparāntikā;
seeing them, he attained stability while remaining in the sky, marked by the signs of his banner.

Beholding the welcome offered by the army, the Lord Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, rejoiced while remaining in the sky, O Rādhikā. Thus ends the third journey, worship, instruction, and meal of Śrī Hari in the city of Muramāṣā belonging to King Kolaka, as well as His simultaneous bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā by assuming many forms at the request of the daughter of Gaṅgā, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.

Chapter One Hundred and Ninety-Nine: The Description of the Occurrence of the Nightly Rest on the Fourth Day of the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Measurement of the Day, the Sun’s Movement toward the Portion of the King, and so forth.
Chapter Two Hundred: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
[Author: Chapter 201.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, in lands where many forests have been devastated and which are exceedingly cold...
This Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who resides among those with very few offspring,
[descended] in his own celestial chariot from the sky with great speed near the city of Aparāntikā by the sea, like a mountain [shining] with the sun at midday. 1–2.
Having seen Hārita-rṣi standing upon the surface of the earth on the path he had shown, he slowly brought [the chariot] down.
At that time, other celestial chariots also descended from the sky.
The king, together with his army, offered a grand welcome to the Supreme Soul;
likewise did the queen and the subjects.
The king beheld Śrīmat Bālakṛṣṇa, known as Hari, traveling in a celestial chariot.
Having approached nearby, he beheld a marvel and was struck with wonder:
the beloved of Śrī, whose beautiful form was exquisite and whom he had never seen before.
Having first gazed upon this divine sight, he remained motionless for a moment.
In the celestial chariot, within the form of Śrī Hari, he remained as if absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi).
(7) Just so, as soon as they were born, the queen, the princes, and the princesses all beheld Bālakṛṣṇa and entered into a state of meditative absorption. (8)
They beheld a splendor equal to ten million lightning flashes facing every direction;
there they saw the lords beginning with Virāṭ, and beyond them, others;
then, after those, the [lords] beginning with Bhūman, and finally the supreme abode, Goloka.
They beheld the Supreme, who is resorted to by millions of cowherds;
and having seen Kṛṣṇa there— the Bālakṛṣṇa— they saw once again Śrī Puruṣottama, situated in the supreme abode known as Akṣara.

They beheld Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all lords, accompanied by the beloved of Brahmā (Lakṣmī) in the midst of the liberated souls, and served by the hosts of emancipated beings. Then their meditative absorption vanished, and they rose up in their celestial chariots.
Those deeply devoted ones beheld Bālakṛṣṇa in their own kingdom;
struck with supreme wonder, the king and the members of the royal family worshipped him in the celestial chariot with necklaces, sandalwood paste, perfumes, and other offerings.
Then Hari, dressed in radiant garments, emerged from the celestial chariot;
captivating with his all-encompassing charm, beauty, brilliance, and smile,
the people and the Gaurīs and Hārītīs honored Acyuta.
With parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, songs, prostrations, and other offerings,
the subjects bowed down to Śrīpati, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. The king, taking Hari’s hand with his own golden hand—
He seated him upon a chariot outside the mechanical device, which was adorned with garlands and other ornaments.
The king’s family also sat upon that chariot.
The king held the parasol, and the queen held the fly-whisk.
The maidens held chowries, and the youths carried the staff.
In other chariots were the two parents of Hari and his entire family.
Having seated Śambhu in another chariot, the assembly of sages was placed in the remaining ones.
And the king seated Kṛṣṇa’s beloved in the inner apartments;
with a great welcome accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and the city resounding with the noise of drums, he caused the Lord to enter the city.
Indeed, a great enthusiasm arose among the subjects at that time from the sight of the new [form].
Hari repeatedly drew the hearts of the people toward himself;
for upon whichever limb of Hari anyone's eye was fixed at that moment, [their heart was likewise drawn].
There, [the Lord’s face] became fixed, motionless, and steady with bliss. 23.
Some, beholding his lotus-face, attained the means of liberation by casting aside [worldly] distractions;
and there, seeing the Lord, who is exceedingly heart-pleasing, they attained a peace that transcends all. 24.
Some, their minds bewildered upon beholding his eyes— resting upon the god of love, wide and drawn with the weight of intense passion— attained a state of stillness and partook of the supreme nectar.
Others, their hearts utterly captivated by gazing upon his lip, which shone like a large, deep-red bimba fruit, [were likewise transfixed].
Women gathered together, and their hearts became filled with longing.

Some, their conduct driven by desire for his limbs which were as beautiful as those of a god, and possessing the realization that he was the Lord, offered to him both their minds and their entire bodies. || 26-27 ||
Beholding him, some among the female devotees and attendants thought, "He is the Supreme Lord;
let us not lead him to our own perishable state," and thus they deliberated together.
Day and night, Rādhikā, Kamalagāramāsatī, Māṇikī, and the others [remained vigilant].
We worship Him, whom these Gaurī-like powers born of Brahmā—the lotus-born ones—serve in many ways;
having abandoned this transient body joined with mental afflictions, there indeed arises eternal happiness here. Therefore, perform the worship of His abode. || 2.200.30 ||
Here, in this cool palace situated by the ocean, the Blessed One has arrived out of grace.
Serve your own Lord through action, mind, recitations, and devotion.
What kind of fiery halo indeed surrounds His face here on all sides?
His body flows with a splendor surpassing ten million moons; he is truly heart-pleasing.

(32) He whose feet are served by countless liberated beings, and whose body is massaged by ten million servants—this one, who is attained only by those rich in the wealth of great merit, must not be forgotten as "the Attained One" (Āpta). (33)
And from the beginning, human beings and the masses have not desired such a one in their hearts;
yet here is this very Umesh, the Supreme Lord, who has been attained—resorting to Him, one finds supreme happiness.
Do not abandon that which is met with, easily accessible, beautiful, and possessed of great, excellent qualities!

"May they increase [their joy] with their hearts and worship Him with flowers, offering all their own wealth! (35). Having thus beheld Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, all those women were captivated; they spoke and drank in the Lord with their senses of bliss. (36)
The king was at the city gate, the chief ministers likewise on the main road; the market-keepers were in the marketplaces, the women at the openings of the streets;
the maidens were in the courtyards, and the common folk on the banks of the river’s edge.
At the four crossroads, all the people worshipped the Supreme Lord.
With parched grains, excellent fruits, flowers, saffron,
and unbroken rice, as well as with garments, sandalwood paste, and fragrances, they honored the Imperishable One.
They gave necklaces of ocean-born jewels to that Supreme Lord;
and other subjects, having paraded them through the city of Āvikā,
honored them and, bringing them to their respective homes, felt their purpose was fulfilled.
Then Hari went to his own residence, the temple of the Sun whose measure is the day (41). And the sage Hārīta, having bowed, said to the Supreme Lord:
"Exquisite foods are available; please eat them indeed" (42).
O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, feed others and satisfy them with milk-rice and other delicacies.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot, you must go to behold the earth with its weight;
you must travel there merely by the sight of it to purify everything on all sides.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One quickly consumed the milk-rice and other foods (44).
He then swiftly fed all those who were honored,
leaving everyone in the royal palace by the command of King Śaṅkara (45).
Accompanied by a limited number of attendants, Kṛṣṇa ascended his own celestial chariot along with the sage and departed upward into the sky.
Even after beholding the region of Vārāṇasī and its surrounding lands, he continued on.
Having beheld the region of Phudrikta, the land of Vilaya, Kāñcana,
the place of Ārṣuka, and the land of Hāyana, he proceeded toward Aparāntika;
thus observing these places, the Blessed One descended from the sky.
The queen rested in the royal palace and came for the sake of worship.
Having worshipped Hari, she then [saw] his two daughters;
while Hari was absorbed in bliss, the two girls gazed with steady eyes and worshipped him.
Upon seeing Hari, they both desired him and chose him with garlands offered;
the Blessed One took their hands as they returned the beautiful garlands.
After the meal, O King, he celebrated that festival during the night.
The king worshipped Gaṇeśa with *dūrvā* grass, sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍuka*), and saffron;
he caused dances to be performed and likewise had musical instruments played.
He honored the auspicious form of Gaṇeśa with vermilion (*sindūra*).
And they caused verses and hymns to be sung at that festival.
When the two maidens had been won, they served Kṛṣṇa with the highest devotion.
When the night had passed and it was morning, he performed his bath and excellent worship.
Then, after drinking milk, Bālakṛṣṇa was ready to depart for the lands of the Aṭakas and the regions of the immortals (the gods),
on the fifth day, during the time of Saṅgava, in the most auspicious bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Then the king bestowed a parting gift consisting of many jewels and other valuables. Hari presented that wealth and so forth to the sage Hārīta;
the king, accompanied by his army, gave him great honor there.
At that time, shouts of victory, words of renown, and songs arose,
filled with sweetness and performed by the Gaurīs and Hāritas.
Hari gave necklaces to the king, to the queen, and also to his sons.
Taking hold of Prajñapti, he ascended the splendid throne;
indeed, the other classes also ascended their respective seats. And the subjects offered counsel for the king's true welfare. (2.200.60)
In ancient times, the camel performed austerities, and Prajāpati appeared before him.
He then requested a boon: "May my neck be one *yojana* in length.
Brahmā said, "So be it," and the camel remained forever in the forest.
Greatly indolent, he sat in one place and devoured trees;
enjoying his ease, he slept at night within a circuit of a yojana.
A jackal arrived in the midst of him and clung firmly to his neck.
My camel, because its throat was split at the mid-neck, became long-necked;
likewise, in this world, one whose thirst is excessive dies, struck by illusion.
Therefore, one should not indulge in thirst, but should practice devotion to Hari.
"Make me your refuge; I shall deliver you, of this there is no doubt.
(65) In a certain forest, there was a preeminent swan belonging to a lion.
A poor Brahmin named Sattvavṛtti went to that forest. (66)
The swan met him on the road and asked, "Where are you going?
He replied, "I am indeed going to another country for the sake of acquiring wealth.
The swan said, "You are a brahmin, O sinless one, and you are worthy of my honor."
"I shall give you here the jewels acquired by the lion from the elephants.
Having said this, the swan took that brahmin along with him into the forest, after having killed the elephants and [taken] the varieties of pearls from their frontal globes. (68–69)
He went to where that lion was, and the swan said to the lion:
"This guest, a brāhmaṇa, has arrived and is worthy of honor;
by giving him [food], the great sin born of violence shall be destroyed."
Thus addressed, the eminent Śārdūla then washed the brahmin’s feet;
having drunk the nectar of the brahmin’s feet, he honored him with gifts of jewels.
As the brahmin was about to depart for his home like a swan, he then spoke to that twice-born man: (72)
"Come back; let no further suffering arise here for me without you.
Having spoken thus, the swan departed. Then, after some time, the twice-born one returned to that forest out of greed, remembering Hari.
At that time, the swan was not the minister; rather, the crow was the minister.
Upon seeing the twice-born one, the crow said to the lion, "Devour him!
The lion replied, "It cannot be so; this brahmin is eternally pure."
Then he drank the water from [the sage’s] feet and placed the dust upon his head.
The crow said: "Indeed, for whomsoever there is the water from the feet, he is truly pure and complete;
he should be eaten in every way."
"By that we shall be purified, and likewise our inner sin shall perish.
Having been addressed thus, King Siṃha devoured that twice-born man.
Therefore, one should not yield to greed; death dwells within the house of greed.
Having abandoned greed and remembering Hari, one should indeed live with contentment;
such a person shall be happy in this world and happy in my abode hereafter.
For one who is content and devoted to service, the supreme abode is certain.
Once, the Ocean said to the rivers, the trees, and the reeds: "Do you come [to me] when carried by water? Indeed, the rivers do come, but the reeds do not.
The rivers and these trees replied: "We remain here on the bank at all times. (2.200.80–81)
Moreover, they never bow even when we are in a state of prosperity;
having uprooted them from their very foundation, we shall cast them into the depths of the ocean.
Reeds in the form of hollow stalks, however, do indeed bend when fallen into a flood.
But when their previous momentum has passed, they gradually rise up again.
We do not indeed lead those who bend like reeds;
rather, it is those people who, at the proper time, bow down before the great and the impetuous.
Those who possess stability do not suffer the destruction of their roots; rather, they remain firm.
Likewise, those who bow down during the time of the force of *māyā* and *kāla* attain a gradual rising and continue to live as embodied beings in this world.
Just as they do not perceive suffering, so too should people here conduct themselves.
Having taken refuge in Me, one should gradually abandon illusion and surely go to My divine abode, that blissful residence which is indeed a perfectly stable refuge.
One who desires happiness must act only after carefully considering the place and time.
"I am Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; the Master is always to be worshipped.
There is no doubt that I deliver the one who worships me and comes to my feet.
The fool became a boar on his back, solely for the purpose of seizing the jackal.
Then, at that opportune moment, the jackal ran with great speed;
leaping into the well, he reached the opposite bank.
A boar with a stout body, running with great speed, fell into a well;
he sank into the midst of the water and died, overcome by ignorance.
Therefore, people should never act with haste in any undertaking.
For by taking refuge in me, a human being may gradually cross over saṃsāra.
But here in this world, a person should not resort to the force of greed, which is like a jackal—fault-ridden, a great rogue, and one that causes one to fall into a pit. (92–93)
"Having abandoned desire, anger, pride, greed, and arrogance, one shall become happy;
having taken refuge in me, the Lord, the virtuous man, and the virtuous woman, one shall become happy.
Having spoken thus, Hari gave the mantra to the king and his family.
And Lomaśa, being commanded, gave the mantra to the subjects;
Maheśvara gave the mantra to the subjects who had been carried away.
Then, having drunk the water, the Blessed One appeared in the sky.
Worshipped by elephants and others with offerings of flowers, the Supreme Lord,
having repeatedly bestowed his blessings, ascended his own celestial chariot.
At that time, all the others likewise remained in their celestial chariots in the sky.
Musical instruments were indeed sounded with great force for his honor.
There, in that place, shouts of victory, cries of glory, and the sounds of mechanical instruments arose; meanwhile, Hari quickly [ascended] the celestial chariot.
They propelled [the chariots] through the path of the sky toward the site of Kenāṭaka;
indeed, having crossed the ocean and the regions of the Kenāṭaka country,
the swift celestial vehicles arrived at midday.
Seeing the lands scattered in the water, he reflected upon Hari:
"The sacrificial ground must first be visited where it is located; thereafter, the great seer Lālāyana and whatever other task remains shall be attended to. (101–102)
Then Lālāyana, having remembered the circle of celestial chariots (*vimāna-maṇḍala*),
quickly caused the royal armies to offer cries of welcome.
Hari, moreover, [crossed] the ocean of foam and the island of foam (*dviphena-dvīpa*).
Having crossed the Haḍḍikāsana, he went to Vinipārasara. (1.04) There musical instruments were being played for the sake of welcoming Hari;
there, countless men were waiting for the Supreme Lord. (1.05)

O Rādhikā, shouts of joy then resounded, reaching to the ends of the quarters; people with far-sighted vision and other such powers beheld them in the sky at that time. There were also harsh sounds of trumpets that caused the wind to tremble.
And the sounds of musical instruments and singing arose for the honoring of Hari.

(107) Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Descent in the City of Aparāntikā, His Wandering, Worship, Feeding, and Resting; His Travel by Air-Vehicle throughout the Country; His Breakfast after Resting at Night; His Departure; and His Return to Lake Vinipāra in the Regions of Kenāṭaka," in the section on the Majesty of King Arka regarding the Measurement of the Day, within the second book, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (200)
← Chapter 200: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 201 [[Author:
→ Chapter 202
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Beloved, O Beloved, ocean of mercy, Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Ramā!
What did Mādhava do in the regions of the immortals? (1)
Where, when, and to what place did he go or stay, and by whom was he served? What wonders were displayed there by the Supreme Soul, the Lord Hari?
And what was done by the subjects when the Supreme Lord arrived there? (2)

To which lands did this Blessed One, the creator of beings, travel? (3) Tell me of the regions of the immortals and the deeds of the Blessed One performed there, while he was devoted to that which is dear to Brahmā. (4)
Having heard the noble discourses of this Lord, I become greatly satisfied;
yet, my thirst to hear His deeds remains ever present.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, as I recount your deeds to you:
the sacrifice, worship, hospitality, the offering of gifts, and the giving of commands;
wandering, the imparting of mantras, and divine visions.
I shall describe to you in brief these wonders that bring liberation to embodied beings, as well as the auspicious sanctification of rivers, lakes, and oceans. (7–8)
The Blessed One performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice on the shore of Lake Vinipāra,
upon a vast and auspicious ground adjacent to the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest,
which grants satisfaction to all the gods and to living beings here.

The embodied beings and others residing within the three worlds, both insentient and sentient, attained eternal satisfaction through the two hands of Bālakṛṣṇa. By whom [was this done] for the sake of the sovereign ruler of the regions and districts of Aṭaka? (2.201.10–11)
King Pañcasara, known as Rāya-kinnara,
and the sage Divimānāyana both rendered assistance at the sacrifice;
for those two were supreme Vaiṣṇavas due to their association with Lālāyana.
By the power of Tuṣita, the two became supreme devotees.
At the command of the sage, King Lālāyana, desiring to perform a sacrifice, sent auspicious letters to him. (13–14)
By means of the Lālāyana yoga, the regions of the Cāmarīs are inhabited by Vaiṣṇava subjects who are righteous;
in every district, there are kings and subjects such as yourselves.
Oh, how great is our fortune that we have attained the state of being Vaiṣṇavas!
Indeed, he who is the supreme Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa among all Nārāyaṇas,
and whose devotees we are here, is Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa.
"Having arrived in my kingdom, he will indeed perform an auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
therefore, everyone must come to that sacrificial festival.
The commencement of the rite will take place on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada."

On the fifth day, that Supreme Self will arrive from his celestial chariot. On that previous day, all the kings who travel through the air must assemble there, along with all the subjects and the Sāttvatas, for the purpose of welcoming Hari.
The worship of Hari should be performed together with a magnificent military display;
the conclusion of this sacrifice shall take place on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).
By the command of Lālāyana, I, Rāyakinnara, write this down.
"Both women and men, whether mentioned or unmentioned, must all come here.
Thus did that king of the Rāya-kiṃnaras send well-written letters to the regions of the *cāmarī* women by means of messengers.
Upon receiving the invitations, the people— including men, women, and others— arrived in haste, eager to see their kinsmen.
They came by means of celestial chariots, vehicles, and carriages, bringing with them various offerings.
Accompanied by gold, silver, grain, and other such items, as well as gems, diamonds, and excellent liquids,
along with suitable sacrificial materials fit for offering, millions of people arrived at the bank of the Śeṣa river in the forest of Kāṣṭhavana. (25–26)
At that time, even kings arrived at the confluence of the Vinipāra lake;
the multi-colored armies of the rulers had assembled.
Well-dressed and ready for the welcome of Hari, they stood waiting nearby.
Adorned with musical instruments, banners, and flags, and beautified by moats;
with weapons in hand, mounted on elephants, horses, and camels, [they gathered] in a newly constructed city ten yojanas in extent. (28–29)
Then, on the banks of the rivers and forests of Śeṣakaṣṭha,
and on the shores of the lakes, there was a great throng of millions of women of the Nara clan who were mourning for their deceased husbands.
At that time, the new city of sacrifice shone like heaven itself.
Then Hari-Kṛṣṇa repeatedly gazed from the sky at that city;
having observed the ground between two lakes for the purpose of the pavilion,
he looked for a level piece of land in the direction indicated by the divine chariot-archer.
Having arranged the circle, he caused the celestial chariot to descend above everyone;
there were the sounds of musical instruments and the songs of the gods,
as well as shouts of victory from the people and the yogis of the sky.
The sounds of trumpets and the clatter of machines arose during the honor paid to Hari.
Ten preeminent sovereigns of the entire earth were present there, having brought offerings consisting of principal items in golden vessels. (34–35)
King Rāyakinnaranṛpati, King Rāyarokīśvara, King Rāyaraṇajit, and King Rāyavākakṣaka;
King Rāyamārīśa and King Rāyabāleśvara. (36)
King Rāyalambāra, King Rāyanavārkabhu,
King Rāyahaṇḍeśa, and King Rāyakūpeśa— all these,
well-equipped with their armies, were then there for the purpose of welcoming Hari. || 37–38 ||
Having arrived there by means of celestial chariots, they had already assembled beforehand with well-adorned bodies on elephants, horses, chariots, and other mounts; at that time,
the army stood ready for the purpose of welcoming them.
Debate-masters and authors of treatises, seekers of fire and collyrium; performers of water-instruments and those making loud noise with dance and music;
those skilled in the power of throat-instruments, and players of the peacock and flute. (2.201.40)
They were highly skilled in the playing of the *tāra* drum and produced the sound of the *paṭaha*;
they moved in accordance with their physical gestures, bearing weapons and seeking to bow down.
There were those wearing the dress of the Gaṇas holding staffs, as well as those in the guise of tigers and leopards.
Clad in tawny garments, with radiant halos, they appeared in the form of ascetics;
some bore tridents and discs, while others likewise carried shields and swords.
They were also distinguished by their rattling cymbals, hand-claps, and flutes.

Some bore conchs and others held thunderbolts; some wore the dress of virgins, while others wore matted locks. Some were resplendent in the attire of warriors, some were clad in white garments, some in red, and others were adorned with variegated ornaments.
There, immortal women of pale luster and exquisite youth stood ready to welcome him, honoring him with triple fans, chowries, flower clusters, and mirrors.
The maidens wore red lower garments and were filled with intense passion from their previous momentum;
they were dressed in blue, yellow, and green colors, adorned with golden ornaments,
and highly beautified by garments such as garlands of networks of small bells.
Holding vessels for the purpose of worshipping Hari, they brought parched grain and unbroken rice,
along with *kahlāra*, *padma*, and *kumuda* lotuses, as well as *kādamba*,
*pārijātaka*, *kunda*, *sāhasrapatra*, and land-lotuses (*sthalapadma*) with beautiful filaments.

Adorned with campaka flowers, kāmala blossoms, pearl necklaces, crests, and garlands; provided with saffron groves and sandalwood fit for worship—hundreds of thousands of divine women, who were like immortals, arrived there. (2.201.50–51)
Thousands of royal ladies and countless women of the common folk were present;
at that time, all the regions were filled with auspicious invocations in the excellent sacrifice held in the palace of King Kinnara, the sovereign.
In order to obtain a vision of the approaching Lord Bālakṛṣṇa-Hari,
men from the young to the old— numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions—
arrived and stood waiting to welcome Hari. (53–54)

At the confluence of the Śeṣakāṣṭhavana river with the Vinipāra lake, they arrived upon the exceedingly vast surface of the earth. There stood a city, many yojanas in extent, fit for the residence of those who had come from afar. ||55||
It shone forth like another heaven, known by the name Makhasevā.
Previously, from the lake near the city of Maṇisevā, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, [proceeded] along the path shown by the king. (56–57)
He brought down from the sky a celestial chariot resembling the sun;
it illuminated all directions and shone with a golden hue.
Having reached stability upon the earth, it appeared like the moon.
Other celestial chariots also descended from the sky.
Skilled artisans captured the likeness [of the figures] using image-capturing machines;
meanwhile, the kings, standing upon a single thread, performed their prostrations.
With their armies, with music, dancing, and other arts,
all the kings together with the emperor went into his presence.
Both Īśāna and Lomaśa proceeded to the front of the celestial chariot.
Both Vṛkāyana and Nīlakaṇa arrived from behind.
The gatekeepers and attendants stood in the courtyard with staffs in hand.
Having reached the ladder, the kings stood there as spectators. (62–63)
Then Hari Bālakṛṣṇa, accompanied by his parents,
arrived ahead at the splendid eastern gate upon a celestial chariot,
his form radiant with the splendor of ten million times ten million suns, moons, fires, and lightning bolts.

And having slightly touched with his hand the beloved one standing beneath the archway, who possessed the luster of flickering lightning, that King of the Rāya-Kinnaras beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, who was wearing a charming, gentle smile. (65–66)
Having prostrated, she placed upon his neck a garland of *mālatī* flowers abundant with fragrance and variegated colors; then she gave him a necklace of jewels.
She placed a cluster of flowers in his hand and applied sandalwood paste to his forehead.
With a vessel filled with fragrant essences and fine garments, the king performed the rite of worship:
he placed golden unbroken rice (akṣata) at his feet, excellent grains upon his head, and flowers upon his body. (68–69)
He offered water, milk, betel-leaf, and fruit in his presence;
with palms joined in reverence, he requested that the earth be inspected for the sake of the sacrifice.
Hari slowly descended by means of golden stairs.
Then, having been offered a lion-throne, he sat upon it for a moment.
Rāyarokīśvara worshipped him with garlands of flowers and jewels,
and King Rāyaraṇajit worshipped him with gems and other offerings.
King Rāyavākakṣaka honored him with gold and other treasures;
King Rāyamārīśa also honored him with jewels and other gifts;
and King Rāyabāleśvara honored him with diamonds.
And King Rāyalambāra honored him with wealth and other gifts;
(74) and King Rāyanavārkabha honored him with rubies;
and King Rāyahaṇḍeśa honored him with pearls. (75)
And King Rāyakūpeśa honored him with silver;
then all the chief ministers also worshipped him with ornaments and other gifts.
The merchants likewise honored the Lord with wealth, food, and the essence of fine flavors.
The groups of subjects also worshipped Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, with oblations for the gods and ancestors, sacrificial fuel, and many other materials. Then,
at the conclusion of their worship and welcome, Śrī Hari questioned them.
Having bowed down with devotion, the king and others spoke these words out of compassion: "May there be freedom from illness, great well-being, security, spiritual practice, and happiness;
today, on this very day, every kind of great joy is present here. (79)
Today the rising of the golden sun has occurred, since your compassion has arisen;
today the eternal gain has been attained, which is this very sight of you here.
Today the fourfold aims of man have been perfected, and the four goals of human existence have been achieved.
Today, through the attainment of what was yet to be gained, the fruit of the burden of sovereignty has been obtained;
indeed, today all prosperity that bestows even the station of Indra has come to our home.
Furthermore, by the sight of you, imperishable merit has been acquired this very day.
O Lord, by your arrival today, our lands have indeed been purified.
Today all the riches bestowed by you have become meaningful;
all various and constant fortunes have surely borne fruit through this noble deed.

"Indeed, by the sight of Mādhava today, men and women, children and the young, the elderly, and even animals, trees, and creepers—all have fulfilled their purpose; they are truly most meritorious this day. (89)
Whether they be birds, aquatic creatures, those that move upon the earth, or even forest-dwellers—
since your feet touch this ground and its like, this earth, possessing great fortune, rejoices as if it were the very abode [of the gods]. (86–87)
Today she has become richly endowed with horripilation, especially through the offering of fragrances;
indeed, today on this day, even trees, grasses, and clumps of weeds have become blessed and fortunate, for they have been purified by the dust of your feet. (88)
Blessed are even the ants and other small creatures who partake of your grace! (89) Blessed are these regions where the arrival of Nārāyaṇa has occurred;
today, the manifestation of you, Hari, which bestows liberation, has begun. (2.201.90)

Wealth, grain, sovereignty, prosperity, sons, cities, elephants, and so forth, as well as the abundance of vehicles and mounts—all these are indeed fruitful only through your arrival, O Blessed One; what, indeed, could possibly be lacking? || 9.1 ||
Everything we possess is already complete, for the attainment of Hari is indeed difficult to achieve.
Having performed this sacrifice, purify us and grant us eternal well-being.
We, as your followers, desire that you always dwell in this land.
Having spoken thus, King Kinnata offered his salutations,
and the other kings likewise bowed down; then the Blessed One himself rose and walked about to inspect the suitable ground.
On the ground to the south of the confluence of the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest river,
extending for many yojanas, he beheld an auspicious site fit for a pavilion and indeed commanded the king to prepare it for the pavilion. (95–96)

The messengers of Indra, the messengers of Viṣṇu, and others who were messengers of Śiva were remembered there and arrived quickly; Viśvakarman also arrived. Having commanded them to construct nine sacrificial pits and an excellent pavilion, [he departed].
Before morning had passed, all of this was fully prepared;
then, at midday, Hari went to his residential palace. There, he took his meal and other refreshments, and then rested together with his companions.
They all constructed a most beautiful pavilion during the night itself,
adorned with sacrificial pits, altars, and great platforms, along with houses for the ritual jars;
it was enchanting, provided with storage rooms and fire-chambers.
Having constructed a pavilion within the city of Maṇisevā,
the attendants went out in all directions to fetch sacrificial fuel; likewise, the sages residing throughout the Gaṅgā as well as the disciples of Lomaśa departed.
The gods and goddesses, composed of that [divine essence], prepared the materials for the sacrifice.
On the sixth day, having performed his daily rites, Kṛṣṇa,
seated upon the back of an elephant and accompanied by kings, set out to behold the new city of Mahīmāna.
He beheld kitchens, broth-halls, and vast bathing-chambers;
sleeping-quarters, halls for peace, and sacrificial chambers. He saw dining-halls filled with kings, as well as great kitchens.
Having observed that all preparations had been completed with perfect materials,
Hari remembered the Lord of the Gods (Indra) along with the nectar at dawn. Mahendra, accompanied by the nectar, arrived there swiftly.
There was a lake of nectar there, which provided inexhaustible satisfaction on all sides. (107) The wish-fulfilling creepers, when remembered, arrived there laden with fruit;
indeed, mountains of fruit were fashioned by them for the sake of the sacrifice. (108)
The *puṣpakaṇada* trees, as well as the *vṛkṣa*, *sasya*, and *druma* trees, were remembered; these *kalpavṛkṣas* indeed fashioned mountains from flowers, grains, and other such things.
Those who grant all desires (*kāmadugdhadhra*) arrived, having been summoned from their own abodes.
In the sacrificial halls, rivers of clarified butter, rivers of curd, and rivers of milk were prepared by the cows,
filled with inexhaustible materials.
At that time, the goddess who is full of food was remembered as the auspicious Lakṣmī.
Having arrived, they fashioned mountains composed of cooked food;
the Earth herself, having come in personified form, created a mountain of sweet sugar.
At the word of Hari, she [the Earth] produced flavors, and the goddess of water produced juices.
All the medicinal herbs, including *veṣavāra* and others, gathered there.
Brahmā himself, the four-faced one, being remembered, arrived at that place; he fashioned suitable dwellings as well as the necessary implements.
Kubera deposited gold, silver, and other treasures for the purpose of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Likewise, the other guardians of the realm, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and the lords of subjects, being summoned,
arrived swiftly to fulfill the offerings to gods and ancestors (*havya-kavya*).
