On the sixth day, when midday had arrived, everything became fully complete and powerful.
It was perfectly accomplished; not even the slightest deficiency existed.
The king [provided] millions of men and kinnaras with delicious foods.
Hari, accompanied by his family and joined by the circles of great sages, gratified all those subjects in many ways.
Together with his own retinue, he partook of the meals there.

Then King Rāya-kiṃnara-bhūpati requested Kṛṣṇa: "O Kṛṣṇa, please come to my palace with Your army and be honored; and also, O Kṛṣṇa, please wander through the city. At that moment, Kṛṣṇa said "Om" (so be it).

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Sending of the Auspicious Letter for the Sacrifice by Keṇāṭa; the Welcome, Inquiries after Welfare, and Instructions for the Construction of the Pavilion, as well as the Preparation of Food and the Collection of Ritual Implements, upon the Arrival of Hari," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 201. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 202 [Author:
Chapter 203 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, King Kinnara quickly mobilized his army,
which was resplendent with elephants, horses, and chariots, and where the various mounts were sounding their musical instruments.
There was a white elephant with four tusks, as lofty as a mountain peak.
That elephant, adorned with a most wonderful and variegated howdah and beautifully decorated with a golden saddle-cloth,
was urged forward by the mahout at the king’s command for the sake of Hari.
It arrived swiftly before him, and Hari mounted the elephant.
Likewise, six other elephants stood there; their parents, brothers, sister, and even the brother’s beloved wife mounted those very elephants,
as did Lomaśa and Tuṣita.
Likewise, Īśāna himself mounted the excellent elephant Lālāyana.
The beloved wives of Brahmā also ascended human vehicles,
as did young women in the bloom of their youth, riding in covered carriages.
Maidens who were fair-complexioned, tawny, and greenish-yellow,
as well as other great sages descended from Gaṅgā, sat upon the chariots,
fully endowed with happiness, to roam through the city of Maṇipattana.
When all those of great honor had thus taken their seats,
the armies of the people of the world were then brought forward,
well-equipped with musical instruments and adorned with banners, flags, and the like.
The attendants were singing the great glory of the primordial Nārāyaṇa;
then followed the magnificent elephant of Lord Īśāna.
Behind him came the elephants of the householders, and after them, the elephants of the great sages.
Indeed, for those such as Brahmapriya and others, human vehicles proceed;
chariots rich in splendor, equipped with golden jars, covered with variegated silken cloths, auspicious, and drawn by white horses, move forward. (11–12)
Then the great elephant, adorned by Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa, proceeded;
there King Kinnāraka held the umbrella over its back.
Standing at its sides, holding chowries, were two princes.
Then the splendid mounts of the kings indeed set forth.
Behind them followed the immortal maidens, who sang of Nārāyaṇa,
adorned with festive attire and auspicious with the sentiments of love.
Seated upon pearl thrones, holding water-pots filled with fruit and auspicious sprouts,
and adorned with all manner of beautiful garments and ornaments, they proceed singing the praises of the Lord.
They chant the hymns of the Lord of Kambharā, the Consort of Śrī and the Master of Kamalā.
Among those divine vehicles, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Satī, Pārvatī,
Māṇikī, Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Saguṇā, Ambikā, Santoṣā, Amṛtā, Muktidevī, Lalitā, and Jayā [are seated]. (17–18)
These and other women, adorned and radiant, proceed along the royal road; others, horsemen and guards, also go forth.
Moving along the great highway as commanded by the king’s decree, the people follow.

Then Śrī Hari, possessing the splendor of the sun and honored by the people, shone forth. Thus this army of Hari marched from Maṇipura; first, that force, rich in royal majesty, proceeded to the royal palace.
Descending from his horse onto the royal throne, which was made of exquisite gold and resplendent with jewels and gems, the king seated Hari there.
Cheers of "Victory! arose, and likewise a rain of flowers fell.

The principal queen, Satī, together with Pradhānā and others, as well as the Kumāras and the other queens, performed the supreme worship of the Supreme Lord. She honored him with a forehead mark made of saffron and sandalwood, as well as with unbroken grains of rice. || 23–24 ||
He placed his joined palms upon the forehead of Śrī Hari to dispel suffering;
having scattered flowers over the head of Kṛṣṇa, he performed a prostration.
Having washed His feet with milk, he brought the milk into a pot.
That royal family quickly drank the pleasing water;
afterwards, having washed their feet with water, they placed a wealth of ornaments such as necklaces and other articles, amounting to ten million, in the presence of the Supreme Soul.
"O Kṛṣṇa, that which was offered by me at the sacrifice by the king's command belongs to you.
Having spoken thus, she approached his side and, with a steady gaze, beheld him. Then King Rādhika bowed at the feet of Hari.
At that time, during the worship, he gave his family jewels and gems;
then Bālakṛṣṇa gave them two most divine eyes,
which were capable of perceiving the forms of others and were His own transcendental.
Kṛṣṇa granted a vision that was most divine and exceedingly beautiful,
with limbs corresponding perfectly to his form, as lovely as ten million gods of love;
it was the supreme state, served by ten million liberated souls and ten million Śaktis.
It is the supreme abode, frequented by infinite and endless liberated souls, as well as by Īśvara and others;

it is worshipped by Brahmā and the rest, resplendent with divine garments and ornaments, attended by Rādhā, Ramā, and others, and possessing a beauty that surpasses even the most beloved of lovers. (32–33)
Beholding that [manifestation] of Mādhava, frequented by incarnations, divine arrays, gods, and spies, those born of royal lineage were bewildered;
seeing that supreme wonder, they remained for a moment as if paralyzed.
Then, impelled by a divine state, the king offered this hymn of praise:
"Victorious is He who dwells in the supreme abode consisting of a mass of great splendor, resplendent, and pleased by the service and attendance of the great liberated ones. (35)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bearer of infinite qualities, the Supreme, the Lord of the Imperishable,
whose state is attained through Śakti and other powers,
reigns supreme. You alone abide in Your own divine abode, the supreme imperishable realm.
He alone remains there as the emaciated one of two excellent arms, the bestower of supreme bliss;
in the world of cows, he remains in his own abode where the hosts of cowherd girls offer him arghya; and in the Vaikuṇṭha abode, he remains served by Lakṣmī. || 37 ||
O Infinite One, you alone abide in the state of the Lord, completely filled with immortality; you alone abide in the unmanifest realm as the one whose body consists of the manifested emanations;
and you, O Hiraṇyagarbha, exist as the Virāj and as the Puruṣa.
O Viṣṇu, you move like a stride for the benefit of human beings.

The gods, the Daityas, others, the ancestors, the Brahmins here, the hosts of sages, the kings, and those dwelling in the netherworld— all that which is designated as insentient and sentient is your body.
The sages here, such as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who possess self-knowledge, worship you in the form of Badarīśa; those desiring liberation worship you in the form of the Yugalas.
Likewise, in the world of Śveta, your people have bodies of white luster.
They serve the Lord who rests upon the serpent, whose feet have been served by Lakṣmī;
you alone are He. You are the halo around the moon, you are within the fire, and you are Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of darkness. (2.202.40)
O Viṣṇu, by the power of even a slight fragment of Your supreme grace, I behold this divine form of Yours abiding within my dull consciousness through my own vision;
for You alone existed in the beginning as the creator of the principles (tattvas) and all else, along with their attendants.
Having entered [the world], you become the nourisher; even in withdrawal, you are the cause of dissolution.
You alone remain, assuming excellent forms through countless incarnations, acting out of compassion as the creator of the supreme good for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence.
O Blessed One, you alone are attained here as the embodiment of sacrifice;
as the enjoyer in this sacrifice, please bring about the happiness of your own people.
Indeed, the substance offered by me was intended for your enjoyment from of old.
This entire kingdom and all else has been placed at your feet;
indeed, O Great King, I remain in this kingdom merely as a constant guest, while you are truly the master of your own domain. 42.
Having thus praised Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, that king then observed a vow of silence; and then the Lord of divine vision caused himself to disappear,
whereupon they beheld him upon a golden throne.

With tears in their eyes and hearts throbbing with emotion, they all suddenly bowed down and prostrated themselves. Then all the queens, having recognized him as the Supreme Lord Śrī, took hold of the feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow and, out of love, licked both his palms.
And there, fifty-one excellent maidens of the king were present as witnesses; they were enchanted by Puruṣottama.
Placing the garland of choice upon their hands, they hung it around the neck of Hari.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa, commanded by the king, indeed collected the taxes.
Having obtained their beloved Lord Kṛṣṇa, those women felt their purpose was fulfilled.
There, Śrī Hari bestowed blessings upon the king.
Having assigned the sacrificial materials and the measurement of time to the Ṛṣi,
the king rose from his seat and felt that he had fulfilled his duty.
At that time, the Blessed Lord was everywhere in the palace and the king's residence.
He wandered through the multi-storied palace complex, which consisted of a hundred floors and more;
he traversed the royal garden, having first purified it with his feet.
Then he went first to the royal residence and thereafter to the principal palace.
Then, having placed his feet in the dwellings of the guild-leaders and the city-dwellers, and having accepted offerings for the sake of the sacrifice in their houses,
he proceeded along the royal highway, through the marketplaces, the squares, and at every spot.
Having received the worship, Hari offered it all for the sake of the sacrifice.
Thus, as he wandered throughout the city with great honor,
he captivated the hearts of the people.
Seeing the Lord seated upon a great elephant as he wandered along the royal highway,
all the women sang his glory as if they were goddesses:
"Blessed are those princesses who have chosen the Lord, the Consort of Śrī!"
How else could they have obtained the fruit of the penance and worship performed previously?
For here in this world, a husband such as the beloved Lord Nārāyaṇa may be found by women—He whom Rādhā, Kamalā, Padmā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī [desire]. (57–58)
Māṇikyā and the others have attained him through the weight of their good fortune—
him whom the beloveds of Brahmā serve, whom other maidens serve,
and whom the Gaurikās also serve. ||59|| They have attained him through the weight of their good fortune.
Whom even the Hārita goddesses, who possess innumerable virtues, serve;
let them behold his supreme face, radiant as the orb of the moon.
Upon his brow rests the arrow of Kāmadeva, poised for action.
The curve of his eyebrows resides upon his body,
and his loveliness is such that his smile possesses a great wonder, captivating and enchanting.
A beautiful and wondrous luster shines from the corners of his eyes.
Behold the extreme beauty of his lips, which causes great attraction;
behold also his broad chest and his powerful, enchanting body, which serves as the support for the splendor of the Kaustubha gem. (63–64)
Let the women behold the palms of Hari’s hands, rich with a beauty surpassing that of red lac; let them behold his thighs, rich with the splendor of plantain trunks.
His fullness, pervaded by supreme luster, rests beyond the range of vision.
But his form is pervaded by supreme splendor and rests upon the far-reaching vision;
this is not a human body, it is divine, the Supreme Lord.
In his form, no limbs joined by joints are perceived.
"Friends, behold the beauty on the outside and within, on all sides!
(67) This stainless one, devoid of the construction and arrangement of bones, channels, and so forth, shines as the single reality; he is surely the illustrious Puruṣottama. (68)
He who is of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss, the Supreme Lord higher than the highest,
who has been heard of in the declarations of the scriptures— he alone is now being contemplated.
Indeed, by the mere sight of him, infinite happiness is attained.
This is indeed a mass of bliss, the substratum of all fragrances and tastes;
it bestows the light of the Self and carries away our inner mind.
This must be attained in every way at the end of death in the supreme Imperishable.
"We shall certainly receive his mantra during the sacrifice;
for we shall obtain that supreme beloved, Bālakṛṣṇa Janārdana.
What kind of extraordinary mass of splendor issues forth from his body?"
"O gentle one, he is blissful, captivating the heart, bestowing virtue and peace, and imperishable.
Thus, O Rādhā, the women of the city of Maṇipura, belonging to the race of the immortals, spoke to one another, utterly infatuated. (73–74)
Along every path, at the front of every house, at every crossroads, and near every palace,
they honored the Supreme Lord with parched grain, unbroken rice, and beautiful flowers;
uttering shouts of victory, they delighted the Lord of the virtuous.
They bow down from the windows, beholding their beloved Lord,
the giver of enjoyment and liberation, the Lord of the lords of gods, who dwells in the cave of the heart.
Having thus wandered through the city named Maṇipūra, Hari—
Then he went forth to behold the preeminent city of sacrifice;
and the men and women of the earth, having seen the Lord of the lords of gods,
honored him with desired gifts and offerings.
They worshipped him exceedingly and offered him the highest welcome.
With wealth, goods, juices, salts, spices, grains such as *kaṇa*, with products of the cow, sacrificial offerings, rice, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and the like, they honored the Lord. (2.202.80)
With garments, auspicious seats, vessels, blankets, tunics, and jackets;
with armor, ornaments, crowns and the like, and earrings;
with sandalwood paste, most delicious foods, fruits, and dried fruits and such.
With mouth-perfumes and fragrances, as well as with strings of jewels and garlands,
and with various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) consisting of gold, silver, and copper,
all the subjects indeed worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa. (82–83)
Encouraged by his army, Kṛṣṇa, having thus granted a supreme audience and having joined the people with blessings and likewise received their gifts,
returned to his own abode accompanied by the assembly of kings and others.
Hari gave the royal palace, fit for the residence of Ruma and equal to heaven;
and all the wealth, grain, and other items that had arrived for the sacrifice, the King joyfully caused to be distributed as if for evening recreation. (85–86)
At night, he organized a great festival with enthusiasm for dancing,
and furthermore, he made a gift of wealth for the purpose of bestowing his daughter.
Then Hari, having eaten himself and having fed his family members and dependents, [proceeded].
After all the great sages, the women dear to Brahmā,
and the subjects had happily retired, he slept upon the bed of Amarikā;
then the immortals attended upon that new beloved with most devoted service.
At dawn, musical instruments were sounded to awaken the Lord;
women performed auspicious recitations and songs.
At that time, the sweet sounds of the musical instruments became pleasing even to the ear.
Having performed his morning rites, Hari-Kṛṣṇa woke up and went to the assembly hall.
(91) Having partaken of milk and other refreshments, he went to behold the pavilion, which was most beautiful and had been constructed by Viśvakarman and others during the night. (92)
It is vast, ten *krośas* in extent, adorned with ten thousand seats,
frequented by ten million deities, and endowed with variegated banners.
Therein are nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), as well as one supreme, ultimate pit.
Having observed the altars, the vessels, the halls, and the sacrificial kitchens;
having examined the oblations for the gods and the fuel for the fire-offerings, and indeed having looked upon the offerings for the ancestors,
the Blessed One was gratified, became serene, and was filled with great joy.
Likewise, there were hosts of Yoginīs possessing both divine and non-divine perfections,
as well as circles of goddesses, Mātṛkās,
and virtuous women; and circles of Sāṃkhya-Yoginīs who possess the power of sovereignty.
They exist for the protection of the kitchens and for the accomplishment of cooking.
Seeing that, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, became exceedingly pleased;
he then summoned Goddess Dharaṇī and appointed her as the presiding authority over them.
Hari gave Annapūrṇā and Lakṣmī as assistants to Dharaṇī for the sake of providing food and other necessities for all the worlds;
he gave Varuṇa the waters and Kubera for the sake of sacrificial fees.
There, Hari appointed the two Aśvinī sons for the sake of health;
Dharmarāja for protection; Vighneśa for the pacification of obstacles;
Sūryadeva for the sake of inexhaustibility; and the wielder of the trident (Śiva) for the purpose of instruction.
He appointed Viṣṇu for the purpose of giving, Brahmā for the purpose of establishing order,
and Mahendra for the purpose of honoring those who have arrived. He appointed the god Agni for the purpose of cooking and Pārvaṇa for the purpose of illumination.
In order to increase the volume of the sound and other qualities, he employed electric lights.
Thus, O Rādhikā, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada at dawn, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa directed his employees. (103–104)

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Pastimes, Worship, Feeding, and Resting at Night in Maṇisevāpuri and Yajñapattana, as well as the Mobilization of Laborers in the Morning on the Sixth Day of the Bright Half of Bhādrapada," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*. Chapter 203 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 203]
[The Author: Chapter 204.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, then in the morning, having performed his daily rites and taken his meal—
Having performed his devotions, Bālakṛṣṇa went to the assembly hall.
(1) The king arrived there quickly, longing to behold the worship;
having offered worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings, he then spoke to Hari with humility. (2)
"O ocean of compassion, O Lord, command me today regarding my duty;
I shall accomplish everything for the sake of the sacrifice with all my power. Hari said to him: "A beautiful and auspicious golden image..."
Today, have a golden image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa made, complete with jewels;
have a golden image of Nārāyaṇa made measuring nine fingers in height and having four arms,
and likewise have one of Lakṣmī made measuring eight fingers.
Have a beautiful image of me made, ten fingers in height;
have a ruby and a golden form fashioned, reaching above my ears.
Have Lakṣmī made as far as my shoulders, and the lotus-born goddess reaching above my ears.

"O King, for the sake of the sacrifice, have a very beautiful golden image made: one of Ramā reaching up to my shoulders, Rādhā rising to the height of my neck, your daughter Amarīśā as my eldest [daughter] reaching up to my face. (7–8)
Having caused the eight forms to be fashioned, have Satī and Śiva made; likewise, have Gaṇanātha and [the others] made of gold,
and properly have Nandin and Kārttikeya fashioned.
O King, having likewise caused the five forms to be made, as well as the Sun-god,
have Viṣṇu fashioned from gold and Brahmā fashioned from gold;
and also my mother Kambharā and my father Gopāla.
Then, have a beautiful golden *pañcaka* constructed;
likewise, have a vast golden image of Vāstudeva made.
Furthermore, have a golden *yūtha* built as a dwelling place for all the gods.
Thus Kṛṣṇa gave his command: "Have a temple for the gods constructed.
Having received the command, the king quickly had the sculptors work;
then Bālakṛṣṇa remembered Nārada, the knower of the worlds.
Sanatkumāra, the virtuous Garuḍa his own vehicle,
the Sudarśana discus, and the yogi Saccidānanda— these five, possessing divine awakening, quickly arrived there before him.
Having performed their duties, they prostrated like staffs and respectfully awaited the appropriate command.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa gave them a meal of grace,
as well as drinks and necklaces, placed his hands upon their heads, and thereafter assigned them their tasks.
He gave them an invitation leaflet indicating the purpose of the sacrifice:
"On the seventh day, a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice will commence here on this earth,
in the region of the immortals, at the place named Kenāṭaka."
In the vicinity of the city of Maṇisevā,
upon a vast expanse of land at the confluence of the Śeṣakāṣṭha forest and the river Vinipāra,
on the shore of this lake, there was a festival of pearls performed by the liberated ones residing in that abode.
With all his incarnations, as well as with the attendants of those [incarnations],
with all the female incarnations and their female attendants,
with the divine manifestations (vyūhas) and the female manifestations, and with all the Nārāyaṇas; ||21||
All the Nārāyaṇīs must come to the festival of the sacrifice;
likewise the Viṣṇus and Vaiṣṇavīs, the Īśvaras and the powers of Īśvara, Vairāja with Vairājī, Satya with her attendants, and Śiva. (22–23)

One must come by all means through illusion (*māyā*), through illusory principles (*māyikatattva*), through the *puruṣa*, and through the great energies of Brahmā; likewise, one must come through celibate students (*brahmacārin*), ascetics (*yati*), sages (*ṛṣi*), and holy men (*sādhu*).
The fathers and mothers, as well as the gods and goddesses;

the guardians of the directions and the protectors of the worlds, accompanied by their beloveds; the male and female deities dwelling in heaven and those residing in the Bhuvarloka—all must come. (25–26)
It should be attended from all sides by the planets, constellations, and stars; by the grahas, pretas, and piśācas; by the bhūtas, kuṣmāṇḍakas, vināyakas, and gaṇas;
as well as by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas.
By the subjects of Kāśyapa, by the Vetālakas, and by the Śaktis;
by men of passionate and ignorant natures together with their families;
by ascetics and yogins, as well as by trees, grasses, and creepers. (28–29)
"Let it be visited by shrubs, grasses, and insects—even those born of old age or from castor-oil plants;
likewise by those born of sweat, those born of particles, those born of bulbs, and those born of water;
and also by mountains, rivers, and lakes."

The guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), the household deities (gṛhadevas), the ancestral deities (kuladevas), the temples, the gandharvas, the cāraṇas, and others must come from all sides, along with sacred fords, groves, forests, and lakes— both natural and artificial. (3.1–3.2)
With bards, Magadha minstrels, heralds, dancers, and actors;
with wrestlers assuming many forms, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others;
with throngs of courtesans and groups of helpless beggars. (33)
Vaninīs dwelling on the earth, those residing in the netherworld (pātāla),
and powerful serpents must also assemble with respect.
Furthermore, the Śāstras, the Vedas, the sciences, and worldly affairs from all sides [must gather].
"All insentient and sentient beings must come to this great sacrifice.
I am Brahmāpati, the Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, the Supreme Sovereign;
as Bālakṛṣṇa, the Incarnate One, I invite you all to the ritual."
"O preceptors of the gods and daityas, endowed with sovereign power,
O brahmins, sages, and those devoted to Brahmā, you must come to my sacrifice on the morning of the seventh day, beginning from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada. (37–38)
The sacrificial rite is considered supreme; therefore, the householders must come.
To those who do not come, I, Narayana, utter a curse.
Let these sanctifiers certainly purify the land of Amari.
May Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others, as well as Śeṣa, Nārāyaṇa, and the rest,
together with their respective liberated souls and attendants, come here, bestowing happiness.
May Śrī, Ramā, Rādhikā, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Tulasī, and Prabhā likewise arrive.
May all the Yoginīs, the Mothers, the Kula-devis, and the Caṇḍikās, who dwell in their respective abodes, come to this great sacrifice.
May all those who are indeed celibate practitioners also come to my sacrifice.

"May they come to the sacrifice—along with their wives, sons, kinsmen, and followers—for the sake of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. A great assembly shall be held here, graced by the Lord of the Cosmic Egg. || 43-44 ||
May Brahmā and the others, as well as Viṣṇus with hundreds of thousands of faces,
and all those who are supreme, come together to this Śrī-Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
I, Acyuta, invoke them, address them, and summon them.
"The Supreme Brahman, beyond the imperishable, the beloved of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
(46) Thus, O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa indeed gave this excellent letter for the purpose of inviting the sacrifice to Nārada and the others. (47)
He swiftly granted them the most wonderful power of assuming infinite forms,
as well as sovereignty, the ability to travel anywhere at will, and omniscience.
Accepting the command of Hari, they all departed, seeking his invitation.
At midday, the Supreme Lord remembered Yamarāja;
by his command, he caused the realm of Yama to be freed from all bondage and liberated all living beings who had fallen under Yama's control. (2.203.49–50)
Then, at the sacrifice, he appointed the messengers of Yama as the ritual assistants.
Having thus completed his midday meal and other duties, the Blessed One himself then caused all those seeking the merit of the sacrifice to eat.
Then he partook of food and thereafter obtained rest for a moment.
Then Hari commanded Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śaṅkara regarding all embodied beings who were arriving there.
He likewise gave instructions for the welcome of men and women seeking the sacrifice,
as well as for Satī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī;
and he also gave instructions for the welcome of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

He also gave instructions to Dharmadeva and Vāsudeva for the purpose of welcoming all those who had arrived seeking the sacrifice. Then he spoke to the venerable Lomaśa and likewise to the sage Bhāradvāja.
"May you all welcome the inhabitants of heaven, the sons of Gaṅgā who follow Yavakrīta, as well as all embodied beings;
for those who have arrived, provide hospitality with water, food, fruits, flowers, and dwellings. (57)
With respectful offerings of dwellings and necessary articles,
he spoke of the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the wish-granting creepers (*kalpalatā*), the wish-granting jewels (*kalpamaṇi*),
and the celestial rivers (*kalpagā*) throughout all the residences surrounding the sacrificial city.
Let them all attend everywhere, endowed with the intent to welcome [the guests],
providing ever-new things according to their requirements and as they desire;
let them then offer everything wished for to those of great honor.
Hari spoke of the Brahma-lake, the Virajā, the Rasakūpa, and likewise the Amṛta;
he said that these should remain at various locations and indeed provide everything desired and all that is to be drunk.
To Pavana and Vahni-deva he said: "Become the fans;
become the providers of heat here as well, for you shall assume many forms.
To Vyoma he said: "You indeed must provide the power of hearing from afar here."
"O Siddhis, you must perform the welcoming rites here!
Thus he then spoke these mantras: "Let various auspicious sounds be proclaimed in the sacrificial arena for the honor of those who have arrived. (64–65)
Then Śāradā said, "Let them perform auspicious songs;
let them indeed play musical instruments for the sake of welcoming those who have arrived.
And Hari said to the kings, "Let them pay honor with their armies."
"Welcome to all the people from every world who have come seeking the sacrifice!
Let them show great honor with musical instruments and the sounding of mechanical drums.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, Bālakṛṣṇa spoke thus. (67–68)
Quickly fashion dwellings for the liberated ones in the sky;
likewise, fashion dwellings for the Lords of Incarnation in the sky. Fashion dwellings for the gods, the best of sages, and the ancestors in the sky.
"O you who dwell within the cosmic egg, upon the surface of the earth at the city of sacrifice,
do indeed fashion higher and higher regions of the ground in an instant!
I grant you divine power, which consists of the fruits arising from mere resolve."
"Accomplish quickly by means of that [knowledge] which is the most excellent, known as the *Kalpaklṛpti*.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One ceased speaking and remained upon his own seat.
At that moment, King Rāyarokīśvara made a fervent supplication to Hari.
If you have the desire today, sanctify my kingdom by coming to my city on the bank of the divine Mahākañjī river— a forest of radiant women—
and by visiting my realm of Dvimānāyana.
"O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, purify me; there is nothing that you cannot reach.
"So be it," Hari replied, and having drunk the cool water, he ascended the celestial chariot together with his mother and father.
Accompanied by Lālāyana and likewise by Māṇakya,
he departed together with his attendants of divine bodies, his servants, hundreds of female slaves,
and his twelve principal virtuous wives.

In the city of Sphūrtinārīvana, in an instant from the sky, the king and the sage, together with their attendants, then offered them due honor. Having descended into the garden near the royal palace, they [remained there].
They welcomed Viṣṇu with their army according to the prescribed rites.
Having washed his feet according to the rule, they drank the nectar-like water.
With sandalwood paste, flowers, and garlands, they honored him with great devotion.
The king and the sage also honored his other companions;
then they led the Lord of Śrī from the palace to the royal residence.
There, the ten queens performed the *ārātrika* ceremony for him.
Then the princes and princesses performed the lustration ceremony (nirājana).
Hari then revealed his own divine four-armed form to them;
and the twenty-one princesses were struck with wonder and amazement.
The princess, subject to her mother’s will and deluded by her mother’s command,
then placed the garland of choice around the neck of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having obtained Janārdana as their beloved, they became fulfilled in their purpose.
The king indeed celebrated that beautiful festival in the royal palace.
The monarch placed wealth numbering ten million at the feet of Hari,
and likewise gave him a dowry consisting of golden necklaces and other ornaments.
He gave him ornaments and garments and performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
Then, having bowed to Hari, he quickly sought forgiveness from the Lord:
"I have been purified; you have taken my hand and accepted my daughter."
"O Blessed One, I have been brought near; always protect me from Māyā.
(88) Then the queens, having bowed to Hari, placed the moon-mark upon their foreheads;
they begged for forgiveness from Hari, entreating him, "Please lift us up. (89)
Hari said, "I shall uplift you and lead you at the end to the supreme state.
Thereupon, he caused his own divine four-armed form to disappear.
After that, he wandered through all the royal palaces.
The Imperishable Lord went personally to the houses of the principal leaders and caused them to be purified.
Accepting the worship performed for him, the Lord, resplendent with his army,
proceeded along the royal highway toward the city of Sphūrtinārīvana.
He was highly honored by spectators, worshippers, and the common people;
his feet were saluted and adored, and he was presented with offerings such as wealth and other gifts.
He was delighted by the goddesses who sang of his glory and by their acts of worship.
Strengthened by blessings, strewn with flowers, and highly honored;
praised with shouts of "Victory! and the sounds of musical instruments, the Supreme Lord, drunk in by the lotus-eyes and drawn forth by their inner feelings, departed. (94–95)
Then all the leading merchants, the common people, and the women,
having received honors and having wandered through the city,
arrived at the royal palace and drank the water of the great Kāñcī.
Honoring the lordly sage named Mahākāñcana,
the king gave him wealth there; the sage, for his part, took that riches and,
having placed it upon a celestial chariot for the sake of the sacrifice, conveyed it to the sacrificial ground.
Then Hari, having ascended his celestial chariot together with his family,
traveled through the sky with the king, the queen, and the maidens, traversing the entire kingdom and observing various regions and lands.
In the evening, he arrived at the shore of Lake Vinipāra;
having descended from the royal palace, Hari went to rest.
Those maidens, whose truth was as firm as Brahmā’s, took up their residence with their beloveds.
Then both Rāyarokīśvara and the great sage Mahākāñcana indeed gave riches to Kubera for the purpose of the sacrificial rites. Then,
from the great sky, celestial chariots of the earth appeared in the atmosphere.
From Akṣara, from Goloka, from Vaikuṇṭha, and even from Amṛta;
from the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta), from the world of Īśa, from Vairāja, and from Hiraṇmaya;
from Satya, from Svarga, from Janaloka, and from Meru and all the directions—103–104.
From the eightfold city and from the intermediate spaces of the worlds they arrived;
from the nether regions and from the three creations, celestial chariots arrived.
Hundreds of millions and billions of vehicles belonging to those who had been invited also arrived.
The sky, indeed, attained a state of being covered by tens of millions of celestial chariots.
At that time, there was heaven after heaven, great heaven, and the heaven of Brahmā;
shining like the sun, it truly became a second heaven.
O Rādhikā, the creation of living beings, the supreme creation of the Lord,
and every kind of creation of Brahmā indeed came there at the invitation;
meanwhile, the night dissolved into a single hair-pore of Śrī Hari.

"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara offered a welcome; the great deities descended from the sky to their appropriate places. (109) Thus, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*: the instruction for King Rāya-Kinnara to commission a golden image; the dispatching of Nārada and others, accompanied by invitation letters written in saffron ink, to the various worlds; and the arrival of Hari in the kingdom of King Rāya-Rokīśvara, where He was worshipped in the city of Sphūrtinārī.
The two hundred and third chapter, titled "Description of the Wandering through the Country, the Return to the Sacrificial Ground, and the Arrival of the Great Honorees," [ends].
