Chapter 204.
[Author: Chapter 205.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the liberated ones have arrived from the supreme imperishable abode (paramākṣaradhāman).
Others, liberated souls, arrived there seated in divine celestial chariots.
Śrī Hari offered them a most magnificent welcome.
The lords of the abodes, the incarnations resplendent with their divine powers, also arrived.
O Rādhā, accompanied by you and surrounded by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, I ascended a celestial chariot along with my divine consorts and departed.
Śrīpati Nārāyaṇa also came there from Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, accompanied by all his attendants and joined by the Ramas,
Vāsudeva and the other Vyūhas arrived at that sacrifice;
likewise, all the incarnations came as well, attended by their respective Śaktis.
The glorious Bālakṛṣṇa himself personally offered them honor and a welcome;
so too did Mahāviṣṇu, Bhūmā, Virāṭ, and Hiraṇmaya.
Even the lords residing within the eight enclosures, though subject to Māyā, [did the same].
And those who had gone to the world of Śiva, being his very portions, also arrived there.
Śrī Hari himself performed a welcome reception for all those created by Īśa and for the inhabitants of the creation of Brahmā.

The incarnate Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, provided a dwelling in the city fashioned within the ether of consciousness-bliss for those residing in Brahmā’s Satyaloka as well as for the inhabitants of other worlds. (9)
The ṛṣis, the ancestors, and the perfected ones (siddhas) indeed arrived there at that sacrifice.
The gods, the lords of the gods, the guardians of the quarters, and the protectors of the world—
those who dwell in the intermediate space (bhuvarloka)— also arrived at the ritual in their celestial chariots (vimānas).
From the sky, the planets and stars arrived at Meru,
as did the lunar mansions, the gods led by the Suras, the Vasus, and tens of millions of Rudras;
the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, Dharmarāja, and other deities likewise came.
And they arrived at the sacrifice, accompanied by their own retinues;
the hosts of Kailāsa, the Gaṇas, the Yoginīs, the Caṇḍikās, as well as the Bhairavas and those with bodies of spirits—all these followers of Śaṅkara arrived there. (13–14)
Hari gave suitable dwellings to these millions of gods. Brahmā, Āja, and Viṣṇu offered them a most cordial welcome and great honor.
The sages, headed by Lomaśa, also bestowed abundant respect upon them.
They paid great honor to the Vālakhilya maharṣis, to the sages of sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), to virtuous women, to the righteous, and to the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
they provided them with abundant dwellings and pleasant comforts, including Lakṣmī and others. (16–17)
Charioteers, bards, panegyrists, and others; Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and the like;
Kim-puṃsas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and various classes of professional singers;
storytellers, entertainers, and wrestlers—all arrived.
Dancers and actors likewise arrived;
people of all castes and inhabitants of all lands came there,
as did men from Saurāṣṭra and those dwelling in the southern region.
The people of Uṣṭrālaya and the people of Brahmabhūmi, those residing in the kingdom of Śiva and the inhabitants of the ancient kingdoms,
the residents of Rāśiyāna and the dwellers of Ketumāla. (21)
Likewise, the inhabitants of Abrikta, those dwelling in the region of Ārakta;
the residents of Ārātrika and Guhāvāsa, and those of Cāmarī;
as well as the Hāritas, the forest-dwellers, and the mountain-dwellers. (22–23)
Those dwelling in the water, those dwelling on land, and those dwelling in the sky all arrived together.
To them, Śiva and the other deities granted dwellings and showed them honor.
Likewise, trees, creepers, clumps of grass, bulbs, roots, and so forth [did the same].
Those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and those with divine bodies arrived;
so too did beasts and birds of the *haṃsa* and *garuḍa* species, as well as other creatures with divine bodies, who came there. (25–26)
Hara and the other gods assigned them dwellings and paid them honor;
all the progeny of Kaśyapa and all the inhabitants of the Atala and other nether regions,
as well as the serpents, the Nāgas, and the lords of the Nāgas, arrived as mounts.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and fierce Rākṣasas arrived;
Śaṅkara and Satī likewise bestowed upon them dwellings on the southern shore of the lake and accorded them honors as was appropriate.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others, as well as Śeṣa, Nārāyaṇa,
and other incarnations likewise arrived at that great sacrifice.
Among them, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was filled with eagerness.
He offered him honor and a welcome, and bestowed upon him auspicious dwellings.
(3.1) At that time, the rivers, streams, oceans, and the fundamental principles (tattvas) arrived there;
as did the sacred fords (tīrthas), the best of brahmins, and the great sages with their divine bodies. (3.2)
Clouds and flashes of lightning arrived there at that sacrifice;
Brahmā then offered them a welcome according to their respective rank.
Time itself—moments, hours, days, fortnights, and years—was present.
The ages and the months arrived, and Śaṅkara offered them a welcome. Then the artisans residing in ten million worlds arrived at that sacrifice;
Viśvakarman honored them well and provided them with dwellings.
Vāsudeva Nārāyaṇa then indeed bestowed upon all those of great splendor gifts and other honors as was appropriate.
O Rādhikā, in those dwellings, everything was truly complete.
There were lamps, vessels for drink, and various kinds of food—both solid and soft;
there were sweetmeats, drinks, foods to be licked, and foods to be sucked, as well as seats and other furnishings, and very soft, suitable beds. (37–38)

There were male and female servants with vessels of milk, excellent rivers of nectar, and most beautiful gardens; there were attendants, maidservants, and workers, all established as laborers in every residence, remaining obedient to their commands. (39)
By the mere resolve of Bālakṛṣṇa, millions of infinite servants appeared;
there were instruments for hearing from afar and instruments for seeing from afar, aerial vehicles, and those possessing the supernatural powers of touching all things and so forth. (2.204.40–41)
There were streams of ghee and streams of milk, as well as mountains of sugar,
all prepared on every side for the delight of the lords of the earth.
O Rādhikā, how can I describe the mountains of golden ornaments and other such things?
Likewise, mountains of garments were fashioned there by the glorious Supreme Soul;
at that time, troughs for fragrant lac-dyes were created there,
and there were supreme mountains consisting of every kind of cosmetic substance.
There were indeed long ponds, lakes of juices,
and rivers of liquids for the enjoyment of those seeking the sacrifice;
they were just like those that exist in the imperishable realms of Goloka and Vikuṇṭha.
On the white plateau of Kailāsa,
such splendors appeared that all the inhabitants of every creation forgot their own respective worlds, having attained a far greater prosperity at the sacrifice of Hari. (46–47)
And thus, until morning, a most excellent welcome was indeed extended.
At that time, the provision of food, service, drink, bedding, clothing,
and even the gift of male and female servants— all was provided in full.
Then, being honored and delighted, they cast off their fatigue.
Having reached those supreme and pleasant dwellings, they became exceedingly happy.
At night, here and there in that place, there were pleasure-pavilions for their delight.
During the night, there were entertainments consisting of dancing and other such performances, as well as tales of warriors,
displays of physical forms, comedies, singers, narrative recitations,
and dramatic plays.
On the morning of the seventh day, likewise auspicious and dear,
O Rādhikā, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, having been awakened, performed his bath,
offered worship and salutations, and summoned the sage Lomaśa. (52–53)
And he commanded the Ṛṣi, his guru who had performed his salutations:
"Apply yourself to the sacrificial rites, you supreme seer of all.
And Lomaśa said to Kṛṣṇa: "That great sage is your disciple."
He was a treasury of the Vedas and Śāstras, yet beyond the scope of ritual action (karmakāṇḍa);
he knew the three periods of time, was a knower of mantras, and was endowed with the perfection of meditative absorption (samādhi).
Possessing all sovereign powers, he was a portion of Kṛṣṇa, a yogi united with the Supreme Lord.
Appoint here in this sacrifice that most excellent one who is steadfast, capable of assuming many forms, known by the name Svayamprakāśa, the supreme witness of all,
and endowed with the power of universal movement.
"Unite him with that peaceful one, the storehouse of virtues, the worthy witness.
Then Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, Bṛhaspati, Kumāra,
and Gaṇeśa indeed rejoiced in that worthy union.
Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Vaiśvānara,
as well as the Viśvedevas and the Maruts, likewise rejoiced in him. The Lord,
self-luminous and the great treasury of omniscience, [was present].

Being humble, he accepted the words of his guru and the words of Hari, which bestow the power of all-seeing vision. Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s beloved gave him a necklace for his neck and a helmet for his head that served the same purpose.
He gave him a cloak enriched with gold stars, a silken garment,
and likewise a washed cloth that signified his status as an all-seeing witness;
and there in that pavilion, he prepared for him a great and excellent seat.
Then he had him seated and sent him to the sacrificial pavilion.
Lord Mādhava himself offered the seat of honor to Lomaśa,
who is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and the beloved of Lakṣmī.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa indeed granted his own representative status;
at that time, the king considered himself the patron (yajamāna).
Accompanied by the noble queen Satīdevī, he went to the sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa).
All musical instruments were sounded as an auspicious sign. (67) Those authorized for the sacrifice arrived from all directions at the sacrificial ground;
the earthly gods, the celestial gods, and the gods of truth all assembled there. (68)
The lords, the gods, and all the deities of the gods assembled;
likewise, the liberated ones and the incarnations, the lords accompanied by their consorts,
the sages, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings accompanied by their wives [all arrived].
The gurus of all the worlds, as well as the Vyāsas and those even more extensive than Vyāsa, arrived;
the Vedas, the Ṛks, and the Sāmans—those whose very selves are worthy of worship—arrived;
and those advanced in age, advanced in knowledge, and proficient in ritual action, also arrived.
Those advanced in voice, advanced in prosperity, and advanced in virtue arrived;
those advanced in wealth, advanced in righteousness, and advanced in worldly standing arrived.
Those advanced in yoga, advanced in austerity, and advanced in their station arrived.
Those advanced in song, those advanced in the Vedas, and those advanced among the aged arrived;
those advanced in spiritual existence also arrived, as did the kings.
Likewise, reciters, ritual workers, performers of fire-sacrifices, and givers of gifts came together.
The gatekeepers and those guarding the pavilion, both principal and subordinate, arrived;

the carriers of ritual materials and the bearers of oblations, with kindled fires, arrived; and those who had prepared the sacrificial pits at night and filled them with decorative creepers arrived. (75)
All those who carry banners and flags arrived there;
those who fetch water, those who prepare collections of vessels, those who carry goods, and those who carry fruits and flowers arrived there. (76–77)
Carriers of juices, carriers of dairy products, and carriers of sweets arrived while musical instruments thundered loudly and the sky resounded with noise.
All of them, eager to see the grounds of the pavilion, indeed came forth.
Then those who move through the sky remained in the sky, the Antarayogins in the intermediate space;
those dwelling in the Bhuvarloka stayed having come together on the wind-path,
while the Vaimānikas, dwelling in the heavens, remained in their celestial chariots amidst the luminous realms.
Then they all arrived and stood facing the pavilion:
virtuous, chaste, and fair women, beloveds of Brahmā, and those who had been abducted;
immortal maidens and goddesses—all had assembled there.
The wives of the gods, having donned their finery and adorned themselves with various ornaments,
all arrived at the sacrificial pavilion, filled with the weight of perfect bliss.
There were also the wives of the lords, the liberated women, and the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs as well.
The daughters of Manu and the mothers, as well as the Yoginīs, arrived;
the female ascetics, the wives of Brahmā, and the Brāhmaṇī women also arrived.
The deities of the site, the deities of the sacrificial pits, and the deities of the branches all arrived.

The deities of the gates, the deities of the archways and so forth, the deities of the pavilion, the deities of the pillars, the deities of the banners, and the deities of the sacrificial posts arrived; as did the thirty-three subordinate deities and the deities of the five abodes. (85–86)
Hearing the sounds of musical instruments, ten kings, accompanied by their wives and endowed with many jewels, arrived at the sacrificial pavilion;
appearing as the very embodiments of the sacrificers, they entered the sacrificial pavilion.
The elemental principles beginning with earth, as well as the objects of the senses such as sound,
the fires, and those possessing physical forms, all arrived at the sacrificial pavilion.
There were also various kinds of fire-pits and altars, including the principal altar.
The sacrificial altars and the offering vessels also arrived in embodied form;
the ladles, the *sruva* spoons, and other ritual implements, as well as the leaves and the deities of the *kuśa* grass;
the fuel-sticks, the grains, and even the oblations—all arrived there.
The sacrificial grasses (*caru*) and purifiers (*pavitra*) arrived there in embodied form;
the purities of cow-products and the seven types of earth also arrived.
Seats and ritual implements likewise arrived in embodied form. (91–92)
Then the Jyotirpuruṣa, possessing a physical form and bearing a divine appearance,
arrived while making all the quarters resound with the beating of a drum.
And the Svarṇayūpapuruṣa also arrived there in bodily form.
All sacred fords (tīrthas) arrived there in personified forms.
The auspicious blessings, the ancestral spirits (śrāddha-puruṣas), and the states of satisfaction also came there;
indeed, all unprecedented things gathered for the sake of attaining the supreme wonder.
The *madhyāpūrva*, the *trikāpūrva*, and ten thousand others arrived there;
all the *kāṇḍikās* and ritual injunctions (*vidhis*) arrived there in due order.
All the things to be offered as oblations arrived there, having taken on embodied forms.
The subjects and the lords of the people, including children, the elderly, and the youth—
both men and women— arrived at the sacrificial ground amidst the sounds of musical instruments; it was refined, endowed with beauty, and rendered as if immortal by the radiance of the heavens.
It was filled with pairs and singles, providing new life;
it shone with pavilions and was exceedingly proud of its sacrificial cities;
it was the most excellent earth, inhabited by the dwellings of all creation.
O Rādhikā, when that auspicious moment— the best for the commencement of all undertakings— had arrived, which was sovereign, equal to the divine abode, and pertaining to the Supreme Lord,
the auspicious sounds of conch shells arose.
Then there arose sounds of trumpets accompanied by the thundering of lightning,
which served as omens for the commencement of the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa).
[At that time,] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama...
He arrived quickly at the pavilion, accompanied by the swelling sounds of victory;
he sat upon a divine seat within the pavilion near the sacrificial pit.
Then the kings, having arrived, also took their seats near the pits.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Welcome and Accommodation of All Guests, the Preparation of Necessities, the Ordinance for the Self-Luminous Incarnation of Hari to Witness Everything at the Sacrifice, the Sounds of Auspicious Musical Instruments, and the Arrival of All the Goddesses and Gods at the Sacrificial Pavilion," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 205: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 205.
[The Author: Chapter 206.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, in the morning, in the pavilion near the sacrificial pit.
The king of the Rāyakinnaras,
accompanied by his wife, arrived together with the sage Dridhamāna as a patron of the sacrifice;
likewise, King Rāyarokīśvara came along with Mahākāñcanakarṣin.
Likewise, King Rāyarājajit, accompanied by his wife and together with the sage Ālārāya, went to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Similarly, joined by his wife, he proceeded to the pavilion near the pit.
King Rāyavākakṣaka,
together with his wife Cārulāṣarṣiṇī, likewise went to the pavilion near the sacrificial pit;
and King Rāyamārīśa also went to the sacrifice accompanied by Dānavarṣi.
Then King Rāyabāleśvara, accompanied by Queen Mālāvanarṣi,
went together with his wife to the pavilion near the sacrificial pit.

Then King Rāyalambāra, accompanied by his wife, went to the sacrifice in the vicinity of the sacrificial pit along with the sage Rūpartu. And King Rāyanavārkabha, together with Vāśṛṅgatanukarṣin, [went there as well]. || 7–8 ||
King Rāyahuṇḍeśa went with his wife to the sacrificial pavilion near the fire-pit, accompanied by Vīrākaja, the son of Karṣin;
he arrived at the pavilion near the fire-pit together with his wife.
And King Rāyakūpeśa,
together with the sage Heyatāna and his wife, went to the sacrificial pavilion near the fire-pit.
In this manner, the ten kings [beheld] the ten fire-pits that had been prepared.
Then, each of them sat down in the vicinity of their respective fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*).
At that time, Śrī Hari, a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) youth,
was present at the teacher’s (*ācārya*) fire-pit together with Lomaśa and King Kinnara.

Together with his wife, he sat upon the supreme throne (1.3). The kings, who were devoted to the Vedas and accompanied by other ṛṣis from various sacrificial pits, sat down as was appropriate, in pairs, as described by Lomaśa (1.4).
O Rādhikā, the celestial brāhmaṇas, the earthly brāhmaṇas,
and the brāhmaṇas born of the soil then began auspicious rites there with melodious voices.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa sat upon an excellent throne.
In the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala, Hari thus installed the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and likewise had all the other forms set up,
including a golden Garuḍa, as well as the gatekeepers and the attendants.
Hari established those endowed with power in the presence of Viṣṇu;
the installation of Gaṇeśa was in the northeast, while the pedestal of Rudra was in the east,
the pedestal of Kṣetrapāla was in the southeast, and the pedestal of Śaktipra was in the southeast.
On the right is the Gaṇeśa-pīṭha, and in the southwest is the Vāstu-pīṭha;
in the northwest is the Yoginī-pīṭha, and likewise the Snāna-pīṭha in the north.
All the Graha-pīṭhas are located in the center of the womb within the intermediate corners.

And having placed those gods there, the Supreme Lord established them; he sprinkled the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, and the altar, as well as the ritual substances within the pavilion. He also established the principal items, such as grains and fuel-sticks.

Barley, rice, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, honey, sandalwood, mustard seeds, white mustard, yellow pigment (rocanā), fruits, as well as sugar, perfumes, flowers, betel nuts, incense, lamps, and so forth. 22–23.
There, the preceptor Lomaśa performed an auspicious svastika ceremony,
as well as the presentation of garments, woolen cloth, a ring, a vessel, madhuparka,
and other offerings; likewise, he provided gold, a lamp, a bathing vessel, a conch, and so forth.
Sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and saffron;
(25) a vessel for clarified butter, a vessel for the sacrificial porridge, rice grains, and various utensils;
a sacred thread, seats, ritual hand gestures, ornaments, and flowers. (26)
There Hari placed the betel leaves and whatever else was required;
thereafter, the patron, together with his wife, went to the bathing hall.
Having bathed, he then came to the pavilion and approached Gaṇapati.
Then the king performed the worship of the Mothers and also conducted the śrāddha for them.
Having performed the worship of the Mothers, he then received the Vaiṣṇava initiation.
He then performed an expiation and subsequently performed the vṛddhi-śrāddha.

Then the king performed the protection against planetary influences, the hoisting of banners, and the pitching of the camp; thereafter, he conducted the formal selection of the preceptor and other officials. Having proclaimed the place and the time, he then offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka).

He performed the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and likewise the selection of the Brahman priest; he also performed the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya*), provided the seats, and offered the ritual fees (*saṃvaraṇa*), the sacrificial gifts (*upahāra*),
and the materials for the priestly compensation (*niṣkraya*).
He performed the selection of reciters and readers in that same manner;
he conducted the selection of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Brahmins.
And the Brahmins, masters of the four Vedas, chanted the mantras appropriate for themselves.
The Brahmins, who were well-versed in the Agamas, performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite;
they uttered words of "Svasti" and then bestowed blessings.
Likewise, all the seven Ṛṣis and hundreds of thousands of great Ṛṣis [did the same].
The king released the *vardhinī* pitcher filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Then he placed gold, sprouts, and jewels therein.
Thereupon, Śrī Lomaśa [invoked] the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa there.
He established a golden image accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Bhū, and Pārvatī, and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites.
There, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa himself shone in person. (37–38)
He installed a golden image of Śrī Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Rādhikā, and Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Śrī; indeed, they appeared there in person.
At that time, he also installed the various incarnations together with their respective Śaktis.
All of them stood there in person at the sacrifice upon their own seats.
Then he indeed established the Vāsudeva and other vyūhas;
those four were present, and others likewise attended.
He established Bhūmā, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vairāja, and the lords of the Āvṛtis;
they all appeared there in person,
accompanied by their respective powers and attended by their respective retinues.

Īśāna, Viśvasṛj, and Viṣṇu, each endowed with their respective powers, having been invoked, arrived and shone forth within the range of perception. So too did Mahāmāyā, Puruṣa, and the principles (tattvas) along with their constituent elements (tāttvikas). ||43-44||
The Śaktis also appeared in person, having been summoned;
all the beloved consorts of Brahmā likewise arrived at the sacrifice, having been summoned.
They all shone resplendently in person upon their own seats within the pavilion.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, remained personally in the station of Brahmā;
and Rudra, possessing eleven forms, remained in the station of Rudra,
accompanied by the Rudrāṇīs and by the Gaṇas, such as Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, and others.
Even the divine golden [deities] sat down visibly upon their own seats; likewise,
the ancestors and the great seers were also invoked and appeared there in person at the sacrifice upon their respective seats.
The Maruts, Vasus, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and lords of the gods;
the lords of the quarters, the world-protectors, and those who have been invoked and move within the field of perception—
all arrived accompanied by their wives and sat down upon their seats.
Then the Siddhas, the Nidhis, the Grahas, the Upagrahas and others,
the Tārakas, and the Gocaras, together with their wives,
were summoned and all sat down visibly upon their respective seats, composed in meditation.
The Seven Sages, the Vālakhilyas, the Kṛttikās, and likewise the Directions;
the Ādityas, Kāmadeva, the Manus, and the lunar days— having been invoked,
they appeared in person and attended the sacrifice.
The constellations and the digits, as well as the thirty-three gods and their followers;
the qualities, the circle of Yoginīs, the sacred fords, and likewise the rivers;
the oceans, the oblong ponds, the wells, the lakes, the mountains, and so forth.
And having been invoked, they all arrived in person with their beautiful forms:
the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Vināyakas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vetālas, and others, at that great sacrifice. (55–56)
Accompanied by their respective families, they arrived in person at that sacrifice;
having been invited, they then sat down fearlessly in the pavilion.
Sūtas, Māgadhas, bards, and others—hirelings, wandering minstrels, and Kinnaras—[also gathered there].

The Vidyādharas, Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, and crores of Siddhas were personally summoned; they arrived and took their places in the pavilion. There were also ascetics of the four castes and holy men such as Sanaka and the others.
All those lifelong celibates who had been invoked stood within the pavilion;
likewise, Garuḍa, the swan, the elephant, the horse, the lion, the bull,
and the rat— these who were invoked arrived.
They shone in person upon the well-adorned pavilion where seats had been provided for them.
Hanumān and the others— long-lived ones who possess the splendor of Brahman— were all invited and arrived in person at the pavilion.
Likewise, the castes, the stages of life, the duties, Dharmarāja with his attendants and sub-attendants,
together with Citragupta and others, joined by Śrāvaṇa and the rest;
Time, the years and so forth, and the Yugas, all manifest in embodied forms.
Having been summoned, all beings present themselves in the pavilion:
creatures dwelling in water and on land, even grasses and the like;
creepers, trees and the like, as well as kalpa-roots and medicinal herbs. (64–65)
The deities of the pillars and so forth, having been invoked, appeared in person within the pavilion;
likewise the household deities, the village deities, the forest deities,
those dwelling at the boundaries, the wild deities, and the deities of the branches and the archways.
Then the deities of the pillars, the deities of the doors, and the deities of the sacrificial pits (67);
likewise the deities of the thresholds and the deities of the *pālikās*;
all the deities of the ramparts and all the deities of the gate-towers (68).

Then, in that sacrifice, there were the deities of the courtyard, the deities of the corners, the deities of the beams, the deities of the slabs, the deities of the banners, and the deities of the jars;
as well as the deities of the staffs and the deities of the pedestals, each accompanied by their respective goddesses.
Once invoked, they appeared in person, standing there in embodied form.
Then Dharma-deva, together with his wives, daughter, and son, arrived there in embodied form; having been invoked, they came to that place.
The Dānavas and the hosts of Daityas, the progeny born of Kaśyapa and others,
as well as birds, beasts,
living creatures, reptiles, snakes, Nāgas, and all the rest, having been summoned, arrived.
They sat down in the pavilion upon the seats prepared for them, having taken embodied form.
Dwellers in all abodes, inhabitants of all worlds,
and residents of all created realms were invited there into that pavilion.
Indeed, sentient beings with physical forms stood upon the seats provided;
likewise, the insentient, the classes of inanimate objects, and embodied beings who were wretched and helpless arrived at the pavilion,
having been granted access, and offered words of praise.
Kāśa grass, kuśa grass, leaves, splinters, and likewise fuel-sticks; sacrificial offerings for the gods and the ancestors, fruits, flowers, grains, and so forth;
juices, substances, sweets, sweet foods, and likewise barks. (76–77)
Then, at the sacrifice, all the essences of fragrance arrived in embodied form within the pavilion; they were invoked and stood there visibly present.
Likewise, the herds of wish-fulfilling cows and the wish-granting creepers also appeared in personified forms.
The wish-fulfilling trees arrived, as did the thought-gems;
there were personified treasuries of the world-age and millions of inexhaustible vessels.
There were weapons such as the conch and the discus, as well as the sacrificial implements for the rites.
All the ritual means, millions of vessels for the limbs of worship,
and all [deities] invoked, stood in embodied form within the pavilion.
The mantras, the Vedas, the injunctions, and the various forms of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) were present as well.
The Purifications (Śuddhis) and the unprecedented Devas, possessing embodied forms, were invited into the pavilion;
they arrived and took their seats as appointed.
Likewise, the vowels, the Vidyās such as Śāradā and others, as well as the Brahmavidyā and so forth [were present].
The Gītis, the Sāman hymns, the Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ families,
and all types of fires were summoned into the pavilion;
they then sat down upon the offered seats in embodied form.
The preceptors of the gods and the Daityas, and the Vyāsas who are the embodiments of exposition;
penances, methods of yoga, knowledge, and even dispassion; devotion and all supernatural powers—having been summoned, they arrived. (85–86)
Multitudes of women stood there visibly, as if personified; obstacles appeared in the form of non-obstacles, diseases took on the appearance of health,
and sufferings arrived in forms that were not suffering, having been summoned.

Then Dharma’s lineage, as well as Adharma and his wives, and those belonging to their lineages, arrived at that sacrifice having become gentle. At that time, Adharma assumed the form of Dharma, transforming his appearance. ||88-89||
Then Ānanda, happiness, peace, contentment, satisfaction, and the like were invoked and arrived in embodied forms within the pavilion;
as did the objects of the senses, such as sound, as well as the six sheaths and other constituents residing in the body.
Summoned to the pavilion, they all arrived in embodied form.
O Rādhikā, this pavilion, endowed with the entirety of creation, shone like a divine abode upon the arrival of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa. || 91-92 ||
In the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
the Lord of all— whoever abides in Him, what partiality can there be for them?
Whether they be insentient, sentient, or a mixture of the insentient and the sentient.
All lineages belong to Hari; He abides equally within all.
Even embodied beings—whether characterized by passion (rājasa), ignorance (tāmasa), or goodness (sāttvika)—are indeed all holy ones, divine beings, bliss itself, and yogis in embodied form.
Having been invited, they arrived and sat down in the beautiful pavilion.
The giver and the priest were both Kṛṣṇa himself, the eternal Supreme Lord.
Therein, there was indeed no deficiency; even the narrowness was expanded.
Then poverty itself was transformed into magnanimity;
even the word "no" (na) there was transformed into the sound of "give" (hā); and even doubt there was transformed into certainty. (97–98)
Then fear suddenly vanished and attained fearlessness; deficiency was revealed and reached a state of abundance.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the deities and others were there in that pavilion.
Having arrived in embodied form, they sat down at their own installation. Indeed, all those very beings who were previously invisible perceivers appeared there in person by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa.

O Rādhā! Thus, for all the gods, the installation upon the altars and other sites took place as required within the pavilion at the ten sacrificial pits. All the kings likewise performed that very same sacrificial rite.
Then the worship commenced, impelled by those respective sages.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Kings and Sages at the Pavilion, the Installation of the Divine Seats, the Selection of the Officiating Priests and Preceptors, and the Manifest Splendor of the Visible Deities," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 205. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (The Tretā-yuga Lineage).
Chapter 206 [Author: Chapter 207 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa established His golden parents in the pavilion,
as well as Sūrya, Candra, Śaṅkara, Satī, and Gaṅgā;
[He then installed] the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa according to the procedure prescribed by Lomaśa.
The king of the Kinnaras worshipped the Supreme Lord;
there he also worshipped the mother and father of Hari.
Then he offered the invitation, the seat, water for the feet, and the respectful oblation.
He gave water for sipping (ācamana), and water also for the purpose of purification;
then, for the sake of cleansing, he gave milk, curd, ghee, and sugar-candy.
After that, he gave honey and sacred water (tīrthavāri) for the purpose of consecration (abhiṣeka).

Even the cleaning of clothes, the rubbing with fragrant oil, the offering of garments and ornaments, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and vermilion; flower garlands, collyrium and the like, incense, lamps, and saffron. (59–60)
He offered Tulasī, lotus garlands, food offerings, and a sacred thread;
an umbrella, chowries, fans, excellent food offerings, and fruit;
as well as water, betel leaf, the waving of lights (ārārtika), and a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa with various modes of adoration— including praise, forgiveness, prostration, falling like a staff, and offering handfuls of flowers—
he then [honored] the incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, the gods, the sages, and the celestial beings.
The king worshipped the ancestors, the goddesses, and the deities;
then he performed the *vyāhṛti-homa*, which is a constituent part of the expiation.
He then performed the *viṣṇu-śrāddha* and conducted the ceremony of beholding the face [of the deity].
The king gave the vessel of clarified butter as a gift to the preceptor. He heard the recitations for peace performed by the brahmins, which bring about happiness;
having heard the auspicious recitations for well-being, he indeed paid homage to his guru.
Then the sage Lomaśa performed the primary ritual act of the sacrifice;
he caused the king to make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and the subsidiary resolves (*aṅga-saṃkalpa*).
The king established the place for the lamps and performed the worship of Bhūmi, Kūrma, and Ananta.
Having taken mustard seeds in his left hand, he performed the protection of the directions;
scattering them on all sides with his left hand, he caused obstacles to be driven away.
Then, O King, the monarch prepared the ground and performed the worship of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
Having invoked the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) into the water, he performed the sprinkling upon his own body;
with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he performed the sprinkling of the sacrificial materials.
He likewise performed the worship of Gaṇeśa directly with *dūrvā* grass and other offerings.
Then, with sixteen types of offerings, he performed the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇa-pūjana).
Thereafter, he performed the worship of the Mothers beginning with Gaurī.
Having performed the worship of the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, the king then [proceeded]. (17–18)
He performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors, which brings them satisfaction;
then he offered the respectful salutation (*argha-vandana*) and wound a thread around the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
He placed medicinal herbs and flowers within it, along with the five sprouts (*pañca-pallava*) and the five gems (*ratna*).
And he threw a golden fruit, clay, grain, and dūrvā grass.
Then he performed the selection of the preceptor, followed by the selection of Brahmā and the others,
the selection of Gaṇeśa, and the selection of the gatekeepers.
He chose the officiating priests and performed the honoring with *madhuparka*;
he partook of the *madhuparka* and then performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Then the king indeed gave wealth for the purchase of the cow to the Brahmin.
And he requested blessings from his venerable preceptor, Bālakṛṣṇa, and Lomaśa.
Then the sage Lomaśa applied the *tilaka* mark upon the king,
and he tied a protective thread on the queen’s left wrist for her protection.
Then he also performed the *puṇyāhavācana* ceremony;
he placed a water-filled jar together with a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) upon grain. He worshipped that jar and performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with its waters.
Lomaśa performed the consecration of the sacrificer and also arranged for the placement of the *vardhanī* pitcher.
Having circumambulated it, the king established it within the pavilion.
Lomaśa then caused a water-procession to be performed, accompanied by ceremonial jars,
auspicious women, musical instruments, vehicles, and the chanting of hymns. Having worshipped Varuṇa, Gaṇeśa, and the Mother of Waters at the sacred ford, [he proceeded].
And he worshipped Jīvamātṛ and Sthalamātṛ.
"May the Mothers of Water—the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the frog, the crocodile, the leech, and the spider—be satisfied. (2.206.30)
May these seven Mothers of Life— Kumārī, Dhanadā, Nandā, Vimalā, Maṅgalā, Calā, and Padmā— be fully satisfied. Also [may] Urmī, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Pānadevī, and Vāruṇī [be satisfied].
"May Nirmalā and likewise Godhā, as well as the Mothers of the Land, be satisfied.
Then he worshipped the circle of the sixty-four Yoginīs;
he also fully honored the Kṣetrapāla, the host of Tīrthas, and Varuṇa.
He performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) and the worship of the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
Then, having arrived at the pavilion accompanied by the water-pot,
the king worshipped the deities presiding over the door-posts.
Having adorned the threshold with circular beauty and having prostrated before the Vāstu deity,
the sage Lomaṣa then performed the ritual installation of the Vāstu;
having prepared the Vāstu-pedestal, he also worshipped Gaṇeśa.
Having invoked the sixty-four deities of the site (vāstu-devas) and worshipped them thoroughly, the sage Lomaśa fully honored the water-pot (kalaśa).
Within the pot, he worshipped the form of Vāstu with the sixteen-fold offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and others.
Then, having performed the external fire-oblation (bahir-homa), the sage offered a bali-offering to him.
Thereafter, he performed the worship of the pavilion and the worship of its pillars;
he worshipped the deities of all the corner-pillars as well as the central deities.
Then the king worshipped the deities of the gates and archways;
he performed the worship of the Vedas, the worship of the insignia, and the worship of the branches.
He worshipped the deities of the tree in the water-pot according to the prescribed rites.
He offered an oblation of beans to the spirits and other beings and then withdrew it.
He worshipped the thirty-three deities within that beautiful, auspicious mandala, which was filled with divine powers.
In the center, he worshipped the primordial Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the source of all incarnations, along with Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, the glorious Nārāyaṇa accompanied by all his consorts,
as well as the various incarnations and the Lords endowed with their respective powers.
Likewise, she worshipped all the goddesses of the lords (Īśvarāṇīs) as well as other Śaktis.
The Muktas and Muktānikās also worshipped the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma), and Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhikā, accompanied by the hosts of Gopas and Gopīs. ||44-45||
Then the king worshipped the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who was accompanied by His beloved consort, His attendants, and Garuḍa;
he also worshipped the female attendants along with the goddesses Ramās.
The king then performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the propitiation of the Vāstu deity;
thereafter, he performed the worship of the lords,
as well as Brahmā, Soma, Īśāna, and Indra.
He worshipped Agni Vaivasvata, Rakṣas, and Varuṇa; he also worshipped Vāyu, Kubera, the Vasus, and the eleven Rudras.
He likewise worshipped the twelve Ādityas and the two Aśvins there.
He worshipped the ancestors, the Viśvedevas, and the seven sacrifices;
he worshipped the serpents, the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, and Skanda;
as well as Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Śūla, and the group of seven beginning with Dakṣa.
He likewise worshipped Durgā and Viṣṇu, as well as Vaiṣṇavī;
he fully honored Svadhā, Svāhā, Mṛtyu, Rogas, and Gaṇeśa.
He also worshipped Varuṇa, the Lord of Sacrifice (Indra), and the Maruts.
The king also worshipped the earth, the river Gaṅgā, and all other rivers;
he worshipped the seven oceans and Mount Meru;
and he worshipped all weapons and sacred fords (tīrthas).
He worshipped the divine ornaments that had become manifest in bodily form,
and he also worshipped the eminent great sages, such as Bhāradvāja and others;
likewise, he worshipped Arundhatī and the other goddesses present there.
The king honored all the wives of the world-protectors (dikpālas) correctly;
he likewise honored the lords, all the ancestors, sages, gods, and seers, as well as virtuous men, virtuous women, and all the practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. ||56–57||
He worshipped all the Kuṣmāṇḍakas, Vināyakas, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and Pretas who dwell in the Bhuvarloka,
as well as the messengers of Yama, both those born of the lineage of Dharma and those born of the lineage of Adharma.
There, that king honored all the women and men;
he also honored the mountains, forest trees, creepers, and varieties of grass, as well as the clusters of bamboo and those who provide nourishment. 2.206.60.
He worshipped the creatures born from roots and tubers, those born from trees bearing fruit, as well as those born from the womb and those born from eggs;
he honored both minute and massive beings, including the inhabitants of the waters. He also paid great honor to all creatures born from sweat and to all the progeny of Kaśyapa.
He worshipped all embodied beings— those born on land, those born from the wind, those born from fire, and even those born from the sky; those of the earth, those born from water,
as well as those characterized by goodness (*sattva*), those who are impure, those characterized by passion (*rajas*), and those with bodies of darkness (*tamas*).
Then he honored the poor, the helpless, and even the mendicants—
those who were without refuge, dependent on others, and living off the fortune of others.
He also honored the groups of servants, the distant relatives, and the groups of slaves.
He honored those who knew the arts, masters of crafts, performers of drama and dance,
as well as the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, bards, and storytellers.
He also honored the insentient specific principles (*tattva-viśeṣa*), the qualities (*guṇas*), and the primordial vowels (*svaras*).
The king honored all the mantras and the objects of the senses;
he venerated the songs, the personified Vedas, the sacrificial vessels, and the excellent grains;
he also worshipped the crops, all the fuel-sticks, and the oblations.
Whatever beings were then invited by Hari himself into the sacrificial pavilion for that festival arrived there—
even those of lowly names and those possessing lowly bodies. (68–69)
Then the Supreme Lord worshipped His entire creation, which had assumed the form of His own offspring, in His own Śrī-Vaiṣṇava sacrifice; likewise,
He worshipped the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas residing in Pātāla, who possessed the forms of Nāgas.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of happiness, honored all those who had gathered in the pavilion from their respective abodes and worlds;
indeed, Hari himself honored even the insects, moths, and other such creatures.
Having offered the *bali* to all, he indeed gratified those present at his own sacrifice:
Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others, as well as the yogis headed by Sanaka,
all the attendants beginning with Viśvaksena, and the deities of the ritual diagrams.
At that time, the king worshipped Śuka and others who are masters of the yoga of knowledge, as well as Matsya and others who are forms of Keśava;
he worshipped all those beginning with Praṇava and the incarnations of Śāradā, those beginning with Ṛṣabha, and all those beginning with Viśvāmitra. (74–75)
Then the king worshipped the powers beginning with Brāhmī, as well as the siddhis such as aṇimā,
the guardians of the directions along with their weapons, the Vedas, the Gaṅgā and other rivers,
the deities of the mantras, and his family members.
Then he performed the rite of fire-transference (agnyuttāraṇa) and applied ghee to the embodied forms.
Having performed the consecration with streams of water, he [invoked] the vital breaths along with their seed-syllables:
"iha prāṇāśca āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ. (77–78)

With the mantra "saḥ so 'ham" and other such formulas, he performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using seed-syllables (*bīja*). In this manner, Hari also performed the worship once again for all those golden images that had been installed there in the pavilion.
[He saw] the auspicious [form] of himself, of his father, of his mother, and likewise of his sister;
of the host of brothers, of Gaṇeśa, and likewise of Rādhākṛṣṇa;
and also of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and of Padmā.
For the sake of consecration, he worshipped the golden images of Ramā, as well as Māṇikī;
likewise the golden images of Sūrya, Candra, and Īśāna;
and the golden image of Satī.
For the sake of dwelling within the sixteen vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he worshipped all the forms;
then he recollected the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of the individual soul (*jīva*).
At that time, Kṛṣṇa then brought to mind the forms of his incarnations (*avatāra*).
All the divine deities, who consist of all essential principles, arrived and took their places within the pavilion upon the images and other objects.
Having thus installed the forms according to the prescribed rite, they were endowed with life.
Having made those arrangements, Bālakṛṣṇaka entered. Then the king, with the approval of Kṛṣṇa, performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā),
the worship of the Supreme Deity, and the worship of the Guru.
He worshipped Vedavyāsa, Garuḍa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī; likewise, he honored Yama, Vāyu, Śiva, Indra, Nirṛti, and Rudra.
He also worshipped Śakti, Kūrma, Ananta, Pṛthivī, and the Mountain.
He worshipped the Ocean of Milk, Śvetadvīpa, the pavilion, and the lotus; likewise, he worshipped Narāyaṇa as the golden solar orb, and the divine Narāyaṇa-Viṣṇu as the lunar orb. (2.206.89–90)
In the sacrificial fire, he worshipped the god Agni, Nṛsiṃha, and Narāyaṇa;
he worshipped Sattva-śrī, Rajas-bhūmi, and Tamas-durgā.
He worshipped the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), and the Supreme Self (Parātman).
Vimalā and the other Pīṭha-śaktis worshipped him whose nature is knowledge;
he worshipped Pradhānapuruṣa, the primordial person of Prakṛti. He also performed the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the worship of Viśvakarman.
Mekhalā worshipped Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra;
she then performed the worship of the yoni, the worship of the throat, and the worship of the navel.
She likewise worshipped the Vāstu deities, as well as Brahmā and the others, the Vedas, and the Tortoise and other [deities].
Then the king named Rāyakinnara performed worship;
having worshipped Dharma and the others, he then established the fire. Having gathered the fire into a casket and whirled it around three times, ||95-96||
He established the fire in the southern pit and Svāhā in the other; he then worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, followed by the bringing forward of the Praṇītā vessel,
as well as the strewing of grass and the placing of the sacrificial vessels.
Also the purification, as well as the sprinkling with water;
the turning over, the lifting up, the sprinkling, and likewise the washing;
the pouring, the placing on the fire, and likewise the circumambulation with fire.
The divine Lomaśa performed the installation of the planetary deities;

he worshipped the nine planets and likewise worshipped their presiding deities (adhidevas). Then he offered worship to the secondary presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās) and to the guardians of the world (lokapālas).
He performed the installation of the Kṣetrapāla and likewise the installation of the Lokapālas;
he performed the installation of Mahārudra and their worship.
Thereafter, he performed the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs.
Then he performed the worship of the fifty guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas),
as well as the Supreme Lord, the incarnations, the Īśvaras, and the deities.
The king meditated [upon them] and then applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) of Hari.
He also gave him a garland of *tulasī*, and then he offered a [sacred] wreath.
Having presented the conch, the discus, and other symbols, the king indeed worshipped him;
he also offered the mark of the fish, the trident, the bow, and the arrow.
Then he worshipped the svastika, the banner, the wheel, and the thunderbolt;
he performed the worship of the bell and conducted the worship of the water-pots. Lomaśa then caused him to perform the purification of the ground and likewise the *namas* [prostration].

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Hari said that this entire world created by me is transitory;

The Great Self is imperishable, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it is composed of innate bliss within the body, yet it consumes the fruits that follow from karma.
As long as karma remains stable, it proceeds from there to another abode.
For that which is performed here, one indeed experiences its fruit in the other world. (4) Having abandoned everything, all must certainly depart for another realm;
therefore, one should perform those spiritual practices by means of which happiness may be attained once gone there. (5)
Indeed, all the other worlds, beginning with Svarga, which are full of happiness,
are attained through abundant merit, through acts of giving, through deeds of benefiting others,
and likewise through service rendered to the aged and the virtuous.
Through blessings and one's own merit, one is born in the highest heaven.
Even higher than that is the supreme heaven of Vaikuṇṭha, or beyond that, Goloka, the imperishable abode, or even my own supreme realm. (7–8)
In Vaikuṇṭha, my auspicious families indeed exist,
as do the circles of male attendants and female attendants;
there are divine couples, and I too am a couple.
There, indeed, I am served by millions of maidservants headed by Lakṣmī.
Likewise, in Goloka, I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa, united with Rādhā and fully served by millions of couples consisting of cowherds and cowherd-maidens.
I abide as the sovereign of kings, a great ocean of eternal bliss;
therein exists the supreme, perpetual happiness of the Yugala.
Through my yoga, everything is divine—a state of liberation from which there is no returning.
That supreme bliss, which is eternally increasing and devoid of diminution,
likewise exists forever on Kailāsa, in the realm of Śaṅkara inhabited by eternal yogis, situated directly below Goloka. (13–14)
I, Śaṅkara, dwell there on the auspicious Kailāsa, served by hosts of male and female divine yoginīs. Indeed,
I have assumed that very form which demonstrates the yoga of the householder.

I remain as a householder in the state of a yogi, though my very nature is that of Śaṅkara. That eternal bliss is certain for virtuous couples; as the Lord and Master of yoginīs, I accept the service of Satī.
Thereafter, he dwells in the most excellent happiness, superior to the three worlds, in my imperishable and eternal abode, according to his desire— the supreme state of the Lord,

Assuming forms at will, they enjoy manifold forms, proceeding from bliss to bliss.

There is no end to happiness anywhere, nor does it ever diminish;

These divine objects of the various senses are designated as imperishable. (21)
Indeed, sounds, touches, tastes, scents, and visible objects become divine;

There, within the Imperishable, the pleasure is even greater than that of ten million lotus-like Golokas.
Likewise, all kinds of happiness— exceeding that of Koṭi, Abja, Vaikuṇṭha, and Kailāsa, and desired by the mind— resides in the liberated souls. Yet,

Through my yoga, for my devotees there is a bliss that is the most supreme of all,

O Rādhā, [the goal] may be attained according to one's desire, either as a single form or as a pair;

Herbs, trees, and shrubs do not suffer defeat; likewise, by becoming conscious, one may overcome an enemy who has already advanced. By swallowing adversity, victory is always attained.
By enduring in every way, one gains the merit of good deeds;
by always bowing down, one destroys the effects of evil deeds—

One should also avoid a wolf, an elephant, one who observes the vow of an enemy, and one who follows a wrong path.

(37) He whose entire circle of servants is skilled in theoretical and practical knowledge, who seeks his welfare, is devoted to his word, and is affectionate—he becomes happy. (38)

That [debt] must never be forgotten by him or her anywhere.

"O Sage, fear of this cat arises within me;

"Be a dog," he said; and immediately he became a dog, remaining fearless at all times. (55) Then one day a wolf arrived and pounced upon him to seize him.

Then, when he had become a wolf, a tiger, distressed by hunger, arrived in the forest to kill the wolf;
the wolf, filled with fear, [approached] the sage.
Seeking a state of fearlessness, the sage granted him the form of a tiger.
Having become a tiger, he became fearless and lived happily in the hermitage of the sage.
Once, however, [he was encountered] by a rutting elephant with great tusks.
Seeing him approaching swiftly with great speed to strike him, he went to the sage and said, "This elephant will kill me!
The seer replied, "You are right here; this elephant is powerful and of massive form."
The tiger quickly attained the state of an elephant, possessing exceedingly great strength and vigor.
At that time, a certain lion once saw an elephant;
just as the lion approached to seize it, the elephant turned toward the sage.
Having approached, he spoke of his fear and begged for freedom from fear;
the compassionate sage quickly granted him the state of being a lion.
Then, at one time, by chance, a śarabha arrived there.
While the lion, out of fear, was seeking to seize the maned one [the lion], the compassionate sage, desiring a state free from fear, spoke to him:
"O son, become a śarabha; let there be no fear at any time. (64–65)
Then he was born as a *śarabha*, the destroyer of the life-force of lions;
for seven days he remained fearless in the forest, and there was excessive rain so that the *śarabha* could find no food. (66)
Then he thought, "I shall indeed devour this ṛṣi.
But the great ṛṣi, perceiving that thought through the power of meditation and yoga, said to the mouse: "By the power of my sovereignty, you [shall not harm] me."
He has granted you the state of a śarabha, which is supreme among all and free from fear;
likewise, he is the Lord who, out of compassion, is the bestower of sovereignty and the protector.
Since he is sinless and the giver of life, how can you wish to harm him? (69)
"Therefore, O you born of a sinful womb, return once more to the state of a mouse! Thus cursed, he attained the state of a mouse;
having reached that condition, he fell into a state of wretchedness and was subsequently cast out by the ṛṣi.
Having understood this, one should give vessels and other items that are either pure (*sāttvika*) or devoid of purity; likewise, one should never bestow excessive power upon them.
Trust placed in such people does not lead to one's welfare.
A master, a merchant, or a king who desires happiness must indeed understand this:
never, without prior examination, should anything be given to an unworthy recipient. One who has fallen into the snare of an unworthy recipient shall never attain happiness.
Even one of noble birth who is base here, or even one who has encountered suffering at some point,
does not set his mind upon evil if he is sattvic, even when being torn asunder.
A man of noble birth who is divided [in mind] is devoid of intelligence and is the most foolish of kings.
Even one who has attained what is difficult to obtain may fall into enmity with those he serves.
[But one should employ] a man of noble birth, well-trained, wise, a master of theoretical and practical knowledge, grateful, patient, contented, and one who has conquered his senses. (76–77)
One who seeks the welfare [of others], serves the virtuous, honors his father, is devoted to the service of Brahman, is endowed with the virtue of offering all actions to his chosen deity,
follows disciplined conduct, is intent on auspicious thoughts, and understands humility.
The wise lord who employs one who understands gestures, is endowed with policy, skillful, and filled with virtues;
who knows how to serve, perceives gain and loss, is grounded in integrity, and possesses rare sovereignty—[that lord is truly wise]. (2.208.79–80)
Whether he be a master, a king, or someone else, he always becomes happy.
Having thus recognized such a disciple, O King, I bestow upon him here my own nature,
which consists of the mastery of yoga established in samādhi.
"Behold my eternal divine nature, O Raṇajit, always!
By this, supreme perfection that grants liberation shall come into your hands.
Having spoken thus, Hari bestowed his divine nature upon Raṇajit. (82–83)
To his father-in-law, the high-souled husband of twenty maidens, he—
having attained that divine state and possessing divine, beautiful eyes—
beheld the divine, prosperous, and great city of Kuṅkumavāpī.
He beheld divine Vaikuṇṭha as well as the imperishable Goloka;
[he saw] Kāṃbhareya, the Lord of the Imperishable, Bālakṛṣṇa, the husband of his daughter.
Then Hari granted his own divine vision to the subjects.
At the end of a moment, having attained human form, he gave them his own mantra.
Then those thousands of subjects became Vaiṣṇavas.
Then the son of Gopāla went to the Yukāsanā river to bathe.
Having bathed and performed the meditation and worship offered by the king, he quickly accepted the offerings;
then, having partaken of the milk and other drinks, he ascended into the sky in a celestial chariot provided for him, and after receiving due honor, he departed from there. (88–89)
Accompanied by Ālāya and Sarṣi, as well as the mountain-dweller (Bhūbhṛt),
Hari, joined by twenty maidens and attended by his ancestors,
arrived at the sacrificial ground with hundreds of thousands of millions of gold coins.
He entrusted the treasury to the guardian for the purpose of making gifts during the sacrifice.
At night, he partook of a meal and likewise held a most excellent great festival;
having fed all the people, the Supreme Lord went to sleep.
Then, in the seventh [age], the people born in that land as well as those from other lands—
sages, seers, and others devoted to the narration of dharma—
[will recite] the narrative accounts of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
There, filled with great enthusiasm, they sang in that most magnificent sacrifice.
Indeed, there were hymns consisting of divine sports and wonders,
on the bank of the Śeṣakāṣṭhavana river, the dwelling place of the virtuous.
All the Apsarases take delight in the form of donkeys;
indeed, the denizens of hell perform a dance at night in the form of actors.
Then, O Rādhā, twenty maidens serve Hari.

At night, having served their new Lord— the husband of Śrī, the Lord of Īśāna, the beloved who is enchanting with beauty, the eternal bliss, and one who blazes with the sovereignty of yoga— they attained that state and became fulfilled. (97–98)
At dawn, Hari abandoned his sleep due to the auspicious sounds arising from the auspicious musical instruments, the voices of the *sūtas* and *māgadhas*,
and the songs of the virtuous women who are dear to Brahmā. (9)
Janārdana was awakened by hymns of praise (*kīrtana*) and acts of worship (*bhajana*).

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Hari instructed the people, including Rāyaraṇajit and others, in the city of Mīnārkakṛṣṇapattana during the Tretā lineage in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; how He arrived at the sacrificial ground, slept at night, and was awakened in the morning," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (Tretā-yuga Lineage), Chapter 208.

Chapter 210 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: in the morning, having performed the ritual of bathing, the Lord sat upon a beautiful golden throne to perform worship. There, he worshipped Yajñanārāyaṇa with various offerings.

Then, accompanied by sixteen and other eminent [sages], the sage Lomaśa arrived there for the purpose of worship and worshipped the Supreme Lord. Likewise, kings who were dear to Brahmā also arrived and paid their respects.
Meanwhile, musical instruments were played during that great festival of sacrificial rites.
And the kings, the subjects, as well as the great sages,
and all the lords beginning with Brahmā, quickly went to the sacrificial ground for the purpose of proceeding there.
In the sacrifice, even the kings made their desired offerings into a single mass.
Milk, sacrificial fuel such as wood, grains, fruits, and rice—all these were provided there in an instant by the gods and others. (5–6)
The preceptor, all the deities, the officiating priests, as well as the reciters,
the performers of rituals, the sacrificers, and their assistants, stood nearby. There, the Brahmins, bestowing auspiciousness, uttered words of benediction.
Then there were proclamations for an auspicious day and the chanting of the Vedas;
while all the sacrificial priests remained in their respective places,
[the king] performed the purification of the body, the ten-fold ritual bathing, and the salutation at the feet of his guru.
The ritual resolve, the protection of the directions, and likewise the worship of the water-pot;
the worship of Gaṇeśa and also the worship of the Mothers;
the Nāndī-śrāddha, as well as the offering of water (arghya) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka)—these then took place.
Consecration, worship of the Vardhinī vessel, worship of the Vāstu deity;
(11) then the worship of the pavilion and the worship of the Sarvatobhadra diagram;
worship of the deities and likewise the honoring of the deities of the yantra. (12)
Then follows the removal of the fire and the worship of the deities of the seat (pīṭha).
Next is the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the worship of the deity, and then the auspicious worship of the fire.
Then comes the worship of the planets, the Yoginīs, and the Kṣetrapāla.
The worship of the liberated ones, the incarnations, and the lords;

the worship of the goddesses and the wives of Brahmā; the honoring of celibate students, the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the virtuous women; and the worship of the righteous. (14–15)
The worship of the ancestors, the sages, and the guardians of the directions;
the honoring of the world-protectors and the worship of those dwelling in heaven;
as well as the worship of the thirty-three gods and the five deities. (16)
Likewise, the worship of the *rakṣasas* dwelling in the *bhuvarloka*,
the honoring of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and human beings, as well as the worship of those living beings residing in the four oceans and the classes of servants. (17–18)
The worship of shrines, both inanimate and animate;
the propitiation of all stationary objects that bestow nectar;
and likewise the [worship] of living beings and of the principles (tattvas) residing in the subterranean realms and below.
The worship of Śrī Mahāviṣṇu and likewise the worship of Viṣṇu;
the honoring of the conch and the bell, the worship of the vital breaths (prāṇas), and the offering;
as well as the oblation with many kinds of delicious foods, clarified butter, ghee, and so forth.

The lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the offering of oblations (balidāna), the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), as well as the priestly fee (dakṣiṇā), prostration (namaskāra), hymns of praise (stuti), the bestowing of blessings (āśīḥpradāna),
the dismissal (parihāra), and the meals— all these occurred in due order at the sacrifice.
In that great sacrifice, millions and hundreds of thousands of gods attained satisfaction.
Having likewise performed the entire ritual procedure at midday on the eighth day itself,
the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa ate together with his family.
He took betel and rested for a moment;
meanwhile, the king arrived there, eager to make his request,
accompanied by the beautiful Lāṣarṣi and the prince Rāyavākakṣaka.

He then requested Hari to sanctify his own kingdom, which was situated in the water like an island, as well as the city of Viṣaturīyaka and the city of Tūryapadā. Hari said, "So be it," and he then quickly made himself ready.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā—
may His parents, brothers, sister,
and likewise His brother’s wife Amṛtā, as well as the virtuous beloveds of Brahmā, all be satisfied. (28)
Śaṅkara, Lomaśa, and the lovely Ṛṣi Lāṣa,
as well as King Rāyavākakṣaka, then quickly ascended two celestial chariots; they all departed together with a limited number of followers.
Having crossed the ocean expanse, they reached an island known as Viṣaturīya; the king went ahead of them.
In the city of Turyapada, he performed a welcome reception for the sake of the horse.
Accompanied by the queen and the army, the king paid his respects.
Having alighted from the celestial chariot in the garden precinct near the royal palace,
Śrī Hari emerged from that vehicle.
The king performed worship with flowers and other offerings to the illustrious Mādhava;
likewise, the immortals worshipped the Supreme Lord with saffron and other substances.
Then, shouts of "Victory! and the sounds of musical instruments arose on all sides.
They honored the Lord of Īśas with flowers, parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
And the subjects honored the Supreme Lord with shouts of joy.
Then the king caused Hari to ascend a small celestial chariot.
And he likewise caused his family to ascend the celestial chariots;
having approached every house in the city with the chariots,
he indeed purified the dwellings of the people.
Having received worship, great offerings, wealth, and excellent jewels,
and having performed purificatory rites in his own home,
he once again wandered through the divine city and granted his own vision.
Then Hari came to the royal residence, a celestial palace;
he rested for a moment and drank milk, and thereafter they all drank it—
the king, the queen, the princes, and even the three princesses.

They worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa (41). With various offerings— sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, saffron, other necklaces, and great jewels— they then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) (42).
The three maidens placed the charming garland of choice around the neck of Hari;
Hari, indeed, took their hands with the consent of the queen.
Having obtained a handsome husband, the maidens became fulfilled in their purpose.

The king rejoiced in many ways, and the queen indeed rejoiced greatly. During the festival, Hari sat upon the great lion-throne in the royal palace and gave them perfect instruction that bestows happiness.
Devotion to Hari, the imperishable Lord, should always be practiced by those who have taken refuge in me;
the service of the virtuous should always be performed, for it is auspicious, bestowing merit and liberation.
One should daily protect all living beings with compassion.
Whatever is beneficial for a particular purpose should be accepted therein, and never anything else.
Self-restraint through the intellect, acting with the understanding that all is to be grasped, and liberation through discernment— these are what must be attained by the embodied being in this world.
One should apply oneself to those duties consisting of the knowledge of Dharma,
as taught in the scriptures and as instructed by the guru;
one should act for the benefit of all without contradicting any of the principles of Dharma.
A virtuous man should indeed protect the Dharma and accomplish his own purpose.
The scripture is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa, while punishment is the duty of a Kṣatriya;
agriculture is the duty of a Vaiśya, and service is the duty of a servant.
Truth is indeed the dharma for all; those rich in dharma are remembered as deities.
Such humans are equal to gods, for they embody the vital breath of all beings.
A scripture is that which provides instruction, characterized by the authority of its teacher.

In ancient times, at my command, Brahmā established this for the sake of protecting the world. Furthermore, for the sake of facilitating legal proceedings and providing a basis for trust in one's master, he fashioned the auspicious rod of punishment, which is the very essence of the duty of the Kṣatriya.
Furthermore, another form of activity, consisting of enterprise, has been established;
it sustains all people by means of various coins acquired through policy.
That [activity] consists of the production of revenue and is characterized by trust in the ruler.
A third person was also created as an instrument for pleasure;
another person was likewise fashioned, consisting of commands and instructions, serving as a source of confidence for all the low-caste people. (56–57)
Established in their respective offices, they obtain the means of sustenance from all the worlds— including gods, asuras, and rākṣasas—
as well as humans, serpents, and even stationary beings. (58)

This fourfold conventional usage, characterized by reliance on the Lord, was established by me in the past for the sake of a continuous flow of happiness and prosperity. It belongs to one who is endowed with dharma, possessed of devotion to me, and solely intent upon me. (2.209.60)
Having become that, I shall indeed constantly abide as its sustainer;
I am the sustainer of actions, of inherent natures, of meritorious undertakings, and of efforts—
and even the sustainer of those who themselves sustain.
"I am the Teacher and the Guide; I am also the one who sustains the course of the world.
Knowing me thus, people should indeed take refuge in me, and they shall cross over [the ocean of existence].
Righteousness (dharma) is always the root of wealth (artha), and likewise, pleasure (rati) is the fruit of wealth."
In this world, all [pursuits] of dharma, artha, and kāma arise from the root of the mind.
All these factors, such as dharma and the rest, which consist of active engagement (pravṛtti), are bound to worldly existence.
Indeed, liberation is said to be the cessation [of activity] from those very things, along with their roots.
The connection with the body through the practice of dharma is the bodily purpose that acts as an aid.
Desire is the fruit; these are all great bonds, and they are all characterized by passion (rajas).
Abandoning those specific distinctions and being free from passion, one is devoted to me.
One whose self is disciplined by yoga proceeds toward becoming Brahman.
If dharma does not grant me attainment, nor does artha likewise;
if kāma does not grant me attainment, then they are considered useless to me.
One should either apply those objects, whether they appear as beneficial or harmful, to Me, or else abandon them.
Otherwise, the intellect of one who indulges in sense-objects will surely wander among them;
thus, the intellect that was withdrawn for the sake of liberation will indeed meet its destruction.
The great delusion that destroys the intellect, which is characterized by darkness (tamas), increases further.
From that arises atheism, and from that comes immoral conduct.
Indeed, through such immoral conduct, the progeny becomes ruined and mixed-race (sāṃkarī).
The virtuous do not enter the home of one who has fallen into wicked conduct.
Indeed, his sins increase, his life becomes miserable,
and even while living, this is hell for him, since his existence is devoid of happiness.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying those defects, for the sake of happiness, and out of a disposition toward all beings,
one should serve those people who are devoted to Brahman and endowed with devotion to Hari.
One should constantly chant my name here and likewise offer everything unto me.
For indeed, that [discipline] conduces to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
One should always propitiate the virtuous through action, mind, and speech;
one should constantly say, "I am yours," bow down, and practice service.
Through the benedictions of the virtuous, through their grace, through service,
through association, and through yoga, a person becomes purified.
This company of the virtuous is sinless and cuts away all defects.
It shall pacify even the most grievous sins; of this there is no doubt.
(77) In this world, virtuous gurus are the best and grant me liberation.
Gold is excellent in every respect, and likewise, the virtuous are excellent in every way. (78)
Those purifying forms of Kṛṣṇa, extending from the feet to the hair,
will grant me union with Him if they are obtained by any means whatsoever;
they will cause me to practice devotion and lead me to my own abode.

Therefore, one should serve saintly persons who are endowed with devotion and my mantras. Those gurus shall explain to you my supreme dharma, the great bhāgavata; those who practice it will attain the supreme imperishable state.
Indeed, through the grace of their gurus, they shall attain the supreme good.
Morality (*śīla*) is the highest of all dharmas, for the virtuous are those whose nature is morality.
By means of morality, the three worlds can indeed be conquered; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in this world that cannot be accomplished by those possessed of virtuous conduct (śīla).
This virtue is the nectar upon the earth, the most excellent of all things;
such is the supreme good as it exists for one established in virtue.
The constant study of the lives of the virtuous, the incarnations, and saintly women; service—this is declared to be the supreme character, the supreme vow of the nature of Brahman.
Indeed, there is nothing else equal to it when performed with proper conduct toward the guru. (85)
In a former kalpa, there was a king named Prahlāda who was always virtuous.
At that time, his supreme vow was solely the practice of good conduct.
Once, in the past, the auspicious Bṛhaspati approached him. (86–87)
He bestowed upon Prahlāda eternal knowledge in the form of devotion.
When the Guru had departed, the King then spoke regarding the sacrificial fee;
Bṛhaspati indeed requested a fee in the form of virtuous character.
And as soon as Prahlāda gave away his virtue (*śīla*),
that divine virtue emerged from his body, and Śrī also departed along with it.
Thereupon, Prahlāda became devoid of splendor and bereft of righteousness.
Deprived of both virtue and prosperity, he asked that man:
"Who are you, and why are you going thus? Tell me the truth.
Virtue replied: "I am Vow; I am being sent by Charity."
When I depart, this Dharma also departs, and Puruṣa as well.
O King, behold: these others, the descendants of Dharma, also depart when I have gone.
When I depart, the devoted wife Dharma likewise departs, as does Ramā.
"Lakṣmī, Śrī, Bhū, and all the beloveds of Hari surely depart from one who abandons good character.
Hearing this, Prahlāda became filled with fear regarding the abandonment of virtue:
"Where there is no service to the virtuous, nor good character, nor restraint of the senses..."
There is no malice toward any living beings, and there Nārāyaṇa is not present.
Where Nārāyaṇa is not, and where my Ramā is not, there indeed liberation does not exist; therefore, let people be virtuous in character. (95–96)
Let the virtuous always perform service for me, who am worthy of it;
for in brief, that is the conduct which consists of favoring all beings.
Those of virtuous character enjoy eternal prosperity through my grace.
If those lacking moral conduct obtain [wealth], they indeed do not enjoy it for long.
That which was given for the sake of rites such as sacrifice and charity should be consumed by the virtuous;
let the people of this land truly subsist upon the fruits of sacrifice.
"Happy, generous, and likewise endowed with the excellence of virtuous conduct"—
having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One then became silent.
Honored by the subjects and esteemed by the king and queen, Kṛṣṇa [departed].
He bestowed mantras upon the subjects and caused them to drink milk.
Having placed his feet within the royal palace and performed a purifying rite,
Hari was received with a welcome and honors in the evening, accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments and other festivities.
Having ascended his own celestial chariot (*vimāna*), accompanied by his entire caravan,
[he went to] Dvinaska, Pārśvarājya, and also the island of Milvila;
likewise to Vilāsadvīpa and Bulandadvīpa.
Then, having traveled by celestial chariot and sported in the sky,
Śrī Hari, beholding [the scene], quickly descended from the air at night on the eighth lunar day and swiftly returned to his auspicious abode, the sacrificial ground.
Hari performed his bath and the twilight rites, and he took his meal;
likewise, others ate, and Hari provided the materials for the sacrifice.
At night, served by the three maidens, he rested happily.
Under the influence of yogic sleep, Kṛṣṇa awoke at dawn to auspicious sounds:
with songs, the chanting of the Vedas, the blare of trumpets, and hymns of praise;
thus was the Supreme Lord awakened by the Sūtas, Māgadhas, bards, and others.

O Rādhikā, for a moment he meditated upon his own nature as that which is higher than the highest, whose form transcends the imperishable, and which consists of the perfect Brahman, the Supreme Self. (1.09)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Performance of All Rites up to the Final Oblation at the Sacrifice on the Eighth Day of the Bright Fortnight of Bhādrapada in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," wherein it is related how, after the meal, Lord Hari, requested by King Rāyavākakṣaka, went to the kingdom of that king, to the island of Viṣaturīya, and to Dvinaska and Milvilā; having purified those places and given instructions, He returned to the sacrificial ground at night and rested. || 209 ||
