Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; having bathed in the morning and performed His daily worship, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa went to the sacrificial ground. (1)
The sages headed by Lomaśa, kings acting as sacrificers, subjects, gods,
lords of the gods, and those devoted to ritual action all attended there. Fresh sacrificial offerings were brought from every direction.
There, juices were offered by the wish-fulfilling trees and others;
there were also words of benediction and declarations of an auspicious day;
there were the sounds of musical instruments as well as the resonance of the Vedas.
And the sacrificing kings, on the morning of the ninth day,
having assembled at their respective places with devotion for the ritual section,
became attentive; and the rites gradually commenced.
Sprinklings, worship, and offerings of food and oblations were presented;
(6) the offerings into the fire became sacrificial oblations.
The gratification of the deities occurred, and the gods and others attained satisfaction. (7)

Then, at the sacrifice, the embodied beings existing within the creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśvara, and the creation of the individual soul attained manifest satisfaction through the oblations of the ritual.
Likewise, Hari offered the final oblation and a handful of flowers in the sacrifice.
Then the Lord made his reply and offered various foods:
auspicious rice, food from the vessel of delusion, mung-bean water-fritters,
delightful powdered fritters, pearl-like sweets, and likewise *śaṣkulī* cakes.
Cloths, ghee-filled cakes, honey-cakes with a hundred holes, *piṇḍakas*, *barphikas*, sweet-filled *polīs*, and *pūrikās*; *khājakas*,
milk-porridges, milk, *saṃyāvas*, and *birañjakas*.
Kaṃsāra, *bundikā-laḍḍu*, and sugar-and-ghee *laḍḍukas*;
*śrīkhaṇḍa*, *rājikā-rāddha*, *kvathikā*, and soup; as well as rice, many vegetables, leaf-dishes, and other foods. (12–13)
Chickpeas and black gram, both boiled and roasted,
as well as *vaṭikās*, *phullavaṭakas*, *polikās*, and *amṛtas*—
these divine foods are for those who have attained liberation, while these are the foods for the lords of beings.
The food of the gods is nectar (sudhā); the food of the ancestors is the soma-juice (cāma).
The food of the principles (tattvas) is essence (rasa); the food of the rākṣasas is intoxication (mada).
Likewise, the food of all embodied beings is according to their respective fitness.
At that time, there appeared various forms of clarified butter (*yajñaprasāda*) that bestow satisfaction:
many kinds of bright buttermilk, which is sour, desirable, and fragrant;
likewise, there was cooking oil, pacifying substances, and curd-cream (*āmikṣā*).
There were honeyed offerings of many forms, as well as *madhuparka* preparations;
at that time, there were bitter, sour, and pungent powders, savory snacks,
delightful fermented gruels (*āranāla*), and various kinds of fruits.
Lord Hari caused divine betel leaves to be given to the guests;
having thus fed everyone, the Lord then partook of a meal himself.
Accompanied by his family, the Lord of Śrī rested for a moment.
At midday, King Rāyamārīśa requested Acyuta [to come]. Hari became ready to return to his own island;
the Lord likewise prepared the others who were established in eternal yoga, according to their requirements.
Having taken his father and other elders, the Lord Śambhu, Satī, his own family,
and the sages headed by Lomaśa, he ascended the celestial chariot.
At that time, the king, the queen, and the sage of the Dānavas likewise stood before him.
They traveled ahead by celestial chariot to the island named Mālīsmara.
At that time, the city of Ṛddhīśā was adorned with various splendors,
and a reception was quickly prepared for them by the army.
Then Hari’s celestial chariot, having crossed over Vardhi and Khāḍikā,
and having traversed various high and low islands as well as a most beautiful kingdom,
reached Ālīsmara; there, Hari brought the chariot down to the surface of the earth.

In the great garden of Ṛddhiśā, in the vicinity of the royal palace, musical instruments were then sounded and shouts of victory arose; there were songs from the women of the city and the war-cries of the subjects. (27–28)
With warm welcomes, banners and other flags, victory standards, parched grain and unbroken rice, archways, flower garlands and the like,
as well as with joined palms, prostrations, and offerings of flowers, the honoring of Śrī Hari took place. (29)
When Śrī Hari quickly emerged from the celestial chariot,
Queen Kuśalakuṇḍalā— the wife of King Rāyamārīśa—
immediately washed his feet with the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites.
The kings and others drank the water arising from Hari’s feet;
having anointed their feet with saffron, they took up the sacred marks (mudrās).
He likewise gave them flower garlands, fragrant water, and sandalwood paste.

With hands joined in salutation, those women who were like reminders of Kṛṣṇa worshiped him alone with great devotion; so too did the maidens, their hearts filled with emotion. Then the king seated Kṛṣṇa for a moment upon a magnificent palace terrace.
Having led him to his own lion-throne, he gave ten million pieces of gold, as well as garments made of fine cloth and all manner of household goods;
he then bestowed three auspicious maidens along with a hundred thousand jewels.
She affectionately offered three garlands around her husband’s dark neck.
Having understood this and received the words of his mother, the king obtained three maidens as wives—the most excellent beloveds of Kṛṣṇa—and was filled with satisfaction. (36–37)

The queen was born having fulfilled her purpose; then the Lord drank the milk, and others also quickly drank the milk. Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his army, remained for a short while in the city of Ṛddhīśā within the celestial chariot.
Requested by the subjects, he then visited houses everywhere;
having performed purifying rites and bestowed his auspicious sight, he received worship from the subjects with various kinds of offerings. (2.210.39–40)
Taking [the throne], the Lord Hari, the Sovereign, arrived at the royal palace;
seated upon the royal throne, he gave instruction to the subjects and others:
"Through great merits, my yoga has been established here in this great ocean."
Drawn by your meditative cultivation, I have arrived from afar.
(42) Everything given for my sake becomes eternal;
indeed, through my yoga, it becomes free of qualities and bestows liberation. (43)
"Having abandoned hope for all other illusory things, he delights in the yoga of the Self and finds the path to liberation.
Hope is a house of perpetual suffering; it is as immovable as the Himalayas. (44)
Like the great ocean, it is unfathomable and filled with faults;
like the sky, it is boundless. Raurava remains present for the living, even for a king established in his kingdom, who pursues the hunt out of desire. (45–46)
In the forest, one experiences suffering just like the base hunter;
even though his senses are fully gratified, he remains tormented by the destruction of his desires.
By the pursuit of unrighteous sensual pleasures, one incurs great misery.
"Between the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*) and desire (*kāma*), which of the two might be superior?
To this question, [the answer is]: "The intermediate space is indeed superior; desire is not [superior] anywhere.
For practitioners of yoga reach the further shore of the intermediate space, but [they do not reach the further shore of] desire anywhere. (48–49)
Those who follow after hope never attain its further shore.
In ancient times, a devotee of mine named Ṛṣabha came from the auspicious Badarī forest to my divine hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
Where my delightful Badarī is, where the Vaihāyasa lake is stainless,
where the sage Aśvaśiras dwells, and where the most purifying Gaṅgā flows—
having arrived there at that beautiful hermitage in the pavilion in my presence, [he spoke].
Having bowed and seen a small hut belonging to a virtuous sage for the sake of a place to stay,
he went toward a leaf-hut with the desire to practice long-term breath-retention (dīrghavāsa) once more.
On that path, he saw a sage named Tanu, whose wealth was his asceticism.
In his body, he was eightfold taller than usual, yet when he became thin, he was like a blade of grass.
His vision became truly marvelous, reaching as far as the little finger.
Having bowed to him, Ṛṣabha stood by; when a seat was offered, he sat down.
When questioned, he spoke only of his well-being as a consolation;
likewise, he said, "I indeed wish to build a leaf-hut here,
and I desire to perform asceticism so that I may find peace."
"I wish to do all of that; instruct me in this matter, O Sage.
The body replied: "This hut made of leaves was not built by me at all.
Since everything is indeed perishable, for whose sake is a hut made of leaves?"
As long as you remain intent on the construction of a leaf-hut according to your desire, so long will there be no peace for you, being enclosed within the hut of craving.
For one who is free from craving, devoid of effort, and without desire, there is great happiness.
Even through austerity, there is no happiness at all if desire for it remains awake.
For one dwelling in a hut of leaves, there can be no entry into Brahman;
but for one who has abandoned the hut of worldly hope, there shall be entry into Brahman.
For one whose world has been permeated by Brahman, peace is eternally united with him.
Therefore, having abandoned hope even for a pond from the midst of the sky,
find rest in the Imperishable One within the leaf-hut of the space of consciousness.
Thus addressed by me with the eye of knowledge,
that Ṛṣabha abandoned his leaf-hut and took refuge in me, the Supreme Lord.
Being a portion of me and my very own form, he thereafter attained liberation.
Therefore, having abandoned hope, one should surrender the mind to Me;
by surrendering everything to Me alone, one shall attain eternal bliss.
He who has rendered hope emaciated is, in my view, one whose self is nourished.
He whose hope is nourished will undoubtedly become emaciated.
That hope which is attached to all beings—even to the ungrateful, the lazy, the cruel, the violent, and those who do harm—[is what causes this]. (66–67)
In sons, wives, wealth, and mansions; in the body, the senses, and enjoyments;
in old age for those without sons; in the kingdom for kings;
and in beautiful amusements for maidens longing for marriage. (68)
The hope that greedy children place in their mother regarding their favorite object is certain;
he by whom such a hope has been made thin attains peace.
Gautama practiced austerities for sixty thousand years. (2.210.70)
The King of Dharma approached that sage of fierce austerities;
Gautama, having paid homage to the King of Dharma, offered him a seat.
He then inquired after his welfare and extended a welcome.
The King of Dharma questioned Gautama: "O sage, what is your purpose, and why do you perform such difficult penance?
Gautama replied: "I practice this arduous austerity for the sake of peace."
"By which [path] shall I go to the worlds of the merit-makers, filled with happiness and the like?
Yama replied: "Your deliberation leads you toward a wrong path;
it is the same for the worlds of both the merit-makers and the non-merit-makers. (74)

Great suffering born of craving afflicts even those who possess merit. (75) Except for the Imperishable Abode, craving and suffering are found elsewhere. Therefore, having abandoned all hope, remain motionless in Brahman. (76)
Through the yoga of Brahman, you shall attain all imperishable peace;
for there is no happiness for one possessed by hope, even though they may practice austerity.
As long as there is hope and craving, as well as this greed for one's own self-interest, [so long is there suffering].
Desire, longing, and passion— how can there be happiness for an individual as long as these exist? For one from whom every object of desire has entirely ceased,
the eternal ocean filled with bliss shall manifest.
Therefore, those in whose will Nārāyaṇa himself is established—
even if they are knowers of Brahman— they alone enjoy peace.
Having heard this, Gautama abandoned his asceticism and became established in devotion.
Then, free from desire and with a peaceful heart, he attained supreme tranquility.
Therefore, I am to be worshipped by kings, subjects, men, and women alike through great sacrifices, and to be propitiated through service.
I alone am to be worshipped directly through the surrender of one's will;
having thus attained Me, one should accomplish one's own liberation through services.
And you all—every person, subjects, kings, and so forth—[should do likewise].

Having surrendered everything— through action, mind, and speech— to me, Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, let them worship Kṛṣṇa, free from all lethargy. I shall grant them my supreme, great peace, which abides in the imperishable Supreme.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari spoke a mantra to Rādhā regarding the subjects and others;
thereafter, the Great Lord bestowed his own devotion upon them and became silent.
Then the king, the queen, and the subjects also fed Acyuta.
They fed the merchant caravans, and the king and others partook of food.
Then, having accepted the worship, he caused [the deities] to ascend into the middle of the celestial chariot;
he himself also ascended it to go to the sacrificial ground.
The subjects, the armies, and the women paid him manifold honors.
Then Kṛṣṇa proceeded together with the king and the ṛṣi;
traveling from island to island, he indeed reached Kāśī in the evening.
He traveled two *vāmas* further west and arrived at Mīlavīla. Then, during the final watch of the night, he reached the sacrificial precinct;
having bathed there, he performed his twilight devotions and took his meal in his own residence.
And the three daughters of Rāyamārī fell into a deep sleep; they served their beloved, the Blessed One, as their new husband.
At dawn, there arose the chanting of the Vedas and the sounds of auspicious musical instruments.
Hari remained awake with songs, the sounds of musical instruments, and hymns of praise. Then the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of kings, having performed the ritual of bathing,
worshipped his parents and granted an audience to his devotees.
Having performed his daily rites and being well-attired, he arrived at the sacrificial ground;
then, to the Dānava Ṛṣi as well as King Rāyamārīśa, he spoke these words:
"This wealth amounting to ten million which has come for my worship—"
"May everything belonging to you and to the subjects be offered into this sacrifice.
Having said this, he summoned Kubera, the lord of the treasury, and gave that wealth to him;
the king of riches then employed all of it for the expenses of the sacrifice.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself,
having purified people, lands, men, and likewise women,
gathers those worthy of liberation into his refuge through his grace.
Having purified children, the elderly, those of middle age, and the young—all embodied beings—the Supreme Lord makes them fit for liberation;
even the innocent daughters of kings were themselves surrendered [to Him]. (2.210.10)
Even though he is divine and the refuge of all people, appearing as an ocean of compassion, he accepts his own yoga according to the prescribed rule and bestows it [upon others].
Even while assuming non-divine human bodies, he grants liberation.
"O beloved of Hari, compassion is that which gives; it belongs to Him, the ocean of bliss.
For the Lord of Time and Māyā, who is untainted, there is no stain anywhere.
Indeed, His entire body, as well as all objects of enjoyment, are likewise under His control. (102–103)
Having specially embraced those who approach with devotion, he indeed purifies them;
for one who is eternally satisfied, there is no satisfaction dependent on another.
He, the bestower of all bliss, is truly victorious everywhere.
O Rādhā, by devotion alone the Blessed Lord becomes subject to His devotees. (105) In whatever way one takes refuge in Him, the Lord honors them in that same way;
in whatever way a person serves Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa serves them in that same way. (106)

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure for the City of Ṛddhīśa on the Island of Ālīsmara in the Kingdom of King Rāyamārīśa after the Sacrificial Rites, the Wandering, the Worship, the Instruction, the Purification of the Islands of Kāśima, Dvivāma, Mīla, and Vīla, the Return to the Sacrificial Ground, and Resting at Night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 211] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (The Continuation of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 211.
[Author: Chapter 212.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, this Bālakṛṣṇa [will perform] the sacrifice on the morning of the tenth day.
He went and sat upon his own golden throne;
and then there arose the sounds of musical instruments, the songs of excellent women,
the chanting of the Vedas by great sages, and the melodies of celestial singers.
The sounds of the mantras as well as those of the lions were likewise heard;
the gods were ready, having performed their daily rites, and the fire-priests were intent on their duties. The sacrificers, offering the oblations, stood within the sacrificial pavilion.
The recitation of benedictions (*svastivāca*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of materials, and likewise the bringing forth of objects;
the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) by the Brahmins, the hymns of praise to the gods, as well as wakefulness,
the actual presence [of the deity], and worship.

Gradually, the worship of the living beings belonging to the world of the living— those who dwell in the creation of the Lord residing in the abode of the Imperishable (akṣara)— came to take place in due order,
through offerings of the sixteen secondary articles and through food and other such gifts.
Worship is performed with offerings of clarified butter, oblations, and juices;

with gifts of nectar, garments, fruits, food, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and the like; and with offerings of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and appropriate gifts of barley, black gram (*māṣa*), and other grains. (7–8)
By the giving of foods to be chewed and swallowed, and by the giving of foods to be licked and sucked;
by the giving of foods to be relished and drunk, and by the giving of foods that satisfy the sight;
by the giving of things to be contemplated and reached, and by the giving of things to be fashioned and prepared.
Through offerings that are gross or subtle, and those consisting of sentient or insentient things,
the gods and other inhabitants of all the created worlds become satisfied. The fires consume abundant, oily food of many varieties.
And there, within the sacrificial fires, there were innumerable and most excellent offerings of oblations, presented with many hands and with devotion.
Having performed the final oblation and likewise having given abundant gifts, ||| 12 || [he departed].
Hari provided golden sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) as exemptions;
kings and sacrificers gave gifts by the millions.
When the sacrifice had thus proceeded, there were meals at midday.
They all indeed prepared pleasing food offerings for the sacrifice;
likewise, the liberated male and female incarnations beloved by Hari,
as well as the male and female attendants and the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs.
The truthful ones, the virtuous women, the sovereign ladies, and likewise the sovereign gods;
the sages, the ancestors, the deities, the guardians of the quarters, and the protectors of the worlds; humans, Daityas, Yakṣas, Dānavas, beasts, and birds. (16–17)
Even insects, moths, and the like, as well as trees, shrubs, and creepers— all principles of existence, whether insentient or sentient—
are entirely composed of name and form, whatever has been fashioned by Hari. (18)
Having attained complete serenity, he reached a state of satisfaction at the sacrifice.
Hari, together with his family, accompanied by his followers and servants,
and joined by the beloved wives of Brahmā, partook of the sacrificial food (caru).
Bālakṛṣṇa partook of all kinds of sweet foods, vegetables, and those things that were savory and rich in flavor, as well as all the divine delicacies;
immediately after eating, he remained right there in the presence of Śrī Hari.
King Dvaipāyanadvīpapati, accompanied by his queens,
together with the sage Mālāvana, sought refuge in the Supreme Lord at the city of Vāyuphena. ||22-23||
To bring Śrī Kṛṣṇa back to his own kingdom, she made him forget his husband by causing him to lose consciousness;
"So be it," Hari replied, and he immediately became ready.
Then the Lord, together with Lomaśa, his family, and Śaṅkara—
In a moment, having ascended a divine celestial chariot (vimāna), he was in the sky;
the sage and the king were together with their families in that chariot.
Previously, for the sake of offering a welcome gift, he had quickly gone to his own city. (25–26)
He quickly made the army ready for the reception;
likewise, the subjects became prepared, taking up flowers and other materials.
[27] [The army] was stationed in a garden near the city of Vāyuphenā.
Then they went into the vast courtyard of the royal palace; at that moment,
Hari’s celestial chariot, exceedingly brilliant and radiant as the sun, was seen in the sky, and various musical instruments were indeed sounded.
Then sounds accompanied by cries of victory were sounded;
meanwhile, the subjects were eager to behold [him] with one-pointed vision.
At that moment, a celestial chariot swiftly arrived in the sky nearby.
Following the path shown by the king, he descended near the palace.
First, the sage Mālāvana adorned the celestial chariot with garlands;
thereafter, the subjects from all sides honored it with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
The king offered a garland and a golden necklace upon the neck of Hari;
having washed His feet, Hari drank [the water] and came outside.
The subjects quickly honored Him with garlands and other offerings, as well as words of welcome.
The king, having led Hari to his palace, worshipped him with abundant wealth.
Then, seating the Supreme Lord in a golden chariot,
the king brought his family, Lomaśa, and Śambhu into the city.
Accompanied by his army, Śrī Hari was honored along the way by the subjects;
he was worshipped and saluted, gazed upon with eyes full of devotion, and presented with abundant wealth such as many jewels, gold, and silver. (36)
Honored by the chief officials and having wandered through the city,
he then arrived at the royal palace and sat upon the king’s throne;
and then he imparted words beneficial to the subjects.
Kṛṣṇa is sought by many, yet He is not attained without merit;
He is attained through much merit, yet His state is not served without devotion.
He is served by many through various states of being, yet one is not attached [to Him] without faith.
I am moved by all these offerings; therein lies the cause of my favor. Even though I am myself the Lord, I become helpless through that very act of favor.
Your land has been beheld by me, who am endowed with such grace.
Service performed with love is indeed devoid of [worldly] qualities and bestows liberation;
for my yoga always grants liberation to every embodied being.
And having attained me here, embodied beings serve according to their knowledge.
To them, I am likewise the giver and the bestower of grace.
Being pleased, I indeed grant happiness and protect them from obstacles; I provide for the acquisition and preservation of what is needed for this devotee, my servant.
For a devotee rich in the power of service, all that is auspicious is present.
One should indeed desire to exist within the power of service, for everything is under the control of the powerful.
The power of service, when established within oneself, protects one from great fear.
Dharma is the strength arising from all phenomena; it is the initiator of all happiness.
Dharma abides in the power of service, and I always abide in Dharma.
As long as I abide, so does Śrī, the means for achieving all happiness.

Just as smoke follows the power of the wind, so does dharma follow service. Service to the powerful is a dharma that prevails even in the face of all calamities. For servants who possess a pleasing disposition, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished.
Indeed, as one worthy of my grace, he shall quickly become highly esteemed.
In this world, he receives honor, and in the hereafter, great fruit;
thereafter, he shall enjoy manifold and eternal happiness. (2.211.50)
Service must be rendered with truthfulness to the gods, the ancestors, ascetics, guests, the virtuous, the helpless, and likewise to women.
One must never fail to perform service; indeed, failure to serve is itself an act of malice.
Distress arises from malice, and because of that, they become enraged.
When teachers and others are enraged with someone, that person’s fortune perishes;
there is no protector whatsoever for them in the three worlds. (52–53)
He who would speak ill of them and even desire their destruction shall himself go to ruin,
just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun.
He is one who perceives the future and possesses a mind directed toward the present.
Through service, both happiness and prosperity increase; deprived of it, they perish.
(55) Service should be performed when the time has arrived; that service is considered to bestow liberation.
When the time has passed, when the Lord has departed, and when the source of fortune has gone, then... (56)
That gain which is sought for the sake of favor is not gain at all.
One should serve those who know Brahman, those advanced in knowledge, and ascetics;
one should serve the virtuous who are rich in sacred learning, conduct, and behavior, for the sake of one's own welfare.
Through affection, divine glory arises; through lack of affection, there is the destruction of all that is auspicious.
(58) That wise person should perform service to the virtuous in order to produce affection;
for when the virtuous or even Hari are pleased, they protect one who has sought refuge. (59)

In the forest, a cruel and harsh hunter of the Śabara tribe, a man of sinful conduct who had long been abandoned by his own kinsmen, was honored with offerings of flesh by a pigeon seeking refuge. (2.211.60)
Then, as he went to the forest, there occurred a rain that surpassed all others.
Indeed, everything became water; it was as if the entire world were composed of vast water.
No living beings could be found, neither birds nor even beasts.
Then, at evening, that hunter found a female dove in the forest;
having placed her in a cage, he took refuge under a tree.
That hunter, then during the night, considered the tree to be a deity.
With palms joined in reverence, he bowed down and spoke these words to the lord of the forest:
"I seek refuge in whatever deities reside in this lord of the forest;
may they protect me here, one who has come to you for shelter and is without any other support."
Hungry, he fell asleep with his head resting at the root of the tree;
meanwhile, a bird named Citrakapotaka remained perched on a branch.
His wife had gone out to forage for food, but she did not return.
Afflicted by the rain, the pigeon grieved in many ways during the night:
"I believe my wife has surely died today from the winds and rains; is all well with that beloved of mine in the forest? (67–68)
Today my house, though filled with sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, servants, slaves, and the like, appears truly empty, for it is bereft of my wife.
Indeed, they say that a house is not a "home"; rather, it is the wife who is the home itself. (69)
Without his wife, the house stands like another empty forest.
Without her, my life is indeed seen to be purposeless;
for she, firm in her vows, does not eat when I have not eaten, nor does she bathe when I have not bathed.
She does not remain standing when I am present, but sits down when I lie down;
she rejoices when I am joyful, and grieves when I am in sorrow;
her face becomes dejected when I have gone abroad, yet she speaks kindly when I am angry.
Devoted to her husband, taking refuge in her husband, and intent on what is dear and beneficial to her husband—blessed is that man who always has such a wife.
And that ascetic woman knows that I am afflicted by hunger and exhausted. (73–74)
A tree, even though it be a fine dwelling, shines and brings happiness when joined with a woman who is devoted, steadfast, faithful, affectionate, and renowned;
indeed, one devoid of her appears like a wilderness, even if it be a magnificent palace. (75)
In matters of dharma, artha, and kāma, a wife is a man’s companion;
even when traveling abroad, she is indeed his vessel of trust. A wife is truly the supreme wealth of a man at all times. (76–77)
In this world, for one who is without a companion, a wife remains as a helper;
indeed, she is the supreme medicine for one overcome by the hardships of disease.
There is no kinsman equal to a wife as a companion in the accumulation of dharma.
In this world and in the next, she is a companion in both diversion and in the afterlife.
He who possesses a virtuous, chaste wife—one who is beautiful and speaks kindly—has nothing lacking in his home; therefore, he should certainly not go from here to the forest. (2.211.80)
"Or must I die?"—thus he lamented profusely during the night.

A female dove, held in a cage within the forest, overheard that lament while she slept and spoke these words out of affection: *The female dove, staying in her cage, heard that [lament] while fast asleep in the forest; full of affection, she spoke these words.* (8.1)

"Aha! I am exceedingly fortunate, for my beloved husband speaks thus of my very virtues despite my failure to obey his commands. Indeed, that woman is not to be esteemed in whom her husband finds no pleasure. (82-83)
"When the husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women;
that woman for whom the husband is not pleased is reduced to ashes.
Having reflected thus, the female dove spoke these words to her husband.
"O Lord, I shall speak that which brings happiness; you ought to act accordingly.
Be entirely devoted to the service of one who has come for refuge.
This hunter, a seeker of prey, has arrived at your dwelling."
Serving one afflicted by hunger through the gift of food bestows merit.
It is held that the merit of serving one who has come for refuge grants heaven.
Therefore, O dear one, serve this enemy by giving him your body. || 86-87 ||
"Offer worship to him; do not harbor any longing for his body.
Having heard these affectionate words, the pigeon went down.
Raising him up, [the cat] said, "May it be well with you; let me offer you a welcome."
"You are here in my own home; what do you wish for? I shall do it for you.
You have come here into the midst of my forest as one who has sought refuge.
Hospitality is a duty that must be performed even toward an enemy when he arrives at one's house."
"The fruit for that householder who provides hospitality is equal to that of a sacrifice.
Having heard this, the Kirāta said: "Indeed, cold and hunger are afflicting me today;
if there is a way, let an effort be made to alleviate them."
The pigeon quickly flew up and went to the blacksmith’s house;
taking a glowing iron bar with its beak, it returned to the tree.
While the hunter was heating a fire among dry leaves, the bird set it ablaze.
When the cold had passed, he said, "O dear one, give me food.
The pigeon replied, "I have no store, for I am a forest-dweller.
I live by the constant practice of gleaning; how could I satisfy my hunger?"
But do you perhaps think that you should satisfy me by the offering of your own self?
(95) One should perform worship even with the surrender of one’s own self for the sages, the deities, the ancestors, the great-souled ones, the virtuous women, and the righteous. (96)
Having spoken thus, the bird circumambulated the fire three times and entered it,
repeatedly bowing to his guest while uttering the words, "Eat me!
Then the hunter beheld the pigeon roasted by the fire.

Filled with compassion, he said: "The sin born of murdering a friend has arisen within me, a cruel man; what indeed might be the expiation for it? Oh, by the gift of my body, hospitality has been shown! (98–99)
"Therefore, I too, having stayed in the forest, shall practice that which pertains to the world beyond;
I shall perform righteous deeds, for devotion to dharma is the supreme goal.
Having spoken thus, he quickly [released] that cage and the female dove.

Having released [the pigeon], the devoted woman chanted "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" as was fitting. Then, seeing her husband consumed by fire, that female dove, taking recourse in the dharma of a virtuous wife, entered the fire in her grief. (101–102)
Then she beheld her husband wearing variegated armlets,
seated upon a celestial chariot, honored by goddesses and high-souled beings;
having attained a divine form like that of the gods, she ascended the celestial vehicle.
The hunter beheld those two gods seated in their celestial chariot in the sky.
Having witnessed the fruit of the duty of service, even the Kirāta performed austerities;
he practiced the service of guests who dwelt in the forest.
He practiced the tending of cattle and birds and the protection of those who sought refuge.
Then, when the forest was consumed by a wildfire, he was reduced to ashes;
yet, having recited the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, his sins were utterly destroyed.
"By serving those who serve Brahman, one indeed attains the divine state.
Thus, let them practice service and go to the supreme station of liberation.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa then became silent for a moment.

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Meal Following the Worship and Fire-offerings (*homa*) to the Deities of the Sacrifice in the Second Section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; and thereafter, the Departure for the Kingdom of Rāyabāleśvara and Dvaipāyana Island, as well as the Wandering, Worship, and Instruction in the City of Vāyuphenā," Chapter 211.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

The king paraded him through the city along the royal highway;
the leading merchants and others congratulated the Lord, as did all the subjects and the Vakriṇī maidens. ||52-53||
Then Hari honored everyone with necklaces, fruits, wealth, blankets, garments, and ornaments;
he gave all that wealth to the sage Rūpa, and he took it along as his dowry.
Having arrived at the royal palace, he found rest during the night.
Attending upon the six maidens, he indeed woke up at dawn. Having performed his morning rites and drunk water, Hari prepared to depart. (55–56)
At sunrise, honored by the army, he arrived quickly;
having received worship on the sacrificial ground, he descended into his own abode.
O Rādhikā, having thus acted, he then went to the auspicious city of Ujjayinī.
At dawn on the twelfth day, he beheld the purifying sacrificial ground.
He summoned the great lords who rule over the entire earth to the assembly hall;
there were the liberated ones, the divine manifestations, the Nārāyaṇas, and likewise the Īśvaras.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the Daityas, and likewise human beings;

those who move through the air, those who dwell in the water, and all those who inhabit the netherworld; both the immobile and the mobile, as well as the insentient and the sentient—all arrived there. (2.213.60)
The male servants, the attendants, the masters, and the mistresses went to the assembly hall.
Likewise, the female lords, the Nārāyaṇīs, the Satīs, the Surapriyās, the Sarvapriyās, the Apsarases, and the Mātṛkās also arrived. (61–62)
The female ascetics from the Brahma-lake, those who practice celibacy, as well as the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and the various emanations arrived at the assembly hall.
The blessed Lord Hari was pleased; [he manifested] the wish-fulfilling tree, the celestial cow, and the creeping plants.
He caused the Kalpamanis, male servants, male attendants,
and female attendants to be brought into the assembly; they then arrived at that hall,
seated upon divine thrones that blazed like the sun.
When they had all taken their seats, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the Lord Mādhava, spoke to all the incarnations who had arrived:
"I offer my honor and gratitude to you all here."
"Even having left their own abodes, they have come here for the sake of the sacrifice.
I offer my respects from afar to these lords and goddesses who have arrived for the sake of the sacrifice, regarding them with a sense of blessedness. (67–68)
I offer honor and thanks to the sages, the ascetics, the ancestors, and likewise to the women, who have come to this sacrifice;
as well as to the gods, the inhabitants of the earth, and all human beings.
I offer honor and thanks to you, for you have come to this sacrifice.
Likewise, I offer honor and thanks to the trees, the grasses, the creepers, and the shrubs, for they too have come to this sacrifice.
I offer honor and thanks to the sacred fords, to the deities, and even to the insentient beings, since you have come to this sacrifice;
likewise to those dwelling in the depths of the netherworld, and to those who inhabit the waters and the land. (72)
Of the sacred fords (tīrthas) inhabited by fire and wind, as well as of the mountains;
of the worlds, the guardians of the directions, and those who perform ritual actions;
and of the attendants, the hosts, the lords of the hosts, and the yogins.
I offer honor and thanks to all those who have come to this sacrifice—
the servants from every side who have exerted themselves for the sake of the rite,
as well as all the female attendants and the guardians of the field from every direction.
[He gave instructions] to the female slaves, the groups of male servants, and the guards on all sides;
likewise to those who had attained all authority over the alchemy laboratories,
the protectors of the storehouses of materials, and those who provided the objects required by his will.
Of donors, of kings, of sovereigns, and of the wives of Brahmins; of Brāhmaṇas, of Vedic mantras, of sacrificial offerings, and of those who possess the vessels for the sacrifice;
of the principles, of the knots of inertia, of shrines, and of the architects of the universe.
I offer honor and thanks for having come to this sacrifice.
I grant leave, with palms joined in reverence, and the favor of my own presence along with auspicious blessings.
I bestow upon you my own form, gold, silver, and other materials, as well as nectar and ambrosia. (2.213.79–80)
He bestowed crowns, bracelets, and beautiful earrings;
he gave ornaments, garments, vessels, and even clothes.
He also gave parasols, divine vehicles, and shawls and other such items.
She gave beautiful helmets and silken garments;
she gave elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels, as well as diamonds;
and she gave various ornaments such as bodices and the like.
I gave you inexhaustible vessels, as well as wish-fulfilling trees and the like;
I gave you wish-granting creepers, wish-granting cows, and wish-granting gems.
I also gave you divine knowledge, great sovereignty, and divine splendor.
"I grant you divine supernatural power, eternal peace, devotion, and service;
I grant you divine perfections, great gain, and my own nectar.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, Kṛṣṇavallabhācārya, the fulfiller of desires, [bestowed these upon them]. || 85-86 ||
Then he gave divine crowns and earrings made of gold and precious gems to the primordial Lords who had taken incarnations,
and after that, to the world-protectors and the kings.
Thus, in accordance with what was appropriate and desired,
Hari indeed bestowed rewards upon all the men and women gathered there;
and thereafter, in the morning, he performed the act of giving in this manner.
The Lord bestowed wealth upon his servants, slaves, and other dependents;
he gave them suitable golden necklaces and jeweled necklaces again and again. To the women, he gave gold ornaments appropriate for ladies.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa gave food in every way even to those who possessed alms-bowls for food,
and he gave garments in every way even to those who possessed alms-bowls for clothing; furthermore,
he bestowed gifts of houses upon many.
Through royal authority, he caused dwellings to be granted to the twice-born;
thus the Lord himself brought all the acts of giving to completion.
Then, he likewise caused a universal feast to be prepared.
For the breaking of the fast, he fed him auspicious and sweet milk-rice (pāyasa);
he also fed him flavorful food, food with honey-offerings (madhuparka), and sweet delicacies;
he fed him food like nectar (sudhā), food like immortality (amṛta), and food like the essence of the moon (pīyūṣa).
He caused them to eat food of merit, food of meditation, and also food of fruit;
he caused them to eat food of grains, food of sages, and also food of leaves;
he caused them to eat food of parched grain, food of sprouts, and also food of crops.
He caused him to eat food of the waters, purifying food, and food of fire;
he caused him to eat food of light, food of splendor, and food of the mode of goodness (sattva).
He awakened him with the food of pure being and the food of the divine play of manifestation.
He fed him seasonal food and non-seasonal food, as well as food born of the body;
he fed him ritual food, perfected food, and the food of the Siddhas;
he fed him the food of contemplation, the food of satisfaction, and the food of contentment.
From the bliss of great happiness, he fed everyone with food; 2.213.100.
He served buttermilk, sugar, milk, soup, as well as rice and the like, and he fed them with *pūrikās*, *polikās*, and various side dishes. 101.
He fed him with sweet dishes, boiled preparations, *caṭanīs*, *parpaṭas* and the like, as well as *sevikas*, cakes (*apūpas*), and *saṃyāva*;
he also fed him with chickpeas, *phullavaṭīs*, and roasted grains.
He fed those who were inauspicious as well as those who grant happiness, and he fed those established in delusion.
He fed those who follow the wheel, those who are steadfast, and even the authors of treatises.
He also fed those who subsist on black mustard and those who consume whey.
He served curd, clarified butter, fresh butter, molasses, and honey;
he offered sour drinks and the juices of mangoes to be drunk during the autumn;
and he also served fruits, both fresh and dried, as well as seeds.
The Lord caused them to eat mouth-perfumes, aromatic grains, and betel-leaves;
he made them all drink the water of the Brahma-lake.
Having thus fed them, Hari himself then ate.
Accompanied by his family and joined by Brahmapriyā, he was joined by Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Pāravatī;
and he was joined by Māṇikī, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, Mañjulā, and Amṛtikā. || 108 ||

Accompanied by Saguṇa, Āśāradā, Haṃsa, Durgā, and Sarasvatī, the parents and the supreme gurus headed by Lomaśa partook of the meal; indeed, all the embodied beings who were honored there likewise ate. (2.213.110)
The descendants of Gaṅgā, the descendants of Atri, the great sages, and the maidens;
the rivers, the streams, and the sacred fords—all partook [of the feast] with great eagerness.
At midday, Śrī Hari caused the kings there to eat most excellently.
At the time following midday,
he ordered the attendants of the sacrifice to go to their respective worlds and their own abodes,
with the exception of all the beloved wives of Brahmā and those such as Lomaśa and others.
Except for His own family— Īśāna, Satī, and Gaṇeśvara—
and except for the Cāmarikarṣīs as well as Tuṣita,
and except for You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who are Saccidānanda, and Rādhikā.
"Except for Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, and except for the people of Aśvasaras," (1.15).
Having thus received permission in every way, O Rādhikā, they departed on their own celestial chariots; by evening, [the place] had become as if empty. (1.16)
At night, those ever-ready workers performed the dismantling of the pavilions by Viśvakarman; by morning, the site had become a bare ground.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the blessings of Agni, the meals, the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), the rewards, the evening departure of Hari for the kingdom of King Rāyalambāra, and his wandering through the city of Kimuvakra.

Chapter Two Hundred and Thirteen: Description of the Worship, the Feasting, the Night’s Rest, the Arrival at the Sacrificial Ground in the Morning, the Performance of the Great Honor-Ceremony, the Bestowal of Honors, Praises, Gifts, and Rewards, the Meals, and the Farewell;
Chapter 213 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Chapter 215 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: on the thirteenth day, having performed his morning rites, Hari took his seat and became established in worship. At that moment, King Rāyanavārka arrived there.
He entreated the Blessed One to bring him back to his own kingdom. Hari replied, "So be it," and made everyone ready;
having summoned the sovereign of the Rākṣasas and Kinnaras, he instructed him on the procedure for that.
Then the king, having honored Kṛṣṇa, granted him leave to depart. Hari quickly descended from his celestial chariot and remained in the sky.
At that time, musical instruments were sounded for the departure of the Supreme Lord.
Rokīśvara, Raṇajit, Mārīśa, Vāyukakṣaka,
Bāleśvara, and Lambāra— these lords of the earth then gave leave and dowry to their daughters for Hari.
Honored by his armies and celebrated with musical instruments and songs,
he traveled swiftly by celestial chariot accompanied by his entire caravan to the kingdom of King Rāyanavārkabha, known as Miśrasura.
At the confluence of the Miśra and Surasari rivers, near the Supārīya lake,
and in the garden situated on the outskirts of the city of Ciñcāgopurikā,
the sage named Vāyuśṛṅgatanu was indeed together with Kṛṣṇa. (8–9)

The king arrived there in his celestial chariot (vimāna), having previously set out; he quickly and properly prepared his army to offer a formal welcome to Hari. At that time, musical instruments were sounded and the subjects expressed their joy.
The sounds of musical instruments resounded, traveling to the very ends of the quarters.
Young maidens and women sang auspicious, melodious songs;
and those prepared with auspicious unguents approached the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
The celestial chariot descended to earth by the path of the King’s Awakening;
at that time, indeed, there was a rain of unbroken parched grain and flowers.
Shouts of "Victory! and cries of "Live long! issued from all mouths. (13)
Then Kṛṣṇa emerged from the steady celestial chariot and stood before them outside.
At that time, praised by the people, the kings, and the maidens and others,
the king washed his feet and drank the water, placing it upon his head.
Then she gave milk for everyone to drink;
and together with his army, they joyfully paraded Kṛṣṇa through the city. The subjects, as well as the leading merchants, honored him with pure love.
Men, women, and even immortals, as well as mixed groups and female deities,
worshipped [him] with substances, flowers, garments, fruits, gems, diamonds, various crowns, and ornaments. (17–18)
They honored him with joined palms, with the devotion of offering their hearts,
with prostrations, with gifts according to their capacity, and with various forms of worship.
Having thus wandered through the city and granted his supreme audience, [he departed].
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa arrived at the royal palace accompanied by his followers.
The king honored him with jewels and other gifts, as well as golden necklaces,
divine garments, excellent wealth, and celestial offerings with great respect.
He performed the nightly lamp-offering and worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
then, declaring "I am fulfilled," he prostrated at his feet.
His four queens also worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Then the seven daughters of the king, their faces like the moon,
were enchanted by the beloved Lord of Śrī; they took him as their husband in their hearts and,
filled with great joy, placed the garland of choice upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
Both the king and the queens became fulfilled;
they were indeed satisfied and considered their good fortune to be supreme.
At midday, he celebrated a royal festival filled with joy.
Then the king fed them all with most delicious food;
having given betel and other refreshments, he bestowed wedding gifts and presents.
Hari accepted all of that and gave it to his father-in-law.
He placed them each in their own appropriate celestial chariot (vimāna).
After resting for a moment, the king then went to his own city of Svarlatikā;
he spoke to Hari to depart, and Hari became ready in an instant.
The king first went there in that city and offered him honor with the sounds of musical instruments, the joyful shouts of the subjects, and offerings of flowers and other gifts.
Then the Blessed One descended from his celestial chariot in the great garden.
In accordance with the king’s command, he wandered through the city, bestowing his vision upon all;
honored, saluted by the people, and presented with material gifts, the Supreme Lord was beheld and firmly held within their own hearts. (2.214.30–31)
The Supreme Lord, being pleased by the various offerings of the people,
bestowed his grace upon Vāyuśṛṅga, who had come for worship.
He took rest in the king’s divine, golden palace.
Then Rāyahāṇḍeśvara, the ruler of the kingdom of Mākṣika, arrived there. He then petitioned Hari to grant him his own kingdom.
Hari quickly prepared himself in the evening, accompanied by his caravan. (33–34)
King Rājanavārka gave him a parting gift as a dowry.
Hari quickly traveled through the sky by means of a celestial chariot and,
at the onset of night, arrived at the city of Mākṣika.
The king Rāyahaṇḍeśa went forth to meet him and offered a welcome to that great city, which was shining all around with the brilliance of lightning,
accompanied by his army, the sounding of musical instruments, and banners, flags, and the like. (36–37)
Then the king offered a welcome to Śrī Hari with flower garlands, shouts of victory, auspicious songs, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.
As the celestial chariot descended to the earth, Hari emerged from it.

And when it was illuminated by lightnings with infinite branches, resembling the day, the Blessed One shone upon the top of the celestial chariot like the moon in the sky. Beholding him, the Supreme Brahman, the women and the subjects were filled with wonder. (2.214.40)
They honored Hari exceedingly with sandalwood and flowers,
with unbroken grains, parched rice, and delightful essences of fragrance.
During the night, the king indeed caused Mādhava to be paraded through the city.
The eager subjects honored Kṛṣṇa as he proceeded with his army;
at the city gates, in the courtyards, in the center, at the crossroads, on the royal highways, before the market stalls, and in the palaces, they joyfully celebrated him in their eagerness. (42–43)
With substances such as gold coins, fruits, saffron, and sandalwood;
with garments, coconuts, and other fragrant essences;
with garlands of flowers, necklaces of jewels, and priceless, excellent articles.
Thus, after wandering through the city, the Blessed One arrived at the king’s palace (verse 45). He entered the assembly hall and, during the night,
gave instruction regarding the purpose desired by everyone for their own livelihood (verse 46).
Happiness and the absence of suffering—both of these are indeed the purposes [of dharma].
Dharma is sought for the sake of happiness, for from dharma happiness is born.
One should indeed strive to prevent the arrival of future suffering.
Unrighteousness is declared to be the giver of suffering; indeed, unrighteousness bears the name of demerit (apuṇya).
Violence, the affliction of others, malice, and sin are indeed unrighteousness.
Theft, the telling of falsehoods, and deception are indeed sinful.
Furthermore, acting unjustly, performing deeds that cause the destruction of others,
destroying the livelihood of others, and the destruction of another's property;
as well as the loss of one's own liberation and the like, as well as the abandonment [of the path] through false knowledge.
Folly, failing to serve one’s own parents, and indeed sinful acts;
the misappropriation of others' property and the failure to protect those who have sought refuge; the forgetfulness of the God of gods and the disparagement of those worthy of worship. 51–52.
The oppression of women, the useless oppression of children,
the destruction of trees, creepers, and the like, and the setting of fire in a great forest—
whereby living beings are consumed by flames— all that is a great sin.
A human being should not inflict such suffering upon himself.
Whether it be happiness arising from the body, from the senses, or from the self,
a person surely accomplishes every purpose for his own sake.
Impermanent happiness will surely meet with destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Having reflected thus, one should not pursue that [transient pleasure], but rather pursue eternal happiness.
Sacrifice, charity, compassion, the gods, truth, service, and austerity—[these are the means]. 56.
Good conduct bestows happiness; these are considered the duties of a yogin.
(57) These eight are indeed purifying, granting excellence and grace.
Visiting sacred pilgrimage sites bestows happiness and is beneficial for eternal welfare. (58)
Visiting sacred places is purifying and bestows prosperity;
if a mortal lives in abundance with food, wealth, clothing, and the like, then,
by performing sacrifices and other rites, he may acquire eternal happiness.
Holy pilgrimage sites truly exist, and virtuous people who benefit the worlds truly exist;
sacred lands truly exist, and images of Hari exist within temples.
By going there, one attains liberation, and through that, indeed, eternal happiness.

The destruction of sin arises through the fear induced by expiatory rites; if one does not commit it again, one is liberated from future sin. (6.2) If one cultivates the company of the virtuous, one is completely freed from evil association.
Having bathed at Sādhutīrtha, one is liberated from the affliction of Yama.
By bathing at Sādhutīrtha one becomes virtuous; by bathing at Haritīrtha one becomes Hara (Śiva).
By using fragrant substances one becomes fragrant, and thereafter one becomes endowed with the fragrance of Kṛṣṇa.

Having performed an action, if a conscious person should think, "I am not [the doer]," he is not stained by that action at all, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. He who covers even the open flaws of the virtuous—
Even one who has committed evil and most heinous sins attains what is auspicious;
just as the sun is the destroyer of darkness, so too is the person who performs auspicious deeds—
the remover of all sins and the destroyer of every evil.
A person devoted to service constantly receives blessings;
through such service, one then attains long life, food, wealth, and happiness.
Through service to the saintly, there is eternal happiness by means of union with Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, a man endowed with far-sighted vision should become a true seeker of the sacred ford (sādhutīrthī).
Those who take refuge in Keśava always abide in that eternal treasury of bliss;
for those who rely upon Him, that eternal treasury becomes present before them.
I am the eternal treasure-chest, overflowing with great bliss;
the virtuous, endowed with my bliss, cause others to be joyful.
Indeed, liberation and eternal happiness are the primary purpose among these.
"Only among the virtuous can [the truth] be found; therefore, one should constantly serve the saintly.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One then became silent.
At the conclusion of the assembly, the king performed worship with millions of precious objects.
With vessels of gold and silver, garments, and ornaments,
he placed a crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa;
he offered necklaces set with gems and made of gold around the neck of Śrī Hari.
He presented [to him] woolen garments of soft appearance and adorned with gold;
excellent parasols and fly-whisks with golden handles and cane shafts; and he gave beautiful garlands set with diamonds and pearls. (75–76)
She gave rings, water-pots, and various types of coverings;
she worshipped with fragrant essences, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Queen Hīravatī performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa and the traditional waving of lights (ārātrika).
She applied a saffron *tilaka* mark along with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and a crescent moon on his forehead;
she performed the highest worship upon his head with unbroken grains, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, she placed morsels of sweet food into Kṛṣṇa’s mouth.
The Queen of Men spoke to the nine maidens standing at her side:
"O maidens! This Lord of Śrī, the Master of Rādhā, truly shines forth;
indeed, he is obtained for the sight of even those who have performed meritorious deeds over many lifetimes. (2.214.80)
By his grace, he has now directly met them in their own home.
Let them dwell upon him in their hearts and never abandon him; let them worship Hari with love and serve Janārdana. (8.1–8.2)
"May they always practice devotion, just like Śrī, Ramā, and Kamalā.
Upon hearing this, the young maidens became deeply infatuated with Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa;
and by their mother's words, they attained nourishment for that beloved Acyuta.
With their faces blooming and filled with joy, those nine maidens chose [Kṛṣṇa] by offering garlands. They placed the bride-garlands around Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
thereafter, the Blessed One took their hands according to the prescribed rite.
Having accomplished his purpose, the king indeed celebrated a festival at night;
then the monarch provided food for all the caravans.
The subjects also performed the worship of Hari there with great devotion.
Then Rādhā and the others took their meal, and thereafter Kṛṣṇa, attended by the maidens, slept for but a moment;
he was quickly awakened at dawn by auspicious sounds and the resonance of musical instruments. (87–88)
On the thirteenth day, having performed his ablutions and worship, he drank milk;
others also drank milk and other drinks in the palace of King Huṇḍeśa.
In the morning, the sage [Vīraka] and the people went to see the lord, the illustrious Hari.
He worshipped with various articles and Vedic mantras.
Having performed the great worship, he chose eternal liberation.
Hari said: "O sage, remain in meditative absorption; attain liberation."
Thus addressed, that sage immediately became steady in meditation; in an instant,
he beheld within his heart the auspicious, divine form of Hari,
composed of celestial splendor and adorned with divine pearls and other ornaments.
They beheld a celestial chariot known as the Imperishable (Akṣara), enveloped in splendor.
O Rādhikā, the Blessed Lord, taking him by the hand upon that celestial chariot,
led him and instantly caused him to reach his own abode, the Imperishable Realm.
The king and others cast the sage’s body into the middle of a pit;
O Rādhā, I shall tell you of the miracle that occurred there in the body.
From that body, heroes emerged, fully equipped with weapons.
Possessing massive bodies and great strength, they bowed to Hari and stood before him.
Those sons of the Vīrāka people requested a dwelling from the Lord;
Hari granted them a permanent residence among the attendants of Śambhu.
Those heroes and those people,
having received permission from the Lord, all departed for the eternal abode of Kailāsa;
for they were always Vaiṣṇavas who had attained the grace of Śambhu, yet remained indeed characterized by tamas.
The devotees indeed became renowned as heroes of Hara.
Then the king prostrated like a staff before the glorious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Kambharā, and he indeed performed service at His feet.
Having performed service, that king then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana);
he drank the divine water used for washing the feet and stood nearby.
At that moment, King Rāyakūpeśa arrived there.
To lead Hari to his own highly splendid city named Havāna, [Huṇḍeśa] spoke;
Hari said, "So be it," and quickly became ready.
Huṇḍeśa gave him a dowry and requested forgiveness from Hari.
Hari, having bestowed the gift of fearlessness, ascended the celestial chariot;
by the command of Keśava, the members of the caravan also came to be situated within the chariot.
King Rāyakūpeśa likewise went there for the purpose of paying his respects.

Having previously gone there and led his own army away, he remained steady in the garden. Then King Rāyahuṇḍeśa gave him leave, along with honor, amidst shouts of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, and songs.
When Hari’s vehicle arrived near Hāṭakeśvarapura,
musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory were raised by the people.
O Rādhikā, there were also recitations of mantras in the great garden.

Then the subjects and others, their hearts filled with joy, became eager to see Kṛṣṇa. (1.08) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, on the thirteenth [chapter], it describes: the morning departure from the kingdom of King Rāyanavārka; the wandering through the city of Ciñcāgopurikā, where He was worshipped; the subsequent journey to and wandering through the city of Svarlatikā, where He was worshipped; and then, in the evening, the departure for the kingdom of King Rāyahaṇḍeśvara and the arrival at the city of Mākṣikā.

Wandering, worship, instruction, resting at night, the liberation of the Vīrākaja sages on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, and the journey to Rāyakūpa, the king, and the kingdom— this is the description of these matters in the two hundred and fourteenth chapter,
titled [Chapter 214]. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga), Chapter 215.
