Then, by means of water-machines, vehicles, and boats, the subjects went to a garden in the vicinity of the city of Havānā. 1–2.
Then the celestial chariot descended upon the auspicious ground near the shore of the ocean;
from there, the king went into the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He bowed at his feet and placed garlands of flowers around his neck.
The queen worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers, parched grains, unbroken rice, and other offerings.
(4) The royal sage Heyatāyana worshipped the Supreme Lord.
The king caused Śrī Hari to be carried through the city on vehicles. (5)
Having seated Śrī Hari, who was adorned with an umbrella and chowries, in the middle of a golden chariot, the people worshipped him with devotion using offerings such as fruits,
garments, jewels, sandalwood, and saffron. (6)
With betel nuts and the like, coconuts, sugar, and other offerings,
the king himself then placed Kṛṣṇa upon a boat and took him out for recreation upon the ocean near the island. (7–8)

Then, at the time for the midday meal, the Blessed One took his food together with the caravan. At that moment, the queen arrived there for the purpose of worshipping Hari and gave her daughter to Hari.
She indeed placed betel and a beautiful garland upon the neck of Hari.
Having obtained Kṛṣṇa as her husband, that maiden became one who had fulfilled her purpose;
her mother also became exceedingly joyful and celebrated a royal festival.
Then, having attained rest in that most excellent abode, the Blessed One remained there;
at that time, the king who was the maternal uncle of the maiden arrived for the purpose of seeing her—
the lord of the kingdom of Kulambāyana and the ruler of the city of Vigoṣṭhā.
Known by the name Kālīmaṇḍalīna, he also worshipped Mādhava. He indeed petitioned Śrī Hari for permission to return to his own kingdom. Hari said, "So be it," and he then quickly made himself ready.
And Kūpeśa gave a farewell gift as a dowry to Śrī Hari;
accompanied by Pūrṇā, Āsana, and the sages, he went before [the Lord].
Seated in his own celestial chariot, the Blessed One traveled through the sky to the assembly.
Having crossed the ocean, he reached that city in the evening;
the king, accompanied by his army, paid him great honor in many ways.
The Blessed One alighted upon the ground near the assembly hall.
The subjects caused him to prosper exceedingly with unbroken grains and other auspicious offerings.
The Blessed One, descending from his celestial chariot, sat upon a divine seat offered by the golden [throne];
the king bowed at his feet.
He placed flower garlands upon their necks and likewise gave them sandalwood paste;
he also gave betel and water to the traveling merchants.
Accompanied by his army, the king caused them to be paraded about on vehicles.
With elephants, horses, carts, and likewise with human-carriages,
the people indeed honored Acyuta in the city named Vigoṣṭha;
they honored Kṛṣṇa as he sat upon his elephant-vehicle, along with his parents and his family.
[He saw] Īśāna and Lomaśa, as well as Satī, Lakṣmī, and the others;
other excellent sages who were servants seated on horse-drawn carriages;
and all the women, such as the beloveds of Brahmā, seated in palanquins.
The subjects— the Brahmins and others who were preeminent, as well as the wealthy merchants—
along with all the poor men and women, worshipped according to their means,
through prostrations, hymns of praise, and with their hearts, eyes, and hands.
With offerings of flowers, garlands, and the like, as well as fruits such as sugar and other delicacies, they worshipped the Supreme Lord who had arrived, an ocean of divine qualities.
Having thus wandered through that entire city, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, [proceeded further]. (25–26)
Hari arrived at the dwelling of the Ṛṣis and constructed a beautiful assembly hall;
there, Hari gave fitting and most appropriate instruction.
For those who have faith in the Lord, the Creator of the universe bears fruit.
But for those who have no faith, the fruit does not arise.
And because of your great faith, my arrival here has become a source of happiness for you,
brought about by Kālīmaṇḍalīnabhūbhṛt, who appears in the form of the gateway.
I am indeed the Supreme Lord, the Master who assumes all incarnations;
I am the Supreme Brahman residing in the heart, the inner controller, and the bestower of fruits.
[In my] worship, service, sight, salutation, and offering— 2.215.30.
In granting the gift of massaging the feet, I am the giver of fruit; of this there is no doubt.
In former times, Mahādeva, my devotee, restored a child to life even at the word of a trusting jackal; such indeed was it.
The gods are worthy of universal worship, and kings abide by trust;
for those who have sought refuge, trust is the primary condition.
After that, the choosing [of a preceptor] is declared, and after that, the surrender [of oneself].
Furthermore, one should serve him like a wretched person, and thereafter maintain a state of steadfastness.
One should follow him in whatever manner pleases Hari, but avoid whatever manner does not please him. (34–35)
Such actions and means for liberation exist here within the human state, and such a condition prevails everywhere.
Therefore, O gods, I alone am to be served here for the sake of liberation and prosperity.
I, the Supreme Lord, am to be served for the sake of attaining eternal bliss.
When served with faith and gladdened by trust, I bestow the entirety of my auspiciousness; indeed, I grant my own Lakṣmī.
I grant life, wealth, prosperity, health, the expansion of one's lineage, enjoyments, objects of pleasure, and the power to experience them; of this there is no doubt.
This applies even to those who previously committed sins but later devoted themselves to meritorious deeds.

"Even though they died long ago, it is certain that they are indeed alive. Those who were doers of merit in the past but later became practitioners of evil are considered to have been alive before and dead thereafter. (2.215.40–41)
Therefore, he who grants life to those whose hope for living has perished—
that giver of life should be understood as the Guru, the Supreme Lord. Even while living, such a person does not know Hari, the Lord, who is the object of perception.
Though breathing, he is indeed dead; he is considered merely like a bellows.
Even such a person, through association with the virtuous, approaches the Blessed One. Devoting himself [to Him], even if remaining inactive, he truly lives, for he is immortal.
Life that is truly life-giving is indeed sweet through the service of Śrī Hari;
however, life that is parched and addicted to sense objects and the like must be abandoned.
Even when death is near, one who remembers Me goes to My abode.
In that manner, one should indeed remember me with the intellect; through faith, I become united [with him].
Formerly, at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the field of Akṣara, there was the son of an old brahmin named Vṛddhadeva, who had only a single son during his old age.
The son went into the water to bathe, and he fell indeed into the midst of the water.
He was dead, yet by drinking that water he became as if dead. His breath remained in his head, but it did not enter his eyes.
The channels no longer circulate, nor does any vital heat remain.
He appears as dead or nearly dead when placed upon the ground.
When he has been smeared with cow dung, people recognize him as dead. (2.215.50)
They took the portion of the dug-out earth along with their father to where the cremation ground was; there,
an old vulture was also present and saw the dead child being held on his lap by the weeping father, who was then letting him go.
The father was indeed unable to go away, having abandoned the child;
others as well were unable to depart after leaving the infant behind.
Then a vulture arrived and said, "Go indeed to your home. (52–53)
In this world, women and men—indeed, more than a thousand—constantly arrive;
yet, having abandoned those who have died, they always depart for their own homes.
No one at all returns again to the body once dead.
Since the entire world exists as such, constructed [by ignorance], and is pervaded by pleasure, pain, and the like, what cause for lamentation is there?
Those who have died have gone; those who carry away the dead will themselves die in another moment. (55–56)
Knowing this, those who take refuge in Hari shall be long-lived;
for no one endowed with life has ever emerged from the mouth of Mahākāla.
Such is the course of Time: it is the same toward both the beloved and the unloved.
Indeed, every embodied being born here must certainly depart.
Once life has passed away at the conclusion of one's karma, that living soul cannot be recovered again.
Let them abandon their homes and go; let them go toward peace as they approach the corpse of the dead.
Having thus obtained this knowledge and casting it aside on the ground,
the men went crying out to the bathing pool, for they realized he was indeed dead.
There, an old jackal arrived and spoke to those people:
All these men are pitiless, merciless, and devoid of affection.
How is it that your hearts are set on departing?
The day and its moments turn in many forms.
"Sometimes even one who is dead departs from the cremation ground while still appearing to live;
how is it that you, being devoid of compassion and merciless, depart after abandoning him?
For his eyes, ears, nose, and entire body are still present."
Do you have no affection for this [body], even that which is shared with beasts and birds?

It is not even like the affection of children who, though devoid of self-interest, increase their own welfare; nor is it like the affection found anywhere among quadrupeds, birds, or insects, even when they are being nurtured.
There is no attainment of fruit, nor is there any virtue whatsoever;
nevertheless, as long as they behold those dead children upon the ground,
they do not abandon them— at such a time, you possess no such affection.
Therefore, do not depart, leaving behind this most excellent son who will sustain our lineage.
Behold that son for a long time while the body remains unimpaired;
for relatives stay only where others do not remain.
Having heard the words of the jackal, those men, though already bathed,
overcome by affection for their son, returned to the cremation ground. Then the vulture, beholding the people filled with grief, spoke to them.
"Alas! Having become human beings, why have you come here so deluded?

This corpse, consisting of the elements, has been abandoned by the vital breaths and the senses; it has become dry and attained the state of mere wood. How can you, who possess knowledge, grieve for it? (2.215.70–71)
Why do you not grieve for yourselves? Why indeed do you grieve for that which is transitory? Evil is destroyed by austerity, and [the sins] of other lives by devotion.
What indeed can be gained by lamenting for a child who has passed away?
Having given away or taken away [wealth], embodied beings depart from this earth;
likewise, this child has departed after leaving behind infinite grief—the home, gold, cows, offspring, jewels, and all prosperity. (73–74)
All austerity is indeed to be acquired; likewise, it is held that [the goal] is attainable through devotion.
Everything is indeed obtainable through merit; therefore, purify that merit which is beneficial.
Through one's own performed dharma or sin, one becomes happy or miserable.
A father, a son, or even a kinsman becomes happy or miserable through their own actions.
Therefore, O best of beings, go to your own homes and practice righteousness;
abide in devotion to Hari, to the virtuous, to the gods, and to your ancestors.
Abandon grief and turn away from delusion, casting it aside.
Whether learned or ignorant, whether a king or wealthy or poor—everyone falls under the power of time and never returns again. (78)

"Death enters all—youths, children, the elderly, fetuses, women, and men alike—and leads them away never to return. Having been told this, those humans then depart, leaving the corpse behind. (2.215.80)
Then the jackal said: "By what has your affection been destroyed?
How have you, who were once full of affection, been made affectionless by the words of one devoid of affection?
"Destiny, human effort, faith, and trust—these are [the four pillars]. (8.1)
They even cause Death himself to flee far away at times.
One must indeed remain free from despondency; for what fruit is there in despondency?
Everything is attained through effort; let them not become merciless in any way.
This corpse, produced from the flesh of your own bodies, is the means for the accomplishment of your paternal lineage.
Once the sun has set, where will you go, you merciless ones, leaving it behind?
For when the sun has gone down, one must either depart or remain right here.
"Even the gods, when propitiated, being compassionate, grant life.
Having been told this, they believed it to be the truth and approached the corpse.
Then the vulture said to them, "It seems to me that you are fools. (85–86)
Indeed, many years have passed for me since being born here;
yet I have never seen life after death, whether as a woman, a man, or a neuter.
Embryos, infants, adolescents, youths, and even the elderly—[all have perished].
Once dead, they do not return to life, even though they were loved by their kinsmen and friends.
When they have been mourned, the relatives, kin, and others depart for home.
O son, let even this body be abandoned; it is empty and like a piece of wood. (88–89)
"Having abandoned [us] and gone elsewhere, why do you not return home?
Why do you not depart now, having abandoned your senses and your vital breaths here?
O best of beings, exert yourselves indeed for the sake of happiness in the next world."
Having heard this, they turned back, and then the jackal said to them:
"Alas! These pitiless ones are indeed departing, abandoning a son who is like gold;
even Rākṣasas do not depart after abandoning their own son."
What is the use of instructions for those who possess no wisdom of their own?
Indeed, the son of Śvetarāja was restored to life;
likewise, Satyavān was restored to life by his wife Sāvitrī as her husband once more.
The son of Hariścandra also, having died, was restored to life again;
the son of Rukmāṅgada also, having died, was restored to life again; and the son of Naciketas also, having died, was restored to life again. (94–95)
The gods known as the Maruts were killed in the womb and yet restored to life;
likewise, by some stroke of fortune, one might obtain life again for one who was dead. A god may show compassion toward the wretched and grant them their breath of life.
Having been addressed thus, those affectionate ones returned with their hopes restored.
Then the vulture, having approached again, spoke to them who were overcome by hope:
"Even those endowed with ascetic power, possessed of sovereignty, and great in intellect—" (97–98)
Once they have gone to death, they do not return again from the city of the departed;
enough with this bond of hope for the living of one who is dead here.
Not even a hundred jackals will bring a corpse back to life.
Even if Īśāna, Hari, Brahmā, Yamarāja,
or the other lords were to revive him, he would live only then and not otherwise;
for there is no life here through mere residence or even through weeping.
"Whether through shedding tears, gasping for breath, or even by crushing [ourselves], we shall live on.
United and endowed with righteousness, let us perform the worship of the Lord.
If there is life, we shall indeed perform it until the break of dawn."
Having heard this, they became despondent and departed, leaving the corpse behind.
Then the jackal approached and spoke again with words of peace:
"Do not depart in despair; fie upon the vulture who is devoid of affection!"
Suffering follows immediately after happiness, and happiness follows immediately after suffering;
it arises inevitably, therefore do not depart from here, abandoning me.
I shall see you alive even a moment later, of this there is no doubt.
Thus, all were joined by hope and remained waiting once more.
Then the vulture named Śmaśāna said: "This place is indeed dreadful;
casting off hope and casting off the corpse, perform the funeral rites."
"When the sun has set, the fierce *preta*s, *yakṣa*s, *bhūta*s,
and *rākṣasa*s who devour flesh will assault you.
If you place your trust in the words of the jackal, you will all perish quickly."
Having been addressed thus, they were about to depart when the jackal said:
"Do not flee, do not flee, you who are deluded by the words of the flesh-eater!
Having driven you away, the vulture, seeking his own interest, will surely devour the corpse. (2.215.110)
The vulture said: "I am certainly not seeking my own interest;
rather, it is the jackal who seeks his own interest—he desires his own prey, the corpse, through deception in the darkness.
Having been told this, they understood that those two were intent on accomplishing their own ends.
Bound by their own interests and greed, hungry and talkative,
they were convinced that the corpse must not be given to those two deceivers.
Agitated by affection for their son, they remembered Śambhu in the evening.
Then, urged by the Goddess, the illustrious Śambhu arrived there;
they bowed to Śambhu and reported their suffering,
whereupon Hara granted him life for ten thousand years.
Selfish and deceitful, they were cheated; yet their son obtained life.
Having propitiated Hara, they obtained a son and became happy.
Having returned home full of confidence, they indeed obtained the fruit of life.
But that which has been obtained by the two deceivers is brought about by their own actions.
Therefore, placing your trust in me, Hari, the Supreme Person, worship me with undivided devotion;
I shall protect you, of this there is no doubt.
"And I shall grant you a life within my abode, filled with eternal bliss.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord himself bestowed the mantras upon his subjects;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa made those who had taken refuge in him his own Vaiṣṇavas.
O Rādhikā, having heard the words of Śrī Hari, the subjects then took refuge in Him;
after worshipping Hari, they returned to their own homes.
And the four daughters of the king [chose] Kṛṣṇa as their beloved, the Great Lord.
They placed a garland of choice flowers around his neck and made him their own lord and master.
They celebrated a royal festival during the night and provided food and other comforts;
the maidens attended upon him, and Kṛṣṇa indeed fell asleep.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Journey to the Kingdom of King Rāyakūpeśa in the Tretā-santāna of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including His wandering through and worship in the city of Havānā, His journey to the kingdom of King Kālīmaṇḍalīnabha, His wandering through and worship in the city of Vigoṣṭhikā, as well as His instruction, meal, and rest at night.
Chapter 215. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 216 [Author:
Chapter 217 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the fifteenth day at dawn, Bālakṛṣṇa was awakened with auspicious songs, musical instruments, and hymns of praise.
Having performed his ablutions, offered worship, and drunk milk and other refreshments, [he arose].
Having paid obeisance to his parents, he sat upon the lion-throne.
At that moment, the king arrived before Hari to perform worship;
he placed a crown upon [the deity’s] head, as well as earrings and bracelets.
He also gave golden rings, chains, pearl necklaces, jeweled diamond necklaces, and wealth exceeding a hundred thousand;
he offered himself as well, and likewise presented flower garlands.
Having washed his feet, the king, accompanied by his kinsmen, drank [the water].
Then he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), bowed, and sang, "Protect me!
The queen offered worship and a dowry, and chose as her boon that he always protect her.
This being the case, his brother— the elder brother of Kālīmaṇḍalin,
the former ruler of the kingdom, the lord of Vanajaleśa,
the master of the region of Vanajvālā, and the sovereign of Oṣṭrīpurī along with his younger brothers— [acted]. (7)
Then he arrived in his own celestial chariot to bring Hari.
Having arrived, he prostrated like a staff, placed a garland of flowers around [Hari's] neck,
and offered a hundred golden rings in a golden vessel.
And Hari prayed to the Supreme Lord to sanctify his own regions; "So be it," the Lord replied, and in a moment He became ready.
King Kālīmaṇḍalīna made his obeisance with a face beaming with joy.
She performed a great worship with sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice,
and saffron; with various materials, gems, necklaces, crest-jewels, and earrings, as well as wedding gifts and offerings, she then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having performed the worship of the caravan of Hari with his army and musical instruments, and likewise having offered honors and leave-taking with shouts of victory,
Śrī Hari then remained there in the sky, seated upon his celestial chariot.
The subjects gazed upon him, bowed, and praised him with longing;
they said again and again, "Please come; we must be protected.
Then Hari, by the path shown [to him], moved the celestial chariot through the sky.
The great sage Rākāsaṇa and the royal preceptor arrived at the palace together with Kṛṣṇa; the king had previously departed for the city.
There, the army was likewise made ready for the purpose of honoring Hari.
All the subjects, adorned with fresh flowers and garlands,
stood in the great garden near the camel and their younger brother to welcome him;
they remained there before him, waiting for the direction of Hari.
The sage Pūrṇāsanaka, the preceptor of the assembly of Kālīs,
arrived together with Hari, as did the sage Rākāsana.
Beholding the celestial chariot in the sky, the people were indeed filled with great joy.

The king, accompanied by his army, offered a welcome with the sounds of musical instruments, cries of victory, banners, small flags, and the like; with prostrations, offerings of flowers, songs, and auspicious rites. (2.216.20–21)
The celestial chariot attained stability upon the surface of the earth, and Hari went outside.
The king placed auspicious flower garlands around the neck of the young Kṛṣṇa and performed an ablution with water at his feet; that water was like nectar.
He drank [the water] together with his family and prostrated like a staff.
The queen bowed to Kambharā and worshipped her as Mahālakṣmī;
thereafter, the king worshipped his father, Gopālakṛṣṇa.
The householders honored their families and the beloved wives of the brāhmaṇas.
The king placed Lord Hari upon an elephant-vehicle made of gold;
likewise, he placed the others upon horse-drawn carriages, palanquins, and other conveyances.
Having worshipped [the Lord] with necklaces, crest-garlands, flower-clusters, and other offerings, the king, accompanied by his army,
led Hari into the city amidst the sounds of musical instruments and hymns of praise.
At the city gate, the princes each individually performed worship.
At the crossroads and on the great square,
the leading merchants and the people there performed the worship of Hari with processions,
offerings, and garlands; the women honored him with necklaces, flowers, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and excellent fruits.
They worshipped with saffron, with their hearts, and with meditations and the like;
likewise with garments, ornaments, and golden materials.
They touched his feet and placed them upon their heads—acts that destroy suffering and increase prosperity.

Beholding the beloved Bālakṛṣṇa, who was most exquisitely adorned with form upon form, they worshipped him with their joined palms, their eyes, and their meditations. The beloved women held him in their hearts forever, never forgetting him.
Others, standing at a distance, beheld Acyuta—
composed of divine splendor, peaceful, as beautiful as ten million Cupids,
Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā and others, and worshipped by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses. (32–33)
Likewise, some beheld him as Nārāyaṇa with four arms, worshipped by Ramā;
others saw the Lord as the Master of Badarī;
some saw Śrī Hari as an ascetic; others saw Kṛṣṇa; and still others saw Him reclining upon Śeṣa.

Some other young women beheld the golden Lord Hari situated within the sun; likewise, others saw the divine, excellent Person, the Lord, standing in the midst of fire—beloved, and the bestower of the bliss of fulfilled desires. (35–36)
The devotees beheld that Lord dwelling in the Great Imperishable;
likewise, the subjects— both men and women— beheld Him in the form of Viṣṇu,
served by Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Śrī.

There they beheld Hari in various forms mounted upon his elephant-vehicle, honored by the beautiful and virtuous qualities of Ramā, Padmāvatī, and Hāsā; he was worshipped by Māṇikī, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, Durgikā, and Kamalā. (38–39)
The women beheld the Lord, who was worshipped by the Brahmapriyās and others, and honored by the Piśaṅginīs, as well as by the Gaurīs,
the Cāmarīs, and the maidens; indeed, they saw him as the divine Śrī Hari himself.
Thus Hari then granted his own vision in many ways;
indeed, while sporting repeatedly among the subjects in the city of Uṣṭrī,
accompanied by his younger brother, he wandered through the city in this manner and arrived at the royal palace.
The queen shone resplendent upon the lion-throne and performed worship;
her five daughters also gave her water to drink.
They worshipped their beloved husband, the Lord of Śrī, who was beautiful and desired by their hearts.
They placed a garland of *pārijāta* flowers around the neck of Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, they chose him who was difficult to obtain, yet easily accessible as he had come to their own homes;
and having obtained Hari as their beloved, they became fulfilled in all their desires.
The king, the queen, and the princes considered their own good fortune;
he held a royal festival and provided a meal at midday.
Having eaten, the caravans attained complete rest after three o'clock in the afternoon.
The king gave both a dowry and a gift of leave to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then men and women came to his abode for the sake of a vision;
to them Hari gave spiritual awakening and the auspicious Vaiṣṇava mantra.
The power of Hari must always be protected, for it bestows all happiness upon men in times of calamity,
at the time of death, at the time of Yama, and during the course of an evil destiny.
My very refuge is my strength, which wards off misfortunes and other such evils.
In the past, even though the śālmali tree was devoid of strength, it became victorious by taking refuge in Brahmā;
indeed, it brought about the defeat of the god Vāyu.
On the Himālaya mountains, there was a great tree known as the śālmali. (2.216.50–51)
He was a tree with branches, a trunk, and leaves, providing refuge for beasts and birds;
through his flowers, fruits, and other resources, he satisfied the hunger even of those who took shelter with him.
Indeed, as Nārada was traveling toward Viśālā, he encountered that Viśālin.
He asked: "O tree, how is it that you remain fearless and happy?
For I see that your branches have not been broken by the wind at all.
Is there perhaps some wind that is your friend, who protects you?"
For the wind is indeed mighty and could destroy even mountains;
yet it exists here having left you behind, and therefore it will be the cause [of your safety].
Elephants, gayals, and other wild animals are standing below you.
You shine forth, for you are worthy of being served by others and are indeed a benefactor in every way.
(56) I conjecture that the Wind is your kinsman, or perhaps your companion or friend;
or else, you must surely have sought refuge with the Wind. (57)
Having heard this, Śālmali said: "Vāyu is neither my friend nor my well-wisher; he is neither my kinsman nor my refuge, by whom I was not protected.
My splendor and strength are superior, exceeding that of Vāyu by eighteenfold. (58)
"By him the wind was obstructed; thus has he been overcome by me. Therefore, I am afraid of the wind, not because it is angry, but because of its extreme velocity.
Then Nārada said: "This which I have heard is truly a great marvel."
Varuṇa, Yama the King, and Kubera are not equal to the Maruts;
yet you have indeed conquered Vāyu, the performer of all activities.
Or perhaps, O Drupada, you speak falsely out of a deficiency of intellect.
I shall go and tell Vāyu exactly what you have spoken so ill.
Indeed, the wind has never been obstructed by mountains, nor by oceans, nor by planets, nor even by the celestial trees, in the manner that you have described it.
"They all pay homage to him; you, out of delusion, boast fruitlessly.
Having said this, Nārada went to where Vāyu was staying and spoke these words of Śālmalī, which were full of provocation.
Having heard this, Pavana arrived at the place where the Śālmali tree stood. Enraged, he said: "O tree, because you spoke words of reproach to Nārada, I shall show you my power; stand firm!"
Since the Grandfather rested upon you during the creation of beings,
I always abandon you with speed, seize you, and carry you away.
Having cast off those qualities of yours, you now exert your strength against me.
"Today I shall lead you away, root and all, stripped of the expansion of your lineage.
Thus addressed, the Śālmali tree replied: "I have no fear at all.
Come with all your might; let your anger toward me be abandoned."
"I have no fear of you, O Vāyu; my strength is even more powerful than yours.
For those who are strong in wisdom are always truly strong.
Those whose strength consists merely in their physical bodies are not strong in the truest sense."
Thus addressed, the Wind became enraged and turned into a violent tempest.
Upon seeing him, the Śālmali tree indeed stripped away its own leaves,
branches, flowers, fruits, and even its small twigs.
Becoming as motionless as a staff, he stood there, thinking, "What can the wind do?
Meanwhile, the exceedingly swift wind saw that the tree was stripped of its branches and its leaves were withered;
laughing, it spoke to the lord of the forest.
Behold my strength and sovereignty, through fear of which you were shattered.
Yet, by taking refuge in Brahmā and through a mere fraction of my compassion, you have become happy here.
Having abandoned the refuge of the great, you now despise the great.
Therefore, you have become miserable, deprived of the expansion of your lineage.
I am capable of consuming you; do not harbor pride at all.
I am also capable of uprooting you; do not harbor fruitless pride.
Having spoken thus, he blew with force by means of his own exceedingly swift current.

(2.216.80) Thus, even one who is devoid of strength, or even one as inert as a tree—

"If even when all has been abandoned there is no refuge for me, then there will indeed be fear from the wind of time; therefore, one should obtain a refuge. Having been thus instructed, the king and others—the people, men, and women—[acted accordingly].

Long ago, the King went to the city of Gatainārāṣṭra for the purpose of honoring [him].

The impetuous ones, the forest-dwellers, and even the women arrived swiftly.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

With garments, ornaments, and other such things, as well as sugar and desired objects—
having thus wandered through the city, the Blessed Lord returned to his residence;

"Meritorious virtue must indeed be acquired by everyone through whatever action possible;
likewise, sin—which is an obstacle to spiritual welfare—must certainly be avoided. (9)
Greed is the foundation and the instigator for the creation of evil.
Greed alone is most wicked; from greed, sin proceeds.
Greed is the root of destruction, by which people go to their ruin.
From greed, there arises in some cases anger, lust, and craving;
as well as pride, deceit, delusion, arrogance, and even hostility toward others. There is also intolerance, the destruction of modesty, and the depletion of prosperity, fortune, and dharma.
Ill-repute, wretchedness, and subjection arise from greed.
So too do non-giving, lack of renunciation, thirst, engagement in improper actions, intoxication, malice, contempt, distrust, and likewise crookedness. (13–14)
The seizure of another's property and so forth, censure, impetuosity, lack of self-restraint, envy, contempt, boastfulness, and malice— all these,
as well as rashness, deception, and theft, proceed entirely from greed. (15)
That which cannot be filled even by ten thousand lifetimes;
as one ages, greed ages along with them, yet it never abandons its persistence.
It always reaches greater depth when applied to objects, remaining unimpaired. (16–17)
When directed toward an object of enjoyment, it always generates passion;
through greed, a human being incurs extreme attachment and thirst.
That greed, together with delusion, must be conquered by one who desires the highest good.
Hatred and anger have their basis in greed; they destroy the conduct of the virtuous.
(1.9) They are cruel within, like hidden wells, and bring about the destruction of the worlds.
People who rely on greed deceive others here by means of various pretexts. (2.217.20)
They plunder and destroy the paths of the virtuous and their own innate virtues;
they fall into terrible suffering and cause others to fall as well.
For the sake of achieving their own selfish ends, they even assault their fathers and kinsmen who are superior to them.
Likewise, greed and other vices cause those who are disciplined to become undisciplined.
By that, merit is lost, and one who has become such perishes.
Therefore, one should rely upon virtuous people who are pure in their vows and free from craving.
One should indeed serve those who are free from greed and delusion, who have attained the highest welfare therefrom,
who are established in truth, who are bulls of dharma, endowed with the conduct of the virtuous,

One should worship the ancestors, the gods, guests, and likewise all benefactors;

Those devoted to the activities of the body think, "This must certainly be done";

They are devoted to truth and uprightness, and likewise devoted to my own form.

One should devotedly serve those whose minds are equanimous toward gain and loss, pleasure and pain, the pleasant and the unpleasant, and birth and death;
one should also take refuge in those of great soul, the divine, and the virtuous.
For the sake of one's welfare, one should take refuge in divine gurus who remove ignorance.
Ignorance is rooted in greed and is the producer of sin;
moreover, due to ignorance, a person does not perceive even the destruction of his own self.

Both of these—ignorance and excessive greed—are equal in their results, equal in their defects, and most formidable; they are considered the destroyers of stability. Ignorance has its origin in greed, and it increases as greed increases.
When greed is exhausted, one goes to destruction; otherwise, one follows the paths of the lotus-born [gods].
Greed is not truly diminished merely by the restraint of the senses;
rather, the root of greed perishes through the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Self-restraint bestows auspiciousness; self-restraint should be understood as the most excellent of dharmas.
Through self-restraint, success is surely attained; self-restraint excels even generosity.
Through self-restraint, one's splendor increases, and one becomes a man of brilliance.
The self-controlled person finds supreme happiness both in this world and in the next.
The self-controlled person sleeps in peace and wakes in peace;
he moves through the worlds in peace, and his mind remains serene. (2.217.40–41)
For an undisciplined person repeatedly encounters suffering;
moreover, an undisciplined person brings forth many other misfortunes.
The fruit of honoring one's teacher is said to belong to the virtuous person who is disciplined and possesses good conduct.
Lust, anger, pride, greed, wrath, envy,
contempt, malice, and other such evil qualities do not reside at all in one who is self-controlled.
The self-controlled person is like the ocean, by whom the fish-like senses have been destroyed.
By whom even worldly and forest activities have been truly destroyed—
he who is well-conducted, endowed with virtue, serene in soul, a knower of the Self, and wise—
having attained honor in this world, he attains a happy state in the hereafter. (45)
The action practiced by the virtuous is the way of life for the self-controlled.
The auspicious path that bestows well-being flourishes for the virtuous and the self-controlled.
Having shaken off [worldly attachments], being established in the Self, and devoted to the service of the righteous, the self-controlled person [attains liberation].
The devotee who is intent on the Middle Path is fit for becoming Brahman;
for he grants fearlessness to all beings and receives fearlessness from all beings.
Whether in the body or beyond the body, he has no fear from any source whatsoever.
Having attained friendship with all, he indeed cultivates my service.
For one who has entered the path of the virtuous, my state is always commensurate. Having abandoned greed born of ignorance and become self-controlled, let him worship me. (2.217.50)
Or rather, for him, there are eternal worlds consisting of light.
Having surrendered his actions to me, having indeed surrendered his austerity to me,
having surrendered his knowledge to me, he is serene in soul and takes refuge in me.
Having attained the enjoyments existing in heaven, he certainly finds my own heaven;
or else, the station of the Grandfather (Brahmā), or the Vairāja realm beyond that, or the abode consisting of the mass of Brahman, the unmanifest, or the immortal state. ||52-53||
Through devotion and self-restraint, one attains Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha—
[the state] of that devotee who delights in knowledge and does not oppose any embodied being.
For such a person, there is no fear here again, nor any fear of the next world.
The peace of one who has mastered self-restraint is not equal to that of one who strives for it.
(55) Regarding self-restraint, there is a common worldly saying which must be endured by the virtuous:
people consider one who is endowed with patience to be weak. (56)
Through lack of power, the supreme quality of forbearance arises in him as a certainty;
by means of forbearance, vast worlds that are otherwise difficult to attain become easily won.
This virtue of endurance is the duty of the virtuous, and it is difficult for others of evil nature to achieve.

Of what use is the forest to one who is self-controlled? For him, wherever he dwells is the forest. Self-control is declared to be the highest austerity; it is the great conquest when it subdues the great desire.
The restraint of the impetuous senses is the great battle. (58–59)
Indeed, that accumulated austerity bestows all desires;
those perfected through austerity and endowed with self-restraint behold the three worlds.
Whatever may be difficult to attain, all that one may obtain through austerity.
Indeed, all sovereign powers have their root in austerity;
for all sins, when heated by it, are consumed by austerity.
For one whose group of sense-faculties has been withdrawn, austerity is that which is called fasting.
It increases one's strength and is the supreme enhancer of divine splendor.
There is no austerity more difficult than giving, nor any greater than fasting. There is no skill equal to attaining liberation for oneself, and no happiness greater than contentment.
Through austerity, one is able to attain the state of liberation from the Lord of Gods and other such states.
Speech is austerity; truth alone exists, for truth is established among the virtuous.
Truth is dharma, austerity, yoga, sacrifice, and the eternal Brahman.

All that is indeed of the nature of truth when austerity is offered to Kṛṣṇa; through union with Hari, one becomes true to one's vows by serving the virtuous. To perceive Me in all things is called the vow of equanimity.

Through the destruction of desire, the vow of self-restraint is attained; through the destruction of craving, the vow of fearlessness is indeed achieved by means of firmness rooted in the Self. Furthermore, through knowledge, stability, profundity, and fortitude are also acquired.
Non-avarice is attained through the state of selflessness in every respect;
goodness is attained through patience, and virtuous conduct through the absence of worldly intention.
Prosperity is attained through wisdom, and well-being through meritorious deeds. (69)
Modesty is obtained from the Dharma, and likewise, patience is acquired through fortitude.
(2.217.70) Renunciation is the abandonment of affection as well as the abandonment of sense objects;
it is attained through freedom from passion and hatred, and by means of dispassion. (71)
Fortitude is the state of being free from agitation even when encountering objects that bring both pleasure and pain;
it is an invincibility attained through the power of one's own self-nature.
(72) One should be patient in every respect, and one should be devoted to truth.
One should remain free from joy, fear, and anger for the sake of attaining what is auspicious.
One who desires welfare should always be free from malice and likewise full of compassion; one should abide in truth, righteousness, and virtuous conduct. (73–74)

One who desires the highest good must cultivate service to the virtuous, must cultivate union with devotion to Me, and must indeed cultivate self-surrender. One should receive a Vaiṣṇava mantra and likewise take refuge in Me, Hari.
"By that, both the higher good (*śreyaḥ*) and the pleasant (*preyaḥ*) shall become supreme for you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), ceased speaking;
and the subjects, out of love, honored him and received the mantra of Hari.

Those assembled there engaged in a feast of riddles and witty replies.
Then they all slept, while the maidens attended upon Kṛṣṇa.

When Hari had performed his daily rites and worship and was composed,
the King arrived there to honor Kṛṣṇa and paid him homage.

Hari said, "So be it," and he showed them due honor.
At that moment, the chief minister Yājaneśvara arrived—

Bowing down along with Patra, he prayed to the Supreme Lord:

"May the Blessed One fulfill [this vow]; it will be for the welfare of all creatures. Through the sight of you, through worship, and through service, the fortunes of the immortals shall also become auspicious. (91–92)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "Welcome to you and to the king.
O best of ministers, I honor your words, which are worthy and desired.
On the morning of the fifth day, having arrived there for the sacrificial festival—"

"Having brought Lomaśa as well as the best of great sages, and having brought Īśāna and Satī, go and inform the king; and also cause the collection of all necessary materials to be prepared and issue a proclamation. || 94-95 ||
Prepare an auspicious and suitable site on the riverbank for the purpose of the sacrifice.
Let the commencement of the sacrifice take place at dawn on the fifth lunar day, and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) of the rite on the eleventh day. Proclaim this in every way.
Having received the command, the minister departed quickly for his own residence (97).

as did Lomaśeśānadeva, Lālāyana, and Vṛkāyana (98).

(2.217.100) Then Kṛṣṇa, having drunk milk together with his family, became ready to depart for the kingdom of Ekadvāra as well as the kingdom of Pārūpara. (101)
The king, who drinks from both shores [of the ocean], gave him a parting gift as a dowry;

Having received a welcome and honor, Hari ascended his celestial chariot.
At that time, Koṭīśvara went first to pay his respects to Hari;
Śrī Satīśa also departed for his own kingdom. Then Hari, accompanied by Mṛtyu, Harṣi, and Suyukta, as well as Koṣṭhaka and Ṛṣi, [departed].

and then, by her mother’s command, the two auspicious daughters [placed them] around Kṛṣṇa’s neck. (14)

"Anger, greed, the relish for flavors, pride, theft, and slander— these,
when intoxicated, constantly afflict both man and woman."
From these arises suffering; from these arises evil.
From greed arises anger, and from pride it is born in great measure.
Likewise, anger toward the faults of others arises as an obstacle to one's desires.
Anger arises from being insulted, as well as from hearing harsh words.
Through forgiveness, anger quickly turns away from the virtuous person.
Sometimes the root of anger is indeed desire, once it has been separated [from its object].
Volition is indeed the root of desire; it increases when its causes flourish. When indulged in, it grows further; when abandoned, it perishes.
Envy arises from pride as well as from the disparagement of one's reputation.
Due to poverty, one’s own lowliness, and being situated in a state of degradation,
delusion arises from ignorance and proceeds from the habitual practice of evil.
When struck down by the path of knowledge, delusion is eradicated from its very root.
The desire to perform action, when its fruit is offered to Me, does not cause bondage. Likewise, grief arises from affection due to the separation from desired objects;
when that object is no longer sought, all grief ceases. (24)
Dependence on others arises from craving, greed, desire, or the pursuit of pleasure;

Having obtained their portion which bestows happiness, one should avoid any other portion.

Indeed, compassion arises in the world from the discernment of having rendered assistance.
Likewise, in the case of the miserly and others, greed turns back due to their lack of virtue.
Wherever greed, which originates from ignorance, arises, one should contemplate in each such instance its instability and its quality of bestowing suffering. (33)

One should always avoid the cruel, having understood things as they truly are;

He is deceitful, mean-spirited, dishonest, and erratic; he is boastful, fond of company, disrespectful toward those worthy of honor, ungenerous in sharing, suspicious of everyone, and merciless.
He is miserly, hateful, given to violence, and full of falsehoods. (36)
Greedy, proponents of heretical doctrines, revilers, and these cruel men—[they are such]. (37) He who perceives one of virtuous character and endowed with qualities as being sinful;

He does not trust anyone on the basis of his own experience with treachery; he who speaks of even a slight fault of the virtuous as being great, and he who considers a helpful friend to be a supreme deceiver. (39)

Those who perform the duties toward their teacher as toward a father, and those who live on what has been given for the sake of dharma—

The attainment of all sovereignty and the state of being a lord arise from taking refuge in that [Lord].
Those virtuous ones are indeed my own form, in whom my auspicious and excellent qualities reside.

I shall speak of those people who must be abandoned, for association with whom brings fear:
one who is greedy, cruel, devoid of dharma, and bereft of devotion to me;
one should avoid such a person who is deceitful, treacherous, base, and of sinful conduct.

One should avoid the lazy, the suspicious of everything, and the procrastinating; as well as the crooked, the ever-abusive, the violator of the teacher’s wife, the one addicted to vices, the evil-minded, the parricide, and the shameless. (2.218.49–50)
One should abandon a person who has eyes for evil everywhere, an atheist, a slanderer, a rogue, one whose senses are unrestrained, one addicted to sensual desires, one who is negligent,
one of wicked conduct, one who is hostile, and one who is unstable in observing the rules of discipline. (51)
One who is slanderous, lacking wisdom, envious, and sinful;
one of bad character, undisciplined, deceitful, and cruel;
one who betrays friends and is possessed by a greedy longing for the wealth of others—[these should not be befriended]. (52–53)

One should abandon even a person who hates giving and is dissatisfied; likewise, one should abandon the undisciplined, the weak, and those intent on inappropriate anger. One should abandon the imprudent, the undiscerning, and those who become hostile without cause. (54)
One should avoid that which produces what is unwholesome, that which is wicked, and that which is full of calamities;
likewise, one should avoid the fool who is intent on doing harm and who causes the destruction of merit.
One should also avoid him who is an enemy with the face of a friend, and even a friend who hates his own kin.
One who looks askance, who seeks only his own self-interest, and whose fame is in decline;
a man who praises one in his presence but reviles him behind his back;
and one who is mild when it serves his own purpose but becomes stubborn once that purpose is achieved—one should abandon such people.
One should abandon a drinker of intoxicants, one who is hateful, wealthy, merciless, and harsh.

A wise person should avoid from afar one who causes distress to others, one who is addicted to the slaughter of living beings, one who is ungrateful, one who is base, and one who looks for faults. 58–59.
"Therefore, there is indeed no loss in this world, nor any distraction of the self anywhere;
there is neither destruction of the intellect, nor any obstacle to his prosperity.
Having examined things thus, the wise man should take refuge with virtuous and beneficial people."
Those who are of noble birth, endowed with knowledge, learned, and highly erudite;
(61) possessed of virtues, free from greed, unconquered, and likewise those who have overcome fatigue;
good friends, grateful, all-knowing, and devoid of avarice. (62)

One should rely upon those who are endowed with the quality of sweetness, who are true to their word, who have conquered their senses, who are habituated to physical exercise, who are faultless, and who follow virtuous conduct;
but not those who are prone to anger at the wrong time or for no reason, nor those who are devoid of passion.
Those who are dispassionate, knowledgeable in matters of state, and devoted to the welfare of their friends;
those who are trustworthy, free from malice, protectors, and lovers of righteousness;
those for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal in value, and who are firm in their resolve—such are the true friends. (64–65)
Having reflected, one should take refuge in virtuous people who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of their master.
That person who forms an alliance with such devotees of the Lord will always experience prosperity,
well-being, and likewise liberation.
Those who are constant in the scriptures, who have conquered their faults, who are contented, and who abide in Hari;
who are endowed with the virtues of good character and tranquility—these are the best of men and are to be allied with.
Likewise, those who are cruel, wicked, and those described as even lower than that [are to be avoided].
Those who are ungrateful, betrayers of friends, and devoid of dharma must be abandoned.
Whence can there be fame for the ungrateful? Whence a place of standing? Whence happiness?
For the ungrateful person is not to be trusted; indeed, there is no atonement for ingratitude.
A man, especially, must not commit treachery against a friend.
One who betrays a friend goes to a terrible hell, experiencing suffering that brings about misfortune.
Therefore, one should always be grateful and truly desire the welfare of one's friends.
From a friend one obtains everything; from a friend one receives honor;
from a friend one attains enjoyments; through a friend, misfortune perishes.
Friends in this world are virtuous beings who destroy the sins of living creatures.
They are the washers away of latent impressions (vāsanā) and likewise the bestowers of heaven and liberation;
they are the removers of worldly existence and death, and the protectors of those who seek refuge.
They are the removers of suffering in every way, compassionate, and exceedingly pure in nature (sāttvika).
By men— whether young or old— and by women, the virtuous who are adorned with good character,
who are free from all faults, divine, endowed with divine qualities, and who bestow divinity upon those who take refuge in them, should always be served. (75)
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and these are my devoted servants.
Even their grace is divine, their sight is indeed divine, their touch is indeed divine, and their service is likewise divine. (76–77)
Salutation, service, obedience to commands, and the nectar of their feet—all these are divine through divine union; therefore, they should be constantly served by people.
There is no higher merit like this, nor is there any dharma superior to this.
"And may I have supreme devotion toward the virtuous; the virtuous are the ones who deliver one from worldly existence.
Having thus instructed him, the Blessed One gave him the most excellent Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Then King Koṭīśvara caused Hari to be fed.
Then he gave all kinds of honors, as well as betel leaves;
he also gave sacrificial fees consisting of gold coins and other items, along with fine garments.
At the time following midday, Kuṣṭhakārṣi then [worshipped] Hari.
Requesting that you come to his own kingdom named Pārūpa, King Śrī Satīśa had previously gone there to welcome you;
Hari then said, "So be it," and immediately became ready. (82–83)
King Koṭīśvara gave him much wealth as a dowry; having received his dismissal and gold, jewels, and other gifts, Hari, accompanied by his own kin,
ascended a celestial chariot and proceeded toward the eastern direction.
Then, by the king’s command, musical instruments were sounded;
shouts of "Victory! were raised by the subjects, and Kṛṣṇa, bowed to by the people and exalted by their devotions, departed through the path of the sky.
He arrived from the neighboring kingdom toward the city of Sañcala.
In the great garden of the royal palace, the king, accompanied by his army, became composed;
indeed, a celestial chariot arrived swiftly for the purpose of welcoming him.
Upon seeing him, who was like the sun, the subjects and the troops on all sides raised shouts of victory and showed their obeisance; eager, they also displayed their banners and small flags. (88–89)

Then, along the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari beheld celestial chariots in the sky— gleaming like the moon, variegated with household designs, and adorned with *vāvaṭikās* and *vāvaṭas*— displaying his fame and glory.
He slowly brought it down from the front of the temple onto the ground in the garden.
Then the subjects honored and worshipped that auspicious celestial chariot with flowers, leaves, and other offerings, bowing with palms joined in reverence.

The Supreme Lord Śrī Hari, resembling the sun in brilliance yet possessing a mind as cool as the moon, swiftly arrived before them in his celestial chariot out of compassion, in order to grant his vision to all the worlds. (93)
Lord Hari has eyes like lotus petals, a face graced with a gentle smile,
and a form encompassed by a halo of splendor; he possesses the radiance of gold,
the beauty of ten million Cupids, and is the Lord who is an ocean of parental affection.
He granted an audience to the people and accepted their prostrations and other marks of respect;
he then took to heart the devotion offered by them with their hearts.
Then the king placed garlands of flowers and golden necklaces upon his own neck.
He sprinkled cool, fragrant essences upon [the Buddha’s] head and other parts;
he placed clusters of flowers in his hands and applied a saffron tilaka mark.
He performed the washing of the feet and drank the nectar of grace.
The queen also worshipped the Lord of Śrī, the husband of Pārvatī;
she performed the *ārātrika* ceremony there in the celestial chariot with many wicks.
At that time, they performed worship and offered adoration with necklaces of pearls and other such ornaments.
Then Kṛṣṇa drank that cool, sweet water.
O Rādhikā, then the army set out toward the city;
for the king was eager to lead Hari away from his camp.
The Blessed Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa descended from the celestial chariot and sat upon a golden throne on a white elephant adorned with ornaments.

(102) Thus ends the eighth [chapter] in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, titled "Description of the wandering through the city of Peyisthāna, the worship, the instruction, the meal, the farewell, and thereafter the arrival in the kingdom of Pāru at evening and the worship there," and so forth.

218. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, [this is] the [pastime] of Anādikṛṣṇa upon the back of an elephant, amidst other elephants.
Then his two parents and his three brothers followed within the interior of the elephant.
Then there were the palanquins and other vehicles for Brahmapriyā and the others;
afterwards, there were the celestial beings who delighted in songs.
At the front, sharp-edged spears and the like, as well as kettledrums and other instruments, were present; military drums were sounded and shouts of victory arose.
The clatter of machines and the loud cries of the Brahmins produced a thunderous roar.
In the watchtowers, at the gate-towers and so forth, in the upper chambers, and among the trees;
on the carriage-roads, on the royal highways, in the houses, and even in the turrets;
on the joyful altars, in the shrines, and on the summits of the fortresses. (4–5)
In the mansions, on the main roads, and in the gardens on all sides,
men and women, seeking knowledge, gathered then to behold Bālakṛṣṇa;
they arrived having taken offerings in their hands and other limbs.
In the city, the circle of ministers worshipped Kṛṣṇa at the gate-tower (gopura). At the crossroads, the wealthy men worshipped; in the gardens, the leaders;
on the streets and in the marketplaces, these [merchants]; and at the crossroads, the common people.

They worshipped Hari with flowers, garments, ornaments, fruits, and so forth; likewise with necklaces of flowers, diamonds, and other gems, as well as with strings of jewels. (9) The immortals and the maidens also worshipped him with unbroken grains and other offerings.
With necklaces of land-lotuses and the like, rings, sugar-candy, and other delicacies—
having thus wandered through the city, the Blessed One then quickly arrived at the palace of the king and partook of a drink of water. (2.219.10–11)
At nightfall, the Blessed One taught the delightful true Dharmas— which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation— to the subjects, beginning with the king.
Indeed, in that place, at that time, and for those specific individuals, the succession of time was intense.
Even that which is undesirable always comes about as a producer of dispassion.
This world is full of many defects; indeed, the virtuous here are free from defects.
They are united with the yoga of the Blessed One and are liberated from the noose of time.
Indeed, by means of my yoga, those who are intent on their own liberation truly come into being.
Having observed that everything is devoid of essence and filled with an abundance of suffering,
a wise person should strive for the sake of their own liberation.
When wealth, wife, son, father, or master has perished,
this deluded world, dragged down by the sense of "mine-ness," undergoes suffering.
Only a virtuous person, and no other, can truly destroy that grief.
Just as two pieces of wood might come together upon a great body of water and,
having met, drift apart again— such is the meeting of embodied beings.
In this way, grandsons, sons, wives, daughters, and kinsmen [are likewise transient].
Truthful and even masters of their own destiny, they are determined to part.
One should not form an attachment there, for separation from them is indeed certain.
Having never been seen before, he has now arrived; once gone, there will be no seeing him again.
Knowing thus that the entire world is of the same nature as the earth,
wise people should conduct themselves in such a way that sorrow does not arise.
Indeed, the suffering born of craving and affection leads from one misery to another, again and again.
When pleasure is attained, pain follows; sorrow and pain arise again and again.
Indeed, pleasure and pain arise for people repeatedly like a wheel.
The body exists as the abode for these two as they revolve.
That suffering shall not arise again; one must proceed thus upon the path.
Śrī Hari, who is without beginning, is the path that destroys all suffering.
He is to be taken as refuge, for I am the medicine at the end of suffering.
But those virtuous ones who do not take refuge in me, the Supreme Lord,
indeed become partakers of suffering and are devoid of happiness;
for they are bound by many snares of affection and by the desire for sense objects.
For those who have not achieved their goal falter, deluded by the mirage of water;
through attachment, everything is crushed like sesame seeds in a press during creation.
Bound by affection, one performs for this [world] actions that result in a burden of sin.
By that, one repeatedly encounters afflictions both here and in the next world.
(28) All embodied beings who are attached to sons, wives, and family are submerged in an ocean of grief; they truly do not possess happiness. (29)
Just as a forest fire that has broken out upon the loss of what is desired, so too does a person burn in vain,
reduced to ashes without any auspicious fruit; indeed,
neither friends nor kinsmen are able to bestow happiness.
Neither enemies nor others are capable of inflicting suffering;
neither wealth nor even the means for its acquisition are capable of bestowing happiness.
Only the wise man, and no other, knows that poverty is the giver of misery.
One who possesses discernment, who is free from attachment, and who is truly my devotee shall indeed be happy.
I am the form of the cow; those who milk me are happy.
I am the cow for the calf, for the cowherd, for the master, and even for the thief.
Just as one who drinks milk receives daily nourishment that bestows happiness, so too shall the one who performs the drinking [of my name] through devotion to me be happy; of this there is no doubt.
Relying upon the intellect, which is discerning, nurturing, and like a mother, [one attains this].
The wise person should acquire happiness so as not to be burdened by affliction in the interim;
through discernment (*viveka*), one attains peace, happiness, and even bliss.
Those who have attained the happiness of discernment transcend dualities and are free from worldly striving.
Neither those things which are beneficial nor those which are harmful ever cause them distress.
But the ignorant, the undiscriminating, the deluded, who are dragged down by their own nature—however much they rejoice, they suffer a hundred times more intensely. (37–38)
Peace born of discernment, accompanied by contentment,

prosperity, abundance, and fortune— these dwell together with Lakshmi in the capable man, not in the lazy one. [The wise man avoids] the fool, the one who has lost his memory, the one possessed by craving, and likewise the one who is envious.
Sorrow enters a person possessed of envy in a thousand ways.
But sorrow never touches one who has taken refuge in Me, who is devoted to the virtuous, discerning, wise, and free from malice and envy.

Grief cannot touch one who is endowed with the existence of the Self, who is devoted to the practice of Brahman, and who frequents the company of the virtuous. Whatever cause might give rise to grief, distress, suffering, and despondency— [that cause is absent in such a person].
One should abandon that from which unrest arises; by doing so, one will become happy.
Whatever is imagined through the sense of "mine" for the sake of one's own self-interest, or whatever effort is exerted for it, immediately results in torment within one's own self.
One who renounces desires here is always filled with happiness;
one who pursues desires and remains full of craving perishes along with those very desires.
The destruction of craving is declared to be the great form of bliss for yogis.
For one who possesses craving and runs hither and thither in this world,
there will surely come great sorrow— just as for a proponent of the selfhood of the body who wishes to lick with his tongue nectar smeared upon the edge of a sword. (46–47)

Non-attainment, separation, and hardship—thus threefold suffering arises for a person who is immersed in sensual desires regarding beloved objects. Indeed, suffering may arise in an instant; therefore, having abandoned desire, one should become happy.
One should indeed loathe all desires; desire born of the mind is death.
Having withdrawn desires and volitions, and having abandoned fear, one becomes happy.
When there is neither longing nor aversion, then one has attained Brahman.

Happiness belongs to one who abandons that craving which is difficult for the foolish to relinquish, which does not grow old even as one grows old, and which is a disease that devours life itself. (5.1) The world is constantly struck down by death and enveloped by old age.
Even when seized by death, one does not know how to accomplish the welfare of one's own self.
For embodied beings, day and night pass in vain without devotion.
Knowing this, one should worship me, Hari, as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (52–53)
As each day passes away, the life-span of living beings is constantly diminished.
Without devotion, the day is rendered fruitless for the embodied soul in every respect.
Driven by excessive craving, the seeker of happiness wanders through the dense thicket of worldly existence.
Indeed, when one's desire remains unfulfilled, Death approaches as a devourer.
Having found one who is searching for pleasure, who is attached to it, and whose mind is distracted by things far away—just as a snake seizes a frog—Death swallows him and departs. (55–56)
One should perform what is beneficial this very day; the wasting of time brings no profit.
Death will come and depart while one's tasks are yet unfinished.
Therefore, one should today diligently carry out one’s own purpose with promptness and heedfulness.
Time does not perceive that "this work of mine is incomplete";
no one at all knows when death will come for whom.
Therefore, a wise person should first perform the work intended for liberation.
From childhood indeed, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, must be worshipped;
when Kṛṣṇa is pleased, there shall be eternal happiness and stainless fame.
[He who is] possessed by delusion and deeply immersed in wealth, wife, sons, and fields—
Death will seize one who is rich in fields, cattle, and other possessions while they are asleep.
Pursuing him as he runs—insatiable, striving for the sake of desire, and possessed of great speed—death indeed takes him and departs. (61–62)
"I shall perform the primary task tomorrow, and another after that, and yet another after that.
While he is thinking thus, Kṛtānta (Death) will bring him near.
He has not obtained the fruit of the undertakings begun, being attached instead to other actions.
Yama takes away and departs with the one who experiences the fruits of their own deeds.
Whether it be a king or a pauper, a wise man, a servant, or one who is helpless—even if protected in every way, death takes them away and departs. (64–65)
Seeing death, old age, infirmity, dependence, humiliation, disease, and incapacity within this body, the wise man should worship Hari.
One is born as an indeterminate child, and likewise, death is indeterminate.
Death will surely come unexpectedly; having reflected upon this, one should worship Hari.
For embodied beings, attachment to sense objects is indeed the seat of death, while detachment is like a great forest that bestows peace upon yogis.
The noose-like rope of the senses, rich with sense-objects, is the constant mode of existence for embodied beings;
having severed that, the wise man should take refuge at the feet of Śrī Hari.
No warrior can conquer the approaching river of death.
The warrior of truth conquers through this; in Hari, who is Truth, immortality resides.
Truth is indeed declared to be Brahman; one should become devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Established in the vow of truth and relying upon the yoga of truth, [one attains liberation].
One who delights in the company of the virtuous shall conquer death through true yoga;
having conquered the death that is delusion, one attains immortality through association with the good.
One who seeks the goal of the righteous, the Supreme Lord, and service, becomes established in the Self.
Having crossed over death, he attains the nectar of great bliss and rejoices.

(73) Established in the sacrifice of the virtuous, self-controlled, and having found delight in the sacrifice to Brahman, one who is immersed in the offering to the Supreme Brahman indeed attains the Great Liberation. (74)
He with whom Kṛṣṇa is always pleased, who possesses the grace of the saintly, and whose parents shower compassion upon him—he indeed shall attain everything.
Knowledge is his eye, the divine vision; the vow of Brahman is his supreme austerity.
Service to the virtuous is the supreme merit; renunciation is eternal happiness.
(76) For one who lives by the Self, who abides in the Supreme Lord, who is free from passion and liberated—what need is there for any other savior? (77)
Wealth is divine; indeed, the virtuous are divine jewels; Hari himself is the jewel.
For one whose engagement is devotion to Him, what need is there for any other means?
One who possesses nothing sleeps happily, and likewise wakes up happily.
Having attained Kṛṣṇa—who is blissful, wholesome, and auspicious—one rejoices as one who is truly happy.
He for whom there is no possession other than Hari is indeed a pauper (akiñcana);
that state of absolute poverty is the supreme happiness, transcending even the three worlds.
Between poverty and sovereignty, there exists a great difference:
one who possesses a kingdom is constantly anxious, whereas one who is destitute is free from agitation.
He has no fear of fire or death, nor even of thieves or calamities.
Neither from an enemy nor from the force of time does fear arise for him.
Śiva and the other gods praise one who is renounced, a devotee of the Lord, whose body and home are a refuge for Hari, who is intent on serving the virtuous, and who is peaceful. (82–83)
Without renunciation one does not attain happiness; without renunciation one does not find Brahman;
without renunciation one does not abide free from fear; having attained renunciation, one becomes happy.
(84) For one who is drawn by worldly striving and is wretched, delusion enters deeply.
For great calamities come upon one who is negligent and has abandoned the bounds of propriety.
The best medicine to destroy them is the service of the virtuous;
by association with them, the attainment of knowledge occurs and the dissolution of worldly desires takes place.
May there be a stream of affection for me, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign, who is full of eternal bliss;
through my yoga, may my devotee become happy and full of eternal bliss—this is the task that should be performed by men here on earth. (87)
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, the Lord Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, gave this mantra—
“Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā”— to all the men and to all the women as well. (88–89)
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge forever"— in this way, He granted refuge to all from the fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and the wicked-hearted. (2.219.90)
"Endowed with the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika," [he said].
Thus he then bestowed this protective mantra upon the people:
"I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband.
In this way, indeed, Hari bestowed upon her the mantra of the nature of Brahman:
"Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is truly my eternal husband."
"May he be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian.
Hari himself bestowed upon her the mantra for self-surrender:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Master."
Thus he caused [the mantra] to be heard as an act of salutation and worship:

"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhasvāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge.
Thus the Lord himself bestowed his own mantras.
Then the subjects, having bowed to Hari, worshipped him with reverence.

Queen Śrī Satīśanṛpa worshipped the Supreme Lord; and the three daughters of King Śrī Satīśanṛpa, while still young women, likewise worshipped him. Having obtained Hari as their beloved and the object of their hearts' desire, they placed garlands around his neck. ||99||
Having offered the garland of choice, they presented their own self-offering.
Hari, taking their hands, became their lord;
the queen and the king rejoiced, and the maidens felt their purpose fulfilled.
The king celebrated that festival and bestowed many kinds of wedding gifts; then he performed the *ārārtrika* ceremony and provided a feast.

The monkey rested during the night, and the three daughters served him.

When Hari had completed his daily rites and performed his worship, the king indeed approached him;
the monarch then caused milk to be drunk by all of them with ease.

Just then,
the royal sage Tretākarkaśa, accompanied by the sages Karṇaphāla and Ṛṣi,

The king granted him leave and honored him with his army.
