they offered gold coins, offered necklaces, and presented excellent flowers; they performed prostrations, beheld him, gave gifts, and carried out worship. (17–18)
The songs of the immortals resounded throughout the sky,
and celestial women, endowed with divine splendor, offered praise to Acyuta.
The leaders, the merchants, and the subjects also [honored] the Supreme Lord.
They worshipped [him] at various places with all kinds of jewels and meditative visualizations.
(2.220.20) Having thus made a grand procession through the city of Phāṅkalāśī, the king arrived at the royal palace; there he worshipped the Supreme Lord. (21)
With joy, Karṇaphāla Ṛṣi seated the Lord upon a beautiful golden throne and honored Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme.
Then the Queen [of Karṇaphāla] applied a tilaka of saffron and unbroken grains to Kṛṣṇa.
With saffron, she fashioned a necklace and placed it around his neck.
(23) Then seven young maidens, beholding the enchanting Kṛṣṇa and determining in their hearts that he was their beloved, chose him as their husband. (24)
At their mother’s command, they joyfully placed the garlands of choice around Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
they performed the *ārārtrika* ceremony and repeatedly exclaimed, "They have been offered!
The queen and the king were pleased, and the maidens felt they had fulfilled their purpose.
"O Rādhikā, Mādhava, who was to be attained in liberation, has now been attained here.
Thus the king celebrated with festivals of dance, song, and other arts during that day;
and Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa gave his instruction.
The fruit of attaining a human body is the happiness of Lord Hari;
following devotion comes great liberation, and service to the virtuous is the supreme fruit.
It also consists of a state free from attachment and aversion, and a constant relish for the narrations of Kṛṣṇa.
That person who possesses both forbearance and discernment shall be happy.
Freedom from passion is the highest happiness; the absence of hatred brings peace.
One who is free from resentment and endowed with forgiveness sleeps happily, even when despondent. (2.220.30)
He who should obtain all desires and he who should renounce all desires—of these two, the renouncer finds great happiness, but not the one who possesses them all.
There is no end to desires; there is neither a first nor a last.
One should achieve happiness through the destruction of craving, thinking, "It will pass away.
No one reaches the end of desire, even when it has been enjoyed and then abandoned; no one reaches the end of accumulated wealth either. (3.2–3.3)
Having abandoned all undertakings, a person attains happiness.
Attachment arises for one who possesses nothing, but once wealth is acquired, it increases further.
Upon the loss of what has been gained, there is either death or constant grieving.
What indeed could be more painful than this: that what has been gained is not kept?
For there is no satisfaction in what is acquired; rather, one seeks even more.
One who is insatiable here becomes truly miserable again and again. (35–36)

The loss of wealth brings greater suffering than all else, as does the contempt shown by everyone; whatever fraction of happiness exists in wealth is the progenitor of a thousand sorrows. Robbers strike down the wealthy man, and others carry him off.
Therefore, having abandoned hope, one should take refuge in Mādhava.
One should also resort to world-weariness, renunciation, contentment, peace, forgiveness, self-control, and satisfaction;
thus, indeed, one shall always be happy in this world.

Having abandoned desire, greed, thirst, longing, and even miserliness, a person in this world may become happy, just like one who is liberated. Long ago, the blessed Nārada questioned his own inner light.
"How, O Brahmin, do you abide in that happiness where there is no sorrow?
Whenever I look at you, I see you indeed in happiness;
I have never seen you in grief. Tell me, what is the cause of this?"
His own light said to him: "Listen, O wise one, to my thought:
I always see him as happy; what indeed is his happiness?
What is his means [thereto], and how does he remain so happy? (43)
I asked the bull, as he was pulling the cart, "How are you happy?
He replied to me, "I have no concern at all regarding food, clothing, house, and so forth;
for that cart is drawn by a farmer who remains under the power of my strength."
Thus, I reflect upon the threefold purpose, but not in every respect;
therefore, I am always happy with food, clothing, houses, and so forth.
[The King] asked the one who eats at the sacrificial session: "How do you live happily?"
And he said: "This wealthy man earns wealth for the sake of providing food for me;
another person here constantly cooks and gives it to me.
Therefore, I have no concern whatsoever regarding money, food, or cooking. (47–48)
Having reflected on that, I shall not act in vain;
for I asked the parrot in the forest, "Why do you rejoice in the woods?
and he replied to me, "I have no bonds; I roam wherever I please. (49)
Whether in a nest or in the hollow of a tree, I sleep according to my desire. Having flown up and gone to the forest, I eat fruits and the like.
I have no anxiety regarding accumulation, nor do I have any concern for protection.
"I have no concern for a house or the like, nor do I have a family;
therefore, free from anxiety, I always rejoice in happiness. Having reflected on this, I too have abandoned her, and I am now without attachment."
Then, being asked, "How do you appear so happy, O Great Lion?
he replied: "Having obtained food by the turn of fate after three days had passed, I sleep thinking, 'No one in the forest shall be my slayer.'"
Having reflected upon that, I have abandoned all fear of time and other such causes;
therefore, I wander about happy and fearless, and even sleep in peace.
The sages who have taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman live in happiness.
Knowing that these states pertaining to living beings— decline, growth, destruction, and birth—
do not affect me, I always move about happy. [I know] that unions end in separation and accumulations end in decay.
Knowing that those who have arisen are likewise destined for destruction, I neither grieve nor rejoice;
having abandoned these three— sleep pervading the bed, weeping stained by loss,
and joy born of acquisition— I am always happy.
"Satī was questioned by me regarding how she could find happiness while dependent on another.
She said to me: 'I have indeed made firm my obedience to the command of my lord;
for me there is no other duty, and he alone is favorable to me.'"
Therefore, great happiness is experienced by me in my very mistress alone;
having reflected upon that, I have performed every kind of the most excellent vow of devotion to my husband toward the Supreme Lord, who is favorable to me. (61)
I have offered myself to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
His will is indeed my fortune; all thought regarding my welfare is entrusted to Hari.
And especially by Him, the very refuge of bliss, am I made happy.
Having heard this, Nārada also adopted such a state;
wandering without support in the world, the sage became ever blissful.
Likewise, the Lord Sanatkumāra is his own self-luminosity.
Lomaśa, Ṛṣi, as well as Śambhu—they are indeed eternally happy.
For those who have their senses and their objects under control, and who have the powers and the elements under control. (65–66)
Those for whom wonders and supernatural powers are indeed under control;
those for whom time, karma, inherent nature, and illusion are always under control;
those for whom the self is indeed under control—these are they who are under the control of the Supreme Self.
They are always happy, whether in this created world or in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman).
Satī, Ramā, the beloveds of Brahmā, and likewise the liberated ones (muktas) are of such a nature;
they are eternally happy because they have offered their very selves for the sake of Hari.
"Therefore, all should become subject to Hari alone, not following others. Hari, who possesses eternal bliss, makes his servants happy.
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One then gave them the mantras.
The king ceased [his activities] and worshipped Rādhikā with great joy.
At that moment, the ruler of the Cilīrāṣṭra kingdom, the monarch named Āṇḍajara, arrived there by celestial chariot for the purpose of making a request.
Accompanied by his mantra and the fire that draws [all things] toward him, we bow down with great devotion.
Having received a welcome and due honor, the king requested Hari:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, purify my city which formerly stood within."
"So be it," Hari replied; he quickly became ready for action.
And King Tretākarkaśa gave him leave and wedding gifts, and with his army, he paid honor to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Hari, together with his family, was in a celestial chariot in the sky;
likewise, he was accompanied by Mantra, Agni, Karṣi, and his caravan.
And King Cāṇḍajarābha, who had previously offered a welcome, [was there].
Then he went quickly to that kingdom and first mobilized his army.
At that moment, Hari arrived, riding upon a magnificent celestial chariot;
seeing him, the subjects cried out, "Victory to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!"

They raised shouts of joy, cries of victory, and the sound of trumpets. Following the path shown by the king, Mādhava, together with the sage, [entered] his own [palace] in the garden situated within the city. 79.
Hearing the sounds of "Welcome! being uttered, he caused the celestial chariot to descend.
Then Śrī Hari quickly came out from the front of the chariot;
there, women with disheveled hair greeted the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, with cries of joy. (2.220.80–81)
With words such as "May you live long! and with thoughts of "Protect us, protect us!", they honored Acyuta from their hearts, saying, "Grant us happiness.
First, the king performed worship with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and flowers.
The queen also performed worship, and the subjects bowed with devotion.
Then the king seated Bālakṛṣṇa upon a great elephant accompanied by the golden Ambālikā, as well as others upon chariots and other vehicles.
Then the king, accompanied by his army, led them all— honored with clusters of necklaces— to his own city, which was adorned within and without,
so that they might be paraded along the royal highway amidst the sounds of musical instruments, proclamations, and songs.
Then the principal merchants worshipped Kṛṣṇa at the city gate;
likewise, the wealthy worshipped him at the crossroads and in the marketplaces, while the female vendors and women, overflowing with emotion, did so at the entrances of the streets. (86–87)
They worshipped the Supreme Soul with necklaces, sandalwood paste, and saffron;
with unbroken grains and other offerings, coconuts and other fruits, and sugar and other sweets.
Having beheld and fully worshipped Mādhava, they became fulfilled in their purpose.
Then the king led Kṛṣṇa to his own spacious palace.
He then performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and placed a crown upon His head;
at that time, the king also gave Him necklaces of gold and jewels around His neck.
Having offered worship, she drank the nectar of his feet;
then, saying "I am fulfilled," the queen caused the worship to be performed.
She placed a plate of gold coins at the feet of Śrī Hari.
She worshipped the Supreme Lord with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, by her mother’s command, Mālikā took those four maidens—who were young women filled with devotion—and held them in her heart. (92–93)
Delighted, they placed their husband around the neck of Hari according to the rite of offering;
having attained their goal and accomplished their purpose, they became inspired by good fortune.
And the king was exceedingly pleased and caused a great festival to be held.

Then Hari instructed Rādhā regarding the subjects at night. (95) Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure from the City of Phānkalāśī on the Morning of the Second Day of the Dark Fortnight of Āśvina, the Wandering, the Worship, the Meal, the Instruction, the Farewell, and After Midday the Journey to the City of Aṇḍajarānṛpa, and the Wandering and Worship in the City of Antaḥprāga," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.
← Chapter 220: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 221 [Author: Chapter 222 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari, established in his own nature and seated upon a golden lion-throne, imparted instruction that brings great benefit to the subjects known as the Cillīs.
Wisdom is the foundation of living beings; wisdom is considered the bringer of liberation.
Having attained a human body, one may reach Hari through wisdom.
Wisdom is the supreme good and pure; wisdom bestows the bliss of heaven.
Through wisdom one attains wealth, and the wise person is indeed always happy.
(3) In this world, a man endowed with hands and feet is considered meritorious;
having understood through his two hands and through wisdom, he should serve the virtuous lord. (4)
One should never have a mind attached to anything else, having abandoned the Supreme Lord.
Some indeed become exceedingly happy, while others are intensely miserable.
In this world, absolute happiness never occurs for anyone, anywhere.
Having attained great wealth, people desire supreme sovereignty;
from that, they desire divinity, and then the state of being worshiped by Indra and the other gods.
They desire the status of Brahmā and the nature of Īśvara, but they never desire liberation at all. (6–7)
Therefore, wisdom endowed with discernment becomes the giver of liberation;
through wisdom, liberation is attained, as well as the permanent state in the world of Brahman.
"Wisdom is Brahman"—this very truth is established even within the heart.

The supreme, eternal Brahman is to be constantly worshipped. For one who is devoted to the essence of Brahman, no other desire ever arises, whether through contact, sight, or even hearing of Brahman. (2.221.10)
Through service and the practice of meditation, one becomes intent upon the essence of Brahman;
without that, there can be no satisfaction anywhere else, even upon obtaining other pleasant things.
Indeed, thirst is not quenched by water, and it only flares up further through worldly enjoyments.
By means of wisdom, that [thirst] is indeed destroyed along with its root; of this there is no doubt.
Having severed the karma born of desire and having fully restrained the senses, one should abide in the nature of the Self; for such a person, thirst perishes.
Not eating, not touching, not seeing, as well as not tasting,
not hearing, not smelling, and not feeling— such a discipline,
performed with wisdom, becomes the supreme good. (14)
Embodied beings, though possessing water, strength, and wealth, become slaves to craving and suffer through slaughter and imprisonment.
They weep, yet they take delight; they rejoice, and they laugh as well. (15–16)
Thus, people possessed of great strength, having acquired knowledge and captivated the mind,
resort to a loathsome, miserable, and base way of life;
they exert themselves, they prosper, they fall, and they weep.
Neither a frog, nor a boar, nor a dog desires to abandon its own body;
even a *puṣkasa*, a *caṇḍāla*, or a bound insect, being highly content with its own womb, wishes to remain within that form through the power of *māyā*. (18–19)
Having seen those who are maimed, those whose wings are broken, those with withered arms, and even those afflicted by leprosy,
one who is healthy does not resort to Hari at all, being struck down by Māyā. Therefore, having reflected with the mind and reached a conclusion through wisdom—
One should worship me, the Supreme Self, having abandoned attachment and delusion.

Desiring to attain the highest good, one should perform meditation, purification, recitation, worship, service to elders, parents, and others, as well as service to the virtuous and devotion to me. (21–22)
While one possesses a kingdom and domestic prosperity,
one should perform meritorious deeds at an auspicious constellation, during a holy time, on a favorable lunar day, and at a propitious moment.
Those of virtuous character strive for merit through sacrifices, charity, and other such acts.
Their wisdom shines forth quickly through union with the Supreme Brahman.
By means of that wisdom, they go to my supreme abode, which is eternal bliss—even those who were born under inauspicious stars, among the Asuras, or at ill-fated moments. (24–25)
Devoid of wisdom and hating sacred rites, they fall into an asuric womb;
they go to the burrows of jackals and dogs, and for them no higher good exists.
One who is contented, vigilant, and fond of sacrifice, charity, and austerity—
One devoted to the service of the virtuous and relying on wisdom attains the supreme goal.
(27) Those who are dear to the gods, hospitable to guests, devoted to servants, and fond of the virtuous—having dedicated all their possessions for the sake of Hari—they go to the supreme goal. (28)

Those who serve the virtuous go from festival to festival, from joy to joy again and again, and from heaven to a higher heaven; whereas the wicked, the deceitful, the rogues, the deceivers, and those who are sinful— [The verse continues: ...go from misery to misery, from sorrow to sorrow again and again, and from hell to a lower hell. Thus, O King, is the fruit of association with the virtuous and the wicked. (30) Therefore, O King, you should always associate with the virtuous and avoid the wicked. For by associating with the virtuous, one attains supreme bliss. (31) Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Virtuous," in the *Sādhucaritramahodadhi*, a work concerning the conduct of the virtuous, composed by Śrī Vāsudeva. (32) [Chapter 33 begins: Then, having heard these words of the sage, the king, filled with great wonder, spoke again to the sage with palms joined in reverence. (1) "O holy one, tell me once more in detail about the nature of the virtuous, as well as the characteristics of the wicked. (2) The sage said: "O King, listen attentively; I shall describe the characteristics of the virtuous and the wicked. By knowing their true nature, one may avoid the wicked and serve the virtuous. (3) The virtuous are those who are compassionate toward all beings, free from malice, devoted to truth, and firm in their vows. (4) They are self-controlled, pure, and devoted to the service of the gods and the twice-born; they are ever intent on the welfare of others and are free from envy. (5) They are grateful, forbearing, and wise; they do not abandon dharma even for the sake of their life. They are contented, humble, and always engaged in the performance of righteous deeds. (6) They are free from greed, anger, and pride; they are truthful and possess great fortitude. They are devoted to the worship of Śiva and Viṣṇu, and are always intent on the practice of yoga. (7) They are devoted to the service of the guru and the elders, and are always engaged in the study of the Vedas. They are free from hypocrisy and deceit, and are always intent on the welfare of all creatures. (8) Such are the characteristics of the virtuous; now hear the characteristics of the wicked. The wicked are those who are cruel, deceitful, and full of malice, who delight in causing harm to others and are devoid of compassion. (9) They are greedy, prone to anger, and arrogant; they are liars and breakers of their own vows. They are intent on the destruction of dharma and are always engaged in sinful acts. (10) They are envious, ungrateful, and fickle; they are devoid of shame and always speak harsh words. They are addicted to vice and are never satisfied; they are always intent on the acquisition of wealth through unjust means. (11) They are hostile toward the gods and the twice-born, and are always engaged in the pursuit of sensual pleasures. They are devoid of faith and are always intent on the deception of others. (12) Such are the characteristics of the wicked; therefore, one should avoid them at all times. One should always serve the virtuous, for by serving the virtuous, one attains the highest state. (13) Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Virtuous and the Wicked," in the *Sādhucaritramahodadhi*, a work concerning the conduct of the virtuous, composed by Śrī Vāsudeva. (14)
Possessed by their own lack of purpose, they enter into sinful deeds;
and having again created defilement, they come to exist in a world of suffering. From famine to famine, from affliction to affliction, they wander thus again and again.
From fear they go to fear, and from agitation to further agitation;
from death to death again go those who are poor and performers of evil deeds.
They are like husks among grains of rice, or like gadflies among birds.
Such as they are among men, devoid of righteous deeds,
they are roasted like grains of grain in the fire of the womb by the power of time.
Without wisdom, they do not attain the supreme good by any means whatsoever.
Agitated, they run forth, facing toward the forest of saṃsāra;
yet karma, having become their follower, runs after them from there to seize them.
It does not let them go, whether they are asleep, in deep sleep, in solitude, or even while awake.
Like a shadow, it never leaves him once it has clung to him.
Seeing him dragged by karma, dependent on others, and enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), Great Time (Mahākāla) drags him away into the ocean of suffering.
Time bestows upon the doer the fruit of his own actions,
just as flowers and fruits appear in trees through time;
so too, previously performed karma arises and does not bypass its fruition.
And with the remainder of what was performed by oneself, one enters the bed of the womb. As a child, a youth, and an old man, one experiences the fruit of that [action].
For one purified by the fire of wisdom, there is long-lasting and infinite happiness. (2.221.40)
For the virtuous who have shaken off evil through wisdom, whose passion and hatred have perished,
and who are devoted to the Supreme Lord, imperishable happiness is attained.
Whatever a person of wisdom does, all that leads not to bondage.
For one who is united with me through wisdom, no action exists.
Just as the track of fish in water or of birds in the sky is not seen,
so too the action of a devotee who knows me is not perceived.
This is the goal of those who possess knowledge, having the abode of Brahman as their supreme refuge;
it is to be attained through virtuous wisdom by men who desire liberation.
Indeed, I dwell within as the inner self, hidden in all beings.
Indeed, it is attainable only through supreme wisdom that perceives reality.
Having received nourishment from my grace and having attained union with me through my good deeds, one who applies himself to me, the Lord of the self, becomes equal to Brahman. 45–46.
And by means of the serenity of his mind, having offered his heart to me,
he remains with a stainless self, a tranquil self, and a self dedicated [to me].
Abiding in me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme, he enjoys infinite bliss.
One of steady conduct attains infinite and boundless bliss.
Through all means, one should always conquer great craving, greed, and anger;
then indeed, the knowledge produced by wisdom attains purity.
Self-restraint alone is the supreme bull (the best path) whose nature is liberation.
By means of that self, one should always abide within the Self—in Me, Nārāyaṇa.
For one who conducts oneself in this way, liberation is held in the palm of the hand.
"Abiding in his heart, I myself shall indeed become the milker of liberation for him.
Having thus instructed [him], the Lord Kāmbhareya, the Great Master,
gave mantras to the subjects, and the subjects performed the worship of Hari.
The subjects presented various articles, garments, and ornaments;
they gave gold and silver to Śrī Hari.
Then, during the night, the king indeed feasted Mādhava.
He fed his family, the great sages, and the maidens.
Then Keśava attained rest and fell asleep;
those maidens served their own beloved, the Supreme Lord.
Then Hari was awakened by the sounds of morning musical instruments, by songs, auspicious chants, and by the Vedic recitations of the Brahmins.
Having performed his morning rites, having offered worship, and having consumed milk and fruit, he arose.
Honored by the king throughout the night, he sat upon a golden lion-throne (57).
The king then caused other worthy men to drink the milk.
At that time, the subjects arrived for the purpose of worship and to behold him (58).
Then, during the mantra-ritual for attracting [wealth], Kṛṣṇa bestowed riches and other gifts.
And the brother of King Aṇḍaja-rāja arrived, bowing to Hari;
prostrating himself like a staff, he spoke of his own most beautiful city. (59)
To purify the limbs of his ministers, the king named Bālyarajas said,
"May Hari be so," and the Lord, honored by Cāṇḍaja and Rāma,
was joined with them through a parting gift and a dowry.
Endowed with great majesty, he quickly ascended the celestial chariot;
then the king and his younger brother departed together through the sky by means of that chariot.
Musical instruments were sounded repeatedly as they played.
Then the celestial chariot of Hari spread out in the sky before him;
the king’s chariot likewise proceeded with great speed ahead,
toward the city of Mantriṇāga, following the path of the ocean.
An army had already been stationed there for the purpose of welcoming them.
Upon seeing that celestial chariot, which was exceedingly brilliant and equal to the sun,
the men welcomed it with banners, small flags, and other such ornaments.
The king first descended from the celestial chariot of Hari;
then he descended into the garden near the assembly of his ministers.
There, the queen stood before him and paid him due honor.
Having bowed to Hari seated in the celestial chariot, she worshipped him with garlands, flowers, unbroken grains, and sandalwood paste; having washed his feet, she drank the water from them.
Having led Hari to the royal palace, the sovereign lady caused him to dwell there.
Then one young maiden, being virtuous, performed the *ārārtrika* rite;
she placed a garland of choice offerings upon the neck of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. At that time, the king caused a great festival to be held.
Thereafter, he gave food to Bālakṛṣṇa and the others; then, having seated him upon a horse-chariot, he paraded him through the city. The subjects joyfully honored the Lord, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

At midday, Hari indeed rested, and then the king himself performed the massaging of Bālakṛṣṇa’s feet. In the evening, having ascended the celestial chariot, he wandered through the sky above the ocean.
Then, on the evening of the third day,
Rāyasomanabhūpati, the lord of the kingdom of Pātragonaya,
arrived to take Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa to his own country in order to purify it. (74)
After sporting about, Hari returned to his abode;
there the king bowed to him and prayed to the Supreme Lord for wealth and happiness.
Hari, having drunk water from the celestial chariot, said, "So be it."
Accompanied by his entire caravan, he quickly mounted [the chariot] and then became ready to go to the city of Vāyumāna. With joy, the king bestowed upon him leave-taking, honors, and wedding gifts.
Awakened by the sound of the lute, Kṛṣṇa urged the celestial chariot forward;
hearing the various musical instruments being played, the Blessed One himself arrived at the divine city, Vāyumānā, which was most beautiful.
Seeing the beautiful celestial chariot situated on the riverbank, Kṛṣṇa,
following the path shown by the king, brought it down onto the river's edge.
Then musical instruments were played, and a grand welcome was offered in many ways.
The subjects greatly increased his prosperity with offerings of flowers, unbroken grains, and other gifts.
(81) Then Hari descended from the celestial chariot and sat down upon a golden throne;
the king himself worshipped him with a garland of flowers. (82)
With sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and the like, as well as with sprinklings of fragrant liquids,
the queen worshipped him with affection and performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Having seated the king upon an elephant, she caused him to be paraded through the city.
The leaders worshipped Śrī Hari there at the city gate;

likewise, the wealthy merchants worshipped him on the main highway; the women worshipped him at the openings of the streets, and the local residents worshipped him in the vicinity of their homes. 84–85.
The women worshipped the Lord of Śrī with songs and sang hymns of praise.
Having thus paraded Hari through his own city,
the king brought Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to his palace at night.
The queen also performed the *ārārtrika* rite and honored [the deity] with various offerings.
(87) Then the three maidens placed the bridegroom’s garland around the neck of Hari;
having obtained their husband as the lord of their lives, those auspicious women felt they had accomplished all that was to be done. (88)
O Rādhikā, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was present;
at that time, during the night, He partook of meaningful meals together with His companions.
On the third night of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, He attained rest.
And the three maidens served their own lord with great devotion.
In the morning, Hari woke from sleep to auspicious sounds:
the resonance of musical instruments, songs, Vedic mantras, and hymns of praise.
Having performed his morning ablutions and daily rites amidst the panegyric verses and poetry of the bards, heralds, and minstrels, Kṛṣṇa paid homage to his own parents;
on the fourth day, he partook of milk and other refreshments right at dawn.
The subjects indeed came early in the morning for the purpose of worshipping the Lord of Lords.
First the king worshipped him, and then the subjects honored the Imperishable One.
Thereafter, Hari gave wealth and riches to the young and eminent brahmin.
King Rāyasoma and the young brahmin sage likewise became supremely satisfied; the subjects also became contented. Then Hari, the benefactor of Rādhikā, gave instruction at that time.

"Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the avatāras. (96) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, [is described] the instruction in the city of Āntaḥprāgsthāna, the meal, resting at night, and on the morning of the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the departure for the kingdom of King Bālyarajas.

Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-One: Description of the Ministers’ Tour of the City of Aṅga, their Worship, Feasting, Farewell Gifts, and Dower; and the Journey to the Kingdom of King Rāyasoma, as well as the Welcome, Tour, Worship, Feasting, and Night’s Rest in the City of Vāyumāna. *Śrī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga), Chapter 222.
[Author: Chapter 223.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa instructed his subjects as follows.
Early in the morning, in the vast royal palace,
the benevolent lord, King Rāyasomana, listened together with his family;
thousands of men, women, and leading citizens also listened.
Renunciation must always be practiced, as well as the relinquishing of active worldly duties.
One who thus renounces attains freedom from the qualities of nature (nirguṇya), which is the means to liberation.
For one whose action is offered in renunciation, that action shall not yield fruit.
Having completely abandoned all persistence, one should always be free from passion.
By means of that, the sorrowless Supreme Brahman shall abide in me, which is great bliss.
The wise man, unattached amidst attachments, should conquer the unconquered mind.
Whatever is perceived by the senses should be abandoned, not grasped as a reality;
having indeed restrained the mind and the vital breaths, one should fix them upon the Supreme Self.
Through such concentration, there shall indeed be eternal bliss, which is liberation.
Indeed, bliss is to be attained from Brahman by means of the offering unto Brahman in every way.
(7) Truth is always to be grasped as Brahman, and falsehood must certainly be abandoned.
Falsehood is said to be darkness; it bestows blindness and leads one into a pit. (8)

For one bound by the rope of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a fall into the pit is inevitable; for one free from impressions and satisfied, it is taught that there is the light which bestows the abode.
Having firmly taken hold of that light, one should strive for the destruction of suffering.
For the constant destruction of darkness, one should rely on association with the virtuous and other such means.
(2.222.10) But he who does not tremble at physical or even mental sufferings—he, being united with me, knows true happiness; he alone is a traveler upon my path. (11)
Where there is suffering, that is hell; but happiness is the supreme state.
For one who has abandoned the undertaking of suffering, heaven is not difficult to attain.
Having burned away defects through the vow of Brahman, one shall conquer the supreme state.
He who practices the stage of liberation with a liberated intellect is dear to Hari;
having offered everything into Hari, that person attains the world of Brahmā.
The virtuous who are devotees of Brahman should be served; by that, the attainment of Brahman is produced.
Being devoted to right conduct and intent upon devotion to me, even householders must always maintain auspicious conduct for their own welfare.
Purity must be practiced as an essential duty, as well as the worship of the gods. (15)
One should also perform the libation for the ancestors (tarpaṇa) as well as honor the elderly.
One should always worship the Sun at the time of the twilights and remember Hari.
Being pure, one should take food and should not revile human beings or others.

One should always perform circumambulation around a temple, a guru, a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a bull, a crossroads, a righteous person, and a divine being. Furthermore, one should protect guests and servants by providing them with food and other necessities.
If one is capable, one should provide assistance to those who are helpless.
Eating either twice or once a day, but not in between,
he is declared to be one who observes the fast and is always happy.
One should be a giver during a sacrifice and a donor during the fertile season, but not otherwise.
Thus, being self-controlled and a celibate student, one is always auspicious.
Indeed, that which is consumed by the gods is nectar; likewise, nectar is considered to be wholesome.
He who accepts that which is consistent with the fivefold path is like a god among men and is happy.
The virtuous, moreover, worship the grace of the gods which bestows long life;
indeed, the virtuous are to be worshipped by one who desires their favor.
Service to the guru must be performed, as must the act of salutation.
For by honoring the gurus, one is indeed endowed with long life, fame, and prosperity.
Among all sacred fords, the gurus are the sacred ford; among all pure things, the gurus are the pure.
That which has been prepared by the learned is praiseworthy; that cow’s tail is always purifying.
Indeed, one should constantly serve a virtuous teacher upon seeing or touching him.
For the head, hair, and body hairs of a virtuous man are truly purifying. (25–26)
The dust from the feet of the virtuous bestows liberation and destroys sin;
the touch of the holy is meritorious, and their eyes are always considered auspicious.
Indeed, the ears of the holy are meritorious, and their nose possesses a sacred fragrance.
The forehead of the virtuous is indeed meritorious, and the cheeks and jaw are likewise meritorious. (28) The temples are in every way meritorious, and their smile is meritorious and captivating.
Their teeth, tongue, and lips are givers of merit and purifiers for the virtuous. (29)
The throat is meritorious, as is the sound; the speech is the meritorious Sarasvatī.
Indeed, the discourse of the virtuous is meritorious, and association with the holy bestows merit.
The shoulders are meritorious, as are the arms and hands, along with the fingers and nails.
The nails and the lines are meritorious, and likewise the forearm bestows merit. (3.1) The elbow and the wrist are always meritorious for the virtuous;
the palm of the hand always bestows merit, and the chest brings about merit. (3.2)
The breasts are always meritorious; the navel is meritorious and purifying. The abdomen is also merit-bestowing, and the waist is the most meritorious part for the virtuous.
The private region is well-purifying, and the hips are always purifying.
The two hips are purifying, and the two thighs are likewise purifying;
the sense organs are purifying, and the two knees are always purifying; the two shanks bring about purification, and the two ankles are likewise purifying. (34–35)
The soles of the feet, the toes, and the nails are purifying;
the skin, flesh, blood, and likewise the divine skeletal framework,
as well as the marrow, fat, and lymph— these constituent elements (dhātus) are purifying for the virtuous.
Like Śrī Hari, the company of saintly persons is purifying for all.
(37) There are three kinds of sons of the Lord who are as purifying as the Lord himself: the saintly, those initiated in Vedic rites, and householders. (38)
Thus, those three sons born of the lineage were the most excellent purifiers;
the fourth was also a purifier, endowed with devotion to the Lord.
They were all fully possessed of initiation, ritual action, devotion, and knowledge.
Those holy ones are equal to Śrī Hari; they are considered the purifiers of the worlds.
Their grace removes sin, and their water is superior even to the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Service to them all destroys sin; offering to them is the same as offering to Brahman.
But whatever trees and such the virtuous touch,
even those trees become divine in this world, bestowing liberation and destroying sin.
Whatever garment— whether made of cotton or wool— is worn by the virtuous, [it likewise becomes sacred].
Silk is of the nature of the tree’s bark; it is divine and always purifying.
(43) Whether a beast, a bird, or any other person who has been touched by a holy man, he indeed quickly becomes divine—a mundane body that has transcended the world. (44)
That which is impure becomes pure through contact with a holy person;
even sin or greater evil is purified by the touch of a saint.
Whatever is worn upon the body by a holy person is pure; of this there is no doubt.
Water becomes a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha) as soon as it is used by a virtuous person for their service.
Likewise, the earth becomes exceedingly sanctified when served by the righteous.
Furthermore, leaves, flowers, fruits, water, or whatever else may be eaten or worn [by them] becomes pure.
Whatever is indeed obtained through association with the virtuous is considered pure;
one who always serves the virtuous is pure, for the virtuous woman is a divine body of Hari. A vehicle or a seat that has been used by the virtuous is also to be called pure.
Worshiping holy men morning and evening bestows heaven and liberation.
Service to the virtuous is the supreme dharma; service to the virtuous is the highest wealth;
service to the virtuous is the ultimate desire; and even liberation comes from serving the virtuous.
The heart of those of virtuous conduct attains goodness in every way;
the accumulated substance of goodness provides assistance in one’s station and abode.
Goodness toward all beings bestows peace and brings about security.
Therefore, one should cultivate goodness, which is a companion on the path to the divine abode.
Goodness is the source for the gods, sages, and ancestors who serve Brahman; it is the source for those who are liberated. A wise person should always practice that goodness. (52–53)
Death is indeed certain; that which was done and enjoyed has already passed away.
No new merit has been earned—what will you eat [in the hereafter]?
Having reflected thus, the virtuous are indeed bestowers of merit.
For one's parents and likewise the deities must always be served. (55) The great fruit of such service is that one will certainly dwell in heaven hereafter;
the fruit of pleasing one's guru is that one will certainly dwell in his presence hereafter. (56)
Having thus concluded, one should constantly serve pure holy men (sādhus).
Holy men are well-established embodiments of the Lord;
from them this creation was born, and from them have millions of incarnations (avatāras) emerged.
Because having attained sovereignty, the lords and others are born;
because the sages, ancestors, and gods constantly worship him;
and because from him even the sun and other luminaries, whose primary quality is splendor, come into being. (58–59)
From whom all beings are born and into whom they are withdrawn,
from whom the senses, the mind, and the intellect arise and exist—
therein stands the conscious Lord as a witness, intent upon no action.
Having restrained that [mind], he abides within as the Lord, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
by whom all this is pervaded, and who exists and moves [within it].
By taking refuge in that Lord of Gods, one attains supreme peace.
Having indeed abandoned the material nature and attained the divine state,
that devotee who finds delight in the Self shall go to the supreme goal;
just as an aquatic bird is not smeared by water.
One who has cultivated wisdom remains thus in the world and is not defiled.
A person who possesses contentment and satisfaction obtained through the grace of their chosen deity remains like a spider in its web, neither grieving nor exulting.

Having severed the firm knot called latent impression (vāsanā) residing in the heart of one's own self, one should dwell in happiness; he shall attain the supreme abode. Just as a person who is soiled becomes pure by taking water and bathing, [so does the soul become pure].
Likewise, even one defiled by illusion attains purity through the acceptance of the virtuous.

(67) Just as one who knows the far shore of a great forest is not at all deluded therein, so too one who has realized the end of illusion is not at all deluded regarding the principles of reality. (68)
For one who has understood the three aims of life, having seen them and enjoyed them, he is released;
for him who is unbound and free from desire, the path of Brahman shines forth.
For the wise there is no fear, but for those ignorant of this, there is indeed no freedom from fear.

For both [of these], when joined with Hari, there is indeed no ultimate fear. Whatever action arises in the world without being preceded by intentional desire— that, whether pleasant or unpleasant, does not lead to bondage, as it is regarded as equal.
Having observed the world to be afflicted and the virtuous to be likewise unafflicted,
he who should worship me by resorting to the conduct of the virtuous will indeed cross over [suffering].
He should certainly not look upon those who grieve, so that his own grief may not perish.
One should always observe those who do not grieve, by which one may attain the happiness of the virtuous.
Those people here who proceed according to the path of the virtuous attain the goal of the virtuous and go to the supreme state.

"O Rādhikā, where I, the great Hari, eternally reside in splendor, served and meditated upon by infinite millions of liberated souls"— having spoken thus, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, [continued].
He then personally ceased [speaking] and gave Vaiṣṇava mantras himself.
The king and his subjects again worshipped Kṛṣṇa with many offerings.
Hari then desired to depart, and the king gave him a gift.
Hari gave him excellent wedding gifts and became ready;
at that moment, King Rājarāya arrived there together with the sage Rājagiri to entreat the Lord Hari.
He then requested the Blessed One to lead him to his own abode, Ārṣaja-tanu-rāṣṭra,
and to reside there permanently on the bank of the river Parībhāsā in the city of Vyenojarāśāna. || 2.222.79-80 ||
Hari, moved by compassion, declared to him, "So be it.
"Indeed, the time has not yet come; you must go quickly to the lower realm.
Tomorrow, on the fifth day, the commencement of the sacrifice shall take place in the kingdom of Brāhmīla."

Therefore, O King, having completed the sacrifice on the morning of the thirteenth day, I shall arrive in your kingdom in the evening; of this there is no doubt. According to your wish, I shall remain for a longer time in your abode.
"But you must come to that sacrifice on the morning of the fifth day;
the conclusion will take place at midday on the eleventh.
Having been addressed thus by Hari, the king accepted the words of Hari.
Having performed worship, he departed swiftly for his own kingdom, traveling by celestial chariot (vimāna).
Then, a second king also approached Śrī Hari—
the sovereign of Urugavākṣa and the lord of the city of Rāyagrāmā.
Urogamana, the lord of the kingdom, prayed to the Supreme Lord;
and Mānatriveda, the king of sages, also prayed to Mādhava:
"O Keśava, come and purify my kingdom and its subjects as well."
Hari said, "So be it," and became ready, ascending his celestial chariot (vimāna).
At that time, the people of the community and the subjects also ascended their celestial chariots.
Having bid farewell to the king and the others, the people raised a great shout.
Many instruments were played, and a celestial chariot appeared in the sky;
it was bowed to by the people and honored in the air with flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
Then, the army of Urogamana set forth ahead.
"He has indeed arrived very quickly," [thinking thus], the king descended from the city.
The lord of the city of Rāyagrāma offered him honor and a welcome.
The city was adorned and the palace became resplendent. (91–92)
With banners and the like, with leaf-patterns, plantain pillars, arches, and svastikas; with water-pots, colored creepers, and likewise with sprinkling vessels—
in the vicinity of such a city, near the edge of the ocean.
By means of a secret sign, he brought Śrī Hari’s own celestial chariot to the earth.
At that time, musical instruments were sounded, shouts of "Victory!
arose, kettledrums and other drums resounded, and auspicious songs by women were sung.
The sounds of musical instruments, thunderous roars, and the joyful, auspicious voices of the subjects arose as a welcome, causing the celestial chariot to ascend.
The subjects offered flowers, consecrated rice, and other gifts, while Hari proceeded ahead.
Having been saluted, honored by the king, the queen, and even the subjects,
the illustrious Lord then sat upon an auspicious golden throne.
O King, Rādhikā then placed flower clusters and necklaces upon the neck of Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction and Farewell to the Subjects of the Kingdom of Pātragona, the Acceptance of the Request to Depart for the Kingdom of Ārṣajatānu, and the Journey to and Reception by the Kingdom of Urogamana," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 223 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Tretā-yuga Lineage) [Chapter 223 begins]
[Author: Chapter 224.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in order to cause Śrī Hari to wander through his own city, the king—
In the city of Rājagṛha, he indeed brought forth his army ready for battle. There, he seated Hari upon a beautiful chariot drawn by white horses;
likewise, he placed his family and his daughter, the beloved of Brahmā, upon other chariots.

Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and songs, the king paraded Kṛṣṇa joyfully through the city; meanwhile, at the city gate, the principal officers honored the Supreme Soul, and in the marketplace,
the most excellent merchants worshipped Him.
At the openings of the streets, on the roads, and indeed in the marketplaces,
the women and the subjects [honored him] with gold and silver coins, sandalwood, unbroken grains, and saffron; with garments, flower garlands, coconuts, fruits, and the like.
Having thus wandered through the city, Hari went to the royal palace;
King Urukṣavakṣa worshipped the Supreme Lord and performed an ablution with water for the feet of the Supreme Soul.
Then, with sweet water and indeed pure water,
the royal family and others drank the nectar from the feet of Śrī Hari.
Then the queen performed worship and also offered the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).

Then the two maidens placed upon the neck of Kṛṣṇa a long, flower-made garland, serving as a bridegroom’s wreath, O observer of auspicious vows. Having obtained the beloved husband of Śrī, they both felt their purpose was fulfilled.
Then the king and the queen felt in their hearts that they had accomplished all they needed to do.
At that time, the king caused a magnificent festival to be held;
he fed Kṛṣṇa and the honored guests from all around.
Hari gave all his wealth to the sage Mānatri-veda;
thereafter, Mādhava also instructed the subjects there. When their means of livelihood were destroyed, Kṛṣṇa shone eternally within their hearts.
Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, is indeed attainable through meditation alone.
In ancient times, sages attained supreme perfection through the yoga of meditation;
likewise, other yogis have attained it and will continue to do so.

People who are greatly satiated by the knowledge of meditation and whose hearts are set on nirvāṇa do not return to saṃsāra; for they are liberated from the mire of worldly existence. Free from passion and hatred, they remain established in the true nature of the self.

Established eternally in sattva and liberated, they do not return anywhere again. By performing actions that bestow peace, which are free from attachment and devoid of dispute and deceit, the devotee comes to me.

Having risen early in the morning and restrained the mind, one should indeed fix it upon my form in my presence and contemplate my image. One should likewise disregard sound, touch, form, taste, or smell as they present themselves.

One should not grasp anything from Me, nor should one think of any other object. (1.9) Having gathered the senses and the mind into a single mass, he who performs restraint within Me—within his heart—there shall arise the vibration of My form. (2.223.20)
If the mind, being indeed fickle, becomes like a fish in meditation,
one should forcibly turn it back and fix it again upon the form.
First, one should practice meditation upon me as adorned with ornaments and richly arrayed in garments.
Then, having dissolved the attire, one should contemplate [the deity] as mere form.
Then one should contemplate me as divine, laughing, and speaking;
and thereafter, one should contemplate me as the bestower of bliss, of a single form.
In this way, the senses, mind, ego, and intellect gradually dissolve into the form [of the Lord] through love; then one attains liberation.
This is the progress of yogis, while for those engaged in ritual action, it is characterized by renunciation.
The senses, which are directed outward, have Kṛṣṇa as their object and are equal [in nature].
They are offered and brought under control by those engaged in action through the offering of everything.
Through the offering of everything, one becomes pure, perfected, and my devotee.
Wherever the collection of the senses may become forcefully attached, even slightly,
one should recognize that object and mentally transform it into a form.
There, in each respective place, the mind should be made steady, gradually and step by step.
Satisfied by the offering of his desired object, it will attain stability.
Then, having dissolved that object into my image in the form [of the deity], the devotee should contemplate it slowly; in this way, he becomes purified over time. (28–29)
When my mind has become serene through yoga, it becomes the supreme source of the arising of sattva;
by that, affection for me arises, by that comes devotion, and subsequently, liberation shall be attained.
[Meditation, austerity, self-restraint, forbearance, worldly activity, reflection, and so forth...]
One should offer speech, action, movement, and every activity unto Me.
Having thus surrendered this impelling sacrifice to Me, one shall become happy;
or else, casting all duties behind oneself, one may remain inactive.
Having become [thus], one should indeed contemplate me with the mind and always mutter my name;
one should pay homage to sense objects and not dwell upon worldly affairs.
Having visualized my form within the heart, one should thereafter remain absorbed in it.

Thus, having attained union with me, he goes at the end to the supreme state. And for the yogin who has renounced everything and is free from desire, there is the attainment of the body of Brahmā; he becomes equal to me in the imperishable.
One should constantly remember my form and chant my supreme name;
performing everything for my sake, one shall attain my world.
Remaining untainted by the persistence of the Brahman and having ascended above the disease of *māyā*.
One attains the nectar, the state of immortality, and the Supreme Self. (37) Among all attainments, the highest attainment is a constant inclination toward the Supreme Lord;
it is the attainment of the virtuous, the attainment of Hari, and the attainment of His abode, and nothing else. (38)
All worlds created by the ego go to hell;
all worlds created by Brahman, however, go to the Imperishable.
The person who slays the self goes to the hells guarded by Yama.

Having attained a connection with Brahman, he is indeed neither a self-killer nor one who has gone to [a lower] abode. Wherever there may be meditative contemplation (*abhidhyāna*) even in the state of a ghost (*preta*), the living soul (*jīva*) undergoes rebirth; therefore, one should practice the meditative contemplation of Brahman.
One who is intent on meditation for the sake of supernatural powers attains a *sāttvika* illusion that grants rebirth;
therefore, one should be intent on meditation upon Brahman.
Overwhelmed by supernatural powers and possessed by intoxication and pride, [he falls].
He who exists through illusion— that indeed is his hell.
He in whom the Yakṣiṇī of craving and the Rākṣasī of seeking reside,
and he in whom the Piśācī of anxiety dwells— these three are of the nature of hell.
He who possesses passion as his rakshasa and delusion as his yaksha,
and he who possesses hatred as his pishacha— these three are of the nature of Raurava.
Wherever these three exist for him, there he is reborn.
Through those [senses] and through those [objects], a corrupted intellect arises and the turning of delusion occurs.
By that, the one of unrefined wisdom indeed goes to the Raurava hell.
Through such lack of wisdom, many hells indeed come to be here.
The flames here burn embodied beings moment by moment;
for one who is not satisfied, true happiness free from suffering never arises.
That pleasure which is mixed with suffering is considered here to be what is called hell.
Illusion exists only in hell; it is never free from suffering.
For one possessing a body of illusion, happiness is neither absolute nor eternal. Therefore, apart from the immutable state, happiness is of the nature of hell. (2.223.50)
I shall indeed describe the hells— both high and low, which are illusory, material,
subject to dissolution, and rendered fruitless by the state of Brahman.
For human beings, the objects of sensory enjoyment are nothing but hells.
Just as are the abodes and dwellings of the gods and the sages,
so too are the hells situated within the bodies of embodied beings.
Likewise, [there are those] of the world-protectors, the guardians of the quarters, the planets, and the winds.

And the celestial, pleasure-acting aerial chariots, assembly halls, and residences of the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Gandharvas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Siddhas, and the Parameṣṭhin; ||54||
Gardens, lotus ponds, and houses made of gold;
nectars and enjoyments, as well as garments of radiant luster; the prosperities of the gods and others, and their bodies that feed upon nectar. (55–56)
Divine women, divine beds, and divine perfumes, flavors, and so forth—these are considered hells that ripen from illusion when compared to the abode of Brahmā.
This is true even for the lords, the Virājas, and the Pradhāna-puruṣa. (57)

And those enjoyments belonging to the realms of *māyā*, which consist of *sattva* yet are illusory—all of these are born from the principle of *mahat-tattva* and are designated as "hell. They are considered inferior to the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (58–59)
Likewise, those worlds consisting of māyā that are near the abodes of Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha— those enjoyments are considered hells.
There is no other divine and eternal abode equal to Brahmaloka.
Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are indeed of the nature of the abode of Brahman;
they are truly devoid of the hell of māyā, free from illusion, and bestow liberation.
I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa in person, served by Rādhā and the others.
In Goloka, I am served by the cowherds and cowherd-maidens who possess my own form;
there I exist in a divine and eternal form where Māyā does not exist.
In Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme realm, I abide in the form of Nārāyaṇa.
Well-served by divine powers such as Lakṣmī and Ramā,
and attended by attendants of divine form, I am the divine and eternal one;
I am of divine and eternal form, where Māyā does not exist.
I am the very nature of Vāsudeva, abiding in that supreme, unmanifest state where Māyā does not exist at all; such am I, possessing a divine form.
Thus, wherever I have established my presence, that indeed is my divine abode.

Through union with me, it has attained divinity; therefore, hell does not exist there. Mansions, dwellings, and riches devoid of me—all these masters and inhabitants are hells destroyed by my illusory power (māyā). //67-68//
Having thus reflected with the wisdom bestowed by me, one should practice my yoga in every way; hellish existence dissolves,
and even divinity is attained for one who has entered the yoga dedicated to my purpose.

Wherever there is no connection for me, even that which consists of surrender, there time is fully operative; it has no power over what is connected to me. I am the ruler of time; it does not operate within me.
Wherever I am, my devotee who goes there indeed never grieves;
such is this supreme abode of the virtuous who are connected to Brahman.
But all other places, distinct from that, are indeed hells, each according to its nature.
Having reflected upon this, the wise man should establish a connection with Me.
Whether it be an insentient object or a sentient being, he should cause it to be made connected to Me.
That alone is declared to be the "non-hell" (aniraya), for through its divine union, it becomes divine.
Having understood this and having offered [themselves] to Me, My devotees have attained divinity;
they are not born again in creation, nor do they pass away when Time devours all.
Having attained a bliss free from suffering, they abide in eternal happiness.
In my supreme abode of bliss, they enjoy all their desires.
Those who perform my recitation and are devoted to my form become immortal;
having attained immortality, they become one with Brahman.
My yogins go to that station of Brahmā, which is non-returning, known as the single syllable, free from suffering, ageless, and peaceful.
One who is still possessed of passion perceives all worlds as being characterized by hell.
Joined with me and liberated from everything, he rejoices happily in the Imperishable (akṣara). He rejoices constantly with me in my manifold form;
liberated and filled with my bliss, there exists nothing inferior to him. (2.223.80)
Having thus instructed them, Hari then imparted the mantras to the subjects, to the king’s family, and to the king himself.
Then Kṛṣṇa set his mind on departing; the king, however, [remained] there once more.
He gave various kinds of wealth, dowry, and parting gifts;
through the medium of his subjects, he offered manifold honors amidst the sounds of musical instruments.
Just then, the king named Parāṅvratā arrived there.
Then Āśanāpurīśvara, together with Alaṃtra and Tṛṣi,
as well as Pārāvātarāṣṭrapati, entreated the Supreme Lord:
"O Abode of Mercy, come to my lands and purify us!"
Having heard this, Hari said, "So be it," and together with his family, he became ready.
Then, having quickly accepted the worship, he ascended the celestial chariot (vimāna).
At that time, the daughters beginning with Brahmapriyā and all the sages likewise [prepared].
They were situated in celestial chariots, and their chariot sped forth.
Then the king [beheld] Pārāvātarāṣṭra approaching with great speed;
for he had suddenly turned away from the sky and descended first to the earth.
"Welcome to the illustrious Hari along with his own army! [Thus they cried]. (88) Then musical instruments were sounded and shouts of victory arose;
the subjects, standing well-composed, offered their welcome with folded hands. (89)
Following the path shown by the king, the celestial chariot descended into a beautiful garden near the city of Āśāsanapura.
Having seen Hari, the subjects, the king, the queen, and the principal ministers likewise [welcomed him].
All others who had arrived also offered their greetings and salutations.
(9.1) The king honored him with flowers and other offerings, as well as golden necklaces and fine pearls;
the queen performed the *nīrājana* ceremony, and then she seated Hari upon his throne. (9.2)
On an elephant accompanied by the golden Ambālikā, and on other chariots and vehicles,
he caused Mādhava to be paraded through the city at his command.
In the evening, all the people honored him with jewels, garments, and other offerings.

Having caused Keśava to be carried around the royal palace with gold coins, flowers, unbroken rice grains, garlands, and other offerings, the king brought him back in; he honored him once more and then fed him. (94–95)
Then, by the command of the king’s mother, the two maidens worshipped the Supreme Lord Hari and chose Him as their husband with an excellent garland.
Having placed that garland around His neck, those two maidens were then bestowed upon Him.
When Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of All and Supreme Controller, himself became their [son and daughter],
the king rejoiced in his heart and the queen attained great joy.
Once the two children were born, having fulfilled their purpose, the king held a great festival.
Indeed, he caused [the festival] to be performed at night, and Hari gave instruction:
"O Rādhikā, in this royal palace is the means of liberation for all.

Thus ends the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning Hari’s wandering through the city of Rāyagrāma, his teaching, his worship, and his departure; and thereafter, his journey to the kingdom of King Parāvāta and his arrival in the city of Āśāsanā.
