Chapter Two Hundred and Twenty-Four: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Section Two (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 224.
[Author: Chapter 225.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the Blessed Lord spoke to all the subjects, beginning with the kings.
"Tomorrow there is a great and most excellent sacrifice in the auspicious kingdom of Brāhmī.
That region where a sacrifice takes place becomes a bestower of merit.
Sacrifice is Nārāyaṇa himself, and he is I, Puruṣottama."
I am indeed constantly pleased and attain satisfaction through sacrifice;
for all actions dedicated to Me are themselves sacrifice, there is no doubt.
Indeed, no purpose whatsoever is ever accomplished by means other than the proper method.
"Through the performance of sacrifice, this sacrifice shall be accomplished here; of this there is no doubt.
Just as deer are captured by deer, birds by birds, and elephants by elephants, so too is sacrifice grasped by sacrifice. (4-5)
Just as the moon is indeed not seen on the new-moon day because it lacks a visible form,
so too am I not at all visible within a heart that is turbid.
But just as the moon shines forth upon reaching the full lunar day, [so do I shine when the mind is pure].
Having attained a mind filled with devotion, I shine forth as the Supreme Lord.
(7) Even when eclipsed by Rāhu, the moon becomes brilliantly radiant;
likewise, even when seized by Māyā, the individual soul (jīvātman) becomes luminous. (8)
One who lacks discernment and has not cultivated wisdom is drawn outward;
dwelling among sense objects, he is never satisfied.
For one who is unsatisfied there is no peace, and for one who is not at peace there is no happiness. (9)
For one who is not free from suffering, there is indeed no liberation; rather, there is the state of going to hell.
(2.224.10) Sense objects are the first hell, the senses are the second, the mind is the third hell, and latent impressions (vāsanā) are the fourth. (11)
The fifth is karma, and the sixth is hell; the seventh is bad qualities, while the seventh is suffering in the home and the eighth is poverty.
The ninth is disease as a hell, and the tenth is subjection to others.
The eleventh is ill-repute, and the twelfth is deficiency of intellect;
the thirteenth is [dependence on] family and the like, while the fourteenth is servitude;
the fifteenth is physical deformity, and the sixteenth is the enemy.
The seventeenth is indeed the manifest body known as hell;
the eighteenth consists of the transformations born of the body—these are the hells.
Thus, in this world, these hells are attached to embodied beings here.
Having reached one sacrifice through another sacrifice, one becomes free from the hellish state.
As long as impurity remains, thirst is not cut off;
that thirst ceases only when the impurity has come to an end.
Through association with sense objects, thirst always increases;
through detachment from sense objects and through knowledge, the absence of thirst grows.
In the mirror of knowledge, the seer beholds his own self as pure.
By the restraint of the senses, a human being becomes happy.
One who withdraws the self from the senses and their objects by means of the self, and abandons the realms of material nature, abides in Me and partakes of immortality.
Having experienced the sublime path through action, or having abandoned it within me,
one shall attain either eternal heaven or my own supreme abode. When the self, divested of qualities that ought to be relinquished, functions within me, [it attains liberation].
Then one attains my abode, the world of Brahman;
all forms, along with the functions of the mind and intellect,
become dissolved when the Supreme Brahman shines forth within the Self, which is of the nature of Brahman.
When an object of the senses has arrived, one should contemplate it as suffering; it does not turn away [from the mind] on its own.
The medicine for this is the non-contemplation of these things.
Life, wealth, union with loved ones, houses, and so forth are all impermanent.
Having reflected upon this consumption of time, the knower of the Self should not crave it.
Therein, suffering may be abandoned, yet that pleasure which arises from sense objects is mixed with suffering and is, moreover, abundant in suffering. (25–26)
Having deliberated upon both, one should abandon them, for he indeed approaches me; when devotion to the state of Brahman— which transcends all illusion— arises within oneself,
then Brahman is realized and attained through meditative absorption.
And having reached the touchstone of the state of Brahman, one attains meditative absorption (dhyāna).
When I am meditated upon by this meditator, I indeed ascend into that interval;
I appear within his own self when all the gates [of the senses] are restrained.
The dissolution of his qualities occurs effortlessly;
he becomes devoid of qualities yet possessed of divine qualities, manifesting in my own form. All embodied beings, possessing qualities, proceed from Prakṛti.
All those who are worthy of heaven are indeed devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and are worthy of my honor.
As long as this possession by a spirit, which causes extreme suffering, remains here,
so long does his mind dwell upon the objects of this miserable cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
When his separation from the elements— both gross and subtle— occurs completely, he then attains Brahman through dharma,
devotion, and dispassion; thus the highest good is realized by the self.
One who is enriched by his own excellence approaches Hari, the treasure-house of supreme excellences; do not [approach] me, for I am the storehouse of others' excellences.

Just as the earth, though possessing the essence of equality, follows the various essences of the seeds sown within it, so too the Self, though possessing the essence of equality, enters bodies produced by diverse karmas.
Just as gold mixed with base metal becomes purified by fire,
so too does the embodied soul become purified through devotion to me and wisdom.
The ancient wisdom bestowed by me shines forth for one who has been thus purified.
Relying upon the path of wisdom, the devotee takes refuge in me.
(37) Furthermore, the fruit of both wisdoms and forms of devotion is the vision of my divine form;
those who lack wisdom and are not devoted do not see me at all. (38)
Those characterized by *sattva* are superior to those who merely perform ritual actions; even more so are those born of pure *sattva*.
Greater than they is Time, my power, all-devouring and mighty.
But beyond Time is my abode, the imperishable and divine dwelling place.
Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end is found for that abode (dhāman).
Where there exists no suffering born of birth, death, and old age—that is Brahman, the supreme station; that is the abode, the highest state.
Placing their feet upon the head of Kāla, my devotees go to that state.
Having fully resorted to the auspicious dharma characterized by renunciation and consisting of self-surrender to me,
they proceed from there to the infinite, supreme, imperishable.
That Brahman is not to be accomplished through effort; it is considered equal to the Śabdabrahman (the Brahman of Sound).
Indeed, that Brahman is to be attained through compassion, for it leads to the Supreme Brahman.
[It is obscured] by sin, by the lack of means, by attachment, and by the bondage of karma.
Mortals do not perceive their own stainless, innate nature because they find rest in sense objects and harbor the conceit of "I" and "mine.
Due to the forceful flow of craving, they do not realize that Brahman is the Self.

Through serving the virtuous, through meditation, through the contemplation of devotion to my form, through the practice of Brahman, through supreme dispassion, and through affection, Brahman is revealed. Those who are struck by the thirst for sweetness perceive only the desired quality. 46–47.
Yet they do not desire even the supreme, immortal, and infallible state; endowed with inferior qualities, they do not perceive those who have reached the further shore.
Remaining on this side, they are repeatedly tossed about here among the multitudes of cosmic eggs.
In ancient times, many reached the further shore through the practice of the virtuous.
The virtuous always walk before those who tread the path to the highest good;
if they indeed take them as their refuge, they shall quickly attain the supreme state.
Through the power of blessings, the force of merit, the fruit of service, and virtuous deeds, if they have taken refuge [in Him],
then they quickly attain the auspicious body of Brahmā.
This applies to those who meditate, those who serve, those who possess affectionate devotion, and those who abide in Brahman.
"They shall attain that immortal, eternal goal which exists.
Having thus instructed them, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, ceased speaking;
and having drunk water and performed other such acts, the Blessed Lord slept.
Then, in the early morning, the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, served by young maidens,
was awakened by auspicious sounds of musical instruments and songs.
Having performed his daily rites and worship, he desired to depart quickly.
The king gave him leave to depart and likewise bestowed upon him a dowry.
Accompanied by his own retinue, Śrī Hari prepared himself for the auspicious moment known as Brāhma and ascended the celestial chariot.
Then musical instruments were sounded and the people offered him honor.
Śrī Hari was glorified, and he gave wealth and ornaments to the Ṛṣi.
Hearing his own fame in the sky, he caused his celestial chariot to move swiftly.
On the morning of the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina,
he quickly arrived at the sacrificial ground in the auspicious vicinity of Goyājānagara in the Brāhmīla kingdom, on the bank of the Āmrajānikā river. (58–59)
Then that celestial chariot appeared, possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns;
the sages, the king, and the subjects awaited it.
Seeing the chariot arrive, they ran toward the place of welcome.

On the vast ground by the riverbank, which was inhabited by countless people, the people became steady and composed; then the celestial chariot descended. Indeed, shouts of "Victory! from the subjects then spread throughout the sky.
The sound of *tūryas* and the sounds of lutes, accompanied by joyful songs, resounded on all sides as echoes born of that initial noise;
and the songs of women, filled with joy, were also heard.
At that time, various sounds of musical instruments indeed arose;
there were the blasts of conchs and the loud resounds of bugles on all sides, as well as the auspicious chants of the brahmins when Hari arrived. (64–65)
The celestial chariot was enlarged and honored by the kṣatriyas;
it was offered handfuls of flowers by the gods and the hosts of deities,
sprinkled with sandalwood, marked with sectarian tilakas, and illuminated by saffron.
Saluted, worshipped, and honored by meditative contemplations,
Śrī Hari indeed stepped outside from his celestial chariot for just a moment;
at that time, the great sages likewise placed necklaces upon Hari’s neck.
Lomaśa applied the *tilaka*, Śambhu gave him a garland of flowers,
and King Īśānapānaśiṣṭa gave him a golden garland.
The sage Śāntārāma placed a garland of *vṛndā* flowers around Kṛṣṇa’s neck.
Then the king honored the feet of his parents,
and the queen performed worship for those dear to Brahmanas;
likewise, the princesses offered honor to all the women.
The great sage Lālāyana, Tuṣita the best of gods,

and the Lord Svīyaprakāśa— these spoke to the Supreme Lord regarding the pavilion for the sacrifice, the sacrificial pit, and the oblations such as fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass, and other offerings. (72)
"O Lord, quickly inspect the dwellings of the people and their food and provisions.
According to your command, everything shall be provided; there is nothing lacking. Purify all things with your glance. (73–74)
Thus entreated, the Blessed Lord, traveling in his celestial chariot, went swiftly to the twenty-yojana regions of the people's dwellings to observe them closely,
by means of a letter of invitation that announced the auspiciousness of the sacrifice.
He beheld the imperishable Brahman, the Great Liberated One, who had assembled there;
he saw the liberated female consorts of Brahman who had come to the sacrifice, as well as all the sovereign powers and all the virtues embodied in beautiful forms. (76–77)
The Blessed One saw all his ornaments, all his weapons in their embodied forms, and also his own incarnation, Kṛṣṇa,
who had arrived together with Rādhā and others, accompanied by cowherds, cowherdesses, and cows.
The Lord beheld Nārāyaṇa, who was playfully accompanied by Ramā and the two Śrī-Kamalās,
as well as Bhū-lakṣmī, Tūlasi, Vṛndā, Padmā, and others,
together with his male and female attendants. (2.224.80)
He likewise beheld the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva, the primary principles beginning with Puruṣa, the conventional times beginning with Mahākāla, and the Infinite One (Bhūman);
as well as Mahāviṣṇu, the Vairāja, and the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā.
He likewise beheld Māyā together with Śakti, endowed with the [supreme] principles;
all the Siddhas and Yogins, the great seers, the ancestors and deities, the gods and lords of the gods, the guardians of the worlds and the guardians of the quarters. (82–83)
The Lord beheld those of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa);
the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts;
as well as the Vidyādharas, divine Gandharvas, the quarters of space, and the inhabitants of the Bhuvarloka.
He beheld oceans, rivers, trees, creepers, and grasses;
sacred fords, the wish-fulfilling cow and others, the vowels, the Vedas, and the qualities and so forth;
mines, mountains, men, kings, women, and all living beings. (85–86)

He beheld the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars, as well as the stationary beings and those born from eggs; likewise, he saw those born from a womb, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts.
He also saw the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and other such groups, as well as the lords of those hosts.
All the sacrificial deities, as well as the Mātṛkās and Devikās;
the Yoginīs of the Brahma-lake and all the Apsarases;
the Ṛṣis’ wives, the Vidyādharīs, the Śaktis, and the Sāṃkhya-Yoginīs. (88–89)
He likewise [saw] all kinds of fires, the offspring of Kaśyapa,
those dwelling in the netherworld (talaloka), as well as yakṣas, rākṣasas, dānavas, daityas, those who have abandoned food, ascetics, and officiating priests.
He saw the sacrificers, the men, the singers, and the patrons;
he also saw the *hotṛ* priests, the chanters, and the great guests.
There were streams of clarified butter, channels of curd, and likewise cascades of buttermilk.
He beheld lakes of nectar-like milk and even rivers;
he saw heaps of desirable foods such as rice and mountains of gathered fruits.
He saw coconuts and other fruits, both dry and fresh, as well as their juices.
He beheld the laboratories for alchemy, the wives' quarters;
he beheld the sacrificial post-hall, the hall for oblations, and the temple of the gods. And having observed that everything was indeed complete and ready, [he entered].
He praised Lomaśa, Viśvakarman, Lālāyana, Śaṅkara,
Svīyaprakāśa, and other great sages;
he then beheld the assembled rulers of the earth who had come for the performance of the sacrifice.
[He saw] the kings of the regions of Amarī, Rāśiyāna, and likewise Ketumāla;
of the eastern lands and Uṣṇabhū;
of Prāgjyotiṣa and the region of Ajanābha. || 97–98 ||
The Lord beheld the kings of the intermediate regions, those born in lands that were neither white nor red; he saw the rulers of the continents and sub-continents,
and he especially beheld those who had not yet attained the acquisition of the stainless [state].
The kings of the regions of Dakṣa and Amarī, who were engaged in sacrifice; King Kālīmaṇḍalīna, the king of Vanajaleśa;
King Pārāvārapiba, and likewise King Koṭīśvara.
He beheld King Śrī Satīśa, the king fierce in the Tretā age; he saw King Parāṅvrata and King Rājārāyapati;
as well as King Rāyasoma and King Aṇḍajara.
He saw Bālyarajonṛpa, Corugavākṣa, and likewise Bhūbhata;
he saw Īśānapāna together with his wife, and all those born in the region of Dakṣāmarī accompanied by their wives and others. (103–104)
Mahākṛṣṇa said to the kings, "May you be the sacrificers. They accepted the auspicious word of the Supreme Lord with "Om.
Having thus honored those who had come to the sacrifice, he [honored] the guests.
Having caused the deficiency to be paid, he quickly went to his own abode.
(106) Meanwhile, musical instruments were sounded for the auspicious hour of the sacrifice; having prepared themselves, the people quickly arrived at the pavilion. (107)

Likewise, the liberated ones, the incarnations and other lords, the most excellent of the Siddhas, the sages, the ancestors, the gods, the lords of the gods, those who bring the gods under their control,
the goddesses, those who subjugate goddesses, humans, Daityas, and Dānavas.
And all the subjects of Kāśyapa, both the stationary and the moving,
those who perform sacrifices for the sake of sacrifice,
the performers of rites, the ritual implements, the mantras, the offerings to gods and ancestors— all these were present at the sacrifice.
O auspicious and most excellent Rādhikā, while the necessary duties were being carried out,
Śrī Hari arrived at the pavilion, honored by all those present.

(111) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [is described] the instruction, worship, feeding, and resting at night for the people of the Pārāvāta kingdom and others, along with the distribution of gifts, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, in the kingdom of Brāhmīlā.

The two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival at the Sacrificial Ground and the Reception of the Mahīmānas and Others," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 225.
[The Author: Chapter 226.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, at the auspicious and most excellent moment of the morning of the sacrifice—
The sages and the deities also arrived at the sacrificial pavilion. Chanting the name of Śrī Hari, reciting the sections of the Vedas,
and muttering the Veda-born mantra, they joyfully entered the pavilion.
The gods, the Lord of Gods himself, Brahmā and the other lords of lords,

the sovereigns, the principal ones, their consorts, the goddesses, and the attendants— all arrived there at the sacrificial pavilion, filled with joy. (3) Indeed, they came in person to that sacrifice.
The ritual ingredients and the auspicious sacrificial offerings, having assumed embodied forms, arrived;
likewise, the seats, the implements, and the fuel sticks arrived.
The banner appeared in person, the water-pot appeared in person, and the pavilion likewise appeared in person.
Makha himself, the sacrificial altars themselves, and the king of sacrificial posts itself;
the fire-pit itself and Vāstupuruṣa himself indeed arrived.
The Vedas themselves, the ritual injunctions themselves, and the mantras themselves came together.

The *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses arrived in person, well-prepared for their respective uses; (7) the sacrificial vessels, the cooked offerings (*caru*), and the fires also arrived in person. Then, all the necessary implements appeared within the pavilion. (8)
Auspicious time, season, place, and a holy day arrived;
likewise, the earthly sacred sites and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) arrived.
All the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu) were present at his sacrifice.
Kalpalatās, Kalpavṛkṣas, and Cintāmaṇis arrived;
all inexhaustible vessels and caskets that fulfill every wish came forth; and imperishable treasuries and stores of nectar arrived. (2.225.10–11)
The flavors, varieties of fruits, leaves, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth— all these,
having taken on physical forms, arrived there at the sacrifice for Rādhikā. Indeed, they were employed exactly according to their respective functions.
All forms of prosperity, all branches of knowledge, all truths, and all supernatural powers,
as well as wonders and perfected beings, arrived at that sacrifice.
There were all varieties of honey-mixtures (madhuparka) and mountains of cooked foods.
All the liquid substances appeared in personified form, all fragrant;
gold and silver coins, as well as products of the cow, arrived in personified form.
Thus, while all these things were indeed present in person within the pavilion—
The auspicious rites of the Brahmins took the form of songs by the women;
there, the most auspicious benedictions of the learned priests were uttered. The sage Lomaśa performed the ritual declaration of the place, time, and other necessary details.
In the pavilion, the patron of the sacrifice— remaining under the instruction of Īśāna—

and the king in the form of a husband and wife, being the principal figures there, performed the auspicious rite; likewise, urged by the sage, he [the king] presided over the assembly of other monarchs.
Performing the procedure for the secondary rite (anukalpa) in the pavilion near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
Lomaśa caused the primary formal resolve (saṃkalpa) to be made;
he also performed the protection of the quarters and the worship of the water-pot (kalaśa).
He had the installation and worship of Gaṇeśa performed;
he also conducted the recitation of the Svasti-vāca and the Puṇyāha-vācana. Lomaśa then caused the consecration of the patron and the others to be performed.
He caused the installation and worship of the Mātṛkās to be performed;
likewise, he had the Nāndī-śrāddha, the selection of the preceptors and others, as well as the offering of the Arghya,
prostrations, and the Madhuparka ceremony conducted.
He also caused the placement of the *vardhanī* jar and the *kalaśa* vessel;
the entry into the pavilion, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the pavilion and so forth,
the establishment of the *vāstu*, and the worship of Vāsudeva.
There, within the Sarvatobhadra mandala of the pavilion,
Lomaśa performed the worship, the installation of the deities, and the ritual adoration of the gods,
as well as the installation of the deity of the yantra and the worship of the gods. (25–26)
The worship of the pedestal, the worship of the altar, the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
as well as the honoring of the deity of the pit and likewise the installation of the fire within the pit;
the installation and worship of the planets, and the installation of the Yoginīs and so forth.
He also caused the installation and worship of the guardians of the field (kṣetrapas).
He performed the worship of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the girdles (mekhalās), and so forth, as well as the worship of the deities,
the worship of the fire, and likewise the worship of the planets.

Lomaśa ṛṣi performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the ritual fuel-adding (*anvādhāna*); then Lomaśa performed the *āghāra* and *ājyabhāga* oblations. Likewise, he performed the invocation for the deities of the sacrificial site (*vāstu-maṇḍala*) and for the *yoginīs*.

There, the sage Lomaśa performed the principal oblation as well as the oblation with the *vyāhṛti* mantras; he offered the ritual bali and excellent sacrificial food (*naivedya*). Then followed the erection of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the consecration by immersion in water (*jalādhivāsana*).

He performed the water-offering and water-worship for the Mothers, as well as the worship of the conch, the bell, and other implements; he likewise performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā),
and he conducted the worship of the golden image of Bālakṛṣṇa.

He performed the sixteen-fold ritual service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā*) and offered cooked rice as a food oblation (*caru-naivedya*). He also performed the complete fire sacrifice (*sarva-homa*) with a thousand oblations (*sahasra-āhuti*), saying:
"I offer this food to the liberated ones (*muktas*). (34–35)
I offer this food as an oblation to Brahmā.
I offer this food as an oblation to the liberated souls (muktātmans).
I give this food as an oblation to the incarnations (avatāras).

I offer this food as an oblation to the [energies] that cause descent; it is dedicated to me. (37) I offer this food as an oblation to the qualities, sovereign powers, and manifestations; it is dedicated to me.
I offer this food as an oblation to the ornaments, weapons, and specific powers; it is dedicated to me. (38)
I offer this food as an oblation to the male lords and the female goddesses; I offer this food as an oblation to the divine manifestations and their attendants;
and I offer this food as an oblation to the wives of Brahmā and to the virtuous women.
To all those who are dear to Brahmā, this food is offered as a salutation.
To the powers such as Rādhā and Lakṣmī, this food is offered as a salutation.
And to the virtuous women such as Māṇikī and others, this food is offered as a salutation.
This food is offered as *namaḥ* to Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Śrī; this food is offered as *namaḥ* to them together with their male and female servants.
This food is offered as *namaḥ* to Mahāviṣṇu, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Virāṭ.
Salutations to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; let this food also be offered to them.
(43) Salutations to Sāvitrī, Kamalā, Durgā, and the others; salutations, let this food be offered to them.
To Kaṃbharā, the Great Lakṣmī; salutations, let this food be offered to her. (44)
To Santuṣṭā and Amṛtā, this food is offered as obeisance;
to Padmāvatī and Ramā, this food is offered as obeisance. To Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, Hāsā, and Ambā, this food is offered as obeisance.
"Also [offerings] to Bālakṛṣṇa, Aṅganāduḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, and the others.
This food is for all the wives; this is my salutation to the Siddhas and Ṛṣis.
This is my salutation to the ancestors, and this food is for the Pitṛkās. ||46-47||
This food is for the sages; salutations, this food is for the gods.
This food is for the goddesses, the divine women, and the deities.
This food is for the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds; salutations.
To the Ādityas and the Rudras, this and this is the food;
to the Vasus and the Aśvins, this and this is the food;
and to the Directions and the Tattvas, this and this is the food.
To the treasures and to the dwellings, this and that food;
to the attainments and to the great seers, this and that food;
to the Kṛttikās and to the Manus, this and that food.
To the Maruts and to the Kalās, this and that food;
to the Tīrthas and to the Vālakhilyas, this food is offered by me.
To the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Pretas, this food indeed.
To the Kūṣmāṇḍas and the Piśācas, this and this is the food; to the Vināyakas and the Gaṇas, this and this is the food;
and to the Vetālas, the Cāraṇas, and the Sūtas, this is the food.
And this food is for the Māgadhas, the bards, and the servants;
it is food for the Ḍākinīs, the Śākinīs, and the Tāmasīs;
and it is food for the Vidyādharas, the Gandharvas, and the Kinnaras.
"Let this food be for the Viśvedevas, malevolent spirits;
let this food be for the Daityas, the Dānavas, and the Nāgas;
and let it be food for the serpents, the hooded snakes, and the crawling reptiles. (57)
Food from trees, from creepers, and from grasses and the like;
food from sacred fords, from mountains, and from oceans;
and this food from rivers, from ponds, and from shrines. (58–59)
To the Kalpalatā creepers and the wish-fulfilling trees, to the Kāmadhenu cows, to the Cintāmaṇi gems, and to the inexhaustible vessels—
this food is offered as an oblation to the sacrificial pits and the deities of the pits; to them, salutations.
This food is for the pavilions and for the deities residing in the pavilions;
likewise for the gateways and for the deities of the gateways, as well as for the spirits of the [door]posts;
this is also for the deities of the banners and for the deities of the sacrificial posts.
To the implements such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, this food is offered with the words "namama.
To the pillars and the deities of the pillars, this food is offered with the words "namama. Likewise, to the *mātṛkās*, the *satīs*, and the virtuous wives, [this is offered] with the words "idam."
This food is for the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; salutations again and again! (64) This food is an offering to the goddesses who are devoted to their husbands.
This food is an offering to Kāmadeva and to the Seven Sages; salutations! (65)
Food for Īśāna, Varuṇa, and Mahendra;
food for Agni, Kuvera, and Nairṛta;
[food] for Vāyu and Yama, and this food indeed for the messengers.
To the aquatic creatures dwelling in the wind, this food is offered as an oblation.
To those dwelling on the earth and those dwelling in the snow, this food is offered as an oblation.
To those born from the womb and those born from eggs, this food is offered as an oblation.
To those born of sweat and those born from sprouts, this food is offered as *namaḥ*.
To the minute beings such as insects and moths, this food is offered as *namaḥ*. To the insentient and the sentient, and to the gods (*makhi*), this food is offered as *namaḥ*.
To the clouds and the thunderclaps, this offering of food;
to all beings, including the gods and the asuras, this offering of food;
and to those established in the creation of Brahmā, this offering of food. (2.225.70–71)
To those created and sustained by Īśa, this food is my offering;
to those created and sustained by Jīva, this food is my offering.
To the eighty-four thousand species born from the earth, this food is my offering.
To those who remember [the tradition] and to those who do not, this food is offered as my own.
To those who are distinguished and to those who are refined in essence, this food is offered as my own.
To all of them, both collectively and individually, this food is offered as my own.
And to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are, this food is offered to them;
to the diligent Brahmins, this food is offered to them.
Svāhā! To Agni, the soul of all, this is offered.
"By these thousand streams, this oblation is offered to Agni, Svāhā!
(76) Thus indeed were the oblation, clarified butter, fuel-sticks, fruits, sweet foods, juices, and even liquids offered to Agni. (77)
Then the sage Lomaśa performed a sacrifice with many oblations;
thereafter, the sage caused a sacrifice of great oblations of clarified butter to be performed.
At that time, the gods and others, though already satisfied, appeared in person again and again.
They accepted the excellent oblation offered together with the fire.
Then the venerable sage Lomaśa performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
and the sounds of musical instruments arose on all sides.
The sounds of the Vedas arose, as did the songs of the women;
then the king offered handfuls of flowers to the gods.
The Brahmins performed the purifying consecration of the sacrificer.
They performed the bestowing of blessings, and the king gave the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then the brahmins, filled with an abundance of joy, sang words of benediction;
having bowed to the fire and offered salutations to the gods, they requested forgiveness.
Having performed the rites, Lomaśa indeed caused the dismissal [of the deities];
at that time, the sky became filled with lotus-like celestial chariots from the gathering, on all sides,
of the inhabitants of the three worlds.
O Rādhikā, on the fifth day, after the conclusion of the sacrificial rites,
Hari fed the honored guests, the great sages, the twice-born,
all the visitors, and those residing in Dhāma, Dhāmādi, and other places. (85–86)
Having fed those who were worthy, he then took his own meal;
the Blessed One himself ate together with the royal sacrificers.
Thus, O Rādhikā, was the sacrifice commenced on the bank of the river.
The propitiation of the ancestors through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and other rites was accomplished.
Then the Blessed One performed his evening bath together with all human beings and embodied deities, after having fully worshipped Varuṇa.
Having worshipped the water, the Blessed One bathed together with everyone;
then he returned to his own abode and gave gifts at that time:
sandals to the liberated ones and crowns to all the incarnations.
The Lord gave golden garments to the female attendants who had descended from the Muktānīs;
he gave crowns to the male attendants of the Īśas,
and he gave necklaces as well as chains and girdles to the female attendants of the Īśānīs.
To the ṛṣis [he gave] golden jars; to the female ṛṣis, golden necklaces;
to the Siddhas, golden garlands; and to the female Siddhas, golden bodices.
To the Pitṛs, he gave vessels of nectar; and to the female Pitṛs, inexhaustible jars.
The Lord gave golden umbrellas to the gods and neck-ornaments to the goddesses;
he also gave bracelets to the lords of the gods and canes to the spirits,
ghosts, and piśācas, and bestowed tunics upon them.
He gave gold coins to the men and jewels to the Daityas;
then he gave golden necklaces to the bards, panegyrists, and minstrels.
To the helpless, the children, and the elderly, he gave wealth and garments.
There, the Blessed Lord gave to each whatever was required;
to both the insentient and the sentient,
the Supreme Self, that treasure-house of compassion, granted everything after forming a resolve.
He caused all the great gifts (*mahādāna*), as well as the intermediate gifts (*madhyadāna*)—such as the giving of land, daughters, and so forth—to be bestowed upon his teachers.
And the kings gave everything: wealth, food, and houses.
He gave many gifts of maidens, as well as gifts of cows, horses, and elephants.
In this manner, the Lord bestowed gifts until the end of the night;
then, O Rādhikā, the *ārārtrika* ceremony for Bālakṛṣṇa took place.
Afterwards, meals were prepared by the kings once again.
Then, during the night, the Blessed Lord imparted instruction to the subjects.

(10.2) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, in the morning, the arrival of the great souls toward the sacrificial ground with Hari, the presence of all in the pavilion, and the *svasti*—all is concluded.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari.

I shall declare to you that instruction which brings about one’s own welfare— the instruction which the Lord bestowed upon his subjects by means of the imperishable Brahman uttered by Brahmā, who was himself impelled by the Supreme Brahman.
The Person, abiding in the Abode, is impelled toward the act of creation;
He joined Himself with His own power, Māyā, and by that [power], the illusory beings were produced.
Those beginningless selves who are merged in Māyā [are driven] by their own karmas.
Impelled, they become either gods or embodied living beings.
(4) Regarding this aggregate known as the body, senses, internal organ, subtle elements, and gross elements as its own self, one is bound therein by karmas. (5)
Living beings repeatedly grasp at composite material forms;
they undergo separation once more and revolve like a wheel.
They encounter states that are peaceful, terrible, or delusive in every respect.
Hair, blood, and flesh are indeed states produced from the mother;
marrow, bone, and sinew are states that arise from the father.
[The body] is always filled with pleasure, pain, and delusion, and is subject to cold, heat, and burning.
Even after encountering those various states of being, he who is not permeated by them—
reflecting "I am that, I am that"— shall become free from the bondage of mental constructs.
[9] The delightful city of nine gates is endowed with all those respective states of being.
Pervading all, this conscious Self, the Puruṣa, is said to lie within.
I am superior to those infinite ones designated as Puruṣas;
I am the inner self within the Virāj, just as I am in the world of Brahmā.
I alone am the Supreme Person, the teacher of all;
for just as I dwell within all sentient beings,
so too do I abide within all insentient matter as the embodied one who discerns the true nature of reality.
Knowing Me as such, the devotee of Videha shall soon be born [as Myself];
he is undecaying, immortal, subtle, and endowed with My virility.
By offering everything to My form and to My devotee, one is liberated.
Fire always resides within wood, yet it is separated when the wood is destroyed;
likewise, upon the destruction of the body, the self surely departs to the supreme reality.
Even sinners, by taking refuge in me, that supreme Self, [attain liberation]. (15)

Those who possess merit indeed become like embers through contact with fire. Through association with the virtuous, through the extraordinary application of my sovereignty, and by obtaining a portion of my qualities, my devotee shall attain equality with me. (16–17)

Just as one who has seen objects in a dream abandons them upon waking, so too does the Self abandon illusion and its like and abide in the Witness of all. Just as water, having left the earth, reaches the great ocean by way of a river.

In that same way, having abandoned this body, the self departs from me, the best of men. (1.9) Just as laborers indeed return once their work is done, so too do embodied selves return once they have experienced their enjoyments. (2.226.20)

Just as an arrow deprived of its momentum moves toward the ground without further action, so this individual soul (jīva), deprived of the momentum of latent impressions (vāsanā), goes to my imperishable state. Just as one becomes free from desire when desisting from ritual action, so too does he become free from longing. (21)
One who has turned away from all desires in the world and has desisted [from worldly activity] indeed approaches me;
one who is devoid of all states of being then goes to my abode.
Through constant practice of me, being attached to me, he does not return again to material nature.
Seeds scorched by fire do not sprout in any way;
likewise, all the seeds of this [person] truly do not sprout again.
Attached to the taste of the nectar of immortality, he does not cling to other tastes.
One who is attached to my own essential taste does not cling to the taste of the material qualities.
Indeed, those who know me are rare in this world;
everywhere, living beings who nourish only their bodies, senses, and objects are easy to find.
Just as currents of water flow with great speed toward low ground,
so too do people generally proceed with great haste toward what is low and vulgar.
But those who know Brahman, possessing the nature of fire, ascend upward.
"Through association with the virtuous, my devotees go upward to my imperishable abode.
Having reflected thus, one should constantly worship the Supreme Lord;
through the company of the virtuous, my devotion—which bestows the divine realm—should be practiced.

For those who offer everything unto Me, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, Māyā shall certainly not be an obstacle. Whatever affection one has for children, wealth, and the like, and whatever affection one has for women and so forth— [let that all be offered to Me].
Whatever affection one has for one's own body and so forth, let that affection be directed toward me;

||| 3.1 || whatever thirst there is for sensual objects and pleasure, whatever thirst there is for the means of enjoyment, and whatever thirst there is for honor and fame—that thirst should be directed toward me, Mādhava. ||| 3.2 ||

Whatever impulse there is for the attainment of one’s own ends, whatever impulse there is in the conquest of enemies and the like, and whatever impulse resides in egoism— that should be directed toward me, Keśava.
Whatever satisfaction exists in the acquisition of desired objects, and whatever satisfaction exists in the departure from enjoyments—
That satisfaction which comes from great contentment—that must be cultivated toward me in every way.

That happiness which exists in a state of pure goodness (*sattva*), that happiness which is free from the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), and that happiness which arises through discernment—all that must be cultivated toward me in every way. (34–35)
Whatever nourishment comes from prosperity, whatever nourishment comes from the accumulation of strength,

and whatever nourishment comes from the subjects of the scriptures— that should always be directed toward me. And that place which I constantly resort to, and that place which provides assistance— [may it be so].
That state which resides within one's own heart must be established in me in every way.
That sense of identity with the body and so forth, that sense of identity with honor, and that sense of identity with one's own pleasure—all that must be directed toward me, the true Lord. (37–38)
The hope you have for your own son, the hope you have for future happiness,
and the hope centered on gain— let all that be placed in me at all times.
The sense of "mine-ness" regarding what has been acquired, and the sense of identity [with it]— [let that too be placed in me].
That sense of "mine-ness" which is directed toward what is desired should be directed toward me for the sake of liberation.

Whatever effort is made for the sake of sense objects, whatever effort is made for the sake of wealth, and whatever effort is made for the sake of life—let that be directed toward me, Mādhava. (2.226.40–41)
One who possesses a body takes up all forms of possession out of delusion;
by that indeed bondage arises, and he goes to hell.
Therefore, one desiring the supreme state of Brahman should not practice impurity.
A person of sound intellect should not desire the fruit of actions that take the form of obstacles.
He who performs action out of greed, delusion, pride, or envy,
having strayed from the path to liberation, perishes along with his kinsmen.
Therefore, a person of discernment should never be joined with passion;
one should certainly not be childish, nor deluded, nor dull-witted.
Just as a house made of clay is plastered over with clay, so it is.
Likewise, this body composed of food must be nourished by foods;
and this body, being made of earth, indeed attains growth through earthly substances.
Nevertheless, one should not form an attachment to the body on account of such ownership.
Sweet, bitter, ghee, oil, unctuous substances, grains, fruits, and the like,
as well as soft preparations and soft earths, are indeed necessary for the body;
they should be used in such quantities as are free from binding properties.
Having thus brought his journey to completion, he indeed proceeds to the further shore of existence.
Just as a yogi who has gone to the forest takes food from a town but is not bound by attachment even there, so it is in this case. (2.226.50)
Dwelling in the forest of saṃsāra like a weary traveler,
one should take food for the sake of the journey so that it does not lead to bondage.
Having examined even the sense objects with the senses, the mind, and the intellect, [one should proceed].
One who desires peace should not be greedy; then one will become free from attachment.
(5.2) Overcome by latent impressions and deluded by my Māyā, people wander like a wheel in the cycle of birth, death, and existence. (5.3)
Therefore, having abandoned the defects born of ignorance as well as all bonds,
one who possesses discernment should take refuge in my path and become a partaker of liberation.
For everything arises from the Untimely Person (akāla-puruṣa), and even the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) revolves therein.
And one experiences the fruit born of egoism, and again enters into illusion (māyā).
The place consisting of heaven, produced by rajas, is indeed a supreme bondage; the place consisting of the realms of Rākṣasas and the like, produced by tamas, is indeed a supreme bondage. (55–56)
Therefore, one who possesses self-mastery should avoid both *rajas* and *tamas*.
When the *sattva* is freed from *rajas* and *tamas*, it attains purity;
through this purity, consciousness becomes perfectly serene.
One who is of the nature of serenity shall attain the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Having attained a state of constant serenity, one reaches liberation.
The Self is declared to be the man, while latent desire (vāsanā) is considered the woman.
For this is a terrible sorcery that leads those full of desire into a pit;
its form consists of passion and ignorance, and it bestows strength upon the senses.
This wicked *ḍākinī* of latent impressions casts man into the ocean.
Whether in a male body or a female body, she is the cause of delusion;
she casts one down indeed into the impure assembly, into the filthy abode,
upon the unadorned great path smeared with the passion for form.
Falling through delusion, a man sows illusory seeds;
from those seeds are born creatures named "son" and "daughter.
Even though there is similarity here, there is a distinction between these and children born from sweat.
Worms are said to be born from sweat, while those known as "sons" are born from the bodily constituents (dhātus).
One who seeks liberation, possessing a state of equanimity toward these worms and sons born of his own body, should abandon them through dispassion and discernment and take refuge in me. (64–65)
In childhood, there is suffering due to dependence on others; even in infancy, there is misery.
In youth, there is subjection to the senses through desires for sense-objects.
And in old age, with its attendant helplessness, there is yet further suffering beyond that.

Having recognized this palace of suffering—characterized by suffering at its beginning and end, and suffering in its middle, both physical and mental—a person should disregard it and take refuge in Me.
[This occurs] through grasping, through the efficient cause, and also through the cooperative cause. (67–68)
For indeed, everything within the body is merely suffering arising from filling [the senses];
disregarding such [suffering], one should resort to restraint through renunciation.
For the discerning person who has attained restraint in Me and is free from thirst [for sense objects], [there is liberation].
For me, a devotee, liberation through yoga is certain; there is no doubt.
For one who partakes of the nectar of the knowledge of reality, who drinks the essence of devotion, and who is anointed with the ambrosia of love for Me, My imperishable abode is ordained.
Celibacy is the form of Brahman; ethical conduct is considered the sky of consciousness. Having taken hold of the space of consciousness, one should approach my own space.
Likewise, there is the space of the body and the space of the senses, which expand within.
Having united it with the space of Brahman, the adept should offer it into the space of Hari.
Thus he indeed becomes liberated, having attained my yoga.
Having performed this practice constantly, nothing further remains to be done.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, ceased;
O Rādhikā, he then bestowed upon his devotees the mantras they had requested.
Thereafter, at night, he entered into supreme peace, consisting of yogic sleep.

At dawn, with auspicious musical instruments, hymns of praise, and the hearing of glorious deeds, the Lord himself awoke; he brought about auspiciousness for the three worlds. Having performed his morning rites, offered worship, and received honors, the Master [arose]. (76–77)
Having honored all his devotees and guests, he proceeded to the pavilion;
then musical instruments were sounded to inspire enthusiasm for the sacrifice, and auspicious songs were sung by the women of the Brahmins. (78)
The sounds of the Vedas arose on all sides from those who were learned in the Vedic lore.
And the performers of the sacrifice, skilled in ritual action, quickly arrived at the site of the rite.
There were incarnations, liberated souls, lords, gods, and great sages.
The Pitṛs, humans, Daityas, Yakṣas, Suras, and Dānavas;
all the progeny of Kaśyapa, the goddesses, and the wives of Brahmā;
the Nāgas, serpents, and those born from the earth—both insentient and sentient—indeed arrived.
Then, on the sixth day, at dawn, the sages commenced the sacrificial rites as before,
preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers (svastivācana) and performed according to the proper requirements.
Likewise, the worship of the gods and the offering of oblations (balinivedana) took place.
The offering of oblations into the fire and likewise the presentation of sacrificial libations,
as well as the libation for the ancestors, the handful of flowers, and the ritual fees— all these were performed,
including the waving of lamps and the dismissal, exactly as was appropriate.
There was also the feeding of the brahmins, as well as the feeding of the honored guests;
furthermore, the auspicious meals for the worlds of the sacrificers and others took place.
Then, having rested well, Hari went to the auspicious assembly hall in the evening.
There, the Lord himself, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, caused [the temple] to be built;
the venerable and eminent Ācārya bestowed the *mantras* upon the people. Then he indeed instructed them in that which grants liberation and brings about welfare.
O Rādhikā, [He is] the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the cowherd child;
Śrīkṛṣṇavallabhācārya, saluted by millions of liberated souls, the Lord of the abode of abodes, the cause of all incarnations. (88–89)
The Supreme Lord, who was propitiated by the service of innumerable Brahmās;
the Master who grants liberation, being satisfied by sacrifices and worshipped by the gods and others;
the compassionate Hari, son of Kambharā, the Lord of infinite power.
"At the moment of instruction, he was gazed upon by all with single-minded attention.

(91) Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction to the Subjects on the Fifth Night, Resting at Night, and on the Sixth Day Morning, the Performance of All Ritual Duties Following the Daily Observances, Eating, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
