Chapter 228 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa taught the vow of Brahman;
listen, for that auspicious state of Brahman is superior to all other vows.
(1) It is renowned as *brahmacarya*, which indeed stands at the very pinnacle of all.
And being devoted, one should indeed resolve upon stainless celibacy (brahmacarya).
One who observes the vow of Brahman, who is a student of Brahman, who serves Brahman, and who is virtuous—
having conquered time, illusion, and karma— shall attain my abode.
For that is indeed easy for a yogin, as well as for those who have attained perfection and for virtuous women;
it is easy for the virtuous, yet difficult for those who crave sense objects.
This is especially so regarding the assembly of the senses, which is intensely inflamed and exceedingly powerful.
One who restrains [the mind] with vigilance indeed conquers that which brings death.
(5) One should not contemplate the nature of desire, nor its objects; one should not look for the signs of desire and should avoid the portions of passion. (6)

One who possesses a body in this world should avoid those objects of enjoyment that nourish the *rajas* quality; likewise, one should completely renounce those enjoyments that nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
This should be done with a mind endowed with knowledge and accompanied by dispassion.

Having utterly destroyed the state of passion, one who possesses self-mastery should conduct himself [thus]. One should certainly not place trust in this body, which is joined with a corpse and impurities, which is the locus of desire, and which will cause one to be cast into hell in the future. (8–9)
Knowing this body to be a house of wind, bile, and phlegm; a vessel of blood, skin, and flesh;
rich with marrow, sinews, bones, and channels; filled with impurities such as excrement and urine; a locus of desire, and base—one should abandon passion for it. (2.227.10)
The channels (dhamanīs), which carry impurities, extend in all directions.
Like rivers flowing toward the ocean, they nourish the body with external [substances].
Among them, however, there is one channel in the heart called the "carrier of the mind" (manovāhā).
It resides with its basis in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and emits semen produced by conceptualization (kalpa).
Semen is said to be of many kinds; that which has gone to the eyes is fiery (taijasa). That which is in the form of a fluid in the ears is indeed the grasper of sound.
Thus, it has entered the abode of the other sense organs and bestows power upon them.
Likewise, oil resides in water, and ghee in milk;
yet that very same substance, in the form of semen, is produced through intense churning.

Even in a dream, that portion of *rajas* produced by the mind and born of volition likewise occurs; however, the semen, having been discharged with force, enters [the womb] even when devoid of strength.
Indeed, there are three seeds of semen: food, its essence (*rasa*), and the mind-carrying [channel]. (16)

Having understood these three, one should repeatedly relax this triad. Then, through the non-production of semen, one fully cultivates the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya). The mind is the subtlest part of that which is to be consumed; therefore, it is the most nourishing.

Having indeed rendered it free from latent impressions (vāsanā), one should conquer that mind through dispassion (virāga). The mind, becoming luminous and stainless, attains the state of its own true nature;
having turned away from being composed of passion (rajas), it becomes composed of purity (sattva).
And that which is permeated by the nature of being becomes existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
To the extent that this [state] shines forth as something recently attained and characterized by passion (rājasa),
one should practice the yoga of meditation for the sake of its dissolution.
One-pointed practice must be performed; by that, youth dissolves. Having reached a state of ripeness, it becomes devoid of strength.
Then, having taken refuge in the Self, one becomes endowed with the power of the living Self.
Then, having cast off the self, it does not go anywhere to the sense objects;
nor does it approach the senses, nor the wonders of the Lord and so forth, nor the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), nor speed and the like, nor *māyā*, nor its qualities. (23–24)
When one's own mind becomes thus devoid of momentum, then,
having transcended the extremely difficult path that follows the kingdom of the qualities,
it reaches the supreme path belonging to the realm of the Self.
And by transcending the path up to the boundary, one partakes of the nectar in the Imperishable.
For one who lives in this manner, the world of Brahman is held in the palm of the hand;
indeed, for one devoted to celibacy (brahmacarya), the world of Brahman exists right here.
Embodied beings who are attached to the objects of the senses sink down during their existence;
but those who are unattached and whose nature is Brahman go to my supreme abode.
Having seen the continuous creation [afflicted] by birth, death, old age, and so forth—
One who is pervaded by the sufferings of mental anguish, physical disease, and affliction should strive for liberation.
Having united the aggregate of the body and senses, as well as the internal organs, with the Lord of Śrī, the devotee should wander happily, free from all expectations. (2.227.29–30)
One who desires liberation should not, even out of compassion, form an attachment to the mind;
for one should practice equanimity toward attachment, knowing that the world is the fruit of such attachment.
Even while remaining an active practitioner of action, one should proceed having abandoned the fruits of attachment.
The liberated soul is not bound at all, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. He who possesses forgiveness and straightforwardness, and is free from malice, shall be happy.
Having known the escape from suffering, he who escapes it shall be happy.
One should not harbor ill-will, nor covet, nor contemplate what is improper or evil.
One should indeed meditate upon the Supreme Brahman and listen to the nectar of my teachings. One should speak words free from malice and follow the dharma of Kṛṣṇa.
One should utter the name of Śrī Hari and contemplate its supreme meaning.
One should avoid that which brings about misfortune and leads to the hells.
Recognizing it as contrary to one's true nature, one should abandon all that pertains to worldly existence.
Free from worldly effort and thus constantly liberated from all possessions, wandering in solitude, observant of discipline, and having burnt away his sins with the fire of knowledge,
he— becoming self-possessed and steadfast— should seek the light within the heart.
Where the gods shine, there Brahman shines.
Having thus attained this state, one is born for the realization of Brahman;
or else, one should practice the great function of yoga very gradually.
Having established restraint over food, one should likewise establish restraint over thought;
having attained the increase of meditation, one should acquire the light of one's own self.
When joined with the light of knowledge, the light of the self flourishes.
Mixed with the light of devotion, it shines forth like the sun.
First possessing the light of the deity, then becoming the illuminator of the self, thereafter it becomes self-luminous; such a one is indeed beloved by Kṛṣṇa. (41–42)

Thus, having traversed the higher heavens by way of the path of light, he becomes eternally the light of consciousness, for he possesses the light of Brahman. When the swan, endowed with qualities, beautiful, and possessing a further shore, is its own master; ॥43॥
Free from passion and knowing the path to liberation, he shall indeed come to me, the Lord.
Having transcended the qualities (guṇas) and conquered old age and death, he reaches the city composed of Māyā;
he attains that which is the imperishable nectar, the eternal Brahman.
All this is eternally attainable through celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
One who desires celibacy must completely abandon sleep, for sleep destroys the vow.
When the mind is overcome by passion (*rajas*), it becomes distracted and ensnared by sleep.

When the state of *rajas* is weakened, agitation (*vyagratā*) comes to an end. There arises tranquility (*śānti*), characterized by the predominance of the function of *sattva*, and a sense of heaviness;
through that, there is the onset of sleep, for one sleeps even by means of the function of knowledge (*jñānavṛtti*). (47–48)
When the functioning of saṃsāra dissolves, the dream state becomes utterly remote.
Therefore, becoming intent upon Brahman, one shall attain the supreme Brahman.
Whatever the mind conceives with a serene heart, [that it attains].

Having attained those respective impressions, one remembers [Me] again and again. Even among those of a sattvic nature, one should contemplate Me as the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord, abiding within the Self of all beings; by that, one shall attain Me in the higher state.
The devotee, desiring with his mind my yoga which brings happiness,
as well as self-clarification, gentleness, and the vision of the gods within the heart,
attains through such constant practice the purification of those impressions by the gods.
Then, seeing those established within the heart, Brahman shines forth.
They call that very thing celibacy (brahmacarya) which is abiding in Brahman,
as well as abiding among the virtuous beings created by Brahman.
That Brahman is the supreme knowledge and the realization of the immortal, imperishable;
having known one's own self in this way, they go to the highest goal.
To abandon illusion (māyā), one should know the imperishable through wisdom for the sake of liberation.
Having completely abandoned worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), one becomes imperishable and shall go to the Imperishable.
Activity leads to rebirth; cessation (*nivṛtti*) is the supreme goal.
The dharma characterized by cessation bestows Brahman and grants eternal liberation.
One desiring to attain divine splendor should remember me, the Lord of Śrī, within the heart.
For the sake of attaining me, one should perform penance through my yoga with total devotion.
Celibacy and non-violence are considered the austerity of the body.

Constant mindfulness of Me and the restraint of the mind—that indeed is mental austerity (mānasa-tapas). Through My grace, this austerity is truly the most excellent, for it destroys sin. Furthermore, the churning away of latent impressions (vāsanā) from the intellect is considered the highest austerity. (2.227.60)
The steadfastness of consciousness in the Self is declared to be the supreme austerity;
and constant effort for the sake of my yoga is the highest austerity.
He whose intellect is unimpeded by other dull-witted beings who are different from me—
Having attained an existence equal to that of Brahmā, he shall indeed follow after me.
That which is the course in the creation of Māyā does not exist in the supreme creation;
there he rejoices through divine states such as the qualities of self-knowledge.
At the end of their lives, some men here worship the existent (Sat); some worship the Self as the imperishable state;
and others, indeed, worship Me, the Supreme God, at the time of departure.
All these beings of other natures attain the supreme goal.
They obtain the body of Brahmā, which is liberated and free from grasping.
Endowed with my wisdom and intent upon my propitiation, they reach this state.
Having obtained my supreme refuge, they go to the highest goal;
having attained the supreme knowledge and become one with Brahman, they go to the highest goal.
Worshipping according to their own nature, all go to the highest goal.
Free from passions, tranquil, and devoted to me as their refuge,
they are liberated from the afflictions of the gunas and attain the supreme goal—
the divine Lord Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the unborn Bhagavān. (68–69)
Having known Me and Hari as abiding within themselves, those endowed with pure love and satisfied by that state go unto Me; they do not return, for they are imperishable.
Those who take refuge in Me, or in My holy persons who are portions of Myself—
Having attained that supreme abode, they rejoice in the imperishable and immutable.
The entire world, bound by craving, revolves like a wheel;
for one by whom the thread of craving has been burnt, there is the seeking of my abode.
Just as a weaver passes the thread through cloth with a needle,
so too is the thread of saṃsāra extended by the needle of craving.
Therefore, the person liberated from that [craving] goes even to Me through devotion.
"Out of affection, I shall lead him by means of a celestial chariot to my own abode.
Having thus instructed them, the Blessed One then paused for a moment;
thereafter, Śrī Hari himself bestowed the mantra upon the newcomers, O Rādhikā.
He brought the assembly to a close and performed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*).
And at night, all those who had gathered for the sacrifice took their meal. During the festivities, there were entertainments everywhere throughout the night.

Śrī Hari, served by Brahmā, his beloved consort, and others, went to sleep. (77) In the camps of those who had come for the sake of the sacrifice, actors and others performed excellent dances at night, illustrating his previous incarnations. (78)
The wrestlers engaged in a wrestling match employing many maneuvers.
In the music pavilion, the singing of singers took place;
in some places, however, there were discourses and narrations by the learned.
In the pavilion during the night, there were the poetic compositions and historical narratives of the bards, panegyrists, heralds, wandering minstrels, and learned scholars;
and in another place, there were the songs accompanied by dance performed by courtesans.
At that time, in the assemblies of the royal class during the night,
there occurred in certain places the songs and dances of gods, goddesses, celestial women,
and the Apsarases of Brahma’s lake.
In some places, indeed, there are great festivals for the creations of the Lord;
in other places, there are various amusements that delight the Dānavas and Daityas, as well as games that signal the onset of festivities. (83–84)
Manifestations appeared for the worlds, as well as for beasts,
birds, women, men, and all embodied beings; in some places, they appeared for forest creepers, trees, grasses, and leaves.
There were displays of various fruits and palanquins;
in some places, there were likewise displays of works of craftsmanship made from wood, stone, and clay, as well as cotton, diamonds, silk, bark, and wool. (86–87)
Likewise, there were visions of elephants, horses, cattle, lions, as well as śarabhas, garuḍas, and camels;
and visions of reṇḍīyas, swans, and parrots.
And he saw sights of armies, of queens, and of wild animals—
such new things arising from many lands, and whatever other objects were produced by the multitude of people. (2.227.89–90)
O auspicious lady, at that time all those things consisting of the arts, those which are primary causes, and others consisting of mechanical devices,
were displayed there on the ground extending for a *gavyūti* by the guardians.
Thus the entire sixth night passed, filled with great enthusiasm.
Then, when half [of it] had elapsed, the people were happily absorbed in sleep. Then, on the morning of the seventh day, various kinds of musical instruments were sounded. (92–93)
There were auspicious recitations, songs, and likewise the praises of the panegyrists; there were the sounds produced by musical instruments,
the chanting of the Vedas by the Brahmins, and the true worship of the virtuous.
The songs of the women were filled with the glory of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
the songs of the goddesses consisted of narrations and accounts of divine deities; and the songs of the sovereign ladies then became recitations of remaining stories. (95–96)
Even though they were sleepless throughout the night, having embraced great joy,
they attained silence, peace, and cessation during the period called night.
And at dawn, [they were awakened] by various auspicious sounds and the like.
Having become composed, they then performed their ablutions and completed their daily religious rites.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari, having bathed, performed his daily rites, and completed his worship, Kṛṣṇa prostrated himself at the feet of his own parents. || 98–99 ||
Then the king and others, having accomplished their purpose, arrived at the great palace, the auspicious abode of Śrīnivāsa, to worship Hari.
With affection they worshipped Śrī Hari and indeed drank the water from His feet.
The assembled nobles performed the *ārārtrika* ceremony in the palace;
having offered handfuls of flowers and bowed down, they were accompanied by words of blessing.
Likewise, the fortunate queens, having likewise worshipped him, [did the same].
The Lord himself arrived at the sacrificial pavilion,
and the sages, the performers of ritual acts, and the deities likewise came there.
O Rādhikā, all the oblations, the fuel-sticks, and the deities of the mantras were present.
All the sacrificial fires also arrived there in the pavilion.
Then, indeed, the sacrificial rite began from the very start,
proceeding with vigilance according to its previous sequence in the sacrifice.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Evening Instruction and Feeding on the Sacrificial Ground on the Sixth Day, and the Arrival at the Sacrificial Pavilion on the Seventh Day in the Morning," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 227. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 228 [Author:
Chapter 229 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the morning of the seventh day, during the most excellent *muhūrta*,
the sacrificial rites were performed by Lomaśa and others, just as they had been on the previous day;
likewise, the sprinkling, the recitation of blessings, and the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) were carried out.
The awakening of the deities and their worship according to the prescribed rules; the waving of lights (ārātrika), the offering of bali, the great food offerings (mahānaivedya);
likewise, the offering of water, the offering of betel-leaf, and the libations for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa). || 2–3 ||
Furthermore, there were oblations into the fire for all [the deities] to receive their sacrificial offerings;
the waving of lamps before the gods; and for the brahmins, the distribution of ritual fees and so forth.
Then followed the offering of handfuls of flowers and the ritual circumambulation, occurring in due order.
When the task had thus been completed by the kings acting as sacrificers,
then, by the command of Śrī Hari, all those foremost among the great and honored ones partook of the sacrificial offerings and sweet foods.
Tens of thousands of people belonging to the lowly classes enjoyed themselves there;
then, having found rest in the evening, the assembly gathered.
There sat the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇasvāmī, the sovereign Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Devoted to compassion, he issued instructions for the welfare of all creatures:
"I am the sacrifice and the Supreme Brahman; fire, however, is considered my mouth.
Through that mouth, I swallow and consume all the oblations."
In my body, at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), the imperishable abode shines forth.
All liberated souls reside in my hair; those who are liberated yet distinct from them are upon my eyebrows.
[They are likewise] in my mouth, eyes, cheeks, jaws, and ears.
All the incarnations also dwell in my beard, and they all reside upon my head. The female incarnations dwell in my chin and the bridge of my nose;
and in my throat dwell the Lordly manifestations, Vāsudeva and the others.
That which is proclaimed as Mahāmāyā, Prakṛti, Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Kāla, Bhūman, Puruṣa, Mahāviṣṇu, Rudra, Sadāśiva, and Virāj resides upon the shoulders and back. (13)
All these, however, dwell at my sides, residing in my belly.
These sovereign goddesses, the great deities, and the great Lakṣmīs— the Śrīs—
are all female powers who reside in the region of my chest.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as millions of perfected beings (siddhas) and lords,
dwell with their wives within my navel and my belly.
The sages, the ancestors, and the gods dwell in my hips.
Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas dwell within the secret hairs;
the gods, beginning with Kāma, reside in the secret [parts]; and the kings characterized by passion (rājasa) dwell there as well.
On the hips reside the Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and tens of millions of Pretas and Piśācas.
In my two thighs dwell the Mānavas and others, and in my two knees the Cāraṇas and others;
indeed, the Daityas and others, as well as the Talavāsas, reside in my two shanks.
Furthermore, serpents, nāgas, and reptiles dwell in my feet and hoods.
Trees, creepers, and the like dwell within my pores;
insects, moths, locusts, birds, and likewise beasts always dwell all around me, situated within the cavities of my body.
Thus, all creations—both insentient and sentient—dwell within me;
when I am satisfied, all those whose self is me are satisfied.
Having worshipped me, the Supreme Lord, in the great sacrifice of Viṣṇu, ||| 22 ||
Whoever feeds my devotees obtains the fruit born of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whoever, having worshipped me as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa during the ritual, feeds the twice-born,
shall obtain here the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Whoever worships me in this sacrifice as Kāṃbhareya Bālakṛṣṇa and feeds the virtuous, for him there is the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
One should worship me here in this sacrifice as Gopālabāla Govinda.
One should feed virtuous and chaste women, for that yields the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice.
Likewise, one should worship me, known as Puruṣottama, in this sacrifice;
he who feeds children shall obtain the fruit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Whoever worships me, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, in a sacrifice,
and likewise feeds the helpless, shall obtain the fruit born of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Whoever worships me, the Lord of Brahmapriyā, here in this sacrifice in that same manner—
He who feeds young maidens shall obtain the fruit of [feeding] a thousand cows.
He who worships me, the beloved of Piśaṅgī, with devotion here at this sacrifice,
and feeds Brahmins and ascetics, shall obtain the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
One should worship me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhāmāṇikī;
having fed the cowherds and cowherd-maidens, one shall attain the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
Likewise, one should worship me, the Lord of Prabhā and Pāravatī, during the sacrifice.
And by feeding the honored guests, one obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
Whoever worships me, the Lord of Gaurī, with devotion during this rite, shall attain the fruit of the Rudrayāga; indeed, by feeding those proficient in ritual action, one gains that same merit.
Whoever worships me here in this sacrifice as Amarīsvāmin,
and feeds the Apsarases, shall obtain the fruit of the Brahma-yajña.
Likewise, one should worship me with devotion here in this sacrifice as Brāhmīnātha.
Having fed virtuous Brāhmaṇa women, one obtains the fruit of the Mahārudra rite;
likewise, one should worship Lakṣmī, Svāmin, and me here at this sacrifice.
By feeding Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, one obtains the fruit of Nārāyaṇa. (35–36)
One should likewise worship me, the Lord of Ābrikta, and [the deity] in this sacrifice;
by feeding the water-carriers, one obtains the fruit of a rain-cloud.
One should likewise worship me, the Lord of Uṣṇālī, and [the deity] in this sacrifice.
He who feeds the Pācinīs shall obtain the fruit of the Anna-sacrifice (Annakrata).
Likewise, he who worships me, the Lord of Īśvarī, in this sacrifice,
and feeds the servants of the sacrifice, shall obtain the fruit born of the sacrifice.

Whoever worships and feeds all these at the sacrifice— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the source of all incarnations, the Lord of the liberated, the destroyer of suffering, and the Beloved of Lakṣmī— shall obtain the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
Having gratified me here at this sacrifice while I am present in embodied form within the field of perception, whatever my devotee may desire, all that he shall obtain.
I am the giver and the Lord of all; I bestow everything upon my servant.
In this sacrifice, gifts should be given according to one's capacity to the performer of righteous deeds;
whatever merit is gained here through these gifts shall certainly become inexhaustible.
O householder, in the ritual of sacrifice, [one should offer] that which is adorned with a network of divine tinkling bells.
Having ascended a celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun, he goes to my abode.
Likewise, the gift of various kinds of food, fruits, sacrificial fuel, medicinal herbs, garments, and leaves is also [meritorious]. 44–45.
One who gives becomes long-lived, a partaker of heaven, and thereafter a partaker of liberation.
He who makes a gift of a manuscript of the *Saṃhitā* goes to heaven,
truth, dispassion, liberation, and my imperishable state.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beloved in the home—
each of those should indeed be given for one's own sake by one who desires that very gift to be inexhaustible.
One should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor out of greed.
For the sake of benefit in the next world, a gift should be given to a worthy recipient for the sake of liberation—
to one possessed of learning, to one who is destitute, to a petitioner, and to one endowed with virtuous conduct.
When given to such a virtuous person, that gift becomes inexhaustible and yields great fruit.
My devotees are all-enduring, free from desire, and have conquered their minds;
they are virtuous and intent on the welfare of all beings. What is given to them yields great fruit.
When these virtuous ones are satisfied, they deliver the donors along with thousands of their ancestral lineages.
One should cause temples, dharma-halls, and excellent monasteries to be built solidly.
For as many bricks as are piled there in those temples and other structures,
for that many thousands of years the virtuous person rejoices in the heavens.
The builder of my temple goes to my abode.

Through the consecration [of an image], one attains the state of Brahmā; through the construction of a temple, the station of Īśvara; and through the practice of worship, one reaches the world of Brahmā—of this there is no doubt. (53–54)
Having coated [the image] with lime and other substances, one should carry out its restoration;
one should sweep it, smear it, and serve my image.
One should also have wells, step-wells, and tanks constructed for my sake.
Cows drink the water, as do virtuous men;
indeed, all living beings afflicted by thirst drink there.
And at that abode of holy fords, immeasurable merit is surely produced.
Indeed, leafy trees should be planted all around the palace,
and gardens should also be established for the rest of embodied beings;
likewise, there should be trees useful for their fruit as well as those useful for their flowers.
The consumption of sacrificial fuel and leaves provides enjoyment for the ancestors and the gods.
This merit is indeed infinite; it bestows all prosperity.
When performed with devotion, it leads to my own abode.
Householders, the wealthy, and especially kings,
must always ensure that the sacred ground of the pilgrimage site is provided with sustenance through great festivals.
The sacrificial ground is always meritorious, as is a river or the bank of a river where a sacrifice has been performed.
That earth extending for eight *yojanas* is always considered to be the bestower of liberation.
Even while living here, people indeed have no vision of the messengers of Yama.
For that Vaiṣṇava by whom Manu is upheld here, there is liberation.
Whoever performs worship for me shall also attain liberation.
Whoever has offered a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or food in my sacrifice—
for him I shall effect release and lead him to my imperishable abode.
"O, what a sacrifice!"—thus even a wise man becomes a seeker of virtues.
O Keśava, I shall cause the very ocean of his sins to blaze up, including the garment, the vessel, the milk-rice, and everything else used in that sacrifice. || 65-66 ||
"Whosoever shall bestow this with devotion, I shall lead him to my imperishable abode.
He shall perform the gift of a cow, the gift of the earth, and the gift of a house;
likewise, the gift of a daughter, the gift of a son, and even the gift of a youth."

Whoever shall perform here at this sacrifice the gift of gold, the gift of silver, the gift of vehicles and mounts, the gift of groves and gardens, the gift of umbrellas, and the offering of elephants— to him I shall lead to the imperishable state. (68–69)

Whoever, with a devoted heart, shall offer themselves, as well as offerings to Brahman and to the guru, and whatever else they can according to their ability in this sacrifice, to him I shall grant the imperishable state. (2.228.70)

Having spoken thus, O Rādhā, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa then bestowed Vaiṣṇava mantras upon the human participants there. Thereafter, Hari performed the twilight rituals and offered the evening worship to the gods.
Īśāna, Pāna, Śiṣṭa, and the others, as well as the kings and others,
performed the *ārārtika* ceremony for Śrī Hari and offered handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
They also fed the subjects and the great men who had assembled there.
The people and others provided food for the gods who were worthy of sacrifice and skilled in ritual action, as well as for all embodied beings,
for the guests who had come out of curiosity to observe, and for those who had arrived and then departed. (74–75)
They caused the families of Hari to be provided with an abundance of various kinds of sweet foods and other delicacies appropriate for each creation.
Furthermore, those lords fed all the inhabitants of every created world.
Then they gave sweet drinks and betel leaves.
Thereafter, there were narrations of stories at night and indeed performances;
then all embodied beings truly became fond of sleep during the night.
Having rested as was appropriate, they quickly awoke at dawn amidst auspicious sounds of musical instruments, the songs of celestial women, and the singing of the praises of bards,
panegyrists, and heralds on all sides.
On the morning of the eighth day of the month of Rādhika, Hari himself awoke.
Having performed his daily rites and offered worship, he honored his own parents;
and all the others, beginning with Brahmā and Lakṣmī, worshipped Lord Hari.
Śrī Hari, having bowed to Lomaśa, then received his words of blessing.
The kings, the royal servants, and the queens worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord,
with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and drank the nectar of His feet.
Then, after a short while, having heard the auspicious sound of musical instruments,
Hari went to the pavilion at the site of the sacrifice accompanied by his devotees. Hari, as well as the kings and the ritual experts, performed the rites of purification.
Tens of millions of other goddesses and tens of millions of incarnations of Īśvara,
as well as humans, sages, gods, ancestors, immovable beings, and moving beings— both men and women— quickly arrived at the pavilion. (84–85)
The ritual ingredients in the form of oblations, the fires that carry the oblations, the givers of oblations,
and the sacrificers all assembled there at that sacrifice.
The Brahmins who performed the rites, the Vedas, the musical notes, and the chants were also present.
And all the subjects of Kāśyapa arrived there at the pavilion.
There, the sprinkling of water, the recitation of benedictions, the declarations of an auspicious day, and the ritual invocation of the deities accompanied by mantras took place. (87–88)
One should perform the ritual bathing and worship with leaves, flowers, unbroken grains, and other such materials;
likewise, with all the auspicious services (upacāras), including incense, lamps, and so forth;
as well as the waving of lights (ārātrika), the food offering (naivedya), and the drinking water at that time.
The offering of betel leaves and other items became like the presentation of a great oblation;
at that time, the offering of sacrificial butter into the fire became even more abundant than before.
There was also the offering of cooked rice (caru), the giving of milk-rice and other foods, and the presentation of fruits.
In this manner, offerings were presented as far as the Pradehis;
thereafter, there was abundant libation for the satisfaction of the ancestors (Pitṛs),
as well as for the Goddesses, the Mothers (Mātṛkās), and the Sovereign Ladies (Īśvarīs).
There was indeed a *śrāddha* ceremony and a libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the *śaktis* and the *vāminīs*.
Then, after the three worlds had been heated by it, Śrī Hari performed the concluding rite (*parihāra*) of the sacrifice; thereafter, the meals were served. (93–94)
At the time of the post-noon meal, all the people partook of various kinds of sweet foods that were like nectar and ambrosia;
likewise, they enjoyed divine flavors and auspicious, celestial elixirs. (95)

The gods dwelling in the three worlds drank and enjoyed the supreme, excellent juices of the Brahman, the juices of the light-worlds, and the juices of the perfected ones (siddha-rasa). Having obtained this food, they were satisfied; thereafter, they partook of the drinking water.
They partook of buttermilk and fruit thereafter;
having taken betel-leaf, they rested in their quarters.
Then, in the evening, Bālakṛṣṇa arrived at the assembly hall.
Hari gave his own instruction to the subjects, O Rādhikā.

(99) Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Sacrificial Duties on the Seventh Day, the Instruction by Śrī Hari on His Being the Soul of All and Other Matters, the Meal, the Night Festival, and Then the Completion of the Sacrificial Duties and the Meal on the Morning of the Eighth Day," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, how Mādhava instructed the worlds:
renunciation alone is considered by Him to be the bestower of supreme happiness for all. (1)
Abandoning is indeed renunciation, as is the act of distancing oneself;
even non-appropriation is, in fact, renunciation in its true sense.
Through the renunciation of craving comes great peace; through the renunciation of desire comes cessation.
Through the renunciation of material possessions comes the cessation of karma; through the renunciation of enjoyments arises the vow.
Through the renunciation of pleasure one attains austerity; through the renunciation of everything comes liberation.
Indeed, the path of renunciation leads to the complete abandonment of sufferings. (3–4)
Wherever and by whatever means suffering may arise, one should abandon each of those and become happy.
Having abandoned illusion (māyā) and transcended the qualities (guṇas), one becomes filled with the bliss of Brahman.
Through the conjunction of the qualities, there arise states of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Upon the abandonment of the qualities (guṇas), there occurs for the self the destruction of the state of being conditioned by those qualities.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the means for [experiencing] cold, heat, and glowing coals; likewise, exhilaration, affection, bliss, happiness, and tranquility of mind [are the effects]. (6–7)

These arise as *sāttvika* from detachment or from the attainment of what is desired: discontent, remorse, grief, greed, and likewise intolerance. These arise as *rājasa* from passion or from the attainment of what is disliked.

Lack of discernment, as well as delusion, negligence, sleep, and lassitude—these arise from the quality of darkness (tamas), whether through dullness or the confusion of the intellect. When those characterized by goodness (sattva) abandon what is desired, their dissolution occurs. (2.229.10)
Upon the abandonment of aversion, there is the dissolution of those characterized by passion (rājasa);
upon the abandonment of delusion, there is the dissolution of those characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
Thus, through the relinquishing of the three qualities (guṇas), one abides beyond the qualities.
The conscious being spontaneously realizes its own nature as truth, consciousness, and bliss.
This being so, at that time it truly possesses no form, name, or shape;
nor does it possess the ego born of form, name, and shape, nor even the sense of "mine-ness."
Upon the renunciation of those two, the state of liberation arises for the conscious being;
he is not smeared by actions at all, nor is he bound, but is liberated.
The firm fetters arising from his body and senses have passed away.
When those [impurities] arising from the internal organ have departed, then one becomes liberated while still on the path.
Possessing immediate experience, he transcends the fear of time and death;
devoid of the provisions of merit and demerit, he is free from the fruits [of karma].
Having attained the Self that is the ether of consciousness, one rejoices in the space of consciousness;
for like a spider, once released from its own web, one is truly free. Indeed, he is just like a stone fallen from a mountain, entirely devoid of bondage.
The old horn of Ruru was cast off, yet it did not lead to bondage for him.
Just as the sloughed-off, worn-out skin of a snake does not lead to bondage, so too the cast-off tail-feather of a peacock does not lead to bondage. (18–19)
Just as a tree falling into a river is abandoned by the birds,
so too one who has abandoned the abode of the body is truly liberated and possesses great bliss.
Even while remaining in the body, he who conducts himself by relying on this wisdom [is liberated].
This one who is unattached to the qualities is indeed liberated like one already liberated, possessing great bliss.
(21) Moreover, even while remaining in the world, he conducts himself through the application of the qualities;
for him too, self-restraint is indeed the means for an abundance of happiness. (22)
Action, austerity, happiness, truth—all these are established in self-restraint (*dama*). Self-restraint increases one's vital energy (*tejas*), and it cuts away fear and evil.
(23) One who is self-restrained sleeps in peace and wakes in peace.
Happiness follows one from the worlds, and happiness becomes serene within the heart.
Through self-restraint, the strength of the self increases and good fortune arises. All the fruits of virtuous deeds are established in the self-restrained person who possesses restraint.
These qualities are eternal for the embodied being disciplined by self-restraint:
freedom from meanness, absence of agitation, contentment, faithfulness, absence of anger, straightforwardness, gentleness, lack of excessive speech, and absence of backbiting. (26)
Neither pride nor envy, but compassion and reverence for the guru;
avoidance of public gossip, falsehood, praise, and blame; desiring what is good, free from longing, without enmity, and well-behaved. (27–28)
He was firm in his vows, possessed of virtuous conduct, free from idle chatter, and possessed of a very serene heart.
With a tranquil soul and self-mastery, having conquered his defects, he remained established in self-abidance.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, he harbored no hatred toward anyone else. (29)
Like a great lake, he is unshakeable, satisfied by wisdom, and serene. Possessing self-mastery, he should wander through the worlds awaiting his time, free from calamity.
With such qualities as these, one who is self-controlled is like heaven and like liberation itself. (2.229.30–31)
Worthy of homage by all beings, he rejoices happily like Brahmā.
Renunciation is declared to be the highest austerity; self-restraint is the supreme austerity.
Uprightness is the best of austerities; silence and good character are the highest austerity.
Eating nectar is another austerity, as is serving the virtuous.

(33) For one whose wisdom is perfected, who is self-controlled, free from thirst, and devoid of desire, who is habituated to meditating on Śrī Hari—stability for such a person is the supreme austerity. (34)
Through sincerity, vigilance,
serenity, service, attendance upon the elders, and tranquility, the highest austerity is produced.
Indeed, through the attainment of wisdom, a person destroys all evil.
The deceitful man gains no peace; he who abides in tranquility becomes serene.
One obtains only what is to be obtained, one goes only where it is to be gone, and one experiences only those sorrows and joys that are destined to be experienced.
Having understood this in its entirety, the embodied being who does not become deluded remains forever well-being; he indeed is considered to possess all wealth.
Therefore, having acquired virtues, one should serve the virtuous and avoid the wicked.
"Through association with the virtuous, there shall be an increase in qualities that lead to Brahman.
By this total surrender unto Mādhava, the attainment of Brahman shall occur.
Having spoken thus to the subjects, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa— 2.229.40.
He caused those Vaiṣṇavas to hear [the teachings] correctly and had them perform [the rites].
Then, on the night of the eighth day, having bestowed the instruction,
the Blessed One fed all the honored guests.
He fed the subjects as well as his own family;
having eaten himself, he obtained rest in the sleep of profound yoga.
On the ninth day, amidst auspicious sounds and the songs of bards and panegyrists, ||43||
The Great Lord was awakened by the multitude of songs of praise from the prisoners;
having performed his morning rites, his worship, and the honoring of the elders,
he arrived at the magnificent pavilion of the sacrifice during an auspicious hour.
The king and others, acting as the sacrificers, arrived at the pavilion.
All the sacrificial rites proceeded exactly as before.
At midday, having offered the oblation, the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa—
The Lord caused them all to eat and ate himself;
then, having ascended his celestial chariot in the sky above the ocean at evening,
the Blessed One departed with the kings for the sake of recreation.
Having returned to his own place, Keśava performed the twilight rites (saṃdhyā).
After feeding the people and eating himself, he took rest at night.
On the morning of the tenth day as well, that Supreme Lord performed his daily ablutions.
Having arrived at the sacrificial pavilion together with the patrons,
and having had the great sages perform the rites of the sacrifice as well as the oblations,
he fed the Brahmins at the time of midday after making the offerings.
Then the Lord, the Master, himself enjoyed all the honors;
there he bestowed the *mantras* upon his devotees,
caused the *śrāddha* rites to be performed, and offered abundant libations to the Brahmins.
Having partaken of food at night and obtained rest, Mādhava,
the lord of the gods, rose quickly at dawn on the eleventh day.
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord Hari.
Having performed his daily rites and completed his worship, he quickly went to the pavilion.

Having caused the sprinkling of the materials, the recitation of benedictions (*svastivācana*), and the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) to be performed, as well as the awakening and worship of the gods and others, [he entered]. (54–55)
Then the Blessed Lord offered the animal sacrifice, the great oblation of food, and likewise the handful of flowers;
he performed the fire-sacrifice with various special offerings and gratified the deities with thousands of streams of clarified butter.
Then those gods and others, as well as all things mobile and immobile, having eaten, attained satisfaction through those excellent oblations, appearing visibly before them.
And this [is offered] as an oblation with the words "Salutation" to the Lord of the Imperishable Abode.
We offer these oblations even to those who are already liberated; we praise them. We offer these oblations to all the incarnations; we praise them.
These are the oblations to the Lords; to them, salutations upon salutations.

These offerings are for all the sages; we bow to them. (2.229.60) These offerings are for the ancestors; repeated salutations to them. These offerings are for the gods; repeated salutations to them. (61)

We offer these oblations to those who dwell upon the earth, and we praise them. We offer these oblations to those born of the human race, and we praise them. We offer these oblations to those who dwell on the seven continents, and we praise them.
We praise those [beings] for whom these offerings are made from all trees, as well as from creepers and grasses (63);
we praise those for whom there are offerings even from as much as bulbs, roots, and so forth;
and we praise those for whom these offerings are made from insects, moths, and the like (64).
We offer salutations to all women dwelling within the three worlds;
we offer these salutations even to the elements, both insentient and sentient.
May these oblations offered to you bring satisfaction indeed to all embodied beings.
Thus, having placed the finest clarified butter in the *sruc* ladle, as well as *śrīphala*, fuel sticks,
leaves, flowers, fruits, and sweet offerings of every kind, one should offer the great *pūrṇāhuti*. Having bowed down, one should perform the visualization.
"Agni is Nārāyaṇa himself; to him I offer salutations.
This [offering] is for Agni Vaiśvānara, the Supreme Self.
Having spoken thus, Hari offered the coconut and other items into the fire.
Then the kings also presented him with auspicious fruits and other offerings.
"Salutations to you, the Gārhapatya fire; salutations to you, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
salutations to the Āhavanīya fire and to you who are established upon the great altar."
Salutations to Brahmā as the Gārhapatya fire, to Viṣṇu as the Dakṣiṇāgni,
and to Śiva as the Āhavanīya fire stationed upon the sacrificial altar.
Salutations to you in the form of the Sabhya fire, and salutations to you in the form of the Gṛhya fire.

Salutations to you, the Supreme Self, who takes the form of the five fires. Salutations to you in the form of the Agnihotra sacrifice; salutations to you in the form of the Parva-iṣṭi; salutations to you whose very nature is the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; salutations to you in the form of the Paśu-iṣṭi.
Salutations to you, O Sautrāmaṇi; salutations to you, O Agniṣṭoma.
Salutations to you who take the form of the Atyagniṣṭoma and who possess the form of the Uktha.
Salutations to you who take the form of the Ṣoḍaśin; salutations to you, O Vājapeya.
Salutations to you, whose nature is the Atirātra sacrifice and whose essence is the Sarvamedha.
You are the mouth of all living beings; through you, when consumed, one may satisfy the gods.
That which is considered the creation of individual souls, the creation of the Lord, and the creation of Brahmā [is all you]. (75–76)
You are indeed the provider of satisfaction to them; O consumer of oblations, carry forth the sacrificial offerings.
May the offerings go to all through the utterance of *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and so forth.
Kālī, Karālī, Dhūmrā, Manobhavā, and Sphulliṅginī—
Your tongues are tawny and red; with them, swallow the oblation repeatedly!
(78) Betel nuts and whatever other fruits there were, they then offered into the fire, saying: "May the Supreme Lord be satisfied! (79)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the great lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
then offered the final great *pūrṇāhuti* oblation to the Lord of Śrī.
Having thus performed the *homa*, he made the offering of the vessel to Brahmā.
Śrī Hari performed the consecration of Brahmā as the patron of the sacrifice.
Having performed the consecration with nectar, he then bestowed blessings.
Furthermore, Hari also performed the offering of the sacrificial fee within the pavilion.
The Lord caused gifts of gold, cows, land, sesame seeds, and other such items to be bestowed;
at that time, the kings gave gifts worthy of royalty.
Then, the sages, headed by Lomaśa, performed the consecration ceremony.
Then the sages sang the Pavamāna hymns and uttered blessings;
having bestowed abundant gifts, they likewise gave these benedictions:
"May there be for you divine prosperities, inexhaustible and bestowing eternal happiness. (84–85)
May your family lineages expand and flourish, free from disease;
may you have male and female servants as the cattle of your royal majesty.
May there be long life, divine fame, and at the end, heaven and liberation.
May all objects of enjoyment be yours here at all times.
May all be happy; may all be free from disease.
Having enjoyed heaven for a long time, may they finally attain the imperishable state.
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa and the others offered a handful of flowers to the deities of the sacrifice, and then the ritual dismissal took place.
All partook of the sacrificial remains and the oblations at the rite.
Whatever offerings belonged to whichever [deities],
those very ones Hari-Kṛṣṇa gave to each of them by means of his own powers—
every kind of food, sacrificial oblations, and things like nectar.
He bestowed various kinds of nectar-essences and millions of vessels for drinking ambrosia upon those who were worthy, satisfying as many as there were;
thereafter, he gave even more food to the wandering mendicants.
He gave food to the mendicants and to helpless women;
on the eleventh day, after midday, he gave all kinds of food to everyone, and thereafter he performed the ancestral śrāddha ceremony.
He bestowed many fruits and other offerings, as well as water and other gifts.
In the evening, the Blessed One sat upon an auspicious seat in the assembly hall;
he gave mantras to the people and established them as the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas.
He granted his own divine vision to him who had gone to the imperishable abode;
[a vision] belonging to the Supreme Lord, served by the beloveds of Brahmā and by the liberated souls.
Then, he indeed manifested there once again in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And she proclaimed the majesty of Yajñatīrtha to the people;
O Rādhikā, at that time, the three worlds indeed heard it with joy.

Thus ends the description, in the second section on the Tretā Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, concerning the performance of sacrificial rites and other duties on the ninth, tenth, and eleventh days of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the offering of the great final oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti), the dismissal of the priests, the feast, and so forth.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, those holy places (tīrthas) which resided upon the sacrificial ground—
The illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa spoke of them on the bank of the river Āmrajānī:
"That land where I, Nārāyaṇa, the performer of sacrifice and Supreme Lord, reside,
is equal to the imperishable (akṣara) and is divine, bestowing a divine goal."
The divine river Āmrajāninī, the celestial Gaṅgā born from Badarī,
and the divine Apsaras Āmrajānī were formerly produced by Nara through his own power,
having been kneaded with *āmramañjarikā* flowers.

In former times, Mahendra came to Badarī accompanied by many apsarases for the purpose of ensuring that no obstacles would arise during the practice of asceticism before Śrī Hari. All those dancing women were directed by Nārāyaṇa at the command of Indra.
Then, for the purpose of shattering their pride,
I indeed manifested Urvashi at Badari through Narada;
in her presence, they all then became as if dark-complexioned.
Abandoning their pride in their beauty, they then requested forgiveness from her.
At that time, I indeed transformed them all by means of a Vaiṣṇava mantra;

That [first] one was offered by me to Mahendra in her singular form;
my second daughter, established in celibacy, remains in my presence.
She dwells indeed at Badarī, while here she exists in the form of water.
She has arrived for the purpose of bestowing the fruits of the Pārāka penance she performed.

For the sake of satisfying his ancestors and for the sake of water, he also prepared [an offering];

Immersed in meditation with great devotion, he praised my form.
With a serene heart, I remembered my daughter who had taken refuge in me.
By my command, that daughter of mine then became the very form of water;
having manifested as seven streams, she became Brāhmī upon the earth.
Wherever the ancestors went by the flow [of the river],
there they were liberated and they attained the imperishable state.
This very divine Āmrajanī river exists as a bestower of liberation.
Her forms here are seven, the most excellent among those born of the Āmra tree.
The second is proclaimed as Rākāntikāsanā;
the third is Gonikaṣā, and the fourth is Goyājñī.
The fifth is Mādvārikā, and the sixth is considered to be Sāpuruṣā;
the seventh is Mānāsanā, for all of them indeed bestow liberation.
This city is Śāntārāmā, and the town is Pāreśvara.
The confluence of the Āmrajānī and the ocean is always a bestower of liberation.
Indeed, this confluence is the cleanser of great sins and even the most heinous crimes.
On this earth, it is the foremost among sacrifices, sacred fords, and likewise among mountains.
"Since I have already ordained the dwelling of Mount Meru and other peaks, as well as of lakes and rivers, let the holy fords (tīrthas) indeed dwell here.
Let the six other rivers dwell here at their confluences with the Āmrajā."
"Let the liberated ones, as well as the incarnations, the lords, and the gods dwell here;
let the goddesses, the powers (śaktis), the oceans, and the rivers likewise have their residence here—let this place be the abode of all sacred fords (tīrthas). Such was the command.
The site of Bālakṛṣṇa lies between Śāntārāma and Pāreśvara;
it is indeed the abode of all sacred fords (tīrthas) and is as pure as the imperishable Brahman.
As far as the earth extends between Goyājanyā and Gavākṣā, [so great is its extent].
Extending for three hundred *krośas*, it is entirely auspicious and bestows liberation.
(25) By bathing here—in the step-well, the well, or the pond—a person shall attain release; by drinking the water of the rivers, one shall go to my abode. (26)
By the act of giving even a small amount of food, one obtains the fruit born of sacrifice;
by the gift of a cow and the gift of gold, one attains heaven—of this there is no doubt.
The gift of a daughter, the gift of land, the gift of clothing, and the offering of a cow [yield similar results].
He will perform the gift of ornaments, the gift of food, and the gift of vessels;
on this earth, he shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. Furthermore, there shall be the giving of medicinal herbs, the gift of knowledge, and the offering of water.
The gift of liquids, the gift of an umbrella,
the gift of utensils, the gift of a house, the gift of vehicles, and the gift of knowledge—
he who performs these shall obtain here the fruit of all sacrifices.
That person who causes the planting of trees, the giving of fruit, the construction of a dharma-hall,
an altar, a house, a mansion, or a landing-place on a river—
his attainment of heaven shall be certain, and in the end, even liberation shall be his.
What is given here at an auspicious time and to a worthy recipient becomes inexhaustible.
By giving a bed, a grass mat, or a gift of woolen cloth,
one shall attain heaven and prosperity in this world.
There are various royal enjoyments and the prosperity of an expanding lineage.
Those people who, at this sacred ford (tīrtha) where the seven rivers flow, shall drink the water and perform their ablutions, will go to heaven.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari ceased there, O Rādhikā.
The Lord and the others, who are the very embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites, returned to their own abodes.
At that very moment, the seven rivers arrived there as young maidens.
With sandalwood and other offerings, they worshipped their father Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. Bowing at his feet, they said, "May you always dwell here.
The self-effulgent Lord himself, in the form of that very image, replied, "So be it, O Hari! (37–38).
From that time forth, Śrī Hari Acyuta always resided in those very temples and bestowed golden images upon the kings.
Those maidens, who were themselves embodiments of sacred pilgrimage sites, returned to their own homes.
Then the kings also built palaces on the riverbank;
in those [palaces], the monarchs installed golden images according to the prescribed rites.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, [resided].
Then, having instructed him, he bestowed as rewards large golden platters, water-pots made of gold,

Golden garlands, earrings, chains, and bracelets;
gold and jewels, ornaments, golden threads, and garments;
vessels made of gold, diamonds, and excellent gems, as well as water-pots. 43–44.
He indeed bestowed as rewards such things as garments, shawls, bodices of silk, golden ornaments,
vehicles, mounts, male servants, female servants,
and likewise finger-rings. ||45||
Then, at the sacrifice, he bestowed expressions of gratitude upon those of high honor;
he also joined those who had assisted in the ritual with blessings.
There, during that night, there were meals of milk-rice and fruits.
Indeed, the Blessed One caused all those festivities to take place there;
and at the conclusion of the celebration of dance and song, the Supreme Lord rested.
The Blessed One fell asleep and woke in the morning with auspicious sounds.
Having performed his daily rites and offered worship, and having attended upon his parents, he sat down upon his seat. Then the kings and others arrived there;
they performed the worship of Śrī Hari and placed their offerings before Him.
Then, on the twelfth day, the Lord himself fed them all various kinds of sweet foods, juices, drinks,
and many sorts of edibles and delicacies in every way.

Having performed his bath and daily rites, Kṛṣṇa sat down upon an excellent seat. Then, the King, the Queen, and the princesses— having partaken of the remnants of the food offered to Īśāna— arrived there in the morning to worship Hari.

afterwards, the monarch bestowed parting gifts upon them.
Seated in their celestial chariots, the kings departed for their own respective lands.
There, on the thirteenth day, the illustrious King Rāyapati,

Hari was honored and worshipped with *brāhmī* leaves, parched grains, and other offerings; and being made to hear shouts of "Victory!", he ascended his own celestial chariot along with his family and the great sages, Śaṅkara, and others. Then he ascended his celestial chariot and proceeded ahead through the sky;
by the king's command, the sounds of the mechanical engines resounded intensely.

at the city of Vyenojarāśā in the vast Mahodyāna park.

people ran about from all sides with eagerness to behold him.
By the path shown by the king, Śrī Hari’s celestial chariot descended to the earth.

The Supreme Lord, having been honored with unbroken rice and other offerings by the subjects,
placed a golden garland around Kṛṣṇa’s neck and bowed down.

having granted them his vision, he rose from the throne at the crossroads.
The king joyfully approached that well-adorned, noble elephant;
he then settled the family of Śrī Hari upon elephants and other mounts, while the women were placed upon carts and vehicles as was appropriate. || 95–96 ||
He seated him upon palanquins as well as divine litters;
then, greatly magnified by the sounds of musical instruments,
songs, shouts of joy, cries of "Victory!", and the chanting of bards.
In the city of Vyenojarāśā, the illustrious Lord Hari was surrounded on all sides:
at the gateway by the nobles, throughout the city by the leading citizens, in the courtyards by the common folk, and at the front of the marketplaces by the wealthy merchants. (98–99)
And the beloved of Kṛṣṇa was honored at the front of the street by women with gifts of gold coins and the like, as well as coconuts and other fruits,
garments, vessels, ornaments, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and water. (2.230.100)
Having been honored throughout the city and having paraded his army in splendor,
Hari then arrived at the royal palace, that auspicious abode.
After drinking water, the protector of dharma took his rest.
Having taken his meal, Keśava, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is served by Brahmā, Lakṣmī, and others, went to sleep at night. (103)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Residence and Greatness of the Divine Tīrthas in the Seven Rivers beginning with Āmrajānī, the Avabhṛtha Bath, the Reward, the Passing of the Night, the Morning Farewell, the Removal of the Mahīmāna Pavilion and other items, and then the King’s Departure for his Kingdom, his Wandering in Vyenojarāśāpurī, Eating, and Sleeping at Night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 230. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (Tretā-yuga-santāna).
Chapter 231 [Author:
Chapter 232 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the morning of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, O Rādhā,
Bālakṛṣṇa was awakened by auspicious sounds of musical instruments and songs; having performed his ablutions and worship, he took his seat upon his throne.
The lord of kings and birds approached to worship Kṛṣṇa.
He bowed with devotion at His feet and then performed the consecration of those feet with water; thereafter, he drank the nectar of His grace.
Together with his family, he applied a sandalwood tilaka to that Lord of Śrī; likewise, he placed collyrium with a moon-design upon His beautiful eyes.
He also placed a crown upon His head and earrings upon His ears.
She placed upon his neck necklaces rich with gold and jewels, as well as chains;
on his arms, bracelets and rings for the fingers; and on his waist and at his ankles, a girdle and anklets. (5–6)
The king honored the Blessed Lord, the husband of Ramā;
he then anointed his limbs with fragrant sandalwood paste and other unguents,
and offered fragrant flower garlands as was appropriate.
The king put on a beautiful royal costume.
(8) Hari joyfully assumed [the guise] for the sake of increasing the king's affection.
Then the king, accompanied by the queen, performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*). (9)
Thirty-three maidens performed the great *nīrājana* ceremony for him;
the charming girls placed the bridegroom’s garland upon the chest of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having obtained the Lord as their husband, they then became fulfilled.

Having seated him upon a beautiful golden lion-throne honored by kings, the king placed the royal crown upon the head of Śrī Hari. "O Kṛṣṇa! This kingdom and these maidens are bestowed upon you for the sake of your liberation."
From this moment forth, we are your kingdom and your male and female servants.
O Blessed One, ocean of mercy, supreme beyond the supreme, remain right here!
You are considered the Self, the inner self, and the supreme self, the Lord.
O Viṣṇu, Lord of all living beings, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra! (14) The kingdom granted by you has been administered by me until the completion of the sacrifice;
now, O Blessed Lord, Master, come and bear the burden yourself. (15)

I shall obey your command like a servant; remain as the protector of the kingdom. By our good fortune, the Blessed One has been obtained by us without effort through his grace—He for whose sake yogis undergo austerities difficult to accomplish. (16)
Even though they perform fire-sacrifices for the sake of their own longevity, you are not attained by them.
(17) Even though the perfected ones (siddhas), absorbed in meditative concentration, constantly worship you, nevertheless, you do not become visible to their eyes. (18)
O Lord, this very person has come here to my house without performing penance, solely by Your grace,
for the sake of my own liberation and that of my family members.
Therefore, having surrendered everything into Your hands, I shall have fulfilled my purpose.
"O Blessed One, accept this kingdom given by me; grant me liberation.
I have recognized you as one of divine form yet acting in human fashion; you are the source of all incarnations, the Supreme Lord described in the Vedas. (2.231.20–21)
O Lord of Brahmapriyā, you who are indeed the Lord of the female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; O Kṛṣṇa, beloved of Lakṣmaṇī, you who are the Lord of the red-complexioned women, protect me!
O Kṛṣṇa, beloved of the dark-complexioned women, O Lord, you who are the Lord of the tawny-complexioned women!
O Lord of the Prācīnīs, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of the Hāritīs, protect me!
O Beloved of the Gaurīs, O Blessed One, O Lord of the immortals, O All-pervading One!
O Lord of those merged in Brahman, O Lord of the perfected ones, O Lord of Rādhā, protect me! (23–24)
O Lord of Lakṣmī, ocean of mercy, Master of Ramā, Lord of the virtuous,
King of the gods and others, and Lord of Īśa— protect me!
Those two feet of yours which Kamalā and Lalitā also serve.
O Keśava, by means of great merit, these two divine daughters of mine have been reunited—those who serve Lakṣmī, the destroyer of sorrow, namely Jayā and Mañjulā;
those two divine ones, endowed with excellent qualities, have been united with me, O Nārāyaṇa. ||26-27||
Māṇikyā serves those two who grant liberation, as does her friend Muktā;
the virtuous Padmāvatī and Hāsā also serve those two givers of supreme release.
There are four hundred and ten million others as well.
Indeed, the inhabitants of the three worlds become your maidservants;
even the lords, incarnations, liberated beings, gods, and great seers serve your feet if they are flooded by your grace. (2.231.30)
O Kṛṣṇa, those two purifying feet have been well-attained by me in my home—
those feet upon which former kings made the total surrender of themselves.
Since they have indeed been reached by me, O Lord, please accept me from this point on.
It is capable of driving far away the fear of Mahākāla, the fear of illusion, and the bondage of karma—nothing else can do so; therefore, worship me alone.
O Janārdana, you are the protector of those who have come for refuge; you are the worthy refuge.
O Maheśvara, lift me up as I have fallen into the stream of worldly existence!
By your yoga, my divine kingdom, home, wealth, and so forth,
have become a great sacred place (tīrtha) on earth, equal to the imperishable abode.
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for King Rāya upon this earth, in whose house dwells Śrī Puruṣottama himself, the beloved of the maiden!
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune even for the river Pārīṇasari! || 35-36 ||
Where all sacred fords (tīrthas) come together by your power,
there the great fortune of the lineage of the Ṛṣis and the kingdom flourishes;
where Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord himself, resides.
O Lord, by your presence, the city of Ayodhyā has become free from old age and death;
today it has truly become meaningful, for through your residence it has become the destroyer of all sins and has been rendered devoid of death, old age, and the like. (38–39)
"O Hari, stay here forever; I shall perform service unto you.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself like a staff before Śrī Hari.
Then, O Rādhikā, that queen likewise performed the daṇḍavat prostration to Hari.

Then, on the fourteenth day, he celebrated a most magnificent festival. At that time, the subjects— both women and men— arrived from all directions, even from lands exceedingly far away, for the purpose of witnessing it.
To them Hari gave the mantras as well as the bliss born of his vision;
by means of attracting them entirely into his own form,
he caused them to cultivate a permanent contemplation of the Lord.
The Supreme Lord accepted the excellent worship performed by them;
having bestowed his grace upon them, Keśava satisfied them and granted his own divine vision, which belongs to the Supreme Lord.

Likewise, the omnipresent Lord [manifests] His own form as residing in the Imperishable (akṣara), as staying in Goloka, as going to Vaikuṇṭha, as abiding in the unevolved (avyākṛta), and likewise as dwelling in the nectar (amṛta); furthermore,
as golden and as situated within the orb of fire.
He showed himself in many forms as the Supreme Lord: residing in Viśālā, situated in Śvetadvīpa, dwelling in the Ocean of Milk;
likewise, he manifested as Bālakṛṣṇa in Kuṅkumavāpī, within the range of perception. Thus indeed did he reveal his own self through various manifestations.
By that, those men and women indeed became ones who had accomplished their purpose;
to them, the illustrious Svāmī Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha gave the mantras.
Then the king, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, fed him.
All the queens, their purpose fulfilled, waited upon that husband.
Hari said to the king: "O King, this kingdom is mine without a doubt;
it was entrusted to me by you, and having received it, I now give it back to you."
"By my command, govern this great kingdom as is fitting;
and cause a firm temple with seven peaks to be constructed.
There, indeed, install me together with Śrī in a golden form."
"I shall always remain within the golden image and accept whatever you offer;
O King, worship me at all times and observe my command.
"So be it," the king replied immediately, O Rādhikā. (53–54)
Right there, in her presence, he had a golden image fashioned;
Kṛṣṇa himself entered that place together with Śrī, becoming perceptible to the senses.
Then the king protected her in his own home, and subsequently in the temple.
Thus he settled Hari and served him with the utmost devotion.
On the fourteenth day, at midday, the king fed him;
and at the time of sunset, he performed the ancestral rites on the bank of the Parnā river.
The Blessed One himself performed various *śrāddha* rites;
Keśava brought satisfaction to the ancestors with water, funeral cakes, and other offerings.
Then he performed his twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) and thereafter went to his palace.
During the night, all those maidens attended upon their own husband.
In the morning, Hari was awakened by auspicious songs and the sounding of musical instruments, as well as by hymns of praise; thereafter, he bathed in the waters of the river.
On the day of the new moon, he indeed performed the offering of water to the ancestors;
at the foot of a *plakṣa* tree, he gave water to all created beings.
The ancestors arrived there from the hand of Hari for the sake of satisfaction.
The liberated ones who possess the consciousness of the syllables are the cowherds dwelling in Goloka;
the attendants (pārṣadas) dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, as do those residing in the Unmanifest (avyākṛta). Likewise, there are liberated ones dwelling in nectar (amṛta) and those residing in other Vaikuṇṭhas.
Those established in truth, those designated as Brahman, the Siddhas, and the great seers;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as the sages and the deities;
Aryaman and the other ancestors, the Mātṛkās, and the wives of the ancestors.

Likewise, others dwelling in the realm of Yama and those situated everywhere throughout the three worlds came there for the sake of satisfaction, desiring the waters of Nārāyaṇa. He offered water with his own hands in the form of añjali-offerings to Śrī Hari.
All the ancestors drank [the offerings], and those seeking liberation attained liberation; those established in their stations obtained satisfaction and departed for their own realms, such as heaven.
All those who were then situated in the state of the ancestors attained satisfaction.
Then the illustrious Blessed One returned to his own residence, the palace.
Thereafter, he performed various kinds of ancestral *śrāddha* rites with offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*),
milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and meals of milked rice and other foods.

He gratified them with offerings of fruits, flowers, and grains, along with sugar and other sweet, delicious flavors, as well as with nectar-like delicacies, choice foods, and the simple fare of sages.
Having performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) according to the prescribed rules, he then offered his formal dismissal.
She fed the Brahmins with delicious, pleasing foods; likewise,
she provided for the poor, the helpless, the wretched, virtuous women, holy men, ascetics,
dependents, maidens, boys, and laborers.

The Lord indeed caused all his devotees and servants to be fed; he also fed the king, the royal retinue, and the Vaiśyas devoted to service. By the command of Hari, that king likewise caused them to be fed.
By his grace, Hari indeed partook of that food immediately after midday.
He then established a very great assembly hall and gave this instruction:
"A mother and likewise a father must always be served by householders."
Furthermore, the guru must be served, and one should abide by his command as is appropriate through mind, speech, body, and wealth.
One preceptor (upādhyāya) is said to be equal to ten śrotriyas.
In this world, a father is considered great as being equal to ten preceptors;
the mother who protects her son is ten times more excellent than the father.
Indeed, he was held by the mother in the womb and likewise nurtured by her in childhood.
Because he was united with his wife during her youth, the mother is considered more venerable;
yet the teacher who imparts knowledge is regarded as ten times more venerable than the mother.
He is the one who destroys the bonds of latent impressions and delivers one from birth, death, and old age.
The Guru, who destroys sin, is worthy of worship; he brings about the liberation of the living being.
(2.231.80) Mother, father, and guru are to be honored and worshipped by those who desire their own welfare.
For one by whom these three are worshipped, prosperity shall never fail. (2.231.81)
These three are indeed of divine form, and they are considered to be the three fires.
By him who has performed service to them, the auspicious fruit of birth has been attained.
They are not to be reviled by sons, nor are they ever to be struck.
These three are neither to be feared nor to be nourished here.
He who performs a circumambulation and likewise offers salutations to his mother has, by that act, performed a circumambulation of the entire earth; of this there is no doubt. (83–84)
By whomsoever the father is fully honored, by him Viṣṇu is honored;
and by whomsoever the guru is honored, by him the gods and others are worshipped.
To them, one should give wealth, food, and clothing according to one's ability.
Whatever is appropriate should be sought after in that manner, for all such things must certainly be given.
Those in whose home the three sacred sites reside suffer in vain by visiting external pilgrimage places;
through the service of these three, the merit of all sacrifices is surely attained.
By receiving the blessing of the triad, the obstacles of Yama depart to a great distance;
all kinds of fortunes come from elsewhere into his house.
These three are declared to be the living ancestors for the sake of service.
He by whom these have been served attains a beautiful world hereafter;
he by whom these have been made miserable shall suffer misery in the next world as well.
And those who, served by sons and others, pass away satisfied, [attain a happy state]. (2.231.90)
Your ancestors shall indeed become liberated, destined for heaven and other higher realms;
they shall certainly not remain in the state of a *preta*, nor shall they have any lower rebirth.
For those who have passed away with a serene mind, birth shall no longer cause them suffering.
Those people who have died while being unpurified, suffering,
or possessed of cruel dispositions— verily they drink the blood of those situated in their lineage.
For the sake of securing a good rebirth for them, sons and others should offer the *śrāddha* rite.
May obstacles in the lineage perish and may there likewise be growth for the lineage.
Today, the *śrāddha* performed and offered—food, water, and fruit—reaches heaven wherever the ancestors indeed reside. (94)
There the ancestors are always satisfied and happy upon receiving [these offerings].

Therefore, the śrāddha ceremony should be performed for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors; food, water, clothing, fruit, and even milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered under their names. || 95-96 ||
Beds, vessels, grains, and juices should be given, especially so;
indeed, meals should be offered for the sake of satisfying the ancestors.
At sacred sites and toward worthy recipients, one should give according to one's capacity and as is appropriate.
Gold, silver, copper, and wealth should especially be given;
even a vehicle or any conveyance that was dear to him should be given to a worthy recipient, for such merit shall be infinite. (98–99)
Having spoken thus, he then ceased; the subjects then performed worship with wealth, food, garments, vessels, and the like, as well as sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, and flowers.
Then, the wealth that had arrived specifically for the purpose of worship was presented.
Kṛṣṇa bestowed gifts upon the sage Rājagiri.
That night, the son of the cowherds found sleep and rest;
the Supreme Lord was served by Rādhikā and all his beloveds.

Harikṛṣṇa was awakened by auspicious morning instruments and the songs of women; he then performed meditation within his own heart. Having completed his bath and other rites, having finished his daily devotions, and having offered praise to his guru—
The king sat upon the divine throne; at that moment, [the Lord] arrived.
He performed a great worship of Śrī Hari with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and he caused all the honored guests to drink milk-rice (pāyasa).
The queen performed worship, and then the subjects worshipped as well; the king endeavored to lead Acyuta into other cities. Hari said, "So be it," and immediately became ready.
O Rādhikā, he remained in his own celestial chariot together with his family.

(1.07) Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Hari, the Instruction on [the Rituals of] Śrāddha for the Ancestors, the Giving of Water, and so forth, performed on the New Moon day; resting at night; and the worship and other rites performed on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
