Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
at the request of King Rāya-nṛpa, Śrī Hari became ready.
From the kingdom of Khaṇḍarāṣṭra,
he went to the city of Lāṭalātrī on the shore of the ocean;
there, in a palace resembling a small island within a great garden, he alighted.
The king honored him with various kinds of gold as a dowry,
as well as with diamonds, the finest gems, pearls, and jewels;
and amidst the sounding of musical instruments throughout the city, he did so with great ceremony.
King Rājārāya caused Kṛṣṇa to wander everywhere; there in that great garden, Hari, having performed service and exerted himself,
and having cultivated the grove, spoke for the sake of peace for two days.
On the third day of the month of Āśvina, there was indeed a Daitya named Navajīvana;
he was a master of illusion, possessed of great speed, and had a body like a massive mountain.
He drew along many clouds with the hair growing from his head.
Striking the force of the lightning with his mace, which was heavy with many living beings,
making the sky roar with his laughter, and agitating the ocean with his claws,
he came at night, covering the houses with the bulk of his body.
Having recognized the celestial chariot, he lifted it with a single hand.
Rudra, perceiving that Daitya, let out a roar:
"Who is this that touches my chariot? Go far away, or you are dead! || 2.232.10 ||
Having heard this, he quickly let out a loud, boisterous laugh;
thundering in the sky with his mace, he spoke, causing terror:
"Who are you? Are you the lord of a celestial chariot? Tell me, to whom does this chariot belong? (11)
"I shall lead you to the celestial chariot; be resolute for the sake of battle!
Śaṅkara said: "Do not desire war; go far away!
In battle there is no welfare for you; abandon the chariot immediately."
The Daitya said: "In this world, victory cannot be achieved without battle.
I shall take away the celestial chariot and carry off all these women from here.
Having spoken thus, he struck Rudra violently on the head with his mace.
The swift Śaṅkara quickly pierced her with his trident.
(15) When the Daitya’s mace was shattered and fell into the ocean, at that moment the tides of the sea became flooded with water. (16)
Then indeed, deprived of his mace, the Daitya fell into agitation;
he thought, "Having done what, or having taken what, shall I flee?
[He went] to the great garden of the royal palace of King Rājarāja.
Having lifted up his youngest sister, who was sleeping with their mother,
and placing her upon his shoulder, he ascended into the sky. Vidyunmaṇi, the young maiden carried away by the Daitya, wept bitterly.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the men who were crying out, "Save us! Save us!
Indeed, their clamor was then filled with fear.
Within a moment, the king, the lord of kings, heard it and woke up.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also arose;
the subjects likewise woke up, filled with a great clamor,
and the honored women all around became awakened from their sleep.
Having heard the account told by Śaṅkara, the king of the Daityas, taking the maiden, indeed runs swiftly through the sky under the name Navajīvana.
He is not very far away; he is moving through the western sky.
"O Kṛṣṇa, having received your command, I shall by all means slay him.
Hari, the king of kings and lord of men, said, "So be it.
Then Mātā said, "Indeed, this maiden has been given to you."
"Protect, protect, O Great Kṛṣṇa! Protect! Quickly ward it off!
Kṛṣṇa said to the king as he was entering his prepared celestial chariot:
"I am departing for the sake of protection; you [should remain] here in this auspicious chariot of mine."
"Or else, follow me here in your celestial chariot along with your mother.
Having spoken thus, Hari quickly followed the Daitya toward the western quarter, accompanied by his family.
The king also, followed by his servants, then caused his own celestial chariot to speed through the sky; equal to the sun, he became the follower [of Hari].
Upon seeing both the chariot of Hari and the chariot of the king, [the gods were amazed].
Driven by fear, the Daitya fled through the sky even while accompanied by his daughter;
lightened by his body’s speed like that of the wind,
he flew over the ocean at night for a thousand yojanas.
After the celestial chariot of Śrī Hari,
the chariot of the king also pursued with great speed in order to seize that foremost of the Daityas.
The Daitya, too, fled with immense velocity until the very break of dawn.
Then a great island emerged from within the ocean;
it was a provider of new life that descended upon that land,
spanning a hundred yojanas and dividing the waters into two parts.

Having quickly entered that city, which was as beautiful as a fortress or a capital, yet terrifying due to the wretchedness of the Daityas, and which was rich with the splendor of royal palaces and other structures— a city consisting entirely of the dwellings of the Daityas— the Daitya indeed roared and alerted the others.
He struck the kettledrum that announces the commencement of battle.
Hearing Jarā’s great roar, the Daityas roared with excitement;
grasping their weapons for the sake of combat, they went forth like mountains.
Navajīva also quickly cast that maiden into a cave and,
accompanied by the Daitya army, came forth for the sake of battle.
Śrī Hari, assuming youthfulness and beauty, took up his Sudarśana discus.
He went to that cave and took the maiden to his own celestial chariot.
Having fashioned another illusory maiden out of clay exactly as she was,
the Lord placed her in the cave, she who was capable of deluding all the Daityas.
She quickly presented her sister to the king exactly as she was;
meanwhile, the Daityas, unaware of this, rushed forward by force to do battle.
And that girl had been informed of her surrender by her brother and her mother.
Placing her hand upon the neck of Hari on the celestial chariot, she chose him as her husband.
Grasping the garland of choice as the garland of betrothal, she became the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
thereafter, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa became the Supreme Lord.
Then Śaṅkara gave the command to Īśāna to slay the Daityas in battle; instantly, out of wrath,
he loosened his matted locks and created ten lakhs of terrifying beings in the form of Rudras who became the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Then he gave the command to fight against those weapons born of [his] resolve.
Leaping up again and again, those Daityas struck him with their tridents.
Indeed, a great battle took place until midday, which brought about the destruction of the Daityas.
All twenty lakhs of Daityas were destroyed;
there was a great cry of "Alas! and the weeping of the women.
Then the compassionate Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, for their sake, [created] the hosts... [to bring them happiness].
He issued a command for them to dwell in that region in the householder stage of life (gṛhāśrama).
The attendants (gaṇas) performed the marriage rites with all the wives of the Daityas.
All those sons of Śaṅkara were Vaiṣṇavas, as impelled by Kṛṣṇa.
Taking each of those wives with them, all the Gaṇas went to the houses in their respective regions; there,
Mādhava made the Gaṇa named Kāmanāyaka the leader of the king.
Having consecrated him in the great kingdom, he likewise gave ten million villages.
Having performed an auspicious and grand festival, the Lord Śrī Hari wandered through Vallīliṅgapura and rendered everything holy.
Then, having ascended his celestial chariot and crossed over Khāḍikā,
the Supreme Lord went to the city of Dinediṣṭhā; there he wandered among the lords of the Gaṇas,
caused them to dwell [there], and received the excellent worship performed by them.
Having given the king permission to eat, the Lord of Māyā,

Hari, gathered together in his own celestial chariot and provided food for all the inhabitants of the vimānas; having bestowed wealth and the gift of fearlessness upon them in the evening, he gave the meal.

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, Śrī Hari abandoned his sleep at dawn and, having surveyed the island on all sides from his celestial chariot, stayed the night in the royal palace in Dvinediṣṭhapura.
Having commanded the king, his mother,
and their army to depart for their own kingdom, Hari, accompanied by his family and joined by Mahīmāna, ascended his celestial chariot. ||57-58||
Having swiftly crossed the ocean by way of the path of the sky,
they arrived at the city of Hambārtana on the island of Trāsamaṇa.
Indeed, at midday, those traveling in celestial chariots took their meals.
Then the great sages, his devotees born in the regions of the hot lands,
who had previously been protected by him, arrived in celestial chariots for the sake of a vision [of him].
Hari joyfully offered them a welcome.

Having received worship and bestowed his blessings, Hari swiftly crossed the ocean by means of his celestial chariot and went to the city of Allālī. [6.2] He arrived at Uṣṇālaya, in the region of Bhūśiras, the abode of those who offer salutations.
Having stayed for one night and taken his morning meal,
Narayana— whose worship was performed in the morning by Vṛndāraka— the lord,
arose and departed in a celestial chariot accompanied by his family.
In the northern direction, at a distance of fifty yojanas,
Hari reached the island named Siṃhala situated in the midst of the ocean;
having taken his meal at midday, he flew away, traveling in his celestial chariot.
Having reached Lake Pampā in the evening, he spent the night upon its shore.
Then, on the morning of the seventh day, the Lord ascended his celestial chariot and went to his own sacred site in Saurāṣṭra for the sake of concealment.
At midday, having performed worship and a feast for the Lord of Gopas,
on the evening of the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the Lord,
traveling by way of the sky, slowly arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.

Afflicted by the pain of separation from the people of Kuṅkumavāpī, they constantly undergo emaciation at every moment, never ceasing their longing for Śrī Hari. Those men, women, young girls, and maidens who serve their Master [attain this state]. (2.232.70)
Beholding a mass of light in the sky, they inferred the arrival of their beloved;
with great joy, they ran toward the vicinity of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake in the magnificent garden,
eager for a vision of her.
At that very moment, a celestial chariot arrived in their presence.
Then, shouts of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, the blares of conchs,
and the songs of women arose from all sides.
The guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*), sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and the deities residing there;
likewise the liberated ones (*mukta*), the lords (*īśvara*), incarnations (*avatāra*), and their attendants (*pārṣada*);
as well as the great seers (*maharṣi*), the kṣatriyas, the brahmins, and the virtuous and truthful ones.
There were yogins and perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas), as well as those established in their vows;
maidens and youths residing in the imperishable realm, and women endowed with good fortune, all possessed of every auspicious quality. (75–76)
The ascetics dwelling in Lomaśa’s hermitage as well as those residing in the mango grove set out quickly toward the lake to welcome Kṛṣṇa;
delighted that Kṛṣṇa had arrived, they all went forth.

Having taken sandalwood, flower garlands, and the like, as well as perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and fruits—indeed, even having taken these precious substances—one must abandon them within the house;
having cast them out at the boundary, the farmers and others may likewise take them in the forest. (78–79)
Abandoning their forest duties and commercial activities, all the merchants quickly went toward Aśvapaṭṭasara to see Lord Hari;
leaving their own homes, they went there for the purpose of welcoming and worshipping Him.
The aerial chariot of Hari descended swiftly to that spot on the ground.
It was adorned with sandalwood paste and other offerings, as well as flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and saffron.
Then the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari quickly took his place at the front of the chariot.
He granted his audience to all people from every side;
filled with affection, he inquired after the welfare of everyone.
All of them, full of eagerness, asked after the health of the Lord of Life.
Then, embracing Hari repeatedly with tears of love,
they placed flower garlands upon His neck, adorned with sandalwood and saffron;
they then performed worship with unbroken grains, fragrant essences, and other offerings.
The group of men prostrated at the feet of the illustrious Gopāla; the group of women repeatedly prostrated at the feet of Kaṃbhārā;
and then the group of attendants prostrated at the feet of Īśāna.
She bowed to the virtuous Īśvarī, the foremost of the Yoginī-maṇḍala;
indeed, all the women paid homage to all the beloved wives of Brahmā—
Gaurī, Hārītakī, Cāmarī, and likewise Brāhmilī.
Indeed, all the women there were like new brides of Kṛṣṇa;
then, with instrumental music, songs, and auspicious rites,
the noble Ārṣya joyfully led Hari into the temple of Hari along with his family.
All the sages and seers prostrated themselves like staffs in worship.
The subjects, distressed by their separation, arrived and inquired after his welfare;
Hari, having likewise inquired after their well-being, bestowed auspicious honors upon them.
Having announced that his tasks were accomplished to his devotees at the onset of night,
the Lord then arose and proceeded to perform his bath and twilight prayers. After completing those rites, he subsequently caused meals to be served.
Having honored Lomaśa, Śaṅkara, and his parents,
Mādhava fed the great sages, Yavakrīta and the others;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa fed the maidens who were dear to Brahmā.
Having fed all those beloved women in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa,
he then sent them all to the assembly of the Brāhmaṇīs;
and Bālakṛṣṇa gave them all divine articles of use.
Assuming many forms, Kṛṣṇa bestowed happiness upon them during the night.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, having purified all devotees everywhere in every land upon the earth, he shines resplendent, dwelling in the imperishable realm.
Blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā; blessed are those maidens as well;
and blessed are those lands that have come into direct contact with Nārāyaṇa.
Those men on earth who shall hear this divine narrative—
Those people who, filled with the weight of devotion, shall read and even recite [this], for them there shall be the destruction of sin and, indeed, the most excellent worldly enjoyment here;
and in the end, liberation in the imperishable world shall surely occur—of this there is no doubt. (2.232.100)
Some men will recount the divine stories of sacrifices, as well as those of the sages, the kings, and the devotees; for them,
there shall be the fruit of sacrifice, and prosperity shall dwell in their homes.

Having heard the life-story of those dear to Brahmā, they shall attain the supreme heaven. O beautiful lady, by listening to this, one obtains the fruit of the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), the fruit of visiting sacred fords (tīrtha), the fruit of religious observances (vrata), and likewise the fruit of all forms of worship.
This divine and preeminent conduct of the Supreme Lord indeed first appeared on earth as a universal sovereign; others will likewise appear,
manifested through incarnations such as myself and those of the lineage of the Blessed One.
O Rādhikā! [These] bestow auspiciousness upon both devotees and followers of the Bhāgavata. 105.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, Hari went to the city of Lāpalātrī. There, a Daitya from the ocean arrived and abducted the king’s sister, named Vidyunmaṇi. Both the King and Hari pursued him in their celestial chariots; having reached Navajīva-dvīpa, they fought with the Daitya. Twenty lakhs of Daityas were destroyed by ten lakhs of Gaṇas sent forth by Śaṅkara. Hari then bestowed the kingdom upon Kāmanāyaka-gaṇa.

A maiden named Vidyunmaṇi chose Hari as her husband. After purifying the city of Dvinediṣṭha, she arrived at Trāsamāna Island by celestial chariot on the fifth lunar day; from there she went to Vṛndāruka, then to Siṃhaladvīpa, and finally to Lake Pampā.

On the evening of the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, she reached Kuṅkumavāpikā. [The Lord offered] welcome, inquiries after her welfare, food, bedding, and so forth. This is the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Days," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Divine, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and raining down the bliss of devotion—

I shall relate those supreme deeds which bestow bliss—deeds of Hari, the protector of the cowherds and Kṛṣṇa’s joy, the beloved husband of Brahmāṇī, the Lord of all, and the Supreme Ruler; listen to me with a focused mind. (12–13)

For those characterized by tamas, he appears as tamasic; for those seeking liberation, he is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).

He went to his side to worship him, and having worshipped him, he attained his favor.
(15) Having received his command, he quickly conceived the idea of a divine pavilion;
for the command had been given to construct an unprecedented pavilion, and so it was done. (16)

"I shall construct a divine pavilion upon the four ritual sites so that the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake may be situated beneath it. Having thus conceived the image within the pavilion in his heart, [he proceeded].
There he recalled four bows, each a yojana in length:
the bow of Indra, the bow of Śaṅkara, the bow of Viṣṇu, and the firm, auspicious bow of Manobhava, capable of bearing great weight. (18–19)
To the east of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ,
he established the very temple of Indra, extending from south to north and long in dimension, consisting of masonry;
and likewise, he established the temple of Īśa to the north.
In the west, he established the Vaiṣṇava shrine exactly as it was; and in the south, he established the shrine of Kāma exactly as it was.
On a stretch of land one yojana in length, he caused eight boundary markers to be placed.
Having thus constructed a square quadrangular courtyard in the form of a base,
he caused sunbeams— those repositories of splendor— to be placed there,
as well as sun-stones, moon-stones, and crystals.
Having laid out that square grid with equal lines as the very foundation of the wall,
he quickly had a golden rampart constructed, complete with gate-towers and adorned with mechanical devices; in its center, he caused a magnificent assembly hall to be built.
It possesses a canopy of nectar-substance produced by the rays of the moon;
it is endowed with pillars whose beauty is enriched by creepers born of ambrosia;
its middle is circular and resplendent with a golden seat situated at its side.
It was resplendent with the planets, constellations, stars, and other celestial bodies serving as its lamp-stands;
it was graced by the shadow of a canopy formed by the mass of *kaustubha* gems;
and it bore a garland whose beauty was commensurate with the very nature of Lakṣmī herself. (27)
[He saw] the fourfold assembly of the gods—Sudharmā, Brāhmabhauma, Īśī, and Sabhā—which was characterized by the dancing, worship, and singing of apsarases;
[he saw it] endowed with the wish-fulfilling cow, the desire-granting creeper, and the thought-jewel. (28–29)
Adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers, wish-granting trees, inexhaustible vessels, and other such treasures;
endowed with fragrances from all quarters, the taste of all flavors, and pleasant breezes;
auspicious, and the refuge of all powers such as hearing and seeing from afar.
In as many objects as were visible there, the Lord Hari appeared in embodied form.
The self-luminous Blessed One, the king of devotees, was Bālakṛṣṇa himself;
and just as he had commanded, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned those forms.
All liberated forms are the very nature of the Imperishable;
likewise, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the forms of the various liberated souls.
Within them, the auspicious Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa is perceived as the inner self.
All types of incarnations, as well as the women who are those incarnations,
the expansions (vyūhas) and the consorts of the expansions, and likewise the lords and their mistresses—
in all of these, the auspicious Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa is seen as the inner self.
The Siddhas, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, the truthful ones, the Sādhyas, and the holy ones;
the Ṛṣis, the Pitṛs, the gods, and their divine consorts;
the humans, the guardians of the quarters, and the world-protectors together with their wives.
And Kāśyapa created all living beings and all divine principles in their entirety.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Gaṇeśas, and other mountain-dwellers,
as well as the renowned kings, were all established by Viśvakarman.
Within all of them, the divine Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was visible.
Having thus prepared such a brand-new assembly hall, complete with pavilions,
he announced it to his father on the seventh day when half the night had passed.

Seeing the staircases on all sides, as well as the paths for vehicles, the spaces for celestial chariots in between them, the routes for elephants, and the paths for chariots and foot-soldiers, his father became delighted. (2.234.40–41)
Seeing the paths with their resting places for repose, the father indeed rejoiced;
seeing the gardens laid out on all sides, filled with fruits and flowers and variegated with many colors, the father truly exulted.
In all those places, he beheld his own son dwelling within his heart.
Everything exists as the essence of reality; this is a distinguished illustration of that, fashioned on earth by Tvaṣṭṛ at the command and through the inspiration of Hari.
A divine lake is seen below the summit of the terrestrial mountain,
rich with the splendor of ten million lotuses and graced by the tortoise Śeṣa;
likewise, a radiant veil is fashioned, abounding in the beauty visible from the netherworld (pātāla).
Thus, having beheld the divine pavilion and the lion-throne of Hari,
they gazed upon the supreme, most divine seat,
which was higher than all other thrones, fashioned from gold produced by divine beings, and supported by an elephant pedestal.
Within the parts of the lion-throne, all divine, auspicious, and celestial lion-thrones were indeed fashioned, together with their presiding deities:
the one belonging to Kṛṣṇa, the one belonging to Nārāyaṇa, the one belonging to Vāsudeva, the earthly one, and the infallible one.
The Sādāśaiva, the Hairaṇyagarbha, and likewise the Vairājaka;
the Brāhma, the Aindra, the Vāruṇa, the Yāmya, and the Kauberaka; as well as the Āgnika, the Anilīya, the Aiśāna, and the Nairṛtika. (2.234.49–50)
The remnants of that solar throne, as well as all other thrones, were contained within the interior of Kṛṣṇa’s seat. Indeed,
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned such a divine elephant-throne.

In a most beautiful, divine, and fragrant pavilion, adorned by throngs of celestial maidens standing upon elephant-thrones with hands joined in reverence, and by those holding handfuls of flowers and hands bearing unbroken grains and sandalwood paste. ||52-53||
Within that which was blazing on all sides with luminous,
imperishable substances, the great Lord Kṛṣṇa, possessing infinite forms, shone forth.
The glorious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, beholding the supreme seat for his son, [proceeded].
Indeed, the most excellent divine being rejoiced, and his family rejoiced as well;
his wives, led by Brahmapriyā, rejoiced to the highest degree upon seeing the imperial dignity bestowed upon their own husband’s throne. (55–56)
Then, having made such an arrangement, Tvaṣṭṛ was filled with joy;
seeing his own unprecedented creation, he indeed attributed it to the grace of Hari.
For that great throne had arisen, which was beyond the reach of his own intellect.

He considered the Lord residing within him to be the creator of that [maṇḍapa]. Then Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa also, seeing the pavilion pervaded by splendor and that field of the maṇḍapa as indeed imperishable through its brilliance, [perceived it as such].
Shining like the sun during the day, he quickly became bewildered at dawn;
he then awakened Gaṇeśa, Īśāna, Satī, Lomaśa,
Saccidānanda, Tuṣita, and Sadāśiva.
He also quickly commanded Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī, Sanatkumāra, and Ṛbhu: "May you all go forth in every direction in an instant,
intent upon bestowing blessings on the occasion of Kṛṣṇa’s Janmajayantī."
May those created by Brahmā, those created by Īśvara, and those created by the individual soul who reside upon this earth come together in Saurāṣṭra to the temple of Gopālakṛṣṇa;
having assembled on the eighth day during the festival, may they all offer their congratulations.
Having thus fulfilled their hopes, they quickly departed for other worlds.
Those who were liberated went to the abode [of Brahman], Gaṇeśa went to the station of Śaṅkara,
Īśāna went to Satyaloka, and [Gaṇeśa] went to the dwellings of the virtuous Sati.
Lomaśa went swiftly to the worlds of the great ṛṣis, the Tuṣitas, and the assembly of Pitṛs;
Sadāśiva went to the worlds of the Īśvaras;
and he who is liberated, being existence-consciousness-bliss, indeed went to the abodes of Viṣṇu.
Then Lakṣmī went to all the goddesses and throughout the worlds;
Nārāyaṇī went to Badarī and to Śvetadvīpa in the Milk Ocean.
Then the blessed Sanatkumāra traversed all the worlds in an instant.
Assuming various forms, they departed swiftly in every direction;
having reached those respective places and received the honors offered by the local residents,
they delivered their messages of invitation and proceeded to the Field of Akṣara.
And all of them, having been invited, accompanied by their families,
with hearts blooming with joy, quickly prepared themselves with ornaments and the like;
they were provided with divine offerings and vehicles such as celestial chariots.
They arrived at the divine pavilion in the sacred precinct of Kuṅkumavāpī.
In the very morning, Hari bathed, performed worship and salutations,
attended upon the elders, and was fully adorned with ornaments.
Thus bowed down by all those beloved of Brahmā and likewise filled with great joy,
he was joined by his mother’s blessings;
having performed the auspicious rites of protection and having assumed a divine form, he was attended by hosts of great sages.

Accompanied by the resonant sounds of musical instruments, the songs of women, and Vedic mantras, Kṛṣṇa proceeded to that pavilion and sat upon an elephant-throne; having arrived, he sat down, and then shouts of "Victory! arose.
Lomaśa honored him with Vedic mantras and sandalwood paste.
All the great sages also honored the Imperishable One; they magnified him with blessings and performed worship with unbroken grains of rice.
His mother applied the *tilaka* to him, and his father placed a crown upon him; the wives of Brahmā offered garlands of flowers, and Śrī then fashioned a crescent moon for him.
All those who had gathered at the pavilion performed the *ārārtika* ceremony.
Then, beholding him of such divine form, the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra became absorbed in him, having attained supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*). There,
the sounds of the Vedas arose on all sides from the Brahmins.
The elder brother, the Blessed One, Śuka, and Vallabha also followed;
there they all gave great gifts and charities in their entirety.
Then, at that time, the liberated souls arrived from the imperishable realm (Akṣara-loka).
Then, having performed worship and the *ārārtika* rite for Bālakṛṣṇa,
they sat down upon beautiful seats pointed out by the attendants (*pārṣadas*).
Thereupon, the incarnations arrived, accompanied by their wives and their attendants.
O Rādhikā, I then went there together with you;
Nārāyaṇa also arrived there, filled with joy, accompanied by Lakṣmī.
All the other Nārāyaṇas likewise came, each joined by his own Śakti.
They arrived, offered worship, and entered when seats were shown to them.
(85) Likewise, the military arrays and the lords headed by Īśvara, as well as the goddesses of sovereignty, arrived there;
they worshipped with offerings and entered when seats were shown to them. (86)
Brahmā and the other lords of the three worlds, indeed innumerable, arrived;
they honored him with offerings and sat upon the seats that were shown to them.
The sages, the women of those [gods], and likewise their fathers arrived.
The gods and goddesses, the world-protectors and guardians of the quarters, together with their families;
the Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras, accompanied by their Śaktis, all arrived.
They worshipped him with offerings and entered when seats had been shown to them.
Virtuous men and women, as well as truthful men and women, arrived;
those dwelling in the netherworld, those dwelling in the forests, and those dwelling on the mountains, all arrived.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas [also came].
The Kinnaras and Kiṃpuruṣas arrived and worshipped the Imperishable One (Acyuta).
The sacred fords, the oceans, the rivers, the lakes, the various types of shrines, the trees, the divine creepers, the cows, and likewise the birds [all came]. || 91-92 ||
Divine vehicles, as well as male and female servants, arrived;
they honored him with offerings and greeted him with blessings.
They sat upon seats and other furnishings within the pavilion, which was endowed with divine splendor.
Indeed, the forms of the gods and others dwelling in the worlds and sub-worlds,
having been beheld everywhere within the pavilion upon their elephant-thrones, and having seen their own true forms, were struck with extreme wonder. (94–95)
For this is not the work of the gods, nor of the divine Tvaṣṭṛ,
since we have no access to his craftsmanship regarding the nature of the syllables and so forth.
Therefore, its creator must indeed be Tvaṣṭṛ, who resides within the syllables.
"By his dwelling in the abode of Brahmā, he is perceived as having been fashioned [by him].
Thus did all those adorned within the pavilion become filled with doubt;
for they gazed upon Bālakṛṣṇa amidst those very principles (tattvas).
Indeed, everyone became bewildered upon seeing Kṛṣṇa within the womb.
Until midday, there was worship with benedictions and celebrations;
likewise, the dancing of Hari and the Apsarases continued there.
There was divine singing as well as the recitation of the *Saṃhitās*; there were also narrative tales and the chanting of Hari’s glories,
performed by Vetradhāra, Hemanta, and Vasantaka.
The one named Ninādana, possessed of great fame and rich in victory, was proclaimed;
and there, Satyāmbikā stood with palms joined in reverence to dispel his sorrow.
His mother placed the Sucandraka mark, accompanied by unbroken grains of rice, upon his forehead.
Thus blessings were bestowed and betel was likewise offered.
In the assembly hall, sugar and other sweets, as well as *khārī* measures of grain and so forth, were distributed; and appropriate refreshments, such as drinks and betel, were duly prepared.
Then, for all those who had arrived, the Lord of Nāthas offered a warm welcome and blessings, expressing his deep affection with sweet words.
He provided them with a magnificent feast of ambrosia, nectar, and delicious foods.
There was the offering of drinks, sweet-smelling substances, and betel leaves (106). There was also the offering of garlands, flower wreaths, and bouquets;
indeed, great honor was repeatedly bestowed upon those who had come for the sake of the pavilion (107).
The entire three worlds were present there at that festival;
then, in the morning, according to the ritual injunctions, Rādhikā was released.
The honored guests departed for the dwellings that had been assigned to them.
They found rest for half a day in divine palaces.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Splendor of the Divine Pavilion, the Arrival of the Invited Guests, the Worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Bālakṛṣṇasvāmī, and the Honors and Hospitality," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 234. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 235 [Author:
Chapter 236 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: the people and others who had gathered there all received the grace of Hari and were filled with joy.
At midday, the brāhmaṇas performed the rite of offering blessings for Bāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Then the women sang songs, and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) took place.
At that time, Bālakṛṣṇa indeed revealed His own form—
divine, the most excellent of the excellent, residing in the supreme abode beyond the Imperishable (akṣara).
Whatever deities, worlds, world-protectors, and the powers of the incarnations of Īśvara were stationed within the pavilion and upon their respective seats—
all those [deities] and all those [powers] became fully present in Bālakṛṣṇa as he sat there.
Those dwelling in all the creations were seen to be liberated from the syllable (akṣara).
There, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) consisting of fourteen levels was seen;
the surface of the earth was seen, and likewise Saurāṣṭra was seen.
"The saffron pond is seen, and likewise the assembly hall is seen;
the pavilion is seen, and Kṛṣṇa’s beloved is seen.
In this way, everything regarding Śrī Hari came within the range of the eyes of his attendants.
Then, they beheld Bālakṛṣṇa within their hearts:
the divine Great Lord, the son of Kaṃbhari, the abode of divine qualities, the cowherd boy, the Lord and Master of Brahmapriyā and the other goddesses. (8–9)
Then, having displayed his divine form, Hari thereafter assumed his own form as a child; indeed, the dismissal from the assembly took place. Śrīmat Gopāla Kṛṣṇa gave food to everyone.

There were various kinds of sweet foods and various kinds of drinks. Then, having honored them with gifts and respect, he granted them leave to depart. Those who resided in the other world went away in every way to different regions.
There, a festival of the people of Saurāṣṭra was established.
At night, a wrestling match took place before Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
likewise, various dramatic performances were then held before Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (13)
There were various songs and musical performances;
and there, throughout the night, food and drinks were served repeatedly.
In this manner, indeed, there were dances by courtesans during the night.
Indeed, rewards were given to the laborers;
having completed everything, at midnight the people succumbed to sleep and exhaustion.
Rising in the morning, they performed auspicious rites with musical instruments and other ceremonies.
Having bowed to Hari and received his leave, they departed for their homes.
And Viśvakarman, having received the command, made that excellent pavilion vanish even as he stood there, in the very next moment at dawn.
To him, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa gave an excellent reward:
a golden crown and a most exquisite necklace for the neck. He also bestowed upon him divine intelligence and granted him a supreme state everywhere.

And out of compassion, the Lord granted him the power to behold the three worlds. (2.235.20) As soon as the pavilion was removed, Aśvapaṭṭasara was instantly visible. All the people, observant of the duty of twilight prayers, bathed there in the morning. (21)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the fifteenth Janmāṣṭamī festival passed away,
coinciding with the fifteenth year of Śrī Hari’s reign.
Indeed, many people came for the sake of beholding Śrī Hari.
Consequently, a great thronging of people occurs there day and night;
from the lowliest to the outcaste (caṇḍāla), they all come and go after receiving the compassion of the King of Kings in the form of his grace. || 23-24 ||
Having obtained food and other such things, they became happy;
O Rādhā! On that Jayantī day, a certain Cāṇḍāla arrived there, named Tāmasākṣi, accompanied by his wife and son.
Since he is a devotee of Hari, he never commits theft in any way;
he does not speak untruth, nor does he practice deceit.
Dwelling constantly in a moving temple, he performs the work of sweeping the village.
With the food he obtained, he constantly maintained his body alone;
however, the food earned through his sweeping was never sufficient.
Furthermore, there was no other outcaste in the village who was considered fit to perform such work.
For he does not commit violence, nor does he even act unjustly.
Like a mendicant, he does not wander about for the sake of acquiring food;
and people, regarding him as a Cāṇḍāla and an unworthy recipient, do not give [him anything] either. (2.235.30)
Then, having encountered hardship and being excessively emaciated by the pain of hunger,
he, together with his family and accompanied by five sons,
as well as two daughters, remained there despite their lack of effort.
Accompanied by his wife, he himself arrived on the ninth day at Jayantī;
taking refuge in the shade of a banyan tree on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
he beheld Bālakṛṣṇa in ever-new splendor.
Together with his family, he even performed the ritual of spinning garlands;
on that festive day, from morning until night, he obtained plenty of alms-food.
On the ninth day he received much, and on the tenth day as well.
On the eleventh day, because of his vow, he did not obtain any food at all.
Hungry along with his family, he remained in the observance of the vow day and night.
At night, accompanied by his wife and children, he was overcome by a state of darkness (tamas).
With his heart broken by hunger and other afflictions, and desiring to die with great haste, he fell right into the lake; his wife fell as well to hold him up.
Their sons and daughters also fell, weeping for their parents.
Then, by virtue of the depth of the water, they reached the bottom;
at that time, during the latter part of the middle of the night, no one knew of this.
Having drunk that water, they then became as if dead.
Remembering Bālakṛṣṇa within their own hearts, they were as if dead;
then the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also quickly awakened.
O Rādhikā, leaving His bed during that night of darkness, He went to the lake.
Then Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, whose true nature is Vāsudeva,
entered the midst of the water with four arms, taking the outcaste devotee with him;
and that true Lord brought his wife back onto the shore outside.

Again Hari went into the water and drew out the two daughters as well as the son from the water; having placed them on the bank, he entered the water once more. Then Hari quickly [drew out] the four sons as well.
And he brought them out onto the bank and protected them for a moment.
Then the Blessed One—Vāsudeva, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṅkarṣaṇa—[protected] the children, the wife, and the husband. || 44-45 ||
Having assumed the fourfold posture and holding each of them separately by the feet, he lifted them up and turned them face-down; for the duration of a single *ghaṭikā*,
he held them in that very manner until the water he had drunk had completely drained out.
Having caused them to be placed in every way with their faces upward so that they have regained consciousness,
one should place them below the excellent [bed] and, for the sake of removing the cold,
arrange small sticks (*kāṇḍikā*) along with *vaṭa* leaves and other items, as well as splinters (*śalākā*), all around.
Having gathered [the materials], the Lord quickly kindled a fire there;
having placed logs therein, he performed the heating.
Śrī Hari himself then gradually heated them all.

He brought his life-breaths from the crown of his head into the cavity of his heart. Having regained their waking power and beholding the fourfold form beginning with Vāsudeva, they quickly bowed at the feet of the Lord.
There, at the end of the night on the eleventh day, they praised Hari:
"O Lord, protector, and sustainer of the distressed, the helpless, and the poor!
We, though outcastes, bow with reverence at Your feet."
You are the Ordainer, you are the giver of food, you are the sustainer, and indeed you are the nourisher.
You alone are the giver of breath and the one who brings us back to life through water.
We are always miserable from the lack of food, suffering from the pain of hunger, and distressed by the struggle for existence.
Out of a state of detachment from sufferings, they indeed offered their lives into the water for the sake of ending their existence; yet,
having regained consciousness in the waters,
you, the Lord of our lives, arrived there and performed our deliverance.
Just as protection has been afforded to your body, so too has protection been afforded to your life.
O Lord, grant us protection through the gift of life and by providing for our livelihood;
or else, lead us, your devoted followers, to the world of Brahmā.
Protection was afforded by you in the womb, even during the formation of the embryo;
protection was afforded on the path of birth, and we were protected even in our state of childhood.
Even until this very moment, we have indeed been protected by you with food and other necessities.

O Lord, even the trees, creepers, animals, insects, and birds are protected by you; therefore, protect us here! You are the one who uplifts the lowly and the remover of the suffering of those in pain. (2.235.59–60)

To those who have no support, you are considered the father who provides a refuge; you are the stay for the young, and you are the life of all living beings. You are the protector of those fallen into calamity, and the savior of those sinking [in the ocean].
O Lord of the World, you are the remover of suffering for the afflicted; take away my pain.
Be the provider of food and clothing to those destitute of food and clothing.
O Lord of the World, be the bestower of good fortune upon the unfortunate.
"O Blessed One, I was submerged in a lake due to the suffering caused by lack of food, along with my family, during the night; I have been rescued by you, the compassionate one.
Therefore, O Acyuta, having shown full compassion, [relieve] the hardship regarding food and clothing."
"Destroy [the fear] of me, your devotee who has fallen for refuge.
Having spoken thus, placing his head upon the ground with joined palms and joyfully gazing at the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, he prostrated himself again and again. (65–66)
The Blessed One manifested forms such as Vāsudeva and others;
then, assuming the form of Bālakṛṣṇa, he spoke in the hearing of Tāmasa:
"Dwell here in this city forever together with your family."
"Perform here the cleaning and other tasks on the streets and the royal highways.
Your livelihood, consisting of new garments and the like, shall be provided for you.
In the morning, I will give you a beautiful house suitable for your residence. (68–69)
"Do not be distressed, O devotee; never do so again.
There is no other sin equal to suicide, which causes great destruction of liberation. Therefore, do not commit suicide."
There is no other merit greater than the gift of one’s own life;
therefore, one should indeed protect one's life.
Accept this food, as well as this sweet meal, which is a fulfillment of religious duty.
Having spoken thus, he, being full of compassion, gave the sweet food brought by Vāsudeva’s wife and also gave garments to him and his family.
He said, "Come to the front of my gateway tomorrow morning; I shall give you a house."
"I am going to my palace; enjoy me and fall asleep," O Rādhikā, having spoken thus, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa vanished.
And the Cāṇḍāla became filled with joy and performed the worship of Hari.
With the sounding of cymbals, they all performed the glorification of Kṛṣṇa.
Having bathed in the morning, all those deeply devoted ones went to the gateway of Hari.
Indeed, Bālakṛṣṇa himself [came] for the protection of his devotee.
Rising from his elephant-seat, he then proceeded to the city gate.
He envisioned a most beautiful house within the mango grove—a lovely, new dwelling adorned with trees, creepers, and grass. (77–78)
It was spacious, equipped with a broom, a hearth, a mortar, and other such items; it was provided with a water-jar and a grinding stone, as well as a bed and other furnishings.
It was filled with grain stored in granaries and supplied with all kinds of food and soups.
Abounding in vegetable gardens and the like, graced by the water of wells,
provided with milch cows, delightful, circular with four enclosures,
and filled with his own various wonders— thus did Kṛṣṇa create that excellent mansion. (2.235.80–81)
He gave everything beautiful to that dog-cooker;
having reached his home, the devotee became pleased and rejoiced.
Then he indeed received the Vaiṣṇava mantra from Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.

"Obeisance to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; I am His servant, O Lord, deliver me!"—this mantra the Blessed One, the son of Kaṃbhārā, gave to him. [He granted him] the right to perform tasks such as cleaning in the village and at the Kumakuma pond in the city. (83–84)
He indeed appointed that devotee of his, who was untainted by tamas, to perform [this task].
Having obtained this auspicious gain, he too practiced devotion day and night;
and his family constantly served Śrī Hari in embodied form.
A certain maiden, the goddess Dugdhikā, remained there as a celibate ascetic (brahmacāriṇī).
Through her devotion to Kṛṣṇa, she became established in meditative absorption (samādhi) and attained a divine body.
This goddess Dugdhikā was the family deity (kuladevikā) of the Cāṇḍālas.
But there was always in the world a girl named Mantrikā, who served Bālakṛṣṇa and was proficient in many mantra-rituals;
through the practice of worshipping Hari, she indeed became possessed of great spiritual power.
Whatever mantra a speaker of truth prepares and teaches to another,
that very mantra becomes powerful and likewise yields fruit. Thus she became a master of mantras, capable of manifesting the power of mantras.
From that [mantra], there then arose the ṛṣi of the mantras of the Cāṇḍāla caste.
All five sons were born in their own hermitage as virtuous men, endowed with devotion and engaged in worship; they became leaders of the maṇḍalīs.
For they were indeed virtuous and, out of devotion, became the gurus of the Cāṇḍālas.
After a long time had passed, their parents—filled with devotion, serving them, and possessing divine hearts—abandoned their bodies. (92–93)
Yayāti and his wife attained liberation and went to the eternal abode of Śrī Hari.
O Rādhā, in the course of time, their sons and daughters, being virtuous and devoted,
cast off their bodies and went to the eternal realm of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Thus the illustrious Blessed One indeed protected the devotees of Rādhā;
He provided for their nourishment and likewise granted them their livelihood.
Furthermore, at the end, the Great Lord even bestowed liberation upon those who were outcaste dog-cookers.
Those who are helpless, poor, wretched, or devoid of fortune— even they,
having gone to the imperishable land of Hari at Kuṅkumavāpikā,
shall perform worship and offer their own respective [devotions]. (97)
Bālakṛṣṇa will certainly protect their bodies, lives, hearts, wealth, and families in every way. Having granted them enjoyment in this world, he will indeed bestow liberation thereafter. (98–99)
"From reading and hearing this, from chanting and even from teaching it, there shall surely be enjoyment and liberation, O Rādhikā; of this there is no doubt.

(2.235.100) Thus ends the [section] in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, concerning the removal of the sacrificial pavilion, the departure of the Mahīmānas, and the protection and nourishment of the outcaste devotee named Tāmasākṣin along with his family when they were submerged in water.
The two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation and Other Matters," [Chapter 235].
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 236.
[Author: Chapter 237.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the day of Dhanatrayodaśī, Bālakṛṣṇa—

He performed the worship of Dhanalakṣmī according to the prescribed rites. He had a golden image of his own beloved Śrī-Lakṣmī fashioned according to the rules for the purpose of giving it away as a gift.
He worshipped [them] with the sixteen primary services and offerings such as sandalwood paste,
and he fed them abundantly with various kinds of cooked food made from fresh grains. Then, he beheld his own wife Lakṣmī, who was Śrī herself in visible form.
Having seated them upon a golden throne, he worshipped them with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
Kṛṣṇa himself indeed arranged the hair-styles and attire of the two women;
having fashioned their braids (*kabarī*), he personally tied their topknots (*dhammilla*).
And there she strung together flower garlands and ornaments,
using excellent jewels for amorous decoration, diamonds, collyrium and the like, saffron,
sandalwood paste and other fragrances, filaments, and *karaka* fruits.

He performed the erotic rite for the two of them with flower garlands, drops [of unguents], and other offerings. He performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) before those two maidens who were visibly present;
for both of them were well-pleased and indeed bestowed their words of blessing.
They both said: "O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Lakṣmī, perform the marriage!
O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Lakṣmī, come together with the auspicious moment (lagna).
Become the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Padmāvatī."

Become the husband of Māṇikī and the husband of Brahmapriyā as well. By means of the marriage rite, become the Lord of Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering; through this union, become the husband of countless brought-forth wives.
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa, this time for your marriage has arrived;
today you have become a fit youth, possessing the sprouts of manhood.
At this auspicious moment, O Śrīkṛṣṇa, quickly become Lakṣmīkṛṣṇa. (12)
"We maidens are all awaiting our marriage.
May you become prosperous, wealthy, excellent, affluent, and possessed of a noble lineage.
Even now, you are praised as a celibate student and a great yogi."
Moreover, by the power of our yoga, you shall become a fulfiller of our desires;
it remains forever unimpaired—what indeed is impossible for a yogi?
Nevertheless, O Kṛṣṇa, perform the wedding festival according to the prescribed rite.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa said, "So be it," and spoke as follows:
"In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, I shall fix the auspicious moment for my marriage with all the women;
meanwhile, you two and the others must maintain your composure."
Having spoken thus and performed the worship, he dismissed him after giving a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
He also gave various kinds of fees to the venerable sage Lomaśa,
and he gave two golden images to the venerable sage Lomaśa as well.
He gave sacrificial fees, golden vessels, and wealth to the brahmins.
Having thus performed a great festival, Hari went to the lake,
to the Vāsudeva-tīrtha where the outcaste had been uplifted.
Having bathed there at the Vyūha-tīrtha, Hari went to the banyan tree.
There, all the beloveds of Brahmā had arrived to sport.
Having given them wealth indeed brought by Kubera, he remained there.
Having honored all his wives with gifts such as fees for the bride-price (*dakṣiṇā*),
and having propitiated them by providing all necessary materials, he went to the edge of the riverbank.
Under the pretext of cleaning his teeth, he approached a *barbura* tree to sport there.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa indeed went to touch Rādhikā;
all those women, beginning with Brahmapriyā,
watched Mādhava as he went to the top of a barbur tree and touched it.
Then the women saw him taking hold of and pulling up a terminal branch suitable for cleaning the teeth; at that moment, that *barbura* tree sprang up together with its very roots. (25–26)
He prostrated himself upon the ground, and from that [spot] there suddenly appeared another great divine being, resembling Indra. Seeing Hari, he paid homage and fell to the earth at his feet.
He quickly prostrated himself like a staff and praised the Supreme Lord:
"O Supreme Lord, ocean of compassion, having remembered You, I have been delivered by You. You are the savior of all living beings, the bestower of liberation, the Supreme Ruler. (28–29)
You abide here as a bestower of grace, ready to uplift all people;
yet one with the eye of flesh does not recognize you, the Supreme Person.
I have attained you, the Supreme Lord, the deliverer from birth in the form of a tree.
"Today, indeed, by your command, I shall go to the divine heaven.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself and, offering flowers at the feet of Mādhava, desired to depart.
Just then, all those beloveds of Brahmā arrived there, filled with supreme wonder; they questioned their beloved:
"Who is this who has emerged from the tree, and how was the tree felled?"
"O Lord, we have a great curiosity regarding this; please tell us the cause of it.
Having heard this, Bālakṛṣṇa commanded that man to describe his entire history and his own story before them.
The king, having prostrated before them all, related this wondrous account:
"Formerly, I was indeed a sovereign emperor on the banks of the Sābhra river in Gaurjara;
my name was King Barbura, and I was devoted to righteous deeds."
He was skilled in protecting his subjects and a devoted worshiper of the gods and the virtuous.
He was constantly intent on religious vows and charity, always serving the elderly, and likewise devoted to the stories of Kṛṣṇa; he was a Vaiṣṇava who punished the wicked. (37–38)
Once, in a vast forest on the banks of the Sābhramatī,
I went forth with only a few attendants to survey the woods;
having traveled far into the deep wilderness on foot, I beheld a horse.
Divine, with a body of seven colors, its hair and skin were radiant:
white on the face, black on the hooves and lips, red on the tail and back, dark brown on the belly, and blue on the neck. (2.236.40–41)
Yellow at the ear and on the side, tawny on the shank,
green in the channels of the veins, and variegated at all the joints of the limbs—
such is that horse, diverse in appearance, firm, well-nourished, and endowed with strength.
Having observed him closely, I set my mind on capturing him.
Then, having slowly approached his side so that he might become confident,
I seized him by the ear and then by the neck with a rope.
Having taken hold of it, I made him my back-seat companion;
he went along exactly as I directed him.
Yet I do not know from where his such simplicity or his straightforwardness has come.
Just as I would move it, so did he go forward.
Having understood that the horse was driven by destiny, he led me to my city;
considering it his own good fortune, he became repeatedly filled with joy.
"I shall certainly not leave that horse, who is under divine protection, even for a moment.
Thereupon, he became enraged and cursed me, speaking in fury:
"Since you do not release me, nor do you recognize me at all... (48)
Even upon seeing me bound, you do not reach satisfaction;
nor, having understood my true nature, do you give me what is sweet with sincerity.
Recognizing me as a beast here in this bondage, you have made me your own and hold me captive.
"Then, O King, by my curse, become a thorny *barbura* tree in that forest;
endure suffering there day and night.
Having been addressed thus, I quickly recognized that the sage was most venerable.

I fell at his feet for the sake of the horse’s swift release. "O Lord, whether you are a god, a sage, or whoever you may be, though unknown to me, you are worthy of my worship; please grant forgiveness to this fool. (52–53)
Act so that the suffering of this curse may be quickly averted.
O Lord, reveal your own true form to me; I bow before you.
O Master, this offense was committed by me in ignorance, and not otherwise.
"Therefore, having practiced supreme forbearance, reveal your own true form.
Thus entreated repeatedly, that horse vanished and became the great ṛṣi named Āśvalāyana himself,
the preceptor of the royal lineage.
Realizing that he was my family preceptor, I wept profusely;
becoming most humble, I entreated him for the sake of revoking the curse. A son reconciles his offenses, but a father forgives day and night. (57)
For even teachers desire the defeat of their disciples.
O venerable one, I have committed an offense against you out of ignorance, greed for a horse, and my royal status;
please forgive me and grant me peace.
Thus entreated, the venerable sage Nāśvalāyana, having granted me forgiveness, said to me there: "O King, what shall I tell you?
Indeed, from the slighting of the great and from the transgressing of their seats, [great calamity arises]. (2.236.60)
And through the neglect of honoring those worthy of honor, merit is entirely destroyed.
Indeed, all of your merit has been lost by mounting my back;
you no longer possess devotion to the king, and you too shall be consumed by a curse.
After you have experienced the effects of the curse, heaven will swiftly be yours.
O King, from union with another's wife, from the humiliation of one's gurus, and from causing suffering to others, the destruction of one's lifespan indeed occurs. (65)
Furthermore, from adhering to false doctrines, from censuring gods and virtuous men,
from committing acts of malice toward the righteous, from causing suffering to one's parents, and even from tormenting one's wives, the destruction of one's lifespan indeed occurs. (64–65)
Indeed, from the commission of violence, the destruction of life-span occurs;
likewise, from the faults of intoxicants, meat, sexual indulgence, and so forth, and from the oppression of dharma, the destruction of life-span arises.
Furthermore, from the fault of possession by spirits and the like, the destruction of life-span is produced.
"You have committed a great offense, yet I did not speak out of shame;
for I am her preceptor, and I am here in the forest in the form of a horse.
This king saw me, so that he might not recognize me as his preceptor. (67–68)
"Thus, I did not change my form in your presence;
for immediately after that moment, the king will depart from here.
Having reflected thus, the horse assumed my form."

I wandered through non-existence for so long until I came into your presence. Having arrived, I was welcomed and led toward your home; yet even then, I thought that I must not reveal myself to him at all.
When he releases me from his house into a stable or into a secluded place in darkness, I shall assume my own form and depart for the forest;
by this means, he will have no grief.
"O King, I thought thus: 'This is a most grievous offense against my guru.
Yet you, out of a spirit of greed, did not abandon me in that desolate place; instead, you cast me into prison like a thief, keeping me there as if I were a permanent prisoner. (73–74)
Then, overcome with anger, I indeed cast a curse upon you;
by that, your merit has been destroyed—tell me, how much compassion have I shown?
Consequently, your kingship has been burnt away this very day due to the cause of your fault.
"Your body shall become like that of the Varbuḍru tree.
I shall grant you this favor here for the swift destruction of the curse, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, on the imperishable ground near the lake. (76–77)
"O Indra among kings, may you become hairy and enjoy the pleasures of drinking water and other such things.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord, shines there; you shall attain union with Him. (78)
He will take a branch from you for the purpose of cleaning his teeth.
When you, having truly attained a divine state and a divine body through the direct touch of his own hand, become a deity indeed— (2.236.80)
"Quickly you shall go to the celestial realm where Indra ever dwells;
having enjoyed the bliss of heaven there for a kalpa, you will proceed to the imperishable state.
Abandon anxiety, mental impressions, and attachment even to your kingdom, son, and beloveds."
"Indeed, kings have gone before, and others shall go as well.
Those who have attained liberation through union with Hari have truly gone; others have not.
Having spoken thus to me, the sage then departed for another forest.
Seeing me depart after I had said to him, "May it be well with you," even though I was dead,
I became a barbara tree on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Ten years have passed for me here in this barbara body.
O Kṛṣṇa, you have rescued me; the sin of the curse has been destroyed.
O bestower of liberation, by your touch I have become a possessor of merit.
I am your servant; you are my refuge—grant me the Vaiṣṇava mantra.
"Act in such a way that my liberation may occur at the end;
I am a king, so show me your own true form—that very nature which, by constantly meditating upon it, I might attain liberation from heaven. (87)
Thus entreated then by Rādhā, Hari, assuming the form of a king,
became King Pṛthu indeed in order to fulfill the desire of his devotee.
And he gave him that Vaiṣṇava mantra consisting of sixteen syllables.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Having taken this mantra and ascended the excellent celestial chariot, he indeed honored Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, with flowers and other offerings.

Then all those beloved of Brahmā, honored by the gods, went to heaven. At that time, the beloved of Brahmā beheld Bālakṛṣṇa, who possessed a vast form, as their own husband, the sovereign lord and king of the three worlds.
Then those wives, having fallen into a state of delusion, took pleasure with the broad-chested Pṛthu, who was Viṣṇu himself— bearing the bow and discus, firm, youthful, and infallible. Afterward,
in a mango grove, they worshipped that ocean of compassion for a long time.
They went to the shore of the lake and bathed together with their husband.
That sacred ford (tīrtha) was named Varbu, and from that time it became known as Pṛthutīrtha.
By residing there, one attains heaven, the destruction of curses, and liberation.
The beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having bathed and put on his garments,
then gladdened the beloved wives of Brahmā and sent them back to their hermitage;
thereafter, he returned to his own home at night and performed the worship of Lakṣmī once again.

The Blessed One made offerings of ghee lamps at night; he indeed performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and offered food oblations (*naivedya*), praying then for Śrī. Lakṣmī became pleased, and prosperity flourished in every house.
Thus, O Rādhikā, having celebrated the festival, he fell asleep.
By reading or hearing this, one becomes possessed of fortune and attains liberation.
For those who have been cursed, there is release from the curse and the destruction of their offenses.
"Even for those devoid of merit, there shall be the attainment of merit; of this there is no doubt.

(2.236.10) Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Dhanalakṣmī by Hari on the Thirteenth Day of the Fortunate Fortnight, the Worship of Brahmapriyā, the Liberation of King Barbura—who had been cursed by the sage Āśvalāyana and turned into a *barbura* tree—and the Establishment of Pṛthutīrtha and the Dispatching of Barbura to Heaven," in the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 236: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 237 [Author: Chapter 238 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, then on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Śrī Parameśvara performed the worship of Śambhu, the protector of his own sacred field.
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped his parents,
he then summoned Lord Īśāna and likewise the Rudras;
he also summoned the god Śaṅkara, the protector of the field (Kṣetrapa), together with Satī.
He established Lord Śambhu upon a golden lion-throne.
Bālakṛṣṇa worshipped that yogi, the husband of Padmā,
and offered him water for the feet, the arghya-offering, sandalwood paste, sacred ash, and unbroken grains of rice.
He placed a garland of *dhattūra* flowers around the neck of Hara,
and on his forehead he fashioned a lunar tilaka, a triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*), and an upright mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍraka*).
The illustrious Lord made Maheśvara laugh as he performed these acts for him.
He also gave him two earrings and *karṇikā* flowers for his ears;
he gave a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads to that Hara as well.
The Blessed Lord himself gave him a tiger skin and an elephant hide.
Hari gave betel-nut and offered sweet foods and sweet drinks;
he also gave flower garlands and likewise bestowed ornaments.
He gave the essence of fragrance and presented golden garments.
He gave golden necklaces to Satyā and likewise gave her ornaments;
he bestowed new garments and all kinds of desired decorations, as well as various articles for personal adornment.
Then he performed the *ārārtrika* rite and offered pearls and diamonds;
having thus worshipped the Lord Bhūtanātha together with Satī,
Hari then held a festival during the day and at night.
Having fed and worshipped Śambhu, Satī, and the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa),
as well as Kārttikeya, Nandin, and the circle of Yoginīs,
and having also fully worshipped the nine Durgās and the Ganges who belongs to Śaṅkara.
Likewise Vīrabhadra, Jālandhara, and the Asura Tāraka;
Tārakākṣa, Gaja, Mahiṣaka, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍaka;
as well as Śṛṅgin, Bhṛṅgin, Rīṭin, and Kirīṭin.
Agni, the Moon, and Maṅgala, as well as poison;
his skull-bowl (kharpara) and the gods, as well as a garland of skulls;
a lion, rudrākṣa beads, and Vāsuki, the progeny of Śaṅkara.
He worshipped Hanumān and likewise Niṣādī;
he worshipped Bhairava, known as Kāla, and Mahākāla.
He also worshipped the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the kūṣmāṇḍas.
He worshipped the Vaināyakas, the Vetālas, the Gaṇas, and diseases;
he worshipped Death (Mṛtyu), the nooses of death, Caṇḍī and the other goddesses, the Mothers (Mātṛkās), the planetary spirits (Grahās), and likewise the Pretas.
She worshipped the female deities of disease, such as Mahāmārī and others;
she also worshipped the Kṛtyās, Kālikā, and Brahmacāriṇī.
She worshipped all the inhabitants of Kailāsa, beginning with Śītalā.
He worshipped the Gaṇas, the wives of the Gaṇas, and the Rākṣasīs. Then he gratified them with cooked foods such as flour-cakes made of black gram.
Likewise, he gratified the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the wives of the Bhūtas, and the Ḍākinīs.
He worshipped the Śākinīs, the Yoginīs, and indeed the Vetālas;
likewise, he worshipped Kālarātri and all the night-faring spirits.
Having thus performed the worship and offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), Hari then—
The Lord performed the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rites for the satisfaction [of the deities] with ghee and other offerings.
With mustard seeds and the like, black gram and the like, black sesame, fruits and the like,
and also with black flowers and the like, he gratified the gods.
Having thus performed the worship, the offering of oblations, and likewise the invocation,
the glorious Lord, the Master, offered lamps everywhere. In this manner, on the night of the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika—
Having worshipped Kālī on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, Hari himself,
after worshipping Mahālakṣmī, performed the ritual dismissal. Then, on the day of the Dīpotsava festival, he slept during the night and [arose] at dawn.

Then, awakened by the sounds of beautiful musical instruments and by hymns of praise, the Lord performed his morning rites and worship; having completed these, he performed the worship of the ancestors.
Then Brahmā’s consorts, Lakṣmī, and others arrived before Śrī Hari.
Having performed the auspicious marriage rites for their own beloveds,
all of them, O Rādhikā, worshipped them with every kind of service.
And having received blessings and fed their own husbands, they [departed].
Having accepted the favor bestowed by him, they returned to the hermitage.
In the evening, Keśava celebrated the Festival of Lamps together with all the women.
The entire Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was filled with lamps within its waters.
Indeed, such a city shone like heaven itself.
At night, the illustrious Lord likewise performed the worship of Śāradā,
[offering praise] to the manifest Śrī, Śāradā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Satī.
Having summoned the five supreme goddesses, Kṛṣṇa honored them with betel leaves,
areca nuts, sweet foods,
fragrant essences, ornaments, fine garments, excellent liquids, and other offerings.
The Blessed One gratified him with gifts of whatever objects he desired; he performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, delighted him with jests,
gave gold and other sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and fed him milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Then he offered an explanation and thereafter slept peacefully;
the maidens, having gone to the hermitage, fell asleep full of longing.
At dawn, Hari quickly woke up and went to the lake.
Having performed his ablutions in the waters of the lake, he remembered his own eternal true nature, the protector of all, on the shore;
for by his own yoga, that great holy place (tīrtha) exists within the lake itself. (2.237.39–40)
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari meditated upon Himself within Himself there;
at that moment, the army of King Saṃparka arrived on the bank, distressed by the suffering of the great pestilence and crying out "Alas! Alas! (Hā Hā).
"Emaciated, overcome by hunger and thirst, exhausted, and on the verge of death.
Śrī Rādhikā said: "How indeed did he come there accompanied by his army?"
Of which country was he the king, and how did this disease arise among his army?
What indeed did Bālakṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa do for him then?
O beloved, tell me the entire auspicious story of Hari in brief.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā; that king was Saṃparka, born in the land of Kaccha.
For the purpose of a pilgrimage, he indeed went to Somanātha. (49)
He constantly worshipped his preceptor Dattātreya, a portion of myself from a former kalpa,
while ruling his kingdom free from thorns on the riverbank.
He was devoted to bathing at dawn and intent upon the worship of the gods.
Devoted to the duty of giving, he honored guests at food-distributions;
he was constantly intent on meditation and a provider of food to the poor and the helpless.
Devoted to serving the virtuous, he followed the instructions of his elders and others.
He was devoted to serving cows and Brahmins, a worshiper of virtuous and faithful women,
non-violent, truthful in conduct, and honored by his subjects;
and upon seeing or hearing of holy men, he would rise and approach them like a servant.
And he serves them with gifts of clothing, as well as gifts of food and the like.
Furthermore, throughout his kingdom, there are circles of virtuous people everywhere who are solely devoted to the worship of the gods and intent upon the stories of Kṛṣṇa.
O Rādhikā, that which occurs every year on the bank of the Nārāyaṇa lake within the kingdom is a preeminent Vaiṣṇava sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
this very king, O Rādhikā, attends it together with his entire military host.

Resplendent with elephants, horses, camels, bulls, carts, and vehicles, he set out for Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra during the month of Āśvina for the sake of pilgrimage. Accompanied by thousands of people and joined by Brahmins and virtuous men, he departed. (53–54)
Having performed the libations for the ancestors at the holy ford where the Hiraṇyā confluence meets,
and having likewise performed bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth, and having worshipped Someśvara;
and having visited the Mūladvārikikā ford and worshipped Gopati.
Having gone to Prācīsarasvatī, he performed the Nārāyaṇa-bali sacrifice.
Then, having seen Vāmanabhūmi and the Svarṇarekhā river, and having established Cakratīrtha, he proceeded to Indreśvara.
Then, having visited the Sītāphala forest and the Tūrikā tīrtha,
one should proceed to the Āmravaṇa forest to bathe in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
On the way, due to the particular fatigue of the journey and the lack of regular meals, [one may experience exhaustion].
And by the power of that heat, the army then became afflicted;
oppressed by great pestilence and major diseases,
and overcome by illness, they approached the edge of the lake in their misery, seeking the merit of the sacred ford.
Having observed his servants and others, as well as the animals shedding blood,
and seeing himself wounded, the king remembered his own spiritual preceptor,
the blessed Dattātreya, who was present on the earth as Bālakṛṣṇa.
Protect the men afflicted here at this sacred site;
O True Guru, come quickly and grant us the gift of life. This disease is destructive and robs our servants of their strength. (62–63)
Even the slaughterer of animals is a most terrible source of bloodshed.
Protect me, protect me, O ocean of compassion, Dattātreya, Teacher of the World!
May Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also protect me, who have come to you for refuge.

Having thus urged [his men], the king, accompanied by his army, took up residence among the *kadamba* trees in the vicinity of the lake. Having reached the shore of the lake and drunk water on its bank at dawn, [he remained there]. (65–66)
Accompanied by his caravan, the king performed the chanting and worship of Hari, consisting of rhythmic clapping and cymbals, as well as descriptive praises of His names:
"O Bālakṛṣṇa! O Hare Kṛṣṇa! O Nārāyaṇa! O Remover of Distress! (67)
"O Dattātreya, O Guru, protect us! O Supreme Lord, save us!
(68) Thus did the king perform his worship together with a thousand men;
and this roar of his reached to the very ends of the quarters. (69)
Having heard this, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa remained steadfast;
yet, although he had set out toward the city, he stayed to observe the worship and other rites.
A great throng gathered around the lake, like that of the inhabitants living along its shores.
On the shore of the lake, those who were visiting the saffron pond became absorbed in the worship of Rādhikā; they saw nothing at their sides,
nor before them, nor even behind them, for they did not even open their eyes.
For they performed worship with one-pointed concentration for the sake of pacifying their disease,
and they bound Lord Hari within their own hearts by means of the rope of devotion.
Seeing and hearing this there, the Lord Himself, Hari, who is Bālakṛṣṇa—
He quickly appeared in the form of Dattātreya,
carrying a small water-pot at his waist, a water-jar in his hand, as well as matted locks, a loincloth, a rosary for recitation, and auspicious sandals. (74–75)
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," he approached the presence of the king.
Upon seeing him, the king quickly prostrated himself on the ground like a staff,
and the soldiers also prostrated themselves on all sides.
With a serene countenance, the divine Dattātreya spoke to them:
"How have you remembered me? Tell me the reason quickly.
The king replied, "There is the affliction of a great pestilence; therefore, protect us from it."
Then the blessed Dattātreya, having opened his belly and stomach-cavity,
gave the king a small amount of ash which was there;
"Throw it into your mouth," he said, and the king threw it into his mouth.
The Great Plague (Mahāmārī), having emerged in embodied form with a distorted face,
bowed to that god and fled toward Śaṅkara in fear;
and at that moment, the army became free from disease in an instant.
Just then, Dattātreya, the son of Atri, arrived there;
at that moment, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the descendant of Kaṃbharā, was born.
Seeing Hari, the Lord of Ramā, there in such a form, the king—
Then, accompanied by his army, he attained a great and wonderful protector;
Dattātreya worshipped the great lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa,
and the gracious Śrī Hari spoke to him for the purpose of granting a boon.
Then Dattātreya said: "Protect me here in your presence;
I am a portion of you and wish to dwell forever in your sacred field.
Hari replied: "So be it; dwell in the waters of the Aśvasaras lake."
The great sacred ford (tīrtha) of Dattātreya shall be known by your name.
Thereafter, you will take up residence upon the peak of Mount Revata;
the mountain Raivata shall also come to be called Mahendra.
And in Saurāṣṭra, Kumuda and others shall dwell all around him;
then, O Dattātreya, your residence shall be upon that peak.
That mountain ridge of Dattātreya shall always be a great sacred site (tīrtha).
"Here, at my place, a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the form of water shall remain forever.
And there, on Mount Raivata, that sacred ford shall remain for you in the sky forever.
Having been addressed thus, the Blessed One Dattātreya dwelt in those waters.
Indeed, that great holy ford of Dattātreya arose within that lake;
through its contact, it became a sacred bathing place (Samparkatīrtha) that truly provides protection.
That king had [a temple] constructed on the bank of that tank.
To the south is a beautiful temple graced by Dattātreya.
Having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, Nirug indeed returned to his own country.
O Rādhikā, thus Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa protects those who are suffering.
The Lord, the source of all incarnations and higher than the highest, assumes their very form and effects the protection of His devotees.
All incarnations belong to Him alone; everything proceeds from Him.
The Lord of All provides protection from everything when he is merely remembered.
Whether in a forest, on a mountain, by a river, in the ocean, or even in a wood;
in a treacherous and fearful place, the Lord of Men protects one when remembered. (95–96)
When one is in the midst of enemies, at the mouth of Death, in fire, during the agitation of the winds,
in an earthquake, or in a great battle— the All-pervading One, when remembered, provides protection.
In cases of the three humors being disturbed, in crushing calamities, in wells, in disease, or in years of famine.

The All-Seeing One, when remembered, protects one from shackles and the snares of others. Indeed, when remembered, He who dwells within the self protects one from the mouth of poison, the mouth of a predator, the falling of weapons, the thunderbolt, the fall from the sky, and from precipices. (98–99)
In fear of kings, in fear of the home, and even in the fear of being driven away;
in fear for one's life, and in every kind of fear—the Almighty One, when remembered, provides protection.
O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa becomes the true kinsman of those who have become His own.
For the sake of its protection, he indeed maintains great anxiety day and night.
(101) From reciting and hearing this, the fruit of visiting sacred fords shall arise;
there is no doubt that protection and the destruction of suffering will surely occur. (102)

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Śāradā during the Great Festival on the Kālī-Caturdaśī in the Tretā Cycle of the Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, Following the Worship of Śaṅkara and His Gaṇas, Servants, and Slaves; the Offering of Lamps by Śrī Hari on Dīpāvalī; and the Dispelling of Disease for Kings and Others Afflicted by the Mahāmārī Plague through the Bestowing of a Vision in the Form of Dattātreya on the Pratipadā Day, as well as the Dattātreya Tīrtha. || 237 ||
