Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in the new year, the Lord, the husband of Brahmā’s beloved,
celebrated the festival of the mountain of food (annakūṭa) in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
He fed all the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā—
men, women, children, youths, and the elderly from every side;
as well as animals, guests, birds, and aquatic creatures.
Hari indeed fed all the conscious beings dwelling on the earth.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa spoke to Lakṣmī and likewise to Annapūrṇā in his own abode, desiring them to eat.

"Today a desire has arisen in me for the sake of feeding everyone at the time following midday; if it may be so, please do accordingly. Having received this command, Annapūrṇā spoke to the illustrious Supreme Lord.
"O Blessed One, indeed five *ghaṭikās* are required for the sake of the food being cooked;
today the time is exactly such. We shall prepare the entirety of the meal; there is no doubt that it is already boiling. (6–7)
Having spoken thus, that Annapūrṇā remembered her friend Bhūmi;
she quickly remembered Śrī, and there she also remembered Vārkṣī;
she remembered Sudhā and swiftly remembered the Lakṣmī of grains.
He remembered all his companions, the hearth-stones, and likewise the sacrificial fuel;
he remembered the leaves for the vegetables, and all the various spices;
he remembered the Ganges and other rivers, and he remembered the wish-fulfilling cows.
Pākalakṣmī remembered the fires,
and there she also remembered the vessels named Akṣaya, as well as the excellent flavors;
and Annapūrṇikā remembered all those who are dear to Brahmā.
She remembered the female cooks, she remembered the waitresses, (12) and she remembered all those who prepared sour gruel and the like, and those who provided drinks of buttermilk;
at that time she remembered them all, and they arrived. (13)
She also commanded the earth, "Quickly prepare a kitchen!
and within a moment, she made it half a *krośa* in circumference and circular; she likewise did so.
She spoke to the rivers for the sake of water, and they brought the waters.
The cooking-pots said, "We are situated to remain on a suitable place.
The fires said to the pots, "We are situated within the pots for the sake of dwelling.
The cauldrons said, "We are situated to remain upon the tops of the cooking-pots."
The ladles and other utensils were instantly appointed to their respective tasks;
the grains, cereals, and juices were placed in vessels, and likewise, the clarified butter and other substances were prepared to remain in the cooking pots. (17)
Then, from all sides, the attendants of Lakṣmī stood before her;
at that time, all those dear to Brahmā became her benefactors.
And by the will of all the Lakṣmīs, [they provided] ghee and other offerings.
And in the cauldrons and vessels,
grains and other such things, as well as flour and the like, come together and cook according to their requirements;
having assembled there for the purpose of being cooked, they enter from all sides.
Likewise, sweets such as sugar-candies, cooked dishes,
and even minced meat preparations (veśavāra), quickly arrive and enter there at the will of Annapūrṇā.
Furthermore, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) attend upon her, stationed on all sides.
At the end of two *ghaṭīs*,

the attendants (*pārṣadas*) and guardians of the field (*kṣetrapas*) of Śambhu presented many prepared cooked foods as invitations to all those dwelling in the sacred precinct (*ākṣarakṣetra*) for the sake of a meal. (23)
Mountains of cooked foods indeed arose in the kitchen;
from that, many varieties of sweets and other preparations were produced in abundance.
Furthermore, countless kinds of snacks were born there as well.
Edible foods were also quickly prepared there in countless varieties; likewise, many kinds of lickable foods were made,
and all types of chewable foods were prepared in great abundance.
Then, all kinds of gruels were quickly prepared;
likewise, various soups such as *āranāla* and others, along with boiled salted chickpeas, black gram, and similar items, were served there. (27–28)
There were various kinds of vegetables, as well as diverse preparations for frying; many savory curries rich with the essence of sugared juices,
and curds, ghee, fresh butter, milk-rice, milk, and buttermilk.
Everything, both cooked and uncooked, was prepared according to their respective requirements.
All the wives of Brahmā, including Lakṣmī, the maidens, and others,
as well as the virtuous *sati*s and the *siddhi*s, stood guard over everything that had been done.
Within five *ghaṭikās*, everything beneficial had been accomplished.
The goddesses prayed to the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama:
"Everything here has already been achieved; people of all different castes are present. (32)
Perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and cause the ringing of bells.
Let there be rows of people everywhere for the purpose of eating.
For at midday, O Rādhikā, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa [is present].
Having bathed, performed the Vaiśvadeva rite, and offered libations to the fire and the ancestors,
and having gratified all the deities, he caused the sound of a bell to be made:
"O highly fortunate ones, please come to the rows for the sake of the meal."
Then, according to their rank, all the vessels were indeed arranged in rows.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other human beings also arrived there quickly from all sides for the sake of eating. (36–37)
The members of the Brahmin class served the food to the brahmins; they fed the men and women there in great abundance from all sides. Indeed, Bālakṛṣṇa gave them rings as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Laddukas, śaṣkulis, and hundred-holed khājakas;
meśubhas, mohanasthālas, and pieces of parpikās; as well as piṇḍakas, excellent guḍakas, granthikas, and modakas. (2.238.39–40)
He also offered *kalikāḍaḍū* cakes, *mudgalaḍū* cakes, *maṇḍaka* pancakes,
*sohilaka* sweets, *saṃyāva* pastries, *kaṃsāra* fritters, *ghṛtapūraka* cakes, savory *sevikā* rolls, sweet *polikā* cakes, *pūrikā* pancakes, and likewise *pāyasa* rice pudding.
Virañja, the pleasure-giving pheṇī, gundrapāka, and apūpakas; ||42|| pūpas, ghurghuras, vaṭakas, and sesame flour-cakes;
śāṭakas, sthirakas, and the fruits of the plantain and mango trees. ||43||
Leafy vegetables such as bhiṇḍaka, svarṇadugdha, kośātakī, and likewise rājakośātakī; gavāhārā and mārgarī;
as well as karkoṭikā, śimbikā, karkaṭī, and cirbhaṭa.
Red yams, black gram and other pulses, the fruits of the *śimbī* and *bimbī* trees; sugar-cane, the *kharbūja* melon, and the *kāravellaka*;
the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the *sūraṇa*, the *muniśimbī*, and the *paṭola*. (45–46)
Also water-melons, methikā, pāravalla, and radish;
śatapuṣpā, sour loṇī, jīvantī, and likewise syandikā;
and fried eggplant, as well as those things smeared with black mustard.
Dates mixed with sugar, balls of wheat flour mixed with curd, flower-balls, various foods, and fragrant rice;
as well as soups, broths, buttermilk, and curd-mashes. 48–49.
Fried *harimantha* beans, flat peas, and likewise *parpaṭas*;
fresh butter, *āranāla*, and *caṭanī* made from coriander and other spices;
sweet boiled milk, curd, and ghee with saffron.
Marīca peppers that are very bitter, as well as cardamom and grains of long pepper;
seeds of bhūphalī and sugar-candy; valla beans and small vaṭa nuts; flower-buds, sweet polīs, ghārikās, and sweet jambukas. 91–92.
There, the brahmins and others [prepared] one hundred and one items, including *roṭakas*, *mūśalīpākas*, *vāsudevī*, *mallikā*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *taralā*, *māṣalaḍḍukas*, and *kalāvaka*. (53)
Having eaten and attained supreme satisfaction, they then indeed went to their homes.
The kṣatriyas, the classes of vaiśyas, and the śūdras feasted with joy;
so too did the wretched, the classes of orphans, the beggars, and those without support.
Then all the groups of male servants and female servants enjoyed [the offerings];
all those situated within the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā partook.
In each and every article there, no deficiency whatsoever arose.
It increases when served into an inexhaustible vessel;
everything being given becomes inexhaustible and imperishable.
Thus did the great seers, the virtuous, and the holy women partake.
Then everyone, from children to the elderly and even the cowherds, partook of the meal;
the guardians of the fields, the deities, and all others likewise ate.
And the entire family of Hari also ate, by the will of the Lord of Śrī.
Then all the women, led by Brahmapriyā, full of enthusiasm, came before Lord Bālakṛṣṇa in order to feed their beloved husband;
they brought vessels set upon golden plates for the sake of Hari.
They placed vessels filled with cooked food before Hari;
the Lord Hari, having sat properly upon a golden seat and a woolen rug,
began to eat after sipping water (ācamana), preceded by the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis).
They worshipped Śrī Hari with sandalwood, saffron, and saffron filaments;
out of extreme devotion, they fed Him with garlands of love.
Lakṣmī placed a vast golden platter before Him.
O Rādhā, small pavilions have been established by you on all sides;
Māṇikī placed a water-pitcher along with a drinking vessel filled with water.
And Ramā, holding a fan, indeed provides a cooling breeze.
Padmāvatī stood by his side, holding a garment;
likewise, all the beloved wives of Brahmā, hailing from every land,
then performed the serving of all the various dishes.
The goddesses, led by Annapūrṇā, said to the illustrious Supreme Lord:
"O Lord, beloved of compassion, please eat; we, being purified, desire to behold you here.
Then Kṛṣṇa, taking a morsel in his hand, ate it with joy.

"Oh, how sweet! Oh, what a delicious meal! By whom has this auspicious food been cooked? (69) Having asked the names of its makers, he praised them repeatedly; and having commended it as being made exceedingly savory, he ate of it again. (2.238.70)
Brahmā’s beloveds and all the other women beheld Hari eating; gazing upon their husband, the lord of their lives, those women were struck with wonder.
When Hari, having eaten very little, desired to rise, ||| 71 ||
Establishing him [in his seat], Śāradā sang the hymn of praise, saying, "Eat.
Sarasvatī, accompanied by musical instruments, sang verses for the meal specifically to please Śrī Hari and to feed him. (72–73)
"O Lord, prepare food; O Yogi, grant your grace! O Beloved, Master of my heart, O Yogi!
Take this mouthful, Kṛṣṇa—this most delicious, most desired [food]."
Taste this heap of food of exquisite fragrance!
O Blessed One, bestower of the goals of human life, enjoy this at will; it is entirely ripe, O living yogi! (74)
O Lord, provide food for the life of this yogi; O Beloved, Master of my heart, O Yogin, grant your grace!
[Give] the auspicious vessel of enchantment, filled with mangoes, milk-rice, and fine food. 75.
O Lord, O Yogin who is my very life, partake of this well-prepared *śaṣkulī*, the *pheṇī*, the sandalwood-scented *iṣṭapolī*, and this meal;
O Beloved, O Yogin who is my very life, grant me this grace! 76.
O Lord, O Yogi who sustains our lives, please partake of this meal: *suparpikā*, *rasāḍhyā*, sweetmeats, *virañja*, the beloved *sugandhapāka*, fine *suśāṭaka* garments, and *ghurghurā*.
Grant your grace, O beloved, O companion of my life!
[Give us] delicious and sweet chickpeas, excellent mung-bean cakes, and flower gardens filled with various vegetables, greens, and other edible delights. //77//
"O Lord, provide food for the life of the yogin; O Beloved, Master of my heart, grant your grace to the yogin.
[78] "Parched grains, roasted flour, and auspicious sour gruel..."
All foods are accompanied by buttermilk and milk;
O Lord, O Yogin, grant me this meal for my life! O Beloved, O Master of my Heart, O Yogin, bestow your grace! 79.

O Lord, O yogi who is my very life, partake of fragrant water, sweet soup and rice as you desire, along with blooming fried cakes and other well-cooked delicacies such as *ghurghura*. Please accept this meal.
"O beloved, lord of my heart, O yogi, grant me your grace!
Eat today this betel leaf mixed with cardamom and cloves, anointed with nectar, until it fills your throat; and give the remainder to me."
"O Lord, O Beloved, O Master, please take your meal; O Dear One,
O Lord of Desire, O Enjoyer, grant us your favor!"—
in this manner, Rādhikā caused her virtuous husband to eat with all of them.

Then the Blessed One ate his fill; thereafter, all the women also took morsels in their hands for the sake of feeding their own husband, the Sustainer of the Universe, and they exerted themselves there with sheer force. (82–83)
To fulfill the mental desires of those wives, Hari, the Lord of Yoga,
assumed as many forms as there were wives— indeed, an infinite number of forms.
From the hands of all those wives of Brahmā, morsels of food [were taken].
He enjoyed them at the same time, delighting them with affection.
Hari drank water and betel leaf from each of their hands; there he partook, and they were thus fulfilled in their desires. (85–86)
Then the Blessed One, with his own hand, repeatedly fed cooked foods and delicacies to all his companions;
and having fed them, he gave them betel juice and betel leaves.
He caused all those daughters of the lotus—numbering in the millions and billions—to drink [the nectar].
Thus, those beloved wives of Brahmā and other women became fulfilled;
likewise, the women who served food and those who prepared the cooking [were also satisfied]. (88–89)

Women who assist in cooking, those who fetch articles, those who display goods, and likewise those who provide flavors— whichever of these were summoned there by Annapūrṇā and the others, [they arrived]. || 2.238.90 ||
Having obtained the grace of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa— which is indeed difficult to attain—
they easily received it, and having partaken of it, they were fully satisfied. Having thus eaten, they made a heap of food and set it aside.
He granted supreme grace even to aquatic creatures,
and to birds, beasts, and insects on all sides;
there the Blessed One bestowed his favor without any restriction.
From the trees, the forest creepers, and the clusters on all sides,
Hari indeed gave delightful, flowing food at their roots;
for the sake of receiving this grace, the gods and the great sages likewise gathered.
The ancestors also, being liberated and possessing divine bodies, arrived;
wherever that prasāda was seen, they appeared in such a manner. Having become so, they all received the prasāda while remaining unobserved.
Having thus received this favor, they indeed departed for their respective worlds.
Having enjoyed all those supernatural powers and obtained the supreme command of the Lord,
they then brought about the disappearance of the kitchen area.
Everything indeed became still, and the city attained a state of contentment;
filled with great joy, it sang the cry of victory for the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having gone to their own homes, they truly found rest.
Thus did Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhikā, celebrate a great festival.
By reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of a mountain of rice;
and by offering libations to Bālakṛṣṇa, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of the Mound of Food (*annakūṭotsava*) Instituted by Śrī Hari and the Feeding of All Creatures," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 239: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 239.
[The Author: Chapter 240.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, now listen to another marvel of the Lord Hari.
At the end of the night of the eleventh day of the month of Kārttika, the Lord performed [this act].
Puṇḍarīka became a great Vaiṣṇava king of Gūrjara;
endowed with all virtues, he protected his kingdom on the edge of the earth.
Every morning he indeed performs the worship of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī with excellent materials;
having honored the virtuous and the elderly, he always takes his meal.
Guests constantly come to and depart from his house.
Having performed the worship of Hari’s names, they eat your food.
They also observe the vows associated with the festivals of Hari’s birthday.
By that king, a auspicious drum was caused to be sounded throughout his own kingdom.
All the subjects, with the exception of the elderly, children, and the sick, must observe all the Ekādaśī fasts without food.
Upholding their virtuous vows, all the subjects indeed obeyed his command.
His subjects, devoted to Viṣṇu, also partook in his vow and worshiped Hari. That king went to Aśvapaṭṭasara for the purpose of a pilgrimage;
there, in the sacred field known as Akṣara, he observed the Ekādaśī of the month of Kārttika.
Having gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā on the tenth day,
he fed the virtuous ones, the brāhmaṇas, and Bālakṛṣṇaka;
with devotion, he honored Lomaśa and the circle of sages.
He bathed in the sacred ford (tīrtha) and beheld the gods and other deities. He gazed upon the divine city of Kuṅkumavāpikā and performed a circumambulation of the lake on all sides.
He worshipped all the deities situated on the bank with offerings;
at night, the king performed the *ārātrika* ritual for the lake.
Having rested in the hall, he rose quickly in the morning.
Having performed his daily rites, bathed, and honored the Brahmins,
and having completed the ritual at the sacred ford, he then went for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa.
He worshipped the Lord Bāleśa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The king gave infinite gifts of gold, silver, and garments;
he bestowed wealth upon the brahmins and those who follow the sacred fords,
as well as clothing and vessels upon the virtuous, and whatever was desired by the destitute.
The king also gave gifts of cows and gifts of food;
he likewise had the concluding rite (udyāpana) of his vow performed with excellent fruit,
including the giving of golden jars and the like, as well as the offering of golden images.
The king gave gifts of wealth, grain, clothing, and vessels,
as well as listened to the narration of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, the monarch performed these acts during the day.
He attended upon the sages and likewise attended upon virtuous women.
The king performed salutations to his devotees and offered worship in the evening;
he also performed the *ārātrika* ceremony and kept a vigil at night.
Without water and without food, accompanied by his entire caravan, he performed worship at night preceded by the playing of cymbals, chanting:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord, Sovereign Lord! (21)
O Supreme Soul born of Kambharā, O delighter of Śrīmat Gopālā;
O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Rādhā, O Master;
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Svāmī, O All-pervading One! 22–23.
Thus he performed worship, chanting, and glorification;
then, in his own heart, he meditated upon the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa whom he had seen directly.
Having performed worship until dawn, he became absorbed in meditation.
And all his followers went to the lake for the purpose of bathing.
At the hour of Brahmā (brāhme muhūrte), the king, having meditated upon Śrī Narāyaṇa within his own heart, chanted: "I am He, I am He, I am He, I am He."
Thus, being both *haṃsa* and *haṃsa*, I chanted *haṃsa-haṃsa*.
Hearing this chanting, the Blessed Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, who dwells within the heart,
became instantly pleased upon remembering His ancient form as the *haṃsa*.
There, Hari himself quickly assumed the form of a swan;
white in color, with white luster, possessing the very appearance of a white swan,
with both divine and human faces, he was a swan-bodied being endowed with splendor.

With limbs proportioned to his form, as beautiful as ten million gods of love, he was a treasure-house of all sciences as well as a treasury of the Vedas and other branches of knowledge. And he approached the presence of the king, walking very slowly on foot.
The king saw a region on the shore of a lake within his own heart;
he also saw the approaching swan with Lakṣmī by its side.
His heart was filled with wonder and his body was suffused with love.

Having risen, he became filled with haste to approach the Blessed One; at that very moment, he attained the state of wakefulness. And as soon as he opened his eyes, O Rādhā, he beheld [him] in close proximity.
He beheld a great mass of splendor in all directions.
In an instant, his own eyes became capable of perceiving that light;
then, within that womb of radiance, he saw the Lord of the worlds.
Seeing one of white complexion, in the form of a swan, laughing and endowed with splendor,
the king suddenly rose and fell prostrate like a staff.
Saying, "I am fulfilled," he placed the dust of [the swan's] feet upon his face.
He rolled repeatedly upon the ground near his feet;
the king also shed tears from his eyes out of great joy.
Lakṣmī then consecrated the king’s head with water from her water-pot.
Having obtained grace, the king, filled with joy, drank that water. Having attained his goal through this vision, he spoke:
"Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for me, this very body of a king! (39)
Upon seeing whom supreme bliss arises— the Full Brahman, the Supreme Lord,
in the form of a swan, endowed with splendor, who has come here manifestly out of compassion—
I have been purified, I have been liberated, and I have been rescued from the ocean.
Having spoken thus, he grasped the feet of the swan and observed a vow of silence.
The swan said, "O King, choose a boon, whatever you desire.
The king replied, "O Hari, grant me liberation here and lead me to Your state."
I have no desire for a kingdom, nor do I possess any longing for worldly existence. (43) All other desires are fully satisfied; bring about my liberation.
That gain which belongs to yogis does not exist even when the age has passed away. (44)
"Today I have obtained that very gain through the observance of the Ekādaśī vow.
Therefore, O ocean of mercy, grant me liberation here by all means.
Having accepted these words of the king, Rādhikā, the Supreme Lord, [acted accordingly].
"So be it," he said with a smile; at that moment, the king’s followers and others arrived.
Beholding his splendors, they gazed upon Hari.
Indeed, having seen him in the form of a swan, they became fulfilled.
Just then, a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun arrived there;
the king, having cast off his body,
attained a liberated form and, in an instant, became four-armed and equal to Viṣṇu, seated within that chariot.
Then the queen, having attained that touch, quickly grasped the celestial chariot with her own hand to go along with him; even as she did so,
casting off her physical body, she became possessed of a divine form.
Then, that celestial chariot (vimāna) immediately appeared there in the sky.
Haṃsa, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, also became the four-armed Viṣṇu.
With that chariot, he led the king straight to Vaikuṇṭha.
He stood upon the bank of the lake in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa.
His splendor vanished, and the caravan was struck with wonder.
All the members of the caravan and the king’s followers performed the funeral rites for his body.
Then the kings went to their own country and told their son this entire account; having heard it again, he rejoiced greatly.
O Rādhikā, that Haṃsatīrtha is in the waters of Tvaśvapaṭṭasaras.
In the southeastern corner, there was an auspicious place that bestows liberation.
Through bathing, giving gifts, immersion, drinking the water, and frequenting it, enjoyment, heaven, and liberation shall be attained; of this there is no doubt. (55–56)
There, self-knowledge arises from bathing and drinking the water;
and at Haṃsatīrtha, the merit of a sacrifice is obtained through the gift of food.
Indeed, on the twelfth lunar day, by feeding even a single virtuous person, one gains supreme merit.
There is no doubt that the merit of feeding a hundred virtuous people [is attained];
by the gift of fruit on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), the fruit is equal to the gift of gold.
And here, the fruit from the gift of gold shall be equal to the Rājasūya sacrifice. 58–59.
Listen, O Rādhikā, to another marvel of the Great Lord:
the King of Utkala, named Rolā, set out with his army for the sake of pilgrimage to Somanātha,
arriving there very slowly over many months.
Having visited the great pilgrimage site of Somanātha, the Prācīsarasvatī,
the Mūladvārikikā-tīrtha, Vāmanasthalī, the great pilgrimage site of Bhadrāvatī, and Kuṅkumavāpikā; ||61–62||
He arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa on the full moon day;
having arrived in the evening, he performed the ritual ablution according to rule and drank the water.
His army was satisfied by the drinking of water, and he himself took his meal at night. (63)
He heard the sounds of the gods' nightly litanies and well-composed hymns of praise.
Having found rest during the night, he then fell under the power of sleep;
and the army, having slept, arose at dawn on the bank of the lake.
There was a garden of fruits and flowers belonging to the King’s elephant-keepers;
the king’s cattle went there to graze upon the grass.
The trees of the garden were devoured by the beasts and even destroyed.
At sunrise, the king, having woken from his sleep, went to the Horse-lake (Aśvasaras).
Having performed his ablutions, charities, and rites, he returned to his own residence.
Meanwhile, that goddess whom the lord of the earth used to worship daily— || 67-68 ||
There, that image of Śrī Nṛsiṃha vanished from sight.
The king grieved in his mind, thinking, "Surely some offense has been committed by me here;
otherwise, the disappearance of the image would not have occurred—of this there is no doubt. (69)
With a grieving heart, he praised Nṛhari:
"O Lord, O ocean of compassion, why indeed are you angry with me today?
I do not know what offense I have committed here that you have come [to this state]."
"I shall die; having abandoned food, I will not take water or fruit.
May I indeed be an offender; this is my penance.
When he had spoken thus, a voice from the sky arose.

"O King, here in the eastern direction there is certainly a garden of fruits and flowers belonging to Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. Behold, its destruction is being carried out by your cattle and other animals; do not delay."
"Restrain them quickly and have a great garden constructed.
You have committed this offense; hear now another thing you have done:
here, you did not perform worship of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa."

He of whom I am an incarnation is the cause of my incarnation. If my worship were to take place without first honoring him, it would be an offense against you; consequently, I would meet with destruction. Therefore, first worship him.
Therefore, worship me here; by that I shall be pleased with you.
Install my image here on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
In that beautiful temple, I shall dwell in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.

"For the purpose of guarding the garden and also for the protection of the forest, O Rādhikā, I shall indeed come with you; not otherwise. Having been addressed thus, the king honored the celestial voice. (2.239.80)
Having gone quickly to the vicinity of the army, he restrained those beasts.
Seeing the garden utterly devastated, he fell into great sorrow.
Then, having swiftly reported the incident to the army commanders, [he departed]. (81)
Having issued orders for the protection of the garden and for the construction of a new garden,
and likewise having given the command for the swift building of a palace,
he— equipped with the materials for worship— went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Seeing Rola approaching, the Lord of the virtuous smiled and said:
"O King Rola! Tell me, when did you arrive in this field?
Is all well with you, and is it likewise well with your army? (84)
"Are your animals, men, and dependents well?
O Lord of Men, please accept food in my house today.
Thus addressed, King Rola shed tears and said to him: [86]
O Nārāyaṇa, ocean of mercy, I have indeed committed an offense against you here;
the garden was destroyed by my soldiers and beasts. Therefore, grant me forgiveness.
I shall cause a garden to be made, and I shall cause a temple to be built.

"The installation of your form as Nṛsiṃha shall always remain here for the protection of the sacred field and its grove, while I shall go to my own kingdom. O Kṛṣṇa, without your worship, Nṛsiṃha has entered into dissolution within me. (88–89)
"O Puruṣottama, forgive this offense of mine.
Having spoken thus, Rādhikā worshipped the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa with royal attire, garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings. (2.239.90)
Then he performed the offering of food like a staff, and gave the ritual balls (piṇḍas).
He also offered betel nut and accepted the grace of Hari.
Having been told by Hari, "You are forgiven," he went to his own home.
Then the Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha, manifesting in bodily form upon His own throne, accepted the king’s worship with heartfelt devotion.
The king, for his part, had a new and very sturdy temple constructed.
He installed Nṛsiṃha in the temple and provided for its maintenance.
Then, having planted a garden and appointed a guardian, that devotee of Kṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, departed for the land of Utkala. (94–95)
Thus, that Nṛsiṃha-tīrtha came to exist within the waters of the lake; likewise,
that beautiful Roḷa-tīrtha and the temple of Nṛhari became entirely composed of sacred fords through the majesty of Bālakṛṣṇa.

There, those who perform the ritual bathing, as well as donors who plant fruit-bearing trees, will surely attain enjoyment, liberation, and an auspicious state. So too shall those who plant clusters of flowers and establish great gardens. (97–98)
For all those men— even those who merely water the roots of trees— shall go to the eternal and immutable abode of Brahman;
having reached heaven and enjoyed its pleasures for a long time, they shall go to my imperishable state.
From reciting or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of planting a garden.
Those who plant trees and creepers anywhere on earth, within the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara or upon its banks, shall attain the supreme goal.
Those without lineage will obtain a lineage, and likewise the poor will become wealthy;
and through the protection of the earth, those who are flavorless will become full of flavor.
They will be enriched with wealth and grain, and they will enjoy the fruit of desirable food.
Those who plant trees near horses, cloths, and lakes,
O Rādhikā, shall become my beloveds;
I dwell among the hosts of cowherd girls in the forests, within the fruits and flowers.

"I dwell in the house of those people who protect trees, endowed with prosperity; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, upon their destruction, I depart. Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Puṇḍarīka—who attained Lord Hari in the form of a swan through the vow of the eleventh day of the month of Kārttika—of Haṃsatīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara, and of the Installation of Nṛsiṃha on the bank of Aśvapaṭṭasara by the Cōla King through the Nṛsiṃha Yoga, as well as Nṛsiṃhatīrtha," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen to another miracle concerning the Lord of Śrī that occurred at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā regarding Yogeśvara.
Vītihotra, a great yogi and lord of yoga, dwelt in the forest;
on Mount Himālaya at Badarī, he performed most rigorous penance.
He attained all the arts of yoga and became just like Śambhu.
By the power of that yoga, he indeed beheld with his divine eye:
the sacrifices performed in Ketumāla, the rituals performed even on Mount Kailāsa, and whatever was done by Hari in the regions of the immortals.
Having perceived all this— the great festival for the birth of Ūrjakṛṣṇāṣṭamī that was celebrated,
as well as the worship of Śāradā and the grand festival of the mountain of food—
with his divine vision, the Supreme Lord [spoke].
He came in person to see Bālakṛṣṇa of Kāṃbhareya.
At the sacred site of Kuṃkumavāpī, that Vītihotra, possessing a thousand forms and endowed with meditative absorption, approached Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
On the third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having reached the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and taking recourse at the Setu,
he assumed his own seat beneath a banyan tree.
Assuming a thousand forms, he sat down there after making his solemn resolve.

May the Lord of Ramā come and embrace my own fundamental form. Then, may that Lord again embrace me with His thousand forms, provided that others cause me to behold the True Guru, who is like a bull among men.
Then I shall dwell here forever as a constant follower in the presence of Śrī Hari;
I shall attain liberation right here at Badarī, for there is no need for any other place.
Indeed, there is no other guru than the Guru, since the Guru alone is the bestower of liberation.
One should take refuge in that teacher by whom one’s own self may attain nourishment, by which one crosses the ocean,
and from whom comes the great peace of the self;
from whom comes the destruction of sin, and from whom comes the destruction of ignorance.

One should take refuge in that Guru from whom comes the cessation of mental fluctuations, from whom comes the destruction of latent impressions, and from whom comes the self-manifestation [of the Self];
and from whom one may obtain instruction, as well as sovereignty and wonder. (14)
One should take refuge in that Guru who abides in a divine state.
(15) There are many gurus, both worldly and unworldly;
for those established in the world must indeed be treated as gurus according to worldly custom. (15)
Unworldly gurus were sustained by unworldly disciples;
likewise, I too must sustain this extraordinary Lord as my guru, in whom every duty is indeed brought to completion within Hari. (17)
The mother is indeed a guru because she gives birth; the father is indeed a guru because he provides the seed.
Others who provide protection for the body are also gurus; others, such as kinsmen and women, are gurus because they impart knowledge of speech. (18–19)
Likewise, there are others who provide instruction, those who bestow knowledge,
and even teachers who impart training in the arts and crafts;
these indeed become one's gurus in the course of maintaining the body.
He who bestows the knowledge of the Self, he who bestows the mantra of Viṣṇu,
and he who bestows righteous conduct— such a Guru is indeed considered the most excellent.
He who bestows the state of Brahman and he who bestows the perfection of Yoga [are likewise preeminent].
He who bestows fearlessness regarding the Buddha is indeed a most excellent Guru;
having purified one's latent impressions (vāsanā), he reveals the Supreme Lord.
He is the one who leads the self to the Supreme Self and grants divine liberation. (23)
For that Guru is indeed the most excellent, the one who sends [the disciple] to the world of Brahmā.
(24) The letter *ga* signifies blinding ignorance, while the letter *ra* signifies radiant knowledge.
The Guru, who destroys ignorance and bestows knowledge, is considered worthy of honor. (25)
He leads one to the imperishable abode, even while dwelling in the realm of pleasure through his splendor.
This very Guru is the bestower of liberation; there is no other teacher superior to him.
The Guru is a yogi, a celibate student, a follower of dharma, a man of knowledge, and one possessed of dispassion.
The teacher of virtuous conduct is also Nārāyaṇa, the supreme teacher. Hari, the teacher, is the giver of worldly enjoyment, the giver of liberation, and the giver of everything.
Since he is the one who brings about the direct realization of the teacher, he is therefore the teacher of the teacher. (27–28)
He alone is this glorious Hari, the supreme teacher of the liberated;
he is the teacher of all incarnations, the teacher of virtuous women and the virtuous;
likewise, he is the teacher of lords, of abodes, of yogis, and of those who possess creative consciousness. (29)
He is the supreme teacher of the ancient creators, the great seers who dwell in heaven, the lords of progeny, the performers of ritual action, and the devotees;
he is the foremost among all teachers and the teacher of even the teacher of Nārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha, the son of Kāṃbhari, who is higher than the highest.
This very Lord, the glorious Gopālabāla, is indeed the master of all embodied beings.
"He has been found by me; he will surely fulfill my heart's desire.
Thinking thus, Vītihotra became absorbed in meditation in a thousand ways, intending, "I shall dwell at his feet and attain the imperishable abode. (33–34)
Having seen him born with a thousand forms on the bank,
the men who were bathing went away in great amazement, wondering, "Whose are these forms indeed? Who are these thousands of yogis who have arrived here?"
They have similar dress, similar bodies, and similar limbs; they are alike.
(36) They have similar hair, similar meditations, and similar proportions;
these either become brothers or they become liberated from their abodes. (37)
Are they perhaps the inhabitants of Badarī, white as pearls;
or are they the attendants of Śaṅkara;
or are they gods in the form of ascetics; or are they the Sādhyas, or those ascetics who dwell upon Mount Meru?
Who indeed could these be— moon-faced and radiant as the sun— who,
though they be thousands of yogins or lords of yoga engaged in the practice of meditation, neither speak nor look, nor even move their vital breaths? (2.240.40)
"Who are these lords, so steadfast in their silence and so firm in their minds?"—
thus did the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā speculate as they arrived in great crowds, filled with curiosity, to behold them. (41)
Some, upon merely seeing him, bow down, offer praise, and say:
"This is the majesty of Bālakṛṣṇakṛpānātha;
yogis constantly come for the sake of obtaining a vision of him. (42–43)
All these who were previously invisible have now become visible:
thousands of Rudras, thousands of Viṣṇus,
and even thousands of Brahmās come to behold the excellent boon.
Likewise, the great seers, the ancestors, and the deities;
the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts come constantly to behold [him].
Even the sacred fords and the world-protectors who guard the creation arrive there perpetually.
Alternatively, the divine attendants residing in Goloka and other realms arrive,
as do the eternal attendants of Vaikuṇṭha;
and the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, along with thousands of suns and moons, [also come].
Are they celestial beings (vaimānika) arriving with reverence from other worlds?
Or are they the Vālakhilyas, or perhaps Brahmin sages from the assembly of Brahmā?
Or could they be Gandharvas, Yakṣas, or even the Dhanadas? 48–49.
Whether they be wandering minstrels dwelling in the mountains or sages established in the forest,
it is their extreme resemblance [to one another] that constitutes their novelty.
On the forehead is the Vaiṣṇava sectarian mark, and on the head is the matted hair of an ascetic.
The eye-gestures (netramudrā), nourished by yoga, reveal the portion of the Imperishable (Acyuta).
Whoever they may be, those who have been directly perceived here by us—meritorious and fortunate ones through the power of destiny—[are indeed the recipients of this revelation]. //51-52//
"Surely their realization will occur at this very moment"—
saying thus, those thousands of yogis then beheld the subjects gathered there in groups on the shore of the lake.
Then Śrīmad Bālakṛṣṇa, the teacher of Nārāyaṇa’s teacher,
arrived at that time on the shore of the lake in the presence of the yogis;
knowing the heart's desire, he quickly beheld him in his original form.
O Vītihotraka! Having lifted him up and called him by name,
saying "Arise!", he took the hand of that yogi, placed him upon his chest,
and embracing him quickly with a laugh, he himself became a thousandfold.
Embraced by those who had arisen in a thousand forms,
Acyuta then quickly became one single form;
Vītihotra also suddenly manifested as a single form.
The people, struck with wonder, raised shouts of victory;
at that moment, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa became the venerable Ṛṣabha—an old man with white matted hair, naked, and grey with dust. (59)
Like one distracted or intoxicated, the ascetic has conquered all his senses.
Pervaded by the splendor of his own nature and devoted solely to the realization of Brahman, that man remains among embodied beings as if he were not of this world, or as if he were absent-minded.
Vītihotra, too, beholding his guru Ṛṣabha, prostrated himself like a staff and offered many praises there to the Supreme Lord:
"You are the Guru, you are the inner self, and you are Ṛṣabha, the king of yogis. (69)
You alone are the Lord of Yoga; you are the Ruler, you are the Supreme Lord.
You are the liberated one, you are the Greatly Liberated, and you are indeed the Lord of the Liberated.
You are the Imperishable, you are Brahman, and you are also the Supreme Brahman.
You alone are the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, and you are Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
You are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
O All-pervading Lord of Śrī, Ṛṣabha and the others are indeed your incarnations.
You alone are the Lord of Rādhā, and you alone are the Lord of Lakṣmī;
you are the Lord of Vāsudevī and likewise the Lord of Nārāyaṇī;
you alone are the Lord of the Liberated, the Lord of Brahman, and the Lord of the Abode.
You are the cause of Mahākāla and the cause of Mahāviṣṇu;
you are the cause of Sadāśiva and the cause of Vairāja.
You are the Abundant One (Bhūman), known as Puruṣa, and also as Puruṣottama.
You are the creator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the Rudras;
you are the creator of the gods, the world-protectors, and the ancestors;
you are the creator of the great seers, the ascetics, and the virtuous ones.
You are indeed the lord and protector of the virtuous, of the lotuses and other such beings;
likewise, you are the sustainer of the gods, of human beings, of animals, and of birds.
You are the life-giving essence of the creepers and the trees, the one who bestows their sap.
You are the creator of the wish-fulfilling cow, the vine of desire, the thought-gem, and so forth;
you are the creator of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas who move through the sky;
and you are the progenitor of those born from water, those dwelling in forests, and those dwelling within the earth.
O Janārdana, you are the progenitor of the Daityas and Dānavas;
you are the protector and nourisher of the wretched, the helpless, and the poor.
You are the giver of food to those who have taken refuge in you, and the one who provides sanctuary to those afflicted by suffering.
You are the giver of desires to those who long for them, and the fulfiller of those whose wishes are already formed.
You are the woman and you are the man; you are the embryo and you are the young child.
You are the seed, you are the form of the harvest, and you are the flower as well as the fruit.
You are Indra; you are the sense-faculty (indriya); you are sleep and you are wakefulness.
You are deep sleep (suṣupti), you are great bliss (mahānanda), you are affection (prīti), and likewise you are delight (rati).
You are the god of love (manmatha), you are born of the mind (manoja), and you also abide within the mind.
O Supreme Lord, you alone are knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge.
You are the season, you are the day and the night; you are exertion and rest.
You are trust and refuge; you are the mother, the father, and the teacher.
You alone are wealth and grain; you alone are power and strength.
You indeed are policy, devotion, virtue, passion, and detachment as well.
You are the vital breath and the life-force; you exist both manifoldly and as one.
You are illumination; you are activity; you are cessation; you consist of the *guṇas*.
You alone are beyond the *guṇas*, yet you are the locus of all perfections and qualities.
You are the wonder, you are the marvel, you are sovereignty and lordship.
You are earth and water; you are fire, wind, and likewise ether.
You are the subtle elements, you are the intellect, and you are the threefold desire.
You are examination and endurance; you are hunger and the longing for liberation.
You are affection; you are the activity of meditation; you are the samādhi higher than the highest. You are worship; you are the mind and its mental objects; you are dullness and likewise atomicity.
You are equilibrium and you are disequilibrium; indeed, you alone are everything.
I am you, Vītihotra; you are the Guru and likewise Ṛṣabha.
Whatever is seen, experienced, or even dissolved—all this arises from the manifestation of your own portions, fragments, and incarnations. (86)
Since you alone are that which, wherever, by whatever means, and for whatever purpose [exists],
therefore I perpetually offer myself, who am named Vītihotra, to that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Brahman, the Supreme Brahman.
"I offer myself to you alone— not as a deposit, nor as a loan to be repaid— but as something fit for your disposal according to your will.
Having thus praised him, O Rādhikā, she fell at the feet of Hari.
Then Hari raised Vītihotra, who was black, up;
having embraced him and placed his hands upon his head,
Hari directed Vītihotra toward the attainment of boons.
Then Vītihotra said: "I shall remain here at your feet;
O Lord, at the end, you will attain liberation and reach your imperishable abode.
"Grant me a dwelling here forever," he said, and Hari replied, "So be it."
O Rādhikā, that great holy place named Ṛṣabha in the lake became famous by these names:
Vītihotra-tīrtha and Sahasrayogin-tīrtha;
thus it was renowned as a beautiful bestower of liberation.
Hari suddenly assumed the form of Bālakṛṣṇa and,
standing on the bank of the Vītihotra, proceeded to his own abode;
there, the ascetic Janadarśana took refuge by embracing a banyan tree.
Having bathed at that sacred ford (tīrtha), they shall attain the supreme goal.
They shall obtain perfection in yoga even without the practice of yoga.
O Rādhikā, by bathing there, their sins shall go to destruction.
Whether it be wet or dry, great or small, and whatever causes suffering to others—
all that sin perishes quickly even from drinking that water.
Furthermore, by giving food there, one obtains a fruit equal to that of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
"May my abode, which is the dwelling-place of Ṛṣabha, become imperishable.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the Blessed One spoke regarding the majesty of this sacred ford (tīrtha).
By reading or hearing this, the fruit born of that sacred ford shall be attained. (2.240.100)

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hari’s Appearance to Vītihotra-Yogeśvara in the Form of Ṛṣabha and in His Thousandfold Forms, the Consecration of Ṛṣabha as a Tīrtha, and His Praise," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 241 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga Santāna*) — Chapter 241.
[Author: Chapter 242.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen now to another marvel of the Lord.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
there appeared that which is known as the Vyūha-incarnation named Vāsudeva, belonging to that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable.
A portion of that [Supreme Being] is Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose activity consists of creation, withdrawal, and maintenance;
he who is described in the scriptures as Saṃkarṣaṇa is born.
He repeatedly assumes the form of Rudra and likewise repeatedly assumes the form of Śambhu.
He alone remains as the soul of dissolution, and he exists under the name of Śeṣa.
Where Hari reclines, he is indeed Śeṣanārāyaṇa;
he himself is born as the great yogi Patañjali.
The sage Patañjali is indeed a portion (aṃśa) of Hari, the teacher of yoga;
that Lord, possessing a divine body, dwells here on earth eternally in Kāśī.
And he [is there] daily at dawn for the purpose of beholding Hari through yogic vision.
He arrives at the site of Aśvapaṭṭasara for the purpose of worship.
(7) Having fully worshipped the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Nārāyaṇa, and having performed the *ārārtika* ceremony and received the sacred remains (*prasāda*) from Him, (8)
In a moment, he departs from Kāśī to his own abode through *samādhi*;
thus the great sage Patañjali comes there constantly.
O Rādhikā, [he sees] the Lord Hari worshipping that sage there.
The king of yogis, traveling through the sky, saw one named Camasa.
He descended to the earth and asked that Patañjali:
"O Blessed One, is the illustrious Puruṣottama worshipped here by you?"
"Bālakṛṣṇaka is the direct sovereign of all incarnations;
how can he go again to Kāśī, having abandoned the Great Lord?
O learned one, tell me the reason for this, for I have come here for the sake of pilgrimage."
"Having established a sacred ford there, I shall then go with Revā;
I shall worship the Lord, and thereafter I will indeed depart with you.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated like a staff and worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having worshipped both [the deities] and received their command, the two went to the bank of the Aśvasaras lake; there, at the eastern embankment, they took refuge beneath a Dhātrī tree.
Then the sage Patañjali spoke of the reason for his residence in Kāśī.
O Camasa, hear the reason why I am going to Varāṇasī:
she is the embodiment of the great sovereignty of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and she who bears half of His own form.
She who is the foremost among all powers, the supreme sovereign of them all; she who is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī, the beginningless one, the half-body of Hari;
the mother of the worlds, of the realms of Brahmā, and of those who take incarnations through yoga.
She is the remover of suffering, the creator of happiness, and the bestower of power upon those who are liberated.
She is the embodiment of all the capacities of all the Nārāyaṇas,
and she who rests upon the chest is the foremost among all those dear to Brahmā.
It shines forth as that of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa alone.
For a moment it does not go far away; once liberated, it is never born again.
It exists in both visible and invisible forms, joined in an inseparable relationship.

The supreme sovereign, worthy of being served by the goddesses Rādhā, Ramā, and others, remains today in embodied form as a maiden, the beloved of Śrī Hari. In the house of Śivasvāmī, the young girl Satī, the daughter of Narāyaṇa, dwells. (22–23)
By name she is Dhanalakṣmī, the destroyer of all suffering;
that goddess of the earth dwells there, arisen as a divine being.
She is the auspicious younger sister of Vijaya, Śaśin, and Kṛṣṇā.
She was waiting for the garden of Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, I am going to perform her worship, service, and servitude;
I am truly going by the command of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
O Camasa! You know that Hari, who is attainable through yoga—that very same Supreme Self (Paramātman) shines here upon this ground smeared with saffron.
Indeed, the constant vision of Him is non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpaka-samādhi).

Direct service to Him is the supreme fruit of samādhi. As for the observances (yamās), my view is that they consist in remaining constant in this [service]. Non-violence (ahiṃsā) consists in accepting Śrī Hari, whose essence is the state of being pleased with Him. || 28–29 ||
Truth is the constant refuge for one whose very nature is truth, which belongs to Hari;
non-stealing is conduct with the spirit of servitude before Śrī Hari. Celibacy is considered to be being attached to Him with love through His image.
Even non-possessiveness itself cannot be attained without him;
nor can my observances consist of service to Kṛṣṇa, nor my purity through touching him and bearing him in my heart. (3.1–32)
Contentment is the constant presence in the heart of Śrī Hari through His grace; austerity is indeed the effort to restrain the [sensual] tendencies toward that very same object;
and self-study consists of His words, hymns of praise, worship, and so forth. ||33||
And that vow is indeed the fixing of the mind upon His form.
Thus, in Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, there are the auspicious restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas);
likewise, the posture (āsana) consists of abiding within His command and remaining in His presence.
Prāṇāyāma is the offering of the vital breaths to the Lord of Prāṇa;
pratyāhāra is the withdrawal of the senses into the Supreme Lord as their sustenance.
Dhāraṇā is when the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, is held within one's own self.
And may my meditation on Hari always consist of one-pointedness of conviction.
May there be meditation on the form of Hari’s image, meditation on the flavor of Hari’s taste, meditation on the fragrance of Hari’s scent, and meditation on the touch of Hari’s touch. (37–38)
Meditation on the word is meditation upon the speech of Hari; meditation on the hand is meditation upon the deeds of Hari;
meditation on the foot is meditation upon the purpose of Hari; and meditation on the voice is meditation upon the qualities of Hari.
Meditation on delight is meditation upon the yoga of Hari; the destruction of obstacles is the dismissal [of impediments].

Contemplation of Hari within the heart, reflection upon Him in the mind, constant awakening to Śrī Hari, and always maintaining the sense of "I" in relation to Hari; with one's mental state fixed on the latent impression and meditation of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.241.40–41)
From that supreme lord Nārāyaṇa comes great enjoyment and bliss;
from union with Him comes the transcendence of the *guṇas*, as well as the divine nature of those very *guṇas*.
Service for the sake of Śrī Hari, whether performed through the *guṇas* or beyond them, constitutes *nirguṇya*.
The discernment of the Puruṣa is indeed the constant vision of Hari;
freedom from craving for the guṇas is indeed attachment to the qualities of Hari; proficiency is the clarity of the intellect, and that which is firm mindfulness is the remembrance of Hari. (43–44)
The obstruction of mental fluctuations is that very state which consists everywhere in the manifestation of Hari;
it is indeed samādhi with conceptualization (savikalpa), for it is service mixed with one’s own personal interests.
Worship of the gross form is accompanied by discursive thought (savitarka), while worship of the mental form is free from discursive thought (nirvitarka).
With reflection is devotion as praise; without reflection is the contemplation of the limbs [of the Lord].
With bliss is the taking up of the aesthetic flavor (rasa); without bliss is the offering of the aesthetic flavor.
With the sense of "I-am-ness" (sāsmitā) is the appearance of Hari as distinct from the master and the servant. 46–47.
There is no dissolution of the state of servitude into the eternal Kṛṣṇa through the ego-sense (asmitā),
as long as there is no oneness with Kṛṣṇa for one who is absorbed in Him, nor any sense of separateness from me.
The fruit [of such absorption] is the attainment of Kṛṣṇa’s own nature, as well as sālokya and sārṣṭi.
Proximity is inseparable connection, and there is always a state of dissolution therein;
from that, the attainment of all sovereign powers, wonders, and so forth occurs, yet there is no difference [between them].
Thus, everything consisting of yoga has been attained by me in this manner. (2.241.50)
"O Camasa, nothing other than Śrī Hari shines for me, nor for you;
therefore, worship Him with that disposition and dwell here at Lake Aśvasaras.
Thus instructed by the practitioner Patañjali, Camasa [acted accordingly].
Patañjali always made his residence on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa;
Camasa went to Kāśī, and Patañjali [went] to the shore of the lake for the sake of rest and for the sake of a gathering.
He constructed an excellent hut made of wood and leaves for Patañjali;
from that time on, that sacred site became renowned in the world as Pātañjala-tīrtha,
where Camasa would constantly hold assemblies of yogis.
Having stayed together with the illustrious Patañjali, the knower of Yoga,
King Vaivasvata Manu then arrived there for the sake of visiting sacred sites (tīrthas).
Upon seeing the purifying abode of Camasa and Patañjali, [he was filled with devotion].
Then King Manu caused a firm temple made of stone to be built; there,
amidst a vast grove of trees,
he installed the sages Śeṣa and Patañjali according to the prescribed rites of consecration.
[He beheld] Śeṣanārāyaṇa, adorned by a multitude of a thousand hoods;
on each and every hood there was the mark of a svastika, made of gold, silver, green, and white. (58–59)
With a red face and pearl-like eyes, served by the Śeṣikas,
beautiful, soft, and charming, seated in the kuṇḍalika posture—
thus is the divine Śeṣa, the sage Patañjali, the Guru.
He established the great sage, a yogin, in that temple;
by his side, he established his beloved Kuṇḍalinī in Siddhi;
and likewise, that Manu established his son named Yoga.
Likewise, he installed the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, resplendent with a mace, a lotus, and other emblems,
together with his beloved Saṃkarṣaṇī, in the temple; and he also installed Rudra,
three-eyed and accompanied by Rudrāṇī.
He installed Īśāna, accompanied by Īśinī, in the temple (64).
For their livelihood, he also granted large fields and gardens;
he appointed Brahmins for their worship, providing them with wages and other means of support (65).
During that consecration, Manu caused the auspicious Mahārudra sacrifice to be performed according to the prescribed rites; he had the Rudrikā mantras recited,
and he also caused sacrificial pits and beautiful pavilions to be constructed.
He summoned the lords of yogis, sages, and the most excellent great seers;
the brahmins, the foremost of the kṣatriyas, the gods, the divine Prajāpatis,
all the hosts and attendants, and all the disciples of Rudra.
[He saw] all those residing on Kailāsa and all those residing in the Ocean of Milk,
as well as the nāgas of the Śeṣa lineage, the supreme yogins devoted to Śambhu,
and also the yoginīs and goddesses— all virtuous and chaste women in every respect.
Manu also summoned all the Avadhūtānikas and Mātṛkās, as well as Vīrabhadra and the others, Nandin and the rest, the Gaṇeśas, and the Kārtikeyas, to the sacrifice. (2.241.70–71)
And the great preceptor Pulastya was there as the leader;
he was indeed a beholder of the Mahārudra and an expert in all branches of medicine.
The ritualistic sages, having gathered all the necessary materials there, [proceeded].

Benedictory words were spoken, and auspicious sounds likewise arose. (73) Then there occurred the purification of the body, the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the worship of the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the adoration of Gaṇeśa, and the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā*). (74)
Then there followed the Nāndī-śrāddha, the Madhuparka offering, the recitation of the Puṇyāha, the placement of the Vardhinī jar, and the water-procession;
thereafter came the consecration of the site (Vāstu), the worship of the pavilion, and the adoration of the deities of the Maṇḍala.
Then followed the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā), the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍapūjā), and the ritual placement of the fire (vahninyāsa).
Thereafter came the placement within the house (gṛhanyāsa), the installation of the Yoginīs, the installation of the Kṣetrapāla,
the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the ritual placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa).
The recitation of the Śatarudrīya, as well as the Rudra-nīrājana,
the Krama-homa, the Sarvadeva-homa, and the Ūrdhvā’rhaṇā took place.
With either goat’s milk or doe’s milk, [the rites were performed] over the bricks.
In the northwestern corner, likewise, an oblation was offered upon a *arka* leaf;
and the Adhvaryu priest, reciting the *Śatarudrīya*, performed the offering for Śambhu with a stream of clarified butter and a stream of *arka* sap. (2.241.79–80)
He offered an oblation to the assembled gods, beginning with Rudra;
thereafter, the handful of flowers became a great full-oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti), and the fire-sacrifice was completed.
Then there was the beholding of the deities in the temple and the presentation of offerings.
Then there was the bestowal of great sacrificial fees (mahādakṣiṇā);
there were also meals for all those present at the sacrifice. Then followed the honoring of the earth, the welcoming ceremony, and the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Thus, O Rādhikā, Vaivasvata Manu indeed installed Śaṅkara,
Śeṣa, Patañjali, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and Īśāna in a new temple with great celebration.
To the east of Aśvapaṭṭasara lies a purifying region;
from there arose the great and divine Śeṣasthalī.
In Aśvapaṭṭasara itself is the supreme Pātañjala Tīrtha. (85–86)
Cāmasa is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha), as is the great Śeṣatīrtha;
Sāṃkarṣaṇa is a supreme sacred ford, as is the Śatarudrīya-tīrtha.
Avabhṛtha is a great sacred ford, and Śambhu-tīrtha bestows happiness.
Likewise, the Vaivasvata Tīrtha and other such sacred sites became forever bestowers of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
they became renowned throughout the Aśvapaṭṭa Sarovara. (88–89)
Wherever there were groups of bathers, those became Gaṇatīrthas;
likewise, there was Gaṇeśatīrtha and Skandatīrtha as well.
Similarly, there was Nāgatīrtha and Pārṣadatīrtha in that place.
The Satītīrtha and Devikāsutīrtha became truly purifying.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this auspicious circle of holy places (tīrthamaṇḍala) has arisen in the eastern region through the power of Śeṣa, bestowing all spiritual perfections (siddhis).
Where, by bathing, drinking the water, sipping it, or even by touching it,
there arose a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) that bestows the fruit of yoga and indeed brings about the attainment of the Self;
there, through giving, one surely attains the state of eternal Kailāsa.
There, by receiving initiation (*dīkṣā*), one attains residence in Vaikuṇṭha.
There, by performing sacrifices, one indeed obtains the eternal heaven. There, by the consecration of an image, one attains the abode of Sāṃkarṣaṇa.
Because one dwells there eternally, there is indeed no fear of Mahākāla.
By performing vows and other rites there, the fruit shall be infinite—
especially for ascetics, yoginīs, and Vaiṣṇavas.
Through the gift of a means of livelihood, there shall be eternal liberation leading to Brahman.
O Rādhikā, by bathing with her menstrual blood, one's sins are destroyed;
and it is held that even animals who die in that place attain birth as gods. (97–98)
"O Patañjali, O Śambhu, O Rudra, O Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, O Manas, O Śeṣa, O Camasa, may you all bring about my auspiciousness!
Having spoken thus, one should sleep at night; then no evil dream shall arise.
He who conducts his business by keeping them in mind gains profit at every step.
Having reflected upon them in the morning, he should engage in buying and selling goods;
by applying his hand [to the transaction], he shall gain profit moment by moment.
"May the goddess Annapūrṇā, Satī, Pārvatī, Śeṣiṇī, Śivā, Sāṃkarṣaṇī, and Yoginī grant me auspiciousness.
Having spoken thus, a woman— whether a maiden or a young wife— should conduct herself [accordingly].
Whether she be a married woman or a widow, her gain occurs moment by moment:
the destruction of suffering and poverty, the fulfillment of all desires, and the increase of happiness, prosperity, and lineage—all arise from even a fraction of his grace. (103–104)

O Rādhikā, by reading this, by hearing it, by causing others to hear it, and even by reflecting upon it, there occurs the destruction of all sins, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation; furthermore,
one quickly attains the desired objects of the mind and the dissolution of Māyā.
"Self-realization shall arise through the grace of Saṃkarṣaṇa.

(106) Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Temples of Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, Śeṣa, and Others Built by Vaivasvata on the Eastern Bank of Aśvapaṭṭasara during the Patañjali-Camasa Conjunction, as well as the Collection of Tīrthas for Saṃkarṣaṇa, Śeṣa, and Others in the Water," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 241.
