Chapter 243 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, to another story—purifying, supremely wonderful, born in the supreme field of Akṣara, and exceedingly ancient. (1)
There was a brahmin seer named Paṅkila whose lifespan lasted for five kalpas.
His mother was a virtuous woman who had been a servant attending upon the great seer. Being an unmarried girl whose father had died, she wandered about within the circle of the seer's hermitage.
From her childhood she was without a protector and without kinsmen, her mother having died;
she was a Brahmin woman who had mastered the Veda and had attained awakening from a great seer.
She was devoted solely to self-realization, a mistress of yoga, whose true wealth was meditative absorption (samādhi).
She took refuge in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, was a treasure-house of discrimination between the self and the insentient,
remained equanimous in pain and pleasure, was devoted to the dharma of serving her elders,
and was virtuous in thought, word, deed, and even in her qualities. (5)
Through diligent effort and generosity, she was devoted to the service of the sages;
her inner being was consumed by the fire of great divine knowledge,
and she remained ever undisturbed by dualities, meditating upon the glorious Nārāyaṇa.
Thus that young woman was born,
free from the state of passion (rajas) and devoid of desires or volitions.
Devoted to celibacy, virtuous, auspicious, and subsisting on the alms of sages, she lived.
Her garment was always dried in the air by the wind;
her alms-bag hung in the sky, catching the breeze.
Indeed, she possessed such a wondrous accomplishment of supernatural power.
She heard that divine discourse in the assembly of great sages;
she listened to the truthful account of Gaṇeśa regarding the awakening of his son,
as well as the story of Sanaka and the others who were born from the mind of Brahmā.
She heard the divine and purifying story of Añjanī’s son.
Then, having heard those accounts of women who possessed sons, she reflected:
"May I too have one son in my mind who is an abode of virtues."
"I shall become a vessel of honor in the midst of the assembly of women who possess sons;
indeed, the fruit of having a son is the very support for women.
Thus she thought, "I must obtain a son who is a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata)."

In the fourth previous kalpa, during that Tretā age, he obtained a mind-born son from the sage Vāmadeva by the mere touch [of his hand]. Born without a womb, that boy was immediately a youth, exceedingly handsome. (15–16)
Endowed with both wisdom and discernment, devoted to the contemplation of Brahman,
he constantly traversed the path of the sky, performing the act of leaping across the four oceans;
likewise, he partook of the northern [portion] according to the ritual of the great pilgrimage site of the four abodes.
He was born capable like his mother and likewise possessed of spiritual perfection like his father. He was the founder of the Vāmadeva lineage and possessed divine power;
he [honored] his mother Dākṣīdevī and his father Vāmadeva.
Having worshipped [the deity] constantly both within his heart and externally, he would then go eagerly to the forest every day for the sake of wild fruits and other offerings.
Having gathered sacrificial wood, fruits, and flowers, he would place them in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having made his seat in the mud, he indeed entered into meditative absorption (samādhi) during the night.
Because of that, he was celebrated by the goddess Dākṣī by the name Paṅkila;
thus the renowned brahmin-sage known as Paṅkila came into being.
Once, even during the day, he placed his seat in the midst of the mud and,
having entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), remained motionless by restraining his vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
At that time, five *satyas* arrived there on the riverbank by chance.
These virtuous women were devoted to Brahman, possessed of character and vows, and equal to Nārāyaṇī.
They were female masters of yoga, disciples of Vāmadeva, and had attained the refuge of spiritual perfections (*siddhi*).
The first was Āpastambī, the second Drumastambī, and the third Marutstambī. (24–25)
Phenastambī was the fourth, and Dhūmrastambī was the fifth.
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, they stood for a moment upon its bank.
At midday, they beheld a young boy in the mud within the mire.
Resplendent, established in Brahman, possessing a form like that of the sun,
absorbed in meditation, and divine in appearance— that yogi born of Vāmadeva—
those sisters quickly approached his side and bowed down to that sage.
The sage, seeing them near his own seat while he was in meditative absorption, quickly emerged and, having approached, offered them a seat and bowed down.
"O sisters, knowers of Brahman, I salute my elder sister again and again. (29)
Having spoken thus and placing his eyes upon their feet,
that sage set the dust of his feet upon the heads of his sisters;
he then quickly prepared seats for the sake of welcoming them.
Just then, other non-sacrificial seats arrived there;
he then remembered water held in a water-pot for the purpose of washing the feet. When that was presented, he then remembered the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Then, sweetmeats, desired foods, honey, various fruits, sugar, and so forth—
the *madhuparka*— was presented to them;
and all the materials for worship arrived there instantly, as if by the power of thought.
Paṅkila honored his sisters with all kinds of articles;
he provided them with delightful food, consisting of various cooked and savory delicacies.
Then he also gave them delicious nectar-like water for their drink.
He gave beautiful bark garments for the purpose of making lower and upper cloths,
as well as suitable bracelets for the female ascetics;
he likewise requested their blessings and their favor.
Having been offered hospitality, they were pleased and gave their brother auspicious blessings.
Then one said, "O brother! May you live for a kalpa and be happy! A second also spoke likewise: "May you live for a kalpa and be happy! (38)

The third, the fourth, and likewise the fifth, spoke with hearts full of grace: "May you live for five kalpas and be happy! By the auspicious blessings of his sisters, he lived for five kalpas. (2.242.40)
O Rādhikā, Paṅkila-Ṛṣi became so through the worship of his own sister;
thus, possessing a lifespan of five kalpas and endowed with dharma, knowledge, and detachment,
that sage remained devoted to the worship of Brahmā and lived in the world as he pleased.
In some cases he goes to Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise to Badarī;
he goes to Śvetadvīpa, as well as to Svarga, and he also goes to the world of Yama.
He goes to the world of Indra, the world of the Sun, and he also goes to the world of the ancestors.
In some places he goes toward Mount Meru, in others toward the mountain known as Lokāloka;
in some places to the world of the Seven Sages, and in others to the world of Dhruva;
in some places he goes to the cool world of the Moon, and in others even to Pātāla.
This king of yogis wanders at will through the mud;
sometimes he remains in meditative absorption for ten thousand years,
sometimes on the ground, and sometimes in the water, bearing a body as hard as a diamond.
In some places he was in fire, in some in wind, and in others he remained in the sky;
like Brahmā, his movement was that of Brahmā, due to his service to his sisters and mother.
Indeed, through the power of his father and the power of yoga, his gait became unimpeded.
He possesses many bodies and forms, and his body may even appear withdrawn;
like the sun, he shines sometimes in the sky and sometimes on the earth;
sometimes he has the form of a god, and sometimes he possesses the form of a human.
In some places he has the form of a parrot, and in some places the form of a bull;
in some places the form of a deer, and in some places the form of a swan.
In some places he is equal to a mountain, and in some places he has the form of an atom.

Thus, possessing independent authority, he who is established in Brahman remains like Vāmadeva, a treasury of all sovereign powers, yet he is indeed defiled. And in this very fifth Kalpa of his, at the very break of dawn— ||51-52||
Wandering along the path of the sky, he beheld Lake Aśvasaras—a vast expanse of pure water, with tranquil and intensely radiant waters;
shining like the moon and beautifully adorned with many lotuses. (53)
It resounded with the sweet calls of royal swans, royal parrots, and cranes;
it possessed the fourfold beauty of excellent bridges; its waters were as unfathomable as the netherworld (pātāla);
it was the sacred ford of the Kṣīrasarasvatī, consisting of the water used for washing the feet of Brahmā.
It was resplendent on all sides with great gardens of fruits and flowers;
it was the dwelling place of the God of gods, frequented by hosts of great sages,
and constantly purified by the bathing and ablutions of those dear to Brahmā.
It was provided with divine staircases for descending to bathe;
its banks were shaded by the dwellings of ascetics and by banyan trees and others;
and that great place shone brilliantly on all sides with women carrying water.
To the west of the city of Kuṅkumavāpikā, it resembles the Imperishable (Akṣara);
to the south, it is exceedingly purifying due to the hermitages of the great sages;
and to the north, it is filled with the dwellings of the guardians of the field (Kṣetrapālas) who embody the principles of Śiva (Śivatattva).

He beheld the Aśvasaras lake, adorned with divine palaces and formerly inhabited by virtuous men and women; it was constantly filled with yogis, ascetics, those free from passion, renunciants, and those who have surrendered themselves.
He beheld great mansions with golden pitchers,
and all around he saw temples richly adorned with gold.
He heard the sounds of musical instruments, the blasts of conch shells, and likewise hymns of praise.
Having heard the songs of the Apsarases and the grandeur of the praises of the virtuous,
and having observed everything both collectively and individually as far as his strength permitted through the sky,
he then descended from the heavens into the Paṅkilāśva lake.

Having drunk the water and likewise bathed, he attained supreme peace while remembering Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. O Rādhikā, being covered in mud, he took pleasure in dwelling within the water.
Indeed, fearing the crowds of people everywhere outside,
he stays by day on the water or on the ground; at night, he even resorts to the bridge,
and he wanders as he pleases among the dwellings of ascetics.
Sometimes he wanders in the evening through the regions of the great sages’ hermitages;
every morning, he goes to the temple and worships Bālakṛṣṇa.
At times, he travels mentally to the most purifying Somanātha.
In some places he suddenly enters through the main gate with his physical body;
in some places, having himself become a maiden, he stays among the beloved wives of Brahmā;
and in some places, having become a young boy, he dwells with the cowherd children.
Thus, O Rādhā, that king of sages took up his eternal residence at the auspicious Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, taking refuge in Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then one day, the glorious sage Lomaśa beheld him.
To her who had assumed the form of a maiden and arrived at his own hermitage, he said:
"Who are you, and from where have you come here? Tell me, O maiden.
She replied: "I am Paṅkilā; indeed, I am the daughter of the goddess Dākṣī."
"I have come to your hermitage for the sake of seeing the maidens;
at other times, however, I am indeed Vāmadevī.
Having said this, Paṅkila abandoned the form of a maiden and became [his usual self].
Lomaśa, too, recognizing him as one already known to him from former times,
closed his eyes in meditation and then bestowed great honor upon him.
Having received the mantra of Hari from the sage Lomaśa, he [Paṅkila] was purified.

He chanted, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya," and having offered salutations, he departed for his dwelling within the water and made his abode in the waters. Then, on the second day, Lomaśa approached him.
He spoke indeed for the sake of a leaf-hut; thereupon the muddy sage said:
"Until evening is my livelihood, and this is my fifth mealtime.
Even as the day of Brahmā passes away, what need is there for a leaf-hut?"
Therefore, I shall dwell in the water, in a home free from care like a pool of mud;
for until now, neither has a leaf-hut ever been built by me anywhere in this world, nor indeed shall one ever be made at the end.
"If there is only a very short time remaining, and I were to build a leaf-hut,
those sages who live for many kalpas would laugh at me.
Having said this, he resolved to dwell constantly in the water.
Fixing his mind on Śrī Hari, he attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the water.
While he remained in that absorption, a full age (*yuga*) passed;
at that time, King Bali became powerful in the world through Vāmana.
Having manifested at the sacrifice in Saurāṣṭra and being entreated for the sake of the earth,
Bali gave the world to Vāmana, who was holding an umbrella.
Vāmana, acting with guile, increased his own stature.
The toes and fingers of his feet sank into the water of that lake, which was filled with cranes;
by his majesty, the ground of the lake was filled [with fire],
and the waters quickly receded from all sides toward the surrounding earth.
Varuṇa indeed brought about the pacification of those waters.
Having emerged from the mud when the lake was drained of water,
Paṅkila became attached to Vāmana’s big toe like a nit.
He too, having gone out, praised the lotus with his thumb for a moment;
meanwhile, Vāmana, assuming the form of a child, appeared after having conquered the three worlds.
Upon seeing him, Paṅkila became overwhelmed with love and joy.
Furthermore, while he was desiring to bathe in a lake abundant with water, Śrī Vāmana said: "Build a beautiful temple for me, and establish me as Vāmana upon the bridge; reside there."
"By my command, become my servant and dwell in my palace.
Having thus commanded him, the Lord Śrī Vāmana went to Vastrāpatha.
By the power of his yoga, he made the ground free of mud and constructed a palace there during the night.
There he installed the beautiful Lord Śrīvāmana;
indeed, he installed Paṅkila in the service of Vāmana.
For the sake of service, Paṅkila appointed Jālakīlaka as his disciple.
There, the sage remained eternally invisible in the abode of Vāmana;
as time passed, he, the long-lived one,
entrusted the various yogic perfections to Jālakīla, for Jālakīla was also a king among yogis.
Indeed, that twice-born Jāleśvara became one whose lifespan was equal to a Brahmakalpa.
He also made his permanent residence on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Thus, O Rādhikā, that holy place of Jāleśvara became filled with mud.
Vāmana-tīrtha, Aṅguṣṭha-tīrtha,
and Kanyaka-tīrtha, as well as the waters of Aśvapaṭṭasaras,
became bestowers of liberation, destroyers of sin, and grantors of happiness.
It bestows the perfection of yoga, bestows prosperity, and likewise bestows heaven.
By bathing there, by giving gifts, and by worshipping Vāmana, a person may obtain the sovereignty of heaven, the supreme status of Brahmā, or the sovereignty of the earth. (2.242.99–100)
Remembering Bālakṛṣṇa of Kāṃbhareya, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa,
whoever bathes at the Vāmana Tīrtha shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Remembering Vāmana Paṅkila, one should perform bathing, giving, and other such rites.
Having likewise remembered Goddess Dākṣī, one should perform the giving of a daughter in marriage and other rites.
One should give food to young maidens and also food to the virtuous;
one should give food to chaste women, and thereby obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the second section concerning the lineage of the Tretā age, [is described] how Paṅkila— the mind-born son of the goddess Dākṣī and Vāmadeva— attained long life for five kalpas through the blessings received from honoring his five elder sisters; and how, after remaining in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at Lake Aśvapaṭṭa until the end of the Yuga, he was awakened by the touch of a toe of Lord Vāmana’s foot.
The two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Vāmana Temple Built by Command and the Vāmanāditya Tīrtha," etc.,
from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen now to [the account] of Vāmadeva’s daughters.
Having learned of their brother's residence at Lake Aśvapaṭṭa,
and having questioned their mother Divyamuktānī— who dwells eternally in Satyaloka— they all returned to Lake Aśvapaṭṭa.
To behold, to choose, and to attain the state of having fulfilled one's purpose the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
[they became] possessed of divine bodies like the Kaumudika stars, such as those belonging to the moon.
Having performed every kind of adornment for the pleasure of Nārāyaṇa,
and though free from the portion of *māyā*, yet deluded by the portion of the Supreme Brahman,
the long-lived ones suddenly arrived by way of the celestial path. (4–5)
On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while Akṣarakṣita was protecting [the realm], they arrived and bowed to their own brother, the Lord Vāmana;
they worshipped him with supreme devotion, and the brother offered them a welcome. (6)
They indeed spoke these words even to their younger sister:
"Since our brother has attained such joy because you sisters are dear to Hari, it is by your grace that he has become one whose life shall endure until the end of five kalpas. (7)

Indeed, having heard of their status as Nārāyaṇīs, she rejoiced exceedingly. On the seventh day, at the very break of dawn, having adorned themselves with beautiful ornaments, they went together with their mother to the magnificent abode of Bālakṛṣṇa early in the morning.
With offerings for worship in their hands and likewise adorned with choice garlands,
they were intent on surrendering all they possessed in the presence of Kṛṣṇa’s beloved. There, they first [saw] their mother, the venerable Kambharā, who was standing.
They worshipped with supreme affection and offered their personal introductions.
Having bowed to their father, as well as to their sister and their two elder brothers,
and then to Amṛtā, the wife of their brother, they repeatedly prostrated before Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed down again and again, they performed worship with many articles;
presented by their brother, they arrived having offered their very selves.
Hari, perceiving their devotion, accepted it, saying, "So be it."
Their hands were offered to Lord Hari by their brother, the sage Paṅkila. Then, with love, he indeed took hold of their hands.
Āpastambī was the first, and Drumastambī was the second.
Marutstambī was the third, Phenastambī the fourth, and Dhūmrastambī the fifth; these were the beloved wives of Hari.
Having honored their own husband, they placed the garland of choice around his neck.
Hari seated them by his side and bestowed excellent garlands upon them;
he then placed them around their necks and granted them his grace.
Having partaken of that, they went with their brother to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
O Rādhā, by the command of Hari they dwelt among the beloved wives of Brahmā;
thus, having obtained the Lord of Rādhā, they became like Rādhā herself forever.
Now, O beloved, hear another sacred and beautiful narrative.
Born in the lineage of King Svarṇāṅgada of Saurāṣṭra,
he became a king named Haimakalpa, who possessed the armor of righteousness (*dharmavarmavān*).
Indeed, he was a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and a follower of the Sāttvata path.
She constantly worships the Lord of Śrī even during her daily activities day and night;
she does not keep the rosary far away, nor does she ever abandon His remembrance.
During eating and sleeping, she keeps Kṛṣṇa well-guarded within her heart.
"O Bālakṛṣṇa! O Kṛṣṇa! O Harikṛṣṇa!"—thus he indeed says repeatedly;
day and night he says, "O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! At the end of every sentence, he always says, "O Bālakṛṣṇa! O Kāṃbhareya! (23–24).
He proclaims, "It is indeed so," and thus he utters the roar of the Supreme Self.
At the time of His worship—whether in any house or in a forest, on the shore of a lake, in a garden, in a pavilion, or in a temple—[he does so]. || 25 ||
Whether in a solitary place, among people, in a crowd, or in private, the bond of love [remains];
for Bālakṛṣṇa himself indeed goes and stands before one, and he accepts all the articles offered during worship. || 26–27 ||
Having eaten all the offerings— fruits, various foods, milk-rice, *pūrikās*, and so forth— Bālakṛṣṇa gives the remainder to the king.
Then, [the deity] indeed vanishes, and the king takes the meal.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the Lord Śrīpati,
being well-pleased by the devotion of Hemakalgi, remained under his control;
likewise, his queen, named Kumudākṣī, remained so as well.
She too, rising quickly and bathing, cooked excellent,
sweet food with great devotion for the pleasure of Bālakṛṣṇa—
milk-rice, cow's milk with sugar, and boiled rice.
She offers *pūrikās* fried in ghee, as well as other foods appropriate for the season;
having prepared even *guṇḍra*-cooked rice, *laḍḍukas*, and cakes made from mung-bean flour,
she presents them to the King in the morning during the offering of worship.
She always provides betel-leaf, water, and sweet, pleasant, cool, and warm refreshments, as well as whatever substances are required for anointing the body, at the appropriate times.
She constantly sings praises of his glorious deeds among her friends within the palace.
His friends, accompanied by the playing of cymbals, sing after her:

"Victorious is Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharī, who brings happiness to the people, who removes the sins of the world, the sovereign of kings, the sustainer of my fortune, the cowherd boy, Murāri! (36)
He who sports with Rādhā, who removes the fear of worldly existence, who dwells among the gopīs, and who provides for my nourishment;
who spreads affection, who delivers His own devotees, and who is the means for dispelling the suffering of women;
who illuminates the eyes, who shines within the heart, who resides in realized wisdom, and who dwells in manifold splendors. (37)

The one who releases from illusion, who is a slave to his own devotees, whose light radiates toward those desiring service, who expands through devotion, who dwells in his own true form, and who speaks as a servant to the world—he says:
"O you who dwell constantly in exile, remain as a resident in my house; become a dweller within me. (38–39)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the queen, accompanied by her friends, constantly sings and indeed praises the virtues of that very possessor of virtues.
And Bālakṛṣṇa, having heard that, becomes delighted in his mind.
When time had passed in this manner, Kṛṣṇa gave him armor that destroys all fear;
wearing which, the king, together with his queen, always remains fearless.
Even Mahākāla, upon seeing that armor, flees far away.

Upon the head of that armor shines the Sudarśana [discus], which possesses a continuous stream of yogic accomplishments, with the Kaustubha gem resplendent in its center and endowed on all sides with the eight sovereign powers at its borders. (43)
Upon whose shoulder shines a mace, and upon whose belly a noose;
such is this [discus], made of gold, exceedingly golden, fiery, yet soft;
it is fierce in its protection, gentle in appearance, and light when worn.
Indeed, King [Nala] continuously wore that armor, which was in the form of a garment bestowed by Bālakṛṣṇa, as if it were a tunic; for by means of it,
old age and even the staff of Yama depart far away.
Even the destruction of Saṃkarṣaṇa retreats far from this armor;
the noose of the god Varuṇa encounters fear from the armor;
and the hosts of Śaṅkara tremble before the armor even when they are traveling on the road. (47–48)
If death itself enters the path of armor, it goes to the state of death;
for such is that armor, endowed with the power of a child.
O Rādhikā, having donned it, the king was liberated and rejoices upon the earth.
"O Rādhikā, tell me, what fear can there be for one who has Kṛṣṇa himself by his side?
O beautiful lady, tell me, what fear can there be for one who has Nārāyaṇa by his side?
Like Rādhikā or like Ramā herself, this king is fearless in the forest. (2.243.50–51)
Dwelling in the forest while worshipping Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
the king then went to the tiger forest with the desire to roam there;
thereafter, traveling by aerial chariot through the sky, he went to the lion forest as well.
He departed for the Daṇḍaka forest, and from there he went to Dharmāraṇya;
then to Naimiṣāraṇya and also to Māhendrāraṇya.
Having thus wandered about together with the queen, he went to Saurāṣṭra.
Beholding that great celestial chariot, which was filled with the splendor of the Kṣatriyas,
Paraśurāma, the slayer of Kṣatriyas, trembled, impelled by Time;
he quickly took up his own axe from Mount Mahendra.
Grasping his bow and arrows, and wielding his sword with great fury,
he descended swiftly from the sky onto the back of the celestial chariot. Indeed,
that one of immense splendor approached rapidly upon its back.
The king, traveling in his celestial chariot, was indeed fearless and did not perceive this;
yet within the hearts of the subjects there was agitation, as if a wind were blowing in the sky.
At that time, the circle of planets became disturbed, portending a future terror.
The earth also trembled then, unable to endure the two splendors.
At the collision of these two indestructible energies, a dissolution was imminent;
thus did the gods and the yogis with divine vision tremble at that time. (2.243.60)
Then the great seers were deeply agitated out of fear for what was to come;
the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of the fields, and others perceived the destruction of the world.
At that time, the Siddhas offered praise to the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa.
"Let there not be the destruction of the worlds through the clash of the axe and the armor!
(62) Then, in an instant, the king’s aerial chariot, swift as thought, arrived and descended at the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. (63)
The king drank water while joyfully remembering Bālakṛṣṇa;
the queen also took her drink after having made her lord drink.
Just then, by way of the sky, a cruel orb appeared like the sun.
Blazing with splendor and red in hue, he descended with great speed.
Then the earth trembled and the waters of the lakes were agitated;
the dwellers of the sacred fords perceived fear and thought that some terrible calamity had arrived.
Seeing the iron ball in the path of the sky, they speculate:
"Is this a planet that has become agitated, or has it fallen from its own place?
Or is a fragment of the sun approaching, accompanied by flames of fire? (67)
Or is it that the fire itself remains there, or perhaps it is filled with wrath?
Or is it the divine Saṃkarṣaṇa, or the serpent Śeṣa, who approaches in a rage?
Or has the Brahmāstra been discharged by someone, unimpeded? (68–69)
Has he come here so that the worlds shall not be born again? Or perhaps it is the Vāḍava fire that has risen from the ocean;
who is this one of cruel appearance who comes to burn the worlds?
While the embodied beings were thus reflecting in their minds,
there appeared before them one with a clearly manifest form:
his face was terrifying, he held an axe in his hand, and he wore matted locks.

Who is this man, wearing a loincloth, armed with weapons, and endowed with the sacred thread; his eyes wide, his fangs bared at the corners of his lips, and his body bristling with excitement? Who dwells in a kṣatriya family while the wielder of the axe still lives?
"Disguised in this manner, he appears here in a celestial chariot for the sake of destruction.
Speaking thus, he quickly descended to the shore of the lake.
At that moment, he was recognized by the local people as the twice-born Paraśurāma, the bringer of death.
Terrified men, beasts, and even birds fled;
on the summit of Mount Hemakūṭa stood Parśudhra at the front of his celestial chariot,
on the lovely slope of the horse-silk mountain, [the protector] of the one who wields the Śārṅga bow and humbles pride.
In the field known as Akshara, Bālakṛṣṇa was a Brahmin who wore only a loincloth;
as soon as he, bearing an axe, set foot upon the ground, the nail of his big toe was pierced by a thorn. (77–78)
That birth of the brahmin was indeed inauspicious for one seeking victory;
nevertheless, out of pride, he came to strike the golden [image].
"Who are you, O scion of the kṣatriyas? You shall be consumed by the hunger of my touch."
"Speak quickly! Fight! Become one who goes to the realm of Yama!
Thus addressed, King Haima, with the swift energy of a warrior, spoke to him so that no offense might be committed against the brahmin.
O son of Jamadagni, Brahmins are to be honored; do not suffer defeat at the hands of the Kshatriyas.
You too are worthy of honor; do not employ the battle-axe or your strength against them in this improper manner.
For one who has been highly esteemed, defeat in an unworthy cause is a death worse than physical death.
"O Brahmin, I am a Kṣatriya; I do not wish to commit an offense against a Brāhmaṇa.
Do not be angry, O lord of sages; do not wash away your merit, O twice-born one.
You are worthy of worship and indeed inviolable, for you are a protector of the earth. (83–84)
"Therefore, you accept my worship and ought to forgive this transgression.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhā, just as the King of Gold went forward to honor the brahmin,
that twice-born one appeared bearing a battle-axe.

Intent on slaying him, he became filled with rage through the gesture of battle. (86) Having quickly remembered the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who wears a golden garland, he bound Parśurāma with the rays of his Sudarśana discus. (87)
The divine Sudarśana-cakra, which had been bestowed by Śrī Hari,
formed a net with its own fiery rays and bound Parśurāma—
along with his weapons and his army— in an instant, while he was still full of wrath. (88)
There, his power obstructed by the splendor of the discus,
Parśudhra became as if inert for a moment and fell to the surface of the earth.
The illustrious king said, "Forgive me here, O sinless one, for I am an offender."
"O Brahmin, release your anger toward this offender and depart quickly!
Parśudhra replied, "I shall not release him; my power does not function [against you].
O King, I am pleased with you; I grant you a boon."
"I worship and approach the god Cakradeva with nooses and nets.
Release me quickly, for I am being scorched by the rays of the discus!
O King, do not seek to kill this devotee of Hari. || 9.2-9.3 ||
The Kṣatriya power has arisen from the Brāhmaṇa; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must not kill one who is devoted [to him].
Rather, observe this one boon: dwell right here in another form.
Abide in the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, assuming the nature of an embodied image.
Thus addressed, Paraśurāma then granted two boons.
Thereafter, Paraśurāma was established in the king’s palace;
he was bathed in the waters of the horse and honored with ritual offerings.
O Rādhikā, thereafter, to the east of that place, there was the Paraśurāma-tīrtha and the Haimakalpi-tīrtha.
Having worshipped Hari, Paraśurāma indeed departed for Mandara.
There, in the Aśvapaṭṭasāgara, he dwells eternally in embodied form.
Then the king went to the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
having worshipped Hari, bowed down, and related the news, [he departed].
Having established a sacred ford (tīrtha), he went to his own capital, Himāvatī.
By bathing, giving gifts, and sipping water at this sacred ford, one shall attain victory.
By reading or hearing this, the defects of the heart are indeed destroyed.
One shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, health, wealth, and sons.

(101) Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as Consort by the Five Daughters of Vāmadeva in the Second Tretā Lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; King Haimakalgi’s Eternal Vision of Hari through Devotion; the Defeat of Paraśurāma by the King; and the Description of Paraśurāma-tīrtha and Haimakalgi-tīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara. (243)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; thereafter, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the commencement of the sacrifice took place at Lake Aśvasara. || 1 ||

Indeed, a Vaiṣṇava king named Aśvapāṭala came from Mount Arbuda with his followers toward Lomaśa for the purpose of performing a sacrifice. He was one who possessed a hundred elephants in his home, as well as vast forests and numerous fields.
He possessed a vast kingdom produced from the region of Arbuda.
Accompanied by a thousand men and likewise a thousand bulls,
he arrived for the sake of the sacrifice, bringing with him many ritual materials.
On the auspicious and purifying northern shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara,
he established his military camps in the Pālāśaka forest;
having summoned Lomaśa and obtained the vision of Hari.
Having summoned the great sages, he performed that most excellent sacrifice.
O Rādhikā, he performed that Soma-sacrifice for five days;
having gathered living Soma plants, he placed them in water-pots.
They were nourished and also fed by the king on the bank of the Aśvasaras lake.
On that shore, he performed the five-day Soma sacrifice known as the Ahīna;
in a very spacious pavilion, he had an excellent sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed.
The king, together with his wife, having performed the preliminary rites,
dispatched a *somapravāka*— a learned Brahmin— to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) for the purpose of choosing them. That Brahmin, having gone there, brought back the gods among men (the Brahmins).
Having offered the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the king performed the formal selection (*varaṇa*):
he chose the *adhvaryu*, the *pratiprasthātṛ*, and the *neṣṭṛ*;
then he also chose the *unnetṛ* and the *brahman*. (11)
He chose the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Āgnīdhra, and the Potṛ;
likewise, he chose the Hotṛ and the Maitrāvaruṇa. He also chose the Acchāvāka, the Grāvastut, and the Udgātṛ.
He chose the *prastotṛ*, the *pratihartṛ*, and the *subrahmaṇya*;
the king also chose the *sadasyas* and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) there.
Having worshipped the deities and having consigned the sacred fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), [he departed].
Having gone to Somakratusthalī and then rubbed the two fire-sticks together, the Adhvaryu established that very fire which had arisen in the Gārhapatya hearth;
thereafter, having led it forward, he established the Āhavanīya fire. (186–187)
Having offered twenty-four oblations and dismissed the fire,
and having brought it from the Gārhapatya fire, he performed seven more oblations;
then, having released that fire, he performed the Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi sacrifice.
He had a sacrificial cake prepared on eleven potsherds;
thereafter, he offered oblations to Agni and Viṣṇu.
Having constructed a sacrificial hall with its beams pointing eastward, the sacrificer [proceeded]. (18–19)
And having had her head shaved in the northern outlying region,
the queen bathed at a sacred ford; then, when the Adhvaryu priest presented her with two auspicious silk garments, she put them on, as well as her nail-clippers and other such items.
Having bathed, they put on two beautiful silken garments.
Then the husband and wife ate food in the pavilion,
and there they indeed anointed their own limbs with fresh butter.
Then, after applying collyrium to his own eyes with ointment,
the Adhvaryu priest offered six initiation oblations into the fire there and presented two black antelope skins to the sacrificer.
The sacrificer, having taken hold [of the materials] and approached the Āhavanīya fire,
then spread [the grass], sat down, fastened the girdle around his waist,
and likewise held a deer-horn as well as a staff made of Udumbara wood. (24–25)
The wife likewise held a net of *iṣīkā* reeds and a girdle of *muñja* grass;
the sacrificer made the binding of his fist, and the *adhvaryu* priest said:
"This sacrificer is consecrated; these Brahmins are consecrated. (26)
The sacrificer remained restrained in speech until the rising of the stars;
then he drank the milk offered by the Adhvaryu priest. The wife also drank it, and thereafter the husband and wife released their speech.

There, the husband and wife partook of their meal as they desired— curd, parched grains, flour-cakes of udumbara fruit, and boiled rice. And the beggars, including the Brahmins and the gods, gathered for the sake of obtaining the sacrificial materials.
Then, having gone for the purpose of begging, the husband and wife remained awake during the night. They observed their vow, thinking, "One should not speak a falsehood.
Likewise, they did not eat meat or drink liquor, nor did they approach a woman.
He did not sleep on a bed or similar furniture, nor did he wear a black antelope skin and such;
likewise, on the eighth day, the king performed the ritual duties of the Soma sacrifice.
Then, during the night in the assembly hall, Lomaśa gave his instruction.
He gave [this teaching], which is filled with knowledge and realization, for the sake of attaining the Self.
(3.3) Sacrifices should always be performed by those possessing wealth for the sake of happiness;
sacrifices that bring about the liberation of the self should always be performed by embodied beings. (3.4)
Those people who perform the sacrifice of liberation, who seize merit, and have conquered their senses,
attain the supreme abode of Hari, which is eternal and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
They are not pleased when being praised, nor do they become angry even when reviled.
Having attained this wisdom, they reach the abode of Hari.

Those people whose knowledge is mature, who have conquered their defects, who do not commit offenses, who are free from envy, who do not cause harm, and who are not tormented by the prosperity of others—[they reach that state]. (36–37)
They do not engage in blame or praise, nor are they affected by them;
being perfectly tranquil, they delight in the welfare of all beings.
They neither become angry nor rejoice, nor do they deceive others.
Having untied the knot of the heart, they go to the abode of Hari.
(3.9) Those who have no kinsmen whatsoever, nor are they the kinsmen of others; those who have no enemies, nor do they become the enemies of others. (2.244.40)
Those who conform to the Dharma live happily and without anger;
yogis should be as satisfied with dishonor as they would be with nectar. The wise should recoil from honor as if it were poison. (41)
Those who have cast off all faults lie in happiness, free from fear from any quarter;
being liberated from all defects, they go to the imperishable state.
Having attained these vows, the virtuous prosper in happiness.
Having performed all sacrifices and rendered their minds perfectly pure,
they attain the supreme and eternal abode of Hari, which transcends primordial nature (prakṛti).
Neither the gods, nor the Gandharvas, nor the sages, nor even the ancestors can reach it.

And they descend to that station which belongs to those who have attained the supreme state. (45) Those in whom there is no egoism regarding qualities or conduct, and whose speech and heart are not at variance, are honored both here and in the hereafter. (46)
Those who know the reality of the internal discipline, who are patient, capable, and have conquered their senses;
who are upright and truthful in speech— they are honored both in this world and the next,
through their splendor, fame, intellect, knowledge, and humility.
Those endowed with noble birth and austerity are honored both here and in the hereafter.
(48) Those of good character, who sleep peacefully, who possess a sense of self-respect and devotion, who speak kindly, and who are free from envy, are honored both here and in the hereafter. (49)
They perform what is beneficial for others, where no evil is found;
they do not take pleasure in the sufferings of others, and they are honored both in this world and the next.
They are patient, even-minded, and likewise endure both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Those who speak for the benefit of others, who are tranquil, are honored both in this world and the next.
(51) Those who are not dejected, free from anger, devoid of greed, and helpful to others;
those who do not quarrel even over wealth or desire, are honored both in this world and the next. (52)
Those whose defects have been completely eradicated, who possess firm devotion to Hari,
and who are free from delusion and pride, are honored both in this world and the next;
likewise, those who are unattached to all worldly ties and whose doubts have been destroyed.
People who are not intent on self-praise are honored both in this world and the next;
those who do not envy anyone, who walk the path of justice, who make their time fruitful, and who are gentle, are honored both in this world and the next. (54–55)
Those who have exerted effort and perfected their wisdom find no satiety in chanting the glories of Hari;
ever-disciplined and vigilant, they are honored both in this world and the next.
They are free from shamelessness, do not obstruct the welfare of others, and are generous givers.
Those who do not disclose the secrets of others are honored both in this world and in the next.
(57) Thus, even the gods worship those who are endowed with all virtues, who are skillful, who seek their own welfare, who know the proper time, and who understand what is pleasing. (58)
Those people who have that as their goal and offer themselves to it surely attain the eternal, divine Supreme Brahman, which is without beginning or end and unborn.
For them, austerity is the means to the highest good, as are tranquility and self-restraint, which are its roots.
By that [penance], one obtains whatever may be most desired.
Through austerity, an embodied being becomes capable of sustaining all living creatures;
by means of that same austerity, the lords and the great seers were likewise born.
Those devoted to the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) attain the upward-leading Brahman;
the Kṣatriyas are considered protectors of the sacrifice, while the Vaiśyas are regarded as performers of the oblation-sacrifice (Haviryajña).
The Śūdras perform sacrifices of service, and the Brahmins perform sacrifices of austerity.
In the Tretā age, sacrifices were performed collectively; they were auspicious and granted the attainment of Brahman.
Through austerity, knowledge, sacrifice, or charity, people attained unbroken fame and established that fame upon the earth.
Those who go to the highest heaven enjoy infinite happiness;
here, it is the donors alone who establish the source of fame within the sacrifice. As long as that source of fame exists, so long does the heaven remain unbroken.

For the sake of gods, sages, ancestors, and teachers; for the sake of the elderly, the sick, and guests; for the sake of the helpless, the wretched, and the noble; and for the sake of chaste women, virtuous ones, and the good—for those who have nothing that should not be given to these, they have attained heaven. (66–67)
Gautama, having always served the Brahmins with food and other offerings during times of drought,
subsequently attained the divine heaven and reached the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Rantideva, having given water that bestows happiness to Vasiṣṭha...
Indeed, through that blessing, having enjoyed heaven, he attained the abode of Hari.
(69) And Indradyumna, having bestowed infinite wealth upon the sacrifice, went to the divine heaven by means of devotion, having reached the state of Nārāyaṇa. (70)
Śibi, having given his son for the sake of a brahmin, went to the highest heaven;
Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, having given his eyes to a twice-born,
enjoyed heaven through devotion and then went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Having offered his head, Dharmāṅgada went to the imperishable state;
Svarṇāṅgada, having given a golden umbrella to a Brahmin, departed for the supreme abode of the Lord along with his entire kingdom. || 72-73 ||

And Sāṃkṛtika, having instructed his disciples and established the Supreme Brahman within himself, indeed departed for the divine, supreme abode of Hari. Ambarīṣa, moreover, gave a herd of cows to the brahmins.

Having enjoyed heaven for as many Arbudas as there are Arbudas, Vṛṣādarbhi went to the imperishable state after bestowing all his jewels upon a Brahmin. Yuvanāśva likewise [went to the imperishable state] after giving away his beloved women and beautiful dwellings.
Having bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins, he then went from heaven to the imperishable realm.
Nimi, having given away his kingdom, became Janaka of Videha. Even the son of Jamadagni, having given away the earth, became Nārāyaṇa.
Having given [the earth] to a twice-born man, Gaya went to heaven and attained the station of Śiva.
The royal sage named Marutta, having offered his daughter to Aṅgiras,
went to the celestial realm and from there proceeded to the imperishable state.
Brahmadatta, the king of Pañcāla, having given the treasure Śaṅkha to a twice-born man,
enjoyed heaven for a long time and then went to the supreme state of the Lord. And the royal sage Mitrasaha gave his own beloved wife to Vasiṣṭha.
Having given Madayantī away, he went to the imperishable state together with his wife.
Likewise, the pure King Sahasrajit gave up his dear life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa; having gone to heaven, he enjoyed its pleasures and then attained the state of liberation.
King Śatadyumna, having given his own golden palace along with its furnishings to Mudgala, enjoyed heaven and went to the imperishable state.
King Dyutimat, likewise, having bestowed his kingdom upon Ṛcīka—
Having enjoyed heaven for a long time through devotion, he then went to the imperishable abode (84).
Having given his daughter Śāntā to the yogi Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Lomapāda enjoyed divine heaven and then went from there to the imperishable abode (85).
The royal sage Madirāśva, having given a most beautiful maiden to the ṛṣi Hiraṇyākṣa, went from there to the imperishable heaven.
Prasenajit, having given a gift of a hundred thousand cows to a twice-born man, [went to heaven].
Having enjoyed heaven, he then went to the imperishable abode of Śrī Hari.
The Pitṛs, the great ṛṣis, the gods, the kings, and the subjects, having given their own daughters to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, resided on the fourteenth level.
In previous kalpas they have gone to the supreme Goloka;
they will go there again by giving even their entire possessions or whatever little they have for the sake of Hari alone. Through devotion, they shall go to that very abode.
Through gifts, austerities, and devotion, many indeed have gone to heaven;
their fame remains established forever in the world of Brahmā,
and likewise their renown abides upon the earth as long as the sun and other celestial bodies endure.
Those who have acquired wisdom from the virtuous, who are disciplined and dedicated to Nārāyaṇa,
and who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of Hari, abide eternally in the imperishable realm.
These people are steadfast, vigilant, self-controlled, and knowers of the Dharma.
Those who are free from joy, pride, and anger never come to grief at all.
(92) Through giving, study, sacrifice, austerity, modesty, self-control, and uprightness, one increases one's own vital energy (*tejas*), and all evil is destroyed. (94)
Those who have shaken off evil, who are endowed with devotion, who have conquered their senses through withdrawal,
and who are not overcome by desire and anger, go to the eternal Brahman. One should always bow down to fire, a brāhmaṇa, a virtuous woman, a holy person, a deity, and an elder.
One should avoid harsh speech; thereby one attains Brahman.
Established in wisdom and established in the Self, even while acting, one is not tainted.
One should strive to cross the river of worldly tendencies and the body.

[This river] brings in the waters of all the senses, has greed and delusion for its banks, mud consisting of anger, is long in duration due to time, and has the affection for one's family as its crocodiles;
[one crosses it] by means of the raft of service or through devotion, with the assistance of the virtuous. (98)
The Sātvatas—tranquil, steadfast, and possessing vision of the further shore—cross over. But those who are neither devoted nor wise do not cross this river.
Therefore, one who possesses the virtue of charity should strive for the sake of emerging [from the flood]. (2.244.100)
One who takes refuge in the Eternal (Sadāśiva) may cross over that [ocean of worldly existence] through sacrifice, devotion, and renunciation;
one should abide by the dharma of the virtuous and perform the actions of the virtuous.
Those who possess knowledge of the distinctions between dharma and devotion cross the river that is difficult to traverse.
"By means of devotion to Śrī Hari, the virtuous are like rafts that carry the ignorant across.
Having thus instructed, O Rādhikā, the glorious preceptor Lomaśa himself ceased speaking; thereafter, the matter was resolved.
The foods provided were indeed such as to grant complete satisfaction according to their desires;
thereafter, O Rādhikā, all the people attained rest in every respect.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of King Aśvapāṭala Commencing the Soma Sacrifice on the Bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa Lake on the Eighth Day of the Dark Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa in the Tretā Age, the Second Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," including the rites of the first day and the instruction given by Lomaśa.
