Chapter 246 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; on the second day, the sage Lomaśa performed whatever duties were required for the Soma sacrifice.
Having first performed the necessary preliminary rites and other virtuous deeds,
Lomaśa indeed performed the Prāyaṇīyeṣṭi sacrifice in the very morning;
he then established and worshipped the five deities beginning with Pathyā.
Pathyā Svasti is the first; Agni Sura is the second;
Soma is the third; Savitṛ is the fourth; and Aditi is the fifth.
The sacrificial material for Aditi is boiled rice (odana), while for the other four it is clarified butter (ājya) alone.
Having cooked the rice, he then offered it as an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire;
thereupon, the king purchased Soma with ten articles:
a one-year-old cow, gold, and a goat.
The lord of the earth purchased Soma indeed with a cow together with her calf, and also with a bull;
with an ox capable of drawing a cart, and also with a young male calf, a young female calf, and a garment. || 6–7 ||
Having purchased the Soma and seized two thieves by the right hand,
the sacrificer placed it upon the Soma-cart and proceeded to the sacrifice.
Standing before the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, he performed the *ātithyeṣṭi*.
And he gave to Viṣṇu the sacrificial substance, a cake on nine potsherds. Then he caused that Soma to be placed upon the royal throne.
The officiating priests and the sacrificer took an oath for the sake of non-enmity.
Then the Pravargya rite proceeded with all its implements:
three vessels called Mahāvīra, two milking bowls,
a vessel for clarified butter, as well as two horses and two earthen potsherds.
The wooden implements made from *udumbara* wood are as follows:

the royal throne (*samrāḍāsandī*), two large offering-ladles (*srucau*), two small offering-ladles (*srucāv*) for the pits, two side-pieces (*śaphau*), two fire-stirring sticks (*dhṛṣṭī*), the central post (*methī*), and three pegs (*śaṅkavaḥ*). || 12–13 ||
Three fans, two golden ornaments, as well as one Abhidhānikā,
the Nidānas, the Śākhadāmas, and likewise Muñja grass—
thus the Adhvaryu then brought the materials for the Pravargya rite.
Permitted by Brahmā, he then proceeded with the Pravargya rite;
he prepared the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) known as Rauhiṇa according to the prescribed rules.
Having fixed four stakes near the door, he likewise prepared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having kindled the fire and placed the *mahāvīra* vessel right there,
having filled its mouth with clarified butter (*ājya*) and covered it with gold,
the *adhvaryu* priest should perform this repeatedly; thereafter—
Having tied a cow, a calf, and a goat to stakes, he milked them;
he poured that milk into the *mahāvīra* vessel, and from it, steam arose. When the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) was heated, the pouring of the milk is called *pravṛñjana*.
The Adhvaryu alone performed this Pravargya rite;
thereafter, the Pratiprasthātṛ offered the Rauhiṇa cake into the Āhavanīya fire with a ladle that was not fashioned from a tree-trunk.
Having performed the call for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response of the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*,
O hero, he offered into the fire the clarified butter mixed with milk.
The milk contained in the *mahāvīra* vessel, once offered, is designated as the *gharma*.
The Aśvins and Mahendra are proclaimed as its deities;
with what remained, he performed the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation.
Having filled the Mahāvīra vessel with curds, he performed that sacrifice.
Having placed the remainder on the altar,
the Pratiprasthātṛ then performed a small portion of the offering of the Rauhiṇa sacrificial cake;
thereafter, the Adhvaryu indeed performed the six Śalākā offerings.
Having performed the Agnihotra and the Homa, as well as the consumption of the remnants,
he did so together with the Hotṛ, the Brahmā, the Agnīdhra, and the Yajamāna. Thus, at that time, the Pravar-gya ceremony was duly completed in the morning.
In the evening, the Pravargya rite shall likewise take place in that same manner.
(27) The Pravargya is for the purpose of rejoining the severed head of the sacrifice.
O Rādhā, in ancient times, Viṣṇu was the sacrifice while the gods were performing a sacrificial session (sattra). (28)
Viṣṇu alone attained glory; the gods did not attain anything beyond that.
They fought with Viṣṇu, but Viṣṇu [defeated] the gods with his bow.
Having conquered them, he placed the tip of the bow below the chin.
Then the ants stood upon the ground where the bowstring lay;
and from the edge of the earth, they tore away the bow as it sprang upward with force.
Viṣṇu’s head was severed from the region of his neck and went into the sky.
When the gods found their worship of Viṣṇu, whose form was the sacrifice and whose head had been severed,
to be fruitless, they then petitioned the Aśvins.
To restore his head, the two of them then spoke to the deities.
"Let there be a portion of the sacrificial oblation for us two from this day forward in the Soma sacrifice.
Let the gods grant us a share and join our heads [to the sacrifice].
This very act is indeed the joining of the Pravargya rite to the head of the sacrifice."
O Rādhikā, Mahāvīra is the embodiment of the head of the sacrifice, and Bodhya is likewise;
from him, moreover, the morning *upasat* and the *iṣṭi* sacrifice were born.
Agni, Soma, and Viṣṇu—these three are the principal deities.
He offered clarified butter as the sacrificial substance for the oblation to those very gods.
Having performed the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā, he then ceased;
likewise, at the time of evening, he performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites.
Then he performed the invocation of Subrahmaṇyā;
thus did the ritual proceed on the ninth day of the Soma sacrifice.
Thereafter, they all partook of meals consisting indeed of sweet foods.
At night, Śrī Lomaśa instructed him in the means to liberation:
"Therefore, for one who is devoid of the method of worship, there shall be decapitation;
thus, the Blessed Lord, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign, must be worshipped."
When one maintains the practice of devotion to Śrī Hari by obtaining one's livelihood from others,
then a state of single-minded steadfastness toward the Supreme Lord arises.
Through the withdrawal of the senses and the cessation of the intake of food, the withdrawal of the mind [is achieved].
Indeed, through a mind free from egoism, knowledge of the Self arises.
By means of that knowledge, one should restrain the self; thereby, one shall attain peace.
One who is steady, observing both the external and internal senses, [attains this].
One who sees the Self by means of the self crosses over the difficult-to-cross hardship;
whether by nature one is a tiger, a dog, or even a boar;
or a lion, a śarabha, an elephant, a cat, or even a monkey. (44)
Whether it be a jackal, a crow, an elephant, or even a scorpion;
whether it be a crane or a donkey—whatever being possesses such a nature, whether it be a sinner or a doer of merit, or one who is afflicted or in the midst of affliction. (45–46)
Whether free from afflictions, or active, or poor, or even a deceiver;
whether inferior in his former state, yet having resorted to the Sāṃkhya dharma,
being a practitioner of yoga, associating with the virtuous, and devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa.
One indeed crosses over the difficult terrain of latent impressions, the ocean of mental tendencies, and the great sea—
[by means of the chariot] whose seat is sacrifice, whose fender is modesty, whose pole is dharma and dispassion,
whose yoke-pins are the vital breaths, whose axle is inquiry, whose path is wisdom, and whose interior is well-constructed. 48–49.
One should cause the chariot of the living being— whose rim is right conduct, whose vehicle is the senses, whose hub is knowledge, whose whip is tranquility, whose charioteer is merit,
and which is mounted by the horses— to reach the end of the long path, being well-guided.
One should establish him in the Garden of Syllables (Akṣarodyāna) and protect him in the Supreme Abode.
He is firmly established in the knowledge of Brahman, devoted to all sacrifices, endowed with infinite sovereignty, and his inner being is won over by devotion. || 51–52 ||
Kṛṣṇa shines within the heart and manifests both internally and externally;
in such a supreme devotee, indeed, the entire universe is contained.
There is nothing whatsoever equal to this state of possessing such greatness.
Having conquered the earth, and likewise having conquered water, fire, air, and space; then,
having conquered the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the ego-sense (ahaṃbuddhi),
he who also conquers the state of being a lord shall go to the station of the Supreme Lord.
Having conquered human effort, destiny, time, and the planets,
and having overcome inherent nature, latent impressions, and illusion, one shall go to the imperishable state.
Those devoted to austerity and dharma are indeed said to belong to the Satya Yuga.
Those devoted to the duty of sacrifice are said to belong to the Tretā age;
those devoted to the duty of giving are said to belong to the Dvāpara age; and those devoted to the destruction of dharma are said to belong to the Tiṣya (Kali) age.
Those who are devoted to the Brahman and the Dharma are said to be indeed yogins seeking liberation.
If they are devoted to the Supreme Brahman, they become established in the Imperishable.
There is no knowledge or austerity without it, nor is there any restraint of the senses without it.
A human being does not find liberation until all things have been renounced.

(2.245.60) In the beginning, at the moment of creation, the Creator bestowed all the principles (*tattva*) upon the individual soul (*jīvātman*) for the sake of enjoyment, heaven, and final release. (2.245.61)
Earth is situated in the region of the body, water in the belly, fire in the mind, and air in the vital breath; space is placed in the cavities of the ears and so forth.
Indeed, all the subtle elements (tanmātras) are held within the sense-organ spheres (golakas).
Even the objects of the senses and the sensory domains were renounced among all things.
Viṣṇu was placed in the foot, Śukra in the strength, and Indra in the hand;
Agni was placed in the stomach, the quarters in the ear, and Sarasvatī in the tongue.

Candra is placed in the *manas*, Brahmā in the intellect (*buddhi*), and Hari likewise in the heart (*citta*). All those gods are established in the individual soul (*jīva*), while Keśava is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) therein.
Thus, all these are established, yet the Imperishable (*akṣara*) resides in the aperture of Brahman (*brahmarandhra*).
But the supreme light is established within the heart in the *suṣumṇā*.
Indeed, everything exists here, yet one who seeks it is difficult to find.
One should seek the Supreme Lord, the path to Brahman, through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Having mounted the chariot of devotion, the successful seeker shall go to the imperishable abode;
by the light of his own lamp, he shall behold the Supreme Self.
Seeing thus, he indeed becomes fit for absorption into Brahman after death.
The Supreme Lord, the Master, dwells within all moving and stationary beings.
Having perceived that Self as supreme, one attains the highest Brahman. To the extent that the self is dedicated to the Self, to that same extent is it dedicated to the Supreme. (2.245.70)
One who constantly places their trust in Kṛṣṇa is fit for immortality.
Time ripens all beings, yet it is by Time that Time itself is ripened.
Having attained that Supreme Ripener, one is never again subject to being consumed.
Having become the imperishable Brahman, he indeed attains the Supreme Brahman.
He is subtle; he is the great gross; he is the Lord within and without.
Abiding as the eternal amidst the transient, he does not shine by means of external manifestation.
And he is seen within as a luminous radiance, sought by the self;
by the power of grace, Kṛṣṇa converses within through devotion. Though abiding here in the divine, immortal, and imperishable state, he remains present right here.
And in that very Self, which is the locus of lordship, equal [to all], and free from impurity—
[he who is] tranquil, self-controlled, whose cloth of spiritual conduct is [well-prepared], who rejoices in the Self, and for whom Kṛṣṇa has been realized— he goes to that supreme state. (75–76)
One should conquer desire, anger, fear, greed, pride, sleep, and worldly attachment through lack of volition, tranquility, and vigilance.
One should conquer the triad [of qualities] through magnanimity, discernment, and fortitude.
One should conquer the genitals and the belly through fortitude; the hands and feet through the eyes;
the eyes and ears through the mind; the mind and speech through action;
and all actions through total surrender unto Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
One should perceive all that consists of the splendor of Brahman as Hari, whose essence is rasa.
Splendor increases through meditation; meditation increases through devotion.
Devotion increases through affection; affection arises from the realization of His majesty.
And awakening arises for the virtuous through association with the good, and the goodness of the good comes from a fragment of Hari’s grace.
(8.1) Grace, in turn, arises from taking refuge [in Him], and likewise from the attainment of one's purpose.
The purpose is happiness for the living being—that for the sake of which one exerts oneself. (8.2)
If there is activity, it arises from desire; desire arises from knowledge; and knowledge, however, is born from the scriptures.
Through the greatness of hearing the divine narrative, a divine disposition is produced.
Therefore, a wise person should listen to the divine narrative constantly.
What more need be said of him by whom the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) has been obtained in the form of this narrative?
Through these [teachings], one's splendor, sovereignty, and the ultimate truth increase;
indeed, all goals are accomplished and the splendor of Brahman shines forth.
Having conquered *prakṛti* through spiritual splendor (*tejas*), one should proceed to the eternal Brahman.
Indeed, the senses are like leaks that cause wisdom to flow away;
one should restrain them by fixing the mind upon the Supreme Self within one's own self.
The inner reality becomes serene; through that, Brahman shines forth.
Indeed, within the divine Brahman and within their own eternal selves, the two perceive each other like two liberated practitioners.
Thus, having practiced in solitude, one should attain identity with the Imperishable;
disregarding the supernatural powers, lordly dominions, and obstacles that arise, one should proceed toward the Imperishable.
Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon Hari on that very same seat.
Having performed the sacrifice of sacred knowledge (*brahmayajña*), the sacrifice of meditation (*dhyānayajña*), and the sacrifice of worship (*pūjāyajña*),
one should thereafter perform the sacrifice of material offerings (*dravyayajña*), while restraining the speed of the mind. One should not become attached, even mentally, to objects situated nearby.
One should not contemplate contempt or honor, nor the impulses of joy or fear;
rather, one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Lord, who resides within the self and is supported by the sacrifice.
For the virtuous person whose nature is thus absorbed in meditation and who is devoted to equanimity— (92) — [the goal is attained].
Swiftly, the stainless Supreme Brahman shines within its own profound cavern.
By this very path, whether a woman or even a person of neutral gender, having propitiated the Supreme Brahman, one shall attain the supreme goal. (93–94)
Having become liberated, one should behold the liberated Hari, who is without beginning;
having become Brahman, one should behold Brahman, the imperishable abode of bliss.
The sovereign of the liberated should behold the Supreme Brahman with the eye of Brahman.
A living being is bound by action that has not been offered to Hara;
indeed, a living being is liberated by that same [action] when it is offered to Hara.
Therefore, both types of yoga related to Hari must be practiced here by an ascetic.
Those two divine ones, who receive everything offered, lead him to their own abode,
reaching which there is no death, no sorrow, and no rebirth.
Then one should know oneself as a portion of that Supreme Self.
"Therefore, one should offer the sacrifice, the ritual action, the invocation, and one's very being unto Hari.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa fell silent. Then followed the dismissal of the assembly and the distribution of food.
They became truly providers of satisfaction, bringing rest during the night;
the people chanted the name of Śrī Hari and meditated upon Hari.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Second Day of the Soma Sacrifice, including the Subrahmaṇya, Upasada, and Pravargya rites, as well as the Instruction on the Avoidance of the Homa-offering by Lomaśa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 245: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 246 [Author: → Chapter 247
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, then, on the third day of the sacrifice,
on the tenth lunar day, the performance of the Soma ritual commenced once again.
Lomaśa arrived, and King Kṛtapuṇyaka also arrived.
In the morning, the preceptor performed the Pravargya, Upasada, and Avabhṛtha rites. Furthermore, the construction of the great altar was six paces away from the pavilion.
The Guru positioned himself both far away and in front, according to the prescribed rule.
That [mandala] is considered to be seventy-two squares in length from east to west,
and sixty squares in width from south to north.
Extending forty-eight [units] across both the hip region and the shoulder region,
he then constructed such a complete altar. Thereupon, the sacrificer undertook the vow consisting of the consumption of milk alone.
He performed the *havana* and all other rites that must be performed;
likewise, he performed the evening *pravargya* and *upasad* rituals.
Having observed the milk-vow (*payovrata*) and addressed the deity Subrahmaṇyā, ||| 6–7 ||
Having invoked the one whose essence is Indra, he then undertook a vow;
thereafter followed the cessation [of the rite], the relinquishment [of restrictions], and the meal of grace.
For as many dignitaries as there were, there was sweet food consisting of milk-rice and other delicacies.
Then the venerable sage Lomaśa, whose soul was never satiated with wood, instructed them in the assembly hall during the night on how liberation is achieved:
"Indeed, by means of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the supreme seers conquer the worlds. (2.246.10)
And thereafter they attain the eternal, supreme good;
subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest, they perform extensive austerities,
dwelling in temples of the gods and contemplating the welfare of all beings.
Those who are immersed in the assembly of the virtuous are prepared for union with Brahman.
Holy men—whether practicing the life of a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller—who remain attached to Hari while following their prescribed conduct, attain the supreme goal. (1.2–1.3)

For those who perform their daily duties, whose fruits have been burnt away by knowledge, and who are free from the defects of desire and hatred, they are established in the supreme Imperishable. Indeed, the four-stepped ladder is the means for ascending to Brahman.
Having ascended that, Hari, supporting him, leads him indeed to the world of Brahmā.
A celibate student who remains steadfast in the vow of Brahman shall obtain everything;
for the Guru is Brahman, the vow is Brahman, the Veda is Brahman, and likewise Hari is Brahman.
One should serve them constantly; thus one shall go to the world of Brahmā.
One should indeed perform service to the guru, for one will obtain fruit equal to that of a sacrifice.
Whatever must be done by a disciple or a servant, that he should perform.
A servant should be one who performs all tasks, free from pride, and exceedingly devoted.
When summoned, he should set aside everything else and approach his teacher.
He should speak what is pleasing and gaze upon the teacher with eyes full of love. (18–19)
Having fed the gurus, he should then eat and likewise drink;
he should perform a foot-massage and touch their feet gently.
He should serve them, saying, "Command me, O Blessed One, what shall I do? (2.246.20)
He should remain close by and dwell there solely for the purpose of serving the Guru.
Even a householder should indeed serve the Guru as a god, his virtuous wife as his lord, and practice dharma and irreproachable conduct with tireless devotion. (21–22)
One should give cooked food to a god, to one’s guru, and to a traveler;
one should also give it to a trustee (nyāsī), but one should never cook for one’s own sake alone.
No guest who has come to the house should dwell there unhonored.

One should also offer sacrificial oblations to the gods (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya) for those worthy of worship, for the poor and children, and likewise for the helpless and guests; as well as for virtuous men, virtuous women, and chaste wives.
Righteous people and ascetics are always to be honored. (24–25)
Likewise, one who dwells in a house should give to those who do not cook for themselves;
he should be an eater of *vighasa* and thus become an eater of *amṛta*.
*Vighasa* is what remains after the servants have eaten, and likewise, that which remains from the gods is *amṛta*.

One should not engage in disputes with relatives, family members, or kinsmen. (27) The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahman; one should not engage in dispute with him. The father is the lord of the world of Prajāpati; one should not engage in dispute with him. (28)
The guest is indeed the lord of Indra’s world; one should not engage in dispute with him.

The officiating priest is the lord of the world of the gods; one should not engage in dispute with him. And the kinsman is the lord of the world of the Apsarases; one should certainly not quarrel with him.
One should not cause division among kinsmen, for they are the lords of the world of the Viśvedevas;
one should not oppose relatives and friends, for they are the lords of the directions.
One should not cause division among the groups of maternal uncles and maternal aunts, for they are the earth itself. (2.246.30–31)
One should not cause a rift with the elderly, children, the sick, or the emaciated;
nor with one's brother, who is like a father, one's wife, son, daughter, or one's own body.
One’s own shadow, the circle of servants, dependents, and wretched people [should likewise not be alienated]. (32)

Therefore, when reviled by these, one should endure it and not retaliate. (3.3) Indeed, while performing all the duties prescribed for the householder's life, if one should act with a mind free from desire, greed, and fear, (3.34) [then he attains success].
If one who is free from dualities and devoid of pride conducts himself like a virtuous person,
and has found refuge in Hari, he is liberated and not bound.
He indeed attains the supreme goal in this world marked by the discus.
He attains a beautiful destiny befitting those who have conquered their senses.
For householders who practice giving, heaven consists of fruits, flowers, and essences;
and for such householders, there is also a second, supreme, and eternal heaven.
That householder, seeing his own body overcome by wrinkles, grey hair, and infirmity,
should indeed worship the Supreme Lord like one dwelling in the forest.
He should eat sparingly, subsist on pure food, and consume roots and fruits.
One should protect the Dharma rooted in the Upaniṣads, which is cherished by Brahman.
Having made one’s dwelling in the forest, the wilderness, or at home like a great seer,
and being fully absorbed in the Supreme Brahman, one shall attain liberation.
Having performed a sacrifice, a fire-oblation, and likewise provided all ritual fees,
or even if he be a virtuous man or a son of Brahmā who is not subject to human limitations,
he should perform the *jīva-śrāddha* (the funeral rite for the living), for he is one whose self is established in the Self.
Having established [the deity] within one's own self, the practitioner of vows should perform the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
There should be constant devotion, worship, meditation upon Nārāyaṇa,
sacrifice, recitation, remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, and contemplation on Brahman.
For that purpose, one should perform all actions while remaining established like one who is liberated;
having attained fearlessness and steadfastness within the self, and having bestowed [fearlessness] upon the proud,
one who possesses the dharma of the virtuous should take up the life of renunciation for the sake of the next world.
His worlds consist of light, each succeeding one providing greater supreme bliss.
Even while remaining in this world, he possesses inexhaustible satisfaction;
having cast off the body through union with Hari, he attains the imperishable infinity.
In this state, the embodied one always exists as the fullness itself, like space;
he should neither become angry nor rejoice, remaining pure and abiding like Brahman.
He should neither welcome death nor the life born of nature.
One should wait upon the Brahman alone, just as a servant waits upon his master.
One should be of unassailable mind, always liberated from evil,
and should grant fearlessness to all beings, both for oneself and for what has been done by others.
For one who is freed from delusion, no fear exists from anything whatsoever;
he dwells eternally in the immortal, the refuge of all embodied beings.
Satisfied by wisdom, free from worldly effort, liberated from attachment, he has transcended death.
He whose life is for the sake of Dharma, and whose Dharma is indeed for the sake of Hari—
he, being liberated from bonds and becoming a Brahmin who knows Brahman,
offers the substance of his own existence arising from the self into the Supreme Self.
Through the satisfaction born of the *homa* offering, Hari attains a state of serene contentment;
and by accumulating that merit, he goes to the eternal Brahman.
The gods nourish him alone and long for the supreme goal.
Having attained that fruitful longing, he beholds the Supreme Self;
seeing that the modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti) have perished and having reached the immortal, he—
tranquil and indifferent toward worldly objects— attains indeed the immortal state.
Having thoroughly subdued all volitional thoughts, one should direct the mind toward sentient beings;
by conquering time through the assistance of the Supreme Lord, one shall attain the deathless state.
Upon attaining clarity of mind, both the auspicious and the inauspicious cease to exist.
Having taken refuge in the divine Self alone, one enjoys infinite happiness.
(57) For him whose sleep is attained with ease, there is serenity within his own self;
and Hari, being propitiated, bestows upon him a treasure-trove of bliss. (58)
For one for whom even the invitation to a formal seat possesses worthlessness, his grace remains constant, like the Imperishable (Akṣara).
When one restrains the rays of the senses with the mind... [59]
When the mind is restrained by the intellect, then the Self is fully revealed.
Freed from internal and external qualities and defects, one is no longer stained.
For one who is unstained, delight arises in that Supreme Self.
With the functions of the qualities (guṇas) utterly destroyed and no longer active toward the works of the qualities,
and being free from the knot of the heart, he attains the knot of Brahman;
he attains the supreme peace of the Supreme Brahman as well as its sovereign power.
Self-knowledge and tranquility are the supreme means for attaining the state of Brahman.
There is no doubt that this state of Brahman leads to the attainment of the Supreme Brahman;
indeed, there is no higher attainment than the attainment of Hari.
Whatever one performs without prior intention is devoid of qualities;
however, that which is preceded by devotion to Hari is divine and indeed bestows liberation. For there is no dharma superior to this dharma directed toward Hari in this world.
The duty of Brahman is the supreme duty, the shroud that covers all duties.
(66) The dissolution of all activities into Hari is the supreme austerity;
being satisfied with the Self through austerity, one enjoys the bliss of the fruit. (67)
Having attained the inner path, he reaches the supreme Lord dwelling within the palace—
the self of all, revealed as his own self.
Then, indeed, the inner self bestows its entire being upon him.

To him who possesses the brilliance of knowledge and has attained his own innate nature, this very ocean of worldly existence—this world composed of *māyā*—has been crossed; he has reached that which consists of Brahman, and here and now, Brahman shines forth within him. (2.246.70)
The Self is neither female nor male, nor indeed is it neuter;
it is neither inert matter nor inherent nature, but is the eternal form of Brahman.
It is protected by the Supreme Brahman and awakened by the Supreme Brahman.
Nourished by the Supreme Brahman and likewise eating the Supreme Brahman;
possessing the flavor of the Supreme Brahman and rejoicing in the Supreme Brahman; having the body of the Supreme Brahman and immersed in the bliss of the Supreme Brahman. (72–73)
He is a friend of the Supreme Brahman, a traveler on the path to the Supreme Brahman, one whose purpose is the expansion of the Supreme Brahman,
and one who has made his dwelling in the Supreme Brahman; indeed, he goes into the Supreme Brahman.

One who possesses the supreme Brahman as his true all-in-all attains liberation consisting of that very essence. (75) When one indeed does not form a separate conception toward any living beings, and [abandons] both suffering and evil, then one attains Brahman. (76)
Latent impressions (vāsanā) are indeed the sole bond, for they are the greatest of all bonds. One who is liberated from the bond of latent impressions is fit for becoming Brahman.
Peace is the secret essence (upaniṣad) of knowledge, and happiness is the secret essence of peace.
Contentment is the secret cause of happiness, and renunciation is the secret cause of contentment.
(78) The renunciant, whose self is serene and who is established in Hari, does not enter into bondage.
With his soul fixed in the Supreme Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss. (79)
He enjoys an imperishable bliss that is uncreated, indestructible, eternally perfected, and unmixed; it is to be realized through the attainment of the Supreme Brahman.
He whose mind is free from agitation has its firm foundation in the Supreme Lord.
For one who finds satisfaction in the Supreme God, there is indeed eternal contentment.
A wise person should choose that Hari by whom one who has not eaten is satisfied, by whom one who possesses no wealth is satisfied, and by whom one who lacks affection is endowed with strength.
Restraining one's own senses, one should open the door to the Imperishable;
thus, with the provisions for the journey consisting of delight in the Self, one attains the imperishable Acyuta.
When one has found perfect rest in the Supreme Kṛṣṇa, having offered all desires to the Lord Hari, [one attains that state].
From that inexhaustible ocean of bliss, happiness arises on all sides. For one who has suppressed the illusory nature [of the world], whose personal impurities have been suppressed,
and whose meditation on Hari remains unimpeded, old age and death do not exist.
Thus, indeed, being liberated from all sides, Brahmā shines forth unliberated;
and for him, O lady of noble nature, the Supreme Brahman remains unliberated.
Having thus transcended the three qualities and attained the imperishable abode here—
Having attained the supreme state, he does not return again.

That tree which has ignorance as its root is said to be like a desire-tree (kalpavṛkṣa); the attainment of sense objects is its cluster of blossoms, and the sense objects themselves are considered its branches.
Enjoyment is its stalk, flavors are indeed its leaves;
joy is its flowers, and happiness is truly its fruit.
Therein, the mixture of suffering is the foul mire of putrid moisture.
Delusion, thirst for sensual pleasure, and illusion are the matrices of ignorance.
Having reached Hari, the traveler should indeed banish that illusion;
by that means, everything belonging to the traveler truly attains dissolution.

While remaining in his own home, Kṛṣṇa, the jewel of heaven, shines forth. Having attained that cooling radiance which bestows the imperishable, one shall go to that bliss known as the Imperishable (Akṣara), which is concentrated within the Supreme Brahman. || 92 ||
In that [state], one's own self, which is the very form of Brahman, becomes the vessel wherein [the Self] is placed;
it is flawless, exceedingly firm, bound by the plaster of devotion and worship, fully ripened in the essence of love, and filled with the nectar of affection. (93–94)
It is inhabited by the divine form known as single-minded concentration on Hari;
it is protected by those who have attained the state of liberation, and thus it does not perish.
It is imperishable, immortal, and filled with eternal bliss.
One’s own innate bliss is filled by the fulfillment provided by the glorious Hari.
Whether this [bliss] is attained through His grace or even by means of spiritual practices,
there is no longer any outflow from his treasury, due to the favor of the Supreme Self.
"Indeed, this alone is to be attained through sacrifices, gifts, and oblations;
for there remains nothing else to be attained by the self.
Thus spoke the illustrious Lomaśa himself, the true guru, O Rādhikā.
Having thus instructed them, he ceased speaking; at night, he provided milk for them to drink.
The king caused all of them to drink the milk, and then those performers of the sacrifice took rest during the night.
Remembering the supreme Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa within their own hearts,
the great kings and other great sages fell asleep.

(101) Thus ends the forty-sixth [chapter] in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*, titled "The Description of the Instruction on Eating and Other Duties Following the Rites of the Soma Sacrifice on the Tenth Day of the Third Day."
The Two Hundred and Forty-Sixth Chapter.
Chapter 246: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 247.
[The Author: Chapter 248.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having risen in the morning, the patron Aśvapāṭala—
The king, having performed his daily rites, as did Lomaśa and the other great sages,
arrived at the sacrificial ground with composed minds on the fourth day,
the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), when all the necessary materials were assembled.

They performed the recitation of auspicious verses, the sprinkling of water and so forth, the purification of their own limbs, and all other daily rites as prescribed, exactly as they had been taught.
Now I shall speak specifically; listen to this in brief.
In the morning, having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, and thereafter,
having removed the Pravargya and cast the vessels into the northern fire,
the Guru commenced the ritual procedure for the Agniṣoma sacrifice involving the fruit-offering and the animal victim.
Having placed fuel-wood upon the Āhavanīya fire and kindled it so that it shone brightly,
he took the blazing fire along with Sīmā and caused the fire to be deposited upon the altar situated within the Mahāvedi.
He established the Gārhapatya fire and that known as the Prājahita;
he also placed the Soma upon the oblation-carrying cart. Having taken the earth from the Cātvāla pit, he scattered it over the Dhiṣṇya hearths with those very particles.
Having performed the offering of the omentum (vapā), the Adhvaryu priest then proceeded with the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā;
thereafter, for the sake of the Soma-pressing and the excellence of the juice,
he drew the Vasatīvarī water from the pond into a jar.
Then, at midday, they established the fire at the entrance of the sacrificial hall (śālāmukhīya).
He indeed commenced the sacrifice of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa),
and even in the evening, he performed the sacrifice of the heart and other limb-offerings.
Having performed the ritual limbs up to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, he did not complete them.
All of them partook of their meals as was appropriate and according to their vows.
At night, the *adhvaryu* priest likewise [prepared] the *vasatīvarī* water-jar.
Taking up the sacrificial post and walking around the altar on all sides, he set it down.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the rites beginning with the driving away of the calves, as well as the preparation of the curds intended for the *āmikṣā* required for the following day. (13–14)
He prepared thick curd for the sake of the *dadhighraha* offering,
and he procured sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the purpose of the *savanīya* oblations.
Then, at that time, the conclusion of the sacrificial rites took place.
Accompanied by his wife, the sacrificer performed a vigil during the night,
preceded by the festival of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He performed the worship of Śrī Hari with sixteen and other ritual articles.
Likewise, at night, the king carried out the concluding ceremony (udyāpana) of the vow;
the sages and the people also engaged in the congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana) of Hari.
In the morning, Hari himself appeared first;
he was indeed Muralīdhara, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, joined by Rādhā and Ramā.
He bore a divine form and was adorned with a circle of divine splendor.
Hari appeared visibly before them all, adorned with ornaments and smiling;
on his right was Kambharā and on his left Gopālakṛṣṇaka, while Māṇikya and others—Brahmā and Satya—stood around him. (2.247.20–21)
"I am pleased today by your vow, and especially by your sacrifice.
I shall be the bestower of the fruit you desire—whether it be liberation, heaven, or whatever else.
Then, O King, they worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the objects they had obtained.
Lord Hari, accompanied by His own retinue, attained invisibility.
Then Lomaśa instructed them all in that which purifies:
"Dharma is manifold, existing both among the worlds and among men. (23–24)
The dharma of sacrifice is itself the essence of Nārāyaṇa and bestows the world of Brahmā;
the dharma of service, through the medium of great blessings, grants heaven.
Indeed, the dharma of non-malice toward all beings truly bestows supreme happiness.
Indeed, serenity toward others bestows the great power of supreme bliss (16).
Likewise, the satisfaction of the gods and of the great seers is of such a nature;
and the satisfaction of guests is a companion on the journey to the next world (27).
Formerly, a great sage named Jaṭilāyana, dwelling in the forest,
practiced various forms of austerity with a steady body, always remaining motionless.
A pregnant sparrow built her nest within his matted locks.
Then that compassionate great seer watched her closely;
for while she was in a nest made of grass and fibers within his matted locks,
that sparrow dropped her eggs, and the seer indeed became aware of it.
Even though he understood this, his mind remained fixed on righteousness, and thus he did not move from his place.
Righteousness consists in providing shelter to all beings and protecting those who seek refuge.
Then, from the fully developed eggs, young birds were born.
They grew right there until their wings were fully formed;
then, flying up again and again at evening, they would return at night,
rest, and depart again at dawn in search of food-grains.
Then, when time had passed and those birds had departed on their journey, they did not return; thereupon the sage set out.
He reflected: "This dharma has been perfected by me, who am devoted to austerity."
Having established a hermitage filled with trees, he indeed provided a dwelling place;
and he himself respectfully honored guests of every kind.
Then Nārāyaṇa himself arrived there in order to test him.
Assuming the form of a hunter, he arrived carrying a dead deer upon his shoulder.
"Give me a place to stay, as well as a hearth, a vessel, and likewise fuel," he said.
"I am a *caṇḍāla*, a dog-eater; give these to me if it pleases you."
Having reflected thus, Jaṭāyana gave him a hearth and fuel;
he also gave him a vessel, fire, and likewise a leaf-hut,
so that there would be no deficiency in his service to the people who had come for refuge.
Having made the resolve, "This is my dharma known as *itivrata*," he then gave [the meat] away;
having cooked it all, the dog-eater ate it with satisfaction.
He likewise threw all the remaining meat onto the floor of the hut.
Having made everything completely impure, he sat down on the ground outside.
He then carried out the great sage’s command, saying, "Wipe it clean.
The great sage, being well-pleased, had that hall made pure.
The dog said, "If you have anything required, I shall give it to you.
The dog replied, "My two feet require a massage.
The sage then performed a heartfelt massage of his feet.
Furthermore, with true devotion, he offered fruits, leaves, and water for drinking, saying:
"May the Lord, the Master dwelling here within this shelter, be pleased.
Having spoken thus, he gave the water and immediately vanished from sight.
His body pervaded by splendor, he indeed assumed a divine form;
the glorious Lord Hari, the four-armed master served by Lakṣmī and Śrī, [appeared].
Even as Jaṭilāyana, he bowed at the feet of the Lord.
"O Hari, you have shown compassion here, and I have been made one who has fulfilled his purpose by you.
"O Lord, grant me the imperishable abode immediately after seeing you.
"So be it," Hari replied; and the sage, casting off his body, [departed].
He went to the imperishable abode there through the practice of service in every way.
Therefore, guests should be served with sacrifices, gifts, houses, and likewise with material goods;
there one may meet Nārāyaṇa.
Protecting those who have come for refuge is indeed the service of Nārāyaṇa.
The Blessed One, whose inner self is that [refuge-seeker], certainly becomes pleased. Observing him and with him in mind, a person should serve the embodied being. (2.247.50)
And that sacrifice remains great, auspicious, and bestowing the attainment of the true sacrifice;
indeed, without Hari, even great sacrifices become non-sacrifices.
Furthermore, others also consider the purchase, sale, and liberation [of animals] as part of it.
Everything performed for the benefit of the worlds is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Indeed,
the Supreme Lord dwells within all embodied beings, situated in their midst.
Whether as buyer or seller, Nārāyaṇa himself is present and no other;
having obtained profit, the supreme Lord experiences joy as the taker, and likewise, the supreme Lord experiences joy as the giver upon receiving wealth. (53–54)
Formerly, there was indeed a certain merchant named Śākavikraya who,
having resorted to the path of truth, conducted his buying and selling.
That merchant would first worship his parents every morning.
Having fed [his guests] and received their instructions, he goes to the marketplace. There, he weighs out vegetables for the purchaser—
whether that purchaser be a child, an old man, a youth, or anyone else.
Whether it be a woman, a maiden, or anyone else of immature intellect who has arrived,
they say "Salutations to you, O Viṣṇu" and indeed give whatever is requested.
Therein, not even the slightest deficiency occurs upon the scale.
Indeed, by virtue of his lordship, he bestows fruit even upon a mendicant.
He gives to all in due order, and never out of disregard; he gives exactly as is appropriate, perceiving Narayana to be present therein. (2.247.60)
And by constantly performing this sale, he indeed imparts knowledge:
"O buyers! You should all worship the Supreme Lord in every way—He who is eternally the friend of all and who delights in the welfare of all. (6.1)
Worship the Inner Self through action, mind, and speech.
Abandon hatred and desire; remember the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara. Do not follow after anyone, nor do you enter into conflict with anyone.
Knowing Nārāyaṇa to be equal [to all] therein, worship that Hari;
become possessed of divine disposition, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
Just as the blind and the deaf neither see nor hear, [so should you remain indifferent to worldly distinctions].

Thus should one always contemplate the objects [of the senses] as if blind and deaf; yet toward the Supreme Lord, one should never be blind, but rather possess the power of hearing when listening to His stories.
Toward other objects one should be mute, but toward the Supreme Lord, one should possess eloquence.
In this way, everything—both the sentient and the insentient—is to be ordained within Nārāyaṇa;
for men in this world, that which pertains to sense-objects is to be attained as something insentient.
Just as the elderly, the sick, and the emaciated are by their very nature devoid of desire.
In this world, one should exist as a person free from longing for sense objects.
(68) When one has no fear of oneself and no fear from anything else, for one who is void of passion, hatred, and the like, the attainment of Brahman is certain. (69)
For one who is free from the nature of evil, there is the supreme attainment of Brahman;
he who possesses that great dharma which is fearlessness attains the state of fearlessness. But for him from whom others have fear, great fear shall come upon him.

In this world, virtuous people who practice non-violence are never a source of fear to anyone. (7.1) Therefore, adopt such a way of life and proceed toward the eternal Brahman. [This consists of] a disposition free from malice, abstention from theft, honesty in purpose, and freedom from deception. (7.2)
For one in whom these qualities have taken root, Brahman is revealed.
Through the gift of fearlessness to both [sides], other sacrifices and the like become equal;
for he who in this world bestows the sacrificial fee of fearlessness upon all embodied beings.
Having performed all sacrifices, he attains the gift of fearlessness.
Indeed, Nārāyaṇa, who has become the self of all beings and is the witness,
grants the imperishable, fearless state to the giver of fearlessness.
For those whose conduct is that of agriculture, who possess a violent disposition, and who perform tasks such as cutting grass,
who serve as draft animals for bulls and the like, are indeed givers of suffering and filled with fear.
People drive these animals, bind them, and subdue them.
Humans employ other humans as slaves;
having made horses and other animals their mounts, they lead them through deep mud.
Since those worlds are terrifying and full of predators, they indeed reap that very fruit: fear.
"Aghnyā" is the name for cows; who is worthy to kill them?
Agni and Soma are the dear names of the calves, while whatever fruit of the tree there is, that indeed is the driving away of the calves—the heart is the ripening of the essence.
Even the limbs [of the sacrifice] are for the sake of the fruit alone; by that, Kṛṣṇa is well-pleased.
(2.247.80) "I do not kill even a blade of grass or even a fruit with my hand, nor with a weapon, nor by any other means, because I protect [all beings] by granting them fearlessness. (81)
Leaves of the *śāka* tree and the like, when fit and ripe, fall from the tree;
having purchased those very items, I indeed carry out their sale.
Happiness and suffering are equal to me; neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant exists for me.
"O people, protect the Dharma in this way by bestowing the gift of fearlessness.
By doing so, you who walk the path of fearlessness will attain liberation;
for the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is always pleased by that."
Salutations to the sacrifice of the Brahmins, and salutations to the ritual of progeny;
salutations to those people skilled in service, and repeated salutations to them.
Through good deeds and excellent offerings, the gods are always satisfied.
Indeed, being well-satisfied by prostrations, oblations, hymns, the heart,
and the sacrificial offering, the Ādityas cause rain to fall;
from that come the juices of the crops and food, which lead to the increase of progeny.
Beings perform sacrifices, and therein the Brahman is pleased;
those devotees who bring satisfaction to the Brahman also satisfy others.
Therefore, let them practice devotion toward everything that has the Brahman as its deity.
When Brahman is satisfied, the entire universe is indeed satisfied; of this there is no doubt.
(89) For him who performs the satiation of Brahman during a sacrifice, all the gods become satisfied;
for him who is satisfied through wisdom, there is eternal satisfaction that gives rise to happiness. (2.247.90)
Those who are the support of the Dharma, the source of the Dharma, and devoted to the meditation of Brahman;
who are endowed with devotion and wisdom, and desire to cross to the further shore.
Having seen, attained, and reflected upon the Supreme Brahman that abides in all things,
they reach the imperishable state, a station more meritorious than merit itself;
having gone there, there is no sorrow, no decay, no affliction, and no death.
For such as these, sacrifice is neither for the sake of heaven nor for the sake of fame.
That sacrifice which is practiced by the virtuous is free from malice;
it is intent on the satisfaction of Brahman and consists of sacrificial fuel, herbs, fruits, and roots. (93–94)
For the sake of heaven there is merit alone, whereas freedom from the qualities (*nairguṇya*) leads to liberation.
Having placed that *nairguṇya* in my heart, I indeed practice it.
Others, having made their resolve, perform sacrifices in rituals for the sake of prosperity.
By that path leading to the gods, they go again to heaven;
they reach the realm of no-return and do not return, being devoid of qualities.
Having themselves procured the sacrificial posts, they perform sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Again to heaven, again to earth—the whirlpool of transmigration does not cease.
Therefore, let them indeed be performers of the sacrifice to Brahman, not sacrificers to other deities;
having made Brahman their deity, let them attain liberation through sacrifice.
"Let them perform the pure sacrifice at the sacred ford of the Self through divine contemplations.
Having received this instruction, the merchant who sold vegetables became constantly devoted to serving all and worshipped Puruṣottama.
Once Śrī Hari, having become a buyer, came into his presence;
he said to him, "Give me eternal vegetables.
The merchant, recognizing Pāravāla, gave the vegetables to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the power to cross over, who strides forth, and who seeks the goal. Salutations to You, who indeed brings one to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having spoken thus, he who possessed divine vision prostrated himself like a staff before the Wielder of the Discus.
Then Hari, assuming four arms, touched him with his hand—
marked with the signs of the fish, the banner, the bow, the trident, the svastika, and the discus.
Having placed him in a celestial chariot and established him in the divine, imperishable state, he led him away.
Thus, those steadfast ones who always worship Hari by way of sacrifice go to the abode of Hari together with Hari. Therefore, one should constantly worship Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within.
I bow to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Gopāla,
the child of Kambharā, the Lord of Śrī, the Master beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
to the Lord beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Protector, the Blessed One, higher than the highest.
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa departed for the lake during the Brahma-muhūrta.
Then all of them, O Rādhikā, went to the lake for the purpose of bathing,
having performed the vigil and completed their daily worship.
On the fifth day, the great sages, the sacrificer, and other ritualists arrived at the pavilion for the sake of the Soma rites;
having performed the daily requirements, they carried out the special ceremonies.
"O Rādhikā, I shall declare to you that auspicious [rite] which bestows all merit.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vigil, the Concluding Rite, the Instruction, and Other Duties on the Eleventh Day of the Soma Sacrifice during the Fourth Day of the Tretā Age," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 248 [Author:
Chapter 249 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
On the fifth day, O Rādhā, in the morning, I shall explain the entire procedure for the subsequent Soma sacrifice, which Lomaśa performed.
On the twelfth day, at the commencement of the Brahma-time, all the officiating priests [assembled].
Having awakened and bathed, and commencing the rites of the Soma-pressing,
the Adhvaryu arranged those vessels upon their respective stands;
then the Hotṛ began the recitation known as the Śastra.
And he performed the pouring out of the oblations for the *savanīya* offerings with five types:

with parched grains (*dhānā*), with flour-mash (*karambha*), with the *parivāpa* grain-offering, as well as with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*). || 4 || The Pratiprasthātṛ likewise [performed it].
Dhānā should be understood as parched barley; karamba is barley flour mixed with curds.
Parivāpa is indeed parched grain (lāja), and payasyā is considered to be āmikṣā.
Their deities are five: Indra is the first because he is green (haritvan).
Indra accompanied by Pūṣan is the second; Sarasvatī is the third;
Indra is the fourth; and Mitra and Varuṇa are the fifth deity.
Having worshipped them, he then performed the ritual procedure for the *dadhi-graha* libations.
Just as one might take excellent curd in an udumbara vessel,
he indeed offered it with an udumbara [ladle] to Prajāpati as the deity. Then, just so, he made the Adābhya cup-offering to Soma as the deity.
Having filled the vessel with either curd or milk and likewise bound it up,
and having taken three portions of the stalks of the Soma plant,
he placed them in the sacrificial cup (graha-pātra) and drew that libation five times.
Having shaken that vessel seven times, he indeed offered it as a libation.
Then, having taken the Aṃśu-graha and the Ekagraha-Soma,
and having thrown them into a stone and sprinkled them with the water of the Vasatīvarī jars.
Having pressed [the soma] with the stones and placed it in the *ādābhya* vessel,
he then offered it as an oblation to Prajāpati as the deity.
Having taken that very vessel and entered the assembly hall (*sadas*) thereafter, he remained there.
Having indeed consumed the soma juice contained in the vessel,
he then set the vessel down upon the donkey and performed the *upāṃśu* libation.
Thereupon, that which had been purchased was likewise placed in a cloth and tied up.
Having untied the *soma* and taken it all,
he should specifically divide it into two parts for the sake of the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*),
and then set aside a small portion for the sake of the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*).
In the morning, indeed for the sake of a single draught from the Soma used for praise,
having taken the Soma and placed it in the Hotṛ’s cup,
he then sprinkles it with the Vasatīvarī waters and grinds it with the pressing-stones.
Having squeezed it and extracted the juice, the Adhvaryu himself took it in his joined palms,
poured it three times into the Upāṃśu vessel, and offered it as an oblation.
This very act of drawing the Āghāra libation is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa) of the deity.
Having given that to her, they then performed the *dhārā-grahas* ending with the *dhruva*.
This is considered the great pressing (*mahābhiṣava*) of the Soma-pressing;
then the *adhvaryu* priests sat down at the place of pressing.
The Adhvaryu sat facing west in front of the pressing stones,
and the Pratiprasthātṛ sat facing north on the south side.
The Hotṛ sat facing east on the west side, and [the Maitrāvaruṇa] facing south on the north side.
The Unnetṛ sat down after placing the Soma upon a stone;
having sprinkled it with the Vasatīvarī waters and ground it, they should press it in that manner.
Dakṣa, having performed this same procedure three times, [proceeded].
Having placed crushed pieces of the Soma plant into the *ādhāvanīya* vessel and a clay bowl,
and having squeezed them to extract the juice,
he took that juice in another vessel and cast the husks aside.
Then, having taken a navel made of goat's hair, fashioned to the measure of a span,
and having spread it out upon a vessel of a *droṇa* capacity over a piece of purifying cloth, the Udgātṛ priests thereafter held it up. (26–27)
The Unnetṛ, having taken the Soma juice from the Ādhavanīya vessel with a ladle,
poured it into the Hotṛ’s cup;
he should draw it out in such a way that the juice falls upon the fringe of the straining cloth.
Then, having poured the stream from the flowing vessel into the cup named Antaryāmin,
the Adhvaryu offered the remnant as the Antaryāma libation;
and having collected the residue along with the remainder in the Āgrayaṇa vessel, he performed the pouring together.
Then, after that, the Guru himself deposited the remaining portion of the cup into the fire for the deity named Indra; he personally offered that oblation.
Thereafter, they prepared the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.
Having drawn the Aindravāyava cup from the stream,
the Guru then wiped it on the outside with the fringe of the *pavitra* filter and set it down upon the *khara* mound.
In this same manner, he [prepared] the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Śukra, and the Manthin juice.
He placed the Āgrayaṇa, as well as the Āgneya, Aindra, Saurya, and the Ukthya, along with the Dhruva, in due order upon the mound (khara) according to the Gṛhya ritual;
and after the drawing of the Dhruva cup, he performed the cessation of the stream.
And from the Havirdhāna shed, five officiating priests went outside.
They crept forward, holding onto one another, for the sake of the Bahiṣpavamāna chant.
First the Adhvaryu, and then the Prastotṛ followed, holding onto his girdle.
Having grasped the handle, the Pratihartṛ then followed after the Udgātṛ;
thereafter the Brahman and the Sacrificer followed along with the handle.
Having gone to the site of the Cātvāla pit and sat down, they released the handle.
The Udgātṛ, the Prastotṛ, and the Pratihartṛ—these three were indeed at that time purified by the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra;
by that [purification], the two Aśvin cups became fit for the sacrifice. || 38-39 ||
Having performed the rite for the Aśvins once the Āgnīdhra fire has been ignited among the hearths (dhiṣṇya),
the Adhvaryu, having set down the cup, places it upon the mound (khara) from the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa).
Then, he performs the rites beginning with the presentation of the sacrificial portions (phalīkaraṇa) for the Savanīya offering.
After that, for the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), which concludes with the offering of the omentum (*vapāyāga*),
the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Sacrificer, and the Sadasya enter the sacrificial hall (*sadaḥsthala*) and likewise take up the vessels such as the *graha* and *camasa*.
Then, having held the ritual substances, Brahmā, acting as the patron (*yajamāna*),
performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) with the respective mantras for all the vessels; thereafter,
he proceeded by the northern path of the *havirdhāna* shed and likewise by the eastern path.
Having entered the *sadas* through the door, they sat down each in his own place. Then they performed the ritual procedure for the *savanīya* oblations,
and likewise carried out the distribution of the *dhārā-grahas* in the prescribed manner.
Having performed the rites ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
the Adhvaryu proceeded to draw the three portions (*trigrāha*) for Indra-Vāyu, Mitra-Varuṇa, and the Aśvins.
After the Adhvaryu had drawn the portion for Indra-Vāyu, [the ritual continued] thereafter.
The Pratiprasthātṛ,

having taken the Aindravāyava and Nigrābhya portions from the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa) into the Āditya vessel, offered them together; subsequently, he poured their mutual juices into the Āditya vessel.
The Guru gave the vessel containing the *sampāta* residue to the Hotṛ;
in this manner, the performance and the pouring out of the subsequent two cups were carried out.
Then the Unnetṛ [took] the cup belonging to the Acchāvāka as well.
Having set aside the nine *camasa* vessels there, he filled them as well:
for the *hotṛ*, the *brahman*, the *udgātṛ*, and likewise the *yajamāna*;
for the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* and the *maitrāvaruṇa*.
Likewise, nine cups for the Potṛ and the Agnīdhra were filled;
having caused the Soma juice to flow from the *kalaśa* vessel by means of the *pariplavā* ladle,
they then took Soma from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel into those cups.
Having filled the *droṇakalaśas* and placed [the contents] into the *camasa*s,
he first causes the flow that consists of the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*);
the second flow is considered to be the place for the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*).
In this manner, the entire drawing [of the soma] must indeed be performed for the purpose of filling [the vessels].
Then the Adhvaryu, having taken the Śukra vessel containing Soma,
and the Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken the Manthin vessel together with the Soma.
Facing each other well at the eastern door of the Havirdhāna shed,
standing with their own houses [behind them] at a distance of one aratni from one another,
and having followed in front of the Mantrakṛt and the Āhavanīya fire; ||56–57||

The two five-faced [offerings] became ready for the purpose of the *graha-homa*; at that time, the nine *camasādhvaryu* priests were indeed equipped with their cups (*sacamasāḥ*). Then, having gone to the location of the *āhavanīya* fire, they stood facing the east.
They prepared for the *homa* sacrifice and likewise performed the *āśravaṇa*.
They performed the *pratyāśravaṇa* and so forth; then the preceptor gave the *praiṣa*.
When the *vaṣaṭkāra* had been made by the *hotṛ* priest and the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* had been performed... [2.248.60]
Having performed the second offering, the *camasa* cups were brought to the *sadas* by the *adhvaryu* and those appointed to the *hotṛ* group for the purpose of consuming them. Then,
the *maitrāvaruṇa* and other *adhvaryu*-related priests filled the *camasa* cups.
Bringing [the oblation] for the sake of the fire-sacrifice, they quickly approached the Āhavanīya fire;
then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the offering:
"Svāhā to Indra as the deity! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!"
The Pratiprasthātṛ performed the offering of the remnants upon the embers with the mantra,
"Svāhā to Rudra. Then the Adhvaryu, having finished the cup,
offered oblations in succession, saying, "Svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa."
All the Adhvaryu priests offered their respective goblets, saying:
"To Indra, to the Maruts, to Tvaṣṭṛ, and to Agni, Svāhā! Obeisance!
Thereafter, they indeed consumed the remnants from those goblets.
Then the Acchāvāka also indeed consumed the cup;
thereafter, the two performed the ritual procedure for the Ṛtu-grahas.
Then the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ offered the auspicious oblations.
Svāhā to Indra Mādhava and to the Maruts Mādhava;
svāhā to Tvaṣṭṛ Śukra and to Agni Śuci;
svāhā to Indra Nabhas and to Mitra-Varuṇa Nabhasya. 68–69.
Svāhā to Draviṇodas for food; svāhā to Draviṇodas for strength;
svāhā to Draviṇodas for the month of Sahas; svāhā to Draviṇodas for the month of Sahasya.
Svāhā to the Aśvins for the heat; svāhā to Gṛhapati for the cold season.
Then the consumption of the *camasa* cups took place according to the prescribed rule.
Thereafter followed the recitation of the *śastra* and the chanting of the *pratigara*:
"O Adhvaryu, *śoṃsāva-ūm*; *śoṃsāmoda-iva*."
"Oṃ mo3thāmoda iva, othāmoda iva.
Reciting the text beginning with "Oṃ othāmoda iva," the Adhvaryu priest then performed the Nārāśaṃsa oblation.

"To Indra and Agni, this Svāhā! To the ancestors, Svāhā! Homage! (74). Having thus performed the Nārāśaṃsa rite, he recited the Prauga Śastra and offered the oblation, saying, "To the Viśvedevas, Svāhā! (75).
Then they drank from the *camasa* cups until nothing remained;
they performed the ritual procedure for the *ukthya-graha*, the oblation, and the consumption of the entire contents;
and they carried out everything, including the washing and the placing [of the vessels] upon the mound (*khara*).
"Oblation to Mitra and Varuṇa! Likewise, oblation to Indra and Agni!

(77). Having thus performed the rites for the officiating priests up to the conclusion of the *sādana* ritual, they completed the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*) and then went out from the pavilion. (78)
And at midday, they performed the Mādhyandina pressing;
having performed everything just as in the morning, they carried out the pouring of the streams [of Soma], saying:
"To Śukra, to Manthin, and to Āgrayaṇa—Svāhā! Adoration!"
They sang the *pavamāna* hymns and then performed the *dadhi-yāga* (curd-sacrifice).
They made the consumption [of the offerings] at the place of sacrifice and performed various rites;
the patron of the sacrifice also gave the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Cows, horses, mules, donkeys, goats, and sheep;
sesame, beans, rice, barley, elephants, clothing, and gold (8.2);
indeed, one's entire possession including the kingdom and so forth, as well as daughters, houses, and gardens.
Then, at that sacrificial festival, the sacrificial fees were bestowed by the king.
Thereupon, indeed, the ritual movement for the Marutvatīya cups took place;
the Adhvaryu priest performed the Vaiśvadeva offerings and the five oblations.
Having offered the oblation, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ performed the consumption [of the portion].
They performed the fire-offering and the ritual shaking, saying: "Svāhā to Indra accompanied by the Maruts!
Svāhā to the Pitṛs of the thighs! Salutation and Svāhā to Mahendra!"
"Oblation to Agni and Indra, svāhā! And oblation to the Red One, svāhā! Homage! (86).
Having performed the ritual observance of the Ukthya sacrifice, the recitation of the five stotras, and the concluding oblation at the end of the Sava ceremony, they then went outside. (87)
They also performed the third libation, the oblation, and the consumption [of the soma], saying:
"Svāhā to the Ādityas! Homage! This is milk, curds, and Soma.
Then they proceeded with the Arbhavapavamāna chant.
They kindled the sacrificial fires, concluding with the consumption of the *iḍā* offering.
(89) Having performed the offerings of the *savanīya* oblations, the Adhvaryu priest indeed performed the single *sakṛddhoma*, and thereafter he performed another *homa*. (2.248.90)
The *camasins* dedicated [the offerings] to their respective ancestors and established them there;
then he performed the *homa* for Savitṛ and the *viśvedevas*. Following that, the consumption [of the remnants] took place, and indeed the sacrifice of the *saumya-caru* proceeded.
He offered as an oblation a *caru* of boiled rice grains cooked without being drained,
saying, "Svāhā to Agni Patnīvat! and the Guru caused the *Prakha* chant,
accompanied by the twenty-one-fold hymn (*stoma*), to be sung.

They also offered oblations from the cups, saying "Svāhā to Vaiśvānara Agni" and "Svāhā to the Maruts," followed by the ritual consumption. Thereafter, they performed the distribution of the Hāriyojana cup.
The Unnetṛ priest offered the Soma juice mixed with parched barley and other ingredients (95).
Others likewise smelled [the remnants], as did the wives and the Jāyā.
He performed the Yajus-homas and other such rites, as well as the expiatory homas (96).
Then, for the patron of the sacrifice, they performed the Viṣṇukramaṇa and other rites;
having thus completed the ceremonies at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana) as well as the meals, all the great lords and the people dwelling at the sacred ford (tīrtha) carried out these acts. 97.
And from that, the final purificatory sacrifice (avabhṛtheṣṭi) took place.
The sacrificer, together with his wife, and the other officiating priests and people, having taken up the Soma vessels upon the royal throne and having grasped the *jīṣaka*, [proceeded]. 98–99.
Singing the melodies of the Sāmaveda, they went to the water's edge;
there, they offered portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) to Agni and Varuṇa.
They performed four fore-offerings (prayāja) and likewise two after-offerings (anuyāja).
"I offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) to Varuṇa; indeed, salutations to the water! (101).
Having thrown the *ṛjīṣa* and other remnants into the water, the king and his wives bathed, as did others; they also bowed down to the Sun. (102).
Having assembled at the entrance of the hall, they performed the *udayanīya* sacrifice;
thereafter followed the *ānubandhya* fruit-sacrifice and the *āmikṣā-yajña*.
Having offered the appropriate oblation (*bali*) with the words "Svāhā to Mitra and Varuṇa," [they proceeded].
Then the sacrificer, having had his hair, beard, nails, and body hair shaved,
and having bathed according to the ritual procedure, [worships] the five [deities]:
Dhātṛ, Anumati, Ākāśī, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū.
Having worshipped those deities with clarified butter,
he likewise performed the Udavasānīya sacrifice, which has an eight-potherd sacrificial cake (aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa) as its substance;
and having offered the Agnihotra at night with the mantra "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," he continued his practice.
Then the sages made an exception regarding the Soma sacrifice.
At that time, the king, accompanied by his wife, partook of the Soma drink,
and all the performers of the sacrifice took their meals at the ritual.
Thus, O Rādhikā, on the twelfth day,
the Soma sacrifice was completed during the night; Yajñanārāyaṇa himself appeared before the king and granted him a boon.
"May there be well-being for you always, O King; at the end, may you attain the state of liberation.
"And establish me here in this palace in the form of an image of Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhikā, that king quickly had a temple constructed.
There, Yajñanārāyaṇa, accompanied by his sacrificial wife, was installed according to the prescribed rites; thus that very sacred site became known as Yajña-tīrtha.
Likewise, Soma-tīrtha came to exist there, bestowing the fruit of sacrifice through its ritual bathing.
Indeed, in the northeast corner of Aśvapaṭṭasara lies a purifying place.
There, King Aśvapāṭala received from the hand of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa a Vaiṣṇava necklace and received the mantra from Lomaśa. (113–114)
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Then, having worshipped the Lord of gods and given gifts in every way, O Rādhikā, the king departed happily for his own kingdom.
Other sages, deities, and others departed for their own respective regions.
(11.6) There, through giving, drinking water, immersion, eating, and even through worship, one may attain heaven; in the end, one shall go to the imperishable state. (11.7)

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Savana, the Midday Savana, the Subsequent Savana, the Full Oblation, the Concluding Bath (Avabhṛtha), the Sacrifice, and the Expiation," in the second section, the Tretā Continuum, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa during the Soma sacrifice.
