Chapter 249 [Author:
Chapter 250 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rādhikā, everyone there indeed fell asleep;
having performed their ablutions and worship on the thirteenth lunar day, they attained awakening.
In the assembly, the sage Lomaśa indeed instructed all embodied beings.

Sacrifices performed with faith are fruitful, while those lacking faith are devoid of fruit. (2) In this world, sacrifices become fruitful through clarified butter, milk, curd, soma, and fruits, as well as by the final oblation and, above all, by faith. (3)
Those who were unable to participate in that sacrifice,
however, indeed crossed over by means of the sprinkling on the tail, or by the consecration, or even by the dust of the feet;
having made Faith their wife through the vow of perfect truth.
The sacrificer who worships Īśa certainly crosses over [saṃsāra], there is no doubt.
Having made the deity the object of his worship, he who performs sacrifice with constant faith and with a disposition of total surrender through the rite of offering,
that performer of sacrifice certainly crosses over.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is always pure and brings satisfaction to the gods.
All rivers are Sarasvatīs; all mountains are meritorious.
For the embodied soul established in Brahman, the entire earth is the abode of Hari.
Faith, when nourished by one, in turn nourishes that person.
But he who destroys faith in the Dharma—faith, once destroyed, destroys that person—even as the virtuous, full of faith, perform the expansion of sacrifice. (8–9)
For she is the progenitor from whom every fruit is produced.
One who is mature in knowledge, mature in mind, and possesses faith in the Divine is protected by Him.
Hari Nārāyaṇa never abandons one who is mature in faith.
One who lacks faith in the gods is not worthy of offering oblations. (11) And food from one who does not offer oblations must never be eaten under any circumstances.
Lack of faith is the supreme sin; that which is permeated by it should certainly not be accepted. (12)
Faith is the purifier, the most excellent, the giver of cessation [from worldly existence], and the bestower of happiness;
indeed, faith is the form of the Supreme Brahman and is holy.
Faith likewise bestows Brahman, and non-violence is the giver of Brahman.

Non-violence is considered superior to all dharmas for living beings. (14) Indeed, among all sacrifices, Viṣṇu partakes of the oblation, which is milk-rice; [he is offered] milk-rice, flowers, fruits, gundra-roots, and juices as the sacrificial offering. (15)
One who possesses pure intent becomes a purifier and a source of satisfaction for Viṣṇu;
indeed, all things such as medicinal herbs are sacred and worthy of the gods.
One should sustain the body with medicines in such a way that it does not become emaciated.
One should always satisfy the sacrifice with bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like.
Faith is indeed the mother, the means for attaining all fruits;
non-violence is her sister, for both of them grant a vision of the Divine.
A mother who always benefits her child must never be killed;
non-violence is the supreme dharma, and one’s own duty is the protection of one’s mother.
Who indeed could ever be happy after killing his mother, the very embodiment of faith?
The mother is the cause of the body; she is one's constant refuge through her maternal care.
Even a virtuous man, though bereft of fortune, seeks his home;
and even a child, accompanied by sons and grandsons, turns toward his mother. (2.249.20–21)
Or, if the mother protects the embryo at an improper time,
then he reaches old age accompanied by suffering and defects.
At that moment, when he is separated from his mother, the world appears empty to him.
There is no support equal to a mother anywhere upon the earth.
(23) There is no refuge equal to a mother; she is the beloved vessel for one's life.
Because she sustains [the child] in her womb, she is called *dhātrī*; because she gives birth, she is indeed the *jananī*. (24)
Ambā is so called because she nourishes the limbs; she is the mother who bestows honor upon her child.
She is faith (*śraddhā*) and the nurse (*dhātrī*) within the womb of heaven, and among the divine beings, she is the progenitor.
She is Ambā because she bestows the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), and she is the mother because she grants liberation (*mukti*).
"One who desires heaven should sacrifice"—this is considered the sacrifice performed with faith.

Herbs, sacrificial fuel, trees, creepers, clarified butter, milk, curd, the oblation, the earth, the directions, faith, time, the Ṛg verses, and the Yajus formulas [are the materials of sacrifice]. (26–27)
In the sacrifice, Viṣṇu is indeed pleased by the Sāman chants, the sacrificer, the fire, the seventeen-limbed ritual,
and by offerings of clarified butter, milk, curd, cow-dung, curds mixed with whey, fruits, juices,
and faith during the rite.
Sacrifice originates from the Brahmin and is dedicated to the offering to Brahman.
The entire world follows sacrifice, and sacrifice follows the world.
"Om" is the name of Brahman; [so too are] Namaḥ, Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ. (2.249.30)
For one in whom these are employed, no fear exists;
for him, the Lord Śrīmat Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the bestower of fearlessness.
Kāṃbhareya Hari is manifest, higher than the highest Akṣara.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, he was beheld by you during the sacrifice.
That very Lord indeed knows the fruit of all sacrifices;
permitted by his mother, he surely bestows the fruit in its entirety.
Therefore, one should sacrifice and cause others to sacrifice for Yaśas, who is dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For one who sacrifices according to the prescribed rite, there is eternal heaven, which is beyond the imperishable. Neither this world nor the next is certain for those who do not sacrifice.
"Nor is there any dharma here on earth that leads to a higher state for those who do not perform sacrifices.
Aśvapāṭala said: "How is this world surpassed, and how is the next world attained?"
"How can Dharma be the giver of a [favorable] destination on earth? Tell me that here. Śrī Lomaśa said:
"For one of virtuous conduct, who has conquered the self and is impartial toward all embodied beings..."
This world is considered the most excellent for one who performs all acts of honor;
and for the devotee who perceives Brahman everywhere, who delights in the worship of Brahman, and who is established in Brahman, the next world shines forth. (37–38)
For one who is worthy of universal faith, who is endowed with all forms of assistance,

and whose dharma consists of non-violence and truth, that very dharma shall indeed become the means to the ultimate goal. For one who is free from the state of illusion and has attained the state of the Imperishable (akṣara).
Indeed, for one who has taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman, those three are held in the palm of his hand.
This very Upaniṣadic knowledge is the means of union with Hari, by which the Supreme Brahman is attained—the imperishable and eternal abode. (2.249.40–41)
Brahman is attained through knowledge, and knowledge is considered to be the Upanishad;
Brahman is reached through devotion, and devotion is considered to be the Upanishad.
Through the dharma of the Bhāgavata, Kṛṣṇa is attained—he alone is that [Upanishad].
If, through detachment and by means of [overcoming] suffering, one goes toward Hari, that by which residence [in Him] is produced is considered an Upaniṣad;
it is that by which residence in the abode of the Lord is brought about. (43–44)
A pure intention is indeed considered the cause, the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) for attaining Brahman.
If a child goes to the temple out of a desire for favor,
that very desire for favor becomes his secret doctrine for being in the presence of Hari.

That by which the presence of Hari may be attained— whether through ritual action, or even through an enemy, or through desire, or even through effort— that is considered the Upaniṣad. Whether by sacrifice, or by service, or by a collective purpose, or even for one's own sake.
Whether by means of charity or even through desire, proximity to the gods is attained;
indeed, whatever [means] achieves this is considered on earth to be the Upaniṣad. Association with the virtuous, which brings about the attainment of Brahman, is truly supreme.
And that is proclaimed as the Upaniṣad which grants Hari to those who associate with the virtuous.
Here, for women, merely listening to the narrative bestows the yoga of Brahman;
and that Upaniṣad must be understood by which one may meet Nārāyaṇa.
If affection, devotion, meditation, conduct, and even passion lead to the attainment of Brahman, then all of these are considered by the Upaniṣads to be valid paths.
For the cowherd women, it was attained through desire; likewise for the brahmins, it was attained through sacrifice.
For the cowherds, [the attainment was] through loving-kindness; for the Daityas, even through hatred;
for Sudāmā, through greed; and for the elephant, for the sake of his livelihood.
For Dhruva, it was through austerity; and for Prahlāda, through resolute conviction. (52–53)
Due to Pūtanā’s state of enmity and Nārada’s act of chanting, Hari was attained by them both.
Thus, by whatever cause whatsoever Hari may be reached,
that cause is considered to be the Upaniṣad, which brings about the attainment of Brahman.
Knowledge, devotion, or action, contemplation, or surrender—whatever is proclaimed in the Upanishads by which Brahman is indeed attained;
O Aśvapaṭṭala! [is attained] through sacrifice to Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. 55–56.
Indeed, you have attained here this divine form, beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Right here, the Soma sacrifice and the Upaniṣad are established as eternal for you.
In His grace toward living beings, the Lord intends that there may be union with Him somewhere.
In some cases there may be a connection through effort, and in others through birth;
that is considered by those yogins to be the cause of the pure Upanishad.
Just as all actions reach their completion in their fruit, [so too does this yoga]. 58–59.
The fruit [of action] lies in tranquility; that [tranquility] is completed in enjoyment, and that [enjoyment] is completed in Brahman alone.
The state of Brahman is completed in the Supreme God, the Parameśa.
Yogis know Him, they behold Him, and they go toward Him.

Free from dualities, free from bonds, liberated, pure, and stainless; having reached the ultimate goal in liberation, devoted to Brahman and dwelling in Brahman; free from delusion and become one with Brahman—their destiny is eternal. (6.1–6.2)
Free from worldly undertakings, steadfast, pure, and identified with Brahman,
those who seek no untruth gratify the Supreme Lord, the God, with sacrifices.
For one who has become the self of all beings, seeing both himself and others as such—
The devotee, possessing the eyes granted by Him, proceeds along that path.
Having secured the closure of the nine gates and opened the heart, he who has traveled by way of Brahman finds his abode in the house of the Supreme Brahman. (64–65)
The Agnihotra, the Paurṇamāsa, the Darśa, as well as the Prayājas,
the Sviṣṭakṛt, the Anuyājas, and the Pitṛyajña consisting of subsidiary sacrifices;
the Cāturmāsya, the Vaiśvadeva, the Sākamedha, and the Vāruṇa.
The Soma sacrifice, the Savana, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi,
the Avabhṛtheṣṭi, the Uktha, the Ṣoḍaśī,
the Atirātra, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Vājapeya, and the Viṣṭuti.
The Vāyavya, the Śatarudrīya, the Vāsava, the Rājasūya, the Sautrāmaṇi, the Aśvamedha, the Puṃmedha, the Sarvamedha, the Gomedha,
the Brahmamedha, and whatever other sacrifices are devoted to ritual action.
Those sacrifices which are devoted to knowledge, those devoted to austerity, and those devoted to ritual materials; likewise,
those acts of hospitality and services, as well as gifts and priestly fees— all these, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, become bestowers of liberation for those who follow the path of Brahman.
Whether [rites] have been performed or not, nothing remains to be instructed for him;
Hari has been propitiated by him, and thus everything that is to be attained has indeed been attained.
Even when sacrifices have been performed and the gods have been gratified with libations.
If it is performed without Kṛṣṇa as its light, it does not grant liberation.
Therefore, among those sacrifices, Kṛṣṇa is the eternal dharma; the saintly ones are practitioners of Brahman-yoga who block the external gates [of the senses].
Those seeking immortality satisfy that Kṛṣṇa in all sacrifices.
Having closed every other door, one should open wide the door of Brahman.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Lomaśa, tell me how the doors are to be closed; and after they have been closed, what further duty must be performed or what fruit will result? Śrī Lomaśa said:
The supreme nectar exists within the treasury of Brahman, protected by the Self;
yet, with its door covered, it goes elsewhere and becomes difficult to attain.
That which is called "playing" is indeed [running] elsewhere with the hands and feet.
The desire is base, and the seat is elsewhere in the courtyard (78).
The description concerns another object, the metaphorical representation is mixed with worldly things;
the tasting is by others through favor, and the smelling is of a body moist with rain (79).
Touching is the result of subtle illusion; hearing is the fruit of agitation; reflection is the cause of the sense of "mine"; and awakening leads to the thought, "May there be much for me.
Contemplation results in the notion, "I possess two chowries," while the realization "I am" leaves no room for one such as I.

Thus, while all this nectar flows incessantly both in the waking state and even in dreams, the vessel will surely become empty. Therefore, the wise person who possesses discernment must provide a lid for it. 81–82.
One should not gamble with dice, nor run through muddy ground;
one should not desire low land, nor sit in the square of delusion. One should not describe another with envy, nor should one fashion a likeness [of another].
One should not relish anything other than the offering, nor should one smell anything pertaining to the body.
One should not touch a soft bed, nor hear nor speak anything else.
One should perform meditation upon the Lord of Māyā, and [the thought] "May there be Brahman for me" should be the awakening.
"May my reflection be nectar, and may I dwell within it"— in this way,
one should indeed perform the protection of the door, which is the form of Śrī Hari.
Just as terrestrial water increases through rainwater, so too does the self expand.
Likewise, through protection, one's own nectar increases by means of the protection of Brahman.
Just as terrestrial water dries up and vanishes due to the heat of summer, so too, when the gates [of the senses] are closed, one's own nectar reaches dissolution [within]. (87–88)
One should indeed not go about in vain in this world, nor should one ever take anything in vain;
one should not indulge in desire in vain, nor should one sit down anywhere in vain.
One should certainly not utter speech that is devoid of truth and devoid of Kṛṣṇa.
One should not look upon form in vain when it is devoid of Kṛṣṇa; indeed, such looking is useless.
One should not accept pleasant taste that exceeds what is necessary for the maintenance of the body.
One should not take up fragrance in vain, but should practice that which is filled with the breath of the Lord.
One should never engage in useless touch except for the touch of Hari; one should never apply one's ears to useless things except for the hearing of the Supreme Lord.
One should direct one’s reflection toward Śrī Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Consort of Kamalā.
One should awaken the Lord of Śrī and always contemplate Śrī Hari.
"I am indeed His very self (ahantā), and never that of another.
Thus, everything belongs to the Lord of Lakṣmī, and I am of the nature of Him. (92–94)
"May my abiding in all the senses be truly within Narayana, the Supreme Lord"—
thus should the guarding of the gates be understood by one seeking immortality;
for him whose gates are all [guarded] or who is free from worldly diversion.
The attainment of Hari occurs for him; he drinks from the ocean of immortality.
The nectar of the eternal belongs to the devotee whose gates are guarded. All sacrifices are completed by one who seeks the eternal state of immortality.

Of what use are his austerities, hardships, sacrifices, and other such afflictions, when the nectar of Nārāyaṇa has indeed been acquired and held within his heart? O Aśvapāṭala! Having recognized that your own nectar is contained within your treasury, [why do you seek it elsewhere]?
One should not discharge [semen] through an improper path, nor should one lead it to futility.
(99) Just as clothing is used according to need, and a grass seat according to need, so too is a pillow used according to need, and food taken only for the sake of sustenance. (2.249.100)
Abandoning delight in dualities, one should always resort to the inner delight;
abandoning the external caravan, one should take refuge in the inner caravan.
By that means, the excellent traveler shall reach the further shore of the long path.
"In this very way, O Rādhikā, Lomaśa spoke this nectar to the king.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge Given by Lomaśa to King Aśvapāṭala, Consisting of the Secret Nectar of Faith and the Upaniṣads," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 251 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having heard Śrī Lomaśa again, Aśvapāṭala asked about the path of renunciation that likewise yields immediate fruit. 1.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Great Sage, tell me here: what is the direct perception and what is the fruit that arises through the path of renunciation?
And what is it that you yourself perceive most directly as you practice here?

Indeed, equality is observed among all beings in the realm of direct perception. (3) Just as you experience both sorrow and joy here, so too are your sense objects identical to those of all embodied beings. (4)
"Among all those who are equal, what is directly perceived as being free from affliction?
For what superiority do you possess merely by being a householder?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
The path of renunciation is indeed centered on Hari; what else is there to be renounced?
This renunciation, consisting of the offering of one's all to Hari, is the most excellent of all.
By that very act, one’s own true nature is indeed directly revealed through the vision granted by Him.
And by the grace of the Supreme Lord, may there be both the fruit [of liberation] and personal happiness.
(7) I worship the manifest Bālakṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā. (8)
He who is indeed most directly perceived here by both the eye and the mind,
that very one is the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī, abiding within the Self alone.
He is the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Master of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, and the Supreme Sovereign.
He who is fond of the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the husband of Brahmapriyā, the Lord of the Self, the Lord of Knowledge, the Sovereign; the Lord of Liberation, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of the Abode—the Master Hari.
"O King, he is most directly evident to me here; look upon him.
O King, I experience joy and sorrow like the costumes of a drama.
Even though the senses are the same and the body is the same,"
Nevertheless, although the worldly activities such as grasping and so forth are common [to both],
I always move about by means of the Supreme Self, like one possessed by a spirit.
He is the enjoyer, He is the controller, and He alone possesses the power of perception and so forth.
"Since I move about possessed by that which is the overlord of all beings, it is He alone who experiences joy and sorrow here in this body, not this embodied one.
Nevertheless, I display everything within me as if in a drama. (15)
I know it, and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya knows it likewise;
Sanatkumāra knows it, as do Nārada and Nārāyaṇa.
Śambhu himself, who is self-luminous, knows it; no one else dwelling on earth knows it.

Kapila and others exist in the water like lotuses; they are untainted, whereas we, though smeared by Kṛṣṇa, are full of defilement. Kings and others, though smeared with their own self-interest, are visibly seen to experience pleasure and pain.
We are saintly persons who have eternally taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. We have dedicated our entire being for His sake; we are absorbed in Him and distinguished by Him.
Therefore, no mental anxiety or disease exists for us, who are true saints.
That disease which exists here for those who live as proponents of the body, the senses, or the self—that disease has departed from us;
therefore, we are free from ailment.
And the root of that disease is latent desire (*vāsanā*), and that has been offered unto Nārāyaṇa.
O King, a pulse has been applied on all sides by Dhanvantari, the great physician;
because of it, we here are free from disease—be you likewise so.
Through the knowledge bestowed by Hari, we move about here within these bodies.
Impelled by that, we perform every purposeful action free from affliction;
every practice performed by that [impulse] remains entirely free from affliction.
And the wisdom bestowed by that [impulse] abandons sorrow at its very root.
Without him, knowledge arising from the pursuit of one's own self-interest destroys living beings.
Therefore, O King, we are indeed possessed of knowledge and free from affliction; for we have attained the stainless oneness with Brahman, Nārāyaṇa. (25–26)
Not having realized the truth, many have fallen under the sway of egoism; though strong in debate, they do not know such a state of freedom from affliction.
Therefore, having fallen under the sway of delusion, they become thieves of Brahman.

For those who are submerged in the cultivation of darkness, this is their ultimate destination: darkness itself. Even those who abide in the higher realms of Brahmā, though they are practitioners of the Vedic path, inevitably return to their own material nature, which consists of defects characterized by hypocrisy, falsehood, and pride. (28–29)
Thus, through internal awakening, they abandon both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
beholding the supreme goal, these virtuous ones are devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (2.250.3) Charity, study, sacrifice, progeny, continuity of lineage, and uprightness—
If, even after performing [all these], there is no liberation from that disease without Hari, then this is indeed a ground for reproach;
all such exertion is useless.
[So too is it] regarding kingdoms, women, the worlds, and the enjoyment of the objects of the body and senses.

Even if one is currently living, if everything is offered to Kṛṣṇa, that life is free from affliction— even if one is without clothing, without companions, without a vessel, and without possessions. Conversely,
even if one endures all hardships, without offering them to Kṛṣṇa, there will be decay and disease.
Therefore, O King, become free from affliction through your sons and your wives.
(34) What freedom from affliction could possibly come through dry intellectualism or ritual action?
One will certainly become free from affliction through devotion to Kṛṣṇa and through the devotion of self-surrender. (35)
The chanting of the Name is to be understood as the stainless Śabdabrahman;
having attained proficiency therein, one reaches the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, through such pure conduct, the self becomes a true Brāhmaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, he who possesses the practice of renunciation and is free from grasping;
whose perfection is achieved through mental resolve, and whose certainty is pure awakening;
for whom birth, action, and knowledge are considered pure in relation to Hari. (37–38)
One who has realized Brahman through direct perception, who is full of faith in the higher and the lower,
who has attained the company of the virtuous, whose self is purified, and who is devoted to good conduct,
contentment, and noble vows— he who practices the Bhāgavata dharma here in this world, even when it involves hardship.
For that very son of Brahmā, who reclines upon the lap of Brahmā,
there exists indeed an eternal state free from disease and devoid of affliction;
for him, nothing whatsoever remains to be accomplished regarding heaven.
There is no need for atonement for him, because he has offered his actions unto Hari.
Thus, O Brahmins, there are many kinds of people devoted to sacrificial rites—
pure, observant of vows, performing the three-fold offerings, and established in Hari.
Sacrificing day after day with sacrifices, free from the bonds of desire,
upright, tranquil, and self-controlled, they are devoted to the duties of Brahman.
For them, Brahman is the supreme dharma, and their constant aim is Brahman.
Desire is Brahman, and liberation is the eternal Brahman for these;
whether in deficiency or in excellence, their very conduct is the perpetual Brahman.
Even the disorder and the order of those for whom Brahman is the supreme beyond the supreme [is Brahman].
For those best of Brahmins whose nature is dark, there is the eternal heaven—
the supreme heaven, constant, free from affliction, and full of great bliss;
they go to that highest state, which is filled with perpetual joy.
Whether in the home, in the forest, or in the renunciant stage (*nyāsa*),
those who are established in Brahman go, O King, to the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord. Those with desires, however, are seen as gods consisting of light in heaven.
In the celestial abodes, the hosts of constellations and stars possess manifold enjoyments;
yet, being devoid of desire, they are not seen [as such], having gone to the farthest, supreme beyond.
But those who possess desire, having become pure once more, shall go to that state.
For those who are free from craving for the self of Brahmā, there is that immutable, eternal,
and supreme abode of the highest Brahman, which is stainless and free from all affliction.
For the sake of one who is subject to temporal conditions, Dharma is known as service to others.
The giver of merit bestows birth in the house of one whose character is meritorious;
and by virtue of such a meritorious birth, the attainment of merit arises for him.
Furthermore, desire devoid of passion arises for the self-realized person.
There shall be the perfection of renunciation and contentment, and wisdom shall become confident.
There shall also be the mind intent on liberation, and one shall be devoted to the dharma of Brahman.
Seeking the state of Brahman, one proceeds to the world of Brahman.
Seeking security as he goes, the weak man perishes here.
If he eats, gives, and performs sacrifices with the things he has acquired,
even his auspicious possession is not equal to the bliss of renunciation.
The ripening of karma is indeed the body; the ripening of knowledge is dispassion.
The ripening of devotion is Brahman-hood, and the ripening of Brahman is the supreme state.
Compassion, forgiveness, contentment, truth, peace, and non-violence.
Uprightness, modesty, forbearance, and the abandonment of pride and arrogance;
association with the virtuous, a spirit of devotion, service to the good, and worship of the gods—these are the paths to Brahman; by means of these, one attains the supreme state. (58–59)
The state to which the virtuous go is called the supreme goal.
Saṃsāra is the aggregate of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), while contentment is liberation (*apavarga*).
O King, even when the group of senses is in a state of equilibrium, one who possesses equanimity remains free from disease.
"These [qualities] have been described here; they bring about freedom from affliction.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"In this world, embodied beings constantly pursue virtue, wealth, and pleasure."
"Some desire liberation; therefore, these three are indeed powerful.
Among them, by resorting to which one does an embodied being obtain a distinguished gain?
What is the fruit, and of what nature is it? O Lomaśa, show me that. || 62-63 ||
Lomaśa said: O King, formerly, in a previous kalpa, I went into the interior of a forest known as Puṣkarāraṇya; there, a brahmin named Viśālika [dwelt].
He, an ascetic who was weak, poor, and full of passion, offered me worship with fruits, water, and other offerings.
Then I asked him about his welfare, and he spoke to me.
"Poverty brings suffering in this world; therefore, O Lomaśa, dispel it!
(66) Then, taking him with me, I went toward the northern direction through the sky to the divine city of Kubera, desiring wealth. (67)
Kubera welcomed him and gave him wealth as much as he desired;
Viśālika was pleased and took the treasure-trove of riches.
Then, in his own auspicious city, during the night, by the King of Wealth—
"Stay here in this beautiful palace and sleep; you two shall be protected.
I know everything that was seen by the Brahmin while you were asleep—that great marvel, indeed full of impurity—listen to it. (2.250.70)
He saw some people rich in dharma with pure minds;
some overcome by desire, devoted to dance and song;
and some adorned with ornaments made of gold, gems, jewels, and wealth.

As they were returning toward their own city, taking wealth from Kubera, an earthquake occurred repeatedly, causing the destruction of living beings; those who had gone into the pits of the earth were indeed crushed by the soil and died. (72–73)
The messengers of Yama arrived there to lead away the many who had died;
they led away those full of desire, having bound them with firm fetters.
They also led away the wealthy, even without any such bonds.
Then he beheld Desire, Anger, Greed, Fear, and Pride;
as well as Sleep, Drowsiness, Great Sloth, and Sin—standing there, enveloping those [heavenly realms], obstructing the paths to heaven, and bestowing fear and the sufferings of Yama. (75–76)
The Brahmin saw those very same men, who were known as hell-beings and stood all around him, merged into his own body.
Having seen these faults in the dream, the Brahmin was indeed seized with fear.
At that moment, the gods arrived specifically to lead away the righteous;
having honored the deceased ascetics—who were equal to deities—by means of celestial chariots of auspicious splendor and great opulence, they indeed led them away. (78–79)
Beholding those righteous ones, joyful and having attained the divine worlds, that brahmin reflected: "Austerity is the supreme wealth; happiness is its fruit.
Wealth, however, is fraught with faults, and desire is filled with impurity. (2.250.80)
For the sake of hell, those two—wealth and desire—are not givers of peace.
Furthermore, desire is essentially harmful and its nature is suffering;
asceticism and virtue lead only to heaven. Therefore, I practice virtue.
Then, by the power of Lomaśa’s compassion, I shall practice the Dharma;
having obtained his grace alone, I shall attain the bliss born of the Bull (Śiva).
Or else, [I shall obtain] the earth filled with jewels or a great collection of gems.
"Having reached the gateway of the world of Yama, I shall never return.
Having spoken thus, the twice-born man left his wealth right there in the mansion at dawn,
and after paying homage to Kubera, he departed for ascetic practice.
Together with Lomaśa, he performed supreme and divine asceticism;
he was constantly devoted to the worship of the gods and always honored his guests.
Having taken refuge with Lomaśa, he subsisted on a diet of leaves.
Then he subsisted on water and subsequently became one who feeds only on air.
With divine vision, the twice-born man also saw the kings who had gone to the city of Yama,
thousands of them submerged in a pit within that hell.
By means of his ascetic power, he also beheld the denizens of hell, who were deluded by desire;
then, in an instant, that dream vanished right there for him.
Viśālākṣa quickly left his bed and approached the venerable sage Lomaśa.
He bowed down and said: "O Guru, I have seen everything that is undesirable. Desire and wealth always bring suffering in the world of Yama;
I have seen them in the city of Yama. Dharma alone is considered the bestower of heaven."
From righteousness comes the highest state, and through austerity, heaven is attained.
Here, the deities together with their celestial chariots honor those who are righteous;
they do not honor the wealthy, nor even those who are full of desire.
A fraction of happiness resides in the Dharma; I shall practice the beneficial path of the Bull (Dharma).
This wealth must not be accepted by me, for it is attended by the faults of suffering.
O Teacher, I have seen that all defects dwell within wealth.
Today I have indeed seen an earthquake in a dream;
that vision here at the commencement of wealth, which bears a great burden of sorrow,

Then there is the path of the stages (*bhūmikā*) and the path of preeminent human effort (*prādhānapauruṣī*);
thereafter is the path consisting of the divine manifestations (*vyūha*), followed by the path through superior worship (*adhikopāsanā*).
Then there is the path consisting of the cowherds and cowherdesses (*gopagopīmayī*), as well as that consisting of the personal attendants and others (*pārṣadādimayī*). (2.252.60)
She is the descent and likewise the goal whose nature is liberation;
she is the embodiment of the descent and the embodiment of Muktānikā.
Brāhmī, who is the beloved form of Brahmā, also arises as the goal.
By the power of worshiping Hari, both the unchanging state and the goal extending up to Brahman are attained;
yet the Supreme Brahman is not born.
He alone is the one Supreme Self, the Lord who dwells within all as the inner controller. (62–63)
He is the incarnation of the Supreme Brahman, known as the Supreme Lord;
he is the highest of the highest among millions of Nārāyaṇas.
O Aśvapāla, whenever an embodied being here takes recourse to unrighteousness, [he manifests].
Then he goes to the womb of an animal or an insect, or even to the state of an immobile being;
or he undergoes a low birth as a demon or a human.
Thereafter, having reached the realm of Yama, he indeed proceeds according to what remains of his karma.
Whether one's birth be impure or pure, the performer of dharma is liberated after a long time; however, one who follows the path of unrighteousness is never released from a low birth.
But he who meditates on Brahman, seeking Kṛṣṇa with a pure heart, [is liberated].
One attains that which is pure, eternal, the imperishable Brahman, and supreme.
All creation proceeds from the world of Hari, and into Him alone it enters.
Worship Him alone, who dwells within, who is perceptible, and who is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
Weave a thread for as long as you have need, like a spider with its web;
swallow it back again when your task is finished, yet remain persistent within the net.
When you have cast off the snare of delusion, reveal yourself anew.
Abandoning even that which is righteous, reveal something else that bestows happiness.
Having abandoned both the net and the repository of the net, O Lord of the Earth, become happy;
enjoy infinite joy within the eternal Brahman.
The knots of the heart here exist based upon latent impressions (vāsanā).
Once destroyed by the realization of Brahman, they do not arise again as something new.
Freed from the bondage of these knots, one proceeds to the eternal Brahman.

The wise and virtuous who have taken refuge in Hari do not indeed suffer at all. (74) But those worlds, possessed of delusion, hope, and the like, and those who perceive only the past, the future, and even what is yet to be, suffer indeed from the waves [of worldly existence]. (75)
The commencement, the conclusion, and the emergence of results—whether equal or unequal—for those actions, as well as their suffering or agitation, do not arise for one who does not understand them.
The destinies of actions are diverse: some are rich in wealth, others are destitute of wealth.
Those with very firm bodies, or those afflicted by unwholesome diseases, or those deprived of food;
the poor, or those with many sons, or a virtuous wife whose husband is wicked; kings who are childless, or gods oppressed by Daityas and other such beings. (77–78)
The learned are devoid of honor, and servants are lazy;
those of handsome form are malicious, and the famous are thieves.
Even those with a thirst for royal enjoyments—behold the downward pull of saṃsāra!
Those with thousands live, and those with hundreds live as well;
even the poor become lords of millions, and all live by eating food.
All go to their death, whether they are full of exertion or devoid of effort.
Having reflected upon this, O Great King, do not resort to imprisonment.
Neither kinsmen, nor gold and such wealth, nor noble lineage, nor prowess, nor wisdom, nor strength are able to protect one from suffering; therefore, one should take refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
One should always abandon that which is pleasant if it generates excitement and bestows pride.
One should always cultivate that which is pleasant if it bestows Brahman, bestows liberation, and grants peace.
Wealth and desire are great fetters that turn one away from dharma and liberation. (83–84)
Those very two, when applied in the month of Mādhava, are considered to bring about merit and liberation.
And for one who conducts himself in this manner, neither death nor even Time (Kāla) causes any affliction.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"Tell me here that by which the welfare of one who is devoid of knowledge of reality, possessed of many doubts, and has not attained certainty in this world may be secured.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
One should always serve the virtuous, the gurus, and the elders;
likewise, one should constantly worship the deities and listen to the scriptures. One must always serve one’s mother and father with sincere devotion.
Service to one's husband, service to virtuous women, receiving the blessings of those worthy of worship,
and the worship of Hari— these indeed bestow prosperity; however,
supreme liberation arises through devotion to the Supreme Lord.
Even secondary benefits arise from auspicious means;
for the virtuous, blessings of well-being are constant, being naturally characterized by generosity and merit.
Dwelling in a temple of the gods is also a blessing that bestows ultimate liberation.
The state of being Brahman everywhere and the performance of service to all;
(9.1) likewise, the honoring of gods, ancestors, guests, and dependents as a means to the highest good;
freedom from the delusion of *māyā*, contentment, and the cessation of all seeking; (9.2)
Dwelling within the inner self, meditation on the self—which bestows the supreme good—and likewise the undertaking of vows that are means to liberation;
the wealth of knowledge and steadfastness in the self—these bestow the supreme good. (93)
One should indeed desire the welfare of all and practice that which leads to universal excellence.
One should speak of the virtuous states of others with extreme praise;
one should bestow honor and encouragement upon others and perform acts of worship for them.
Devoted to honoring his own teachers and considering others worthy of honor,
intent on attaining wisdom, he always finds the highest good.
He should desire to dwell among the virtuous and cultivate straightforwardness toward the learned.
One should cultivate loving-kindness toward those of virtuous conduct, for it bestows the highest good. One should not take pleasure in dwelling where people lack spiritual excellence;
rather, one should indeed dwell where the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* prevail. (97–98)
Where there is happiness, there indeed people dwell for the sake of liberation;
liberated and free from bonds, they move about in bliss.
O King, even insects and other such creatures exert effort toward the accumulation [of merit].
Those who are unattached are happy, while those who are attached are afflicted by the ocean of suffering.
(2.252.10) A wise and discerning person seeking their own welfare should certainly not worry about their own kin, thinking, "How will they live without me? (101)
All abide under the power of karma; through karma one meets with death.
Union and separation also occur according to karma.
Death is true in every respect; for the sake of the highest good, death is auspicious.
Having performed many auspicious deeds, that death leads to further death.
He who has constructed a fortress for the sake of others but resorts to his own pit for his own benefit—
how could there be prosperity for him in this world, much less the supreme, ultimate liberation?
Therefore, O King, having abandoned negligence, devote yourself to that which leads to the supreme good. Day after day worship Kṛṣṇa, and night after night worship Hari.
Perceive your own nature as the nature of Brahman; being liberated, take birth here [in this state].

He who has no desire to remain in this world as its foremost leader, who has no regard for the maintenance of life, medicine, or recreation, and for whom sense objects are like those of one devoid of consciousness— he is certainly liberated in this state. (106–107)
Food, clothing, dwellings, and the like are to him as worn-out skins;
even the acquisition of human prosperity leads only to the piercing of his vital organs. And though his senses are intact, he possesses the nature of one who is senseless.
When there is the attainment of enjoyments such as food and the like, discernment is like a calamity.
(109) O King, this very person is liberated here and also in the hereafter;
indeed, through union with him, even other people may attain liberation. (2.252.110)
Having enjoyed the earth as sages, kings, and great emperors, they have gone to their death.
Seeing this, one becomes liberated, freed from bondage and devoid of hope.
In this world, sufferings are easily obtained, while happinesses are difficult to find.
Since those things acquired through effort perish, how could one not honor liberation?
When wealth is present, everyone on all sides exclaim "Aho! and, addressing him with auspicious words such as "O brother! or "O father!", they pay him homage. (1.12) (12)
When wealth has departed, those who are hostile are intent solely on their own interests;
or in times of poverty, they do not know where their brother is or where their father is.
How could a wise person, having understood that they are devoted only to self-interest, not become disenchanted?
Human existence is as if without essence, and life itself is fruitless.
Therefore, the dharma of the Blessed One is superior both in this world and the next;
for the dharma of the virtuous and devotion always bestow the highest good.

"O Rādhikā, thus the glorious Lomaśa instructed Aśvapāṭala in many ways; the King questioned him again. (2.17) Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, within the *Lomaśa-gītā*: the inquiry regarding the means for attaining the state of the Imperishable (*akṣara*) by Aśvapāṭala; the inquiry regarding the destination resulting from either renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) or the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*); the inquiry regarding the creation of the threefold manifestation (*sṛṣṭi-traya*); and the inquiry regarding the highest good (*śreyas*).
The two hundred and fifty-second chapter,
titled "The Determination of the Answers Given by Lomaśa," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 253.
[Author: Chapter 254.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, having heard this supreme, ultimate liberation, Aśvapāṭala—
He questioned Lomaśa again regarding liberation for the self.
Aśvapaṭṭala said:
"Tell me here once more that which is the highest good, bringing happiness both in this world and the next."
That which is to be accomplished through duty brings about ever-increasing prosperity.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
A cart carrying a heavy load for travelers proceeds with its charioteer.
For one on this earth who is intent only on the journey of maintaining the body and remains unsatisfied, hunger and thirst are the two draft-oxen; sorrow and delusion are the two wheels;
pleasure and pain are the front and back parts [of the carriage]; and latent desire resides in the middle. (3–4)

The charioteer himself, having taken up the cart, goes for the sake of profit; greedy for more than the mere cost of the journey, he reaps sixfold [the gain] here in this world. For this very reason, the driver is always distressed and knows no sleep.
Carrying countless goods repeatedly with a cart,
one becomes helpless when plundered in the forest by the thieves of the senses;
the thieves carry away entirely the wealth consisting of happiness and peace.
Therefore, the two bulls need not be guarded, nor does the cart require protection.
By abandoning these, for one whose journey is merely for the sustenance of the body, there arises happiness and peace like that of a yogi;
indeed, this occurs for the traveler who employs only what is necessary for his journey.
One should not desire more than [necessary] clothing, food, water, and shelter.
One should perform meritorious deeds and those rites dedicated to the gods; one should carry out acts of service for others according to one's own capacity. (2.253.10)
This human life is difficult to obtain; one should not waste it in a pit of misery.
One should strive for liberation and for the sake of excellence and worldly prosperity.
Through meritorious action, both excellence and prosperity are attained. (11)

Through vows, effort, practice, good fortune, and the blessings of the virtuous—(12)—one should not emulate the non-actions of the gods, the sages, and likewise of the great and radiant ones; yet there is no fault in them. (13)
One should never disparage the seemingly impossible deeds of the great;
with a tranquil mind, one should perform auspicious acts, for such a person perceives only what is beneficial.
One should not acquire wealth, honor, or authority through cruel deeds.
For all of that will surely result in suffering in the world of Yama.
Therefore, one should perform everything that is praiseworthy, renowned, and conducive to merit—whether it pertains to the gods, the ancestors, guests, humans, or animals. (15–16)
The virtuous great seers attain perfection through selfless action;
kings through expenditure on ritual action; and yogis through worship.
Śūdras attain it through service to women, and likewise, servants through servitude. (17)
The wise [serve] by means of the path of knowledge; artisans, by their craft and science;
(18) cows and the like, by the giving of milk; trees and the like, by the giving of fruit;
shrubs, by the giving of leaves; and creepers, by the giving of flowers. (19)
And when human beings assist one another through acts of kindness,
they indeed attain supreme perfection and proceed toward the perfection of liberation.
Even sages of firm vows, having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire, [attain this].
They attain supreme perfection by aiming for the illustrious Narayana.
Wife, self, mother, father, progenitor, son, teacher, daughter, and gods— these are to be served by one who desires the fruit of happiness.
All these are declared to be fires; that is the sacrifice, and that indeed is the office of the Hotṛ priest.
When they are satisfied, Hari, who dwells within, becomes satisfied as well.
The fruit of that satisfaction is happiness in this world and eternal bliss in the hereafter.
Whether by devotion, or by service, or by charity, or by sacrifice,
or by austerity known as *kṛcchra*, even those unworthy have attained worthiness;
Uśanas, Viśvāmitra, and Vālmīki have all attained the state of the virtuous.
Through ascetic penance, Uśanas attained the state of Śukra from Śambhu; thereafter, he was born eternally in heaven as Śukrācārya, the preceptor of the Daityas.
And the Kṣatriya Viśvāmitra indeed attained the status of a Brahmarṣi.
Both Vālmīki and Śabara became eternally liberated.
Through service to women, Śūdras attain the supreme, auspicious goal;
association with the virtuous always bestows the rise of fortune and grants great merit.
Through association with the virtuous, a person indeed becomes good;
even a single cowrie-coin earned through honest labor brings happiness, whereas gold acquired through unjust means brings suffering and the imposition of shackles. (29)
Food acquired through unjust means leads to disease and vomiting;
a field acquired through unjust means leads to fire and hell;
a woman acquired through unjust means leads to death and infamy.
Wealth acquired through unjust means leads to the destruction of one’s roots.
In ancient times, Brahmā indeed created Dharma as a son for the happiness of all creatures. All social classes who abide by their own respective duties shall indeed dwell in heaven and be happy.
Then, for the sake of their liberation, He created Dharma from His own body (3.3).
[He also created] Bhakti, so that people might attain the eternal heaven of Hari;
through those two, one may reach heaven for a long time and eventually attain the eternal state (3.4).
One should exert effort in this manner so that victory over the two heavens may be attained;
when action becomes free from mental attachment and devoid of egoistic intent, then,
having taken refuge in the Inner Controller dwelling within the heart, one should, being pure, acquire spiritual merit.

O King, for the most part, the bondage of virtuous men who are renouncers and dispassionate does not become firm, whether through the power of wisdom or through devotion. And loosening is attained through knowledge, discernment, and the study of the scriptures.
For householders or for the dull-witted, bondage becomes firm;
by taking recourse to houses, cattle, fields, and wealth,
as well as to wives, sons, and servants, their bondage becomes firm.
Attachment and aversion always increase through the delusions of sensory enjoyment and the like.
Delight indeed arises from them, and one becomes attached to vulgar pleasures and such.
For one does not know what is for the sake of the Self—neither discernment nor even liberation. (2.253.40)
But one who strives for enjoyment perishes once again;
therefore, one should remain unattached to home, wife, wealth, and the like.
Prosperity and the fruits of austerity bind people here in this world.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the Manus;
the Viśvedevas and the Aśvins, the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and great Ṛṣis;
the Kimpuruṣas and Gandharvas, as well as Vahni, Indra, Sūrya, and Candra. (2–3)
The ancestors, the world-protectors, the rākṣasas, yakṣas, and kinnaras;
the hosts and attendants, as well as the planets, gods, and dānavas;
kings, elders, teachers, perfected beings, and virtuous women.

All those who have attained perfection through austerity enjoy the fruit of their austerities. Those born into great families, prosperous and powerful, rejoice in garments of fine silk, and in ornaments of gold and diamonds. (45–86)
Vehicles, seats, and foods; drinks, women, male and female servants;
excellent and soft beds; garments upon the floors of palaces—all these desired things are entirely the fruit of those austerities.
Everything arises for the sake of enjoyment, for the sake of action, and for the sake of hell.
Likewise, discontent leads to great suffering and is the destroyer of wisdom;
it becomes a source of delusion, exhausting one through futile wandering.

For the heat-induced pleasure born of desire, lasting no longer than the flight of an arrow through contact, leads entirely to suffering and to hell. Therefore, having understood it to be momentary and full of suffering, [one should abandon it].
Even one who follows the duties of a householder should strive for liberation if he is wise.
But those men who do not aim for liberation and are instead obsessed with the pleasures of desire—
even if they perform meritorious deeds, they destroy them like swine.
They employ a worthy vessel, yet they do not realize it is equal to the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā).
Indeed, those unfortunate ones crush, wither, and destroy it—
this body which has arrived as a wish-granting gem (cintāmaṇi), though it is veiled by the illusion of a queen.
Men and women exhaust themselves, having rendered liberation fruitless.
O King, although people are by nature possessed of desire and other such impulses, they cannot be restrained; being powerless, they constantly engage in actions. || 54–55 ||
Although there are many worldly activities that bestow physical pleasure,
nevertheless, by the word of the Guru,
one should perform another activity among them called devotion (*bhakti*), which is superior, by means of which one is liberated.
Abiding by the conduct of the virtuous, even those who have fallen may desire to be uplifted; having attained merit, happiness, and tranquility, they shall reach the supreme heaven—
even if they are attached to sense-objects, provided they are free from malice.
Performing actions for the sake of Hari, the cowherd women seem to uplift themselves by ascending the path of action leading to the supreme good— the chariot of Hari.
Devoted to Him, they belong to the company of the virtuous and practice the method of total self-surrender.
They go to the ageless and imperishable abode, ascending to heaven.
Devotees are victorious everywhere, whether they possess qualities or are devoid of them;
sons, disciples, and even women who are full of devotion are indeed victorious.
The father, friend, teacher, wife, king, mother, husband, and deity—these do not find satisfaction in those who lack devotion, even if they are virtuous.
Indeed, devotion is the supreme means for pleasing them; service is auspicious.
In this matter, service and servitude are indeed the best means for attaining [the Lord].
Therefore, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa must be quickly propitiated through devotion and other such means by one who is conscious of this very body.
O King, no one can save one who has fallen into the snare of death;
while merit and demerit remain, no one can drag them away.
O King, there exists no enemy here equal to ignorance.
Under its influence, a person constantly commits terrible violence.
By that [violence], they undergo sufferings, new births, and new deaths.
Therefore, in this world, one should indeed attend upon the virtuous elders for the sake of restraining it.
Having attained wisdom, one should banish that enemy along with its retinue;
then, having cast the wish-fulfilling gem into a pit, one will certainly not fall from liberation.
Even in the state of a *caṇḍāla*, human birth is auspicious for the sake of devotion.
The human womb is indeed the most excellent means for self-preservation.
This body should not be wasted in vain through sensual enjoyments;
as long as it has not perished here, we must perform the highest good.
Having obtained such a human form, which is the seed for a kalpa,
he who hates his own liberation is considered forever deceived. Indeed,
for the sake of the world, one should perform beneficial service through acts of giving.
One should provide assistance with wealth and goods for the sake of one's family;
one should undertake appropriate business endeavors for the sake of one's sons and others;
but for one’s own sake, one should perform the supreme practice that grants liberation.

One should always perform sacrifices, giving, officiating at sacrifices, meritorious deeds, rites for the ancestors, and rites for the gods, as well as worship and service, for the sake of the highest good.
(174) Aśvapāṭala said:
"What is the root of all that is auspicious, and what, once performed, never perishes?
To where has one gone from which there is no return? Tell me this, O Guru.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Virtuous conduct, detachment, service to the good, and association with them;
receiving the blessings of the elders—these are the inexhaustible roots of all that is auspicious.
Likewise, austerity, devotion, the gift of fearlessness, and taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa [are such roots]. (76)
And this self-surrender that has been performed shall never perish.
Among all austerities involving bodily hardships, this is the supreme austerity:
indeed, the restraint of one's activity within Hari bestows direct vision [of Him]. (77–78)
That direct realization, once attained, never ceases;
and the supreme gift of fearlessness surpasses all other gifts.
For one who bestows fearlessness upon all, there is imperishable fearlessness both in this world and the next.
Even while dwelling in the midst of sense-objects, the wise man does not dwell [in them] at all;
whereas the ignorant man dwells excessively even in non-existent objects.
Sense-objects do not overpower a person who is wise and full of spiritual luster. (2.253.80–81)
Even very slight [faults] indeed surge powerfully against one who lacks wisdom;
the evil deed never at any time leaves its perpetrator.
Those who have disciplined their selves are not divided by sense objects, even by tens of millions of actions.
In this world, fear never leaves one whose self is unrefined.
Indeed, for one who is free from passion, liberation is certain because birth is no longer seen;
even while living, there is no stain upon him from the actions he has performed.

Even after death, there is indeed no enjoyment of karmas for one who has set out upon the path of devotion; his destination is considered to be the supreme abode. Elaborate paths are joined with affliction, while concise ones bestow happiness.
One should resort to the abandonment of extensive activities for the sake of others—which are fraught with suffering—and instead take refuge in what is beneficial for oneself.
(86) In this world consisting of day and night, the embodied being stands at the mouth of death;
he is swallowed constantly, and his life-span is perpetually being consumed. (87)
Bitten by the many snares of worldly attachment and by the venomous scorpions of delusion,
one who is agitated by their poisonous sting finds no happiness anywhere.
Having cut the snares, abandoned the home, and renounced all possessions, and having offered salutations—
He who proceeds upon the path of Hari shall indeed reach the further shore.
O Aśvapāṭala! This world, when in a state of well-being, seizes the portion of well-being;
yet in a state of ill-being, it remains far removed, devoted solely to its own self-interest. (2.253.90)

That which is for the sake of others is always considered superior to that which is for one's own sake; moreover, one who is devoted to the welfare of others and is patient is distinguished as even more excellent.
Furthermore, the wise man is superior to the merely patient, and the one possessed of devotion is superior to the wise man.
That indeed is the protected Brahman to be realized; rich in devotion, it always effects liberation.
It is the supreme treasury of the nectar of immortality, the highest gateway to liberation, the most excellent vehicle to heaven, and likewise the storehouse of dharma.
Indeed, in the world of humans, the devotee remains liberated like one who is already liberated.
Through association with devotees, those who are devoted indeed become destined for Brahman.
Whatever kind of person a living being serves, such a person he himself becomes.
If a virtuous person here serves the holy, he himself becomes holy.
(95) The gods are satisfied by the holy, as are the ancestors and the millions of Siddhas;
the liberated ones are satisfied by the virtuous. Therefore, one should embrace the state of being virtuous. (96)
Gods abandon from afar those people who are intent solely on their own self-interest;
gods and the liberated dwell together with the virtuous.
Thus, through union with the virtuous, one proceeds to the world of Brahmā.
"Established in the Supreme Brahman, the liberated one enjoys infinite bliss.
(98) Having thus instructed Aśvapāṭala, O Rādhikā, the illustrious Lomaśa ceased speaking; the king then questioned him once again. (99)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Inquiry Regarding Prosperity, the Inquiry Concerning the Root of Welfare and Other Matters, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 254 *Section 2: The Tretā-yuga Continuation* of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*
[Author: Chapter 255.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Aśvapāṭala inquired about the propitiation of the deities.
"And by what means does one's own delight also arise without obstacle?
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Great Sage, residence in the worlds of the gods belongs indeed to those who sacrifice with wine."

And for those who sacrifice to Brahmā, residence arises in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka). For those who sacrifice to the various Īśvaras, there is residence even in the world of those respective Īśvaras;
and by sacrificing to the abodes of the Avatāras, one shall dwell in those very abodes. (2–3)
"Please show me compassion and tell me, as well as for other luminaries, by what means the satisfaction of the gods may be achieved.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
The gods are pleased by sacrifice, by worship, and by ritual service;
likewise by offerings of food and oblations, as well as by the propitiation of mantras and their associated vows.
[They are pleased] by truth, non-violence, purity, good conduct, and virtue. (5)

O King, the gods are pleased by the surrender of one's self, as well as by honor, seeking refuge, and so forth; by the performance of difficult austerities, by giving gifts, by remembrance, by festivals, and by chanting praises and the like. (6–7)
Through self-purification, discernment, meritorious deeds,

and devotion, the gods, being pleased, bestow their own happiness pertaining to this world and to heaven. The lords and the ancestors [are satisfied] by ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and by great acts of ritual completion (*udyāpana*).
Through recitations of the *pārāyaṇa*, studies of Vedic knowledge, and the honoring of images;

through the ritual installation of deities in temples according to rule, worship and other rites, great festivals, and the duties prescribed by the Vedas—ten million Lords are thus pleased. (2.254.10)

The manifestations of Hari are attained through devotion, worship, and likewise through the service of His image and other such acts, by visiting sacred fords, observing His vows, and cultivating the proper disposition;
also by following His command, by the method of self-surrender, and by listening to His narrations and so forth. (11)
By taking refuge in no other, by being intent on the singular path,
by constant following, by mindfulness, by meditation, by service, and by a pure way of life joined with stainlessness at all times; (12–13)

Through service to His powers, His attendants, and so forth; by means of offerings, taking refuge, and other mental acts of worship such as the presentation of various amorous gestures (*śṛṅgāra*) and gifts;
and through serving and offering food to His male and female devotees. (14)
The incarnations, when pleased by devotion, bestow their respective sovereignties;
they become the givers of their respective abodes when gratified by devotion.
But the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O King— || 15–16 ||
In this matter, the Lord of Śrī is pleased solely by devotion consisting of total self-surrender;
[He is pleased] through trust, devotion, the act of entrustment (*nyāsa*), servitude, steadfast service, compliance, following after Him, choosing Him as one's own, and worship. (17)
He is pleased by selfless service, by worship, and by virtuous conduct;
indeed, He is gratified by meditation, by devotion, and by the surrender of the self.
However, contemplative realization is the great cause, for affection is what truly brings Him satisfaction.
Whether it be very small or even great, worship accompanied by meditative devotion certainly pleases Govinda, who is uniquely manifested through all modes of existence;
for by whatever disposition one may have, through constant remembrance [of Him].
Through a continuous flow of identification with Him, through the rope of divine love,
through the vision of the Self in all beings, through acts that bring satisfaction to everyone, through welcoming those who belong to Him, and through serving the saintly; ||| 21–22 ||
By pleasing the Sātvatas, by helping the distressed, by nourishing the helpless, and by being free from malice toward all embodied beings;
and by means of all the duties of the Bhāgavatas, the knowledge of reality, and self-realization. (23)
Furthermore, by engaging in discourse about him, by describing his virtues, by chanting his names,
by applying the principles of his purpose,
by functioning with a mental state absorbed in him, and by protecting the dharma of his creation; (24–25)
The Supreme Brahman is pleased by the offering of all one’s affection and possessions,
as well as by acts of charity and virtue toward the categories of sentient and insentient beings—
bestowing upon them what each requires through vows of goodness, non-malice, honesty, and the like. (26)
Through the dharmas of the virtuous and by pleasing his male and female devotees,
Hari, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, abides within all beings.
Indeed, all things— both insentient and sentient— are but manifestations of this very Kṛṣṇa.
Men, women, and all other embodied beings existing within the entire creation—
everywhere, even within the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— I serve as that very form with my intellect; may He indeed, my Lord, be pleased.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā;
the delighter of the cowherds, the beloved and most dear Lord of Kṛṣṇa;
the Lord of Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Māṇikya, Ramā, and Padmā. (2.254.30–31)
"He is the beloved husband of Brahmā’s wife, the Lord of the Liberated, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Lord of the virtuous,
the Lord of the Self, the Lord of all, and my own Lord. Thinking thus, one should indeed worship Him, the Inner Controller within all embodied beings.
With that vision, with that meditation, and through acts of offering and so forth, one should remain free from desire for rewards in every aspect of worship.
In this way, Kṛṣṇa is indeed pleased; He is honored in all embodied beings.
"I am yours; protect me, save me!"—thus one should always pray.
"O Lord Hare, O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, I am yours!
Just as You cause me to act, so do I act according to Your command. (35)
"All this belongs to you alone; there is nothing here other than you.
Everything within the range of my vision is yours, and you yourself are that very thing.
Thus is it for the embodied soul who has been permeated by the vision of the Blessed One.
Whether it be out of desire, anger, delusion, self-interest, devotion, or even for the sake of refuge, for one who has fallen into shelter and surrendered their very self,
the compassionate Lord, who is affectionate toward His devotees, is quickly pleased.

For the purpose of pleasing Him, no other means, nor material substance, nor oblations and the like are required; He is pleased with whomever [He chooses]. The thought "this is for Me and not for another" is indeed born from the grace of Hari. (2.254.40)
By mercy Kṛṣṇa is attained; by mercy one is led to the Imperishable;
and by mercy the Lord of the virtuous bestows His own abode as well.
Indeed, by the conception of being insignificant, the demigods and others do not appear at all.
Satisfied with all things through external ritual action,
the gods and other lords indeed take delight together with their devotees, as masters do with their servants, and even the controllers with their slaves. (42–43)
For those beings shrouded by ignorance, stained by the ink of envy and the like,
and dragged down by defects such as greed, neither heaven nor liberation provides satisfaction.
The wise devotee goes to the Imperishable and rejoices with the blissful ones.
Having obtained the power of one’s own chosen deity, one attains peace.
Indeed, whatever action embodied beings perform for the sake of Kṛṣṇa is divine;
devotion to Kṛṣṇa is divinity itself, as are purity and the study of sacred texts.
Vows, moral conduct, and the conquest of the senses are considered virtuous by the wise.
Quarreling, reviling, deceit, roguishness, and the like—these should be known as non-virtue; death dwells together with them.
Having examined where death resides, the wise man should abandon those [objects] and,
by taking refuge in Hari, drive death far away from this world;
then, free from the fear of death, he should practice the means for attaining the Imperishable.
O King, one should practice that by which the attainment of the abode of the Supreme Brahman may occur;
for one who conducts oneself in this manner, there is no turning back from that eternal attainment of the imperishable world. 2.254.50.
"Through devotion, one attains that abode from which there is eternal residence.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"By means of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, what indeed would liberation be like?"
O Guru, what kind of liberation might arise through the worship of Hari?
Or what kind of liberation might there be through the practice of yoga? Please tell me this.
Furthermore, what kind of liberation is considered to result even from taking refuge in mere dharma alone? (52–53)
"By the mere taking of refuge in the Guru, does that [liberation] occur or not?
O Guru, tell me: by what means is the attainment of liberation certain and free from doubt?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
The body is indeed considered a composite of the five elements, as well as the internal sense organs,
the instruments of action, the vital breaths, the three qualities (guṇas), and the subtle elements (tanmātras).
The Self (ātman) is distinct from these, eternal, conscious, and unconditioned.

Always liberated, always pure, and always awakened, dwelling eternally [in that state], through the practice of reality (tattva-abhyāsa), one shines forth with the realization: "I am not, nothing is mine, and there is no 'I'," because of the destruction of ignorance regarding the consciousness of the insentient and the sentient. (56–57)
Through the exhaustion of karma, one is indeed liberated from the body; truly liberated, one is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Indeed, having the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), one is free from produced illumination.
The self of liberation attains a state that lasts as long as its own essential nature.
Indeed, one who is not happy nor possesses a [refined] form will always be a locus of dullness.
If one worships Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord who removes dullness,
one becomes perfected in the nature of the Supreme Lord within the abode of Brahman.
As is Hari, so is the devotee; he attains residence in the same world (sālokya), equality of power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), and similarity of form (sārūpya), and enjoys all delights.
Having bathed in the lake of Brahman and having indeed assumed a body of Brahmā—
Released by Brahmā, he attains divine qualities through the will of Hari.
For there, this aggregate body caused by material nature no longer exists;
rather, the Self alone becomes a single manifest reality through its own power. (62–63)
Through the yoga of worshiping Hari, one who is capable and possesses a physical form becomes liberated;
indeed, upon liberation, Māyā no longer exists there.
[One attains] the tasting of the essence of all desires and the abiding in the bliss of all fragrances.
Endowed with all sovereignty, he is a treasury of the fragrance of eternal bliss;
immersed in imperishable joy, he rejoices together with Brahman.
Possessing the very nature of Brahman, he enjoys all desires established within himself.
And through the attainment of union with the Supreme Brahman, one becomes filled with all bliss;
for there, indeed, nothing is lacking for the liberated devotee of Śrī Hari.
Thus, by means of the yoga of worship, the supreme and highest liberation is attained.

If yogins established in the effort of yoga worship Kṛṣṇa, then they attain the supreme liberation described above; there is no doubt in this matter. And if they worship others, such as Īśvara or Vairāja, [they attain their respective goals]. 68–69.

Just as lords attain worlds created by a Lord, that liberation consisting of natural sovereignty brings about destruction in the Great Abode (Mahālaya). Having attained supernatural powers and stability, at the end, it remains as one's own residue.

They attain either dissolution, or the state of another Īśvara, or divinity; they enjoy powers such as multiplying themselves a thousandfold and so forth. That [liberation] is inferior and leads to a fall, whereas liberation from the low ground is supreme.
Or else, through the yoga of meditation upon the form of Hari, there arises a state of absorption characterized by being merged into Him;
for these [practitioners], liberation as oneness occurs through the samādhis beginning with "non-differentiation" (abhinnādi),
which is produced free from such states as that of master and servant.
O King, in the Supreme Lord they are never separate, for their nature is always one with His concealment (tirobhāva). By the power of meditation, they become absorbed in Him and identified with Him;
thus, as supreme lords within the Supreme Lord, they attain the state of non-becoming once again.
This is the most excellent liberation, which is the state of the Supreme Lord;
here, service in the form of a servant is by no means enjoined.
That liberation which consists merely of dharma, however, is not free from worldly enjoyment.
Indeed, it is merely dwelling in bodies within worlds such as heaven and Satyaloka.
Having enjoyed the fruits of dharma, there is again birth upon earth and the acquisition of merit;
thus, heaven and earth follow one another in a continuous cycle.

Even when such a thing has arisen, if that dharma consists of devotion to the Lord (bhāgavata), or takes the form of a connection with Brahman, or is designated as being beyond the qualities (nirguṇya);
or if it consists of service to Hari, or takes the form of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in a ritual sacrifice; [then it is acceptable]. (79)
Then, through the nature of giving, there is eternal liberation for the sake of pleasing Hari.
Indeed, dharma performed merely for one's own sake does not lead to liberation;
when practiced with the intention of benefiting others, it gives rise to auspiciousness.
If performed with the intention of offering to the Supreme Lord, [actions] grant liberation in the Imperishable.
O King, in this way, all actions— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
born of a state of non-attachment and offered to Kṛṣṇa, lead to fulfillment.
For all those [rites] which are accomplished through the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa indeed bestow liberation.
(83) Even the master of a field prepares the field, ploughs it, sows the seeds and ears of grain, reaps them, and also eats [the fruit]. (84)
Having offered everything as an oblation to Brahman, whatever one does— whether like the King of the Kurus,
or like Janaka, or like the brahmin-sage Kūrmi—
all that becomes faultless and free from taint.
A goldsmith produces an ornament through his honest craft;
if that craftsmanship is offered to Kṛṣṇa, it becomes a bestower of liberation.
Whatever is done for the sake of Hari is considered devoid of worldly qualities (*nirguṇa*) and a giver of liberation. (86–87)
Everything performed without Hari is fruitless or even a source of suffering.
If the twice-born practice the Vedas while devoid of the constant remembrance of Hari,
then that practice becomes like the devouring by a dog.

Without the greatness of jewels, a cowherd might tie a pebble around the neck of a buffalo, thinking it has value, yet there is no fruit from that; likewise, even by regarding a Śālagrāma stone as the eternal Viṣṇu, [there is no fruit without its true nature]. (2.254.89–90)
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas indeed protect [the Lord] and serve Him day and night;
for Viṣṇu, perceiving their service as fully realized,
appears before them with four arms and becomes visible to the range of their eyes.
If that very [Lord] is separated from one's inner disposition, He immediately vanishes from view.
But if that same Supreme Lord is bound by the noose of devotion through worship—He, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is indeed the descent of the Supreme Brahman—[He remains present]. || 92-93 ||
Just as an incarnation descends from its source, so too does that which is beginningless, endless, and internal manifest within the heart and before one; thereafter, it leads one to the Imperishable.
Therefore, O King, ritual yogas are performed by means of the body, senses, and so forth.
For these [worldly] bonds indeed bind for the sake of one's own self-interest, whereas they grant liberation for the sake of Hari.
Through association with Kṛṣṇa, the virtuous become divine, their very souls absorbed in the heart of Kṛṣṇa;
sustained by Kṛṣṇa’s sovereignty, they become bestowers of liberation and givers of happiness. (95–96)
They bestow the divine realm, grant divine bliss, and bestow the imperishable;
they grant the yoga of the Lord’s image and are givers of knowledge.
They destroy obstacles, annihilate worldly cycles, and ward off delusion.
They ward off suffering and faults and bestow the world of Brahmā.
One should serve them all without any doubt, with the firm conviction that they are indeed specific manifestations of the Blessed One’s form. (98–99)
Just as affection exists toward one's wife, son, parents, and one's own kinsmen—
affection driven by self-interest and the notions of "I" and "mine"—
so too should one always cultivate such affection for the true guru, for that indeed bestows liberation.

Whether it be Dharma, the sacrifice of Dharma, merit, charity, or auspicious action—(101) one should offer all of this to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Then there is liberation, the great liberation, in the form of union with Brahman. (102)
She possesses the same power and form as Brahmā and bestows the world of Brahmā;
she creates a form equal to the Supreme Brahman and is the most excellent of the excellent.
She is attained by a powerful human being even while still in this very body.
"Union with the Lord—nothing more remains to be attained.
(1.04) The gopīs have indeed attained the supreme yoga; likewise, the beloveds of Brahman have attained liberation.
Having attained the supreme yoga, they have no desire for any other form of yoga. (1.05)
"Thus, O King, apply yourself here to yoga directly before my eyes;
having assumed a supreme, divine, and eternal body, apply yourself to yoga.
O Rādhikā! Having thus granted this interval to the king, Lomaśa—
The king ceased his instruction and rejoiced greatly.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Question Regarding the Cause for Pleasing the Gods and Others, the Question Concerning What Kind of Liberation is Attained through the Teachers of Discrimination, Devotion, Yoga, and Dharma, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 254 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* – Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*)
Chapter 255 [Author:
Chapter 256 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:

Then Rādhikā and Aśvapaṭṭala asked the sage Lomaśa about the nature of the power and the lack of power of yoga. Aśvapaṭṭala said: 1. Then Rādhikā and Aśvapaṭṭala asked the sage Lomaśa about the nature of the power and the lack of power of yoga.
