Aśvapaṭṭala said:
"O Sage, what is the nature of the power of yoga? I wish to know its strength, by which one may be liberated or, being weak, may be held fast.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Purity, austerity, compassion, truthfulness, non-violence, abstention from theft,
breath control, restraint of the senses, and meditation are indeed equal for yogins.
(3) Yoga is perfected for one whose practice is powerful.
The practice of one who is weak is itself weak; by that, bondage is produced.
(4) Although one may sever desire, greed, delusion, affection, anger, and passion through yoga, the weak person becomes attached to them once again. (5)
Just as fish with large bodies, having broken through the net, enter the water again,
so too do those who are weak enter the sixfold [realm] once more;
and just as powerful deer, having burst their bonds, [return to the forest].
Just as [birds] go to another forest, so too do the best of yogis reach the supreme state.
Devoted to the most powerful Self, they surely cross over the ocean of *māyā*;
whereas those who are weak, such as the hares and other small creatures, remain indeed in bondage.
Likewise, once yogis have entered [the body], they are not able to exit;
indeed, being weak, they are not capable of escaping from the net.
And even fish, when weak, do not go forth at all after having cut through the net.
In the same way, weak yogis do not proceed after cutting through *māyā*.
Powerful birds, having cut through the net, go to the ends of the quarters;
indeed, powerful yogis, having cut through *māyā*, go to the sky.
Just as a powerful fire consumes everything that comes before it,
so too do the most powerful yogis burn away illusion by means of their own splendor.
But just as a weak fire is extinguished even by pieces of wood, [so is the weak yogi overcome].
Even one who is capable, if weak against the group of six, surely meets with defeat.
Just as a watercourse lacking strength is dragged away by the current into the water,
so too the group of six, being weak, drags one away into the realm of illusion.
An elephant, though powerful, is both held back by the current and carried along;
likewise, a yogi who is most strong proceeds after having warded off the six [internal enemies].
Those who are powerful are liberated, while those who are weak fall into bondage.
Just as the great sun arising at the time of dissolution dries up the world,
so too does the yogi, arisen through the power of liberation, dry up the defects.
By the power of yoga, the yogis enter the abode of the Lord.
Whether it be the abodes of the gods or the stations of Prajāpati,
the power of yoga increases for one who is always habituated to practice.
Then, having once again pierced through illusion, they proceed to the Imperishable.

Just as a skilled archer who has practiced well reaches victory after piercing the target, so too does he reach the Imperishable. And just as one who has practiced well places a vessel of oil upon his head, [he remains steady]. (2.255.20)

Just as a dancer proceeds without stumbling along a rope and attains victory, so indeed does the yogi, through the power of the perfection of practice, proceed to the Imperishable. Just as a helmsman reaches the further shore with a boat through practice... [2.1] ...so too [does the yogi reach the goal].
Likewise, one who is thus disciplined reaches the further shore of the world by means of strength.
Just as a skilled and powerful charioteer proceeds with certainty after restraining the horses,
so too the best of yogis, being thus disciplined, goes to the imperishable and eternal state.
The knower of yoga who indeed perceives the Supreme Lord within his own self,
having truly severed the net of illusion, attains the supreme state.
Having withdrawn the impurities from the wheels situated within the body...
Having repeatedly burned away [all obstructions], he indeed proceeds along the path of Brahman and departs by his own power. And whenever he wills to go to the Imperishable (akṣara), then,
having abandoned the body, he goes to that abode as one who is independent.
Through the worship of one’s chosen deity, one may obtain strength; likewise, through practice, self-yoga, restraint, and virility,
as well as through austerity, the yoga of meditation, and absorption, one shall attain strength.
But, O King, some indeed reach the further shore in the great forest;
for those who dwell in the forest are conquerors of the powerful.
Yet, without Nārāyaṇa, it is a state fraught with doubt to reach the further shore.
Even those who are most powerful are indeed carried away by enemies who are even more powerful—
those who dwell in the abode of the source of divine sovereignty, wonder, and spiritual perfections.
This occurs when Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa stands before them.

Advancing, he surely leads away even the most powerful beings after conquering them to his own divine, eternal, and supreme state of liberation. O King, considering the qualities within the body to be such, never become bound.
The body, which is the abode of variegated elements, must be scrutinized through discernment.
Here, understand my tenfold state of *sattva*; I shall describe them:
bliss, joy, exultation, luminosity, and the performance of meritorious deeds.

Contentment, straightforwardness, faith, renunciation, and sovereignty—know these to be my ninefold nature of *rajas*. Now listen as I describe them: belief in the scriptures, lack of miserliness, and likewise the pursuit of dualities. (34–35)
Lust, hatred, intoxication, pride, dispute, and likewise harshness; as well as shadow, darkness, and non-existence—understand these as mine; I shall speak to you.
Delusion, the state of being tamasic, smokiness, and the loss of intelligence.
Sleep, negligence, laziness, and destruction—such are its forms.
Understand from me the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) as having seven states; I shall describe them to you:
egoism (*ahantā*), possessiveness (*mamatā*), pride (*māna*), prolixity (*dairghya*), hope (*āśā*), and self-worship (*svapūjyatā*). (37–38)
I shall describe to you the six states of the mind: lordliness, fickleness, impetuosity, doubt, independence, and untrustworthiness; these are always considered to reside in the mind.
Understand from me the sense-faculty and its fivefold state; I shall speak to you.
Lack of satiety, attachment, indifference, perception, and movement—understand from me these four states of the reality of the elements as I describe them. (2.255.40–41)
Support, bondage, destruction, and procreation— these six sheaths, which constitute the reality of the sheaths (*kośatattva*), always possess these three states and reside within the body:
hair, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, and sinew.
The *bhāvas*, however, are moisture, impurity, and likewise the state of being an object of enjoyment.
Know from me that these two *bhāvas*—vitality and indeed the dual nature—are life and wandering; thus have the principles (*tattvas*) been declared to you. (43–44)

O King, through the discernment of reality, those states which take the form of defects are indeed obstacles on the path to the liberation of the self, if they appear as such to you. Having discerned them, one should indeed realize that singular state of being, which is the state of bliss belonging to one's own self.
One should offer [the mind] with devotion to the Supreme Lord; for him, liberation is certain.
Alternatively, having observed all states of being, one should bring about the end of the desire to see:
all human objects of sense, as well as those of the Piśācas. 46–47.
The realms of the yakṣas and likewise the realms of the nāgas;
the realms of the gandharvas and likewise the realms of the ancestors;
the realms of the animals and likewise the realms of the Maruts.
And also the realms of the birds, as well as the realms of the royal sages (rājarṣi),
the realms of the brahmin sages (brahmarṣi), and likewise the realms of the Asuras;
the realms of the Viśvedevas and the realms of the yogins.
Having fully understood the objects of the senses pertaining to Prajāpati, Īśvara, and Brahmā— those born from millions of lords— and having experienced pleasure and pain,
and having observed their merits and defects, one attains peace thereafter.
And by means of discernment, one should establish oneself in liberation.
(52) Endowed with knowledge and realization, and having cultivated himself through the means, he attains divine liberation, the imperishable state of eternal bliss. (53)
O King, one who possesses discernment should withdraw the vital breath along with the six sheaths within the elements;
he should dissolve the elements together with their constituent parts, the senses, and the mind—
including the sense of "I-ness"— into the intellect.
One should offer one's intellect into one’s own true nature, which is designated as the Self;
and one should place that Self, in the form of Brahman, within Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the heart.
By means of that, one should unite [the Self] with liberation, through which one goes to the imperishable abode.
Having known that the gods, the Prajāpatis, the Ṛṣis, the Seven Sages, and even the royal and celestial Ṛṣis are always cast down by the jaws of Time;
and having known that the Brahman-Ṛṣis and Lord-Ṛṣis are likewise brought to their end by Time—
One who travels the path of liberation should certainly not practice meditation there [in hell].
Having understood the fate of sinners enveloped in the world of Yama, and having observed the births in various wombs and the states of hungry ghosts, [one should turn away from evil]. (58–59)
Having truly understood the wretched sufferings of the womb for living beings,
as well as their terrible calamities, the falling of stars and constellations,
and likewise the miserable and sudden separation of couples.
Having observed the pitiless devouring of living beings by one another,
the wickedness of sense objects, the lack of life for those whose breath has departed,
and the terrible, suffering-filled destinies of sinners; ||61-62||
Observing the suffering of animals and the exhaustion of their lifespans day by day;
seeing the decay of embodied beings and beholding the misery of death;
and having fully understood the defects of the body as well as its nature as a prison-house of hell.
Having cast off the body from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should go to the supreme state.
One should then take refuge in the deity of Prāṇa, and thereafter in the deity of Vāyu;
then also in the deity of Vyoman (Space), and thereafter in the rays of the Sun.
Then also Cāndraraśmi, and after that Puṇyaraśmi;
then also Satyaraśmi, and after that Sattvaraśmi;
then also Īśvaraśmi, and after that Brahmaraśmi.
Then, having released the rays, one should attain the Supreme Brahman.
Having reached the Supreme Self, pure as the abode of that Being, one attains the supreme immortality from which there is no return. (67–68)
O King, that is the supreme goal for the virtuous, for yogis as well,
and for the Sāttvata devotees who perform all actions for the sake of Hari.
Therein indeed lies knowledge, omniscience, and the accumulation of a multitude of sovereign powers.
Satisfaction is that which transcends all else, even the measure of bliss itself, being utterly full.
For omniscience is held to belong eternally to one who is unattached and free from the pairs of opposites.
Therefore, by virtue of possessing omniscience, they are forever contented.
They are eternally blissful, eternally peaceful, eternally satisfied, and free from desire;
though they are indeed all-seeing, they do not perceive the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
And even when perceiving the cycle of worldly existence, they are devoid of attachment to those various states.
They are devoid of the transformation of states (bhāva-vikṛti) and have attained the perfections such as withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Capable of grasping both the graspable and the ungraspable, they are free from the defects of creation.
They do not at all bind themselves to the objects created by the lower levels of creation within their own knowledge.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O learned one, what is that imperishable abode from which one does not return again?
And what is the perishable, distinct from that, from which one returns again? (75)
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, that is the imperishable, auspicious abode of the Supreme Lord, of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is the source of all avatars. (76)
This belongs to the Supreme Brahman himself, to that Lord Nārāyaṇa, known as Puruṣottama, who is beyond the imperishable (akṣara) and eternal;
it is auspicious, secure, brought about by one's longing, and endowed with all perfections.
That is the abode of the Lord of all lords, the dwelling of liberation, higher than the highest;
it never perishes at any time in the past,
nor is it ever seized by the future— it is that immutable realm of Brahman.
Above both Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha lies the infinite and infallible realm,
where indeed exist infinite abodes created by Nārāyaṇa, fashioned by Nārāyaṇa himself.
In those abodes where millions of incarnations dwell, they shine forth;
that all-pervading abode is the Imperishable (akṣara). It is the world of Brahman, the space of consciousness, a treasury of undivided splendor.
Where the Lord shines forth as both the imperishable Brahman and in embodied form—
that is the supreme abode of the Imperishable, dearer even than Hari himself.
Indeed, there exists that supreme abode where the seat of the Supreme Brahman is eternally established.
The most excellent and auspicious throne, the elephant-seat (*gajāsana*), exists everywhere.
Indeed, all those dear to Brahmā serve there as maidservants of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who grant liberation. (84–85)
Indeed, other than the Lord, there are the liberated souls, the powers of Hari’s form, and infinite perfections;
there dwell the perfected ones in infinite numbers, as well as the deities who are still striving for perfection.
Those beginningless liberated souls reside in that supreme abode.
But those who are liberated from the beginning always dwell in that imperishable abode (dhāman).
This is known as the Imperishable (akṣara), for that abode is beyond Māyā;
it transcends the qualities (guṇas), is great bliss, and is filled with eternal bliss and other such qualities.
Indeed, by the mere pleasure of a single hair-pore [of this state], all other abodes become filled with the bliss of the nectar of bliss;
and other worlds known as the realms of the Lord (Īśvara) are likewise filled with that same bliss.
Then all types of creations were delighted by that bliss.
Indeed, the creations consisting of *māyā* are subject to decay;
they are characterized by the three qualities (*triguṇa*), darkness (*tamas*), and *māyā*, as well as the unmanifest (*avyakta*) placed within the *puruṣa*. || 91 ||
The principle of Mahat indeed becomes manifest as the "I" (ahaṃkāra), as well as knowledge and ignorance, merit and demerit, and likewise the two others: injunction and prohibition.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established in the manifest.
And likewise, everything opposed to that [unmanifest] is established in the manifest:
sound, touch, taste, form, and smell—the subtle elements of the [gross] elements; as well as the mind for the purpose of perception, and the ear, skin, eye, and tongue. (93–94)
The nose, and likewise the others—speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ—for the sake of action; as well as space, air, fire, water, and earth;
and thereafter the others who bear bodies composed of the six sheaths.

All of this wastes away day and night; therefore, it is called *kṣara* (the perishable). Indeed, for all those who possess a body, the twenty-four elements are either deficient or subject to decay; because of that, it is declared to be *kṣara*.
Whatever possesses form is entirely subject to the nature of decay,
whether it be in water, on earth, in space, in air, or in fire, or even in the highest [element],
in the most meritorious [realm], in the realm of supernatural powers, or in the sphere of pure being (sattva). (98)
This entire manifest world, which is known by that name, flows away as a stream of the perishable.
Within the perishable, the imperishable always abides; for the Self is also called the imperishable.
He who has his station in the imperishable Self is the Supreme Lord.
That very Hari dwells within the hearts of all forms;
O King, worship Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is accompanied by Ramā, the Lord of the lotus-born Brahmā, and the Master of the white, red, and black creations. 101.
Pāraga, Antarastha, Kāṃbhareya, Priya, Prabhu;
Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha, Nātha, Kuṅkumavāpīkeśvara; Gopālabālaka, O King, Lomaśeṣṭa, and Patīśvara. || 102-103 ||
[I bow to] Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the Sun of the Aśvapaṭṭasara field, the beloved husband of Brahmapriyā, the Lord of Akṣara, the Master who dwells within all as the inner controller;
and [to Him who], at the beginning of creation, enjoyed this earth of Surāṣṭra.
The glorious son of Mahāviṣṇu, the sole child of Mahālakṣmī; then him who possesses manifold forms and assumes many incarnations;
then that Kṛṣṇa, the son of Dharma, the son of Devakī, and Hari.
To Nara and Nārāyaṇa as well, who are devoted to the conduct of Brahman;
to the Master, the Renouncer, and likewise the Omniscient Guide;
to the Preceptor, the True Guru, the Lord of the Abode, and the Sovereign of the Noble Mandala.
"O King, practice the vow of celibacy (*brahmavrata*), which sustains life, perceives all things, and is infallible. Attain supreme liberation by a mere drop of my grace.
Thus did the sage speak to King Aśvapāṭala, O Rādhikā. (1.08–1.09)
Having instructed him thus, he ceased, remembering the Beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The king also, his inner being filled with joy from the abundance of bliss,
attained a supreme savor by drinking the nectar of the discourse on the Supreme Brahman.
Like one parched with thirst, he questioned Lomaśa once again.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Inquiry Regarding the Strength and Weakness of Yoga, the Inquiry Concerning the Worlds of the Perishable and the Imperishable, and the Answers Given by Lomaśa," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 255: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 256 [Author:
Chapter 257 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, I shall now relate in brief that which King [Nala] then asked Lomaśa; understand it from my heart. 1.
Aśvapāṭala said:
This transmigratory existence is indeed perishable, while the conscious self within it is imperishable.
Why then does he not abandon this perishable [existence] and attain that which is imperishable? (2)
Lomaśa said:
In the womb, one who is asleep is cooked by the power of karma like a ripe grain; as if having attained identity with the impressions of the elements, he is roasted. (3)
Having encountered perishable phenomena and being overwhelmed by a state of ignorance,

the perishable self falls into the delusion that "this is I" and is consequently born again. Strengthened by external sounds such as "I am a child," "a man," or "a woman," [it continues in this cycle].
Dulled by the delusion of perceiving objects as white, red, or black;

fallen into confused conceptualization and rendered inert by association with worldly objects; emaciated or stout, miserable or happy, awakened to the notions of "mine" and "I" and "you"—[such is the state of the mind]. (5–6)
Bound by the ropes of the life-span of the noose of karma, he is rendered powerless;
tied by the knots in the chest-casket of the vital breaths, he remains indestructible.
Afflicted by the sprinkling of the heat of illusion, he is made firm.
Smeared with the fluids of the six sheaths and having taken his seat right there, he was further anointed with great unguents;
unable to depart, he was powerless.
Right there, he experienced states that were either tamasic, rajasic, or sattvic.
This [mind] attains a continuous flow, a ripened flavor, and a cultivated taste;
thereafter, it reaches nourishment through those various excellent essences brought by the senses.
It thrives with the joys of happiness and indeed runs toward that very object.

And for that purpose, he strives again and again to know it, to attain it, to enjoy it, to abandon it, to renew it, and to accumulate it anew. Thrown by the momentum of those latent impressions, the fool—perishable and consisting of perishable nature—is thus driven. (11–12)
Indistinguishable and inseparable [from his body], he exists as one dragged by his hair;
devoted to the attributes of the body, he rejoices in bodily pleasure.
Again, he performs meritorious deeds for the sake of attaining a divine body and the like.
Thus, as one goes by means of the wheel, from body comes action, and from that, a new body;
again action, again a body—in this manner, within the pit of transience, the ignorant self falls repeatedly and repeatedly desires joy. (14–15)
For one who conducts himself in this manner, liberation from the perishable can never occur;
on the contrary, delusion, bondage, and worldly existence only increase.
Following from delusion to further delusion, he perceives nothing but ever-new [objects of attachment].
One strives to acquire and to enjoy that [object], and thus binds karma consisting of that very thing.
Through such actions, one undergoes thousands of bodies from one body to another—among animals, among the hosts of gods, among humans, and among birds. (17–18)
He is born again and again among the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas;
though free from dualities, he encounters dualities within those very same wombs.
He experiences the enjoyments of the gods, the enjoyments of the Sādhyas, and the unsurpassed enjoyments of the Siddhas.
Likewise, in order to obtain the enjoyments of lords, it churns everything in every way.
In sickness, enjoyment, recreation, agitation, decay, impairment, or injury, the embodied self—disturbed by delusion—conceives the notion of "mine. (2.256.20–21)
Indeed, when bodies have been split apart, he dwells exercising sovereignty over them as they lie scattered—
on a bed, on a ball, in some hole, in a cleft,
or in the mud; on a brick, in the sky, in a pit, in a cave, or upon the earth.
On thorns, in ashes, in dwindling water, on fruits, in the wind, or on reeds;
wearing beautiful garments, woolen blankets, mats of grass, silken cloths, those made of mud-fiber, and skins. (23–24)
Whatever womb one may be born into, one regards that very thing as a garment;
likewise, one considers various foods, both fragrant and foul-smelling,
as well as the consumption of moisture and moss, to be one's own through delusion.
For the sake of perfection, he undergoes various hardships and observes vows;
he performs his desired rites and follows them with zeal, [seeking] the qualities of his own form and various gains that are dear to his heart. (26–27)
It runs about for the sake of enjoyment, thinking, "I must experience these things.
Constantly enveloped by the sense of "mine," it revolves right there through thousands of millions of creations and within the three worlds; such is the fruit thereof.
One experiences the fruits of one’s actions within bodies that endure until death.
Even though devoid of food, one becomes as if possessed of food;
and though lacking sense organs, one perceives oneself as having sense organs and being possessed of wounds. (2.256.30)

The signless one regards the possessor of signs; the deathless one regards him who is beset by the fear of death; the sorrowless one regards the sorrowful; and the imperishable one regards the perishable.
Thus, through the conceit of being perishable, he does not at all emerge from the perishable.
O King, for one whose nature is ignorance, no end to this state exists anywhere (32),
except through the secret instructions of the guru, the thorough study of the scriptures,
association with the virtuous, the attainment of sacred discourse, and service to the holy devotees of Hari (33).
Grace, following after the liberated souls who reside in the heart of Hari, the propitiation of Hari, and meditation upon that Supreme Self—
these indeed are the divine means that bestow divinity.
The self is joined with the self, and therein the supreme self is joined.
(35) Then one goes to the further shore, to the Lord who stands beyond the imperishable.
As long as one does not take refuge in Hari, nor practice the company of the virtuous, (36) so long [one remains bound].
One should not perform devotion nor practice worship; as long as one does not serve Hari who is directly present, nor serve the guru, nor likewise the virtuous,
so long indeed will one’s worldly existence not dissolve.
Thousands of millions of creations go to their end in destruction;
by means of one abode, he goes to thousands of abodes that likewise end in death.
Through the service of Māyā and her products, he becomes possessed of the three qualities (guṇas) and full of conceit.
Through the application of connection with Māyā, he becomes composed of the qualities of Māyā;
through the union for the sake of passion, and by resorting to each other's qualities,
he repeatedly assumes an illusory form within the womb during the fertile season.
Thus, for one who is born in this manner, how could there be the dharma of liberation?
Therefore, having severed and split asunder the knot called latent impressions (vāsanā), one should proceed;
having brought about the destruction of craving through austerity alone, or indeed through knowledge.
Having distinguished through discernment and realized the Self as indeed free from illusion,
one should proceed by the path of the light of knowledge and upon the way of truth.
Then, the qualities are separated from the attributeless conscious Self.
From the very moment of conception, through merit, one perceives [the Lord] as distinct from all qualities;
likewise, like Prahlāda or like the young Madālasā,
or else by the grace of Śrī Hari, the divine eye is manifested.
Through the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, and by the abandonment of the qualities (guṇas), each disciplined soul perceives its own true nature;
likewise, it beholds Hari, who is higher than the highest.
One-pointedness is the strength therein, and the power of meditation is the cause.
Freed from all attachments and remaining steady during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa within the heart during the final watch of the night;
having stabilized the activity of the intellect through discernment, one should become unshakable and motionless. (47–48)
When he perceives Hari dwelling within, then he becomes one who is disciplined (yukta). For the disciplined one, there is a constant manifestation centered on the Supreme Lord;
he hears nothing else, smells nothing, tastes nothing, and sees nothing else.
He neither touches, grasps, moves, speaks, nor urinates;
he does not perceive, nor does he form volitions, nor does he think.
At that time, the Self does not cognize, yet it rejoices within the Supreme Self.
The sun shines in the sky like a lamp in a windless place;
the sages, who are masters born of Brahman, behold it.
Then they see that Supreme Self with the vision of the Self.
The view of a self is considered ignorance (*avidyā*), while the vision of the mind is knowledge (*vidyā*).
Ignorance is characterized by creation and destruction; knowledge is indeed eternal liberation.
Ignorance produces the unmanifest, whereas knowledge attains the Self. (53–54)
Through ignorance one goes to death; through knowledge one attains immortality.
Upon the acquisition of knowledge, indeed, a manifold discrimination regarding the self arises in one who has perfected the self;
listen, O King, as I speak to you.
What has been done by me, who am indeed illusory, during all this time?
Like an ignorant fish, I have followed the net here.
A fish that finds its life in the water knows nothing other than the water. || 56–57 ||
Likewise, obscured by delusion, I did not know anyone else;
fie, fie upon my pursuit of delusion and my following after infatuation regarding my own conduct!
Having succumbed to the persistence of delusion, I did not recognize the Supreme Lord.
Concealed by Māyā, I remained hidden and deceived regarding the Supreme Self.
Controlled by Māyā for all this time, I did not realize it;
indeed, I have been cheated by her, for I did not attain the path to liberation.
This is not her fault, nor is it my own;
rather, it is because I dwelt here attached, greedy, and possessed by the latent impressions of sense-objects.
Though formless and incorporeal, I became endowed with form and body through her.
I was then overcome and deceived by natural selfishness (mamatva).
Having cast myself into liberation, what have I done that I have obtained hell instead—by me, who am devoid of the sense of "mine" (mamakāra), yet possessed of the notion of "mine"? (62–63)
"I have no further need for this courtesan, who deceives me by manifesting herself in many forms to unite with me.
Now, however, I am awakened through the grace of the true guru, Hari. (64)
Departing from this woman, I shall today take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the Guru, the Master.
I shall attain equality with the Divine, and not with this deceitful woman.
I shall find security through Kṛṣṇa; I shall go to the supreme state.
Having thus reached this conclusion regarding solitude by means of one's own self,
one attains through association with Hari a state equal to Hari due to that very association.
This is called the Supreme Brahman, from which one does not return again.
O King, he by whom this supreme knowledge, which bestows liberation, has been attained—
by him the perishable and the imperishable are known, and for him no fear exists;
nor indeed does fear exist for one who performs what is beneficial in this world.
For him, fear never arises in the world beyond;

indeed, for men who take refuge in the Dharma that is beneficial to the virtuous, there is truly no fear. For those who desire the sweet [pleasures] of sense-objects, freedom from thirst [for them] is always fearless.

For one who cultivates familiarity with knowledge and the Dharma, there is no fear anywhere. (7.1) Indeed, for one who constantly gives much, who always serves the virtuous, and whose nature is to honor the good, there shall never be any fear. (7.2)
For one who bestows justice upon the worthy, whose heart is pure, who possesses true knowledge,
who is dispassionate and free from attachment, there shall never be any fear. For one who has eradicated all defects and serves all living beings, [there is no fear].
For one whose nature is to help others, fear shall never arise anywhere.
(74) Fear does not come upon an embodied being who is patient, enduring, free from anger, upright, and a doer of good. (75)
For a donor who possesses a virtuous basis, who is self-restrained, compassionate,
and free from pride in all circumstances, there shall never be any fear.
[This applies to] one who is steadfast in soul, tranquil, wise, and who conducts himself with devotion.
Indeed, no fear whatsoever arises for the ascetic servant.
For one who is liberated from merit and demerit, who has destroyed all doubts, and who is freed from birth and death, the supreme good is certainly attained. (77–78)
For one who is liberated from merit and demerit, who possesses the yoga of Brahma’s grace,
and who is distinct from the three bodies, the supreme good is indeed certain.
[This occurs] within the principle of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and the sixteen transformations.
Furthermore, he who is bound by both nature and its transformations is liberated.
He who knows the other body as distinct from his own self is not defiled.
One should know the gnat to be one thing and the fig tree another. (2.256.80–81)
By means of contact with a fresh fig, a mosquito becomes smeared there;
yet one should know the fish to be one thing, and the water another.
Even through its association with the water, the fish is not smeared by it.
The fire on the hearth is one thing and the fire of the hearth is another; the hearth-fire is not defiled by the former.
Water is one thing and the lotus is another; the lotus is not defiled by the water.
Indeed, their coexistence and their dwelling are merely mutual. (83–84)
Nevertheless, he who perceives this as a state of separateness truly sees;
for one who sees thus, there is no bondage when the substratum is destroyed.
If, moreover, a life-force greater than that which fills the current life should meet [him], [he is not bound]. 85.
Then, having attained the life-force (*jīvana*), one rejoices there in happiness.
Indeed, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the life-force that bestows all bliss and immortality. Having reached that refuge, there is neither fear nor death, nor destruction. (86–87)

The supreme good, the supreme Brahman, supreme liberation, the supreme state, the world of the ageless and immortal, and the ocean of imperishable bliss—one who is disciplined attains all this here, eternally within one's own self. 88. One who is liberated always experiences [this] here in one's own soul.

Ever serene, with a satisfied soul, tranquil in his sleep and at ease—just as a rock is not moved by clouds, so too is he of such a nature; he would not tremble at the sounds of shouts, thunder, songs, or instrumental music. (2.256.89–90)

Holding a vessel of oil in his hand, the dancer proceeds along with a rope; even though he is bound by the pot, his mind is composed, and he is indeed fearless and free from trembling. Not even a single drop of oil falls from his vessel.
Joined with that [state], he proceeds to the northern limit and shall obtain victory.
(92) One who is thus united with Brahman perceives Brahman right here;
having attained the Supreme Brahman, being liberated, he shall reach final liberation. (93)
Having thus instructed the king regarding Rādhikā, Lomaśa attained peace, and the king, in turn, asked about the path of those [liberated ones]:
how the great-souled ones, seeking the supreme good, become liberated. (94)
And they depart by means of the upward exit (*utkramaṇa*) and other such methods; Lomī asked about these things.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Inquiry as to How the Self's Release from the Perishable and its Journey to the Imperishable Occur," followed by the Exposition of that Release and that Journey, in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 258 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the pure self indeed departs, having become separate from the body, O Rādhā, how does it depart? Thus the king questioned Lomaśa. 1.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Sage, what is the nature of this soul's departure? How and for what reason does it go forth? Having emerged from the body, tell me that, O Lord.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Whatever [object] emerges from its place, according to the power of yoga and austerity, according to the power of devotion, and also according to the power of merit;
according to the power of sin, and also according to the power of karma. (3)
Just as by the power of illusion and also by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā),
one goes to the worlds of the various deities residing in those respective places; for instance,
if one departs on foot, one indeed goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
If he departs by means of his two calves, he goes to the abode of the Vasus;
if he departs by means of his two thighs, he goes to Prajāpati;
if he departs by means of his anus, he attains the station of Mitra.
If he departs through the linga [the organ], he reaches Satyaloka;
if he departs through the jaghana [the perineum], he attains the station of Meru.
And if he indeed ascends from the navel, he shall attain the heaven of the gods.
If he departs through the two sides, he reaches the worlds of the Maruts;
if he ascends by way of the two arms, he shall attain the world of Indra;
and if he departs through the chest, he shall attain the world of Rudra.
If he departs by way of the neck, he shall attain the world of men;
if he departs by way of the mouth, he shall attain the Viśvedevas.
And if his departure is through the ears, he shall become a guardian of the quarters (Dikpāla).
By departing through the nose, one attains the world of Vāyu;
by departing through the eyes, one reaches either the world of Sūrya or the abode of Candra;
and by departing through the cheeks, he goes to the world of Vahni. || 11–12 ||
By departing through his two eyebrows, one attains the world of the Aśvins;
by departing through the forehead, however, there is access to the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka).
And by exiting through the crown of the head, one goes to the eternal world of Brahmā.

If he departs from the wheels, having taken recourse to the path of the *suṣumṇā*, then he indeed proceeds to the worlds of those respective lords. This departure has been described, O lord of men, by virtue of the power of the [respective] stations. (14–15)
Furthermore, by the power of worship, the departure [from the body] is indeed distinguished;
and by the power of merit and demerit, the journey is indeed differentiated.
Through the worship of Śambhu, one goes to Kailāsa, which is adorned by the Gaṇas.
Through the worship of Viṣṇu, one goes to Śvetadvīpa, the ocean of milk;
through devotion to Nara and Nārāyaṇa, one goes to the Lord of Badarī;
and through devotion to the Sūryagāyatrī, one goes to the solar orb. (17–18)
Through the practice of worship such as sacrifice, one who performs the rite goes to heaven;

indeed, by the worship of the ancestors, a human being goes to the world of the ancestors. Through celibacy, one reaches the world of the Siddhas, and through the performance of austerity, the world of Truth (Satyaloka).
By means of the *Puruṣasūkta*, one goes to the abode of Vairāja;
by the worship of Mahāviṣṇu, a human being goes to Vaikuṇṭha;
and through the upāsanā of Nārāyaṇa, one reaches Mahāvaikuṇṭha.
Indeed, by the worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one attains Goloka;
by the worship of Māyā, one attains the worlds of Māyā, such as Āvaraṇa and the rest;
and by the worship of Bhūman, a human being goes to the Unmanifest (avyākṛta).
And by the worship of Vāsudeva, one goes to the immortal abode. (23) By the worship of the incarnations beginning with Kapila, one goes to their respective abodes;
and by the worship of the Imperishable (Akṣara), one goes to the eternal, imperishable abode. (24)
Through the worship of the Supreme Brahman, one attains the supreme abode;
through lack of worship and by means of ritual acts alone, one becomes subject to birth within various wombs.
By means of tamasic actions, one becomes a Daitya, a Dānava, or a Rākṣasa.

Through rajasic actions, he goes to the state of a king or even to that of a merchant; likewise, he reaches the Vasus, the worlds of the Gandharvas, the world-protectors, and the inhabitants of heaven. (26–27)
Through *sāttvika* qualities one is born as a Brahmin, a virtuous person, or a deity of merit;
through sinful acts, one is born as a bird, an animal, an insect, or even a wild beast.
Through meritorious deeds, one is born as a king, a god, a teacher, a chaste woman, or one who observes vows. (28)
Those who owe debts are reborn as draft animals such as stallions and bulls;
those who give gifts are reborn as venerable persons adorned with seats.
Thus, indeed, they go to their broken dwellings by means of broken carts.
Even those abiding in the householder’s life, when endowed with the fire of knowledge,
burn away all karmas and, having illumined the Self within the self,
proceed to the supreme Brahman just like stainless renunciants.
"For those who have not renounced are indeed renounced when they have taken recourse to the renunciation of knowledge.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, how is it that those who have not renounced are called 'renounced'?"
"And how do those established in the householder's life attain that supreme goal?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"Listen, O King, to this most wonderful story."
Formerly, we two were indeed the skillful Yoginīs of King Ānarta.
In Saurāṣṭra, there was a king named Ānartaka who was a devotee of Kṛṣṇa;
it was by him that this land of Surāṣṭra was settled after he had brought [the people] from the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
That king was a devotee of Viṣṇu, faithful to his wife and a follower of the twice-born;
for he had indeed attained true knowledge from the brāhmaṇa Patnīvrata.
Devoted to that knowledge, he remained present in the assembly of the virtuous.
Having completely severed the continuous bond of "I" and "mine" by means of the science of knowledge,
one remains eternally established in yoga within the supreme Lord in meditative absorption (samādhi). Furthermore,
there arise for holy men and great sages the expositions of knowledge (jñānavārtikāḥ).
O King, because of that [performance] which was held every evening in the assembly hall at Camatkārapura,
the fame of Anarta-yogin spread to the ends of the quarters.
Having heard of it, the virtuous and skillful Yoginī, endowed with supernatural powers, [went there].
The Goddess of the Supreme Lord dwells in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
she is perfected in the arts of yoga, capable of entering the bodies of others,
assuming desired forms at will, possessed of realized wisdom, and a treasure-trove of the meaning of the knowledge of reality.
The aged Vaiṣṇavī ascetic, having transcended the attributes of the body, became one whose nature was the Self; she was profound, invulnerable to the laws of elemental existence, virtuous,
and abiding in the state of Brahman with her characteristics unperceivable— she was Nārāyaṇī.
O Kṛṣṇa, she has attained the state of supreme being and abides in the renunciation of all things.
Just as the entire world is under the control of Lakṣmī, so too is she of such a nature;
she is the Goddess who descends as an incarnation, the virtuous Satī, and the power of Śiva.
That virtuous woman, known as Kuśalā, having assumed an exquisite form of supreme and blossoming youth, went to the city of Camatkārapura;
she reached King Ānarta, who was seated in an assembly surrounded by the virtuous.

Having beheld her supreme delicacy and youthful age, all the yogis, renunciants, great sages, and those learned in the Vedas were filled with wonder, asking: "Who is she? To whom does she belong? And from where has she come here? (46–47)
The king also welcomed her and offered her a seat in the assembly. Having been honored with marks of respect, the virtuous Yoginī Kuśalā,
desiring to question the king, bound him with yogic bonds.
"This king is renowned in the *Maukṣadharma* and is celebrated everywhere.
"This liberated king, Sāttvata—how does he sit? Let me observe.
She immediately entered the *buddhisattva* of Ānarta with her own intellect. (2.257.50)
Restraining the rays from his two eyes with [his own] rays, he entered into the functions of his opponent's intellect by means of the arrows of knowledge in order to conquer them.
A dispute concerning the intellect arises in the hearts of two practitioners of yoga.
"Of those two, one shall possess mastery [of yoga], while the other shall suffer defeat.
A non-yogi does not attain victory; this king is either such a one or he is not.
Having reflected thus, and her intellect being firm, she brought that king under her control. (52–53)

The king, perceiving her intention, thought, "I shall render this yoginī mute," and with that thought, he seized her intellect by means of the great powers of yoga. Having entered the body of the king, she took possession of his intellect. || 54 || Having honored her who had entered the form of the king's intellect, [he said: "I shall make this yoginī mute. Thus resolved, he seized her intellect through the powerful forces of yoga. Once she had entered the king's body, he treated her with respect within the framework of his own intellect.
Having established [his consciousness] within the subtle body (liṅgadeha), the king remained there with her.
At that time, those two, unattached to their gross bodies and abiding in the subtle body, engaged in a mutual debate as yogis for the sake of self-conquest. (55–56)
Ānarta said:
"O you who are true to yoga, where has this practice been performed, and where will you go?
Whose are you, from where do you come, what are you, and how indeed have you arrived? (57)
"O yoginī worthy of honor, though I am a king, I too am free from those [royal] marks and have resorted to yoga. I desire to know you quickly;
for I have specifically received this [knowledge] from my teacher named Patnīvratā. (58)

Listen to me regarding the vast knowledge of yoga and liberation as well. Having attained stability in these three—knowledge of reality, the power of yoga, and the methods of sovereignty—which bestow liberation, I move about free from passion. (2.257.59–60)
The cause of liberation is the absence of passion, and this is attained through knowledge.
By means of knowledge, through the gateway of passionlessness, the accomplishment of liberation has been achieved by me.
Free from dualities and unattached, I abide with an unwavering intellect.
Just as a dry field devoid of water, even when sown with seed, cannot produce a sprout;
so too have I become parched.
I take no delight in sweet things, nor do I feel distress at harsh ones.
One should worship with sandalwood paste on the right and pierce with a weapon on the left.
"O virtuous lady! A certain truth exists there for me: I am equal [to all].
I am happy, having accomplished all my goals, regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same. (64)
Though I abide in the state of kingship, I remain unattached; I dwell in the company of the virtuous.
The triad that serves as the cause for liberation consists of knowledge born of discrimination, the renunciation of actions, and devotion to the Supreme Self.
I have received the Trika from my guru, which, when integrated, leads to liberation;
and I perform every action endowed with devotion and discernment.
Just as the best of renunciants have indeed resorted to actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), [so do I].
Likewise, regarding restraint, observance, desire, hatred, possessiveness, pride, hypocrisy, attachment, and affection—I have attained freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*).
If those [others] are destined for liberation, why am I not likewise going that way? (68–69)
If liberation were to arise in every way for those dwelling in a leaf-hut,
then how could liberation not be within my grasp as I dwell in this magnificent mansion? Whatever a person has need of, that very thing they rely upon.
One [carries] a staff and a garland, another an umbrella and chowries.
Having perceived the defects in the householder’s life, one becomes an ascetic who has gone to the stage of renunciation;
abandoning the former duties and undertaking the subsequent ones as are appropriate.
Having attained union through the cessation of attachment, he would be liberated, not while still attached.
Sovereignty over my kingdom is indeed equal to their life in the forest.
Tell me, if that mendicant is truly liberated, why am I not liberated?
Food, clothing, drink, sleep, and the gathering of what is required—
wherever there is sovereignty equal to that of a mendicant,
if they indeed possess liberation, then mine too is surely liberation.
If you truly possess a share in bondage, then you are equal to householders;
if liberation comes through knowledge alone, then the wearing of saffron robes is in vain.
The abandonment of worldly entanglements is useless, and the maintaining of matted hair is in vain.
The renunciation of gold and fine garments is in vain; the wearing of fire-like robes is in vain.

The renunciation of a mouthful of cooked food is in vain, and consequently, begging for alms is in vain, if knowledge—which is indeed the cause of liberation—does not exist within the tongue [of the seeker]. (77–78)
My knowledge, enriched with the marks appropriate to the stages of life (āśrama), is the cause of liberation;

or rather, having observed sufferings and sins, my mind is set upon the stage of renunciation (tyāga-āśrama). Likewise, having observed pleasures and merits, it is equally inclined toward the householder’s stage (gṛha-āśrama).
Or rather, activity impelled by passion and hatred is the same in its binding effect. (2.257.80) Knowledge without possession is not found anywhere, even in a stage of life (*āśrama*).
Possession is bondage; it is equal in all stages of life, both for me and for you. (2.257.81)
Therefore, O virtuous one! Know me to be unattached, even though I abide in every way within the very abodes of bondage—namely, virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Sovereignty over a kingdom is a constant snare, a bond consisting of affection, action, and the like.
With the sword of knowledge, which flows like a stream of liberation, I have severed [the bonds] while existing.
Through knowledge, I move about in renunciation and do not incur attachment at all.
Even in a kingdom, I do not fall as one bound, though appearing like a king.
The knots of latent impressions have been burnt away by me with the fire of knowledge;
therefore, I move about within the kingdom of the body with the senses and other faculties as my kinsmen. Established in the company of the virtuous, I wander free from all attachment.

I am established in liberation, neither in bondage nor even in sovereignty within the forest. Thus, being eternally liberated, I have developed a sense of reverence for you, O virtuous one; therefore, I ask you: how is it that you, though liberated, assume such contradictory forms? (86–87)
Your beauty is enriched with a golden luster, your body possesses fresh delicacy, and your youth is preeminent; endowed with such form and wealth in every way, how can you be a virtuous woman?
If one were virtuous, she would not be passionate; if she were passionate, she could not truly be virtuous.

Seeing both of these, as well as her yogic power, the assembly was filled with doubt, wondering whether she was truly liberated or not. [She was] rich with the splendor of the assembly of the King of Enjoyment (Bhogarāja) and endowed with the essence of erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra). (2.257.90)
How do you proclaim yourself to be one perfected in yoga and a virtuous woman,
when you have fallen from my yoga and are completely enveloped by the defects of touch? How indeed can you be a teacher of yoga, acting as a restrainer of my heart?

"The person who caused you to enter my kingdom and assembly has brought you under his influence; thus you appear to have fallen from your virtuous character. Having obtained me again as a Kṣatriya, do not bring about a confusion of castes."
"You are a virtuous woman devoted to the dharma of liberation, while I am a householder following the dharma of kingship.
If there were unity between our hearts, a second kind of confusion of dharmas would arise.
O Yoginī, your knowledge of the Dharma and other teachings is now being subverted.
Out of passion you desire to conquer me, yet your hope for victory is bound by fetters;
you are already bound like me, for you are not within the grasp of my hand.
Or else, if you are so arrogant as to show that you have conquered all those on my side once you have defeated me,
then you are truly deluded;
for, filled with indignation yet bewildered by infatuation, you desire to conquer [me].
That which is called yoga is like poison, yet that very same thing, when established in you, is nectar.
For one who desires it, yoga is supreme; for one who does not desire it, however, it is like poison.
Do not display your own excellence, for he is either a liberated soul or a king.
The strength of kings is great sovereignty; the strength of women is beauty and youth;
the strength of the liberated is indeed Brahman. Show me that strength!
(2.257.10) For the powerful should be approached with straightforwardness, for they are givers of happiness.
The powerful destroy the Tathāgata through dishonesty.
Therefore, casting aside all audacity, tell me truly about your birth, lineage, learning, austerity, conduct, disposition, status, desire, and purpose.
Lomaśa said:
Thus, though disregarded by Ānarta with many such improper and inconsistent words, Kuśalā did not indeed give way to fear.
Then that virtuous Aśvapāṭalā, who was even more beautiful to behold than Cāru, possessing lovely wisdom, proceeded to answer him even more extensively.

Thus ends the [section] on the demonstration of the cause for the soul’s departure from the body, within the inquiry into renunciation and non-renunciation, concerning the King of Ānarta and the Yoginī Kuśalā, in the *Lomaśagītā* of the second section, the *Tretāsantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter,
titled "The Dialogue," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 258.
[Author: Chapter 259.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, [the tīrthas] Lomaśa and Aśvapāṭala follow after that.
He spoke a reply to Kuśalā according to the circumstances.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"O Aśvapāṭala! Kuśalā has reached the further shore of yoga."
He whose impurities had been burnt away by the fire of the knowledge of reality spoke; listen to that.
Kuśala said: "Listen, O Ānarta! You stand as the foundation for two pairs of scales."
By your words you maintain the state of a householder, yet you expand upon the nature of a yogi.
You awaken the unskillfulness of one who is skilled through your censures. O King, if such is your defilement, how can it exist in you who are liberated?
The word of a trustworthy person (*āptavākya*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided it is endowed with appropriateness and other such qualities;
it is augmented by power, honored by its genus, similarity of form, and so forth;
it is free from defects such as equivocation (*jalpa*), and has not arisen from a field of error. (5)

Listen with one-pointed mind to such a statement of mine, which is clearly endowed with explicit meaning through the presence of indicative marks (*lakṣaṇa*), connection (*āśleṣa*), and other factors, and which serves as authoritative evidence:
"Just as flour [is not stone], and a cloud [is not] a circle of smoke. (6–7)
Likewise, O Ānarta, they are closely joined; the sustainers of life are closely joined.
Sound, touch, taste, smell, form, space, water, earth, wind, and fire—O King, these are joined within the self like flour or like stones.

They dissolve like clouds and scatter like smoke. (9) They do not recognize their own nature; how then could they perceive another? At that time, the mind, conjoined with them, follows after them in the external world. (2.258.10)
In that case as well, the state of being produced, magnitude, external conjunction,
and the conjunction of the self are the causes regarding the object to be grasped.
Thus, indeed, these are the causes for the perception of all external objects everywhere.
Having formed a volition through the mind regarding my nature, the intellect then effects a firm determination;
through the ego-sense, it conceives of this as its own opinion within itself,
and then this self projects it [onto objects], thinking, "This is mine."
From those [impressions] seen and released, a latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises that produces memory;

and there is ignorance (*avidyā*), or even darkness (*tamas*), which is the subsequent state of non-cognition in deep sleep. Furthermore, in that state, a memory consisting of delusion arises repeatedly.
Then, pleasure and pain, gain and loss, as well as the pleasant and the unpleasant—
among these, time shall be the cause and nature the fulfiller.
Whatever the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) may be, from that a corresponding fruit is produced.
The twenty-fourfold aggregate is indeed the cause of sensation;
it does not perceive the unmanifest, but perceives that which has a manifest form.
That is said to be the one who sees only the gross, and it is that which is mixed with the notions of "mine" and "I."
He who understands the Unmanifest perceives the Self;
as one who contemplates the inner self, he shall reach the further shore.
Manifest are the constituent elements derived from primordial nature—both we men and women. (18–19)
Seated upon the seat of the *bindu*, they consist first of a mass of semen and blood;
after ten nights, there is the *kalala*, then the bubble (*budbuda*), and then the *peśī*.
From that, the limbs arise, including the nails and the ends of the hair.

In the ninth month, whether it be a child, a female, a male, or otherwise, names are dependent upon gender; thereafter follows childhood and so forth. The name for those with delicate limbs is designated as "kumāra" (boy).
Indeed, that very fool possesses the foolishness of one who is unawakened;
he is considered "young" because he is joined with desire through his youthful state.
Remaining [in this world] again and again, he truly departs, having become a hero and then an elder.
Thus, O King, because other constituent parts (kalās) undergo transformation moment by moment,
this subtle differentiation of name, form, and so forth is not perceived;
neither their passing away nor their arising is observed.
For this entire world, which is always rushing about like the flame of a lamp, who is it?
What is this? From where does it come? For what purpose? To whom does it belong? By what means?
Whence does it not come? How is it? Of whom is it? By what is it not? Who is it? And what indeed is it? (26)
Indeed, these very connections of living beings, even with their own limbs, cannot thus be known through mutual power by those who move about;
just as rays [proceed] from the sun, or fires from fuel. (27–28)
Indeed, those things which are momentary cannot be determined with certainty;
likewise, all ordinary beings, whose nature is composite,
are born and die in every single moment as mere aggregations.
The self is eternal, everlasting, established in its own nature, and indeed not a composite.
If that discerning one has attained yoga and remains as if liberated, he perceives the composite as transitory and his own self as eternal. (2.258.30–31)
If you perceive your own self by means of the self within the self alone;
or if you perceive it as non-self, as something separate, or as momentary—[then you do not see the truth].
In this very way, one perceives the self by means of the self as the supreme self, which pervades all.
If you perceive the eternal through the attainment of disciplined yoga,
and likewise resolve upon the equality between yourself and others,
then who are you, whose are you, and for what purpose do you ask me?

"O King, for you who are liberated from the dualities of 'this shall be mine' and 'this shall not be mine,' what is the purpose of such words as 'Who are you?', 'From where?', or 'For what reason? (35) Nevertheless,
do so without forming any attachment, having understood that the state of being separate is transitory.
Having identified oneness with the body, what liberation can there be for you in this inquiry?

(36) Whether in sovereignty, in an enemy, in a friend, or in one who is neutral; whether in defeat or in victory—what indeed is your liberation, O Kṣatriya, while you still perceive "I" and "mine"? (37)
For you, who are attached to the pursuit of dharma, wealth, and pleasure, who follow after the attachment to fruits,
and who are most arrogant with the sense of being a king— what indeed is your liberation?
You perceive distinctions between man and woman, and between the beautiful and the ugly.
When you are completely pervaded by the state of having a body, what indeed can be called liberation in you?
(39) What indeed can be called liberation in you when, having assumed a material nature, you set aside the attributes of the body and speak of the faults of attachment? (2.258.40)
Even while you exist through yoga, you are mocked by non-yoga;
having encountered ordinary sensory contact, what liberation indeed can there be in you?
You are truly a treasury of knowledge, yet you speak to me as if I were a mere woman created by artifice.
O Indra among kings, having reflected and observed, what indeed can be called liberation in you?
For he who possesses a common nature has a common state, and he who possesses consciousness has a conscious state;
since you possess no eye that is equal [to all], what liberation can there be for you? (42–43)
This conscious principle here is skillful when the aggregate is transformed.
O King, know me to be the divine consciousness, free from attachment.
Who belongs to whom, from where, by what means, for what purpose, and why is there this conjunction with a body?
"I am distinct from that; behold this Self as it abides within the body.
(45) "If you cannot see it thus, then you are merely one who is enveloped by the aggregate [of the constituents].
Therefore, O King, your desire for liberation is fruitless for one such as you who is improperly situated. (46)
The virtuous should restrain you from that [conduct], for it is unwholesome food for you.
Since there is no such thing as conduct apart from knowledge, and no knowledge apart from that [conduct], there is certainly none at all in worldly affairs; so what fruit of yoga could there be? 47.

If you perceive the body as the self, then your exertion is in vain, your pride is in vain, and likewise your verbal abuse is in vain; even your effort to associate with the virtuous is in vain. For the Self is neither woman, nor man, nor neuter, and yet it does not exist [as a material entity].

And if you remain thus, O King, why do you not likewise perceive others? Having observed common things and distinguished them from the reality of the Self, one should see the Self everywhere; what else is the characteristic of liberation?
One should perceive all objects of attachment within the Supreme Lord, who is one's own Self.
For one who is liberated, sporting in the Self and delighting in the Self is indeed the characteristic mark.
Now hear from me also about those places rich in attachment for one established in liberation.

For the kingdom is a bond compared to the realm, and the capital city is indeed a bond compared to that; even more than that is the royal palace, for it is a common bond. Even more than that is one's own home, and therein one's own bed is truly a bond. (53)
Even that [enjoyment] is half [complete] when accompanied by a woman; without a woman there is no bondage.
Even in the three [worlds], bondage is merely the act of desire and nothing beyond that.
Even in that case, if there should be latent impression (*vāsanā*), then bondage is rooted in attachment.
The cause for obtaining the elements is food, medicine, and so forth;
likewise, there is indeed bondage from a king, and bondage from servants and the like. In this way, one is joined here with results through attachment to women and other such things.
There is bondage regarding food, clothing, garments, and ornaments;
even the king’s power to punish and favor exists only within the confines of imprisonment.
Furthermore, the king is always subject to dependence on others, even in matters of his own minor affairs, due to the constraints of protocol. (57–58)
Even in matters of subduing servants, in war and peace, in women, in sports and diversions, and in counsel within the circle of ministers—
where is the independence of a king who merely follows what others say? (59)
He remains under the control of his ministers and acts against his own will;
he finds no sleep at the proper time, being preoccupied with people seeking their own interests,
and even while asleep upon his bed, he is awakened by the messengers of his enemies.
And in some places, she is constantly brought under control by female slaves at his command:
"Arise! Bathe! Take hold! Drink! Eat!
Speak! Listen! Come! Look! Desist! Delight! (6.2)
Thus, this king is always dependent on others and under the sway of attachment;
supplicants arrive, yet he does not even venture to give.
If he gives, there is anxiety over the depletion of the treasury; if he does not give, enmity arises. (63–64)
Constantly preoccupied with protection, the king is always bound by anxiety;
driven by the fear of death, the king indeed suspects everyone.
Thus, both the king and his subjects live in mutual fear.
Everyone is a king in their own home; everyone is a householder in their own home.
In every household, all possess the power to punish and to favor.
Sons, wives, the home, the self, the treasury, friends, and accumulated wealth—[all these belong to each individual].
For all of them, those associations are indeed equal states of bondage:
"My country is destroyed, my village is ruined, my horse is killed;
my wealth is lost, and the crops have been burnt by the fire of frost."
The field has been devoured by birds, and the cows have been carried off by thieves;
my food has been ruined by diseases, and my independence has been destroyed by enemies.
I have been assailed by the arrows of their words and ousted from my royal throne.
Thus, he is indeed tormented by states of attachment and by false cognitions,
as well as by mental sufferings born of passion and anger produced by a ruler or by others,
and he is truly consumed by the pains arising from disease and humiliation.
One who is constantly attached to worldly ties forcibly experiences suffering.
Therefore, what knower of yoga would undertake a kingdom—which offers little pleasure, is exceedingly full of pain, and is devoid of essence—being like a seat of glowing embers? (72–73)
"You consider this city, kingdom, and supreme wealth to be yours;
tell me, O knower of the Self—who are you, and to whom do this wealth, kingdom, and city belong?
This body of yours, composed of the five elements, shall enter the fire."
And for me as well, there is equality in that regard, not distinction.

For one who desires the destruction of the natural state of the relationship between container and contained, there can be no non-attachment to the body, which is by nature subject to attachment. (75–76)
But for the conscious one who is unattached, there is no attachment whatsoever;

for him who is devoid of the relationship of container and contained, who is non-material, and who is eternally existent— O King, speak, for I am capable of explaining this in a thousand ways through knowledge.
I have no attachment to the female body; how then could I have any toward you as my wife?
You ought not to speak so plainly of a state of attachment while considering me a woman.
Surely you have heard from Pativratā that liberation is attained in its entirety through devotion to one’s husband.
You are without attachment and free from bonds; how then are you attached to kingship?
All that you have heard has become fruitless for you, as you dwell in the state of identifying with the body.
Or perhaps what was heard has merely passed through your ears, and you act out of sheer deceit.
Or rather, neither has anything been worn nor cooked by you yourself,
yet you now remain attached to worldly and bodily things;
O Self, you appear bound like an ordinary beggar.
I myself have entered into you, who are the Self and the Lord.
Tell me, what harm has been done there to me, who am eternally liberated?
O King, it is a constant rule for the virtuous to dwell in emptiness.
"Having entered into the void, what fault have I committed against you here?
(84) I do not touch you at all, neither with my arms, nor with my thighs, nor with any of my limbs.
You must not speak of good or evil between us in this assembly. (85)
Whatever has been done between a man and a woman, whether good or bad, is called a mutual union.
These are virtuous elders, and you are the king, the most excellent of gurus.
Indeed, one should never speak of the talk of yogis among yogis.
Just as water remains upon a lotus leaf without attachment,
so shall I dwell within you with my own self free from attachment.
I shall dwell there in the manner of a yogi for the sake of attaining the supreme perfection of the Self.
Where indeed those virtuous, steadfast ascetics who have reached the further shore of yoga dwell,
having ascended to the station of the Supreme Lord and remaining present in embodied form—
who that possesses a self would not desire to reside there through the practice of yoga? (89)
"O King, if you perceive my touch while dwelling within me,
then all the knowledge you have acquired is seedless, being merely an ornament of speech.
You have indeed fallen from the state of a householder, yet you do not find the station of liberation."
Standing here in the interval between both, you are a mere mimic;
for when one who is liberated meets another who is liberated, or when one who is wise meets another who is wise,
no confusion of dharma arises, since it is only the union of two who possess the same dharma that constitutes such a meeting.
The union of one being with another being, and likewise the union of the self with the Self;
the union of one yogi with another yogi—in these cases, there is indeed no confusion of castes.
O King, you are a knower of Brahman, and I, Savarṇikā, am likewise a knower of Brahman.
In our union, no confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) is considered to occur.
Indeed, Brahmā himself took on the form of the daughter of Brahmā (the Gaṅgā) at Somanātha.
Long ago, he was summoned by the Moon for the purpose of consecrating Somanātha.

At that time, the mental, skillful activity produced at the sacrifice was none other than myself in the form of Satī; I am known as Kriyā and called Kuśalā. I am the wife of Kratu—the sacrifice—existing in this manner through the state of a body.
I am virtuous by nature and have reached the further shore of yoga;
therefore, O King, I exist here as the Self and am not a woman. Furthermore, when the state of equanimity has arisen, there is no longer any confusion whatsoever here.

Having heard that your intellect is cultivated for liberation and seeks what is wholesome, I, Kuśalā, have come here desiring to know about your liberation. [I am here] at this imperishable sacred field of Saurāṣṭra, at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. (2.258.100)
Having established my abode on the bank of the pool named Kuṅkuma, I dwell there;
having stayed for one night within your body, I shall return to my own place.
O King, I am a Brahman-yoginī and do not remain long with a greedy person.
Honored with hospitality and with the gift of my very self through the food of knowledge,
tomorrow I shall go to my own abode before reaching one who stands in equal yoga—
there where Lomaśa, the best among those who know yoga, dwells in that same state.
"The Lord is my own light and the supreme knower of the Self.
Having become one with Him therein, O King, I, being skilled, indeed carry the bliss of Brahman; yet I have assumed this form for the sake of this assembly, which possesses but limited yogic power.
Wherein the foremost vision of the body perceives all that is to be seen;
for these sages are indeed rigid, being practitioners of the yoga of bodily perception.
What shall I say to you? Do not be rigid, O King!
O King, the strength of the self does not increase in this way for those who perceive only the body;
nor can there be the attainment of the self for those who associate with their equals.
Furthermore, liberation cannot arise from the life of a householder as long as one has not realized the nature of the self.
As long as one remains attached to worldly existence, one indeed continues to act with a sense of "mine-ness.
O Ānarta, do not harbor anger; eat what is true and digest it.
Go to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake for the sake of attaining the perfection of mastery over yoga.
Worship the Lord of Yogis, Lomaśa, who is your own self-luminous spiritual preceptor, and the Goddess Yoginī who is ever-contented; thus become one who never falls from his state.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
To her who was speaking thus, the King of Ānarta then did not grant his heart, which was worthy of her dwelling, for he remained there in meditative composure.
And there, both of them indeed engaged in a conversation with one another at dawn.
Then the sages, their purpose understood, departed for their respective abodes.
O Aśvapāṭala! Ānarta, having realized his own lowliness, attained the supreme pinnacle through the company of a yogin.
Then he set out with her for Aśvapaṭṭasara, where,
having attained full yogic power from the sage Lomaśa and having gained his own supreme awakening through his own inner light.
Having become satisfied with the Yoginī and having been instructed in the state of Brahman,
Ānarta departed for his own city of Camatkārapura.
Therefore, O King, householders must cultivate renunciation.
Or rather, through the yoga of those who possess renunciation, liberation comes into one's hand;
from association with the virtuous, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa will certainly be met.
Even for one who is incomplete, perfection is attained through every effort.
Indeed, householders who have not renounced may become renunciants through the yoga of their guru.
Just as dancers are born skilled through practice,
so too do householders attain the supreme goal through association with such virtuous men.
"They will surely depart, there is no doubt— even those who are greedy for illusion," having spoken thus to Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa observed silence.
King Aśvapāṭala also attained satisfaction upon hearing this.
That sacred ford is known as Kuśalatīrtha and also as Ānartatīrtha.
It is also called Yogitīrtha, and it is situated within the waters of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
by bathing there or by drinking its water, one attains the vision of the Self.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Discussion between King Ānarta and the Brahmin’s Daughter Kuśalā-Sādhvī, and the Exposition that Liberation Occurs Either through Renunciation Even in the Householder State or through Association with the Holy," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
