Chapter 259 [Author:
Chapter 260 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to what the King of Horses then asked Lomaśa once more; I shall relate that which is for the benefit of the virtuous.
The Horse Pāṭala said:
"O Guru! How did the weariness with one's own manifestation arise, which has the eternal as its refuge, and how did the certainty regarding the reality of the formless Hari come about?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
To the ascetic named Brahmakallola, a devotee of the Brahmins, there was born in a former kalpa a son, the lord Trivikrama;
he was an incarnation of Śrī Hari, and again in another kalpa, he became Hari himself.
Then he became Trivikrama, the one who seized the kingdom from the powerful Bali.
Suddenly, on the bank of the Golden River (Svarṇanadī), at the site of the Nārāyaṇa lake, he beheld a superhuman man within his heart through yoga.
He is endowed with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, trident, and arrow;
his right hands bear the marks of the banner, svastika, thunderbolt, and so forth.
He is laughing, pervaded by splendor, gracious, and long-eyed.
With arms reaching down to his knees, exceedingly radiant and endowed with splendor,
the Lord beheld within himself his own manifestation as Vāmana,
who is Brahman in form, Trivikrama, and the preceptor of the powerful Iṅguda.
Then, upon seeing his own form within the glorious Nārāyaṇa,
he suddenly became bewildered for a moment and thought, "Who is this [separate being]?
Thereafter, with divine vision, he realized his own original form.
He praised Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva, his Lord and Supreme Controller:
"O Inner Self, O Supreme Self, You are the sustainer of all incarnations;
You are the cause of all manifestations, residing within the heart of all. (2.259.10–11)
Everything, including your body which consists of both the Brahman and the non-Brahman, resides within your heart;
I am your separate dwelling, yet I am also your inseparable abode.
You alone are the supreme reality, who by your grace have become the object of my vision.
Within my field of experience, form is endowed with direct perception.
Having attained the vision of the self, and having attained the vision of the supreme self—
having attained both visions, I have today become one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Give me your command, O ocean of compassion, O friend of the world, O Janārdana!
Having attained You, the Supreme Self, nothing remains to be attained.
Having made Your yoga my garden, nothing remains to be done.
Thus praised, the Lord, the glorious Śrīśa Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa,
then showed him his own radiant form and his own abode, as well as the entire wheel of worldly existence, all within that single unity. (16–17)
The lords, the persons of Brahmā, the liberated ones, the many abodes,
the gods, the sages, the hosts of ancestors, the lords of the gods, and human beings;
the serpents, the rākṣasas, the daityas, the dānavas, and even the asuras.
He showed him animals, birds, and even stationary beings, both insentient and sentient;
all the great elements, the principles, stable primordial nature, the transformations, and those possessing bodies, along with their dissolution into that [nature].
Having thus demonstrated this, he indeed vanished.
Having revealed this very knowledge— which is immediate, eternal, and pertaining to the Self—
he established it firmly within his heart.
He granted him this boon: "May you always possess a nature consisting of light;
and may this knowledge, known as self-luminous, never be obscured.
From that time forward, this Lord Trivikrama has been self-radiant.

He became renowned among yogis as one possessed of self-luminosity. Having beheld that sacred field known as Akshara, which was charming, rich with the abode of Hari, and endowed with the Ashvapattha lake, he made his request. (24)
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "So be it," for the purpose of his own dwelling; and there, Narāyaṇa assumed such a divine form as was required,
possessing a celestial body with four arms.
The mental son of Śrī Hari, who is the refuge of eternal knowledge,
having bathed there in the Nārāyaṇahrada together with Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, then quickly proceeded to the site of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He attained [this state] through yoga, speed, power, and the grace of Hari.
Thus, having obtained another birth, another body, and likewise another mode of life, he indeed assumed a physical form, though with the designation of "liberation," as the son [of the Lord]. (28–29)
Having always attained, by way of his incarnational form, the divine form of Viṣṇu— the mental-born form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— Nārāyaṇa was born as soon as he appeared.
Endowed with detachment from worldly objects and full of devotion, he was sixteen years of age.
In the field of Kuṅkuma, the Lord became one whose complexion was like saffron.
Indeed, he became a natural treasury of all branches of knowledge.
He is the very locus of omniscience, endowed with all sovereign powers;
he is the creator of all that is auspicious, devoted to the dharma of the yogis;
his actions transcend all others, and his description transcends all others. (33)

Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa moved within that field of the imperishable (akṣara-kṣetra) and instructed him in all duties— those pertaining to the world, those pertaining to the Vedas, those of the mind, and those that follow them— in order to establish his lineage beginning with his guru. (34–35)
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "O son, practice the Sāttvata duties which bring about your welfare.
Conquer your vital breath, and endure hunger, thirst, cold, and heat. (26)
Having conquered the senses through austerity, protect truth and self-restraint;
protect freedom from malice, lack of envy, and straightforwardness as your character.
Offer oblations to the gods, the ancestors, and guests, and subsist on the remnants of that food.
Worship Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord; do not sleep in the darkness of ignorance.
O son, since consciousness is as unstable as a bubble on the surface of water and is fleeting, do not place your trust in it like an ignorant man, for it is accidental. || 38–39 ||

For enemies who are vigilant, sleepless, and ever-exerting find a vulnerability in this body; do not be overcome by them. The days pass away in succession, truly cutting short the lifespan of living beings.
Life perishes constantly; go for refuge to the Guru.
The ignorant desire the nourishment of flesh and blood through the body and its like, yet at the end all this must depart, while they remain fast asleep regarding the means to liberation.
O son, do not proceed as an ordinary man would by means of that alone—
merely through the singular suffering at the end, which carries one away from the state of non-becoming.
Go instead to the great-souled yogis who abide in the virtue of the righteous.
Therefore, properly attend to this path that is righteous, which bestows liberation and leads to the ultimate Imperishable;
inquire about it and retain its words.
Restrain the churning of the mind and bring forth steadfastness toward the Lord of the virtuous.
Taking hold of the ladder of Dharma and ascending the stage of devotion,
proceed to the eternal abode with the impetus of self-realization.
O best of Brahmins, cast those who are atheistic and devoid of devotion to your left.
O son, abandon from afar hope, craving, anger, and delusion.
Taking hold of the boat of yoga, cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
This world is led away by death and crushed on all sides by old age.
One is indeed carried away in the Vaitaraṇī river; cross it with the boat of knowledge.
Whether he is standing, moving, drinking, or lying down on his bed, death watches for the mortal—do not fall into its power.

Death, arriving unexpectedly, seizes and departs with one who is still asleep— while he is amassing things for the sake of pleasure, unsatisfied, greedy, conceited, unfulfilled, oppressed by obstacles, most arrogant, and treading upon a wrong path.
The interior of the cosmic egg is a chamber filled with darkness;
to exit from it, you must hold fast to the lamp of knowledge.
Indeed, while many cycles of bodies pass away fruitlessly, [you must seek the light].
"O you who carry the essence of Brahman, through divine merit you have attained the state of a Brāhmaṇa.
This great and most excellent body of Brahman is not suited for petty desires;
it is intended for liberation, the attainment of dharma, austerity, and the highest good. (53–54)
Such a priceless jewel, which grants the fruits of one's desires,
must not be treated with contempt or deemed worthless, like a petty cowrie shell.
(5) Concealing her face from above, she is filled within with longing.
She displays modesty toward this eater in the presence of other people.
Pervaded internally by both poison and nectar, she strives to bind him and is intent upon her own gain; yet, having eaten, she causes him suffering.
Even as one abandons it, this [desire] does not leave; it goes along with him to another place.
Though treated with contempt, it remains attached, bound by the root of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Called "Hell," she makes her guest dwell for a long time within her own palaces.
Behold this deceptive display of intoxication, which renders one heedless!
Who indeed would be bound or impassioned therein, possessing divine vision? Never allow yourself to be led astray by that which is attached to the body as if it were a worthy vessel. (2.259.59–60)
The body is bound by karma and is the producer of further karma;
it has desire as its limit and anger as its end—observe that as your own nature. Where there is fear of kings and likewise fear of thieves, [there too is this nature].

Abandoning that divine wealth, acquire instead the provisions for the journey—that certain, imperishable substance by which one lives in the next world and is never separated from it; gather that, my son. (62–63)
For mother, father, friends, and kinsmen do not follow one into the state of mingled existence;
indeed, only one's karma goes with one. Therefore, practice that which is beyond action (naiṣkarmya).
Accumulations of gold, kingdoms, male servants, female servants, and beloved offspring—[none of these follow].
When the body perishes, they depart; therefore, worship the Lord who is your companion.
Worship always the Supreme Lord, the witness dwelling within, the bestower of the bliss of Brahman, the deliverer, and the treasure-house of joy.
Those who follow the duties of a householder go to the worlds of Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati,
and Śatakratu, only to perish at their end.
O son of Brahmā, do not fix your livelihood upon the state of a householder.
Bear the vow of Brahman, which is fearless, infinite, and a treasure-trove.
Being unattached and possessing divine vision, bring about the presence of Brahman.
Having surrendered all action unto me, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme.
Enjoying the supreme state beyond the qualities (nirguṇya), you shall become liberated in the Imperishable as it were.
Living in a village is indeed bondage; having severed that, enter the forest.
What use have you for wealth, friends, kinsmen, or even a son?
Having become self-luminous, enjoy your own light.
Beholding those who are dying and those who are equal to you standing in this world,
and reflecting upon those who will die, seek the Self that resides within the cave of the heart.
One should perform auspicious deeds quickly; indeed, what is to be done tomorrow should be done swiftly today.
I know not what death will seize and depart in another moment.
For this worldly existence is the cresting flame of Death, the Great Time, in his act of devouring.
Taking refuge in the Guru, being possessed of discernment, attain liberation with your whole being. (74) Death is the liberation of the self; therefore, strive for that alone with diligence.
The wise man is intent on attaining liberation, while one devoid of that is of the class of the dull-witted. (75)
Human birth is indeed difficult to obtain here as a staircase to heaven;
by means of it, accomplish this liberation, which is infinite and eternal bliss.
He whose mind does not run elsewhere than toward the path of liberation—

He alone is a performer of meritorious deeds and is not to be grieved for by any human beings. (77) He whose mind is pure and firm regarding the goal of liberation, who has commenced the practice thereof, and who is free from other dispositions—such a person has no fear of time. (78)
For one who has been struck down by merit and demerit, who is greedy, whose soul is attached to sense objects,
and who is immersed in bonds of affection, there exists danger from time.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and tens of thousands of sons and wives—
"Who were those who existed in past times, and whose is this present one?
I am alone, known as the Self; you too are yourself the Self, solitary.
Others have gone elsewhere, and they do not see one another."
They have no business with you, nor do you have any business with them here.
They have gone by their own actions; you shall go by your own deeds.
This world is full of self-interest, affectionate toward its own interests, and engaged in its own pursuits.
Having swiftly accomplished their own purpose, they abandon a person devoid of merit.
(83) For those who are prosperous and wealthy, even a stranger acts as a kinsman; for the poor and destitute, even a kinsman acts as a stranger. (84)
Having entered into union with a wife, a person accumulates inauspicious karma;
from that arises a birth fraught with afflictions, followed by suffering and yet another birth.
Thus, for one who is immersed in this cycle and impelled by latent impressions (vāsanā), [the wheel of existence continues].
Indeed, from the middle of the ocean, no journey to the shore is possible.
Therefore, my son, having attained Dharma accompanied by dispassion, and with the eye of the lamp of knowledge, go to the supreme state through devotion. (86–87)
Time cooks all beings in the cauldron known as delusion, by means of the sun-fire, the fuel of days, and the ladles of months, seasons, and years.
In this, I see no protector; you do not see one, nor does anyone else.
I do not see anyone whom I do not see, nor do I see anyone who does not see me.
Therefore, in this land of action, always worship the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign of Śrī, so that you may go to the imperishable abode. (2.259.90)
Of what use is birth, or the body, or knowledge, or virtue,
or austerity, or dwelling in the forest, if through them liberation does not occur?
He who is called Aśvapāṭala is indeed self-luminous.
Having attentively grasped what was spoken by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he constantly set his mind upon liberation while always dwelling in celibacy.
Sometimes visible and sometimes invisible, he indeed moved about upon the earth.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, he possesses a divine body that is exceedingly radiant;
he is long-lived, a great liberated soul, and conducts himself beyond the reach of ordinary men. Free from all attachments, he has attained union with Brahman.
Having become twofold, with one body he went to the supreme Imperishable (akṣara),
while with the other he always remains here in this field known as Akṣara,
devoted in spirit to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 95–96 ||

O King, having quickly attained the knowledge of reality through my yoga, [know that] the preceptor is the refuge of all sciences, a lord who is a treasury of wisdom; he may have four arms or two arms, being a treasure-house of bliss according to one's desire. (97)
Worship this Supreme Self, and here you shall possess a divine body.
O King, that sacred ford known as Svataḥprakāśa exists within the waters of Aśvasaras; it bestows divinity through bathing, drinking, and other such acts. || 98–99 ||
Having attained this knowledge, liberation will surely occur; there is no doubt.
There shall be the illumination of all sciences and the self-illumination of the Self.
It shall be the illumination of the Deity and the illumination of the consciousness of the Intellect.
"O son, that which cannot be attained through knowledge, nor through dharma, nor even through austerity,
is indeed obtained from even a small fraction of the grace of the Guru.
Having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the glorious Lomaśa became silent.
Then the king, exceedingly gratified and drawn by the sweetness [of what he had heard], while remembering Hari within his own heart,
inquired regarding the fruits of the deeds performed.

(10.3) Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Purifying Study Arising from the Instruction of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the State of Liberation for the Son of Brahmakallola," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Fifty-Nine (259).
Chapter 260: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 260.
[Author: Chapter 261.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O illustrious Rādhikā, to the story of King Aśvapāṭala.
Furthermore, he asked Lomaśa about the means for attaining happiness.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"Gifts, sacrifices, austerity, and service to the guru, and so forth—"
"Even that which is performed by a yogi for the sake of liberation is either fruitless or yields its fruit.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"O King, that which has been performed is never fruitless, nor does it perish here."
Having experienced the fruit, it suddenly dissolves even for yogis.
(3) For all beings in all creations, there is the experience of the fruits of their actions;
however, when a gift is given, there is indeed no such experience for the giver in that regard. (4)

All actions, whether merit or sin, should be offered and surrendered to the Lord of the Good; once surrendered, they are no longer experienced. When offered to Hara, this very state becomes free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇya).
The fruit of that offering is the grace of Hari. (6) Through that grace, the attainment for the devotee who has offered it is the state of having Hari as one's refuge;
residence in the abode of Hari is considered the fruit, which is the bliss of liberation. (7)

If ordinary karma yields extraordinary fruit when offered to Kṛṣṇa, yet this very same [karma] is experienced among the lords and others— among gods, humans, and other species, whether high or low— only when it has not been offered to Kṛṣṇa. (8)
The doer, when the time has come, is led into affliction and defilement.
(9) Indeed, the wicked repeatedly go from poverty to poverty, from disease to disease, from fear to fear, and from famine to famine. (2.260.10)
From prosperity to prosperity, from joy to joy, from heaven to heaven,
and from happiness to happiness, those who perform meritorious deeds proceed indeed to great festivals.
Those who do not give are handless, like serpents, reptiles, and the like.
Those who possess bodies that yield the fruit of their own atheism are born as *tāmasa* beings.
Indeed, those who are givers, deities, those to be accomplished, residents of sacred sites, lords, lovers of the gods, guests, brahmins, and the virtuous come into existence. (12–13)
In this world, those people who do not give are like chaff among grains,
or like jackfruit eaten by an elephant, or like rotten eggs among birds—
those for whom there is neither dharma, nor faith in the hereafter, nor generosity, nor even beneficence. (14)
Those who merely fill their bellies will indeed obtain no new higher rebirth.
In this world, people who only nourish their own stomachs consume nothing but sin;
they will not give what was not given to others in future births.

The king named Śveta did not obtain food or water in heaven because he had given very little in charity here on earth; for although he had given gold, diamonds, and the like, as well as vehicles and mounts, he considered those gifts to be insignificant. (17)
He indeed obtained all of that [in heaven], yet there was neither food nor water.
Then, having returned from heaven hungry, he made an effort to satisfy his hunger by licking the ashes produced from his own corpse.

Seeing him, Nārada also caused his sons to perform an excellent *śrāddha* for his sake, including the abundant offering of food, water, and other gifts. Thereupon, that king named Śveta indeed attained satisfaction.
Therefore, O King, everything given in the land of action (karmabhūmi) is obtained;
nothing that is not given is obtained anywhere. Therefore, one should give according to the prescribed rule. A performed deed—whether white or black—runs after the doer.
Each respective experience is consumed like a shadow belonging to the self;
though veiled by karma and accompanied by mental agitation, it seeks the prospect of happiness.
Enveloped by various aggregates of beings, Time drags it away.
Just as flowers and fruits belong naturally to a tree,
so do the results of past actions remain with the embodied soul through the power of time.
And their fruit— be it happiness or suffering, gain or loss, decline or prosperity— likewise persists.
Honor and dishonor, poverty and prosperity, festivals and sorrows—these continue until death; they do not cease even when struck.
Furthermore, the suffering earned by oneself, beginning with lying in the womb and so forth, [persists].
Furthermore, one experiences all that was previously done, again and again, in successive order.
Just as a calf seeks out its own mother even among thousands of cows, so too does karma reach its own doer. (27–28)
The staining of cloth is dissolved by alkaline water;
internal impurity dissolves through austerity accompanied by righteousness.
O ascetic, the footprint of a fish is not seen in water.
Likewise, the category of action does not manifest at all within the treasury of knowledge.
Enough with unattainable instruments; enough with arduous practices.
By the mere service of the Guru, every accomplishment rests in the palm of one's hand.
Whatever kind of perfection a person attains through austerity and the restraint of the senses,
a human being attains that same perfection multiplied a thousandfold through yoga;
thereafter, by the grace of the Guru, one attains it multiplied ten-thousandfold.

The fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and the like is comparable to but a fraction of yoga. O King, without yoga, without knowledge, and even without higher realization (vijñāna), as well as without service to the guru, liberation is indeed difficult to attain.
Having acquired knowledge from the guru and having served the supreme teacher,
and having offered devotion to Hari, one shall swiftly attain the highest liberation.
With his soul purified by theoretical and practical knowledge, he becomes a vessel for the guru’s blessings.

Even having become a Brahmayatī, one shall quickly attain liberation. (36) Indeed, if one possesses good conduct in the first stage of life, one attains liberation swiftly through the grace of the guru; what need is there for the efforts of other stages of life? (37)
Having abandoned states characterized by passion and darkness while established in the hermitage of the Brahman-vow,
and having firmly set out upon the path of purity, one should perceive the Self by means of the self;
[one should perceive] the Self as the soul of all beings and the Supreme Lord abiding within the self.
And having perceived that which abides in all things, one should cast off the bondage of karma.
Just as clouds, having left the ocean,
go toward the dry land, so too those who are liberated, having abandoned the earth, go toward the station of Brahman.
The light joined within the Self shines in all bodies;
it can be seen through austerity, devotion, and also through grace.
One has no fear of others from oneself, nor does one have any fear of oneself from others.
The Supreme Brahman shines forth for one who is free from hatred and attachment. Indeed,
the Supreme Brahman shines forth for one who is devoid of the state of sin, endowed with the state of Brahman, and firmly established in self-abidance.

Having united the self with Śrī Hari and abandoned the deluding Māyā, the Supreme Brahman shines forth for one who is immersed in the lake of Brahman. Having attained equanimity toward both the external and the internal in the primordial state, [the Self is realized]. //44//
Even in adversity, he remains equanimous; then he attains Brahman.
Praise and blame, iron and gold, pleasure and pain, the agreeable and the disagreeable, gain and loss, cold and heat, as well as life and death—[all these he regards with indifference]. 45–46.
When one perceives one's own self, the supreme, the inert, the external, and even the internal with equanimity, then one attains Brahman;
just as one might perceive a cave pervaded by darkness through one's own light.
Likewise, Brahman can be perceived by means of the lamp of self-knowledge.
There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no home equal to Brahman.
There is no suffering equal to craving; there is no happiness equal to contentment.
The cessation of latent impressions, constant adherence to the conduct of Brahman, virtuous behavior, and service to the holy—this is the highest good that bestows liberation.
If someone, having become attached, should think, "I am happy," [he is deluded]. (2.260.50)
One should not think, "This person is happy," for attachment is the source of suffering.
The intellect of one who is attached wavers, and it spreads the net of delusion.
For one caught in that net, indeed, misfortunes converge from all sides.
For both desire and anger destroy the welfare of the embodied being;
consisting of attachment and aversion, these two defects are considered to lead to hell.
Therefore, one who is pure and composed should constantly protect himself from them.
A virtuous man is always devoid of these two; likewise, a chaste woman is then devoid of them.
He who abandons these two achieves a great abandonment, becoming one who has renounced everything.
He who remains unattached to these two attains the imperishable state.
Devoid of those two, he is devoid of [worldly] beings; having abandoned the drawing together of the multitude, he is liberated and before long abides in the supreme good.
Freedom from possessiveness, perfect contentment, desirelessness, and lack of fickleness—these are his qualities.
This has been declared as the highest good; by means of it, one shall attain the supreme state.
There would be sorrow in possession, and when that is empty, how could there be grieving?
Noble persons, citizens, and those born in the kingdom do not take refuge in that which is devoid of qualities.
Even a beloved wife becomes despondent upon realizing [the Self] to be devoid of qualities and tranquil;

even Māyā, having abandoned attachment to that which is devoid of qualities and tranquil, dissolves away. Those possessed of passion do not leap about in the sky when it is free from bait, but they do so when there is bait.
They do not speak to one who is indifferent, nor do they even cause him to speak.

People, like those deprived of their senses, abandon one who is satisfied with wisdom, satisfied with knowledge, and overflowing with the bliss of Brahman, as if he were a delusion, a source of confusion, or mere pleasure. (2.260.60–61)
There is no end to thirst; contentment indeed is the supreme happiness.

Having attained the contentment of wisdom, one becomes immersed in the bliss of Brahman. One should dwell and conduct one's affairs with those yogis who are skilled in the knowledge of the inner self.
Having established friendship with the best among the knowers of Brahman, one shall attain the bliss of Brahman.
(63) In every respect, people are seen to be of the nature of passion (*rājasa*), or of darkness (*tāmasa*), or even half-possessed of goodness (*sāttvika*);
being devoid of the guru’s blessings, they are fit for hell. (64)
Those who dwell in deception, whose minds are intent on violence,
and who disregard their teacher and the Dharma, are defeated for the sake of hell.
Prosperity attends only certain individuals among those groups who are fully characterized by sattva.
Where Nārāyaṇa dwells, there is perfection and liberation.
(66) Everyone desires to go higher and higher above the world; they strive by various paths, yet they do not reach their desired goal. (67)
Therefore, O King, having fully embraced the path of yoga— the path of Hari, which is higher than the highest—
a yogi should set forth, equipped with the provisions of compassion.
For without yoga, it is not possible to attain the eternal Brahman.
Without yoga, even the bondage of karma cannot be cast off.
O King, dwelling of the mind in Kṛṣṇa is yoga, which bestows supreme liberation.
O King, dwelling of the self in Kṛṣṇa is considered that eternal liberation.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, born of Dharma— these brothers too, having meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, attained identity with it.
So too did Kapila, Ṛṣabha, Datta, Sanaka and the others, and Nārada.
Pṛthu, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, and others,
as well as Śveta, Vyāsa, and others, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
having accomplished the yoga of the Supreme Brahman, they attained identity with it.
The cessation of all phenomena is considered the supreme Nirvāṇa;
for that very activity is offered unto the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Rādhā, Bhū, Līlā, Pārvatī, and Satī—[are His consorts].
Ramā, Kṛṣṇā, Māṇikī, Gaṅgā, Durgā, Sarasvatī,
Jayā, Virajā, Brahmapriyā, and all others—
having accomplished the yoga of the Supreme Brahman, they have attained identity with it. (75–76)
Sacrifice is of the nature of worldly engagement (pravṛtti) when it is offered to the Supreme Deity;
however, O King, this [sacrifice] was fashioned by you as being solely of the nature of renunciation (nivṛtti).
Therefore, you have indeed obtained the supreme fruit of all sacrifices.
O King, that the Blessed One, the beginningless and glorious Narayana,
the Supreme Lord, came here at dawn and granted you his vision;
and that all the gods were satisfied when Hari was satisfied— that is the fulfillment of your sacrifice.
"Today you have accomplished all that was to be done regarding the four aims of human life.
May there always be well-being for you and for those people who constantly practice the dharma of service.
Aśvapāṭala said:
How did the Blessed One become the foremost recipient at sacrifices?
And how were the deities made by Hari entitled to shares in the sacrifice? Śrī Lomaśa replied:
Listen to how it truly occurred at the beginning of the eon and at the commencement of creation:
the deities, together with Brahmā, and the sages whose wealth is austerity, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, desiring an increase in their splendor. (8.2)
They performed austerities with their gaze fixed upward and their arms raised, standing together on one leg.
At the end of a thousand years, they heard a voice from the sky:
"O gods, including Brahmā, and you sages whose wealth is penance!"
The work of active engagement must be performed to increase your strength;
you shall enjoy the supreme fruit of my propitiation and asceticism.
All of you, sacrifice to me and fashion yourselves as my own portions.
And at the sacrifice, you must honor me; for service to me bestows strength.
O King, having come to this auspicious land of Kṛṣṇamaṇi, they performed a sacrifice in the region called Surāṣṭra, where [the fire] was established by you.
O King, I was then present here in this assembly of great sages.
At that time, a divine sacrifice was performed here by the gods and others;
it was a Vaiṣṇava Sarvamedha sacrifice, conducted according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas.
In that sacrificial session, Brahmā himself assigned a portion for Hari;
the gods and the celestial sages likewise assigned portions for Hari.
All of them offered their respective shares to the Supreme Soul for the sake of the sacrifice.
Those portions, characterized by the dharma of the Kṛta Yuga, then became divine;
offered entirely to Śrī Hari, they then assumed the form of Brahman.
Those liberated souls praised the Supreme Lord.
The Supreme Person, resplendent like the sun and beyond darkness—
then that Hari, the bestower of boons, remaining bodiless in the sky for the sake of granting a boon to the gods, spoke from near the Horse-sacrifice lake.
Whatever portion was assigned by each of you has all come to me.
I am pleased; I grant you here a boon that bestows strength.
All of you yourselves shall perform sacrifices accompanied by excellent sacrificial fees.
In age after age, you shall partake in the fruits of worldly activity (pravṛtti).
Other people who perform sacrifices according to your ritual procedures, having assigned portions to you, shall attain the supreme fruit. (95–96)
And you shall obtain those portions being given to you;
in age after age, you shall be partakers of the fruits of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*).
Devotion (*pravṛtti*) in the form of renunciation (*nivṛtti*), when offered to me, shall come to pass.
Just as those portions have been assigned here by you,
so shall the portions be assigned by me in the sacrifice to those who bestow the portions.
You, who provide the fruits of the sacrificial shares, must nourish the worlds.
"O gods, having obtained your share of the fruit from this sacrifice, you shall repeatedly increase your strength and sustain the worlds. Indeed,
you shall be honored by men through sacrifices in all their rites."

"You shall cultivate this [meditation] upon me; this meditation of mine is intended for you. Indeed, I have established that very meditation, which is identical in nature to the injunctions of Vedic sentences, within the Vedic texts.
Having performed sacrifices and partaken of the offerings in the ritual, contemplate the welfare of all beings. (101–102)
The sages such as Vasiṣṭha, the great seers such as Sanaka,
the lords such as Brahmā, the deities such as the Ādityas,
and others such as Manu— all who are entitled to the path of sacrifice. (103)
"Go forth and perform your respective duties; conduct the great sacrifices.
Let the ritual sacrifices proceed, and likewise let the prescribed ordinances be set in motion.
This age called Kṛtayuga, the most excellent of times, is now unfolding."
"The entire four-footed divine Dharma proceeds here.
Having spoken thus to Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa revealed his own form;
indeed, in the form of Hayagrīva, he recited the auspicious Vedas.
Embracing him, he said, "O Brahmin, I cast this burden upon you;
for when the task of the gods becomes unbearable, I shall repeatedly manifest myself through you, who possess the gift of knowledge. Having spoken thus, he vanished.
The great holy site of Hayagrīva was born within that lake;
by bathing there and drinking its water, one becomes possessed of Vedic knowledge.
Brahmā went to his own world, and the gods departed for heaven and other realms.
Thus, O King, Hari became the foremost recipient of the sacrificial offerings.

Then Kṛṣṇa himself established the path of action (*pravṛtti*) and the path of withdrawal (*nivartana*), as well as the state of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*) which bestows strength. || 2.260.110-111 ||
This very one is the Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he, the son of Kambharā, has been described to you by me as the bestower of liberation upon the worlds.
O King, let my words be followed, and let Bāla-Kṛṣṇa be served.

"Kṛṣṇa should be constantly sung of, and He who dwells within should be worshipped; one should go to the imperishable abode and enjoy eternal bliss. Having thus instructed Rādhā, Lomaśa became silent.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of how even Yogins obtain the fruits of serving their chosen Guru and others, and the arising of the portions for Hari and the deities in the sacrifice," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 262 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: thereafter, the King of Āśvapaṭṭala questioned a sage regarding the realization of Śrī Hari as manifest before his eyes. (1) Aśvapāṭala said:
O Sage, this Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the manifest Bhagavān who is without beginning, resides here; O Master, cause me to realize Him.
I perform my worship under His name every day, seeking its true meaning.
"Teach me, who am endowed with all goals, that supreme consciousness belonging to the Lord.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"O King, those wise ones who have reached the further shore of the Vedas are not exclusively devoted [to one path alone]."
Ordinary people do not understand the etymological meanings of Hari’s names;

for those who are single-mindedly devoted are superior, being those who have no other deity, whose very selves are He, who are intent on Him, whose character is His, and whose actions are performed together with Him.
They know when, where, how, and by whom [the scripture] was produced;
thereafter, the devotees praise it as previously revealed by them.
The beginning consists of the origin of birth and the conjunction of the body, senses, and so forth.
That which exists prior to emission and after emission, and which is not found within any form;
that which is the imperishable time (kāla) at the beginning, and in which nothing whatsoever dissolves—that is the primordial, supreme Lord of all others. (7–8)
Since there was nothing else prior to him, he is indeed beginningless;
and he who is possessed of eternal glory, upon whom rests the most excellent of divine splendors,
whose divine attire, arrangement, speech, and prosperity are manifestations of his majesty.
All sovereign powers and all qualities reside there where the glorious feet are found.
Therefore, He is Śrī; because of His identity with Śrī, He is the refuge of Ramā, Lakṣmī, and the rest.
That Blessed One alone is indeed declared to be the Supreme Lord, the Possessor of Glory (Śrīmān).
This is indeed the ancient refuge of men and of the self;
all divine forms are *nārāḥ*, which are its powers (*śaktayaḥ*), and that is their dwelling place.
For those who have attained liberation, there is no *arā*—neither illusion (*māyā*) nor poverty—therein.
Men are liberated [by it], and its abode is Nārāyaṇa; he is indeed so regarded.
He draws forth the entire world, and sometimes all emanations reside within his body; he leads everything back to dissolution, and for that reason he is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa.
Agriculture (*kṛṣi*) is the destruction of impurity, and that is said to be liberation (*nirvṛtti*).
Such is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
"Kaṃ" refers to eternal bliss, or alternatively, to Kaṃ, the Supreme Lord who is Brahman. (15)
She who bears [the world] within her own womb and in her heart is Kaṃbharā.
And here, the son of Kaṃbharā is indeed Kāṃbhareya, for he is Hari himself,
who personally protects the rays— the "cows" (gāḥ) of Kṛṣṇa.
He protects the cows, the milch-cows, the earth, speech, and the divine goal;
his father is Nanda, the cowherd who delights in protecting the cattle.
He protects cities, bodies, and both sentient and insentient beings.

Indeed, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is truly present within them. Because of his greatness, his all-pervasiveness, and his transcendence— he who is the supreme Brahman, Hari, the Supreme Brahman, he is indeed the Blessed Lord himself.
Therein exist all supreme and complete sovereignties;
He alone is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who is renowned as the Highest Lord (Pareśvara).
All that is perishable consists of Māyā, while that which is beyond it is the Imperishable Abode (Akṣara-dhāma).
Hari, who transcends that [unmanifest], is said to be beyond the imperishable (akṣara).
(22) The incarnations of Hari alone manifest from the totality;
the Incarnator himself is called the root of them all, Śrī Hari. (23)
This Hari indeed carries away the minds of his devotees;
he also removes all sufferings, and thus he is celebrated as Hari.
From him arises Hara, who is Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Lord who performs all actions.
Thus addressed by him, the Lord Hari, who possesses sovereign power, replied:
"He who dwells within all things and sports [within them], abiding in their midst—he indeed is called Vāsudeva, the eternal Supreme Lord. (25–26)
He whose nature is desire and whose power is indeed the *śāla* tree—
his *māyā* is that very nature, and he alone is its husband, Mādhava.
The Lord is also declared to be the soul of time (*kāla*), possessing the power to create everything.
In whom all creations enter, or from whom they proceed—he is indeed Viṣṇu.
Because he pervades and encompasses all, he is called the pervasive Viṣṇu.
By self-restraint, people ascend to my supreme abode.
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa is Dāmodara because he delights (ramati) in giving (dāna) and in joy (muda).
His hairs (keśāḥ) are said to be his rays (aṃśavaḥ); indeed, Kṛṣṇa possesses them, and thus he is Keśava.
Fire and the Moon are my two forms; both of them are my mouth and my taste.
Therefore, the sacrifice named Agniṣṭoma is Nārāyaṇa himself.
Fire is the Kṣatriya and the twice-born, while Soma is the Brāhmaṇa; the unity of these two is Hara and Hari.
Fire is the woman and Soma is the man; thus, Agniṣṭoma is Nārāyaṇa.
In ancient times, he recovered the lost cow and the earth;
therefore, he became renowned as Govinda. Because he protects the cows, he is called Gopāla. Furthermore, because he rules over the *hṛṣīkas*, which are the senses, he is Hari.
Hṛṣīkeśa became the master of the senses in the place of austerities (34).
Because he perceives everything below and everything beyond, he is therefore called Adhokṣaja.
Dharma is the bull (vṛṣa), and its abode is the boar (kapin), this one who has the form of a boar (35).
Yogis delight therein; the Lord Rāma is the possessor of delight.
Through the application of qualities and actions, His names are infinite.
Worship the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman.

Kṛṣṇa himself, in the form of a child, shines eternally in the imperishable field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; worship that Bālakṛṣṇa always. Because Māyā (the syllable *bā*) attains dissolution here in Kṛṣṇa, he is therefore called Bālakṛṣṇaka.
Having directed people who are children enveloped in ignorance onto the path of truth,
he draws them to the ground of the imperishable abode and bestows supreme bliss.
Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, Śrīkṛṣṇa, and Puruṣottama.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of the beloved of Brahmā; the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of all, Janārdana;
the Lord of devotees, the Lord of His own—O King, let Him be served and attained! (2.261.40–41)
Aśvapāṭala said:
Oh, what knowledge! Oh, what awakening! Oh, what nectar, what elixir!
This divine [teaching], which grants divine liberation, has been constantly made to drink by my heart. 42.
O treasury of austerity, you have spoken to me the nectar of the stories of Nārāyaṇa;
such a Lord has been shown to me and awakened within my heart.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa has been directly beheld.
This Lord, whose nature consists of Agni and Soma, has been gratified by me;
likewise, he has been propitiated and has truly been attained in person.
There is nothing superior to him, nor is there anything else equal to him.
Indeed, there exists no other narrative equal to this story even within the three worlds;
it is the supreme purifier of all sacred fords and the bestower of all fruits.
Moreover, my own merit has not increased by a small amount here, but has been greatly augmented by you.
"O Rādhikā, having reached Kuṅkumakṣmā, by which means I have seen Hari"—
thinking thus, his own king, considering himself to have fulfilled his purpose, fell prostrate like a staff on the ground before his guru, Lomaśa.
Then Lomaśa spoke to him, who was covered with horripilation and tears of joy:
"Blessed are you; you have been graced, since you have beheld Hari.
Indeed, it is His very compassion that is the cause for seeing Him there, where He is otherwise invisible. (49)
For the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, who descends as an incarnation, is difficult to behold. There is no one in the world dearer to him than his devotee;
therefore, O best of kings, he has himself revealed his own self.
From that, O King, arises forbearance which resides upon the earth;
from that arises taste, by which the waters are composed of flavor;
and from that arises form, by which the sun and other luminaries possess beautiful forms.
From that arises touch, by which the vital breaths of the well-yoked practitioner are sustained;
from that arises sound, by which the worlds utter praise;
from that arises the mind, which maintains the quality of luminosity.
Therefore, the intellect that effects the determination of reality arises;
having known through that intellect Kṛṣṇa, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of the Sātvatas, O King,
those who are composed enter the Supreme Self residing in the heart.

O King, worship that Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—him who is the supreme deity, the sacrifice, the transcendental Self, and the eternal one. He, the Lord of the universe, is eternally sought after in all sacrifices. 56–57.
Those who worship the gods, the ancestors, teachers, the virtuous, as well as guests;
cows, Brahmins, the wretched, the earth, and the chaste mother;
sages, servants devoted to service, wives, husbands, and children— [58]
Those who worship the venerable, the helpless, the destitute, as well as beasts and birds, pillars, trees, and winged creatures—they worship Viṣṇu alone.
For that Blessed Lord resides within and is established in every single body. (2.261.60)
He accepts what is given with faith and brings about the satisfaction of life;
He is this very Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, renowned in the Vedas. O King, worship that Supreme Self who is perceptible to the senses.
Who else in this entire circle of the earth could go about performing great sacrifices and delivering and liberating people, were it not for this very teacher of ours, Kaṃbharānanda? (62–63)
How could thousands and millions of princesses choose that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who enchants the entire world, in his absence?
And how could the gods, the sages, the lords, and the lords of lords [do so]? 64.
How could they come and perform worship in his sacrifices without Hari?
And how could Rādhā, Ramā, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, and the others—crores of them, the wives of Kṛṣṇa—perform service to him without Nārāyaṇa? (65–66)
How indeed could all the marks that ascend through the three worlds exist so directly upon his form without Nārāyaṇa? He,
Kṛṣṇa, is truly the treasury of the Vedas and the very treasury of austerities.
He is the treasure-house of the knowledge of yoga, and he alone is the belly of all.
(68) The Vedas have the Supreme Brahman as their ultimate goal; the sacrifices have the Supreme Brahman as their ultimate goal;
liberation has the Supreme Brahman as its ultimate goal; and austerity has the Supreme Brahman as its ultimate goal. (69)
The Supreme Brahman is the ultimate truth; the Supreme Brahman is the ultimate reality.
The Supreme Brahman is the supreme merit; the Supreme Brahman is the supreme goal.
The dharma of engagement and withdrawal has the Supreme Brahman as its ultimate refuge.

O King, fragrance, which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, is the most excellent quality in earth (71). The auspicious qualities of water, consisting of taste, are likewise devoted to the Supreme Brahman; and the form of luminous bodies is similarly supreme, being dedicated to the Supreme Brahman (72).
Touch, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, is the follower residing within all that is tangible.
Sound, whose essence is the Supreme Brahman, is enveloped by all that is audible. The mind, intellect, ego, and the sovereign consciousness are likewise the Supreme Brahman. (73)
The constituent elements (mātrās) have the Supreme Brahman as their essence; the qualities (guṇas) have the Supreme Brahman as their essence.
Time has the Supreme Brahman as its essence; form is devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Fame, Śrī, the goddess Lakṣmī, and the earth are likewise devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Bhūti, Līlā, Sarasvatī, and Satī are devoted to the Supreme Brahman;
likewise, all the Ṛgvedic verses dear to Brahman are devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
Knowledge, yoga, renunciation, and auspicious actions are supreme, being devoted to the Supreme Brahman. (76)
All causes are directed toward the Supreme Brahman.
For those desiring to know the truth, the Supreme Lord is the ultimate reality. That supreme Master knows the intention of everyone. (77–78)
Hari himself is the sacrifice for the gods, the sacrifice for the ancestors, austerity, charity, and the refuge of all.
He is the abode of all beings, whose dwelling is Kuṅkumavāpikā;
he is the abode of the imperishable Brahman—he is indeed that very Bālakṛṣṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of Nārāyaṇa. Indeed, the Blessed Lord Hari gratifies all those who are single-mindedly devoted to Him;
the Blessed Lord Himself accepts the excellent worship performed according to the prescribed rites.
For those people who are single-mindedly devoted attain the abode of Śrī Hari—
the essence of the religion of exclusive devotion, dedicated to the Supreme Brahman,
equal to the Sāmaveda, and established in the beginning during the Kṛta Yuga. (82)
Indeed, he is sustained by Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa. In ancient times, on the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā, at the Nārāyaṇahrada, Nārāyaṇa performed the divine and ancestral sacrificial rites.
In the ancient age, the sages, the deities and others, as well as Soma and human beings, took refuge in Hari and established the dharma of sacrifice.
In the Kṛta Yuga, Rudra protected the dharma of Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, in the first Kṛta Yuga, Hara instructed the Brahmins;
and the great sage named Suparṇa, having received the dharma of sacrifice from Śrī Puruṣottama,
established that righteous ritual on earth.
Then, O King, Samudra set forth the sacrificial duties;
after him, the sage named Āraṇyaka also set them forth;
and thereafter, the virtuous Manu set forth the sacrificial duties.
The blessed Sanatkumāra set them in motion;
Vīraṇa, Suvrata, Barhiṣad, Dakṣaka,
and Vivasvat established this eternal dharma.
The *sāttvata* dharma, which consists of total surrender, is difficult for people to practice;
yet it is upheld by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa and established once again upon the earth.
By the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, it is made manifest in the form of sacrifice.
O King, when the Dharma consisting of total surrender is established upon the sphere of the earth,
that very Lord, having firmly established the imperishable Dharma in the world,
thereafter sports and indeed governs the subjects as He pleases. (92–93)
Thus, O best of kings, the doctrine of single-minded devotion has been declared to you.

O King, those people on earth who are single-mindedly devoted to Viṣṇu are difficult to find. If this world of Viṣṇu were indeed filled with such single-minded devotees, [it would be a sight to behold].
And there shall be the City of Brahmā, the flawless Kṛta Yuga;
where men, women, animals, birds, deities, and others are all single-mindedly devoted to the Supreme Brahman. (95–96)
All castes there are indeed Vaiṣṇavas, and that place is considered the imperishable state (akṣarapada).
There is no unrighteousness at all there, nor even those born of an unrighteous lineage. All the interactions between men and women there consist of millions of liberated beings.
Whether it be Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, Śveta-dvīpa, or the Badarī forest—
if all people on this earth were exclusively devoted,
being true Sāttvatas possessed of devotion, they would certainly attain liberation.
For having attained their desire, they shall worship the Supreme Person—
those who are exclusively devoted, constantly intent upon the Supreme Brahman. For those who are firmly established in Hari, Hari provides for their acquisition and preservation.
He whom Hari regards as His own being at the very moment of his birth becomes a Sāttvata here; he is possessed of exclusive devotion to Dharma,
and from that, he attains the supreme goal in liberation, which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman.

He who is beheld by Nārāyaṇa indeed becomes awakened; O King, one does not become awakened anywhere merely by one's own will. Hari himself does not look upon one who is still joined with the characteristics of worldly activity.
Mahāmāyā, Brahmā, the gods, and human beings behold him;
thereafter, they all indeed become transformed and bound by Māyā.
However, if they perform service to the Sātvatas with true devotion, [they are liberated].
Then, after some time, having attained freedom from the qualities (*nairguṇya*), they go to the Imperishable;
or else, when they are looked upon with compassion by the Sāttvata [Lord] within the assembly of the Sāttvatas,
they become those who are looked upon with the singular compassion of the Sage.
Then, their hearts will surely undergo a transformation quickly;
of this there is no doubt—either through the food of [Hari’s] grace, or by consuming even a mouthful of water or food from Hari or his devotees. || 107–108 ||
Pure intellect, directed toward the state beyond the qualities (*nirguṇa*), gradually arises;
it becomes stainless and serene within the circle of the Sāttvatas.
By dwelling there, one gradually attains the state of a Sāttvata and liberation.
"They will go, there is no doubt, for that state is to be accomplished through compassion.
Having spoken thus, the great sage Lomaśa then became silent.
O Rādhikā, Aśvapaṭṭala then worshipped the sage Lomaśa.
Having fulfilled his purpose through many ritual preparations, he then,
desiring to visit the sacred fords on the northern shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara,
requested Lomaśa; and together with Lomaśa, he proceeded from there.
Accompanied by his entire caravan, he proceeded to the lakes and sacred fords (*sarastīrthāni*).

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Lomaśa’s Revelation of the Primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the Manifest Supreme Lord to Aśvapāṭalā, and the Instruction on Dharma Devoted to the Supreme Brahman," in the *Lomaśagītā* within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 262 [Author:
Chapter 263 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: the king named Aśvapātala first went to Somatīrtha together with Lomaśa. Having bathed there according to the prescribed rites and having given various gifts, [he remained].
Having paid homage to the site of the sacrificial post (yūpasthalī), he then proceeded to Rāmatīrtha.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O great sage, how did this sacred ford (tīrtha) bearing the name of Rāma come to be?"
"Relate this ancient story in brief.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"In former times, there was a king of the Siṃha lineage named Bhānuvīrya."
King Dharmadhara rules the kingdom of the Gopanātha and other regions splendidly;
he governs the territories of Śatruñjaya, constantly uttering "Rāma, Rāma," "Rāma, Rāma," and "Rāmāditya. (4–5)
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa, the Sun!"—thus indeed does the Vaiṣṇava chant together with his family.
His subjects dwell in happiness, they are abodes of joy, and remain established in bliss.
They always worship Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, and Acyuta. Bhaṇavīrya constantly practices righteousness even toward guests;
he performs acts of charity, fire-offerings, and circumambulations for the sake of the virtuous and for the rites of the gods.
While he was living in this manner, once indeed a physical hardship arose for that king, who was a bearer of the earth, by the name of Bhāladeśa;
he set out with his own army toward the ocean for the sake of victory.
Having crossed the Sābhramatī river and conquered the regions known as Dhavala,
he advanced to conquer the kingdom of Bhāṇuvīrya;
he [then] subdued the army of that king, as well as its haughty villages and cities.
Having made his own territories secure, he marched toward Siṃharāyikā; indeed, in order to conquer it, he quickly drew near. A circle of troops was stationed all around the city of Siṃharājya.
Having besieged the capital, he sent a messenger to the king. The messenger delivered the king's words: "Submit to our authority, or else give battle here, or else surrender the entire kingdom."
Bhāṇavīrya also spoke to the messenger of the king:
"In my kingdom, no injustice exists, nor does any unrighteousness exist.
The Lord Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are always worshipped by me. (15)
All virtuous people are protected, and guests are always honored.
It is perceived that the kingdom has been entrusted by me for the sake of Rāma’s refuge;
herein there is no subjection to another, nor indeed any war with men. (16–17)
The gift of the kingdom was made to Rāma; how could it be enjoyed by another?
I am indeed his foremost servant, yet the Blessed One himself will fight.
Speak! I shall certainly not give up the kingdom, nor shall I submit to your control.
"The Blessed One himself will perform the battle for his own purpose.
O Indra among kings, be prepared and do not harbor pride," he said to the lord of the earth; "or else, say what you wish and return to your own abode. (2.262.20)
"Or rather, I shall welcome you in the form of a friend;
tell me again what you desire here," he said, looking about.
Then the messenger went and reported these words exactly as they were spoken. 9.
He dispatched a messenger to the king, saying, "Prepare yourself!
Having waged war, I shall seize the kingdom; do not indulge in pride.
For Nārāyaṇa will certainly not protect his devotee in battle. (22-23)
Having thus dispatched the messenger who signaled for battle,
he caused the sounds of kettledrums, cymbals, and conchs to resound simultaneously;
and he had various mechanical noises produced in the vicinity of the fortress.
Having bound the fortress-guards, those stationed at the gate-towers, and likewise the door-keepers,
and having brought them under his own control, the king, the upholder of the earth,
entered the city of Siṃharājya together with his army.
Trembling with fear, the subjects remembered the infallible Rāma—the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Protector and Supreme Sovereign.
Having proceeded directly to the royal palace, the king, accompanied by his forces, [entered]. (27)
Out of his valor in speech, he requested either a wrestling match or the kingdom.

Then, from his body, hundreds of hideous, naked women of black complexion emerged in the form of female elephants;
they blazed up instantly and were reduced to ashes right there. (63)
Then, from his body, there emerged from that place beings whose physical forms were withered:
old men with large heads, emaciated bellies, and thin chests; men of sinful appearance, swarming with flies and mosquitoes. (64–65)
Dark-complexioned, hungry, merciless, and embodiments of evil,
they suddenly burst into flames from the fire that had arisen;
they too were reduced to ashes from his body.
Indeed, streams of phlegmatic threads consisting of blood-born organisms quickly issued forth from there, for they were the very nature of that house of disease;
then, having become smoke, they blazed and vanished into the sky. (67–68)
Pārṣṇirada became pure, possessing a body equal to that of a god;
he was made divine by Nārada through the power of the divine holy site (tīrtha).
He then quickly bathed in the water there and drank the auspicious water.
Having washed the feet of Nārada, he drank the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana).
He became endowed with golden garments, adorned with golden earrings,
his face possessing the luster of the moon, his radiance like that of the sun, and worthy of the abode of the gods.
Though his body was divine, he danced while covering himself with dust;
repeatedly perceiving the greatness residing at the feet of Nārada, he cried out:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa! Bāla Kṛṣṇa! Nārāyaṇa! Hare! Hare! (72)
"O Vāsudeva, Supreme Brahman, Supreme Self, Lord of Śrī!
He constantly chanted [this] alone and spoke nothing else at that time. Having become divine, he did not even forget the chanting. (73–74)
Nārada, too, having seen such a devotee—the best among devotees—was struck with great wonder; he stood for a moment in his presence.
"Aha! This man is truly a devotee, one who is worthy of Vaikuṇṭha itself."
"After beholding the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I shall indeed lead this man to Vaikuṇṭha as a companion in his kīrtana. Having reflected thus, he took him and went to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (76–77)
With supreme devotion, he worshipped the Supreme Lord with flowers and other offerings; having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, as well as dancing and singing,
and having offered the chanting of His names, he received a welcome and honor.
Having received the command to lead Pārṣṇi and Rada to Vaikuṇṭha,
Nārada, accompanied by him, bowed down to his father, his mother, and the goddess Kaṃbharā— the glorious Gopāla Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed to Īśāna and Lomaśa, as well as those dear to Brahmā,
and having reminded Kṛṣṇa of the moment of his wedding on the road,
she laughed and propitiated him on the fourth day of the bright fortnight.
Pārṣṇirada went to the place of Pārṣṇirada and spoke to him:
"In this spot, there shall be a holy ford (tīrtha) named after you, Pārṣṇirada;
likewise, there shall be a holy ford called Nārada and a holy ford called Nṛtya."
"O devotee, dwell right here for one month and construct a hut of leaves for me.
Having installed a clay image of Nārada and witnessed the marriage of Kṛṣṇa,
you shall then go to Vaikuṇṭha with a divine body and four arms."
Having spoken thus and left him on the bank, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then went back to Hari and said, "I am a servant who wishes to speak:
in Kāśī, there is Śrī Duḥkhahā Lakṣmī, the daughter of King Śiva. (85–86)
O Lord, the beloved of Brahmā likewise observes the marriage ceremony on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, which is a treasury of auspiciousness;
at that time, O Blessed One, perform the rite of marriage there.
"Out of devotion, I remind even the Blessed One, the Omniscient;
he has been informed by my mind of all those who are dear to Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed at that very moment. (88–89)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said to Nārada:
"Go to Kāśikā, toward the abode of Śiveśvara.
Having gone there and understood everything as it truly is, report it back to me."
Having received the command, "So be it," the sage Nārada departed,
O King, on the pretext of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in order to ascertain the news.
This is that *Nārada-tīrtha*, and there is also the sacred ford known as *Pārṣṇirada*.
This sacred ford (tīrtha), which destroys evil and brings about its exhaustion, is called Devatīrtha.
Indeed, by bathing here, all sins are destroyed;
and through giving gifts here, prosperities comparable to heaven arise.
In this matter, indeed, through austerity, worship, chanting, and dancing, one shall obtain a divine body resembling that of a god;
moreover, one’s lifespan increases and good fortune likewise shines forth. (94–95)
O King, from residing here, one gains a benefit equal to serving the virtuous;
moreover, there is the attainment of the peaceful ones who bestow liberation.
One who is free from desire attains liberation, while one with desire attains heaven.
A devotee of Viṣṇu attains Vaikuṇṭha; of this there is no doubt.
O King, having drunk the water here, bathed, and bowed to Nārada, give gifts of cows, which indeed yield the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
When Rādhikā had spoken thus, the king indeed gave gifts of cows;
having likewise given other gifts, he performed the ritual of bathing and so forth.
Then, together with his family, he went to the western holy ford.
Accompanied by Lomaśa, King Aśvapāṭala remained pure.
By reciting or hearing this [account], there shall likewise be the destruction of sin;
one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and obtain whatever destination is desired.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cure of Consumption through Bathing and Other Rites at Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake by the Śūdra Cowherd named Pārṣṇirada, as well as the Nārada Tīrtha," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
