O Rāseśvarī, beloved one! Afterwards, the king went to that foremost of holy places (tīrtha).

There he asked Lomaśa about its greatness and also its name. Aśvapāṭala said: 1. O Rāseśvarī, beloved one! Afterwards, the king went to that foremost of holy places (tīrtha). There he asked Lomaśa about its greatness and also its name. Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, tell me in brief: when did this holy ford (tīrtha) attain fame here, what is its power, and by whom was it established?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, in ancient times, at the commencement of creation, Vyāsa himself, Hari,
came here in the form of Śvetavyāsa with a desire for the sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having established a supreme sacred site here, he bathed and worshipped Mādhava.
Having bowed down to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he then proceeded to Vastrāpatha, Somanātha, and Mūla-Dvāravatī; likewise, having visited Gopanātha, Stambhatīrtha, and Puṣkara.
He went to Kurukṣetra, where indeed his own residence was located.
At that time, he had many disciples on earth who were knowers of the Vedas and other scriptures;
they acted by bestowing knowledge and so forth for the sake of the liberation of the world. (6)
In this place, at a distance of two yojanas from the city of Arka,
there lived a brahmin named Dharmasumantuka, a disciple of Śvetavyāsa. That great sage, who was equal to Vyāsa himself, resided constantly on the bank of the lake.
Having made his own abode beneath a banyan tree, he constantly instructed many people on the path to spiritual welfare— which consists of knowledge, devotion, and is endowed with righteousness—
and he was served by Brāhmaṇas.

The people of the village of Pārśva, eager to hear the story there, always arrived in the evening and departed once again. Without Hari there is no auspiciousness; without devotion there is no liberation.
Without knowledge, there is no dissolution of darkness within this illusory home;
indeed, without a saintly person (sādhu), there is no direct attainment of the Lord at all.
For the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa truly dwells within us.
"Worship Hari, that Kṛṣṇa who exists in the form of Śvetavyāsa!
(1.3) Thus he gives instruction and even causes the Saṃhitā to be recited;
he goes daily to Aśvapaṭṭasara for his morning bath. (1.4)
Having performed the rites for the sacred bathing sites and having bowed to Śrī Puruṣottama,
and having paid homage to the sages and honored the gods, he departs for his own home.
Thus indeed it is for the brahmin who knows the Vedas and conducts himself in this manner.
On the path, a snakebite occurred for the pilgrim in that desolate place.
Quickly becoming intent on yoga and sitting in meditative absorption (samādhi),
he performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) while a hooded serpent was passing along the bank of the road.
That brahmin summoned him and forcibly brought him under his control;
even though the powerful serpent was terrified, he could not flee from that spot,
for despite his efforts to escape, he was unable to run away.
Then, having become dependent on the Brahmin, he ran again and again toward the presence of the twice-born;
arriving there, he fell down, crying out, "Protect me! Protect me!
He said, "O Brahmin, I am indeed a gnat who has committed an offense against you here."
"Do not kill me, O best of Brahmins; my life-breaths are as dear to you as they are to me.
I beg your forgiveness, for I am of a *tāmasa* nature and my disposition is such.
You, however, are *sāttvika*; your very nature is the dharma of compassion, O twice-born one."
"When shall my liberation come as I wander in the womb of animals?
(22) "By means of your yoga, my liberation shall occur even though I am an offender here;
O Brahmin, act in such a way that my liberation may indeed be achieved. (23)
"Or rather, having bestowed knowledge upon me, make me pure;
I pray that you do not kill me here with the intent of an enemy.
Having heard the serpent's words, Dharmasumantu then—
Becoming compassionate toward him, he asked about the cause of his birth:
"Who are you? Why have you attained this serpent womb, and by what karma?
You know everything; tell me, if you do not act for your own welfare. (25–26)

"What is the reason for this, O serpent? Being one who knows, why do you wander about? Knowing me, you have bitten me; what benefit do you consider yourself to have gained from this? The serpent replied:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything afterwards exactly as it is.
I shall relate the news of my gain; this question is of no use.
By the Creator, the creation was fashioned in three ways, consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Those of the nature of *sattva* desire peace; those of the nature of *rajas* desire passion;
and those of the nature of *tamas* desire affliction—this is their inherent disposition, which is difficult to overcome.
Fire simply blazes forth; what gain indeed is there in its burning? (2.266.30)
Water always wards off the thirst of living beings;
rain pours down—tell me, what is the benefit of water here?
(3.1) The wind blows sometimes harshly, cruelly, gently, or with great force.
What benefit could there be in that case, since such is its very nature?
A sattvic being attains peace; water carries coldness, the moon is cool, and stone is cold—what benefit is there in that for their sake? (32–33)
The ocean is salty by nature, yet its water is sweet; the neem tree is bitter, and ginger is pungent—what gain is there for it in that?
The flower of the hibiscus is red, saffron is red, and blood is red.
The classes of gods are characterized by *rajas*; what indeed is the gain from *rajas*?
Lightning-strikes, thunderbolts, time, destruction, death, and darkness are indeed *tāmasa* by their very nature. (35–36)
Bhangā, gañjā, and dhattūra are born of *tamas* by their very nature. Tell me here, O learned one, what benefit indeed arises from these things born of *tamas*?
No benefit of one's own is seen in the vow of darkness.
Beings act according to their qualities, like water flowing downward;
their activity proceeds according to their own nature, like the chewing of teeth; but innate action occurs like the striking down by a falling sword. (38–39)
Since this was done by me in that manner, you ought not to be angry with me;
for even you have no news of gain, just like a bull among Brahmins who has performed his ritual bath.
At night there is surely sleep, and likewise, during the day, there is wakefulness.
But this [world] is fashioned by inherent nature; what gain is accumulated therein?
In childhood the mind is intent on play, in middle age on desire, and likewise at the end on delusion.
What gains are there that have been destroyed? One proceeds according to inherent nature.
Some are virtuous, while others are engaged in acts such as theft;
some possess the nature of lords—tell me, what is the gain in that?
Indeed, the serpent is of the nature of *tamas*, and my fangs are considered to be of the nature of *tamas*.
And that [fang] certainly causes a wound; what is considered the gain here?
Indeed, the poison has the nature of fire, appearing as saliva and flowing forth;
it is like lightning upon entry and like thunder upon its spreading.
Just as water and other fluids flow through the network of channels in the blood, such is the very nature of poison;
what gain, indeed, is there in this poison?
Furthermore, those elements such as earth and the rest, though conjoined, possess a nature characterized by separation.
The channels (nāḍīs) are of the nature of food; what gain is there in the accumulation of poison?
Tell me, O Brahmin, when life is destroyed and the body is destroyed by its own nature—when both I am destroyed and you are destroyed—what gain is there here for our two selves?
Upon the destruction of the body, there is no attainment of the self; the physical form is perishable and transitory.
It departs by its very nature, so do not grieve, O protector of the earth!
Indeed, it is through this transitory body that the embodied soul attains liberation.
"You are capable and have fulfilled your duty; O sinless one, grant me liberation!
The attainment of liberation is the supreme gain for you, as it is for me and for all embodied beings.
Do not harbor anger, O best of Brahmins; indeed, wrath leads to hell."
"O Brahmin, it was indeed through my anger that I attained this womb, so full of poison, known as hell; therefore, do not direct your wrath toward me.
Dharmasumantu said:
"Aha! O learned one, though you are a serpent, you appear like a sovereign sage.
Who are you, appearing in the form of a serpent, who takes away my life? Tell me—is it Death, or Great Time (Mahākāla), or a messenger of Yama, or Yama himself? || 5.3 ||
Tell me, are you my own *prārabdha* (past karma), or are you a forest deity?
Are you Saṃkarṣaṇa, or Śeṣa, or some wise man, or are you a human being?
Or are you a *preta*, or a real serpent; who indeed are you here, one who remembers his past lives?
Even in the state of a serpent, you speak that which is natural and in accordance with the scriptures;
for those of dull nature who have succumbed to their own inherent tendencies, there is no gain.
Indeed, "gain" means attainment through association; what indeed is the use of such a thing for the dull-witted?
Gain is considered to be the acquisition of pleasure and the like, and enjoyment is indeed held to reside within the self.
This experience of pleasure and pain occurs in the individual soul (*jīva*) and constitutes its enjoyment.
A foolish person of delusive nature believes that peace arises from the destruction of enemies. (57–58)
The unborn Self exists as the supreme state beyond pleasure and pain;
it neither gains nor loses anything through the union with or separation from the body.
However, the human form is regarded as the means for attaining liberation.
If death should occur midway before one has accomplished liberation or the means that bestow the highest good, there would be a loss of liberation; in this case,
it would be a failure to attain [the goal], having encountered the cause for it therein.
O serpent, you are the sharer in the sin of Brahmin-slaughter; you are the one at fault here.
You remain bound and unreleased from this state, being sinful and certainly not gaining anything.
And if I were to kill you, even for me no benefit would be found.
"If the body is destroyed, there is no gain, nor is there liberation; indeed, there is no such thing.
Thus, the lack of gain is equal for both of us. Tell me, who are you, one so full of activity?
Or what kind of gain have you seen here? Tell me, O serpent."
The serpent said: "O Brahmin, by nature you are gentle and compassionate;
in wisdom you are equal to Bṛhaspati and like the venerable Vyāsa. (6.5)
You are free from attachment and aversion regarding the discernment of gain and loss.
I shall speak in the form of a sūtra; listen here to what gain and loss are.
Gain is honor according to the convention; loss is the departure from that convention.
When the proper time had arrived, he did not honor him with due respect.
That opportunity has since passed; once gone, it does not return.
And for me, there was an occasion here regarding this human being in the form of a Kṣatriya.
In Arkagrāma, your prosperous village endowed with every abundance,
my sons, kinsmen, servants, slaves, and so forth,
as well as horses, houses, and fields, are found in your city.
"All those illusory beings released by me do not know me;
I, remembering my past births, know all of you, as well as others, the villages, and all the worlds, yet you do not know me here. (2.266.70)
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell you:
I was indeed the village king named Śārdūlacandra, a ruler of men. I was an atheist, a reviler, and one who treated Brahmins with contempt. (71)
Deprived of both dharma and ritual action, you were always devoted to the doctrine of causality (hetuvāda).
O Brahmin, while residing in my village, you would discourse on stories and instruct the people; moreover, you frequently approached me and taught me concerning the purpose of dharma. (72–73)
"For the sake of giving, for the sake of sacrifice, and even for the sake of helping others—
I have indeed spoken these words to you, yet at that time they were not accepted by you anywhere.
You were treated with contempt there and severely censured by me."
Then once, you indeed made a beautiful request for the sake of a sacrifice;
having learned that you were a deceiver regarding gold, wealth, and other things, you were angrily expelled from the village by me and took refuge under a banyan tree outside.
"This tiger cursed me, saying, 'May the reviler meet his death. Because of that, I met my end while filled with anger toward you;
and thus, O King, I have attained this state of a serpent, a birth among the lower animals."
I perceive suffering and I remember all my kinsmen;
I even manifest myself, yet these people do not recognize me at all. Brahmins devoted to Brahman must never be treated with contempt. (78–79)
The wise, who are embodiments of the fire of knowledge, must never be treated with contempt.
For one who treats them with contempt meets destruction, and the destroyer himself is destroyed.
When water falls upon a powerful fire, it is consumed by the fire itself.
"I was consumed by a curse and entered the womb of a serpent.
I still remember my enmity and I have been searching for you to kill you.
Today, having found you in this secluded place, I have bitten you out of hostility. (81–82)
"O twice-born one, death is certain for you in order to exact vengeance;
a living being experiences the fruit of its own actions in some physical body.
[This has come about] through your anger, the utterance of a curse, and the murder of a king."
The life-span of one such as you, who has failed to perform expiatory rites, has come to an end.
(84) Through the sorrow of me, your queen, your life-span has reached its exhaustion; for even Brahmins are set ablaze by the sighs of virtuous women. (85)
O best of Brahmins, your lifespan has indeed perished in that very manner;
for those whose lifespan has vanished do not live even for a moment.
The messengers of Death, dispatched [by Yama], arrive with great speed.
The messengers, who are mere omens, destroy one's remaining lifespan.
Serpents, scorpions, poison, dogs, poisonous herbs, spirits, ghosts, piśācas and the like, the messengers of Yama, the planetary deities (grahas), and so forth—[all these are but signs]. (87–88)
Fire, water, fever, and even enemies are merely instrumental causes;
one is slain by an instrument, and there exists another, higher or lower, who is the slayer.
Indeed, failing to understand this reality, people hate scorpions and the like.
Therefore, O Brahmin, my death here is certain, and my death is also certain for you.
You are capable of bringing about liberation for me, for yourself, and for others;
for a human body is the field of action, and by means of it, everything is attained.
Even at the cost of one's life, a good deed surely protects the doer.
Death is indeed certain; therefore, perform that which will liberate us both.
Truly, the gift of fearlessness to living beings yields a fruit greater than that of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, grant me liberation indeed.
Then the Brahmin, being thus addressed, quickly [poured] water from the pitcher for the serpent, saying:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (93–94)
Having consecrated it with this mantra, he gave it for the purpose of drinking;
he also sprinkled it upon his body, and the serpent, abandoning its body,
quickly assumed a divine form and then went to heaven.
And the Brāhmaṇa, consumed by poison, remembered the Lord Hari;
he cast off his body right there in the desolate wilderness on the path,
and his soul reached the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
There, at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he remained until the end, according to his understanding.
Then, the farmer observed that the brāhmaṇa was dead;
the farmer went to the village and told the brāhmaṇas what had occurred.
Having taken the corpse, the twice-born went to Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara to cremate it.
All the kinsmen arrived and wept on the shore of the lake;
having laid down the corpse, they all indeed sang the praises of the twice-born man's virtues.
This brahmin is equal to Śvetavyāsa, devoted to the practice of dharma, and a bestower of liberation to the worlds; such a person is rare to find.
He is a disciple of Śvetavyāsa and has reached the further shore of the state of meditative absorption (samādhi).
And that one should die because of a snakebite is indeed a marvel;
for once the life-force has reached its end, it cannot be joined back together by anyone except the Supreme Self and the yogi who is the Guru. 102–103.
Speaking thus, they called to mind Śvetavyāsa;
they also remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Then, O King, his Brahmin wife was overwhelmed with grief.
With the desire to attain the state of Satī, she approached the vicinity of the funeral pyre there.
She remembered Śvetavyāsa as well as Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa;
having worshipped the corpse according to the prescribed rites, she offered it upon the pyre.
Having kindled a fire, as he strove to burn [him] from the tips of his feet upward, at that moment the Lord, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa,
who is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, appeared there in a white form by the power of devotion.
Then Śvetavyāsa himself arrived there together with Dharma and Sumantu. Having gone to the side of the funeral pyre, he said to Satī:
"This husband of yours is indeed here; take him, do not follow me into the flames."
At that moment, the brahmin rose up, breathing, living, and laughing in an instant; Satī also became submerged, and the brahmins were likewise delighted.
Then, having performed their ablutions at the sacred ford, they all departed toward Arkapura.
"O King, that is the holy ford known as Śvetavyāsa, and likewise Satītīrtha;
here also exists Jīvatīrtha—bathe and perform the ritual for these sacred sites. Thus commanded, O Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭala proceeded there.
He performed worship of Śvetavyāsa, undertook his ritual bath, and gave many gifts; thereafter he went to another place. Together with Lomaśa, he remained at another sacred ford on the riverbank.
He remembered Śrī Hari, yet he did not bow to the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) nor the temple.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Serpent’s State for King Arkapurī due to the Curse of the Sages Dharmasumantu and Ṛṣi; the Brahmin’s Bite by the Serpent; the Liberation of the Serpent; the Revival of the Brahmin at Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara at the Request of the Brahmin’s Wife Satī by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; and the Description of Śvetavyāsa-tīrtha, Satī-tīrtha, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

"Then I shall worship Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of existence;
I shall worship Vyāghreśvarī and I bow to Vighnarāja.
Having thus resolved, he quickly bathed and worshipped them.

Having paid homage to the deities, she prayed for protection; she repeatedly sought from the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) the destruction of all inauspiciousness. Queen Rāṇikā likewise bestowed various gifts.
Then she caused the propitiation of the planets to be performed by the twice-born and others.
Thereupon, the Great Goddess Mahālakṣmī appeared visibly before her and was pleased. She said to her: "An obstacle to your kingdom shall arise from the Mleccha tribes."
And there shall also be a battle between both of these two armies.
O King, let not Aṅgāraka go forth to the fray;
let him not indeed go outside the fortress, for then victory will truly be yours.
"The enemies shall perish on all sides outside the fortress;
your victory shall be within the fortress, while defeat shall lie without.
Having been told this, that virtuous woman related everything to the king.
The king also remained vigilant within his own palace.
At that time, the Mlecchas arrived with their armies in five divisions;
numbering in the tens of thousands, they were armed and mounted upon elephants.
Mounted on horses and stationed in chariots, they blocked the gates of the fortress on all sides;
having secured the closure of the gates, they remained steadfast.
Indeed, the proud royal officers, together with their armies, were within the city.
Having thus blocked the gates, they stood there armed with weapons.
From various positions, the numerous enemies hurled many destructive mechanical balls from the siege engines in order to conquer that impregnable city.
Even after many days, they were not at all able to enter.
Then those foremost of Mlecchas employed a stratagem of sowing dissension;
by means of speech, they gave wealth—gold and silver—to the villages.
Having learned from a spy the secret path for entering the city,
the Mleccha tribes breached the fortress, entered through its gate,
fought, plundered, and proceeded to the royal palace.
Then the royal armies fought with the sacrifice of their lives;
indeed, many were slain according to their will, and many royal soldiers were killed.
Even the commanders of the armies were slain by the blows of weapons.
When the army known as the Mleccha people reached their own abode,
the king then descended into the fray to fight for his own protection; thereafter,
the subjects too, together with their forces, slew many of the Mlecchas.
The great army of the Kṣatriyas, joined with protective embers,
fought against the great Mlecchas and slew them while they were still alive;
others, moreover, fled right into the midst of the city.
Abandoning the fortress, the Mlecchas fled in all directions.
The king, intoxicated by the battle, having indeed forgotten the words of his virtuous wife,
went out from the fortress to fight and slay the fleeing Mlecchas.
Turning back, they then fought by giving up their lives;
with blows from their weapons, they struck Rakṣāṅgāraka on all sides. The king died upon the ground, casting off his life-breaths as he fell.
Rāṇikā was indeed performing worship of the deity in her own palace.
For the sake of protecting her beloved, she then observed two marks on his feet—red and uncrushed—which were like two lines upon the ground. 41–42.
Seeing her own saffron-stained feet upon the ground, Satī was overcome with fear;
crying out "Alas, my Lord!", she beheld the truth of Satī’s nature.
In that very moment, Satī became established in the state of Truth.
Then, having seen her husband’s subtle body with divine vision,
she quickly emerged from her own dwelling and the hole, having taken him back to her own home,
while being overcome by the defeat [she had suffered].
Indeed, that virtuous Satī, having departed from that place in male attire,
went outside and by the power of her fortune reached a great camel;
then, taking a secret path through the trees, she emerged from that land of fear.
Having abandoned her kingdom, she went toward the Aśvasaras lake to experience suffering.
Reaching the northern shore of the lake in a single day,
she disembarked on the bank of the lake, bathed, and wept within.
There she offered a handful of water to her beloved who had gone with her,
and then to Him in His subtle form; thereafter, having remembered, bowed to, and entreated the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, she stood firm on the bank with a steady resolve.
"In the presence of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa here,
I shall kindle the fire of my body and depart for the auspicious heaven.
Having thus resolved in the evening, she remained devoted to her virtuous vows.
Then he praised Satī, the truth, as Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa:
"I bow to Nārāyaṇa, the truth of truths, the eternally true.
Oṃ, salutations to the creator of Brahman; salutations to you, the protector of the truthful. (52)
Salutations to You, who are the very essence of devotion to one’s husband, and salutations to You as the five sacrificial fires (pañcāgni).
Salutations to You as the three sacred fires (tretāgni), and salutations to You whose nature is the seed.
Salutations to You in the form of the embryo, to You in the form of childhood, and salutations to You in the form of youth.
Salutations to you who are the beloved and the Beloved, together with your entire lineage;
salutations to you who are the Couple, the Ancient One, and the Threefold Self.
Salutations to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, and salutations to you, the Blessed Lady.
Homage to you whose form is virtue, who are the Dharma, and who are the attainment of the Dharma.
Homage to you whose nature is the funeral pyre, homage to you who are the husband’s form.
Homage to you who are the caravan for the traveler, homage to you who are the guide across the way.
Salutations to the Sun, to the cloud, to the lightning, and salutations to the Moon;
salutations to you whose nature is day and whose form is night.
Salutations to the one whose form is the two solstices, who sets the ages (yugas) in motion.
Salutations to the Divine, the Truth; salutations to the Dweller in Vaikuṇṭha.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of virtuous women and the Sovereign of the world of the virtuous.
Salutations to the Beloved of Goloka; salutations to the Dweller in the Imperishable.
Homage to the one worthy of worship by the liberated, and homage to the Lord of the virtuous!
Homage to you, the Lord of the lords of the liberated, the beloved of Brahmā!
Homage to the Lord of Lakṣmī, who possesses rubies and pearls! 6.1.16–17.
Salutations to the Lord of Padmāvatī, Satī, Lakṣmī, and Rādhā.
Salutations to the All-pervading One, the Supreme Lord; salutations to the Śrī Paramātman.
Salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī; salutations to You, the Śrī Puruṣottama.
Salutations to the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations again and again to You, the inner controller, who is united with all.
O Lord, salutations to You, the son of Gopālā, Kaṃbhārāja.
Salutations to you, the moon of the horse-skin, the illusory sun!
Salutations to you, the bestower of prosperity, the dispassionate one, and the remover of all things!
I am this house known as "I," and you, O Truth, are my home.
O Aṅgāraka, you are my protector; whatever songs are devoted to you, having obtained you as my supreme helper, I offer this [oblation]; accept me!
Whether they know it or do not know it, they ultimately offer everything.
By both [means], I shall indeed perform the oblation for you here according to the injunction.
You are the sacrifice; you are present in the sacrificial pit in the form of the Āhavanīya fire;
you are the Gārhapatya fire by nature, and you possess the nature of the Āvasathya fire.
You alone are the fire of the sacrificial pit, and you are indeed the fire of every pit.
Lead me by means of the dharma of truth; have mercy on me! For the dharma of a faithful wife is that which brings about the upliftment of the world.
In ancient times, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, was born; her body was consumed by fire.
Reṇukā was also born as Satī, and Śabarī likewise in former times.
Women who take refuge in performed righteousness attain the state of Satī.
"O Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, in that same way I shall attain the state of a virtuous wife (satītva). O King, as Rāṇikā, whose limbs were so delicate, spoke thus and ascended the funeral pyre,
she desired to kindle the fire.
At that time, the divine Śrī Lomaśa, Īśāna, and the gods and others,
as well as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, became visible there in their presence; Satī bowed to them on all sides.
"O Satī, may you attain victory; you shall go to the world of the virtuous (Satī-loka). Together with your husband, enjoy happiness as long as heaven exists.
Having spoken thus, they bestowed blessings, flowers, and sandalwood paste.

Having paid obeisance to Viṣṇu, she then remembered her husband once more. At that time, Nandin, an attendant of Śaṅkara who possessed a gross physical body, went and quickly brought from the sky the charred corpse of Rakṣas. || 77-78 ||

She gave that [garland] to Satyabhāmā upon the funeral pyre; she too, delighted, embraced her body as it was united with the deceased according to the prescribed rite, even as the gods and men looked on.
Then, while the people were watching, she produced fire from her foot.
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Rādhākṛṣṇa! she sang.
Having said, "O Lord of the Gopīs, O Beloved of the Virtuous, O Lord of Ramā, look upon me!", Lambikā lay down upon the funeral pyre with the corpse.
The fire did not touch her; she shone only at her feet. At that moment, Hari Kṛṣṇa became Rādhākṛṣṇa there.
Accompanied by Muralī, the Lord remained there, granting his vision.

There, with his own hand, the Blessed One himself offered water, clarified butter, flowers, sesame seeds, and sandalwood upon the funeral pyre. The two souls, the beloved of Satī, became possessed of divine forms.
They departed from the place of the corpse and stood for a moment in the sky;
then a divine celestial chariot, radiant as the sun, arrived from heaven.
They sat there and beheld the cremation of the corpse.
Having bowed to those two Supreme Lords, Agni burned their two bodies;
they both went to the world of Satī, where they shall remain for the duration of a kalpa,
and from there they will proceed to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self.
And there the gods, having established the Satī-tīrtha and gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, worshipped the glorious, beginningless Śrī-Nārāyaṇa;
they then departed for their own divine world, and Kṛṣṇa vanished.
The attendants of Śambhu indeed threw the ashes from the funeral pyre into the water.
That very spot became the Rāṇikā Tīrtha, also known as Rakṣāṅgāraka Tīrtha; it is supremely famous as a signifier of the chastity of women.
O King, here, by bathing and giving gifts, and especially by drinking the water, one protects the dharma of virtuous women (*satī*), destroys the torment of sin,
and by performing the worship of the *satī*, one attains the fruit of the world of the *satīs*.
Any widow here who, remembering her husband, shall bathe [in this place],
will indeed lead him to the world of chaste women (satīloka) by means of that merit.
And any maiden who shall drink the water or perform a bath here, [shall obtain her desired fruit].
Having attained the state of a virtuous wife and obtained a husband who bestows happiness,
she will enjoy a full lifespan here and then go to the worlds of the *satīs*.
Furthermore, a woman endowed with good fortune [attains this] here through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts.
Having obtained the fruit of her devotion to her husband, Satī shall go to the worlds of the virtuous.
Even an elderly woman, by merely bathing there, grants liberation to a hundred families;
and even a man, by merely bathing there, becomes devoted to truth and righteousness.
Having recovered his beloved who had passed away and died, he shall proceed to the heavenly realm.
Such is this Satī-tīrtha, which is indeed a purifier for women.
Let the queen and others perform here ablutions, acts of charity, and the offering of water-libations.
Just as the Satī-tīrtha is most great in the celestial Gaṅgā,
and as the Reṇukā-tīrtha is likewise in the river Revā,
so too here is the Rāṇikā-tīrtha, the supreme purifier in the three worlds. (98–99)
"O King, when the Kṛta Yuga had begun, the ancient [Rādhikā] was born," he said;
and Aśvapāṭala, along with his wives and even his female servants,
bathed in the waters of the Satī-sthala lake on the day of Rādhikā.
Then, having bestowed gifts, they performed the libations;
the king and the others proceeded ahead toward that supreme, purifying holy site,
accompanied by Lomaśa, who was well-acquainted with the majesty of the sacred ford.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Satī-bhavana and Satī-tīrtha at the Shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake by Rāṇikā-satī, the Wife of King Rakṣāṅgāraka, after he was slain by the Mlecchas in Svarṇapattana in Saurāṣṭra," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
(Chapter 267, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2: The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 268 [Author:
Chapter 269 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O Rādhā, having gone to that holy place (tīrtha) frequented by the virtuous, King Aśvapāṭala questioned Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said: 1. Then, O Rādhā, having gone to that holy place (tīrtha) frequented by the virtuous, King Aśvapāṭala questioned Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"What is this most purifying sacred site (tīrtha) pervaded by the virtuous?
O Guru, tell me of these two types of sacred sites: the immobile and the mobile.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
King Amohākṣa lived in the vicinity of the Himalayas;
having approached a teacher named Prabodha, he gratified him with service.
The teacher granted him a vision of Śrī Hari in his own form.

He had four arms, resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and other [emblems]. (4) Then, in another moment, he again assumed the form of his guru; filled with wonder, the one named Amoha lay reflecting upon the Lord of Śrī. (5)
"This guru is a human being and appears with four arms;
I consider him to be Nārāyaṇa himself, encountered through my good fortune. Therefore, I shall indeed worship him and serve him in every way. (6)
"Having meditated upon and worshipped [him] with devotion, I shall indeed attain the supreme good.
Having thus made this awakening resolution in his heart,
the king served his guru, Janārdana, with supreme devotion.
The queen, the sons, the subjects, and the daughters served the Guru Hari by providing food and water, by massaging his feet and the like,
by obeying his words, and by washing his clothes and other such services. (9)
By providing beds and seats, by offering leaves, fruits, and petals,
with sandalwood paste, unbroken grains, and oils, with fragrant garlands and ornaments,
and with all the royal enjoyments, they [honored] the entire royal family at all times.
Considering his master to be Lord Hari himself, he served him tirelessly;
he worshipped him by reciting the names [of the Lord] known as *prabodha*.
The Guru reflected that a bond had been established.
Royal enjoyments arise as fetters leading surely to hell;
therefore, enjoyments that obstruct liberation must be avoided from afar. One ought not to disparage the awakening to the illusory nature [of these things]. (13–14)
Having thus made this firm resolve, Prabodha gradually abandoned worldly enjoyments through spiritual instructions and observances;
and for the sake of the destruction of delusion, he spoke to him of the auspicious discourse on Dharma.

O King, the duty of kings is one thing, while the duty of ascetics is another. (16) I am a seeker of truth and enlightenment; worldly enjoyment is not fitting for me. Indeed, the ornaments of householders are truly the blemishes of the virtuous. (17)
Indeed, the faults of householders are the ornaments of the virtuous;
the duty of the virtuous is said to be forbearance, while the duty of kings is indeed governance.
The duty of the virtuous consists of the three daily ablutions, whereas the duty of kings consists of the final purificatory bath.

The dharma of the ascetic is the guarding of moral conduct; the dharma of the householder is association with women. (1.9) Furthermore, the dharma of the ascetic is contempt, while the dharma of the householder is honor. The ascetic lives on alms, whereas the householder eats food earned by his own labor. (2.268.20)
A holy man may wear tattered rags, yet a householder may possess golden garments and the like;
a holy man may be inclined toward wandering, yet a householder may dwell in a magnificent mansion.
A holy man may be devoid of affection, yet a householder may be possessed by a deep attachment to his family.

A virtuous householder is always devoted to his own self, whereas another is devoted to his household. A virtuous householder may also be homeless, while one who is attached to kin is established in a home. A virtuous householder always eats in moderation, whereas another always eats for the sake of physical nourishment.

The virtuous householder is always free from dualities, whereas the [ordinary] householder is possessed of dualities; the virtuous householder is always free from desire, while the [ordinary] householder is enveloped by desires.
The dharma of the virtuous bestows liberation, whereas the dharma of the household indeed bestows heaven.
"Thus, indeed, there exists a distinction between us two regarding the paths of dharma.
Now, O King, listen to the distinction between us even with respect to knowledge:
'He is my son,' 'She is my wife,' 'This elephant and other property are mine.'"
Indeed, for a householder, "my field," "my kingdom," and so forth appear as real;
yet for a holy person, it appears that "I have no son, no wife, no wealth such as elephants, no field, and how could there be a kingdom? (27)
"These are my relatives and likewise my family members;
these are my servants and my subjects"—thus it appears to the householder.
But [for the one who has renounced], there are neither his relatives nor his family members. (28–29)

"I have no servants, much less subjects; indeed, this world shines for the virtuous. My body, my form, my command, and my strength—all my very existence and everything else—shines as belonging to the householder."
I have no body, I have no form, nor do I have command or strength. I have no existence; how then could anything belong to me? Indeed, it is the world of the virtuous that perceives [these things].
"My nourishment," "my disease," "my sweet," "my cool"—[these are merely designations].

"Mine is suffering, mine is pride"—thus does the householder appear. "Neither nourishment nor disease is mine; neither sweetness nor coolness is mine, nor mine"—thus does the world of holy men appear. (33) Mine is no suffering, mine is no pride—thus indeed does the world of holy men appear.
"I am maimed," "I am fat," "I am leprous," "I am lame"—thus does the notion of a householder appear: "I am intelligent," "I am dull-witted.
But [in truth], I am neither maimed, nor fat, nor leprous, nor lame. (34–35)

Indeed, the Buddha is not dull-witted, nor does he appear so to the world of the virtuous. [The thought] "May there be my birth, my death, and my heaven," as well as "my worship and my fame"—this indeed shines forth for the householder. (36)
I have no birth, I have no death; for me there is neither heaven nor bondage.
(37) I have no worship, nor do I possess the fame of the world of the virtuous.
Indeed, yours is the village, yours the grove, yours the garden, and yours the land. (38)
"This is yours and this is mine"—such indeed appears to the householder.
But for you there is no village, nor for you a garden, nor for you a grove, nor for you land.
"This is yours and this is not mine"—this indeed does not appear to the world of the virtuous.
Thus, O King, listen to the distinction regarding knowledge as well as dispassion:
"My wife is desirable, my home is desirable, and my body is desirable; for such is the attachment of a householder. (2.268.40–41)
"My wife, my home, and my body—wherein is there any desirability? On the contrary, they are moist, impure, and loathsome.
In this way, the absence of passion arises from the very nature of virtuous people.
"Oh, what wealth! Oh, what enjoyments! And oh, what means for attaining them!
Oh, and I myself—for what a wonder is this householder's life, dedicated as it is to my sake!
What indeed is wealth? What are enjoyments? And what, indeed, are the means? (43–44)
What egoism or sense of "mine" can there be for a virtuous person? There is no wonder in this:
"Today is a festival! Today is a wedding! Today is dancing and singing!
"Today is a theatrical performance! Today is a drama!"—such is the delusion of a householder.
The festival of the self is the vehicle to liberation; there is always dancing and singing for Hari.

(46) In the divine drama, the virtuous man’s offering of everything to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of the Supreme Lord—thinking "this is a stake," "this is won," "this is lost," or "this is made one's own"—[is the true game]. (47)
For a householder, there is both giving and receiving, as well as the state of possessing passion;
yet he has his own splendor, has attained Brahman, has conquered his mind, and has made it steady.
For the virtuous one, however, there is neither giving nor receiving, for he is devoid of passion.
Constantly reclining upon pleasure, bound by the threads of craving;
following a state of greed, the householder possesses passion. Constantly reclining upon the self, he is bound by the sacrificial thread. (2.268.50)
The virtuous person always follows the state of goodness and maintains constant detachment.
Observe likewise the distinct nature of detachment even within devotion:
for the householder, devotion is found in the home; for the virtuous person, however, devotion is fixed upon Mādhava.
For the householder, devotion is directed toward sexual pleasure, whereas for the virtuous man (sādhu), it is indeed directed toward renunciation.
For the householder, devotion is for his own sake; for the virtuous man, devotion is for the sake of others.
For the householder, devotion is directed toward worldly matters; for the virtuous man, that devotion is directed toward the supreme goal (paramārtha).
The householder’s devotion is fixed on his own station, while the saint’s devotion is fixed on the station beyond.
The householder’s devotion is toward aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), while the saint’s is toward that which is the self of all flavors.
The householder’s devotion is toward delusion (*bhrama*), while the saint’s devotion is toward that which transcends delusion.
For a householder, devotion is during the fertile season; for a saintly person, devotion is without Hari.
Indeed, the devotion of a saintly person leads to the non-returning state, whereas that of a householder leads to the cycle of rebirth.
The devotion of a householder is within the womb; the devotion of a saintly person is in the golden realm.
The virtuous householders who eat at home are worshippers of the planets;
indeed, the virtuous householders who eat only what is offered as food are those who subsist on food taken at night.
Furthermore, the virtuous householders who eat many times a day are those who take but a single meal.
Householders are indeed devoted [to worldly objects], whereas saintly persons are always free from such devotion.
Householders are devoted to everything, while saintly persons are truly devoid of such attachment.
Thus, O King, there is a distinction between householders and the virtuous on the path of devotion. (58–59)
Even regarding their destination, there is indeed no companionship whatsoever:
the destination of the householder is downward, while the destination of the virtuous man is always upward.
The householder has a garden as his destination, whereas the virtuous man always has the mountain as his destination.
The householder follows the path of passion, while the ascetic always follows the path of purity.
(61) Likewise, the householder moves within the realm of dualities, while the ascetic is free from dualities.
The householder is subject to the influence of the planets, while the ascetic is forever beyond them. (62)
The path of action belongs to the virtuous householder, while the path of Brahman belongs likewise to the virtuous one.
The path of the Self belongs to the virtuous householder, and the Self is the true path for the virtuous one.
The goal of the virtuous one is the Blessed Lord; the goal of the householder is the *bhaga*.
Thus, O King, since there is such a distinct separation between the movement of the virtuous householder and that of others,
how could there be a simultaneous conjunction with you here?
For passion and dispassion do not coexist, nor indeed do light and darkness.
Bondage and liberation do not exist together; they never exist at all.
Therefore, I have taken pleasure in dwelling in the forest, which is approved by the virtuous.
Behold, O King, how this body is indeed a *kalala*, born from a *kalala*.
Through the region of the *apāna* wind, [the embryo] is produced by way of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
In the womb, which is the site of the *apāna*, it is constantly cooked by the *kalala* stages;
it attains nourishment and emerges [from the womb] having been matured by milk and cooked foods. (67–68)
Everything is pervaded by the *kalala*; indeed, it is a repository of the *kalala*.
There exists the *kalala*, as well as impurity and water; and that which extends from the feet to the nails is composed of the elements and is foul-smelling. (69)
A treasure consisting of impurity is seen to belong to impurity alone.
(70) Rich with fragrance when first consumed and swallowed, yet having descended below the throat, it quickly becomes foul-smelling; having become impurity, it preserves itself. (71)
That fragrance and essence of scent which fills the nostrils becomes foul-smelling within the stomach and exits through the outside. Indeed,
there are foul-smelling impurities everywhere at all nine gates [of the body].
For indeed, for everyone, that which is the hellish cauldron is ever flowing.

Behold the loathsomeness of your own limbs; do not associate with others. [This body] is fit for receiving water and food only while it remains unaltered by the moisture of the *kalala* stage. (73–74)
And what pure impression could there be in the discharge of feces and urine?
Through ignorance, one delights in the impure as if it were pure, just as one might take pleasure in a fetter.
Indeed, [this arises] from saliva, which is essentially water, and is merely a transformation of what has been eaten.
From the mixture of earth, fire, and air, the embryo (kalala) is born.

From that [embryo] arises the body, and therein the sense organs, such as the physical seats (golaka), as well as the subtle elements (tanmātra) and so forth; likewise, their powers of movement and speech are produced. (76–77)
Indeed, the states of the grasped and the grasper arise from that very source;
therefore, what conscious person could find delight therein against their will?
For moment by moment, objects of entirely different forms are seen, truly beyond the reach of logical thought.
At what moment will this aggregate meet its destruction?
Having understood that this mass of the body is like a cloud, like smoke, or like a veil of dust, the wise man should not place his trust in it. (2.268.80)
Yet this body becomes empty the very next moment upon the departure of the vital breath;
for suffering is directly perceived, since that is indeed its intrinsic nature.
If such is the case with the body itself, what need is there to speak of those who are related to it?
Therefore, O King, I shall dwell here within that which is known as the "forest" (araṇya) within your own self;
thereafter, I shall find my abode in the Supreme Lord, who is beyond the forest.
If what I have said is pleasing to you, then cultivate that excellent path.
O wise one, grant me this boon: let there be no grief at our separation.
For if the mind is always as it has been described toward the Guru, then the body remains exactly the same even in the forest; indeed, association with others is what brings fear.

If you dwell in his company, even in the forest, your residence will be possible there. Since the forest is as much my home to you as my own house, O Lord, please do not go; instead, establish your permanent dwelling right here.
Prabuddha said:
"O King, what you have spoken is indeed true, and what I have said is likewise so.
Having gone to Bhavana without obstacle, I shall attain liberation, which is difficult to obtain. (87)
"O King, your palace is seen to be full of many obstacles, whereas the forest indeed has few obstacles; I shall strive according to my strength.
Having attained self-knowledge, I shall enter into the knowledge of Brahman."
"By means of the knowledge of Brahman, I shall realize the eternal Supreme Brahman.
Amohākṣa said:
"How may I obtain the vision of the one whose nature is the perfect Brahman?"
"O Guru, grant me here the vision of the full Brahman.
The Awakened One said: "Through the burning away of the impurities of karma, the full Brahman shines forth."
"O King, I am not thus engaged, being entangled in the web of karma.
Amohākṣa said:
"There is no trust in this body; it perishes at the end of a moment."
If there is no attainment from the presence of the Guru that pertains to the Supreme Brahman,
then when and where will that attainment ever be reached by the disciple?
O Guru, grant me the direct knowledge of the Supreme Self.
Prabuddha said:
"I am not capable in such a way; capability rests upon devotion.
But thousands of incarnations like me have already been born as Buddhas. (94)
O King, through devotion and the worship of that very Supreme Brahman, you shall cross over [samsara] by means of that practice; of this there is no doubt.
O King, if you so desire, I shall go quickly to the forest.
Right here, even without the perfection of spiritual means, I shall out of compassion describe the vision of Brahman in the land known as Surāṣṭra,
in the field of Aśvapaṭṭasara, that auspicious field of the Imperishable. (96–97)
At the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Lord himself is manifest:
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
He shines as the Supreme Brahman, having assumed a human form.
By these [means], you will quickly go to that region where you shall meet the Supreme Brahman.
Having established me, your Guru, there in the temple, you shall thereafter proceed to the world of Brahman; go quickly indeed, do not delay.
"I shall go, O King; may you always have well-being.
Having spoken thus, O King, the Buddha departed for the forest expanse.
Amohākṣa, having quickly prepared himself, arrived there.

Having arrived at this sacred field, he beheld the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa directly before his eyes; he likewise resided here in this holy place, and having established the Awakened One here, he departed for the supreme liberation beyond the highest.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, one reaches the imperishable, eternal abode.
This indeed is the ford of Buddhahood, as well as the ford that dispels delusion;
it eternally effects the destruction of delusion and brings about the attainment of the perfect Brahman.
"O King, bathe after meditating upon your guru, and also bestow gifts.
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭalaka then performed an auspicious bath and gave gifts according to the instructions of Lomaśa.
Then he went suddenly to yet another sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
By reciting and hearing this, one attains the state of the Supreme Brahman;
discernment (*viveka*) arises, and likewise, one comes to abide in Brahman.
There shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and eternal heaven shall also be attained.
(108) Here, through giving, austerity, worship, and immersion, as well as by drinking the water, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). (109)
"Even if a sinful person comes here and gives up their life,

having become awakened in this place, they shall proceed to the state of liberation. (2.268.11) Thus ends the description of the arrival at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī through the instruction of the enlightened Guru to King Amohākṣa, the attainment of the Supreme Brahman in person, the Buddhatīrtha, and liberation, etc., in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter Two Hundred and Sixty-Eight [268] The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga — Section 2 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā Chapter Two Hundred and Sixty-Nine [269]
[Author: Chapter 270.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; having gone to that sacred ford (tīrtha), Aśvapāṭala—
He asked Lomaśa again: "What is the name and other details of this sacred ford (tīrtha)? Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, by what name is this famous ford known, and when did it come into being?"
Tell me all that in brief, and what the fruit of this is.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe a most purifying sacred site (tīrtha).
Likewise, O King, there is Lakṣmītīrtha and this Nārāyaṇatīrtha.
Formerly, there was a king named Abhayākṣa, the lord of the Pañcāla land,
who was devoted to the practice of righteous deeds and endowed with charity and devotion toward Hari.
In whose house hundreds of guest-like holy men and wretched beings constantly eat and attain eternal satisfaction;
where Nārāyaṇa himself shines in the form of a saint.
He is unknowable to all the worlds, the Lord served by the Brahmins.
Lakṣmī and Rādhā likewise shine forth in the form of virtuous women;
the gods and goddesses know Him, but mortals do not.
Only those sages who possess divine vision know this, and no others;
the king constantly serves the illustrious Lord Śrī Puruṣottama,
and he worships Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed husband of Śrī.
He constantly listened to discourses from virtuous Brahmins.
Together with his family, the king became devoted to self-knowledge,
intent on serving the righteous, and dedicated to the protection of his subjects.
Among his subjects there was no unrighteousness, nor theft, nor even violence.
His people maintained purity and protected one another, being content with their own possessions. Indeed, the brahmins and ascetics partook of his food.
Constantly devoted to the sound of the Vedas and dedicated to the six duties and other rites,
and likewise intent on sacrifices and offerings, the people were devoted to Nārāyaṇa and committed to the conduct of Brahman; they did not highly esteem desire at all.
Indeed, they acquire only the wealth required and nothing more than that;
all the remaining time they devote entirely to the pursuit of liberation.
In his kingdom, there is no widow, nor any woman without a son, nor any childless person.
Householders were without wives, and their offspring were not endowed with wealth or grain.
(15) In every part of the city, auspicious sounds of "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! arose in the morning;
auspicious ceremonies took place, and hymns of praise were heard. (16)
There is no one who exists without having bathed, nor likewise anyone who exists without worship;
on the foreheads of men, there is seen the auspicious sandalwood tilaka accompanied by a crescent moon, serving as a reminder of Śrī Hari. (17)
Indeed, garlands of *tulasī* are seen upon the necks of all people;
on the hand as well, there is a *tulasī* rosary that awakens one to the practice of recitation (*japa*).
On the tongue is the name of Śrī Hari, and even in prostration, there is indeed Hari.
In acts of charity and in helping others, people remember Śrī Hari; likewise,
those girls and boys who are devoted to the study of knowledge first perform kīrtana of Śrī Hari in the school, and only thereafter proceed with their studies.
The preceptors, who have taken refuge in Hari, practice [these names] and teach them.
Even in the court of justice, it is constantly heard at the beginning and at the end:
"O Hari, O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, obeisance be unto You! || 21-22 ||
On the banks of rivers, in houses, fields, gardens, and even in forests—farmers, artisans, wood-gatherers, and those who collect grass and other materials—all are devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, they perform their labors while remembering Kṛṣṇa. (23)
The female cooks, who are devotees of Hari,
having placed all kinds of cooked food— whether grain, fruits, roots, water, or other items— in a vessel, offer them to Hari and afterwards feed their household masters. (24–25)
Having first offered everything to the Lord, they eat and drink;
even the eminent merchants stationed at the marketplace perform the worship of Gaṇeśa,
and having lit a lamp of ghee, they then perform the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They engage in their labors by day and worship Mādhava at night. Having bowed to Hari and honored the cow, the herdsmen then behold the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and subsequently obtain a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Devoted solely to the remembrance of Hari, wood-gatherers go to the forest regions;
indeed, on the path they proceed while worshipping Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa.
Washermen, while washing bundles of clothes, [chant] the name of Rāma.
Having uttered "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," the parrots and other birds likewise wash themselves in the reservoir; the beasts also low, O Śrī Narāyaṇa,
for these Vaiṣṇavas indeed utter the syllable Om.
Performers of the triple arts played songs in praise of Kṛṣṇa; poets, bards, and others composed compositions concerning Kṛṣṇa.
Then the king himself, having explained his own name as "The Eye of Fearlessness," [spoke].
He proclaimed the name of Hari as "Adhokṣaja," and that became his secondary name (upanāma).
He also caused the subjects to receive names endowed with the meaning of the Supreme Lord;
thus, the kingdom truly became a Vaiṣṇava realm.
Having thus reflected that the home is perishable, and that wealth, kingdom, prosperity, and even his own body are transitory, this devotee of Abhaya,
overcome by dispassion, went to Aśvapaṭṭasara.
The subjects, the brahmins, and the elders followed after that king.
Seeing them approaching with such devotion and chanting on the road,
the people from the villages along the way were filled with curiosity.
Together they returned with eager anticipation to the Aśvasaras tīrtha;
on the northern bank of the lake, they took up residence in a dwelling among the trees.
Having visited all the sacred fords, they went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then they went to the temple of Anādikaṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having bowed to their mother and father and having beheld the Kuṅkumavāpikā, they worshipped the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with supreme devotion. (2.269.40)
Having drunk the water of Kuṅkumavāpikā and performed the worship of Śrī,
they gave gifts and returned once more to the shore of the lake.
There, on that spot, King Adhokṣaja indeed prepared to perform a sacrifice.
In order to propitiate Nārāyaṇa through a great sacrifice,
that Adhokṣaja (Kṛṣṇa) requested Lomaśa for the sake of the ritual;
he indeed performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice with hundreds of thousands of gold coins.

He gratified the gods with oblations, the ancestors with *śrāddha* rites, the virtuous with food, and the people with gifts; likewise, he honored the holy men and the lords of the gods with self-surrender.
At the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), Kṛṣṇa himself appeared as the four-armed Nārāyaṇa.
The Lord was seen in the fire, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
accompanied by Lakṣmī, he partook of all the sacrificial offerings, served by Ramānanda, Sunanda, and others, and joined by Garuḍa. 45–46.
With a serene countenance, dark-complexioned, youthful, and radiant as ten million suns, he appeared;
and all the other brahmins and people were filled with wonder.
"Oh, how great is the king's devotion and his love for Nārāyaṇa! [47]
"Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa himself partakes of the sacrificial offering presented by you, O King.
The Blessed One said to the king, "Have a temple built here;
I shall dwell together with Lakṣmī. O King, have me consecrated."
"Having indeed received the initiation of a virtuous ascetic, perform worship for me;
O King, I shall remain under your control. O virtuous one, O Adhokṣaja, accept me.
Having spoken thus and having been addressed by the Lord, the Blessed One then [accepted] the sacrificial offerings.
Then King Adhokṣaja vanished from the presence of the brahmins and the others;
having bestowed sacrificial fees and fed everyone,
he received the initiation of renunciation from the self-luminous sage.
He observed a fast and performed a purification of the body;
he had his head shaved, and having bathed, he offered oblations into the fire.
He also worshipped Nārāyaṇa within a *sarvatobhadra* mandala.
He gave gifts of cows, gifts of land, and gifts of gold and other such things (54).
For the sake of the temple of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa as well,
he gave a gift of one hundred thousand gold coins to his preceptor (55).
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā!
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times.
[56] "From fear of Time, Māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and wicked-hearted beings..."
He possesses a trident, a fish, a banner, a bow, a discus, and a swastika.
(57) "I am Brahmā; I am an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my Master. (58)
"Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; He is indeed my eternal Lord.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian.
(59) "The beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, the venerable Master, is my refuge."
"I am a devotee of the Beloved of Kṛṣṇa; Śrī Hari is my refuge.
"Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabha Svāmī, Śrī Hari, is my refuge"—these mantras he received from his self-manifested true guru.
Then, observing virtuous vows, he donned saffron robes;
he wore a sacred thread around his neck, a garland of tulasī on his hand,
an ointment of sandalwood as a tilaka, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and rings bearing the discus and other emblems.
For the purpose of worship, he took up a golden image of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Ramā,
and he performed worship of his guru;
he indeed preserved his own name as "Adhokṣajaprakāśa."
Having duly completed the two-fold initiation (*dīkṣā*) as an ancillary part of the rite on the bank of the lake,
he made his permanent residence there in a leaf-hut at that sacrificial site.
With supreme devotion, he chanted the name of Śrī Śaṅkara Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa.
He caused a beautiful temple for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa to be built;
he installed Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa within that shrine.
O King, this very temple, inhabited by Śrī Hari, shines resplendently.
Indeed, behold there the presence of Śrī and Hari.
O Indra among kings, bestow gifts and perform your ablutions here.
This sacred ford is a great holy place that grants the fruit of all sacrifices.
Yajñatīrtha, Sādhutīrtha, and Lakṣmītīrtha are likewise considered [sacred], as well as the tīrtha named Adhokṣaja and the tīrtha named Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, Dīkṣātīrtha is renowned; indeed, this very place is purifying.
Having worshipped Keśava here according to the prescribed rite during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one indeed obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice through bathing and giving gifts in Mārgaśīrṣa.
And by bathing and giving gifts in Pauṣa, one worships Nārāyaṇa who is endowed with Śrī.
By worshipping [Mādhava], one obtains the merit arising from the Vājapeya sacrifice;
and by bathing and giving gifts in the month of Māgha while thoroughly worshipping Mādhava,
one becomes a maker of sacred sites (tīrthakṛt) and attains here the supreme fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By bathing and giving gifts in the month of Phālguna, and having fully worshipped Govinda,
the performer of the rite shall indeed obtain the fruit arising from the sacrifice known as Atirātra.
Likewise, by bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Caitra, and having worshipped Viṣṇu, [one obtains that same fruit].
O King, that performer of the pilgrimage, having bathed and given gifts in Vaiśākha and having worshipped Madhusūdana, attains the purifying fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice;
he obtains here the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By bathing and giving gifts in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and by worshipping Trivikrama,
one obtains here the fruit of the Gavāyana sacrifice performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
By bathing and giving gifts in Āṣāḍha, and by thoroughly worshipping Vāmana, [one likewise attains that fruit].
By bathing and giving gifts here in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and by fully worshipping Śrīdhara, the performer of the pilgrimage obtains the fruit born of the Soma sacrifice. Furthermore,
the performer of the pilgrimage obtains here the fruit born of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
By bathing and likewise by giving gifts in the month of Bhādrapada, and having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa,
one obtains here the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice. By bathing and giving gifts in the month of Āśvina, and having worshipped Padmanābha— || 2.269.80 ||
A holy place-maker (tīrthakṛt) obtains various merits born of the conjunction with the moon by bathing and giving gifts in the month of Kārtika, and by worshipping Dāmodara. Furthermore,
one who sleeps at this holy place obtains the fruit arising from the sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
By bathing and giving gifts during the intercalary month (adhimāsa), and having worshipped Puruṣottama,
one who has performed the rites of a holy place obtains the supreme fruit of all *medha* sacrifices.
Furthermore, on whatever day it may be during this [month], through bathing, giving, recitation (*japa*), and other such acts— || 82–83 ||
O King, a pilgrim indeed obtains the fruits of all sacrifices;
by bathing and giving gifts on Śivarātri, the fruit of the Mahārudra rite shall be attained.
This is the purifying sacred field proclaimed by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
"Perform a bath and likewise worship Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Meditating upon all the Blessed Lords, you shall obtain all merits.
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, the king indeed became as pale as a horse. ||85-86||
Accompanied by his family, he bathed in the water and worshipped Hari in the temple,

together with Śrī, using the sixteen types of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and the waving of lights (nīrājana), and so forth. At that time, indeed, fourteen [manifestations] appeared within the image of Śrī Hari.
Indeed, the Blessed Lords beginning with Keśava appeared exactly as described.
After granting their vision for a moment within the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
all those incarnations merged into him, and he too vanished from sight.
King Aśvapāṭala experienced great wonder;
he then considered himself to have accomplished his purpose through the holy site of Adhokṣaja.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Lomaśa, here my vision born of Keśava and the other [deities] has arisen;
I have truly accomplished my purpose. What need is there for other holy places or extensive acts of charity?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, understand that all this has arisen through the power of sacred fords (tīrtha).
One who lacks a sacred ford possesses no strength, no merit, no purity,
no state of stainlessness, and no grace from Kṛṣṇa.
There is no devotion for one who has not visited a sacred ford (tīrtha), nor is there liberation or even heaven [for such a person].
Whether moving or stationary, a sacred ford is the destroyer of impurities. Once impurities have been destroyed, the pilgrim attains fitness [for higher states]. (93–94)
When fitness is truly perfected, Brahman indeed shines forth within the heart;
in that state, love for the devotee who is of the nature of Brahman arises.
A natural proximity to the Supreme Brahman comes to be born for him.
Then the vision of Hari, which is otherwise difficult to obtain, becomes easy to attain.
Thus, for one who has obtained such a vision, sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) are always prescribed as duties to be performed for the sake of gathering the world.
Therefore, one who is possessed of compassion should perform pilgrimages and acts of charity.
Whether he be a liberated one, a perfected being (*siddha*), a god, or a celestial being assuming the form of Brahmā—
whatever he practices that bestows liberation or grants heaven [should likewise be done].
Another person, however, practices by taking hold of that very merit.
Through that, liberation will surely occur, and it shall also become the gift of fearlessness.
One should practice at a sacred ford through action, mind, speech, and inner disposition. (2.269.100)
Having spoken thus to King Aśvapāṭala, Lomaśa led him to another sacred site, an excellent temple of Viṣṇu,
where indeed resides the eternal white form of Viṣṇu, O Rādhikā.
It shines, joined with Lakṣmī and adorned by Garuḍa.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Abhayākṣa’s Devotion, Renunciation, and Sacrifice on the Banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara Lake; His Taking of the Vow of Renunciation; His Vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Others; The Construction of the Temple; and the Lakṣmī-tīrtha and Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
(Chapter 269, Section 2: The Tretā-yuga-santāna).
Chapter 270 [Author:
Chapter 271 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā: afterwards, King Aśvapāṭala asked Lomaśa about the origin of the holy ford at the front of the sacred site. Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Lord, what is the name of this holy ford (tīrtha), when and by whom was it created?
O Guru, tell me what its fruit is and what ritual procedure must be performed here.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
O King, listen to the majesty of this sacred site; I shall tell it to you.
There was a Vaiśya named Devānīka, a cultivator who was exceedingly devoted.
He resided in the village of Ujjvala, staying day and night in his garden.
During the rainy season, the protector indeed remains having made his own dwelling there.
He constantly worships Śrī Hari; having bathed in the morning, he also performs worship.
At midday, having offered all food to Hari, he eats it.
Indeed, whatever crops, leaves, petals, vegetables, bulbous roots, and fruits there may be during the rainy season,
whether in the fields or in the garden, he [consumes] those that are fresh.
After offering [these] to Hari, the householder then partakes [of them].
Sugarcane stalks, ears of grain, seeds, vegetables such as bhājikā and the like, food fit for sages, sacrificial offerings, sacrificial fuel, and likewise juices—[all these he offers]. (7–8)
Honey, sugar-cane juice, molasses, *gundra*, and whatever milky plants there may be;
*bhājikā*, roasted grains, and likewise roasted pulses;
stalks, creepers, and whatever species of grasses there may be. (9)
Month after month, having offered his offspring to Hari, he would eat them.
Thus, O King, that king of devotees, who had surrendered himself, became a farmer.
Once, at the end of the rainy season, rain fell suddenly.
Violent winds, laden with large raindrops, blew throughout the night until dawn;
likewise during the day, and then again at night.
Day and night, due to the heavy downpours, the surface of the earth was filled with water.
The fields took on the form of water, and likewise the rivers overflowed their banks. Indeed, paths that were no longer passable appeared, as water surrounded the villages on all sides.
The roads became like rivers, and the trees stood as if situated in a lake.

When such a rain, causing extreme terror, had fallen, that farmer, trembling with his clothes soaked by the cold, took refuge at the base of a tree. Abandoning the waters of the rivers and leaving the path that was truly impassable, he remained there.
At night, they indeed arrived from all sides at the garden.
There were trees standing in the water; a farmer, having climbed that very tree for his own protection, remained firmly perched upon its three branches.
At night, by the turn of fate, a storm of wind and rain broke out.
A tree was tossed, whirled about, and felled by the wind.
Its branches were broken, yet the farmer, remembering Hari, [clung to] a small branch.
Having grasped it, he became firmly attached to the branch above the water.
Previously the branch had been pulled up, but now that it had gone into the midst of the water,
it was dragged along with the plowman and carried away into the middle of the river.
While being carried away by the force of the overflowing current, the horse-saddle tree branch,
though laden with fruit, sank into the waters of the lake.
But the farmer, finding himself without support, then knew how to swim across.
He indeed began to float in the midst of the water; was he perhaps afflicted by the cold? (22) But, exhausted by the waves and with his arms paralyzed, he sank.
"O Hara! O Nārāyaṇa! O Kṛṣṇa! O Bālakṛṣṇa! O All-pervading Lord! O Master! (23)
O Viṣṇu, Satyavrata was then rescued by you when he was submerged in the waters of the elephant;
formerly, O Lord, the earth was also rescued by you when it was submerged in the waters. (24)
Indeed, you rescue embodied beings here from the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Lord, you lead the water-born lotuses upward;
having yourself previously slept upon the waters, you then brought forth the Vairāja egg.
O Viṣṇu, you lie upon the serpent Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk during the dissolution;
today I too am asleep, so lead me quickly to that ocean.
Protect me at your own head, above the heavenly realm of your own world.
I have no desire to remain in the mortal world; lead me, however, to Your abode.
Homage to Śrī Viṣṇu, the conqueror of the worlds, the Supreme Self!
Homage to You, the omniscient one, the inner self and the supreme self!
"Here I renounce my very life-breaths; I surrender them at your feet.
Having spoken thus, he meditated in his mind upon Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
At that moment, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, arrived there.
Four-armed, youthful, and gentle, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
Hari, Viṣṇu, the delighter of the cowherds, took his own devotee Karṣuka by the hand from the midst of the water and led him to the shore. (3.1–3.2)
Having led the servant into his house, he even warmed him with fire;
then he fed him delicious foods and gave him garments.
He laid him upon a bed and protected him in every way.
There, a devotee was drawn from the water onto the bank and set down for a moment by Kṛṣṇa in the form of Viṣṇu; thus this supreme sacred site became known as Viṣṇutīrtha,
truly a savior from the ocean.
The farmer, having been protected, later went home;
having returned and caused a temple adorned with Viṣṇu to be built through the gift of wealth,
he installed the four-armed Viṣṇu here.
O King, this very temple, adorned with Viṣṇu, shines here;
it is renowned as the Tāraka Tīrtha, the most excellent of the excellent.
By bathing here one certainly crosses over [saṃsāra], and by giving gifts one also attains prosperity. (37–38)
And by performing the worship of Viṣṇu, one attains Vaikuṇṭha as well.
Therefore, perform your bath here and give gifts as you desire.
Having beheld Viṣṇu, perform the worship of the Teacher of the World.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭala indeed worshipped Viṣṇu with flowers and other offerings and bestowed gifts of gold;
thereafter, he proceeded to the holy site named Puruṣottama.
Aśvapāṭala said: How did this holy place (tīrtha) come to be known by the name Puruṣottama?
At what time and for what reason did it arise? Tell me its ritual procedure and its fruit.
Śrī Lomaśa said: Listen, O King, I shall describe the most excellent of all holy places (tīrthas), known as Puruṣottama, where the Supreme Person himself is truly present. 43.
In the regions of Ānarta, indeed in the city of Bhadrāyana,
the great Ṛṣi Brahmastamba was born into the house of a Brahmin.
From his very childhood, he was immersed in Hari, who is called the Imperishable Brahman.
Brahmā, whose self is Brahman and who is established in Brahman, worshipped the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Constantly intent on meditation, the yogi, abiding in the state of yogic absorption,
beholds indeed the divine form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa within his heart.
He for whom there is no obstruction by walls and no confinement by water, who possesses the power of traveling through space and the accomplishment of invisibility—
he indeed beholds Hari constantly at the time of his own performed worship.
The Supreme Lord comes before him and accepts the sandalwood paste and other offerings he gives;
He directly partakes of the milk-rice and other foods offered.
Such is the Brahmin who is like the Brahmastamba (the cosmic pillar) within his own mind.
A desire for penance, which grants peace through the propitiation of Hari, arose within him;
having gone there, he remained at the Karamardī lake for one year.
Then he went indeed to the famous Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having arrived here, he stayed upon the bank and took up residence at Āmraka (51).
At the foot of a mango tree with auspicious shade, he became intent on steady meditation.
He performed bathing, meditation, recitation, worship, libations, and the dedication [of all acts] to the Lord (52).
One indeed performs one's own purifying action that bestows merit:
the constant vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. One does so eternally in the morning and also worships Him directly.
For one who worships Him in this manner every morning,
the Supreme Lord Hari— the Soul of the Universe— manifests in person, assuming a divine form.
Those who know yoga, possessing divine vision and superhuman insight, behold Him.
There, by Brahmastamba, a beautiful leaf-hut was made;
on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, a small shrine for Puruṣottama was built. There, he then constructed this splendid temple.
Where Puruṣottama himself shines forth in embodied form,
that is the Puruṣottama-tīrtha on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
It is called the Brahmastamba-tīrtha, which bestows divine liberation.
By bathing here, one attains [the vision of] Puruṣottama, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
by giving gifts here, one attains the eternal world of Brahmā.
O King, the fruit of worshipping Puruṣottama cannot be described.
Indeed, the worshiper of this [Lord] is born as the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa;
the devotee is born as the embodiment of Brahman, a great enjoyer.
O King, perform here the bathing, giving, chanting, and worship of Hari.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, King Aśvapāṭṭala performed with all his being the rites of bathing, giving, and worship. Then, afterwards, he went to the holy ford known as Mahāviṣṇupratīrthaka.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, at the confluence of the Kṣīrikā, there is an auspicious place.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, why is this holy site named after Mahāviṣṇu?"
"Tell me also how she was born from a frog and what her fruit [the result of her actions] was.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"The daughter of the god Mūla-bhakta was an immortal maiden (amarakanyā)."
In former times, she performed difficult penance here to attain Hari;
that virtuous woman, devoted solely to Mahāviṣṇu, lived on fruits and roots, dwelt in the open air, wore matted hair, and was clad in fine bark garments and the like. (65–66)
Afterwards, subsisting on air alone, she remained standing on one foot,
constantly closing her eyes and devoted to the recitation of the *japa* rosary.
When much time had passed in this manner, Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, [appeared].
The Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet was seen,
possessing a serene countenance, resplendent in the midst of light,
well-formed, and the Lord adorned with weapons and ornaments such as a beautiful crown.
Then he became two-armed and spoke to the celestial maiden:
"Speak, O Goddess; I am pleased. What is in your heart?
Whatever you desire, I shall grant it here, for I have come for your sake."
Then, opening her eyes, Sundarī beheld Hari—the Great Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, appearing with two arms;
a beloved one worthy of a beautiful form, a youth who is the abode of all virtuous qualities. (71–72)
Thus entreating him, saying, "O Blessed One, be my husband," Satī fell at the feet of Mahāviṣṇu. Then Hari said to the ascetic woman, "So be it," and took her hand in his own.
She too, overcome by love, seized it for a moment and gave her own rosary to Viṣṇu; she became attached to Kṛṣṇa’s chest.
The Blessed Lord, taking her as his own, spoke to that virtuous Vaiṣṇavī.
"I shall take you, O fortunate one, O daughter of the immortals, O most beautiful one!
On this earth, I am the Lord in the form of Mahāviṣṇu;
indeed, I dwell before Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (76)
"Worship me; I shall now accept you as that Blessed Lord according to the prescribed rite.
