(77) Then the Goddess placed a mental flower-garland around his neck, and Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa appeared before her. (78)
And I, Lomaśa, was present there at that time;
having quickly manifested the fire,
I caused the celestial vehicle to be brought forth by Viṣṇu, and that Satī shone within the house.
And the Lord Mahāviṣṇu shone forth, having become a human being.
Having obtained as her husband the Blessed One, the elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with all virtues,
that daughter of the immortals felt she had accomplished her purpose and was filled with happiness.
This very place is a station of austerity, frequented by the daughters of the immortals; it is known as Amarī-tīrtha, as Bhagavat-tīrtha,
as Vivāha-tīrtha, and likewise as Mahāviṣṇu-tīrtha.
By bathing here, by giving gifts, and by the worship of Mahāviṣṇu,
one attains the station of Mahāviṣṇu and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
O King, in this beautiful abode, one should worship Viṣṇu as Amarīviṣṇu.
"The devotee shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, and become a partaker of eternal bliss.
Having been told this, O Rādhikā, the king bathed, gave gifts, and worshipped Him.
Then he went to the supreme holy place known as Sanatkumāra.
"It bestows a mass of merit, is most excellent, and destroys all sins.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"How and when did that Sanatkumāra-tīrtha come into existence in ancient times?"
"O Guru, tell me here of its majesty, the procedure for its worship, and the fruit thereof.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"In this forest there lived a wood-gatherer who carried water from a well."
Living as a wood-gatherer in the forest, he was always devoted to his axe as his only tool.
He worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world—that virtuous son of Brahmā who is Sanatkumāra in form. (88–89)
Devoted to the service of the virtuous, he indeed cultivates the company of the good;
for with action, mind, speech, and body, he serves the saints.
The Blessed Lord is indeed the saint; the saint alone is the supreme goal.
Service to the virtuous is a source of great merit, for the virtuous are purifiers. (9.1) A wood-gatherer and his wife used to serve a circle of holy men;
having performed their tasks, such as splitting wood, during the day, they would attend them at the onset of night. (9.2)
Devoted to Nārāyaṇa, the two of them performed service for the virtuous;
they were intent on serving the holy men who were disciples of Sanatkumāra.
Then, they indeed went into the forest to gather firewood.
Supported by an elephant, the wood-gatherer suddenly remembered his true guru,
the Lord Sanatkumāra, who dwells in Satyaloka. The blessed Sanatkumāra immediately became visible to him.
In the forest, he said to the elephant: "O beast, what indeed are you doing?
Do not pointlessly cast this wild one, who is a friend in form, into distress here.
'Do not, do not, do not kill me, O wood-slayer! He is certainly not your enemy. (96)
The elephant said:
"O Sanatkumāra, I shall now discharge my enmity against the Blessed One.
This Brāhmaṇa was once a man living on this marshy bank, devoted to righteous deeds and the like. (97)
Devoted to the ritual section of the Vedas and intent on meritorious acts such as the gift of knowledge,
I was once a king named Rāyadhaneśvara.
This man, acting as my guru, issued a command to me.
But I, unable to tolerate this, forbade him from entering the teaching.
Then he cursed me: "Become an elephant in the midst of the forest!
Cursed by me, he replied: "Then become a wood-gatherer in that very forest. (2.270.100)
"Therefore, I, the king, shall kill the wood-gatherer; of this there is no doubt.
O virtuous one, do not create an obstacle for me in the execution of my enmity.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O slayer of men, what fruit would there be for you here in merely enduring this enmity?
Do not act thus, O lord of the forest; accept liberation from me.
Thus spoke the venerable Sanatkumāra, who had arrived there.
"Accept the mantra and, casting off this body, go to the supreme state.
The elephant said:
"O ocean of mercy, grant me the mantra; grant me liberation; have compassion!"
Furthermore, just as there would be no rebirth for me, nor any cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Sanatkumāra said:
"Come, O elephant, to the shore of the lake; having drunk the water that provides a refuge of comfort."
"Having received the mantra, go indeed to the supreme abode, the imperishable state.
(1.05) Thus, O King, Sanatkumāra, the elephant, and the wood-cutter—these three arrived there together; [the third being] the sage Sanatkumāra. (1.06)
He indeed caused him to drink water and bathed him there;
he bestowed the Vaiṣṇava mantra and granted liberation to Hastin.
Having become composed, the wood-gatherer performed the worship.
There he established that virtuous Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā and Supreme Lord, within a wooden leaf-hut.
The blessed Sanatkumāra shone there in the form of an embodied image. (108–109)
Having attained a divine form through truth, he went there; this is his supreme holy site (tīrtha).
Indeed, there is the Sanatkumāra-tīrtha and likewise the auspicious Hasti-tīrtha. Furthermore, the Kāṣṭhahāra-pratīrtha is proclaimed as the most excellent of the excellent.
Thus, a sacred ford (tīrtha) has arisen right here; O King, bathe indeed in this place!
Worship the sage Sanatkumāra, the Supreme Lord. Through bathing, giving, and worship here, worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained.
Thus addressed, the king there performed his bath in the Rādhikā [tīrtha],
worshipped the sage Sanatkumāra, and likewise gave gifts.
Then he proceeded further to another sacred ford (tīrtha) that purifies one of sin.
From remembering, reciting, and hearing this, liberation shall come to pass.

Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*: [the account of] Viṣṇutīrtha, where Devānīka Karṣuka, who was submerged in water, was rescued by Viṣṇu; Puruṣottamatīrtha, where the Brahmin Brahmastamba, a resident of Bhadrāyana village, attained the vision of Puruṣottama while performing austerities; Mahāviṣṇutīrtha, where the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu, propitiated by the maiden Amaryā of Devamūlaka who remained steadfast in penance, accepted her according to the rites of marriage; and [the account of] Kūpyavālaka, the wood-gatherer.
The two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Sanatkumāra-tīrtha, where Sanatkumāra provided protection from an elephant," etc.
[End of Chapter 270]. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 271.
[Author: Chapter 272.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; thereafter, King Aśvapāṭala [will appear].
He proceeded to the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Kuṅkumeśvara, which is the refuge of Sadāśiva.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, tell me why this sacred ford exists and how it came to be."
"According to the prescribed rule, its fruit and all its observances (niyama) and so forth are in every way [attained].
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"Listen, O King, in former times there was a certain killer from a distant land."
Afflicted by the suffering of his kinsmen's afflictions, he arrived in Saurāṣṭra.
Having recognized that sacred site, he dwelt there at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
thereafter, abandoning all acts of violence, he became a mendicant who subsisted on alms.
"O Hare Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Brahman, Lord of Śrī, Supreme Lord!"— by reciting this name through the association of the virtuous,
he performed japa, engaged in devotional worship, and likewise performed ritual bathing at sacred fords and other such rites. || 5 ||
Having thus performed meritorious deeds and service to the virtuous day and night,
he died there in that sacred field known as Akṣara.
By virtue of his connection with that holy site (tīrtha), he indeed went to heaven and attained divinity.
Then, once again in human form, he became a Brahmin named Kuṅkuma;
he was devoted to righteous deeds and attentive to his duties toward the gods.
Furthermore, being one who remembered his former births, he likewise worshipped Śaṅkara.
Having fashioned an earthen image of Śaṅkara, the brāhmaṇa installed it there.
At the end of a year, at the end of five years, and likewise at the end of ten years,
he indeed performs a great festival, including the feeding of brāhmaṇas and other rites.
On Śivarātri, he performed the annual festival for Śaṅkara.
Thus, at the end of twenty years, Śaṅkara appeared before him in person:
"O Brahmin, I am pleased with your devotion; choose whatever you desire."
The Brahmin said: "O Lord of Pārvatī, grant me great liberation.
Śambhu replied: "Listen, O devotee; I am the God who is the Supreme Lord.
Kailāsa is my abode, and beyond that is the Gavāyana."

Goloka is the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; beyond that is the Imperishable (Akṣara). If you desire to go to Goloka, worship the Lord of the Cowherds—the Lord Gopāla, the husband of Śrī Rādhikā, who holds a flute in His hand. (14)
If you desire to go to the Imperishable One, worship Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Kailāsa is my abode, the dwelling place of Sadāśiva. (15–16)
"If you desire to go there, where that place equal to Vaikuṇṭha resides, I shall lead you among my attendants and establish you there; tell me what you desire.
Kuṅkuma said:
"I shall go to that abode which is imperishable, consisting of liberation, and higher than the highest.
I have no desire for any other abode; therefore, tell me here the means to achieve that.
Śambhu said:
"O sinless one, receive this divine mantra of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa:
'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and you shall go to the imperishable realm. (19)
"Worship Him, chant His name, and remember Him, the Supreme Lord.
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin Śaṅkara quickly vanished;
[there remained] Mahādeva in the form of stone, named Kuṅkumeśvara.
Having established [the deity] in the temple, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
This very place is a purifying holy site (tīrtha), the abode of Sadāśiva.
And having established the Kuṅkumeśvara-tīrtha, that twice-born man indeed became known as Kuṅkuma.
Having worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he went to the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma).
By bathing here as well as by giving gifts, Mahādeva becomes pleased;
and having bestowed the Vaiṣṇava mantra, He causes one to attain the imperishable state.
"Therefore, O King, bathe quickly and give gold in charity.
Thus addressed by Lomaśa, O Rādhikā,
Aśvapaṭala performed his bathing, giving of gifts, and worship, and went to the foremost of holy fords.
"It is indeed renowned by the name Satīśatīrtha, the supreme purifier.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, how did this auspicious holy place (tīrtha) come to be known as Satīśa?"
"Tell me briefly its ritual procedure and its fruit as well.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you this which originates from the Satīśa-tīrtha."
O King, here in the vicinity of Derikākheṭa, families of wandering minstrels as well as families of cowherds dwell;
they tend hundreds of cows and likewise thousands of goats. (28–29)
They tend to the bulls and the young calves as if they were their own wealth;
they graze them on the borders of the fields and provide them with water to drink here.
At night, they rest them on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
In the morning, they would indeed go back again to the forest for tending the cattle.
Thus, those cowherds and wandering minstrels lived beneath trees on the embankment surrounding the lake at Kuṅkumeśvara.
Once, while staying in Parṇapallī, that chaste woman Cāraṇī was asleep;
she was a devoted wife named Satīśā and a devotee of the illustrious Mahādeva.
In the morning, she performed her ritual bath and consecration with the milk of Mahādeva.
She indeed performed [her service] for the Lord of Pārvatī with her innermost heart and true devotion.
Then, thieves entered her house while it was empty of her husband and, finding the virtuous woman alone, they violated her—she who was possessed of such devotion. (34–35)
Her husband had gone to another village, to the house of a relative.
Having thus found an opportunity, the thieves assailed the virtuous woman.
That chaste lady, devoted to righteousness, remembered the virtuous Pārvatī.
O Mother, you who are Caṇḍī, the yoginī of Śaṅkara and the destroyer of the wicked,
quickly grant me protection from thieves indeed.
Having boiled milk this morning, I shall offer it as an oblation to you.
Thus remembered, Satī Durgā then swiftly took a sword in her hand and went from the side of Kuṃkumeśvara to the abode of Śiva.
Armed with a sword, a dagger, and a mace, she was accompanied by Siṃhikā.
Roaring with eight hands, she seized the thieves;
she suddenly struck down the thieves and protected those who were virtuous.
The thieves were slain by the sword, and five men then died.
Satīśā arrived at the waters of the lake together with Durgā.
Having both drunk the water, they went to Kuṅkumeśvara.
There, Durgā remained hidden while Satīśā stayed in the temple.
In the morning, the Gaṇas returned to their own home and carried away the slain people. That virtuous Satī, who had drunk water at that place where Durgā was present,
established the goddess Durgā on the bank there.
Durgātīrtha, Satītīrtha, Satīśātīrtha,
and likewise Pārvatītīrtha became indeed the protectors of righteousness.
By bathing here, by giving gifts, and by beholding Satīśa, [one attains merit].
The destruction of fear from thieves and other dangers, as well as the protection of Dharma, will certainly come to pass.
O King, perform ablutions, likewise practice charity, behold the virtuous,
and also carry out the worship of Durgā at the sacred site of Durgā-tīrtha.
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, the king bathed, gave gifts, and performed worship.
Then the king went to another holy site on the Setu in the foremost region.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, O Lord, instruct me regarding this best of holy fords (tīrtha):
how, why, and when did it arise, and what indeed is the fruit of this purifying place?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Dhanyeśvarī, the wife of a merchant, was devoted to service and devotion;
she was a true Vaiṣṇavī and a faithful devotee in Kuṅkumavāpī.
Yet, under the influence of greed, she would occasionally take the property of others.
Once she went to the house of Kambharā Mahālakṣmī.
Having entertained Bālakṛṣṇa and bowed to the virtuous Śrī Kambharā,
she took ten jewels by stealth and returned to her own home.
In a householder's jar where jewels and wealth were kept,
he even placed those things brought by theft within that very jar.
Then, after some time had passed, on the auspicious occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), ||53||
Having taken a water jar,
a housewife arrived here at the bank of the Āśvapatta lake to bathe and to give gifts.
As she was bathing and about to place her own hand into the jar to give the offerings, || 54-55 ||
Having caused [them] to enter, he took the jewels; yet at that very moment,
all the jewels became stuck to the jar,
and then everything within the jar became like a single solid mass.
The hand was joined within the ball, and the ball was situated within the jar;
the jar rested upon the earth, and indeed everything became one.
Dhanyeśvarī was seized with fear, wondering, "What is this that has come into my hand?"
The beautiful woman made an effort to withdraw her hand;
she became exhausted and weary, watched by the many people.
Then, indeed, an auspicious sound arose from within the jar.
"Indeed, you have placed jewels here in this jar by means of theft. The fruit of that has now arisen for you: your state as a physical body shall not perish.
O friend, if you have the desire to separate yourself from it," [he said].
"I am Lakṣmī herself; build my temple and, having summoned Lomaśa, give him all the wealth.
Then your hand shall be released, but never otherwise."
Having been addressed thus, she then summoned me, Lomaśa, to this place.
She made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the donation of a water-pot intended for the temple;
thereafter, her hand became separated from the pot at that spot.
Then Lakṣmī herself, four-armed, was revealed from the jar;
having displayed her form for a moment, she vanished right there on the spot.
Thereafter, the temple of Lakṣmī was caused to be built here by me.
And Lakṣmī herself dwells here, having been worshipped as Dhanyeśvarī.
Thus, the Lakṣmītīrtha, the Dhanyeśvarītīrtha, and Ghaṭasthalī became renowned; this [place] is the remover of the sin of theft. (66–67)
Furthermore, the offering of the "lump of sin" (pāpapiṇḍa) and so forth bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
likewise, bathing, giving gifts, and other rites here bring about the destruction of sins.
By worshipping Lakṣmī here, one becomes possessed of fortune and wealth.
One shall attain the world of Lakṣmī and become devoted to the service of Lakṣmī.
"O King, bathe, give gifts, and worship Śrī with what is fitting.
Thus addressed, Aśvapaṭala bathed, gave gifts, and worshipped her.
O Rādhikā, he then went ahead with Lomaśa to the great holy site of Śālagrāma, which was resplendent with temples.
Aśvapāṭala said:
"O Guru, this sacred site (tīrtha) where the Śālagrāma resides is most excellent.
When and how did it come into being? Teach me its ritual procedure and its fruit.
Śrī Lomaśa said:
There was a twice-born man named Caityabrahmā who followed a degraded way of life;
he dwelt among the lowly and subsisted on lowly food.
Having encountered sinful company, he became constantly devoted to sin.
He drank liquor and committed theft through association;
likewise, he committed adultery. Thus, following the conduct of a *cāṇḍāla*, even though he was a Brahmin, he became fallen from his caste, family, and other such status.
Then one night, a holy man arrived at his house;
the brahmin treated that guest with contempt, as if he were a low-born person.
Recognizing his wicked conduct, the holy man summoned a messenger of Yama.
Then, O King, the messenger of Yama quickly arrived at his house.
He then killed him in many ways, like the slaughter of an animal; but when that virtuous man, devoted to compassion, begged for forgiveness, [the messenger] then [acted]. || 77–78 ||
Then he liberated that wicked man from the fear of Yama’s messengers;
the virtuous one departed by the proper path, while the wicked brahmin went to my hermitage, to me, his guru, desiring deliverance. (79)
He then prayed in many ways for his own deliverance from the image.
Lomaśa granted him an expiation lasting one year;
he, moreover, performed the vow of twelve *cāndrāyaṇas*.
He gave a Śālagrāma stone to that pure brāhmaṇa for the purpose of worship,
and that brāhmaṇa worshipped it appropriately.
Then, out of devotion to Viṣṇu, I gave him a mantra.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā.
(83) He performs the recitation of this mantra and the worship of the Śālagrāma stone;
he also practices meditation and devotional service to Hari day and night. (84)

In the early morning, during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, he would indeed go there to the bank with a *śālagrāma* stone; and there, on the Setu near the *tulasī* tree, he would always perform worship until the rising of the sun.
Thus, when much time had passed, Śālagrāma became pleased upon beholding his devotion; he indeed became the divine Viṣṇu,
while the Śālagrāma stone then attained dissolution there, O twice-born one.
"Protect, protect, O ocean of mercy! Grant me deliverance, O Lord!
Having spoken thus, he then fell at the feet of Viṣṇu.
At that very moment, the goddess Lakṣmī emerged from the tulasī tree.

Śrī said to the brāhmaṇa: "Indeed, have a temple for Tulasī built here, as well as a shrine for Śālagrāma on the bank of the lake. By that means, you will attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (2.271.90)
Having spoken thus, she vanished and indeed took the form of a tree;
Viṣṇu also vanished and became a Śālagrāma stone.
O King, this very temple was caused to be built by that brāhmaṇa.
In its midst shines the divine Tulasī in the form of a tree.
At its root resides the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu in the form of the Śāla-stone.
By bathing here, by giving gifts, and by worshipping the Lord Tulasī, [one attains the highest goal].
By joining one's hands with *tulasī*, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
all sins are destroyed, and one attains heaven and even beyond heaven.
Śālagrāma is an auspicious holy site, as is the *tulasī* holy site.
This purifying holy site known as Caityabrahma also exists here. O King, bathe and offer worship to Tulasī and Kṛṣṇa, who reside in the temple; thus attain the favor of Kṛṣṇa. (95–96)
Thus addressed by Rādhikā, the king bathed, gave gifts, and performed worship;
having received the nectar of the water as well as the nectar of the divine grace,
he performed circumambulation and prostrated like a staff before the other sacred ford.
Yoked with Lomaśa, he indeed traveled joyfully across Lake Mānasa.
"Aha! All these sacred fords are truly composed of the Blessed Lord; they have been visited by me, a fortunate one who is a vessel of Hari’s grace. (98–99)
Thus, the king, filled with wonder, attained great peace within his heart; for a moment, he meditated in his own heart upon Lomaśa, the knowledge-bestowing guru,
and upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
The King, situated in the northwestern corner, remembered Lake Nemi-sarovara.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "Description of the Kuṅkuma-viprakṛta Kuṅkumeśvara Tīrtha, the Durgā-satī Tīrtha established by Satī Śācāraṇī, the Lakṣmī Tīrtha established by Dhanyeśvarī, the wife of a merchant, and the Śālagrāma Tīrtha established by Caitya Brahmadvija," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (271)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā; thereafter the king, having gone to the holy place called Nara-Nārāyaṇa, questioned the best of sages, Lomaśa.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Lord Lomaśa, tell me how and why this sacred ford (tīrtha) is named after Nara and Nārāyaṇa; what is the ritual procedure here, and what is its fruit?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the holy place that is the most excellent among the best of holy places.
Here indeed were Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa, the master of the cows and the father of Hari.
First, indeed, for the sake of a son, he performed severe penance;
and that deity Nara-Nārāyaṇa who dwells on the Himālaya mountains, the protector of the dharma of ascetics and devoted to the vow of celibacy. (4)
Having meditated upon the supreme excellence of ascetics, he indeed practiced penance.
First he abandoned food; thereafter he became devoted to eating roots; then he subsisted on leaves, and after that, he ate only withered leaves.
Thereafter he subsisted on water, and then he arose as one who subsists on air.
He constantly chanted the names of Śrī Nara and Nārāyaṇa within his heart.
Thus, at the end of a hundred years, Nara and Nārāyaṇa [appeared] there.
Kṛṣṇa and Hari—these four Blessed Lords—arrived together.
Having come into his presence, they said to that cowherd Kṛṣṇa:
"O Mahāviṣṇu, O Nārāyaṇa, why indeed do you perform penance? (8–9)
"O Vāsudeva, sustainer of the world, what is the reason for your ascetic penance? We four Nārāyaṇas are truly pleased with you.
Speak as you wish; we shall grant you here whatever boon you desire."
Having heard this, Gopāla Kṛṣṇa spoke for the sake of the welfare of the worlds,
of the gods, of the ancestors, as well as of women,
birds, animals, creepers, and trees.
"May you become my sons from the pillars and the grasses. "So be it," they replied, and then those four supreme lords— Nārāyaṇa and Nara as well— entered into his body.
Kṛṣṇa and Hari were his mind-born sons;
and the Kaṃbharā-boys were portions [of him] for the sake of the world's welfare. Nārāyaṇa was the eldest, known by the name Śrī Bhagavān.
From him was born a man named Śukadeva as the second;
and Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
is this third incarnation, the Lord of Akṣara.
Then Hariścandra was the fourth, and his name was Śrīvallabha.
O King, those boys there were indeed supreme lords; they were equal in status, equal in sovereignty, and endowed with equal bodily splendor. (17–18)
This ground is purifying because it is here that Gopālakṛṣṇa performed most rigorous penance, and this very place is his temple.
Here, that Gopālakṛṣṇa [worshipped] Nārāyaṇa as well as Nara.
He installed images of Kṛṣṇa and Hari in the temple.
This is the preeminent of all holy places, the abode above all sacred sites;
having found rest here, take up the fourfold masters in meditation.
From remembering, seeing, bathing here, drinking [the water], worshipping, giving gifts, and also from serving, liberation alone is the great fruit. Indeed,
there is no fruit equal to this among sacrifices or religious observances.
There is no fruit equal to this for sacrificial fees and initiations.
O King, here on this earth there once was a vast region known as Brahmasaṃjñita,
which is seen today as this Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Aśvapāṭala said:
O Sage, when did this beautiful lake, which contains all holy fords (tīrthas) and is the refuge of all Nārāyaṇas, truly come into existence here upon the earth? 25.
Śrī Lomaśa said: Formerly, while I was in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha,
I once heard that there is the Lord of the Imperishable, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the universe of the four-faced Brahmā, within the abode of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
one becomes a human being for the sake of the welfare of the world.
At that time, all the Nārāyaṇas and likewise all the Īśvaras are liberated.
The sages and the ancestors also assembled here upon the earth.
(28) So too did the goddesses, the wives of the lords, the liberated ones, and the cowherd women;
the daughters of Nārāyaṇa, the daughters of Brahmā, the celestial nymphs, and the wives of the gods. (29)
All the beloveds of Brahmā, the beloveds of Hari,
and all the powers (śaktis) belonging to Viṣṇu also arrived there for the sake of a welcome,
for the sake of worship, and likewise for the sake of dwelling together.
Thus, for the sake of service, they and those women worshipped the Supreme Lord.
Then both they and those women awaited His very manifestation;
and at that time, He said: "I beheld this entire festival."
Then, in the supreme abode of the Imperishable, Māṇikī realized:
"My Lord is the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all lords;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is descending to the earth. (33)
Formerly, she had come to the Vyāghra forest on earth by her own power.
Desiring to become the vehicle for this vow of celibacy, Satī wished to take the form of Aśvinī and desired the form of a maiden according to her choice. (34–35)
Having become a mare, she wandered through unknown regions of the earth;
here, at this auspicious sacred site (tīrtha), she remained seeking Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
She, the beloved of Hari, possessed of a divine form, was beheld by Īśvara and the other gods. (36)
Wherever she was, that ground became a horse-collar (aśvapaṭṭikā).
It also became a sacred ford (tīrtha), and this was our conclusion:
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shall dwell here.
At that moment, Brahmahrada arrived there from the imperishable state (akṣara-pada),
taking the form of water, possessing a divine luster, and consisting of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
here on this earth, he became that divine lake whose essence is water.
"Remember, O King, that which is the Brahmahrada and the divine lake;
he who is the performer of the Soma sacrifice, King Aśvapāṭala, is none other than you yourself, shining upon the earth having assumed a human form. (2.272.40–41)
Thus addressed, O Rādhikā, that king indeed looked at himself;
he beheld the lake of Brahmā, released by Brahmā, which serves as a descent for the waters of the celestial lotus-lake.
He considered it a supreme wonder, for in that moment, true knowledge had indeed arisen within him.
Furthermore, he considered everything that had dissolved back into its own primordial nature.
Then Śrī Lomaśa said: "O King, this supreme holy place is the purifying Māṇikītīrtha and also known as Aśvinītīrtha."
I have seen all this directly with my own eyes: the great holy ford of Brahmahrada and the Aśvapāṭala ford;
beyond that, I have established my permanent residence here in this auspicious hermitage.
Likewise, the incarnations, the liberated souls, and the lords such as the deities—
all of them resided in the imperishable Akṣarāśvapaṭṭasāgara, the field of Hari,
after the manifestation of Hari. ||46-47||
With supreme love, they worshipped Anādikṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Padmā, Ramā, Jayā, Rati, Lalitā, Padminī, Rambhā, Māṇikī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī. (48)
Gaṅgā, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Saṃjñā, Yamunā, Rohiṇī, Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, Hāsā, Haimī, Śānti, Supuṣpikā, Manu, Kastūrikā, Devī, Campā, Ambhojasvatī, and Vṛjā. (49–50)
All the goddesses, the wives of Brahmā, numbering in the hundreds of billions and trillions,
arrived and dwelt right here in this lake at the foot of Hari.
The Gaṇḍakī, the Svarṇarekhā, the Narmadā, and the Tuṅgabhadrī [also settled there].
The Godāvarī, Brahmaputrā, Kāverī, Phalgu, and Īśvarī;
the Kṛṣṇā, Śoṇā, Gomatī, Sindhu, and likewise the Coralikā; the Śoṇabhadra, Cerāvatī, Sālvī, Nā, Menakā, and Aṅgikā.
Mannāmnī, Cāṅgaśikṣāṅgī, and likewise Kāñcanagaṅgikā;
Tryaṅgahā, Āmūrakā, Vīṇā, Yānāsanā,
as well as Ombā, Trivalī, Āmū, Vālagā, and Nīparā.
Devikā, Ubā, Utkrośī, Nāilī, Prapattikā, Sevikā, Nāstijarā,
Kaṅgukī, Kyubagaṅgā, Rañjikā, Viṣatūrā, and Jampikā. (54–55)
Śvetā, Nārāyaṇī, Matkuñjā, Yūkanāyikā, Niraśāṇā, Miśrajālā, Āmajanā, Parānikā, Śvānā, Grāsakāyānā, Viṣatūryā, and Kaliṅginī. (56)
Likewise, other rivers such as the Mūrā,
all of them taking the form of sacred fords (tīrtha), came to that lake for the purpose of dwelling there forever.
[Also present were] Mānasa, Indradyumna, Nārāyaṇa, and Puṣkara.
Pampā, Indraprastharūpa, Sudarśana, and Revata;
likewise Śivasaras, Citkṛtsaras, Kaulārakasara, Śivaśīla, Mīnakaṅgasaras, and Sābharakasara. ||58–59||
Also Bālakṛṣṇa Lake, the Dvikala lake,
the Saṭālapha lake, and the Viṣatūra lake;
likewise the Urala lake and the Triguṇoraska lake.
Pherumaṇḍa, Lūrāsara, the lake called Maśaka,
Rukma, Trināsika,
Eṣāla, Saṭālpaka, Alparūkṣa, and the lake Ārdravārta. (61–62)
Furthermore, there is Tryaṅgānaka, Mayūrasa, and likewise Saras;
Bangapāla, Nyūnajāmī, Śirāvāsa, and likewise Saras;
Aitasa, Caunīyāgara, Lenduga, and likewise Pāyuga.
Yonigama, Aurasa, Tūronasa, Gaura, and likewise Saras;
Gogrāsa, Bālarīśa, Ubarāsa, and likewise Saras; Jayaśāna, Grātavāra, Grātaslāva, and likewise Saras. (64–65)
The lake Krītastāva, Ceṣṭavāsa, Pīlipārśva,
Supārayāra, Kālīya, and the lake Itarīśa—
these lakes also stood there, having indeed arrived at that place.
Vṛndāvana, Mahākālavana, and likewise Tapovana;
Indraprasthavana, Dharmāraṇya, and Pauṣkaraka-vana;
Siṃhāraṇya, Badaryāraṇyaka, and Sundaraka-vana. (67–68)
Prāgjyotiṣāraṇyaka, Kāśamāraṇya, Irāraṇya, Śikṣāraṇya, Rāśavana,
Uralāraṇyaka, and Khāsīnāraṇyaka.
Bālāyana-mahāraṇya, as well as Sahārāraṇya;
Vālajīvāraṇyaka, and likewise Śādayānavana; Amarīvana, and also Abriktāraṇyaka. (2.272.70–71)
Likewise, Siṃhāraṇya and the Daivavana forests arrived there;
having offered a welcome and worship, they established a residence for Hari here at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, remaining there forever.
Thus, O King, this Aśvapaṭṭasara is a supreme holy site (tīrtha).
It is the purifier of all holy sites, auspicious, and consists of the Brahma-lake.
Whatever [holy sites] exist on earth, in the heavenly world, or elsewhere— [this is superior to them]. (73–74)
There are sacred fords there, such as Viraja and others;
and oceans of divine waters dwell here perpetually within these waters.
Therein resides the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Therein abide all the incarnations and whatever abodes there are;
the lords and goddesses, the gods and goddesses dwell there; all sovereign powers and spiritual accomplishments reside there as well. (76–77)
That is indeed the supreme Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha;
here the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama took up His residence.
At that time, all His auspicious beloveds were present with Him in bodily form.
One hundred and twenty-five noble ladies, who occupy the left side of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
arrived at the beautiful western lake situated within the Setu region.
They entered [the waters] which were the very embodiment of sacred fords; therefore, that place is called Śatatīrtha.
On the day of the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived there accompanied by cowherds and cowherd women.
It is known as Gopītīrtha, Gopatīrtha, and Golokatīrtha;
it is also called Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and it bestows supreme liberation in Goloka.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived here, he spoke to Rādhikā. (82–83)
"O Rādhikā, listen to this," he said to his beloved Rādhikā:
"Thousands of universes have been created by Vairāja;
and in each of them, Hari has been established for the purpose of entering and presiding over them. (84)
He prayed to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa:
"O Hari Kṛṣṇa, Hari Kṛṣṇa, O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of lords!
You are the sovereign master in all the universes created by me. (85–86)

O Mādhava, as long as you do not arrive, who will establish the order for those performing righteous deeds, for living beings, and for worldly transactions? And who will provide instruction to the Daityas and those characterized by darkness?
Who other than you will effect the destruction of the sins of sinners?
(88) Who other than you will perform the injunctions for Vedic initiation and the like, as well as the divine rites such as sacrifices and oblations, and the ancestral rites that bestow merit? (89)
And who, apart from you, will establish the boundaries for embodied beings?
Who will provide the gift of self-knowledge to the virtuous and protect the dharma?
Who will arrange the proper rites for chaste women and perform the work of marriage?

For embodied beings who are submerged in passion and hatred and wandering in delusion, who else but You and Your association will grant liberation? [The paths of] the dharma of worship, the dharma of protection, and the dharma of what has arisen—[all depend on You]. (9.1–9.2)
Who, indeed, apart from you, will proclaim to humanity the dharma of service,
the dharma of virtuous conduct, the dharma of the householder, the dharma of the forest-dweller, the ritual duties of the ascetic,
the dharma of renunciation, self-surrender, and the ancient code of ethics? (93)
And who but you could compose the *Paddhati* and the *Vārṇikī*?
Even without your manifestation, those cosmic eggs, all the cremation grounds, and the birthplaces of life and death [would exist]. (94–95)
Without you, the perfected ones (sādhus) who have attained liberation will not depart from the imperishable state;
likewise, the attendants (pārṣadas) and the goddesses of fortune (lakṣmīs) will not go to the millions of cosmic eggs (aṇḍas).
Without you, there will be no auspiciousness whatsoever among the gods and others.
Without you, protection will certainly not exist as it truly is.
O Blessed One, without you, the entire household will become empty; even the dwellings of yogins will no longer exist in any way whatsoever. (97–98)
Likewise, those incarnations will also pass away;
and among them, who else but the sovereign of all creation would go first?
O Lord, [there is no one else] regarding the knowledge of the path to liberation and so forth, as well as the methods of worship and the like.
Even the sattvic gods and others will certainly not understand at all; for,
having encountered the veil of *māyā* and being enveloped by it, embodied beings abandon their own divine nature and fall into the realm of darkness.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, may You manifest in all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas). Go forth, O Lord, O Ocean of Mercy, O Anādi Śrī Puruṣottama!
Thus entreated, Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [remained] in the Imperishable Realm (akṣara).
Abiding in the supreme abode, having heard [the request] from Virājaka through a divine voice, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord of the supreme abode, said:
"So be it; I shall go to the millions of cosmic eggs.
Having spoken thus, [he departed]. (10.3–10.4)
He desired to become manifold for the sake of all auspiciousness;
thus the Supreme Lord became a distinct form in every cosmic egg.
In all the many cosmic eggs, He exists everywhere through His qualities, sovereignty, and manifestations.
Together with his attendants, divine beings, wives, and Śaktis,
along with devotees, the fruits of dharma, and modes of worshipful devotion—
He indeed manifested, O Rādhā, as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (106–107)
Where Brahmā the Self-born, Śaṅkara Somanāthaka,
and Viṣṇu Nara-Nārāyaṇa reside, there dwells Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
This is in the western region of Surāṣṭra, within the section concerning Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
On the surface of the earth, in the Akṣara-kṣetra, to the east of Bhāvi-Revata, at the holy site of Kukkuṭavāpikā, on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
and in the city of Kuṅkumā, that Śrī Hari manifested himself. (2.272.110)
"This very one is the Supreme Kṛṣṇa, from whom infinite dark forms manifest, O Rādhā; understand indeed His greatness. Thus did Kṛṣṇa Himself then speak to His beloved Śrī Rādhikā.
He spoke: "O lord of men, I have heard that directly:
this very Śrī-Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī-Kambharā, the Lord who is the delight of Gopāla, the youth beloved by Kṛṣṇa, is performing the sacrifice."
All incarnations, abodes, and liberated beings, as well as the lords and others,
gods, sacred fords, the virtuous, and the truthful indeed dwell here.
Liberation and the state of being liberated shine forth here on this earth in embodied form.
"Therefore, O King, whatever small amount [of wealth] you have here at this sacred ford, please bestow that as well.
Having been addressed thus by Lomaśa, the king, having abandoned delusion, his kingdom, and his home, undertook the Vaiṣṇava initiation according to the prescribed rite.
Having received initiation from the Vaiṣṇava preceptor named Citprakāśa, O Rādhikā, that king became a perfected saint (sādhu) and subsequently became a seer (ṛṣi).

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of Naranārāyaṇa-tīrtha, Harikṛṣṇa-tīrtha, Māṇikī-tīrtha, and the Previous History of Aśvapāṭala; the Arrival of All Tīrthas at Aśvapaṭṭa; the Arrival of the Supreme Brahman through the Praise of Vairāja; and the Initiation of Aśvapāṭala as a Sādhu," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (Chapter 272)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, five hundred other sages, who have taken refuge in Hari, were impelled by the initiation into the light of consciousness at Kuṅkumavāpī. (1)
Having bowed to the true guru Lomaśa, they quickly requested initiation.
Lomaśa also bestowed upon them that auspicious Vaiṣṇava initiation at that very spot—an initiation endowed with all mantras, characterized by saffron robes, and esteemed by the virtuous. (2)
Having observed fasts and purified their bodies,
all of them performed fire-offerings (homa) and, wearing saffron robes, took up the mantras:
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times."
Thus, with firm minds, they firmly adopted this refuge-mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
After that, they also adopted the mantra known as *samarpaṇa*.
"From fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, the enemy, Yama, and the wicked-hearted,
[we take refuge in] you who bear the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika. Thereafter, they received this protective mantra.
"I am Brahmā, an eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and Master.
At the end, they received this mantra known as the state of Brahman.
"Bālakṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman; He is indeed my eternal Lord.
May He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. Then they received from him this mantra of self-surrender.
Then, O Rādhā, those sages, having bowed to the sage Śrī Lomaśa, inquired about the duties of a protector; thereupon Lomaśa spoke:
"The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the glorious Puruṣottama."
He himself will proclaim all the dharmas worthy of the virtuous.
(12) Then, O Rādhikā, that queen, the king’s wife, thereafter took up the auspicious initiation of a virtuous woman on the shore of that lake. (12)
Then many women took the vow of virtuous discipleship;
for that became the holy ford of initiation, the holy ford of the virtuous, and indeed the holy ford of the female disciples.
Then there were five hundred virtuous men and likewise five hundred virtuous women.
Having gone together with Lomaśa to the auspicious and glorious abode of Bālakṛṣṇa,
they all— both men and women— honored and sat down before Hari, and listened as he explained the duties of the virtuous in response to their questions. (15–16)
In the gross body resides the subtle body; in the subtle body resides latent impression (vāsanā);
in latent impression resides the individual soul (jīva); and in the individual soul resides the state of being the witness (sākṣibhāvanā).
In the state of being the witness lies freedom from the qualities (nirguṇatva); and in freedom from the qualities lies the absence of all taint (lepavarjana).
In the state of non-clinging there is devotion to Brahman, and in the state of Brahman there is liberation. In liberation there is supreme bliss produced by the Supreme Brahman.
Thus, having ascended the tenfold altar, one enjoys bliss. (18–19)
The virtuous should always practice the tenfold concentration;
they must bring the body under control through austerity and restraint,
as well as through endurance, forgiveness, good conduct, and constant service.
One should bring the subtle senses under control through the cultivation of fortitude (21).
This is achieved by the non-engagement with sense objects, by the mind’s refusal to accept them,
as well as by discernment, inquiry, and constant tranquility of mental activity (22).
Therefore, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) must always be accomplished through lack of desire,
by means of non-recollection, by the final recollection, through protracted duration, and over a long period of time.
Living consists of the movement of the vital breaths and the arising of the fruits of karma.
O Kṛṣṇa, by the offering of fruits and by the restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃyamana),
as well as by taking only what is necessary for sustenance and by means of kuṃbhaka and other techniques again and again,
one should practice the restraint of the vital breaths and abandon the defects of the vital breaths.

One who is endowed with selflessness should abandon the sense of being a witness to pleasure and pain, as well as one's own egoistic identification with them; thus one becomes free from the "I"-notion.
For witnesshood exists only when there is a concern for one's own interest; how could there be witnesshood when acting for the sake of another?
In this way, the ascetic wins the state of being a witness by abandoning the sense of "I" regarding the "mine.

Then, for him, the contacts with the qualities (guṇas)—which cause pleasure, pain, and delusion, and which consist of illumination, activity, and restraint, as well as cold, heat, and their middling states—[no longer bind]. || 27–28 ||
Since he is not born [again], his very state of being free from the modes (nairguṇya) has been attained;
for the offering of the modes to Kṛṣṇa results in freedom from the modes even within the internal self.
That mental reflection which is offered to Kṛṣṇa does not cause further attachment.
Thinking with the mind, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, does not create attachment; nor does awakening through the intellect, when offered to Kṛṣṇa, create attachment;
and even the identification through the sense of "I," when offered to Kṛṣṇa, does not create attachment.
That mere perception does not, by that very fact, become a source of attachment at all.

Even when meditation, latent impressions, or mental formations are directed toward Hari, they attain a state of supreme divinity; being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they do not cause any taint whatsoever.
Thus, in the offering of everything, everything becomes devoid of qualities through union with Hari.
This must be performed in every way here by virtuous men and virtuous women,
provided there is no lapse caused by the qualities of *māyā* and no lack of connection to the fruits [of such practice].
The state of Brahman, steadfastness in Brahman, conduct like that of Brahman, and abiding therein—
these arise in every way for the virtuous one at all times, along with equality with the Imperishable.
Just as all creations indeed arise within the Imperishable and dissolve back into it, so too does this occur.
In Brahman there is no contact with creation, nor even contact with *māyā*.
Therefore, for him there is no bondage at all, for contact with *māyā* is indeed bondage.
For the virtuous one who is free from *māyā*, there is the constant absence of dualities.
Direct realization and immediate perception arise in the very self of consciousness (cidātman).
Through this immediate experience, all that is false dissolves.
By that, there is the destruction of defects and the cessation of worldly activity.
There is the destruction of the connection with the fruits [of action] and the destruction of all suffering and the like.
When a person here becomes a perfected one whose focus is solely upon the Self, he is indeed then liberated and is called "living liberation" even while alive. (2.273.39–40)
For one who practices in this manner, the bliss of Brahman arises;
for one who has attained his own self as the form of Brahman while remaining here in this world, the mind indeed becomes permanently absorbed in identity with the supreme Brahman. (41)
A supreme identity, as it were, arises [between them].
Just as the tongue, though distinct from honey, perceives the taste of honey, and just as the eye, situated within its socket, perceives the form of an object. ||42||
Just as the mind perceives that which is situated within and that which is distant,
so too the intellect, directed toward the Self, becomes the knower of the Supreme Self;
it becomes its own perceiver and its range of operation extends beyond its own self.
Likewise, the Self is self-luminous; it is its own knower and it illumines itself.
(45) Endowed with self-luminosity, it illumines Kṛṣṇa, who is not itself but is joined with it.
Kṛṣṇa illumines this [Self], and thus they illumine one another. (46)
When two manifestations are unified, a state resembling identity arises;
through the identity with the commonality of qualities, the possessors of those qualities attain such a nature.
In this manner, according to the principle of "possession by the element" (bhūtāveśa), there is identity with the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, through that [practice], it arises for both the virtuous—the self and the Supreme Self.
By means of the state of being the Supreme Brahman, one partakes in the bliss of Brahman.
This ten-limbed yoga is indeed the ever-supreme dharma of the virtuous.
This state, which is to be served by the virtuous and dwelt in by those established in the Supreme Brahman, has been described.
If there should be a lower state consisting of both self-luminosity (*svabhāna*) and other-luminosity (*parabhāna*),
then that other-luminosity, free from self-luminosity, should be understood as the supreme state.
Such a person would be a perfected being (sādhū) known as asamprajñāta;
he is celebrated in the Vedas and scriptures as being of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa.
He is likewise Sanatkumāra, Śambhu, and Śeṣanārāyaṇa.
This great sage Lomaśa and these others are considered Nārāyaṇas;
likewise, all those who are dear to Brahmā, such as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, and the rest,
as well as Garuḍa and my other vehicles— all these are Nārāyaṇas.
The entire city of Kuṅkumavāpī is mine, O Nārāyaṇī.
Here, virtuous men and noble women of equal merit dwell;
they are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, my own playful manifestations (līlāvibhūti). ||54-55||
Some here indeed become my thousands of qualities; some here indeed become my sovereign powers and accomplishments;
some here indeed become my divine ornaments.
Some here are indeed my powers born of my form;
some here are indeed my splendors, my lusters, and my radiances; and some here are indeed the various objects of enjoyment belonging to me.
This entire Kuṅkumavāpī is my very instrument;
my entire form exists here, untainted, beyond qualities, and supreme.
Indeed, she is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, dwelling in the abode of Brahman.
"This earth is the abode of Brahman; it is my own body, O virtuous ones.
Thinking and meditating thus upon their own form as being eternally identical with the Supreme Brahman, they attained supreme bliss.
Thus have these divine, subtle, and knowledge-perceivable dharmas been declared by me here for you virtuous ones; for the virtuous are indeed regarded as such.
The virtuous said:
"O Blessed One, indeed the subtle dharmas have been understood by me here;
but what are the gross dharmas like, and how are they to be protected? Tell me, O Lord.
The Supreme Brahman said:
Whether it be a man or a woman, when one is established in the state of a holy person (sādhu),
then indeed the defects of the body must be abandoned and its virtues embraced here.
Always in the early morning, having abandoned laziness, negligence, and lethargy—
Having become free from sleep and acting with haste, one should perform the bath pertaining to Brahmā (brāhma-snāna).
One should indeed effect the purification of the body by means of water, ashes, wind, or by wiping, as well as by the application of oil and other unguents. 65–66.
One should always practice internal meditation on the Blessed Lord as the highest form of purification;
thereafter, one should indeed perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
Hari, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, Gaṇeśa, Lakṣmī, and likewise of Sūrya.
One should perform the worship of the virtuous, the waving of lamps (ārārtika), and the offering of food (naivedya).
One should practice hymns of praise, the chanting of the Lord's names, and the circling with a garland.
How should one perform the service of Hari? Indeed, one should practice begging for alms and the preparation of cooked food.
One should perform the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to the gods, and the sacrifice to the ancestors;
having performed the sacrifice to Brahman and the sacrifice to men, one should partake of food.
In the evening, one should perform the auspicious ninefold worship of Śrī Hari.
One should perform every auspicious act with faith as is appropriate;
one should sustain oneself with contentment, gentleness, and non-possessiveness.
One who follows the dharma of the virtuous should practice neither excessive eating nor excessive austerity.
One should not practice improper conduct, nor should one do what ought not to be done.
One should indeed avoid affliction, violence, falsehood, censure, and speaking ill of others.
And one should perform service to others through body, mind, and speech.
Through action for the sake of the supreme happiness of others, one should practice what is beneficial and conducive to well-being.
One should especially establish the path of the self and the path of liberation.
For the sake of destroying the sins of others, one should always be a source of refuge. (74–75)
One should bestow my mantras and grant my initiation;
one should practice the study of the scriptures that grant liberation and likewise acquire knowledge.
One should also wander to sacred fords and partake of pure food.
One should drink pure, filtered water and milk and other such liquids.
One should never harbor passion, thirst, pride, or greed.
Indeed, one who contemplates Brahman should never show contempt toward anyone.
One should certainly not practice deception, nor should one ever harbor hatred.

One should give gifts according to one's ability, including the gift of liberation and the gift of fearlessness. One should accept the affectionate devotion of those who have sought refuge, which leads to the yoga of liberation.

The virtuous are purifiers, and the company of the virtuous is also purifying. By always bringing embodied beings to one's own assembly and purifying them with supreme love, one should send them to my abode.
One should withdraw the senses, the internal organs, and so forth, into the heart;
one should constantly perform meditation upon me and accumulate the bliss of Brahman.
One should effect absorption into my form; this is the supreme duty.
And you should constantly perform meditation upon Me, consisting of reflection.
Thus should you virtuous men abide and act for My sake;
and likewise, the virtuous women here should perform service to the holy ones.
For women, the constant granting of liberation, the imparting of knowledge, instruction, and the initiation of virtuous men and women shall lead to emancipation. Furthermore,
those vices which obstruct liberation must not be committed.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the husband of virtuous women and of the righteous at all times.
Through the dharma of devotion to one's husband, I am to be served as the granter of desired boons.
One should offer oneself to me for eternal happiness.
"I must enjoy [the fruits] together with you because of my divine union;
I am never to be abandoned by you at any time or in any activity.
Thus is this "living liberation," which brings about supreme liberation.
O virtuous ones! I have declared this auspicious refuge, consisting of the divine Dharma.
The attributes of the body must indeed be maintained by the righteous in a fitting manner;
they should not be pursued in excess, for such things are obstacles to my service. (2.273.90)
"May there be well-being for you, O virtuous men; and may there be well-being for you, O virtuous women," having spoken thus, O Rādhikā, the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa became silent.
Thereupon, the saintly ones performed the ritual worship and the waving of lights (nīrājana).
"You must protect us and liberate us," they cried out;
and having received his blessing, they departed from the shore of the lake for their own homes.
Just then, Nārada, who had gone to Kāśī, arrived before Hari.
Then, together with his teacher who held an auspicious letter, he eagerly performed the prostration like a staff (daṇḍavat) before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having bowed to his father and mother, he uttered words of auspiciousness.
Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, having offered his salutations and received due honor,
[offered] a welcome, the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and so forth, and having inquired after his well-being,
he paid homage to Śiveśvara and his daughter Lakṣmī, wishing them happiness. (95–96)

O Rādhikā! Having given a leaf encircled with saffron thread and adorned with jewels, he announced the auspicious news of their meeting—the eternal well-being of Lakṣmī and the momentary union of the Divine Couple. (97)
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, he presented [the offering].
Having increased that leaf-offering and having worshipped Bṛhaspati,
Gopālakṛṣṇa there also honored Nārada.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of how the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa bestowed mantra-initiation, knowledge-instruction, and other gifts upon the saintly men and women in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; and how Bṛhaspati, accompanied by Nārada and bearing an auspicious letter sent from Kāśī by Śiveśvara, arrived at Kuṅkumavāpī and presented that letter. Chapter 274 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 274: The Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa at the Abode of Brahmā and the Bestowal of the Veda-Saṃhitā. Śrī Nārada said: O great sage, please describe in detail how the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arrived at the abode of Brahmā and what He did there. Śrī Sūta Gosvāmī said: O best of sages, I shall now relate everything exactly as it occurred. Listen with focused attention. At that time, the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Vasudeva, was seated on His throne in Dvārakā. He was surrounded by His divine consorts, headed by Śrī Rādhikā, as well as by the gopīs, the residents of Dvārakā, the kings, the sages, and the celestial beings. He was adorned with all ornaments and garments, and He shone with the splendor of millions of suns. At that very moment, the divine messenger of Brahmā arrived at the gate of Dvārakā. He was radiant, wearing a crown, earrings, and a sacred thread, and he was adorned with a garland of forest flowers. Carrying a message from Brahmā, he stood before the gatekeeper and announced his arrival. Upon hearing this, the gatekeeper immediately informed the Lord. Then, the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Vasudeva, spoke to the gatekeeper: "Let the messenger of Brahmā enter; he is My own devotee. Hearing these words, the gatekeeper ushered the messenger into the assembly hall. Seeing the messenger, the Lord, who is the embodiment of all opulences, smiled and spoke to Him: "O messenger of Brahmā, welcome! Tell Me what you have brought from the creator of the universe. Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā! Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa rejoiced upon seeing the letter."
He bowed down to Bṛhaspati and placed a necklace of jewels around his neck. Bṛhaspati observed the birth-day of that Hari on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the lunar month of Kārtika.
The birth of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa from the womb of Satī Śrī Kambharā occurred; fourteen years, one month, and six days have passed since then,
and today it is the fourteenth lunar day.

On the day of the conjunction of the two [planets] during the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, there will be the acceptance of the marriage proposal (verse 4). And from here, on the fifth day—the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, at an exceedingly auspicious moment—there will be a great festival in Kāśī. (Verse 5)
Likewise, the letter conveys most auspicious news:
"I have been sent with this letter by the Lord Śiveśvara.
O Gopālakṛṣṇa, may everything be entirely auspicious, fortunate, and excellent! (6)
Gopālakṛṣṇa, beholding the divine sage Lomaśa,
the muni, quickly called him; that sage arrived there, and having been shown respect and having performed worship to the gods and his guru, he sat upon an auspicious seat.
He sat down and inquired after the welfare of Bṛhaspati;
he then examined the letter given by Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. Lomaśa read that letter, which contained the praises of Nārada.
He caused auspicious news to be proclaimed and increased his prosperity;
Bālakṛṣṇa rejoiced, Kaṃbhārā rejoiced greatly,
and the members of the household were filled with joy upon hearing that letter of union.

All those who were dear to Brahmā, having heard this, attained supreme joy; Pārvatī, Hārītī, Śakti, Amā, and others likewise experienced great delight. At that time, Gopālakṛṣṇa indeed played musical instruments.
He presented an auspicious gift and sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor. Then,
according to the prescribed rite, he fed him most delicious milk-rice (pāyasa) and subsequently honored him with sandalwood paste and other offerings.

The Blessed Gopālakṛṣṇa questioned the sage Nārada regarding the qualities and characteristics of a maiden; Nārada then spoke. Brahmā’s partial incarnation, the divine Lord Śiva, shines forth as the Sovereign of Śivā.
Mahālakṣmī is indeed a great devotee of the Lord, as is Pārvatī;
both are portions of Nārāyaṇa, most venerable and most excellent, honored by all the worlds, and the supreme lords who are most worthy of reverence. (16–17)
Their daughter was Lakṣmī herself, the destroyer of misery and poverty;
she was the most excellent among maidens and women, and exceedingly beautiful.
What praise could I possibly offer, especially for the daughter of Śambhu? (18)
She is delightful and exceedingly beautiful; among women, that Ramā is most honored.
Her fresh youth has blossomed, and she is indeed a treasury of all prosperity.
Adorned with thousands of marks of Lakṣmī, she is the Supreme Sovereign.
Having the luster of the color of a yellow campaka flower, adorned with jewel ornaments, she was like a flash of lightning, graced with the playful charm of a smile and restlessness;
endowed with the brilliance of molten gold, she was radiant with splendor. (21)
Divinely-limbed and possessing divine reality, she is always endowed with pure being;
truthful, compassionate, merciful, and virtuous, she is an ascetic devoted to the vow of Hari.
Peaceful, self-controlled, fortunate, and a treasury of infinite magnanimity. (22–23)
Her head was adorned with a svastika mark and resplendent with hidden golden lines; it shone with hair that was curved and long, beautiful with dark tips and a golden hue,
radiant and shimmering with luster.
Bearing upon her broad forehead a beautiful tilaka as lovely as a streak of gold, she shines like the natural moon;
is she Rādhā, or Lakṣmī, or Māṇikī, or perhaps the daughter of the Sun? || 25-26 ||
She is Pārvatī or Sāramā, Sarasvatī or Śāradā;
Vairājī or Vāsudevī, Nārāyaṇī or Sadāśivā;
Padmā or Virajā, and Sāvitrī or Vaiṣṇavī.
Is she Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Candrāṇī, or Rohiṇī?
(28) Or is she Kubera’s consort, the wife of the Sun, Svāhā, or Ahalyikā?
Is she the sky itself, or perhaps Brāhmī Śakti, or even Śīlikā herself? (29)
Or rather, even if there were other women who were most excellent and captivating,
they would all not equal even a sixteenth part of this daughter of Śiva.
She is enriched with the splendor of the full autumnal moon, and her eyes are like autumnal lotuses.
"Is this form, which is like your own son, has entered into that body?
This young woman is most beautiful and fit for marriage;
she possesses a divine body, free from even a trace of material elements."
She is indeed the very form of Bālakṛṣṇa; she is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī.
I believe this Supreme Brahman shines forth, having manifested in two forms.
What more is there to describe here? For she is indeed Hari himself in person.
O Gopālakṛṣṇa! Your son is fortunate; he is the Blessed Lord himself.
He is celebrated under the name Puruṣottama throughout all creations.
This very Śrī Lakṣmī, who embodies all limbs, is his portion, the consort of Puruṣottama.
Manifested here in this world by Bālakṛṣṇa, she bestows liberation upon men;
she is the Mother of the Universe, the Mother of All—how then can I possibly describe her here?
Listen to all the signs by which she may be recognized as such.
What kind of thing is it, or who is it, that must be determined, since nothing higher exists?
Having heard which things, people undoubtedly attain liberation;
I shall describe those states of the Guru as seen by me through divine vision. (37–38)
In the heart of Śivakanyā there is an auspicious form of Bālakṛṣṇa;
on her two feet are beautiful and auspicious upward-pointing lines resembling lotuses.
On her hips there is a line like an arrow, and on her forehead a mark shaped like a crown.
On his right cheek and forehead, a crimson mark shines brilliantly.
On his chest is the Viṣṇu-line, and on his left arm is an auspicious mace.
On his left thigh is a sandal, and the Vaijayantī garland rests upon his heart.
In her hand there is a lotus, and likewise another mark of an elephant;
on her right foot there is the mark of a conch, a boat, and a celestial chariot;
as well as a mace, a fish, a temple pinnacle, a large fish, and a betel vine.
On the left foot, there are lines of barley, a temple, and an umbrella;
likewise, upward lines, a lotus, a banner, a goad, and a jar;
as well as a water-lily, a bilva fruit, a land-lotus, and the moon. (43)
The ten fingers are complete with golden lines;
on the forehead is a golden necklace and golden-lined dots.
On the chin is a dot, and on the hand-line above the right breast is a dot.
A discus is on her left breast, a necklace on her neck, and a golden ornament on her chest.
A banner, a fish, a flute, and a svastika are on her right hand;
likewise, a bow, a fish, and a pitcher are also present on her right hand.
On the right foot there are a wall, a gateway, and a lotus;
likewise, on the left foot there are a horse, a plow, and an elephant.
Furthermore, on the [other] foot there are a tree, a sacrificial post, an arrow, and a javelin.
In her hand there is the mark of a rosary, the mark of a lamp, and a fly-whisk;
(48) as well as a mark of good character, earrings, an altar, and a wheel—these indeed are auspicious.
She possesses other beautiful and pure marks as well. (49)
No other such woman has been seen in the three worlds except for Kamalā;
indeed, no such marks as these exist anywhere except in Śrī.
O Gopālakṛṣṇa! This son of yours is the Supreme Lord himself.
He knows all that has occurred there and always goes to offer worship;
he accepts what is offered by her as well as what is done by her parents.
Nevertheless, Hari himself remains here like one ignorant, manifesting his divine power (māyā).
The king of sages named Hemaśālāyana knows this;
and Hanumān also understands Lakṣmī’s penance performed for the sake of Hari.
At that time, Bālakṛṣṇa granted a boon for the purpose of his own yoga.
All this auspiciousness resides in the offering of prosperity to Nārāyaṇa.
O Gopālarāja! Behold this preceptor of the gods, Bṛhaspati, who has brought a letter to your house for this highly auspicious undertaking.
Since the lords of the gods worship the lotus-feet of one who has arrived here,
your home is blessed, meritorious, and glorious, and has been sanctified by him. Oh,
I consider my own fortune to be great, for I am steadfast in milking the cows!
I shall become fortunate enough to behold the festival of the union of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, I shall dwell forever on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa,
and I shall serve Śrī Puruṣottama, the Lord of countless consorts.
With pure devotion, I shall cause that Bālakṛṣṇa to hear these songs;
and during festivals, I shall always wander together with the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. Indeed, this is the fulfillment of my birth: that there may be union with Hari right here.
The Supreme Lord is to be worshipped by anyone through whatever state of being.
(2.274.60) O Gopālakṛṣṇa! You are blessed; blessed is Śiva, the bestower of happiness. Blessed is Kambharā-Lakṣmī; blessed is the goddess Pārvatī. (61)
Blessed is the Kuṅkumavāpī pond, and blessed is the land of Vārāṇasī;
blessed is Bṛhaspati as well, and blessed is the celestial sage Nārada—
those in whose hearts and eyes the illustrious Narāyaṇa dwells.
The fourth day shall become blessed and worthy of worship by all. Future incarnations as well will celebrate a festival on this occasion.
A daughter offered on that day shall become equal to Lakṣmī.
Having spoken thus, Nārada observed silence, and Bṛhaspati likewise;
thereafter, they both took rest in the abode of peace.
Then, the venerable sage Nārada [considered] that secret of the gods spoken by Lakṣmī.
He went to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa to inform Kṛṣṇa [of this].
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, too, was anxious to understand what Lakṣmī had said and waited, thinking, "When will Nārada speak that which is dear to my heart? (66–67).
At that moment, the illustrious Nārada arrived there at Kṛṣṇa’s palace;
having bowed to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and uttered "O Blessed One, obeisance!
with a smile, he was filled with joy and sat down upon the ground.
Then Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, having quickly raised him up,
seated that celestial sage upon his own golden couch;
placing the great muni upon his chest with joy, he embraced him closely.
He asked about Lakṣmī’s welfare: "Tell me, Nārada, what is in her heart?
How is she faring in happiness, and how much is she filled with joy for my sake?
Is the daughter of Śiva occupied with thoughts concerning me?"
"Did she say anything, or was some secret revealed by her?
O Nārada, tell me quickly what you wish to know, for it shall bring me joy.
Thus addressed, O Rādhā, Nārada, desiring to speak, was filled with great delight.
He related everything exactly as it had been told by the daughter of Śiva.
"Listen, O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, she who desires you is well;
when I went to Kāśī on the auspicious bank of the Varaṇā..."
In a delightful garden area near the temple of Śiveśvara,
within a beautiful Viṣṇu shrine adorned with golden pitchers,
she then stayed together with her mother, her sister, and Kṛṣṇā. ||75–76||
Or perhaps you had come for the purpose of seeing Viṣṇu; having bowed to him,
I suddenly saw you performing a circumambulation, beautiful in your graceful movement— Lakṣmī herself, sharing half his body, recognized by the marks upon her form.

At that time, I was indeed a child of variegated form; being of equal age with him, I remained engaged in childhood play. Under the pretext of circumambulation, I went to the temple together with her.
And Bālakṛṣṇa spoke repeatedly with great speed: "Abhrama!
and "The lake of the horse-breeders! and "The daughter of Śiveśvara!
Indeed, she then heard these words from my mouth.
He questioned me: "Salutations to you! O youth, from where have you come here?
Tell me, do you know Bālakṛṣṇa? Who dwells at Aśvapaṭṭasara? Tell me the truth quickly. (81-82)
Then I assumed there a form approved by Nārada;
she, recognizing me as a being, laughed and bowed down to me.
Thereafter, I again became a child there, and so did she.
In the open area of the square, adorned with *kadamba* trees, he summoned him under the pretext of playing and spoke to him privately:
"O great sage, tell me here—how and why did that happen? Speak if it is for your own sake. (84–85)
"O virtuous lady! I have been sent by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa;
I have come for the purpose of inquiring about the auspiciousness of the marriage.
Speak quickly what is in your heart, so that Satī may not know. (86)
"Speak without delay under the pretext of the five products of the cow, betel, spittle, and so forth!
O Kṛṣṇa! As soon as she saw me, she was filled with joy and delight and said: 'The Lord of my life is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (87–88)
"When will he come quickly? When will he accept me?
Indeed, I am not at all able to endure even a moment's separation.
Tell Kṛṣṇa quickly and with haste that he must indeed come swiftly."
"O Guru, tell me this: what is my time for giving?
For he has granted me this word: 'The Blessed One himself will come and take my hand fourteen years from now.'"
"If Kṛṣṇa does not accept me this year,
I shall certainly give up my life and come there in a divine form.
Tell this to my father and inform my mother as well."
"O wise one, do not make my words known before those two!
Quickly arrange matters in such a way that he may become mine.
Having spoken thus, her limbs bristling with joy, she was then overwhelmed with love.
With eyes filled with tears of affection, as if absorbed in meditative concentration, she spoke again briefly:
"O Nārada, report this which has been entrusted to you; speak no more in the presence of Śrī Hari, and depart. (95)
"Tell my mother and father that you have come to my house there.
Having spoken thus, she playfully prostrated at my feet,
rose up, and, intent on her play, quickly performed a circumambulation.
Having seen Hari again in that temple along with his mother, she went to her own home; O Kṛṣṇa, after that, I became Nārada.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Varaṇā and the Gaṅgā, I went there.
Addressing him by his true form as "Nārāyaṇa," Nārada spoke thus.
Upon seeing me wearing matted locks, Satī offered her salutation;
and when she saw me, she was filled with joy after I had bestowed my blessing upon her. (2.274.100)
He inquired after my complete well-being as I stood upon the seat offered to me, having suddenly arrived there while accepting the *madhuparka* and other honors.
I said: "O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Lord!"
Then, proclaiming "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," I drank a little water,
O Kṛṣṇa, while recollecting all your names which are purifying and auspicious. (1.02–1.03)
Then, having attained peace, whenever I wish to speak, the goddess Lakṣmī, the bestower of happiness, will listen with longing before me in the assembly;
likewise Jyeṣṭhā, Kṛṣṇā, and my other divine-sighted friends.

They sat down all around me, even though I was a chaste woman. (105) Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious Letter Given by Bṛhaspati, the Ritual Worship and Recitation Performed by Lomaśa, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa and Others Welcoming Him with Madhuparka and Feasting Him, and Nārada Explaining to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa the Sovereignty, Qualities, and Divine Marks of the Maidens, as well as the Secret Meaning of What the Maidens Said to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
