Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā! Whatever Nārada indeed told them, I shall relate all of that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind. (1)
Nārada said:
I have come from Satyaloka to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake in western Saurāṣṭra on earth, where Puruṣottama resides.
Together with him, I wandered upon the earth for the sake of sacrificial rites,
where those liberated from their abodes as well as the attendants (pārṣadas) of other realms had arrived;
likewise the attendants of Satyaloka, the lords, and the deities.
The daughters of Manu, the beloveds of the Nāgas, virtuous women, and those who have attained supreme siddhi;
all the incarnations, the Īśvaras, and the holy ones (sādhavas);
the perfected ones (siddhas), those devoted to the vow of Brahman, the ancestors, and likewise the ṛṣis.
The Ṛṣis, all the gods, and those others who had assembled;
the humans, the guardians of heaven, the world-protectors, and the great lords;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise their wives.
The fires, the winds, the treasures, and likewise the planets;
the directions, Kāma, the Mānasas, the lunar days, and likewise the Kalās;
the principles (tattvas), all sacred fords, rivers, lakes, and oceans.
The mountains, the Vālakhilyas, those with bodies of air, the Asuras and others,
the Daityas, the devotees, the Dānavas, the birds, and likewise the Rākṣasas;
the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras as well.
Serpents, *kiṃpuruṣas*, trees, grasses, and creepers;

those devoted to Dharma and others, those devoted to Yama and others, the devotees of Śiva who dwell on Kailāsa, those who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, those who dwell in the White Ocean of Milk, and those who dwell at Badarī.
Dwellers of Meru, dwellers of Āvaraṇa, and inhabitants of Pātāla—
countless crores of deities indeed flocked to every sacrifice.
They all praised Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
They bow to him, honor him, and praise the Son of Kaṃbhārā.
Then those guardians of the world, guardians of the abode, guardians of creation, and Nārāyaṇas drink his grace, which is the nectar of his feet. (13–14)
The Nārāyaṇas and those who carry out his command— all this was witnessed by me there directly. Indeed,
Śaṅkara himself resides in his imperishable field (akṣarakṣetra).
He dwells as the guardian of the field (Kṣetrapāla) all around Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Rāmadeva, Nara, and likewise Nārāyaṇa; the Vyūhas beginning with Vāsudeva, and Sanatkumāra, the king of yogis. (16–17)
Likewise, other supreme lords such as Saṃkarṣaṇa and others,
as well as Mahāviṣṇu, Bhūman, Vairāja, and Sadāśiva—
those lords of time, māyā, and the ego— all carry out his command. (18)
For from him all beings arise, by him they are nourished, and into him they enter.
He who is called the inner self, the Lord himself who is the witness,
and who is called the Supreme Brahman, by whom all this is pervaded.
The lights of lightning, the sun, the moon, fire, and likewise Dhruva—
all those luminaries that shine forth by its splendor—
become endowed with knowledge through entry into it. 21.
He by whom the world of living beings is indeed illumined within his own self— he,
the bestower of all light, that Blessed One who is truly beyond the imperishable, shines resplendent in the place of Kuṅkumavāpikā. (22–23)
"In his own human form as the cowherd boy Kṛṣṇa"—
thus did those who honor the Great One praise him at the sacrifice.
Even that Janārdana, Kṛṣṇa the Child, assumed ten million forms.
And it surely meets with many hundreds of millions of devotees upon his chest.
Indeed, I have seen that directly; I have heard everything and praised it;
and I have heard the voices of women at every sacred site during the great festival.
Blessed are we, for today we behold the vision of Surūpa, the Lord of All and the Yogin, whose merit is beyond measure.
Oh, from the sight of him, eternal peace arises!
Today, indeed, the length of our eyes finds its fulfillment;
even from afar, great bliss arises upon beholding him—a bliss that is ever-increasing, rich with the force of an unbroken flow. (28–29)
And we experience great happiness for all our senses;
since such supreme bliss arises from merely seeing her from afar, then what must it be like when one lies by the side of her, his wife, in person? (2.275.30)

What would be the nature of Lakṣmī, the daughter of Śiveśvara and the divine one? She who is indeed the sovereign Nārāyaṇī, the supreme mistress, whose cheeks and temples resemble the sun and the moon. (31–32)
Her body is like gold, resembling the *campaka* flower;
likewise, the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet are like red lac.
Her lips, which are the dwelling place of love, resemble the ripe *bimba* fruit.
Her two beautiful thighs are like the trunks of plantain trees;
her eyes are as expansive as lotus petals, and her form is indeed unsurpassed.
That supreme goddess dwells upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
And she who dwells upon her own breast with her beloved Kṛṣṇa—
she who is united with him in every limb— how truly happy she must be!
Oh, how blessed is the daughter of Śiva, who enjoys such bliss from Kṛṣṇa!
Blessed is that goddess Pārvatī, who through her happiness is happy with Śiva.
That happiness belongs neither to Ramā, nor Kamalā, nor Śrī, the consort of Kṛṣṇa; nor to Vṛndā, nor Tulasī, nor even to Bhārgavī. ||37-38||

That which was written on our foreheads by Kṛṣṇa, and which Lakṣmī has always inscribed— oh, no such fortune as this exists for others, that it is not perceived! Nor is He our husband, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Birth in this world is in vain for a woman without the bliss of union with Kṛṣṇa.
All devotion to her husband is in vain if her husband is not Kṛṣṇa.
Oh, how truly fruitful is the daughter of Śiva’s dignity! (2.275.40–41)
She enjoys all tastes, all fragrances, and all touches filled with bliss;
she enjoys all sounds, all sights, and all joys,
having obtained as her beloved husband Kṛṣṇa, the abode of all bliss, who has conquered his senses.
That daughter of Śiva, who enjoys the company of the Lord of All whose vigor is unbroken,
though she resides in Kāśī, O Kṛṣṇa, remains always attached [to Him] and unmanifest;
yet virtuous and chaste women with divine vision behold her day and night.
Thus indeed have I heard of your fame repeatedly from groups of women;
as such, I was desirous of seeing you and sought to know more of you again and again.
Having inquired repeatedly and gradually, I have now come to your house.
The name "Duhkhalakṣmī" was indeed heard by me repeatedly.
"What is she like? Whose daughter is she? What kind of virtues does she possess? [I thought].
"If that goddess were here, she must certainly be seen by me. (46–47)
Where does she dwell? What is her true nature? What is her condition and what are her garments?
What is her disposition, what is her physical form, and what is her configuration?
Furthermore, what is her appearance, what is her radiance, and how many years of age is that beautiful woman?
What was her face like, what was her speed, what was her disposition, and what were her auspicious marks?

What arts did she possess, what was her voice, and what was her complexion? How radiant were her feet, what was her forehead like, how beautiful were her hair, what was her nature, and what was her supreme accomplishment? (2.275.49–50)
What is her power, what is she enriched with, what is her splendor, and what is her awakening?
What is her duty, what is her devotion, what is her divinity, and what is her inner nature?
What is her knowledge, what is the beauty of her signs, what is her height, and what is her course?
What is her dress, what is her companion, what are her ornaments, and what is her array of vessels?
(52) What is her strength, what is her goodness of character, what is her food, and what is her asceticism?
What is her contentment, what is her purity, what is her study of sacred texts, and what is her virtue? (53)
What is her heart? What is the object of her love? What is her skill and what is her intellect?
What are her limbs? What is her wealth? What is she fickle at? What indeed is her writing?
What is her taste? What is her speech? What is her livelihood? And what is her activity? (54)
What are its three components? What are its beginning, middle, and end results?
What is its action? What is its distinction? What is its commonality? What is its intermediate state?
What is its basis of trust? What is its yoga? What is its awakening? And what is its worship? (55–56)
Is she one who seeks propitiation? Is she one who seeks adornment? Is she one who seeks dispassion? Is she contented? Is she greedy? Is she full of hope? Is she full of desire?
Is she one who speculates? Is she one who has reached certainty? Is she one who engages in debate? Is she one who relies on valid means of knowledge? || 57 ||

What is its object of knowledge? What is its application? What is its established doctrine? What is its point of defeat? (58) What are its Vedas? What is its means of proof? What is its beloved? What does it utterly conquer? What are its restraints (*yama*)?
What are its observances (*niyama*)? What is its meditation (*dhyāna*)? And what is its posture (*āsana*)? (59)
"What is her life-force, what is her delight, and what is her desire? Such a curiosity has arisen in me to see the daughter of Śiva;
for that reason, O Blessed One, this divine sage Nārada has come to my mind."

And the son of Brahmā, the brother of Rudra, renowned among divine sages, was a devotee of Viṣṇu; yet he lacked steadfastness and was entirely fond of quarreling. "If those in whose house I go honor me," [he thought]. (6.1–6.2)
Indeed, I have spoken these words; I am the one who brings them happiness.
If people do not respect my words and do not satisfy me, then, having created unbearable quarrels within their homes, I shall afflict them.
I shall go to another house where I may receive honor. (64) My daughters show their hands so that I may examine their fortune;
having seen everything, I shall tell them what brings happiness. (65)
Whatever unhappiness there may be, I shall destroy it;
yet by treating me with disrespect, people do not obtain happiness.
Those who follow my words receive great honor.
Indeed, my stay and my clothing are produced in one place for only as long as it takes to milk a cow;
nevertheless, beholding your devotion, I dwell there day and night.
Therefore, a special residence for me shall become the bestower of prosperity and heaven.
Even more than that, my abode grants the attainment of Nārāyaṇa;
even more than that, my abode bestows the Supreme Brahman.
I grant liberation by my word; I grant liberation through my glorification.
I bestow affliction with a fraction [of my power], yet I grant happiness through being propitiated. I administer poison when I am not satisfied by one's livelihood;
but I cause even nectar to be drunk where I have been served.
"Wherever my desire for knowledge is fulfilled, there I shall grant the supreme bliss of heaven and then depart elsewhere; let them know this to be my vow.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
O Lord of Śrī, son of Kaṃbhārā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Hari, Hari!
(73) O Beloved of the daughter of Śiva’s Lord, Hari, delight of the cowherds!
O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Brahmā’s beloved, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, Hari! (74)
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Brahmā, O Hari!
O Lord of all beloved women, Beloved Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Hari!
O Master, Beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, You who possess the form of Prince Kṛṣṇa!
"O Guide, O Vedic scholar, O Self of all, O Soul of all, O Abode of the Residue!
Having thus offered his worship, Nārada ceased;
and Lakṣmī likewise [worshipped] toward Nārada with her mind, speech, and action.
At that time, the functioning of her other senses had become absorbed in Him;
being present, Śivā said to the divine sage, "O Sage, blessed is my fortune!
Since you, who are the very form of Kṛṣṇa, have come to my home. (78)
"My daughter possesses great fortune, since she has had the sight of you, a holy man, here.
I am Nārada; I know that if the merit accumulated from a hundred births is combined with it, one indeed attains a human birth. (2.275.80)
Furthermore, if one were to perform a hundred sacrifices there,
one would indeed attain heaven for a duration equal to that of Indra; thereafter, upon this earth,
by the power of the remaining merit, one would obtain the status of an excellent human being.
There, through the majesty of the Brahmins and also by the blessings of the virtuous,
one shall obtain a kingdom that is supreme, filled with devotion, auspicious, and bestowing happiness.
Therein lies service rendered to the gods and service to guest-folk.
It surely leads to virtuous understanding and brings prosperity to the creeper-like lineage;
even in that regard, sons and daughters come into being through the satisfaction of their fathers.
By the power of serving the virtuous, people become happy.
Service to the virtuous bestows wealth; the gift of land bestows happiness.
(85) And that service is attained through righteousness, devotion, austerity, and likewise through vows;
otherwise it is not attained at all, for service to the virtuous is indeed difficult to obtain. (86)
Service to the virtuous is undertaken through favor and compassion; service to the virtuous is undertaken through the dharma of devotion to one's husband.
[This is the case] for those whose nature is to assist others and who provide perpetual feasts of food.
For those who are always devoted to giving, gain arises.
(88) For virtuous people who are devoted, gentle in disposition, dedicated in the practice of offering everything, and who show honor to the virtuous, gain arises. (89)
For those who are constantly devoted to the nature of sacred fords, who always listen well to sacred narratives,
and who are ever disposed toward salutation, gain arises for the virtuous;
likewise for those who are constantly engaged in the worship of the gods and who always perform acts of hospitality.
The gain of those who are virtuous and possess constant mindfulness of the good arises;
likewise, for those who desire their own spiritual welfare, those who subsist by the practice of service, and those seekers who serve the virtuous, such gain arises. (91–92)
For those who are mindful, seeking [the truth], and endowed with virtuous qualities,
the attainment of the wise occurs in the homes of the wise,
in the yoga of the wise, in the dwellings of true gurus, and at the great festivals of the wise. (93)
From constant association with the virtuous, the attainment of the virtuous arises.
For those established in the vow of truth, who sacrifice to the supreme Brahman, and who are associates of Hari—the virtuous arise. (94–95)
The attainment of the virtuous arises in the home of those devoted to Hari, in the house of female devotees, and among assemblies of dispassionate saints;
it comes through association with noble friends and by dwelling in a holy land.
Through the application of favorable time, service to the virtuous arises.

Through the occasion of initiation by the virtuous, through the reception of mantras from the virtuous, and even through the power of affection for the virtuous, service to the virtuous arises. (97–98)
Through faith, through respectful address, through fame, through noble lineage, and through connection with the great, service to the virtuous arises;
or else, it arises through the grace of Śrī Hari or by taking refuge in the consort of Hari. (99)
"Or rather, by the constant residence of Hari, the service of the virtuous is attained.
Today, O Nārada, this cremation ground, the abode of Śaṅkara,
has been purified by you, O holy one, a virtuous devotee of Hari."
By the grace of your feet, the entire world has been purified;
it surely proceeds upon the path to liberation, and even my home has been sanctified.
All that is auspicious has been made known to me—the bliss born of the connection with Kṛṣṇa.
The purifying glory of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has been proclaimed by you.
My heart has been purified here, as has that of my daughter, the golden-complexioned Lakṣmī, who stands in your presence; O Nārada, live long! (1.03–1.04)
"Oh, what great fortune for my daughter, that her name is celebrated among all beings throughout the three worlds! I am blessed, O my little daughter.
Daughter Lakṣmī, offer your salutations indeed to Śrī Nārada."
"Perform the massaging of my feet and the anointing of my limbs with oil.
Give me water, food, and whatever is sweet, desirable, and most excellent; do not delay.
Grant me a couch, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), drink, and likewise contentment of mind."
"O best among the virtuous, just as this Nārada himself desires,
so do you grant him the opportunity to perform his examination of you.
O daughter who causes me grief, you are indeed the daughter of Śambhu, the brother of Brahmā."
"This son is the son of Brahmā and my own son, yet he is your elder brother.
By virtue of this relationship, he is indeed a great preceptor and a supreme ṛṣi.
This Nārada is a portion (aṃśa) of Hari; he is worthy of worship by you and by me as well."
"O daughter, serve him in such a way that he becomes well-satisfied. Having been addressed thus, Lakṣmī Ājākarī bowed to Nārada and offered him water for drinking, sweet food, and a comfortable seat.
She gave him a golden-colored couch and flower garlands and other offerings. Lakṣmī massaged the feet of the illustrious Nārada,
and after resting, O Rādhikā, Nārada dispelled her fatigue.
Nārada also examined the characteristics as they had been described;
indeed, all those previously seen there were most excellent.
And Satī and Jānakī quickly [beheld] their own husband, Śiveśvara.
With joy, she called out to Viśveśvara, who was in the great garden.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of Events such as the Majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as Spoken by Nārada to Pārvatī and Satī, the Majesty of Lakṣmī, the Causes for Attaining the Company of the Virtuous, and the Honoring of Nārada," in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 277 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, Nārada then spoke thus to the Lord of Śrī regarding everything that had occurred in the house of Śiva concerning Bālakṛṣṇa.
Nārada said:
O Hari, I have now rested;
the creator of Śiva, the world-hero with three eyes and a divine body, has arrived at my home.
I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose; indeed, a Vaiṣṇava has come to my house today.
Even there, my affectionate brother has arrived today. (3) Oh, Nārada, my son! From where indeed have you come? Is all well and auspicious with you and likewise with my brother? (4)
"Is Viṣṇu well, and are his family members happy?
Having said this, Śiva suddenly embraced me with his chest.
Then, by me [was told] of Satyaloka and likewise of my father Brahmā.
And the welfare of his mother Sāvitrī was also proclaimed.
Then indeed the welfare of Sanaka and the others, as well as that of Rudra, was proclaimed; and thereafter the welfare of Dakṣa and the others was also proclaimed.
Then, the entire account of Viṣṇu and Mahālakṣmī,
as well as their happiness and welfare while residing in Vaikuṇṭha, was proclaimed.
Thereafter, the events that had previously occurred in Vaikuṇṭha were recalled once again.
Indeed, at the time of Śiva’s Tāṇḍava dance, there was the curse of Lakṣmī and so forth;
[there was] the birth of Śiva on the surface of the earth, with the thought, "You shall become Śiveśvara," and also the abandonment of Lakṣmī which was performed by Nārāyaṇa. (2.276.10)
Indeed, for the sake of His devotees, Nārāyaṇa arrived upon the earth;
through that pretext, the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa,
the Supreme Brahman, came to Aśvapaṭṭasara.
I have indeed proclaimed that, and Lakṣmī has also arrived.
This daughter was born in the house of Śivasvāmin; she too has been proclaimed by me.
She is Śivā, the goddess Pārvatī—all of this has been proclaimed by me.
Remembering [her] again and again, the Lord of Śivā shed tears as well; embracing me firmly, he cried out, "O son! O son! and embraced me.
Having bowed to Śaṅkara, I indeed made known what was in my heart.
The Blessed One knows this maiden and he is indeed free from disease;
the time for her giving away has truly arrived.
What is appropriate and right must be done by him, so that happiness may be attained.
O Śambhu, you perform worship of Kṛṣṇa constantly;
indeed, that very divine and beautiful one has been seen by you again and again.
Janārdana is certainly the Supreme Brahman himself for you.
"He who possesses a human form was seen by me and has been seen by you as well.
There remains nothing further to be seen in his true nature as the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
Nevertheless, if you have the desire, you may come. || 18-19 ||
When I had spoken thus, Śambhu remembered Bṛhaspati;
and Hara, having quickly arrived, offered the madhuparka and all other honors to the preceptor, reporting everything that I had said.
Bṛhaspati declared everything to be auspicious and most excellent.
Then Śambhu, having made his decision, spoke repeatedly in my presence and also before the Guru regarding the oral betrothal of the maiden.
Having observed an auspicious moment, I indeed presented ornaments, garments, a bilva fruit, and a tilaka to the girl;
she, being pleased with you, put on those garments.
Then, having been instructed by her preceptor regarding various excellent ornaments, she too became filled with joy;
considering herself beautiful among her friends and desiring a husband, she was delighted.
Hara then said to Bṛhaspati, "When shall this great festival take place? || 24-25 ||
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, Bṛhaspati spoke this to him.
Having heard it, all who remained steadfast in the words of Bṛhaspati attained great joy.
Then, having deliberated with me, Vācaspati quickly [acted].
Having taken up the vessel for yoga and observed the mind of the maiden,
and having observed the mind of Pārvatī and worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas,
he made the liquid moist with saffron and waited for an auspicious moment.
He drew up the document itself with Nārada as the sole witness;
by the command of Hara, people there played musical instruments,
while women sang auspicious songs and the wives of the gods likewise sang.

The illustrious Nārada, Bṛhaspati, Śaṅkara, and all the others likewise partook of that auspicious Gūḍadhāna and other offerings. Then this king of preceptors of the gods was joined by Śiva with the yoga-leaf.
"He was sent by me along with you to the abode of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
that very lord, the preceptor of the gods, has certainly arrived.
Having made her your own—she who was given to you in word—O Kṛṣṇa, bring your beloved here."
Waiting for your path, she remains as if distraught.
(33) "When will Kṛṣṇa arrive? When will he perform his own duty toward me?
Having been abandoned before, when shall I obtain him, the very life of my life? (34)
When will that Lakṣmī, whose hair is like a braid, look upon me with love?
She who, having come twice and gazed at me, has departed again and again.
And when Hari arrives from the sacrificial grounds by means of his celestial chariot— 35.‬
Furthermore, she who was worthy of worship does not come; why does she not even remember me?
Previously, when I saw her, I was still a young girl;
thinking, "She is suitable for my son," she placed me upon her lap. (36–37)
I believe that goddess remains ever firm in her resolve;
she is content, serene, and satisfied, and thus she does not forbid me at all.
O Nārada, when you arrived, she was Kambharā, who is indeed Ramā.
"What did he say to me or to my mother? Tell me the truth. Thus she questioned me repeatedly regarding that secret. O Kambharā, I must relate all of that to you.
"O ocean of mercy, act quickly; everything will bear fruit for your heart.
Thus addressed there by the celestial sage, Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, rose up and went swiftly toward his mother Kaṃbharā.
Having bowed to his mother, Nārada said, "He is eager to summon me to his palace to inform me of a secret;
he likewise summons my sister, who is well-pleased, as well as my virtuous brother’s wife. (42–43)
"Taking Amṛtā and Śrī along with Sahasrā, come to my abode.
Thus addressed by Bālakṛṣṇa, the mother, accompanied by her sister,
joined by her brother’s wife, and united with Bālakṛṣṇa, [departed].
"O virtuous Rādhā, come eagerly to the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa!
(45) Upon merely seeing her, Nārada smiled gently and bowed to the virtuous lady.
Rising up with his neck bowed, he welcomed her with his voice. (46)
Then, with his hands joined in *añjali*, he stood up as soon as his mother sat down upon the golden throne; thereafter,
his sister and his brother’s wife likewise sat down.
Honored, worshiped, and saluted, the sage Nārada, having prostrated himself in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, spoke according to the truth:
"O Mother, I bow at your feet; I shall tell you a secret."
That Śaivī, who spoke to me repeatedly regarding a secret matter—
Śrī Kaṃbharā Lakṣmī said:
"O Great Sage, is that girl Nārāyaṇī, the Supreme Sovereign?"
Relate here everything that she said for my sake:
Is that young woman beautiful, free from physical defects, and endowed with all auspicious marks?
What indeed is her state of health, and what is the nature of her pure mind?
"What does she desire for my son? What is that heart-born woman doing here? Is she still possessed of affection for me? Is her mind still fixed on my son?
Is she dwelling with a serene heart, even as she remembers me?"
When the sacrifice took place in the forest, Piṅgā was there at that time as Satī.
Seeing her arrived there, I became exceedingly joyful;
and having manifested my state as her daughter-in-law, she took me onto her own lap.
Again, having returned to my own country and then during the course of a sacrifice,
I went to the regions of Rāśiyāna and once more reached that place.
Indeed, upon seeing her there together with my own son, I was filled with joy.
Having requested her in private for the sake of her own son,
and having then related everything concerning him to his mother as well,
she returned after reaching a firm conclusion as if it were already settled; she did not go back to her again.
"Is that maiden suitable for my son?
Tell me everything regarding her—what virtues she possesses and what training she has received.
What kind of intellect does she have, and what arts is she endowed with? || 58 || Then he asked: "Does she exist [as such]?"
"Tell me everything here that ought to be understood for the sake of my daughter-in-law.
Nārada said:
"O Mother, having heard the name of that Lakṣmī, Kambharā, out of great reverence..."
Out of love, she became both thrilled and filled with tears;
after remaining thus for a moment, she regained her composure, smiled at me, and said:
"Is all well with me, who am worthy of honor? Does he even remember me?"
"O Great Sage, tell me what is the news concerning my venerable mother—what is her disposition toward me?
Is she striving for my sake, and is she well-disposed toward me?
Tell me, according to the actual state of those who abide in the stages of virtue."
"Or rather, if there is something else that ought to be known, tell it to me.
Then I spoke to the maiden, whose mind was fixed on listening:
"O Lakṣmī! Goddess Kambharā never forgets you at any time. (63–64)
Constantly remembering you while eating, she even causes you, Kṛṣṇa, to be remembered;
and here and there, absorbed in talk of you, the description of your virtues arises.
With eyes filled with tears of affection, what indeed can I say to you?

Your mother-in-law always dwells in happiness and awaits you, who are yourself happy. O Lakṣmī! She, whose every account is auspicious, who possesses a body, a home, and sons, and who is enriched with all prosperity, awaits you. (66–67)

Just as Kambharā Satī was always satisfied with her daughter, so too does she possess an even greater affection for you. She is constantly striving for your sake, wondering, "When will my beloved daughter come to me? (68)

The noble lady Kaṃbharā remains ever gracious toward you; indeed, she is your sovereign mistress. (6.9) Sometimes the auspicious one says: "What vow must my daughter-in-law perform? Without her, my Kṛṣṇa does not shine at all, for she is his worthy beloved. (2.276.70)
"O Mother, in this manner I indeed reported everything to her;
and when she bestowed the blessings you mentioned, I spoke then.
She remained gracious, affectionate, and endowed with excellent virtues. (71)
When I had spoken thus to her, she replied to me: "Offer salutations to her;
report my prostrations at her feet.
Report that my life-breaths reside in your son, and likewise report this to the noble lady."
"Tell the venerable lady that I have indeed come there;
inform her that my ignoble childishness must be forgiven.
Whether I am such as I am, or whether I belong to those who dwell in the mountains and forests," ||| 74 ||
"O noble lady, inform [him] that I, his daughter, am composed of dullness and must be forgiven.
I am not learned, O noble lady; I am not a repository of arts;
I am not endowed with discernment, nor am I beautiful in my cleverness. (75–76)
I am neither a practitioner of illusion nor one who employs harsh means;
I am not Kṛṣṇā, nor am I worthy of Kṛṣṇa. Nevertheless, do not forget me. I am the daughter of one worthy of worship and the wife of the son of one worthy of worship.

"I am a maiden; quickly make me your daughter-in-law, for such as I am worthy. Having spoken these words of the maiden, and noting that the time for giving had indeed arrived, he gave me sweet fruits of nectar.
"Gifts should be given to Kambharā-Lakṣmī and to her son, Viṣṇu. Having said this, he prostrated before me. This secret has been told to you.
That virtuous woman never passes even a single moment without Kṛṣṇa.
That Lakṣmī was indeed equal to Lakṣmī, but never equal to any other;
for all splendors exist as concentrated masses within her very form. She remained so radiant, like a sprout emerging from youth.
She always abides in the state of the virtuous, the supreme garment of the sky of consciousness;
she is of eternal nature, the condensed mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
She exists as the very seat of Brahman, having the form of liberation and the splendor of Hari.
Having reached twelve excellent years and considering herself the best of women,
she shines with the force of her affection for Hari due to her devotion as a faithful wife;
and within the center of her heart dwells Hari, marked by the characteristics of Kṛṣṇa.
O Mother, how could I possibly describe her who is perfected in every art?
She knows the science of cooking, she knows the arts of weaving,
she knows the duties of the household, and whatever tasks belong to the accountant.
She understands the treatises of the young and even the arts born of passion;
she knows every arrangement of costume and all methods of beautification, as well as all the duties of servants and even those tasks of slave-girls. (87–88)
All acts of service and all that provides mental delight; all theatrical performances and whatever dance performances there may be;
all instrumental music and all forms of singing in every respect.
All festivals and whatever matters concern the assembly; all expositions and likewise all logical arguments; all forms of self-knowledge and the arts arising from yoga. (2.276.90–91)
He knows all supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and medicine;
he understands Āyurveda and sacrificial rites in their entirety. He knows all the Vedas as well as all forms of exchange.

He understands all causes, all seasons, and all transformations and evolutions; he knows every craft, and he speaks all systems of ethics. He knows all meters, the origins of lineages, and domestic rituals.
He understands the hospitality due to guests, the offerings to the ancestors, and the worship due to the gods; he also understands how to offer welcome and respect, as well as honor.
He understands the origin of charity and the act of benefiting others.
She understands affection, love, devotion to her master, wifely fidelity, and her own virtue;
she knows all mixed flavors and sweet foods, as well as the preparation of buttermilk and the cooking of milk dishes. (96–97)
She understands weaving, purification, and religious observances directly;
she is endowed with wisdom, remains composed, and is seen to be deeply learned.
Is she Śāradā? Or is she Rādhā, who truly delights the heart?
He understands the art of painting and knows how to tend to cows and the like;
he knows agricultural work, the growth of crops, and forests as well; he knows all medicinal herbs, sacrificial fuel, and even the attainment of health. (2.276.100)
He understands the power of water and knows the power of fire; he thoroughly understands all the powers of mantra and the various migrations [of beings].
He well discerns gain and loss, as well as the four aims of human life.
She also understands conciliation, bribery, and other such means of discernment;
she knows all forms of discourse as well as the arts of the great gardens.
With a throat of sweet sweetness, she possesses an exceedingly melodious voice.
Golden-hued, with the complexion of Brahmā, her hands and palms are red;
she in whose body the brilliant autumnal moonlight dwells eternally;
her forehead is broad, elevated, and resembles the moon, shining like the moon and other luminaries.
She has black hair and a black soul; she is the one who bestows the perfections of black sovereignty and other powers.
She possesses the majesty of all prosperity and is endowed with the bliss of Brahman.
She is the radiance of the Supreme Brahman and the awakener of the Supreme Brahman.
Muktānikā, who is always devoted to Hari and whose activities are prosperous,
has Lord Bālakṛṣṇa— the Lord who grants liberation— residing within her. And she, O Kaṃbharā, remains established in the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Equipped with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and trident (1.08),
she possesses the previously mentioned marks and is adorned with the emblem of Kamalā.
Her entire body is beautified by thousands of the signs of Lakṣmī (1.09).
There, indeed, are seventy-two principal leaders;
and Bālakṛṣṇa shines forth, reaching up to his neck.
He possesses the gait of an elephant and a swan, and always maintains the gait of a supreme sage (parahaṃsa).
Svarṇavāsā, Sugandhā, Koṭyabjasakhikā, as well as Rādhā,
Ramā, Satī, Padmā, Māṇikī, Padmajā, Śrī, Śāradā, and other such female companions— all wives of Kṛṣṇa— attend upon her. (111–112)
Adorned with all ornaments and resting upon every artistic composition, she is endowed with a flash of wondrous brilliance and possesses the strength of the black Śīla.
Consisting of pure sattva, she is Brāhmī, who eternally consumes the bliss of Brahman.
She is virtuous, subsisting on milk-rice and other offerings, and she restrains herself for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
She is devoted to the penance of meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, finding satisfaction in the welfare of the child Kṛṣṇa.
She finds contentment through the destruction of all cravings; she is free from deceit, pure, and radiant.

She is one who has thoroughly studied the Vedas and sciences, a great being of virtuous conduct, whose heart is fixed on liberation, whose heart is devoted to self-surrender, who is intent on offering herself,
who is a vessel for the love of Nirvāṇa, and who is solely dedicated to the love of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
She is skilled in the means of attaining Kṛṣṇa and possesses the noble intelligence of future enlightenment.
She has limbs as dark as Kṛṣṇa’s and her wealth is Acyuta; she is always fickle toward those who are not devotees.
She is endowed with the fickleness of Kṛṣṇa and likewise sports for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Delight in liberation, discourse on the stories of Kṛṣṇa, a stable disposition,
and engagement with the Supreme Brahman— these are endowed with the three goals of human life;
they ordain the threefold creation and result in the abandonment of effort and enjoyment.
She has as her fruit the sacrifice, heaven, and liberation, and she possesses the activity of fulfillment;
she is distinguished by the attainment of Brahman and equalizes the bliss of creation;
she is subtle, centered in the bliss of the Self, and is the yoginī who breathes through Mādhava.
She is united with Kṛṣṇa, possessing all-encompassing realization and devoted to the worship of the Omniscient One;
she is eternally intent on honoring her elders and is resplendent with the amorous grace of Kṛṣṇa.
She is detached from anything other than Kṛṣṇa and finds perfect contentment in Nārāyaṇa.
Muktā was eager for the company of the virtuous, while Kṛṣṇā desired the hope of Kambharā. (123) She wished, "When indeed shall I see the home of the fortune of Kambharā?
If I am not for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, then what is the point of my life? (124)
"Since my very life exists for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, I am His servant"—this is my reflection;
"The pair of thighs of the Supreme Brahman is my home"—this is my firm conviction.
At every step, there is only the discourse of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The glorious Bālakṛṣṇa is directly perceived; He is the divine and eternal authority.
O Mother, His alone is that [authority], and all other things are rooted in Him.
Everything remains eternally a distinct object of knowledge for His sake.
That which is equal to, yet not surpassed by, the Supreme Brahman— the Great Reality— is its well-practiced yoga, which accomplishes the goal of Kṛṣṇa’s doctrine;
it is the perfected conclusion of the Kṛṣṇa-tantra, free from all selfish attachments.
Bound by the grasp of Bālakṛṣṇa, she is sustained by the Vedas and the commands of Kṛṣṇa.
Nārāyaṇa is her goal, and her means of attainment is not mere tranquility or the like.
She is the beloved of Bālakṛṣṇa, the lovely one who bestows everything other than what is unlovely.
She is the Yama of the great Bhāgavata dharma, endowed with the discipline of Kṛṣṇa;
she is fixed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, observing the vows of Kṛṣṇa, and relies on no other.
She meditates upon the face of Bālakṛṣṇa and sits at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
In your son Kṛṣṇa, she is endowed with life and engaged in the acts of love.
She dwells within the desires of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
she is the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, exceedingly dear to him, and as dear to her as he is to her. (132–133)
O Mahālakṣmī! She dwells in Kambharā, endowed with virtues. The separation from Kṛṣṇa is her ailment, and by that she suffers mental affliction.
A desire for a hundred million sons shines within her heart. (134)
Sarvasnehā is full of love and affection for Kambharā and for you, her son;
she is constantly intent upon your marriage and is ever cheerful at heart.
O Mother, she remembers you, her son, always and again and again.
She spoke to me with great urgency: "Listen again, Kaṃbhare!
When the sacrifice took place in the Piṅgā forest, my mother-in-law arrived there;
having displayed the role of a daughter-in-law, she took me onto her own lap. (136–137)
Having gone to the regions of Rāśiyāna and returned once more,
she approached me in private to make a request on behalf of her own son;
having secretly placed an unbroken *candraka* flower [in my hand], she departed as soon as she had gone.
"Even now my mother has not yet arrived; she is venerable, noble, and supreme. O Nārada, tell me quickly when the illustrious lady will come.
And my salutations must be conveyed to her," he said again and again. (2.276.139–140)

"Mother, she who is endowed with all virtues, trained in all duties, and proficient in household tasks, is manifest as worthy of being given away. Therefore, having gone quickly, let her be informed by means of the festival invitation. (141)
"Considering today to be the fourth day, perform the auspicious rites for the two of them.
Having spoken thus to Rādhikā and having bowed to her, the brahmin Nārada returned to his own seat and once again attained rest.
Then Kaṃbharā attained peace and rejoiced in contentment;
Amṛtā also then gave her joy and approval.
And Bālakṛṣṇa became delighted upon hearing the news.
And then they all slept happily on the night of the fourteenth day.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of how Nārada told Bāla-Kṛṣṇa the account of Lakṣmī’s secret speech as related in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, and how he subsequently told it to Queen Kambharā."

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; on this New Moon day at dawn, the cowherd girls, the daughters of brahmins, and young maidens sang auspicious songs indeed. (1)
Likewise, the young married women, the elderly, and the girls,
having heard the auspicious news of the arrival of the *yogapatra*,
indeed sang auspicious songs in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā due to the auspicious arrival of Bṛhaspati.
Having heard of Hari’s auspiciousness, they sang songs in every house.
All the beloveds of Brahmā, as well as all the maidens,
and the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, sang songs bringing auspiciousness to their beloved.
All the gopīs gathered together and came to the house of Śrī Kambharā, as did virtuous women, celibate students, and those singing auspicious songs;
also the wives of kṣatriyas, the noble women of vaiśyas, the pāṭala women, and other female attendants. (5)
Filled with great enthusiasm,
the goddesses who dwell eternally in the imperishable field arrived at the house, singing songs with longing upon hearing the news of Hari’s wedding. (6–7)
The friends born from the four oceans, assuming forms at will,
and the Kāmavallīs came to Kṛṣṇa’s palace singing;
so too did the Mātṛkās dwelling at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Having heard that their preceptor had arrived at the auspicious moment and knowing it to be highly propitious,
the noble ladies— worthy of worship, including the wives of kings and maidens— dressed in divine attire, sang as they proceeded to Kṛṣṇa’s palace. (2.277.9–10)
The women of Kuṅkumavāpikā arrived there singing;
all the young women of every caste and all the ladies came together.
They [prepared] for Satī, Śrī, Kaṃbharā-Lakṣmī, who had already performed her bath and worship.
Having bowed down and seated themselves upon a golden palace,
they sang auspicious hymns consisting of the glory of Kṛṣṇa, the Black One. He had performed his bath and worship by his mother, and the auspicious *candraka* mark had been applied to him.
With their foreheads adorned with saffron and unbroken grains of rice, and having dressed Acyuta in festive finery,
all the women, full of longing, sang praises and honored the Supreme Lord, their beloved Master, who had been attired by his brother’s wife. (13–14)
They placed a crescent moon upon his forehead, adorned with unbroken grains of rice and flowers;
and having sung songs of praise and manifested their inner joy, they offered blessings and bowed to the preceptor Bṛhaspati, who had completed his daily rites. (15)
Having drunk the milk mixed with sugar and saffron offered by their mothers,
and having taken their desired betel leaves, they departed for home after speaking auspicious words.
In every house here in Saurāṣṭra, there was talk of the festival of Kṛṣṇa.
The arrival of Bṛhaspati and Nārada spread swiftly;
hearing this, all the subjects attained great joy and celebrated a festival.
Immersed in bliss, they gathered together for the sake of seeing them.
Auspicious musical instruments were sounded in the palace (19).
All the celestial instruments, those used by kings,
as many as there are household instruments, and whatever regional instruments there may be— (20).
Musical instruments played with the hands, those played by blowing, and those that purify; all those played with sticks, and those played with lightning;
those played with the limbs, and those played with the various parts of the body—[all these were present].
Musical instruments from various regions resounded on all sides;
indeed, the sweet sounds of conch shells arose, as did the sounds of water-machines,
and the high-pitched notes of flutes were produced in every house.
Singers sang and those like celestial nymphs danced;
at that time, having heard of the festival for Bālakṛṣṇa, the women were exceedingly joyful.
The peacocks danced and the cuckoos warbled as well.
Birds—parrots, peacocks, and cranes—sang forth;
the planets shone brightly, as did the radiant fires.
The virtuous, pervaded by affection and luster, sang his praises. (25–26)
The learned Bhaṭṭas, Bhūsuras, and Vidyādharas, who were knowers of the Vedas, then sang the Sāman chants, while the Cāraṇas recited poetic verses.
Others cried out toward the Lord, "Victory! Victory to you, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa!"
Thus, O Rādhikā, joyful words arose among every person.
Having heard that the letter concerning the festival of Bālakṛṣṇa had arrived, and having heard that the preceptor Nārada was coming, others also approached for the sake of seeing him.
Uttering blessings and saying, "May you live long!
even the frogs, resembling frogs, caused the water-lifting machines to resound;
and those resembling *tammarikā* birds then sounded their lip-organs.
Playing cymbals, they uttered cries of victory.
What need is there for much speaking before you, O Rādhikā?
For the sake of establishing righteousness, He will take up the duties of a householder.
"That supreme reality which is distinguished is always distinguished;
in order to make it known to the world, he will practice the dharma of a householder.
Having reflected thus, he celebrated with a festival for the selection of the auspicious day.
Desiring to make it manifest, they joyfully performed the Rāsa festival.
Men and women, men and women— consisting of a succession of men and women—
they wandered about, and while wandering, they sang of the virtues of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having previously seen [the Lord] in the cities and other places through his divine vision at Kuṅkumavāpī, the Guru was filled with wonder regarding Saurāṣṭra and the sovereign ruler there:
"Aha! How great is this devotion to the Bhagavat on earth, consisting of such abundant affection! (36)
In the course of visiting great holy sites, I have seen among the people here such devotees as these;
they are liberated in this world, there is no doubt, for within their hearts resides the divine, most divine state of being toward Hari. (37–38)
Oh, blessed is that Lakṣmī, the daughter of Śiva, who is Nārāyaṇī;
for she shall indeed obtain the Lord of the Abode, the renowned, beloved, and eternal one.
I know her to be even higher than Rādhā, and the very stepping-stone for Him.

She whose husband is supreme stands upon the upward path; for even a maiden who is the consort of Kṛṣṇa is proclaimed the Mother of the World. Even an old woman, though hunchbacked in the world, is praised when she is joined with Kṛṣṇa.

Vṛndā and Tulasī were indeed the two wives of the demon Jalandhara and likewise of Śaṅkhacūḍa; they were equal to Lakṣmī in their union with Viṣṇu. Worthy of worship, adored by the world, and bestowers of liberation, they have always been so.
Oh, how great is the majesty of Kṛṣṇa! There are countless beloveds of Brahmā, yet they do not attain even a fraction of the dignity of this Lakṣmī;
for it is for her sake alone that the horoscope is written, unlike any other.
For the sake of fortune, Bṛhaspati was approached by none other than you;
for the sake of fortune, even your fame is sung today by none other than him.
For the sake of fortune, this joy-inducing [deed] was performed by you in the past, equal to which there is nothing else.
For the sake of Lakṣmī, the heart of Bālakṛṣṇa is unlike any other. (46) For the sake of Lakṣmī, his worldly speech is now perceived as divine;
for the sake of Lakṣmī, his worldly fickleness is seen to bring about auspiciousness. (47)
Aha! By the glance of Lakṣmī and Kṛṣṇa, the worldliness of the world today attains its true nature, for it is indeed of the essence of divine vision.
Aha! My fortune is supreme; that station of mine has truly become meaningful.
"And the Guru was always born superior due to the sending forth of Lakṣmī’s leaf.
Thus, that Brahmin Bṛhaspati, who was filled with wonder, having seen all that, O Rādhikā, became even more devoted to Bālakṛṣṇa. (2.277.50)
The great devotee and worshiper, having offered himself, attained the state of one who has surrendered his self; he offered his very own form to Hari by means of the gift of all that he possessed.
Then Bṛhaspati, intending to depart, [approached] Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
He said, "I wish to go to Kāśikā today; please inform [the Lord].
For on the new moon day, the Sovereign Śiva indeed awaits me there.
Gopāla replied, "So be it," and spoke further to Bṛhaspati.
"Go quickly, O Guru! Inform Śiveśvara of Kāśī.
May your desire be fulfilled; I shall honor your word.
Having thus honored the marriage document, I accepted it with devotion.
"For gods such as yourselves, that [union] is certainly conducive to happiness;
conversely, if it were otherwise, it would result in the opposite and cause distress.
Since the girl is suitable and the prince is also suitable, let it be so."
Having spoken her verbal acceptance, she then gave him a written agreement.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"What kind of yoga-agreement is that, and what kind of counter-agreement is it?"
"Therefore, I wish to hear that message and its reply.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you of both auspicious letters."
When the [donative] record was written, true to its meaning and adorned with excellent qualities such as profundity—
in the auspicious, venerable, and glorious dust of the Brahmākṣara-kṣetra,
where the illustrious Śrīpati shines within the preeminent place named Śrīmat-kuṅkumavāpikā— 58.
In whose house the Supreme Lord, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa Hari, sports— the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa, who is saluted by millions of lords of the lotuses, may He be victorious! He who,
being the father of Vairāja, shines forth as Mahāviṣṇu himself.

I bow perpetually to you, the illustrious Lord of Kaṃbharā, who, by the command of Hari, exists as the first human being in creation; whose fame is sought after for the sake of the three worlds, and who is renowned here as the abode of auspicious qualities. (2.277.60)
For those whose treasure-trove of a well-accumulated mass of merit manifests here in this world;
for whom the abundant blessings of holy men bear fruit in the long duration of time;
and for whom the fruit of sacrifices and austerities, as well as the fruit of serving the elders, truly arises—
But for them, a connection with a Viṣṇu such as you would be difficult to attain.
(6.1) Such that the virtuous offer their merits and even their blessings at the feet of your son,
and the lords of the quarters offer the crowns resting upon their heads in worship.
The gods [bestowed] divine prosperity, supreme jewels, gems, and so forth;
kings [gave] unsurpassed sovereignty; mountain-dwellers [offered] gold and the like; and merchants [presented] wealth to that Blessed One, the Lord of all lords, who dwells in the Imperishable. (6.2)
To the worthy Hari, the abode of supreme virtues, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa;
indeed, I, Śiveśvara residing in Kāśī, the sovereign of the gods and lord dwelling on Kailāsa, offer my daughter—an unblemished gift—to you daily, O Lord Śrī Pārvatīśa. (63)
That Lakṣmī who formerly came here from the abode of Hari by the will of Nārāyaṇa and manifested herself in my auspicious home, a devotee of Hara—
she is now present, worthy of being chosen as a bride and fit for the giving and receiving of gifts.

The procedure for its gift was determined by us on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month, during the most auspicious of auspicious moments for the festival of that act of giving— a most excellent and most propitious time distinguished by its preeminence.
"May you, illustrious ones whose hearts are gladdened by the presence of virtuous kinsmen and friends, come to my palace and fulfill my purpose by taking my son by the hand.
I am a devotee of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa on this earth, and here Hara is indeed a Sāttvata."
Day by day, I shall provide for you all excellent service according to my ability and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having seen the sacrifice brought to its conclusion without obstacle through the grace of Gaṇanāyaka, I shall behold great satisfaction; therefore, please accept this my prayer. (65)
Indeed, this beautiful letter of mine, which awakens my thought, inscribed with auspicious words like drops of glorious saffron and intended for delivery,
was sent by me after being placed in the hand of Bṛhaspati two years ago, accompanied by witnesses.
May she, having come into your hands, bring about for you and for my son the auspiciousness of a daughter.

Having quickly dispatched me along with this Devaguru, who has been treated with great respect, and having entrusted me as a festive pledge for the fulfillment of our higher purpose, may she grant us consolation.
May the residents of glorious Kāśī grant us that which is most worthy to be done:
that we become devotees intent on Brahman, disciples who uphold the teachings of Hari, and virtuous servants.
Or else, may there be another day, auspicious with welfare and the like, which is beautiful for the illustrious ones.
"Let that which is worthy of being given be announced most swiftly to the True Guru along with me;
furthermore, let everything else that has come into my own possession according to family custom and whatever is fit for me be offered as well.
Speaking thus, Śambhu attains peace—Om. (69)
Thus, O Rādhikā, this letter of donation sent by Śaṅkara has indeed been spoken by me to you at his request;
now hear the reply-letter which the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa wrote to Śaṅkara.
Listen to [this hymn], which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and is filled with manifold meanings:
Oṃ! Formerly, on the land of Goloka, the fortunate abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, He manifested from Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and on Kailāsa, He became half the body of His own consort.
In his own abode, Śiva, known by the name Sadāśiva, shines as a devotee of Viṣṇu;
in Vaikuṇṭha, in the presence of Hari, he performed a most excellent dance accompanied by music.
Indeed, Śrī Lakṣmī perceived that his untimely arrival was an obstacle to Hari’s amorous play. || 72 ||
Having heard that he was cursed to be born in human form and would be joined by his wife,
Śrī Hari himself became a follower of his devotee, even though he had abandoned his own glory (Śrī).
That Lakṣmī, following out of a desire to attain Hari, has become your daughter.
Thus may Lord Kṛṣṇa always grant auspiciousness here to Śrī Pārvatī’s noble husband, who possesses the very form of Śiva, and also to Lakṣmī;
and may your son Gaṇādhipa, together with his consort, bestow welfare and auspiciousness.
Gopālakṛṣṇa, whose residence is in the illustrious Kuṅkumavāpikā, makes this request:
"Indeed, you have increased my good fortune by giving your daughter to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow—my son Narāyaṇa, who is Hari himself, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa. (74)
Even after Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, had visited my home and been honored by me,

and even after he had affectionately accepted the deed of gift offered here by me, [I departed]. Then, having reached the city of Kāśī at a most auspicious and excellent time appointed for that purpose, ||| 75 ||

O Śambhu! Today, by attaining Your supreme vision, may there be auspiciousness that bestows peace. Having thus brought to completion all the various rites at this sacred site, I shall indeed behold the eternal happiness ordained for the couple.
O Lord of Umā, I shall come there swiftly by means of celestial chariots on the third day of the bright fortnight, after midday, accompanied by my family and the lotus-born Brahmā;
as well as whatever other kings on earth have performed sacrifices and are devoted to the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Even here, thousands of crores and billions of men have been carried away;
countless lords who dwell in the abode of liberation, Nārāyaṇas, as well as Siddhas, hosts of Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, gods, and likewise humans.

Even the divine hosts of conscious beings, though endowed with bodies, are indeed sacred sites; even the goddesses, though established beyond creation, shall pass away even beyond the highest limit (parārdha).
Likewise, the millions of maidens and the women who are the beloveds of Brahmā, though situated here—
They will come to your abode, eager for the yoga of Brahman from time immemorial.

O omniscient one, whose form is Śiva, what secret could there be between you and me? O Hari, who dwells on the Vaiśālī ground, what need is there for me to speak of your welfare, for you are a perfected yogin? (79)
Having thus bowed down and likewise made this petition to the Lord of Kāśī,
I now respectfully present this letter to my Guru along with ten thousand jewels.
Whether there be deficiency or excess, whether the reply be unpleasant, sweet, weighty, or harsh— [I offer it].
"O Śambhu, you who are disciplined in soul, my playful conduct must be forgiven by you in every way.
Thus, O Rādhikā,
the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, encouraged by Nārada, gave this reply to Hara in a letter.
He performed a great worship of Bṛhaspati with millions of jewels,
as well as with fine garments, sandalwood, pearls, necklaces, and offerings;
he delighted the true guru with meals and hospitable drinks.
He gave him a beautiful celestial chariot (vimāna) filled with jeweled ornaments;
the true Guru ascended that lovely vehicle, which was provided with wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatā),
and on the morning of the first lunar day, he traveled through the air to Kāśī.
He gave a letter in reply to the letter from Śambhu, and Hara rejoiced;
he read the auspicious letter and rejoiced yet again at the salutations and other marks of humility, affection, and devotion toward himself.
The true guru related [the history] of Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, as well as Bālakṛṣṇa, Lomaśa, and others. "A great arrival here is imminent—a universal river [of grace]. (86–87)
"When both [types of] fame exist, the three worlds will surely come under the influence of generosity," the Guru said at that time.
Śambhu, with a gracious heart, spoke to the Guru according to his strength: || 88 ||
Indeed, the three worlds shall come into the courtyard of this vessel of merit.
We shall perform appropriate, auspicious, and supermundane service.
And my hosts, numbering in the millions, tens of millions, billions, and trillions, dwell in the world.
Tens of millions, billions, and trillions of goddesses become my forms as virtuous women;
Saṃkarṣaṇa, Mahākāla, Mahārudra, Rudraka, and Hara— I am they,
and my forms exist even by the tens of millions.
Kṛṣṇa is my father before my very eyes, and Goloka is mine in every respect.
Mahāmāyā is my creation, Hanumān is indeed my son, and Gaṇeśa is likewise; my attendants (pārṣadas) number in the millions, billions, and trillions.
"Everything is auspicious for me, and you are likewise my preceptor among the gods.
What is lacking for me today? Everything is accomplished for me.
Having spoken thus, he honored Bṛhaspati as he sat upon his seat.
Śaṅkara caused [the guests] to be fed and had a pavilion constructed;
he caused the sounds of musical instruments to resound in all directions and dispatched messengers throughout the three worlds to issue invitations. (95–96)
O Rādhikā, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was accompanied by Kuṃkumapatrikā;
and all auspicious things were present in the abode of Hara. || 97 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious Songs of the Women of the Three Worlds in Every House During the Great Festival at the Abode of Gopālakṛṣṇa on the New Moon Day in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Honoring of Bṛhaspati, the Description of the Deed of Donation, the Return of the Honored Bṛhaspati to Kāśī after his departure, and the Invitation Extended by Śambhu Throughout the Three Worlds. || 277 ||

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā! On the first day of the lunar fortnight, women indeed sang auspicious hymns of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the morning. || 1 ||
All musical instruments were played everywhere;
in every house and courtyard, festive archways were filled with people,
and beautiful gateways adorned with fresh sprouts were erected.
In every house, women placed lamps filled with ghee at all the doors; banners and small flags were raised, and festoons,
beautifying the arena, were fastened to the heights of the sky.
The entire splendor of Kuṅkumavāpikā was like that of the celestial abodes;
it was fashioned with wonderful arrangements by the subjects who were filled with great joy. The carriage-roads, the royal highways, the side-streets, and the alleys—
They were swept clean and sprinkled with water, and decorated with colorful paintings;
market stalls were established, adorned with arches,
colored creepers, curds, sprouts, and betel leaves, all possessing an auspicious character.
The dwellings, temples, palaces, rows of mansions,
vast halls, and beautiful gardens were adorned by the people;
even the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was decorated with various colors.
The crossroads were purified by means of rafts and auspicious lamps;
the balconies, altars, and door-frames were made difficult to scale,
and the beautiful gate-towers were adorned with seven-tiered finials.
Indeed, they were adorned with leaves, sprouts, creepers, and fruits;
and there was the auspicious abode of Bālakṛṣṇa, made of moonstone and other precious materials,
surrounded at that time by groves of wish-fulfilling vines and fruit-bearing trees.
That palace of Śrī Hari, which possessed a thousand and one golden pitchers, was adorned on all sides with sun-crystals and other precious gems;
at that time, it was further embellished everywhere with new articles of beauty and splendor.
Was it Vaikuṇṭha, or was it another? Was it Goloka, or yet another? Was it the abode of Brahmā, or the immortal realm, or something else?
Or was it some other heaven entirely? Thus did the subjects speculate.
In such a city, indeed, the women and men were clad in new garments;
they possessed new ornaments and new colors, beautified by new finery, and were then endowed with new enthusiasm, new strength, and new prosperity. (15–16)
There were new foods and drinks, new songs and chants, noble new intentions, and those endowed with ninefold virtues;
even the beasts possessed new vigor, as did the birds. (17)
On the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the cows yielded fresh milk; the buffaloes were newly vigorous;
the bulls possessed fresh virility; the elephants and other animals were full of new curiosity;
and the horses and other creatures experienced fresh joy. (18–19)
The trees were laden with new fruit, and the creepers were covered in fresh blossoms;
the branches possessed every new flavor, as did the crops and the ears of grain.
At that time, honey was abundant from the fresh flowers everywhere.
The Brahmins were indeed ninefold in their joy, virtuous, and possessed of ninefold devotion;
they were learned, possessed of a ninefold intellect, and their principles were truly new.
At that time, they became radiant with a ninefold splendor.

In particular, O Rādhikā, the inner hearts of people became truly stainless; through the intensity of their emotion, they indeed became bestowers of eternal bliss. Thus, Kuṅkumavāpī was like something newly created.

Endowed with fresh youth and adorned with every ornament, the divine Lakṣmī arrived as something truly new; indeed, it was for the sake of her new co-wife’s attainment of fresh joy that she appeared as a novelty. (24–25)
For the sake of the affection of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
a divine pavilion from the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣaradhāma) arrived there.
He did not bow to the Blessed Lord, nor did he bow to Gopāla Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed to his mother, that pavilion, which had been composed of liberated souls, vanished;
and by the mere will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, within a moment, it manifested again as a divine form composed of liberated souls. (27–28)

"Having come to propitiate the Supreme Self, I pray that by His command I may become a beautiful pavilion leading to the abode of the Imperishable. Hari said, "So be it; you have indeed been remembered for that very purpose."
"Let him create a beautiful pavilion that shines as it does in the Imperishable.
Having received this command with "Om," O Rādhikā,
the Great Liberated One, whose self is the pavilion, assumed the form of the pavilion itself.
Having grasped both forms, the small and the large, the small form indeed became stable in front of the temple of Bālakṛṣṇa.
It was adorned with a hundred kalaśas and beautifully graced by a hundred pillars. || 32 ||
It was seven stories high, surrounded on all sides and in the center by a path in the sky;
it shone above with a priceless central pinnacle,
like the moonlight of the full moon spreading across the earth.
Likewise, its white luster, resembling water, spread everywhere across that ground, like the world of the moon;
in its center, a natural sun-gem shone brilliantly. (35)
It shines forth with a thousand gentle and soft rays.
Then, stalks of lightning,
possessing the brilliance of lamps and white as milk, flash forth on all sides.
The gems, set in their sockets, were white, red, and variegated;
blue, yellow, green, and tawny, with diverse radiances.
Fastened in every corner, they shone indeed like stars.
In various ways, diverse leafy creepers grow at its side.
Medicinal herbs and leaf-lamps shine here and there upon the ground.
There are pillars serving as bases for sacrificial pits, and the pits themselves are adorned with cloth bands.
The water-carrying strips, the secret conduits for fire,
and the secret channels for flames shine forth according to their respective locations.
There are bamboo poles, pillars, statues, mechanical devices, and arched gateways.
The branches, sub-branches, and lineages shine forth through their carriers.
There is no deficiency in their brilliance; they shine just as they do in the Imperishable (akṣara), for that liberated one is indeed the single self of the pavilion.
They become radiant with heat, and likewise they become cool;
they manifest as both cold and hot, and as neither hot nor cold.
They possess the touch of sweet nectar and bestow the bliss of Brahman.
And they also bestow bliss upon all the senses.
Thus, in this pavilion of great splendor illuminated by lamps, there were pillars in the form of plantain trees, joined with unbroken leaves. (45–46)
Even among hundreds of seven-storied mansions situated in distinct divisions,
there were indeed divine seven-colored cloths enveloped in garments.
In their midst, within that abode of splendors and in the flow [of light], all creations reside.
They are seen within the pillar like the abodes of the gods on Mount Meru.
For in some parts of the pillar there are sages, and in others there are perfected beings (siddhas);
in other places, there are infinite liberated souls in the form of lions.
In some places dwell the incarnations; in some places dwell the attendants (*pārṣadas*).
In some places indeed are the groups of liberated women, the virtuous beloveds of Brahmā;
in some places is Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka, and in some places Vaikuṇṭha as well.
In some places the indeterminate abode shines forth, and in some places the immortal;
in some places the golden abode, and in some places the realm of Vairāja;
in some places the abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra shines forth.
In one pillar is Satyaloka, in another the abode of the ancestors;
in some are the gods and guardians of the directions, and in others the lords of the universe.
In certain pillars shine the planets, such as the sun, the moon, and the rest.
In some places the Vasus and Indras dwell, and in others the great ṛṣis;
in some places there are men, and in others Daityas and Dānavas;
in some places there are oceans, rivers, and wild forests.
In some places there were mountains; in some, beings dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla);
in some, those who dwell in water; and in some, even those who dwell on land.
In certain caves there, elephants and other creatures were also seen.
Garuḍas, parrots, sāras cranes, peacocks,
bhāsas, swans, and cātaka birds— beings of divine origin— are seen there; and in some places, apsarases from the lake of Brahmā appear as dancers.
Within the interior of the pillars and upon the rows of paintings,
the threefold creation is indeed seen, contained within the pavilion that is composed of the Imperishable.
Upon the ground, on the golden earth, the divine realms truly shine forth.
In some places water shines, in some fire, and in some the earth;
in some places there are oceans, and in some there are forests;
and in some places there are mountains, as well as lakes and rivers.
In some places, most delightful gardens and even cities are seen within the interior of the earth, as well as upon its level surface above. Likewise,
the Ocean of Milk and the Lord Nārāyaṇa are found there.
In the center of that pavilion, Hari is seen within the womb of the earth (bhūgarbha).
At the bases of all the pillars, the deities of the site (vāstudevatās) are seen;
they are also observed in their respective places within the pavilion’s foundation.
The deities of the branches are seen, and there are also the deities of the door;
likewise, the female friends of the archway and the goddesses of the couch, adorned with garlands, are beheld.
These youthful women, the supports for the painted arts, are observed there.
Well-attired with garments and ornaments, illuminated by divine light,
and surrounded by circular hanging lamps,
the goddesses, filled with the sentiment of laughter, shone brilliantly in the gateway. (66–67)
All the women born of delight, diverse as if they were sentient beings,
shine forth, situated upon the support of the mirror at its rounded tip.
There also exist Gandharva singers, existing in the form of couples.
The floors within the pavilions shine brightly with banners.
In every corner, seven golden jars each, arranged along a single cord, gleam as brilliantly as the sun. (2.278.70)
Fruit-bearing branches hang down there, supported by pillars and posts; and ropes are fastened there, adorned with garlands of gems and pearls.
A wonderful variety is seen here throughout the pavilion upon inspection.
On one side were millions of Lakṣmīs, and on the other, even more than a million;
on one side were Sarasvatīs, and on the other, a million Durgās.
All of them were seen bearing weapons and adorned with every ornament.
Upon the upper floors of the archways were all manner of enchanting celestial beings;
above them were the attendants (*pārṣadas*) and the cowherds (*gopas*) in their own forms,
as well as all the *gandharvas* and the hosts of Śiva (*śāṅkaragaṇas*).
And all those divine weapons which exist even throughout the three worlds are indeed situated above that;
and above that are the regions of Dhruva, accompanied by twelve suns.
The circular pavilions, enriched with splendor and canopies, shine forth;
likewise, the delightful quadrangles and the brilliantly radiant upper chambers.
All the staircases are covered with carpets of gold and silver.
The walls of cloth-paintings, jewels set in golden filigree,
and all kinds of canopies made of silk shone brilliantly;
and just as on the upper floor there was another divine Vaikuṇṭha.
In the great garden, it was in full bloom and graced by the Rāsa-sport;
there were the excellent, delightful, and auspicious vehicles of the celestial dwellers, such as elephants, lions, and Garuḍas. (2.278.80)
All of those were as if placed in succession upon the higher levels.
[There was] a beautiful place endowed with wish-creepers, wish-trees, and wish-lamps;
distinguished by the splendor of the *kalpa* age, and likewise bestowing the fruits of the earth of the *kalpa*.
Indeed, this pavilion came to be adorned with garlands of wish-fulfilling pearls;
it possessed the pleasant touch of the *kalpa* wind and was resplendent with the fragrance of the *kalpa* tree.
It bestowed garments like the *kalpa* tree and was provided with the creepers of the *kalpa* betel vine. (83)
He is the giver of garments and drink, and his celestial palace lasts for an eon (kalpa).
He provides bedding and coverings for an eon, and is adorned with royal couches for an eon.
He bestows eon-long cushions, bolsters, and seats, and he accomplishes all that is required for an eon.
He was seated upon a lion-throne as soft as a celestial grass mat (bṛsī), endowed with the splendor of a celestial assembly hall and adorned with celestial plaques;
he was joined by celestial parasols, banners, and unbroken canopies of cloth. 86.
It was provided with archways made of glass and archways adorned with jewels and gems;
its walls were enriched with panels and door-panels set with precious stones; and it shone with side grounds resplendent with swings, hammocks, and other such amusements. (87–88)
Equipped with lightning-sight instruments and lightning-voice machines,
possessing lightning-hearing devices and excellent instruments for perceiving lunar touch,
he rendered the *kalpa* piercing [of the target] as if it were already accomplished, through the application of secondary methods. 89.

Rich in the machinery for the conception of time, he is the initiator of omniscience. Within the microcosm of the body and the macrocosm of the universe, he possesses the power of yoga within the supreme wheels;
he manifests the sounds of musical instruments, the self, and songs through the mechanism of his creative imagination.
Adorned with the yantra that reveals the entire essence of both the individual body and the cosmic egg, it bestows the satisfaction of desire through its touch and grants the highest wonder.
It grants to the beloved the moment’s fulfillment merely by being remembered for an instant. (92)
Filled with the wonder of primordial creation, His consciousness is being, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
He is the bestower of eternal bliss, possessing the bell, conch, and drum; He is endowed with a heart filled with all objects of enjoyment and is perfectly sustained by the ocean of nectar.
Whatever excellent women exist throughout the entire creation, and of whatever kind they may be—
all those of diverse forms were caused to be fashioned there.
In one corner stands a pillar named Māṇikya, which is made of gold.
Resplendent with a red hue, possessing four ears and a beautiful crest,
he is worshipped with vermilion flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), lotuses, and other offerings; likewise, upon a sandalwood plaque and within a circle of unbroken grains.
A golden water-pot (*vārdhinīkalaśa*) filled with water and accompanied by a *pūjikā* [offering]; adorned with a neck-thread and cloth, and filled with water in its center;
provided with mango, *aśoka*, beautiful *campaka*, and betel-leaf vines. (98)
Adorned with *śrīphala* fruits, jewels, and minerals, it was beautifully fashioned;
it was worshipped by Gaṇeśa with gold, and was graced by the presence of the gods, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, and endowed with the attainment of auspiciousness. (99–100)
Thus, that divine pavilion there became truly magnificent;
whatever splendors exist in the world through variety were created there by him himself.
O Rādhikā, its description cannot possibly be accomplished.
Carrying vessels of unbroken rice, saffron, and all auspicious sprouts,
and bearing the complete collection of materials for worship and hospitality,
he shone brilliantly as he went before the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa. (102–103)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Morning Auspicious Rites on the First Day of the Bright Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Splendor of the Kuṅkumavāpī Lake and the Divine Courtyard Pavilion," etc., in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 278. [End of] Section 2 (Tretā-yuga-santāna), Chapter 279.
