Śrī Rādhikā said:
How is it that a ruby pillar is placed here in this pavilion?
For what purpose indeed is the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) prescribed there?
Likewise, the installation of Gaṇeśa, the installation of the Mothers (mātṛkā),
the installation of Vāstu, and also the installation of Viṣṇu.
And how, O Kṛṣṇa, is the installation of a family deity (kuladeva) performed?
What fruit is said to result from its installation, and what is the undesirable consequence of not installing one?
Tell me all that, O Kṛṣṇa, which is the cause of happiness for those in the cycle of worldly existence.
Knowing this, the worlds beyond,
along with the sages and the devotees of the Blessed One, establish the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala together with the deity according to the prescribed rite; what, O Lord, is the reason for this?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe the happiness that brings benefit to both husband and wife, especially for the householder, and most particularly for the husband. 6.

In the house of a householder who provides wealth such as jewels and gold, [the pillar] is always worshipped as having Indra as its deity, as having Agni as its deity, and even as having the Cow as its deity; thus it is called a ruby-pillar (māṇikya-stambha). 7.
This [pillar], installed in the pavilion, has Indra, Agni, and the Cow as its presiding deities.
(8) It shall always make the householder equal to Indra in prosperity, and his family shall forever be as radiant as fire. (9)
May the cow always yield milk; may the house indeed be full of flavor.
May the prosperities of Indra always be present in the home of the householder.
May the prosperities of Agni always be present in the home of the householder.
"May there always be abundance of cows in the house of the householder.
Thus do the deities stationed there bestow their blessings;
otherwise, a threefold poverty arises for him.
Indeed, a home would become impoverished, lacking food, and devoid of flavor;
it would surely consist entirely of suffering here due to the failure to worship the *māṇikya* jewel.
Wherever the *māṇikya* resides, there the residence of Hari is always present.
Wherever Hari dwells, there is the dwelling of Lakṣmī;
wherever Lakṣmī dwells, there is the dwelling of prosperity.
Therefore, those who know the ancient lore worship the ruby pillar (māṇikya-yūpa).
Many earthly defects— sleepiness, laziness, heaviness,
dullness, and dryness— dissolve through the worship of that [deity].
Destruction, widowhood, misfortune, and illness [are likewise removed].
By worshipping him, these [misfortunes] dissolve: namely, childlessness itself;
by worshipping him, they dissolve as well—being an exile, having no refuge, the emptiness of one's home, and the absence of fruit-bearing trees and the like. (17–18)
The absence of love between husband and wife, lack of mental focus in the excellent dwelling,
and the bride’s lack of good fortune— all these dissolve through its worship.
Likewise, the bride’s exclusion from the ground and her exclusion from the home [are likewise removed].
By worshipping this [Māṇikya], the bride’s lack of fortune within the family perishes;
furthermore, through the worship of the Māṇikya, one is released from the debt to the Rākṣasas, the debt to the goddess Kumārī, and the debt to the ancestors, such as the father.
O Rādhikā, one should understand that the testimony of Indra, Agni, and the Cow establishes the existence of the next world and other realms;
from that, even all the duties of domestic life become fruitful.
Such is the fruit to be understood from the worship of Māṇikya.
Listen now to the auspicious fruit of worshipping the water-pot (kalaśa).
Within the water in the pot, Varuṇa indeed shines resplendently;
all sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas), as well as the oceans and rivers, come there as well. (23–24)
The lakes, the deities, and the lords of the jars also brought that which was required for the marriage rite which bestows peace and happiness;
it was a giver of water and food, and a provider of all flavors.
Even the bodily acts of desire performed by him become purifying through his worship.
His entire household always bestows the prosperity of sons and remains sanctified.
Furthermore, whatever natural impurity exists in the bodies of women or even men [is likewise purified].
By sprinkling with the waters of Varuṇa, all that [impurity] is removed.
Through this, the husband becomes a sacred ford (tīrtha), bestowing the fruit of all holy fords;
the wife likewise becomes a sacred ford, bestowing the fruit of all sacred fords.
The deity Varuṇa declared that Yugala-tīrtha itself exists [there]:
"Where indeed is the station of Varuṇa, there no debt arises;
all flavors and all fragrances there belong to Varuṇa. (2.279.30)
The abode of Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Maheśa shall be in that house where there is a place for a water-pot (kalaśa) filled with water;
and [where there is] always milk, ghee, or even fresh butter.
Nourished by curd, buttermilk, Soma, and nectar, he shall dwell [therein].
In this manner, minerals of the nature of jars—gold, silver, and gems—reside within him due to his worthy offering of the jewel-encrusted jar. || 32–33 ||
The house of one who possesses auspicious jars and daughters supported by sons-in-law shall be endowed with prosperity of lineage and adorned with golden jars.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, have I described the fruit of being worthy of the jar.
If the ritual vessel (kalaśa) is not established, everything that has been prescribed fails to take effect.
Everything becomes the opposite, increasing suffering and poverty.
O Gaṇeśa, I shall state the fruit of the worship: I am indeed Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Gaṇas.
The Blessed One is the bestower of prosperity, the fulfiller of all desires;
he is the granter of every success and likewise the giver of spiritual accomplishments and supernatural powers. He is the provider of auspicious gains and the destroyer of all obstacles.
I am also a protector at all times for one who worships me.
(38) One who performs my worship shall have desirable foods such as *laḍḍukas* and the like;
for that worshiper of mine, houses made of gold and silver come into being. (39)
There shall be an abundance of elephants, horses, and chariots, and his house shall be rich in vehicles.
His attire shall always be resplendent with yellow garments and other such finery.
The face of Gaṇeśa, endowed with a trunk, bestows cattle and wealth.
The abdomen is equal to a woman; it bestows food and grants sons and other blessings.
The region below the waist, up to the genitals, fulfills all desires.
Through the worship of Gaṇeśa, even the onset of adverse karma (duṣṭaprārabdha) shall be destroyed. 41–42.
"No harm shall come to him from the wicked yogis of the *gaṇas*.
Thus, O Rādhikā, has this supreme fruit been declared here regarding the worship of Gaṇeśa; for I myself, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, abide as Gaṇeśa within the home.
In all those places, the householder obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Rādhikā, listen now to the excellent fruit of the installation of the Mātṛkās:
the sixty-four Yoginīs of Śaṅkara. (44–45)
The Mātṛkās and other mother-goddesses who are the wives of the sages,
as well as other water-deities, and others such as Caṇḍī and the rest;
the Mātṛkās such as Koṭarā and others, who take the form of child-seizing spirits (bālagraha).
The goddesses beginning with Ṣaṣṭhī, as well as the Rākṣasīs and the Mātṛkās—thus they exist in many forms, worshipped and always bestowing happiness;
yet when unworshipped and provoked to anger, they devour the household, the child, and the fetus. (47–48)
In some houses, they even consume the bride or the groom when they are angry;
therefore, these women must be honored, for when pleased, they bestow prosperity.
They ward off danger arising from both water and fire.

In this way, the family goddesses (kuladevyaḥ) are always to be worshipped. Family goddesses are worshipped for the sake of increasing the lineage, for the sake of increasing prosperity, and for the sake of averting destruction. (2.279.50–51)
Having always worshipped Vāstudeva, the Person, for the constant satisfaction of the Earth,
[one should perform this] in the house, the pavilion, the altar, and the sacrificial pit.
The worship of Vāstu is the destroyer of the sins arising from the destruction of living beings during these rites.
O Rādhā, the defects of the quarters, the defects of the earth, and the defects of the elemental spirits are entirely destroyed on all sides by the propitiation of Vāstu; indeed,
it becomes a provider of residence for the couple for a very long time.
On the ground, there shall be good fortune for the bride and the groom, as well as for one named Dhruva.
When the ritual of offering all activities to the deity Vāstu is performed, auspiciousness shall prevail.
Thus has been described to you here the disease-destroying worship of Vāstu.
The installation of Viṣṇu alone bestows Lakṣmī and grants auspiciousness.
Wherever Viṣṇu resides, there dwells prosperity that grants all happiness.
When worshipped and saluted, Viṣṇu makes one’s home like Vaikuṇṭha.
Viṣṇu, the eternal one, shall bestow devotion upon his family, as well as the welfare of the husband and wife; he shall grant fame, renown, and a virtuous disposition.
Being duly worshipped, he shall provide protection with his Sudarśana discus.
One should bestow the Dharma, and likewise bestow knowledge gathered through discernment;
being well-honored, one should bestow even the internal, divine eye;
and when propitiated by the offering of everything, one should bestow nirvāṇa. (2.279.60)
Thus has been described, O Rādhā, the fruit of worshipping the gods and other deities.
Now listen, O Rādhā, to the auspicious fruit of the pavilion (maṇḍapa):
the pavilion is said to be a refuge; the pavilion is the abode of the deities. (66.1)
And the pavilion is proclaimed as the abode of all emanations;
it may be a cloth pavilion, or even a mineral pavilion, or even a meritorious pavilion, or even a wooden pavilion. (62–63)
There was a pavilion of jewels, as well as a pavilion of houses;
there was indeed a pavilion of trees, and likewise a pavilion of gardens.
There was also a pavilion of reeds, and likewise a pavilion of earth.
Indeed, even within the Kalpamaṇḍapa, those very pavilions come to be. There, in every place, the gods and all other beings,
existing within the three qualities (guṇas), arrive for the great festival.
Therefore, the worship of the pavilion indeed bestows the fruit of all worship;
through the honoring of the pavilion, all the gods and others certainly become pleased.
The temple shall become auspicious, and heaven itself shall meet with auspiciousness.
All prosperity shall also converge through the thorough worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
When receiving guests and offering honors, the pavilion is considered to be at the forefront;
it brings peace to the mind and bestows tranquility upon this person.
The auspicious Maṇḍapa always bestows the nectar of buttermilk;
he gives curd-whey and also causes the performance of fire-sacrifices.
That Maṇḍapa always brings about supreme prosperity rooted in that.

O Rādhā, for a householder, the fire-sacrifice (havana) is always considered to grant satisfaction and happiness to all the gods; it is declared to be the destroyer of sins, the bestower of all enjoyments, and the increaser of all longevity. (71–72)
It is considered bestower of all health and the liberator from all debts;
the auspicious Sarvatobhadra diagram is also installed in the pavilion.
Its fruit is the destruction of afflictions caused by the planets and the eradication of sin.
It bestows gold, silver, and utensils, as well as houses;
it grants supreme merit and prosperity, providing beds and furnishings,
as well as vessels, ornaments, umbrellas, and chowries.
This great and auspicious circle of omens (*bhadramaṇḍala*) bestows royal prosperity, sovereignty, and power, as well as welfare;
it is the supreme giver of merit among meritorious things and is itself a performer of merit. (76)
The Bhadramaṇḍala is indeed the supreme among heavens and the bestower of heaven;
it is [the fruit] of liberation, of devotion, of dharma, and of sacrifice, as well as of all meritorious works (iṣṭāpūrta) and the planting of trees. || 77-78 ||
The auspicious Maṇḍala bestows indeed all merit from the giving of a daughter, as well as from the giving of a son, and from all religious duties.
It likewise bestows merit upon yogas and merit upon services.

The auspicious maṇḍala bestows merit for deeds performed for the benefit of others. By worshipping the auspicious maṇḍala, a maiden shall always behold what is auspicious, a husband shall always behold what is auspicious, and the family shall also behold what is auspicious. (2.279.80–81)
A maiden obtains good fortune, and a man attains the status of a householder;
through the worship of Bhadra, she becomes a virtuous woman endowed with a husband and sons.
Through the worship of Bhadra, there shall be no separation between wife and husband.
This indeed wards off obstacles and fulfills all prosperities.
Wherever Kṛṣṇa is worshipped, there the deities, the sages, the attendants, the incarnations, the planetary spirits, and others are likewise worshipped. (83–84)
Wherein the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) are worshipped, as well as other household protectors;
where male lords (īśvaras) and female goddesses (īśvarīs), such as Śāradā and others, are worshipped;
and wherein the Ekādaśīs and the great powers (suśaktis) such as Rādhā and others are fully honored.
The divine lineages are worshipped, as is the auspicious Bhadramaṇḍala.
Therefore, O Rādhikā, in that pavilion the Bhadramaṇḍala must be worshipped according to the prescribed ritual, and likewise Hari is to be worshipped. (86–87)
In whatever engagement with ritual action, in a great festival or a joyful celebration,
at a wedding, during the procession for the bridegroom, in the giving away of a daughter, at a site sacred to a virtuous woman,
in the bestowal of the Veda, the imparting of mantras, the conferring of initiation, or in the observance of vows and the like— (88) [one should perform these acts].
Hari should always be worshipped during a great gift-giving ceremony and on one's birthday.
Indeed, the worship of the Supreme Lord bestows the fruit of all worship;
it grants the fulfillment of all intentions and completely satisfies every desire.
The worship of Śrī Hari at the beginning [of any rite] always bestows the fruit of all sacrifices and fulfills every duty; it is rich with the fruits of all undertakings.
Likewise, the worship of Lakṣmī at the commencement of any task should be performed, as it bestows happiness.
This [worship] bestows prosperity, as well as peace and good fortune;
it destroys misfortune and eliminates suffering and poverty. Indeed, through the full worship of Lakṣmī, even meanness shall be destroyed.
"Through the initial worship of Lakṣmī, the jewel of a daughter, the jewel of a bridegroom, and whatever jewels of wealth there may be shall become free from obstacles.
Thus, O Rādhikā, has the fruit been declared, since you have asked about it."
Abundance of happiness will surely arise from worship wherever it may be.
(95) Generally, people possess a latent desire for physical pleasure;
through the aforementioned forms of worship, their abundance of happiness increases. (96)
By reading or even by hearing this chapter on the fruit,
that same fruit is obtained which arises from worship as well as from giving.
In the three worlds, there exists no gift equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
That which is the support of all phenomena and the expansion of the lineage;
that upon which the entire world rests and which all creation depends;
without which dissolution is proclaimed, and without which emptiness is considered [to exist]. //98-99//

Just as there is no state of Indrahood without women, so too there is no kingdom for the self without a woman; the self is made a king by her. Therefore, O Rādhā, a woman is indeed taken in marriage by a man.
Then the excellent king indeed finds his firm foundation through a woman.
Even without a kingdom, the excellent king remains an excellent man, for his beloved wife becomes his queen;
thus, the kingdom shall be established here upon the prince, the excellent king.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the great king who both bestows and receives gifts, will appear for two days;
He shall be the husband of my son and of Śambhu’s daughter.

"O Rādhikā! Joy arises in you upon hearing this, and it arises in me as well upon speaking it. Having said this, the supreme Lord, the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa, adorned his own abode with that small pavilion. 104–105.

Thus, in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, [this concludes the account] of the worship of the ruby pillar, the pinnacle-vase, Gaṇeśa, the Mothers, Vāstu, Viṣṇu, the family deity, and the *Sarvatobhadra* diagram within the pavilion.

The two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Declaration of Fruits," from the second section of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga). Chapter 279.
Chapter 280 [Author:
Chapter 281 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā! Hear also of another auspicious and great pavilion.
The one called Maṇḍapa is endowed with great power and assumes its own form.
It is ten yojanas wide and ten yojanas long.
Extending upwards for one *yojana*, it consists of fifty-six stories.
(2) There, golden jars numbering ten thousand—equipped with banners and flags and resembling a thousand suns—shine resplendently. (3)
In the center, hundreds of jars shine one above the other;
or rather, are the planets and stars shining like jars?
And there shines a divine golden canopy.
Just as the sky of consciousness is merged with the great physical sky,
so too ten thousand peaks shine forth in the supreme ether.
Like clouds at the waist, they enter the pavilion within and proceed, stainless.
On each level, there stand [deities] equal to a thousand moons—
full, white, and white-shining, consisting of the nature of the imperishable. Their moonlight flows into the inner chambers within the pavilions.
All the walls are made of gold, and all are suffused with the radiance of Brahman (8).
They flow with the nectar of Brahman and rain down great bliss. The circular canopy consists of ten thousand Vaikuṇṭhas (9).
In the upper portion of the pavilion, within the inner sanctum, auspiciousness is indeed beheld;
in the center are jeweled pillars possessing the luster of the moon,
while around the peak-structure, pearls truly shine forth.
Kalpavallīs, kalpavṛkṣas, and likewise cintāmaṇis—
fulfilling every desire— shine upon the capitals of the pillars.
Upon the pillars, streams of ghee and streams of curd flow on all sides.
Rivers of honey, rivers of water, and rivers of drink flow forth;
and channels for autumnal drinking and streams of nectar flow as well.
There are also channels of ambrosia, channels of fresh butter, and ponds of the essence of milk.
Streams of nectar dwell within the interior of the pillars and flow forth;
rivers that carry the essences of various foods and drinks for the inhabitants of those respective abodes stand there on all sides at the archways.

There, wish-fulfilling vines were fashioned, as well as male and female slaves who grant all desires; all these were designed to provide every object of sensual enjoyment. All the archways, moreover, were adorned with variegated colors.
There, in that pavilion, they were prepared by the yogi known as Maṇḍapa:
a water reservoir, bathing halls, and even the requisites for bathing; these shone like Indra’s hall and were endowed with fragrant substances. (17–18)
The halls are provided with ointments, soot, musk, sandalwood, and other such substances, as well as fragrant essences and juices;
and there are dining halls and drinking saloons for the inhabitants of those respective abodes. (19)

In each of those abodes, dining halls are fashioned like wish-fulfilling creepers and jewels; they yield fruits according to one's resolve, bestow whatever is desired, and abound with the delights of various enjoyments. (2.280.20–21)
Equipped with various vessels, utensils, seats, and implements,
there were beds, gardens, halls, and rest-houses,
as well as celestial couches and divine lamps.
Adorned with the splendor of divine coverings and possessing divine veils;
suited for divine attire and wearing divine garments; consisting of substances for divine play and producing a divine state of being. || 23–24 ||
In that pavilion, the garments are divinely fragrant, they provide divine pleasure, and they indeed bestow divine bliss—
whether one remembers them while eating, drinking, sleeping, or even during sexual union. ||25||
For all the couples, everything divine was present.
Wondrous gambling halls and auspicious performance halls,
complete with every necessary implement, shone forth within the pavilion.
There were various theaters for drama and separate wrestling arenas;
likewise, there were dance halls, costume rooms, and dressing areas.
There were indeed endless galleries for visual spectacles and mechanical chambers for auditory performances.
There were pleasant dwellings for news, as well as fragrant chambers;
delightful hermitages for touch, various abodes for taste,
and beautiful halls for song were all present there in that pavilion.
The five elements, the principles, and the objects— both gross and subtle—
as well as the principles that are effects and causes, were fashioned within the pavilion.
There, the Brahma-lakes were created, and indeed the Virajā and other lakes were fashioned.
And rivers of nectar were created in various places, as were ponds;
there were also wonderful gardens filled with fruits and flowers,
and groves of sugarcane juice and stalks within those pavilions.
In the pavilion, there indeed shine sweet and sour juices, betel nuts, areca nuts, and cloves; portions of cardamom, cinnamon, and other delicacies are present.
Within that pavilion, there are dwellings for each and every one of those [guests].
In that pavilion, there were even miniature temples for their various weapons; likewise,
the toys of those various young girls and the play-grounds of the children shone brightly within the pavilion.
Royal highways, carriage roads, squares, and balconies,
as well as great courtyards and pleasure gardens, shine forth within the pavilion.
Beloved mansions, moon-chambers, and windows are situated on all sides.
There were door-frames both short and long;
some were shaped like umbrellas, gentle, and situated like groves.
These door-frames, with their upper coverings, shone there in that pavilion.
Parrots and cranes, as well as peacocks and pheasants;
swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, as well as *garuḍas* and vultures;
hawks, divine pigeons, ruddy geese, and partridges.
Blue-throated birds, cātaka birds, divine pigeons,
and likewise other such birds, all fresh and beautiful to behold, were perched upon the archways on every side, shining brightly and filled with joy.
Cuckoos warble and others coo;
they dwell upon the tops of pillars and in the sightlines.
Elephants, śarabhas, lions, maned beasts, and cows [are present].
There were dvīpas, tigers, nāra-dvīpas, bears, and likewise gavayas;
gaṇḍakas, deer, rhinoceroses, and variegated animals bearing horns and manes; reṇḍakas, rabbits, and even white horses of various breeds.
Bulls, camels, crocodiles, tortoises,
as well as *timiṃgila* fish and large fish, shine forth on all sides,
adorned with jewels, diamonds, pearls, and various precious gems.
Then, in the sky above every dwelling, the central regions shone forth;
there were garlands, clusters of flowers, and divine, highly fragrant wreaths.
Radiant with splendor, they gleamed, and here and there stood Kaustubha jewels.
Then divine women, sovereigns, celestial beings, and the most excellent maidens—
virtuous and true— shone forth, stationed at the entrances of the gates;
they were accompanied by moon-chambers and palaces that moved at will.
In the pavilion, hundreds of thousands of creepers from the garden groves shine forth, reaching toward the sky; even the clusters of flowers become pillars,
and the abodes of lotuses perfume the pavilion with their fragrance.
Filling the air with cool breezes carrying a gentle fragrance,
they come from the forest paths into every house and pavilion.
There is no deficiency in the objects of enjoyment, whether in dress, ornaments, garments, or the self.
In this pavilion and in every house, there are heaps of sweet foods,
indeed suitable for the enjoyment of the inhabitants of those various abodes;
there are portions of mirrors and looking-glasses, as well as liquids that reflect images.
Indeed, the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* shine forth in the pavilion;
there are infinite male and female servants,
and even crores of maidens who bestow the bliss of nectar, all present in the pavilion at that time.
O Rādhikā! Listen to the wonderful novelty that was there:
in every house, a single jewel was placed upon the threshold, through which the entire pavilion could be seen clearly. (56–57)
All the sections of the pavilion, all those who preside over the pavilion, and all the honored guests [gathered] during the day, but certainly not at night.
O Rādhikā! What more need I say? There are women as numerous as the Arbuda mountains who are your equals.
Other maidservants and attendants were present there.
Even though I was situated in Goloka, upon remembering and seeing this, I fell into a state of delusion; your playful charm appears as if it were empty in my presence.
In various places, Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha also exist;
there, a higher realm has been established for the inhabitants of Akṣaradhāma,
and below that, for all the inhabitants of Goloka from all the abodes.
Below that was established the auspicious and glorious Vāsudeva-sthala;
below that was established the beautiful and supremely auspicious Vaikuṇṭha;
and below that was established the divine, auspicious, and unmanifest (avyākṛta) region.
Then the nectar was made below, and from that the terrestrial ground was formed;
then the realm of Hiraṇyagarbha and the realm of Vairāja were indeed established beneath it. Furthermore, the plane of Mahāmāyā and likewise the plane of Sadāśiva were created.
The Vaiṣṇava realm has been established, and Vaikuṇṭha is the second;
then the Brāhma, Raudra, Śaiva, and Saiddha abodes, situated below those;
and further below those are the dwellings of the Īśvaras and the Ṛṣis.
And [the abodes] of the ancestors (pitṛs) are below those, as well as those of the gods (surās);
the stations of the thirty-three deities are below even those;
and the abodes of the humans dwelling in Bhuvarloka are below even those.
[He is the refuge] of the devotees dwelling in the netherworlds (atala) and below, of the sons of Diti,
of the Danujas, of the Nagas, of the aquatic creatures, and likewise of the beings of the earth;
[he is the refuge] of all wild creatures who assume forms at will.
The abodes of the wish-fulfilling cows, the multitudes of stationary beings, as well as of the self-souls, the holy fords, the mountains, and so forth,
were established even below within the pavilion by the liberated one named Maṇḍapa in his own pavilion.

Indeed, by the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, new sacrificial halls, divine temples, and halls for chanting were established; likewise, halls for the Vedas, halls for medicine, and halls for piercing [the body] were constructed. (71–72)
Rows of marketplaces and cooking halls were likewise constructed;
many pleasure-grove halls were also built down upon the earth.
Staircases made of all kinds of jewels were fashioned in various designs.

There were variegated ladders, as flickering as one’s own volitions; there were houses for ascending and descending, provided with chains according to one’s will, and attendants who manifested whatever was imagined, stationed here and there. (74–75)

Carriers were appointed for those who were weary to relieve their fatigue; and in the Brahma-maṇḍapa, there was equal prosperity for the king, the pauper, and Lord Hari. There were also dwellings for holy men, ascetics, and celibate students.
Auspicious rites were performed for the virtuous, faithful, and liberated women;
forest-dwellings were established within the pavilion, as were hermitage residences;
and likewise, garlands were prepared for the bards, panegyrists, and minstrels.
Likewise, abodes were constructed for those who play musical instruments, for panegyrists, and for Vedic scholars;
and similarly, abodes were made for all branches of knowledge and for the fulfillment of all desires.
Abodes were also made for servants, for the elephants of the quarters, and for serpents.
And likewise, dwellings were made for the remaining tortoises who were without food,
as well as for the great seers, ascetics, devotees, and Brahman-yogins,
and for those who had renounced the world and the avadhūtas. (2.280.80–81)
For the subjects of diverse castes, dwelling in various lands, and possessed of different natures, residences were established in the pavilion;
dwellings for those requiring protection from cold, heat, and other elements were constructed according to their needs. (82)
Dwellings have been made according to need for those whose forms are gross and subtle;
dwellings have been made according to need for those whose forms are divine and non-divine;
and dwellings have been made according to their bodies for those who are illusory and those who are beyond illusion. (83–84)
Great highways for the celestial chariots were constructed in the pavilion and in the sky; following the pattern of staircases, even pathways for the feet were fashioned.
Furthermore, the names of the worlds and the designations of the inhabitants were likewise established.
In each house there, natural inscriptions consisting of syllables were made;
just as they are in the Veda, so too were names assigned here in the pavilion.
There were woolen coverings and the like, as well as soft silken cloths.
Indeed, beautiful footstools made of gold and silver were fashioned there,
as were splendid lion-thrones in the pavilion;
and there were also garments of silk and fabrics made of fine cotton.
All syllables are deposited here and there.
Whatever foods there are—whether chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked; all those things that are to be drunk or tasted, and whatever is cooked by fire. (2.280.90)
All forest-grown fruits, as well as those that have been roasted; uncooked flour-dusts and whatever betel-leaves there may be;
all intoxicants, and all cooked foods in every way.
All preparations of meat-soups, those made with leaf-vegetables,
the delightful preparations of alkaline decoctions, those cooked in ghee,
all varieties of milk-rice, and likewise those prepared with sugar. (6, 93)
All kinds of sugarcane products prepared by confectioners,
as well as fried snacks and soups, were placed in the kitchen;
likewise, all varieties of desired foods and various kinds of honey were provided.
All the Gundrapāka fruits were placed in the storehouse of food.
O Rādhikā! What more need be said? That which was displayed in the pavilion is superior even to what exists in the world of Brahmā and superior to that which exists in the world of Śiva. 95–96.
Whatever is most excellent in the world of truth (Satyaloka), what is most excellent in the world of humans,
and what is most excellent in the netherworld (Pātāla) and the celestial realms— that which is named Ratna—
all that was deposited there in the pavilion in the form of the pavilion itself.
Long ponds were laid out there, as well as beautiful lakes;
pathways of light were established, filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss;
and there were sections for the discourses of the learned, as well as halls for exposition.
All those assembly halls throughout the creations that are renowned and esteemed by the inhabitants have been displayed here within this pavilion, in the very form of the pavilion itself.
O Rādhā, I have seen an even greater wonder than that!
In every chamber, however, there was a beautiful gem placed upon the threshold (101),
through which the entire pavilion could be seen clearly;
and in that very pavilion, I beheld yet another auspicious gem (102).
There, I beheld the threefold creation consisting of the insentient and the sentient; I saw all abodes, which are the domains of the Lord of All.
I also beheld all the worlds of living beings in their entirety.
Whatever indeed has been seen by me, nothing remains to be seen. There is a jewel on the threshold, and there is a pavilion made of jewels;
everything is contained therein, for such is this very variety.

That great wonder—the vision of everything—is indeed not found in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in other abodes; it exists only in one's own home. For this very reason, even those liberated in the imperishable realm (akṣara-muktas) become truly omniscient.
"All those who see with their own eyes perceive the jewel within the jewel.
"O Rādhā! I have shown this to you; why do you not remember it now?
Thus, O Rādhā, was described the inspection of the pavilion.
Even upon hearing it, one may attain divinity, the desire for knowledge, the desire for liberation,
liberation itself, the state of Brahman, and even fitness for dwelling in Brahman.
This [teaching] of the Supreme Self must not be held by one of small intellect.
"The nature of the pavilion is indeed auspicious and composed of all abodes.

(2.280.110) Thus ends the two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "Description of the Divinity of the Great Pavilion Constructed by the Great Liberated Souls," in the second section, the Tretā-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 282 → Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, when the pavilion had thus come into being, illuminating all the world,
the splendors of the sun turned away from the sky and from the heavens.
The very splendors of the pavilion brought about the day in Saurāṣṭra.
Then the night departed for another region, its radiance having been withdrawn.
But the perception of night by the people dwelling in the imperishable field was inferred from the rays of light streaming forth from the pavilions. (2–3)
When that universal vision within the jewel— which belongs to those situated inside the pavilion—
does not arise at all, then it is like the inference of night.
And when, within the jewel, the creations shine forth in the jewel...
Then the light of day arose for those dwelling within the pavilion. (5) When such a thing has occurred in a mere pavilion, what wonder is there in the house of Hari?
Everything indeed is possible for Him; this pavilion is but a small thing. (6)
Thus, during the construction of the pavilion, various divine musical instruments as well as worldly musical instruments were sounded therefrom.
And people arrived from all directions to behold that pavilion.
The gods, indeed, having assumed the forms of swans, came through the sky and departed again.
(8) Then the father of the Blessed One summoned Lomaśa and the great sage Nārada and drew the *kuṅkumapatrī* (the saffron-leaf diagram). (9)
At that very moment, after one and a half ghaṭīs following sunrise, he questioned the self-luminous Lord. Then,
having observed the muhūrta of the first lunar day (pratipad), those three spoke.
"The time that brings victory over all is now present, auspicious and favorable. The propitious moment has arrived; let him write the letter.
Having spoken thus, those eminent brahmins [recited] the mantras of well-being and auspiciousness. (11–12)
Eagerly, they all worshipped the hymns contained within the Ṛgveda, which are beautiful and auspicious in every way,
as well as the leaf, the pen, the vessel for liquid, the tablet,
and the red liquid. (13)
They performed the worship of Gaṇeśa with incense, lamps, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
(14) They likewise performed the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu, as well as the worship of Gopāla; and at that time, they indeed performed the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa. (15)
Bālakṛṣṇa, together with his father, also honored them;
the sages, the brahmins, and others were likewise respected and seated upon the offered seats.
Those venerable groups sat down, while the women sang songs.

Śrī Mahāviṣṇu Gopālakṛṣṇaka, his father, having bowed to the gods, sages, and elders, and having remembered Śrī Puruṣottama, wrote this saffron leaf-letter for the purpose of invitation, which provides awakening through yoga. (17–18)
For the Lord is indeed the sovereign of the glorious city of Brahmapura, the master of all incarnations;
he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Śrī Vāsudeva,
Śiva, Śrī Viṣṇu, the elder brother of Nara, and Nārāyaṇa residing on the White Island (Dhavaladvīpa).
May Hari, who remains as the Residue, and Gaṇeśvara grant us auspiciousness. May the Goddess,
who is identical in form to the glorious Brahman, the sovereign of all incarnations—
Śrī Rādhā, Nārāyaṇī, Hariṇī, Śrīvāsudevī, and Śivā— grant us auspiciousness.
May Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Ramā, and Nārāyaṇī who dwells on the White Island (Dhavaladvīpa),

as well as Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī, and those residing in heaven, bestow auspiciousness upon us. May the Beloved of Śrī, Puruṣottama, the manifestations of power (vibhava), the emanations (vyūha), and the lords of the abodes (dhāmādhipa) [grant us blessings].

May Lakṣmī and the Lords, the Pitṛs and the Ṛṣis, the gods and their wives, the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Aśvins, the guardians of the quarters, the Rudras, and the lords of the three classes of gods— may they all extend this auspicious blessing, born of the domestic dharma of the married couple. ॥21॥
May there be supreme auspiciousness for Lakṣmī, the daughter of the illustrious Śrīnidhi Śaṅkara— who is himself worshipped by the wise as the Lord of the holy city of Kāśī—
through my son, the venerable Bālakṛṣṇa, in the city of Kāśī.
On the night of the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the son [Viṣṇu] departed from the field of Akṣara.
Indeed, in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he resides upon the lotus-seat of the four-faced Creator (Vidhi);
and likewise on the earthly realm (bhūloka), in the region to the south of Meru, upon the navel of the Unborn (Ajā).
May they indeed come quickly, accompanied by their own kin, to me, Gopālakṛṣṇa, who am staying in the famous city known as Kuṅkumavāpikā in Surāṣṭra.
Today, on this first day, is the time for the pavilion and for the consumption of betel-leaf.
Tomorrow there will be the ceremonial kneading of fine flour upon the body of the illustrious son;
on the third day, the worship of the deities and the procession toward Kāśī;
and on the fourth, the taking of the hand in marriage—therefore, please illuminate these events, I entreat you. (24)
Those indeed who belong to the creation of Brahmā, the imperishable beings dwelling in the abodes and so forth;
those who belong to the creation of Īśvara, including the insentient and those situated within the eight coverings;
and those who belong to the creation of Jīva—the various worlds and the lords of the worlds.
"Let the kings, their own subjects, friends, and kinsmen come—
each endowed with his own sovereignty, accompanied by his own servants, joined by all his followers,
together with his own divine attendants, and accompanied by his wives, sons, and daughters."
Accompanied by their respective friends, joined by those of measured age, and including both the young and the old—
let these bringers of splendor surely come here on all sides for the auspicious occasion of my son’s marriage.
Also present are the eminent Śrī Bhagavān, his elder brother, and the radiant Śuka.
O sinless one, you are our beloved kinsman named Śrīmad Vallabha, and all your followers are likewise our kinsmen;
indeed, so too are all other members of your family. We offer this request to everyone:
may we certainly have the sight of you here. || 27 ||

Those liberated ones who have attained the state of Brahman and reached the abodes of the Lord of Śrī, those attendants of the Lord of the World who have gone to the realms of Īśa, Īśāna, and others, and who possess great sovereignty and are liberated;
those esteemed by Brahmā and others, the perfected beings (*siddhapuruṣas*), and those who are virtuous and saintly— [all these are present].
"May they bring auspiciousness and eternal well-being, full of great blessings, to the couple.
Thus, O Rādhikā, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa wrote there and dispatched the saffron-smeared letter throughout all of creation.

Having honored her with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, and other offerings, he dispatched the sages Nārada and others to the spheres of the universe, to the abodes of the imperishable liberated ones, and to the worlds of the Lord. (2.281.30)
Having taken that [liṅga] which was wrapped in a leaf-cup, bound with a cord,
joined with a *tulasī* leaf, and was the likeness of ten million times ten million [Brahmās],
they all departed at the speed of thought, having been thus commanded. (31–32)
Having received saffron leaves, they arrived with due honor;
O Rādhā! then, in that pavilion during the festival, Gopāla Kṛṣṇa gave them milk to drink, sweet food, and betel leaf.
To the assembled kings, devoted brahmins, the people, and the subjects;
to the merchants, the helpless, and even those who were great yet poor;
to the venerable, the worshipful, and the worthy of salutation—namely the vaiśyas, the male servants, and the female servants. (34–35)
To the servants, the laborers, the local residents, the pilgrims, the guests, the dignitaries, and those who had arrived by chance—
[he offered] drink, betel nut, milk, milk-rice, and sweet food. (36)
Gopālakṛṣṇaka gave fruits, water, and even leaves.
There, various musical instruments and wind-instruments were played,
and songs were sung by all the women in the pavilion.
O Rādhā! During that festival there—the festival of betel leaves—all people from Saurāṣṭra and every single city arrive and depart after having obtained betel leaves and other such gifts. || 39 ||
O beloved, betel-leaf offerings were given there constantly.
Even at midday, rows were formed for the purpose of eating,
and thousands of people arrived there to behold the pavilion.
All of them— the dignitaries residing in the city as well as those who had arrived from various countries— took their meals in the house of Śrī Hari.
Having offered praises to Bālakṛṣṇa and received a most gracious welcome, they then [partook of the feast].
Having partaken of the meals, they attained supreme rest.
The Brahmins, others besides them, the servants and those of the master’s lineage, the wretched, the helpless, and the beggars all took their food. (43–44)
They partook of sweet foods, milk-rice, milks, and various edibles—
salty and delicious— to their complete satisfaction. Then, having received betel leaves and areca nuts, they indeed enjoyed them.

Having partaken of the guest-offerings (āgantuka-bhojana), they depart for their own abodes. Those who are honored today at the ancestral rite (paitrya)—whether residing in one's own country, in foreign lands, among different peoples, or in different worlds—[all partake]. (46–47)
Yogis, swift as thought, arrive there at that festival;
in the pavilion, they partake of the *madhuparka* offerings with devotion.
Having likewise received betel and beheld the pavilion, [they remain].
Having honored Bālakṛṣṇa and taken the foods,
they gathered with the great dignitaries; then, having offered them seats,
they departed while the unsurpassed sounds of musical instruments arose unceasingly.
Songs of young maidens resounded everywhere:
"Give! Give! and "Eat! Eat!
Even the cries of "Accept this hospitality! did not cease.

From the path of the earth, from the path of the wind, from the earth, and from the sky, the cowherds and servants of Kṛṣṇa arrived in aerial chariots and other vehicles swift as thought; they were led into the center of the great pavilion by the cowherd-servants of Kṛṣṇa. || 52-53 ||
And they indeed cause them to dwell in houses prepared according to their needs;
and the attendants stand constantly before them for the sake of welcoming them.
At that time, maidens, male and female servants, and skilled attendants serve them.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā!

until evening there was the giving of drinks, the offering of betel leaves and other items, the serving of food, and the exchange of conversation; thereafter followed the twilight worship and the waving of lights before Hari.
Then, during the night, a great festival was held.
Singers accompanied by instrumentalists sang in accordance with rhythm and measure;
at that time, female singers skilled in the Gandharva arts also sang songs.
Well-dressed and fond of flowers, the dancing women perform their dances;
the Apsarases of Brahma’s lake sing songs,
and likewise the Nṛsarasas sing songs accompanied by dance.
The maidens, of various heights and having dispelled their fatigue through diverse gestures,
displayed their postures by stretching out their slender bodies.
Thus, O Rādhikā, when this had occurred, they then arrived for the sake of the *rāsa* dance.
In the middle of the performance pavilion, those maidens performed the *rāsa* dance.
(6.1) All of them were identically attired, possessing equal luster and wearing identical garments;
with uniform ornaments and identical moods, they indeed danced the *rāsa* within the pavilion. (6.2)
The instrumentalists were indeed playing their instruments, and likewise the singers were singing;
meanwhile, two dancing women in the midst were performing a dance.
Others sang and whirled about in the manner of a spinning wheel.
They take delight in the circle with clapping of hands, the stamping of feet, and heroic strides;
with their hind legs, with bent legs, and with crooked bodies;
and also with curved necks and crooked eyes. (64–65)
When the *rāsa* dance had thus been performed, the wrestlers subsequently arrived there;
they were powerful, mountain-like, robust, and resounded with their shouts.
By nature restless, they caused laughter by leaping upon each other's backs.
Then, in that circular arena, two by two they approached;
and in combat, they engaged in dragging and pulling away,
as well as tossing each other face-upward and throwing each other face-down onto the ground.
By throwing their own faces, by pulling at the master’s limbs and so forth,
by striking him on the back, and likewise by striking him on the thighs;
by hurling themselves forward with speed, and likewise by tossing themselves into the air.
With whirling movements, as well as with discharges and the exertion of their feet and arms;
with chest-to-chest grappling, they were intent on victory and defeat.
Others bore heavy loads, while some carried the weight of tusks upon their shoulders.
There were wrestlers who split stones with their chests, those who rode upon the backs of elephants, those who obstructed carts with their hands, and those who supported ten men on their shoulders;
in this way, the wrestlers displayed many such diverse feats.
Then the auspicious actors, wearing their stage costumes, arrived;
and both boys and girls performed the auspicious dressing rites for the drama of the incarnation of Bālakṛṣṇa exactly as it occurred.
They created something exceedingly beautiful, captivating, and enchanting;
it was like the arrival of Nārāyaṇa with Lakṣmī from Vaikuṇṭha,
and likewise the arrival of Śambhu’s exquisite dance upon the surface of the earth.
The penance of Lakṣmī, as well as the vision of the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa—
thus indeed did they perform that drama based on the ancient events of Hari.
When the performance on the stage had concluded, the learned scholars arrived there.
Charioteers, panegyrists, bards, and poets likewise recited entirely new poems before the assembly;
they also recounted the virtues of Nārāyaṇa and his ancient deeds.
And they spoke of the virtues of Lakṣmī, the destroyer of suffering, as well as those of Satyā and Śiva;
likewise of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, Kaṃbharā, and Hari.
Then there were delightful discourses concerning those matters established in the Saṃhitās. (2.281.80)
Then, at midnight, the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa took place with the offering of drinks and other gifts,
as well as garments, clothes, and ornaments. At that time,
there were indeed offerings of betel leaves, foods, and sweet beverages.
And Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa gave [gifts] to all the limbs [of the body].
Whether one was a child, or intoxicated, or distressed, none were left out;
everyone received food, betel-leaf, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 82–83 ||
The Lord’s father gave excellent rewards to the performers and the artists who held the prize vessels:
gold, silver, gems, jewels, pearls, and diamonds.
The father of Hari gave him priceless necklaces, ornaments, and even divine garments; he also gave neck-garlands, golden bracelets for the forearms, rings, and other articles of use. (85–86)
The spectators were satisfied, as were those who added beauty to the stage;
the performers, though laboring, were satisfied, being masters of their artistic skills. Displaying their respective sciences and arts, they attained satisfaction through wealth.
Exclaiming, "Blessed! Blessed! they bowed down to Kṛṣṇa and the cowherd [Nanda].
They prostrated before their father, as did the women skilled in the arts, the dancers, and the singers, who offered garments, ornaments, and fine clothes.
Having received rewards consisting of garlands of gems and pearls, diamonds,
silken garments, and bodices made of gold thread,
they attained great satisfaction upon obtaining these articles of adornment.
Having drunk, eaten, and offered their salutations, they then departed for their respective dwellings.
The dignitaries went to their great pavilions and residences; the city-dwellers went to their own homes, and the great sages to their huts.
The virtuous ones went to their own hermitages, and the servants returned to their respective homes.
Then Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, having partaken of a sattvic meal himself,
fed his household members, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the others.
Having transformed his priceless attire and assumed an ordinary dress,
he went to his own abode for the sake of rest and fell asleep.
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also attained the yogic sleep.
The musicians also ceased their playing, and having taken their meals,
they returned to their own dwellings, even as they fell asleep.
The guardians of the field, Śaṅkara and the others, as well as the hosts of deities, likewise finished their meal.

Having enjoyed their respective mansions, they found rest during the night. The confectioners, the servants, the tax-collectors, and the laborers, having finished their meals, slept in their own places. (97–98)
Then at night, O Rādhikā! those guards and protectors who roam by night remain awake and perform inspections of the precincts;
armed and with their mounts and so forth, they wander about in such a manner. (99)
"Vigilant, they protect the dwellings of those who sleep.
Thus, O Rādhikā, that radiant night passed away;
then morning dawned, filled once more with all manner of divine auspiciousness.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Sending the Saffron Letter to All Creations after Writing It, the Great Festival of Betel Leaves, Areca Nuts, and Other Items; the Night Festivals of Singing, Dancing, Instrumental Music, Drama, Martial Arts, Poetic Recitals, Prizes, and Feasting; as well as Leisure and Sleep," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 281. [End of] Section 2 (*Tretā-yuga-santāna*) of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*.
