Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, then the glories [of the Lord] became fully awakened.
At dawn, the people were awakened by auspicious musical instruments, by the songs of *sūtas* and *māgadhas*,
by the recitations of bards, by the natural sounds of trumpets,
and by melodious hymns of praise.
At dawn, the people remained awake to the sound of musical instruments played for four *ghaṭikās* that evoked the memory of Brahmā, and to the resonant chants of Kṛṣṇa’s glories;
they were awakened by the songs of fortunate women and the hymns composed by maidens.
At dawn, the people stayed awake with the songs of singers;
at dawn, the people stayed awake on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake with the kīrtanas of the maṇḍalīs and with the sounds of hymns from the sacrificial altars.
At dawn, the people remained awake through their zeal, reflections, dispositions, acts of faith, virtuous impulses, and gentle endeavors; likewise,
through the inspirations of the Inner Controller and the weight of their feelings of love.
The people woke at dawn from the thundering of celestial chariots;
they woke at dawn from the sweet warbling of birds, from visions of Kṛṣṇa’s festival in their dreams, and from the songs of housewives. (7–8)
At dawn, the people remained awake amidst the sounds of milch cows and their calves, the playing of musical instruments, singing, and the proclamations of the arrival of the great festival,
as well as through the inspirations of merit and the restless movements of the senses. (9)
And with the intensity of their desire to know [the Lord], the people remained awake at dawn.
Having bathed in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and performed the twilight prayers and other rites,
they adorned themselves with beautiful ornaments and offered auspicious benedictions and other ceremonies at the gates.
They also fashioned colorful garlands by rubbing them with curd and powders,
and likewise placed multi-colored archways in the courtyards.
With eyes anointed with collyrium and their hair arranged in braided ornaments, they [prepared themselves].
Adorned with ornaments and radiant garments, the women sang auspicious songs.
The brahmins performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the worship of the pavilion;
they performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa. (13–14)
They performed the worship of their family deity, Puruṣottama,
as well as the worship of Śrī Śaṅkara and of Sūrya. Thereafter, they also carried out the worship of the deities of the Sarvatobhadra diagram.
Then they performed the worship of cows, the worship of maidens, the worship of the Mothers (Mātṛkās),
and the worship of Viṣṇu;
they offered the lustration ceremony (Nīrājana), excellent food offerings (Naivedya), and gifts such as priestly fees (Dakṣiṇā).
They performed the worship of the Brahmins as well as the worship of turmeric;
the women, having ground it, prepared knots of turmeric paste.
[They also used] sandalwood, sesame paste, musk, and saffron.
And eager, they mixed in excellent fragrant oil.
Then, for the sake of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa’s bath,
women adorned with the splendor of good fortune brought water from the sun and water from sacred pilgrimage sites.
The maidens brought auspicious water in golden jars;
indeed, they carried the water accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and songs.
Having placed the deity of the waters upon a golden seat, they worshipped her.
Having placed the five jewels as well as fragrant substances [therein],
and having invoked the gods, the oceans, the sacred fords (tīrthas), and nectar—
having also invoked the ambrosia (sudhā) upon the cloth— they bathed Acyuta.
Then the women massage his radiant body in its entirety—
his form possessing the splendor of ten million suns, his auspicious face like ten million moons,
his limbs like ten million flashes of lightning, and which is the abode of ten million fragrances. (24)
He bears the form of the ultimate limit (koṭi) and is distinguished by the essence of that limit;
he is the treasury of all excellent qualities and the repository of all loveliness.
He is the vessel of all beauty and the locus of all desirable attributes.
They thoroughly massaged Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord who bestows all prosperity—
the removers of impurity for the stainless one—
with oils, fragrant essences, and aromatic substances that cleanse away dirt. (27)
Eagerly, they bathed [the image] with *āmalaka* fruits, sesame pastes, brilliantly shining alkaline substances,
soft unctuous materials such as fresh butter, nourishing mud-pastes, and fragrant sandalwood and other perfumes. (28–29)
Then the barber performed the shaving as was appropriate;
thereafter, this Lord bathed himself with honey, then with water mixed with sugar,
and also with milk, ghee, and curd.
Then he bathed again with honey, and also with sugar;
then with alkaline substances, and thereafter with fragrant pastes.
Then he bathed with oils, musk, sandalwood, and saffron.
By rubbing himself with flour paste, Campaka became clean;
having thus performed his bath with flour paste, he put on his garments— namely,
all his ornaments and clothes, as well as his forehead mark and the moon-shaped tilaka.
Then the Lord himself sat down upon the golden throne.
At that time, people came for the purpose of applying the *tilaka* and for the worship of Hari;
likewise, women, great lords of the earth, and others also arrived. (34–35)
Thus was the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, accompanied by Piṣṭika, worshipped.
Indeed, a sweet fragrance issued forth from his body in every direction.
Consequently, even from afar, the entire region of Saurāṣṭra became perfumed with that fragrance.
Then those great-souled ones arrived by means of aerial chariots from all directions, from every land, and from all the worlds. Śaṅkara, Kṣetrapāla, and the great sage Nārada also came. (37–38)
The Blessed One, as well as Bhāvayicāpi, Śuka who follows him,
the self-luminous Blessed One, Santuṣṭika and the others,
and all those dear to Brahmā, eagerly offered their welcome. (39)
Meals are served, and indeed drinks of milk as well;
all kinds of foods, both solid and soft, are distributed from the kitchen.
Rows are even formed by the inhabitants of all the worlds.
They enjoy many kinds of sweet foods with feelings of affection;
they lick all things to be licked and sucked, and even savor various flavors.
They drink milk-based preparations and the like, and they eat foods roasted in alkaline ash.
They relish curds and the like, as well as fresh butter and clarified butter;
they eat cakes, balls of food, and fried pastries;
and with deep devotion, they drink nectars that possess the flavor of ambrosia. (583–584)
They secretly eat leafy vegetables, various kinds of rice, fragrant boiled grains, blossoming *vaṭī* cakes, and desired *prapolikā* sweets;
they consume *pūpa*, *apūpa*, *laḍḍu*, *khājaka*, and *mohanasthala* cakes.
At that time, people consume many unwholesome as well as desirable foods.
Rivers of clarified butter, rivers of curd, and rivers of honey flow there;
those with digestive power drink them, and those who enjoy such pleasures partake of them.
For those dwelling in each respective abode, all things appropriate to them are indeed provided here by the celestial architects, such as Lakṣmī and others,
using vessels of desire and the like, as well as inexhaustible vessels and so forth.
Betel leaves are given to them, along with mouth-cleansers to be chewed;
likewise, auspicious water for drinking and powder that purifies the mouth are provided.
Then the honored guests proceed to their residence quarters.
Thus, O Rādhikā, a magnificent festival then takes place;
indeed, millions of honored guests arrive there from all directions—both those liberated souls who have reached the abode of Brahmā and those residing in other realms. (51)
And the liberated ones dwelling in all abodes gathered there;
other liberated ones, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, and likewise the beloveds of Brahmā arrived.
The Īśvaras and the Īśvarīs also arrived, full of eager anticipation.
The incarnations and their consorts arrived there with eager anticipation;
the lords of lords and the goddesses of lords arrived in great numbers.
Those liberated souls who dwell in the realm of Māyā and their liberated consorts also arrived.
Those liberated from the eight enclosures, and others who were likewise liberated, arrived there.
The virtuous ones who had reached Satyaloka, the great ṛṣis, the holy men devoted to celibacy, and the perfected beings (siddhas) all assembled there.
The ancestors, sages, elders, and perfected beings (siddhas) arrived;
truthful, virtuous, and dispassionate goddesses arrived there.
The Mothers, yoginīs, noble women, and yogins also arrived.
The gods, the lords of the gods, and the deities also assembled;

those dwelling in Dhruva, those residing in the world of the stars, those inhabiting the planets, those situated in the intermediate space, and those dwelling in the circles of the sages [all came]. (58–59)
The gods who dwell in the sun and the moon arrived there;
the daughters of Brahmā, the daughters of the gods, and the daughters of the Pitṛs arrived. Those who dwell in lightning, those who dwell in clouds, and those who dwell on Mount Meru arrived.
The guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds, as well as the lords of the eight cities, arrived.
Those who dwell in the Bhuvarloka and those whose bodies are composed of wind also arrived;
so too did the Gandharvas, the Cāraṇas, the lords of the Siddhas, and the ascetics.
Aquatic creatures, land-dwellers, and sky-goers arrived;
likewise, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas,
and those devoted to Vināyaka, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Vaiṣṇavas came there.
The household deities, the village deities, and the forest deities arrived;
likewise, the forest-dwelling gods, sages, and even human beings arrived.
All the Gandharvas and others, as well as the ascetics, also arrived. (64–65)
The Siddhas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Kinnaras, and Kiñjanas,
as well as the Vidyādharas, Kāmadeva and others, and their wives, all arrived. Dharma, the lineage of Dharma, and the wives of Dharma also arrived.
Animals, beasts, and birds likewise remembered their former births;
insects, moths, trees, creepers, and even blades of grass arrived there.
The wish-fulfilling cows, the celestial kalpa-creeper, and the vessels of plenty also arrived.
The aesthetic sentiments, the varieties of the erotic sentiment, the goddess Śāradā, and likewise the musical notes;
the qualities and the types of weapons arrived there in embodied form.
The ritual procedures, the sacrificial beings, and the Vaiṣṇava fires likewise appeared.
The implements for ritual service arrived there in personified forms.
Rivers, streams, oceans, ponds, wells, and lakes,
as well as sacred fords, mountains, and forest retreats, also came there.
People of the four castes, both men and women, also arrived;
they came from the southern and eastern regions, from Prāgjyotiṣa, from the land of the Uṣṇas,
from the region of the camels, and from the land of the Brahmas.
They arrived from the eastern land of Piṅga and from Jalapāna;
they arrived from Rāśiyāna, Trivitta, and Śāmbhava; they arrived from the snowy regions, from Kashmir, and from the land of Orola.
They arrived from Kiṃpuruṣa and Ketumāla, from the oceans and the islands,
from Ārakta and Āvrikta, as well as from Sāmudradvīpa; likewise,
they came there for that great festival from the northern region of Tarka.
They arrived from the region of Ārārtrika and from the interior of the earth;
they also came from Uttarakuru and likewise from Kenāraka;
[they came] from the region of Brāhmīla and from the region of Hārītaka.
They came there for the great festival from the land of Amarika,
from the region of Varāsana, from the region known as Mākṣika,
and from the land of Arajas; all of them arrived full of eager anticipation.
Those dwelling on islands in the ocean arrived, traveling by celestial chariots;
kings and their retinues of servants, fathers of maidens, and householders such as the fathers-in-law of Bālakṛṣṇa all came together. (2.282.79–80)
The ṛṣis, the zodiac signs, the male rivers, the female rivers, and the maidens;
as well as the prosperities and the supernatural powers, all arrived from every direction.
Furthermore, the gods, daityas, and dānavas who dwell in the subterranean realms such as Atala also came.
The Asuras and the devoted Bhaktas arrived there;
the Nāgas, serpents, and the elephants of the quarters, as well as the Śaktis who protect the creation, arrived; all the Vedas, the sciences, and every single art arrived as well. (82–83)
Those belonging to the mother’s side, the father’s side, and likewise those on the daughter’s side; those on the sister’s side and the son-in-law’s side, as well as their respective relatives—
relatives connected through successive lineages— all arrived there.

Those belonging to the side of the disciples, those belonging to the side of the devotees, and those belonging to the side of the sages arrived. Those belonging to the side of the mantras, those belonging to the side of the regions, and those belonging to the side of the subjects arrived. And there were those who followed the sides of the members of the family, and those who followed the sides of the followers of those [family members]. (85–86)
Men and women, gods and goddesses, arrived there for that festival;
likewise, they came with their servants, friends, companions, and followers.
Those who were joined in yoga, those engaged in worldly affairs, and those living together all assembled there.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the beloved Mādhava of Śrī.
On earth, Śrī Kṛṣṇa bears Lakṣmī, who is Kṛṣṇā and born from Śiva.
She is the daughter of Śiveśvara, the Śrī-Śāla-Lakṣmī who is herself Narāyaṇī.
Lakṣmī is offered unto the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning;
she shall always remain united with Him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Lakṣmī is half the body of Kṛṣṇa, and indeed she is Kṛṣṇa’s very self.
Kṛṣṇa has Lakṣmī as half of his body; he is indeed Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
On this earth, the identity of Kṛṣṇā with Kṛṣṇa is brought about.
Oh, even though they must depart, what a perfect union of the two Kṛṣṇas!
Likewise, the lords who have been liberated from their abodes, as well as gods and even humans,
come with eager hearts, thinking, "A great union of the two Kṛṣṇas is occurring.
So too do children, the elderly, the young, and those established in the third gender.
"Men and women are coming together; there will be a fine union of the two Krishnas.
Thus spoke the ants on the bridge over the lake, as heard by Nārada:
"We shall obtain food and shelter; there will be a fine union of the two Krishnas."
The messengers of Dharmarāja indeed heard these words in hell:
"We shall quickly attain liberation; there is a great union of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna. Having heard these very words from the prison, they became observers.
"We shall encounter an obstacle; there is a great union between the two Kṛṣṇas.
"Even the words of mendicants who are virtuous and learned declare that we shall receive the best of gifts; there is a great union between the two Kṛṣṇas. (97–98)
Even from the poor and those burdened by debt, words were heard:
"We shall attain freedom from debt; this is a most auspicious occasion for the two Kṛṣṇas.
From the servants as well, words full of enthusiasm were likewise heard.
"We shall receive a reward when the conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas occurs.
Such words were heard as news from the caravans that had reached the road:
"One must travel very quickly, very quickly, so that the conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas may take place."
Families of maidens also come to Lake Aśvapaṭṭa;
"We shall arrive by boat at the auspicious conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas," such were the words heard by the great sages at the time of the aquatic creatures' bathing.

"We shall obtain food in the auspicious conjunction of the two Krishnas"—such words of joy were heard from the ancestors at the *śrāddha*: "We shall attain satisfaction in the auspicious conjunction of the two Krishnas. (103–104)
In the forest, the voices of the predators were heard observing their vows:
"Nothing must be harmed for seven days; this is an auspicious conjunction of the two dark fortnights.
For eight days, even the voices of the gods were heard proclaiming words of righteousness.
"Devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), we must be protected during the excellent union of the two Kṛṣṇas"—
thus were the eager words of the wise indeed heard.
"In that very place we shall sing the Sāman, during the excellent union of the two Kṛṣṇas."
We have heard the words of those devoted to ritual action: "We shall indeed go to behold the two Krishnas; we shall learn their path well during this auspicious conjunction.
Thus they speak, while inauspicious realities contend with one another.
"Inauspiciousness must be abandoned when there is auspiciousness regarding the two Kṛṣṇas," they say;
having gathered together at their own place, they quickly [dismiss] ill omens.
"Evil disposition must be destroyed during the ritual application regarding the two Kṛṣṇas. (2.282.110)
Even the planets quarrel; cruelty must be abandoned during the eight days [of the dark fortnight].
No fruit whatsoever should be offered on the day of Maṅgala (Mars) or during the two dark fortnights.
A certain old man, with a withered body and a crooked waist, leans upon a staff.
"Breathing heavily and speaking quickly, he goes along saying, 'The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas is at hand!
(1.12) "Upon seeing the saffron leaf-messenger, the inhabitants of all the worlds become ready for its arrival, thinking, 'The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas is at hand! (1.13)
The wish-fulfilling cows, along with their calves, approached slowly and eagerly to the beautiful Aśvasara lake, thinking it to be an auspicious omen for the two Kṛṣṇas.
Even those engaged in business abandoned their own work and set out [to witness the event].
"The field of Aśvapaṭṭasara is auspicious for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
(11.5) And the farmers, abandoning their cultivation and even carrying the fruits from the gardens, go joyfully to Aśvasaras, thinking, "It is auspicious for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. (11.6)
Having shaken off the impurity of birth and the observances of their vows with great difficulty,
those dwelling in all the worlds go joyfully to Lake Aśvasaras during the auspicious conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas, presenting their offerings there.
"Gifts must indeed be given according to one's ability during the auspicious conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas.
"Even after accomplishing the impossible, one must go quickly to the pavilion"—thus do the beings proclaim, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas is at hand! (118–119).
"Thus, O Rādhikā! words devoted to the Blessed Lord were heard.
From reading and hearing these, there shall be attainment of heaven and liberation.

(2.282.120) Thus ends the section on the morning auspicious sights, the worship of the gods, the kneading of flour, the bathing, the adornment, and the feeding of Mahīmān and others, in the second book, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Eighty-Two: The Arrival of the Three Creations; and the Description of the Attainment of Enthusiasm by Kṛṣṇa and Māṅgalya through Yoga.
Chapter 283: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 283.
[The Author: Chapter 284.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Just as it is at midday, so too at night, one should partake of excellent foods.
Having eaten all kinds of suitable foods and drunk water and other drinks, they took betel leaves and eye-ointments for the night;
then everyone went to the theater and beheld ever-new spectacles. (1–2)
Then, having avoided the sights and topics of awakening that were like mere fragments,
they took up sleep and tranquility; and the morning of the third day arrived during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, constantly accompanied by auspicious sounds from musical instruments.
And the embodied beings were awakened by songs and the voices of bards.
All the musical instruments that exist in the universe were indeed played there.
And the great sages, having bathed, being joyful, and having performed their twilight prayers, [assembled].
They came indeed to bestow their blessings upon Bālakṛṣṇa,
who had performed his ablutions, was dressed in his finery, and was seated upon a supreme throne.
Having offered words of blessing, the brahmins applied the *tilaka* and *candraka* marks to him.
They performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the thorough consecration of the water-pot (kalaśa). They performed the Nāndī-śrāddha and other rites, and they carried out the worship of the preceptor.
They performed the honoring of the family deities and likewise conducted the chanting of the Vedas.
They performed the worship of the gods Sarvatobhadra and Viṣṇu;
the dignitaries everywhere partook of milk and other refreshments.
Furthermore, from morning onwards, the embodied beings prepared their meals.

Then, in the third watch of the night, after having cleared the area on all sides, the people— numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, trillions, and even beyond that to the highest count (parārdha)— became ready in every respect at an auspicious moment. (2.283.10–11)
At that time, there were thousands upon thousands of aerial chariots for those following the yogic journey toward Kāśī;
all the vehicles were fully adorned and ready for departure.
"All those who are indeed traveling through the air for the purpose of a yogic pilgrimage—let them all come to the purifying Kāśī!
Śiveśvara desires that all those engaged in yogic travel assemble there. (13–14)
Śaṅkara, accompanied by his Gaṇas, will protect this sacred field in every way;
he will also protect the city, the hermitages, the pavilions, and so forth.
Having heard this, all the great-souled ones indeed became ready.
The foremost subjects of Surāṣṭra and the most excellent of all created beings were worthy of honor;
they were all dear to Brahmā and entirely devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
All their ancestors and others lived throughout every land. (16–17)
Listen, O Rādhā, then a wonder occurred that bestowed great amazement;
a voice from the sky was heard clearly on all sides:
"By those who, throughout the three worlds, have offered their own daughters to the Supreme Self..."
Within fifteen years, [they shall come] to Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
(1.9) Since all of them, including their father and others, must certainly come there, they will indeed become firmly attached through union with the Fortune of Śambhu. (2.283.20)
To the extent that it is according to the Vedic injunction, the injunction of Manu,
the injunction of Agni, and the procedure for the giving away of the maiden;
and for the sake of avoiding deficiency, in accordance with the laws of the country.
"Having circumambulated the fire, the ritual shall be performed.
And it shall be performed by all the maidens who dwell in the hermitage of Lomaśa—indeed, by those who are the beloved consorts of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (22–23)
"You must indeed come together with the army of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, along with your fathers, families, and kinsmen; there shall be no obstruction.
Having heard this, all the fathers and their families [prepared] with all necessary articles.
Equipped with all necessary articles, all were eager and accompanied by women;
they became ready, and the maidens likewise became ready in every respect.
So too did Lomaśa, the other sages, and the virtuous great seers.
The virtuous guests from all directions were ready,
accompanied by millions of others with ornaments, garments, celestial chariots, and so forth. O Rādhā, at that time, the joy of the maidens could not be contained within their bodies.
Equipped on all sides with chests containing all kinds of ornaments and finery, they quickly became ready and proceeded to the abode of Kṛṣṇa;
at that time, the fathers and mothers of the maidens also arrived there in haste. (28–29)
Having arrived at Kṛṣṇa’s abode along with the maiden and the army,
they reached a firm decision and became joyful in heart. At that time, auspicious omens appeared repeatedly for everyone there.
For indeed, all [omens] for all [the queens] were auspicious;
they were bestowers of the highest yoga, bringers of fame and renown, and they indicated the successful fruition of their undertakings without obstacle. (31–32)
With faces radiant with joy, filled with bliss, and accompanied by their calves, the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) gathered together, shedding streams of milk.
Adorned with every kind of erotic ornament and overflowing with all-encompassing delight. (33)
The young girls gathered there, as did the courtesans; the crops were lush and ripening, and there was curd. Adorned elephants arrived, accompanied by the royal queen along with her mother.
Swans, royal swans, and maidens accompanied by water,
as well as celestial nymphs (gandharvīs), all beautifully adorned, gathered together and sang;
and the vision of the gods also became manifest in the sky.
At that time, there were visions of Lakṣmīs and lotuses;
the auspicious sounds of musical instruments were heard, and the Vedic mantras of sacrificial oblations, which bring forth well-being, were heard. (37–38)
A white object appeared spontaneously, and the sacrificial fires blazed favorably; the winds blew propitiously, and there the most auspicious words of the guru’s blessings were heard. (39)

All the men and women had gathered their belongings; staying at Kuṅkumavāpikā, they had finished eating and drinking. Having prepared offerings and dressed in their finest attire, the people were together with their families. (2.283.40–41)
All the classes of people, along with their servants, friends, and kinsmen, became ready; they quickly prepared ten million celestial chariots.
Then, at that time, [the sound] of the auspicious conch Pāñcajanya indeed [resounded].
At the commencement of the journey, there was indeed a great clamor for the sake of auspicious rites.
Then Gopālakṛṣṇa gave gifts by the millions,
especially to the maidens, the Brahmins, and the children.
He then gave sweet foods, sugar, and various kinds of fruits;
garments, ornaments, vessels, jewels, and wealth;
as well as gifts of cows and donations of gold and silver.
At the commencement of the journey, he performed the worship of Gaṇeśa;
likewise, the worship of the Sarvatobhadra diagram, the honoring of the elders, salutations, and the worship of the family deity as well as Puruṣottama, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 46–47 ||
He beheld Lord Viṣṇu and likewise performed the worship of Śrī;
there he made offerings and gave away innumerable gifts.
Having paid obeisance to the deities of the sacred sites, he worshipped the deities of the gateway.
Having worshipped the cows, Bālakṛṣṇa then fully honored the celestial chariot; he also worshipped the Vedic deities at that time.
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and adorned with a crown, [he remained there].
He came to possess earrings on his hands and held a golden sword;
he quickly assumed a magnificent attire, adorned with diamond necklaces and other ornaments.
That most excellent of men was dressed in garments of pure silk and gold.
Having applied a tilaka of saffron and possessing a well-perfumed fragrance,
adorned with ornaments on his forearms, arms, waist, limbs, and fingers,
and marked with unbroken rice grains upon his forehead, he shone, endowed with splendor. (52–53)
His mother, Śrī Kaṃbharā Lakṣmī, applied the *tilaka* upon him;
his sister, named Santuṣṭā, placed a moon [mark] on his forehead and gave him a garland for his neck.
Ujjayinī and Śukapatnī likewise gave him necklaces of gems and pearls. (54)
Amṛtā placed [the ornament] upon the neck of Hari and applied collyrium to his eyes; Śaṃvatī prepared his hair with oil,
and Ramā likewise applied red lac to the palms of his hands.
Then Māṇikī applied red lac to the soles of her feet; Lakṣmī gave her lotus-garlands and golden necklaces;
Hāsā gave her a cluster of flowers; and Mañjulā gave her armlets. (57)
Ambā placed the jewel of splendor (tejomaṇi) upon her head, and Sugandhā cast the guṇākṣī [ornament].
Having thus adorned themselves, the beloved wives of Brahmā and the other maidens, having dressed in their finery, stood ready.
Likewise, there were other brothers, as well as the elder brothers of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa;
and other brothers born of Bālaka-Kṛṣṇa’s father as well;
and hundreds of daughters, as well as young boys and girls.
Sons, grandsons, sisters, and thousands of kinsmen quickly prepared themselves at that time, having taken their food and drink.
Those kings who were the fathers of the maidens, as well as the other rulers of the earth, likewise made ready. (61)
They too became ready, having indeed partaken of food and drink.
At that moment, there arose the sound of kettledrums and likewise the blast of conchs—
a deep resonance indicating their ascent into the celestial chariots.

Then Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, Lakṣmī, and the virtuous Śrī-Kambharā ascended a magnificent celestial chariot together with their family and belongings; indeed, all the beloved wives of Brahmā also ascended that celestial chariot. 64.
The sages, headed by Lomaśa, ascended the magnificent celestial chariot;
the virtuous Aśvapaṭṭavāsas ascended the celestial chariot; and the people of Kuṅkumavāpikā ascended the celestial chariot.
King Svarṇāṅgada also ascended, along with the full extent of his lineage;
Raṇaṅgama also ascended, and Lakṣmaṇa indeed ascended;
the deities of the sacred fords ascended, and the subjects ascended as well.
Proud and exalted, they ascended tens of thousands of celestial chariots.
Listen, O Rādhā, to the names of these foremost ones in brief:
fourteen thousand were prepared with the roar of clouds.
The sixth is Manasādevī, who always provides protection for children.
Her forms are indeed the millions of Kanyās and Dīpāvalīs;
they were then prepared and brought from the hermitage of Lomaśa in celestial chariots.
Having dressed themselves and filled with enthusiasm, they ascended by the command of Acyuta.
Talajā, the daughter of Tala, who was a Rākṣasī that had attained divine status,
she too ascended a celestial chariot here by the command of Mādhava.
Then, by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, ten million maidens who were like wish-fulfilling cows quickly ascended the celestial chariot there;
likewise, the hundred daughters of the Rākṣasa Arjuna accompanied Vasumatī.
Then, by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, she ascended the celestial chariot;
and by the command of Mādhava, the daughter of Hara, Krodhanā, ascended.
Ten thousand daughters of the Earth, accompanied by the Earth herself, also ascended.
Then ten million divine beings known as Gahvaras,
adorned with all ornaments and garments and being encouraged, ascended the celestial chariot;
and the daughter of Brahmā, named Sūcī, also ascended the chariot.
A hundred thousand daughters of the forest goddesses ascended the beautiful celestial chariot.
Indeed, the maiden named Oṣadhī, together with her mother the forest goddess, as well as a hundred thousand maidens of the Damanas and other Rākṣasas known by new names, [ascended]. (76–77)
Adorned with ornaments, garments, and other finery, they ascended the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Six young maidens of beautiful form ascended,
as did ten thousand divine women, including Kaṅkatālī and others.
Adorned with all ornaments, they ascended the celestial chariot;
and hundreds of thousands of divine maidens belonging to the Pitṛs, such as Aryaman and others,
seated themselves upon the chariot along with their fathers, beautifully decorated.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, five thousand daughters of the Daityas of the netherworld, beautifully adorned, ascended the celestial chariot;
likewise, sixteen spring-born maidens, also adorned, [ascended it].
Then, by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa,
five hundred daughters of the Daitya Tālamāla,
well-adorned, ascended the celestial chariot at the word of Kṛṣṇa.
Twenty thousand Naga maidens, beautifully adorned, ascended the celestial chariot by the command of Mādhava. Likewise, a thousand daughters of Śāvadīna, well-ornamented, [ascended]. 84.

Then, by the command of Bālakṛṣṇa, she ascended the celestial chariot (vimāna). And then, adorned with ornaments, a thousand daughters of illusionists ascended the celestial chariot by the command of Kṛṣṇa.
Sarasvatī, as well as the maidens known as the fourteen branches of learning and sixty other beautiful maidens, ascended the celestial chariot.
Then, King Lakṣmaṇa emerged there from within the earth.
He too quickly ascended his own most excellent celestial chariot (vimāna) along with two thousand of his own maidens;
indeed, there were seventy-two thousand maidens known as Nāḍikās.
The daughters of the Creator ascended their own celestial chariot;
and Viśvāvasu, filled with longing, then ascended his chariot together with his three hundred daughters who were arrayed in their finery.

A thousand maidens, adorned with the beauty of ornaments prepared by their own fathers, ascended the celestial chariot of King Jumāsemla. One hundred other maidens, likewise adorned by their brahmin fathers, also ascended.
Then the three daughters of Mahābāleśvara, accompanied and adorned, ascended the celestial chariot together with their father;
they ascended the well-decorated and embellished aerial vehicle.
King Dakṣajaṅgharo, the sovereign of Uṣṇālaya,
took his hundred beautiful daughters and a thousand daughters of his subjects, and ascended a magnificently adorned celestial chariot. 94–95.
Aryaman had twenty daughters, and another ten thousand;
all of them, together with Aryaman, ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna).
Prācīnabarhis’s progeny consisted of ten million daughters, who were likewise adorned.
Each ascended a divine celestial chariot together with their respective fathers. The two daughters of the brahmin Santāraṇa, adorned and accompanied by their father, also ascended the chariot.

Thus, O Rādhikā, the maidens residing at the hermitage of Lomaśa sat quickly upon their celestial vehicles by the command of Kṛṣṇa, their beloved, along with their fathers, mothers, and the ṛṣi Lomaśa. 99.
Adorned with ornaments and filled with longing, they thought, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas has begun" (2.283.100).
Considering their own Draupadī to be [the other] Kṛṣṇā, they offered themselves for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
bound by an inseparable connection to Kṛṣṇā, they thought, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas has begun" (101).
Filled with enthusiasm and exerting every effort, all the women sang of their own festive joy, saying, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas has begun!
Then other maidens as well ascended the celestial chariot.

"O Rādhikā, I shall describe to you those who are adorned by Kṛṣṇa’s beloveds. Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Morning Duties on the Third Day of the Bright Fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa in the Tretā Age, the Midday Meals and other rites, the Preparations for the Auspicious Journey toward Kāśī, the Adornment of Śrī Hari, the Auspicious Obligations, and the Ascension of the Brahmapriyās and Dākinyas into their Celestial Chariots," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā! Even those maidens who were born in distant lands such as Rāśiyāna, being beloved of Kṛṣṇa, ascended the celestial chariot. || 1 ||
Then King Śibi-deva, together with his hundred daughters and accompanied by his family and others, ascended his own celestial chariot.
Likewise, the great king Ṛkūṭastha, accompanied by fifty maidens, [ascended his].
The great king, the paramour of Vīra’s daughter, eager for the bridegroom’s procession, ascended his own celestial chariot accompanied by a hundred maidens. (3–4)
Śaktākṣi, the lord of the earth,
also ascended his own celestial chariot, eager for the bridal procession, accompanied by sixty maidens and likewise joined by one hundred and one Piśācī maidens.
Two hundred daughters of King Kālimāśa and a celestial chariot ascended [to heaven],
all beautifully adorned and accompanied by their parents.
At that time, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa [ascended] with Rādhikā.
On the ruby [throne], she beheld Śrī, Ramā, Lakṣmī, and Padmajā;
and on the celestial chariot, Ambā, Hāsā, Sadguṇā, and Mañjulā.
Furthermore, there were the four hundred and forty goddesses beginning with Parāvidyā.
King Uralaketu,
accompanied by thirty maidens, seated himself upon the celestial chariot with every mark of splendor;
he then ascended that beautiful and supreme vehicle for the sake of his journey.
King Kratha, accompanied by five maidens, ascended an excellent celestial chariot;
likewise, the gentle Saumya ascended for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Kāśī. Then King Pṛthu indeed ascended his own celestial chariot.
Accompanied by twenty maidens, that best of travelers [departed].
Ten maidens mounted the palanquin of Uṣṭrāla,
while King Haṃkāra was accompanied by five maidens.
And he ascended the celestial chariot for the very purpose of a pilgrimage to Kāśī.
Then King Jayakāṣṭhala, accompanied by his five daughters,
also ascended the celestial chariot for the sake of the pilgrimage to Kāśī.
King Tīrāṇa, accompanied by six maidens,
ascended a celestial chariot for the very purpose of a pilgrimage to Kāśī.
Ālvīnara, joined by five maidens, likewise ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Likewise, King Jīnavardhana,
accompanied by his family and seven daughters, ascended a celestial chariot,
eager for that purpose, to perform the pilgrimage to Kāśī. (16–17)

Then, together with that one orphaned girl who had been scattered among the Rākṣasas, she indeed ascended the celestial chariot for the sake of the chariot procession. (18) These were the girls who had been liberated from the Rākṣasas.
Two hundred and one thousand ascended their celestial chariots (vimānas).
King Alapaketu ascended a chariot with seven maidens,
and the royal sage Jayakṛṣṇa likewise ascended with a single maiden.
And King Parīśāna, accompanied by twenty-one maidens, ascended a single,
magnificent palanquin; he mounted that vehicle which was laden with every kind of ornament.

King Indurāya, exceedingly joyful, ascended a celestial chariot adorned with every ornament, accompanied by his two daughters. King Mudrāṇḍa, likewise, ascended accompanied by fifteen maidens. (22–23)
Then Gaṇḍarāja, accompanied by the nine maidens, ascended that excellent celestial chariot for the purpose of a yogic journey;
he also ascended that magnificent vehicle for the sake of a pilgrimage to Kāśī.
King Līnorṇa, accompanied by his four daughters and eager for the journey to Kṛṣṇa, ascended a celestial chariot. King Vṛhacchara also ascended, joined by his eleven sons. (25–26)
Then King Balalīna, accompanied by forty maidens, ascended his own opulent and adorned aerial chariot for the sake of his yogic journey.

Then King Varasiṃha, accompanied by five maidens, ascended a celestial chariot for the sake of a pilgrimage to Kāśī; and at that time, King Rāyagāma, likewise joined by five maidens, did the same. (28–29)
Accompanied by three other maidens, he ascended the celestial chariot;
the two queens also ascended the chariot,
as did King Phenatantu together with his two daughters.
Then he indeed ascended that magnificent [palanquin] for the sake of the pilgrimage to Kāśī.
And King Stokahoma, accompanied by his only daughter,
then ascended a splendid celestial chariot for the purpose of the pilgrimage to Kāśī.
A daughter of King Kāṣṭhāyana, accompanied by her father,
ascended a magnificent celestial chariot used for yogic travel. At that time, a daughter of King Kolaka also [ascended] a celestial chariot.
Then, for the sake of the pilgrimage to Kāśī, they ascended that magnificent [palanquin].
O Rādhikā, in this manner those Gaurīs, eager for the sake of their beloved Kṛṣṇa,
having performed their adornments and being beautifully decorated, attained great joy.
King Arkamāna, accompanied by two maidens,
ascended his own celestial chariot for the sake of a successful journey of yoga.
And Rāya, the king of the Kinnaras, [ascended] a celestial chariot endowed with every prosperity.
Adorned with great splendor, King Rāyarokīśvara ascended [the chariot] along with fifty-one maidens;
taking twenty-one maidens and his own celestial vehicle (vimāna), he indeed ascended it at that time.
And King Rāyaraṇajit, accompanied by twenty thousand maidens,
ascended his own magnificent celestial chariot for the sake of the supreme expedition. King Rāyavākakṣaka, likewise, was accompanied by three maidens.
He indeed ascended his own celestial chariot for the sake of a divine journey.
(2.284.40) And King Rāyamārīśa, accompanied by his three daughters, ascended his own opulent chariot for the sake of the journey as well. (41)
King Rāyabaleśvara, accompanied by three daughters,
ascended his own celestial chariot, eager for the pilgrimage to Kāśī.
At that time, King Rāyalambāra also departed, joined by six daughters.
Then King Rājanavārka,
accompanied by his seven daughters, ascended his own magnificent celestial chariot for the sake of the journey. (43–44)
Then King Rāyahuṇḍeśa, accompanied by nine maidens,
ascended a celestial chariot endowed with all prosperity.
And King Rāyakūpeśa, accompanied by one maiden, likewise ascended.
Then King Kālīmaṇḍalī,
accompanied by his four daughters, ascended a magnificent celestial chariot for the purpose of the pilgrimage to Kāśī. || 46-47 ||
And King Vanajeśa, accompanied by five maidens,
himself ascended that beautiful celestial chariot at that time.
And Pārāvārapibakṣmeśa, accompanied by three maidens, [ascended].
Then he ascended a celestial chariot endowed with every prosperity.
(49) Then King Koṭīśvara, accompanied by his two daughters, ascended that auspicious celestial chariot, which was likewise filled with all splendors. (284.50)
Then the three daughters of King Satīśa, together with their father,
ascended a magnificent and auspicious celestial chariot intended for the journey.
And King Tretākarkaśa, accompanied by his seven daughters, [ascended as well].

Then the king, accompanied by his four daughters, ascended a magnificent celestial chariot for the purpose of the pilgrimage. King Āṇḍaja also, together with his four daughters, ascended his own celestial chariot for the sake of the pilgrimage to Kāśī.
Then King Bālyaraja, accompanied by his only daughter, ascended a magnificent and auspicious celestial chariot for the sake of the pilgrimage to Kṛṣṇa.
King Rāyasomana, likewise, was accompanied by three daughters.
Then, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s journey, the king ascended his own magnificent aerial chariot, which was equipped with wide windows; he was accompanied by his two daughters. (55–56)
Then King Parāṅavrata, accompanied by his two daughters,
ascended a celestial chariot for the purpose of a pilgrimage to Kāśī;
and King Īśānapāna likewise ascended his own opulent celestial chariot.
And the king, the lord of wealth and sovereign, ascended his own magnificent aerial chariot accompanied by forty-one maidens;
he also ascended the ceremonial vehicle together with thirty-three daughters.
The maiden Maṅgalā, the sister of King Rājārāya, and the wife of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, ascended her own celestial chariot along with Lalitā,
Revā, Bhārgavī, and Sarasvatī.
Ramā, Gaṅgā, Dayā, Bhakti, Muktī, Ekādaśī, Rati, Kāmadughā,
Tulasī, Kamalā, Virajā, Satī, Mūrti, Gomatī, Svarṇarekhā, Jayā, and Nandinī. (61–62)
Vanitā, Mohinī, Dolā, Puṣpā, Prīti, Kalāvatī, Mādhavī,
Badarī, Campā, Kuśalā, Manu, Maṇi, Śānti,
Śāntā, Ramā, and Haimī— these were seated upon the celestial chariot, full of vigor. (63)
Others were also adorned by Lomaśa and brought to a state of peace;
indeed, there were billions of female companions for all those who had been mentioned.
Adorned likewise were the daughters of Kubera, the daughters of Mahendra, and the daughters of Yama.
The Vāyavyas, Vaiśvakarmyas, Vārkṣyas, Raudryas, and those born of fire;
the Śrāvaṇyas, the Khānijyas, the Sāṃvatsaryas, and the Gopikās;
the Prācīnyas, the Piśaṅginīs, the Rāśiyānyas, and the Samuṣṭrikās.
The Romāyanīs, the Pāraśvīs, the Dhaivaryīs, and the hosts of Kinnarīs;
likewise the Amaryas, the Gaurīs, the Paryas, and the Hāritikas;
also the Ābriktyas, the Pātālyas, the Svargyas, and the Apsarases. (67–68)
The daughters of Brahmā, the Gandharvīs, and the adorned daughters of Arbuda,
together with Lomaśa and each of their own fathers,
ascended their respective magnificent and opulent aerial chariots, which were fully equipped with all necessary provisions.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa then became ready. (2.284.70) Then other great personages who had come for Kṛṣṇa’s procession—Ṛṣis such as Hemaśālāyana and others—sat upon the palanquin. (71)
Cakravākī and Urvaśī, Hanumān along with Agastya, the sages beginning with Maṅkaṇaka, Devāyatana,
the sages beginning with Meṣāyana, and the sage Pradhī, son of Lālāsana.
And five thousand others, such as Vṛkāyana and his peers,
as well as Yavakrīta and others, Śvetavyāsa and his like,
and Sanatkumāra and the rest, sat down upon the celestial chariot.
Tuṣita, Hārita, Divimāna, Āyana, and so forth; Kuśala, Yoginī, and also Sāṃkhya-yogin;
Śāvadinī, Mahākālī, Vārinara, and Kṣetrapa. (75)
Then, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s procession, the sages headed by Āryāyana, the gatekeeper Brahmanādaka,
the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, and likewise those such as the Vālakhilyas,
ascended their celestial chariots.
O Rādhikā! Then the liberated ones who are beyond the syllables (akṣara), as well as all other liberated souls from every direction,
and likewise all male and female incarnations,
ascended their celestial chariots, adorned with every kind of ornament.
All the attendants who dwell in his abode, as well as those residing in Vaikuṇṭha;
Vāsudeva and the others, the Infinite Viṣṇu, the Sovereign Virāṭ;
the Sāttvika sages, the Siddhas, and likewise the virtuous ones.
Adorned and highly opulent,
the Pitṛs, beginning with Aryaman, as well as the world-protectors who guard the quarters,
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Kumāras, and likewise the Aśvins, ascended their celestial chariots.
Then, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa’s journey,
the Maruts, Siddhas, Nidhis, and auspicious planets ascended their celestial chariots;
as did the Sun and Moon, the Seven Sages, Dhruva, the Mothers, and the Quarters.
Kāmadeva, the Manus, the Kalās, and likewise the Tithis;
the Tattvas, the lunar mansions, the Guṇas, the sacred fords, the rivers, and the streams;
the Brahmachārins, those possessed of the Nyāsa-mantras, and the trees known as the divine deities.

The wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpavallī*), the wish-fulfilling stones (*kalpaśilā*), the household deities and others, as well as temples and shrines (*caitya*), ascended the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
Likewise, the *nāgas*, serpents, *daityas*, *dānavas*, and *rākṣasas* [also ascended]. (84–85)
Charioteers, bards, panegyrists, and wandering minstrels; Brahmins and learned scholars, as well as Kiṃpuruṣas and Kinnaras;
Gandharvas and storytellers, and male and female servants by the millions.
Adorned with every kind of ornament, they ascended celestial chariots.
Artisans, goldsmiths, wealthy men, as well as performers of sacrifices, and the preceptors mentioned by Lomaśa— all these went to the entire Kuṅkumavāpikā grove.
They ascended their celestial chariots, saying, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas has begun.
The Earth herself, remembered as Medinī, arrived there;
and the Seasons arrived, as did Dharma himself, the god of righteousness.
Then Nara also arrived from the Badarī forest,
and the Goddess Akṣaravāsinī arrived with the pedestal;
they ascended the well-formed seats and the liquid substances.
Then the one known as Maṇḍapa arrived, and he who is remembered as Mukta likewise came; even Māṇikya-stambha appeared before Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
as did Sudarśana the discus and Hara, the protector of the sacred field.
Having bowed down in the presence of Śrī Hari and taken their seats upon auspicious thrones, they sat there. Then the venerable Gopālakṛṣṇa, their father,
spoke to these nine for the purpose of protecting the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
"Protect this field indeed; we shall go to Varāṇasī.
Having said this, and having given suitable provisions, weapons, and rewards, he made the sun-shaped celestial chariot ready for departure.
He beheld the youthful Kṛṣṇa adorned with ornaments, his brothers headed by Bhagavān,
the wives of his brothers, the groups of his paternal kinsmen from children to the elderly,
and all his family members and relatives seated upon celestial chariots.
He seated the successive groups of men and women related to him upon celestial chariots and caused them to raise shouts of victory;
drums were also sounded, signaling the commencement of the procession.
Then auspicious sounds from the *vyaṅgula* instruments, providing a connection for all to hear, arose;
and the resonant sounds of the musical instruments of the *gandharvas* occurred, and the sounds of kettledrums were like thunderclouds during that expeditionary march. (2.284.99–100)
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be ever victorious!"—
thus spoke a divine voice then, moving through the sky.
[He was] honored with flowers, consecrated rice, and other auspicious items by Devikā and the others.
And the celestial chariot of Bālakṛṣṇa proceeded toward the eastern direction.
Then, in the sky, the celestial chariots, resounded with songs and graced by joyful people, followed behind it.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the celestial chariot carrying them moved forward;
that procession for Kṛṣṇa’s journey, as if swiftly ascending to heaven, appeared exceedingly beautiful.
Joy could not be contained within the heart of every single embodied being.
A great joy arose regarding the wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas.
(105) Having crossed the Maru country, the Kośalas, and the Madhyadeśa regions, and having passed beyond Prayāga, the army proceeded toward Kāśī. (106)

Seeing Kṛṣṇayānī, who resembled a thousand moons, roaring and appearing in the form of a celestial chariot (vimāna), Śiveśvara was exceedingly delighted. The inhabitants of Kāśī also went forth toward her with great eagerness.
"O Rādhikā! Let us go; the wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas is at hand! (108).

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ascension of the Great Kings, the Maidens, and the Sages into the Celestial Chariots, and the Departure of Kṛṣṇa and Others for Kāśī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (284)
