Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā! Beholding the army in the sky in the form of celestial chariots, there were the great devotees of Śaṅkara as well as King Śiveśvara. (1)
Then, having quickly paid homage to Kṛṣṇāyānī for her welcome,
he commanded all those skilled in musical instruments, as well as the cowherds and others,
to play the finest musical instruments and trumpets.

Then, pleasant sounds of musical instruments arose throughout the sky; auspicious sounds produced by *tāra*, *bherī*, and *vyaṅgula* drums resounded beautifully, as did the far-reaching sounds of conch shells. (3–4)
Likewise, sounds arising from peacocks, the resonance of flutes and lutes,
those produced by water-machines and the like, and those originating from the throat are auspicious.
So too are those produced by mṛdaṅga drums, hand-claps, and the like, as well as those generated by fire-machines.
The sounds produced by the wind and the songs of the sky became manifest.
There were the vocal tones of the Apsarases and the songs of the Yoginīs,
as well as the sweet sounds of the speech of women such as Vedā and others, like the resonance of Sarasvatī.
There, pleasant sounds reached far, traveling to the ends of the sky; those auspicious sounds were heard from the celestial chariots in the atmosphere.
Hearing those sounds, the inhabitants of the chariots were filled with wonder.
They all, traveling in their celestial chariots, beheld that vast and beautiful land of Vārāṇasī— the city situated amidst the banks of the Gaṅgā,
ten yojanas in extent, and then resembling Vaikuṇṭha itself.
And five days later, they beheld the vast, newly constructed City of Śiva on the bank of the Varaṇā, extending for twenty yojanas;
it had been caused to be built by summoning Maya, the architect of the universe.
Is it another Kailāsa, or perhaps another Goloka?
It stands fashioned like ten million moons, yet possesses the radiance of ten million suns;
it is situated in the sky with many stories, or perhaps it rests upon a trident.

Those traveling in the celestial chariot considered that very place to be the divine Kailāsa. Indeed, that city had been constructed by Śiveśvara for the sake of his daughter’s auspicious festival of marriage and as a residence for his own majesty.
It was resplendent with golden walls and adorned with ten million palaces;
it possessed beautiful golden halls and was endowed with golden domes;
it was distinguished by golden banners and featured a hundred stories on all sides. (14–15)
Wherever the city of Kubera is, there likewise is the city of Īśāna;
in the corner is the city of Indra, and in the intermediate corner is the city of Agni.
Where the city of Varuṇa is, in the intermediate corner is the city of Dharma.
The city of the Maruts is in one corner, and the city of Brahmā is in the intermediate corner (17).
Likewise, the city of Sūrya and the city of Viṣṇu shine in the [other] corners.
In the center are the abodes of the gods, palaces with a hundred stories (18).
Surrounded by gardens and situated beside water-stations, they were filled with exquisite fragrances;
like the white Himalayan mountains, they were as radiant as the moon.
All the palaces, newly constructed, were endowed with every prosperity.
The moon-chambers shine like those situated on the path of the planets.
There, the gems in the walls emit their natural radiance,
and the lattices indeed possess their innate brilliance.
In the archways there are wish-creepers dripping with nectar;
upon the upper portions of the pillars stand trees of desire;
and in the balconies flow rivers of milk born of longing.
Just as there is the heat arising from the wish-fulfilling tree as desired,
so too in Śivapura, within every palace and upon the ground of every palace,
there exist wish-granting cows (kāmadhenus). // 23–24 //
Divine beings, capable of assuming any form at will, moving through the sky, and bestowing happiness, exist there; likewise, Kalpa-maidens are found stationed upon each level.
Furthermore, male and female servants of divine complexion exist as attendants.
Then all the divine beings born of his resolve were stationed there for the sake of service;
likewise, those who massage the body, the singers, and the dancing women—all of them born of resolve, they were placed there by Śaṅkara. (26–27)
All flavors, all fragrances, and all forms are most beautiful;
there are palaces with all sounds and all tactile sensations.
There is the splendor of golden seats, as well as lion-thrones and elephant-seats.
There are couches soft and delicate where the altars stand;
there are various kinds of grass mats and comfortable beds, with divine silk coverlets spread on all sides. (2.285.29–30)
There were woolen rugs—soft, delightful, variegated, and auspicious;
colorful with many hues, shimmering in appearance, and serving as individual seats.
There were also balls for play, cushions, and soft bolsters.
And those secret, priceless golden cages which were placed by Śambhu within those very palaces—
there were also swings and hammocks with creepers, provided with soft beds. || 32–33 ||
There, even small-bodied celestial chariots, adorned with creepers hanging down for the purpose of swaying, descend to the earth;
and in every house there are vehicles capable of movement through the path of the wind. (34)
And by means of which gates people enter and exit their respective dwellings in the higher realms from the path of the sky in celestial chariots;
there are also staircases and ladders constructed of precious gems. (35–36)
All the vessels were made of gold, as were the ritual cups; there were inexhaustible bowls and auspicious jars. In every house, all the floors were inlaid with jewels.
Mirrors with transparent surfaces shine in every house;
the doors of the gods consist of the vision of creation, and chests, caskets,
and the like are indeed filled with inexhaustible wealth.
In every house there were all kinds of most beautiful garments,
as well as vessels for fragrant substances, oils, and saffron. Indeed,
in every house there were bowls containing musk and camphor.
In every house there are channels of juice, channels of curd, and channels of honey, as well as granulated sugar; there are stalks of sugarcane, channels of clarified butter,
pools of nectar, jars of cream, and likewise lakes of ambrosia.
There were also collections of fruits, flowers, and lotuses; likewise, reservoirs of water;
stores of bulbs, both fresh and dried, and of seeds;
as well as weapons, beautiful stage-props, and the implements for gambling.
In every house there are machines for hearing and seeing;
there are statues of deities in every house, along with laborers.
There are alchemy laboratories, cooking kitchens, schools of learning, and underground chambers.
In every house there were secret chambers, bath-halls, and kitchens;
in every house there were halls for drinks, halls for peace, and halls for pleasure;
and in every house there were beds for secret sleep and raised balconies.
There were various pleasure halls and diverse chambers for the women;
there were easily accessible halls for the elderly, provided with all necessary articles, as well as purification halls and cleansing rooms in every house. (47–48)
In every house there were diverse pleasure-halls equipped with all necessary implements, as well as assembly halls and recreation chambers;
and there were all kinds of vehicles, both those moving on land and those born of the sea.
And there were wind-born creatures placed at every door;
great lions were at the gate-towers, elephants stood at the crossroads, Garuḍas were atop the mansions, and tigers were upon the gate-towers.
The Paryas, the Apsarases, the Gaṇyas, and the hosts of Yoginīs—these sentient beings dwell there, serving the Great Lord.
O Rādhikā! A special distinction has been ordained there by Śaṅkara.
But he whose house exists merely for the sake of his own residence, wherever that may be,
he alone shines with his own family like a consecrated image—
like a king in action, or like a god, a Daitya, or even an Asura.
Likewise, that reality is hidden within the secret walls of the palaces.
Whosoever dwells in the palace becomes double-formed.
A delusion arises for everyone; here, what is real and what is other?

Those who do not know the original object (bimba) wander among its reflections; having turned away from the fruitless [reflections], they indeed seek the original object. Deprived of the valid cognition of that very [object], they mistake the delusion for valid cognition.

Land appears as water in the water, and water as land on dry ground; fire is perceived in water, and the appearance of space is seen upon the earth—thus do those who pride themselves on their greatness wander.
Yet, Śaṅkara is also seen everywhere, manifesting in subtle form.
This was a divine illusion created by Śiva, manifested there within the palaces.
There, the god of wind attends to the service of the images with fans;
he remains present as required, delighting the minds of all.
Aditi and the Giver of Food exist in the form of young girls;
having appeared through the power of resolve, they bestow [their gifts] and then vanish from sight.
The medicinal herbs were placed by Śaṅkara in every palace and every house.
Golden trees bearing fresh clusters of *vijaya* flowers were set up.
In every house, beautiful skins of lions, tigers, and other beasts were displayed within the palaces as if they were living beings. (62–63)
The ornaments of women, as well as their charming garments,
and vessels filled with the essence of love were placed in every house.
All kinds of foods— those to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked— were likewise provided.
And delicious drinks were placed in every house.
In every house, Śaṅkara established a single vessel of moonlight, a cloud that bestows nectar, full and granting happiness. (65–66)
And Vāsanta was summoned and established in Śivapattana. All those traveling through the sky beheld such a wondrous city of Śiva, the residence of the bridegroom’s party, built by Viśvakarman.
They beheld the second [city], the beautiful and excellent Pārvatīpattana, which had been constructed for the purpose of providing a residence for the assembly of the maidens' party;
it was not inferior to this [first city] in any respect, nor even slightly in its various objects. (68–69)
On the ground of the Varaṇā plateau, twenty yojanas in extent,
and situated between two divine, newly built cities,
the palace of Pārvatīśa shines forth, possessing ten thousand peaks.
Built by Viśvakarman and adorned by Maya,
it shone like a peak of Mount Meru situated between the Moon and the Sun.
O Rādhā, this indeed belongs to Śiva in the city of Pārvatī.
And those who belonged to the side of Kanyā stayed there,
O beautiful one; indeed, Śaṅkara, the Lord of Beings, accompanied by ten million hosts,
as well as Piṅgarāja, Śaṅkara, and Īśāna, who dwells upon Ketumāla.
Being capable of assuming any form at will, Kāmākṣi and they all dwelt there.
Navajīvadvīparāja, whose name was Kāmanāyaka—
these were all the Śaṅkaras who resided in the city of Pārvatī.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed the manifest father of Śaṅkara;
he dwelt there together with millions of cowherd women and cowherds.
The Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose form is the cosmic manifestation (vyūha), was accompanied by ten million attendants (pārṣadas).
Accompanied by ten million Kṛṣṇas, he dwelt in the city of Pārvatī;
and Mahāmāyā, the power (śakti) of Kṛṣṇa, also resided there.
So too did Mahākāla, the sustainer of the world, accompanied by Old Age and Death.
And there dwelt the Lord Sadāśiva, endowed with sovereignty equal to ten million Śaktis; for he is indeed the father of Vairāja.
He too, accompanied by Śivā, resided right there in the city of Pārvatī.
All the Rudras, as well as the Rudrīs and the hosts created by Rudra,
along with the Mahāmānas, dwelt happily in the city of Pārvatī.
Śiva, residing on Kailāsa, was likewise accompanied by ten million attendants.
Yamarāja dwelt in that city accompanied by ten million messengers;
Agni and all the various deities also resided in that city.
Kubera, Nirṛti, and even the circle of Yoginīs were there as well.
Yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas;
vaināyakas, kūṣmāṇḍas, vetālakas, and likewise the gaṇas;
vetālīs, śākinīs, ḍākinīs, caṇḍikās, and others. (83–84)
The Brahmācaryas, the Mothers, the Durgās, and those who are the Śaktis; the Kālīs and Mahākālīs, as well as the Bhairavas and Bhadrakās—
they all dwelt happily, sleeping at ease, in the city-palace of Pārvatī.
The lords, the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, and those beyond the unmanifest (avyākṛta);
likewise, those dwelling in immortality, the followers of the Sun, and the followers of the Moon resided there.
There were also sages, perfected yogis, ascetics free from worldly ties (avadhūtas), and those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgins).
The yogins, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors also dwelt there;
the planets, the stars, the lunar mansions, and the comets were there as well.
At that time, the Daityas and the Dānavas also resided in that city.
The celestial world-protectors and likewise the guardians of the sacred fields (kṣetrapālas) and others;
the purifiers dwelling in the atmospheric realm (bhuvarloka), along with the family deity Hanumān;
the human kings as well, and the lords of serpents residing in the netherworld (pātāla).
Likewise Hāṭakeśa, the Jyotiḥ-svarūpas, and the Praśaktis;
the Gāndharvas, Gaṇikās, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and others;
the Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and the mountains such as Himālaya.
Sages, fevers, obstacles, and those who employ poisons;
trees, creepers, and the principles (tattvas); cruel forms of Time, scorpions and other creatures capable of assuming any form at will—all these dwelt in the city of Pārvatī. (92–93)
These and other great beings, the attendants and followers of Śaṅkara,
all residing in the city of Pārvatī,
beheld the sky and perceived that Kṛṣṇa’s army was approaching through the air.
Quickly becoming ready with sounds from their two-fingered cymbals, they went to the temple of Śiva.
Accompanied by their families and others, taking refuge in auspicious instrumental music, and adorned with beautiful ornaments and attire, they arrived for the sake of a welcome. (95–96)
Then all the people of Vārāṇasī also arrived,
considering their own fortune and merit blessed because of the wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas; they brought gifts,
fruits, flowers, and garlands.
They quickly followed the Lord of Pārvatī to his abode.
Śiveśvara swiftly [reached] his own Kailāsa, the divine person,
as well as the Himālaya mountain and the vast, divine person.
And in the sky, he spoke to the support of the celestial chariot so that it might become most divine there for a moment as a welcome;
"O Rādhikā! Let these Kailāsa and Himālaya mountains [be brought] here immediately."
In the intermediate space, they fashioned another Kailāsa, a divine celestial expanse with the form of earth and a firm foundation. There,
Śiva and his followers quickly ascended into that sky to reach their new abode.
In the new and beautiful abode, the people following [the Lord], situated in celestial chariots, witnessed a marvel in the sky as the army arrived.
Beholding the supreme majesty of Śiveśvara, they were then filled with wonder. (103)

Then Śrīmad Gopāla, Kṛṣṇa, and the others praised Hara, who is the very form of Brahman, whose self is Brahman, the father of Mahālakṣmī, and the husband of Pārvatī— seeing him thus enriched with all splendors, they were filled with joy.
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa’s consort, Śaṅkara and the others were indeed filled with joy;
and beholding her supreme majesty, they then became utterly bewildered.
O Rādhikā, she is the maiden Lakṣmī who removes the pride of both [Śiva and Viṣṇu].
Bālakṛṣṇa himself is the remover of pride, and he is also Kumāraka.
When there is a fitting union here between these two portions of the Lord, their respective parts indeed blossom; this is the marriage of the two Kṛṣṇas.
Wherein I am your beloved—Kṛṣṇa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Śiva;
wherein Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the Supreme Lord reside; and wherein all the directors of creation dwell—what wonder indeed could there be in that place?
"Everything falls into place, O Rādhā, since the marriage of the two Kṛṣṇas is at hand! (2.285.11).

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sounding of Musical Instruments Caused by Śiveśvara for the Purpose of Honoring the River Kāśī; the Vision from the Sky of Kāśikā, Śivapura, and Pārvatīpura; the Description of the City; and the Construction of Mount Kailāsa in the Sky for One Ghaṭikā to Welcome the River, along with Śiveśvara and the Dignity of the Maidens of Pārvatīpattana," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Eighty-Five:
285. Chapter 286 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
[Author: Chapter 287.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, there on that vast Kailāsa situated in the sky...
In a beautiful golden pavilion, auspicious and worthy of royal entry, situated within a magnificent garden fifty *yojanas* in extent and endowed with every conceivable supernatural power,
Śrī Śaṅkara and the others took their stand upon the royal highway.
And they showed him these [beings] seated in celestial chariots nearby,
as well as a divine land fashioned in the sky for a slow descent—
entirely golden in color and appearing like another Mount Kailāsa. (3)
It was adorned with a golden city and wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas),
enriched at that time by trees bearing fruit in all seasons; it was graced with millions of resting-houses and auspicious, great inner groves.
It was endowed with trees beautiful with blossoms and fragrant with scents,
and it was surrounded on all sides by the landing-places for celestial chariots;
such was that vast city shown to him at that time.
On level ground and on sites suitable for standing nearby,
O Rādhikā, Bālakṛṣṇa and the others, as well as the great sages, kings, maidens, holy men, deities, and so forth, [prepared their respective celestial chariots]. (7–8)

The liberated lords, as well as the sovereign goddesses, the ancestors, Manu, and the others, being filled with eagerness, brought down their own aerial chariots— which were the very embodiments of their respective armies—
upon the ground of Kailāsa.
Then, indeed, hundreds of thousands of auspicious musical instruments—
both fierce and sweet, bestowing blessings— were sounded;
as were those belonging to Goloka, Amṛta, and Avyākṛta.
Of Kailāsa, of Kubera, and of the earth; of the worlds of the asuras, of the daityas, of the classes of beings, and likewise of the hosts and yogins;
of the yoginīs, of the courtesans, and of the women of the gandharvas. 12.
Musical instruments were sounded on all sides for Caṇḍī and the others.
On the top of the golden city wall, which was lined with trees,
and at the front of the great palace, stood the celestial chariot of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And it descended slowly and came to rest firmly within the circle of trees;
likewise, other celestial chariots also descended individually into the various groves of trees and,
having alighted, each came to rest steadily upon its own respective palace roof.
Then, O Rādhikā, I beheld a great wonder of Śaṅkara:
he assumed as many forms as there were celestial chariots, and Bṛhaspati likewise assumed as many forms there. 16–17.
I, however, stood before the palanquin of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa,
together with Śaṅkara, my preceptor, Vāmadeva and others,
as well as Vyāsas, Brahmins, and sages who held vessels worthy of worship. (18)
With flowers, unbroken rice grains, liquid offerings, parched grain, saffron, and bilva fruits;
with fragrant flower garlands and the like; accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas and auspicious words; and provided with jars of water for worship—(19–20).

For the sake of sweet food and drinking water, [he was served] by numerous groups of attendants provided with golden vessels and the like, as well as by servants holding platters, and by countless female slaves carrying sweet dishes and similar items. (21)
Accompanied by female attendants bearing water-vessels and other items, adorned with the form of those [deities], and provided with fly-whisks, fans, and the like;
and by hosts of divine servants equipped with parasols, vessels, and other such articles.
Together with hosts of cane-bearers, weapon-bearers, and those who obeyed his commands— all of whom were skilled in the offering of perfumes and honors, provided with fruits and betel,
full of respect and courtesy, and endowed with all pleasing speech— (24).
With attendants who provided excellent and superior seats and knew how to wash his feet; with groups of servants who understood his gestures, carried out his tasks, and gave him what he required;
and also with young male and female attendants.
There, joined by the wicks of my own volitions, I was Śaṅkara, as well as Bṛhaspati and others; we were there seeking to welcome [the guest].
Just as all that occurred together with me, so indeed did everything happen.
At every spot, there was a celestial chariot to welcome them.
28. Listen, O Rādhā, to another marvel born of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa:
then the Lord, beholding Śrī Śaṅkara assuming many forms, [was amazed]. 29.
The Lord Bālakṛṣṇa also, accompanied by his family and joined by Lomaśa,
assumed those respective forms and suddenly descended from the celestial chariots, one by one.
Śaṅkara too was struck with great wonder upon beholding Mādhava.
Indeed, Śaṅkara had then assumed various forms along with all the embodied beings situated in their celestial chariots, for the sake of honoring him.
However, because those who travel in celestial chariots have indeed offered themselves [to the Lord],
they do not take even a leaf or anything else without first offering it to Bālakṛṣṇa.
Otherwise, their acceptance of that worship material would constitute an act of disrespect.
Śaṅkara would incur the fault of failing to receive the food offered by himself;
therefore, to avoid that fault, the Lord and Master Bālakṛṣṇa, having understood this, [acted] separately for each in order to accept the worship. 34–35.
Then, from all the celestial chariots, Śaṅkara, the foremost one, descended with all his manifestations and all his possessions;
he indeed performed the worship due to Kṛṣṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman itself.
Having received worship, Hari then bowed to the venerable ones, beginning with Hara;
having inquired after their welfare and announced his own well-being,
and having received words of blessing, he vanished from that spot to another place.
Then the Lord Śambhu remained steady in his own principal celestial chariot,
while Bṛhaspati and others performed the worship of the great ones and conducted the auspicious rites according to the rules with Vedic mantras. (39)
The father of the bridegroom and the father of the bride inquired after each other’s well-being and health;
likewise, all the relatives and kinsmen asked after their welfare and then embraced one another with their chests.
"Welcome! they exclaimed, speaking beautiful words with great eagerness;
they quickly offered him honor by washing his feet and other such rites, providing seats, offerings of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and gifts of fragrant water. (42)
With offerings of flowers and garlands, sandalwood paste and the like, and by presenting flower wreaths,
parched grain, and unbroken rice, the lords honored Him;
likewise with the offering of handfuls of flowers and by pressing Him against their chests.
On the appropriate ground, Niṣādas [offered service] upon golden lion-thrones and the like;
in groves and golden palaces, by means of offering mouthfuls of water;
then likewise with the giving of sweet foods and the drinking of milk and other such things.
They also performed auspicious and excellent hospitality by offering betel leaves;
they offered various forms of welcome with fans, chowries, the display of the honor of staff-bearers, and the massaging of feet and other services. ||46-47||
Then the glorious primary palanquin of Bālakṛṣṇa was indeed adorned with fine parched grain, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings;
and amidst shouts of "Victory!", the Lord of Śrī descended from the palanquin.

With welcoming words, flower garlands, and even handfuls of flowers, as well as with barley sprouts and sandalwood paste, he was honored; and Śambhu inquired after the welfare of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (1.286.49–50)
The followers of Kṛṣṇa were questioned by the devotees of Śaṅkara regarding their welfare and health;
then likewise the goddesses and maidens, such as Kātyāyanī and others,
as well as Durgā and the rest, and Sati, Kambharā, and other women [were questioned].
The maidens also inquired after their welfare and health.
They welcomed them with water for the feet, the offering of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the gift of desirable food;
they honored them with betel leaves and the like, and worshipped them with garlands and other offerings.
Then, with various seats and acts of service, the women honored the wives of the earth-dwellers and increased their comfort; likewise,
the remover of sorrow [the king] did so with folded hands and by pressing them against his chest.
With the offering of all suitable gifts, honeyed words, and services,
Jaya, Candra, Dhenupāla, and other devotees of Śiva paid honor and extended a warm welcome to the family of Bālakṛṣṇa. (55–56)
Then Queen Aśokasundarī and her female friends welcomed the maidens, beginning with Santuṣṭā;
and ten million maidens of Śāṅkarī also offered them welcome at that time.
They welcomed the maidens with hospitality, offerings, food, and service.
They indeed inquired after the welfare of the subjects and of their offspring;
likewise, the kings then inquired after the well-being of the other monarchs.
Then the gods among the gods, millions upon millions of liberated souls,
and the sages among the sages, inquired after his welfare;
and the lords among the lords offered him a welcome and other marks of hospitality.
Then the groups of women offered their respects to the women.
Śaṅkara said: "I am blessed that the Blessed One himself has come to my house as a mendicant, a worthy recipient of merit for the sake of my daughter."
Blessed is this delightful city of Kāśī and its people as well;
blessed indeed is the goddess Lakṣmī, in whose house the Blessed One himself resides.
I am blessed, for today in my house the liberated souls have truly become the very abode.

For Vāsudeva is the Lord himself, and indeed Viṣṇus and Nārāyaṇas dwell in his house— saints who are equal to Nārāyaṇa. Since sacred pilgrimage sites reside in his home today, I am truly blessed and fortunate.
Blessed are the trees and likewise the creepers; blessed are the insects and the winged creatures;
blessed are those who honor the earth, for here they have union with the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Blessed indeed are those households where there dwell Sāttvatas, devotees of the Lord, and saintly persons.
Even the sages purify the three worlds when they dwell in his house;
today my Kailāsa has become supremely Vaiṣṇava,
for there now dwells in the sky my Lord of Life.
"Today all my attendants have become supreme Vaiṣṇavas;
today my name 'Śiva' has truly become meaningful for me forever.
Having said this, he shed tears of love from his own eyes.
And with joy, he made the three-eyed Lord, who was turbid, free from turbidity.
Then the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa said to Śaṅkara: "O Rādhikā!
We are blessed, for today we have obtained the sight of you."
He who is the very form of the Supreme Brahman, the self-effulgent Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa,
and whose nature is that of Mahākāla— our meeting has taken place in his abode. O Great Yogin, O Cause of the dissolution of the universe, we are blessed!
By a mere fraction of your grace, this son of mine is now worthy of your gift.
Blessed is my young Kṛṣṇa, who shall obtain your daughter—
she who is the mother of all the worlds, the virtuous Brāhmī, the Nārāyaṇī.
"Harikṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka, is present here today together with Rādhā, the gopīs, and others; so too is your father, Śiveśvara.
You shall behold this Supreme Person, whose nature is infinite."
"Having obtained this, we are blessed; what other supreme fortune could we possibly possess?
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kambharā bowed down to Śaṅkara, as well as to Kṛṣṇa and Satī, and then spoke of the greatness of her good fortune.
And Satī spoke of the auspicious greatness of her own fortune:
"Oh, how blessed is my daughter, since the virtuous Kambharā is to be served by her!
Today my home has become sanctified through the arrival of Mahālakṣmī. (78)
And my family shall be sanctified by the arrival of the entire creation;
the sacred field of Kāśikā shall become a bestower of liberation for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman. (1.286.80)
Likewise, from the assembly of the Lords, of the virtuous who bestow liberation,
and from the assembly of chaste women, maidens, and goddesses;
and from the arrival of the Mothers, the Apsarases, and the celestial nymphs of Brahmā.
And from the arrival of the sovereign goddesses, and from the union of Rādhā and Ramā;
from the arrival of Kamalā, Tulasī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, and Śāradā; and from the arrival of Ramā, Padmāvatī, Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, and Vibhūti. (82–83)
Indeed, through the arrival of the Muktānīs, and especially the Vaiṣṇavīs,
as well as the arrival of the devoted queens, I am blessed here today.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and today my actions have become fruitful.
Today my prosperity has become fruitful through the union with Kambharāśrī.
Today my learning has become fruitful; my sovereignty has become fruitful for me.
My male servants and female servants have become fruitful through the union with Kambharāśrī.
Indeed, I am Pārvatī, married in the house of Śiveśvara;
together with my family, I have attained fulfillment, and as the mother of Lakṣmī, I am most auspicious.
Today, Pārvatī realizes her own supreme fortune.
"Since the blessed Lord will indeed take as his daughter the child Kaṃbharā," having said this, she and the others bowed down to Śrī Kaṃbharā.
Then Śrī Kaṃbharā said: "Today, even our own [efforts] have reached fulfillment."
"In whose house we come and behold the virtuous Girijā,
in my house the daughter of Satī, Lakṣmī, will also arrive.
She who nourishes all the worlds— surely this is my supreme good fortune here."
The virtuous Brāhmī shall become worthy of honoring my son.
Since the three worlds are dissolved by the mere glance of her eye,
she is today worthy of honoring my son, and my son is worthy of honoring her.
"Aho! My good fortune in the three worlds is such that no other possesses its equal!
Having said this, the virtuous Kaṃbharā then bowed down to Satī.
Then the goddess Pārvatī, having honored all the women who had arrived for a moment, [dismissed them].
Having repeatedly offered a welcome with the *madhuparka* and other honors,
and by providing them with the drinking of nectar and the serving of sweet milk,
the two brothers, Jayacandra and [his companion], then rested in joy. (94–95)
Reflecting upon their own good fortune, the two rejoiced intensely;
the party of the bridegroom ceased, and a sound of "Brahman" arose.
Then, indeed, the army of Kṛṣṇa set out toward the city of Śiva.
Nandīśvara indeed uttered the Brahma-sound again and again.
Then Bṛhaspati, having worshipped Hari, arose; and after resting, the men and women then stood up.
O Rādhā! Listen to how it became a source of great wonder, a marvelous and extraordinary marvel for all to return to their dwellings:
everyone said that they must go toward the city of Śiveśvara.
By what method did [he] leave Kailāsa from the sky?
At that very moment, indeed, Śambhu swiftly brought down the entirety of Kailāsa slowly by means of his power of yoga.

Then, having descended toward the earth as was appropriate— toward the city of Śiveśvara and the entire city of Kailāsa, which is a city created by Śiva— he entered into internal absorption within that formless state.
In the gardens there were then other gardens, and in the groves,
other groves; likewise, in the palaces there were then invisible palaces,
and in the abodes of celestial chariots, there were then celestial chariots.
Indeed, those very lords of the earth for whose sake the dwellings had previously been prepared sat there in those residences,
filled with happiness; and the maidens sat in the maidens' quarters.
In the dwellings of kings, there were kings; in the dwellings of the virtuous, the virtuous;
in the dwellings of sages, the sages; in the dwellings of gods, the deities;
in the dwellings of lords, the lords; and in the dwellings of the liberated, the liberated. (1.06–1.07)
O Rādhikā, Hari resides in the abode of Kṛṣṇa, while others reside in other abodes; indeed, according to their respective fitness, they dwell throughout the three worlds,
for at that time, residence in the three worlds became their natural state.
Mount Kailāsa appeared as if it had dissolved away, and the city of Śiva was visible.
Having quickly reached their dwellings, they performed the purification of bathing;
thereafter, they indeed took their meals in magnificent mansions.
They took betel-leaf and then took their rest;
having beheld sights that delighted the mind, they then fell asleep.
At that time, male and female servants performed services such as massaging their bodies.
Śiveśvara and the others returned to their own homes at night.
(1.12) The honored guests from the bride’s side, having partaken of an excellent meal, obtained rest and sleep; O Rādhikā, we became happy. (1.13)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Welcome, Celebration, Worship, and Honor accorded by Śaṅkara in his many forms to Kṛṣṇavāhinī with musical instruments on the celestial Kailāsa; the mutual inquiries regarding welfare and health among the men and women; the disappearance of Kailāsa; the descent into Śivapura; the taking of food and so forth; and the rest at night," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. 286.

Chapter 288 →
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā! Having attained happiness through their services, those great souls then became enjoyers of unprecedented bliss in the city of Śiva. 1.
On the morning of the fourth lunar day, people gather there in the divine city of Śiva, where everything follows one's intention;
they do so with auspicious musical instruments and songs that proclaim his glory.
Those who considered themselves great abandoned sleep and bathed with prior purification.
They worshipped Hari, performed their private Vedic study, and engaged in recitations and other rites.
Auspicious songs of maidens also arose there.
In every house and courtyard, decorative patterns were created using curd, barley sprouts, saffron filaments, and various pigments such as saffron; likewise,
svastikas and lotuses were fashioned in every city.
Arches were erected and banners were fastened;
the sounds of musical instruments resounded in the pavilion and in every house.
Then, in the morning, the ritual preparations were also carried out with warm water and other materials.

In the morning, however, all of them partook of milk and sweet foods as they desired, which were provided by Śivasvāmin; at that time, the honoring of the elders was also performed in a fitting manner. (8)
Then the daughter of Śiva, having bathed, adorned, and decorated herself, bowed again and again to her father and likewise to her mother; accompanied by her friends,
she was beautiful with a face like ten million moons and graced by every ornament.
Accompanied by the ritual materials for the worship of the family deity,
the virtuous Durgā set out on foot to worship Hanumān;
she was joined by ten million maidens and attended by women endowed with great beauty and auspicious fortune.
Accompanied by female singers and delighted by the sound of musical instruments,
she was surrounded by women with golden jars upon their heads; indeed,
she was also surrounded by virgins carrying the five products of the cow and other offerings.
Accompanied by those who possessed the materials for worship and were endowed with beauty, 13.
and who were radiant like fire, clad in fine garments, and increased her good fortune—she first went and worshipped the supreme goddess Durgā. 14.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), sandalwood paste and other substances, milk, and waters from sacred fords;
with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, musk, and liquid saffron filaments;
with fragrant flowers, garlands, and other offerings, as well as milk-pudding (pāyasa) and other food offerings. || 16 ||
With sweet foods, drinks, and the like, with betel leaves and gold, (16) with sacrificial fees,
vessels, and lustration rites, as well as with hymns of praise,
circumambulations, prostrations, and requests for forgiveness for one's offenses. (17)
Then he worshipped Durgā, and likewise offered her a skirt and a bodice; having presented a girdle, a night-garment, anklets, and rings,
as well as chains, a waist-belt, golden necklaces, and auspicious gems.
Bracelets, bangles, finger-rings, and lotuses;
strings of pearls, necklaces, golden earrings, as well as leaf-patterned ornaments, crescent-moon ornaments on the forearms, armlets, and other such decorations. (2.287.19–20)
He gave everything to the goddess Durgā and then spoke:
"O Mother, may there be no obstacle to my union with the Blessed One and to our marriage. O Durgā, you must always look after me wherever I go."
Durgā also, O Rādhikā, laughed there and said, "So be it.
(22) Having thus worshipped Durgā and obtained her gracious blessing, she went to Śrī Hanumān for the sake of penance, he who provides refuge. (23)
Having gone and bowed to the son of Vāyu, the divine brother of Śaṅkara,
he offered the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), water, sandalwood paste, a garland of arka flowers,
saffron, unbroken grains of rice, a golden garland, and vermilion.
Having given oil, fragrant essences, ornaments, and garments;
having given sugar, *vaṭaka* cakes, and auspicious sweet foods;
and having given drinking water, mouth-cleansing materials, fruit, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), as well as hymns of praise and circumambulation, Lakṣmī requested forgiveness from him who is the companion to the perfection of asceticism:
"O brother, you who bring about the yoga of the Blessed One, protect me always. (27)
"May my excellent union with Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, be free from obstacles;
may I be happy with the Lord of the World as my protector—act accordingly.
Thus entreated, Hanumān indeed spoke to his sister: |||29||

"So be it; may you always be possessed of good fortune, O remover of sorrow! Then, having bowed and received his favor, she returned with her companions to the Lord of the Universe, her father, who was staying in his palace.
Having bathed Viśveśvara in many ways with milk,
honey, curd, ghee, sugar, and water from sacred fords (tīrtha),
and having worshipped him with sandalwood paste, he offered the ritual food (naivedya).
Then, having performed the *ārārtrika* rite, he asked for forgiveness and entreated for compassion;
he also prayed for freedom from obstacles in his auspicious undertaking, and [the deity] replied, "So be it.
His father, Viśveśvara, spoke thus, and he then went to Annapūrṇikā.
Having thus worshipped the Mother and likewise offered her ornaments,
he presented the food offering and then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
He then drew a crescent moon with unbroken grains of rice upon her forehead, making her "Annapūrṇā" (the one who is full of food).
"May you possess unbroken good fortune and eternal life," he said,
and then the girl, having bowed to Gaṇeśa, gave her blessing.
Having worshipped Sarasvatī with dūrvā grass, vermilion, and sweetmeats, [she offered the same to him].
He went to the Gaṅgā and to Pañcagaṅgā, and he worshipped the god Dharma. Having bowed down and having given gifts consisting indeed of gold and silver,
as well as necklaces of gems, rubies, pearls, and jewels.
Then, having received the blessings of the subjects,
the virtuous lady bowed to Śivapura and departed for her own home.
At midday, she then gave food to all her female companions.
Lakṣmī, eager for the service, performed the distribution of food to her female companions.
Then, millions of women from the cities and mountain regions of Himavat sat in rows on all sides and ate sweet foods.
Indeed, from children to the elderly, the women became fully satiated with the foods;
likewise, the women destined for the city of Śiva and the noble ladies,
as well as all the maidens and others, partook of the meals.
Then the people dwelling in both cities ate;
so too did the subjects residing in the palace of Śiva-rāja and those of Kāśī.
The lords, the gods, and human beings—by the crores, by the billions, and by the hundreds of millions—partook of the meal.
Unwholesome and deluding foods such as black-gram *laḍḍūs*, fine pearls (*sumauktika*), powdered *laḍḍūs*,
milk-preparations (*dugdhapāka*), rice-puddings (*pāyasa*), milk-balls (*kṣīrapolikā*),
sweet *polīs*, *pūrikās*, *sūtrapheṇī*, and *barphikā*.
Dugdhasāra, biraja, śaṣkulī, khājaka, and baṭī; apūpa, pūpa, saṃyāva, bindu, laḍḍu, and prabharjikā;
śrīkhaṇḍa, śatacchidra, jāmbūka, and likewise ghevara. ||46–47||
Balls of flour (*piṇḍaka*), as well as knotted sweets (*granthaka*), *kalikā*, and *ghurghura*;
*vaṭa* cakes, *phullavaṭī*, and almonds coated in sugar;
chickpeas, rice, and both roasted and boiled grains.

Soup and rice, various boiled dishes and diverse vegetables; (49) various kinds of vessels, as well as *sudhā* and *amṛtaka* sweets; buttermilk, drinkable substances, foods to be chewed, and excellent fruits. (2.287.50)
Savors, linctuses, edible grains, and sour gruels; parched grains, fried snacks, and prepared alkaline preparations;
likewise, sweet fruits and whatever seeds are fresh.
Likewise, śimbikā, vallā, gundrapāka and so forth;
various kinds of kandapāka, the most excellent phalapāka, even rājikārāddha, and whatever fruit powders there may be. (52–53)
They ate wild tubers and cultivated roots, as well as medicinal herbs that ripen without being tilled;
they consumed various delicious foods produced by the wish-fulfilling trees,
and they drank, especially, the nectar of immortality.
Hara bestowed upon each of them the various foods characteristic of their respective worlds; Hara gave to each of them the various drinks belonging to those specific regions;
and he provided beautiful betel leaves, along with sweet-smelling mouth-cleansers.
The illustrious Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, gave vegetable gardens;
then the great lords, as well as the guests, the mendicants, the wretched people, the destitute, and both men and women, partook [of them]. (57)
The laborers, as well as the servants, male and female slaves, attendants, and sub-attendants;
the courtiers, gatekeepers, and likewise the servers; the guards and the lookouts—all of them partook [of the meal] with delighted minds. (58–59)
Inanimate beings as well as sentient ones, lords, gods, and humans;
those dwelling in the three worlds and all the great beings here—
every one of them became truly fully satisfied by those excellent foods.
Then, for a moment, all the great lords attained rest. Thereafter, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śivā, assuming the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, went quickly to ascertain the firmness of Śiva’s devotion.
Going to Lord Śiva in secret, he said: "Listen, my dear one!
Whether my son is worthy or unworthy, listen here as I speak of him.
May you know him; however I describe him, you shall know him. (63)
"This son of Patnīvratā is indeed a brahmin who lives as a mendicant.
He is Bālakṛṣṇa by name, a youth of humble birth.
A daughter must never be given to a mendicant by a king under any circumstances. (64–65)
A daughter should never, under any circumstances, be given in marriage to one residing abroad; rather, the giving of a daughter in happiness is auspicious when it is to one of equal caste.
But in this world, there would be suffering through union with one of a different caste—of this there is no doubt.
Moreover, this Kṛṣṇa appears weak in body;
even though he is the son of you, Dhavalā, he does not shine in his youth. Furthermore, I shall tell you another thing: he appears ancient.

O Indra among kings, how can this delicate girl, who has seen but few years, be given away? Furthermore, if you desire the eternal happiness of the maiden, then the princess must not be given to the prince. ||69||
Bālakṛṣṇa has indeed arrived here together with ten million wives.
In that context, how insignificant will this young girl be in the calculation?
Furthermore, the quarreling of co-wives is more unbearable than fire.
Listen further: likewise, he indeed possesses the nature of devouring all;
he consumes everything offered by all, yet he does not possess even a single dharma.
Furthermore, he is always free from deceit and devoid of the guṇas.

Moreover, he constantly abides devoted to the conduct of a sage; he does not even know how to enjoy pleasures, for he is devoid of desire. He possesses the nature of illusion, yet he does not know how to employ that illusion. (73–74)
Behold, his father is a cowherd whose occupation is like that of a cowherd;
he is named Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, one who relies on a different occupation.
A daughter should not be given by a Kṣatriya to a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of a different occupation. (75)
"Having understood this in every way, do as you wish.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Bālakṛṣṇaka ceased speaking.
But Viśveśvara, having bowed to his father, reflected and spoke.
O Father, the destiny of your daughter was ordained long ago;
her marriage shall take place there with one in the form of a brahmin.
Indeed, Mahāviṣṇu himself, devoted to his wife, dwells here upon this earth.

By my very vision of yoga, I know that son to be the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). He is always a mendicant for his devoted followers who are full of affection; yet he himself abides as the Supreme Brahman. How then could my daughter not be given to him? (2.287.80)
Lord Hari, the bestower of welfare upon the ignorant, remains for the sake of the distressed;
He brings about both worldly prosperity and liberation for those who are pure yet possessed of a childish nature.
Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the Master and Sovereign of the Imperishable Abode, dwells there.

"O Great King, my daughter must be given by me to the mendicant Śārṅgin; for in that there lies the arising of the attainment of fame. Since he is a foreigner and the imperishable Brahman, why indeed should she not be given to him? (82–83)
By birth my daughter is equal to a Brāhmaṇa; indeed, she is a Brāhmaṇī.
Birth is never found to be inherent in the body alone; it always arises from one's qualities.
My daughter is the Fortune of Brahman (Brāhmī Lakṣmī); she is united with Brahman.
This one is Kṛṣṇa because he draws away (saṃkarṣaṇa) evil, and likewise because he leads [beings] to his own abode,
just as you do.
He is the ancient Puruṣa, known by the name Puruṣottama.
My ancient maiden is Nārāyaṇī, the supreme among persons;
all the bodies of the one known as Puruṣottama are considered to be his progeny. All those wives of the capable Hari are likewise his offspring; there is no fault in this.
Today, the offering of Bali is seen by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is capable of accepting it;
he is the foremost among all [goddesses], and that status is most excellent.
There is no rivalry before Kṛṣṇa, for he is the remover of passion and hatred.
Indeed, it is fitting that this Supreme Self is the devourer of all;
for the Lord, whose nature is all-dharma and who upholds dharma, has ornaments as his very adornment. Where Māyā, which bestows bondage, does not exist, its qualities do not exist either.
He alone is one who conducts himself rightly, the bestower of the fruits of all actions. He alone conducts himself according to justice and remains non-violent.
He always abides as a silent sage (muni), for the Vedas are indeed his very breath.
They constantly sing his excellent qualities, and silence itself is his ornament.
O Father, desire arises repeatedly in one who is incomplete;
but for him who is filled with all prosperity and who bears all bliss, [desire does not arise]. (93)
The absence of desire in Kṛṣṇa, who is the soul of all, is indeed a great virtue;
for he, who is supreme, does not know that pleasure which arises from sense objects.
My daughter likewise remains so, being devoted to Māyā and consisting of the nature of Ramā.
This Supreme Lord is the giver of bondage and the destroyer of *prakṛti*;
He never practices deception, for He is indeed beyond *māyā*.
You are Gopāla, and He is your father; He too is Gopāla, and He is his father as well.
The union of the two Vaiśyas here has come about solely through destiny (bhāgya).
Since the root *viś* means "to enter," He is the Lord who enters within as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*).
Lakṣmī is the one who has entered into all three worlds as their internal regulator.
The union of these two is always considered appropriate and is ever praised;
for the Kṣatriya is the perpetual protector of those who dwell in his shelter.
How indeed could the Blessed Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa not be a Kṣatriya?
"My daughter is a Kṣatriya, and the Blessed One is also a Kṣatriya.
By good fortune, there is a union between these two dark-complexioned ones; their marriage appears auspicious to me. Therefore, father, I do not approve of your suspicion. (2.287.100–101)
Upon hearing him speak thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his heart gladdened within, said to his son, "So be it," and departed from there.
Then, O Rādhikā, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself [proceeded].

And Śāṃbhavī, wishing to understand [the situation], departed for her home having assumed the form of a woman. Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious Rites Performed at Dawn on the Fourth Day in the Second Section (Tretā-santāna) of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the worship of the family deity performed by the girls, the feeding of the honored guests, the dialogue between Bāla-Kṛṣṇa (in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa) and Śiveśvara regarding the non-giving of the girl, and their subsequent replies. *** **Chapter 288** Then Śāṃbhavī, having become a woman, went to her own abode. There she saw her husband, who was seated upon a throne, surrounded by his ministers and attendants. She approached him with great humility and spoke these words: "O Lord of the World, O Bestower of Boons, please grant me this favor. I have come here to see you; I am your wife, Śāṃbhavī. I have been born as a woman due to a curse. Therefore, O Great God, please show me compassion. Hearing these words of his wife, the lord of the world smiled and said: "O Goddess, do not grieve. You shall soon regain your own original form. Having spoken thus, he gave her a divine garland and sandalwood paste. He then bestowed upon her a boon that she would never again experience the suffering of old age or death. Having granted her this supreme blessing, the Lord vanished from that place. Meanwhile, the father of the girl, having heard everything that had transpired, became filled with joy. He then summoned all the elders of the lineage and the priests and said: "Today, my daughter has attained a most auspicious state. Let the marriage rites be performed according to the prescribed rules. The elders and the priests, being highly pleased, replied: "O King, this is indeed a great fortune for you. Today is an excellent day, and the moon is in a favorable position. Let the wedding be celebrated with great splendor. The king, delighted by these words, immediately ordered the preparation of the wedding pavilion and the necessary materials. He then invited the bridegroom’s party, including the groom’s parents and kinsmen, and welcomed them with great honor. On the appointed day, the marriage ceremony commenced. The bridegroom, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, appeared resplendent in his divine form. The father of the girl offered the hand of his daughter to the groom. After the sacred fire was kindled and the mantras were recited, the couple were united in marriage. The gods showered flowers from the heavens, and celestial music resounded everywhere. After the marriage was concluded, the bridegroom’s party stayed for several days. They were provided with every luxury—exquisite food, garments, and ornaments. Finally, taking leave of the bride’s family with affectionate blessings, they returned to their own abode, praising the magnanimity of the host. Meanwhile, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa remained with his wife in the palace, enjoying the fruits of their union. Thus concludes the description of the marriage of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa and the fulfillment of the divine plan. *** **Chapter 289** One day, while Bāla-Kṛṣṇa was seated with his wife in a secluded chamber, the sage Nārada arrived there. Seeing the sage, the Lord rose to greet him and offered him a seat. Nārada, having accepted the hospitality, sat down and began to speak: "O Child of the Yadu dynasty, I have come to see you. I wish to hear from you about the nature of the Supreme Reality and the path to liberation. Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, bowing before the sage, replied: "O Holy One, you are the knower of all things. Please instruct me in the truth of the Self and the means to attain eternal peace. Nārada then explained the nature of the three qualities (guṇas), the cycle of birth and death, and the necessity of detachment from worldly objects. He described the practice of yoga, the importance of devotion (bhakti), and the ultimate goal of realizing the identity of the individual soul with the Supreme Brahman. Upon hearing these teachings, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa attained a state of profound realization. He understood that all forms are manifestations of the one Absolute, and that true happiness lies in the service of the Divine. The sage Nārada, having imparted this wisdom, took his leave and departed. Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, now firmly established in spiritual knowledge, continued to rule the kingdom with righteousness and compassion, bringing prosperity to all his subjects. Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Sage Nārada and the Instruction on Spiritual Knowledge," in the second section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. *** **Chapter 290** In the course of time, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa and his wife Śāṃbhavī begot many sons and daughters. As the children grew, they were educated in the traditional sciences and arts. The king ensured that his offspring were virtuous and well-prepared to carry on the lineage. Once, during a festival, the sage Vyāsa visited the city. Bāla-Kṛṣṇa received him with great reverence and requested him to perform the thread ceremony (Upanayana) for his sons. Vyāsa, being pleased, initiated the princes and taught them the Vedas and the sacred scriptures. Under the guidance of Vyāsa, the princes became learned in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. They mastered the art of governance and the principles of warfare. The king was deeply satisfied with their progress and entrusted the administration of various provinces to them. As the years passed, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa realized that his life on earth was drawing to a close. He called together his ministers, his sons, and his spiritual preceptors to discuss the future of the kingdom. He advised them to remain united, to uphold justice, and to always remember the divine grace that sustained them. Finally, after making arrangements for the succession and offering prayers to the Lord, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa ascended to the heavenly realm, where he rejoined his divine parents, Śiva and Pārvatī. His wife Śāṃbhavī, following him, attained the same exalted state. The descendants of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa ruled the earth for many generations, spreading the fame of their ancestor. Their lineages multiplied, and their stories became legends told by the wise. Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Lineage of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa and the Attainment of Liberation," in the second section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. *** **Chapter 291** Now, let us turn our attention to the other side of the narrative. When the news of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa’s departure reached the mortal world, the people mourned his loss. However, the divine plan was fulfilled, and the balance of the universe was restored. In the meantime, the sage Śukra, who had been observing the events from afar, came to the court of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa’s father. He wished to offer his condolences and to advise the king on how to console his subjects. Śukra spoke: "O King, do not grieve for your son. He has returned to his eternal abode. His deeds were noble, and his legacy will endure. Remember that all beings are subject to the laws of time and destiny. By performing righteous acts and remaining devoted to the Divine, you shall find peace. The king, comforted by these words, resolved to live a life of virtue. He dedicated himself to the service of the people, ensuring that no one suffered want or injustice. Under his rule, the land prospered, and the citizens lived in harmony. This chapter concludes the account of the earthly life of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa and the impact of his presence upon the world. It serves as a reminder of the transient nature of human existence and the enduring power of divine love. Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Consolation of the King by Sage Śukra and the Legacy of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa," in the second section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Sa
