Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, thereafter the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa,
having himself assumed the form of Rādhā, went to the home of Śrī Pārvatī.
Seeing you, her daughter-in-law Pārvatī rose and offered a seat.
In private, Rādhikā said to her, "Listen to what is beneficial:
she is called 'mother' because she should always be a bringer of welfare to her daughter. (2)
One should not look merely at the act of giving; rather, one must consider its future consequence. (3) It is the considered opinion that a daughter born later will be eternally happy.
Among women, if there is suffering, co-wifely rivalry is the greatest of all. (4)
Today I have heard that he to whom my daughter is to be given is indeed a husband who, since childhood, has been the lord of ten million women on this earth;
and all those women have come here together with their fathers and other kinsmen.
This is evident: there, your daughter would be sorrowful.
I have a misgiving regarding that; therefore, O Pārvatī, she should not be given.
For in the company of many women, enjoyments indeed become divided.
Even if there were divisions of wealth sufficient for them, they would not be satisfied;
for indeed, the women of a man who possesses many wives do not reach satiety. Truly, everything belongs to kings who possess sovereignty over the earth.
"But this brahmin here is a son-in-law who performs the duties of a vaiśya.
He has no village, nor a garden, nor a field, nor a shop or the like. His livelihood consists solely of alms; how then can my daughter be happy? (2.288.10)
Indeed, she possesses no wealth within her home, yet she displays great abundance outwardly;
even though she was offered in marriage according to Nārada’s words, she is separated from him at the very moment of the betrothal.
Therefore, Lakṣmī should not be given away, for though she appears most happy, she will become a source of misery.
"Speak, daughter-in-law, what is your opinion in this matter, as I have spoken with a burning heart:
A daughter should be given to one who is free from disease, a youth of good character, well-disciplined, wealthy, handsome, and who has not yet taken a second wife. (12-13)

To one who has a family, who is established in stability, who possesses wealth in cattle, who is endowed with great intelligence, who is joined with prosperity acquired by his own arms, who is distinguished by virtues,
who is renowned, who is capable, and who fulfills desires. (14)
Regarding the wife as a deity, a daughter should be given to the illustrious Rāma, who is endowed with righteousness and possesses great wisdom;
thereafter, other qualities should be examined, foremost among them being the absence of co-wives. (15–16)
Rivalry between co-wives is indeed the foremost corruption in a household and leads always to hell;
furthermore, the respect due to one's children may certainly not exist at all, or it may be as unstable as the moon’s partiality toward Rohiṇī. (17)

"O daughter-in-law, just as in former times Kali was born from Virajā and Rādhā, so too did he exist in Goloka; because of that, there was indeed the suffering of co-wifely rivalry. Therefore, do what is appropriate for me, as it has occurred to my mind. (18–19)
Thus, O Rādhikā! Having heard these words of Rādhā, Pārvatī—the beloved of Śiva and Īśvara, the worshipful one—spoke this supreme conclusion:
"This Bālakṛṣṇa is meritorious; he is the eternal Supreme Brahman."
The Lord is full bliss, like the ocean is to rivers;
he shines forth, replete with prosperity, replete with valor, and replete with qualities.
Indeed, the entire circle of creation has arisen from him alone.
O Lord, for that master whose desires are fulfilled, there is indeed neither disease nor anxiety;
for this undisturbed yogin, the state of perpetual youth always abides.
Moreover, his vow known as *śīla* is proclaimed in the Upaniṣads.
And this yogi, a knower of yoga, is always possessed of cessation.
He by whom all wealth was created is indeed the most excellent of merchants;
by him the earth was made, and by him the Vasus were fashioned.
And because he was fashioned as Kubera by him, he became the wealthiest of all; moreover, for however many wives he may have, he possesses that many bodies,
and he enjoys each wife separately and always remains distinct from one another.
Therefore, having two wives is not a defect for him, who is like the moon;
he, being possessed of beautiful form, became a counterpart to every form.
And his family exists in the imperishable abode, being beyond counting.
Of whom alone there exist reflections in the form of millions of incarnations—
lords, Manus, Rudras, world-protectors, and Viṣṇus;
of this very one there are also the incarnations of the Ādityas and the stainless sages.
"I have heard that his family is universal;
yet this Supreme Person dwells with equanimity toward all,
or even with greater affection until satisfaction arises."
Whether situated in a state of prosperity or adversity, he is the bestower of happiness upon his wife. Furthermore, you and I both consider the wealth of cattle to be the most excellent in Goloka;
it is well-known that wish-fulfilling cows are always present for his service.
The entire earth belongs to him, for kings are his fathers-in-law;
the wealth acquired by his own arms is seen here in person.
Indeed, his pilgrimage to Kāśī is accompanied by ten million creations.
His mother is Mahālakṣmī herself who shines forth;
his father is Mahāviṣṇu Gopāla, the creator of the universe.
Furthermore, the eight great qualities taught in the Vedas are present here.
In the Supreme Lord, there are eternal qualities such as being free from sin;
likewise, truth, purity, and other such qualities— thirty-nine in total—
and indeed innumerable qualities exist here, eternally united with Him.
His fame exists in the Vedas, in his abodes, and even among the lords;
among the gods, in the world of men, and even in all the netherworlds.
He is capable and he is the giver of liberation; for the sake of liberation, this maiden has been offered by me.
"She has been given, and she is even being given; what cause for lamentation is there?
This Supreme Lord exists as the fulfiller of desires;
He is the one who fulfills the wishes of His devotees and the fulfiller of all desires. (2.288.40)
That true lord considers his wife to be equal to a deity;
he is the giver of happiness, endowed with fame, for he is indeed Rāma, the one who brings delight.
He bears the burden of all dharma, he is wise, and he is ancient.

Moreover, there is never any rivalry among co-wives here, even when one is joined with many wives. (42) Here, there is no deficiency in qualities or sovereignty, by which [the state] remains constant like that of Dhruva;
nor can it ever be otherwise than like the Moon or like Goloka. (43)
In his hand there are signs— the fish, the banner, and the bow—

as well as the arrow, the trident, the svastika, the wheel, the staff, and other marks belonging to the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, the physical characteristics described in the *Sāmudrika* [treatises] are indeed present upon his body.
I have heard all of that from the mouth of Nārada:
that the girl was given to the Supreme Lord, the worthy recipient in that particular place.
Therefore, O Mother, my daughter is truly fortunate and blessed with happiness.
Having obtained the most excellent boon, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
she formerly performed severe penance in her childhood on the Himālayas at Hanūmat’s hermitage; there he appeared, assuming a divine form.
Having granted his boon to Lakṣmī as her husband, he vanished from sight.
Then my daughter returned home and told me that news;
since then, she has waited for twelve years.
The fourteenth year of Kṛṣṇa’s own [cycle] has been declared to be complete.
Indeed, this most excellent time has arrived;
the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, has come to my home. (2.288.50)
Today I have accomplished my purpose, for the Supreme Person is worthy of my worship.
His mother, Mahālakṣmī, is endowed with great fortune.
And my daughter—your granddaughter, O noble lady—is likewise one who has fulfilled her life’s task.
Thus addressed, Rādhikā observed silence and, having offered her blessing, departed for her own abode; she too vanished from sight.
Bālakṛṣṇa, however, firmly perceived the deep affection of his two elderly parents for him.
Extremely delighted,
Bālakṛṣṇa, in the form of a brahmin, went in private to Lakṣmī and spoke words that reached her heart:
"Listen, daughter, I have heard that your marriage is about to take place."
"A Brahmin has also come here to marry the princess.
I have heard that this mendicant, deprived of his kingdom, is staying on the shore of the ocean;
indeed, he is just like a fisherman, and so too is this cowherd. || 55-56 ||
"In his house there is indeed no abundance, yet he observes the vow of a bridegroom;
however, even though he is a prince, he is not the husband of ten million women.
I have heard that he is of such a nature, and women have indeed come here for him."
For there are indeed women here who stand with you for the same purpose;
they will come to the pavilion and circumambulate it clockwise.
Having established the fire as witness here, those two daughters of yours shall [face] their co-wives.
"What is this that pleases you? Why do you choose that brahmin as your husband in the pavilion when he has many wives? O princess, do not choose him;
rather, choose a king, O queen of kings, for he is indeed a portion of Nārāyaṇa."
He is most righteous, venerable, and a bestower of all prosperity.
And you, O beautiful one, remain there— charming, honored among beautiful women,
endowed with fresh youth, and radiant with splendor, a virtuous lady.
She possessed the luster of molten gold and was the very embodiment of pure being;
she was devoted to her husband, truthful in character, peaceful, and endowed with the most excellent virtues.
She was Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Rohiṇī, and Kalāvatī.
You are Svāhā, Saṃjñā, Sāvitrī, and Kuberaṇī; you are known as such.
Among other excellent beauties, you shine forth as the most excellent.
Rich with the splendor of the full autumn moon, you have eyes like autumn lotuses.
"O Indra among kings, do not choose a Brahmin, a mendicant who dwells afar.
Having heard this, the maiden spoke to her husband in his own Brahmin form:
"You are a Brahmin; you are worthy of my worship. Do not speak those words again."
Otherwise, you would deserve punishment, since you have come here as a mendicant; for whether he be of such a kind or of another,
he was first examined by me and subsequently accepted by me.
He whose sovereignty indeed extends over the entire earth and comprises the three worlds—
this omniscient lord, a fisherman, dwells upon the shore of the Ocean of Milk.
And he shines as the protector of both cows and splendors.
And all prosperities belong to him, because this world belongs to the Lord (Īśāvāsya).
Indeed, he who is devoted to his beloved always observes the vow of devotion;
even though he is the husband of ten million women, he is ever possessed of the highest state of being.
"This youth always remains [here]; I know him from a previous birth.
Thus he is indeed known as one whose vital energy is unbroken and upward-directed, and who is skilled in ritual application.
O Brahmin, even if there were tens of millions of women here in my pavilion,"
They shall wander about at my back, and therein I shall have honor;
for among all my co-wives, I shall be the one most highly revered.
Let there be ten million women in the presence of Agni as witnesses to my equality! 73–74.

May my respect for him increase even further than this; for if the Lord were to appear in his full perfection, what wish could I possibly choose? Just as he is a dweller in a distant land, so too am I a dweller in a distant land.
O Brahmin, do not harbor anxiety; the union of these two is indeed fitting.
Indra and the other gods are under his control, while Brahmā and the others are under his control as well.
The Vairāja and other beings are under his control, and even the Vyūhas are under his control.
Under his influence, what maiden would not choose him as her husband?
You surely know the ancient narrative declared in the Vedas; do not hear it again.
Out of compassion, the Lord himself, the Consort of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), [has acted].
Indeed, for the sake of uplifting all people and his devotees in every way,
this very Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Being,
dwells in the noble home of Gopālakṛṣṇa by the side of Śrī Kambharā.
He is the Supreme Lord, the husband of the virtuous Rādhā and Ramā;
he is the creator of the Creator, worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Śeṣa.
The Blessed One is the very nature of light, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest.
Untainted, desireless, and the witness of all actions, he dwells in the heart and resides in all things; for his sake have I come here.
From before, I choose him alone as my abode, and no other.
O Brahmin, I have surrendered my very self to that Supreme Self alone;
the line inscribed by the Creator for His sake is mine.
Behold that Supreme Self, whose form consists of grace toward His devotees.

O best of Brahmins, by beholding him— who is the cause for following the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and who eternally possesses a divine and beautiful form— effect the destruction of the karma of your own birth. He is one whom the four Vedas and even the virtuous deities do not know.
Even the lords of the senses, the lords of sages, the gods beginning with Brahmā,
and even yogis absorbed in meditation, do not reach him whom they contemplate.
Sarasvatī herself becomes paralyzed when it comes to describing him.
Even Śeṣa has a thousand faces, and Sadāśiva has five;
the Creator of the world has four faces, as do Kumāra and Kārtika.
The sages and the seers are also devotees who are supreme Vaiṣṇavas. (88–89)
O best of Brahmins, he whom even the gods are unable to praise and who is unattainable through meditation by yogis—I am but a young girl; what can I say of his hosts?
O Brahmin, I have always chosen him, and for his sake alone am I a woman of passion.
And I, a maiden, am for that purpose—the daughter of the Lord of the Universe.
Having become a devoted daughter here on earth, I seek the Blessed One.
For that which is called "chastity" (pātivratya) is indeed that which resides in the heart while one is still a maiden.
The Lord, held within the mind, is indeed one's constant life;
the offering of the heart is truly accomplished by means of the heart.
The offering of the gross body, however, occurs later through the gross body.
For the sake of the flow of worldly transactions, this gross [self] has been imagined to exist in the world.
Know this very thing from me today; go and behold it, until you have seen the Great Lord who is the beloved of all. (94–95)
"O Brahmin, you have spoken here to me something that should not be heard; therefore, bear my forgiveness—[the Lord] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of the Life-breath of Śrī.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: 'If such steadfastness as this exists in you...'"
"Whatever I have said must be forgiven; I am departing, so look upon me again.
Having spoken thus, he gave her a golden ring engraved with his own name, and he granted her a vision of his divine form as a token for recognition.

Seeing her lord, the son of a brahmin, shining with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments, and graced by the conch, discus, mace, lotus, yellow garments, and so forth— seeing him as he truly was, Lakṣmī [was filled with joy].
She quickly fell at his feet and embraced him for a moment.
Having spoken these sweet and pleasing words, "My dear, I shall return in the evening," she,
overflowing with joy, suddenly vanished from sight.
With her mind absorbed in Him, she did not perceive herself there for even a moment;
gradually attaining His manifestation, her body filled with joy,
O Rādhikā, that best of women considered her own fortune to be blessed.
Guarding her dignity, she did not speak this when it was revealed.
Thus, the Blessed One, knowing her state of mind while assuming another form,
became subject to the devotion of those devotees who offer themselves to Him.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between Bālakṛṣṇa in the form of Rādhā and Pārvatī regarding 'A Daughter Must Not Be Given,' the Dialogue between [Bālakṛṣṇa] in the form of a Brāhmaṇa and Lakṣmī regarding 'Do Not Choose a Brāhmaṇa Beggar,' their Subsequent Responses, and the Firmness [of Their Resolve]," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 289: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 289.
[The Author: Chapter 290.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Now indeed, O Rādhikā! during that third watch...
Having drunk the milk-water, the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa was then [honored] by great souls,
eminent persons, deities and the like,
together with kings and auspicious women. (1–2)
In spacious vessels made of gold and silver,
he prepared divine garments and ornaments for the sake of the maiden,
as well as all kinds of jewelry and various necklaces.
All jewels of good fortune and all articles that bring about auspiciousness;
indeed, hundreds of kinds of fresh substances for auspiciousness and perfumes; and all varieties of sweet foods, betel leaves, and so forth. (4–5)
He also placed within golden vessels excellent and auspicious objects that were the very height of wonder,
as well as beautiful golden bells of many different colors.
There were garments purified by fire, numbering in the hundreds, as well as gold-embroidered cloths (7). Others were made of silk, featuring various colors and diverse patterns;
they were adorned with rows of golden stars, possessed golden borders, and were set with diamonds (8).
There were golden-colored and red-colored bodices set with jewels;
silken garments beautified by knots and strings of silver necklaces; and likewise delightful *colikā* tunics, shining with a hundred silver ornaments.
And there were priceless hair-cloths and also priceless *kucalī* garments;
there were also priceless *caṭṭikā* cloths and golden coverings.
There were also golden tubes and golden waist-bands for the body.
Garlands with their clusters, armlets, and priceless hair-bands;
breast-covers, waist-bands, and whatever else was intended for concealment;
silken garments and fine clothes cut into hundreds of pieces.
Then the father had those two golden garlands placed in golden vessels,
and he also had two soft sandals,
dyed and resembling land-lotuses, laid down in a hundred places.
All those very beautiful hair-preparations,
as well as other Viṣṇu-oils and likewise fragrant essences,
and the pastes of musk and the like, and those made from sandalwood and so forth— 15.
Various types of collyriums and whatever red substances there are;
saffron, auspicious vermilion pastes,
shimmering soft powders, and liquid butter.
Also [substances] fit for massaging, liquid substances, as well as pills fit for bathing; principles for coloring the nails, liquid substances for the soles of the feet;
various [dyes] such as lac, and liquid substances for the purpose of making leaf-patterns.
Then the father had all the shimmering *dhīraka* gems, the sparkling powders, the ripe *sthalapadma* fruits, and fragrant waters placed upon golden platters. (2.289.19–20)
Likewise, there were hundreds of beautiful golden rings set with emeralds, rubies, pearls, and other gems; as well as bracelets,
waist-bands, and auspicious finger-rings.
Also forearm-bands and bracelets, as well as golden *vyaṅgīḍīs*;
armlets beautiful with set diamonds and excellent upper-arm bands; golden arm-enclosures and very splendid chains. (22–23)
There were leaf-patterns joined by chains, colored and with blossoming leaves; lion-faced ornaments, beautiful bracelets, and many bangles;
as well as *natthikas*, *cibukīs*, *ṭibakīs*, and *bindukīs*.
And stars, the beautiful Sucandra, and many lovely serpents;
golden ear-garlands, earrings, and ear-chains;
as well as golden ornaments for the head, *troṭikas*, and *phullagranthikas*.
There were also golden clusters, *śiṅghoṭakas*, and *kadambakas*;
*ārāyakas* and *subuṭṭikas* set with gold and diamonds;
as well as *vālikās*, *tārikās*, *kuñcikās*, and *rūpyakānakīs*.
The string made of fortune, lunar, belonging to the moon-leaved one, and likewise extended;
also a golden lotus and a very beautiful golden garland;
and a golden sun, rich in splendor, residing above the forehead.
And hair-pins and needles made of gold as well as silver; golden hair-ornaments for binding the tresses in braids consisting of chains;
crescent-moon ornaments for the sides of the braided hair; and locks of hair concealed by garments.
Eager for the sake of the maiden, he placed in vessels powder for coloring the lips, powder for the cheeks,
necklaces adorned with leaves, and fruits tied in knots. (31–32)
Also [offer] chains and necklaces, a golden *plakṣa* leaf,
a golden auspicious mark (*maṅgala*), likewise a golden *mādalī*,
a golden *svastika*, and indeed a golden wheel.
The lotus of the hand, the lotus of the throat, the golden [ornament], and the lotus of the forehead;
a golden necklace for the neck, as well as the face of Siṃhikā; and necklaces of sesame, necklaces of mung beans, necklaces of black gram, and beautiful beads. (34–35)
And [he saw] delicate leaf-shaped ornaments,
beautiful pearl necklaces, golden breast-plates, and locks of hair adorned with spears;
as well as a golden vessel with a sun-like face and golden jars.
Golden bands, golden garlands, and excellent strings of pearls;
golden waist-bands, as well as chains, girdles, and beautiful golden triple-stranded belts. || 37-38 ||
Anklets joined with small bells, golden jhañjharī ornaments,
plantain-shaped figures, staffs, śṛṅgalās, and likewise ghurghuras;
all kinds of auspicious and new ornaments.
[He gave] betel-boxes and small baskets, as well as combs;
mirrors, leather bags, and hair-ornaments made of *maujika* grass;
coverings, helmets, and beautifully adorned horse-tethers.
Flower-ornaments and buds, as well as golden fillets of fine cloth;
a beautiful back-plate, a hip-band, and an exquisite ivory leaf-pattern;
pearl necklaces and splendid strings of rubies.
Also garlands of emeralds and strings of lapis lazuli gems;
strings of sapphires and leaf-patterns of topaz and other stones;
wreaths fashioned from karketana stone and garlands of coral and crystal.
He had trays set out with leaves adorned with coral,
as well as beautiful *gālīcaka* and *hārītaka* cloths;
likewise, there were woolen and silken coverlets.
Red *gulāla* powders and auspicious saffron,
very sharp unbroken grains (*akṣata*), as well as auspicious garlands of barley, flower wreaths, vessels, and golden incense burners. 46–47.
Thus, O Rādhikā, her father had a *śṛṅgāraka* (ornamental vessel) placed [before her], which was worth billions upon billions of lotuses; then he had another vessel worth a single lotus set down.
Having placed them in platters as radiant as the sun, the husband of Kaṃbhārā [presented them].
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and likewise by the songs of maidens,
he then went to the residence of the maidens, the abode of Śivasvāmin.
And everything for the sake of the maiden had been obtained from Kṛṣṇa by Śiva.
Then Hara, having performed a warm welcome, honoring, and acceptance for them with great affection,
caused them to drink water and partake of a small auspicious meal of sweet foods.
He gave betel-leaf as well and spoke many times, "Much! Much! (52). Delighted, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa gave everything to Śiva;
having received his permission, he then quickly returned to his own abode. (53)
In the fourth watch of the night, while she was performing her adornment there,
all her friends gathered together and, full of eagerness, spoke what was appropriate to her.
"It is fitting that Kṛṣṇa’s father also had his own adornment prepared."
His father adorned the auspicious elephant Suvāhana, which had four tusks and a beautiful golden girth-band, making it white and preeminent in every respect;
it was equipped with a golden moon-patterned howdah and a golden girth-band. ||55-56||
On his trunk was a variegated spear, and on his forehead the *sudarśana* [discus];
likewise, on his ears were fans, and on his temples two suns.
On his tusks were golden bracelets, and around his neck were golden bells.
On the feet were the attendants of variegated forms, and on the belly was a mace;
on the tail were golden garlands, and likewise a ladder on the flanks.
In this manner, the father then adorned the elephant. (58–59)
Then, with joy, his father decorated slow-moving chariots with wheels touching the ground for the sake of the army; at that time,
there were also excellent elephants adorned with pearls and [vehicles] shaped like Garuḍas.
As soon as they were remembered, they arrived, adorned and beautifully decorated:
horses, camels, swans, cranes, and cātaka birds;
likewise bulls, gayals, deer, and crocodiles.
Likewise, geṇḍūka deer, lions, tigers, and śarabhas—
those very mounts which are remembered as being present upon the Kalpa tree—
were fashioned from the wish-fulfilling cow and quickly arrived there.
There were beautiful celestial vehicles and small ground-based ones;
all were adorned with ornaments, as were the chariots and their riders. There were palanquins, foot-stools, and men-carriers, all well-decorated.
The banners, standards, swords, and other items such as canes and umbrellas were all quickly adorned and made ready.
At that time, the men and women stationed in the army were likewise beautified with ornaments.
Then, with their garments and colors shimmering in nine ways and resplendent with ornaments and the like, they were indeed filled with joy, possessing every mark of amorous grace in its entirety.
The musicians, dancers, actors, and those who sounded the kettledrums [were likewise present]. (67–68)
All the gods and goddesses dwelling in the three worlds, adorned with various garments and ornaments, were experts in all musical instruments;
at that time, they became elegantly decorated, as befitting a noble wedding procession.

At that time, there were maidens suitable for the marriage ceremony numbering four crores (40 million), as well as others by the tens of millions and even by the number of atoms in a hundred thousand crores; they were all adorned with ornaments by their fathers and other relatives, as well as by their female companions. (2.289.70–71)
All were adorned with garlands of skulls and decorated with every kind of ornament; by the will of Hari and at the command of Lomaśa, they all circumambulated the fire while dancing,
adorned with every ornament.
And just as Lakṣmī was a maiden worthy of being given in marriage,
Kṛṣṇa, having performed wonderful adornments at the end of the fourth watch, departed from Śivapura at an auspicious moment. (73–74)
Accompanied by hundreds of millions of billions of people, he was honored and praised by the masses; he was worshipped and saluted with offerings of fruits, flowers, and wealth.
Then, having wandered through Vārāṇasī along the great royal highway, [he departed].

Having beheld the deity and bowed down to Viśveśvara, and having drunk the auspicious water of the Gaṅgā, he— mounted upon ten thousand and ten million vehicles, accompanied by a hundred thousand celestial chariots,
and surrounded by all the men and women— [proceeded].
Accompanied by all the necessary honors, he proceeded to the Yoga-maṇḍapa on the delightful bank of the Varaṇā,
at the site of Kāpiladhārikā—
a vast field of excellent form, indeed beautified by gardens. || 77–78 ||
And before the temple of Śivasvāmin, there was a pavilion made of Kailāsa,
ten thousand *yojanas* in extent, which took the form of Mount Kailāsa itself;
it appeared in the sky in the likeness of Kailāsa for the purpose of welcoming him.
That very eternal Kailāsa pavilion shines forth here. O Rādhā, what deficiency could there be in that pavilion where the entire city of Śiva and likewise the city of Pārvatī are present on all sides?
And the city of Kāśī also attained an internal splendor;
such was the beauty fashioned there by Śambhu within that pavilion.
Indeed, the pavilion extended across the region between the Gaṅgā and the Gograrā.
It was a hundred yojanas in width, adorned with sacrificial pits and altars;
it was one yojana in height, filled with divine splendor,
and replete with all the requisites belonging to Goloka.
He was seated upon a lion-throne and other such seats, resplendent with the brilliance of jewels;
he was surrounded on all sides by his attendants and hosts of gaṇas intent on service,
and attended by all the wish-fulfilling cows and celestial kalpa-trees.
It was resplendent with cowherds and cowherdesses, enriched by the beauty of the *rāsa*-circle;
it was adorned with the effigies of all the inhabitants of the worlds, and it shone with streams of ghee, streams of curd, and streams of honey. 86–87.
It was furnished with all kinds of soft seats, such as cushions, mats, and strips of cloth;
it was carpeted with woolen rugs and silken coverlets;
and it was captivated by songs endowed with enchanting melodies.
It was graced by those skilled in the arts of dance and drama, and by those who knew the art of comedy;
it was constructed with vehicles visible from afar, audible from afar, and touchable from afar,
and was attended at every moment by chariots that travel according to one’s will.
It was illuminated in every way by cool streams of lightning,
and it was surrounded on all sides by lofty [pinnacles] raining down nectar and ambrosia.
It was provided with seats upon the pillars, the archways, and the upper portions.

It was as if one were seeing a reflection of the marriage of a noble maiden. (92) As many stars as there are in heaven, so many jewels shine here in that pavilion on Kailāsa, within the pavilion of yoga. (93)
Indeed, Viśvakarman constructed within that pavilion as many assembly halls as there were for the creators of the worlds;
and in the central sphere, he fashioned seats for the maidens worthy of receiving gifts.
Viśvakarman had prepared them nearby for the purpose of a necklace for his neck.
There, Mount Kailāsa also shone forth in embodied form;
indeed, it was brought there to that great festival for the purpose of bestowing all worthy objects.
Such a pavilion as this has never existed before, nor will it ever exist anywhere; yet,
visible to those who see both the near and the far, it stands established like a celestial abode,
adorned with sacrificial posts, pinnacle-vases, the consecration of deities, svastikas, and other such ornaments.
It was presided over by the citizens of Pārvatīnagarī who were full of great honor,
and crowded with the people of Kāśīnagarī and those dwelling in the three worlds, all of whom were saying, "The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas has taken place! || 98-99 ||
In the most excellent and auspicious main gate of the pavilion,
Vīrabhadra spoke from the sky regarding the welfare of the two Kṛṣṇas:
"Let the celestial machines descend for the great festival!"
"Behold the Supreme Self; this is the bestowal of the two Krishnas.
Standing in the sky, the Sāmaveda in embodied form offers salutation:
"Victory to that Hari, the illustrious Lord of Śārṅga, who is arriving! 102.
And the Ṛgveda, stationed at the front of the gateway, beheld the vast army approaching and signaled it to Śiva and the others.
Then the virtuous goddess Śrī Pārvatī ascended to the upper level.
"What is its extent, and what is it like?"—with such thoughts she entered the procession.
Having taken up [the image] from Śivapura toward Kāśikā, near the pavilion, she beheld the exceedingly long line and stood motionless for a moment. (104–105)

[The Author: Chapter 291.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, seeing Pārvatī ascending upward, millions of women [beheld her].
Other women, for the sake of beholding Kṛṣṇa, ascended from their own residences to the upper chambers of the pavilion, eager for a sight. While they stood there,
Pārvatī spoke the Ṛgveda in the presence of Bṛhaspati.
But what is that which is seen before me? Tell me that, for it brings me peace.
For the sake of my daughter, who indeed are the great ones present here today?
Who are they, and of what nature are they; and what is the state of the Lord of my daughter as well?
"There is one who is the greatest of all; I desire to know that—tell me everything. Thus questioned by Satī, Śrī Girijā, the omniscient Ṛgveda attained great joy and then began to speak in due order.
Behold, O Mother, first of all the attendant named Maṅgala:
four-armed, adorned with a tilaka mark, decorated with all ornaments, accompanied by the goddess Maṅgalādevikā, and endowed with every auspiciousness. (6)
Chanting the Sāman mantras, the bringer of auspiciousness indeed approaches;
mounted upon a very small swan and endowed with every splendor,
so too do Maṅgalā and Sarasvatī, mounted upon swans.
And Śāradā arrives, adorned with all ornaments;
this vision is indeed the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Then, the instruments of Vaikuṇṭha were indeed played by the musicians.
Indeed, the sounds and echoes of that [conch] resound throughout the three worlds as they arrive.
Behold! Then comes a magnificent elephant with its banner;
released from Akṣara, it shines like a great mountain.
Behold, then, these thousands of *snātaka*s, devoted to celibacy, who arrive from that direction proclaiming cries of victory.
Behold, furthermore, the auspicious drum *ḍaṅkā* arrives from there, sounding its deep resonance.
For the white horse with black ears is indeed standing ready, unbridled.
Behold behind him the chariot drawn by bulls,
golden, adorned with a banner bearing a golden pitcher, and beautified by its fender.
"Behold, O Mother, then thousands of horsemen equipped with weapons;
behold then the Nirṛta-Rākṣasas mounted upon camels—Vaiṣṇavas, servants of Viṣṇu, all richly adorned with ornaments. (15)
Behold, O Mother, the Yakṣas there, foot-soldiers who practice generosity (dāna),
showering rains of gold, silver, and other riches, possessing abundant wealth,
numbering in the thousands, adorned with crowns and golden ornaments. (16–17)

Behold, O Mother, the Vaiṣṇava people gathered there for the rāsa dance by the thousands, along with their musical instruments, chanting the virtues of Hari. Behold, O Mother, the Vaiṣṇava women there, intent upon singing songs.
Behold those thousands of women, adorned and engaged in chanting the praises of Kṛṣṇa;
and then behold thousands of venerable great sages seated in palanquins and human-littered carriages, intent on meditation upon Brahman.
Behold, O Mother, the ancestors and the gods together with Aryaman,
seated upon golden celestial chariots along with hundreds of thousands of maidens;
and behold thereafter the virtuous Siddhas stationed upon their chariots and other vehicles.
O Mother, behold more than a thousand divine, purifying, and world-sanctifying [beings],
as well as the youthful attendants adorned in celestial attire, accompanied by the playing of the flute and gentle [instruments]. (22–23)
"Behold, O Mother, the thousands of Daityas stationed upon Śarabhas, who are devoted to Viṣṇu, adorned with ornaments, and uttering cries of victory.
Behold, O Mother, the fierce Gaṇas thereupon, whose vehicle is the bull."
Behold the Vaiṣṇavas of many forms and appearances, resembling Śiva;
behold the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas who are servants of Viṣṇu.
Then, O Mother, behold the divine gandharvas, the instrumentalists and singers. (25–26)
"Behold, O Mother, those possessing the luster of the golden campaka flower and reaching the height of a palm tree; then see all the sacred fords (tīrthas) arriving there in personified form—
hundreds of thousands of them, purifying and divine."
"Behold, O Mother, ten million goddesses there, accompanied by songs;
auspicious, adorned with divine attire, and seated upon human vehicles.
Behold, O Mother, those auspicious elderly men from Saurāṣṭra."
Behold the gods seated upon their vehicles, adorned with parasols and chowries;
they number in the hundreds of thousands, possessing the hue of the sun, and are accompanied by male and female servants.
Some are situated in celestial chariots of exquisite design, while others move upon the ground or through the sky.
O Mother, behold those gods who have gone there, possessing the luster of the moon, the sun, and fire; and behold the serpent-bearers dwelling in Pātāla,
who have arrived here by the millions, possessing many forms and able to assume any shape at will.
Behold, O Mother, the worlds of the Sūtas, the Māgadhas, and then the Kinnaras;
behold the Kiṃpuruṣas and the Vidyādharas who sound the musical instruments of the gods.
Behold, O Mother, then the Brahmins, the twice-born who utter the resonance of the Vedas.
Behold, therefore, the kings who rule over the earth seated upon elephants;
likewise, behold King Jummasemla mounted on an elephant, and around him, the thousand maidens dear to Hari, traveling in their chariots. (34-35)
"Behold, O Mother, King Dakṣajaṅghara on his elephant,
as well as the more than thousand maidens seated in their vehicles.
Behold, O Mother, the handsome King Śibi mounted upon his elephant."
Behold one hundred adorned maidens mounted upon human vehicles;
and behold the great king Ṭharkūṭastha, accompanied by fifty maidens, seated upon a golden lion-throne supported by the shoulders of Viṣṭi. (37–38)
Then behold King Vīrajāra, accompanied by a hundred thousand maidens, seated upon a human vehicle and adorned with every ornament.
Likewise, behold King Śaktyakṣi together with sixty thousand maidens.
Behold the highly resplendent Śatapiśācinī, accompanied by ten thousand maidens.
Behold King Kālimāśa, attended by two hundred maidens,
seated upon a golden chariot and adorned with every ornament.
"These kings from Rāśīyāna, of the Kimpuruṣa lineage,
who are equal to the gods, have arrived at your house.
Now, listen to the sounds of musical instruments and behold these most excellent [beings]."

Behold King Uralaketu, who travels on a small vehicle, accompanied by thirty maidens, moving amidst a multitude of flutes and lutes; he possesses beautiful Ketumālīya-jāti flowers that are played upon like musical instruments. (43–44)
Behold King Krathaka, auspicious and accompanied by five thousand maidens; behold the broad King Uṣṭrāla, mounted upon a small vehicle and accompanied by twenty maidens;
and behold King Uṣṭrāla, accompanied by ten maidens.
Behold the syllable *haṃ*, joined with the five maidens, upon the vehicle.
O Mother, behold King Jayakāṣṭhalabha, accompanied by the five maidens, and the king of Tīrāṇa, joined with the six maidens. 46–47.
Behold King Alvīnara accompanied by seven maidens;
behold King Jīnavardhin seated in a vehicle with a single maiden.
Then, O Great Queen, behold the circle behind the kings.
Adorned with two hundred thousand maidens,
the entire great celestial chariot, decorated with every kind of ornament,
traveled upon the surface of the earth, beautifully graced by wish-fulfilling creepers.
Behold King Alpaketu, accompanied by seven daughters;
and behold, O Mother, King Jayakṛṣṇa, who has but one daughter. Behold King Parīśāna, who has twenty-one daughters.

Then behold King Indu, auspicious, seated in a small celestial chariot adorned with every kind of beauty and ornament, accompanied by two maidens. After him is King Mudrāṇḍa, joined by fifteen maidens. 52–53.
Behold King Gaṇḍa, adorned with all ornaments, traveling in a small celestial chariot; behold him accompanied by nine young maidens, traveling in a celestial chariot.
And behold King Līnorṇa, traveling in a celestial chariot accompanied by four maidens.
Behold King Bṛhacchara, accompanied by eleven maidens;
then behold Balalīna, who has forty beautiful maidens, traveling in a small celestial chariot, auspicious and adorned with every requisite.
Behold indeed King Varasiṃha with five daughters; behold the auspicious King of Rāyagāma with eight daughters;
and behold King Phenatantu accompanied by two daughters.
Likewise, behold Stokahoma; and one auspicious Kanya, who travels by vehicle.
Behold Kāṣṭhayānanṛpa; and one Kanya, the king Kolaka.
And one Kanya—these are the kings belonging to Ketumāla. 58–59.
"Understand from me that all these great masters are in your house.
Moreover, behold those skilled in musical instruments, born in the land of Gauri;
and behold, O Mother, the auspicious Hārītakas of divine attire, one after another."
Then behold the king traveling in a celestial chariot, accompanied by his two daughters;
behold him, O Mother, as he proceeds— the independent lord of kings, equal to the sun in majesty, beautifully adorned, and followed by a multitude of *rāya-kinnaras*.
Behold the king of the Kinnara-nāṭaka regions, accompanied by fifty-one thousand maidens traveling in golden celestial chariots and joined by the Amarīs;
then behold the kings of Uttarakuru, born in the land of the Amarīs.
[He saw] auspicious beings dwelling in great celestial palaces that touched the surface of the earth;
King Rāyarokīśvara with twenty-one daughters, and King Rāya-raṇajit accompanied by twenty daughters. 64–65.
Behold Rāyavākakṣaka, the lord of the three maidens, who dwells in a magnificent celestial chariot; and behold Rāyamārīśa, the king of the three maidens, who dwells in a celestial chariot.
Behold Rāyabāleśvara, the king of the three maidens, who dwells in a celestial chariot.
And the king Rāyalambāra, possessing six daughters, indeed travels by celestial chariot; the king Rāyanavārka, possessing seven daughters, travels by celestial chariot;
and the king Rāyahūṇeśa, possessing nine daughters, travels by celestial chariot.
"Behold King Rāyakūpeśa and his daughter traveling in their own celestial chariot;
see them, resplendent with the beauty of parasols and accompanied by male and female servants.
O Mother, behold then the musicians dressed in black."
Look, O Mother, at the kings born in the region of Dakṣiṇakuru;
behold King Kālamaṇḍalin accompanied by his four daughters,
mounted upon an elephant, and endowed with every splendor.
And behold King Vanajeśa, accompanied by five maidens,
mounted upon an elephant, adorned with a parasol and other regalia, O Mother. Behold King Pārāvārapiba, accompanied by three maidens.
Behold him seated upon an elephant-vehicle, accompanied by all his servants and attendants;
behold the king, a lord of ten million, accompanied by two daughters, seated upon an elephant-vehicle and surrounded by all his servants, O Mother. (73–74)
Behold King Śrī Satīśa accompanied by three daughters,
and likewise King Tretākarkaśa joined by seven daughters;
and behold King Āṇḍajara accompanied by four daughters.
Behold King Bālyaraja, who has one daughter and travels by elephant;
[76] behold the auspicious King Rāyasomanan, accompanied by three daughters; and behold King Urugavākṣa, accompanied by two daughters. [77]
Then behold King Parāṅavratu accompanied by two maidens;
and King Īśānapāna seated upon a vehicle consisting of four great elephants, attended by forty-one maidens. (78)
Behold the king, the lord of kings, well-served by female and male attendants with chowries, umbrellas, and other honors;
behold him who possesses thirty-three beautiful maidens, seated upon a great vehicle drawn by four elephants, and adorned with umbrellas and other regalia. (2.290.79–80)
O Mother, behold also the subjects of the eastern region traveling in celestial chariots—
all ten million maidens and adorned by ten million youths—
in whom the gaze of everyone, from children to the elderly, cannot reach its end.
Behold this vast army that has arrived at your courtyard.
Behold the Mahābāleśvaras and behold the Suratīyas;
behold the Sāntapanī offspring and the five thousand maidens.
Behold, O Mother, the vast aerial chariot of King Bhūgarbha Lakṣmaṇa, adorned with ornaments and filled with two thousand maidens, all seated within their palanquins. (84)
Behold the thousand daughters of Śāvadīna traveling in celestial chariots;
and behold the thousands upon thousands of chariots belonging to the Nāga maidens, with the Nāgas themselves mounted within them, here in your very courtyard. (85–86)
"Look, Mother, at those gods there, adorned with parasols and chowries, riding in human vehicles, accompanied by their own musical instruments and attendants bearing canes.
This Kubera is approaching; he is a devotee of Viṣṇu who belongs to a previous kalpa. (87)

"Accompanied by his own family and endowed with every splendor, here comes this Mahendra; behold him, attended by the gods, seated upon a great lion-throne, the king of heaven, radiant as the sun. (88-89)
"Behold, O Mother, the wind-god approaching there accompanied by the gods;
behold Rudra, resplendent as a king of kings, accompanied by his hosts. Then behold Agni departing, and behold the Sun traveling in his celestial chariot."
Behold the Moon, Mercury, and Venus, frequented by ten million gods;
and behold, O Mother, the lord of sages, Ṛbhu, seated upon a great celestial chariot, accompanied by Sanatkumāra and ten million virtuous beings.

Then listen also to the musical instruments situated in Satyaloka. O Mother, behold the ancestors dwelling among the people, indeed ten million maidens, stationed within their celestial chariot-armies; and then behold Viśvāvasu.
Behold the three hundred maidens accompanied by throngs of Gandharvas;
behold the Daityas of the netherworld who have come as devotees;
and here, King Prahlāda and others with five thousand maidens. (94–95)
Behold, O Mother, the earth Saṃvaraṇā, endowed with ten million kanyās, adorned and seated upon a supreme celestial chariot;
and behold the families of the wish-fulfilling cow, whose natures are liberated.
"Millions of families come to your home, which is a refuge of happiness.
Behold, O Mother, Viṣṇu approaching from there, accompanied by ten million attendants and preceded by people richly adorned with the musical instruments of Vaikuṇṭha. (97–98)

O Mother, behold Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, proceeding from there, augmented by the sounds of victory, accompanied by rows of ten million lamps, joined by hundreds of Ārjanīs, and attended by ten million Ramās.
It was augmented by the guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, by the tens of millions;
it was accompanied by the lakes of Brahmā along with Sarasvatī and the other [rivers];
it was joined by seventy-two thousand maidens and moved upon a celestial chariot.
Behold, O Mother, the one adorned even by a thousand illusory daughters of magicians, and the hairy one (Lomaśa) served by ten million great sages;
and behold the Guru of the Lord, the Master of Lakṣmī, seated upon a magnificent celestial chariot.
Behold, O Mother, upon his back millions of groups of maidens (103),
as well as hundreds of thousands of groups of forest goddesses and their daughters.
Behold also the trees, the clusters of blossoms, and the wish-fulfilling creepers— all embodied beings among the immobile world (104).
O Mother, behold those of great majesty, beautiful and with forms like the gods; then behold that supreme assembly of a hundred thousand maidens.
Behold the supreme host of lightning-flashes, the Dāmanīs, stationed upon their celestial chariots.
Behold, O Mother, then those ten thousand Kaṅkatālīya maidens,
seated in celestial chariots, adorned and intent upon singing;
likewise the Sālamālīya maidens and the Vāsantika maidens.
Behold, O Mother, thousands of others likewise stationed in celestial chariots;
behold, O Mother, the daughters born of Yama, those born of Vāyu,
and then the fourteen thousand daughters of the clouds, as well as others.
The Vārkṣyas, the Raudryas, the Khānijyas, the Sāṃvatsaryas, and the Gopikās;
the Śrāvaṇyas, the Vaiśvakarmyas, the Prācīnyas, and the Piśaṅgikas; the Rāśiyānyas, the Romāṇyas, the Pāraśyas, and the hosts of Kinnarīs.
There were also Dhaivaryas, Pārthas, Amartyas, and adorned Gaurīs;
likewise Hārityas, Svargyas, Pātālyas, and those born from the Ābhiriktas;
as well as Bhaumyas and Dānavīs, numbering in the millions, billions, and hundreds of billions.
"Behold, O Mother, those women are here for the sake of your daughter's honor;
they all come eagerly, thinking, 'The wedding of the two Kṛṣṇas is taking place.
Behold, O Mother, as it proceeds with a thousand jars."
O Mother, behold then that supreme Person, Vairāja, in his glorious great celestial palace (vimāna),
accompanied by many lords and adorned with a thousand arms; indeed,
behold the unborn one who possesses a thousand faces as he proceeds.
And likewise, O Mother, behold the thousands of auspicious Viṣṇus who are Brahmās;
behold all the lords of the universe. Behold Mahāviṣṇu, O Mother, and behold Bhūmāna, the Supreme Lord, traveling in his celestial chariot.
Behold Pradyumna and Aniruddha, accompanied by ten million lords;
behold likewise, O Mother, Vāsudeva together with his family.
Then behold Prakṛti and Puruṣa, endowed with all the principles (tattvas).
"Behold, O Mother, the drummers of the lords there;
and behold, O Mother, the circles of the lord's consorts beyond that,
seated in celestial chariots, mounted on Garuḍas, and riding upon elephants."
"O Mother, behold the adorned female attendants standing upon the chariot.
O Mother, behold then the eternal Blessed One;
behold him in the form of a fish, in the form of a tortoise, and then as Nṛsiṃha."
Then behold the Boar, and look upon the Swan and Hari;
then behold Kapila, and after that behold Pṛthu;
then behold Dattātreya, and behold Ṛṣabha and Vāmana.
Then behold Paraśurāma; thereafter behold the sacrifice.
Then behold Rāma, O Mother, and look upon Hayagrīva.
Behold Nārada, O Mother, and look upon the King of Kings.
"O Mother, behold Vyāsa, who is white; behold Buddha, the son of Aśvinī.
Then behold Dhanvantari, and behold the many Nārāyaṇas.
Behold the attendants and their beloved consorts, traveling in tens of millions of celestial chariots."
Behold, O Mother, those liberated ones who dwell in the abodes of light;
behold, O Mother, likewise the female liberated ones who possess the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. Behold, O Mother, others who are friends of Brahman and beloved of Brahman.
Behold these forty-one women, a group of six;
see Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmāvatī, Śrī, and likewise Māṇikī.
See these daughters of Kṛṣṇa, O Mother; they have all come together to your home.
Mādhavī, Suguṇā, Hāsā, Dayā, Śāntā, Sumā, Ambikā,
Campā, Haimī, Muktikā, Devikā, Lalantikā, Jayā— O Mother,
see these and hundreds of other [goddesses] who have come to your home.
Drawn by Kṛṣṇa, their lives belonging to Kṛṣṇa, they perceived your daughter as their sister:
"O Mother, behold this great celestial chariot with its elephant-vehicle, wherein are our father, mother, brothers, and the entire family! (2.290.130–131)
Indeed, the splendor of Śrī Hari is equal to ten million suns;
behold it, O Mother! Then there is a divine celestial chariot, drawn by a thousand elephants, adorned with jars, and endowed with a thousand peaks.
Surrounded on all sides by thousands and tens of thousands of vehicles,
increased and served by millions of women endowed with great fortune,
behold the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is gazed upon and possesses divine splendor. || 132–134 ||
[He saw] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Vallabha, and all [the forms] whose nature is that of Svāmī Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
[he saw Him] further augmented by brothers, wives, sisters, and others.
"He is indeed Puruṣottama himself, the cause of all manifestations.
(1.36) "Oh mother, your good fortune has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again!
Such a Kṛṣṇa as this has truly never been before, nor will he ever be again. (1.37)
"Look, mother, at those who are measuring the earth as they proceed toward Kṛṣṇa;
and look at the horsemen, born of all the worlds, by the tens of millions.
Look, mother, then at the noble women singing songs."
"Behold all the inhabitants of the earth adorned with ornaments, and then behold the spectators!
(139) Śrī Girijā said:
"Oh, what supreme good fortune is mine! My eyes [are fixed] upon Bālakṛṣṇa!"
"O *Ṛk*, I do not see the other one who has ceased; speak to me here!
(2.290.140) A blessed daughter has been born to me, for whose sake I, though a lord, come here. Go quickly to welcome her, and you too, come near the pavilion! (141)

Having spoken thus to Rādhikā, Himajā (Pārvatī) immediately descended into the house below for the sake of honoring and welcoming her. Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to the Majesty of Kṛṣṇa as Narrated by the Ṛgveda to the Goddess Śāṅkarī," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā! Having seen Hari, the youthful Supreme Lord, by the millions upon the river Kṛṣṇavāhinī, the throngs of women were utterly enchanted. (1)
Filled with millions of splendors, beautiful with millions of charms,
nourished by a weight of millions of blisses, adorned with millions of ornaments,
the Lord is the abode of millions of excellent virtues and the bearer of millions of desires.
Gazing again and again with steady vision, the young women became absorbed in him;
as many maidens as there were, they too entered into meditative absorption.
Even the men, the worlds, and the lords attained a state of absorption.
All the gods were bewildered; what then need be said of women?
Even the saintly, the yogis, the liberated ones, and even the personal associates [of the Lord]—even the ascetics were bewildered;
what then need be said of the liberated women?

Mahāmāyā, Pradhāna, Prakṛti, Dhāma, and Yoṣit—these deluders themselves were deluded; what then need be said of worldly women? From their birth until they reached maturity, these young women went forth together with their families.
Eager indeed for the sight of the two Kṛṣṇas, they spoke thus;
even they were bewildered there by the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman.
There were ten thousand kings and princesses as well.
And other women who had arrived there also recognized him as their own lord.
Likewise, ten thousand daughters of subjects there,
being utterly infatuated, recognized the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa as their own master.
Intent upon that, they indeed stood holding garlands of *kaṇṭha* flowers,
saying, "In the presence of fire as witness, we shall become the handmaidens of Kṛṣṇa, surrendered to him. Thus, at that time, there were indeed crores and billions of maidens intent upon that.
Having fully prepared their attire, they awaited the auspicious moment.
(12) Millions of Vidyādharīs were transfixed upon beholding Mādhava; millions of Apsarases were transfixed upon beholding Keśava. (13)
Even millions of celestial nymphs (gandharvīs) were bewildered upon seeing Acyuta;
even millions of kinnarīs were enchanted upon seeing the granter of desires;
and even millions of dancers were infatuated upon seeing the Master of Illusions.
The artisans were bewildered, and likewise the eloquent women were bewildered;
the flower-bearing women were bewildered, as were tens of millions of female ascetics;
the virtuous wives were bewildered, and likewise tens of millions of female renunciants.
The Brahmin women who were celibate maidens were bewildered, and likewise [others] were stupefied;
O Rādhā! upon seeing Bālakṛṣṇa, the entire world was deluded.
Some, merely by gazing at Hari, were drawn toward Keśava.
Someone, beholding that steady golden silk garment,
tawny and pervaded by rays of light, remained fixed right there.
And [he saw] the crown of Lakṣmī, made of gold and set with ten million diamonds.
Beholding that auspicious [palace], radiant like the sun and pervaded by various jewels and gems, some women there became transfixed, while others remained motionless as if submerged.
Some [beheld] jewels set in crowns, necklaces of gems, and beautiful flower-garlands.
Beholding rows of flowers, buds, crests, and floral garlands that indicated the act of offering, they stood there motionless and were enchanted;
some [beheld] beautiful locks of hair endowed with a shimmering luster. (21–22)
Having seen those that were black, curved, rich in folds, fine, captivating to the eye, and auspicious;
those drinking fragrant oil up to the tips of their ears like archways;
and the fans placed in the fifth part, serving as covers.

Seeing those [trees] refined with *dantika* [wood], made level, and uniform at their ends—some with reddish-brown tips—even those who were very steady there were bewildered. Others, seeing a great and blazing halo of light, were likewise struck with wonder. (24–25)

Having beheld that divine [form], which was a thousand *paridhi*s in extent, filled with the luster of millions of rays, multicolored, and possessed of the wonderful charm of sweet attraction, they were struck with wonder right there and became motionless. (26)
Some, having observed the forehead to be broad like a half-moon, radiant, enriched with a single line, and possessing the luster of the moon at its edges;
while in the center it is brilliant like the sun, intensely glowing, and elevated—such a forehead is considered auspicious. (27–28)
Beholding him then—nourished, beautiful, and captivating—the innocent women became steadfast.
Some, seeing the moon-like splendor of saffron situated in his center, most magnificent;
others, seeing him like the rising sun, those innocent women became firm in their devotion.

Seeing some with beautiful *sutilaka* marks and golden *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*s, others with sandalwood paste the color of gold, and others with slender bodies adorned with saffron mixed [with other pigments],
the charming women there then became filled with steady bliss.
But some women, having observed two leaf-patterns made of sandalwood at the edges—
beautiful with a profusion of tiny dots of saffron in their centers—
became transfixed by those very leaves and remained fixed upon the dots.
Some charming women remained fixed upon the pair of her lovely eyebrows— which were composed of the very essence of the workings of desire, adorned with a fine, dark, and shimmering line of hair,
and possessing delicate, slender, and pointed tips. (33–34)
Some, fixed there, were enchanted by the junction of the eyebrows, which shone with white light and possessed a beauty equal to the orb of the moon;
others were captivated by the charming region at the base of the nose, where the eyebrows meet.
Some, though naturally steady, were bewildered as a light shone between their eyes (36).
Others, seeing the nose of those possessing radiance— which was like a sesame flower and adorned with jewels—
remained there, charming and motionless, as they gazed at that sunken [point] (37).
Some had cheeks like those of a cow, beautifully colored and radiant; others had high, well-rounded breasts, worthy of a kiss, adorned with jewels.
Some bore smiles and were uplifted, possessing a luster like that of the sun and the moon.
Seeing their well-nourished, intoxicating arms so steady and charming,
some [maidens] fixed their eyes— eyes reaching to the ears, perfumed by passion, with sharp corners, flowing with love, and heavy with expressive gestures. (2.291.40)
With red lines rich in collyrium, with white globes that are tremulous,
with lovely black pupils, knowing emotions and awakening emotion;
perceiving the ultimate and filled within with the measure of activity.
O attractor, filled with passion, shining with the opening and closing of the eyelids;
endowed with a protective *chajjikā* (veil) resplendent with a fine line of hair;
auspicious, the substratum for the reflections of all the creations of the worlds. 42–43.
The two oceans, which are the repositories of rivers of love and the abodes of all splendors,
and the foundations of all measurements and forms— there they remained steadfast,
and some [goddesses] then became fixed within the cavities of their ears.
With golden earrings, golden pendants, and golden crest-ornaments (cippi),
as well as with golden chains and surfaces inlaid with jewels,
the steady [gods] there were enchanted by the two moons joined together. ||45–46||
Some women, beholding the turret adorned with golden ground,
fell into a state of infatuation right there and remained fixed in that place.
Others, seeing the back of the upper chamber, radiant with gold, [were likewise transfixed].

There, those who were well-composed became infatuated with her row of extremely fine hairs, which evoked passion, and with her tawny-colored line of beard-stubble. Some gazed at her lips, which were symmetrical, long, and perfectly proportioned. (48–49)

Filled with blood, resembling a ripe bimba fruit, and brimming with essence; worthy of a kiss and possessing a savor fit for consumption, it was positioned in the middle of the bow like the central part of a bow.
The two ends were firmly joined at the two ends of the bow, just as they should be.
Bearing the form of all bows, he is the treasury of love;
(51) slightly curved, revealing his state of affection, and a temple of smiles;
the refuge of serenity, beautiful, and adorned with the luster of betel-juice. (52)
In some places he performed a beautiful kiss with his teeth, in some with his tongue,
and in others with his lower lip;
at the central point, he pressed down the lower part with the stalk of his nose.
Beholding his upturned lips, the women there stood motionless and were utterly enchanted.
Other women [beheld] his fragrant breath as he sighed,
spreading in all directions and perfuming the lords.
Having smelled [the scent] that intoxicates and brings peace, the charming women became steady; beholding that friend of the lower lip— the red-colored lower lip that knows the taste of betel—
those charming women became steadfast.
The chin is adorned with golden spots and tawny marks;
it is beautiful, well-proportioned, and graced by appropriate depressions.
It is rendered exceedingly lovely by the splendor of its symmetrical jawline.
Beholding him, who was divine, with the luster of fresh butter and the radiance of a land-lotus, the women were enchanted; they remained fixed, holding him within their hearts.
With his conch-like neck and melodious voice, the flesh of his throat below the chin was full and well-fleshed.
Seeing his neck as firm as a mountain peak, those steady women were struck with wonder;
likewise, seeing Hari’s lion-like shoulders, muscular and well-developed,
some were bewildered and remained there motionless.
Some gazed upon his excellent chest—high, well-developed, and broad;
auspicious, filled with the luster of milk and campaka flowers, and the refuge of all strength;
which for a moment revealed his manhood and caused agitation in the minds of the heroes.
It is not desired by other women, yet it is manifested by the embrace of Rādhā and Ramā;
it is endowed with golden lines and possessed of hair-coils curling to the right; it is filled with the affection of Śrī and resplendent with breasts shining like the sun and the moon. (63–64)
It is indeed broad and long, resplendent with firm joints;
it possesses a softness in the belly and is pleasant to the touch due to the tenderness of its sides.
The position of the spine is firm, and the base of the arms is exceedingly beautiful.
Beholding such a chest of Hari— a supreme abode of bliss,
rich with the desire for the happiness of all perfections— the throngs of beautiful women were utterly enchanted;
they became submerged right there, remaining steadfast in that joy.
A golden neck-ornament set with jewels upon his neck,
as well as a golden leaf-patterned chain and a golden five-stranded cord.
(68) Furthermore, a golden leaf-patterned cord and a golden five-stranded cord.
A golden garland of jujube fruits (*badarī*), likewise a wreath of *gokṣura*,
a golden garland of fine leaves, a garland of mung beans,
a golden garland of barley, and a golden garland of kidney beans.
A golden necklace with a silver pendant, a garland of eight-cornered gems,
a tulasī necklace, a necklace of fine golden jewels,
a golden rosary, and fragrant flower necklaces.
Beholding the necklaces worn upon golden breastplates and silken bodices—
necklaces adorned with gems, jewels, diamonds, and the like,
as well as pearl necklaces and *kaustubha* stones— the women gazed upon them indeed. (72–73)
Beholding the auspicious moonstones, sunstones, and firestones worn around their necks there, the celestial women were truly enchanted;
all the others rejoiced for a moment and remained motionless there.
His two arms and back were like the core of a plantain tree—beautiful, radiant, and full.
They were adorned with bracelets and resplendent with chains; auspicious, they shone with ornaments bound upon them like the necks of lions.
Indeed, upon seeing him, the women were bewildered and remained motionless for a moment;
[he was adorned] with forearms like the fruit of desire, encircled by golden bracelets, and endowed with auspicious ornaments rich in gems, pearls, and jewels. (77)
Seeing the [palace] richly adorned with the beauty of floral decorations, the charming women stood still;
likewise, they gazed upon their nails, red as lac upon the palms of their hands, and their fingers, which resembled small moons and were encircled by strings of finger-rings. || 78–79 ||

Likewise, the women were adorned with golden rings set with gems and jewels; their soft, reddish fingertips were graced by these signets. Seeing them—endowed with beautiful joints, pleasant to the touch, charming, and steady—the [men] were captivated.

Seeing his two beautiful hands marked with five fingers and endowed with blue spots, the women were enchanted and remained fixed there. Seeing on the palm of his right hand a fish, a banner, and a trident, [they were further amazed]. (81–82)
A bow, an arrow, a svastika, a thunderbolt, a staff, a discus,
a mace, a lotus, a conch, a sword, and a scimitar adorned with gold—
seeing these, all the women were indeed bewildered and became motionless there at that time.

Beholding the sword-sheath, the shield bound with split gems, and likewise the [other] equipment, all the celestial women were bewildered; even upon seeing the auspicious thread around his neck and the auspicious cord on his arm, the charming goddesses were struck with amazement. (84–85)
The women possess tongues that are red, fit for tasting, and endowed with every flavor;
they are broad, the foremost cause of delusion, resembling land-lotuses, and full of longing.
Their teeth, appearing like jasmine buds or pomegranate seeds, manifest in their smiles.
Beholding them endowed with white luster and shimmering radiance, they were infatuated;
indeed, they conceived a longing to obtain [such beauty] and remained fixed upon that state.
Their bellies were beautiful, radiant, auspicious, and adorned with the three folds. || 87-88 ||
Seeing her cool [complexion], with a deep navel and a waist enriched by folds, they were then enchanted there and became motionless;
and a golden necklace was worn upon her neck in a half-split fashion.

Then, seeing the ends of their garments hanging down over their shoulders, some innocent women stood still; others, having contemplated their concealed hips and the dark skin of their two buttocks while their garments were tied around their waists, became bewildered there. (2.291.90–91)
On a costly cushion joined with gold and silver,
upon a divine seat worthy of a king, fashioned from the finest silk;
resting on ten million jewels, adorned with golden cushions and pearls.

When the nāḍikā joined with the *phullaphummakikā* was introduced and held within the beautiful bow, the young women were enchanted; indeed, all women were captivated by that desirable inner [instrument] which is the locus of all desires. (93–94)
Deluded by total infatuation, they did not perceive anything else for even a moment;
[they gazed] at the lovely foreparts of the feet, which resembled the *karmāṇika* jewel.
On the two feet, the two parts marked by the *pañcaja* [ornament] were resplendent with fine hair.

Seeing those two [feet] well-fitted with soft sandals, adorned with the beauty of gold ornaments, and dyed [red], the charming women became steadfast; yet, upon seeing the base of the thighs and the middle of the thighs—parts not belonging to the body—they were utterly bewildered by passion. (96–97)

Beholding the finger-rings with their golden ornaments, as well as the women themselves, and seeing the golden foot-ornaments equipped with tinkling bells, the bracelets, the armlets, and the earrings, they stood motionless, utterly enchanted.
With hands reaching down to their knees and hips like the trunks of elephants,
seeing the women’s arms and palms resembling the limbs of an elephant,
they were bewildered there and became steadfast, as if absorbed in meditative concentration.

Seeing the lord, the most excellent king of kings, seated upon a golden throne on a soft spot within the elephant-palace, all the charming women came toward the city gate as he approached. (2.291.100–101)
Beholding the glorious Supreme Lord, who was enriched by drops of saffron and unbroken rice grains,
the people indeed beheld him and sang shouts of "Victory!
O Rādhikā, in this manner they reached the great gateway.
And amidst the sounds of musical instruments, delightful to the minds of the people, the Lord, who understands all internal states, remained upon His throne during that procession.
O Rādhikā, listen now to the various ways He granted His vision there. (103–104)
In the form of Puruṣottama, he gave his vision to those who were liberated;
in the form of Kṛṣṇa, he gave his vision to the cowherds and the cowherd women;
and to his personal attendants, he gave his vision as being identical with Nārāyaṇa.
To the lords (Īśvaras), He gave His vision in the form of Vāsudeva;
to the hosts of Siddhas and Sādhus, He gave that [vision] in the form of Viṣṇu;
and then to the great seers (Maharṣis), He gave His own vision as the Self of Brahmā.
To the ancestors, he gave his own vision in the form of Aryaman; to the gods, he also gave his own vision in the form of the Lord of Milk (Viṣṇu);
and to human beings, he gave that [vision] in the form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
To the inhabitants of the world of Pātāla, he gave his vision in the form of Śvetaprabhu;
to the women, he gave his vision in the form of Kāmadeva;
and to the maidens, he gave his vision as Mālādhara in the form of their own husband.
To those worthy of worship, he granted a vision in the form of a youth;
to his devotees, he granted a vision of the Lord’s form that bestows liberation.
With four hands holding all weapons, he was served by Ramā and the Vṛndāvanas.

He granted to men a direct vision in His form as Nārāyaṇa, and He revealed the nature of the Inner Self within the hearts of embodied beings. Thus, O Rādhikā, did the glorious Lord Hari, Bālakṛṣṇa, act. (112–113)
For that sovereign lord was indeed recognized as belonging to the city named Maṇḍapa;
he arrived at the front of the gateway and then attained stability for a moment.
The entire army also stood still for a moment, having been duly honored.

[They were seen] by the most excellent brahmins, Kṛṣṇa and Bṛhaspati, who had come into his presence. Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Bewilderment of Men and Women through the Attraction of Every Limb of the Adorned Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, His Divine Appearance, and His Arrival at the City Gate," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (291)
