Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā! Śrī Bṛhaspati stood before Lord Hari together with millions of sages, holding vessels for the worship of unbroken grains and other offerings.
The beautiful city named Maṇḍapa, extending for fifty yojanas,
was filled with subjects who had gathered to behold the King of Lords.
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself bowed down to Śrī Hari, while I [bowed] as well.
Then the Brahmins prostrated and chanted Vedic mantras.
They also placed barley sprouts into the hand of Bālakṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa then took a cluster of flowers in his hand and a garland for his neck.
Bṛhaspati placed a garland of *kādambara* flowers around his neck;
likewise, the Guru applied vermilion, unbroken rice grains, and sandalwood paste upon his forehead.
The women from the bride's maternal kin increased his prosperity with parched grain.
There Bṛhaspati gave water for drinking to the Lord.
He caused Bālakṛṣṇa’s army to enter the city;
and the subjects beheld it entirely as possessing a divine form in every respect.
Daughter-goddesses of the gods, daughter-goddesses of the *nāgas*, princesses, daughters of sages, and daughters of *Īśa*—all these women beheld the Lord Hari with eyes that did not blink.
8. All the women indeed gazed [upon him] without blinking.
Śivasvāmī arrived before the gopura for the purpose of worship;
having performed the worship and inquired after his well-being, he made him joyful, as did Vasu, his father, and the other dignitaries of the earth. (2.292.10)
The women of Mahimā bowed down, beholding the Supreme Lord—whose face was gracious, who was lovely, captivating, and beautiful of form;
who was endowed with every splendor, worthy of worship, the fulfiller of all desires, and dear to the heart. (11)
The Lord, the Supreme Self of all, who is accessible through his grace to his devotees, was seated upon a celestial chariot on the ground, richly adorned with the finest essence of jewels;
he was as white as the new moon and beautified by rows of necklaces. (12–13)
With all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with many garlands,
he was radiant with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and necklaces of gems;
his cheeks were made to shine by the ornaments of jeweled earrings.
Adorned by the tinkling of anklets fashioned from the finest essence of precious gems, smiling, holding a cluster of flowers in his hand, and gazing into a jeweled mirror;
he was served by white chowries and a parasol made of pearls. (15–16)
Beside him, he was graced by the Primordial Lord, who is self-luminous;
he was endowed with fresh youth, possessed eyes like autumn lotuses, a face equal to the full moon of autumn, and was the bestower of grace upon all. (17)
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, he is beyond the syllables and is imperishable.
Purified by sacred fords and purified by his own glory, he is worshipped by the lords of the gods and others;
he is the Lord of Devas who brings supreme delight and is a treasure-trove of beauty. (18–19)
He wore a silk thread made of *dūrvā* grass and a bright cluster of blossoms from a plantain tree upon his crest;
he bore a garland of flowers offered by a woman, an excellent and fragrant bouquet.
Seeing Hari in such a state, the women then fell into a swoon. They spoke these desired words: "The life of Lakṣmī is blessed and praiseworthy.
The daughter of Himavat (Pārvatī) also gazed upon Tāraka again and again.
Śiveśvara, separated from his beloved, arrived together with his ministers and priest and bowed down before Hari, the Lord of gods.
In a long pavilion at the front of the hall, he caused a dance to be performed.
He caused the most delightful performances of dancers, the singing of musicians,
the songs of female singers, the dances of female dancers,
and various distinctions of instrumental sounds to take place before him.
Then Śiva went to the front of the army and caused the cracking of hand-claps, the flashing of lightning,
the bursting sounds of mechanical devices,
and the loud roaring of kettledrums.
They indeed caused the subjects to prosper under Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa. Thus, at that time, the holy procession arrived at the rest-house;
Kṛṣṇa, descending from his celestial chariot, took his place upon the gateway.
Pārvatī repeatedly increased his joy with her folded hands,
while she washed the feet of Hari with the water of sacred fords.
He was then worshipped with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other auspicious substances.
He was honored with barley sprouts, dūrvā grass, and fragrant substances;
likewise, he was then worshipped with parched grain and the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana).
He was then further strengthened by the brahmins and his preceptor with words of blessing.

Then, having been sprinkled with water, he led Hari and all those most worthy of worship for a moment to the rest-house by his side, where he seated them upon auspicious golden thrones that bestow all peace. (32)
He honored his parents with a welcome, as did Śiva, the Lord of Gods.
Then Śivasvāmī, for the sake of peace and in accordance with worldly custom, offered them food known as *madhuparka* along with water for drinking.
Then, even millions of maidens adorned themselves with their own finery;
eager for the occasion, they donned garments and ornaments suitable for yoga.
Their bodies were fragrant with perfumes, and likewise, they were dyed with colorful pigments.
Then they remained present, joined with drops and possessing drops [of water].
(36) "When Hari shall accept the gift from Lakṣmī, at that time Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa will take our hands. (37)
Thus, at that time, her friends performed auspicious adornments for Lakṣmī;
they dyed her beautiful nails, which resembled land-lotuses,
as well as the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet, with red lac.
They indeed dyed their lips with red pigment;
they likewise smeared both their cheeks and ears with saffron paste,
and they certainly anointed their eyes with collyrium.
They adorned their foreheads with saffron and sandalwood paste,
and they made their bodies fragrant with sandalwood.
Furthermore, they rendered their bodies richly scented with camphor.
They adorned their hair with fragrant, refined oil;
they fashioned it into a beautiful, radiant, and auspicious braid.
They bound their hair into a topknot, adorned with a garland of land-lotuses.
It was likewise adorned all around with strings of jasmine buds,
joined with *mālatī* flowers and woven with variegated threads;
at its edge was a beautiful piece of silk cloth, decorated with diverse patterns.
It was resplendent with a crest of *pārijāta* flowers;
that auspicious abode was encircled by golden jewel-garlands.
There, they placed a moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*) for the sake of illumination. (45–46)
They placed a sun-crystal (sūryakānta), radiant with light, at the site of the *brahmarandhra*;
and they placed upon her head a beautiful crown suitable for a woman,
rich with jeweled necklaces and gems, made of gold, and shimmering with color.
There, crests made of flowers of gems and pearls hung down.
They wore upon their foreheads, or indeed had fashioned for themselves, tiaras of gold and silver set with many jewels. 48–49.
In the center, they drew a dot of beautiful moonlight with liquid saffron;
likewise, on her broad forehead, they fashioned auspicious curved lines—
upward-pointing, angular, and crooked— along with saffron filaments, all adorned with unbroken grains of rice.
At intervals, within each group of four, they drew vermilion bindus and cakras;
they scattered a small amount of shimmering powder that produced a dazzling luster,
and they placed flower garlands suitable for offering during the auspicious ceremony.
They also wore very small, exquisite *natthikās* made of gold, enriched with pearls,
and likewise excellent *vālikās*.
They likewise offered a golden *cibuka* adorned with *harikas*.
They placed a pearl necklace upon her neck and gave her earrings for her ears;
they also gave her two golden ear-ornaments (*īrika*) set with diamonds and other gems, as well as five-stranded pendants and ear-rings (*karṇaśṛṅkhalā*).
They gave him two leaf-patterned *phullikas* set with fine diamonds;
then they gave him a golden neck-ornament (*kaṇṭhahaṭhikā*) inlaid with gems,
as well as a silk bodice for binding the breasts and a silken tunic (*kañcukī*).
They placed upon their shoulders a hair-ornament (keśāvalī) adorned with the splendor of golden bells, set with rows of golden stars,
interwoven with divine diamonds and gems, and featuring diamond knots,
complete with side-tassels (cipikā). || 57–58 ||
They gave her a binding hairpin made of gold and silver;
likewise, the attendant (kārpaṭika) gave her a woolen garment enriched with golden stars.
They applied saffron to her breasts, which were dyed and possessed a brilliant red luster.
Eagerly, they wore beautiful golden garments filled with fine diamonds,
as well as soft ones made of fine silver; they fastened their raiment with ties of kamsa-cord and other ornaments.
With thin, fine needles, they likewise bound the inner garments between the arms,
between the chest, and between the hips;
they even fastened the *ghargharī* (a small bell) within.
He also [offered] a large *ghargharī* (water-pot) set with gold and silver,
auspiciously inlaid with small mirrors and jewels;
it was red in color, adorned with variegated patterns, and likewise had a yellowish-brown rim.

Upon her hips, which were adorned with a sash of saffron silk and bound with a golden girdle, they placed two leaf-shaped ornaments made of gold and set with jewels, fashioned in the likeness of two lotuses, soft and beautiful as land-lotuses. 65.
Then they gave a golden ring, complete with chains for each finger, sufficient to fit all five fingers;
and above the two joints of the fingers, they gave a golden tortoise-shell ornament.
They also placed rings set with diamonds and other gems;
lotus-shaped ornaments on their hands, and anklets and bracelets upon their forearms— bracelets made of gold, richly adorned with lions and resonant with a network of tiny bells.
They placed golden *kāmbika* and *kaṭakika* bracelets, set with rubies, upon the two forearms of Śrī; and they also placed a golden girdle, adorned with pearls, around her waist. (2.292.70)
Upon the wrist-bracelets set with diamonds and fashioned from gold, they placed small golden ornaments;
likewise, upon the armlets fastened with gems and diamonds on both forearms,
and upon the bracelets adorned with lotuses, they gave various rings.
They gave golden armlets and auspicious leaf-shaped ornaments;
they gave beautiful golden bracelets and even chains.
They also gave a golden svastika and crescent-shaped ornaments for the arms.
They gave golden necklaces adorned with gems and diamonds,
as well as garlands of mung beans, barley, and rose-apples; likewise,
they offered a golden leaf of the *plakṣa* tree, a necklace, and strings of pearls.
They offered a necklace of seven chains, a beautiful *sūkṣmapatrī*,
a *catuṣkikādalī* garland, a *badrīmālā*, and a *māṣikā*— excellent golden necklaces set with diamonds, each worth ten million [gold pieces]. (75–76)
They put on for her a bodice with a sash that enhanced all her beauty and stole the very eyes [of onlookers],
and they even gave her a veil and gloves for her hands.
Thus adorned by her companions like Lakṣmī herself, the maiden appeared as Lakṣmī.
Then all the maidens, even by the millions, became adorned with ornaments, thinking,
"Kṛṣṇa will marry us during this auspicious conjunction of the two Kṛṣṇas. Then, all the musical instruments of those traveling for the sake of wealth were sounded.
In an auspicious and favorable moment, under a most excellent constellation that brings about well-being,
during a conjunction that bestows all good fortune, in the Māhendra yoga which grants prosperity,
at a time that yields great bliss, with an excellent rising, and endowed with spiritual perfection.
When the ascendant is conjoined with the lord of the ascendant and is auspicious for marriage;
when it is purified by the aspect of benefic planets and devoid of the aspect of malefic planets;
when it is endowed with the purity of the moon and stars and free from the defects of *vedha* (piercing) and the like. || 81-82 ||
And at that moment, which was free from even the slightest obstacle such as a [divination] stick, which always bestows happiness,
and which was a time most suitable for the pleasure of the couple, Bālakṛṣṇaka arrived at the courtyard of Śivadeva’s Kailāsa palace.
Hari was entreated at night by Bṛhaspati, the brahmins, and the ṛṣis;
accompanied by Lomaśa and others, as well as his kinsmen and relatives, together with his father, mother, kings, connexions, and friends. (84–85)
Together with the gods, the ancestors, virtuous ascetics,
the attendants, the lords, the liberated ones, the bhaṭṭas, and the family priests,
as well as all the guardians of creation, he went to the sacrificial altar-pavilion.
It was adorned with thousands of plantain pillars decorated with golden bands,
with archways of campaka, aśoka, mango, and sandalwood trees,
and beautifully embellished with garlands of flowers possessing every exquisite form. (87–88)
With auspicious golden pitchers adorned with fruits and sprouts,
worshipped with musk, unbroken grains of rice, parched grain, dūrvā grass, and saffron, and accompanied by flowers,
leaves, sandalwood paste, jewels, and garments; || 89 ||
It was exceedingly beautiful, adorned on all sides by those who were resplendent;
it was surrounded by all the great-souled attendants of Śambhu who move through the sky, as well as by his personal associates and incarnations headed by Saṃkarṣaṇa.
By the lords, the deities, the seers, the kings, and the guardians of the quarters;
by those dwelling on Kailāsa and those inhabiting the three worlds;
and by the domestic priests, the brahmins, the ascetics, and the avadhūtas.
Together with the Gaṇas, the Yoginīs, and even the fathers of the maidens,
[he established] that auspicious abode provided with an altar fashioned from the finest essence of jewels,
adorned with pigments, sandalwood powder, musk, saffron, and other such substances.
It was made fragrant and beautifully colored with fragrant heartwoods;
it was pervaded by the luster of various jewels and scented with the sweet aroma of incense.
Endowed with wonderful beauty, it was delightful and filled with the songs of celestial musicians.
Resounding with the music of song, beautifully adorned by the dances of Vidyādharīs, and watched on all sides by young women, it was a source of auspiciousness;
and the preceptor, together with the family priest, held an auspicious water-pot. ||96-97||

The gift-pavilion was adorned with celestial wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavallī*) and other ornaments; it was graced by the king, who stood ready to give with *kuśa* grass in hand, accompanied by the articles for the gift.
Likewise, the sacrificial pavilion was beautified by those same items for the gift.
On all sides and in the upper parts,
with millions of lotus-maidens and others, led forth and adorned, accompanied by their fathers and kin—
Bālakṛṣṇa [entered] that beautiful pavilion where the consecration had been performed. (2.292.100)
Honored and celebrated by the twice-born, he arrived at the main gate;
there, Śiveśvara came forward to offer him worship.
Indeed, the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, having reached the appointed time, proceeded with haste.
Then he commanded all those beloved women who were his own:
"Wearing all the garments, ornaments, and finery offered by me—all things suitable for the wedding—come to the beautiful pavilion. (102–103)
"The marriage of you all must indeed be performed by me along with Śrī.
Having heard this, they all prepared themselves and arrived at the pavilion for the prosperity-rite,
accompanied by their respective fathers and others, having presented themselves for the purpose of giving the bride-price.
At that time, during the ritual for his own daughter performed by Śivasvāmin,
the Creator himself presided over this ceremony for all of them.
O Rādhikā, listen to this wonder regarding the wives of those who possess minds as vast as millions, billions, and trillions of lotuses.
In the Kṛta age, Kṛṣṇa displayed wonders and such;
indeed, Śiveśvara set in motion the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa) everywhere.

Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described is] the worship and vision of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa at the city gate, his dancing and clapping before it, his resting in the rest-house, the offering of Madhuparka, and [the arrival] of all the maidens.
The two hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of Lakṣmī’s Ornamentation and the Deity’s Return to the Main Entrance of the Gift-Pavilion," etc., [ends here].
Chapter 292. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 293.
[The Author: Chapter 294.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Śiveśvara was a great devotee who knew the majesty of Hari.
O Rādhikā, reciting this at that time, he considered his own fortune to be blessed:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my actions have become fruitful;
today everything of mine has become fruitful, since Puruṣottama is in my home."
Today my life has truly come to birth; everything has been well-lived, since that which was born from ten million lifetimes—accompanied by the dissolution of the root of karma—is now present.
That lotus-foot of Yours, which sages constantly meditate upon within their hearts.
"Today, indeed, Śrī Hari, the bestower of all fruits, has appeared in my courtyard.
And today, the three worlds have become the most excellent sacred site (tīrtha) in my courtyard.
Oh! Until the end of the kalpa, my courtyard has become a sacred place! || 4-5 ||

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord, Hari— who was invisible to the eyes until now— is visible to me today in my courtyard. You are the bestower of the fruits of actions, the eternal one whose form is light.
"I bow to the Supreme Self residing within, who is my very own self.
(7) Having thus praised Rādhikā and remembering Hari, whom Śiva had praised, she joyfully offered water for the feet at his lotus-feet, which were worshipped by Lakṣmī. (8)
There he offered *arghya* accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and fruits;
he also gave a small portion of *madhuparka* and applied a beautiful crescent-moon mark (*sucandraka*) upon his forehead.
He then bestowed a *tilaka* made of saffron, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and musk.
She applied sandalwood paste, fragrant and the very essence of scent, to his body.
She placed a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, her own favorite, around his neck,
as well as a necklace of jewels upon his throat and a gem-encrusted ornament on his wrist.
He gave him divine garments purified by fire, a radiant crown,
earrings, bracelets, anklets, rings, and so forth;
as well as a pair of jeweled chowries and a golden parasol.
He placed necklaces of gold and pearls, along with the Kaustubha gem, garlands, and ornaments at the feet of Kṛṣṇa; he offered millions upon millions of gold pieces,
incense, jewel-lamps, and likewise performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
He indeed gave a beautiful golden lion-throne as a gift to Hari,
as well as water from seven sacred fords, madhuparka, and likewise water for sipping,
betel, drinking water, and fragrant scents.
Then she gave him an excellent bed and ornaments;
she also offered a handful of flowers and likewise bowed at his feet.
Girijā too honored her daughter’s beloved with great respect.
She washed his feet, honored him with parched grain,
worshipped him with sandalwood paste and other offerings, and gave him gold coins and the like;
she even lifted household utensils from her head [as a sign of devotion].
The key to the treasury, as well as a pen, a sword, a pestle, a grindstone, a broom, and likewise a winnowing fan;
a ladle, a chain, a wedge, and likewise a staff. (2.293.20)
A trident, a conch, a discus, a mace, and a shield;
a rope, a small bell, a mirror, and likewise a water-pot;
a cooking vessel, a pill of good fortune, dūrvā grass, a stalk, and a flute.
Fruit, food, water, vegetables, ornaments, and likewise sacrificial fuel—
having removed all such things from his head,
he then performed the *nīrājana* rite over Kṛṣṇa’s head.
With palms joined in reverence, he meditated five or six times upon the destruction of suffering;
then he caused [the door] to enter there upon the surface of the earth—
a casket of the universe fashioned from two skull-halves.

Seeing it bound by threads of illusion and set up there, Mādhava placed his foot upon it and then Hari broke it. Having utterly destroyed the obstacle, he [revealed] the excellent, divine golden lion-throne.
He took that seat which had been placed near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and sat down right there; he also bowed to the sacrificial post (yūpa),
as well as to the water-pot (kalaśa), the Mothers (mātṛkāḥ), Gaṇeśa, and the deities.
He bowed down from all sides to the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, and the preceptor.
Śiveśvara and the twice-born honored him with unbroken grains of rice.
Thus, having received the formal invitation, the Blessed Lord Hari shone with splendor.
In the meantime, Lakṣmīsukhadā, the daughter of Śiva, arrived at the edge of the altar in the pavilion along with her female companions. Beautiful musical instruments were played and songs were sung.
And the sounds of the Vedic mantras arose for those who know the Vedas.
Then the beautiful Lakṣmī arrived there, accompanied by her companions;
she came on foot with devotion, adorned with ornaments of excellent jewels.
Wearing garments purified by fire, adorned with her heavy braid of hair,
that virtuous woman, having smelled the mirror and being fragrant with sandalwood and other perfumes,
was marked on her forehead with a drop of musk and a dot of vermilion.
Having the luster of molten gold, beautiful with a halo of radiance,
wearing all her ornaments and accompanied by the garlands and other items for worship,
she arrived in the presence of the bridegroom together with her brothers and others. (34–35)
Millions of great souls beheld her, who was like the moon;
indeed, Rādhā is the most radiant and supreme among all women in every creation.
Seeing her even more radiant than that, they praised her again and again.
That Lakṣmī, devoted to her husband, having bowed to the pavilion,
likewise bowed to her own husband and the gods, and performed seven circumambulations;
she sprinkled [them] with cool water and with tender leaves of fragrant sandalwood.
Bālakṛṣṇa sprinkled that beloved Lakṣmī, who was smiling beautifully.
At that auspicious moment, the lover beheld his beloved, and she beheld her lover.
O Rādhikā! Listen now to how a supreme wonder then arose in every way.
When the Blessed One sprinkled Lakṣmī, at that time there was an ablution;
it fell from all sides upon the heads of all the maidens who were being led out in marriage, and they all became truly joyful then.
Then Lakṣmī, having bowed to Kṛṣṇa, sat down upon a seat;
standing to his left, accompanied by her Lord, she performed the worship of the deity.
Bṛhaspati and Lomaśa both officiated for them.
Having proclaimed the place and time for the successful completion of the gift of the daughter,
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, they both caused the worship of Gaṇeśa and likewise the worship of Śrī Viṣṇu to be performed.
There is also the worship of Rudra and likewise the worship of the Mātṛkās;
the worship of the pavilion, of the gods, and of the Yoginīs;
as well as [the worship] of the planets, the guardians of the directions, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The worship of the Ādityas, of the Ṛṣis, and of the Pitṛs and the gods;
likewise the worship of Brahmā, the worship of the Īśvaras,
the worship of all the lords, and likewise the worship of the Vighnas.
Likewise, there was the worship of the *rakṣasas* who protect maidens,
as well as of the fires, the deities of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), those dwelling in the branches and the archways, the gatekeepers,
those stationed within the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and those residing in the ruby pillars.
They also had the worship of Lakṣmī performed,
as well as the worship of Pārvatī, the worship of Hanumān,
the worship of Durgā, and likewise the performance of the Śrāddha rites.
In whatever manner the worship was performed,
all the maidens, being Kṛṣṇa’s daughters, observed it and performed it exactly in that same way.
Having thus completed the worship, they then [approached] the fire situated within the sacrificial pit.
Having worshipped the Āhavanīya fire, the maiden rose and placed a very extensive garland of flowers upon the neck of her beloved;
she also prostrated at his feet and marked his forehead with saffron and unbroken grains of rice.
She applied a tilaka and a crescent mark, offered a handful of flowers,
and said, "I am yours," as she sat upon her own seat.
Kṛṣṇa, for his part, placed a garland together with unbroken rice grains and saffron around her neck.
Having taken moist earth, he applied it as a mark upon her forehead;
he placed auspicious vermilion in her braid of hair,
offered a handful of flowers, and gave her a pinch of gulāla.
She too gave an auspicious handful of clay to Kṛṣṇa;
then the two priests joyfully recited the mantras for the gift.
All the maidens who were to receive the gifts likewise performed the same action.
Then, at Kāmaphala, the two gurus bound the ends of their garments in knots upon the forearms of both [the princes];
likewise, they fastened a single long garland of flowers around the necks of both. (58–59)
And at that time, O Rādhikā, when all those maidens— numbering many millions and billions—
fell into a moment of anxiety before their own beloved in his absence,
then the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa displayed a miracle.
He was born bearing ten million forms, adorned with millions upon millions of garlands.
For as many maidens as had been acquired previously, he became a handsome lover for each maiden, possessing a form like that of a lotus.
Whichever [goddesses] were situated wherever, he placed them there according to the prescribed rite;
just as Lakṣmī was on the right side, so it was for the side of all [the others].
He took the necklace for the neck and gave her the vermilion and other [ornaments].
In his forearm, he also wore a bracelet made of *candraka* from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kāmaphala*).
Indeed, everyone there who beheld him obtained all these things.
Now hear, O Rādhikā, of another wonder that occurred there. (64–65)
Then, by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa, Bṛhaspati and Lomaśa became the pillars of the pavilion in the form of lotuses;
likewise, the deities, including Brahmā, became the lotus-pedestals and other parts of the structure, appearing somewhat startled.
The fathers of the maidens were likewise struck with great wonder.
Having beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s status as the Supreme Lord, Śiva and Pārvatī,
as well as the other great souls, beheld the majesty and sovereignty of the Supreme Soul.
Contented and serene, they offered salutations again and again;
and the simple-minded beheld the entire ritual for the giving away of the maidens.
The fathers of the maidens stood there for the purpose of the gift.
But for those whose fathers who had passed away had no [other] sons at all,
they were remembered by Bālakṛṣṇa; having arrived there quickly with excellent forms,
they were all seen to be auspicious and filled with joy at the time of the gift.
Lomaśa also attained great wonder, as did Bṛhaspati;
such a marvel had never occurred before, nor will it ever occur again, as it was witnessed openly by all the worlds. 72.
Then, in this manner, when the time for union with their beloveds had arrived, the fathers gave away their own daughters according to the ritual of gifting. Those maidens,
radiant and auspicious with splendor, stood with faces bowed in modesty.
All of them gave their respective daughters to the Most Perfect One (Paripūrṇatama).
Then all the fathers placed the hands of the maidens into the right hand of Bālakṛṣṇa; Śiva’s lord (Śambhu) also gave his daughter.
O Rādhikā, they gave her away with the formal gift-offering and Vedic mantras:
"This daughter is given by me to the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul, the sage Bālakṛṣṇa."
Having thus recited this and then taking water in their hands, they poured it upon the ground in the presence of Gaṇeśa, with fire as witness.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa, by his father’s command, said, "May there be well-being! (svasti).
Indeed, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa took hold of the maidens;
at that moment, however, there were as many as a hundred million lotuses, each assuming his own form.
Having seen such great sovereignty, the most excellent Śiva offered praise.
Having attained the state of Śiva and assumed a divine form,
he took his own *ḍamaru* drum in his hand, sounded it, and danced.
For he is the witness of the entire universe and the one who sets in motion the wheel of creation.
You alone are that Supreme Lord, shining in the imperishable abode.
You have come to my house for the sake of accomplishing ten million maidens;
today my home is blessed, and likewise, my sacrifice here is eternal.
In whose house tens of millions of maidens are offered to the Supreme Lord with divine knots— blessed indeed is this most excellent Śiva!
[I take refuge in] you alone, the protector of the protectors of lords, known as the Supreme Lord, the ancient Puruṣa.

I bow to the beloved of my daughter, and likewise the beloved of the daughters of Arbuda. (85) Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, golden-hued, the inner self of the universe, dwelling in the hearts of all beloved ones—I bow to You, who possess infinite forms. (86)
Oṃkāra by name, the seed-syllable of liberation, you are self-luminous; you are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
You are the Lord of all, with ten thousand heads; you are the eternal, you are the Supreme Person.
Today I know you alone as that ancient one, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness.
"You have come here for the sake of liberating me; indeed, she was your own beloved in former times.
I am your ancient devotee, and you, having accepted us all, have surely delivered us.
I take refuge in You, who possess infinite forms, who grant birth in excellent forms, and who are worthy of supreme worship. (88-89)
Having spoken thus to Śrīmat Bālakṛṣṇa, O Rādhikā, Śaṅkara gave him a dowry, and all the kings then likewise gave gifts:
ten million pieces of gold and a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun.
The wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā), a parasol for the head, chowries with jeweled handles,
a golden vessel for betel, as well as an inexhaustible vessel,
the wish-granting jar (kalpaghaṭa), golden sandals, and a jewel-gem.
A thousand wish-fulfilling cows together with their calves,
a thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses,
and the entirety of household requisites such as beds and the like.
Śambhu gave what was in his hand to Hari, to Bālakṛṣṇa.
The kings also gave there auspicious beds that provide pleasure,
as well as various treasuries, gold, diamonds, and pearls.
Then the partisans of Hari also gave everything to Kṛṣṇa:
hand-clasps, wealth, gold, silver, thrones, and so forth;
Vāsudeva gave a divine crown and an elephant-throne.
There, Mahāviṣṇu gave him a celestial aerial chariot;
Vairāja gave him two golden earrings and a golden parasol;
Brahmā gave him the Kalpa-pitcher, and Viṣṇu then gave him the discus.
The ancestors gave various golden vessels;
the gods gave coffers of nectar and divine garments;
and then the guardians of the quarters gave divine gold coins.
The oceans gave strings of pearls as well as garlands of pearls;
the trees there gave forth juices, and the kings joyfully bestowed jewels and gems, along with cows, horses, elephants, and bulls in infinite numbers.
Then they also gave ten million female and male servants;
whatever was most excellent in the three worlds, and whatever each person possessed at that time, they all gave as handmaidens, excellent gifts, and sacrificial offerings.
And those belonging to the side of the maidens then gave dowries;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa bestowed a thousand gopīs adorned with jewels,
as well as diamond necklaces, strings of gems and jewels, and ornaments.

And Saṃkarṣaṇa likewise gave her a crown worthy of a virtuous woman; Sadāśiva gave jeweled necklaces, and Kāla gave her garments. [He also gave] a divine skirt free from old age and a bodice of fresh youth.
He also gave him an eternal [garland], and the Rudras likewise gave him garlands;
the Rudras gave countless golden divine wreaths and ornaments of adornment, while Śaṅkara gave him a small parasol.
The goddess gave a lion-throne, and Kubera gave a *koṭikānaka* [drum];
then Lakṣmī was given wealth, and the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) gave riches.
The celestial dwellers of the nether regions and Śeṣa and others gave jewels.
Then all the hosts of *bhūtas* and *pretas* gave ornaments for the sky;
men and women, according to worldly custom and divine tradition as appropriate,
gave abundant gifts to the maidens and to the groom as well.
The Supreme Brahman himself, whose very form is the universe, has today accepted this gift; indeed, it could not have been contained within the pavilion.
Thus, after the gift, the fathers of the brides then [placed their hands] in his hand.
Then, taking water, they indeed spoke [his] lineage,
name, and so forth: "To the Great Soul, Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, whose supreme lineage is Parabrahman, and whose pravaras are Kṛṣṇa, Akṣara, and Narāyaṇa."
To the eminent Brahmin learned in the Sāmaveda, who belongs to the Patnīvratīya branch,
the illustrious Gopālabāla— to him, Śiva himself bore witness in the presence of the sacred fire. (1.14) I am of the Śrīkṛṣṇa lineage and a descendant of Sadāśiva.
He who possesses the three *pravaras* known as Rudra, Kāla, and Yama, and who is a knower of the Rigveda, has given me his daughter Śrī Lakṣmī, whose very form is Lakṣmī herself.
By this gift, may the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, be pleased. (1.15–1.16)
Having spoken thus, he again released water upon the ground;
and there Hari spoke once more, saying, "I have taken it.
In this manner, all the Janakas likewise spoke and released water.

Then the two family priests tied divine knots upon the garments of the Lord’s two daughters. There, the two gurus caused the two girls, who wore garlands around their necks, to circumambulate the fire four times.
Having bowed to the fire, the couples indeed sat upon their respective seats;
there, at that auspicious *gārhapatya* fire,
they performed the oblation with clarified butter, sesame seeds, sugar, and excellent fruits.
They performed the oblation with rice and various sacrificial materials.
Then they received from one another the gracious madhuparka offering and accepted the morsel placed into the mouth by Kṛṣṇa’s beloved.
Then, having touched each other’s hands with palms joined in reverence, they both bowed;
at that moment, perspiration quickly appeared on the forearms of Śrī,
and a thrill of horripilation arose even in Kṛṣṇa.
All the maidens, adorned with garlands of *kaṇṭha* flowers, performed the circumambulation of the fire;
the monkeys likewise took mouthfuls of food, and they both performed the oblations and other rites simultaneously. (1.24–25)
"O Rādhikā! Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Ramā, Māṇikī, and Padmāvatī—these six truthful maidens together performed a circumambulation of the fire in the pavilion along with Kṛṣṇa. (1.26)
Hemanta gave both Ramā and Padmāvatī here;
Nārāyaṇa also gave those other women to Hari. Together with Agni, they all performed the circumambulation of the fire with their husband.
All the other lovely women performed the circumambulation of the fire;
seeing the rite which bestowed such great joy, they rejoiced together with their beloveds.
And there were one hundred and forty maidens residing in the temple.
They performed circumambulations together and offered morsels of food to Hari.

Likewise, all the daughters of Brahmā, the daughters of Īśa, as well as others—the daughters of kings, the daughters of the world, and those of miscellaneous origins—performed circumambulations. (2.293.1–30, 131)
They made morsels for one another and gave excellent betel to their own kin;
and following the consumption of the morsels by the bridegroom and the young brides,
the beauty of finger-rings appeared upon the water of the stage-pool.

"In that regard, O Rādhā! Listen here from me concerning the wives of Kṛṣṇa who were joined in marriage. (133)" Thus ends the section on the worship of Kṛṣṇa performed by Śiveśvara, the removal of household furnishings performed by Goddess Pārvatī, Kṛṣṇa’s sitting upon the seat in the pavilion, and [the arrival] of the bride and the maidens in the *Śrī-lakṣmī-nārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*, in the second part, the *Tretā-santāna*.

Chapter Two Hundred and Ninety-Three: Description of the Tradition of Kṛṣṇa-worship as Divine Worship, the Bondage of the Fruit of Desire, the Giving Away of Maidens, Gifts at the Taking of the Hand, Kṛṣṇa assuming so many forms for the sake of crores, billions, and trillions of maidens, the taking of the hands of all maidens, the wearing of all neck-garlands, the circumambulation of all fires, and the offering according to the rules of lineage and so forth.
[End of] Chapter 293 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 294.
[Author: Chapter 295.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"Tell me here all those beloved ones who have attained maturity."
By the mere remembrance of whom people are liberated from illusion (māyā).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, together with Bālakṛṣṇa at that time.
Just as Lakṣmī, Ṣaṭka, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī;
Ramā, Padmāvatī, and Śrī—these one hundred and forty principal daughters, beginning with Aśanā, who are dear to Brahmā, have been offered. (2–3)
Adorned with flower garlands, they circumambulated the fire;
fourteen thousand Meghanādas were offered up,
as well as the sixty Manasas, the Dīpāvalyas, and the Kanyakās.
Ten million [cows] were offered after circumambulating the fire.
Then, one named Kāmadhenu was offered, as well as ten million cows known as Vasumatī and others, which were being milked.
Śāṃbhavī, Krodhanā, the daughters of Dharā, and the Gahvarās— numbering ten million— were joyfully presented there by Dharā. Furthermore,
a hundred thousand daughters of Vedhas, Sucī, and Vanadevī were also present.
Adorned with excellent garlands offered by the forest goddesses and filled with happiness,
one hundred thousand Dāmanī Rākṣasa maidens, presented by Damana,
circumambulated the fire while wearing those flower garlands. (8–9)
Six thousand maidens, each holding a *kaṅkatālī* fan, and ten thousand *kāṅkatālikā* fans were offered by the *kaṅkatāla* bearers; having circumambulated the fire,
they were joined with Bālakṛṣṇa while adorned with flower garlands.
Twenty-one lakhs of the daughters of his father’s kinsmen were given by Aryaman and made his own;
twenty thousand daughters of his paternal uncles were also made his own; and ten thousand female slaves of his father were likewise made his own there. (11–12)
Rāsātalya gave five thousand maidens born of Daityas;
having circumambulated the fire, they were offered along with flowers and oblations.
Indeed, sixteen maidens, lovely as springtime, were likewise offered.
Then, having circumambulated the fire, Vāsanta gave him five hundred maidens of the Daitya Sālamālin; these girls,
along with a hundred Mothers (Mātṛs), were surrendered by the Daitya and made his own there.
Twenty thousand Svastika Naga maidens, adorned with flower garlands, circumambulated the fire;
likewise, a thousand daughters of King Śāvadīna, wearing beautiful wreaths, did the same. || 16 ||
Having circumambulated the fire, the maidens presented by the king were made his own;
and the thousand daughters of Śambhu, presented by Śambhu himself, adorned with flower garlands, were made his own in the presence of the fire as witness. (17–18)
Sarasvatī and the fourteen branches of knowledge— these sixty maidens were offered by Brahmā with fire as witness and adorned with garlands.
Furthermore, there were two thousand Lakṣmaṇī maidens from within the earth.
There, seventy-two thousand Nāḍikās, the daughters of Brahmā, were offered by Lakṣmaṇa in the presence of fire as witnesses and were taken as his own wives;
they were bestowed by Brahmā and accepted in the presence of fire as witnesses.
Three hundred Gandharva maidens, presented by Viśvāvasu,
performed a circumambulation of the fire while holding flowers and incense.
A thousand princesses from the Jumma and Semal kingdoms were also presented by Jummalā.
Having circumambulated the fire,
five thousand Rākṣasa maidens, adorned with garlands and accompanied by their Sāntapanī wives,
were presented as brides by the Sāntapanas in the presence of the fire as witness, adorned with their own garlands.
Sauratya performed a circumambulation of the fire one hundred times. Then,
the three maidens— Kanyā, Suratarṣyarpitā, and Sapuṣpasraṅnijīkṛtā—
were given by Mahābāleśvarī with the fire as witness.
Offered to Baleśvara, she was adorned with a garland of flowers and made his own.
Then, the sole daughter of Ilavila,
accompanied by a garland of flowers, was offered there by Ilavila and made his own in the presence of the fire as witness.
The hundred daughters of King Aṅga, the son of Dakṣa, adorned with beautiful flower garlands,
as well as the thousand daughters of Uṣṇālaya, were made his own wives;
having circumambulated the fire, they were accompanied by their floral wreaths.
Maidens from eastern lands, daughters of kings, and those born of common folk—
numbering in the tens of millions— were offered by their fathers with fire as witness;
they were bestowed by King Piśaṅga and made his own with the garlands of the bridegroom.

Two daughters of the Santāraṇa brāhmaṇas, adorned with flower garlands, were offered there by Santāraṇa in the presence of fire as witnesses; they were then made his own. At that time, one hundred daughters of King Śibi-deva were also offered by Śibi.
Then, in the presence of the fire as witness, the fifty daughters of King Tharkūṭastha were made to undergo the ordeal; provided with flower garlands, they were restored to life by the fire.
(32–33) The fifty daughters of King Tharkūṭastha, having been offered to the fire as witnesses, were restored to life when joined with the flower garlands. (33)
One hundred daughters of King Vīrajāra were indeed given with fire as witness;
they were presented by Vīrajāra, adorned with flower garlands, and made his own.
Furthermore, sixty daughters of King Śaktyakṣi were also given with fire as witness.
One hundred Piśācinī maidens were presented by Śaktyakṣin;
having circumambulated the fire, they were adorned with their own flower garlands.
Two hundred daughters of King Kālimāśan were offered by the king.
In the presence of the fire as witness,
thirty maidens of King Uralaketu,
accompanied by Yogamālā, were made his own there, having been bestowed upon him by the king.
The five daughters of King Kratha were indeed given by their father with fire as witness; they were united with him there and made his own wives. Pṛthurāja gave twenty of his own daughters to Agnika.
Having performed the circumambulation,
the daughters of Uṣṭrāla were made his own by Daśoṣṭrāla;
in the presence of the fire as witness, they were wedded there, adorned with flower garlands.
There were five [daughters] of King Haṃkāra and five of Jayakāṣṭha;
six of King Tīrāṇa and five of Alvīnara;
and likewise seven of King Jīnavardhin, as well as Anāthā and Ekalā.
Having circumambulated the fire offered by their respective kings,
those two hundred and one thousand auspicious maidens were united with Bālakṛṣṇa in the garland of yoga.
|| 43 || Two hundred and one thousand auspicious maidens [were thus wedded].

The seven daughters of Alpeketu, who had been seized by Rākṣasas and brought before the fire as witnesses, were made his own wives along with Sumasraṅgī. Likewise, there were twenty-one maidens belonging to King Parīkṣit, excluding Jayakṛṣṇā. (44–45)
At that time, King Indurāya also had two beautiful daughters;
King Mudrāṇḍa had fifteen adorned daughters;
King Gaṇḍa had nine; and Līnorṇaja had four.
King Bṛhacchara also had eleven daughters;
King Balalin had forty daughters;
Varasiṃha had exactly five; and Rāyagāma had eight daughters. (47–48)
For the king Phena-tantu there are two, for Stoka-homa one;
for the king Kāṣṭhāyāna there is one, and for Kolaka also one.
For the king Dinamāna there are two maidens, together with the Yogamālikās.

Having circumambulated the fire, those fifty-one daughters of the king of the Rāyakinnaras were presented by their respective fathers; they were offered by the kings and accepted as his own by Bālakṛṣṇa. (2.294.50–51)
Likewise, there were twenty-one daughters of Rāyakoṭīśvara,
and twenty daughters of Rāyaraṇajidbhya.
At that time, there were also three daughters of King Rāyavākakṣa.
King Rāyamārīśa had three beautiful daughters;
King Rāyabaleśvara likewise had three other daughters;
and King Rāyalambāra had six daughters endowed with youth. (53–54)
King Rāyanavārka had seven very beautiful daughters;
King Rāyahūṇḍeśa had nine very delicate daughters;
and King Rāyakūpeśa had one virtuous and auspicious daughter.
Likewise, King Kālīmaṇḍa had four daughters;
King Vanajaleśa had five very pale daughters; and Pārāvārapiba also had three daughters who were deep red.
King Koṭīśvara had two daughters, King Satīśa had three,
and King Tretākarkaśa had seven beautiful daughters.
King Āṇḍajarā also had four auspicious daughters.
King Bālyaraja also had one daughter who was endowed with righteousness.
King Rāyasomanabhūpa had three most beautiful daughters, and likewise, King Ūrugavākṣa had two beautiful daughters. (2.294.59–60)
King Parāṅvṛta had two daughters; King Rājārāja had one daughter;
King Īśānapāda had forty-one beautiful daughters;
and King Rājārāyapati had thirty-three beautiful daughters. (6.1)
Then all these women there, adorned with garlands of yoga,
radiant with royal elegance, and presented by their respective fathers,
circumambulated the fire and were taken as wives by Bālakṛṣṇa.
Thirty maidens, beginning with Maṅgalā, were presented by the great sages;
they became the wives of Bālakṛṣṇa for those various sages.
Furthermore, the radiant daughters of kings from the region of Ājanābha [were also taken].
Ten thousand [daughters] were presented by their respective fathers and other relatives;
ten thousand daughters were presented by the subjects—
richly adorned with all ornaments and beautified by garlands of yoga.

Having circumambulated the fire, those who had been made their own by Bālakṛṣṇa then performed the marriage ceremony for all of them individually in separate sacrificial pits, with individual fires as witnesses. (67)
O Rādhikā! And likewise there were thousands of others belonging to Kubera;
thousands belonging to Mahendra; thousands of daughters of Yama;
those of Vāyu, Vaiśvakarman, the Trees, Rudra, and those born of Fire.
There were also the Śrāvaṇyas, the Khānijyas, the Sāṃvatsaryas, and the Gopikās;
the Prācīnyas, the Piśaṅginyas, and the Rāśiyānyas by the millions;
and the Raumāyanyas, the Pāraśvas, and the Dhaivaryas by the thousands.
There were also Kinnarīs and Apsarases by the millions—Gaurīs and Pārṣvas, Ābhriktyas and Hārityas, those of the netherworld (pātālya) and those of heaven (svargya);
likewise, Apsarases from the Brahma-lake and Gāndharvīs by the millions. (71–72)
Vidyunmaṇiśca, the skillful Yoginī, and two others besides;
as well as Bhaumyas and Dānavīs numbering in the billions, trillions, and hundreds of millions—what person with limited vision could possibly calculate their number there? (73)
All of them, having remembered their fathers and other elders, stood in the presence of the Pitṛs; adorned, having tied the ends of their garments, and being in the full bloom of youth,
they were equipped with yoga-garlands and then performed circumambulation of the fire.

Then, while everyone was looking on, the Supreme Soul Bālakṛṣṇa individually accepted each of them— those who had been offered by their respective fathers and others— with the taking of their hands in marriage by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

O Rādhikā! At the beginning of creation, they were made to hear [the truth] by the Supreme Soul in the presence of fire as witness and with all beings as witnesses. Indeed, all these beloveds of Brahmā were wedded according to the sacred rites. (77–78)
Those [goddesses] are indeed the very powers (śakti) of Hari, arisen from the form of Hari;
they have come to the earth for the sake of Hari throughout the entire creation,
and at the proper time, they remain as they desire, in every way beloved by Kṛṣṇa.
They have taken refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa at Kāśī. In the courtyard of Śiveśvara, time does not exert its power over them;
for Śiva is indeed the embodiment of Time, and therefore they have been offered by Him as those who transcend it.
All those forms of Kṛṣṇa that transcend time are indeed bestowers of liberation.
Saurāṣṭra was born from my jewel; here Bālakṛṣṇa shines forth.
Having undergone his marriage in Kāśī, he manifests throughout the three worlds.
All of them, having been waiting and having now attained the wedding ceremony,
became fulfilled and filled with eternal bliss.
Lakṣmī, the daughter of Śiva and Īśvara, obtained her own beloved on earth.
Padmavatī, daughter of the quarters; Subhāsvarā, daughter of the Sun; Śrī, daughter of the Kalpa-tree; Lakṣmī, daughter of the Ocean of Milk;
Māṇikyā, daughter of divine splendor; and the virtuous Akṣarī.
Likewise, Kamalā and the others, having obtained the auspicious Hari as their beloved,
became fulfilled and were endowed with every object of enjoyment.
All of them were wedded there during that auspicious and excellent union of the two Kṛṣṇas.
Listen, O Rādhā: at that time, Kāśīrāja Śivachatruka, as well as Dhenupāla—the supreme king of devotees of Śiveśvara—beheld the infinite, supreme lordly power within Bālakṛṣṇa. (88)
At that very moment, the King of Kāśī gave ten maidens as well;
meanwhile, Dhenupāla gave three in the presence of fire as witnesses.
Accompanied by Yogamālā, they were all brought into this pavilion.
Then the king gave him a dowry of one hundred thousand gold pieces, as well as a palanquin, a hundred female slaves, and ornaments. Furthermore,
the subjects also gave gifts to that Bālakṛṣṇa in the pavilion.

Then, after performing various kinds of gifts, he offered oblations into that sacrificial pit (92). Having offered into the fire those excellent virtues of a householder as instructed by his guru, the bridegroom, together with his wife, heard there the duties to be protected on all sides (93).
O Mādhava, protect the indivisible Dharma of this couple;
and you, who possess these women as your own half-bodies, protect them all.
O Supreme Lord, behold happiness in happiness and likewise sorrow in sorrow.
The beloved and the lover are indeed not distinct; bring about the unity of the two bodies.
(95) Regard all beloved women as your own self and gladden them; for within the bodies of those beloved ones, your own body shines resplendent. (96)
Head to head, face to face, heart to heart; belly to belly, waist to waist, and foot to foot—regarding the body of your beloved as your own body, protect her. 97.

Perform here together with them those duties that serve to increase the lineage. O beloved, one's own wife should be regarded as dear as one's own life; she should always be served like a lord in every way. 98–99.
Devotion to the husband must always be maintained by wives for the sake of happiness;
the command of the Lord must always be obeyed even at the cost of one's life and all other activities.
With a sense of oneness, the Lord himself should be meditated upon and worshipped.
Thus, having observed this, couples should conduct themselves without interruption;
rivalry should never be provoked between one another at any time. Toward co-wives, one should always behave as toward a sister. || 101–102 ||
O sons, one should always be content after giving happiness to others;
they should indeed be regarded as portions of the Lord and as His own parts, never otherwise.
One should abide in this alone as the highest dharma; may there be well-being for you, and may there be happiness and peace.
Having spoken thus, the two gurus performed a sprinkling with water from the sprouts.
Kṛṣṇa then gave them abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as maidens,
ten million jewels, gems, and ten million measures of gold.
Then the preceptors performed the concluding rites of the sacrificial ritual;
thereafter came the dismissal of the deities and the dismissal of all [the participants].
Then Hari quickly brought about the dissolution of the many forms.
In the meantime, the goddess Girijā arrived quickly,
preceded by virtuous women who possessed sons and husbands;
at that time, the Mothers who dwell within all creation also arrived.
Having performed all auspicious rites there, such as the ritual sprinkling (*nirmañchana*) and others,
they caused the couple to enter a palace fashioned of jewels, which was illuminated like a dwelling fit for ten million, a hundred billion, and a hundred thousand maidens.
It was instantly fashioned by Viśvakarman like a second Goloka,
renovated with the assistance of the liberated one named Kailāsa;
and they indeed caused [the deities] to dwell upon jeweled lion-thrones.
The maidens also fed together with their master;
they offered camphor, betel-leaf, and scented water.
Then Sarasvatī spoke to all the mothers of creation: ||| 112 ||

May the goddesses who are truthful, virtuous, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, faithful to their husbands, and blessed with good fortune—may these maidens bestow the highest auspiciousness. Just as the Lord is, so is the maiden; they have been joined together by the Supreme Self.
"Let the meetings of the wise with the wise be auspicious.
(1.14) Then the Lord of Śivā honored all the distinguished men and women according to the prescribed rite and fed them with great respect. (1.15)
"Let it be eaten! Let it be enjoyed! Let one's own desire be sucked! Let it be licked again and again!
Let it be given, let it be given, and let it be taken! Let there be satisfaction!"—the sound "Let it be drunk! Let it be tasted! arose incessantly.

In the halls there arose a sound of auspicious instrumental music and singing. (1.17) Thus, at the end of the night, when the meal was finished and even the betel had been set aside, the honored guests attained supreme peace, rest, and auspicious sleep. (1.18)
Both sides took their places in the vast city that had been prepared;
and in the palace of the royal couple, the glorious Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, who is infinite, assumed as many forms as there were beloved wives. He, the Lord, assumed as many forms as there were consorts.
Served by them upon soft beds, he became the giver of happiness.
O Rādhikā, even millions of billions of crores of consorts are never able to overcome that yogi of infinite being and infinite power.
In that city, during the night, there were dances, sports, and other excellent arts of wrestling,
the sounding of musical instruments, and performances of dramas,
all undertaken as part of the wedding festivities.
From the midpoint of the night onwards, everything indeed becomes peaceful within the circle of truth.

(123) Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Those Married with Fire as Witness," "Instruction on Domestic Duties," "Renunciation of the Duties of Marriage," "The Feeding of the Couple," "The Universal Feeding," "Renunciation of the Forms of Koṭi, Arbuda, and Abja," "The Sport of Kṛṣṇa in All His Forms with All of Them in the Couple's Chamber," and "The Universal Reclining," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (294)
← Chapter 294: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) Chapter 295 [[Author: → Chapter 296
Śrī Rādhikā said:
How many beloved maidens were enumerated at that time in the chamber of love? How many indeed were previously obtained, and how many were obtained thereafter?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, those maidens who were offered by their own fathers and others number four crores, that is, four hundred thousand, and they are indeed my beloveds.
Furthermore, fifty-five thousand,
six hundred and twenty-two additional new maidens were brought under his control.
Then there were other maidens from the three worlds, such as Kauberī and the rest.
Arbuda, Svāgatā, Abja, and Sūkṣmavartikā—these indeed were the friends of Rādhikā in the palace of Bālakṛṣṇa;
they remained there upon the bed of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (4–5)
All those beautiful women, numbering in the hundreds of billions of trillions, were indeed present in the chamber of delight;
they remained there for that long, endowed with boons, upon couches numbering in the hundreds of billions of trillions.
Then, when morning had dawned on the fifth day, Śrī Hari then—
With auspicious rites and songs, with the sounding of fine musical instruments,
with the chanting of the fame of bards, minstrels, and panegyrists, with Vedic hymns and chants uttered by the twice-born, and with the praises offered by the staff-bearers; (7–8)
The Lord also woke up, and all the mistresses woke as well.

Having performed their morning ablutions and daily rites, and having adorned themselves with ornaments, they were accompanied at dawn by their beloved wives, who were likewise resplendent with their own finery. (9) Bālakṛṣṇa [arose]. (10) Accompanied by his beloved wives, who were radiant with the beauty of their ornaments, he arose at daybreak.
Having honored the elders, the venerable, the gurus, the preeminent, and the virtuous and faithful women,
and having received the blessings of the elders, he— accompanied by ten million women and men— prepared for a procession to wander through the city. (2.295.10–11)
Then, at the command of his elders, the traveler prepared his own carriage according to tradition;
it was made ready, beautiful, adorned with full-blown flowers, and most splendid.
Then, with a virtuous heart, he ascended that vehicle, which was as magnificent as an elephant.
It was vast and exceedingly beautiful, created by the Architect of the Universe (Viśvakartṛ).
It was long enough for travel, extending for many yojanas in length,
and was well-frequented by rivers numbering in the millions, billions, and hundreds of billions.
The Supreme Lord shone upon that celestial chariot, Bhūsparśa, which had been sent by Śiva—the one known as Kailāsa—and was newly established;
it was beautified by the fragrance of saffron paste, saffron, musk, and sandalwood. (15)
It shone with rows of flower-offerings, beautiful and perfectly circular in every respect (16).
It was adorned with countless golden lion-thrones, a sight captivating to the mind;
it was fashioned like a casket of saffron, complete with troughs for scattering flowers (17).
It was preceded by the songs of women who were the foremost among those honored on earth, while it was led at the front by men who were the foremost among those honored on earth;
likewise, it was accompanied by parents and other relatives of the bridegroom and bride. (18)
The celestial chariot of the illustrious Śaṅkara, honored by all and resounded with the sounds of every musical instrument, was worshipped in the courtyard of his palace;
it was attended by a husband and wife who were scattering handfuls of full-blown *gulāla* flowers.
Advancing slowly at first, revealing great bliss,
that army proceeded forward from the temple of Śiva.
The people of the settlement honored the couples with fruits and other offerings.
Then, with offerings of precious substances, necklaces, gifts for the hands, flowers, and auspicious blessings,
the blossoming procession of pilgrims, having circumambulated the entire city of Girijā and received all the worship offered by the people, increased its splendor. || 22-23 ||
Then, having wandered throughout the entire city of Kāśīpattana along with his family, he likewise beheld the goddess Durgā, the tutelary deity of his lineage;
he beheld Hanumān and beheld Viśveśvara.
There was a vision of Annapūrṇā and also a vision of Gaṇeśa;
on the bank of the Pañcagaṅgā, there was also a vision of Dharmadeva,
along with his worship through wealth, gifts, flowers, leaves, fruits, and other offerings.
Having performed [these rites] everywhere, he then went to Bindumādhava.
There, having worshipped the illustrious Mādhava and given gifts and sacrificial fees,
he departed upon a celestial chariot over the purifying waters of the Gaṅgā.
The beloved women were as if bound by the knots of yoga, and the beloved [husband] likewise [drank] the water of the river.

(28) Having taken up the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana), having worshipped that most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha), and having asked forgiveness from the glorious Gaṅgā, he offered the gift of a lamp. (29)
They placed a gift of much gold, accompanied by mantras, into his mouth;
there, the true guru Lomaśa untied the knots of yoga.
Then the Lord [departed] again from the center of the city by means of a celestial chariot.
He departed by way of the royal road accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments.
Men and women stood everywhere, eager to see him;
having seen him again and again—so beloved, so worthy, and so exceedingly beautiful—they gazed upon him.
They praised in many ways the supreme happiness of the couple.
There, being enchanted by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they said to one another:
"This very Lord, the ocean of mercy, has arrived. (33)
"O friend, when will that Lord meet us?
This Master has been obtained here by many young maidens through His grace alone, and certainly not from the accumulation of their own merit. (34)
O friend, having obtained this human body which is so difficult to attain, if the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is not served,
then the bonds of worldly existence will never find peace.
Let this Lord be beheld with your own eyes—
He who is eternally worshipped by infinite attendants in the supreme imperishable realm, and by the bliss-bestowing, virtuous consorts of the Lord.
Worshipped by maidens even in other worlds, this bestower of happiness has arrived here; let him be sprinkled with water.
For he indeed possesses the power to assume many millions of forms. || 36 ||
For he is the fulfiller of the essence of all desires;
though dwelling within the heart, he has become visible to one's own eyes. Let him be grasped here by you with devotion. (37)
In former times, the Śrutis attended upon him with songs of his glories; moreover, celestial maidens in human form, along with the wives of the gods and royal princesses, served him together.
Behold these vehicles that carry one like horses!
Is it not indeed easy to travel by means of the wealth of meritorious coins?
Yet we are here destitute of such wealth.
For those who have not attained the supreme imperishable state here,
it is desired through both worship and absorption;
O friend, just as millions of beloveds are enjoyed here— ||39|| [so too is that state].
Even by one's own actions, Hari is not attained;
even if He is attained, if He is not enjoyed here, then one's own birth is seen to be in vain. (2.295.40)
May they, adorned with beautiful garlands, triumph for many years, immersed in an ocean of happiness;
may they possess the splendor of a most excellent form, like a hundred crores of Kamadevas.
May they find happiness and may they attain true bliss.
O friend, a longing for his lotus-face arises within me; what means is there here to achieve this?
This is my petition: you reside within our hearts; therefore, please grant us a new union there.
O brides! You who have offered salutations to the Lord—
Indeed, let our own maidservants look on; at some time, in the place of love, let them remember their own master—this indeed is our prayer. (43)
Having praised them, saying "O Rādhikā," and having bowed and placed Hari within their hearts, they honored the Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with flowers and other offerings.
Listen, O Rādhā: having beheld the Supreme Brahman, the courtesans—
In their eagerness, they worshipped him by the thousands and offered him praises;
likewise, three hundred and four maidens, remaining unblemished, were also enchanted.
Then, by their mothers’ command, they [honored] the Lord, the bridegroom, at every stage along the way.
Having worshipped him, they placed flower garlands around the neck of the Lord; offered by the Mothers, these garlands caused them to ascend into the middle of the celestial chariot.
And those wives of Kṛṣṇa became Gāndharva attendants forever.
Thus, O Rādhā, the wives of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa numbered four crores,
four lakhs, and even more than that— increased by fifty-six thousand, totaling 40,456,000. (48–49)
Those numbered in the millions, billions, and trillions, as well as others, have been rendered soulless;
they now rejoice together with those who are equal in form and entirely identical. (Millions, billions, and trillions). || 2.295.50 ||
By the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇas and Śrī Bāla Kṛṣṇas,
the army of Phullayātrī then proceeded from there to the unsurpassed city of Śivasvāmipura, their own abode.
Then the avoidance of the Phulla festival occurred, which brought auspiciousness.
Śiveśvara and the others, full of eagerness, returned to their own abodes.
Thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the others departed for the auspicious city of Pārvatī.
Then Śaṅkara indeed caused all the great lords to partake of foods consisting of many kinds of delicious dishes according to the prescribed rite—
various types of milk-rice and excellent boiled rice as well.
Śaṅkara caused [them] to eat vegetables and pulses, as well as all kinds of foods to be chewed and swallowed,
things to be licked and sucked, and all sweet drinks—
even nectars of every kind. (55–56)
Then Śaṅkara fed all the dignitaries, the parties of the bridegroom and the bride, the village folk, the poor, and the mendicants;
likewise, he fed all the groups of servants as well as the troupes of dancers and the like.
He [honored] all the groups of panegyrists and all the musicians;
all the carriers and all the guards, as well as the singers,
the laborers, the ascetics, the virtuous men, and the guests who had arrived.
Śivarāja fed all the Brahmins, all his elders, those dear to Brahmā, as well as the Lord,
Kṛṣṇa’s father, his brothers, and his entire family;
he also provided them with drinks.
He fed all those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), all those dwelling on earth,
all those dwelling in heaven and other realms, all those dwelling in the abodes of the lords (īśvara),
and all those dwelling in the imperishable (akṣara) in many ways.
She fed sages, virtuous men, chaste women, and likewise those who maintain celibacy; she fed groups of renunciants, groups of yogis, and lords.
She also fed even insects, moths, and the like, as well as beasts and flocks of birds.
[He saw] those born of sweat, those born of water, those born of the earth, and the stationary and moving beings;
sacred fords, mountains, rivers, streams, and oceans; all the *kalpalatās* and other such things, as well as all the gods and shrines. (64–65)
Śaṅkara fed the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others, as well as the gandharvas, kinnaras, and the cāraṇas who dwell in Kāśī;
he also gave them drinks and presented them with betel leaves.
Then Śiva gave there as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) even greater quantities of gold, silver, and fine pearls;
he also gave golden rings, ornaments, garments, and garlands, numbering in the tens of millions, billions, and trillions.
Thereafter, he gave her as a dowry ten million gold coins,
a casket of divine recipes, a vessel of divine recipes, an inexhaustible cooking pot,
an imperishable treasury, and likewise an unimpeded royal umbrella.
The *pātrikā* containing all flavors, the *suvallikā* containing all fragrances; the *puttalī* containing all forms, and the pill (*guṭī*) that bestows eternal youth;
the fly-whisk that grants movement through the sky, and the armor that wards off time.
Then the King of Kāśī gave to Bālakṛṣṇa a bed that was a treasury of bliss, a pearl necklace, and also a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi);
he also gave him a celestial chariot with wheels as bright as the sun.
A hundred elephants, a thousand horses, a thousand wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), a hundred thousand bulls, a hundred thousand horses with black ears,
a thousand female slaves, and likewise a jeweled lion-throne. (73–74)
The kings as far as Ājanābha gave her dowries such as the great staff that devours death and the cane-stick that destroys disease; likewise,
the subjects as far as Ājanābha also gave her dowries.
The fathers, brothers,
and mothers of the maidens also gave them dowries, as well as beautiful ornaments, garments, and the like; likewise, jewels, diamonds, garlands, necklaces, and those made of precious gems.
Golden, silver, and jeweled vessels, as well as pearls;
celestial chariots, excellent vehicles, and beds adorned with couches;
likewise, liberated souls, lords, incarnations, and hosts of goddesses.
The gods, the ancestors, the great seers, and human beings all gave wedding gifts (yautaka) in every way, according to what was appropriate. Then,
when the distribution of the wedding gifts had been completed, Hari himself [bestowed further gifts].
He bestowed golden rewards upon those worthy recipients according to their merit; he gave ten thousand to each of his slaves, his circle of servants, and his attendants,
and likewise he gave gold to the laborers as well.
To singers, barbers, and even porters;
to those in the world who massage the body, as well as to female servants, female cleaners, female washers, and female dyers—he gave wealth. (82–83)
He gave wealth to the female dancers, the instrumentalists, and the singers;
he gave wealth to the bards, the wandering minstrels, the captive women, and the Vidyādharas;
likewise, he gave wealth to the musicians and the artisans and painters. (84)
He bestowed wealth upon those who showed him the way and those who were victorious;
he gave wealth to those who carried water, those who fanned him, and those who performed acts of pacification.
He granted wealth to those who drove carts, those who traveled in celestial chariots, and those who rode in chariots.
He bestowed wealth upon the banner-bearers, the musicians, and the charioteers;
he gave wealth to the guards, the companions, and the mendicants.
He bestowed wealth upon the maidens, the youths, and the virtuous women.
She gave wealth to the *nālinīs*, the *śodhinīs*, and the *tālinīs*;
she gave wealth to the *vaṃśinīs*, to the twice-born (*dvijas*), and to the followers of various sects (*tairthikas*);
