Having beheld the delightful ground adorned by the Badarī forest,
having looked upon the grove of Bakula trees and gazed upon the Jambū forest,
and likewise having observed the Gundrā forest and the Sītāphala forest.
They arrived at Aśvapaṭṭasara joyfully at the onset of night.
Having descended from their celestial chariot, they performed their evening prayers.
Then, accompanied by Bālakṛṣṇa, they went to their own dwellings.
Then they all partook of their meal and thereafter adorned themselves with finery;
Bālakṛṣṇa then went to the great pavilion to attend upon the honored guests,
accompanied by his father, brothers, and others.
He caused them all to be fed with great respect.
He offered betel and other items, and gave whatever else was required there.
Indeed, everything was fully provided; what could possibly be lacking in the house of Mādhavī?
Filled with great honor and serene through their discernment of the Supreme,
the men and women attained supreme rest during the night. Then, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa arrived at the palace.
Then those newly-wed brides awaited their beloved in order to bring him pleasure;
and the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, assumed forms numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions to fulfill the desires of all his new wives. (51–52)
In every single house, that bestower of delight,
the Lord of the Great Lords of Yoga, manifests during the night.
Listen, O Rādhā, for at that time a certain divine maiden arrived.
Indeed, she had come to behold the praised pavilion, which was commended by the gods in the form of swans;
for she had approached to see both the small and the great,
yet first, appearing as ten million forms, she beheld the great pavilion.
Having become so, she then beheld everything as a great wonder;
yet again, she looked upon the small pavilion with a steady gaze.
Having truly observed the three worlds, she once more became a great wonder.
Having offered salutations to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), she remained silent for a moment.
Śrī Rādhikā said: "Who was that girl? How did she come there, and where has she gone again?"
"Tell me everything, O Blessed One, if it is something that may be heard, for there is nothing higher.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, having seen the pavilion, the deities indeed assumed the form of swans."
Having gone to heaven, they praised the highly beautiful pavilion.
Upon hearing that, Dyaus quickly made up her mind to see it for herself.
Dyaus herself, having become a young maiden, arrived at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Adorned with earrings, a crown, and chains, and graced with ornaments,
she was filled with all splendor and replete with the essence of nectar;
her limbs were proportionate to her form, like another enchanting goddess.
Whether it was Rādhā, Kamalā, or some other woman who had come there,
she beheld everything that she had never before seen or heard anywhere;
having witnessed all of that in the pavilion, the virtuous lady was filled with great wonder.
In a very small pavilion, the Goddess stood by the side of the sacrificial post.
With a salutation, the pavilion offered a welcome to the Goddess:
"Come, O Goddess who bestows heaven; let me offer you a welcome."
"Accept water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), food, and water.
Having spoken thus, she offered her a throne, water, and so forth;
she gave her the honey-mixture and also provided auspicious food.
Having reached the pavilion, she said: "O Pavilion of the Liberated King, listen!
If Bālakṛṣṇa possesses a pavilion such as this, what would his palace be like, and what would his riches be?"
And what would those celestial women who enjoy them be like?
And what would their beloveds be like, and what would his own splendors be like? Indeed, I wish to see all this. (68–69)
"He alone is the lord of hundreds of millions of billions of beautiful women;
I have heard this today from the mouth of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.
How might he become accessible to all? I desire to see him, O Heaven."
"The gods dwell within me; what power does he possess compared to them? What is his sovereignty, what is his heroism, or what is the strength of his yoga?
Of what form is he who now stands alone, for he is indeed the Lord of all? ||71-72||
"I have heard that even Indra, my husband, is not capable in such a manner.
Thus, urged by Urvaśī, I have come here to see him.
And having been told so by the Preceptor of the Gods, I have come here, unable to endure [the situation]. (73)
"I have been insulted by the gods, for you are not like this pavilion (maṇḍapa).
Nor do you possess even a ten-millionth part of the sovereignty of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Therefore, having come here today and beheld this pavilion, I [have spoken thus]. (74-75)
"Though never seen nor even heard of before, that jewel rests upon the threshold;
indeed, I have become free from pride and now desire to behold its splendor—its riches, that divine beauty, and those millions of lotus-eyed women.
(76) [I wish to see] those riches, that divine loveliness, and those millions of women with eyes like lotuses.
"I especially wish to see the new Lakṣmī; I am Dyu.
Having been addressed thus, Maṇḍapa went quickly to the palace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself and informed the staff-bearer at the door of Lakṣmī’s residence.
The cane-bearer, endowed with jewels, having gone and received the command,

caused that maiden— who was like the sky itself, possessing the form of ten million, a hundred million, and a trillion [stars], and who was truly coeval with it— to enter that beautiful palace of Lakṣmī.
She then entered all the houses to look about;
in every house she beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, possessing a divine form, standing with each individual woman, yet appearing to have distinct activities in each dwelling.
In the house of Lakṣmī, Dyaus saw Acyuta swinging upon a swing together with Lakṣmī; he worshiped him and bowed down.
In the house of Māṇikī, she saw Kṛṣṇa eating.
In the house of Padmāvatī, she saw her beloved seated upon a couch;
in the house of Ramā, she indeed saw him drinking milk;
and in the house of Rādhā, she saw Kṛṣṇa reclining upon his bed. (83–84)
In the House of Fortune (Śrīgṛha), she saw him sporting with Śrī in the very act of gambling; and in the Palace of Skill (Kuśalāsaudha), he was indeed chewing betel-leaf.
And in the House of Sarasvatī, she found him seated, singing to the accompaniment of a lute.
In the house of Gaṅgā, she saw him massaging her feet with his own;
in the house of Virajā, she saw him wandering here and there;
and in the house of Durgā, she saw him laughing with playful words.
In the temple of Śāradā, he indeed saw him chanting his rosary;
in the houses of the daughters of the King of Kāśī, he saw him in the form of Kṛṣṇa, delighting the women and bringing them joy. (88)
Dyau beheld him in various forms within the dwellings of Ājanābhi—
residing in the accounts of the Itihāsas and engaged in the mastery of the arts— and she saw him in the houses of his three hundred wives, who were each more than a hundred years of age.
She indeed saw the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa delighting in the state of playful union with His bed; and then Dyaus saw the Lord performing the dressing of His hair in the houses of auspicious women.
Then he saw the Lord, who had been massaged by the women of the Uṣṇālaya region in their home,
bathed with the finest oils and the like, and adorned with ornaments,
in the palace of the beautiful women of Prācīnīya. (92–93)
The fortunate lady of heaven beheld her husband Hari being colored and decorated by those women with lac-dye and other substances;
she saw him sporting and making them laugh within the houses of the lovely women of Rāśīyāna.

She saw the beautiful son of Kambharā immersed in the local customs of those various regions (95). At that time, she saw him in the houses of the wives of the Kimpuruṣas, absorbed in music together with them all (96).
In the palaces of the beloved women of Ketumāla, he saw him— conforming to royal custom— wearing the ornaments of a king and accompanied by parrots;
and in the dwellings of the immortals, he saw him dancing together with them.
Together with her female attendants, she beheld the sky filled with bliss;
and in the dwellings of the Hārītīs, she saw him seated upon a throne, surrounded by women and attended by his kinsmen. (98–99)
In the dwellings of the Ābhīras, he saw that Lord, devoted to the worship of the gods, at night; and Dyau beheld the Master wearing a divine form.
In the temples of the Ābhīris, he was singing with instrumental rhythms.
She beheld Kṛṣṇa, who was immersed in her own state of being filled with passion;
she saw Kṛṣṇa in the house of his paternal ancestors, engaged in the ancestral rites (śrāddha);
and she beheld Mādhava endowed with the erotic sentiments and other states of the goddesses.
In one place she saw him watching a theatrical performance with a woman,
and in another she saw him touching her with an expression of love. Then, in yet another place, she saw him immersed in meditation like a yogi.
In one place she saw him fast asleep in slumber;
in another, indeed, instructing the women in the knowledge of Brahman;
and in yet another, then filling the hearts of the women [with love].
Somewhere he saw one weaving a garland from various kinds of flowers;
the sky beheld him standing alone in the courtyard of a house. Then, elsewhere, it saw him coming from one neighboring house to another.
In some places he saw the Lord within the house, glowing with fire;
in others, he saw him just outside at the doorway;
and in some places, he saw him adorned, walking together with his wife.
In one place she saw him showing his own wife her face with a mole in a mirror, and making a mole appear on it;
in another place, he was applying collyrium to the eyes of a woman.
In one place he was then applying a leaf-design upon the forehead of his beloved;
in another place he was anointing her feet with red lac; and in yet another place, out of intense identification, he was embracing her.

In one place he saw Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa feeding his own dependents with morsels of food, and in another place offering the essence of betel-leaf from His own mouth; while the Sky-goddess stood fanning Him with a fan.
In one place he saw that king of kings seated upon his throne;
in another, being massaged and rubbed by many women; and in yet another, beckoning his own beloved wife under the pretext of a glance from his eye.

In some places he saw the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa writing on a leaf with subtle and hidden gestures; thus, in all the palaces, the sky beheld the omnipresent Lord in ten thousand different activities.
With supreme affection, she worshipped the divine couple in every house.
And Lakṣmī and the others, recognizing her as their own representative on heaven and earth,
joyfully offered her a most cordial welcome and fed her with eager devotion.
And they gave excellent rewards such as garlands of flowers;
the women bestowed the remembrance of their lovely pastimes, which grants liberation. Dyaus beheld that prosperity, the most supreme of all.

Those various riches— garments, ornaments, seats, couches fit for reclining, vessels, jewels, and diamonds— which exist neither in heaven, nor in the realm of truth, nor even among the lords; (2.297.1–20)

Having beheld treasuries, four-sided pavilions, excellent mechanical devices, golden caskets, and celestial chariots, she was filled with great wonder. [She saw] the palace of Indra, the mansion of Brahmā, the abode of the Sun, and the residence of the Moon.
Having beheld in a single house that prosperity which does not exist even in the eternal abode of Kubera, the heavens became divested of its pride. Then,
having received blessings and forgiveness, it returned to the pavilion.
She departed for heaven, illuminating the ten directions as she traveled through the sky.
Thus, O Rādhikā, was the glorious deed of Bālakṛṣṇa,
endowed with millions of opulences and possessing hundreds of millions of billions of wives.
Together with as many [consorts] as there are, eternally filled with the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*),
he is indeed to be understood as divine, devoid of material qualities (*nirguṇa*), auspicious, and the bestower of liberation. Thus,
the Blessed One is indeed the eternal bestower of happiness upon those who serve him with devotion.
The Lord, who fulfills all desires and is within the scope of good fortune, slept soundly as the companion of the night for the newlywed brides.
Then, O Rādhikā, even though she had gone to heaven, she was enchanted by Hari.
From then on, she constantly strove day and night to become his wife.
Once, having developed a desire for sensual enjoyment, she approached Śrī Hari in private;
after eating and bringing her satisfaction, Hari sent her back, and she went to heaven delighted.

Thus, in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*: On the morning of the sixth day, the beloved wives performed their daily rites and received the mantras; there was a feast for the great sages (*mahīmānas*); the young women traveled through the sky in celestial chariots (*vimānas*) to view the forests; they took their evening meal; the maiden Dyau arrived to witness the divine play (*līlā*); having beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa displaying diverse pastimes within the palaces of hundreds of millions of billions of women, the enchanted Dyau returned to heaven; and Hari fell asleep.

Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga).
Chapter 298.
[The Author: Chapter 299.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, [I am] the one who simultaneously bestows happiness upon my own wives during the night.

At dawn, Hari was awakened by auspicious musical instruments and hymns of praise. Then, at the hour of Brahmā, those who were intent on their duties also awoke. Hari said to them all, "Remain in meditation before me for a moment."
"By my yoga, you women have today become divine;
you are liberated, freed from illusion, and devoid of all veils.
O Rādhikā! Thus were all the women of Kṛṣṇa and Mādhava addressed.
Having received the command of their beloved husbands, those devoted wives remained absorbed in meditation for a moment.

(4) Then, at that time, all of them, under the influence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the channels (*nāḍī*), withdrew the breaths from the channels and entered into the heart in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). (5)
Having forgotten their perception of the body due to the presence of their beloved in their hearts,
they beheld him, radiant with the splendor of Brahman, residing within his own form.
There, he became a mass of effulgence like great oceans of light.
There, they gazed upon heaven and all the abodes of the gods;
then, further ahead, together with their lord in their own celestial vehicle,
they proceeded, beholding the regions of the ancestors, which were radiant with merit.
Then, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa as their beloved, they all proceeded further ahead; they went to Satyaloka and were honored by its inhabitants.
Having attained a divine state, they passed through the firm covering of the earth.
Then, having pierced through, they all proceeded toward the covering of the waters.
At the junction of that covering, those servants of Śrī Rāma beheld Vaikuṇṭha in the proximity of light. (2.298.10–11)
Sītā, Rāmā, and the others joyfully offered them a welcome;
Rāmāditya also extended a welcome to the Supreme Soul.
Then, leaving behind the Marutpaṭa mountain, they proceeded further on their way.
Leaving behind the cloth of the sky as well as the wall of the ego, and rising upward,
they abandoned even the covering consisting of the principle of Mahat;
accompanied by their beloved, they went to the auspicious palace of Vairāja.
There, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, was honored by him,
as were all the royal women of the Vairāja class who worship Hari.
Then they all proceeded further toward the realm of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Therein lies the great kingdom of Mahāviṣṇu, where Gopālakṛṣṇaka is his own lord; there he shines forth together with his queen, the illustrious goddess known as Mahālakṣmī,
as well as with the goddess Śrī Kambharā.
And having been honored by them, the god was then indeed honored by Kānta’s father; Kānta’s mother was also honored, and by those two, the Śrīs were likewise treated with hospitality.
They were fed, embraced, and properly attended with blessings.
Having honored their husband and received his command, they ascended to the upper story. Accompanied by their husband, they traveled in celestial chariots to the vast realm of Bhūman.
There, they were honored by the goddess Bhūmi, and Hari was likewise honored by Bhūman.
Having beheld those manifestations before them, they went to the abode of Vāsudeva.
Vāsudevī, filled with great devotion, performed a hospitable reception for them;
Vāsudeva and Narāyaṇa likewise offered them a most gracious welcome.
They caused drinking fountains of nectar and meals of ambrosia to be prepared;
likewise, the wives of Vāsudeva performed worship.
Then, after the Blessed One had revealed his various incarnations and abodes, he [departed].
Having bathed [the Lord] in the Brahma-lake and drawn him out into the imperishable splendor, Hari indeed entered his own supreme, imperishable abode;
then, having dissolved all [the deities] into his own form, he remained there.
Then, having been liberated and endowed with a divine form corresponding [to their nature], they were established in their own true forms, freed from all veils;
they became the state of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) and were of the essence of the Supreme Brahman. || 25-26 ||
O Rādhā, Hari then created here, by his very self, all the forms, natures, and qualities of his own consorts just as they were;
what indeed can I say to you regarding that field of Kuṅkumavāpikā? His own bodies [appeared] there as those of his wives.
They have become fit for sustenance, and their illusory nature has dissolved.
They are eternally composed of the bliss of the single essence of consciousness; indeed, they are enriched by the expansion of the mass of self-knowledge that is omniscience. (28–29)
Truly perfected and fully accomplished, they have reached their destined abode;
born from that [state] and through bathing in the Brahma-lake,
they exist as liberated souls with the very form and nature of the body of Brahman.
Those [Vedas] are indeed of the nature of the imperishable Brahman and consist of light;
having been produced, they became even more abundant through the attainment of their formal existence.
Having attained the form of the Blessed Lord, they are truly the Bhāgavatas.
For these [realms] known as Prajātāni are indeed composed of consciousness and belong to Brahman;
they are designated as Jñāna, Tejas, and Susārūpya.
Therein, He is attended by these innumerable liberated female beings.
The glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, served by the liberated souls,
revealed to them his imperishable sovereign realm—
a universal empire, a great kingdom situated above the three worlds. (34–35)
Mādhava revealed all his own sovereign powers and every one of his manifestations— eternal, blissful objects of enjoyment—
including divine opulences and circles of liberated souls on every side. (36)
Kāntaka showed him millions of circles of pearls;
Kṛṣṇaka showed him various gardens, auspicious palaces, and the private dwellings of all the women.
He displayed all divine prosperities and all sources of good fortune, as well as *kaustubha* jewels that fulfill every desire like wish-fulfilling gems;
he also manifested the nourishing rays of his own form in every direction.
The Lord indeed showed her those things that grant satisfaction, bestow the attainment of happiness, and give joy;
those that provide pleasure, love, and delight; those that fulfill desires like a wish-fulfilling tree;
and those which are truly filled with eternal bliss. (2.298.40–41)
He showed all kinds of halls, ever-new and worthy of service,
as well as auspicious grounds for pleasure-gardens that were desirable and unobstructed;
indeed, these were pervaded by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He showed them divine garments, ornaments, attire, and finery;
he also showed them secret chambers, dwellings, and beautiful beds. Having shown them everything situated there, after that—
The Lord gave them food consisting of the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, excellent drink, betel-leaf, and provided them with the pleasure of amorous sport;
He also bestowed upon them absolute happiness born of the secret union.
Then, in the presence of those liberated women, the Blessed One accepted the auspicious worship offered by the great liberated ones;
and they also accepted the worship offered by the liberated men and women.
Those of divine form received him with a warm welcome and great honor.
Having thus shown his entire abode,
the Blessed Lord Hari then departed from Akṣara for the glorious realm of Goloka.
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, offered a warm welcome;
there, Rādhā and the others paid honor to the wives of Hari. Then Rādhā and the others gave them the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu, to drink. (2.298.50)
They likewise offered him foods such as milk-rice and various delicacies;
then the Lord quickly went to Vaikuṇṭha along with them. There, he was welcomed by Lakṣmī and Kamalā.
By Bhārgavī Śrī, Vikuṇṭhā, and others as well, and by Nārāyaṇa himself, honor was then bestowed upon Śrī Hari;
having received worship and praise, they displayed their auspicious splendors. ||52-53||
The Lord himself went to the divine Kailāsa, the abode of Sadāśiva. There,
the Blessed One showed him all his beloved manifestations (vibhūtis),
including those of Śiva and Durgā and others, whom he then worshipped.
All the Gaṇas there indeed performed the worship of Hari.
Then Śrī Hari himself went together with them to the auspicious abode of Mahāmāyā, which is composed of Māyā, for the sake of curiosity. (55–56)
They beheld millions of beautiful women equal to the beloved of Hari;
all of them, the dear consorts of Brahmā, received great honor there.
Adored with various illusory powers and by the maidens, they were highly esteemed.
There, she was served in many ways by those skilled in illusion with excellent objects:
with foods, drinks, and fine enjoyments; with garments, ornaments, and cosmetics;
and with all kinds of stimulating powders that increase the erotic sentiment. || 58–59 ||
The women were served and honored with all kinds of costumes and implements, with all objects of good fortune, and with states that bestow all bliss.
There, Mahāmāyā herself performed the massaging of Hari’s feet.
All the wives of Hari experienced great wonder as she performed [this act].
Indeed, that queen— the sovereign of the queens of kings, the mistress of all, and the supreme lady—
was seen by everyone while serving her own husband.
Having displayed his abode of *māyā*, Hari then quickly departed from there and went to the abode of Viṣṇu; there, the Vaiṣṇavīs paid him their respects.
They offered a welcome to all of them, as well as the *nīrājana* rite and worship. (63)
They gave him desirable food, drink, and garments of fine cloth. Then that glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, adorned by his beloveds,
departed for the abode of Viṣṇu with a hundred heads and a thousand faces, who wields the Śārṅga bow.
Hari indeed [sustains] the cosmic eggs of the lotus-eyed Śambhu, of the thousand-faced Viṣṇu, of the ten-million-faced wielder of the Śārṅga bow, of the lotus-faced Creator (Brahmā),
and of the Creator whose faces shine with a number of worlds equal to a parārdha.
He indeed displayed all the infinite manifestations of creation.
Worshipped by each of them, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, his own beloved son,
revealed to them the divine glories bestowed by himself.
All these manifestations, offered to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
were enjoyed by all of them together with the beloveds of Brahmā; for indeed,
O Rādhikā, that was witnessed directly by me in samādhi at that time.
Then, having taken up those planets, beginning with the sun and the moon,
he showed them as they exist in the world, situated within the nature of hell.
Upon seeing them, their minds were indeed not attached to that place.
He quickly brought them to his own auspicious palace, the pavilion known as Divyākṣara, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā. There, in that imperishable place, he indeed attained steadiness of mind.
And through their meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they all then awakened from their own bodies;
they beheld those supreme, non-human beings who had entered their divine abodes, who were free from the state of being veiled and were non-material (*abhautika*).

They are always free from illusion, uniform in nature, devoid of hunger and thirst, and stripped of the qualities of *māyā*; they are endowed with splendor and sovereignty, possess the inherent nature of all abodes, and consist of a bliss equal to that of the Imperishable (*akṣara*). (75)
Filled with the bliss of Brahman and adorned with divine raiment, they possessed sovereignty equal to that of their Lord; established in a state that was a treasure-trove of divinity,
they became filled with great bliss and capable like Bālakṛṣṇa himself.
Having thus attained divinity and obtained their husband at that time,
those wives— whether they were young brides or even elderly matrons— obtained omniscience.
In this way, Hari indeed bestowed upon them his own eternal equality.
O Rādhikā, just as you have been made by me to shine with my own likeness,
so indeed has Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa made his own wives.
[He created] the covering of the earth, the covering of the walls, and the enclosure of the house.
For those [women], there is no obstruction by the closing of doors;
nor is there any affliction to their bodies from water in the midst of oceans and the like, from the currents of rivers, from ice, or from rain and other such elements. (8.1)
Fire does not burn them, nor do the sun’s rays scorch them;
even the submarine fire or lightning does not consume them.
They are independent to travel among the sun, the moon, and the other planets. (82)
These [energies] are not dependent on breath, nor does the wind dry them up;
these wives of Brahman exist as the higher states of *prāṇāyāma*.
Drowsiness, laziness, and heaviness do not exist there at all.
Nor indeed does defeat come to them by means of poison;
nor does a wound from a weapon ever arise anywhere to pierce their bodies. Furthermore, even illusory diseases are unable to remain within them. (85–86)

The accomplishment of hearing from afar, the accomplishment of direct perception from afar, the accomplishment of grasping objects from afar, and the accomplishments of distant conversation and so forth;
as well as the power of moving with the speed of thought and the state of being subtle through meditation. (87)
Greatness of being, as well as the power of bringing all desires to fruition,
mastery over everything, the assumption of forms such as those at the limits of existence, the ability to travel within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and immunity to cold and heat. (88–89)
The power to create by mere volition and whatever perfections of supernatural powers there may be— all these manifest for them through the grace of Bālakṛṣṇa.
[2.298.90] The wish-fulfilling creepers, the wish-granting cows, and the vessels that grant all desires—
"Furthermore, wish-fulfilling gems exist for them, functioning according to their will.
O Rādhā! Such incomparable sovereignty as this occurred for them moment by moment; those who had emerged from meditation then beheld it.
Observing that their bodies were liberated from the abode and were no longer subject to rebirth,
they all became serene, freed from the pride born of *māyā*.
Then, they all rose up [to behold] Bālakṛṣṇa, their own Lord.
In a divine manner, they served [the guests] with baths, worship, and meals.
Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the others likewise offered these to the distinguished guests who had completed their ritual baths and daily duties.
Having received honors, food, hospitality, wealth,
and betel-leaves that satisfied them, all those great men requested Acyuta to depart for their respective countries and regions. || 96 ||

And to the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa and the virtuous Śrī Kambharā, Hari’s father begged for forgiveness regarding his deficient service. "By your arrival, this festival has become truly magnificent. (97–98)
"When will there be another opportunity for me to see the Blessed Ones?
Knowing that I must certainly come here once my own [disciples] have been brought under my control," having said this,
he prostrated himself and gave many parting gifts.
He performed worship in many ways and likewise bestowed various materials.
For the worship, his father gave gold, silver, and diamonds;
he also gave rewards to the laborers.
He gave as much as they desired to the classes of the poor, the helpless, and guests;
and he bestowed wealth to bring satisfaction upon his servants, employees, and artists.
He also indeed gave excellent crowns to all the kings.
The Lord bestowed crowns upon the gods and the Īśvaras;
he also gave garments, ornaments, and the like to the goddesses and the women.
To everyone, he gave their own desired things as a reward for what was desired by all.
The incarnations as well as the manifestations, the stages [of yoga] beginning with *bhūmi*, and the sovereign Virājas;
the Viṣṇus, the unborn ones, the ancestors, the gods, the Siddhas, and the great seers;
human beings, those dwelling at the base [of the tree], and the sacred fords, mountains, rivers, and so forth.

All were delighted and said, "We have always been well-pleased with you, O Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa! We shall now depart; may there be well-being for your son, and likewise may there be well-being for the maidens. May it ever be well with you all. (106–107)
Having spoken thus, those great-souled ones, with their hearts prepared and their equipment ready,
had their celestial chariots made ready and were, at that very moment, on the verge of departure.
The honored guests, kinsmen, and friends [prepared themselves] for one another.
The women likewise pressed their breasts against his chest.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Display of the Three Worlds, the Imperishable Abode, and so forth, to all [the women] in their meditative absorption at dawn on the seventh day of the second Tretā cycle in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; the transformation of them into the nature of eternal, divine liberation; and the granting of greatness, food, worship, gifts, forgiveness, and other honors, as well as rewards for the deities of the sacred field. 298.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā! At the time of departure, all the girls were embraced by their mothers and fathers, their hearts filled with affection. (1)
Having shed tears of separation, they remained silent like those deprived of sensation;
though divine and possessing celestial bodies, they were previously born from the qualities of the lotus.
Beholding the affection of their kinsmen, which had increased even further at that moment—
At that time, they became unable to bear their separation even for a moment.
Then, seeing their daughters distressed by the pain of separation,
their mothers— those simple women— petitioned Bālakṛṣṇa.
He took his own daughters with him for only a short time,
in order to visit his kingdom, his family members, and his friends; likewise,
he repeatedly gazed upon his noble elder brother Śrī Hari for the sake of seeing him, along with his sisters born of the same womb.
"O Lord, send us your daughters for the sake of our happiness.
Furthermore, we shall send them here again quickly at the end of the month.
O Kṛṣṇa, O merciful one, grant this request of ours as they serve you. (6–7)
Hari said, "Let it be so," for the sake of their affection;
he then commanded them all to go along with their mothers and others.
Hearing the magnanimity of the Lord, they were all then filled with joy.
Suddenly approaching Hari, they bowed and embraced the Lord.
Having said, "We shall return quickly," they remained in his presence for a moment, providing him with satisfaction so that he would indeed come back again. (2.299.10)
Having repeatedly attended upon their own beloveds, those women became ready, adorned, and beautifully decorated;
they worshipped the Supreme Lord,
as well as the parents of Viṣṇu and his venerable sister.
Having bowed to all the elders residing in the household and addressed them with "Welcome," and having also spoken of their well-being in a fitting and appropriate manner, they,
provided with suitable garments and ornaments, ascended the celestial chariots as directed by their Lord.
"Everyone must indeed come," the Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, then said;
though beyond illusion, he shed tears through his illusory power.
Then musical instruments were played, and worship was performed with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
And there was a construction of celestial palaces (vimāna) by Saubhāgyika and others.
[There were also] the Seasons, Dharmadeva, Nara, and Devī as the pedestal;
Mahī as the pavilion, and Muktā as the ruby pillar.
Sudarśana, the Discus, Hara, and the leader of the Gaṇas—
these nine indeed approached for the sake of beholding the Mothers. Having prostrated themselves like a staff, they said, "The guardians of the field must be forgiven."
Having spoken thus, they stood there; then Hari,
as well as all those dear to Hari, including Vāsudeva and the others,
bestowed blessings and gave them rewards.
Jewels of many forms, as well as garlands of diamonds and the like; beautiful crowns, vessels, ornaments, and garments;
and likewise name-plates inscribed with golden letters.
Having gathered wealth and excellent, auspicious implements,
those sons of the field became established in happiness;
then there arose the sounds of two-fingered [beings] as well as the sounds of mechanical devices.
The sounds of drums and shouts of victory resounded everywhere in the sky;
at that time, the joyful maidens, seated in their fathers’ celestial chariots,
gazed upon their beloved even in the region of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
They honored Lomaśa with a rain of flowers and with prostrations.
Then, celestial chariots appeared in the sky, moving through the air;
all those crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of maidens were there together with their fathers and other kinsmen.
Except for Kāśīśvarī, the other goddesses departed for their respective regions along with their mothers; however, the Brāhmī goddesses, who were like indestructible syllables,
remained in their own beautiful abodes without the Lord, resolving that they must not go.
O Rādhikā! Bālakṛṣṇa, as the inner self (antarātman), remained present;
together with the women who had surrendered their souls, he departed invisibly.
Then those beloveds of the three worlds returned each to her own world.
In that field known as Kuṅkumavāpī, everything became as if empty in an instant.
Then, by the command of Hari, even the pavilion vanished;
that very small pavilion also quickly disappeared from that place.
Thus was the solution quickly brought about by the will of Bālakṛṣṇa. Meanwhile,
those friends, the daughters of Kāśī, who had been living in the service of their husband,
now joyfully and incessantly served Śrīkṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Divine and of celestial form, devoted solely to their husbands,
they performed service with action, mind, speech, and body. Lakṣmī, moreover, serves the Supreme Lord with particular distinction.
Even though there were six thousand maidservants who were all equal [in status],
[he performed] the bathing, the giving of garments, the anointing with oil, the dressing of the hair,
the arranging of attire, the washing of clothes, and even the cleaning of the teeth. (33–34)
Applying collyrium to the forehead, massaging the body with oil, rubbing the feet, providing water for drinking, offering food, giving betel leaf,
fanning with a fan, and providing a night-garment. (35)
The offering of fruit, as well as the bed and bedding and the presentation of the water-pot—
whatever may belong to her own person, she herself performs it all.
She is solely devoted to the service of her own Lord in its entirety.
Lakṣmī herself is indeed Lakṣmī; there is no other like her anywhere.
While such Lakṣmī is present with Kṛṣṇa, no deficiency whatsoever is seen in his service, for that service is truly distinguished.

Nevertheless, Kṛṣṇa remains impartial toward all, endowed with equanimity; he bestows happiness and is full of affection, yet he is not partial. That same supreme magnanimity always resides in that Beloved. (2.299.40)
She fulfills all desires and grants satisfaction according to one's wish;
indeed, the service rendered to Padmāvatī and Ramā exceeds that of Lakṣmī herself.
By these two, who are ever devoted to their master’s interests, even Lakṣmī has been put to shame.
Then, O Rādhā, in the springtime Kṛṣṇa celebrated a festival;
he also performed the delightful festival of the flower-swing,
and he likewise observed the Cāturmāsya festival consisting of vows.

"The month of Kārtika has arrived; it is the eighth lunar day that awakens one's birth, and Kṛṣṇa’s sister remains nearby. Having reflected thus, all the women quickly ascended a magnificent celestial chariot from their father's house.
Accompanied by their fathers and others, they arrived at the house of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having reached the master’s home, they were indeed filled with happiness;
it was a joyful reception for all those who were the most eminent of the great ones.
Then the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa indeed performed everything according to the prescribed rites;
the kings likewise acted in accordance with the majesty of the Lord Śrīkṛṣṇa.
In the fifteenth year, during the celebration of the sixteenth birthday, [the festival was held].
All the fathers of the sons, inhabitants of all the worlds,
arrived at the field known as Akṣara to magnify Hari.
On the eighth day, having performed his ablutions early in the morning, he observed the auspicious rites.
Having adorned himself with elegant attire, Hari entered the assembly hall;
he was honored by Lomaśa and others, and further gladdened by auspicious blessings.
Purified by offerings and gifts, he was delighted by hymns of praise for his glory.

The Supreme Lord, enriched by the splendor of a king of kings, shone forth. (2.299.50) And thus, while the great festival of his birthday was taking place in the morning, gifts such as elephants, horses, cows, and so forth were being distributed there. (2.299.51)
There, vehicles and mounts consisting of cows, buffaloes, bulls, and camels,
as well as houses, fields, gardens, groves, wealth, and gold, were displayed;
musical instruments were played there, and his glories were sung.

When that obstacle had been removed, at midday there occurred for all the people, including their beloveds, the most excellent of meals and other provisions. Hospitality was rendered to guests with food, clothing, and other necessities. (53–54)
At night, there was a captivating spectacle of dance,
as well as the wrestling of athletes, the sounds of musical performances,
the poetry of eminent poets, and the dances of courtesans.
And there were instructions from the virtuous on the occasion of the birth festival.
O Rādhā! At this festival, Nārāyaṇa—the father of Ramā and Padmāvatī—and his son Cārudeva [were present] in the imperishable sacred field (akṣarakṣetraka). ||56-57||
He who is celebrated as a divine incarnation and a portion of the Sun himself came from Kāśī, having remembered the words of Hari;
for Śiva himself is one who remembers his past births, having come there for the sake of liberation.
Having cast off his human state, he aspired to the state of Śiva.
Then even Dhenupāla, having given his own kingdom to his son Dharmapāla, who was a yogi, departed together with him. (2.299.60)
Having all made their resolve for the sake of liberation, they were then in haste;
having performed the auspicious birth festival,
they prayed to the Supreme Self for the purpose of release from the body.
Beholding the sun situated in its northern course, Hari said:
"I must go to my own abode; for now, you and the entire family of Śrī should remain here in this house. Thus he placed his hope upon their heads.
Śiva remained constantly in the vast inner chamber of Lakṣmī’s house;
there, Śiva himself asked Hari, his son-in-law’s husband, about the means for liberation.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to him, his own dear friend, concerning that very liberation.
Listen, O Śambhu, I shall tell you the supreme means for liberation.
(64) Indeed, those who are established in liberation and are free from the state of illusion—by associating with them and by serving them, liberation is attained. (65)
I, who dwell in liberation, always dwell within all selves;
by constantly worshipping me, a human being attains liberation.
Time, action, and dharma are mine, as are these powers.
Realizing this, whoever takes refuge in me, the omnipotent one, is liberated.
He who has offered himself to me entirely— with body, action, speech, mind, and his own possessions— is swiftly and completely released.
May he see me, may he taste me, and may he always proclaim my name;
may he smell me, touch me, hear me, and contemplate me;
may he grasp me, serve me, and always massage me.

He should approach me in secret and gladden me within his heart; he should establish me there, contemplate me, and resolve upon me within the inner heart. He should desire me constantly and dwell forever in union with me.
One should meditate upon me, embrace me with full affection, and gaze upon me; having unified oneself with me, one should take up all objects of enjoyment and cast them into me.
Having made me manifest as one's own self, one should perform every action for my sake.
Śivarāja, having thus attained my yoga, shall attain liberation.
[Therein lie] delighting, wandering, sporting, dancing, fighting, waking, sleeping, proceeding, and returning. (73–74)
"Going forth, wandering about, practicing virtuous conduct, and moving about—
one should certainly do all this for my sake and shall surely attain liberation.
Thus was this King Śiva addressed, O Rādhikā, as well as Śītajā.
Jaya, Candra, Dhenupāla, and Aśokā became steadfast in Hari;
they attained steady meditation and were devoted to constant service.
Having reached a divine state, they served Him by offering their very selves. (76–77)
Then, when the sun had entered its northern course, they became eager; desiring liberation, they embraced their daughter Lakṣmī,
bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, and performed worship to Hari.
Then the cowherd, having addressed his three daughters,
withdrew all their worldly activities; they became absorbed in meditation,
for the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the giver of knowledge and the master of all, was dwelling within their hearts.
Thus, having perceived them before his very eyes— those whose minds were set on Nirvana but who remained attached to their own [worlds]—
he swiftly mounted his divine celestial chariot and arrived in his own divine form to grant them liberation.
Then Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, caused them to ascend divine celestial chariots in those very bodies while the virtuous looked on. At that time,
the drums of the gods resounded in every direction.
Sadāśiva attained supreme liberation, which is eternally free from all fatigue.
All those who had been honored by the gods and others went to the most excellent Kailāsa.
The attendants likewise went eternally to Vaikuṇṭha, as did Kṛṣṇikā.

Likewise, Lakṣmī and the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇārya are capable of accomplishing everything; indeed, with that very body, O Rādhā, they have led them to liberation—this has truly been a great wonder. (85–86)
There, together with her own lord, the daughter performed the subsequent rites,
including worldly gifts, śrāddha ceremonies, festivals, and so forth. Then,
at the winter solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa also [performed] for the cows...
There he performed worship for the sake of initiating meritorious deeds.
At that time, he gave fresh fodder and grain to the cows,
and he had secret provisions of grain distributed everywhere.

Then, from all the worlds, cows with divine forms who were dwelling on earth arrived swiftly, longing for his grace. Having eaten, bowed to Hari, and received worship, they departed for their respective abodes.
Then the Blessed One gave gifts in abundance to the twice-born;
he gave garments and excellent foods to the virtuous,
and he gave in every way to the poor, the helpless, and even to the mendicants.
At that time, one should provide sweet foods, garments, silver, gold, and vessels;
having thus performed the rite of giving, [one should offer] fresh [food] accompanied by the seven grains,
as well as savory, cooked, and ghee-filled dishes along with *parpaṭas*.
Hari ate his meal together with Sudadhna and Āranāla;
he also fed all his beloved wives the excellent dish known as *kṛsara*,
which was prepared with *kvathikā*, delicious, and fragrant.
Thus, O Rādhikā,
the noble Kṛṣṇakānta, born of the cowherds,
celebrated a great festival for the conjunction of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) in his sixteenth year, accompanied by the beloved of Brahmā.
He who brings about all auspiciousness enjoyed manifold pleasures.
O Rādhikā! The women of Nara should remember that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the sixteen pastimes of Hari arising from his sixteenth year, which bestow liberation and peace. (97–98)
From hearing these, the imperishable fruit of complete liberation arises;
from hearing these, the imperishable fruit of the worship of Brahman arises.
This is the Yoga of the Supreme Person, the highest among all yogas.
This is the yoga of universal descent, the most supreme among all supreme knowledges.
It bestows all prosperity and likewise grants all liberation;
it bestows all good fortune—having heard this, Ramā was filled with joy. (2.299.100–101)

Desiring for himself the most excellent liberation that is eternal, the Blessed Lord liberated him and likewise went to his imperishable abode. Then his kinsmen, their minds fixed upon Hari, performed the funeral rites for him.
O Rādhikā! This union with Śrī Hari bestows liberation upon all;
it grants all auspicious fortune and is known as the "Tretā-santāna.
It [surpasses] all vows, sacrifices, gifts, and meritorious deeds. 103–104.
He is the bestower of the fruits of all austerities, of the applications of initiation, of the duties of renunciation, of the duties of world-renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and of devotional practices;
he is considered the giver of the fruit resulting from hearing the duties of all the stages of life (āśrama).
This is indeed the heart of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*;
it is the life-breath of all living beings, consisting of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. It bestows the fruit of all consecrations and grants the merit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
It bestows the fruit of all service and grants the fruit of all knowledge;
it yields the fruit of the dharma of virtuous wives and grants the fruit of devotion to one's husband.
By hearing this, one will certainly obtain all enjoyments and all prosperity.
It brings about divinity, causes the destruction of all latent impressions (vāsanās),
and is the kindler of all sins while bestowing great merit; indeed,
the constant hearing of this is itself action performed without desire for fruit (niṣkāma-karma).
Likewise, its worship and the giving of it yield great fruit;
its preservation within the home destroys time, illusion, and the like.
By listening to this fragment with devotion, Śrī Hari himself [is attained].
Abounding in the power of Brahmā, such as Lakṣmī and others, he shall grant his divine vision. His story must be narrated, and likewise the *puraścaraṇa* rite should be performed.
For those who have no other recourse, there shall be liberation; for spirits and the like, there shall be deliverance. (112–113)
There shall be the destruction of suffering and poverty, and the prosperity of one’s lineage and family;
wherever this [mantra] resides, there one shall always find an abode.
There shall be the increase of the lineage, along with the fortune of sons, wealth, wife, and husband.
Wherever this Khaṇḍa is worshipped and recited,
O Rādhikā, there resides Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
all the beloveds of Brahmā, and the entire circle of the liberated (Muktamaṇḍala). (1.15–1.16)
I am Kṛṣṇa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa, who encompasses the entire maṇḍala;
together with all the lords of the gods, we both dwell here to hear this narrative.
Furthermore, the reciter must be honored according to the prescribed rites.
Ornaments for men and women, garments, and even wealth;
houses, fields, villages, gardens, elephants, horses, diamonds, and so forth—these should be given according to one's capacity to the reciter by those desiring to hear [the teaching]. (1.18–1.19)
Indeed, for one who seeks the supreme goal, everything should be given as an offering for the sake of liberation.
Likewise, the concluding rite (udyāpana) should be performed, along with an auspicious and great festival.
By hearing this even once, Māyā is surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.

O Rādhikā! I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and I declare here that through the service of the lineage of Tretā, I am indeed the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā), the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), the wish-fulfilling cow (kalpadhenu), the wish-fulfilling gem (kalpamaṇi), the wish-fulfilling vessel (kalpapātra), and a portion of Tretā itself. (121–122)
"I shall give the station of Rādhā to the noble woman, and the station of Viṣṇu to the man:
'Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul.

(123) Thus, in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [described is] the departure to their own country of the beloved wives who had long resided in the hermitage of Lomaśa along with their fathers and others; the relinquishing of the pavilions and other structures; and the [departure of] Lakṣmī and the other women of Kāśī.

The ninety-ninth chapter after two hundred [Chapter 299], titled "Description of the Manner of Performing Service, the Arrival of All People on the Eighth Day of the Dark Fortnight of Kārttika during the Sixteenth Birthday Festival, the Great Festival, the Liberation of Śiveśvara and Others through the Instruction on Liberation, the Gift of the Uttarāyaṇa in the Sixteenth Year, and the Majesty of the Tretā Lineage of the Saṃhitā. [Chapter 300] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 2 (The Lineage of the Tretā Yuga) — Chapter 300.
[The Author:
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Beloved Kṛṣṇa! Tell me all these stories in brief.
"Indeed, a profound peace arises within me upon hearing this section concerning Tretā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Rādhikā, the Blessed Lord became Śrīmat Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa."
When the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is united with Lakṣmī,
those who lack the vision of the heart do not truly know this very Supreme Self, the eternal Supreme Brahman. (2–3)
Thus, out of compassion, he has appeared upon this earth for the sake of liberation,
and likewise for the fulfillment of the hearts of devotees— both men and women.
Blessed are those bodies here by which Hari himself has been attained.
Blessed indeed are those senses that have attained union with Hari;
blessed are those prosperities, and likewise blessed are those lands;
and blessed are those householders who are united with Puruṣottama.
Wherever the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* is recited, that very land is blessed; indeed, it is the same as the place where Puruṣottama resides.
[This occurs] in the second section of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
In the lineage of Tretā, the first [chapter] named Sumaṅgala was proclaimed;
then the universal majesty of the Supreme Brahman was recounted;
and thereafter, the origin of the sheath and the filaments of the golden egg was described.
Then the two asuras named Hiraṇyakūrca and Hiraṇyāṇḍa fought with Saṃkarṣaṇa using maces. Those portions of Mount Meru that were severed became the planets.
Requested by all the worlds, Kṛṣṇa manifests from his abode;
he accepts service both on earth and in the home of Śrī Kaṃbhārī.
On the festival of his manifestation, Jayantī, there are offerings, hymns of praise, and other such rites.
On the tenth day, while the gods and goddesses were being born from the trees, creepers, and other plants upon the earth, the Daityas committed an offense against the Lord;
by means of the remnants of the impurity following the birth of the Ṣaṣṭhī, they caused the forest of Bālakṛṣṇa to be destroyed.
The birth of Sūtaka and the granting of boons to the soul of Sūta;
at the festival for the naming ceremony, the demons Sāṇa and Vyāghra were slain;
on the eleventh day, the mounting upon the swing was performed by those whose forms are infinite.
For the noble lady Talājārākṣasī, there was delusion regarding Hari and devotion to him;
by the power of his grace, that very puffed rice (lāja) became a performer of auspicious rites.
On the day she drank milk, she consumed the milk of cows in many forms.

The Rākṣasīs in the form of cows drank the milk still containing his vital breath. During the rite known as Hari’s seating upon the earth, Siṃhikā and other women also attended upon the Lord, the infant Kṛṣṇa.
During his ear-piercing ceremony (*karṇavedha*), even the deities beginning with Sūcī performed service and took refuge in Kṛṣṇa, their lord who assumes many forms.
During the food-eating ceremony (*annaprāśana*), He gave them abundant foods.

Having fed him with herbs, they approached their beloved Kṛṣṇa. Indeed, to demonstrate his mastery of livelihoods, he simultaneously grasped thirty-two objects with as many hands; his divinity is thus proclaimed.
Then the widowed wives of the Daityas arrived to wage war;
a tumultuous battle ensued between the Rākṣasīs and the maidens.
When the maidens were victorious, the Rākṣasīs sought refuge.
Divinity was bestowed upon them by Śrī Hari in the form of maidens.
Then Śrī Lomaśa spoke to them concerning service and the boons of liberation.
Thereafter, all the maidens belonging to the hermitage undertook their vows during the rainy season.
The Kaṅkatālās, who dwelt on Mount Śatruñjaya, were slain in battle;
yet the divine Kaṅkatālī Rākṣasīs became beloved of the monkeys in the fight.
They remained there and eventually settled in the hermitage of Lomaśa, where they became knowers of the self.
The daughters of the Pitṛs performed the worship of Hari and the liberation of the deceased;
the worship performed by the multitudes, the description of Kṛṣṇa’s favor, the splendor of the great pavilion, and the description of Hari’s adornment. (26–27)
The battle of Prahlāda with Nārāyaṇa, his victory through devotion,
the liberation of the Dānavas, and the choosing of Hari by the maidens;
the tonsure ceremony of Śrī Hari, and the fact that the hairs [of his body] are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
The body hairs of living beings are proclaimed to be the trees known as *agha*.

At the festival of the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*), there was the destruction of the Sāla, Māla, and Asura [demons], and the seizure of their women by Hari; likewise, the various tribes such as the Sāla, Māla, and others were [slain] by the Daityas.
Likewise, the teachings on liberation as described by Lomaśa;
the narrative of Sukeśin; the Aśūnyaśayana vow;
the sleeping of the gods; and worship performed on various different lunar days.
Then followed the destruction of Kāraṇḍava, the lord of Pātāla;
the maiden was protected at the abode of Lomaśa for the sake of the daughter of the poor youth,
the prince of the king of Ārakta-deśa.
The worship of the goddess Śāvadīnā was performed with the offering of a child;
then the destruction of the king and others was carried out by the goddess. [She went] to Badarīvana, to Kuru-kṣetra, to the abode of Hari, and she returned toward Kuṅkumavāpī.
The offering of a child to his ancestors is said to be the liberation of mothers.
In ancient times, during an unrighteous age, the boundaries of conduct were demonstrated by Śvetaketu;
likewise, Aśmaka, the son of Vasiṣṭha, was born from the wife of Saudāsa, as was Vṛṣa.
Bṛhaspati forcibly took possession of Utathya’s wife;
Dīrghatamas begot many sons upon the wife of Bali.
All those who are by nature various types of child-seizing spirits (bālagraha) have been described.
Then, indeed, the destruction of the Vyāghrāsuras was accomplished by Hari.
During the festival of the fifth year, there were songs performed by the Gandharvas;
and from the skins of lions, tigers, and other beasts, living lions were brought forth.
Then Hara, joined by Naṭa and Naṭī, performed dramatic dances;
he was always made to dwell in that sacred field by the gratified Hara.
Śrī Hari attained all branches of knowledge through the power of his penance at Varāṭaka.
The destruction of Varāṭaka’s army and the account of Daṇḍa and others have likewise been narrated.
O twice-born ones, it is told how Hari brought about the slaughter of the Dikpālas and the Mlecchas when Śaṅkara was naked and had gone to the hermitage of the sages.
Due to Satī’s curse, those Rākṣasas indeed struck the Lord;
thereafter, their state as Rākṣasas was destroyed by Śrī Hari.
On the occasion of the celebration of the beginning of the sixth year, worship was performed by Kṛṣṇa and the others.
The outcaste status of the Brahmin Devāyana and his wife was destroyed [by the power of the story].
In the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, the wonder of the narrative is proclaimed, as well as the hymn of praise, the pilgrimage site, and the *ūrjavrata* performed by the sage Ṛṣi. ||44-45||
The conduct of Kanthādharas is wonder; their transcendence of death is marvelous.
Their lordship over the bodies within the heart is atheism resulting from the deer [of ignorance].
The life of the dead son of a Brahmin named Vṛṣaparvan— 46.
Due to his atheism, he would have been reborn as a barbarian at death, but because of his son,
he was rescued from both states. Having become a Vaiṣṇava through the sage Lomaśa,
he obtained a vehicle provided by a Yakṣa maiden for the sake of a sacrifice performed on the battlefield.
The seventh birth festival of Śrī Hari was celebrated most excellently when Raṇaṅgama had departed with the desire to behold the Southern Pole Star (Dakṣiṇadhruva). There,
he received hospitable honors from Lakṣmaṇārya, the king of Antārki-deśa.
From the Rākṣasa who committed offenses against his wife and mother, [Śrī Hari] protected his wife and mother;
the protection of his wife and mother by Śrī Hari has been described.
Then, victory in battle was achieved by him alone as he entered the field of combat, and [the kingdom] was entrusted to Lakṣmaṇa.
Indeed, the instruction of Lomaśa to the two thousand maidens;
the description of sons, daughters, husbands, wives, disciples, and disciples’ disciples;
and the piercing of the channels Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā through the state of being the Master. ||52||
Having beheld Hari, they departed in their celestial chariots to explore various regions.
Having heard of Hari from them, seventy-two maidens of Brahmā set out in a vehicle to behold him clearly. ||53-54||
The aerial chariot was obstructed in the sky by the armies of Abhiketu;

there, the discourse of the messengers and others, the description of Śukra’s curse and the punishment for pride, and the description of Viśvakarman, Citrāṅgada, and the Asura chariots [are recounted]. (55)
Then, in that battle, tens of millions and even hundreds of thousands of Mlecchas were destroyed.
Both right discrimination and lack of discrimination were described, as was the taking of refuge.
Furthermore, in the battle of guile, the Mlecchas died by the thousands. (56–57)
Even hundreds of thousands of Mleccha women fought and were bewildered by Hari;
then, they were destroyed by means of magical spells (*kṛtyā*). Furthermore, the king’s vision of Śrī Hari, as well as his merits from previous births, was indeed recounted in this context.
Hari bestowed the empire of Abrikta upon his two devotees.
And Dharmarāja, having conquered the regions of Ārabīja in battle, granted those realms to the gods and the Maruts who had been born as Daityas.
There, the story of his previous births was narrated by the gods and the Maruts;
then followed the accounts of the Daityas Raktabīja, Ārabīja, and others,
as well as the story of King Udaya, who was like a boat crossing a river in flood.
It has been described how Hari provided protection for the subjects;
indeed, the demoniac nature of the cruel lion was cast off by Hari.
In the eighth year, he bestowed health upon those who were afflicted by diseases and physical defects.
Then, the protection of Vasumedha’s preeminent merchant who was submerged in water was described;
thereafter, the great pilgrimage site of Gopanātha in Saurāṣṭra was described;
and then, the grand festival of Bālakṛṣṇa’s sacred thread ceremony (*upavīta*) was described.
Therein is described the instruction on the supreme knowledge (parāvidyā) spoken by Nārada;
likewise, the bestowal of rewards and the presentation of offerings, as well as the fruit of service, worship, and adoration of the Lord, are fully recounted. 65–66.
Through giving gifts with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn as an illustration, one indeed attains freedom from dullness within six lifetimes.
The diversity of former natures has been thoroughly explained in detail.
Furthermore, the yoga of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya-yoga) and spiritual knowledge (jñāna) have been fully proclaimed.
Through devotion manifested by the surrender of the self, the liberation of the king and queen was accomplished;
likewise, the protection of the one named Sudhana, who dwelt in the city of Āmoda, from thieves was performed by Hari in a divine form. (68–69)
By the yoga of Kauśikāmbarṣi, there was the liberation even of a low-caste man with his wife from the three-fold eightfold [sins], and the destruction of leprosy and dropsy;
and Hari [destroyed] the Rākṣasas who were the destroyers of six hundred Brahmin children.
He destroyed [the demons] in battle and restored the children to life once more.

Hari declared that the fruit resulting from the terrible acceptance of gifts by Brahmins—which had been described as being caused by Kṛpī—had been neutralized by the rivers made into lunar days and astrological divisions (tithis and karaṇas). || 71-72 ||

The testing of King Bāleśvara was performed by Śrī Hari through the cooking of his son and the taking of his daughter as a wife; this has been narrated. In the sacrifice of Jayadhvaja, the vision of Śrī Hari is described.
And at the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the Droṇa and other mountains, there occurred the destruction of sins.
Furthermore, Kolāra, Cila, Śambhala, and Nārāyaṇasara attained divinity and liberation; this story has been beautifully narrated.
The characteristics of the four yugas have indeed been declared and demonstrated by Pulastya;
the greatness of Akṣarakṣetra, known as Kauṅkumavāpika, has been proclaimed;
and the residence of the subjects of the Harivaṃśa on the Sahya mountain has been described.
The son of Kharā, who lived unrighteously, displayed atheism toward Hari;
subsequently, he was shown an evil fate as a consequence of his conduct, yet a boon was granted for the sake of his future destination.
Then, at the confluence of the Kuṃbha and the Prayāga, ten million holy sites and others arrived.
Following the words of Sanatkumāra, they went to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Then there was the harassment by the Rākṣasīs dwelling in Siṃhala;
[the two of them] were destroyed by Mahāmārī and others when Hari had gone to Badarī.
Having arrived, they were restored to life by Hari, though they had previously been dead.
Now, the knowledge of qualified non-duality (*viśeṣādvaita*) is considered the bestower of liberation;
therefore, the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of Hari, which grant liberation, have been described.
The self-luminous nature of even the fourfold array (vyūha) has been described in the *Kuṅkumavāpī* as being sanctified by its character as a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). Furthermore,
[this occurs] in the great desert of Uṣṭrālaya during a mighty storm.
Protection was provided by Śrī Hari for those who had died at that time and were thus restored to life.
Furthermore, Urvaśī’s transformation into a female cakravāka bird and the sage Sanatsujāta’s transformation into a cat were mutually averted through their respective curses. (83–84)
The water on the mountain peak was indeed made drinkable for the female ruddy geese,
and protection from the fire was provided for the kittens of the female cats;
furthermore, liberation from the curse was truly accomplished by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then, in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the greatness of the mother was also described; indeed,
while Nārāyaṇa was reclining upon his bed with Lakṣmī, the cowherds and others arrived there for the purpose of beholding him.
When the time for the dance and other festivities had passed, Lakṣmī cursed them in anger;
consequently, Śiva and the others took human birth upon the earth.
Abandoning Lakṣmī, the Blessed Lord went to where Śiva and the others were.
Lakṣmī and her companions, having indeed experienced grief, took on various births.
Lakṣmī and Urvaśī went to the Śrī Hanumat forest for the sake of performing penance.
Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, arrived there to grant them the fruit of their merit.
On the peak, Hari offered water for drinking to the female cakravāka birds;
likewise, there was the arrival of Śivavarma’s family and others in Kāśī.
Having obtained a splendid residence and other comforts, Hari returned to his own home.
He arrived at the sacred field known as Kuṅkumavāpī. In the great region of Uṣṭrālaya, at the house of Hemaśālāyana, King Dakṣaja Vaṅgara indeed performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu. ||92-93||

Having bestowed a hundred royal maidens and a thousand daughters of the subjects upon Kṛṣṇa, the king and the others went to Kuṅkumavāpikā. Having performed their ablutions at the sacred ford, they returned to the abode of Uṣṭra by means of celestial chariots.
Then the daughters of the Pitṛs arrived there for the purpose of seeing him.
The Rākṣasas who were obstructing their celestial chariot were slain by Hari.
Hari’s arrival by means of the celestial chariot took place in the regions of Prāgjyotiṣa.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, a great battle took place there, in which millions of asuras were destroyed;
thereafter, Vaiṣṇava kings were established in the kingdom.
Having performed the sacrifice, Hari then placed his own city within his own body.
Having shown them to the young maidens, he indeed caused them to be drawn toward himself.
Proclaiming the greatness of the installation of the forms of the rivers of laughter and grace,
he established the ninefold aspects of devotion as well as the destruction of obstacles and their fruits.
The identity of the virtuous with one's own self-nature and their preeminence over all else have been proclaimed.
For those whose abode is the elements, there is the kingdom of the King Śyāmādi, who is free from desire.
Thereafter, the kingdom of Brahman has been determined, followed by the scripture concerning the imperishable field (akṣarakṣetra).
He celebrated the festival of the flower-swing and performed the birth-festival. Meanwhile, King Samīraṇa, having gone out for the sake of hunting in the forest,
was indeed transformed into the skin of a Śarabha by the curse of Pārṣṇigraha.

On Mount Raivata, this [account] of the visit to Haridatta Ātreya at Aśvapaṭṭasara has been related, including the excellent holy ford of Dattātreya (Dattātreyasutīrtha) and the Vārāha-tīrtha, together with its narrative. (103)
And the holy ford named Pavamāna arose in Aśvasaras;
because the Brāhmaṇas who were submerged in the water were rescued by [the deity] in the form of a tortoise through his assistance,
it thereafter became known as the Kacchapa-tīrtha.
It is proclaimed that by one devoted to the temples of the gods, the subjects of the world-protectors (dikpālas) are established;
indeed, by the recitation of the names of Śrī Hari during the month of Śrāvaṇa, they are liberated.
This applies to the twelve zodiac signs (rāśis) in regions such as Rāśiyāna and others.
The story of Katherita and his liberation at the Bālakṛṣṇa lake are told;
likewise, the Mahāyajña sacrifice and the dance of Devāyana are described.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, Śibi indeed gave a hundred maidens as a gift to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Furthermore, the virtues of the noble yogins have been described;
the sacred fords (tīrthas) have been mentioned, and likewise, the liberation of the ancestors was accomplished at the lake.
Then, Śrī Hari went to the site of the lake known as Dvikalā for the sake of a sacrifice.
Therein, there was the teaching of the Dharma and likewise the deliverance of the hungry ghosts (pretas);

the instruction in political ethics (nīti) for the king; the arrival at the third sacrifice; and at that sacrifice, [the appearance] of those dwelling in the world of the Sun and the celestial beings such as Vīraja and Arā.
Liberation has been declared, as well as the giving away of daughters and their instruction;
the true meaning of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) and its fruits have been told.
Then, in the fourth sacrifice, his own forms and other attributes were subsequently taught.
In the fifth sacrifice, indeed, all the Piśācinīs were delivered.
The causes for their state as Piśācas were explained: the initiation into mantras and the worship [of the deity], whereby their own divine and true form was revealed there.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, the saint named Lālāsana arrived;
he then received the Vaiṣṇava initiation of Hari.
Five thousand other saints likewise received that holy initiation.
Lālāyana went to the Northern Kurus out of a desire for Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Hari, together with His family, arrived at the realm of Akṣara by means of a celestial chariot; there, indeed, He became the very embodiment of Devāyana’s temple.
Hari has demonstrated the essential nature of the temple along with its ancillaries;
the description of the temple, beginning from the excavation and ending with the flagstaff (dhvaja), has been proclaimed.
Its true form and the internal divisions have been made clear.
The gods and others occupy lion-thrones, their palaces being indistinguishable from [the peaks of] Meru;
indeed, the palaces belonging to the Meru class have been described in their entirety,
as well as the embodied forms of the Vedas and the deities.
Furthermore, the weapons and other such items have been described;
thereafter, the banners and so forth were mentioned, as well as the sacrificial pits according to the number of oblations.
The configuration of the Vāstupuruṣa, enriched with the rites for the deities, has been declared.
The selection of the preceptor, the worship of the venerable Gaṇeśa and others,
the installation of the deities, the Nāndī-śrāddha and other offerings, the worship [of these],
the installation of the deities situated upon the Vāstu-pīṭha, and the recitation of the Svasti-vācana. (122–123)
The worship of the yoginīs, the worship of the kṣetrapālas and others, the worship of the deities of the pillars, and the worship of the respective deities of the branches;
the installation of the fire, and the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), its limbs, the yoni, the grahas, and so forth. (124)

The worship of the fifty-six deities and the adoration of the presiding deities (pratyadhidevatā) [are performed]; the invocation and worship of the world-protectors (lokapāla) and the planets (graha), as well as the oblation to the singular deity consisting of the Yoginīs, Kṣetrapālas, and others, have thus been described. (1.25–1.26)
The group of six beginning with Rādhā, the one hundred and forty-two [deities] beginning with Parāvidyā,
and the incarnations of the Supreme Lord and so forth were worshipped with the offering of bali;
the collyrium for the eyes, ornaments, and various nyāsas have been described.
The final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the ceremonial bath with the horns (*śṛṅgasnāna*), the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and so forth;

mounting the chariot, wandering through the village, the union with the vital breaths (*prāṇayojana*); the waving of lamps (*ārātrika*), the full oblation (*pūrṇahoma*), the benedictions, and the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

The ascending of the water-pot (*kalaśārohaṇa*), the climbing of the pride-pillar (*mānastaṃbha*) and the flagstaff (*dhvajādhirohaṇa*), the consecration of mobile images (*calamūrti-pratiṣṭhā*), and the restoration of ruined temples (*jīrṇoddhāra*) are thus proclaimed.
By the grace of Turīlakṣmī, the fisherman became a cloud of wealth.
Liberation was granted by Lord Hari at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha (131).
The attainment of knowledge through austerity for those who carried the palanquin is proclaimed;
likewise, the protection from a lion of a cowherd who provided rest under a tree and tilled the soil (132).
And then Hari spoke thus: "Vṛkāyana and the others went to Ketumāla, where there was a gathering of sixty descendants of Gaṅgā.
In Ketumāla, a great sacrifice was performed and described by Hari."
The arrival of all the kings at that place, the movement of Hari to those regions,
the birth of all created beings, the delights of the mind,
and the meals taken in the evening and morning, as well as the bestowal of mantras in their entirety. (1.34–1.35)

Therein, the worship of all the gods and others according to the prescribed rites, the fire-oblation (*havana*) at the sacrifice, and the forms assumed by Hari as Koṭirudra, Abja, and others were described; likewise,
the birth of Avabhṛthakumāra and Tṛptikumārikā.
Once this prince was born, his marriage was performed.
(1.37) Then, in the capital city of Orala-ketu, a grand welcome was given to Hari;
Śrī Hari brought about the liberation of the ancestors of the king. (1.38)
The knowledge of one's own true nature and the establishment of the tradition have been declared; now follows the movement of Hari in the capital city of Krathaka.
Regarding the construction of temples and other such works, the auspicious times and other factors have been proclaimed.

The constellations, planetary conjunctions, the divisions of time (karaṇas), the lunar mansions, the planets, and the stars— both auspicious and inauspicious— have been well explained, as have the auspicious moments (muhūrtas).
In the capital city of Jarasthālī, there was a welcome reception and worship of Hari.
The account of the previous births of the twenty-six kings has been told. Then the Lord, together with his family, went to the kingdom of Uṣṭrāla;
having received due honors there, he then proceeded to the capital city of Tīrāṇā.
Indra declared that for yogis, the duties of householders and other such practices grant liberation.
Then Hari, having received worship from Āyayāvalvī,
went from the kingdom of men to the city of Arthaśrī, and [bestowed] liberation upon Tuṣita and the Rākṣasa.
Having given [the land], he then went to the capital city of Jinavarddhibhūbhṛt;
after wandering through Rāmapurī,
the Supreme Lord went to Mount Cāpināya for the sake of destroying the *rākṣasa* named Janahārī.
He slew the Rākṣasas by means of Rudra through the fire-wheel of the mountain;

[then followed] the making of the bow, the acceptance of the gift of the maiden, and the protection of the subjects. Thereafter, the release of those held in fetters is proclaimed as his protection of the world. (146–147)
The gift of life from the bones of the deceased, the journey to the city of Jīvanī;
the theft of what was written in Śaṅkhavāṭī resulted in the severing of the hands, while bathing in the Bāhudā led to the regrowth of those very hands once more. (148)

Having witnessed the city of Varaṇā belonging to King Jayakṛṣṇa, Hari went to the kingdom of Pariśāna; from there he wandered, and after purifying Cāpapūjana, he went to the kingdom of Parijara. (2.300.149–150)

There, by means of the water of the Indirā, the bathing of Hari was performed for the Vāyūnānagarīyas, and the liberation of the Vetālas was accomplished. Thereafter, the vision of the four-armed Lord was granted to the king.
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Mudraṇḍa, he beheld the city of Madrirā;
having received worship there and given instruction, he then beheld the city of Śaivāla.
Having visited Līśavana, he reached the city of the lord of Gaṇḍaka.
Having received worship and given instruction, he then departed for Līnorṇarāṣṭraka;
after wandering through Vāruṇīpuryā, he went to Dhīvarāpurikā.
Having also wandered through Milīndānagarī, he proceeded to Vālinīpurī.
He indeed received great honor in the kingdom of King Balalīna.
Then followed the instruction on vows, the journey to Śīlāpurī, the teaching on worship, and his travels through the kingdoms of Rāya and Āmalaka. (155–156)
Then there was the journey to that city of Rīmāna, where a grand welcome was received; the arrival in the kingdom of King Phenatantu, along with worship and other honors.
Then followed the wandering through the city of Trinayā, the giving of instruction, and further worship.
The analogy of the crow is mentioned here; his destination was the site of a small fire-offering (stokahoma).
He wandered through the city of Umāpurī and the kingdom of Kāṣṭhayāna, and after roaming about, he gave his instruction in the city of Tunnavāya. 158–159.
Then followed Hari’s journey to the kingdom of King Kolaka;
in the city of Muramāṣā, he received a grand welcome, worship, and other honors.
Hari performed his ablutions in various forms in the Ganges, the Yamunā, and other sacred waters.
Then, in the Hārita regions, at the city of Aparāntikā,
the Lord, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, traveled by celestial chariot across the surface of the earth to the presence of the royal sage Ārkarāja, whose greatness was renowned upon the earth. (161–162)
In the city of Aparāntikā, he was welcomed by the people of the land;
in the regions of Aṭaka, his movement was free from all disease.
And in Yajñapattana, he sent forth a proclamation for the sake of the sacrifice.
The images of Kṛṣṇa’s wives are said to have been the performers of duties at the sacrifice.
However, by the will of Rāyarokīśvara, they were brought back to the city of Sphūrtinārīnagarī;
furthermore, there was the wandering of the sacrifice and its subsequent return to the sacrificial ground.

In that sacrifice, the gods themselves shone forth visibly as the witnesses of the self-luminous Brahmin, who was the seer of all; they were present in the fire where the oblation to the gods was offered.
Then followed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), which wins wealth and brings about the vision of the world of sovereign power.

The worship of twenty maidens, the offering of flower garlands, the seizing [of enemies], and so forth—[these were performed] during the reign of King Rāyavākakṣaka over three continents. Under King Rāyamārīśa, he moved through a fourth continent as well. (167–168)

In the kingdom of Rāyabāleśvara, at the city named Vāyuphena, he was welcomed; thereafter, the great final oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*) of the sacrifice was performed. Benedictions, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth were given, followed by the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
In the kingdom of Rāyalambara, his destination was the city of Uvakrā;
in the kingdom of King Rāyanavārka, his destination was the city of Svarlatikā;
