and in the realm of the lord of Rāyahaṇḍa, his destination was the city of Makṣikā.
In the kingdom of Rāyakūpeśvara, the destination is the city of Havānāya;
in the kingdom of Kālīmaṇḍalīna, the destination is the city of Vigoṣṭhikā;
and in the kingdom of Vanajvālā, the destination for one with younger brothers is the city of Sānujyoṣṭrī.
Then his destination was the city of Kāyanī in the kingdom of Gatainasara (173).
His destination for Hari was the city of Peyisthā in the kingdom of Koṭīśvarakṣmeśa;
in the kingdom of Pārūpa, he performed the welcoming rites and so forth in the city of Sañjālā (174).
Hari went to the kingdom of Bālāvittaka, then to the city of Phāṅkalāśī, then to the kingdom of King Āṇḍajara, and to the city of Prāgastha;
thereafter, he arrived at the city of King Bālyarajas. (175)
Then, in the city called Aṅganagara, there was again the welcoming reception for the ministers;
likewise, in Vāyumānapura, there was the instruction for King Rāyasomana and for the subjects of the Pātra and Gona districts.
Then the illustrious Blessed One proceeded from there to Rājārāyapati-rājya, Ārṣaja-tanurāṣṭraka, and Urogamana-rāṣṭra;
he received a welcome in the city of Rāyagrāma and in the city of Āśāsana-pura.
In the kingdom of King Parāṅvṛta, there was a welcome and a wandering about;
then, in the land called Brāhmīla at the site of a sacrifice, there was instruction, the arrival of the gods, their installation, worship, and so forth. (2.300.179–180)
The mantras for offering oblations, as well as the instructions and so forth, have been proclaimed;

therein in that sacrifice, the greatness of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been proclaimed. Furthermore, his own nature as the self of all and the great final oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*) have likewise been proclaimed. (181)
The rescue of Adhvara, the sanctity of the seven rivers,
the journey to the city of Lāṭalātrī, the destruction of the ocean-dwelling Daitya, the seizing of the lightning-gem with his hand, and the arrival at the city of Dvinediṣṭha. (182–183)
Having arrived at the island of Trāsamāna, the island of Vṛndāruka, Siṃhala, and at Lake Pampā, he then proceeded to Kuṅkumavāpikā; there,
he engaged in the autumnal full-moon festival pastimes with Hari and his own consorts.
On the eighth day of the Caturdaśajanmajayantī festival, a celebration was held.
[Therein occurred] the description of the wonder of the divine assembly, the conclusion of the great festival, and the liberation of the Tāmasa-akṣi outcaste together with his family. (185–186)
By the command of the sage Aśvalāyana, who had assumed the form of a horse,
King Barbura was released from his state of being a barbura-tree.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, there is the worship of Śaṅkara and other deities.
On Dīpāvalī, the festival of Śāradā was established by Hari.
(188) The destruction of King Saṃparka’s disease was accomplished by Śrī Hari;
moreover, in the form of Dattātreya, he also established an auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha). (189)
Then the festival of the mountain of grain was described by him in the form of a swan;
thereafter, the liberation of King Puṇḍarīka was told by him in the form of Nṛhari.
Furthermore, the liberation of the Cola king was recounted; those two are indeed holy places of pilgrimage.
By Hari, who possesses a thousand forms and is a yogi for Vītihotra,
a vision was granted in his thousandfold form and also in the form of Ṛṣabha, and praise was likewise uttered. (191–192)
On the bank of the lake, at the Śeṣamandira established by Vaivasvata,
there is the installation of Śeṣa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, and others;
that particular holy site is likewise declared to be the Vāmanāṅguṣṭha-tīrtha.
In connection with the sage Paṅkila, [his] birth and [his] conversation are related.
The defeat of King Haimakalgi by Paraśurāma is proclaimed;
the performance of the Soma sacrifice by King Aśvapātaratna is described. 1.94–95.
The Pravargya and Upasad rites, the invocation of the Subrahmaṇyā, have been described;

as well as the pressings (savana), the great full oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti), the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), and so forth. [1.96] Faith, the Upaniṣads, realized knowledge (vijñāna), and the manifestation of the vast [reality].
The dialogue between Lomaśa and Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, along with Aśva and Pāṭala, has been related.
This very song of Lomaśa, which demonstrates the liberation of all, was spoken;
herein [is told] the story of King Ānarta and the virtuous female yoginī.
Then, the dialogue of the one endowed with self-luminous yoga was shown;
the account of past events was told, as well as the instruction of the Guru.
[199] There is also the narrative of Bhāṇavīrya and his devotee, arising from the occasion of Rāmāditya.

The *Ūrjavrata* [treatise] of Kāyastha effects the destruction of leprosy. This *Saṃhitā* named after Śārṅgadhara is the work of a Śūdra who was a mute Brahmin; it is said to be composed with illustrative narratives by one whose soul was purified through austerity.

The consumption disease of this Śūdra, Pārṣṇiraḍa, was cured by the serpent moving through the curse of the Brahmin, the lord of Arkapura. Furthermore, the Brahmin suffered a snakebite and death, yet his life was restored by Kṛṣṇa.
The protection of King Aṅgāraka and the account of Rāṇikā are related;
[then] the liberation of King Amohākṣa through the words of the teacher Prabuddha, and also the description of the renunciant initiation for King Abhayākṣa. ॥203–204॥
Then, having been praised by the host of gods submerged in the waters of a lake,
Mahāviṣṇu, being pleased, beheld Puruṣottama— the Brahmin known as Brahmastamba— and married the immortal maiden.
The protection of an elephant from one who was stealing water-pots, children, and wood;
the account of Kuṅkuma, Satīśā, and Dhanyaiśvarī; and the wonders concerning the Caitya, the Brahmin, and the twice-born—these are proclaimed. (206–207)
Likewise, the Harikṛṣṇa-Naranārāyaṇa Tīrtha was proclaimed;
then there is Māṇikī Tīrtha, and the determination known as Aśvapaṭṭa.
Following that, the virtuous initiation of the one named Aśvapāṭala was proclaimed.
Having brought from Kāśī the journal named *Yoga*, sent by Śiva and Śambhu,
both Bṛhaspati and Nārada reached Hari;
and Nārada described the maiden’s sovereignty, virtues, and divine characteristics.
The yogapatrī and the pratipatrī, replete with virtues, have been shown;
the divine pavilion has been described, as well as the worship of the rubies of its pillars (211).
[Therein is] the worship of the water-pot, of Gaṇeśa, and of the Mothers.
The worship of the site (vāstu), Viṣṇu, the family deity, and the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] is prescribed;
[this concludes] the description of the great pavilion (mahāmaṇḍapa) accompanied by the declaration of the fruits [of the rite].
Then follows the sending of a saffron-leafed letter and the festival of betel leaves.
At night there were songs, dances, instrumental music, wrestling matches, poetry recitations, feasts, and festivals;
the kneading of flour-doughs, amorous dalliance, and the arrival of people from Hari’s city; preparations for the pilgrimage to Kāśī, and the adornment of countless maidens. (214)
The Yogavāhinikā reached Kāśī and remained in Śivapura.
Herein is also described Pārvatīpura and Śivapattana. [There occurred] honors, inquiries after welfare, and the descent of Kailāsa. (2186–2187)
Then, in Śivapurī, Hari performed the worship of the family deity;
and in the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā,
he conducted the test [to determine] that the girl must by no means be given to Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then, having spoken before Śiva, Śambhu, and also before Girijā, as well as before Lakṣmī, Hari tested his firm resolve;
the sending of garments, ornaments, and other gifts for the sake of the maiden was fully described. (218–219)
The description of the Yogavāhinī was shown to Pārvatī through a verse;
the women who witnessed it were enchanted upon beholding Him within the limbs of Kṛṣṇa.
In the resting pavilion of Kṛṣṇa, the madhuparka offering took place.
The beautiful adornment of the maidens and Hari’s arrival at the pavilion; (221) and with forms numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion, Hari accepted the maidens.
All the rites were performed, and the description of the beloved was proclaimed. (222)
The dissolution of all forms and so forth, the perfection of the rite of marriage, resting and sporting together with all [consorts] without a single form,
the morning procession of the blossoming maiden, and the loosening of the knots of yoga. (223)
On the Gaṅgā, the distribution of rewards and other gifts to all classes [of people] (224).
On the bank of the Pañcagaṅgā is the excellent holy site named Bālakṛṣṇa;
there, alms were given to Śambhu, and he arrived at Śivapura (225).
There was also the honoring with hospitality, the parting gift, and the request for forgiveness;
then the arrival at the Kuṅkumavāpikā field for those traveling on their spiritual journey (yogayātrins);
the entry into the house of their beloveds, and finally, the monastery and recreation.
She received the guru-mantra and beheld the forests.

Having seen the sky in the form of a maiden, she was infatuated upon seeing the playful pastimes of Hari, who assumes the forms of millions of billions of lotuses, as he sports with his beloveds. (227–228)
Then Hari induced the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of all the maidens;
Hari revealed to them the abode of the syllables of the three worlds and so forth,
as well as the knowledge of the greatness of the earth and their mutual requests for forgiveness.
All the maidens were requested by their mothers and bestowed by Śrīhṛt.
There was the avoidance of the ceremonial pavilion and other such rites; it was a service rendered to Lakṣmī.
At the sixteenth birth-festival of her own chaste wives, there was a return once more.
The fruit of hearing the *tretāsantāna* [is] liberation through Śiva, Śambhu, and the others;
the enumeration of the subject matter of the *tretāsantāna* is the conclusion of the section.
The greatness of the *tretā* has also been declared; these, then, are the subjects in brief. (232)
O Rādhā, in this Tretā-santānaka, there are indeed thousands of divine accounts concerning kings, devotees, sacrifices, women, and sacred fords, all of which truly bestow liberation. (233–234)
In this *Santānaka*, there are thirty-two thousand verses and exactly three hundred chapters dedicated to the Supreme Brahman.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reciting it—
Indeed, by guarding [the sacred texts] in their homes, they become endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
There are five hundred and ninety Saṃhitās consisting of four chapters each;
when these are reduced to three chapters each, they indeed become eight hundred and ninety.
There will be eighty-seven thousand verses in the Saṃhitā. Then, O Rādhā, the third section, called the *Dvāpara-santānaka*, concerning Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, shall be completed. (238)
[This is] a description of the nature of Kṛṣṇa in his sixteen-year-old state.
By connection with this narrative, women become the beloved consorts of Kṛṣṇa and men become the servants of Kṛṣṇa; indeed, I, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, declare this. (2.300.239–240)
May the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, grant you well-being; may he bring you prosperity.
May your mother, father, husband, wife, and lineage be auspicious for you.
For the sake of liberation, one should give one’s entire wealth to the reciter of this [work], who is like Vyāsa.
For the sake of prosperity, let the listeners pay homage with faith and divine understanding.
(242) Gold, jewels, beds and the like, diamonds, pearls, elephants, horses, cattle and so forth, celestial palaces, and vehicles. (243)
A vehicle, a mansion, a garden, and so forth should be given to Vyāsa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
for Vyāsa himself is indeed the beloved Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his true form.
All forms of good fortune should be bestowed upon him by one who listens [to this].
For wealth, prosperity, sons, a wife, and even sovereignty are indeed obtained [through this].
May this scripture—which brings about the attainment of Brahman, is enriched by all branches of knowledge, is the lineage of the Tretā age, and has Kṛṣṇa as its soul—be most victorious! (245–246)

Through hearing [this] and likewise through giving it, there is the destruction of all suffering for him, as well as the attainment of total peace and the production of all accomplishments. Hearing [this] bestows the fruits of the gifts of knowledge, land, maidens, and gold. (247)
She is the giver of liberation, the giver of the fruit of charity, and the bestower of the lordship of Kṛṣṇa.
Om! The noble one, the child of Kambharā, the Lord of all, the Master of the virtuous, the embodiment of the good, the Supreme Self—the Lord is victorious day and night. (248–249)
May this second lineage, offered unto that very Supreme Brahman, perpetually extend here for you, O fortunate one; may it be well.
Indeed, thirty-two thousand, two hundred, and fifty [years].
And there are four verses here concerning the offspring of Tretā.
(251) Thus ends, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, within the second section on the lineage of Tretā,
the majesty of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and a concise indication of the subjects contained in the Tretā-santāna-khaṇḍa.
The three hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Introduction to the Lineage of Dvāpara and the Benedictions," is concluded.
Thus ends the second section, the Tretāyuga-santāna-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Oṃ, may this be offered unto Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī.
This is the table of contents for the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā.

1. A description of the universal sovereignty of the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa. 2. The destruction of the two demons Hiraṇyakūrca and Hiraṇyāṇḍa—born from the beard and the testicles of the progenitor of the manifold lineage of the Lord of the Imperishable Supreme Abode (Akṣara Paradhāma)—by means of Saṃkarṣaṇa; and how, with the southern portion of the terrestrial globe centered on Meru remaining as the sole residue, Śrī Kṛṣṇa introduced Rādhikā to Him, and so forth. 4.

3. The existence of Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa in all creations as the perfect form (*sumūrtatayā*), and His manifestation by grace in Saurāṣṭra, in the great sacred field of Ānarta (the field of Lomaśāśrama), and so forth.

4. On the day of the Supreme Lord’s manifestation, the incarnations (*avatāras*), the gods (*īśvaras*), the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), and the subjects (*prajāḥ*) assembled, along with various gifts (*dānas*), and so forth.

5. The protection of the Lord in His infant form performed by Ṣaṣṭhī; the abduction of Him by the demons to Pātāla through the medium of a *sūtaka* (impurity) man; the origin of the *sūtaka* and others; the protection provided by Śeṣanārāyaṇa; and the devotion of the *sūtaka*.

The ritual procedure for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa-saṃskāra*) of the Supreme Lord; the destruction by means of His discus (*cakra*) of the demon Sāṇāsu, who had assumed the form of a tiger and desired to kill Hari; the performance of rites for pacification (*śānti*), and so forth. 17.7.

At the festival of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s mounting of the swing (*preṅkhā-ārohaṇa-utsava*), the granting of liberation and other blessings to Talā, the daughter of Talaja, a Rākṣasī who arrived in disguise and was nonetheless enchanted by Hari; and so forth. 20.0. [Fragmentary heading]

8. At the commencement of the second month of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, during the festival of drinking milk, the Blessed One drank the milk of divine cows in various forms; there was a great festival for the cows, and the Blessed One brought about the destruction and liberation of the wives of the deceitful Rākṣasas who had assumed the form of cows by making them run and drink milk while it was still alive.

In the third month of the bright fortnight, during the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) sacrament performed by women outside the house for the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, there occurred playful fondling; [the Lord displayed] manifold forms and divine visions. In the hermitage of Lomaśa, Suraprabhā took Kṛṣṇakānta and departed. There, the asura Krodhana, having become a maiden named Krodhanā, abducted Hari. She was incinerated in the sky by Hari and released him;

having made that divine woman threefold in form, He established her in the hermitage of Lomaśa, [attained] liberation, and [experienced] the birth as Durvāsas—thus He acted. [There were also] the vision of lightning, wonders, and so forth. 26.

10. During the consecration ceremony for Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa’s seating upon the earth, ten thousand daughters of the earth, including the caves such as Siṃhikā, attained Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and so forth.

29. 11. The ear-piercing ceremony (*karṇavedha-saṃskāra*) of Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa; the display of wonders by the needle; the Aśvinīkumāra Tīrtha; the consecration ceremony for the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana-saṃskāra*); the feeding performed by the forest deities; the manifestation of many wonders through various forms by the forest deities; the attainment of a beloved; and [the account of] taking up the garments, weapons, and other objects held before Hari in order to test His livelihood.
31. 12. The manifestation of various forms and so forth;

the paralyzing of the Daitya Damana—who had come to the hermitage of Lomaśa to abduct the daughter of the one situated by the Southern Ocean—by Lomaśa; and the destruction of him along with his army, followed by his liberation, performed by Bālakṛṣṇa with the Sudarśana discus, and so forth. 34. 13.
The commencement of a tumultuous battle between the Rākṣasīs and the maidens in the vicinity of Aśvapaṭṭasara, and so forth. 37.

14. In the battle with the Rākṣasīs, accompanied by innumerable maidens capable of combat, there is the seeking of refuge at the conclusion of the Rākṣasīs' defeat and imminent destruction; [the attainment of] the state of liberation and the state of a maiden through the grace of Bālakṛṣṇa, and so forth. 40. 15.
Regarding the new maidens, [the account begins with] the greatness of the Ekādaśī vow shown by Lomaśa, their devotion to their husbands, and their service to cows, gurus, and others. 44.

16. On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, [the Lord] performed worship by means of His own daughters; assumed many forms; observed vows; engaged in battle with and liberated the Daityas known as Kaṅkatālas residing on Mount Śatrūñjaya; and caused the remaining ones, who had assumed the forms of maidens, to dwell in the hermitage of Lomaśa, and so forth. 46 17. Regarding the wives of the Kaṅkatāla Daityas, [the Lord] manifested the state of being the beloved of Kṛṣṇa in the field of Lomaśa during the battle; and Lomaśa imparted the instruction concerning the offering of Himself as Bālakṛṣṇa, and so forth. 49

18. On the paternal side: the worship of Hari performed by the daughters of the ancestors; the libations for the ancestors and other rites performed by Hari; the liberation of those in hell; the acquaintance with the lineage of the ancestors' wives; the deliverance of the *pretas*, and so forth. 52 19. On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, during the festival marking the beginning of the second year of the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa: the dispatching of invitation cards to all the worlds; the construction of a great pavilion for the presentation of offerings arranged according to the zodiac signs (*rāśi*), and so forth.
56 20. A description of the splendor of the pavilion; the seating arrangements for the assembly; the adornment of the form of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and so forth. 60

21. Description of the magnificent throne in the pavilion during the great festival marking the beginning of the second year of Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as all the performed worship and blessings, etc.

(63) 22. By means of the yoga of descent, Prahlāda’s arrival on earth from the subterranean realm (rasātala) for the sake of pilgrimage; his battle with Nara-Nārāyaṇa; the defeat of Nārāyaṇa through devotion; and the arrival of Prahlāda and Cyavana at the hermitage of Lomaśa, etc. (66) 23. The liberation of ten thousand dānavas residing in the subterranean realm and elsewhere, and the taking of five thousand maidens into the protection of Bālakṛṣṇa. (69)

24. The narrative concerning the sins residing in the body hairs during the tonsure ceremony (*caula-saṃskāra*) of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and how the hairs of Hari are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and so forth.

(72) 25. The blossoming of spring, the festival of the flower-swing (*puṣpa-dola-utsava*), and the destruction by Hari of the demon Sālamāla—who had assumed the form of a whale (*timiṅgila*) and arrived for the purpose of slaying Hari—and so forth.

(75) 26. On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the festival of the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra-utsava*) on the bank of a lake, the arrival of the Daityas belonging to the lineage of Sālamāla, the battle, their destruction by the Lord, and the teachings on the path of liberation (*mokṣadharma*) imparted by Lomaśa, and so forth. (78)

27. The narrative of Sukeśī regarding the instruction in dharma for the wives of the Daityas; the Aśūnyaśayana-vrata, the Śivapuṇyaka-vrata, and others; the sleeping of the gods on specific lunar days (tithis), their worship, and so forth.

81 28. At the festival marking the commencement of the Lord’s fourth year, the liberation from distress of Svastika, a Nāga of Pātāla, who had arrived via Garuḍa from Sumadhu, the minister of the King of Pātāla; the bringing of the Nāga maidens to the hermitage of Lomaśa, and so forth. 84

29. King Āraktadeśīya’s journey to Śrī Hari for the sake of obtaining a son, for the purpose of offering children as a sacrifice to the goddess Śāvadīnākālī, and for the liberation of the bound children; [and] the affection of the thousand maidens toward Hari, and so forth. 87. 30. The consecration of the queen as a sacrificial animal performed by the king for the Lord; the destruction of the king and others by the queen; the return to Badarī, Kurukṣetra, and the hermitage of Lomaśa; the restoration of the boys to their fathers; the liberation of the mothers, and so forth. 90.

31. The milk-vow (*payovrata*) for young girls; the boundaries established by Śvetaketu regarding the principles of ancient dharma; Aśmaka, the son of Vasiṣṭha, born of the wife of Saudāsa; the wife of Utathya touched by Bṛhaspati; Dīrghatamas procreating sons upon the slave-girl and the queen of Bali; and the subsequent establishment of social boundaries (*maryādākaraṇa*), and so forth. 93 32. The manifest arrival of the child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) and others during their worship; and the description of them by way of names, forms, and other characteristics. 96

33. Regarding the worship and dismissal of Gaurī: the destruction [of the demon] Vallīdīna, known as Vyāghrāsura, along with a host of demons assuming the forms of tigers and lions, numbering one hundred, and so forth.

99 34. During the great festival marking the Lord’s fifth year: the singing of various Gandharvas; the bringing to life of lions and other creatures from the skins of lions, tigers, and so forth by thousands of sages such as Dālbhya and Baka; and the manifestation of those respective skins from his thumb, and so forth. 102

35. At Lomaśakṣetra, the Lord was pleased by the Kailāsīya Ardhanaresvara dance troupe’s extraordinary performances; being thus gratified, He became the destroyer of Śaṅkara’s pride and the bestower of liberation, and [the place became known as] Naṭanāṭyatīrtha, and so forth.

105 36. Upon the commencement of the Lord’s education, all the sciences in embodied form arrived; there was an examination of His intellect, Bṛhaspati’s instruction to the Daitya Varāṭaka regarding the necessity of diligence, the obstruction of the Daitya’s penance, and so forth. 108

37. The defeat of the army of the asura Varāṭaka and the subsequent punishment, as well as the destruction of the mlecchas of the Ḍaphphara tribe, and so forth. 111. 38. The harassment in the garden by the great sages Vanaspati, Nabhaspati, and Saraspati, who had attained the state of rākṣasas due to the curse of Satī; their release from the curse by the Lord; the wandering of naked Śaṅkara through the hermitages of ascetics; the offense committed against the sages; the felling of the *liṅga*; and the cause of the curse, and so forth. 114.

39. At the commencement of the Lord’s sixth year, on the eighth lunar day, there was a great festival and worship performed by Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, the Vyūha deities, humans, and others; furthermore, the twice-born Devāyana, together with his wife, was delivered from birth as a Cāṇḍāla, and so forth.
40. During the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while listening to the narration of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* performed during the Ūrja-vrata, there occurred a divine vision of the Lord.
The hymns of the sages, the sacred fords (tīrthas) due to their habitation, and so forth.

121. 41. King Kaṇṭhādhar’s attainment of the staff of death through devotion to Śaṅkara; his long life through service at Puṣkara by the blessing of Vasiṣṭha; the bringing back of the Brahmin’s son who had gone to the abode of Yama and the gift of his own lifespan; his marriage with Yamunā, the daughter of King Yama; and, in connection therewith, his atheism (nāstikatā), and so forth. 124.

42. Through his association with Hṛḍḍakāyinī, the wife of Kaṃthādharasvāmin, [Raṇaṅgama] became extremely atheistic; due to the cessation of Vedic rites and other duties, his sovereignty was destroyed and he died in the forest, taking birth as a *mleccha*. He was subsequently liberated at the Aśvapaṭṭasara Tīrtha by his son, Raṇaṅgama. — 127 43. Raṇaṅgama performed a sacrifice; it was the seventh birth-festival of the Lord (*prabhu*). Raṇaṅgama married a Yakṣa maiden and obtained a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and other such boons. — 130

44. [The account] beginning with the Lord’s vision upon entering a fissure in the earth in the midst of the circular region of Antariksha while traveling by celestial chariot (vimāna) to behold the southern pole star at Raṇaṅgama; and the departure from the earth for the journey of King Lakṣmaṇa along with his family by means of that same celestial chariot, and so forth. 133.

45. In the middle [of the section], the wicked account of the Rākṣasa Mātrāgaskara, who obstructed [the path] and committed acts such as beating his own sister, mother, and others; and the protection afforded by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to Māñjāmbikā and her daughter-in-law when they were cast into the ocean, and so forth.

136 46. The battle between Raṇaṅgama and Mātrāgaskara; the victory of Raṇaṅgama; the arrival at the hermitage of Lomaśa; the worship of the Lord; Lakṣmaṇa’s seeking refuge with two thousand maidens in the Lord; the six-footed bees, and so forth. 139
47. From the daughters of Lakṣmaṇa, Lomaśa [obtained] the discernment of sons, daughters, disciples, wives, and so forth, as well as self-knowledge and other [realizations].

142 48. The Creator had three daughters—Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā—who, having arrived by celestial chariot (*vimāna*), bowed to the Lord, considered him their own, worshipped him, and departed, and so forth.

145 49. Suṣumṇā and the others, having observed the regions of the earth by means of the celestial chariot, went to Satyaloka; furthermore, seventy-two thousand maidens set out through the sky by celestial chariot for the purpose of beholding Śrī Hari.

148. 50. The king of the Abrikta region had his aerial chariot (*sarvakāmavimāna*) blocked by his own army commanders; the message delivered by the messenger and Nārada’s reply; and therein the account of Śukra, Araja, Daṇḍa, Viśvakarman, Citrāṅgada, and the Asura chariots, and so forth.
151. 51. In the Abrikta regions, along with the Brahma-aerial chariot, eleven crores and eleven lakhs of warriors, Nagaras, and Mlecchas perished, and so forth. 154.

52. The manifestation of the discernment and higher knowledge produced by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā. 158 53. The Daityas’ feigned surrender; the departure of Śaṅkara and others toward their capital city; their welcome; and the battle in the aerial chariot (*vimāna*) from behind, and so forth. 160 54. The battle waged by the Daitya women on the seventh floor of the aerial chariot; the destruction of the female Daityas by means of magical rites arising from the *kalpavallī* (wish-fulfilling creeper); the vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; the King’s prayer; and the instruction, and so forth. 164

55. An account of how Śrī Hari, having wandered through the lands of Abrikta, established sacred fords (*tīrtha*), effected the liberation of those who had died, and brought about the salvation of the royal family, divided the kingdom into two parts, and bestowed them upon his two devotees, and so forth.

166 56. The birth of the Marut deities in the form of Daityas, their subsequent attainment of divinity, the narration of their various births and lives, and the history of the principal Daityas born in Abrikta, and so forth. 169

57. The destruction of ten thousand Daityas, beginning with Raktabīja, at the gates of King Yama; the granting of the kingdom to the messenger named Āra; the protection of the Ṛṣi Bakadāna; the birth of the lineage of Ārava, and so forth. (172) 58. The origin of Asuras such as Raktabīja and Ārabīja; the birth of the Daitya Dhundhu; the sin consisting of the destruction of seeds, and so forth. (175) 59. The liberation of Pretas through a Śrāddha ceremony performed on the eleventh day of the month of Bhādrapada at the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake; the dialogue between the Pretas and a merchant, and so forth. (178)

60. King Udayapattana’s vision of the Lord while staying on the shore of the Dhīravīra lake during the Cāturmāsya period; his being submerged in water due to excessive rain; and how the Lord provided protection by means of a boat, and so forth. 181.

61. Having rescued two hundred men who were submerged in the waters by means of a boat, the Lord traveled via the Mahī river, circumambulated Stambha, Akhāta, and the ocean gate, and reached Somanātha, Svarṇapura, and Camatkārapura; then, by means of his boat-vehicle, he brought them to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī. [This section also includes] the protective hymn (rakṣāstotra) instructed by Lomaśa, and the liberation of the Rākṣasa Krūrasiṃha through the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by means of a Brāhmaṇa, and so forth. 184.

62. [The Lord] performed the restoration of health for those rescued from the water who offered praise, as well as for the sick, the maimed, the eunuchs, and others during the festival of the eighth year; He accepted their hymns of praise, received a prayer composed by Āryāyana, brought those lifted up by the waters back to their own country, and granted liberation to King Udayana, and so forth. 187 63. Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa rescued the merchant Vasumedha, a resident of the city of Candrodaya, along with his family, after they had been submerged in the waters of the Saurāṣṭra ocean while traveling by boat to a sacred pilgrimage site via the Narmadā River; He bestowed upon them the gift of liberation, and so forth. 190
64. In the *Gopanāthamāhātmya*, a description of the sacred fords, holy sites, and other locations where Śrī Kṛṣṇa was born among all classes of people in Saurāṣṭra.
(192) 65. In the eighth year of the Lord’s life, during the great festival of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in Vaiśākha, the arrival of everyone through auspicious invitation cards and so forth.
(194) 66. The ritual procedure for the offering of the sacred thread to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, including worship and other rites. (197)
67. The giving of food to the honored ones, the assembly meeting, and the instruction in the supreme knowledge (parāvidyā) as spoken by Nārada, and so forth.
200 68. The granting of rewards to the honored ones, the worship of the Lord, the presentation of offerings, the divine vision, and the dismissal, and so forth.
203 69. A description of the greatness and the fruits of service, worship, giving, and adoration of the Lord. 206

70. The description of the previous nature [of the soul], characterized by dullness, is elucidated through six births by means of the example of Agha. 209 71. King Jyāmagha related to his wife Dhanālasā the knowledge previously spoken by the Blessed One to the brahmin Indradyumna, beginning with the statement that it is the means to liberation. 212 72. The liberation of Jyāmagha and his wife through devotion manifested at the sacred field of Lomaśa, and so forth. 215

73. The protection from thieves granted by the Lord to a devotee named Sudhana, a resident of Āmodapura, who attained the state of devotion to the Bhāgavata through the yoga of the great seer Varcakāyani; as well as the Lord’s divine vision and other such occurrences. (218) 74. What more need be said? On the bank of the Anadyā river, through the yoga of the seer Kauśika Ambarīṣa, a sick outcaste, Tryaṣṭakāru, together with his wife, attained the station of liberation due to his devotion to the Lord, and so forth. (221)

75. When six hundred young disciples of Hiraṇyakeśin, who were staying in the preceptor’s hermitage, were destroyed by Rākṣasas, Śrī Hari undertook efforts such as battle for the sake of destroying those demons. 224 76. The restoration to life of the disciples of Hiraṇyakeśin who had been killed by the Daitya Santāpana; the destruction of the Daityas; and the consecration of rivers, lakes, and sacred sites (tīrthas) in the southern direction and elsewhere. 227 77. Through the union with the sage Suratāyana, the thousand Brahmins—who had assumed the form of black cranes after accepting a terrible gift from King Bṛhadvarcas on the banks of the Tāpī river—returned to their original state. 228

78. The instruction given by the sage Suratāyana; the appearance of the Lord, the arrival of the two Aśvinīkumāras, the purification of the brahmins, the clarification regarding renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and so forth.

(231) 79. The arrival of the five thousand brahmins, headed by Suratāyana, at Lomaśa-tīrtha; their auspicious instruction, and so forth. (234) 80. King Baleśvara’s attainment of supreme *bhāgavata*-hood through the yoga of the Blessed Lord Kapila; the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the guise of a forest-dweller for the purpose of testing [the king] during the Kārtika vow through the yoga of the great sage Tārakāyana; and [the account] of the king...

237. 81. King Baleśvara, together with his family, offered praise to Śrī Hari; [he attained] the vision of the Lord by surrendering his sons, daughters, wife, and family, and so forth. 240. 82. By the power of the worship of the Supreme Brahman taught by Viśvāmitra, King Jayadhvaja attained Hari at the sacrifice; there was the destruction of the Rākṣasa Videha, and the concluding purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*) at the four mountains, and so forth.
243. 83. The knowledge bestowed by Jayadhvaja [was received] by Droṇa, Eḷa, Nīla, and Śrīparvata.
The divine nature of the holy sites of Kolāṭa, Cila, Śambhala, Nārāyaṇa, and Saras, as well as devotion and liberation; the liberation of Jayadhvaja, and so forth. (246) 84.
The duties of the four yugas as spoken by Pulastya, the granting of boons to Ailavilā and others, her ascetic practices, and so forth. (249) 85.
The majesty of the imperishable realm (*akṣara-kṣetra*) and other matters told to Ailavilā by the Lord Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (252)

86. Ailavilā’s arrival at the hermitage of Lomaśa, her assumption of two forms, and the residence of the descendants of Hari on the Sahya mountain, and so forth. (255) 87. The atheism of Adharmajīva, the son of Khara; the attribution of faults to the qualities of Hari; his hatred toward Śrī Hari and his consequent miserable state; and subsequently, the granting of a boon for the sake of his future attainment of a good state, and so forth. (257) 88. A description of the pilgrimage from Prayāga to Lomaśatīrtha, surpassing all other holy places, by means of the majesty of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake as revealed by the sage Śrī Sanatkumāra, and so forth. (260)

89. The arrival of all the gods and others from various holy sites (*tīrtha*) for the pilgrimage to the hermitage and sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Lomaśa, the festival on the birthday of Śrī Hari, and so forth.

262. 90. The Lord’s journey to Badarī; the arrival of the *rākṣasīs* at the sacred field of Lomaśa; the destruction of the *rākṣasīs* by Mahāmārī Bhairavī; and thereafter, His manifestation as the pervasive one (*vyāpaka*) for the purpose of devouring sinful people, and so forth. 265. 91. When many humans were destroyed by the great plagues (*mahāmārī*), groups of virtuous women, holy men, and Brahmin sages went to Badarī, informed the Lord, and brought Śrī Hari [there]; Hari restored the dead to life, and so forth. 268.

92. In the *Vāsudevagītā*, [there is] the attainment of that state (*tatpada*) and so forth through the realization of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) and non-duality (*advaita*) regarding the Supreme Brahman.
(p. 271) 93. In the *Vāsudevagītā*, there is a description of the manifestations (*vibhūtis*) consisting of spiritual practices for the sake of attaining the Lord.

(p. 274) 94. In the *Vāsudevagītā*, [there is] the arrival at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) of Śrī Lomaśakṣetra by the fourfold manifestation (*vyūhacatuṣṭaya*) and the fourfold Śrī, as well as the Self-luminous Tīrtha (*svataḥprakāśatīrtha*), the Tīrtha of the fourfold manifestation, and so forth. (p. 276)

95. In the section on the Uṣṇālaya-khaṇḍa: Agastya’s departure; the dissolution of the waters there due to the agitation of the ocean and violent winds caused by the host of local ṛṣis; and how Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was remembered, and so forth. 279 96. The prayer of the people and great sages of the Uṣṇālaya-bhū-khaṇḍa; the Lord’s journey; the pacification of the calamities; and the granting of life to all, and so forth. 282 97. In the land of Uṣṇālaya, at the Hemaśālāyana hermitage, the descent of Lord Hari’s celestial chariot (vimāna); and the narration of the account of their own protection, and so forth. 284
98. In the region of Uṣṇālaya, the narration of the previous births of the female ruddy goose (cakravākī) and the female cat (mārjārī), as requested by Hemaśālāyana, and so forth.
287 99. The protection of the female cat’s offspring from the fire of the potter’s discarded vessels by Nārāyaṇa, the liberation of the female cat from her curse, and so forth.

290 100. During the pilgrimage to sacred fords, the female ruddy goose’s meeting with her mother Lakṣmī on the banks of the Gaṇḍakī river, the description of the greatness of the mother, and so forth. 293

101. While the Lord was reclining upon His bed with Lakṣmī in Mahāvaikuṇṭha, the devotees headed by Dhenupāla, as well as Satī and Śaṅkara, arrived; consequently, the pleasure of Lakṣmī’s reclining with Nārāyaṇa was interrupted, and due to Lakṣmī’s curse, Aśoka and others descended among human beings, and so forth. 296 102. Following the curses issued by Śrī Lakṣmī against Śambhu and the others, Śrī Nārāyaṇa abandoned Kamalā and departed from Vaikuṇṭha, and so forth. 299

103. From Vaikuṇṭha, there was the arrival of Lakṣmī, the male attendants (pārṣadas), and the female attendants (pārṣadīs) at Satyaloka; from there, their arrival at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake; and subsequently, the manifestation of Lakṣmī in the temple of Śiveśvara in the snowy region, as well as the manifestations of her attendants and others in various locations, and so forth.

302 104. Having received the permission of her parents, Lakṣmī and Urvaśī went to Hanumān’s hermitage in the Himalayas for the purpose of performing penance; at the end of a year, Nārāyaṇa himself went there to bestow the fruit [of their austerities], and so forth. 304

105. By the water consecrated by Nārāyaṇa, the life-force of Lakṣmī and Cakravākī was restored; and when Cakravākī was addressed for the sake of granting a boon, she chose the drinking of water upon the mountain peak, and thereafter she chose liberation. Then, having caused the region to submerge with rains, Hari bestowed water upon the peak; having drunk it, [Cakravākī] was released from the curse. Under the pretext of fear of the rains, the family of Śivasvāmin, the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Vaikuṇṭha and others who had assumed human forms, came to Kāśī and took up residence on the banks of the Varaṇā, in the palaces of the King of Kāśī, and in the mango groves, where they were honored by Viśvanātha, Annapūrṇā, and other deities of Kāśī.

And so forth. 307. 106. The granting of boons to Hanumān; following that narrative, in the *Uṣṇālayakhaṇḍa*, the Lord’s bathing, wandering, and the consecration of holy sites (*tīrtha*) among all the rivers, lakes, and mountains; the performance of a Viṣṇu-sacrifice by the sovereign King Dakṣaja-vangara in that region; thereafter, the arrival of the king—accompanied by a hundred celestial chariots and ten thousand subjects—at the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ along with Hari; the offering of worship, gifts, and other tributes on the twelfth birthday of the Lord; and [the birth of] a hundred daughters for the king and a thousand for his subjects.
The maidens of Bālakṛṣṇa were brought to safety by the king and others, as was the return of the king and his followers to their own country, and so forth. 310.

107. To end the confinement inflicted upon the daughters of the fathers by Rākṣasas and others in the Kimpuruṣa region, a battle was waged by Brahmā and the other gods; he restored life to those who had died, and they offered prayers for liberation through their lives, [realizing] that the bestower of supreme liberation is indeed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and so forth. 314.

108. The dispatching of sages from the sacred field of Śrīlomaśa; thereafter, Hari’s journey with his parents to regions such as Prāgjyotiṣa and others; and the outbreak of war at the conclusion of the sacrifice, and so forth. (317) 109. The death of fifteen kings, including Makaraketu and Madādi, along with their four-quarter army of forty million soldiers, in battle against Śambhu and the others; the seeking of refuge by the remaining twenty-five lakhs [of followers], and so forth. (320) 110. The establishment of Vaiṣṇava kings in regions such as Prāgjyotiṣa and others, the establishment of sages, and the divine vision granted out of compassion, and so forth. (322)

111. Hari granted divine vision to the daughters of the Pitṛs, beginning with Brahmaputrī; twenty-one thousand maidens sought refuge in him; he bestowed the kingdom of the Kaśmīra region upon Aryaman; these rivers, such as Brahmaputrī, came into existence in the form of streams; Hari performed ablutions in all of them, consecrated them as *tīrthas*, and granted boons to them, along with the fruits of visiting those sacred sites (*tīrtha*), and so forth. 325 112. The majesty of the second sacrificial ground, consisting of the Upala, Asha, Hasa, lakes, and rivers, including their worship through forms and icons, their consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and so forth. 328

113. Description of the various limbs of devotion that cause the grace of Śrī Hari. 331 114. The Lord’s manifestation of His own true nature and supreme devotion to virtuous people before the rivers who were formerly His father’s daughters.

334 115. The Lord bestowed the kingdom of Bhūtāsana upon Bhairava, the kingdom of Nagna-parvata, and the kingdom of Sāma upon the disciplined warriors; having commanded the rivers to go to their own regions in the Sundara forest, He proceeded toward the sacred field of Lomaśa, where He celebrated the festival of the flower-swing and the festival of Śrāvaṇa, and so forth. 337

116. The thirteenth birthday festival of the Lord; the transformation of King Samīraṇa into a Śarabha due to the curse of the Ṛṣi Pārṣṇigṛha while he had gone out for hunting; his subsequent liberation at the sacred field of Śrī Lomaśa on Mount Raivata through Dattātreya; the Dattātreya-tīrtha, and so forth. (339) 117. King Pavamāna’s journey toward Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, taking the Lord Varāha with him, in order to avert the curse bestowed by the Ṛṣi Picchala; the liberation from the curse through the grace of Hari; the Varāha-tīrtha, the Pavamāna-tīrtha, and so forth. (342)

118. On the festival of Hari’s fourteenth birthday at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, in the form of a tortoise, performed the rescue and deliverance of the Brahmins who had been submerged; and so forth. (375) 119.
Devāyatana, a devotee of the sages, by chanting the names of Śrī Hari in the city of Yama, liberated all those bound for the realm of Yama; and so forth. (348)

120. Bālakṛṣṇa, being pleased by the devotion of the sage Devāyatana, came under his influence and rescued him from the water; furthermore, having caused the name of Śrī Hari to be proclaimed to the subjects of the eight guardians of the quarters, he brought about their liberation through that means, and so forth. 351 121. In the Kiṃpuruṣa-khaṇḍa, in the regions of Rāśiyāna, the sage Devāyatana was sent by [the Lord] for the purpose of awakening the chanting of the name of Hari; there occurred the meeting with the twelve fierce great sages (maharṣis), beginning with Meṣāyana, and other events. 364

122. Having traveled by celestial chariot (*vimāna*) through the regions of Rāśiyāna together with great sages and kings, the sage Devāyana proclaimed the name of Hari among the subjects and bestowed mantras upon them, and so forth.

(357) 123. On the shore of the Bālakṛṣṇa lake, the construction of the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*) and other structures took place; there was the arrival of the *mahīmānas* and the arrival of the venerable Bālakṛṣṇa and others, and so forth. (360) 124. In the kingdom of Śibi, at the Bālakṛṣṇa lake, during the great sacrifice (*mahāyajña*), the arrangements for the officiants were made and the sacrificial rites were completed; furthermore, the king offered one hundred maidens to Śrī Hari, and so forth. (362)

125. The instructions and blessings bestowed by the Lord in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa; the command for the performance of the second sacrifice; and the greatness of the Bālakṛṣṇa-saras tīrtha, etc. (365). 126. The performance of the second Viṣṇu-yajña at Dvikalasarovara during the reign of the great king Tharkūṭastha; and the bestowing of mantra-instructions upon the subjects, etc.
(368). 127. The liberation of a deceased spirit (pretoddhāra); and the instruction in royal policy and true dharma to King Tharkūṭastha, etc. (371).

128. In the kingdom of King Vīrajāra, at the confluence of the Obīrā and Triśā rivers, the performance of the third Viṣṇu-sacrifice took place; [this section contains] the bestowal of mantras and so forth, as well as the majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha). 374. 129. Through the offering of a divine body fit for the attainment of the imperishable state by means of a golden image of the deity, liberation was attained by Śūrajāra, the father of Vīrajāra, together with his family.
376. 130. In the kingdom of King Śaktyakṣin, the performance of the fourth Viṣṇu-sacrifice took place, including the greatness of the avabhṛtha bath and other rites. 379.

131. Following the fourth sacrifice, the dispatching of Kālī to the ocean for the sake of the fifth sacrifice of the celestial sages (*devarṣis*); the attainment of refuge in Śrī Hari by sixty maidens through the King of Śakti’s eyes; and the liberation of one hundred and one female spirits (*piśācinīs*). 382 132. In the kingdom of King Kālimeśa: the performance of the fifth sacrifice; the ritual ablution (*avabhṛtha*); the feast; the narrative; the worship; the gift of two hundred maidens; the divine vision; the worship performed by the subjects of many islands; the meal at the seat of Sādhulāla; and the sounds of natural conchs and other musical instruments, and so forth. 385
133. Śrī Hari gave initiation to Sādhulālāsanayogin as well as to five thousand others, including the female practitioners (sādhavī), and so forth.

388 134. The honoring of all great souls, the proclamation of Vaiṣṇavism, the dispatching of Saccidānandalālāyaṇa toward Uttarakuru, the liberation of the couple Śūra and Jārā, the transformation of the thirty sons of Raudrī and Rudra into Vaiṣṇavas, and the designation of those places as sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha), and so forth. 391

135. [The account of] Śrī Hari’s departure from the Bālakṛṣṇa lake toward Kāśī, his arrival at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, and his return; the threefold abode of Hari—within the hearts of the perfected ones (santaḥ), within the temple-form, and in the imperishable realm (akṣaradhāman); the fact that the great sage Devāyana was the very embodiment of the temple; the blessing given to the sage Devāyatana that he should become the embodiment of the temple; and the blessing for the stability of the deities who are the limbs of the temple. 394 136. Regarding the construction of a temple in the form of a palace: the description and measurement of the temple components, beginning from the excavation (khāta) up to the pedestal (pīṭha) and the corner-projections (karṇa). 397
137. Description of the constituent parts of the temple-form, such as the *maṇḍovara*, *kuṃbhī*, *chajju*, *nāsā*, pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), door-lintel (*udumbara*), and so forth.
400. 138. [Description of] the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), smoke-temple (*ghūmmaṭa*), lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), the deity therein, and so on, along with the measurement of their respective parts.
402. 139. Description of the pinnacle (*śikhara*), lotus-bud (*padmakośa*), finial (*kalaśa*), banner (*dhvaja*), and so forth, in the form of the temple. 408.

140. Description of palaces in the form of Mount Meru and other such types, as well as those of other types such as the Akṣara (Syllable) class and others. 408 141. At the festival of consecration (*pratiṣṭhotsava*), description of the measurements and proportions for the superior, middling, and inferior Meru temples, as well as for the images of Gaṇeśa. 411 142. At the festival of consecration, the measurement of the images of Brahmā, the Vedas, the gods, and goddesses, as well as the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and the abbreviated rites of consecration. 414
143. The procedure for the installation festival, including the placement of the Vāstupuruṣa and the deities, and so forth.
417 144. At the installation festival of an image: the selection of the preceptor (ācārya), the gathering of sacrificial materials, the worship of Gaṇeśa, and so forth.

419 145. At the installation festival: the placement of the water-pot (kalaśa), the recitation of the Puṇyāha formula, the invocation of the Mothers and other deities, the Nāndī-śrāddha, the worship of the seat, the offering of food, the giving of priestly fees (dakṣiṇā), the dismissal of the deities, and so forth. 422

146. In the consecration festival (*pratiṣṭhotsava*), there is the selection of the preceptor (*ācārya*), officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and others; the sprinkling of the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*); the recitation of benedictions (*svastivāca*); the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*); and the invocation, salutation, and so forth, of the deities of the *vāstu-pīṭha*. (425) 147. In the consecration festival, there is the installation of the water-jars (*kalaśa*); the installation and worship of the *vāstu* deity; the worship of the *vāstu* deities; the offering of food (*naivedya*) and oblations (*bali*); the encircling of the pavilion with the triple-thread (*trisūtrī*); and the recitation of mantras, and so forth. (429) 148. In the consecration of a deity, there is the invocation and worship of the sixty-four *yoginīs*, the fifty *kṣetrapālas*, and the deities of the sixteen pillars of the pavilion, and so forth. (433)

149. The worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) of the arches (toraṇa), the water-pots (kalaśa), the door-frames (dvāraśākhā), the thresholds (dehalī), and their respective deities, and so forth.

436 150. The installation of the fire (agnisthāpana), the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), its girdle (mekhalā), and its womb (yoni), as well as the worship of their respective deities, the fire, the nine planets (navagraha), and their presiding deities (adhideva), and so forth.

441 151. The invocation of the secondary deities (pratyadhidevatā), the invocation of the world-protectors (lokapāla), the three gods and goddesses, and the planets; the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭa); the worship of the Sarvatobhadra mandala; and the worship of the fifty-six deities, and so forth. 444

152. The worship of the water-pots (*kalaśa*), their presiding deities, and the gatekeepers; the selection (*varaṇa*); the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and other implements; the sacrificial porridge (*caru*); the oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*); the warding off (*vāraṇa*); and the fire-offering (*homa*) for the planets, the presiding deities (*adhideva*), the secondary deities (*pratyadhideva*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), and so forth.

448 153. The fire-offering to the deity of the site (*vāstudeva*); and the offering to the Yoginīs, the Field-Protector (*kṣetrapāla*), the Mothers (*mātṛkā*), the Vasus, Ādityas, Rudras, the host of Mothers (*mātṛgaṇa*), Gaṇeśa, Pitāmaha (Brahmā), Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Sūrya, and others. 514 154. The worship and presentation of offerings (*bali*) to the six [deities] beginning with Rādhikā, the one hundred and forty [deities] beginning with the Supreme Vidyā, the two Kaṃbharās, the incarnations of the Supreme Lord (*parameśavatāra*), Viṣṇu, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the elemental beings (*bhūta*), and so forth. 454

155. The erection of the sacrificial pillar (yūpa), the worship of that deity and others, the ritual immersion of the image in water (jalādhivāsana), its procession through the city, the bringing of it to the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and so forth. 457 156. The placement of the pitchers for the ritual bath, the offering of oblations (bali) to the guardians of the directions (dikpāla), the application of the golden probe, the collyrium for the eyes, the bathing with many jars, the bathing with sprouts (pallava), worship, the offering of ornaments and food (naivedya), the fire sacrifice (homa), and the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the Praṇava, the Mātṛkās, and the constellations (nakṣatra), and so forth. 460

157. Regarding the physical form (mūrti), there are: the months, seasons, pairs [of deities], castes, Vedas, Vasus, directions, world-protectors (lokapāla), field-protectors (kṣetrapāla), incarnations of the Lord (bhagavad-avatāra), sacrifices, fires, weapons, ornaments, beloveds, principles (tattva), root-mantras, the two Gāyatrīs, the mantras of offering (arpaṇa), the Puruṣasūkta, ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, the offering of oblations (bali), and the fire-sacrifice (havana), etc.

463 158. The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), ritual placements (nyāsas), the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), the waters from the pitcher (kuṃbhajala), the bathing of the pinnacle (śikharasnāna), the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caruśrapaṇa), meditation on the temple as having the form of the Supreme Person (prāsādapuruṣākāratādhyāna), worship, the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā), the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), the pedestal (piṇḍikā); gems, the water-offering for the deity (devārghya), and so forth. 466

159. The installation of the deity upon the chariot, the procession through the city, the placement of the deity upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and the throne, the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), the ritual depositions (nyāsas), the invocation of the life-force (jīvāvāhana), the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the fire sacrifice (homa), the offering of the great final oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti), the pronouncement of blessings, peace, and auspiciousness, the dismissal of the deities, the declaration of completion, and the concluding purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). 469 160. The mounting of the golden pitcher, the erection of the victory pillar and the flagstaff, the procedure for the installation of a mobile image (calamūrti), the restoration of ruined temples (jīrṇoddhāra), and so forth. 472

161. Through the blessing of Turīlakṣmī, the fisherman Dhanamēda attained wealth; thereafter, Yātrālu beheld the descent of the Fish incarnation in the divine pond, attained liberation, and established the Matsya-tīrtha, and so forth.

476 162. By means of the penance performed by the hundred bearers of his palanquin, the mute son obtained a carrier; at Aśvapaṭṭa-saras, the bearer beheld Śrī Hari in the form of Kapila through his own austerity, and attained the perfection of the speech of Sāṃkhya knowledge, and so forth. 479

163. The Lord, assuming the form of a lion, protected the cattle of the farmer known as Dyuviśrāmākhyakṛṣika when they were attacked by lions; this and other deeds are known as Haritīrtha and Gotīrtha. (482) 164. During a great deluge, the Lord provided protection for the family of Nīlakarṇacāṭvāla through the sage Vṛkāyana; Nīlakarṇa and his hundred attendants, having reached Lakṣmīvāpī, attained divine status, and the Lord sent him to the region of Ketumālakhaṇḍa. (485)

165. The departure by celestial chariot toward Ketumāla with the great sages Vṛkāyana, Nīlakaṇṛṇa, and others; the surveying of the region; the reunion with the sixty offspring of Gāṅgeya, and so forth.

487 166. The account of the origin of the Gāṅgeyas and their names; Vṛkāyana’s arrival at Lomaśakṣetra and his invitation to Hari; Vṛkāyana’s journey to Ketumāla together with Sudarśana; the determination of the site for the sacrifice as indicated by Sudarśana’s steadfastness; the proclamation of the sacrifice, and so forth. 490

167. The arrival of the great sages headed by Lomaśa, as well as the gods, Viśvakarman, the kings of Ketumāla, and the subjects, at the sacrificial ground; the presentation of the pavilion, the sacrificial pits, the oblation materials, and so forth.

493 168. The proclamation of the auspicious invitation for the sacrifice; the arrival of all the inhabitants of the created world; the arrival of Śrī Hari, together with his family and the people of Saurāṣṭra, in celestial chariots at the sacrificial ground; his welcome, his walking about, his rest, his entertainment, and so forth. 496

169. In the sacrifice (yajña), there is the worship of the ground, the worship of the deities of the site, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and so forth; the worship of those created by Brahmā, those created by Īśvara, and embodied beings created by the individual soul (jīva); the fire-oblation (havana); the offering of the great final oblation (mahāpūrṇāhuti); the distribution of food, and so on. 499 170. In the seven-day sacrifice (saptāhayajña), there are the offerings presented, Bālakṛṣṇa’s assumption of forms numbering in the millions and billions, the majesty of the sacrificial ground, and so forth. 502

171. Hari was present in person as he received the great final oblations (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*), the meals for all, the purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*), the manifestation of the boy named Avabhṛtha, the manifestation of the girl named Tṛpti, the giving of the boy named Avabhṛtha to the girl who was requesting him as a husband, the gifts given to the boy during the marriage rites, the great gifts (*mahādāna*), and their resting in their respective places, and so forth. 509.

172. The ritual for the marriage of the prince, the dismissal of the honored guests, the Lord’s journey to Mokṣikā, the capital city of King Uralaketu; his wandering through the city, the worship [of the Lord], and the liberation of the king's ancestors, and so forth. 508 173. Hari bestowed upon King Uralaketu, the great sage Yavakrīta, and the subjects the knowledge of His own true nature and the knowledge of His eternal character, and so forth. 511

174. Having gone to the royal capital of Krathaka, Oṃkāreṣṭā, and having received worship and rested there, on the morning of the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, Hari, when questioned by the king, declared the auspicious times and other factors for the construction of temples and similar edifices, and so forth.

514 175. [He described] among the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) the auspicious and inauspicious actions, their results, the conjunctions (*yoga*), the *karaṇa*, the *bhadra-cakra* with its auspicious and inauspicious results, the strength of the stars (*tārā-bala*), the strength of the moon (*candra-bala*), the revolution, the accomplishment of yogas (*siddhi-yoga-cakra*), auspicious and inauspicious yogas, the conjunctions of the sun (*ravi-yoga*), strengths, and so forth. 517

176. The twenty-eight yogas beginning with Ānanda; the inauspicious yogas arising from lunar days (tithi), weekdays (vāra), and asterisms (nakṣatra); the three types of Gaṇḍānta yogas; the Kulikā and other such inauspicious muhūrtas; and [the determination of] Abhijit, Siddha, Chāyā, and other muhūrtas. 520 177. The results of planets in their exaltations and debilitations; the results of the planets situated in the birth chart (lagna-kuṇḍalī) at the time of consecration (pratiṣṭhāna); the results of the Moon; the Āpīḍa and other yogas; the defect of conjunction (yuti-doṣa); the strength of the ascendant (lagna-bala); the examination of whether the earth is "asleep" (suptā); and thereafter, the circumambulation of the city, the worship, the dismissal (vidāya), and the arrival at the ancient capital (jarasthalī) of King Pṛthu, and so forth. 522

178. Having gone to Jarasthalī, the capital of Pṛthu, and having received a welcome, Hari gave him instruction; He spoke of how twenty-six kings in a previous kalpa attained the status of Ṛṣis, Manus, and Sūryas; then, after resting, He proceeded to the kingdom of Uṣṭrāyana on the full moon day, and so forth. 524 179. [The account of] the journey by celestial chariots to the capitals of King Uṣṭrāyana, Haṃkāra, and Jayakāṣṭhala; their wandering through the cities and receiving worship; and their departure for the capital of Tīrāṇa at dawn on the first lunar day, and so forth. 527

180. Having gone to the city of Tīraṇapura, Hari wandered about in the guise of an army welcome party; after taking food and so forth, he spoke in the evening assembly on the teaching of the dharma of eating leftovers (*vighasāśitva*), describing the state of being free from bondage. Having rested at night, he performed worship in the morning, ate, and being ready, arrived at the kingdom of the monkey-king, and so forth. 530.

181. On the second day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādra, the illustrious Hari went to the kingdom of Alvinara; having wandered through the city of Arthaśrī, partaken of food, and granted liberation to a Rākṣasa, he dispatched that Tuṣita deva to Uttarakuru. Then, sitting in the assembly hall and receiving worship, and after sleep, receiving further worship and resting, he set out toward the royal capital of Jinavardhin on the morning after his meal, and so forth. 533.

182. Having purified Rāmapurī within the kingdom of King Jinavardhin, having instructed the people, partaken of food, rested, and accepted worship, Hari—the destroyer of the demon who oppresses the people—went with Viḍāya to Mount Apināya for the sake of destroying that Rākṣasa, and so forth.

183. A battle took place between the two kings and the Rākṣasas along with their armies; a battle took place between the Rākṣasīs and Durgā; the destruction of the Rākṣasas was accomplished by means of the discus (cakra); and the protection of the subjects held in fetters was provided by the splendor of the Sudarśana mountain.
[The text describes] the state of being composed of mercury and stone, and so forth. 539. 184.

For the sake of rescuing helpless children, following the destruction of the *rākṣasa*, there is the taking of refuge in Hari by one thousand one hundred and twenty maidens; the restoration to life of those who had died from the bones of those killed by the *rākṣasa*; the establishment of the kingdom of Īśāna; the greatness of Sunday (*ravivāra*), worship, and blessings; resting at night; and in the morning after eating, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, the departure toward the city of King Alpaketu. 542.

185. In the city of Jīvanī belonging to King Alpaketu, Śrī Hari wandered about, was worshipped, gave instruction in the assembly using the example of Śaṅkha and Likhita, and took his meal; at night He rested, and in the morning after breakfast, He arrived in the city of Varaṇā on the sixth day in the region of His own beloved elder sage, King Jayakṛṣṇa, and so forth.

545. 186. Hari, descending from His celestial chariot into the kingdom of the royal sage Jayakṛṣṇa, wandered through the city of Varaṇā, accepted worship, and gave instruction; having obtained food and rest at night, He performed His daily rites in the morning and [drank] milk—
After the drinking and other festivities on the sixth day, he went to the regions of the Phērūnas and the Sārṣis, and then to the kingdom of King Parīśāna, and so forth.

547. In the city of Parīśāna, there was a great gathering of the people; there was the splendor of Hari, his mounting upon an elephant, the drawing of the people [toward him], his wandering through the city, and his arrival at the royal palace, and so forth.

550. He gave instruction to the people of Parīśāna and others, performed the worship of Hari, and on the morning of the seventh day, he traveled through the sky over the kingdom of Parīja by means of celestial chariots (vimānas).

189. In the kingdom of Indurāya, [there occurred] the worship of Hari in his palace, a meal, wandering through the city of Vāyūnā, instruction, and a farewell; on the seventh day, an evening bath in the Indirā river, the raising of the Vetāla, and the journey to the kingdom of King Mudrāṇḍa, and so forth.

557 190. Wandering in the city of Madrirā, visiting the royal courtesan, worship, instruction, and a meal; departing after the night and following the morning rites, wandering through the city of Śaivāla and the regions of the sage Gaṇḍarṣi, the Lord’s journey toward the city of Līśavana belonging to King Gaṇḍa, and so forth. 560
191. The journey toward Līśavana, the capital city of Harigaṇḍaka; the wandering, the worship, the eating, the giving of instruction, and resting at night, and so forth. 163.

192. [The account includes] the journey to the kingdom of Harilīna; wandering through the city of Vāruṇī, worship, eating, and taking leave; thereafter, the arrival at the kingdom of King Bṛhacchara and wandering through the city of Dhīvarā, worship; then the journey toward Milinda, the city of the King of Aṅga, wandering, teaching, eating, and resting at night; on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, at two watches of the night, the journey to the kingdom of King Balalīna, and so forth. 565.

193. Hari’s wandering through the city of Bālī, his worship, the keeping of the vigil, the giving of instruction, the breaking of the fast on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, and thereafter the journey toward the city of Vāśīlā, and so forth.

568 194. In the city of Vāśīlā, King Varasiṃha’s [encounter with] Hari’s wandering, his worship, the instruction on the Yuga, the meal, the rest, and after sleep, the departure for the kingdom of Rāyagāmala before midday on the thirteenth day, and so forth. 571

195. [The account of] Hari’s wandering, worship, teaching, eating, resting, and passing the night in the city of Rīgā within the stainless kingdom of Rāyaga; and on the morning of the fourteenth day, after drinking milk and other drinks, his arrival at the kingdom of King Phenatantu.

574 196. [The account of] the descent of Śrī Hari into the city of Trinayā in the kingdom of King Phenatantu; his wandering, worship, teaching, eating, and resting; and after the night, on the morning of the new moon (amāvāsyā) of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, after drinking milk, his arrival at the kingdom of King Stokahoma, and so forth. 577

197. For King Stokahoma, there was the descent of Hari in the city of Umā, his wandering, worship, instruction, and eating; at night, he rested; on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, King Kāṣṭhayāna arrived with his kingdom, and so forth.

198. For King Kāṣṭhayāna, there was the wandering of Śrī Hari in the city of Tunnavāya, his worship, instruction, and eating; after nightfall, in the morning, he proceeded to the kingdom of King Kolaka, and so forth. 582.

199. In the city of Muramāṣā belonging to King Kolaka, [the Lord] performed a circumambulation, worship, gave instruction, and took a meal on the third day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa; at the request of the daughter of Gaṅgā and others, he assumed many forms and simultaneously performed ablutions in their waters, thereby sanctifying those holy sites (*tīrtha*). He rested during the night, and on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, he departed for the region of King Arka, whose duration of reign was measured by the day. Thus it continues. 584.

200. On the day of the Sun-king (the twenty-first day), in the region of Garima-khaṇḍa, there was the descent of Hari into the city of Aparāntikā; then wandering, worshiping, eating, and resting, he traveled by celestial chariot through all directions, rested at night, ate in the morning, set out, and returned to the Vinipāra lake in the regions of Kenāṭaka, and so forth. 587.

201. In the drama: the sending of auspicious letters regarding the sacrifice (kratu); the welcome accorded by the ten kings and others to Hari upon his arrival; inquiries after his welfare and so forth; the orders for the construction of the pavilion and other structures; the provision of food and such; and the gathering of sacrificial implements.

590 202. In Maṇisevāpuri and Yajñapattana: Hari’s wandering, worship, and dining; resting at night; and on the morning of the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the appointment of the ritual officers and so forth. 593

203. The command to commission a golden image for King Rāyakinnara; the dispatching of Nārada and others to the various realms with letters of invitation written in saffron; Hari’s journey to the kingdom of King Rāyarokīśvara, his worship there, and his wandering through the land of Sphūrtinārīnagarī; his return to the site of the sacrifice and the arrival of the great honors (mahīmānas), and so forth. 597.

204. Welcoming all guests and providing them with lodging and prepared provisions; the arrangement for the self-luminous Lord to be the witness of all at the sacrifice; the sounding of auspicious musical instruments; the arrival of all the gods, goddesses, and others at the sacrificial pavilion grounds, as well as the arrival of Śrī Hari, and so forth.

600 205. The arrival of kings and sages at the pavilion; the installation of the divine seats and the deities; the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and preceptors (*ācārya*); and the radiant presence of the manifest deities, and so forth. 602

206. Worship of the golden image; worship of Gaṇeśa and others; the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) or the mandala; the installation of Vāstu; worship of the Lord of all lords, the gods, and others; worship of the deities of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the branches [of the tree], and other male and female deities; worship of the Yoginīs, Kṣetrapālas, and others; self-worship, purification of the body, and so forth; worship of Brahmā, the establishment of the fire (agnisthāpana), and so on. 605

207. At the sacrifice of Śrī Hari, there was worship, the offering of oblations into the fire, the giving of oblations to all embodied beings of the three worlds, the dismissal of the guests, the meal, and the journey toward the kingdom of Rāyaraṇajit; furthermore, there was wandering and worship in the city of Mīnārkakṛṣṇa, as well as the act of offering, and so forth.

608 208. In the city of Mīnārkakṛṣṇa, Hari instructed the people, including Rāyaraṇajit and others; thereafter, he went to the sacrificial ground, slept at night, and woke up in the morning, and so forth. 611

209. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, at a sacrifice, he performed all rites up to the final oblation (*āhuti*). After that, having gone to the island of King Rāyavākakṣa—which was one-fourth of his kingdom and comprised two days' journey—and having purified and instructed [the people], he returned to the sacrificial ground at night and rested there, and so forth. 614.

210. On the ninth day, following the conclusion of the sacrificial rites, there was a journey to the city of Ṛddhīśā in the island of Ālīsmara within the kingdom of Rāyamārīṣa, followed by wandering, worship, and teaching; after purifying the islands of Kāśima, Dvivāma, Mīlavīla, and others, there was a return to the sacrificial ground and rest during the night, and so forth. 617 211. On the tenth day, following the worship of the deities of the sacrifice, the *homa* offerings, and other rites, there was a meal; then a journey to the island of Dvaipāyana in the kingdom of King Rāya-Bāleśvara, followed by wandering, worship, teaching, and so forth in the city of Vāyuphenā. 620

212. On the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), there was the offering of the great final oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*) for all sacrificial rites, the satiation of all, the dismissal [of the priests], and so forth. 623 213. There were blessings from the fire, the meal, the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and rewards. In the evening, Lord Hari arrived with King Rāyalambāra and his kingdom; he wandered through the city of Kimuvakra, performed worship, ate, and rested at night. On the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), in the morning, he returned to the sacrificial ground, where the *mahīmāna* ceremony was performed. This included honoring him, giving thanks, presenting gifts and rewards, meals, and the granting of leave (*vidāya*). 627

214. On the thirteenth day of the month of Hara (Jyeṣṭha), in the morning, he traveled to the kingdom of King Rāya Navārka; there was wandering and worship in the city of Ciñcāgopurikā, followed by a journey to the city of Svarlatikā, where there was wandering, worship, and instruction, and at evening, a journey to the kingdom of King Rāyahaṇḍeśvara, with wandering and worship in the city of Mākṣikā, and rest for the night. On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, in the morning, there was the liberation of the sage Vīrākajanarṣi; thereafter, he traveled to the kingdom of King Rāyakūpeśa, and so forth. 630.

215. [The account] of Hari’s wandering through the city of Havāna, his worship there, then his journey to the kingdoms of Kālīmaṇḍalī and Nabhūpa, his wandering through the city of Vigoṣṭhikā, his worship, his teaching, his meal, and his rest at night, and so forth.

633 216. On the morning of the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, Hari’s awakening, his performance of daily rites, and his worship; then his journey to the kingdom of Vanajvālā, his wandering through the city of Sānujyoṣṭrī, his worship, his divine vision, his teaching, and his meal; then his journey to the kingdom of Gatainasa and his welcome, and so forth. 637

217. Hari’s wandering through the city of Kāyanī, His worship in the royal palace, His instruction, His meal, His sleep, and His departure in the morning; on the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, His journey toward the kingdom of King Koṭīśvara, and so forth. 639 218. Hari’s wandering through the city of Peyisthāna, His worship and instruction, His meal, and His departure; thereafter, His arrival in the kingdom of Pārūpa, His welcome, His worship, and so forth. 642
219. [The Lord] Hari’s wandering in the city of Sañcālānagara, His worship, teaching, taking food, resting at night, departing on the morning of the second day, receiving honors, and so forth.

645 220. On the morning of the second day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the journey to the city of Phānkalāśī, wandering, worship, taking food, teaching, and departure; thereafter, in the afternoon, the journey to the kingdom of King Āṇḍajarā, wandering in the city of Antaḥprāga, worship, and so forth. 648

221. [The Lord] gave instruction in the city of Antaḥprāgastha; there was a meal and rest at night. On the third day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, in the morning, there was a journey to the kingdom of King Bālyarajas, followed by the ministers' wandering through the city of Aṅga, worship, a meal, and their departure with wedding gifts. In the evening, there was a journey to the kingdom of King Rāyasomana, where they were welcomed in the city of Vāyumāna; there was wandering, worship, a meal, and rest at night, and so forth. 651.

222. The morning instruction, the farewell, the kingdom of Rājārāyapati, the acceptance of the request for permission to depart for the kingdom of Ārṣaja-tanu, the journey toward the kingdom of Uroga-mana, and the honor bestowed by King Urugavākṣa, and so forth.

653 223. Hari’s wandering through the city of Rāyagrāma, the instruction, the worship, the meal, the farewell, and then the departure for the kingdom of Parāṅvrata; the wandering and worship on the evening of the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina in the city of Āśāsana, and so forth. 656

224. [There was] instruction, honoring, feeding, and resting at night for the people of the kingdom of Pārāvāta and others; the distribution of gifts on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina; and the journey toward Makhasthalī in the kingdom of Vrājhīla, along with the reception of the Mahīmāna and other dignitaries, and so forth. 659 225. On the morning of the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the arrival of the Mahīmānas together with Hari toward the sacrificial ground; the arrival of everyone in the pavilion, the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastivācana*), and so on; and the performance and completion of all rites up to the offering of the great oblation of clarified butter (*mahāghṛtāhuti-homa*). 662.

226. On the fifth night, there is instruction for the subjects and rest; on the sixth [night], in the morning, after the daily rites and the completion of all sacrificial activities, there is the meal and so forth. 665 227. On the sixth [night], in the evening, there is instruction and so forth in the assembly hall, followed by the meal and retiring to bed; on the seventh [night], in the morning, there is the arrival at the sacrificial pavilion, and so forth. 667

228. On the seventh day, having completed the sacrificial rites in the morning, there is the instruction by Śrī Hari on his being the self of all and so forth, followed by a meal; then at night there is a festival, and thereafter in the morning of the eighth day, the completion of the sacrificial rites, a meal, and so on. 670 229. On the ninth, tenth, and eleventh days of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, there is the completion of sacrificial and other rites, the offering of the great final oblation (*mahāpūrṇāhuti*), the ritual withdrawal (*parihāra*), a meal, and so forth. 673

230.
