At the seven rivers beginning with the Āmrajānī, there was the residence of the deities, the holy bathing sites (*devatīrtha*), the greatness of the occasion, the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*), rewards, gifts, a meal, rest at night, departure in the morning, a meal, travel, honors, the avoidance of pavilions and the like, and thereafter the journey to the kingdoms of Rājārāya and Patirāṣṭra; on the thirteenth day, wandering and sleeping at night in the city of Vyenojarāśā, and so forth. 675.

231. Having performed the worship of Hari, instruction, and on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the ancestors, the offering of water, the *śrāddha* rites, and so forth, and having rested, after sleep, one should perform the worship and other rites on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) in the morning.

[678] 232. On the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, Hari went to the city of Lāpalātrī. There, the ocean-dwelling Daitya abducted the king’s sister named Vidyunmaṇi. Both the king and Hari pursued him with their celestial chariots (*vimāna*). In the battle at Navajīvadvīpa, two million Daityas were slain. The king’s sister sought refuge with Hari; [the text continues with the mention of] ten million Gaṇas of Śambhu... [text fragment ends].

He gave his kingdom to the host of Kāmanāyaka for the sake of sovereignty; having purified Dvārakāpurī, on the fifth lunar day he traveled by celestial chariot to Uṣṇālaya and reached the island of Trāsa. From there he went to Vandāru, then to Siṃhaladvīpa, and arriving at Lake Pampā, he reached the sacred field of Śrī Lomaśa on the evening of the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina. [There he received] welcome, inquiries after his welfare, food, bedding, and so forth. 681. 233. On the night of the full moon of the autumn month of Āśvina, the description of Bālakṛṣṇa’s playful amorous sport in the bliss of the *rāsa* dance with all his wives, and so forth. 684.

234. On the eighth day, the anniversary of the fifteenth birth of Śrī Hari, there was the decoration of the divine pavilion, the invitation of those invited, their arrival, the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and the offering of hospitality and honors, and so forth.

687 235. The conclusion of the pavilion, the dismissal of the great devotees, and the protection, nourishment, and liberation from the waters of the outcaste devotee named Tāmasākṣin along with his family, and so forth. 690

236. On the thirteenth day of the month of Dhanus, Śrī Hari performed the worship of Dhanalakṣmī and the worship of Brahmapriyā; He brought about the liberation of King Barbura, who had been cursed by the sage Āśvalāyana and turned into a *barbura* tree, established the site of Pṛthutīrtha, and sent Barbura back to heaven, and so forth. 693.

237. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, Śrī Hari performed the worship of Śaṅkara, his attendants, servants, male and female slaves, and so forth; on the festival of Dīpāvalī, he performed the worship of Śāradā and others; and on the first day (pratipad), in the form of Dattātreya, he destroyed the disease that afflicted those tormented by the great pestilence (mahāmārī) and their contact with kings, armies, and the like, and established the Dattātreya Tīrtha, and so on. 696 238. Śrī Hari instituted the festival of the mountain of food (annakūṭotsava) and caused all the subjects to partake in feasting and other such pleasures, and so on. 699

239. Through the Kārttika-ekādaśī vow, King Puṇḍarīka attained liberation upon beholding Hari in the form of a swan; at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake is the Haṃsa-tīrtha. Furthermore, by means of the Nṛsiṃha-yoga, the Cola king established an image of Nṛsiṃha on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, which became known as the Nṛsiṃha-tīrtha, and so forth. (702) 240. To Vītihotra, the Lord of Yogins, Hari granted a vision of Himself in the form of Ṛṣabha and in thousands of other forms; this is celebrated as the Ṛṣabha-tīrtha, and so forth. (705)

241. In the *Patañjali-camasa-yoga*, it is stated that on the eastern bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, there is a temple for Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, Śeṣa, and others, built by Vaivasvata; furthermore, in the water, there is a collection of holy bathing places (*tīrtha*) such as those dedicated to Saṃkarṣaṇa, Patañjali, and Śeṣa, and so forth. (707)

242. By means of the blessings obtained through the service of the five elder sisters of the sage Paṅkila—the mind-born son of Dākṣīdevī and Vāmadeva—he attained long life for five kalpas until the end of the Yuga. While he remained in meditative absorption (samādhi) at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, [the Lord] touched him with the big toe of His foot while he was awake; thus He caused the construction of the temple of Vāmana and other works, as well as the establishment of the Vāmana-tīrtha and other sacred sites. 710.

243. The five daughters of Vāmadeva obtain refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa; King Haimakalgi has the Lord constantly manifest before him through his devotion; the defeat of Parśurāma by the king; and the establishment of Parśurāma-tīrtha and Haimakalgi-tīrtha at Aśvapaṭṭasara, etc. (713) 244.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, King Aśvapāṭala commenced a Soma sacrifice on the bank of Aśvapaṭṭasara; the performance of the rites on the first day; the instruction given by Lomaśa, etc. (716)

245. On the second day, on the ninth [lunar day], Lomaśa performed the duties of the Soma sacrifice, such as the Pravargya rite, the oblation, the ritual avoidance, the meal, the instruction, and so forth.
719. 246. On the third day, on the tenth [lunar day], following the duties of the Soma sacrifice, there was the meal and the instruction of Lomaśa, and so forth.
721. 247. On the fourth day, on the eleventh [lunar day], the duties of the Soma sacrifice were performed, including the vigil, the concluding rite (udyāpana), the instruction, and so forth. 724.

248. On the fifth day, the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the Soma sacrifice, there was the morning libation (prātaḥsavana), the midday libation (mādhyandinasavana), the subsequent libation (taduttarasavana), the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the purificatory bath (avabhṛtheṣṭi), and so forth. 727 249. In the *Lomaśagītā*, Lomaśa instructed King Aśvapāṭala on the secret protection of the nectar of the pure Upaniṣads and other matters. 730 250. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there are the questions posed by Aśvapāṭala regarding the path of renunciation (*tyāgamārga*) and its perceptible fruits, his question concerning freedom from disease, and his question as to which is the best among the three aims of life (*trivarga*), along with the answers given by Lomaśa, and so forth. 733

251. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there are the questions posed by the king regarding the soul’s nature as sinful or virtuous, its state of liberation, and its state of destruction of defects, along with the answers provided by Lomaśa, and so forth.

(736) 252. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the question posed by the king concerning the means for attaining the path of the Imperishable (*akṣara*), the question regarding the destination resulting from renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) or the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*), the question regarding the creation of the three worlds, and the question regarding the highest good (*śreya*), along with the answers given by Lomaśa.

(739) 253. In the *Gītā*, there is the question posed by the king regarding prosperity (*abhyudaya*), the question regarding the root of the highest good (*śreya*) and other matters, and the answers provided by Lomaśa. (742)

254. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the question regarding the cause for pleasing the gods and others; the question concerning what kind of liberation is attained through discernment (*viveka*), worship (*upāsanā*), yoga, and dharma, as taught by the guru; and the answers provided by Lomaśa, and so forth. (745) 255. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the question regarding the relative strength and weakness of yoga; the question regarding the perishable (*kṣara*) and imperishable (*akṣara*) worlds; and the answers provided by Lomaśa, and so forth. (748) 256. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the king’s question as to how one attains liberation from the perishable (*kṣara-mocana*) and liberation from the imperishable (*akṣara-mocana*). There follow the answers provided by Lomaśa regarding that liberation and the destination [of the liberated soul], and so forth. (791)

257. In the *Lomaśagītā*, the demonstration of the cause for the Self’s departure from the body; and the dialogue between King Ānarta and the virtuous Yoginī regarding the inquiry into renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and non-renunciation (*asaṃnyāsa*).

[754] 258. In the *Lomaśagītā*, the debate with the daughter of Brahmā, the virtuous Kuśalā, by King Ānarta; and that liberation is attained through the company of the saintly even while remaining in the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), due to renunciation [of worldly attachments]. [767] 259. In the *Lomaśagītā*, the purification and imperishability resulting from the instruction of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa received by Anādiśrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the son of Brahmakallola, as well as his attainment of the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). [760]

260. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the account of how even a yogin attains the fruit of serving his chosen preceptor and so forth, as well as the description of how the gods receive their shares in the sacrifice of Hari.

(763) 261. In the *Lomaśagītā*, there is the account of Lomaśa bestowing upon Aśvapāṭalā the realization that Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the beginningless Supreme Brahman, and the imparting of the knowledge of Dharma centered on the Supreme Brahman.

(766) 262. In the *Lomaśagītā*, King Aśvapāṭala reaches the Rāmāditya-tīrtha, hears the story of the devotee Bhāṇavīrya, and performs ritual bathing, charity, and other duties according to the prescribed rules; it also includes the dialogue between the two kings. (770)
263. Through the worship of the Sun, the leper named Ūrjavrata, a scribe (kāyastha), attained freedom from disease, liberation, the Sūryatīrtha, and so forth.

772 264. A Śūdra who was a reviler and a killer was reborn as a mute Brahmin in Dharmāraṇya after dying in the Godāvarī. Having his sins washed away through austerity, he gained knowledge of medicinal herbs at Kuṅkumavāpī, his muteness was destroyed, he composed the Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā, and [attained] the Śārṅgadhara-tīrtha, the Āśvaśirasa-tīrtha, and so forth. 775
265. Pārṣṇiradanāmaka, Ajāpāla, and Śūdra’s prevention of consumption disease through bathing and other rites at Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara, Nārada-tīrtha, and so forth.

778. 266. The king of Arkapurī’s transformation into a serpent due to the curse of the sage Dharmasumantu; the Brahmin’s snakebite; his liberation from the snake; the restoration of the Brahmin to life by Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa at Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara at the request of Satī, the Brahmin’s wife; Śveta-vyāsa-tīrtha, Satī-tīrtha, and so forth. 781.

267. In Saurāṣṭra, at the city of Svarṇapattana, when King Rakṣāṅgāraka was slain by the Mlecchas, his wife Rāṇikāsatī maintained her chastity on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake; [this section covers] her devotion as a virtuous wife, the greatness of Satītīrtha, and so forth. 784. 268. Through the instruction of Guru Prabuddha, King Amohākṣa attained the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma) upon arriving at the sacred site of Śrī Lomaśakṣetra; [this section covers] liberation, Buddhatīrtha, Amohatīrtha, and so forth. 787.

269. King Abhayakṣa’s devotion, renunciation, and sacrifice; his taking of the vow of a renunciant on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake; his vision of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and others; the construction of temples; and [the establishment of] Lakṣmītīrtha, Nārāyaṇatīrtha, and so forth. 790.

270. Viṣṇutīrtha is where Devānīkakarṣuka, who was submerged in water, was protected by Viṣṇu on dry land; Puruṣottamatīrtha is where the Brahmin Brahmastamba attained Puruṣottama while performing austerities at Bhadrāyana village; Mahāviṣṇutīrtha is so called because the Lord Mahāviṣṇu, propitiated by the maiden Amarīdevī through her penance at Devamūlaka, accepted her according to the prescribed rites; and Sanatkumāratīrtha is where Sanatkumāra provided protection to Kūpyavāla, a wood-gatherer, when he was seized by an elephant—and so forth. 793.

271. There is the Kuṅkumeśvara-tīrtha, which was established by Kuṅkuma; the Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha, established by Satī Śācāraṇī; the Durgāsatī-tīrtha, established by the merchant’s wife Dhanyeśvarī; the Lakṣmī-tīrtha, established by Caityabrahma the twice-born; the Śālagrāma-tīrtha, and so forth. 797. 272. There is the Naranārāyaṇa-tīrtha, the Harikṛṣṇa-tīrtha, and the Māṇikī-tīrtha. [The text recounts] the account of Aśvapaṭṭa, the arrival of all the holy places (sarvatīrthāgama), the descent of the Supreme Brahman through the praise of Vairāja, and the initiation of Aśvapaṭṭa as a saint (sādhu). 800.

273. The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa bestowed mantra-initiation, the teaching of knowledge, and other instructions upon the *sādhus* and *sādhvīs*. From Kāśī, Bṛhaspati—accompanied by Nārada and carrying the *Yoga-patrikā* sent by Śiveśvara—arrived at Lomaśa-kṣetra; the presentation of the letter, his welcome, and so forth are described here. (803) 274. Lomaśa performed the worship and reading of the letter provided by Bṛhaspati according to the prescribed rites, followed by the honoring of the people and other ceremonies. Nārada then spoke to Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa regarding His various divine powers, qualities, and auspicious marks, and he also explained the secret meaning to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, and so on. (806)

275. The greatness of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as spoken by Nārada to Śivā; the greatness of Lakṣmī; the causes for attaining the company of the virtuous; the account of the honoring of Nārada, and so forth. 809 276. Nārada spoke the divine secret to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, and thereafter spoke it to Śrī Kaṃbharādevī; the description of such qualities and so forth. 812

277. On the new moon day, at the abode of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, auspicious songs by the women of the three worlds were sung in every house, there were great festivals with the playing of musical instruments, and Bṛhaspati was honored. After receiving and reading the published letter and its reply, he returned to Kāśī after having worshipped Bṛhaspati; meanwhile, invitations had been sent throughout the three worlds, and so forth. 816 278. On the first day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the morning, there were auspicious rites, the splendor of the Kuṃkuma-vāpī lake, and the beauty of the pavilion adorned by celestial maidens, and so forth. 819

279. The fruit of worshipping the ruby pillar in the pavilion, as well as the pinnacle (kalaśa), Gaṇeśa, the Mothers (Mātṛkās), Vāstu, Viṣṇu, the family deity (kuladevatā), and the Sarvatobhadra diagram, and so forth.
822 280. A description of the divinity of the great pavilion constructed by Mahāmukta, and so forth.

825 281. The writing of the letter, its worship, and its dispatch throughout all the worlds; the great festival of offering betel leaves, areca nuts, food, and feasting; and at night, singing, dancing, instrumental music, wrestling matches, acrobatics, and the composition of poetry—[and so forth].
[These include] festivals such as the distribution of *toṣika* gifts, the giving of food, and acts of avoidance, and so forth.

828. 282. On the second day: auspicious sights in the morning, worship of the gods, the great bathing, massage, and bathing of Bālakṛṣṇa; his adornment, the feeding of the *mahīmāna* guests and others, the arrival of the three worlds, and the attainment of auspicious joy by the two Kṛṣṇas, and so forth. 831.

283. On the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the morning rites were performed; at midday, the meals and other activities took place. Preparations were made for the journey toward Kāśī, including personal adornment and auspicious ceremonies. Then, the daughters, such as Brahmapriyā and others, ascended the palanquin along with their fathers and other relatives, and so forth. 834 284. The names of the dignitaries, the ascent of the daughters and the sages into the palanquin, and the departure of Kṛṣṇā and the others toward Kāśī, and so forth. 837

285. The sounds of musical instruments played by Śiva for the purpose of honoring the followers of the Yoga-yāna; the vision from the sky of Kāśī, Śivapura, and Pārvatīpura; a description of the city; and how Kailāsa was fashioned in the sky by Śiveśvara, along with his retinue, to remain there for a *ghaṭikā* to welcome Kṛṣṇa, and so forth. 840.

286. On the Kailāsa of the sky, Śaṅkara, assuming many forms, performed a grand welcome, worship, and honoring of Yogavāhinī with musical instruments; he also provided sweet foods, drinks, and betel-leaf. Men and women exchanged greetings of mutual well-being. Then Kailāsa vanished, and everyone descended to Śivapura, where they took their meals and rested at night, and so forth. 843.

287. On the fourth day: in the morning, the performance of auspicious rites and the worship of the family deity (*kuladevatā*); at midday, the feeding of the honored guests (*mahīmāna*) and so forth; rest; and the debate between Bālakṛṣṇa in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Śiveśvara, along with its subsequent conclusions.

846 288. The dialogue between Bālakṛṣṇa in the form of Rādhā and Girijā; the dialogue between [Bālakṛṣṇa] in the form of a Brahmin and Lakṣmī, along with its subsequent conclusions, the strengthening [of faith], and so forth. 849

289. The sending of ornaments, garments, and requisites; the grand procession, the measurement of the ground, and the decorations; the departure toward the pavilion and the beautification of the pavilion, and so forth. 852 290. In the moon-chamber (*candraśālā*), Pārvatī was made to worship the Goddess with the *Ṛgveda*; furthermore, the acquaintance with the grand measurements of the city of Kṛṣṇāyati was demonstrated. 855 291. While Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa was beautifully adorned, there was the bewitching charm of men and women as they were drawn toward each of his limbs; [he beheld] the divine vision and returned toward the city gate (*gopura*). 859

292. The worship and sight of Bālakṛṣṇa at the city gate (gopura), dancing before him, the clapping of mechanical instruments, resting in the rest-house, the offering of madhuparka, the decoration, and Śrīkṛṣṇa’s arrival at the main door of the pavilion. 862.

293. The worship performed by Śiveśvara; the removal of household utensils performed by Śivā; the sitting of Śrī Hari upon the seat in the pavilion; the arrival of the maidens; the worship; the worship of the deities; the gift of the binding of the fruit of desire; gifts in the hand; assuming the form of Arbuda; the taking of all taxes; the wearing of all garlands; the circumambulation of the fire; and the offering of the procedure for the proclamation of the lineage and so forth. 865.

294. The instruction on the fire-witnessing rite, the teaching on domestic duties, the avoidance of ritual acts, the meal for the couple, the universal meal, the avoidance of various forms in the pavilion, and the sleeping of the couple in their chamber following the gift of ten million, hundred million, and ten billion [coins], and so forth. 869.

295. The enumeration of gifts: on the fifth day, the morning excursion for the Phullaka procession; the untying of knots; midday meals and rest at Śivapura with rewards and the like; bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha) in the Gaṅgā and giving gifts at Pañcagaṅgā; the Yoga-tīrtha; the offering of alms to Śaṅkara; the arrival at Śivapura, and so forth. 872.

296. [The sequence includes] the crossing at the Prodvāha-tīrtha, the Koṭi-tīrtha, and the Yajña-tīrtha; the dismissal of those of high status, mutual requests for forgiveness, grief at separation, the departure of celestial chariots, arrival at the Lomaśa-kṣetra, the giving of gifts, auspicious rites, entry into the home, meals, joyful pastimes, sleep, and so forth.

On the sixth [day], following the morning bath and worship, there was the reception of the mantra; the *mahīmāna* feast; the wandering in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) for the purpose of viewing the forest; the evening meal; the maiden named Dyauḥ arrived to witness the divine play (*līlā*); having beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa performing various pastimes in millions, billions, and trillions of abodes, she was enchanted, worshipped Him, and returned to heaven; and finally, the sleep of Hari. 878.

298. On the morning of the seventh day, within meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the manifestation of the threefold creation, the imperishable abode (*akṣaradhāman*), and so forth; the transformation of those [powers] into the nature of eternal, divine liberation; the honoring, feeding, and worshiping of the *mahimānas*; the granting of forgiveness and gifts; and the presentation of rewards to the deities of the sacred field (*kṣetradēva*). 882.

299. After a long time, the departure for their own country together with their father and others who were staying at the hermitage of Lomaśa; the removal of the pavilion and other structures; the manner in which Lakṣmī and the others performed service to the daughter of Kāśī; the arrival at the palace until the eighteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika on the occasion of the sixteenth birth-festival; the great festival; the instruction on liberation and the attainment of liberation by Śiva, Śambhu, and others; the giving of gifts during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) in the sixteenth year; and the greatness of the *Saṃhitā* as the continuation of the Tretā Yuga, and so forth. 885
300. The majesty of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; a brief indication of the narratives contained within the Tretā-khaṇḍa; the introduction to the lineage of the Dvāpara age; and the benedictions. 888.
Thus ends the table of contents for the subjects of the second section, consisting of the lineage of the Tretā Yuga, of the Śrī-Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā.
